## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, complete, uniform, convenient, economical library, of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the times of Innocent III;** a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and corrected with the utmost diligence; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the very extensive editions published during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes, following each individual volume or author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself and with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the material treated below; enlarged with works both doubtful and apocryphal, as well as with those possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is immediately clear to the reader which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, have commented on the several texts of the books of Scripture.

This edition is exceedingly accurate and readily to be preferred to all others, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the extremely convenient form of the volumes, consistently alike throughout the work, their low price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and little works hitherto scattered here and there, gathered for the first time in our library from works pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.

**Second series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, editor of the universal library of the clergy, or complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical science. Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. One thousand two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; one thousand three hundred of the Greek-Latin edition for eight hundred francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, Western and Eastern alike; the latter, however, are given in it only in Latin translation.

## About the year of the Lord 1152: Zacharias, bishop of Chrysopolis

[Col. 0009]

## Notice

(Fabricius, *Library of Medieval and Late Latin* [*Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*], vol. VI, p. 332.)

Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, or Goldsborough, an Englishman of the Order of Premonstratensian Canons at the abbey of Saint Martin of Laon around the year 1150, wrote a Commentary on the evangelical harmony of Ammonius of Alexandria, which was printed at Cologne in folio in 1535 and afterward in the Libraries of the Fathers.

[Col. 0009]

## Second notice

(*Literary History of France*, by Benedictine religious.)

Zacharias, called Chrysopolitanus [Note: [Col. 0009] Oudin (*Script.*, vol. II, p. 1442) calls him Goldsborough, on the authority of a manuscript in the Bodleian Library (*Catalogue of English Manuscripts*, part I, no. 1235). Was this an attempt to make Zacharias English, because Goldsborough is a place in the diocese of York? But can a single manuscript prevail against countless others, as old and even older, that contradict it?], from the ancient name for Besançon, where he was probably born, was contemporary with Ralph of Flaix [Note: [Col. 0009] Alberic, *Chronicle*, under 1157.]. Several make him bishop of Besançon, but without foundation [Note: [Col. 0009] Crowoeus (*De sacra scriptura*, p. 343), by a rather gross mistake, makes him a Greek bishop: “Zacharias Chrysopolitanus,” he says, “a Greek bishop.”]. Besides the fact that his name does not occur in the list of that city’s prelates, it seems certain that he never left the Premonstratensian order, which he had entered at the abbey of Saint Martin of Laon. Zacharias distinguished himself in that retreat by his devotion to study, and that devotion was not fruitless. It produced two works that have come down to us.

One is a Commentary on the harmony of the Gospels. It is preceded by three kinds of preface. The first treats the excellence of the Gospel; its difference from the Law; the figures of the evangelists, *de figuris evangelistarum*, that is, the emblems under which they are represented; their style; their manner of writing; the matter of the Gospel; its purpose; and the branches of philosophy to which it relates. The author speaks there of a writer of his own time who is otherwise unknown to us, named Enipius. According to Zacharias, he was a man of wide reading, possessed a large library, and had made an exposition of the Gospel drawn almost wholly from Saint Augustine. The life of the four evangelists serves as a second preface. In the third, Zacharias reviews those who had made harmonies of the four Gospels before him: Ammonius, Tatian, Theophilus of Antioch, and Saint Augustine. He does not positively venture to affirm who was the author or arranger of the harmony that he takes as his guide, but, from a passage of Eusebius of Caesarea, he supposes it to be Ammonius. It seems to him deserving of preference over all the others because of the singular art and wonderful precision with which all the evangelists’ words are joined in it, without any mixture of alien terms. He adds that Ammonius took care to distinguish what belongs to each evangelist by capital letters placed at the head of each chapter.

A brief warning to the reader follows, in which the author says that, since there are many versions of Scripture differing among themselves, he has always used the same ancient version in his Harmony, but has followed that of the moderns in his explanations. He thought this should be observed so that readers of the text and gloss would not be tempted to correct one by the other. After the table of chapters for the first and second book comes another warning naming the sources from which the commentary is drawn: Saint Jerome; Saint Augustine on Saint John; Albin, or Alcuin, his abridger; Origen; Saint Chrysostom; Saint Gregory the Great; Saint Ambrose; Saint Hilary; and Rabanus Maurus. This work, less literal than allegorical and moral, is nevertheless made with taste. Father Lelong (*Bibliothèque sacrée*, vol. II, p. 747) says it was published under Tatian’s name—he doubtless means the Harmony, not the explanations—but gives no such edition, and we do not believe it real. The first known edition was printed at Cologne in 1535 by Eucharius Cervicornus, in one folio volume of 377 pages, under the title: *Zachariae Chrysopolitani, [Col. 0011] viri suo tempore celeberrimi, in unum ex quatuor, sive de Concordia evangelistarum libri quatuor jam nunc primum excusi* [“Four Books by Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, a man most celebrated in his own time, on making one [Gospel] out of four, or On the Harmony of the Evangelists, now printed for the first time”] [Note: [Col. 0011] The following is immediately added: “That you may understand more clearly what you are to find here, remember that the four Gospels, reduced by Ammonius into one continuous work, are here explained by Zacharias in four books. When you have read them, you yourself will judge how highly you should value them; for good merchandise needs no herald.”]. It was adopted in the Libraries of the Fathers at Cologne (vol. XII) and Lyons (vol. XIX).

Zacharias’s second work is a collection of homilies preserved in manuscript at the abbey of Aulne, in the diocese of Liège. We do not think it has yet been printed, and we know only the single copy just mentioned.

Dom Bernard Pez published, in the fourth volume of his *Anecdotes*, p. 17, a sermon on Saint George composed by a certain Zacharias described as a bishop. But the editor rightly observes that this designation itself shows that the discourse belongs to another Zacharias, not to our author.

[Col. 0011]

# Zacharias Chrysopolitanus: Four books on making one [Gospel] out of four, or On the harmony of the Evangelists

(*Library of the Ancient Fathers of Lyons*, vol. XIX, p. 732.)

## Note

That you may understand more clearly what you are to find here, remember that the four Gospels, reduced by Ammonius of Alexandria into one continuous work, are here explained by Zacharias in four books; when you have read them, you yourself will judge how highly you should value them.

## Zacharias’s preface to the following four books

[Col. 0011A] Reason requires us to set forth the excellence of the Gospel and its difference from the Law; the figures of the evangelists and their manner of writing; the matter, purpose, and end of the Gospel; and the branches of philosophy to which it pertains. The matter of the Gospel is the mystery of the Holy Trinity; Christ according to his divine and human nature; his sayings and deeds; and the sayings and deeds of others that relate to him. John reveals its purpose and end when he says: “But these things are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Son of God, and that, believing, you may have life in his name” (John 20). For its end—that is, the final cause of the Gospel—is surely to believe, to love perfectly, and to be marked by the sacraments; and the final cause of these three is eternal life. The evangelical purpose in preaching and writing was to attain these things.

[Col. 0011B–0012A] Let us now speak of the Gospel’s excellence and its difference from the Law. Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*: “Among all divine authorities the Gospel deservedly excels. For what the Law and the prophets foretold as future is shown in the Gospel as rendered and fulfilled.”

From Isidore’s *Book of Differences*: “This is the difference between Law and Gospel: in the Law, the letter; in the Gospel, grace. The former had the shadow, the latter the truth; the former was given because of transgression, the latter because of justification; the former shows sin to the ignorant, the latter helps the person who recognizes it to avoid it; the former rebukes those devoted to disgraceful acts, the latter by its own goodness frees those who sin; the former decreed that retaliation should be returned, the latter commanded prayer even for enemies; the former commanded the possession of many wives, increase, and begetting, the latter recommended continence. There circumcision of the flesh is proclaimed; here a washing for the cleansing of heart and body.

[Col. 0012B–0013A] “There the kingdom of Canaan and promises of temporal things are contained; here eternal life and the kingdom of heaven are promised. There Sabbath leisure and rest are celebrated; here Sabbath rest is possessed in Christ, who said: ‘Come to me, all who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you; and you shall find rest for your souls’ (Matt. 11). There unclean animals are forbidden to the saints; here, in Christ’s body—that is, in his saints—whatever those unclean animals signify in human conduct is not admitted. There sacrifices of flesh and blood were offered by slaughtering cattle; here the sacrifice of Christ’s flesh and blood is offered, which was prefigured through those animals. There Passover is celebrated from the flesh of the lamb; here ‘Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed’ (1 Cor. 5), he who is the true spotless Lamb.

[Col. 0013B] “There the beginnings of the new moons are celebrated; here the new creation in Christ is received, as Paul says: ‘If anyone is a new creation in Christ, the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new’ (2 Cor. 5). What more need be said? In the Law, events performed were announced as figures signifying future things; but in the grace of evangelical truth, the things announced are fulfilled.

“Again: In the Law commandments and promises are written; but in the Law the commandments are observed which command the Law’s fulfilment or preservation, whereas the promises are brought to completion in the Gospel’s fullness. Again: the Law showed sin, but did not remove it; under its terror it made people slaves, and the Apostle teaches that the former people thus had the spirit of slavery (Rom. 8). But when the Gospel came, it removed the Law’s severity, remitted through the spirit of adoption the sins which the Law punished through the spirit of slavery, made sons out of slaves, and gave all people love for fulfilling the Law. If thereafter they commit things deserving punishment, it grants pardon through that same spirit of adoption.

[Col. 0013C] “It gave a pattern of right conduct and pours in the assisting Spirit, so that what it teaches may be done. For legal precepts, in comparison with the Gospel, are even called not good, because they do not accomplish what they command; whereas the Gospel’s grace inwardly assists the fulfilment of what it outwardly commands. For by Ezekiel’s testimony it is said: ‘I gave them precepts that were not good’ (Ezek. 20). They were not good, certainly, in comparison with the Gospel, because certain useless things were allowed in them to be done by weaker minds; as, for example, where God permitted the Israelites’ desire to be satisfied with Egyptian spoils (Exod. 3).

[Col. 0013D] “For because the carnal people exceeded the measure of vengeance, the Law permits carnal persons to return evil for evil; the Gospel forbids this to the stronger.”

Junilius, in his book to Bishop Primasius: “The intention of the Old Testament is to show forth the New by figures and enigmas; but that of the Gospel is to kindle human minds toward the glory of eternal blessedness.”

Jerome, to Paula and Eustochium in the *Epistle to the Galatians*: “Let us not suppose that the Gospel lies in the words of the Scriptures, but in their meaning; not on the surface, but in the marrow; not in the leaves of speech, but in the root of reason.”

Hence Ambrose, on Luke: “Although the Church has four books of the Gospel, she has one Gospel and teaches one God.”

Remigius, on Matthew: “It should be known that, just as there is one faith and one baptism, so there is one Gospel, because there is one doctrine. And the Lord shows that it is one when he says, ‘Go: preach the Gospel to every creature’ (Matt. 16); and again, ‘The kingdom shall be preached throughout the whole world’ (Matt. 1). And Paul: ‘I make known to you, brethren, the Gospel which was preached by me, because I did not receive it from man,’ and so forth (Gal. 1). Whenever we speak of ‘Gospels’ in the plural, we do not divide the doctrine, but distinguish the books.”

[Col. 0014A] Bede also, on Luke: “Although there are four evangelists, they published not so much four Gospels as one Gospel harmonious in the truth of four books. For just as two verses which have precisely the same subject are two by reason of the difference of metre and words, yet contain only one meaning, so, although there are four books of the evangelists, they contain one Gospel, because they make one doctrine concerning the Catholic faith, the communion of the sacraments, and the reward of virtues.”

Similarly Jerome says on Mark: “The four Gospels are one, and the one is four. For though they are called four, because four men wrote them separately and in various sequence, they are nevertheless one in the sum of the Catholic faith.”

So Augustine says also on Psalm 150 that many churches are one Church: “They are many indeed in variety of tribes, languages, and peoples; they are one by participation in faith and sacraments.”

*Evangelium* means “good announcement.” For in Greek, εὐ means “good,” and ἀγγέλιον means “announcement”; hence *angelus* also is interpreted “messenger.”

[Col. 0014C] Concerning the figures of the evangelists, we shall set forth not contrary but differing opinions of the Fathers, so that the reader may choose what seems best to him. Jerome, in the introductory argument before the Gospels: “The book of Ezekiel proves that the four Gospels were foretold long before, for its first vision is thus composed: ‘And in the midst, as it were, the likeness of four living creatures; and their faces were the face of a man, the face of a lion, the face of a calf, and the face of an eagle’ (Ezek. 1). The first, the face of a man, signifies Matthew, who began to write as it were from a man: ‘The book of the generation of Jesus Christ’ (Matt. 1). The second signifies Mark, in whom the voice of a lion roaring in the wilderness is heard: ‘The voice of one crying in the wilderness’ (Mark 1). The third, that of the calf, foreshadows that Luke took his beginning from Zacharias the priest (Luke 1). The fourth signifies John, who, hastening to higher things, speaks of the Word of God (John 1). The same signification occurs in the Apocalypse, where it is said: ‘The first living creature was like a lion, the second like a calf, the third like a man, the fourth like a flying eagle’ (Rev. 1).”

Sedulius:

> Matthew, at work, generally fulfills the man.  
> Mark, as the mighty voice of a lion, roars through deserts.  
> Luke holds the priestly rights in the mouth of the young bull.  
> John, flying in the manner of an eagle, seeks the stars with the Word.

Juvencus, otherwise:

> Matthew established conduct by the path of virtues,  
> and rightly gave laws for good living in orderly sequence.  
> Mark loves to fly between earth and heaven,  
> and, a vehement eagle, cuts through all things in headlong flight.  
>
> [Col. 0015A] Luke more fully describes the battles of Christ,  
> rightly the sacred calf who speaks of ancestral walls.  
> John, like a roaring lion, thunders aloud,  
> revealing the mysteries of eternal life.

Augustine, however, writes thus in *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*: “Matthew treated the Lord’s incarnation according to the royal lineage. Mark seems to be his attendant and abridger, saying nothing with John alone. Luke dealt with the Lord’s priestly lineage, ascending to David; he did not follow the royal stock, but went through the kings to Nathan, son of David, who was not a king. Matthew, on the other hand, descended through King Solomon and followed the remaining kings.

“Luke did not have an attendant abridger as Matthew did. Perhaps this was not without a mystery, because kings are not accustomed to lack the service of attendants. But the priest entered the Holy of Holies alone. These three are chiefly occupied with deeds of Christ’s humanity, John with his divinity. Therefore, since there are two powers of the soul, one active and the other contemplative, signified by Jacob’s wives—Leah, interpreted ‘labouring,’ and Rachel, ‘the principle seen’—we are given to understand that the three evangelists were occupied with the active power, but John with the contemplative.

[Col. 0015B] “Accordingly, those who understood the lion in Matthew, the man in Mark, the calf in Luke, and the eagle in John seem to me to have taken the more probable view than those who assigned the man to Matthew, the eagle to Mark, and the lion to John. The latter wished to draw an inference from the beginnings of the books, rather than from the whole intention of the evangelists, which ought rather to have been examined. For Matthew, who especially commends Christ’s royal person, is much more suitably signified by the lion. Thus in the Apocalypse the lion is named with the royal tribe itself: ‘The lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered’ (Rev. 1).

[Col. 0015C] “According to Matthew, the Magi are said to have come from the East to seek and worship the king who appeared to them as born by a star; and King Herod himself fears the infant king and, in order to kill him, murders so many little children (Matt. 2). No one doubted that Luke is signified by the calf, an animal allotted to sacrifices; for the movement of his narrative is especially concerned with the temple and Jerusalem. At the beginning he places a priest praying at the altar while the people stand outside. Having conceived the Lord, he sends Mary to Jerusalem, to the house of the high priest. There he reports the Baptist’s birth (Luke 1); there he brings the newborn Lord with an offering; there he takes him with his parents every year; there, at twelve years old, he places him among the assemblies of teachers in the temple (Luke 2); and, after the rest, he closes the Gospel with the disciples praising God in the temple.”

[Col. 0015D] Augustine’s *Harmony*, book four: “Mark therefore seems to represent the person of the man and to be Matthew’s companion, because he says much with him by reason of the royal person, which is not accustomed to be without an attendant; or, more probably, because he goes with both. For though he agrees more often with Matthew, in some things he agrees more with Luke, so that thereby it may be shown that what Christ is as man belongs to the lion and the calf—that is, to the royal person indicated by Matthew and the priestly person indicated by Luke—while Mark bears the figure of the man and belongs to both.”

[Col. 0016A] Augustine, on John, chapter 86: “Many before us have understood the lion among the four living creatures as representing the king, since he appears to be king of beasts by reason of his terrible strength. This person was assigned to Matthew because, in the Lord’s genealogy, he traced the royal line (Matt. 1). But Luke, because he began with the priesthood of Zacharias, mentioning the priest who was the father of John the Baptist, was assigned the calf, since the calf was a great victim in priestly sacrifice (Luke 1). Christ as man was rightly assigned to Mark, because he said nothing either of royal power or of priestly power, but began simply from Christ as man. All these spoke little of divinity. John is the eagle, the contemplator of eternal light.

[Col. 0016B] “For eaglets are said to be tested by their parents in this way: they are suspended by the father’s claw and placed before the rays of the sun. The one that gazes steadily is acknowledged as a son; if its sight flickers, it is released from the claw as illegitimate.”

Ambrose, on Luke: “Many think that our Lord is figured by the four forms of living creatures. He is man because he was born from Mary; lion because he is strong; calf because he is a victim; eagle because he is resurrection.”

[Col. 0016C] Jerome, on Mark: “Christ is man in being born, calf in dying, lion in rising, eagle in ascending.”

Let us now set forth the matters that may suitably be referred to the manner of writing. From Augustine’s letter to Volusianus: “The very manner of speech in which the Gospel is composed is accessible to all. What it contains openly speaks, like a familiar friend, plainly to the hearts of unlearned and learned alike. Yet the things which it conceals in mysteries do not elevate themselves even by proud eloquence, so that a slow and uneducated mind might not dare approach, as a poor person approaches a rich one. Rather, with humble speech it invites all, feeding them not only with things manifest but exercising them also with hidden truth. By these, small minds are beneficially corrected and nourished, and great minds delighted.”

[Col. 0016D] According to Isidore in the sixth book of the *Etymologies*, the subject-matter of the Gospel is divided in three ways: history, morals, and allegory. These three are again variously divided: into what was done and said by God, angels, or human beings; what was announced by the prophets concerning Christ and his body; concerning the devil and his members; concerning the old and new people; and concerning the present age, the future kingdom, and judgment.

Jerome, on Mark: “There are four kinds of material of which the holy Gospels are composed: precepts, commands, testimonies, and examples. In precepts is righteousness; in commands, charity; in testimonies, faith; in examples, perfection. Precepts are such as: ‘Do not go into the way of the Gentiles’ (Matt. 10), that is, ‘Turn away from evil’ (Ps. 33). Commands are such as: ‘I give you a new commandment, that you love one another’ (John 13), that is, do good and fulfil charity. Testimonies are those established in the mouth of two or three, such as: ‘John bears witness of me, but I have a testimony greater than John’s’ (John 5): ‘The Father himself, who abides in me, bears witness of me.’

[Col. 0017A] “Examples are such as: ‘Learn from me, because I am meek’ (Matt. 11); and: ‘Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect’ (Matt. 5). And elsewhere: ‘For I have given you an example, that you also may do likewise’ (John 1). But David says of these: ‘The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes’ (Ps. 18). And elsewhere: ‘Your commandment is exceedingly broad’ (Ps. 118), because the person who loves his neighbour has fulfilled the whole Law (Rom. 13).

[Col. 0017B] “Again: ‘I have understood your testimonies’ (Ps. 18); and elsewhere: ‘The testimony of the Lord is faithful’ (Ps. 118), because testimony requires faith of the mind more than eyes of flesh. Fourthly: ‘The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves’ (ibid.), so that examples of our judgments may be justified in the same manner as we find them established in God’s judgments. Hence the same author says elsewhere: ‘For I was afraid of your commandments’ (Ps. 118). For with whatever judgment we judge, judgment shall be made concerning us (Matt. 7).

“In these four kinds are fear, faith, hope, and charity. We begin with fear; by faith we keep what we begin; by hope we are raised up; by charity we are brought to completion. For ‘the end of the commandment is charity’ (1 Tim. 1). These are the four months which Christ declared before the harvest, saying: ‘Are there not four months until the harvest?’ (John 4).

[Col. 0017C] “Thus may we too, through God’s precepts, commands, testimonies, and examples, joyfully reap in heaven the ripe fruits, carrying our sheaves of charity; we who have cast the seeds of repentance into the earth amid tears of fear (Ps. 125).”

From Junilius’s book to Primasius: “On the surface of evangelical Scripture four modes of discourse must be observed: historical, prophetic, proverbial, and simple teaching. Gospel reading is principally woven in the historical mode, the other three occurring secondarily. For what was first said according to the other modes is later related by the evangelists as history. Thus the prophecies of Zacharias and Elizabeth [Col. 0017D] were spoken by them in the prophetic spirit, but Luke, who relates them, narrates them in historical order (Luke 1). Similarly, the evangelists bring the Lord’s proverbs and his simple teaching back to the sequence of history.

“It should be known that history is sometimes narrated in the prophetic spirit, as there: ‘In the beginning God created heaven and earth’ (Gen. 1); and sometimes parabolically, as: ‘A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho’ (Luke 10), and so forth. Prophecy is the disclosure by divine inspiration of hidden things—past, present, and future. Of present things, as there: ‘How has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?’ (Luke 1).

[Col. 0018A] “Of past and future things, where she says: ‘Blessed is she who believed, because the things spoken to her by the Lord shall be fulfilled’ (ibid.). For, by calling her the mother of the Lord, she understood in the present that she bore the Saviour of the world in her womb. By saying, ‘Blessed is she who believed,’ she plainly indicates that through the Spirit she recognized the angel’s words to Mary. By adding, ‘shall be fulfilled,’ she foresaw future things.

“The proverbial mode is figurative speech which seems to say one thing but is understood to mean another, and offers instruction concerning the present time. In it the meaning is taken allegorically, so that the surface of the words is, as it were, removed. We recognize allegory in the Gospel in four ways: by transference, by representation, by comparison, or in the proverbial mode.

[Col. 0018B] “Transference occurs when movements of the soul or human limbs are transferred to God in order to convey meanings. Wherever Sacred Scripture describes in God a head, eyes, eyelids, ears, mouth, lips, tongue, heart, image, womb, hands, right hand, left hand, fingers or finger, arm, wings, shoulders, back parts, feet, likewise movements of the soul—anger, fury, forgetfulness, remembrance, repentance, and other such things—they are not to be understood carnally and literally by those who understand rightly, as they are by Jews and by many heretics who think carnally and suppose God to be corporeal and locally confined. Rather all are to be understood and confessed spiritually of him whose nature is simple and immutable, who is not one thing himself and another thing what he possesses.

[Col. 0018C] “Representation is found in: ‘A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho’; and again in the parable of the vineyard and the husbandmen (Matt. 21). For the order of things done by Christ is recounted, as by an image, as fulfilled in another person and affair. Comparison occurs in: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like mustard seed,’ and so forth (Matt. 13). There no narrative is composed, as in the preceding example, but merely the effects of causes are compared. A proverb occurs, for example: ‘He who does not enter by the door into the sheepfold, but climbs up another way, is a thief and a robber’ (John 10).

“Simple teaching is so called in distinction from the other modes. It teaches faith and morals without composing history, containing prophecy, or employing proverbs; rather, it sometimes commands or forbids, sometimes persuades or dissuades. A command is: ‘Love God and your neighbour’ (Exod. 20). A prohibition is: ‘You shall not kill’ (ibid.). Persuasion is: ‘Sell whatever you have and give to the poor, if you wish to be perfect’ (Luke 18).

[Col. 0018D] “Dissuasion is: ‘Do not swear’ (Matt. 5). The same applies to similar cases.”

Of commands and prohibitions Jerome says in his letter to Cellantia that all righteousness is expressed in them: “Just as evils are prohibited, so goods are commanded. There the mind is restrained; here it is stirred up. There having acted is culpable; here having failed to act is culpable. In any vocation, at any rank, it is an equal sin either to commit prohibited acts or not to do what is commanded.”

The style of evangelical reading is likewise divided into three figures—grand, moderate, and restrained—according to Augustine’s teaching in book IV of *On Christian Doctrine*. For he says: “The same great matter is spoken of restrainedly if it is taught, moderately if it is commended, and grandly if an adverse mind is impelled to conversion.” These modes are most manifest in the Gospel. For evangelical preaching taught the world what it did not know; persuaded it of what it did not wish; and finally compelled it to glory in Christ’s cross (Gal. 6), which was a stumbling-block to Jews and folly to Gentiles (1 Cor. 1).

[Col. 0019A] Bede, on Mark: “It should be noted that, though kindled by one Spirit, the evangelists established different beginnings and different conclusions to their narrative. Matthew, beginning from Christ’s human birth, narrated as far as the resurrection. Mark, beginning from evangelical preaching, proceeded as far as the ascension. Luke, beginning his Gospel from the birth of the Forerunner, ended with the Lord’s ascension, while the disciples awaited the coming of the Holy Spirit. John, from the eternity of the Word of God, reaches as far as the resurrection.”

## Ambrose II on Luke

“John descended from heavenly beginnings to earthly matters, saying when the Word was, how he was, what he was, what he had done, what he was doing, where he was, where he had come, how he had come, at what time he had come, and for what reason he had come. ‘In the beginning was the Word’ (John 1): there you have when he was. ‘And the Word was with God’: there you have how he was; you also have what he was, for he says, ‘the Word was God.’ What he had done: ‘All things were made through him’; what he was doing: ‘He was the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world.’ And where he was: in this world; whither he had come: he came to his own; how he had come: ‘the Word became flesh’; when he had come, John the Baptist says: ‘This is he of whom I said, He who comes after me was made before me; he was before me’; and for what reason he had come, John bears witness: ‘Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world.’”

## Augustine, in *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*

“It must be understood that one evangelist omitted what another narrated, and there is no contradiction in this; nor did they preserve the same order in many matters, and here too there is no opposition.”

Again, in the same work and section: “It is probable that each evangelist believed he ought to narrate in the order in which God willed to suggest the matter to his memory. Therefore, where the order of times does not appear, it should make no difference to us which order any of them followed.”

Again, in the same work and section: “We must commit this to memory: if we should ever find such individual accounts in the several evangelists where contradiction cannot be resolved, we should know that another event occurred, as in Matthew: ‘As Jesus passed from there, two blind men followed him’ (Matthew 9). The two blind men about whom the others narrate are not these; rather, a similar event took place.”

We have also taken up these rules, which are not foreign to the manner of writing, both from Augustine’s *On the Agreement of the Evangelists* and from other authorities.

The evangelists very often recapitulate what has gone before. Thus Matthew, after the sermon delivered on the mountain, brings back into the narrative the man who had been called before the sermon (Matthew 9). And, when recalling the Passion, he inserts the account that Mary poured precious ointment upon the Lord’s head (Matthew 28). The same applies to similar cases.

The evangelists also very often anticipate what is to be said much later. Thus Luke, before the Lord’s baptism, mentions John’s imprisonment (Luke 3); and shortly after the baptism, by anticipation, he places: “Physician, heal yourself; the great things we have heard done at Capernaum, do also here in your own country” (Luke 4). The same applies to similar cases.

In anyone’s words we should attend to nothing except the intention which the words serve. A person does not lie if he expresses in other words what the one whose words he is not repeating intended. Hence Matthew expresses John’s humility and the Lord’s majesty in this way: “Whose sandals I am not worthy to carry” (Matthew 3). Others say: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (Mark 1; Luke 3). Likewise Matthew says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 17); Mark: “You are my beloved Son, in you I am well pleased” (Mark 9); Luke: “You are my beloved Son, in you I am well pleased” (Luke 3, 4). The meaning is the same, and so in similar cases.

Sometimes, according to common usage, names are applied to things by way of opinion, as where it says: “Your father and I, grieving, were seeking you” (Luke 2)—father, that is, the one who was thought to be his father. And where it says: “Give me the head of John the Baptist on a platter. And the king was saddened” (Matthew 14), that is, he was regarded as having been saddened. The same applies to similar cases.

Very often in the Gospel a cause is designated by the name of its effect, as the following examples show: “Come out, deaf and mute spirit” (Mark 9), that is, the spirit that makes a person deaf and mute. “I am the resurrection” (John 11), that is, I make people rise. “Of that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels nor the Son” (Mark 13): the Son does not know, that is, he does not make his own people know. “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times” (Matthew 26), that is, you will have the cause—namely, fear compelling you to deny me three times. Similarly it is said: “Whoever looks at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her” (Matthew 5). “It was the third hour, and they crucified him” (Mark 19), that is, they firmly determined that he should be crucified. The kingdom of heaven is sometimes called the preaching of the Gospel, and sometimes other things by which one reaches the kingdom. The same applies to the rest.

[Col. 0020D] The name of a cause is also used for its effect, as where it says: “What was made in him was life” (John 1), that is, it was preordained by Life, which is the living mind, the primal reasoning of things, and eternity. Again: “The Lord cast demons out of Mary” (Mark 16), that is, the vices which are sent by demons. Again: “I chose you twelve, and one of you is a devil” (John 6), that is, he is the devil’s instrument and servant. Again: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27), that is, may the vengeance whose cause will be the shedding of his blood fall upon us and our children.

## Further rules for reading the Gospel

Of different things placed in the same succession, Scripture often speaks of one and the same matter, as here: “Down to the blood of Zechariah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar” (Matthew 23). They themselves had not killed him, but their fathers had. Again: “I have come in the name of my Father and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John 5), namely Antichrist. Again: “I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28). The same applies to the rest.

Very often a signified thing receives its name from the likeness of the thing signifying it, as where he says: “I am the true vine” (John 15), and then, “I am the vine, you are the branches” (ibid.). So also Christ is called a lamb, a rock or stone, a lion, a calf, an eagle, and by similar names.

A signifying thing is also understood by the name of the thing signified, as where it says: “He saw the heavens opened” (John 1), that is, the things which signified the opening of heaven to those who were baptized. “I saw the Spirit,” that is, the sign of the Spirit, descending like a dove, namely, like the thing that truly was a dove. In this way it is said, “his glory as of the only-begotten” (ibid.), that is, truly the glory of the only-begotten from the Father. Again: “Some of those standing here will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom” (Mark 9), that is, until they see him signifying through the Transfiguration his future coming in the kingdom of glory. Again, when Judas had received the morsel and gone out, Jesus said: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified” (John 13), that is, now the future glorification of the Son of Man has been signified, namely in the separation of the reprobate from the saints. Hence Augustine says to Bishop Boniface: “If the sacraments did not possess a certain likeness to the things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all. From this likeness they often take the names of the things themselves, in accordance with which the sacrament of faith is called faith.” The same applies to similar cases.

The whole is understood from a part, as where it says: “The Word became flesh” (John 1). What is “flesh” here understood to mean except a human being? And, “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isaiah 40): what can this mean except every human being? Similarly: “The Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights” (Matthew 12), that is, within the three periods made up of three days and three nights. Again, “the evening of the Sabbath” (Matthew 28), that is, the night which follows the Sabbath day. Numbers also, which Sacred Scripture commends more prominently, are used, either by themselves or through multiplication, for universality [Col. 0021D], as the number seven is used when it says: “The Lord cast seven demons out of Mary” (Mark 16), that is, all vices. The same applies to the rest.

Sometimes the plural is found in the Gospel in place of the singular. What Matthew and Mark say—“The robbers who were crucified with the Lord reviled him” (Mark 15)—Luke explains thus: “One of the robbers who hung there blasphemed him” (Luke 23). What Luke says, that the soldiers came and offered vinegar, Matthew and Mark say, that one ran and gave him vinegar to drink. A universal expression is also sometimes referred only to the elect, with the multitude of the reprobate silently omitted, as though it did not exist. Hence: “He enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1), meaning everyone who is to be enlightened by eternal light. Again: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12), meaning all things that are to be drawn by me to the vision of the Father. Similar is: “All things that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15), as though he said: You will know through me all things made known to me by the Father in which the salvation of the elect consists.

In divine Scripture, sons and fathers are so called according to imitation, adoption, nature, and teaching. By imitation, all good people are sons of Abraham, while all evil people are sons of the devil. Hence: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8). By adoption: “All peacemakers shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5). By nature, fathers and sons are such as James and John, who were sons of Zebedee. By teaching, there are sons and fathers, in accordance with Paul’s saying: “In Christ Jesus through the Gospel I begot you” (1 Corinthians 4). Thus of those concerning whom the Lord says, “They sit upon Moses’ chair; what they say, do, but what they do, do not do” (Matthew 23), even if they do not beget sons by example, they beget them by teaching.

Brothers too are so called in four ways. By nature, as the James and John mentioned above. By nation, as all Jews are called brothers among themselves. Hence in Exodus: “If you buy your brother who is a Hebrew, or a Hebrew woman, he shall serve you six years; in the seventh you shall let him go free” (Exodus 21). By kinship, as those who belong to one family; hence James the younger is called the Lord’s brother, because he is shown to have been born of Mary, the sister of the Lord’s mother, Cleophas. Brothers are also so called by affection, which is divided into spiritual and common affection. Spiritually, all Christians are called brothers, as in: “Behold how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together” (Psalm 132). Commonly, all human beings are called brothers because they were born from one father. Hence the Apostle says: “If anyone is named a brother who is a fornicator,” and so forth (1 Corinthians 5).

## Christological senses and the divisions of philosophy

In what is read about Christ, Scripture refers some things to his divinity and others to the humanity he assumed, so as to display their distinct properties without confusion. Sometimes it mentions both together, to assert their unity. His divinity is meant by: “Before Abraham was, I am” (John 1). His humanity is meant by: “They will hand him over to the Gentiles to be crucified” (Matthew 20). Both are mentioned where it says: “The Word became flesh” (John 1), followed by, “full of grace and truth” (ibid.). Sometimes statements that seem to concern his humanity must specially be referred to his deity, as: “The Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3). Conversely, things sometimes seem to be attributed to divinity which specially refer to the flesh, as: “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2). Some things are also understood according to Christ’s soul and others according to his body. His soul is meant by: “My food is to do the will of the Father” (John 4), and, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Luke 4); that anointing was spiritual, not bodily. His body is meant by: “The Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12), “When I am lifted up from the earth” (John 12), and, “They have taken my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him” (John 20). In accordance with Paul’s words—“May your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless at the coming of the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 5)—soul and spirit are to be considered in Christ’s humanity. Hence: “He entered into agony” (Luke 22), and, “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26). The voice of the soul is: “Let this cup pass from me” (ibid.); the voice of the Spirit: “If this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done” (ibid.). Christ is also often signified together with his members in one person; then the prudent reader should understand what belongs to the head and what to the body.

It remains now to discuss the disciplines of philosophy.

## Origen on the Song of Songs

“There are three general disciplines: moral, natural, and contemplative. Some have called logic, that is, rational philosophy, a fourth; others have not, saying that it is inserted throughout the whole body of the three mentioned above and cannot be separated from them. As I see it, the Greeks received these from Solomon, and Solomon himself from the Holy Spirit. Solomon therefore, wishing to distinguish these three disciplines, published them in three little books: in Proverbs, the moral discipline; in Ecclesiastes, the natural; in this little book, the contemplative. In this book he also seems to me to have remembered logic, by which the property of each expression is distinguished and in which it is especially fitting for children to be instructed, because one who is trained in these matters necessarily governs himself rationally by what he has learned and recognizes the various forms of speech in the divine words, namely tropes and figurative expressions.

“This threefold form of philosophy was prefigured in the three patriarchs: in Abraham, the moral, through the obedience he showed (Genesis 22); in Isaac, the natural, through digging wells and searching out the depths of things (Genesis 26); in Jacob, the contemplative, through seeing the ladder extended from earth to heaven and the ways of the angels (Genesis 28); hence he was also named Israel.” Thus far Origen.

## Boethius, in his Commentary on Porphyry

Boethius defines and divides philosophy as follows: “Philosophy is love and pursuit of wisdom—not of the wisdom occupied with certain arts and subtle knowledge, but of that which needs nothing, is a living mind, and is the primal reason of things. It is the illumination of an intelligent soul and its withdrawal into itself. Philosophy has two species, theoretical and practical, that is, contemplative and active.

“The theoretical, or contemplative and speculative, has three species: one concerning the intellectible, another concerning the intelligible, and another concerning natural things. The intellectible is that which, remaining one and the same in its own divinity, is grasped not by any senses but solely by mind and understanding. This concerns the contemplation of God and the incorporeality of the soul; the Greeks call this part theology. The second part is intelligible: it embraces intellectible understanding. It concerns all rational souls which, through contact with heavenly and earthly bodies, have declined from intellectible things to intelligible things, and are happier whenever they apply themselves to intellectible things. The third species concerns knowledge of bodies and is called natural philosophy. Intelligible things are rightly placed in the middle, because they possess both the animation of bodies and the contemplation of intellectible things.

“Practical, or active, philosophy likewise has three species. The first, caring for itself, raises, adorns, and increases itself through every virtue, admitting nothing in life over which it would not rejoice and doing nothing of which it would repent. The second undertakes care of the commonwealth and ministers to the welfare of all through prudent care, the balance of justice, the steadfastness of courage, and the endurance of temperance. The third arranges and distributes the duties of the household in moderate order. There are other subdivisions of these, but for now we should refrain from pursuing them.” Thus far Boethius.

We may call the first practical species solitary, the second public, and the third domestic. Solitary practice is reflected in the fact that Jesus led a solitary life in the desert for forty days, went up the mountain to pray, spent the night in prayer (Luke 6), and, when they wanted to seize him and make him king, fled (John 6); after dismissing the crowd, he went up the mountain alone to pray, and in the other acts by which the singular perfection of his holiness is made clear. Domestic practice is reflected in: “Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I, grieving, were looking for you”; he went down with them to Nazareth and was subject to them (Luke 2). It is also reflected when, after dismissing the crowds, he explained parables to his disciples, sometimes rebuked and sometimes praised them, and from the cross entrusted his mother to a disciple. The same applies to similar cases.

Public practice is indicated in parables, as: “There was a householder who planted a vineyard and surrounded it with a hedge” (Matthew 21), and: “Whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the door but climbs in another way is a thief and a robber” (John 10). The same applies to other examples. For in parables understanding is twofold: principally one must understand what is received by likeness, but this cannot be done unless one also understands what the force of the words signifies according to ordinary usage. Such matters properly concern common practical life, as the discernment involved in sowing, lest seed fall beside the road and the birds of heaven eat it, or fall on rocky ground and dry up in the sun, or among thorns and be choked by them, but, falling on good soil, bear fruit (Mark 4). The same applies to the rest. Public practice should also be considered wherever the Lord teaches everyone generally about morals. In accordance with the foregoing, some virtues are political, some purgative, and some belong to the purified soul.

## Ambrose on Luke

As for theoretical philosophy, the Gospel pertains to it through the intellectible species called theology wherever it indicates divinity, whether through words or miracles—that is, wherever it reveals the Trinity and proves Christ to be true God. Through the intelligible species the Gospel reading makes us theoretical wherever Christ is proved to be true man and souls are taught to attend to themselves, considering their animation in bodies and their contemplation of eternal things. To natural philosophy pertains the statement: “Do you not understand that everything entering the mouth goes into the belly and is cast out into the sewer?” (Matthew 15; Mark 7).

Ambrose, on Luke: “There are three things which the philosophers of this world considered pre-eminent: namely, that wisdom is threefold, either rational, natural, or moral. We can observe these three in the Old Testament. What else do those three wells signify—one of vision, another of oath, and the third of abundance—except that this threefold virtue existed in the patriarchs? The well of vision is rational, because reason sharpens the mind’s sight and cleanses the soul’s vision. The well of oath is natural wisdom, which comprehends and affirms the things of nature as though by oath, when the Lord of nature, that is, God, is introduced as witness of faith. The well of abundance is ethical, because, when the Philistines, whose figure represents bodily vices, withdrew, Isaac found a living stream of water (Genesis 26). Good morals flow pure, and goodness itself, public (*popularis*; [*pluralis*, ‘of many’]), abounds for others while more restrained for itself.

“What else do Solomon’s three books show except that Solomon was skilled in this threefold wisdom? He wrote of ethics in Proverbs, of natural matters in Ecclesiastes—for creation has been subjected to vanity (Romans 8)—and of wondrous and rational things in the Song of Songs, because when the love of the heavenly Word is poured into our souls and the holy mind is joined to reason, wondrous mysteries are revealed.

“Do you think wisdom was lacking in the evangelists? Though they are filled with various kinds of wisdom, each excels in a different kind. Natural wisdom is in John, who found the Word in the beginning (John 1), transcending angels and the powers of heaven. Matthew, following each detail according to the human order, gave us moral precepts for living. Mark, rationally, thought it should be placed immediately at the beginning: ‘Behold, I send my angel’ (Mark 1), and, ‘the voice of one crying in the wilderness’ (ibid.), to arouse wonder and teach in John the Baptist the humility that pleased God. Luke, however, kept the order of a historian, embracing every kind of wisdom.

“It belongs to natural wisdom that he revealed the Holy Spirit, the Creator, also to have been the author of the Lord’s incarnation (Luke 1). Hence David, teaching natural wisdom, says: ‘Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created’ (Psalm 103). He teaches morals in the Beatitudes and shows in the Lord’s sermon that even an enemy must be loved (Luke 6). He teaches rational matters when he says: ‘Whoever is faithful in the least is faithful also in the greater’ (Luke 16). Thus spiritual wisdom possesses every principality that human prudence falsely claims for itself, especially since the mystery of the Trinity itself cannot exist without this principality. Naturally the Father begot the Son; morally the Son became obedient to the Father unto death; rationally the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, pouring into human hearts the reason for worshiping the divine and governing life.”

The divisions of philosophy made by Ambrose and Boethius mutually include one another. Moral philosophy contains the three species of practical philosophy; rational, that is, contemplative, philosophy contains the intellectible and the intelligible. Natural philosophy is the same as physiology.

## Augustine, in his Letter to Volusianus

“From these two commandments—‘You shall love God and your neighbor’ (Matthew 5)—Christ says that the whole Law and the Prophets depend. Here there is physics, because the causes of all natures are in God the Creator. Here there is ethics, because a good and honorable life is formed nowhere else than when the things that ought to be loved are loved as they ought to be loved—that is, God and neighbor. Here there is logic, because God alone is the truth and light of the rational soul. Here also is the admirable welfare of the commonwealth. For the best city is neither founded nor preserved except on the foundation and bond of faith and firm concord, when the common good is loved, which is God, the highest and truest good, and when people sincerely love one another in him, since they love one another for his sake, and cannot hide from him with what spirit they love.

“The same point is made in the eighth book of *The City of God*. Perhaps those who praise Plato for understanding more sharply than the other philosophers of the nations have thought something of this kind about God: in him are found the cause of existing, the reason of understanding, and the order of living, of which one is understood to belong to the natural, another to the rational, and the third to the moral part. If the human being was created so that, through what is highest in him, he might reach what is highest of all—namely, the one true and supremely good God, without whom no nature exists, no teaching instructs, and no use is effective—then God himself should be sought, where all things are secure for us; God himself should be seen, where all things are certain for us; God himself should be loved, where all things are right for us. Plato therefore rightly said that the wise person is an imitator, knower, and lover of this God, by participation in whom he becomes blessed. He rightly declared God to be the highest good and wanted the philosopher to be a lover of God, so that, since philosophy tends toward the blessed life, the one who enjoys God may be blessed.

“It must be understood that, although Christians do not use the terms of certain philosophers—physics, that is, natural philosophy; logic, that is, rational philosophy; or ethics, that is, moral philosophy—they nevertheless know that from the one true and supremely good God we have nature, by which we were made in his image; teaching, by which we know him and ourselves; and grace, by which, cleaving to him, we are blessed. Therefore, whether Platonists or any others, once they have known God, have found in him the cause by which the universe is established, the light by which truth is perceived, and the fountain of living happiness: when they think these things about God, they think with us.”

## Why the Gospel was written

[Col. 0027A] Let us now consider the reasons why the Gospel was written. Jerome, in his *Argument before the Gospels*: “Especially for the sake of those who had believed in Jesus from among the Jews but were in no way observing the shadow of the Law, as the truth of the Gospel followed, Matthew published his Gospel. Before he passed with the other apostles to the Gentiles, he confirmed in writing for the churches of Judea what he had preached by word, lest false preachers and corrupters of the churches should sow errors over them.”

The same author, in the same work: “When John was in Asia and the seeds of the heretics Ebion and others were sprouting, he was compelled by the bishops of Asia to write about the Savior’s divinity. Ecclesiastical history tells that, when he was urged by the brothers to write, he replied that he would do so if, after a fast had been proclaimed, all together prayed to God. When this was completed, he poured forth: ‘In the beginning was the Word,’ and so forth.”

Bede, on Mark: “When the light of God had arisen for the city of Rome through the preaching of the Apostle Peter, the minds of the hearers were so delighted by the divine word that they could never be satisfied by it. Therefore they asked Mark, his disciple, to commit to writing what Peter preached, so that at home and abroad they might continue in meditation on such words. Peter was greatly pleased by this.” Clement, in Book IV of his *Institutions*, describes these events in the same way.

Bede, on Luke: “In his prologue Luke signifies that his chief reason for writing the Gospel was to prevent false evangelists from having the opportunity to preach falsehood, men who, under the name of the apostles, tried to introduce sects of unbelief. Thus some are found falsely to have prefixed to their writings the name of Thomas, others of Bartholomew, some of Matthias, and others the title of the twelve apostles. Basilides and Apelles also, one of whom taught that there were 365 heavens and the other two mutually opposed gods, among other abominable doctrines, left behind Gospels polluted by the error of their names. Among these it should be observed that the Gospel called ‘according to the Hebrews,’ which the Nazarenes use, should be counted not among the apocrypha but among ecclesiastical histories. For Jerome himself, interpreter of Sacred Scripture, thought it right to take many testimonies from it and translate it into Latin and Greek. Luke refutes the false Gospels in his preface.” Thus far Bede.

Since, besides the four books of the Gospel, the Church receives a fifth used by the Nazarenes, it does not seem unreasonable for us to receive the Gospel in summary form in a single work by Bishop Theophilus, or Tatian, or Ammonius of Alexandria, or any other person who composes one account from the four narratives in a suitable order. For a theology of the Gospel, let us place before it a brief introduction, to be believed both from the testimonies of the saints and from the judgments of teachers.

## Alcuin, *On the Trinity*, book II, chapter 11

“What always was and always is is either unbegotten or begotten, or neither unbegotten nor begotten. These are three, eternally three. The unbegotten is the Father alone, who receives from no one what he is, except from himself. The begotten is the Son, whose being what he is comes from the Father. What is neither unbegotten nor begotten is the Holy Spirit, whose being consists in proceeding from the Father and the Son. These three are truly one Trinity, consubstantial and co-eternal. Since begetting is one thing, being born another, and proceeding another, distinct from begetting or being born, it is clear that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. Trinity therefore refers to the persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; unity pertains to the nature of the eternal Godhead.”

## Justinian, in the Edict of Faith

“In three subsistences or persons we adore one Godhead or nature, substance and power, distinguishing the properties but uniting the Godhead. Again, we must confess one God, one nature or substance and form, and proclaim three subsistences or three persons, each with its own property.
