“The Wisdom of God is called the Word, both because nothing in the substance of its nature is visible or bodily, and because through it the Father founded or commanded all things, and because through it the Father was made known.”

## Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, chapter 23

“When God is called wise, and is called wise from wisdom—without which it is wicked to believe that he ever was or could be—he is not called wise by participation in wisdom, as a soul may be wise or not wise, but because he himself begot the wisdom by which he is called wise.”

Again, in the same work, chapter 16: “God is the cause of all things that exist. Since he is the cause of all things, he is also the cause of his wisdom. God is never without his wisdom. Therefore he is the eternal cause of his eternal wisdom. Further, if being Father is eternal in God, and he was never at any time not Father, he was never without the Son. The Son therefore has always been begotten, because he is always Son. He is not only the image of the Father because he is from him, and likeness because he is the image, but also an equality so complete that not even an interval of time is an obstacle. For through him times were created.”

## Augustine and Alypius, in a letter to Maximus, physician of Thamugadi

“Just as a flame does not precede in time the brightness it generates, so the Father was never without the Son. He is the Wisdom of God the Father, of whom it is written: ‘He is the brightness of eternal light’ (Wisdom 7). He is therefore undoubtedly co-eternal with the light whose brightness he is, that is, with God the Father. Thus it is not said, ‘In the beginning God created heaven and earth’ (Genesis 1), that in the beginning he made the Word, but, ‘In the beginning was the Word’ (John 1).”

Again, in the same letter: “The Father begot the Son from himself in such a way that he remained wholly in himself and was in the Son as great as he is alone. Likewise, by proceeding, the Holy Spirit neither diminishes him nor, by abiding in him, increases him. The whole Trinity is therefore as great in the Father alone, or in the Son alone, or in the Holy Spirit alone, as it is together in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Therefore God must in no way be called threefold.”

[Col. 0029C] Jerome, in *Whosoever Will*: “God the Father begot God the Son, neither by will nor by necessity, but by nature.” Gregory, *Morals on Job*, XXIII: “In that the Father begot the perfect Word, he spoke; in that he always begets, he speaks. The only-begotten Son of God is said to have been born with respect to perfection, and is declared always to be born with respect to eternity.” Augustine, Book XVI of *The City of God*: “For God’s utterance before his work is the unchangeable rational principle of that work: it has no noisy and passing sound, but a power that remains eternally and works in time.” Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*, chapter XXX, on John chapter II: “Just as we know the Father alone to be always unbegotten and without beginning, so we confess the Son always to have been begotten from the Father and without beginning. Nothing except this makes a division of the persons: the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten; the one is Father, the other Son.” The same, Book XV of *On the Holy Trinity*, chapter XXVI: “That the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son is evident from what the Apostle says: ‘God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts’ [Gal. 4]. And when he had risen and appeared to the disciples, he breathed on them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ [John 20].” The same, in the same chapter: “Although we do not call the Holy Spirit begotten, we nevertheless do not dare call him unbegotten, lest someone suppose that there are either two fathers in that Trinity, or two who are not from another.” The same, in the same work, chapter XVIII: “Just as we properly call the one Word of God by the name Wisdom, although both the Holy Spirit and the Father are wisdom, so the Holy Spirit is properly designated by the term love, although the Father and Son are love. Most rightly the Holy Spirit is also called the gift of God.”

Enipius, from Augustine’s sayings in an exposition of the Decalogue: “No sanctification is divine and true except from the Holy Spirit. For it is not without reason that he is properly called the Holy Spirit, although the Father too is holy and the Son holy. This proper name was received by the Spirit so that the third person in the Trinity might be called the Holy Spirit.”

Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter XIII: “God’s grace was therefore to be signified through the Holy Spirit, because he is so God as also to be called God’s gift.”

[Col. 0030B] The same, Book V of *On the Holy Trinity*, chapter II: “Other essences or substances admit accidents, by which change occurs in them; but God does not.”

The same, chapter V: “Although being Father and being Son are different, the substance is not different, because these are not said according to substance but according to relation. Yet this relation is not an accident, because it is not mutable.”

The same, Book IX, chapter IV: “Mind, its love, and its knowledge are three things. And these three are one. When they are perfect, they are equal. Love and knowledge, or cognition, are not present in the mind as though in a subject; rather, they too are substantial, just as the mind is. For when the mind knows itself wholly, it knows itself perfectly; and [Col. 0030C] when it loves itself perfectly, its love is throughout its whole being.”

The same, in a sermon on the Old and New Scriptures against the Arians: “In the sun there are three things which cannot at all be separated: the sun, brightness, and heat. Fire likewise has three indivisible things: motion, light, and heat. If, then, as a heretic, you cannot divide the creature, how will you be able to divide the Creator? You have in the Psalm: ‘By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power’ [Ps. 32].”

The same, against Arius: “Let us understand God as far as we can: good without quality, great without quantity, Creator without need, present without position, wholly everywhere without place, eternal without time, making mutable things without changing himself, suffering nothing. If anyone thinks of God thus and still cannot discover what he is, let him nevertheless devoutly beware, as far as he can, of thinking anything about him that he is not.”

From the foregoing and very many other ordinances of the holy Fathers, some say that by the name Father is designated the power of the divine majesty, by which God can effect whatever he wills. For God cannot do unjust things, because he himself is supreme justice and goodness. By the title Son, or Word, they understand God’s wisdom to be signified, by which he can discern all things so that he can be utterly deceived in nothing. By the designation Holy Spirit is understood God’s very love or benevolence, by which, namely, he wills all things to be done and ordered in the best way.

[Col. 0031A] Thus it is a description of the highest good, whose fullness lacks nothing: a distinction of omnipotence, supreme wisdom, and supreme goodness. For all things said of God are contained in these three. That he is called ineffable, unchangeable, unfailing, eternal, belongs to power. For to be capable of change or failure belongs to impotence. Again, that he is provident, foreknowing, and measured belongs to wisdom; for to know things themselves only from their outcomes or effects is human foolishness. That he is called kind, merciful, and compassionate belongs to goodness, though “compassionate” is said more from the exercise of mercy than from goodness. So too with the rest.

Certainly, this distinction of the Trinity greatly advances our devotion in divine worship; and for this reason especially divine Wisdom itself, incarnate, decreed to employ it in its preaching. For there are two things that make us wholly subject to God: fear and love. Power and wisdom chiefly instill fear, when we perceive God to be judge, know that he can punish whatever he wills, and recognize that nothing is hidden from him. Benevolence, however, belongs to love, so that we may love most especially him whom we hold to be most kind. From this one may also observe that he wills to avenge impiety: for the more justice pleases him, the more injustice displeases him, according to the saying: “You loved righteousness and hated iniquity” [Ps. 54].

Again, this distinction of the Trinity is highly effective for commending all [Col. 0031C] God’s works: whatever he does should be believed to be excellently done, since he can effect whatever he wills, knows how to preserve measure in all things, and wills all things to be done or to proceed in the best way. Hence the works of the whole Trinity are called undivided—that is, common—because whatever power performs, wisdom governs and goodness brings into being. Therefore, in the things we do, or ask God to do, we fittingly make mention of the Trinity, saying: “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” or, “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity,” so that, as the operation of the three persons is undivided, their invocation too may be inseparable.

Thus Moses, after first saying, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” [Gen. 1], added: “And the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” [ibid.]. In God the Creator, he intimates the Father and fittingly recalls the divine power by which he could create all things from nothing. For the name *God* is interpreted “fear,” and the reverence of fear is shown especially to power. By the name “beginning,” however, he designates the Son—that is, the divine reason or wisdom—in which all things in some manner first had their subsistence through providence before they came into the effect of works. By “the Spirit of the Lord” he plainly intimates the Holy Spirit, that is, the goodness of divine grace.

In the creation of humankind, too, he did not say, “I shall make humankind,” but “Let us make humankind” [ibid.], in order to designate the plurality of the Trinity. Yet although the whole Trinity has one power, one wisdom, one goodness, and one and the same operation, those things assigned to power are specially attributed to the Father; those pertaining to wisdom, to the Son; and those belonging to goodness, to the Holy Spirit, as is shown by the examples set below.

[Col. 0032A] The Son says: “Which the Father has placed in his own power” [Acts 1]. And elsewhere: “As my Father has appointed for me” [Luke 22]. Whenever the Son’s humanity itself implores the aid of the divinity united to it, or pours forth prayers to it, it uses the title Father alone, recalling, that is, the power by which God is able to effect what is asked; as when it is said: “Holy Father, keep them” [John 17]; “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” [Luke 23]; and similar expressions belonging to prayer. Hence the Church’s practice directs its speech to the Father alone in the special prayers offered in celebrations of the Mass.

Likewise, when the Apostle says that the Father raised Jesus from the dead, will make our bodies alive, sent the Son or the Holy Spirit, or that the Son obeyed him—when, I say, he says such things—he ascribes in a proper and special sense to the Father’s distinctive property those things that seem to pertain to power. So also, things relating to reason or wisdom are specially assigned to the person of the Son, according to the saying: “The Father has given all judgment to the Son” [John 5]. For the power of Wisdom takes precedence in the discrimination of judgment, where equity must be examined more than force and power exercised. The further statement, “because he is the Son of Man,” declares that judgment especially rests on this fact: among their other evils, the impious rejected even the Son sent by the Father. Hence the Son says: [Col. 0032C] “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” [John 15].

The Psalm’s superscription, “for the hidden things of the Son” [Ps. 9], also pertains to this; that is, to the judgments of which it is said: “Your judgments are a great deep” [Ps. 35]. For, as has been said, it belongs to wisdom to judge—that is, to know what is due to each person in justice. The Apostle calls Christ “the power of God and the wisdom of God” [1 Cor. 1]: wisdom, indeed, by which he knows all things completely; power, by which he brings the efficacy of all good things to completion. Hence: “All things were made through him” [John 1]; and elsewhere: “You made all things in wisdom” [Ps. 103]. Thus he is called the Father’s right hand or hand, through whom the Father works all things. He is also fittingly called the Father’s mind, reason, or Angel of Counsel, because in this wisdom the Father rationally orders all things, whether creating the world or repairing it after its fall. And in this the Father gave true counsel to our ignorance when the incarnation of Wisdom visited us.

The operation of divine grace, however, and all things that more clearly concern the goodness of divine love, are ascribed to the Holy Spirit—for example, the remission of sins and the distribution of every good thing that proceeds from his goodness rather than from our merits. Hence we are said to be regenerated “by water and the Spirit” [John 1], not by water and the Father or the Son, although the operation of the whole Trinity in each case is the same.

[Col. 0033A] Finally, all the sacraments performed in the Church through God’s goodness must be attributed to the Spirit, so that it may plainly appear from this that the affection of the Father’s majesty—that is, the sweetness of divine goodness—is expressed by the name Holy Spirit. For through the spirit of our mouth—that is, through breath—the emotions of the mind are especially disclosed: when, for example, we sigh from love or groan under the distress of grief or labor. Therefore in this place “spirit” is used for a good affection, according to that saying of Wisdom: “The spirit of wisdom is kindly” [Wis. 1]; and in the Psalm: “Your good Spirit shall lead me” [Ps. 152]; and the Apostle: “God is love” [1 John 4]. For, as Gregory attests, spirit itself is love: by this love, according to John, the Father loves the Son; and hence the Holy Spirit is a certain communion of Father and Son. He is also called the eternal gift of both, that is, capable of being given; but “given” temporally.

The vigilance of learned doctors offers the following traces of this Trinity, of the Son’s generation from the Father, and of the Spirit’s procession from both.

Augustine, Book XI of *The City of God*: “In every creature these three questions are asked: who made it, through what he made it, and why he made it. The Father, therefore, is he who made all things through the Son, for the sake of his goodness. Since this goodness is understood as the Holy Spirit, the Trinity is made known to us. For in creating, the immensity of things chiefly displays power; in governing created things, wisdom; and in bringing them to the best outcome, benevolence is manifested from the creatures themselves.”

[Col. 0033C] Likewise: “From our mind is born wisdom, which is in the mind itself; and from mind and wisdom proceeds love, by which the mind itself loves the wisdom it has begotten from itself. These three are together in the one indivisible substance of the soul.”

Likewise: “As is apparent in the sun, from the substance of fire the force of fiery heat is born, and brightness proceeds from it in the same substance.”

Likewise: “An image made from bronze for sealing—what is an image, that is, bronze thus formed—derives from bronze as from matter; and that which is sealable or seals proceeds from both. Therefore, in one and the same essence there are three things distinct in property: for it is one thing to be this bronze, another to be this image, and [Col. 0033D] another to be this sealable thing. Knowledge or wisdom, since it is the power of discerning, necessarily requires power for its own existence; but power does not require wisdom. This may readily be seen from the analogy of matter and that which is made from matter. For since a statue consists of bronze and form, bronze does not require a statue for its existence; but a statue requires bronze. Thus one might, improperly and figuratively, say that the statue has been born or produced from bronze, and that every thing made of matter is from matter. From power and wisdom proceeds the affection of good will, because, when these require it, we consequently will to do what we can and know how to do, unless vice prevents us, if we recognize that it ought to be done.

“But what is the purpose of the analogies proposed? Will anyone presume to explain the generation [Col. 0034A] of the Son from the Father and the procession of the Spirit from both? For Jerome, in *Whosoever Will*, and Ambrose, in the book *On the Trinity*, say: ‘How the Father begot the Son, even angels do not know.’ But perhaps you will suppose that this was said because power, to which all things are possible, is incomprehensible; and wisdom, which sees all things and discerns each individual thing, is incomprehensible; and moreover its generation, insofar as it is eternal, is beyond understanding.

“Yet perhaps, according to the analogies set forth above, you will suppose this can easily be understood, and say: Since wisdom, because it is the power of discernment, is that which is from power itself, divine wisdom is said, metaphorically, to be born or begotten from divine power and is called Son, insofar as sons are, as it were, the express images of their fathers and possess mutual love. And divine power, because wisdom is from it, is of course metaphorically called Father. For very many names are transferred from creatures to the Creator.

“But this must firmly be known: the one God is one power, from whom are all things. He is not called omnipotence or omnipotent as though by an aggregation of powers, but because he can do all that he wills. Therefore the Son, through whom are all things, is omnipotence equally with the Father, since he is divine power insofar as he is the power of discerning and governing all things. Do not marvel that God can do all things by one power, see and order all things by one act of mind, and embrace all things with one affection of benevolence, when you too see the moon, stars, and other such diverse things with one glance of the eye.

[Col. 0034C] “The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son because God wills all that he does precisely because he can and knows. This procession consists in the extension of the benevolent affection of divinity, from power and wisdom, to the creation and governance of things and to the distribution of graces. For God eternally wills that all things which he accomplishes in time should come to be, and his will is the cause of all good things. Therefore this affection of divinity, considered in relation to creatures, proceeds from the Father and also proceeds from the Son: not as born, but as given through grace conferred upon creatures. The Son, however, proceeds from the Father as born.

“Since, then, God’s goodness is the cause of all divine creation and cooperates with power and wisdom in every divine operation, it is clear from the authorities stated above that the three subsistences, or persons—that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are of one essence, one majesty, one indivisible nature, and eternal Godhead. Although being powerful, being wise, and being benevolent are different, yet because these three, distinct in their properties, are of one substance of divinity in God, it is evident that the whole Trinity is supreme power, the whole is supreme wisdom, and the whole is supreme goodness. For to say that God is power, wisdom, and goodness is no different from saying that God is powerful, wise, and benevolent. For he is powerful, wise, and good not by participation but by nature.

[Col. 0034D] Therefore, in respect of substance, what the Father is, the Son and Holy Spirit are also, and conversely. Relation, however, prevents us from saying that he who is Father is Son or Holy Spirit, or that he who is Son is Father or Holy Spirit. For one person is not another, although he is the very same thing as the other. For the property of power is one thing, the property of wisdom another, and the property of goodness another; so the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another.

“Note here that the Father has one property, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another: some things are true of the Father alone, others of the Son alone, and others of the Holy Spirit alone. When we say that it is a property of the Holy Spirit that he is neither begotten nor unbegotten, we do not say that this property is either substance or accident. Likewise, it is a property of the Father—that is, it is properly said of the Father alone—that he is neither born nor proceeding.

[Col. 0035B] “Thus, because it is false that the Father is the Son or the Son the Father, it is false that God begot himself. But because one person begot another—the Father, namely, the Son—God begot God, and he is God from God, light from light. Likewise, since the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and Son, God proceeds from God, but neither from himself nor from another. Not from another, because there is only one God; nor from himself, because the person proceeding is not the one from whom he proceeds. The Father is related to the Son, the Son to the Father, and the Spirit to both jointly.”

Augustine, Book V of *On the Trinity*, chapter XIV: “Just as the Father and Son are one God and, in relation to creation, one Creator, so, in relation to [Col. 0035C] the Holy Spirit, they are one principle. In relation to creation, however, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one principle, just as they are one Creator. It should therefore be known that, if a coin, without being changed itself, begins to be the price of the thing bought, much more does God, without changing himself, begin to be Creator when creatures first come into being; he begins to be Lord when a creature begins to serve him; and he begins to be compassionate when there is first someone on whom he may have compassion. He was eternally immense, just, and merciful, but in relation to creatures he is called Creator, Lord, and compassionate.”

Likewise Augustine, *On the Trinity*: “Insofar as the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Spirit proceeding, neither equality nor inequality is considered. But insofar as the persons are one God, one nature, one substance, they are coequal and consubstantial with one another. Although, therefore, the Son is from the Father, he is neither later than nor inferior to the Father, but coeternal and co-omnipotent. So too the Holy Spirit: although he is from the Father and Son, he is in no way lesser or [Col. 0036A] later, but consubstantial, coeternal, and co-omnipotent.

It should be noted that “person” is used in several senses. A person is an individual rational substance, as any human being is. In rhetoric, however, a person is anyone brought into controversy on account of a particular saying or deed. In grammar, person is described thus: “A person is one who speaks to another, one to whom another speaks, or one about whom some speak.” Therefore, when it happens that the same person speaks to another, speech is addressed to him, and speech is made about him, then one and the same thing is first, second, and third person. Yet the first is not second or third, nor conversely.

In God, however, a person is either unbegotten, begotten, or neither unbegotten [Col. 0036B] nor begotten. Therefore the one and same divine substance is three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, such that the Father is not the Son or Holy Spirit, nor conversely.

And it should be known that persons in the Godhead are called persons not by relation, but in themselves.

Augustine, Book VII of *On the Trinity*, chapter VI: “To be God and to be person are not different things, but entirely the same. Nor, when in this Trinity we speak of the person of the Father, do we say anything other than the substance of the Father. Therefore, just as the Father himself is the substance of the Father—not in respect of that whereby he is Father, but whereby he is—so also the person of the Father is nothing other than the Father himself. For person is said in relation to itself, not to the Son or Holy Spirit. Why, then, do we not call these three together one person, just as we call them one essence and one God? It is because we wish one particular term to serve for that signification by which the Trinity is understood, so that we might not be entirely silent when asked, ‘What three?’ although we confess that there are three.”

Thus far concerning the unity of the divine essence and the properties of the persons, according to the judgment of the masters and the assertions of the saints.

## BRIEF EPILOGUE

The nature of the highest good is, above all things, simple.

This same nature is the Father, the Begotten One, and the goodness of both.

The Father is light and source, supreme power not born.

The brightness, image of the Father, Word, is Wisdom born.

The goodness of both is the gift of Father and Begotten.

[Col. 0036D] The Father, or the Begotten One, or the gift of the two, is as great

as is the Son with the Father and their Spirit.

Thus God is by no means threefold, but three-in-one and one.

Three in persons; in nature eternal and one.

Therefore the three persons do everything that God does.

## THE SAME AUTHOR’S SECOND PREFACE, BRIEFLY OUTLINING THE LIVES OF THE FOUR EVANGELISTS

[Col. 0035]

[Col. 0035D] Matthew, surnamed Levi, whose calling to God was from the occupations of tax collectors, was the first to write the Gospel in the Hebrew [Col. 0036D] language in Judaea. In Christ’s genealogy he took the beginnings of two men: one whose first circumcision was in the flesh; the other whose election was according to the heart. Thus, arranging the number fourteen in threefold fashion, he extends the beginning from faith in belief to the time of election, directs it from election to the day of the deportation, and concludes from the day of deportation to Christ, displaying the genealogy traced through the Lord’s coming.

Then Mark, God’s evangelist, Peter’s son in baptism and disciple in the divine word, a Levite by birth, wrote the Gospel in Greek in Italy, showing in it what he owed both to his lineage and to Christ. For, by establishing the beginning of evangelical preaching in the voice of prophetic proclamation, he displayed the order of Levitical election. He foretold John, the son of Zechariah, as sent forth in the voice of the angel proclaiming [Col. 0037B] the Word made flesh, and the Lord’s body animated by the word of the divine voice, so that in himself the flesh might find the Word which it had lost amid consonants [reading uncertain].

Beginning to preach God from the Lord’s baptism, he set forth the fasting in the wilderness, the Devil’s temptation, the gathering of beasts, the ministry of angels, and the rest so compactly that he neither diminished the authority of the event nor denied the fullness of the work’s accomplishment. Finally, after embracing the faith, he is said to have cut off his thumb so that he might be considered unfit for the priesthood. But election, predestined in accordance with faith, had such power that he did not thereby lose in the work of the Word what he had earlier merited by birth. For he was the first bishop of Alexandria, since in each action he knew both how to order within himself the things said in the Gospel, recognize the discipline of the Law, and understand the divine nature in the Lord’s flesh. There he died and was buried in Nero’s eighth year.

Luke, however, a Syrian of Antioch, a physician by profession, disciple of the apostles, and afterward follower of Paul up to Paul’s passion, serving the Lord blamelessly, wrote the Gospel in Achaia after Matthew and Mark, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit. Beyond what the order of Gospel arrangement requires, the chief necessity of his labor was first to work for Greek believers, lest, intent on Jewish fables, they should be held fast in the desire for the Law alone, [Col. 0038A] or, deceived by heretical fables, fall away from the truth. Then he intended, by taking up John’s birth at the beginning of the Gospel, to indicate for whom he was writing, testifying that those things had been fulfilled in him which many had presumptuously begun.

Not undeservedly was Luke also given the grace of writing the Acts of the Apostles, as one whose every word is medicine for the languishing soul. Having never had wife or children, he died in Bithynia at the age of eighty-four, full of the Holy Spirit.

John, apostle and evangelist, a virgin chosen by God, whom he called from his wedding when he was about to marry, wrote the Gospel in Asia after all the others, after he had written the Apocalypse on the island of Patmos [Rev. 1]. [Col. 0038B] A twofold testimony to his virginity is given in the Gospel: he is called especially beloved by God, and from the cross Christ entrusted his mother to him, so that a virgin might preserve the Virgin [John 1]. Finally, in the Gospel he reveals what he himself was: alone, he began the work of the incorruptible Word, testifying that the Word was made flesh and that the light was not comprehended by darkness [John 1]. He places first the sign which God performed at the wedding, so that, when the old things were changed, all the new things instituted by Christ might appear.

Accordingly, he for whom there was an incorruptible beginning in Genesis at the beginning of the canon is also granted an incorruptible end through the virgin in the Apocalypse, Christ saying: “I am Alpha and Ω” [Rev. 1; 22]. This is John, who, knowing that the day of his departure had come, summoned his disciples in Ephesus, descended into the excavated place of his burial, prayed, and was laid with his fathers in the sixty-eighth year after the Lord’s passion, as free from the pain of death as he was untouched by the corruption of flesh.

Therefore it is highly useful for those who desire God to know in the Gospel the first things, the intermediate things, and the perfect things in such a way that, reading throughout, they may understand both the Gospel’s work and the love of God born in flesh, and may recognize in it that for which they have been apprehended and which they seek to apprehend.

## THE SAME AUTHOR’S THIRD PREFACE

[Col. 0037]

[Col. 0037D] Ammonius of Alexandria, who is also said to have invented the Gospel canons, composed with illustrious care one Gospel from the sayings of the four evangelists. Eusebius of Caesarea, in the letter prefixed to the edition in which he published the aforementioned Gospel canons, wrote to Carpianus in imitation of that man’s endeavor. Tatian also, a most learned man endowed with elegant eloquence, whose commendation blessed Jerome did not omit in his book *On Illustrious Men*, compiled one Gospel from four, as ecclesiastical history relates, and published splendid books against the gentiles. While blessed Justin the philosopher and martyr was still alive, Tatian was his disciple. Later, however, puffed up with doctrinal arrogance, he rushed into heresies.

Indeed, if this heresiarch’s Gospel work, which perhaps he composed while closely attached to blessed Justin, had survived, nothing would prevent one from safely reading it and carefully embracing in it the words of the Lord Jesus, whose voice his sheep recognize. For just as sacraments are received by evil people without their being corrupted, so the words or sayings of truth, whether spoken or written, cannot in the least be deprived of their proper tenor by heretics. Hence the perversity of Origen’s errors did not at all disfigure those aspects in which his scholarship shone. Likewise, [Col. 0039A] the monstrous character of Solomon’s life in no way obscured the wisdom—indeed, God’s wisdom—in him. Very many examples make it plainly evident that truth will not be rejected because of falsehood.

Moreover, Father Jerome, introducing Theophilus’s expositions in a homily on the unjust steward, bestowed this praise upon him: “Theophilus, seventh bishop of the Church of Antioch after the apostle Peter, left us monuments of his genius by combining the sayings of the four evangelists into one work.”

Blessed Augustine likewise, in the second book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, making one narrative from diverse sayings insofar as seemed good to him, says: “Whether by this example, either as I have done it, or in some other manner it may be done more conveniently, let each person see; and let him see that it can be done in other places also.” By his example and persuasion, then, some perhaps have outlined a single narrative from the four. But who was the author—indeed, the arranger—of this work is of no importance to know. For both the words and the meanings belong only to the evangelists. For Matthew’s sayings are joined with excerpts from the other three—something which anyone who investigates can easily discover—by a marvelous art, and even more marvelously by brevity.

Eusebius writes to Carpianus that the aforesaid Ammonius did this. Receive, therefore, worshipper of Christ, in this natural work—or, if you can more conveniently, in another—the “word shortened” which the Lord accomplished upon the earth [Rom. 9]. Gather, then, in concise form the history, commandments, and promises of the incarnate Word. In these possess the way, the truth, and [Col. 0039C] the life. Therefore, by Christ’s example, know how one may live well through commandments and promises; know and desire to live well, so that the light of the Lord’s countenance may be marked ever more abundantly upon you [Ps. 4].

By these three, three things must necessarily be driven away: impotence, ignorance, and negligence. “For one who is ignorant shall be ignored” [2 Cor. 14]; the negligent person will not be known; and the wicked pretender of impotence will likewise be cast out. See, then, with the prophet, the four living creatures, full of eyes throughout their bodies [Ezek. 1]. That they have four faces while being one, and that their appearance is like fire—this new sequence explains by marvelous art. Here the wings are joined equally; the wheels likewise seize one another and turn by no other art. Wherever the spirit gives direction, there they go, and there is no turning back; now descent, now ascent is in them. They send out flashing sparks as rays, and lightning flashes upon the impious: terror for them, brightness for the sons, is in them.”

So that the studious mind may use this volume without scruple and in security, I have taken care diligently to distinguish the sayings, persons, and locations of the evangelists by numbers. One set, expressed by certain signs commonly called *cifras* (“figures”), indicates the numbers themselves in the Eusebian Canons. The other, represented below in rather heavy letters and proceeding only as far as ten, indicates in which canon the number set above it is found. For the numbers make clearer than light what the evangelists said individually, jointly, and similarly. The letters also show that they ought to be distinguished, for brevity as well as difference, by the following designation: Mark by the letter R; Matthew by M; the supreme evangelist, the eagle, by A; and Luke by L.

Moreover, let no one find fault because the natural order of the history is not everywhere preserved here. Each of the evangelists, as also Juvencus and Sedulius, distinguished versifiers treating the same subject, related many things in an inverted order. It should therefore be understood that the rules of anticipation and recapitulation, and many others besides, of which Doctor Augustine teaches in *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, must often be applied to this work.

## ADMONITION TO THE READER

[Col. 0039]

[Col. 0039D] Just as the Creator is known from creatures, and through their infinite variety is without doubt understood to be incomprehensible, so the sacred Scriptures are a straight path directed toward that same end, and are therefore manifold because they lead to the immeasurable. There are seven translations from Hebrew into Greek, greatly differing from one another; many more from Greek into Latin, likewise differing among themselves; and, in addition, Jerome’s one translation from Hebrew into Latin, word for word.

Since such a perplexing diversity of Scripture is evident in the divine books, we have nowhere intentionally placed one reading or another according to different exemplars while treating the harmony of the Gospel. The text interposed with exposition therefore contains chiefly the reading according to modern usage; but in both text and exposition many established readings [Col. 0040D] are taken from the old library or extracted from expositions. We have taken care to note this so that those who read both text and exposition may not wish to correct one by means of the other.

We make known to the reader that we have drawn the light of this exposition from Jerome, Hilary, and Rabanus on Matthew; from Jerome and Bede on Mark; from Ambrose and Bede on Luke; and on John, from Augustine and his abridger Albinus. Moreover, [Col. 0045B] Augustine’s *Harmony of the Evangelists*, Augustine’s *Sermons on the Words of the Lord*, Augustine’s *Questions on the Gospels*, and the homilies of Origen, Gregory, John Chrysostom, and very many others also illuminate the work. Therefore, where divisions of thought are somewhat lengthy, we have attached in the margin, or above the beginnings of the statements, the names of the commentators or their first syllables or letters, so that even thus it may be distinguished whose opinion each is. Rabanus did this, and Bede also, gathering the weightier sayings of the saints in graceful language, like bees gathering the sweetest flowers to make honey.

Accordingly, let the letter H indicate to the reader Jerome on Matthew; the letter A, Augustine on John and on the sermon delivered by the Lord on the mount; and B, Bede [Col. 0045C] on Luke, in which Ambrose’s exposition is explained in clear language. These are indeed the writers whom we have chiefly followed. The letter M signifies what is gathered piecemeal from the aforesaid or other expositions, or the opinion of any teacher whatever. For, since it is written, “Do not quench the Spirit; do not despise prophecies” (1 Thess. 5), I have endeavoured to include things well said by anyone as words, so to speak, of [Col. 0046A] the Holy Spirit himself. Thus the clarity with which the statements are presented will deservedly excuse any lack of polished composition. For what benefit is there, as blessed Augustine says, in a golden key if it cannot open? And what harm is there in a wooden one if it opens well?

We insert only a few interpretations, because at the end of the work we shall arrange alphabetically all those relating to the Gospel, [Note: [Col. 0045] They have been omitted, but nearly all are found near the end of the sacred Bibles.] so that the reader may draw from them arguments as occasion permits. For Arator says:

> From a name we often see  
> Arguments drawn and very great proofs produced.

Here too we judged it necessary to note what Jerome says in his preface to Pope Damasus:

> “The Canons which Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, following Ammonius of Alexandria, [Col. 0046B] arranged into ten numbers, we have set forth as they are found in Greek. When you have read them, you will be able to know both the agreements and the distinctive features of the Evangelists. In the first canon all agree. In the second, three agree: Matthew, Mark, and Luke. In the third, three: Matthew, Luke, and John. In the fourth, three: Matthew, Mark, and John. In the fifth, two: Matthew and Luke. In the sixth, two: Matthew and Mark. In the seventh, two: Matthew and John. In the eighth, two: Mark and Luke. In the ninth, two: Luke and John. In the tenth are the passages peculiar to each one. In each Gospel book, beginning from one and continuing to the end of the books, a distinct number increases. This number, expressed in numerals, has beneath it [Col. 0046C] another number indicated by letters, which, proceeding up to ten, shows in which canon the former number is to be sought. Therefore, when you open the codex and wish to know to which canon a chapter belongs, you will be instructed by the number placed beneath it; and, returning to the books of the individual Evangelists, you will find in which places they have said either the same things or related matters.”

Thus far Jerome.

# Book I

[Col. 0045]

## Prologue of Luke the Evangelist

[Col. 0045C]

[Col. 0045D] “Since indeed many have undertaken to arrange a narrative of the events fulfilled among us, just as those who from the beginning themselves saw them and became ministers of the word delivered them to us, it seemed good to me also, having carefully traced everything from the beginning, to write to you in orderly fashion, most excellent Theophilus, so that you may know the truth of the words in which you have been instructed.”

“Many” refers not so much to their number as to the diversity of their heresies: men such as Basilides and Apelles, who rashly presumed to write concerning the matters of our salvation, which have been fulfilled and abound among us through God. What abounds is lacking to no one, and no one doubts what has been fulfilled, since the result establishes faith. Thus the completed Gospel overflows throughout the whole world, watering and strengthening the minds of believers.

But one “undertakes” who begins and does not complete; who relies upon his own powers rather than the grace of God which gives increase. He does not merely undertake who, with the divine Spirit supplying events and sayings, completes what he has begun. Those who from the beginning saw the deeds done by the Lord, both with bodily sight and with the perception of the mind, and who were ministers of the word by word and example, transmitted them to us by teaching. Not only Mark and Luke learned by hearing what they wrote; John and Matthew also learned much concerning the infancy, childhood, and genealogy of the Saviour from the reports of others.

“It seemed good to me also to write,” through the prompting of the Holy Spirit, by whose grace it comes about that what is good also appears good to us. He says that he has traced not a few things but “everything,” that is, many things, from which he wrote those he judged suitable for confirming the faith of readers. Theophilus means “one who loves God” or “one loved by [Col. 0047A] God.” Whoever, therefore, loves God or desires to be loved by God, should obey the Gospel as though it had been written for himself. Heretics promise novelties; but to Theophilus is promised the truth of the words in which he has been instructed.

## Chapter I

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God.”

The Word—that is, begotten Wisdom, ordering all things—was in the beginning, namely before the things to be created came into being. In it the Word was eternally, so that it might be the beginning, that is, the origin and cause, of things to come. He himself says of this: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8). It is as though he said: [Col. 0047B] “I am that supreme Wisdom in whose ordering all things are first formed in the mind before they are completed in deed.” Hence it is written: “He who made the things that were to be.” And elsewhere: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 130).

The Evangelist determines from whom this Word was begotten—that is, whose Wisdom it is—when he says: “And the Word was with God,” as Wisdom is in him whose Wisdom it is. But lest that Wisdom of God be thought to be something other than God, just as the wisdom of a human being or an angel is something other than the human being or angel himself, in whom it inheres accidentally, he adds: “And the Word itself was God.” He had stated three things separately; he recapitulates them jointly in order to proceed to what follows: this Word, existing as God, was in the beginning with God.

[Col. 0047C] He then shows of what things the Word itself was the beginning: namely, of all natures made afterwards. And this is:

> “All things were made through him.”

Every creature, bodily and incorporeal, and everything naturally inherent in substances—such as quantity, quality, motion, and so forth—began to exist through God’s Word. Evil, however, was not made through him, because it is contained under no form and subsists by no nature of its own, but is only the privation of good. For as the absence of natural light is called blindness of the eye, as darkness is the absence of light, and hunger the lack of food, so we call evil the absence of good, which, if it were present, would naturally belong to a rational creature.

For when the will arises in the mind, its motion is natural; and if grace is present to cooperate with free choice, [Col. 0047D] directing and ordering the movement of the will in things belonging to justice, the will is good and worthy of reward. But if the movement of the will seeks to retain or obtain what justice forbids, then certainly the absence of grace—which directs and orders the movement of the will—is the disorder of the will: it is evil, it is sin, yet it is none of the things that subsist. Of this grace the Psalmist says: “His mercy will go before me and follow me” (Ps. 58).

And lest anyone perhaps think that some or all of the things which began to exist through God’s Word are outside him, as though they subsisted by themselves, he added:

> “And without him nothing was made.”

Thus, “without him nothing was made” means: [Col. 0048A] nothing that has been made subsists outside him. For “Wisdom reaches mightily from end to end” (Wis. 8), that is, from the least creature to the greatest. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23).

Jerome, on the essence of God: “He who fills heaven and earth has, without doubt, no place absent from his presence. He presides over every creature, ruling and commanding; he is beneath all things, supporting and bearing all things—not by the weight of labour, but by untiring power. For no creature can subsist by itself unless it is sustained by him who created it. He is outside all things, but not excluded from them.” The Greek book does not have “without him,” but “outside him.” Likewise, there: “Outside me you can do nothing” (John 15).

[Col. 0048B] But, so that you may understand that the origin and change of creatures takes place without any change in the divine mind—which is the unchangeable and primordial principle of things—he adds:

> “What was made in him was life.”

We must know that effects are said, improperly and figuratively, to have existed where their original causes preceded them. Thus one commonly says: “We were all in Adam’s loins,” that is, we were propagated from the cause which preceded there. Likewise, an ark is said to have existed in the mind of its maker, because its plan and arrangement had already existed there. In the same way it is said: “What was made was life in him”; that is, what was made derived both its coming-to-be and its subsistence from the life possessed in the Word.

By “life in the Word” he means the rational principles and causes of things, unchangeable and eternal. Hence Augustine, in the *Eighty-three Questions* [Col. 0048C]:

> “All things have been created according to rational principles, and not by the same principle is a human being made as a horse; for it is absurd to suppose this. Individual things, therefore, were created by their own proper principles. These principles must be understood to exist in the very mind of the Creator. For he did not look upon something placed outside himself, in order to establish according to it what he was establishing. But if the diverse principles of all things to be created are contained in the divine mind, and nothing in the divine mind can be other than eternal and unchangeable, these chief principles of things remain eternal and unchangeable; through participation in them comes it about that whatever exists, exists in whatever manner it does. These principles may indeed be called ideas, forms, species, or rational principles; many are allowed to use these names, but very few to see what is true.”

> “And the life was the light of men.”

[Col. 0048D] That is, it was that by which rational creatures were to be enlightened so as to become blessed. For in the future life, which alone is truly to be called life, the knowledge of God’s Wisdom and of its rational principles—by which all things were most excellently created and ordered—will make each person more blessed in proportion as it has become more known to that person and has enlightened that person more fully by participation in itself. For then, through a kind of savour of spiritual tasting, it will be known by experience in the thing’s own reality what is now held by faith. Of this knowledge Truth himself says to the Father: “And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the true God, and [Col. 0049A] Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17). This is also customarily called the gift of the Spirit of wisdom.

> “And the light shines in the darkness.”

That is, it shines where it is neither seen nor noticed by those who remain, as it were blind, beneath the sun. For “who has known the mind of the Lord?” (Rom. 1): that is, who is sufficient by himself to perceive the rational principles which God has in creating or ordering all things? Hence it follows:

> “And the darkness did not comprehend it.”

[AMBROSE.] Those, namely, who have not yet been enlightened by it are wholly unable to perceive it. We may also understand “darkness” to mean this entire present life outside the future vision of God, by comparison with that future brightness. God’s Wisdom thus shines even in this life, [Col. 0049B] but its light does not appear through the darkness of our ignorance. For all things have been created and ordered so wisely by God that in themselves they already possess the means by which they could furnish this knowledge of themselves—a knowledge reserved for future blessedness.

But so that the darkness might be enlightened by the light, John was sent to bear witness to the truth. John’s nobility, therefore, is shown not only by his parents but also by his ancestors: he is exalted not by worldly power but by religion, so that he might proclaim, as by hereditary right, the faith in Christ’s coming which had been instilled into him.

## Chapter II

“There was in the days of Herod, king of Judaea, a certain priest named Zachariah, of the course of Abijah; and his wife was of the [Col. 0049C] daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth.”

[BEDE.] The dignity of Aaron, the first high priest under the Law, is well known; but let us say a few words about Abijah. The eighth lot fell to Abijah’s family, from which Zachariah sprang, when David enlarged the worship of God’s house, dividing the ministries of the priests into twenty-four lots (1 Chr. 24). Appropriately, then, the herald of the New Testament is born in the course of the eighth lot, because the New Testament is often understood through the number eight because of the sacrament of the resurrection, just as the Old is understood through the number seven because of the Sabbath.

“And they were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without reproach.”

[Col. 0049D] They were righteous before God, who sees the heart and is not deceived; but before human beings they bore reproach, because the Law cursed the barren. First comes the commandment, then the ordinance. We walk in the Lord’s commandments when we obey them; but when we judge fittingly, we observe his ordinances. This praise is complete: it includes ancestry in their forebears, character in uprightness, office in priesthood, action in commandment, and judgment in ordinance.

Concerning the addition “without reproach,” the Apostle says: “Providing good things not only before God but also before men” (Rom. 12). And Ecclesiastes says: “Do not be excessively righteous” (Eccl. 1), because harsh justice often provokes people’s complaint; whereas tempered justice avoids even the complaint of envy.

[Col. 0050A] “And they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both had advanced in their days.”

[BEDE.] It was divinely arranged that John should be born to persons advanced in years and long deprived of the fruit of marriage, so that God’s gift might be more welcome to them and the wonder of the miracle might designate to others the prophet who was to come.

“And it came to pass, when Zachariah was performing the priestly office before God in the order of his course, according to the custom of the priesthood, that by lot he went in to place incense in the Temple of the Lord; and all the multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of incense.”

When, by Moses’ command, one priest was required to succeed another upon his departure, it was established in David’s time that those serving in turn should minister for eight days, from Sabbath [Col. 0050B] to Sabbath. During the period of their course, each was to practise continence and not visit his own home. Zachariah receives his lot, not a new one but an ancient one: namely, that by which he succeeded in the course of Abijah when he first came to the high-priesthood.

This solemnity is celebrated on the tenth day of the seventh month reckoned from the paschal month; it is called the day of expiation or propitiation, when the high priest alone entered the second tabernacle with blood. In this Jesus the priest is signified: having fulfilled the dispensation of the flesh, he entered heaven’s hidden places in order to make the Father propitious toward us and to intercede for the sins of those who still pray and wait outside the doors, loving his coming. Fittingly, therefore, his descent is announced by an angel on the day when his ascent was prefigured by the Law, because [Col. 0050C] “he who descended is the same also who ascended” (Eph. 4).

Bede, in his treatise on the election of the apostle Matthias:

> “The high priest was commanded to be sought by lot, so that it might be prefigured that the true Priest was to be sought until he came who entered once into the holy places through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption (Heb. 9). His sacrifice was offered at the time of Passover, but was consummated on the day of Pentecost when the Holy Spirit appeared in fire. For it was the ancient custom that sacrifices accepted by God should be consumed by heavenly fire. Therefore, until the truth was fulfilled, it was lawful to practise the figure. Hence Matthias, who was ordained before Pentecost, was sought by lot; but the seven deacons, who were later ordained, were chosen not by lot but only by the disciples’ election (Acts 1), and by the apostles’ prayer and laying on of hands (Acts 6).”

[Col. 0050D] “And an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right side of the altar of incense.”

[AMBROSE—BEDE.] God’s angels are said to appear because they cannot be foreseen; but it is in their power both to be seen when they wish and not to be seen when they do not wish. He fittingly appeared at the right side of the altar, because he announced both the coming of the true priest and the mystery of the universal sacrifice and the joy of the heavenly gift. For as present things are often denoted by the left hand, so eternal good things are denoted by the right, according to that saying in praise of Wisdom: “Length of days is in her right hand; riches are in her left” (Prov. 3).

“And Zachariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell [Col. 0051A] upon him. But the angel said to him: ‘Do not be afraid, Zachariah, for your prayer has been heard.’”

Just as it is a human weakness to be frightened, so it is angelic kindness gently to comfort one who is afraid at its appearance. Demons, by contrast, if they perceive anyone frightened by their presence, shake them with greater terror. The prayer made for the redemption of the people was heard, not a prayer for offspring, since he despaired of being able to have them. But because the people’s salvation was to come through Christ, a son is announced to Zachariah who, by preaching repentance and faith, would prepare a people for the Saviour.

“And your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John.”

A mark of singular merit is given whenever a name is either bestowed upon or changed [Col. 0051B] for human beings by God. Thus Abraham, because he was to be the father of many nations, was called Abraham (Gen. 17); thus Jacob, because he saw God, deserved to be called Israel. John means “in whom is grace,” or “the grace of the Lord.” This declares both that grace was granted to his parents and that it was granted to John himself, who was to be filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb.

“And you will have joy and exultation, and many will rejoice at his birth.”

Joy pertains to the mind; exultation to the body’s gladness. At the birth of the Forerunner many rejoice; at the birth of the Lord, “great joy” is announced, which “will be for all the people” (Luke 2). [Col. 0051C] For this man proclaims salvation to many; the other grants it to all.

[AMBROSE.] It should be noted that Jacob rejoices at the begetting of twelve sons, and that sons are likewise given to Abraham and Zachariah. Thus the fruitfulness of a parent is a divine gift. Let fathers therefore give thanks because they have begotten children; children, because they have been begotten; and mothers, because they are honoured with the rewards of marriage.

“For he will be great before the Lord, and he will drink neither wine nor *sikera*, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.”

[BEDE.] It is a great virtue before the Lord to preach heavenly joys in the wilderness, to despise earthly delights, and to be beheaded for the truth. The Hebrews call *sikera* every drink capable of intoxicating, whether made from fruit, grain, or any other material. The Law of the Nazirites required abstinence from wine and *sikera* [Col. 0051D] during the time of consecration. But John, Samson, and Jeremiah, so that they might always remain Nazirites—that is, holy persons—always abstained from these things. For it is fitting that one who desires to be filled with the new wine of the Holy Spirit should not be made drunk by any drink. “He will not drink *sikera*”; and, beyond this virtue, even from the womb he will be filled with the Holy Spirit.

“And he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God; and he himself will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of fathers to children, and the unbelieving to the prudence of the righteous, to prepare for the Lord a perfect people.”

[BEDA.] He turned those to the Lord to whom he gave baptism in faith in the One who was to come. He is said to go before in the spirit of Elijah, because, just as Elijah will come as the herald of the Judge, so John was made the herald of the Redeemer. Their power too was very similar [Col. 0052A]: both were in the wilderness, both sparing in food, both rough in dress, and both endured the madness of kings. Elijah divided the Jordan when he was about to seek heaven; John turned many toward the washing by which heaven is sought. To turn the hearts of fathers to children is, by preaching, to instil into the peoples the spiritual knowledge of the saints of old. But the wisdom of the righteous is not to presume upon righteousness from the works of the Law, but to seek salvation from faith, so that, although they live under the Law and fulfil its commands, they nevertheless understand that they are to be saved through grace by Christ. “For the righteous shall live by faith” (Hab. II; Rom. I; Heb. X). Hence Peter says: “We believe that we shall be saved through the grace of the Lord, just as our fathers were” (Acts XV). Since the Jews, instructed by this teaching through John and yet to be instructed through Elijah, were to remain unbelieving for longer, Malachi predicts almost the same words about Elijah as the Angel speaks about John (Mal. IV). Read the sentence thus: “He will go before, to prepare for the Lord a perfect people.”

And Zechariah said to the angel: “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in her days.”

[BEDA.] Hesitating because of the greatness of the promises, he seeks a sign, though the angelic address ought to have been enough for him. He therefore deservedly paid the penalty in the silence he had incurred, so that he who had spoken in unbelief might now learn to believe by keeping silence.

And the angel answered and said to him: “I am Gabriel, who stand before God, and I have been sent to speak to you and to proclaim these good tidings to you. And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day when these things take place, because you did not [Col. 0052C] believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their proper time.”

When angels come to us, they so perform their ministry outwardly that inwardly they never cease from contemplation. Though sent, they stand before God, because wherever they go, they run within him who is everywhere.

And the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they wondered that he delayed in the temple. But when he came out, he could not speak to them. And they recognized that he had seen a vision in the temple; and he kept making signs to them and remained mute. And it came to pass, when the days of his service were completed, that he went home.

[AMBROSE—BEDA.] The Jewish people resembles mute Zechariah, being unable to give an account of its actions. The high priests, however, observing continence during the time of their course, necessarily returned to their homes and wives after the temple service was completed, because at that time priestly succession was sought from Aaron’s stock. But now, because for priests not carnal succession but spiritual perfection is required, so that they may always be able to stand at the altar, perpetual chastity is commanded.

Now after those days Elizabeth his wife conceived.

That is, after the days of Zechariah’s service were completed. These things happened, John Chrysostom says, in September, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [24 September], on the eleventh lunar day, when the fast of the Feast of Tabernacles is observed at the equinox, when the day begins to decrease, because he was conceived who said: “I must decrease, but he must increase” (John III). For the light had been diminished by darkness when sacrifices were being offered to God according to the Law—sacrifices which now had to cease [Col. 0053A] when the Baptist was conceived. Therefore his father, a priest of the Jews, was struck mute, because priestly sacrifices had now to cease with the coming of the Priest who would offer himself for the sins of all. John’s conception is announced on the day of fasting because through him the affliction of repentance was to be preached.

And she concealed herself for five months, saying: “Thus has the Lord dealt with me in the days when he looked upon me, to take away my reproach among people.”

[AMBROSE—BEDA.] Elizabeth shows how great is the saints’ concern that they should admit nothing shameful of which they ought to be ashamed. She is ashamed of God’s gift and blushes at having conceived in old age, lest she seem to have given herself to lust in her old age—a thing which ought never to be practised even in youth, except for the sake of offspring or to avoid [Col. 0053B] fornication.

[BEDA.] Allegorically, Zechariah signifies the Jewish priesthood; Elizabeth, the Law. Exercised by the teaching of priests, as though with a husband’s aid, it ought to bear spiritual children for God. But it was as though barren, because it led no one—[or, “nothing,” an uncertain reading]—to perfection (Heb. VII), nor opened the gate of heaven. Both were righteous, because both the Law and the priesthood were good in their own time. Both were advanced in days, because legal devotion, under Moses, flourished with the priesthood as in youth; but with Christ’s coming the Law and priesthood were in old age, since the order of the priesthood was confused through the ambitions and quarrels of the high priests, and the Law was transgressed through Pharisaic traditions. Zechariah enters [Col. 0053C] the temple because it belongs to priests to understand God’s sanctuary and to enter it by understanding. The multitude prays outside because, unable to penetrate the mysteries, it must humbly attend to the warnings of teachers. While he places incense upon the altar, he learns that John will be born, because while teachers are kindled by divine reading, they discover that God’s grace, to come through Christ, will issue from the inner marrow of the Scriptures, as though from Elizabeth’s womb. This is through an angel, because “the Law was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator” (Gal. III). By not believing, he becomes mute, because the person who does not understand the spiritual sense in the letter is mute. Such a person cannot teach the people as a master, but merely makes signs, because he neither considers the meaning of sacrifices nor takes care to know the sayings of the prophets. When [Col. 0053D] Zechariah is mute, Elizabeth conceives John, because, although the high priests and Pharisees neither enter the inner meaning of the Law nor permit their hearers to enter it, the inner meaning of the Law nevertheless abounds in Christ’s sacraments. Elizabeth conceals her conception for five months, either because Moses the lawgiver sets forth the mysteries of Christ figuratively in five books, or because the Law itself figures Christ’s dispensation through the deeds and sayings of the saints in the five ages of the world. And because Christ’s incarnation was to occur in the sixth age of the world for the fulfilment of the Law, the angel rightly announces to Mary, in the sixth month from John’s conception, that the Saviour will be born.

## CHAPTER III

Now in the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent by [Col. 0054A] God to a city of Galilee called Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary.

[THE GREEKS.] Understand the sixth month as March, on the twenty-fifth day of which the Saviour is traditionally said to have been conceived and to have suffered. Angels are designated by their individual names in order that their names may show what service they come to perform. Thus Gabriel means “the strength of God,” because he announces the one who was to defeat the powers of the air. The virgin was betrothed for many reasons. First, because she was related to Joseph, so that through him the virgin’s lineage might be known; for both were of the house of David, and it is Scripture’s custom not to set forth women’s genealogies. Second, lest she be stoned by the Jews as an adulteress. Third, so that in fleeing into Egypt she might have a husband’s comfort [Col. 0054B] and protection of her integrity. Fourth, lest her childbirth become known to the devil. Therefore, because a reputation for chastity is precarious, the Lord did not wish the credibility of his birth to be established through insults to his mother; rather, he permitted some to doubt his birth rather than his mother’s chastity. In this, an occasion is also removed from unchaste virgins, lest they say that the Lord’s mother had been defamed.

[BEDA.] Mary is interpreted in Hebrew as “star of the sea,” and in Syriac as “lady,” because she brought forth to the world both the light of salvation and the Lord, having been instructed by an angel; whereas, conversely, a woman deceived at the devil’s urging introduced the darkness and slavery of sin. Mystically, Mary, betrothed yet a virgin, is a type of the Church, which is immaculate yet married. A virgin conceives us, but by the Spirit; a virgin bears us without groaning.

[Col. 0054C] And the angel entered to her and said: “Hail, full of grace. The Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.”

She was full of grace in the exclusion of vices, knowledge of truth, and love of virtue; she was the first among women to offer God the glorious gift of virginity. The Lord is with you in mind, the Lord is with you in womb, the Lord is with you in help—you who are his holy temple. Blessed above all women is she whom angels and human beings alike venerate as the Mother of God and as a virgin.

When she heard this, she was troubled at his saying and considered what kind of greeting this might be.

[BEDA.] A virgin unaccustomed to a man’s greeting is frightened by the novelty of the words. It belongs to virgins to be alarmed at every man’s approach and to fear every address by a man. [Col. 0054D] Mary therefore marvelled at this new formula of blessing, which had nowhere previously been read.

And the angel said to her: “Do not fear, Mary, for you have found grace with God.”

He calls her by name more familiarly, as one known to him, persuading her not to be afraid. You have found grace: you are to conceive the author of all grace. Hence follows:

“Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.”

You will conceive and remain incorrupt; you will bear and suffer no loss of virginity. Jesus is interpreted “Saviour” or “salutary,” because he was to save his people from their sins.

“He will be great and will be called Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father.”

[Col. 0055A] John will be great before the Lord, as a human being; but this one will be great as God, the Son of God. Jesus received David’s throne so that he himself might call to an everlasting kingdom the people over whom David had temporarily exercised rule. That he is said to be both Son of the Most High and to have David as father shows that the one person of Christ possesses two natures, namely divine and human.

“And he will reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.”

In the present life he will reign by dwelling in hearts; in the life to come, by calling people from exile to glory. Hence Isaiah: “And there will be no end of peace” (Isa. IX). By the house of Jacob he means the whole Church, which belongs to the inheritance of the patriarchs through faith and confession of Christ: both those born from the good root of the patriarchs and [Col. 0055B] those cut from the wild olive of the Gentiles and grafted into the good olive tree of the Jews (Rom. XI).

And Mary said to the angel: “How will this be, since I do not know a man?”

She did not say, “How shall I know this?” but “How will this be?” because she did not doubt the angel’s words. She had read, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. VII), but she had not read how this would happen, nor had she heard it from the angel.

And the angel answered and said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”

He calls the gifts of the Holy Spirit “the Holy Spirit.” Thus, as often happens, the name of the cause is attributed to the effect. He also calls the same Spirit the power of the Most High, in accord with the Lord’s promise to his disciples concerning the coming of that Spirit: “But remain in [Col. 0055C] the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke XXIV). A shadow is produced from light and a body when we place some sort of screen between ourselves and the sun, thereby making its light more bearable to us. Thus the incorporeal light of the Godhead, invisible in its own nature, assumed in the virgin the veil of our weakness—that is, human nature—so that in some manner it might be seen in our substance. This is what he says: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you,” that is, the inestimable gift of the Holy Spirit—a new and singular grace—will be bestowed upon you. And thus the Holy Spirit himself, whose work is to distribute and preserve every good thing and to establish it in the best end, is called the power of the Most High; he will overshadow you, that is, he will form from your flesh, as though a sheltering covering [Col. 0055D] for the radiance of eternal light, the human body of the Wisdom of God. And this will happen to you—that is, for your immense glory, you who will be enlightened beyond all others.

“Therefore the holy thing that will be born from you will be called the Son of God.”

[BEDA.] Though we become holy, we are not born holy, as the Prophet says: “I was conceived in iniquities” (Ps. L). But Jesus alone was born holy, because he was not conceived through the mingling of carnal intercourse.

“And behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman has also conceived a son in her old age; and this is the sixth month for her who is called barren, because no word will be impossible with God.”

[Col. 0056A] [BEDA.] The construction is: “And behold, even [*et*, meaning ‘also’] Elizabeth your kinswoman has conceived a son.” So that the virgin may not doubt that she will give birth, she receives the example of an old barren woman who will give birth, in order to learn that all things are possible to God, even those that seem contrary to the order of nature. Or otherwise: the angel does not urge her to faith by examples as though she were unbelieving; rather, to one who believes he recounts further and greater miracles, so that she who, being a virgin, would bear God might also know that the forerunner would be born from an old barren woman. It should be known that Aaron, of Levi, took as wife Elizabeth, the sister of Nahshon, from the tribe of Judah; and Jehoiada the high priest had as wife Jehosheba, daughter of Joram, from the royal tribe. Through these, and others besides, the two tribes, royal and priestly, were joined. Hence Mary and Elizabeth were kinswomen; and it is fitting [Col. 0056B] that the Mediator should be born from both tribes, he who reigns for ever and is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. CIX).

And Mary said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.” And the Angel departed from her.

She who is chosen as the Lord’s mother calls herself a handmaid, ever mindful of both her own condition and God’s condescension; and with great devotion she desires the angel’s promise to be fulfilled. Augustine, in the sermon beginning *Legimus et fideliter retinemus* (“We read and faithfully hold”):

> “Once the virgin’s consent had been received, the angel immediately returned to the inhabitants of the heavenly region. And behold, suddenly an ineffable power penetrated the virgin’s secret chamber, because the eternal sun descended from the supreme height of the Father’s radiant glory, opened the entrance of the virgin’s womb, and drove back the darkness of the whole world with brilliant flashing light. The Maker of the world enters the narrow confines of a human womb; the untouched mother becomes pregnant. Mary surrounds a man by giving credence to the angel, because Eve lost her man by consenting to the serpent.”

Gregory, in the letter beginning *Quia charitati nil longe est* (“Because nothing is far from love”):

> “The flesh was not first conceived in the virgin’s womb and then divinity came into the flesh. Rather, immediately the Word came into the womb; immediately, preserving the power of his own nature, the Word became flesh and a perfect human being—that is, possessing the reality of flesh and a rational soul. Hence he is said to be anointed above his companions (Ps. XLIV), namely with the gift of the Holy Spirit. For this very being conceived from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin’s flesh was his anointing by the Holy Spirit.”

ORIGEN:

> “If this human and bodily word, when it is sent into the ears of many, is not divided among individuals, so that one part is in one person and another part in another, but is possessed whole and complete by all, so that the whole is complete in each one [*plenum*, perhaps repeated in the source], how much more is the only-begotten Word of God wholly everywhere—in heaven and on earth, with the Father and in the Virgin?”

Now Mary arose in those days and went with haste into the hill country, to a city of Judah.

[BEDA.] Rejoicing at the example, she hastens to visit pregnant Elizabeth. That she went into the hill country, to a city of Judah, where she was to remain for three months, teaches that every soul which conceives the Word of God ought immediately to ascend the heights of virtues and enter the city of Judah, that is, the citadel of confession and praise, [Col. 0057A] so that it may be able to remain there, as it were, for three months—until it reaches the perfection of faith, hope, and charity.

And she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. And it came to pass, when Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, that the child leaped in her womb; and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit.

Mary greets Elizabeth in order to display her humility. Elizabeth heard the voice of greeting first, but John felt grace first in the womb. She heard according to the order of nature; he leaped in the womb. She perceived Mary’s arrival; John perceived the Lord’s conception. The mother was filled with the Holy Spirit, but the son was filled first.

And she cried out with a loud voice and said: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.”

[Col. 0057B] Because she recognized God’s great gifts, she cried out not so much loudly as devoutly, aflame with the Holy Spirit with which she was filled. Observe that Mary is blessed by Elizabeth in the same words as by Gabriel, so that she may be shown worthy of veneration by angels and human beings and to be preferred above all women. The fruit of her womb is blessed, as the Apostle says: “He who is over all, God blessed for ever” (Rom. IX).

“And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?”

Elizabeth does not inquire into these things as though ignorant, but struck by the novelty of the miracle.

“For behold, as soon as the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the child leaped for joy in my womb.”

[Col. 0057C] By the Spirit with which she was filled, she understands that the child’s leap signifies that the mother of the one whose forerunner he was to be had come. Therefore she who previously blushed and hid herself because she had conceived a son now boasts because she has borne a prophet.

“And blessed is she who believed, because the things spoken to her by the Lord will be fulfilled.”

She plainly indicates that by the Spirit she had learned the angel’s words to Mary. The virgin believed and thereby gained the fruit. Having heard Elizabeth’s reply, which pronounced her blessed, called her the Lord’s mother, and praised her strong faith, she now, at the fitting time, gave expression to the gifts she had received, which virginal modesty had hidden in silence.

And Mary said: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Saviour.”
