[Col. 0057D] Spirit is the same as soul; hence it is said in the Passion: “And, bowing his head, he gave up the spirit” (John XIX). Yet it is sometimes understood as the rational faculty and higher excellence of the soul, as in: “Bless the Lord, spirits and souls of the righteous” (Dan. III). For we live by the soul, but discern and understand by the spirit. Therefore Mary, devoted to God in soul and spirit, devotes all that lives and feels, all that understands and discerns, to contemplating God’s greatness, observing his commands, and offering the praises of thanksgiving. This is to sing to God on harp and psaltery (Ps. CL), according to the Psalmist. Mary’s soul magnifies—that is, thinks great things of and praises—the Lord, namely God the Father, from whom are all things. And her spirit rejoices in God her Saviour, that is, in the Son, through [Col. 0058A] whom are all things and through whom salvation is restored to the world in her. Thus she says with the Psalmist: “My soul shall rejoice in the Lord and delight in his salvation” (Ps. XXXIV).

“For he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid; for behold, from this time all generations will call me blessed.”

[BEDA.] The Lord regarded humble Mary with the gaze of the Holy Spirit, when that Spirit overshadowed her. For God’s regarding is the granting of grace. She therefore rightly rejoices that she is to be called blessed by all. She says this so that, just as death entered through Eve’s pride (Gen. III), the entrance of life might be opened through Mary’s humility.

“For he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name.”

[Col. 0058B] Therefore my soul magnifies the Lord, because he who is mighty in himself and not through another—that is, God the Father—has deigned to do great things for me; and holy is his name, that is, the Son, who is the Father’s name, for through him the Father became known to the world. Therefore: “Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name” (Ps. XXXIII). The Lord’s name is holy because by singular power and holiness he transcends every creature.

“And his mercy is unto generations and generations for those who fear him.”

From her particular gift she turns to general matters, describing the condition of the human race: what the proud and the humble deserve; what the children of Adam are through freedom of choice and what the children of God are through grace. He has not done great things for me alone, but in every generation the person who fears God and does righteousness is acceptable to him (Acts X), and his mercy—that is, the Holy Spirit, distributor of mercies—dwells in that person.

“He has wrought might with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thought of their heart.”

The Son is signified by the arm, not because he is attached as a limb to a body, but because the Father works through the Word—that is, through the Son. The proud person is one who wishes to be raised above what he is, as the devil did. Thus the Father, who says in the psalm, “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. XLIV), has powerfully scattered the proud by his arm—that is, in the thought of his heart—in which he both works and judges all things calmly. Since the Word of the divine mind is good, it rejects and [Col. 0058D] condemns pride, which is the beginning of all evils (Ecclus. X). Jerome, *On the Essence of God*:

> “The heart of God the Father mystically indicates the hidden place of his wisdom, from which, without suffering and without beginning, he begot his Word—that is, his Son—as he himself says through the Prophet: ‘My heart has uttered a good word.’ Or thus: by his arm he scattered the proud, both hidden and manifest, because they were raised up against him in the thought of their heart—that is, in the understanding by which they ought to have seen God.”

“He has put down the mighty from their throne and exalted the humble. He has filled the hungry with good things, and sent the rich away empty.”

[BEDA.] He connects with “unto generations and generations,” which he stated before, by saying that through all the generations of the age he casts proud mighty people down from the throne of pride and, by his gracious ordering, exalts the humble. “For whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” [Col. 0059A] (Luke XIV; Matt. XXIII). By the hungry he means the Gentiles, who had neither Law nor prophets; by the rich, the Jews, rich in Law, prophets, and psalms. The Lord sent the latter away empty when they were cast out, but filled the former with good things when they received the preachers. He said “filled” and “sent away” in the prophetic spirit, using the past for the future.

“He has received Israel his servant, mindful of his mercy.”

[BEDA.] He fittingly calls Israel a servant, namely an obedient and humble one, as Hosea says: “Israel was a child, and I loved him” (Hos. XI). Whoever refuses to humble himself cannot be saved, nor can he say with the Prophet: “Behold, God helps me, and the Lord is the upholder of my soul” (Ps. XXXV). The Lord will receive Israel at Elijah’s coming, “mindful,” that is, so that he may be shown mindful of his mercy. It is not that remembrance of mercy departs from God; rather, he is said to remember when, after a long time, he has mercy on someone as though he had previously forgotten.

“As he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his seed for ever.”

The Lord spoke to Abraham and his seed for ever—that is, through long ages—concerning the mercy of our salvation, bestowed in Christ upon all nations. Abraham’s spiritual seed means those who have followed Abraham’s faith, whether in circumcision or uncircumcision. Hence the Apostle says: “If you are Christ’s, then [Col. 0059C] you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. III). Thus what God deigned to reveal to his saints, both Gentiles and Jews, after Abraham, concerning faith in the Incarnation, he spoke to Abraham’s seed.

And Mary remained with her about three months, and returned to her own house.

[BEDA.] She remained until she saw the forerunner’s birth, for which she had especially come, and so that Elizabeth’s and John’s spiritual progress might grow through so long a stay. For if they were filled with the Holy Spirit at Mary’s first arrival, much was added to them by so lengthy a remaining.

## CHAPTER IV

Now Elizabeth’s time to give birth was fulfilled, and [Col. 0059D] she bore a son.

The term of fulfilment is customarily used only of good things: “Mary’s days were fulfilled for her to give birth” (Luke II); “Solomon completed the building of the house” (III Kings IX); “Abraham died full of days” (Gen. XXV); “when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son” (Gal. IV). By contrast, the days of the impious are empty, as it is written: “Men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days” (Ps. LIV).

And her neighbours and relatives heard that the Lord had magnified his mercy with her, and they rejoiced with her.

At the birth of a righteous person, the grace of virtue that will follow is signified by the foreshadowing joy of the neighbours.

And it came to pass, on the eighth day they came to circumcise [Col. 0060A] the child, and they were calling him by his father’s name, Zechariah. But his mother answered and said: “By no means; he shall be called John.”

The mother was not ignorant of her son’s name, she who had already prophesied that Christ was conceived. For by the spirit of prophecy she knew what name should be given, though she had not learned it from her husband, who was mute and to whom it had been foretold by the angel.

And they said to her: “There is no one in your family who is called by this name.” Then they made signs to his father, asking what he wished him to be called. And requesting a writing-tablet, he wrote, saying: “His name is John.” And all were amazed.

[BEDA.] “His name is John”—as if to say: We do not give him this name; it has already been given by God. For this is not a family name but a prophet’s name. They marvelled at the agreement of father and mother. Those who determined that the child ought to be called by his father’s name rather than John represent those who, when the Lord declared the gifts of new grace, wished him instead to proclaim the customary ordinances of the old priesthood. Zechariah is appropriately interpreted “remembrance of the Lord,” because he represents remembrance of the old observance given by the Lord. A *pugillaris* is called either a stylus or a tablet which may be enclosed in the fist.

And immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he spoke, blessing God. And fear came upon all their neighbours.

[BEDA.] Faith loosed the tongue which unbelief [Col. 0060C] had bound. Allegorically, John’s celebrated birth is the beginning of the exalted grace of the New Testament. The mother declares John’s name—that is, “God’s grace”—in words, and the father in writing, because the Law, the prophets, and the psalms proclaim Christ’s grace. Zechariah fittingly speaks on the eighth day after his child’s birth, because through the Lord’s resurrection, which took place on the eighth day, the mysteries of the legal priesthood were opened.

And all these sayings were spread abroad throughout all the hill country of Judaea; and all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying: “What, do you suppose, will this child become?” For the hand of the Lord was with him.

The signs which went before prepared the way for the forerunner of truth. Thus those who heard, stirred by the miracle and stunned by fear, silently awaiting the outcome, say: “What, do you suppose, will this child become?” By “the hand of the Lord” his Son is understood, as in Isaiah: “My hand has made all these things” (Isa. LXVI). In another sense the hand of the Lord is understood as his scourge, as in Zephaniah: “I will stretch out my hand over Judah” (Zeph. I); and hence Job says, “The hand of the Lord has touched me” (Job XIX). Here, however, the hand of the Lord means [Col. 0060D] his power, of which he says in Jeremiah: “As clay is in the potter’s hand, so are you in my hand, house of Israel” (Jer. XVIII).

And Zechariah his father was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and wrought redemption for his people.”

[BEDA.] What Zechariah knew would shortly be done, he relates in prophetic fashion as though already accomplished. For what is prophesied is future in time, but according to the prophet’s knowledge must be regarded as accomplished. “He has visited,” he says, his people, wasting away as though under a long sickness; and he redeemed them, sold under sin, by the blood of his Son. They are called his people, not because he found them already his when he came, but because by visiting them he made them his. Similar is that passage at the end of Proverbs: “Who can find a valiant woman?” (Prov. XXXI). He did not find the woman—that is, the Church—valiant, but made her valiant by espousing her to himself.

“And he has raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant.”

By “horn” he means firm loftiness, because a horn is firm and projects beyond the flesh, while all other bones are covered with flesh. The kingdom of the Saviour, by which the world and pleasures of the flesh are overcome, is therefore called a horn of salvation. As its figure, David and Solomon were consecrated with a horn of oil unto royal glory.

“As he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets who have been from the beginning of the age.”

“From the age,” that is, from the beginning of the world, because the whole Scripture of the Old Testament went before as prophecy concerning Christ; and from Adam’s time onward the holy fathers have each borne witness to his dispensation by their deeds.

“Salvation from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us.”

He explains what he had said, “He has raised up for us a horn of salvation”; that is, he has raised up for us salvation from our enemies, namely from the power of all who hate us, whether [Col. 0061C] unclean spirits or perverse human beings. For now we have been saved in hope (Rom. II); in the future we shall be saved in actuality.

“To show mercy to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant, the oath which he swore to Abraham our father, that he would grant us, delivered from the hand of our enemies, to serve him without fear.”

He raised up salvation in the house of David, to show us mercy together with our fathers, who await the Redeemer’s coming in darkness. He thus raised up salvation “to remember,” that is, that he might be known as mindful of his covenant, in order to fulfil the oath which he swore to Abraham, that he would give to us—that is, accomplish in us. I say “accomplish” in such a way that, delivered from fear of eternal death, we may serve him. For God’s covenant, that is, the declaration of his will, and his oath, that is, his firm promise, was what he said to Abraham: “In your seed, which is Christ, all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII). Indeed, God’s promising is his swearing.

[BEDA—AMBROSE.] Having said that the Lord would be born in David’s house in accordance with the prophets’ sayings, he now says that the same Lord will deliver us in fulfilment of the covenant he made with Abraham, because to these two patriarchs especially were promised both the blessing of the nations through their seed and Christ’s incarnation. Matthew also briefly indicates this when he says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. I). Here [Col. 0062A] it should be noted that in both evangelists David is placed before Abraham, because although he is later in time, he is greater in promise. To Abraham, still in uncircumcision, who abandoned what was his own, knew God, and attained the testimony of faith, were specially promised the faith of the nations and the holy assembly of the Church, when the Lord said to him: “In you all the kindreds of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII). But David heard the higher oracle that Christ would be born from him according to the flesh: “When,” he says, “you have fulfilled your days, I will raise up your seed and establish his throne for ever; I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me” (I Chron. XVII). Abraham therefore received principally the promise concerning the Church, but David the promise concerning Christ, through whom the Church itself exists. Thus Abraham is accorded primacy with respect to the faith of the peoples, while David is accorded the special prerogative of Christ’s generation according to the flesh.

“In holiness and righteousness before him all our days.”

Holiness concerns religious worship; righteousness, the moderation of judgment or punishment. These are before the Lord when one seeks no reward other than God’s.

“And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways.”

[BEDA.] Suddenly, while speaking of the Lord, he turns his words to the prophet, in order to indicate that the benefit of his becoming a prophet would come from the Lord. It is no wonder that he addresses an infant eight days old, because the child could well hear his father’s voice after birth, having heard Mary’s greeting while still enclosed in the womb. Zechariah should also be understood, for the instruction of those present, to proclaim as soon as he could speak the future gifts of his son which he had learned through the angel. He calls the one before whose face John went “the Most High,” according to the Psalmist: “Mother Zion will say, ‘A man and a man was born in her,’ and the Most High himself founded her” [Col. 0062C] (Ps. LXXXVI).

“To give knowledge of salvation to his people in the remission of their sins.”

Desiring to commend the Saviour’s name, he frequently mentions salvation. And lest he seem to promise a carnal salvation, he says: “in the remission of sins.”

“Through the tender mercy of our God, whereby the rising sun from on high has visited us.”

You will go before the Lord’s face to give knowledge of salvation, not through human merits but through tender mercy, through which the rising sun from on high—that is, the Word of the Father, opening the dawn of true light—has visited us in assumed flesh, making children of light out of children of darkness and night. Hence follows:

“To give light to those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, to direct our feet in the way of peace.”

[BEDA.] He visited in order to give light: the rising sun gives light to those who are depressed in the darkness of sins and in the shadow of death, that is, in the blindness of ignorance. By excluding the darkness of errors, he poured in the true light of his own knowledge and opened the sure path to the heavenly homeland. [Col. 0063A] Our feet are the affections of the mind; if they accord with the grace of our illuminator, they are directed into the way of peace—that is, into works which are for us the way to the everlasting peace of heaven. Hearts are fittingly enlightened first, and then directed into works of peace, as the Psalmist says: “Seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. XXXIII).

But the child grew and was strengthened in spirit, and was in the wildernesses until the day of his manifestation to Israel.

[HIERON.] As one who was to be a preacher of repentance, he sought the rigors of solitude as soon as he could, so that he might withdraw both himself and his hearers from the enticements of the world. The birth of the Forerunner having been set forth—he who is born first, preaches first, and dies first—the generation and birth according to the flesh of the Savior are fittingly added [Col. 0063B]. But concerning the generation of his divinity Isaiah says: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. LIII).

## CHAPTER V

**The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.**

[RABANUS—ALCUIN, *On the Homilies.*] Matthew’s book is called the “book of the generation,” in accordance with the custom of the Hebrews, who give volumes names from their opening words. Jesus is called *Soter* in Greek, *Salvator* in Latin, and in Hebrew Jesus: this is the proper name of our Redeemer. Christ, moreover, is called “Anointed” in Latin and Messiah in the Hebrew tongue; it is a title of dignity, because in ancient times kings, prophets, and priests [Col. 0063C] were anointed with the oil of consecration (Ps. XLIV). But Christ himself was anointed by God above his fellows as king and priest, because it pleased God that the fullness of divinity should dwell in him (Col. I).

David, king and prophet by divine election, is rightly set before Abraham, both because far fuller and clearer promises concerning Christ were made to him, and because David and the promises he had received were especially upon the lips of the people. This is shown in the Gospel, where those who seek healing from Jesus call him Son of David.

[HIERON.] Or otherwise: when it says, “Son of David, son of Abraham,” the order is reversed, but necessarily so. For if Abraham had been placed first and David afterward, Abraham would have had to be repeated in order to continue the genealogy, thus: “Jesus Christ [Col. 0063D], son of Abraham, son of David, son of Abraham.”

**Abraham begot Isaac; Isaac begot Jacob; Jacob begot Judah and his brothers.**

Abraham is the beginning of the account, because with him the promise began. The Evangelist passes over in silence Ishmael and Esau, brothers respectively of Isaac and Jacob, because they did not remain in the worship of the one God. Judah’s brothers, however, are worthily mentioned, since they were patriarchs.

**Judah begot Phares and Zara by Thamar.**

In the Savior’s genealogy not righteous women but sinful women are named, in order to suggest that he who wished to assume the form of a man from a woman, so as to save men and women, deigned to be born of sinners in order to blot out sins. Moreover, the Lord is born [Col. 0064A] from righteous persons and sinners, in accordance with Moses’ command that the sacrificial lamb be taken from a flock of sheep and goats.

**Phares begot Esrom; Esrom begot Aram; Aram begot Aminadab; Aminadab begot Naasson; Naasson begot Salmon; Salmon begot Booz by Rahab; Booz begot Obed by Ruth.**

Because the Lord is born of Ruth the Moabitess, the prophecy was fulfilled which says: “Send forth the lamb, O Lord, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the wilderness” (Isa. XVI); that is, from the Gentiles, who are called a rock because they worship idols, and a wilderness because they live without the Law.

**Obed begot Jesse; Jesse begot David the king.**

[Col. 0064B] The Evangelist preferred to call David’s father Jesse rather than Isai, although he bore both names, in order to indicate that the prophetic saying was fulfilled in Christ and Mary: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. XI). He calls him David the king because he was the first king from the tribe of Judah, through whom the course of the genealogy runs.

**David the king begot Solomon by her who had been Uriah’s.**

That is, by Bathsheba, who is not named here because she sinned more grievously than the other women named. For while she was Uriah’s wife, David joined himself to her in adultery.

**Solomon begot Roboam; Roboam begot Abiam; Abias begot Asa; Asa begot [Col. 0064C] Josaphat; Josaphat begot Joram; Joram begot Ozias.**

[HIERON.] In the Fourth Book of Kings one reads that Joram was father of Ochozias, Ochozias father of Joas, Joas father of Amasias, and Amasias father of Azarias, who was also called Ozias. But because Joram joined himself to the family of the utterly wicked Jezebel by marrying her daughter, three kings are removed from the middle. Or this was done because the Evangelist intended to set down three groups of fourteen—that is, three numbers of fourteen, making forty-two.

**Ozias begot Joatham; Joatham begot Achaz; Achaz begot Ezechias; Ezechias begot Manasses; Manasses begot Amon; Amon begot Josias; Josias begot Jechonias [Col. 0064D] and his brothers at the deportation to Babylon.**

He calls it the deportation to Babylon because the sons of Israel were led captive to Babylonia; and before that captivity this Josias was killed by Pharaoh Necho, king of Egypt. Therefore, when it says, “Josias begot sons at the deportation” (IV Kings XXIII), either “at” is used in the sense of “before,” or, as some wish, he begot them—understand, men who would go into deportation. Consult the history near the end of the Book of Kings.

**And after the deportation to Babylon, Jechonias begot Salathiel.**

[HIERON.] If we wish to place this Jechonias at the end of the second group of fourteen, there will not be fourteen in the following group. Let us therefore understand the earlier Jechonias [Col. 0065A] to be the same person also called Joachim, and the latter to be his son. The former is written with K and M, the latter with *ch* and N; through scribal error and the passage of time these have become confused among Greeks and Latins. What is K among us is C among the Greeks; and what we call *ch* is called *chi* among them.

Jerome explains this more readily in the beginning of Daniel against Porphyry: “Joacim,” he says, “son of Josias, was also called Heliacim; he was succeeded on the throne by his son Joachin, surnamed Jechonias. Therefore, no one should suppose that the Joacim at the beginning of Daniel is the same as the Joachin named at the beginning of Ezekiel. For the former has the final syllable *-cim*, the latter *-chin*. Hence in the Gospel according to Matthew one generation seems to be lacking, because the second group of fourteen [Col. 0065B] ends with Joacim, son of Josias, and the third begins with Joachin, son of Joacim.”

Augustine, however, in his book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, in order to turn the discussion toward allegory, said that “the same Jechonias is counted twice here.”

**Salathiel begot Zorobabel; Zorobabel begot Abiud; Abiud begot Eliachim; Eliachim begot Azor; Azor begot Sadoch; Sadoch begot Achim; Achim begot Eliud; Eliud begot Eleazar; Eleazar begot Mathan; Mathan begot Jacob; Jacob begot Joseph, husband of Mary, from whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.**

[AFRICANUS.] Africanus, *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*: [Col. 0065C] “Mathan,” he says, “and Mathat, at different times, had one son each by one wife named Esta. For Mathan, who descended through Solomon, had first married her and, leaving a son Jacob, died. After his death Mathat, who traced his line through Nathan, son of David, being of the same tribe, took the same Esta as his wife and begot by her a son named Eli. Thus Jacob and Eli were uterine brothers. Jacob, in accordance with the command of the Law, took the wife of his brother Eli, who had died childless, and begot Joseph by her. Thus Joseph is called the son of Eli according to the Law, but the son of Jacob according to nature. Matthew therefore rightly says, ‘Jacob begot Joseph’; and Luke, ‘As was supposed, son of Joseph, who was of Eli, who was of Mathat’ (Luke V).”

[Col. 0065D] **Abraham was son of Thare, who was son of Nachor, who was son of Seruch, who was son of Ragau, who was son of Phaleg, who was son of Heber, who was son of Sale, who was son of Cainan, who was son of Arphaxad.**

Bede, *On Luke*: “The name and generation of Cainan, according to the Hebrew truth, are found neither in Genesis nor in Chronicles; rather, Arphaxad is said to have begotten Sela, or Sale, as his son, with no one intervening. For thus you have it: ‘Arphaxad lived thirty years and begot Sale.’ Likewise in Paralipomenon: ‘Arphaxad begot Sala, who begot Heber.’ Know, then, that blessed Luke took this generation from the edition of the Seventy interpreters, where it is written that Arphaxad, at one hundred and thirty-five years of age, begot Cainan, and Cainan himself, when he was one hundred and thirty years old, begot Sela. But which of these is true, or whether both can be true, [Col. 0066A] God knows.”

**Who was son of Sem, who was son of Noe, who was son of Lamech, who was son of Mathusale, who was son of Henoch.**

This is Henoch, who, with death deferred, was translated into paradise (Gen. V).

**Who was son of Jared, who was son of Malaleel, who was son of Cainan, who was son of Enos, who was son of Seth, who was son of Adam, who was of God.**

M. 2[X]

**Therefore all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; and from David to the deportation to Babylon, fourteen generations; and from the deportation to Babylon to Christ, fourteen generations.**

[Col. 0066B] In the first set of fourteen, Abraham is first and David last. In the second, Solomon is first and Jechonias last. In the third, Jechonias son of Jechonias is first, and Jesus last—he who came into the world through elect and circumcised fathers. For election is shown in David and circumcision in Abraham.

Do not wonder that Luke set down more successions from Christ to David, and Matthew fewer—that is, one forty-two and the other twenty-seven. One recounts persons different from the other; and it could happen that some fathers lived longer than others and begot children later. By descending, Matthew indicates that Christ descended to this mortality in order to govern us. But Luke, ascending, as if designating him a priest, recounts the generations from Christ’s baptism [Col. 0066C] until he comes to God, to whom we are reconciled after cleansing. And he rightly took up the origin of adoption, because through adoption we become sons of God, whereas through carnal generation the Son of God became Son of Man for our sake.

Accordingly, in Matthew’s generations is signified Christ’s taking upon himself our sins; in Luke’s, their abolition. Therefore the latter recounts while ascending, the former while descending. For what the Apostle says—“God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. VIII)—is the taking up of sins. But what he adds—“that he might condemn sin in the flesh” (ibid.)—is the expiation of sins. Matthew consequently descends through Solomon, in whose mother David sinned; but Luke ascends through Nathan, the prophet of that name through whom God expiated that sin.

[RABANUS.] It should be known that the fathers named above signify Christ’s incarnation by their deeds and names, and that, as the Apostle says, all things happened to them in a figure (I Cor. X). Alcuin the deacon therefore adapts their names to allegory as follows:

“Christ, taking up the office of the patriarchs, willed in the interpretation of their names to indicate our salvation. In Abraham, he is the father of all believers, and it is fitting for all to cry and say, ‘Abba, Father’ (Rom. VIII). In Isaac, he is the joy of all the faithful, of whom the angel sang: ‘Behold, I announce to you great joy, which shall be for all the people’ (Luke II). In Jacob, he is the supplanter, because he overthrew and crushed the devil, destroyer of the human race, and distributed his vessels. In Judah, confession, [Col. 0067A] as he himself said: ‘I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth’ (Matt. XI). In Phares, division, because he separates the sheep from the goats (Matt. XXV). In Zara, the rising for our salvation, as it is said: ‘For those who fear the name of the Lord, the sun of righteousness shall rise’ (Mal. IV). In Thamar, the palm of victory, as he himself says: ‘Take courage, for I have conquered the world’ (John XVI). In Esrom, directing arrows of salvation, as it is said: ‘The sharp arrows of the mighty’ (Ps. CXIX). In Aram, the chosen one, concerning whom the Father says: ‘Behold my chosen servant, whom I have chosen; I have placed my Spirit upon him’ (Isa. XLII). In Aminadab, the willing people, because he freely laid down his life for our salvation, to make us a praiseworthy people of the Lord (John X). In Naasson, the augur—that is, the mighty prophet—who says: ‘When [Col. 0067B] the Son of Man comes in his majesty, then he shall sit upon the throne of his majesty, to judge the world in righteousness’ (Matt. XXV). In Salmon, the perceptive—that is, the intelligent one—who said to the Jews: ‘What are you thinking in your hearts?’ (Luke V), and who knows past, present, and future. In Booz is expressed strength of virtue, as he says: ‘I shall draw all things to myself’ (John XII). In Rahab is signified the breadth of the Church. In Obed, serving, because he came not to be served but to serve (Matt. XX), as the Apostle says: ‘Taking the form of a servant’ (Phil. II). In Ruth, hastening to our salvation. In Jesse, fire, as he says: ‘I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I will but that it should burn?’ (Luke XII). And John says: ‘He shall baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire’ [Col. 0067C] (Luke III). In David, beloved, because it is said: ‘Beautiful in form above the sons of men’ (Ps. XLIV); likewise, a mighty warrior, while he conquered the devil and humbled our accuser. In Solomon, peaceable, as he himself said: ‘I give you my peace; I leave you peace’ (John XIV). Likewise the Apostle: ‘He is our peace, who made both one’ (Eph. II). In Uriah, ‘my light is God.’ In Bathsheba, ‘son of the oath,’ concerning whom it is said: ‘The Lord has sworn and will not repent’ (Ps. CIX). In Roboam, the breadth of the faithful people. Hence he says: ‘Many shall come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven’ (Matt. VIII). In Abia, ‘the Lord is my Father,’ who says: ‘Call no one your father upon earth; for one is your Father, who is in heaven’ [Col. 0067D] (Matt. XXIII). In Asa, lifting up, of whom John says: ‘Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world’ (John I). In Josaphat, judge, because he himself shall judge the world in righteousness (Ps. XCV). And likewise: ‘The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son’ (John V). In Joram, exalted, because he ascended into heaven (Acts I). In Ozia, strength of the Lord, because he freed the captivity that held the human race captive and led it up to the heights of heaven (Eph. IV). In Joathan, perfect, as he says in the Gospel: ‘It is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness’ (Matt. III). In Achaz, grasping, because he measured heaven with his palm and enclosed the earth in his fist (Isa. XL). In Ezechias, strength of the Lord, who says: ‘Take courage, for I have conquered the world’ (John XVI). In Manasse, forgetful of our iniquity, as is read in Ezekiel [Col. 0068A]: ‘On the day when the sinner turns from his iniquity, all his iniquities shall be handed over to forgetfulness’ (Ezek. XVIII). In Amon, faithful, because he says: ‘Ask, and it shall be given to you’ (Matt. VII). Likewise Paul: ‘That he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God’ (Heb. II). In Josia, salvation of the Lord, because ‘whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved’ (Joel II). In Jechonia, preparation of the Lord, who says: ‘If I go and prepare a place for you’ (John XIV). In Salathiel, ‘my petition is God,’ as he himself says: ‘Holy Father, keep in your name those whom you gave me’ (John XVII). In Zorobabel, teacher of sinners and tax collectors, in order to call them back from the error of their way. In Abiud, ‘my father,’ who said: ‘I and the Father are one’ (John X), and who is the father and head of all believers. In [Col. 0068B] Eliachim, the resurrection of the Lord, who says: ‘Whoever believes in me shall not die forever’ (John XI), and ‘I shall raise him up on the last day’ (John VI). In Azor, helped, who says: ‘I am not alone, because the Father is with me’ (John VIII), and he himself is the helper of all who hope in him. In Sadoch, righteous, as it is written: ‘That he may be righteous, justifying those who are in the faith of Abraham’ (Rom. III). In Achim, ‘my brother,’ who says: ‘Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, that one is my brother and sister and mother’ (Matt. XII; Mark III). In Eliud, ‘my God’: this he said to the Father from our weakness, ‘My God, my God, from the dawn I watch for you’ (Ps. LXII), that is, I rise again to you. In Eleazar, ‘God, my God, helper,’ and protector of all believers in him, who said: ‘The Father who sent me is with me’ [Col. 0068C] (Ps. XVII). In Mathan, gift, because through him the Father gave all things (John VIII); and he himself, ascending on high, gave gifts to men (Rom. VII). In Jacob, supplanter of the ancient enemy, who gave believers power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy (Luke X). In Joseph, increase and increase of eternal life, as he himself says: ‘I came that they may have life and have it more abundantly’ (John X). But in the holy and perpetual virgin Mary, from whom he was born, ‘star of the sea’—that is, the light of this world, which enlightens every human being coming into this world (John I).

“For through these dwelling places he came into the world, in order that, coming through them, he might lead us into the land of eternal promise [Col. 0068D]. Morally, too, the interpretations of the patriarchs’ names signify our progress. In Abraham, that we may be fathers of many virtues and possess by right of inheritance an abundance of good works (Gen. XVIII). In Isaac, that we may have joy, as the Apostle says: ‘Rejoice always in the Lord; again I say, rejoice’ (Phil. IV). In Jacob, that as supplanters of our vices we may tread under our vigorous foot carnal desires and the devil’s power. In Judah, that we may come before the face of the Lord in confession, confess his name, and praise him for ages of ages (Ps. XCIV). In Phares, that we may be divided from the wicked and separate our actions from their fellowship. In Zara, that the morning star may rise in our hearts and the sun of righteousness shine everywhere [Col. 0069A] in our minds. In Thamar, that with the palm of victory we may overcome the devil’s pomps and the world’s desires. In Esrom, that we may be arrows of the Lord’s salvation, so that it may be said of us: ‘The sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals’ (Ps. CXIX). In Aram, that we may be the Lord’s chosen and a chosen race, a royal priesthood (I Pet. II), by Christ’s exalted merit. In Aminadab, that we may be the Lord’s willing people in the building up of his body. In Naasson, that, abandoning the worldly auguries of the Gentiles, we may put faith in divine promises. In Salmon, that we may be found perceptive—that is, intelligent—of God’s truth and doers in him (Col. II). In Booz, that we may confess the Lord and act manfully (Ps. CXVIII), triumphing over the aerial powers in Christ. In Rahab, that we may observe the broad commandment [Col. 0069B] of the Lord by loving God and neighbor. In Obed, that we may serve the Lord with gladness (Ps. XCIX), through the spirit of love and holy affection. In Ruth, that we may hasten to enter unto God (Heb. IV) while we have time (Gal. VI). In Jesse, that we may offer the incense of our prayers to the Lord on the altar of the cross, as the Prophet says: ‘Let my prayer be directed as incense before you’ (Ps. CXL). In David, that we may be found beloved by our God, strong against the spiritual Goliath (I Kings XVII). In Solomon, that, as far as lies in us, we may have peace with all (Rom. XII), because ‘blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God’ (Matt. V). In Uriah, that God may be our light. In Bathsheba, that we may keep the oath (Gen. [Col. 0069C] XXI). In Roboam, that, fulfilling the place of charity, we may rejoice in the breadth of spiritual goods. In Abia, that we may be brothers having God as Father, and heirs of God, indeed coheirs with Christ (Rom. VIII). In Asa, that we may direct our meditation from vices to virtues, from earthly things to heavenly. In Josaphat, that we may judge every person rightly. In Joram, that we may seek the things above (Col. III), think on things above, be exalted in the Lord in effect, and have our manner of life in heaven. In Ozia, that we may be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might. In Joathan, that we may perform perfect works, according to the Gospel: ‘Be perfect, as your Father is perfect’ (Matt. V). In Achaz, that we may lay hold of discipline, lest the Lord at any time be angry (Ps. II); and may love the way of our salvation, which is Christ, who says: ‘I am the way and the truth’ [Col. 0069D] (John XIV). In Ezechias, that we may praise God’s strength fighting for us and continually beg him to strengthen us. In Manasse, that we may forget our injuries and, forgetting what is past, always attend to what lies ahead (Phil. III). In Amon, that we may stand in the faith by which we can extinguish the fiery darts of the devil’s deceit (Eph. VI). In Josia, that with all strength and power we may attain the Lord’s salvation, which he deigned to grant us. In Jechonia, that we may be ready at the Lord’s coming (Luke XII), watching and praying lest we fall into temptations (Matt. XXVI). In Salathiel, that we may ask one petition of the Lord: that we may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of our life (Ps. XXVI).

[Col. 0070A] “In Zorobabel, that we may be teachers of truth, opposing the teaching of heretics, which is confusion. In Abiud, that God may be a father to us, and we sons to him. In Eliachim, that we may rise from the death of sin and live to God in the Holy Spirit. In Azor, that, with God’s help, we may conquer the enemies of our salvation. In Sadoch, that we may deserve to be justified by him who justifies the ungodly. In Achim, that we may be Christ’s brothers, mothers, and sisters in him, by doing his will (Matt. VII). In Eliud, that we may have no God except our Lord Jesus Christ. In Eleazar, that we may confess that our salvation consists in the Lord Jesus alone, saying: ‘Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth’ (Ps. XII). In Mathan, that, receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit, we may not [Col. 0070B] desire evils as the Gentiles do. In Jacob, that we may overthrow the rulers of this darkness by our strength. In Joseph, that, as the outward person wastes away, the inward may be renewed day by day, until Christ is spiritually formed in us; and that through Mary—that is, the light of faith—we may be led by divine grace to the ineffable vision of God Almighty.”

Thus far Alcuin.

In Thare, Christ explores and feeds, because “the Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II), and “will place them in a place of pasture” (Ps. XXII). In Nachor, he rested in the tomb in hope of the light of immortality. In Seruch, he was a perfectly knotted cord, because no one fully knew the mystery of the incarnation. In Ragau, he is the good shepherd who gives his life for all his own (John X). In Phalog, he divides spiritual persons from carnal persons. [Col. 0070C] In Heber, he passed from death to life. In Sale, he dissolved the enmities between God and human beings. In Cainan, he possesses heaven and earth and all that is in them. In Arphaxad, he healed us from the wounds inflicted by the devil laying us waste. In Sem, a good name, because he is the merciful and compassionate Creator and Re-creator. In Noe, eternal rest for angels and human beings alike. In Lamech, humble even unto hell; hence: “O hell, I shall be your bite” (Hos. XIII). In Mathusalem, the Lord was sent forth from death by rising again. In Enoch, he consecrated the temple which we are (I Cor. III). In Jareth, he descended from heaven and strengthened the Church. In Malalehel, he praised the Lord; hence: “And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives” (Matt. XXVI). In Enos, despairing, [Col. 0070D] to whom the two disciples going to the village of Emmaus said: “But we had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke XXIV). In Seth, placing, as Simeon says: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and resurrection of many” (Luke II). In Adam, he was earthly, because he assumed a true body from the Virgin.

M. IV[V] L. 11

**Now the generation of Christ was thus.**

[AUGUSTINE, *in a Sermon.*] The first condition of humanity was that Adam was formed from the earth. The second was that woman was created from the side of man. The third was that a human being was born from man and woman. But Christ’s generation was thus: he was born from a woman without a man [Col. 0071A], conceived through the Holy Spirit. The first and second generations fell; from their fall they generated the third; in the fourth they found salvation.

**When Mary his mother had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit.**

[RABANUS—ORIGEN.] “Before they came together,” that is, before they celebrated the marriage ceremonies, she was found to be with child: first by the angels guarding her, and then by Joseph, as a man solicitous about his betrothed. The Evangelist, writing of past events, rightly calls Joseph the husband of Mary and Mary the mother of Jesus according to his own time. For it is certain that at the time of the betrothal she was not yet a mother, nor was he yet a husband.

[Col. 0071B] M. 4[X]

**But Joseph her husband, being righteous and unwilling to expose her, wished to put her away secretly.**

[ORIGEN.] If he suspected her, how was he righteous? If he did not suspect her, why did he wish to put her away? For it would have been unjust for him to wish to put away one who was undefiled. He therefore wished to put her away because he knew that a great mystery was present in her. He judged himself unworthy to draw near to it, just as blessed Peter, humbling himself before the Lord, said: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke V); and the centurion: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (Matt. VIII). And Elizabeth said to Mary: [Col. 0071C] “Whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?”

[AUGUSTINE, *On the Words of the Lord.*] Or otherwise: if you alone know that someone has sinned, when you wish to accuse that person before others, you are not a corrector but a betrayer. Therefore Joseph did not wish to make Mary public, although his suspicion of adultery was certain; rather, he wished to benefit one who had sinned, and this was reckoned to him as righteousness.

**But while he was considering these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in sleep, saying: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife.”**

[RABANUS.] This is as though he said: “Take Mary, your betrothed, as your wife.” The angel appears to one who is awake by assuming a visible body, but to one asleep by impressing an image upon the mind. Joseph is called son of [Col. 0071D] David so that Mary too may be shown to be from David’s tribe, as it is written: “Let no one marry a wife except from his own tribe” (Num. XXXVI).

**For that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit.**

That is, what was conceived in her is from the operation of the Holy Spirit. To be born *in* her is to be conceived; to be born *from* her is to come forth into the light.

**And she shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he shall save his people from their sins.**

He explains the etymology of the name. For he is called Jesus—that is, Savior—because he saves.

**But all this happened in order that what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son; and they shall call [Col. 0072A] his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isa. VII).**

As if to say: God is in our nature, because this son of the Virgin is God and man. The very word *behold*, which the prophet uses, expresses amazement at the greatness of so great a mystery. All this—that the Virgin should be betrothed to her kinsman, that Joseph should be instructed by an angel, and so forth—happened so that both through these things and through those that follow the prophecy might be fulfilled.

**But Joseph, rising from sleep, did as the angel of the Lord commanded him.**

Whoever is admonished by God should delay no longer: let him rise from sleep and do what is commanded.

**And he took his wife, and did not know her [Col. 0072B] until she had borne her firstborn son; and he called his name Jesus.**

[RABANUS.] Joseph at first, wishing to dismiss Mary, because he was righteous, did not wish to expose her publicly or have her condemned by the Law. But now, lest any uncertainty about her childbirth should arise, he is received as a witness to Christ’s conception by the Holy Spirit when he takes his betrothed as his wife. He therefore took her with the title of wife for the reasons already stated; and he did not know her in marital intercourse because of the mysteries he had learned.

“He did not know her until she had borne” does not mean that he knew her afterward; rather, *until* is used in the sense of *and*, or it excludes that time about which greater suspicion would arise, as David says: “Until I place your enemies” (Ps. [Col. 0072C] CIX), and so forth. Firstborn are all who first open the womb, whether brothers follow them or none at all.

L. 1[X]

**And it came to pass in those days that an edict went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled.**

[BEDA.] According to the testimony of histories, Augustus reigned in such great peace for twelve years around the time of the Lord’s birth that, with both foreign and civil wars throughout the world stilled, that prophetic saying seems to have been fulfilled even literally: “They shall beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into sickles. Nation shall not lift sword against nation” (Isa. II). Christ is fittingly born in a most peaceful time because “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” [Col. 0072D] (II Cor. V).

This peace which Augustus made signified the peace which our Mediator would make, both personally and through his disciples, between God and human beings. It was also fitting that the disciples, wherever they went to preach, should be protected by the formidable shadow of the Roman name. For as a declaration for the census was required by Caesar from the whole world, so a declaration of faith was to be required by Christ throughout the world. Hence: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI).

**This first enrollment was made by Cyrinus, governor of Syria; and all went, each to make declaration in his own city.**

This enrollment is called the first with respect to the time of [Col. 0073A] Cyrinus. For before this, many regions of the earth had often been enrolled. Cyrinus, sent by Caesar to administer justice among the nations and to become censor of property, came to Syria. And because Judaea is, as it were, the navel of the whole earth, the tax assessment is first required in the middle of the earth, so that afterward it may be sought thence even to the ends of the world.

[BEDA.] At this point Judaea first became tributary to the Romans. While Augustus was emperor and Cyrinus governor, all went to the enrollment so that, each returning to his own city, they might declare the tax due. Therefore, if now, with Christ reigning and promising rewards through the governors who are teachers of the Church, we declare the assessment of righteousness, take up his yoke which is light, and we shall find rest for our souls (Matt. XI). A denarius, containing ten coins and bearing Caesar’s image, was paid to Caesar; let us likewise offer our King the Decalogue of the Law, in which we shall find the face of our King—that is, the knowledge of his will.

**And Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, to the city of David called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David, to make declaration with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant.**

[GREGORY.] The Lord wished to be conceived in one place and born in another so that he might more easily escape the fury of Herod, who lay in wait. At the Lord’s birth the world is enrolled, because he was appearing in the flesh who would inscribe the elect in eternity. Conversely, of the reprobate it is said: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous” (Ps. LXVIII).

**And it came to pass, while they were there, that the days [Col. 0073C] were fulfilled for her to give birth, and she bore her firstborn son.**

[BEDA.] The Lord is rightly born in Bethlehem, both because of the judgment concerning the royal stock and because of the mystery of the name. For Bethlehem is interpreted “house of bread”; and there the living bread which came down from heaven (John VI) appears in the flesh, refreshing the minds of the elect with inward fullness.

Every day the Lord is conceived in Nazareth and born in Bethlehem when any faithful person, receiving the flower of the Word, makes himself a house of eternal bread. Every day he is conceived through faith in the mind of believers as in a virginal womb and born through baptism. Every day the Church, like the Mother of God, accompanies her teacher as Mary accompanied Joseph, ascending from the ruin of worldly life—which is what Galilee signifies—to the city of Judah, that is, of confession and praise [Col. 0073D], and pays to the eternal King the tribute of devotion.

This Church, after the example of blessed Mary, is as though betrothed to one but made fruitful by another: she is joined to the bishop set over her, but filled with the power of the Holy Spirit. Thus Joseph is rightly interpreted “increased,” indicating that the effort of a teaching master avails nothing without the increase of heavenly help.

**And she wrapped him in swaddling clothes and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for him in the lodging.**
[GREGORY—BEDE.] He who clothes the world in varied adornment is clothed in lowly garments, that we might receive the robe of immortality. His hands and feet are bound in swaddling-clothes, so that our hands may be directed to good works and our feet into the way of peace. He is laid in a manger, that he might refresh all the faithful—that is, the holy animals—with the grain of his flesh: he who is the bread of angels. He is contained in a narrow manger, that he may enlarge us through the joys of the heavenly kingdom. The Lord was not born in his parents’ house, to show that through the humanity he assumed he was born, as it were, in a place not his own—not according to his power, but according to the nature of his humanity. For of his power it is written: “He came unto his own” (John 1). And because “all flesh is grass” (Isa. 40), God, made man, turned our grass into grain, saying of himself: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone” (John 12). Hence, having been born, he is laid in a manger.

John Chrysostom (in a homily): The mother laid down the child. But Joseph did not dare to touch him, whom he knew had not been begotten by himself. Whoever you are that are poor, take comfort. Joseph and Mary, the Lord’s mother, have no male servant, no maidservant, no beast of burden: they themselves are both masters and servants. Timid poverty does not dare approach among the rich; they go to an inn. He who raises the needy from the dunghill is born in a stable (Ps. 112). Job sat upon a dunghill and was afterwards crowned (Job 2).

## CHAPTER VI

L. 3[X]

“And there were shepherds in the same region, keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock. And behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside them, and the glory of God shone around them.”

[Col. 0074C] [BEDE.] When the Lord was born, the shepherds keep watch and guard their flock, in order to show that the time had come which he had formerly promised, saying: “Behold, I myself will seek my sheep and visit them, as a shepherd visits his flock” (Ezek. 34). By the flock the people are meant; by the night, the world; by the shepherds, priests, who are to provide for souls with wakeful care. The angel’s appearance with so great a light—a thing not found throughout the whole course of the Old Testament—mystically foretold what the Apostle later stated openly: “The night is far spent, but the day has drawn near” (Rom. 13).

“And they feared with great fear. And the angel said to them: Do not fear. For behold, I proclaim to you joy which shall be for all the people, because there is born to you today [Col. 0074D] a Savior, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David.”

Everlasting joy is announced to all the faithful people being gathered from every diversity of nations. Although it was night, the angel did not say, “this night,” but “today,” because he announced great joy. But where sad events occur, mention is usually made of night, as in: “This night you shall suffer scandal” (Matt. 26).

“And this shall be a sign to you: You shall find an infant wrapped in swaddling-clothes and laid in a manger.”

The Savior’s humility, opposed to the pride through which came death, is a sign of salvation to the faithful.

“And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: Glory to God in the highest [Col. 0075A] and on earth peace to people of good will.”

While one angel proclaims the Gospel, a multitude bursts forth into harmonious praise, both rendering its service to God and instructing us that, whenever we hear sacred teaching from a brother’s mouth, we should render praise to God in heart, speech, and deed. The term “heavenly host” is apt, because they were soldiers: he was ordering the hosts of angels against evil spirits for our protection. Because God and man has been born, peace is sung to humankind and glory to God, who is glorified by the angels for our redemption. And because neither Jews nor Gentiles possess peace—for “there is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isa. 48)—it is specifically said, “to people of good will,” namely, those who receive the newborn Christ.

[GREGORY.] Because through sin we had become strangers to God, the angels counted us as strangers. But because we have acknowledged our king, the angels have acknowledged us as their fellow citizens; and an angel fears to be worshipped by human nature, which it beholds in its king (Rev. 19). Thus Lot (Gen. 19) and Joshua (Josh. 15) were not forbidden to worship angels, but John was forbidden in the Apocalypse: “See,” he says, “that you do not do this, for I am your fellow servant and that of your brothers” (Rev. 22).

“And it came to pass, when the angels had departed from them into heaven, that the shepherds said to one another: Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this Word which has happened, which the Lord has made and shown to us.”

[BEDE.] They did not say, “Let us see the child,” but “the Word”; [Col. 0075C] as though they said: “The Word was in the beginning, and became flesh.” What the Lord—that is, the Father, the Word himself, and the Holy Spirit—made, namely determined should be incarnate, he thus showed as accomplished, though it could not be seen in his divinity.

“And they came with haste, and found Mary and Joseph, and the infant laid in a manger. And when they saw, they came to know concerning the Word which had been spoken to them about this child.”

Some who seek Christ do not find him because they seek sluggishly. But the shepherds found him because they ran with unfeigned faith. Thus the shepherds of the Church—indeed, all the faithful—raised by heavenly teaching, as though entering the gates of Bethlehem, find the catholic [Col. 0075D] Church as Mary, the company of teachers as Joseph, and the humble coming of the Mediator, set in the pages of Scripture as in a manger. When they saw the child, they came to know the Word which had been spoken; and we too, through faith in the incarnation, shall come to behold the glory of the Word.

It should be noted that things worthy of report and narration are sometimes called “words.” Thus in Isaiah: “There was no word,” that is, no thing worthy of mention, which Hezekiah did not show the Chaldeans (Isa. 39). Similarly, the shepherds say here: “Let us see this Word which has happened,” that is, that event worthy of narration, which the Lord himself, most exalted, performed and signified to us through angels. Therefore, where it says, “They came to know concerning the Word which had been spoken,” understand “word” as speech.

[Col. 0076A] “And all who heard wondered at those things which had been spoken to them by the shepherds.”

[BEDE.] They wonder both at the mystery of the incarnation and at so great a testimony from the shepherds, who did not know how to embellish what they had heard, but preached true things with simple eloquence. Thus the Lord appointed not rhetoricians but fishermen to preach the Gospel. So too, in the Old Testament, he appointed shepherds as messengers of his dispensation; therefore the shepherds’ testimony is not to be lightly esteemed.

“But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart.”

Mary, no less modest in speech than in body, silently compares what she had seen happen around her with what she had read in the Scriptures was to happen. She had read in Isaiah: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7). She had read: “The ox knows [Col. 0076B] its owner, and the ass its master’s manger” (Isa. 1). She saw her son, her only son, crying in God’s manger. She saw that she was descended from David’s stock, that she had conceived by the Spirit in Nazareth, and had given birth in Bethlehem: testimonies to all these things she had read in the prophets. She therefore compares the prophets’ words with the events, and in all of them finds grounds for faith. If Mary learned from shepherds, let us also learn from priests.

“And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things they had heard and seen, as had been spoken to them.”

For what they had heard from the angels they praised God, and for what they had seen in Bethlehem they glorified him. Likewise, the teachers of spiritual flocks now survey the camps of the faithful, seeking examples of uprightness; now they return to their pastoral office by teaching.

## CHAPTER VII

“And after eight days had been completed for the child’s circumcision, his name was called Jesus, which had been called by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.”

The rite of circumcision began with Abraham, when he also received an enlargement of his name. In imitation of this, names were given to boys on the day of their circumcision. Thus it was done also to Jesus himself. He is rightly circumcised on the eighth day, that both his resurrection might be celebrated on the eighth day and our future eighth age might be prefigured. For there are six ages [Col. 0076D] in which people labor for the Lord; the seventh is that of souls until the time of the resurrection; the eighth is the resurrection, when the perfect glory of circumcision shall shine forth and the whole person shall cleave to the vision of the Creator.

But now one who looks upon a woman in order to desire her (Matt. 5) has uncircumcised sight. Their ears are uncircumcised to whom Truth says: “He who is of God hears the words of God. Therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John 8). Their tongue and hands are uncircumcised whose mouth has spoken vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity (Ps. 143). Their taste is uncircumcised whom the prophet rebukes, saying: “Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine, and strong men at mixing drunkenness” (Isa. 5). Their smell and touch are uncircumcised [Col. 0077A] who, anointed with varied perfumes, follow the embraces of the harlot who sprinkles her bed with cinnamon. Their steps are uncircumcised, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace” (Ps. 13).

But he who had come “in the likeness of sinful flesh” did not reject the remedy by which sinful flesh was cleansed; rather, he was circumcised, “made under the law,” that he might prove it just and redeem those under the law (Gal. 4). Note that circumcision under the law bestowed against the wound of original sin the same healing aid that baptism now confers in the time of grace—except that entry into the kingdom was not yet open to the circumcised as it is now to the baptized. Yet baptism does not do this alone, but also the addition of the Passion; [Col. 0077B] and if this had been added to circumcision, the same would have occurred there as well.

The reason it was done in such a member was that no other limb should either be weakened or expose anything shameful publicly, and that Christ’s coming might be signified through chastity. Circumcision was also performed in the flesh of the foreskin because concupiscence rules more strongly in that part, through which original sin is propagated. Therefore, where the way of sin is, there the remedy for sin was fittingly marked; and by circumcision of the flesh is signified the circumcision of the mind, by which the soul is cleansed from vices.

There are, then, clearly three circumcisions. One is the sacrament; the realities belonging to that sacrament are, namely, circumcision from sin, which takes place daily in the soul, and circumcision from sin and from every punishment of sin, which shall occur at the resurrection [Col. 0077C] in soul and body. Joshua circumcised those entering the promised land with stone knives (Josh. 5), because “the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10), who takes away the sins of the world (John 1).

“And when the days of Mary’s purification according to the law of Moses had been fulfilled, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord.”

Moses said: “A woman, if having received seed she bears a male child, shall be unclean seven days, and on the eighth day the infant shall be circumcised; but she herself shall remain thirty-three days in the blood of her purification.” He did not say, “every woman giving birth,” but “she who, having received seed, bears”; distinguishing her from the one who conceived and bore as a virgin. Therefore neither mother nor [Col. 0077D] son needed purification by sacrifices; but that we might be freed from fear of the law, they were made subject to the law.

It was also decreed by the law that a child be brought to the temple from the thirty-third day after circumcision and that a sacrifice be given for him; but every firstborn male was to be made holy to the Lord. This indicates that no one except those circumcised from vices is worthy of the Lord’s presence, as the Psalmist says: “The wicked does not dwell beside you, nor shall the unjust remain before your eyes” (Ps. 5). “To present him to the Lord,” that is, to offer and consecrate him.

“As it is written in the law of the Lord: Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.”

The law commanded every firstborn, both of humans and beasts, [Col. 0078A] of the male sex to be consecrated to the Lord and belong to the priest, so that the priest should receive a price for a human firstborn, should cause an unclean animal to be redeemed, and should offer clean animals to God. A firstborn was redeemed for five silver shekels, and a shekel contains twenty obols.

[BEDE.] Yet it should be noted that little children of the tribe of Levi were not redeemed, but were held permanently for the service of the house. All those firstborns signified Christ, who, though the only-begotten Son of God, deigned to become “the firstborn of all creation”; who alone is holy to the Lord, because he “did no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth.” Morally also, firstborns signify the good beginnings of our actions, as though born in the heart and to be attributed to the Lord’s grace. We are commanded to redeem evil deeds by the fruits [Col. 0078B] of repentance.

“Opening the womb” is a customary expression, not an assertion—as heretics maintain—that the Lord, by leaving the lodging of the sacred womb, is to be believed to have destroyed virginity. Mystically it signifies that the Lord opened the generative secret of the virgin Church, so as to beget for himself peoples through water and the Holy Spirit.

“And to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the law of the Lord: a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.”

It was said in the law that for a male child, on the fortieth day after birth, and for a female on the eightieth day, a spotless year-old lamb should be offered as a burnt offering, and a turtledove or young pigeon for sin. But anyone who could not offer a lamb because of [his] poverty [Col. 0078C] was to offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a burnt offering and the other for sin. The Lord wished this sacrifice of the poor to be offered for himself, having become poor for us, in order to make us rich here in faith and heirs of the kingdom in heaven.

Morally, whether a person has performed strong works, distinguished by the masculine name, or weak ones, denoted by the feminine term, so that these may be consecrated to the Lord, let that person offer the sheep of innocence and the turtledove or pigeon, signifying the groaning of compunction and the tears of the humble, since these birds have groaning rather than song. For we need tears even in good things, because we do not know by what end we are to be brought to completion. There are two kinds of compunction: when, recalling the punishments of evils, we fear; and when, burning with desire for heavenly things, [Col. 0078D] we groan at delay. Hence two young birds are commanded to be offered: one as a burnt offering, when we are inflamed with love for heavenly things; the other for sin, when we groan over evils committed.

The pigeon, which lives in a flock, signifies the active life; the solitary turtledove, the contemplative life, which belongs to few. Since each sacrifice is acceptable to God, each bird is wisely offered for the Lord. One who prays to the Father in secret behind a closed door offers a turtledove; one who seeks companions in work brings a pigeon to the altar.

[BEDE, in a homily.] Jesus is first circumcised and then, after intervening days, brought with sacrifices to Jerusalem, because he first trampled down the corruption of the flesh by rising again and, after intervening days, ascended to the heavenly city with the flesh which he had made [Col. 0079A] a sacrifice. We too are first circumcised from sins in baptism; then, as grace advances, we enter the altar to be consecrated by the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood. At the end of the world, the whole Church too shall first put off in the resurrection the stain of earthly corruption and afterwards be transferred to the heavenly Jerusalem, commended to the Lord by the victims of good works.

“And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon; and this man was just and devout, awaiting the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was in him.”

[BEDE.] He was just and devout, because justice is difficult to preserve without fear. I do not mean servile fear, which charity casts out, but the holy fear of the Lord which remains for ever and ever; by it the more a just person loves God, the more carefully he avoids offending him.

“And he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he should not see death before first seeing the Lord’s Christ; and he came in the Spirit into the temple.”

To see death means to experience and feel it. Happy is the one who shall see death after first striving to see the Lord’s Christ with the eyes of the heart, by living in the heavenly Jerusalem and sighing with the Psalmist, who says: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord” (Ps. 26).

“And when his parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the law, he took him into his arms.”

By the same grace through which he had known beforehand that he would come, he recognized him when he came. He whom heaven and earth cannot contain is borne in the arms of an aged man. Figuratively, the old man received the infant, to teach us to put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new in the righteousness and holiness of works signified by the arms. The old world received the innocence of Christian infancy, that it might be renewed like the eagle.

“And he blessed God and said: Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace.”

He knew how blessed were the eyes that would see Christ; and therefore, until he saw him, he did not wish to be released by death. But as soon as he saw him, he desired to be released from the body and to have peace in Abraham’s bosom.

“Because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared [Col. 0079D] before the face of all peoples.”

Him whom you afterwards prepared to be sought by all peoples with love and beheld by faith, I now behold as Savior with the eyes both of flesh and mind. Blessed are those who see what Simeon saw; blessed are those “who have not seen and have believed” (John 20).

“A light for the revelation of the Gentiles and the glory of your people Israel.”

By salvation I mean a light for revelation: that the blind eyes of the Gentiles, raised by no hope of the Lord’s coming, may be opened; and that Israel may glory in receiving its promised and desired one. The revelation of the Gentiles is rightly placed before Israel’s glory, because when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then Israel shall be saved. Hence in the Psalm: “In the sight of the Gentiles he revealed his righteousness, remembering mercy toward the house of Israel” [Col. 0080A] (Ps. 27).

[AMBROSE.] Whoever wishes to be dismissed in peace, let him come to Jerusalem, having his manner of life in heaven; let him come to the temple—that is, let him be fashioned after the example of those in whom God dwells. Let him await the Lord, receive the Word of God into his hands, and embrace him with the arms of faith, hope, and charity; then he shall be dismissed so as not to see death, because he has seen life.

“And his father and mother were wondering at the things spoken concerning him. And Simeon blessed them.”

[BEDE.] Since Joseph was the foster-father and preserved Mary’s reputation, he is called the Savior’s father according to common opinion.

“And he said to Mary his mother: Behold, this one is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, [Col. 0080B] and for a sign that shall be contradicted.”

The Lord is set for the fall of many, because he is the stone of offense and rock of stumbling—that is, ruin—to those who stumble at the word and do not believe. Of them he himself says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin” (John 15). But he is set for the rising again of those who, believing in him, have risen from sins through him. He is also set in his preachers for fall and rising again, as the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are saved and among those who perish” (2 Cor. 2). By one good fragrance some are saved, others perish. By “a sign that shall be contradicted,” understand the faith of the Lord’s cross, concerning which the Jews said to Paul: [Col. 0080C] “As to this sect, it is known to us that everywhere it is spoken against.”

“And a sword shall pierce your own soul.”

That is, the grief of the Lord’s Passion; for she could not see her son crucified without the feeling of maternal sorrow, even though she hoped that he would rise again. Until the end of the age, the sword of tribulation pierces the soul of the Church when the sign of faith is contradicted by the wicked and when she sees many fall.

[ORIGEN.] Alternatively: The Lord is set for the fall of vices and the rising again of virtues; and there is no rising again unless a fall comes first. Everything related about Christ—that he was born of a virgin, that he rises again, that he enters through closed doors—all these, I say, are a sign contradicted by unbelievers.

[AMBROSE.] “A sword shall pierce your own soul,” [Col. 0080D] namely, the Word of God, revealing mysteries to you. The Lord is set for fall and rising again. Hence it follows:

“That the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.”

[BEDE.] Before this it was uncertain which Jews would receive Christ and which would reject him; but when his birth was heard of, thoughts were revealed, as Herod and his people were troubled. Later, when his teaching and power had become widely known, some regarded him as a teacher of truth, while others withdrew from him as from a deceiver.

“There was Anna, a prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She had advanced in many days and had lived with her husband seven years from her virginity. And she was a widow until eighty-four years of age, and did not depart [Col. 0081A] from the temple, serving with fastings and prayers night and day.”

According to the historical sense, Anna is described as worthy to bear testimony to the Lord, both because of her devout manner of life and her venerable age. Mystically, however, she signifies the Church, which in the present life is widowed, as it were, by the death of her bridegroom and Lord. Seven times twelve makes eighty-four: seven belongs to the course of the world, which revolves in seven days; twelve, to the perfection of apostolic teaching. Whoever therefore devotes the whole time of life to apostolic institutions is praised as though keeping the thresholds of the heavenly temple for eighty-four years, awaiting the Lord’s coming while absent from the Lord.

The seven years during which Anna lived with her husband signify the perfection [Col. 0081B] of that time in which the Church is taught by the Lord while he lives in the flesh. Those years were afterwards multiplied by twelve because of the apostolic teaching that thereafter governed the Church.

“And she, coming in at that very hour, gave thanks to the Lord and spoke of him to all who awaited the redemption of Israel.”

At the very hour Simeon took the child, Anna came in and gave thanks—that is, praised God. And to all the faithful who, burdened under the yoke of the foreigner Herod, awaited deliverance, they promised that redemption would shortly occur through Christ’s coming. Not angels alone, but every sex and age bears witness to the child at his birth; and, just as he was foretold by the faithful of every age, so, when he came, he is proclaimed by the praise of all the saints.

[BEDE.] That aged Simeon and Anna receive and praise Jesus signifies the synagogue of the faithful, which after long expectation of the promises received with unfeigned faith him who had been foretold.

“And when they had completed all things according to the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own city Nazareth.”

## CHAPTER VIII

M. 4[X]

“Now when Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of King Herod, behold, magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?”

[BEDE.] The time of Herod also bears witness to [Col. 0081D] the Lord’s coming. For it had been foretold that “a ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. 9). From the time the fathers departed Egypt, they were governed by leaders of their own nation until Samuel the prophet, and afterwards by kings until the Babylonian captivity. But after the return from Babylon, supreme affairs were conducted by high priests until Hyrcanus, who was both king and high priest. When he had been killed through the treachery of Herod—whose father Hyrcanus himself had elevated from a lowly foreigner, that is, one of the Idumaean nation—the kingdom of Judaea was entrusted to Herod himself by order of Caesar Augustus. In Herod’s thirty-first year, he who was to be sent came.

It is called Bethlehem of Judaea because there is another [Col. 0082A] Bethlehem in Galilee. “Magi came from the East,” that is, from regions lying toward the East. For they were from the land of the Persians and Chaldeans, where the river Saba is, from which the region is called Saba.

“For we saw his star in the East, and have come to worship him.”

This was said to shame the Jews: “We saw his star,” so that they might learn Christ’s birth from the Gentiles.

[AMBROSE.] The magi were successors of Balaam, who knew the star through his prophecy. He saw the star in the Spirit; they saw it with their eyes and believed. Certainly they would not have worshipped him if they had believed him merely a little child.

[GREGORY.] An angel appeared to the shepherds when the Lord was born, but a star to the magi; because to the Jews, as those who used reason, a rational creature ought to preach, while signs were to be given to the Gentiles, as though lacking reason. It was fitting that, when the Lord was already speaking, apostles should preach to the Gentiles; but while he was not yet speaking, the elements should preach. The magi were called eastern kings, either because they were of Balaam’s stock and knew much about incantations, or because they deceived Herod by returning to their country by another way. Those are also called magi who suppose that they can know certain things through stars, birds, or any other signs.

“But when King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.”

[GREGORY.] When the king of heaven is born, the earthly king is troubled, because earthly exaltation is confounded when heavenly exaltation is revealed. Jerusalem is troubled because it favored Herod, whom it feared, according to Solomon’s saying: “An unjust king has all his ministers wicked” [Col. 0082C] (Prov. 29).
