“And gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he asked them where Christ was to be born.”

M. 3[VII] A. 83

“But they said to him: In Bethlehem of Judaea. For thus it is written through the prophet: ‘And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come forth a leader who shall rule my people Israel’” (Mic. 5).

Bethlehem is indeed a very small village, but it is by no means least among the rulers—that is, in the excellence of the dignity of Judah’s rulers. For the Savior is born there. This testimony is from the prophet Micah, but the Evangelist, according to his custom, adopts the prophet’s sense [Col. 0082D] and changes the wording.

M. 6[X]

“Then Herod, having secretly summoned the magi, carefully learned from them the time when the star had appeared to them. And sending them to Bethlehem, he said: Go and inquire carefully concerning the child; and when you have found him, report back to me, that I too may come and worship him.”

Having learned the place and time, he does not wish to remain ignorant of the child’s identity. Herod signifies hypocrites, who say one thing and think another; while they seek God falsely, they never deserve to find him.

“When they had heard the king, they departed. And behold, the star which they had seen in the East went before them, until it came and stood over the place where the child was.”

[Col. 0083A] As the magi approached Jerusalem, the star disappeared, because whoever approaches hypocrites and heretics loses God’s light. But after withdrawing from them, one recovers the divine light, so as to believe that Christ was born of a virgin. Since it distinguished the house, the star did not follow the courses of the stars; rather, standing near the house above it, it indicated—the phrase is understood—the place where the child was. This star, as Fulgentius says, had never appeared before it was appointed to lead the magi; it was created then and, its task completed, immediately ceased to exist.

“And when they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. And entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother. And falling down, they worshipped him.”

“Entering the house,” that is, the lodging mentioned by Luke, they found the child and his mother. [Col. 0083B] Joseph is silent here either because none of the duties proper to a foster-father is mentioned, or perhaps because he was absent, lest there be occasion for evil suspicion. And falling down in mind as well as body, they humbly worship the Word in the flesh.

“And opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.”

[RABANUS.] In gold understand a king; in frankincense, God; in myrrh, one who is mortal. Gold belongs to tribute, frankincense to sacrifice, and myrrh to the burial of the dead, since bodies are customarily prepared with myrrh lest they decay.

[HILARY—GREGORY.] In these, then, you have no small understanding of the mysteries: in the man, death; in God, resurrection; in the king, judgment. In gold also understand wisdom, as Solomon says: [Col. 0083C] “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. 21). In frankincense, understand the power of prayer, as in: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. 140). In myrrh, understand the mortification of our flesh. Hence: “Your hands have dripped myrrh” (Song 5).

[HILARY.] Mystically, the rising of the star first understood by the magi signifies that the Gentiles would soon believe in Christ. For the star signifies the prophetic utterance confessing Christ’s birth. Herod signifies the devil, who, having learned of Christ’s birth, persecutes him in his members. The magi depart from him when the Gentiles withdraw from idolatry and come to the house where Christ is—that is, to the catholic Church. Entering it through faith, [Col. 0083D] they find Christ with Mary his mother. Christ’s mother means the fellowship of the faithful, in which Christ dwells through faith. Having opened their treasures—that is, their learning in letters—they offered him earthly gifts, namely physics, logic, ethics; or history, allegory, tropology; or faith in the Holy Trinity.

The names of the three magi in Greek are Apellius, Amerus, and Damascus. Apellius means “faithful,” Amerus “humble,” Damascus “merciful.” In the Hebrew language they were called Magalath, Galgalath, and Saracin. Magalath means “messenger,” Galgalath “devout,” Saracin “grace.”

“And having received an answer in a dream not to return to Herod, they returned to their own region by another way.”

[RABANUS—JEROME.] Desiring with devout affection to know what the divine will commanded, they receive an answer—not through an angel, but are divinely instructed by the Lord [Col. 0084A] not to return to Herod.

[HILARY.] In this we are admonished to place all salvation and hope in Christ, and to abstain from the path of the former life.

[GREGORY.] We return to our own country by another way through obedience, from which we departed through disobedience.

## CHAPTER IX

“After they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying: Rise, take the child and his mother, flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you. For Herod is going to seek the child in order to destroy him.”

Note that when the angel commended the virginity of Mary, who was betrothed, he said to Joseph: “Do not fear to take Mary your wife.” But after she had been recognized as a wife, so that the venerable chastity of the just Joseph might also be commended, she is called not his wife but “the child’s mother,” as here: “Take the child and his mother.” And again: “Return with the child and his mother.” And again in Luke: “And there was Joseph, and his mother.” Whenever, after the birth, both are mentioned together, the mother of Christ is not called Joseph’s wife.

“He arose, took the child and his mother by night, withdrew into Egypt, and remained there until Herod’s death, that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Out of Egypt I called my son.’”

This testimony occurs in the prophet Hosea. After the magi departed, the time of purification was completed; [Col. 0084C] then Joseph, warned by an angel, fled into Egypt with the mother and child.

[BEDE.] The Lord’s being taken into Egypt so as not to be killed signifies that the elect are often driven from their homes by the malice of the wicked or condemned to exile. At the same time, an example is given to the faithful, that they should not hesitate, when it is expedient, to avoid the rage of persecutors by flight. Hence: “When they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. 5). Egypt means “darkness” and figures the Gentile world darkened by sins.

[JEROME.] Joseph typologically represents the apostles, to whom Christ was entrusted to be carried about.

[BEDE.] Therefore, for the child Jesus and his mother to be carried into Egypt by Joseph is for faith in the Lord’s incarnation and the fellowship of the Church to be entrusted to the Gentiles through holy teachers. Their being in Egypt until the king’s death signifies that faith in Christ will remain among the Gentiles until their fullness enters in, and thus Israel is saved. Herod’s death signifies the end of the malicious purpose by which Judaea now rages against the Church. The child is taken away by night, leaving the night of ignorance to the unbelievers from whom he departs. But when he returns, no mention of night is made, because at the end of the world the Jews, receiving the light of faith as Enoch and Elijah preach, will be enlightened.

## CHAPTER X

“Then Herod, seeing that he had been deceived by the magi, was exceedingly angry.”

[Col. 0085A] Cassiodorus, on Psalm forty-seven, says that there was then a violent wind, when Herod, enraged because the magi did not return to him, caused the ships from Tarsus of Cilicia to be shattered, since the magi were believed to have returned secretly in them.

“And sending, he killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem and throughout all its borders, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had ascertained from the magi.”

It is likely that, when the Magi reported nothing to Herod, he believed that they had been deceived by the vision of the star and had therefore been ashamed to return to him; and so he ceased searching for the child. But later, when he heard what had happened in the Temple, what Simeon had said, and what Anna had prophesied, he realized that he had been deceived by the Magi; and, hastening toward Christ’s death, he killed all the children [Col. 0085B] throughout the whole territory of Bethlehem, from a child one night old up to children two years old. For *bimatus* denotes a period of two years; for in Greek *imatos* is called “a year” in Latin. [BEDA.] The killing of the little ones figures the passion of all martyrs, who, little—that is, humble and innocent—were killed by the ungodly, whom Herod signifies. That the little ones were killed but Christ escaped indicates that bodies may be slain, but Christ, for whose sake persecution rages, can by no means be taken away from the faithful. For whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s.

Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: “A voice was heard in Ramah, much weeping and wailing. Rachel weeping for her children [Col. 0085C] and unwilling to be comforted, because they are not” (Jer. XXXI).

The question arises how Rachel is said to have wept for her children, since the tribe of Judah, which possessed Bethlehem, descended not from her but from her sister Leah. The solution: children were slaughtered not only in Bethlehem but also throughout all its territory. Now the tribe of Benjamin, which descended from Rachel, was adjacent to the tribe of Judah. Hence it should rightly be believed that many of Benjamin’s stock were killed, for whom Rachel’s offspring wept. Or, because Rachel was buried near Bethlehem, by a prophetic manner of expression she is said to have done what was being done in that very place. Ramah here is not the name of the place near Gibeah; rather, because *ramah* is interpreted “high,” the sense is: “A voice was heard on high,” that is, scattered far and wide. [Col. 0085D] Rachel’s offspring wept for the children and would not be comforted because they were not—that is, on account of their death. [JEROME.] In Genesis Rachel bore the type of the Church, whose voice and weeping are heard. The Church weeps for her children, not because she grieves that they have been slain, but because they were slain by those whom she had first wished to retain as her firstborn. Yet in the end, she who grieved refused to be comforted. For these were not “not,” because they were believed dead; rather, through the glory of martyrdom they were being borne onward into the increase of eternity. Consolation should be offered for something lost, not for something increased. Therefore she neither wished nor could be comforted because they are not—that is, on account of their not being—but rejoices because they happily are. [BEDA.] Or otherwise: the Church daily weeps over the removal of the saints from this world, yet she does not wish to be comforted [Col. 0086A] because they are not—that is, because they are dead—in such a way that those who have conquered the world by death might return again to endure with her the world’s defilements.

## CHAPTER XI

But when Herod had died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying: “Rise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel; for those who sought the child’s life are dead.”

From this passage we understand that the scribes and priests, together with Herod, had plotted the Lord’s death.

And he rose, took the child and his mother, and came into the land of Israel. But when he heard that Archelaus reigned in Judaea in place of Herod his father, he was afraid to go there; and, being warned in a dream, he withdrew into the regions of Galilee.

[Col. 0086B] [RABANUS.] When Joseph heard from the angel, “Go into the land of Israel,” he understood Judaea to be called the land of Israel, especially since it seemed to him that such a child ought not to live anywhere but in Jerusalem, where the Temple and the observance of the prophets were. But after he learned that Archelaus reigned there, he did not wish to expose himself to that danger, since “the land of Israel” could also be understood in such a way as to include Galilee, for the people of Israel inhabited it too. There are two Galilees: one near Tyre, of which it is written, “Galilee of the Gentiles” (Isa. IX); the other around Tiberias and the lake of Gennesaret.

And, coming, he lived in a city called Nazareth, [Col. 0086C] so that what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: “He shall be called a Nazarene.”

[JEROME.] He would not have said in the plural, “through the prophets,” if he had cited a fixed example from the Scriptures. He therefore took the sense from Scripture, not the words. For *Nazareus* is interpreted “holy,” and all the Scriptures call the Lord holy. Or it may be understood according to Isaiah, who says: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a [flower], a Nazarene, shall rise from his root” (Isa. XI). The part of Judaea in which Archelaus ruled indicates the followers of Antichrist. Nazareth of Galilee, however, to which the Lord is transferred, signifies the nation which at that time was to receive Christ through faith. [BEDA.] It should be known that in the forty-second year of Octavian Caesar Augustus—who was the second king of the Romans and reigned fifty-six and a half years—Jesus Christ, as is found in ancient chronicles, consecrated the sixth age of the world by his coming, assuming flesh; this was the forty-fifth year of Augustus’s reign. Herod killed the children aged two years and under, according to the time which he had learned from the Magi. Histories also relate that Herod himself died miserably of dropsy beneath the skin and worms swarming throughout his body, in the forty-seventh year of Augustus’s rule, that is, in the second year after the slaughter of the innocents. In his place Augustus appointed his son Archelaus, who ruled nine years, that is, until Augustus himself died. Then, when the Jews accused his savagery before the Romans, he suffered exile in the Gallic city of Vienne. Next the Romans, in order to diminish the power of the Jewish kingdom, divided the province into four parts and appointed the four brothers of Archelaus to govern it. [Col. 0087A] Each was called, from his rule over a fourth part, a *tetrarch* in the Greek language. One of these was Herod, who beheaded John and gave his assent to Pilate in the Lord’s passion; the second was Antipater, the third Lysanias, and the fourth Philip, as writers of the times report. Yet it should be noted that some hold the opinion that Herod, after a full year had elapsed following Christ’s birth, killed infants two years old and under. For, they say, he feared that the child whom the stars served, being somewhat above or below that age, might alter his appearance. Augustine too seems to think that the slaughter of the children occurred in the very year of the Lord’s birth, not long after that birth. For in his sermon on the Epiphany, which begins, “The coming in the flesh of our Lord and Savior,” he says that the Magi saw the utterly unfamiliar star not a few days but nearly two years earlier, as they disclosed to Herod when he questioned them. Hence, according to the time that he had learned from the Magi, he killed children aged two years and under.

## CHAPTER XII

L. 3[X]

And the child grew and was strengthened, full of wisdom; and the grace of God was upon him.

[BEDA.] Understand this as growth in body and strengthening in human age. “Wisdom” is the divinity itself with which he was full; “grace” is the union of divinity and humanity [Col. 0087C] in one person. John wrote something similar, namely, “full of grace and truth” (John I), calling the same thing “truth” that Luke calls “wisdom.”

And his parents went every year to Jerusalem on the feast-day of Passover.

The question arises: since they feared Archelaus, how did they dare go there? The answer is that, on the feast day, they could have gone up secretly among the enormous crowd, intending to return at once. Thus, even on the day when they went up to the Temple after the days of purification had been completed, they are believed to have escaped Herod’s notice, while he was awaiting what the Magi might report to him. Or royal concern may have been distracted by so many and such great occupations that Herod was either turned away or prevented from searching for the child. But while Archelaus reigned, all were silent about the persecution of the child. Therefore, when Luke says that they went to Jerusalem every year, we should understand this to have happened when Archelaus was no longer feared.

And when he had become twelve years old, as they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast day, and when the days had been completed and they were returning, the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem.

[BEDA.] When he reached twelve years of age, he began to reveal what he owed to his heavenly Father and what he owed to his earthly mother. The age of twelve was a type of the twelve apostles, through whom his divinity and humanity were to be proclaimed throughout the world. Rightly, therefore, in the number twelve the radiance of his perfection begins to be disclosed. He remained in Jerusalem without his parents in order to teach us [Col. 0088A] that he had God as Father before the world was made.

And his parents did not know it. But, supposing him to be in the company, they travelled a day’s journey and sought him among their relatives and acquaintances; and, not finding him, they returned to Jerusalem seeking him.

If anyone asks how his parents left him, whom they had nourished with such care, we answer that it was the custom of the children of Israel, when going to Jerusalem at the festivals or returning from there, for the men to travel separately and the women separately, while children went with either parent. Thus Mary and Joseph each in turn supposed, as they returned, that Jesus was with the other parent.

And it came to pass that, after three days, they found him in [Col. 0088B] the Temple, sitting in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and questioning them.

[AMBROSE.] As the fountain of wisdom, he sat in the midst of the teachers; but as an example of humility, he questions and listens before instructing, lest the young be ashamed to learn from elders and lest the weak dare to teach. After three days he is found in the Temple, giving the indication that he who was believed dead would rise after the three days of his triumphant passion.

L. 4[II] M. 62 R. 13

And all who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers; and, seeing him, they were amazed.

They were the more astonished at the wisdom of his answers because they saw how few were [Col. 0088C] his years. His speech brought forth divine wisdom, but his age displayed human weakness.

L. 2[X]

And his mother said to him: “Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I have sought you in sorrow.” And he said to them: “Why did you seek me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that are my Father’s?”

He does not rebuke them for seeking him as a son, but compels them to lift the eyes of their minds in order to seek what he owes to the eternal Father, showing that the Temple and all things belonging to the Father belong no less to himself than to the Father, whose majesty is one.

[Col. 0088D] And they did not understand the saying which he spoke to them. And he went down with them, came to Nazareth, and was subject to them.

They do not understand what he says concerning his divinity; and yet he condescends and is subject to them, so that he may fulfill the duty of filial devotion. How greatly, then, ought we to obey God, since God himself obeys human beings.

And his mother kept all these words in her heart.

Everything that she learned concerning the Lord, or spoken or done by the Lord—whether understood or not understood—she stored in memory, so that in due time she might understand all things as they had happened and explain them to those who asked.

[Col. 0089A] And Jesus advanced in wisdom and age and grace before God and human beings.

Wisdom pertains to the soul, age to the body, grace to the salvation of both. He advanced in age, therefore, as belongs to flesh, which receives the increase of age. But insofar as he advanced in age, he revealed more and more to human beings the gifts of grace and wisdom that were present in him. This was for wisdom and grace to advance not in himself but in others, before God and human beings—that is, to the honor of God and the salvation of human beings. In himself, however, he did not advance in wisdom or grace through intervals of time, since from the hour of conception he was full of grace and truth. Note that teachers commonly affirm that Christ’s soul, when united to the Word of God, received as much wisdom and goodness [Col. 0089B] as it was possible for a creature to receive. For in it, as the Apostle says, are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; in it the whole fullness of divinity dwells (Col. II). To others the Spirit is given by measure, but to Christ, as John the Evangelist says, it was given without measure (John III). Many therefore maintain—as Alcuin does in his book *On the Trinity* addressed to Charles—that Christ’s soul possesses as much knowledge of all things as divinity itself possesses; namely, divinity is wise by nature from itself and not from another, whereas Christ’s soul is wise by grace from divinity. Others, however, do not think that any creature can be capable of the whole of divine knowledge or of the whole of divine goodness, just as it cannot be capable of omnipotence. For they judge it unfitting that a creature should even in this manner [Col. 0089C] be made equal to the Creator, by receiving from him as much knowledge as the Creator himself has.

## CHAPTER XIII

L. 6[III] M. 7 A. 2

In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate governed Judaea, Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, Philip his brother tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene; under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came to John, son of Zechariah, in the wilderness.

In the twelfth year of Tiberius Caesar, Pilate was sent into Judaea and undertook the governorship of the nation; and he remained there as governor for ten successive years. Annas and Caiaphas were high priests when John began preaching. But Annas administered that year, whereas Caiaphas administered the year in which the Lord went up to the cross. At that time the high priesthood was granted to no one for merit of life or lineage; Roman power conferred the priesthood on whom it wished. Between Annas and Caiaphas three others held the high priesthood, as Josephus reports. And the entire time during which our Lord is described as teaching on earth is confined to a space of four years, within which the successions of high priests mentioned by Josephus were scarcely administered one year each. [BEDA.] Since John preached him who was to redeem both some from Judaea and many from the Gentiles, the times of his preaching are indicated by the ruler of the Gentiles and the rulers [Col. 0090A] of the Jews. And because the Gentiles were to be gathered and Judaea scattered, this is shown by the description of earthly rule: one is described as presiding in the Roman commonwealth, while many ruled over fourth parts in the kingdom of Judaea. The priests too are fittingly mentioned because John preached him who was both king and priest.

The word of the Lord came to John.

Paul was caught up above himself to the third heaven, hearing secret words (II Cor. XII). John likewise ascended in mind to contemplate above himself the grace which he preached. John heard the Word of the Lord by the hearing of the mind, by grace alone, with God speaking to him from above. [AMBROSE.] The Word first works in John, revealing [Col. 0090B] to him what it wishes to be proclaimed by him; then through John the Word of the Lord comes into the wilderness, proclaiming the consolation of redemption to abandoned and forsaken Judaea. Therefore, when the Son of God was about to gather the Church, he first works in his servant, so that the Church might begin not from a human being but from the Word. She herself, once deserted, now has more children.

L. 7[I] M. 7 R. 2 A. 10

And he came into all the region of the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, saying:

M. 7[III] L. 6 A. 6

“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.”

John preached repentance and the baptism of repentance, [Col. 0090C] in which remission of sins is effected—that is, Christ’s baptism—but John could not give remission of sins. Thus he is a figure of the Law, which announces sin but does not forgive it; John is Christ’s forerunner, just as the Law announces the grace of the Church. To repent is to grieve over past evils and to wish to avoid what must be lamented; this is effected by love of God and hatred of sin. To do repentance is to make satisfaction for sins. The kingdom of heaven draws near—that is, reigning in heavenly things through Christ’s humility and obedience, just as death and hell drew near through Adam’s pride and transgression.

M. 8[I] R. 2 L. 7 A. 10

For this is he who was spoken of through Isaiah the prophet, [Col. 0090D] saying: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.”

[JEROME.] John thus preached, to be sure: “This is he,” Isaiah saying, “the voice of one crying,” etc. As a voice first sounds and then understanding is conceived, so John’s preaching went before, announcing Christ’s coming. Thus John is called the voice of Christ, that is, of the Word which was in the beginning with God, which cries out in John to Jews who are deaf, far off through sins, and worthy of a cry of indignation. To Jews stopping their ears, there is a voice and a cry in the wilderness, because they are without the Spirit of God, without prophet, king, or priest. What does Christ cry through John? “Prepare the way of the Lord.” The way of the Lord, by which God descends to us [Col. 0091A] and we ascend to him, is faith, repentance, and love. The paths—that is, intentions—are straight if they are raised purely to God. But they are made crooked if we do for earthly things what should be done for God’s sake. *Phiris* in Greek is called “vision” in Latin. Hence *prophet* means “one who sees from afar”:

“Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; and crooked things shall become straight, and rough things smooth ways. And all flesh shall see the salvation of God.”

[GREGORY.] The valley denotes the humble; mountain and hill, the proud. The hearts of the humble will be filled with the word of sacred teaching and the grace of virtues, according to: “He sends forth springs in the valleys” (Ps. CV); and again, “the valleys shall abound with grain” (Ps. LXIV). For water flows down from mountains, because the truth of teaching abandons proud minds. [Col. 0091B] Crooked things become straight when hearts twisted through injustice are directed toward justice; rough things are changed into smooth ways when cruel and angry minds return to gentleness through the infusion of grace, so that the preacher may find a smooth road there where formerly, because of roughness, he could not set foot. “All flesh,” that is, every human being, will see the salvation of God at the judgment—that is, Christ on the throne of majesty—so that the righteous may be rewarded and the wicked groan eternally.

A. 2[III] M. 7 L. 6

He came as a witness, to bear witness concerning the light, so that all might believe through him.

The Word of God itself is called “light,” namely that which is capable of illuminating. But “lamp” means, as it were, light already placed in the vessel of our mortality and made human. John therefore bore witness not merely concerning the light but also concerning the lamp, because he visibly showed as made human the one whom he preached as God, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God.” Hence he was also called more than a prophet.

He was not the light, but came to bear witness concerning the lamp.

John was not the light—that is, not one illumining by himself and sufficient through himself to illumine others, as is the true light of which we have spoken. Rather, he came to bear witness to that light, now, as we have said, made a lamp. Before it became our lamp, that light was from eternity the true light, whose office is to illumine everyone who is truly to be illumined; and this is:

[Col. 0091D] A. 3[III] M. 1 L. 13

The true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world, was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him.

That light—that is, the wisdom of God, through whom the world was made—was in the world from the very beginning of the world. That is, it shone in all creatures through the principle by which they were created and governed; and the world—that is, the human being inhabiting the world—did not know it. But in order that it might be known, it humbled itself by taking the form of a servant. Hence follows:

A. 4[X]

He came unto his own, and his own did not receive him. But to as many as received him, [Col. 0092A] he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name.

From the beginning of the world there have always been some who received the divine Word, believing in his name—that is, trusting that they would be saved through the knowledge of him. A thing is known by its name, and therefore “name” is used for knowledge.

Who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.

That is, in becoming children of God they were not born from “bloods,” namely, the material of the father’s and mother’s blood; this he explained by saying, “not from the desire of the flesh,” that is, of the woman, nor of the man. Because flesh is supported by bones and has less strength, the weaker sex is therefore denoted by it.

[Col. 0092B] A. 5[III] M. 1 L. 14

And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us.

He explains how the Word came unto his own, namely, not by a local coming but by humbling himself through the assumption of our weakness, saying that the Word was made flesh—that is, that he joined a human being assumed into unity of person with himself. Thus he dwelt among us—that is, he entered into a permanent dwelling with our nature, so that he might never thereafter be wholly separated from our nature by a division of person. For even if he laid aside the flesh for a time, the union of soul and Word did not fail. Or, he will dwell in us through grace, as he himself promised, saying: “Behold, I am with you [Col. 0092C] until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.

[BEDA.] When the Word so veiled himself beneath the covering of flesh, as though wiping our eyes with salve, we who were humble understood in him, thus made human, his glory—that is, the excellence of his divinity—because the proud were unwilling to believe on account of the weakness of his flesh. I say, his glory as of the Only-Begotten—that is, truly Only-Begotten by nature, not by adoption, from God the Father. Therefore, according to the excellence of divinity, the Son of God is Only-Begotten from the Father; but according to fellowship with the brethren he is the firstborn of every creature. Only-Begotten in the substance of the Godhead; firstborn [Col. 0092D] in the assumption of humanity. Only-Begotten in nature; firstborn in grace. Hence he is called both brother and Lord: brother because firstborn, Lord because only-begotten. Thus the Evangelist calls the Word made human itself—that is, Christ—full of grace and truth. According to humanity, full of grace, that is, of the gifts of the Holy Spirit; according to divinity, full of truth, that is, of immutability, although he joined a mutable nature to himself. For he so assumed ours that he did not abandon his own.

A. 6[I] M. 40 R. 4 L. 10

John bears witness concerning him and cries, saying: “This was he of whom I said: He who is to come after me has been made before me, because he was before me.”

[Col. 0093A] He who is to come after me in preaching has been made before me. I do not mean, “He was made before I existed,” but, “He has been set before me and surpasses me in humanity,” because he was before me in the eternity of divinity.

A. 7[X]

The Evangelist returns to the testimony of his assertion: “We saw him full of grace.” From this fullness of gifts which he possessed, all we elect have received, as it were, certain streams in portions: namely, grace for grace. That is, because of that singular grace of gifts bestowed upon that man, grace by which we are saved has also been bestowed upon us as members of this head. That great grace of our advocate obtained for us gifts of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0093B] above our merits, because in all things he deserved, on account of his own worthiness, to be heard by the Father. Or, we have received grace from him for grace: that is, faith, love, and sacraments, for the attainment of eternal life.

For the Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.

[AUGUSTINE.] As one commonly says, “Because I promised, I gave,” so we understand this: through Moses, the faithful servant, the Law was given by God, containing knowledge of good and evil, and the promise and shadow of good things to come. Beyond doubt, through Jesus, who is Lord and Son of God, grace came to be, by which we turn away from evil and do good; and the truth of things came to be, promised and prefigured in the Law. Or understand truth as the immutability of the blessedness above, [Col. 0093C] in which we shall be like God.

A. 3[III] M. 112 L. 119

No one has ever seen God. The Only-Begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has made him known.

Seeing God is beyond the human condition. Therefore Paul was caught up beyond the human condition, that he might see mysteries which it is not permitted a human being to utter (II Cor. II). Moses saw a cloud, an angel, and fire, not the presence of the Lord himself. [AUGUSTINE.] Why, after all that he had seen, did he say: “Show me yourself” (Exod. XXXIII)? By “bosom” he means the Father’s secret place. From there the Son came through the assumption of flesh and recounted what he saw there—that is, he revealed to his own what they presently behold by the faith of eyewitnesses concerning the Trinity of the Godhead, and that he will bring them into the manifest vision [Col. 0093D] which will make them blessed. For elsewhere he says: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV). Again: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matt. XI). Thus grace and truth came through Jesus.

M. 9[VI] R. 3

John himself wore a garment of camel hair and a leather belt around his loins; and his food was locusts and wild honey.

[HILARY.] The wilderness is John’s place, and meditation his occupation. He proclaims repentance, through which there is a return from error, withdrawal from sin, and, after shame for vices, a profession of ceasing from them. He was clothed in hair, not wool: this signifies austerity, not luxury. [Col. 0094A] The leather belt with which Elijah also was girded is a girdle made from the dried skins of animals (IV Kings I). John was therefore girded around the loins in order to mortify luxury. He ate locusts and wild honey because it befits a wilderness-dweller to follow not riches but necessity. A cheap, rough garment of camel hair, or of whatever animal skins, signifies the contrite and humbled heart of the penitent. [HILARY.] The fastening of the belt admonishes us to be girded for every service of Christ’s will. The swift-moving locusts chosen for food figure us, who formerly, in a will that wandered, were carried about as if by certain leaps of the body—useless in deeds, complaining in words, strangers in our dwelling. But now we are the food of saints and the nourishment of prophets, chosen together [Col. 0094B] with wild honey, because we are to offer a most sweet food, not from the hives of the Law but from ourselves, as if from the trunks of the wild trees of Gentile life.

Then all Jerusalem, all Judaea, and all the region around the Jordan went out to him, and they were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins.

[BEDA.] John baptized, not in order to give his own baptism for the remission of sins, but in order to precede Christ’s baptism, which would remit sins. [RABANUS.] They were baptized in the Jordan, which is interpreted “descent,” descending from the pride of the old man to the humility of confession and amendment.

M. 10[V] L. 8

But seeing many Pharisees and Sadducees [Col. 0094C] coming to his baptism, he said to them: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come?”

The Pharisees are “separated” or “separators,” that is, Jewish priests who separated themselves from the people through hypocrisy. The Sadducees are “justified” or “self-justifiers.” They receive the five books of Moses, reject the prophets, and do not believe in the resurrection. [BEDA–GREGORY.] Therefore both are called offspring of vipers, because, imitating the deeds of evil parents, they envy and persecute the good; and thus they are venomous children born from venomous parents. Since they stood in the greatest need of repentance and correction, they are rebuked because they do not first lay aside their poison before coming [Col. 0094D] to baptism. The wrath to come is God’s final vengeance, from which the sinner will then be unable to flee if he does not now resort to the tears of repentance.

“Therefore bear fruit worthy of repentance. And do not wish to say within yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones.”

He speaks of fruit not of just any kind but worthy of repentance: the more gravely one has sinned, the more one should repent in accordance with the kind of guilt, and perform good works with greater gain. But the Jews, glorying in the nobility of their descent, did not recognize themselves as sinners because they descended from Abraham. By “stones” are understood the hearts of Gentiles, insensible to the understanding of God. Thus it is also said to certain Jews: “I will take away [Col. 0095A] the stony heart from your flesh” (Ezek. XI). The Gentiles are rightly compared to stones, since they worshiped stones, changed into a stony nature not through bodily use but by the disposition of their minds. Hence: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. CXIII). Children of Abraham were raised up from these stones because the Gentiles were united through faith to his seed, namely Christ. Thus Paul says to the same Gentiles: “If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s seed” (Gal. III). [HILARY.] John therefore rebukes the Pharisees so that those who had begun, through unbelief, to have the devil as father might again become children of Abraham through faith, together with those raised from stones.

For now the axe has been placed at the root of the trees.

A tree signifies the human being; the root, the will from which [Col. 0095B] the fruit of works proceeds; and the axe, the preaching of the Gospel. It is said to be placed at the root because it examines the purity of the will. For it teaches that reward consists in good will, but punishment in evil will. Works which the Law of Moses condemned or rewarded are certain evidences of the will.

“Therefore every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire.”

[BEDA, from GREGORY.] The meaning is: whoever scorns to do good here will be cut off from the assembly of the faithful, or from the present life in which he is planted, and will be burned in hell. Or otherwise: the trees are the human race. The axe is our Redeemer, who is held, as it were, by handle and iron in his humanity, but cuts [Col. 0095C] through his divinity. This axe has already been placed at the root because, though he waits in patience, he nevertheless knows what he will finally do. He says that the axe is laid not to the branches but to the root. When the children of the wicked are removed, what else is this but the cutting off of the branches of an unfruitful tree? When the entire offspring is removed along with the parents, the tree is cut down by the roots, lest anything remain from which some shoot might grow again. [RABANUS.] Some branches worthy of fire are dry, as pagans; others are green but fruitless, as hypocrites; others bear fruit, but bitter fruit, as heretics.

L. 9[X]

And the crowds asked him, saying: “What then shall [Col. 0095D] we do?” John answered and said to them: “Let one who has two tunics give to one who has none, and let one who has food do likewise.”

[BEDA, from GREGORY.] Since a tunic is more necessary for our use than a cloak, it belongs to fruit worthy of repentance that we share with our neighbors not only external and less necessary things, but even the things very necessary to us—namely food and a tunic. For the Law says: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. XIX). It could not be said of one tunic that it should be divided, because then no one would be clothed with it. Concerning food, Truth says: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke XI).

Tax collectors also came to be baptized, and they said to him: “Teacher, what shall we do?” And he [Col. 0096A] said to them: “Exact nothing beyond what has been prescribed for you.”

There is great power in John’s word, which compels even tax collectors and soldiers to seek counsel concerning their salvation. He therefore commanded them to demand nothing beyond what had been prescribed for them. Tax collectors are those who either exact public taxes or lease the revenues of the treasury or public property. Those who pursue the profits of this world by commerce are also designated by the same name.

The soldiers too asked him, saying: “And what shall we do?” And he said to them: “Do violence to no one, make no false accusation, and be content with your pay.”

[AUGUSTINE, *On the Words of the Lord*.] Some, when they sin grievously, excuse themselves with this plea: “I am a soldier,” and say that they are occupied with wicked deeds—as though military service, rather than the will, were at fault. But serving as a soldier is not a sin unless they serve for certain wrongful ends; nor is administering the commonwealth criminal unless they administer it in order to increase their family property. Likewise, whatever rulers or clerics seek more than has been decreed for them are condemned by John’s judgment as false accusers and extortioners. For we are soldiers of Christ. Hence the Apostle: “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in worldly affairs” (II Tim. II).

But as the people were expecting, and all were pondering in their hearts concerning John whether perhaps he was the Christ—

[Col. 0096C] A. 9[X]

The Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to him to ask him, “Who are you?” And he confessed and did not deny; and he confessed: “I am not the Christ.”

[GREGORY–BEDA.] He confessed that he was not Christ, and he did not deny what he was, namely that he was the forerunner, as what follows makes clear. Here John’s humility is commended: as he strove humbly to acknowledge his own weakness, he deserved to attain the height of God. Wonderful is the blindness of the Jews: although they believed John to be Christ, they were unwilling to believe that Christ was the Savior, even while John himself testified to it, despite Christ’s approval by so many signs and powers.

[Col. 0096D] And they asked him: “What then? Are you Elijah?” And he said, “I am not.” “Are you the Prophet?” And he answered, “No.”

The Lord said to his disciples: “John himself is Elijah, because John was Elijah in spirit, not in person”; in that latter sense he says here that he is not Elijah. John therefore denied that he was the prophet, because he was more than a prophet, showing forth what others had foretold; or because the messengers meant to ask whether he was Elisha, in whom a figure of baptism had preceded, or some other ancient prophet.

Therefore they said to him: “Who are you, so that we may give an answer to those who sent us?”

A. 10[I] M. 8 R. 2 L. 7

“What do you say about yourself?” He said: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord,’ as Isaiah the prophet said” (Isa. 40).

John is the voice in which the Word sounds: that is, the manifestation, prophecy, and lamp of the Word of God present in John, through whom he cries—the Word present in assumed flesh, to whom John bears testimony—according to the saying, “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” (Ps. 131). He makes straight the Lord’s way who prepares his life for His commandments. Hence: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John 14).

A. 9[Z]

And those who had been sent were from the Pharisees; and they questioned him and said: “Why then do you baptize, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?”

The Pharisees had heard in the prophets that Christ would come and baptize [Col. 0097B]. They also knew that the Jordan bore a figure of baptism, and that Elijah and Elisha had crossed it dry-footed as a figure of baptism; they therefore supposed that these men had now risen in order to baptize. Since John declared himself to be none of these, they ask by what authority he baptizes.

A. 12[I] M. 40 R. 4. L. 10

John answered them, saying: “I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance.”

M. R. L. A.

“But he who is to come after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. Yet he stands in your midst, and you do not know him.”

[Col. 0097C] M. 12[V] L. 11

“He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and in fire.”

As though he said: Let not what I do be attributed to presumption. I baptize with water unto repentance; that is, as a sign of repentance cleansing souls, I wash bodies and institute the practice of baptism, preparing the way for one mightier than I, whose sandals I am unworthy to carry: so great is his excellence above my lowliness. But he whom I proclaim stands among you, and you do not know him, because you misuse his humility. He will baptize in the Holy Spirit and fire.

[Bede.] That is, both with the cleansing of sanctification and with the testing of tribulation. Or, “in the Holy Spirit,” that is, in the fire which he came to cast upon the earth (Luke 12). The Holy Spirit is understood through fire because he both inflames hearts through love and enlightens them through wisdom. Some explain it thus: in the Holy Spirit in the present, in fire in the future. For just as we are now reborn of water and the Holy Spirit for the remission of sins, so then, from the lesser sins with which we die, we shall be cleansed by purgatorial fire, as though by baptism. Hence the Apostle: “Fire will test what sort of work each person has done” (1 Cor. 3).

The Evangelist John wrote: “whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to untie.” This has a mystical meaning. [Albinus.] It was an ancient custom that, if someone did not wish to take as wife a woman whom it was his right to marry, the man who by right of kinship would betroth her to himself should untie his sandal. But Christ was the bridegroom of the Church, as John says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” [Col. 0098A]. Therefore, since John was thought to be Christ, he rightly declares himself unworthy to untie the strap of his sandal. It is as though he said: “I am unable to uncover the footsteps of the Redeemer, because I do not claim for myself the name of Bridegroom.”

Or thus: sandals are made from dead animals. The Lord appeared, as it were, shod, after he assumed flesh. No one has ever been able fully to investigate the mystery of this incarnation. The sandal-strap is the binding of so great a mystery. Thus John is unable fully to untie the strap, because he is insufficient to investigate the mystery of the incarnation.

“His winnowing-fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing-floor, and gather his wheat into the granary; but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.”

[Col. 0098B] [Hilary.] The work of the winnowing-fan is to distinguish fruitful things from unfruitful. Its being in the Lord’s hand indicates the judgment of his power: he stores the wheat—that is, the perfect fruits of believers—in granaries, and burns the chaff—that is, the emptiness of unfruitful people—with the fire of judgment. By the winnowing-fan is figured the discrimination of righteous examination, and by the threshing-floor the present Church. The cleansing of this threshing-floor is even now taking place, when the perverse are expelled from the Church because of manifest sins, or, after death, are condemned by divine severity.

There is a difference between chaff and tares: chaff comes forth from the seed of pure wheat, while tares spring from a different origin. Thus chaff signifies those who are instructed in the mysteries of faith but, through the frivolity of unbelief, differ from the elect; tares signify those separated from the elect in work [Col. 0098C] and profession. These are not removed by this winnowing-fan, because they have already been judged; but the chaff is winnowed.

L.

And exhorting them in many other ways as well, he proclaimed the good news to the people.

A. 13[X]

These things took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.

## CHAPTER XIV

M. 13[X]

Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him.

[Col. 0098D] [Jerome.] The Savior was baptized by John for several reasons: that, as man, he might fulfill both righteousness and the humility of the law; that he might approve John’s baptism; that in the washing of believers he might show the coming of the Holy Spirit; and that you might not disdain to receive the baptism of the Lord when he himself received the baptism of a servant.

L. 14[III] M. 1 A. 5

And Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years old, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph.

[Bede.] Jesus is baptized at thirty years of age and begins more openly to perform signs and teach, thereby showing the lawful age for those who think every age suitable either for priesthood or for teaching [Col. 0099A]. This is not so, unless it happens on some occasion through a miracle of God, as in Jeremiah and Daniel, who received the spirit of prophecy while children. The age of thirty in the baptized Savior suits us because of the mystery of the Trinity and the working of the Decalogue. Therefore whoever is baptized, or rejoices to have been baptized, should be thirty years old in this manner: that in the faith of the holy Trinity he may understand and fulfill the Decalogue.

M. 13[X]

But John tried to prevent him, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” But Jesus answered and said to him: “Permit it now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he allowed him.

[Bede.] The Lord came to be baptized in order to impart to us [Col. 0099B] the mystery of baptism and sanctify the waters. But the servant was afraid when he came to him to be baptized, since there was no fault in him. Thus what John says here, “I ought to be baptized by you,” is understood to be the same as what he says elsewhere: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” John himself therefore ought to have been baptized by him, that is, cleansed from original sin.

“Permit it now,” says the Lord: let me be baptized by you in water, so that afterward you may be baptized by me in the Spirit. “For thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness,” that is, to teach and furnish an example of every righteousness. Whoever receives Christ’s baptism has mercy on his own soul by pleasing God (Ecclus. 30), receiving the remedy of salvation; he humbly submits to his Creator, obeying his institution, and edifies his neighbor by example. Thus he fulfills all righteousness [Col. 0099C], because he does what he owes to God, himself, and his neighbor. Therefore, when John recognized that righteousness ought to be fulfilled in this way, he then allowed himself to baptize him and consented. For true humility is that which obedience, its companion, does not abandon: obediently he performed the office at which he had first trembled.

L. 13[I] M. 14 R. 5 A. 15

And it came to pass, when all the people were being baptized, that Jesus also, having been baptized and praying, immediately came up from the water. And behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending in bodily form, like a dove coming upon him. And behold, a voice from heaven:

L.

“You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased.”

[Bede.] Jesus, having been baptized and praying, rose from the waters, to which by the touch of his pure flesh he had given the power to wash away sins; so that whoever comes to Christ’s washing may lay aside sins and afterward rise through the increase of virtues. [Jerome–Bede.] The heavens are opened, not by an unclosing of the elements, but to spiritual eyes; for when he entered the waters, the power of his divinity opened for us the gates of heaven. Heaven did not then begin to be opened to him, to whom the inner things of the heavens lay open; rather, by these words the power of baptism is shown, because the heavenly gate is made known to the baptized.

Christ prayed not for himself, but to instruct us to pray, that we may be victorious after baptism. For, as though the Red Sea had been crossed, we rejoice that the Egyptians have been slain; yet in the wilderness of this world other enemies meet us, who must be conquered until we come to [Col. 0100A] the eternal homeland. Hence, after the grace of the Holy Spirit is conferred in baptism, a fuller grace of the same Spirit is given to those reborn through the laying on of the bishop’s hand.

The dove appeared over Jesus, in order to teach that the anointing of the Holy Spirit would be present only for those baptized in simplicity. It descended in bodily form, like a dove, in order to show that those baptized into his body, which is the Church, receive the Holy Spirit. Notice also that it was not a raven but a dove that brought an olive branch into Noah’s ark, because among the baptized some leave the Church, while others remain peacefully in the Church. The olive branch with green leaves in the dove’s mouth signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, abundant in words of life.

What Luke says, “in you I am well pleased” (Matt. 3), is as though he said: “In you I have established my good pleasure”; that is, through you I accomplish what pleases me. But what Matthew says, “in whom I am well pleased,” is explained thus: one who corrects by repentance what he has done wrongly regrets what he has done, and is displeased with it. Since the almighty Father spoke in human fashion, saying, “I regret that I have made man” (Gen. 6), he seems to have been displeased with himself in sinners. But in Christ alone he was well pleased, because he did not regret having created him as man, since there was no sin in him. Hence David: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: you are a priest forever” (Ps. 109).

Understand that, although the Evangelists did not report the same wording, they reported the same meaning. This diversity of expressions is useful, lest a statement expressed in only one way be understood less fully and interpreted otherwise than the matter itself warrants.

[Bede.] [Col. 0100C] The mystery of the Trinity is shown in Christ’s baptism. The Son is baptized, the Holy Spirit descends in the form of a dove, and the voice of the Father bearing witness to the Son is heard. The dove appeared over Jesus’ head so that the Father’s voice might not be thought to have been addressed to John rather than to the Lord. Moreover, when the paternal voice sounded, it did not teach the Son; rather, it is shown to us what we ought to believe: namely, that he who was baptized by John is truly the Son of God, and that we too, through the water of washing and the Spirit of sanctification, may by the adoption expressed in the Father’s voice become children of God.

Read the text thus: Jesus, and those who were with him, saw the Spirit of God—that is, a thing signifying the Holy Spirit—descending like a dove; that is, like a thing which was truly a dove and had been assumed for the purpose of signifying this. Whether the dove was newly created and, after performing its office, dissolved into the elements, or not, is of no concern to us.

[Bede.] Likewise Marcus must be read thus when he says, “He saw the heavens opened” (Mark 1), that is, the opening of heaven is signified for the baptized. Let us consider the nature of the dove, that from it we may take rules for life. It harms no one with beak or claws—not even the smallest flies or worms. Let us see that our teeth are not weapons and arrows; let us restrain our hands from plundering. “Let the one who stole steal no longer, but rather labor, working with his hands, so that he may have something to give to one in need” (Eph. 4). For the dove is even said often to feed the young of others as if they were its own.

It feeds on the fruits and seeds of the earth. Let us hear [Col. 0101A] the Apostle: “It is good neither to eat meat nor to drink wine” (Rom. 14). It has groaning instead of song: “Let us weep before God who made us” (Ps. 94 [printed LXLXIV]). “Let our laughter be turned into mourning and our joy into sorrow” (Jas. 4). “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5). It is accustomed to sit upon waters so that, seeing in the water the shadow of a hawk about to swoop down, it may avoid being seized. Let us also sit upon the streams of the Scriptures, taught by their mirrors to recognize and beware the snares of the ancient enemy. Hence: “Her eyes are doves washed with milk, dwelling beside abundant streams” (Song 5).

They also make their nests in the holes of the rock, in the hollow of the wall. “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10), whose hands were pierced with nails on the cross and whose side was pierced by a lance [Col. 0101B] (John 19). His wall is the united strength of the saints; its hollow is the bosom of brotherly love, in which, while they nourish those tender in faith, they open a place within themselves as nesting doves. Hence: “Arise, my friend, my beautiful one, and come; my dove, in the holes of the rock, in the hollow of the wall” (Song 2). We have rightly mentioned these seven examples of virtue, because the grace of the Holy Spirit, who descended in a dove, is sevenfold.

The question is asked why baptism succeeded circumcision. For, as blessed Gregory says in the fourth book on Job: “What baptismal water accomplishes among us, formerly either faith alone accomplished for little children, or the power of sacrifices for adults, or, for those descended from Abraham’s stock, the mystery of circumcision.”

Solution: It was fitting for a new king to institute a new law and to resolve the hostility between Jews and Gentiles, so that the two peoples might be joined into one and become one people. Therefore it was necessary to abolish the causes of hostility, namely Jewish rites, which the Gentiles abhorred, and substitute other sacraments common to both. Baptism also took the place of circumcision because circumcision was an imperfect sacrament, applying only to males. Baptism, however, is a perfect sacrament because it is administered without pain to both sexes.

Baptism is uniformly consecrated in water because water flowed from Christ’s side, because no liquid is so effective for washing [Col. 0101D] as water, and because it is easily obtained by everyone, lest anyone excuse himself on grounds of poverty. Note that baptism is understood in several ways. There is only one baptism in water, such as John’s, which did not grant remission of sins. Another is in fire or the Spirit, by which the Apostles were baptized on the day of Pentecost. Hence: “You shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit” (Acts 1). A third is in water and Spirit, with which the Apostles baptized. A fourth is in the shedding of blood. Three visible things are in baptism—the priest, the person to be baptized, and water—and three invisible things—faith, the soul, and the Holy Spirit.”

But the Lord, as Ambrose says in the first book *On the Sacraments*, descended into baptism before the Holy Spirit, whereas now the reverse occurs, because the Lord did not need to be cleansed [Col. 0102A]. In us, however, the power and presence of the Trinity, manifested in Christ’s baptism, works invisibly in the visible sacrament of baptism.

A sacrament is a visible sign of invisible grace. Thus, when someone is baptized, the outward washing of the body which we see is a sign of the inward washing of the soul, consisting in the remission of sins. Water, which cleanses bodily defilements outwardly, is likewise a sign of faith, which cleanses sins inwardly. The priest washing with water also signifies the Spirit forgiving sins through faith. Yet concerning this sacrament, as concerning others, it must be seen that it makes no difference by whatever minister it is given. For the minister performs the ministry, but Christ baptizes. Hence: “This is he who baptizes.” Therefore, whether it is given by clerics, laymen, or even women when necessity presses, it is not repeated.

Some receive this sacrament, like the sacrament of the altar, unto life, and others unto death. Those who approach truly receive both the reality and the sacrament; those who approach falsely receive the sacrament alone. Therefore, if they later come to their senses, they are not rebaptized. The form of baptism consists in these words: “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” or words of equivalent force. For the Lord, instituting baptism generally, commanded: “Go, teach the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 23 [as printed]). Baptism has its power and efficacy from Christ’s death and shedding of blood, as do the other sacraments, whether before the law or under the law. For through it Christ forgives what has been done [Col. 0102C], helps lest it be done further, leads to where it can no longer be done at all, causes the law to be fulfilled, nature to be set free, and sin not to reign.

A. M. R. L.

And John bore witness, saying: “Because I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and he remained upon him. And I did not know him.”

[Augustine.] He did not know him—understand, not so deeply, not so subtly, as he came to know him when the Spirit descended upon him. For then he learned that the Lord would retain for himself the power of his own baptism, as of the other sacraments, whether present on earth or absent bodily in heaven, and would give it to no servant. You will find none of the Apostles saying, “my baptism”; but you will find one saying, “my Gospel” (2 Tim. 2). And this is what he says:

“But he who sent me to baptize with water said to me: ‘He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’ And I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God.”

[Bede on Mark.] He fittingly added, “remaining upon him.” For it is peculiar to our Mediator that the Holy Spirit never departs from him. But it is sometimes conferred upon his faithful and sometimes withdrawn. From some, however, it is never absent for preserving love of God and neighbor. Hence he himself said to them: “But you shall know him, because he will remain with us and be [Col. 0103A] in you” (John 14). John, moreover, according to his hearers’ capacity, elsewhere proclaims Jesus a man mightier than himself, but here the Son of God. Hence Paul says: “As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3). “But among the mature we speak wisdom.”

## CHAPTER XV

M. 15[II] R. 6 L. 15

Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, to be tempted by the devil.

Luke deliberately placed first: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan,” so that there might be no doubt by what spirit he was led into the wilderness according to Matthew, or driven according to Mark. Beyond doubt, Jesus was not moved into the wilderness by the power of an evil spirit, but by the will of his own Spirit, in order to overthrow the adversary. Here he shows us beforehand that after baptism we should arm ourselves courageously against the devil, abandoning the enticements of the world and the company of the wicked.

M. 19[V] L. 19

And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry.

He offered himself to the tempter for forty days and forty nights, to signify that whether prosperity flatters us here—which pertains to the day—or adversity strikes us—which accords with the image of night—the adversary is always present to believers, never ceasing to hinder them through temptation. [Jerome.] He was hungry in body so that the devil might be given an occasion for tempting him and might be conquered by the man [Col. 0103C] over whose death and sufferings he boasted.

[Hilary.] The devil was stirred by the fast of forty days. He knew that for the same number of days the waters of the abyss had been poured forth, the land of promise had been explored, the law had been given by God to Moses, and the children of Israel had lived in the wilderness upon the bread of angels for the same number of years. But when after his fast he sensed that the Lord was hungry—something not said of Moses or Elijah after their fasts—he approached to tempt him, far from the fulfillment of his malicious desire.

[Bede.] The commandments of the law are ten, and the world is fourfold; this signifies the grace of Christ now spread throughout the world, he who fasted for forty days. In this fast he seemed to cry: “Abstain from the desires of this age.” In eating and drinking after the resurrection he seemed to cry: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 8 [as printed]). Therefore, although we do not boast, we are nevertheless already fed through hope. The fast of Lent was fittingly established as adjoining the Lord’s Passion, because it signifies that we ought to restrain ourselves from friendship with the world, so that we may be able to follow God.

[Gregory.] The number forty is observed in abstinence because the power of the Decalogue is fulfilled through the four books of the Gospel when the Gospel is kept. Or because through the Decalogue we are commanded to love God and neighbor, and because love of God and neighbor is violated through the movement of the body, which consists of four elements, a time of repentance rightly rises to the number forty for the cleansing of sins.

[Col. 0104A] And the tempter came and said to him: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves.” But he answered and said: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.”

[Bede.] At one point the devil believed that his conqueror had come into the world, as he said through the possessed man: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come before the time to torment us?” (Matt. 8). Yet, as Christ underwent mortal sufferings, he doubted that he was God.

[Jerome–Hilary.] “It is written,” said the Lord, because he had purposed to conquer the devil by humility, not by power. The prince of demons intended, through the transformation of stones into loaves, to recognize in God the power of authority and, through the pleasure of food, to mock in the man the endurance of hunger. But the Lord, taking testimony from Deuteronomy, showed that the nourishment of eternity is to be hoped for not in this bread alone but in every word of God [Col. 0104B] (Deut. 8).

[Gregory.] Temptation takes place in three ways: suggestion, delight, and consent. But Christ was tempted by suggestion alone, because the delight of sin did not bite his mind. It was not unworthy of him to be tempted, since he had come to be killed, so that by his temptation he might overcome ours, just as by his death he bore our sins.

Then the devil took him into the holy city and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple.

It is no wonder that he allowed himself to be taken, led, and set there by him whose members he endured crucifying him. It may also be understood thus: “The devil took him,” that is, assailed him by temptation; “and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple,” that is, the devil was the occasion why the Lord was led and placed there by his own Spirit. A *pinna* or pinnacle is a summit, that is, a height. For the ancients used, as is still done in many places, to make the upper parts of houses or temples with a flat surface, so that people might stand there and do what they wished. Hence the Lord says to the Apostles: “What you hear in the ear, preach upon the rooftops” (Matt. 10). The holy city was called Jerusalem, in which the temple and worship of God according to the law of Moses were found.

And he said to him: “If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down. For it is written: ‘He has commanded his angels concerning you, and they will bear you up in their hands, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone’” (Ps. 90).

In all temptations the devil seeks to learn whether he is the Son of God. But the Lord so tempers his reply that he leaves him uncertain. In saying, “Cast yourself down,” he who strives to cast down everyone reveals himself weak: he can persuade, but cannot cast down. The testimony he adduces is prophecy not only concerning Christ but concerning every holy man.

Jerome explains Psalm 90 thus: “Whoever has believed that the two natures of God and man are perfect in the Savior, being guarded by angelic hands, does not strike his foot against the stone—that is, Christ—who is a stone of stumbling and rock of offense” (Isa. 8). Augustine, on the same psalm: “The Lord was borne in the hands of angels when he was taken up into heaven, not because he would have fallen if they did not carry him, but because they rendered service [Col. 0105A] to the king.” If you say, “Those who carry are better than the one carried,” I shall reply: “Then beasts of burden are better than human beings.”

[Jerome.] The equivocator, however, kept silent concerning his own trampling; he did not add that the Son of God would walk upon the asp and basilisk and trample the lion and dragon.

Jesus said to him: “Again it is written: ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God’” (Deut. 6).

With the true shields of the Scriptures he breaks the devil’s false arrows drawn from Scripture; for the devil either proposes falsehoods or attempts to persuade with falsehoods by means of truths. The Lord brought forward testimonies from Deuteronomy in order to show the mysteries of the second law [Bede]. He was being urged, as though he were a man, to test by some sign how much he prevailed with [Col. 0105B] God. But it is written for man that he must not dare to tempt God when he has something he can do to escape what ought to be avoided. Hence: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. 10). But once human provision fails, if a person entrusts himself wholly to divine power, it should not be called temptation. Now Christ could have come down from the temple in another way than by vaingloriously hurling himself down.

Again the devil took him onto a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory; and he said to him: “All these I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me.”

He showed him the kingdoms upon, that is, above, the mountain—not because he enlarged the sight of him who sees all things, but because, so far as was in his power, by word and promise he showed the vanity of human pomp, which he loved as something beautiful, persuading the Lord that even thus he might subject him to himself. It is well that Luke records that temporal things are shown “in a moment of time,” because human powers quickly fall. In saying, “All these I will give you,” he speaks proudly, not because he could give all kingdoms. “Falling down, you will worship” is said because the one who would worship the devil had first fallen.

[Ambrose.] Note that every power and ordering of powers is from God, but ambition for power is from evil. Thus power permitted to the devil for a time is not evil; but one who makes evil use of power by ambition is evil.

Then Jesus said to him: “Go, Satan. For it is written [Col. 0105D]: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’”

Satan and Peter are not, as some think, condemned by the same sentence. For Peter is told: “Go behind me, Satan,” that is, “Follow me, you who are opposed to my will.” Here “behind” is not said, so that it is understood: “Go into eternal fire.”

[Bede.] It is written for every human being that he should worship God and serve him alone. In Greek, that service which belongs to God alone, not to a creature, is called *latria*. Hence idolaters are so called: those who render to idols sacrifices due to the one God. But *dulia* is service common to God and humankind. Thus in Latin a slave is called *servus*, which is called *doulos* in Greek. Therefore we are commanded through charity to serve one another—Greek *dulium*—and God alone—Greek *latrium*.

[Col. 0106A] L.

And when he had completed every temptation, then the devil left him until a time.

M. L.

And he was with the wild beasts.

R. 7[VI] M. 17

And behold, angels came and ministered to him.

It says that every temptation was completed because in these three temptations are contained the origins of all vices, as John testifies when he says: “Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2). And in the Gospel parable three wicked pursuits exclude people from the feast of eternal life [Col. 0106B]. The first said: “I have bought a farm,” etc. (Luke 14). Another said: “I have bought five yoke of oxen.” Another said: “I have taken a wife” (ibid.). The desire for a wife pertains to concupiscence, as does gluttony. The purchase of a farm pertains to avarice and pride. The testing of five yoke is referred to the desire of the eyes, where curiosity and vainglory are found.

Against the enemy’s threefold weapon set the same number of weapons of defense: let the desire of the flesh be driven away by fasting, avarice by almsgiving, and boastfulness by prayer.

[Gregory.] The devil overcame the old man through gluttony in the forbidden apple; he overcame him through vainglory, saying, “You shall be as gods” (Gen. 3); and through avarice, when he said, “knowing good and evil.” For avarice is rightly called the height of ambition. Thus he also tempted the Lord, but departed defeated. David struck down Goliath with three stones from the stream (1 Sam. 17); Christ struck down the devil with three testimonies from the law. Which temptation was first, which middle, which last, and in what form the tempter came—whether in his own form or in an assumed human appearance—is of little consequence to know.

The devil left him until a time, intending afterward openly to attack him through the Jews. Likewise, when he does not prevail in temptation, he withdraws from us until another time. [Bede on Mark.] The Lord lives among wild beasts as man; he makes use of angelic ministry as God. And we, when in the wilderness of holy conduct we endure the beastly manners of people, deserve the ministry of angels, by whom, once freed from the body, we may be carried over to eternal joys.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0106D]

A. 16[X]

The next day John was again standing with two of his disciples. And, looking at Jesus as he walked, he said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world.”

[Bede, Homily.] Typologically, John—that is, the people of grace—on the next day, that is, after the law, recognizes the Lamb by whom it is redeemed. Jesus’ walking signifies the dispensation of the incarnation, by which he gave us examples of life, just as his remaining signifies the eternity of his divinity. But the standing of John and his disciples shows that he himself had ascended the citadel of virtues, from which no temptations could cast him down, and that [Col. 0107A] the disciples followed his teaching in their hearts.

[Bede, Homily.] Or otherwise: John stood, that is, the law ceased, yet still bore witness to Christ. Jesus walked about, that is, grace gathered people from here and there. The innocent Lamb to be sacrificed was prefigured in the paschal lamb. The Apostle Peter shows how he takes away sins, saying: “You were redeemed from your futile manner of life handed down by your fathers, not with corruptible silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of an immaculate and unstained Lamb” (1 Pet. 1). And John says in the Apocalypse: “He who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1).

He not only washed us when he gave his blood for us, or when we are baptized into the mystery of his passion; he also washes us daily in his blood when the memory of that blessed passion is repeated at the altar, when the created bread and wine are transformed into the sacrament of his flesh and blood by the ineffable sanctification of the Spirit. The sin of the world is called original sin, which entered through the first human being into the whole human race.

And the two disciples heard him speaking and followed Jesus. Then Jesus turned and, seeing them following him, said to them: “What do you seek?”

[Bede.] To those desiring to receive the word of grace from himself rather than from John, he gives them confidence to ask whatever they wished. [Albinus.] He turned, as it were, offering his face, when he descended from majesty [Col. 0107C] so that he might be seen, when he offered the light of the Gospel in place of the shadow of the law.

They said to him: “Rabbi”—which, translated, means “Teacher”—“where are you staying?” He said to them: “Come and see.”

They did not wish merely in passing to enjoy the teacher of truth, but sought his dwelling in order that they might be more fully instructed by him. They therefore admonish us that whenever we call to mind the Lord’s passage in the incarnation, we should ask him with an attentive heart to deign to show us the dwelling of eternal abiding. “Come,” departing from the law through John’s testimony; come by believing, by persevering in good works, and you shall understand.

They came and saw where he was staying, and remained with him that day.

It was about the tenth hour.
