They remained with the Lord that day, happily awaiting evening; because all the elect, after the completion of good works, will spend with him that day of which the prophet says: “One day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83). They rightly followed him at the tenth hour, because the time had come for the law, which has ten commandments and which the Jews did not fulfill through fear, to be fulfilled through love. Hence the Lord: “I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5).

And Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, was one of the two who had heard from John and followed him.

[Albinus.] In faith neither a greater nor a lesser number of years is considered. Andrew was younger in age than Simon, yet he found Jesus first. And immediately [Col. 0108A] he announces the one he has found to his brother, so that he may be a brother not only in blood but also in faith. And this is what it says:

A. 17[I] M. 146 R. 82 L. 94

He first found his brother Simon and said to him: “We have found the Messiah,” which is translated, “Christ.” And he brought him to Jesus. Looking at him, Jesus said: “You are Simon, son of John; you shall be called Cephas,” which is translated, “Peter.”

[AUGUSTINE.] Cephas is Hebrew and Syriac; Peter is Greek and Latin; and in both languages the name is derived from “rock.” He is called Peter on account of strength of mind, because he clung to Christ, the most solid Rock. It should be noted that Peter received his name here, not where Jesus said to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16). Nor did he receive it where Mark, individually naming the twelve disciples, said that He gave him the name Peter. Recalling this name, he says:

## CHAPTER XVII

A. 18[X]

On the next day he wished to go out into Galilee; and he found Philip and said to him, “Follow me.” Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.

Galilee means “a migration having taken place,” or “revelation.” A person migrates from vices to virtues, and then from virtue to virtue; and thus revelation comes to him, so that the God of gods may be seen in Zion (Ps. 13). Therefore, when the Lord was about to call disciples to follow—that is, to imitate—him, he left Judaea, where John was baptizing, and went into Galilee. By the name of the place he indicated that, just as he himself advanced in wisdom and entered into glory through sufferings, so too would his followers. Bethsaida means “house of hunters,” whereby their disposition and office are indicated. For they were God’s hunters in catching souls. Thus Philip, before he became an apostle, called Nathanael.

Philip found Nathanael and said to him, “We have found Jesus, son of Joseph, from Nazareth, of whom Moses wrote in the Law and the prophets.” Nathanael said to him, “Can anything good be from Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.”

[AUGUSTINE—ALBINUS.] Because Nathanael was skilled in the Scriptures, when he heard “from Nazareth,” he was immediately raised to hope, both by the interpretation of that name and because the Scriptures call Jesus a Nazarene; and he said, “Can anything good be from Nazareth?” This may correctly be pronounced either as a question or without interrogation. Nazareth means “purities,” or “its flower,” or “separated.” [AUGUSTINE.] For this reason Nathanael was not one of the twelve: he was skilled in the Law, whereas the Lord chose unlearned men by whom he might confound the world. Or perhaps Nathanael, wondering that a prophet should arise from Galilee rather than Judaea, said, “Can anything good be from Nazareth?”

Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said of him, “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit.” Nathanael said to him, “How do you know me?” Jesus answered and said to him, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.” Nathanael answered and said, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel.”

[ALBINUS.] Because Nathanael recognized that the Lord, though bodily absent, had seen what he himself had done elsewhere—namely, how and where he had been called by Philip under a certain fig tree—which is evidence of divinity, he confesses him not only as Rabbi, that is, Teacher, but also as the Son of God and King of Israel, that is, Christ. In this he is proved to be an Israelite—that is, a man who sees God—who was without deceit, that is, without pretence. For if he had sins, he confessed them. But the Pharisees are deceitful, who proclaim themselves good when they are evil. We find the fig tree cursed because it had no fruit (Matt. 21; Mark 11). And when Adam and Eve had sinned, they made themselves girdles of fig leaves. [Col. 0109B] Those leaves, therefore, are understood as sins. [AUGUSTINE.] Nathanael was under the fig tree as though under the shadow of death, when light rose for him. Nathanael means “gift of God.” [ALBINUS.] Unless each person is called by God’s gift, he will never escape the guilt of the first transgression.

Jesus answered and said to him, “Because I said to you, ‘I saw you under the fig tree,’ you believe. You will see greater things than these.” And he said to him, “Amen, amen, I say to you: you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending above the Son of Man.”

[AUGUSTINE.] It is a greater thing that the Lord justified us when called than that he saw us lying beneath the shadow of death. When Jacob saw the ladder and angels ascending and descending, and anointed the stone placed beneath [Col. 0109C] his head, the whole thing was a signification (Gen. 28). The stone, therefore, is understood to be Christ. The good angels are preachers in the Church, who, by preaching the Son of Man, ascend and descend when they proclaim both the loftiness of his divinity and the weakness of his humanity. [ALBINUS.] They ascend when they teach that “In the beginning was the Word”; they descend when they add that “the Word became flesh.”

L. 17[I] M. 23 R. 27 A. 46

And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee. And his fame went out through the whole region concerning him. And he taught in their synagogues and was glorified by all.

[Bede.] Understand “the power of the Spirit” as the signs of miracles, just as elsewhere the Jews say, “Whence has this man this wisdom and this power?” (Matt. 13), referring wisdom to teaching and power to works.

## CHAPTER XVIII

L. 18[X]

And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and according to his custom entered the synagogue on the Sabbath day.

[BEDE—AUGUSTINE.] Jesus entered with the others, so that by heavenly grace he might fulfil the rite of the Law. Synagogue is ordinarily and properly the name for the Jewish assembly, although it is also called Church. But the apostles never called ours a synagogue; they always called it Church, either to distinguish them or because there is some difference between “gathering together,” from which synagogue takes its name, and “calling together,” from which Church takes its name. For cattle too are accustomed to be gathered together, while calling together more properly belongs to beings endowed with reason, such as human beings. Therefore teachers thought that the people of the new grace ought to be called the Church, called together with greater dignity into the unity of faith.

And he stood up to read, and the book of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him.

It was a sign of humility to undertake the office of reader. Yet Scripture concerning him had to be opened and fulfilled for us by himself.

And when he unrolled the book, he found the place where it was written: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he anointed me” (Isa. 61). “He sent me to proclaim good news to the poor, to preach release to captives and sight to the blind, to send the broken forth into release, and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense.”

He received the prophet’s book closed, but read it when unrolled; because the mystery of his Incarnation, obscure in the prophecies, he first undertook to fulfil and afterward opened for mortals to understand. He was anointed in his mother’s womb with the Holy Spirit above his companions; and the sacrament and manifestation of that anointing was that, at his baptism, the Holy Spirit appeared over him in the form of a dove. To the poor—that is, the Gentiles—he proclaimed through his heralds the resurrection; to captives—that is, the Jewish people captive in sins—he preached the forgiveness of sins. To the blind—that is, Pharisees who did not understand the Law—[Col. 0110C] he proclaimed sight, namely, understanding of the Scriptures. By “the broken” he means either those contrite in heart or those oppressed by the burden of the Law; by “the year of the Lord,” the time of his preaching; by “the day of recompense,” the last judgment. Hence it is written: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8). And concerning the broken: “A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50). And: “He heals those broken in heart and binds up their wounds” (Ps. 46). David also says concerning the Lord’s year: “You will bless the crown of your goodness’s year” (Ps. 64). Concerning the day of recompense it is written: “The Son of Man will come in his glory with his angels, and then he will repay each according to his works” (Matt. 16).

[Col. 0110D] And when he had folded the book, he returned it to the attendant and sat down.

While the Lord was in the world, he spoke, teaching in the synagogue; but, about to return to the heavenly kingdoms, he left the office of evangelizing to the ministers of the Gospel and sat down at the right hand of the Father. Standing, he read; when the book had been returned, he sat. For by standing in the world he wrought for us the way of progress and the meaning of doctrine; but by sitting at the right hand of the Father he taught us that after labour we shall have rest. Standing belongs to one who works; sitting, to one resting or judging. Therefore every preacher of the word should rise, read, and sit down: that is, he should labour, preach, and then await the rewards of rest. He read the book when unrolled, because, when the Spirit had been sent, the Church taught all unity. He returned the book [Col. 0111A] folded to the attendant because not everything is to be said to everyone, but he entrusts it to teachers to dispense according to their hearers’ capacity.

And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed upon him. And he began to say to them that today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.

He says that Scripture is fulfilled because he himself was doing what it had foretold.

M. 20[VI] R. 9

From that time Jesus began to preach and say: R. “For the time has been fulfilled.” M. “Repent.” R. “And believe the Gospel.” M. “For the kingdom of heaven will draw near.”

That time was fulfilled, undoubtedly, of which the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under [Col. 0111B] the Law, that he might redeem those who were under the Law” (Gal. 4). The sweetness of the fruit compensates for the bitterness of the root; hope gives delight amid the perils of the sea; hope of health alleviates the pain of treatment. Whoever desires the kernel must break the nut. Similarly, one who wishes to attain the good must repent. Those who have deserved to reach the palm of pardon can proclaim Christ’s praises; hence preachers are chosen after repentance. “Believe the Gospel”: for unless you believe, you will not understand (Isa. 7, according to the Septuagint). Good works do not come first so that faith may exist; rather, faith comes first so that good works may follow. “For without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11). Poverty succeeds an earthly kingdom, but the everlasting kingdom succeeds the poverty of Christians. Hence: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18). For every earthly honour is foam, smoke, and a dream.

## CHAPTER XIX

Now as Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea; for they were fishermen.

M. 21[XI] R. 10 L. 32

And he said to them, “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of human beings.” And they immediately left their nets and followed him.

[HILARY.] From their craft the work of their future office is made known. For as fish are drawn from the sea, so human beings must be drawn from the world into a higher place, that is, into the light of the heavenly dwelling. [JEROME.] Fishermen and unlearned men are first sent out to preach, so that faith may be believed to rest in God’s power and not in eloquence. But because Scripture does not say, “having left everything,” but only, “having left their nets, they followed him,” it is an indication that they still wished to return to what was theirs and perhaps returned to those same nets.

M. 22[VI] R. 11

And going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them. And they immediately left their nets and father and followed him.

[Col. 0112A] L. 29

And it came to pass, when the crowds pressed upon him to hear the word of God, that he was standing beside the Lake of Gennesaret.

[BEDE.] They say that the Lake of Gennesaret is the same as the Sea of Galilee or the Sea of Tiberias. It is called the Sea of Galilee from the adjoining province, and the Sea of Tiberias from the nearby city. Gennesar, moreover, is said in Greek to mean, as it were, “generating a breeze for itself,” from the nature of that lake, which, when its waters ripple, raises frequent breezes from itself. The water is fresh; but in Hebrew linguistic usage every collection of waters, whether fresh or salt, is called a sea. This lake, with the Jordan running through it, extends one hundred and forty [Col. 0112B] stadia in length and forty in breadth. Therefore, because the lake or sea signifies the present age, the Lord stands beside the sea after he has attained the steadfastness of eternal rest, having conquered the mortality of this transitory life. The gathering of the crowds is a type of the nations converging in faith, of whom Isaiah says: “All nations shall flow to him, and many peoples shall go and say: ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord’” (Isa. 2).

And he saw two boats beside the lake.

The two boats are circumcision and uncircumcision. Jesus saw them because he knows those who are his from each people, and mercifully brings them forward to the tranquillity of the future life, as it were to the shore.

But the fishermen had gone down and were washing their nets.

[Col. 0112C] The fishermen are teachers, who will bring us, caught in the nets of faith and lifted from the deep into the light, to the shore, as it were, of the land of the living. For the interwoven utterances of preachers are like nets, holding in faith those whom they catch. Nets are so called as things that retain. These nets are sometimes cast loose for catching and sometimes, washed, folded up, because at one time the teacher’s tongue must be exercised, at another he must attend to the care of himself.

And entering one boat, which was Simon’s, he asked him to put out a little from land; and sitting down, he taught the crowds from the boat.

Simon’s boat is the primitive Church, of which Paul says: “He who worked through Peter in the apostleship of the circumcision also worked through me among the Gentiles” (Gal. [Col. 0112D] 2). It is called one because “the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4). From it he taught the crowds, because by his authority the Church teaches the nations even to this day.

L. 30[IX] A. 219 and 222

And when he had ceased speaking, he said to Simon, “Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch.”

That he asked Simon to put the boat out a little from land signifies either that the word should be used moderately with the crowds, lest one go so far into the depths of the sacraments that hearers do not understand; or that preaching must first be done in nearby regions, so that the words “put out into the deep” apply to more distant nations, to whom preaching was later brought. John Chrysostom: “We have the Church for our ship, the cross for our steering gear, Christ for our helmsman, the Father for our net, the Holy Spirit for our wind, grace for our sail, the apostles for our sailors, the prophets for those sailing, and the Old and New Testament for our sea. Therefore let us entrust ourselves to the depth of this sea, to seek out the pearl hidden in the divine Scriptures.”

Simon answered and said to him, “Master, though we have laboured all night, we caught nothing; but at your word I will let down the net.”

[BEDE.] Unless the Lord illumines the hearts of hearers, the teacher labours in the night. Unless arguments are cast forth in heavenly grace, the preacher hurls words in vain; for faith does not arise from wisdom of speech [Col. 0113B] but from the divine gift.

And when they had done this, they enclosed a great multitude of fish. But their net was breaking.

The net was breaking because now, at the confession of faith, so many reprobate persons enter together with the elect that they rend the Church by heresies. The net is torn, but the fish does not slip away, because the Lord preserves his own even amid the scandals of persecutors.

And they signalled to their partners in the other boat that they should come and help them.

The other boat is the Church from among the Gentiles, because not so many will believe from Judaea as have been predestined to eternal life. For the net is torn in the Church of the circumcision because Judas the betrayer and Simon Magus—the worst fish—and Ananias and Sapphira, and [Col. 0113C] many others, went back before Barnabas and Paul had been set apart for the apostolate to the Gentiles.

And they came and filled both boats, so that they were sinking.

This filling increases until the end of the age. “They are sinking” means that they are burdened with the danger of submersion; for they were not submerged but endangered. Hence the Apostle says: “In the last days perilous times will come, and people will be lovers of themselves” (2 Tim. 3). Thus the sinking of boats means that people lapse back into the world; Peter, still placed in weakness, shows this in the following words.

L. 31[X]

When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at the knees [Col. 0113D] of Jesus, saying, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord.” For astonishment had surrounded him and all who were with him at the catch of fish which they had taken; and likewise James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were Simon’s partners.

Carnal people in the Church in some fashion drive away from themselves the governance of spiritual persons, in whom Christ’s person especially shines forth—not with their tongue, but by their habits and deeds—fearing that they cannot endure their governance. Yet they honour such persons especially, although they differ from them in habits and actions. Peter expressed honour by falling at the Lord’s feet, but dissimilar habits by saying, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord.” Yet the Lord did not depart from him, signifying that spiritual persons ought not [Col. 0114A] be moved by the sins of crowds so as to abandon their ecclesiastical office.

L. 32[XI] M. 21 R. 10

And Jesus said to Simon, “Do not fear. From now on you will catch human beings.”

Carnal people must be encouraged by spiritual people, lest, fearing because of awareness of their own guilt and astonished at others’ innocence, they should dread to undertake the path of holiness. The words that follow—“From now on you will catch human beings”—apply especially to Peter, to whom the Lord explains that the catch of fish signified the catching of people through him.

A. 18[X]

And his disciples believed in him.

[Col. 0114B] L. 30[XI] M. 21 R. 10

And when they had brought the boats to land, they left everything and followed him.

[GREGORY—HILARY.] Those left much who strove to love nothing in this world. In them we are taught to follow Christ and not to be held by concern for secular life or by the familiarity of the paternal household. Note that, when they saw the miracle of the catch of fish, those who were called believed more firmly and followed Jesus to remain with him, leaving not only their nets but everything. Yet they brought the boats to shore, though they would not afterward return to their possessions, so that they might be more carefully preserved for use until they passed into someone’s possession. For it was fitting that the apostles, [Col. 0114C] whom God established as a model of true religion for the whole world, should not contemptuously, nor with less care, despise the world in the way we read that philosophers did. For Crates of Thebes, as Jerome says in his work against Jovinian, threw no small weight of gold into the sea, saying: “Go to destruction, evil desires! I shall drown you, lest I myself be drowned by you.”

## CHAPTER XX

M. 71[XI] R. 21 L. 28

And as Jesus was passing on from there, he saw a man sitting at the tax office, Matthew by name, and said to him, “Follow me.” And rising, leaving everything, he followed him.

[Col. 0114D] [BEDE, *On Mark*.] *Telos* in Greek is called *vectigal* (“tax”) in Latin. Matthew, who was also called Levi, was sitting at the tax office, that is, in charge and administration of taxes, obstinately intent on gain. For he had two names. [BEDE, *On Luke*.] Understanding what it is truly to follow the Lord—namely, to imitate him—Matthew follows him less by his steps than by his affection. For he left his own possessions, though he had been accustomed to seize those of others; and he despised the danger that might befall him from the authorities because he had left the tax accounts unsettled. Thus Matthew, who was a tax collector, shows that no one ought to despair of salvation if he turns back. [BEDE, *In a Homily*.] Tax collectors are those who are either publicly defiled by [secular] crimes, or entangled in public business, which can scarcely, or not at all, be administered without sin.

A. 24[X]

After these things Jesus and his disciples came into the land of Judaea, and he remained there with them and baptized.

A. 25[III] M. 7 L. 6

Now John was baptizing in Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there. And people came and were baptized.

A. 26[IV] M. 18 R. 9

For John had not yet been put into prison.

[AUGUSTINE.] Aenon is a place where water is abundant. Salim, however, is a town situated near the Jordan, where Melchizedek formerly reigned (Gen. 14). If John had baptized no one except the Lord, it would be said that his baptism was better than the Lord’s baptism, who baptized many.

A. 27[X]

Therefore a dispute arose between John’s disciples and the Jews concerning purification.

John sent to Christ to be baptized those who came to him; those coming to Christ were not sent to John. And from this John’s disciples were disturbed.

And they came to John and said to him, “Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore testimony—behold, he baptizes, and all are coming to him.” John answered and said, “A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given him from heaven.”

A. 28[I] M. 11 R. 4 L. 10

You yourselves bear me witness that I said, “I am not the Christ,” but that I have been sent before him.

A. 29[X]

He who has the bride is the bridegroom. But the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice.

He stands who humbles himself. See John standing: “I am not worthy,” he says, “to loosen the strap of his sandal.” The whole Church is called a virgin. For God’s gifts are diverse, so that one who does not have bodily [Col. 0115D] chastity may have chastity of soul. What is virginity of mind? Whole faith, firm hope, sincere charity. The Apostle says concerning the Church’s chastity: “For I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 2). The Church, then, is the bride; Christ the bridegroom; John the bridegroom’s friend, standing in faith in Christ and hearing—that is, understanding—and fulfilling the bridegroom’s voice—that is, his commandments. Hence he says:

Therefore this joy of mine has been fulfilled. He must increase, but I must decrease.

[ALBINUS.] That is: he must give, but I must receive; he must be glorified, but I must confess. Christ’s renown grew after he rose from the dead. John’s renown diminished after it was believed that he was not Christ, as had been supposed. This is attested by the fact that John was born when the days were decreasing and Christ when they were increasing; and that John is diminished by the head, while Christ is exalted on the cross.

He who comes from above is above all. He who is from the earth is from the earth and speaks from the earth. He who comes from heaven is above all. And what he has seen and heard, this he bears witness to. And no one receives his testimony.

This proves that a person cannot receive anything unless it has been given him from heaven. He who is from the earth—that is, earthly—is from the earth and speaks from the earth: that is, he is earthly, and he thinks and says earthly things. And no such person—that is, no one persisting in being earthly—receives the testimony of the Son of God; for “the natural person does not receive the things that are of God” (1 Cor. 2). Hence Paul says: “The first man is from the earth, earthly. As is the earthly man, such also are the earthly” (1 Cor. 15): that is, mortals from a mortal, [Col. 0116B] condemned to the penalty of disobedience unless the grace of heaven supplies a remedy. A little later the Evangelist calls this condemnation God’s wrath remaining upon unbelievers. The words “he who comes from heaven” explain “he who comes from above,” so that “above” is understood as heaven. He who comes from heaven into the world. Hence the Psalmist: “His going forth is from the highest heaven” (Ps. 18), which the hymn explains thus: “His going forth is from the Father.” He is above all because he is heavenly, equal to the Father. And because he is heavenly, he teaches true and heavenly things. This is what follows: “What he has seen”—he to whom all things are naked and open—“this he bears witness to.” But since seeing in some sense proceeds from ourselves, whereas we hear from others, in order that you may understand that the Son sees from the Father, from whom he has the very being that he is, he therefore defines it thus: “What [Col. 0116C] he has seen,” that is, known; “and heard,” that is, understood from the Father, “this he bears witness to.”

He who receives his testimony has set his seal that God is true.

[ALBINUS.] “Has set his seal” means that Christ himself has placed in that person’s heart, as though a singular and special mark, that he is the true God, sent to us by God the Father. Hence follows:

For he whom God sent speaks God’s words. For God does not give the Spirit by measure.

[AUGUSTINE.] God gives the Spirit to human beings by measure, as the Apostle says: “To one, indeed, is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom; to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit” [Col. 0116D] (1 Cor. 12), and so forth. But to the incarnate only-begotten Son it is given without measure; therefore he speaks nothing but God’s words. Therefore, as he himself is heavenly, so people become heavenly through him: through the obedient one, obedient; through the immortal one, immortal. Hence follows:

A. 31[X]

He who believes in the Son has eternal life. But he who does not believe the Son shall not see life; rather, the wrath of God remains upon him. Therefore, when Jesus knew that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John—although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples—

[Col. 0117A] A. 8[VII] M. 26

And that John had been handed over, he left Judaea and went again into Galilee.

[AUGUSTINE.] Augustine, in the letter to the handmaid of God at Seleucia: “Having read your letter concerning your welfare, both things are written concerning the Lord: that he baptized more than John, and that he himself did not baptize, but his disciples did. Thus we understand that he did indeed baptize by the presence of his majesty, but not with his own hands—for the sacrament of baptism was his—while the ministry belonged to the disciples.” The Lord left Judaea, in which were the unbelieving Pharisees, by whose counsel John was seized and who were also considering persecuting him because his baptism was increasing and because they understood that through his teaching the Law was being made void. Therefore, after choosing a few from the Jewish people, he left the unbelievers who followed the letter of the Law, which brought no one [nothing: uncertain reading] to perfection, and went into Galilee (Heb. 7), that is, into the spiritual understanding of that letter.

M. 18[IV] R. 8 A. 26

[Note: [Col. 0117D] Here others begin Chapter 21.] Now when he had heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee.

## CHAPTER XXI

M. 19[VII] A. 19

And having left the city of Nazareth, he came and dwelt in Capernaum by the sea, in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali, that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: [Col. 0117C] “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles. The people sitting in darkness saw a great light; and for those sitting in the region and shadow of death, light arose” (Isa. 9).

He preached in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali, where Israel’s first captivity by the Assyrians had occurred, and from these two tribes he called certain apostles. Hence in the Psalm: “The princes of Zebulun and the princes of Naphtali” (Ps. 67). Understand the land of Zebulun as Galilee, which is around Tiberias and Lake Gennesaret; and this is the way of the sea because it lies beside the lake. But the land in which the tribe of Naphtali was adjacent to the Tyrians was called Galilee of the Gentiles after Solomon gave in it twenty cities, from the allotted territory of the tribe of Naphtali, to Hiram king of Tyre. [Col. 0117D] Read it therefore thus: “The land of Naphtali of Galilee of the Gentiles”—that is, which is in Galilee, or which itself is Galilee of the Gentiles, and which is the way of the sea beyond the Jordan—“saw the light.” The people sitting in the darkness of sins are the Gentile people, of whom Isaiah prophesied that they would see the great light, that is, believe in Christ, who is the light of the world (John 8). The worship of idols and every evil work are the shadow of death, because they signify the death of the soul, just as a shadow signifies some body.

## CHAPTER XXII

M. 23[I] R. 27 L. 45 A. 46

And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in [Col. 0118A] their synagogues and preaching the Gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every infirmity among the people.

[HILARY.] Jesus manifests himself by deeds, so that those accustomed to read of him in the books of the prophets might behold him present in his works. [RABANUS.] He goes about in order to teach that a teacher must be ready to move and must not show partiality. A disease is a prolonged illness; an infirmity is any illness, even a momentary one.

And his report went through all Syria, and they brought to him all who were ill, afflicted with various diseases and torments, those who had demons, lunatics, and paralytics; and he healed them. And great crowds followed him from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judaea, and beyond the Jordan.

His report—that is, his fame—went through all Syria. [Col. 0118B] Syria is the entire region from the Euphrates to the Great Sea, and from Cappadocia as far as Egypt, containing among other provinces Palestine, where the Jews live. By “torments” he means sharp, not prolonged, sufferings. Lunatics properly are those who do not always lose their senses, but sometimes do so with the phases of the moon; thus demons, by causing people to observe lunar times, sought to disgrace the creature. Paralytics are contracted persons or those whose limbs are weakened. The Decapolis is a region of ten cities. “Beyond the Jordan” means from the place on the far side of the river Jordan.

L. 28[VIII] R. 17

And they detained him, lest he depart from them. But he said to them, “I must proclaim the kingdom of God to other cities also, because for this I was sent.”

M. 24[X]

And when he saw the crowds, he went up the mountain. And when he had sat down, he called to himself those whom he himself wished. And they came to him, and he appointed twelve to be with him, whom he also named apostles.

L. 44[II] M. 80 R. 30

Simon, whom he surnamed Peter, and Andrew his brother; James of Zebedee and John, James’s brother, to whom he gave the name Boanerges, that is, “sons of thunder”; Philip and Bartholomew; Matthew and Thomas; James of Alphaeus; Simon who is called the Zealot; Judas of James; and Judas Iscariot, who was [Col. 0118D] the betrayer.

[JEROME.] He ascends the heights in order to draw the crowds toward higher things. But since the crowds are unable to ascend, the disciples follow. He speaks to them while seated, for they would not have understood him had he spoken in his majesty. Yet it is plausible that the crowds followed at some distance and, together with the disciples, heard in some level place on the mountain’s side the discourse which Matthew and Luke narrate differently, after the Lord had chosen the disciples on the mountain; and perhaps he then said to them many things that we do not have in writing. If anyone insists on affirming that Matthew and Luke reported not one but two discourses, nevertheless nothing prevents their being collected into one in this work according to the rules of anticipation or recapitulation. This mountain is either Tabor or another mountain in Galilee. [AUGUSTINE—BEDE.] The mountain signifies greater commandments; sitting belongs to the teacher’s dignity. He called those whom he wished, because their call to the apostolate was not due to their own striving but to divine grace. Hence: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15). He appointed twelve, so that they might mark the four-cornered world with faith in the holy Trinity and also commend by their number the salvation which they would preach. For perfection is signified both by the number seven and by twelve, because the parts of seven, multiplied together, make twelve. [RABANUS.] Their figures were the twelve sons of Jacob (Gen. 35), the twelve leaders of the people of Israel (Josh. 3), the twelve stones [Col. 0119B] in the priestly garment (Exod. 15), the twelve springs found at Elim (Exod. 23), the twelve loaves of presentation (Num. 33), the twelve scouts sent by Moses (Exod. 23), the twelve stones of the altar (Num. 13), the twelve stones taken up from the Jordan (Exod. 24), the twelve oxen beneath the bronze sea (Josh. 4), the twelve stars in the bride’s crown (1 Kgs. 7), the twelve foundations (Rev. 12), and the twelve gates of the city (Rev. 21). By many other figures also the apostles were prefigured for dispensing the divine mysteries. It should be noted that Scripture calls apostles not only the twelve, but also all who have been sent by God to preach. [BEDE.] For *apostoli* in Greek means “those sent” in Latin. [JEROME.] Hence elsewhere the Lord says: “As the Father sent me, I also send you” (John 20). [Col. 0119C] The paired yokes of the apostles are joined not so much in flesh as in spirit. [BEDE.] Peter is a surname, to distinguish him from Simon the Canaanite. The sons of Zebedee are called Boanerges in Mark because of the steadfastness and greatness of their faith; their sublime merit was to hear upon the mountain the Father’s thunder concerning the Son through the cloud: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 17). James of Alphaeus is the one called the Lord’s brother, because Mary the wife of Alphaeus was the sister of Mary, the Lord’s mother. Simon the Canaanite, from the Galilean village called Cana, is called the Zealot in Luke. Thaddaeus is called Judas of James by Luke and elsewhere Lebbaeus, because he had three names. This Judas was brother of James the Lord’s brother, and of Joseph and Simon; hence they too were called brothers [Col. 0119D] of the Lord. Judas Iscariot took his name either from the village in which he was born or from the tribe of Issachar, so that he was born, as it were by a prophecy, for his own condemnation. For Issachar means “payment,” signifying the price of betrayal. He was deliberately chosen among the apostles because truth is so great that not even an opposing servant weakens it.

M. 25[V] L. 46

And his disciples came to him. And lifting up his eyes toward them, opening his mouth, he taught them, saying:

M. 26[V] L. 47

Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

[Col. 0120A] The disciples were so called from learning. The Lord raises His eyes toward them, so that those who receive the word with the attentive ear of the heart may receive more abundantly the light of inward savor and plainly understand what they have heard. For these are mountains upon the height of the mountain, receiving in their hearts peace written for the people from Him who is especially the Mountain of mountains and the Holy of holies. Thus Moses also, understanding the law spiritually, received it on the summit of the mountain, where God spoke to him through an angel, but written upon stones. [HILARY.] For that law was given to servants, this one to sons. He is said to open His mouth who, established in the loftiness of paternal majesty, taught the precepts of heavenly life, so that, at the prompting of the speaking Spirit, the office of the human mouth might be shown to have obeyed. For He opened His own mouth here who, in the old law, [Col. 0120B] opened the mouths of the prophets. The opening of the mouth also signifies that the Lord’s discourse was lengthy.

The poor are those who are poor willingly for God’s sake, not through the compulsion of need. [AUGUSTINE—JEROME.] The poor are the humble, whom the spirit of pride does not puff up. The saying begins well, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110), just as “pride is the beginning of sin” (Prov. 19). Those poor for Christ’s sake abstain from sins, trample upon the world, and do not seek seductive things; and thus they are rightly declared worthy of the heavenly kingdom, because they have stripped themselves of the desire for human pleasure, as the Prophet says: “But I am needy and poor” (Ps. 69). And elsewhere: “But it is good for me to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. 72).

[Col. 0120C] M. 27[X]

Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.

[CASSIODORUS.] The gentle are called *mansueti*, as though “accustomed to the hand” (*manu consueti*), that is, enduring injuries and not returning evil for evil. But the meek are those disturbed by no stirring of anger, but who continually persevere in gentleness of mind. [HILARY.] To the meek the Lord promises the inheritance of the land of the living, where no one dies; that is, the kind of bodily dwelling which He Himself assumed when He rose again. For if Christ dwells in us through the meekness of our mind, we too, glorified, shall be clothed with the glory of His body.

[Col. 0120D] M. 28[V] L. 48

Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.

[Bede.] Eternal consolation is prepared for those who mourn, not temporal losses, but their own sins and the losses of spiritual virtues—who weep, that is, over their present misery and over the delay of good things. We are commanded, moreover, to lament not only our own sins but also the offences of our neighbour. Thus the Lord wept over the sinful city that was to fall (Luke 19), and over Lazarus, whom He raised, sharing the grief of Lazarus’s sisters (John 11).

Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled.

[AUGUSTINE.] Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness shall be filled with [Col. 0121A] the glory of God and with the water of the fountain springing up into eternal life. Here we are plainly instructed that we must never consider ourselves sufficiently righteous, but must always love daily progress in righteousness. For to hunger and thirst for righteousness is to desire it intensely. Hence the Psalmist says: “But I shall appear before You in righteousness; I shall be satisfied when Your glory appears” (Ps. 16).

M. 29[X]

Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.

[HILARY.] The merciful are those who aid the wretched in whatever circumstances; God delights so greatly in their kindly disposition toward all that He will bestow His mercy upon them.

Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.

[AUGUSTINE, *On the Words of the Lord*.] God will be seen not with outward eyes but with the heart, as it is written elsewhere: “Seek Him in simplicity of heart” (Wis. 1). For the pure heart is the simple heart. And just as this light cannot be seen except by clean eyes, so neither can God be seen except through purity of heart—a heart which the consciousness of sin does not accuse, but which is the holy temple of God.

Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.

Certainly sons ought to bear the likeness of their father. Therefore the sons of God, subjecting every movement of their minds to reason, ought to be at peace within themselves, as God is. And this is the peace given on earth to people of good [Col. 0121C] will (Luke 2).

Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

Whoever, for God’s sake, flourishes in the seven virtues mentioned above will be blessed if they persevere. Therefore the eighth saying invites us to perseverance, whatever tribulations may arise. The eighth saying appropriately exhorts us to martyrdom, in which there is true circumcision from every sin; for the Jews were circumcised on the eighth day, as a sign of true circumcision. [AUGUSTINE.] The sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit fittingly corresponds to the seven stages of perfection that have been assigned. For fear corresponds to the poor, piety to the meek, knowledge to those who mourn, fortitude to those who hunger and thirst, [Col. 0121D] counsel to the merciful, understanding to the pure in heart, and wisdom to the peacemakers. [AUGUSTINE, *On the Words of the Lord*.]

For the poor in spirit—that is, those not puffed up and not aspiring to high things—fear lest after this life they proceed to punishments. From there one comes to the knowledge of divine Scripture, where the soul ought to show itself meek through piety, lest it become unteachable through stubborn disputes. In the third stage, in which there is knowledge, one mourns the loss of the highest good. In the fourth stage, in which righteousness is hungered for, fortitude is necessary, because that which is retained with pleasure is not abandoned without pain. In the fifth stage, counsel for escape is given to those who labour; for unless each person is aided by one above him, he is not fit to free himself from miseries. Therefore it is just counsel that one who wishes to be helped by someone more powerful should [Col. 0122A] help one who is weaker. In the sixth stage there is purity of heart arising from the consciousness of good works, able to contemplate the highest good with serene understanding. In the seventh stage there is wisdom itself, that is, contemplation of truth, receiving the likeness of God in the sonship of peacemaking.

There are therefore seven stages which make a person perfect; hence the one reward, which is the kingdom of heaven, has been named in various ways. But the eighth, namely perseverance, proves and makes the perfected person manifest. This, however, is the difference between the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit and the seven virtues named above: the gifts are the first motions in the heart and the origins of virtues; virtues are the effects of gifts and dispositions of mind already confirmed. They are also called gifts of the Spirit, as John saw [Col. 0122B] in the Apocalypse the seven spirits proceeding before the throne of God (Rev. 1). They are called spirits, that is, inspirations which precede virtues; and they are gifts only, not merits. Virtues are both gifts and merits. For in the former God works without us; in the latter He works with us. Thus humility is born from fear, which is the beginning of wisdom (Ps. 110). So it is with the rest.

M. 30[V] L. 49

Blessed are you when they curse you, L. and when people hate you, M. and persecute you, and falsely say every evil thing against you. L. And when they separate you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man.

[Col. 0122C] He sets forth general sayings, applicable not only to those present but also to those absent and to future persons. Nor does it matter that He changes the form of speech, saying above, “For theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” and adding here, “Blessed are you,” and so forth. They will curse you in your presence, and falsely speak every evil in your absence. To persecute is to inflict violence or to attack by plots. They will separate you by excluding you from the synagogues. Hence elsewhere: “They will put you out of the synagogues” (John 16). By “your name” He means the name of Christians, which was often cast out by Gentiles and Jews for no other cause than the Son of Man.

Rejoice on that day and exult, for your reward is great in heaven.

This is said to those who went rejoicing from the presence of the [Col. 0122D] council because they had been deemed worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus (Acts 5). For there is great reward in heaven for those who endure much on earth for righteousness’ sake.

For so their fathers persecuted the prophets who were before you.

He strengthens them by the example of the prophets, because those who speak truth are accustomed to suffer persecution; yet the prophets did not for that reason cease from preaching.

## Chapter XXIII

L. 51[X]

But woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation.

[Col. 0123A] [BEDE.] Since above the kingdom of heaven is said to belong to the poor, it is clear from the opposite that one who seeks consolation in temporal things alienates himself from this kingdom. For it is not riches but the love of riches that is at fault, as Ecclesiastes says: “He who loves riches will not reap fruit from them” (Eccl. 5); that is, one who does not know how to distribute to the poor will lack in the future. And elsewhere we read: “Blessed is the rich man who has been found without blemish, who has not gone after gold and has not put his hope in money and treasures” (Ecclus. 31).

Woe to you who are full, for you shall hunger.

The rich man clothed in purple was full, feasting splendidly every day (Luke 10); but he endured a dreadful woe when he sought from the finger of Lazarus, whom he had despised, a drop of water. Certainly, if those who always hunger [Col. 0123B] for righteousness are blessed, unhappy are those who feel no hunger for the true good.

Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep.

Hence Solomon says: “Laughter shall be mingled with sorrow, and mourning occupies the end of joy” (Prov. 14). And again: “The heart of the wise is where there is sorrow, and the heart of fools where there is gladness” (Eccl. 7).

L. 51[X]

Woe when all people bless you.

The Psalmist laments this thus: “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked man is blessed” (Ps. 9). No small part of that person’s punishment is that not only are his crimes not reproved, but they are even praised as though they had been well done. For flattery, the very nurse of sin, commonly supplies fuel to those burning in guilt just as oil does to flames. And as poor persons who hunger and weep are tested by the wickedness of evildoers, so those at leisure amid riches, feasts, and laughter are further nourished for punishment by the patronage of wickedly compliant dependants. [Col. 0123C]

For their fathers did these things to the prophets.

He means false prophets, who sought popular favour as though foretelling the future. Hence Ezekiel says: “Woe to the foolish prophets who follow their own spirit and see nothing” (Ezek. 13).

But I say to you who hear.

## Chapter XXIV

[Col. 0123D] M. 31[V] R. 102 L. 185

You are the salt of the earth.

The apostles, seasoning the human race, are rightly called the salt of the earth through the power of their teaching to salt, preserving human nature for its Creator, uncorrupted for eternity. For salt seasons foods and dries flesh; and preaching preserves human nature unharmed by the worms and decay of vices.

But if the salt has lost its savour, with what shall it be salted? It is good for nothing any longer except to be cast out and trodden under foot by people.

[BEDE.] Since a human being is subject to change and only one who perseveres to the end is blessed, the apostles are therefore warned to persist in the strength of the power entrusted to them, [Col. 0124A] lest, having lost the perception of the flavour they received, they be unable to restore what is corrupt to life and, cast out of the Church, be trodden underfoot by people—that is, be regarded by people as worthless, like something trampled down. If the salt loses its savour—that is, if a teacher, refreshed by the seasoning of truth, returns to apostasy—by what other means shall he be corrected? Hence the saying of a certain wise man: “Who will show pity to a snake-charmer bitten by a serpent?” (Ecclus. 12). By this saying you may rightly think Judas and his companions indicated, he who, conquered by love of money, did not hesitate to betray the Lord (Matt. 26).

[JEROME.] Just as tasteless salt, when it has ceased to be effective in seasoning foods, will no longer be suitable for any use—neither for soil, as Luke says, since it prevents it from producing, nor for manure, since it does not allow farming to be fruitful (Luke 14)—so one who falls away from the knowledge of truth can neither bear the fruit of good work nor cultivate others. Rather, he is cast out of the Church and mocked with these words: “This man began to build and was unable to finish” (ibid.). [BEDE.] We read that certain cities were sown with salt in the wrath of conquerors, so that no growth might arise in them. Thus salt sometimes harms, and unless it seasons it is good for nothing. So the salt of wisdom without peace is not a gift of virtue but an increase of condemnation. For the one who could have avoided sin if he had wished will deserve punishment without excuse. Therefore Mark says: “Have salt in yourselves and peace among yourselves” (Mark 9).

## Chapter XXV

M. 32[II] R. 39 L. 133

[Col. 0124C] You are the light of the world. A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden. Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a measuring-basket, or under a bed, or in a hidden place, or under a vessel; rather, they put it upon a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house. So let your light shine before people, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

[RABANUS.] He teaches confidence in preaching, lest the apostles conceal themselves through fear and resemble a lamp under a measuring-basket; rather, they are to show themselves with complete freedom, resembling a city set upon a mountain and a burning lamp upon a lampstand. Therefore they are the light of the world, because enlightened by Christ they openly dispense, by word and example, the light of faith and knowledge [Col. 0124D] wherever they go, seeking not their own glory but God’s.

Mystically, the mountain is understood as Christ; the city as the Apostles, who receive the laws of heaven. Hence we too have become fellow-citizens of the apostles and members of God’s household (Eph. 2). [BEDE.] Christ lights the lamp when He fills the earthen vessel of human nature with the flame of His divinity. Good teachers daily light this lamp for others—that is, they freely preach the lamp already lit. To place the lamp under a measuring-basket is to confine the word of faith within the boundaries of the one Jewish nation. *Modium*, neuter, is the vessel in which something is measured. *Modius*, masculine, is the thing measured, whether grain or wine. Therefore the law, measuring for the Jews alone a fixed measure of observance, is rightly compared to a measuring-basket.

[Col. 0125A] [BEDE.] By the name of a vessel or bed is signified the flesh in which the soul rests. Therefore one who conceals the word of God through love of present seduction, as it were covers a lamp under a bed, because he prefers to it the desires of the flesh. One places a lamp in a hidden place who strives to mingle the shadow of the old law—that is, its observances—with the evangelical light. But one who conceals the Word through carnal fear puts flesh itself before the manifestation of truth, and so covers it, as it were, beneath a vessel when he trembles to preach. One puts a lamp upon a lampstand who subjects his body to God’s service, so that the preaching of truth may be above and the servitude of the body below. Hence Paul says: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” (1 Cor. 9). Or, to put a lamp upon a lampstand—that is, upon the Church, in which the sevenfold [Col. 0125B] grace of the Spirit shines—is to preach the incarnate Word as the head of the Church, so that it may give light not only to the Jews under the measuring-basket of the law, but also to all who are in the house, that is, in the Church or in the world. Therefore the sign of faith is customarily affixed to the foreheads of believers, so that one who wishes to enter the Church may openly behold the light of truth.

M. 33[X]

Do not think that I have come to destroy the law or the prophets; I have not come to destroy but to fulfil.

[JEROME.] He fulfilled what had been prophesied concerning Himself; and He made clear those things which, because of the weakness of the hearers, had formerly been imperfect or less well understood. This answers what might be said to Him: “Will you say that something is contrary [Col. 0125C] to the law?” “No,” He says, “I have not come to destroy,” that is, to abolish.

Observe that for Christ to fulfil the law was for it to cease and for its works to be set aside. For Christ caused the promises of prophecy to cease when He brought what had been promised. He likewise brought the figures of the law to an end when He established that the realities figured should succeed them. Hence the saying: “The law and the prophets were until John” (Matt. 11): understand, they prefigure and promise; but from then onward, the things prefigured and promised succeed. The moral precepts also cease in respect of the imperfection which they previously had, when what is perfect is added, as where He says: “But I say to you, love your enemies” (Matt. 5).

Moses, then, seeing that Christ would be the end and fulfilment of the law and the minister [Col. 0125D] of a better covenant, commanded that He be heard in everything without exception when he said: “God will raise up for you a prophet; listen to Him” (Deut. 18). Concerning the same one Jeremiah says: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall complete over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah a new covenant, not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers when I brought them out of the land of Egypt. And I shall give my laws into their mind, and I shall write them upon their heart; and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people” (Jer. 31).

M. 34[V] L. 194

For truly I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the law, until all things are accomplished.

[Col. 0126A] [AUGUSTINE.] *Amen* is neither Greek nor Latin, but Hebrew, and means “true.” Yet for this reason neither the Greek nor the Latin translator dared translate it by saying, in place of “Amen, I say to you,” “Truly, I say to you,” lest it become cheapened when stripped bare. *Ioth* or *iotha* is called the smallest letter of the Hebrew language, and also of Greek, just as among us I is called the smallest letter. One stroke is one line of a letter at its upper end, as in *b* or *d*, or a single accent-mark.

[JEROME.] Therefore the meaning of “until all things are accomplished” is: understand, the things written concerning Me. No form of a letter, nor any part of a form, shall fail in the law before heaven and earth pass away. Thus it is shown that even things considered least in the law are full of spiritual mysteries, and that all things are recapitulated in the Gospel. [BEDE.] The Lord also declares that the greatest elements of the world will pass away more easily than the least sayings of the law. It is said of the form of this world that it will pass away, not of its matter. Hence elsewhere: “We await new heavens and a new earth, according to His promises, in which righteousness dwells” (2 Pet. 3). [AMBROSE.] Mystically, the least commandments are signified by one iota and one stroke.

M. 35[X]

Therefore whoever destroys one of these least commandments and teaches people accordingly shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven. But whoever does and teaches them shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.

Since nothing in the law will pass away as superfluous, whoever destroys even one of these least [Col. 0126C] commandments—that is, of the law—and teaches accordingly, that is, according to what he destroys, not according to what I teach and he himself reads, shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven, where none can be except great; that is, the citizens of heaven will regard him as utterly contemptible, though here he may be exalted. [JEROME—AMBROSE.] He marks out the Pharisees, who despised God’s commandments and established their own traditions. But whoever does and teaches, as I am about to say, shall be great in heaven, though here he may be rejected.

Those also will be great, though not quite so great, who do but do not teach; for “the doers of the law shall be justified before God” (Rom. 2). But those who destroy the least commandments, whether they teach well or neither well nor badly, shall be judged small, as worthy of condemnation, yet not altogether least. Finally, it profits nothing to teach righteousness which the least fault destroys. [JEROME.] Or thus: the kingdom of heaven is the Church, in which the heavens reign—that is, the righteous, who declare the glory of God (Ps. 18). In it, the one who destroys a commandment is called least, even if he has taught people as I have taught them; because when a person’s life is despised, it follows that his preaching is despised.

But I say to you that unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.

This is as if He said: Strive to fulfil the commandments and to teach them. For I, whose words do not change, tell you that unless you surpass in righteousness the scribes and Pharisees, who are considered more righteous on account of their new traditions, you shall not reign in heaven. Observe that, since righteousness is the virtue that renders to each what is his own, it has many parts, by whose union it is constituted. Religion, by which we render to God what is His; piety, rendering to parents what is theirs; likewise the virtue which renders to superiors and inferiors what is theirs; and also the virtue which gives the poor what is theirs—all these, I say, are referred to righteousness as integral parts.

## Chapter XXVI

You have heard that it was said to the ancients: “You shall not kill. But whoever kills shall be liable to judgement.” But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgement.

[Col. 0127B] [HILARY.] With a fine beginning He began to exceed the work of the law, not to abolish it. For He declares that the movement of the mind toward anger with a brother is counted as homicide, whereas previously they did not regard homicide as anything except the destruction of a human body. The sense is: one who kills in deed is liable to the judgement of the Mosaic law; but I say to you that, by the judgement of the heavenly law which I teach, everyone who is angry with his brother is liable. [JEROME.] In certain manuscripts “without cause” is added; but it must be erased, because anger is altogether removed and we are commanded to love even our enemies. But if anger should arise, one should be angry not with one’s brother but with sin, as the Psalmist says: “Be angry,” namely with sin; whence follows: “Do not sin” (Ps. 4; Eph. 4).

[Col. 0127C] But whoever says to his brother, “Raca,” shall be liable to the council. And whoever says, “Fool,” shall be liable to the hell of fire.

[JEROME.] *Raca* is properly a Hebrew word. For *raca* is called *kenos* (κενός), that is, “empty” or “vacant”; in ordinary insult we may call such a person “brainless.” [HILARY.] Therefore whoever says this reproach of emptiness to a brother filled with the Holy Spirit shall indeed be liable to the council and to the judgement of the saints, destined to pay the penalty for an insult to the Holy Spirit. [JEROME.] Our brother is one who believes in Christ. But the person who says “Fool” to one who believes in God is impious in matters of religion. [HILARY.] Therefore whoever provokes with the insult of a foolish mind one whom God calls salt shall, unless he makes satisfaction for it, be fuel for eternal fire on account of such a curse.

[Col. 0127D] The righteousness of the Pharisees is that one should not kill; the righteousness of those who are to enter God’s kingdom is that they should not be angry without cause. One who does not kill is not thereby great and fit for the kingdom of heaven, but he has nevertheless ascended some degree. He will be perfected, however, if he is not angry without cause. It is less serious to be angry without cause with one’s brother than to say “Raca”; and it is less serious to say “Raca” than “Fool.” First there is anger alone; then there are two things, anger and the utterance of indignation; then there are three, anger, utterance, and a definite expression. Judgement pertains to anger, in which room is still given for defence. In the council the matter is no longer argued with the accused himself, but the judges deliberate among themselves about the punishment. In Gehenna condemnation is certain. Thus different abodes in eternal condemnation are expressed according to the degree of sin.

Observe that although anger with a brother is less than reviling him, anger is nevertheless very often kindled to such a degree that it takes upon itself both the name and guilt of homicide. Hence John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3). *Raca*, as some say, is an interjection signifying a movement of an indignant mind; but because interjections are not easily transferred into another language, it compelled both the Greek and Latin translator to retain the Hebrew word itself. The name Gehenna is not found in the old books, but is first used by the Saviour to signify the torments of hell. [JEROME.] It is derived from the name of a most horrible and foul place because of the slaughter of people killed there, called *gehennon*, that is, “the valley of the sons of Ennon,” and it signifies future punishments. In this valley there was a grove dedicated to the idol Baal, to whom the madness of Israel sacrificed, burning their own children to demons. The place itself is near Jerusalem, at the foot of Mount Moriah, where Siloam flows. The Book of Kings, Chronicles, and Jeremiah write very fully of this; and God threatens to fill that place with corpses, so that it shall no longer be called Topheth and Baal, but Polyandrium, that is, “the tomb of the dead.” Since the one who says “Fool” to his brother shall be liable to the hell of fire, reconciliation must therefore be sought from the brother who has been injured. And this is what follows:

## Chapter XXVII

Therefore, if you offer your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first [Col. 0128C] to be reconciled with your brother; and then, when you come back, you shall offer your gift.

[AUGUSTINE.] It is absurd to suppose that, if this should happen, a brother overseas must be sought out. Therefore we are compelled to take refuge in spiritual meanings, so that the saying, “Go first to be reconciled with your brother,” may be understood without absurdity. We are the temple; the altar is inward faith. Therefore, when we wish to offer prayer to God in our heart, if we have injured a brother in anything, we must proceed to reconciliation not with the feet of the body but with movements of the mind. But if he is present, he must be called back into favour by asking pardon, provided you have first done this before God.

M. 36[V] L. 16

[Col. 0128D] Be well-disposed toward your adversary quickly, while you are on the way with him, lest perhaps the adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be cast into prison. Truly I say to you, you shall not come out from there until you have paid the last farthing.

[JEROME.] In place of “well-disposed,” the Greeks have εὐνοῶν, which means “benevolent” or “kindly disposed.” While we run on the way of this world, because it is still permitted to work, we are admonished to have peace with all people, insofar as it depends on us. [AUGUSTINE.] “Lest the adversary hand you over to the judge,” that is, lest he be the cause why you are handed over for punishment into the hands of Christ, to whom the Father gave all judgement (John 5). By “officer” he means the angelic host which will come with Him for judgement. By “prison” he means the outer darkness.

[HILARY.] A *quadrans* is a kind of coin [Col. 0129A] containing two *minuta*. Thus, when one Evangelist says that the widow put a *quadrans* into the treasury (Mark 12), while another says two *minuta* (Luke 21), there is no contradiction. The meaning is: you shall not leave the prison until you have paid even the least sins. [AUGUSTINE.] In the last farthing it is understood that nothing remains unpunished, just as we say “down to the dregs” when we wish to express something so exacted that nothing is left. Or earthly sins may be understood by the farthing, because earth is the fourth element from heaven. The word “until” here is of the same kind as in: “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. 109). It does not therefore signify here an end of punishment, but that one always pays the last farthing and will never pay it, because there is no place of pardon there.

[BEDE.] Or otherwise: the adversary on the way is the word of the Lord, opposed to our carnality in this life. The person freed from it is the one who submits to its commandments. The judge is Christ, who will hand over one resisting His words to the exactor, that is, to the devil. The devil in turn will cast him into prison, that is, into hell. The devil is His officer in this respect: that he tortures souls in hell until the day of judgement; and afterward the fire of hell will torture demons and souls in bodies together. Literally, this chapter may also be understood thus: while you are on the way—that is, while you are going to judgement with a legal injury—come to terms with your adversary who has a just claim against you, lest you then be sent to prison and pay there in torments whatever [Col. 0129C] you have taken, down to the last farthing.

## Chapter XXVIII

M. 37[X]

You have heard that it was said to the ancients: “You shall not commit adultery.” But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

[HILARY.] Passing over the outward acts of the law, He forbids the movement of the mind toward desiring, just as the preceding matters forbid the movement of the mind toward doing harm. For Truth plainly shows that adultery is committed even by sight alone when we desire shamefully. What the law commands, “You shall not desire your neighbour’s wife” (Exod. 20), the Jews thought they fulfilled as long as they did not carry off another man’s [Col. 0129D] wife.

[JEROME.] The difference between passion and pre-passion is this: passion is counted as a vice; pre-passion is at the beginning of fault, though not yet a crime. Therefore one who is aroused by a woman has been struck by pre-passion. But if he passes from thought into an affection of the heart, as David says, “they passed into an affection of the heart” (Ps. 72), he has passed from pre-passion into passion, because he lacks not the will to sin but only the opportunity; and thus he commits adultery in his heart.

[AUGUSTINE.] For the Lord did not say, “Whoever desires a woman,” but “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her”; that is, with this end in view, that he may desire her and, if opportunity is given, be satisfied in her. Sin is completed by suggestion, delight, and consent. Suggestion occurs through memory or through bodily senses. The suggestion came from the serpent; delight was in carnal appetite, as it were in Eve; consent was in reason, as it were in the man. Delight before consent either does not exist or is so slight as to be nearly nonexistent without consent. If it proceeds into deed, it is satisfied; but when the suggestion is repeated afterward, greater delight is kindled. Just as one arrives at sin through three stages, so there are three kinds of sin: in the heart, in deed, and in habit, like three deaths—one as though in the house, another as though outside the gate, and a third as though in the tomb.

[GREGORY, *Morals on Job*, book 21.] Under the designation of an adulterer every carnal desire ought to be understood, when the soul, having abandoned the higher law, is corrupted by prostituting itself to the shameful pleasure of lower things. For one who desires an unmarried woman with such a disposition that, even if she were married, he would nevertheless have intercourse with her if he could, is already an adulterer, which in Greek is called *moechus*.

[Col. 0130B] But if your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it away from you. For it is expedient for you that one of your members should perish rather than that your whole body be cast into Gehenna. And if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it away from you. For it is expedient for you that one of your members should perish rather than that your whole body go into Gehenna.

[HILARY.] Since desire is compared to an efficient cause, bodily mutilation would be useless if the impulse of the will remained. Therefore, by the eye and the right hand, affection for any friends is indicated. [AUGUSTINE.] We must cut them off from ourselves if they wish to keep us from God, lest, while we want to gain them, we perish with them. Therefore, whatever you love as much as your right eye, which is dearer to you than the left: if it hinders you from blessedness, cast it away from you, lest you enter Gehenna. Or your right eye means your counsellor, who instructs you in divine things. Reject him too if he tries to lead you into some heresy. The right hand is a helper and minister in divine works. By your whole body understand yourself and the friends who serve you, just as members serving one another are one body in any person.

[JEROME.] Or thus: because He had spoken of desire for a woman, He calls the thought and sense that flit in different directions the eye; by the right hand He understands the beginning of the will moving toward effect. These are called, as it were, members of the soul, “right” by comparison with the body, through whose frailty we are more prone to sin. There are also those who understand by the right eye the pursuit of contemplation, and by the right hand the occupation of the active life. One for whom it is advantageous may therefore pass from one to the other.

## Chapter XXIX

It was also said: “Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce.” But I say to you that everyone who dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery. And whoever marries a woman who has been dismissed commits adultery.

Moses commanded that a bill of divorce be given because of the hardness of husbands, not conceding separation but preventing murder. For it is far better that discord, though sorrowful, [Col. 0131A] should occur than that blood should be shed through hatred. Hence, when elsewhere questioned on this matter, the Lord replied: “Moses did this because of your hardness of heart” (Matt. 19). [AUGUSTINE.] However hard a man might be whose wife displeased him, when he considered that, once a bill of divorce had been given, she could now marry another without danger, he would readily restrain his rash anger, so that he would neither kill his wife nor cast her off, but would either abandon the intention entirely or defer it. Therefore, he who sought delay in dismissing her showed that he did not wish for separation. It seems that the bill contained, among other things, the grounds for divorce and permission for her to marry another. But the Lord, surpassing the works of the Law, commands that every hardship, except the cause of fornication, be endured for the faithfulness of marriage, and forbids an adulteress to marry a second husband. [Col. 0131B] If anyone marries such a woman while her former husband lives, he is under the charge of adultery. Therefore it is permitted to dismiss a wife on grounds of fornication, because she who did not keep faith with her husband was unwilling to remain the first man’s wife; and because Scripture says: “He who keeps an adulteress is foolish and impious” (Prov. 18). Yet whoever wishes to cast off his wife because of fornication must first himself be cleansed from fornication.

Jerome, in that letter to Oceanus: “It has been many years since the Lord commanded that a wife ought not to be dismissed except on account of fornication, and that, if dismissed, she should remain unmarried. Whatever is commanded to men consequently applies also to women. For neither is an adulterous wife to be dismissed nor an adulterous husband retained. The laws of the Caesars are one thing, those of Christ another. Among them the restraints of chastity are loosened for men; among us, what is not permitted to women is equally not permitted to men, and the same bondage is assessed under an equal condition. And since it is written, ‘You have destroyed everyone who commits fornication away from you’ (Ps. 72), fornication is not merely sexual immorality, but generally whatever causes one to depart from the law of God. Therefore, if a wife compels someone to sacrifice to idols or to share in other crimes, she certainly ought to be dismissed on the ground of such fornication, according to the saying, ‘If your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it away from you.’ But if a wife does not try to involve her husband in crimes, she is not to be cast off on the ground of fornication of this sort.”

Marriage is a good of nature, widespread among all people, even among unbelievers. Hence John’s saying to Herod: “It is not lawful for you to have [Col. 0131D] your brother’s wife” (Mark 6). For, as John Chrysostom says on that passage, it was adultery. Philip, Herod’s brother, was Herodias’s husband and the son-in-law of her father, King Aretas, as Jerome asserts in the same place. The Apostle teaches that marriage also exists between a believer and an unbeliever, saying: “If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her” (1 Cor. 7).

Marriage is the lawful union of a man and a woman, through which they may join in sexual intercourse according to divine and human laws. Observe in marriage a trace of the Holy Trinity. For the man is a principle from which comes the woman; both are a principle from which a third proceeds. Marriage was instituted in paradise before sin for the work of procreation; after sin, [Col. 0132A] it is also a remedy for avoiding fornication. That one man was permitted in the time of the Law to have many wives occurred so that the people of God might increase; but now it is by no means permitted, because God’s people have now increased. Then too it was commanded that each man should take a wife from his own tribe, lest the tribes be mixed and the possession of one pass into the possession of another, since the land was divided among the tribes (Num. 36). But now the Church has ordained that a man should take a wife not from his own but from another lineage, so that charity may increase; for through the wife whom a man marries, he loves her entire family more deeply.

Marriage is constituted by the manifest consent of persons lawfully capable of marrying. Many things indeed impede marriage: kinship, a public vow, sacred orders in the Latin Church, and incapacity to render the marital debt. The latter results from illness, lack of bodily members, or natural frigidity. The goods of marriage are fidelity, the hope of offspring, and the sacrament. Fidelity of the marriage-bed is the bond of chastity—that is, the marital covenant by which neither may join with another before the death of the other. In the hope of offspring lies the religious upbringing of a child who has been received. The sacrament is that of Christ and the Church: for as a wife belongs to one husband and a husband to one wife, so Christ is the bridegroom of one bride—that is, the Church—and the Church is the bride of one bridegroom—that is, Christ.

## CHAPTER XXX

“You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not swear falsely, but you shall render your oaths to the Lord.’ But I say to you: Do not swear at all—neither by heaven, because it is [Col. 0132C] God’s throne; nor by earth, because it is the footstool of his feet; nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King. Nor shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black. But let your speech be: Yes, yes; no, no. Whatever exceeds these is from evil.”

[HIEROME.] In the Law it is commanded that one swear only by God, not because this is good, but lest the Jews, swearing by created things through a most wicked custom, should think them worthy of veneration (Deut. 6; Exod. 25). But the Gospel does not admit oaths, since every truthful utterance of the faithful person should serve as an oath.

[AUGUSTINE.] This is not contrary to the Apostle, who often swore, saying: “Behold, before God, I do not lie” (Gal. [Col. 0132D] 1); and: “He who is blessed for ever knows that I do not lie” (2 Cor. 11), unless someone says that this is not swearing because he did not say “by God” or “by anything.” That defense is ridiculous. He also said: “I die daily through [for] your glory” (1 Cor. 15). The Lord commanded that one should swear only from necessity, when people appear reluctant to believe.
