Hence he did not say, “It is evil,” but, “from evil”; that is, if you are compelled to swear, it arises from the necessity caused by the weakness of those whom you are persuading. You do not sin when you make proper use of an oath. Although it is not good, it is nevertheless necessary; but the person sins whose weakness compels you to swear.

“Neither by heaven.” He added this in condemning the superstition of ancient obstinacy. [HILARY.] For the Jews had a religious custom of swearing by the names of heaven and earth, Jerusalem and their own head, to which they gave the reverence of oaths, in contempt of God. For what force was there in swearing by heaven, God’s seat; by earth, the footstool of his feet; or by Jerusalem, a city soon to be destroyed because of the arrogance and sins of its inhabitants, especially since it had been established as a prefiguration of the Church, which is the city of the great King? [RABANUS.] He therefore forbids any cause to lead us to swear by created things. Heaven is called God’s throne because by its height and beauty it signifies holy souls (Isa. 66), in whom God judges. For the spiritual person judges all things and is judged by no one (1 Cor. 2). Earth is called the footstool of his feet because mystically it signifies sinners, who are ordered in lowly places through justice and punished under the Law.

[HILARY.] Removing the practice of swearing, he establishes the affairs of our life in truth; setting aside the desire to deceive, he prescribes simplicity of speech, so that we may say that what is, is, and that what is not, is not. For then our speech is “Yes, yes; no, no,” when with the twofold truth of heart and mouth we affirm or deny.

## CHAPTER XXXI

“You have heard that it was said: ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ But I say to you, do not resist evil.”

[HIEROME.] In the Law there is retribution; in the Gospel, grace. Since the Jews exceeded due measure in vengeance, they were permitted, if they utterly refused [Col. 0133C] to forgive their wrongdoers, at least to observe equality rather than excess: namely, to take from an enemy a corresponding limb for a limb removed. But in the Gospel we ought not to resist evil—that is, not by means of evil—but to overcome evil with good (Rom. 12). Nor is this contrary to judges ordering robbers to be hanged, provided they attend there only to justice and not to hatred or some advantage of their own. For it is just that each person receive what he has done; but because the appetite for revenge is vicious, the discernment and punishment of this ought to be reserved to God and to his judges.

M. 38[V] L. 53

“But if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, [Col. 0133D] offer him the other also.”

[BEDĒ.] The physician of souls, who instructs people to heal their neighbours, commands them to endure everything that can avail for their neighbours’ salvation. It belongs to mercy that they should suffer much, as though from sick and frenzied children, if their salvation requires it, until the weakness passes. What is so astonishing as to offer one’s cheek to one who strikes? [HIEROME.] Does not every onset of anger thereby break, become calmed, and through patience invite the offender to repentance? According to mystical interpretations, we are commanded to offer the other right cheek, for the righteous person has no left cheek. If a heretic strikes us in disputation and wishes to wound [violate] right doctrine, another testimony from the Scriptures should be set against him.

[AUGUSTINE.] Nobility according to God is the right side; worldly nobility is the left. Therefore whoever is despised because of Christianity should not be troubled at being despised with respect to worldly honours.

“And to the one who wishes to contend with you in court and take your tunic, yield your cloak as well.”

By tunic and garment understand everything that we possess temporarily. For if this is commanded concerning necessities, how much more does it concern superfluities? There is a serious question whether this should also be understood of slaves. If they may be governed more fittingly by this master for God’s service than by one who wishes to take them away, I do not know whether anyone would dare say that they ought to be disregarded like clothing. In Greek the word is [Col. 0134B] *pallium* (“cloak”); Luke, however, uses “garment.”

M. 39[X]

“And whoever compels you to go one thousand paces, go with him another two.”

To avoid contention, offer not only what is yours but yourself to the one compelling you; be ready to serve far more than he commands, not so much with your feet as with a mind disposed in compassionate affection. By the thousand paces—because this is the Sabbath journey, on which servile works are prohibited—we understand lawful work; this is also signified by the number one thousand, which denotes perfection. Therefore he says one thousand and two thousand, so that we may serve God perfectly not only in body but in spirit and soul, meekly enduring what our neighbour inflicts through weakness. [Col. 0134C] The vengeance that serves correction is not prohibited here, but no one is fit for such vengeance unless he overcomes hatred with love. For a father does not hate his son when correcting him.

“Give to the one who asks of you; and do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow from you.”

[BEDĒ.] He embraces two kinds of beneficence: when we give willingly, and when we lend to one who will repay. “Give to everyone who asks of you,” says Luke (Luke 6). He does not say, “Give everything to the one who asks,” but give what you can justly give. [HIEROME.] If he asks for unlawful things, justice must be pointed out to him, lest you send him away empty. Therefore this must not be understood only of almsgiving, since even the wealthy could not always give; but of money that never fails—that is, wisdom, [Col. 0134D] which you retain all the more as you distribute it more generously to those who ask for it for God’s sake. Therefore do not turn away from one who wishes to borrow wisdom from you in order to teach others, because what he teaches others through you will be repaid to you by God.

L. 53[Y] M. 38

“And from the one who takes what is yours, do not demand it back.”

[BEDĒ—HILARY.] He spoke of clothing, land, a beast of burden, and money generally. For he teaches that the judgments of human courts should be avoided, together with the willingness to sustain loss, so that, despising worldly possessions through hope of future goods, we may condemn the empty greed of the nations.

[Col. 0135A] L. 54[V] M. 54

“And as you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them.”

Since charity is patient and kind (1 Cor. 13), it not only bears the injuries of enemies courageously but also graciously anticipates the favour of friends, so that others may be drawn to love by kindnesses. Hence he does not say, “Do as they do,” but, “As you wish them to do to you, do to them.”

## CHAPTER XXXII

M. 40[V] L. 52

“You have heard that it was said: ‘You shall love your neighbour and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you: Love your enemies.”

[Col. 0135B] [BEDĒ.] Every human being must be regarded as a neighbour. Many think that it is sufficient for virtue not to hate enemies, but that human nature cannot endure loving them. They do not see that Moses, Samuel, and Stephen prayed for enemies (Num. 21), and that David mourned dead enemies (1 Kings 15). They do not see that the Lord did not command impossibilities. Paul testifies to this, saying: “We are cursed, and we bless; we are reviled, and we entreat” (Acts 7).

“Do good to those who hate you.”

Accordingly Paul says: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink” (1 Cor. 4; Rom. 12). [HIEROME, in the Epistle to the Romans.] Do not refuse what God refuses to no one, even if he is a blasphemer and impious. Let us simply give without distinction to all persons in need, asking not to whom we should give but why we should give. For whoever can help someone dying in any need and does not do so, kills him.

“And pray for those who persecute and slander you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven.”

[AUGUSTINE.] The Scripture, “May his children become orphans and his wife a widow” (Ps. 108), and the Lord’s words elsewhere, “Woe to you, Capernaum and Chorazin” (Matt. 11; Luke 10), are not contrary to this, because such words of Scripture are found not as wishes but as predictions. The apostle John, saying, “If anyone knows his brother to commit a sin not unto death, he shall ask, and God will give him life” (1 John 5), plainly shows that prayer is not to be made for every brother. Therefore, since the Lord commands prayer for persecutors, it is clear that some sins of brothers are more grievous than the persecution of enemies. A sin unto death occurs when a Christian attacks a Christian against the grace of God and never repents. Therefore the Lord on the cross said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke 23), and blessed Stephen prayed for those stoning him, because they had not yet believed in Christ (Acts 7). And for this reason, I think, the Apostle does not pray for Alexander, because he was no longer a brother, when he says: “Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils; God will repay him according to his works” (2 Tim. 4).

This difference distinguishes Judas from Peter: not because one who repents ought not to be forgiven—for then we should oppose the Lord’s judgment, by which he commanded that a brother asking forgiveness should always be forgiven—but because the enormity of his sin drove him into despair, when he said: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 27). This may perhaps be sinning against the Holy Spirit: namely, attacking brotherly charity through envy. This sin will be forgiven neither here nor in the future.

“Who makes his sun rise upon good and evil, and sends rain upon just and unjust.”

It is more probable that this is to be understood of the common sun and of rain-water than of the sun of righteousness and the rain of the teaching of truth. For the spiritual sun rises only upon the good, as the wicked lament in Solomon’s Book of Wisdom, saying: “The sun has not risen for us” (Wis. 5).

[Col. 0136B] M. 41[V] L. 55

“For if you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this? L. And if you do good to those who do good to you, what favour is there for you? For sinners too do this. And if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what favour is there for you? For sinners also lend to sinners, in order to receive equal things. And if you greet only your brothers, do not even the Gentiles do this?”

[BEDĒ.] If such people know how to be beneficent to one another under nature’s guidance, how much more, because of the surpassing rank of our profession, must the care of virtue be more abundant, so that you may embrace even those who do not love you in the bosom of charity? [Col. 0136C] “Sinners” are very wicked people, burdened by heavy loads of sins. There is a great difference between those who sin and sinners, as between those who laugh and mockers, between those who write and writers; for even the righteous sin. “They lend” means they make a loan. “You greet” means you wish them health. *Ethnici* in Greek are called *gentiles* in Latin.

L. M.

“Nevertheless love your enemies, do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return.”

[BEDĒ.] It should be known that many have not lent, not because of wickedness, but because they feared being defrauded. Divine authority remedies this weakness, saying: “Lend, expecting nothing in return”: that is, fix your hope of reward not in a human being but in God, who will repay you for what you do at his command. Hence: “The sinner borrows and does not repay; but the righteous is merciful and lends” (Ps. 36).

“And your reward will be great, and you will be children of the Most High, because he is kind to the ungrateful and evil.”

There is one Son of God by nature; the righteous, however, are his children by adoption, heirs indeed of God and co-heirs with Christ (Rom. 8). Therefore, the more exalted the reward, the more earnestly must the service be rendered. The most high God is kind to the ungrateful and evil, either by granting temporal goods or by inspiring them toward heavenly things.

“Therefore be merciful, as your Father is merciful.”

[Col. 0137A] [AUGUSTINE, in the Treatise on Patience.] God’s nature is incapable of suffering. Yet, as he is jealous without any envy, angry without any disturbance, and repents without correction of any fault of his own, so he is patient without any suffering and merciful without any pain.

“Therefore be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.”

This is likeness, not equality of degree. The sense, therefore, is this: Be perfect as far as you are able, so that you seek to benefit even enemies, which God is plainly seen to do.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

M. 42[X]

[Col. 0137B] “Take heed not to do your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them. Otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.”

[AUGUSTINE.] That is: do not perform righteousness before people with this end, that you may seek human praise from them. “Otherwise” means: if you perform righteousness other than in such a way that God alone is the motive, you will not have a reward from him for it. Human praise ought not to be sought, but to follow, so that others may be invited by one’s example. By “righteousness” understand fasting against the desire of the flesh; almsgiving against the desire of the eyes; and prayer against the pride of life—concerning which he immediately adds the intention with which they ought to be done.

[Col. 0137C] “Therefore, when you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before yourself, as hypocrites do in synagogues and streets, that they may be honoured by people. Amen, I say to you: they have received their reward.”

[HIEROME.] It is not virtue but the motive for virtue that has a reward before God. When hypocrites give alms, however, they sound a trumpet before themselves: that is, they do so openly, just as one who blows a trumpet gives a public signal, so that they may be honoured by people and not by God.

“But when you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand does, so that your almsgiving may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.”

[HIEROME—AUGUSTINE.] The reward of hypocrites is human praise. The left hand signifies love of praise, while the right hand signifies the intention of fulfilling God’s commandments. Therefore, when you fulfil a divine command by giving alms or doing any good thing, do not mix human praise with it. “In secret” means in the conscience. If inward things belong to the right hand, outward things belong to the left.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

“And when you pray, do not be like the hypocrites, who love to stand praying in synagogues and at the corners of streets in order to be seen by people. Amen, I say to you: they have received their reward.”

[RABANUS.] He teaches that prayer, like almsgiving, must be made with a pure heart. A hypocrite is one who feigns what he is not, an actor representing another character while seeking praise under an appearance of goodness.

[Col. 0138A] “But when you pray, enter into your chamber; and, having shut the door, pray to your Father in secret, and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.”

When he says, “Enter into your chamber,” he commands us to flee vain glory. [HIEROME.] Yet this seems rather a command to pray with one’s thought enclosed and one’s lips restrained, as is read of Hannah in the Book of Kings: “Only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard” (1 Kings 3). [AUGUSTINE.] The door must be shut: that is, carnal perception must be resisted. The chamber is the secret place of the heart, which we enter in prayer when, through divine contemplation, we regard all outward things belonging to the world as though they were nothing in comparison with heavenly glory. The door of the mind is the virtue of fortitude; it must be shut against the tumults of the world and against human favour, lest secret prayer be hindered, and so that it may be poured forth in divine contemplation. Prayer is the soul’s sweet entreaty, with compunction of heart. Or thus: prayer is “the reason of the mouth,” by which we humbly disclose our vows, and it is brought forth from the secret depths of the breast.

M. 43[V] L. 123

“But when praying, do not speak much, as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard because of their much speaking. Therefore do not be like them. For your Father knows what you need before you ask him.”

[Col. 0138C] [RABANUS.] We are admonished to pray to God with conscience, not with much speaking like the Gentiles, who think that they can bend God by words as an orator bends a judge. [HIEROME—AUGUSTINE.] Here the objection is made: if God knows what we need, we speak needlessly to one who knows. We answer that we are not informants but petitioners. The very intention of prayer makes our heart serene and more capable of receiving divine gifts.

L.

Then one of his disciples said to him: “Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples.”

Where Matthew says, “Then Herod, seeing that he had been mocked by the magi, was greatly enraged” (Matt. 2), he does not assign a definite, fixed time through “then”; it is equivalent to saying: “In those days it happened that Herod was angered.” Thus a prudent reader should interpret “then” wherever the reading requires it.

M. L.

And he said to them: “When you pray, say:

‘Our Father, who are in heaven.’

[AUGUSTINE.] Whoever says, “Our Father,” should take great care not to be unworthy of so great a Father. The noble and wealthy cannot truly and devoutly say “Our Father” unless they recognize that they are brothers of the low-born and poor. “In heaven” means in the holy and righteous. For although God is everywhere by the presence of his divinity, he is present in the holy especially through indwelling grace. When we stand for prayer, we turn toward the east, so that the mind may be reminded [Col. 0139A] to turn toward the higher nature—that is, toward God.

‘Hallowed be your name.’

We pray that the name which is always holy may be made known to all and be hallowed in us. God’s name is knowledge of him: by manifest vision among angels, but by Catholic faith in the present pilgrim Church. Therefore, when we are hallowed in the knowledge of God, so that he is Father, we are children, we are gods like him, and he is God of gods, then God’s name is glorified and made manifest as most holy.

‘May your kingdom come.’

That is, may it be manifested. For as present light is present to the blind and to those who shut their eyes, so God’s kingdom, although it never departs from the earth, is absent to those who do not know it. [HIEROME.] Or thus: “May your kingdom come”—that is, may sin not reign in us, but you. [AUGUSTINE, to Proba, On Prayer.] Otherwise: when we say, “May your kingdom come,” we arouse our desire toward the future kingdom, that it may come to us and that we may deserve to reign in it. For whether we wish it or not, it will certainly come.

‘May your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.’

May it be done, I say, so that as angels serve you blamelessly in heaven, so we too may serve you on earth. Or thus: as the righteous, understood by “heaven,” do your will, so also may sinners, understood by “earth,” do it when converted to you. Nor is it unreasonable to understand “heaven” as the spirit and “earth” as the body, so that as the good spirit does not resist God, so the body may not resist the spirit, lest, while flesh and spirit contend, we be less able to fulfil God’s commandments. Or understand heaven as Christ the bridegroom, and earth as the Church his bride: so that as the Father’s will is done in Christ, so it may also be done in the Church.

‘Give us today our supersubstantial bread’ L.; ‘our daily bread’ M.

[HIEROME.] In Greek there stands *epiousion*, that is, “supersubstantial”; in place of this, in Hebrew stands *sogolla*, which they have translated “chief,” “excellent,” or “peculiar.” [AUGUSTINE.] Supersubstantial bread is he who says, “I am the living bread who came down from heaven” (John 6), who indeed surpasses all creatures. Daily bread is called either the necessary support of this life, or the sacrament of Christ’s body, or spiritual food, of which the Lord says: “I am the bread of life who came down from heaven.” Which of these three is more probable should be considered.

Concerning temporal sustenance the Lord says: “Do not be anxious about what you shall eat or what you shall wear” (Luke 11). And when he says, “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 16; Luke 12), he does not say, “Then seek these things”; rather, he says, “All these things will be added to you,” namely even to those who do not seek them. But I do not see how anyone who prays to God does not seek them. Let us now consider the sacrament of the body. Eastern Christians do not receive the Lord’s supper daily, yet the rulers of Churches do not condemn them on that account. For without scandal they may do this or not do it: that is, receive daily or not receive daily. Therefore this bread is not understood as daily bread in those regions, for those who do not receive it daily would be charged with the guilt of a great sin.

Since this is so, who would dare say that this Lord’s Prayer is to be said only up to the hour when we communicate in the Lord’s body? For after receiving it, we could no longer say, “Give us today” what we are already receiving; or else that sacrament would have to be celebrated again in the final part of the day. It remains, then, that we understand daily bread as spiritual: namely, the divine commandments which we ought daily to meditate upon and perform, according to the saying, “Work for the food that does not perish” (Job 6). This food is called daily so long as this life lasts. For after [Col. 0140B] this life it will not be daily, since in that life one day does not succeed another through any movement of time. “Today” means: as long as it is called today, according to the saying, “Today, if you hear his voice” (Heb. 3; Ps. 94). If anyone also wishes to understand the preceding two senses, all three must be understood together: namely, that we ask at once for daily bread necessary to the body, sacramental bread, and the visible and invisible bread of God’s Word.

‘And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.’

He calls sins “debts.” Therefore no one is here compelled to forgive money owed by debtors, except those so unwilling to pay that they wish to litigate over it, as was said above: “If anyone wishes to take your tunic and contend with you in court, yield him your cloak as well” (Matt. 5). For the servant of the Lord ought not to litigate. Therefore one who acts moderately to have money restored is concerned not so much for the money as for correcting the debtor, who refuses to return what he can return; he not only does not sin but does the debtor much good by correcting him, lest he suffer loss of faithfulness. And since every sin is here understood as a debt, if a debtor sins against you by refusing to repay money when he has the means to do so, you cannot say, “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors,” unless you forgive him this sin. For since you ask forgiveness from the Lord, you ought to forgive those who ask forgiveness from you.

‘And do not lead us into temptation.’

It is one thing to be led into temptation, another to be tempted; for no one is proved without temptation. Hence it is written: “God tests you, that he may know whether you love him” (Deut. 13)—that is, that he may make it known. Therefore we do not pray here not to be tempted, but not to be led into temptation, as if someone who must necessarily be tested by fire prays not that he should not be touched by fire, but that he should not be burned up. For the furnace tests the vessels of the potter, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people (Ecclus. 27). A person is led into temptation when things happen to him that he cannot endure. Therefore we ask that we may neither consent to a temptation when deceived nor yield when afflicted.

‘But deliver us from evil.’

We must pray not only that we may not be led into the evil from which we are free, [Col. 0141A] but also that we may be delivered from that into which we have already been led.

Amen.

[HIERONYMUS, Letter to Marcella on the Diapsalma.] Among the Hebrews, one of three words is customarily appended at the end: either they write *amen*, or *sela*, or *salon*, which means “peace.” Hence Solomon too is called “peaceful.” For *sela* the Greek says *diapsalma*, and among us it is always so rendered. *Amen* means “truly” or “faithfully.”

[AUGUSTINE, *Enchiridion*, ch. 53.] Of these seven petitions, the first three will remain for eternity; the rest belong to temporal life, though they are necessary for attaining eternal life. Certainly, in that eternal life in which we always hope to be, both the hallowing of God’s name, and his kingdom, and his will [Col. 0141B] (Luke 11) will abide perfectly and immortally in our spirit and body. They begin here, and, insofar as we make progress, increase within us. Daily bread, however, is so called because it is necessary here. And perhaps it is called bread rather than drink because bread is turned into nourishment by being broken and chewed, just as the Scriptures nourish the soul by being opened and expounded. Drink, however, passes into the body as it is prepared. Thus here this bread is truth acquired with some labor; there it will be drink, with no labor of disputation.

Here also is the forgiveness which we ask, where there is the commission of sins. Here are temptations, which either entice or impel us to sin. Here, finally, is the evil from which we desire to be delivered; there, however, none of these things exists. Luke, in the Lord’s Prayer [Col. 0141C], comprises not seven petitions but five, in which the seven are understood to be included (ibid.). For God’s name is hallowed in the spirit, while his kingdom will come in the resurrection of the flesh. Thus Luke wished the third petition to be understood in those two. Then he adds the petition for daily bread, forgiveness of sins, and avoidance of temptation, leaving out “but deliver us from evil,” so that each person may understand that he is delivered from evil insofar as he is not led into temptation.

This is also the meaning intended by the wording, “but deliver.” For it does not say, “and deliver,” as though it were a single petition, as when one says, “do not do this, but do that.” Observe how closely the seven petitions correspond with one another: the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, the seven virtues by which the seven principal vices are repelled, and the beatitude thereby obtained, as is explained at the beginning of this sermon.

We ask that God’s name be hallowed in us through chaste fear that endures for ever, so that through fear of God we may be poor in spirit and vain glory may be driven far away. From vain glory arise disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, quarrels, obstinacies, dissensions, and presumptions of novelty. We ask that God may reign in us, so that through piety we may become gentle, envy having been removed. From envy are born hatred, whispering, detraction, rejoicing in a neighbor’s adversity, and grief at his prosperity. We pray that God’s will may be done in us, so that through knowledge we may mourn for ourselves and every forbidden anger may be excluded from us. From anger proceed quarrels, swelling of mind, insults, shouting, [Col. 0142A] blasphemies, and indignation.

We pray to be refreshed by daily bread, so that through the spirit of fortitude we may hunger and thirst for righteousness, with sadness swallowed up—the sadness that commonly swallows sinners. From sadness are born malice, rancor, faintheartedness, despair, sluggishness toward the commandments, and wandering of mind toward unlawful things. In counsel, by which we are merciful, there is purification of the soul. At this stage love of neighbor must be exercised even to the love of one’s enemy, all avarice being excluded. Therefore we ask to be forgiven by God, as we forgive our neighbor. From avarice arise betrayal, fraud, deceit, perjuries, restlessness, violence, and hardenings of heart against mercy.

Understanding, with a pure heart, contemplates divine things as far as one who is dead to the world can see them; for while we are pilgrims in this life, although our citizenship is in heaven, we walk more by faith than by sight. [Col. 0142B] Therefore, lest the heart become double through temptations, we ask not to be led into temptation, through either pleasant or harsh things, so that gluttony may thus be wholly cast away. From gluttony spring foolish mirth, buffoonery, uncleanness, talkativeness, and dullness of perception. But because wisdom itself is enjoyed only by one who is peaceful and tranquil, we pray to be delivered from every evil, and especially, while we live, from the evil of lust. From lust are generated blindness of mind, thoughtlessness, inconstancy, rashness, love of evil, hatred of God, attachment to the present age, and horror and despair concerning the age to come.

Just as smelling differs from tasting, so understand the spirit of understanding and the spirit of wisdom to differ. The seven petitions are also fitted in reverse order to the seven gifts and the seven beatitudes: thus the final petition corresponds, in fear of God, to the first beatitude; the next-to-last, in piety, to the second; and so with the rest.

[AUGUSTINE, to Proba, on prayer.] Whatever other words may either precede, so as to form the praying person’s disposition clearly, or follow, so as to increase it, we say nothing other than what is set down in the Lord’s Prayer, if we pray rightly and fittingly.

M. 44[VI] L. 126

For if you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will forgive you your debts. But if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive you your sins.

[Col. 0142D] [AMBROSE, on the Athanasian Creed.] The whole prayer bears no fruit unless we forgive our debtors—that is, those who sin against us. In Scripture, “man” sometimes signifies nature, as in: “A rational soul and flesh are one man”; sometimes frailty or guilt. It signifies frailty, as in: “Man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. 9). Guilt is indicated, as in: “But you shall die like men” (Ps. 81). Therefore it says here, “If you forgive people,” that is, sinners, who through sinning have become men from gods; then you too will be forgiven.

## CHAPTER XXXV

M. 45[X]

But when you fast, do not become sad like hypocrites. For they disfigure their faces, so that they may appear to people to be fasting. Amen, I say to you: they have received their reward. But you, when you fast, anoint your head. And wash your face, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting, but to your Father who is in secret. And your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.

“They disfigure their faces,” that is, they make them unsightly and, as it were, draw them beyond their proper bounds, so that they may look pale and sad—as though mourning for their own sins and those of others. “Anoint your head.”

[HIERONYMUS.] He speaks according to the custom of the province of Palestine, where on feast days people used to anoint their heads. Therefore he commanded that, while fasting, we should show ourselves cheerful.

[AUGUSTINE.] In this chapter it should be observed that boasting exists not only in bodily finery but also in filth itself. And because anointing the head in this manner is most unbecoming, the precept concerns inward things. Thus one anoints one’s head who rejoices in mind and reason, which is rightly understood as the head of the soul. One washes one’s face who cleanses one’s heart, so as to be able to see God. But a person who, in Christian profession, draws people’s attention to himself by unusual squalor and dirt through choice alone and not necessity, may be judged from his other deeds as to what sort of person he is. Hence the Lord commanded that wolves beneath sheep’s clothing be avoided: “By their fruits,” he says, “you shall know them” (Matt. 7). We rightly take the mind as the head of the soul, by which thoughts are governed.

L. 151[X]

Do not fear, little flock, for your Father has been pleased to give you the kingdom.

[Col. 0143C] [BEDE.] Do not lose confidence in almsgiving, prayer, or fasting, for the Father, in his gracious goodness, will give you the kingdom. He calls the flock of the elect “little,” either in comparison with the greater number of the reprobate, or rather because of the devotion of humility by which the heavenly kingdom is attained.

L. 152[II] M. 194 R. 108

Sell what you possess, and give alms.

Whoever despises all worldly things for heaven should sell what he has and distribute it. Whoever does not possess such great virtue should give alms from what he has.

[BEDE.] For it is not commanded that the saints reserve no money at all for necessary uses, since even the Lord himself, to whom angels ministered, is recorded to have had a money-box for the instruction of the Church [Col. 0143D] (Matt. 4; John 12).

L. 152[V] M. 46

Make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven.

The sense is: Hide alms for yourselves—that is, for your own benefit—in the bosom of the poor; their reward remains in heaven, that is, in spiritual and eternal things.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

M. 45[X]

Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where rust and moth destroy.

[Col. 0144A] M. 46[V] L. 153

But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves neither break in nor steal.

[RABANUS.] This should be understood not only of money but also of all possessions. Every earthly thing is either consumed by rust, as gold and silver are; or destroyed by worms and decay, as garments are; or, if it is immune from these, taken away by thieves, as precious stones are. Thus every kind of avarice is reproved in these things. By “heaven” he means not this airy heaven, but the spiritual firmament which will never pass away.

For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.

[Col. 0144B] [HIERONYMUS.] This has also been said concerning passions. The glutton has his heart in his belly; the wanton person in amusements; the lover in lust; the miser in money.

[AUGUSTINE.] Therefore, if the heart is on earth—that is, if a person acts from such a heart as to gain earthly advantage—how can it be pure when it wallows on earth? A thing becomes defiled when it is mixed with a lower nature; for even gold is defiled by pure silver if it is mixed with it. Thus too our mind is defiled by desire for earthly things, although the earth itself is clean in its own kind. Therefore, if the treasure is on earth, the heart is below; but if it is in heavenly things, the heart is fixed in Christ Jesus. For it is necessary that wherever the treasure of love has gone before, the affection of thought should follow. Therefore gifts given out of love for Christ bring eternal fruit in heavenly things [Col. 0144C], where the future riches of the saints are incorruptible.

[RABANUS.] Mystically, rust signifies pride, which darkens the beauty of virtues; the moth that secretly gnaws garments signifies envy, which tears apart good zeal and scatters the unity of harmony. The thieves are heretics and demons, intent upon stripping us of spiritual things. “To destroy” means to dissolve and consume.

M. 47[V] L. 134

The lamp of the body is the eye. If your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark.

[Col. 0144D] [HIERONYMUS.] He continues the theme of purity of heart. Those with inflamed eyes are accustomed to see many lamps; a sound eye sees simple things. All this is transferred to the understanding. Therefore, just as the whole body is in darkness if the eye is not sound, so, if the soul loses its brightness, the whole understanding remains in gloom. Hence elsewhere it is commanded: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, because life proceeds from it” (Prov. 4).

[BEDE.] By the eye understand intention; by the whole body, all works. For the Apostle also calls the works he condemns “our members,” saying: “Therefore put to death your members which are on earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust” (Col. 3), and things like these.

[AUGUSTINE.] Therefore, if with a pure intention you direct your works to God, [Col. 0145A] to whom all things must be referred, they are works of light because of the proper end of intention, even if they do not so appear to people. But if the intention is perverse, whatever you do is wrong, even if it appears right. Therefore they are called works of darkness, because their outcome is uncertain.

Therefore, if the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be?

That is, if intention is defiled by the desire for temporal things, the darkness of deeds will be foul and exceedingly dark, both because the end of the intention is base and confused, and because the result of the work is itself uncertain. What Luke says, “If your whole body is full of light, it will be wholly bright” (Luke 11), understand thus: If all your works shine to you through good intention, then they will also be bright before God, and from him you will be granted the grace of light.

M. 48[V] L. 191

No one can serve two masters. For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will endure the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and Mammon.

The same work does not suit the differing wills of masters. In Syriac, *mammon* is called “riches.”

[HIERONYMUS.] Let the miser hear this. He did not say, “the one who has riches,” but “the one who serves”—that is, who keeps them as a servant and does not distribute them as a master. Among the Hebrews *mammon* means riches; in Punic, *mammon* means gain.

[AUGUSTINE.] Whoever serves Mammon serves the devil, whom the Lord calls the ruler of this world. “And he will love the other,” that is, God. For who loves the devil? Yet someone may endure him, like a man joined in a great house to another’s slave-girl: because of his own desire, he endures harsh servitude, even though he does not love the slave-girl’s master. “And he will despise the other.” Who can hate God? Yet someone despises him—that is, does not fear him—when he presumptuously relies too securely upon his mercy. Hence: “My son, do not add sin to sin and say, ‘God’s mercy is great’” (Ecclus. 5). Luke has “cling to” where Matthew says “endure”; and both refer to the devil, whom those who wickedly acquire riches endure by clinging to him.

## CHAPTERS XXXVII–XXXVIII

[Col. 0145D] M. 49[V] L. 150

Therefore I say to you: Do not be anxious about your life, what you shall eat, nor about your body, what you shall wear.

[HIERONYMUS.] This must be understood of bodily food and clothing, because concerning spiritual things we must always be concerned. Work must be performed, but anxiety about bodily things must be removed. Some add: “nor what you shall drink.”

Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing?

[AUGUSTINE.] The sense is: He who supplied the greater will supply the lesser. He uses “life” for this life, as in: “He who loves his life will lose it” [Col. 0146A] (John 12).

Look at the birds of heaven: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they?

[HILARY.] This must be understood literally, because the Lord plainly removes every concern about present things and teaches us to attend only to hope for the future.

[AUGUSTINE.] A rational creature to which eternity is promised is greater than an irrational creature. “Worth much more” means that you are of far greater value than the birds of the airy heaven.

But which of you, by thinking, can add one cubit to his stature? Therefore, if you cannot do even what is least, why are you anxious about the rest? And why are you anxious about clothing?

[BEDE.] Leave the care of covering the body to him whose care brought it into being.

Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they do not labor, nor do they spin.

[RABANUS.] No allegory should be sought here, any more than in the birds; rather, an argument is made from lesser things to greater.

But I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.

[HIERONYMUS.] What royal purple, what embroidery of weavers, can be compared with flowers? The very color is called the garment of flowers, just as one says, “blushing covers him.”

[Col. 0146C] But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which exists today and tomorrow is cast into the oven, how much more you, of little faith?

God “clothes,” that is, adorns, the grass—that is, herbs—with both beautiful color and pleasant fragrance. When dried, it will be cast into the oven, that is, into a heap resembling an oven. Little faith is faith that is not certain even about the smallest things, much less hopes for eternal things.

Therefore do not be anxious, saying: “What shall we eat?” or “What shall we drink?” or “With what shall we be clothed?” For the nations seek all these things. For your Father knows that you need all these things. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added [Col. 0146D] to you.

The Gentiles have no concern for future things, but seek present things; it belongs to children, however, to seek the kingdom. All these things will be added by fatherly grace even to those who do not seek them, so that no grace may be lacking to them either in the present or in the future.

[AUGUSTINE.] Yet if present things are taken away, it is for testing; if they are added, it is for thanksgiving, because all things work together for good. For the heavenly physician knows what he is to give us for consolation and what he is to take away for training. A man does not without cause withhold fodder from his beast of burden. When he said, “Seek first the kingdom of God,” he indicated that temporal things are to be sought second—not in time, but in dignity. The former as a good, the latter as a necessity; but the necessity is for the sake of that good. He plainly shows that temporal things are not to be sought in such a way that we ought to do good for their sake, though they are necessary. For whatever we do, we are instructed to do for the kingdom of God. We ought not to preach the Gospel so that we may eat, but to eat so that we may preach the Gospel. For whatever is sought for the sake of something else is less valuable than that for whose sake it is sought.

Not everyone ministers for the salvation of the Church; some do so for temporal things, or for both purposes. But it was said above: “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6). Therefore we ought to work good solely for the kingdom of God, and in this work not consider temporal reward either by itself or together with the kingdom of God. He included all these temporal things under the name of “tomorrow” [Col. 0147B], saying: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow.” For “tomorrow” is not spoken of except in relation to time.

Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow. For tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own evil.

[HIERONYMUS.] We are allowed to be concerned about present things, not future things. Hence the Apostle: “Working with our own hands night and day, lest we burden any of you” (1 Thess. 2). In Scripture, “tomorrow” means future time, as Jacob says: “My righteousness will answer for me tomorrow” (Gen. 30). By “day” people are understood, whose day it is, as the Apostle says: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. 5). Thus the sense is: The day of tomorrow—that is, people of future time—will be concerned for themselves. But you should be concerned with the matter presently at hand.

“Anxious” in the preceding passages signifies distress; here it signifies foresight, which future time brings with it, so that when it is necessary to take some temporal thing, it may be available, because God knows what we need.

[AUGUSTINE.] He calls the care of present things “evil” because it is burdensome and belongs to mortality, which we have deserved by sinning. It is sufficiently burdensome in itself, even without adding concern for future things. At this point we must be especially careful not, when we see a servant of God making provision lest these necessities be lacking either to himself or to those entrusted to him, perhaps to judge that he acts contrary to the Lord’s commandments. For the Lord himself deigned to have a money-box with money, lest anyone take offense at this [Col. 0147D] (John 12). Paul too seems to have thought about tomorrow when he says: “Concerning the collections, do as I directed” (1 Cor. 16). Therefore the whole precept is reduced to this rule: even in providing these things, let us think of the kingdom of God; but in the service of God’s kingdom, let us not think of these things. Thus labor and foresight are not condemned, but care that chokes the mind.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

M. 50[II] R. 41 L. 56

Do not judge, so that you may not be judged; for with whatever judgment you judge, you shall be judged. Do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned.

[BEDE.] He utterly forbids us to judge doubtful matters and to condemn persons under suspicion as though they were guilty. Therefore, let us interpret doubtful matters in the better sense; for we are permitted only to judge manifest things, such as sexual immorality, blasphemies, thefts, drunkenness, and the like. Of doubtful matters it is written: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes and brings to light the hidden things of darkness” [Col. 0148A] (1 Cor. 4).

There are two cases in which we must avoid rash judgment: when it is uncertain with what intention actions are done that may be done either well or badly; or when it is uncertain what a person who now appears either good or bad will become. Surely, if we judge that we ought to fear, God will not judge us rashly? Far from it. Rather, it must be understood that the rashness by which you punish another necessarily punishes you. Hence elsewhere he says: “He who strikes with the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. 26), namely, the sword of sin, with which he commits the deed.

Forgive, and you shall be forgiven; give, and it shall be given to you.

[Col. 0148B] Forgive injuries and give benefits, so that your sins may be forgiven and eternal life given to you.

They will give into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over.

This resembles what is said elsewhere: “So that they too may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16). Those to whom you give alms will give—that is, they will be the cause why God gives—into your bosom, that is, into great security; a good measure, namely eternal life; pressed down, namely bestowed upon all the saints; and shaken together, that is, joined with the angels; and running over, that is, abounding beyond your merit. “Bosom” is understood as security because we are very secure about things that we keep in our bosom. Or understand “bosom” as conscience [Col. 0148C] or as the assembly of saints.

M: L: R:

And with the measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you.

[BEDE.] This may be understood generally of everything that we do with mind, hand, or tongue, because God will render to each according to his works.

M: 31[V] L: 59

Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not see the beam in your own eye? Or how do you say to your brother, “Brother, let me take the speck out of your eye,” while behold, there is a beam in your own eye?

[AUGUSTINE.] If someone sins through anger, you should not rebuke him through hatred [Col. 0148D]. For anger differs from hatred as much as a speck differs from a beam. Hatred is anger grown old.

Hypocrite, first cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see to cast the speck out of your brother’s eye.

That is, first cast hatred out of yourself—namely from your intention and heart—so that, once the beam of a deadly sin has been removed from the light of the mind, you may be able to teach, more by example than by words, that the lesser sins signified by the speck should be excluded. Whenever necessity compels us to rebuke someone, we should first consider whether we have ever had such a fault; and if we never have, we should consider that we could have had it. For we are human. Hence the saying of the wise man (TERENCE, *Heauton Timorumenos*): “I consider nothing human foreign to me.” But if we have had it, let remembrance of our shared frailty move us, so that mercy, not hatred, may precede that rebuke. If we have the very fault in which we wish to rebuke someone, we should not rebuke him but mourn with him; and invite him not to obey us, but to strive together with us.

[BEDE.] Many people, overtaken by crimes, undertake to accuse everything out of hatred or envy and wish to appear advisers, while without the example of their own praiseworthy conduct they censure and condemn lesser sins in their brothers [Col. 0149A].

M. 52[X]

Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine, lest perhaps they trample them under their feet and, turning, tear you apart.

[CHRYSOSTOM.] Swine are those who have enslaved their life to filthy lust and to the pleasures of this world. Dogs, however, are all heretics who utter blasphemies against their Creator.

[HIERONYMUS.] Some understand dogs as those who, after faith, return to their vomit; swine as those who have not yet believed, to whom the Gospel should not quickly be preached.

[AUGUSTINE.] Some people, by disclosing things that their hearers cannot bear, do more harm than by remaining silent. Hence the Lord says: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16). And the Apostle: “As to little ones in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3). What is holy is that which it is unlawful to violate, such as the Gospel. Pearls are [Col. 0149C] allegories, drawn up, as it were, from the deep. The same thing, therefore, may be called both holy and a pearl: holy because it ought not to be corrupted; a pearl because it ought not to be despised. Everyone attempts to corrupt what he does not wish to remain intact, and to despise what he regards as worthless. Dogs are attackers of truth; swine are those who despise it. Therefore care must be taken that nothing be disclosed to one incapable of receiving it. For it is better that he seek what is closed than that he either attack or neglect what has been opened.

But because our Lord is found to have said certain things which many who were present did not receive, either because they resisted or because they despised them, we should not suppose that he gave what is holy to dogs. For he did not give it to those unable to receive it, but to those who could receive it. “To trample” applies to despisers of pearls; “to tear apart,” to attackers of truth. By “feet” he means evil affections; by those “turning,” those who turn from the good they hear to evil, so as to tear you apart in faith.

## CHAPTER XL

L. 124[X]

Which of you has a friend and will go to him at midnight and say to him, “Friend, lend me three loaves, because a friend of mine has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him”; and he from within says, “Do not trouble me; the door is already shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot rise and give you anything”? And if he persists [Col. 0150A] in knocking, I tell you, even if he will not rise and give him because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needs.

Some make a question of the words: “I cannot rise and give you?” But the whole chapter may also be read under one construction: “Which of you”—that is, if any of you has a friend, and so forth; and if the other from within says, “Do not trouble me,” and so forth; and if he persists in knocking, and so forth. The Savior teaches not only a form of prayer but also persistence and frequency in prayer, even by comparison with importunity. He employs an example from the contrary case, as with the judge who neither feared God nor respected people and yet, overcome by weariness, granted justice to the widow [Col. 0150B] (Luke 18).

[AUGUSTINE, in a homily.] A friend comes from a journey—that is, from the evil life of this world—not finding the truth by which he might become blessed. He comes to you, a Christian, and says, “Give me an explanation, and I shall become a Christian.” He asks you something that perhaps you do not know, and you have nothing with which to refresh the hungry person; but when you wish to teach, you are compelled to learn. Where will you learn the truth except in the Lord’s books? Yet perhaps what he asks you is obscurely stated in the books, and you cannot question Paul or Peter, because that household now rests with its Lord. Midnight is profound ignorance. The hungry friend who presses you must not therefore be abandoned; rather, you must knock at the Lord himself, with whom the wise household rests. Even if he delays giving, he nevertheless wishes to give; but he wants you to desire more intensely what is delayed, lest what is quickly given become cheap.

But when you attain understanding of the Trinity, you have three loaves with which to feed your travelling friend. Nothing is better than that God gives you himself.

[BEDE, on Luke.] Or thus: the friend who comes from a journey is our mind, which departs from us as often as it wanders outside to seek earthly things. But it returns and desires to be refreshed with heavenly nourishment when, coming back into itself, it begins to meditate upon heavenly and spiritual things. Concerning this mind, the petitioner aptly adds that he has nothing to set before it, because it has followed worldly things to such an extent that it has neither food of the divine word for itself nor for another who asks it. And because it can receive instruction neither from itself nor from another except through God’s grace, it must ask God, in the night of tribulation, for three loaves [Col. 0150D]—that is, understanding of the Trinity—by which the labors of this present life may be consoled.

The friend’s door is understanding of the divine word, which is closed to every person who does not understand, until it is opened to him. Hence the Apostle prays that a door may be opened to him for speaking the mystery of Christ (Col. 4). “Do not trouble me.” It is as though God says: “If you wish to receive what you ask, do not trouble me further; do not, as you have done until now, put me after worldly things. ‘Return to me, and I will return to you’” (Mal. 3; Zech. 1). “Ask as you ought, and I will give you more than you hope.”

“I cannot rise,” that is: I cannot help you through righteousness unless you ask through right faith. God’s rising is his help. Although the Lord, being powerful, does not immediately give him help because he is his friend, according to the fact that he is his creature, nevertheless he should not be understood thereby to deny mercy, but to delay it for a more welcome reception and in order to impress the petition upon him. Hence it follows: “Yet because of his importunity”—that is, because of his persistent asking—he will help him and give him what he needs. God wishes to be faithfully asked for what he has resolved to bestow upon those who ask.

M. 53[V] L. 125

And I say to you: M. L. Ask, and it shall be given to you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you.

[AUGUSTINE.] As though someone said: “Why do you forbid what is holy to be given to dogs, when we still know nothing?” Therefore he urges people to ask for spiritual things, after earlier forbidding them to seek carnal things. Asking concerns obtaining health and strength of soul, so that we may be able to fulfill what is commanded. Seeking concerns finding truth; knocking, possession. To illustrate these three things, suppose someone cannot walk because his feet are infirm. First he must be healed, and this concerns asking. But what advantage is there in now being able to walk if he does not know the way? He will not reach where he wishes. This concerns seeking. But if he finds the place where he wishes to dwell closed, it will not benefit him to have walked and arrived unless it is opened to him. This concerns knocking.

For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and it shall be opened to the one who knocks.

[Col. 0151C] [BEDE.] According to the parable of the friend who asks, perseverance is necessary: that we may receive what we ask in prayer through faith, find what we seek by living rightly through hope, and have opened to us that upon which we knock through charity. Whoever is not given receives no answer because he does not ask rightly.

M.

Or which of you is the person whose son asks him for bread, and would he offer him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, would he offer him a serpent?

L. Or if he asks for an egg, would he offer him a scorpion?

He gives confidence in asking and explains what ought to be asked for, rising from lesser things to greater [Col. 0151D], as above in the case of the birds of heaven and the lilies.

Therefore, if you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?

[AUGUSTINE.] He calls lovers of the world evil; their gifts may be called good according to their own understanding, or all things made by God are naturally good. Therefore, if we, though evil, know how to give what is asked of us, how much more does God?

[HIERONYMUS.] He called the Apostles evil, or the human race under the person of the Apostles, in comparison with divine mercy.

[BEDE.] What Luke says, “will give the good Spirit,” where Matthew has “will give good things,” shows that the Holy Spirit is the distributor of all spiritual goods. Mystically, bread is understood as charity [Col. 0152A], because its desire is so necessary that without it the other things are nothing, just as a table is poor without bread. Its opposite is hardness of heart, which he compared to a stone. The fish is faith in invisible things. For just as a fish is born, lives, and is nourished beneath the covering of waters, so faith in God is invisibly born in the heart; it is consecrated by the invisible grace of the Spirit through the water of baptism; it is nourished, lest it fail, by the invisible help of divine protection; and it works well through the invisible prospect of rewards.

[BEDE.] Because faith is not broken by the waves of this world that bark around it, it is rightly compared to a fish. He sets against it the serpent, because of the poisons of unbelief, which also first sowed themselves by giving evil counsel to the first human being (Gen. 3). Hope is compared to an egg: for it has not yet reached the reality, just as an egg is not yet a chick but is hoped for by being warmed. He sets against it the scorpion, whose poisoned sting must be feared behind it, just as it is contrary to hope to look backward when hope stretches forward toward good things.

M. 54[V] L. 54

Therefore all things whatsoever you wish people to do to you, do also to them. For this is the law and the prophets.

Strength is established in good conduct. He concludes accordingly: If you wish your requests to be granted, what you seek to be found, and what you knock for to be opened to you, then do to others what you wish them to do to you. For this is the law—that is [Col. 0152C], the fulfillment of natural law, Mosaic law, and prophetic preaching. The saying is: “Love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. 19), which must be done from love of God.

M. 55[V] L. 17

Enter through the narrow gate, because the gate is broad and the way spacious that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it. How narrow the gate and constricted the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it.

[HIERONYMUS.] It was said above: “Seek the kingdom of God” (Matt. VI); if you wish to enter it, enter by the narrow gate. The broad way is the pleasures of the world; the narrow way, holy labours and fasts. Many find [Col. 0152D] the narrow way, but do not enter it, because, captivated by worldly pleasures, they turn back from the path of truth. The broad way is not sought, because it presents itself of its own accord. “The way is spacious,” you are to understand. “How narrow it is,” that is, how exceedingly narrow it is. The confined way is he who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). It is confined for those to whom his commandments seem unbearable; yet for those who love, the Lord’s yoke is sweet. Few find this way to their benefit, because few are saved. Hence Luke: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke XIII). The gate may be understood either as the same one who elsewhere says: “I am the door” (John X); [BEDE.] Or as the Church of the righteous, through which one enters paradise. He rightly said, “Strive,” because unless the intention of the mind burns fervently, [Col. 0153A] the wave of the world is not overcome. Many seek to enter, stirred by love of salvation, but they cannot, frightened by the harshness of the journey, as it appears to them.

## CHAPTER XLI

M. 59[X]

“Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves. By their fruits you shall know them.”

[HILARY.] Because it belongs to few to find the narrow way, he exposes the deceitfulness of those who pretend to seek it. “Beware,” that is, take care. [HIERONYMUS.] This may be understood of all hypocrites, but especially of heretics, who prey upon the fruits of souls. Hence they are compared with wolves. [AUGUSTINE.] [Col. 0153B] Heretics are especially to be guarded against, since they promise knowledge of the truth which they do not possess. Sheep’s clothing consists of the flattering words of harmful persons and the other signs of religion. [BEDE.] Yet sheep ought not for this reason to hate their own clothing, because wolves often hide themselves beneath it, displaying one thing in order to deceive and bringing forth another in order to plunder. But under temptation of temporal advantage or in time of persecution they are stripped bare, and what they are is revealed. Their fruits are their evil works.

M. 57[V] L. 61

“Do men gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?”

The wise do not gather grapes from thorns—that is, [Col. 0153C] sweet words from heretics, who are therefore called thorns and thistles because they wound souls through verbal flatteries. Thistles are a kind of thorny plant. Luke: “Neither do they gather figs from thorns, nor harvest grapes from a bramble” (Luke VI). [BEDE.] Thorns and brambles are worldly cares and the pricks of vices, of which it was said to the sinner: “Your land shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. III). But the fig and the grape are the sweetness of the new manner of life, for which Christ hungers in us, and the fervour of love which gladdens the human heart. Hence it is written: “The fig tree has put forth its early figs; the flowering vines have given fragrance” (Song III). No fig is gathered from thorns, nor grape from a bramble, because a mind still weighed down by the habit of the old man may pretend, but cannot bear the fruit of the new man [Col. 0153D]. And if at times the deeds or words of evil people benefit the good, it is not the evil people who bring this about.

M. 58[V] L. 60

“So every good tree produces good fruits; but a bad tree produces bad fruits. A good tree cannot produce bad fruits, nor can a bad tree produce good fruits.”

Just as it is true that figs are not gathered from thistles, so it is true that a good tree produces good fruits. The good or bad tree is a human being—not by nature, which God created good in all things, but by good or bad will. The fruits are deeds, which cannot be good when they proceed from an evil will, nor evil when they proceed from a good will. [HIERONYMUS.] Therefore, so long as the good tree—that is, the good person—remains good, [Col. 0154A] it does not produce bad fruits; and so long as the bad tree—that is, the bad person—does not turn to repentance, it remains in the fruits of sins. [AUGUSTINE.] Snow cannot be warm: when it begins to be warm, we no longer call it snow, but water. Therefore it can be changed, but it cannot be warmed. Thus one who was evil can cease to be evil, yet an evil person cannot do good. For even if he is sometimes useful, this is not done by himself but by divine providence. The fact that the Pharisees were usefully heard was not theirs, but God’s; concerning them the prophet says: “You sow wheat and reap thorns” (Jer. XII). Thus their hearers did not gather grapes from thorns, but through thorns from the vine: as if someone drew a grape toward himself through a thorny hedge, [Col. 0154B] that grape would not belong to the thorns but to the vine.

L. 62[V] M. 125

“A good man brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart, and an evil man brings forth evil things from evil. For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.”

[BEDE.] The treasure of the heart is the same thing as the root of the tree; and what is brought forth from the heart is the same as the fruit of the tree. Therefore one who possesses in his heart the treasure of patience and perfect love pours forth the finest fruits: he loves his enemy, does good to one who hates him, blesses one who curses him, gives what is his own to everyone who asks, and patiently corrects one who errs. But one who keeps an evil treasure in his heart hates his friend, harms one who loves him, and curses one who blesses him [Col. 0154C]. Thus neither the devil can do good works nor Christ evil ones. By speech of the mouth the Lord signifies everything that is brought forth from the heart in deed or thought. For it is the custom of Scripture to put words for things, as Isaiah says of Hezekiah: “There was not a word which he did not show them” (Isa. XXXIX): he revealed, of course, the secrets of things, not of words.

M. 58[V] L. 60

“Every tree that does not produce good fruit shall be cut down and thrown into the fire; therefore, by their fruits you shall know them.”

If one who does not produce good fruit is to be separated from the righteous as kids from lambs and thrown [Col. 0154D] into the fire by that saying, “Depart, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV), what will become of the one who does every evil he can? For a bad tree cannot produce good fruits. Therefore, by their fruits—that is, by the fruits of false prophets—you shall know them to be false.

## CHAPTER XLII

M. 59[III] L. 63 A. 116

“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he shall enter the kingdom of heaven.”

[HIERONYMUS.] Just as false prophets who possess an appearance of good life must be avoided because of their wicked doctrine, so also, conversely, must those who have sound faith and doctrine but live shamefully. For both are necessary: deed must be proved by word, and word by deeds. Luke: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke VI). [BEDE.] As though he said in other words: “Why do you display the leaves of right confession when you show no good fruits?” Hence the Apostle, distinguishing the perfect disciple from the hypocrite, says: “I will come to you and shall know, not the speech of those who are puffed up, but their power” (I Cor. IV). Therefore he properly says, “Lord, Lord,” who declares the will by the sound of his voice. In this sense the Apostle says: “No one says, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (I Cor. XII). For truly to say “Jesus is Lord” is to believe with the heart, confess with the mouth, and bear witness by deeds; for one without the other is denial.

[Col. 0155B] M. 60[V] L. 121

“Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and perform many mighty works in your name?’ And then I shall confess to them: ‘I never knew you; depart from me, you who work iniquity’” (Ps. VI).

[HIERONYMUS.] “On that day,” that is, on the day of resurrection. To prophesy, cast out demons, and perform mighty works is sometimes not the merit of the person performing them; rather, the invocation of Christ’s name accomplishes this either for the condemnation of those invoking it or for the benefit of those seeing and hearing. For Saul, Balaam, and Caiaphas prophesied without knowing what they were saying. [AUGUSTINE.] The Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses performed many miracles [Col. 0155C] (Exod. VII), as did many others. Antichrist too will perform many miracles. These, then, must especially be guarded against. God never knew them, because he is said to know those whom he approves, as in: “God knows the way of the righteous” (Ps. I). But he is said not to know those whom he does not approve in his love. [HIERONYMUS.] He did not say, “you who have worked,” lest he seem to take away repentance; but “you who work,” that is, who at the present day of judgment, although you no longer have the power to sin, nevertheless retain the disposition.

## CHAPTER XLIII

M. 61[V] L. 64

“Therefore everyone who hears these words and does them shall be likened to a wise man, who built his house [Col. 0155D] upon a rock; and the rain descended, the floods came, the winds blew, and they rushed against that house, and it did not fall, for it had been founded upon a rock.”

Therefore, lest you depart from me with the workers of iniquity, hear my words and do them. For everyone who hears and does—that is, fulfils the commandments—is like a wise man, namely, myself. [BEDE.] As Christ builds, teaches, and governs one Church for himself out of persons of various kinds, intending to bring it into life, so the good hearer builds for himself a heavenly dwelling from various virtues, to rejoice with Christ at its future dedication. [AUGUSTINE.] The rain is dark superstition, full of the obscurity of hypocrisy; the floods are carnal desires; the winds are vain reports of men. [HIERONYMUS.] Or otherwise: the rain striving to overthrow the house [Col. 0156A] is the devil; the floods are antichrists; the winds are spiritual wickednesses in heavenly places. [HILARY.] The devil attacks in three ways: by the desire of the flesh, by outward delights of the world, or directly, when he unleashes the assault of all the winds. The rain of desire, by which each person is tempted, gradually softens the firmness of faith; and if it does not prevail, floods and winds follow—that is, the wickedness of false brothers and the open attack of external enemies. These three are called in Luke a flood’s inundation (Luke VI), and elsewhere “the gates of hell.” Hence: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against the Church” (Matt. XVI). For the rushing of the river gladdens the city of God: “The Most High has sanctified his tabernacle” (Ps. XLV). [BEDE.] The rock is Christ; the house is [Col. 0156B] the Church. Of this rock the prophet says: “The rock is a refuge for hares, or hedgehogs” (Ps. CIII), that is, for the timid. [AUGUSTINE.] The person who hears the Lord’s commandments and does them has his house founded upon the rock, attributing its firmness not to himself but to Christ. Luke: “He dug deep and laid the foundation upon the rock” (Luke VI). [BEDE.] The wise builder digs deep because he removes from his heart everything earthly, lest he serve God for some temporal thing. The foundations signify teachers, of whom it is said: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI). But the teacher of teachers and foundation of foundations is himself called the foundation—namely Christ, of whom it is said: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” [Col. 0156C] (I Cor. III). Morally, however, the foundations of the house are the intentions of a good way of life. Having, through Christian humility, cleared away the rubble of superfluous thoughts, the perfect hearer of the word firmly plants himself in fulfilling Christ’s commandments, saying with the Psalmist: “He drew me out of the pit of misery and the mire of the dregs, and set my feet upon a rock” (Ps. XXXIX). Each of our houses is daily assailed either by unclean spirits, wicked people, or the agitation of its own mind or flesh; insofar as they trust in their own strength, they are inclined to fall, but insofar as they cling to the invincible rock, they cannot be shaken.

“And everyone who hears these words and does not do them [Col. 0156D] shall be like a foolish man, who built his house upon sand; and the rain descended, the floods came, the winds blew, and they rushed against that house, and it fell; and its ruin was great.”

The one who hears Christ’s sayings and does not do them, whether initiated into Christ’s mysteries or wholly estranged from Christ, and who builds himself badly, is like the foolish man of whom it is said: “An enemy has done this” (Matt. XV). The devil’s house is the world lying in wickedness. He builds it upon the earth because he drags down to earthly things those who obey him. Sand is the instability of vices, such as worldly vanity. He builds without a foundation because sin subsists in no nature of its own: it was not created by God, but is merely the lack of good. Or he builds without a foundation—that is, without a bottom [Col. 0157A]. If a soul falling into some sin remained fixed there, that sin would have, as it were, a bottom, just as someone submerged in a well is held by the bottom of the well. But because it is not content with one sin and is daily cast down from sin into sin, toward worse things, it finds no bottom on which to be fixed. Hence: “When the sinner comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. XVIII). The house fell because every conscience that does not remain fixed in hope in God cannot endure temptations; and it is driven all the more as it is more separated from higher things into those of the world. And indeed the evil and the falsely good become worse when temptation comes upon them, until at last they fall into everlasting punishment. The rushing of the river may therefore be understood as the separation effected by the final judgment, [Col. 0157B] when both houses have reached their end: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke XIV). The wise and good man may also be understood as any righteous person, just as the foolish man may be any perverse person.

M. 62[II] R. 13 L. 24

“And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these words, that the crowds marvelled at his teaching. For he was teaching them as one having authority, and not as their scribes and Pharisees.”

[BEDE.] “At his teaching,” that is, concerning his teaching. A teacher speaks with authority when he practises the things he teaches. For one who destroys his own words by his deeds is despised. Hence Paul says: “Let no one despise your youth” (I Tim. IV). The scribes gave the people the precepts which they had learned through the Law [Col. 0157C]. But Christ, as author of the Law, freely instituted things that seemed deficient, either changing or increasing them. [AUGUSTINE.] This is what is said in the psalm: “I shall act confidently in him. The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, proved in the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. XI). Whether these commandments are referred to the seven beatitudes at the beginning of this sermon, as the exposition of blessed Augustine relates, or whether there is another order, what the Lord commanded must be done, and what he promised must be believed.

## CHAPTER XLIV

M. 77[VI] R. 63

“But seeing the crowds, he had compassion on them, because they were [Col. 0157D] harassed and lying helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.”

[HIERONYMUS.] The affliction of the flock is the fault of the shepherds and the failing of rulers. Seeing with a gaze of compassion the people harassed by the violence of unclean spirits, burdened beneath the yoke of the Law, and benumbed through various errors by a vain security, the Lord had compassion on it by opening the way of truth and removing bodily afflictions. Here the seventy-eighth chapter of Matthew is passed over, because in the parable of the sower and in the thirty-third chapter of John it will become clear that the peoples are the harvest and the preachers the labourers.

M. 79[II] R. 29 L. 86

“And having called his twelve disciples, he gave them power over unclean spirits, to cast them out, [Col. 0158A] and to cure every sickness and every infirmity. And he sent them to preach the kingdom of God.”

[HIERONYMUS.] There is a great difference between possessing and receiving. God drove away illnesses by his own power; the disciples did so in his name. [BEDE.] Having first granted them the power of signs, he sent them to preach the kingdom of God, so that the greatness of the deeds might bear witness to the greatness of the promises: those who preached new things performed new things.

“And he said to them: ‘Take nothing for the journey.’”

Such should be the preacher’s confidence in God that he carries no provision for the present life. According to Luke, he is also forbidden to greet anyone on the road, in order to show with what urgency he ought to hasten to preaching. It should be known that one who greets on the road greets from an occasion, not from an earnest desire to obtain salvation. Therefore, one who preaches salvation not from love of the eternal homeland but from ambition for rewards is, as it were, greeting on the journey.

M. 84[X]

“Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

There were then people from Judaea who were to be called; people from the Gentiles were not yet to be called. But after the resurrection it is said: “Go, teach all nations” (Matt. XXVIII). First, indeed, it was necessary to preach the Gospel to the Jews, lest they have the excuse that they had been rejected. [HIERONYMUS—HILARY.] According to the tropological sense, to abstain from the ways of the Gentiles is to abstain from the conduct and life of Gentile ignorance; [Col. 0158C] not to enter Samaritan cities is not to go to the churches of heretics.

M. 82[II] R. 53 L. 87 A. 110

“And as you go, preach, saying: ‘The kingdom of heaven has drawn near.’”

[GREGORY.] Certainly it draws near to those who, through fellowship with Christ, reform in themselves the image of God. If the world is falling like a collapsing house, and we embrace it in love, we wish to be crushed rather than to dwell in it, because no reasoning separates us from its ruin when love binds us to its sufferings.

“Cure the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons.”
