[HIERONYMUS.] Lest anyone believe that unlearned men lacking eloquence possessed the kingdom of heaven, he gives them power to perform miracles, so that the greatness of the signs may prove the greatness of the promises.

“Freely you received; freely give.”

[GREGORY.] Some receive no monetary rewards for ordination, yet confer holy orders for the sake of human favour. Such people plainly do not give freely, because they seek the coin of favour. Hence the prophet fittingly describes as righteous the person “who shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isa. XXXIII). And he rightly added, “from every,” because one gift comes through service—that is, undue submission; another comes through the hand, which is money; another through the tongue, which is favour.

“Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money [Col. 0159A] in your belts; nor a bag for the journey, nor bread, nor two tunics, nor shoes, nor a staff. For the labourer is worthy of his food.”

If the apostles possessed gold, they would be thought to preach, not for people’s salvation, but for gain. “No bag for the journey.” [HIERONYMUS.] By this he rebukes the philosophers commonly called *bactroperitae*, because, although they despise the world and reckon all things as nothing, they carry a store-room with them. “Nor two tunics.” He does not say this so that anyone in Scythian cold must be content with one tunic; rather, we are to understand clothing by “tunic,” so that, while dressed in one garment, we do not keep another in reserve through fear for the future. “Nor shoes.” Plato also instructed that the two extremities of the body should not be covered and that the head and feet should not be accustomed to softness. [Col. 0159B] For when these have firmness, the remaining parts are stronger. “Nor a staff.” One who has the Lord’s help—why should he seek the protection of a stick? “The labourer is worthy of his food.” Receive only as much as is necessary for your food and clothing. [BEDE.] It is sufficiently shown that the Lord did not forbid them to carry what they needed to sustain this life, for use when necessary; rather, he showed that these things were owed them by those to whom they preached. This is the historical sense. But according to the anagogical sense, gold often signifies understanding, silver speech, and bronze voice. We ought to possess these gifts bestowed by the Lord and not adopt the teaching of heretics. Money shut up in belts is wisdom not distributed. And it is written: “Hidden wisdom and hidden treasure—what benefit is there in either?” [Col. 0159C] (Ecclus. XX). By the bag are indicated worldly burdens; by bread, temporal luxuries. [AUGUSTINE.] Therefore no one undertaking the office of teacher ought to be burdened by the weight of worldly business, relaxed by fleshly desires, or hide beneath the idleness of a sluggish body the entrusted talent of the word. When the wearing of two tunics is forbidden, we are expressly warned to walk not duplicitously but simply. [BEDE.] Shoes signify examples of dead works, lest the preacher regard the examples of fools and so cover and fortify his feet—that is, his affections—as though with deadly bindings. In the prohibition against carrying shoes, according to Matthew, care is forbidden; in sandals or soles, according to Mark, there is a mystical significance: the foot should be neither covered nor bare upon the ground, that is, the Gospel should neither be hidden nor rest upon earthly advantages. Yet literally it was necessary for the apostles to bind soles beneath their feet, because the land of Palestine is sandy and excessively hot in summer. [HIERONYMUS.] We must not have a staff which is changed into a serpent, nor lean upon the staff of fleshly support, which, when pressed, soon breaks and pierces the hand of the one resting upon it. Matthew says, “nor a staff” (Matt. X), while Mark says, “except a staff only” (Mark VI). This is resolved as follows: temptation is understood in two ways, as in “God tempts no one” (Jas. I), and “the Lord your God tempts you” (Deut. XIII). The former is temptation by seduction; the latter by testing. Judgment likewise signifies both condemnation and discernment. Thus “staff” has two meanings: in Matthew it is understood as the smallest thing, as though he said, “Carry none of the necessities with you, not even a staff”—that is, not even the smallest things; but in Mark the staff signifies authority received from the Lord. Therefore there was no contradiction.

M. 83[II] R. 54 L. 87, 112

“Whatever city or village you enter, inquire who in it is worthy; and remain there until you depart. L. Eating and drinking what is set before you, and cure the sick who are there.”

[HIERONYMUS.] A host should be chosen by reputation, lest the preaching be disgraced by the ill repute of the one who receives the preacher. It is fitting that they should remain there and receive earthly things from those to whom [Col. 0160B] they offer heavenly things. For, as Luke says, the labourer is worthy of his wages. [BEDE.] Here the reward of preaching begins and is perfected in heaven, because two rewards are due for our one work: one on the way, the other in the homeland. It is clear, however, that the Lord did not command this as though evangelists ought not to live from any source other than the provision of those to whom they preach; otherwise the Apostle would have acted against this command, since he earned his living by his own hands so as not to burden anyone. For when something is commanded by the Lord, failure to do it is the sin of disobedience; but when authority is given, anyone may relinquish his own right. “Until you depart,” understand: from the city or village.

L. 113[X]

[Col. 0160C] “And do not go from house to house.”

[BEDE.] He gives a command of constancy, that they may observe the laws of hospitality. For it is foreign to a preacher to run about from house to house and change lodgings.

M. 84[V] L. 111

“And when you enter a house, greet it, saying: ‘Peace to this house.’ And if the house is worthy, your peace shall come upon it; but if it is not worthy, your peace shall return to you.”

[HIERONYMUS.] He has covertly expressed the greeting of Hebrew and Syriac speech. For what is said in Greek, *chaire*, and in Latin, *ave*, is in Hebrew and Syriac *salomlach* or *samalach*, that is, “peace be with you.” [BEDE.] [Col. 0160D] The peace offered from the preacher’s mouth either rests in the house, if there is in it a child of peace, or returns to that same preacher; for either someone will be predestined to life if he follows the word he hears, or, if no one is willing to hear, the preacher himself will not be without fruit.

M. 85[II] R. 55 L. 114 and 82

“And whoever does not receive you or hear your words, as you go outside from that house or city, shake the dust from your feet. L. As a testimony to them. M. Amen, I say to you: it will be more tolerable for the land of the Sodomites and Gomorrhites on the day of judgment than for that city.”

[HIERONYMUS.] “Shake off the dust” is said as a testimony, because the preaching reached that city. Or the dust is shaken off as a sign that they should receive not even necessities from those who despise the Gospel. He says “more tolerable” because Sodom and Gomorrah did not have preaching. Luke: “Shake off even the dust of your feet as a testimony against them” (Luke X), that is, display and declare even the smallest part of the journey and labour which you endured for them, because it will be the occasion of greater condemnation for them. This is to shake the dust off upon them, and it is among the other testimonies by which they will be without excuse. Such is the saying: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have had sin” (John XV).

M. 86[V] L. 109

[Col. 0161B] “Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves. Therefore be prudent as serpents and simple as doves.”

The scribes and Pharisees, who are the Jewish clergy, are wolves. By the serpent’s prudence avoid snares; by the dove, be innocent. [HIERONYMUS.] The serpent conceals its head, in which its life resides, with its whole body; and you, even at the peril of your whole body, preserve your head—that is, me. The serpent also, squeezing itself through narrow places, sheds its old skin and is renewed; so those entering through the narrow gate that leads to life put off the old man.

M. 87[V] R. 139 L. 250 A. 46

[Col. 0161C] “But beware of men. For they will hand you over in councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you; and you will be brought before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles.”

[BEDE.] Here he explains whom he called wolves. This was the cause of destruction for the Jewish people: after the killing of the Saviour, they harassed his heralds with impious cruelty. In councils they forbade Christ’s name to be preached; in synagogues, under the appearance of correction, they beat preachers with scourges, as is read of Paul (Acts XVI); and they delivered them to governors and kings for condemnation, as they did James to Herod. These things are a testimony to them and the Gentiles (Acts XII): namely, of the perversity of the Jews and the correction of the Gentiles. For the death of the righteous helps the good; it is [Col. 0161D] a testimony against the evil, so that the perverse perish without excuse from the very thing from which the elect take an example by which to live.

M. 88[II] R. 141 L. 148 A. 251

“But when they hand you over in synagogues and before magistrates and authorities, do not be anxious how or what you should answer, or what you should say. M. For in that hour you will be given what you should say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.”

Having foretold future adversities so that, once foreseen, they may wound less, he adds consolation against fears. [BEDE.] When we are brought before judges on account of Jesus, we must offer our own will for Christ; [Col. 0162A] but Christ himself, who dwells in us, speaks for himself, and the grace of the Holy Spirit is supplied in answering.

M. R.

“But brother will hand brother over to death, and father son; and children will rise up against parents and put them to death; and you will be hated by all because of my name.”

[HIERONYMUS.] In persecutions we frequently see this happen, because there is no faithful affection among those whose faith differs. [GREGORY.] The torments we suffer from those in whom we had confidence rage more fiercely within us, because, together with bodily harm, the evils of lost love torment us.

“But he who perseveres to the end, he [Col. 0162B] shall be saved.”

The end, not the contest, crowns; hence the tail of the victim is commanded to be placed in the sacrifice, teaching that a good work must be brought through to its end.

M. 89[X]

“But when they persecute you in this city, flee to another. Amen, I say to you: you will not finish the cities of Israel until the Son of Man comes.”

This must be referred to the time when it was said to the Apostles: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles.” The sense is: if the Jews persecute you in this city—that is, in some city of Judaea—flee to another, not merely avoiding persecutions, but rather so that tribulation may become the seed-bed of the Gospel. Paul indeed fled Damascus in this way (Acts IX). “Until the Son of Man comes”: by bringing you urgent aid. [HIERONYMUS.] Spiritually, by this city we may understand the New testimony [Testament] of the Scriptures; by the cities of Israel, the many books.

M. 90[III] L. A. 118

“A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master. It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher and the servant like his Lord.”

[BEDE.] If the teacher, who is God, does not wish to avenge his own injuries but instead, by suffering them, wishes to make his persecutors gentler, it is necessary that disciples, who are mere human beings, follow the same rule. [Col. 0162D] He calls the Apostles and their imitators until the end of the age “disciple” and “servant,” but himself “teacher” and “Lord.”

M. 81[X]

“If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more his household? Therefore do not fear them.”

[HIERONYMUS.] Beelzebub is the idol of Ekron, called in the Books of Kings the idol of the fly. For *zebub* means “fly,” signifying uncleanness. *Beel* is the same as what is called Baal, namely the god of Ekron. He is called the god of flies because, when sacrifice was made to him, the annoyance of flies defiled the sacrifice. Christ calls himself the master of the house, that is, of all the righteous.

[Col. 0163A] M. 92[II] R. 40 L. 80

“For nothing is covered that shall not be revealed, and hidden that shall not be known.”

[HIERONYMUS.] The sense is: do not fear the savagery of persecutors or imitate pretenders, for the day of judgment will come in which both your virtue and their wickedness will be made manifest. [BEDE.] Therefore hold firmly in mind that day of recompense, when God “will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the thoughts of hearts.” Then praise from God awaits you, and eternal punishment awaits the enemies of truth. “Covered” concerns thoughts; “hidden,” deeds.

M. 91[V] L. 145

“What I tell you in darkness, say in the light; and [Col. 0163B] what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops.”

“In darkness,” that is, in mystery, or while you are still in fear. Preach “in the light,” that is, openly, with the confidence of truth after receiving the Holy Spirit. What you hear “in the ear,” that is, in secret, preach “upon the housetops,” that is, steadfastly and publicly, having trampled down the dwelling of the flesh. He speaks according to the custom of the province of Palestine, where people commonly sit on flat roofs. [BEDE.] They do not make roofs raised into high ridges as we do, but level in a flat design. Hence the Law commanded that whoever built a house should put a wall around the roof, lest innocent blood be shed there when someone slipped and fell headlong.

L. “But I say to you, my friends”: M. “Do not fear [Col. 0163C] those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.”

Those who desire nothing earthly are called God’s friends. There are two kinds of persecutors: one openly cruel, the other deceptively flattering, which belongs to the hypocrisy of the Pharisees. The Lord commands that neither be feared, because they have no power over the souls of the righteous. Once fear of the world has been expelled, serve the Lord through fear of Gehenna until love casts that fear out, while chaste fear remains—that is, reverence to be offered to God without end. That Gehenna is twofold, of fire and cold, we read most fully in Job (Job XXIV).

“Are not two sparrows sold for an *as*? Yet not one of them [Col. 0163D] falls to the ground without your Father.”

Luke: “Not one is forgotten before God” (Luke XII). If no sparrow dies apart from God’s providence, in which all things are contained, how much more you, who were made in God’s image? Luke: “Five sparrows are sold for a *dipondius*” (ibid.), that is, are sold. A *dipondius* is a very small kind of weight, composed of two *asses*. What one is in numbers, an *as* is in weights; and what two is in numbers, a *dipondius* is in weights.

“But even all the hairs of your head are numbered.”

To say nothing of the body’s mass, even its smallest parts are preserved by God’s providence. All things are numbered to God—not by an act of counting, but by the ease of his knowledge—that is, they are known. Things which he preserves are rightly called numbered, because we count what we wish to preserve. [Col. 0164A] Here those who deny the resurrection mock us, as though we said that the material which becomes a corpse when the soul departs must be restored in such a manner that the things which waste away and are changed into other forms must return to the same parts of the body in which they previously were. Otherwise, if what frequent cutting removes returns to the hairs, and what is removed returns to the nails, an unseemly resurrection results. But just as, if a metal statue were ground into powder and an artisan wished to restore it, he would not seek which particle should be returned to which limb of the statue, provided only that he restored the whole from the material of which it had consisted; so God will wonderfully restore us from the matter of our flesh. Nor will it concern wholeness whether hairs return to hairs and nails to nails, provided only that by God’s providence [Col. 0164B] we are fittingly restored.

“Therefore do not fear; you are better than many sparrows.”

Luke: “You are worth more than many sparrows” (Luke XII), that is, you are of greater dignity before God.

“Therefore everyone who confesses me before men, I also shall confess before my Father who is in heaven, L. and before his angels.”

For torturers of the flesh are not to be feared; therefore confess me. For everyone who confesses me before men—that is, not only by faith of heart, but by word and deed, not refusing, that is, to die for me—I too shall confess him before the presence of the heavenly city and the eternal King and Judge, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25). [Col. 0164C]

M. 94[II] R. 86 L. 87 and 146

But whoever denies me before men, R. and has been ashamed of me in this adulterous and sinful generation, M. I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven, L. and before his angels. R. and the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.

Whoever, before men—where confession of my name ought to be of benefit—denies that I am God or man, I too shall deny him before my Father and the angels; that is, I shall not reveal the Father to him, nor myself in the majesty of the Father. Whoever has been ashamed because of me, as though I were crucified—for which reason I am a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles [Col. 0164D]—the Son of Man shall be ashamed on his account; that is, he shall cast him into outer darkness, and thus he shall be put to shame because of his presence. “Who has been ashamed of me,” that is, holding me as shameful; or “ashamed,” that is, causing shame, namely blushing: the Son of Man “shall be ashamed,” that is, shall be regarded as putting him to shame. Or the passive is taken as an adjective. “He shall be ashamed,” that is, he shall put him to shame and, as though blushing at his presence, shall exclude him from glory. The Father is in heaven, that is, in the fellowship of the saints. There are some who say, “We are not ashamed to confess God”; yet for proof of faith the voice of Christian profession is insufficient when they disdain to endure injuries, and when they are ashamed, if a quarrel arises, to make satisfaction first.

[Col. 0165A] M. 95[V] L. 150

Do not suppose that I came to send peace upon the earth. I came not to send peace, but a sword.

[Jerome.] “Brother will hand over brother,” as was said above. For I did not come in order to confirm carnal affections, but to separate them by the spiritual sword of the word of God. He thus shows what follows preaching. At faith in Christ the whole world was divided against itself, because every household had both unbelievers and believers. Thus a good war was sent, so that an evil peace might be broken. [Bede.] Something similar is read in Genesis concerning those who wished to build the tower: God divided their languages (Gen. 11). Hence David: “Scatter the nations that desire wars” (Ps. 67). Hence [Col. 0165B] Isaiah: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a cloud and enter Egypt; and Egypt’s idols shall be moved at his presence, and he shall set Egyptians against Egyptians” (Isa. 19): the former, plainly, fighting for the faith, the latter against it.

L.

For from this time five in one house will be divided, three against two, and two against three.

M.

For I came to separate a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are those of his own household.

“Against two and against three” means against two and against three. The mother of the son is the mother-in-law of his wife, and [Col. 0165C] thus the same woman is divided against her daughter, who is her daughter-in-law. Allegorically, the three belong to those who keep faith in the Trinity; the two suit those who do not attain to completeness of faith. Therefore the good and the evil, thinking and acting contrary to one another, are divided from each other. Our father was the devil, because we imitated him; but the sword of God’s word came, which separated us from him and showed us another Father, who is in heaven. The Synagogue is the mother, whose firstborn daughter is the Church; between them there was great opposition. The same Synagogue was mother-in-law, and the Church from the Gentiles was daughter-in-law, because Christ, the bridegroom of the Church, is according to the flesh the Synagogue’s son. Therefore the Synagogue is divided against daughter-in-law and daughter, because it persecutes believers from each people [Col. 0165D].

M. 96[V] L. 182

Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me. And whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me, L. nor can he be my disciple.

[Jerome.] No one ought to prefer filial affection to religion. It is read in the Song: “He set love in order within me” (Song 2). The right order is to love father and friends after God. But if necessity requires that both cannot be preserved, hatred toward one’s own is devotion toward God. By “cross” he means the ardour of faith. The cross is so called from torment, and it must always be carried, so that love for Christ may be shown. [Col. 0166A] [Bede.] We carry the Lord’s cross in two ways: either when we afflict the flesh through abstinence, or when, out of compassion for a neighbour, we account that person’s need as our own. But because one who mortifies the flesh for empty glory does not follow the Lord, nor one who has carnal compassion on a neighbour so as to favour sin, the words “and follows me” were added.

M. 97[II] L. 211 A. 105

Whoever finds his life shall lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake shall find it.

Whoever finds his life by preserving it for the present through denying me shall lose it eternally. But whoever, setting all things aside for [Col. 0166B] love of me, is ready to lose life here, undergoing temporal death for my sake, shall find it safe in the world to come.

M. 99[I] R. 96 L. 116 A. 120

And whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.

[Hilary.] Because Christ is in the apostles, and God is in Christ, whoever receives the apostles receives God. He says this lest the reception of the apostles be considered contemptible by those from whom he had said above that they ought to receive support.

M. 99[X]

Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward. And whoever receives a righteous man in the name [Col. 0166C] of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward.

[Jerome.] Jews, understanding the prophets carnally, do not receive the prophets’ reward. Alternatively: in every profession tares are mixed with wheat. Therefore we ought to receive both false prophets and Judas the traitor, and supply them with food. In providing for this, the Lord says here that persons are not to be received but names; and those who receive do not lose their reward, even if the person received is unworthy. By “righteous man” he means any worthy preacher. He will deservedly receive a prophet’s and righteous man’s reward who, by supporting some people lest they fail through want, establishes them for himself as labourers in prophecy and in works of righteousness.

[Col. 0166D] M. 100[VI] R. 98

And whoever gives one of these little ones only a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple, R. because you belong to Christ: M. R. Amen, I say to you, he shall not lose his reward.

[Jerome.] He excludes an excuse based on poverty, lest someone plead lack of means, saying that because he has nothing with which to heat water, he cannot give it; let him at least give cold water to one asking for God’s sake. Therefore, just as he announced the danger of those who do not receive them by the testimony of shaken-off dust, so he commends, beyond expectation, the merit of those who receive them with good intention.

[Col. 0165] End of the First Book.

## SECOND BOOK

[Col. 0167]

## CHAPTER XLV

[Col. 0167A]

M. 101[X]

And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished giving commands to his twelve disciples, that he departed from there to teach and preach in their towns.

He calls those towns the disciples’ towns in which they had either been born or educated. Therefore, preaching to Jews, not Samaritans or Gentiles, he did what he had taught: in accordance with the promises, the opportunity of salvation was first to be offered to the Jews.

R. 56[VIII] L. 89

And going out, the disciples preached that people should repent; and they cast out many demons, and anointed many sick persons with oil, and healed them.

[Col. 0167B] [Bede.] James says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him call in the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the Lord’s name; and if he is in sins, they shall be forgiven him” (Jas. 5). It is therefore evident that this practice of the holy Church was handed down by the apostles themselves: sick persons are anointed with oil consecrated by episcopal blessing. Thus the visible anointing is the sacrament; but the reality of the sacrament is forgiveness, bestowed upon the soul through the spiritual anointing of grace.

A. 81[X]

And a wedding took place at Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. Jesus and his disciples were also invited to the wedding.

The Lord wished by his presence and also by a miracle [Col. 0167C] to commend marriage, lest heretics presume to condemn it.

[Albinus.] Mystically: through the desire of the fathers who preceded the Law, under the Law the bridegroom was called to come to the Church, his bride; and he came in the grace of the Gospel. The disciples too were called, as ministers at the wedding.

[Augustine.] The bridegroom joined this bride to himself in the virgin’s womb. For the Word is the bridegroom, and human flesh is the bride.

[Albinus.] At Cana of Galilee—that is, in the zeal of migration—the wedding takes place. For those are worthy of Christ who, in the fervour of devotion, migrate from vices to virtues, from earth to heaven.

And when the wine failed, Jesus’ mother said to him: “They have no wine.” [Col. 0167D]

As though she said, “Give them wine.” The wine failed because the spiritual understanding of the Law had begun to lie hidden beneath the deceptive exposition of the Pharisees.

And Jesus said to her: “What is that to me and to you, woman? My hour has not yet come.”

What do you, my mother according to the flesh, and I, the eternal power and wisdom of God—from which will come the miracle you request—have in common? My hour will come: that is, the fitting time for my passion, when indeed [Col. 0168A] the weakness of which you are mother begins to hang upon the cross; then I shall acknowledge you as my mother, as a son, entrusting your care to a disciple. But after the Gospel had been preached and divine power shown to the world, the hour of the passion came: not an hour of necessity, as heretics maliciously allege, but of will. Hence: “I have power to lay down my life and to take it up again” (John 10). For the author of times is not governed by the fate of time.

His mother said to the servants: “Whatever he tells you, do it.” Now there were six stone water-jars standing there for the Jews’ purification, each holding two or three measures.

Confident in her son’s kindness toward her, that what she asks will be done, his mother confidently commands the servants. *Hydor* is Greek for “water,” whence *hydria*, “a water-vessel.” He calls it the Jews’ purification because they frequently washed hands and vessels. *Metron* in Greek means “measure,” whence *metreta*, the name of a measure.

Jesus said to them: “Fill the water-jars with water.” And they filled them to the brim. Then Jesus said to them: “Draw some now and take it to the master of the feast.” And they took it.

[Col. 0168B] The *architriclinus* is the chief of the triclinium, that is, of those reclining in the dining hall. A *triclinium*, they say, is a hall divided into three rooms, or three houses or chambers made with a vaulted roof, in which the reclining diners sat, as if beneath three arches.

When the master of the feast tasted the water made wine, and did not know where it came from—though the servants who had drawn the water knew—the master of the feast called the bridegroom and said to him: “Everyone first serves the good wine, and when they have become drunk, then that which is inferior. But you have kept the good wine until now.” Jesus performed this beginning of signs at Cana of Galilee and revealed his glory.

Among the many signs Jesus performed at Cana of Galilee, this was the first; and by the singular dignity of transforming the elements he revealed his glory, that is, his hidden deity. [Augustine.] We marvel at water changed into wine, but do not marvel that every year God does this in vines, making many things from one grain; and, what is greater, he created heaven and earth from nothing and governs them wonderfully.

Therefore, because people, attentive to other things, had lost consideration of the Lord’s works, in which [Col. 0168D] they ought daily to praise him, God reserved for himself certain unusual things to do, that by wonders he might awaken people, as though sleeping, to worship him. Jesus changes water into wine when he imbues the tasteless mind of carnal people with the flavour of heavenly knowledge. For we were water, that is, without wisdom; and he made us wine, that is, wise through faith in him. [Albinus.] Or water signifies knowledge, cleansing hearers from the stains of sins. It is changed into wine when someone wholly forgets past evils, so as not to fall again [Col. 0169A] into them, and begins to grow warm in God’s love; for wine, when it intoxicates, makes drinkers forgetful and warms them. Christ changed water into wine when he showed that things which appeared carnal in the Law were spiritual, and made the surface of the letter appear full of heavenly power. For Christ, not yet manifested in the prophecies, lay hidden like wine in water; but when he opened his disciples’ understanding that they might understand the Scriptures, Christ himself, revealed in the Law and prophets, was intoxicating wine. Thus, while Christ lies hidden in Scripture beneath the veil—that is, the covering—of the letter, it tastes like insipid water. But when the veil is removed, it is intoxicating wine.

The six water-jars are the six ages. They would run their course in vain unless Christ were preached in them. The first age is from Adam to Noah; the second to Abraham; the third to David; the fourth to the Exile; the fifth to John the Baptist; the sixth from there to the end of the age. Let us see how prophecy in each age, as though water without flavour in the jars according to the letter, is changed into wine when referred to Christ and to all nations. Whatever was prefigured in Adam concerning Christ belonged to all nations, as in Genesis: “A man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2). Christ cleaved to the Church, that they might be two in one flesh; and he left the Father, not appearing to people in that form in which he is equal to the Father. He left his mother when he passed from the Synagogue to the Church. The Lord could have removed a rib from waking Adam without pain; but undoubtedly Christ’s sleep upon the cross was signified in this, for from his side the sacraments of the Church flowed forth as from a bride. [Col. 0169C]

Let us drink wine from the other jars. Christ was prefigured in Noah. For this reason every kind of animal was enclosed in the ark (Gen. 7): that all nations to be saved through Christ might be signified. God did not lack the power to create anew every kind of animal; but they were saved through wood because we too were to be saved through wood. In the third jar Abraham heard: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22). Who does not see whom his only son prefigured, carrying the wood for the sacrifice to which he was being led to be offered? For the Lord carried his own cross. In the fourth jar David says: “Rise up, O God; judge the earth, for you shall inherit among all nations” (Ps. 81). It is as though he were told: “You slept, judged by the earth; rise up, that you may judge the earth.” In the fifth age Daniel saw a stone cut from a mountain without hands, which broke all the kingdoms of the earth; that stone grew and became a great mountain, so that it filled the whole face of the earth (Dan. 1). From what mountain was it cut, if not from the kingdom of the Jews, from which Christ was born according to the flesh without human action, because without marital embrace? To the sixth age belongs John the Baptist, saying: “Do not say, ‘We have Abraham as our father’; God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. 3). By “stones” he means the Gentiles, not because of firmness but because of the hardness of their foolishness, [Col. 0170A] while they worshipped idols and became like them. Hence: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. 113).

[Albinus.] Likewise, the six water-jars are the perfect hearts of the saints, prepared in these ages as receptacles of God’s Scriptures, set forth as an example for living and believing. They are stone, that is, strong in Christ the stone. “For the Jews’ purification” is said because the Law was given only to the Jewish people, whereas grace through Christ was bestowed upon all (John 1). Therefore it was not said that some held two measures and others three, but two or three, so that the same ones called two might be called three. There are two measures in Scripture when Father and Son are named, but the Spirit—who is understood to be the Father’s and the Son’s—is there also; as in: “You made all things in wisdom,” that is, in the Son (Ps. 103). There are three measures [Col. 0170B] when, with the Holy Spirit named, the Trinity is more clearly understood; as in: “Baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). Alternatively, the two or three measures are all nations, to whom the Scriptures belong: two on account of uncircumcision and circumcision; three because they were dispersed from Noah’s three sons. That the jars were filled at the Lord’s command signifies that the Old Scripture is from him.

[Albinus.] One who creates all things from nothing could have filled empty jars with wine; but he preferred to make wine from water, so as to teach that he came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it, and in the Gospel to do or teach what prophecy had foretold. The water-jars are filled to the top because no age was empty of saving teaching. By the master of the feast are understood leaders skilled in Scripture, which contains histories, moral teachings, and allegories. Therefore, when the word of the Gospel is offered to one such as Nicodemus, Gamaliel, or Saul his disciple, wine made from water is served to the master of the feast. Some, however, understand the water as John’s baptism and the wine as Christ’s passion. Thus wine is first brought to the master of the feast—that is, to John himself, who drank the passion before Christ.

[Albinus.] The triclinium, that is, the three orders of persons reclining at the wedding, distinct from one another in rank, signifies the three orders of believers in the Church: the married, the continent, and the teachers. And because it is the teachers’ office to prefer the Gospel’s grace to ancient institutions, the master of the feast, when he had called the bridegroom, said that the good wine had been kept. But the statement that he did not know where it came from [Col. 0170D] must be understood thus: Christ’s disciples, who had drawn the water by wisely understanding and faithfully expounding the Old Scripture, proclaimed the Gospel to many skilled in the Law according to the letter. “Everyone first serves the good wine” was said literally, according to many people’s custom. Mystically, the man—that is, the carnal man—drinks worse wine after good: he descends from true things to false. But the spiritual person is daily intoxicated by the invisible wine first washed in the Scriptures, and progresses.

[Maxim.] Bishop Maximus, in his sermon *On the Epiphany*, which begins, “Many things, brethren,” says: “As faithful antiquity handed down to its posterity, today the Saviour was worshipped by the Chaldeans; today he consecrated the flowing waters of the Jordan by the blessing of his own baptism; today, invited to a wedding, he changed water into wine.”

## CHAPTER XLVI

M. 63[II] R. 18 L. 33

But when he had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. And behold, a leper came, bent the knee, and worshipped him, saying: “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me.”

[Jerome.] Miracles rightly follow teaching, so that the word may be confirmed by power. [Bede.] According to Mark the leper bends the knee; as Luke says, he fell upon his face. This belongs to humility and shame: each person ought to blush at the stains of his life; shame does not suppress confession, but, with the wound exposed, seeks a remedy. The leper attributes the power of healing to the Lord’s will. Nor does he doubt as an unbeliever; but, conscious of his own foulness, he does not presume to say, “Cleanse me, Lord, and I shall be cleansed.” Since one excluded from the Law asks to be healed by the Lord’s power, he indicates that grace is above the Law. For as authority of power is displayed in the Lord, so steadfastness of faith is shown in this man. [Col. 0171B]

And Jesus stretched out his hand, touched him, and said: “I will; be cleansed.” And immediately his leprosy was cleansed.

Stretching out his hand in mercy, he touched him in humility, teaching us to despise no one because of bodily defilement. The Law forbids touching lepers, but it was not forbidden to him who is Lord of the Law. Therefore he touched him, not because he could not heal without touch, but in order to show that he was not under the Law—indeed, that he was Lord of the Law—who did not fear contagion, since he rather frees others from it. In compassion he said, “I will,” healing in the manner in which he had been asked. Since it had been said, “If you will, you can cleanse me,” he added the command, “Be cleansed,” in which the power of majesty is disclosed. For there is nothing intermediate between God’s work and his command, since among his commands is the work itself. For he said, and they were made (Ps. 32). [Col. 0171C]

And Jesus said to him: “See that you tell no one; but go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.”

There was no need for him to proclaim by speech what he displayed in his body. The Lord taught that our good deeds should not be publicized but concealed, so that we may abstain not only from the reward of money but also from that of praise. Avoiding boastfulness prevents leprosy from passing to the physician. [Hilary.] Silence is commanded also because it is better to seek salvation through more spontaneous faith than to be invited by benefits. [Bede.] The leper is commanded to show himself to the priest, that the priest might understand that he was healed not by the order of the Law but by God’s grace. He is commanded to offer a sacrifice, to show that the Lord came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it, walking according to the Law and healing above the Law. For the Law commanded that those cleansed from leprosy should offer gifts to the priests; therefore he humbly sends him to them.

Bede—Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels.* Significant sacrifices ought not to have been removed before the true sacrifices prefigured in them had been confirmed in Christ and the Church by the testimony of the apostles and the faith of believers. The offering is made as testimony to those who see the leper cleansed: if they believe, they are saved from the leprosy of sins and offer themselves to God; but if they do not believe, they shall be without excuse. [Hilary.] Or thus: he offers the gift which Moses commanded to be offered to them, namely the priests, as a testimony—that is, as a sign of a spiritual offering. As the healing of leprosy testifies to the healing of sin, so he offers that gift, I say, not only in sign but also in reality, so that you yourself, cleansed from the filth of sin, may become God’s sacrifice. For Moses commanded a testimony whose effect you bear in yourself. [Bede.] No definite place is specified where the leper was cleansed, in order to show [Col. 0172B] that not merely one people of some particular city, but the peoples of many cities, were healed. Since the leper typically signifies the human race sick with sins, he is rightly described in Luke as full of leprosy. For all have sinned and lack the grace of God (Rom. 3). The stretching out of the hand signifies the Saviour’s incarnation, extended for the salvation of all human beings. Hence elsewhere: “You are already clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” (John 15). Christ himself is priest forever (Ps. 109); all who have been cleansed from the manifold character of ancient error ought to show themselves to him, confessing that they are his temple, and offer their bodies to him as a living sacrifice (Rom. 12).

[Col. 0172C] R. 19[X]

But when he had gone out, he began to proclaim and spread abroad the report, so that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town, but stayed outside in deserted places; and people came to him from every quarter.

[Bede on Mark.] Jesus said, “Tell no one”; but he, performing an evangelist’s office, immediately went out and began to preach, teaching that he had been healed inwardly and outwardly, so that his salvation drew many to the Lord. This was done as an example of teaching: although the elect should in their intention desire to remain hidden in the great things they do, which belongs to humility, they are, despite themselves, revealed so that they may profit others, which belongs to great sublimity, when their works cannot be kept silent even if they wish it. [Jerome on Mark.] In avoiding towns, the Lord flees the tumultuous minds of carnal people and visits those secluded from worldly cares. Therefore the Lord’s glory shall be revealed to those who come together from every side—that is, by level and difficult ways—whom nothing can separate from Christ’s love. [Col. 0172D]

## CHAPTER XLVII

M. 64[II] L. 65 A. 37

When Jesus had entered Capernaum, a centurion came to him, entreating him and saying: “Lord, my servant lies at home paralysed and grievously tormented.”

[Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists.*] It is not contradictory that Luke says he sent the elders of the Jews to Jesus with this request, since we commonly gain access to someone through a friend. Nevertheless, Matthew’s mystical wording must also be carefully considered, according to which it is written in the psalm: “Draw near to him and be enlightened” (Ps. 33). Thus the centurion came by faith. Yet it may be said that he also came bodily; and that he entrusted his message to the Jewish elders, as Christ’s acquaintances, as Luke explains, as is usually done before persons of power. [Col. 0173A] [Rabanus.] The paralytic lies ill, tormented by an acute suffering. He expresses this in such a way as to indicate both the distress of his own soul and to move Christ to mercy. From this let us learn compassion for servants. As Luke says, the servant was about to die, had he not been restored to life by his master’s faith and Christ’s compassion, as King Hezekiah, to whom the Lord added fifteen years (Isa. 38).

Jesus said to him: “I will come and heal him.”

[Col. 0173B] He refused to go to heal the royal official’s son, lest he seem to have honoured wealth; he consented to go to a servant, lest he seem to have despised servile condition. But on the way he healed him by a word, lest he be thought to go through inability rather than humility.

And the centurion answered: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only speak the word, and my servant shall be healed. For I too am a man under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”

Because he was conscious of his Gentile life, he feared burdening the Lord. The Lord saw the centurion’s faith, humility, and discernment: faith, because as a Gentile he believed; humility, because he judged himself unworthy for the Lord to enter under his roof; discernment, because he recognized divinity veiled by a body. In this discernment he also said, “I am a man and send men,” knowing that the Lord could send angels. Hence follows:

When Jesus heard this, he marvelled, and said to those following him: “Amen, I say to you, I have not found such faith in Israel.”

[Bede.] Jesus’ marvel signifies that we ought to marvel. When such emotions are predicated of God, they are not indications of a disturbed mind, but of a teacher instructing. [Jerome.] He says concerning those then present: “I have not found such faith in Israel,” not concerning the patriarchs and prophets—unless perhaps, in the centurion, the faith of the Gentiles is set above Israel. [Bede.] The centurion’s faith is preferred to those present because they had been taught by the admonitions of the Law and prophets, whereas he believed voluntarily with no one teaching him. [Col. 0173D]

M. 61[V] L. 172

But I tell you that many shall come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; but the children of the kingdom shall be cast into outer darkness. There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Not only this Gentile centurion rightly believes in God, but many Gentiles will yet come to right belief. [Jerome.] He speaks of the nations that will believe: many will come and rest, feasting happily. By the children of the kingdom he means the Jews, among whom God previously reigned. Darkness is always inward, [Col. 0174A] not outward; but it is called outer because the person whom the Lord expels outside has left the light. In saying “weeping and gnashing of teeth,” he shows a true resurrection, since weeping belongs to the eyes and teeth are bones.

M. 66[V] L. 66

And Jesus said to the centurion: “Go; and as you have believed, so be it done for you.” And the servant was healed in that hour. And the centurion returned to his house and found the servant who had been sick well.

The Lord’s merit comes to the servant’s aid. Let us understand that the centurion at last came bodily to the Lord and returned home with those who had been sent, when the Lord said to him, “Go”; or let it be understood that, just as he approached through messengers, so he returned through messengers. [Col. 0174B] [Bede.] In divine providence Jews were sent, so that, having seen the miracle and the Gentile man’s faith, they might be without excuse if they did not believe. The elders intercede with the Lord for the centurion, and the saints for us. The centurion’s soldiers may be understood as natural virtues, which many bring with them when they come to the Lord. Of Cornelius the centurion it is said in praise that he was “a righteous [devout] man, fearing God with all his household, giving many alms to the people, and praying to God always” (Acts 10). Those who do not use these virtues rightly are by no means worthy of God’s visitation. The centurion signifies the elect from the Gentiles, who, as though surrounded by a hundred soldiers, are exalted by the perfection of spiritual virtues and seek for themselves and their own only the joys of eternal salvation. For the number one hundred, which is transferred from the left to the right, signifies heavenly life. Hence Noah’s ark was built in a hundred years (Gen. 6); Abraham at a hundred received the son of promise; Isaac sowed and found a hundredfold in that same year (Gen. 26); the court of the tabernacle was a hundred cubits long (Exod. 27); and in the hundredth psalm mercy and judgement are sung to the Lord (Ps. 100). [Col. 0174C]

## CHAPTER XLVIII

M. 67[II] R. 15 L. 26

And when Jesus came into Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying sick with fever; and he touched her hand, and the fever left her; and she rose and ministered to them.

[Jerome.] It is human nature to be weak after fevers; but health bestowed by the Lord gave Peter’s mother-in-law strength to minister. Luke: “They asked him concerning her” (Luke 4). [Bede.] At times the Saviour heals the sick when asked, at times of his own accord, showing both that he yields to believers’ prayers against the sufferings of sins and that he forgives those things which people least understand in themselves. Hence the Psalmist says: “Who understands transgressions? Cleanse me, O Lord, from hidden faults” (Ps. 18). Morally, the woman healed from fevers signifies the flesh restrained from the heat of desire by the precepts of continence, so that members which had served uncleanness may serve righteousness. [Rabanus.] Allegorically, Peter’s house is the circumcision entrusted to his apostolate; the mother-in-law is the synagogue, which is in some manner the mother of the Church [Col. 0175A] entrusted to Peter. It has a fever because it labours under the burning heat of envy while persecuting the Church. The Lord touches its hand when he converts its carnal works to spiritual use; and thus raised up, it ministers in the Spirit.

## CHAPTER XLIX

L. 67[X]

And it came to pass afterward that he went into a city called Nain; and his disciples and a large crowd went with him. And when he approached the gate of the city, behold, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother; and she was a widow, and a large crowd from the city was with her.

[Bede.] Nain is a city of Galilee. The dead man carried out before many people beyond the gate signifies one sinning criminally and revealing his sin to many people’s knowledge through words and deeds, as through the gates of his city. He is rightly called his mother’s only son because, although Mother Church has many children, good and bad, the evil are nevertheless regarded as one person in respect of their wickedness; just as the good are regarded as one person in respect of goodness. Any one of the elect, when instructed in faith, is a son; when instructing others, is a mother. Hence Paul: “My little children, for whom I am again in labour” (Gal. 4). Therefore, when the good unanimously endeavour to recall the evil, the good are called mother and the evil an only son. The gate of the city through which the dead man is carried out is one of the senses through which a person falls into sin: for example, one who sees in order to lust; one who gives an ear to idle or shameful hearing; one who lends the tongue to quarrels; and all others who do not guard their senses open for themselves the entrances of death. Everyone who remembers that the Church was redeemed by the death of her bridegroom recognizes her as a widow. There were many witnesses to this miracle, that many might become praisers of God. [Col. 0175C]

When the Lord saw her, moved by compassion for her, he said to her: “Do not weep.”

The evangelist beautifully testifies that the Lord was first moved by compassion for the mother and then raised her son, so that in the one act he might give us an example of piety to imitate, and in the other establish faith in his wondrous power.

And he approached and touched the bier; and those who carried it stood still.

[Col. 0175D] The bier in which the dead man was carried out is the wrongly secure conscience of a desperate sinner. Those who carry him to burial are either unclean desires that snatch a person away to destruction, or the poisonous flatteries of those who flatter, which bury sinners as though under a mound of earth. When the Lord touches the bier, the bearers of the funeral stand still, because conscience, touched by fear of the heavenly judgement, returns to itself, restraining carnal pleasures and unjust praisers.

And he said: “Young man, I say to you, arise.” And he who was dead sat up and began to speak; and he gave him to his mother.

The one who was dead sits up when the sinner comes to life through inward compunction. He begins to speak when he shows that he is returning to true life. He is restored to his mother when, [Col. 0176A] through priestly judgement, he is joined to the Church’s communion.

And fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying: “A great prophet has arisen among us,” and, “God has visited his people.”

All were magnifying, that is, praising God; for the more serious the fall, the more welcome is the mercy of the one who raises up, and the more certain is the hope of salvation for penitents. God has visited his people, both when he determined once for all that his Word should be incarnate, and when he daily sends the Holy Spirit into our hearts so that we may be raised up.

## CHAPTER L

L. 68[X]

And this report concerning him went out through all Judaea [Col. 0176B] and throughout all the surrounding country.

[AMBROSE.] That is, throughout all the country around Judaea. Allegorically, Jesus’ approach to the gate of the city signified that the Word, having become flesh, led the Gentile people through the gates of faith into the heavenly Jerusalem. Behold, the younger Jewish people, dead through unbelief, are carried out; their mother, the Church, possessing nothing in the world as though it were her own, surrounded by great crowds of peoples, weeps for them in pious affection and labours to restore them to life. This she obtains both meanwhile in the conversion of a few Jews and finally in their fullness. The bier on which he is carried is the human body; those who carry it are evil habits which draw toward death. But Jesus touches the bier when he raises frail nature upon the cross. Or the place of the dead man is touched by [Col. 0176C] God—that is, the wood of the cross—because man perished through the wood of Paradise. The bearers of the dead man are the four elements, whose imbalance is an incitement to sin in man. The bearers stand still because they can no longer draw him toward death as they did before. Jesus’ speaking is the pouring in of counsels of salvation; thus the sick person is raised to life by good works and is so restored to Mother Church. All are afraid, because many are corrected by the example of one.

M. 67[II] R. 15 L. 26

[Here some begin Chapter L.] Now when evening came, they brought to him many possessed by demons; and he cast out the spirits by a word, and healed all who were ill, so that what had been spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: “He took our infirmities and bore our diseases” (Isa. 53).

[JEROME.] Now when evening came, the sick are healed when, that is, the grain of wheat dies in the earth. The setting of the sun, which Luke mentions, signifies the death of him who said: “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world” (John 12). More sick people are healed after Christ’s death than before, because, having trampled down the kingdom of death, he sent the gifts of faith throughout the world through his ministers. Hence the Psalmist sings: “Make a way for him who ascends above the setting” (Ps. 67). The Lord ascends above the setting because from that in which he set in the Passion, he will reveal his greater glory by rising again. [RABANUS.] In the literal sense, according to the present passage, he took lesser infirmities—that is, removed them by healing [Col. 0177A] them—and bore long-standing diseases, removing them as though by carrying them away. Mystically, he took our infirmities on the cross and bore our diseases, because he endured suffering for our lesser and greater sins.

But Jesus, seeing many crowds around him, ordered them to depart across the sea.

## CHAPTER LI

M. 68[V] L. 105

And one scribe came up and said to him: “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.” And Jesus said to him: “Foxes have dens and birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.”

[JEROME.] This scribe of the Law, who knew only the letter [Col. 0177B], was not a spiritual hearer of the Lord; rather, he thought him one of the more learned teachers, and therefore there was no place where the Lord might lay his head. He was crafty, certainly, not simple and humble, one in whom the Godhead might dwell in a familiar abode. He was rejected for this reason: seeing the greatness of the signs, he wished to follow the Saviour in order to seek profit from miracles, like Simon Magus (Acts 8). He is therefore rightly condemned by the Lord, as though he were saying: “Why do you wish to follow me for riches, when I am so poor that I do not even have lodging?” [BEDE.] Or, moved by miracles, he wished to follow for empty display, which the birds signify; and he feigned that he would render a disciple’s service, and this pretence is figured by the fox. [ALBINUS.] For the fox is a deceitful animal [Col. 0177C], intent upon ambushes, practising the robberies of fraud, and dwelling in dens even among human habitations. So too the heretic, having no house of faith, draws others into his fraud and seduces them from the faith.

But he said to another: “Follow me.” And he said: “Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father.”

[BEDE.] The former calls him Teacher; this man calls him Lord. He does not reject discipleship, but desires, out of filial devotion, to bury his father; he is worthy of one in whom Christ may lay his head—that is, in whom divinity may dwell. Or the laying down of the head signifies Christ’s humility, which had a place in this man, not in that pretender and proud man.

But Jesus said to him: “Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead. But go and proclaim [Col. 0177D] the kingdom of God.”

The Lord teaches us that lesser goods are to be set aside for the usefulness of greater ones. For it is a greater good to preach than to bury one’s father. He who buries his father hides flesh in the earth; but he who preaches raises the dead to life. [JEROME.] Dead is the one who does not believe. Therefore we must beware lest, while we are concerned about the dead, we too die. [ALBINUS.] The Lord rejected the deceitful man and chose the innocent one; but the man whose father he knew to be dead—that father of whom it is said: “Forget the house of your father” (Ps. 44). Mystically, the disciple was not recalled from the duty owed his father, but the faithful person is separated from communion with the unbelieving, whose throat [Col. 0178A] “is an open grave” (Ps. 15); such also was the heretic, compared to foxes and birds. There is a burial proper to the righteous, of which it is said: “For in pouring this ointment upon my body, she has done it for my burial” (Matt. 26). Therefore, one who buries Christ within himself by good faith, so that he may rise with him, must by no means bury within himself the unbelief of the devil. [GREGORY.] The dead bury the dead when sinners flatter and soothe those like themselves, and crush them beneath the heaped-up weight of utterly evil flattery.

L. 106[X]

And another said: “I will follow you, Lord; but first permit me to take leave of those who are at home.” Jesus said to him: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and [Col. 0178B] looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”

[BEDE.] If a disciple intending to follow the Lord is reproved for taking leave of his household, what will become of those who, for no useful purpose, do not fear to revisit the home they had left? To put one’s hand to the plough is to break up the hardness of one’s heart, as with an instrument of compunction—the wood and iron of the Lord’s Passion—and to open it for the production of the fruits of good works. But if anyone, having begun to cultivate, delights with Lot’s wife in looking back at abandoned vices (Gen. 19), he is deprived of the reward of the kingdom to come.

## CHAPTER LII

M. 69[II] R. 47 L. 83

And when he went up into the boat, his disciples followed him. And behold, a great storm arose on [Col. 0178C] the sea, so that the boat was covered by the waves. But he was asleep in the stern upon a cushion.

A cushion is called either a small pillow or any other thing placed beneath the neck of one reclining to sleep. The boat seemed to be covered and filled by the waves; therefore fear disturbed the disciples all the more.

And they came and woke him, saying: “Lord, save us, for we are perishing.” And he said to them: “Why are you afraid, you of little faith?” Then, rising, he commanded the wind and sea, and said: “Be silent and be still”; and there was a great calm.

Although the evangelists recount it in differing words, the sense is one, and the whole may have been said. He rebukes the wind and the sea, concerning which it is said: “You rule over the power [Col. 0178D] of the sea” (Ps. 88). He commanded them not in the error of heretics, who think all things living, but with the majesty by which they are perceptible to God. [JEROME.] We read a type of this sign in Jonah: while the others are in danger, the Lord is secure and sleeps; he is awakened, and by the command and mystery of his Passion delivers those who awaken him. Thus he deigned to show both natures in his own person: sleeping as man, restraining the sea as God.

Moreover, the people marvelled and said to one another: “Who or what kind of man is this, that he commands even winds and sea, and they obey him?”

They are rightly called people, whoever had not yet known the Saviour’s power, whether they are understood as sailors, or others who were in the boat, or even the disciples themselves. [Col. 0179A] Allegorically, the sea is understood as the surge of this age. The boat is the tree of the Passion, by whose help the faithful transcend the waves of the world and arrive at the shore of the heavenly homeland. That the disciples go up into the boat with the Lord is explained elsewhere when he says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke 9). As the disciples sail, Christ sleeps, because, while the faithful, in hope of eternal rest, tread down the world and eagerly cast its pomp behind their backs, the time of the Lord’s Passion comes. Hence Mark reports that this happened in the evening, so that not only the Lord’s sleep but even the hour itself might signify the setting of the true sun. When he ascends the stern of the cross to take the sleep of death, [Col. 0179B] waves of blasphemers, stirred up by demonic storms, arise. [JEROME, On Mark.] His patience is not troubled by them, but the disciples’ weakness is endangered. The stern covers the living with dead skins, keeps off the waves, and is strengthened with wood: these indicate that the Church is saved in the Lord’s cross and death. Understand the cushion as the body, upon which the divinity, like a head bending down, reclines. [BEDE.] The disciples awaken the Lord lest they perish, because with the greatest longing they sought the resurrection. The Lord, rising, rebuked the wind because he cast down the devil’s pride when he destroyed his dominion. He caused the storm of water to cease because he checked the rage of those crying, “If he is the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Matt. 27). Those who were afraid while Christ was present are rightly reproved; hence after [Col. 0179C] the resurrection some of them also heard: “O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken” (Luke 24). The Lord also often seems to sleep while we sail amid the roar of the sea: when, amid efforts after virtues, through the frequent assault of unclean spirits, wicked people, or thoughts, the brightness of faith is darkened, the height of hope wastes away, and the flame of love grows cold. But then it is necessary to have recourse to God, so that he may restore us to calm and grant us the harbour of salvation.

## CHAPTER LIII

And when he had crossed the sea into the region of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee, and had come ashore, two men possessed by demons met him [Col. 0179D] as they came out of the tombs, exceedingly fierce, so that no one could pass along that road.

[AUGUSTINE, On the Harmony of the Evangelists.] Gerasa is a city of Arabia beyond the Jordan, adjoining Mount Gilead in the tribe of Manasseh, not far from the Lake of Tiberias, into which the swine were cast headlong. Matthew records that two met him, Mark and Luke that one did; because one of them was of more notable person and greater madness, and therefore his healing was more famous.

For one had had demons for a long time, and did not wear clothing; nor did he remain in a house, but among tombs. No one could any longer bind him even with chains, because he had often been bound with fetters and chains, but had broken the chains and shattered the fetters [Col. 0180A]; and no one could tame him. Always, night and day, he was in the mountains, crying out and cutting himself with stones. But seeing Jesus from afar, he ran and worshipped him; and crying in a loud voice, he said: “What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? Have you come to torment us before the time?” For Jesus was saying to him: “Come out, unclean spirit.”

[BEDE.] The Jews say that he casts out demons by the prince of demons; the demons deny that they have anything in common with him, because there is no peace or fellowship between them and him. [JEROME.] Arius maintains that he is a creature, whom the demon confesses to be the Son of God. Yet this is not a confession of the will, followed by the reward of confession, but a compulsion of necessity forcing the unwilling. The Saviour’s presence is torment [Col. 0180B] to demons; and it is a great torment for them to cease from harming a human being. They depart all the more grievously the longer they have possessed him. Some ridiculously suppose that demons know the Son of God while the devil is ignorant of him, because they are retainers of less wickedness than he whose retainers they are; but both demons and the devil conjecture more that he is the Son of God than they know it.

“Tell me what your name is.” And he said: “Legion,” because many demons had entered into him.

He asks for the name not as though ignorant, but so that the healing power might appear more welcome through the confession. Even priests of our own time, who know how to cast out demons through the grace of exorcism, are accustomed to say that sufferers cannot otherwise be healed, unless, insofar as they are able to understand, they set forth in confession all that they have endured from unclean spirits, whether awake or asleep.

And they begged him not to drive them out of the region, and not to command them to go into the abyss.

The demons knew that they would one day be sent into the abyss, recalling the words of the prophets.

Now not far from them there was a large herd of swine feeding. And the demons begged him, saying: “If you cast us out, send us into the herd of swine.” And he said to them: “Go.” Then, going out, they went into the swine; and with great violence the herd, numbering about two thousand, rushed headlong into the sea, and they were drowned in the sea.

He permitted what they requested, so that the destruction of the swine [Col. 0180D] might be an occasion of salvation to people. Note that the unclean spirits could not enter even into swine without the Saviour’s permission, so that we may know that they are far less able by their own power to harm human beings. [AUGUSTINE.] There is no contradiction in Mark’s saying that the swine were around the mountain, while Luke says that they were on the mountain. For the herd was so large that part of it was on the mountain and part around it. Fearing the punishments due to them before the time, the demons ask to be sent into the swine, and are sent. Thus every sinner is himself the agent of his own punishment. Hence Isaiah says: “Enter into the flame which you have kindled for yourselves” (Isa. 50).

But those who fed them fled and reported everything in the city and in the countryside. And behold, the whole city came out to meet Jesus; and, seeing him, they found the man from whom the demons had gone out sitting [Col. 0181A] clothed and in his right mind at his feet. They were afraid and begged him to depart from their borders.

[JEROME.] Their request that he depart from their borders does not arise from pride but from humility, because they judged themselves unworthy of the Lord’s presence.

R. 48[VIII] L. 84

And when he went up into the boat, the man from whom the demons had gone out begged him to let him be with him. But he did not permit him; instead he said to him: “Go to your home, to your own people, and tell them how great things the Lord has done for you and how he has had mercy on you.” And he went away, proclaiming throughout the Decapolis how great things Jesus had done for him; and all marvelled.

[BEDE.] Mystically, Gerasa, or Gergesa as some [Col. 0181B] read it, is interpreted “casting out the settler” or “the stranger drawing near.” Therefore, after the sleep of the Passion and the glory of the Resurrection, the Lord comes through preachers into the region of the Gerasenes when he is preached to Jews and Gentiles. Both are Gerasenes, casting out the settler—that is, the devil—who dwelt in some through idolatry and in others through transgression of the Law. Thus those who were far off were made near in the blood of Christ and, by free choice, came to meet him in faith. They lived among tombs, not in a house, because they did not rest in their conscience but delighted in dead works—that is, sins. For the bodies of unbelievers are, as it were, tombs of the dead, in which the soul, dead through sins, is shut up. They were exceedingly fierce, because in the frenzy of desire they persisted against divine and human [Col. 0181C] laws, obstructing the way of faith so that no one might pass along it. This one man of greater madness represents the Gentile people, who for many times—that is, almost from the beginning of the world—were tormented by a demon and did not wear clothing because they had lost the covering of virtue, of which the first parents are read to have been stripped after their sin. This robe is offered to the returning son. The hard and heavy chains and fetters are the laws of the Gentiles, by which sins were restrained even in their commonwealth. When the chains were broken, as Luke writes, he was driven by the demon into desert places, because, having transgressed those laws, they were carried away by desire into crimes which exceeded even ordinary custom. The demoniac raged always by night and day, because whether the Gentile world [Col. 0181D] suffered adverse circumstances or prosperity smiled upon it, it did not know how to cast off the neck of its mind from the slavery of demons. Through the foulness of deeds it lay as though in tombs; through pride it wandered as though in mountains; and through the harshest words of unbelief it cut itself as though upon rocks. That many demons had entered the man signifies that the Gentile people had been enslaved to many cults of idolatry. In the destruction of the swine are indicated unclean people devoid of reason, who delight in muddy deeds upon the mountain of pride. Demons rule such people: for unless they lived like swine, the devil would not receive power over them to destroy them, though at times he receives it to test them. The herdsmen flee because [Col. 0182A] neither the philosophers of the Gentiles nor the leaders of the Synagogue can offer a remedy to those perishing; and although they flee the Christian law, they nevertheless proclaim its power by marvelling at miracles. The man seated at Jesus’ feet, clothed and in his right mind, signifies the faithful people healed from their former way of life, clothed with fitting reason, and, through the practice of virtues, following the footsteps of Christ and Christians. Seeing these things, they marvel and fear because they are unable to fulfil the Christian law. The healed man is sent home and preaches in the Decapolis. Thus, after remission of sins, let each person return to a good conscience and serve the Gospel for the salvation of others, so that afterward he may rest with Christ, lest, by wishing too hastily already to be with Christ, he neglect the ministry of preaching suited to the redemption of his brethren [Col. 0182B].

M. 70[I] R. 20 R. 37 A. 38

And going up into the boat, he crossed over and came to his own city.

Christ crosses over in the ship of the Church, ever to calm the surge of this age, so that he may bring those who believe in him by tranquil voyage to their heavenly homeland. Mark says that the Lord healed the paralytic in Capernaum; Matthew, in his own city. This question would be harder to solve if Matthew had named Nazareth. But now who doubts that Capernaum was the Lord’s city, which he made his own not by being born there but by making it illustrious with miracles? Finally, in [Col. 0182C] comparison with foreign [other] regions, any town of Galilee could rightly be called the Lord’s city, much more Capernaum, which so excelled in Galilee that it was regarded as a kind of metropolis.

## CHAPTER LIV

And behold, four men carrying on a bed a man who was paralysed sought to bring him in and place him before Jesus. But, unable to find a way to bring him in because of the crowd, they went up upon the roof and lowered him with the bed through the tiles into the midst before Jesus. When he saw their faith, he said: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you.”

He called the paralytic whom he healed “son,” not because of his own faith—for he was without sensation—but because of the faith of those offering him, and because his sins had been forgiven. Consider how much another’s faith avails, if it availed so greatly here. Therefore, let one burdened by sin call upon the Church to pray for him. Here we are given to understand that many bodily infirmities arise because of sins. Thus perhaps sins are first forgiven so that, when the causes of infirmity have been removed, health may be restored. Hence this paralytic is called “a man” in Luke, as though a sinner; and to the other paralytic at the pool it is said: “Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5). There are five different causes for which we are afflicted by bodily troubles in this life. Either the righteous are burdened with bodily weakness in order that their merits may increase through patience, as Job, Tobit, and the martyrs; or for the safeguarding of virtues, lest they become proud, as Paul says: “Lest I be exalted by the greatness of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (2 Cor. 11); or for the correction of sins, as Miriam, Aaron’s sister, was struck with leprosy in the wilderness because of her rash words (Num. 12), and as this paralytic was; or for the glory of God who saves, whether through himself or through his servants, as with the man born blind, who neither sinned nor did his parents, but was so afflicted that the works of God might be manifested in him (John 11), and Lazarus, whose illness was not unto death but that the Son of God might be glorified through it (John 11); or as the beginning of eternal condemnation, which is peculiar to the reprobate, as Antiochus and Herod, whose miserable afflictions showed what they would suffer forever in Gehenna [Col. 0183B] (2 Macc. 9). To these applies the prophet’s saying: “Crush them with a double destruction” (Jer. 17).

And the scribes and Pharisees began to think, saying: “Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins except God alone?”

The scribes speak truly, because he alone can forgive who also forgives through those to whom he grants the power of forgiving. They thought that the Lord blasphemed by arrogating to himself what belongs to God; but by revealing their thoughts, and by a visible sign—by which it is equally evident [the text is uncertain: “a visible [sign], by which it is equally evident”] that he has divine power, as it is to forgive sins—he shows himself to be God.

And when Jesus knew their thoughts, [Col. 0183C] he answered and said to them: “Why do you think evil things in your hearts? Which is easier to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? But that you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the paralytic—“I say to you: Rise, take up your bed, and go to your home.”

Whether the paralytic’s sins had been forgiven was known only to him who forgave them. But rising and walking was evident to all who saw. A visible sign is therefore performed to prove what is invisible. “Take up your bed,” so that what was evidence of infirmity may become proof of health. “But that you may know,” and so forth down to “he said to the paralytic,” are words of the evangelist, as though he were saying to the readers of the Gospel: “They murmured about his having said, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ but I tell you that he said to the paralytic, ‘Rise,’ so that through his healing you may know that the Son of Man then had and now has the power to forgive sins.” Or Christ’s words may be understood thus: “You think that I cannot forgive sins; but that you may know that the Son of Man—that is, I—can do this, he says”—that is, the Son of Man himself says to the paralytic—“Rise.”

And immediately, rising before them, he took up the bed on which he had been lying and went to his home, magnifying God. Amazement seized them all, and they magnified God; filled with fear, they said: “We have seen marvellous things today.” And they glorified God, who had given such power to human beings.

God’s great power is shown where healing is accomplished without delay at his command. Therefore those present, [Col. 0184A] abandoning blasphemies, rightly turn in astonishment to the praise of so great a majesty; nor would they be afraid if they believed soundly and loved perfectly. The healing of the paralytic signifies the salvation of a soul longing for Christ after the lethargy of fleshly enticement. It first needs ministers to offer it to Christ—that is, teachers to suggest the hope of intercession. Mark reports that there were four bearers, whether because the power of preaching is strengthened by the four Evangelists, or because the confidence of the mind is raised to obtain health by the four virtues, of which it is said in praise of eternal wisdom: “She teaches sobriety and wisdom, justice and virtue” (Wis. 8). Some call these prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice.
