When those wishing to offer the paralytic to Christ are blocked by the crowd [Col. 0184B], this is because the soul, often wishing after bodily sloth to be renewed by heavenly grace, is held back by an old habit of sins; often amid prayers and sweet converse with the Lord, a crowd of thoughts blocks the mind’s sight lest Christ be seen. Therefore the roof of the house in which Christ teaches must be ascended—that is, the loftiness of sacred Scripture must be sought, and the Law of the Lord meditated upon day and night (Ps. 1). When the roof has been opened, the sick man is lowered before Jesus, because through the mysteries of Scripture being unlocked one arrives at the knowledge of Christ. Jesus’ house is described as covered with tiles because beneath the lowly covering of the letters, if there is someone to unlock it, the power of divine spiritual grace is found. That he is lowered with the bed signifies that Christ must be known by a person still placed in this flesh [Col. 0184C]. To rise from the bed is for the soul to draw itself away from carnal things. Therefore he says: “Rise from the numbness of negligence, lift up for the exercise of good works the body in whose desires you lay, and so enter the home of eternal dwelling.” Or to go home is to return to inward self-guardianship, lest one sin again.

## CHAPTER LV

A. 36[X]

He came again, therefore, to Cana of Galilee, where he had made water into wine.

A. 36[III] M. 64 L. 65

And there was a certain royal official whose son was ill [Col. 0184D] at Capernaum. When he heard that Jesus had come from Judaea into Galilee, he went to him and begged him to come down and heal his son, for he was beginning to die. Jesus therefore said to him: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.”

The royal official believed him to be the Saviour, from whom he sought salvation; but he doubted in faith insofar as he requested his presence. The Lord, therefore, knowing the heart of the doubter, rebuked his distrust, saying: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.” [AUGUSTINE.] Wonders are things which portend something. They are called *prodigia*, as though *porrodicia*, because they say beforehand—that is, signify—something that will be. Therefore, the things then performed portended those now performed. Every wonder is a sign, but the converse is not true [Col. 0185A], because a sign may concern the past or present as well as the future, whereas a wonder concerns only the future. A sign of the present occurred when the Lord turned water into wine, thereby indicating his glory, just as a circle presently signifies wine for sale. A sign of the past is a footprint appearing in snow.

The royal official said to him: “Lord, come down before my son dies.” Jesus said to him: “Go; your son lives.”

[GREGORY.] Showing that he is not absent where he is invited, he heals by his word alone. Therefore, in not disdaining to go to the centurion’s servant, while disdaining to go to the royal official’s son, our pride is checked; for among people we honour not the nature in which they are made in God’s image [Col. 0185B], but rank and wealth. Observe the distinction. [ALBINUS.] This royal official wished the Lord to come down into his house; the centurion said that he was unworthy. Here pride was rebuffed; there humility was granted its request, as though this were said to the official: “Do not trouble me; you wish my presence in your house when I can heal your son by a word. The foreign centurion believed that I could do this by a word; you do not believe unless you see signs and wonders.”

The man believed the word which Jesus spoke and went. And as he was now going down, his servants met him and reported that his son was alive. He asked them at what hour he had begun to improve, and they told him that the fever had left him yesterday at the seventh hour. [Col. 0185C] Then the father knew that it was at that hour when Jesus said to him: “Your son lives.” And he himself believed, and his whole household.

The man began to believe that the Lord could heal as effectively while bodily absent as when present, and so he obtained healing for his son. He does not therefore distrust mercy by asking the servants about the hour; rather, he wishes the divine power to become known to many through the servants’ testimony. Or he asked lest the healing might have happened by chance, because perhaps he did not yet believe perfectly. In the figure of the sevenfold Holy Spirit, in whom all salvation consists, the fever left him at the seventh hour. This royal official, slow to believe, represents the Jews, who come to faith with difficulty—such as Thomas, when he heard: “Come, put your hand here, and do not be unbelieving but believing” (John 20).

## CHAPTER LVI

L. 39[II] M. 72 R. 22

And Levi made him a great feast in his house.

[BEDE.] Whoever receives Christ in the inner dwelling is nourished with the greatest delights. Therefore the Lord gladly enters and reclines in that person’s affection.

And it happened, as he reclined in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and reclined with Jesus and his disciples. For there were many who also followed him.

The Lord often went to the meals of sinners in order to provide spiritual food. Those reclining there saw [Col. 0186A] that a tax collector converted from sins to better things had found a place for repentance; and therefore they did not despair of salvation, especially those who, already repentant, followed the Lord.

And when the scribes and Pharisees saw that he ate with sinners and tax collectors, they said to his disciples: “Why does your teacher eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?”

[BEDE.] The Pharisees and scribes, glorying in fasting, err in two ways: they think themselves righteous though they are proud, and they regard the Lord’s guests as guilty though they have already repented. Here first the difference between Law and grace is made clear: those who follow the Law suffer eternal hunger, but those who receive the word of life are refreshed by heavenly food and cannot hunger. Then the future recompense is prefigured: when the elect feast with Christ, the fasting will be tormented above them, to whom it is said: “Harlots and tax collectors shall go before you into the kingdom of God” (Matt. 21). The Pharisees disdain sinners, because true righteousness has compassion, whereas false righteousness has disdain. The righteous, too, are accustomed rightly to be indignant with sinners; but there is one thing done as a type of pride and another from zeal for discipline.

M. 73[II] R. 23 L. 40

When Jesus heard this, he said to them: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill do. Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice’ (Hos. 6). For I came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.”

[Col. 0186C] The teacher answered for his disciples, calling himself a physician, because “by his wound we are healed” (Isa. 53). He calls well and righteous those who are ignorant of God’s righteousness and establish their own; but he calls ill and sinners those who, conscious of their weakness and seeing that they cannot be justified through the Law, submit themselves penitently to Christ’s grace. Therefore this is what he says in rebuke of the scribes and Pharisees: “I do not turn aside toward you because you do not think you need a physician; but I help these humble people because through repentance they make room for grace. But if you too wish to be healed, go from your rash condemnation and learn the sayings of the prophets more carefully, so that through works of mercy you may seek mercy; and while you neglect to help your neighbour [Col. 0186D], do not trust that you can appease God through sacrifices of the Law.” Hence that saying: “You did not require even a burnt offering for the blotting out of sin; then I said, ‘Behold, I come’” (Ps. 39), namely, to perform mercy. And elsewhere: “Indeed, you will not delight in burnt offerings” (Ps. 50). And: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. 49). The sacrifices of the Law were instituted in order to be a sign and approach to the true sacrifice of the cross, in which is the salvation of the world; and in order to recall God’s people from idolatry, since they would sacrifice victims to demons if not to God. Or it may be understood thus: “I desire mercy,” in forgiving sins, “and not sacrifice,” that is, the destruction of sinners. Hence elsewhere: “I do not desire the death of a sinner, but rather that he be converted and live” [Col. 0187A] (Ezek. 18). This may also be read thus: “I came not to call the righteous to repentance, but sinners.” For he calls sinners so that they may be corrected through repentance; he calls the righteous, such as Nathanael and John the Baptist, so that they may be made still more righteous.

But they said to him: “Why do John’s disciples often fast and make prayers, and likewise those of the Pharisees, while yours eat and drink and do not fast?”

Matthew reports that John’s disciples said to the Saviour what, according to Luke, the Pharisees said to him; hence it is clear that both said it. But John’s disciples are especially to be reproved in this matter, because they glory in fasting: they bring a slander against one whom they know was proclaimed by their teacher, and they join themselves to the Pharisees, whom they knew had been condemned by him. Spiritually, the disciples of John and of the Pharisees fast, but Christ’s disciples eat and drink, because those who reject Christ’s proclamations are not refreshed by spiritual food; but whoever faithfully adheres to Christ does not fast, but is nourished by his flesh and blood. Otherwise, John does not drink wine or strong drink (Luke 1), because he increases merit but cannot forgive sins; whereas the Lord eats and drinks with tax collectors and sinners (Matt. 4), because he can purify them. Yet Christ fasted, lest you should reject the command of fasting; he ate with sinners, so that you might recognize his power to purify.

To these he said: “Can the children of the wedding feast fast while the bridegroom is with them? [Col. 0187C] But days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.”

The bridegroom is Christ; the bride is the Church. Through this spiritual marriage the apostles were brought forth by the washing of regeneration. They cannot mourn while they see the bridegroom in the bridal chamber, since his presence benefits them far more than bodily abstinence. But when the wedding has passed and the time of the passion and resurrection has come, then the bridegroom’s children will fast in the humility of tribulation. Hence some think that Lent should be observed after the forty days following the Passion, even though Pentecost intervenes; others, such as Maximilla, after Pentecost. But the Church’s [Col. 0187D] custom comes to the resurrection through the humbling of the flesh. When Luke says, “Can you make the children of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them?” he elegantly intimates that those speaking would themselves be destined to fast in mourning, because they would kill the bridegroom. Afterwards, however, when the Holy Spirit had been given, they fasted in the joy of minds raised to spiritual things and thereby, in a sense, estranged from bodily food. The following comparisons concern this. Tropologically, while the bridegroom is with us, we are in joy and can neither fast nor mourn; but when he has withdrawn from us because of sins, then we must fast and mourn.

And he also told them a comparison: “No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth onto an old garment; otherwise [Col. 0188A] the new patch pulls away from the old, and a greater tear results.”

Otherwise—that is, if he sews an unshrunk, namely new, cloth patch onto an old garment—the new material is pulled away from the old, and the tear becomes greater, that is, more blameworthy. For both the piece of unshrunk cloth is harmfully torn from the remaining fabric, and a larger hole than before is made in the old garment because of the mismatch between new and old. By *assumentum* he means that which is sewn on, just as a garment is that which is put on. Matthew and Luke call such a piece a joining; if it is from new cloth and joined to an old garment, according to Matthew it removes its fullness—that is, it tears it broadly apart—and so the tear becomes worse. The Lord therefore says that the disciples are still like old [Col. 0188B] garments: that is, carnal persons not yet strengthened by faith in the Passion and Resurrection. For this reason they cannot bear severe fasts and precepts of continence, lest through excessive austerity they lose even the faith they possessed. Until one puts off the old man and puts on the new through Christ’s Passion, one cannot bear the new teaching, which must be observed whole and not in parts. The new teaching is not merely to fast from the desire for food, but also from every delight of temporal temptations. Therefore he says that the cloth of this teaching—that is, the part concerning food—ought not to be imparted to people still devoted to their old way of life; for there too a kind of tearing seems to occur, and, as Luke says, it does not suit the old condition. [Col. 0188C] For the actions of the old and new person must not be mingled. A variegated garment does not please the bridegroom. Hence the Apostle says: “Put off the old man with his deeds, and put on the new with his deeds” (Col. III).

“And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. Otherwise the new wine will burst the wineskins, and it will be spilled, and the wineskins will perish. But new wine must be put into new wineskins, and both are preserved.”

Here he compares the disciples to old wineskins and says that they could quickly be burst if they were filled with spiritual precepts, because unformed minds cannot bear the mysteries of the new life. Thus the teaching is spilled—that is, it does no good—and minds are choked by the weight of sins, which is for the wineskins to perish. [BEDA.] [Col. 0188D] After the Lord’s Ascension they became new wineskins, and then received the Holy Spirit as new wine. Hence it was said of the Jews that they were full of new wine (Acts II). Therefore, when teaching is entrusted to memory and the mind is not without fruit, then both are preserved.

Otherwise: the teacher must beware of committing the secret matters of the new mysteries to a soul still persisting in the oldness of malice. [HIERON.] Or thus: the old garment and old wineskins are the scribes and Pharisees; the new garment and new wine are the precepts of the Gospel, which the Jews cannot bear, lest a greater tear occur. [BEDA.] There is, however, a difference between new wine and new cloth: wine refreshes us, while clothing covers us. Spiritually, therefore, the garment signifies good works, by which we shine before people; [Col. 0189A] while in wine is expressed the ardor of faith, hope, and charity, by which we are inwardly renewed.

“And no one who drinks old wine immediately wants new; for he says, ‘The old is better.’”

This signifies the Jews, who, imbued with the flavor of the old life, found the precepts of new grace distasteful. Defiled by the traditions of their ancestors, they were wholly unable to perceive the sweetness of spiritual words.

## CHAPTER LVII

M. 127[X] L. 128

Then some of the scribes and Pharisees answered him, saying: “Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you.”

“Then,” that is, at that time, they answered him—that is, they added this [Col. 0189B] after his words. Testing him, they ask for a sign from heaven, as Luke writes, as though the things they had seen were not signs. Or they desired fire to come down from above, as in Elijah’s time two captains of fifty were destroyed by fire from heaven (IV Kings I); or, contrary to the custom of that land, thunder to roar, lightning to flash, and rains to pour down in summer, as happened under Samuel (I Kings XII)—as though they could not slander even those things and say that they had occurred through hidden and diverse disturbances of the air. But you, who slander things that you see with your eyes, hold with your hand, and experience by their benefit—what will you do with things that come from heaven? Certainly you will answer that the magicians in Egypt also performed many signs from heaven (Exod. VII).

[Col. 0189C] M. 198[V] L. 132

He answered and said to them: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given it except the sign of Jonah the prophet” (Jonah II). “For as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights.”

He fittingly said “adulterous,” because, having left her husband, she had joined herself to many lovers, according to Ezekiel. [HIERON.] To understand the whole from the part: “three days and three nights” means that within three periods, consisting of three days and three nights, the Son of Man was in the tomb, as though in the heart of the earth. [BEDA.] These Jews were not worthy to see a sign from [Col. 0189D] heaven, but one from the depths of hell: Jonah signified it in that he was shipwrecked and swallowed by the devouring sea-monster. But in being delivered from the abyss of the sea and the jaws of death, he gave a sign of the incarnation of Christ, who was to rise from death. The Lord gave his disciples a sign from heaven when he was transfigured on the mountain (Mark IX; Luke IX). By this comparison he showed that the Jews, like the Ninevites, were entangled in grave sins and near to overthrow, unless they repented; but if they repented, they would obtain forgiveness. Jonah was indeed a sign to the Ninevites: as he himself was delivered from bodily death by the sea-monster, so they might be delivered from death of the soul by repentance. The Son of Man was likewise a sign to the generation of the Jews: as he [Col. 0190A] rose from death of the flesh, so they might rise from death of the soul if they repented.

“The men of Nineveh will rise in judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because they repented at Jonah’s preaching. And behold, one greater than Jonah is here.”

[HIERON.] He rightly says “greater,” because Jonah preached for three days, while Christ preached for a much longer time. The men of Nineveh, who are Assyrians, will therefore condemn—not by authority to pronounce sentence, but by the example of comparison—that generation called the people of God, because they repented at Jonah’s preaching (Jonah III). Jonah, performing no signs, was accepted by a foreign people. Christ, performing so many signs, was rejected by his own nation. In old books one finds *Ninevitae*, not *Ninivitae*, as some read.

“The queen of the South will rise in judgment with this generation and condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom. And behold, one greater than Solomon is here.”

[Col. 0190B] [BEDA.] “Here” is an adverb, both here and above, meaning “in this place.” The queen of the South rises in judgment with the reprobate; since she herself is undoubtedly among the elect, this shows the resurrection of both good and evil. Scripture recounts through how many difficulties the queen of Sheba came to hear Solomon’s wisdom (II Kings X); bringing him many gifts, she received still more from him. She will therefore condemn the Jews by comparison with herself, because from the uttermost ends of the earth she learned that he was famous for wisdom [Col. 0190C] and sought him out; whereas they, having God’s wisdom and power in their midst, not only did not listen but blasphemed him and laid snares for him. For many came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom, as the Third Book of Kings relates, and brought him gifts. In the Ninevites, through repentance which abolishes sin, and in the queen of Sheba, through the pursuit of wisdom which avoids sin, the Church is preferred to the Synagogue. For the Church consists of these two things: either that you cease to sin, or that you do not know how to sin. Some are reconciled to God through wisdom or repentance; but the devil, returning to the Jews, will rule over them. This is what the following comparison says.

[Col. 0190D] M. 129[V] L. 130

“But when an unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it walks through dry places, seeking rest, and does not find it.”

[BEDA.] These words may suitably be understood of any heretic or schismatic, or even of an evil Catholic. When an unclean spirit has gone out of such a person at the time of baptism, it travels through waterless places—that is, it circles the hearts of believers, cleansed of the softness of unstable thought. It seeks rest and does not find it, because it cannot inhabit chaste minds, nor rest except in a perverse heart. Hence the Lord says of it: “It sleeps under shade, in the shelter of the reed, in moist places” (Job XL). By shade he signifies dark consciences; by the reed, which is fair outside [Col. 0191A] and hollow within, hypocritical minds; by moist places, wanton and soft ones.

“Then it says, ‘I will return to my house, from which I came out.’”

“I will return to that person’s conscience, from which I was cast out in baptism, and in my accustomed way subject to myself my former possession.”

“And coming, it finds it empty, swept, and adorned.”

Empty, namely, of good works through negligence; swept, of former vices through the grace of baptism; adorned, with counterfeit virtues through hypocrisy.

“Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself; and, entering, they dwell there.”

By the seven spirits he indicates all vices, which are rightly called worse than the devil by comparison [Col. 0191B] with the former habitation [the printed reading *habitaris* is uncertain/corrupt]. Since the devil is evil and makes people evil before baptism, whomever he seizes after baptism through heretical perversity or worldly greed, he immediately casts down into the depths of every vice. Such a person will not only have seven vices contrary to the seven spiritual virtues, but through hypocrisy will pretend to possess those very virtues.

“And the last state of that person becomes worse than the first.”

“It would indeed have been better for him not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back” (II Pet. II). We read that this was especially fulfilled in Judas the traitor (Luke XXII) and Simon Magus (Acts I). The conclusion indicates the point of this parable:

“So it will be also with this most evil generation.”

[Col. 0191C] [HIERON.] That is: what I have related particularly of one person will happen in the nation of this people. The unclean spirit went out from the Jews when they received the Law, and passed over to the Gentiles. But when later it found no place among the believing Gentiles, it returned to the Jews, empty of Christ and—as they thought—cleansed and adorned with superfluous observances of the Law. In order to possess them more firmly thereafter, it takes with it the entire host of demons. The Jews therefore now act worse, possessed by a greater number of demons, than before; for it was a lesser evil not to believe that Christ would come than not to receive him after he had come.

## CHAPTER LVIII

[Col. 0191D] L. 131[X]

And it happened, as he said these things, that a certain woman from the crowd raised her voice and said to him: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked.”

[BEDA.] This woman is shown to possess great devotion and faith. While the Pharisees blaspheme the Lord, she confesses his incarnation with such sincerity that she confounds both the unbelief of those present and that of those to come. For if the flesh of the Word of God were foreign to the flesh of his virgin Mother, as many heretics have said, the womb which bore him and the breasts which nursed him would be called blessed for no reason. Hence the Apostle says against heretics that “God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the Law” (Gal. 4). Nor should those be heard who think the reading should be “born of a woman,” rather than “made.” [Col. 0192A] Otherwise he would not be a true son of man unless he had drawn flesh from his mother. According to natural philosophers as well, milk for nourishing children and seed for begetting them flow from the same source. Therefore he who could be nourished by the virgin’s milk could be conceived from her seed. This woman bore the type of the Church, which believes that Christ was born true God and true man. Truly blessed is Christ’s parent, who, as someone has said, is the mother who gave birth to a king:

> Who rules heaven and earth [“holds,” Sedulius] through the ages, whose  
> Name and dominion, embracing all things in their eternal circuit,  
> Remain without end; she who, in her blessed womb,  
> Possessing a mother’s joys with the honor of virginity,  
> Was seen to have neither an equal before her nor one to follow.

[Col. 0192B] But he said: “Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.”

The Savior beautifully assents to the woman’s testimony, affirming not only that his mother is blessed, but also that all who conceive him, the Word of God, through the hearing of faith, and bear and nourish him in their neighbors’ hearts by the keeping of good works. By this statement he secretly strikes at the Jews, who deny that Christ is the Son of God. Indeed, the whole perfection of heavenly life is comprehended in these two things: that we hear the word of God and do it.

## CHAPTER LIX

M. 130[II] R. 35 L. 82

While he was still speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother and brothers [Col. 0192C] stood outside, seeking to speak with him. And someone said to him: “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you.”

While the Lord was occupied in the work of preaching, someone prompted him concerning his mother and brothers, who were laying snares for him, to see whether he would prefer flesh and blood to spiritual work.

But he answered the one speaking to him: “Who is my mother? And who are my brothers?” And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said: “Behold my mother and my brothers. For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, that person is my brother and sister and mother.”

He does not refuse to obey his mother, he who says, “Honor father and mother” (Exod. XX); but he shows that he owes more to his Father’s mysteries [Col. 0192D] than to maternal affections. Nor does he despise his brothers, but puts spiritual work before kinship, teaching that the union of minds is better than that of bodies, so that we too may prefer spirit to flesh. He did not deny his mother, as though born from a phantom, as Marcion and Manichaeus wished; rather, he answered the one laying a snare. It is as though he said: “My mother is the person who begets me in believers through preaching; my brothers are those who do the works of my Father.” “Sister” and “brother” are said on account of both sexes, although the Lord distinguishes rather by deeds than by sex. Whoever is Christ’s brother or sister through faith becomes his mother through preaching, while through preaching such a person, as it were, gives birth to him in the hearts of hearers, if faith or love of Christ is brought forth there. Some, following the absurdities [Col. 0193A] of apocryphal books, suppose that the Lord’s brothers standing outside were Joseph’s children by some woman. But here we must understand them as the Savior’s cousins, namely children of his maternal aunt—that is, of the mother of James the Less, Joseph, and Jude. [GREGOR.] In gathering believers from the Gentiles, the Lord does not acknowledge carnal Judaea as his mother. Hence she stands outside, because, having lost spiritual understanding, she clings outside to the letter. [BEDA.] By the crowds, then, we may understand the Gentile world that flocked to Christ; and the nearer it came in faith, the more fully its mind drank in the mysteries of life, in accordance with the Psalmist: “Come to him and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII). But Christ’s mother according to the flesh—that is, the synagogue—and his brothers—that is, the Jewish people—standing outside, wish [Col. 0193B] to see the Lord; but because they do not seek the spiritual sense in the Law, they fasten themselves outside to the observance of the letter, and as if compel him to go out to teach carnal things rather than themselves consenting to enter to learn spiritual things.

## CHAPTER LX

M. 74[II] R. 49 L. 85

As he was saying these things to them, behold, one ruler of the synagogue, whose name was Jairus, came and worshiped him, saying: “My daughter has just died; but come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live.”

That is, while the Lord was saying the things just mentioned—here not nearly all the matters set down before, but some of them—behold, the ruler of the synagogue reports that his daughter is near death, [Col. 0193C] as Mark and Luke relate. Since, therefore, he despaired of finding his daughter alive, according to Matthew he speaks of her as already dead, asking the Lord either to heal her while dying or to raise her when dead.

And Jesus rose and followed him, and so did his disciples. And behold, a woman who had suffered a flow of blood for twelve years, who had suffered much from many physicians and spent all that she possessed, yet could not be cured by anyone but was becoming worse, came up behind him in the crowd and touched the fringe of his garment. For she said within herself, “If I only touch his garment, I shall be healed.” And immediately her flow of blood stopped, and she felt in her body that she had been healed of the affliction. And immediately Jesus, knowing within himself, said: “Who touched me?” [Col. 0193D] Peter and those with him said: “Master, the crowds press and afflict you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” And Jesus said: “Someone touched me, for I too know that power has gone out from me.” And he looked around to see the woman who had done this. But when the woman saw that she had not escaped notice, she came trembling and fell at his feet; before all the people she told why she had touched him and how she had immediately been healed. But he said: “Your faith has made you well. Go in peace, and be healed of your affliction.” While he was still speaking, someone came to the ruler of the synagogue, saying to him: “Your daughter is dead; why trouble the teacher any further?” But Jesus, hearing this report, said to the ruler of the synagogue: “Do not fear. Only believe, and she will be saved.” And he allowed no one to follow him except Peter, James, and John the brother of James. And when he came [Col. 0194A] into the ruler of the synagogue’s house, he saw flute-players and a crowd in tumult, weeping and lamenting greatly. Entering, he said: “Go away. The girl is not dead but sleeping.” And they mocked him, knowing that she was dead. But after putting them all out, he took the girl’s father and mother, and those who were with him, and went in where the girl lay. Taking her hand, he said to her: “Talitha cumi,” which is translated, “Girl, I say to you, arise.” And her spirit returned, and the girl immediately arose and walked. She was twelve years old; and they were all struck with great amazement. And he sternly ordered them that no one should know it, and commanded that food be given to her. And this report went out through all that land.

[BEDA.] No one is more suitably understood by the ruler of the synagogue than [Col. 0194B] Moses; hence Jairus is appropriately called “enlightening” or “enlightened.” For, receiving words of life to enlighten others, he is enlightened by the Holy Spirit. The ruler of the synagogue fell at Jesus’ feet, as Mark and Luke record, because the lawgiver recognized that Christ must be preferred to himself, declaring that saying of the Apostle: “What is weak in God is stronger than men” (I Cor. I). Christ’s feet signify his incarnation, because God is his head. He asks him to come in the flesh and lay the hand of mercy and power upon his daughter, that is, the Jewish people. Moses longed by continual prayers for Christ’s coming into the synagogue. Hence: “My soul shall rejoice in the Lord and delight in his Jesus” (Ps. XXXIV). For he who lives for himself makes others live. [Col. 0194C] Abraham, Moses, and Samuel pray for the dead people, and Jesus follows their prayers. The synagogue, formed solely by legal instruction, was, as it were, born as Moses’ friend; nobly reared by the prophets, after she reached the age of understanding and ought to have borne spiritual offspring for God, she languished in errors and was dying in sins.

As the Lord went toward the girl, the woman with the issue of blood met him on the way, because under the Law menstruating women and those flowing with blood were excluded from towns. The woman with the hemorrhage is the Church from the Gentiles, which had been defiled by the flow of pleasures and separated from the assembly of the faithful; but on receiving the word of God, she snatched away salvation of soul from the Jews. According to the Psalmist: “Ethiopia will hasten her hands unto God” (Ps. [Col. 0194D] LXVII). And according to: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI). It should be noted that the woman had been flowing with blood for twelve years, and the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter was twelve years old: that is, when this one was born, the other began to be ill. For at one and the same age of the world the synagogue began to be born in the patriarchs, and the Gentiles began to be defiled throughout the world by the prostitution of idolatry and the pleasures of the flesh. She had spent all her resources on doctors, that is, the powers of natural ingenuity. By doctors he means either false theologians, philosophers, and teachers of secular laws, who promised much concerning virtues but supplied no remedy to souls; or unclean spirits, who insinuated themselves as gods to be worshiped, as though they were giving people counsel.

[Col. 0195A] The Church came up behind, that is, drew near to Christ through faith. It is said to have come behind either according to his saying: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John XII), and elsewhere the command: “You shall walk after the Lord your God” (Hos. XI); or because, not seeing the Lord present in the flesh, it began through faith to follow his footsteps. Through touching—that is, through participation in his sacraments—it deserved healing from sins. She touched the fringe of his garment because she first received a portion of his teaching through his ministers. The fringes of his garment are the words that depend upon Christ’s incarnation, with which divinity is clothed. Therefore whoever perfectly loves and believes the mysteries of the incarnation, until he comes to receive greater things, touches the fringe. [HIERON.] Hence the bells hanging [Col. 0195B] from the outer edges of the high priest’s tunic signify confession; and the pomegranates, the will to martyrdom and the brightness of virtues. [BEDA.] The flow of blood causes barrenness. Hence to the Church of the Gentiles: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear” (Isa. LIII). The fountain of blood is the origin of sin, that is, the beginning of unclean thought, from which every sin is born. The Lord uproots not only evil deeds but even the evil root of thoughts. The Lord does not ask who touched him in order to learn something unknown to him, but so that the power of the woman’s faith may appear and benefit many.

As he goes to the girl, he is pressed by the crowd because, in visiting Judaea, he is burdened by the harmful habit of carnal things. [Col. 0195C] He whom crowds press is touched by one believing woman, because the Lord is pressed by diverse heresies but sought by the faithful heart alone. For many who touch do not touch, just as those who see do not see and those who hear do not hear. Hence he says to Mary Magdalene, who did not yet believe fully: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John XX). The person who truly touches him is one who believes him equal to the Father. “I know that power has gone out from me.” Pelagius says that, if he chooses, he can be saved by his own effort; but let us say that human salvation is vain: “In God we shall do valiantly,” he who forgives all our iniquities and heals all our infirmities (Ps. LIX). “And he looked around to see her.” The Lord deigns to look upon all who deserve to be saved. “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears toward their prayers. This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him” (Ps. XXXIII). [Col. 0195D] “She fell before him.” See the purpose of the Lord’s question: namely, that the woman might openly confess the truth, be strengthened in faith, and provide many with an example of salvation.

Once the woman was healed, the girl was immediately reported dead: because once the Church of the Gentiles was cleansed of the stain of vices, the synagogue was immediately overcome by the death of unbelief and envy—unbelief, because it did not believe; envy, because it grieved that the Church had believed. Hence in the Acts of the Apostles: “When the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and contradicted what was said by Paul” (Acts XIII). This messenger is anyone who, seeing the synagogue abandoned, believes that it cannot be restored and therefore that prayer should not be made for it. But what is impossible with human beings is possible [Col. 0196A] with God. Hence Jesus’ reply to the girl’s father follows: “Do not fear.” The father of the girl is the body of teachers of the Law, of whom the Lord says: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat” (Matt. XXIII). If they had believed, the synagogue subject to them would have been saved. None but believers are allowed to accompany the Lord, so that mysteries may be revealed to those who honor him. Hence elsewhere: “Wisdom is justified by her children” (Matt. XI; Luke VII).

Because through deserved unbelief the synagogue lost the joy of the Lord’s indwelling, it lies as though dead to this day among mourners and lamenters—that is, grieving persons. Yet heavenly mercy will not allow it to perish utterly, but toward the end of the age will save its remnant. Hence it follows: “Entering, he said: ‘Go away.’” Those who appear to be teachers are the flute-players, [Col. 0196B] that is, singing a dirge while soothing their followers in error. The crowd of Jews is the tumultuous crowd, murmuring and rebelling against Christ’s teaching. The girl is not dead to God, to whom all live. Thus she who is dead to people unable to raise her is asleep to God, in whose disposal both her received soul lives and her flesh, destined to rise, rests. Christian custom has indeed prevailed that the dead are called sleepers because they will rise. Hence the Apostle: “We do not want you, brothers, to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, lest you grieve as others do, who have no hope” (I Thess. IV). Allegorically also, although a soul that has sinned dies, it may be said to sleep to God if he deigns to raise it.

The crowd is put out because those mocking him were not worthy to see the miracle. The crowd is put out so that the girl may be raised, because a dead soul does not rise unless the importunate multitude of worldly cares is first expelled. Peter, James, and John signify faith, hope, and charity. The father is the bishop; the mother, the Church. The Lord took the girl’s hand, and she arose, because unless the blood-stained hands of the Jews are cleansed, the dead synagogue will not rise. In the Syriac expression, “Talitha cumi” means nothing more than “Girl, arise”; but the Evangelist, explaining it, inserted on his own part, “I say to you,” perhaps to express the force of the Lord’s command. It is customary for those citing testimonies from the Old Testament to attend more to the sense than the words. The girl rightly rose and walked, because [Col. 0196D] anyone whom heavenly mercy raises from death through sins ought not merely to rise from the filth of crimes, but immediately to advance also in good works, according to the Psalmist: “He who walks without blemish and works righteousness” (Ps. XIV). He commanded food to be given her as proof of life, so that she might be believed to be not a phantom but reality. If anyone is likewise raised from spiritual death, that person must immediately be satisfied with heavenly bread, having become a participant both in the divine word and in the most holy altar.

In the moral sense, the three dead persons whom the Savior raised bodily signify three kinds of resurrection of souls. He raised the girl still shut up in the house: that is, a soul that has given only consent, not action, to evil pleasure. He raises the young man already carried outside the gate: that is, a sinner who has already carried consent into action. He raises Lazarus, already stinking: that is, a soul foul-smelling through long habit of sinning and corrupting others by its reputation. He speaks to the girl before few people, because he easily raises one whom he both declares not dead and shows that a similar soul is quickly raised. He strengthens the young man with more words when he says, “I say to you, arise,” because such souls return to life somewhat more difficultly. At the tomb of Lazarus, dead four days, he groaned in spirit, troubled himself, shed tears, and cried with a loud voice: “Lazarus, come forth” (John II). [BEDA.] Likewise, one oppressed by long habit is raised only with difficulty and, as it were, with labor. It should also be noted that a public offense requires a public remedy. Lesser sins, however, are removed by lighter and secret repentance. [Col. 0197B] The girl lying in the house rises with few witnesses, who are also ordered not to publish the miracle. The young man is raised outside the gate with a crowd accompanying him; but Lazarus became so well known among the people that because of him many Jews believed in Jesus.

## CHAPTER LXI

M. 75[X]

As Jesus passed on from there, two blind men followed him, crying out and saying: “Have mercy on us, Son of David.” And when he came into the house, the blind men approached him; and Jesus said to them: “Do you believe that I can do this for you?” They said to him: “Certainly, Lord.” Then he touched their eyes, saying: “According to your faith, let it be done to you”; and their eyes were opened.

[Col. 0197C] [HIERON.] As Jesus went toward his house at Nazareth, two blind men cried out. They are not healed in passing, but their faith is examined at home. Both peoples were blind while the Lord passed through this age, and unless both believe, neither will receive light. What is crying out to the Lord except corresponding to his grace by good works? [AUG., *On the Words of the Lord*.] The person who despises worldly pleasures cries out to Christ. The person rightly cries, “Have mercy, Son of David,” who truly believes that the Word took flesh from David’s seed. The Lord passes by when he administers to us temporal sacraments, by which we are admonished concerning eternal things. He passes from the house of the ruler, which is the synagogue, into his own house, that is, the heavenly Jerusalem, in which, [Col. 0197D] after he had placed his flesh, certain blind persons from both peoples approached him through faith. Through preachers he says to them, “Do you believe?” and so forth. To touch their eyes is to instruct their minds through preachers with divine words. The Lord asks whether we believe so that faith, by prayer, may obtain what he is ready to give.

And Jesus sternly charged them, saying: “See that no one knows.” But when they went out, they spread word of him through all that land.

[HIERON.] Seeking to avoid the glory of boastfulness, he gave this command; but they could not remain silent because of their remembrance of grace. Observe, then, that in one respect one righteous person may be contrary to another righteous person.

When they had gone out, behold, they brought to him a mute man possessed by a demon. And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke. And the crowds marveled, saying: “Never has anything like this appeared in Israel.”

M. 120 L. 82

“Is this man the Son of David?”

It is as though the faithful crowds were saying: This man is not merely the Son of David, but also the Son of God. [HIEROM.] In Greek “deaf” sounds better than “mute”; but Scripture uses one indifferently for the other. When they had gone out—understand, from this age—the preachers brought to the Lord a mute man, namely a people mute because it had as yet said nothing of God’s glory, since it had had no preachers. This people is understood to have been from the Gentiles; hence follows the crowds’ amazement [Col. 0198B] at themselves saying that such a thing had never appeared in Israel, namely, that so many from it should be converted together to Christianity.

## CHAPTER LXII

M. 121[II] R. 32 L. 127

But the Pharisees said: “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, this man casts out demons.”

[BEDA.] While less educated crowds marvel at the Lord’s deeds, the scribes and Pharisees perversely interpret the Lord’s deeds, attributing his miracles to Beelzebub, who was the god of Ekron (IV Kings I). *Beel* itself is Baal; *zebud* means “fly.” Nor, according to certain corrupt copies, should an *l* or *d* be read at the end of the name, but a *b*. *Beelzebub* means “man of flies,” or “one having flies,” on account, that is, of the filth of sacrificial blood; from this utterly foul rite or name they gave the prince of demons his surname. Note that King Ninus, founder of Nineveh, dedicated a statue to his father Bel and instituted divine honors for it. The Chaldeans, adopting the likeness of this image, called it Bel. Hence the Palestinians, adopting it, called it Baal; the Moabites, Beelphegor; while the Jews, worshipers of the one God, called it Beelzebub in derision of the Gentiles, asserting that the prince of demons dwelt in this image.

L. 129[II] M. 122 R. 33
He himself, seeing their thoughts, said to them: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and [Col. 0198D] a house divided against itself will not stand.”

[Jerome.] He answered the thoughts of the Pharisees, so that even in this way they might be compelled to believe. In the literal sense it is clear that every solid and firmly established kingdom, if divided into factions, when some are destroyed or oppressed by others, is reduced to desolation, emptied of inhabitants. [Sallust, *Jugurthine War*.] The same principle applies to a household or city, as Matthew writes: “By harmony small things grow; by discord the greatest fall apart.” He explains the spiritual bearing of this as follows:

“But if Satan too is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? It cannot stand, but is coming to an end, because you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebub.”

[Col. 0199A] Let them choose whichever they wish. If Satan cannot cast out Satan, let them say nothing against the Lord. But if he can, let them depart from his kingdom, which cannot stand if divided, lest they be involved together in its ruin.

“But if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they shall be your judges.”

By “sons” he means either the Jewish exorcists of that nation or the apostles born from their stock. As though he said: If, in the case of your sons, you attribute the expulsion of demons to God, why do you not do the same in my case? The apostles—who are the insignificant and despised things of this world, in whom not malice but the simplicity of my power appears—will be my witnesses that I cast out demons in the Holy Spirit. And they will be your judges concerning your charge that I work through Beelzebub [Col. 0199B]. Or the exorcists who are your sons and drive demons from the possessed will be your judges—not by power, as are my disciples, but by comparison: while they attribute the expulsion of demons to God, you attribute it to Beelzebub, the prince of demons.

“But if I cast out demons by the finger of God, then surely the kingdom of God has come upon you.”

[Augustine.] If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, and your sons cannot cast them out otherwise, then without doubt the kingdom of God has come upon you—a kingdom by which the devil’s kingdom is overthrown, and with it you too are overthrown. The kingdom of God is the power by which the wicked are condemned and separated from the faithful. Or thus: the kingdom of God signifies either himself, of whom he says elsewhere, “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17); and, “There stands among you one whom you do not know” [Col. 0199C] (John 1); or the kingdom of Scripture, taken away from the Jews and given to us; or the kingdom of heaven. As though he said: If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, know beyond doubt that entrance into the heavenly kingdom has been opened to believers.

The finger of God is that which the magicians acknowledged when they performed signs against Moses and Aaron, saying, “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 7); and by it the stone tablets were written on Mount Sinai. For he himself wrote who dictated what was to be written. The hand of God and the arm of God are his Son; and his finger is the Holy Spirit. He is called the finger because of the participation [variant: division] of gifts which are given in him as proper to each, whether human beings or angels. For in no members is division more apparent than in the fingers. [Col. 0199D] But just as the finger with the hand or arm, and the hand with the arm and body, are one in nature, so the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are indeed three persons, but one substance of divinity. The fingers of God, in the plural, are understood to be the holy prophets, through whom the Holy Spirit, by his inspiration, writes the books of the Law and the Prophets. Of these it is written in the Psalm: “I will behold your heavens, the works of your fingers” (Ps. 8). By “heavens” he mystically indicated the books of the Law and the Prophets; by “fingers,” the holy prophets, as has been said.

“Or how can anyone enter the house of the strong man and plunder his goods, in which he trusted, unless he first binds the strong man, and then plunders his house?”

[Col. 0200A] [Bede.] The Lord shows by an obvious parable that he frees human beings from the devil by the power of his divinity. The strong man is the devil; his house is the world lying in wickedness, in which, until the Savior’s coming, he rested as though in peaceful dominion, without opposition. Hence the Lord says: “The prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (Job 14). And again: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12). The Lord himself was stronger than he, taking away his weapons—that is, the cunning and deceits of spiritual wickedness—and thus, by removing his power, compelling him to cease from seducing the elect. This was the binding of the strong man.

The spoils or goods are the people deceived by him, whom Christ the conqueror distributes—an emblem of a triumphant victor—because, “leading captivity captive, he gave gifts to [Col. 0200B] men,” appointing some apostles, others evangelists, others prophets, others pastors and teachers (Eph. 4). Therefore, to plunder the strong man’s house was to gather into the Church those snatched from the devil and to advance them through the distinct dignities of ranks.

“He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters.”

This consequently refers not to heretics but to the devil, whose works cannot be compared with the works of the Savior. For he desires to hold human souls captive, whereas the Lord sets them free; he draws them toward vices, whereas the Lord calls them back to virtues. How then can they agree, whose works are opposed? He who does not gather—that is, who does not gather my sheep with me—scatters, that is, disperses them from the assembly of the faithful. [Col. 0200C] Here he indicates that one does not possess the Holy Spirit who does not gather with him, however much one may assemble under his name. Here he altogether compels us to understand that remission of sins can occur nowhere except in Christ’s gathering, which does not scatter.

M. 123 R. 134 L. 147

“Therefore I say to you: Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven human beings, but blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the age to come.”

[Col. 0200D] Because you say that I cast out demons only by Beelzebub, therefore I say to you: “Every sin,” and so forth. [Bede, *On Mark*.] Yet not all sins are indiscriminately forgiven to everyone, but to those who repent worthily in this life. Here Novatian is refuted, who denies forgiveness to penitents undergoing martyrdom.

[Augustine, *To Consentius*.] Blasphemy is that by which false things are said about God himself; and therefore it is worse to blaspheme than to swear falsely. For in false swearing God is falsely invoked as witness; in blasphemy, falsehoods are uttered concerning God himself.

[Jerome—Bede.] The meaning, then, is this: Whoever takes offense at the weakness of my flesh, because he calls me a carpenter’s son, a glutton, or a wine-drinker, may obtain forgiveness. But whoever clearly understands the works of God and, from envy, attributes works of the Holy Spirit to Beelzebub [Col. 0201A], will never be forgiven—not because forgiveness is denied him if he repents, but because this blasphemer, as his evil deserts [variant: many] require, will no more come to forgiveness than to repentance. For a fall into contempt of the good is so deep that no one rises from it. Hence: “When a sinner has come into the depth of sins, he despises” (Prov. 18). Conversely, in love of the good there is a highest degree from which no one falls. In that condition Paul said: “Who shall separate me from the love of Christ?” (Rom. 8).

[Bede.] That blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, therefore—when someone, in likeness of the devil and his angels, does not fear, against his own conscience, to assail the majesty of the Godhead—does not have forgiveness for ever, but [Col. 0201B] will be guilty of an eternal sin, as Mark explains, adding after the Lord’s saying: “Because they said, ‘He has an unclean spirit’” (Mark 3). But those who, through human ignorance, believe and say that the Holy Spirit does not exist, or is less than the Father, are not held guilty of an unforgivable crime.

The Lord says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6). [Augustine, homily on this chapter.] Does one who receives unworthily the sacrament of his flesh and blood—who eats and drinks judgment upon himself, as Paul says—abide in Christ and Christ in him? (1 Cor. 11). Certainly there is one manner of eating that flesh and drinking that blood unto salvation, and another manner unto judgment. [Col. 0201C] Thus likewise there is a manner of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit which merits forgiveness, and one which does not merit it. For the unclean spirit is cast out in the Holy Spirit; if anyone speaks impenitently against this grace, that very impenitence is blasphemy against the Spirit, which will never be forgiven. For repentance obtains forgiveness.

Yet no judgment can be made concerning this impenitence while the impenitent person lives. Is he today a pagan, a Jew, or a heretic? What do you know whether tomorrow he may be a believer? God does not snatch from this life the wicked person whom he wills to be converted and live (Ezek. 18).

[Gregory, Book XVII on Job.] But if someone remains impenitent to the end of life and so dies, he will not be forgiven either here or hereafter. “There is sin unto death,” John says; “I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John 5). “Unto death” means unto death itself, because forgiveness is sought in vain for the sin which is not corrected here. [Col. 0201D]

[Augustine, in the homily mentioned above.] Nor should it trouble you that the Evangelist says “a word” in the singular, although prolonged impenitence weaves blasphemy together with many words. Scripture often calls many words “a word,” as in the phrase, “the Word which came to this or that prophet.” For no prophet spoke only one word. And James does not say “doers of words,” but, “Be doers of the word and not hearers only” (James 1). Therefore, whatever words a person may have spoken, whether with the mouth or only in thought, with an impenitent heart against the forgiveness of sins which occurs in the Church, he speaks a word against the Holy Spirit. How can that be forgiven which even prevents [Col. 0202A] the forgiveness of other sins? A word against the Holy Spirit is therefore spoken when one never comes from scattering to the gathering which received the Holy Spirit for the remission of sins.

Those who are baptized in schismatic or heretical gatherings—or rather separations—although they are not reborn of the Spirit, like Ishmaels, who was born to Abraham according to the flesh (Gen. 16), and not according to Isaac, who was born according to the Spirit, through promise (Gen. 21), nevertheless, when they come to the catholic Church and are joined to the fellowship of the Spirit, whom beyond doubt they did not possess outside, do not receive again the washing of the flesh. This form of piety was not lacking even to those outside; but unless they are within, the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace cannot be given to them. [Col. 0202B] Of such persons the Apostle says: “Having the form of piety but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3). The visible form of a branch can indeed exist even apart from the vine, but it cannot have the invisible life of the root except in the vine.

Accordingly, the bodily sacraments which those separated from the unity of Christ’s body bear and celebrate can display the form of piety; but the invisible and spiritual power of piety cannot be in them, just as sensation does not accompany a human limb when it is cut off from the body. Since these things are so, forgiveness of sins—because it is given only in the Holy Spirit—can be given only in that Church which has the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0202C]

[Augustine, *Enchiridion*.] Therefore, one who does not believe that the Church forgives sins despises so great an abundance of divine gift; and if he closes his final day in this obstinacy of mind, he is guilty of that unforgivable sin against the Holy Spirit, in whom Christ forgives sins.

What Augustine says concerning those baptized among schismatics or heretics should be understood of adults imbued with their error, or likewise of little children who are neither presented for baptism with a right intention nor baptized with a right intention, even though outwardly they receive the complete form of baptism.

[Bede, *On Mark*.] Just as the desire to fornicate is called a spirit of fornication, and the love of pursuing drunkenness a spirit of drunkenness, so the will knowingly to attack the truth is called a spirit of blasphemy, the forgiveness of which will never be granted to many for eternity. Here Origen is reproved, for asserting that, after the universal judgment and after innumerable revolutions of ages have passed, all sinners will obtain pardon and go to heaven. But the statement, “neither in this age nor in the age to come,” gives us to understand that some faults are forgiven in this age and some in the age to come. For what is denied concerning one case is consequently granted concerning certain others; yet this should be believed only of the least sins, such as an idle word or excessive laughter. [Col. 0202D]

M. 124[X]

“Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad; for a tree is known by its fruit.”

You see me doing good works and yet you blame me: [Col. 0203A] in this a great inconsistency appears. Therefore either make—that is, call—me good, like my work; or, if you can, make both me and my work evil. [Jerome.] For there is no middle position: the works of a good doer are only good, and those of an evil doer evil. Therefore, if the deeds you see are good, the devil is not the one who does them. He calls himself the tree and his work the fruit.

“Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.”

Here he shows them to be a bad tree and to bear bad fruit, since malice abounds in the intention of their hearts.

M. 125[V] L. 62

[Col. 0203B] “A good person brings forth good things from a good treasure, and an evil person brings forth evil things from an evil treasure.”

Thus neither can Christ perform evil works, nor the devil good works. [Remigius.] The treasure is the intention of the heart, from which God judges works, so that sometimes a greater reward follows lesser acts, and sometimes a lesser reward greater acts.

M. 126[X]

“But I tell you that for every idle word which people speak, they will render account for it on the day of judgment.”

[Jerome.] You cannot speak good things because you are evil, and therefore—*autem* meaning “and”—I tell you that every idle word people may speak [Col. 0203C] is understood to be of such a kind that they shall render account for it on the day of judgment. If an idle word is not without peril to the speaker, what will become of you who slander the works of the Holy Spirit? An idle word is one said without benefit either to the speaker or the hearer, as when tales are told. But one who dissolves his mouth in loud laughter, utters something shameful, or repeats buffooneries will be held guilty not of an idle word but of a criminal one.

“For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.”

Hence the saying: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. 18). Here he calls not only utterances of the mouth but also those of the heart “words.” Even before human beings it often happens that a person is judged from the words of his mouth either righteous or [Col. 0203D] guilty.

## Chapter LXIII

L. 122[X]

It came to pass, as they were going along, that he entered a certain village; and a woman named Martha received him into her house. She had a sister named Mary, who also, sitting at the Lord’s feet, listened to his word; but Martha was occupied with much serving.

[Augustine.] Mary sat at the feet of our Head; and the more humbly she sat, the more abundantly she received. For water flows down to the lowliness of the valley from the swelling heights of the hill. Mary was attentive to how she might be fed by the Lord; Martha, to how she might [Col. 0204A] feed the Lord. The one prepares a meal for the Lord; the other already delights in the Lord’s meal. It should be known that in these two women the present and future lives are figured: the laborious and the restful, the hardship-ridden and the blessed. In Martha was the image of present things; in Mary, of things to come.

Or thus: these two sisters represent the two spiritual lives through which the Church is exercised in the present. Martha represents the active life, through which we are joined to our neighbor in charity; Mary, the contemplative life, through which we sigh in love for God. The active life is to give bread to the hungry; to teach the ignorant by a word of wisdom; to correct the erring; to call back the proud neighbor to the way of humility; to care for the sick; to provide each individual with what is needed; and to see to the sustenance of those entrusted to us. The contemplative [Col. 0204B] life, however, is to retain with one’s whole mind the love of God and neighbor; to rest from outward action; to cling solely to desire for the Creator; to burn to see the Creator’s face; and to long to be admitted among the heavenly choirs.

The teacher of the Gentiles recounts his dangers in the active life; and, also commending visions and revelations of the Lord, he indicates that he had been perfected in the contemplative life. Hence he said: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are sober-minded, it is for you” (2 Cor. 1).

She stood and said: “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her therefore to help me.”

He speaks in the person of those who, still ignorant of divine contemplation, regard as pleasing to God only the work of brotherly love which they have learned. Martha is fittingly described as standing and Mary as sitting at the Lord’s feet, because the active life toils in laborious struggle, while the contemplative life already enjoys repose of mind in Christ. Mary does not prepare a speech in reply, lest she relax her attention to listening. But he who had been appealed to as judge became her advocate. Hence it follows:

The Lord answered and said to her: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things. But one thing is necessary.”

The Lord’s words remind us that there is one thing toward which we should strive when we labor amid the multiplicity of this age. Hence David: “It is good for me to cling to God” [Col. 0204D] (Ps. 72), “that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 22). Therefore there is one theoretical—that is, contemplative—knowledge of God, to which every pursuit of virtues should rightly be subordinated. The repetition of Martha’s name is an indication of affection, or a summons to attention, that she might listen more carefully.

“Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her.”

Martha’s part is good, but Mary’s is best; it will not be taken away, just as the active life ceases with the body. When a person serves, he sometimes wishes to do what he cannot. What is lacking is sought, what is available is prepared, and the mind is distracted. If what she desired had been sufficient for Martha, she would not have asked for her sister’s assistance. The burden of necessity is taken away; the sweetness of eternal truth never—[text incomplete or corrupt]. [Col. 0205A] The labor of multiplicity passes, and the charity of unity remains. For the fire of love which begins to burn here, when it sees him whom it loves, burns still more intensely in love. Then works of mercy will be necessary for none of the saints—for example, that food be given to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, and so forth.

## Chapter LXIV

M. 102[V] L. 69

Now when John had heard in prison of Christ’s works, summoning two of his disciples, he sent them to the Lord, saying: “Are you he who is to come, or should we expect another?”

The meaning is: Tell me whether I ought to announce you to the underworld, whither I am about to descend; or whether it is not fitting [Col. 0205B] that you taste death, since you are the Son of God. Gregory, *On Ezekiel*: The spirit of prophecy sometimes touches the mind of one prophesying concerning the present and not the future, as when John said: “Behold the Lamb of God” (John 1). Yet, about to die, he asked through his disciples: “Are you he who is to come, or should we expect another?” This shows that he knew the Redeemer had come, but doubted whether he would descend into hell in person. For through such a lapse of piety and love, not of unbelief, even the saints did not believe that Christ would die. Hence Peter, prince of the faith, said: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you” (Matt. 16).

John also sends his disciples to Christ in order to provide for their ignorance, so that, seeing the signs, they might believe. For they were scandalized because they had heard Jesus preferred [Col. 0205C] to their master. This became known when they said: “Rabbi, he to whom you bore witness—behold, he is baptizing, and all are coming to him” (John 5).

At that very hour he cured many of diseases, afflictions, and evil spirits, and gave sight to many who were blind. And answering, he said to them: “Go and report to John what you have seen and heard: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, and the poor are evangelized.”

These matters are directed to the scandal of the messengers, not to the questions asked. By “poor” he means either poor in spirit or poor in possessions, so that in preaching there may be no distinction between noble and lowly, rich and needy. “The poor are evangelized,” that is, they are drawn by the Gospel and [Col. 0205D] converted to faith.

“And blessed is he who shall not be scandalized in me.”

Here the Lord answered concerning the humility of his death. Blessed, indeed, are those whose faith is brought no temptation by the cross, death, or burial. [Gregory.] He rebukes John’s messengers, who did not believe that he was the Christ, for the scandal of their unbelief; and he explains to John what he had asked, because God is a God of salvation, and “to the Lord God belong the issues from death” (Ps. 67). Having seen so many signs, each person could avoid scandal and instead marvel. Yet the minds of unbelievers were greatly disturbed when they saw the Lord die after so many miracles. Hence Paul: “But we preach Christ crucified: a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles” (1 Cor. 1). The Lord did wondrous things, yet did not disdain to die. [Col. 0206A]

[Jerome.] But since many think that John at least knew from the Scriptures of the prophets that Christ would die, let us read it in this way also: just as the Lord said concerning Lazarus, “Where have you laid him?” (John 11), so John questions Christ not at all for his own sake but for that of his disciples. The question may likewise be understood thus: Are you he whom the Law foretold would come, or is another Christ to be expected? The Lord answers by deeds rather than words.

[Ambrose.] The miracles seen undoubtedly give full testimony that he is the Son of God. Before the Gospel, such things were either rare or nonexistent. Tobias alone received his sight (Tob. 11), and this was healing by an angel, not a human being. Elijah raised a dead person (3 Kings 17), yet he himself prayed and wept; this man commanded. Elisha caused a leper to be cleansed [Col. 0206B] (4 Kings 5), but there the authority of a command was not effective; rather, it was a figure of mystery. After the matters mentioned above, he adds concerning the cross, death, and burial, which is the fullness of faith. For no testimony of the Lord is greater than that he offered his whole self as one offering for the world. By this alone the Lord is fully declared. Thus he was also declared by John: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1).

As they went away, he began to say to the crowds concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed moved [variant: shaken] by the wind?”

[Jerome.] Since the surrounding crowd did not know the mystery of the question and thought that John doubted Christ, he said this in praise [Col. 0206C] of John so that they might understand that John had asked not for himself but for his disciples. By the reed he denotes a soul empty of the knowledge of God and wandering at the breath of unclean spirits. John did not possess such a soul, for he was not elated by prosperity and did not know how to bend beneath adversity.

“But what did you go out to see? A man clothed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear costly clothing and live in luxury are in kings’ houses.”

Did one who lives on locusts and wears camel hair seek gain for food or clothing, led by vain glory? Here it should be noted that the pursuit of costly clothing is not free from sin. Hence Peter says in his Epistle to women: “Not in costly clothing” (1 Pet. 3). A strict life and preaching ought to avoid the palaces of the luxurious, frequented by those clothed softly: flatterers who put cushions beneath the elbow (Ezek. 12), soothing rather than pricking the lives of sinners, in order somehow to catch something for themselves. [Col. 0206D]

“But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.”

John is greater than a prophet in this: he pointed with his finger to the one whom the others had foretold would come. [Hilary.] The two clauses, “But what did you go out to see?” are mystically read as “and.” The Law, bound by the people’s sins and shut up in the breasts of sinners as in prisons emptied of light, was kept from being understood as referring to Christ. [Ambrose.] He therefore sends the disciples to behold the Gospel, that it may receive its completion, because Christ is the fullness of the Law (Rom. 13). [Col. 0207A] Since truth was often unsteady without deeds, faith is presented in its fullest form through the testimony of acts accomplished. John was not clothed softly, because he did not foster the lives of sinners with flatteries but rebuked them severely. Hence Solomon: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply” (Eccl. 12).

M. 103[II] R. 1 L. 70

“This is he of whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way before you.’”

John is indeed more than a prophet, because he is called an angel not by nature but by the dignity of his office. In Malachi the Father says thus to the Son: “Before your face”—that is, before your manifestation—“he shall prepare the way” [Col. 0207B] (Mal. 3); that is, by preaching repentance and baptizing, he will make the hearts of hearers passable for you.

[Gregory.] All those who bear the title of priest are also called angels, as the prophet testifies: “The lips of the priest shall preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2). Likewise, if a believer recalls his neighbor from wickedness and exhorts him to good, or announces to one who has strayed either the eternal kingdom or punishment, then in doing this he is certainly an angel—that is, a messenger—of the Lord.

M. 104[V] L. 72

“Amen I say to you: among those born of women no prophet greater than John the Baptist has arisen.”

[Col. 0207C] To sum up his virtues: among those born of women—that is, born from sexual intercourse, not of a virgin—none was greater than he. John bears no comparison with the Son of God. John is not preferred to the other prophets and patriarchs, but is their equal. Whether anyone afterwards has been holier than he, or is yet to be, is left undecided.

“But he who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.”

[Bede.] John is greater among human beings and is an angel; but he who is an angel on earth is lesser than the least of the angels who minister to the Lord in heaven. Likewise, every saint already with God is greater than one who still stands in battle. [Col. 0207D] Some wish to understand this of the Savior: he who is lesser than John in the time of his birth is greater in dignity, in the Church of saints, which endures from the first righteous person to the last elect.

L. 72[X]

“And all the people, hearing him, and the tax collectors, justified God, having been baptized with John’s baptism.”

In baptism God will be justified, in which there is confession and forgiveness of sins. In this God is justified—that is, he appears righteous to human beings—because he forgives not the obstinate but those seeking remission of sins, as it is written: “Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Isa. 43, according to the Septuagint). Therefore the person who rejects injustices by accusing them, humbly asking grace from God, is justified; and “the righteous Lord loves righteousness” (Ps. 10). [Col. 0208A]

“But the Pharisees and lawyers rejected God’s counsel against themselves, not having been baptized by him.”

“Against themselves,” that is, to their own harm: for one who rejects God’s grace acts against himself. Or they foolishly refused to receive the counsel of God sent to themselves. For God’s counsel was to save the world through Jesus’ death; this the Pharisees and lawyers rejected.

M. 105[V] L. 193

“But from the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.”

[Col. 0208B] [Augustine.] The kingdom of heaven is said to suffer violence because the guilt which the letter without the Spirit produced by commanding is loosed by believing, and the Holy Spirit is obtained by the violence of faith. It is indeed great violence for those born on earth to seek heaven and, by virtue, to possess what we did not hold by nature. Everyone who loves the kingdom of God more than earthly goods does violence to it—that is, labors with strength and virtue so as finally to arrive there. “From the days of John” means after John began to preach. Christ does not say “until now” because the violence upon the kingdom of heaven then ceased; it will endure until the end of the world. The violent—that is, those who do violence—seize it when they do violence to their nature, so that it may not sink down toward earthly things but raise itself toward those above. [Col. 0208C] It is like robbery to acquire, where we have no right, what is the possession of angels. [Hilary.] Or the kingdom of heaven is said to suffer violence because the glory of the Lord owed to the fathers of Israel, announced by the prophets and offered by Christ, is occupied and seized by the faith of the Gentiles, while through the repentance preached by John they return to life for the heavenly homeland, as though entering a place belonging to another.

M. 106[X]

“For all the prophets and the Law prophesied until John. And if you are willing to receive it, he is Elijah who is to come. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

[Jerome.] He does not say this in order to exclude prophets after John. For we read in the Acts of the Apostles that Agabus prophesied [Col. 0208D] (Acts 11). But because the time of Christ had come, whom the prophets foretold would come down to John, who pointed him out, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God” (John 1). John is called Elijah because he came in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1); they were alike in firmness of mind, and both lived in the wilderness. [Remigius.] Some think John is called Elijah because, as Elijah will announce the Lord’s second coming, so John announced the first. By saying “ears,” he seeks ears of the heart, that John may mystically be understood as Elijah.

M. 107[V] R. 73

“But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplace, who cry out [Col. 0209A] to their companions: ‘We played for you, and you did not dance; we lamented, and you did not mourn.’”

[Bede.] The generation of Jews living in Christ’s time is compared with ancient Jews, among whom there was great division. The children are the prophets and teachers who lived before Christ’s coming, of whom it is said: “The unfolding of your words gives light and gives understanding to the little ones” (Ps. 118). “Little ones” means those humble in spirit. The marketplace is either the synagogue or Jerusalem, where the ordinances of God’s commandments were established.
