There the prophets, as in a public assembly in the marketplace, reproached their companions—that is, peoples of their own race—in their native speech, because they did not rise, with devout hearts and bodily agility, to praise God when attracted by psalms, as the dancing signifies; nor were they converted to repentance by threnodies—that is, prophetic lamentations—over destructions already accomplished or still to come. [Col. 0204C] [Col. 0209B]

“We played for you,” namely the wedding song, where the soul and spirit are married to the Word of God. The Psalmist, as though placed in the very act of the wedding, dancing with a certain joy, urged us to make merry, saying: “Rejoice in God our helper; sing aloud to the God of Jacob” (Ps. 80), and the rest. But what follows? “My people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not attend to me” (ibid.). The prophet cries: “Thus says the Lord: Return to me with all your heart, with fasting and weeping and mourning; rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2). And again: “My belly aches; the feelings of my heart are troubled within me” (Jer. 4). And a little later: “My foolish people have not known me; they are senseless and foolish children” (ibid.).

[Hilary.] Because bodily movement in dancing is suited to the duty of those who sing, it is said: “We played for you, and you did not dance”; that is, we urged you to the confession of singing psalms to God, and you did not obey by conforming and establishing yourselves in the teaching. [Col. 0209C]

“For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Behold, a gluttonous man and a drinker of wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.’”

[Bede.] As then, he says, so now you have rejected both ways of salvation. “We lamented” applies to John, whose abstinence signified the sorrow of repentance. But what Luke says, “We played pipes” (Luke 7), concerns the Lord, whose eating and drinking with others signified the joy of the kingdom.

“And wisdom has been justified by her children.”

[Jerome and Bede.] Whatever you may think of me, I am nevertheless understood by the apostles to be the power of God and the wisdom of God, acting justly. Here the Lord shows that the children of wisdom understand that righteousness does not consist in abstaining or eating, but in temperance—not taking things which may rightly be reproved—and in equanimity in enduring need. For the kingdom of God is not food and drink (Rom. 14), whose use is not reproved but whose lust is; rather, it is righteousness, peace, and joy (ibid.). Wisdom is justified: God’s dispensation [Col. 0210A] and teaching are approved by the faithful; it resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (1 Pet. 5). In some manuscripts it reads: “Wisdom has been justified by her works” (James 4), because wisdom seeks not the testimony of speech but of works.

## Chapter LXV

M. 108[V] L. 115

Then he began to reproach the cities in which most of his mighty works had been done, because they had not repented.

[CASSIODORUS.] To reproach is to revile someone to his face; to speak against someone is to bite them deceitfully in their absence. The Lord therefore reproaches in order to correct, foretelling what is to come, not wishing evils upon them.

[Col. 0210B] “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes. Yet I say to you: it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you.”

[JEROME.] “Woe to you” means, “You shall be condemned.” Chorazin and Bethsaida are cities of Galilee in which the Lord performed signs while he went about the villages and towns healing the sick, as was said above. [BEDE.] Tyre and Sidon, which possessed only the natural law, are preferred to these. Tyre and Sidon, once allied with David and Solomon, believed when Christ’s disciples preached the Gospel; they embraced the faith with such devoutness that, when the apostle Paul departed from Tyre, all the citizens, with wives and children, accompanied him [Col. 0210C] as far as the ships (Acts 21).

Sackcloth, woven from camel and goat hair, signifies the remembrance of sin, which painfully pricks; while in ashes the Lord shows the consideration of death, through which the whole mass of the human race is to be reduced to dust. Moreover, sitting, in Luke, signifies humiliation, of which the Psalmist says: “Rise up after you have sat down” (Ps. 106 [Vulgate]; 107 [Hebrew numbering]); that is: “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation” (1 Pet. 5).

“And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted even to heaven? You shall descend even to hell.”

Either you will be cast down because, being exalted, you proudly resisted my preaching; or because, exalted by the renown of my lodging among you, you refused to believe the mighty works you saw [Col. 0210D]. As Luke says, it was exalted to heaven (Luke 10), according to the estimation of those who thought it could therefore be saved because it had seen many miracles of Christ. But the more signs distinguished it, the more severely it will be punished if it does not believe.

M. 109[X]

“For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, perhaps they would have remained to this day.”

Certainly their overthrow would not have occurred if correction had intervened. When the Lord says, “perhaps they would have remained,” he has no doubt; rather, he follows ordinary human usage, which often expresses as doubtful what it knows most certainly.

[Col. 0211A] “Yet I say to you that it will be more tolerable for the land of the Sodomites on the day of judgment than for you.”

“To whom much has been given, much will be required” (Luke 12); and: “The mighty will suffer mighty torments” (Wis. 6). Although the Sodomites burned with vices and, as Ezekiel testifies, were inhospitable (Ezek. 16), they would nevertheless readily have consented had grace been offered to them, unworthy though they were. Indeed, Lot among them, though righteous, neither taught nor performed signs (Gen. 19).

Why, then, was preaching given to those who would not believe, and not given to those who would believe? He knows whose every way is mercy and truth (Ps. 24 [Vulgate]; 25 [Hebrew numbering]). He has mercy on whom he wills, not by justice but by grace; whom he wills he hardens (Rom. 9), not through injustice but through the truth of retribution. [AUGUSTINE.] Yet mercy and truth thus meet [Col. 0211B] together (Ps. 48 [as cited; cf. Ps. 84/85]), so that mercy does not hinder the truth by which the worthy are punished, nor truth hinder the mercy by which the unworthy are delivered.

God, eternally knowing that human conduct would be evil, and that people could be saved neither by severity alone nor advance in merit by mercy alone, decreed what should be preached in each age, allowing each person to his own judgment—that is, to the natural law. But because the natural law had grown dull through the habit of sinning, the Law was preached to restrain sinners. And because man again did not restrain himself through the severity of the Law, but rather was held guilty by the prohibition, mercy was preached: mercy that would save those fleeing to it and blind those rejecting it, sending the Gentiles toward the promises made to the Jews, so that the Jews themselves [Col. 0211C] might at least be converted through emulation of the Gentiles. This is the depth of God’s counsel (Rom. 11), by which in wondrous providence he restored Jews and Gentiles to the life they had lost in Adam.

## CHAPTER LXVI

R. 61[VIII] L. 91

“And when the apostles came to Jesus, they reported to him everything that they had done and taught.”

The apostles come to Jesus as streams to their spring. “The rivers return to the place from which they go forth” (Eccl. 1). They report to him what they had done and how they had taught, always giving thanks for what they had received.

[Col. 0211D] R. 62[X]

“And he said to them: ‘Come apart into a deserted place and rest a little.’ For there were many coming and going, and they had no opportunity even to eat.”

The need for rest is shown when it says: “For there were many coming,” and so forth. He leads apart those whom he chooses, so that amid those living wickedly they may not attend to wicked things—as Lot in Sodom (Gen. 19), Job in the land of Uz (Job 1), and Obadiah in the house of Ahab (3 Kings 18). “Rest a little,” he says, like birds in the branches of the mustard tree. Here the saints’ rest is slight and their labor long; but later it will be said to them that they may rest from their labors (Rev. 14).

Many were coming and going. In Noah’s ark, animals that were within [Col. 0212A] were sent outside (Gen. 7), and those outside burst in: so in the Church Judas departed (Matt. 27), and the thief drew near. So long as persons fall away from the faith, the Church has no rest without sorrow; Rachel, weeping for her children, refused to be comforted (Jer. 31). Yet the saints will have opportunity to eat at the banquet in which new wine will be drunk, when a new song is sung in a new heaven and a new earth by new people (Rev. 14).

## CHAPTER LXVII

L. 107

“After these things the Lord appointed another seventy-two, and sent them two by two before his face into every city and place where he himself was about to come.”

[Col. 0212B] Just as the twelve apostles are the pattern of bishops, so the seventy-two are the figure of presbyters—that is, priests of the second rank—although in the earliest times of the Church both were called presbyters and both were called bishops. The seventy-two are well sent, either because the Gospel was to be preached to an equal number of nations, so that just as the twelve were first sent on account of the twelve tribes of Israel, these might be sent on account of foreign peoples; or because the number of preachers indicated that the whole world was to be illumined through the Gospel of the Holy Trinity, just as the sun completes seventy-two hours of its light in a three-day circuit.

For the Lord himself calls himself the day, but his apostles hours: “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” (John 11). Through three days, moreover, the mystery of the Trinity is shown: hence the Lord rose on the third day; the ancient people, arriving at Mount Sinai (Exod. 19), received the Law on the third day; and on the third day after arriving, it crossed the same river Jordan [Col. 0212C] (Josh. 3), by which the grace of baptism was commended.

They are sent two by two, which suggests to us that one who does not have charity toward another ought never to undertake the office of preaching. Charity cannot exist among fewer than two; for no one is properly said to have charity toward himself. He sends them before his face because words of exhortation go before, by which truth is received in the mind. Often the tongue of preachers is restrained through their own wickedness; often through the fault of their subjects. Concerning their own wickedness the Psalmist says: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recite my righteous deeds and take my covenant in your mouth?” (Ps. 49 [Vulgate]; 50 [Hebrew numbering]). Concerning the vice of subjects the Lord says to Ezekiel: “I shall make your tongue cling to your palate, and you shall be mute and not like a man who rebukes, because they are a provoking house” (Ezek. 3). It is as if he said: The people are not worthy to receive exhortation.

“And he said to them.”

L. 116[I] M. 98 R. 96 A. 120

“He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me. But he who despises me despises him who sent me.”

[BEDE.] In hearing or despising the Gospel, hearers should learn that they do not hear or despise insignificant persons, but the Savior himself and his Father. For in the disciple the teacher is heard, and in the Son the Father is honored. Or thus: Whoever does not show mercy to one of these my brethren does not show it to me, who assumed for their sake the form of a servant and the clothing of poverty. “He who despises me despises him who sent me,” because “I and the Father are one” (John 10).

L. 117[X]

“But the seventy-two returned with joy, saying: ‘Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name.’ And he said to them: ‘I was watching Satan fall like lightning from heaven.’”

Then I saw him when he fell. His saying that he fell like lightning signifies his fall from the heights; and, though cast down, he still transforms himself into an angel of light [Col. 0213B] (2 Cor. 11). The disciples attribute the honor to Christ’s name; but because, still weak in faith, they rejoice in powers and are lifted up by the working of signs, they are frightened by this example and recalled to humility, so that they may recognize that, if they become proud, they who are earthly must be humbled, remembering that the devil was cast out of heaven because of pride (Isa. 14).

“Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy; and nothing shall harm you.”

By serpents and scorpions he signifies every kind of unclean spirit, to be expelled from the possessed, although this may also be understood literally. Paul, attacked by a viper, suffered no harm (Acts [Col. 0213C] 28), and John, having drunk poison, remained unharmed. Serpents, which injure by the tooth and rage openly, are either people or demons who cast the poisons of perverse persuasion before virtues in their beginnings. Scorpions, which harm by the tail and lie hidden in ambush, are those who strive to corrupt virtues already brought to completion.

“Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that spirits are subject to you. But rejoice that your names are written in heaven.”

Casting out spirits and performing other miracles are sometimes not due to the merit of the one who performs them; rather, they are granted through the invocation of Christ’s name, either for the condemnation of those invoking it or for the benefit of those who see and hear. In this God is always honored, through whose name miracles are performed, even though those performing the signs are despised. In the Acts of the Apostles the sons of Sceva cast out demons (Acts 19), and Judas the betrayer is said to have performed many signs. Christ’s disciples should therefore rejoice, not at the humiliation of demons, but at their own exaltation: raised up from where the demons fell, they may ascend through humility. For their names being written in heaven means that they are predestined. Although all things are eternally fixed in God’s memory, yet by a certain prerogative it is said: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2).

M. 110[X] L. 118

“At that very hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said: ‘I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden [Col. 0214A] these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones.’”

Rejoicing in the Holy Spirit over the salvation of the humble people to whom he spoke, he gives thanks and rejoices in the Father because he disclosed to the apostles the mysteries of his coming—mysteries unknown to the Scribes and Pharisees, who seemed wise to themselves. Hence above: “Wisdom is justified by her children” (Luke 7). Confession does not always signify repentance, but sometimes thanksgiving. In saying “Father,” he shows himself begotten of God, not created, as heretics say; in calling him “Lord,” he shows him to be the Creator of heaven and earth. [BEDE.] He aptly set not the foolish and dull, but little ones—that is, the humble—in opposition to the wise and prudent, in order to show that he condemns pride, not keenness of understanding [Col. 0214B]. For humility is the key of knowledge, of which he says elsewhere: “You have taken away the key of knowledge” (Luke 11), that is, the humility of faith in Christ, by which you could have attained knowledge of his divinity.

“Yes, Father, because thus it was pleasing before you.”

The meaning is: Certainly, Father, you did these things because thus it pleased you—that is, it pleased you in your sight. By these words we receive examples of humility, lest we presumptuously investigate the heavenly counsels concerning the calling of some and the rejection of others. He did not give a reason, but said that it so pleased God, showing that what pleases the Just One cannot be unjust. Therefore, in paying wages to the laborers in the vineyard, he says: “I wish to give to this last one as to you” (Matt. 20). Thus, in all things ordered by God, the manifest reason is the will of hidden justice [Col. 0214C].

M. 111[III] L. 119 A. 148, 30

“All things have been delivered to me by my Father.”

[JEROME.] Therefore I confess to the Father, because the Father has delivered all things to me. He does not speak of the elements, but of those who come to the Father through the Son and were formerly rebellious. Of all these he says elsewhere: “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me” (John 6). [AMBROSE.] Or thus: When you hear “all things,” you acknowledge the Almighty—not one unlike the Father, not degenerate from him. When you hear “delivered,” you confess the Son, to whom all things rightly belong by nature, through the unity of substance, rather than being bestowed as a gift by grace.

Note that Christ, insofar as he is man, confesses—that is, gives thanks—to the Father, indeed to the undivided Trinity. But insofar as he himself is the radiance that shone from the Father beyond understanding, he gives no thanks, although he has all things from the Father, because he has them by nature [Col. 0214D].

M. 112[III] L. 119 A. 3 and 44 and 61 and 67 and 87 and 90 and 142 and 154

“And no one knows the Son except the Father; nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him.”

[JEROME—BEDE.] Let Eunomius be ashamed, who says that he possesses full knowledge of the Father and the Son. This must not be understood as though the Son could be known by no one except the Father alone, whereas the Father could be known not only by the Son but also by those to whom the Son reveals him. Rather, “and to whom the Son wills [Col. 0215A] to reveal” must be referred to both clauses, so that you understand both to be revealed through the Son. For the Father makes himself known through his Word, and the Word makes himself known, because he is the light of our mind.

[HILARY.] The things delivered to the Son are not other than those which are known in him to the Father alone. And the things known to the Son alone are those which belong to the Father. Thus, in this secret of mutual knowledge, it is understood that nothing existed in the Son unknowable except what is unknowable in the Father. Observe that where the Father alone is said to know the Son, or the Son alone to know the Father, creatures alone are excluded. For neither is the Son excluded from knowledge of himself, nor is the Father excluded from knowing himself; and the Holy Spirit, consubstantial with both, is in no way separated from the complete knowledge of either. Hence Paul: “The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God” [Col. 0215B] (1 Cor. 2).

“And turning to his disciples, he said:”

M. 113[X]

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.”

[JEROME.] He speaks of the burden of sin, or invites those pressed under the yoke of the Law to the Gospel. In what way is the grace of the Gospel lighter than the Law, when adultery is punished under the Law but lust under the Gospel; murder there, but anger here? Under the Law works are required; under the Gospel, the will. Even if it does not achieve its effect, it nevertheless does not lose its reward: thus, if a virgin is violated against her will, she is received as a virgin under the Gospel, but under [Col. 0215C] the Law is rejected as though defiled. “You who labor” means either in the difficulties of the Law or in acquiring riches. “I will refresh you,” that is, I will restore you once unburdened through the Gospel, promising the eternal kingdom.

“Take my yoke upon yourselves, and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart; and you shall find rest for your souls.”

The yoke is called Christ’s Gospel, joining Jews and Gentiles in one faith, so that they may cultivate the soil of their heart with the ploughshare of sacred speech. “Take the yoke upon yourselves”—namely, upon the higher part of your mind, holding it in honor. Learn also from my example to be meek in heart and humble in heart, lest a serpent lie hidden beneath the appearance of a dove. The humble despise no one; the meek, persevering continually in gentleness of spirit, injure no one. Thus through tranquility of mind they finally find eternal rest for their souls [Col. 0215D].

“For my yoke is sweet, and my burden light.”

[HILARY.] What is sweeter than Christ’s yoke? What lighter than his burden? To become approved; to abstain from crime; to will good and refuse evil; to love all, hate evil, pursue eternal life, not be captivated by present things, and not wish another to suffer what would be burdensome to oneself. Although the way leading to life is narrow in its constrained beginning, as he says elsewhere (Matt. 7), in the course of time it is widened by the inexpressible sweetness of love. The yoke of faith is sweet compared with the Law, because there children are wounded, but here those to be saved are washed. The burden of the Gospel is light in comparison [Col. 0216A] with the Law, because there adultery is punished by stoning, but here it is cleansed through repentance.

L. 182[V] M. 96

“If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters—yes, even his own life—he cannot be my disciple. And whoever does not carry his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.”

[GREGORY.] It is worth asking how we are commanded to hate parents when we are also commanded to love our enemies (Matt. 5). And Truth says concerning a wife: “What God has joined, let no man separate” (Matt. 19). Paul says: “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the Church” (Eph. 5). If we consider the force of the command, we can do both: love our neighbors and, in obeying God’s way, disregard those opposed to us. We must indeed apply hatred to our neighbors in such a way that we love in them what they are, but hate what hinders us on God’s path.

To show that this is what must be done, the Lord immediately added: “Yes, even his own life.” For we rightly hate our own life when we do not yield to its fleshly desires but follow the Lord while carrying the cross. Thus what is despised in order to be led to something better is, as it were, loved through hatred. To this teaching concerning contempt for the world and rejection of the body is attached, under the comparison of building a tower, a teaching about perseverance, for which patient endurance joined with humility is necessary. It is as though he said: You ought so to hate, carry the cross, and come after me, because thus the edifice of faith will be completed, and thus one comes to the kingdom. This is what follows.

L. 183[X]

“For which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the costs necessary, to see whether he has enough to finish it? Otherwise, after he has laid the foundation and is unable to complete it, all who see it may begin to mock him, saying: ‘This man began to build and was unable to finish.’”

We ought to anticipate everything we do by consideration. Therefore, if, upon the foundation of faith, we wish to complete the lofty structure of a perfect life through assumed patience [repentance], we must first prepare ourselves for the adversities of the world. For this is the difference between an earthly and a heavenly building: an earthly building is constructed by gathering resources, but a heavenly one by distributing them. Let us therefore sit down and calculate; that is, resting from the tumults of the world, let us carefully discern that temporal substance must be given away, the heart turned from desires, and the soul prepared against the world’s adversities. Otherwise, failing in the building of good works, we shall suffer mockery from enemies who rejoice in our failure; for, in Paul’s words, “we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men” (1 Cor. 4).

“Or what king, about to engage in war against another king, does not first sit down and consider whether he can meet with ten thousand the one who comes against him with twenty thousand? Otherwise, while he is still far away, he sends an embassy and asks for terms of peace.”

If a king seeks peace from a king, much more should we, who are weak, have peace with God. To understand that someone is saved by God justly because of merits is, as it were, to wage war with God. But this comparison shows that no one can attain glory unless the sentence of the severe Judge is tempered by mercy. For in his sight every human being is imperfect. Therefore, just as forethought is necessary to avoid an enemy’s mockery, so it is necessary to obtain the Judge’s mercy. Perhaps we cut off an evil deed from ourselves; but can we sufficiently render an account of our thoughts? A person meets God, as it were, with ten thousand when he offers the works of the Ten Commandments that he has outwardly done; but God comes against him, as it were, with a doubled number, when he examines one scarcely prepared in outward deed concerning both deed and thought. He is said still to be far away because he is not yet seen as present in judgment. Let us therefore send an embassy to propitiate him: namely, tears and works of mercy from a pure affection.

L. 184[V] M. 96

“So therefore, everyone of you who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple.”

Since one who does not calculate the cost cannot build well, nor can one safely meet the opponent without first sending an embassy, neither can one be my [Col. 0217C] disciple who does not renounce all things. Here we are taught that building a tower and making peace with the stronger one are nothing other than being Christ’s disciple; while preparing resources or sending an embassy to make peace is nothing other than renouncing everything we possess. Included among these are love of neighbors and our own life, which some understand as temporal life; and we must possess it in such a way that it does not hinder us from eternal things.

There is, however, a difference between renouncing all things and leaving all things. It belongs to the few who are perfect to leave everything and desire eternal things alone; but it belongs to all faithful people to renounce all things—that is, to conduct earthly affairs in such a way that their whole mind nevertheless tends toward heavenly things.

## CHAPTER LXVIII

[Col. 0217D]

L. 41[II] M. 114 R. 24

“And it happened on the second-first Sabbath, as Jesus passed through grainfields, that his hungry disciples plucked ears of grain and ate them, rubbing them in their hands.”

[JEROME—BEDE.] The Lord’s disciples rubbed ears of grain because, as Mark says, chapter 52, they had no opportunity to eat on account of the excessive importunity of those who came to be healed (Mark 6). Thus they hungered as human beings. That rubbing signifies a more austere life: a life seeking not prepared meals but simple food. Note that the first apostles abolish the letter of the Sabbath against the Ebionites, who accept the other apostles but reject Paul as a transgressor of the Law.

[BEDE.] Luke aptly calls the Sabbath which the apostles were setting aside *deuteroproton*, that is, “second-first.” He wished to indicate that the observance of the legal Sabbath ought henceforth to cease, and that the liberty of the natural Sabbath, which existed until Moses’ time and was like the other days, ought to be restored. He calls the Sabbath of this time, on which useful work may lawfully be done as on other days, “second-first” to distinguish it from the Jewish Sabbath: first, that is, preferred; second, either in chronological order or in the gift of grace. Thus understand “second-first Sabbath” as nothing other than what is higher in relation to what is lower. Hence one does not err if one wishes to call Jesus Christ the second-first Adam: he rightly preceded Adam through merit and grace, not in the order of human birth [Col. 0218B].

It may also be understood in this way: the Sabbath of the New Testament is second and first—second because it follows the legal Sabbath, first because it was observed by the righteous of old before the decrees of the Law. Mystically, the disciples pass through grainfields—that is, through the Gentiles—hungering for their salvation. Hence: “Rise, Peter; slaughter and eat” (Acts 10). There is a wonderful harmony of mystery: animals are slaughtered and ears of grain rubbed, just as Paul says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth, and put off the old man with his deeds” (Col. 3). To pluck ears is to draw people away from earthly intention; to rub them in the hands is to strip the purity of the mind even from the lust of the flesh, as from the coverings of the ears. To eat the grains is to incorporate into the members of the Church, through the mouths of preachers, each person cleansed from every defilement of flesh and spirit.

In Mark the disciples are reported to have done this while going ahead of the Lord (Mark 2), because the teacher’s word goes before and the grace of heavenly visitation follows. [BEDE.] This is fittingly done on Sabbaths, because preachers labor in hope of eternal rest, to which they also invite others. Or thus: The field is the world; the crop of the field is the fruitfulness of the human race; the ears are the fruits of the Church, with which the apostles are satisfied as they feed themselves upon our progress.

Otherwise: Those walk through grainfields with the Lord who, obeying the divine commands, delight in sacred words. They hunger in the grainfields when, as they pass through the sacred words by reading, they desire to find matters through which, more intensely kindled, they may be fed as if with bread by the love of God [Col. 0218D]. They pluck and rub ears when they take up and examine the testimonies of Scripture until they draw out the marrow of love, veiled beneath the lowliness of the letter as beneath the bristling husks of ears. But those who follow only the surface of the letter—the foolish defenders of the Sabbath—know neither refreshment of mind nor seek rest for souls. Therefore it follows:

“But some of the Pharisees said to them: ‘Why do you do what is not lawful on Sabbaths?’”

The other Evangelists report this objection as addressed to the Lord. But whether it was said to him, to his disciples, or to both, the answer belonged to him as teacher; in it, through the gift of new grace, he shows that the leisure of the Law is the work of grace, rebuking the teachers of the Law for not knowing the Law. No question is raised concerning the wasting of crops, because the Law permits one to eat from a neighbor’s vineyard or grain, but not to put in a sickle or carry anything away.

“And Jesus answered and said to them: ‘Have you not even read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God, took and ate the loaves of offering, and gave them to those who were with him—loaves which it was not lawful to eat except for priests alone?’”

David, fleeing Saul, came to Nob and asked the priest Ahimelech for food [Col. 0219B] (1 Sam. 21). [BEDE—AMBROSE.] Since he had no common bread, he gave him consecrated bread, which priests and Levites alone ought to have eaten; yet he first asked whether David’s young men had kept themselves from women since yesterday and the day before (ibid.). For he did not doubt that human safety is a sacrifice pleasing to God, according to the prophet’s saying: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Hos. 6). That is: I prefer to rescue a person from the danger of hunger than to offer sacrifice to God.

The meaning is: If David is holy, and Ahimelech the high priest is not reproved by you, but both transgressed the Law’s command with a commendable excuse, and hunger is the cause, why do you not approve in the apostles what you approve in others? The loaves of offering were baked before the Sabbath, offered on Sabbath morning, and set upon the sacred table—six on one side and six on the other, facing one another—with two golden bowls placed above them, full of incense; they remained until the next Sabbath. Then others were set in their place, and the former loaves were given to the priests; and, when the incense had been kindled on the sacred fire in which burnt offerings were made, other incense was added over the other twelve loaves.

At the hour when David came, received the consecrated loaves, and ate them, he figuratively showed that priestly food would pass into the use of the peoples; or that we all ought to imitate priestly life; or that all the sons of the Church are priests. For we are anointed into a holy priesthood, offering ourselves to God as spiritual sacrifices. Abiathar, son of Ahimelech—or Abimelech, as some codices have it—was present with his father when David asked for and received the loaves. But after Saul killed Abimelech, along with eighty-five men of his household who were of priestly descent, Abiathar fled to David and became the companion of his exile. Later, under David’s reign, he received the rank of high priest, becoming more eminent than his father; and for this reason he was worthy that the Lord, as Mark relates, should mention him as high priest, even while his father was alive.

“And he said to them.”

M. 115[X]

“Or have you not read in the Law that on Sabbaths the priests in the temple violate the Sabbath and are without guilt? But I say to you that one greater than the temple is here.”

[JEROME.] The priests violated the Sabbath by slaughtering bulls and circumcising boys. Here *hic* must be read not as a pronoun but as an adverb of place, as though he said: I, the Lord of the temple, who am here, am greater than the temple—that is, better. Therefore, if the figurative temple could defend the priests serving it, why cannot the spiritual temple defend disciples who believe in it?

R. 25 M. 116 L. 42

“The Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath.”

Therefore greater care must be given to human welfare [Col. 0220B] than to the keeping of the Sabbath. The command to keep the Sabbath was given in such a way that, if necessity existed, one who set it aside was not guilty. Circumcision on the Sabbath was not prohibited when necessary. Joshua marched around Jericho’s walls with the army for seven days (Josh. 6), and the Maccabees fought on the Sabbath through necessity. Thus what was not lawful in the Law became lawful for the hungry disciples through the necessity of hunger. Today also, if an ill person breaks a fast, he is not held guilty.

## CHAPTER LXIX

“And it happened on another Sabbath that he entered the synagogue and taught. And there was a man there whose right hand was withered.”

[BEDE.] The Lord especially teaches and performs miracles on Sabbaths, not only to signify the spiritual Sabbath but also because the people’s gathering was larger. The man with the withered hand signifies the human race dried up in good work because the hand of the first parent was extended toward the forbidden fruit; but through the Lord’s mercy it was restored to salvation by the innocent hands stretched out on the cross. The hand was fittingly withered in the synagogue, because where there is a greater gift of knowledge, there the transgressor is subject to greater guilt.

[JEROME.] This sick man is said to have been a mason, earning his livelihood by his hands; and the hand of the Jews, to whom the care of the spiritual building had been entrusted, was withered until the Savior’s coming, but afterward was made right in the believing apostles.

[Col. 0220D] “But the Scribes and Pharisees watched him, to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find an accusation against him.”

Because he had plausibly excused his disciples, they watched him, so that if he healed on the Sabbath they might accuse him of transgression, but if he did not heal, of cruelty or weakness.

“But he knew their thoughts. And he said to the man who had the withered hand: ‘Rise and stand in the middle.’ And he rose and stood.”

Hence: “The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain” (Ps. 93 [Vulgate]; 94 [Hebrew numbering]). The sick man stood in the middle so that all might see him.

“And Jesus said to them: ‘I ask you whether it is lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do evil; to save a life or to destroy it?’”

[Col. 0221A] [BEDE.] That is, to heal a person or not to deliver him from destruction? Anticipating the calumny prepared against him, he rebukes the Jews, who thought that on the Sabbath one must rest even from good works, whereas the Law says: “You shall do no servile work on it” (Lev. 23). But “servile work” is said of sin, for “everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8). In the customary manner of Scripture, he used “life” for “person,” as in: “These are the lives that went out from Jacob’s thigh” (Exod. 1).

Or he asks about the saving of the soul when he is about to heal the body because the healing of the hand itself signified the salvation of the soul, which, ceasing from good works, seemed in a sense to have a withered right hand. The supremely merciful one destroys no one; but when he does not save, he is said to destroy, according to Scripture’s customary manner—just as he “hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. 10), that is, he did not soften it but permitted it to be hardened [Col. 0221B].

“But they were silent. And looking around at them all, he said to the man: ‘Stretch out your hand.’ And he stretched it out, and his hand was restored sound, like the other.”

Having nothing to answer, they are silent; and the Lord looks around at them all, as though angry at their unbelief. The hand is commanded to be stretched out because the weakness of an unfruitful soul is healed in no better way than through the generosity of almsgiving. Hence Ecclesiasticus: “My son, let not your hand be stretched out to receive and drawn back in giving” (Sir. 4).

[JEROME.] This man signifies the greedy, who, unwilling to give, wish to receive; to plunder, and not to distribute. They are told to stretch out their hands—that is: “Let him who stole steal no longer; rather, let him labor, working with his hands what is good, so that he may have something to give to one who is in need” (Eph. 4). Before Christ’s coming, the man had his right hand weak because he was sluggish in almsgiving; his left hand sound because he attended to his own advantage. But when Christ came, his right hand was healed like the left, because what he had greedily gathered he now distributed in charity [Col. 0221C].

“And he said to them: ‘What man among you, having one sheep, if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? How much more valuable is a man than a sheep?’”

Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath. By a fitting example he shows that those who accuse him of violating the Sabbath in a work of charity themselves violate the Sabbath in a work of greed. He equates doing good on the Sabbath with saving a life. The observance of the Sabbath was indeed a figure: after doing good through the six ages of the world, in the seventh rest they would cease only from evils. For the fruit of a good work will not be idle when it rests in the praise of God. [AUGUSTINE.] Where Matthew says that the Lord was asked whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath, this does not conflict with Mark and Luke, who relate that they were questioned by the Lord whether it was lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do evil. For it must be understood that they first questioned the Lord, and then the Lord questioned them; and, as they remained silent, he proposed the comparison of the sheep.

But they were filled with folly, and discussed among themselves what they might do to Jesus.

[Col. 0222A] [JEROME.] Envy was the cause. For neither was the man at fault for stretching out his hand, nor Jesus for healing; but it was great folly to deliberate about putting to death one whose benefits they so greatly needed.

M. 118[X]

But Jesus, knowing this, withdrew from there; and many followed him, and he healed them all.

Jesus did not wish to give the Pharisees an occasion for impiety against himself. Therefore he fled those who hated him and came where he found people following in love, and thus deserving to be healed.

And he charged them not to make him known, that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled:

> Behold my servant, whom I have chosen,  
> my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased;  
> I will put my Spirit upon him,  
> and he shall proclaim judgment to the nations.  
> He shall not contend or cry out,  
> nor shall anyone hear his voice in the streets.  
> (Isaiah 42)

Silence about the healing was not commanded, for the health restored to each person was itself its own witness. [HILARY.] By commanding secrecy, therefore, the Lord avoids boastful self-display, yet nonetheless grants knowledge of himself precisely in warning that people should be silent about him; for the observance of silence proceeds from the matter that is to be kept silent. Indeed, by this wish that people be silent concerning him, the fulfilment of Isaiah’s words is accomplished. Isaiah speaks in the person of the Father: “Behold my servant.” [REMIGIUS.] That is, in the form of a servant, he was a child in malice, not in understanding; chosen to restore the human race, for which no one else was fit. Hence he is shown to be specially beloved by God, and the Father’s will to have taken pleasure in him. For he alone is the Lamb without blemish. By “the soul of God” is understood the affection of his will. By “Spirit” he means the Holy Spirit, of whom it is elsewhere said: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him” (Isaiah 11). Through the preaching of the New Testament he shall proclaim to the nations the future judgment and the just judgments now being carried out, though hidden. The streets are the broad way of life; those who dwell there and refuse to be converted do not hear the Lord’s voice. Therefore he sometimes spoke to them not in his own direct voice but in parables. Against such people he did not contend or cry out: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2); rather, “like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and he did not open his mouth” (Isaiah 53).

> He shall not break a bruised reed,  
> and he shall not quench a smoking flax,  
> until he brings judgment forth unto victory;  
> and in his name the nations shall hope.

[JEROME.] Whoever does not stretch out a hand to a sinner or bear a brother’s burden breaks the bruised reed; and whoever despises the small spark of faith in little ones quenches the smoking flax. Christ did not do this; rather, he came to seek what had perished (Luke 19). For he preserved patience until the judgment being carried out in him should attain victory, and, once the prince of this world had been cast out, he should return to the kingdom and sit at the Father’s right hand, until he places his enemies beneath his feet (Psalm 109). [HILARY.] Or thus: by the bruised reed which is not broken he means the nations, shaken by the wind of vanity and tossed about in sins, but preserved for salvation through Christ. By the smoking flax which is not quenched he means that the small breath remaining from the remnants of ancient grace was not taken away from Israel, because in the time of repentance there is the possibility of recovering the whole light. The reed may also signify the Jews, yielding to every wind and scattered through their disagreement with one another. [REMIGIUS.] The smoking flax, however, is the nations, which the exceedingly bitter smoke of error enveloped after the heat of the natural law had almost died out, until Christ raised them from a small spark to a great flame of charity. Indeed, his preaching, overcome by no snares, will shine upon the world until he brings forth—that is, reveals—the final judgment, for a complete and irrevocable victory over all his enemies. The name of Christ is knowledge of him in Christian faith, in which the Christian nations shall hope.

## CHAPTER LXX

L. 43[II] M. 149 R. 60

And it came to pass in those days that he went out into the mountain to pray; and he spent the whole night in prayer to God.

[BEDE.] He heals as God; he prays as man. When he prays, he indicates the contemplative life; when he heals, the active life: lest anyone, because of care for a neighbor, grow slack in the pursuit of contemplation, or, because of the pursuit of divine contemplation—though it is higher—neglect care for a neighbor. Since the Father has placed all things in the hands of the Son, he is judge: this is the mark of provident power. Yet, to fulfil the form of man, the Son entreats the Father for us, because he is our advocate, in whom the office of loving mercy consists. Hence John says: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ” (1 John 2). If he is advocate, he ought to intercede for our sins. Therefore he does not entreat as though weak, but as one who obtains what he asks, prescribing a pattern of prayer that we ought to imitate. He who seeks God in prayer goes out to the mountain, suppressing the rising tumult of vices and advancing to the summit of a higher court, so that, when outward tumult has ceased, he may silently speak with the Lord, through inward desires, in a certain hidden place of the mind. But whoever prays for riches, worldly honor, or an enemy’s death lies in the depths, and his prayer becomes sin to him (Psalm 108).

M. 131[II] R. 36 L. 76

And going out of the house, he sat beside the sea; and great crowds gathered to him, so that, entering a boat, he sat down. And the whole crowd stood on the shore.

Whether the Lord, on the same day on which he called the disciples after prayer, or at another time, went out of the house and did what follows, does not trouble one who knows the Evangelists’ manner of anticipating and recapitulating in narrative. Matthew, indeed, immediately after the account he gives of the Lord’s mother and brothers, adds these words: “On that day Jesus went out of the house and sat by the sea,” etc. (Matthew 13). But, according to the practice of Scripture, in using “day” for “time,” he seems to have anticipated. Luke, however, certainly places the election of the apostles before the sermon delivered on the mountain, recounting it in the manner in which omitted matters are customarily recapitulated: “And when day came, he called his disciples and chose twelve of them, whom he named apostles” (Luke 6). [JEROME.] It is therefore probable that the proper order of the history is preserved here. Yet nothing prevents an artificial order from being observed here, as often elsewhere. The merciful Lord goes out of the house—that is, from profound mysteries—and sits beside the sea of this world, so that he may at least be heard on the shore. For the sea is the world: bitter when tasted, restless with the waves of vices. Yet the predestined are rescued from it by the Lord himself, who sweetens bitterness, turns sorrow into joy, and sickness into health. Whenever the word “crowds” is inserted in the Gospel, just as there is diversity of persons, so also diversity of wills is indicated. For they followed Christ for different reasons. [HILARY—BEDE.] Yet the gathering of the crowds prefigured the multitude of peoples to be assembled to Christ through the apostles, into whose minds he would ascend through faith, as is signified by his boarding the boat. For the ship upon the sea presents a type of the Church, to be built amid unbelievers and opponents; within it the word of life is set forth and preached, and by the grace of his visitation he illumines it and consecrates in it a dwelling beloved by himself. But those outside lie alongside it like barren, useless sand, and cannot receive the understanding of the divine discourse. Nevertheless, those standing on the shore—neither in the sea nor in the boat—bear the figure of those who have withdrawn from the bitterness of the reprobate but have not yet been instructed in the heavenly mysteries for which they long.

And he spoke many things to them in parables, saying:

## CHAPTER LXXI

Behold, the one who sows went out to sow.

[JEROME—BEDE.] He speaks many things in parables, because if he spoke everything parabolically, his hearers would depart without profit. A parable is a comparison, made by means of some likeness, of things differing in nature. The sower who went out to sow is understood to be Christ, the Son of God, who, going out from the bosom of the Father, came into the world to sow, through himself and through his own, the word of truth among human beings—the word which he saw with the Father.

And while he sowed, some fell beside the way; they were trampled down, and the birds of heaven came and devoured them.

Some fell—understand, grains or seeds—beside the way. The way is the mind, worn down and dried out by the continual passage of evil thoughts. There the seed perishes in two ways: it is trampled by the passage of carnal thoughts, and demons devour it—that is, seize and swallow it up with a certain pleasure—so that the mind does not retain in memory what it neglected to practise in action. Demons are called birds of heaven either because they are of a heavenly and spiritual nature, or because they dwell in the air.

But others fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil. And they sprang up at once, because they had no depth of soil. But when the sun rose, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered.

The seeds falling on rocky ground—that is, soil abounding in stones—can indeed germinate quickly, but their root does not take hold, because it has no depth of earth, that is, no profundity; and therefore it withers in the heat of the sun. Here the rock signifies the hardness of an obstinate mind; the soil, the gentleness of an obedient soul; the sun, the heat of persecution. Thus the seed of the word falls upon rock when the sweetness of promises moves an untamed heart, not penetrated by the ploughshare of true faith. [Col. 0225B] There, as Luke says, it finds no moisture (Luke 8), that is, no love of virtue. It sprang up immediately through mere recollection, not through effectiveness, because it had no depth of soil, that is, no profundity of a good heart in which it might be firmly founded. And when the sun rose—that is, the heat of persecution or of any tribulation—it was scorched, that is, came to dryness and wholly withered, because it had no root of steadfast desire. The depth of soil is the uprightness of a mind trained in heavenly disciplines and tested in temptations.

But others fell among thorns; and the thorns grew up and choked them.

Other seeds fell among thorns. The word of God also falls among thorns when it is received by a heart anxiously occupied with concern for riches; and then multiplied riches, which are understood by the thorns, occupy the mind so that spiritual fruit cannot grow in it.

But others fell on good soil, and yielded fruit: one a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, another thirtyfold.

Just as there were three kinds of bad soil, so there are three kinds of good soil. For one person is good, another better, and another best. Since the number ten is customarily taken for perfection, because observance is contained in the ten commandments of the law, the number one hundred, which arises through ten multiplied, denotes great perfection. Therefore good soil bears fruit a hundredfold when a gentle and teachable heart attains the active life through love of neighbor and the contemplative life through love of God, and is adorned with the perfection of spiritual virtues. In the number six, however, because the adornment of the world was completed in six days, the sixtyfold fruit fittingly signifies the perfection of good action in fulfilling the Decalogue; while the thirtyfold fruit is fulfilment of the law in faith in the holy Trinity.

As he said these things, he cried out: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

Wherever this admonition is inserted, it shows that what is said is mystical and should be sought with greater attention. Therefore, whoever has ears of the heart—that is, understanding of mind—let him hear; that is, let him understand these words spiritually.

## CHAPTER LXXII

[Col. 0226A]

M. 136

He set before them another parable, saying: “The kingdom of heaven has become like a man who sowed good seed in his field.”

[RABANUS.] Understand the kingdom of heaven to be Christ, who grants reign in heavenly places; and to serve him is to reign. Only a good person sows what is good, striving to bring the seed of good will to good works.

But while people slept, his enemy came and oversowed tares in the midst of the wheat, and went away. Morally, this teaches the need for vigilance. The sleepers are teachers of the Church when, through sloth and negligence, they neglect those entrusted to them, or when they undergo the sleep of death. Then, though the name of Christ has gone before, the devil oversows tares amid the wheat: that is, he introduces heretics among the righteous. They are called wheat because by faith they have been shaken free from the chaff of unbelief. And he went away because he could not remain long among the righteous.

But when the blade had grown and borne fruit, then the tares also appeared.

The blade grows when the word of the faithful’s preaching advances; it bears fruit when it displays works of good hope; and then the doctrines of heretics begin to show themselves. On seeing this, good people—but not yet spiritual people, who judge all things, according to Paul’s words, “The spiritual person judges all things” (1 Corinthians 2)—are disturbed because heresies exist under Christ’s name. Hence follows:

The servants of the householder came and said to him: “Lord, did you not sow good seed in your field? Where, then, did it get tares?” And he said to them: “An enemy has done this.”

On hearing of the deceit, the householder did not blaze with anger or immediately desire vengeance; likewise, when injured, let us bear it patiently. The devil is called an enemy-man because he desired to be God. Hence it is written of him in the ninth Psalm: “Arise, O Lord; let not man prevail” (Psalm 9). Therefore let the rulers of the Church keep watch, lest the enemy-man sow tares—that is, heretical doctrines. But the servants said to him: “Do you wish us to go and gather them?” And he said: “No, lest perhaps in gathering the tares you uproot the wheat along with them.”

[RABANUS.] Here room is given for repentance and an example of discernment. For the wicked are to be patiently borne where there are some good people who may be helped. Moreover, one who errs today may perhaps defend the truth tomorrow; and the wicked must necessarily be mixed with the good, by whom the good are tested or by comparison with whom they strive toward what is better.

“Let both grow until the harvest; and at harvest time I shall say to the reapers: Gather the tares first, and bind them into bundles to burn. But gather the wheat into my barn.”

He says that the tares are bound into bundles because each person will be punished according to the degree of his perversity; but those who have loved the unity of faith will be gathered into heavenly dwellings. Here justice is indicated. Long-suffering, however, is indicated where he says: “Let both grow until the harvest.” [JEROME.] This seems contrary to what Paul says: “Remove the evil person from among you” (1 Corinthians 5), and that no fellowship is to be maintained with those who are called brothers and are adulterers or fornicators; but it is not contrary. For before wheat comes into ear, there is a great resemblance between it and the tare which we call *lolium*, and they can scarcely be distinguished. Thus “let both grow” is spoken of ambiguous cases, whereas “remove the evil” concerns manifest cases. Therefore the wicked are to be endured among the good until their wickedness becomes manifest, lest the righteous be uprooted with the unrighteous. For judgment must not be passed upon doubtful cases until the day comes when the hidden things of hearts and the pretences of the ungodly will be revealed. Yet some, having zeal for God but not according to knowledge, presume to avoid those not yet convicted or confessing guilt—as though saying, “Do you wish us to go and gather them?” that is, “Shall we excommunicate them?” But divine Scripture, and likewise the mature judgment of prelates, rebukes such persons, as the Lord rebuked James and John when, not received in a certain city, they said: “Lord, do you wish us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” (Luke 9).

## CHAPTER LXXIII

M. 137[II] R. 44 L. 167

He set before them another parable, saying: “To what is the kingdom of God like, and to what shall I judge it comparable? Or to what parable shall we compare it? It is like a mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his garden. It is indeed the least of all vegetables, yet it becomes a tree, so that the birds of heaven come and dwell in its branches.”

The kingdom of heaven is the preaching of the Gospel. Hence the Lord says to the Jews: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to the nations” (Matthew 21). [JEROME.] The sower is the Savior, who sows in the souls of believers; or it is the person himself sowing in his own heart. The preaching of the Gospel is the least of all teachings, because at first one scarcely believes the preacher of a crucified Christ. Philosophical teachings, however, though believed at first, are finally found to contain nothing useful, and, like the herbs of the field, quickly fall away (Psalm 36). But the preaching of the Gospel, appearing small at the beginning, eventually grows—not like herbs, which quickly dry up and collapse, but like a tree enjoying long life and excellent fruitfulness. The birds are the souls of believers; the branches are the various doctrines, so that there may be a different medicine according to the variety of diseases. [BEDE.] Or thus: the kingdom of God—that is, the faith by which one comes to God—is compared to a mustard seed, either because it is said to expel poisons, that is, every doctrine of perversity, or because of its similar pungency. For faith is at first like something despised and bitter in taste, because of Christ’s weakness; but, crushed by adversities, it pours forth the grace of its power and fills those around it with its fragrance, while the glory of the resurrection and ascension is proclaimed throughout the whole world even after death. The man is Christ; the garden is the Church, to be cultivated by disciplines so that the plants of virtue may grow. He is rightly said to have received the grain that he sowed, because the gifts which he grants us together with the Father from his divinity he received with us through his humanity. Hence: “You received gifts among men” (Psalm 67). The power of faith grows throughout the world and in the mind of every believer, because no one suddenly becomes supreme. “He has set ascents in his heart,” says the Psalmist; “they shall see the God of gods in Zion” (Psalm 83). The birds, therefore, are righteous souls, which tend upward on the wings of virtues and rest there. Hence: “Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly and rest?” (Psalm 44). The humility of the Lord’s incarnation may also be understood in the mustard seed. A man took it and placed it in his garden because Joseph, having received the body of the crucified Savior, buried it in a garden. But he who was considered least among other people, who are understood by the vegetable, according to the saying “all flesh is grass” (Job 19), grew and became a tree because he rose again and ascended into heaven. He spread branches in which birds might rest, because he sent preachers throughout the world, in whose teaching and consolations faithful hearers might take breath from the weariness of this life.

## CHAPTER LXXIV

M. 138[V] L. 168

[Col. 0228C] He spoke another parable to them: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, until the whole was leavened.”

[JEROME.] Human tastes differ, and therefore different foods are offered, so that one who is not pleased by one may be pleased by another. Leaven comes from flour and imparts to the mass of its own kind the power which it has received. [HILARY.] The Lord compared himself to this. The woman, namely the Synagogue, received him and hid him through a sentence of death, charging that the law and the prophets were dissolved by the Gospel. But he, working together with—or, perhaps, hidden within—the three measures of meal, that is, the harmonious equality of law, prophets, and Gospel, makes all things one, so that what the law established and the prophets announced may be fulfilled by the Gospel’s progress. For all things are done through the Spirit of God, of one and the same power and meaning; and nothing leavened in measures of equal proportion will be found discordant from another. Scripture is called meal because it refreshes its readers.

Otherwise, this woman is understood as the Church or the wisdom of God, which hides the leaven—that is, knowledge of the Scriptures—in three measures of meal: that is, in the spirit, soul, and body of the people, until the whole is leavened, so that the three, directed to unity, may not disagree among themselves. The spirit is the mind and rational faculty of the soul. Meal resembles the people because, just as it is made from different grains, so the people consists of different ages. Or the three powers of the soul, like three measures of meal, are reduced to one flavor when through knowledge of Scripture we possess prudence in reason, hatred against vices in anger, and desire for virtues in appetite. Otherwise, the Church mixes the faith of the Name into three measures of meal: that is, into belief in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. And when it has been leavened into one, it leads us not to knowledge of a threefold God but of one Godhead. Flour denotes divinity because it satisfies faithful souls. The three measures are the three persons, because one must speak of them with measure, as the Apostle says: “Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think unto sobriety” (Romans 12). A *satum* is a measure, according to the custom of Palestine, holding one and a half *modii*. [BEDE.] Or thus: leaven signifies love, which makes the mind fervent. We, all of us who are ground, as it were, by the upper and lower millstones of the exercise of fear and hope, are signified by meal, so that we may be one bread, though many, in Christ. Therefore the Church hides the leaven of love in three measures of meal because she commands us to love God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength. The three measures of meal may also signify the three fruits of the Lord’s seed—the thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold: namely, those of married people, continent persons, and virgins. Or the three measures are the three kinds of people: Noah, Daniel, and Job. But charity hidden in the mind must continue growing until it transforms the whole mind into its own perfection, so that it loves and remembers nothing but God. This begins here but is completed in the other life. [HILARY.] Otherwise, the three measures of meal are the human race, restored from Noah’s three sons. To it the wisdom of God commends faith, love, and sound doctrine, until the whole is leavened: that is, until at the end of the world all believers attain the glory of the perfect resurrection.

M. 139[VI] R. 45

Jesus spoke all these things to the crowds in parables. R. And with many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it.

M. And he did not speak to them without parables, so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled:

> I will open my mouth in parables;  
> I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world.  
> (Psalm 77)

He spoke to the crowds even in such parables, so that through earthly likeness they could easily perceive heavenly things. He did not speak to them without parables, because scarcely any saying of his is found in which something parabolic is not intermingled. In the seventy-seventh Psalm it is said in the Lord’s person: “I will open my mouth in parables.” Therefore one must consider more attentively that he spoke parabolically: “I will utter things hidden,” proclaiming mysteries from the treasury of my secret counsel.

M. 131[II] R. 31 L. 76

And the disciples came and said to him: “Why do you speak to them in parables?” He answered and said to them: “Because to you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given.”

[BEDE.] The mysteries of the kingdom of heaven—that is, the hidden meanings of the Scriptures—will be revealed to you who are with me, and to your followers who enter spiritually into me through understanding. But to those who are outside, as Mark writes, all things are done in parables. By “outside” he means not only those who did not care to enter the boat or know the truth, but also all like them, who follow bodily senses alone and understand nothing spiritually. Note that, when he says that all things occur in parables for those outside, he indicates that there are parables—that is, signs of mystical realities—not only in the Lord’s words but also in his deeds, into which the perverse do not penetrate.

R. 46[X]

But privately he explained everything to his disciples.

For they were worthy to hear mysteries in the inner sanctuary of wisdom who, removed from the tumult of thoughts, remained in the solitude of virtues.

M. 133[I] R. 37 L. 77 A. 109

“Therefore I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear or understand; and in them the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled, which says:

> By hearing you shall hear and shall not understand;  
> and seeing you shall see and shall not perceive.  
> (Isaiah 6)

[JEROME.] “Seeing they do not see” means that, presuming to see by their own intelligence, they are deprived of spiritual understanding; and, while hearing outwardly, they do not hear in the heart, which is not to understand. Hence Isaiah says: “With outward hearing you shall hear Christ’s preaching and shall not understand; and often, with outward sight, you shall see his miracles and shall not see with the eye of the mind.”

> For the heart of this people has grown dull,  
> and they have heard heavily with their ears,  
> and they have closed their eyes,  
> lest at any time they should see with their eyes,  
> hear with their ears, understand with their heart,  
> and be converted, and I should heal them.

He calls the heart of the Jews “grown dull” because of an abundance of wickedness; thus they received the Lord’s words ungratefully, which was to hear heavily. They are said to have closed their own eyes, lest we suppose the fault to belong to nature rather than will. For though they could think and understand, they turned away the gaze of the mind through envy; and thus they themselves became the cause of God’s blinding them by abandoning them. [AUGUSTINE.] Hence John says: “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said: ‘He has blinded their eyes, that they should not see’” (John 12; Isaiah 6). Because Isaiah, in the spirit of one foreknowing all things, foretold the Jews’ blindness, they could not believe—not that they could not do so by necessity, and therefore bore no guilt, but because they were unwilling. They could not believe because, ignorant of God’s righteousness, they wished to establish their own. They are blinded and hardened because, by refusing divine help, they are not helped. That they are said not to be able to believe is a fault of human will, just as the statement that God cannot deny himself is praise of the divine will. Therefore, unwilling to open eyes and ears to truth, they deserved never to see with their eyes, hear with their ears, or understand with their heart—that is, neither to see nor to hear—and not to be converted to repentance or healed of sins, so as to receive innocence. [AUGUSTINE.] Or thus: many heard the parables because they were blinded, and they were blinded because through pride they had a heart grown dull. Yet their blindness and the obscurity of the parables became an occasion for them, lest perhaps—that is, lest at some time—they should be converted more beneficially through him who is terrible in his counsels over the children of men, who has mercy on whom he wills and justly abandons whom he wills. For because they did not understand what was obscurely spoken, they did not believe in him, and so crucified him; and thus, after the resurrection, frightened by miracles and pierced by the guilt of a greater crime, they burned with greater love after receiving pardon. Of others the Lord says: “I will speak to them in other tongues and with other lips” (Isaiah 28), namely through the plain teaching of the apostles, “and even so they will not hear me” (1 Corinthians 14); but of these he can say: “And perhaps even thus they will hear me.”

M. 134[V] L. 120

“But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear. Amen, I say to you: many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it.”

[BEDE.] He calls those eyes blessed which know the sacraments of Christ. The prophets and righteous, such as Isaiah and Abraham, saw in a riddle and not face to face. “Abraham rejoiced that he should see Christ’s day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8). Isaiah and the other prophets saw the Lord’s glory, and hence they are called “seers.” But they saw in a riddle, not in presence, as the apostles did, who had no need to be taught through angels or various kinds of visions. Those whom Luke calls kings Matthew calls righteous, because great kings are those who know how to rule over the movements of their temptations rather than succumb to them. Note that the prophets had lesser grace and lesser knowledge of Christ’s sacraments than the apostles, who especially, having received the Holy Spirit, also illumined the world. Nevertheless, some prophets, at certain times lifted above human capacity, contemplated the Godhead in intellectual vision without a riddle, just as the apostles did. Hence the Lord says in the book of Numbers: “If there be among you a prophet of the Lord, I shall appear to him in a vision or speak to him through a dream. But my servant Moses is not such; I shall speak with him mouth to mouth, openly, not through riddles and figures; he sees the Lord” (Numbers 12).

## CHAPTER LXXV

M. 135[II] R. 38 L. 78

“Therefore hear the parable of the sower. Everyone who hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it—the evil one comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart. This is the one sown beside the way.”

[RABANUS.] Everyone who hears the word of the eternal kingdom and neglects to understand it is such a person—that is, one to whom the evil one, the devil, comes. “This is the one sown” means the one upon whom seed fell beside the way. For, disdaining to receive the word of God that he hears, he by no means receives it within the path of his heart, worn down by most evil thoughts. Or thus: the word is sown outside the way which is Christ’s truth, and not in the way, when hearers do not take care to retain or understand it. Whoever does not enter that way but travels around it falls into error. We must take care, wherever the Lord expounds his own sayings, not to desire to understand anything other than, or beyond, what he himself expounds. Yet he expounded them in order to teach that meanings are to be sought also in things he did not explain.

“But he who was sown upon rocky ground is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy. Yet he has no root in himself, but is temporary. Then, when tribulation and persecution arise because of the word, he immediately falls away.”

A person who receives the seed of the word is called “sown,” just as soil is called “sown” after it has received seed. Therefore those sown on rocky ground—that is, upon thoughts full of hardness, incapable of retaining what they gladly hear—are called temporary, because they believe for a time and fall away in time of temptation; that is, they fall from tranquillity of mind. [JEROME.] There is indeed a great difference between one compelled to deny the Lord by many tribulations and one who falls at the first persecution.

“But he who was sown among thorns is the one who hears the word, and the anxiety of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it becomes fruitless.”

[GREGORY.] Though riches sometimes delight, they are thorns because they tear the mind with the pricks of their thoughts; and when they drag it into sin, they make it bleed as though a wound had been inflicted. The Lord rightly calls them deceitful, because they cannot remain with us for long or banish the poverty of the mind. Only those riches are true which make us rich in virtues. Anxieties, riches, and pleasures choke because, with their importunate thoughts, they strangle the throat of the mind; and, because they do not permit good desire to enter the heart, they kill by closing, as it were, the entrance of vital breath. In riches there are two contrary things: anxieties and pleasures, which make their possessors both afflicted and unstable. But because the will does not accord with affliction, at one time anxiety afflicts through hope of acquiring or fear of losing; at another, pleasure softens through abundance and causes dissipation. Many indeed, on hearing an argument against avarice or luxury, say that those who despise the world and live chastely are blessed; but when desirable appearances are presented to their gaze, whatever sound thought they had immediately departs from them. Those sown upon rocky soil and among thorns, therefore, are people who both approve the word and taste it with desire, but whom either this life’s adversities, through fear, or its prosperities, through flattery, hold back from attaining the word’s benefit. Against both kinds of loss Paul sought to protect the seed he had received when he said: “Through the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left” (2 Corinthians 6).

[Col. 0233A] “But he who was sown in good soil is the one who hears the word and understands it and bears fruit, producing one a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, and another thirtyfold.”

The varieties of good soil are the souls of those who believe devoutly. They receive and preserve the word of God and, as Luke records [says], “bear fruit in patience,” because they do good and calmly endure the evils inflicted by their neighbours, so that after humbly accepting scourges they may be received into rest. Thus a grape is crushed beneath the feet and liquefied into the flavour of wine. [GREGORY.] Thus an olive, pressed by crushing, leaves behind its dregs and becomes rich in the liquid of oil. Thus, by the threshing of the floor, grains are separated from chaff and, purified, reach the granary. Whoever therefore desires fully to conquer vices [Col. 0233B] should strive humbly to endure the scourges of his purification. We assign the hundredfold fruit to virgins, the sixtyfold to widows and the continent, and the thirtyfold to holy marriage. [BEDE.] That thirty is assigned to marriage is suggested by the joining of the fingers, which, as though embracing each other in a tender kiss, portrays husband and wife. Sixty belongs to widows, who receive a greater reward in proportion as they abstain more. The hundredth number, transferred from the left hand to the right, represents the crown of virginity. [AUGUSTINE.] Otherwise: the hundredfold fruit belongs to martyrs, because of the holiness of their life or their contempt for death. The sixtyfold belongs to virgins because of inward repose, since they do not fight against the habit of the flesh. For exemption from service after military duty is customarily granted to those aged sixty. [Col. 0233C] The thirtyfold belongs to married persons, because this is the age of those who fight, and their conflict is greater, lest they be overcome by lust.

## CHAPTER LXXVI

R. 43[X]

“So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed upon the earth, and should sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should sprout and grow, while he does not know. For the earth bears fruit of itself: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. And when it has produced fruit, immediately he puts in the sickle, because the harvest is at hand.”

The kingdom of God is the Church, which is governed by God and [Col. 0233D] itself governs human beings and tramples vices underfoot. The man who casts the seed is the Son of Man; the seed is the word; the earth, human hearts; and the man’s sleep is the death of the Saviour. The seed rises night and day after Christ’s sleep, because the number of believers is multiplied more and more amid adversity and prosperity. The seed sprouts through good intention and grows in action, while he does not know—that is, while he makes us not know what fruit each person will bring forth at the end, when he says: “He who perseveres to the end, he shall be saved” (Matt. X). The earth bears fruit of itself while God awaits our will, saying: “If you wish to come to life, keep the commandments” (Matt. XIX). This earth first produces the blade, that is, fear: for “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CI). Then the ear, [Col. 0234A] that is, tearful repentance; then the full grain, namely charity. For “charity is the fulfilment of the law” (Rom. XIII). At harvest time he cuts it with the sickle, because by sending the sentence of death he cuts off temporal life, bringing the grain to the heavenly granaries. [BEDE.] Or thus: the sickle is judgment, which cuts all things, because the harvest is at hand—that is, the consummation of the age—in which the righteous who sowed in tears will rejoice. But any person casts seed into the earth when he implants a good intention in his own heart; he sleeps because he now rests in the hope of good work. The seed rises night and day because it progresses amid adversity and prosperity. It sprouts and grows while he does not know, because, while he is still unable to measure his own growth, the virtue conceived is led onward to progress. [Col. 0234B] The earth bears fruit of itself because, grace going before, the human mind voluntarily rises to the progress [fruit] of good work. This earth first produces the blade, still possessing the tenderness of a good beginning; then the ear, when the virtue conceived in the soul draws itself toward the fruit of good work; then the full grain, when virtue has now advanced to vigorous and perfect work. He puts in the sickle who, already prepared for martyrdom, desires “to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. I).
