He cuts the harvest with the sickle when through death he ceases from working, harvesting the fruit of good work, namely eternal life. Then the harvest is at hand, because all his good deeds are presented before him in the presence of the angels of God.

[Col. 0234C] M. 140[X]

“Then, having dismissed the crowds, he came into the house. And his disciples approached him, saying: Explain to us the parable of the weeds in the field. He answered and said: He who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. The field is the world. The good seed are the children of the kingdom. But the weeds are the children of the evil one. The enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the consummation of the age, and the reapers are angels. Therefore, just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so it will be at the consummation of the age. The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all stumbling-blocks and those who commit iniquity, and will cast them into the furnace of fire. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

The good seed are those—understand, those who are children of the kingdom. “All stumbling-blocks,” that is, those who unceasingly commit evil with an evil disposition of mind. The angels are said first to gather them, because at the resurrection itself the reprobate will be weighed down by the burden of their sins, whereas the elect will be caught up to meet Christ in the air (1 Thess. IV). Thus on earth the unjust will be separated from the just; then in the air the good will be joined to Christ, shining in their own measure through holiness without failing, just as the sun is the most luminous body in its own kind. By the furnace of fire he means hell. Good angels, indeed, are understood to perform the offices of vengeance with a good disposition, like a judge; evil angels do not perform offices of mercy.

## CHAPTER LXXVII

[Col. 0235A]

“The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field, which a man, having found it, hides; and for joy over it he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.”

[HILARY.] By the likeness of a treasure in a field he shows the riches of our hope placed within us. The treasure in the field is understood as the Son of God hidden in flesh, or in the holy Scriptures. [GREGORY.] To have found it is gratuitous; but since heavenly riches are possessed only at the cost of the world, he who finds it must despise worldly things, so that he may have the power to use the treasure together with the field. Or thus: the treasure is heavenly desire; the field in which it is hidden is the discipline of heavenly study. He buys that field after selling all things who renounces the pleasures of the flesh and tramples earthly desires through observance of heavenly discipline, so that he may apply himself more freely to the study of understanding. We ought to hide the treasure, not on the road but in our heart; for in this life we are, as it were, on the road to our homeland, lest malignant spirits, like brigands lying in wait upon our route, strip us if we carry the treasure publicly on the road. I do not say that we should conceal our good works from our neighbours, since it is written, “Let them see your works and glorify your Father” (Matt. V); rather, that in good works we should not seek outward praise. [REMIGIUS.] Otherwise: the treasure in the field is the two Testaments of the Law in the Church; for the sake of understanding them, temporal things are despised so that they may be studied at leisure. Philosophers too are understood to have done this for the sake of human knowledge.

“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls. Having found one precious pearl, he went away, sold all that he had, and bought it.”

The same reasoning applies to pearls and to the treasure; but above, “the kingdom of heaven” is understood as Christ himself, or the heavenly Church, or heavenly desire. [JEROME.] Here, however, and below, it is the Church still present, in which even now the virtues of heavenly citizens reign. The fine pearls are the Law and the Prophets; the most precious pearl is knowledge of the Saviour. The merchant is like the apostle who despised his former observances for Christ’s sake. This is not because finding the new pearl condemns the former pearls, but because in comparison with it every gem is cheap. The merchant went out from his house to the marketplace; the churchman went out from his possessions to the school of the wise. The former sold everything; the latter renounced everything, even himself, because the price of this one desired stone must be purchased by the loss of all other labour. [REMIGIUS.] Otherwise: you seek, as fine pearls, holy men to whom you may conform yourself, or good precepts and spiritual understandings in which salvation lies. You find, therefore, before all things Christ, the precious pearl; and among precepts, the commandment of love; and beyond every understanding, you discover—after the shell of flesh has been pierced through—the understanding of the Word who will be with God.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII

[Col. 0236A]

“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind. When it was full, they drew it out and, sitting by the shore, chose the good into their vessels but cast the bad away.”

The Church, or evangelical preaching, is compared to a net cast into the sea: it draws people, as fish, from the sea of the world into the light of the true sun. From both Testaments the apostles wove for themselves the net of the Gospel, and to this day it is stretched out amid the waves of this world, catching both good and bad. [REMIGIUS.] But at the end of the world it will be drawn to shore, and the good fish will be distinguished for heaven, the bad for Gehenna. Through the resurrection the angels will draw forth the filled net, because then the Church will contain all the predestined. Sitting by the shore—that is, after the end of the world, in a sense judging by the office laid upon them, which is signified by sitting—they will choose the good into their vessels, that is, into everlasting dwellings; but the bad, lest they see the glory of God, they will cast out, namely into hell. This is what follows:

“So it shall be at the consummation of the age. The angels will go out and separate the evil from among the righteous, and cast them into the furnace of fire. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

[BEDE.] Weeping is customarily caused by heat, gnashing of teeth by cold. Here a twofold Gehenna is shown to exist, of excessive cold and heat. The saying of blessed Job agrees with this: “From snowy waters he will pass to excessive heat” (Job XXIV). Or the gnashing of teeth reveals an indignant state of mind, because each person repents too late, groans too late, and is angry with himself too late, having sinned with such obstinate wickedness.

“Have you understood all these things?” They say to him, “Yes.” He said to them: “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder [is like a man] who brings out of his treasure new things and old.”

The Apostle gives testimony suitable for future teachers, not merely hearers but those who understand, comparing himself under the name of a householder and calling them scribes because of their knowledge. It is as though he said: Because you have understood, I therefore tell you that every scribe instructed—that is, everyone who writes in his heart what he hears from me, as you and others do—in the kingdom of heaven, which is the Church, is like me, who am the householder, because I am the Lord of hosts, namely of human beings and angels, and because I bring from the treasure of my heart things new and old—that is, knowledge of the New and Old Testaments. The apostles also, when they preached the Gospel, confirmed by the voices of the Law and the Prophets what they drew forth from the treasure of doctrine. [GREGORY.] Otherwise: it was old for the human race to descend into hell; it is new for those who live righteously to enter the kingdom of heaven. Therefore the learned preacher knows how to bring forth both new things concerning the sweetness of the kingdom and old things concerning the terror of punishment, so that penalties may frighten those whom rewards do not invite.

[Col. 0237A] “And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these parables, that he departed from there.”

## CHAPTER LXXIX

M. 141[I] R. 79 L. 79 A. 59

“And coming into his own country, he taught them in their synagogues, so that they were astonished and said: ‘Where has this man this wisdom and such mighty works, which are accomplished by his hands? Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas, and his sisters? Are they not all with us? Whence, then, has he all these things?’ And they took offence at him.”

The Lord is dishonoured by his own people, although both the wisdom of his teaching and the power of his works stirred their admiration. Yet, though they can recognize from his words and deeds that he is Christ, they despise him merely because they know his family. For unbelief, seeing greatness on one side and lowliness on the other, does not receive the truth of judgment, but takes offence—that is, the decision of the mind is impeded. Mark says that the Lord was called a carpenter; Matthew, the carpenter’s son. [AUGUSTINE.] Both could have been said: they believed him to be a carpenter because he was a carpenter’s son. Yet truth lies hidden in their error. For he truly was the son of a carpenter who made all things through him in the beginning, who works through the Holy Spirit and fire, who fashioned the dawn and the sun, the primitive Church and the Church that followed. The Father of Christ and Christ fashion vessels of different kinds in the great house of this world; and, softening vessels of wrath with the fire of the Spirit, they transform them into vessels of mercy. Hence Malachi, speaking in the person of the Father, says of the Son: “He will sit refining and cleansing silver; and he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them as gold and silver” (Matt. V). It is clear that relatives are, in the manner of Scripture, called brothers and sisters; and low birth often accompanies contempt, as it was said scornfully of David: “Who is this son of Jesse?” (3 Kings XII). But: “The Lord looks upon the lowly, and knows the lofty from afar” (Ps. CXXXVII).

L. 20[X]

“And he said to them: ‘Surely you will say to me this proverb: Physician, heal yourself. What we have heard done in Capernaum, do also here in your own country.’”

Because we have heard that you healed many in Capernaum, heal yourself—that is, do the like in your own city, where you were conceived and reared. It is as though they said: We do not believe what uncertain report has spread abroad, since you have done nothing of this sort among us, to whom such benefits ought more fittingly to have been granted. Christ is the true physician because he restores the fallen, so that after wounds we may be whole.

M. 142 R. 51 L. 21 A. 35

“Amen I say to you, that no prophet is accepted in his own country and in his own house.” And he did not perform many mighty works there because of their unbelief, except that he cured a few sick persons by laying hands upon them; and he wondered at their unbelief.

[BEDE.] Not only the Lord himself, the head of the prophets, of whom Moses foretold, “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren” (Deut. XV, 1), but also Elijah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets were held in less esteem in their homeland than in foreign cities. For it is customary for fellow citizens to envy their fellow citizens, and to consider neither a man’s present deeds nor his virtue, but to recall the weakness of his childhood. He performed few mighty works there because, if he had performed none, the unbelievers by whom he was mocked might perhaps have been thought excusable; whereas if they had seen many signs, they would have become wholly inexcusable and would have been condemned all the more. And because they believed neither the prophets nor Christ himself, whom they saw present, he marvels at their unbelief—not as though it were unforeseen, but showing before human beings that he marvels at what he wishes to make seem marvellous to them.

L. 22[X]

“Truly I say to you: There were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when heaven was shut for three years and six months, when a great famine came over all the land; and Elijah was sent to none of them except to Zarephath of Sidon, to a widow woman.”

[BEDE.] That I withdraw divine benefits from fastidious fellow citizens is not contrary to the deeds of the prophets. For just as, in the time of famine, no one in Judaea was found worthy to receive Elijah as a guest (3 Kings XVII), but a widow of a foreign nation was sought; and just as, though there were many lepers there, Naaman the Syrian alone was deemed worthy to be cured by Elisha (4 Kings V): so you too, because of your faithlessness, will be deprived of the gift from above. The widow to whom Elijah was sent signifies the Church of the Gentiles. Long abandoned by her Creator, she supported, with scanty provision, a people ignorant of faith as though it were a poor son—that is, she taught it by the word of worldly learning without the fruit of benefit. Thus the widow is rightly said to have dwelt in Zarephath of Sidon. Sidon indeed means “useless hunting”; Zarephath, “fire” or “narrowness of bread.” By these is expressed Gentile life, which, devoted to useless hunting—that is, serving the gains and commerce of the world—endured the fire of fleshly desires and scarcity of spiritual bread, until Elijah—that is, prophetic speech—was sent to it, he who in Judaea had been endangered by famine, with heaven’s gate shut—that is, with the understanding of the Scriptures having ceased because of the faithlessness of the Jews. Therefore prophetic speech came to the Church so that, being received, it might be fed and might refresh the hearts of believers. Where formerly there was scarcity of spiritual bread, there flour and oil are blessed by the mouth of the prophet; that is, the fruit and gladness of charity, or the grace of the Lord’s body and the anointing of spiritual gifts, are made fruitful by the unfailing gift of the heavenly word. These gifts have not failed in the Church even to the present. That this woman, about to make the mystical bread, declares that she wishes to gather two sticks signifies the wood of the cross, by which for us the bread of eternal life was prepared.

“And there were many lepers in Israel under Elisha the prophet, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.”

Naaman also the Syrian, whose name is interpreted “sorrow,” represents the people of the nations, once stained with the leprosy of faithlessness but later cleansed from every defilement through the sacrament of baptism. At the counsel of the captive girl—that is, through the grace of heavenly inspiration, which the Gentiles seized from the Jews who kept it wrongly, for their salvation—he is commanded by Elisha to wash seven times, because baptism alone saves, regenerating through the sevenfold Spirit. Hence after washing his flesh is recorded to have appeared like the flesh of a little child: either because the one mother of grace gives birth to all who are baptized in Christ into a single infancy, or because Christ is understood as the child to whose body the whole offspring of believers is joined through baptism. He is said to have carried away with him a portion of the holy land because those baptized ought to be conformed [confirmed] through participation in the Lord’s body.

“And all in the synagogue were filled with anger when they heard these things. And they rose up, drove him out of the city, and led him to the brow of the mountain on which their city was built, in order to throw him down headlong. But he, passing through their midst, went away.”

What the Lord testifies concerning the Jews in word, they themselves testify in deed, repaying evil for good. O inheritance of disciples worse than their master! The devil had said, “Cast yourself down” (Matt. IV); the Jews tried to cast him down by their action. But when the minds of those raging people were suddenly struck dumb, the Lord went down, preferring to heal rather than destroy them, so that, their wickedness frustrated, they might thereafter desist from seeking his death. For the hour of his passion had not yet come, nor had he chosen to die by this kind of death.

## CHAPTER LXXIX, SECOND PART

M. 144[II] R. 59 L. 12

“At that time Herod the tetrarch seized John and bound him in prison because of Herodias, the wife of Philip his brother, because he had married her.”

An old history relates that Philip, son of Herod the Great, under whom the Lord fled into Egypt, and brother of that Herod under whom Christ suffered, had married Herodias, daughter of Aretas, king of the Arabs. Afterwards, however, her father, certain hostilities having arisen against his son-in-law, took back his daughter and joined her to Herod, his enemy, both to the grief of her former husband and because he was greater in power and renown. Therefore John, who had come in the spirit and power of Elijah, rebuked Herod and Herodias with the same authority by which Elijah had rebuked King Ahab and his wife Jezebel (3 Kings XVIII).

M. 145 R. 60

“For John said to Herod: ‘It is not lawful for you to have her.’ But Herodias plotted against him and wished to kill him, but could not. M. For he [i.e. Herod] feared the people, because they regarded him as a prophet. M. R. Likewise Herod, wishing to kill him, was afraid. R. Knowing him to be a just and holy man, he kept him safe. And when he heard him, he did many things, and they gladly heard him. B. M. And when an opportune day came, Herod gave a supper on his birthday for the leading men, tribunes, and chief men of Galilee.”

We find that no one else observed the day of his own birth except Herod and Pharaoh, so that those whose impiety was one might also have one festival. But let us not celebrate the day of birth in luxury; rather, let us always commemorate and fear the day of death. For “man is born for labour” (Job V), and the saints pass through death into the kingdom.

“And when the daughter of Herodias herself came in and danced, she pleased Herod and those reclining with him. The king said to the girl: ‘Ask of me whatever you wish, and I will give it to you.’ And he swore to her, ‘Whatever you ask, I will give you, even half my kingdom.’ When she had gone out, she said to her mother: ‘What shall I ask for?’ But she said: ‘The head of John the Baptist.’ And immediately, coming in hastily to the king, she asked, saying: ‘I want you to give me at once, on a dish, the head of John the Baptist.’ And the king was grieved; yet because of his oath and those reclining with him, he did not wish to disappoint her. And he sent an executioner, who beheaded John in prison. His head was brought on a dish and given to the girl, and she gave it to her mother. And his disciples came, took his body, and buried it in a tomb. Then they came and reported it to Jesus.”

Fearing that Herod might one day, through John’s admonition, come to his senses, Herodias desired to have in her power the tongue which rebuked the unlawful marriage. [BEDE.] Nor does the oath in any way excuse Herod’s crime, for perhaps he swore for this very purpose, to prepare devices for a future opportunity. Otherwise, if he says he acted because of the oath, what if the girl had asked for her mother’s death? Certainly, if we happen carelessly to have sworn something whose observance would turn out more badly, we should know that it may freely be changed by wiser counsel, and that under pressing necessity we should rather commit perjury than, in avoiding perjury, turn aside into another and graver crime. David swore by the Lord to kill the foolish and impious man Nabal (1 Kings XXV) and to destroy everything belonging to him; yet at the first intercession of Abigail, a prudent woman, he withdrew his threats from Nabal. This moderation must be observed more carefully not only in swearing but in everything we do: if we happen to fall into such a predicament that we cannot escape it without some sin, we should choose rather the means of escape in which we see less danger. So those enclosed by hostile walls, when they desire to escape but see that access to the gates is barred to them, must choose a place to leap down where the wall is lower, so that in falling they incur the least danger. [JEROME.] He said, “And the king was grieved,” because it is the historian’s custom to relate the opinion of the many just as it was then believed by everyone. Where it says, “because of those reclining with him,” it means that Herod wished all to be accomplices in his crime. We read in Roman history that Flaminius, a Roman commander, was expelled from the senate by the censors because he agreed to have a man accused of a capital crime beheaded during a banquet, at the request of a prostitute who said she had never seen a man beheaded. [JEROME.] How much more criminal were Herod, Herodias, and the girl! This is according to the letter. But even today we see, in the head of John the prophet, that the Jews lost Christ, who is the head of the prophets. The head of the Law, which is Christ, is cut off from its own body—that is, from the Jewish people—and given to the girl from among the Gentiles, that is, to the Roman Church; and the girl gives it to her adulterous mother, namely the Synagogue, which will believe at the end. John’s body is buried, his head is placed on a dish, because the letter is as though covered in earth, but the spirit is received and honoured at the altar. [HILARY.] For when the times of the Law were ended and buried with John, his disciples—that is, the hearers of the Law—having put to death within themselves their carnal observances, as though John’s body were buried, come from the Law to the Gospel, from the letter to the Spirit; and, progressing therein, are joined to the Lord. [BEDE.] Ecclesiastical histories relate that John was taken bound to the fortress in Arabia called Machaerus and beheaded there. His body was buried at Sebaste, a city of Palestine formerly called Samaria; his head, however, was buried at Jerusalem. But in the time of Julian the Apostate, pagans, envying Christians who diligently frequented John’s tomb, invaded the monument and scattered the bones; gathering them again, they burned them and scattered them more widely. But God’s providence was present: certain monks from Jerusalem, mingling with the pagans as they gathered the bones, collected the greater part and brought them to their father Philip at Jerusalem. He immediately sent them through his deacon Julian to Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria. Later Theophilus, bishop of that same city, preserved them there; after cleansing the temple of Serapis from its filth, he placed them there and consecrated a basilica in honour of Saint John, when, by order of Emperor Theodosius, the shrines of the Gentiles were destroyed. In the time of Emperor Marcian, John revealed his head, near the former dwelling of King Herod, to two eastern monks who had come to Jerusalem for prayer. Found and taken up there by them, but not long afterwards lost through neglect, it was brought by others to Emesa, a city of Phoenicia, and was for a considerable time ignobly stored beneath the ground in a jar in a certain cave, until John again revealed himself and his head to a certain religious abbot and priest, Marcellus, while he lived in the same cave. It is established that this head was found for Lulioramus, bishop of the same city, through the aforesaid priest. From that time the beheading of the Forerunner began to be celebrated in that city, on the very day, as we suppose, on which the head was found or elevated. They say that a *discus* is a round vessel, very broad at the top. Serapis was called a god of Egypt.

M. 143[II] R. 56 L. 90

“Now Herod heard the report about Jesus and all that was done by him, and he was perplexed because it was said by some that John had risen from the dead; by others, that Elijah had appeared; and by still others, that one of the ancient prophets had risen. R. L. And Herod said: ‘I beheaded John. But who is this of whom I hear such things?’ And he sought to see him.”

In Mark, Herod expressly says ironically: “The John whom I beheaded—he has risen from the dead.” [BEDE.] He could also have spoken ironically to his servants, who had beheaded John with their own hands, as Matthew relates it thus: “Herod said to his servants: ‘This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead, and therefore mighty works operate in him.’” But if we understand these words as an affirmation, we must think that after his uncertainty Herod confirmed in his mind what others were saying. They rightly thought that saints risen from the dead would possess greater power than when burdened with fragile flesh. How great was the Jews’ envy against the Lord, we learn from the Gospel (Matt. XXVIII): they believed that John had risen from the dead, but proclaimed that Jesus, who had worked so many signs, had not risen but had been stolen away secretly.

M. 146[III] L. 62 A. 47

“When Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a deserted place by himself. And when the crowds heard it, they followed him on foot from the cities. And going out, he saw a great crowd, had compassion on it, and healed their sick.”

[JEROME.] It is well said that he “withdrew,” not that he fled, so that he may be shown to avoid persecutors rather than fear them. Awaiting the fitting time of his passion, he avoided having his own murder joined to the murder of John. Or he withdrew in order to give us an example of avoiding the rashness of voluntarily handing ourselves over. For not all persevere with the same steadfastness in torments with which they offer themselves to be tormented. In seeking solitude, moreover, he tests whether the crowds care to follow him in faith, and rewards their proven faith with a worthy recompense. The crowds, however, take the road through the wilderness not on beasts of burden or in vehicles but by the labour of their own feet, showing their desire for salvation. In turn, by receiving the weary, teaching the ignorant, healing the sick, and refreshing the hungry, he shows how greatly he delights in the devotion of believers. Otherwise: after prophecy lost its voice among the Jews, it passed over to the desert of the Church, which lacked a husband. The crowds left the cities—that is, their former ways of life and the variety of doctrines. His “going out” means that the crowds had the will to come to him, but lacked the strength; therefore the Saviour went out to meet them.

## CHAPTER LXXX

M. 147[I] R. 63 L. 93 A. 49

“When evening came, the twelve approached him and said: ‘Dismiss the crowds, so that they may go into the surrounding villages and hamlets, lodge there, and find food, for we are here in a desert place.’ But Jesus said to them: ‘They have no need to go; give them something to eat yourselves.’”

[BEDE.] He invites the apostles to the breaking of the loaves so that, as they testify that they have nothing, the greatness of the sign may become better known; and at the same time he indicates that we are daily to be fed through them. For what do Peter and Paul do through their Epistles, if not feed our minds with heavenly nourishment? He refreshes the crowds at evening because, either as the end of the age draws near or when the sun of righteousness set for us, we were freed from the hunger of spiritual starvation by divine aid. [HILARY.] Observe the order of the mystery. After the failure of the Law, evangelical food begins; but first, through forgiveness of sins, medicine is given to wounds, and afterwards the nourishment of the heavenly table is distributed. Therefore we need not seek food in villages and hamlets—that is, we must not abandon the bread of life in order to buy, at the price of study and labour, the doctrines of philosophers fortified by their own arguments, and delight in their food. That the disciples call the place deserted signifies the Jews murmuring against the conversion of the Gentiles. Hence Isaiah speaks in their voice: “Behold, the nations are as a drop from a bucket” (Isa. XL). Again: “All nations are as though they were not before him” (ibid.).

A.

Philip answered him: “Two hundred denarii worth of loaves are not enough for them, for each one to receive a little.” R. And he says to them: “How many loaves have you?” A. One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, says to him: “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are these among so many?” L. “Unless perhaps we should go and buy food for all this crowd.” M. He said to them: “Bring them here to me.” R. L. And he commanded them to make everyone recline in groups upon the green grass. And they reclined in sections, by hundreds and by fifties.

[AUGUST.] The Lord had asked Philip, testing him—as John relates—where food could be obtained for the crowds. For the people’s ignorance lay in the Law: “as long as Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts.” Therefore that testing by the Lord displayed the disciple’s ignorance. Andrew speaks with the same simplicity as Philip; but the Lord shows that he freely bestows food upon the believing people by the same gracious power by which he heals them through freely redeeming them. The boy carrying the loaves and fish was one of his disciples, or perhaps someone from the [Col. 0243D] crowd. What Philip or Andrew says individually in John, the other Evangelists report as said by the disciples in the plural, understanding one to speak for the rest, or using the plural number for the singular. Understand the companies to be the different groups of people who had come from different villages, just as soldiers sharing fellowship in the same tent are customarily called tent-companions. The five loaves are the five books of Moses, because in the works of the Law life was, as it were, derived from bread. For through the Law the knowledge of divine eternity, the creation of the world, the course of the passing age, and the true religion of serving God were made known to humankind.

[AUGUST.] In the two fish, however, the Psalms and the Prophets are understood, tempering the harsh taste of the Law; for they fed the people trained in God’s Law [Col. 0244A] with the sweetness of grace, through the promise of the Lord’s incarnation, cherishing hope for human life as if through the power of water. Hence the Lord said after the resurrection: “It was necessary that all things written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms should be fulfilled” (Luke 24). Here also, when he commands the loaves and fish to be brought to him, he mystically commands that the understanding of the Old Testament be referred to him. Those who prophesied about our age are appropriately represented by aquatic creatures, since in this age the people of the faithful cannot live at all without the waters of baptism. The loaves, moreover, were of barley, a food for beasts of burden and country people, because coarser precepts must, as it were, be entrusted to unlearned hearers. “The natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2). Therefore the Lord, giving each person gifts according to his capacity [Col. 0244B] and always summoning them to greater perfection, first feeds five thousand with five loaves; secondly, four thousand people with seven loaves; thirdly, he entrusts to his disciples the mystery of his flesh and blood; and finally, he grants them to eat and drink at his table in his kingdom.

AUGUSTINE. Or thus: the loaves were of barley because they belonged to the Old Testament; and just as one reaches the marrow of barley only with difficulty, so the Old Testament is clothed in a covering of carnal things, yet it satisfies when one reaches what is within. The two fish, which gave the bread a pleasant flavor, are the two offices of priest and king, by which the people of Israel were governed, so that through them they might receive the guidance of counsel. As these were buffeted among the crowds of the surging age, after the manner of fish, yet did not fail, Christ was prefigured as the true [Col. 0244C] priest and ruler. The boy carrying them is that people childish in understanding: not eating what they bore closed up as a burden, nor feeding others. Hence follows:

“But what are these among so many?”

[JEROME.] It is as though it were said: “What use is the old letter to the very many who will seek spiritual nourishment above every bodily sense and every letter?” Because they thought carnally and rested in carnal hope, to whom the Law had promised temporal things, they are commanded to recline upon green grass. For “all flesh is grass, and all human glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40). Therefore the person reclining upon grass tramples down his flesh and crushes its flowers like withered grass, subjecting the pleasures of the age to himself. The different reclining groups of the diners [Col. 0244D] signify the different congregations of churches. They recline in groups of fifty who, still engaged in repentance, receive the word they have heard; for the number fifty is the number of repentance and forgiveness.

[AUGUST.] Those reclining in hundreds, however, are those who, having been fifties through repentance, ascend to the perfect summit of the hundredfold number and now yearn only for the desire of eternal life.

M. L. R.

R. A. “And having received the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and blessed them; and he broke them and distributed them to the disciples, and the disciples to the crowds. And all ate and were satisfied. They took up twelve baskets full of fragments left over. The number of those eating [Col. 0245A] was about five thousand men, besides women and children.”

[HILARY.] The Lord looked to heaven, acknowledging the honor of the Father from whom he himself was, so that those present might understand from whom he had received the effect of so great a power, and might themselves direct the eyes of their minds there.

[JEROME.] Unless the loaves were broken, they would not feed so great a crowd; likewise, unless the Law were opened, it would not feed the many whom, once opened, it does feed. Each Apostle fills his own basket from the remnants, either so that he may have material later to provide food to the nations, or so as to show from the remnants that the loaves had been real. The five thousand men are the perfect; the weaker sex and younger age are unworthy of the number.

[Bede.] Thus in the Book of Numbers, whenever priests, Levites, and [Col. 0245B] fighting multitudes are enumerated, servants, women, little children, and the common rabble are omitted. The Savior does not create new food, but blesses what is present, because in coming in the flesh he does not proclaim other things, but shows that the words of prophecy are pregnant with mysteries of grace. Hence it follows that he broke them: for he opened the closed mysteries of the Law and the Prophets. The loaves are multiplied by being broken, because many books were produced in expounding the Law. Breaking them, he distributes them to the disciples; and they, breaking what had been broken beforehand, distributed it to the crowds. For he opened the understanding of the holy teachers so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24), and they faithfully dispensed what they understood to hearers throughout the world.

[AUGUST.] The disciples gather up what remains for the crowds, because [Col. 0245C] mysteries which the unlearned cannot grasp are investigated by the perfect. For the fragments which the people could not eat are certain more hidden meanings, with which the twelve Apostles were filled as with baskets.

[JEROME.] The Apostles are represented by the baskets, and through the Apostles the companies of subsequent teachers: outwardly despised by people, but inwardly filled with saving food to nourish humble hearts. For servile tasks are customarily performed with baskets. But the Lord will fill baskets with fragments—he who chose “the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1). And because there are five senses of the outward person, the five thousand men who followed the Lord signify those who know well how to use the outward things they possess in the world. They are rightly nourished with five loaves, because such persons must necessarily [Col. 0245D] still be instructed by the precepts of the Law. But those who renounce the world completely are the four thousand, refreshed with seven loaves—that is, exalted by evangelical refreshment and taught by spiritual grace.

[JEROME.] For the sake of this signification, I think five gilded columns were commanded to be made at the entrance of the tabernacle, but four before the oracle—that is, the Holy of Holies—because beginners are disciplined through the Law so that they may not sin, while the perfect are admonished through grace to live in greater devotion to God.

M. 148[VI] R. 63

“And immediately he commanded the disciples to get into the boat and go ahead of him across the water to Bethsaida, until he had dismissed the crowds.”

[Col. 0246A] [BEDE.] Mark does not have “commanded,” but “compelled,” which shows that the disciples withdrew from the Lord unwillingly.

[HILARY.] The disciples went on ahead to Bethsaida, the city of the Apostles Andrew, Peter, and Philip, in Galilee near Lake Gennesaret.

[BEDE.] Therefore, where Luke reports that memorable miracle as having taken place in the desert place of Bethsaida, it is rightly understood that he did not mean the city itself, but a desert place belonging to it. John relates that the crowds ate near Tiberias and that the disciples came to Capernaum. Both cities are in Galilee beside Lake Gennesaret, which is also called the Sea of Tiberias after the city of Tiberias.

[BEDE.] It must therefore be understood that they passed through Bethsaida to Capernaum. It should also be carefully noted [Col. 0246B] that the Lord fed the Jews as those who would thereafter receive new food from the Law; but the fact that the miracle occurred in the wilderness of Bethsaida expressly prefigured that the Lord would bestow the pasture of the Word in the wilderness of the Church, which has no husband. Bethsaida is fittingly interpreted “house of fruits.” Hence Isaiah says: “The desert and trackless place shall rejoice; the wilderness shall exult and blossom like a lily” (Isa. 35). And shortly afterward: “They shall see the glory of the Lord and the beauty of our God” (ibid.).

A. 50[X]

“Therefore, when those people had seen the sign that he had performed, they said: ‘This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world.’ Jesus therefore, when he knew [Col. 0246C] that they were about to come and seize him in order to make him king, fled.”

[AUGUST.] They rightly perceived that so great a prophet would come into the world through proclamations of salvation—that is, into the common knowledge of humankind. The disciples and crowds who believed in the Lord thought that he had come in order to reign already. This is what it means that they wished to seize him and make him king: they wished to anticipate his time, which he kept hidden within himself until the end of the age. Hence: “It is not for you to know the times or seasons” (Acts 1).

[JEROME.] By fleeing, he gives us an example that we should avoid in ourselves the recompense of human favor for what we do; at the same time he indicates that his exalted nature cannot be understood.

[Col. 0246D] M. 149 R. 66 L. 35 and 43

“And when he had dismissed the crowd, he went up the mountain alone to pray.”

Had Peter, John, and James been with him, perhaps they would have gone up with him; but the crowd cannot follow him into the heights. This makes it understood that, when the Lord sat on the mountain with his disciples, as John records, and saw the crowds coming to him, he had come down from the mountain and fed the crowds in the lower places.

## CHAPTER LXXXI

M. 150[IV] R. 67 A. 51

“And when evening had come, he was there alone. But the boat was being tossed by waves in the middle of the sea, for the wind was contrary. And in the fourth watch of the night, seeing [Col. 0247A] them struggling, he came to them, walking upon the sea. And he intended to pass them by.”

[JEROME.] The Apostles had rightly departed from the Lord unwillingly, lest they should be endangered. Military watches are divided into periods of three hours. Thus it is shown here that the disciples were endangered throughout the whole night and received help from the Lord at the end of the night, which signifies the consummation of the world.

[HILARY.] The first watch was that of the Law, the second that of the Prophets, the third the coming of Christ, and the fourth the return in glory. Then he will come to the Church, wandering and shipwrecked, wearied by the spirit of Antichrist and tossed about by the disturbances of the entire age.

[BEDE.] Otherwise: they are endangered all night because, while a person considers himself, he finds nothing but the darkness of distress and the heat of hostile enemies rising up. But when [Col. 0247B] he lifts his mind toward the light of heavenly help, he sees, as it were, amid the shadows of night, the sudden rising of the morning star, which announces the approaching day—that is, Christ. For the morning star is said to illuminate the three hours of night, that is, the whole morning watch. The Lord, on land, saw his own struggling at sea and did not immediately help them; for although he seems for a time to delay help for those in distress, he nevertheless strengthens them at last. Hence, when he came, he intended to pass the disciples by, so that, troubled briefly and then immediately delivered, they might marvel more greatly at the miracle of their rescue and give greater thanks to the Lord. The same happens in the storms of sufferings inflicted by unbelievers. Hence the Church, laboring in the contest of martyrdom, says: “Why have you cast me off? [Col. 0247C] Why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me?” (Ps. 42). But how could the Apostles have understood that the Lord wished to pass them by unless he was proceeding in another direction? Who does not perceive the mystical meaning? How, then, did he wish to pass by those whom he strengthened, except that this apparent intention of passing them by served to draw forth the cry to which help had to be given?

M. R. A.

“And when they saw him walking upon the sea, they were troubled, saying, ‘It is a phantom’; and they cried out in fear. Immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying: ‘Take courage; I am; do not be afraid.’”

He did not add who he was, because they could understand him either from his familiar voice or from the fact that they knew that he had spoken thus to Moses: “Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: ‘He Who Is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3). They cried out in fear, naturally, because confused shouting and an uncertain voice are signs of great fear. Their being troubled even while seeing the Lord walking upon the sea mystically indicates that, when a long-standing tribulation is suddenly calmed, true deliverance is often not immediately believed. Therefore, while the former dread persists, earnest prayer should be directed toward deliverance, because “the Lord is near to all who call upon him” (Ps. 144). Their saying that it was a phantom signifies that some who believed the devil doubted Christ’s coming. Hence: “Do you think the Son of Man will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18).

[Col. 0248A] M. 151[X]

“But Peter answered and said: ‘Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.’ And he said: ‘Come.’ And Peter, descending from the boat, walked upon the water to come to Jesus. But seeing the strong wind coming, he was afraid; and when he began to sink, he cried out, saying: ‘Lord, save me.’ And immediately Jesus stretched out his hand and took hold of him, and said to him: ‘O you of little faith, why did you doubt?’”

[HILARY.] In Peter we must observe that he surpassed the rest in faith. For before the others he was the first to answer: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” First, he rejected the Passion, thinking it an evil. First also, he promised that he would die and would not deny him. First [Col. 0248B] he forbade the washing of his feet; first likewise he drew the sword against those who were arresting the Lord.

[JEROME.] Let those who think that the Lord’s body was not real because he walked upon the waters answer how Peter walked, whom they do not deny to have been a human being. When he began to sink, faith in his soul was burning, but human frailty was drawing him into the depths. Concerning the Lord Dionysius says in the *Short Treatises on the Divine Names*: “We do not know how, from virginal blood, he was formed by another law beyond the natural order; nor how, with bodily weight and material burden, and with feet as though not immersed, he walked upon the wet and unstable substance of water.”

The sea is the world; wind and storm are each person’s own desire. The wind rages and the waves rise, yet the ship continues onward. “The one who perseveres to the end shall be saved.” Do you love God? The fear of the world lies beneath your feet. Do you love the world? It swallows you. When your heart is tossed by desire, call upon God. Peter’s entreaty that he not sink signifies that the Church will be purified by certain tribulations even after the final persecution. Hence Paul says: “He shall be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 3).

M. 152[VI] R. 68

“And when they had entered the boat, the wind ceased.”

A. 51 M. 150 R. 67

“And immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going.”

[Col. 0248D] M. 152[VI] R. 68

“And those who were in the boat came and worshiped him, saying: ‘Truly you are the Son of God.’”

[BEDE.] It is no wonder that when the Lord enters the boat, the wind ceases; for in whatever heart he is present through the grace of his love, all the wars of vices, of the hostile world, and of evil spirits immediately become quiet.

The Lord shows himself to be the Creator of things in the miracle of the loaves; in walking upon the waves, he shows that he has a body free from every weight of sins; in calming the winds and the fury of the waves, he shows himself ruler of the elements.

[HILARY.] When, by his presence, the boat passes from the waves to the firm security of harbor, this signifies the peace and tranquility of the eternal Church after his return in glory. And because he will then come visibly in glory, all rightly say in amazement: “Truly you are the Son of God.”

## CHAPTER LXXXII

M. 153[II] R. 69 L. 36.

“And when they had crossed over, they came into the land of Gennesar. And when the men of that place recognized him, they sent throughout that entire region, brought to him all who were ill, and begged him that they might only touch the fringe of his garment; and all who touched it were made whole.”

[JEROME.] They recognized him by report; indeed, because of the greatness of his signs, very many also knew him by sight. Mystically understand the fringe of his garment as the least commandment, or the distribution of graces.

[HILARY.] [Col. 0249B] Just as a fringe comes from a garment, so the power of the Holy Spirit proceeds from Christ; given to the Apostles, it supplies salvation to those who desire to touch it. Gennesar is the same as Gennesaret; but the province was named from its proximity to the lake: the land of Gennesar, or the land of Gennesaret.

A. 52[X]

“On the following day, the crowd which stood across the sea saw that no other boat was there except one, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples had gone away alone. Other boats, however, came from Tiberias near the place where they had eaten bread after giving thanks to God. Therefore, when the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they boarded the boats and came to Capernaum, seeking [Col. 0249C] Jesus.”

[AUGUST.] To the crowds still on the other side of the sea, from which the disciples had come, this miracle—that Jesus had walked upon the waters—was made known, because there had been only one boat there and Jesus had not entered it with his disciples. How, then, had he come across the sea except by walking upon the waters? The one boat signifies the Catholic Church. The other boats arriving from Tiberias, in which the crowds are transported, signify the assemblies of those who do not seek Jesus sincerely.

“And when they had found him across the sea, they said to him: ‘Rabbi, when did you come here?’”

[AUGUST.] He presents himself to the crowds from whom he had fled to the mountain lest he be seized; this confirms for us [Col. 0249D] that all these things were done in a great sacrament.

“Jesus answered and said: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were satisfied.’”

[AUGUST.] “Answered” means that he added this after their words. How many seek Jesus only in order that he may do them temporal good, for example by fleeing to the Church when they are oppressed by the more powerful.

“Work not for the food which perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you.”

That is: seek me for my own sake, not for something else. For he is the food by which even angels live, which endures unto eternal life, as he will shortly say openly. He therefore strives to satisfy the minds of those whose [Col. 0250A] bellies he had satisfied. Truly the Son of Man gives spiritual food. Hence follows:

“For him God the Father has sealed.”

[AUGUST.] What does “sealed” mean? He gave him something proper to himself, so that he should not be compared with other human beings. Thus it is said of him: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44). Therefore, to seal is to hold him as set apart above his companions, because he who is Son of Man is Son of God.

“Therefore they said to him: ‘What shall we do, that we may perform the works of God?’”

Because they understood that that food was a work of God, they ask by what work they could fulfill this command.

“Jesus answered and said to them: ‘This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent.’”

[Col. 0250B] [AUGUST.] This is to eat the food which endures for eternity. Why do you prepare your teeth and stomach? Believe, and you have eaten.

“Therefore they said to him: ‘What sign, then, do you perform, that we may see and believe you? What work do you do?’”

[AUGUST.] They knew that what he had done from five loaves was great, but they preferred manna to this food. Moreover, they were troubled because Jesus promised more than Moses, placing himself above him by promising food which endures unto eternal life.

“Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness, as it is written: ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat’” (Exod. 16).

It is as though they said: “Do not think manna something small, which the Psalm calls ‘bread of heaven’” (Ps. 77).

[Col. 0250C] “Jesus therefore said to them: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you bread from heaven. The true bread is that which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world. My Father gives you the true bread. For the bread of God is that which descends from heaven and gives life to the world.’”

The bread from heaven is the Word of God, “whose going forth is from the height of heaven” (Ps. 18), that is, from the Father; and it is turned into milk when it descends into flesh—which was its descent from heaven. Moses, however, did not give manna thus from heaven but from the air, as a figure of this true bread that gives life to hearts. Angels eat the Word itself as solid food; we eat the same Word, but turned into milk, because if we cannot eat, we can suck. For unless he had been incarnate, he would not have been known [Col. 0250D] by us or tasted by us.

“Therefore they said to him: ‘Lord, always give us this bread.’”

[AUGUST.] They sought bread which would refresh them and would not fail, just as the Samaritan woman, wishing to be free from need of water, understood the water physically, though the Lord said of it that whoever drank it would never thirst (John 4).

“But Jesus said to them: ‘I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me shall not hunger; and whoever believes in me shall never thirst. But I told you that you have seen me, and yet you have not believed.’”

Just as coming to Jesus is believing in him, so not hungering and not thirsting signifies, plainly, that same eternal satisfaction. “I said that I am the bread that refreshes, [Col. 0251A] but I said, to reproach your unbelief, that you see and do not believe; and thus the fault is yours. But that others come, whom I receive, is from grace.” Hence follows:

“Everything which the Father gives me will come to me; and him who comes to me I will not cast out.”

The Father gives to the Son—that is, he draws those who therefore believe in the Son because they think of him as having God for his Father. Such people will not be cast out, but will remain within in the hidden place of blessedness. Hence it is said: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25). But the proud, whose lot is to be cast outside, have neither here nor in the future any inward good of mind—that is, grace poured out through the Holy Spirit into our hearts—and this arises because they do their own will rather than God’s [Col. 0251B] will. But the humble person does not fail to do God’s will instead of his own, and therefore “I will not cast out” the humble person who clings to me, because I came to do not only my own will but also the Father’s will. This is what he says:

A. 57[I] M. 295 R. 176 L. 282

“Because I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.”

[AUGUST.] God became man and came down from heaven, so that the one ashamed to follow a humble man might follow the humble God.

“And this is the will of him who sent me, the Father: that I should lose none of all that he has given me, but should raise it up on the last day.”

[Col. 0251C] The humble have been given to him, in whom the first resurrection takes place when the soul knows God. He loses none of them—which would happen if one were cast out—but will gloriously raise him in the second resurrection. Those who are puffed up perish, but none of the little ones does. Hence elsewhere: “It is not God’s will that one of these little ones should perish” (Matt. 18).

“For this is the will of my Father who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life; and I will raise him up on the last day.”

Through me as mediator, the Father wills to give both kinds of life to believers. For whoever sees and believes in me, who am life just as the Father is, already has life in the mind [Col. 0251D] and will be raised in the body. Hence he says: “Whoever sees the Son and believes in him” (John 6); and elsewhere: “Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life” (John 5), because whoever believes in the Son believes in the Father, and conversely; and as the Father has life in himself, so also has the Son in himself (ibid.).

A. 36[I] M. 141 R. 50 L. 19

“Therefore the Jews murmured about him because he had said: ‘I am the bread which came down from heaven.’ And they said: ‘Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then does he say: “I came down from heaven”?’”

These people were far from the bread from heaven; though their ears were open, they were deaf; they saw, yet stood blind. For this bread seeks the hunger of the inward person. [Col. 0252A] Hence elsewhere: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. 5). Therefore, as the Lord was about to give the Holy Spirit, he said that he was the bread who came down from heaven, exhorting us to believe in him. For to believe in him is to eat the living bread; and the one who is invisibly reborn is invisibly nourished; inwardly renewed and inwardly satisfied.

A. 60[X]

“Jesus therefore answered and said to them: ‘Do not murmur among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up on the last day.’”

[AUGUST.] Whom the Father draws, and whom he does not; why [Col. 0252B] he draws this person and not that one—do not wish to judge this, if you do not wish to err. This drawing has no violence, but is an exercise of the will. A person can enter the Church unwillingly; he can receive the sacrament unwillingly; but he cannot believe except willingly. Peter was drawn by the Father, nevertheless through the incarnate Son, when he said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” For he heard: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16). This revelation is itself the drawing. You show a green branch to a sheep, and you draw it. Nuts are shown to a child, and he is drawn. Hence it is said:

> … Each person is drawn by his own pleasure.  
> (VIRGIL, *Eclogues*)

[Col. 0252C] Therefore we are drawn by God not by force but by the bond of the heart. “I will raise him up,” so that, while he is being drawn, he may see what he believes, eat what he hungers for, and possess what he desires.

“It is written in the Prophets: ‘And they shall all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me.”

[ALCUIN.] “In the Prophets,” that is, in some prophet, or in the plural, “in the Prophets,” because Joel gives the words and others along with him give the sense. All people of that kingdom—that is, of the Christian faith—will be taught by God (John 6), because although people speak outwardly, God alone inwardly opens the understanding and inwardly instructs through knowledge and love of the truth. Thus everyone who hears and learns from the Father comes to me. But lest anyone excuse himself by saying, “I have never seen the Father; how then [Col. 0252D] do I learn from him?” he adds:

A. 61[III] M. 112 L. 119

“Not that anyone has seen the Father, except he who is from God; he has seen the Father.”

[AUGUST.] I have seen the Father, not you; yet you will not come to me unless you are drawn by the Father. To be drawn by the Father is to learn from the Father; to learn from the Father is to hear from the Father; to hear from the Father is to hear the Father’s Word—that is, me.

A. 62[X]

“Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever believes in me has eternal life.”

[Col. 0253A] That is, he has me, who am eternal life. He wished to reveal what he was, namely, life. To believe in God is to be united to him through faith and love, and to tend toward him by imitating him.

A. 63[I] M. 64 R. 165 L. 266

“I am the bread of life.”

He is truly fed until he joins those who have been fed to life.

A. 64[X]

“Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness, and died. This is the bread that came down from heaven, so that whoever eats of it may not die.”

[AUGUST.] Why do you boast? Is it because your fathers ate manna? Why did they die? Because they believed what [Col. 0253B] they saw, but did not understand what they did not see. They are therefore rightly called your fathers, because you are like them. He speaks of the death of the soul; for in bodily terms all have died, both righteous and unrighteous. But the righteous did not die in soul, because they understood visible food spiritually, as Moses and Aaron did. Even today we receive visible food, but the sacrament is one thing and the power of the sacrament another. Many receive from the altar and die. Hence the Apostle says: “He eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11). The Lord’s morsel was not poison to Judas when the enemy entered into him (John 13); rather, an evil man received a good thing badly. Therefore, to eat the heavenly bread spiritually: manna signified this bread, and God’s altar [Col. 0253C] signifies this bread.

The sacraments differ in their signs; in the reality signified they are equal. Hear the Apostle: “Our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food” (1 Cor. 10). The same spiritual food, certainly, though another bodily food; but “our fathers,” not their fathers. And he adds: “And all drank the same spiritual drink.” They had one thing and we another in visible appearance, yet with spiritual efficacy it signified the same thing. How the same drink? “They drank,” he says, “from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ.” From it came bread and from it drink. The rock was Christ in sign; the true Christ, in Word and flesh. And how did they drink? The rock was struck [Col. 0253D] twice with the rod, signifying the two timbers of the cross. This, then, is the bread which came down from heaven, so that whoever eats of it may not die eternally—namely, as concerns the power of the sacrament, not the visible sacrament: the one who eats in the heart, not the one who presses it with the tooth. “This” means, in this place, “bread”; and he subsequently defines which bread.

A. 65[I] M. 284 R. 165 L. 266

“I am the living bread which came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live forever.”

By descending to earth, he offered himself as living bread—that is, life-giving and eternal—so that a human being might eat the bread of angels. For Truth itself, Wisdom, [Col. 0254A] and the Power of God are the food of angels and human beings. Whoever therefore eats this heavenly bread through faith and love and is united to him shall live forever through righteousness, truth, and wisdom.

“And the bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world.”

How could flesh grasp his saying that bread was flesh? What flesh cannot grasp is called flesh; and flesh grasps it all the less because it is called flesh. According to the explanation of Augustine and Alcuin, the Lord here calls both his bread and his flesh the fellowship of the faithful in his body, which is the Church. He calls it bread because the Church daily refreshes those whom it receives; and within it, until they reach complete satisfaction, each feeds the other by word and example. Hence the Lord said to [Col. 0254B] Peter: “Feed my sheep” (John 21).

[AUGUST.] The Church is called Christ’s flesh because, united to the incarnation of the Word by faith and sacraments, it lives by the Spirit of Christ. For just as each person’s body lives by his own spirit, that is, by his soul, so faithful souls live by the Holy Spirit. Hence Paul says: “Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. 8).

A. 66[X]

“Therefore the Jews disputed among themselves, saying: ‘How can this man give us his flesh to eat?’”

[JEROME.] They disputed because they did not understand the bread of concord. “One bread, one body”—or one flesh of Christ—we are many. [Col. 0254C] Do you wish to know how we are made one body with Christ? If you believe as the Apostles believed, you will become one body of Christ with them. In this, as John says, we know that we remain in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit. Augustine also teaches in his *Sermon on the Sacraments of the Faithful*, on the Monday of Easter, how we become one bread:

> You were brought together by the labors of oxen—that is, by those who proclaim the Gospel. You were threshed when you became catechumens. You were stored in the granary when you gave in your names. You began to be ground by fasts and exorcisms; you came to the water, when, sprinkled in baptism, you were made one; with the [Col. 0254D] heat of the Holy Spirit added, you were baked, and thus made the Lord’s bread.

Therefore, as you were made one, so be one: holding one faith, one hope, and indivisible love.

[AUGUST.] When, disputing among themselves, they ask how the Lord can give his flesh to be eaten, they do not immediately hear the answer; instead, they are told something that troubles them still more. Jesus therefore said to them:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you do not have life in yourselves.”

[AUGUST.] You do not know how it is given, nor what manner of eating this bread is; nevertheless, unless you eat, you will not have life in yourselves. And lest they understand this life [Col. 0255A] in a merely temporal sense, he added:

“Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.”

[AUGUSTINE.] He who does not eat the flesh of the Lord nor drink his blood has no life in himself; and he who eats and drinks has life. It is not so with temporal food: for one who does not take it will not live, yet neither will one who takes it live. By food and drink which give eternal life, the Lord wishes us to understand the fellowship of his body and members, which is the Church among the predestined, called, justified, and glorified. Of these, the first has already taken place, namely predestination; the second and third have taken place, are taking place, and will take place, namely calling and justification; but the fourth is now in hope and will be future in reality, namely glorification. The sacrament of this matter—that is, of the unity of the body [Col. 0255B] and blood of Christ—is prepared in some places daily, in others at fixed intervals, upon the Lord’s table; and from the Lord’s table it is received by some unto life, by others unto destruction. But the reality of which it is the sacrament is unto life for every person, and unto destruction for none.

“And I will raise him up on the last day.”

He added this lest they should think that they would not die bodily.

A 67[I] M. 284 R. 165 L. 266

“For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.”

[AUGUSTINE.] Since human beings seek food and drink in order not to hunger or thirst, this food and drink alone truly accomplishes that end, making those [Col. 0255C] who receive it immortal and incorruptible: that is, the fellowship itself of the saints, where peace and perfect unity shall be. For this reason, as the men of God before us also understood, Christ commended his body and blood in those things which are made one from many. One thing is made into one from many grains; another flows together into one from many grapes.

A. 68[X]

“He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.”

[AUGUSTINE.] He now explains what it is to eat his flesh and drink his blood: namely, to eat that food and drink that drink—to remain in Christ [Col. 0255D] and to have him remaining in oneself. Accordingly, one who does not remain in Christ, and in whom Christ does not remain, undoubtedly neither eats his flesh nor drinks his blood, even if he eats and drinks the sacrament of so great a thing to his own judgment. Eating and drinking are complete refreshment for us; and by the flesh of Christ we understand the Church, as was said above; likewise, by the blood of Christ we understand the Church, because blood is the seat of the soul, and the Church is in a certain sense the seat of the Holy Spirit, who is as it were the soul of all the souls of the faithful. Therefore we eat Christ’s flesh and drink his blood if we especially and uniquely rejoice in participation in the Church, in which Christ is as the head and the Holy Spirit as the soul, and in which there is communion of the sacraments and [Col. 0256A] forgiveness of sins.

These words may also be referred in a particular sense to Christ’s person: “The bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world.” It is as though he said: “The refreshment which I offer, so as to bring one to the fullness of divine contemplation, is my incarnation, accomplished so that the world may live.” “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves”: that is, unless you are nourished in faith in the incarnation, you will not attain eternal life. By “blood,” understand the soul, since blood is the seat of the soul. “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.”

[AMBROSE.] It is as though he said: “He who gladdens and nourishes his mind—because I assumed flesh and soul in order to save the whole human being—is on the way of salvation.” “My flesh [Col. 0256B] is truly food, and my blood is truly drink”: that is, through my flesh and blood I shall give true satisfaction, namely sufficient and eternal satisfaction. For the Savior’s flesh was offered for the salvation of our body, and his blood was shed for our soul, so that he might make us whole in soul and body, as was prefigured by Moses. “The flesh,” he says, “shall be offered for your [our] body, but the blood for the soul” (Deut. 12); therefore blood is not to be eaten. Thus from this comes our spiritual food and drink; from this comes the voice of rejoicing and the sound of feasting, because without ceasing we chew over in a kind of mental mastication the flesh of Christ and his blood as the price of our redemption, and as the way of immortal life, in which there will be neither thirst nor hunger. But an animal that does not chew the cud [Col. 0256C] is unclean.

Augustine, Book III of *On Christian Doctrine*: “In figurative expressions this rule shall be observed: what is read must be considered with diligent reflection until the interpretation is brought to the kingdom of charity. ‘Unless,’ he says, ‘you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.’ He seems to command a crime and an outrage; it is a figure, commanding participation in the Lord’s passion and the sweet and beneficial storing up in memory that his flesh was crucified and wounded for us.”

“He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me” through conformity of life, “and I in him” through indwelling grace; surely, faith in your heart is Christ in your heart.

“As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father. [Col. 0256D] And he who eats me, he also shall live because of me.”

[AUGUSTINE.] The Father sent me as his equal, that is, he made me man. Therefore, in order that I may refer my life to him as greater than myself, my self-emptying, in which he sent me, brought this about. We eat him—that is, we receive him as eternal life. Or the Son lives because of the Father because he is from the Father. For as the Father does not lack life, so the Son does not need another’s life. For both are one life, because they are one God.

“This is the bread which came down from heaven. Not as your fathers ate manna and died. He who eats this bread shall live forever.”

“This,” that is, in this place; or “this,” namely the Son of Man, concerning whom above it was said that he is bread from heaven. Those who eat me, the heavenly bread, will not die [Col. 0257A] in soul as your fathers ate manna and died.

“He said these things in the synagogue, teaching at Capernaum. Therefore many of his disciples, hearing, said: ‘This saying is hard. Who can hear it?’”

[AUGUSTINE.] That is, who can obey it? The disciples are disturbed; what then of his enemies? Behold, the wheat is being winnowed; but God’s hidden purpose ought to make us attentive, not turn us away. The Lord’s words are indeed so profound that they disturb all the perverse and exercise all upright hearers. The disciples said among themselves that the Lord’s saying was hard, in such a way that he did not hear them. Hence follows:

“But Jesus, knowing within himself that his disciples were murmuring about this, said to them: ‘Does this scandalize you?’”

[Col. 0257B] [AUGUSTINE.] Namely, that I said: “I give you my flesh to eat and my blood to drink.”

A. 69[I] M. 310 R. 121 L. 297

“If, then, you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before?”

[AUGUSTINE.] Here he resolves what had troubled them. Here he discloses the source of their offense. Here the matter would be plain, if they understood. For they thought that he would distribute his body. But he said that he would ascend into heaven, certainly whole. “When you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before,” then at least you will see that he does not distribute his body in the way you suppose. Then at least you will understand that his grace is not consumed [Col. 0257C] by bites.

There would be no question here if he had said, “If you see the Son of God ascending where he was before.” But now he said “the Son of Man.” Was the Son of Man, who began to be on earth—as in the words, “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. 84)—previously in heaven? Yet elsewhere he says: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who came down from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3). Here he did not say “was,” but “is”; and yet when he said this he was speaking on earth, and he did not say “the Son of God,” but “the Son of Man.” All this pertains to our understanding that Christ, God and man, is one person. For Christ is one: Word, soul, and flesh; and according to the unity of his person, the Son of Man was in heaven while speaking on earth, just as [Col. 0257D] the Son of God was on earth in assumed flesh, and the Son of Man in heaven in the unity of person.

A. 70 M. 297[IV] R. 188

“It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing.”

[AUGUSTINE.] In the sense in which they understood it, it profits nothing. For they understood flesh as it is torn apart in a corpse or sold in a butcher’s shop, not as it is enlivened by the Spirit. Thus it was said, “The flesh profits nothing,” just as it was said, “Knowledge puffs up” (1 Cor. 8). For knowledge without charity is useless; likewise flesh without spirit.

A. 71[X]

“The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life.”

[Col. 0258A] That is, they are to be understood spiritually.

“But there are some among you who do not believe.”

[AUGUSTINE.] Because they do not believe, they do not understand, as the prophet says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7). By faith we are joined together; by understanding we are made alive. Let us first cling through faith, so that there may be something to be made alive through understanding.

A. 73[X]

“And he said: ‘For this reason I told you that no one can come to me unless it has been given him by my Father.’”

For faith is not from oneself as one’s own possession, but from God as grace.

“After this many of his disciples went back and [Col. 0258B] no longer walked with him. Therefore Jesus said to the Twelve: ‘Do you also wish to go away?’”

A. 74[I] M. 166 R. 82 L. 94

“Then Simon Peter answered him: ‘Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we have believed and known that you are Christ, the Son of God.’”

[AUGUSTINE.] Refreshed by the Holy Spirit, Peter understood. “You have the words of eternal life”: that is, you have eternal life in the administration of your body and blood. “We have believed, so that we might know.” For if we wished first to know by the Spirit and then to believe, we would be able neither to know nor to believe. What have we believed? That you are Christ, the Son of God—that is, that you yourself are eternal life, and in your flesh and blood [Col. 0258C] you give nothing other than what you are. One spoke for all.

A. 75[X]

“Jesus answered them: ‘Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?’ But he spoke of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot. For he was about to betray him, though he was one of the twelve.”

He answered in order to test them. He chose twelve to remain, with that choosing of which it is said: “Many are called, few are chosen” (Matt. 20). But he chose Judas—that is, called him—so that through him the dispensation of divine mercy for the salvation of the world might be fulfilled. Hence the goodness of God made good use of his wickedness, as in the selling of Joseph he made good use of his brothers’ wickedness (Gen. 37). [Col. 0258D] Conversely, the wicked make evil use of God’s good things, such as fire, water, and the rest. Therefore Judas, when he perished, destroyed himself; he did not violate the sacred number (Gen. 50).

All that the Lord said concerning his body and blood; and that in the grace of their distribution he promised us eternal life; and that by this he wished it understood that those eating and drinking his flesh and blood should remain in him and he in them; and that those who did not believe did not understand; and that, interpreting spiritual things carnally, they were scandalized; and that, when they were scandalized and perishing, the Lord was a consolation to the disciples who remained—all this, beloved, may avail to this end: that we do not eat Christ’s flesh and blood only in the sacrament, as many wicked people do, but [Col. 0259A] eat and drink even unto participation in the Spirit, so that we may remain in the Lord’s body as members, be enlivened by his Spirit, and not be scandalized, even if many now eat and drink the sacraments with us temporally who shall have eternal torments at the end. For Christ’s body is now mixed together like a threshing floor, but “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2).

It should be noted that some teachers incidentally refer certain of the foregoing matters to the sacraments of the altar, but none does so in a continuous exposition. In the one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter of this work, however, the sacrifice of the altar is treated specifically.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII

[Col. 0259B] L. 135[V] M. 236

“Now a certain Pharisee asked him to dine with him; and entering in, he reclined. But the Pharisee began to say to himself, wondering why he had not been baptized before dinner.”

[AUGUSTINE.] That is, washed, according to Jewish custom. The Pharisees were the more eminent and learned Jews.

“And the Lord said to him: ‘Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of cup and dish, but your inward part is full of robbery and iniquity.’”

[AMBROSE—BEDE.] You observe outward bodily cleanliness, yet retain the foulness of the soul. A cup is a glass vessel; a dish is earthenware, made from earth. By these is signified the frailty of the human body, in which they outwardly [Col. 0259C] display holiness and pretend righteousness, while inwardly they are disfigured by the filth of vices.

“Fools, did not he who made the outside also make the inside?”

He who made both natures of the human being desires both to be cleansed. This is said against the Manichaeans, who think that the soul alone was created by God but the flesh by the devil. It is also said against those who detest bodily sins—namely, fornication, theft, and robbery—as though they were most serious, but scorn as light sins the spiritual ones which the Apostle no less condemns: namely anger, pride, and greed, which is the service of idols (Col. 9).

“But give alms from what remains, and behold, all things are clean to you.”

[Col. 0259D] Give to the poor what remains beyond the necessities of food and clothing, according to John’s command: “He who has two tunics, let him give to one who has none” (Luke 3).
