Or thus: Make of what remains a remedy for your crime. Give alms, because “as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. 3). He who wishes to give alms in proper order ought to begin with himself and first give it to himself, that is, show mercy to himself. For almsgiving is a work of mercy, and it has been said most truly: “Have mercy on your soul by pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30). The first almsgiving occurs when we are reborn; the second is every good thing we do afterward. Therefore, when hearts have been cleansed through faith, all things are clean: that is, nothing defiles the mind.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV

[Col. 0260A]

R. 70[X]

“The Pharisees and some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem, when they saw some of the disciples eating bread with common hands—that is, unwashed hands—rebuked them, saying:

M. 154 R. 71

‘Why do your disciples transgress the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread.’”

[BEDE.] The Pharisees understood spiritually spoken words carnally: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. 1); and “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 59). They did not rightly understand this cleansing, for it was said [Col. 0260B] concerning the purification of heart and deed, not merely the washing of the body, as they imagined. Thus, though outwardly washed with water, they were polluted by the bruising stain of conscience; they came together not to hear the word, not as to a physician, but for battles of controversy. Therefore they rebuke the disciples about their body’s unwashed hands, although they find no uncleanness in their works. For they diligently washed the hands of their souls, that is, their deeds. The Jews called all unclean things “common.”

“But he answered and said to them: ‘Why do you also transgress the commandment of God because of your tradition?’”

Since you neglect God’s commands for the sake of human tradition, why do you accuse my disciples because, in order to keep God’s ordinances, [Col. 0260C] they make little of the elders’ commands?

“For God said: ‘Honor your father and mother’ (Exod. 20); and, ‘He who curses father or mother shall surely die’ (Exod. 21).”

In the Scriptures, “honor” is understood not so much as the rendering of greetings and services as the giving of alms and offerings. Hence the Apostle says: “Honor widows who are truly widows” (1 Tim. 5). That is, give to them. Therefore one who judges his parents unworthy of the services owed them shall die an eternal death.

“But you say: ‘Whoever says to father or mother, “Whatever gift is from me will profit you,” and does not honor his father or mother’—and you have made void the commandment of God because of your tradition.”

[Col. 0260D] The Lord, providing for the weakness and poverty of parents, commanded that children honor them even in the necessities of life. Overthrowing this law in order to clothe impiety with the name of piety, the Pharisees taught children that they did better if they vowed to God, the true Father, what ought to have been offered to their parents. Thus the parents themselves became needy, while the children’s offering, under the pretext of God, passed into the priests’ profit.

Read the passage thus: God commanded—namely through Moses—that parents be honored; but “whoever says to father or mother,” etc.—you say this because, whoever says it, you instruct him to say it. You, I say, teach wicked children in this matter to say: “O father, O mother, whatever gift is offered from me”—understand, in the Temple—“will profit you in soul.” Or thus: You compel children [Col. 0261A] to say to their parents: “Whatever gift I ought to offer to God, I spend on food for you, and it benefits you, O father and mother,” so that they may fear to receive things consecrated to God, lest they incur the crime of sacrilege.

Or it may be read as a question: “O father, O mother, will the gift given from me to you for food and clothing profit you toward saving your soul?” Certainly not, because you care only for the body. Otherwise: Young people, presuming to offer despite their parents’ loss and dishonor, said at the priests’ instigation: “The gift which is for me will benefit you, father; do not offer it yourself.” It is as though they said: “We have reached the age at which, by the priests’ judgment, we may now make offerings for ourselves.”

[Col. 0261B] R. 70[X]

“For the Pharisees and all the Jews, unless they wash their hands frequently, do not eat, holding the traditions of the elders; and when they return from the marketplace, unless they baptize themselves, they do not eat. And there are many other things handed down to them to observe: baptisms of cups, pitchers, bronze vessels, and beds; and they do many other similar things.”

[BEDE.] “From the marketplace” means, understand, after returning from it: unless they wash, they do not eat. In vain are they so baptized, since they are not washed in the Savior’s name. By “baptisms of pitchers and cups” he means washings of vessels, which the Jews perform so that they may appear clean in body, without caring to cast out from themselves the sins of unbelief. Yet those who neglect the filth of their hearts and bodies observe in vain the baptisms of vessels. [Col. 0261C] Hence Paul says: “The will of God is that you abstain from fornication, that each one of you may know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor” (1 Thess. 4). Superstitious human tradition commanded frequent washings for eating and other useless practices of this kind; but the necessary teaching of truth commands those who wish to eat the bread of life frequently to cleanse their works through the fostering help of almsgiving, tears, and the other fruits of righteousness.

M. 154[IV] R. 71

“You have made void the commandment of God because of your tradition. Hypocrites, Isaiah rightly prophesied concerning you, saying: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me’ (Isa. 29). In vain [Col. 0261D] do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men. For, leaving the commandment of God, you hold the tradition of men.”

[AUGUSTINE—JEROME.] He blunts the Pharisees’ barking with the fork of reason—that is, with the rebuke of Moses and Isaiah—so that we too may overcome heretics with the words of Scripture. The hypocritical Jews indeed say with a clamor of lips, “Teacher, we know that you are true” (Matt. 22), and commend external cleanliness; but because they oppose the truth with an unclean mind, they will by no means receive a reward with true praisers.

“And having called the crowds to him, he said to them: ‘Hear and understand. It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person; but what proceeds from the mouth, this defiles a person.’”

[AUGUSTINE.] If this statement is understood wholly of the bodily mouth, [Col. 0262A] it is absurd. For food does not defile one, nor does vomit defile one. Food enters the mouth; vomit proceeds from the mouth. But without doubt the former words concern the mouth of the flesh, where he says, “What enters the mouth does not defile a person.”

[JEROME.] The latter words concern the mouth of the heart, where he says, “But what proceeds from the mouth defiles.” In this way the saying is true. Why, then, do we not eat things sacrificed to idols? The Apostle says: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons” (1 Cor. 8). We must understand, therefore, that foods and every creature of God are clean in themselves, but the invocation of idols and demons makes them unclean.

M. 135[X]

“Then his disciples came to him and said: ‘Do you know [Col. 0262B] that the Pharisees were scandalized when they heard this saying?’ But he answered and said: ‘Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be uprooted.’”

The Pharisees, whose religion lay in distinguishing foods, were scandalized—that is, offended. For *skandalon* or *scandalum* may be called an offense, a fall, a striking of the foot, or, as some wish, a stumbling block. By “plantation” he here means doctrines and commandments of men, which are not from God.

M. 136[V] L. 57

“Leave them; they are blind, and guides of the blind. But if a blind man gives guidance to a blind man, both fall into a pit.”

[Col. 0262C] That is, if a fool teaches a fool, both sink into the depths of sins. “Leave them,” understand, to their own choice, because they are incorrigible. Hence Paul: “Avoid a heretical person after a first and second correction” (Titus 3).

M. 157[V] R. 72

“And when he had entered the house away from the crowd, Peter questioned him: ‘Explain this parable to us.’ But he said: ‘Are you also still without understanding?’”

The apostles thought what was plain had been spoken parabolically. Therefore they are rebuked by the Lord. From this we understand that a hearer is faulty if he wishes to understand obvious things obscurely, or obscure things obviously.

“Do you not understand that everything which enters the mouth goes into [Col. 0262D] the belly and is discharged into the privy?”

Certain heretics calumniate this passage, alleging that the Lord, ignorant of natural science, thought that all foods go into the belly and are digested in the privy, whereas food immediately after being swallowed is distributed through limbs, veins, marrow, and sinews. Thus they say that many people who, through a stomach ailment, suffer continual vomiting, vomit immediately after suppers and meals what they have eaten, yet are corpulent because, at the first contact, liquid food and drink are distributed through the limbs.

But although the moisture is very thin and the food fluid, nevertheless, when the food has been cooked and digested with the moisture in the veins and limbs, it descends through the hidden passages of the body—which the Greeks call *poroi* (“pores”)—to the lower parts and goes into the privy. Any evacuation of humors [Col. 0263A] as by sweat or in any other way may also not improperly be understood as a “discharge.” For the elements that flow in flow out. Alternatively, let us take *emittitur* (“is discharged”) as an impersonal verb, as if the sense were: “Everything that enters through the mouth indeed goes into the belly; afterward there is a discharge into the privy.”

“But those things which proceed from the mouth come out of the heart, and they defile a person. For from the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, greed, wickednesses, deceit, indecency, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, foolishness. These are what defile a person. But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile a person.”

[JEROME.] Plato thought that our rational faculty dwelt in the brain, anger in the gall, and desire in the liver. [Col. 0263B] But if evil thoughts come out of the heart, then the ruling faculty of the soul is not, according to Plato, in the brain, but, according to Crates, in the heart. Here also those are refuted who think that thoughts are implanted by the devil, who may be an assistant but not their author. For he does not search out the secrets of the heart, but conjectures the matter from the body’s bearing: if he sees us repeatedly look upon a beautiful woman, he understands that the heart has been wounded.

Murderers also are those who hate their brothers unto death. Hence John: “He who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3). To commit adultery is to violate another’s marriage bed; fornication is love loosed from lawful marriage and wandering at large. Fornication is so called from the arches (*fornices*) in which pagans practiced their shamefulness. Theft is everything acquired at another’s loss. [Col. 0263C] Greed, moreover, the root of evils, is the service of idols (1 Tim. 6), because just as the belly is the god of the gluttonous, so money may most justly be called the god of the covetous. Wickedness is a lack of good; hence a wicked slave (*nequam servus*) says that he is unable (*nequire*) to do something. Deceit is hidden malice adorned with flattering words. Indecency is every lack of self-control connected with lust, such as unlawful touching of the flesh, shameful words, and shameful thought. The evil eye means envy: being tormented by another’s prosperity. The forms of pride are wishing to rule, refusing to be subject, and refusing to have an equal. The difference between a fool (*stultus*) and an unwise person (*insipiens*) is this: however great a philosopher may be, he is unwise if deprived of God’s wisdom; but a fool has no shrewdness even in temporal matters.

Mark uses *communicat* (“makes common”) instead of “defiles” (Mark 7), an expression proper to Scripture but not current in ordinary speech. The Jews call “common” those foods that all people use, such as hares and animals of that kind which do not divide the hoof, do not chew the cud, and, among fish, do not have scales. Hence in the Acts of the Apostles: “What God has made holy, do not call common” (Acts 10). Thus they regard “common” as “unclean.” Yet apostolic communion extends its branches, unwashed, as far as the sea; but Pharisaic cleanliness is barren.

## CHAPTER LXXXV

M. 157[VI] R. 72

“And rising from there, he went into the district of Tyre and Sidon. And [Col. 0264A] behold, a Canaanite woman, a Gentile, Syrophoenician by race, cried out, saying: ‘Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is grievously tormented by a demon.’”

[HILARY.] The Canaanites inhabited the land in which Judea lies. Whether consumed by war, scattered into neighboring places, or subjected to slavery by the condition of the conquered, they carry about only their name and no homeland. Among other consequences of that dispersion, this Canaanite woman is Syrophoenician by origin—that is, born from Syrians and Phoenicians. She is therefore a Gentile, although mingled with Jews and bearing the appearance of proselytes. She is rightly thought to have learned from the Law what she confesses: that Christ is both Lord and David’s son.

[BEDE.] In a typological sense she signifies the Church from the Gentiles, which asks for her daughter [Col. 0264B] when she supplicates heavenly mercy on behalf of souls not yet believing, that they may be freed from the devil’s deceits. Fittingly, according to Matthew, she went out from her own borders, and according to Mark, fell at the Lord’s feet, so that from both accounts it may be inferred that those rightly pray for the erring who leave behind the former dwellings of their unbelief and transfer themselves to the Church in devout commitment.

“But Jesus did not answer her a word. And his disciples came and begged him, saying: ‘Send her away, for she cries out after us.’”

The Canaanite woman uttered her pleading cries after the Lord as he walked along, and afterward fell at his feet in the house, as Mark records. The Lord’s failure to answer her was not from proud disdain, but lest he seem to contradict himself after saying, “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. 10), and lest he give slanderers an occasion, reserving the Gentiles’ complete salvation for the time of the resurrection. The disciples pleaded for the Canaanite woman, unaware of the Lord’s mysteries, either moved by compassion or wishing to be rid of her importunity.

M. 158[V] R. 226

“But he answered and said: ‘I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.’”

This means that he was first sent to Israel, which he would abandon for neglecting the Gospel and pass over to the Gentiles.

[Col. 0264D] M. 159[V] L. 74

“But she came and worshiped him, saying: ‘Lord, help me.’ He said: ‘Let the children first be filled. For it is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.’”

[BEDE.] It is as though he said: “You Gentiles also will obtain salvation, but first it is necessary that at least some Jews, who are called children of God by the ancient election, be refreshed with the bread of heaven; and only then that the food of life be supplied to the Gentiles.” The heathen are called dogs because of idolatry; devoted to eating blood and to the corpses of the dead, they are borne into madness. O wonderful reversal! Israel was once the son, we the dogs; and later it was said concerning him: “Many dogs surrounded me” (Ps. 21).

[Col. 0265A] “But she said: ‘Yes, Lord. For even the little dogs eat from the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table.’”

The sense is: Certainly, Lord, what you say is true: it is not good to give the children’s bread to dogs. But for that reason I do not cease to seek your mercy, which you may fittingly extend to me according to the comparison of bread and dogs. For “even” means “indeed,” that is, certainly: little dogs also eat crumbs. Therefore, if I am unworthy for you to give me the whole bread, at least grant my daughter’s health as a crumb in comparison with the many marvelous things you have done.

[BEDE.] Mystically, the table is Holy Scripture, which ministers the bread of life. Hence the Church says: “You have prepared a table before me” (Ps. 22). The crumbs are the inward mysteries of the Scriptures, [Col. 0265B] by which humble hearts are refreshed, according to the words: “He satisfies you with the fat of wheat” (Ps. 147). The little dogs therefore do not eat crusts, because those from the Gentiles converted to faith seek not the surface of the letter but the spiritual marrow. And this is “under the masters’ table,” while, humbly subject to the words of sacred utterance, they place beneath it the services of body and heart in order to fulfill the commandments. Or the masters of the table may be understood as the composers or interpreters of the Scriptures.

“Then he said to her: ‘O woman, great is your faith; let it be done to you as you wish.’ And her daughter was healed from that hour.”

[JEROME.] Under the person of the Canaanite woman, the Church’s great faith, great patience, and humility are proclaimed: she believed that her daughter could be healed; though so often rebuffed, she endured to persevere in prayer; and in humility compared herself not to dogs but to little dogs. Therefore her daughter was delivered.

[BEDE.] Here an example is given for catechizing and baptizing infants, who through their parents’ faith and confession are delivered from the devil in baptism. The Lord’s healing, without coming to them, of the centurion’s servant and the Canaanite woman’s daughter signifies that the Gentiles, to whom he did not come in bodily presence, were to be saved through his Word.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI

R. 74[X]

“And again, going out from the district of Tyre, he came through Sidon [Col. 0265D] to the Sea of Galilee, through the midst of the district of the Decapolis.”

[BEDE.] Decapolis is a region of ten cities beyond the Jordan, to the east, around Hippos, Pella, and Gadara, opposite Galilee. Therefore, the statement that the Lord came to the Sea of Galilee through the midst of the district of the Decapolis does not mean that he entered the actual territory of Decapolis. For he is not said to have crossed the sea, but rather to have come as far as the sea and reached the place facing, across the sea and at a distance, the central territory of Decapolis; *inter* means “opposite.” Or it refers to Galilee, which lies amid the central boundaries.

“And they bring to him a deaf and mute man, and beg him to lay his hand upon him. And taking him aside from the crowd, he put his fingers into [Col. 0266A] his ears; and spitting, he touched his tongue. And looking up to heaven, he groaned and said to him: ‘Ephphatha,’ that is, ‘Be opened.’ And immediately his ears were opened, the bond of his tongue was loosed, and he spoke rightly.”

A deaf and mute person is one who opens neither ears nor mouth for hearing and uttering the words of God. The first gateway of salvation is to lead the infirm person away from the crowd. This occurs when the Lord, taking hold of a mind weakened by sins, calls it away from accustomed habits and summons it to his commandments. He puts his fingers into the ears when, through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, he opens the ears of the heart to understanding. The Lord spits and touches the sick man’s tongue when he instructs the mouths of catechumens for the confession of faith. For spittle is the savour of wisdom. [Col. 0266B] Hence the saying: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Ecclus. 24). The Lord looked up to heaven in order to teach that speech for the mute, hearing for the deaf, and healing for all the infirm must be sought from there. He groaned, that he might give us an example of groaning both for ourselves and for our neighbours. *Ephphetha* properly concerns the ears; hence it is added: “And immediately his ears were opened.” Here both natures of the Redeemer are indicated: he looks to heaven as man; he heals as God. One who is thus healed may rightly say: “Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise” (Ps. 50).

[HIERONYMUS.] Otherwise: The human race, as though one man infected by the plague contracted in the first-created man, is blinded while it sees; becomes deaf while it hears; while it smells, suffers a running nose; becomes mute while it speaks; becomes maimed while it raises its hand; is bent over [Col. 0266C] while it is raised upright; becomes dropsical while it lusts; lame while it advances; is covered with leprosy while it is stripped naked; is filled with a demon while it seeks divinity; dies by death while it makes a bold excuse. But the patriarchs and prophets, desiring the Incarnation, pray that the hand of mercy may be laid upon it. The person worthy to be healed is always led away from turbulent thoughts, disordered actions, and incoherent words, as though from the crowd. The fingers put into the ears are the words of the Holy Spirit, of whom it is said: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 7); and: “The heavens are the works of your fingers” (Ps. 8). The spittle descending from the head is Wisdom from the Father, which loosens the lips of the human race so that it may say: “I believe in God the Father,” etc. Looking up [Col. 0266D] to heaven, he groaned; that is, he taught us to groan and to raise the treasure of our heart to heaven. After compunction it is cleansed from the frivolous joy of the flesh, as is said: “I roared from the groaning of my heart” (Ps. 37). The ears are opened to hymns, canticles, and psalms. The tongue is loosened so that it may pour forth a good word, which neither threats nor beatings can restrain. Hence Paul: “I am bound, but the word of God is not bound” (2 Tim. 2).

“And he commanded them that they should tell no one.”

R. 75[VIII] L. 100

But the more he commanded them, the more zealously they proclaimed it. And they were all the more astonished, saying:

[Col. 0267A] R. 75 M. 160

“He has done all things well; he makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.”

He taught that one should not glory in miracles, but in the cross and humiliation. For humility always precedes glory. The order of the words is: “But the more he commanded them, the more they proclaimed.” (Matt. 5). [BEDA.] For a city set upon a mountain, visible from every side, cannot be hidden. Therefore he who knows all things before they happen knew that they would proclaim all the more; but by giving this command he wished to show the slothful how much more earnestly and how much more frequently those ought to preach whom he commands to preach, since those who were forbidden could not keep silent.

CHAPTER LXXXVII

[Col. 0267B]

A. 33[X]

“It was necessary for him to pass through Samaria. Therefore he came to a city of Samaria called Sychar, near the estate which Jacob gave to his son Joseph. Now Jacob’s spring was there.”

Whether the Lord passed through Samaria from Judaea into Galilee, or from Galilee into Judaea, when the events which follow occurred, is by no means certain from the Gospel account, because it very often changes the sequence of times in reverse order. In a figure of Christ, the rightful heir of the patriarchs, who possesses an inheritance among the Gentiles, Joseph received from Jacob the inheritance of an estate, which the Gentiles inhabit [Col. 0267C] and in which, through the type of the Samaritan woman, they cleave to Christ. Where water flows on the surface of the ground, it is called a spring; but where it is in the depths, it is called both a spring and a well.

“But Jesus, weary from the journey, sat thus beside the spring. It was about the sixth hour.”

The Lord is weary according to the flesh, though he made us by his strength. For he assumed, without sin, all that belongs to our weakness, and as one weak he nourishes the weak. That Adam was made in flesh, while Eve was made from his side, signifies that we shall become strong through Christ’s weakness. For his strength created; his weakness re-created. Strength made what did not exist to exist; weakness ensured that what existed [Col. 0267D] should not perish. Thus, weary from the journey, he sat as a humble teacher, about to teach and to take possession of those who approached. The sixth hour signifies that the Lord came in the sixth age.

“A woman came from Samaria to draw water. Jesus said to her: ‘Give me to drink.’ For his disciples had gone into the city to buy food.”

The Samaritan woman comes as a figure of the Church from among the Gentiles. Formerly she drew water with the vessel of desire from the well—that is, worldly pleasure from the dark depth—but now Jesus thirsts for her faith and asks to drink from her. He asks as one about to receive, and pours forth as one about to satisfy. In the city, the disciples buy food from the Jews, whose hearts they labour to win for God through the preaching of faith.

[Col. 0268A] “Therefore that Samaritan woman said to him: ‘How is it that you, being a Jew, ask a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?’ For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.”

[AMBROSE.] The Samaritans accepted the Law alone, that is, the five books of Moses. They were of Persian and Assyrian origin. When the king of the Assyrians had carried the children of Israel away into captivity, he settled them in the places of Samaria to inhabit (4 Kgs. 17); and therefore they worshipped fire in the Persian manner. Accordingly the Jews detest them, abstaining from their food and vessels; and they call them supplanters, because they lay claim to the inheritance of the patriarch Jacob. The woman recognized Christ as a Jew because Jews wore fringes on their garments, by which they were distinguished.

[Col. 0268B] “Jesus answered and said to her: ‘If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, “Give me to drink,” perhaps you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.’”

[AUGUSTINE.] Although Jesus thirsted bodily, he nevertheless sought only the drink of faith, in return for which he desired to give the Spirit; and therefore he admonishes the Samaritan woman to ask. The gift of God is the Holy Spirit, and the living water is that of which it is said: “With you is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35).

“The woman said to him: ‘Lord, you have nothing with which to draw, and the well is deep. Whence, then, have you living water? Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well and drank from it himself, with his children and his cattle?’”

As though she said: You cannot give me the water which you promise from this source, since you have no vessel for drawing and [Col. 0268C] the well is deep. For she understands “living water” to mean water which is collected where it springs up. But lest he seem to promise another spring, she adds: “Are you greater than our father Jacob?” She calls him her father both because she possessed his inheritance and because she lived under the law of Moses. Men and cattle drink from the well. Likewise, from reason—which is, as it were, corrupted and darkened, and is dug out and exercised with great labour—those drink as human beings who use it for good; those drink as cattle who use it for evil.

“Jesus answered and said to her: ‘Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again. But whoever drinks from the water which I shall give him will never thirst; rather, the water which I shall give him will become in him a spring of water leaping up into [Col. 0268D] eternal life.’ The woman said to him: ‘Lord, give me this water, that I may not thirst or come here to draw.’”

[AUGUSTINE.] The Lord now speaks more plainly, yet the woman still thinks carnally. Nevertheless, she longs to have water from that spring, so that after drinking she may not need water. Jesus promises the satisfaction of the spirit which will take place in the resurrection. Hence: “We shall be satisfied with the good things of your house” (Ps. 94). And elsewhere: “They shall be made drunk with the abundance of your house” (Ps. 35). Bodily water flows downward, but spiritual water leaps upward—that is, makes one leap upward—when it bears those who drink it up into eternal glory. To drink this water, then, is to delight exceedingly in faith and the other gifts of grace, and thus to pass into the fullness of glory.

[Col. 0269A] “And Jesus said to her: ‘Go, call your husband, and come here.’”

That is, with your husband as guide, ascend to contemplation of spiritual understanding. A carnal husband is not meant here, but the husband of the soul, namely its understanding. As though the Lord said: What I say is grasped by understanding alone; call your husband—that is, bring forth your understanding. For it is no great thing to have a soul without understanding. Hence David: “Do not become like horse and mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31). Life without understanding is beastly. The husband who governs the soul is understanding. Yet the understanding of the soul is not something other than the soul, but something belonging to the soul; just as the eye is not something other than flesh, but part of the flesh, pouring light upon the other members. Therefore the understanding [Col. 0269B] that enlightens the soul is itself enlightened by God.

“The woman answered and said: ‘I have no husband.’ Jesus said to her: ‘You have rightly said, “I have no husband”; for you have had five husbands, and the one whom you now have is not your husband. This you have truly said.’”

In truth she had no husband, but was joined to some unlawful man, an adulterer. According to some, the five husbands are the five books of Moses, which the Samaritans also used; for from them they had circumcision. But because what follows constrains us—“and the one whom you now have is not your husband”—it seems to me that the five husbands of the soul are the five bodily senses. For when someone is born, he cannot use reason, but is governed only by the senses of the flesh: as a child, he desires what pleases him and flees what offends him. Therefore the senses are lawful husbands, since they are given to the soul by God. But when one reaches the years in which reason is to be exercised, if it is most properly disciplined, the true husband succeeds, governing toward eternity and teaching not so much to avoid offences as to distinguish good from evil, such as love and hatred. But if this husband does not succeed, error then rules—the error that was tossing this woman about—not as a husband but as an adulterer. For while the Lord spoke of the Holy Spirit, she thought of water.

“The woman said to him: ‘Lord, I see that you are a prophet. Our fathers worshipped on this mountain, and you say that Jerusalem is the place where one ought to worship.’”

The husband had now begun to come and to exclude the adulterer. [Col. 0269D] Therefore she calls him a prophet and asks the question that troubled her. The Jews preferred themselves to the Samaritans because of the Temple built by Solomon, in which they worshipped. Conversely, the Samaritans boasted against the Jews because of the mountain on which the fathers who pleased God prayed long before the Temple was built.

“Jesus said to her: ‘Woman, believe me: the hour is coming when you shall worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.’”

As though he said: The Church will come and pass from nation to nation. Believe me; for unless you believe, you shall not understand (Isa. 7), and the husband who can believe is already present. “The hour is coming,” that is, the time; so that you may understand the whole from the part, as is read in the Epistle: “It is the last hour” (1 John 2).

[Col. 0270A] “You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, because salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and now is, when true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father also seeks such as worship him.”

He speaks in the person of all the prophets who believe in Christ. Hence he says: You worship the Father whom you do not know, because no one worships the Father unless he worships the Son, through whom one comes to knowledge of the Father. But we know the Son, and through the Son, the Father. Hence it follows: “Because salvation is from the Jews,” whose are the knowledge of God, the covenant, prophecy, and promises; from whom Christ is according to the flesh (Rom. 9), and from whom faith and the primitive Church arose. Although not all Jews but the elect surpass the Samaritans, [Col. 0270B] I do not nevertheless prefer the place of the Jews to the place of the Samaritans. And this is what he says: “But the hour is coming, and now is,” in which, through the illumination of my teaching, true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth—that is, in the love of the Holy Spirit and in knowledge of the truth of the Son of God.

“God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”

Since God is Spirit and not body, he seeks a pure mind, not a bodily place, in which he may be worshipped. Therefore let no one choose either Jerusalem or the mountain as a place for worship; but worship in spirit and truth—that is, in the spirit of the heart, which is everywhere with us, and in knowledge of the truth of those things whose figure and shadow have been removed. For the command that the people in the Law should be cleansed [Col. 0270C] by the sprinkling of a lamb’s blood was a shadow; the truth is that Christ, suffering on the cross, washed us from our sins in his blood. So too, with the other figures cast aside, may we be illumined by the truth of the things prefigured.

“The woman said to him: ‘I know that Messiah is coming, who is called Christ. When he comes, he will announce all things to us.’”

[ALBINUS.] She knew who could teach her, but did not yet recognize the one teaching her. Therefore she was worthy to receive the manifestation. “Messiah is coming,” as though she said: He will come. *Messias* is Hebrew, *Christus* Greek, “anointed” Latin. Hence in Punic *messe* means “anoint.” For Hebrew, Punic, and Syriac are related languages. Messiah [Col. 0270D] will announce all things concerning his worship and that of the Father: namely, how, with Temple or mountain set aside, we may present ourselves inwardly as God’s temple, where we pray in spirit and truth.

“Jesus said to her: ‘I am he who speaks with you.’”

I am the Messiah whose coming you await. When she received this disclosure, the husband at once became the woman’s head, and Christ the husband’s head. Therefore she left the vessel of desire and ran to preach.

“And immediately his disciples came, and they marvelled that he was speaking with a woman. Yet no one said: ‘What do you seek?’ or: ‘Why do you speak with her?’”

They marvelled at good, not suspecting evil. For he who teaches the erring Gentile woman had come to seek what was lost. And they marvelled at this, not knowing [Col. 0271A] the mystery of the Church to come from among the Gentiles. The disciples did not dare question the woman, “What do you seek?” or the Lord, “Why do you speak with her?” fearing that, if they questioned incautiously, he might rebuke them.

“Therefore the woman left her water vessel, went into the city, and said to the men: ‘Come and see a man who told me all that I have done. Can this be the Christ?’”

[ALBINUS.] Little by little she leads these unlearned people to the truth; she does not immediately affirm that he is Christ, lest they become angry and indignant. Greek *hydor* is Latin *aqua*, “water”; hence *hydria*, that is, a water-vessel. What she had formerly regarded as useful, she now counts as a burden and throws away. From this those who are about to evangelize should learn first to lay aside the care and burden of the world.

“And they went out of the city and came to him. Meanwhile [Col. 0271B] his disciples begged him, saying: ‘Rabbi, eat.’ But he said to them: ‘I have food to eat which you do not know.’ Therefore the disciples said to one another: ‘Has someone brought him something to eat?’”

What wonder if the woman did not understand the drink of the spirit, but that of the flesh? Behold, the disciples who had brought food for the belly do not yet understand that the teacher speaks of food for the mind. Therefore he instructs them openly, rather than indirectly as he did her, who lacked a husband.

“Jesus said to them: ‘My food is to do the will of him who sent me, to complete his work.’”

[ALBINUS.] The Father’s will is that men should believe in him, that is, in the Son whom he sent. The Father’s work is our salvation. Christ’s food and drink—that is, his delightful refreshment—is our faith and [Col. 0271C] our salvation. He therefore does the will by teaching men to believe in himself; he does the work by bringing the mystery of the Incarnation to completion, until through the Passion and the rest he fulfills it.

“Do you not say that there are still four months and then the harvest comes?”

You reckon four months until harvest, but I show you another harvest, white and ready.

“Behold, I say to you: Lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for harvest.”

Consider with the eyes of your heart that, the winter of unbelief having passed, the warmth of faith is present, and hearts are prepared for you to gather works of righteousness from them.

“And he who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit [Col. 0271D] unto eternal life, so that he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together.”

The prophets who sowed and the apostles who reaped had labours at different times; but they will alike receive eternal life as their reward.

“For in this is the saying true: one sows and another reaps. I sent you to reap that for which you have not laboured; others have laboured, and you have entered into their labours.”

In this the Gospel saying is shown true: the apostles reaped where the patriarchs and prophets had sown, namely in Judaea. Thus this woman too was ripe fruit when she said, “I know that Messiah is coming”; and the harvest was ripe when gold was brought [Col. 0272A] to the apostles’ feet. A few chosen grains from that harvest sowed the whole world; and another harvest arose, to be reaped at the end of the age. Of that harvest it is said: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Ps. 122). Not only the apostles but also the angels will be reapers of this harvest, which grows among tares and awaits its cleansing at the end. On the day of judgment the granary will be filled; and then all who reap will rejoice with the angels.

“Now many Samaritans from that city believed in him because of the testimony of the woman, who declared: ‘He told me all that I have done.’ Therefore, when the Samaritans came to him, they begged him to remain there; and he remained there two days. And many more believed because of his word, and they said to the woman, [Col. 0272B] ‘We now believe no longer because of your report; for we ourselves have heard and seen that this is truly the Saviour of the world.’”

At first we heard a report; now we see his presence. So it is done today with those who are outside. Christ is announced to them as through the woman, that is, through the Church. They come to Christ through the report, and Christ remains with them two days—that is, he gives them the two commandments of love.

CHAPTER LXXXVIII

A. 38[I] M. 70 R. 20 L. 37

“After these things there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Now there is at Jerusalem the sheep-pool, called in Hebrew Bethsaida, having five porticoes. In these lay a great multitude of sick persons—blind, lame, and withered—waiting for the moving of the water. For an angel of the Lord descended into the pool at a certain time, and the water was stirred. Therefore whoever first descended after the stirring of the water was made whole from whatever infirmity held him.”

[ALBINUS.] Greek *probata* means “sheep” in Latin. Hence the pool is said to be called *probatica*, that is, the sheep-pool, because the priests washed the sacrificial victims in it. [AUGUSTINE.] A pool is water without fish, gathered in some hollow. The water surrounded by five porticoes signifies that people [Col. 0272D] enclosed, as it were, by the five books of Moses. Many sick persons lay there because the Law does not heal but exposes the sick, so that they may eventually seek a physician. The blind are there, who do not possess the light of faith; the lame, who cannot perform what they see; and the withered, who, whatever they do, lack the richness of love. They waited for the moving of the water, in which healing came through an angel, because, convicted by the Law, they desired the grace of redemption. The invisible angel troubled the water because the Son of God, hidden in flesh, troubled the Jews by performing many miracles, to such an extent that they crucified him. To descend into the troubled water, therefore, is humbly to believe in the Lord’s Passion. One is healed, to commend unity, because no one can be healed apart from the unity of faith. Otherwise it would have been scant kindness and no great power for one among so many to be healed by him who could raise all with a single word; but in these bodily matters he directs his attention especially to the eternal salvation of souls.

[Col. 0273A] “Now there was a certain man there who had been in his infirmity for thirty-eight years.”

In the number forty, composed of four tens, the perfection of works is signified, because the Law was given in ten commandments and is fulfilled through the Gospel of the four Evangelists. Therefore he has two fewer than forty, because forty has the perfection of the Law and the Law is not fulfilled except through the twofold commandment of love: he lacks love of God and neighbour, and thus is deservedly sick.

“When Jesus saw him lying there, and knew that he had already been so a long time, he said to him: ‘Do you wish to be made [Col. 0273B] whole?’ The sick man answered him: ‘Lord, I have no man to put me into the pool when the water has been stirred; for while I am coming, another descends before me.’”

The sick man is asked whether he wishes to be healed, so that he may be raised to hope of health, of which he had already despaired. Hence he complained that he had no man to put him into the water. The sick man needed a man—but a man who was God.

“Jesus said to him: ‘Rise, take up your bed and walk.’ And immediately the man was made whole, took up his bed, and walked. Now it was the Sabbath on that day.”

Rise in mind from vices—that is, leave sins; rise in body, which is the activity of health. “Take up,” he says, [Col. 0273C] “your bed,” that is, love your neighbour. We should not be disturbed if love of neighbour is commended through an inanimate thing, since the Lord himself is called a stone. When you were sick, your neighbour carried you; now that you have been made whole, carry your neighbour. “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 8). Walk in the love of God from strength to strength, hastening to his vision.

“Therefore the Jews said to him who had been made whole: ‘It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to carry your bed.’”

They did not object that he had been made whole on the Sabbath, but that he carried his bed, lest it should be urged against them that they themselves would draw an animal out of a pit on the Sabbath if it fell in.

[Col. 0273D] A. 39[X]

“He answered them: ‘He who made me whole said to me: “Take up your bed and walk.”’”

Obeying the healer’s commands, he sets the authority of his healing against those who slander him.

“Then they asked him: ‘Who is the man who said to you, “Take up your bed and walk”?’ But the man who had been made whole did not know who he was, for Jesus had withdrawn from the crowd gathered in the place.”

He had been healed through faith, yet did not know how to identify by name or bodily appearance the one who had healed him. So we too, while carrying our neighbour and walking toward God, do not yet see the one toward whom we walk. God is still seen by intention alone, not amid the clamour [Col. 0274A] of the crowd. Therefore whoever wishes to attain the vision of God should flee the crowd of wicked affections and evil people, and enter the temple of inward prayer, as follows:

“Afterwards Jesus found him in the Temple and said to him: ‘Behold, you have been made whole; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you.’”

He indicates that he had been sick because of sins; but Jesus healed him inwardly as well as outwardly. Hence he warns him that, by sinning again, he may be judged more severely.

“The man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him whole. Therefore the Jews persecuted Jesus, because he did these things on the Sabbath.”

This man announced the salvation so that they might follow it; but they, on the contrary, persecuted him.

[Col. 0274B] “But Jesus answered them: ‘My Father is working until now, and I am working.’”

That is, in none of the things done thus far has my working been absent from the Father’s working; rather, in all things I work together with the Father, since the divine power does nothing except through its Wisdom. As though he said: If you dare to censure me in anything done through me, censure also God my Father who works, whose special people you boast yourselves to be. [ALBINUS.] God has not worked only for six days, as you suppose, but works until now. For he who created new things in six days, from which he rested on the seventh day, thereafter works until the end by governing, sustaining, renewing, and propagating them, so that the created things may endure. Since God always works, it is evident that what is read concerning the rest of the Sabbath is a sacrament. Perhaps, then, the Lord is said to have rested from his works on the seventh day because on the sixth day before the Sabbath he yielded up his spirit, and on the Sabbath rested in the tomb. As though he said to the Jews: What are you waiting for, that I should not work on the Sabbath day? The Sabbath day was commanded to you as a sign of me.

“Therefore the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God.”

[ALBINUS.] He set aside the Sabbath from the commandments of the Law, which were no longer to be observed according to the letter. Those who attend only to the form of a servant charge him with making himself equal to God by usurpation; but by nature, being born, he is equal.

“Jesus therefore answered and said to them: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: the Son can do nothing from himself except what he sees the Father doing; for whatever he does, the Son likewise does.’”

Just as he showed that the Father does nothing without him, so conversely he says that he does nothing without the Father, so that the operation of Father and Son may be understood as altogether the same—that is, of divine power and Wisdom. And this is the meaning: “The Son” (that is, the Wisdom of God, which I am) cannot do anything by himself, but can do only what he sees the Father doing together with him—that is, what he recognizes as being done with him by the Father. For the Father, that is, divine power, does nothing except through his Wisdom.

[Col. 0275A] “For the Father loves the Son and shows him all things which he himself does; and he will show him greater works than these, that you may marvel.”

He shows him all things to be done—that is, he places all things in his counsel, as one consulting someone shows him what he is about to do. He will accomplish by his counsel greater things than those now done: this is what it means to show them to him. Hence Wisdom itself says of itself in Proverbs: “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel” (Prov. 6); and again: “I was with him, arranging all things” (ibid.). He will do greater things, that you may marvel—that is, that you may have still greater cause for wonder if you know them. Or in the life to come you will marvel at this, when, with the other damned, you say: “How have these been reckoned among the children of God?”

“For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills.”

He says what those greater things are: namely, the resurrection of souls from sins, which is greater than the aforesaid bodily healing of the sick man, at which they marvelled greatly; or than that setting aside of the Sabbath which they slandered. “The Son gives life to whom he wills.” For the will of Father and Son is one, as are power and operation. Truly the Father loves the Son, because he does so to such an extent that he grants him all judgment. And this is the meaning:

“For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honour the Son as they honour the Father.”

In rendering judgment, where it must be considered what is due to each according to merits, Wisdom rather than power is to be exercised; so that all, observing that judgment belongs to the Son, may revere the judge as much as the Father—if not from love, then at least from fear—whose power it is to reward anyone according to merits. [ALBINUS.] Or thus: The Son not only gives life in the first resurrection, namely that of souls, but will also judge in the second resurrection, which will be that of bodies. And this is the meaning: “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” For the person of the Father will not appear in the judgment; nor will Christ appear in that by which he is consubstantial with the Father, but rather in the form of a servant, which stood before a judge, so that he may also be seen by the ungodly. Connect the text thus: “The Son gives life to whom he wills, that all may honour the Son as they honour the Father.”

[Col. 0275D] A. 40[I] M. 98 R. 90 L. 116

“He who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him.”

[ALBINUS.] Christ as man is honoured, but not as God the Father is honoured. For he said according to his humanity: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14). According to divinity, Father and Son are equally honoured. What is it to honour the Father, except that he has a Son? You take honour away from the Father when you give lesser honour to the Son. For if he did not wish to beget one equal to himself, he was envious; but if he wished it and could not, he was deficient.

A. 41[X]

“Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word [Col. 0276A] and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life.”

He returns to the commendation of the resurrection of souls. Why does he say, “hears my Word and believes,” not “believes in me,” but “believes him who sent me”? Because his Word is in me—indeed, I am his Word. Therefore whoever believes him believes his Word, that is, me; and thus has eternal life, that is, the cause that grants eternal life, namely faith and obedience. Therefore he will not come into a judgment of condemnation, but here passes from the death of unbelief to the life of faith and righteousness.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who have heard shall live.”

[Col. 0276B] He makes clear that he speaks of the resurrection of souls. Do not await the last hour. The hour is coming, and now is, in which those dead in sins shall hear through me, and afterwards through the apostles, the word of salvation; and those who hear, that is, obey, shall live. For they will not live merely because of hearing unless they obey. Truly they will live through the voice of the Son. Hence it follows:

“For as the Father has life in himself, so he also gave the Son to have life in himself.”

That is, he begot the Son having life in himself. This alone is the difference: the Father is life without being begotten; the Son is life by being begotten. But the life which is Father and Son gives life, enlightens, feeds, and satisfies alike souls and angels, whose nature it is to apprehend the life of Wisdom by reason. Bodies, however, are given life by souls.

[Col. 0276C] “And he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of man.”

As life begot life, so one powerful to judge begot one powerful to judge. And this is the meaning: “He gave him authority to execute judgment.” Father and Son, and likewise the Holy Spirit, therefore judge indivisibly. Yet because power yields to Wisdom in the discrimination of judgment, where equity must be examined more especially than power exercised—though power is also to be exercised and goodness not excluded—the distinction of judgment is assigned more particularly to Wisdom. Accordingly he said above: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” But the addition, “because he is the Son of man,” declares that judgment depends especially on the fact [Col. 0276D] that the ungodly also crucified, and daily trample underfoot, the Son sent by the Father. [ALBINUS.] Or thus: Insofar as he is the Son of man, the Father gave him authority to execute judgment. For in judgment man will be seen by all, but God is to be seen only by the righteous.

“Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs shall hear his voice. And those who have done good shall come forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment.”

Here he plainly treats of the resurrection of the flesh, as above of the resurrection of the mind. Do not marvel that I speak so freely of the Son’s execution of judgment, for at the end of the age the hour is coming in which all will rise bodily: some to life, that they may see God as he is; [Col. 0277A] others to condemnation. Then the discrimination of judgment will appear. They will hear his voice—that is, they will perceive it through its manifestation. Either the judge himself will utter a human voice, or it will be formed through angels, according to the Psalmist’s saying: “The Lord ascended with the voice of a trumpet.”

“I can do nothing from myself; as I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just.”

He explains what he had said: “He gave him authority to execute judgment.” “I can do nothing from myself”: as though he said, I am not from myself, but from the Father, from whom and with whom I do all things. “As I hear,” that is, as I understand through unity of substance from him from whom I am, so I judge. [ALBINUS.] Or thus: I, the Son of man, can do nothing from myself; but as I hear from God, I judge.

[Col. 0277B] A. 43[X]

“If I bear witness concerning myself, my witness is not true.”

But how is it not true, except according to the flesh? Hence elsewhere: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing.”

“There is another who bears witness concerning me, and I know that the witness which he bears concerning me is true.”

In what follows he shows who that other is, where he says: “The Father who sent me himself bears witness concerning me.” This testimony occurred at the baptism. Because God is truth, his testimonies are true.

“You sent to John, and he bore witness to the truth. But I do not receive testimony from a human being; [Col. 0277C] nevertheless I say these things to you, that you may be saved. He was a burning and shining lamp, but you were willing to rejoice for a time in his light.”

[ALBINUS.] John bore witness to Christ as a lamp, in order to confound his enemies. For it had already been foretold in the Psalm, under the person of the Father: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ; I will clothe his enemies with confusion, but upon him my sanctification shall flourish” (Ps. 131). All the prophets and apostles are lamps; Christ is the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1). I do not receive testimony from a human being as something necessary; yet I say these things about John’s testimony so that through a human being you human beings may be led to Truth itself and, believing, may be saved. For John [Col. 0277D] was a lamp burning with the spirit of charity and shining with the light of truth, showing that people were to rejoice in the sun of righteousness. But you wished to remain, as though that were sufficient, in the lamp’s light, while you believed John to be Christ.

“But I have testimony greater than John’s. For the works which the Father gave me to complete, those very works bear witness concerning me that the Father sent me. And the Father who sent me, he himself has borne witness concerning me.”

John’s testimony was indeed true and very useful to many, but I have greater testimonies. For the Father’s works which I visibly perform attest that the Father sent me. And it is the testimony of the Father—who displayed me outwardly as a human being visible to the eyes—which inwardly kindles human hearts to know me.

A. 44[III] M. 112 L. 119

“You have neither ever heard his voice nor seen his form.”

In this he shows that the substance of divinity is incomprehensible and invisible, and that its voice is not apprehended by the bodily ear but understood only spiritually.

A. 45[X]

“And you do not have his word abiding in you, because you do not believe him whom he sent.”

The Word which was in the beginning, and through which you could attain knowledge of the Father, does not remain in [Col. 0278B] your hearts, because you do not believe what you have heard from me, nor even the Scriptures. Hence it follows:

“Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life. And they are those which bear witness concerning me; and you are unwilling to come to me, that you may have life.”

While rejecting me, who am life, you will not find life in the Scriptures; yet through what they teach you are unwilling to come to me—that is, to believe in me—so that you may have the life which you seek in them.

“I do not receive glory from human beings; but I have known you, that you do not have the love of God in yourselves.”

I do not seek human praise or carnal honour, for I came to give what is spiritual. Rather, I grieve for you in your error [Col. 0278C], because you do not have love for God, and I desire to lead you back to the way of truth.

“I have come in my Father’s name, and you have not received me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him.”

He proves that the love of God is not in them. I came so that through me the Father might be glorified, and you did not receive me—that is, you did not believe in me. But this will be the punishment of your sin: when Antichrist comes in his own name, because he will seek his own glory and call himself God, you will receive him. This is what the Apostle says: “That those who did not believe the truth might believe a lie” (2 Thess. 2).

“How can you believe, who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory which is from God alone?”

[Col. 0278D] They do not disbelieve because the truth is not plain, but because pride blinds them, as does ambition for praise, which seeks to be thought to possess what it does not possess and to exalt itself above others. Humility, by contrast, seeks the glory of God alone and desires to please him alone.

“Do not think that I will accuse you before the Father. Moses, in whom you hope, is the one who accuses you. For if you believed Moses, perhaps you would also believe me; for he wrote concerning me.”

The word “perhaps” is the mockery of one confronting unbelief, not uncertainty on the speaker’s part. Therefore I do not accuse, because I came not to condemn but to save. Moses, however, accuses you because you disbelieve his voice, which says: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren, like myself; you shall hear him. Every soul that does not [Col. 0279A] obey that prophet shall be cut off from the people of God” (Deut. 18).

“But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?”

Certainly much less so: for in the Law you presume to be teachers, whereas in my words you are willing to be neither teachers nor disciples. There is the beginning of the perfect life; here, its consummation. There I was prophesied; here I tell you: behold, I am present.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX

M. 160[VI] R. 76

“And having left them, in those days, again when there was a great crowd, he called his disciples together and said: ‘I have compassion on the crowd, for behold, they have now remained with me for three days, [Col. 0279B] and have nothing to eat; and I do not wish to send them away fasting, lest they fail on the way.’”

[HILARY.] Since the error of unbelief held the minds of the insolent, it is written that he left them rather than dismissed them. [JEROME.] He calls the disciples together in order to teach masters to share their deliberations with their inferiors; or else so that, through the conversation, they may understand the greatness of the sign. [BEDE.] The crowd remains with the Lord for three days on account of the healing of the sick; and the elect, in faith in the Trinity, entreat the Lord for the infirmities of their own souls or of those belonging to them. Or the crowd remains with the Lord for three days when the faithful are converted in deed, speech, and thought. Those who have been converted fail on the way of this present life if they are dismissed without the nourishment of teaching. Mark relates that they came from far away. [Col. 0279C] The more a person has wandered, the farther that person has withdrawn from the Lord. Likewise, believing Jews came from nearby, being instructed by the Law and the prophets; believers from the Gentiles came from far away, as not having been instructed.

“And his disciples said to him: ‘Where then can we get enough bread in this wilderness to satisfy so great a crowd?’ Jesus said to them: ‘How many loaves do you have?’ They said: ‘Seven, and a few little fish.’ And he ordered the crowd to recline upon the ground.”

[AMBROSE.] Nourishment of heavenly grace is imparted not to those who are idle, nor to those sitting in the city of the Synagogue or in worldly dignity, but to those seeking Christ amid desolate places. For those who are not disdainful are received by Christ and are healed, both spiritually and bodily, if they are in need. Mystically, preachers, wondering at the Church’s progress, say: “Whence have we such eloquence that we may suffice for so many thousands and such eager hearers in this wilderness of the world?” Yet the seven loaves—that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit—suffice for all, joined with apostolic authority as with the flavour of a few fish; these refresh us by the example of their life or death. Those, however, who belong to the seven loaves are commanded no longer to sit upon grass but to press the earth. [BEDE.] For in the New Testament we are commanded, if we are to be perfect, to leave even the earth itself and temporal possessions.

“And taking the seven loaves and the fish, and giving thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples, and the disciples gave them to the people.”

[Col. 0280A] The Lord gave the loaves to the disciples to distribute to the crowd—that is, spiritual teaching. He broke the loaves—that is, he opened the mysteries, namely himself, who is the bread of life. He gave thanks in order to show how greatly he rejoices in human salvation, and to instruct us always to give thanks to God, whether we are refreshed in body or in soul. If, in the seven loaves, which are not said to have been of barley, the sevenfold grace of the New Testament is signified, what should we understand by the little fish except the holy authors of that Scripture? Or those whose faith, life, and sufferings that Scripture contains: rescued and consecrated from the turbulent waves of this age, they have provided us inward refreshment through the example of their life or death, lest we fail in the course of this world.

[Col. 0280B] “And they all ate and were satisfied.”

We eat by listening attentively and contemplating examples; we are satisfied by storing them in memory and acting upon them. To this refreshment accords the Psalmist’s saying: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord who seek him” (Ps. 21). That the people are satisfied while eating signifies that hunger is to be driven away from the elect for ever, when one who has received Christ’s food shall not hunger. And they took up seven full baskets of the fragments that remained. The seven baskets left over are the higher commandments or counsels, which the multitude cannot attain by observing them, but only those who are filled with greater grace. To them it is said: “If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have and give to the poor” (Matt. 19). And because baskets are customarily woven from rushes and [Col. 0280C] palm leaves, they are rightly placed as a sign of the saints. Rush grows over water, and the elect place the root of their heart in the very fountain of life, lest it wither from the love of eternity. The palm adorns the hand of a victor, and the elect retain in their hearts the memory of eternal recompense, having conquered the world. [AMBROSE.] Why, then, is there more left over for five thousand persons, but less for four thousand? Because the four thousand were with Christ for three days and therefore received more of the heavenly food.

“Now those who ate were four thousand men, apart from little children and women; and he dismissed them.”

In the earlier sign there were five thousand, according to the number of loaves, because they were near to the five senses. These, who are fed from seven loaves—that is, from the sacred number—are four thousand. This number is always used in praise: a four-sided stone is not unstable, and the evangelists are four in number. Thus the number of those refreshed teaches that they are fed with evangelical food, and likewise indicates the innumerable multitude that will gather from the four quarters of the world to receive the gift of heavenly food. This, therefore, is the typical difference between this feeding and the other: there, the old letter was signified as full of spiritual grace; here, the grace of the New Testament is shown as to be ministered to believers, adorned with four virtues. The first of these is knowledge of things to be sought and avoided; the second, restraint of desire for things that delight temporarily; [Col. 0281A] the third, steadfastness against the troubles of this world; the fourth, which is diffused through them all, love of God and neighbour. Here and there women and children are excepted, because in both the Old and New Testaments those are not admitted to the number who do not persist in advancing toward the perfect man, whether through weakness of strength or levity of mind. Each feeding was celebrated upon a mountain, because both Testaments proclaim to us in harmonious voice the loftiness of God’s commandments and the height of that mountain which is “the mountain of the house of God upon the top of the mountains” (Isa. 2).

“And immediately, entering the boat with his disciples, he came into the district of Dalmanutha.”

The satisfied crowd is dismissed; and since the Lord remains with us throughout all the days of our life, he enters the boat—that is, the Church of believers—having accompanied the people. Where Matthew has Magadan, Mark has Dalmanutha. [AUGUSTINE.] The same place has two names; consequently most manuscripts of Mark have Magadan. It should be understood that those chapters whose canonical material is contained in this work are not to be thought entirely absent. Moreover, certain passages have fittingly been omitted, such as chapter 162 of Matthew, because, as Jerome says, it is not found in most manuscripts. Here too, undoubtedly, Matthew’s one hundred and sixty-first chapter is omitted; its meaning is contained in the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter of the same work, according to which the Lord often said the same things at different times and in different places. But when things have been said many times, it is sufficient in this work for some of them to appear once. Therefore, too, what Mark alone relates in chapter 81 concerning the blind man who received sight is appropriately passed over in this book, which reports very much concerning the healing of blind persons. The same applies to similar matters. For it is the practice of one writing a Gospel deliberately to omit certain things, plainly in order to indicate that many things remain. Hence John says at the end of his book that there were many other things which Jesus did; and that if all were written, the world itself would not suffice to contain them (John 21).

M. 163[VI] R. 78

“And when his disciples had come across the water, they forgot to take bread, and they had only one loaf in the boat.”

[Col. 0281D] [BEDE.] This indicates how little concern they otherwise had for the flesh: in their eagerness to accompany the Lord, they did not even take provisions for the journey. The one loaf signifies the bread of life. The Lord went across the water when the people of the Gentiles followed him.

M. 79[II] R. 164 A. 144

“And he commanded them, saying: ‘Look, and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees, and of the leaven of Herod.’”

Whoever guards against the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees does not observe the precepts of the letter, but disregards human traditions in order to fulfil God’s commandments. For the leaven of the Pharisees is to put the decrees of God’s law after human traditions, or to preach the Law [Col. 0282A] in words and oppose it by deeds. [BEDE.] Their leaven also consists in testing the Lord and believing neither his teaching nor his works. Herod’s leaven is adultery, murder, rashness in swearing, and the pretence of religion. Of this leaven the Apostle says: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5). As the force of a small quantity of leaven mixed with flour makes it rise and draws it into its own flavour, so a small spark of heretical teaching, if cast into your breast, will quickly grow into a huge flame and draw you wholly to itself.

M. 165[VI] R. 80

“But they were reasoning among themselves, saying: ‘Because we have no bread.’”

[Col. 0282B] They reasoned, “We have no bread; therefore he tells us to beware of leaven,” that is, of Pharisaic bread. But Jesus, knowing that they had misunderstood “beware of the leaven of the Pharisees,” rebuked them for this and led them to a sound understanding. This is what follows:

And Jesus, knowing this, said: “Why do you reason among yourselves, you of little faith, because you have no bread? Do you not yet understand or remember? Do you still have your heart blinded? Having eyes, do you not see? And having ears, do you not hear? Do you not remember when I broke five loaves for five thousand, and how many baskets full of fragments you took up?” They said to him: “Twelve.” “And when I broke seven loaves for four thousand, how many baskets of fragments did you take up?” And they said: “Seven.” [Col. 0282C] “Why do you not understand that I did not speak to you about bread: ‘Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees’?” Then they understood that he had not said that they should beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.

Certainly, one had to beware lest the teaching of the Pharisees, which does not know Christ, corrupt the effect of evangelical truth. But if the leaven of the Pharisees and Herod signifies perverse traditions and heretical doctrines, it is clear that the foods with which God’s people were fed signify true and uncorrupted teaching. Since faith is frequently mentioned in the Gospel, lest it should be nowhere explained, let us briefly set forth what faith is, what its objects are, and in what respect it is called little or great. Faith is an estimation of things not apparent—that is, not subject to the bodily senses—situated above opinion and below knowledge. Above opinion, because it is more to believe than to opine; below knowledge, because it is less to believe than to know. For we believe, and at some time come to know. Things apparent, however, do not involve faith but knowledge. For that is properly said to be believed which cannot be seen; what can be seen can no longer be believed. Yet from things which we see, faith is produced in us concerning things we do not see. Augustine repeatedly affirms these points in his commentaries on John and in his letter on faith to the most illustrious Marcella; Gregory does so in the fourth book of the *Dialogues* and the second book of his Gospel homilies, [Col. 0283A] as do other teachers.

Faith, therefore, is to believe what you do not see: “for we walk by faith, not by sight.” But when that which is perfect has come, you will see what you believed. And, because believing is less than seeing, faith will cease, because the reality will be seen. The estimation involved in belief will cease when knowledge of the truth is manifest. Faith, then, as the Apostle says, is “the evidence of things not apparent” (Heb. 11), that is, a showing. For the ancients used *arguere* in the sense “to show.” Bodily senses, accordingly, indicate to us things apparent; faith, by contrast, extends to things not apparent, showing them in its own way until the true vision of understanding succeeds it. Faith is therefore “the substance of things hoped for,” because, while we believe that things we do not see either have been, are, or will be, faith itself makes them subsist within us through belief. For example, although the general resurrection has not yet occurred, nevertheless through faith it already subsists in our soul, as though we held it before our eyes. Faith, therefore, concerns present and past as well as future things, good as well as evil things, as Augustine discusses at the beginning of the *Enchiridion*.

Hope, however, concerns only good things and future things. Hope is the expectation of future goods, with confidence in attaining them through God’s grace and a good conscience. Hope without merits is not hope but presumption. The expectation of some misfortune is not called hope but despair—that is, distrust of the good. The difference, therefore, between hope and that part of faith which concerns future goods within us is this: by faith we understand the good things that are to come to us, and by hope we confidently await them. Once the thing is possessed, there will no longer be hope’s expectation. From faith, however, as the foundation of all good things, hope and charity arise. For what can be hoped for, or loved as hoped for, unless it is believed? Something may be believed, however, even if it is neither hoped for nor loved. Thus we love because we believe; and we also hope because we believe and love. Since hope is the confident expectation of a future good, the capacity to await arises from faith, and confidence in obtaining it arises from charity.

Hence Augustine, in chapter 54 of the *Enchiridion*: “One who loves rightly undoubtedly believes and hopes rightly. But one who does not love believes and hopes in vain, although these belong to true blessedness. For although hoping cannot occur without love, it may occur that a person does not love that without which he cannot arrive at what he hopes for: as when someone hopes for eternal life and does not love righteousness.”

The same author, in Book I of *On Christian Doctrine*: “These are the three things to which all knowledge and prophecy are subordinate: faith, hope, and charity. But faith is succeeded by the sight which we see, and hope is succeeded by blessedness itself, which we shall attain; whereas charity, even when these have passed away, will rather increase. For if by believing we love what we do not yet see, how much more when we begin to see it? And if by hoping we love that to which we have not yet come, how much more when we have arrived? Therefore charity is greater, because, when faith and hope have passed away, it remains.” The same author, in Book VIII, chapter 8, of *On the Trinity*: From one and the same charity we love God and neighbour: God for God’s sake, but ourselves and our neighbour for God’s sake.

It should also be known that the name “faith” is sometimes transferred to designate the certainty of manifest vision which we shall have. This occurs either according to the rule by which the name of a cause is used for its effect, or according to another by which the thing signified receives, by likeness, the name of the thing signifying. For the faith by which we now see God “through a mirror in an enigma” is the sacrament of that future vision by which we shall see God face to face as he is; and we are led there through faith.

Augustine, in Book II of *Questions on the Gospels*, chapter 200, on Luke: “There is also a faith of things, when belief is given not to words but to the realities themselves as present. This will occur when God’s Wisdom itself, which is to come, offers itself to the saints for contemplation by manifest sight. Perhaps Paul speaks of this faith of realities and of the presence of light itself when he says: ‘For the righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith to faith’ (Rom. 1). For he says elsewhere: ‘We all, beholding with unveiled face the glory of God, shall be transformed into the same image from glory to glory’ (2 Cor. 3). As here he says ‘from glory to glory,’ so there he says ‘from faith to faith’: namely, from the glory of the Gospel, by which believers are now enlightened, to the glory of manifest truth.

“There are also many things pertaining to God which make no difference to us whether they are believed or not. For whether we believe that God will send rain tomorrow or not; whether we believe that Christ was of this or that height, or not; or that he preached in this or that city, or not—we incur no danger. But precisely those things which concern the catholic faith, if they are not believed, produce condemnation. Catholic faith—that is, universal faith—is so necessary for all that no rational person can be saved without it. Therefore Athanasius, after stating, ‘This is the catholic faith,’ immediately explained why it is called catholic by adding: ‘Unless each person believes it, he cannot be saved.’ Or it is called catholic, that is, common, in distinction from the faith of heretics, which is not spread everywhere with the Church but lurks, as it were, in a corner.

“Catholic faith consists partly in the nature of Divinity itself, and partly in the divine benefits and all God’s most righteous dispensations or ordinances, which have been set forth for us in the creeds of the apostles and holy Fathers. It should be known that faith is not called great or small because it concerns many or few things, but because those things are believed firmly or lukewarmly.
