The Lord praises intense and steadfast faith when he says: ‘O woman, great is your faith’ (Matt. 15); and concerning the centurion’s faith: ‘I have not found so great a faith in Israel’ (Matt. 8). But he rebukes the weak faith of the apostles, who believed many more things, when he says: ‘Why do you reason among yourselves, you of little faith, because you have no bread?’ Certainly, if among other things they firmly believed that what enters the mouth does not defile a person, they would not have thought that the Lord was forbidding the bread of the Pharisees.”

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0285]

## CHAPTER XC

[Col. 0285A]

“And Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi.”

[JEROME—BEDE, in a homily.] Philip, brother of Herod, tetrarch of the regions of Ituraea and Trachonitis, imitating his father Herod—who named a city Caesarea in honour of Caesar Augustus, though it had formerly been called Strato’s Tower—founded a city on the northern border of Judaea, which he named Caesarea Philippi in memory of his own name and in honour of Tiberius Caesar, under whom he himself ruled. This place, Caesarea Philippi, is now called Paneas and lies in the province of Phoenicia, where the Jordan rises at the foot of Lebanon. There are two springs there, Jor and Dan, which, when joined, produce the name Jordan.

“And he asked his disciples, saying: ‘Whom do people say [Col. 0285B] the Son of Man is?’”

[BEDE.] Intending to examine the disciples’ faith, the Lord first asks the opinion of the crowd, lest the faith of the apostles should seem to have been established by popular opinion rather than by knowledge of the truth. [JEROME.] Therefore Peter is told: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you”—that is, human teaching. He aptly said “people,” because human beings speak concerning the Son of Man; but those who understand the divinity are gods.

“They said: ‘Some, John the Baptist; others, Elijah; others, Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.’”

To one asking why this opinion existed concerning John, Elijah, or Jeremiah, we answer that it is not ours to give an account of another person’s error.

[Col. 0285C] “He said to them: ‘But whom do you say that I am?’”

[BEDE, in a homily.] The apostles were above human beings, as gods, according to the Psalmist’s words: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High’” (Ps. 81). The Lord asks them, not because he does not know their opinion concerning him, but in order worthily to reward their confession of faith.

Simon Peter answered and said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

[BEDE.] Peter answered for the others, although the other apostles knew. The limit of my faith concerning Christ is that he is the Son of God. I am not permitted to know the secret of his generation; yet I am not permitted to be ignorant of faith in that generation. [JEROME—BEDE, in a homily.] “Of the living God,” that is, the unchangeable and eternal God, is said in distinction from the gods which the madness of paganism has established for worship, whether from dead human beings or from works of hands. [HILARY.] The Lord called himself the Son of Man, because the sight of his body was presented; but by adding, “Whom do you say that I am?” he indicated that beyond what was visible in him there was something else, hidden, which was to be understood, concerning which the question was asked, and to which believers’ faith ought to extend. Peter’s faith, therefore, seeing the Son of God in the human being, embraced both, saying: [Col. 0286A] “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” This principle of confession must be maintained: as we remember the Son of God, so also we must remember the Son of Man, because neither apart from the other gives any hope of salvation. [AUGUSTINE, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*.] It may cause difficulty that Luke says the Lord asked his disciples whom people said he was when he was praying alone, whereas Mark says that they were asked this on the road. But this troubles only one who has never prayed on the road. The Lord is nowhere found praying with his disciples; everywhere he prays alone, because human petitions do not comprehend God’s counsel, nor can anyone share Christ’s inward things.

M. 167[X]

[Col. 0286B] “And Jesus answered and said: ‘Blessed are you, Simon Barjona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.’”

[JEROME.] In Peter he rewards all the others for the true confession. It is as though he said: “What flesh and blood could not reveal, the grace of the Holy Spirit has revealed to you.” Therefore he receives a name from his confession, because *Barjona* means “son of a dove.” Others say that Simon, that is Peter, was the son of John, as in: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John 21). They hold that this has been corrupted through scribal error, so that *Barjona* has been written instead of *Barjoanna*, “son of John,” one syllable having been removed. *Joanna* means “the grace of the Lord.” Both names are understood mystically, because the dove signifies the Holy Spirit and the grace of the Lord signifies a spiritual gift. The Father revealed this to the son of the dove, because the grace of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one. *Barjona* is Syriac and Hebrew.

“And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.”

[JEROME, in the letter to the Galatians.] You said that I am the Son of the living God. And I, whose saying is doing, say to you that you are Peter. The chief of the apostles is now called Peter, now Cephas, not with a different meaning; for what we call *petra*, “rock,” in Latin and Greek, the Hebrews and Syrians call *cepha*. [JEROME.] Peter rightly receives this name because he believed in Christ the rock; and according to the metaphor of the rock it is said to him: “I will build my Church upon this [Col. 0286D] rock,” that is, upon this foundation of faith. [BEDE, in a homily.] Or thus: upon this rock which you have confessed—that is, upon myself. Hence the Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3).

“And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.”

The gates of hell are sins and heretical teachings. By “the keys of the kingdom of heaven” he means the knowledge and power of discernment by which Peter was to admit the worthy into the kingdom and exclude the unworthy from it. Hence follows:

“And whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

[JEROME.] He says “upon earth”; for in the act of binding he nowhere said that one who has died is to be absolved. Bishops and presbyters, not understanding this passage, assume for themselves something of the Pharisees’ arrogance, so that they either condemn the innocent or imagine that they can loose the guilty, although before God it is not priests’ judgments but the life of the accused that is considered. We read in Leviticus concerning lepers, where they are commanded to show themselves to the priests and are declared unclean if they have leprosy (Lev. 14): not because priests make them leprous and unclean, but because they have knowledge of the leprous and the non-leprous, and can discern who is clean and who unclean. Therefore, as there the priest makes the leper unclean, so here the bishop or presbyter binds or looses—not those who are innocent or guilty in themselves, but, by virtue of his office, when he has heard the varieties of sins, he knows who should be bound and who should be loosed.

The sense, therefore, is this: whomever, while living, you bind upon earth by excluding him from the Church, shall be bound in heaven; that is, all the Church members who know of it will avoid him. Or, “shall be bound in heaven” means that the heavenly judgment will confirm that the present Church should avoid him. And whomever, while living, you loose from excommunication by reconciling him, shall be loosed in heaven; that is, the churches which know this will communicate with him. Or, “shall be loosed in heaven” means that the heavenly judgment will confirm that he should be received by the present Church. Great is the honour, but heavy the burden. It is hard indeed for someone unable to govern the course of his own life to become judge of another’s. Thus, one who exercises this grace of binding and loosing according to personal favour or hatred, rather than according to the merits of those subject to him, deprives himself of that power.

Hence the prophet says: “They put to death souls which do not die, and make alive souls which do not live” (Ezek. 15). One puts to death a person who does not die when one condemns the righteous; one attempts to make alive someone who does not live when one seeks to absolve the guilty. The disciples loosed Lazarus alive, whom the Master had raised (John [Col. 0287D] 11); for if they had loosed him dead, they would have displayed a stench rather than power. Therefore we ought to loose those whom we know, in confession, to have been made alive by God’s grace. [BEDE, in a homily.] Thus Lazarus is not told, “Come back to life,” but “Come forth.” Peter therefore receives in a special manner the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the primacy of judicial authority, so that all believers may understand that whoever separates themselves from the unity of faith and fellowship with him can neither be loosed from the chains of sins nor enter through the gate of the kingdom of heaven.

[AUGUSTINE, Book III of *On Baptism*.] For the peace of the Church remits sins, and alienation from the Church’s peace retains sins—not according to human judgment, but according to God’s judgment. The rock retains; the rock remits. The dove retains; the dove remits. Outside [Col. 0288A], indeed, nothing can be bound or loosed, because outside the Church there is no one who can bind or loose. It should be known that the knowledge of discernment begins to be a key of the Church when the authority to bind and loose is added to it. This happens through episcopal ministry in the ordination of presbyters, or, what seems truer, when care of souls is imposed upon them. No one may excommunicate another’s parishioner, for such an excommunication has no force. No one can be bound or condemned by the judgment of a judge other than his own. Some say that the power of binding and loosing—that is, of closing the Church to sinners or opening it to them—is called “two keys” in the plural on account of these two effects: by one the sinner is bound, that is, expelled from the Church; by the other he is loosed, that is, restored to the Church.

M. 168[II] R. 83 L. 95 and 206

“Then he commanded his disciples that they should tell no one that he was Jesus Christ.”

[AMBROSE.] He commands that it be kept silent that he is the Son of God, in order to deceive the prince of this world, to teach humility, and to prevent disciples still untrained and imperfect from being overwhelmed by the burden of a greater preaching. But after the mystery of the Passion has been completed, the apostles are more fittingly told: “Go, teach all nations” (Matt. 28).

“From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, scribes, and chief priests, and be killed, and rise on the third day.”

[Col. 0288C] [JEROME.] “From that time,” that is, so that the disciples might better retain the Lord’s command, Jesus began to show the matter of his Passion. At the same time, he did so lest they should dread the danger of death if they loved the glory of the kingdom. It is as though he said: “Preach me when I have suffered, because it does not profit to publicize his majesty among the people when afterwards they will see him scourged and crucified.” [AMBROSE.] The wisdom of God took human nature as an example by which we might live rightly; and it belongs to right living not to fear things which ought not to be feared. Death ought not to be feared. Therefore this same truth had to be shown by the death of that human being assumed by God’s wisdom. There are people who, although they do not fear death itself, nevertheless dread a particular kind of death. Yet, just as death itself is not to be feared by a good and upright-living person, so neither is any kind of death to be feared. Therefore this too had to be shown by the cross of that human being. For among all kinds of death none was more accursed or more terrifying than that kind. The Lord also came in the flesh in order to show us the hope of resurrection. This could not happen otherwise unless he assumed mortal flesh; for God could not die.

M. 169[VI] R. 84

“And Peter, taking him aside, began to rebuke him, saying: ‘Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you.’”

[HIERON.] In the Greek it reads: “Be gracious to yourself, Lord.” This is better than “Far be it from you, Lord.” [Col. 0289A] Peter does not think it possible that the Son of God should be killed; he takes him aside in his affection, or leads him apart, lest he seem to rebuke his teacher in the presence of his fellow disciples.

And turning, he said to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling-block to me, because you do not think the things of God, but the things of men.”

Because you speak contrary to my will, you ought to be called an adversary. *Satan* means “adversary” or “opponent.” Many suppose that Peter was not corrected, but rather that an evil spirit was suggesting these words to him. But it will never seem to me that an error arising from affectionate devotion is an incentive of the devil. “Get behind me,” that is, follow my judgment, so that the grain of wheat falling into the earth may bear much fruit. [Col. 0289B] For in wishing to go before me, you are a stumbling-block to me—that is, you offend me. Let the discerning reader know that this blessedness—“whatever you bind on earth,” and the rest—was promised to Peter for the future. For had it been given to him immediately, the error of a perverse confession would never have found a place in him.

M. 170[II] R. 85 L. 96

Then, having summoned the crowd together with his disciples, he said to them: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.”

[BEDA—GREGORY.] After predicting his passion and resurrection to the apostles, he exhorts both them and the crowd to follow him. Whoever puts off the old person with his deeds denies himself, becoming another person [Col. 0289C] from the former one, saying: “Now I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2). For we deny ourselves when we avoid what we were through oldness and strive toward that to which we are called through newness. Whoever was proud leaves himself behind. For converted ungodly people will not be ungodly—not because they cease to exist in essence, but because they will no longer be in the guilt of ungodliness. Unless someone departs from himself, he does not draw near to him who is above himself; nor can he grasp what is beyond himself unless he knows how to put to death what he is.

But whoever denies himself in respect of vices, so as to grow in virtues, should take up his cross: either by afflicting the body through abstinence, or the soul through compassion. Hence Paul says: “I chastise my body and bring it into slavery” (1 Cor. 9). Of compassion for one’s neighbor he says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” [Col. 0289D] (2 Cor. 11). Bearing the cross, moreover, we ought to follow the Lord by laying down our life for our brothers and for love of him, just as he did for us. For whoever wishes to save his life here will lose it in the future. And this is what he says:

“For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it. But whoever loses his life for my sake will find it.”

Whoever, in a time of persecution, loses the present life of the flesh for my sake will find it—that is, receive it back safe—in the resurrection. This is said to the believer as though it were said to a farmer: “If you keep your grain, you lose it; if you sow it, you renew it.” What decays in [Col. 0290A] the dust becomes green in renewal. Life must be lost in this world for my sake—that is understood—not retained for earthly desires.

“For what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers loss to his own life?”

This was said because, while one is permitted to live, one also delights in striving after things. It signifies two periods of the Church: one of persecution, when life must be laid down rather than deny God; the other of peace, when earthly desires must be broken.

“Or what will a person give in exchange for his life?”

For the human life, the only recompense is that sung by the Psalmist: “What shall I repay to the Lord for all that he has repaid to me? I shall take the cup of salvation [Col. 0290B] and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115).

M. 171[X]

“For the Son of Man is to come in the glory of his Father with his angels. And then he will render to each according to his work.”

[HIERON.] Do not be afraid, for joyful things follow sorrowful ones. It is as though he said: “Do you fear death? Hear of the glory of the victor. Do you dread the cross? Listen to the ministry of angels.”

CHAPTER XCI

M. 172 R. 87 L. 99

“Amen I say to you: there are some standing here who shall not taste death until they see the Son [Col. 0290C] of Man coming in his kingdom.”

The apostles could have endured such a scandal in silent thought: “You now say that slaughter and death are coming; yet the glory which you promise is deferred to distant times.” Therefore, lest they be broken by despair or weariness, he who knows hidden things compensates their present fear with a present reward.

[BEDA.] It is as though he said: “Because of your unbelief, I shall show you in the present time what manner of glory I shall possess in the kingdom.” Or he promises that some of the disciples will see the extension of the Church before they depart from the world by death, so that, seeing it raised up in the present against the glory of the world, it may be believed more certainly to reign in heaven.

[HILARY.] The word “taste” is aptly used, [Col. 0290D] because those standing with Christ taste bodily death but retain the life of the soul. Or, by the condition of tasting, he indicates a certain slight draught of death for believers.

“And after six days Jesus took Peter and James and John his brother, and led them apart up a high mountain, to pray.”

[HIERON.] Luke gives eight days; Matthew and Mark, six. There the first and final days are included; here the intervening days are counted.

[BEDA.] On the eighth day the Lord reveals to the disciples the future glory of blessedness, because on the eighth day the joy of resurrection was to come. We too, after the six ages of this world and the seventh age of the soul’s rest after death, shall rise as though in an eighth age. According to Matthew and [Col. 0291A] Mark, the saints must rest after six ages. The sixth psalm is entitled “for the eighth,” concerning the resurrection, because during the six ages in which work is permitted we must persist in prayer, lest in the eighth time of recompense we be rebuked by the angry Judge. Thus the psalm begins: “O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger” (Ps. 6).

[HIERON.] That we may persist in prayer, we are instructed here by the Lord, who went up the mountain to pray. The mountain which he ascended signifies that those who desire to see Christ in his beauty should dwell in their minds upon things above. In the three apostles is displayed the privilege of their rank.

[BEDA.] They are led apart because many are called but few chosen. The Lord takes three with him so that the world may believe through three suitable witnesses, [Col. 0291B] and to signify that those who are here imbued with faith in the Holy Trinity will there rejoice in eternal vision. Or Peter represents leaders or married persons; James, penitents or those in the active life; John, virgins or contemplatives. It should be noted that Matthew here calls James the brother of John, because some have falsely imagined that another James was present—the one first ordained by the apostles as bishop of the Jerusalemites.

“And it came to pass, while he was praying, that he was transfigured before them; and his face shone like the sun, while his garments became white as snow, shining exceedingly white, such as no fuller on earth can make white.”

[Col. 0291C] [HIERON.] He is said to have been transfigured because he appeared to the apostles as he will be in the judgment, when all, both good and evil, will see the Judge himself, each for his own recompense. Let no one suppose that he lost the reality of his body and assumed a spiritual or airy body. For where the brightness of the face and whiteness of the garments are described, the substance is not removed. The transformation therefore added splendor; it did not take away his face.

The Lord’s garment is the choir of saints, as the Apostle says: “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3). This garment, despised on earth, shines on the mountain, because “what we shall be has not yet appeared; but when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3).

[Col. 0291D] Mark aptly says of his garments, “such as no fuller on earth can make white,” because Christ, the true fuller, cannot—because by right judgment and true promise he ought not—give the faithful on earth the brightness that awaits them in heaven. The fuller is the teacher of souls and their cleanser from the defilement of flesh and spirit.

“And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him in majesty; and they spoke of his departure, which he was to accomplish at Jerusalem.”

[HIERON.] To increase the apostles’ faith, he gives them a sign from heaven: Elijah descending from where he had ascended, and Moses rising from the lower regions. Achaz too is commanded through Isaiah to ask for a sign for himself from on high or from the depths (Isa. [Col. 0292A] 7). The living man and the dead man appear in order to signify that Christ would die and conquer again, so that we may be alive to God and dead to the world.

[BEDA.] Moses, that is, the lawgiver, and Elijah, the outstanding prophet, appear to show that he is the one promised by the writings of the Law and the Prophets. They appear not in the low places but on the mountain, because only those who seek Scripture with an elevated mind are worthy of God’s majesty. Thus the Jews could not follow Moses ascending the heights to the Lord. But Elisha alone, with the sons of the prophets, contemplated the triumph of Elijah’s ascent. They spoke of the things to be fulfilled at Jerusalem; and the Law and the Prophets still teach the mystery of the Lord’s dispensation.

According to Luke, the disciples, having awakened, [Col. 0292B] saw the vision. For the saints, raised after death, will see the Lord’s majesty. Then they will behold Moses and Elijah in glory, because then they will understand more fully how not one iota or one stroke has passed away from the Law, and how the Lord did not come to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them (Matt. 5).

Otherwise: Moses, who was dead, signifies the saints who died from the beginning of the world until the day of judgment and who are to be raised in that judgment; Elijah, who was alive, signifies those who will be found alive. They are seen in majesty and speak of the Lord’s departure, because the saints will reign gloriously with Christ and praise his mercy, since for their salvation he deigned to suffer.

Then Peter answered and said to Jesus: “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, let us make [Col. 0292C] three tabernacles here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.”

[HIERON.] Having gone up to the heights, he does not wish to descend to earthly things. You are mistaken, Peter, as Mark and Luke testify. There is only one tabernacle of the Gospel. If you seek three tabernacles, make one as though it were three—for Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—without equating servants with the Lord.

O how great is the happiness of being perpetually present among the angels at the vision of the Godhead, if even Christ’s humanity and the company of two saints, glimpsed for a moment, delight Peter so much that he wishes to render them service lest they depart! Though as a human being he does not know what to say, he nevertheless shows the indication of the ardor implanted in him. He had forgotten that the kingdom of God [Col. 0292D] was promised to the saints not on earth but in heaven, and that a house made with hands was unnecessary, but rather a heavenly dwelling. Even today, whoever wishes to make three tabernacles for the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel is marked by ignorance, since these cannot be separated from one another and have one tabernacle: the Church of God.

It should be noted that some believe Moses and Elijah appeared in forms supplied through the ministry of angels, while others believe that they themselves appeared in their own bodies. The apostles, who had not known them before, distinguished their forms in majesty by that gift of grace through which each of the saints will know all the others after the resurrection.

“While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them.”

[Col. 0293A] [BEDA.] He who sought a material tabernacle received the overshadowing of a cloud, that he might learn that in the resurrection the saints are protected not by the covering of houses but by the glory [grace] of the Holy Spirit. Hence the Psalmist says: “But the children of men shall hope in the shelter of your wings” (Ps. 35). And John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw no temple in it, for the Lord Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb” (Rev. 21).

“And behold, a voice from the cloud saying: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.’”

[HIERON.] Because Peter had questioned foolishly, he does not deserve an answer; rather, the Father answers for the Son, so that the Lord’s word may be fulfilled: “I do not bear witness concerning myself, but the Father who sent me.” The sense is: A tabernacle of obedience has been established for my Son; Moses and Elijah are his servants. Hence Moses wrote of him: “You shall listen to him in all things whatsoever he shall speak to you” (Deut. 18).

[BEDA.] Notice that, just as the mystery of the Trinity was declared when the Lord was baptized in the Jordan, so it is declared on the mountain. For we shall see in the resurrection the glory which we confess in baptism. Nor without reason does the Holy Spirit appear here in a bright cloud and there in a dove: for whoever now preserves faith with a simple heart will then behold in the light of open vision what he has believed.

“And when the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces and were greatly afraid.”

[HIERON.] They are terrified for three reasons. They knew that they had erred; the bright cloud covered them while they were seeking a tabernacle [Col. 0293C] of branches or tents; and, upon hearing the Father’s voice, frail human beings could not endure the sight of greater glory. Indeed, the more one seeks things beyond one’s measure, the more one falls down to lower things, if one does not know one’s own measure. Whoever wishes to make a tabernacle for God should prepare for him the inner chamber of his own heart.

“And Jesus came near, touched them, and said to them: ‘Rise, and do not be afraid.’”

By his consoling touch and word he drives away fear and strengthens their limbs, so that teaching may afterwards be given.

“But lifting up their eyes, they saw no one except Jesus alone.”

If Moses and Elijah had not vanished, it would seem uncertain to whom the Father’s voice had borne witness. They rightly see them vanish, because after the shadow of the Law and the Prophets had departed—the shadow which had covered the apostles as a cloud—the Gospel remained. “Jesus alone” is said because, when he reveals himself to the elect, God will be all in all; indeed, Christ himself will be one in every respect with his own—that is, the head will shine together with the body. [Col. 0293D] Because of this unity he says elsewhere: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3).

“And as they came down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying: ‘Tell the vision to no one until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.’”

He does not wish this to be proclaimed to the people at that time, lest it seem incredible because of the greatness of the event, and lest the cross which followed [Col. 0294A] such great glory become a stumbling-block to the inexperienced. It is certainly the teacher’s task to consider the persons of his hearers, lest he be mocked before he is heard.

M. 173[VI] R. 89

“And the disciples asked him, saying: ‘Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?’”

The sense is: Since Elijah departed from us so quickly, what then is this which the scribes say about Elijah? How are we to understand it? According to the prophet Malachi, the scribes hand down that Elijah will precede the Savior’s coming (Mal. 4). Therefore the disciples suppose that this is the glory of his coming which they had seen, and say: “If you have now come in glory, how does your forerunner not appear?” They say this especially because Elijah had departed.

“But he answered and said to them: ‘Elijah indeed will come and restore all things.’”

This is said in accordance with Malachi, where it is written that he will turn the heart of the fathers to the children and the children’s hearts to their fathers, and restore all things to their ancient state.

[BEDA.] Here Mark adds that, just as many wrote concerning Christ’s passion, so Elijah too, when he comes, will suffer many things and be despised by the ungodly.

“But I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they wished. So also the Son of Man will suffer from them.” Then the disciples understood that he had spoken of John the Baptist.

[Col. 0294C] [HIERON.] He who is to come bodily at the Savior’s second coming has already come through John in power and spirit. And just as the Pharisees’ party agreed to John’s death, so Herod joined his will to the Lord’s death, sending him back to Pilate in contempt to be crucified.

R. 90[X]

“And when he came to the crowd, he saw the scribes disputing with them. And immediately, when all the people saw him, they were astonished and alarmed; and running to him, they greeted him. And he asked them: ‘What are you disputing among yourselves?’”

He knows and yet asks, so that confession may bring forth salvation and the murmur of our heart may be released in words; as it is written: [Col. 0294D] “Tell your iniquities first, that you may be justified” (Isa. 43, according to the Septuagint). But the evangelist does not say what they were disputing about.

CHAPTER XCII

L. 174[X]

“And some of the Pharisees came to him, saying: ‘Go out and depart from here, because Herod wishes to kill you.’”

[BEDA.] “Leave Galilee, where Herod rules, and pass into a place where he has no authority.”

“And he said to them: ‘Go, tell that fox.’”

He calls Herod a fox because of his deceit and snares. This animal is full of craft, hiding and stinking in its den, and running not by straight paths but by winding turns. All these things suit heretics, of whom Herod is a type: they strive to kill Christ—that is, to take from believers the humility of Christian faith. [Col. 0295A]

“Behold, I cast out demons and accomplish healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am consummated.”

These words are to be understood mystically. It is as though he said: “Neither Herod nor the heretics, of whom he is a figure, will be able to disturb what I intend to do. I intend to cast demons out of human hearts, so that, leaving vanities behind, they may believe in me; and to accomplish healings, so that they may live according to my commands. Afterwards I shall be consummated in my body, which is the Church, when on the day of resurrection I bring her, glorified, into the fellowship of angels.” The first day, then, is to renounce vanities through God’s grace; the second, to conform one’s conduct and life to truth; the third is the final glorification.

[Col. 0295B] “Nevertheless, I must walk today and tomorrow and the following day, because it is not possible for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem.”

Herod will not be able to prevent me from acting and being consummated in this way; but neither will he be able to bring about the death of my body, which must occur in Jerusalem, where Pilate, not he, rules. For it is not possible—understand, according to some Scripture—for me, a prophet, to perish outside Jerusalem. We have often said, and still say, in answer to the importunity of those who contend over the sequence of the narrative, that chapters which seem not to occupy their proper places are to be understood, in the manner of this Scripture, as placed by anticipation or recapitulation.

[Col. 0295C] M. 174[II] R. 91 L. 99

“And it came to pass, on the following day, that a man came to him, falling on his knees and crying out: ‘Lord, have mercy on my son, for he is my only son and is lunatic; a spirit seizes him, throws him down, and he foams, grinds his teeth, wastes away, and suffers severely. For he often falls into fire and frequently into water; and suddenly he cries out, and it tears him apart, and scarcely departs from him, lacerating him.’”

[BEDA—HIERON.] In supplication and lamentation, he sets forth his son’s afflictions. The places suit the events. On the mountain the Lord prays; he is transfigured on the plain; he is besought by the weeping of the wretched. Above, he opens to the disciples the mysteries of the kingdom; below, he reproves the crowds for the sins of unbelief.

This lunatic signifies those of whom it is written: “A fool changes like the moon” (Ecclus. 27), who, never remaining in the same state, are altered now into these vices, now into those, waxing and waning. The sinner foams with folly, grinds his teeth in anger, wastes away through sloth, and is now borne into the fire of adulterers, now into waters unable to extinguish charity. Such waters are the multitude of foolish idol-worshipers, [Col. 0295D] or the pleasure of the flesh, which by softening dissolves the mind’s strength.

“And I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they could not cure him.”

He indirectly accuses the apostles; but the inability to heal is sometimes attributed not to the weakness of those who heal, but to that of those who are to be healed, as the Lord says: “Let it be done to you according to your faith.”

[Col. 0296A] Jesus answered and said: “O unbelieving and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you and endure you?”

He says this not from weariness, but like a physician seeing a sick person act against his prescriptions. Through one person he rebukes the Jews for unbelief.

“Bring him to me.” And when he approached, and the spirit saw him, immediately the spirit convulsed the boy; and, thrown down upon the ground, he rolled about foaming.

[BEDA.] “Bring the boy,” he says, because he had plainly been made far from salvation through sins and for that reason handed over to a demon. And when he approached, the demon threw him down. For often, when after sins we turn to God, we are attacked more fiercely by the devil, either that he may shake our virtue or avenge his own expulsion.

“And he asked his father: ‘How long has this been happening to him?’”

He asks so that, once the long duration of the illness is displayed, the healing may be more welcome.

“But he said: ‘From childhood. But if you can do anything, help us, having compassion on us.’”

Let Julian be ashamed, who dares to say that all people are born without any contraction of sin. For what had this boy done, that from childhood he was tormented by a demon, if he was held by no original sin, when it is evident that he could not yet have committed any personal sin?

But Jesus said to him: “If you can believe, all things are possible to one who believes.”

All things conducive to human salvation are possible to the believer, because they are asked [Col. 0296C] and given in the name of Jesus. In saying, “If you can believe,” he indicates freedom of choice.

And the father of the boy cried out with tears, saying: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief.”

Because faith grows through the hidden inspiration of grace by degrees of merit, at one and the same time the man who did not yet believe perfectly both believed and was unbelieving in the imperfection of his faith. Or thus: he believed, and, by comparison with consummate faith, called himself unbelieving.

And when Jesus saw the crowd running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it: “Deaf and mute spirit, I command you: come out of him, and do not enter him again.”

[Col. 0296D] [HIERON.] By his power he rebukes and commands the spirit, imputing to it what he grants the man, since he neither heard nor spoke. As the spirit leaves, lest it return again, let us say to the Lord with a heart strengthened by humility: “Be for me a protecting God and a fortified place, that you may save me” (Ps. 30).

“And crying out and tearing him violently, it came out of him.”

The devil tears apart those approaching salvation, whom he desires to draw into his belly as though they were food beloved by him, through terrors and losses—as with Job.

“And he became like a dead person, so that many said: ‘He is dead.’”

It is said to those who have been healed: “For you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3). Hence [Col. 0297A] even the weakness of Christians is not death but a likeness of death.

“But Jesus, taking his hand, raised him. And he arose; and the boy was healed from that hour, and he gave him back to his father.”

[BEDA.] Whoever wishes to heal a sinner must rebuke and drive away the vice, but lovingly restore the person, until healed, to the Church’s spiritual fathers.

M. 175[V] L. 200

Then the disciples came to Jesus privately and said: “Why could we not cast it out?” He said to them: “Because of your unbelief.”

[HILARY.] While the Lord remained on the mountain and they stayed [Col. 0297B] with the crowd, their faith had grown lukewarm.

“For amen I say to you: if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move; and nothing will be impossible for you. But this kind of demons is not cast out except by prayer and fasting.”

[BEDA.] Bodily passions are healed by fasting, and the diseases of the mind by prayer. Thus the devil’s more grievous insolence is overcome; thus also the Lord’s anger, when it has been kindled to avenge our crimes, is appeased as though by a singular remedy.

[HIERON.] Since Paul says, “If I have all faith, so as to remove mountains” (1 Cor. 13), the faith compared to a grain of mustard seed is great, not small, as some suppose. The removal of a mountain does not signify the mountain which we see with the eyes of the flesh, but the one removed by the Lord from the lunatic.

[BEDA.] Therefore those are foolish who say that the apostles did not possess even small faith because none of them moved mountains. A mustard seed, ground and sifted, mixed with lukewarm rich mead, if one gargles with it while fasting in the sun or in a bath, purges every harmful humor from the head and averts the dangers of approaching illnesses. Thus faith, tested in the mortar of temptations, purified by the sieve of discernment from every surface of frivolous thoughts, and sweetened with the honey of perfect love, not only drains away at present all cesspools of vices from the heart—which is the head of our inner person—but also provides beforehand against their gathering again in the future.

[Col. 0297D] Therefore read it thus: “If you have effective faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to the mountain”—that is, you will be able to command the proud devil to depart from the possessed person—“and nothing harmful will be impossible for you to heal.”

[AMBROSE.] In Luke it reads: “You will say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and transplanted into the sea,’ and it will obey you.” The fruit of the mulberry is white in blossom, ruddy when formed, and black in ripeness. So the devil, flourishing in the angelic nature and bright with power, became black with a foul odor through transgression; he is excluded through faith.

[BEDA.] Or through the mulberry tree, whose fruit and shoots are red—and hence it is also called *rubus*, “bramble,” by the Latins—the Gospel of the cross is expressed. Uprooted from the Jewish people by the words of the apostles’ preaching, it was transplanted into the sea of the Gentiles. Mulberry leaves placed upon a serpent bring death. [Col. 0298A] For the word of the cross, as it bestows every saving benefit, so removes harmful things.

Otherwise, by the mountain to be moved and the mulberry tree to be uprooted and transplanted, this may be understood: that the mark of consummate faith is to command gently where reason requires; so that what is said specifically of these things may be understood generally of all things.

CHAPTER XCIII

M. 177[V] R. 93 L. 101

And while they were staying in Galilee, Jesus said to them: “The Son of Man is to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.” And they were greatly distressed.

The Lord always mingles sorrows with blessings, so that when they come suddenly they may not terrify the apostles. And if his being killed grieves them, the resurrection ought to make them glad. That, according to Mark and Luke, some did not understand the Word arose not so much from slowness of mind as from love: because they knew him to be the true God, they could not believe that he would die. And because he often spoke in figures, they thought this was said figuratively.

M. 177[X]

And when they came to Capernaum, those who collected the didrachma came to Peter and said to him: “Does your teacher not pay the didrachma?” He said: “Yes.”

[HIERON.] That is, truly, he does not pay it. After Augustus Caesar, Judea was made tributary. But because of the greatness of his signs, they did not dare address the Lord [Col. 0298C] about the tax. They therefore approach the disciple. Or they did this maliciously, wishing to know whether he would oppose Caesar.

And when he had entered the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying: “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute or tax—from their sons or from strangers?” And he said: “From strangers.” Jesus said to him: “Then the sons are free.”

Our Lord was a king’s son both according to the flesh and according to the Spirit. Therefore he did not owe the tax, but paid it in humility. Jesus anticipated Peter, not wishing to wait for the request for tribute, lest the apostles be scandalized.

“But lest we give them offense, go to the sea, [Col. 0298D] cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up. When you open its mouth, you will find a stater; take it and give it to them for me and for yourself.”

I do not know what to wonder at first here: the foreknowledge of the stater in the fish’s mouth, or the greatness of the power, if at his word the stater was at once created in the fish’s mouth. This fish, which was in the sea’s depths, is mystically understood to be the first Adam, freed by the second Adam. Peter, fisher of men, cast the hook of doctrine into the world, so that by the sweetness of the bait he might draw from its waves those wandering and tossing there.

The stater is confession. A stater is so called because it contains two didrachmas, by which the flesh of servant and Lord are freed. The same price is fittingly given, but divided: for the Lord passed through voluntary sufferings [Col. 0299A] to the impassibility of his flesh by confession of the truth; but he freed us from the captivity of sin and necessary corruption. Or, understood simply, this edifies the hearer: the Lord was in such poverty that he had nothing from which to pay the taxes. If anyone objects that Judas carried money in the purse, we answer that the Lord considered it wrong to turn the property of the poor to his own use.

CHAPTER XCIV

R. 64[X]

“At that hour, when they were in the house, he questioned them: ‘What were you discussing on the way?’ But they kept silent. For on the way they had disputed among themselves which of them was the greater.”

[BEDA.] The disciples’ dispute about precedence seems to have arisen because they saw Peter, James, and John taken apart up the mountain, as though something secret were to be entrusted to them. They had also heard that Peter had been promised the keys of the kingdom of heaven, that the Church was to be built upon the rock of faith from which he had received his name, and that the tribute had been paid jointly for Peter and the Lord. Therefore they thought that either those three were set above the rest, or Peter above them all. [Col. 0299B] Understanding this, the Lord wishes to heal their desire for glory by the contest of humility.

M. 178[II] R. 95 L. 92

And the disciples came to Jesus, saying: “Who do you think is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?” And Jesus, calling a little child, placed him in their midst and said: [Col. 0299C] “Amen I say to you: unless you are converted and become like little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.”

[HIERON.] As they were going, they had disputed about supremacy. In the house the Lord teaches them to change pride into humility. Rulers labor; the humble rest. A little child does not persist in anger, does not remember an injury, does not delight in a beautiful woman, and does not seek honor through ambition.

[BEDA.] Therefore this is the meaning of the saying: “Unless you possess the innocence of a child, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.” That Mark relates that he embraced the child signifies that the humble are worthy of his embrace; they can truly glory and say: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2).

“Whoever therefore humbles himself like this little child [Col. 0299D] is greatest in the kingdom of heaven. If anyone wishes to be first, he shall be last of all and servant of all. And whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me.”

In the future fellowship of the saints there will indeed be no precedence of offices. Yet there you will be greater in holiness than some, or even one of the foremost, insofar as here, aided by the effort of reason, you seek more earnestly the form of virtue which a child follows by nature’s guidance. Those saved without merits by the grace of baptism alone will indeed be great, but not greater than any others.

Therefore, whoever wishes to be among the greater should receive little children for Christ’s love—which is to receive Christ himself in them—that is, should nurture toward greater things those still weak [Col. 0300A] [lowly] in childlike simplicity. Hence Paul calls the Philippians his joy and crown. Understand the statement, “This one is greatest in the kingdom of heaven,” and the earlier question, “Who do you think is greatest?” according to that usage by which we speak of things certainly future as though they already existed. Or thus: “This one is greatest,” that is, he possesses the cause which makes him greater.

M. 196[II] R. 99 L. 127

“But whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it is better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths of the sea.”

[Jerome.] Whoever is caused to stumble is a little one. For the greater do not admit stumbling-blocks. Rightly, therefore, one who can be caused to stumble is called little, because a great person, whatever he suffers, does not turn aside from the faith. He speaks of an ass-millstone according to the custom of the province, among the ancient Jews, where this was the punishment for greater crimes: criminals, with a stone bound to their neck, were submerged in the deep. This judgment is general, applying both to all and to the apostles: if they persisted in contending for honor over which of them was greater, by their stumbling-block they would destroy those whom they called to faith. The sense is: It is expedient—that is, far better—to receive a brief punishment for one’s fault than to be reserved for eternal torments. For will not God judge the same thing twice? (Nahum 1, according to the Septuagint.) Or thus: It is expedient—that is, much more advantageous—for an innocent person to end bodily life by a most dreadful but merely temporal punishment, than, by harming a brother, to deserve the perpetual death of the soul. Yet if a stumbling-block is occasioned by truth, it is more useful to allow the stumbling-block to arise than to abandon the truth. [Col. 0300C]

[Hilary.] Otherwise: By the ass-millstone is expressed the circuit and toil of secular life, and by the depth of the sea is signified final damnation. Therefore, for one who has been brought to an appearance of holiness and destroys others by word or example, it would be better for earthly affairs to bind him beneath an outward appearance unto death. For if he alone fell, he would be tortured more tolerably in hell.

[Hilary.] Otherwise: The work of the mill is the labor of blindness. For beasts, with their eyes shut, are driven in a circle. Under the name of an ass, moreover, the Gentile people is frequently designated in the Scriptures. It is bound to the mill, that is, to stony gods, around whom it is dragged in the circular course of its error with blind eyes, [Col. 0300D] and so, with its sacrilegious mill, is submerged in the waves of the world’s judgment. The sense, therefore, is: It would be better for a Christian through whose stumbling-block his brothers or subjects perish to be a pagan, because pagans do not suffer in hell as great a punishment as false Christians.

## Chapter XCV

**R. 97[VIII] L. 103**

But John answered and said: “Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we forbade him, because he does not follow with us.”

But Jesus said: “Do not forbid him. For no one who performs a mighty work in my name can quickly speak evil [Col. 0301A] of me. For whoever is not against you is for you.”

[Augustine.] It is not contrary that elsewhere he says, “Whoever despises you despises me,” and, “Whoever is not with me is against me.” For he means that a person is not with him insofar as he is against him, and is not against him insofar as he is with him. Thus this man, in performing mighty works in Christ’s name, was not opposed to the disciples; but in not being in their communion, he was opposed in that respect. Hence the Lord said to them, “Do not forbid him.” They ought to persuade him toward the unity of the Church, not forbid what he had in common with them. Thus the Catholic Church does not disapprove in heretics the sacraments held in common, in which they are with us, but their separations from [Col. 0301B] us and their judgments contrary to the truth.

[Bede.] Taught by this saying, the Apostle declares: “Whether Christ is proclaimed from pretext or from truth, in this I rejoice and shall rejoice” (Philippians 1).

**M. 179[II] R. 99 L. 197**

“Woe to the world because of offenses. For offenses must come; nevertheless, woe to the person through whom offense comes.”

Just as fire must be hot and snow cold, so it is necessary that the iniquity of the world, full of errors, should produce offenses, while the love of the perfect should shine in works of piety. Yet because no necessity compels human hearts to be wicked—although, since they are wicked, they necessarily stir up offenses—therefore woe to the person through whose fault they come. In this general judgment Judas is struck. He says especially that offenses must come because, for the sacrament by which eternity is restored to us, every humiliation of the Passion had to be fulfilled in him. For human ignorance is held fast especially by this: that, beneath the ugliness of the cross, it refuses to receive the Lord of eternal glory. And what is so perilous to the world as not to have received Christ?

**M. 180[VI] R. 100**

“But if your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter into life maimed or lame than, having two hands or [Col. 0301D] two feet, to be cast into eternal fire.”

[Bede.] Since above he taught that we should not cause believers to stumble, he warns how carefully we must avoid those who cause stumbling, since there is little difference in guilt between deceiving and being deceived. A person causes stumbling when, by a word or deed that is less than right, he gives occasion for ruin. Either take *good* here as “better,” or understand *than* in the sense of “rather than,” as there: “It is good to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in man” (Psalm 17).

“And if your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter life one-eyed than, having two eyes, to be cast into the Gehenna of fire.”

[Augustine.] It should be noted that the man reported by John was not so separated from the disciples as to disapprove of them as heretics. Rather, he was like those who, not yet daring to receive Christ’s sacraments, nevertheless favor the Christian name. Although such people ought not yet to regard themselves as safe on account of this goodwill, because they have not yet been washed in baptism, nevertheless God’s mercy already guides them in such a way that they attain it and thus depart this world secure. Indeed, even before they become Christians, they are sometimes more useful than false Christians who persuade others of things that draw them along with themselves into eternal punishment. The Lord commands that these people, who cause stumbling under the name of bodily members—like a hand or eye causing stumbling—be plucked from the body, that is, from the fellowship of unity, so that one may go to life without them rather than with them to Gehenna. And if their perversity is known to all good people who know them, [Col. 0302B] they should be completely separated from everyone’s fellowship and from participation itself in the divine sacraments. But if their perversity is known to some and unknown to many, they must be tolerated as chaff is tolerated on the threshing floor before winnowing: neither consenting to them in a fellowship of iniquity nor abandoning the fellowship of the good because of them. This is done by those who have salt in themselves and have peace with one another.

**R. 101[X]**

“Where their worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished. For everyone shall be salted with fire, and every sacrifice shall be salted with salt.”

[Bede.] By the worm he indicates the corruption of Gehenna, and by the fire its burning. For he calls the worm the late repentance for sins, which in torments will never cease to gnaw the conscience: fire is the punishment outwardly, the worm pain inwardly. Therefore, by the fire of tribulation, remove friends as useful to you as hand, foot, or eye if they wish to draw you to Gehenna; for everyone who is God’s sacrifice will be tested by purgatorial fire, and meanwhile is salted by the reason of wisdom while the corruption of blood—which preserves decay and is the mother of worms—is consumed. For the stench of worms is accustomed to arise from the corruption of flesh and blood. Thus fresh meat is seasoned with salt, so that, when its bloody moisture is dried, it cannot breed worms. Flesh and blood, therefore, create worms, because carnal pleasure, against which the seasoning of continence does not resist, produces eternal punishment for the lustful. Whoever desires to escape its stench should strive to purify the body with the salt of continence and the mind with the seasoning of wisdom from the stain of error and vices. [Col. 0302D]

Otherwise: “Everyone shall be salted with fire” is wonderfully said. For a sacrifice that is salted wards off the corruption of worms; but that which is treated with fire and sprinkled salt consumes the flesh also (Leviticus 2). This was done according to the Law with offerings burned upon the altar, where salt was commanded to be offered with every sacrifice. Salt, therefore, signifies the sweetness of wisdom; fire, the grace of the Holy Spirit. Thus everyone shall be salted with fire, because the elect are consecrated to God as a worthy sacrifice through the love of the Holy Spirit. And because they cleanse themselves from vices with the salt of wisdom, he fittingly adds, “and every sacrifice shall be salted with salt.” Such a sacrifice is therefore not only sprinkled with salt but consumed by fire, because not only is the contagion of sin driven away, but from the minds of the elect even the pleasure of this present life in the flesh is taken away. Hence the Apostle says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3).

Or thus: the altar of God is the heart of the elect; the offerings to be made upon this altar are good works. Salt must be offered in every sacrifice, because no good work exists without wisdom. Fire consumes sacrifices upon the altar; of it John says: “He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matthew 3). Or it is the fire of tribulation, by which the patience of the faithful is exercised, that they may have a perfect work. Everyone, therefore, who wishes to avoid the worm of eternal torment will be chastened by fire, so that all his work may be a sacrifice seasoned with salt for God.

## Chapter XCVI

[Col. 0303B]

**M. 181[X]**

“See that you do not despise one of these little ones.”

He tempers the severity with which he commanded that friends be cut off for God’s sake, saying: Thus I command severity that I may teach mercy. So far as lies in you, do not despise them; rather, seek their healing also through your own salvation. If you cannot do so, it is better that you be saved than that you perish with them.

“For I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven. For the Son of Man came to save that which had perished.”

As if he said: If you despise one of the little ones, [Col. 0303C] their angels will see it and my Father will take vengeance. I say this to you because you ought not despise what I came to save. Great is the dignity of souls, since every soul has, from its birth, an angel assigned to guard it.

[Isidore.] Individual nations or Churches also are believed to have angels set over them. This is shown by the testimony of the angel speaking to Daniel: “I came,” he says, “to tell you, but the prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me” (Daniel 10).

[Jerome.] And afterward: “There is none to help me except Michael, your prince” (ibid.). And in the Apocalypse: “Write these things to the angel of Ephesus and Thyatira, and to the angel of Philadelphia, and to the angels of the four remaining Churches” (Revelation 2). The Apostle likewise commanded women’s heads to be veiled in the Churches because of the angels (1 Corinthians 11).

**M. 182[V] L. 187**

“And he spoke this parable to them, saying: What do you think? If someone has a hundred sheep and one of them goes astray, does he not leave the ninety-nine in the mountains or in the wilderness and go to seek the one that wandered? And if he happens to find it, he lays it upon his shoulders rejoicing; and, coming home, he calls together his friends and neighbors and says to them: Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep which was lost.”

Because the number one hundred is perfect, the Lord had one hundred sheep after he created human beings and angels. But one sheep perished when humankind sinned. Yet the rich shepherd left the ninety-nine in the mountains—that is, in the heavenly places—or in the wilderness, when he emptied himself; for we all are the hundredth portion, and he left the choirs of angels in heaven. Why is heaven called a wilderness except because a wilderness is called an abandoned place? For humanity abandoned heaven when it sinned.

The sheep which [“Whom” in the text] the Lord placed upon his shoulders signifies that, by assuming human nature, he bore our sins. Christ’s shoulders are the arms of the cross. There I laid down my sins; upon that noble neck of the gibbet I rested. Having found the sheep, he returned home, because, after restoring humankind, he entered heaven. The angels are his friends because they steadfastly keep his will. They are also his neighbors because they enjoy the brightness of his vision. Note that he does not say, “Rejoice with the sheep,” but “with me,” because our life is his joy.

**M.**

“Amen I say to you that he will rejoice over it more than over the ninety-nine that did not go astray and do not need repentance.”

Although the shepherd undoubtedly loves the ninety-nine sheep much more than the lone hundredth, he nevertheless shows, while the others are unmentioned, that he rejoices in many ways over the restored one. So too the Savior rejoices more over the restoration of the human race—that is, he displays his joy more and by more proofs—than over the steadfastness of the angels. Or thus: “He rejoices more,” that is, he causes us to rejoice more over it.

“Thus it is not the will before your Father who is in heaven [Col. 0304C] that one of these little ones should perish.”

Just as it is not the shepherd’s will that one sheep perish, so it is not the will before the Father; that is, the Father does not will that one little one perish.

**L. 189[X]**

“Or what woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her women friends and neighbors, saying: Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma which I had lost.”

[Bede.] A drachma is a coin of fixed value bearing the image of a king. The woman, therefore—that is, God’s Wisdom—had ten drachmas, when man was added as the tenth to the nine orders [Col. 0304D] of angels, so that the number of the elect might be completed. The woman lost the drachma when man, who had been made in God’s image, sinned. But the woman lit a lamp because God’s Wisdom appeared in flesh. The lamp is light in an earthen vessel: that is, divinity in flesh. Of this vessel of her body Wisdom herself says: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Psalm 21). A potsherd is hardened in fire, and her strength dried up when she strengthened the assumed flesh through the tribulation of the Passion unto the glory of the Resurrection. Once the lamp was lit—that is, once the flesh was glorified by divinity—the house was swept because human conscience is disturbed by consideration of its guilt. Thus the drachma is sought again, because in humanity the likeness of the Creator is restored. By women friends and neighbors he means the angelic powers, which are so much nearer to supreme Wisdom as they contemplate her more closely. He calls them together when, by displaying grace bestowed upon humanity, he kindles them more ardently in love for himself.

**L. 189[V] M. 181**

“So I tell you, there will be joy in heaven before the angels of God over one sinner doing repentance, rather than over ninety-nine righteous persons who do not need repentance.”

Often those who know themselves to be oppressed by no heavy masses of sins remain sluggish in doing good, secure because they have not committed more serious evils. Conversely, those who remember that they have done unlawful things are sometimes, pierced by that very grief, set ablaze with love for God. Therefore greater joy occurs in heaven over a converted sinner than over a righteous person who remains standing. Indeed, in battle a commander loves more the soldier who, after flight, returns and vigorously presses the enemy than one who has never turned his back and has never done anything bravely.

[Albinus.] That angels, being rational beings, rejoice over a human being reconciled to them kindles us toward uprightness, that we may do what is pleasing to those whose protection we ought to seek and whose offense we ought to fear. In the third parable concerning the receiving of sinners, the Lord shows not only his own joy and that of his own people, but also rebukes the murmuring of those who envy.

## Chapter XCVII

[Col. 0305C] **L. 190[X]**

“And he said: A man had two sons; and the younger of them said to his father: ‘Father, give me the portion of the property that falls to me.’ And he divided his property between them.”

[Bede.] The man who had two sons is understood to be God the Father, creator of two peoples. The elder son is the one who remained in the worship of the one God; the younger, the one who worshiped idols. The divided property is rational understanding in humanity. The younger son asked this of his father when he thought that through free choice he could govern himself without God’s grace. To believers God gives the aid of his grace; to unbelievers, he grants the benefit [Col. 0305D] of natural intelligence.

[Augustine.] Whoever wishes, then, to use his own power so as to live with no one governing him, as God has no one by whom he is governed, fades away by departing from truth. This the devil did. Likewise humankind, to whom nothing was lacking except that it wished to use its own power, so that, with no one ruling it, it might become like God, touched through disobedience the fruit forbidden to it and found punishment.

“And not many days afterward, the younger son gathered everything together, departed into a far country, and there squandered his property by living luxuriously.”

[Bede.] Not long after the creation of humankind, the soul chose to extend its powers into wandering. The younger son thus departed far away [Col. 0306A] not by changing place but in mind; for the more anyone sins, the farther he withdraws from God’s grace, and the more quickly he consumes, through luxury, nature’s adornments.

[Ambrose—Bede.] Nor should one suppose that any age is too weak to possess the kingdom of God, or that faith is burdened by years. Whoever departs from the father, however, becomes an exile from his homeland and a citizen of the world, and rightly squanders his inheritance.

“And after he had consumed everything, a severe famine came upon that region, and he began to be in need.”

He had received from the Father the ability to know God’s invisible things through visible things and, from the beauty of creatures, consequently to understand the Creator. But famine in the far country is a lack of the word of truth amid forgetfulness of the Creator. He began to be in need [Col. 0306B] because nothing is enough for prodigal pleasure.

“And he went and attached himself to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his field to feed swine.”

The one citizen who voluntarily ensnared himself is he who, deservedly set over earthly desires because of his wickedness, is called the prince of this world. He sent him into his field by subjecting him to desire for worldly possessions.

[Jerome.] To feed swine is to perform those things in which unclean spirits delight. For as a pig delights in filth, so the devil feeds upon the blood of animals in idols, but is especially satiated by human death. Thus he sent him into his possession—that is, made him his slave—that he might feed swine by sacrificing his own soul to him.

“And he desired to fill his belly with the pods which [Col. 0306C] the swine ate, and no one gave him any.”

[Bede.] The pod, food of swine—that is, of demons—is drunkenness, fornication, and similar things, which are enticing and invite one to use them. Hence the lustful especially strive to fill their belly, “whose god is their belly” (Philippians 3); yet in these there is no satisfaction, because pleasure always hungers for itself. Moreover, when the devil makes someone his own, he no longer urges him onward to an abundance of vices, knowing that he is already dead.

Or the pods are secular teachings, resounding with barren sweetness, in which demons delight, woven together by the varied speech of tales and songs. Therefore, though he who fed swine desired to be satisfied and to find something solid for the blessed life, he could not, [Col. 0306D] because no one gave him any straight path to blessedness.

“But, returning to himself, he said: ‘How many hired servants in my father’s house abound in bread, while I perish here from hunger!’”

[Augustine.] If God is our blessedness, what can belong to one who departs from him but misery? Return, then, after misery, and say: “Lord, who is like you? How many great and grievous tribulations you have shown me; and, having turned, you revived me and brought me back again from the depths of the earth” (Psalm 70).

[Bede.] Returning to himself, he recognized that his father’s hired servants abounded in bread, because those who labor to do things worthy of God are refreshed by the nourishment of heavenly grace. But those who live without faith and devote themselves to empty philosophy [Col. 0307A] are full of vanity, just as a pod is empty within and soft without. A pod, however, is not, as some suppose, the fruit of a tree, but a kind of legume with resonant, empty husks, which burdens the belly more than it refreshes it.

“I will arise and go to my father, and say to him: ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants.’”

Until now I lay fallen because I departed from my father; but now I will arise and serve him. To sin against heaven is to forsake God in the presence of angelic spirits and holy souls.

[Bede.] One sins before God even by thinking of doing evil. He desires to become a hired servant because he does not presume to call himself a son.

[Col. 0307B] “And rising, he came to his father.”

To come to the Father is to return to the Church, where confession is fruitful.

“But while he was still far off, his father saw him.”

Before he understood God, yet while he was already seeking piously, his Father loved him through foreknowledge of the future. For only those who are loved are customarily said to be kept before one’s eyes.

“Moved by compassion, he ran and fell upon his neck and kissed him.”

The Father runs through the mercy of the incarnation of the Word, lest anyone impede the one who comes. He fell upon his neck and kissed him, because he humbled himself in mercy [Col. 0307C] and restored his grace to him.

[Jerome.] The Father leaned upon the neck of the returning son because he humbled his arm—that is, his Son—in that one’s embrace; or because he laid upon him the light yoke of love. The returning son receives the kiss of love from the Father when, through grace, he is assured of forgiveness.

“And the son said to him: ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’”

“I have sinned against heaven, because I abandoned the heavenly Jerusalem; and against you, because, having forsaken you, I worshiped idols.”

[Bede.] Established in the Church, he makes confession. Nor does he say what he had promised that he would say: “Make me as one of your hired servants,” because by grace he aims to become what by merits he had proved unworthy to be. For he understands that there is no small difference between a son, a hired servant, [Col. 0307D] and a slave: namely, a slave is one who, through fear of Gehenna or of present laws, does not dare to sin; a hired servant is one who restrains himself from vices by hope of the kingdom of heaven; a son is one who has the affection of goodness through love of virtues. Hence the Apostle says: “Now there remain faith, hope, love, these three; but the greatest of these is love” (1 Corinthians 13). Faith shuns vices through fear of judgment and punishments; hope despises pleasures in expectation of heavenly rewards; love kindles us unto death and unto the fruit of spiritual virtues.

“And the father said to his servants: ‘Quickly bring forth the first robe and put it on him; put a ring on his hand and shoes on his feet; bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let us eat [Col. 0308A] and feast, because this my son was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.’ And they began to feast.”

The first robe is the garment of innocence which humankind received when well created, but lost when badly persuaded. The servants are the preachers who proclaim the robe to the reconciled person. The ring is the seal of Christ’s likeness and the expression of truth, or the pledge of the Holy Spirit because of the division which is fittingly marked by the finger. Or thus: the ring is the sign of faith, or the pledge of the Church’s marriage joined to Christ. It is rightly given on the hand, so that faith may shine through works and works be strengthened through faith. The shoes signify the office of the Gospel, so that the course of the mind, tending toward heavenly things, may be kept unharmed from earthly things; and, fortified by examples of the godly, it may walk safely over serpents and scorpions.

The fattened calf is the Lord himself. He is rightly called fattened because his flesh is so rich in spiritual virtues that it was sufficient to be offered for the salvation of the whole world as an odor of sweetness. To bring and kill the fattened calf is to preach Christ and make known his death. For he is, as it were, freshly slain for each person when that person believes that he was slain. His flesh is eaten when the sacrament of his Passion is received both with the mouth for cleansing and pondered in the heart for imitation. Not only does the found son feast—that is, receive refreshment from the flesh of the most holy calf—but so do the Father and his servants, because our salvation is the Father’s food and the forgiveness of our sins is the Father’s joy.

Note that the first robe, the ring, and the shoes are bestowed before the calf is sacrificed, because unless one has put on the hope of immortality, fortified one’s works with the ring of faith, and preached the faith by confession, one cannot participate in the heavenly sacraments. These feasts are celebrated through the enlargement of the Church throughout the whole world.

“But his elder son was in the field.”

That is, he was far from the Father’s counsel in earthly works. This son is the Israelite people, which, although it had not gone away to worship idols, was nevertheless not at home because it did not understand the inward meaning of the Law and Prophets but clung to the earthly letter by expecting earthly things.

[Jerome.] This is the one who bought a field and five yokes of oxen and, burdened by the yoke of the Law, [Col. 0308D] takes delight in earthly understandings and takes a wife in carnal affection.

“And as he came and drew near the house, he heard music and dancing.”

Drawing near the house—that is, the Church—after rejecting the labor of servile work, he heard music, that is, the harmony of Law and Gospel; he heard dancing, that is, the ecclesiastical assembly living in the harmony of love. Some Latin writers wrongly suppose that *symphonia* is a kind of instrument; for *symphonia* is rendered in Latin by *consonantia*, “harmony.” A chorus, moreover, is where diverse strings make one song.

“And he called one of the servants and asked what these things were. And he said to him: ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf because he received him back safe.’ But he was angry and would not go in. Therefore his father came out and began to entreat him.”

[Bede.] The one servant whom he calls is some prophet whom he reads, seeking to learn why such feasts are celebrated in the Church. When he finds it there, as though the prophet were answering him, he is angered and refuses to enter—that is, to believe. Yet the Father goes out to him through preachers and entreats him to enter; but even today, because of envy toward his brother and ignorance of the Father’s will, he stands outside. Nevertheless, he will enter at the end, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered.

“But he answered and said to his father: ‘Behold, for so many years I serve you, and I have never transgressed your command.’”

It is asked how that people [Israel] never [Col. 0309B] transgressed God’s command; but the solution is readily available. This is not said of every command, but of that command by which it was ordered to worship no other God than the Creator of all things. This son represents those who never turned from the one God to images. Although they were or are in the field, desiring earthly things, they nevertheless desired and desire that these be given them by the true God. Hence it immediately follows: “Son, you are always with me.” Many likewise kept the Law as hired servants, lest God withdraw earthly prosperity because of their transgression of it.

“And you never gave me a kid, that I might feast with my friends.”

A kid commonly signifies a sinner, but here it signifies Christ, not because he ever committed sin, but because the Jews considered him a sinner. This kid has not yet been given to the Jews for feasting because they do not yet believe in him. The phrase “with my friends” is understood either in the person of the rulers, that they might feast with the people, or in the person of the people of Jerusalem, that they might feast with the other tribes of Israel.

[Jerome.] Israel, you err in the field because you are silent about the Father’s feast, as though true joy could exist apart from him. Those who at the end of the age sacrifice the kid—that is, Antichrist—for themselves will be filled without the Father together with their demon friends. Hence it is said: “You crushed the dragon; you gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia” (Psalm 73), that is, to those unwilling to be converted.

[Col. 0309D] “But after this son of yours, who devoured his property with prostitutes, came, you killed the fattened calf for him.”

The prostitutes are the superstitions of the Gentiles, with whom he says that his younger brother committed fornication. Israel’s complaint to the Father is therefore this: For me, who remained with you and earned merit, there was never for refreshment the one whom I regard as a kid and a violator of the Law. But that same person, whom you call your son, you killed for idolaters unto the full joy of redemption.

Otherwise: a kid may be called any saint in comparison with the Son of God. Israel therefore says to the Father: So much blood of the righteous has been shed, and none of them has restored freedom to us. Behold, we still lie subject to the Roman empire. So many saints have been slain, and none of them—neither priest nor prophet—has been sacrificed for our salvation. But for the luxurious son, that is, for the undeserving Gentiles, as the world cries out, the glorious blood of your Son has been shed.

“But he said to him: ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But it was necessary to feast and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.’”

[Bede.] Dead through unbelief, he came to life through faith; lost by withdrawing from the fellowship of the righteous, he was found when restored to mother Church.
