The Father does not rebuke the elder son as though lying, but praises his perseverance with himself and invites him to share in a higher rejoicing. When he says, “All that is mine is yours,” it should not be thought that this is said as though those things were not also the brother’s. But if the younger has a share there, how are all things the elder’s? After this life, the righteous possess all things in such a way that all things belong to each individually. Therefore, when we obtain that blessedness, the higher things will be ours for living, equal things for fellowship, lower things for ruling.

Let the elder brother, therefore, rejoice together over the younger’s return, whether one prefers to understand the two brothers as the two peoples, or as any two persons—a penitent and a righteous person, or one who seems righteous to himself. For as soon as the world was made, there began to be citizens of Babylon and of Jerusalem, that is, evil and good people. Thus the younger son can signify all evil people who come to repentance; the elder, all those who persist in God’s worship, although they deviate into certain sins, such as envy of their brother. Accordingly, by the fattened calf we understand the greater gifts of grace, and by the kid, in comparison with them, lesser gifts, just as all human righteousness, compared with God, is accounted unrighteousness.

[Albinus.] Three parables are concluded by one end of mercy. The sheep that slipped away from the shepherd is recalled; the drachma which was lost is found; the son returns to his father by his own footsteps and is honored by his father. We are sheep: let us seek pasture. We are a drachma: let us have value. We are sons: let us hasten to the Father.

## Chapter XCVIII

**L. 198[V] M. 183**

“Take heed to yourselves. If your brother sins against you, go [Col. 0310D] and rebuke him between you and him alone. If he listens to you, **L.** and does repentance, forgive him, **M.** and you will have gained your brother.”

Because God rejoices over a converted sinner, take care not to despise the little ones; instead, rebuke the sinner so that he may be converted, and gather the penitent into the fellowship of love. Thus, through another’s salvation, salvation is gained for yourselves.

[Bede.] It must be keenly observed that we are not commanded indiscriminately to forgive one who sins, but one who does repentance. Therefore, first comes rebuking the sinner, that afterward we may forgive the penitent.

[Ambrose—Augustine.] For one sins who sees a sinner and keeps silent just as does one who does not pardon the penitent. For he who said, “If he repents, forgive him,” first said, “If he sins, rebuke him,” so that forgiveness may be neither difficult nor indulgence lax.

[Jerome.] We shall therefore forgive our debtors the debts of sin’s punishment if they repent of having sinned against us.

[Augustine.] But to forgive what someone sins against God is not within our discretion. A brother sins against us if he sins even with our knowledge, because, so far as lies in him, he corrupts by his example those whom he makes witnesses of his iniquity. When someone, within my hearing, wrongs my brother, far be it from me to think that wrong foreign to myself. Therefore, as the Apostle commands Timothy, sins committed before all are to be rebuked before all, that the rest may have fear (1 Timothy 5). But if you alone know your brother’s sin, then he has truly sinned against you alone. What does “he has sinned against you” mean? You know that he has sinned. And because he sinned against you in secret, correct him in secret. For if you alone know it and wish to accuse him before everyone, you are not a corrector but a betrayer. Perhaps what you know I also know, but I do not rebuke him before you because I wish to heal, not accuse. There are adulterous men in their homes; they sin secretly, and their wives reveal them to us, often from jealousy, sometimes seeking their husbands’ salvation. We do not expose them openly, but rebuke them privately. A brother should likewise be rebuked separately, lest, once he has lost shame, he remain in sin.

**M. 184[X]**

“But if he does not listen to you, take with you one or two more, so that every word may stand upon the testimony of two or three witnesses. And if he does not listen to them, tell the Church.”

[Bede.] We read something similar in Deuteronomy: “Do not hate your brother in your heart, but rebuke him publicly, lest you bear sin on his account” (Leviticus 19).

[Jerome.] A third person should be brought in, either with the purpose of correction or to confront him before witnesses. If he does not listen then, it must be told to many, so that one who could not be saved through shame may be saved through reproaches.

“But if he does not listen to the Church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector.”

Tax collectors, in the tropological sense, are those who pursue worldly gain, frauds, thefts, and perjuries. [HILARY.] And when it is said, “let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector,” this shows that one who, under Christ’s name, performs the works of unbelievers is more detestable than those who are openly Gentiles. Israel had advanced by observing that order. For he rebuked the Jewish people, sacrificing to foreign gods, by the coming of his majesty, although that same people, positioned outside the mountain, could not bear the terror of his present power. Then the Law, the Prophets, and John came together against the disobedient people as witnesses, that it might cease from sinning. Thirdly, it was admonished by the Lord’s own coming, as though by the assembly of the Church looking on. And, these rebukes having proved fruitless, it is disregarded with the contempt due tax collectors and Gentiles.

M. 185[VII] A. 215

“Truly I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

[Col. 0312A] [JEROME.] He gives authority to the apostles so that they may not be despised by anyone. It is as though he said: If anyone refuses to hear your correction, and you bind him on earth with the bond of anathema, he will also be bound in heaven—that is, with the heavenly sentence confirming it. Or, as above: whomever you cast out of the Church in this life, or bring into the Church, the sentence will be ratified also in heaven, that is, throughout the whole Church. But whether this is done justly or unjustly makes no difference: the person subject to it must obey. [GREGORY.] For the judgment of the shepherd, whether just or unjust, is to be feared, lest one who was not previously guilty become guilty afterward through a proud reply.

M. 186[X]

[Col. 0312B] “Again I say to you: if two of you agree on earth concerning anything whatever that they ask, it shall be done for them by my Father who is in heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, I am there in their midst.”

[REMIGIUS.] Truly, your judgment shall stand firm, both in rejecting the obstinate and in receiving the penitent; for once two of you agree, I speak not only of these matters but of everything that may be asked: by reason of unity, the request of their agreement shall be granted by my Father. For I am peace and charity; I am the highest and common good; I have established my dwelling among the peaceful. [JEROME.] See the reward of concord, to which this entire discourse summons us. This may also be understood typologically: wherever spirit, soul, and body agree, they obtain every good thing that they ask.

M. 187[V] L. 199

Then Peter came to him and said: “Lord, how often will my brother sin against me and I forgive him? Up to seven times?” Jesus said to him: “I do not tell you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.”

[Bede.] That is, four hundred and ninety times, so that forgiveness may be granted to one’s brother as often as he can sin in a day. Alternatively: seven commonly denotes the totality of every matter or time. Thus what is sung in the Psalm, “Seven times a day I have spoken your praise” (Ps. 118), means nothing other than “His praise is always in my mouth” (Ps. 33). Eleven, however, signifies transgression, because it departs from ten, in which the Decalogue [Col. 0312D] consists. Therefore, when it is multiplied by seven, so that seven times eleven makes seventy-seven, every transgression is understood. Thus forgiveness is commanded seventy times seven—that is, seventy-seven times: in other words, every transgression. Where it says, “and shall I forgive him?” *et* is used in the sense of “also.”

## CHAPTER XCIX–C

M. 188[X]

“Therefore the kingdom of heaven has been likened to a man, a king, who wished to settle accounts with his servants.”

[JEROME.] It is customary among Syrians, and especially among Palestinians, to attach parables to all their discourse, so that one who cannot be held by a simple command may be held through a comparison. Understand the kingdom of heaven as Christ, compared therefore to an earthly king in order to show that forgiveness must be given without number to penitent fellow-servants, since through the grace of the Gospel God has bestowed upon us, by his gift and not by our merit, forgiveness for absolutely all sins.

“And when he had begun to settle accounts, one was brought before him who owed ten thousand talents. But since he had nothing with which to repay, his lord ordered him to be sold, together with his wife, children, and all that he had, and payment to be made.”

[REMIGIUS.] Christ, the examiner of merits, now settles accounts with his servants through the Scriptures. He owed ten thousand talents who was to render an account for innumerable sinful or criminal acts. But when he lacked the means and grace with which to make satisfaction, he learned from the Scriptures that God commands such persons to be sold—that is, handed over to eternal fire with wife and children, namely, with folly and evil thoughts. But he promises that he will glorify the righteous with wife and children—that is, with wisdom and good thoughts. The price of the one sold is understood as the punishment of the condemned.

“But that servant fell down and begged him, saying: ‘Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.’”

Humbled by fear of Gehenna, he says: “Spare me, Lord; and I, believing and repenting, shall cover a multitude of sins by charity.”

“But the lord of that servant, moved with compassion, released him and forgave him the debt.”

[Col. 0313C] The sinner who asks receives the gift of ten thousand talents—that is, forgiveness of his offenses—when he takes upon himself the remedy which God instituted for this purpose. This occurs if he receives the washing of baptism without pretense, or if, after baptism, he devoutly receives the baptism of repentance. Released, therefore, from the bonds of his former fear, he goes forth into hope of salvation.

“But that servant, having gone out, found one of his fellow-servants who owed him a hundred denarii; and seizing him, he choked him, saying: ‘Pay what you owe.’”

The debtor of a hundred denarii was one who ought to make satisfaction to his brother for certain offenses. To choke one’s fellow-servant is to burn against one’s brother in vindictiveness.

[Col. 0313D] “And his fellow-servant fell down and begged him, saying: ‘Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.’”

“I shall amend what I have done wrong, namely, by the counsel or judgment of the Church.”

“But he refused, and went and threw him into prison until he should repay the debt.”

He refused to consider himself, so as to act mercifully in a spirit of gentleness; rather, he departed from the good grace that he had received, casting his fellow-servant into the prison of dire tribulation—perhaps in order that he might thereby repay the debt of sin, leaving nothing to be avenged more severely in the future. Thus it happens, according to the Apostle, that the one is swallowed up by sorrow, while the other perishes because he hates his brother and exceeds the bounds of strict justice (2 Cor. [Col. 0314A] XXI). Of this excess it is written: “And the righteous man who perishes in his righteousness” (Ezek. 33).

“Now when his fellow-servants saw what had happened, they were greatly grieved; and they came and reported to their lord all that had happened.”

Those who are spiritual, who judge all things, seeing such deeds are grieved and report them to the Lord, imploring help for correction.

“Then his lord summoned him and said to him: ‘Wicked servant, I forgave you the whole debt because you begged me. Ought you not, therefore, to have had mercy on your fellow-servant, just as I had mercy on you?’ And his lord, angered, handed him over to the torturers until he should repay the whole debt.”

This summons takes place inwardly in the conscience, namely, when someone falls into despair. But God, with whom there is no change or shadow of variation (Jas. 1), is said at one time to have mercy because he bestows works of mercy, and at another to be angry because, in just judgment, he hands a person over to infernal ministers to be punished forever.

“So also my heavenly Father will do to you, unless each of you forgives his brother from your hearts.”

It is certain that, if we do not forgive from the heart what is committed against us, that which we rejoiced to have already been forgiven through repentance is required from us anew. For the double-minded and unstable in all their ways will deservedly pay the whole debt; these are the persons especially struck by the parable and its conclusion. For, while falsely converted within [Col. 0314C] the Church, they neither love their neighbor with sincere affection nor do anything purely for the sake of God alone. Therefore, although God had forgiven those who asked him—insofar as he granted them communion in the sacraments—they rejoice in vain that it has been forgiven them, since their pretense prevented them from receiving true forgiveness. It will therefore be demanded again, even though it is reckoned to have been forgiven through repentance. For prayers, fasts, almsgiving, and the like, though they are remedies for sins for those who seek the highest good directly, are turned in hypocrites, through the wandering fluctuation of their minds, into the security of false hope and an incentive to sin. Hence: “Let his prayer be made sin” (Ps. 108).

Moreover, after receiving full forgiveness of sins and the adhesion of inward grace, many fall criminally, as Peter and David did, who rose more strongly. For “though the righteous man fall, he shall not be cast down,” because the Lord, who snatches the righteous person away lest evil change his understanding, places his hand beneath the one who falls (Ps. 36), so that one who falls through weakness of the flesh may rise through repentance. Who, then, would dare to say of those thus received into grace that God permits anyone to fall as far as condemnation?

Yet if any happen to be condemned, some say, according to the parable, that sins previously forgiven and even temporarily punished by the judgment of the Church return in order to be punished eternally. For just as righteousness blots out previous sins, so subsequent unrighteousness destroys righteousness; once righteousness has been condemned, no remedy against earlier sins remains. For the Lord says through the prophet: “On whatever day the righteous man sins, all his righteous deeds shall be forgotten” (Ezek. 33). Therefore, where perseverance in charity is lacking, no repentance is sufficient. Hence it is said to the person released from sins: “Go, and sin no more” (John 8).

Civil laws also, on account of certain acts of ingratitude, restore freed persons to their former slavery. But the prophet’s saying is objected: “A second affliction shall not arise” (Nah. 1), or according to another translation, “God shall not judge twice in the same matter.” But, they say, this is not a double affliction but one affliction and one punishment, when one who has not been punished sufficiently here is punished afterward. They also do not unreasonably think that former sinful inclinations return, according to the parable in which the unclean spirit, taking seven other spirits more wicked than itself, says: “I shall return to my house, from which I went out” (Luke 11). Indeed, a sinner appearing in the act of one crime should be understood to possess many such tendencies in affection, just as a righteous person possesses many more virtues in affection than in act.

Others, however, consider that a person is no longer to be punished for those sins for which he has made satisfaction to God through repentance; and that, if after them he commits sins similar or more serious, he indeed becomes a sinner as he was before, and through ingratitude for mercy bestowed becomes more guilty. They therefore say that the whole debt to be repaid is not that which had already been forgiven, but rather the mercy which he ought to have shown to others because he himself had received mercy. Hence also elsewhere: “With what measure you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Matt. 7). The parable, then, has this meaning, as though it said: [Col. 0315C] “If you are unwilling to have mercy on others, as God had mercy on you in forgiving your sins, the heavenly Father will exact this debt from you.” They therefore judge that it was said as a warning that what had been forgiven through repentance would be demanded again—a point commonly affirmed by commentators.

Now let us consider forgiveness of sins more carefully. In the reconciliation of a sinner to God three things must be considered: contrition of heart, confession by the mouth, and satisfaction by works. Scripture commands us to rend our hearts, not our garments (Joel 2); to confess sins to one another (Jas. 5); and to bear fruits worthy of repentance (Matt. 3). It should be noted that many groan over their sins, not because sin displeases them on account of God, but on account of punishment. Such sorrow or groaning is not contrition of heart unto salvation, but dismay of mind unto condemnation. For in this way the wicked will grieve in the future. Some also regret having sinned solely because of the shamefulness of sin, in accordance with the philosopher [SENECA.]: “If I knew that the gods would forgive and that men would remain ignorant, I would not sin.” But fruitful contrition of heart exists when someone grieves and is troubled over the sin by which he has offended God, because iniquity displeases him through love of righteousness. Hence: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. 18). For with God nothing happens slowly and nothing is absent: as soon as anyone truly repents, so soon does he who is present forgive. Hence David also says: “I said, ‘I shall confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the impiety of my sin” [Col. 0316A] (Ps. 31). That is, I deliberated in my heart and firmly resolved to abhor, for God’s sake, what I had committed by despising God, accusing myself. Hence: “The righteous man is the first accuser of himself in his speech” (Prov. 18).

For God to forgive sin is to remit the eternal punishment due for it by the bestowal of present grace. This indeed happens in little children when they receive the washing of baptism; it also happens in adults when the blindness of the mind is dissolved by compunction. Therefore teachers of sacred doctrine have written that original sin passes away in baptism as guilt, but remains in operation, because the dissolution of the body and the numerous multitude of temporal defects remain. This is of great value because “all virtue is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. [Col. 0316B] 12), and also lest anyone seek baptismal grace for the sake of happiness in the present life and so neither possess even that worthily nor attain eternal life.

Likewise, once the eternal punishment of actual sin has been remitted through the quickening of the mind, temporal punishment remains, so that what was committed through unlawful delight of the soul or even fleshly pleasure may be worthily cleansed by a human being through the bitterness of satisfaction while it is still possible, lest he be punished more strictly by God in the future. For no evil passes unpunished. Confession, therefore, was suitably established so that one who, being in his own power, had departed from God might return, being subject to another, with humility and devotion. Thus God established the priest as his representative and, as it were, a physician, to whom the wounds of sins should be uncovered for healing, so that the sinner might receive the medicine of satisfaction not from himself but from another, for the sake of greater humility. For the sacraments are like certain plasters.

Thus a heart previously contrite and humbled is strengthened in confession; and often a sinner brought before a priest merely through fear or through the custom of the Church is truly pierced through by the priestly office and departs full of charity. Some do not return from the heart even then, yet the form of repentance which they undertake gradually nourishes humility together with charity in them. Likewise, baptism benefits many when they come to their senses, even though they approached it hypocritically. The canons assign the duration of penitence to the discretion of an understanding priest because, before God, the measure of time does not matter as much as the measure of grief, nor abstinence from food alone as much as the mortification of vices. [Col. 0316D] Therefore they command that periods of penitence be shortened in proportion to the faith and conduct of penitents, and judge that they should be prolonged through negligence. Nevertheless, fixed modes of penitence have been imposed for certain faults; other faults are to be weighed by these, since through the same measures it is easy to estimate the punishment and canonical censure.

It should nevertheless be known that the longer anyone remains in sins, the longer penitence he must perform. Therefore, since the temporal punishment of sin is prolonged or shortened at the discretion of priests, many understand the following to refer to it: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 2). For the punishment of sin is called “sin,” by the transfer of the name of the cause to its effect. From what has been said it is therefore clear that God forgives some persons, through the ministry of priests, both sin and the punishment of sin; others, only temporal punishment, because he had already loosed the darkness of sin and the bond of Gehenna. This he showed through Lazarus. For he came and called him; having called him, he gave him life; and to him once alive he said, “Come forth”; and concerning him he said to the disciples, “Loose him and let him go” (John 11).

Likewise, he comes to the sinner and calls him by inward inspiration; and, when the death of sin departs, the sinner is made alive. And to the one made alive he says to come forth—that is, to show himself to priests through confession; and concerning him he says also to the priests, “Loose him,” that is, restore him to the Church, “and let him go,” that is, let him live and remain among the other [Col. 0317B] faithful. Therefore God forgives sins of himself and through himself whenever he wills. Hence he says through the prophet: “I, the Lord, alone blot out the iniquities and sins of the people” (Isa. 43). Hence Ambrose: “He alone forgives sins who alone died for sins.”

Yet priests are sometimes said to forgive sins, not from themselves but by the grace working in them and through them, according to the decision not of themselves but of God. So also: “You alone do wonderful things” (Ps. 71), although many people have worked miracles, but not of themselves as God does. Likewise: “No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10), because he is good of himself; and many people are good, but not in the way God is. Therefore no one but God can save another, which he would do if he forgave sins of himself. That no one except ourselves can condemn us is also shown there: “My soul is always in my hands” (Ps. 118).

It should be noted that if one who wishes to confess cannot do so when a pressing emergency arises, the invisible priest does not disdain to supply what the visible priest would administer if present. Of him it is said in Ecclesiasticus: “Behold the great priest” (Ecclus. 50). And the Apostle says: “Many have become priests because death prevented them from continuing. But this one remains forever, having an everlasting priesthood” (Heb. 7). But if someone does not confess out of contempt or negligence, it is certain that he lacks true contrition of heart, and he is shown to deserve eternal punishment both for the sin he refuses to confess and because [Col. 0317D] he disregards the Church’s ordinance.

Leo, Ambrose in *On the Sacraments*, and Maximus say: “I read of Peter’s tears; I do not find his confession.” Therefore Peter’s tears blot out the sins which it is shameful to confess. But it should be known that the institution of confession had not yet been promulgated in the primitive Church; or Peter may have confessed although Scripture does not relate it, just as we are compelled to believe that the Apostles were baptized, though we do not read when or how this occurred. Some nevertheless think that, by dispensation, Peter kept silent about the confession of his denial because, if others still weak had known that this singular architect of the Church had fallen so grievously, they would have been greatly scandalized against him.

Thus, by a salutary dispensation, someone might keep silent about a matter for which he would not thereby be eternally punished, when his conscience testified that, if he told anyone, it could not remain concealed and, if known, would scandalize the Church. But if he did so for his own sake, lest he become infamous or contemptible in the sight of others, this would be most blameworthy pride. From what has been said it is clear that repentance is the medicine of a wound, the hope of salvation; and its name itself is derived from punishment, by which the soul is afflicted and the flesh mortified, and it is called *poenitentia* as though *punientia*, “punishing.”

Those who perform repentance let their hair and beard grow, to display the abundance of crimes by which the sinner is burdened. Haircloth indicates remembrance of sins because of the goats destined to stand on the left (Matt. [Col. 0318B] 25). The sprinkling of sinners with ashes shows that they are ashes and shall return to dust (Gen. 3). The tears of penitents are reckoned before God in place of baptism. The groaning of repentance is twofold: either when we lament what we have done badly, or when we lament because we did not do what we ought to have done. But that person performs repentance who neither neglects to repent of past acts nor commits acts requiring repentance.

Whoever continually sheds tears yet does not cease to sin has lamentation but not cleansing. For when he despises the forgiveness which he could obtain by weeping, he deprives his tears of cleansing and makes even those tears themselves foul in God’s sight. Those who cut off certain vices from the desire of their mind while persevering grievously in others indeed love fewer evils than before; but unless they love evil less, they do not become less evil. For attachment to evil in one sin is sometimes so great that it alienates from God more than even many sins do. It is certain, however, that while anyone lies in the death of one sin, he cannot, in respect of another, be watered and made alive so that it may be utterly erased; but he is sometimes rained upon for the reduction of punishment, according to the prophet’s saying: “The Lord rained upon one city and did not rain upon another” (Amos 4).

Those whose sins are public ought to perform public penitence for the periods determined by the bishop. Their reconciliation, too, ought to be public, performed by the bishop or by priests at the bishops’ command, as the canons of the African council testify. Augustine, in his letter to Macedonius, says that the statement, “There is no place for a second repentance,” should be understood of this solemn penitence. Although it has therefore been prudently and beneficially provided that the place of this most humble penitence be granted once in the Church, lest a remedy be too cheap or less useful to the sick—a remedy all the more healthful the less contemptible it is—who would dare say to God: “Why do you spare once again this person who, after the first repentance, again binds himself with the snares of iniquity?” Who would dare say that in their case the Apostle’s words are not at work: “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance?” (Rom. 2); or that the following does not apply to them: “Blessed are all who trust in him” [Col. 0319A] (Ps. 2), and: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord” (Ps. 30)?

But a person whose sins are hidden and disclosed by voluntary confession only to a priest or bishop ought to perform hidden penitence, lest the weak in the Church be scandalized by seeing the penalties of persons whose reasons they utterly do not know. And it must be known that Satan likewise deceives by excessive harshness, so that sinners perish through despair, just as he does by excessive leniency in correction. Hence Solomon: “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left” (Prov. 4).

M. 69[VI] R. 103

“And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these sayings, that he departed from Galilee and came to the borders of Judea beyond [Col. 0319B] the Jordan. And great crowds followed him, and he healed them there.”

[REMIGIUS.] He wished to heal Galileans in Judea so that he might admit the Gentiles to the forgiveness prepared for Judea. Indeed, the whole territory of the Jews, in distinction from other nations, is called Judea; but more particularly the southern region, as distinct from Samaria, Galilee, Decapolis, and the other regions of the same province.

“And the Pharisees came to him, testing him and saying: ‘Is it lawful for a man to dismiss his wife for any cause whatever?’”

[JEROME.] The faction of the Pharisees wished to catch God as though by a horned syllogism, so that they might show either that he taught things contrary to chastity or that he spoke contrary to Moses. But the Lord passed through their snare by tempering his answer.

“He answered them: ‘Have you not read that he who made human beings from the beginning made them male and female? And he said: “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.”’”

God said this through Adam, for whom he formed not women but a woman from his side. For this reason—namely, because the wife is from the man—a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife. He did not say “wives,” in order to show that one woman is not to be taken in addition to another—that is, that the first should not be abandoned and another taken. [CHRYSOSTOM.] As plants are born and grow from moisture, so human beings begin and increase through love. Moisture ascends from the roots into the plant and passes into the seed, but does not return to the root; so affection rises from parents to children but does not return. Parents therefore love their children more than they are loved by them, because children transfer their affection to begetting others.

“Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh.”

Just as the souls of many who love one another spiritually are said to be as one, as in: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4), so husband and wife, because they love one another carnally, are called one flesh. Or they are one flesh because they are bound by one law to render the debt of the flesh: for just as a woman has no authority over her own body, but the husband does, so a husband has no authority over his own body, but the woman does.

“What therefore God has joined together, let no human being separate.”

[JEROME.] A human being separates when, out of desire for a second wife, he dismisses the first. God separates when, by mutual consent for the service of God, we have wives as though not having them.

They said to him: “Why then did Moses command that a certificate of divorce be given and that she be dismissed?”

They reveal the calumny they had prepared, as though saying: “Since God established things thus, why did Moses enact an additional ordinance?”

He said to them: “Because of the hardness of your hearts, Moses permitted you to dismiss your wives. But from the beginning it was not so.”

He did not say, “Because of the hardness of your hearts God permitted you,” but “Moses.” For when Moses saw that they were killing their first wives because of desire for more beautiful women, he gave them counsel. [CHRYSOSTOM.] Divorce is an evil; nevertheless, it is lawful with reason. A husband should correct and retain a wife of bad conduct. How? In three ways. First, by teaching according to God; if she does not feel the fear of God, by reproaching her, so that she may at least be ashamed before people; if, frequently shamed, she does not even feel shame, let him do to her what Solomon commanded: “Strike the stubborn one with a rod.” “Have you not read,” both here and above, therefore ought not to be read as a statement but as a question: *nonne*, “have you not?”

M. 190 R. 105 L. 91

[Col. 0320C] “But I say to you that whoever dismisses his wife, except for fornication, and takes another commits adultery; and whoever takes a dismissed woman commits adultery.”

From this passage some think that a man who dismisses an adulterous wife may lawfully take another while she is alive. But anyone who dismisses his wife not because of fornication but for another reason does what is unlawful; and if he takes another while the first lives, he is certainly an adulterer. Whoever takes a woman dismissed for any cause incurs the guilt of adultery. For if a husband repudiates her, though not for fornication, the marriage remains on both sides, but she suffers violence through repudiation. If, however, the wife was repudiated because she divided one flesh into another and separated herself from her husband through fornication, then, by her own fault, she releases the man from the marriage bond, as they maintain, though she herself remains bound.

Hence Ambrose, on the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “This is what the Apostle intends: if a woman departs because of her husband’s bad conduct, she should either remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. A woman is not permitted to marry if she has dismissed her husband because of fornication or apostasy, or because, driven by lust, he seeks to invert the use of a wife, because the inferior party does not at all employ the same law as the superior. Yet if the husband apostatizes or seeks to invert the use of a wife, the woman can neither marry another nor return to him [Note: [Col. 0319D] This passage should be read cautiously.].” And “let not the husband dismiss his wife” is to be understood with the exception of fornication. Thus he did not add, as he did concerning the woman, “But if she departs, let her remain [unmarried]” (1 Cor. 7), because it is lawful for a husband to take a wife if he has dismissed a sinful wife: a man is not bound by the law in the same way as a woman, for the husband is the head of the woman.

The same author, on the same epistle: “It is certainly lawful to have a wife; but if she has committed fornication, she must be put away.” So too it is lawful to eat flesh; but if it has been offered to idols, it must be rejected. Many authorities indeed seem capable of being opposed to this view; but they say that it is not an assertion but a salutary admonition, so that one who dismisses his wife not from lust but because of injury, having experienced the unhappiness of an earlier marriage, should not expose himself to the danger of a new one. It should be noted that the Lord here speaks only of marriage [Note: [Col. 0321D] As it was established by God’s decree.] contracted between believers; and, because divine law does not remove secular status, a marriage of slaves without their masters’ permission is not valid. Nor is marriage between free persons and slaves secure unless the free person knows the servile condition and wishes to cohabit.

M. 191[X]

His disciples said to him: “If this is the case of a man with a woman, it is not expedient to marry.” He said: “Not all receive this word, but those to whom it has been given.”

[JEROME.] That is, virgins do not become such by chance or fortune, but those who ask God for virginity and labor to receive it. In other things we may ascertain what they are like before we possess them; this is less permitted with a wife. Thus it is not expedient to marry, since a wife may in no way be dismissed except for fornication. If she is irascible, drunken, quarrelsome, abusive, or anything of that kind, whether we wish it or not, she must be endured. For when we were free, we voluntarily subjected ourselves to slavery.

“For there are eunuchs who were thus born from their mother’s womb; there are eunuchs who were made such by human beings; and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let him who can receive this, receive it.”

There are three kinds of eunuchs: two bodily kinds and a third spiritual kind. No reward at all is due to the first two; it is promised to the third, because, though able to be men, they voluntarily become eunuchs. The first kind comprises eunuchs said to be of a nature so cold that they do not desire lust. The second comprises those who have either been cut or, through heretical persuasion, feign chastity under counterfeit religion. But reward is promised to none of these three unless he makes himself a eunuch for God’s sake. Therefore, encouraging his soldiers, he adds: “Let him who can receive this, receive it,” so that each person may consider whether he can fulfill the precepts of virginity.

## CHAPTER CI

M. 192[II] R. 106 L. 216

“Then little children were brought to him, that he might lay his hands upon them and pray.”

[CHRYSOSTOM.] They brought children untainted by chastity, for they thought that he would praise them only because they were pure in body and not by their will, not knowing that the Lord did not pronounce blessed eunuchs chaste through the necessity of childhood, but those chaste through the virtue of continence.

“But the disciples rebuked them.”

[JEROME.] They rebuked them not because they did not wish them to be blessed, but because, not yet having the fullest faith, they thought that God was wearied by importunity.

But Jesus said to them: “Let the little children be, and do not prevent them from coming to me.”

[CHRYSOSTOM.] If they are going to be holy, why do you prevent children from coming to the Father? If they are going to be sinners, why do you pronounce a sentence of condemnation before you see their guilt? What they are now belongs to me; what they will be belongs to themselves. Therefore honor what is mine; pity what will be theirs.

“For of such is the kingdom of heaven.”

[Col. 0322B] [JEROME.] He did not say “of these,” but “of such,” in order to show that it is not age which reigns, but character; and he promises the reward to those who possess similar innocence and simplicity, concerning whom Paul says: “Do not become children in understanding; but be little children in malice, while in understanding be perfect” (1 Cor. 14).

“And when he had laid his hands upon them, he went away from there.”

[REMIGIUS.] He laid his hands upon the little children to signify that the humble are worthy of his blessing. And he lays them on daily when he grants the grace of help to the humble. [HILARY.] Mystically, these children represent the Gentiles, to whom salvation is restored through faith and hearing. But the disciples, who had pleaded for the Canaanite woman, perhaps already knew the mystery that both peoples were destined to be called; yet, because they did not yet know the order, they prevented the children from approaching out of their desire that Israel should first be saved. “Of such is the kingdom of heaven.” For the gift and bestowal of the Holy Spirit through laying on of hands and prayer, after the work of the Law had ceased, was to be granted to the Gentiles. Here Mark and Luke add that we should receive the kingdom of God—that is, the teaching of the Gospel—as a child does, because a child, in learning, neither contradicts teachers nor frames arguments against them, but receives faithfully, obeys, and rests.

M. 186[II] L. 72 A. 22

“Now many tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to him to hear him. And the scribes and Pharisees were murmuring, saying: ‘This man receives sinners [Col. 0322D] and eats with them.’”

A. 75[X]

“After these things Jesus was walking in Galilee, for he did not wish to walk in Judea because the Jews were seeking to kill him.”

He had not lost his power, but was comforting our weakness. For it would happen that some believer would hide himself; he therefore went before in the head, lest the member afterward be reproached as guilty.

## CHAPTER CII

L. 163[X]

[AUGUSTINE.] Now some people were present at that very time, reporting to him [Col. 0323A] about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices.

[BEDA.] Those Galileans who were killed by the impious governor amid their own sacrifices paid the penalty for their crimes by a criminal death. Yet it was not death itself that harmed them, so as to send them into the second death, but their wicked life. For the glory of martyrs shows that good persons too often die in this way, either for the correction of the living, so that “when a pestilent person is scourged, a fool may become wiser” (Prov. XIX); or as an example to those unwilling to be corrected and therefore destined to perish most miserably: thus many die and are punished by a most grievous death. Hence it follows:

And answering, he said to them: “Do you suppose that these Galileans were sinners above all the Galileans, because they suffered such things? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you shall all perish in like manner: as those eighteen upon whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them.”

The sense is: I tell you, the Galileans alone were not sinners; nor, likewise, did only those Jerusalemites upon whom the tower fell sin; but all you Jews will perish as did those Galileans, unless you are willing to repent. He continues concerning the Jerusalemites:

“Do you suppose that they also were debtors beyond all the people dwelling in Jerusalem? No, I tell you; but unless you do penance, you shall all likewise perish.”

Those crushed by the tower’s fall signify the Jews who would refuse repentance and perish together with their walls. [Col. 0323C] Nor is it without significance that there were eighteen: among the Greeks this number is expressed by *iota* and *eta* (ι and η), with which the name of Jesus begins. For they indicate that those who despised the Savior’s name deserved condemnation. That tower signifies him who is the tower of strength; indeed the very name Siloam, interpreted “Sent,” designates the same one sent by the Father into the world (John IX), who will crush all upon whom he falls. Pilate, moreover, signified that after the Lord’s Passion the Romans, beginning from Galilee, would kill the unrepentant Jewish people and would destroy the courts of sacrifice and the Temple itself, defiling them with human blood.

Pilate also signifies the devil, the interpretation of whose name is “the mouth of the hammerer,” ever ready to kill souls. Blood represents sin, [Col. 0323D] and sacrifices good actions. Thus Pilate mingles the blood of the Galileans with their sacrifices when the devil defiles the alms, prayers, fasts, and other good works of the faithful—whether through the deadly delight of flesh and blood, the brooding of hatred, the frenzy of envy, ambition for human praise, or any other accursed plague—so that, though they appear to be offered to the Lord, they profit their offerers nothing, and indeed sometimes become sin. Of Judas, who amid sacrifices was plotting the betrayal of the Lord’s blood, it is written: “And let his prayer become sin” (Ps. CVIII).

L. 164[X]

And he spoke this parable: “A certain man had a fig tree [Col. 0324A] planted in his vineyard; and he came seeking fruit on it, and found none.”

[AUGUSTINE.] The fig tree is fittingly understood as the human race, because when the first man sinned he covered his shame with fig leaves (Gen. III), and from him we are born. [GREGORY, BEDE.] This tree is rightly called planted, because it was created in the likeness of its Maker; and though it refers generally to humankind, it bears in particular the type of the Synagogue. For just as a barren fig tree, luxuriant in leaves, deceives its owner with the hope of fruit, so the teachers of the Synagogue, unfruitful in works and glorying in the empty shade of the Law’s words, provide their subjects with no example of good work. Therefore the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, while the Synagogue, established within that same house, is the fig tree [Col. 0324B] in the vineyard. The Lord sought fruit on it, but found none in the minds of the Pharisees.

And he said to the dresser of the vineyard: “Behold, these three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none.”

The dresser of the vineyard is the order of apostles and teachers, through whose prayers and admonitions concern for God is urged upon the people. For the Lord often complained to them of the fruitless Jews: that throughout the three years of his visitation they had proved negligent amid the legal commands, prophetic testimonies, and the grace of the radiant Gospel. Or thus: for three periods no fruit could be found in the Synagogue, because those who did not seek circumcision of heart could not be purified in the time of circumcision; those who pursued only carnal things in the Law were not sanctified through the Law; [Col. 0324C] nor were those unwilling to repent of sins justified through grace. Therefore, since they deserved to be cut down—which indeed was done by the Romans—those who labored in circumcision are commanded, by announcing the disaster of cutting down, to urge repentance. This is what follows:

“Cut it down, therefore. Why does it also occupy the ground?”

That is, announce to the Jews that they will lose their place and nation—the very things they kill Christ and his people to preserve. Why do they also enjoy temporal abundance? One occupies the ground who does not exercise with good works the place he holds, and who by the example of his depravity creates an obstacle for others. The Jewish people may also be figured by ground occupied by barren fruit: [Col. 0324D] oppressed by the harmful shade of its rulers, so that it might not receive the light of truth or be warmed by the sun of heavenly love, according to that saying: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven before men” (Matt. XXIII).

But he answered and said to him: “Lord, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put in manure.”

That is, I shall call to its mind the abomination it has committed, so that it may be aroused to compunction, as it were, by the rottenness of manure. Sins of the flesh are called manure. Hence the prophet says: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel I). That is, carnal people ended their lives in the stench of their lust. He knows how to cultivate the ground [Col. 0325A] who knows how to rebuke vices. Understanding, therefore, that the hardness and pride of the Jews were the cause of their barrenness, the dresser promises to dig until he humbles the root of the unfruitful mind with the hoe of two-edged rebuke, namely by striking it with both the pressure of present affliction and the terror of eternal damnation. For a trench lies low, and rebuke humbles the mind when it shows the mind to itself.

“And if indeed it bears fruit; but if not, in the future you shall cut it down.”

Whoever here refuses to become fruitful through interpretation will fall there, where through repentance he will not rise again. When he said, “And if indeed it bears fruit,” he added nothing, but left the sentence suspended, because he saw that the Synagogue was readier to deny God [Col. 0325B] than to confess him. But when he added, “but if not,” he immediately joined the judgment of coming condemnation: “In the future you shall cut it down.” After “and if indeed it bears fruit,” understand: “though this can scarcely be believed, preserve it.”

## CHAPTER CIII

And he was teaching in their synagogue on the Sabbaths. And behold, there was a woman who had had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years; and she was bent over and could not at all look upward.

After the parable concerning the fig tree had been spoken, the Lord is said to have taught in the Synagogue, to make known that seeking fruit in the fig tree and finding none means that the word was preached to the Synagogue but not received. Yet, lest you should suppose [Col. 0325C] that it was wholly to be uprooted because of barrenness, rather than know that a remnant was to be saved through grace, its healing in part immediately follows there under the figure of the bent woman. For the preserved fig tree signifies the same as the woman made upright; and the Lord’s coming a third time to the barren fig tree signifies the same as the woman’s having been bent over for eighteen years. For the number six, in which the creation of the world came to rest as complete, signifies the perfection of works; multiplied into a triangle, it makes eighteen. Therefore, because man, made on the sixth day, willed to possess perfect works but languished through feeble works during the three periods of the Lord’s visitation—namely before the Law, under the Law, and at the beginning of dawning grace—the woman was bent over for eighteen years. Nor could she look upward, [Col. 0325D] because Judaea, thinking earthly thoughts, did not reflect upon heavenly things, hearing through the prophet: “If you are willing and hear me, you shall eat the good things of the earth” (Isa. I). In contrast the Apostle says to the members of the Church: “Set your minds on things above, not on things upon the earth” (Col. III).

When Jesus saw her, he called her to himself and said to her: “Woman, you are released from your infirmity.” And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made upright and glorified God.

He saw her by predestining grace; he called her by enlightening teaching; he laid hands upon her by helping her with spiritual gifts; he raised her up in good works for the glorification of God. “Those,” says the Apostle, “whom he predestined, them he also called; and those whom he called, them he also justified; and those whom he justified, them he also glorified” (Rom. VIII). This woman could not be raised up until after eighteen years, because human nature could not put off this corruption and be raised to the incorruption of eternal blessedness until it had first fulfilled the Law, which is contained in the ten commandments, and grace, in which Christ’s resurrection took place and ours is awaited.

L. 165[II] M. 116 R. 25

But the ruler of the synagogue answered indignantly, because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, and said to the crowd: “There are six days in which one ought to work; therefore come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.”

[JEROME, BEDE.] Jesus healed on the Sabbath, showing that the time had now come when, according to the prophecy of the Song of Songs, the day should breathe forth and the shadows be removed [Col. 0326B] (Song II). The ruler of the synagogue did not know that the six days signify the six ages in which it is lawful to work, whereas the Sabbath signifies eternal rest, in which the righteous will not cease from good work when they praise God. Certainly God rested from the works of the world on the Sabbath, but in works of sanctification—calling, justifying, and governing—he continually perseveres. Hence the Law prohibited not healing a person on the Sabbath, but performing servile works, that is, being burdened with sins.

But Jesus answered and said: “Hypocrites, does not each one of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or ass from the stall and lead it away to water it? And ought not this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound, behold, these eighteen years, to be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?”

In a deeper sense, the ox and the ass signify the Jew [Col. 0326C] and the Greek, concerning whose calling it is written: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger” (Isa. I). Each, released from the bonds of sin through preaching, laid aside the thirst of this world by drinking from the Lord’s fountain. The daughter of Abraham is the Church drawn from both peoples; when the time of the Law and of the Lord’s resurrection was fulfilled, she escaped the bonds of long captivity through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

L. 165[X]

And when he said these things, all his adversaries were ashamed, and all the people rejoiced in all the glorious things done by him.

Those ashamed at the Savior’s words show themselves comparable to the barren fig tree; those who rejoice in his miracles declare themselves to belong to the daughter of Abraham, that is, to the Church [Col. 0326D] of faith.

## CHAPTER CIV

A. 73[X]

Now the Jewish feast of *scenopegia* was near.

[AUGUSTINE.] A *scena* is a shelter; hence *scenopegia*, that is, the construction or setting up of tabernacles. *Scenopegia* was the feast at which, in the seventh month from March, the Jews dwelt seven days in tabernacles in remembrance of those in which their fathers had lived in the wilderness. According to their custom, moreover, the seven days are called a feast day on account of the single festival:

His brothers said to him: “Depart from here [Col. 0327A] and go into Judaea, so that your disciples also may see the works you do. For no one does anything in secret while he himself seeks to be publicly known. If you do these things, reveal yourself to the world.” For not even his brothers believed in him.

When you hear “the Lord’s brothers,” think of their kinship with Mary. True disciples knew that the Lord’s works were to be exalted by divine praises and not by popular favor; but these brothers of the Lord—that is, the Lord’s relatives—did not know this. Because they refused to believe, they gave him advice for attaining worldly glory. It was as though they said: You do wonderful things, but in secret. Go into Judaea, where the leadership of the people is and the capital city of the kingdom, so that you may be praised by all and we, your relatives, may become sharers in glory: “If you do these things, then reveal [Col. 0327B] yourself.” Or *if* is read in place of *because*.

That is: the worldly glory you seek is always ready. But when I receive the time of glory, which must be attained after humility has been fulfilled, “I shall judge justices” (Ps. LXXIV). For now is not the time for judging, but for bearing with the wicked.

“The world cannot hate you, but it hates me because I bear testimony concerning it that its works are evil.”

I do not indeed accuse the world before the Father, but I reprove it for sins; and so this is not now my time but yours, because you are lovers of the world and false witnesses, calling good evil and evil good.

“You go up to this feast day. I do not go up to this feast day, because my time [Col. 0327C] has not yet been fulfilled.”

“Go up to this feast day” is not a command but permission: go where you seek human glory, where you wish to extend carnal joys. But the time of my glory will abide forever, that festival itself without a cloud.

Having said these things, he remained in Galilee. But when his brothers had gone up, then he too went up to the feast, not openly but as though in secret.

He did not say, “to this feast day,” because he did not desire to glory temporally, but to teach something salutary. His going up secretly is not without meaning, nor is what was hidden in that feast day. All ancient things were shadows of things to come; therefore *scenopegia* too was such a shadow. For we were led out of Egypt, where we served the devil as Pharaoh. Christ cried to us as though we were making bricks: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. XI). We were led out through baptism, as through the Red Sea, consecrated by Christ’s blood, with our enemies—that is, our sins—dead. Therefore, before we come to the promised land, that is, the eternal kingdom, we are in the tabernacles of this wilderness. But since Christ’s body is ourselves, Christ is in tabernacles when we are in tabernacles. Yet then he was there secretly, now openly; for the shadow has been removed and the light has come, in which we now recognize all things.

The Jews therefore sought him and said: “Where is he?”

[Col. 0328A] His failure to go up with the brothers who were advising him about glory gave them occasion to seek him. Hence he said to them: “I shall not go up to this feast day which you desire,” that is, the first or second day.

And there was much murmuring about him among the crowd. Some said, “He is good.” Others said, “No; rather, he deceives the crowds.”

The same is said of all Christ’s servants, because our life is hidden with Christ in God (Col. III), though God will at last come openly.

Yet no one spoke openly about him for fear of the Jews.

Namely, none of those who said, “He is good.”

But when the feast was already halfway through, Jesus went up into the Temple and taught.

[Col. 0328B] When, that is, as many days of that feast as were to pass had already passed, he went up. His concealment is an example of avoiding evil people; his public speech, and his not being seized by those who sought him, are evidence of his power.

And the Jews marveled, saying: “How does this man know letters, when he has not learned?”

They marveled because many knew how he had been brought up and had never seen him learning letters.

Jesus answered them and said: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.”

He seems to speak contrariwise. If he had said, “This teaching is not mine,” there would be no question. But the solution lies in this: the Father’s teaching is the Father’s Word, that is, the Son from the Father. It is as though he said: I am not from myself but from the Father. For what is so much yours as yourself? And what is so little yours as yourself, if what you are belongs to another? Hence elsewhere the Lord says: “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he has sent” (John VI). Whoever believes in him believes him, but the converse does not hold, because demons believe him, not in him. We also believe Peter and Paul, but we do not believe in Peter and Paul. What, then, is it to believe in God? To go into him by believing and to be incorporated into his members. This statement—that the Son is the Father’s teaching—refutes the Sabellian heresy, which dared to say that Father and Son are two names but one reality. For the Son’s teaching belongs to another if it is not his own.

“If anyone wishes to do his will, he shall know concerning the teaching whether it is from God, or whether I speak from myself.”

The sense is: if anyone believes me to be the Son of God, he will understand that my teaching is his.

“He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory.”

He speaks of Antichrist, who, not sent by God but permitted to come, will exalt himself, as the Apostle says, above everything called God or worshiped (II Thess. II).

“But he who seeks the glory of him who sent him, he is true, and there is no unrighteousness in him.”

[Col. 0329A] In saying this of himself, he gives an example of humility, that we may attribute every good thing to God.

“Did not Moses give you the Law? Yet none of you keeps the Law. Why do you seek to kill me?”

You glory in the Law, indeed; yet against the Law—which forbids killing and which proclaims me—you deliberate concerning my death.

The crowd answered and said: “You have a demon. Who seeks to kill you?”

What else could the turbulent crowd say? What else could stirred-up mud smell of? The brightness of light disturbed the crowd of bleary-eyed people. For eyes lacking health cannot bear the brightness of light.

Jesus answered and said to them: “I have done one work, and [Col. 0329B] you all marvel. Therefore Moses gave you circumcision—not because it is from Moses, but from the fathers—and on the Sabbath you circumcise a man.”

The one work was that I made a man whole on the Sabbath. Therefore, namely on account of such a work—that a person’s salvation may result—it was rightly done that you received circumcision from Moses. Moses convicts you: by the Law you received the command to circumcise on the eighth day, and you also received the command to rest on the seventh day. What then will you do if the eighth day after birth falls upon the Sabbath? I know that you circumcise. For circumcision pertains to a certain sign of salvation. And people ought not to rest from salvation on the Sabbath. Therefore do not be angry with me because I made the whole [Col. 0329C] person well on the Sabbath. This is what he says:

“If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath so that the Law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because I made the whole man well on the Sabbath? Do not judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment.”

One must not judge according to appearance, that is, by respect of persons, but with righteous judgment, that is, according to the truth of things. Once this is known, you will condemn neither me nor Moses, nor call me opposed to him. In reproving them in this matter, he instructs us not to show partiality in judging cases—not that we should not honor persons differently according to differences of rank. [AMBROSE.] It should be noted that Abraham, believing that he would have a son, received circumcision as the sign of this, so that it might be seen that he was justified by believing. The children of Israel received this sign so that they might be known as the children of the one who, by believing God, had received it. [JEROME.] Circumcision was also commanded so that God’s people might be recognized among the nations, or so that their bodies might be recognized in war. [AUGUSTINE.] Finally, when they were alone in the wilderness, they were not circumcised. Moreover, circumcision performed upon the male member, through which mortal creatures are generated, indicates that chastity of mind ought to be observed. Each person is born with a foreskin because each is born with the defect of propagation.

Therefore some of the people of Jerusalem said: “Is this not the one whom they seek to kill? And behold, he speaks openly, and they say nothing to him. Have the rulers truly recognized that he is the Christ?”

[Col. 0330A] Those who knew with what savagery he was sought wondered by what power he was not seized.

“But we know where this man is from; whereas, when Christ comes, no one knows where he is from.”

This opinion, “no one knows where he is from,” did not arise without cause. For the Scriptures said that he would be called a Nazarene; thus they foretold where he would be from. Again, when Herod summoned the scribes and asked where Christ would be born, they said: “In Bethlehem of Judaea” (Matt. II). But Isaiah also said: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. LIX). This concerns his divinity. Thus in this respect they did not know where Christ was from, though they recognized him according to the flesh.

[Col. 0330B] A. 76[III] M. 112 L. 119

Therefore Jesus cried out as he taught in the Temple, saying: “You both know me and know where I am from; and I have not come from myself, but he who sent me is true, whom you do not know. I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me. And if I were to say that I do not know him, I would be a liar like you.”

“You know me” was said concerning the appearance of his humanity, which was familiar to them. “You know where I am from,” namely, from Nazareth. “I have not come from myself” is as if he said: According to divinity you do not know me, for no one has ever seen God. Yet I know him because I am truth from him who is true of himself. Therefore seek him from me; believe in me, because the Son reveals the Father to whom he wills.

A. 77[I] M. 220 R. 122 L. 261

[Col. 0330C] Therefore they sought to seize him, but no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come.

He did not mean the hour at which he would be compelled to die, but that at which he would deign to be killed.

R. 78[X]

But many of the crowd believed in him and said: “When Christ comes, will he perform more signs than this man does?”

Certainly, if there will not be two Christs, this is the Christ. This crowd was stirred by his miracles and, believing in him, said this.

## CHAPTER CV

L. 149[X]

[Col. 0330D] Someone from the crowd said to him: “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” But he said to him: “Man, who appointed me judge or divider over you?”

This brother is rightly rebuked for wishing to impose upon the teacher of heavenly peace the trouble of an earthly division. He is rightly called “man,” that is, carnal, as Paul says: “For while there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal? Are you not men, and do you not walk according to man?” (I Cor. III). He rightly declines earthly matters who had descended for divine ones; nor does he deign to be judge of disputes or arbiter of property, who possesses judgment over living and dead and discernment of merits.

And he said to them: “See and beware of all covetousness, [Col. 0331A] for a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of what he possesses.”

A human being lives not by bread alone, but by the word of God; nor is the span of life extended by an abundance of riches. “See,” he says, with the eye of reason; and he does not say, “Beware of covetousness,” but adds *all*, because some actions seem simply permissible to people, while the inward Judge sees with what intention they are done. Who would count it a crime for an inheritance to be divided with one’s brother, or the fruits of a field to be stored in barns? But God himself is witness that this man did it [here] without a good intention. Hence he sets before him the example of his folly.

And he told them a parable, saying: “The field of a certain rich man yielded abundant crops, and he considered within himself, saying: ‘What shall I do, because I do not [Col. 0331B] have where to gather my crops?’”

Behold, excessive anxiety, striving from covetousness to reserve his goods for future luxury; and deliberation follows from anxiety.

And he said: “This I shall do: I shall destroy my barns and build larger ones, and there I shall gather all the things produced for me and my goods; and I shall say to my soul: ‘Soul, you have many goods stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast.’”

“I shall gather,” he says, “what has been produced for me more than usual”—that is, by my labor, or for myself alone. In saying, “Rest,” he joins the plague of idleness to the plague of covetousness, so that he may not even call upon God for temporal things. “Eat and drink,” against hunger and thirst; “feast,” luxuriously, with a great provision of delights.

[Col. 0331C] But God said to him: “Fool, this night they shall demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared—whose shall they be?”

What a person cannot take away with oneself are not one’s goods; mercy alone accompanies the dead. Yet this rich man is not rebuked because he cultivated the soil and wished to preserve its fruits, but because he placed all his life’s confidence in his abundance and determined to distribute nothing to the poor, in accordance with the Lord’s command: “Give alms from what remains” (Luke XI). His soul is taken in the night because he neglects to possess the light of reflection, so as to foresee what he may suffer. Hence Paul says: “But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that that day should overtake you as a thief. For you are all children of light [Col. 0331D] and children of the day” (I Thess. V). Likewise, after first saying of any covetous person, “and he is troubled in vain,” the Psalmist adds: “He heaps up treasure and does not know for whom he shall gather it” (Ps. XXXVIII). God’s speaking to the perverse is his checking their evil schemes by sudden punishment.

“So is he who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.”

Such is the fool, who is to be snatched away in the night by divine judgments: one whose hope is not the Lord, and who does not distribute transient goods to the poor so as to be received by them into eternal dwellings. But that person is rich toward God whose substance—that is, the possession of conscience by which one is sustained and nourished—is with God, not amid the ages of earth.

## CHAPTER CVI

[Col. 0332A]

R. 107[II] M. 193 L. 219

And when he had gone out onto the way, a certain man ran up, knelt before him, and asked him: “Good Teacher, what good thing shall I do to have eternal life?” He said to him: “Why do you ask me about the good? No one is good except the one God.”

[AUGUSTINE.] Both forms could be said: according to Matthew, “Why do you ask me about the good?” and according to the others, “Why do you call me good?” The former refers to the questioner’s words, “What good thing shall I do?”; the latter to his words, “Good Teacher.” [BEDE.] Since, therefore, he had called him a good teacher, and not God or the Son of God, he says that any holy person, by comparison with God, [Col. 0332B] is not good. Of God it is said in the psalm: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good” (Ps. CXVII). God alone is good by nature; others who are good do not possess goodness from themselves but from God. Thus Christ does not deny that he is good, but indicates that he is God; nor does he deny that he is a good teacher, but declares that apart from God no one is good.

“But if you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.” He said to him: “Which?” And Jesus said: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness. Honor your father and mother; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

Note that the righteousness of the Law, observed in its own time, conferred not only earthly goods but eternal life. It should also be noted that Paul commands husbands that each should [Col. 0332C] love his wife as himself. If, then, everyone must love a neighbor and a wife as oneself, there will be no difference between love of neighbor and love of wife—which is utterly absurd. But in “your neighbor as yourself,” *as* is an adverb of comparison. In reference to a wife, however, *as* conveys not similarity but approval and affirmation with a certain emphasis, as when we say, “he acted like a man.” And concerning the Savior: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” (John I)—not as though the Savior possessed glory by comparison with another only-begotten.

The young man said to him: “I have kept all these things from my youth. What do I still lack?”

R. 180[II] M. 194 L. 291

[Col. 0332D] But Jesus, looking upon him, loved him, and said to him: “One thing you lack. If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.”

This man should not be thought to have lied concerning his observance of the commandments, but to have made a straightforward confession; for if he were guilty of the fault of lying, Jesus, looking into the secrets of his heart, would by no means be said to love him. For he loves those who keep the commandments of the Law, but adds what is lacking there for those who wish to be perfect. Whoever, therefore, wishes to be perfect must sell what he has—not in part, like Ananias and Sapphira—and give it to the poor (Acts V). Nor does this suffice for perfection unless he follows the Savior: that is, unless, leaving evil things behind, [Col. 0333A] he does good things.

[JEROME—CHRYSOSTOM.] Or thus: this young man was rich, proud, and a tempter; and through empty boasting, as one glorying in the Law, he falsely claimed to have kept the commandments. But Jesus, as though accepting his words as true, taught him the things that belong to perfection. Looking upon him with the eyes of mercy—those by which he deigns to justify the ungodly, by which he looked upon Peter so that he wept bitterly (Luke XXII)—he loved in him not what had formerly been there through pride, but what had begun to be there through grace. [CHRYSOSTOM.] Accordingly, whatever is said about that young man is to be understood also of the Jewish people, who were young not in age but in levity, immature in character rather than years. Consider that he asks not what he should believe, but by doing what he may possess eternal life; for the Jew places all his hope in works without faith. Hence the Apostle: “The Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness attained the righteousness of the Law, because not by works but by faith. But Israel, pursuing the righteousness of the Law, did not attain to the law of righteousness, because not by faith but by works” (Rom. IX). The first righteousness is to know the Trinity; the last is to act well. The infancy of the Jews extended from Abraham’s time to the departure from Egypt, and until then they were like an infant. Their youth extended from Moses’ time to the kings. Their manhood extended from the kings to the Babylonian captivity. Their old age extended from then to Christ, when that people died by killing its own life. Thus it lies in saying it kept the commandments from youth; it does not keep them even now in old age. Yet Jesus [Col. 0333C] looks upon and loves it, namely so that a remnant may be saved. [HILARY.] In being commanded, for perfection, to sell his goods and give them to the poor, he is admonished to leave behind confidence in the Law and sacrifices, which he used carnally. All things are commanded to be exchanged in a blessed transaction, and he is told to remember that they contain the shadow of truth, which henceforth must be distributed spiritually among the Gentiles, poor through the truth of his own body. But he indicates that no one can accomplish this unless he begins to follow Christ. Yet the Jewish people, having heard these things, withdrew sorrowful, for it had great confidence in the wealth supplied by the Law.

M. 19[II] R. 109 L. 220

[Col. 0333D] But when the young man heard the word, he went away sorrowful, for he was very rich and had many possessions.

Many indeed leave riches out of love for God, yet do so grieving and weeping. Although they love their neighbor, they rightly love themselves more; and therefore they desire riches for their own use rather than for others, though they distribute all their possessions to those others, at the urging of God, whom they prefer to themselves. So too martyrs, who surely love their own flesh, unwillingly [in life] give it over to martyrdom; nevertheless, for God’s sake they do not hesitate to surrender it.

And Jesus, looking around, said to his disciples: “How difficult it is for those who possess riches to enter the kingdom of God! Amen, I tell you, a rich man shall with difficulty enter the kingdom of heaven.”

[Col. 0334A] On the occasion of this man who possessed riches, he begins a discourse about the covetous under the name of the rich. Thus when he says “difficult,” he does not assert impossibility but indicates rarity: riches are discarded with difficulty, and scarcely anyone attains worldly possessions without the vices of the world itself. These are the thorns and briars that choked the seed of God; therefore it is safe neither to have nor to love riches.

“And again I tell you: it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven.”

“Easier,” that is, less difficult—and therefore less difficult because less impossible. For it is more impossible for a covetous person to enter the kingdom of heaven than for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle. For charity, whose expansiveness joins one to God, is contrary to covetousness, whose narrowness separates one from God. Therefore, just as it is utterly impossible for what is black, while it remains black, to become white, since black is contrary to white, so nothing is more impossible than for a covetous person to be joined to God while remaining covetous. Who does not see degrees of comparison even among impossibilities? [BEDA.] Certainly it is more impossible for a horse to be changed into a stone than into an ass, from which it differs less. How then did very many rich people enter the kingdom of God, unless, God inspiring them, they regarded riches as nothing? Did David place confidence in riches, when he sang of himself: “For I am alone and poor” (Ps. XXIV)? He also exhorts others thus: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. LXI). Mystically, [Col. 0334C] it is easier for Christ to suffer for lovers of the world than for lovers of the world to be converted to Christ. Christ is called a camel because, humbling himself willingly, he bore the burdens of our weakness. Hence: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. III). By the needle he signifies the piercings endured in the Passion. The eye of the needle therefore means the straits of the Passion, through which he deigned, as it were, to mend the torn garments of our nature—that is, to restore it after the Fall. [CHRYSO.] Otherwise: It is easier for the nations, crooked in mind, to enter through the narrow gate of the heavenly kingdom than for Jews, accounted rich in the Law and the Prophets. The nations had the hump of idolatry, just as the camel has a hump, which does not permit it to raise its neck. The needle is the Son of God: its first part, thin and sharp, signifies [Col. 0334D] his divinity; its last part, his incarnation. The Son of God is wholly straight like a needle, having no roughness of sin; through the wound of his Passion the nations entered into eternal life. By him the tunic of immortality, torn in Adam, was sewn together. This needle sewed spirit to flesh, and the Jewish people to the Gentile. Hence the Apostle: “He is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II). This needle joined together the broken friendship of angels and human beings; this needle fastens and passes through, yet makes no wound.

When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished, saying: “Who then can be saved?”

[BEDA.] They understood that lovers of riches, even if they do not possess them, are reckoned among the rich. Otherwise, [Col. 0335A] since the poor are far more numerous than the rich, they would not have said, “Who then can be saved?”

But Jesus, looking at them, said: “With human beings this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”

This must not be understood as meaning that covetous persons will enter the kingdom of God, but that it is possible for God, through his word, to convert them from covetousness for temporal things to charity for eternal things.
