Then Peter answered and said to him: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you. What then will there be for us?”

Great confidence. Peter was a fisherman; he had not been rich, but sought his livelihood by hand and craft. Yet he speaks confidently: “We have left everything.” And because leaving is not enough—for Socrates the philosopher [Col. 0335B] did this also—he adds what is perfect: “And we have followed you,” which belongs to believers. We have done what you commanded. What reward, then, will you give us?

M. 196[X]

And Jesus said to them: “Amen I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit upon the throne of his majesty—

M. 197[V] L. 272

—you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

In the first resurrection the soul is regenerated through faith; in the second, the flesh will be regenerated through incorruption. Hence two adoptions and two resurrections [Col. 0335C] are spoken of. Concerning God’s throne, hear the Prophet: “God shall reign over the nations; God sits upon his holy throne” (Ps. XLVI). All believers are the thrones of his majesty. Observe that he does not speak here of the time of the future judgment, but of the calling of all nations. For he did not say, “when the Son of Man shall come sitting,” but “when he shall sit.” He began to sit on the throne of his majesty from the time when the nations began to believe in him. From that same time the apostles also sat upon twelve thrones—that is, in all Christians, according to the differences of their souls. Those who receive the Word of the Father became his throne. So likewise concerning the other apostles. Hence the Prophet says: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city” (Ps. CXXI), and the rest. Jerusalem [Col. 0335D] is the Church; the apostles are God’s thrones; faithful people are the apostles’ thrones. Thus, by the teachings and examples of the Fathers, those of the twelve tribes of Israel who refuse to believe are condemned daily. The tribe of Levi, which is the thirteenth, is understood within the twelve, because, receiving no share in the division of the promised land, it was distributed among the twelve tribes, from whom it received tithes and offerings. [HIERON.] Otherwise: To sit upon the throne of majesty will be for the King of Glory to appear in judicial authority; for sitting belongs to one judging. Therefore they shall sit—that is, they shall appear as judges—who “instruct many unto righteousness,” shining “as the stars for everlasting eternities” (Dan. XII). Thus, by the dignity of their merits, they shall be above twelve thrones—that is, above the whole body of the good whom [Col. 0336A] they taught in Christ. For the number twelve signifies totality, as does seven; its parts, namely three and four, multiplied one by the other make twelve. Therefore what was thought insignificant by the Jews—the holy teachers—shall condemn on the day of judgment the despisers of the Gospel from the twelve tribes of Israel, not to mention the other nations.

M. 198[III] R. 110 L. 221

“Amen I say to you, everyone who has left house or parents, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands for the kingdom of heaven, and for my name and for the Gospel, shall receive a hundredfold: now in this present time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands with [Col. 0336B] persecutions; and in the age to come he shall possess eternal life.”

[HIERON.—BEDA.] The sense is: Whoever has left all riches for the Savior and despised carnal affection shall receive a hundredfold in spiritual things, which, by comparison with bodily things, will deservedly be as a hundred compared with a small number. Those who despise temporal things for the kingdom of God will taste, even in this life full of persecutions, the joys of that kingdom with sure faith, and will enjoy the sincere love of all the elect. Since, therefore, they receive from companions in their purpose a love much more welcome, they regard everything as their own, being bound together by a spiritual bond; for “the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and there was none needy among them” [Col. 0336C] (Acts IV). Likewise, in marital continence there is greater sweetness in the honor of sanctification than is offered by the lustfulness of the flesh. [CHRYSO.] Mystically, the father is the devil, the mother ignorance, through which the devil begets children; brothers and sisters are companions, male and female, in error. If one who was a pagan priest believes, he leaves idolatry as his wife, through whom he begot sons and daughters. If a master of any evil profession believes, he leaves that profession as a fruitful field. Leaving rank and wealth, he despises them as a house sheltering him. The graces of God receive the one leaving sisters, as most beloved sisters. No sister embraces a brother as sweetly as the graces of God embrace a holy soul.

[Col. 0336D] M. 199[II] R. 111 L. 173

“But many who are first shall be last, and the last first.”

Many are fervent at first and later grow sluggish; many are cold at first and suddenly burn with zeal. Consider Judas, an apostate turned from an apostle, and the thief on the cross made a confessor. Otherwise: Many despised in this world will be glorified in the future; others glorious in human eyes will be condemned in the future; or the Gentiles, who had long lived without the Law, are to be called to faith, while the Jews are to be blinded.

L. 192[X]

Now the Pharisees, who were covetous, heard all these things and mocked him.

[Col. 0337A] They mocked him as he disputed concerning contempt for the world, because the Law promised earthly goods to its observers; they did not consider that in the Law lesser things are rightly commanded to the carnal, whereas in the Gospel greater spiritual things are commanded to spiritual people.

And he said to them: “You are those who justify yourselves before human beings, but God knows your hearts; for what is exalted among human beings is an abomination before God.”

Those who despise sinners and assert that they themselves are righteous justify themselves before people, while neglecting the remedies of almsgiving. But how justly this proud covetousness is to be condemned is taught in the following example by him who “will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (I Cor. IV).

CHAPTER CVII.

[Col. 0337B] L. 196[X]

Again he said: “There was a certain rich man, who was clothed in purple and fine linen, and feasted splendidly every day.”

In riches is marked the lust of the eyes; in costly garments, the pride of life; in splendid feasting, the lust of the flesh. Therefore this rich man, as though unknown to God, is not identified by name. [AUGUST.] What is this greed, when even beasts have a limit? For they seize only when hungry, and spare their prey when they feel satiety. The avarice of the rich is insatiable: it always seizes and is never satisfied; it neither fears God nor respects a human being. It spares neither father nor [Col. 0337C] recognizes mother; it obeys no brother and keeps faith with no friend. It oppresses the widow and invades the orphan’s property. [BEDA.] What madness is this—to acquire gold and lose heaven? Yet this rich man is reproved not for taking what belonged to another, but for not giving what was his own, although under the Law it is robbery, not stinginess, that is condemned. Marine shellfish, cut around with iron, emit purple tears with which wool is dyed, from which purple cloth is woven. Fine linen is a kind of very white and soft flax, which the Greeks call *papaten*.

“And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, who lay at his gate, full of sores, desiring to be filled with the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him anything. But dogs also came and licked [Col. 0337D] his sores.”

[CHRYSO.—AMBR.] He could not even drive the dogs away from himself, nor was there any visitor to remove them. Note that, although parables do not assign proper names, the Lord names this poor man in approval of his humility; this is therefore not a parable but an account of an event. The fastidious rich man recoils from the beggar’s sores, lest amid costly feasts and perfumed guests he should endure the stench of sores being licked by dogs. [BEDA.] Thus, as Lazarus lay before his gate, the sight of the poor man brought an added weight of condemnation upon the rich man, who had no pity; and conversely, by the daily sight of the rich man the poor man was tested. For a greater testing of him, poverty and illness together, the visible abundance of the rich man, and the absence of all consolation for himself, afflicted him. We must therefore beware of despising the poor, even if we see things blameworthy in them; perhaps those wounded by weakness of character are healed by the medicine of poverty.

Now it came to pass that the beggar died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried in hell.

Abraham’s bosom is the repose of blessed poor people; burial in hell is the depth of punishments for the proud and merciless. Hence Gregory, in the twelfth book on Job: “We do not say that the souls of the righteous descended to hell to be held in places of punishment, but that they might rest in higher places.” The same, in the thirteenth: “The longing by which the righteous desired to see the Savior Job calls darkness, where he says: ‘In darkness [Col. 0338B] I have spread my bed’” (Job XVII). The same, in the eighth: “As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so one who descends to the underworld does not come up.” As though Job were speaking plainly, saying: One who runs upward fails if, through pride, he tends toward destruction. If guilt once drags such a person to punishment, mercy no longer restores him to pardon.

And lifting up his eyes, while he was in torments, he saw Abraham far away and Lazarus in his bosom.

[BEDA.] Since we call Abraham our father according to faith, Abraham’s bosom was the assembly of believers awaiting the Deliverer; Lazarus was directed there by the ministry of angels, becoming rich from being a beggar. But unbelievers, placed according to the variety of their faults in different abodes in the depths of punishments, see believers resting above them from afar, because they do not attain that place by merit.

And he himself cried out and said: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water, that he may cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame.”

Just as the divinity is said figuratively, by metaphor, to have eyes, tongue, fingers, and other human members, so too are souls separated from bodies. The rich man therefore asks that his tongue be cooled—that is, that the punishment which he earned with his tongue be relaxed. Since talkativeness commonly abounds at feasts, the rich man is said to burn more grievously in his tongue. Therefore he desires to be touched by the tip of a finger—that is, to be refreshed even by the least [Col. 0338D] work of the righteous, and thus to receive merciful aid through the living water of God’s grace.

And Abraham said to him: “Son, remember that you received your good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted, and you are tormented.”

He is tormented before judgment, because for a sensual person to lack pleasures is punishment. Abraham and the other faithful fathers by no means seek, according to the flesh, to free from torments children whom they see to have wandered from the faith. Perhaps this rich man had some good thing, for which the prosperity of his passing life rewarded him; and Lazarus had some evil thing, but the fire of poverty purified it. Or he received his good things in this respect: he regarded all his joy as transient prosperity. But even if the righteous have worldly goods, as they burn with holy desires for eternal things, the things at hand seem to them by no means good.

And in all these things a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that those who wish to pass from here to you cannot, nor can any pass from there to us.

“Chasm,” or *chaus*, as the ancient manuscripts have it, signifies the perpetual dissimilarity between the wills of good and evil people, because merits cannot be changed after death. There is no doubt that the reprobate would wish to pass from punishments, as they still do, into the lot of the blessed. But the passing of the righteous is to go in mind through mercy to those placed in torments and to wish to free them. Yet they cannot, because the souls of the righteous, although they possess mercy in the goodness of their nature, are nevertheless so bound by the righteousness of their Creator [Col. 0339B] that they are moved by no compassion toward the reprobate. Otherwise: The righteous are thought by many to wish to pass over to them, especially to rescue from punishments those to whom they were joined by greater affection in this life.

And he said: “Then I beg you, father, to send him to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torments.”

After hope has been taken away from the burning man concerning himself, his mind turns to his relatives. For the punishment of the reprobate sometimes teaches their minds, though uselessly, toward love, so that then at last they love their own even spiritually, though here, while loving sins, they did not even love themselves. Thus the rich man’s knowledge of the poor man whom he despised, and his memory of the brothers whom he left behind, are preserved for his punishment. The good will indeed know the good, the evil the evil, the good the evil, and the evil will know the good. In this mutual knowledge the fullness of recompense for both sides grows: the good rejoice more because they see those whom they loved rejoicing with them; while the evil, tormented with those whom they loved in this world, are consumed not only by their own punishment but also by theirs. Yet something more venerable happens in the elect: they not only recognize those whom they knew here, but recognize as though already seen and known good people whom they never saw.

And Abraham said to him: “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them.” But he said: “No, father Abraham; but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.”

[Col. 0339D] [AMBROS.] This rich man begins to be a teacher too late, when he has neither time to learn nor to teach. And because he had despised God’s words, he judges that his followers cannot hear them.

But he said to him: “If they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead.”

[BEDA.] Those who despise the words of the Law will refuse to believe even one who has been raised. This rich man signifies the Jewish people, who possessed an outward way of life and made useless use of the delights of the Law received. Lazarus, full of sores, is the Gentile people: when converted to God and confessing its sins, it emits outwardly, as though through burst skin, the poison that lay hidden within. Lazarus desired the rich man’s crumbs, and no one gave him any, because proud Israel despised the Gentile people. While puffed up over the teaching of the Law as though over received riches, words of knowledge flowed to it like crumbs falling from the table. Dogs in sacred speech commonly signify preachers: when they instruct those confessing sins, they touch, as it were, the wound of the mind with their tongue; and when by speaking they rebuke people for sins, they lead them back to salvation, just as dogs heal wounds by touching them with the tongue. Thus Lazarus is rightly interpreted “helped,” because those Gentiles are helped who heal their wounds by correction of the tongue. The licking of dogs may also signify the tongue of flatterers, who lick wounds when they extol our evils with wicked approval. Abraham’s bosom signifies the rest of heaven, in which those coming from east and west shall recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; but the children of this kingdom, clothed in purple and fine linen, [Col. 0340B] shall be cast out (Matt. VIII). The unbelieving people held the Law in its mouth but despised keeping it in deed; and therefore it will burn more intensely there. The rich man, begging for a drop of water in this life, says in the other that he has five brothers, because the Jewish people, now for the most part condemned, knows that its followers remain upon earth, devoted either to the five books of Moses understood carnally or to the five bodily senses. [AUGUST.] Therefore, just as an innumerable multitude of saints is understood in the five virgins (Matt. XXV) and in the one hundred fifty-three fishes (John XXI), so in the rich man’s five brothers many thousands of the Jewish people are understood, whose failure to rise to spiritual understanding he laments. [BEDA.] He therefore desires Lazarus, or another of the faithful, to be sent to them; but they would not believe him if they do not hear Moses and the prophets. The Lord rose from the dead, but because the Jewish people did not believe Moses, it despised believing the Lord. And since it refused to understand Moses’ words spiritually, it did not come to him whom Moses foretold. Hence Truth says: “If you believed Moses, you would indeed believe me” (John V).

CHAPTER CVIII.

L. 190[X]

And he said to his disciples: “There was a certain rich man who had a steward, and this man was accused before him as though he had wasted his goods.”

[Col. 0340D] Now the Lord speaks to the covetous and proud Pharisees, now to the disciples, with the former hearing, that they may come to their senses. [HIERON.] A *villicus* is properly the governor and guardian of an estate, and derives his name from *villa*, “estate.” Here, however, it is used for an *oeconomus*, that is, a steward, who administers the entire substance of a household. For *oeconomus* denotes the administrator both of money, grain, and everything the master possesses. The steward, therefore, is one to whom God has entrusted certain wealth for distribution. He dissipates it either by collecting it badly or by not spending it well.

And he called him and said: “What is this that I hear about you? Render an account of your stewardship, for you can no longer be steward.”

[Col. 0341A] God calls when he instills fear of eternal condemnation. A person renders an account if, considering that stewardship must end with this life, he gives more thought to making friends than to accumulating riches.

But the steward said within himself: “What shall I do, since my master is taking the stewardship away from me? I am unable to dig; I am ashamed to beg. I know what I shall do, so that, when I have been removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses.”

[BEDA.] When stewardship has been taken away, we cannot dig, because after this life we are not permitted to seek the fruit of good conduct with the hoe of devout compunction. It is shameful to beg, in the manner in which the foolish virgins begged. The houses of the saints, on whom we bestow mercy during the time of this stewardship, are the heavenly dwelling places in the Father’s house (Matt. XXV).

Therefore, having summoned each of his master’s debtors, he said to the first: “How much do you owe my master?” And he said: “A hundred measures of oil.” And he said to him: “Take your bond, sit down quickly, and write fifty.” Then he said to another: “And how much do you owe?” He said: “A hundred cors of wheat.” He said to him: “Take your document and write eighty.”

“Take your document”—understand, the one in which you had written the debt. A bond is whatever safeguards against injustice so that justice may be maintained. A *cadus* is Greek for an amphora containing three urns; a *corus* contains thirty bushels. That half is remitted to one debtor, and a fifth part to the other, taken simply, teaches that everyone who relieves the need of any poor saint by either half or a fifth part shall receive a sure reward for his mercy. Or it may be understood thus: since the Jews say that tithes ought to be given to priests and Levites, we, abounding above their righteousness in the righteousness of Christ, should give half our goods, as Zacchaeus did (Luke XIX), not only from income but from all our possessions. Or at least let us double their tithes by giving fifths to the Church.

And the master praised the unjust steward because he had acted prudently; for the children of this age are more prudent in their generation than the children of light.

[Col. 0341D] Everyone is called the child of the one whose works he performs. Thus the good are children of eternal light; but the evil are children of this age, that is, of darkness, concerning whom Solomon says: “Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and prudent in their own sight” (Isa. V). We ought not to take from this steward an example to imitate, so as either to defraud the Master or give alms from fraud. But illustrations are sometimes drawn from a contrary case, as here and in the case of the unjust judge, treated by Luke in the eighteenth chapter. Therefore, if the master, though suffering loss, nevertheless praises the steward’s prudence—not because he acted fraudulently against him, but because he acted prudently for himself—how much more will Christ, who cannot suffer any loss and is inclined to mercy, praise his disciples if [Col. 0342A] they are merciful in obedience to his command. Hence follows:

“And I say to you: Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings.”

[HIERON.] In the Syrian tongue, *mammon* is the name for riches; “of iniquity” is added because they have been collected through iniquity. Hence the common saying: a rich person is either wicked or the heir of a wicked person. He therefore teaches that we should make friends from unrighteous riches, not merely any poor people, but those who can receive us into heavenly dwellings. [ALBINUS.] Or thus: Let us make friends from unrighteous mammon, so that by giving generously to the poor we may gain for ourselves the favor of angels and all the other saints. [GREGOR.] Some, misunderstanding this, plunder in order, as they suppose, to dispense well; but they are burdened rather than helped. For the sacrifices of the wicked are abominable. Hence Solomon says: “One who offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son in his father’s sight” (Ecclus. XXXIV).

“He who is faithful in the least is faithful also in the greater; and he who is unjust in a little is unjust also in the greater.”

[BEDA.] He is faithful in the least who has bowels of compassion and works of mercy, giving alms and loving poor neighbors. He is faithful in the greater who clings wholly to the Creator and desires to become one spirit with him. For whoever does not love the brother whom he sees, nor pity the needy person, how shall he love God whom he does not see (I John IV), and how [Col. 0342C] shall he give himself to God?

“If therefore you have not been faithful in unrighteous mammon, who will entrust to you what is true?”

[AUGUST.] The riches of the world, however they are gathered, are called unrighteous mammon and deceive, because they either leave us or are left by us. But heavenly and spiritual riches are true, and once we possess them, we cannot lose them.

“And if you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own?”

[ALBINUS.] The resources of the world are alien to us, that is, situated outside our nature. For “we brought nothing into this world, and we shall take nothing out of it” (I Tim. VI). But ours are those things properly reckoned as belonging to a human being. Christ is ours, because he is our life; and therefore blessed is the one whose Lord is his God (Ps. CXLIII). The virtues are ours, because, as Solomon testifies, “the redemption of a man’s soul is his own riches” (Prov. XIII). Therefore let us give what is alien, that we may receive what is ours; let us offer small things, that we may receive great ones; let us sow in blessing, that we may reap blessing. For whoever sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly (II Cor. IX). [HIERON.] Theophilus of Antioch, who compiled the sayings of the four Evangelists into one work, spoke as follows in his commentaries on this parable: The rich man who has a steward or administrator is the Almighty. Paul was his steward, learning the Law of God under Gamaliel. When he began to persecute Christians and [Col. 0343A] to dissipate his master’s substance, he was corrected by the Lord, hearing: “It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts IX). And he said in his heart: “What shall I do? I was a teacher and steward; now I am compelled to be a disciple and a laborer. I cannot dig, for the commands of the Law, binding one to earth, have been destroyed. I am ashamed to beg, because I who was a teacher of the Jews must now begin to beg Ananias for the teaching of salvation. Therefore I shall act so that Christians may receive me when I have been cast out of my stewardship.” And he began to tell those who had formerly lived under the Law and thus believed in Christ, imagining that they were to be justified by the Law, that the Law was abolished, the prophets had passed away, and that the things formerly counted as gain were to be considered dung. Therefore he summoned two among the many debtors. The first, who owed a hundred measures of oil, namely those gathered from the Gentiles and needing God’s mercy. And from the number one hundred, which is full and perfect, he caused the number fifty to be written, which properly belongs to penitents, according to the year of jubilee and that parable in the seventh chapter of Luke, in which five hundred denarii are forgiven to one debtor and fifty to another (Luke VII). But he summoned second the Jewish people, nourished on the wheat of God’s commandments, which owed him the number one hundred; and he compelled it to make eighty from a hundred—that is, to believe in the Lord’s resurrection accomplished on the eighth day. For eighty consists of eight tens, and to pass from the Sabbath to the first day of the Sabbath. For this reason he is proclaimed by the Lord to have acted well, [Col. 0343C] because he was changed from the severity of the Law to the clemency of the Gospel. If you ask why he is called an unjust steward in the Law of God, know that he was an unjust steward who offered well indeed but did not divide well: believing in the Father but persecuting the Son; possessing the almighty God but denying the Holy Spirit. Paul, therefore, was more prudent in his transgression of the Law than the sons formerly of light, who, occupied with the Law, lost Christ, who is the true light of God the Father. But if people are received into eternal dwellings through unrighteous mammon well administered, how much more shall the divine word, in which there is no unrighteousness, entrusted to the apostles, raise good stewards to heaven? Therefore, one faithful [Col. 0343D] in the least—that is, in bodily things—will also be faithful in the greater, that is, in spiritual things. But one unjust in a small matter, by not giving brothers for use what God created for all, will likewise be unjust in distributing spiritual wealth, dividing the Lord’s teaching not according to need but according to persons. To be faithful in the least is a great thing. [AUGUST.] For just as the principle of circularity—that from the central point all lines are drawn equally to the circumference—is the same in a large disk as in a very small coin, so where small things are rightly done, the greatness of justice is not diminished.

L. 159[X]

“But that servant who knew his master’s [Col. 0344A] will and did not prepare, and did not act according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes.”

[BEDA.] Many, thinking they will be beaten less if they do not know what they ought to do, turn away so as not to hear the truth. But since they could know, if they wished to apply themselves diligently, they are judged not as ignorant but as despisers.

“But he who did not know and did things worthy of stripes shall be beaten with few.”

One should be called ignorant who wishes to comprehend but is unable. He is deservedly punished less to whom less was entrusted. For one who sins ignorantly sins in the night; but one who sins knowingly sins as in the day. Therefore those who sin knowingly descend alive into hell.

[Col. 0344B] “But from everyone to whom much has been given, much shall be required; and from him to whom they have entrusted much, they shall demand more.”

[BEDA.] The order of the words is: “But from everyone to whom much has been given, much shall be required.” Why did he add, “and from him to whom they have entrusted much”—understand, the divine judgments—unless because this explains what he had said previously? Or perhaps he indicates both orders, namely rulers and subjects. Many subjects are often granted both knowledge of the Lord’s will and the ability to fulfill it. But to prelates, along with their own salvation, is entrusted the care of feeding the flock. [BEDA.] Thus “the mighty shall suffer mighty torments” (Wis. VI); that is, if those endowed with greater grace sin, greater vengeance will follow. But the mildest punishment will be theirs who have not added personal sin to original sin; and among those who have added it, condemnation will be more tolerable in proportion as they have had less iniquity here.

L. 160[V] M. 95

“I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire except that it be kindled?”

Do you not know that I desire the divine fire to be kindled and burn in the hearts of believers? Therefore do not be like the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it; but in charity be faithful in the least and in the greater. By fire he means the fervor of the Holy Spirit, who, illuminating the secrets of the heart, burns sins as though they were thorns and brambles, [Col. 0344D] testing and improving golden vessels, and consuming wood, hay, and straw.

“But I have a baptism with which to be baptized; and how I am constrained until it be accomplished!”

“I came,” he says, “to cast fire into the hearts of believers, so that they may despise earthly things and seek heavenly things, being inflamed by the Holy Spirit; but for this I must first be baptized”—that is, dipped and drenched in baptism, namely the dipping, understand, of my blood. That is to say: Before I send the Holy Spirit, I shall give myself to be crucified. Hence: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified” (John VII). I am greatly constrained until that Passion itself is accomplished, yet nothing can compel me not to do what I have determined [Col. 0345A] concerning myself. Some manuscripts have *angor* (“I am distressed”) instead of *coarctor* (“I am constrained”). He who had nothing in himself from which to grieve was nevertheless distressed by our miseries, so that he might permit himself to be crucified.

CHAPTER CIX.

M. 200[X]

“The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard.”

[GREGOR.] The kingdom of heaven—that is, Christ—is compared with a householder, who made the first last and the last first. For Christ himself, the true householder, having care for the whole human race, calls all people at every time to cultivate the vineyard. When he is not known, he is hidden; but when he is known, he goes out to hire laborers, coming forth from concealment into recognition. The vineyard is the Church, which from righteous Abel to the last elect sends forth as many branches as it produces saints. The laborers are preachers and each individual, so long as he persists in right faith and obedience to the divine Law.

And after agreeing with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard.

[REMIG.] The agreement was the confirmed promise that they would be re-formed in the image of God if, in building the Church, they persevered in the commandments of the Decalogue. Thus in the denarius, bearing the image of the king and formerly reckoned as ten small coins, both the reward of obedience and the fact that it is given to laborers through keeping the Decalogue are plainly signified.

And going out about the third hour, he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, and said to them: “Go also into my vineyard, and whatever is just I will give you.” And they went.

[CHRYSOSTOM.] By the marketplace is understood the world, in which there are always the tumultuous troubles of slanders, wrongs, quarrels, and diverse business affairs, and where everything is for sale. Sinners are called dead, not idle. For as one is called deaf before God who hears not what belongs to God but what belongs to the devil; and blind, through whose eyes the devil sees, not God; so he who lives for the devil is dead to God. A robber is not [Col. 0345D] idle, but dead. A drunkard or fornicator is not idle, but dead. Yet he who takes nothing is idle unless he gives from what is his to those in need. Do you wish not to be idle? Take nothing, and give of your own for God’s sake; live not for yourself, but for God. Do you wish not to be idle? Fast, and give for God’s sake what you ought to eat and drink. Do you wish not to be idle? If you are without a wife, do not seek a wife, but cultivate the vine of chastity. If you say, “I cannot abstain,” I show you how both to have a wife and to cultivate the vine of chastity: abstain from a menstruating woman and from a pregnant woman. Be ashamed to do what animals do not do. Why did the servant who received a mina from his master hear, “Wicked servant”? And why was he sent into darkness? Because he gained nothing from it. If, therefore, he who stood idle in the marketplace will not be unpunished on the day of judgment, [Col. 0346A] what will the sinner do who loses his mina?

Again he went out about the sixth and ninth hour and did likewise. But about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing, and said to them, “Why do you stand here idle all day?” They say to him, “Because no one has hired us.” He says to them, “Go also into the vineyard.”

The first hour denotes Adam sent into the vineyard, and the remaining patriarchs down to Noah. [JEROME.] The third denotes Noah himself and the rest down to Abraham’s circumcision. The sixth, from Abraham to Moses, when the Law was given. The ninth, Moses and the prophets. The eleventh, the apostles and the people of the nations, who previously stood idle all day—that is, throughout all time, neglecting to labour for salvation. [HILARY.] The Law had indeed [Col. 0346B] hired Israel, saying, “Do this, and you shall live” (Luke VI); but no one had hired the nations. For the Gospel was owed to be preached throughout the world, and the nations to be saved by the justification of faith. Alternatively: morning is childhood; the third hour, adolescence rising upward like the sun; the sixth, youth; the ninth, old age; the eleventh, decrepit age. [GREGORY.] Thus the labourers of the first hour seem to be Samuel, Jeremiah, and John the Baptist; those of the third, persons who began to serve God from puberty; of the sixth, those who did so from mature age; of the ninth, those already declining toward old age; and of the eleventh, those in extreme old age. Those who remain sluggish until their final age are therefore rightly reproved for idleness, so that they may repent even at the end. For no one has hired such persons, [Col. 0346C] although the ways of life were preached to them, because it belongs to God alone inwardly to teach those who have not yet obeyed him.

When evening had come, the lord of the vineyard says to his steward:

[CHRYSOSTOM.] That is, either the Father speaks to the Son, or the Son to the Holy Spirit.

“Call the labourers and pay them their wage, beginning with the last and going to the first.”

Observe that he pays the wage in the evening, not on another morning. Therefore judgment will occur while this present age still stands, for two reasons. First, because the blessedness to come is the reward of righteousness; secondly, lest sinners see blessedness, as the prophet says: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. XXVI).

So when those who had come about the eleventh hour [Col. 0346D] came, they received a denarius each.

[AUGUSTINE.] Although all the righteous will receive the happiness of resurrection together, yet, because some receive it after one hour and others after many, those are said to receive first who receive after a short time. Thus the last in labour will be first in reward, and the first in labour last in reward. Since that denarius is eternal life, the first—such as Abel and Noah, called to the kingdom, as it were, at the first or third hour—and the last, who since the Lord’s bodily advent arrive, as it were, at the eleventh hour without delay, will be equal in that reward. They will indeed shine with differing merits, one more and another less; and therefore the householder promised to give each what was just. Nevertheless, [Col. 0347A] eternal life will be equal for all: longer for none and shorter for none, because it will have no end. [GREGORY.] Alternatively: evening comes whenever the end of one’s life arrives. The householder began to pay denarii from the last, for he brought the thief to the rest of paradise before Peter (Luke XXIII). Though that thief did not reach the eleventh hour in age, he nevertheless came late through punishment. Thus those who come late are sometimes rewarded first, because they depart their bodies before those called in childhood.

But when the first came, they thought that they would receive more. Yet they too received a denarius each.

[REMIGIUS.] Those called long ago will receive the same eternity as the justified nations, being conformed to [Col. 0347B] the body of Christ’s glory. Yet, when they came first, because they had been God’s people from the beginning, they thought that the nations, who had previously served idols, would receive less.

And receiving it, they murmured against the householder, saying: “These last have worked one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden and heat of the day?”

[GREGORY.] The ancients who reached heaven after long periods in hell receive the denarius, as it were, after murmuring; but we receive it without murmuring, because as soon as we depart from the body, we receive our reward without delay. Note that this denarius is not received wholly at once: the true cultivators of the spiritual [Col. 0347C] vineyard will have a hundredfold in this life, then heaven, and after the reward of judgment a double robe. Therefore, in receiving the denarius, they do not murmur against the last labourers out of envy of grace, but against the householder out of ignorance of his secrets. Such, then, is the murmuring of a devout inquiry by those above: What reason is there that you delayed so long to send the fire of heaven onto the earth and kindle it? Or why did you not reserve us for this time? Why did the last not have our times with us, or why have we not the last times? Why, too, is equal reward given for unequal callings? And many questions of this kind are asked. [CHRYSOSTOM.] The burden signifies the work of righteousness; the heat, the world’s desire. This is said because in former times the world prospered for all good people. Therefore those who lived then maintained righteousness with greater difficulty, because worldly prosperity hinders the soul. Great indeed was the good person then who could be righteous. But very evil was the one who did not flee to God when he saw the world pressed by many adversities. The burden may also mean the burdensome commandments of the Law; the heat, the burning error of temptations [Col. 0347D] which evil spirits stirred up against the ancients, provoking them to jealousy of the nations.

But he answered one of them and said: “Friend, I do you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what is yours and go.”

He is said to have answered one because the cause of murmuring was equal in all [Col. 0348A]. This friend is understood as the first-formed man, Adam, and those who believed at that time. When he says, “for a denarius,” it is as though he said: “You have received the promised reward, namely my image and likeness; nor is the reward of your merit diminished by another’s participation. What more do you seek? Go,” that is, persevere in the righteousness you have attained.

“But I wish to give to this last one as to you also. Or is it not lawful for me to do what I will? Is your eye evil because I am good?”

I wish the Gentile people to become coequal and incorporated with you. Does not the judge have power either to do justice or to bestow mercy upon whom he wills? Take care, then, lest, on account of my goodness, you look upon your neighbour with an envious eye. But to me alone—the invisible, immortal [Col. 0348B] King of the ages—be honour and glory for ages of ages (I Tim. I).

“So the last shall be first, and the first last.”

[CHRYSOSTOM.] Thus, as has been shown, the last and first will be made equal. For as in a crown there is neither beginning nor end, so among the saints, with respect to time, in that age no one is called last and no one first.

“For many are called, but few are chosen.”

This concerns not the saints mentioned above, but the nations: more people come to the Church [faith], more fill the walls of the Church, but few are brought to the kingdom. Alternatively, some understand “the first” as meaning not only the good but also certain persons who began in the vineyard and did not persevere. These murmur out of envy toward the last [Col. 0348C], like those who, at the beginning of the Church’s birth, set themselves above those called from the nations. Thus some statements made generally refer to the good, such as: “I wish to give to this last one as to you also.” But other statements concern those who falsely think that they will receive the denarius, such as: “And receiving it, they murmured.” [REMIGIUS.] And then: “Is your eye evil because I am good?” “The last,” he says, “will be first, and the first last, because the Jews are turned from head into tail, and we are changed from tail into head.” Hence Moses in Deuteronomy: “The stranger who dwells with you shall rise above you; he shall be head, and you shall be tail” (Deut. XXVIII). Yet that many, both last and first, are rejected [Col. 0348D] is added in the terrible sentence: “For many are called to faith, but few chosen for the kingdom.”

## CHAPTER 110

L. 176[X]

And it came to pass, when he entered on the Sabbath into the house of one of the rulers of the Pharisees to eat bread, that they were watching him. And behold, a certain man with dropsy was before him.

[Bede.] The disease of dropsy takes its name from a watery fluid; for in Greek *hydōr* means “water.” It is a subcutaneous fluid arising from a disorder of the bladder, accompanied by swelling and foul breath. It is characteristic of a dropsical person that, the more he abounds in disordered fluid, the more he thirsts. Therefore he is rightly compared [Col. 0349A] to one weighed down by an overflowing stream of carnal pleasures; he is also compared to the avaricious rich man, who, the more abundant are the riches which he does not use well, the more fiercely he desires such things.

L. 177[II] M. 116 R. 25

And Jesus answered and said to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?” But they were silent.

They rightly keep silent, since they see that whatever they say is said against themselves. For if it is lawful to heal, why do they watch to see whether he will break the Sabbath? If it is not lawful, why do they tend their animals? “He said, saying” is a construction like “I waited expectantly” (Ps. XXXIX), signifying the speaker’s persistence until he accomplishes what he intends.

[Col. 0349B] But he took hold of the man, healed him, and dismissed him. And answering them, he said: “Which of you, if his ass or ox falls into a pit, will not immediately pull it out on the Sabbath day?” And they could not answer him in these matters.

For this reason he heals the dropsical man before the Pharisees and immediately disputes against avarice: so that, through his bodily illness, their illness of mind might be expressed in them, and by the example of bodily healing they might learn to be healed spiritually. He fittingly compares the dropsical man to the animal that fell into the pit, for he suffered from fluid. The ox and ass signify the wise and the dull; or the ox signifies the people worn down under the yoke of the Law, while the ass signifies the Gentile people, not tamed by reason, like a foolish and brutish animal. The Saviour draws these out of the pit of desire, [Col. 0349C] for all have sinned (Rom. III).

L. 178[X]

And he spoke a parable to those who had been invited, observing how they chose the first places at table. He said to them: “When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place, lest perhaps one more honourable than you has been invited by him; and he who invited both you and him comes and says to you, ‘Give this man your place’; and then you begin with shame to occupy the last place.”

Observing how they strove after the first places at table—or observing in his teaching how they ought to choose places in the Church—he teaches humility not only before God but also before [Col. 0349D] human beings. Since this admonition is called a parable by the Evangelist, we must consider what it signifies. The wedding is the union of Christ and the Church; hence Matthew says in the twenty-second chapter: “The kingdom of heaven was made like a king who made a wedding for his son.” Whoever is invited to this wedding—that is, joined to the members of the Church—must not recline in the first place: that is, he must not exalt himself by glorying in his merits as though higher than the rest. Let him strive to be clothed in a wedding garment—that is, to shine with the splendour of virtues—but with humility. He gives place to one more honourable when, recognizing better things in others, he accounts as small whatever exalted thing he had thought of his own conduct, and humbles himself with the Prophet, saying: “I am poor and in labours from my youth; but having been exalted, [Col. 0350A] I was humbled and troubled” (Ps. LXXXVII). With good reason, the penitent who exalts himself above others more than he ought occupies the last place in the Church with shame.

“But when you are invited to a wedding, recline in the last place, so that, when he who invited you comes, he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will have glory before those reclining with you.”

“The greater you are, humble yourself” (Ecclus. III), saying with the Psalmist: “I have been humbled utterly; Lord, give me life according to your word” (Ps. CXVIII). When the Lord comes for judgment, or for the Church’s daily visitation, he commands to ascend the one whom he finds humbling himself more. Hence: “Whoever humbles himself like a little child, he is greater [Col. 0350B] in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVIII). He aptly says, “Then you will have glory,” lest you wish now to receive in full that which is to be rendered to you at the end. Hence Solomon says: “An inheritance hastily acquired at the beginning will lack blessing in the end” (Prov. XX). Even in this life the humble Church is exalted to obtain the greater gifts of the Holy Spirit.

L. 179[V] M. 231

“For everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted.”

He who rashly elevates himself because of his merits will be humbled by the Lord, even if not before men; and he who prudently humbles himself because of his good deeds will be exalted by him.

[Col. 0350C] L. 180[X]

And he also said to the one who had invited him: “When you give a dinner or a supper, do not invite your friends, your brothers, your relatives, or rich neighbours, lest perhaps they also invite you in return and repayment be made to you. But when you give a banquet, invite the poor, the weak, the blind, and the lame; and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.”

The poor do not have—supply, “the means by which”—to repay you; but God will repay you. He does not forbid friends and brothers as though they were wicked, but shows that this accomplishes nothing for winning the rewards of heavenly life. Hence elsewhere: “If you do good to those who do good to you, what grace is there for you? For sinners also do this” (Luke [Col. 0350D] VI). There are also certain banquets which are not merely repaid in the present but even produce condemnation in the future. Thus Paul, denouncing works of darkness, says: “Not in revelries and drunkenness” (Rom. XIII). Therefore whoever invites gluttonous and lustful persons for the sake of wantonness will be punished with eternal punishment. But one who invites friends and rich persons in order that he too may be invited by them receives his reward. Yet if he does this for God’s sake, after the example of the sons of blessed Job (Job I), he who commanded it rewards this as he does the other offices of brotherly love.

When one of those reclining with him heard these things, he said to him: “Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God.”

Drawn by the sweetness of the resurrection and glorious [Col. 0351A] recompense of the righteous of which he had heard, he bursts forth in praise of them. The bread eaten in the kingdom of God is not bodily bread, as Cerinthus held; but rather it is he who says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John VI).

## CHAPTER 111

A. 48[I] M. 274 R. 156 L. 260

After these things the feast day of the Jews, Passover, was near. Passover (*pathein*, “to suffer”) is not a Greek name but a Hebrew one. Yet in this name there fittingly coincides an agreement of both languages. For one who suffers is said in Greek to *paschein*. Hence Passover was thought to mean “passion”; but in its own language, that is, Hebrew, it is called “passing over,” because God’s people first celebrated Passover when they crossed the Red Sea (Exod. XII). Thus [Col. 0351B] Passover is called in Hebrew *phase*, that is, “passing over,” because the destroyer, seeing the blood on the doors of the Israelites, passed over and did not strike them. Or it is named from passing over because the Lord, giving help to his people, walked above them. But our passing over occurs if, leaving behind the Egypt of the world, we hasten to heavenly things.

L. 201[X]

And it came to pass, as he was going to Jerusalem, that he passed through the midst of Samaria and Galilee. And as he entered a certain village, ten leprous men met him. They stood at a distance and raised their voices, saying: “Jesus, Master, have mercy upon us.”

[Bede.] Lepers are those who, lacking knowledge of the true faith [Col. 0351C], profess various teachings of error. They indiscriminately mingle true things with false, as though displaying the various colours of leprosy. The Church must avoid these persons; being kept far off, they must cry out with great effort until, through knowledge of the Master, they return to the form of health.

When he saw them, he said: “Go, show yourselves to the priests.” And it came to pass, as they went, that they were cleansed.

The Lord is found to have sent only lepers to priests, because the Jewish priesthood was a figure of the priesthood that now exists in the Church. Whoever has been cleansed by God’s grace from heretical perversity, Gentile superstition, Jewish unbelief, or even a brotherly schism must come to the Church [Col. 0351D] and show the true colour of faith, like that of the others. Thus Paul was sent to Ananias in order to receive the sacrament of faith and to have his true colour approved (Acts IX), not because the Lord cannot do all things by himself, but so that the fellowship of believers itself, communicating with one another, may confirm in faith one appearance of the true colour. Cornelius too, though his prayers had been heard, was commanded to send for Peter, for the sake of confirming unity (Acts X).

But one of them, when he saw that he was cleansed, returned, glorifying God with a loud voice; and he fell on his face before his feet, giving thanks. And he was a Samaritan.

The one who returned giving thanks signifies the humility of the Church’s unity. Samaritan is interpreted [Col. 0352A] “guardian,” by which name is signified the person who attributes all his strength to God, in accordance with the Psalmist: “I will keep my fear for you, because you are the God who receives me” (Ps. LVIII). He falls on his face who is ashamed of the evils he has committed. But of the Lord’s persecutors it is written: “They went backward and fell” (John XVIII). He who falls before himself sees where he falls; but one who falls backward does not see. Therefore the wicked fall backward, because the heart is exalted before ruin, so that they do not see what follows them; but the righteous fall forward, because, pierced with compunction, they are humbled.

And Jesus answered and said: “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner?” And he said to him: “Rise, go; your faith has made you [Col. 0352B] whole.”

If faith saved this man, unbelief destroyed the nine. If one is added to nine, a certain image of unity is completed, producing so complete a number that it cannot proceed further unless it returns to one. Thus nine need one for a kind of unity, while one does not need them for the unity proper to itself. Therefore the one who gave thanks signifies those who are in the unity of the Church, whereas the nine signify those outside it. The Lord asks where they are because for God to know is to choose, while not to know is to reject. When they were cleansed, they knew God, but went backward. Of such persons the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Rom. I). It should be known that one is called the first [Col. 0352C] unity and ten the second. The former is attributed to God, because, multiplied within itself, it neither increases nor decreases; the latter to the Church, because, multiplied within itself, it grows into a hundred. Therefore, because in ten—which is the unity of a hundred—variety is generated by its own multiplication, ten lepers are aptly said to have existed, since they were divided from faith in the one God. And just as all believers can be designated by the number ten because of keeping the Ten Commandments, so all unbelievers can, conversely, be designated by the same number because of neglecting those same commandments. The one who returned to the Lord when healed is called a foreigner, either because he had formerly been alien to the Church or because he made himself alien from the unbelief of his companions.

## CHAPTER 112

[Col. 0352D]

M. 201[II] R. 112 L. 222

And taking the twelve again, he said to them: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and all things written through the prophets concerning the Son of Man shall be fulfilled. For he shall be delivered to the chief priests and scribes, and they shall deliver him to the nations; he shall be mocked, flogged, spat upon, and crucified; and on the third day he shall rise again.”

[CHRYSOSTOM.] If the apostles, though so often forewarned of the Lord’s death, nevertheless abandoned him when he was seized, how much more would they have been scandalized had they not been forewarned? [BEDE.] He therefore repeatedly foretold both the punishment of his passion and the glory of his resurrection, so that, when they saw him dying, they might not doubt that [Col. 0353A] he would also rise again. He showed this from the prophecies of the prophets, for the overthrow of heretics who would arise in the Church.

M. 202[VI] R. 113

Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee approached him with her sons, worshipping and asking something of him.

[CHRYSOSTOM.] The mother of Zebedee’s sons is Salome; her name means “peaceful,” because she bore sons of peace. Zebedee died between the time of the apostles’ calling and the Lord’s passion, and so she followed Jesus.

He said to her: “What do you wish?” She said to him: “Command that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.”

[Col. 0353B] [JEROME.] The Lord asks so that her unconsidered petition, once confessed, may be corrected. The woman had heard that he would rise on the third day, and she thought that what is promised at the second coming would be fulfilled at the first. Therefore, through feminine eagerness, forgetful of future things, she desires present things. It is not surprising that this woman is reproved for ignorance when Peter, wishing to make three tabernacles, was mistaken.

But Jesus answered and said to them: “You do not know what you ask.”

[CHRYSOSTOM.] I called you from the left to the right, and you run to the left. You wish to reign though you have not deserved the summit of honour. The mother asks, but the Lord speaks to the disciples, understanding that the mother’s prayers arose from her sons’ desire. Perhaps [Col. 0353C] the matter was pursued through a woman because the devil could not prevail against them through themselves. As he stripped Adam through a woman, so he wished to separate these men through their mother. But destruction could no longer enter through a woman, since our salvation had proceeded from a woman.

“Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink, or be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” They say to him: “We can.”

The cup is the passion; baptism is death. It is called baptism by likeness to wool that is dyed. For as wool is dipped and receives the distinction of some colour, so we descend bodily into death and rise spiritual. Hence the Apostle: [Col. 0353D] “We are sown in weakness; we rise in power. A natural body is sown; a spiritual body rises” (I Cor. XV). Every death involves suffering, but not every suffering involves death; for confessors suffered but were not killed. Therefore all drank the Lord’s cup, but not all were baptized with his baptism. Cassiodorus, on Psalm X: “It is called a *calix* [cup] because it is accustomed continually to receive a hot drink.” Macrobius Theodosius says that the people of the Cylicrani [possibly “Ciriclani”] were near Heraclea, their composite name deriving from drinking, *cylicos*; with one letter changed, this name of a kind of drinking vessel gave *calix*, “cup.” Thus the name is known to have been fixed in memory. The same author, on Psalm LXXIV: “A *calix* is so called from the hot drink used by diners.” The same, on Psalm CXV: “A cup [Col. 0354A] signifies passion and martyrdom, because it is drunk in measure.”

He said to them: “You shall indeed drink my cup, and you shall be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized.”

[JEROME.] It is asked how both drank the passion, since James was beheaded by Herod, whereas John ended his life by a natural death. But if we recognize that he was sent into a cauldron of boiling oil, we shall see that his spirit did not fail in martyrdom and that he drank the cup of confession. Hence Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*: “As the merit of patience is not unequal in Peter, who suffered, and John, who did not suffer, so the merit of continence is not unequal in John, who experienced no marriage, and Abraham, who begot children.” Jerome [Col. 0354B] also says in the larger breviary, on Psalm CXV: “Monks ought to possess the purity of martyrs, since they too are martyrs.” For what angels do in heaven, monks singing psalms day and night do on earth.

“But to sit at my right and left is not mine to give to you, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.”

“It is not mine to give to you” by a particular prerogative, as you intend, because there is no respect of persons with God, but only of those who fear him. Therefore you too will receive the kingdom of God if you are worthy. Or thus: “It is not mine to give to you,” namely, to the proud, for such they still were. If you wish to receive it, first humble yourselves.

[Col. 0354C] M. 203[II] R. 114 L. 270

And when the ten heard it, they were indignant at the two brothers.

[CHRYSOSTOM.] If the apostles were disturbed because these men dared to ask this through their mother, how much more would they have been disturbed if their petition had been granted? Therefore he neither said, “You shall not sit,” lest he shame the two, nor, “You shall sit,” lest he provoke the rest. Rather, like a gracious father, he answered in such a way that concord among the brothers might not be broken, but all might hope. For what is not promised specially to one or two is hoped for by all.

But Jesus called them to himself and said: “You know that [Col. 0354D] the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and their great men exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you. But whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your servant; and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your slave.”

[JEROME.] Both their immoderate request and the others’ grief at it were in vain, since one comes to the summit of virtues not by power but by humility. [BEDE.] We are given this model so that we may not imitate secular rulers but humble ourselves both to one another and to those entrusted to us. Thus one of the wise rightly says: “Have they appointed you leader? Do not be exalted, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclus. XXXII). Peter likewise says: “Not lording it over the clergy, but becoming an example to the flock” (I Pet. V). Yet sometimes one sins more grievously if, among the perverse, equality is maintained more than discipline. For because Eli, overcome by false pity, was unwilling to strike his offending sons (I Sam. II), before the strict Judge he struck himself and his sons with a cruel condemnation. It is therefore necessary that a ruler show both the compassion of a mother and the discipline of a father toward subjects; and one must diligently take care that discipline not be rigid or compassion lax. “The rulers of the nations lord it over them,” that is, over the peoples of the nations; the pronoun refers to the implied sense.

M. 204[II] R. 115 A. 91 and 135

“Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

[Col. 0355B] He sets forth his own example. “For many,” he says—that is, for believers, not for all human beings. God indeed wills all to be saved, but only if they come to him. He does not will them to be saved against their will, but willingly. A physician publicly shows that he wishes to save, provided that he is sought by the sick. For salvation is not true if it is bestowed upon one unwilling. Faith gives salvation; unless the mind receives it with its whole will, it will not only profit nothing but will even harm.

## CHAPTER 113

L. 178[V] M. 55

(Read chapter 40 of this work.) And someone said to him: “Lord, then are there few who are saved?” But he said to them: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate, [Col. 0355C] for many, I tell you, seek to enter and will not be able.”

M. 171 L. 60

“But when the householder has entered and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, open to us,’ he will answer and say to you, ‘I do not know where you are from.’”

Light does not know darkness—that is, it does not look upon it; for if it looked upon it, darkness would not exist. The householder is Christ, who in his divinity is wholly present everywhere. He is therefore within for those whom he gladdens in the heavenly homeland, but is still, as it were, outside for those whom he secretly helps while they struggle in this pilgrimage. He will enter when he brings the whole Church to contemplation of himself; [Col. 0355D] he will shut the door when he removes from the reprobate the opportunity for repentance. Standing outside, they will knock—that is, separated from the righteous, they will vainly implore the mercy which they despised.

“Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank before you, and you taught in our streets.’”

This may be understood simply of the Jews, who despise the mysteries of faith and suppose that they please the Lord if they bring sacrifices to the temple, feast there before the Lord, attend to the reading of the prophets, and do not know that the kingdom of God is not in food and drink but in righteousness and the Holy Spirit (Rom. XIV). Or, mystically, those are understood to eat and drink before the Lord who eagerly receive the food of the word [Col. 0356A] but do not perform works; hence follows, “You taught in our streets.” Holy Scripture is food in its more obscure places, because by expounding it is, as it were, broken and swallowed. But it is drink in clearer places, because it is imbibed as it is found.

“And he will say to you, ‘I do not know where you are from. Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity.’ There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

Feasting at legal festivals does not help one whom the godliness of faith does not commend; knowledge of the Scriptures does not make known to God one whom the wickedness of his works shows unworthy of God’s regard.

L. 172[V] M. 65

“When you see Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and all [Col. 0356B] the prophets entering into the kingdom of God, but yourselves cast out, and when they come from east and west and north and south and recline in the kingdom of God.”

L. 173[II] M. 199 R. 111

“And behold, there are last who were first, and there are first who were last.”

## CHAPTER 114

L. 225[X]

And Jesus, having entered Jericho, was passing through it. And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus; he was chief of the tax collectors and was rich. He sought to see who Jesus was, but could not because of the crowd, since he was small in stature. Running ahead, he climbed a sycamore tree to see him, because he was about to pass that way.

[Col. 0356C] Behold, the camel, having laid aside its humped burden, passes through the eye of a needle: that is, the rich man and tax collector, abandoning the burden of riches and despising the income of fraud, ascends the narrow gate and constricted way that leads to life. Because, through faith’s devotion, he supplies by climbing a tree what he lacks in natural stature in order to see the Saviour, he justly receives the blessing of the Lord’s hospitality which he desired, though he had not dared to ask for it. Moreover, since the crowd is the confused multitude of ignorant people, unable to see the summit of wisdom, he rightly sees the one he desires not in the crowd but after passing beyond the unknowing populace [or: “in knowledge”]. Zacchaeus is interpreted “justified” and signifies believers from the nations: depressed and small through preoccupation with temporal affairs, but sanctified by the Lord. They seek to see the Saviour entering Jericho when they desire to share in the grace of faith which the Saviour brought; but the crowd of the harmful habit of vices delays them. Therefore the small man must pass beyond the crowd’s obstacle, leave earthly things behind, and climb the tree of the cross. The sycamore is called the “foolish fig”: a tree whose leaves resemble a mulberry’s but which surpasses it in height, whence it is called *celsa* (“lofty”) by the Latins. Christ’s cross is to believers like a fig tree, but is derided by unbelievers as foolish. For, says the Apostle, “We preach Christ crucified: to Jews indeed a stumbling block, and to nations foolishness; but to those called, Jews and nations alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I). The small man [Col. 0357A] climbs this tree when anyone humble and conscious of his own weakness cries: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI). He sees the Lord as he passes by when, in the mystery of the cross, he applies himself as far as he can to heavenly wisdom. Finally, he was about to pass that way—that is, in that region where the sycamore stood, or where someone would believe—both to preserve the mystery and to sow grace; for he had come so as to pass through the Jews to the nations.

And when he came to the place, Jesus looked up and saw him.

For already, through the sublimity of faith, he stood out amid the fruits of new works, as though in the height of an unfruitful tree. Through the heralds of his Word, among whom Jesus was present and speaking, he came to the people of the nations; [Col. 0357B] and this man, now exalted by faith in his Passion, burns also to acknowledge his divinity. Looking up, he saw him: for through faith he chooses those raised above earthly things who choose him, and loves the one who loves him.

And he said to him: “Zacchaeus, come down quickly, for today I must stay in your house.” And he came down quickly and received him joyfully.

The one invited invites, because, though he had not yet heard the voice of the one inviting him, he had heard his disposition. Thus today he must stay in the house of the lowly Zacchaeus; that is, with the new grace of light shining forth, he must rest in the humble heart of the believing nations. That he is commanded to come down from the sycamore and thus prepare lodging in his house for Christ is what the Apostle says: “Even if we have known [Col. 0357C] Christ, yet now we know him no longer” (2 Cor. 5). “For although he died through the weakness of the flesh, yet now he lives through the power of God” (2 Cor. 13).

And when they all saw it, they murmured, saying that he had turned aside to lodge with a sinful man.

It is evident that the Jews have always hated, or failed to understand, the salvation of the nations. Thus even believing brethren said against the chief of the apostles: “Why did you go in to men who have the foreskin and eat with them?” (Acts 11).

But Zacchaeus, standing, said to the Lord: “Behold, Lord, I give half my goods to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.”

Zacchaeus standing—that is, persevering in the faith he had received—shows that he has turned wholly to [Col. 0357D] the Lord. Therefore, if he has defrauded anyone of anything, he restores it fourfold, because in the ancient statutes of the Church it is decreed that one who seizes another’s property shall not go unpunished, but shall restore everything with increase. The laws of the secular realm also provide that one who steals another’s property shall restore it elevenfold [fourfold] to the person from whom he stole it. But when Zacchaeus readily promises to distribute half his goods to the poor, he indicates that he would not refuse even to give the whole.

Jesus said to him: “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham.”

He is called a son of Abraham not because he was begotten from Abraham’s line, but because he imitated Abraham’s faith. The salvation that was once the Jews’ has today shone upon the people of the nations, believing [Col. 0358A] in the Lord. Hence the Apostle: “But if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s seed” (Gal. 3).

158 M. 226[V] L.

“For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.”

Hence elsewhere: “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matt. 9).

## CHAPTER CXV

M. 205[II] R. 116 L. 224

And as they were going out from Jericho, a great crowd followed him.

[HIERONYMUS.] There were many robbers in Jericho, who used to kill and wound those going down from Jerusalem to Jericho. [Col. 0358B] Therefore the Lord came with his disciples to deliver the wounded.

And behold, two blind men, one of whom was Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus, sitting beside the road, heard that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by. And they cried out, saying: “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David.”

[AUGUSTINE.] The fact that Mark says nothing about the other blind man is resolved in the same way as the question concerning the two men possessed by a legion of demons in the country of the Gerasenes. For it is clear that one of the two blind men was especially well known, because Mark even records his father’s name. Luke, however, although he relates the event concerning the blind man in an entirely similar way, must be understood to recount the same kind of miracle in another blind man.

[Col. 0358C] But the crowd rebuked them, telling them to be silent. Yet they cried out all the more, saying: “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David.”

[CHRYSOSTOM.] Such is the nature of faith: the more it is forbidden, the more it is kindled; for the power of faith is confident amid dangers.

And Jesus stood still, called them, and said: “What do you want me to do for you?” They said to him: “Lord, let our eyes be opened.”

The Son of David cannot give light to the blind, but the Son of God can. Therefore I ask: “What do you want?” Then they no longer said, “Lord, Son of David,” but only, “Lord, let our eyes be opened.” So long as they said, “Son of David,” healing was suspended; as soon as they said only, “Lord,” it was bestowed. He also asks this in order to stir the heart to prayer, because he wishes us to ask for what he knows beforehand that he will grant. Or he asks in order that we may believe that none but one who confesses can be saved.

But Jesus, having compassion on them, touched their eyes; and immediately they saw, and followed him, glorifying the Lord. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.

[GREGORY—BEDE.] He touched their eyes bodily, not by a word, because they called him David’s son. He healed as God, because they believed. While passing by, he hears the blind; standing still, he gives them light. For through his humanity he has compassion on the cries of our blindness, but through the power of his divinity he pours into us the light of grace. The person who sees and follows Jesus going before him is one who performs, under his gaze, the good [Col. 0359A] that he understands. Such a person both advances and kindles others to praise God. The people praise God not only for the gift of light obtained, but also for the merit of the faith that obtained it: that is, not only because he gives light powerfully and mercifully, but because he also hears the cry of faith crying out steadfastly.

[HIERONYMUS.] In a figurative sense, those are called blind who could not yet say, “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35). It says, “beside the road,” because they seemed to possess knowledge of the law, but did not know the way, which is Christ. Some understand them to be the Pharisees and Sadducees. Others understand them as the two peoples, one of whom had the written law, the other the natural law. If the blind are referred to the Jews, then the crowd must be understood as the Gentiles. But if they are referred to both peoples, the crowd was from both [Col. 0359B] peoples.

[CHRYSOSTOM.] Alternatively, according to some, the blind men signify the two peoples from the Gentiles: one from Ham, the other from Japheth. They were blind because the light of the Only-Begotten had not appeared to them. The nations heard of Jesus’ passing through the apostles’ proclamation, in accordance with the testimony of the prophets, when he had already departed from Jericho—that is, from this world. For Jericho is interpreted as “moon,” by which the waning of our mortality is understood.

[BEDE.] Therefore, according to Luke, as the Lord approached Jericho, he restored light to the blind man, because before his Passion he preached only to the people of the Jews. But as he departed from Jericho, he gave light to the blind men, because after the resurrection and ascension he disclosed through the apostles to both Jews and Gentiles [Col. 0359C] the mysteries of eternal divinity and assumed humanity. Mark’s writing that one man was given sight looks especially to the salvation of the nations, whose blindness was most notorious. Matthew rightly says that two were enlightened, writing for Hebrews (Matt. 21); for he knew that knowledge of God would come to the nations. Hence he also relates that both the ass and the colt were brought together to the Lord, whereas the other three Evangelists mention only the ass, since they write for the Church of the nations. The Lord calls to himself, according to Mark, the blind man who cries out, when he entrusts the word of faith through holy preachers to the people of the nations longing for the knowledge of truth. They say with the Prophet: “Draw near to him and be enlightened” (Ps. 33). And again: “Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ shall give you light” (Eph. 5). By the garment understand worldly possessions and restraints. *Animaequior*, that is, “of a more even mind,” namely, more steadfast.

[BEDE, *On Luke*.] While our Creator approaches Jericho, the blind man returns to the light; for while divinity assumed the frailty of our flesh, the human race received again the light of eternal brightness which it had lost. The blind man sits beside the road when he begins to believe in him who says: “I am the way” (John 14). He begs when he asks. Hence it follows: “And he cried out.” Those who go before Jesus as he comes and rebuke the blind man signify the tumult of carnal vices, which scatter our thoughts and disturb the heart’s voice in prayer, lest Jesus come to enlighten the heart. The phantasms of sins that we have committed often come upon the heart [Col. 0360A] and trouble the mind; but then we must persevere all the more ardently in the cry of prayer. When the phantasms occur, we sense in some measure that Jesus is passing by; but when we persist forcefully in prayer, then Jesus stands within us, and thus lost light is restored.

## CHAPTER CXVI

M. 206[II] R. 117 L. 232

And when they had drawn near to Jerusalem and had come to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, saying to them: “Go into the village opposite you, and immediately you will find an ass tied up, and her colt tied with her, upon which no human being has ever sat. Untie it and bring it to me. And if anyone says anything to you, tell him that the Lord [Col. 0360B] needs its service, and he will immediately send them.”

[HIERONYMUS—BEDE.] Bethphage was a village of the priests and bore the figure of confession, because it is interpreted as “house of the cheek.” Its location on the Mount of Olives is aptly reported, since the olive is by nature a minister of light and a solace for labors and pains; for those who confess their sins cleave to Christ, who refreshes us with spiritual anointing and the light of knowledge. But lest the city set upon this mountain should remain hidden, he sends disciples into the village opposite them, so that through them he may penetrate the strongholds of the whole world set over against them.

[CHRYSOSTOM.] The ass and colt are the Jews and the nations, because of certain resemblances. This animal is unclean and, among beasts of burden, especially foolish, weak, ignoble, and burden-bearing. Such were human beings before Christ. They were also bound by the devil and could not escape by their own power.
