For as a ship, when its rudder is broken, is carried wherever the storm drives it, so a human being, having lost through sin the help of divine grace, does not do what he wills but what the devil wills. And just as it is initially within a people’s power to make whomever it wishes its king, but, once he has been made king, it is no longer within its power to depose him from the kingdom, and thus the people’s will is turned into necessity; so before a human being sins, he has free choice whether he wishes to be under the devil’s kingdom. But when, by sinning, he has been subjected to him, he cannot leave his power, because will has been turned into necessity. This is what sinners are accustomed to say: “We would like to be holy, [Col. 0360D] but we cannot.” They speak truly, but have no excuse, because at first they could have avoided being under the devil’s power, from which no one but God alone can deliver them.

No human being had ever sat upon the people of the nations, entangled in the bonds of unbelief: that is, none of the teachers had applied the bridle of correction by which it might be compelled either to restrain its tongue from evil or to go in the way of life. For a human being would sit upon it—that is, would rest upon it for its benefit by teaching—if someone rational corrected its foolishness by subduing it. Hence not without reason the two disciples are understood as the two orders of preachers, sent respectively to Jews and Gentiles. Some, however, understand these two as Peter and Philip, because they first brought the Gentiles to Christ: Philip, Samaria as the ass [Col. 0361A] (Acts 8), and Peter, Cornelius as the colt of Samaria (Acts 10).

[BEDE.] The apostles are called in pairs and sent in pairs, because charity is not in one person alone. Hence it is written: “Woe to one who is alone” (Eccl. 4). Two lead the Hebrews out of Egypt; two carry the cluster from the Holy Land, so that those set over others may always join knowledge to work; they may bring forth the two commandments from the two tablets; be washed and wash with two fountains; carry the ark of the Lord with two poles; and acknowledge the Lord between two cherubim, singing with spirit and mind. “Untie them,” he says, through teaching and miracles. As if it were said: “Whatever you untie on earth shall be untied in heaven.”

[CHRYSOSTOM.] Strangers bind in order to possess; Christ unties in order to hold. “He will immediately send them”: namely, the Lord, because by right of creation he desires [Col. 0361B] every creature to be devoted to his service. First people are called through the teaching and miracles of the apostles; afterward the Lord dismisses them to their own choice, that they may either remain in the faith to which they were called or return to their former practices: the Jews to their superstitions, the Gentiles to their impurities. For our being called is God’s work; but our living worthily in that calling is both ours and God’s. This is what he means by “he will send them,” not to the devil, but to their own choice.

M. 208[II] R. 118 L. 233

And the disciples went and did as Jesus commanded them. But as they were untying them, their owners [Col. 0361C] said to them: “Why are you untying the colt?” They said: “It is needed by the Lord,” and they let them go. And they brought the colt to Jesus, and throwing their garments upon the colt, they made him sit upon it.

[BEDE.] Mark writes that the colt was found tied outside before a door, at a crossroads. The door is he who says: “I am the door of the sheep; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved and will find pasture” (John 10). The people of the nations lacked these pastures while they stood tied outside the door at the crossroads. Aptly at the crossroads, because they did not hold one way of faith, but, wandering, followed uncertain paths of error. He stood at the crossroads who, in freedom of choice, wavered between death and life. Indeed, he had many masters, because, carried away by many errors through many doctrines, he served as many vices as demons possessed him. Yet those whom guilt, not nature, had made masters could not claim lordship for themselves; therefore, when “the Lord” is spoken of, the one Lord is recognized. For although there are many gods and many lords, nevertheless in general there is one God and one Lord.

Therefore those who objected to the untying of the colt, when they heard the Lord’s name, became quiet, because the teachers of error who opposed Christ’s teachers defended their darkness only until, with miracles bearing witness, God’s power shone forth. Thus the free people of believers, who bear God in their heart, are brought forward. The apostles’ garments are the divine precepts and spiritual grace by which the shamefulness of our flesh is covered. These people were formerly naked, but are now adorned through the apostles; they have Christ as their rider, so that sin may not reign in the wanton [Col. 0362A] flesh, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.

M. 207[VII] A. 101

Now this was done in order that what was said through the prophet might be fulfilled: “Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, meek, seated upon the colt of a yoked ass” (Isa. 62).

[AUGUSTINE.] This is written in the prophet Zechariah, from whose sense Matthew and John do not depart at all, even though they use different words. And because Jerusalem itself is Zion, he calls the good among that blind people “the daughter of Zion.” Say to her, you preachers, that she should not fear but, rejoicing, recognize her king, who governs minds and leads them to the kingdom of heaven, lest with the reprobate [Col. 0362B] she say: “We have no king but Caesar.”

[CHRYSOSTOM.] For he comes meek, not seated in a golden chariot flashing with purple, nor upon a horse that loves discord, but upon a beast friendly to peace.

[HIERONYMUS.] According to the letter, the Lord does not appear to have sat upon both animals during a short journey; rather, it is more fitting that he used the colt for riding, while the ass was led free. Mystically, however, he sat upon both peoples humbled under his dominion, Peter and Paul having been sent to them. Since the wanton and untamed Gentile people believed through the example of the faithful from the Synagogue, which had borne the yoke of the law, the colt is rightly said to have been the son of the yoked ass.

[CHRYSOSTOM.] Consider that, just as this kind of beast, if it goes astray, goes astray in simplicity and not in fierceness, so the people who believed in Christ from both peoples sinned before Christ not through malice but through ignorance.

A. 102[X]

The disciples did not understand these things at first; but when Jesus had been glorified, then they remembered that these things were written concerning him, and that they had done these things to him.

[AUGUSTINE.] That is, after he had shown the power of his resurrection, the disciples, recalling what they had seen, understood that according to prophecy he sat upon the colt, and that they had done to him nothing other than those things written concerning him.

M. 208[II] R. 118 L. 233

[Col. 0362D] And as he went along, many spread their garments in the road. Others cut branches from the trees and spread them in the road.

[CHRYSOSTOM.] Observe that the apostles placed their garments upon the beast, while the others placed theirs beneath the beast’s feet. Christians are spread out and adorned by the apostles’ commandments. But the commandments of the law—circumcision and the other Jewish observances—are trampled underfoot. For the garments of the crowd are the commandments of the law, trampled by Christians in the way, that is, in Christ. The crowd spreading its garments in the road are believers from the circumcision, who, seeing and recognizing Christ, cast down to earth the glory they had from the law, humbling themselves and saying with the Apostle: “Whatever things were [Col. 0363A] gain to me, these I have counted loss for Christ; and I reckon them dung, that I may gain Christ” (Phil. 3).

Those who cut branches from the trees are believing and instructed teachers who, taking examples from the prophets as branches from trees, spread them before the Gentile people in the way—that is, in Christ—so that it might enter the sanctuary of God without stumbling.

[BEDE.] Or thus: The Savior, seated upon the beast, goes toward Jerusalem not only when, governing the soul of each believer, he leads it to the peace of inward vision; but also when he presides over the holy Church universally and kindles it with longing for heavenly peace. The beast’s feet are the lowly persons whom the Apostle appoints to judge; though they are not the back upon which the Lord sat, they are nevertheless instructed together with the soldiers by John. Many indeed spread garments in the road, because the army of martyrs gives their bodies—the coverings, that is, of their souls—for the Lord, so that they may make a path of right living for the elect who follow. Finally, those spread garments in the road who tame their bodies through abstinence, that they may prepare a way to the mind for the Lord or provide good examples to those who follow. Those cut fronds or branches from trees who gather the sayings or examples of the Fathers and place them by humble preaching in God’s way before the mind of the hearer who is coming. For the righteous shall flourish like a palm tree, narrow in their roots and broad in [their leaves] and fruits; because they are the good fragrance of Christ and spread the way of God’s commandments by their good reputation.

[Col. 0363C] M. 209[I] R. 119 L. 234 A. 100

And when he was now drawing near to the descent of the Mount of Olives, all the crowds of those coming down began joyfully to praise God with a loud voice.

As the Lord comes down from the Mount of Olives—that is, humbles himself to the weakness of our flesh, though he is in the form of God—the crowds come down with him; that is, those who need mercy humble themselves under his hand, that they may be exalted by him.

M. R. L. A.

But the crowds going before and those following cried out, saying: “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes, the King, in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest! Blessed is the kingdom of our father David that comes! Hosanna in the highest!”

[HIERONYMUS.] The prophets go before; the apostles follow. “Deep calls to deep” (Ps. 41): that is, law calls to another law. The Jewish people went before; the Gentile people followed. All believers cry, “Hosanna,” to the Son of David—a word which in Latin means “salvation”—because they believe that the Son of David, the Son of God, the one Son, saves those on earth, so that the righteous may be built up in place of the fallen angels. They also confess: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” that is, of his Father, because the Son receives his name from the Father, and the Father from the Son. Blessing rendered to God is only confession and praise of the good things [Col. 0364A] bestowed by him. But blessing rendered by God is fulfilled in us when we are filled with his benefits. The one whom the faithful Jews believed would come, we believe has come. In his praise heavenly and earthly things sing together, because at his birth the heavenly powers sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to human beings” (Luke 2); while, as he was to triumph over the ruler of this world, mortals return the tribute of praise, saying: “Peace in heaven and glory in the highest.”

[BEDE.] The crowds fed with the five loaves and two fish wanted to seize Jesus and make him king, but he fled to the mountain (John 6). Now, however, he does not check the voices of those who sing that David’s kingdom is to be restored in him. In this he openly teaches that he was king of an everlasting empire [Col. 0364B] in heaven, not merely on earth, an empire which he would reach through contempt of death, the glory of the resurrection, and the triumph of the ascension. Hence after the resurrection he says to his disciples: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28). The crowd’s praise agrees with Gabriel’s words, who said to the Lord’s mother: “He will be great, and will be called Son of the Most High; and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever” (Luke 1). Therefore they rightly cry, “Hosanna in the highest,” that is, “Save us in the heavenly places,” where every knee of beings in heaven, on earth, and under the earth shall bow to him (Phil. 2).

It should be noted that *hosanna* is a Hebrew word, compounded from a corrupted and a complete element. For “save” or “make saving” is called *hosi* among them, and *anna* is an interjection of one beseeching. [Col. 0364C] Thus in Psalm 117, where the Seventy translators rendered, “O Lord, save me,” it is written in Hebrew: *anna adonai osi anna*. Our translator Jerome, explaining this more carefully, rendered it thus: “I beseech you, O Lord, save, I beseech you.” “O Lord” has the same force through the interjection of a petitioner as “I beseech you, Lord” has through the actual word of entreaty. Therefore *hosanna* means “Save, I beseech you,” the vowel ending the preceding word being elided when *osi* is spoken in full. Metrists call this *synaloepha* in scanning verses, although in scanning they pass over a written letter. But in the word *hosanna* the letter *i* is not written; rather, while the speakers’ meaning remains intact, it is entirely omitted.

On the next day, the great crowd that had come for the feast, hearing that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, crying: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel!”

[AUGUSTINE.] Palm branches are praises, signifying the victory by which the Lord was to overcome death and triumph over the devil. *Hosanna*, as some Hebrews say, is the cry of one rejoicing or beseeching, indicating rather an emotion than signifying any particular thing, just as *raca* is said to be an interjection of indignation.

[CHRYSOSTOM.] Hence neither Greek nor Latin could translate it according to its sound; but according to its sense some translate *hosanna* as “glory,” others as “redemption,” others as “make saving” or “save me.”

L. 233[V] M. 213

And some Pharisees from the crowd said to him: “Teacher, rebuke your disciples.” He replied: “I tell you: if these should be silent, the stones would cry out.”

[BEDE.] They call the Lord teacher because they knew that he taught what was true. Thus it is remarkable madness to say that the disciples of truth ought to be rebuked. When the Lord was crucified, those known to him, standing at a distance, did not dare confess him as God; but the rocks that were split apart, as the tombs were opened, openly proclaimed God and Lord of the world. Mystically, “the stones will cry out” means that the converted nations [Col. 0365B] will proclaim God while the Jews are partially blinded.

L. 236[X]

And when he drew near, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: “If only you too had known! And indeed, on this your day, the things that make for your peace; but now they are hidden from your eyes. For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart, hem you in on every side, and cast you and your children within you to the ground.”

Read the sentence thus: “If you had known that days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you,” etc., “you too,” understand, “would weep”—you who now, because you do not know what threatens, rejoice while surrendering your flesh to pleasures. “And indeed, on this your day,” that is, amid this splendor of your prosperity, “which makes for your temporal peace,” understand, “you would weep if you had known that these evils were to come upon you; but now they are hidden from the eyes of your heart.” Or the beginning of the chapter may be read as one sentence as far as “that make for your peace,” as follows: “He wept, saying, ‘If only you too had known with me’”—understand, “the ruin which threatens”—“and indeed,” that is, “even certainly,” “on this your day, for the peace that is yours,” understand, “you would weep.” “But now they are hidden” begins another sentence, continuing to the end of the chapter.

L. 237[II] M. 242 R. 137

“And they will not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not know the time of your visitation.”

[BEDE.] We know that the destruction of Jerusalem was carried out by the Roman leaders Vespasian and Titus. The very removal of the city now built outside the gate where the Lord was crucified bears witness that the former Jerusalem was utterly destroyed. This was the cause of its destruction: it did not know the Lord when he visited it. Hence that prophetic saying: “The kite in the sky knew its appointed time; the turtledove, swallow, and stork observed the time of their coming; but my people did not know the judgment of the Lord” (Jer. 1). The Lord wept once over the city when he foretold that it would perish, but every day through his elect in the Church he laments the reprobate, who do not know why they are lamented, who, according to Solomon, “rejoice when they have done evil and exult in most wicked things” (Prov. 2). If they foresaw their condemnation, [Col. 0366A] they would lament themselves with the tears of the elect.

The perverse soul has its own day here, rejoicing in a passing season. Its present circumstances make for peace, because while it rejoices in temporal things, is elevated by honors, gives itself up to the pleasure of the flesh, and is frightened by no fear of future punishment, it has peace in its own day; but on the final day it will suffer the grave scandal of condemnation. The enemies are evil spirits, who besiege the soul as it departs from the body—the soul which, while still in the flesh, they encouraged with deceptive pleasures. They surround it with a rampart when, setting before its eyes again the wicked deeds it committed, they constrain it into the fellowship of their condemnation. They hem it in on every side when they rehearse to it not only the wickedness of its acts but also that of its speech. Then the soul is cast down to the earth through awareness of its guilt when the flesh is pressed into dust. Then its children fall into death when unlawful thoughts proceeding from it are scattered in the final retribution, as it is written: “On that day all their thoughts shall perish” (Ps. 145). A stone upon a stone means a hard thought upon a hard thought. God visits the perverse soul daily—at times by command, at times by chastisement, at times by miracle—so that one who does not know may hear, or, pierced by suffering, may return, or, overcome by benefits, may be ashamed of the evil done.

## CHAPTER CXVII

M. 110[X]

[Col. 0366C] And when he had entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred, saying: “Who is this?” And the people said: “This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth of Galilee.”

[HIERONYMUS.] The city marvels at the size of the crowd, not knowing the truth about him whom they meet with praises. Yet confession begins with the lesser people, so that it may reach the greater.

A. 211[I] M. 121 M. 238 L. 21

And Jesus entered the temple of God.

Entering the temple, he gave us an example: wherever we go, we should first visit, if it is there, the house of prayer, and, commended to God through prayers, then depart for the business to be done. Next, he showed in the temple that the foretold ruin arose chiefly through the fault of the priests, and that the root of destruction proceeded from there.

[CHRYSOSTOM.] When a physician enters a sick person’s house, he immediately inquires about the stomach, lest, if it is unhealthy, the whole body become unhealthy.

[BEDE.] The priesthood is understood by the heart and stomach, through which the people ought to be governed spiritually. Thus, if the priests sin, the whole people turns to sin. Each Christian gives an account for his own sin, but priests do so not only for their own sins but also for the sins of all who are subject to them. And just as, on seeing a tree with pale, withered leaves, you understand that some fault lies at its root, so when you see an undisciplined [Col. 0367A] people, know without doubt that its priesthood is not sound.

And having made something like a whip out of cords, he drove out all those selling and buying in the temple, together with the sheep and oxen; he overturned the money-changers’ tables, poured out their coins, and overturned the seats of those selling doves, and said to them: A. “Take these things away from here, and do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.” R. M. L. “It is written: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations’; but you have made it a den of robbers.” R. And he did not allow anyone to carry a vessel through the temple.

[HIERONYMUS.] He prohibited vessels of commerce, not vessels dedicated to God. It should be known that, in accordance with the commands of the Law, when the Jewish people streamed to the Temple of the Lord—famous throughout the whole world—from almost every region, [Col. 0367B] innumerable sacrificial victims of bulls, rams, and goats were offered, especially on feast days. The poor, lest they be without a sacrifice, offered young pigeons and turtledoves. But because those coming from afar often did not have sacrificial animals, the priests devised a way of making profit from the people: namely, selling animals to those who lacked animals for sacrifice and then taking them back again. But when it happened that certain poor persons did not even have the means to buy birds, the priests placed money-changers there, who would lend money on security (Deut. 15). Yet because the Law commanded that no one should take interest, they devised another trick: [Col. 0367C] they made them *colybistae* rather than money-changers. The Latin language does not convey the precise sense of this word. Among them *colybia* denotes what we call petty gifts—for example, roasted chickpeas, raisins, and fruits of various kinds. Thus the *colybistae* received various articles in place of interest, so that they might exact in such goods, purchasable with money, what was not permitted in money itself—as though Ezekiel had not expressly warned against this, saying: “You shall not take interest or excess” (Ezek. 22). The Lord drove all these out of the Temple. For in a house of prayer no one ought to do anything except that for which it was made; hence it has its name.

[BEDE.] A robber is one who turns God’s Temple into a robbers’ den, pursuing profit from religion. [Col. 0367D] Certainly there was no doubt that those sitting in the Temple, when some did not give, sought means of injuring them.

[HIERONYMUS.] According to the mystical sense, Jesus enters the Temple of his Father daily and drives out of the Church all who seek their own interests in it rather than those of God; and therefore he holds sellers and buyers alike guilty of one crime. Whoever adds sins to sins, as it were joins a rope by which he is scourged. The cords, then, by which the merchants are expelled are the accumulations of evil deeds. Hence Isaiah: “Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity” (Isa. 5). And Solomon: “Each person is bound with the cords of his own sins” (Prov. 5). By oxen are signified the preachers of heavenly doctrine. Hence the Apostle: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out grain” (1 Cor. 9). Therefore those sell oxen who expound the Scriptures for a price, [Col. 0368A] or in order to receive praise and honor from the people. They also sell sheep—that is, the common people. To whom? To the devil. Or thus: innocent sheep supply their wool for clothing. By these, then, works of purity are here signified when they are performed for human praise. Since the Lord shows the life and teaching of such people to be reprobate, he is accordingly said to cast out both sheep and oxen. Those lend money in the Church who serve, not hypocritically heavenly pursuits, but openly earthly gain. Jesus therefore overturns their coins and tables, because in the end the very things they loved will be destroyed. Because of priests’ greed, God’s altars are called the tables of money-changers.

[CHRYSOSTOM.] He overturned, then, the tables of the money-changers, signifying that in God’s Temple there should be no coins except spiritual ones—[Col. 0368B] that is, those bearing God’s image, not the image of the devil. Or, certainly, by “the tables of the money-changers,” that is, of the priests, he means the Scriptures: for when the New Testament succeeded the Old, their Scriptures were overturned. What are the many pigeons doing for sale in the Temple, now that the one freely given dove has descended into the Temple of Christ’s body? The Temple—that is, the Church—will no longer be pleasing to God in a sacrifice of pigeons, but in the Holy Spirit. Hence the prophet: “I will not take calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks; for all the beasts of the forests are mine, the cattle on the mountains and oxen. I know all the birds of heaven” (Ps. 49). God does not desire sacrifices but faith. One bull has been offered for the whole flock.

[HIERONYMUS.] Those who sell pigeons in the Church [Col. 0368C] are those who sell the grace of the Holy Spirit so that they may devour the people subject to them. Of these it is said: “Who devour my people as bread is eaten” (Ps. 13). In the teachers’ chairs is indicated a dignity reduced to nothing when it has been mingled with profit.

[GREGORY.] The Lord likewise detests within the holy Church those who, drawing near to him through sacred orders, seek from those same orders not the merits of virtues but the resources of this present life.

[AUGUSTINE.] Therefore, when they suffer anything on account of their iniquities, all those who either feign good deeds or openly do evil in the Church should recognize that the Lord has made a scourge out of the little cords of their sins; he admonishes them to change and not be merchants, [Col. 0368D] lest at last they hear: “Bind their hands and feet, and cast them into the outer darkness.”

[BEDE.] Further: God’s Temple in the city is the religious life among the people. Many, while receiving a place in sacred orders because of the appearance of religion, turn the office of religion into the commerce of earthly trade. They sell in the Temple who grant for reward what is rightly due to certain persons. They buy in the Temple who disdain doing what they ought, and purchase release from patrons. To them it is said: “You have made my house a den of robbers,” because, while perverse persons occupy the place of religion, they kill there by malice where they ought to give life by prayer. The mind of the faithful person is God’s Temple; it becomes a den of robbers when, abandoning holiness, it endeavors to do that by which it may harm its neighbors. [Col. 0369A] Let there be, then, no commerce in the house of our breast: no trading of sellers and buyers, no greed for gifts. It should be noted whether this expulsion from the Temple occurred once or twice, as some have thought, because John recounts it in an order far different from the others. Yet nothing conflicts with the narrative, since at one time he recapitulates what preceded and at another anticipates what followed.

A. 21[X]

But his disciples remembered that it was written: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. 68).

[AUGUSTINE.] He is consumed with zeal for God’s house who strives to correct everything perverse there. If he cannot correct it, he endures it; he groans and bears the chaff, so that he may enter the [Col. 0369B] granary. For example: do you see a brother running to the theater? Forbid him, warn him, grieve for him. Do you see him running to drink? Forbid him, if you can. Is he a friend? Let him be warned gently. Is he a wife? Let her be restrained most severely. Thus zeal for God’s house consumes you. But if, cold and dull, you say in your heart, “What concern are other people’s sins to me? It is enough for me to preserve my own soul for God,” then surely that servant who hid the talent has not come to your mind.

M. 212[X]

And the blind and the lame came to him in the Temple, and he healed them.

[HIERONYMUS.] Among all the signs, this seems more wonderful: that one man, with blows of a scourge, drove out such a great [Col. 0369C] multitude, although those whose profits he was destroying raged against him. For something fiery and star-like shone from his eyes, and the majesty of divinity gleamed in his face.

M. 213[V] L. 235

But when the chief priests and scribes saw the wonders that he did, and the children crying out in the Temple and saying, “Hosanna to the Son of David,” they were indignant and said to him, “Do you hear what these are saying?” But Jesus said to them, “Certainly. Have you never read: ‘Out of the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise’?” (Ps. 8).

[CHRYSOSTOM.] How moderately he tempered his reply. He did not say what the slanderers wanted to hear: “The children do well to bear witness to me.” [Col. 0369D] Nor again did he say, “The children are mistaken,” as though to say, “You ought to pardon their age”; rather, he brought forward testimony from the Psalm. If we remember the crowd before and behind him crying aloud above, we understand that they were infants not in age but in simplicity of heart. For nursing infants neither understand nor praise. But those children were called nursing infants because they cried out, stirred by the delight of miracles as a child delights in the sweetness of milk. And every simple teaching is called milk, because it gives delight as milk is sucked without the pain of teeth.

A. 23[IV] M. 141 R. 77

Therefore the Jews answered and said to him, “What sign do you show us, that you do these things?”

[Col. 0370A] Not daring to lay hands on him, they seek a sign to justify his casting the customary trade out of the Temple. Rightly indeed does he cleanse the figurative Temple, because he will, together with the Father as God, raise up the most pure Temple of his own body, dissolved in death by human beings. This is what follows.

A. 24[X]

Jesus answered and said to them, “Destroy this Temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” Therefore the Jews said, “This Temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?” But he was speaking of the Temple of his body.

[ALBINUS.] After the Temple, which Solomon completed in seven years, had been destroyed by the Chaldeans, and after the captivity had been relaxed after seventy years, rebuilding began by command of Cyrus the Persian. [Col. 0370B] But the children of the exile could not complete it before forty-six years, because of attacks by neighboring nations. This number corresponds to the human body. For natural philosophers report that the form of the human body is completed in such a number of days. During the first six days from conception it has the likeness of milk; in the following nine it changes into blood; in the following twelve it is solidified; and in the remaining eighteen it is formed into the outlines of its limbs.

[AUGUSTINE.] Here are forty-five days; add the day on which the body, differentiated into limbs, begins to grow. This number is also found in the letters of Adam’s name in Greek: α, *alpha*, denotes one; δ, *delta*, [Col. 0370C] four; likewise α, *alpha*, one; μ, *mu*, forty. These four letters signify Adam scattered through the four parts of the world in his children; hence these four letters are found at the beginnings of the names of the parts of the world: ἀνατολή (*anatolē*), the east; δύσις (*dysis*), the west; ἄρκτος (*arktos*), the north; μεσημβρία (*mesēmbria*), the south. Since Adam is understood in the number forty-six, as though in something built, Christ under this number took from Adam, through the Virgin Mary, the Temple of his body. To Adam it is said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3); and Christ says of himself, “You will destroy this Temple, and I will raise it.” Thus scattered Adam is raised in Christ and gathered from the four parts of the world into the one body of Christ, which is the Church. [Col. 0370D] Hence it is said that the elect are to be gathered from the four winds.

## Chapter 118

L. 207[VIII] R. 136

And looking up, he saw rich people putting their gifts into the treasury.

[BEDE.] The *gazophylacium* is called the place where riches are stored, because in Greek φυλάσσειν (*phylassein*) means “to keep,” while *gaza* means “riches” in Persian. It was a chest with an opening on top, placed near the altar on the right side for those entering the house of the Lord. Into it the priests guarding the doors put the money brought to the Temple, and it was [Col. 0371A] kept for the restoration of that same Temple; see the Book of Chronicles.

And he saw a certain poor widow putting in two small coins, which make a quadrans. And summoning his disciples, he said to them, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all.”

Accountants call a *quadrans* a fourth part of anything—for example, of a place, a period of time, or money. Perhaps, then, it here signifies a fourth part of a shekel, that is, five obols. In the moral sense it is intimated how pleasing to God is whatever we offer with a good disposition. For God weighs the heart, not the substance; nor does he consider how much is offered in his sacrifices, but from how much it is produced. According to allegory, the rich who put gifts into the treasury signify Jews proud of [Col. 0371B] the righteousness of the Law; the poor widow, however, signifies the simplicity of the Church. She is rightly called poor because she has cast away both the spirit of pride and the riches of the world. She is a widow because her husband died for her. She puts two small coins into the treasury because she brings before God love of him and of her neighbor, or faith and prayer.

For all these gave from their abundance into God’s gifts; but she, from what she lacked, put in all the livelihood that she had.

“From what she lacked” means her good will: for she gave what she could, and desired what she could not give. The Jew offers riches from abundance, as if praying within himself: “God, I thank you [Col. 0371C] that I am not like the rest of humanity, robbers, unjust persons” (Luke 18), and so forth. The Church puts all her livelihood into God’s gifts, as if praying: “I attribute nothing to my own merits, Lord God; be merciful to me, a sinner” (ibid.).

L. 214[X]

And he also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves as righteous and despised others: “Two men went up to the Temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.”

“They went up,” he says; and the ascent of the Temple had fifteen steps. He carefully shows that one ought not glory in works, but humbly trust in God’s grace. The tax collector pertains to the humility [Col. 0371D] of the Church, the Pharisee to the wickedness of pride.

Standing, the Pharisee prayed these things within himself: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity—robbers, unjust persons, adulterers—or even like this tax collector.”

There are four forms by which all the swelling of the arrogant is revealed: either they think they possess good from themselves; or, if they believe it given from above, they suppose it was given to them for their merits; or they boast of possessing what they do not possess; or, despising others, they wish to appear uniquely to possess what they do possess [or: do not possess], as this Pharisee did. Therefore he departed from the Temple without justification, because he boastfully preferred himself to the tax collector.

[Col. 0372A] “I fast twice in the week; I give tithes of all that I possess.”

Ezekiel says that the living creatures shown to him were full of eyes (Ezek. 1), because the conduct of the saints ought to be visible from every side. But we often neglect some things while attending to others. The Pharisee had an eye to abstinence and mercy, but did not have one for guarding humility. And what use is it for a city to be guarded if one opening is left through which enemies may enter?

And the tax collector, standing at a distance, would not even lift his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” I tell you: this man went down justified to his house rather than the other.

That is, by comparison with the other, or more justified than [Col. 0372B] he; for the one was justified in his own eyes by works, while this man was justified before God by faith. To stand at a distance and not lift one’s eyes are signs of humility, which God beholds from near at hand. This man presses down his conscience but raises up his hope; he strikes his breast, exacting punishment from himself so that God may spare him; he confesses so that God may forgive him. God does not know what this man acknowledges. But what is it to strike the breast except to accuse what is hidden in the breast and, by a visible blow, punish the hidden sin? Typologically, the Pharisee is the people of the Jews, who exalts its merits from the justifications of the Law and withdraws in pride. The tax collector, however, is the Gentile, who, humbly confessing his sins, approaches God and is exalted.

L. 215[V] M. 231

[Col. 0372C] “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

After the controversy of the Pharisee and the tax collector had been set forth, the Judge’s sentence was given and confirmed, so that pride might be avoided.

M. 214[VI] R. 120

And leaving them, when it was already evening, he went out beyond the city to Bethany and remained there.

[HIERONYMUS.] Leaving the unbelievers, he went to Bethany, which is interpreted “house of obedience,” already prefiguring the calling of the Gentiles. At evening he went away, because, as the sun departed, he left darkness among the Jews. In the great city he found no host, but in a small rural place, with Lazarus and his sisters, whose village [Col. 0372D] was Bethany.

M. 140[VI] R. 76

And when the crowd knew that he had gone out beyond the city, they followed him; and receiving those who needed care, he healed them.

When the Lord entered the city, very many met him with the greatest eagerness; and afterward they saw the wonders that he performed. Who, then, would dare deny that at least the crowd requiring care followed him as he went out? For he healed every illness, so that works might persuade those whom his word had not persuaded to believe. Hence John says: “When he was in Jerusalem at the Passover, on the feast day, many believed in his name, seeing the signs that he did” (John 2). They recount a similar healing: [Col. 0373A] Matthew in chapter 160, and Mark in the corresponding canon.

## Chapter 119

A. 24[X]

Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. He came to Jesus by night and said to him: “Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher. For no one can do these signs which you do unless God is with him.”

[AUGUSTINE.] Nicodemus came to Jesus at night either because, being one of the rulers, he feared to offend the people; or because he was a teacher in Israel and was ashamed to learn openly. Night, therefore, signifies the letter of the Law, or ignorance of heart, or fear. Nicodemus, however, [Col. 0373B] one of those who believed through signs, is a figure of catechumens: although they believe, they nevertheless reach baptism through a certain night of the sacraments, where, reborn, they pass from the trackless way of darkness to the way of heavenly light. For if the figure of baptism was so powerful that those baptized through Moses in the cloud and in the sea were brought to manna, can one not arrive at the same goal through true baptism? What is manna? “I,” he says, “am the living bread that came down from heaven.”

Jesus answered and said to him, “Amen, amen, I tell you: unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.”

That is, he cannot know me, who am the kingdom of the Father, who am the vision of truth. Since Nicodemus wisely observed the manifest signs, he deserved to be more fully taught about the second birth [Col. 0373C] and the other mysteries of faith.

Nicodemus said to him, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?”

The Spirit speaks to him, but he savors his own flesh, not Christ’s—like those who thought that the Lord could be cooked and eaten in pieces like a lamb, when the Lord said: “Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he shall not have life in himself” (John 6); and immediately, withdrawing, they no longer followed him. But the Lord explained this to those who remained, saying: “What I have spoken is spirit and life; for the spirit gives life, but the flesh profits nothing” [Col. 0373D] (ibid.), lest they understand carnally what he had said. Thus Nicodemus did not yet know the parents who beget unto life. One generation is carnal; the other is spiritual. It should be known that just as the womb cannot be entered again, neither can baptism. Whoever is born from the Catholic Church is born, as it were, from Sarah; but whoever is born from heresy, as it were, from the slave woman. Consider why the Lord says, “I am the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (Exod. 3), as though Noah, who was before them, and Moses, who came after them, were not holy patriarchs. For in these three we find free women and slave women giving birth; and all this is a figure, as the Apostle says: “These things happened to them in a figure” (1 Cor. 10). And: “They were written,” he says, “for our sake, upon whom the end of the ages has come” (ibid.). In the generations of free women [Col. 0374A] and slave women are four classes of people, in which the pattern of all Christianity is fulfilled. Let slave women represent the evil, free women the good. Thus either free women bear good children, as Sarah bore Isaac (Gen. 21); or both evil and good, as Rebecca bore Esau and Jacob (Gen. 25); or evil women bear evil children, as Hagar bore Ishmael (Gen. 16); or evil women bear both good and evil children, as Jacob’s slave women did (Gen. 30). Correspondingly, either good people baptize good people, as Ananias baptized Paul (Acts 9); or evil people, as Philip baptized Simon Magus (Acts 8); or evil people baptize both good and evil, as do certain preachers whom the Apostle says customarily proclaim the Gospel not chastely. He tolerates them in Christian fellowship and says: “What then, provided that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed? And in this I rejoice” (Phil. [Col. 0374B] 1). He did not rejoice in another’s evil, but because truth was preached. If such men baptized those like themselves, then evil people baptized evil people. But if they baptized persons such as the Lord admonishes us about when he says, “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23), then evil people baptized good people. Therefore, just as it did not harm those sons of Jacob who were born of slave women, so that they held the land of promise equally with brothers born of free women—rather, their father’s seed prevailed—so whoever are baptized through evil persons, although born from evil persons, yet because they are born from the seed of God’s Word, which is figured in Jacob, will, if they are willing to be good, possess the inheritance with their brothers.

[BEDE.] Therefore, whether a heretic, schismatic, or any criminal baptizes in confession of the holy Trinity, [Col. 0374C] that person cannot validly be rebaptized by Catholics, lest the confession or invocation of so great a name seem to be annulled. And in the womb of the Church there is a great struggle between good and evil, just as Jacob and Esau struggled (Gen. 25); and the evil always persecute the good, as Ishmael persecuted Isaac. For this reason Sarah said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave woman and her son,” because she saw mockery in the play, not because Ishmael was playing with her son (Gen. 21). Hence the Apostle: “As then he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so it is now” (Gal. 4). Those born according to the flesh are lovers of the world; those born according to the Spirit, lovers of Christ. Those who deceive us through mockery persecute us all the more: “Come, come, [Col. 0374D] be baptized here; here you have true baptism.” Ishmael, then, was not disinherited because he was born from a slave woman, but because he was proud. For if he had been disinherited for that reason, Jacob’s sons would not have been admitted to the inheritance. But when Sarah afflicts the slave woman Hagar, this is not called persecution but correction. Hence the angel also says to her when she flees: “Return and humble yourself under your mistress’s hand” (Gen. 16). Thus good rulers justly afflict heretics and all who are harmful to the Church with exile and other legal penalties.

Jesus answered: “Amen, amen, I tell you: unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.”

[Col. 0375A] The sense is this: whoever scorns to be reborn through the visible sacrament of water and the Holy Spirit, and ends life in this neglect, will be excluded forever from God’s kingdom. But those who die for confession of Christ without having received the washing of regeneration obtain, for the forgiveness of sins, as much as if they had been washed in the sacred font of baptism. For he who said, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven,” made these persons exceptions by another statement, where he says no less generally: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I too will confess him before my Father” (Luke 12). Indeed, the blood and water that came from the wound in Christ’s pierced side alike bore the type of martyrdom and baptism, by which one goes to heaven. Finally, if the moment of death excludes from the sacrament [Col. 0375B] of baptism persons rooted in faith in Christ and unfeigned love, it is clear that they are not excluded from salvation. For they are martyrs before God if they were ready for martyrdom with a pure heart; and they have been baptized in fire and Spirit, according to what the Lord foretold to the Apostles: “But you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts 1). Hence Ambrose says concerning Valentinian: “My belly aches” (Jer. 4), to use the prophet’s example, “because I have lost the one whom I was going to regenerate.” Yet he did not lose the grace for which he had asked. Augustine, in Book Four on Baptism: “Considering the thief to whom it was said, ‘Today you will be with me in paradise’ (Luke 23), I find that not only suffering for Christ’s name can supply what is lacking of baptism, but also faith and conversion of heart, if, in the constraints of time, help cannot be obtained for celebrating [Col. 0375C] the mystery of baptism.”

[BEDE.] How much force there is, even without the sacrament of visible baptism, in the Apostle’s saying, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10), is fulfilled invisibly when not contempt for religion but a crisis of necessity excludes the ministry of baptism. It should be known that Augustine did not retract this statement, as some falsely think; rather, the point he made in the example—that the thief had not been baptized—rests on the fact that it is uncertain whether he had been baptized or not. Therefore when elsewhere he says that we do not believe a catechumen, though dead in good works, to possess life unless he is a martyr, this and similar statements were spoken of those who despise the sacrament of baptism.

[Col. 0375D] “What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of spirit is spirit.”

He distinguishes spiritual birth from carnal birth. From the Holy Spirit our spirit—that is, the soul—is born in God when its sins are remitted through God’s grace, which is understood as the Holy Spirit, lest it incur the punishment of condemnation because of them. For it is not the flesh but the soul that can feel or be punished, and the penalty of sin is remitted only to that which can be punished.

“Do not wonder that I said to you: you must be born again. The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes. So it is with everyone born of the Spirit.”

[Col. 0376A] The Spirit has power to impart the grace of forgiveness to whom he wills, and you hear his bodily voice when he speaks in holy preachers, according to the saying: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10). Yet you do not know whence that voice comes through understanding to certain persons—that is, why, though the same Spirit is acting, some perhaps less learned persons understand that voice—or whither it goes from others who are equally present—that is, why it passes by them without understanding. In this manner occurs that birth which is from the Spirit: you do not know how to examine how the Spirit works invisibly, when he himself performs nothing bodily. Do not wonder, then, about what the Spirit does in that generation if you do not know it.

[Col. 0376B] [BEDE.] Or thus: the Spirit has it in his power to enlighten the heart of whomever he wills; and if, while you are present, he fills someone for a time, you indeed hear the Spirit’s voice, but do not know whence it comes or where it goes—that is, how it entered that person’s heart or how it withdrew. For its nature is invisible. Thus, through the Spirit’s action, one who was not reborn begins invisibly to be reborn, so that the unbeliever does not know whence he comes or where he goes: by what grace he comes into the adoption of God’s children and goes into the reception of the heavenly kingdom. Because these things are unknown to the carnal person, he asks again.

Nicodemus answered and said to him, “How can these things happen?” Jesus answered and said to him, “Are you a teacher in Israel, and do you not know these things?”

[AUGUSTINE.] Why did the Lord seem to mock this [Col. 0376C] teacher? He wished him to be born of the Spirit, which cannot happen unless one is humble. But he was puffed up and seemed to himself to be a person of some importance because he was a teacher of the Jews.

“Amen, amen, I tell you: we speak what we know, and testify to what we have seen, and you do not receive our testimony.”

If they were humble and born of the Spirit, they would believe what the Lord, with the prophets and Apostles, testifies outwardly to the world concerning things seen in God’s hiddenness. The Evangelist John customarily doubles *amen* in confirmation of divine words, observing what the Lord says: “Let your speech be, Yes, yes” (Matt. 5)—that is, say nothing with duplicity, but believe in your heart as you utter with your mouth. Therefore, *amen, amen* is as though he said: “I pronounce it with a twofold truth, of both mouth and heart.”

“If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?”

[AUGUSTINE.] The sense is: If you neither believe nor even understand that I can raise up the Temple destroyed by you—which is an earthly thing—how will you believe that people can be reborn through the Spirit? Yet, having invited him to humility through rebuke, he continues to instruct him about his divine and human birth, his passion and ascension, and many other matters. Hence follows:

“And no one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.”

[Col. 0377A] “No one ascends”—that is, no one causes ascent to the height of heavenly life—except he who descended from there by humbling himself: namely, the Son of God, the Father’s Word, assuming our weakness, according to which he is called less than the Father. He descended, I say, by becoming the Son of Man, though he remains in heaven—that is, in that equality with the Father which he had before. For by assuming what he was not, he did not lose what he was.

[AUGUSTINE.] In another sense: God did not consider his divinity unworthy of the name “Son of Man,” just as he deemed his flesh worthy of the name “Son of God,” lest Christ be spoken of as though he were two Christs. Thus, by the distinction between divinity and weakness, the Son of God remained in heaven and the Son of Man walked on earth. But through the unity of person, by which Christ is one in two natures, the Son of God also walked on earth; and that same Son of Man is said to have descended from heaven and, before the Passion, to have been in heaven. The sense, then, is: no one ascends into heaven unless he descended, so that those who were to ascend through him might be one in him and with him. The Lord ascended, but the body did not ascend; it was lifted into heaven by him who ascended.

[AUGUSTINE.] For if someone descends, for example, naked from a mountain and, when he ascends, clothes himself, we rightly say, “No one ascends except the one who descended.” We do not consider the clothing he lifted with himself; we speak only of the person who was clothed as having ascended.

“And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

[ALBINUS.] The people of Israel, wearied by their long labor in the wilderness, murmured against the Lord and Moses; therefore the Lord sent fiery serpents among them. When Moses had prayed, the Lord commanded him to make a bronze serpent and for those struck by bites to look upon it, so that they might live.

[AUGUSTINE.] Who are the biting serpents? Sins. Who is the lifted-up serpent? The Lord dead upon the cross, figured by the image of a serpent because death came from a serpent. Therefore those who look upon him in faith are delivered from the wounds of fiery serpents—that is, from the incitements of vices that sting the soul to death.

“For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.”

[Col. 0377D] He reveals the cause of human salvation: namely, the love of God the Father, from which every restoration or institution comes through his Son in the Holy Spirit. He says concerning believers’ attaining this from the Son of God the same thing that he said above concerning the Son of Man: that we who were created through him in divinity might be restored through that same one in manhood.

“For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him.”

The Savior came to save, not to judge—that is, not to condemn. But if a person is judged, he has this from himself, because he did not believe.

“Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe [Col. 0378A] has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.”

Judgment has not yet appeared, but it has already been made. For “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2).

[AUGUSTINE.] He knows who will remain for the crown and who for the flame. He knows the wheat in his threshing floor; he knows the chaff; he knows the crop and also the weeds. Let us not listen to those who deny, from this passage, that a day of judgment is still to come. For they say: “If one who believes will not come into judgment, and one who does not believe has already been judged, whom will the Lord judge on the day of judgment?” They do not understand that the past tense is used for the future. For “has been judged” means “has been condemned by God’s foreknowledge,” who knows what awaits unbelievers; and where it says, “will not come into judgment,” [Col. 0378B] it should be understood as “will not come into condemnation.”

“And this is the judgment: that light has come into the world, and human beings loved darkness rather than light, for their works were evil. For everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved.”

By “judgment” he means eternal condemnation, which will consist in not knowing God, just as eternal life is knowing him. Because the light—that is, the Word in flesh—has come and rouses and moves people to recognize their evils, in which all are involved, those who hate the admonishing light are certainly judged. They drive it away, lest their evils be reproved: namely, impiety, unbelief, hatred of the eternal light, and refusal to look upon it, preferring to remain in the darkness of sins. Certainly everyone whose intention is evil, acting with love for that evil, hates the light that exposes evils; and so does not come to the light in order to be joined to it, but flees lest the evils he loves be reproved.

Whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be made manifest, because they have been done in God.

Because the beginning of good is the accusation of evil, whoever, admonished by the light, accuses his own evils does the truth—that is, he does what truth commands—so that this accusation of his and the other good things that he does may be made manifest as wrought by divine illumination. [AUGUSTINE.] Therefore, whoever wishes to come to the light should not merely abstain from grave sins, but should also make a true confession even of lesser ones; for many small sins, [Col. 0378D] if neglected, kill. Small drops fill a river, and small grains of sand, if they are many, overwhelm a ship. This is also what a neglected bilge does: water gradually enters through the bilge, but by entering for a long time and not being pumped out, it sinks the ship. And because God chastises sinners in this age for their cleansing, bear with a father who disciplines you, lest you experience a judge who punishes you.

A. 86[X]

And they returned, each to his own house. But Jesus went to the Mount of Olives; and at daybreak he came again into the temple. And all the people came to him, and, sitting down, he taught them.

When all who had followed him from the city had returned, he reached Bethany, which is on the Mount of Olives. [Col. 0379A] Do not wonder that he came there at night, since he preached to Nicodemus at night; and elsewhere we read of him that he spent the night in prayer to God (Luke 6). You also read that before the Passion, after supper had been completed at Jerusalem and a hymn sung, he went out with his disciples, according to his custom, to the Mount of Olives (Matt. 6). [ALBINUS.] The Mount of Olives signifies the loftiness of the Lord’s loving-kindness and mercy; from it comes to us chrism—that is, the anointing by which we are anointed to contend against the devil. In Greek *eleos* means “mercy”; an olive grove is called *oleon*; and an anointing with oil brings relief to weary and aching limbs. Oil rises above and immediately surpasses whatever liquid you pour over it. But the Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are [Col. 0379B] over all his works (Ps. 144). The time of daybreak shows the light of the Gospel having risen and the shadow of the Law removed. Every day the sun of righteousness rises at daybreak in the temple, when he mercifully enlightens sinners who come to him by the illumination of the Holy Spirit. His sitting signifies the humility of the Incarnation, by which he has mercy and teaches.

## CHAPTER 120

But the scribes and Pharisees brought a woman caught in adultery; they set her in the midst and said to him: “Teacher, this woman has just been caught in adultery. Now in the Law Moses commanded us to stone such persons. What, then, do you say?” They said this to test him, so that they might be able to accuse him.

[AUGUSTINE.] They thought that the Lord would be either merciful [Col. 0379C] in judging or unjust. If he decided according to the Law that she should be stoned, they would mock him as lacking the gentleness which he preached and for which the people loved him. If he forbade her to be stoned, they would call him an enemy of the Law and an opponent of Moses—indeed, of God its author—and thus guilty of death together with the adulteress.

But Jesus, bending down, wrote on the ground with his finger. When they persisted in questioning him, he straightened up and said to them: “Let the one among you who is without sin cast the first stone at her.”

The Law was written by the finger of God, but, because of hard people, on stone. Now the lawgiver himself, stooping from the seat of the Father into the world in order to remove the sins of the human race, [Col. 0379D] wrote on the ground because he sought fruit. Every day he furrows the ground with his finger when he touches the hearts of his hearers by the Holy Spirit. [AUGUSTINE.] Further: he wrote on the ground, as though signifying that the accusers were to be written on earth, but we in heaven. The bending of his head demonstrates humility. [ALBINUS.] Further: by the finger, which is flexible through the arrangement of its joints, the subtlety of discernment is expressed; by the ground, the human heart, which is accustomed to yield fruit. [AUGUSTINE.] Therefore, before we judge anyone, let us examine our own conscience and decide the matter by a just scrutiny. Thus he says to them: “Let the one among you who is without sin cast a stone at her.” It is as though he said: Let each person ascend the tribunal of his own mind, and he will find himself a sinner. Therefore either dismiss this woman, or [Col. 0380A] undergo with her the penalty of the Law. Let the sinful woman be punished—but not by transgressors of the Law. Behold complete justice: a just person should punish evils. Even if an accused official puts accused persons to death, he nevertheless ought not to do so, because he himself is accused.

And again, bending down, he wrote on the ground. But when they heard these things, they went out one by one, beginning with the elders; and Jesus alone remained, with the woman standing in the midst.

He remained alone from them, of course, for the disciples remained with him, in whose midst the woman stood. He wrote on the ground again, according to ordinary human custom, turning his face elsewhere, so that those whom he foresaw would leave sooner than ask further questions might be free to depart. Thus, with his face turned away, he does not deign to look upon those who fall, but gives them an opportunity to flee.

[Col. 0380B] Then Jesus, straightening up, said to her: “Woman, where are those who accused you? Has no one condemned you?” She said: “No one, Lord.” Jesus said: “Neither will I condemn you. Go, and sin no more.”

First standing upright in the judgment of justice, he then stands upright to pronounce the sentence of mercy, because to do both belongs to divine power. Since the woman could fear that he who was without sin would punish her, he says to her, as the merciful one forgiving what is past, “Neither will I condemn you”; and, as the just one forbidding her to sin again, “Go, and sin no more.” For those who despair, the Lord set forth the draught of pardon; for those endangered by hope and deceived by delay, he made the day of death uncertain.

## CHAPTER 121

[Col. 0380C] M. 204[VI] L. 120

Now, returning to the city in the morning, he became hungry. And seeing a fig tree by the road, he came to it and found nothing on it except leaves only. For it was not yet the season for figs. And he said to it: “May fruit never grow from you again for ever.” And immediately the fig tree withered. Seeing this, the disciples were amazed and said: “How did it wither immediately?”

[JEROME.] What the Lord did on the road when he returned to the city in the morning had been passed over, but is here supplied in recollection. Hungry, he came to the fig tree; thirsty, he had come to the well—showing in both cases the reality of his human flesh, and at the same time suggesting that he hungered for the salvation of human beings and thirsted for the faith of the Church, [Col. 0380D] burning with grief at Israel’s unbelief. The tree is the Synagogue, which stood by the road: for it possessed the Law. Its leaves are the noise of Pharisaic traditions, the boasting of the Law, and the ornament of words. By the same power by which he dried up the tree, the Savior could also have dried up his enemies, had he not awaited repentance. [HILARY.] Further: the fig tree is the Synagogue because of its likeness to the many seeds; it is by the road, that is, beside the world. Therefore Christ found no fruit in the Synagogue, because it lived according to the world, which is the common passageway of all who are born. [HILARY.] The first flower of the fig tree appears in fruits commonly called early figs (*grossa*). Afterwards, when the power of inward fertility grows abundant, fruits of the same form emerge and advance toward ripeness; when these emerge, the earlier fruits fall, their roots being loosened. Yet if it happens that, clinging in the folds of the little branches, they do not fall from their roots, they outstrip the other fruits in ripeness. Thus this is a fitting likeness of the Synagogue. For the first fruits it had produced from the beginning were lost under the image of the early figs, because the faithful people of the Gentiles, abiding until the consummation of the ages, displaced its useless people. Nevertheless, the first believers from Israel—the apostles—clinging like early figs between the Law and the Gospel, will precede the rest in the glory and time of the resurrection. In the figure of this matter Adam and Eve covered their shame with the leaves of this tree, because the unbelieving Synagogue, transgressing the commandments of the Law, was to cover the foulness of its shamelessness and the confusion of its disgraces [Col. 0381B] with barren coverings of words, as with fig leaves. [AUGUSTINE.] Whoever says that Christ performed miracles only in order that they might be mere miracles may also say that he did not know it was not the time for fruit when he sought figs on the tree. Did the cultivator of the tree know what its Creator did not know? Therefore, when he sought fruit while hungry, he signified that he was seeking something else. For what fault was the tree’s barrenness, when he cursed it? The barrenness is their fault whose fruitfulness depends upon their will. A person is proved not by reputation or the pomp of words, but by the testimony of deeds; just as a tree is known not by flowers and leaves, but by fruit. Therefore Judaea, which uttered the words of Scripture [Col. 0381C] without works, deserved the punishment inflicted on it, which it ought to have avoided by being frightened at the tree’s barrenness. Let us therefore understand that Christ’s miracles signify something other than the miracles themselves. [HILARY.] And it should be noted that he commended the hope of things to come and the salvation of the soul amid the anxieties of present afflictions; but he indicated the danger of unbelief through the loss of the tree, so that it might be taught without loss to those for whose redemption he had come. Mark does not inappropriately introduce him as answering the fig tree, since the thing itself cried out that it had not yet fruit but leaves only. Therefore, when he says, “Let no one ever again eat fruit from you,” do not interpret it as concerning the whole Synagogue universally, but concerning the larger part which he knew would never be converted: “You have now come to this, O Judaea, that henceforth no one will ever eat fruit from you”—that is, that no just person may delight in your fruit.

R. 123[X]

When evening came, he went out of the city. And when they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree dried up from the roots. Peter remembered and said to him: “Rabbi, look: the fig tree you cursed has withered.”

[BEDE.] The fig tree was dried up from its roots, to indicate that the wicked people were to be deprived utterly, not only of outward human glory but also of inward divine favor.

[Col. 0382A] M. 215[VI] R. 124

Jesus answered and said to them: “Have faith in God. Amen I say to you: if you have faith and do not waver in your heart, you will not only do this to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Lift yourself up and cast yourself into the sea,’ it will happen.”

[JEROME.] In their writings the barking dogs of the Gentiles rail against us, maintaining that the apostles lacked faith because they could not move mountains. We answer them that, according to the testimony of John the Evangelist, the Lord performed many signs which, if they had been written, the world could not contain (John 21)—not because the world could not contain the volumes, which, however numerous, one bookcase [Col. 0382B] or one dining room could hold, but because, given the magnitude of the signs, it could not bear them on account of astonishment and unbelief. Therefore we also believe that the apostles did these things; but they were not written lest unbelievers be given a greater occasion for contradiction, since they do not believe even the lesser signs which have been written. We read that through the prayers of the blessed father Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, a man outstanding in merits and powers, a mountain gave way over as much ground as the inhabitants of the city needed. For when, wishing to build a church in a suitable place, he saw that it was narrower than the undertaking required—being confined on one side by a sea-cliff and on the other by a neighboring mountain—he came to the place at night and, bending his knees, reminded the Lord of his promise, that he would move the mountain farther away in accordance with the faith of the petitioner. When morning came and he returned, he found that the mountain had left the builders as much space as they needed for the church. This is against the faultfinders. But we understand the mountain to be the devil, who can be removed by the apostles and those like them from a possessed human soul into the sea, that is, into bitter places. Hence the Psalm says: “We shall not fear though the earth be shaken and mountains be carried into the heart of the sea” (Ps. 45).

L. 200[V] M. 175

And the apostles said to him: “Lord, increase our faith.” And Jesus said:

[Col. 0382D] R. 125[IV] M. 21 A. 128, 150, 153 and 127

“Whatever things you ask in prayer, believe that you will receive them, and they will come to pass for you.”

When they were about to enter the land of promise, it was said: “Every place upon which your foot treads shall be yours” (Deut. 11). But here we are told that every place of mercy which, advancing toward God, you tread with the foot of the mind shall be ours. Therefore, that we may lean more firmly upon this foot, would that the other foot, by which the mind advances toward earthly things, might be weakened, as the angel blessing Jacob is recorded to have done (Gen. 32).

R. 126[VI] M. 44

“And when you stand to pray, forgive, if you have [Col. 0383A] anything against anyone, so that your Father who is in heaven may also forgive you your sins.”

Since perfect faith is that which works through love, drives out demons, and obtains forgiveness of sins, the following parable fittingly exhorts us always to pray and believe, and to place our confidence not in ourselves but in God. The Apostle also says: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 3). [BEDE.] But who can pray always? Therefore this must be understood either of the daily hours according to the rite of the Church, as the Psalmist says: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33); or certainly that whatever the just person does according to God is to be reckoned as prayer.

## CHAPTER 122

[Col. 0383B] L. 214[X]

He also told them a parable, that they ought always to pray and not lose heart, saying: “There was a judge in a certain city who did not fear God or respect anyone. There was a widow in that city, and she came to him saying, ‘Vindicate me against my adversary.’ For a long time he refused. But afterward he said to himself, ‘Although I do not fear God or respect anyone, yet because this widow troubles me, I will vindicate her, lest by coming continually in the end she wear me out.’”

That is, lest she come again and again and choke me with wearisome cries. *Sugillare*, derived from *sugo* and *lamiae*, means “to strangle.” The Lord presents parables either by similarity—as concerning the man who had two sons, the elder in the field and the younger in a far country (Luke 15)—or proves something by dissimilarity, as there: “If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith?” (Matt. 6). [Col. 0383C] The former type is connected thus: “as that, so this or that”; the latter thus: “if that is so, how much more—or how much less—this or that?” The judge here is an argument from dissimilarity, since an unjust person is never likened to God. The widow herself can bear the likeness of the Church, which appears deserted until the Lord comes, although even now he cares for her in secret.

And the Lord said: “Hear what the unjust judge [Col. 0383D] says. And will not God grant vindication to his elect, who cry to him day and night, and will he have patience with them? I tell you, he will quickly grant them vindication.”

If anyone is troubled that the elect pray to be avenged, when we are most plainly instructed to pray for persecutors (Matt. 5), it must be understood that the vengeance of the just consists in the destruction of evil people. Evil people perish, however, in two ways: either by conversion to righteousness or by loss of the power through which they prevail temporarily against the good.

“Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you suppose that he will find faith on the earth?”

Although the omnipotent Creator is always ready to bring vengeance, yet on the day of judgment the ruin of evil people will be more severe. “Do you suppose?” is not said here as an expression of doubt, [Col. 0384A] but as a rebuke. For we also sometimes use a word of doubt in rebuking concerning certain matters: for example, if you say indignantly to your servant, “Do you despise me? Consider—perhaps I am your master.” And the Apostle says: “But I suppose that I too have the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 7).

## CHAPTER 123

M. 217[XI] R. 127 L. 240

When he had come into the temple, it happened that, while he taught the people and preached the Gospel, the chief priests and elders of the people came to him and said: “By what authority do you do these things? And who gave you this authority?”

[JEROME.] In different words they construct the same calumny as above, when they said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, prince of demons”; for they imply that he works through the devil. [Col. 0384B] [CHRYSOSTOM.] Everyone judges another by himself. A fornicator thinks no one chaste; a chaste person does not readily suspect another of fornication. A proud person thinks no one humble; a humble person thinks no one proud. Thus, one who is not a priest from God thinks no one’s priesthood comes from God. Hence he despises others.

Jesus answered and said to them: “I too will ask you one question. If you answer it for me, I too will tell you by what authority I do these things. Whence was John’s baptism—from heaven or from human beings?” But they reasoned among themselves, saying: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ But if [Col. 0384C] we say, ‘From human beings,’ we fear the crowd, for all regarded John as a prophet.” Answering Jesus, they said: “We do not know.”

[JEROME.] The Lord could have refuted them with an open answer, but wisely asks a question so that they may be condemned either by their silence or by their own verdict.

And he said to them: “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.”

He did not say, “Neither do I know,” which would have followed their answer; for Truth cannot lie, as they lied when they said that they did not know. [BEDE.] “I do not tell you,” he says, “what I know, because you are unwilling to confess what you know”—namely, that John received prophecy from heaven, and thus bore testimony to him and showed by what authority he did these things. [Col. 0384D] It should be noted that knowledge of the truth is to be hidden from questioners for two reasons: either the questioner is too incapable of understanding, or, because of hatred or contempt for the truth, is unworthy for it to be disclosed to him. Of the first the Lord says: “I have still many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16); of the other: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine” (Matt. 5).

M. 218[X]

“But what do you think? A man had two sons. Going to the first, he said, ‘Son, go today and work in my vineyard.’ But he answered, ‘I will not.’ Afterwards, moved by repentance, he went. Going to the other, he said likewise. But he answered, ‘I am going, lord’; and he did not go. Which of the two did the father’s will?” They said: “The latter [the former].” Jesus said to them: “Amen I say to you, tax collectors and prostitutes go before you into the kingdom of God. For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him. But tax collectors and prostitutes believed him; and you, seeing this, did not afterwards repent so as to believe him.”

[JEROME.] These are the two sons also described in the parable in Luke—the dutiful and the prodigal—and of whom the prophet Zechariah says: “I took for myself two staffs; one I called Beauty and the other I called Cord, and I fed the flock” (Zech. 11). The command is first spoken to the people of the Gentiles through their knowledge of the natural law: “Go [Col. 0385B] and work in my vineyard”—that is, “Do not do to another what you do not wish done to yourself” (Tob. 4). They answered proudly, “I will not.” But afterwards, at the coming of the Savior, having repented, they worked in God’s vineyard and corrected the defiance of their words by labor.

The other son is the Jewish people, who answered Moses: “We will do all the Lord’s commands” (Exod. 24). Yet they did not go into the vineyard, because, after killing the householder’s son, they thought themselves the heir. Others refer the parable to sinners and just persons, as the Lord himself explains: “Amen I say to you, tax collectors and prostitutes”—that is, sinners—“go before you into the kingdom of God” through repentance. The Pharisees, who boasted that they kept God’s Law, despised John’s baptism. But concerning the written reading, “They say to him: the latter,” [Col. 0385C] it should be known that in the true copies there is not “the latter” but “the former,” so that they may be condemned by their own judgment. If, however, we choose to read “the latter,” the interpretation is plain: we may say that the Jews understood the truth, but equivocated and refused to say what they thought, just as, though knowing John’s baptism to be from heaven, they refused to say so. [CHRYSOSTOM.] The vineyard is righteousness, which God planted above human nature; but he gave it in a special way to the Jews in the book. Since powers differ, kinds of righteousness also differ.
