In this vineyard each person works according to his strength, cultivating few vines or many; but I do not know whether any human being is sufficient to cultivate the whole vineyard. “I will not,” he said in thought. I think that the tax collector is set forth as representing all male sinners, and the prostitute as representing all female sinners. Although there are many sins in both sexes, greed especially abounds among men and fornication among women. In the tax collectors and prostitutes the people of the Gentiles may be understood. It is as though he said: “The people of the Gentiles are more pleasing to God than you.” Laypeople and priests also can be understood as the two sons: first the people, the son; then the priests who govern them. For the people of God began from the time of Abraham, but priests from the time of Aaron. A priest or any cleric, even if he does not expressly promise to obey God, nevertheless, because he is appointed as a teacher of others, seems silently to promise God on behalf of human beings. Therefore a layperson [Col. 0386A] is better who outwardly professes a secular life but in truth strives for a spiritual one, than a priest who outwardly professes a spiritual life but in truth embraces a carnal one. And a repentant layperson is better before God than a cleric who remains in sins. For on the day of judgment the layperson will receive the priestly stole: for this reason all are anointed in chrism into priesthood. But the sinful priest will be stripped of the dignity of priesthood which he possessed and will be among unbelievers and hypocrites. Who has ever seen a cleric quickly repent? Even if, when caught, he humbles himself, he does not grieve because he has sinned, but is ashamed because he has lost his glory. Those who have enslaved themselves to worldly desires and carnal pleasures are often converted more quickly. Observe that he said in the present tense, “They go before you”; and observe that where someone goes before, someone seems to follow. By this word, then, the priests too were signified as about to enter the kingdom of God—that is, as about to believe in Christ. But because the priests did not believe John and those baptized by him, when tax collectors and prostitutes did believe, they are announced as entering after tax collectors and prostitutes, as indeed happened: for after the Lord’s Ascension many believed. The tax collectors who went before are Matthew the tax collector and Zacchaeus, chief tax collector. Understand the prostitutes through blessed Mary Magdalene.

## CHAPTER 124

M. 219[II] R. 128 L. 241

[Col. 0386C] “Hear another parable. There was a man, a householder, who planted a vineyard, put a hedge around it, dug a winepress in it, built a tower, leased it to tenant-farmers, and went abroad.”

God, who with paternal love cherishes all the peoples he created, is called shepherd in one parable and householder in another; in one he leases a vineyard, in another he invites to a wedding; and by different likenesses he signifies the same matter, so as to reprove the pride of the Jews and approve the common repentance of all sinners, whether Gentiles or Israelites. Thus this householder is called “a man” by likeness, not in truth. Let no one think that Christ had a human soul because he is called a man, for God the Father also [Col. 0386D] is called a man. Since, therefore, heretics were going to blaspheme Christ because of the designation of the human name, as though he were a mere human being, God the Father was also called a man, so that God the Son might thus be freed from the blasphemies of heretics. The vineyard is the house of Israel, around which he put a hedge—that is, the city wall or the aid of angels. [JEROME.] Or thus: he gave them as a hedge the guardianship of their righteous fathers, because it was made for them like a wall. [CHRYSOSTOM.] For because of the promise made to them, they were possessed by God, beyond their own merit, through the hedge of their fathers. The winepress is the Church, in which the fruit of the vineyard—that is, the works of God’s servants and proven faith—is conveyed to God’s glory. The Church becomes a winepress because it has in itself the word of God; so that not the Church alone [Col. 0387A] may seem to be the winepress, as much as the word itself which has been given and dug in it. For if the word of the New Testament, which is light, torments a person opposing the nature of the flesh, how much more the word of the Old, which was unbearable? Therefore where the word of God was placed in the Law, establishing a manner of life, there a winepress was dug. But where faith was prophesied, a tower was built. For just as those who stand in a tower neither easily suffer an enemy’s attack nor fail easily to crush enemies from the tower, so those who stand in faith are neither overcome by demons nor fail to wound the demons with the arrows of good works. [JEROME.] The farmers are those whom elsewhere he called laborers, hired at the first, third, sixth, and ninth hours—that is, sent to the vineyard at different callings. [Col. 0387B] [CHRYSOSTOM.] Alternatively: he dug a winepress in it, namely the prophets, from whom the grace of the Holy Spirit flowed down like must. He built a tower, namely the assurance of the Law, from which the priests watched for Christ who was to come. [JEROME.] The tenants are the priests, to whom the people planted in Abraham were leased. He went abroad, not by a change of place, since he is everywhere, but he appears to depart when he grants the vinedressers free choice to work.

“When the season of fruits drew near, he sent his servants to the tenants to receive his fruits. But the tenants seized his servants: they beat one, killed another, and stoned another.”

They beat Jeremiah; they killed Isaiah; they stoned Naboth and Zechariah, whom they killed between the temple and the altar (Matt. 23). We read that Naboth was not merely wounded but also put to death by them. [BEDE.] He aptly says “the season of fruits,” not “the produce,” for no fruit of the vineyard of the Law was found in many Jews. The first servant sent is understood to be Moses the lawgiver, who for forty years sought fruit from the cultivators of the vineyard and found none, but, beaten by their harsh words, was sent away empty. For “they provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord. And Moses was troubled because of them, because they embittered his spirit” (Ps. 105). What this servant thinks of the vineyard’s fruit they declare thus: “Their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster is most bitter. Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom [Col. 0387D] of asps” (Deut. 32).

“Again he sent other servants, more than the former, and they did the same to them.”

He shows the patience of the subsequent sending, so that they might be called to repentance. The second servant was David, who, after Moses, together with the other psalmists sought by psalmody to stir the tenants to good work. He too, suffering insult, was sent away empty, the tenants saying: “What share have we in David? Or what inheritance in the son of Jesse?” (3 Kings 12). Although beaten by their poisonous tongues, he nevertheless prayed thus: “God of hosts, turn again; look down from heaven and see, and visit this vineyard. And perfect that which your right hand has planted” (Ps. 79). Understand the third servant to be the company of prophets, who announced [Col. 0388A] the Savior’s coming. One of them, Jeremiah, says: “I planted you a choice vineyard; how have you turned into a foreign vineyard?” (Jer. 2). In these three ranks of servants, openly distinguished in Mark and Luke, we understand all the teachers who were under the Law. Hence elsewhere: “It is necessary that all things written concerning me in the Law of Moses, the Psalms, and the Prophets be fulfilled” (Luke 24).

“Finally he sent to them his son, saying: ‘Perhaps they will respect my son.’”

[JEROME.] What can the householder not know, when God the Father is understood here? But he is said to be uncertain so that free will may be reserved for humanity. Let us set this against Arius and Eunomius. Behold, the Father is said not to know; and whatever answer they give for the Father, let them understand the same of the Son, who says that he does not know the day of consummation.

[Col. 0388B] “But when the tenants saw the son, they said among themselves: ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance.’”

[BEDE.] The leaders of the Jews crucified the Son of God out of envy, he to whom it was said: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. 2). The Son’s inheritance, then, is the Church from the Gentiles. After the Lord was killed, these evil tenants sought to seize it for themselves when they tried to extinguish the right faith, to prefer their own righteousness from the Law to faith in Christ, and to incorporate the Gentiles into themselves.

“And seizing him, they cast him outside the vineyard and killed him.”

That Jesus suffered outside the gate (Heb. 13) [Col. 0388C] was prefigured by Moses through the altar of burnt offering, upon which the blood of victims was poured out (Num. 19), in that he placed it not inside the tabernacle but at its entrance. But the altered order in Mark—“they seized him, killed him, and cast him outside the vineyard”—indicates their obstinacy: even after the Lord had been crucified and raised from the dead, they refused to believe the apostles who preached him, but cast him out like a worthless corpse; for, insofar as it lay in their power, excluding him from their own borders, they handed him over to be received by the Gentiles. Envy indeed killed the Son of God, whom it found guilty of no offense; yet if they had definitely known that he was the Son of God, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2). For just as the highest good hates none of the things it has made, so it seems that no conscience can, in itself, have hatred of that same good. Hence the apostle Peter said to them: “I know, brothers, that you committed this evil through ignorance, as did also your rulers” (Acts 3). Yet they did not fail to know that what they were doing was impious, nor did they persecute flesh alone, but him who worked through the flesh. Therefore when they say among themselves, “This is the heir,” they say it by comparison with the other saints, and because many were already believing him to be the one promised in the Law. But why did the perverse refuse to believe what they could not contradict by reason? It would not be a fault if it were not devoid of reason.

“When, therefore, the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?” They say to him: “He will miserably destroy those wicked men, and lease [Col. 0389A] his vineyard to other tenants, who will render him its fruits in their seasons.”

[CHRYSOSTOM.] Luke records their spoken answer, “May it never be!” But Matthew writes according to the answer of their hearts. For in heart and conscience they said, “He will miserably destroy those wicked men.” [AUGUSTINE.] Alternatively: let us understand that some gave the answer Matthew records, but others gave that recorded by Luke. For Matthew, for the sake of brevity, passed over what Luke does not pass over: namely, that the parable was spoken not only to those who deceitfully questioned the Lord concerning his authority, but also to the people. Matthew’s words, “They say to him,” should not be understood with “they” in the plural as though this were the answer of those who deceitfully questioned the Lord concerning his authority; rather, as the Greek manuscripts show without any ambiguity, *to him* is singular—that is, those who were already members of the Lord say such things to the Lord himself. For he had already baptized many. Mark says, “He will destroy the tenants,” in the voice of the Lord himself; for it can be understood that, after they had first spoken the truth, the Lord himself, who is Truth, also confirmed it afterwards.

Jesus said to them: “Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This was done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?” (Ps. 117).

[BEDE.] How, he says, will this prophecy be fulfilled, which declares that a stone rejected by the builders is to be made the head of the corner, unless Christ, [Col. 0389C] rejected by you, is to be preached to the Gentiles who will believe, so that, like a cornerstone, he may join in himself two walls from the two peoples and build for himself one temple? Of this stone Isaiah says: “I will lay in the foundations of Zion a chosen, precious cornerstone; and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame” (Isa. 28). Those called tenants above are here called builders, because they were commanded to cultivate the people so that it would yield fruit and, as it were, to construct a house worthy for the Lord himself to dwell in.

“Therefore I say to you that the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.”

[HILARY.] The householder’s manifest return will be the glory of the Father’s majesty, present in the Son at the time of judgment. He also comes daily to some by the benefit [Col. 0389D] of grace, and to others by the vengeance of their obstinacy—as when he then transferred the kingdom of God, that is, the understanding of the Scriptures, from the Jews to the Gentiles. Therefore the vineyard is given to others: those coming from east and west, south and north, and reclining with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of God.

“Everyone who falls upon this stone will be broken; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him.”

[CHRYSOSTOM.] What falls, falls heavily for two reasons: either because of its own weight or because of its height. Christians fall upon the stone by sinning; but by believing in Christ they stand upon it as upon their own foundation. Nor are they crushed as completely as Christ can crush them, [Col. 0390A] but according to their sins—either because of the greatness of a grievous sin, or because of the loftiness of their rank, as with clerics, monks, widows, and virgins. But the stone—that is, Christ—falls upon unbelieving Jews and pagans, who perish not according to their deeds nor according to their persons, but perish as completely as Christ is able to destroy those who do not believe in him. Of them the Prophet says: “Not so the ungodly, not so; but like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” (Ps. I).

[JEROME.] Therefore, one who is a sinner and yet believes in Christ falls upon the stone through consenting to evil and despising God, and is broken so that he does not walk uprightly, yet is not utterly crushed. But the one upon whom this stone falls from above with the punishment of destruction—the stone which he denies—will be completely [Col. 0390B] crushed, so that not even a shard remains.

What Matthew calls a winepress, Mark calls a pit, because just as wine is pressed out in a winepress, so water is pressed out of the ground in a pit. For the winepress, as it were, vomits forth new wine, and the earth, as it were, vomits forth a pit. “He dug it,” that is, he staked it out or planted it; or, what seems better to me, he provided it with pasture—that is, he manured it with dung. God the Father, as it were, fed the children of Israel with dung when he satisfied them with the flesh for which they themselves had longed. Hence: “They ate and were exceedingly filled; and he brought them their desire: they were not deprived of their desire” (Ps. LXXVII).

“He dug,” that is, by digging the earth he made a winepress or pit; because, by digging into the hearts of the Jews and casting out from them the dung of vices, he gave them prophecies [Col. 0390C] through which they might distinguish good from evil, just as in a winepress new wine is distinguished from grape-skins and oil from lees; and through which, as though by a pit, they might be cleansed from the filth of wicked desires. They wounded David and the other prophets in the head—that is, in the heart, which is called the head of thoughts—or in Christ, who is the head of all believers, when they did not believe the prophets speaking to them of Christ’s coming. Hence David himself says: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, thy consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. XCIII).

M. 220[I] R. 122 and 129 L. 239 and 242 and 261 A. 77 and 85 and 88

[Col. 0390D] And when the chief priests and Pharisees had heard his parables, they understood that he spoke of them. And, seeking to seize him, they feared the crowds, because they regarded him as a prophet.

[JEROME.] The crowd is fickle and is carried about after the fashion of waves and winds. The one whom they now venerate, later they cry out against: “Crucify him!”

CHAPTER CXXV.

M. 221[V] L. 181

And Jesus answered and again spoke to them in parables, saying: “The kingdom of heaven has become like a king who made a wedding-feast for his son.”

[GREGORY.] They hear in parables what they did not deserve to hear plainly. Although the Lord knew the will of those raging against him, he nevertheless rebuked them. This king is God the Father, who made a wedding for his Son when, in the Virgin’s womb, he joined him to human nature. This union arose from two natures, not from two persons. More plainly, the wedding is the fellowship of Christ and the Church, gathered both from Jews and from Gentiles. The bridal chamber of this bridegroom was the Virgin’s womb. The assembly of the righteous is called the kingdom of heaven because heavenly powers reign within it. It is like God the Father in this respect: as he joined the Church to his Son, so that assembly joins to the Church of the faithful its own children, whom it begets for God through the word of preaching and joins through the sacraments of faith.

“And he called many; and at the hour of the supper he sent his servants [Col. 0391B] to call those invited to the wedding, and they would not come.”

[GREGORY.] Luke describes under the name of a supper what Matthew calls a luncheon, since among the ancients the daily meal was taken at the ninth hour and was called supper.

[CHRYSOSTOM.] The luncheon or supper is the teaching of righteousness and the divine words. Manna, which prefigured the Word in the wilderness, was called manna because in Hebrew it means, “What is this?” Thus whenever we hear the Word, its very name admonishes us to inquire, “What is this that we hear?” And just as, after we have chewed food, we send it down into the stomach, so the Word, when properly considered, must be entrusted to memory as though to the stomach.

The invitation occurred when God said to Abraham: “Go out from your land and from your kindred, and come into the land which [Col. 0391C] I shall show you; and I shall give it to you and to your seed” (Gen. XII). What land? The eastern land, flowing with milk and honey. This is not literally true of the land of Judaea, for it never flowed with milk and honey. Rather, it is the rational land which Christ assumed, from whose incarnation milk and honey flowed forth. Milk means the work of miracles, by which the unlearned, as little children, are sustained; honey means the utterance of doctrine, as the Prophet says: “How sweet are thy utterances to my palate, above honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII).

It was therefore rightly said to Abraham, “Go out from your land and from your kindred”; that is, whoever wishes to be saved must understand that he must depart from Judaism and circumcision. Not only Jews, but no human being can eat God’s milk and honey unless he leaves his land and kindred, as in the saying, “Unless someone leaves father and mother and the rest, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV); and again: “Whoever wishes to be my disciple, let him deny himself” (Luke IX). Therefore, one leaves one’s kindred not by despising it, but by loving God more than one’s parents. One leaves one’s land by not following the pleasure of one’s flesh.

From the time of Moses this banquet began to be prepared, when the Law was given. That feast was adorned with diverse kinds of righteousness, just as a royal luncheon is embellished with diverse foods. From that same time the inviters went out—that is, the prophets.

“And all began together to make excuses.”

Those who refused to come make excuses, and thus shut themselves out [Col. 0392A] from the eternal banquet, which God freely offers without being asked to those who are willing. Everyone makes excuse who loves earthly things more than heavenly things, even if he says that he is striving toward heavenly things.

“The first said to him: ‘I have bought an estate, and I must go out and see it. I beg you, hold me excused.’”

The estate signifies earthly property, which some acquire for themselves at great labor or even at the cost of their faith, whether through pride or for bodily sustenance. Thus the person who leaves inward contemplation and thinks only of outward things goes out to inspect it.

“And another said: ‘I have bought five yokes of oxen, and I am going to test them. I beg you, hold me excused.’”

[GREGORY—BEDE.] The five bodily senses are rightly called yokes, since they are doubled in both sexes. [Col. 0392B] Since these senses know only outward things and not inward ones, they rightly signify curiosity. Curiosity is a great vice: while it investigates a neighbour’s life, it draws the mind outward, neglecting its own inner state. Note that when they say, “I beg you, hold me excused,” humility sounds in their speech; but when they disdain to come, pride appears in their action. So the sinner who says, “Pray for me, a sinner,” and does not wish to abandon sin, displays humility in words but acts in pride.

“And another said: ‘I have taken a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’”

In the wife, pleasure of the flesh is understood—not because marriage is not good for the propagation of offspring, but because some seek in a wife not the fruitfulness of children [Col. 0392C] but the desires of pleasure. Marriage, therefore, is not condemned, but virginity is called to greater honor.

Likewise, dominion is indicated in the purchased estate, and pride is rebuked. The first man wished to rule, because he did not wish to have a Lord. What is ruling except delighting in one’s own power? The five yokes are in the senses; three are easily apparent: there are two eyes, two ears, and two nostrils. Even in taste there are two instruments, the tongue and the palate. The pleasure of the flesh, which belongs to touch, is doubled more secretly, for it is both external and internal. They are called yokes of oxen because earthly things are sought through these senses, and oxen turn the earth. There are people who wish to believe nothing except what they perceive through the senses. The wife pertains to bodily pleasure, which hinders many.

“Again he sent other servants, saying: ‘Tell those invited: Behold, I have prepared my luncheon; my bulls and fattened animals have been slaughtered, and all things are ready. Come to the wedding.’”

The first servants were the prophets who foretold the Incarnation; the second are the apostles, who affirm what has been done.

[GREGORY.] Therefore it is said here: “My luncheon is prepared,” that is, the mystery of the Incarnation is fulfilled and the entrance into the kingdom, previously closed, has been opened.

[CHRYSOSTOM.] The bulls and fattened animals that have been killed are understood as saints who have been killed. All the prophets and Christ were killed so that this spiritual tabernacle might be firmly prefigured. For just as people did not eat the entrails of the lamb—that is, Christ’s sayings—until after he had been killed, but after his death they preached his Gospels, so too the entrails—that is, the sayings of the prophets—were not received until after they had been killed. For if they had received Isaiah’s words, they would never have sawn him asunder; but after he was killed, the Jews began to mourn him. Just as the entrails of no living animal are eaten, so no one received the sayings of prophets while they lived.

The fattened animals are those full of God’s grace. He did not say “bulls and fattened animals” because the bulls were fattened; rather, not all the fattened animals were bulls. Some were prophets only, while others were both prophets and priests, such as Jeremiah and Ezekiel. Therefore by “fattened animals” he means prophets alone, because they were filled with the Holy Spirit; but by “bulls,” those who were prophets [Col. 0393B] and priests. For just as bulls lead the herd, so priests are leaders of the people.

[GREGORY.] Alternatively, the bulls are the Fathers of the Old Testament, who, by the Law’s permission, struck their enemies back, as it were, with horns of strength. The fattened animals signify the Fathers of the New Testament, striking with evangelical commands, lifted to sublime things upon the wings of holy contemplation, and receiving through grace the richness of eternal abundance; for we call fattened animals *altilia* from *alere*, “to nourish.”

[CHRYSOSTOM.] Note that in the first invitation nothing is said about bulls and fattened animals, but in the second, because when we refuse to hear God’s words, he adds examples. “All things,” he says, “are ready,” because whatever is required for salvation has already been fulfilled [Col. 0393C] in the Scriptures. The ignorant person will find there what to learn; the obstinate person and the sinner will find there the punishments of the coming judgment. Every kind of food is found in the Scriptures, for little ones and for the mature alike.

“But they neglected it, and went away, one to his estate, another to his business.”

He did not say, “They acted maliciously,” but “They neglected it,” because not all Jews crucified Christ or consented to his death. Every human activity is of two kinds: either estate, or business. The estate denotes every earthly occupation, whether in a field, vineyard, wood, iron, or anything produced by manual labor. But whatever we obtain not by manual labor but by other gains—such as remaining in positions of honor, military service, or trade—all this is called business. Thus in two words he has comprehended every human occupation: whether honorable, such as cultivating an estate, of which Solomon says, “Do not hate rural work” (Ecclus. VII); or dishonorable, such as pursuit of rank, military service, or trade—things which the Jews formerly possessed not at all.

But perhaps you say, “Is cultivating an estate also a sin, because it is an impediment?” Cultivating an estate is not sin; rather, by preferring it to God, you make it a sin. Or thus: the estate is this world, around which lovers of the world are occupied; business is the preaching of the Law and the administration of the Temple, which greedy priests and the other Temple ministers regard as a kind of trade.

[Col. 0394A] “But the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them.”

He is silent about his own death because he had mentioned it in the preceding parable; and he shows the death of his disciples, whom the Jews killed after his Ascension.

“But when the king heard it, he was angry; and, sending his armies, he destroyed those murderers and burned their city.”

Those who killed the king’s servants are charged with a great crime. When it comes to vengeance, the man is left unmentioned and only the king is named. By “armies” are meant evil angels, or the Romans under Vespasian and Titus: he destroyed the Jews and burned the treacherous city. Or thus: by “armies” are meant holy angels, through whom he will execute judgment; he will destroy the persecutors and burn in Gehenna, together with the soul, the city—that is, the flesh—in which they dwelt.

“Then he said to his servants: ‘The wedding is indeed ready, but those who had been invited were not worthy. Go therefore to the ends of the roads, into the streets, lanes, and cities; and summon to the wedding whomever you find—poor, weak, blind, and lame.’”

[CHRYSOSTOM.] As many as are the varieties of acts in this world, so many are the roads leading to the devil, namely, the general road of destruction. Therefore he says, “Go to the ends of the roads,” so that people of every condition may be called to faith. For God’s grace is able to correct in mind any barbarians whatsoever; it changed Nebuchadnezzar’s heart to a beastly mind [Col. 0394C] and restored it again to human understanding (Dan. IV).

[GREGORY—REMIGIUS.] Therefore he sends into streets, lanes, and cities, inviting poor, weak, blind, and lame people, so that among those coming to faith in Christ there may be no distinction of places or persons. For bodily weakness excludes no one from the kingdom of God; one who lacks the inducement to sin sins more rarely, and one who has nothing in the world in which to delight turns more readily to God. Alternatively, the poor, weak, blind, and lame signify Gentiles in comparison with Jews, who ought through the Law and prophets to have been rich, strong, enlightened, and upright, though they falsely presume themselves to be so. He sends into streets when he calls sinners from broad ways to the narrow way of life. He sends into lanes when he invites those whom lack of temporal things calls. He sends into cities when he calls those who distinguish cultivated places from uncultivated, who have known how to keep the law of nature amid civic life.

“And the servant said: ‘Lord, it has been done as you commanded, and still there is room.’ And the Lord said to the servant: ‘Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter, so that my house may be filled. But I tell you that none of those men who were invited shall taste my supper.’”

God’s house must be filled with the number of the predestined, but proud sinners who, having been called, refused to come have excluded themselves irrecoverably. The Lord calls through himself; he calls through angels, patriarchs, apostles, miracles, and afflictions. Let no one disdain to come, lest, while called, he makes excuse and then, when [Col. 0395A] he wishes to enter, be unable to do so.

[AUGUSTINE.] Humbled sinners from the Gentiles came from the streets and lanes; let heretics come from the hedges. For those who build hedges seek divisions. Let them be drawn from the hedges and pulled out from the thorns. They do not wish to be compelled; “Let us enter,” they say, “of our own will.” The Lord did not command this, for he said, “Compel them to enter.”

[GREGORY.] Let necessity be found outside and willingness be born within. Thus roads and hedges mean erroneous sects and heresies. It is plain, therefore, that some are called and disdain to come; others are called and come; others are compelled to enter. Those are called and disdain to come who receive understanding into the house of their mind but do not pursue that same understanding in works. Those are called and come who fulfill in action the grace of understanding they have received. Those are compelled to enter whom the Church temporarily punishes, because they turned back after putting their hand to the plough.

“And his servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, bad and good; and the wedding was filled with diners.”

By the good and bad it is plainly shown that the wedding signifies the Church, which now receives people indiscriminately and later, at the departure, separates them. The bad are mingled with the good because the iron of the soul is never brought to the fineness of an edge unless it has been rubbed by the file of another’s wickedness. For the good must endure the bad, just as in Noah’s ark there were diverse kinds of animals, and in the threshing-floor grain is found with chaff.

M. 222[X]

“But the king entered to see the diners, and saw there a man not clothed in a wedding garment. And he said to him: ‘Friend, how did you enter here without having a wedding garment?’”

[CHRYSOSTOM.] The king—that is, God—entered, not because he is not everywhere, but because where he chooses to look he is said to be present, and where he does not choose, absent. He entered to see—that is, to make the merits of each person visible. Here he speaks of the future in past tenses. The day of inspection is the day of judgment, when he will visit Christians reclining at the table of Scripture—that is, resting and being filled with heavenly [Col. 0395D] teachings. Understand the wedding garment as the Lord’s commandments. Therefore, if anyone is found on the day of judgment under the Christian name, clothed with the cast-off clothing of the old man, he will hear: “Friend, how did you enter here?” He calls him friend because he had been invited.

[JEROME.] More fully: the wedding garment is charity, which every baptized person ought to possess. It is contained in the two commandments—love of God and of neighbour—just as a garment is woven upon two pieces of wood, the upper and the lower *linia* [an uncertain textile term]. He says “Friend” as though openly saying: “Friend, and not friend”: friend through faith, but not friend through works.

“But he was silent.”

[CHRYSOSTOM.] Here we hide our deeds and conceal our hearts; but on that day, when the sun, moon, [Col. 0396A] and the whole world stand against us as a testimony to our sins, even if all else is silent, nevertheless our thoughts themselves and our deeds themselves will stand particularly before our eyes before God, as the Apostle says: “Their thoughts accusing one another or even defending them, on the day when the Lord shall judge the hidden things of human beings through Jesus Christ” (Rom. II).

“Then the king said to the attendants: ‘Bind his feet and hands and cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’”

Understand bound hands and feet, the weeping of eyes, and the gnashing of teeth either as confirming the truth of the resurrection, or certainly that hands and feet are bound so that they cease to do evil and to run [Col. 0396B] to shed blood. Those things which are now voluntarily bound in vice will then be bound painfully in punishment. In the weeping of eyes and gnashing of teeth, moreover, the magnitude of torments is shown by a metaphor drawn from bodily members. The outer darkness is the uttermost darkness, that is, the eternal night of damnation, because inner darkness is blindness of heart. Once the one man in whom the whole body of the wicked is represented has been cast out, a general sentence follows:

“For many are called, but few are chosen.”

The sense is this: he does not say that only one of those called was cast out of the wedding, but that this is to be understood of many. For now we partake of the feasts of the divine Word, but on the day of judgment the king, entering, will distinguish us.

Alternatively: from the fact that he did not say, “The king entered to reward,” [Col. 0396C] but “to see,” there arises a possibility that perhaps this should not be understood of the vengeance of judgment. For he did not say, “Cast him into the lower darkness,” that is, into the lower places of hell, of which elsewhere: “And thou hast delivered my soul from the lower hell” (Ps. LXXXV); rather, he said “outer.” Therefore, according to this interpretation, the day of inspection is the day of temptation, when he deigned to test his Church in order to see who has faith and works. Whenever, therefore, he tests the Church, he enters it to see who are worthy of the heavenly wedding; and if he then finds someone unworthy, he questions him. Since human simplicity has difficulty discerning the deceitfulness of a feigned heart, God alone finds this person unworthy of the wedding assembly.

The wedding garment is true faith, as the Apostle says: “Put off the old man with his deeds, putting on the new, who is created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Col. III). Righteousness pertains to good conduct; holiness of truth, to true faith. The questioning takes place in the thoughts of the wicked. It is as though he said: “Why have you become a Christian? Your works are not those of a Christian.” When God sees such a person in the Church, having no answer to give to his own conscience, he hands him over to spirits of seduction. For he repays evils through evil ministers, and they bind his hands—that is, works of uprightness—and his feet—that is, the movements of the soul, by which it proceeds not from place to place but from evil to good and from good to evil, so that it falls into the snare of destruction. Thus [Col. 0397A] he is cast into the outer darkness of either Gentiles, Jews, or heretics. Perhaps the darkness of Gentiles is nearer, because they despise a truth they have not heard; the darkness of Jews is farther out, because they did not believe; that of heretics is farthest out, because they learned it. Now they are cast into outer darkness; afterward they will suffer weeping and gnashing of teeth.

CHAPTER CXXVI.

M. 223[II] R. 130 L. 143.

Then the Pharisees went away and took counsel how they might ensnare him in speech. And they sent to him their disciples with the Herodians, saying: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful, that you teach the way of God in truth, and that you have no concern for anyone; for you do not regard the person of men.”

[REMIGIUS.] You do not fear an exalted person, but speak the truth equally to the great and the small. They call him teacher and truthful so that, as though praised, he may simply reveal the secret of his heart to them and may wish to have them as disciples. By the Herodians understand the Gentiles serving Herod the tetrarch who beheaded John, or another Herod, son of Antipater. Such as was the counsel, such also were its counsellors. The priests thought within themselves: “Everyone knows that we are his enemies, and an enemy’s testimony, even if true, is rejected.”

[CHRYSOSTOM.] Therefore they do not question him themselves, for an open enemy is better than a false friend: he is more easily avoided when he is feared. [Col. 0397C] So they sent their disciples to question him as less suspect, that they might either deceive him secretly or, if discovered, be less ashamed. Yet the disciples were equal to their teachers in malice, though younger in age. For young serpents are smaller in size but equal in venom; and wolf-cubs, still tender though unable to hunt, nevertheless delight in blood and bites. Of such people the Prophet says: “Their words were softer than oil, yet they are darts” (Ps. LIV).

“Tell us therefore what you think: is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?”

The fraudulent question has this meaning: it is not right for us, servants of the supreme King, to serve earthly kings. For if it is unworthy for the servant of one king to serve another king—and if he does so, he wrongs his own lord—how much more unworthy is it that worshippers of God should be burdened by human authorities?

[JEROME.] Others said that taxes ought to be paid to the Romans, who fought for all, for security and peace. Because of this controversy the kingdom and country were later destroyed. Thus the Pharisees provoke him to answer that taxes ought not to be paid, so that he may consequently be held before the Romans as the author of sedition.

But Jesus, knowing their wickedness, said: “Why do you test me, hypocrites? Show me the coin of the tax.” And they offered him a denarius.

The first virtue of one answering is to know the minds of those questioning. A *numisma* is a kind of coin [Col. 0398A] reckoned as worth ten coins, and it bore Caesar’s image.

And Jesus said to them: “Whose image and inscription is this?” They said to him: “Caesar’s.”

He asks not because he is ignorant, but in order to answer appropriately to their words. They call here Caesar Tiberius, under whom the Lord suffered, Augustus’s stepson, who succeeded in the place of his stepfather. All Roman rulers, however, were called Caesars after Gaius Caesar, who seized imperial power.

Then he said to them: “Render therefore the things that are Caesar’s to Caesar, and the things that are God’s to God.”

Caesar’s things are coins, tribute, and money; God’s things are tithes, first-fruits, and offerings. And as Caesar demands the impress of his image, so [Col. 0398B] God desires the soul marked by the light of his countenance.

[AMBROSE.] Since the image of God is one thing and the image of the world another, if Christ did not bear Caesar’s image, why did he pay the tax? He did not pay from what was his own, but returned to the world what belonged to the world. If you do not wish to be bound to Caesar, do not possess the things of the world. But if you possess riches, you are bound to Caesar. If you wish to owe nothing to an earthly king, leave all that is yours, follow Christ, and first rightly determine that Caesar’s things must be rendered. For no one can belong to the Lord unless he has first renounced the world.

And when they heard it, they marvelled; and leaving him, they went away.

[HILARY.] Whereas they ought rather to have believed, they departed in amazement because they had no opportunity for testing him. For it is beyond complaint of injustice that Caesar should receive what is Caesar’s; but we must render to God what properly belongs to him, namely body, soul, and will. For from him these receive both origin and advancement.

CHAPTER CXXVII.

On that day Sadducees, who say that there is no resurrection, came to him and questioned him, saying: “Teacher, Moses said: ‘If anyone dies without children, his brother shall take that man’s wife and raise up seed for his brother.’ Now there were among us seven brothers. The first married and died; having no seed, he left his wife to his brother. Likewise the second died childless, and the third took her; and all seven did so, and they left no seed. Last of all the woman also died [Col. 0398D]. Therefore, in the resurrection, whose wife will she be? For they all had her.”

[JEROME—BEDE.] There were two heresies among the Jews: those of the Pharisees and Sadducees. The Pharisees preferred the righteousness of their own traditions, which they call *deuterōsin*—that is, “second law”—and hence they were called “separated” from the people. The Sadducees, however, whose name means “righteous,” denied the resurrection of body and soul, believing that souls perish with the body. Therefore they devise the indecency of this tale; or it may be that something like this once happened among their people. In the law of the letter they were compelled to marry during life, but in the law of the Spirit chastity is commended. Mystically, the seven brothers who died without children correspond to all the reprobate who, throughout the whole life of this age, which [Col. 0399A] turns in seven days, remain barren of good works; and at last worldly conduct itself, like their barren wife, passes away.

And Jesus said to them: “You err, knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. The children of this age marry and are given in marriage; but those who are considered worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor take wives. For they can no longer die, but are like the angels of God in heaven, and are children of God, since they are children of the resurrection.”

This should not be understood as though the unworthy—that is, sinners—were either not to rise at all or were to be believed to rise for marriage; rather, the Lord wished, in order to stir people toward the glory of the resurrection, to speak only of the elect. Those who rise will be equal to angels both in chastity and in immortality. Marriages exist for children, children for succession, and succession because of death.

[CHRYSOSTOM.] Therefore, where there is no death, there are no marriages. The Sadducees did not believe that there would be marriages after death, since they denied resurrection itself; but they thought they had found a defense of their error when they said to themselves: “Just as it is impossible that a woman who belonged to seven husbands should be the exclusive wife of one or the common wife of all, so it is impossible for the resurrection of the dead to occur.” Why, when the Lord had spoken about fasting, almsgiving, and the other spiritual virtues, did he introduce the likeness of angels only now? Because just as all fleshly acts are the works of animals, especially [Col. 0399C] acts of lust, so all spiritual virtues are angelic things, but especially chastity.

Where Matthew and Mark have “they shall neither marry nor be married,” Latin usage does not correspond to the Greek idiom. Properly speaking, women are said to marry (*nubere*), and men to take wives. But let us understand the expression simply: men shall not marry and women shall not be married. This concerns the power of God; what follows concerns his saying: “You err, not knowing the Scriptures.”

“But concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read in the book of Moses, concerning the bush, how God said to him: ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’” (Exod. III)? “He is not the God of the dead but of the living. For all live to him. You therefore greatly err.”

[JEROME.] In the bush was our likeness, because the fire burned there but did not consume its thorns. Thus the divine word is afire within us, but does not consume our thorns, which sprang up under the curse. In saying, “God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob,” he signifies the Trinity by naming God three times; by repeating “God,” he signifies one substance.

[HILARY.] Those live who claim their portion, which they chose to possess in the land of the living. For if Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had perished when dying, God would not be said to be their God, since they would not exist. But now, how can those be denied to exist—and to exist forever—whom Eternity declares himself to be? He is not the God of the dead [Col. 0400A] who have utterly perished, as the Sadducees supposed, but of those living the blessed life. For all whose Lord and God he is live to him, who by his eternal ordering is the life of souls and the resurrection of bodies. Hence elsewhere the Lord says: “Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, shall live” (John XI). He could have supplied clearer prophetic testimonies concerning the resurrection, but the Sadducees do not accept the prophets.

And when the crowds heard, they marvelled at his teaching. But some of the scribes answered and said: “Teacher, you have spoken well.”

[BEDE.] Note that when the Lord speaks hidden mysteries to plotters and despisers, he nevertheless does not give what is holy to dogs; for worthy persons were present, who ought not to be neglected because of the uncleanness of others.

[CHRYSOSTOM.] Where the withered hand is discussed, Christ first presents an authority to his accusers under a kind of question, then the reason. Here, however, he first gave the reason, saying, “For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are married,” and afterward the authority: “I am the God of Abraham.” He did this so that we may first present authority to accusers and then reason; but when people question us with any purpose, we should first set out reason and afterward confirm it by authority. For accusers must be refuted, but questioners taught; an accuser, even if he understands the reason, does not assent.

CHAPTER CXXVIII.

M. 224[II] R. 131 L. 121

[Col. 0400C] But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. And one of the scribes, a doctor of the Law, came up, testing him and saying: “Teacher, which commandment is great in the Law?”

[JEROME.] Although Pharisees and Sadducees were opposed to one another, they nevertheless agreed with one mind to test the Lord, as we read that Herod and Pilate did in the Lord’s death. Though the Pharisees had often been refuted, malice and envy nourish shamelessness. Thus, stripped of truth, they armed themselves with a multitude, saying among themselves: “Let all of us speak through one, so that if he is defeated, he may seem confounded.” He calls him teacher though he does not wish to be his disciple. This most simple questioner and most malicious plotter asks about the great commandment while observing not even the least. For one ought to ask about greater righteousness only after fulfilling the lesser.

Jesus said to him: “The first commandment of all is: ‘Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God; and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength.’ This is the first and greatest commandment” (Deut. VI). “And the second is like it: ‘You shall love your neighbour as yourself.’ On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (Lev. XIX).

First and greatest is to love the one God above all things; and this we ought to establish before everything else as the single foundation of piety. Therefore he did not say, “You shall know,” but “You shall love,” because to know that there is one God is [Col. 0401A] almost proper to human nature; but to love him belongs to a devout and upright heart. The command concerning love of one’s neighbour is like this, because a human being is the image of God.

[ISIDORE.] Love toward God is the source of love toward one’s neighbour, and love toward one’s neighbour is knowledge of love toward God. Love of God is expressed in three things, so that nothing may remain in a human being which is not subjected to divine love. For when it is said, “Love God with all your heart,” it commands that all thoughts be directed to God. When it says, “With all your soul,” it commands that all the affections of the soul be directed to God. And when it adds, “With all your mind,” it indicates that all human reason, by which we understand and discern, is to be occupied with divine things. Where it says, “With all your strength,” it enjoins the good of perseverance. Likewise, two things [Col. 0401B] must be preserved in love toward one’s neighbour: that he be cherished by the bestowal of kindness, and that he be harmed by no malice. This is what is meant by: “Do not do to another what you do not wish done to yourself” (Tob. IV); and, “Whatever you approve that people should do to you, do also to them” (Luke VI). Therefore, although the precepts are diverse, by which we either usefully desire what ought to be sought or usefully guard against what ought to be avoided, they are nevertheless one at the root of love, because we ought to do everything in love of God and neighbour. Thus it rightly says that the Law and the Prophets are referred to the two commandments of love, because the whole Decalogue and the admonitions of the prophets have their end there. Let us therefore consider the Decalogue:

But because what is grasped in metre is retained better,

Behold, the observance [perhaps “harmony”] of the Law resounds upon ten strings.

[Col. 0401C] The Almighty is one; there is no other God at all.

Take care not to fashion any image of him.

Do not take this name in vain; keep the Sabbaths.

The first tablet comprises these four commands.

The remaining six are thus inscribed on the second tablet:

That you may endure longer, hold your parents in honour.

Do not strike with the sword; be neither adulterer nor thief;

Be no false witness; do not covet what belongs to another.

R. 132[X]

And the scribe said to him: “Well, Master, you have spoken truly: for God is one, and there is no other besides him; and to love him with all the heart, and with all the understanding, and with all the soul, and with all the strength, and to love [Col. 0401D] one’s neighbour as oneself, is greater than all burnt offerings and sacrifices.”

[BEDĒ.] By this answer the scribe shows that there was often a serious dispute among the scribes and Pharisees as to which was the greatest commandment: some praised offerings and sacrifices, while others preferred the works of faith and love, because many fathers before the Law had pleased God, without any practice of victims and sacrifices, solely through faith working through love; whereas no one has pleased him through sacrifices apart from faith and love.

[CHRYSOSTOM.] We call a commandment great or small in respect of dignity. Otherwise the benefit of all commandments is one, and they are so joined together that one cannot exist without the other. Thus we say that the foundation is [Col. 0402A] better, although neither the foundation can exist without the building nor the building without it. The foundation, then, is not more useful than the building, but more worthy, just as the head is more worthy than the members.

But Jesus, seeing that he had answered wisely, said to him: “You are not far from the kingdom of God. You have answered rightly: do this, and you shall live.”

Because our salvation consists in knowledge of truth and love of virtue, the Sadducees are far from the kingdom of God, since they neither know what must be known nor love what must be loved. But this proud tempter is less far outside the kingdom, because by knowledge he has now assented to evangelical perfection. Yet he would be in the kingdom of God if his knowledge of the true and love of the good increased, so that he might receive Christ both as God and as neighbour.

[Col. 0402B] L. 122[X]

But he, wishing to justify himself, said to Jesus: “And who is my neighbour?”

No one is nearer to a human being than God, who knows inwardly and outwardly, and can heal all things; but every unbeliever or tempter has neither God nor human being as neighbour. The lawyer, wishing to gain popular favour by boasting that he had answered wisely, asks the Lord what he ought to do, but does so because he wishes to justify himself. The Lord moderated his answer by speaking to him in a parable, so that everyone who shows mercy might be understood as a neighbour, and especially that the Son of God himself might be designated, who became near to us through his humanity.

[Col. 0402C] And Jesus, taking up the matter, said: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among robbers.”

This man is understood to be Adam. Jerusalem is the heavenly city, from whose blessedness he fell into this mortal life. Jericho, aptly, signifies this life, since its name is interpreted “moon,” uncertain through its various phases of waning. Understand the robbers to be the devil and his angels, into whose hands he would not have fallen unless he had first swelled inwardly with pride. For the saying is true: “Before ruin the heart is lifted up” (Prov. XVI).

“Who also stripped him, and inflicted wounds on him, and went away, leaving him half-dead.”

They stripped him of the glory of immortality and the garment of innocence. The wounds are sins, by which the integrity of [Col. 0402D] human nature was violated. They went away, not by ceasing in any degree from their snares, but by concealing the deceits of those same snares. They left him half-dead because they were unable to abolish his reason. For in so far as a human being can be wise and know God, he lives; but in so far as he wastes away in sins, stained by the deadly wound, he lies as though dead.

“Now it happened that a certain priest was going down by the same way; and when he saw him, he passed by. Likewise also a Levite, when he was near the place and saw him, passed on.”

The priest and Levite who passed by the wounded man signify the priesthood and ministry of the Old Testament, in which the wounds of the ailing world could be shown but not healed. For the Apostle says that it was impossible for the blood of calves [bulls] and [Col. 0403A] lambs and goats to take away sins (Heb. X). Thus the priest, descending into the world through Moses and proclaiming God’s Law, brought no healing to humanity. So likewise the descent of the Levite, who prefigures the prophets: he heals no one, but when he rebukes sins, he passes on, because he does not grant forgiveness.

“But a certain Samaritan, travelling, came near him; and seeing him, was moved with compassion.”

The Samaritan, whose name is interpreted “guardian,” signifies the Lord, to whom the Prophet prays against these robbers: “Guard me from the snare which they have set for me, and from the stumbling-blocks of those who work iniquity” (Ps. CXL). The Lord himself, having become human, undertook the journey of this present life and came near the wounded man: near through his assumption of our compassion, and neighbourly through the bestowal of mercy. [Col. 0403B] But the Law had not mercy, but judgment and vengeance.

“And approaching, he bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine.”

For the sins which he found in human beings he restrained by rebuking them, promising hope of pardon to the penitent and instilling fear of punishment into sinners. Thus he binds the wounds when he commands, “Repent”; he pours in oil when he adds, “For the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. VII); and he pours in wine when he says, “Every tree which does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. IV). Or, he binds up the wounds in baptism and pours in oil and wine—that is, the chrism of the Holy Spirit and the cup of his passion.

[Col. 0403C] “And placing him upon his own beast, he brought him to an inn and took care of him.”

His beast is his flesh, in which he bore our sins upon the wood and, according to another parable, carried the straying sheep back to the flock. Therefore, to be placed upon the beast is to believe in Christ’s incarnation and to be protected from hostile attack by his mysteries. The inn is the present Church, in which travellers returning to their eternal homeland are refreshed in hope. By the name of an inn he pointedly suggests the miseries and foulness of this life, lest a human being rejoice in this exile as though it were a homeland. He took care that the sick man, brought into the Church, should not abandon the precepts he had received.

“And on the next day he brought out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, [Col. 0403D] saying: ‘Take care of him; and whatever you spend beyond this, I will repay you when I return.’”

The next day is after the Lord’s resurrection, which shines more brightly than the preceding time. The two denarii are the two Testaments, in which the name and image of the eternal King are contained. The innkeeper is the company of disciples, to whom he opened the understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures through the Holy Spirit. The innkeeper spends beyond what he receives in the two denarii when the Apostle Paul says: “But concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, yet I give counsel” (1 Cor. VII). Likewise he spends beyond it when he says: “The Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel; but we have not used this authority, lest we burden any of you” (1 Cor. IX). The returning debtor [Col. 0404A] will repay what he promised, when the Lord says in judgment: “Because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV).

“Which of these three seems to you to have been neighbour to him who fell among robbers?” And he said: “The one who showed mercy to him.” And Jesus said to him: “Go, and do likewise.”

No one is nearer to us than he who healed our wounds, as the head is near to the members. Let us therefore love him as God and Lord; let us love him as neighbour; and let us also love all imitators of Christ. What he says, “Do likewise,” means this: whatever you can do to relieve your neighbour’s need, whether bodily or spiritual, do it devotedly, so that you may be shown [Col. 0404B] to be a neighbour. Mercy rightly makes one a neighbour, because it accords with nature. For nothing is so natural as to help one who shares one’s nature.

## CHAPTER CXXIX

L. 239[I] M. 220 R. 122 A. 85

“And he was teaching daily in the temple. But the chief priests and scribes and leaders of the people were seeking to destroy him, and they could not find what they might do to him. For all the people hung upon his words as they heard him.”

[HILARY.] Christ was indeed teaching daily in the temple, whose proper office it is to bring knowledge of God and grant understanding of his name and power. For this purpose he had come, brought forth from eternity. The people therefore hung upon him—that is, they were drawn away from the speech of the leaders, acknowledging Christ’s teaching to be more powerful, while the leaders themselves could find no grounds for condemnation in him.

A. 78[X]

“The Pharisees heard the crowd murmuring these things concerning him.”

A. 79[I] M. 300 R. 197 L. 285

“And the chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to seize him.”

[AUGUSTINE.] The mad leaders, hearing the murmuring by which Christ was glorified by the crowd, seek to kill him.

[Col. 0404D] A. 80[X]

Jesus therefore said: “Yet a little while I am with you, and I go to him who sent me.”

They could not seize him while he did not will it, but they heard him teaching. Christ’s mission from the Father was his emptying of himself—that is, his appearing on earth; his return, however, was the glorification of resurrection and ascension, by which it became known to human hearts that he had been and is with the Father, and equal to the Father.

A. 81[X]

“You shall seek me, and you shall not find me.”

He foretells that after his resurrection they will seek him and will not find him, either by faith or bodily. [Col. 0405A] It should be known that many, pierced with compunction after the Lord’s resurrection, believed, for whom, hanging on the cross, he deigned to pray thus: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke XXIII).

“And where I am, you cannot come.”

He did not say, “Where I shall be,” but, “Where I am,” because his divinity came to us in such a way that it did not depart from heaven. A human being, according to the body, is in a place and moves from place to place; when he comes to another place, he is not in the place from which he came. But God fills all things and is wholly everywhere. Thus Christ was on earth according to the flesh, and in heaven and on earth according to majesty. He did not say, “You will not be able,” lest they despair, but, “You cannot,” while you are such as you are.

The Jews therefore said among themselves: “Where is this man going, that we shall not find him? Is he going into the Dispersion among the Gentiles, and will he teach the Gentiles? What is this saying that he spoke: ‘You shall seek me, and you shall not find me’; and, ‘Where I am, you cannot come’?”

They did not know what they said, but because the Lord willed it, they prophesied. The Lord was going to the Gentiles, not by the presence of his body, but through the preaching of the apostles. He was going to fulfill what they read and did not understand: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. XVII). Those in whose sight the Lord was did not hear him; those in whose ears he resounded heard him.

But on the last, great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers [Col. 0405C] of living water shall flow from his belly.” But he said this of the Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive.

Here he explains to what drink he summoned those who thirsted—that is, those desiring refreshment through divine love. Therefore, whoever thirsts, let him come in the affection of love, withdrawing from love of the world by the steps of faith; and let him drink the Holy Spirit. When he has drunk him, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly. The belly of the inward person is the conscience of the heart; the rivers are benevolence, by which one provides for one’s neighbour from living water—that is, from grace which cleanses and gives life to minds. For living water does not flow from the belly of one who thinks that what he drinks ought to suffice for himself alone. This testimony is in Proverbs, as is read in the prologue to Genesis (Prov. XVIII). Perhaps some will dispute [Col. 0405D] that the Evangelist John here mentions the feast of Tabernacles; but perhaps they will readily refrain from such disputes if they carefully notice how Matthew and Mark report the expulsion from the temple, and other similar transpositions either of times or events.

“For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.”

[AUGUSTINE.] Many had the Holy Spirit before Christ’s coming, but not in the way in which he was later given, so that they spoke in the languages of all nations; and therefore he says, “The Spirit had not yet been given.” Since all who are baptized in Christ receive the Holy Spirit, why do they not speak in all languages? Because the Church now possesses the languages of all; but formerly [Col. 0406A] the Church was in one nation, and when it spoke in the languages of all, it signified that the Church, growing through all nations, would speak in the languages of all. The Church is Christ’s body; you are a member. For the unity of the members agrees in love, and that unity itself speaks, just as one person then spoke. Therefore after his resurrection the Lord gave the Spirit, so that he might show in his body the life which we do not yet have, but hope for in the resurrection.

A. 82[VII] M. 120

Therefore some of that crowd, hearing these sayings of his, said: “This is truly the Prophet.” Others said: “This is the Christ.”

[Col. 0406B] A. 83[VII] M. 105

But some said: “Does the Christ come from Galilee? Does not Scripture say that Christ comes from the seed of David and from Bethlehem, the town where David was?”

A. 84[X]

Therefore a division arose in the crowd because of him.

A. 86[X]

The officers therefore came to the chief priests and Pharisees, and they said to them: “Why have you not brought him?” The officers answered: “Never has a man spoken as this man speaks.” The Pharisees therefore answered them: “Have you also been deceived? Has any one of the leaders believed in him, or of the Pharisees? But [Col. 0406C] this crowd, which does not know the Law, are accursed.”

This is what the Lord said: “I came that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may become blind.”

Nicodemus said to them—he who had come to him by night, and who was one of them: “Does our Law judge a person unless it first hears from him and knows what he does?” (John III).

Nicodemus believed that if they were willing patiently to hear him, they would become like those who had been sent to seize him and believed.

They answered and said to him: “Are you also a Galilean?”

That is, they call Nicodemus a Galilean because he had been misled by the Lord, who was called a Galilean because his parents were from Nazareth, a city of Galilee [Col. 0406D].

“Search the Scriptures and see that no prophet arises from Galilee.”

The Lord of the prophets arose from there, whom Scripture calls a Nazarene.

## CHAPTER CXXX

M. 225[II] R. 134 L. 245

When the Pharisees had assembled, Jesus questioned them, saying: “What do you think concerning Christ? Whose son is he?” They said to him: “David’s.” He said to them: “How then does David, in the book of Psalms, call him Lord, saying: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet’?”

[Col. 0407A] [AMBROSE.] To say, “the Lord said to my Lord,” is to beget a Son equal to himself. David calls him “my Lord,” not insofar as he was born from him, but insofar as he has always been from the Father. That enemies are subjected by the Father, whether willingly or unwillingly, signifies not the Son’s weakness but unity of nature, by which one works in the other. For the Son also subjects enemies to the Father, because he glorifies the Father upon earth. Thus Jesus’ question benefits us against the Jews. But the Jews devise many frivolous things, asserting that the one hundred and ninth Psalm was written in the person of Eliezer, Abraham’s home-born servant, returning from the slaughter of five kings; and they introduce him as speaking thus: “The Lord God said to my lord Abraham, after the slaughter of five kings: Sit at my right hand.” [Col. 0407B] But the subsequent portions of the Psalm do not agree with this. The Jews are therefore rightly opposed, not because they call the Christ whom they confess is to come David’s son, but because they believe him to be merely human and not the Son of God.

M. 226[II] R. 133 L. 244

“If David therefore calls him Lord in the Spirit, how is he his son?” And no one was able to answer him a word, nor did anyone dare from that day onward to question him any more.

Because they are refuted in argument, they no longer question him, but hand him over when openly seized to Roman authority. From this it is clear that the poisons of envy may be overcome, but are difficult to quiet.

## CHAPTER CXXXI

[Col. 0407C]

A. 86[X]

Jesus therefore spoke to them again, saying: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.”

[AUGUSTINE.] The light of the world, proceeding from the Father, is covered by the cloud of flesh; and thus tempered, it is made bearable for human beings, so that through the human being one may come to divinity. Therefore, while that light illumines us, we who were born blind from Adam are now illumined by the eye-salve of faith; and we follow in obedience both to words and examples, so that, the darkness of ignorance or sins being expelled, we may in the future be illumined by the manifest vision of the Godhead.

[Col. 0407D] The Pharisees therefore said to him: “You bear witness concerning yourself. Your testimony is not true.”

Those who said this had weak eyes, because they could not bear the light. They think he ought not to be believed, as though he alone bore witness concerning himself, forgetting the lamps of prophecy which went before and John the Baptist himself, who clearly testified concerning him.

Jesus answered and said to them: “Even if I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is true, because I know from where I came and where I am going. But you do not know from where I come or where I am going.”

He means the Father, by whom his testimony is confirmed. Because they do not know this, they judge according to the flesh, and therefore he seems arrogant to them. Whenever any human being wishes to bear praiseworthy testimony concerning himself, [Col. 0408A] he seems arrogant and proud. Therefore it is written: “Let not your own mouth praise you, but the mouth of your neighbour” (Prov. XXVII). But this was said to a human being who can lie. Light, however, cannot lie.

“You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one.”

Understand: “according to the flesh, as you do.” Or: “I do not judge now.” Hence elsewhere: “I did not come to judge the world, but to save it” (John XII), not denying judgment but postponing it. For mercy had first to be shown, and judgment afterward exercised, as the Psalmist says: “Mercy and judgment I shall sing to you, O Lord” (Ps. C).

“And if I judge, my judgment is true, because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.”

[Col. 0408B] The sense is: my judgment is true because I am the true Son of God. Blush, Sabellian: you hear “Son,” you hear “Father.” Distinguish the persons by understanding, not by faithlessness, lest, as if fleeing Charybdis, you run upon Scylla. Charybdis swallows you if you say that he who is the Father is himself the Son; you are shipwrecked upon Scylla’s rocks if you say that the Son is less than the Father in divinity. Therefore do not say, “The Father is gold, the Son is silver”; for there is one substance, one divinity, one co-eternity, perfect equality. Hear the Son: “I and the Father are one” (John X). Hear both “one” and “are,” and you shall be freed from both Charybdis and Scylla. In saying “one,” he frees you from Arius; in saying “are,” he frees you from [Col. 0408C] Sabellius. When you say, “The Father is one, the Son another,” you speak rightly; but if you say, “The Father is one thing and the Son another thing,” you err.

“And in your Law it is written that the testimony of two human beings is true. I am one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me.”

Even if I postpone judgment now, I do not postpone testimony. He proves from the authority of the Law that his own testimony and the Father’s are true, where there is steadfast truth. He expounded the Law to them, if they were not ungrateful. It is a great question, and the matter seems to me very much established in mystery, where God says: “By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Deut. XIX). This is the customary practice of the human race; yet Susanna was pressed by two false [Col. 0408D] witnesses, and the whole people lied against Christ. Therefore the Trinity is commended through the mystery. Do you wish to have a good cause? Have two or three witnesses: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. This Trinity bore witness for Susanna in her conscience, raising up one witness, Daniel, and convicting two. Let us also choose God as our witness. For he who is Judge does not disdain to be a witness. He is a witness because he needs no one else from whom to learn who you are; he is Judge because he has power to give life and death, condemn and absolve, cast down into hells and raise up into heavens, join to the devil and crown with angels. When he says, “in your Law,” it is said as though he had said, “in the Law given to you by God”; [Col. 0409A] just as it is said, “our daily bread,” and yet we say, “give us this day” (Luke XI).

They therefore said to him: “Where is your Father?”

A. 87[III] M. 112 L. 119

Jesus answered: “You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, perhaps you would also know my Father.”

You think me only human; therefore you seek my Father as a human being. He who knows all things, when he says “perhaps,” does not doubt but rebukes. O human being! When a word is in your heart, it is something other than its sound; but in order to pass to me, it seeks sound as a kind of vehicle. It takes up the sound, so to speak places itself upon the vehicle, passes through the air, and comes to me without departing [Col. 0409B] from you. Yet the sound, in coming to me, departed from you and did not remain with me. Did the word, then, which was in your heart, pass away when the sound passed by? The sound flew across between us; but the word which took up the sound is with me and has not departed from you. Consider this, whoever you are who examine sounds. Do you despise the Word of God when you do not comprehend a human word? God knows all things. He also spoke such a saying to the disciples as he now spoke to the Jews, when Philip asked him, saying: “Lord, show us the Father.” “Philip, he who sees me sees also the Father” (John XIV). Here there was no “perhaps he sees also the Father,” a word of uncertainty, because the Lord was not rebuking unbelief but teaching. Do not then be surprised concerning the Word of God, whether he says “perhaps” or speaks otherwise, since you do not fully comprehend even a human word.

A. 89[X]

“I go away, and you shall seek me, and you shall die in your sin.”

You will not seek me in desire, but in hatred. After the Lord departed, both those who hated and those who loved him sought him: the former by persecuting him, the latter by desiring to possess him.

“Where I go, you cannot come.”

He said this also elsewhere to the disciples, not removing hope as he did from these people, but proclaiming a delay.

The Jews therefore said: “Will he kill himself, because he says, ‘Where I go, you cannot come’?”

[Col. 0409D] Foolish words, as though they themselves were immortal and could not go where he was going if he killed himself. But the Lord was speaking not of death but of the glory to which he was going after death. They, understanding everything carnally, did not understand it.

And he said to them: “You are from below; I am from above.”

Therefore you savour the earth, because, like serpents, you eat earth. What does it mean, “You eat earth”? You feed on earthly things, delight in earthly things, covet earthly things; your heart is not set above. “I am from above,” that is, from the Father, surpassing all things with him.

“You are of this world; I am not of this world. Therefore I said to you that you shall die in your sins.”

He explains what it is to be of the world: to be sinners, [Col. 0410A] unbelieving, and minded toward earthly things. Therefore he, through whom the world was made, is not of this world; for all who are of the world were made after the world. But the Lord is before the world, because “in the beginning was the Word.”

“For if you do not believe that I am, you shall die in your sin.”

Conversely, he gives hope to believers, that they may be raised from the world to him who made the world. Because he added nothing when saying, “that I am,” he gave much to be understood: namely, “I am the Father’s Word, maker of the world, former and restorer of humankind.” Whoever does not believe this dies in sins. To Moses also I said: “I am who am” (Exod. III); that is, I possess true being, because I am not changeable but always the same. In every [Col. 0410B] movement of things I find past and future; in God’s truth, the present alone.

They therefore said to him: “Who are you?” Jesus said to them: “The Beginning, even as I speak to you.”

He is the Beginning, of whom it was said: “But you are the selfsame, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. CI). He knew that some there would believe, and therefore they said, “Who are you?” so that they might know what they ought to believe him to be. He answered, therefore, “The Beginning,” not as though saying, “I am the Beginning,” but as though saying, “Believe me to be the Beginning.” This is evident in the Greek expression, where “beginning” (*archē*) is feminine in gender, just as “law” (*nomos*) is masculine. But the custom of speech varies the genders of words across languages because no sex is found in the things themselves. For wisdom is not truly female [a woman], although Christ is God’s wisdom. Therefore, though to the question, “Who are you?” he seems to have been required to answer, “I am truth,” he answered as though saying, “Believe me to be the Beginning.” And he added, “even as I speak to you,” that is, “I who, made lowly for your sake, have come down to these words.” The Father is Beginning, and the Son is Beginning; yet they are not two beginnings, just as they are not two gods. For if many souls drawing near to God through love are one soul, and many hearts one heart (Acts IV), how much more is the Trinity itself, the fountain of love, one God?

“I have many things to say and to judge concerning you; but he who sent me is true. And what I have heard from him, these things I speak in the world.” And they did not understand that he called God [Col. 0410D] his Father.

I have many things to say: in teaching, if you believe; in rebuking, if you do not believe. And I have to judge the living and the dead in the future. But all this is from the Father, from whom I hear the truth which I speak. For the Son to hear from the Father is the same as to be from him. The sense, then, is: I judge truly because I am Truth, the Son of the True One.
