This Truth is neither greater nor less than that True One, but equal to him—although a devout person is less than piety itself, a beautiful person less than beauty itself, and a chaste person less than chastity. For if the piety which is with God, in which a devout soul participates, departs from that devout soul—or likewise beauty or chastity—God nevertheless neither increases nor diminishes, just as your eye neither diminishes the light when closed nor increases the light when open. By [Col. 0411A] this comparison: if a soul is true, truth is with God, in which it participates; and if it does not participate in it, then every human being is false, because no human being is true from himself. Therefore God the Father is true, not by participating in truth, but by begetting Truth.

Jesus therefore said to them: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you shall know that I am, and that I do nothing from myself, but speak these things as the Father taught me. And he who sent me is with me and has not left me alone, because I always do what is pleasing to him.”

He foretells that some among them, after his passion, would know who he was and believe in him. Here he calls his passion an “exaltation,” not his glorification; the cross, not heaven. “I do nothing from myself,” that is, “I am not from myself.” He said this against the Patripassians, [Col. 0411B] who say, “He who is Father is himself Son. There are two names, but one reality.” “The Father taught me” means, “The Father begot me as one knowing.” Earlier he had said that he was sent; but he often recalls this great matter: although both are together, one was sent and the other sent, since the mission is the incarnation, which belongs to the Son alone and not also to the Father. For nowhere is the Father read to have appeared in any form. The Father’s power, especially manifested from the creation of the world, is not expressly declared by any individual creature, as his wisdom is in Christ’s humanity, or as the manifold grace of his goodness is in the division of tongues or in the dove.

[AUGUSTINE.] Just as heat and brightness in a ray of the sun cannot be separated from each other—yet heat dries [Col. 0411C] while brightness illumines—and just as reason is in the soul, but we live by the soul and understand by reason, so the Son alone assumed flesh, yet did not separate himself from the Father. And because the Father fills heaven and earth, the Holy Spirit also fills them; in the unity of divinity they fill Christ’s flesh by majesty, not by assumption.

While he was saying these things, many believed in him. Jesus therefore said to the Jews who believed him: “If you remain in my word, you shall truly be my disciples; and you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.”

[AUGUSTINE.] “If you remain in my word”—that is, if you persevere to the end in the faith which began to be in you through the word—then you shall be my disciples, so that you may know the truth which you now believe: the truth which [Col. 0411D] now, covered in flesh, speaks to you and is hidden from you. “It has not yet appeared what we shall be”; but at last we shall see him as he is (1 John III), when he has marked us with the light of his countenance. We are God’s coinage, his coins. We wandered from his treasury; through wandering, what had been stamped upon us was worn away. He who had formed us came to reform us; he too seeks his own coin, just as Caesar seeks his. Hence he says: “Render therefore the things which are Caesar’s to Caesar, and the things which are God’s to God” (Matt. XXII). “Will make free”: the Lord used this word in relation to freedom. For just as “he saves” means nothing other than “he makes safe,” so “he frees” properly means nothing other than “he makes free.” This is clearer in Greek. For in Latin we often use *liberare*, “to deliver,” not with reference to freedom [Col. 0412A] but to salvation, when someone is improperly said to be delivered from sickness.

They answered him: “We are Abraham’s seed, and we have never been enslaved to anyone. How do you say, ‘You shall become free’?”

Those who believed did not answer; rather, the unbelievers boast that they are Abraham’s seed. O inflated skin! You understood only temporal freedom, according to which you also lie when you say, “We have never been enslaved to anyone.” Was Joseph not sold? (Gen. XXXVII). Were not the holy prophets taken captive? Did not your fathers serve in Egypt, making bricks? (Exod. I). Were you yourselves not paying tribute to the Romans?

Jesus answered them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.”

[AUGUSTINE.] Whoever sins from love of sin, not from the weakness [Col. 0412B] of nature nor from slight ignorance, is a slave of sin. For some sins arise from weakness, some from ignorance, and some from malice. Weakness and ignorance are contrary to virtue and wisdom; malice is contrary to goodness. Whoever therefore knows what God’s wisdom is can judge what sins are pardonable; and whoever knows what God’s goodness is can judge for what sins definite punishment is due, both here and in the age to come.

[AUGUSTINE.] A human slave, wearied sometimes by his master’s harsh commands, finds rest by fleeing. But where shall the slave of sin flee?

“But the slave does not remain in the house for ever; the Son remains for ever. Therefore, if the Son makes you free, you shall be truly free.”

The Church is the house; the slave is the sinner who is obstinate with an unrepentant heart [Col. 0412C]. He did not say, “is not in the house,” because many sinners enter the Church; but he does not remain [do not remain]. Yet since Scripture says, “Who shall boast that he is clean from sin?” (Prov. XX), will Christ alone be in the Church? Whose head will he be, without a body? Therefore he frightened us, lest we should love sin, by saying: “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin.” He gave hope lest we despair, by saying: “The Son remains for ever.” For our hope is that we may be set free by the Free One.

It must be understood that many righteous persons are called “without reproach,” that is, without crime. For in human affairs no just reproach is made against those who have no crime. Crime, however, is grave sin, most worthy of accusation and condemnation. But by God’s grace sin is consumed within us [Col. 0412D]. It is diminished in the life of those making progress, and is consumed in the life of the perfect. Therefore the first freedom is to be free of crimes. Hence the Apostle, concerning those to be ordained as presbyters or deacons, does not say, “if anyone is without sin”; for if he had said this, no one would be ordained. Rather, he says, “if anyone is without crime” (Tit. I), such as murder, adultery, some unclean act of fornication, theft, fraud, sacrilege, and the like. When a Christian begins to be without these things, he begins to raise his head toward freedom; but freedom is not yet perfect, because eternity has not yet come. Perfect freedom is to be in the Lord, when “this corruptible shall put on incorruption, and this mortal shall put on immortality” (I Cor. XV).

“I know that you are Abraham’s children; but you seek to kill me, because my word has no place in you.”

[Col. 0413A] That is, it does not take hold of your heart, because it is not received by your heart. The divine Word is like a hook: it catches while it is caught. Christ recognizes in these people their fleshly descent, in whom vain freedom coexists with the real slavery of sin; but he does not recognize faith of heart through imitation of Abraham, in which there would be true freedom through the Son himself.

“I speak what I have seen with the Father; and you do what you have seen with your father.”

“I have seen the truth,” namely myself, who am the Father’s truth.

They answered and said to him: “Our father is Abraham.”

They were provoking him to say something evil about Abraham, seeking an occasion to do what they intended.

Jesus said to them: “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham [Col. 0413B]. But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth which I heard from God. Abraham did not do this. You do the works of your father.”

He does not yet say who their father is, but praises Abraham and condemns them as degenerate, because they do not prove themselves to be Abraham’s children by works of faith. Rather, by the opposite they are proved not to be his children, because they seek to extinguish the truth.

Therefore they said to him: “We were not born from fornication; we have one Father, God.”

They had now, in some measure, begun to recognize that the Lord was not speaking of physical descent but of the pattern of life. And because it is customary in Scripture to call service of false gods “fornication,” they said: “We have one Father, God” [Col. 0413C]. I think they were considering: “Whenever we name Abraham, he will say to us, ‘Why do you not imitate the man in whose lineage you glory?’ And because we cannot imitate so great a man, let us say that we have God as our Father, so that we may hear what he says.”

Jesus therefore said to them: “If God were your Father, you would surely love me. For I proceeded from God and came. For I did not come of myself, but he sent me.”

As he had previously shown concerning Abraham, so now he shows that God is not their Father, because they neither know nor love the Son whom he sent. To proceed means that God is the natural source and eternal cause of his Wisdom’s existence; to come, however, means to become incarnate. For God is not wise by participation, as a soul or an angel is [Col. 0413D], but because he begets from himself Wisdom, which is God from God.

“Why do you not understand my speech? Because you cannot hear my word. You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s desires.”

Here the heresy of the Manichaeans must be avoided. They say that there is a certain nature of evil, and a certain nation of darkness with its rulers. This nation dared to fight against God; and they say that the true God sent rulers against that nation and that it was defeated. From this, they say, the devil derived his origin, thinking that the Lord’s saying, “You are of your father the devil,” was spoken in this sense. The Jews, therefore, were called children of the devil through imitation, not through birth. The Prophet said to them: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. XVI) [Col. 0414A], not because the Jews derived their origin from those nations, but because they imitated their impieties.

Perhaps one may ask: whence is the devil? Certainly from the same source as the other angels; but through pride he became the devil. And it should be noted that he was corrupted neither by an intrinsic force nor by external persuasion, but by his own will: from the greatness of his knowledge he took an occasion for self-exaltation. Hence the Apostle says: “Knowledge puffs up” (I Cor. VIII).

“He was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him.”

The devil is called a murderer, not because he came against a human being armed with a sword or girded with iron, but because he sowed an evil word. Therefore do not think that you are not a murderer when you persuade your brother to evil. Hence in the Psalm: “The teeth of the sons of men are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. LVI) [Col. 0414B]. What is said, “from the beginning,” must be understood of the first human being.

“When he speaks falsehood, he speaks from his own resources, because he is a liar and its father.”

From this the Manichaeans deceive the unlearned, saying that the devil has a father; but the Lord said that the devil is the father of falsehood. For the devil begot falsehood, as though a son, when he fell from the truth, which God the Father begot in the Son. Therefore the devil is a liar and the father of falsehood. But if you lie, you have received it from the devil, as the Jews did when they spoke falsehood; and thus you are not the father of falsehood.

[Col. 0414C] “But because I speak the truth, you do not believe me. Which of you will convict me of sin?”

[GREGORY.] He does not disdain to show by reason that he is not a sinner.

“If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me? He who is of God hears God’s words. Therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God.”

There are some who do not deign even to receive God’s commands with the ear of the body. There are some who receive them, but embrace them with no desire of the mind. There are some who, hearing gladly, are pierced with compunction, but after their tears return to iniquity. These certainly do not hear God’s words, because they scorn to put them into practice. Although, therefore, all are children of God by nature—as the parables of the dutiful and prodigal son [Col. 0414D], and of the two sons invited to the vineyard, show—nevertheless those who do not love God’s words are of the devil through vice. But those who are born again of God through the generation of adoption hear and keep God’s word.

The Jews then answered and said to him: “Do we not rightly say that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?”

The Samaritans had received the Lord when he spoke with the woman at the well and had stayed with them. Thus the Jews call him a Samaritan, as though a sinner, because they regarded the Samaritans as sinners and did not count them among themselves.

Jesus answered: “I do not have a demon; rather, I honor my Father, and you have dishonored me.”

[Col. 0415A] [GREGORY.] Of the two charges, he denied one. For “Samaritan” means “guardian,” and he did not deny that he was a guardian. “He who guards Israel neither slumbers” (Ps. CXX). And: “Unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it watches in vain” (Ps. CXXVI). He did not return insulting words, though he could truly have answered: “You have a demon.” But here our pride is put to shame. For what is indicated to us by this, except that when we receive false insults from our neighbors, we should also keep silent about their real evils, lest we turn the ministry of just correction into weapons of rage?

“But I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges.”

[AUGUSTINE.] I do not seek glory as pretenders do [Col. 0415B], who seek to appear to be what they are not. There is the Father, who seeks my glory and judges—that is, distinguishes it from your glory—because you glory according to the world, whereas I do not. Rather, I possess that glory which I had with the Father before the world existed, a glory distinct from human self-exaltation. In respect of punitive judgment, the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son; in respect of discriminating judgment, he judges, as in the Psalm: “Judge me, O God” (Ps. LII). The explanation of this judgment follows: “And distinguish,” he says, “my cause from the unholy nation” (ibid.).

Likewise we understand two temptations: one deceives, the other tests. For it is written: “God tempts no one” (Jas. I); and again it is written: “The Lord your God tests you, that he may know whether you love him” (Deut. XIII). “That he may know” is said in the sense, “that he may cause it to be known” [Col. 0415C]. Job was hidden from himself (Job I), but not from God. God admitted the tempter and made Job know himself. So too there are two fears: servile fear, when you fear suffering punishment; and chaste fear, when you fear losing righteousness. Perfect love casts out the former (I John IV); the latter keeps us before God, remaining for ever and ever (Ps. XVIII). For an adulterous woman fears lest her husband arrive; a chaste woman fears lest her husband depart.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: if anyone keeps my word, he shall never see death.”

[GREGORY.] By his own example he warns us not to cease preaching when the perversity of evil people increases; for the good become better through insults, while the reprobate become worse through kindness.

[Col. 0415D] Therefore the Jews said: “Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham is dead, and the prophets; yet you say: ‘If anyone keeps my word, he shall not taste death for ever.’”

[AUGUSTINE.] He speaks of the second death, the death of Gehenna, the death of condemnation with the devil: neither Abraham nor the prophets died that death. For they died and live; these people were living and were dead. To see or taste death is to experience it.

“Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? The prophets also died. Whom do you make yourself?” Jesus answered: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, whom you say is our God, and you have not known him. But I know him; and if I said that [Col. 0416A] I do not know him, I would be a liar like you. But I know him, and I keep his word.”

As the Son, he spoke the Father’s Word, and he himself was the Father’s Word, speaking to humankind. If, therefore, they had known the Father, they would have received his Son, whom the Father’s voice glorifies at the baptism, on the mountain, and in other such events. Therefore, against their question, “Whom do you make yourself?” he refers his glory to the Father, saying: “If I alone, apart from the Father, glorify myself like pretenders, my glory is nothing.”

“Your father Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad.”

Believing, he rejoiced in hope, that he might see by understanding. What he means by “my day” may be uncertain: whether he means the Lord’s temporal day in the flesh [Col. 0416B], or the day which knows neither rising nor setting. But Abraham saw both. For when he sent his servant to seek a wife for his son Isaac, he said: “Put your hand under my thigh, and swear by the God of heaven” (Gen. XXIV). What does this mean except that it was signified that the God of heaven would come in the flesh from Abraham’s race? Those who condemn Christ’s flesh condemn Abraham’s deed.

[GREGORY.] Abraham saw the Lord’s day when, in a figure of the supreme Trinity, he received three angels as guests.

The Jews therefore said to him: “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” Jesus said to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am.”

He did not say, “I was,” but “I am,” because divinity has no time. He draws them from the perception of flesh to divinity, but [Col. 0416C], hard as stones, they think this is blasphemy.

Therefore they took up stones to throw at him. But Jesus hid himself and went out of the Temple.

[JEROME.] Him whom they could not understand, they sought to overwhelm; but the Lord, who had come to suffer, did not choose to avenge himself. Therefore he hid himself, to give us an example of yielding place to anger; or in order to show that Truth itself is hidden from those who scorn to follow its words, and flees the mind it does not find humble. Note that the thoughtless Jews said to the Lord, “You are not yet fifty years old”; there are some who imagine that there were far more years from the incarnation to the passion than we gather from the histories.

CHAPTER CXXXII.

[Col. 0416D] “And as he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth.”

[ALBINUS.] The Lord is said to pass by because “he did not stand in the way of sinners” (Ps. I). He saw one blind from birth because he had compassion on our mortality. For that blind man is the human race, having blindness from Adam. When Adam sinned, vice grew ingrained in place of nature; hence in respect of the mind we are born blind.

And his disciples asked him: “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” Jesus answered them: “Neither this man sinned nor his parents, but that the works of God might be manifested in him.”

They certainly sinned, but his being born blind was not caused by their sin. The Teacher, seeking a believer in order to make him understanding, gives the cause of the blindness: that the works of God might be manifested in him, namely [Col. 0417A], that by enlightening him, and by signifying through him what he would do in the blindness of the human race, the Son of God might be manifested.

“I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day. Night comes, when no one can work. As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.”

The day is he who says: “I am the light of the world” (John VIII). Therefore, if it is day so long as the Lord is in the world, there will be night when he is not in the world—even though he himself says to the disciples: “You shall do greater things than these” (John XIV). Was Peter working in the night when his shadow healed the sick (Acts V), something the Lord did not do, though he said: “Without me you can do nothing”? (John XV). What then shall we say of this night? This night shall belong to those who hear: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared [Col. 0417B] for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV). Hence also: “Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. XXII). Then no one will be able to work. Therefore let us work while it is still day. For he is still here who said: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXIII).

[ALBINUS.] Further: “While it is day,” that is, while I am in the world, I shall do the works of the Father, preaching him and enlightening the blind. But night was when Christ was both killed by the Jews and faith almost failed. Hence he says to them: “Now is your hour and the power of darkness” (Matt. XXVI).

When he had said this, he spat upon the ground, made clay from the spittle, smeared the clay upon the man’s eyes, and said [Col. 0417C] to him: “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam,” which is interpreted “Sent.”

[AUGUSTINE.] He made clay from spittle because “the Word became flesh.” For the spittle which descends from the head into the mouth signifies Christ’s divinity, because God is Christ’s head. Thus the spittle is wisdom, which comes forth from the mouth of the Most High. The earth, however, is Christ’s flesh. The blind man, when anointed, does not see, but is sent to the pool, whose name is interpreted as “sent by the Lord.” The Lord himself is the Sent One. To be anointed is to become a catechumen; to be washed in the pool is to be baptized in Christ. *Catechumen* is Greek, and is interpreted in Latin as “instructed.” For this reason the untrained are gradually instructed in faith, so that at last, fully enlightened, they may participate in the sacraments with charity. Hence Paul says: “We too were once by nature children [Col. 0417D] of wrath, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. II).

Therefore he went away and washed, and came back seeing. So the neighbors and those who had formerly seen him, because he was a beggar, said: “Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?” Some said, “It is he”; others, “Not at all, but he is like him.” But he himself said: “I am he.”

Some did not recognize him because his opened eyes had changed his face; but he openly acknowledges the benefit, lest he incur the loss of ingratitude.

They therefore said to him: “How were your eyes opened?” He answered: “The man called Jesus made clay and anointed my eyes, and said to me: ‘Go to the pool of Siloam and wash.’ So I went, washed, and saw.”

Siloam is a spring at the foot of Mount Zion, which does not bubble up with continuous waters, but at uncertain times through the hollows [Col. 0418A] of the earth. There the blind man, after washing his face, received light, because the blindness of the Jews, or of any unbelievers, cannot be healed except by the teaching of Christ’s waters, which flows gently without the noise and clamor of words. Hence Isaiah says: “The waters of Siloam, which go softly” (Isa. VIII).

And they said to him: “Where is he?” He said: “I do not know.”

[AUGUSTINE.] His mind still resembled one who had been anointed, not yet one seeing clearly. For he does not know the one whom he proclaims. But those who observed the Sabbath carnally were neither seeing nor anointed.

They brought to the Pharisees the man who had been blind. Now it was the Sabbath when Jesus made the clay and opened his eyes. Therefore the Pharisees again asked him how he had received sight. He said to them: “He put clay [Col. 0418B] upon my eyes, and I washed, and I see.”

He who formed a human being from the clay of the earth re-formed the human race by the same kind of clay.

Therefore some of the Pharisees said: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath.” Others said: “How can a sinful man do such signs?” And there was a division among them.

A division was taking place between light and darkness, because some were already being anointed.

Therefore they said to the blind man again: “What do you say about him, since he opened your eyes?” He said: “He is a prophet.”

They were seeking how to cast him out of the synagogue, but he steadfastly said that he was a prophet, still anointed in heart.

[Col. 0418C] Therefore the Jews did not believe concerning him that he had been blind and had received sight, until they called the parents of the man who had received sight and questioned them, saying: “Is this your son, whom you say was born blind? How then does he now see?” His parents answered them: “We know that this is our son and that he was born blind; but how he now sees we do not know, nor do we know who opened his eyes. Ask him; he is of age. Let him speak for himself.” His parents said these things because they feared the Jews. For the Jews had already agreed that, if anyone confessed him to be the Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue. Therefore his parents said: “He is of age; ask him.” So they again called the man who had been blind and said to him: “Give glory to God.”

[Col. 0418D] That is, deny what you have received—which would be [is] to blaspheme, not to give glory to God. To give glory to God is to speak the truth about someone as before God who is present. Thus they say: “Confess that the righteous one is not righteous as we are, but a sinner.”

“We know that this man is a sinner.” Therefore he said: “Whether he is a sinner, I do not know. One thing I know: whereas I was blind, now I see.” They said to him: “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?” He answered them: “I have told you already, and you heard it. Why do you wish to hear it again? Do you also wish to become his disciples?”

He replied thus, as though indignant and, as though seeing despite being blind, now unable to bear the blind.

They cursed him and said: “May you be his disciple [Col. 0419A]; but we are disciples of Moses. We know that God spoke to Moses; but this man, we do not know where he is from.”

Above they had said, “We know where this man is from”; here they say that they do not know. But we say that we “do not know” the things we reject. Thus, according to their intention, their statement, “May you be his disciple,” is a curse; but what is said is desirable for all, namely that they should be Christ’s disciples.

The man answered and said to them: “This indeed is marvelous: you do not know where he is from, and yet he opened my eyes. But we know that God does not hear sinners. If anyone is a worshipper of God and does his will, God hears him.”

He still speaks as one anointed, for God also hears sinners. For if he did not, the tax collector would in vain strike his breast and say: “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke XVIII).

[AUGUSTINE.] Do not consider it a great thing to be heard by God according to one’s will. The demons were heard according to their will, when they were permitted to go into the swine (Mark V). Their prince, the devil, was heard according to his will when his request that Job be tested was not denied (Job I), so that Job might be proved and the devil confounded [Col. 0419B]. At times God, as if angry, gives what you ask; and graciously refuses what you ask. When you ask for something good, persist in prayer so that you may receive it. The physician knows what is beneficial and what is not.

“From the age it has not been heard that anyone opened the eyes of one born blind. Unless this man were from God, he could do nothing.”

[AUGUSTINE.] Disregarding their anger, he freely confesses the truth. For this could be done only by the Lord, and not even by disciples, unless God were in them [Col. 0419C].

They answered and said to him: “You were wholly born in sins, and do you teach us?” And they cast him out.

They say that his being born with closed eyes was due to his parents’ sin. But Christ heals the whole person outwardly from the eyes, and inwardly opens the heart. By questioning him so often in order that he might speak, they had made a teacher of him; ungratefully they cast out the one teaching them. But because he was expelled, he became more fully a Christian.

CHAPTER CXXXIII.

Jesus heard that they had cast him out; and when he found him, he said to him: “Do you believe in the Son of God?” He answered and said: “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?”

[Col. 0419D] By these words he showed that, although still anointed, his heart had long since been ready to believe, but that he had not known in whom he ought to believe.

Jesus said to him: “You have both seen him, and he who speaks with you is he.” And he said: “I believe, Lord.” And falling down, he worshipped him.

Now the Lord washes the face of the anointed man’s heart; now he enlightens the eyes of his mind; and the man confesses not merely the Son of Man, but also the Son of God.

And Jesus said to him: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may become blind.”

O Lord! You are light; you are day; and therefore you free from darkness the humble, who think that they do not see and seek through you to see. But the proud, wise in their own eyes [Col. 0420A]—such as the Pharisees, stirred by these words—who “see” may become blind: they think they see, but by experiencing punishment they will feel that they are blind. And this is judgment, that is, discrimination, which distinguishes the cause of believers from the proud. For judgment of condemnation will take place not now, but at the end. Hence elsewhere the Lord says: “I judge no one” (John VIII).

Some Pharisees who were with him heard this and said to him: “Are we also blind?” Jesus said to them: “If you were blind, you would not have sin. But now you say, ‘We see’; your sin remains.”

“If you were blind,” that is, if you recognized yourselves as blind and ran to the physician, you would not have sin, because I came to take away sin. But those who think they see and do not seek the physician remain in sin [Col. 0420B]; and this is what it means that those who see may become blind.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: he who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber.”

Because the Pharisees boasted that they saw—which indeed they could do if they were Christ’s sheep—the Lord set forth this likeness against their arrogance. He thus shows that neither wisdom, observance of the law, nor good conduct has any value except through him. Whether a Jew, even a Pharisee, or a Gentile, even a philosopher, teaches people to live well; or whether a heretic does so under Christ’s name, yet does not preach in Christ: all without him plunder and kill. The sheepfold is the Church. Whoever wishes to enter it must enter through Christ, seeking Christ’s glory rather than his own. Christ is the humble [Col. 0420C] door. Therefore let the one who enters humble himself, lest, climbing over the wall, he fall while exalting himself. He certainly climbs in by another way who enters by any means apart from Christ—whether by holding wrong opinions about him, or by seeking not his glory but his own. He is a thief, therefore, because he enters wrongly and calls his own what belongs to another, that is, makes God’s sheep his own. He is a robber because he kills what he has stolen, corrupting the sheep by evil example or perverse teaching.

“But he who enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep. To him the gatekeeper opens, and the sheep hear his voice.”

Wherever the voice of God’s Word sounds, those predestined to life hear it by obeying. And it should be noted that not everyone who enters through the door is a shepherd, because the sheep also enter [Col. 0420D]. Nevertheless, the unity of the universal Church feeds daily by word and example. The gatekeeper is Christ, who opens himself; or Scripture, which leads to Christ; or the Holy Spirit, who teaches all truth.

“And he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. And when he has sent out his own sheep, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, because they know his voice.”

He calls the sheep by name, who says to his disciples: “Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke XX). Hence elsewhere: “The Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II). He leads them out from here into eternal life; he sends them forth by freeing them from the bonds of sins; and he goes before them by rising from the dead. Otherwise: he leads the sheep from darkness into the light of teaching, and goes before them, thus sent forth as if from [Col. 0421A] Egypt, like the pillar of cloud and fire, showing by example what he taught. The sheep follow him wherever he goes, persevering to the end. For those cannot be said to live well who either do not know, through blindness, the end of living well, or scorn it through self-exaltation.

“But they do not follow a stranger, but flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers.” Jesus spoke this proverb to them, but they did not understand what he was saying to them.

In this they are convicted of being blind. For this is the difference between us and them before we recognize these words: we knock, that it may be opened to us; but they do not.

Jesus therefore said to them again: “Amen, amen, I say to you [Col. 0421B]: I am the door of the sheep.”

Just as the Son knows the Father through himself, while we know the Father through him, so he enters the sheepfold—that is, the hearts of the sheep—through himself, while we enter through him. The bodily eye cannot see itself; it sees other things. But the intellect understands both itself and other things. Thus Christ enters into himself, into you, and into the Father through himself. For by the Word, other things that are not the Word are spoken, and the Word himself is spoken. There are many shepherds, such as good bishops, but no one is the door except Christ. In the Apocalypse the saints are called not the door but gates, through which one comes to the door (Rev. XXI).

“All who came are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not hear them.”

Those who came, not those who were sent, were thieves [Col. 0421C]. Hence in the Prophet: “They came, and I did not send them” (Jer. XIV). In those who come there is the presumption of rashness; in those who are sent, the obedience of service.

[AUGUSTINE.] Or thus: “All who came,” namely apart from me, “were robbers.” The heralds of truth did not come apart from him who is the truth; for they believed in him who was to come, just as we believe in him who has come.

[JEROME.] The times have changed, not the faith. There is one canon of Scripture: statements of universality are not always referred to every individual, but to the greater part—as in: “All have turned aside; together they have become worthless” (Ps. XIII). Similarly here: “All who came before me were thieves and robbers.” And Paul says to the Corinthians: “I became all things to all, that I might gain all” (I Cor. IX) [Col. 0421D]. And to the Philippians: “For all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. II). So also is the father’s statement to the dutiful son: “All that is mine is yours” (Luke XV).

[AUGUSTINE.] It should be understood that not all who heard the shepherd’s voice were sheep—for Judas, hearing the shepherd while under sheep’s clothing, was a wolf lying in wait for the shepherd. Yet some of those who crucified Christ did not hear him and were sheep; concerning them the Lord says: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am” (John VIII). Someone resolves this as follows: when they did not hear, they were still wolves; but when they became sheep, they heard. Both can be said. But through Ezekiel, while rebuking the shepherds, the Lord says of the sheep: “You did not bring back the one wandering” (Ezek. XXXIV). He calls it both wandering and a sheep [Col. 0422A]. If it wandered while it was a sheep, undoubtedly it was hearing not the shepherd’s voice but the voice of a thief and robber. Yet the Lord says: “All who came apart from me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not hear them.” Therefore, according to God’s foreknowledge, by which he sees who are his, many sheep are outside and many wolves are within. Many indeed blaspheme Christ who will believe in him: they are sheep outside, but still follow the voice of a stranger. Likewise, many within praise him who will blaspheme later; nevertheless, so long as they think rightly, they hear Christ’s voice.

But there is a particular voice of the shepherd in which sheep do not hear strangers, and in which non-sheep do not hear Christ. What voice is this? “He who perseveres unto the end shall be saved” (Matt. X). His own does not disregard this voice; the stranger does not hear it. For one predestined and foreknown unto life, though he goes astray for a time, eventually returns and perseveres.

“I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he shall be saved; and he shall enter and go out and find pasture.”

The teacher of truth exercises us with obscurities and feeds us with things made plain. Any person without pretence, entering the catholic Church through the brightness of God’s wisdom, shall be saved by persevering; and even before this he was in the sheepfold by divine predestination. He shall enter inwardly by thinking well, according to the Apostle, who says that Christ dwells through faith in our hearts (Eph. III). He shall go out externally by acting well, according to the Psalmist: “Man shall go forth to his work” (Ps. CIII). Otherwise: he shall enter by believing and go out through acting into battle against heretics. Further: he shall enter the Church, in order to live here by faith [Col. 0422C], because “the righteous lives by faith” (Rom. I); and he shall also go out through the door of faith in Christ from this life, in order to live eternally. For where he adds, “I came that they may have life, and have it more abundantly,” he seems to mean that they may have life by entering, and have it more abundantly by going out. Therefore understand “pastures” as the everlasting joys of paradise, the present face of God: when this is beheld without failure, the mind is satisfied without end with the food of life.

“The thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and have it more abundantly.”

The thief comes in order to steal, by appropriating another’s property to himself; to slaughter, by drawing away from life; and to destroy, into eternal condemnation.

[Col. 0422D] “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd gives his life for the sheep.”

[GREGORY.] He is good not accidentally but essentially; he adds the pattern of goodness that we should imitate, saying: “The good shepherd gives his life for the sheep.” He did what he urged; he showed what he commanded. He laid down his life, in order to turn his body and blood into our sacrament and to satisfy with the food of his flesh the sheep whom he had redeemed. The first thing is to bestow our outward goods mercifully upon the sheep; the last, if necessity requires it, is to die for them. Hence John says in his Epistle: “As Christ laid down his life for us, so we too ought to lay down our lives for our brothers” (I John XXX). This is distinctive of the good shepherd, as opposed to the hireling or thief. All who are set over [Col. 0423A] the Church are sons; they are shepherds. If they are shepherds, how is there one shepherd, unless they are all members of the one shepherd, whose own sheep they are?

“The hireling, who is not a shepherd and whose sheep are not his own, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees. And the wolf seizes and scatters the sheep. The hireling flees because he is a hireling and does not care about the sheep.”

Whoever is set over the Church and seeks temporal advantages rather than the things that are Christ’s is a hireling. Of such persons the Lord says: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI). Yet hirelings are necessary, because through them Christ’s voice is heard. Hear the Lord pointing out hirelings: “The scribes,” he says, “and the Pharisees have sat upon Moses’ seat [Col. 0423B]; do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. XXIII). What else did he say but that one should hear the shepherd’s voice through hirelings? For no hireling has dared to say to Christ’s people: “I seek what is yours, not what is Jesus Christ’s.” Therefore he harms precisely where he does evil, not where he speaks good things. Pluck the cluster; beware the thorn. A cluster is sometimes interwoven with thorns, and the thorn bears a fruit not its own when the vine-shoot rests upon thorns. Moses’ seat was the Pharisees’ vine; their conduct, the thorns; true teaching comes through evil men: the vine-shoot is in the hedge, and the cluster among thorns. Choose carefully, lest, while seeking fruit, you tear your hand; and when you hear one speaking good things, do not imitate his evil deeds. “Do what they say”: choose the grapes. “But do not do what they do”: beware the thorns. Hear the Apostle speaking concerning hirelings [Col. 0423C]: “What then, provided that in every way, whether from pretext or from truth, Christ is proclaimed?” (Phil. I). Truth—that is, Christ—is proclaimed by hirelings from pretext, and by sons in truth. Sons patiently await their Father’s eternal inheritance; hirelings hastily desire a temporal payment.

[GREGORY.] Therefore, a hireling is one who occupies the shepherd’s place but does not seek the profit of souls, because he hankers after earthly advantages and delights in the honour of preeminence. Yet whether he is a hireling cannot readily be discerned except when the wolf approaches, who reveals with what disposition each guardian watches over the flock. The wolf comes when any unjust man and robber oppresses the faithful. Thus he who seemed to be a shepherd, but was not, flees—not by changing [Col. 0423D] his place, but by withholding help. For he is silent and does not dare to resist injustice; of him it is said through the Prophet: “You have not gone up against the enemy, nor set up a wall for the house of Israel, so that it might stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Ezek. XIII). To go up against the enemy is to oppose wicked men with a free voice. To set up a wall and stand in battle on the day of the Lord for the house of Israel is, by the authority of justice, to defend the faithful against the injustice of perverse men. The evil spirit too is a wolf: he tears minds, not bodies, continually prowling round the sheepfolds of the faithful; of him it is said, “he scatters the sheep.” For then he scatters them, when he draws one into lust, inflames another with avarice, and exalts another into pride. He spurs this one with envy and trips that one by deceit. Thus the wolf scatters the flock when [Col. 0424A] the devil kills the faithful through temptations.

[AUGUSTINE.] But the hireling, seeing the wolf, flees, because he is a hireling and does not love Christ in the sheep, but their milk and wool. He does not dare freely to rebuke one who sins, nor to excommunicate one who ought to be excommunicated, lest he lose the advantage of human friendship or incur the inconvenience of human enmities. Thus he flees because he is silent; he is silent because he is afraid. Flight is the fear of the mind lest it lose what it loves. He remains in body but flees in spirit. This was not what he did who said: “Though I am absent in body, I am with you in spirit” (Col. II). Shepherds, therefore, do not flee for their own sake, but yield to persecution—as the Apostle himself was lowered in a basket through a wall (Acts IX). For he commended the sheep, while their shepherd was seated in heaven, to him in prayers; and, by fleeing, preserved himself for their benefit [Col. 0424B], as he says elsewhere: “To remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. I). For they had all heard from the shepherd himself: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. X). Thus in the hireling it is not bodily flight that is reproved, but flight of mind: namely, that he seeks his own interests, not those of Jesus Christ.

“I am the good shepherd. I know my own, and my own know me.”

“I know my own,” that is, I love them; and my own love me. Among the good are the door, the doorkeeper, the shepherd, and the sheep. Among the evil are thieves, robbers, the hireling, and the wolf. The Lord says that he is the door and the shepherd; but if we consider the proper meanings, Christ is neither shepherd nor door, but by likeness he is both shepherd and door and [Col. 0424C] sheep.

[AUGUSTINE.] “For he was led as a sheep to slaughter” (Isa. XLIII). He is the door in respect of the head, the shepherd in respect of the body. He said to Peter: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI). As though he said: “What will you give me, since you love me? Give me this: if you love me, feed my sheep. Enter through the door; for he who climbs up another way is a thief and a robber.” In these persons you will find whom to love, whom to tolerate, and whom to beware of. The shepherd is to be loved; the hireling tolerated; the robber avoided. For the hireling enters canonically and teaches the truth, though with a crooked intention. The thief enters wrongly, teaches falsehood, and is therefore an outsider.

A. 90[III] M. 112 L. 119

[Col. 0424D] “As the Father knows me, so I know the Father.”

That the Son knows the Father through himself, and that no one sees God except through the Son, is evident from this chapter and its parallel canonical passages.

A. 91[III] M. 204 R. 115

“And I lay down my life for my sheep.”

This is the proof of his love for the Father and for the sheep. Thus Peter too, after confessing his love a third time, is commanded to feed the sheep and to die for them.

[AUGUSTINE.] Hold fast that Christ is Word, soul, and flesh. There were heretics, called Apollinarians, who dared to teach that Christ was only Word and flesh, without a soul.

[Col. 0425A] A. 92[X]

“And I have other sheep that are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd.”

The one fold is unity in Christ. Hence Paul says: “He is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II). “Not of this fold” was said concerning those in Israel who were to be saved, of whom the Lord said: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV). He said this because he did not offer his bodily presence except to that people. For he did not go to the Gentiles, but sent his own men, in whom he himself spoke.

“Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, that I may take it again.”

[Col. 0425B] Therefore it appears that the Father loves me, because out of love I die for the salvation of the sheep, not compelled by the violence of the Jews. I die, I say, only for a short time, and I shall rise again. From the moment when the Word assumed humanity—that is, flesh and soul—he never laid aside the soul so that the soul might be separated from the Word. But the flesh laid down the soul when he breathed his last; when it returned, he rose. Death, therefore, temporarily separated flesh and soul, but not the soul from the Word of God. For he departed in such a way that Christ, who did not abandon the thief’s soul, was separated from his own soul. Thus he yielded up the spirit—that is, the flesh of Christ remained without a soul. Christ is called flesh; Christ is called soul; Christ is called Word. Yet these three are not three Christs, but one Christ. Make a step from the case of a human being, so that you may understand [Col. 0425C] better, and inquire: Where is the Apostle Paul now? If someone answers, “At rest with Christ,” he speaks truly. Again, if someone answers, “At Rome in the tomb,” he too speaks truly. The former is said of the soul, the latter of the flesh. For from the time when flesh and soul are joined, each receives the name “human being”; and either one, even when separated, retains the name of human being. Therefore Christ’s flesh alone was called Christ: by the power of the Word it laid down and took up the soul again. When any human being lays down his life for his brothers, as Christ did for us, the flesh lays down the soul—yet by the power of the soul dwelling in the flesh. How do you prove that flesh alone is called Christ? Because when we say, “We believe in God the Father,” we add that we also believe in Jesus [Col. 0425D] Christ, his Son, and there we understand the whole. But when we say, “crucified and buried,” only the flesh is understood, for it was buried without a soul.

“No one takes it from me; but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. This commandment I received from my Father.”

He speaks of the commandment to lay down and take up his life. The Word did not receive a commandment from the Word; rather, in the only-begotten Word is every commandment of the Father. For in begetting him perfect, he gave him all things by begetting.

There was again a division among the Jews because of these words. Many of them said: “He has a demon and is mad; why do you listen to him?” Others said: “These are not the words of one who has a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?”

[Col. 0426A] Their eyes had already begun to be opened. But those who said, “He has a demon,” were darkness that did not comprehend the light.

## CHAPTER CXXXIV

Now the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem, and it was winter.

[BEDĒ.] *Encaenia* was the festival of the dedication of the Temple. In Greek, *kainon* means “new.” Whenever something new has been dedicated, it is called an *encaenium*. The word has now entered common usage: if someone puts on a new tunic, he is said to *encaeniare*, that is, to inaugurate it. The Feast of Dedication concerns not the Temple’s first dedication but its last, as can readily be inferred from the fact that it is reported to have occurred in winter. The first dedication was by Solomon in autumn; the middle one, by Zerubbabel and Jesus the priest, [Col. 0426B] in spring; and the last, by Judas Maccabaeus, in winter. At that time it was specially ordained that this dedication should be recalled every year in solemn offices of commemoration.

This was the reason for the second and third dedications. Solomon completed the Temple in seven years; in the eighth year, on the tenth day of the seventh month—which we call September—he dedicated it. This day had previously been appointed by the Law as a solemn day, so that on it the whole tabernacle was to be expiated every year with greater sacrifices. Thus Zechariah, father of John the Baptist (Luke I), while serving at the altar in these same expiatory rites, was instructed by the angel concerning the mystery of the Lord’s birth. But after four hundred and thirty years the Chaldeans burned this Temple [Col. 0426C]; having destroyed Jerusalem, they carried the people of Israel captive to Babylon. After seventy years, when the Persians were ruling, the people were sent back to their country; the Temple was rebuilt over forty-six years, and the work was brought to completion on the third day of the twelfth month, which we call March. Zerubbabel, Jesus the priest, and the prophets Haggai and Zechariah presided over this work.

Then, after nearly three hundred and fifty-six years, Antiochus, the most wicked king of the Greeks, captured Jerusalem by treachery and profaned the Temple with the filth of idols. He removed and broke up the Lord’s golden altar, the table of the Presence, the lampstand, and the other golden objects; he set up an image of Jupiter in the Temple, and slaughtered many [Col. 0426D] for keeping the Law. Among them that mother with seven sons won the crown of martyrdom together with her offspring. But Judas Maccabaeus, of priestly descent, took up arms against Antiochus’s commanders, expelled them from Judaea (II Macc. VII), cleansed the Temple, made new altars and new ornaments, and dedicated them with the Temple on the fifth day of the ninth month, which we call December and which is known to be in winter. He established in every year the day of the *encaenia*, that is, of the invocation and dedication of the Temple. These things, certainly, as the Apostle teaches, happened as a figure of us (I Cor. X), and must therefore be examined spiritually.

Solomon, whose name means “peaceful,” signifies our Redeemer. Of him Isaiah says: “His dominion shall be multiplied, and of his peace there shall be no end” [Col. 0427A] (Isa. IX). The Temple is the Church, which he gathers from all believers, as from living stones, into one structure of faith and charity. The Temple’s construction over seven years signifies that throughout all this time, which revolves in seven days, the building up of the Church increases. The dedication in the eighth year signifies the feast of the heavenly country; and because the Lord rose on the eighth day, the number eight fittingly signifies the feast of our resurrection. The Temple was burned by enemies and then rebuilt: this indicates the various fortunes of the Church, which is now oppressed, now delivered; now endangered by the snares of the ancient enemy, now receives back through repentance those whom it seemed to have lost.

That the Temple was built for a second time in forty-six years signifies the Lord’s body, [Col. 0427B] of which he said to the Jews: “Destroy this Temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II). They relate, indeed, that the human body is formed in the differentiation of its limbs on the forty-sixth day after conception; and therefore it was not by chance, but by divine providence, that the Temple was built in that number of years. The command that the *encaenia* be celebrated yearly admonishes us always to keep in mind the remembrance of the Lord’s resurrection and to hope for our own. Nor should we pass over the fact that, when Solomon dedicated the Temple, fire descended from heaven after he had finished his prayers and consumed the burnt offerings and sacrifices. For we are the burnt offerings and sacrifices of the true Solomon, of whom the Apostle Peter says: “Christ died once for our sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might offer us to God, put to death indeed in the flesh but made alive in the spirit” [Col. 0427C] (I Pet. III). The fire is the ardour of surpassing love in the heavenly country, through which the citizens of heaven rejoice to burn both in their own blessedness and in the brightness of their Creator. Hence certain ranks are called *seraphim*, that is, “burning” or “setting aflame.” When the dedication is complete, therefore, the fire consumes the offerings; for when the time of our resurrection has been completed, the blazing of true love, by which the angelic powers are now inflamed, will absorb the minds of the faithful when they behold the visible glory of their Creator.

Also noteworthy is that Solomon, after the celebration of the dedication, dismissed the people; blessing the king, they departed joyfully to their tents. For after the resurrection is accomplished, the Lord will dismiss the elect into eternal dwelling places—not removing them any longer from his presence, but, having delivered them from the peril of judgment, which, as the Apostle teaches, we know will take place in the air, admitting them to dwell in the heavenly country [Col. 0427D], so that each may receive a place in the kingdom according to his merits (I Thess. IV). Hence the saying: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John XIV). Having departed to their tents, they blessed the king, because it is a most blessed activity to sing hymns to the Creator. Hence: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII). “The Feast of Dedication,” says the Evangelist, “took place at Jerusalem, and it was winter.” Winter is aptly mentioned because the cold Jews were slow to approach the divine fire—that is, to believe in Christ.

[Col. 0428A] “And Jesus was walking in the Temple, in Solomon’s portico.”

That is, where Solomon used to stand to worship. The porticoes surrounding the Temple are customarily denoted by the name “Temple.”

The Jews therefore surrounded him and said to him: “How long do you keep our soul in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.”

They do not desire truth but prepare a calumny. They accuse him of taking away souls when he delivers them. Perhaps because they believe that Christ will come as a mere human being, but will reign above all others: if he said that he was Christ, they wished to hand him over to the authorities for punishment as one making himself king in opposition to Augustus. But the Lord so tempers his reply that it gives them no opening for calumny [Col. 0428B] and makes it manifest to the faithful, for whose sake these things are recorded, that he is the Christ—not merely human, as they suppose, but the Father’s Word.

Jesus answered them: “I speak to you, and you do not believe; and the works which I do in the name of my Father, these bear witness concerning me. But you do not believe me, because you are not of my sheep.”

I speak to you as the Word of God, and I prove what I am by the works which I do in the name of my Father—that is, by confessing him, whose glory alone I seek everywhere, because the glory of the Father and the Son is one.

“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. And I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish; and no one shall snatch them out of my hand.”

[Col. 0428C] The thief and robber, or the wolf, can do nothing against those whom I know as mine. And if some appear to perish in the present life, they shall not perish eternally—understand, as you shall perish, who are not of my sheep.

“My Father, what he has given me, is greater than all; and no one can snatch it from my Father’s hand.”

The Father gave the Son this, greater than all: that he should be his only-begotten Son. He gave it by begetting. Thus the Son has wisdom; thus he has life: he himself is Wisdom making others wise, Life making others live—which is greater than all. But because he whose Word this is is not from the Word, while the Word is from him whose Word it is, he therefore says, “gave to me.” What did he give? That I might be his Word, his only-begotten, his radiance [Col. 0428D]—that which is greater than all.

Is the Father’s hand and the Son’s hand one hand? Or perhaps the Son himself is the Father’s hand? If by “hand” we understand power, the Father’s and Son’s power is one, because their divinity is one. But if we understand “hand” as in the Prophet’s saying, “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII), the Father’s hand is the Son himself. This is not said as though God had a human form, but because all things were made through him. For people commonly call other people their hands, through whom they do what they wish. Even a work made by a person’s hand is called that person’s hand, as in the saying: “Each recognizes his own hand,” when he recognizes what he has written. Since, therefore, God’s hand can be understood in more than one way, in this passage we understand the Father’s and Son’s hand [Col. 0429A] as the power of each, lest, if here we take the Son as the Father’s hand, carnal thought should begin to seek a son of the Son himself, whom it would likewise believe to be Christ’s hand.

“I and the Father are one.” The Jews took up stones to stone him.

Through “I and the Father are,” the distinction and equality of the persons is expressed; through “one,” the unity of the divine substance is understood. This they could no longer endure, though they had endured the rest; hardened, they run to stones. But because Jesus suffers only what he wills, he freely responds to their action.

Jesus answered them: “I have shown you many good works from my Father; for which of these works do you stone me?” The Jews answered him: “We do not stone you for a good work, [Col. 0429B] but for blasphemy; because you, being a man, make yourself God.” Jesus answered them: “Is it not written in your law: ‘I said, You are gods’?” (Ps. LXXXI).

Sometimes the Scriptures are divided into three, as in: “Everything written concerning me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms had to be fulfilled” (Luke XXIV); sometimes into two, as in: “The Law and the Prophets were until John” (Luke XVI; Matt. XI). Here, however, he generally calls all those Scriptures “the Law.”

“God” is said in three ways: by nature, by adoption, and by opinion. By nature, the almighty God; by adoption, those who share in divinity, of whom the Psalm says, “You are gods”; by opinion, demons or idols.

“If he called those gods to whom the word of God came, and Scripture cannot be broken, [Col. 0429C] do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?”

The Father sanctified the Son in the same way as he begot him. He sanctified him—that is, he begot him holy and willed that he should be called holy. Therefore there was never a time when he was not holy. We also say to God the Father: “Hallowed be your name” (Matt. VI).

“If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me. But if I do them, even if you are unwilling to believe me, believe the works, so that you may know and believe that the Father is in me, and I in the Father.”

If you will not believe the words and the innocence of my life, give faith to the works, so that by the merit of faith, through further knowing [Col. 0429D] the works, you may come to faith in the Godhead. The Father is in the Son, as in Wisdom born from himself and equal to himself, by which he knows himself no less than he is. The Son is in the Father as God’s Wisdom in God, not by participation but by nature.

A. 93[II] M. 117 R. 26

They therefore sought to seize him, and he went out of their hands. And he went away again beyond the Jordan, to the place where John had first been baptizing, and remained there.

One who understands him seizes him in order to possess him. But the Jews wished to seize him in order not to possess him.

## CHAPTER CXXXV

[Col. 0430A]

A. 94[X]

And many came to him and said: “John indeed performed no sign; but everything that John said about this man was true.” And many believed in him.

John did not give sight to the blind or raise the dead, but whatever he said bore witness to this man. He was a lamp for the day; through the lamp let us come to the day.

[Here some begin chapter 135.] Now there was a certain sick man, Lazarus of Bethany, from the village of Mary and Martha his sisters. Mary was the one who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair [Col. 0430B]; her brother Lazarus was sick.

Mary anointed the Lord after Lazarus’s resurrection; but because both events had already passed when the Evangelist wrote, he fittingly mentions the later event before relating what happened earlier.

His sisters therefore sent to him, saying: “Lord, behold, he whom you love is sick.”

[ALBINUS.] They did not dare to say, “Come and heal him”; and it is enough to inform one who loves, for he does not abandon the one whom he loves. Lazarus was ill in Bethany, a village near Jerusalem. These sisters of Lazarus signify the Jews sound in Christ’s teaching, or those already received into eternal blessedness, who entreat the Lord for the healing of their brother—that is, for the rest who still wander in the darkness of ignorance.

[Col. 0430C] When Jesus heard this, he said to them: “This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.”

[AUGUSTINE.] Neither the sickness nor even the death that threatened him was unto death, but rather unto a miracle, by which all might believe in Christ. The glorification did not increase the Son of God, since he is fully God, but benefited us.

Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister Mary and Lazarus.

The comforter of the sorrowful, the saviour of the sick, and the raiser of the dead loved Lazarus, by whom the sinner is signified, because he came not to call the righteous but sinners (Matt. IX).

Therefore, when he heard that he was sick, he nevertheless [Col. 0430D] remained in the same place two days.

The time was prolonged until the four days were complete. For that very number of days conveys a certain mystery.

Then after this he said to his disciples: “Let us go to Judaea again.” The disciples said to him: “Rabbi, the Jews were just seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?” Jesus answered: “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks by day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks by night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.”

He reproves their hesitation and unbelief. They wished to give counsel to him not to die, though he had come to die. Hence elsewhere, when Peter says, “Lord, be merciful to yourself,” he says: “Get behind me, Satan; for you do not savour the things of God” [Col. 0431A] (Matt. XXVI). I am the day; you are the hours. Should hours give counsel to the day? If Judas had been an hour there, he would have shone and would not have betrayed the day. Therefore, in this saying the Lord foresaw not Judas himself but his successor.

Further: “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” The sense is as though he said: The human mind is changeable; it does not always will what it wills at one time, but, just as the hours change, one succeeding another, so thoughts pass away as others succeed them. “If anyone walks by day, he does not stumble”—understand, himself—because he sees before himself. Day signifies peace, as though it were said: If anyone walks by day, that is, in peace—in me, who am true peace—he will not be struck by anyone so as to be harmed; and [Col. 0431B] therefore come with me confidently. But if anyone walks by night, that is, in the darkness of the devil, who is night and brings in the darkness of sins and the adversities of wars, he rightly stumbles—that is, is struck and harmed—because the light is not in him: he lacks wisdom, following the night of sin. Therefore he can have no security unless he comes to his senses.

He said these things, and after this he said to them: “Our friend Lazarus sleeps, but I am going to awaken him from sleep.”

[AUGUSTINE.] To those who could not raise him, he was dead; to the Lord, he slept.

His disciples therefore said: “Lord, if he sleeps, he will recover.” But Jesus had spoken of his death, while they thought that he spoke of sleep in the ordinary sense.

They answered according to their understanding. For the sleep [Col. 0431C] of the sick is commonly an indication of recovery.

Then Jesus told them plainly: “Lazarus is dead; and I am glad for your sakes, that you may believe, because I was not there. But let us go to him.”

They could already wonder that the Lord called him dead, though this had not been reported to him. “That you may believe,” he says—that is, more firmly; for their faith was strengthened by miracles.

Then Thomas, who is called Didymus, said to his fellow disciples: “Let us go too, that we may die with him.” Jesus therefore came and found that he had already been in the tomb four days.

This number of four days signifies death. A human being is born with the death of Adam’s sin, as the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death” (Rom. V). Behold one day of death. After people reach the years of reason, they transgress the natural law which says in the heart, “What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another” [Col. 0431D] (Tob. IV). Behold a second day of death. The Law was given through Moses and is despised. Behold the third day of death. The Gospel is preached and despised. Behold the fourth day of death, in which a person stinks; yet mercy does not abandon even such persons.

Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away.

[ALBINUS.] That Bethany—that is, “house of obedience,” where the dead man was to be raised—is near Jerusalem accords with the mystery. For the Jewish people [Col. 0432A], who will be converted at the end of the age, will quickly come to Jerusalem—that is, to the vision of peace—yet not until the fifteen stadia have been completed, that is, through spiritual knowledge of the Old and New Testaments.

Many Jews had come to Martha and Mary to comfort them concerning their brother. Therefore, when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went to meet him; but Mary remained sitting at home. Martha therefore said to Jesus: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.”

I know this: that you can raise him if you will; I leave it to your judgment. For I neither presume nor ask that you raise my brother, because I do not know whether resurrection would benefit him.

[Col. 0432B] Jesus said to her: “Your brother will rise again.”

This was ambiguous: whether he spoke of a present resurrection or of the future resurrection common to all.

Martha said to him: “I know that he will rise in the resurrection on the last day.” Jesus said to her: “I am the resurrection and the life.”

You rightly think of the final resurrection; but he through whom your brother will then rise can rise even now, because I am resurrection—and therefore resurrection because I am life.

“He who believes in me, even though he has died, shall live; and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die.”

Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob live (Exod. III), whose God he is called, as the God of the living. The believer who has died lives, just as the unbeliever, even while living, is dead. Whence is death in the body? Because the soul is not there. Whence is death in the soul? Because faith is not there. For faith working through love is, as it were, the soul of the soul. But faith without works is dead (Jas. II). Therefore God, through faith and love, is the life of the soul just as the soul is the life of the body. “He who believes in me,” he says, even though he has died in the flesh, lives in the soul until the flesh too rises, never afterwards to die. And everyone who lives in the flesh and believes in me, even if he dies temporarily by the death of the flesh, shall not die eternally, because of the life of the spirit and the immortality of the resurrection.

“Do you believe this?” She said to him: “Certainly, Lord; I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who have come into this world” [Col. 0432D].

Though knowing her faith, he seeks her confession. “Yes,” she says, “I believe all these things because I have believed that you are the Son of God, sent for the salvation of the world.”

And when she had said this, she went away and called her sister Mary quietly, saying: “The Teacher is here and calls for you.”

By “quietly” he means in a subdued voice. Martha’s words briefly show that the Lord called Mary.

When she heard this, she rose quickly and came to him. For Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him. Therefore the Jews who were with her in the house and consoling [Col. 0433A] her, when they saw that Mary rose quickly and went out, followed her, saying: “She is going to the tomb to weep there.”

The Evangelist took care to relate this so that we might see what occasion caused the resurrection of one dead for four days to have more witnesses.

Therefore Mary, when she came where Jesus was, saw him, fell at his feet, and said to him: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.” Therefore, when Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her weeping, he groaned in spirit and troubled himself, and said: “Where have you laid him?”

He who, though absent in body, knew that he was dead, knows where he is buried; but by asking this, he signifies that he does not, as it were, know the lost human being—that is, one dead in sins. [Col. 0433B] Hence at the judgment he will say: “I do not know you; depart from me” (Matt. VII). That is: I do not see you in my light. Thus he also said to Adam: “Where are you?” (Gen. III). He troubled himself, whom no one else could trouble. By his own will, the weakness of the flesh is troubled. Christ’s disturbance signifies how much the person weighed down by the mass of sin ought to be troubled. Disturbance is a certain sorrowful movement of the heart accompanied by groaning, which tears commonly follow, just as, conversely, the face becomes cheerful before laughter. To groan in spirit is the onset of anger breaking forth against vices. Christ undertook such passions because he willed it, for our instruction. And because faith in Christ is Christ in the heart, Christ groans and is troubled in a person when the sinner reckons what good things he receives from God, what evil things he repays, and rebukes himself for his sins.

They said to him: “Lord, come and see.” And Jesus wept.

Let a person weep for himself and groan while accusing his own evil deeds. “Lord, come and see,” that is, have mercy, as it is said in the Psalm: “See my lowliness and my toil, and forgive all my sins” [Col. 0433C] (Ps. XXIV).

Therefore the Jews said: “See how he loved him.” But some of them said: “Could not this man, who opens the eyes of one born blind, have prevented this man from dying?”

He could, but he did not will to, because it is greater to raise one who has died than to prevent him from dying.

[Col. 0433D] Therefore Jesus, again groaning within himself, came to the tomb.

He shows the difficulty of justifying a sinner overwhelmed by grave sins.

Now it was a cave, and a stone had been placed over it.

The dead person under the stone is one guilty under the Law, which was written on stone. “For the Law is not laid down for the righteous” (I Tim. I).

[JEROME.] Therefore Moses and the prophets, possessing the Holy Spirit, were not under the Law but in the Law and with the Law; yet they lived as though under the Law, in order to win those who were under the Law. So too is the Apostle’s saying: “God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the Law” (Gal. IV). For he willingly subjected himself to the Law, in order to redeem those who were under the Law. And the Virgin was called “woman” in an improper sense, on account of those who [Col. 0434A] did not know her to be a virgin. Thus, on account of those who thought Christ to be under the Law, he who was as though under the Law is said to have been made under the Law.

Jesus said: “Take away the stone.”

[AUGUSTINE.] Remove the weight of the Law and preach grace. For the killing letter is like a crushing stone.

Martha, the sister of him who had died, said to him: “Lord, by now he stinks, for he has been dead four days.”

She feared that, when the stone was removed, the stench would be stirred up rather than her brother raised.

Jesus said to her: “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?”

[AUGUSTINE.] That is, you would see the stinking man raised. Lazarus, dead four days, is raised because the death of the soul is completed by four stages [Col. 0434B]. The first is like the stirring of pleasure in the heart; the second, consent; the third, the deed; the fourth, habit. Some cast away unlawful things presented to their thoughts so completely that they do not even take pleasure in them. Some take pleasure but do not consent. Death is not yet complete, but has in some manner begun. Consent is added to pleasure; already there is condemnation. After consent it erupts into deed; the deed turns into habit; and a kind of despair results, so that it may be said: “He has been dead four days; by now he stinks.”

They took away the stone. But Jesus, raising his eyes upward, said: “Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me; but I said it because of the people standing around, that they may believe [Col. 0434C] that you sent me.”

By these words he shows, as in his other works, that he seeks the glory of God the Father. For because, according to his humanity, he was less than the Father, he asks him for Lazarus’s resurrection; and therefore he says that he has been heard, so that in this way at least the bystanders might believe in the Son [in the Son] of God.

Having said these things, he cried with a loud voice: “Lazarus, come out.” And immediately the man who had been dead came forth, his feet and hands bound with strips, and his face bound with a cloth. Jesus said to them: “Untie him and let him go.”

[AUGUSTINE.] Do not be surprised that he came forth with his feet bound, he who rose after four days. This signifies that, while the sinner is contemptuous, he lies buried; [Col. 0434D] when he repents, he rises; when he confesses, he comes forth, as though leaving hidden things and becoming manifest. God brings about this confession by crying with a loud voice, that is, by calling with great grace. But because, though made alive and freed from sins, he is still outwardly bound, he says to the ministers: “Untie him and let him go.” For by the ministry of the ministers, the Church is closed against the perverse and opened to those who return, as was done under the Law concerning lepers. He is indeed released from the bonds of exclusion, and goes and associates freely with the other faithful, whom mother Church receives again.

[AUGUSTINE.] Further: just as we understand the human race in the blind man, so also in this dead man. “Where have you laid him?” Here our calling, which takes place in secret, is signified. For the predestination of our calling is hidden; the sign of this mystery [Col. 0435A] is the Lord’s question, as though he did not know, although we ourselves do not know, as the Apostle says: “That I may know even as I also am known” (1 Cor. 13). When he says, “Take away the stone,” he signifies those who live corruptly in the Church and are an obstacle to those wishing to believe. Martha says to him: “Lord, it is already the fourth day, and he stinks.” Earth is the last of the four elements. It signifies the stench of earthly sins, that is, carnal desires. For the Lord said to Adam when he had sinned: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3). His coming out of the tomb signifies the soul withdrawing from carnal vices. His coming out wrapped in bands signifies that even those who withdraw from carnal things and serve the law of God in their mind cannot nevertheless, while established in the flesh, be free from the troubles of the flesh, [Col. 0435B] as the Apostle says: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Rom. 7). His face being covered with a cloth signifies that in this life we cannot have full knowledge, as the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13).
