And Jesus said: “Untie him and let him go.” This means that after this life all veils are removed, so that we may see face to face.

But how great is the difference between the man borne by the wisdom of God, through whom we have been set free, and other human beings, may be understood from this: Lazarus is not untied until he has come out of the tomb; that is, even a reborn soul cannot be free from every sin and ignorance except through the dissolution of the body, so long as it sees through a mirror and in [Col. 0435C] an enigma. But the grave-cloths and face-cloth of the Lord, who committed no sin and knew nothing in ignorance, were found in the tomb. For he alone in the flesh was not so oppressed even by the tomb that any sin could be found in him; nor was he entangled in cloths, so that anything might be hidden from him or delay him on his way.

Many therefore of the Jews who had come to Mary and Martha and had seen what he did believed in him. But some of them went away to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.

[AUGUSTINE.] Some of those who had come reported Jesus to the Pharisees so that they might rage; or some of those who had believed reported it to them so that they might believe.

[Col. 0435D] Therefore the chief priests and Pharisees assembled a council, and said: “What are we doing? For this man performs many signs.”

They were considering how to harm him, not how to provide counsel.

“If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him; and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation.”

They feared losing temporal things and gave no thought to eternal things; thus they lost both. They feared that if Christ’s teaching advanced, the Jews would become of no consequence and the Romans would therefore take their city from them and scatter them into slavery—which afterwards happened.

But one of them, named Caiaphas, being high priest that year, said to them: “You know nothing [Col. 0436A] and do not consider that it is expedient for us that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish.” But he did not say this of himself; rather, since he was high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus was to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but that he might gather into one the scattered children of God.

Caiaphas prophesied concerning the Jewish nation alone, namely the predestined sheep of the house of Israel, to save whom the Lord was sent by his death. But because the Evangelist, when he wrote the Gospel, had seen the calling of the Gentiles, he added concerning them: “But that he might gather into one the scattered children of God,” so that there might be one flock and one shepherd (John 10). Here we are taught that even evil persons may foretell future things by the spirit of prophecy; yet the Evangelist attributes this to a divine mystery, [Col. 0436B] because Caiaphas was high priest for that year. But God established one high priest, to be succeeded by another at his death; later, through ambition, it came about that there were several, serving in turn by yearly rotations. Perhaps even in one year several officiated, from among whom the one who was to offer incense was selected by lot—an act permitted only to the high priest, as is read concerning Zechariah (Luke 1).

A. 95[IV] M. 117 R. 26

From that day therefore they resolved to put him to death. Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went away into the region near the wilderness, to a city called Ephraim, and remained there with his disciples.

They resolved more decisively than before to kill [Col. 0436C] him; but he gave his disciples an example of preserving life. For it is not a sin if believers withdraw themselves from the sight of those persecuting them. His going to Ephraim, which means “fruitfulness,” signifies the transition to the Church of the Gentiles.

A. 96[I] M. 274 R. 156 L. 260

Now the Passover of the Jews was near.

A. 97[X]

And many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover, that they might sanctify themselves.

The Lord commanded the Jews through Moses that, on the day of Passover, in celebrating the feast, they should sanctify themselves. [Col. 0436D] This celebration was a shadow of what was to come. The doorposts of the Jews were marked with blood, because our foreheads are marked with Christ’s blood.

Therefore they sought Jesus, and, standing in the temple, spoke with one another: “What do you think? Is he not coming to the feast-day?”

Forgetting their own sanctification, in the very place of prayer they seek the lamb to be sacrificed. Hence in the Psalm: “Let those who seek my life be confounded and ashamed” (Ps. 34). Of those who seek rightly it is said: “Refuge has failed me, and there is no one who seeks my life” (Ps. 141).

Now the chief priests and Pharisees had given an order that, if anyone knew where he was, he should report it, so that they might seize him.

## CHAPTER 136

[Col. 0437A]

L. 104[X]

And it came to pass, when the days of his assumption were being fulfilled, that he set his face firmly to go to Jerusalem. And he sent messengers before him; and as they went, they entered a city of the Samaritans to make ready for him. But they did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem.

[BEDA.] By “the days of his assumption” he means the time of the Passion; when it was near, with an undaunted mind he sought the place where he had resolved to suffer. The Samaritans did not receive him because they saw him going to Jerusalem, for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans.

[Col. 0437B] But when his disciples James and John saw this, they said: “Lord, do you wish us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” And turning, he rebuked them, saying: “You do not know of what spirit you are. The Son of Man did not come to destroy souls, but to save them.” And they went to another village.

Elijah struck many with death, both by his own hand and by fire divinely obtained (3 Kings 18). Following his example, when the apostles wished to ask for fire from heaven to consume those who had not offered them hospitality, the Lord reproved in them the desire for vengeance, perceiving that they desired revenge not from love of correction but from hatred. At the words of the apostle Peter, Ananias and his wife fell dead, [Col. 0437C] not through hatred but by just vengeance (Acts 5). Paul also delivered a certain sinner to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the soul might be saved (1 Cor. 5). “You do not know,” says the Lord, “of what spirit you are”; that is, you do not rightly recognize by whose Spirit you have been sealed, and therefore you wish, through hatred, to exercise vengeance—a thing not permitted to those who are servants of God. Certainly perfect virtue both counsels piously and judges justly where expedient, because there is no anger where charity is complete.

## CHAPTER 137

A. 97[X]

Jesus therefore came to Bethany six days before the Passover, where Lazarus had been dead, whom Jesus raised.

He who made all things in six days, who created man on the sixth day [Col. 0437D], came to redeem him in the sixth age, and was to die on the sixth day of the week, at the sixth hour. He came to Bethany six days before the Passover, so that Lazarus’s resurrection might be more firmly committed to everyone’s memory and that the Jews, plotting the death of so great a raiser of the dead, might be put to shame without excuse. [JEROME.] He also seeks obedience from us: the young deer, always obedient to the Father unto death, who by his presence exalts Bethany, as a lamb about to come to Jerusalem for sacrifice, that we may have the true Passover.

R. 158[I] M. 276 L. 74 A. 98

And when Jesus was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper.

[Col. 0438A] A. 99[X]

A great crowd of Jews learned that he was there, and they came not only because of Jesus, but also that they might see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead.

[JEROME.] Curiosity brought them, not charity. Simon had once been a leper, but was then clean because he had been healed by the Lord, while his former name remained; just as Matthew is still called the tax collector, though he had ceased to be one. Some understand Simon to represent believers cleansed from sins by the Lord. For his name means “obedient” or “clean.” Through the sin of the first man, the earth became the house of Simon the leper.

A. 102[X]

[Col. 0438B] Therefore the Pharisees said among themselves: “You see that we gain nothing. Behold, the whole world has gone after him.”

[AUGUSTINE.] They prophesy without knowing it. What wonder if the world goes after him, through whom the world was made?

A. 99[X]

But the chief priests resolved to kill Lazarus also, because many of the Jews were going away on account of him and believing in Jesus.

O foolish plot and blind cruelty! He who was able to raise Lazarus cannot raise one who has been killed?

A. 98[I] M. 276 R. 158 L. 74

So they made him a supper there, and Martha was serving; but Lazarus was one of those reclining [Col. 0438C] with him.

[AUGUSTINE.] Lazarus was present at the supper, lest it should be thought that the one who had risen from death was a phantom. Although human beings can only marvel, and cannot define in words, at all the mighty works which the Son of God accomplished on earth in order to reveal his majesty, the miracle performed upon Lazarus surpasses them all: from the very inhabitant of hell, from that pale dwelling-place itself, after the law of Tartarus had been destroyed, he commanded death’s captive to return to the upper world. And so that the miracle of divine power might be increased, while he reclined at the banquet, Lazarus, questioned by the diners, carefully set forth in orderly narration the sorrowful places of punishments and the abodes darkened by deep night; and thus hell, unknown for long ages, [Col. 0438D] at last found one who betrayed it.

[ALBINUS.] Mystically, the Lord’s supper takes place in the faith and devotion of the righteous. Martha serves when any faithful person offers works of devotion to the Lord. Lazarus—that is, those raised from grave sins—feasts joyfully with those who have remained in righteousness because of the Lord’s presence.

## CHAPTER 138

Then Mary, having an alabaster vessel of precious spikenard ointment, broke the alabaster vessel, poured it upon the head of Jesus as he reclined, anointed his feet, and wiped them with her hair; and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.

[BEDA.] Alabaster is a kind of white marble, variegated with diverse colors, usually hollowed out into vessels for ointments; it is said to preserve ointments unspoiled. [Col. 0439A] Nard is an aromatic shrub, with, as they say, a heavy and thick root, but a short, black, brittle one; its leaf is small and dense and smells like cypress, and its tops spread out into spikes. Dealers in spices prize the spikes and leaves of nard. Hence Mark says, “precious spikenard ointment.” For the ointment which Mary brought to the Lord was made not only from the root of nard but, to make it more precious, also from its spikes and leaves. Natural philosophers report concerning nard that it holds first place among ointments. There are many kinds, all of them herbs except Indian nard, which is more valuable. John, however, specified a pound of *pistic* nard ointment. *Pistic* is named from a place and means “faithful,” namely, not corrupted by any admixture.

Mystically, this devotion of Mary [Col. 0439B] signifies the faith of the Church, speaking in the Song of Songs: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song 1). Mary fulfilled these words also by her hands, and the Church fulfils them spiritually every day in her members. “Thanks be to God, who always manifests through us in every place the fragrance of his knowledge, because we are the sweet fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Cor. 2). For the ointment is the most sweet grace of the Holy Spirit, sweetly fragrant, poured out in the hearts of believers. A pound of ointment from *pistic* nard is righteousness from pure faith. For *pistis* is called “faith” in Greek, and fragrant nard signifies the sweetly fragrant confession of faith. The alabaster vessel of ointment is the body of the faithful soul. The broken alabaster vessel is carnal desire, broken upon the head from which the whole body [Col. 0439C] of the Church is joined together.

Therefore, when the Church preaches the power of Christ’s divinity, it pours precious ointment upon the head of him who reclines. “Reclining” means humbling himself, so that the Church’s faith might touch him. For in his majesty he is not visible to understanding; he was made visible in the form of a servant. Therefore, whoever reverences the assumed humanity by devout preaching of sacred discourse pours ointment upon the Lord’s feet. He wipes with his hair who, by a rational arrangement of words, drives all heresies far away from the incarnation of the Word. For just as bodily nature produces hair for its adornment with fitting moderation, so reason dictates a suitable ordering of words for its own beauty. “The house was filled with the fragrance” means the world filled with good repute.

[Col. 0439D] Then one of his disciples, Judas Iscariot, who was about to betray him, said: “Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?” But he said this, not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief; and, having the money-box, he carried what was put into it.

[JEROME.] Under the pretext of avarice, he speaks a mystery of faith. For our faith, multiplied threefold in the ten senses of body, soul, and spirit, is as it were bought with three hundred denarii. What is signified by ten multiplied threefold is signified by three hundred. Therefore, like Gideon (Judg. 7), taking upon ourselves as it were the number of three hundred men, let us, poor in spirit, [Col. 0440A] destroy the camp of the foreigners with our broken jars, trumpets, and lamps; and like Abraham with three hundred men (Gen. 14), let us divide the spoils at evening. Where Judas is said to have been a thief, we are warned to tolerate thieves and sacrilegious persons.

[AUGUSTINE.] Why did the Lord have a money-box except because the Church was to have money-boxes? Why did he admit a thief except that the Church might tolerate thieves? Embezzlement is theft from public property. Whoever steals anything from the Church is compared to Judas the betrayer. Of Judas alone, by synecdoche under a plural number, they think that Mark said: “They were indignant at her” (Mark 14).

But there were some who were inwardly indignant and said: “Why has this waste of ointment been made?”

Others were indignant because of the poor, perhaps [Col. 0440B] persuaded by Judas’s words; Judas himself, however, because of gain.

But Jesus, knowing this, said to them: “Why do you trouble the woman? She has done a good work toward me. For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you wish you can do good to them; but you will not always have me.”

He speaks to both good and evil persons concerning the presence of his body. For he sits at the right hand of his Father after ascending into heaven, and according to the body he is not here, though by the presence of his majesty he is always here. Yet if you belong to the good, you always have Christ present through faith, through the sign, through the sacrament of baptism, through the food and drink of the altar. Hence elsewhere he says to them: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the world” (Matt. 28).

[Col. 0440C] M. 277[I] R. 159 L. 74 A. 98

“For in pouring this ointment upon my body, she did it for my burial.”

It is not a waste of ointment, but an office of burial. The Lord’s patience does not accuse Judas of avarice and of saying what he said not for the poor’s sake, but commends Mary’s service. What John says, “Leave her, that she may keep it for the day of my burial,” is as though he said: Let her do what she does, so that she may preserve this deed in her heart until the day of my burial; and then she will know that this service is a preparation for the burial of my body. Hence according to Mark it is said: “What she had”—that is, what she was able—“she did.” [Col. 0440D] For she anticipated anointing my body for burial—understand, when it was to be laid down. It is as though he said: Let her now prepare me for burial according to the Jewish custom, while she can; what she will then wish to do, she will be unable to do.

“Amen, I say to you: wherever this Gospel is preached in the whole world, what she has done will also be spoken of in memory of her.”

Understand also: what Judas said against her will be spoken to his disgrace. For she commendably expended upon Christ what she had shamefully used for the fragrance of her own flesh, devoted to unlawful acts, before becoming familiar with the Lord. In the whole world, not so much this woman as the Church is preached.

[BEDA.] Observe his knowledge of future things: the Lord, who was to suffer after a few days, knew that his Gospel would be preached throughout the whole world. [Col. 0441A] It should be noted that Judas acquired as much infamy as Mary acquired fame; but the Lord, rewarding the good woman with worthy praise, passed over in silence the future reproaches of the wicked.

But the Pharisee who had invited him, seeing this, said within himself: “If this man were a prophet, he would surely know who and what sort of woman this is who touches him, because she is a sinner.”

Although custom commonly preserves former names, the Pharisee’s false opinion, presuming upon false righteousness, calls Mary a sinner—Mary from whom seven demons had already been cast out—when the Lord had said of her: “Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken from her” (Luke 10).

[AMBROSE.] Since all time is encompassed in seven days, the totality [Col. 0441B] of vices with which she had been full is rightly signified by the number seven.

[BEDA.] Mystically, the proud Pharisee signifies the Jewish people; the sanctified sinner, the converted Gentile world. The Pharisee asked the Lord to eat with him because that same people, who did not wish to believe when he came, hoped that he would come and desired his coming, saying: “Stir up your power and come, that you may save us” (Ps. 79). The Lord’s eating with the Pharisee means his rejoicing in the believing people. Hence elsewhere: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 6).

And Jesus answered and said to him: “Simon, I have something to say to you.” And he said: “Teacher, say it.” “There were two debtors to a certain lender; one owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty. [Col. 0441C] Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both. Which of them therefore loves him more?” Simon answered and said: “I suppose the one to whom he forgave more.” And he said to him: “You have judged rightly.”

By his own judgment the proud Pharisee is convicted within himself, and like a madman he carries the rope by which he will be bound. In human judgment, perhaps the one who owed more offended more; but through the Lord’s mercy the case is changed, so that the one who owed more may love more, if only he obtains so great a grace. The two debtors set before Simon as a comparison signify the two peoples; the lender signifies the Creator, who seeks the profit of that coin which he fashioned in us after his own image. The people to whom the Decalogue of the Law was given through a servant owes less; the people to whom [Col. 0441D] the grace of eternal life was entrusted through the Son owes more. Thus the Jews’ debt is reckoned by the denarius, the Christians’ by the hundredfold number; but both are multiplied by five, because in this life each people must devote its five senses to the service of reason. And because none of us is saved by our own strength but by God’s grace, it is rightly said: “Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both.” Therefore the Church of the Gentiles loves more than the Jew, because both in its present state greater grace is conferred upon it, and from its past it is drawn out of greater foulness. Certainly none can love as much as she who loves amid more gifts and in more persons.

And turning to the woman, he said to Simon: “Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave no water for [Col. 0442A] my feet. But she has bathed my feet with tears and wiped them with her hair. You gave me no kiss; but from the time she entered, she has not ceased kissing my feet.”

[GREGORY.] By this enumeration the falsely righteous man is refuted, and under the figure of the woman both her merit and that of the Church are commended together. She had desired earthly things with her eyes, but, crushing those eyes in repentance, she wept. She had arranged her hair, but now with it she wiped away tears. She had spoken proudly with her mouth, but now she kissed the Lord’s feet. Therefore, as many delights as she had in herself, so many burnt offerings she found from herself. The Pharisee’s house is the keeping of the Law and the prophets, in which the Jews gloried that they lived. The Lord enters it when he comes not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it. In this house [Col. 0442B] the repentant woman, watering the Lord’s feet with tears, is glorified—not the unbelieving Pharisee, who gave not even water for his feet. The moisture of tears is within us, because the converted Gentile world even sheds blood, while the Jew offers not even outward things. He waters the Lord’s feet with tears who, moved by compassion, sympathizes with his saints in tribulation. He wipes the Lord’s feet with his hair who bestows charity from his superfluous goods upon those in need. But he waters the Redeemer’s feet with tears and does not wipe them with his hair who somehow sympathizes with his neighbors’ sorrow, yet does not have mercy on them from his surplus. He kisses the feet who diligently loves those following Christ’s footsteps, giving them what is his, lest his neighbor’s need be burdensome to the giver. Or we kiss the Lord’s feet when we love his incarnation [Col. 0442C] perfectly.

He kisses the Lord’s knee who, with the Apostle, understands that what is weak in God is stronger than all human beings (1 Cor. 1). For the strength for standing resides in the knee. He kisses the Lord’s hand who meditates diligently day and night upon the working of our redemption. He kisses God’s mouth and, as it were, presses lip to lip, who is joined by faith and love to the wisdom and goodness of God the Father. For the understanding of faith grows together with divine wisdom, and the affection of our love is united to the supreme goodness, according to the Apostle’s saying: “He who is joined to God is one spirit with him” (1 Cor. 6). He kisses God’s eyes who casts himself wholly upon him in the predestination of the good and foreknowledge of the evil, tasting the savor [Col. 0442D] of unutterable justice. We must also see, in Christ’s body, who is his eye, who his hand, and who another member; and according to the distribution of graces, as each person is, let some be stamped more and some less with the kiss of love.

“You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment. Therefore I tell you: many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much. But he to whom less is forgiven loves less.”

The more greatly the rust of sin is consumed, the more the sinner’s heart is burned with the fire of charity. If we perform works by which we sprinkle the Church with a good fragrance, we pour ointment upon the Lord’s body. The fragrance of faith, which duly extols both his divinity and his humanity [Col. 0443A], anoints the Lord’s head and feet as with the scent of spices—now ascending from the feet to the head, now descending through faith from the head to the feet.

And he said to her: “Your sins are forgiven.” And those reclining together began to say within themselves: “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” And he said to the woman: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.” And after saying these things, he went away, going up to Jerusalem.

Since the Pharisee still regarded the woman—namely Mary Magdalene, Lazarus’s sister—as a sinner, the Savior introduces the forgiveness of her sins. Faith had saved her because she did not doubt that what she asked could be granted her. She is commanded to go in peace, that she may persevere in the way of truth. But when or where she was converted is not determined from the Gospel [Col. 0443B]. It is probable that Luke narrated the same event as the other Evangelists, because he does not mention another place where it happened; and the name Simon also agrees with the others; neither what precedes nor what follows is at odds with it. Some, however, have thought that two anointings and two women—a sinner and a holy woman—are commemorated, one of whom poured ointment upon the Lord’s feet and the other upon his head and feet. Others say that there was one woman and that she came gradually from the feet to the head: she first anointed the Lord in Galilee and afterwards in Bethany, there approaching as a sinner, here truly justified. If, therefore, anyone thinks that Luke reported not the same event as the other Evangelists but a similar one, he will apply here the rule of recapitulation [Col. 0443C] and explain the continuation of the text thus: “And after saying these things, he went to Jerusalem”—namely, after the things Judas said about selling the ointment and the things the Lord answered in reply.

## CHAPTER 139

A. 102[X]

Now there were certain Gentiles among those who had gone up to worship on the feast day. Therefore they approached Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee, and asked him, saying: “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.” Philip came and told Andrew; Andrew in turn and Philip told Jesus.

A. 103[IV] M. 299 R. 180

But Jesus answered them, saying: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.”

[AUGUSTINE.] The Lord answered in this way in order to indicate that the fullness of the Gentiles would believe after his Passion, when he had been glorified in heaven.

A. 104[X]

“Amen, amen, I say to you: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.”

He called himself the grain to be put to death by the unbelief of the Jews, but to be multiplied by the faith of the peoples. And because he compares himself especially to a grain of wheat, the Church’s custom began of making the Lord’s body from this grain alone.

[Col. 0444A] A. 105[III] M. 97 L. 211

“He who loves his life will lose it; and he who hates his life in this world will keep it unto eternal life.”

He exhorts us to follow the footsteps of his Passion, as though saying: If you desire to keep life in Christ, do not fear death for Christ. Do not love your life in this present world, lest you lose it in eternal life. A remarkable saying: how a human being’s love for his own life causes it to perish, while hatred prevents it from perishing. If you love badly, then you hate; if you hate rightly, then you love. Blessed are those who hate by preserving, lest they lose by loving. But take care not to wish to kill yourself in the meantime, as some perverse persons do, misunderstanding this verse. When, however, the decisive [Col. 0444B] circumstance arises, so that you are faced either with doing something contrary to God’s command or with dying, then choose rather to die than to live, so that in this world you may hate your life and keep it for eternal life.

A. 106[X]

“If anyone serves me, let him follow me.”

Hence Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example that we should follow in his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2).

“And where I am, there will my servant be also.”

The reward for serving him is to be with him, without whom nothing is ever well and with whom nothing is ever ill. Therefore he openly adds:

[Col. 0444C] “If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him.”

With what honor, except that he may be with his Son—not equal to his divinity, but joined to his eternity? When you hear, brothers, “There will my servant be also,” do not think only of good bishops and clergy; you too, according to your measure, serve Christ by giving alms and by preaching his teaching to those whom you can. For every head of a household ought to exercise discipline over his own people by warning, teaching, correcting, and offering kindness.

A. 107[IV] M. 293 R. 154

“Now my soul is troubled. And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour.”

[Col. 0444D] Having foretold his Passion and added an exhortation based upon it, as though he had given voice to his own strength, he adds the feeling of our weakness. He truly assumed it, but willingly for us, lest we despair because of this weakness. In it he also teaches what we ought to say and to whom we should flee: as though, when the soul is troubled, “What shall I say? Whom shall I call upon? Where shall I flee? In whom shall I hope?” In the Father who saves, whose will I place before my own, because for this reason I came to this hour: that I might suffer these things, from which glorification follows both for me and for my members. And this is what he says:

A. 108[X]

“But for this reason I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name.”

[Col. 0445A] “Save me from this hour of Passion,” I ask, but I do not refuse the Passion. Therefore glorify me by raising me, which is the glory of your name.

Then a voice came from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”

“I have glorified it” before I made the world; that is, I begot one who is glorious and purposed to glorify him in rational creatures. Or thus: “I have glorified it” when he was born of the Virgin, adored by the Magi, recognized by the saints, declared by the appearance of a dove, and transfigured on the mountain. “I have glorified it” when he healed many, fed many from a few loaves, commanded the waves, and raised the dead. “And I will glorify it again” when he rises from the dead, ascends into heaven, and is recognized by all [Col. 0445B] as judge, so that every knee may bow to him.

Therefore the crowd which stood by and heard said that thunder had occurred. Others said: “An angel spoke to him.” Jesus answered and said: “This voice came not for my sake, but for yours.”

He shows that this voice did not reveal to him what he knew, but to those to whom it was necessary for it to be revealed.

“Now is the judgment of the world. Now the ruler of this world will be cast out.”

By “judgment” he means here the discrimination of the redeemed, not condemnation, when on the day of judgment he will condemn the wicked. By the ruler of the world he explains the judgment of which he spoke. The devil had indeed been cast out from the righteous of old; but what had then been done in very few [Col. 0445C] is now done in a multitude through the preaching of the apostles. Rightly did Christ’s illumination drive the prince of darkness out of man, because he had no right over him. For because, by wicked fraud and deception, he alienated man from subjection to his Lord, he ought not thereby to have received any power over him; rather, if he had possessed any previously, he ought to have lost it. For one who abuses granted power deserves to lose its privilege. Likewise, God did not make man the devil’s slave, nor could man lawfully make himself the devil’s slave. Although a slave may flee from his master, he cannot lawfully hand himself over to another.

Therefore, the devil is said to have reigned from Adam to Christ’s cross as ruler of the world because the children of Adam, [Col. 0445D] weighed down by the heavy yoke of sin, readily assented to diabolical temptations. But the sacrifice of the cross, pleasing to God the Father through the love it pours into the human race, removed slavery to sin, so that we may truly be free because the Son did not free us. Therefore the devil, envying humankind all the more and consequently to be punished more severely, nevertheless does not cease to tempt; but it is one thing to reign within, another to attack from without. For it is one thing for a captured city to be possessed within, another for it to be attacked by missiles hurled from afar. When the devil is called “the ruler of this world,” he is not believed to be lord of heaven and earth; rather, “the world” means evil people scattered throughout the whole world. Thus we are accustomed to call a house bad where bad people are, and good where good people are; for “world” is also said of good people dispersed in the world. Hence the Apostle [Col. 0446A] says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5)—those from whom the devil is cast out.

“And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself.” But he said this, signifying by what death he was to die.

What “all things,” except those from whom the devil is cast out? He did not say “all people,” but “all things,” because he referred this not to the totality of human beings but to the integrity of the creature: spirit, soul, and body—by which we understand, by which we live, and by which we are visible. For he who said, “Not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke 21), draws all things after himself. Or, if “all things” means human beings, we may say all those predestined for salvation. Or certainly he draws to himself as head all classes of human beings: in languages, ages, [Col. 0446B] ranks of honor, varieties of ability, and professions of lawful arts. “If I am lifted up” means “when I am lifted up,” for he does not speak in doubt. By lifting up he means the Passion on the cross, and he refers to what was said above, that a dead grain bears much fruit.

The crowd answered him: “We have heard from the Law that Christ remains forever. How then do you say, ‘The Son of Man must be lifted up’? Who is this Son of Man?”

They remembered what the Lord had said: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” For here he does not say, “If the Son of Man is exalted,” but, “If I am exalted” [Col. 0446C]. They therefore think Christ’s abiding forever and his exaltation on the cross to be contradictory.

Jesus therefore said to them: “Yet a little while the light is among you. Walk while you have the light, lest the darkness overtake you.”

The darkness consists in believing Christ’s eternity in such a way as to deny the humility of his death. Therefore walk from faith to faith, understanding the whole: that Christ would die in order to redeem, and would live eternally in heaven in order to bring you there. “Walk,” he says, “while you have the light”: that is, advance by believing what I say while I minister to you the light of my words. For the darkness of ignorance and everlasting death will be not to believe me.

“And he who walks in darkness does not know where he is going. While you have the light” [Col. 0446D], “believe in the light, that you may be sons of light.”

## CHAPTER 140

L. 202[V] M. 255

But when he was asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them and said: “The kingdom of God does not come with observable signs; nor will they say, ‘Look, here!’ or ‘Look, there!’ For behold, the kingdom of God is within you.”

[Bede.] Many thought that, when the Lord came to Jerusalem, the kingdom of God would immediately be made manifest. The Apostles too were led into this opinion, when after his resurrection they asked him, “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” (Acts 1). And elsewhere Cleophas says, “But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel” (Luke 24). He therefore says that the kingdom of God [Col. 0447A]—that is, the good reigning in God—does not come through an observable point of time or by local movement, so as to be said to exist locally here or there. For reigning with God is not bodily but spiritual; it has already begun by faith in believers’ hearts. Hence he says, “The kingdom of God is within you.”

Alternatively, he says that the day of judgment does not come with observable temporal signs, nor will a determined place be known, so that anyone may say, “Judgment will occur here,” or, “there.” For neither angels nor human beings will announce the Lord’s coming for judgment, as prophets and angels announced the time of his incarnation. He calls himself the kingdom of God, set among those who believed in him as reigning. For he who will one day come as judge of all even now reigns in the hearts of the faithful.

[Col. 0447B] L. 259[X]

Now he was teaching in the temple by day, but at night he went out and lodged on the mountain called Olivet. And all the people came early to him in the temple to hear him.

By the Lord’s example we ought to teach by day and, in the nights of adversity, pray to God, so that we may say with the Psalmist: “But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in the mercy of God” (Ps. 15). Whether we are in prosperity, signified by day, or adversity, understood by nights, let us always teach and pray to the extent of our ability. “The people came early to him” means that they hastened to come in the morning.

## CHAPTER 141

[Col. 0447C]

M. 227[X]

Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples, saying: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat. Therefore keep and do whatever they tell you; but do not do according to their works. For they speak and do not act.”

[Jerome.] Because of the priesthood and the dignity of the title, he exhorts the people to submit to them, considering not their deeds but their teaching. By the seat he signifies the teaching of the law. It is not the seat that makes the priest, but the priest the seat; it is not the place that sanctifies the person, but the person the place.

[Chrysostom.] Not every priest is holy, but every holy person is a priest [Col. 0447D]. For the sake of the good priests, honour even many priests, lest because of the bad you despise the good as well. It is better to grant the bad what is not their due than to withhold from the good what is due to them. Good teaching often proceeds from a bad person, just as common earth sometimes produces precious gold. As gold is selected but not the earth, so receive the teaching, not the morals. For bees require not herbs but flowers.

Or thus: the scribes and Pharisees were undeservedly established in the rank which Moses had occupied, preaching to others the law that prophesied Christ, whom they themselves did not receive when present. Therefore the Lord exhorts the people to hear the law—that is, to believe in Christ—and not to imitate the Pharisees.

[Col. 0448A] M. 228[V] L. 139

“But they bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them on people’s shoulders, but they are unwilling to move them with their finger.”

[Jerome–Chrysostom.] This saying applies generally against all teachers who command great things and do not perform even lesser ones. The shoulders, finger, burdens, and cords by which the burdens are bound must be understood spiritually. Of burdens it is said elsewhere: “Come to me, all who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11). They commended the burdens of the law by fanciful arguments, but themselves did not fulfil them even with a finger—that is, even by a slight touch.

Such even now are priests who declare every kind of righteousness to the people, but themselves observe not even a small part of it [Col. 0448B]. Such also are those who impose a heavy burden on persons coming to repentance, while themselves doing not even the least of such things. For just as, if you place an unbearable bundle on a young person’s shoulders, he must either throw it off or be crushed under its weight, so a penitent burdened beyond his strength must either reject repentance or, scandalized by his collapse, sin more grievously. Finally, if we err by imposing a light penance, is it not better to render account because of mercy than because of cruelty? Where the master of the household is generous, the steward ought not to be stingy.

M. 229[II] R. 135 L. 137 and 246

“But they do all their works to be seen by people [Col. 0448C]. For they enlarge their phylacteries and make their fringes large.” R. L. “And they desire to walk in robes.”

[Jerome.] Whoever does anything in order to be seen by people is a scribe and Pharisee. When the Lord had given the commandments of the law through Moses, he added at the end: “You shall bind them on your hand, and they shall be immovable before your eyes” (Deut. 6). Its meaning is: Let my commandments be fulfilled in action, and meditate upon them day and night.

Misinterpreting this, the Pharisees wrote the Decalogue of Moses—that is, the ten words of the law—on little pieces of parchment; they folded and bound them on their foreheads, making, as it were, a crown for the head, so that they might always move before their eyes. This is still done by Indians and Babylonians; whoever has such an object is judged to be, as it were, religious among the people [Col. 0448D].

Moses had also ordered them to make violet-blue fringes at the four corners of their cloaks (Num. 15; Deut. 22), so that the people of Israel might be recognized: just as circumcision upon the body gave a mark of the Jewish nation, so the garment too might have some distinguishing feature. Hence those superstitious teachers, courting popular applause and pursuing profit from little women, made fringes and tied very sharp thorns into them, so that while walking and sitting they might occasionally be pricked and, as if by this reminder, recalled to the duties of God.

They called those little labels of the Decalogue “phylacteries,” because whoever possessed them was thought to have them as a safeguard and protection for himself; the Pharisees did not understand that these things ought to be carried in the heart. Otherwise bookcases and chests also contain books [Col. 0449A], yet have no knowledge of God. Such was the short fringe prescribed by the law, which the woman suffering from a flow of blood touched on the Lord’s garment (Matt. 9). But she was not pricked by the superstitious thorns of the Pharisees; rather, she was healed.

“To walk in robes” is to go out in more elegant clothes in public. This is reproved in the rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen (Luke 16).

M. R. L.

“For they love the first places at dinners, the first seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by people.” L. “And all the people listened to him gladly.”

That the people gladly listened to him even in these matters is found in Luke at the beginning of chapter 246. Mark also touches on the same point at the end of chapter 130.

[Jerome–Bede.] Observe that he does not forbid greeting in the marketplace or reclining in the first place to those for whom these are appropriate according to the order of their office; rather, he teaches the faithful to beware those who improperly love such things. We are commanded to guard against those eager for vain glory for a double reason: lest we be deceived by pretence, supposing the things they do to be good; or inflamed by rivalry, taking pleasure in being praised for the good things they merely pretend to do.

M. 230[X]

“But you are not to be called Rabbi; for one is your teacher, and all of you are brothers. And call no one your father on earth; for one is your Father, who is in heaven [Col. 0449C]. Nor are you to be called masters, because your one master is Christ.”

[Jerome.] No one other than God the Father and the Lord the Son is to be called teacher or father. Father, because all things are from him; teacher, because all things are through him, or because through his flesh we have been reconciled to God. Why then did the Apostle say that he was a teacher of the Gentiles, and why in the monasteries of Egypt do they call one another fathers? Because it is one thing to be father or teacher by nature, another by indulgent usage. When we call a human being father, we show honour to age. A person is called teacher by association with Christ the teacher. And as the only Son does not preclude others from being called gods and sons by adoption, so the one Father [Col. 0449D] does not preclude others from being called fathers by adoption.

M. 231[V] L. 179 and 215

“He who is greatest among you shall be your servant. But whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted.”

[Bede.] He who is greater, either in merits or in the office of pre-eminence, should surpass others in service. Hence the Apostle: “Outdoing one another in showing honour” (Rom. 12).

L. 137[II] M. 229 R. 135

“Woe to you, Pharisees, because you love the first seats in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplace.”

Woe to the wretched persons into whom the vices of the Pharisees have passed [Col. 0450A], because, during the short course of this life in which they ought to mourn their sins, they do not fear to contend for precedence.

M. 232[V] L. 142

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, lawyers, hypocrites, because you have taken away the key of knowledge and shut the kingdom of heaven before people. You yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow those who are entering to enter.”

[Chrysostom.] The kingdom of heaven means the Scriptures; their door is understanding. The priests are the key-bearers; the key is the word of knowledge; opening is true interpretation. He did not say, “You who do not open,” but, “You who shut.” Therefore the Scriptures are not closed, but obscure. Hence Peter says in his epistle: “Not as man willed did the Spirit speak, but as the Spirit willed did man [Col. 0450B] speak” (2 Pet. 1).

The reason for obscurity is manifold. We give two causes: first, because God willed that some should be teachers and others disciples; second, lest Scripture be despised if it were understood by those who neither love nor keep it. The Jews shut the door of truth when they decreed that anyone confessing the Son of God should be expelled from the synagogue.

[Bede.] The key of knowledge is Christ’s humility, which the lawyers were unwilling either to understand in the law and prophets or to have understood by others. To enter the Scriptures is not to be content with the surface of the letter, but to penetrate to the hidden things of understanding.

[Jerome.] Or certainly every teacher who scandalizes his disciples by evil works shuts the kingdom of heaven before them [Col. 0450C].

R. 136[VI] L. 247

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who devour widows’ houses under the pretext of lengthy prayer; for this you shall receive a greater condemnation.”

[Bede.] He condemns their pretence by the declaration of their punishment. For “woe” is the cry of one grieving. He does not merely say that they will receive condemnation, but adds “greater,” to indicate that those who pray to be seen by people deserve condemnation; but those who, praying at greater length, paint their avarice with the colour of religion, seeking not only praise but money as well, are to be punished by a greater condemnation. Since they are supposedly to be advocates in a legal matter, in order to retain authority for entering widows’ houses [Col. 0450D], access to saving help is barred to the others, and the kingdom of heaven is locked. Therefore they will receive fuller judgment, because they shall be accountable both for punishment for their own sin and for the guilt of another’s ignorance.

M. 233[X]

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you travel sea and land to make one proselyte; and when he has been made, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves.”

[Jerome.] The scribes and Pharisees, travelling around the world for gain, strove to make proselytes from the Gentiles—that is, to mix newcomers and circumcised persons with the people of God. But when such a person was a Gentile before, he was a son of Gehenna by erring once; seeing the hypocrisy of teachers who destroyed by their deeds what they taught, they returned to their vomit. Having become Gentiles again, they were worthy of a greater punishment as transgressors [Col. 0451A]. He calls him a son of Gehenna because everyone is called the son of that whose works he performs. “You make him twice as much,” understand: “a son of Gehenna,” as yourselves, through whose fault he returns to his vomit.

“Woe to you, blind guides, who say: ‘Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound.’ Fools and blind! For which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold? And: ‘Whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gift that is upon it is bound.’ Blind! For which is greater, the gift or the altar [Col. 0451B] that sanctifies the gift? Therefore whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything upon it. Whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it. And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it.”

Whoever swears by the altar, just as the sanctification of the things offered derives from the altar itself, likewise makes his oath extend to the gifts offered upon it. But whoever swears by the temple is bound by the oath both in respect of container and contained, sanctifier and sanctified. Whoever swears by heaven swears through the created thing that is subject, and through the divinity presiding over creation. In a typological sense, the temple and altar are Christ; the gold and gift are praises and sacrifices offered to God. For he is not sanctified by these things, but these by him.

[Jerome.] The Jewish priests, doing everything for the sake of avarice, are accused of impious injustice [Col. 0451C]. For if anyone in an ambiguous case had sworn by the temple and was afterward convicted of lying, he was not held liable for the offence. But if he had sworn falsely by the gold and money offered to the priests in the temple, they said that he was bound—that is, bound to keep the oath—and for perjury he was immediately compelled to pay over that by which he had sworn. Again, if he had sworn falsely by the altar, he was not held liable for perjury. But if he had sworn falsely by the gift or offerings—that is, the victim and the other things offered to God upon the altar—they pursued these most diligently.

[Chrysostom.] They said that the gold and gifts on which they fed were holier than the temple and altar [Col. 0451D], so that people might be more ready to make gifts than to offer prayers. Foolish Christians still do this. If there is some matter at issue, one who swears by God seems to do little; but one who swears by the Gospel seems to do something greater—as though God were holy because of the Scriptures, and not the Scriptures because of God.

M. 234[V] L. 136

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who tithe mint, dill, cumin, rue, and every herb, and have left aside the weightier matters of the law: judgment, mercy, faith, and the love of God. These you ought to have done, and not have omitted those.”

The word “you tithe” is ambiguous; for both the one who [Col. 0452A] receives and the one who gives may properly be said to tithe. The scribes and Pharisees tithed even the smallest vegetables, so that onlookers might say: “How they give tithes of everything, since they do not neglect to give tithes even of vegetables!”

[Jerome.] Or they are accused here of avarice because they diligently exact tithes even of cheap vegetables, while neglecting judgment in the adjudication [or discernment] of affairs, mercy toward the poor, and faith in God joined with the disposition of love—things that are great. We know indeed that tithes are offered to God for the sake of priests, who ought to minister spiritual things to the people.

[Chrysostom.] Yet even today priests murmur if the people do not offer tithes; if they see the people sinning, they do not murmur. In saying “judgment,” the Lord wills that all should judge justly; in saying “mercy,” he commended good conduct to all [Col. 0452B]; and faith must be adorned with works of love.

[Bede.] “These,” he says, “ought chiefly to have been done, and alms from the fruits of the earth not omitted.” Therefore by almsgiving immunity is not purchased for those persisting in injustice.

M. 235[X]

“Blind guides, straining out a gnat but swallowing a camel.”

[Jerome.] Understand the camel as the magnitude of the commandments, namely judgment, mercy, faith, and the love of God; and the gnat as the tithes of mint, dill, cumin, rue, and the other cheap vegetables. The meaning is: You are blind guides—that is, unseeing leaders—because you strain out, that is, investigate as milk is strained, even the tithes of herbs, while swallowing—that is, concealing, just as that which is swallowed is concealed—the greater commandments [Col. 0452C].

Or thus: to strain out a gnat is diligently to avoid the smallest transgression. For a gnat is a very small fly, excluded from liquid by fine straining. And because a camel is a large and ungainly animal, he swallows a camel who readily incurs a great transgression.

M. 236[V] L. 135

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you cleanse the outside of cup and dish, but within you are full of robbery and uncleanness. Blind Pharisee [Col. 0452D], first cleanse what is inside the cup and dish, that what is outside may also become clean.”

[Jerome.] In different words but with the same sense as above, he accuses them of pretence and falsehood: they speak one thing and hold another in their hearts.

[Chrysostom.] That he means human beings under the image of cup and dish is made clear by what he adds: “but within you are full of robbery.”

[Remigius.] It is as if he said: You vainly display holiness outwardly, like someone who cleans a cup outside but leaves dirt within, though its use is inward. The cup and dish are full of robbery and uncleanness because what you drink and eat you take from others; and therefore your drink and food bear the uncleanness of sins. “Blind Pharisee,” that is, undiscerning one: first cleanse what is your own within, your heart that thinks evil, so that what is outside may become clean—that is, that your deeds may be righteous [Col. 0453A]. For an evil tree cannot produce good fruit. A *paropsis* is a square vessel having equal *apsides*, that is, corners.

L. 138[V] M. 237

“Woe to you, because you are like tombs that do not appear, and people walking over them do not know it.”

[Bede.] Hypocrites are like unseen tombs: while displaying the common surface of the ground, inwardly they are full of the stench of rotting corpses. Those deceived by their teachings who imitate them walk, as it were, unknowingly over tombs.

[Col. 0453B] M. L.

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people, but within are full of dead men’s bones and every uncleanness. Thus you too outwardly indeed appear righteous to people, but inwardly are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.”

[Jerome–Chrysostom.] What he showed in the cup and dish he now repeats more openly through the example of tombs. The bodies of sinners are called tombs of the dead, because the soul is dead in the sinner’s body.

[Bede.] Thus he rebukes the superstition of the Pharisees, who outwardly display the appearance of sound doctrine but conceal what filth they produce within [Col. 0453C].

L. 139[V] M. 229

Then one of the lawyers answered and said to him: “Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also.” But he said: “Woe to you lawyers also, because you burden people with loads that cannot be borne, while you yourselves do not touch the loads with one of your fingers.”

This means: You do not keep, even in the least commandment, what you impose upon others. For you do not seek grace and reject the light yoke; but the law without grace cannot be fulfilled.

M. 238[V] L. 140

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who build [Col. 0453D] the tombs of the prophets and adorn the monuments of the righteous, and say: ‘If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been their companions in the blood of the prophets.’ Thus you bear witness against yourselves that you are sons of those who killed the prophets.”

For you build the tombs of the prophets—understand, hypocritically and not devoutly—since you seek to kill both me and mine. Thus he turns back upon yourselves the sentence of condemnation which you pronounce upon your fathers.

[Chrysostom.] One person quickly understands another’s fault, but his own with difficulty, because in another’s case a person has a tranquil heart, but in his own is troubled. A troubled heart does not permit a person to consider what is good. Christ explains the natural habit of evil people: in almost everyone [Col. 0454A] this evil is found, that they blame others’ errors but not their own. He also lays down a rule of nature when he says, “You are their sons,” because bad people are scarcely born of good parents, or good people of bad ones. And as a tree is known by its fruit, so parents are known in their children.

If the father is good and the mother bad, or the mother good and the father bad, the children sometimes follow the father, sometimes the mother, but more frequently the father. If both are alike, it sometimes happens that bad children come from good parents, or good children from bad, but rarely. Such is human nature: a person is born with two eyes and five fingers, though sometimes, in order that the works of God may be manifested, someone is born blind, or someone with six fingers.

It should be observed that those who build shrines to martyrs and adorn churches, if they preserve God’s justice in other matters [Col. 0454B], if the poor rejoice in their goods, build for God’s glory. But if not, who does not understand that they do not make those buildings for God’s glory, where the poor, having suffered violence at their hands, cry out against them? The martyrs do not rejoice to be honoured by money for which the poor weep. What sort of justice is it to honour the dead and despoil the living? To take from the blood of the wretched and offer it to God is not to offer it to God, but to wish to make God a partner in one’s violence. Do you wish to build God’s house? Give faithful poor people the means to live, and you have built a rational house of God. For in buildings human beings dwell, but God dwells in holy people.

M. 239[X]

[Col. 0454C] “And you, fill up the measure of your fathers—serpents, brood of vipers! How will you escape the judgment of Gehenna?”

[Chrysostom.] As vipers are born from vipers, so you murderers were born from murderers. What was lacking to them, therefore, you must fill up. They killed the servants; you, crucify the Lord. He does not command them to do it, but shows what they would do. As serpents, more cunning than all animals, look about for how to bite and afterward hide themselves, so hypocrites consider how to harm and, after doing harm, behave as though they had injured no one.

They are fittingly compared to vipers, because the nature of vipers is that, once they have conceived, their offspring when born burst their mothers’ wombs and emerge in this way. The offspring themselves suffer the same from their own brood [Col. 0454D]. Therefore, as vipers eat their parents and are eaten by their young, so faithless Jews condemn their fathers and are condemned by their own children. “How,” he says, “will you escape the judgment of Gehenna?” You want to appear good; but just as it does not benefit a prostitute to be called chaste, so it does not benefit a sinner to be called God’s servant.

M. 240[V] L. 141

“Therefore the wisdom of God also said: ‘I will send to them prophets, apostles, wise men, and scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some you will scourge in your synagogues.’”

[Bede.] Because I know that you will fill up the measure of your fathers in the killing of me and mine [Col. 0455A], therefore I, the wisdom of God, said from eternity: “I will send to them prophets and apostles,” so that they may have no excuse that they lacked preachers of the truth, and so that their malice may be an occasion of salvation to others. Behold, he who first sent prophets and afterward apostles. Therefore let heretics cease to preach that the God of the law and prophets was one, and that of the New Testament another.

Scripture also often calls prophets those who preach the coming joys of the heavenly kingdom. The Apostle says: “Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others discern” (1 Cor. 14).

[Jerome.] Further, some disciples were prophets in that they foretold future things, such as Agabus (Acts 21); wise men were those who knew the time for preaching and expounding the Scriptures, according to the Psalmist, “instructed in heart in wisdom” (Ps. 89); scribes were those most learned in the law [Col. 0455B]. Of these Stephen was stoned, Paul killed, Peter crucified, and other disciples scourged and persecuted.

The Lord clearly shows the Jews that he understands their hearts: they will be like their fathers in evil. For before God, one who wishes to kill someone is already a murderer; one who wishes to commit adultery is already an adulterer; one who wishes to swear falsely is already a perjurer. For God judges not only from works, but from thoughts. It is the will that is either rewarded for good or condemned for evil; works are testimonies to the will.

“And you will persecute them from city to city, so that every righteous blood shed upon the earth may come upon you.”

[Col. 0455C] He prophesies the destruction of the Jews. For he had long ago threatened all evils, which he rendered to the last generation. And just as all the good things which all the saints in every generation, from the foundation of the world, deserved were given to those who received Christ, so all the evils which the wicked in every generation, from the foundation of the world, deserved to suffer came upon the Jews who rejected Christ.

What then? Is God unjust? Far be it! But the righteous are said to have suffered what belonged to those people because they deserved what those others deserved; and they alone suffered, though they had not alone sinned. The matter is morally comparable to this: when your servants sin, you despoil one and spare him again, saying, “Unless you keep this command, you will suffer.” You do the same to another. If they do not improve, when one is punished he seems to be punished for them all, because what was threatened to the others he alone pays. Yet in truth he is not punished for the others but for himself. But if someone who had not sinned were punished, he would be said to be punished for others.

Thus this generation seems to have been punished for its fathers, who were frightened but not punished; but in truth it was condemned not for them but for its own sin. For it is not just that one person be punished for another’s sins; on the day of vengeance each person will be punished for his own sin.

[Bede.] Alternatively: vengeance for the blood of all the righteous is required from one generation, although many before the incarnation and after the resurrection of the Saviour were killed by other nations; because it is the custom of Scripture to reckon two generations, namely of the good and of the evil. For all the evil [Col. 0456A] are one generation, one city, one body of the devil; just as all the good are one generation and one body of Christ.

“From the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar. Amen, I say to you: all these things will come upon this generation.”

[Jerome.] The altar of incense was inside the temple; the altar of burnt offerings was outside. Between it and the temple Zechariah was killed. There is no doubt that Abel is the one whom his brother Cain killed (Gen. 4). Some say that Zechariah is the one who is the eleventh of the twelve prophets; others, Zechariah the father of John; others, the Zechariah killed by King Joash of Judah between the temple and altar, as the history of Kings [Col. 0456B] relates, and whom Scripture records as the son of Jehoiada the priest: “Joash,” it says, “did not remember the good which his father Jehoiada had done to him” (2 Chron. 24).

Since the place of the killing agrees in the case of this man, but not in the former cases, we ask why he is called the son of Barachiah. *Barachiah* is rendered in our language “blessed of the Lord,” and by this Hebrew name the righteousness of the priest Jehoiada is indicated. In the Gospel used by the Nazarenes, moreover, we find written “son of Jehoiada” instead of “son of Barachiah.” Because these people acted against the apostles in ways similar to Cain and Joash, they are therefore said to belong to one generation. For, as was said, just as the good are one generation, so the evil are another.

[Bede.] But why it is said, “to the blood of Zechariah,” requires investigation, since after him, up to Christ’s birth, many were killed by this generation, and after Christ was born innocent children as well. But because Abel was a shepherd of sheep, whereas Zechariah was a priest, he wished under their names to indicate martyrs of both ranks: both laypersons and those devoted to the service of the altar [Col. 0456C].

## CHAPTER 142

M. 241[V] L. 175

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you!”

[Jerome.] By “Jerusalem” he means its inhabitants, not the stones and buildings of the city, speaking with a father’s grieving affection.

“How often I wished to gather your children together, as [Col. 0456D] a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling!”

In saying, “How often I wished to gather your children,” he testifies that all the prophets of old were sent by him. Its meaning is: “I willed; you were unwilling; and all whom I gathered, I did so by my ever-effective will even against your unwillingness, because you were always ungrateful.” Or thus, according to the rule that uses the name of the cause for its effect: “I wished,” that is, “I approved, warned, and in many ways and by many means advised you, an apostate, to return to your senses; but you were unwilling. I sent Isaiah to you, and you sawed him asunder; I sent Jeremiah, and you stoned him.”

[Chrysostom.] “I sent Ezekiel, and you dragged him over stones and dashed out his brains. How can you be healed, when you permit no physician to come to you?” The Lord compares himself to a bird and is said to have wings because, in the manner of a bird, he gathers his chosen ones beneath himself [Col. 0457A] as chicks, warms them, and protects them from the snares of the devil and evil people. Hence the Prophet says: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Ps. 16).

Further, he compares the Church to a hen. For as chicks, following their food, wander in various directions and are gathered by their mother’s calls, so the people of God, following carnal pleasure and worldly desire, wander away from Mother Church and are now gathered and nourished through priests, sometimes by rebukes, sometimes by gentleness. And just as the hen warms not only her own chicks but loves as her own those of any bird that have been hatched elsewhere, striving to cherish Christians, so, whether those placed under her be Gentiles or Jews, she gives them life by the warmth of her faith, gives them birth in baptism [Col. 0457B], nourishes them by the word, and loves them with a mother’s charity.

These things said here about the Jews also apply to heretics. For whenever the words of prophets and apostles are read in churches, the prophets and apostles sent speak to us. Since heretics neglect and wrongly interpret them, they kill and stone them, as it were. Whenever a contest arises between believers and heretics, and the Lord wishes to gather them beneath the truth of his wings—that is, the two Testaments—they, not like domestic chicks but like wild and bloodthirsty vultures or hawks, not only refuse to come to the truth but even rush upon the hen, that is, the Church, and scatter her chicks.

“Behold, your house will be left to you desolate.”

[Col. 0457C] When I have been crucified, the veil of the temple will be torn, the secrets of its holy mystery will be made public, and the Spirit of God will depart from it. As a body, when the soul departs, first grows cold, then decays and comes apart, so your temple, when God’s Spirit departs from it, will first be filled with seditions and then collapse. For just as an incurable illness precedes a person’s death, so irreparable sins precede the fall of a place.

And as chicks often called by their mother, when they do not follow her, are either snatched away by a hawk or perish while wandering far off, so, when the Lord repeatedly called the Jews and they did not follow him, the Roman king, like a hawk, consumed some of them by famine and sword, while others were scattered [Col. 0457D] in order to perish.

“For I tell you, you will not see me from now on until you say: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

[Jerome.] The meaning is: Unless you confess that I am the one of whom the Psalmist sang that he would come in the name of the Lord (Ps. 117), you will not see my face from now on—that is, from this time of my passion. This confession and vision, however, are twofold. Jews who will believe, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, will from the judgment onward see divinity in Christ’s human face, because they will first confess in faith and love that the Son of the Almighty came in the flesh as blessed—that is, free from every sin—to glorify the Father’s name. Unbelievers, however, will see only his humanity in the second coming [Col. 0458A]; and yet then, with their consciences testifying to it, they will most certainly say that the blessed Son of the Almighty came in the name of the Lord.

## CHAPTER 143

A. 110[X]

Nevertheless, many even of the rulers believed in him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, lest they should be expelled from the synagogue. For they loved the glory of men more than the glory of God.

[AUGUSTINE.] It should be known that the Lord fixed his cross upon the foreheads of believers, where in some sense the seat of shame is, so that the faithful person may not blush at his name and may love the glory of God more than that of men. In its own time nothing was more intolerable to the [Col. 0458B] flesh than the cross; now nothing is more glorious upon the forehead. Therefore, where the Lord’s cross has been honoured, the cross is no longer a punishment for criminals, because it was thought that even a criminal would be honoured if he were crucified.

A. 111[I] M. 98 R. 96 L. 116

But Jesus cried out and said: He who believes in me does not believe in me, but in him who sent me.

He had already said something similar: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John 7). But now, he says, he does not believe in me—that is, only in what he sees in me—but in the Father. And whoever believes in the Father must believe that he has a Son.

And he who sees me sees him who sent me.

[Col. 0458C] Lest it be thought that he wished the Father to be understood in this manner as the father of sons by grace, rather than of the unique Word equal to himself, he added this. It is as though he said: So completely is there no difference between me and the Father that whoever sees me sees him.

A. 112[X]

I have come as light into the world, that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness.

Elsewhere the Lord said to his disciples: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5). Therefore all the saints are lights, but they are enlightened by him from whom, when they depart, they are darkened. When he says, “may not remain in darkness,” he clearly shows that he found all people in darkness.

And if anyone hears my words and does not keep them, [Col. 0458D] I do not judge him. For I did not come to judge the world, but to save the world.

Now is the time of mercy and gathering; later will be the time of judgment or condemnation, according to that saying: “I will sing to you, O Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. 100). Concerning the final judgment he added:

He who despises me and does not receive my words has one who judges him. The word which I have spoken, that will judge him on the last day; for I have not spoken of myself.

He does not speak from himself because he is not from himself. He made it sufficiently clear that he himself will judge, when he said, “The word which I have spoken,” and so forth. Those who have not heard will be judged in one way; those who have heard and despised it, in another. For the Apostle says: “Those who sinned without the law will perish without the law; and those who sinned through the law will be judged through the law” (Rom. 2).

But the Father who sent me himself gave me a commandment: what I should say and what I should speak.

The Father gave by begetting what the Son received by being born, just as he gave life. For life begot life—that is, the Father begot the Son. He gave a commandment, not because the Son did not possess it, but because in the wisdom of the Father, which is the Father’s Word, are all the Father’s commandments.

And I know that his commandment is eternal life.

Therefore the Son is the commandment of the Father, because he himself is eternal life.

Therefore, the things which I speak, I speak as the Father has told me.

We should not understand this as though the Father had spoken to the one Word by means of words. What then is meant by “I speak thus”? He spoke as the truthful one; this one speaks as Truth. The truthful one spoke to Truth—that is, he begot Truth. Truth speaks—that is, it announces itself. Truth thus speaks inwardly, without sound, to understanding minds, as the Father speaks to it; but so that people might believe what they are not yet able to understand, words sounded forth from the mouth of flesh. Uttered and marked in writing, they raise us in some measure to Truth itself.

A. 108[X]

Jesus said these things, and departed and hid himself from them.

He did not hide himself from those who had begun to believe, but from those who desired to kill him—making provision for our weakness, not detracting from his own power.

Though he had performed so many signs before them, they did not believe in him, so that the saying of Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled which he spoke: “Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53). Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: “He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes and understand with their heart, and be converted, and I heal them” (Isa. 6).

“Who” is used in the sense of rarity or difficulty: that what the prophets heard from the Lord and preached to the people was believed by scarcely a few Jews, even when the Lord was present in the flesh. By “arm” the Son is understood, because all things were made through him, just as you work by means of your arm. Such an arm is neither extended when stretched out nor contracted when drawn in. For the Son, like the Father, is wholly present everywhere. Here some mutter, saying: What fault of the Jews was it, if the saying of Isaiah had necessarily to be fulfilled? We answer them that the Lord, foreknowing future things, foretold through the prophet the unbelief of the Jews; he did not therefore compel them to sin because he foreknew their future sins. God foresaw their evil will, which he announced beforehand through the prophet. For providence imposes no necessity upon events; rather, things are foreseen as they stand with respect to either possibility, namely, occurring or not occurring. This providence—or, what is the same thing, foreknowledge—of God, from the wisdom of one foreknowing all things [Col. 0460A] before they exist, is altogether unchangeable and can in no way be mistaken. Nor does God now know anything that he did not know from eternity; nor will he know in the future anything that he does not know now. For example: if he knows today that you are reading, he knew from eternity that you would read today, and forever will know that you read today. Therefore, because foreknowledge cannot be mistaken, everything foreseen by God must occur. Thus it has been foreseen that Antichrist will be born, and this will necessarily happen. Therefore, it does not follow that it is false to say that Antichrist will necessarily be born. For when we say, “What has been foreseen must necessarily happen,” we mean that it is true; for it cannot at the same time be the case that it has been foreseen and does not happen. Hence it by no means follows that it happens necessarily. Likewise, when I see you running, it is necessary that you are running—that is, it cannot happen at the same time that I see you running and that you are not running. Yet it does not follow from this that you run necessarily. Thus the sophism is excluded which led many into error, causing them to think that all things happen by necessity.

A. 110[X]

Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory and spoke of him.

He foretold these things concerning the blinding of the Jews when he prophesied Christ’s incarnation. Isaiah did not see God as he is, any more than Moses did, unless perhaps they saw him when caught up above the human condition, as Paul was (2 Cor. 12). Hence this John says in his Epistle: “What we shall be has not yet appeared; we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). Therefore, before the incarnation, the Lord showed himself to human eyes as he willed, in a creature subject to himself, not as he is.

## CHAPTER CXLIV

M. 242[II] R. 136 L. 248

And when Jesus was going out from the temple, his disciples came to him to show him the buildings of the temple, saying: Teacher, look at what stones and what structures!

[HILARY.] After the threat that the city would be abandoned, as though he might be moved by admiration for the temple and prevent so great a work from ever being destroyed, its magnificent construction is shown to him. But he says that all things are to be destroyed, for the temple consecrated to him as the eternal dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit was the human being: that is, one made worthy to be God’s dwelling through recognition of the Son, confession of the Father, and obedience to the commandments. Let no one be troubled that Matthew says “his disciples” in the plural, while Mark says “one of his disciples,” for either one spoke for them all, or he used the singular number for the plural.

And Jesus answered and said: Do you see all these great buildings? Amen, I say to you: days will come in which not one stone will be left here upon another which will not be thrown down.

The historical sense is clear. But mystically, when the Lord departed from the temple, the entire ordering [Col. 0461A] of the commandments was so destroyed that the Jews fulfil nothing; and, their head having been removed, the members fight among themselves. [BEDE.] It was also divinely arranged that, once evangelical grace had been revealed throughout the world, the temple with its ceremonies should be removed, lest anyone still immature in faith should lapse into Judaism by seeing the institutions established by the prophets remain.
