Thus the shadow is taken away, and truth, revealed throughout the world, holds the palm.

## CHAPTER CXLV

R. 138[II] M. 243 L. 149

And as he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, the disciples came to him privately and asked him, saying: Teacher, tell us when these things will be, and what will be the sign of your coming, when all these things begin to be fulfilled?

The disciples ask the Lord at what time Jerusalem will be destroyed and what signs will afterward precede his coming, which will occur at the consummation of the age. The Lord sits on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple while discussing the temple’s ruin, so that even the position of his body accords with his words; and mystically he signifies that, while remaining at rest in the saints, he detests the madness of the proud. For who does not see that the Mount of Olives signifies the fruitful height of the holy Church, which the Lord always delights to inhabit? That mountain does not ordinarily produce a barren forest, but one which gives light, relieves infirmities, and refreshes the weary. These things are shown to be done by the Church, as the Psalmist says: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” (Ps. 51). The Church gives light by preaching the Scriptures, relieves the infirmities of sins, and refreshes the weary by promising eternal life.

L. 203[X]

And he said to the disciples: Days will come when you will desire to see one day of the Son of Man, and you will not see it.

[BEDE.] By “one day” he means the kingdom of God, whence the Psalmist says: “For one day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83). We ought indeed to desire the presence of this day; yet the greatness of our desire does not permit us to fabricate dreams as though the day of the Lord were at hand. Often also, because of the importunity of heretics, the faithful desired the Lord—even if it could be done for a single day—to return visibly in the body to earth; and he says, “You will not see it.” For it is enough that he once displayed the light of the Gospel to the whole world, strengthened it by the gift of charity, and works unceasingly and invisibly in his own. Thus the apostles are instructed by the truth of teaching, so that neither in this world of exile may they seek to see the glory of God, nor, in order to see it before God wills, presume to undergo death. “Whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s” (Rom. 14).

M. 243[II] R. 138 L. 249

See that no one leads you astray. For many will come in my name, saying, “I am Christ,” and they will lead many astray.

Many appeared when the destruction of Jerusalem was imminent, preaching many things contrary to the truth and declaring that the day of the Lord was near. Hence the Apostle, in the Epistle to the Thessalonians: “Many Antichrists will come in the name of Christ” (1 Thess. 5). I consider all heresiarchs to be Antichrists. “They will lead many astray” (2 Thess. 2); thus all in Samaria listened to Simon Magus, saying: “This man is the great power of God” (Acts 8).

But when you hear of battles, reports of wars, and seditions, do not be alarmed. For these things must happen first, but the end is not yet.

Battles and expectations of wars concern enemies; seditions concern fellow citizens. It is clear that all three abounded among the Jewish people. But when these things have gone before, the apostles are warned not to be alarmed, because the destruction of the city was to be deferred until the fortieth year.

[Col. 0462B] For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom; and there will be pestilences, famines, earthquakes in various places, terrors from heaven, and great signs. But all these things are the beginning of sorrows.

[GREGORY.] It is clear that all these things happened at the time of the Jewish sedition, before the final overthrow of the province. Some of them come from human beings [enemies], others from the earth, others from heaven, others from the elements. Nation will rise against nation: behold, the disturbance of human beings. Great earthquakes: behold, wrath from heaven. Pestilences: here are inflicted disorders of bodies. Famines: behold, the barrenness of the earth. Terrors from heaven and storms, as some manuscripts have: behold, the disorder of the air. Therefore those who sin in all things are struck in all things. This is not said of winter terrors and storms, which come in their proper season, but of those which do not keep the order of the seasons. For what comes to establish order is not a sign. All these things, fulfilled at that time, are found in Josephus, who recounts that a star resembling a sword hung over Jerusalem for an entire year, and that armed chariots and horsemen, as he reports, were seen moving through the air for forty days. Moreover, a heifer brought forward for sacrifice gave birth to a lamb in the hands of those offering it. [JEROME.] Mystically, “kingdom against kingdom,” and the pestilences of those whose speech spreads like a cancer, the famine of hearing the word of God, the shaking of the earth, and separation from the faith are understood of heretics; by fighting against one another, they bring about the Church’s victory.

M. 234[I] R. 639 L. 250 A. 141 and 146

Then they will hand you over to tribulation, and kill you; and you will be hated by all nations because of my name.

In the apostles the person of all believers is signified. Since the Jews persecuted them after the Lord’s death because of their confession of his name and faith, they are deservedly destroyed. [GREGORY.] First human hearts, and afterward the elements, are disturbed, so that when the order of things is thrown into confusion, the source from which tribulation comes may be shown.

L. 252[II] M. 88 R. 141

And not a hair of your head will perish; and by your patience you will possess your souls.

[Col. 0463A] Since harsh things are foretold concerning the affliction of death, consolation is given concerning the joy of resurrection. It is as though he said to his martyrs: Why do you fear that what hurts when cut off may perish, since even that in you which does not hurt when cut off cannot perish? Flesh hurts when cut; hair does not hurt. Otherwise: not a hair of the disciples’ heads will perish, because not only the courageous deeds of the saints, of whom it is said, “The Lord guards all their bones” (Ps. 33), but also, so to speak, the fleeting and most delicate surface of thoughts—which comes forth from the hidden root of the heart like hair from the brain—will be preserved before the just Judge and rewarded with a worthy recompense. Hence the prophet: “The remnant of thought will keep festival for you” (Ps. 73). Nazirites too are commanded in the Law to let their hair grow, and no razor came upon Samuel’s head (Num. 6), because the good thought of the wise is preserved forever. Patience is the guardian of all virtues; in it we possess the souls which possess the body, when by reason we govern those very souls in enduring. True patience, however, is to endure another’s evils with equanimity and not to be stirred by any resentment against the one inflicting them.

Therefore set it in your hearts not to premeditate how you will answer. For I will give you a mouth and wisdom which none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict.

It is as though he says to his weak members: Do not be afraid. You approach the contest, but I fight; you utter the words, but I speak.

M. 245[X]

Then many will be scandalized, and will hand one another over, and will hate one another; and many false prophets will arise and lead many astray. And because iniquity will abound, the charity of many will grow cold. M. R. But whoever perseveres to the end, that person will be saved.

Many will be scandalized—that is, will fall away from the faith—through fear, the savagery of torments, or wonders. They will hand one another over: an unbelieving brother his believing brother. They will hate one another, sons rising against parents and parents against children, the Lord’s sword separating them from one another; this occurred at the beginning of the preaching. False prophets will arise in order to deceive also by miracles. But let the faithful person, whenever he begins, remain in charity until the end of the present life, a charity which many waters cannot extinguish. And as the evangelist John was a martyr because he preserved in his mind the passion which he did not undergo in his body, so we too can be martyrs.

M. 246[VI] R. 140

And this Gospel of the kingdom will be preached in the whole world, as a testimony to all nations; and then the consummation will come.

Since the Lord knew that the disciples’ hearts would be saddened by the destruction of their nation, he consoles them in this way: they are to know that, once the Jews have been lost, they will have companions in the heavenly kingdom from the whole world. For, as ecclesiastical histories testify, long before the destruction of Judaea all the apostles were dispersed to preach the Gospel throughout the whole world, except James the son of Zebedee and James the Lord’s brother, who first shed their blood in Judaea for the word of the Gospel. Therefore, before the consummation of Jerusalem’s overthrow, the Gospel was preached in the four parts of the world: as testimony to believers of the coming and redemption of the Son of God, and as testimony to unbelievers of their condemnation.

M. 247[IV] R. 142

Therefore, when you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place—let the reader understand—

[Col. 0464B] [JEROME.] When we are summoned to understanding, what is said is shown to be mystical. In the older Scripture an idol is called an “abomination”; and “of desolation” is added because the idol was set up in the desolated temple. Some think this is to be understood either of Antichrist, or of Caesar’s image which Pilate placed in the temple, or of Hadrian’s statue, which stood for a long time in the very place of the Holy of Holies. Luke, however, shows in the following chapter that the abomination of desolation foretold by Daniel occurred when Jerusalem was besieged. [JEROME.] This testimony which the Lord took from Daniel is found at the end of the eleventh vision: “And in the middle of the week my sacrifice and libations shall be removed, and in the temple there shall be an abomination of desolations until the consummation of time” (Dan. 9). [AUGUSTINE.] Expositors of the divine utterances demonstrate, not only by the calculation of times but also by the events themselves, that Daniel’s weeks were fulfilled at the Lord’s first coming. This is especially so because it is written, “The Holy of Holies will be destroyed,” or because Hebrew codices have more expressly in that same prophecy: “Christ will be slain, and he will not be his” (*ibid.*)—that is, he will not belong to that city, since he was so alienated from the Jews, who believed for that very reason that he was not their Saviour because they were able to kill him. But if the weeks have already been fulfilled—since the Holy of Holies has already been anointed, Christ has already been slain so as not to belong to his city, sacrifice has already been removed from that temple, and anointing rightly removed—then, when the apostles ask about the end, the answer is: “It is not for you to know the times or seasons which the Father has set in his own power” (Acts 1). For the times which they could know through Daniel’s prophecy did not belong to the end of the age about which they asked.

L. 252[X]

But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its desolation is near.

[BEDE.] These are the things which were to happen during the forty years before the end had yet come. Here the very end of the desolation wrought by the Roman army is explained.

[Col. 0465A] L. 253[II] M. 248 R. 143

Then let those who are in Judaea flee to the mountains; let those in its midst depart; and let those in the surrounding regions not enter it, for these are days of vengeance, in which all that has been written may be fulfilled.

[BEDE.] Then—that is, at the time near the siege, while flight is still possible, while the Roman soldier has begun to spread through the districts of Judaea—those outside must not flee into Jerusalem; rather, those within it must depart before danger presses so hard that escape is impossible. For these are days of vengeance, demanding vengeance for the Lord’s blood. Ecclesiastical history recounts that the Christians who were in Judaea, warned by an angel when the destruction was imminent, crossed the Jordan and lived in the city of Pella under the protection of Agrippa, who obeyed the Roman government, until the desolation of Judaea was completed.

M. 240[II] R. 144 L. 254

But woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days.

[BEDE.] Woe, amid the captivity at hand, to those who are pregnant and nursing—or suckling, as some translate—since the burden either of the womb or of children in their arms greatly hinders the necessity of flight. Read the history of Kings, where Jonathan’s wife, escaping the evil of captivity by over-hasty flight, received her son after a fall into her lap permanently lame (2 Sam. 4). [AUGUSTINE.] More deeply: when someone desires another’s property, that person’s soul appears, as it were, to have conceived. But if through some wickedness that person can obtain what is desired, that person is known, as it were, to kiss and nurse the child that has been born. Do you wish to be pregnant with desire? Desire eternal life. Let that be your hope, and your birth will be sure.

L. 255[II] M. 251 R. 146

For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people. [BEDE.] Distress, an inseparable companion, clings to the Jewish people, scattered among all nations even to this day.

L. 256[X]

And they will fall by the edge of the sword, and be led captive into all nations; and Jerusalem will be trampled by the nations until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.

The times of the Gentiles are those mentioned by the Apostle when he says: “A partial blindness has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter; and thus all Israel should be saved” (Rom. 11). What follows pertains to the end of the age.

M. 250[V] R. 145

But pray that your flight may not occur in winter or on the Sabbath.

Taken literally, these words do not prohibit flight in Judaea, because there the mildness of winter is more suitable for flight than the heat of summer, and because the Lord had already brought Sabbath observance to an end. [HILARY.] Therefore we are warned to pray that our flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath—that is, that we may not be found either in the coldness of sins or in idleness from good works. Certainly we flee away from God if faith and charity in Christ grow cold, or if we languish idly on the Sabbath of virtues in God’s work. More deeply: “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath,” that is, lest the fruits of your work end with the end of time. For fruit ends in winter, and time on the Sabbath.

M. 251[II] R. 146 L. 155

For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor ever will be.

[BEDE.] Therefore prayer is necessary, because when the times of the Gentiles have been fulfilled, the persecution of Antichrist will occur, when most frequent and bitter torments will be inflicted far and wide upon the faithful.

L. 257[II] M. 258 R. 150

And there will be signs in sun, moon, and stars, and upon the earth distress of nations before the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and waves, while people wither from fear and expectation of what is coming upon the whole world.

“Before the confusion,” that is, before the upheaval: signs and distress among the nations will come first, and then the upheaval caused by the roaring sea and waves will follow. Joel says: “The sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes” (Joel 2). Rightly, when judgment is impending, the roaring of sea and waves is thrown into confusion; the earth’s world is defiled as its inhabitants press upon one another; and the great lights of heaven are disturbed. For as trees driven toward falling ordinarily send forth indications of their crash and movement beforehand, so, as the end of the world approaches, the elements, as though afraid, sway and tremble. Nor is it surprising that people wither from fear, in whom this will be fulfilled: “The whole world will fight for him against the senseless” (Wis. 5). We turn into fault everything we receive for the use of life. We turn the tranquillity of human peace into vain security; we love our earthly pilgrimage as though it were a homeland in which to dwell; we reduce bodily health to an instrument of vices; we employ the abundance of fertility not for the necessity of the flesh but for the perversity of pleasure; we compel the serenity of the air to serve us for love of earthly attachment. Therefore all things rightly strike us, so that for as many joys as we had in the world, we may afterward feel as many torments.

M. 252[V] R. 147

And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved; but for the sake of the elect those days will be shortened.

[REMIGIUS.] The sense is: unless God, who gives the strength to endure, had by his ordering shortened the power of persecution, few or none would be saved. Therefore he does not say this in order that times may be altered according to the ravings of certain persons, who do not observe what is written: “By your ordinance the day endures” (Ps. 118), but lest the delay of malice shake the faith of believers. For as the tribulation in the time of Antichrist will be more severe than all others, so it will be more moderate through the shortness of its duration. The Church will be assailed for three and a half years.

M. 253[II] R. 148 L. 204

Then if anyone says to you, “Behold, Christ is here,” or “there,” do not believe it.

[BEDE.] Some have arisen who, calculating the courses of ages, claimed to have discovered the exact year, day, and hour of the world’s consummation, contrary to the Lord’s authority when he says: “It is not for you to know times or seasons” (Acts 1). Many heretics also will come and have come; the first was Simon Magus, but the last will be Antichrist (Acts 8). Therefore no one is to be believed, either concerning a person—that that person is Christ—or concerning the time of the coming judgment.

M. 254[II] R. 149

For false Christs and false prophets will arise, and they will give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error. Behold, I have foretold it to you.

[BEDE.] These things properly apply to the times of Antichrist, when the working of signs will accompany even those who inflict torments. Hence the Apostle: “Whose coming is according to the working of Satan, in every deception, signs, and lying wonders” (2 Thess. 2). Thus the elect are forewarned so that, knowing beforehand, they may keep watch and their faith may not be shaken, although the persecutor of truth is a worker of power. Perhaps many will fall who appear elect in human judgment.

M. 255[V] L. 202

Therefore, if they say to you, “Behold, he is in the desert,” do not go out; “behold, he is in the inner chambers,” do not believe it.

Antichrist will attempt to restore the ceremonies of the Law in order to destroy the Gospel. This will persuade the Jews to receive him as Christ. Therefore the members of him who will exalt himself above everything called God or worshipped (2 Thess. 2) will proclaim that they have Christ in the wilderness of the letter of the Law. [AUGUSTINE.] More deeply: if anyone tells you that Christ abides in the desert of Gentile and philosophical doctrine, or in the inner chambers of heretics, who promise the mysteries of God, do not go out from your faith to believe them. “Inner chambers” here are the secret rooms of heretics.

M. 265[V] L. 205

For as lightning comes out of the east and appears as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.

He will come suddenly and flashing brightly, so that no one may be permitted to hide in one’s own mind without being penetrated by the Judge’s brightness. The Psalmist also says: “God will come openly; our God will not be silent” (Ps. 149). [BEDE.] It is therefore foolish to believe him hidden who is the light of the whole world. Luke fittingly says, “from under heaven,” because the decision of judgment will occur in the air, as the Apostle says: “We shall be caught up with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air” (1 Thess. 4). [AUGUSTINE.] This can also be understood of that coming of the Lord by which he comes daily into the Church and reigns in the hearts of the faithful. Do not, I say, believe that Christ is hidden, but that his faith shines from east to west in the churches. For it was prophesied of him under the figure of Solomon: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 71)—from the river, namely, where he was baptized, because there he began to preach the Gospel. And elsewhere: “All the nations you have made will come in faith and worship you, O Lord” (Ps. 85). Concerning the same one, Zephaniah says: “Each one from his own place will worship him, even all the islands of the nations” (Zeph. 2). By the name *fulgur* or *fulgor* (“lightning” or “brightness”), understand the manifestation of the sun or of another radiance that drives away the world’s darkness, just as Christ illuminates the Church.

M. 258[II] R. 150 L. 257

But immediately after the tribulation of those days, the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, the stars will fall from heaven, the powers of heaven will be shaken, and then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.

[JEROME, BEDE.] Understand the sign to be the cross, or the banner of victory. Not through a diminution of their light, but by comparison with the true light, all things will be darkened on the day of judgment, of which Isaiah prophesied: “The moon will blush and the sun be confounded when the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem and is glorified in the sight of his elders” (Isa. 24). But when the day of judgment has passed and the glory of the future life shines forth, when there is a new heaven and a new earth, then what the same prophet says elsewhere will occur: “The light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, like the light of seven days” (Isa. 30). [GREGORY.] What does the Lord call the powers of heaven but angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers? At his coming they will visibly appear to our eyes, so that they may then strictly exact from us what the invisible Creator now bears patiently. [BEDE.] What wonder if people tremble when the angelic powers tremble at the sight of judgment? Hence Job says: “The pillars of heaven tremble and fear at his command” (Job 26). What then will planks do when pillars tremble? What does the desert shrub suffer when the cedar of paradise is shaken?

M. 259[II] R. 151 L. 258

And then all the tribes of the earth will mourn.

[JEROME.] Then, namely, when they see the triumphal banner, those who have no citizenship in heaven but are written on earth will mourn for themselves. John Chrysostom says: just as, when a king enters a city, an army goes before him carrying the royal standards and banners, and by the array of martial preparation announces the king’s entrance, so when the Lord descends from heaven, an army of angels and archangels will go before him. Carrying the sign of the cross as a triumphal banner, they will announce to trembling lands the divine entrance of the heavenly King. Then those who crucified the Lord of majesty will recognize the design of their wickedness. Then they will confess their impious blindness in vain, when the King of glory displays his wounds and when they see him whom they pierced.

And they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven, with great power and majesty.

He who formerly descended in humility like rain upon fleece will come in power and glory. And because a cloud received him as he went into heaven, and there the angels said that he would come in the same manner as he departed, he is rightly believed to be coming not only in the same body, but also in a cloud.

And then he will send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice, [Col. 0469B] and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from the highest parts of heaven to their farthest bounds.

[Bede.] The trumpet is the power of raising the dead; the loud voice ensures that none remains unraised and that all may be present at the judgment. “From the four winds,” that is, from the four regions of the world—east and west, north and south. And lest anyone suppose that those from inland regions would not also be gathered, Mark adds: “From the utmost part of the earth to the utmost part of heaven,” that is, from the farthest bounds of earth in a straight line to its outermost limits, where, to those looking from afar, the circle of heaven appears to rest upon the earth. Therefore all, both elect and reprobate, will come to judgment. Matthew says: “From the ends of the heavens to their bounds,” signifying all who are [Col. 0469C] beneath the vault of heaven, as it were along the horizon.

Since it is especially the commentator’s task, in obscure passages, to place differing opinions before the reader’s judgment, let us also read it otherwise. Immediately after the tribulation of those days has begun—not yet ended—the sun of righteousness will be darkened for cold hearts. For just as, according to the capacity of the beholder, the ray of the material sun appears either paler or brighter, so according to the devotion of the believer spiritual light is poured into each one. The moon gives no light when the rays of the sun are excluded by the obstruction of the earth; likewise the Church will not give light when the vices of the flesh stand in the way, so that it cannot borrow the brightness of divine light from Christ’s rays. For in persecutions it is usually love of this life alone that shuts out God’s light. “The stars will fall from heaven” (Gen. XV), that is, from the Church, because the seed of Abraham—to which the stars were compared—will be almost lacking.

[Remigius.] “The powers of heaven will be shaken,” because certain very steadfast believers will be disturbed while the ungodly rage beyond measure. Or the angels will be stirred to the wrath of vengeance, those whom the Son of Man is to send with a trumpet. For to descend “with the trumpet of God” is to wage war in God’s name. By the last trumpet is understood the final war of evil spirits, who have often been defeated by angels, as the apostle John says: “I saw Michael and his angels fighting in heaven against the dragon” (Apoc. XII). Then will be the final battle, because they will be sent into Gehenna. In the time of Antichrist’s tribulation the sign of the Son of Man will appear—in heaven, understand, and not on earth. For the efficacy of the cross [Col. 0470A] will then lie hidden on earth, but in the thousands of saints it is most manifest in heaven. Then all the tribes of the earth will mourn; that is, they will commit deeds worthy of mourning, which mourning must necessarily follow. For no evil goes unpunished.

And at last they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven, that is, in the saints, just as even now he does not cease to come, according to what he says: “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the power of God and coming in the clouds of heaven.” But he will then come with great power and majesty because his greater power and majesty will appear to the saints, to whom he will give great strength so that they may not be overcome by so great a persecution. “And he will send his angels,” that is, his preachers; “with a trumpet,” that is, in open manifestation. For in the Law trumpets are commanded to be made, drawn out from gold, bronze, [Col. 0470B] and silver, so that they may resound with the sublime mysteries of doctrine; and they will gather his elect from the four parts of the world, that is, from the whole earth. Without doubt the steadfastness of the saints will be great when it is heard that Antichrist has been slain by the breath of the Lord’s mouth and that all Israel has been converted to the faith.

“But when these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.”

[Gregory.] When the plagues of the world increase and the terror of judgment is displayed as its powers are shaken, lift up your heads—that is, gladden your hearts. For while the world to which you are not attached is ending, the redemption you have sought is near. In Holy Scripture “head” is often used for the mind, because, just as the limbs are governed by the head, [Col. 0470C] so thoughts are ordered by the mind.

## CHAPTER CXLVI

“Now learn the parable from the fig tree. When its branch has already become tender and leaves have sprung forth, and when all the trees already bring forth fruit from themselves, you know that summer is near. So also you, when you see all these things happening, know that it is near, at the doors.”

Just as approaching summer is recognized from the fruit of trees, so the kingdom of God is recognized as near from the ruin of the world. These words show that the world’s fruit is its ruin. For it grows in order to fall; it buds in order that what it has budded may be consumed by calamities. He rightly compares the kingdom of God to summer, because then the clouds of sorrow will pass away and the day of life will shine with the brightness of the eternal sun. According to the former of the interpretations set forth above, take the passage with this qualification: “When you see all these things happening”—understand, those things said about the time of Antichrist’s persecution—“know that the consummation of the age is near.”

[Bede.] Mystically, the fig tree signifies the Synagogue condemned when Christ did not find in it the fruit of righteousness for which he looked. But when Israel receives the light of faith, the fig tree, long barren, will yield fruit, according to the saying of blessed Job: “A tree has hope: if it is cut down, it will grow green again, and its branches will sprout” (Job XIV). When you see this happen, do not doubt that the summer of true light is near. Before this, too, all the trees will produce fruit of themselves, because the peoples of all nations, according to the prophecies mentioned above, will receive [Col. 0471A] the Gospel before the day of final judgment comes. In it every tree will reveal what it had within itself: what was dry, for burning; or what was green, for planting, with the tree of life whose leaves will be for the healing of the nations—that is, the words concerning which it will be said: “Come, you blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXV).

“Amen I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.”

[Bede.] By “generation” he means either the whole human race, or specifically the Jews. By the heaven that will pass away we should understand not the ethereal or starry heaven, but the aerial heaven, of which we say, “the birds of heaven.” For we should not suppose that the waters of the Flood, which rose only fifteen cubits above the mountain peaks, reached beyond the boundaries of air and ether [Col. 0471B] (Gen. VII). But wherever they could reach, there the fire of judgment will reach. Thus heaven and earth will pass away in the form which they now have, but will remain without end in their essence. Hence Ecclesiastes: “A generation passes away, and a generation comes; but the earth stands for ever” (Eccles. I). The Lord’s words will never pass away; that is, the truth which they express remains eternally.

L. 259[X]

“But take heed to yourselves, lest perhaps your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness and the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly. For it will come like a snare upon all who dwell upon the face of the whole earth.”

[Col. 0471C] If a physician told you, “Take care that no one greedily takes the juice of that herb, for he will die at once,” would you not avoid death? Now the Savior commands the guarding of souls and bodies, and you do not care. No greater madness can exist than not to fear the death of soul and body.

“Watch therefore at all times, praying that you may be counted worthy to escape all these things that are to come, and to stand before the Son of Man.”

R. 153[VI] M. 263

“For you do not know when the time will be.”

[Augustine.] At all times watchfulness of mind is necessary before bodily death, so that we may stand secure in the presence of the supreme Judge. This indeed will be our blessedness.

[Col. 0471D] He did not say, “We do not know,” but “You do not know,” because neither a human being nor an angel knows the day of judgment either for himself or for another; but the Son, in the Father, knows it for himself, although he does not know it for others—that is, he makes no one know it—so that we may always watch anxiously. The Father alone is said to know, because he alone causes the Son to know. This is a familiar rule of speech, as in: “God tests you, that he may know,” that is, make known, whether you love him (Deut. XIII). Thus what follows is clear.

M. 260[VI] R. 232

“But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the Son, nor the angels in heaven, except the Father alone.”

[Jerome.] From this Arius and Eunomius said that the one who knows and the one who does not know are not equal. But since the Word of God made all times, how can he be ignorant of a part when he knows the whole? All the treasures of wisdom are hidden in the Savior because it is not expedient for us to know them (Col. II). Hence he says: “It is not for you to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts I). This shows that he himself knows, but that it is not expedient for the apostles to know, so that, always uncertain about future times, they may live in fear. Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*, in this chapter: “Certainly, when he said, ‘The Father knows,’ he said this because the Son also knows this in the Father. Yet the Son does not know—that is, his body placed on earth, which is the Church, does not know it.” Hence Jerome, in the shorter Breviary, on Psalm CXXXVIII: “The humanity of the Son said in [Col. 0472B] the Gospel that it was ignorant of the end of this world.” Gregory, in the Register, to Eulogius the patriarch: “The only-begotten Son of God knows the hour of judgment, but not from the nature of his humanity.”

## CHAPTER CXLVII

M. 261[V] L. 207

“But as in the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. For as they were in the days before the Flood, eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day on which Noah entered the ark (Gen. VII), and did not know until the Flood came and swept them all away, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.”

[Jerome.] After wars and dissensions and the other things by which the human race is devastated, a short peace will follow, according to the Apostle, in order that the faith of believers may be tested. For he says: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (I Thess. V). Noah builds the ark when the Lord builds the Church by gathering faithful people together as though they were smoothed timbers. He enters it when it has been perfectly completed, when, on the day of judgment, as its eternal inhabitant, he illumines it by the presence of his vision. But while the ark is being built, the wicked live in luxury; when it is entered, they perish. So those who here insult the saints while they struggle will there, when the saints are crowned, be punished with eternal damnation.

L. 208[X]

“Likewise, as it happened in the days of Lot: they ate and drank, bought and sold, planted and built; but on the day Lot went out from Sodom, it rained fire and sulphur from heaven and destroyed them all” (Gen. XIX). “So it will be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed.”

He mentions only offences which might be judged slight or no offences at all, so that it may be understood with what punishment unlawful things will be struck, if even lawful things—without which this life cannot be sustained—when done without moderation are punished with fire and sulphur. Lot in Sodom, that is, the people of the elect, dwells among the reprobate as a stranger, according to the interpretation of Lot’s name, avoiding their crimes. When Lot departs, Sodom will perish, because at the consummation of the age the wicked will be sent into the furnace of fire. The fire that will fall from heaven will not be their everlasting punishment, but one far more severe.

[Col. 0473A] M. 248[II] R. 145 L. 209 and 253

“Then let the one who is on the roof not come down to take anything from his house; and let the one who is in the field not return to take his garment.”

[Remigius.] He is on the roof who, rising in mind above carnal things, lives spiritually in doctrine, a place to which the devil’s darts do not reach. Therefore, especially when judgment is at hand, let him by no means descend into the house of his former manner of life, lest he resume the desires of world or flesh which he had abandoned. For this very flesh in which we dwell, or this world, is our house, of which the Apostle says: “We know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God” (II Cor. V). The field is the Church; the one who labours in it should not look back to worldly things. In the field of spiritual Scriptures also we ought to sow, not seeking the things behind, nor taking a second tunic, which the apostles are forbidden to possess.

L. 210[X]

“Remember Lot’s wife” (Gen. XIX).

[Bede.] Lot’s wife signifies those who look back in tribulation and turn away from hope in the divine promise. Therefore she was made a statue, so that by warning people not to do this she might, as it were, season their hearts lest they become foolish.

M. 262[V] L. 212

“Then two will be in the field: one will be taken, and the other left.”

[Col. 0473C] Then—that is, at that consummation, or, as Luke says, in that night of the children of darkness who will say, “Peace and security”—there will be found two kinds of preachers, labouring in the ministry of the Church as in God’s field. Hence a certain cultivator said: “You are God’s field” (I Cor. III). The one will be taken who has spoken in Christ without adulterating God’s word. But the one will be left by God who proclaimed Christ not sincerely, but from ulterior motive.

“Two women grinding at one mill: one will be taken, and the other left.”

[Maximus.] By the two women we may understand heresies and the Church, since they appear to grind together in the Law and Gospel, and from the same Scriptures to grind out the flour of God’s commandments. Though they share one profession of the Christian name, they will not receive the same reward. The Law, like the stone of the lower mill, would lie slow and heavy among the Jews alone unless the movement of the Gospel, like the upper millstone, had been laid upon it. For without the Gospel the Law did what one stone can do: it could crush but not benefit, as the Apostle says, “The Law works wrath” (Rom. IV), but does not bestow grace. The Gospel laid above it adorns both, and is carried around with such swift motion that by its revolution it traverses the whole world: that is, it visits the lower regions, penetrates the heavens, and illumines earthly things. Understanding this, Paul says: “That the word of God may run and be glorified among you” (II Thess. III). The Gospel, like the upper [Col. 0474A] millstone, receives all who come and sends them inward, as it were through certain channels of the commandments, so that there, with the harshness of Gentile character softened by the saving precepts of the two Testaments on either side, it may bring forth everything pure. By the operation of these millstones the Church shakes off the roughness of sins and draws out from the depths of thoughts the marrow of the worldly heart, offering it to God as fine flour, as David says: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. L). I think Ezekiel touched upon this likeness of the Testaments when he said that a wheel was joined within a wheel.

[Bede.] Alternatively: he calls “grinding” those placed among the common people, who conduct worldly affairs under the direction of teachers. He signifies them also by the name of women because it is beneficial for them to be guided by the counsel of the experienced; and he calls them grinding because of the cycle of worldly business. He says that they grind “at one [mill]” insofar as they supply from their affairs the needs of the Church. They cast forth flour, as it were, from themselves because in a quiet heart they produce very minute thoughts. Of these, that portion will be taken which has practised marriage solely for love of offspring and has distributed earthly substance to acquire heavenly things. But that portion will be left which has served marriage for the pleasures of the flesh and, if it offers anything earthly to the Church or the poor, does so in order that, as though serving the Lord, it may itself abound more greatly.

“Two in one bed: one will be taken, and the other left.”

[Col. 0474C] By the two in bed he signifies those who love leisure and quiet and are occupied neither with worldly business nor with ecclesiastical duties. This is not said of two persons, but of two kinds of disposition. For the one who has pursued continence for God’s sake, so that, living free from care, he may think upon the things of God, will be taken to meet Christ in the air. But the one who, from love of human praise or through any other corruption of vice, has neglected the state of monastic life in which he was trained, will be left. Hence Jeremiah, describing the fall of the idle soul under the figure of Judaea, says: “Her enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lam. I). Nor do I think there are other classes of people of which the Church consists than these three, each having two distinctions on account of taking and leaving. Thus Ezekiel the prophet saw three men delivered—Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezek. XIV)—in whom preachers, the continent, and married persons are respectively signified. For Noah guided the ark amid the waters (Gen. VII), and therefore bore the figure of rulers. Daniel, too, in the royal court devoted himself to abstinence, and therefore signified the life of the continent. But Job exercised care for his own household in marriage (Job I), whence the order of good married persons is figured. We know that Job endured so much not for sins, but to demonstrate his righteousness.

L. 213[V] M. 257

In reply they say: “Where, Lord?” He said [Col. 0475A] to them: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered.”

[Jerome.] The Savior, questioned about two things—namely, where the good will be taken and where the wicked will be left—said one thing and left the other to be understood. For he kept silence concerning the reprobate, who are to be condemned with the devil. Eagles and vultures are said to scent corpses across the sea and gather there. How much more will the multitude of believers hasten to the light of the whole world when the Son of Man comes with intelligible clouds and every eye sees him? Or, by the body, more significantly called a corpse because it falls in death, understand Christ’s passion. The eagles, then, are the elect, who, humbly imitating his passion, are satisfied as it were from his flesh, and whose youth will be renewed like the eagle’s through the resurrection (Ps. CII). Therefore where the Lord is bodily, there the spiritual eagles will be gathered. Saints may also be called eagles because of the flight of the spiritual body.

[Bede.] Furthermore, with all their mind they thirst to contemplate the glory of the heavenly majesty, just as eagles, surpassing other birds in flight, delight to fix their eyes upon the sun’s ray. The eagle also customarily brings to its nest a stone that resists poisons, lest a serpent dare to approach and touch its young and eggs. Thus the wise person defends his actions and thoughts against the assault of the ancient serpent through faith in and love for Christ, who is the stone cut from the mountain (Dan. II) and who overthrew the kingdom of the devil.

[Col. 0475C] R. 154[II] M. 269 L. 228

“It is like a man who has gone abroad, who left his house and gave his servants authority over every work, and commanded the doorkeeper to keep watch.”

[Gregory—Jerome.] Earth is the proper place of the flesh; it is, as it were, taken to foreign parts when through the Redeemer it is established in heaven. Therefore he himself, like a man who has gone abroad, having been lifted to heaven according to the body, left his house—that is, the Church. He gave his servants authority over every work: that is, to the faithful, eight talents according to Matthew and ten minas according to Luke. He commands the doorkeeper who leads into the heavenly house to watch: namely, the preacher, to whom it is said: “If you do not announce to the wicked man his wickedness, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. III).

R. 155[II] M. 264 L. 156

“Watch therefore, for you do not know when the Lord will come: in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning; lest, coming suddenly, he find you asleep.”

[Augustine.] In whatever state one’s own last day finds him, in that state the last day of the world will overtake him, since as each person dies on this day, so he will be judged on that day. Therefore the Savior exhorts us to watch in mind, so that at whatever hour the end of this life brings judgment, it may not find us unprepared.

M. L.

“But know this: if the master of the house knew at what hour the thief would come, he would surely keep watch and would not allow his house to be broken into. Therefore you also be ready, because you do not know at what hour the Son of Man will come.”

[Gregory.] Since the master of the house, if he knew, would keep watch at the hour he suspected, Christ proves by this comparison that they ought to keep watch and be sober, ready without spot or wrinkle. While the master of the house does not know, the thief breaks into the house, because when the spirit sleeps from guarding itself, unforeseen death breaks into the dwelling of the flesh and drags the soul to punishment. Yet he would resist the thief if he watched in mind, because he would meet him by repenting, lest he perish unrepentant. The old manuscripts read *perfodiri* (“to be broken into”), not *perfodi* (“to break into”), as some correct it.

L.

[Col. 0476B] Peter said to him: “Lord, do you speak this parable to us, or to all?” R. “What I say to you, I say to all: Watch.”

[Bede.] Not only rulers of the Church, but all of us are commanded to watch, guarding the doors of our hearts lest the evil suggestion of the crafty enemy enter, and lest the Lord find us asleep.

[Jerome.] One who sleeps sees not bodies but phantasms; and when he wakes, he retains nothing of what he saw. Such are those whom love of the world carries away in life and abandons after life.

L. 157[V] M. 265

“And the Lord said: Who do you think is the faithful servant and prudent steward whom the Lord has appointed over [Col. 0476C] his household, to give them their food at the proper time?”

[Bede.] The Lord generally commands all to watch; but concerning the prelates of the Church he says that one who dispenses faithfully is rarely found: rare is one whom the Lord has appointed by calling, as Aaron was; and one who has not pushed himself forward, who does not feed himself more than the sheep. The faithful servant, by properly distributing his master’s money, serves his master for the Lord’s sake; he feeds Christ’s sheep not for gain but from love of Christ. The prudent person is wise and understanding, foresees the end, discerns the capacity of each person, and gives them food at the proper time—that is, he measures out the food of the divine word and example according to the quality of his hearers.

M. 266[V] L. 157

[Col. 0476D] “Blessed is that servant whom his master, when he comes, finds doing so. Truly I say to you that he will appoint him over all his goods.”

By “over all” he means the joys of the heavenly kingdom: not that they alone may possess eternal goods, but that they may possess them above others, both for their own life and for the keeping of the flock. Even in this age those who labour greatly in teaching ought to be honoured above others. Hence the Apostle says: “Let the presbyters who rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially those who labour in word and teaching” (II Tim. III).

M. 267[V] L. 15

“But if that evil servant says in his heart, ‘My master delays his coming,’ and begins to beat his fellow servants, and eats and drinks with the drunkards, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know; and he will divide him, and assign his portion with the hypocrites and unbelievers. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

[Bede.] “He will divide him”: namely, he will separate him from the fellowship of the saints. Here he calls hypocrites those left in the field, at the mill, and in the bed; but unbelievers are those who never possessed the faith. Just as the order of reward was stated in the case of the faithful steward, so the eternal condemnation of evil prelates is described in the case of the evil servant: they not only live badly, but also provoke their subjects by injuries. Typologically, beating boys and maidservants may also be understood as corrupting the hearts of the weak in faith by the example of wrong action or speech. To eat, drink, and become drunk is to be occupied with the crimes and enticements of the age, which make the mind senseless and cause it to wander.

[Augustine.] Notice that the evil servant is condemned not because he thinks the Lord slow, but because he does not love the Lord’s coming. For there is no difference, perhaps, among those who hold these differing opinions if they thirst for the Lord’s manifestation, await it vigilantly, and love it faithfully. One says, “Let us watch and pray, because the Lord will come sooner.” Another says, “Let us watch and pray, because life is short and uncertain, even though he will come later.” A third says, “Let us watch and pray, because life is short and uncertain, and we do not know when the Lord will come.”

## CHAPTER CXLVIII

[Col. 0477C] M. 268[X]

“Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride.”

[Jerome.] Some take this parable simply as referring to virgins: some are virgins in body and mind; others only in body, either because they do not act rightly, or because they have been preserved by their fathers’ guardianship while being married in mind. But this comparison seems rather to concern the human race as constituted in Church and Synagogue, just as above the two in the field, the two grinding, and the two in bed signified all church members, both just and unjust, and Jews. They are all called virgins because they possess knowledge of the one God and their mind is not defiled by idolatry. They have oil when they adorn faith with works; they lack oil when they do not adorn it.

We may interpret the five virgins as the five senses, by which some hasten toward heavenly things while others, desiring earthly dregs, lack the nourishment of truth by which to illuminate their hearts. Of sight, hearing, and touch it is spoken spiritually: “What we have seen, what we have heard, what we have looked upon with our eyes, and what our hands have handled” (I John I). Of taste: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII). Of smell: “We run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Cant. IV); and: “We are the good fragrance of Christ” (II Cor. II).

Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*: “The whole Church, consisting of virgins, boys, married women, women, wives, and men, has been called virgin under one name.” Hence the Apostle: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (II Cor. XI). He says this not to religious women alone but to the whole Church; and because the devil is the corrupter of this virginity, he immediately adds: “I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the chastity which is in Christ” (ibid.). Few possess virginity in body; all ought to possess it in heart.

Therefore the five virgins seem to signify fivefold continence of eyes, ears, smell, taste, and touch. Since this continence is partly practised before God, so as to please him in the inward joy of conscience, and partly before people for human glory, five are called wise and five foolish—yet both are virgins because of continence. The words “to go out to meet the bridegroom and the bride” should be understood of Christians, for those who are not Christians cannot meet Christ. The lamps are works made bright through continence. The five foolish women did not take oil—that is, joy—except in human praises. Therefore they do not possess oil, that is, the joy of which it is said: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness” (Ps. XLIV). “In their vessels,” that is, in their hearts. Hence the Apostle: “Let a person test himself, and then he will have glory in himself and not in another” (Gal. VI).

Or oil seems to signify charity, because of what the Apostle says of charity: “Though I speak with the tongues of men and angels, but have not charity, I have become as sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (I Cor. XIII). Oil rises above all liquids, just as charity is the surpassing way of attaining heaven. Read the letter thus: “Then”—that is, at the end of the world and at the unknown hour—“the kingdom of heaven,” that is, the Church of that time, will be like ten virgins, that is, church members, from the beginning of the Church to its end.

[Remigius.] A doubled five makes ten, because the multitude of believers is gathered from both sexes. Taking lamps is the display of good works, by which the merely superstitious and the truly religious alike are thought to go out to meet the bridegroom and bride—that is, Christ and the Church already crowned in heaven.

[Hilary.] Every day, through the duties of this life, we prepare to meet in the resurrection which is from the dead. Or understand the bridegroom and bride as God in the human being, according to the sense in which I have explained the parable. For as the spirit is bridegroom to the flesh, so the flesh is bride to the spirit. Finally, when the trumpet sounds, one goes out only to meet the bridegroom, because in Christ the humility of the flesh has now passed into spiritual glory.

“But five of them were foolish and five prudent. The five foolish, having taken their lamps, did not take oil with them. But the prudent took oil in their vessels with their lamps.”

[Gregory.] Holy Church has prudent virgins who work well for God, and foolish virgins who labour for empty glory. Oil is the brightness of glory. The vessels are our hearts. Paul says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I). The foolish [Col. 0479A] did not take oil with them because, while they seek glory from others, they do not store it in their conscience.

“But while the bridegroom delayed, they all became drowsy and slept.”

The bridegroom’s delay is the time for repentance until his second coming. To become drowsy is to languish through infirmities before death; to sleep is to die. For all will be raised from death as from sleep.

“But at midnight a cry was raised: ‘Behold, the bridegroom comes; go out to meet him.’”

[Jerome.] Jewish tradition signifies that Christ will come at midnight, in likeness to the Egyptian time when the Passover was celebrated by night (Exod. XII). Hence I think an apostolic tradition has remained: during the Paschal vigil, the people awaiting Christ’s coming may not be dismissed before midnight; but after that time has passed, in presumed security, the festival day is celebrated together. Hence also David: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you for the judgments of your righteousness” (Ps. CXVIII).

[Augustine.] But we say “at midnight,” that is, with no one knowing, because the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night (I Thess. V). Night is ignorance, of which it is elsewhere said: “It is not for you to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts I). The cry is that of which the Apostle says: “For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise” (I Cor. XV).

[Col. 0479C] “Then all those virgins rose and trimmed their lamps.”

The past tenses are to be read for future ones, in this manner: “A cry was raised,” that is, will be raised. “Then all will rise and trim [their lamps],” recalling how they have acted as they prepare to render account for their works.

“But the foolish said to the prudent: ‘Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out.’”

Those whose deeds are sustained by others’ praise fail when that praise is withdrawn. Therefore the foolish will say to the wise in the desire of their minds: “Give us, if you can, some of the oil of your glory”—that is, help us, because now from our works we recognize that they do not shine before him who sees all things, since you placed your glory better in your consciences than we placed ours in the favour of flatterers.

[Macrobius.] Hence a certain philosopher said: “The wise person places the fruit of a good work in conscience; the less perfect person, in glory.” Those who complain that their lamps are going out show that they shine in part, but do not have unfailing light or enduring works. Therefore the virginal soul ought not to be content with mediocre virtues, lest it wither, but should possess perfect virtues so that it may have everlasting light.

“The prudent answered, saying: ‘Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you; go instead to those who sell, and buy for yourselves.’”

They answered this not out of avarice but out of fear, although they have works of virtue shining before the Judge. For on the day of judgment the virtues of some will not relieve the vices of others; each person will be concerned for himself. Each will render account for himself, and there will be no need for testimony before him who knows all things. The prudent adorn their senses, in which they receive the oil of knowledge; this oil is sold at great price and acquired by difficult labour when they attend to almsgiving, other virtues, and the counsels of teachers.

[Augustine.] When they appear to say to the foolish, “Go to those who sell and buy for yourselves,” it is as though they said: “Let us now see how those who were accustomed to sell you praises will help you.” They should not be thought to give advice, but to recall the foolish women’s fault. Flatterers sell oil to those who do not understand the saying: “Those who call you happy lead you into error” (Isa. III). It is better to be rebuked by a just person than praised by a sinner. Those who, having received some grace, offer its shining glory to their empty praises, as it were sell oil. Hence the Psalmist: “Let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat” (Ps. CXL), that is, let not a flatterer’s favour caress my mind.

“But while they went to buy, the bridegroom came. And those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was shut.”

It is not said here that they go to prepare new works, but to give an account of past ones. Through memory they will turn themselves toward outward things, anxiously seeking joys; and the Judge will come. But those who are ready will enter the wedding feast, where the pure soul is joined to God’s Word. The entrance to the heavenly kingdom will be closed, because after judgment [Col. 0480C] there is no place for prayer. It should be known that the Church is now betrothed and is a virgin to be brought to the wedding, that is, continent from worldly corruption. But at that time she will be wed, when all mortality has passed away and she is made fruitful in an immortal union.

“Finally the other virgins also came, saying: ‘Lord, Lord, open to us.’”

The confession in calling him Lord is indeed noble, and the repetition is an indication of faith; but it is of no use to call upon one whom you deny in deed. These things will not be done in human words, but by consciences speaking to themselves.

“But he answered and said: ‘Amen I say to you, I do not know you.’”

There the person will not be heard by God who here refuses to hear what he commanded. For “the ignorant person will be ignored” (I Cor. XIV), so that one who now rejects ineffable mercy may experience severity without end.

Therefore watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.

See where the parable is directed: because we do not know the day of judgment, and because each person also does not know the day or hour of his own falling asleep, let us diligently prepare for ourselves the testimony of a good conscience, lest the Judge find us unprepared.

## CHAPTER CXLIX

M. 269[II] R. 154 L. 228

For it is as when a man going abroad called his servants and entrusted his goods to them.

Therefore I say that you should watch, because the bridegroom mentioned above, like a man going abroad, entrusted his goods to his servants to yield fruit, intending to require from each an account of what had been committed to him. [JEROME.] This man is Christ, who, ascending into heaven after the resurrection, called the apostles and entrusted evangelical teaching according to the capacities of those receiving it; and in the end he receives with equal joy both the one who made ten out of five talents and the one who made four out of two, considering not the profit but the intention.

M. 150[V] L. 229

And to one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one, to each according to his own ability; and he departed immediately.

[GREGORY.] In the five talents is expressed knowledge of outward things, acquired through the examination of the five senses. The two signify understanding and action; the one signifies understanding. Behold, the distribution of gifts is unequal because those who receive them differ. For although the distributor has departed, in that he has left us free power to act by our own choice, nevertheless he is always ready to give, according as we are willing to advance grace.

Now he who had received five talents went away, worked with them, and gained another five. Likewise he who had received two gained another two.

He went away through the exercise of study, who received earthly senses, and doubled for himself the knowledge of heavenly things, understanding the Creator through creatures. Those of this kind, although they do not know how to penetrate mysteries, nevertheless teach rightly with a good intention. But he who received present knowledge and activity understood types of future blessedness. Or, the other five or other two come as profit in this respect: preaching is bestowed upon both sexes, and the talents received are, as it were, doubled. For some of both sexes flourish through the word and example of teachers in understanding and action; others through the discipline of the senses and contemplation of visible things—both seeking the highest good.

But he who had received one went away, dug in the earth, and hid his master’s money.

The wicked servant put into earthly works the teaching God had given him. For to hide a talent is never to lift one’s heart above earthly things. Hence the prophet says: “They are wise to do evil, but they do not know how to do good” (Jer. IV).

But after a long time the master of those servants came and settled accounts with them.

This will happen at the Lord’s second coming. If the apostles are to render an account and rise again under fear of the Judge, what of us? Each person’s deeds will be examined, as conscience accuses or excuses each one.

And he who had received five talents came forward and offered another five talents, saying: “Lord, you entrusted five talents to me; behold, I have gained another five.”

Coming forward to render a grateful account, he would offer the Lord all those whom he had turned from error, while conscience bore witness that, through the grace given him, he had gained all whom he could.

[Col. 0482A] His master said to him: “Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things; I will set you over many. Enter into the joy of your master.”

Joined to the choirs of angels, rejoice inwardly in a gift which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (I Cor. II; Isa. LXIV), so that you no longer have anything outwardly to grieve over because of corruption. Present things, although they seem great, are nevertheless small and few in comparison with things to come, nor are they without an admixture of some trouble. What joy is greater than to be with the Lord?

Then he who had received two talents also came and said: “Lord, you entrusted two talents to me; behold, I have gained another two.” His master said to him: “Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things; I will set you over many. Enter into the joy of your master.”

“Euge,” that is, “well done”: it is the congratulation of a gracious master to a servant who is good toward himself and his neighbor, and faithful in every respect to his master.

But he who had received one talent also came forward and said: “Lord, I know that you are a hard man: you reap where you did not sow, and gather where you did not scatter. And being afraid, I went away and hid your talent in the earth. Behold, you have what is yours.”

It is as though he said: “You gave me understanding; I have understanding.” Having a most unhappy testimony from his own conscience, when he ought simply to have confessed his idleness and asked forgiveness, he slanders the master’s severity; and thus what he thought to say in excuse is turned into guilt against him. He calls the master hard because the way leading to life is arduous, and because the higher the step, the more serious the fall. [JEROME.] “You reap,” he says, “where you did not sow,” cutting down with the sickle of judgment Gentiles to whom you did not commit the Scripture of the Law. “You gather also into your kingdom from the Gentiles, where you did not scatter the seed of preaching.” From this we understand that the Lord receives even the good life of Gentiles and philosophers, and that, in comparison with those who obey the natural law, those who neglect the written law are condemned. [GREGORY.] There are many within the Church who bear the image of the evil servant: they fear to undertake paths of better life, yet they do not fear to lie in the slothful idleness of their torpor. When they consider themselves sinners, they tremble to take up paths of holiness, yet they do not dread remaining in their iniquities.

[Col. 0482D] His master answered and said to him: “Wicked and slothful servant, you knew that I reap where I do not sow and gather where I have not scattered. Therefore you ought to have entrusted my money to the bankers, and when I came I would certainly have received what was mine with interest.”

He is called a wicked servant because he slanders his master, and in this his pride is noted; slothful because he did not double the talent, and in this he is accused of negligence. If he knew his master to be a hard exactor, why did he not serve him so as to profit from that which had been given him for distribution? Where it is written “my money,” the Greek word signifies both money and silver. Hence: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire, tested in the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. XI). Money, or silver, is preaching, which ought to have been given to the money-changers and bankers—that is, to other teachers. To give money to money-changers, therefore, is to bestow the knowledge of preaching upon those able to exercise it in speech and deeds.

Therefore take the talent from him, and give it to him who has ten talents.

The talent is taken away and given to him who has ten talents, so that we may understand that a greater reward is due to one who labors more, though the joy is equal both for the one who doubled five and for the one who doubled two talents. Hence the Apostle says: “Honor presbyters who are true presbyters, especially those who labor in the word of God” (I Tim. V). [GREGORY.] Or thus: the talent is rightly given to one who rightly ministered outward things; this happens daily in the Church. For many, while ministering outward things well, are also brought by divine grace to mystical understanding. In judgment also, many who seemed fit to teach will, because of their negligence, be reckoned among the untaught; while some simpler persons, because of the devotion of their conduct, will receive the highest rewards among apostolic teachers. “For he who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward” (Matt. X).

M. 271[II] R. 255 L. 230

For to everyone who has, it will be given, and he will abound; but from him who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away.

[JEROME.] Many naturally possess keenness of intellect, yet through idleness corrupt it and lose that good of nature because they do not exercise it; and they see the promised reward pass to those who increase by labor and diligence what they possess in smaller measure. Or thus: one who has faith and a good will in the Lord, even if he accomplishes less as a human being, will nevertheless be granted grace by the good Judge. But one lacking these will lose even the other virtues which he seemed naturally to possess. It is elegantly said, “what he seems to have.” For what is without faith is not truly possessed; it is charged against the evil servant, not credited to his master. Gregory says: one who has charity receives other gifts as well; one lacking it loses even what he had. Let no one say, “I received no talent; there is nothing for which I can be compelled to render an account.” For each person will be called to account for the very thing, however slight, which he received. Does one have understanding for preaching? He must minister from that talent. Does another have earthly substance? Let him distribute from the talent of his substance. Does another have the trade by which he is fed? His trade is his talent. Is another a companion of a rich man? He has the talent of companionship and ought to speak on behalf of the needy. Therefore, to everyone who has as he ought—that is, who uses what he has with generosity—grace upon grace will be given. But every possession which is not diminished by giving, while it is possessed but not given, is not yet possessed as it ought to be possessed. Let him therefore fear who seems to have that which he misuses, lest it be utterly taken from him.

[Col. 0484A] M. 272[V] L. 231

And cast the unprofitable servant into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

The Lord is light; whoever is cast out from him lacks true light. Therefore one who has not paid the last farthing of the word before the end of life will never be released from the prison of darkness. For the coin of eternal life is established upon four parts: what you believe with your heart, confess with your mouth; what you confess, fulfill in deed; and what you fulfill, do not cease to teach. “For whoever does and teaches these things shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V).

## CHAPTER CL

[Col. 0484B] A. 154[X]

Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning.

[GREGORY.] That lust is in the loins for men and in the navel for women is attested by the Lord, who speaks of the devil to blessed Job: “His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly” (Job XL). Thus lust is designated by the name of the loins, the principal sexual region, when the Lord says: “Let your loins be girded.” [BEDE.] Therefore, because the wicked servant is wholly subject to the world, and the foolish virgins serve God with a view to worldly praise, he fittingly teaches his own to gird their loins against love of worldly things and to have lamps, so that they may do and teach these very things with a right intention. [GREGORY.] In another sense, we gird our loins when we restrain the lust of the flesh by continence. We hold lamps in our hands when by good works we display examples of light. For neither one without the other pleases our Redeemer: neither the person who does good deeds but does not abandon the defilements of lust, nor the person who excels in chastity but does not continually practice good works.

And you yourselves be like people waiting for their master when he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may open to him immediately.

The Lord went to the wedding when, ascending into heaven, he joined to himself as a new man the heavenly multitude of angels. He will return then, when he is manifested for judgment. For he comes when he hastens to judgment; he knocks when, through illness, he indicates that death is near. He immediately opens to him who receives him with love. For one does not wish to open to him who trembles to depart from the body, because he remembers having despised him.

L. 155[V] L. 265

Blessed are those servants whom, when the Lord comes, he finds watching.

He watches who keeps the eyes of his mind open to behold the true light. He watches who drives from himself the darkness of torpor and negligence. Hence Paul says: “Watch, you righteous, and do not sin” (I Cor. XV). Again he says: “It is now time for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. XIII).

[Col. 0485A] Amen I say to you, he will gird himself, make them recline at table, and, passing among them, will serve them.

He girds himself, that is, he prepares himself for recompense. He makes them recline, that is, he refreshes them in eternal rest. Hence elsewhere the Lord himself says: “They shall recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (Matt. VII). He will serve while passing among them, because, returning from judgment to the kingdom, after that judgment he will satisfy us with the illumination of his light. For him whom we shall behold in his humanity at judgment, we shall also see in his divinity after judgment. Or certainly he is said to serve while passing among them because he will cause his own to pass happily onward, when he raises them from the contemplation of his humanity to the vision of divine brightness.

And if he comes in the second watch, or if he comes in the third watch, and finds them so, blessed are those servants.

He calls them watches by comparison with those keeping night-watch, because in the night of this age we must always be vigilant against enemies and await the Judge, ready at every age to bestow everlasting light. The first watch, therefore, is the earliest period, that is, childhood; the second is adolescence or youth, which sacred Scripture treats as one, saying: “Rejoice, young man, in your adolescence” (Eccl. XI). The third watch is old age, in which at least in old age a person who did not awake to the ways of life in the first and second stages may come to his senses.

L. 228[II] M. 267 R. 154

He said therefore: A certain nobleman went into a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself and to return.

[Col. 0485C] [BEDE.] The nobleman is Christ. The distant country is the Church from the Gentiles, concerning which the Father says to him: “But I have been established by him as king”; “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. II). This inheritance or possession is called a distant country in two ways: either because it cries to the Lord from the ends of the earth, or because “salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. CXVIII). Though the Lord is everywhere, he is nevertheless far from idolaters; but those who were far off “have been made near in the blood of Christ” (Eph. II). For Christ went away from the blinded Jews to enlighten the Gentiles, and will return at the end, when all Israel will be saved (Rom. XI).

[Col. 0485D] L. 299[V] M. 270

And having called ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas.

The number ten pertains to the Law because of the Decalogue. Thus the master of the house calls ten servants, because he chose disciples instructed in the letter of the Law. He gives them ten minas because he reveals that the sayings of the Law are to be understood spiritually. For after his resurrection he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke XXIV). A mina, according to the Greeks, weighs one hundred drachmas; and the discourse of Scripture, because it suggests the perfection of heavenly life, shines, as it were, with the weight of a hundred.

And he said to them: “Conduct business until I come.”

Offer to the peoples the mysteries of the prophets and the Law, and receive from them confession of faith and uprightness of conduct, according to the psalmist: “Take,” he says, “the psalm and give the timbrel” (Ps. LXXX). That is, receive the praise of preaching in the heart, and bring the devotion of works to the chastening of the flesh. The timbrel is skin stretched upon wood, and signifies that our flesh must be afflicted after the example of the Lord’s cross.

But his citizens hated him and sent an embassy after him, saying: “We do not want this man to reign over us.”

By his citizens he means the Jews, concerning whom he testifies elsewhere: “Now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father” (John XV). They not only hated him in his presence, even to the death of the cross, but after his resurrection they sent persecution against the apostles and despised the preaching of the kingdom of heaven.

And it came to pass, when he returned after receiving the kingdom, that he ordered the servants to whom he had given the money to be called, so that he might know how much each had gained by trading.

When he says “when he returned,” he signifies his second coming. “So that he might know,” he says—that is, so that he might make all know; for then the works and thoughts of all will be openly displayed to all.

Then the first came, saying: “Lord, your mina has gained ten minas.”

The first servant is the order of teachers sent to the circumcision, who received one mina—that is, one God, one faith, one baptism. This mina gained ten minas because it joined to itself the people under the Law.

[Col. 0486C] And he said to him: “Well done, good servant; because you have been faithful in a little thing, you shall have authority over ten cities.”

Little is whatever we receive in the present life, in comparison with things to come. “For we know in part and prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away” (I Cor. XIII). The ten cities are souls arriving through the words of the Law at the grace of the Gospel.
