Yet the one who has worthily commended to God the money of the word among them will be set over them in glory. Hence the Apostle says: “What is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you before the Lord Jesus?” (I Thess. II).

Then another came, saying: “Lord, your mina has made five minas.”

[Col. 0486D] The other servant is the body of those sent to evangelize the uncircumcised, whose mina made five minas because it converted the Gentiles, formerly enslaved to the five senses, to the grace of evangelical faith.

And he said to this one: “And you, be over five cities.”

That is, shine through the faith of the souls with which you have imbued them, and be honored for their progress, in whom you changed the five senses from works of darkness to works of light. Hence Isaiah says: “On that day there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Canaan” (Isa. XIX), that is, with their language changed.

Then another came, saying: “Lord, behold your mina, which I kept laid away in a cloth. For I was afraid of you, because you are an austere man: you take what you did not put down and reap what you did not sow.”

[Col. 0487A] The third servant consists of those who, after Jews and Gentiles have been gathered, negligently use the office of preaching committed to them. They bind the mina in a cloth who, by living softly and delicately, weaken the teaching entrusted to them. Everyone stores money away in a cloth who, though fit to preach, either refuses to undertake the office of preaching or does not perform well the office he has undertaken, but hides gifts received in the idle torpor of repose, saying to himself: “It is enough for me to render an account for myself. What need is there to preach to others and render an account for them?” Before God even those to whom the Law was not given are without excuse (Rom. I), since through creation they can know the Creator. This is like reaping where he did not sow: holding even those guilty of impiety to whom he did not minister the word of Law or Gospel. It is the same thing according to Matthew, “you gather where you did not scatter,” and according to Luke, “you take what you did not put down.” The sense is: you take and gather all things to such an extent that you receive even the fruit of good life, by nature, from those to whom you did not give preachers. And as you receive all good things, so you punish all evil things. This seems to me great harshness and savage austerity. Therefore, fearing the graver danger of judgment, I did not preach what I understood through your gift. Because this servant speaks foolishly, he is judged from his own mouth.

He said to him: “Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant.”

Truly wicked, because he is slothful in exercising his office and proud in accusing the Lord’s judgment.

[Col. 0487C] “You knew that I am an austere man, taking what I did not put down and reaping what I did not sow. Why then did you not give my money to the bank, so that when I came I would certainly have demanded it with interest?”

If you knew me to be so cruel and hard, why did this thought not strike fear into you, so that you might know I would seek my own more diligently? He distributes Christ’s money to the table—which is understood as the minds of believers—who worthily makes evangelical preaching known to God in the ready and prepared hearts of the faithful. Hence the Apostle says: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the utterances of God” (I Pet. IV). But one who buys the money of the Word from a teacher by believing must repay it with interest by acting. Or, one repays interest upon the loan of the Word received when, from what he hears, he also strives to understand further things.

[Col. 0487D] And he said to those standing by: “Take the mina from him, and give it to him who has ten minas.” And they said to him: “Lord, he has ten minas.”

Those standing by are understood to be angels, through whom the Lord punishes the wicked and rewards the good. He rightly loses grace bestowed who neglects to share it with others by preaching. Thus Saul lost the royal anointing through pride, which David earned through obedience, as it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and was directed upon David from that day forward” (I Kings XVI). Mystically, when all Israel is saved, then the whole fullness of spiritual grace, which we now exercise sluggishly, will be bestowed abundantly upon the teachers of that time.

[Col. 0488A] L. 236[II] M. 271 R. 42

But I say to you that to everyone who has, it shall be given; but from him who does not have, even what he has shall be taken away.

[BEDE.] “From him” is repeated here either because of the intervening words or to emphasize the taking away. To one who has love of the Word, understanding will also be given. Otherwise, he will enjoy none of the sweetness of true wisdom, even if he seems to himself shrewd by natural ability or literary study. [HILARY.] Otherwise: to one who has the use of the Gospel, the honor of the Law is also restored. But from one who does not have faith in Christ, even the honor from the Law which he seemed to possess will be taken away. Otherwise: to one who makes good use of God’s gift, grace will be increased. But from one who does not make good use of God’s gift, even what he has will be taken away. [BEDE.] It should be noted that the examination of the returning Lord is even now celebrated in part, because of the change of grace which is given to one and taken from another; but at the general judgment it will be fulfilled universally. For daily he beholds the state of the Church and lends money to traders. He prudently grants greater grace to one who labors, and deprives one pursuing idleness of what he had given.

L. 231[V] M. 272

Nevertheless, bring here those enemies of mine who did not want me to reign over them, and kill them before me.

[Col. 0488C] This signifies that, on the day of judgment, the iniquity of all the reprobate who refuse to be converted to Christ—who prefer either never to hear the word of faith or to corrupt it by interpreting it wrongly—will be punished. By the two faithful servants are meant the teachers of the two peoples; by the ten and five minas, believing peoples; by the wicked servant, evil Catholics; and by the reaping of the field not sown, even those who never happened to hear the word of God. In these five persons every kind of human being to be examined on the day of judgment is represented.

## CHAPTER CLI

M. 251[X]

But when the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty.

[REMIGIUS.] That is, he will reign over the Church, in which his omnipotence will then appear. He who appeared to be judged in the humility of a servant will come to judge in the majesty of divinity. Thus, since he was soon to be handed over to the cross, he rightly sets forth beforehand the glory of the conqueror. Angels will come in his service as witnesses of human actions.

And all nations shall be gathered before him, and he shall separate them from one another as a shepherd separates sheep from goats; and he shall set the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left.

Those who loved eternal things will be established at the right hand of eternal blessedness; but those who desired present things, at the left hand of eternal misery. For even God’s transitory gifts are called things of the left in comparison with eternal things; eternal things, being more excellent, are at the right. Hence: “The heart of the wise man is at his right hand, and the heart of the fool at his left” (Eccl. X). He calls sinners goats because goats were offered for sin. He does not say female goats, which can bear young, but uses an animal that is wanton, unruly, and always ardent for mating.

Then the King will say to those at his right: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

The King of kings will speak without the sound of words—that is, he will reveal consciences and merits. Thus he will speak through the bestowal of glory: “Come, blessed ones, advanced by the favor of my Father to obtain the kingdom of life, predestined for you from the foundation of the world.”

For I was hungry and you gave me food; thirsty and you gave me drink; a stranger and you took me in; naked and you clothed me; sick and you visited me; in prison and you came to me.

The works of mercy concerning bodily miseries are clear. But in respect to souls: refresh one hungering and thirsting for righteousness with the bread of God’s word, or cool him with the drink of wisdom. Recall the erring person to the house of mother Church; adorn with virtues one naked of good works; strengthen one sick in faith. Help one oppressed by any tribulation or by the prison of sorrow, by compassion or consolation in true love.

Then the righteous will answer him, saying: “Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink? And when did we see you a stranger and take you in, or naked and clothe you? Or when did we see you sick or in prison and come to you?”

Thus they will answer in their consciences, not doubting the Lord’s words, but either amazed at the magnitude of the King’s majesty or because every good thing they did appears small to them in comparison with the reward. Hence the Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII).

[Col. 0489D] And the King will answer and say to them: “Amen I say to you: insofar as you did it to one of these least brothers of mine, you did it to me.”

He does not seem to have said this generally concerning the poor, but concerning those who are poor in spirit. For elsewhere he says: “My brothers are those who do the will of my Father” (Matt. XII).

Then he will say also to those at the left: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.”

While the evil are mingled with the good, they seem to be with God; but at last they will be sent into the fire prepared for them from the foundation of the world, and “the wicked shall not see the glory of God.”

For I was hungry and you did not give me food; thirsty and you did not give me drink; a stranger and you did not take me in; naked and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me.

[AUGUSTINE.] Christ is the head of the Church; the Church is his body. In our body the head is above and the feet are on the ground. In a crowd of people, when someone steps on your foot, does not the head say, “You are stepping on me”? Thus Christ the head, whom no one steps upon, will say: “I was hungry and you did not give me food,” and so forth.

Then they too will answer, saying: “Lord, when did we see you hungry, thirsty, a stranger, naked, sick, or in prison, and not minister to you?”

They will strive to excuse themselves from the habit by which they used to deceive people; but those who would not turn from evil and do good have no excuse.

[Col. 0490B] Then he will answer them, saying: “Amen I say to you: insofar as you did not do it to one of these least ones, neither did you do it to me.” And these shall go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.

[REMIGIUS.] What does one deserve who takes what belongs to another, if one who did not give from his own is eternally condemned? “Judgment without mercy shall be given to him who did not show mercy” (Jas. II). Note that, at judgment, there is one order of the perfect who judge with God and are not judged. Of them the Lord says: “You also shall sit upon twelve thrones” (Matt. XIX). Another order judges the reprobate even by its example, and is judged when it is told: “I was hungry, and you gave me food.” But the evil who are within the Church certainly do not judge, but are judged, when they are told: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food.” But concerning those who are found outside the Church, the Psalmist says: “The wicked do not rise in judgment” (Ps. I), either to judge or to be judged. The wicked person is punished by a twofold sentence: either here he is struck with blindness of mind for his merits, so that he may not see truth; or at the end he is condemned to pay the punishments due.

Let us set forth what the holy Fathers thought about the fire of eternal punishment. From the *Book of Prognostics*, from sayings of Augustine: “What kind of fire it will be, and in what part of the world or of created things it will exist, I think no human being knows, unless perhaps the divine Spirit has revealed it to someone.” From the same: “The fire of Gehenna is one, but it does not torment all sinners in one manner. Each person there will experience punishment to the extent required by his guilt. For just as in this world all do not feel the heat of the sun equally, so there is not one manner of burning in that one fire; rather, it burns sinners differently.” Augustine, *City of God*, Book XXI: “It must by no means be denied that the eternal fire will be lighter for some and heavier for others according to the diversity of merits—whether its heat itself is varied according to the punishment deserved by each, or whether it burns equally but is not felt with equal distress.” Gregory, Book XV on Job: “In a most wonderful way, the fire of Gehenna is bodily; it is nourished by no wood, needs no kindling, and was created by God from the very origin of the world as unquenchable.” The same, Book VIII on Job: “The avenging flame has the burning of vices, but it has no light. That fire does not shine for consolation; yet, in order to torment more severely, it shines in some respect. For the reprobate will see themselves in hell, that they may grieve more; for the rich man also saw Lazarus in Abraham’s bosom” (Luke XVI). From the *Book of Prognostics*: “As blessed Augustine says, the substance of the lower world is incorporeal. Therefore it is rightly asked why the lower regions are said to be beneath the earth, if they are not bodily places; or why they are called ‘lower,’ if they are not beneath the earth.” But the same doctor says: “They are said or believed to be beneath the earth because they are suitably shown in the spirit through those likenesses of bodily things. Since souls of the dead worthy of the lower regions sinned through love of the flesh, they are presented with those likenesses of bodily things by which bodies, once dead, are usually buried beneath the earth.”

Some infer from this statement of Augustine that wherever a sinner may be, there the elements will torment him, both in his body and from adjacent places. For it is probable that a soul which voluntarily takes from the flesh an incentive to sin should unwillingly receive from the same flesh an incentive to torment. And because those punishments will be exceedingly sharp and everlasting, they are not improperly called eternal fire. They are rightly said also to be infernal and beneath the earth, because wretched souls will incur them through the fall of earthly pleasure. Augustine, *City of God*, Book XI, chapter XXXI: “Why should we not say that, although in wonderful yet true ways, even incorporeal spirits can be afflicted by the bodily punishment of fire? The same incorporeal fire will torment demons and human beings.” Jerome, to Heliodorus, on the Epistle to the Ephesians: “No one doubts that hell is beneath the earth.”

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0491]

## CHAPTERS CLII–CLIII

[Col. 0491B]

And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished all these sayings, that he said to his disciples:

M. 274[I] R. 156 L. 269 A. 66

You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.

[Col. 0491C] Having completed in word and deed all the discourses from the beginning of the Gospel—or, having completed these teachings concerning the Lord’s second coming, in which he foretold that he would come in glory—he showed that he would suffer, to remind us that the mystery of the cross is joined to the glory of eternity. Let those be ashamed who think that the Savior said, out of fear of his passion, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI). For he foreknew that he would be handed over and did not flee in terror. After two days—that is, after two days—the Jews were to celebrate their Passover, namely on the fourteenth moon after the equinox. There is indeed this difference between the old Passover and unleavened bread: Passover is the name of the single day on which the lamb was killed toward evening, that is, on the fourteenth moon of the first month; but on the fifteenth moon, when that people went out from Egypt, the feast of unleavened bread followed. Its solemn observance was appointed for seven days, that is, until evening of the twenty-first day of the same month. Yet the writing of the Gospel customarily uses “Passover” without distinction, both for the day of unleavened bread and for the days of unleavened bread; hence Luke says, “the feast day of unleavened bread which is called Passover.” Likewise John, when the events took place on the first day of unleavened bread—that is, the fifteenth moon—says: “They themselves did not enter the praetorium, lest they should be defiled, but that they might eat the Passover” (John XVIII), because the Passover day was also commanded to be celebrated with unleavened bread. For after the lamb was sacrificed in the evening on one day, seven successive days of unleavened bread follow, because Jesus suffered once for us and commanded that, throughout all the time represented by the seven days, life should be lived in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

M. 275[VI] R. 157

Then the chief priests and elders of the people gathered in the court of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas, and took counsel how they might seize Jesus by deceit and kill him. But they said: “Not on the feast day, lest perhaps a disturbance arise among the people.”

[JEROME.] Those who ought to have been preparing victims for the approaching Passover, whitewashing the Temple walls, sweeping the pavements, and cleansing the vessels, enter into counsel about how to kill the Lord. They did not wish to agree to his death on the feast day, although they nevertheless did so, lest the people who loved him should rise against them and defend the innocent man.

M. 278[VI] R. 160 L. 264
Then one of the twelve, called Judas Iscariot, went away and spoke to the chief priests and officers, saying to them: “What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you?” [Col. 0492D] When they heard this, they rejoiced and agreed upon thirty pieces of silver for him. From then on he sought an opportunity to hand him over without a crowd.

[REMIGIUS.] Judas was one of the twelve by number, not by merit; in body, not in mind. He was neither invited by the rulers nor compelled by any necessity, but of his own accord entered into the counsel of his wicked mind. Nor, in selling his master, did he demand a fixed price for so precious a thing; rather, as though handing over a worthless slave, he left the matter to the purchasers’ discretion. [BEDE.] Many today shudder at Judas’s crime, yet do not beware of it. For when, in return for gifts, they give false testimony, they surely sell the Lord for money by denying the truth; when they defile the fellowship [Col. 0493A] of brotherhood with the plague of discord, they betray the Lord. And just as John the Baptist suffered martyrdom for truth, and therefore for Christ, who is Truth, so conversely whoever scorns the claims of truth certainly betrays Christ. It should be known that Joseph, contrary to what many suppose, was sold not for twenty gold pieces according to the Septuagint translators, but for twenty silver pieces according to the Hebrew truth (Gen. XXXVII). For the servant could not be more valuable than his master.

## CHAPTER CLIV

A. 112[X]

Before the feast day of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, [Col. 0493B] having loved his own who were in the world, loved them unto the end.

Passover is called “passing over,” because the Lord passed through Egypt, striking its firstborn and delivering the children of Israel, and because the children of Israel passed that night out of Egyptian bondage (Exod. XII). This signifies the Lord’s passage from this world to the Father, and that of his faithful from temporal things to heavenly ones. “He loved them unto the end,” that is, unto himself. For, as the Apostle says, “Christ is the end of the law” (Rom. X). [AUGUSTINE.] He is the end to which we go, not the end in which we perish. Or, “unto the end,” that is, unto death: not because Christ’s love ends in death, but because he loved so greatly that love led him even to death. In this [Col. 0493C] he gave an example, that all should remain in God’s truth until the end.

A. 115[X]

He rises from supper and lays aside his garments. And when he had taken a towel, he girded himself. Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded.

In his great humility he did not disdain to wash even the feet of him whose hands he already foresaw to be engaged in wickedness. What wonder that he laid aside his garments, who, being in the form of God, emptied himself? (Phil. II.) What wonder that he girded himself with a towel, who, taking the form of a servant, was found in appearance as a man? (ibid.) What wonder that he poured water into a basin, to wash [Col. 0493D] the disciples’ feet, who poured his blood upon the earth in order to wash away the defilement of sins? What wonder that with the towel with which he was girded he wiped the feet he had washed, who by the flesh with which he was clothed made firm the footsteps of the evangelists?

Therefore he came to Simon Peter, and Peter said to him: “Lord, do you wash my feet?”

It should not be understood that he came to Peter after some others; rather, the washing began with him. Thus the first of the apostles is astonished that God should wash a man’s feet.

Jesus answered and said to him: “What I am doing, you do not understand now; but you will understand afterward.” Peter said to him: “You shall never wash my feet.”

That is, “You shall never wash them.” As the Lord is humble in serving, so the servant is humble in declining the service.

Jesus answered him: “Unless I wash you, you will have no part with me.”

By “you” he speaks with reference to the feet alone. Whoever is not washed through baptism and the confession of repentance has no part with Jesus.

Simon Peter said to him: “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head.”

Frightened by the Lord’s answer concerning the danger to salvation, he offers his whole self to be washed, troubled by love and fear.

Jesus said to him: “He who has been washed needs only to wash his feet, but is wholly clean.”

This must be understood as excepting the feet. The whole person is washed in baptism; yet, when one afterward lives amid human affairs, human affections—without which life is impossible—are, as it were, feet. For if we say that we have no sin, we lie (John I). Therefore he daily washes our feet, who daily intercedes for us. Hence we also say daily: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. VI). And in the Song of Songs: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song V.) Let those fear to defile their feet who, under the creeping influence of love for human praise, seek to please people. It should be noted that Peter erred, lest we should err when he offered his whole self to God to be washed. God corrected him, showing that one who has been baptized once is not to be baptized again.

“And you are clean, but not all.” For he knew [Col. 0494C] who it was that would hand him over; therefore he said, “You are not all clean.” So, after he had washed their feet, he took his garments; and when he had reclined again, he said to them: “Do you know what I have done for you?”

[BEDE.] Now he wishes to disclose what he had said to Peter: “You will understand afterward.” Mystically, the supper at which the Lord reclined with his disciples signifies the entire period in which he dwelt bodily in the Church, fed all the faithful with the feast of the saving word and the sweetness of miracles, and was himself fed by the faith and love of his hearers. Therefore he rose from supper and laid aside his garments when he laid down the members of his body upon the cross. He girded himself with a towel when he surrounded his members with the labor of the Passion. For [Col. 0494D] the towel, which is made by varied labor, is customarily a figure of the affliction of the Passion. “He poured water into a basin,” and so forth. Dying upon the cross, he poured forth water together with blood from his side, by which he deigned to cleanse and sanctify believers. After he had washed their feet, he took his garments and reclined, revealing to them the mystery of the washing; for after, by suffering on the cross, he had consecrated for us the washing of forgiveness, he received limbs now immortal and, after the resurrection, explained to them the benefit of his Passion.

A. 116[III] M. 59 L. 36

“You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly; for I am.”

[Col. 0495A] A. 117[X]

“If then I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.”

This ought to be fulfilled both literally and in a mystical sense. Literally, we should serve one another through charity, not only by washing the brethren’s feet but by helping in every need. In its mystical meaning, as he forgives us our sins when we repent, so we should forgive our brethren. And as he washed us from sins by interceding with the Father for us, so we should pray for our brethren.

“For I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you also should do.”

[AUGUSTINE.] This, Peter, was what you did not know when you would not permit your feet to be [Col. 0495B] washed. The Lord promised that you would know it afterward. It is customary among many, when they receive one another as guests, to wash one another’s feet. Where this practice is not observed among the saints, they do it in their hearts; but it is better that what Christ did should also be done with the hands. In this we are admonished that, having confessed our sins to one another, we should pray for one another, just as Christ intercedes for us.

A. 118[III] M. 90 L. 50

“Truly, truly, I say to you: a servant is not greater than his lord, nor an apostle greater than the one who sent him. If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.”

He does not mean that Judas will be blessed together with the others by doing what the Lord himself did and taught. This is what follows.

A. 119[X]

“I do not speak of all of you. I know whom I have chosen. But this is so that the Scripture may be fulfilled: ‘He who eats bread with me shall lift up his heel against me.’”

Judas lifted his heel against him; that is, he trampled him as far as he could. But another translation of the psalm reads: “The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my breads, magnified treachery against me” (Ps. XL). The Lord chose Judas indeed for that which was done through him for the salvation of others; but he chose the eleven for himself as followers, that they might be blessed. Hence elsewhere: “I chose you twelve, and one is a devil” (John VI).

[Col. 0495D] “From now on I tell you before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe that I am.”

As though he said: “Until now I have endured and kept silent; but now I identify the betrayer before what he is shortly to do occurs, so that afterward you may believe that I am he of whom that Scripture foretold.” Therefore, after teaching the apostles by his example humility and the suffering of the heel, he adds the honor by which to console them: that he and the Father will be received in them.

A. 120[I] M. 98 R. 96 L. 116

“Truly, truly, I say to you: whoever receives anyone whom I send receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.”

In these words, the unity of nature of the one sent and the sender is not being asserted; rather, the sender’s authority in the one sent is commended. Therefore let each receive the one sent in such a way as to regard the sender in him: Christ in Peter—that is, the lord in the servant—and the Father in Christ—that is, the begetter in the only-begotten Son.

+ It must be observed carefully that at this point the order of this work both teaches and corrects Greeks and Latins alike. The Greeks seem to hold a more correct view than the Latins, in accordance with John’s Gospel: that the aforementioned supper, with the washing of the feet, took place before the feast day of Passover, while leavened bread was still being eaten. But they err in saying that on that occasion the Lord ate the paschal lamb beforehand with his disciples and then instituted the sacraments of his flesh and blood, and that for this reason they sacrifice with leavened bread. They further add that the Lord was crucified at noon on the actual day [Col. 0496B] of Passover; and, to support this, they cite the fact that the Jews did not wish to enter the praetorium—that is, Pilate’s house—lest they be defiled, but might eat the Passover, understanding “Passover” only as the eating of the lamb. Since, therefore, they are plainly opposed to the three evangelists, they shamelessly say that John corrected them on this point. But it is agreed that all spoke by the same Spirit; and if they erred in one matter, they would be believed less in the others.

+ It must be considered carefully whether the aforementioned supper was the same as that recalled a little later: if so, how was it held before the feast day of Passover? But it has been stated above that “Passover” is used both for the Day of Unleavened Bread and for the days of unleavened bread, of which the first and last were observed with greater solemnity. Hence John says, “Before the feast day of Passover,” [Col. 0496C] calling Passover the first day of the ensuing solemnity, namely Friday. The Greeks, however, call not the day on whose evening the fourteenth moon appeared, but only the following day, the day of Passover and of the lamb’s immolation. They say that on Thursday the Lord ate the paschal lamb beforehand with his disciples and then instituted the sacraments of his flesh and blood, while leavened bread was still being eaten; and for this reason they sacrifice with leavened bread. Thus they say that the Lord, etc.

## CHAPTER CLV

M. 278[I,] R. 160 L. 263

On the first day of unleavened bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying: “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?”

[BEDE.] “We have no dwelling; we have no tent.” Let those hear this who are concerned with constructing marble houses and golden ceilings. Let them recognize that the Lord of all had no place where he might recline. Here the first day of unleavened bread is called the fourteenth day of the first month, when, after leaven had been removed, the Passover—that is, the lamb—was slain toward evening. Explaining this, the Apostle says: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V). Though he was crucified on the following day, that is, on the fifteenth moon, nevertheless on this night, when the lamb was slain, he delivered to his disciples the mysteries of his flesh and blood to be celebrated; and, seized and bound by the Jews, he consecrated the beginning of that very immolation—that is, of his Passion.

[Col. 0497A] But Jesus said: “Go into the city, and as you enter, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house which he enters, to a certain man, and say to the master of the house: ‘The Teacher says: My time is near; with you I keep the Passover with my disciples.’ And he will show you a large furnished upper room; prepare it for us there.” And his disciples went and found it as he had told them, and prepared the Passover.

[AMBROSE.] As God, foreknowing all things, he speaks with his disciples about matters taking place elsewhere. [JEROME; BEDE.] Mystically, the city is the Church, surrounded by the wall of faith. The man who meets them is the original people. The jar of water is the law of the letter. Or thus: while they are preparing the Passover, a man carrying a jar of water meets them, [Col. 0497B] to show that the mystery of the Lord’s Passover is to be celebrated for the cleansing of the world. Water signifies the washing of grace; the jar, the measure of virtues, or the full measure of the time fulfilled, at which it was fitting for this to be done. Alternatively, the jar signifies the frailty of those through whom this grace was to be administered. Hence: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (I Cor. IV). The names of both the water-carrier and the master of the house are deliberately left unspoken, in order to signify that all who desire to celebrate the true Passover—that is, to be imbued with Christ’s sacraments and to receive him through the devotion of their minds—are to be given opportunity to do so. The large upper room is the spiritual law, which, rising out of the narrowness of the letter, receives the Savior in a high place. For one who still observes the killing letter and understands nothing in the lamb but an animal plainly celebrates Passover below. But one who follows the water-carrier—that is, the herald of grace—into the house of the Church prepares through the life-giving Spirit a dwelling for Christ in the height of the mind. [Col. 0497C] [JEROME.] “Therefore,” he says, “follow him who leads upward, where Christ is refreshed with his disciples by the delight of exalted virtues.” Hence Rahab orders the spies not to go by the low places but by the heights (Josh. II). Further: the upper room is the great Church, which declares the Lord’s name, spread out with the diversity of virtues and tongues; whence that saying: “Clothed round with variety” (Ps. XLIV). In it the Passover is prepared for the Lord. The master of the house is the apostle Peter, to whom the Lord entrusted his house, so that there might be one faith under one shepherd. [AUGUSTINE.] Whereas Mark says a flask and Luke an amphora, one indicates the kind of vessel and the other its capacity.

M. 279[III] R. 161 L. 121

When evening had come, he came and reclined with his twelve disciples.

Judas does everything so as to remove suspicion that he is the betrayer; for he reclines with the other disciples. The evening of the day signifies the evening of the world; for those who come about the eleventh hour are the last, yet receive first the denarius of eternal life (Matt. XX). Before the cross Abraham was in hell, and after the cross the thief was in paradise. [AUGUSTINE.] Alternatively: it was evening when the true Sun was hastening to his setting, saying: [Col. 0498A] “My time is near, when I shall go from the world to the Father.” He reclined with the disciples because he was preparing eternal life for them.

And while they were eating, he said:

L. 264[X]

“I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.”

[BEDE.] He desires to eat the typical Passover, and thus to declare the mysteries of his Passion, so that he may both show himself to approve the legal Passover and henceforth forbid its carnal observance, teaching that it was a figure of the true Passover. As a figure of this, manna ceased after the children of Israel ate of the fruits of the land and no longer used that food (Josh. V).

[Col. 0498B] L. 213[II] M. 286 R. 166

“For I say to you that from now on I shall not eat it, until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.”

[BEDE.] That is: “I shall celebrate the Mosaic Passover no more, until it is fulfilled in the Church, which is the kingdom of God, as spiritually understood.” In this kingdom the Lord today eats the Passover, because he himself spiritually performs in his members what Moses commanded a rough people to observe carnally.

A. 121[III] M. 289 M. 156

When he had said these things, he was troubled in spirit, and testified and said: “Truly, truly, I say to you, that one of you will hand me over.”

[Col. 0498C] He testifies, that is, he foretells the hidden crime, so that the betrayer, seeing that he cannot remain concealed, may repent of his act. Yet he does not identify him by name, lest, openly rebuked, he become more shameless. He therefore places the accusation among the number, that the guilty man may repent. The Lord was troubled by his own power, taking upon himself the affection of our weakness. [AUGUSTINE.] Therefore when we are troubled, let us not despair. Let the arguments of the philosophers perish, who deny that disturbances of the soul can occur in a wise person. The Christian soul is troubled not by misery but by mercy. For the Lord’s being troubled in spirit signifies that spiritual persons are to be troubled in charity when an urgent cause compels the separation of tares from wheat before the harvest.

[Col. 0498D] R. 162 M. 288 L. 269 A. 122

Then they began to be grieved and to say individually: “Surely it is not I, Lord?”

The eleven apostles knew that they had entertained no such thought, but they trusted their teacher more than themselves; and, fearing their own frailty, sorrowfully inquire concerning a sin of which they have no consciousness.

R. 163 M. 281 L. 268

He said to them: “He who dips his hand with me in the dish, he will hand me over.”

While the others were saddened, withdrew their hands, and forbade food to their mouths, Judas, with the very shamelessness by which he was going to betray his master, put his hand into the dish, so that through boldness he might feign a good conscience. [Col. 0499A] It should be noted that all twelve took food with the Lord from the same dish, sitting around it in the furnished upper room, reclining almost as though lying down, according to ancient custom. Otherwise the betrayer would have been expressly identified by the dipping of his hand, if none of the others had extended a hand to the Lord’s food. [AUGUSTINE.] Whereas Matthew calls it a *paropsis* [dish] and Mark a *catinus* [bowl], one indicates the vessel’s square form and the other that it was earthenware.

“The Son of Man indeed goes, as it is written of him.”

M. 153[V] R. 164

“But woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is handed over.”

[Col. 0499B] [JEROME.] The punishment is foretold so that he whom shame does not overcome may be corrected by fear. [BEDE.] Even today, woe to one who approaches the most holy altars wickedly and with a heart defiled by some crime.

“It would have been good for that man if he had not been born.”

If he had died in his mother’s womb and had not been born alive, in comparison with the evil he afterward incurred, that would have been good for him. [JEROME.] Thus the Pontic Sea is said to be sweeter than the other seas, that is, less bitter. Or it is said in the ordinary and simple sense that it is far better not to exist than to exist badly, as if one said of some utterly wicked person: “It would have been better for him if he had never existed.”

A. 122[I] M. 280 R. 162 L. 269

Therefore the disciples looked at one another, uncertain [Col. 0499C] of whom he was speaking.

L. 269[I] M. 280 R. 162 A. 122

And they asked among themselves which of them it was who would do this.

A. 123[X]

Now one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining in Jesus’ bosom.

[AUGUSTINE.] What he means by “in his bosom” he says shortly afterward, when he speaks of reclining upon Jesus’ breast. This is John, whom Jesus loved—not more than all others, but more familiarly—as a young man, as a kinsman, as a virgin; in him he set forth the pattern of contemplatives. [AUGUSTINE.] For it was the custom for a writer of events, when he came to speak of himself, to speak as though of another person. By the bosom is signified the secret place from which he drank the sacrament of divinity.

Simon Peter therefore signaled to him and said to him: “Who is it of whom he speaks?” So, as he reclined upon Jesus’ breast, he said to him: “Lord, who is it?” Jesus answered: “It is he to whom I shall give the dipped bread.”

Peter questions John not with words but with a bodily signal; John questions the Lord in the intimacy of counsel, and the Lord identifies the betrayer to him in a low voice.

A. 124[IX] L. 262

And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas, son of Simon Iscariot. And after the morsel Satan then entered into him.

[Col. 0500A] By the dipped morsel the Lord points out his betrayer, perhaps signifying through the dipping of bread that man’s hypocrisy. For not everything dipped is washed; some things are dipped in order to be dyed or stained. But if this dipping signifies some good, condemnation rightly followed upon his ingratitude toward that good. Note that Satan had entered Judas’s heart when he made an agreement with the Jews for the price of the Lord’s blood, as Luke says. He came, then, to supper with the devil in his thought; after the bread, however, Satan entered into him, not in order to tempt another, but in order to possess one who was his own. [AUGUSTINE.] For he enters the heart by introducing wicked persuasions into the thoughts of the wicked. But now we must understand Judas to have been more fully possessed by the devil, just as the apostles, [Col. 0500B] who after the resurrection had already received the Holy Spirit when the Lord breathed upon them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX), afterward received him more fully on the day of Pentecost (Acts II).

A. 125[X]

Jesus said to him: “What you are doing, do quickly.”

[HILARY.] He did not command the crime, but foretold it, giving power over himself, so that, because the crime of the will is reckoned as an act, envy might accomplish in deed what it had already done in will. The Lord hastens toward the good of the faithful’s salvation, which Judas brings about, though not for himself. Many indeed do good as Judas did, but it profits them nothing.

But none of those reclining knew why he had said this to him. For some supposed, because Judas had the money-box, [Col. 0500C] that Jesus was telling him: “Buy what we need for the feast day,” or “Give something to the needy.”

[AUGUSTINE.] The Lord had a money-box, preserving the offerings of his faithful for their needs. At that point the pattern for ecclesiastical funds was established, that we might understand that the command not to be anxious about tomorrow was not given in order that the saints should keep no money at all, but that one should not serve God for the sake of money or abandon justice through fear of poverty.

M. 284[X]

Judas, who handed him over, answered and said: “Surely it is not I, Rabbi?”

[Col. 0500D] [AUGUSTINE.] Lest his silence seem to expose him, he asks as the others did. In calling him “Rabbi,” he adds the manner of one who flatters, and calls him teacher as though to excuse the betrayal.

He said to him: “You have said it.”

Something may be said by thinking it, according to the phrase: “They said among themselves.” It is therefore clear that Judas said in his heart, and held it settled, that he was the betrayer. Thus he is confuted when he hears, “You have said it”; yet he is not openly disclosed to the others. For this can be understood as though the Lord were saying: “I have not said it.”

A. 125[X]

Therefore, when he had received the morsel, he went out immediately. And it was night.

[Col. 0501A] [AUGUSTINE.] Because he made evil use of a good thing, this presumption increased his sins, so that he openly departed from the Lord. The night also suits the mystery: for he who went out was a son of darkness, doing works of darkness.

Therefore, when he had gone out, Jesus said: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him. If God has been glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and will glorify him immediately.”

When Judas, on whose account it had been said, “You are not all clean,” had gone out, only the clean remained with their cleanser. In this was signified Christ’s glorification, in which, after the wicked have been separated, he will remain eternally with the saints. For when the world passes away, no unclean person will remain among Christ’s people. And because things signifying are spoken of as though they were the things signified—as the rock is not said merely to signify Christ, but “was Christ”—so he does not say, “Now the glorification has been signified,” but “The Son of Man has been glorified”; that is, God has been glorified in him, because this is the glorification of the Son of Man. Explaining this, as it were, he adds: “If God has been glorified in him,” because he came not to do his own will but the Father’s; and God will glorify him in himself, in God, and this glorification will occur immediately. For immediately after death human nature will rise in immortal eternity, in which it will appear that he has God in himself, who will raise it. Or, because things about to occur are reckoned as already done, it may also be understood thus: “Behold, the betrayer brings in the merchants of death, the scourges, the cross; but this is the glory of the victor.” Now the Son of Man will be glorified, because the saints who await in darkness will see [Col. 0501C] God, through the ministry of his soul as soon as he expires. This is what he means by saying that God is glorified in him. If God will be glorified in him—that is, in his members, as has been explained—it follows that God will also glorify him in himself and glorify him immediately, so that his immortal resurrection, unlike that of others, may not be delayed.

## CHAPTER CLVI

M. 284[I] R. 165 L. 266 A. 67

While they were at supper, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: “Take and eat. This is my body, which is given for you.”

[JEROME.] After the typical Passover had been fulfilled [Col. 0501D] and he had eaten the lamb’s flesh with the apostles, he took bread, which strengthens the human heart, and passed over to the sacrament of the true Passover, so that, as Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God, had offered bread and wine in prefiguration of him, he also might set forth in truth the reality of his body and blood. Bede on Mark: “He blessed the bread by the grace of a certain sacrament before he broke it, because he filled with the grace of divine power the human nature which he assumed in order to suffer. He blessed and broke it because he deigned so to subject the assumed manhood to death that, through his swift resurrection, he might show that the power of divine immortality dwelt in it.” The same, on Luke: “When the solemnities of the old Passover, which were observed in remembrance of the ancient deliverance from Egypt, had been concluded, [Col. 0502A] he passed over to the new Passover, so that in place of the flesh and blood of the lamb he might show the sacrament of his own flesh and blood in bread and wine. He breaks the bread which he offers, to show that the breaking of his body would not occur without his own will. What he says to his disciples means this: ‘Receive, both in mind and body; eat, both in faith and with the mouth; preserving in your heart the price of your redemption—namely, my body, which is given for you.’”

M. 285[II] R. 166 L. 267

And taking the cup, he gave thanks, blessed it, and gave it to them, saying: “Drink from this, all of you. This is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins.”

[BEDE.] Taking the cup, he gave thanks, because the old things were to pass away and new things were to come. Certainly he gave thanks to the Father, giving us an example of glorifying God at the beginning of every good work. Or thus: taking the cup prefiguring his Passion, he gave thanks for the redemption bestowed upon the human race through it. For we have been saved by God through grace, not merits. Let each person, then, consider what he ought to do under the scourge of his own fault, since the Father’s equal bore with equanimity the scourges due to another’s fault. Hence he says: “Drink from this, all of you,” both with mouth and heart, that you may be participants in my Passion. Thus the Apostle says: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (Rom. VIII). The Lord blessed the cup with the same heavenly blessing as the bread, because [Col. 0502C] he established his Passion as the sufficient sacrifice by which the world is reconciled to God. Hence the Apostle: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI). “This,” he says, “is my blood, the confirmer of the New Testament.” But the Old Testament was dedicated with the blood of goats and calves. Therefore, because it is impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of goats (Heb. X), Christ’s blood is necessarily poured out for the forgiveness of sins. It is poured out for many because it does not cleanse all, although it would suffice to cleanse all if they attained its power through faith, love, and participation in the sacraments.

“But I say to you: I shall not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father.”

[Col. 0502D] He passes from carnal things to spiritual things. Scripture testifies that the people of Israel are called a vineyard. The Lord therefore says that he will not drink from this vineyard except in the kingdom of his Father. I think that the kingdom of the Father is the faith of believers. Hence the Apostle: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII). Observe that “Father,” not “God,” was said. Every father is father in relation to a son. Therefore, when they have believed in God the Father, and the Father has brought them to the Son, then the Lord will drink their wine and, after the likeness of Joseph, will be intoxicated with his brothers (Gen. XLIII). The sense is: “Hereafter I shall not delight in the sacrifices of the Synagogue, until it believes in my Father and in me, and in the Church faithfully offers the sacrifice of my flesh and blood.” When it has done this, then I shall drink—that is, I shall delight [Col. 0503A] with you in its renewal through the Church’s faith. Bede on Mark: “The Lord, about to suffer, says: ‘I shall no longer drink of the fruit of the vine.’ As though he plainly said: ‘I shall no longer delight in carnal ceremonies, in which the carnal lamb has its place. For the time will come, when I have risen and been raised into the glory of immortal life, that I shall share with you in the salvation of this people, reborn from the fountain of spiritual grace.’” The same, on Luke: “It may be understood simply: from the hour of supper until the time of the resurrection, he would not drink wine. For afterward he ate and drank, as the apostle Peter says: ‘We ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead’ (Acts X).” Yet it is much more fittingly understood to mean that he denies he will again taste the typical drink until, with the glory of the resurrection revealed, faith in the kingdom of God comes to the world.

L.

“Do this in remembrance of me.”

The Apostle explains this, saying: “As often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (I Cor. I). [JEROME.] He left us this final memorial, as if someone setting out on a journey were to leave some pledge with one whom he loved, so that whenever the latter saw it he could remember both the traveler’s kindnesses and friendship. If that person loved him perfectly, he could not see it without intense longing or tears. Therefore the Savior handed down this sacrament so that through it we might always remember [Col. 0503C] that he died for us. For this is why, when we receive it, priests remind us that it is Christ’s body and blood: that we may not be ungrateful for such great benefits. Bede on Luke: “Bread is understood mystically as Christ’s body, and wine as his blood. But because it is necessary both that we remain in Christ and that Christ remain in us, water is mixed with the wine of the Lord’s cup. Hence John says: ‘The waters are peoples’ (Apoc. XVII). Therefore, lest we be separated from Christ, it is not permitted to offer either water alone or wine alone, just as neither is a grain of wheat made into bread without the admixture of water. If anyone is troubled that, although the Savior gave his body and blood to the apostles after they had supped, we receive the same sacraments fasting, let him hear that it was then necessary for the typical Passover first to be completed [Col. 0503D] and then for the transition to the true Passover to occur. But now, in honor of so great a sacrament, the teachers of the Church have judged it fitting that we should first be fortified by participation in the Lord’s Passion and filled with spiritual food, and afterward refresh the body with earthly food.” [AUGUSTINE.] Luke mentions the cup beforehand, before the blessing of the bread, and afterward, by repeating it, arranges the order according to the others. In mentioning the betrayer after the cup was given, he seems to recapitulate matters previously omitted. For Hilary, in his commentary on Matthew, maintains that the betrayer departed before the Lord gave his disciples the mystery of his body and blood. For those who drank the Lord’s cup were afterward to be with him in the kingdom of the Father, of which Judas was not worthy. Moreover, when they were drinking, he said, excluding no one: “My blood will be poured out for you.” But elsewhere he made an exception, saying, “for many.” Nevertheless, since things may occur together which cannot be narrated together, the arrangement of this book offers no obstacle to those who think that the Lord distributed the sacrament of his body and blood before he identified his betrayer by the dipped morsel. Now, by the grace of so great a sacrament, which preeminently is called the Eucharist—that is, “good grace”—let us see that sacraments were instituted for instruction, humility, and exercise. Instruction consists in the mind’s being advanced through visible things to understand invisible things. It is also a great display of humility to seek salvation from God in these visible things, which are far inferior to human beings—the salvation which pride lost. Since a human being cannot exist without exercise, in order that he might be removed from evil and superfluous things [Col. 0504B] and train himself in good things, God instituted sacraments and their appointed places: so that Mass may be heard in church, the Eucharist received, and the like. A sacrament consists in things, actions, and words. Sacramental things include water, oil, and the like; actions include the immersion and breathing upon those being baptized; words include, for example, the invocation of the Holy Trinity.

And it should be noted how great a transformation occurs in sacramental things through the power of divine consecration. Before consecration they are available without distinction for ordinary uses; but the power of the divine blessing wholly transforms them for spiritual purposes. Hence, according to the ruling of the canons, when the spiritual use of baptismal water has been completed, it is poured out in a separate place; [Col. 0504C] chrism and the Eucharist are burned when old; even the timbers of a dedicated church are not allowed for lay use; and so with the rest. The unity of each sacrament must likewise be considered: for the one Church worships one God in unity of faith; by one baptism—although in different places and at different times—it is regenerated; by one confirmation it is fortified against adversities; and above all it is united to Christ by one saving victim, when the sacrament of his passion is received with the mouth for redemption and is also contemplated with an attentive mind for imitation. Thus we anoint body and soul with Christ’s blood, because the blood of the lamb upon both doorposts of the house delivered the Hebrews from the destroying angel (Exod. 12).

Therefore in the sacrament of the altar one must carefully consider [Col. 0504D] its institution, the cause of its institution, the sacrament, the reality of the sacrament, the manner of consecrating, the manner of receiving, and spiritual eating. Its institution is: “Do this in remembrance of me.” The cause of its institution is threefold: namely, that the memory of the Lord’s passion may be retained; that the human spirit may be cleansed and refreshed; and that human weakness may be strengthened and defended against frequent falls. The sacrament is threefold, because it consists of bread, wine, and water. Bread is the sacrament of the Lord’s body; that body, moreover, is the sacrament of incarnate divinity. The Apostle says: “Great is the sacrament of godliness, which was manifested in the flesh” (1 Tim. 3). Hence Augustine:

> “That visible and tangible body is the sacrament of an invisible form, namely the heavenly bread by which angels live. For since Christ’s soul performed nothing in [Col. 0505A] the body except insofar as the Word to which it was united inspired it, who does not see that the body is the sacrament of the indwelling Deity?”

Wine, however, is the sacrament of the blood, in which the soul is understood. Water signifies either the water which flowed from Christ’s side, or the Church’s faith: so that neither may Christ be without the Church nor the Church without Christ, but that it may be united and conformed to his flesh and soul.

Further: bread is the sacrament of Christ’s body, which is the Church. Hence Jerome on Mark:

> “Jesus took bread, representing his body by bread—which is the Church present here—which is received in faith, blessed in number, broken in sufferings, given in examples, received in teachings. He forms his blood in the cup from wine and water mingled, so that by the one [Col. 0505B] we may be cleansed of guilt and by the other redeemed from punishments. For by the blood of the lamb houses are preserved from the angel’s blow, and by the water of the Red Sea enemies are extinguished: these are mysteries of Christ’s Church. For there are three witnesses: water, blood, and spirit (1 John 5). Water for washing, blood for the price, spirit for resurrection.”

Further: bread is the sacrament of charity, wine of hope, and water of faith. Without these—that is, faith, hope, and charity—there can be no unity with or conformity to Christ. The reality of the sacrament, then, is this threefold conformity to Christ in the unity of the Church’s body, and Christ himself, who is likewise comprehended in a threefold way: according to his human nature, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh; [Col. 0505C] according to his divine nature, through the union in unity of person of the Word with both.

But a distinction must here be made. Christ’s visible form, now an invisible reality for us, is the reality of the visible sacrament of the altar; and the invisible form of heavenly bread, by which angels live, is the reality of Christ’s visible and tangible form. Thus Christ is both sacrament and reality of the sacrament.

It should be noted that the aforesaid conformity of Christ and the Church is jointly called the flesh and blood of Christ, because it is the proper effect of the incarnation of the Word and the final cause of the Lord’s passion. Hence Jerome, to Paula and Eustochium, on the Epistle to the Ephesians:

> “Christ’s blood and flesh are understood in two ways: either as that spiritual and divine flesh and blood of which he himself says, ‘My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly [Col. 0505D] drink’ (John 6); and, ‘Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not have eternal life’ (ibid.); or as the flesh which was crucified and the blood which was poured out by the soldier’s lance.”

The same author, to Ebidia, in Book Twelve of the *Questions*:

> “Let us hear that the bread which the Lord broke for the disciples is his body, and the wine his blood. The Lord himself is both host and banquet, both the one eating and the one eaten; we drink his blood, and without him we cannot bear it.”

Daily, in his sacrifices, we tread the reddening musts from the offspring of the true vine and from the vineyard Soreth, which is interpreted “chosen”; and from them we drink new wine in the kingdom of the Father—that is, in the Church—not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the spirit, singing the new song which no one [Col. 0506A] can sing except the Church. All who are baptized into Christ eat the bread of angels and hear the Lord proclaiming: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4). Therefore let us do the will of the Father who sent us, and Christ will drink his own blood with us in the kingdom of the Church.

The manner of consecration pertains to the rank of priesthood, to the place of the true sacrifice—which is not outside the Catholic Church—and to the Lord’s own utterance. It belongs to the priest to pronounce the Lord’s words with the intention of consecrating and, in the person of the Church, to say: “We offer.” The manner of receiving is likewise divided threefold. One eating occurs by the mouth and is sacramental; another occurs in the heart and is real; another occurs by mouth and heart: in one there is the sacrament, [Col. 0506B] in the other the reality of the sacrament.

Merely sacramental eating belongs only to the wicked. Although they receive Christ’s body under the visible species of the elements, because they neither truly believe nor love, they cannot be united to the heavenly bread. Merely real eating belongs only to the good. Although they do not receive Christ’s flesh under the visible sacrament, nevertheless by faith and love they eat the heavenly bread and are united to it. Hence Augustine: “Why do you prepare teeth and stomach? Believe, and you have eaten.” Real and sacramental eating are joined when those who receive in the bread that which hung upon the wood, and in the cup that which flowed from the side, reach in mind as far as the eating of the bread of life. The reception and incorporation by the mouth, I say, [Col. 0506C] which takes place in receiving the Eucharist, is the sacrament of the heart’s eating, by which, as was said above in Jerome’s words, we eat Christ’s flesh with the Lord and drink his blood with him. That is: through the efficacy of his flesh and blood we abide in him, and he in us.

Thus some receive the Lord’s body unto death because they do not attain to the bread of life; others receive it unto life because they are united with the Word of life. In spiritual eating seven things must be considered: faith, thought, understanding, memory, love, imitation, and adherence. For a person who eats first takes a morsel of bread, then places it in the mouth and grinds it with the teeth; through saliva descending from the head, that food becomes swallowable, and so descends into the stomach. From it the body [Col. 0506D] is strengthened and the spirit sustained.

The morsel of bread is the portion of faith which God places in the mouth of the heart. Thought follows, inquiring, grinding, and repeatedly turning it over within itself. Then comes understanding, which makes the ground bread swallowable. With the help of saliva—that is, grace descending from Christ the head through understanding—it passes and descends into the stomach, that is, memory. Memory nourishes love; love leads to imitation; imitation produces full adherence. Hence, “He who adheres to God is one spirit with him” (1 Cor. 6).

A person strengthened by this bread can drink the cup, that is, endure suffering; food is followed by drink. The cup is suffering in the Lord’s hand, and the surge of suffering soon passes, as drink is quickly consumed. Strengthened by the aforesaid eating, [Col. 0507A] he encounters and is offered the cup; seeing it, people desire and thirst for it. First there is the cup, then thirst; drink follows, for the thirsty drink. Blessed intoxication follows drink, through which a person, estranged from earthly things, is strengthened in heavenly things. Sleep follows intoxication, rest follows sleep. For many sleep who do not rest. Eternal life follows rest, so that one may obtain in actuality what one already possesses in hope.

Certainly, three points must be distinguished, which holy teachers commonly affirm and the Church firmly maintains. First, bread and wine are changed through consecration into the true body and blood of Christ. Thus bodily food passes into food of the soul, the food of the belly into the food of the faithful and spiritual mind; [Col. 0507B] and for this reason it is called *viaticum*, provision for the journey. But, as the Apostle testifies: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the Lord’s cup unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11); and thus “eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (ibid.). Jerome, on this passage of the Apostle:

> “If no one dares place anything in a dirty cloth or vessel, how much more [should this not be done] in a polluted heart, whose uncleanness God abhors above all things? Joseph the just therefore wrapped him in a clean and new linen cloth, because he prefigured that those receiving the Lord’s body should have a mind as clean as it is new.”

Second, the visible species of bread and wine remain subject to our senses after consecration just as they were before. For without any deception our eyes see the form and color both of bread and [Col. 0507C] wine; without falsehood taste and smell prove their flavor; touch perceives heat or cold, softness or hardness; and our ears perceive the breaking. Hence Ambrose:

> “Nothing false must be supposed in the sacrifice of truth, as happens in the tricks of magicians, where the eyes are deceived by a certain illusion, so that what is not may seem to be—utterly so.”

A *praestigium* (“illusion”) is so called, as it were, because it blinds the sharpness of the eyes; Mercury is said to have been its inventor.

Third, Christ’s body, in human form, impassible and incorruptible, is locally and invisibly in heaven until it appears to all at the judgment. Hence Jerome, in the shorter *Breviary*, on Psalm 138, “I arose and am still with you”:

> “It signifies the time during which he is still at the Father’s right hand, until he comes to judge the living and the dead.”

Augustine, on the Song of Ascents, Psalm 127:

> “He who gave us the pledge of his blood—Christ our bridegroom—is absent; absent in body, but present in majesty.”

The same author, in chapter seventy-five on John:

> “The Lord is above, but truth is also here. For the Lord’s body rose in such a way that it can be in one place; his truth is spread everywhere.”

The same, on Psalm 75:

> “If you think of your brother or the Son according to divinity, he is present everywhere. But if you understand the Son as he was seen in flesh among human beings, crucified, risen, and ascended into heaven, then angels are around [Col. 0508A] him.”

The Church therefore holds that the Lord’s body is locally in heaven; it holds that the true body of the Lord which hung upon the wood is upon altars. Christ’s body is impassible and inviolable; death shall no longer have dominion over it. Yet the true body of Christ is sensibly handled by priests’ hands, broken, and wholly and entirely received in every portion. Christ’s body is incorruptible; yet again, Christ’s body is crushed by teeth and swallowed. Read Berengar’s confession of faith, which the Church established for him under Pope Nicholas, and you will find it to be so.

Therefore an interpretation must be sought through a salutary consideration of the truth. Far be it that the holy Church should believe contradictory things when it proclaims such statements as these: God is a simple and incorporeal nature; God is man; God [Col. 0508B] is eternity itself; God was born of a virgin; God is immortal; God died on the cross; God is boundless; God lay in the tomb; God is immutable and non-local; God rose from the dead and ascended into heaven.

Here, in the commentator’s role of presenting many views for acceptance or avoidance, while preserving peace with the Church, we shall note certain opinions. Virtue loves itself and rejects its opposites, and no one can avoid a vice unless it is known. There are some—indeed perhaps many, though they can scarcely be identified—who think the same as the condemned Berengar and nevertheless condemn him together with the Church. They condemn him, namely, because, rejecting the Church’s manner of speech, he provoked scandal through the nakedness of his language. They say that he did not follow the usage of Scripture, which frequently calls things that signify by the names of the things signified, especially in the sacraments, in order to express their powers. Others secretly charge them with failing to understand tropes and figurative expressions and therefore, by the wretched death of the soul, taking signs for realities. They especially ridicule the assertion that the species of bread and wine, some say, appear in the air, while others say that bodily senses are deceived after the conversion of bread and wine into Christ’s flesh and blood. But a certain distinguished poet understood rightly and said:

> Melchizedek offered bread and wine to the Lord.  
> Christ, establishing the same, annulled the old covenant.  
> Between the two there long existed another rite  
> of sacrificing, possessing some power of expiation.  
>
> For the lamb of the Law cleansed fleshly acts,  
> prefiguring the Lamb who washes us, made a victim.  
> Once this had been offered, that former course ended;  
> the present reality drove away what had been a sign.  
>
> What place remains for dawn after the sun has risen?  
> What place remains for vows when the sailor holds the harbor?  
> The Law was dawn; ox and goat were vows.  
> The cross is sun; the cross is harbor: this is so; let those things pass away.  
>
> The cross closed the temple; the cross solved the Law’s riddles.  
> Beneath the cross the ephod ceases, and royal anointing fails.  
> Goat, sheep, sparrow, ram, and calves’ fat  
> proclaim nothing: God is the victim, their end.  
>
> Let the Hebrew spare the sheep: flesh has removed flesh from the altar.  
> It is the act of beasts to sacrifice beasts after Christ,  
> who died once, though he shall die no more.  
> [Col. 0509A] Yet the same is sacrificed daily without wound.  
>
> Let no one doubt that bread is on the altar, God on the cross:  
> Life itself confesses that these are made by the word of life,  
> which gives life to the mind—unless Christ sanctioned empty things;  
> the substance of bread passes into Christ’s flesh.  
>
> In this flesh there is nothing fleshly or bloody.  
> Here the spirit touches, sees, and receives unto the memorial  
> a sacred order, good tradition, the pious victim of bread.  
> Therefore let crime, horror, and empty practice be far away.  
>
> A blessed mystery, a ninth power [reading uncertain], a useful sacred rite,  
> by which liquid has become blood for such a washing.  
> For because we sinners always need medicine,  
> we always have this medicine for sins.  
>
> This is given unto life; but if you, guilty one, fear him  
> who sits at the Father’s right hand and is sacrificed on altars—  
> [Col. 0509B] behold, you see types and signs perish in the Law,  
> and three sacraments return to their proper head.

L. 273[X]

But the Lord said to Simon: “Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, that he may sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail.”

[Bede.] The Lord teaches that no one’s faith is tested by the devil unless God permits it. Satan demands the good in order to sift them; that is, he longs for their affliction. The Lord prays for Peter, not that he may not be tempted, but that after the fall of denial he may rise again to his former state. For it is beneficial to the saints to be tested by temptations, so that either their strength may appear when tested, or, recognizing their weakness through temptation, they may learn to become stronger; and thus, when they have been proved, may receive the crown of life.

L. 274[IX] A. 229

“And you, once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.”

By the example of your repentance strengthen your brothers, lest, after sinning, they despair when they turn back to me.

A. 125[X]

“Little children, I am still with you a little while.”

Before I die, I shall be with you for a little while in this weakness of the flesh; for after the resurrection I shall not be with you in fellowship with human weakness.

“You will seek me, and, as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going, [Col. 0509D] you cannot come,’ so I say to you now.”

That is, you cannot come now. But in order that you may someday follow me—by dying for righteousness and coming to immortal life—keep the commandments.

“I give you a new commandment: that you love one another; as I have loved you, that you also love one another.”

Was it not in the old Law: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself”? Why then is it called new here? Because this love renews the obedient person. In order to distinguish it from carnal love, the Lord added: “As I have loved you.” That greater commandment, by which we are commanded to love God with all the heart, seems to be omitted here. Yet those who understand rightly find both in each individual command. For what did God love in us except that we [Col. 0510A] should possess him? A physician loves nothing in the sick except the health which he desires to restore.

“By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

(1 Cor. 13.) Even those who are not mine possess my other gifts—namely nature, life, sensation, reason, and faith—but because they do not possess charity, they resound like cymbals and gain nothing. This is the fountain in which the outsider has no share.

A. 126[I] M. 189 R. 170 L. 275

Simon Peter said to him: “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered: “Where I am going, you cannot follow me now; but you will follow afterward.”

Having heard the way of love by which the Lord must be followed, Peter, ready to follow, says: “Lord, where are you going?” But he who knows all teaches him not to presume, because he is not yet clothed with power from on high.

M. 287[IV] R. 168 A. 112

Then Jesus said to them: “All of you will take offense because of me this night.”

He predicts what they will suffer, so that when they have suffered it they may not despair. He significantly added, “this night,” because they were scandalized in darkness, like drunken people. But let us say: “The night has passed; the day has drawn near” (Rom. 13).

M. 278[VI] R. 169

“For it is written: ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’ But after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee.”

[Jerome.] In the prophet Zechariah it is written in the person of the prophet addressing God: “Strike the shepherd” (Zech. 13). He asks for the Lord’s passion. The Father answers: “I will strike the shepherd.” For through the prayers of the saints the Son is sent by the Father and struck—that is, he is incarnate and suffers—and the sheep are scattered when the shepherd is taken. The resurrection is promised lest hope be extinguished. For consolation is foretold at the point where those who had heard sorrowfully of the place of suffering will see him glorified by resurrection.

M. 289[I] R. 170 L. 275 A. 125

Peter answered and said to him: “Even if all [Col. 0510D] are offended because of you, I shall never be offended.” L.: “I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.” A.: “I will lay down my life for you.”

[Jerome.] This is not Peter’s rashness, but his ardent devotion toward the Savior.

Jesus answered: “Will you lay down your life for me?” M. R. L. A.: “Amen, I say to you, that on this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.”

[Augustine.] The weak man was boasting of his own will, but the physician was observing his health. If Peter’s threefold denial had begun after the first crowing of the cock, Matthew, Luke, and John, who said that Peter would deny him before the cock crowed, would seem to have spoken falsely. Again, if he had completed the threefold denial before the cock began to crow, Mark would have superfluously narrated the Lord’s words: “Before the cock gives its voice twice, you will deny me three times.” Therefore, because that threefold denial began before the first cockcrow, the other three did not attend to when it was completed, but to when it began—although the whole denial can be understood as already present in his mind before the first cockcrow.

For although the threefold denial began in the denier’s words before the first cockcrow and was completed before the second, yet it was wholly conceived in Peter’s fear before the first. Nor does it matter at what intervals of hours it was uttered in three statements, since his heart as he denied him possessed the whole denial before the first cockcrow. Such great fear had filled his heart that he could deny the Lord not merely once but, when questioned again and a third time, a second and third time. And just as one who has looked at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in [Col. 0511B] his heart (Matt. 5), so Peter had conceived such fear in his mind that it could endure as far as the Lord’s third denial. Therefore the whole threefold denial must be assigned to the time in which fear sufficient for three denials seized him. Accordingly, even if he had begun to deny in words after the first cockcrow, there would still have been no contradiction.

It should not, then, trouble us that the threefold denial began before the first cockcrow and was completed after it—as if someone were told: “This night, before the cock crows, you will write me a letter in which you will insult me three times.” Certainly, if he began to write it before the first cockcrow and finished after the first cockcrow, the prediction would not on that account be said to have been false.

M. 290[VI] R. 170

Peter said to him: “Even if I must die with you, I shall not deny you.” And all the disciples said likewise.

[Jerome.] A spirit without wings attempts to fly on high, but the body weighs down the soul, so that fear of human death overcomes fear of the Lord. Peter nevertheless does not lie, because he believes what he promises to be true. But a liar is one who signifies what is false with the intention of deceiving.

## CHAPTER 157

A. 127[X]

“Let not your heart be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in me.”

[Col. 0511D] [Augustine.] Lest they should fear death as human beings and therefore be troubled, he consoles them, testifying that he too is God. As though he said: “You fear death for this form of a servant; do not be troubled, because God will raise it.”

“In my Father’s house are many dwelling places.”

They were rightly troubled, since it had been said to the more confident man that he would deny the Lord. But when they hear of heaven’s dwelling places, they recover from their distress, assured that after dangers they will remain with God according to their merits. This is signified by the many dwelling places. “For one is the glory of the sun, another of the moon, another of the stars; for star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 15).
