Therefore those must be rejected who think that the many dwelling places were mentioned because there is something outside the kingdom of heaven in which blessed innocents who departed this [Col. 0512A] life without baptism may remain; this is not Catholic faith.

“If it were otherwise, I would have told you, because I go to prepare a place for you.”

[Albinus.] *Quominus* means “not.” If there were dwelling places anywhere other than in the Father’s house, that is, in the righteous, I would have told you. But know that I now go to prepare a place for you by dying, rising, and ascending into heaven. Jerome, *Against Jovinian*:

> “If there were not many dwelling places with the Father, I would have told you, because I go to prepare a place for you.”

That is, if each person did not prepare a dwelling place for himself by his own works, I would have told you. Thus it is not mine to prepare for you, but yours. The prepared place did Judas no good, since he lost it through his own fault. In accordance with this sense must also be understood what was said to the sons of Zebedee: “To sit at my right hand or left is not mine to give you, but [is for those] for whom it has been prepared by my Father” (Matt. 20). “You ask in vain,” he says, “for what lies within you and what my Father has prepared for worthy virtues.”

“And if I go and prepare a place for you, I am coming again and will receive you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be.”

[Augustine.] He is in himself; therefore they were to be in him. For he himself is eternal life, in which we shall be. He departed by hiding through the absence of his flesh; he will come at the judgment by appearing; but he remains by reigning, so that we may advance by living well, and thus a place is prepared. Though departing, he prepares without leaving; because he withdraws and hides himself, so that faith may concern a thing not seen, and therein lies the merit of faith. It is not contradictory that he said, “There are many dwelling places,” and that here he says he will go to prepare a place. For those dwelling places already exist by predestination, and thus do not need to be prepared; yet they must be prepared in operation. This is said as the prophet says that God made things yet to come: he made them by predestining; he will make them by acting.

God therefore now prepares dwelling places by preparing dwellers for dwelling places. By the house is understood God’s temple, of which the Apostle says: “God’s holy temple is what you are” (1 Cor. 13 [as cited]). This is also the kingdom of God, which the Son is to hand over to the Father. Hence the Apostle: “Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ at his coming, [Col. 0512D] then the end, when he hands over the kingdom”—that is, those redeemed by his blood—“to God the Father” (ibid.). Then the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt. 13). The kingdom will shine in the kingdom, when the kingdom comes to the kingdom which we pray for when we say: “Your kingdom come” (Matt. 6). It is already called a kingdom, but then it will possess the power of reigning, when it hears: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25): that is, you who were a kingdom and did not reign except in hope, come and reign in reality. Merit is gathered for the believer; reward is rendered to the one who sees. Desire for the vision is preparation for the dwelling place. Lord, prepare what you are preparing—namely, us for yourself—and [‘et re nobis’: reading and meaning uncertain], so that there may be many dwelling places: so that, according to the diversity of merits, one may participate in you more and another less.

[Col. 0513A] “And you know where I am going, and you know the way.”

Since Christ is God and man in the same person, according to his humanity he came to human beings, and according to his glorified humanity he returns to himself as God, who is truth in the Father and life from life.

Thomas said to him: “Lord, we do not know where you are going; how can we know the way?” Jesus said to him: “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.”

The Lord had said that they knew both things which Thomas says he does not know. The Lord cannot lie. Therefore they knew what they did not know that they knew. For if they knew him, and he himself is the way, truth, and life, they knew all this. He was going to truth and life, that is, to himself, and to the Father through himself. We too go through him both [Col. 0513B] to the Father and to him. In a wonderful and ineffable manner, he who never left himself came to himself.

Take an unequal example, however helpful for understanding. As regards my own mind, since I am what you are: if I am silent, I am with myself; if I speak to you so that you understand, in a certain manner I go forth to you, yet do not leave myself. But when I become silent, in a certain manner I return to myself; and I remain with you if you retain what you have heard. If a creature of God can do this, what can God the Son of God do? “I am,” he says, “the way, truth, and life,” as if to say: “By what you wish to go, I am the way; where you wish to go, I am there as truth. Where do you wish to remain? I am life.”

Every human being desires truth and life but does not find the way. The way itself came to you: rise and walk. Walk by conduct, not by feet. Many walk well [Col. 0513C] with their feet but badly in conduct. Sometimes those walking well fall outside the way, as certain non-Christians do. They run well, but not on the way. If they do not hold the way, however well they walk, it is cause for sorrow. Better to limp on the way than to walk strongly outside the way.

“If you had known me, you would certainly have known my Father also; and from now on you will know him, and you have seen him.”

[Augustine.] It should be noted that some of them knew him and some did not; and he reproves those who did not know him, saying: “If you had known me, you would certainly have known my Father also,” because I am truth in the true Father. But he is understood to have said, “You know where I am going, and you know the way,” to those who already knew the Son; and to these he adds the statement about the Father: “From now on you will know him,” known through me; and “you have seen him,” on account of the complete likeness which he has to the Father, whom they had not yet seen. This is also the force of what is later said to Philip: “Whoever sees me sees the Father”—not because he himself is both Father and Son, as the Sabellians and Patripassians say, but because Father and Son are so similar that whoever knows one knows both. For we customarily speak this way of two very similar people: when one has been seen and someone wishes to know the other, we say, “Have you seen this one? You have seen that one.” Therefore whoever sees the Son with the eyes of the heart also sees the Father, who is most like him. They had seen the Son, who is most like the Father, but needed instruction to understand the Father too as such and not unlike him.

[Augustine.] There is certainly supreme likeness between supreme truth and the supremely truthful, between [Col. 0514A] supreme wisdom and the supremely wise—that is, between the Son and the Father. For God the Father is truthful by the truth whom he begot; wise by the wisdom whom he begot.

Philip said to him: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.” Jesus said to him: “Have I been with you so long, and have you not known me? Philip, whoever has seen me has seen the Father. How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?”

[Augustine.] I see in what spirit you ask that the Father be shown to you: you do not seek another who is similar, but think that he is better than I am. Philip wishes to know the inseparable ones separately, seeking sufficiency in the Father and not in the Son, because he is one of those who do not know the Son. Even if they knew that this one was the Son and that one the Father, they did not think the Son wholly similar, but thought the Father better; and thus they knew neither Father nor Son.

“The words which I speak to you I do not speak from myself. But the Father abiding in me, he does the works.”

Therefore words too are works. For one who edifies a neighbor by speaking performs a good work. Here the Arians say: “Behold, the Son is unequal to the Father, since he does not speak from himself.” The Sabellians—that is, the Patripassians—reply: “Behold, the Father himself is the Son. For what does ‘the Father abiding in me, he does the works’ mean except, ‘I who do them abide in myself’?” But we say that each is equal to the other, since they are one in substance, yet one is naturally from the other and attributes the work to him from whom he who performs it himself is.

“Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? Otherwise, believe because of the works themselves.”

For if we were separate, we could by no means work inseparably.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these, because I go to the Father.”

“He will do greater works than these,” that is, greater works—understand, by the power of these works. Or read the genitive as an ablative, after the Greek manner. [Augustine.] It was greater that Peter’s shadow healed (Acts 5) than that the hem of Christ’s garment did so (Matt. 9). Jesus did the latter through himself, the former through Peter. Thus he himself did both; but what works was he then speaking of, if not the words he was speaking? They believed these words by hearing them, yet later, when they preached the Gospel, more people believed than they themselves had been. And these are without doubt greater works.

Yet he did not say this only to the apostles, for he did not say, “You will do greater works than these,” but: “Whoever believes in me will do greater works than these.” This must be understood thus: the one who believes in me will not be greater than I; but I shall do greater things through that person, so that an impious person becomes righteous, than I now do without that person. This does not concern all Christ’s works, for he made all things. Yet I call the salvation of souls greater than heaven and earth, because when these pass away the salvation of the righteous will remain. Still, I do not dare hastily to pronounce judgment so as to say that salvation wrought by Christ is greater than the angels [Col. 0515A] and archangels, which are Christ’s works. Let whoever can understand whether it is greater to create the righteous or to justify the ungodly, since the latter is a work of greater mercy. This discourse concerns the words of righteousness which he then performed, not all his works.

A. 128[III] M. 216 R. 123

“And whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son.”

Whatever we ask contrary to our salvation, we do not ask in the Savior’s name. Therefore, when the Lord does not do what he sees requested against salvation, he rather shows himself to be Savior. For the physician knows what the sick person asks that is health-giving and what is contrary to health. If we wish him to do what we ask, let us ask for our salvation. [Col. 0515B] “That the Father may be glorified in the Son”: he added this lest anyone should think that the Son would do anything without the Father.

“If you love me, keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you forever: the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.”

How shall we keep the commandments so as to receive him, when, unless we have him, we are unable to keep the commandments? Hear the Apostle: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except by the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12). Who says “Jesus is Lord” in the sense in which the Apostle intended it, except one who loves him? Many say it with the voice, but deny it in heart and deeds. Let us therefore understand that the one who loves has the Holy Spirit, and by having him merits to have more; and by having more, loves more. The disciples had the Spirit in lesser measure, and he was to be given them more abundantly. They had him secretly; they were to receive him openly. Accordingly, a promise is made both to one who has and to one who has not, but to the one who has, so that he may have more. The Spirit is not divided, but his gifts are. For “there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit” (ibid.). *Paraclete* is interpreted “advocate.” And it is said of Christ: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ” (1 John 2), who pleads for us by presenting his obedience. By “the world” here he means lovers of the world, who plainly do not have the Spirit of truth. Whatever is subject to time is vanity. But the Spirit of truth—that is, the unchangeable love of the Godhead—will remain with the saints, so that he will be in them for knowing and for abiding. For although David, overcome by weakness, sinned grievously, yet he truly believed (2 Sam. 11); he loved his neighbor, if not in effect, at least in affection; and perhaps he had Christ as his foundation. He had him—that is, he loved him in such a way that, if the choice had been offered him, he would first have allowed himself to be killed rather than deny God, although for a time he despised him in some respect. When saints sin, the stone is moved, not torn out. Let the righteous fall, let the righteous slip, let the righteous rise again: he will be better. For “all things work together for good for the saints” (Rom. 8).

“ I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you.”

He added this so that it might not be thought that he was sending the Spirit without himself. *Orphans* are *pupilli* (“fatherless children”); the former is Greek, the latter Latin. Thus in the Psalm where we read, “You will be a helper to the fatherless” (Ps. 9), the Greek has “to the orphan.”

“Yet a little while, and the world no longer sees me.”

The world, which now sees with the eyes of the flesh, will shortly no longer see, because after the resurrection he did not wish to show his flesh except to his own. Yet the whole span of time is brief; when it is ended, the wicked person will be taken away so that he may not see the glory of God which the righteous will see. He called it brief because what seems long to human beings is exceedingly short to God.

“But you will see me, because I live, and you will live.”

Because his own resurrection was soon to take place, he used the present tense, “I live”; but because theirs would be deferred to the end, he says, “You will live” [Col. 0516B]. And then, when they live, they will openly know those things which they now believe.

“In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you. He who has my commandments and keeps them, he is the one who loves me.”

He who has them in memory and keeps them in life, who has them in speech and keeps them in conduct, who has them by hearing and keeps them by doing—he loves me. The proof of love is the performance of the deed. Hence John says in his Epistle: “He who says, ‘I love God,’ and does not keep his commandments, is a liar” (John 4).

A. 129[I] M. 98 R. 96 A. 116

“But he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him.”

[Col. 0516C] Now he loves us so that we may believe; then he will love us so that we may see. This vision will be the reward of faith.

A. 130[X]

Judas—not Iscariot—said to him: “Lord, what has happened that you are going to reveal yourself to us and not to the world?” Jesus answered and said to him: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him. He who does not love me does not keep my words.”

This is the Judas whose Epistle is read among the canonical Scriptures. The Lord answered that the holy people are distinguished from the unholy through love. For charity makes persons of one mind in the house in which the Father and the Son make their dwelling [Col. 0516D], they who bestow love itself. There will therefore be an inward glory: a vision and dwelling, not passing but eternal. And this will be the manifestation about which he had asked. God comes to a human being when a human being comes to God. A human being comes by believing, obeying, beholding, and receiving; God comes by helping, enlightening, and filling. [GREGORY.] Nevertheless, he comes into the hearts of certain people but does not make his dwelling there, because through compunction they perceive God’s regard, but fail in temptation.

A. 131[I] M. 98 R. 96 L. 116

“And the word which you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me.”

[Col. 0517A] [AUGUSTINE.] The Son is not less than the Father, but he is not from himself. Nor does this conflict with what he said: “He who does not love me does not keep my words.” Perhaps because of some distinction he there said “words” in the plural. Here, however, he said that the word is the Word of the Father, which was in the beginning.

“These things I have spoken to you while remaining with you.”

While I am still remaining with you in bodily presence, soon to be taken away from you, I have said these things concerning the spiritual dwelling. That dwelling eternally blesses those who have been delivered; this bodily presence visits in time those who are to be delivered.

A. 132[X]

“But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and will suggest [Col. 0517B] to you all things whatsoever I have said to you.”

“In my name,” that is, in knowledge of me: the Father will send the Spirit to those who confess me. Or thus: he will send him in my name, that is, for my glorification in those who love me; or “in my name,” that is, in the name of the Godhead, because the Father, the Holy Spirit, and I are one God. [AUGUSTINE.] Where the Holy Spirit teaches, the Father and the Son teach; but because there is a Trinity, the individual persons had to be indicated. [GREGORY.] *Paraclete* is interpreted “advocate,” because those whom he fills he makes intercessors. Hence Paul says: “The Spirit himself intercedes for us with unutterable groanings” (Rom. 8). Not that he intercedes as an inferior, but that he kindles us to intercede. The same Spirit is called Consoler, because, while he prepares pardon for penitents, he lifts the mind from sorrow. Why does he say “will suggest,” when suggesting is usually the office of one who is inferior? Because *suggerere* sometimes means to supply, as here: not that he brings knowledge to us from below, but from what is hidden. Augustine does not have, “He will suggest to you all things,” but “He will cause you to remember all things”; and he explains it thus: we should understand that the salutary admonitions which we are commanded not to forget pertain to the grace by which the Spirit causes us to remember.

“Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you.”

As I go to the Father, I leave peace to those who follow; I give it to those who arrive. This is what we read in the prophet: “peace upon peace.” He leaves us peace in this age, by which we conquer the enemy and love one another; he will give us his peace in the future, when we shall reign without enemy and without discord. He leaves us peace, lest we judge hidden things; he will give us his peace when he reveals the thoughts of hearts. “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2). But why did he not add “my” when saying “I leave,” as he did when he said “I give”? Perhaps he wished “his peace” to be understood—the peace which he himself possesses, in which there is no opposition—while the peace which he left us is not without sin; hence we say: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6). Therefore peace here is not complete, because according to the inward person we delight in the law of God, but see another law in our members resisting the law of our mind [Col. 0518A] (Rom. 7). Likewise, we have peace with one another, loving one another; but even that peace is not complete, since we do not see one another’s thoughts and suppose certain things which are not in one another, either for the better or for the worse. Nor am I unaware that this can be understood so that there seems to be a repetition and “my” is to be supplied in the first instance. But the world—that is, those who love the world—give themselves peace so that without conflict they may enjoy, not God, but the world. And when they give peace to the righteous so that they may not persecute them, it is not true peace, because their hearts are divided.

“Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid. You have heard that I said to you: I go, and I come to you.”

Because I give you peace, so that you may have one heart fixed above, do not be troubled because I said, “I go,” as though, in the shepherd’s absence, the wolf might attack the flock. [AUGUSTINE.] And though I go bodily from you as a human being, I remain present through that by which I am God. The Arians object that the Son of God is a creature, on the basis of Solomon’s words: “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything” (Prov. 8). But this was said of his humanity: “He created me at the beginning of his ways,” that is, that I might reveal through the Gospel the beginning of his ways and works. What follows, however, belongs to the Godhead: “He established me before the age,” which is to say, “He begot me before all times.” Again they say: Why do you worship with the Godhead the flesh which you do not deny to be a creature? Because it is so united to the Godhead that the Son of God is both God and human being. Finally, if you separate the human being from God, I will never serve him—just as if someone found royal purple or a royal diadem, would he worship it? But when the king has put them on, whoever refuses to worship them together with the king incurs the danger of death. Therefore, whoever refuses to worship flesh united to the Godhead will suffer the punishment of eternal death.

“If you loved me, you would surely rejoice because I go to the Father, because the Father is greater than I.”

[AUGUSTINE.] According to the form of a servant, Christ as a child was also less than his parents. “You would rejoice,” he says, because human nature ought to rejoice that it is raised to the Father’s right hand, in whom the rest hope for the same thing for themselves.

“And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it has happened, you may believe.”

He foretold that he would go to the Father, and after his death they were to see [Col. 0518D] him living and ascending to the Father. Upon seeing this, they would believe that he was the Son of God, who was able to do this. For faith concerns things believed and not seen. They would believe, I say, that he was the Son of God, not with a new faith, since they had believed before, but with faith increased and renewed; for when he said these things their faith was still small, and when he died it was almost gone.

“I will no longer speak much with you.”

“For the ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me.”

The ruler of sinners, not of natures, is coming, having received permission from God to hand me over to the Jews; and I shall follow willingly, since he has nothing in me which belongs to him. The Lord did not wish to have anything which he might lose: he came poor, so that the devil might have nothing to take away. The ruler of this world is the devil; the world consists of lovers of the world. Hence it is written: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this age is made an enemy of God” (Jas. 4).

“But that the world may know that I love the Father, and as the Father commanded me, so I do.”

[AUGUSTINE.] He added this as though someone had said to him: “Why do you die, if you have no sin?” Because the Father commanded it. It should certainly be observed that the Father handed over the Son, the Son himself, the disciple his master, the devil the Savior, and the Jews their king to the Gentiles and to the cross. Behold one common deed, but utterly diverse wills.

## CHAPTER CLVIII

[Col. 0519B] L. 276

And he said to them: “When I sent you without purse, bag, and sandals, did you lack anything?” But they said: “Nothing.” Therefore he said to them: “But now, whoever has a purse, let him take it; likewise a bag. And whoever does not have one, let him sell his tunic and buy a sword.”

[Bede.] The Lord instructs his disciples to maintain discernment, the mother of virtues, so that one rule of life may apply in time of persecution and another in time of peace. There are virtues always to be maintained—mercy, humility, chastity, faith, hope, and charity. There are others to be changed according to time and place: hunger, thirst, vigils, prayers, the labor of working and teaching. Whoever supposes that these must always be practised will not only deprive himself of their fruit, but will also incur [Col. 0519C] the reproach of folly. Therefore the teacher of virtues, in order to instill discernment, commanded the disciples sent out to preach to take nothing on the way, but to live by the Gospel. Yet in time of persecution he determined that they should take money necessary for food, until the time for preaching should return once persecution had subsided. For us, however, travelling through inhospitable regions, it is permissible to carry more for the sake of provisions than to keep at home. Hence here the Lord commands one who does not have a sword to buy one; readers should know that the Lord did not lack the power to resist, but rather possessed the love to suffer. This displays the Savior’s beneficent power: when the servant’s ear was cut off, it was healed by his touch, and enemies persecuting him were admonished toward faith. [AMBROSE.] The sword is spiritual: sell your possessions and buy the word by which the naked inner chambers of the mind are clothed. There is also the sword of suffering: put off the body, and let the crown of martyrdom be purchased for you with the spoils of sacrificed flesh.

L. 277[VIII] R. 216

“For I tell you that this which is written must still be fulfilled in me: ‘And he was numbered with the unjust.’ For the things concerning me have an end.”

[Bede.] Isaiah, describing the Lord’s passion, includes among other matters the statement that “he was numbered with the unjust” (Isa. 33), plainly indicating the thieves. “They have an end,” he says—that is, the things foretold concerning me have their fulfillment [Col. 0520A]—because he was soon to descend into hell in order to call his own back to the realms above, according to another prophet who sang to him: “You also, in the blood of your covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water” (Zech. 9).

L. 278[X]

But they said: “Lord, behold, here are two swords.” And he said to them: “It is enough.”

[AMBROSE.] Two swords suffice as testimony that the Savior suffered willingly: one that would cut off the ear, in whose healing the Lord’s power would be revealed; the other, which was not drawn at all, would show that the apostles were not permitted to do all that they could in defense of their master. Two swords are brought forth: one of the New, the other of the Old Testament, by which we are defended against the devil’s snares. And it is said, “It is enough,” because nothing is lacking to one fortified by the teaching of both Testaments.

A. 132[X]

“Rise, let us go from here.”

[AUGUSTINE.] Still reclining, he spoke to those reclining. “Let us go,” he said, to the place from which he was to be handed over to death.

M. 286[IV] R. 267

“And when they had sung a hymn, they went out, according to custom, to the Mount of Olives.”

[Bede.] The Psalmist says of this hymn: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord” (Ps. 21). Luke reports in his two-hundred-and-seventy-ninth chapter that it was the Lord’s custom to frequent [Col. 0520C] the Mount of Olives. Therefore, about to be betrayed by a disciple, he goes to his accustomed retreat, where he could most readily be found. Jesus is seized on the Mount of Olives and ascends to heaven from there, so that we may know that we ascend to heaven from the place where we keep watch, pray, and are bound, and do not resist on earth. Beautifully, after his disciples had been instructed in the mysteries of his blood and body, he leads them out with a hymn sung to the Mount of Olives, signifying that all baptized into his death are to be strengthened with the most exalted gift of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER CLIX

A. 132[X]

[Col. 0520D] He says to them: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.”

[AUGUSTINE.] He calls himself the head of the Church and the disciples its members. Vine and branch are of one nature; for this reason he became human, so that he might have our nature. Why did he add “true,” when he is called a vine by comparison, as he is called a lion and a lamb, and not by literal property? Because he distinguished himself from that vine to which it is said: “How have you turned into the bitterness of a strange vine?” (Jer. 2). That was not a true vine, which yielded thorns instead of grapes. Christ is the vine according to the saying, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14); but according to the saying, “I and the Father are one” (John 10), he himself is also the husbandman—not working from outside, but giving growth from within [Col. 0521A], as the Apostle says: “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 1).

“Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he will take away; and every one that bears fruit, he will cleanse, that it may bear more fruit.”

The cleaner they are, the more fruitful. God cleanses hearts already cleansed by pouring into them more abundantly the Spirit of charity. But those who have been planted in the vine and yet have withered—that is, who adhere to the Church in faith but do not grow rich in charity—will be cut off for the fire.

“Already you are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you.”

Why did he not say, “because of the baptism by which you were washed,” but “because of the word,” unless because even in water the word cleanses? Without the word there is only water. The word is added, and a sacrament results. Thus, when he washed their feet, he said: “He who has been washed does not need to wash, but is wholly clean” (John 13). Whence does water have such power that it touches the body and washes the heart, except through the working of the word? Not because it is spoken, but because it is believed. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.

“Remain in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me.”

It is the voice of heretics that a human being accomplishes righteousness from himself; but Truth contradicts it.

“I am the vine; you are the branches. He who remains in me and [Col. 0521C] I in him bears much fruit, because without me you can do nothing.”

He did not say “little,” but “nothing,” because we can do neither little nor much without him. We remain in him by persevering in faith and obedience, and he remains in us by giving willing, accomplishing, and perseverance.

“If anyone does not remain in me, he will be cast out like a branch and wither; and they will gather him, cast him into the fire, and he burns.”

The branches of so great a vine are the more contemptible if they do not remain in the vine, the more glorious if they do remain. Hence Ezekiel says: once cut off, they are useful for no agricultural purpose, assigned to no artisan’s work. One of two things befits a branch: vine or fire. Therefore, that it may not be in the fire, let it bear fruit from the sap of the vine.

A. 133[IV] M. 216 R. 125

“If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you will ask whatever you will, and it will be done for you.”

God’s words are then said to remain in us when we do what he commands and love what he promises. But one who touches the words by memory and does not cling to them by obedience does not have them for benefit but as testimony to condemnation. If we ask and it is not done, we do not ask rightly, because what is asked is not abiding in Jesus, nor what his words have in us, but what cupidity and the weakness of the flesh have. For insofar as we remain in Jesus, we cannot will anything except what pertains to salvation.

[Col. 0522A] A. 134[X]

“In this my Father is glorified: that you bear very much fruit and become my disciples.”

This is the Father’s glory—that, since he grants everything, a human being becomes Christ’s disciple by his grace, and, remaining in him, bears fruit through preaching and suffering with him. The Apostle says: “We are his workmanship, created in Christ” (Eph. 2). Whether one says “glorified” or “made glorious,” both are translated from the one Greek word, δοξάζω (*doxazō*).

“As the Father loved me, I also have loved you; remain in my love.”

That is, persevere in my grace. Behold the source of abundant fruit: namely, love. But whence comes love? Because he loved us first. He does not show an equality of our nature with his, such as exists between Father and Son, but grace, because Christ the mediator is human. Christ is the mediator of God and human beings, not insofar as he is God, but insofar as he is human. Hence the saying: “And Jesus advanced in age and wisdom, and grace with God and human beings” (Luke 2). The sense, then, is: as the Father loved me, a human being, by ineffable grace, and you in me, so I have loved you. Therefore remain in my love, because I love you.

“If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love.”

That is, you will know that you are loved by me. No one keeps the commandments who does not love, and no one loves except one who keeps them. Nor do we first keep the commandments in order that Christ may love us; rather, unless Christ loves us, we cannot keep them.

“As I too have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love.”

By this I, a human being, am shown to be loved by the Father: because I am obedient to him unto death on the cross [death].

“These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you and that your joy may be fulfilled.”

God’s joy in us, whom he foreknew and predestined, is always complete. Our joy begins in the faith of those reborn; it will be fulfilled in the reward of those raised again.

“This is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you.”

Why did Christ love us, except that we might reign with him? [Col. 0522D] Therefore, that we may have God, let us love one another. Whether it is called *praeceptum* (“precept”) or *mandatum* (“commandment”), both render the one Greek term ἐντολή (*entolē*). He had already stated this thought when he said: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John 13). This repetition is therefore an emphatic commendation.

A. 133[IV] M. 204 R. 115

“No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends.”

Here he calls the proof of love—namely, the performance of the deed—“love,” transferring the name from cause to effect. Indeed, no evidence of love is greater than to lay down one’s life for friends. [AUGUSTINE.] It follows that, just as Christ laid down his life for us, so we too should lay down our lives for our brothers. This is what is read in the Proverbs of Solomon: “If you sit down to dine at the table of a ruler, consider attentively what is set before you, and so put forth your hand, knowing that you ought to prepare such things” (Prov. 23). The table of the ruler is that from which the Lord’s body and blood are received. To sit down is to approach humbly. To understand what is set before one by considering it is to reflect upon so great a grace. To put forth the hand and know what must be prepared is to know that we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers, just as Christ laid down his life for us. Hence the Apostle Peter also says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, that we may follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2). This is the voice sounding above the firmament in Ezekiel [Col. 0523B], which makes the outspread wings bend down (Ezek. 1). For if martyrs had not had the example of Christ’s death in their own death, they would have thought that they were doing so great a thing that no one could possibly think himself able to do more for God; and therefore there would not have been such humility. But they hear the voice above the firmament: that is, they see Christ, who had all things in his hand, enduring every sort of insult, as the Gospel describes. They see also that he was mortal by a will of mercy, not by necessity of nature: he alone died voluntarily; all others by necessity. That his suffering was more difficult than all others, he himself testifies through Jeremiah, saying: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. 1). Compared with this suffering, the torments of martyrs will appear less; therefore no one in suffering can make himself equal to him. And it is evident that this was done in order to show how great was his love for humankind, so that a human being might draw nearer more fully to love of him. Therefore the Son of God came in order to free humankind from sin and pour his love into it. He did this by offering to the Father as a sacrifice the human being whom he assumed, and by giving a human being, as it were, as the price for humankind. This, then, is found to be the certain cause of the incarnation, which both the Apostle in Romans and Christ in the Gospel taught.

A. 136[X]

[Col. 0523D] “You are my friends if you do what I command you. I no longer call [*dicum*, apparently an OCR error for *dico*] you servants, because a servant does not know what his lord does.”

[AUGUSTINE.] A servant becomes good through charity, and thus a good servant is a friend. As there are two fears, so there are two forms of servitude. There is the fear which perfect charity casts out; there is another, chaste fear, which remains for ever and ever (Ps. 18). The Apostle joined both servitude and the fear which is not in charity when he said: “For you have not received again the spirit of servitude in fear” (Rom. 8). Of chaste fear he said: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. 11). Of unchaste servitude it is said: “I will no longer call you servants” (John 15). Of the other servitude he says elsewhere: “Well done, good servant; enter into the joy of your lord” [Col. 0524A] (Matt. 25). Therefore we are servants and not servants: good servants, not servants such as the one of whom it is written, “A servant does not remain in the house forever” (John 8).

“But I have called you friends, because I have made known to you all things whatsoever I heard from my Father.”

This does not conflict with what he says elsewhere: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16), because here he used the past for the future, as in: “They have pierced my hands and feet” (Ps. 21). The Lord was going to give them the fullness of which the Apostle says: “When that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part shall be done away” (1 Cor. 13). This will be the making known to them of all things, namely, all things sufficient for blessedness. Thus it is said: “God will be all in all” (1 Cor. 15), that is, sufficient for each person.

“You did not choose me, but I chose you, and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit may remain.”

A. 138[IV] M. 216 R. 125

“And that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give you.”

It would not be grace if merits came first. Therefore God did not choose good people; rather, grace makes good those whom he chooses. He places them in himself as branches in the vine, so that, rooted in him, they may go by willing—for to will is to go with the mind—and bear fruit by working. Let love remain, because it is our fruit. This love is now in desire, not yet in satisfaction; and in this very desire, whatever we ask in Jesus’ name, the Father will give us [Col. 0524C].

A. 138[X]

“These things I command you: that you love one another.”

Since the sacred utterances are full of the Lord’s commandments, why does the Lord here speak of love as though it were a single command, except because every commandment consists in love alone and all things are one commandment? For whatever is commanded is established in charity alone. And just as many branches spring from one root, so many virtues spring from the root of charity. [AUGUSTINE.] The Lord’s commandments are many because works are diverse, but they are one in the root of love. This is what the Apostle says: “The fruit of the Spirit is charity” [Col. 0524D] (Gal. 5). He began with the chief thing, then joined together the others as though springing from that head: joy, peace, long-suffering (ibid.), and the rest. Charity is the movement of the mind to enjoy God for his own sake, and oneself and one’s neighbor for God’s sake. To choose this is prudence; not to be turned from it by any troubles is fortitude; not by any enticements is temperance; not by any pride is justice. Here these virtues are in act; in eternal blessedness they are in effect. Here they are in work; there in reward. Here they are in duty; there in fulfillment. Cupidity, however, is the movement of the mind to enjoy oneself, one’s neighbor, or any bodily thing, not for God’s sake. What unrestrained cupidity does to corrupt its own mind and body is called a shameful act; what it does in order to injure another is called a crime. These are the two kinds of all sins; but shameful acts come first, and when they have emptied the mind and brought it to a kind of poverty, one rushes into crimes.

“If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you.”

[AUGUSTINE.] Why does a member exalt itself above the head? Whoever refuses to endure the world’s hatred together with the head refuses to be in the body.

“If you had been of the world, the world would love what was its own.”

If an evil person punishes another evil person’s crimes, in one respect the world hates what is its own, insofar as it punishes; in another it loves it, because an evil person favors evildoers. The world hates nature in itself and loves vice; it loves iniquity and hates its own soul [Col. 0525B]. But concerning nature we are told: “Love your enemies” (Matt. 5); and concerning vice: “Do not love the world” (1 John 2).

“But because you are not of the world, and I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.”

He says this to the whole Church, which Scripture also often calls by the name of “world,” as in: “The Son of Man did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” (John 12); and: “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5).

A. 139[III] M. 110 L. 58

“Remember my word, which I said to you: A servant is not greater than his lord.”

Here the servant is understood to be one belonging to chaste fear, which remains for ever and ever [Col. 0525C].

A. 140[X]

“If they persecuted me, they will persecute you also. If they kept my word, they will keep yours also.”

A servant cannot please one to whom his lord is displeasing.

A. 141[I] M. 244 R. 139[I] L. 258

“But they will do all these things to you for my name’s sake.”

That is, they will hate me in you and persecute me in you. The more miserable, then, are those who do these things, as those who suffer persecution are more blessed. The wicked hate Christ’s name and righteousness in the good; therefore they persecute them.

A. 142[III] M. 112 L. 119

[Col. 0525D] “Because they do not know him who sent me.”

They do not know him with that knowledge of which it is written: “To know you is perfect understanding” (Wis. 8).

A. 143[X]

“If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin.”

[AUGUSTINE.] The order is: If I had not come, and if I had not spoken to them. He means the Jews, of whom he had said: “If they persecuted me, they will persecute you also.” What does “they would not have sin” mean? Were the Jews without sin before Christ’s coming? He means here a great sin: that they did not believe in him, who had come precisely so that they might believe. His coming was to some “the fragrance of life unto life,” to others “the fragrance of death unto death” [Col. 0526A] (2 Cor. 2). “But now they have no excuse for their sin.” Those to whom he did not come or speak have an excuse, not for every sin, but for this: that they did not believe in Christ, who did not speak to them—provided, however, that he did not come to them through his disciples. Hence he says elsewhere: “He who receives you receives me, and he who despises you despises me” (Matt. 10). And Paul says: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13). Certainly those who died before hearing his Gospel have this excuse; yet “those who sinned without the law will perish without the law” (Rom. 2).

A. 144[I] M. 98 R. 97 L. 116

“He who hates me hates my Father also.”

[Col. 0526B] Since it was said above, “They do not know him who sent me,” how can they hate one whom they do not know? They do not know the truth which condemns them. When they hate that truth, they surely hate him from whom the truth they hate was born, in that he inflicts punishment. For the Jews do not wish their deeds to be condemned, while it belongs to truth that such deeds should be condemned. Thus, without knowing him, they hate God as he is in just action; and they think they love him because they love the God whom they conceive through a lying suspicion. Something similar occurs among human beings through suspicions. We can love or hate persons we have not seen, since, though they have not been seen, their goodness or wickedness is known through reputation or the writings of histories. If we hate evils and love goods, we do not err in judgment about things; rather, there is a right rejection of vices and approval of virtues. But it is pardonable if we hold untrue opinions about hidden matters of human beings—this is a human temptation—namely, if we suspect them to be otherwise than they are. Therefore, if a good person thinks a good person evil, he loves him unknowingly, because that person is righteous and righteousness is what he loves; though mistaken, he afflicts a good person as though evil, lest he injure others and so that he himself may become more corrected. Likewise, if an evil person to whom goodness is displeasing thinks a good person evil, he associates familiarly with him and hates him unknowingly.

A. 145[X]

“If I had not done among them works which no one else did, they would not have sin.”

[Col. 0526D] That is, the great sin spoken of above. But what does he mean by saying, “which no one else has done”? Among Christ’s works none seem greater than the raising of the dead, which we know Elijah did (3 Kings 17) and Elisha (4 Kings 4). Yet Christ did perform some things which no one else did: he fed five thousand people with five loaves, and four thousand with seven. He walked upon the waters, and granted Peter to do the same (Matt. 14). He changed water into wine and opened the eyes of a man born blind. But the reply may be made that others did things which he did not do, and things which no one else did: for example, Moses, striking the Egyptians with so many plagues, leading the people through the divided sea, obtaining manna for the hungry, and bringing forth water from the rock (Exod. 15). Who but [Col. 0527A] Joshua son of Nun stopped the moving sun (Josh. 10)? Who but Samson, when thirsty, was satisfied by water flowing from the jawbone of a dead ass (Judg. 15)? Who but Elijah was borne aloft in a fiery chariot (4 Kings 2)? Who but Elisha, when buried, raised a dead man (4 Kings 13)? For certain men carrying a dead body, when enemies suddenly attacked, fled to the place where he had been buried; and when they laid the corpse there, it immediately rose. Who but Daniel lived among hungry lions (Dan. 6)? Who but Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael walked unharmed amid flames (Dan. 3)? It is therefore clear that saints also did certain things which no one else did; but no one among the ancients is recorded as having healed so many ailments and afflictions of mortals by such great power. Hence Mark says: “Wherever he went, they laid [Col. 0527B] the sick, and begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment; and as many as touched him were made whole” (Mark 6). When he says “in them,” it must be understood thus: not merely among them or before them, but actually in them, because he healed them. That he was born of a virgin surpasses every miracle. Whoever considers more deeply the phrase “which no one else has done” will find that Christ did whatever any man of God did. He can do all things by himself; no one, however, can do anything without him.

“But now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father; but this happened in order that the word written in their law might be fulfilled: ‘They hated me without cause’” (Ps. 24).

They saw the works and nevertheless hated, even though they did so in ignorance of the Son and the Father working indivisibly. He calls it their law not because they invented it, but because it was given to them—just as we say, “Our daily bread,” though we ask it from God, adding, “Give us” (Luke 11). One hates without cause when one seeks no advantage from hatred and avoids no disadvantage by it. The righteous love someone without self-interest, apart from him who will be all in all (1 Cor. 15).

“But when the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father—he will bear witness concerning me.”

On the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit came upon one hundred and twenty gathered persons, among whom were all the apostles (Acts 2). When they spoke in tongues, many of those present, astonished by so great a miracle and pierced to the heart as Peter spoke, were converted and received forgiveness. Seeing this, therefore, the Lord spoke as though saying: “They have hated me, but the Paraclete will bear such witness concerning me that he will make many of them believe in me.” The Spirit comes of his own will, as God; for the Son sends him from the Father, to whom he refers both the fact that he himself is from him and that the Spirit proceeds from both.

[AUGUSTINE.] If it was said of the Son through the prophet, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23), where was he sent except where he already was? If it was said of the Father, where could he be without his Wisdom, which reaches from end to end (Wis. 8)? Nor could he anywhere be without the Holy Spirit.

[GREGORY.] Therefore the Holy Spirit too was sent where he already was. Hence the Psalmist: “Where shall I go from your Spirit? And where shall I flee from your face?” [Col. 0528A] (Ps. 138). Nowhere do we read that the Father was sent. It is commonly asked why the Spirit appeared in fire; why in fire and tongues at once; why he is sometimes shown in a dove and sometimes in fire; and why he appeared over the Son of God in the form of a dove and over the disciples in fire. Let us consider these four questions. The Spirit is shown in fire because the Apostle says, “Our God is a consuming fire” (Heb. 12). This is true because through him the rust of sins is consumed. Of this fire Truth says, “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it should burn?” (Luke 12). By “earth” he means earthly hearts, which are trampled down by evil spirits because they heap up low things. He was shown in fiery tongues because a tongue corresponds to a word, and the Word, who is the Son of God, is one substance with the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0528B] Or he was shown in tongues because, just as a word proceeds through the tongue, so one touched by the Holy Spirit confesses God’s Only-begotten Son. Or again, he appeared in fiery tongues because he makes those whom he fills ardent and eloquent. For those who preach God out of love set their hearers’ hearts aflame. He is shown sometimes in a dove and sometimes in fire because he makes those whom he fills simple and ardent. For neither simplicity without zeal nor zeal without simplicity pleases God. Hence Truth says: “Be therefore prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10). Paul explains the serpent’s prudence when he says: “Do not become children in understanding.” And concerning the dove’s simplicity he says: “Be little children in malice” (1 Cor. 14). He appeared in the Lord through a dove, [Col. 0528C] and in the disciples through fire, because the righteous Judge did not wish to strike sinners but gently to correct them. Yet these people, who were simple human beings and therefore sinners, had to be set spiritually aflame against themselves and saved through repentance.

“And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.”

[AUGUSTINE.] That is, from the beginning of my preaching. The charity poured into your hearts through the Holy Spirit will give you confidence to speak (Rom. 5). Peter did not yet possess this charity when he denied the Lord. The Holy Spirit will bear witness in your hearts; you, however, in your voices, so that this may be fulfilled: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. 18).

[Col. 0528D] “I have spoken these things to you so that you may not be scandalized, making you outcasts from the synagogues.”

He sets forth what they were to suffer. Here he announces that the Jews would not receive him and would therefore expel those who preached about him. But he foretold the Spirit, who would strengthen them so that it would not be a stumbling-block to them; for “great peace have those who love” the law (Ps. 118) of God, which is charity itself.

A. 146 M. 244 R. 139 L. 250

“But the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is rendering service to God.”

It is as if he said: “They will cast you out of the synagogues, but do not fear isolation. For, separated from their assembly, you will gather so many in my name [Col. 0529A] that they, fearing lest their temple and law be abandoned, will kill you, thinking that they do well.” This is what the Apostle says: “They have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10).

“And they will do these things because they have known neither the Father nor me. But I have spoken these things to you so that, when their hour comes, you may remember that I told you.”

I foretold them so that unexpected events might not trouble you through ignorance, but, once foreseen, might be borne patiently when the dark hour of evil people comes.

A. 146[X]

“But I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you.”

He had not told them about the Holy Spirit, who would come to them [Col. 0529B] to console them when they suffered evils. When Christ departed, the Holy Spirit was necessary to console them, left bereft of Christ’s bodily presence.

“But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’”

He indicates that he would go so manifestly that there would be no need to ask where he was going. For they would see him ascending in a cloud, more certain of his glory than they had been before.

“But because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.”

Human affection was sorrowful because the bodily sight was being taken away.

“But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go. For if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come [Col. 0529C] to you; but if I go, I shall send him to you.”

If I do not take away the tender nourishment with which I have fed you, you will not hunger for solid food. If you cling carnally to flesh, you will not be capable of the Spirit. The meaning is: You cannot fully receive the Spirit so long as I am with you according to the flesh. Hence one who had already received the Spirit says: “Even if we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5).

“And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment.”

That is, he will give you, once fear is driven away, freedom to rebuke. The works of the Trinity are inseparable, but the Persons are commended individually, so that both unity and Trinity may be understood without confusion.

[Col. 0529D] “Concerning sin indeed, because they do not believe in me; but concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer.”

If a righteous person is at any time reproved, he is reproved concerning sin, not concerning righteousness. Hence it is written: “There is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin” (Eccl. 7). Likewise: “Do not become excessively righteous” [nimium] (ibid.). Here the righteousness of the wise person is not censured, but the pride of the presumptuous person. For whoever makes himself excessively righteous becomes unjust by that excess. One makes oneself excessively righteous either by saying that one has no sin, or by thinking that one becomes righteous not by God’s grace but by one’s own will. The world is thus convicted concerning sin because it does not believe in Christ; it is convicted concerning the righteousness of certain believers, for comparison with the faithful is a reproach to the unfaithful. [Col. 0530A] The sense is: Your righteousness, by which the world is convicted, will be that I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer; for you will believe in him whom you will not see. But when you see me, you will not see me humble as now, but exalted; not mortal, but eternal; not about to be judged, but about to judge. And because of this faith of yours—that is, your righteousness—the Holy Spirit will convict unbelievers. The same applies in the world regarding the baptism of infants. What is this righteousness by which, though they did not see him, the world would be convicted, unless it is that by which “the righteous lives by faith” (Heb. 10), and by which we, looking not at things seen but at things unseen, await in spirit and faith the hope of righteousness?

“But concerning judgment, because the prince of this world has already been judged.”

[Col. 0530B] The prince of this world is the devil, concerning whom elsewhere he says: “Behold, the prince of the world comes, and has nothing in me” (John 14). “World” is used both in a good and a bad sense. For just as a tree is full of leaves and fruit, and a threshing floor of chaff and grain, so the world is full of unbelievers and believers. The devil has been judged—that is, assigned by judgment to eternal fire. The world is convicted concerning judgment because it is judged with its prince. Let people therefore believe, lest they be convicted concerning sin. Let them pass into the number of the faithful, lest they be convicted concerning the righteousness of those whom, though justified, they do not imitate. Let them beware the future judgment, lest they be judged with the prince of the world.

Bede: “It is clear that, while the Son of God was in the world, he convicted the world—that is, the followers of the world—concerning the sin of their unbelief; concerning righteousness, because they would not imitate it; [Col. 0530C] and concerning judgment, because they followed the devil, who had already been judged and condemned. Yet not without reason does he say that the Spirit, when he comes, will do the same; for through his inspiration the minds of the disciples were to be strengthened, so that they would not fear to convict the world raging against them. The devil was judged by the Lord when he himself cast out demons and gave his disciples power to tread upon every power of the enemy” (Luke 10).

“I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.”

[AUGUSTINE.] This is not contrary to what he said above: “All things that I heard from my Father I have made known to you,” because it resembles that prophetic expression: “He who made the things that are to come.”

[Col. 0530D] “But when he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will teach you all truth.”

Some manuscripts read: “He will lead you into all truth.” Hence: “Lead me, O Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth” (Ps. 85). I do not think this truth can be fulfilled in this life. Hence the Apostle says: “Now I know in part; but then I shall know as I also am known” (1 Cor. 13). For what human being understands the Trinity as angels do? It is asked whether spiritual people have anything in their teaching that they keep silent from carnal people and say to spiritual people. If we say no, the Apostle’s words to the Corinthians will be objected: “I could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to carnal” (1 Cor. 3). But if we say that they do, we must fear lest, under this pretext, [Col. 0531A] they teach wicked things in secret. Therefore, once this is recognized—that spiritual and carnal people hear the same things, but each receives them according to their own capacity, the former as solid food and the latter as milk—there is understood to be no necessity that some secret teachings be withheld from little faithful ones and spoken separately to the more intelligent. What the Apostle says must be understood thus: You could not receive what I was saying as spiritual people, but as carnal people. Hence he says to the Hebrews: “You have become those needing milk, not solid food” (Heb. 5). From this it follows that spiritual people do not altogether keep these things silent from carnal people, because of the catholic faith which must be preached to all; yet neither should they expound them so as to weary those able to receive them by trying to bring the matter to their understanding in this way. Christ himself as man is called the pure milk of little ones; when he is rightly apprehended by spiritual people, he is found to be solid food and Lord of angels. Therefore little ones must not be fed milk in such a way that they never understand the Lord Christ; nor should they be weaned in such a way that they abandon Christ the man.

[Col. 0531B] “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak.”

Both the Son and the Holy Spirit are equal to the Father. But to explain at length the difference between proceeding and being born is difficult, and to define it is rash; for if the mind comprehends anything of it, it is nevertheless most difficult for the tongue to express it, however great the teacher who presides or the hearer who is present. The meaning is: “He will not speak from himself,” because he is not from himself. Therefore he will hear from him from whom he proceeds. For him, hearing is knowing; and knowing is being. Nor should it disturb us that a future-tense verb is used, because in that which is eternal, whatever tense of a verb is used is not used falsely. Although that immutable nature does not admit “was” and “will be,” but only “is”—hence, “I am who I am” (Exod. 3), and “He who is has sent me to you” (ibid.)—nevertheless, because of the mutability of times in which our own mutability exists, we do not falsely say that it was, is, and will be.

[Col. 0531C] “And he will announce to you the things that are to come.”

Many have had the spirit of prophecy. But because some heal the sick, raise the dead, and command demons, and yet do not know future things, this may be understood thus: that the Spirit, when he comes, would announce things to come by recalling to mind the joys of the heavenly homeland.

“He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.”

It is as if he said: God will do all these things through the Spirit—that is, through his goodness. “He will glorify me” by taking fear away from you and giving you more ardent love. What they themselves would do in the Holy Spirit, he said that the same Spirit would do, as in the saying: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.” The Greek word δοξάζω (*doxazō*) has been rendered by Latin translators, some as “will glorify,” others as “will make illustrious” (*clarificabit*). For δόξα (*doxa*), from which *doxazō* is derived, is translated both “brightness” and “glory.” And because glory makes people illustrious, and brightness makes them glorious, the meaning conveyed by either word is the same. Glory is widespread renown for someone accompanied by praise. This conferred nothing great upon Christ himself, but upon the world. For it is good to be praised; it benefits not the one praised but those who praise. False glory is threefold: in things, in people, or in both. One is deceived regarding things if one thinks good what is evil; likewise regarding people; and regarding both when a vice is thought to be a virtue and the person praised for it does not possess what he is thought to possess, whether he is good or bad. For giving one’s possessions to actors is a monstrous vice, not a virtue. And you know how widespread praise-filled renown for such people is, as in: [Col. 0532B] “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul” (Ps. 9). Those who praise such people are not deceived about the people but about the things, for what they believe to be good is evil. The vicious persons themselves are such as they appear. Those who praise hypocrites are not deceived about things but about people. But those who praise people believed to free their country by magical arts are deceived in both. True glory does not make the righteous blessed; nevertheless, those who praise may rightly glory because they love what is just. True glory is in the catholic Church. Hence the prophet: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth” (Ps. 56). The Son says, “The Spirit will receive from what is mine,” because the Holy Spirit receives from the Father, from whom the Son receives. The Holy Spirit receives from the Father by proceeding; the Son, by being born. The Father was born from no one and proceeded from no one. As the Father begot the Son—namely, life from life—so the Father gave him that life might proceed from him, as it also proceeds from himself.

[Col. 0532C] Truth is born from the Father; charity proceeds from both, to sanctify the creature.

[AUGUSTINE.] Wisdom is born from the Father; good will extends from both to creatures. Counsel is born from the Father; the gift of love goes forth from both to creatures. The Word is born from the Father; the good of kindness proceeds from both. Eternal splendor shone forth from the Father; from both proceeded the affection of good will [goodness]. Since, therefore, the whole Trinity is spirit—that is, incorporeal nature—the Holy Spirit is individually called “Spirit,” as the breath or breathing (*spiramen seu spiraculum*) of Father and Son. [Col. 0532D] For the Holy Spirit is breathed forth by the Father and Son in order to sanctify; nor does he come without the Father and Son, because the Trinity is undivided. The Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son through the disposition of distributing gifts; he proceeds, is breathed forth, and is sent in time through the infusion [outpouring] of graces. This breathing-forth, this temporal procession or mission, occurs daily, while different gifts are daily conferred upon different persons.

A. 149[III] M. 111 L. 119

“All things whatsoever the Father has are mine.”

[AMBROSE.] The meaning is: The very reality of what the Father is is in me, and I am from him; thus the Father is the Father of the Son, and the Son is the Son of the Father.

[Col. 0533A] A. 149[X]

“Therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.”

I said that the Spirit proceeds from that same source from which I am begotten, lest the Spirit be thought inferior to me or born from me, as I am from the Father.

“A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me, because I am going to the Father.” Therefore some of his disciples said to one another: “What is this that he says to us: ‘A little while, and you will not see me; and again a little while, and you will see me’; and, ‘Because I am going to the Father’?” They therefore said: “What is this that he says, ‘A little while’? We do not know what he is saying.”

This troubled them because he said, “A little while,” but it was revealed later. For in a little while he was to suffer, and they did not see him; again, in a little while he rose, and they saw him.

[Col. 0533B] [BEDE.] Or thus: They did not see him for a short time while he rested in the tomb; and they saw him for a short time when he appeared to them during the forty days after the resurrection. “For a short time you will see me, because I am going to the Father,” laying aside mortality and bringing human nature into heaven. But the statement, “and you will no longer see me,” must be understood as above, where he says: “Concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer”—namely, because they would no longer see him as mortal.

But Jesus knew that they wished to ask him and said to them: “Are you asking one another about this, because I said, ‘A little while, and you will not see me; and again a little while, and you will see me’? Amen, amen, I say to you: you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You indeed will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy.”

They were sorrowful at the Lord’s death, but soon rejoiced at the resurrection. Here “the world” signifies the enemies by whom Christ was killed.

[Col. 0533C] “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her hour has come. But when she has borne the child, she no longer remembers the distress because of joy that a human being has been born into the world.”

Childbirth is compared to joy more particularly when not a girl but a boy is born. The joy is Jesus himself, of whom the Apostle says: “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more” (Rom. 6).

“And so you now indeed have sorrow. But I shall see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you.”

[BEDE.] The Lord explains the comparison which he set forth concerning the woman. For the disciples had sorrow when the Lord suffered; but after the glory of the resurrection had been accomplished, they rejoiced on seeing the Lord (John 20). Their joy is not taken from them because, even if afterward they suffered persecutions and torments for Christ’s name, nevertheless, kindled by hope of the resurrection and of seeing him, they gladly bore every adversity; indeed, they counted it joy when they fell into various trials (Jas. 1). But when he says, “I shall see [Col. 0534A] you again, and your heart will rejoice,” it is understood thus: I shall rescue you from adversaries, crown you as victors, and prove that I have always seen you striving.

“And on that day you will not ask me anything.”

On the day of eternal vision you will not ask or inquire, because then there will be complete knowledge and sufficiency.

[AUGUSTINE.] This word *rogare*, “to ask,” signifies not only to request but also to inquire; and the Greek word from which it was translated has a term that can be understood in both ways. It is therefore ambiguous. These words can also be explained as the Lord speaking in the disciples’ persons to the whole Church, as there: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). “A little while, and you will no longer see me” refers to his saying, “Because I am going to the Father.” That is, by going to the Father I shall withdraw bodily sight, so that the Church may believe fruitfully. “And again a little while, and you will see me” refers to eternal vision. In this sense, understand “a little while” as the duration of this swiftly passing age. “You will weep,” he says, because all good people weep amid the miseries of this life, but lovers of the world rejoice.

[Col. 0534B] [BEDE.] He calls the holy Church a woman because of the fruitfulness of good works and because she never ceases to bear spiritual children to God. She never ceases to be tried by the temptations of the world as long as she persists in advancing in spiritual virtues while in the world. But when, after overcoming the contest of labors, she comes to the palm of victory, she no longer remembers the preceding distress because of the joy of the reward received. “For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory” [Col. 0534C] (Rom. 8), when we shall be like God and see him as he is (1 John 3), as John says in his Epistle.

[AUGUSTINE.] Now the Church labors in childbirth by groaning; then she will give birth in joy. Now she labors in childbirth by praying; then she will give birth by praising. And therefore a male child, because all the offices of action are directed to the fruit of contemplation.

[BEDE.] And as a woman rejoices when a human being is born into this world, so the Church is filled with exultation when a people is born into the life to come. Laboring greatly and groaning in the present for this birth, she suffers as one in labor. Nor should it seem new to anyone if one who has departed from this life is said to have been born: for just as someone is said to be born when emerging from the mother’s womb, so too one released from the bonds of the flesh and raised to eternal light may be called born. Hence ecclesiastical custom has prevailed that we call the days of martyrs and confessors of Christ—the days on which they passed from the world—their birthdays; and their celebrations are called not funeral observances but birthday festivals. It follows: “And you will have sorrow.” The whole Church, through the labors and straits of this life, advances toward the eternal rewards of heavenly joys, because, as the Apostle says, “Through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God” (Acts 14). When the Lord says, “But I shall see you again,” he promises the second coming, in which he will see the whole Church in order to reward it completely. And because in the fullness of that joy we shall not ask, now we must ask to arrive there.

[Col. 0535A] A. 150[III] M. 216 R. 125

“Amen, amen, I say to you: if you ask the Father anything in my name, he will give it to you.”

Whatever is sought contrary to salvation is not sought in the name of the Savior. When he says “in my name,” he does not mean the sound but the meaning of the sound. Thus one who thinks wrongly about Christ does not ask in his name, even if one utters his name. But one who, thinking rightly of him, asks for eternal salvation or anything pertaining to it receives when it is fitting to receive. Nor are certain things denied because they are delayed in order to be given at an appropriate time.

“Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you shall receive, that your joy may be full.”

[Col. 0535B] Whatever else is asked besides the blessed life, or what pertains to it, is nothing in comparison with so great a thing. It can be understood in two ways: “Until now you have not asked in my name,” either because you have not known my name as it ought to be known, or because whatever else you have asked must be counted as nothing in comparison with so great a thing as that which you ought to have asked. He then adds how they can ask for full joy: because he will make spiritual beings out of all living creatures, so that, casting off bodily images, they may cling with the pure sight of the mind to the sincere light.

A. 131[X]

“I have spoken these things to you in proverbs.”

A merely animate human being thinks carnally, not spiritually, about whatever he hears concerning God’s nature. Therefore the things he hears concerning God’s incorporeal substance are proverbs to him—not because he regards them as proverbs, but because he thinks as those do who hear proverbs and do not understand them. But the spiritual person asks in his name because he understands that he is of the same substance as the Father. Spiritual people drive away vanities and fictions as troublesome flies and, with inward vision as far as they can, know the incorporeal God.

[Col. 0535C] “The hour is coming when I shall no longer speak to you in proverbs, but shall openly declare the Father to you.”

He plainly signifies the hour when he was to give them the grace of the Holy Spirit. We may also understand the hour he promises as occurring in the future life, in which he will openly declare the Father to the elect—that is, he will show the Father—where the elect truly ask in Jesus’ name, while they intercede on account of our frailty, that we may attain a share in their salvation. It is rightly said, “on that day,” because there are no dark troubles there, but everlasting light. The same spirits of the elect in that heavenly city may even ask for themselves, because they desire the time of universal judgment to come, so that they may receive also the blessedness of their bodies. Hence John says: “I saw under the altar the souls of those slain for the word of God and for the testimony which they had, and they cried with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, O holy and true Lord, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?’” (Rev. 6). Immediately it is added: “And a white robe was given to each of them, [Col. 0536A] and they were told to rest a little while, until the number of their brothers should be completed” (ibid.). The souls now have individual robes because they enjoy their own happiness alone; then they will receive two, when, after the full number of their brethren is completed at the end, they also rejoice in receiving immortal bodies.

“On that day you will ask in my name, and I do not tell you that I shall ask the Father for you.”

He says this because of his divinity consubstantial with the Father, in which Father and Son together hear those who ask and together grant what is asked—something visible only to spiritual eyes. But what he says to Peter, “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22), and what John says of him, “We have an advocate with our Father, Jesus Christ” (1 John 2), refer to his humanity. Or thus: “I shall not pray for you,” because I shall instead fulfill what I have hitherto prayed for. How did he pray? Because he had not yet ascended. For if he had not ascended, no certainty of our own ascent would have remained. But now his humanity, seated at the right hand of the Father, is both the certainty and pledge that we too shall ascend. Hence Jerome, in his Epistle to the Romans: “The Arians commonly raise the slanderous objection that the one for whom intercession is made is greater than the one interceding. They must be answered that God does not suffer forgetfulness, so as always to be moved on behalf of those whom he himself chose; rather, he is said to intercede in that he always shows the Father the man whom he assumed, as our pledge, and offers him as the true and eternal high priest.”

[Col. 0536C] “For the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and believed that I came forth from God.”
