The Father loves us because we love the Son, although we receive from Father and Son the ability to love Father and Son, through the charity given by the Spirit, whom we ourselves love with Father and Son. He who loves first causes himself to be loved in us.

“I came forth from the Father and came into the world. Again I leave the world and go to the Father.”

He came forth from the Father because he is from him; and, having assumed flesh, he came visibly into the world, yet without leaving the Father. He left the world by bodily departure, not by withdrawing his governing presence. He goes to the Father because he brought his humanity into the invisible realm of the Father’s majesty. He left the world because he took away from the sight of lovers of the world what they had seen. He returns to the Father because he taught his lovers that he must be believed equal to the Father.

[Col. 0536D] His disciples said to him: “Behold, now you speak openly and say no proverb. Now we know that you know all things, and that you have no need for anyone to question you. By this we believe that you came forth from God.”

[ALCUIN.] They thought he was speaking openly, though they were unable to comprehend his mysteries. They clearly show that the Lord was speaking about things which pleased them to hear and which they wanted to ask. Therefore they believed him to be God. For an evident indication of divinity is to know the secrets of thoughts.

A. 152[IV] M. 287 R. 168

Jesus answered them: “Do you now believe? Behold, the hour is coming—and has now come—when you will be scattered, each one to his own place, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me.”

You believe as little children, to whom all high matters are still proverbs. The hour of the Passion is coming and is already near, in which I must tread the winepress alone. But you will be scattered, each to his own place—that is, into the fear of your own unbelief. It is as if he said: You will be so disturbed that what you now think you believe, you will afterward abandon. This appeared in Cleophas, when he said: “We had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel” (Luke 24).

[AUGUSTINE.] A little earlier he had said: “I go to the Father”; now he says: “The Father is with me.” Who goes to one who is with him? But this is a saying for one who understands; for one who does not understand, it is a proverb. For one who understands, it is a word of truth; [Col. 0537B] for one who does not understand, a proverb—that is, a word far from truth. Going to the Father belongs to his humanity; the Father’s being with him belongs to his divinity.

A. 153[X]

“I have spoken these things to you so that you may have peace in me. In the world you will have tribulation; but take courage: I have conquered the world.”

For this peace we endure tribulation, in order that we may reign happily in it without end. This is the peace for which we are Christians; for which we are initiated by the sacraments; for which we are instructed in every way; for which we receive the Spirit as a pledge; for which we believe and hope in Christ and are kindled by love for him. This is consolation and deliverance amid tribulations. Thus [Col. 0537C] he concludes his discourse to the disciples and turns his words to the Father.

Jesus spoke these things and, lifting his eyes to heaven, said: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son.”

The Lord could have prayed silently, but he gave us an example of prayer. The Apostle speaks of this glorification, which took its beginning from his resurrection: “God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2). The meaning is: The hour for sowing humility has come; do not delay the fruit of glory. Of this humility the Apostle says: “He became obedient to the Father unto death” (ibid.). It follows:

“That your Son may glorify you.”

[Col. 0537D] The Father’s glory can neither be diminished nor increased in God; among human beings, however, it was lesser when God was known only in Judaea (Ps. 75). For the children had not yet praised the Lord’s name from the rising of the sun to its setting. Since this was accomplished through Christ’s Gospel, the Son plainly glorified the Father. It is as if he said: “Raise me up, that through me you may become known throughout the whole world.” It follows:

“As you have given him authority over all flesh, that he may give eternal life to all that you have given him.”

“All flesh,” that is, every human being. The whole human being is signified by a part, as the Apostle says: “Let every soul be subject to higher powers” (Rom. 13), that is, every person. The Father gave authority to the Son according to his humanity; for according to his divinity, all things were made through him (John 1).

[Col. 0538A] “And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.”

The order of the words is: that they may know you, and Christ whom you sent, as the only true God. The Holy Spirit is consequently understood as well, because he is the consubstantial charity of both. Life is the knowledge of the one God: here it is from the Father; in the world to come it will be complete. Whoever therefore advances in this knowledge tends more fully toward life. But when knowledge is complete, praise too will be without end. And this is that glorification; yet first he is glorified here, while he is made known to the faithful. Hence follows:

> I have glorified you on earth; I have completed the work [Col. 0538B] which you gave me to do.

The Passion still remained, but he says that he has completed what he knew with absolute certainty that he would complete; as in: “They pierced my hands and my feet,” etc. (Ps. 21).

> And now, Father, glorify me with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world existed.

The Son glorified the Father by preaching to the nations; the Father, by placing the Son at his right hand. In saying, “I have glorified,” “I have completed,” he uses the past tense for the future, and to show that it had already been accomplished in predestination. He disclosed this predestination by adding, “with the glory which I had.” The order of the words is: “which I had with you before the world [Col. 0538C] existed.” This is the force of his saying “now”: as if to say, “As then in predestination, so now in fulfillment.” What exists is destined; what does not exist is predestined and prepared. Thus the Son, according to divinity coeternal with the Father, was predestined before the foundation of the world according to his human nature; and we, in him, that we might be his members, were chosen and predestined before all times. Christ’s humanity therefore asks to possess in you what it possessed in the Father’s predestination.

> I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world.

He says, “I have manifested,” not because the manifestation without parables is already complete, but because it will most certainly come to pass. All this could be said of the future faithful; [Col. 0538D] but that it may be understood of the disciples alone whom he then had, this is pressed by what he says below: “When I was with them, I kept them,” etc. Yet from the beginning of the prayer—“Father, the hour has come”—as far as “And now, Father, glorify me,” he intended all his own to be understood. Let us see what he means to say. It is written: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75). Therefore, “I have manifested,” not that name of yours which is “God,” but that which is “my Father.” This name cannot be manifested without the manifestation of the Son. “Whom you gave me,” he says according to his humanity.

> They were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word.

[Col. 0539A] They belonged to the Father, who predestined them through the Son because of his goodness; and thus they belonged to the indivisible Trinity. From it [or: from him], the Son, inasmuch as he is man, received them to teach.

> Now they have known that all things which you gave me are from you, because the words which you gave me I have given them; and they received them, and truly knew that I came forth from you, and believed that you sent me.

All things which you gave me as man are from you. Or thus: the Father gave all things at once when he begot him who possesses all things. In begetting the Word, that is, the Father gave all things. But in saying, “they truly knew,” he explained it by adding, “and they believed”—understand, “truly.” “I came forth from you” is the same as “you sent me.” “They knew” is the same as “they believed.” “They believed” [Col. 0539B] was added lest anyone suppose that this knowledge was already through hope rather than faith. The disciples were not yet such as he calls them in words of the past tense; but since they were to become such after receiving the Holy Spirit, the past is used for the future. This became plain when their leader denied him three times.

> I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you gave me, because they are yours; and all mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I have been glorified in them.

That is, “I shall be glorified in them,” namely when through them I am made known to all believers as glorified at the Father’s right hand. By saying, “mine are yours, and yours are mine,” he shows in a special way that the saints under discussion belong to him by whom they were created and sanctified—namely, to the Father and the Son. And thus all things subject to them must belong to him whose they themselves are. Note that one should not pray for the evil who are lost, since he says: “I do not pray for the world.”

> And now I am no longer in the world, and these are in the world, and I am coming to you.

“I am no longer in the world,” namely in bodily presence. He shows as certain what was still future. In saying, “I am coming to you,” he explains why he said, “I am no longer in the world.”

> Holy Father, keep in your name those whom you gave me, that they may be one as we are.

As man, he prays to the Father for the disciples; as God, he says that he is one with the Father. He does not say, “that they may be one with us,” or, “that they and we may be one.” Let them be one in their own [Col. 0539D] nature, just as we are one in ours.

> When I was with them, I kept in your name those whom you gave me; I guarded them, and none of them perished except the son of perdition, that the Scripture might be fulfilled.

Judas, by imitation the son of the devil, who is perdition itself, fulfilled the Scriptures which prophesied concerning him. We must not understand that the Father and Son preserve in alternation, as though one succeeds the other. For Father, Son, and Holy Spirit preserve together: they are one God. But Scripture does not raise us unless it descends to us. When it speaks in this way, let us understand it to distinguish the persons, not to separate the nature.

> But now I am coming to you, and I speak these things in the world, [Col. 0540A] that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves.

That is: “That they may be one as we are,” which will be granted them by me. Behold, he says that he speaks in the world, though shortly before he said, “I am no longer in the world.” Therefore, though he had not yet departed, he was still here; and because he was soon to depart, in a manner of speaking he was already no longer here.

> I have given them your word, and the world has hated them.

Still using words of the past tense, he foretells future things. He then adds why the world hates them:

> Because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.

This was granted them by regeneration; for by generation they were of the world. Hence elsewhere: “I chose you out of the world” (John 15).

> [Col. 0540B] I do not pray that you take them out of the world, but that you preserve them from evil.

From this you have that the saints ought not to pray to pass out of the world if it is not yet fitting for them, just as it was not yet fitting for these. He repeats the statement already made.

> They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. Sanctify them in truth: your word is truth.

One may ask how they were not of the world if they had not yet been sanctified in truth; or, if they had already been sanctified, why he asks that they be sanctified. They had been sanctified, but he asks that they become holier and advance in holiness. Hence the Apostle: “He who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of [Col. 0540C] the Lord Jesus” (Phil. 1). Truth is Christ, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). As though he said: “Sanctify them in me.” Hence follows: “Your word”—that is, I, consubstantial with you—“is truth.”

> As you sent me into the world, I also sent them into the world.

That is: because you sent me, I sent them.

> And for their sake I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth.

“For their sake I sanctify myself,” that is, I sanctify them in myself. He says this because they are his members. Hence follows: “That they too may be sanctified in truth,” that is, in me according to divinity, by which the man with whom I am clothed was also sanctified from the beginning of [Col. 0540D] his creation. He says this because the Word and man became one person. Therefore he sanctified himself in himself—that is, himself as man in himself as the Word.

> But I pray not for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word.

Here we must understand not only those who heard the apostles in the flesh, but all to whom their word has come and will come, who have believed and will believe. It may seem that Jesus did not here pray for some of his own, unless we carefully examine his words. For he does not seem to have prayed for those who were not then with him when he said these things, nor afterward believed through the apostles’ words, such as the Apostle Paul, who was made an apostle neither by men nor through man, but through the revelation of [Col. 0541A] Jesus Christ, as he himself says (Gal. 1). Likewise, he does not seem to have prayed for the ancient righteous, nor for those who had already believed, whether through himself or in any manner whatever: Nathanael; Joseph of Arimathea, who asked Pilate for the Lord’s body; his mother and the other women; those who cried with branches, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 117); and the five hundred brethren to whom he appeared at once after the resurrection (1 Cor. 15). The thief also believed on the cross (Luke 23), when the teachers failed. We should therefore understand “through their word” so as to believe that the very word of faith which they preached is signified here. It is called “their word” because it was principally preached and first inculcated by them. Nor is it therefore not the word of God because it is called theirs; for [Col. 0541B] Paul says that the Thessalonians received it from him not as the word of men, but as it truly is, the word of God (1 Thess. 4). It is God’s because God gave it; it is theirs because God first entrusted it to them to be preached. The thief possessed their word in faith; the ancient righteous possessed their word, concerning whom it is established that they could never have been saved unless they had believed in the Mediator who was to come. Thus those already dead who did not doubt that he would rise again are found more faithful than those who, seeing his death, lost the hope they had held concerning his resurrection. Hence some said: “But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel” (Luke 24). We must therefore believe that all who possessed the faith which the apostles preached after Christ’s resurrection belonged to Christ’s prayer. [Col. 0541C] It follows:

> That they all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you.

Understand: “we are one.” The Father and Son are one substantially; we, however, can be in them, though not substantially. We are in them as creatures are in the Creator; we can now be one in them by faith and charity, and in the future by a fuller love. Hence follows:

> That they too may be one in us.

Let them become one temple of God by believing, as he shows by adding:

> That the world may believe that you sent me.

[Col. 0541D] If we place the word “I pray” a third time, the sense will be clearer in this form: “I pray that all may be one; I pray that they too may be one in us; I pray that the world may believe that you sent me.”

> And I have given them the glory which you gave me, that they may be one as we are one.

“Glory,” that is, the immortality which you gave me, I have given them. Because of the immovability of predestination, he signifies future things in words of the past tense.

> I in them, and you in me, that they may be perfected into one.

He briefly shows that he is the mediator between God and human beings, and that through him the Father abides in us. His addition, “perfected,” indicates perfect blessedness.

> [Col. 0542A] And that the world may know that you sent me.

Sometimes “to know” is used for “to believe”; but here, where he speaks of completion, the knowledge to be understood is such as will be by sight, not such as is now by faith. For as long as we believe what we do not see, we are not yet perfected, as we shall be when we see.

> And I loved them as you loved me.

He who loves the only-begotten Son also loves his members whom he adopted. We are not thereby equal to the only-begotten Son because it is said, “as [you loved] me.” For “as” does not always signify equality, but is sometimes used in the sense of “because,” as here and in: “As you sent me into the world, I also sent them into the world.” The Father, by the grace of love, brought the members of his Only-begotten to equality with the angels; [Col. 0542B] but he raised the flesh of his Only-begotten above the excellence of every angel, since flesh and Word are one person. Yet there are some who even prefer us to angels, saying that Christ died for us, not for angels. What is this but a desire to glory in impiety? For Christ, according to the Apostle, died for the ungodly (Rom. 3); in this, not our merit but God’s mercy is commended.

> Father, I desire that those whom you gave me may be with me where I am, that they may see my glory which you gave me.

This he says with respect to the creaturehood in which he was made man. Yet he was not there then, but was soon [Col. 0542C] to ascend there. Or he said “I am” because of the unity of person in which God is man and man is God. But with respect to the form of God, he is everywhere. Hence the thief heard: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23). According to that in which he was man, his soul was that very day to be in hell, and his flesh in the tomb. But according to that in which he was God, he was also in paradise. Therefore, after saying, “that they may be,” he added, “with me.” For even the miserable can be where he is who is everywhere; but only the blessed are with him, because they cannot be blessed except from him. Let us take whatever example we please. Just as a blind person, even if he is where light is, is nevertheless not with the light, so a wicked person—or a pious person not yet fit—although he cannot be anywhere where Christ is not, is nevertheless [Col. 0542D] not with Christ, as Christ is understood here to have meant when he said: “I desire that where I am, they too may be with me.” For he was speaking altogether of that vision in which we shall see him as he is (1 John 3). Hence he adds, “that they may see,” not “that they may believe.” This is faith’s reward, not faith: seeing God’s glory follows.

> Because you loved me before the foundation of the world.

In him he also loved us before the foundation of the world by predestination, because we are his members; and we are loved in him who is wholly loved, if we understand the saying, “I desire that where I am, they too may be with me,” with reference to the Son’s coeternity with the Father. We shall be in the Father with Christ. But he as he is; we as we are. He says, “I desire,” and what the Almighty wills cannot fail to happen. Indeed, all power belongs to him, [Col. 0543A] but only those whom he chose are his own, as he says: “I chose you out of the world” (John 15). The Father gave them to him—that is, drew them to him.

A. 154[III] M. 112 L. 119

> Righteous Father, the world has not known you, but I have known you.

The unrighteous world has not known you; but the reconciled world has known you, not by merit but by grace.

A. 135[X]

> And these have known that you sent me, and I have made your name known to them, and I will make it known, that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.

I have made your name known through faith; I shall make it known through hope. I made it known, with an end, to those on pilgrimage; [Col. 0543B] I shall make it known without end to those who reign. And thus their knowing you is grace, through your having sent me.

## Chapter 160

M. 291[IV] R. 172 L. 279 A. 156

> Then Jesus came with them to a country-place called Gethsemane, across the torrent Cedron, where there was a garden, into which he and his disciples entered.

[Bede.] Gethsemane is a place at the foot of the Mount of Olives, and is interpreted “valley of the fat ones.” There fat bulls surrounded the Lord, and many calves encircled him (Ps. 21). Approaching death, he came into the valley of fatness, he who through the valley of humility and the fatness of charity underwent death for us. [Col. 0543C] [Albinus.] He chose to be seized in a garden in order to blot out the sin committed in the garden of delights. He chose to be apprehended beyond the torrent Cedron, and, according to the Psalmist: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way” (Ps. 109). On the way of this life he drank from the torrent of the Passion; therefore he lifted up his head. *Cedron* is a Greek genitive plural, which in Latin may be rendered “of cedars.”

A. 157[X]

> Judas also, who betrayed him, knew the place, because Jesus had often met there with his disciples.

L. 292 M. 292 R. 173

> And when he came to the place, M. R. he said to his disciples, [Col. 0543D] “Sit here,” L. M. R., “and pray that you may not enter into temptation,” M. R., “until I go there and pray.”

[Jerome.] The order is: “Sit until I go and pray; and pray that you may not be overcome by temptation.” Those who are separated in prayer are separated in the Passion: he prays, while they sleep, oppressed by the fatness of their hearts. [Bede.] When he prays on the mountain, he silently admonishes us that we ought to pray for heavenly goods. When he prays in the valley of fatness, he teaches us that humility must be maintained in prayer, together with the abundance of inward love.

> And taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, James and John, he began to be sorrowful and distressed.

He takes no others here than at the Transfiguration, to whom he reveals more secret things. To prove the truth of the assumed [Col. 0544A] humanity, the preliminary stirring of passion truly makes him sorrowful, yet passion does not rule his mind. It should be known that Christ could by nature have escaped death, as Adam could have escaped death before sin. For in him there was no debt of guilt, no trace of any sin. But he voluntarily assumed our infirmities which do not separate one from God, unlike ignorance or concupiscence, which do separate. As he assumed true humanity, so too he assumed human infirmities, in order to nail them to the cross and make us strong. Accordingly, he assumed our will and sadness. I confidently say “sadness,” since I preach the cross. But there is a kind of sadness and fear that overwhelms reason and leads a person into sin, disregarding God’s commandment, as Peter denied through fear. It is of this kind that interpreters speak when they say that Christ did not fear, he who came to suffer and had rebuked Peter’s timidity. There is another, moderate fear, naturally present in every human being and without sin, like hunger and thirst; and this was in Christ. For he shrank from death. He was also sorrowful on account of the most unhappy Judas, the stumbling of all the apostles, the rejection of the Jews, and the destruction of Jerusalem.

M. 293[IV] R. 174 A. 107

> Then he said to them: “My soul is sorrowful unto death.”

Hence elsewhere he says: “I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished” (Luke 12). [Col. 0544C] He is sorrowful unto death, until his Passion delivers his apostles. For bodily death is release from suffering in Christ and in his own. [Bede.] Christ fears, while Peter does not fear. Peter says, “I lay down my life for you.” Christ says, “My soul is troubled.” Both are true and full of reason: the inferior does not fear, while the superior bears the feeling of one who fears. For the former, as a human being, does not know the force of death; the latter, as God established in a body, displays the frailty of flesh, so that the impiety of those who reject the sacrament of the Incarnation might be excluded. It follows:

> Stay here and keep watch with me.

[Gregory.] Endure the burden of temptation, keeping watch [Col. 0544D] against the sleep of unbelief and the torpor of the mind. The others indeed I ordered to sit there, as inferior to this struggle, preserving them in safety; but you, as stronger, I have brought thus far. Yet I do not wish you to advance farther. You are not yet able. Therefore remain here watching, as I also watch, so that each person may stand in the rank of his calling, since every grace, however great, has one higher than itself. I brought them to this point, especially Peter, so confident in himself, that they might see and hear where human ability lies and how it is obtained. Let them see him falling on his face; let them hear him saying, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” And let them learn not to think highly of themselves, but to esteem humble things; not to be quick in promising, but diligent in worship. For this reason he also led those who seemed more faithful and strong, like Peter, in whom boasting could likewise easily find a place because of confidence in faith. Those of middling strength, however, are safeguarded, as regards the danger of boasting, by the very smallness of their faith.

M. 294[I] R. 175 L. 201 A. 181

> And he went forward from them about a stone’s throw.

[Bede.] Figuratively, he indicates that they should direct the stone toward him—that is, bring the intention of the Law, which was written on stone, as far as himself. For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Rom. 10).

> And kneeling down, he fell upon his face and [Col. 0545B] prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him, saying: “Father, if it is possible; Abba, Father, all things are possible to you; my Father, if it is possible, take this cup away from me.”

[Jerome.] By the posture of his body he displayed the humility of his mind, and humility is the chief means of exaltation. For no one is exalted by God unless he has humbled himself for God’s sake. [Bede.] In saying, “Abba, Father,” he shows God to be the Savior of both peoples. For *abba* has the same meaning as *father*, but *abba* is Hebrew, while *pater* is Greek and Latin. Thus he himself first invokes him in both languages, to teach that he must be invoked by both peoples. For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek. [Gregory.] Insofar as he began [Col. 0545C] to fear and to be sorrowful, he also prays that the cup of the Passion may pass from him, so that he might not taste its bitterness at all—if this were possible according to God’s justice. For when he said, “if it is possible,” he referred this both to God’s power and to his justice; since, in respect to his justice—because he is not only powerful but just—nothing is possible except what is just. But the Father’s justice required that Christ should suffer, and from the foundation of the world this sacrament of our salvation had been set forth in him. Therefore he suffered, not because he willed to suffer—indeed, he recoiled from it—but because he loved the Father, whom he knew to will this, and because through his death he desired the salvation of his neighbor. Nor does it follow that, if he willed to suffer for this reason, he therefore willed suffering itself; as may be seen in the case of a sick person who wills to be cut or cauterized in order to be healed, yet does not will to be cut, but wholly recoils from it. It also happens that someone imprisoned wills his own son to be put in prison so that he himself may thereby escape, yet he does not will his son to be imprisoned, but rather grieves over it. For will is never without love, since we will what delights us; but we commonly abhor what causes distress. Hence in the future life, where there will be no suffering, nothing will happen against the will. Thus the martyrs endured pains and hardships against their will; otherwise there would be no merit in them. They fled their persecutors insofar as they could, yet they willed to suffer because of their love for Christ. But to will to be stoned or burned—if anyone could will it—would still have no merit; rather, to suffer truly for Christ and to will to be mutilated for love of God has merit. [Col. 0546A] For where Christ is laid as the foundation, where God is established as the highest and greater cause, there alone is merit. It is also clear that martyrdom or any external good does not give a good will or love; it displays what is already possessed and sometimes increases it. But because it did not increase [the text appears to read *non plus*] in Christ, he merited no more in the Passion than before, both salvation for us and for himself the state in which after the Passion he can neither be sorrowful nor troubled nor suffer in any way. That martyrdom is not voluntary in itself is also plain because it is not pleasant. Among desirable things, some are pleasant goods sought for their own sake, such as seeing God. Others are goods not pleasant, sought for the sake of something else, such as martyrdom. The Lord made this plain to Peter when he said: “And he will lead you where you do not will to go” (John 21). If it is objected that Christ is said to have been offered because he himself willed it, we say that he willed it—that is, he approved his death as necessary for all. Thus the Apostle also understands “to will.” “What I will,” he says—that is, what I approve as to be done—“I do not do; but what I do not will,” that is, what I do not approve as to be done, “that I do” (Rom. 7). But Jesus, displaying devotion in his prayer, as one loving and pleased with the Father’s dispositions, added:

M. 195[I] R. 136 L. 282 A. 42

> [Col. 0546C] Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will.

[Jerome.] What he had anxiously refused out of human weakness, returning into himself he confirms by obedience and strength of mind. “Let not that happen,” he says, “which human feeling speaks, but that for which I was sent.” [Bede.] He thus shows that when what we do not wish to happen is imminent, we should ask in our weakness that it not happen, so that in strength we may be ready for our Creator’s will to be done even against our own will. [Origen.] For just as we should not be greatly self-confident, lest we seem to profess our own strength, so we ought not to act with excessive faintheartedness or despair, lest we appear to declare the impotence of God our helper. [Bede.] Many are saddened by approaching death, [Col. 0546D] but let them have an upright heart. Let them avoid death as far as they can; but if they cannot, let them say what the Lord said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” Behold, you have human will expressed; see what an upright heart says: “But not what I will, but what you will.” Hence elsewhere: “I came not to do my own will,” namely that which I temporarily assumed from the Virgin, “but the will of him who sent me” (John 6), which I had eternally with the Father and always approve by the rational faculty of my soul. He prays that the cup may pass because he is man; but he accomplishes the dispensation because he is obedient to the Father. The sense is: “If death dies, let the cup pass without my dying.” But because this cannot happen otherwise, let what you will be done. [Jerome.] In another sense, he asks this not so much from fear of suffering as from mercy toward the former people, lest he drink the cup offered by that people. Thus he expressly said: “This cup”—that is, the Jewish people, who can have no excuse if they kill me, since they possess prophets who foretell me. [Remigius.] “If therefore it is possible for the multitude of Gentiles to believe without the destruction of the Jews, I decline the Passion. But if they must be blinded so that others may see, let not my will but yours be done.”

M. 296 R. 177 L. 284

> And when he rose from prayer, he came to his disciples and found them sleeping. And he said to them: “Why are you sleeping thus? Could you not keep watch with me for one hour? Keep watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation.”

[Col. 0547B] [Bede.] He clearly shows that he prayed also for the apostles, whom he diligently admonished to watch and pray. For because of the greatness of their sorrow they cannot overcome sleep, but as they sleep in mind, so also in body. [Jerome.] It is indeed impossible for a person not to be tempted; he does not say, “that you may not be tempted,” but “that you may not enter into temptation”—that is, that temptation may not overcome you and hold you in its snares. The martyr who shed blood for confessing the Lord was indeed tempted, but was not bound in the nets of temptation. If, however, he denied the Lord, then temptation would overcome him.

M. 297[I4] R. 178 A. 70

> The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.

[Col. 0547C] This is said against the rash, who think themselves able to do whatever they have believed. But as much as we trust in the ardor of the mind, so much should we fear the frailty of the flesh; nevertheless, according to the Apostle, let us put to death the deeds of the flesh (Rom. 8).

M. 298[VI] R. 179

> Again, a second time, he went away and prayed.

He went alone to pray for all, who alone was to suffer for all.

L. 283[X]

> But an angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him.

Elsewhere we read that angels ministered to him (Matt. 9). Thus, as evidence of his divinity, they ministered [Col. 0547D] to him; but as evidence of his humanity, he was strengthened by an angel. [Bede.] He is said to have been strengthened in the same manner in which he was said to be sorrowful—namely, for our sake, not for his own.

> And being in agony, he prayed more earnestly, saying:

M. 298[VI] R. 179

> My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done.

In agony—that is, in the struggle of death—he prayed more earnestly, to teach us to pray more devoutly in dangerous conflict. He prays that, if Nineveh cannot otherwise be saved unless the gourd withers, the Father’s will may be done. [Jerome.] That is: if the people signified by Nineveh cannot be saved unless the gourd withers, [Col. 0548A] that is, unless the flesh of Christ dies, let the Father do with it what he wills.

L. 283[X]

> And his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground.

It is contrary to nature to sweat blood; but by the ground watered with blood he declares that earthly people have been redeemed by his blood.

L. 284[II] M. 298 R. 179

> And when he rose, he came again to his disciples and found them sleeping because of sorrow. M. R. For their eyes were heavy. R. And they did not know what to answer him.

[Col. 0548B] [Jerome.] The eyes of the apostles were growing faint, with the denial near at hand.

M. And leaving them, he again went away and prayed a third time. M. R., saying the same words.

[Origen.] Because of the good end that would follow after the cup’s bitterness had been drunk, he prays so often that the Father’s will may be done. [Remigius.] For this reason he had previously consecrated his bodily blood to be shed for remission. He prayed three times so that we too may pray for pardon for past sins, protection from present evils, and safeguard from future dangers, and so that we may direct every prayer to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Likewise, just as the temptation of desire is threefold, so is that of fear. There is the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and worldly ambition; and there is fear of death, fear of disgrace, and fear of pain. Against all these he teaches that we must arm ourselves with prayer. Hence, because of the threefold temptation of the Passion, the Lord may be understood to have prayed three times.

M. 299[IV] R. 180 A. 103

> Then he came to his disciples and said to them: “Sleep now and rest.”

[Hilary.] The reason why, on returning and finding them asleep, he rebukes them at the first return, is silent at the second, and commands them to rest at the third, is this: after the Resurrection, he rebuked them when they were scattered, distrustful, and fearful; secondly, after sending the Paraclete Spirit, he visited their eyes, made heavy for beholding the freedom of the Gospel. For for a while, held fast by love of the Law, [Col. 0548D] they were occupied by a kind of sleep of faith. But thirdly, by the return of his glory, he will restore them to security and rest.

> Behold, the hour has drawn near, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinners.

[Augustine.] It is understood that after saying, “Sleep now and rest,” the Lord was silent for a little while and the disciples rested. For according to the second [Gospel] of Mark, he added, “It is enough; you have now rested,” and then added, “The hour has come.”

> Rise; let us go. Behold, he who betrays me has drawn near.

[Jerome.] As if to say: “They will not find us afraid; let us go of our own accord to meet them, so that they may see the confidence of those about to suffer.” We ought to offer ourselves voluntarily when it is not expedient to flee death, and not before.

## Chapter 161

M. 300[I] R. 181 L. 275

> And while he was still speaking, behold, Judas, one of the twelve, having received a cohort, came; and with him a large crowd, with lanterns, torches, weapons, swords, and clubs, from the chief priests, scribes, and elders of the people.

[Augustine.] The cohort was not Jewish but consisted of soldiers received from the governor, so that no one might dare resist those making the arrest. A large crowd handed over by the Jews also came with Judas, so that if anyone dared resist, he could not stand against so many. Whoever despairs of God’s help places confidence in worldly strength. Yet he betrays his master at night, so that he might be found without the crowds that often came in the daytime. They come with lanterns and torches so that, if he wished to hide, he might be sought by these means.

M. 301[II] R. 182 L. 286

> Now he who betrayed him had given them a sign, saying: “Whomever I shall kiss, he is the one. Seize him, and lead him away carefully.”

[Jerome.] Wretched Judas thought that the signs which the Savior had performed were done by magical arts. And because perhaps he had heard that the Lord was transfigured on the mountain, he feared that by a similar transfiguration he might slip from the servants’ hands. He therefore gives the sign of a kiss with the devil’s poison, just as Cain offered a treacherous and rejected sacrifice (Gen. 4). Hence they put wine with vinegar on the cross.

> And immediately, approaching Jesus, he said: “Hail, Rabbi.” And he came near to Jesus to kiss him. But Jesus said to him: “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss? Friend, for what have you come?” And he kissed him.

[Ambrose.] With shameless and criminal conscience he calls him master and presses a kiss upon him whom he betrays. Yet he retains something of a disciple’s shame, because he did not hand him over openly to the persecutors, but by the sign of a kiss. The Lord receives the kiss, not to teach us dissimulation, but lest he seem to flee betrayal; and he fulfills what is written: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceable” (Ps. 119). His saying, “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” should, I think, be pronounced interrogatively, as though he reproved the traitor with an affectionate feeling. As if to say: “With a pledge of love you inflict a wound; under the office of charity you shed blood; by an instrument of peace you bring about death; as servant you betray your Lord, as disciple your master.” [Jerome.] This word, “friend,” must be understood by antiphrasis: “friend” is said by the contrary, of one who was not a friend but an enemy. Or he is called friend because he was amicably chosen by the Lord as an apostle, just as the man in the parable was amicably invited to the wedding and is told: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” (Matt. 22).

A. 159[X]

> Jesus therefore, knowing all things that were coming upon him, [Col. 0550A] came forward and said to them: “Whom do you seek?”

[Augustine.] He did not fail to know what they wanted, but, prepared to die, he asks so that they might know that he was the one whom they sought.

They answered him, “Jesus of Nazareth.” Jesus said to them, “I am he.” Judas, who was betraying him, was also standing with them. Therefore, when he said to them, “I am he,” they drew back and fell to the ground.

Where now is the protection of armed men? A single utterance—“I am he”—cast down the crowd without any weapon. What will he do when judging, who did this while being judged? [ALBINUS.] What will he be able to do when reigning, who was able to do this while dying? Now Christ says everywhere through the Gospel, “I am he”; and do the Jews, awaiting Antichrist, draw back and fall into the earthly things that they love?

[Col. 0550B] Therefore he asked them again, “Whom do you seek?” They said, “Jesus of Nazareth.” Jesus answered them, “I told you that I am he. If, therefore, you seek me, let these go.” Thus was fulfilled the word that he had spoken: “Of those whom you gave me, I lost not one of them.”

They do what he commands: they allow to depart those whom he does not wish to perish; and what he had said is fulfilled: “I lost none of them.” This is not because they would not die afterward, but because they did not yet believe as those believe who do not perish.

M. 301[II] R. 183 L. 286

Then they came forward, laid hands on Jesus, and seized him.

[Col. 0550C] L. 287[I] M. 320 R. 183 A. 140

But when those who were about him saw what was going to happen, they said to him, “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?”

A. M. R. L.

Therefore Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the high priest’s servant, cutting off his right ear. The servant’s name was Malchus.

[HIERONYMUS.] Peter, with the same fervour as in the other matters, cut off Malchus’s right ear. For he knew how Phinehas, by punishing sacrilegious persons, received the reward of righteousness and an everlasting priesthood (Num. 25).

A. 161[I] M. 294 R. 175 L. 281

[Col. 0550D] Then Jesus said to Peter, “Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me? Put the sword into its sheath.”

[AUGUSTINE.] He commanded that the sword be put away, in order to teach us patience, not vengeance. By the term “cup” he indicates the suffering of the body. For our bodies are marked by the character of earthly and fragile things, which, when cast down in a brief fall, are broken. Hence the Lord says elsewhere: “You Pharisees first cleanse that which is outside of the cup and dish” (Matt. 23). Likewise, those inward things which the mind has willed are readily revealed through bodily acts, just as what a glass cup contains within shines forth outside. Thus he drinks the cup of his body who absorbs bodily frailty through spiritual disposition; and it is, as it were, poured into mind and soul, [Col. 0551A] so that the weakness of outward things may be drawn in by the inward.

M. 303[X]

“For all who take up the sword shall perish by the sword.”

By which sword? Namely, that flaming sword which turns before Paradise: the sword of the Spirit, which is described in God’s armour. Or thus: whoever schemes to injure another strikes himself with his own weapon and falls into the pit which he has dug.

“Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will at once provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?”

[HIERONYMUS.] As though he were saying: “I have no need of the Apostles’ assistance, since, if I wished, I could have twelve legions of angels, in which there are seventy-two thousand.” For among the ancients one legion consisted of six thousand men. Twelve times six thousand makes seventy-two thousand. And because the language of humankind was divided among seventy-two nations, he indicates that there is no need to fear if all nations rise against him, since he can have angelic armies far stronger. Therefore, though he could receive legions, he did not wish to receive them, so that through his patience the Scriptures prophesying concerning him might be fulfilled: that it was fitting for him to suffer thus. And this is what follows:

“How then shall the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen thus? Allow them to proceed this far.”

[Col. 0551C] [AUGUSTINE.] As though he said: “Do not be troubled by what is about to happen. They must be permitted to advance this far, so that they may seize me and what was written concerning me may be fulfilled.”

L. 288[X]

And when he had touched his ear, he healed him.

[BEDЕ.] The Lord never forgets his mercy: he even heals his enemy, teaching that those intent upon his death can be healed if they turn. Allegorically, this servant is the Jewish people, enslaved to the service of the priests, so that they asked for Barabbas to be released but Christ to be crucified. They lost the right ear—that is, the spiritual understanding of the Law—while retaining the left, that is, the letter alone. This ear is cut off by Peter’s sword, not because Peter himself took understanding from them, but because he showed that it had been taken from them by divine judgment. The ear has been restored by God to believers from that people. The ear therefore, first cut off and then restored, signifies hearing renewed after the oldness has been cut away; the text is defective here, followed by: “in newness of spirit and not in oldness of letter” (Rom. VIII). But the one whose understanding is restored shall reign with the Lord; this is signified by the servant whose name is interpreted “king” or “one who will reign.”

M. 304 R. 184 L. 289 A. 170

At that hour Jesus said to the crowds, “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs, to seize me? Daily I was with you, teaching in the Temple, and you did not seize me. L. But this is your hour and the power of darkness.”

[HIERONYMUS.] It is foolish to seek with swords and clubs one who freely offers himself into your hands; and to look for him by night through a traitor, as though he were concealed and avoiding your eyes, though he teaches daily in the Temple. But you assemble against me in darkness because your power, by which you arm yourselves against the light, is in darkness. [BEDE.] It is asked how Jesus is said by Luke to address the chief priests, officers of the Temple, and elders, when Matthew and Mark report that they themselves did not come, but sent servants. But because they arranged the Lord’s death so as to appear innocent—since he was betrayed by a disciple, seized by a tribune and crowds, condemned by a governor, crucified by Romans, and Barabbas was even chosen by the people—Luke, wishing to show most clearly the guilt of those by whose counsel all was done, says that they came to seize the Saviour: not in person, but through those whom they sent to seize him.

M. 305[VI] R. 18

All this happened in order that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.

[HIERONYMUS.] David says: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. 21). And Isaiah: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Isa. 53).

Then all the disciples left him and fled.

[Col. 0552C] [BEDE.] The Lord’s saying, that all would be scandalized because of him on that very night, is fulfilled. For although, with the crowd’s permission, they fled at the Lord’s request, as John writes in chapter 159, nevertheless they showed fearfulness of mind, being readier for flight than for suffering with the Lord. That also was fulfilled: “You have removed friend and neighbour and my acquaintances far from misery” (Ps. 87).

A. 162[I] M. 306 R. 187 L. 290

Therefore the cohort, the tribune, and the officers of the Jews seized Jesus and bound him.

Joseph is present, bound and sold by his brothers; and iron passed through his soul (Ps. 104).

[Col. 0552D] A. 163[X]

And they led him first to Annas. For he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. Caiaphas was the one who had advised the Jews that it was expedient for one man to die for the people.

[HIERONYMUS.] Moses, at God’s command, had ordered that the line of descent among priests be maintained. Josephus, however, reports that this Caiaphas bought the high priesthood for only one year from the Roman ruler, at a price. [AUGUSTINE.] It is therefore no wonder if an unrighteous high priest judges unrighteously. For Annas and Caiaphas, as Luke relates in chapter 6, were both chief priests, serving their respective years in turn; and it was Caiaphas’s year when Christ suffered. Jesus was therefore led to him, but first to Annas—not because Annas was his colleague, but because he was his father-in-law. It should be believed that this happened according to Caiaphas’s will, or that their houses were so placed that Annas could not be passed by those going through.

## Chapter CLXII

R. 186[X]

But a certain young man followed him, clothed only with a linen cloth over his naked body; and they seized him. But he, leaving the linen cloth behind, fled from them naked.

[BEDE.] “In body” is understood here, so that one reads “over his naked body”; for he had no outer garment except the linen cloth alone. The Evangelist does not say who this young man was; but whoever he was, he demonstrated that greater love for the Lord remained in him than in the others who fled, although neither did he possess perfect charity, since afterward he fled. For just as perfect charity casts out fear (1 John 4), so fear shows charity to be imperfect. Yet the Evangelist does not say that this young man fled from the Lord’s company, but that he fled from his enemies. Nor is anything opposed to understanding him as John, beloved above the others. For that he was a young man at the time is indicated by his long life afterward. It could have happened that, slipping from the hands of those who held him, he immediately resumed his garment and returned; and, under cover of night, mingled with the crowds leading Jesus as though he were one of them, until he came to the high priest’s courtyard, where he was known, as he himself records in chapter [Col. 0553C] 165. Just as Peter, who eradicated his denial by confession, provides an example of restoration for those who fall, and the other disciples in fleeing teach those less able to endure punishments that it is safer to seek the protection of concealment than to expose themselves to the danger of conflict; so also this young man, who threw off the linen cloth and fled naked from the ungodly, signifies those who, in order to be more secure from the assaults of enemies, cast aside whatever they possess in this world in order to serve the Lord. So too blessed Joseph, leaving his cloak in the adulteress’s hands, preferred to escape outside naked rather than serve a harlot (Gen. 39). Jerome, in the larger Breviary, on Psalm 37: “And those who sought my life used violence against me” (Ps. 37). The Jews used violence either against Peter when they said, “You too are among them,” or against James [John], who, when he was dragged away, left the linen cloth behind and fled from them naked.

A. 164[V] M. 306 R. 188

Now Simon Peter followed Jesus at a distance, and another disciple, as far as the courtyard of the high priest.

[HIERONYMUS, BEDE.] Peter, being near to denial, followed at a distance; for he could not have denied Christ had he been near him. Now the double-minded man is unstable in all his ways (Jas. 1), and fear draws back the one whom charity draws onward. That he follows Jesus comes from devotion; that he fears, from nature; that he denies, from a sudden failure; that he repents, from faith. He signifies the Church, which indeed will follow—that is, imitate—the Lord’s sufferings, but with a great difference. For the Church suffers for herself; Christ, for the Church.

A. 165[X]

But that disciple was known to the high priest, and he entered with Jesus into the high priest’s courtyard.

[AUGUSTINE.] Since it is not stated here, one ought not rashly determine who that disciple was. Perhaps it was John. For he is accustomed to speak of himself as though of another.

A. 166[I] M. 314 R. 195 L. 291

But Peter was standing outside at the door.

A. 167[X]

[Col. 0554B] Therefore the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out, spoke to the doorkeeper, and brought Peter in.

A. 168[I] M. 314 R. 195 L. 291

When the maidservant who kept the door saw him and looked at him, she said, “Are you also one of this man’s disciples?” He said, “Woman, I do not know him, nor do I know what you are saying.”

[BEDE.] What does it mean that a maidservant first exposed him, though men could have recognized him, except that this sex also might appear to have sinned in bringing about the Lord’s death, and might be redeemed through the Lord’s Passion? Therefore a woman first saw the risen Lord, so that it might be believed that he had abolished the ancient error of transgression even in the female sex. Some, from pious feeling toward Peter, interpret this passage as though he properly said that he did not know him whom no one fully knows except the Father. Again, when questioned he said, “Man, I am not,” which they interpret as meaning that he preferred to deny himself rather than Christ. And when questioned a third time he said, “Man, I do not know what you are saying”; they say that he did not know their sacrileges and condemned them by rejecting them. But both the Lord, who foretold that Peter would deny him three times, and Peter himself, who by his ensuing tears showed that he had not spoken thus intentionally, testify that these interpretations are frivolous. In short, not only does the person deny Christ who says that he is not Christ, but also the person who denies that he is a Christian, who denies that he is his disciple; and thus what the Lord said is fulfilled: “You will deny me three times.”

[Col. 0554D] A. 169[X]

Now the servants and officers stood by a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and warmed themselves. Peter too was standing with them and warming himself, in order to see the outcome.

[BEDE.] There is a fire of love, and there is a fire of desire. Of the former it is said: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it should burn?” (Luke 12). Of the latter: “Behold, all you who kindle a fire, girded with flames, walk in the light of your fire.” The former descended upon believers in the upper room of Zion and taught them to praise God in diverse tongues. The latter, kindled by the prompting of an evil spirit, armed the tongues of unbelievers in Annas’s courtyard to deny and blaspheme the Lord. What the wicked council of priests was doing inside the high priest’s house, the fire materially kindled outside in the courtyard amid the night’s cold symbolically displayed. Peter, benumbed for a time by cold, desired to warm himself at the persecutors’ coals, because he sought the comfort of temporal advantage in the society of unbelievers. But when the Lord soon looked upon him, he left their fire and cast away the unbelief of his heart. [HIERONYMUS.] Matthew says in chapter 307 that he was in the courtyard to see the outcome: he wished to know what would be decided concerning the Lord—whether they would sentence him to death or release him after beating him with scourges.

## Chapter CLXIII

Therefore the high priest questioned Jesus concerning his disciples and his teaching.

[Col. 0555B] [HIERONYMUS.] The one whom they awaited from afar they do not see near at hand, just as Isaac, with dimmed eyes, does not recognize Jacob under his hands (Gen. 27), but from afar sings of what will happen concerning him.

A. 170[I] M. 304 R. 184 L. 289

Jesus answered him, “I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in synagogue and in the Temple, where all the Jews gather; and I have spoken nothing in secret.”

[AUGUSTINE.] A question arises which must not be passed over: how could the Lord say, “I have spoken nothing in secret,” when after supper he said to the disciples, “I have spoken these things in parables” (John 16)? If, then, he did not speak openly to the disciples, how did he speak openly in the world? Moreover, as the other Evangelists testify, he spoke more plainly [Col. 0555C] to the disciples than to the crowds. Thus, when removed from the crowds, he explained to them the parables which he set forth in veiled form to others. What then does “I have spoken nothing in secret” mean? It means: many heard me. Therefore he spoke in one sense openly, in another sense not openly. Openly, because many heard him; not openly, because they did not understand what he spoke separately to the disciples. Even the things he said to a few were not said in secret, because he said them in order that they might be preached from the rooftops, not kept silent.

A. 171[X]

“Why do you question me? Question those who heard what I spoke to them. Behold, they know what I said.”

Why do you question me, when you do not desire to hear the truth from me? Rather question those whose statements will not provoke your envy. Thus he moderated his answer, so as neither to suppress the truth nor to seem to be defending himself.

A. 172[I] M. 314 R. 194 L. 294

But when he had said these things, one of the officers standing by struck Jesus on the face, saying, “Is this how you answer the high priest?”

A. 173[X]

Jesus answered him, “If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness to the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me?”

He speaks wrongly who speaks against truth. “If I have spoken wrongly, give testimony by which you prove me a liar.” By answering humbly, he taught us patience—he who, by command, could have inflicted whatever punishment he wished upon the one striking him. Someone says here: “Why did he not do what he himself commanded elsewhere? He ought not to have answered the striker in this way, but offered the other cheek” (Matt. 5). The answer is that he offered not only the other cheek to be struck, but his whole body to be crucified. For many offer the other cheek in anger. Blessed therefore is the one who, in everything suffered for God, can truthfully say: “My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready” (Ps. 56).

A. 174[I] M. 306 R. 187 L. 290

And Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.

A. 175[I] L. 315 A. 196 L. 292

But Simon Peter was standing outside in the courtyard and warming himself.

[Col. 0556B] This recapitulates what had been said before, and then joins what followed.

Again another maidservant saw him and said to those standing around, “This man also was with Jesus of Nazareth.”

Having said that Annas sent Jesus to Caiaphas, the account returns to Peter, to explain what happened concerning his threefold denial in Annas’s house.

Those who were standing there came forward and said to Peter, “Truly you too are one of them, for your speech makes it clear that you are a Galilean.”

They do not say this because Peter’s language differed from Hebrew, but because every province has its own peculiarities of speech.

And again he denied it with an oath: “I do not know the man.”

[Col. 0556C] Certainly he denied Christ, because Christ was a man—the one who had said, “Until you deny me three times.” Some, from pious feeling toward Peter, think that Peter denied not God but man. Any discerning reader will understand how frivolous this is. For they defend the Apostle in such a way as to make the Lord a liar, who had said: “You will deny me.”

[AUGUSTINE.] Before denying a second time, he went outside before the high priest’s courtyard; and, as Mark alone records, then the cock crowed for the first time. When Peter returned to the courtyard, the second denial occurred. But as he was going out through the gate, as Matthew says, a maidservant noticed him and said to those standing by the fire, “This man was with Jesus of Nazareth.” Returning to them, Peter swore: “I do not know [Col. 0556D] the man.”

And after a little while, about one hour, one of the high priest’s servants—a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off—said, “Truly this man also was with him, for he is a Galilean. Did I not see you with him in the garden?” He began to curse, invoke an anathema, and swear: “I do not know him; I do not know what you are saying; I do not know this man of whom you speak.” And immediately the cock crowed.

Behold, Christ’s prediction is fulfilled and Peter’s presumption disproved. First he says, “I do not know what you are saying”; second, he denies with an oath; third, he began to curse and swear that he did not know the man. For persevering in sin increases crimes, and one who despises small matters falls into greater ones. After the third denial comes the cock’s crow. The mysteries of things are signified by the sequence of times. At midnight he denies; at cockcrow he repents; after the resurrection, in the light, he confessed three times that he loved the one whom he had denied three times. For what he had done amiss in the darkness of forgetfulness he corrected by recalling the light now hoped for [the reading “reward” is also possible]; and, once he attained the presence of that same true light, he fully restored whatever had wavered. Mystically, the cock is one of the teachers who, reproving those who sleep, says: “Awake to righteousness, and do not sin” (1 Cor. 15). Peter’s denial before the first cockcrow signifies those who, before the resurrection, did not think Christ to be God, being troubled by his death. His two denials before the second cockcrow signify those who now deny the truth because in him, according to his humanity and according to his divinity, both substances existed. The first cockcrow is the Lord’s resurrection in himself; the second is his resurrection in the body of the Church.

And the Lord turned and looked at Peter.

[AUGUSTINE.] That look appears to have been divinely effected, so that Peter might remember how many times he had already denied the Lord and what the Lord had foretold to him; and thus, as the Lord mercifully looked upon him, he might repent and weep. So we are accustomed to say, “Lord, look upon me.” [HIERONYMUS.] For the one upon whom the Light of the World looked could not remain in the darkness of denial.

L. 293[II] M. 316 R. 197

And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, who had said to him, “Before the cock crows, today you will deny me three times.”

[Col. 0557C] The word “today” is found in Mark in chapter 170.

And Peter went out and wept bitterly.

[BEDE.] Not only when repentance is being performed, but even in order that it may be performed, God’s mercy is necessary; and his looking upon us is mercy. Hence the Psalmist says: “How long shall my enemy be exalted over me? Look upon me and hear me, O Lord my God” (Ps. 12). That is: have mercy and help me. Therefore Peter goes outside, so that, separated from the council of the ungodly, he may wash away the defilements of denial by unrestrained tears; for he could not repent among the ungodly. [HIERONYMUS.] The recollection of Christ’s word washed away the threefold denial with tears after the cock crowed and, as darkness diminished, the approaching light was announced. The cock crows for us when the preacher recalls our hearts to compunction. We then begin to weep when we are kindled within by the spark of knowledge and go out from what we had been. Peter, before the Spirit was given, yielded to a maidservant’s voice; after the Spirit was given, he did not give way [the text reads dedit, corrected cessit] either to rulers or to kings. We may know what the high priest’s maidservant is if we understand what God’s maidservant is, concerning whom it is written: “I am your servant and the son of your handmaid” (Ps. 115). You can know what the high priest’s courtyards are if you understand what the courts of God’s house are, concerning which it is written: “Behold, now bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Ps. XXXIII). I think the first maidservant signifies the Synagogue; the second, the assembly of the Gentiles; those standing in the courtyards, the ministers of various heresies; and the man of the third denial, the prompting of diabolical power. All these compel the denial of Christ’s truth.

## Chapter CLXIV

M. 317[II] R. 198 L. 295

When morning came, all the chief priests, together with the elders of the people and the scribes, assembled to deliberate.

Here begins the account of what was done before Caiaphas after Jesus had been led from Annas’s house and before he had yet been brought to the governor’s praetorium. Nevertheless, some who have paid insufficient attention to John’s account, and to what the other Evangelists have said by anticipation or recapitulation, have maintained [Col. 0558B] that Peter denied him in Caiaphas’s courtyard.

M. 308[II] R. 189 L. 305

They sought false testimony against Jesus in order to hand him over to death, and they found none. Though many false witnesses came forward, they found none, and their testimonies did not agree.

[HIERONYMUS.] Iniquity lied to itself, as did the queen against Joseph (Gen. 39), and the priests against Susanna (Dan. 13); but fire fails when it has no material.

M. 309[VI] R. 198

Finally two false witnesses came and said, “We heard him say: ‘I can destroy this Temple of God, made with hands, and after three days build another, not made with hands.’” But Jesus remained silent.

[HIERONYMUS.] How are they false witnesses if they say what we have previously read the Lord saying? A witness is false, however, when he does not understand words in the sense in which they were spoken. The Lord had spoken concerning the temple of his body. They alter the Saviour’s words; he had said, “Destroy this Temple” (John 2), but they claim that he said, “I can destroy the Temple of God.” “You,” says the Lord, “destroy it,” not I, because we ourselves ought not to lay hands upon ourselves. Then they change it by saying, “and after three days build another,” so that it may be understood of the Jewish Temple. But the Lord, to show that it was a living temple, had said, “And I will raise it up in three days.” For to build is one thing; to raise up is another.

[Col. 0558D] And the high priest, rising in the midst, questioned Jesus, saying, “Do you answer nothing to what these testify against you?” But Jesus answered nothing.

The high priest, stirred by anger and driven by mental frenzy, rises because the Lord was silent. Christ’s silence indeed provides Adam’s defence. And the more he was silent toward those unworthy of his answer, the more furiously the high priest provoked him to answer, so that from any occasion of an answer he might find grounds for accusation. Therefore he is silent because he knows that whatever he might answer would be twisted into slander.

## Chapter CLXV

And again the high priest said to him, “I adjure you by the living God to tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of the blessed God.” Jesus said to him, “You have said it.”

[Col. 0559A] Why do you adjure him, most ungodly man? In order to accuse, or in order to believe? If in order to accuse, others accuse you of condemning one who is silent [or: those who are silent]. If in order to believe, why were you unwilling to believe one who confessed? [HILARY.] The priest was ignorant of the Law in which he gloried. By adjuring him, he seeks assurance whether he himself was the Christ, as though the Law and Prophets had spoken of him secretly; but he himself too confessed Christ unwillingly, when the Lord said, “You have said it.” For all the Law and the Prophets had proclaimed that Christ would come; and in them the priest had often said that he was the Christ, the Son of God.

L. 296[X]

And he said to them, “If I tell you, you will not believe me; but if I also ask you, you will not answer me, nor will you release me.”

[BEDЕ.] He had often told them that he was the Christ—for example, when he said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10), and, “The works which I do in my Father’s name bear witness concerning me” (ibid.). He had also asked how they could say that Christ was David’s son, when David himself in the Spirit had called him his Lord; and they had not answered him (Matt. 22). Thus they were unwilling either to believe one who spoke, answer one who questioned, or release him who was innocent.

M. 310[I] R. 191 L. 297 A. 69

“Nevertheless I tell you: from now on you will see the Son of Man [Col. 0559C] seated at the right hand of God’s power and coming on the clouds of heaven.”

[HIERONYMUS.] The priest asks about the Son of God; Jesus answers concerning the Son of Man, that we may understand that the Son of God and the Son of Man are the same person, and that we may not make a quaternity within the Trinity, but that man is in God and God in man. [BEDE.] O Jew, pagan, heretic: if contempt, weakness, and the cross in Christ are an insult to you, see him who was born from a virgin sitting at the right hand of God the Father and coming in his majesty for judgment! Hence the Apostle, after describing the abasement of the cross, says: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus [Col. 0559D] every knee should bend—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2). [ORIGEN.] Since he is the everlasting power and right hand of the Father, his sitting in his humanity signifies a certain foundation and royal firmness. The clouds of heaven are the Apostles, showering forth words and watering the hearts of believers. He comes in the clouds of heaven—that is, in the preachers of the heavenly word, where God’s mysteries are always hidden—showing his coming to those worthy of it: God the Word, Wisdom, Truth, and Righteousness. [HIERONYMUS.] He ascended in a cloud (Acts 1); he will come with a cloud—that is, he ascended in the body alone which he assumed from the Virgin, and he will come for judgment with the Church of many forms, which is his body and fullness.

[Col. 0560A] M. 311[VI] R. 192

Then the high priest tore his garments, saying, “He has blasphemed.”

[HIERONYMUS.] The man who had risen in fury tears his garments in rage, thereby showing that the Jews had lost the glory of the priesthood. It is also a Jewish custom, when they hear something blasphemous against God, to tear their garments. [BEDE.] We also read that Paul and Barnabas did this when they were being honoured with divine worship in Lycaonia (Acts 14). In a higher mystery, the high priest tears his garments while the Lord’s tunic could not be torn by the soldiers. For the Jewish priesthood was signified as destined to be torn apart for the high priests’ sins, whereas the integrity of the Church, which is called God’s garment, can never be rent.

M. 312[II] R. 193 L. 299

“Why do we still need witnesses? Behold, now you have heard the blasphemy from his mouth. What do you think?” And they all answered, “He is guilty of death.”

[BEDЕ.] By their own judgment they condemn themselves when they hand over to death the one whom they are able to know as God by the testimony of both his words and deeds.

M. 313[X] R. 194 L. 294 A. 172

Then they spat in his face; and those holding him mocked him, covered his face, and struck him with their fists. Others struck his face with the palms of their hands, saying, “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is it that struck you?” And they spoke many other blasphemies against him.

[HILARY—HIERONYMUS.] To complete the humiliation of the man, every kind of insult was inflicted upon him. They spat in his face, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled which says: “I did not turn my face away from those reviling and spitting upon me” (Isa. 50).

[BEDE.] They covered him, not so that he should not see their crimes, but so that they might hide his face from themselves. That covering remains over their hearts to this day. [HIERONYMUS.] He who was then struck by Jewish fists is now also struck by the blasphemies of false Christians. [BEDE.] They said to him, “Prophesy,” but it was foolish to prophesy to those whose madness was evident. [HIERONYMUS.] Their striking his face with the palms of their hands fulfilled the prophecy: “They shall strike the judge of Israel upon the cheek with a rod” (Mic. 5). By receiving spittle, he washes the face of our soul; by the covering of his face, he removes the covering from our hearts. By the fists with which he was struck upon the head, he heals the head of the human race, namely Adam; and he was struck with open palms so that we might applaud him especially with hands and lips. Hence the Psalmist says: “All nations, clap your hands; shout joyfully to God” (Ps. 46). In mockery, because he wished to be regarded as a prophet, they say to him, “Prophesy”; in this he prepares us to endure derision for his name, he who endured it for us. Even today, all who provoke him by wicked deeds, while thinking that their thoughts and works of darkness are not seen by him, say mockingly, as it were: “Prophesy: who is it that struck you?”

## Chapter CLXVI

M. 318[I] R. 199 L. 300 A. 176

And they led him bound into the praetorium and handed him over to Pontius Pilate, the governor.

It was their custom to hand over bound to the judge the man whom they had condemned to death. Samson is present, bound by Delilah (Judg. 16). [HIERONYMUS.] Samson was the sun of those for whom the sun set at noon. Delilah is interpreted “bucket,” that is, the Synagogue: like a bucket, it does not retain clear liquid but gathers filthy refuse. Our Samson here lays low countless bands of Jews and demons with the jawbone of his word, and opens for us who thirst the fountain of everlasting life—that is, his body.

A. 177[X]

And they themselves did not enter the praetorium, so that they might not be defiled, but might eat the Passover.

[AUGUSTINE.] Those who led Jesus had already begun to observe the days of unleavened bread, during which it was defilement for them to enter a foreigner’s dwelling. O impious blindness! They feared defilement from a foreigner’s praetorium, yet did not fear the blood of an innocent man.

M. 319[X]

[Col. 0561C] Then Judas, who had betrayed him, seeing that he had been condemned, was moved by repentance and brought back the thirty silver coins to the chief priests and elders, saying, “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood.” But they said, “What is that to us? See to it yourself.”

That is: you have seen what you did; or, you will see and perceive that you sinned, but it has nothing to do with us. It is a bold and blind declaration. [ORIGEN.] They hear that they have bought the blood of a righteous man, yet believe themselves free from guilt and locate the crime in the seller. [HILARY.] Judas, seeing through reflection upon the outcome of the matter that Jesus had been condemned—or seeing concerning himself that one who had dared such things had without doubt been judged and condemned by God—brought back the silver coins as though it were in his power to change the persecutors’ decision. [ORIGEN.] He changed his intention, indeed, but not the outcome of his first intention. Perhaps Satan, who had entered Judas after the dipped bread, stood by him until Jesus was handed over to Pilate. But after he had done what he wished, he departed from him, intending to return again for another deception. Therefore, when the devil departed from him, Judas could feel repentance and bring back to those who had given them the thirty silver coins, confessing from heartfelt repentance his sin in having betrayed innocent blood. Yet he did not repent with understanding, as he ought to have repented, because he never guarded his heart or grieved wisely. Instead, he received from the devil, who wished to swallow him up in excessive grief, a more abundant sorrow laid upon him. Therefore the Apostle, knowing the devil’s devices beforehand, advises the Corinthians that one who had already grieved with godly sorrow—which produces a firm repentance unto salvation—should not be swallowed up in excessive sorrow (2 Cor. 2; 2 Cor. 7). Judas’s repentance became a worse sin when he hanged himself; in this he offended the Lord more than when he betrayed him.

And after throwing down the silver coins in the Temple, he departed; and going away, hanged himself with a noose. But the chief priests, taking the silver coins, said, “It is not lawful to put them into the corban (treasury), because they are the price of blood.””

[HIERONYMUS.] Truly, they strain out a gnat and swallow a camel. For if this is why they do not put the money into the corban—that is, into the treasury—because it is the price of blood, why is the blood itself shed? [ORIGEN.] I think that Judas, understanding something great concerning the Savior, threw the silver coins nowhere but in the Temple, because he knew that the Lord had driven sheep and oxen from the Temple and had said to the sellers of doves: “Take these things away from here, and do not make my Father’s house a house of trade” (John 2).

Having taken counsel, they bought with them the potter’s field as a burial-place for foreigners. Therefore that field was called Haceldama, that is, Field of Blood, to this very day.

They saw that this money was more suitably spent in connection with the dead, and upon a place for the dead and for burial, because it was the price of blood [Col. 0562C], than placed in the corban or used for any honorable need. But because there are distinctions even among burial-places—for many are desirably buried, according to their wish, in their ancestral tombs, while others are often buried in foreign tombs because of certain misfortunes—they took the price of Jesus’ blood and used it to purchase a potter’s field, where clay is worked for forming pots and other earthenware, so that foreign dead might be buried in that field. [HIERONYMUS.] But we, who were foreigners to the Law and the Prophets, have turned the perverse designs of the Jews to salvation, and rest in the price of the Lord’s blood. [HILARY.] By Christ’s price a field is bought—that is, the whole world is acquired for him, and all authority in heaven and on earth is given to him.
