Therefore this is the potter’s field [Col. 0562D] (Matt. 28), because all things belong to God, in whose hand it is, from the same clay, to make a vessel for honor or for dishonor (Rom. 9). By Christ’s blood the world is bought as a burial-place for foreigners and the poor; that is, for an abiding place of rest—not indeed for proud Israel, but for those who, as pilgrims in this world, are buried with Christ through baptism (Rom. 6).

Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: “And they took thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one appraised, whom they appraised from the sons of Israel, and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord appointed me.”

[HIERONYMUS.] This testimony is not found in Jeremiah; in Zechariah, however, nearly the same sense occurs in different words [Col. 0563A]. It therefore appears that this testimony was taken from Zechariah, according to the common practice of the Evangelists and Apostles, who, omitting the order of the words, give only the sense from the Old Testament. Hence some manuscripts do not have “through Jeremiah,” but only “through the prophet.” Jerome, in the larger Breviary, on Psalm 77, in Matthew, says: “It is said, ‘that what was written in Asaph the prophet might be fulfilled.’ Thus it is found in the old manuscripts; but the ignorant removed Asaph, not knowing who he was. And so, when a scribe wished to correct it, he made an error, writing Isaiah instead of Asaph. Hence many manuscripts still have, ‘what was written through Isaiah the prophet.’”

The impious Porphyry advances this very point against us, saying: “Your Evangelist Matthew was so unskilled as to say that ‘I will open my mouth in parables’ was written in Isaiah” [Col. 0563B]. Matthew did not err, but unskilled copyists did. Finally, it is written in Matthew and John that our Lord was crucified at the sixth hour; in Mark, at the third hour. This seems discrepant, but it is not, because the error was the copyists’; and in Mark it was written, “the sixth hour.” But many, taking the Greek episēmon (ἐπίσημον), whose figure is ς and which is written for six, though it is not a letter, thought it was the letter gamma, which signifies three. Therefore here too there was a copyists’ error. Likewise there was a copyists’ error in Matthew where Judas returned the thirty pieces of silver. For it is said to have been written in Jeremiah, whereas it was written not in Jeremiah but in Zechariah.

The same writer, on Matthew, says: “I recently read in a certain Hebrew volume, offered me by a Hebrew of the Nazarene sect, an apocryphon of Jeremiah, in which I found these words written word for word.” Origen, on Matthew: “This testimony is found in the secret writings of Jeremiah, just as the Apostle cites certain secret Scriptures, as in: ‘What eye has not seen, nor ear heard’ (1 Cor. 2). For this is found in no canonical book except in the secret writings of Elijah the prophet.” Likewise, what he says—“As Iannes and Mambres resisted Moses” (2 Tim. 3)—is found not in public books but in the apocryphal book entitled *Iannes and Mambres*. Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*: “Zechariah has the thirty pieces of silver, but nothing about buying the field” (Zech. 11). “In Jeremiah chapter thirty-two [Col. 0563D] it is read that he bought a field from the son of his uncle and gave him silver, though not under this designation of price. The Evangelist combines both and shows that they pertain to what was fulfilled in the Lord.”

Some manuscripts read: “Whom the sons of Israel appraised”; in others: “Whom they appraised from the sons of Israel.” Read it thus, therefore: The Jews took the thirty pieces of silver which Judas returned—the price, namely, of the Lord who was appraised, whom they appraised, since they heard from the sons of Israel that he had been sold. Who were those who appraised him? Namely, those Jews who were not present at the sale of the Lord. “And they gave them for the potter’s field, as he appointed”—that is, as the Lord revealed to me what had been appointed. All the words are Jeremiah’s, as is found in the apocryphon; or, according to Augustine [Col. 0564A], some are to be taken as spoken in the person of the Evangelist.

## CHAPTER CLXVII

A. 177[X]

Pilate therefore went out to them and said: “What accusation do you bring against this man?” They answered and said to him: “If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you.”

A. 301[X]

“We found this man subverting our nation, forbidding tribute to be given to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.”

[Bede.] The Jews are convicted of impiety because, accusing the Savior [Col. 0564B], they cannot even find any plausible falsehood to cast against him. [Origen.] False testimony has force when it is presented with some appearance of plausibility. But against Jesus not even an appearance could be found that might support lies against him.

A. 177[X]

Pilate therefore said to them: “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law.” Then the Jews said: “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.” So that the saying of the Lord might be fulfilled, which he had spoken, signifying by what death he was to die.

[Augustine.] Did they not kill the man whom they offered to be killed? If he is an evildoer, why was it not lawful to kill him? [Col. 0564C] If it was unlawful because of the feast, why did you cry, “Crucify, crucify”? Hear the Psalmist: “The sons of men—their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. 56). Yet because they did not wish to kill him with their own hands, as if they were thereby strangers to the crime, the saying of Jesus was fulfilled, which he had foretold concerning his death: handed over by the Jews, he was to be killed by the Gentiles.

A. 168[I] M. 320 R. 200 L. 302

Pilate entered the praetorium again, called Jesus, and said to him: “Are you the King of the Jews?” Jesus answered: “Do you say this of yourself, or have others told you about me?”

A. 179[X]

[Col. 0564D] Pilate answered: “Am I a Jew? Your nation and the chief priests handed you over to me. What have you done?” Jesus answered: “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would certainly fight, so that I should not be handed over to the Jews. But now my kingdom is not from here.”

The vain opinion concerning his kingdom, whether held by Gentiles or by Jews, had to be exposed to us. Pilate had heard that he was a king, as though he were therefore to be punished with death because he had sought an unlawful kingdom; or because rulers are usually jealous of those who are to rule, and it was necessary to guard against his kingdom being hostile either to Romans or to Jews. The Lord could have answered this at the governor’s first question [Col. 0565A], but through Pilate himself he wished to show that the Jews had charged this against him as a crime, exposing before him the thoughts of men. For if he had immediately answered Pilate, he would not appear to have answered the Jews also, but only the Gentiles who held this opinion about him. But now, through Pilate’s words—“Am I a Jew? Your nation and the chief priests handed you over to me”—it is evident that he heard this from the Jews. Then, by saying, “What have you done?” he shows that this had been charged against him as a crime, as though saying: “If you deny that you are a king, why have you been handed over to me?” Thus in his answer the Lord excluded the pretexts of those who envied him, saying that his kingdom was not of this world, so that no guilt whatever might be recognized in him.

[Col. 0565B] A. 180[IV] M. 311 R. 201

Pilate therefore said to him: “Then are you a king?” Jesus answered: “You say that I am a king.”

He was not afraid to confess himself king, but he so weighed his words that he neither denied himself to be a king nor confessed himself to be such a king as one whose kingdom was thought to be of this world. As though he said: “If you think I am a king from here, you, being fleshly, understand fleshly.” Moreover, that Pilate, though asking, nevertheless firmly thought Jesus to be King of the Jews, is confirmed also by what he wrote elsewhere in the title: “King of the Jews,” [in three languages,] Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, so that Hebrews, Greeks, and Romans might know that Pilate too knew him to be King of the Jews. It is therefore apparent with what reverence he inquired [Col. 0565C] concerning Jesus and urged the people to ask more for Jesus’ release than for Barabbas. Pilate’s reverence was also shown when he washed his hands and said: “I am innocent of this man’s blood. See to it yourselves.” [Hilary.] Note that when the Lord was asked by the priest whether he himself was the Christ, he answered as concerning things past: “You have said it,” because he himself had always said from the Law that Christ would come. But to Pilate, ignorant of the Law and asking whether he was King of the Jews, it is said: “You say it,” because by faith in this present confession comes the salvation of the Gentiles.

A. 181[X]

“For this I was born, and for this I came into the world [Col. 0565D], to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice.”

[Augustine.] Therefore I do not deny that I am king, because for this I was born: to show what I am. This syllable *hoc* (“this”) should not be lengthened, as though he said “in this matter”; it should be shortened, as though he had said “for this purpose” or “for this I was born.” For in Greek there is no ambiguity in this expression. Hence it is evident that here he mentioned his temporal birth, not his eternal one. What he adds—“Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice,” that is, obeys and believes me—is a commendation of grace, through which Truth grants belief in itself.

Pilate said to him: “What is truth?” And when he had said this, he went out again to the Jews.

[Col. 0566A] [ALBINUS.] He did not wait to hear what Jesus would answer, because he was not worthy; instead he went out again.

A. 182[V] L. 303

And he said to the chief priests and the crowds: “I find no charge in this man.”

This is what he himself said to his disciples, among other things, on the day before he suffered: “For the ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14). The charge that he forbade tribute to be given to Caesar, as an obvious lie of his envious accusers, the governor dismisses without concern; for he could have heard what the Lord said: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” [Col. 0566B] (Matt. 22).

L. 304[X]

But they grew more insistent, saying: “He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judaea, beginning from Galilee even to this place.”

This speech of the accusers teaches both that the accused is innocent and that the accusers are perverse. For teaching the people is plainly not a charge of crime but evidence of virtue.

When Pilate heard of Galilee, he asked whether the man was Galilean. And when he learned that he belonged to Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent him to Herod, who himself was in Jerusalem in those days.

So that he might not be compelled to pronounce judgment against one whom he knew to be innocent [Col. 0566C], Pilate sent him to Herod, that he, being tetrarch of that country, might instead either acquit or punish him. But by divine providence, lest the Jews retain any excuse, as though Romans rather than they themselves had crucified Christ, Herod, who was a Jew, sent him back to Pilate.

When Herod saw Jesus, he rejoiced greatly. For he had long desired to see him, because he heard many things about him and hoped to see some sign performed by him. He questioned him with many words, but Jesus answered him nothing.

The Lord was silent before Herod because he avoided display, and Herod’s cruelty did not deserve to see divine things. Perhaps Herod signifies the ungodly, who, if they do not believe the Law and the Prophets, will not see Christ’s wonders [Col. 0566D] in the Gospel.

L. 305[IV] M. 308 R. 188

But the chief priests and the scribes stood, vehemently accusing him.

When the chief priests and scribes accused the Lord before Pilate, he answered little; before Herod, nothing, lest he should be released and the benefit of the Cross be delayed. It was fitting that he should answer in some degree Pilate, who pronounced sentence unwillingly; but Herod and the rest, who condemned the innocent contrary to the Law, deserved nothing. Where he is silent, like a lamb to be sacrificed for the flock, he displays patience; where he answers, like a shepherd he fights for the sheep against wolves and robbers.

[Col. 0567A] L. 306[X]

Herod despised him with his army and mocked him, clothing him in a white garment, and sent him back to Pilate. And Herod and Pilate became friends on that day; for previously they had been enemies of one another.

That the Lord is clothed in a white garment is an indication of his spotless Passion, because he is the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world. He is mocked in a white garment because he suffered in chaste flesh. Or thus: that here he is mocked in white, and according to the other Evangelists in purple or scarlet, expresses the twofold kind of martyrdom. Hence the Church says in wonder: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Song 5): white in conduct, namely, ruddy in blood. And the Church herself, blooming with diverse little flowers of her members, bears lilies in peace and roses in war [Col. 0567B]. The most wicked alliance of Herod and Pilate in the killing of Christ their successors preserve as a hereditary right, because Gentiles and Jews, differing in race and religion, agree in persecuting Christians and destroying Christ’s faith within them.

L. 307[XI] A. 186

Pilate, having called together the chief priests, rulers, and people, went out to them and said: “You have brought this man before me as one turning the people away. A. L. Behold, I bring him out to you, that you may know that I find in him no charge among those of which you accuse him.”

[Col. 0567C] L. 380[X]

“Nor has Herod; for I sent you to him, and behold, nothing deserving death has been done to him. Therefore I will chastise him and release him.”

“I will subject him to scourges, as much as you demand; only release him as innocent.” Observe how earnestly Pilate seeks to release Jesus. First he says that he has found no charge in him; then he sends him to Herod; finally he confirms that there is nothing deserving death in him. Yet at last, the one he acquitted in judgment he crucified in service.

L. 310[I] M. 335 R. 204 A. 182

But the whole crowd cried out: “Take him away; crucify, crucify.”

[Col. 0567D] A. 189[X]

Pilate said to them: “Take him yourselves and crucify him.”

A. 190[X]

“For I find no charge in him.”

A. 191

The Jews answered him: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.”

Behold a greater envy, as though the charge by which they accused him of royal power had been slight.

A. 192[IV] M. 321 R. 201

When Pilate heard this saying, he was more afraid [Col. 0568A]. He entered the praetorium again and said to Jesus: “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer.

The Lord was not silent only once before the rulers, that the prophecy concerning him might be fulfilled: “Like a lamb before its shearer, he was without a voice” (Isa. 53). This likeness to a lamb is given so that through his silence he may be regarded not as guilty but as innocent. For he is not convicted as one conscious of guilt, but is sacrificed as one meek for others.

A. 193[X]

Pilate therefore said to him: “Will you not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to crucify you and authority to release you?” Jesus answered: “You would have no authority at all against me unless it had been given you from above [Col. 0568B]. Therefore he who handed me over to you has the greater sin.”

The one who hands over the innocent to be killed sins more through envy than the one who kills through fear of another’s greater authority. Pilate was under Caesar, and the Romans had sent him as governor into Judaea. Thus authority had been given him from above, namely, by the Romans; but all authority is given from above in this sense, because there is none except from God (Rom. 13).

From then on Pilate sought to release him.

He had sought to release him before as well. Therefore interpret “from then on” thus: “on account of this”—that he might not sin by killing the innocent, though he would sin less than the Jews who had handed him over.

But the Jews cried out: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar.”

Pilate could not so readily disregard Caesar as he could the law of a foreign nation, concerning which they had said above: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die.”

When Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus outside and sat upon the judgment-seat, in the place called Lithostrotos, but in Hebrew Gabbatha. Now it was the Preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour; and he said to the Jews: “Behold your king.”

*Parasceve* means “preparation” in Latin. The Jews also, who speak Latin more than Greek, use this Greek word more freely. It was the Parasceve, that is, Friday [Col. 0568D], on which they prepared what was necessary for the Sabbath—the day on which Moses commanded that double manna be gathered because of the Sabbath. And at that time it was the day of Passover, because the Jewish Passover fell on that day, so that the preparation for the Sabbath and the Passover, which had begun on the preceding night, coincided. Or it may be divided thus: “It was the Preparation of the Passover hour,” that is, about the sixth hour of the day of Passover; because the sixth hour had not yet been completed but had begun when Pilate sat upon the judgment-seat. And while Jesus was being led away and the other events were occurring, the sixth hour was completed, from which darkness lasted until the ninth hour. But Mark, saying, “It was the third hour, and they crucified him,” wished covertly to show that those who cried at the third hour that he should be crucified crucified the Lord more than did those who obeyed their governor [Col. 0569A]. By the tongues of the Jews he was crucified at the third hour; by the hands of the soldiers, at the sixth.

A. 194[I] M. 326 R. 205 L. 313

But they cried: “Take him away, take him away; crucify him.”

[Bede.] How great the cruelty that desires not merely to kill him but even to crucify him. They seek to have the Lord fastened to the wood with nails, lest the pain end quickly. What the Jews cannot accomplish by accusing and reasoning, as it were, they accomplish by demanding and shouting. Ecclesiastical history shows that persecutors also maintained this manner of raging in martyrdom.

[Col. 0569B] A. 195[X]

Pilate said to them: “Shall I crucify your king?” The chief priests answered: “We have no king but Caesar.”

[Augustine.] Pilate tries to overcome the terror they introduce concerning Caesar.

R. 201[IV] M. 321 A. 180

And the chief priests accused him of many things, but Jesus answered nothing.

[Albinus.] He who needs no defense is accused and remains silent; nor does he confirm the accusation by silence, but despises it by not refuting it. Let those seek to be defended who fear being defeated. Better is the cause that is not defended and is proved. Susanna was silent and conquered (Dan. 13).

[Col. 0569C] Then Pilate said to him: “Do you not hear how many testimonies they bring against you?” And he did not answer him a word, so that the governor greatly marveled.

[Hieronymus.] He who condemns Jesus is indeed a Gentile, but he lays the blame upon the Jewish people. [Origen.] He marvels at his steadfastness: brought before a criminal tribunal, he remained undisturbed and stood before death, which is thought terrible by all people.

M. 322 R. 202 L. 309

Now at the feast the governor was accustomed to release for the people one of the prisoners, whomever they requested. And he then had a notorious prisoner called [Col. 0569D] Barabbas.

M. 323[IV] R. 203 A. 183

When they had assembled, Pilate said: “A. It is your custom that I release one to you at Passover. M. R. A. Whom then do you wish me to release to you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?” M. A. For he knew that they had handed him over through envy.

[Bede.] The governor was accustomed to release one of the prisoners, not by enactment of imperial law but by the yearly custom of that nation, to which he was pleased to be bound by such a custom. [Albinus.] This custom of release remained among the Jews in memory of their deliverance from Egypt at Passover. Therefore Pilate, wishing to satisfy the people, gave them the choice [Col. 0570A], though he did not doubt that Christ would be chosen, knowing that he had been delivered up through envy. Barabbas was a notorious prisoner, that is, widely known for wickedness.

## CHAPTER CLXVIII

M. 325[X]

While he was sitting on the judgment-seat, his wife sent to him, saying: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man; for today I have suffered much in a dream because of him.”

[Hieronymus.] Dreams are often revealed by God to Gentiles. Thus the wife of a Gentile man understood in visions what the Jews, awake, refused to believe. Therefore Pilate and his wife, confessing Christ to be righteous, provide the testimony of the Gentile people. Pilate sat [Col. 0570B] upon the judgment-seat, that is, to judge, which is the office of one sitting on a tribunal. For a tribunal is the seat of judges, the throne of kings, the chair of teachers.

M. 325[I] R. 204 L. 310 A. 184

But the chief priests and elders persuaded the people to ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus. The governor answered and said to them: “Which of the two do you wish to be released to you?” They said: “Barabbas.” A. Now Barabbas was a robber. L. M. R. He had been bound in prison for a certain insurrection made in the city and for murder.

[Bede.] Iniquity went forth from the elders and judges of the people, and their request, which they obtained—that they should choose a robber in place of Jesus—clings to the Jews to this day [Col. 0570C]. For they have been so overwhelmed by robberies and seditions that they have lost both country and kingdom. [Hieronymus.] These are the two goats: one, the scapegoat, is released with the people’s sin into the wilderness of hell; the other is killed as a lamb for the sins of those released. [HIERONYMUS—BEDE.] The Lord’s portion is always sacrificed; the devil’s portion, he who is their master, is hurled unrestrained into Tartarus. Since Barabbas in the Hebrew Gospel is interpreted “son of their master,” he can bear the type of Antichrist, whom those to whom it is said, “You are from your father the devil” (John 8), will prefer to the true Son of God.

[Col. 0570D] M. 326 R. 205 L. 291 A. 188

Pilate said to them: “What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” They all said: “Let him be crucified.” The governor said to them: “For what evil has he done?” But they cried out still more and more: “Let him be crucified.”

[Hieronymus.] Pilate gave many opportunities for the Savior to be released, and in saying, “What evil has he done?” he acquitted him of evil. But the Jews, neither ashamed that Pilate confessed Jesus as Christ nor observing any limit to their impiety, all said: “Let him be crucified.” Hence the Psalmist: “Many dogs surrounded me; the council of the wicked besieged me” (Ps. 21). And Jeremiah: “My inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest; they raised their voice against me” (Jer. 12). And Isaiah: “I expected them to do justice, but they did iniquity” [Col. 0571A] (Isa. 5). O Jews, we do not blame you for releasing the guilty man, but for killing the innocent one.

M. 327[X]

But Pilate, seeing that he was accomplishing nothing and that a greater disturbance was arising, took water and washed his hands before the people, saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man. See to it yourselves.”

[Hieronymus.] As if he said: “I am a minister of the laws; your voice sheds the blood of the righteous man, and for this you will suffer punishment.”

And all the people answered and said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

The imprecation of this crime and punishment endures to this day [Col. 0571B]. Hence Isaiah: “When you lift up your hands to me, I will not hear you; for your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 10). Pilate acted according to the saying: “I will wash my hands among the innocent” (Ps. 25), so that in the washing of his hands the works of the Gentiles might be cleansed and he might make us strangers to the Jews’ impiety, as though saying: “I wished to release the innocent man; but because an uprising arises and an accusation of treason against Caesar is brought against me, I am innocent of the blood of the righteous man.”

[Note: [Col. 0571] The crime of *perduellio* is taking arms with hostile intent against the commonwealth and its ruler.]

The judge who is compelled to pronounce sentence does not condemn the man brought before him, but indicts those who brought him. Thus Pilate is innocent by comparison with them, although he shared in the deed, because, if he had wished entirely, he could have rescued the one whom he pronounced righteous.

## CHAPTER CLXIX

[Col. 0571C] M. 328[I] R. 206 L. 314 A. 196

Then he released Barabbas to them; but Jesus, having been scourged, he handed over to them to be crucified.

[Hieronymus.] Barabbas, a seditious robber and author of murders, was released to the Jews—that is, the devil, who reigns in them. Why did Pilate hand Jesus over to the Jews after scourging him, when he had first declared himself innocent of his blood? [Augustine.] Because it was established by Roman law that one to be crucified should first be scourged. He is also to be believed to have scourged Jesus so that the Jews, satisfied with his injuries, might desist from the Lord’s death. Hence he also permitted his cohort to mock him, or perhaps commanded it. [Bede.] The column to which he was bound—the one who usually frees those in chains—still displays the traces of the Lord’s blood [Col. 0571D]. [Hieronymus.] Jesus is scourged so that we may be freed from scourges, as Scripture says to the righteous man: “The scourge shall not come near your tent” (Ps. 90). [Augustine.] Why did the Jews earlier refuse to kill Jesus if they now received him to kill? It was not said that they should crucify him, but that he should be crucified by the governor’s authority. Therefore the Evangelist said that he was handed over to them, to show them entangled in the crime from which they tried to appear alien.

M. 329[IV] R. 206 A. 185 and 187

The governor’s soldiers, taking Jesus into the praetorium [Col. 0572A], gathered the whole cohort around him; and stripping him, they clothed him in a purple tunic and draped a scarlet cloak around him. They plaited a crown of thorns and placed it upon his head, and put a reed in his right hand; and bending the knee before him, they mocked him, saying: “Hail, King of the Jews.”

[Hieronymus.] In mockery they strip him of his clothes, as though of his former powers, and clothe him in a purple tunic because he was called king; and with a scarlet cloak in place of the red-bordered garment which ancient kings wore; and in place of a diadem they give him a thorny crown, and in place of a scepter a reed. All these things must be understood mystically. For as Caiaphas said, “It is expedient that one man should die for all [the people],” not knowing what he said, so these men, doing what they do with evil intention, provide us with sacraments [Col. 0572B]. [Bede.] The purple is Christ’s flesh made red by sufferings, concerning which the Prophet says: “Why is your garment red, and your clothes like those of one treading the winepress?” (Isa. 62). [HIERONYMUS—BEDE.] In the scarlet cloak he bears the bloody deeds of the Gentiles; in the crown, the ancient curse. He bears the crown of thorns because, having become mortal for us, he took upon himself our sins. Hence his forerunner says: “Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). That thorns signify sins the Lord showed when, after the first-created man fell into sin, he said: “Your earth shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3). That is to say: “Your conscience will not cease to produce for you the pricks and stings of vices.”

[Origen.] The reed was a sign of the vain and fragile scepter upon which we all leaned before we believed [Col. 0572C]. For we trusted in the reed-staff of Egypt or Babylon (Isa. 36), or of any kingdom opposed to the kingdom of God. He took that reed and staff of fragile rule from our hands, in order to triumph over it and break it on the wood of the Cross, giving us the scepter of the heavenly kingdom and the rod of which it is written: “A rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. 44); or the rod that corrects those who need correction, of which the Apostle says: “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod?” (1 Cor. 4). He also gave us a staff, so that, laying aside the reed-staff which we had before celebrating the Lord’s Passover [Col. 0572D], we might celebrate the Passover according to what is written: “Let your staffs be in your hands” (Exod. 12). Further: he held the reed in order to write down the Jews’ sacrilege; or he kills poisonous animals with the reed. [HIERONYMUS—HILARY.] Further: having taken upon himself all the infirmities of our body, he is then suffused with the scarlet color in the blood of all the martyrs, to whom the kingdom was due with him. And he is clothed in purple with the precious honor of the prophets and patriarchs. He is crowned also with thorns, that is, with the sins of the Gentiles which once pierced them. For the sting of sins is in the thorns, from which victory and a crown are woven for Christ. In the reed, moreover, the infirmity and emptiness of those same Gentiles, grasped in his hand [Col. 0573A], is made firm. [Bede.] That the Lord is clothed before Herod in a white garment, and is said to have been mocked by Pilate’s soldiers in scarlet or purple dress, expresses in the one the innocence and chastity of assumed humanity, and in the other the reality of the Passion. In either garment may also be understood the whole multitude of the elect. For confessors are clothed in white, martyrs in purple or scarlet.

M. 330[VI] R. 208

And spitting upon him, they took the reed and struck his head.

What Pilate’s soldiers did then, the soldiers of the devil—heretics and pagans—do to this day: they strike his head by denying that he is God and by trying to confirm their error with the authority of Scripture, which is signified by the reed [Col. 0573B], for writing is commonly done with a reed. They spit upon his face who reject his presence and deny that he came in the flesh. They mockingly worship him who worship him with firm faith as the true God, but by perverse deeds despise his commandments and set temporal things before his promises.

And after they had mocked him, they stripped him of the cloak and purple, clothed him in his own garments, and led him away to crucify him, A. carrying his cross for himself.

[Hieronymus.] Here Abel is led into the field by his brother to be killed (Gen. 4). Here Isaac is present with the wood, and Abraham with the ram caught among thorns (Gen. 22). Here Joseph is present with the long robe stained with blood (Gen. 37). Here Moses is present with the rod and the serpent raised upon the wood (Num. 21). Here is the cluster carried upon a pole (Num. 13). Here Elisha is present with the wood for finding the axe which had sunk to the bottom and floated up at the wood (4 Kings 6): that is, the human race, which fell into hell through the forbidden wood, floated to paradise through the wood of Christ’s Cross and the water of baptism. Here is Jonah, sent from the wood of the lot into the sea and into the belly of the whale for three days. By his Cross he undid our torment, and through his death he put ours to death. In the form of a serpent he kills the serpent, because when a serpent was made from the rod, the other serpents were swallowed up [Col. 0573D]. Hence he says through the prophet: “I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O hell” (Hos. 13). His reproaches took away our reproach; his bonds made us free. By the thorny crown of his head we gained the diadem of the kingdom; by his wounds we were healed; by his burial we rise again; by his descent into hell we ascend into heaven. Here honey is found in the mouth of the dead lion (Judg. 14); hence the Prophet says: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. 115). Christ is stripped of his garments, that is, of the Jews; he is clothed in purple, that is, in the Gentile Church gathered from the peoples of the sea. Likewise, when that Church causes offense, he is stripped of it at the end and clothed again in the Jewish people. For when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved (Rom. 11).

[Col. 0574A] M. 331[I] R. 209 L. 315 A. 197

As they went out, they found a Cyrenian man coming from the country, named Simon, the father of Alexander and Rufus. They compelled him to carry the cross behind Jesus.

Simon seems to have been a man of great repute, since even his sons are identified by name as though known to all. Some are commemorated for the merits of their fathers—such as the Jewish people through the merits of the patriarchs and prophets—while others are commended through the merits of their children, as Simon here is through the merits of his sons, who were disciples. By this we are admonished that, in the present life, parents are helped by the merits of their children. Simon is rightly described as carrying the cross [Col. 0574B] after Jesus, because Christ himself suffered for us and left us an example, that we might follow in his steps (1 Pet. 2). Hence elsewhere: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9).

Cyrene, from which this Simon came, is a city of Libya, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 2). This Simon signifies the Gentiles: once strangers, but now, through obedience, made fellow citizens and members of God’s household, as is said elsewhere: “Heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs with Christ” (Rom. 8). Thus Simon is aptly interpreted “obedient,” and Cyrene “heir.” Nor should it be passed over that Simon is said to have come from the country. In Greek, a country district is called *pagos*, whence pagans take their name, because they are alien to the city of God. Coming from the *pagus*, Simon carries the cross after [Col. 0574C] the Lord when the people of the nations, abandoning pagan rites, obediently embrace the footsteps of the Lord’s passion.

[GREGORY.] Otherwise: Simon, who carries the cross under compulsion, is the person who labours for human praise. Men compel him to this labour; neither fear nor love of God compels him.

M. 316[X]

Now a great multitude of the people and of women followed him, who were weeping and lamenting for him. But Jesus turned to them and said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me; rather, weep for yourselves and for your children.”

[BEDA.] They did not follow the Lord with one and the same disposition; for a large part of the male populace rejoiced. [Col. 0574D] Even now a twofold crowd follows Jesus as though he were being led to sacrifice: some mock the history of his passion as a fable; others read it with tearful eyes; some receive the mysteries of his flesh and blood as common food; others resolve that they should be received with worthy hearts. It should be noted that not only those women who had come with him from Galilee are called daughters of Jerusalem, but also those who joined him from the city and wept with the others. The weeping of women alone is not introduced as though many men did not also grieve; rather, because the female sex, regarded as more contemptible, could more freely show, in the presence of the chief priests, what it thought against them. Since the Lord truly knows those who are his (2 Tim. 2), passing over the raging crowd of the people, he turned his [Col. 0575A] eyes and speech toward the women who loved and mourned him. “Do not lament,” he says, “that I am to die—my swift resurrection can undo death; my death will destroy death and death’s very author. Rather wash yourselves and your offspring with fitting fountains of tears, lest you be condemned with the faithless in punishment for my cross.”

“For behold, days are coming in which they will say: ‘Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that never bore, and the breasts that never nursed.’ Then they will begin to say to the mountains: ‘Fall upon us’; and to the hills: ‘Cover us.’”

He signifies the days of the coming siege and captivity by the Romans. Josephus relates that the Jews competed in seeking fortified caves and the caverns of the hills, so that he himself testifies that he was found, with forty companions, in a fortified place of the ruined city [Col. 0575B] and captured by the enemy. Moreover, this may be understood in an additional sense: those who have made themselves eunuchs, in either sex, for the kingdom of heaven say to mountains and hills, “Fall upon us and cover us,” when, mindful of their own frailty at the onset of temptation, they seek protection through the examples, admonitions, and prayers of exalted persons—whether through virginity itself, martyrdom, or any other virtue.

“For if they do these things in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?”

By the green wood he means himself and his own; by the dry wood, sinners and ungodly persons. It is as though he says: “If I, free from sin, do not depart from the world without the fire of suffering, what will become of the ungodly and sinners?”

## CHAPTER 170

[Col. 0575C] L. 312[I] M. 336 R. 215 A. 198

And two other evildoers were led with him to be put to death.

What was said is fulfilled: “And he was reckoned among the wicked” (Isa. 53). Detestable in deed is the wickedness of the Jews, who crucify the Redeemer of all as though he were a robber; yet in mystery the robber is good, who lay in wait for the devil in order to seize his goods.

L. 318[I] M. 330 R. 215 A. 197

And after they came to the place called Golgotha, which is interpreted “the place of the Skull.”

M. 333[IV] R. 211 A. 203

[Col. 0575D] And they gave him wine mixed with myrrh and gall to drink; and when he had tasted it, he would not drink.

[AUGUSTINE.] What Mark says—“he did not take it”—is to be understood thus: he did not take it in order to drink, as Matthew testifies when he says: “And when he had tasted it, he would not drink.”

[JEROME.] The bitter vine offers bitter wine. Then was fulfilled: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 58). Having tasted, he would not drink, because he tasted for us the bitterness of death; but on the third day he rose again, and by rising rejected death. Some say that the place of the Skull is where Adam was buried, and that this is why it was so called: because his head is said to have been placed elsewhere. They take this to be what the Apostle says: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give you light” (Eph. [Col. 0576A] 5). This is an attractive interpretation, pleasing to popular ears, but it is not true. Outside the city are places where the heads of condemned persons were cut off, and therefore they were called places of Skulls—that is, of the beheaded. The Lord was crucified there so that, where there had formerly been the execution-ground of the condemned, there might be raised the standards of the martyrs. But that Adam was buried near Hebron, we read in the twenty-first chapter of the book of Jesus son of Nave.

L. 320[X]

And Jesus said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

Because Luke set out to write of Christ’s priesthood under the figure of the calf, it is fitting that in his Gospel the Lord, exercising a priest’s office, intercedes for his persecutors and [Col. 0576B] opens the gate of Paradise to the confessing robber. For he did not pray in vain, but obtained this in those who believed after his passion.

M. 334[I] R. 212 L. 321 A. 201

After they crucified him, they took his garments and made four parts, one part for each soldier, and also the tunic. The tunic, however, was seamless, woven from the top throughout. Therefore they said to one another: “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it, to see whose it shall be,” so that the Scripture might be fulfilled which says: “They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast a lot” (Ps. 21). The soldiers indeed did these things, and, sitting, kept watch over him.

[JEROME—AUGUSTINE.] The carefulness of the guard benefits us, [Col. 0576C] so that the power of the risen Lord may appear more plainly. From the four parts of the Lord’s garments it is evident that four soldiers crucified him. Where it says “and the tunic,” “they took” must be understood. They could not divide it without tearing it; rather than do so, they preferred that it should fall by lot to one person. In saying “lots,” Luke uses the plural for the singular. Mark alone seems to introduce a question by saying that they cast a lot upon them, as though the lot had been cast concerning all the garments. But brevity creates obscurity: it is as though he said that the division of all the garments would not have been complete unless it had been made clear by lot who would take the tunic.

The Lord’s garment, divided into four parts, signifies the Church divided into the four regions of the world. [Col. 0576D] The tunic signifies the unity of all the regions, held together by the bond of charity. The tunic is said to have been seamless, lest charity be torn apart. For if, according to the Apostle, charity is above all commandments, it is rightly reported that the garment which signifies it was woven from above. “Throughout” is added because all believers ought to possess charity in all their deeds. In the lot, moreover, what is commended except God’s grace? For a lot comes to all through one, when the lot is pleasing to all; and grace is cast, as it were, by lot, because it is given to no one by merits, but is bestowed, by God’s hidden judgment, in the unity of faith.

How the Lord was placed upon the cross, and what royal symbolism that position of his most sacred body contains, Sedulius expressed in verses in his Paschal poem:

[Col. 0577A]

Lest anyone fail to know that the form of the cross should be revered,  
which bore the Lord in triumph: by mighty design  
it gathers the four regions of the squared world.  
The radiant East shines from the Creator’s head.  
His sacred feet are bathed by the star of the West.  
His right hand holds the North; his left raises the central axis.  
All created nature lives from his limbs,  
and Christ, embracing the cross, rules the world on every side.

The Apostle also describes the moral figure of the most holy cross when he says: “Rooted and grounded in charity, that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and also to know the charity of Christ which surpasses knowledge” (Eph. 3). Breadth signifies works of charity; length, perseverance [Col. 0577B] in holy conduct to the end; height, hope of heavenly rewards; depth, the inscrutable judgments of God by which this grace comes to human beings. These are fitted to the mystery of the cross as follows: breadth is the transverse wood on which the hands are extended, because of the signification of works; length is from that same beam down to the ground, where the crucified body seems to stand, signifying steadfast endurance; height is from the transverse beam upward, where it rises above the head, signifying expectation of things above, lest good works and perseverance in them be thought to be done for temporal benefits, but rather for everlasting blessings to be hoped for; and depth is that part of the wood fixed unseen in the earth, from which [Col. 0577C] what rises above springs forth. Thus, from the hidden will of God, one person is called to share in so great a grace [glory] in one way, another in another. By the charity of Christ that surpasses knowledge he surely means that peace which surpasses all understanding.

A. 199 M. 335 R. 214 L. 324

Pilate also wrote a title stating his charge, and set it above his head: “This is Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.”

[JEROME.] There are three kinds of inscriptions: one on the tombs of the dead; another on the thresholds of cities or houses; and a third at the victory of a king. Here he speaks of the title of the victory of the king, that is, of Christ. For after the [Col. 0577D] devil had been overcome, it was written over his head: “This is the King of the Jews.” I cannot sufficiently marvel that they killed him because he was King of the Jews [their king]. The title shows that not even by killing him could they bring it about that they should not have him as king.

[BEDA.] The title is fittingly placed above the cross, because he shone with royal majesty even while suffering on the cross; and it indicated to readers that he had not lost his sovereignty through the gibbet of the cross, but confirmed it.

A. 200[X]

Therefore many of the Jews read this title, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city; and it was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. Therefore the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate: “Do not write, ‘King [Col. 0578A] of the Jews,’ but rather, ‘He said: I am King of the Jews.’” Pilate answered: “What I have written, I have written.”

[AUGUSTINE.] Christ indeed is King of the Jews—but of Jews circumcised in heart, in spirit and not in letter. Thus Pilate wrote what he wrote because the Lord said what he said. The prophecy is fulfilled which says: “Do not destroy the inscription of the title.” These three languages stood out above the others: Hebrew, because of the Jews who gloried in the Law; Greek, because of the wise among the Gentiles; Latin, because of the Romans, who at that time already ruled almost all nations. Whether the Jews will it or not, therefore, diverse languages testify that Jesus is King of the Jews—that is, ruler of those who believe in and confess God.

M. 336[I] R. 215 L. 319 A. 198

[Col. 0578B] Then they crucified with him two robbers, one on his right and the other on his left.

[JEROME.] If Golgotha is Adam’s tomb and not the place of the condemned, and the Lord was therefore crucified there in order to raise Adam, why were the two robbers crucified in the same place?

[BEDA.] The robbers signify those who, under faith in and confession of Christ, undertake either the struggle of martyrdom or any disciplines of a stricter life. Those who do so solely for eternal glory are signified by the robber on the right, through faith; those who do so for some other reason by the robber on the left. Of the former it is said: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). But of the latter the Apostle says: “If I give up my body so that I may be burned, but do not have charity [Col. 0578C], it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13).

M. 337[VI] R. 217

Those passing by blasphemed him, shaking their heads and saying: “Aha! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days, save yourself. If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.”

[HILARY.] It was not difficult to come down from the cross. But the mystery of the Father’s will had to be fulfilled, and, while fixed upon the cross, he was accomplishing greater works through the disturbance of all nature.

[JEROME—GREGORY.] Those who go past blaspheme, because they refuse to walk in the straight way of the Scriptures. They shook their heads because they had previously moved their feet, refusing to stand upon the rock. For all heretics pass by [Col. 0578D] and turn aside, blaspheming Jesus. They have no firm head, but move it up and down because they lack wisdom and do not have their eyes in their head, where they ought to have them, as Ecclesiastes says: “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Eccl. 2). It belongs, then, to those passing by to blaspheme the Son of God; for no one speaking in the Spirit says, “Anathema to Jesus” (1 Cor. 12).

M. 338[II] R. 218 L. 322

Likewise the chief priests, mocking with the scribes and elders, said: “He saved others; himself he cannot save.”

[JEROME.] Though unwilling, they confess that he saved others. He who saved others would have saved himself if he had wished.

[Col. 0579A] “If he is King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, that we may see and believe him. Does he trust in God? Let him now deliver him, if he wants him. For he said: ‘I am the Son of God.’”

They distort those words of the Psalmist: “He hoped in the Lord; let him deliver him; let him save him, because he desires him” (Ps. 21).

[JEROME.] It is a deceitful promise that they will believe him if he now comes down from the cross. Which is greater: to come down alive from the cross, or to rise dead from the tomb? He rose, and they do not believe. Therefore, had he come down from the cross, they would not have believed. But I think demons suggested this. For as soon as he was crucified, they perceived the power of the cross and understood that their strength had been broken; and they acted to make him come down from the cross.

[BEDA.] But the Lord remains on the gibbet in order to destroy them. He [Col. 0579B] also declined to come down from the cross because, by dying, he resolved to save even some of those who crucified him. Note also that the Jews, blaspheming, mock the title “Son of God,” which Scripture had entrusted to them; but the soldiers, being ignorant of Scripture, insult not the Son of God but the King of the Jews.

M. 339[II] R. 219 L. 325

Likewise one of the robbers hanging there blasphemed him, saying: “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us.”

[JEROME.] Matthew and Mark introduce the robbers as reviling him, while Luke introduces only one of them. This is because at first both blasphemed, but afterward, when the earth was darkened, one believed. Or it may be understood thus: in those writers the plural [Col. 0579C] is used for the singular. We find this manner of speech in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “They stopped the mouths of lions” (Heb. 11), though Daniel alone is intended; and “They were sawn asunder” (*ibid.*), though it is said of Isaiah alone. So too in the Psalm: “The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers assembled as one” (Ps. 2): “kings” is said because of Herod, “rulers” because of Pilate. For what is more common than for someone to say, “The country people insult me,” even though only one person insults him? The pagans also spoke of “Phaedras” and “Clytemnestras,” though there was only one of each. Thus Luke’s statement about one is not contrary to Mark and Matthew. It would be contrary only if they had said that both robbers reviled the Lord; then one alone could not be understood under the plural number. But the fact that the robber reproaches him with the condition [Col. 0579D] of his suffering signifies that the cross will become a stumbling block even to all believers.

L. 326[X]

But the other answered and rebuked him, saying: “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we receive what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong.” And he said to Jesus: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” And Jesus said to him: “Amen I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise.”

[BEDA.] Nothing in this robber was free except his heart and tongue, by which he confessed the Lord, according to what is written in the Apostle: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10). [Col. 0580A] The Apostle says that three virtues remain in the hearts of the faithful, and the robber preserved them on the cross: faith, hope, and charity (1 Cor. 13). He had faith because he believed the Lord would reign. He had hope because he sought entry into his kingdom. He possessed charity because he reproved his fellow robber for wickedness. He confessed the Lord whom he saw dying with him, though Peter had denied him after seeing him work miracles. Great is the Lord’s grace: it gives more than is requested. The robber asked the Lord merely to remember him, but the Lord promised him Paradise. Where Christ was, there Paradise was.

[JEROME.] In the two robbers both peoples are represented: the Gentile people still blasphemes the Jewish.

[BEDA.] Some associate the two robbers crucified with Christ [Col. 0580B] with two classes of baptized persons. For all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death (Rom. 6; Gal. 3). But some, having works of faith, are crowned through the Lord’s suffering in the flesh; others, refusing, are deprived of the gift of grace.

A. 212

Now beside the cross of Jesus stood his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene. Therefore, when Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing there, he said to his mother: “Woman, behold your son.” Then he said to the disciple: “Behold your mother.” And from that hour the disciple received her into his own.

[AUGUSTINE.] A moral lesson is here suggested. He does what he admonishes should be done: namely, that devout children should bestow care upon their parents [Col. 0580C]. Paul had learned from this teaching what he taught when he said: “But if anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5). What is more closely one’s own than parents to children or children to parents? In place of himself, the Lord provided his mother with another son, as it were: John the Evangelist.

M. 340[II] R. 220 L. 326

From the sixth hour darkness came over all the land until the ninth hour.

[JEROME.] Those who wrote against the Gospel suppose that Christ’s disciples, through ignorance, interpreted an eclipse of the sun—which ordinarily occurs at fixed times—as pertaining to the Lord, although an eclipse of the sun never occurs [Col. 0580D] except at the conjunction of the moon. Yet it is beyond doubt that the moon was full at Passover. And lest it should seem that the shadow of the earth and moon cast upon the sun had produced only brief darkness, a period of three hours is stated, to remove every pretext from disputants. Then this prophecy was fulfilled: “The sun shall set at noon, and light shall be darkened over the earth in daytime” (Amos 8); and elsewhere: “The sun has set while it was still midday” (Jer. 15). The sun withdrew its rays lest it either behold the Lord hanging there or allow the ungodly to enjoy its light.

[BEDA.] It should be noted that the Lord was crucified while the sun was withdrawing from the centre of the world.

[GREGORY.] Since the order of things required that, at the very time when the gate of Paradise had been closed against sinning Adam, it should be opened to the repentant robber; and as, when Moses stretched out his hands toward heaven, darkness came [Col. 0581A] over the Egyptians (Exod. 10), who held God’s servants in bondage, so too, when Christ stretched out his hands toward heaven upon the cross at the sixth hour, darkness came upon the people who had cried, “Take him away from the earth and crucify him”; and they were deprived of every light. Again, under Moses darkness came over all Egypt for three days, while all the children of Israel had light in every place where they dwelt. But under Christ darkness came over all the land of Judaea for three hours, while light was over all the rest of the earth; this light everywhere illuminates the whole Church of God in Christ. For if darkness had then come over the whole earth, surely some such unprecedented event would be found in the histories of those who wrote chronicles [Col. 0581B]. And if the darkness was over all Judaea until the ninth hour, it is clear that light shone upon them again, because when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel shall be saved (Rom. 11). The fact that darkness came over all Judaea for three hours shows this: those who dared to lay hands upon the true Light were, because of their sins, deprived of the light of God the Father, of the radiance of Christ, and of the illumination of the Holy Spirit, as the prophet says: “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see” (Ps. 68).

M. 341[VI] R. 221

And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: “Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?” which is interpreted: [Col. 0581C] “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” But some who stood there and heard said: “This man calls Elijah.”

[JEROME.] I think these were Romans who did not understand Hebrew. But if we understand them to have been Jews, they wished to discredit the Lord’s weakness. For he speaks as a man, weeps as a man, is troubled as a man, and is crucified as a man, lamenting the miseries of the assumed nature, corrupted in the first parents. By this he shows how much those who sin ought to weep, when he who never sinned wept thus. He used the beginning of the twenty-first Psalm. For the words “look upon me,” which occur in the middle of the verse, are superfluous.

[GREGORY.] For it is read in Hebrew: “My God, [Col. 0581D] my God, why have you forsaken me?” Therefore those are ungodly who suppose that the Psalm is spoken in the person of David, Esther, or Mordecai. Since every utterance of Christ the Son of God must be considered great, even if it is quiet, some great hidden thing must be sought in his cry to God: “Why have you forsaken me?” Yet, with respect to those things in which the form of God and the image according to the Father were visible, he was forsaken by the Father when he took the form of a servant; and he was forsaken for humankind, so as to undergo such things and so great things—to come even to death, the death of the cross, which seems most shameful among human beings. The culmination of his abandonment was that he was crucified between robbers; that those passing by blasphemed him, shaking their heads at him; [Col. 0582A] that the chief priests with the scribes said, “He saved others; himself he cannot save”; and further, that even the robbers reproached him on the cross. You can therefore clearly understand what is meant by “Why have you forsaken me?”: it compares the glory that he had with the Father with the disgrace in which, despising it, he endured the cross. For his seat was like the sun before God, like the moon perfected forever, and his witness was faithful in heaven. Then, concerning those for whom he says, “Why have you forsaken me?” he adds: “But you have rejected and brought to nothing, and delayed your Christ. You have overthrown the covenant of your servant; you have profaned his holiness upon the earth,” and so forth (Ps. 21).

Seeing, therefore, that darkness had come, he cried out with a loud voice: “Why have you [Col. 0582B] forsaken me?” By this he wished to show: “You have willingly forsaken me, Father, and delivered me, emptied out amid such calamities, so that the people who had been honoured with you may receive the things they dared to do to me—filling up the measure of their fathers and doing what they did to the prophets—so that they may be deprived of the light of your regard and become in darkness as though you, God, were by no means present to them.” But you also forsook me for the salvation of the Gentiles, so that, with Israel forsaken, salvation might come to the Gentiles.

Or thus: seeing the sins of the human beings for whom he suffered, he said: “Why have you forsaken me? So that I became like one gathering stubble in harvest, and like one gathering grapes in vintage, when there is no cluster to eat, no first-ripe fruit. And I say these things because the devout have perished from the earth, and there is no one among humankind to correct.” [Col. 0582C] Before the ninth hour ended, the Lord cried with a loud voice, as though asking the sun to rise over the earth and dispel the three hours’ darkness, as we have set out above. For, made a curse for us, because “everyone who hangs on a tree is cursed” (Gal. 3), though by nature he was blessing, he consumed, dissolved, and scattered every human curse.

A. 203 M. 333 R. 211

Afterward, Jesus, knowing that all things had now been completed, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said: “I thirst.” Therefore a vessel full of vinegar had been placed there.

He speaks of this Scripture: “In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68).

[AUGUSTINE.] It is as though he said: “You have done too little; give what you are.” The Jews were [Col. 0582D] vinegar, having degenerated from the wine of the patriarchs and prophets, and, as from a full vessel, filled with the iniquity of this world. Everything that ought to have been done before he received the vinegar had already been completed.

M. 342[II] R. 222 L. 323

And immediately one of them ran, took a sponge, filled it with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave it to him to drink.

He found the sponge an image of them: hollow, weak, dry, fit for fires. He fills it with vinegar—that is, with malice and deceit.

[JEROME.] Of this the Lord says: “I planted you as a vine of Soreth; how then have you turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jer. 2). And: [Col. 0583A] “I expected it to produce grapes, and it produced thorns” (Isa. 5).

[AUGUSTINE.] The Jews had a heart like a sponge, deceitful through hidden recesses that were, as it were, cavernous and winding. But the hyssop, on which according to John they placed the sponge full of vinegar, is a lowly herb that cleanses the chest; we understand it as Christ’s humility, with which they surrounded him. Hence the Psalmist: “You shall sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Ps. 50). For we are cleansed by Christ’s humility. The reed on which the sponge was placed signifies Scripture, fulfilled in this deed. Just as “tongue” is used for the speech it expresses, so that we speak of Greek or Latin language, so “reed” can signify the writing that is written with a reed. Thus they place the sponge upon the reed: that is, they join the event to the prophecy previously uttered [Col. 0583B]. Therefore they were vinegar [the text has *erat*, “was”] and full of vinegar, because they themselves were corrupt and full of corruption. With this vinegar the soldiers give drink to the Lord, whom, at their instigation, they hand over to death. With this vinegar the deadly juice of the apple is wiped away.

M. 344 R. 223 L. 329 A. 204

Therefore, when Jesus had received the vinegar, he said: “It is finished.”

The Lord left nothing undone of what had to be done before he died. He therefore rightly said, “It is finished,” concerning that which belonged to the prophets.

[AUGUSTINE—HILARY.] Or he said, “It is finished,” because he had drained every defect of human corruption.

[Col. 0583C] M. R.

But the others said: “Leave him; let us see whether Elijah comes to deliver him.”

Because they misunderstood the Lord’s cry, they waited in vain for Elijah’s coming. Mark says that the person who filled the sponge said this. [AUGUSTINE.] From this we understand that both he and the others said it. Luke anticipated this before the robber’s insult, for he wished to summarize at once what the soldiers did and said. It should not trouble us that he said not one but several offered vinegar, just as John used the manner of speech discussed above, putting the plural for the singular.

[Col. 0583D] M. R. L.

And Jesus again cried out with a loud voice.

L.

“Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.”

A.

And bowing his head,

M. R. L. A.

he gave up the spirit.

[JEROME.] When his flesh was weakened, the divine power immediately prevailed, which says: “Open to me the gates of righteousness; having entered them, I shall give thanks to the Lord” (Ps. 117). We, who are from the earth, die with a low voice or with none; he who descended from heaven [Col. 0584A] breathed out with a raised voice.

[GREGORY.] He bowed his head and, as though resting upon the Father’s bosom, gave up the spirit—he who could cherish and strengthen it in his own bosom. Hence elsewhere he says: “No one can take my life from me, but I lay it down” (John 10).

[BEDA.] By calling upon the Father, he declares himself to be the Son of God; by commending his spirit, he indicates not a failure of his power but confidence in the same power which he has with the Father. He loves to give glory to the Father, so that he may build us up to give glory to the Creator. He commends his spirit to the Father, according to what he says in the Psalm: “For you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor allow your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 15).

M. 344[II] R. 224 L. 328

[Col. 0584B] And behold, the veil of the Temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.

[REMIGIUS.] The mysteries of the Law which were previously concealed were disclosed and passed to the Gentiles. The veil called the outer veil was torn, because now we see in part (1 Cor. 13); but when that which is perfect comes, the inner veil will be torn apart. It was divided into two parts, namely into the Old and New Testaments; and from top to bottom—that is, from the beginning of the world, when man was created, until the consummation of the age.

[JEROME.] In the Gospel of the Nazarenes, which we have often mentioned, we read that the lintel of the Temple, of immense size, was broken. Josephus also reports that the angelic powers formerly presiding over the Temple cried out together [Col. 0584C] at that time: “Let us depart from these seats.”

M. 345[X]

And the earth shook, the rocks were split, the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose; and, coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they came into the holy city and appeared to many.

The magnitude of the signs, according to the letter, shows forth its crucified Lord. Mystically, the hearts of earthly people were shaken; for, as the Prophet says: “All who saw them were troubled”—that is, Christ’s disciples—“and every human being was afraid” (Ps. 61). Those who had formerly been stony and, in understanding, as though dead, afterward acknowledged the Creator when their hearts’ hardness had been softened. [Col. 0584D] Or the rocks were split—that is, the prophecies of the prophets, called rocks because of Christ the Rock—so that whatever had been enclosed in them beneath the hard veil of the Law, when split open might stand revealed to the Gentiles. And just as the dead Lazarus rose, many bodies arose so that they might show the Lord rising again; yet, although the tombs were opened, they did not rise before the Lord, so that he might be the firstborn of the resurrection from the dead (Col. 1). By “the holy city” he means either the heavenly Jerusalem, where they were seen, or the earthly city, which had formerly been holy because of the Temple and the Holy of Holies, and in distinction from the other cities in which idols were worshipped.

[REMIGIUS.] They appeared to many, namely to those worthy to see them. These are believed [Col. 0585A] to have ascended bodily with the Lord when he ascended.

M. 345[II] R. 225 L. 330

The centurion and those who were with him guarding Jesus, when they saw the earthquake and the things that took place, were greatly afraid, glorifying God and saying: “This man was truly righteous, truly the Son of God.”

[BEDA.] The centurion confesses him to be the Son of God, while Arius proclaims him to be a creature. Nor did the centurion alone glorify God, but also the soldiers who were with him guarding Jesus. Thus the last become first, because the Gentiles confess, while the blinded Jewish people deny, so that their error becomes worse than the former one. Therefore through the centurion is rightly signified the faith of the Church, which, once the veil of the heavenly mysteries had been opened through the Lord’s death [Col. 0585B], immediately affirms—while the Synagogue is silent—that Jesus is both truly a righteous man and truly the Son of God.

L. 331[II] M. 347 R. 236

And all the crowd who had come together for this spectacle, seeing the things that took place, went away beating their breasts; and at a distance were many women who had gone up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, among whom were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the Less and Joseph, and Salome, mother of the sons of Zebedee. And when he was in Galilee, they followed him, seeing these things.

[Bede.] “They were returning from a distance,” that is, from places somewhat removed from the very scaffold of the cross. [Col. 0585C] The beating of their breasts may likewise be understood in two ways: either because they grieved for the Lord, whom they had loved, unjustly put to death; or because those who had obtained His death feared His glorification. The Lord had as companions Mary Magdalene, from whom He had cast out seven demons (Mark 16); the mother of the sons of Zebedee, who had asked a kingdom for her children; and others of whom we read in the Gospel (Matt. 20). For it was customary among the Jews that women should provide teachers with food and clothing from their own resources. Paul, however, states that he had renounced this, because it might cause scandal among the nations: “Have we not the power to lead about women who are sisters, as also the other apostles?” (1 Cor. 5). [Col. 0585D] They supplied the Lord with temporal things in return for spiritual things—not because He was in need, but in order to show that teachers ought to be content with food and clothing received from their disciples. [Bede.] The lesser James was called James of Alphaeus, to distinguish him from the greater James, son of Zebedee, who was called among the first apostles. This lesser James was also called the Lord’s brother, because he was the son of Mary, the Lord’s maternal aunt. She is Mary of Clopas, so called either from her father or from kinship; or perhaps because her husband Alphaeus was also called Clopas; or because, after Alphaeus had died following the birth of James, Mary herself married Clopas.

A. 205[X]

Therefore the Jews, because it was the Preparation, asked Pilate that the bodies should not remain [Col. 0586A] on the cross on the Sabbath—for that Sabbath day was a great one—but that their legs might be broken and they taken away.

[Augustine.] Not merely that their bodies should be taken down, but that those whose legs were therefore broken might die, lest their prolonged suffering should defile the feast with horror. [Bede.] *Parasceve* is Greek; in Latin it is called “Preparation.” By this name the Jews living among Greeks called the sixth day of the Sabbath, because on that day they customarily prepared what was necessary for the Sabbath.

Therefore the soldiers came, and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who had been crucified with Him. But when they came to Jesus, and saw that He was already dead, they did not break His legs; but one of the soldiers opened His side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out, [Col. 0586B] that the Scripture might be fulfilled: “You shall not break a bone of it” (Exod. 12). Again another Scripture says: “They shall look upon Him whom they pierced” (Zech. 12).

[Augustine.] The Evangelist deliberately used the word “opened,” rather than saying “struck” or “wounded,” so that from there, as it were, the door of life might be thrown open, whence the sacraments of the Church flowed—without which one does not enter into true life. This door was prefigured in the side of Noah’s ark, and by the first woman being made from the man’s side. They, moreover, who were commanded to celebrate the Passover by the sacrifice of a sheep under the old Law, were commanded: “You shall not break a bone of it.”

## Chapter CLXXI

[Col. 0586C] M. 348[II] R. 227 L. 332 A. 206

When evening had come, there came a certain rich man, a noble councillor, from the city of Arimathea in Judaea, named Joseph, a good and just man, who was himself also a hidden disciple of Jesus because of fear of the Jews, and who himself awaited the kingdom of God. He had not consented to their counsel and actions. He approached Pilate and requested the body of Jesus. Pilate wondered whether He had died already; and, summoning the centurion, he asked him whether He was already dead. When he had learned this, he ordered the body to be given over.

[Jerome.] Joseph was rich, and therefore could obtain from Pilate the body of Jesus, which poor men had not dared to request. Some think that the first Psalm was composed about him: “Blessed is the man who has not [Col. 0586D] walked in the counsel of the ungodly.” [Bede.] A *decurio* is one who belongs to the municipal council and administers its office; he is also called a *curialis*, from civil administration. Arimathea is Ramathaim, the city of Elkanah and Samuel (1 Sam. 1). [Augustine.] By the confidence which his rank gave him, Joseph entered familiarly to Pilate, now caring less for the Jews, although earlier, while hearing the Lord, he had avoided their hostility.

A. 307[X]

Nicodemus also came, he who had first come to Jesus, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds.

[Col. 0587A] The punctuation should not be made so as to say, “first bringing”; rather, “first” belongs to what precedes, thus: “who first came to Jesus by night.” This Nicodemus afterwards became a disciple of Christ (John 3), as is apparent in the revelation of the body of St Stephen.

A. 208[I] M. 349 R. 228 L. 393

Therefore they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with spices, as is the Jewish custom in burying.

[Jerome.] John the Evangelist did not say without purpose, “as is the Jewish custom in burying,” but reminded us that in the rites for the dead the custom of each nation should be observed. [Augustine.] Since others said that Joseph wrapped the body in a shroud, they did not thereby deny that other linen cloths could have been brought by Nicodemus. Indeed, [Col. 0587B] because of the cloth for the head and the bands with which the body was bound, since these were of linen, it could most truly be said that one shroud was there. [Jerome.] From the Lord’s simple burial the ambition of the rich is condemned, for they cannot dispense with riches even in their tombs. Mystically, we may understand that the Lord’s body should be wrapped not in gold, gems, or silk, but in pure linen. Yet this also signifies that the person wraps Jesus in a clean shroud who receives Him with a pure mind. [Bede.] We read that St Sylvester, pope, decreed that the sacrifice of the altar should be celebrated only upon a linen cloth, just as the Lord’s body was buried in a clean shroud.

A. There was, however, in the place where He was crucified, a garden; and in the garden a new tomb. A. L. In which no one had yet [Col. 0587C] been laid. M. R. L. A. And Joseph laid Him there. M. R. And he rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb, and departed.

Joseph placed the body of Jesus in the tomb because, through the nobility of secular power, he was able to receive it, and through the righteousness of his merits was worthy to bury it. Here the evasiveness of the Jews is refuted: for they would have said that He had not been buried, whom they said had been stolen, if the apostles had buried Him. [Augustine.] The burial was hastened lest evening should come, when, because of the Preparation, it was no longer lawful to do such a thing. [Jerome.] He is placed in a new tomb, lest, after the resurrection, while the other bodies remained, someone else might be pretended to have risen. [Bede.] Matthew and Mark also record that the tomb was cut out of rock, lest, if it had been built from many stones, it might be said that He had been stolen by undermining the foundations of the tomb. The Lord alone is enclosed in the tomb, so that His singular burial might differ from ours, as did the other mysteries of His dispensation. Hence: “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. 140). And: “For Thou, O Lord, hast established me singularly in hope” (Ps. 40). [Jerome.] The new tomb may also signify the virginal womb of Mary; and the great stone set against its entrance shows that the tomb could not have been opened without the help of very many persons. [Augustine.] As no one was conceived in Mary’s womb before Him or after Him, so no one was buried in this tomb before Him or after Him. [Bede.] [Col. 0588A] The Lord’s tomb is described as a round chamber cut out of the underlying rock, of such height that a man standing inside could scarcely touch its roof with his outstretched hand. It has an entrance from the east, upon which that great stone was placed. On the north side of this tomb was the sepulchre itself—that is, the place for the Lord’s body—made out of the same rock, seven feet in length and raised three palms above the rest of the pavement. This place was open throughout, not from above but from the southern side, through which the body was brought in. The colour of this tomb and bier is said to have been a mixture of reddish and white.

[Col. 0588B] M. 350[VI] R. 229

Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb.

While the others left the Lord, the women persevered in their service, awaiting God’s promise. [Jerome.] Therefore they deserved to be the first to see Him risen, because “he who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10). Holy women keep the day of the Preparation when humble souls follow the Saviour’s footsteps in this world, in which the future rest must be prepared.

L. 334[X]

They saw how His body was laid.

[Col. 0588C] L. 325[VIII] R. 230

And returning, they prepared spices and ointments, so that when they came they might anoint Jesus; and on the Sabbath they kept silence according to the commandment.

[Bede.] Among the Jews it was commanded that Sabbath rest be observed from evening to evening, that is, from sunset to sunset. This the women also did. Having seen the Lord’s burial, they bought spices on the Preparation before sunset, or on the Sabbath after sunset, and prepared them so as to anoint the Lord’s body in the morning. Thus the faithful remember the Lord’s burial and, as it were, prepare spices if they turn themselves to works of virtue in which Christ delights. They keep silence on the Sabbath, intending to come after the Sabbath with gifts to [Col. 0588D] the Lord, because, when the preparation of this present life has ended, they rejoice in rest while awaiting the day of resurrection, and then offer Christ spiritual actions, like fragrant spices. Man was made on the sixth day; God rested on the Sabbath. Therefore Jesus dies for man on the sixth day. Hence He said, “It is finished”: that is, on the sixth day the work for the redemption of the world was completed, and on the Sabbath He rested in the tomb. Thus we too must suffer for the Lord in this sixth age, and rest in hidden peace during the seventh, which is that of the dead, until the eighth, that of resurrection, arrives.
