In Genesis the seventh day is not said to have had an evening, because in that age the rest of souls is consumed by no sorrow, but is increased by the joy of the future resurrection.

## Chapter CLXXII

[Col. 0589A]

M. 351[X]

On the next day, which is after the Preparation, the chief priests and Pharisees gathered before Pilate, saying: “Lord, we remember that that deceiver said while still alive: ‘After three days I shall rise.’ Therefore command that the tomb be guarded until the third day, lest perhaps His disciples come and steal Him, and say to the people: ‘He has risen from the dead’; and the last error will be worse than the first.”

The Jews seem to have said these things on the day before the Sabbath, which is the Preparation, after the Lord had already been buried. Or, as other books have it, “on the next day, which is after the Preparation,” that is, on the Sabbath, they said these things. It is credible [Col. 0589B] that they said these and other things not written down on both days, their envy being plainly shown in seeking to extinguish the Lord’s renown.

Pilate said to them: “You have a guard; go and guard it as you know how.” And they went and secured the tomb, sealing the stone together with the guards.

[Hilary.] Their fear that the body might be stolen, the guard of the tomb, and its sealing are testimony to their folly and unbelief, since they had already seen, by the Lord’s command, a dead man raised from the tomb (John 11). [Jerome.] That He was to be laid in a tomb is attested by the prophet who says: “He dwelt in the lofty cave of the most strong rock” (Isa. 33). Immediately, two verses later, follows: “You shall see the King in glory” (ibid.).

## Chapter CLXXIII

[Col. 0589C]

M. 352[I] R. 231 L. 336 A. 209

At the evening of the Sabbath, which dawns into the first day of the Sabbath, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene, the other Mary, and Salome came to the tomb, bringing the spices which they had prepared.

[Augustine.] By the term “evening” he denotes the night, understanding the whole from a part. For evening is the beginning of night. Therefore he did not say “which dawns,” but “which [feminine] dawns,” making the reference, according to the sense, to the night, which ends at the dawn of the Lord’s Day. He is understood to have called that night thus because, once the Sabbath had passed, it was already permissible from evening onward for them to prepare and bring [Col. 0589D] spices. [Bede.] The Ordainer of times rose during the final part of this night. What else is it for the Son of God to rise again but to come to life again—that is, to return from death to life? On this night, through the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection, the order of times was changed. Formerly night rightly followed day, because humanity, falling from the light of Paradise through sin, descended into the darkness and miseries of this world. Now day rightly follows night, since through faith in the resurrection, by Christ’s gift, we are led back from the darkness of sin and the shadow of death to the light of life. [Augustine.] Therefore, when it is said that the Lord was three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, as Jonah was in the belly of the whale (Matt. 12; John 2), we must understand it according to this manner of speech in which the whole is understood from a part: namely, through the final part of the day of the Preparation, on which the Lord was buried, the whole day with its already-past night; and, through the following night and the Sabbath, the complete third day. [Jerome.] “The first day of the Sabbath,” or “one day of the Sabbath” or “of Sabbaths,” means the Lord’s Day, because the entire week is divided into the Sabbath and the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth day of the Sabbath. The week itself was also sometimes called “Sabbath” by privilege of the Sabbath, as in: “I fast twice in the Sabbath” (Luke 18), that is, in the week.

And when the sun had now risen, they said among themselves: “Who will roll away for us the stone from the entrance of the tomb?” For it was very large.

[Col. 0590B] [Augustine.] “When the sun had now risen,” that is, when the sky had already begun to whiten on the eastern side. This surely does not occur except near the rising of the sun; for that brightness is what is usually called dawn. [Bede.] That the women came very early shows their great ardour in seeking the Lord. Mystically, moreover, we are given an example: having cast off the darkness of vices, we should approach the Lord’s body. For the tomb signifies the Lord’s altar, on which the mysteries of His flesh and blood are celebrated. The spices brought by the women signify the fragrance of virtues and the sweetness of prayers, with which we ought to approach the altar.

And behold, there was a great earthquake. For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and came and rolled back [Col. 0590C] the stone.

[Bede.] The angel rolled away the stone, not in order to open a door for the Lord who was coming out, but to furnish proof that His departure had already taken place. He who came forth mortal from the closed womb was able, having now become immortal, to come forth from the closed tomb—and did so. That a great earthquake occurred at the Lord’s resurrection, as also at His death, signifies that hearts attached to earthly things and cast down from heavenly hope are to be shaken to repentance through faith in His passion and resurrection, and, stirred by most salutary fear, raised to everlasting life. The rolling away of the stone signifies the unveiling of the mysteries that had been hidden under the veil of the letter. For the Law was written upon stone; when its covering was removed, [Col. 0590D] the glory of the resurrection was revealed.

R. L.

And looking, they saw the stone rolled away from the tomb, and an angel sitting upon it. His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow.

[Gregory.] Because God is fearful to sinners and gentle to the righteous, the angel is rightly shown thus, that by his appearance he may terrify the reprobate and soothe the devout. For in lightning is the terror of fear; in snow, the gentleness of brightness. The brightness of the garment announced the joys of both the angelic feast and our own. For the Lord’s resurrection both restored us to immortality and, by replenishing the number of angels, repaired the losses of the heavenly country. Thus he sat, [Col. 0591A] indicating one who reigns, whereas by standing at the Nativity he had signified one who would fight. [Bede.] He sat upon the stone that closed the tomb, to teach that the gates of hell had been overcome. As Mark specifies, he sat at the right—that is, on the southern side of the place where the body of Jesus had been. For a body lying on its back, with its head toward the west, has its right side toward the south. [Gregory.] What is signified by the left hand but the present life, and by the right hand but eternal life? Hence: “His left hand is under my head, and His right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2). Since our Redeemer had now passed beyond the corruption of the present life, the angel who came to announce His everlasting life rightly sat on the right. God placed His left hand—that is, the prosperity of this present life—as it were beneath the head of the Church, which she presses down by the intention of supreme love. But God’s right hand embraces her, because she is held in complete devotion beneath His eternal blessedness.

M. 353[II] R. 232 L. 337

But because of fear of him the guards were terrified and became as dead men. The angel answered and said to the women: “Do not be afraid. For I know that you seek Jesus, who was crucified. He is not here; for He has risen, as He said. Come and see the place where the Lord was laid.”

[Jerome.] As though he said: If you do not believe words, believe the empty tomb. The angel does not console the guards but the women. “Let terror,” he says, “remain among unbelievers. But you, because you seek Jesus, hear that He has risen.” [Gregory.] Let those fear who do not love the coming of the citizens above; let those be terrified who, burdened by carnal desires, despair of being able to attain their fellowship. Why do you fear, you who see your fellow citizens? He who is not here in the presence of flesh is absent nowhere in the presence of majesty. [Jerome.] The bitter root of the cross has vanished; the flower of life has burst forth with its fruits: that is, He who lay in death has risen in glory. [Bede.] The body of Jesus is not found dead, but is proclaimed living. For even if “we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know Him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5).

L. 336[I] M. 352 R. 231 A. 209

[Col. 0591D] And it happened, while they were bewildered in mind about this, behold, two men stood beside them in shining clothing.

The angels proclaim the glory of the triumphant One not only in word but also in their shining attire. Women who came with spices see angels, because those women behold in mind the citizens above who advance toward God with virtues through holy desires. [Bede.] They were bewildered in mind because they were astonished both at the great stone having been rolled away and grieved at not finding the body. It should be known that, as angels are recorded to have been present at the Saviour’s tomb, so they ought to be believed to stand by the mysteries of the Lord’s body at the time of consecration. Hence the Apostle urges women to be veiled in church because of the angels (1 Cor. 11).

[Col. 0592A] L. 337[II] M. 353 R. 232

But when they were afraid and bowed their faces to the earth, they said to them: “Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but has risen. Remember how He spoke to you when He was still in Galilee, saying: ‘The Son of Man must be handed over into the hands of sinful men, be crucified, and rise on the third day.’”

It is impossible for what He said not to happen; and it is certain that among the disciples the Lord foretold His resurrection even to the women who followed Him. Why, then, do they seek Him, now raised, among the dead—that is, in the tomb, which is the proper place of the dead? By the example of the women, whenever we enter the church we ought to enter with all humility. [Col. 0592B] We bow our face to the earth at the sight of angels when, contemplating the joys of the citizens above, we remember that we are ashes, as blessed Abraham says: “I shall speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18). Note that the holy women are said not to have fallen to the earth, but to have bowed their faces. Hence the ecclesiastical custom has prevailed that, whether in memory of the Lord’s resurrection or in hope of our own, on every Lord’s Day and throughout the whole season of Pentecost, we pray not with bent knees but with faces bowed to the earth. The Lord lay in the tomb for one day and two nights not without reason, because He joined the light of His single death to the darkness of our double death. For He accepted death in the flesh alone, and loosed our two deaths, of flesh and spirit.

M. R.

And go quickly and tell His disciples that He has risen from the dead. And behold, He will go before you into Galilee. There you will see Him; behold, I have told you beforehand.

[Gregory.] The women are told to announce risen life to the apostles because death had been announced through a woman. Galilee is interpreted “a migration accomplished”: the Redeemer had already passed from passion to resurrection, from death to life, from punishment to glory, from corruption to incorruption. After the resurrection He is seen by the disciples in Galilee, because we too shall afterwards joyfully see the glory of His resurrection if we now pass from vices to the heights of virtues. [Jerome.] Or thus: He will go before them [Col. 0592D] into Galilee, that is, into the rolling mire of the nations, where formerly there were error and slipperiness, and they did not set their foot firmly.

L.

And they remembered His words.

M. 354[II] R. 233 L. 338

And they went out quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, running to announce it to His disciples.

[Augustine.] They feared because of the greatness of the miracle, and rejoiced because of the longed-for resurrection. Therefore, when Mark says that they fled from the tomb in fear and told no one anything, let us understand that they had not dared to say anything to anyone about the angels themselves, or about the guards whom they saw lying there.

[Col. 0593A] A. 210[X]

Therefore she ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and said to them: “They have taken the Lord from the tomb, and I do not know where they have laid Him.”

[Augustine.] Some manuscripts have “my Lord,” which may be understood as said with a more fervent affection of love and service. Mary Magdalene was more ardent than the other women. Therefore John mentions only her as coming, passing over the others who were with her; and she thought that Jesus’ body had been taken away because she did not find it. Therefore she ran and announced it to Peter and John, that they might either seek with her or grieve with her.

Therefore Peter and that other disciple went out and came [Col. 0593B] to the tomb. The two were running together, but that other disciple ran ahead more quickly than Peter and came first to the tomb. And when he had bent down, he saw the linen cloths lying there; yet he did not go in. Then Peter came following him and entered the tomb. And he saw the linen cloths lying there, and the cloth that had been upon His head, not lying with the linen cloths, but separately wrapped together in one place. Then the disciple who had first come to the tomb also entered; and he saw and believed. For they did not yet know the Scripture, that He had to rise from the dead.

[Albinus.] He saw the empty tomb and believed what the woman had said, namely, that He had been removed from the tomb. [Col. 0593C] For darkness still remained in their minds, so much so that, even when Scripture was openly taught by the Lord Himself, because they were accustomed to hearing parables from Him, they did not understand. [Jerome.] But how did Peter and John enter while a company of soldiers kept guard? Because, when the great earthquake occurred, the terrified guards either fled or became numb with fear. [Gregory.] John, who ran ahead, signifies the Synagogue; Peter, the Church. John was younger than Peter. For although the Synagogue was earlier than the Church of the Gentiles in worshipping God, nevertheless the multitude of Gentiles is earlier in the course of the world than the Synagogue. Paul bears witness when he says: “What is spiritual is not first, but what is natural” (1 Cor. 15). They ran together because, from its beginning until its end, [Col. 0593D] Gentile society ran alongside the Synagogue by the same path, though not with the same understanding. Throughout the course of this world the Jews ran by the letter of the king; the Gentiles by the law of nature. The Synagogue arrived first at the tomb by hearing the prophecies of the Lord’s passion, but did not enter at all because it refused to believe. The linen cloths are the sacraments of Scripture. The cloth for the Lord’s head is not found with the linen cloths, because, as Paul testifies, the head of Christ is God, and the incomprehensible mysteries of divinity are distinct from the knowledge possible to our weakness. It is found wrapped up because that which is wrapped has neither its beginning nor its end visible. For the loftiness of divinity neither began to exist nor ceases. “In one place” is added because God is not in divided minds. Since a cloth is ordinarily used to wipe the sweat [Col. 0594A] of those who labour, the name “cloth” may also express the labour of God, who is always at rest and unchangeable in Himself, yet declares that He labours when He bears the harsh perversities of human beings. Hence He says through the prophet: “I have laboured in enduring” (Isa. 1). In the flesh He laboured from our weakness. It is rightly found separately, therefore, because the Redeemer’s passion is far different from ours. He endured it without fault; we, with fault. He underwent death willingly; we, unwillingly. John entered after Peter because at the end of the world Judaea will be converted, as Paul says: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and so all Israel should be saved.”

Then the disciples went away again to their own homes (Rom. 11).

[Col. 0594B] A. 211[I] M. 352 R. 231 L. 336

But Mary Magdalene, from whom He had cast out seven demons, stood outside the tomb weeping.

[Augustine.] Since the disciples believed that the body had been taken away, they went back to their own homes—that is, to the place where they lived and from which they had run to the tomb. But Mary grieved more that the Lord had been taken from the tomb than that He had been killed, because no memorial even remained of the Teacher whose life she had lost; and this grief held her before the tomb. [Bede.] In Mark, chapter 233, she is recorded as having been healed from seven demons—that is, from all vices—so that where sin abounded grace might abound still more. For the number seven is customarily used to signify totality. [Gregory.] With burning desire she sought the Lord, in accordance with: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10). The Law commands the tail of the victim to be offered, signifying that a good work must be brought through to its end. Thus Joseph is written to have had a tunic reaching to the ankle (Gen. 37), for a tunic reaching to the ankle signifies a good work brought to completion.

A. 212[X]

Therefore, while she wept, they said to her: “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them: “Because they have taken my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid Him.”

[Augustine.] The angels who, according to Luke, stood and spoke to the women are here understood, according to John, [Col. 0594D] to speak while seated to Mary, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain. What else do they announce there but future joy, forbidding tears? But she, by the force of love increasing the intensity of her search, revealed the cause of her tears, saying: “Because they have taken my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid Him.” She calls the Lord’s body “Lord,” signifying the part by the whole. [Gregory.] The two angels sitting at the head and feet signify that the Gospel is to be proclaimed from the beginning of the Lord’s resurrection to the end of the world. They signify that He is to be proclaimed who is God before the ages and man at the end of the ages. As though at the head, the angel sits when John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” As though [Col. 0595A] at the feet, the angel sits when it is said: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” Or we understand the two angels as the two Testaments, which, in harmonious meaning, announce both that He died and that He rose; as it were, the earlier Testament sits at the head and the later at the feet. Hence too the two cherubim who cover the mercy-seat look at one another, their faces turned toward the mercy-seat (Exod. 35). *Cherubim* indeed is said to mean “fullness of knowledge.” Therefore the two Testaments are signified by the two cherubim; the incarnate Lord by the mercy-seat, of whom John says: “For He is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2).

When she had said this, she turned backward and saw Jesus standing, and did not know that it was Jesus.

She turned backward so that she might see Jesus, because through her doubt she had, as it were, turned her back upon God’s face: she did not at all believe that He had risen, and therefore, though she loved Him, she did not recognize Him when she saw Him. This was not because, according to the heretics, the Lord had changed His form and face, so as to appear different and changeable at will, but because Mary was astounded by the miracle.

Jesus said to her: “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom do you seek?”

The cause of her grief is asked so that the longing of love may increase, in order that, when she named Him whom she sought, she might burn more ardently in love.

Thinking that He was the gardener, she said to Him: “Lord, if you have taken Him away, tell me where you have laid Him, and I will take Him up.”

Perhaps this woman, who in error thought Jesus a gardener, was not mistaken. For was He not spiritually a gardener, who planted in her breast the verdant virtues through the seeds of His love? Before Mary said whom she sought, she said, “Lord, if you have taken Him away,” because the power of love is accustomed to work this in the mind: whoever it continually thinks about, it supposes no one else can fail to know.

Jesus said to her: “Mary.”

After calling her by a common name and not being recognized, He calls her by name. It is as though He plainly said: “Recognize Him by whom you are recognized.”

She turned and said to Him: “Rabboni,” which means “Teacher.”

Earlier she had turned in body and supposed Him to be what He was not; now, turned in heart, she recognized what He was. [Augustine.] [Col. 0595D] Let no one reproach the woman because she called the Lord a gardener and Jesus a teacher. There she was making a request; here she was recognizing Him. There she honoured a man from whom she sought a favour; here she remembered the Teacher from whom she had learned to distinguish human and divine things.

Jesus said to her: “Do not touch Me, for I have not yet ascended to My Father.”

The sense is: You seek One dead and are not worthy to touch Him living. If you still think that I have not ascended to the Father but have been taken away through human fraud, you are unworthy of My touch. [Gregory.] He said this so that she might believe spiritually that He reigns with the Father. For that person truly touches Jesus who believes that the Son is coeternal with the Father. For Jesus had already ascended to the Father in Paul’s heart when Paul himself said: “Who, [Col. 0596A] being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized” (Phil. 2). [Augustine.] Mystically, in Mary the Church from the Gentiles was prefigured, which did not believe in Christ before He ascended into heaven.

“But go to My brothers and tell them: ‘I ascend to My Father and your Father, and My God and your God.’”

He does not say, “our Father.” Therefore He is Mine in one way and yours in another: Mine by nature, yours by grace. “My God,” under whom I too am man; “your God,” among whom I myself am mediator.

## Chapter CLXXIV

M. 355[X]

Behold, some of the guards came into the city and reported to the chief priests all that [Col. 0596B] had happened. Having gathered with the elders and taken counsel, they gave a large sum of money to the soldiers, saying: “Say that His disciples came by night and stole Him while you were asleep; and if this is heard by the governor, we shall persuade him and make you safe.”

If the governor hears that the body was secretly taken away, we shall persuade him not to exact anything from you for negligence in guarding it. [Jerome.] O foolish madness! You produce sleeping men as witnesses. If they slept, how did they see? If they did not see, how are they witnesses? The guards confess the miracle; but those who ought to have been converted persist in wickedness and turn money given for the uses of the Temple into payment for a lie. Therefore all who misuse the Temple fund and what is contributed for the uses of the Church upon other things through which they fulfil their own will are like the scribes and priests who purchase a lie.

But they, having received the money, did as they had been instructed; and this report was spread among the Jews up to the present day.

[Hilary.] From guards who had seen the miracles, money purchases silence about the resurrection and the lie of theft; and these persist among the Jews, lest they believe in Christ. Therefore, because worldly money confers honour, Christ’s glory is denied.

A. 212[X]

[Col. 0596D] Mary Magdalene came, announcing to the disciples: “I have seen the Lord, and He said these things to me.”

[Gregory.] Behold, the fault of the human race is cut off at the point from which it proceeded. In Paradise a woman offered death to a man; from the tomb a woman announces life to men. Brothers, we ought to behold the great mercy of our Creator. Has someone burned with the wickedness of cruelty against a neighbour? Let him look at the thief (Luke 24), who in the very moment of death came by repentance to the rewards of life. Has another, panting with the heat of greed, plundered what belonged to others? Let him look at Zacchaeus (Luke 19), who, if he had taken anything from anyone, restored it fourfold. Has another, inflamed by the fire of lust, lost the purity of the flesh? Let him look at Mary (Luke 9), who burned up in herself the love of the flesh by the fire of divine love.

## Chapter CLXXV

[Col. 0597A]

M. 355[X]

And behold, Jesus met them, saying: “Greetings.” They came up, took hold of His feet, and worshipped Him.

[Hilary.] The Lord met the women after they had been exhorted by the angel, so that they who were about to announce the resurrection to the awaiting disciples might speak not from the mouth of an angel but rather from Christ’s own mouth. [Jerome.] Those who ran thus deserved to have the Lord meet them and to be the first to hear, “Greetings,” so that Eve’s curse might be undone in women. These women approach and hold His feet. But she who sought the living among the dead and did not yet know that He had risen deservedly hears: [Col. 0597B] “Do not touch Me.”

Then Jesus said to them: “Do not be afraid.”

In both the Old and the New Testament this is to be observed: whenever some more august vision has appeared, fear is first driven away, so that what is said may be heard with a tranquil [calmed] mind.

“Go, tell my brethren to go into Galilee; there they shall see me.”

[AMBROSE.] That is, not in Judaea, but among the multitude of the Gentiles. For grace, about to pass over from the Jews to the Gentiles, goes ahead by preparing the way in their hearts: there they shall see me in the members of my body, which is the Church. Since the weaker sex does not possess constancy for preaching, whence women are by no means permitted to teach in the Church, the office of evangelizing is therefore entrusted to men. [Col. 0597C] [REMIGIUS.] He calls brethren those whom previously he had also called servants, in order to teach both that through the resurrection he had resumed the same humanity, and that they were to hope for the same.

L. 338 M. 354 R. 233

When they had gone, they reported all these things to the eleven, who were mourning and weeping, and to all the rest who had been with him. And when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by them, they did not believe them.

And these words appeared before them like nonsense, and they did not believe them.

L. 339[X]

[Bede.] Just as woman was formerly first in guilt, [Col. 0597D] so now she first saw the resurrection. And lest she should bear perpetual reproach among men, as she then transmitted guilt, so now she announced grace. That the disciples were slow to believe in the resurrection was not so much their weakness as our strength. For the resurrection itself was shown to them, though they doubted, through many proofs. While we read these things, we are strengthened by their doubt.

But where Luke says, “Peter, however, rose and ran to the tomb,” it can fittingly be understood that, after he and John returned from the tomb and believed that the Lord had been taken away, and after they again heard from the women that the Lord had truly risen, Peter alone ran there—although what the women reported appeared like nonsense to the other apostles—and then the Lord appeared to him, when he went away wondering at what had occurred. But if Luke and John recount not two journeys but the same journey of Peter, it must be understood that Peter first stooped down and saw what John omits; afterwards he entered before John, in order to examine the interior more carefully. If this is so, why does Luke recount that Peter ran, while passing John over in silence, unless perhaps Mary had first reported it to him?

It should be noted that, especially from the hour of the resurrection up to this point, the sequence of the history has been greatly disputed. Hence Jerome, on Matthew:

> “That different occasions of the women are described in the Gospels is not a sign of falsehood, as the impious allege, but of the duty of diligent visitation: they repeatedly go away and return, and do not endure to be absent long or far from the Lord’s tomb.” [Col. 0598B]

The same writer, to Ebidia, in the twelfth book of *Questions*: “Matthew says, ‘Now late on the Sabbath,’ and so forth; but Mark says, ‘And very early on the first day of the week they come to the tomb, when the sun had already risen.’ There is a twofold solution to this question: either we do not accept Mark’s testimony, since almost all the books of Greece do not have this chapter at the end; or both spoke truly. Matthew states when the Lord rose, namely late on the Sabbath; Mark, when Mary Magdalene saw him, namely in the morning, so that he who, according to Matthew, had risen in the evening might appear to Mary in the morning.”

Ambrose, in the latter portions of his exposition of Luke:

> “The Lord rose not as day was drawing toward evening, but in the evening of the night. For the Greek wording has *sero* for ‘evening.’ Now *sero* signifies both the hour at the setting of day and the lateness of anything, as when you say, ‘He came late,’ that is, tardily. Thus the Lord rose not at the evening time of day, but late, that is, in the depth of night.

> “Therefore the women had opportunity to approach the tomb, now that the guards were resting—and for that reason all the more terrified, as commonly happens to those awakened from sleep. The chief priests themselves confirm that this was done at night, saying to the guards of the tomb: ‘Say that his disciples came by night and stole him away.’”

The same, shortly afterward:

> “That you may know it happened at night, some women know and others do not know that the Lord has risen. Those know who keep watch at night; those do not know who departed. One Mary Magdalene according to John does not know; another Mary Magdalene according to Matthew knows. For the same woman could not know beforehand and afterward not know. In short, you will recognize that they are different women. The one is permitted to hold the Lord’s feet; the other is forbidden. The one deserved to see an angel; the other, when she first came, saw no one. The one announced to the disciples that the Lord had risen; the other that he had been taken away. The one rejoices; the other weeps. Christ meets the one; the other seeks the dead.”

Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*: “Let us arrange all the events surrounding the time of the resurrection according to all the Evangelists, in the order in which they may have occurred. All agree that the tomb was visited at dawn. What Matthew reports had already taken place: the earthquake, the stone rolled back, and the guards terrified. Mary Magdalene came, more ardent than the rest. Thus John mentions her, passing over in silence those who were with her. Seeing the stone removed, before examining more closely, she supposed that Jesus’ body had been taken away. Therefore she ran and reported it to Peter and John. They came and, as Mary had said, believed that the Lord had been taken away. Therefore they returned.

“But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb—that is, before the place of the sepulchre—yet still within the space into which they had already entered, for there was a garden there. Then they saw the angel sitting at the right upon the stone, of whom Matthew and Mark speak. While that angel was speaking to them, Mary, weeping, bent down into the tomb and saw, according to John, two angels sitting in white. After they said to her, ‘Woman, [Col. 0599B] why are you weeping?’ she says to them, ‘They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.’ Here the angels are to be understood to have risen, so that they were also seen standing, as Luke says. After this she saw Jesus standing, and so on, as far as: ‘But go to my brethren,’ and so forth.

“Then she went out from the tomb—that is, from that place where there was the space of the garden before the hollowed-out stone—and the other women with her, whom, according to Mark, trembling had seized. Then, according to Matthew, Jesus met them, saying, ‘Hail.’ Thus we conclude that they received the angels’ address twice, and the Lord’s own address twice: once, namely, when Mary thought him to be the gardener, and now again when he met them on the way, so that by this very repetition he might strengthen them and restore them from fear. Then, according to Matthew, he said to them: ‘Do not be afraid. Go, tell my brethren to go into Galilee.’ Therefore Mary Magdalene came, according to John, announcing to the disciples that she had seen the Lord, along with the others who were with her, whom Luke mentions.” Thus far Augustine.

Whoever thinks that he has appropriately arranged the history will assign in the reading of this work the rules of anticipation and recapitulation most suitably. Nevertheless, since Augustine revised very many matters and nowhere, as he himself often attests, prejudged superior opinions by his own statements, it may not unreasonably be said that the sequence of the history is more diligently recounted in this work.

It appears, therefore, that at the very dawn, when the women first came to the tomb, what Matthew [Col. 0599D] and Mark report concerning the vision and address of one angel occurred, as also what Luke relates concerning two. Then the women, remembering the Lord’s words, departed from the angels, running to announce the news to the disciples. If we say that some of them believed that he had risen but Mary did not, the question which compelled some to invent two Mary Magdalenes is easily resolved. There is a similar solution to the question: “You know where I am going, and you know the way.” The Lord is understood to have said this to those who knew, and not to those who did not know, among whom was Philip, to whom it was said: “Have I been so long with you, and have you not known me?”

Likewise, after he appeared to the disciples with many proofs, when he reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, a similar distinction must be made. For the rebuke does not at all seem to refer to Peter, who saw the Lord on the very day of the resurrection and is nowhere read to have failed afterward firmly to believe that he had risen; rather, those are reproved who were slow to believe, such as Thomas. And it should be noted that, just as Thomas doubted more than the others, so he was more than the others instructed to touch and see. Peter denied singularly, and singularly the Lord appeared to him. Thus Mary, since she did not believe even through the angels, was exceedingly unbelieving regarding the resurrection, and to her the Lord singularly manifested himself. For graver wounds require greater medicine, so that where transgression abounded, grace might superabound.

While Mary was running to Peter and John, whether the other women ran to the other disciples and immediately returned, or whether they waited somewhere for Mary to return shortly, is uncertain. But this is most certainly certain: when Peter and John departed from the tomb, while Mary remained there weeping, she saw two angels, as John relates; and, turning around, she saw the Lord.

## CHAPTER CLXXVI

R. 254[IX] L. 340

After these things he was manifested to two of them as they were walking, going that same day to a village named Emmaus, sixty stadia from Jerusalem; and they were talking with one another about all the things that had happened.

Greek writers relate that the giant Hercules ran one hundred and twenty-five paces in a single breath. [Col. 0600C] When he had completed these, he stopped; and from standing still he called such a distance a *stadion*. A stadium is an eighth part of a mile, and sixty stadia make seven miles and half of an eighth. Reduced to a total, these make three leagues and three quarters of a fourth. Thus sixty stadia signify seven thousand five hundred paces.

This distance of travel fittingly accords with those who walked certain of the Saviour’s death and burial but doubtful of his resurrection. For who doubts that the resurrection, which occurred after the seventh day of the Sabbath, is comprehended in the eighth number? Therefore the disciples walking and speaking about the Lord completed the sixth mile of their journey, because they grieved that he, who had lived without complaint, had reached death, which he underwent on the sixth day of the Sabbath. [Col. 0600D] They also completed the seventh, because they did not doubt that he had rested in the tomb. But they did not at all complete the eighth, because they did not perfectly believe in the glory of the resurrection.

Emmaus is Nicopolis, a distinguished city of Palestine which, after the conquest of Judaea, was restored under the emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and, together with its condition, changed its name.

And it came to pass, while they were conversing and discussing together, that Jesus himself drew near and went with them. But their eyes were held, so that they did not recognize him.

Understand “they were conversing” as “they were speaking.” “They were discussing,” however, means that they were searching the Scriptures concerning Christ. [BEDE.] As they spoke of him, the Lord drew near and accompanied them, both to kindle faith in the resurrection in their minds and to fulfil what he had promised to do: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. XVIII). He did indeed appear, but he did not show a form which they would recognize.

[GREGORY.] Just as they loved him inwardly and yet doubted, so he was outwardly present with them but did not reveal who he was. Therefore, to those speaking of him he offered his presence; but from those doubting concerning him he withheld the appearance by which he might be recognized.

Hence Augustine, in that letter to Bishop Paulinus, concerning “the very prosperous arrival of our brother and fellow-presbyter”: “Your inquiry is accustomed to move many people: how could the Lord after the resurrection be both unrecognized and recognized by certain persons of both sexes? The first usual question is whether something was done in his body, or rather in their eyes, by which he could not be recognized. For we read, ‘Their eyes were held, lest they should recognize him’; and elsewhere it is openly said, ‘He appeared to them in another form.’

“But why is it not troubling that, in the transfiguration before the passion, his face shone like the sun, while after the resurrection it is troubling that his features were somewhat changed so that he could not be recognized, and again that, just as then he resumed his former colour, so after the resurrection he resumed his former features? The three disciples before whose eyes he was transfigured on the mountain would not recognize him if he came to them from elsewhere in that form. If anyone suddenly saw as a young man one whom he had known only as an infant, he certainly would not recognize him. Cannot God’s power accomplish swiftly by changing features what human age accomplishes through the delays [Col. 0601C] of years?”

And he said to them: “What are these words which you exchange with one another as you walk and are sad?” And one of them, whose name was Cleophas, answered and said to him: “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem, and have you not known the things done there in these days?” And he said to them: “What things?” And they said: “Those concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a man, a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people; and how our chief priests and rulers delivered him up to condemnation of death and crucified him. But we had hoped that he was the one who was to redeem Israel.”

[BEDE.] The companion of Cleophas was called Amaon, according to Ambrose’s testimony in his exposition of Luke. They consider him a stranger because they do not recognize him; and he truly was a stranger to them, for through the glory of the resurrection he was already far removed from their frailty, and he remained an outsider to those whose faith was ignorant of his resurrection. They confess that he was a prophet and great, but they are silent about the Son of God, either because they did not yet perfectly believe it or, even if they believed it, because they feared being handed over to the Jews, not knowing with whom they spoke. In a sense, too, they rebuke themselves for having hoped for redemption in one whom they had seen dead and did not see about to rise. They especially grieved that he whom they knew to be innocent had been killed without fault; and for this reason they walked in sadness.

“And now, besides all this, today is the third day since these things happened. But certain women of our company alarmed us: they were at the tomb before dawn, [Col. 0602A] and, not finding his body, came saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who [Latin *quae*; variant *qui*] say that he lives. And some of our people went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said; but him they did not find.”

From this sequence of the account also observe that the women saw the vision of angels first, and Peter and John then ran to the tomb. Thus those to whom the women reported the vision were alarmed, receiving more grief from the body’s not being found than joy and consolation from the announced resurrection.

And he himself said to them: “O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken. Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things and so enter into his glory?” And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.

Here a twofold necessity of humbling ourselves lies upon us: we are neither instructed in the Scriptures as much as we ought nor attentive, as is fitting, to fulfil what we know. For if Moses and the prophets spoke of Christ and foretold that he would enter glory through suffering, how can someone glory in being a Christian who neither investigates the Scriptures insofar as they concern Christ nor desires to attain through sufferings the glory which he wishes to possess with Christ?

And they drew near to the village to which they were going, and he pretended to go farther. And they compelled him, saying: “Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day has [Col. 0602C] already declined.” And he entered in with them.

[GREGORY.] The Lord opened to those two the sacred mysteries of the Scriptures concerning himself; yet, because he was still a stranger in their hearts, he pretended to be going farther. For by “to feign” we mean “to fashion.” Hence we call makers of clay *figuli*, potters. Therefore simple Truth did nothing through duplicity, but displayed himself to them bodily as he was in their minds. They had to be tested, whether they would love at least as a stranger him whom they did not yet love as God. And because those with whom Truth walked could not be strangers to charity, they invited him as a stranger into their lodging—indeed, they compelled him. From this it is inferred that strangers are not merely to be invited, but even drawn into lodging.

[Col. 0602D] And it came to pass, while he reclined with them, that he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and offered it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him; and he vanished from their eyes.

The God whom they did not recognize in the exposition of Scripture, they recognize in the breaking of bread. They were not enlightened by hearing, but by doing, because it is written: “It is not hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but doers” (Rom. II). Therefore whoever wishes to understand what he has heard should hasten now to fulfil in deed what he has understood. The appearance of weakness is withdrawn from carnal eyes, so that the glory of the resurrection may begin to appear to their minds. Hence it follows:

And they said to one another: “Was not our heart burning [Col. 0603A] within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?”

[BEDE.] At hearing the Lord’s discourse, the heart that had formerly been cold through the torpor of unbelief and fear was kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that it might burn with heavenly desire and extend itself to believe the truth. By as many commandments as a person is instructed, so to speak, by so many torches is he set aflame. Yet they did not recognize him until the breaking of bread.

This was done for the sake of a certain mystery: that in that form there might be shown to them one whom they would not recognize except in the breaking of bread; and that no one should suppose that he has recognized Christ if he is not a participant in his body, which is the Church. The Apostle commends its unity in the sacrament of bread, saying: “We, though many, are one bread, one body” (I Cor. X). [Col. 0603B] For then we truly recognize Christ, when through the sacrament of the Church we faithfully understand that he died and rose again for us.

Not incongruously may we understand this hindrance in their eyes to have come from Satan, so that Jesus might not be recognized; but Christ permitted it until the bread, so that we may understand that the obstacle of the enemy is removed from us when in the Church we worthily understand the mystery of the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood.

And rising, they returned that same hour to Jerusalem. And they found the eleven and those who were with them gathered together, saying, “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon.” And they themselves related what had happened on the way and how they recognized him in the breaking of bread; and they did not believe them.

[Col. 0603C] It should be noted that some were there who did not believe those two; but those to whom the Lord had already appeared undoubtedly believed them. As among the women he first appeared to Mary Magdalene, so among the men he first appeared to Peter. And although the Evangelist does not say when or where this happened, he does not keep silent that it happened.

## CHAPTER CLXXVII

L. 261[IX] A. 213

While they were speaking these things, A. when it was evening on that first day of the week and the doors were shut where the disciples were because of fear of the Jews, A. L. Jesus came and stood in the midst of the disciples and said to them: “Peace be with you.” L. “It is I; do not be afraid.”

[Col. 0603D] [AUGUSTINE.] Where divinity was, the mass of the body was not hindered by closed doors. And it must undoubtedly be understood that Thomas had gone out from there before the Lord appeared to the others.

But they were troubled and terrified, thinking that they saw a spirit.

[AMBROSE.] The apostles believed, but were nevertheless troubled at first, because the opinion of the few is excluded by the judgment of the greater part. For Peter, though he believed that he had risen, could still be troubled that the Lord, in a body, had unexpectedly entered among them through closed doors. [BEDE.] Therefore they think that they see a spirit, not flesh, because they do not yet believe either that true flesh could rise from the tomb on the third day, or that, once raised, it could penetrate to them through closed doors.

[Col. 0604A] And he said to them: “Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts?”

Those thoughts did not come down from above, but rose from the lowest part of the heart, like evil grass from the earth. I require the faith which I planted in you; I condemn what has sprung from you. If the resurrection is not true, the fruit of the passion is lost.

“See my hands and feet, for it is I myself. Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have.”

L. A.

And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet and side.

[AUGUSTINE–BEDE.] For the healing of doubting hearts, the marks of the wounds were preserved. Thus by many proofs he persuades them of the resurrection, offering himself both to be seen by their eyes and handled by their hands. By showing flesh and bones to be touched, he signifies the state of his resurrection and ours, in which our body will be both subtle through the effect of spiritual power and touchable through the truth of nature. Hence blessed Job: “And again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God” (Job XIX).

And it should be known that, just as the Lord deigned to reveal to the disciples the places of the nails and the lance, so on the day of judgment he will show both the same tokens of his passion and likewise the cross itself, in order to confound the unbelief of the proud. [Col. 0604C] For many reasons he wished scars to remain in his body. The first reason was to establish in the disciples faith in his resurrection. The second was that, while pleading with the Father for us, he might always show what kind of death he endured for humankind. The third was that through such tokens he might renew his mercy toward us. The fourth was that on the day of judgment he might show the faithless how justly they deserve to be condemned in eternal fires.

If some most valiant soldier, at his king’s command, killed an enemy for the salvation of his people, received many wounds, and brought back the spoils of his people from the defeated enemy, and if he were asked by a physician whether he wished to be healed so that no marks of the wounds appeared, or rather so that the scars remained without any deformity, he would answer that he wished to be healed in such a way that the signs of triumph remained in him, if this could be done without bodily deformity. Thus indeed the Lord acted. Therefore he preserved the scars not from inability to heal, but in order to bear perpetually the triumph of his victory.

[Col. 0604D] L. 342[IX] A. 221

But while they still did not believe and marvelled for joy, he said: “Have you here anything to eat?” And they offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb. And when he had eaten before them, taking the remains, he gave them to them.

It is to be understood devoutly that after the Lord’s resurrection the foods which he took offered him no assistance of nourishment; but just as water thrown into fire is consumed, so they were immediately consumed after being eaten by his spiritual power. Certainly he did not need food after the resurrection, just as neither shall we need it; but he wished to show a true life, not an imaginary one. For thirsty earth absorbs water in one way, and the burning ray of the sun dries it in another. The former absorbs through need; the latter dries through power.

[GREGORY.] The broiled fish signifies our Mediator, who deigned to lie hidden in the waters of the human race, wished to be caught in the net of death, and to be broiled in the tribulation of the passion. But he who was a broiled fish in the passion became a honeycomb in the resurrection. A honeycomb is honey in wax: that is, the sweetness of divinity in humanity. He did not wish to join the honeycomb to the broiled fish in his food, because he receives into eternal rest in his body those who, while feeling tribulations here, do not depart from love of inward sweetness. Those who here are broiled for God like a fish will there be satisfied with true sweetness like a honeycomb.

[Col. 0605B] L. 343[X]

And he said to them: “These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you: that all things written concerning me in the law of Moses and the prophets and the psalms must be fulfilled.”

[BEDE.] “While I was still with you”—understand, in mortal flesh—I spoke these words, namely: that what is written concerning me must be fulfilled. See how the Lord removed all evasions. He was seen, touched, ate, set forth the Scriptures, and expounded them.

Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures. And he said to them: “For thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the [Col. 0605C] third day; and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.”

Having commended the truth of his body, he commends the unity of the Church. He wills that repentance and remission of sins be preached among all nations, so that those who were to preach should begin from Jerusalem—not preaching only to the Jews, but also extending the preaching to the errors of the Gentiles.

“But you are witnesses of these things, and I send the promise of my Father upon you.”

You who have seen and heard the things which are to be preached are witnesses; and, that you may be sufficient for bearing witness, I will send you the promise of the Father, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0605D] A. 214[X]

Therefore the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord. And he said to them again: “Peace be with you.”

[AUGUSTINE.] He offers peace who came for peace. Repetition is confirmation. For he gives peace upon peace, as he promised through the prophet (Isa. XXVII). Or he repeats it to show that by his blood he has made peace both in heaven and on earth.

“As the Father sent me, I also send you.”

[GREGORY.] As the Father sent me, God to God, so I send you, man to men. The Father, loving the Son, sent him to suffer; and the Lord, loving the apostles, sent them not to the world’s joy but to suffering. The Son’s being sent by the Father may also be understood according to the divine nature: for the Son is sent from the Father in the same manner in which he is begotten. For if mission were to be understood only as incarnation, the Holy Spirit, who was not incarnate at all, could in no way be said to be sent. But his mission is his very procession from the Father and the Son. Therefore, just as the Spirit who proceeds is said to be sent, so also the Son who is begotten.

When he had said this, he breathed upon them and said:

A. 215[IX] M. 185

“Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained.”

[AUGUSTINE.] By breathing upon them he signified that the Holy Spirit [Col. 0606B] is not the Spirit of the Father alone, but also his own. The charity of the Church, which is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, forgives the sins of its members; but it retains the sins of those who are not its members.

[GREGORY.] And therefore, after he had said, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” he immediately added concerning the forgiveness and retention of sins. The Spirit is given on earth, that one may love one’s neighbour, and in heaven, that one may love God; and as charity is one and the commandments two, so the Spirit is one and the gifts two. Yet the Holy Spirit was already in the minds of the disciples for faith, but not so manifestly as after the resurrection. Hence the saying: “The Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified” (John VII).

Thus it is also said through Moses: “They sucked honey from the rock, and oil from the solid rock” (Deut. XXXII). Nothing of the sort is read according to the historical sense, if the whole sequence of the Old Testament is reviewed. But because, according to Paul, “the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X), those sucked honey from the rock who saw the Redeemer’s miracles; but those deserved to be anointed with oil from the solid rock who, after his resurrection, received the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. The solid rock gave honey while he was still mortal; but the solid rock poured out oil when, after the resurrection, he was incapable of suffering.

## CHAPTER CLXXVIII

A. 216[X]

But Thomas, one of the twelve, who is called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came. Therefore the other disciples said to him: “We have seen the Lord.” But he [Col. 0606D] said to them: “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”

It was not by chance but by divine dispensation that that disciple was absent then, and afterward, doubting, touched; and, touching, believed. For Thomas’s unbelief benefited our faith more than the faith of those who believed; because, while he is led back to faith by touching, our mind is made firm in faith.

M. 217[IX] R. 341

And after eight days his disciples were again inside, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came, the doors being shut, stood in the midst, and said: “Peace be with you.” Then he said to Thomas: [Col. 0607A] “Bring your finger here and see my hands; bring your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but faithful.”

The Lord’s body entered to the disciples through closed doors, as through birth it came forth from the closed womb of the Virgin. Nor is it surprising that he who would live forever entered to the disciples, since he who would die came forth from the Virgin’s closed womb. The Lord displayed two wonders, very contrary to each other according to human reasoning, when after his resurrection he showed his body incorruptible and touchable. For that which is touched must be corruptible, and that which is incorruptible cannot be touched. Yet in a wonderful manner our Redeemer, showing himself incorruptible, appeared in order to invite us to the reward; and he made himself touchable in order to form us in faith, showing that his body was of the same nature but of another glory.

> A divine deed is not greatly wonderful  
> if it can be grasped or proved by reason.  
> The force of reason is not suited to the merits of faith.

A. 218[X]

Thomas answered and said to him: “My Lord and my God.”

[AUGUSTINE.] He saw and touched the man, and confessed the God whom he neither saw nor touched.

Jesus said to him: “Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed.”

He saw one thing and believed another. He saw the man and confessed God. He did not say, “Because you touched,” but “Because you saw.” [Col. 0607C] For sight is, in a manner, a general term for sense. It is customarily named through the other four senses, as when we say: “Hear and see how well it sounds”; “Smell and see how well it smells”; “Taste and see how well it tastes”; “Touch and see how well it is warm.” Hence here too the Lord says: “Bring your finger here and see my hands,” that is, “Touch and see.” Therefore he saw either merely by looking or also by touching; for it may be said that the disciple then did not dare to touch the Lord. For it is not written, “Thomas touched,” but, “Because you saw, you believed.”

“Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.”

He commends the faith of the Gentiles, but uses words in the past tense because he who knew in his predestination that which was future regarded it as already done. It should be known that the one truly believes who completes faith by works. But concerning those who retain faith in name only, Paul says: “They profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Titus I). And James says: “Faith without works is dead” (James II).

Jesus indeed performed many other signs in the presence of his disciples which are not written in this book. But these have been written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that, believing, you may have life in his name.

The Evangelist sets down what seems to be the conclusion of the book, giving a more eminent place, as it were, to the narrative that follows for the great commendation of its mystery.

## CHAPTER CLXXIX

[Col. 0608A]

A. 219[IX] L. 30

After this Jesus manifested himself again at the Sea of Tiberias. He manifested himself in this way: Simon Peter and Thomas, who is called Didymus, and Nathanael, who was from Cana of Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together. Simon Peter said to them: “I am going fishing.” They said to him: “We also will come with you.” They went out and got into the boat, and that night they caught nothing. But when morning had now come, Jesus stood on the shore. Yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus. Therefore Jesus said to them: “Children, have you anything to eat?” They answered him: “No.” He said to them: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find.” Therefore they cast it, [Col. 0608B] and now they were unable to draw it because of the multitude of fish.

[GREGORY.] Peter and the sons of Zebedee remained fishermen without sin after their conversion. Matthew, however, did not return to the business of the tax office. For there are occupations which can scarcely, or not at all, be conducted without sins. [AUGUSTINE.] Yet they were never forbidden, by their lawful craft, to seek sustenance from the people, preserving their integrity, when they had nothing on which to live. Thus, while they laboured, God added the necessities He had promised to those who first sought the kingdom of God and His righteousness. For who else supplied the fish to be caught? He must be believed to have brought upon them the want that compelled them to go fishing for no other reason than that He wished to display the miracle which He had ordained, [Col. 0608C] so that He might at once feed the preachers of His Gospel and enhance that Gospel itself by the great mystery signified in the number of the fish. The seven disciples present at this fishing signify the end of time, which revolves through seven days.

[GREGORY.] It is also commonly asked [or: may be asked] why the Lord, after His resurrection, stood on the shore while His disciples laboured upon the sea, whereas before the resurrection He walked before them upon the sea. But the sea signifies the present age, in which the disciples were still labouring; the firmness of the shore signifies the enduring rest in which the Lord already was. Twice in the Gospel we read that the Lord commanded nets to be cast for fishing: before the Passion and after it. But on the earlier occasion He does not command that they be cast to the right [Col. 0608D] or to the left. In that fishing, because of the multitude of fish, the nets are many; in this one, they are not. Therefore that fishing signified the present Church, gathering good and evil alike. This fishing, however, signifies the Church of the elect alone, which is not rent by any heresies, resting in the unbroken peace of its Author.

[AUGUSTINE.] What does it mean that the disciples were unable to draw in the net, except that those who belong to the resurrection and are to be set at the right hand will not appear until they rise again? For the Church possesses them after the end of this life, hidden as though in the depth in the sleep of peace, until they appear upon the shore—that is, at the end of the age.

A. 220[X]

Therefore the disciple whom Jesus loved said [Col. 0609A] to Peter, “It is the Lord.” Simon Peter, when he heard that it was the Lord, girded himself with his tunic—for he was naked—and threw himself into the sea. But the other disciples came in the boat; for they were not far from land, but about two hundred cubits away, dragging the net of fish.

What elsewhere is represented by two boats, on account of circumcision and uncircumcision, I think is represented in this place by two hundred cubits, on account of the elect of both peoples, circumcision and uncircumcision, as it were a hundred and a hundred; because the number one hundred passes from the left to the right.

A. 221[IX] L. 341

When, therefore, they came down to land, they saw coals laid out, and a fish laid upon them, and bread. Jesus said to them: [Col. 0609B] “Bring some of the fish which you have just caught.”

It should not be understood that the bread too was laid upon the coals. Rather, they saw—the following must be supplied—thus: they saw coals laid out and a fish laid upon them; they also saw bread.

A. 222[IX] L. 30

Simon Peter went aboard and drew the net to land, full of one hundred and fifty-three large fish. And though there were so many, the net was not torn.

[GREGORY.] Peter draws the net to land because the Church was entrusted to him. Hence he heard in particular: “Simon, son of John, do you love me? Feed my sheep.” He draws the fish to the firmness of the shore because, by words, Epistles, and signs of miracles, he displays the stability [Col. 0609C] of the eternal homeland.

[AUGUSTINE.] In the other catch of fish, which signifies the present Church, great and small fish were caught; but here the good who are to be present in the resurrection of the dead are signified only by the large fish. The Lord made this clear elsewhere, namely where He gave the parable of the net cast into the sea, saying: “So shall it be at the consummation of the age” (Matt. XIII). It should be known that those who teach but do not act will not be among the number of the large fish. But “he who does and teaches shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven,” where one who acts but does not teach will not even be least. In the other fishing the number of fish is not specified, because, as the prophet says, “they have multiplied beyond number” (Ps. XXXIX). Here, however, there is a definite number, [Col. 0609D] and its rationale is this.

The Decalogue of the law consists in ten commandments. Unless that law is aided by God’s grace, it makes transgressors, as Paul says: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (II Cor. III). The Holy Spirit is signified by the number seven. Hence Isaiah: “the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. XI). Therefore, when the Holy Spirit, by the number seven, is added to the ten of the law, seventeen result. When all the numbers from one through seventeen are added together, this number amounts to one hundred and fifty-three. Thus all who belong to grace are figured by this number, because perfection lies in one hundred; the Trinity is contained in fifty and likewise in three. Here the Trinity is doubled [Col. 0610A] on account of the faith of the two peoples. The number fifty is completed by multiplying seven by seven and adding one. That one is added to signify that the Spirit is one, though He is displayed by seven because of His sevenfold operation. Or, by counting seven from one through itself, one likewise reaches one hundred and fifty-three: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, and seventeen together make one hundred and fifty-three.

A. 223[IX] L. 142

Jesus said to them: “Come, dine.”

A. 224[X]

And none of those reclining at table dared ask Him, [Col. 0610B] “Who are you?” knowing that He was the Lord.

[AUGUSTINE.] The truth with which Jesus appeared to them was so evident that none of them dared not only to deny it, but even to doubt; and therefore it would have been foolish to ask.

A. 225[IX] L. 342

And Jesus came, took the bread, and gave it to them, and likewise the fish.

The Lord prepared a meal for the seven disciples from the fish laid upon the coals and from the others which they had caught. The roasted fish is Christ suffering. He is also the bread that came down from heaven. He ate fish and bread in order to show us that He both endured the Passion in His humanity and provided us, from His divinity, with refreshment [variant: resurrection]. To share in blessedness, the Church is incorporated into Him. Therefore it was said, “Bring some of the fish,” so that all of us who hold this hope might, through that sevenfold number of disciples—by which our whole body may be understood—share in so great a mystery [Col. 0610C] and be joined to the same blessedness.

A. 226[X]

This was now the third time that Jesus was manifested to the disciples after He had risen from the dead.

This must be referred not to the individual appearances but to the days. On the day of the resurrection He was seen not only once; after eight days He appeared where Thomas was; and today also, when this event concerning the fish occurred, He appeared. But after how many days He appeared, the Evangelist did not determine. He also appeared thereafter as often as He wished during the forty days.

CHAPTER CLXXX.

When therefore they had dined, Jesus said to Simon Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” He said to Him: “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.”

A. 227[IX] M. 274

He said to him: “Feed my lambs.”

[ALCUIN.] When the Lord asked whether Peter loved Him more than the others, he did not dare answer, “More.” It was as though he said: “You know that I love you with an undivided heart; but how greatly the others love you, I do not know.” Peter answers cautiously because he remembers that, when the Passion was formerly imminent, [Col. 0611A] he had attributed to himself more steadfastness than he possessed, answering that he was ready to go with Him both to prison and to death.

[AUGUSTINE.] Where Peter is asked, “Do you love me?” and he answers, “I love you,” it is shown that *amor* and *dilectio*, “love” and “affection,” are one and the same thing.

A. 228[X]

He said to him again: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” He said to Him: “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.”

A. 229[IX] L. 274

He said to him: “Feed my lambs.”

[AUGUSTINE.] What else is “Feed my lambs” than as if He said: “If you love me, feed my sheep”? Seek my glory in them, not your own. Do not belong to the company of those who love themselves and belong to [Col. 0611B] dangerous times. Heretics and schismatics have made private property for themselves out of the Lord’s stolen goods, and have wished to feed flocks not of Christ but of themselves, against Christ. Certainly, in their very plundering, they have placed His title upon them, so that their prey might seem defended by the title of One who is powerful. What does Christ do when such persons are converted—those who, outside the Church, received the title of His baptism? He casts out the plunderer; He does not remove the title; He takes possession of the house, because He finds His own title there. For why need He change His own name?

A. 230[X]

He said to him a third time: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” Peter was grieved because He said to him a third time, “Do you love me?” and he said to Him: “Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you.”

[Col. 0611C] A. 231[IX] L. 274

He said to him: “Feed my sheep.”

A threefold confession is rendered for the threefold denial, lest the tongue serve love less than it served fear. And just as denying the Shepherd was a mark of fear, so feeding the Lord’s sheep is the duty of love. To feed the sheep is to strengthen believers lest they fail; to provide earthly assistance for those subject to one’s care, if necessary; to furnish examples of virtues; to withstand adversaries; and to correct sinners.

A. 232[X]

“Amen, amen, I say to you: when you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished. But when you grow old, you will stretch out [Col. 0611D] your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish.” Now He said this, signifying by what death Peter would glorify God.

“You will stretch out,” He says, “your hands”; that is, you will be crucified. Moreover, for this purpose another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish. He first stated what would happen, and then how it would happen. For the imposition of bonds by the persecutor is expressed in another’s girding him. Certainly, he was led where he would not wish in order to be crucified; for when crucified he did not go where he did not wish, but rather where he wished—namely, to Christ. Yet if it were possible apart from the pain of death, he would desire eternal life. Therefore, since the force of love overcomes the grave pains of death, martyrs indeed glorify God by their death, showing by it how greatly He ought to be worshipped and loved.

[Col. 0612A] And when He had said this, He said to him: “Follow me.”

Having said these things, Jesus began to depart; and Peter, not yet understanding what he had heard, “Follow me,” began to follow with the steps of his feet. John followed, whom the privilege of the Lord’s love commends.

Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following, who also reclined at supper upon His breast and said: “Lord, who is it that will betray you?” Therefore, when Peter saw him, he said to Jesus: “Lord, what about this man?”

Because Peter had heard that he was to be crucified, he wished also to know the end of his brother.

Jesus said to him: “So I will that he remain until I come; what is that to you? Follow me.”

[AUGUSTINE.] Why is it said to Peter, “Follow me,” and not to [Col. 0612B] the others who were present with him and followed their Master as disciples? Was Peter alone put to death? Was not James, son of Zebedee, among those seven, he who after the Ascension was killed by Herod? Yet someone may say that, because James was not crucified, it was rightly said to Peter, “Follow me,” since he experienced the cross. Let this stand, if nothing else more fitting can be found.

Therefore this saying went out among the brethren, that that disciple does not die. Yet Jesus did not say that he does not die, but: “If I will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?”

[ALCUIN.] I do not wish him to be brought to his end through martyrdom, but to await the peaceful release of his flesh until, when I come, I receive him into eternal [Col. 0612C] blessedness. But that this was not to be understood as the brethren who were present believed—that he would not die but would remain always alive—John himself makes clear, saying: “And Jesus did not say, ‘He does not die.’” Therefore one must not suppose that John did not die in the flesh; rather, although he had previously endured many labours, he ended his old age in peace, with the Lord visiting him in a special manner. For it would not have been a great thing to grant His beloved not to die, when “to be dissolved and to be with Christ is better.”

This is the disciple who bears witness concerning these things and wrote them, and we know that his witness is true.

Here he plainly identifies his own person by his office, [Col. 0612D] though he did not wish to identify it by name.

There are also many other things which Jesus did; if they were written individually, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would have to be written.

[AUGUSTINE.] This should not be understood as meaning that the world could not contain them in spatial extent, but in the capacity of readers. It may also, without injury to the faith, be understood as said through the figure which the Greeks call *hyperbolē*, “hyperbole,” a mode frequently found in the divine books; as here: “They set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue passes through the earth” (Ps. XXVII); and: “the crown of the head of those walking in their offences” (Ps. LXVII).

It is commonly asked why the Lord loved John more, when Peter loved the Lord more. For John, without speaking his own name, wished it to be understood that he was loved above the others; far be it from us to call this a lie. But what greater token of love could Jesus give him than that he should recline upon His breast? Furthermore, that Peter loved the Lord more than the others is plainly evident where it is said: “Do you love me more than these?” This was certainly known to Him who knows all things; nevertheless He asked, so that we too, reading the Gospel, might know Peter’s love for the Lord. But when Peter answered that he loved the Lord, he did not add “more,” because he could not see another’s heart. Therefore, if we ask which is better, one who loves Christ more or one who loves Him less, who would hesitate to answer that the better person is the one who loves Him more? Again, the one whom Christ loves more appears better than one who is loved less by Him. But if, by comparing them with each other, it is asked [Col. 0613B] which of two persons is better—the one who loves Christ less and is loved more by Him, or the one whom Christ loves less, though he himself loves Christ more—the answer is uncertain.

The solution to the question proposed seems to be this. We often see, for certain reasons, that a father shows less familiarity to the son whom he loves more, while conversely he embraces with a greater display of affection one whom he loves less. Likewise it must be said that the Lord loved Peter more than John in affection, and conversely loved John more than Peter in the display of familiarity. Peter, indeed, because he loved more than the others, as the Gospel explains in many places, deserved to be loved with a fuller affection by Him who says: “I love those who love me” (Prov. VIII). John, however, because he was young and the Lord’s cousin, had access to familiarity. Therefore, since he had been called by Him from a wedding feast and had lived most chastely from boyhood, he deserved above the others the prerogative of familiarity as a privilege of love. Thus the Lord loved John above the others—that is, He manifested more familiarly and by greater tokens that He loved him. Peter, therefore, although He loved him more in affection, He loved him less in outward display.

Nor is it devoid of mystery that a lesser manifestation of love was bestowed upon Peter and a greater upon John. To see this, let us begin somewhat more deeply. Peter did not receive his name from *petra*, “rock”; rather, Peter received his name from the Rock, just as Christ was not named from a Christian, but a Christian from Christ. Therefore the Lord says: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” [Col. 0613D] (Matt. XVI)—upon this rock, namely, which Peter confessed when he said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid.). For Christ was the Rock (I Cor. X). Peter himself was also built upon that foundation. For “no one can lay any other foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III).

Therefore the Church founded in Christ received from Him, in Peter, the keys of the kingdom of heaven—that is, the power of binding and loosing sins. For what the Church is in Christ by its proper reality, Peter is in the Rock by signification. In this signification Christ is understood as the Rock, Peter as the Church. While this Church lives amid evils, it is delivered from evils by loving and following Christ. Yet it follows Him especially in those who contend for truth even unto death; but to the whole body it is said: “Follow me.” For this whole body Christ died, leaving us an example that we should follow in His footsteps (I Pet. II). See why it was said: “Follow me.”

But there is another, immortal life, where we shall see face to face what is here seen through a mirror (I Cor. XIII). Thus the Church knows two lives: one in faith, labour, and the way; the other in sight, rest, and the homeland. Therefore the one is good but still wretched; the other is better and blessed. The former, to which it is said, “Follow me,” by imitating the endurance of temporal evils, was signified by Peter; the latter, which has no end and awaits fulfilment, by John.
