Hence the Lord says: “Thus I will that he remain”—that is, thus I will that the heavenly Church wait until, when I come for judgment, I bring it to fulfilment. In this life God loves us in order to deliver us [Col. 0614B] from evils; in that life He loves us more, where there is nothing displeasing to Him. This explains why Christ loved John more than Peter, not why Peter loved Christ more than John.

For if John signified the life in which the Lord is to be loved more, why did John love Him less? Namely because it was said: “I will that he remain,” that is, wait until I come; and because we do not yet possess that love, which will then be fuller. Consequently, since all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. XXIV), we love more the Lord’s mercy, by which we wish to be delivered from misery. This is signified through Peter. But we love less the contemplation of truth as it will be, because we neither yet know it [Col. 0614C] nor possess it. This is signified through John.

Yet let no one separate these eminent Apostles. For both were present in that which Peter signified, and both were to be present in that which John signified. In signification, this one followed and that one remained. But in faith both endured the evils of this misery, and both awaited future goods. Nor do they alone do this; the whole Church does so. Therefore, on behalf of all the saints, Peter received the keys of the kingdom of heaven for the governance of this life, for binding and loosing sins; and on behalf of those same saints, John reclined upon the Lord’s breast for the most peaceful bosom of eternal life. That John is a virgin accords with the future life, where they neither marry nor are given in marriage.

CHAPTER CLXXXI.

[Col. 0614D]

M. 355[X]

But the eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them; and seeing Him, they worshipped Him, but some doubted.

[BEDE.] He appeared on the mountain, signifying that His assumed body had now been raised above all earthly things. But why did He foretell specifically that He would go before them into Galilee and be seen there, when He was neither seen there alone nor first seen there? Because Galilee is called “a passage over” or “revelation,” and both interpretations look to one end. It signifies that, as Christ passed from death to life, so His followers pass over from death to life. And, beholding Him in the form of His divinity, they praise Him without end. “Revelation” is also fitting, because we who now reveal our way to Him and follow His footsteps, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image (II Cor. III). But some doubted, because Luke says: “Troubled and terrified, they thought that they saw a spirit.”

R. 235[X]

And He reproached them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen Him risen.

[GREGORY.] He rebuked the disciples when He was about to leave them bodily, so that the words which He spoke as He departed might remain more firmly impressed [Col. 0615B] upon the hearts of the hearers.

[JEROME.] He reproaches their unbelief and hardness of heart, so that belief may succeed and a heart of flesh, full of charity. Hence the companies of martyrs gladly desire the death of this age, because through temporal destruction they wish to live victorious forever. Most blessed is the passage from this age into eternity.

M. 355[X]

And He spoke to them, saying: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me.”

[BEDE.] What the Psalmist said to the Father concerning the Lord rising again—“You have subjected all things under His feet” (Ps. VIII)—the Lord Himself now says to His disciples. Among “all things,” death itself, which for a time seemed to prevail against Him, has been made subject to His feet. For all [Col. 0615C] power was given to Him who, shortly before, had been crucified and lay buried. Power was given in heaven and on earth, so that He who reigned in heaven might reign also on earth through the faith of believers. Before He rose from the dead, the angelic powers knew that they were subject to the assumed man; but blind human beings disdained to submit to Him whom they knew clothed in mortality. They despised His divine power because they saw human weakness present in His sufferings. Therefore the Mediator, wishing a change to occur because all power had been given Him, sent teachers to preach the word of life to all nations throughout the world.

R. 235[X]

[Col. 0615D] “Going into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every creature.”

“Every creature” is not said with reference to inanimate things or brute animals, but by the name of every creature a human being is signified: he has being with stones, life with trees, sensation with animals, understanding with angels, and consists of hot and cold, moist and dry; for man is called a lesser world. Therefore, since man has something of every creature, the Gospel is preached to every creature when it is preached to man, for whose sake all things were created and to whom all things are in some way similar. Or by “every creature” every nation of the Gentiles may be denoted; for earlier it had been said: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. X). When Truth sends His disciples to preach, [Col. 0616A] He scatters the grains of seed in the world. And He sends forth little in seed so that He may receive the fruits of many harvests from our faith.

M. 315[X]

“Teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you.”

Baptize in the confession of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so that those whose divinity is one may have one bestowal. The proper order is that they first teach, then baptize believers, and afterward instruct them in what must be observed.

[BEDE.] For one who does not have faith cannot receive the power of baptism; and as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith too without works is dead [Col. 0616B] (Jas. II). What great reward for devout conduct and what pledge of future blessedness remain even now for the faithful, He subsequently indicates, saying:

“And behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age.”

[JEROME.] He who promises this does not fail to know the day on which He knows that He will be Judge together with the Apostles.

R. 23[X]

“He who believes and is baptized shall be saved. But he who does not believe shall be condemned.”

[BEDE.] What are we to say here about little children, who by reason of age cannot yet believe? There is no question concerning adults. Therefore little children believe in the Church through others, just as they inherit sins from others, which are forgiven them in baptism.

“But these signs shall follow those who believe: in my name they shall cast out demons; they shall speak with new tongues; they shall take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not harm them; they shall lay hands upon the sick, and they shall recover.”

[GREGORY.] Do we not believe because we do not perform these signs? They were necessary at the beginning of the Church, so that the faith of believers might be nourished by miracles. For when we plant shrubs, we pour water on them until they become established in the ground. Hence Paul says: “Tongues are for a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers” (I Cor. XIV). Yet the holy Church daily performs spiritually [Col. 0616D] what it then did bodily through the Apostles. For priests, laying hands upon believers through the grace of exorcism, cast out demons; and believers, putting away secular speech, sound forth the praises of their Creator, which is to speak with new tongues. Likewise, when by good exhortations they remove wickedness from others’ hearts, they take up serpents. And when they hear deadly persuasions yet are in no way drawn into wicked action, they drink a deadly thing, but it does not harm them. When, moreover, by the example of their conduct they strengthen the life of those weak in faith, they lay hands upon the sick. Therefore these miracles are so much greater because through them not bodies but souls are raised up.

[Col. 0617A] L. 343[X]

“But you, remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.”

[BEDE.] Of this power Luke speaks more plainly in the Acts of the Apostles: “He commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father” (Acts I). And shortly afterwards: “You shall receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, and you shall be my witnesses” (ibid.). It should be noted that some are prevented from the office of preaching by age or immaturity, yet are driven toward it by rashness. They must be warned to consider the deeds of the Saviour, who could suddenly strengthen whomever He wished. Yet, lest the immature presume to preach, after He had instructed the disciples He added: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.” [Col. 0617B] We remain in the city if we confine ourselves within the enclosures of our minds, lest we wander abroad in speech; so that, when we are clothed with divine power, we may go forth from ourselves and instruct others.

And He led them out as far as Bethany; and lifting up His hands, He blessed them.

To bless His disciples, He led them out to Bethany, which is called “the house of obedience,” because He who descended through disobedience ascended through obedience, according to the Apostle: “He died for our offences and rose again for our justification.” Further, the site of that village is said to be on the slope of the Mount of Olives; and the Church, the house of obedience, has laid the foundations of its faith, hope, and love nowhere except on the side of that highest mountain, that is, Christ Himself. From whose most fruitful summit—that is, the height of divinity—it desires the gifts of spiritual anointing and awaits the promises of light and everlasting peace. Thirdly, as John writes, Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away. This number, consisting of seven and eight, is well suited to the mysteries of Scripture, suggesting either the life which now is and that which is to come, or the Old and New Testaments, on account of the Sabbath and the resurrection of the flesh.

And it came to pass, while He blessed them, that He departed from them and was carried into heaven, R. and sits at the right hand of God.

Because our Redeemer now judges all things and will at last come as Judge of all, Mark describes Him as sitting. But Stephen saw Him standing, whom he had as his helper. For sitting belongs to one judging, while standing belongs to one fighting or helping.

L.

And they, worshipping, returned to Jerusalem with great joy.

They returned to Jerusalem because they had been commanded there to await the Father’s promise. They rejoiced because they had learned that their Lord had penetrated the heavens.

And they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God.

[BEDE.] In the place of prayer they awaited the coming of the Holy Spirit, praising Him for His benefits [Col. 0618A] and blessing—that is, magnifying—Him for the divine promises. Let us, then, after celebrating the solemnities of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, take care to become a house of obedience, following the footsteps of Him who, in order to give us a pattern of life, became obedient unto death (Phil. II). Thus we shall merit His daily blessing if daily we remember His triumphant Ascension, praising and blessing God in Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of heavenly peace—by hope like people awaiting their lord when he returns from a wedding feast.

R. 235[X]

And they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed.

[Col. 0618B] [GREGORY.] Obedience follows the command, and signs follow obedience. We read that Elijah was taken up into heaven (4 Kings II), but the aerial heaven is one thing, the ethereal another. The former is nearest the earth, since birds fly through it. Elijah, therefore, was taken up into the aerial heaven, so that he might suddenly be conveyed to a certain hidden region of the earth, where he may live until the end of the world, and then return from there in order to die. For he did not escape death, but postponed it. Our Redeemer, however, did not postpone death but conquered it, and by ascending made manifest the glory of the resurrection. Elijah ascended a chariot, as a mere man needing assistance; for those aids were made and displayed through angels. But our Redeemer is not recorded as having been lifted up either by chariot or by angels, but by his own power. Enoch likewise, [Col. 0618C] translated to the aerial heaven (Gen. V), prefigured the Lord’s Ascension, just as Joseph did his sale (Gen. XXXVII). Thus the Lord had witnesses of his Ascension, one before the Law and the other under the Law. The sequence in the elevation of each is distinguished by certain gradations. For Enoch is said to have been translated, Elijah borne up, so that afterwards there might come One who, neither translated nor borne up, would penetrate the ethereal heaven by his own power. Consider, brethren, how the purity of holiness increased, as is plainly shown in the servants and the Lord. Enoch was translated: begotten through intercourse and begetting through intercourse; for he had a wife and children. Elijah was taken up: begotten through intercourse, but not begetting through intercourse; for he had neither wife [Col. 0618D] nor children. But the Lord was assumed: neither begetting through intercourse nor begotten through intercourse.

Bede, in the homily, “If you love me, keep my commandments”:

> “On the fiftieth day after the slaughter of the lamb the Law was given (Exod. XIX), and on the fiftieth day after the resurrection of our Redeemer the grace of the Holy Spirit was given to the one hundred and twenty disciples in the upper room (Acts II).”

Rightly is perfect peace denoted by this number, because in the Law the fiftieth year was commanded to be called the Jubilee (Lev. XXV; Num. XXXVI), that is, “releasing” or “changed”; in it the people were to rest from every work, all debts were to be remitted, slaves were to return free, and the year itself was to surpass all others in greater solemnities and in divine praises. [Col. 0619A] Therefore the number fifty is suited to signify eternal rest, because it is completed from seven weeks and one unit. For six days the people were to work under the Law and rest on the seventh; for six years they were to plough and reap, and in the seventh were commanded to cease (Exod. XX; Lev. XXV), because the Lord also completed the adornment of the world in six days and rested on the seventh. By all these things we are mystically instructed that those who in this world, which consists of six ages, labour in good works for the Lord are brought by the Lord into the Sabbath to come, that is, into eternal rest. But the fact that seven days or years are multiplied sevenfold signifies the manifold abundance of that same rest, in which that first sublime gift is bestowed on the elect, of which the Apostle says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, [Col. 0619B] what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. II).

Appropriately the grace of the Holy Spirit is described as sevenfold, since assuredly through his inspiration rest is attained, and in the full possession of him true rest is possessed. Moreover, the fiftieth day or year itself, which exceeds the seven weeks and was more venerable than the rest through its greater solemnity, indicates the time of the future resurrection, in which the rest now enjoyed by souls will likewise be crowned with the glory of the bodies of the elect.

Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*:

> “We find in the Evangelists that the Lord was seen by human beings ten times from the resurrection [Col. 0620A] to the Ascension. First, by Mary Magdalene, weeping at the tomb; second, by the same woman and the other women returning from the tomb; third, by Peter, as Luke says, although where is not specified; fourth, by Cleophas and his companion as they went to Emmaus; fifth, by the disciples in Jerusalem, where Thomas was absent; sixth, after eight days, when he was with them; seventh, by those fishing on the Sea of Tiberias; eighth, on the mountain of Galilee, as he had appointed for them; ninth, on the day of the Ascension; tenth, on that same day, when they saw him already raised into the air.”

Let Paul also be compared, so that no question remains. “He rose,” he says, “on the third day according to the Scriptures, and appeared to Cephas” (1 Cor. XV). He did not say, “He first appeared to Cephas,” for that would contradict the fact that he first appeared to the women. [Col. 0620B] “Afterwards,” he says, “to the eleven,” perhaps on the very day of the resurrection. Then to more than five hundred brethren. Whether these were gathered with the eleven behind closed doors for fear of the Jews, whence, after Thomas had departed, Jesus came to them, or after eight days, makes no difference. “Afterwards to James”: we should not understand this to mean that James was first seen by him then, but that there was some special manifestation. “Then to all the apostles”: not that they first saw him then, but that he was now conversing with them more familiarly until the day of his Ascension. “Last of all he was seen also by me.” This was not a short time after the Ascension.

## ZACHARIAS, BISHOP OF AN UNKNOWN SEE, YEAR UNCERTAIN

[Col. 0619]

## NOTICE

(R. P. Bernard PEZ, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum novissimus*, preface to vol. IV, p. V.)

I have turned myself in every direction to discover who this Zacharias was, or at what time and in what place he flourished; but nowhere did I find anything on which I could rest. I know Zacharias surnamed Chrysopolitanus, or Goldsborough, of the Order of Premonstratensian Canons, who, about the year 1157, flourished in the monastery of St Martin at Laon, according to the witness of Alberic the monk in his *Chronicle*, and in that same year completed in four books his Commentary on the Gospel Harmony of Ammonius of Alexandria. But this Zacharias is nowhere recorded as distinguished by the episcopal rank in which the author of the present sermon shone. The others named Zacharias—though very few occur in catalogues of ecclesiastical writers—I deliberately pass over in silence, because they were either Greek writers or lived in such a place and age that they could scarcely have been authors of this sermon.

Of all who can even come under suspicion, the greatest occasion for conjecture seems to be afforded by Zacharias, the twenty-third bishop of Säben, now Brixen. Concerning him Hund, enlarged by Gewold, says in vol. I of the *Metropolis of Salzburg*, p. 441:

> “Zacharias, twenty-third bishop of Säben, lived in great renown about the year 902, under Emperor Louis, son of Arnulf, and Pope John IX. He took part in the expedition of the aforesaid Emperor Louis against the Hungarians, in which he fell at Anaspurg with Dietmar, archbishop of Salzburg, Otto, bishop of Freising, and Leopold, margrave of Austria, in the year of the Lord 907, according to Aventinus, *Annals*, book IV, fol. 480. Nothing further has been discovered concerning him, except that, with five other bishops of Bavaria—namely, Dietmar, archbishop of Salzburg; Waldo of Freising; Erekhanbald of Eichstätt; Tuto [Col. 0621] of Regensburg; and Richarius of Passau—he, third in order, wrote a letter to the aforesaid supreme pontiff John. In it they complained of the withdrawal of the bishops of Moravia and the Slavs from their diocese, namely from the bishop of Passau. Although they obtained nothing, this letter, because it is rare and full of ancient information concerning the ecclesiastical condition of Bavaria, is not unworthy of reading. A copy of it still exists in the archives of the aforesaid churches and in Wolfgang Lazius, book XII of the *Commentaries on the Roman Commonwealth*; it is omitted here for brevity’s sake.”

Such are Hund’s words. From them an easy basis for conjecture is opened to us: that this Zacharias is the very bishop who left to posterity the sermon published by me. The conjecture is strengthened by the fact that I found it in a library of St Emmeram at Regensburg, to which many other ancient monuments of the metropolitan church of Salzburg had long ago been brought together by the most diligent monks of that monastery, although the parchment codex I used does not in date go beyond the twelfth century. But whoever may ultimately have been the author of this sermon on St George the martyr, no one will deny that he is weighty, learned, elegant, and indeed most worthy of public light.

[Col. 0621]

## SERMON OF BISHOP ZACHARIAS ON SAINT GEORGE

(R. P. Bernard PEZ, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum novissimus*, vol. IV, p. 17, from the Emmeram codex.)

[Col. 0621A] I. Today’s feast, most beloved brethren, doubles the joy of Paschal glory and, like a precious gem, adorns the gold into which it is set with the beauty of its own radiance. It was especially fitting that blessed George should be granted triumph at this season, when, after the winter storm’s harshness has passed and the south wind’s heat has dissolved it, the glad earth eagerly brings forth, and, with the bursting blossoms of diverse herbs and trees, comes into bloom, as it were, in the adolescence of its age. For “George” in Greek signifies in Latin speech “tiller of the earth.” In accordance with the presage of his name, he not only cultivated the field of his own mind with the disciplines of spiritual exercise; but also ploughed the earthly hearts of many by the ploughshare of holy exhortation and pious correction; and, rooting out the brambles of vices, planted in them fruitful [Col. 0621B] shoots of virtues.

Rightly, therefore, the soul of this blessed martyr today deserved, after the bloody rage of a furious prince, after the savagery of executioners raging with deadly cruelty, after the refined tortures of his mangled body, after the unjust torments of fire and iron, pitch and sulphur, after finally the blows of scourges and the darkness of prisons—like one emerging after the wintry storms of raging winds and snows—to hear this oracle of the divine summons:

> “Come,” he says, “my dove, my bride, my fair one; for now winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed; flowers have appeared in our land, the time of pruning has come” (Song II.10).

II. Truly, he was transferred from military service to military service, because he exchanged the office of the earthly tribunate which he held for the profession of Christian warfare; and, as a truly valiant soldier, first gave all his possessions to the poor, cast off the burden of earthly wealth, and thus, free, unencumbered, and girded with the breastplate of faith, threw himself ardently as Christ’s warrior into the battle-line of that dense conflict. He kept the proper order: first laying down the weight of possessions, and then fearlessly leaping into the field of battle. Hence the command in the Law that a fearful and faint-hearted man should not go out to war, but, it says, “Let him go [Col. 0622A] and return to his land, lest he make the hearts of his brothers afraid as he himself is terrified” (Deut. XX.8). By these words we are plainly taught that those who still fear to strip themselves of earthly concerns can neither fight bravely nor fittingly in defence of the faith. It is more tolerable that they should, in a manner of speaking, return home and live ignobly and unwarlike, than that through their degenerate example of fear they should turn both themselves and others away from the glory of triumph.

III. But blessed George, kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit and invincibly fortified with the standard of the cross, so entered into conflict with the wicked king that in his henchman he conquered the prince of all the wicked, and stirred the hearts of Christ’s soldiers to act courageously. Diocletian the emperor, indeed, at that time—as is found in the written history of his Passion—

> “whose mouth, according to the Psalmist, was full of cursing and bitterness, and under whose tongue were toil and pain; who sat with the rich in secret places, to kill the innocent, lying in wait like a lion in his den” (Ps. X.7),

first craftily put on, as it were, the clothing of a sheep and so attempted, by a certain art of guile and the painted colours of flattery, to persuade him. But when the illustrious athlete of Christ despised the foaming poisons from the mouth of the ancient serpent and showed that no longer the line of the first parent, but rather the marks of the second, lived in him, Diocletian immediately, like an arrow coming forth from Satan’s quiver, revealed the monstrous wolf that had lain hidden and, a bloody beast, cruelly burst forth to inflict diverse punishments.

Accordingly, executioners having been assembled, the blessed Martyr is stretched out, beaten with scourges, and torn by harsh blows. Then a wheel armed with swords is brought into the midst, so that the bound martyr’s body might be pierced the more cruelly because in more places. Ingenious savagery devises new and refined instruments of punishment; and, to sate the madness of its rage, reasons out ways to exceed the measure of human cruelty—ignorant, of course, that the precious pearl of conspicuous brightness, destined to be set among the living stones of the heavenly Jerusalem, [Col. 0623A] is made to shine all the more gloriously the more it is polished by the rough abrasion of the file or the hammer’s beating.

IV. The heavenly and invisible Judge was indeed present. According to the judgment of his providence, he permitted on the one hand the hands of the ungodly to rage, while on the other he preserved his jewel in the unviolated integrity of its own firmness. Although he handed over the limbs of his martyr to the hands of executioners, he guarded his soul, sustained upon the impregnable citadel of faith, with the tireless defence of his protection. Nor did he permit them to reach that which was hidden, presenting to them the image that appeared outwardly; thus they could flow around it on every side like the waters of the Flood around the ark, yet could not penetrate its inner parts.

Therefore let blessed George say, let him say:

> “Had the Lord [Col. 0623B] not been in us, when people rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive; when their fury raged against us, perhaps the water would have overwhelmed us” (Ps. CXXIII.2 ff.).

These are the waters of which the Saviour says through the Psalmist:

> “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul” (Ps. LXVIII.2).

And through Jonah:

> “You cast me,” he says, “into the deep, into the heart of the sea, and a flood surrounded me; all your whirlpools and your waves passed over me” (Jonah II.4).

But, according to Scripture, the Lord set a boundary around these waters and the sea, because he permits the reprobate to rage against his elect according to the measure of his providence, not according to the desire of human perversity. Hence, in the beginning of the world’s creation, [Col. 0623C] God divided the sea from the dry land. For what does the sea signify in mystery, if not reprobate and unbelieving human beings? They are indeed hot with a certain saltiness of carnal disposition, but are always found bitter towards one another in hatreds and quarrels; and, like the sea, they swell under the various winds of temptations and are shaken by the storms and tempests of carnal desires. What, then, does the dry land signify, if not a soul thirsting for the fountain of faith, or panting towards its Creator with ardent desire, like a thirsty throat? Thus one soul, happily dry with this thirst, cries out in its burning desire:

> “My soul has thirsted for the living God: when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. XLI.3).

Therefore the sea is divided from the dry land when God Almighty restrains the assaults of the reprobate from those thirsting for him, and, as it were, opposes a shore to the waves of the sea by setting the boundary of his governance against the efforts of raging madness. This is certainly demonstrated by that voice of God which says:

> “Who shut up the sea with doors, when it burst forth as though proceeding from the womb?” (Job XXXVIII.8).

And a little later:

> “I surrounded it with my boundaries, and set bar and doors, and said: Thus far you shall come, and you shall proceed no farther; and here you shall break your swelling waves” (ibid., 10).

V. Indeed, the heart of a wicked person is rightly signified by the sea: troubled by fury, bitter with quarrels, swollen with proud arrogance, and darkened by the gloom [Col. 0624A] of malicious deceit. God then divided the sea and restrained its threatening waves from flooding the land, so that the earth might put forth green herbs and fruit-bearing trees, and afterwards yield the fruits of crops. He now likewise separates from his elect the storms of reprobate persecutors and restrains, as it were, the furious assaults of tempests. Although he permits them to rage even to the infliction of bodily tortures, still, lest they harm souls, he keeps them at bay with the invincible and ever-watchful protection of his arm, saying in a manner to the sea: “Thus far you shall come, and you shall proceed no farther; and here, breaking, your swelling waves”; as if he openly said: “I allow you to proceed as far as inflicting tortures upon bodies; but lest you overflow even to the soul with your swelling surges, I set the shore of my law against you, so that, while the threat of the fury of your waves [lacuna] is left free [Note: [Col. 0623D] L. reads *anima* (“soul”); something is missing.].”

And because, as we said above, George signifies a tiller of the earth, the mystery of this allegorical figure is rightly adapted to this most blessed martyr. Though the wave of persecution boiled against him thus far, to the shore of the flesh, the solid ground of his soul was not enveloped by the storm of the tempestuous whirlwind; nor was he swallowed by the abyss of the raging sea, because he fixed his hope not upon the support of crumbling sand, but upon the solidity of the rock which is Christ (1 Cor. X). Hence the Truth says:

> “Whoever hears my words and does them, I will compare to a wise man who built his house upon a firm rock. The floods came, the winds blew, and they struck against that house, and it did not fall, for it was founded upon the rock” (Matt. [Col. 0624C] VII.24).

Truly this distinguished soldier of Christ set his foundations upon the rock of faith: for the prospect of heavenly reward he despised the threats of princes, mocked the promises of wicked flatterers, scorned the tortures of executioners, and trampled underfoot iron, fires, swords, and diverse kinds of punishment with the majesty of unconquered endurance.

VI. Dearest brethren, let us not merely admire this warrior of the heavenly army, but imitate him. Let our spirit now be raised to that heavenly reward, so that, while we fix our heart in contemplation of it, we may not be moved whether the world smiles as a seducer or rages with the adversities of conflict, saying with the Psalmist:

> “As its darkness, so also is its light” (Ps. CXXXVIII.12).

Let us therefore cleanse ourselves, in accordance with Paul’s command, “from every defilement of flesh and spirit” (2 Cor. VII.1), so that we may at some time deserve also to enter that temple of blessedness upon which we now direct the gaze of the mind. Hence Aaron is first washed with water, and afterwards enters the tabernacle to offer sacrifice. Concerning him the divine voice fittingly commands Moses:

> “He shall be clothed with a tunic; he shall cover his shameful parts with linen drawers; he shall be girded with a linen belt; he shall place a linen turban upon his head. For these are holy garments, which he shall put on after he has been washed” (Lev. XVI.4).

For whoever strives to sacrifice himself to God in Christ’s tabernacle, which is the Church, [Col. 0625A] must, after being washed in the laver of the sacred font, also put on the diverse garments of virtues.

> “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI.9),

so that one who is reborn in Christ as a new person through baptism may no longer wear garments of skin—that is, signs of mortality—but, having put off the old person, may put on the new and live renewed in him through devotion to a pure manner of life.

VII. It should be noted that all those garments are described as linen. Linen is brought to whiteness with labour; and the life of virtues is not acquired in the sluggishness of idleness but rather in the exercise of laborious discipline. Therefore, beloved brethren, purified through the sacrament of new baptism, let us put on the linen tunic [Col. 0625B] so that the brightness of holy conduct may adorn us. Let the shameful parts be covered with drawers, so that when the covering of an honourable life is assumed, the foulness of past crimes may be hidden before God’s eyes. Hence David says:

> “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI.1).

Let us be bound, he says, with a linen belt, and let a turban also be placed upon the head, so that, having girded the loins of the mind in truth, we may be protected by the helmet of salvation. If, then, cleansed from the filth of old sin and made conspicuous by the brightness of a new way of life, we thus worthily celebrate the Paschal mystery, we truly imitate the examples of the blessed martyrs.

And do not despair, my brethren: though still weak, though perhaps still entangled in outward occupations, do not despair of belonging to the fellowship of the martyrs, you who recognize that you love the martyrs’ victories from the heart. Certainly the five daughters of Salphaath are known to have received an inheritance among their brothers by Moses’ ordinance (Num. XXVII): five and women, so that external occupation is signified by the number five of the daughters, and weakness by the female sex. Jonathan too stood in a certain middle ground between the two: he neither remained with Saul in evil nor could be made David’s equal in good. Yet, because he was the friend of God’s beloved Prophet and rejoiced with brotherly kindness in the future success of that Prophet, he is believed not now to be divided from his fellowship in spirit, to whom, while he lived in the flesh, he was united in unanimous love.

VIII. But we, beloved brethren, who by God’s help have left behind us the evil spirit that harassed Saul—or rather, who have escaped the army of Pharaoh, drowned in the Red Sea through the power of the Paschal sacrament—still remain in the wilderness because of the weakness of the flesh. Let us pass on to perfection of life, to the land flowing with milk and honey. Having gone out from Sodom, let us not linger longer in Zoar; but, delivered with Lot, let us swiftly ascend the mountain summit. Thus, having already begun amid the very rudiments of our service to rejoice in the triumphs of the blessed martyrs, may we one day be advanced so far that we ourselves learn to triumph with the saints. And may Jesus Christ our Lord himself be our strength as he protects us, just as he became our price when he redeemed us—he who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1153: ROBERT PULLUS, CARDINAL AND CHANCELLOR

## PROLEGOMENA

(*Works of Robert Pullus*, Paris, 1655, folio, edited by Hugh Mathoud, Benedictine monk.)

[Col. 0625]

## DEDICATORY LETTER

To the most illustrious Prince of the Church, Louis Henri de Gondrin, Archbishop of Sens, Primate of Gaul and Germany.

Behold, most illustrious Archbishop, the Phoenix once destroyed by a treacherous death, but now for the first time restored to life beneath your rays in glory no less great. That, when at last he was to be restored to the public good, he chose to begin life under you is a privilege of your virtue. [Col. 0627] To have smiled upon him even once is a sure path to safety; nor will he fear that his memory will perish among later ages when you yourself commend it by the renown of your name. How far that renown will spread among posterity may be inferred from the fact that it has already won the approval of all whose earnest desire is to cultivate or admire virtue. What better fortune could receive him as he is reborn and wrapped in new swaddling-clothes than that he should be cherished in the bosom in which piety has grown up together with all the Muses; to whom wisdom has been a companion from childhood, and excellence of mind no less a natural disposition to virtue?

It is so, most illustrious Archbishop: nature has been more generous towards no one, fortune has cherished no one more; yet everything beneath wisdom lay beneath you. You knew that to be born a prince is commonly the sport of fortune; to become great and illustrious is the offspring of wisdom and the fruit of glory. Hence, although you are pre-eminent in the splendour of your birth, you sought splendour of character as though you had derived none from your lineage. I say that you stand out in nobility of birth: ancient Spain is joined to you in ties of blood, through the illustrious marriage alliance of the Dukes of Cardona in Catalonia—whom you trace as your origin—with the royal lines of the princes of Aragon and the Counts of Foix and Armagnac. A lineage no less splendid is added by the house of Castillon among the Médoc, enlarged by a double marriage alliance with your family: a noble offspring of the Kings of Cyprus from the line of Lusignan. The dukes of Bellogarde, allied with the Termes family, chief equerries and marshals of France, and distinguished by patrician rank itself, are likewise bound to you by new alliances.

But the title by which the natural summit of your nobility rises still higher is the most ancient love of kings for your family and their constant favour. Finding them nowhere degenerate from themselves, and enriched by almost hereditary honours, kings raised them even to the rank of the second dignity in France—yet with such a genius of fortune that they indulged virtue no less than affection. That your father, grandfather, and great-grandfather were governors of Béarn and Navarre was a mark of singular prudence. That your father was pre-eminent in the king’s bodyguard and commander of his sword-bearers was a mark of well-known fidelity. Finally, that all were knights of both orders—the Order of the Shell and the Order of the Holy Spirit, Knights of the Collar—was a sign of outstanding courage. A sufficient example of that ancestral courage is displayed in the severed heads of Moors in the family arms: Louis IX, an eyewitness, granted them as a badge and shield to that eminent knight de Gondrin, who in single combat among the Syrians had slain that number, with the armies drawn up on either side and the most holy king himself present. These, I say, most illustrious Archbishop, are certain ornaments of your nobility; although they would have sufficed to crown another’s glory, they were scarcely the beginning of yours.

You preferred to make illustrious rather than to inspect those many ancestral wax portraits, in recounting which others spend almost their entire lives. You delighted only in the light that you yourself would emit, not in that which you would receive. Hence came your greater impulse toward piety and your constant care to form your mind by divine gifts. Witness is borne by that most blessed ardour of virtues contending among themselves as to which would first fill your breast and adorn your mind. For your so great virtues, the vast clergy was due; for your care, the people; for your learning, the chair; for your prudence, the pastoral staff; for your faith, the ring; for your authority, the mitre; the cross as an example; and finally that see was due to your wisdom, so that in governing, your hand might hold the helm of the Church.

And these, indeed, most illustrious Archbishop, the outstanding ornaments of your mind made the most celebrated cardinal who bears your name envious, so that here you might have his purple garment as a suppliant. But the man whom you consecrate to posterity under your auspices, you will also possess as immortal by the right of gratitude and the pledge of obedience. The book will go safely through all the provinces of the world under its own name, but almost exalted by your authority; and to its own fame, which it possesses in the highest purity, it will add yours, in whose eternity nearly all things concur.

I seem able to claim no small part in the glory of this gift—that is, in earnestly devoting myself to your praises—by a familiar and hereditary destiny. For your interest in us is not slight; no Archbishop of Sens is holier or dearer to anyone than to the monks of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif, among whom whatever dignity you possess begins and whatever sanctity you possess flows back upon us. You know that, following the example of your predecessors, the dedication of your mitres and the birthday of your see flourish here; here dawns the aurora of your light; nor does an entrance into Stephen’s house lie open except by Peter’s keys. Yet your return to us is holier than your departure is illustrious. As the sun is greater at its setting than at its rising, we receive as saints those whom we sent forth merely as bishops; and for those whose inauguration we prepared with a chair, as custom requires, we have raised altars when they return to us.

Thus, most illustrious Archbishop, almost all the saints whom you honour, almost all the illustrious bishops of your metropolitan church whom you number among the ancients, are ours by the title of their education and the authority of our sacred school: because here they were taught letters and piety, sometimes by monastic profession of life, by inauguration to their see, or by the right of burial. Yet we shall belong to you still more because your ready and innate inclination to love is in us an equally strong spur to emulate the affection you bear toward us and the piety of your forebears. According to their judgment, prompted by their supreme goodwill towards us, no house was more religious than ours; none more familiar, more welcome, or holier. How great a flame of love burned in them for us you may sufficiently infer even from their ashes, beneath which our ground rises in forty and more tombs. Under these noble remains of love you will cherish the ancestral fire; nor will incentives be lacking so long as you recognize in us the everlasting reciprocal returns of grateful feeling, obedience, and reverence.

As a pledge hereof, of fidelity sworn among us, we here give our hand as hostage, not only by the dedication of this work, but by the sacrament through which one binds oneself most especially:

To Your Most Illustrious Lordship, the most devoted Brother HUGH MATHOUD, Benedictine religious of the monastery of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif, Congregation of Saint-Maur.

[Col. 0629]

## THE SCHOLIAST TO THE READER

[Col. 0629A] Long ago, kindly reader, I would have satisfied the wishes of learned persons demanding the birth into print of this offspring of Pullus, had I not learned with certainty from the reports of friends that certain other studies by the author lay concealed in England, and one in Sweden. I first endeavoured—and with quite exceptional zeal—to leave no stone unturned during three whole years, in the hope of obtaining even one of them, so that the work might grow to the proper bulk of a volume. A great longing burned in a mind devoted to the good of letters: to restore their Apollo to the Muses. Nor did I consider the delay useless, although it was unwelcome to many, if only I could spur the diligence of the English by my example. Rebuffed by them, I could extract from them only the hope that they would take care that a man worthy among all people to be crowned with the laurel of immortality should not perish any longer among his own countrymen in cheap obscurity. [Col. 0629B]

My effort towards the Swedes was equal; equal also was the ruin of my hopes. Yet the brothers of the distinguished scholar Valesius, to whose kindness I owe much, repeatedly urged acquaintances of theirs among that nation to arrange for the return of the manuscript codex containing the sermons of our Robert—or at least a copy of it—which had formerly been taken away, against the will of its owners, the monks of Fleury, together with many other books.

I wished to mention these things in passing so that you might know, reader, why the birth of this work was so long delayed. You would have received it as early as the year 1651, together with our observations upon it, had I not devoted an equal length of time [Col. 0629C] to recovering from exile that codex snatched away by a hasty hand.

Having therefore undertaken these labours in vain, and wishing to act as midwife for other offspring of this most excellent intellect, no less desirous of light, I offer you, reader, only one part of his studies, but the noblest: the work which, following the custom of his age, he entitled *Sentences*. We had a codex from our celebrated abbey of Saint-Remi at Reims, written in an excellent hand and contemporary with the author’s own pen, whether he dictated or wrote it.

It had happily fallen into the hands of one of our brethren, the Reverend Father Dom Alexis Edouard, renowned among his own people for the eminence of his learning and for the variety of his scholarship. Through continual reading he had grasped the author’s genius; and admiring [Col. 0629D] his free manner of writing, the lights of vigorous reasoning scattered throughout the work, the weightiness of the *Sentences*, and their continuous texture woven from the judgments of the Holy Fathers, especially Augustine, he regretted that the rays of so great a star had until then been withheld from public light. To bring them forth, he had already transcribed the codex with his own hand and would undoubtedly have devoted the remainder of his energy vigorously to completing the work. But, summoned to the sacred pulpit at Corbie, and afterwards [Col. 0630A] to Compiègne, where he publicly taught philosophy with the highest praise, he could not discharge this most welcome task.

Meanwhile the most learned men, especially of the University of Paris, pressed for publication of this work. Our Luc d’Achery had brought this Pullus before them for approval like an eagle brought before the rays of the sun. Ordered to yield to their requests, I undertook a task beyond my strength and, I fear, unworthy of their wishes. Yet I shall briefly state what care and effort I have expended.

First. I feared that in an author not readily accessible, though otherwise most Christian, there were certain obstacles that might hinder unwary readers. Above all, in the most difficult question concerning the order in which the parts of human nature—namely [Col. 0630B] soul and body—were assumed by the divine Word, I suspected that his view, wholly singular, would not be safe for those who know the dogmas of faith only in words, unless someone held out a light from the shore and all matters were reduced to the precise points of law: namely, to the meaning of Holy Scripture as established by the Church or by the unanimous consent of the Fathers who wrote expressly on the matter; to the canons of ecumenical councils; and to the decrees of the supreme pontiffs. These three form a threefold cord, difficult to break.

After consulting in writing and in speech several theologians of the highest repute from both the most eminent house and the royal College of Navarre—who saw nothing worthy of obelus—I nevertheless, guided by their advice, added certain notes and observations. In them difficult matters are explained, obscure ones reviewed, some matters touched upon, and the rest [Col. 0630C] illuminated, especially where Pullus examines the method and practice of the sacred forum.

Second. In the notes we have sometimes adduced the authorities of the holy Fathers of the Church and the author’s thought adhering to their judgments, adding, for the sake of learning and when it seemed useful, the opinions of several others to whom he may also have had regard. This was done more frequently in reference to Augustine, to whose doctrine he was so devoted that he scarcely has a page that does not aim at Augustine’s sayings. But lest any fiction slip in or any ungrateful silence occur, we certainly passed over far more than we included, unequal as we were to this diligence and labour; or because studies planned earlier continually called us elsewhere. Unless it is preferable [Col. 0630D] to pardon this fault, those who imposed a task fit only for mature strength upon a youthful pen will share the penalty with us.

Third. Since it redounds greatly to Pullus’s praise that he published theology before the Master of the Sentences wrote his own work—as, among others, Father Jacob of Saint Charles noted in his panegyrical synopsis of Pullus—we judged it worthwhile to indicate Peter’s *Sentences* in the margins of Pullus’s text; and, where the importance of the matter required it, by asterisks placed on both sides, to show the reader, as it were by pointers, how closely these two stars of nascent scholastic theology were mutually connected, and (if there should perhaps be suspicion of borrowed light) which first shone upon the other.

Fourth. From the prologue composed by the author for the work, it is certain that several numbers, or numerical notes, were appended to the individual chapters, and that the same number of them was prefixed in turn to those chapter-headings immediately following the Prologue itself. But since they are lacking in our manuscript, it was impossible to supply them because another manuscript was unavailable. This is likewise why, besides typographical blemishes, the reader will encounter certain errors, and perhaps mutilated passages; these could most easily have been remedied had other manuscripts been at hand. Nor did we judge that our own understanding should prevail in these matters, thinking that every learned reader would more judiciously offer assistance here, as in other cases.

Fifth. Here the method and course which Pullus pursued throughout this whole work ought briefly to have been explained, and a synopsis of the books, or individual parts, ought also to have been prefixed. But he himself has provided for the latter by setting out at the beginning of the work a summary heading for each chapter.

You have the other matter sufficiently set forth in the observations, where occasion especially offered to touch lightly upon the first impulses of rampant scholasticism, then scarcely emerged from its cradle. Although Pullus granted it very sparingly, he nevertheless sometimes yielded to that age, in which it was scarcely thought unlawful for reason to peer with excessive curiosity into the very sacred inner sanctuary of faith. It will suffice to warn that the context is rendered obscure by the transposition of words, which is unusually frequent in him; therefore less experienced readers will need serious attention when they encounter those intricacies.

Nor, I think, will anyone except some rigid Aristarchus condemn the fact that he not infrequently appears, beneath the cover of the word *perhaps*, to assume the appearance of doubting in matters which we believe with certainty and divine faith. For in the notes we have shown that this mask of disputants is neither hostile nor unwelcome to the genuine gaze of truth, but familiar and almost necessary to theologians. Thus the problem-based mode of disputation has never been banished from their schools—not so that one may freely assent, according to one’s native whim, to either side of a problem, but so that, by that method of inquiry, the brightness of faith, which alone is pleasing, may shine forth more abundantly. Pullus, Thomas, and the other leaders of the schools thus prepare support for truth; but the former more subtly—hence the cause of scruple—the latter with the open coloring of falsehood. Therefore our Peter of Poitiers says excellently, Part III, chapter 21:

> Although the certainty of faith is so great, we may nevertheless doubt concerning the articles of faith, and inquire and dispute. I do not mean that we doubt whether the articles of faith are true, but [we doubt] about the manner, etc.

As to our observations on Pullus, I would have you, reader, be warned of nothing except this: since I have used a miscellaneous apparatus of books, especially of the older edition, which sometimes differs from the more recent both in the headings of books and in the division of chapters, I may perhaps occasion you delay or weariness—or, what is worse, suspicion of bad faith—when you test it, unless I forestall this by this brief token of what has occurred. The monastery of Sens, where for more than a full year I devoted myself to nurturing this Pullus, lacked that collection of books; consequently I had need of outside books, and of the old reading, as I have said—except for those which the most illustrious and most reverend Lord Louis-Henri de Gondrin, Archbishop of Sens, supplied with open-handed generosity. I have many reasons for commending him; but, after the qualities implanted in a most vigilant shepherd, he is especially known for munificence equal to his nobility.

But, reader, lest you remain unaware of the others through whom I have advanced: besides the Doctors de Sainte-Beuve and Jean de Launoy, already mentioned by me in the observations, who poured much light upon one whose sight was dim, the following most learned men also share both the praise and the burden: Lord Charles de Hanniques de Benjamin, Archdeacon of Étampes in the Church of Sens, and likewise vicar-general and official of the same illustrious Lord Archbishop; Monsieur Pereyret, prefect of the Royal College of Navarre; and the Reverend Father Hilarion Le Febvre, my master in theology. Refreshed by their letters or their personal learning, I ventured upon more than my courage had promised. Yet, lest the order of this recension displease, I most sincerely declare that I have followed no order.

I wish to distinguish from this series of thanks the Reverend Father Dom Luc d’Achery, librarian of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, to whom, reader, you certainly owe the chief part of this entire labor. By his assistance, encouragement, private and public efforts on my behalf, and frequent transmission of letters and notes, what I could not have done is here, in whatever manner, accomplished before your eyes. But while I remained stubbornly at Sens, he was present over the press as its superintendent and corrected it with a most kindly hand—this being the sum of my wishes. Though always in frail health and occupied with better Muses, which you enjoy almost every year, he could scarcely have sufficed for so great an office, had he not devoted himself to you and to me. Farewell.

From the Monastery of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif at Sens,  
the Ides of May, 1655.

[Col. 0633]

# TESTIMONIES OF CERTAIN WRITERS WHICH SET FORTH A FEW FACTS CONCERNING ROBERT PULLUS AND HIS WRITINGS

[Col. 0633A] We find Pullus variously named by authors. Some, such as William of Saint-Thierry, friend of Saint Bernard and Pullus’s contemporary, and John, prior of Hexham, call him *Pullanus*. Others write *Pulleinus*, *Pulleinius*, or *Polenius*, as John Pits does; Bale and Gesner write *Polenus*, *Pollen*, *Pulcy*, and *Pully*. Ciaconius writes *Pullenus*, alternatively *Pully*, and also *Bullenus*, together with Claude Héméré in Book 5, page 41, of *On the University of Paris*. But this is erroneous, as also in François Amboise’s *Apology for Peter Abelard*, near its end, where one reads *Robertus Polonus* instead of *Polenus*. Bernard, however, calls him Pullus; so too does our manuscript, written in an excellent hand and which we believe contemporary with Pullus himself. On its opening page one reads most distinctly: “Here begins the Prologue to the *Sentences* of Master ROBERT PULLUS.” After this: “Here begin the *Sentences* of MASTER ROBERT PULLUS, Cardinal and Chancellor of the Holy Roman Church.” The English authors Bale and Gesner, who write *Pully*, do not differ from this.

In Claude Robert’s *Gallia Christiana*, another Robert Pullus is named as the fifty-third Archbishop of Rouen; he was made archbishop in the year of Christ 1208 and died in 1221, commonly called Robert Poullain. Volume II of Jacques-Auguste de Thou’s *History*, Book 29, page 88, mentions another Robert Pullus. Likewise, in de Thou’s index: Robert Pullus, Poulain, who lived in the preceding century, namely in 1562. Whether these men were related by blood to our Robert may remain conjecture for others.

From Saint Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, Letter 205, to the Bishop of Rochester.

It was no empty title of glory that Pullus was considered worthy of Bernard’s praise, for Bernard found acceptable only those who stood out through the merit and eminence of virtue or thoroughly tested learning. Since that letter concerns the author alone and commends his sound doctrine in no small measure, we reproduce it here in full. [Col. 0633C] Bernard’s reason for writing to the Bishop of Rochester, Pullus’s diocesan, was to prevent him from forcing a man highly deserving in learning and at the University of Paris, and still likely to be useful there, to return so soon to England.

The letter reads as follows:

> “You write harshly to one who does not deserve it. What sin have I committed? If I advised Master Robert Pullus to remain for some time at Paris because of the sound doctrine known to reside in him, I thought this necessary and still think so. If I asked your highness to permit this, I would ask the same even now, had I not perceived that you were angered by my former request. If I said that the man was supported by the favor of friends whose influence at court is not slight, I said what I feared for you and still fear. For, after an appeal had been made, you stretched out your hand, as we have heard, against the property of the appellant; I neither approved nor approve this. Yet I neither advised him nor advise him to oppose your will in any respect. Henceforth we are yours, ready always to receive and honor your crown with fitting and due reverence. Trusting in the testimony of this conscience, we still venture to approach you—with petition and counsel only—that Master Robert may be able to remain at Paris for some time, without any diminution of your favor. May the Lord repay you with eternal life because you have cherished our very hearts—I mean the sons whom we sent into Ireland.”

Moreover, the authority of this letter renders the trustworthiness of our manuscript certain and beyond doubt, for there likewise the author is called Robert Pullus, although other writers alter his surname somewhat, as we have already shown.

From William of Saint-Thierry’s treatise against Gilbert of Poitiers, *On Divine Relations*, at the end.

> “To return specifically to the chapters now in hand: when people heard such novel doctrines, ought they not to have considered how many wise and learned men, of sound opinion and doctrine, the Church had possessed not long before these times—men who had plainly thought and taught the contrary? I mean those distinguished men of Laon, Anselm and Ralph; Master Alberic of Rheims, formerly Archbishop of Bourges; Hugh of Saint-Victor, the most faithful interpreter of the divine word; and also Robert Pullanus, chancellor of the Apostolic See; and very many others whose presence still remains, or whose fresh memory is held in blessing. Their common opinion stands thus: whatever is in God is God. Hence Master Ralph of Laon says in one of his writings: ‘By the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit we do not understand that any properties are posited—as was said above concerning Just and Pious—which are something other than the persons themselves,’ etc.”

I owe this testimony of William of Saint-Thierry to the attention and kindness of the most learned Philippe Labbe, priest of the Society of Jesus.

From the *History* of Symeon of Durham, continued by John, Prior of Hexham, under the year of Christ 1147. [Note: [Col. 0633D] In Volume I of the *Writers of English History*.]

[Col. 0634C]

> “In these days Robert Pullanus, chancellor of the Apostolic See, stood preeminent among the Roman clergy, most experienced in every kind of wisdom and learning. A native of Britain, devoted to philosophy from his earliest age, he refused, for its sake, the episcopal dignity offered by King Henry; possessing food and clothing, he was content with these.”

This John wrote under Henry II, King of England, and not long after Pullus’s lifetime.

From Pits, *On the Illustrious Writers of England in the Twelfth Age*.

> “Robert Pulleinius, or Pulleinus, was born in England and educated there until youth. Afterwards, fleeing the civil disturbances which occurred under King Stephen, as may be inferred from John Boston of Bury, he went to France for the sake of study and devoted himself vigorously to learning at Paris for a long time. He both learned, and in part taught, every branch of knowledge, sacred and profane, divine and human. [Col. 0635A] For he was in some sense made and endowed by nature not merely for learning good letters, but also for teaching them and advancing them by every means. When therefore maturity of age, firmness of judgment, and zeal to assist his country had been added to his exceptional learning, he was ordained priest and at last returned to his own people. When he saw the wretched condition of the universities, disfigured by civil wars, he was immediately moved by compassion and resolved to raise anew the University of Oxford, now almost collapsed, and restore it to the Muses. There he opened schools and taught the best disciplines without charge; he summoned hearers and pupils, professors and masters, thither from other parts of the kingdom. He supported not a few of them at his own expense; others he bound to himself and to the Muses by every office of kindness. Meanwhile, he continued to teach, dictate, and write much.

> “By these truly generous actions he acquired a great reputation, which reached the Roman court and the ears of the supreme pontiff himself. Called therefore to Rome, he was created cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church. Yet even then he did not cease from his studies, but wrote much. John Rous bears this testimony concerning him in his book *On the Universities*, and John Leland writes similar things.

> “Among the writings of Pulleinius we find at least the following works:

> “*Sentences on the Holy Trinity*, eight books. [Note: [Col. 0635D] This is the work which we are now publishing.] ‘That the reader may readily find in this volume,’ etc. A manuscript exists in the private library of Walter Cope.

> “*On the Apocalypse of John*, one book. [Note: [Col. 0635D] Bale mentions this in his index of authors who wrote on the Apocalypse.] ‘For the most part, concupiscence, having been lulled to sleep …’

> “*On Certain Psalms*, one book.

> “*On Contempt of the World*, one book. ‘Dear brother, consider,’ etc.

> “*On the Sayings of the Doctors*, four books. ‘The enemy of the human race, on every side …’

> “A book of his sermons. [Note: [Col. 0635D] A manuscript existed recently in the possession of the illustrious S. Petau; but, sharing the fate of many other ancient manuscripts, it was carried off into exile, taken from the French against their will, and is held by the Swedes.]

> “A book of his lectures, and many others.

[Col. 0635C] “He flourished in the year 1146 after the coming of the Messiah, while Stephen and Matilda were contending hostilely for the kingdom of England.” Thus Pits.

In the prolegomena, or introductory stage-setting, of his work, chapter 2, “On the Antiquity of the University of Oxford,” pages 28 and 29, the same Pits writes as follows:

> “Moreover, not many years later, first Danish soldiers and then King Harold himself, surnamed Harefoot, ravaged the city of Oxford with sword and fire so severely that it remained almost desolate until the time of King William I and the coming of the Normans. But then at least it began to flourish again. For it is certain that about the year of the Lord 1070 the most learned monk Ingulf flourished there. Likewise, in the reign of King Stephen, though otherwise calamitous, studies revived as if anew and gradually returned to their former flourishing, chiefly through the industry of Robert Polenius. He summoned there many pupils and hearers, as well as masters and professors, supported them there, and finally taught himself; he spared neither labor nor expense in restoring the study of letters there, which had almost collapsed. Afterwards King Henry II, and after him his son Richard, born in that same city, advanced this very pious work to no small degree. Thus Polenius’s undertaking achieved a happy result.”

This again is Pits, who further mentions the same Robert Pullus in his *Index of Illustrious English Writers Who Were of the Cardinalitial Order*, no. 29: “Robert Pulleinus, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, of Oxford,” etc., 1146.

In Gesner’s *Bibliotheca*, from Bale:

> “Robert Polenus, otherwise Pully, an English cardinal, published certain *Sentences*, eight books; *On Contempt of the World*, one book; *On the Apocalypse of John*, one book; *On Certain Psalms*, one book; *On the Sayings of the Doctors*, four books; a work of his sermons, one book; several lectures, one book. He lived in 1146.”

In Bale’s *Index of Authors Who Wrote on the Apocalypse*, Robert Pully, an Englishman, is listed among the non-regular priests.

From Onofrio Panvinio.

Under the year of the Lord 1134, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent II, in December, at the second creation, he writes that six cardinals were made, Robert being fourth in order; he says that Robert was afterwards made chancellor.

Robert, cardinal-priest of the title of S. [lacuna], afterwards chancellor: when Innocent, pope, died at Rome on the eighth day before the Kalends of October in the year 1143, thirty-one cardinals assembled and named Celestine II pontiff, among whose number was our Robert. When he had been taken from the living after five months and thirteen days, Lucius II was elected pope in 1143 by forty cardinals; Robert is counted among them and is said to have acted as chancellor in that year. When Lucius II was removed, Eugenius III succeeded in 1145, on the third day before the Kalends of March; Robert is listed among the electors and is called archpriest and chancellor through Eugenius’s third year, which was the year of Christ 1147.

From these facts it appears that Robert Pullus held the office of cardinal for about twelve years. Nor was he declared cardinal only in the year 1144, as a recent, otherwise most learned writer has stated; while his notable work *On Penance* was being set for the press this year, its author himself showed it to me hastily.

From Ciaconius.

> “Robert Pullenus—erroneously, Bullenus—otherwise Pully, an Englishman, cardinal-priest of the title [lacuna]. A man highly accomplished in every kind of learning, he was exceedingly distinguished by varied erudition and knowledge of divine matters. He acquired great glory on many accounts, especially because, after the schools of the Oxford academy had formerly been overthrown by Harold, king of the English, he worked vigorously for their restoration. Returning to England, he summoned students there from every part of the kingdom. There, offering instruction in every kind of knowledge, he taught the disciplines of the best arts without charge, and in advancing learning displayed every act of kindness. He wrote many little works for the restoration of letters, through which he made his name widely known there. Called to the City by Innocent II, he was appointed cardinal by his successor Celestine and chancellor of the Apostolic See by Lucius II. He died under Eugenius III, having deserved exceedingly well of literary studies; he wrote, etc.”

As in Pits, but not without errors in Ciaconius.

From Claude Héméré, *On the University of Paris*, chapter 5, page 41.

[Col. 0636D]

> “Nevertheless, the rights and prerogatives of the Church of Paris did not prevent the canons from sometimes associating with themselves other learned colleagues, who were to contend most gloriously in the same arena. Such were Anselm of Laon, Roscelin, who was canon of Tours, Gilbert of Poitiers, Peter Abelard, Fulk of Deuil, Robert Bullenus, etc.”

Louis de la Châtaigneraie, Bishop of Poitiers, also mentions him with splendid praise in his *Nomenclator of Cardinals* and compiled an index of his works.

Aubery too, in the *General History of Cardinals*, published in French in 1642, has an account of this Robert differing in nothing from that of Pits reported above, except that, following Godwin of Llandaff, he assigns him the title of Saint Eusebius and places his death in the year 1150; but this conjecture is not well established, and therefore he does not adhere to it. He further writes that Pullus received the laurels of public teaching at Paris, where he taught for a long time, and that in 1134 he was raised to the insignia of the second dignity.

In several monasteries of the Benedictine order there are original bulls to which Robert Pullus himself, as chancellor, appended the date. Thus, in the Abbey of Saint-Germain at Paris, Eugenius III issued sealed letters approving and confirming its rights, privileges, and immunities, subscribed by our Robert as follows:

> Given at the Lateran through the hand of Robert, cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth Ides of January, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1145 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

Likewise, in the monasteries of Cluny, Fleury, and Saint-Remi at Rheims, and in the cartularies of Marmoutier near Tours, of Blessed Mary of La Ronde outside the walls of Auxerre, and of Bourges, we read similar subscriptions made by the same Robert, all within the years of Eugenius III’s see.

To all these I shall add, in gratitude, the splendid eulogy of Pullus which its author, the Reverend Father Louis Jacob of Saint Charles, Carmelite of Chalon, sent us in a friendly hand, composed in the following words.

Eulogy of Robert Pulleinius, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, taken from the cardinalitial library, manuscript of the Reverend Father Louis Jacob of Saint Charles, Carmelite of Chalon, royal counsellor and almoner, and also librarian to His Eminence Cardinal de Retz, Archbishop of Paris.

> “Robert Pulleinius or Pulleinus, commonly Pollen, Pulley, or Pulcy, and sometimes Bullen, an Englishman by nationality, was public professor in the theological faculty of Paris, famous throughout the world. Afterwards, having returned to England, he resolved, Pits says, to raise anew the University of Oxford, then almost fallen, and restore it once again to the Muses. He opened schools there, taught the best sciences without charge, and summoned hearers and pupils, professors and masters from other parts of the kingdom. He supported not a few of them at his own expense; others he bound to himself and the Muses by every office of kindness. Since this most eminent doctor was a patron of letters and learned men, and a most munificent Maecenas, he taught and dictated much publicly, and also wrote privately for his everlasting remembrance and the benefit of the commonwealth of learning. On account of his highest gifts of intellect and nature, his exceptional candor of spirit, singular uprightness of character, and exact knowledge of the sciences, King Henry I of England loved him greatly. On Henry’s recommendation he was created cardinal-priest of the Holy Roman Church, of the title of Saint Eusebius, by Pope Innocent II at Rome in December 1134—as Onofrio [Panvinio states]—and was later appointed Apostolic Chancellor by Lucius II. A most learned man, an outstanding interpreter of the Sacred Scriptures, and a sublime theologian, he wrote theology before Peter Lombard, Master of the Sentences and Bishop of Paris, easily the foremost of theologians. He was also a great preacher in his age. As the glory and delight of the Muses, he wrote:

> “*On Certain Psalms*, one book.

> “*On the Apocalypse of Saint John*, one book. It begins: ‘For the most part, concupiscence, having been lulled to sleep …’

> “*Sentences on the Holy Trinity*, eight books. They begin: ‘That the reader may readily find in this volume,’ etc. Manuscripts exist in England in the private library of Walter Cope, as Thomas James indicates in his *Oxford-Cambridge Eclogue*, published at London in 1600 in quarto. I saw [one] at Paris in the very extensive library of the Benedictine Fathers of the royal monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, in folio, through the kindness of the Reverend Father Dom Luc d’Achery, the most learned librarian of that monastery. This outstanding work is eagerly awaited by all devotees of the Muses.

> “*On the Sayings of the Doctors*, four books. It begins: ‘The enemy of the human race …’

> “*On Contempt of the World*, one book. It begins: ‘Dear brother, consider,’ etc.

> “A book of his lectures.

> “A book of sermons. In the library of the most illustrious Alexander Petau, son of Paul Petau, Parisian senator, there are manuscript sermons of the same Cardinal Pulleinius *On the Common of Saints*, no. 1434, and [manuscripts] in the Putean Library. There is also a manuscript little work of his there, no. 1223, though its subject has hitherto remained unknown to me.

> “And some other works.

> “He departed this life about the year 1150 of the Lord’s Incarnation, under Pope Eugenius III.

[Col. 0638B] “Concerning Robert Pulleinius’s merits and writings: Onofrio Panvinio, Augustinian, under Innocent II; Alfonso Ciaconius, Dominican, in the same place; Boston of Bury, English Benedictine, in his *Catalogue of Church Writers*; John Leland, *On the Writers of England*; John Bale, in the same work; Francis Godwin, Bishop of Llandaff, *On the Cardinals of England*; John Rous, Englishman, *On the Universities of Britain*; Jacob Middendorp, *On the Universities of the Whole World*; Josias Simler, in the *Epitome of Gesner’s Bibliotheca*; Antonio Possevino of Mantua, S.J., in the *Sacred Apparatus*; Henri-Louis Chasteigner de la Roche-Posay, Bishop of Poitiers, in the *Nomenclator of Cardinals*; Francesco Maria Torrigio, *On the Most Eminent Cardinal Writers*; Fabiano Giustiniani, priest of the Roman Congregation of the Oratory, later Bishop of Ajaccio in Corsica, Book III of *On Sacred Scripture*; Antoine Aubery of Paris, volume I of the *General History of Cardinals*; Ángel Manrique, of Burgos, of the Cistercian Order, Bishop of Pacis Augustae in Spain, volume II of the *Cistercian Annals*, under the year 1446, chapter 3, no. 12; Gabriel Naudé of Paris, in the *Additions to the History of Louis XI, King of the French*, page 162; Pietro Angelo Spera of Remiremont, Book III, *On the Nobility of Professors of Grammar and Humane Letters in Both Languages*. Thus Louis Jacob.”

But of all those whom we have mentioned above, none, in my judgment, seems to provide information more certain or more abundant than a certain English writer, a Benedictine, highly renowned among his countrymen for learning—though he did not wish to be named here. We append his letter, also sent to us, by way of conclusion.

> “To answer your inquiries more particularly, I say:

> “1. This Robert’s surname varies greatly among authors. To say nothing of the Latin declension of the name, the vernacular name itself is pronounced in many ways: now Pollen, now Pullen, now Pulley, now Pulcy, now Pudsy or de Puteaco. Most of these names persist among us even to the present day in families of no mean rank and have not wholly disappeared. But if we agree with Godwin, who wished him also to be called Bollen, there will be not merely nobility in the name, but majesty and something of royalty besides.

> “2. Godwin asserts, even stubbornly, that he was English both in country and descent, as though he thought he must expressly fight against the suspicion that Pullus had come to us from Gaul, from which the Normans, recently victorious at that time, were bringing many men distinguished in learning and uprightness into England.

> “3. You may infer that he had a handsome and ample patrimony from the fact that, after English wealth had been cut down by Norman plundering and wars, Polenus nevertheless had sufficient means, together with the king’s work and resources, to restore the Oxford Studium and support both himself and the learned men whom he had called in to assist with that work. Nor is there doubt that he received this patrimony from his parents; for, devoted as he was to Christian philosophy, he sought no goods other than those by which the mind is cultivated.

> “4. All who write about him agree that he laid the foundations of his earliest education at home in his native country; then travelled to France and devoted himself at Paris to better teachers; and finally returned to his homeland, opened a school at Oxford, and, with the favor and support of Henry I—who was called *Beauclerc*, that is, ‘good cleric,’ because he favored learning and was himself learned—restored the university there, which had completely collapsed.

> “5. It is therefore divination, not a statement of fact, when certain of our countrymen invent that Pullen changed his country by voluntary exile, fleeing the wars under King Stephen, and only then, when affairs were peaceful, began to teach at Oxford after returning from his sojourn in Paris. The truer account is that he returned to his native country and to the University of Oxford under Henry I. For anyone who separates Henry I’s benefactions and Pullen’s labors in restoring the University of Oxford, and places them in different periods, will find it difficult to reconcile the histories and dates.

> “6. Therefore, under Henry I’s auspices and chiefly through Robert Pollen’s industry, studies at Oxford began to flourish again about the year of the Lord 1129. Pullen held the Oxford chair for more than ten years. Afterwards, summoned to Rome by Innocent II, he was made cardinal of the title of Saint Eusebius in 1144 by Innocent’s successor Celestine; [Note: [Col. 0639B] But in this matter the opinion of Onofrio Panvinio seems preferable.] and finally was appointed Chancellor of the Holy Roman Church by Lucius II. Pullen was indeed most thoroughly trained in every branch of learning, especially that concerned with interpreting the opinions of the Fathers and popes. Nor did his theoretical speculations hinder his skill in practical affairs. Hence some rightly suspect that the responses of Innocent II and Eugenius III on sacred matters were drafted by him.

> “7. Pullen departed life full of days and honors, with which he had been heaped: at home by King Henry, and at Rome by the supreme pontiffs Innocent II, Celestine II, Lucius II, and Eugenius III.
