> “8. He was the first of all men from England to be a cardinal of the Roman Church, unless perhaps one should prefer a certain Ulric before him. But the matter is certain concerning Pullen, doubtful concerning Ulric.

> “9. At Oxford, Pullus’s memory is celebrated even down to our own times not merely by annual and solemn student panegyrics, but also by testimonies far weightier. Indeed, those who trace and exalt the origins of the Oxford Studium, once they have become somewhat more defined, beyond or above Robert Pullen scarcely escape mere fables.

> “10. The following writings are enumerated as his by Bale and Pits under Pullen in the twelfth century, and by the *Nomenclator of Cardinals* under Celestine II, page 15, etc.,” as above.

Thus he.

[Col. 0639]

# THE EIGHT BOOKS OF SENTENCES OF ROBERT PULLUS, CARDINAL AND CHANCELLOR OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

(*Works of Robert Pullus and Peter of Poitiers, formerly Chancellor of the University of Paris*, edited by Hugues Mathoud, Benedictine monk.—Paris, 1655, folio.)

## 1. HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE

That the reader may readily find in this volume what he seeks, these distinctions are prefixed, in which matters treated more fully in what follows are first sampled in summary. This book is divided into eight parts, and these prefatory notices are equal in number to its parts. Each part is divided into chapters. Numbers are frequently inserted in these distinctions, and later appear prefixed to the individual chapters, so that it may thus be clearly ascertained which passage here belongs to the discussions that follow.

# THE PREFATORY NOTICES OF THE FIRST PART BEGIN

[Col. 0639C] **CHAPTER I.** In the first part it is shown that God exists and has no beginning of subsistence; that he is not susceptible of contraries, and exists through himself, not through another.

**CHAPTER II.** There is also inserted here an argument against the blindness of idolatry: what and how great absurdities would follow if there were several gods; and thus it is proved that there is only one God.

[Col. 0640C] **CHAPTER III.** It is then added that there are three persons. This is carefully and subtly investigated: properties belong to substance, but do not constitute a person; God is joined to no form; and why we confess only three persons in unity. There is also discussion of the incomprehensibility of the Godhead; the true divinity and humanity of Christ; the procession of the Holy Spirit from both; knowledge, revelation, and the knowledge of faith; the fact that persons are not affected by properties; what properties are; and the manner in which the Father begot the Son as another, not another thing.

**CHAPTER IV.** It is likewise demonstrated that God is not subject to accidents, qualities, relations, and the like; and that wisdom, goodness, and the like are in God nothing other than God.

**CHAPTER V.** It is then shown what we signify when we declare God to be just, omnipotent, and the like; that we understand and speak of the divine essence in diverse ways; those things which distinguish the Trinity in the persons; what the properties are which distinguish the persons; what forms are; the unity of the Trinity; how many properties are constituted; what these three terms, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, denote; what a person is; the operation of the Trinity in the three persons; and how other things differ from one another.

[Col. 0641B] **CHAPTER VI.** This is followed by the statement that there are two processions, and what the procession of the Son and that of the Holy Spirit are; and that something attributed to the persons either belongs to all of them commonly without distinction, or belongs differently: for example, *person* to three; *procession* and *principle* to two. It also discusses how the Trinity is called the principle both of creatures and in relation to itself; how *principle* and *proceeding* are related to one another; and how the Father has certain things proper to himself as well as things held in common.

**CHAPTER VII.** It is next said that the Father sends the Son and the Holy Spirit, while the Son sends only the Holy Spirit; and hence that the Son is both sender and sent; and that the same relation obtains in mission as in principle and procession. It discusses what it is for the Son and Holy Spirit to have been sent; what it is for the Father, for both, and for the Son to have sent the other; and likewise what it means that the Father sent, and what it means that the Holy Spirit is said to have sent.

[Col. 0641C] **CHAPTER VIII.** It is added that the Father is another than the Son, but not another thing, and similar matters. For whatever the Father is in the unity of the Godhead, rather than by a property of personhood, that the Son also is. The masculine gender indicates distinction of person, but the neuter unity of substance. And although three made the world, it must not be said that there are three makers, and similarly in other cases.

**CHAPTER IX.** Finally, it is added that God is not divided or confined in any place, but is wholly everywhere, not only potentially but essentially.

**CHAPTER X.** Likewise, it is carefully proved that the soul is wholly everywhere in its own world, namely the body, and that it lacks parts and always accompanies the body so long as the body lives.

### Chapter XI

To the foregoing is added that God hates none of the things that He has made, and in what manner He loves all; that His love does not change; and that the statements made above, when explained, do not conflict with this: “Thou hatest all workers of iniquity.” It also treats of God’s hating the wicked, and of their hating Him; of how He loves the wicked who are to become good; and why He rescues some from wickedness, but not others. What would become of the evil person whom He loves if he were to die evil? Does He hate a good person who is going to become evil? It is also maintained that He hates one who is to be condemned even before he exists, while He foreknows, wills beforehand, and loves one who is to perish while that person is good—not conversely, that He always hates the unrighteous.

### Chapter XII

There follows a discussion of the wrath and fury of God, and of what they are; likewise, how He judges and has mercy, hates and loves. It treats of His eternal will: whether He wills evil things to be done, whether they please Him, and who performs them; whether He wills a sinner whom He does not will to be converted not to be converted; what He wills and what He does not will; whether He willed Christ to be killed, and whether He willed anyone to kill Him; and that He wills man to be able to do evil.

### Chapter XIII

It is then argued that one who is to be condemned is worthy of salvation while living well; conversely, that one who is to be saved, if he were to die in sins, would be consigned to death. Does God love an evil person when He inflicts evil upon him? It is also considered how, in accordance with the words, “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth,” He deals with both those to be saved and those to be condemned. It is further asked how future goods are rendered according to works.

### Chapter XIV

To these matters is joined the teaching that we are placed here between heaven and hell, where we merit either to ascend to heaven or to descend to hell. It considers what merits and rewards are; that the activity belongs to this life and reflection to the other; why an infant is assigned to condemnation; why God saves these but condemns those; and that at one time He follows justice alone, at another mercy alone. His will and His action are the same. Those whom God hates ought not to be loved by man; yet, while His will is hidden, charity must be followed. It also explains that unbelievers were condemned, and that those who hear the words, “God wills every human being to be saved,” do not thereby contradict this teaching.

### Chapter XV

It is then added that God is almighty, and in what manner He knows and foreknows all things; His wisdom knows neither increase nor beginning. Whatever He foreknows happens necessarily. It asks whether providence, power, and will are equal; whether He could have foreseen things otherwise; whether events therefore happen necessarily; what then becomes of His justice or grace; and whether He can do more than He wills.

### Chapter XVI

Finally, it is stated that God could have foreseen otherwise, just as He is plainly able to do otherwise. His providence, just as it lacks a beginning, will lack an end; and, once what has been foreknown has occurred, His foreknowledge and disposition cease to be called by those names, though they do not cease to exist. It examines what knowledge and disposition are; how His unchanging knowledge comprehends changing things; and how past and future things are present to Him. It also considers that He sees evils only, whereas He both sees and knows goods; that He acts together with the one who acts, yet does not compel; whether He can foresee contraries simultaneously; and that He cannot do, in any present circumstance, what does not pertain to it. The power of God is to be discussed cautiously. He lacks beginning and end. It is further asked how the will is the cause of providence.

## The Preliminary Notices of the Second Part Begin

[Col. 0643]

### Chapter I

In the second part it is shown that God created the world when He willed, and that He could, had He willed, have made it earlier and could have made more worlds. Why did He make only one, and for whose sake did He make it? How, according to Moses, did He make it in six days; and how, according to another Scripture, “He who lives for ever created all things at once”? This is carefully investigated in order to demonstrate it plainly. It also explains how God rested on the seventh day from every work—not from work itself, but from the newness of things.

### Chapter II

It is next said whose the earth and heaven are, and will be; and when God created the angel. Moses could not state simultaneously what God performed simultaneously. Why is heaven called the firmament? It is also asked whether heaven revolves; and, if it does, whether the upper heaven is fixed—the place where the saints rest, according to the words, “Ascending above all the heavens.” Is heaven bodily or spiritual? If bodily, how can it be a fitting dwelling-place for spirits? If spiritual, how can it suit bodily nature? And if heaven is bodily, hell is so by the same reasoning; and as heaven is believed to be above, so hell must be believed to be below.

### Chapter III

It is then made clear what sort of beings angels were created to be; how long they are to minister to God on behalf of human beings; when their power will cease; and why it was bestowed.

### Chapter IV

To the foregoing is added how great a freedom was granted to angels; to whom freedom of choice is necessary, and who lack it. It considers how the first man flourished in freedom of choice and lost his flourishing; that this freedom was depressed, not extinguished; how it operates when divine grace assists; and when a human being, created good, will be perfected. Why did the erring angel not deserve to be recalled as man did? The power to err is indeed good; and why did the good angel deserve to be confirmed?

### Chapter V

After the foregoing, it asks what confirmation and conversion are. It also states what place is appointed for believers and what place for those who see God, and what chiefly hinders the mind. Did created spirits know God immediately? If they foresaw their fall, how did they lose eternal life? It also treats of the torments of human beings after judgment, and how in the meantime they are in this air. They received the faith by which they might merit. How did the good angels, by persevering, change their faith? By the fall of the evil angels they advanced; what sort of beings were they created by God, and whence did they contract their stain? They were perfected at once, whereas man is still to be perfected.

### Chapter VI

To the foregoing is appended Augustine’s authority: that neither an angel after conversion or perfection, nor a human being after resurrection, can sin. Jerome seems to oppose this, saying: “God alone is one in whom sins do not occur.” They are shown not to disagree. Before their fall angels were naturally removed from sin; afterward they are far more removed, yet, though it does not occur, they can sin. It asks whether, as the good can sin and thus be condemned, the evil can likewise repent and be saved. If, according to the Apostle, every creature of God is good, how is the devil evil? If he is good, many unacceptable consequences follow.

### Chapter VII

It is further added from what God formed the first-created man, and why one made one. When is the spirit infused? How is the liquid seed differentiated through the diversity of the members? How is the seed-bed, so that it may exist by itself, separated from both parents? How does the force of nature give form and proportion to the maternal conception before life? The body is subject to death, but the soul is not; yet the soul suffers in the dying person. Necessary and varied arguments establish that the soul is then joined to the body when a human being may fittingly be called sentient.

### Chapter VIII

It is also asked whence the soul comes, and, false views having been refuted, its true origin is shown.

### Chapter IX

It is discussed where the soul is created; after false views are removed, it is finally shown to be created in the body. What is it like, and whence comes its corruption? How was it created good, when it is troubled from the beginning by the body? The souls of the first human beings were not corrupted by their bodies; rather, their bodies were corrupted by them.

### Chapter X

There follows a discussion of what man is. First the opinion of certain persons is set forth and shown to be wholly untenable; then what man is is plainly demonstrated.

### Chapter XI

It is added what belongs to the soul, and the effects of those things upon it; that it is rewarded according to good or evil merit; and that the senses belong to the soul, while their instruments belong to the body, whence each receives different things from them. All the senses embrace the soul. Why are they called bodily? If they are not senses of the living being, how is there sensation? And if they are not the soul’s except in the body, how can the soul perceive outside the body? What is attributed to which element when a living creature is said to be sentient?

### Chapter XII

It is then shown that all the senses serve reason, and that reason itself directs everything unless hindered by its subjects. Wherever reason exists, there is discernment only, because we merit only insofar as we discern. It asks what things will be without recompense; whether the outer person, the inner person, or the whole person discerns; and teaches that all vices belong to the soul, though some are called carnal. The soul is deservedly tormented both in itself and in the body; and, although this should not belong to the body itself, the soul will intensify for itself joy or sorrow from the body. It also treats of what our future condition will be.

### Chapter XIII

To this is joined the question of when reason comes to the soul together with its companions; how the soul of a child is in the image of God; and, if it has reason, why it does not use it. The spirits of brute animals are stated to be more illustrious and excellent.

### Chapter XIV

It is added when the spirits of brute animals perish. If they did not perish, the unacceptable consequences that would follow are shown.

### Chapter XV

It is further added what imagination is, in what beings it flourishes, and in what manner; and that spirits preside over brute animals.

### Chapter XVI

It is shown what man is by nature; what the first man was like when created; what would have belonged to himself and his descendants had he persevered; and what sort of persons it is credible would be born from transgressors. The good advance through the condemnation of the wicked. How many are to be recalled from error? Whence is the number of fallen angels to be made up? Would man have been created if no angel had fallen? If created, would he have been condemned or saved? The state of the future life is perfect. How long will the number of saints increase, and how many saints are to be substituted? The number of those who fell is less than that of those who persevered, although evil human beings are more numerous than good ones. It also considers the size of the number of the blessed.

### Chapter XVII

It is also stated that, had angels not offended, they would have filled the places of those who fell, and how they would have been equal to those substituted for them. Human beings have erred, but God rescued some. It explains how He set those rescued above the number mentioned previously; how the human race grew through Adam’s fault, just as the good angels grew through the fall of evil angels; and that therefore not their fault, but God’s mercy, will be praised. In an invective against the devil it is said that he harmed only himself, and that the loss of the heavenly Jerusalem pertains to the praise of its Creator.

### Chapter XVIII

It also states how man would have lived had he not sinned; how woman would have conceived and borne children; and how works would have been performed.

### Chapter XIX

Paradise is described: how effective it is; why man was expelled from it and to what place; and that he was created outside it. Why is access difficult? Why is there a revolving flame, when no one can come there or is even said to dare attempt it?

### Chapter XX

To the matters already mentioned is added what man was like in paradise in relation to himself and to God; what he was like after transgression; and how he was to die. By obedience, while animal (*animalis*), he was to become spiritual (*spiritalis*). It also considers that one fortified by God sinned grievously, whereas those who resist, when weakened by God, do not deserve much [blame].

### Chapter XXI

It is asked whether, apart from the forbidden fruit, man could have abused freedom in another way. It is stated that the woman was especially deceived, but why the Lord nevertheless reproached the man; why he sinned more grievously; and the difference between inward and outward sin. Why was eating alone forbidden? Why was so great a punishment inflicted for such an act? Did death follow because of eating alone, or also because of the preceding evils?

### Chapter XXII

It is then shown that the words of the threat, although spoken only to the man, also concern the woman and the whole family. Why does the tree of transgression, like the tree of life, occupy the middle of paradise? It is carefully investigated how long this commanded abstinence as obedience was to last.

### Chapter XXIII

It is added that, if the Creator had given the first-created man an inability to turn toward forbidden things, abstinence would have been commanded in vain. It treats of a reward then not owed; and that this would not have benefited his children, although some hold otherwise, whose opinions are appended.

### Chapter XXIV

It is then asked whether God justly commands that whose evil outcome He knows beforehand. It is carefully shown that He commands even such a thing justly.

### Chapter XXV

It is also considered why the first human beings did not need garments; when they were ashamed of nakedness, especially of the genitals; why this was so; why we frequently have misshapen members; and that the first parents stained the brightness of their creation by sin.

### Chapter XXVI

It is further stated in what form the Lord is understood to have walked in paradise after midday; and how greatly they diminished and fell after sin.

### Chapter XXVII

It is also shown that, by sinning, the man yielded to the woman; that, unless each had first been inwardly corrupted, both would have resisted the outward temptation; what would have occurred if the woman alone had sinned; how each was punished; when this punishment, spread to posterity, will be extinguished; and how much benefit comes from it.

### Chapter XXVIII

There is also found there the reason why such children as the first parents themselves were had to be born from them; that propagation, corrupted from its origin, becomes more corrupt through generation; and whether each person is more corrupt the farther removed from the first parent. If man generated without lust, what would conception be like? Why does nature bring one stain of its own, while lust brings another? Are the accidental stains of parents transmitted to children? What kind of human being is born from corrupted seed? Whence does the original stain pass on? If neither the stain of lust nor the original stain is attributable to nature, what follows? And whence did the entire evil of succession take its beginning?

### Chapter XXIX

To the foregoing is joined the proposition that the soul, like the flesh, is corrupted; whether this is just, and how; and finally it is said that the soul participates only in original sin.

### Chapter XXX

It is asked whence evil has its origin for angel and human being; what sort of beings God created them to be; why He made them such; what is due to each if he sins; and concerning their ability and will. It treats of the punishment due to evil; whence evil first drew its origin, and whence afterward; of the unrighteous person when he inclines to forbidden things; of whose power it is for the impious person to turn back; and that the judge does not leave the guilty person unpunished—and why.

### Chapter XXXI

It is also asked whether there is one original sin or many, from which all are corrupted and, as it were, depraved from the root. Authorities prove that there is one by which all became defiled in Adam, in paradise. What was actual in the first parents is called original in their children. It asks whether the other transgressions of the first parents, like original sin—which was actual—are not imputed to descendants. It also treats of the tasting of the forbidden apple and how this is imputed to descendants; of the death born from it; of the remaining sins of the parents; how punishment reaches innocent infants; the tinder of sin; concupiscence, which did not precede the forbidden eating; how we are bound by another’s sin; how the sins of parents are punished in children; how “the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father”; how everyone is liable to death, though not also to the eating; and the original sin of each individual.

## The Preliminary Notices of the Third Part Begin

[Col. 0647]

### Chapter I

In the third part it is shown that the human race turned aside toward the lower regions from the path due to heaven. It considers who brought them back, and how; why this occurred so late; what messengers were sent beforehand and why; why the law was given, what it brought, and what it did not bring; how it benefited some; and those who resisted it. It also considers those before the law, under the law, and in the time of grace; how far they were enlightened by faith in the One to come; and that the nearer one comes to the end of time, the more faith is required.

### Chapter II

It also states what provision was made before the law and under the law for infants and older persons. Though they had not incurred guilt by a personal act, they were originally stained and needed a remedy. Why, although the Creator could save nature without remedies, did He not will to do so? Remedies were rightly established for each period, even for infants.

### Chapter III

It is added on what day circumcision was performed; whether someone dying uncircumcised was damned; and that women were not circumcised. If someone died before the day of circumcision, was that person held by the ancient transgression? How is the authority, “Every soul that shall not have been circumcised shall perish from among the people,” to be understood? It is asked what we must hold among ourselves, among the Gentiles before the law, and among the Jews under the law, concerning those who were permitted to receive life in the womb but were not born.

### Chapter IV

There it is found that God, regarding the purity of the father, remits the wrath due to children; that children’s disgrace does not increase through the foulness of their parents; what parental uprightness contributes to children once born, and what it does not contribute. Just as the equality of baptism now makes infants equal to one another, and just as circumcision without distinction under the law cleansed equally, so it must be believed that Gentile children are equal through reconciliation—unless, rather, their fathers’ varying merits distinguished them among themselves.

### Chapter V

To the foregoing is joined the question why children, both infants and adults, are burned by their parents’ crimes; and why, conversely, parental religion sometimes brings good things to children. Conversely, by reprobation evils are allotted to the offspring of good fathers, followed in the source by “and the good things of the wicked in de…” and a [lacuna]. It seems to conflict with this: “The soul that sins, it shall die,” and, “He will render to each according to his works”; and the difficulty is resolved.

### Chapter VI

After this it is shown why the law and circumcision were established only for the Hebrews; that the new law followed the old; why the new law, rather than the old, is commanded to all; that before the law and under the law salvation existed among Gentiles as among Jews; and that there is one faith, working through love, from which salvation comes in every age.

### Chapter VII

It is added why weak observances were permitted to the weak, yet in such a way that they attained certain corrections while many vices remained. Why did He command easy goods and overlook evils?

### Chapter VIII

It is then asked whether that people ought to have been condemned by merit or saved through mercy. Finally, it is shown that they must be counted among the lost, except for the very few who excelled in Christian perfection, such as the patriarchs; and why divine judgment then overlooked the gravest crimes.

### Chapter IX

It is shown that, as lesser grace formerly instructed the lesser, so the greater grace at Christ’s coming instructed the greater. Why did He send messengers beforehand? The Lord was merciful and just toward the ancients. Why was the very burdensome law of works given to them? Christ’s yoke is sweet and His burden light. In what respect is the old law intolerable, and in what respect tolerable? Why did He order it thus? Who alone were saved in that age?

### Chapter X

To the foregoing is added that many worshippers of God among that people deservedly perished because of earthly things. There were among them some who were good but not perfect, some perfect, and some less perfect, who served God and not Mammon. Just as far more things are imputed to us than to the ancients, so our charity differs from theirs. Their perfect people possessed our charity. Why is the old law called one of servitude, whereas ours is called one of liberty, when in both there are servants?

### Chapter XI

There it is shown what fear proceeds from God and what does not; why the old law is one of servitude while ours is one of grace; that most then were good and some perfect; and how they could have been perfect while enduring that old order.

### Chapter XII

It is also stated that worshippers under the law descended to hell, and why; and that there they had something better than they had while living here.

### Chapter XIII

It is further granted that Christ finally came. Why then and not earlier, and why, since He could have saved His own otherwise? Why did He accept the law in part? It is also said that He afterward honorably buried it with delay, and that the figures of that age are now fulfilled spiritually.

### Chapter XIV

To this is added that the old and new laws each contain three things: sacraments, promises, and commandments, as is shown in considering each. The sacraments must cease—and why. Foods are not to be distinguished, nor is circumcision to be retained. Greater sacraments succeeded those legal observances that were buried; the things signified succeeded the signs. It considers what the law promised, what the prophets promised, and what is now promised to the good; how Christ ended the law; and which commandments are retained. It is also asked: if the law and the prophets were until John, how were they until the Lord’s passion? The difficulty is resolved.

### Chapter XV

It is further said when the sacrifice of the new Lamb began; how the Virgin conceived Him and why it is spoken of thus; that, although He has a Father in His divinity, He nevertheless ought not to have one in His humanity; how He was conceived of the Holy Spirit; why His conception and incarnation are attributed especially to the Holy Spirit; and that the Son alone was incarnate. It is also asked why the Incarnation, though it is a work of the Trinity, is attributed to the Son alone.

### Chapter XVI

It is next asked and shown when the two natures were united; that the Virgin conceived God; what it is to conceive man and what it is to conceive God; and when she conceived each. What does it mean that He was conceived from His mother by the Spirit? What is it that descends? How did He descend from where He remained to where He had been? What is His descent? He was not made flesh by a changeableness of nature, but by union. Scripture customarily attributes to one what belongs to the other, as is evident from examples. Though there are two essences, He is one; and though two natures, there is one person.

### Chapter XVII

From the foregoing it follows why the man is God and God is called man, and how this is to be understood. Christ had a soul; and it considers from what He subsists without being composite. He is called man and God in different respects. What is meant when one says, “Christ is man,” “Christ is God,” or “Christ is God and man”? How is “man is God” to be understood? Man is not God by nature; yet “man is God” and “God is man”: He who is equal to the Father according to divinity is less than the Father according to humanity. It explains how this is said; that divinity is not humanity, nor conversely; yet God and man, man and God, are one Christ. How is “God became man” to be understood? God-man is not God essentially, yet He is God personally. What is meant by “God is man,” “man is God,” and “man is united to God”?

### Chapter XVIII

After these matters it is stated that Christ was God before the ages and became man in time; that He consists of two substances, remaining what He was and assuming what He had not been. One began; the other did not. Hence the Son of God and the person could both die and not die. Thus many contrary things are said of Him, yet they agree in different respects; this is treated at length and carefully, lest error arise on either side. In the union of two natures, “person” is understood differently from its use in the Holy Trinity. Is it more proper to say that the person in the Trinity is a person of three substances, or rather that what always was became united to humanity? In the death of Jesus it is evident that the one person consisted of three substances—divinity, soul, and flesh. Augustine, however, in view of the divine and human nature, commonly calls the person one of two substances. It asks what the name Christ signifies. Although Christ is a creating substance and two created substances—namely soul and flesh—and died for us, the Deity did not die, but the humanity; yet not the whole humanity, because not the soul, though it suffered with it. Therefore the meaning of the foregoing words is asked, and stated.

### Chapter XIX

It is added why God is said to have suffered and been buried as man. Although there is no danger in it, the use of unusual expressions is faulty. While Christ was in the tomb and in hell, the Deity subsisted as one person with both soul and body, although body and soul were not during that interval one person. It is also shown that, although the same person remains, the same designation of person does not remain.

### Chapter XX

Following the foregoing is an inquiry into when one should speak cautiously and conjecturally concerning the articles of faith; when the Incarnation was accomplished; and what it means for Him to be united. It is asked how a fourth person is introduced into the Trinity, subsisting from Deity, flesh, and soul: is the Trinity to be counted as four, or is He rather the same person as the third person in the Trinity—previously existing from one substance only, but afterward from three? A careful inquiry proves that the latter is so.

### Chapter XXI

It is joined to this that Christ assumed every defect except sin. It carefully investigates whether He also had ignorance, and finally proves that He did not. It treats of His purity and clarity, which He had from creation, and how excellent they were. It asks whether, even if no killer had been present, He would have died by dying according to the law of mortals.

### Chapter XXII

It is also asked whence Christ received the privilege of coming forth from the closed womb—a condition belonging neither to our state nor to that which was in paradise. Hence it seems that He borrowed this from the state of immortality, in which He entered through closed doors. Yet He was still mortal: as there are two earthly states, so He had a third, heavenly state.

### Chapter XXIII

It is added that some distinguished men attribute ignorance to the boy Jesus; others attribute complete wisdom to Him, and these are to be preferred. Authorities that appear contrary are explained as not contrary. After His resurrection, His knowledge or holiness did not increase, but blessedness was added.

### Chapter XXIV

It is then asked whether Jesus, by devoting Himself to works of charity, did not increase His merit and make Himself better before God. It also states how He was as a child full of grace, and yet advanced in wisdom, age, and grace. From the beginning He foreknew and willed beforehand all things that were to happen concerning Him.

### Chapter XXV

Likewise it is shown that a person is judged according to a good or evil disposition. Saints in this life continually grow through works of charity; but the child Jesus did not do so, for at the first He shone so greatly in charity that nothing was added to it. Thus it is asked how, being obedient to the Father, He merited exaltation according to the Apostle. This is carefully investigated.

### Chapter XXVI

Since it is established that Christ did not become better through the continuance of good works, just as neither human beings nor angels who have attained perfection do, there follows an inquiry concerning demons: one may perhaps think that the merits of the good angels increased until, when the number of their brethren was complete, their merits too were completed together. The fall of the human race, undoubtedly evil, the good God turned to good. Both the good and the evil angel are perfected: the one in good, the other in evil.

### Chapter XXVII

It is then asked how the child Jesus was full of wisdom and grace, when these belong to a grown man; whether a man of adult age lay hidden beneath the appearance of a child; and it is stated that He assumed the smallness proper to childhood, excepting ignorance and sin—although He could easily have enclosed the stature of a thirty-year-old man within the narrowness of the womb. The reason follows. Though He grew as a child in our customary manner, He was conceived and born in a manner unfamiliar to us.

### Chapter XXVIII

There is also found there the teaching that Christ instructed people to live well by word and example. Why did He perform miracles? Is the knowledge in Christ as man to be equated with that which is in the Deity? Did man perform miracles, or God in man? This is carefully investigated in order that it may be plainly shown.

### Chapter XXIX

It is also asked whether man can, by God’s gift, do everything that God can do. This is carefully examined and finally proved to be so.

### Chapter XXX

It is also asked whether that man possesses power, wisdom, and goodness as great as God’s; and, if so, He is nevertheless less than God, because these are received by His gift.

## The Preliminary Notices of the Fourth Part Begin

[Col. 0651]

### Chapter I

In the fourth part it is shown that, just as that man is superior to all other created beings, so He is so much inferior to God that, in comparison with Him, He should not even be called good.

### Chapter II

It is also said that, just as God surpasses man in goodness, so He surpasses him in power. This is shown by several examples.

### Chapter III

An objection that might be made is introduced and resolved: if the power of God and man is not the same, because God can do what man cannot, how is the power of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit the same, when the Father begets, which the others do not; the Son is begotten, which the others are not; and the Holy Spirit proceeds, which the other persons do not? Christ, who has greater power than man, does not have the same power but a different one.

### Chapter IV

It is shown that none of the three persons can do more than another. What is it for the Father to beget, the Son to be begotten, and the Holy Spirit to proceed? What is it to be Father? How great is it to be God having a Son? How great likewise is it to be God having a Father equal to Himself? What do we find if we seek to distinguish the persons, and what if we consider the substance of the persons? Since a property belonging to God belongs also to the persons, and conversely, why are some things attributed to the Deity and others to the Trinity? Begetting, being begotten, and proceeding from both are properties of the persons, not actions. In their works their power is the same; according to their properties, one can do something another cannot. Yet they do not have divided powers.

### Chapter V

All power was given to the assumed man. How is this said, when a greater power is reserved for the giver? As power is inferior to God, so too is knowledge.

### Chapter VI

It is also interwoven that Christ, though still destined to die, willed what He ought to will, and could do what He willed. According to His divinity, His knowledge was greater than His power, and His power greater than His action. Why did God prefer that certain things which would shine forth if done should remain undone? What does He do with our evils, and why does He permit or not permit them to exist? It is asked how He willed whatever He ought, when, knowingly against the divine will, He asked not to be crucified, saying in Mark: “Father, all things are possible to Thee; remove this cup from me.” This is carefully investigated and plainly explained; likewise: “Not as I will, but as Thou wilt.”

### Chapter VII

It is also asked whether Christ feared death and being cast into hell; and, if not, why He prayed not to be lost, saying, “Do not deliver me together with …” [the quotation is incomplete]. How was He filled with the fear of which it is said, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom”? How did He reasonably pray not to be condemned, when He was certain of salvation?

### Chapter VIII

It is added that the fear of hell, coming beforehand, prepares a place for charity; how it is said to be cast out when charity reigns; that neither exists without the other; and that there is another holy fear, enduring for ever and ever, which is born here and perfected in the future.

### Chapter IX

It is then stated what effects faith, hope, and charity ought to have in us; and that, when all else is abolished, charity never fails.

### Chapter X

It is also asked whether Christ had these three. If He loved all through charity, how did He love the wicked, whom, if He could, He did not free from perdition?

### Chapter XI

It is carefully investigated whether Christ also had faith; and it is finally proved that He enjoyed vision in the place of faith.

### Chapter XII

Indeed, Christ is shown to have seen God as He is even in this life. Therefore the soul of Christ, not weighed down by the burden of flesh and sin, was united to God amid bodily troubles and adorned with the first robe; the second robe, namely that of the body, was deferred for a time for the sake of redemption.

### Chapter XIII

It is also shown why Christ endured adversities and why He chose to be condemned by a most shameful death. If Judaea had dreaded to crucify its Lord, would He have become man in vain? It is also stated why He willed to be killed by the Jews.

### Chapter XIV

It is asked whether He offered Himself as a sacrifice to the devil or to God. It is shown that He offered Himself to the Father, and what the price of this sacrifice was. Why did He endure shameful and harsh things? How did He conduct Himself in the Passion?

### Chapter XV

It is then found that through Christ’s Passion and death the sins of saints before it and after it were forgiven; how this was so; that the Passion without faith, or faith without the Passion, profits nothing; and that ancient and modern saints were saved by faith—and how.

### Chapter XVI

To this is appended that the perfect among the ancients were not only holy but equal to the just persons of our age, and that most of them were greater than most of us. Why did they descend to hell, and what was their condition there?

### Chapter XVII

It is stated that hell is both worse than earth and lower than it. Yet it is said that it was better there for the ancient saints than here, since their only anguish was that they lacked the vision of God. Why they lacked it is also considered; and why, meanwhile, He neither rewarded their good deeds, nor forgave or punished their evil deeds. It is also stated that they were never worthy of heaven before Christ’s coming, whereas ours are always worthy.

### Chapter XVIII

It is said that the merit of the ancients was fulfilled by Christ’s coming. It is also shown [Col. 0654A] that they were not merely righteous, but that some among them were exceedingly righteous.

### Chapter XIX

It follows that Christ’s soul, separated from the body but with the divinity nevertheless united to each, descended into hell in order to free the saints from there. There the lost occupy the lowest regions of hell, while the righteous occupy the upper regions.

### Chapter XX

It is further added that there are many dwelling-places in hell, and that, according to Isaiah, hell is beneath, in the lower parts of the earth. Therefore the Lord did not draw out all souls, but only a portion of them. Some seem to have belonged to these who departed this life repentant, but still needed purification for some time; concerning them it is asked where they then were.

### Chapter XXI

It is then said that the name “hell,” [Col. 0654B] although it is the name of the whole, sometimes signifies the lower region, and more often the upper region, namely Abraham’s bosom. It is also asked where those needing purification were in ancient times.

### Chapter XXII

It is also shown that those who discipline themselves less here are afterwards assigned to purgatorial places. Where these are, and how long they remain there, is asked.

### Chapter XXIII

There too it is found, and demonstrated by the clearest arguments, that, once their penance has been completed, the purified are granted heaven and do not await the resurrection. It is also stated that, according to Abraham’s words, a great chasm lay between the good and the wicked. Hence it appears that those needing purification dwelt outside Abraham’s bosom from Adam until Christ, [Col. 0654C].

### Chapter XXIV

It is also heard that, just as repose is incompatible with the lower regions of hell, so affliction is incompatible with the upper. It is said that a third place for those needing purification is not easily found there. It is therefore asked whether, just as on earth good and evil persons are mingled in place but distinguished by merits, they also dwelt thus in hell.

### Chapter XXV

It is also asked what Christ did, when descending into the underworld and bringing out His own, with those not yet purified. It is said that they too were reconciled through Christ’s death, and when reconciliation began.

### Chapter XXVI

To the foregoing is joined the statement that Christ took with Him those found in hell who needed purification. The evidence for this is shown, as is also how far He went. Having brought out His own, it is considered for what purposes He left the upper region necessary.

## Prefatory Notices of the Fifth Part

[Col. 0653]

### Chapter I

[Col. 0653D] In the fifth part it is said that Christ’s soul, returning from the underworld with the whole multitude of saints, entered His body on the third day and endowed it with resurrection. Thus He became a human being incapable of suffering and immortal. The greatness of His brightness is described, as is why, concealing His own appearance, He showed His disciples His former form. It is asked how He assumed the form of immortality while mortal, and the form of mortality while immortal.

### Chapter II

What should be thought concerning those whom Christ brought out from the underworld with Him is also considered, and it is said what they seem rather to have been.

### Chapter III

It is said that for forty days Christ, frequently appearing to the disciples, remained beneath heaven with the spoils of hell; and what He then did with them is also stated. It is believed that He ascended only after the forty days had been completed and will descend only on the day of judgment. It is said how He again appears to saints—and to holy persons.

### Chapter IV

It is further related that Christ, sitting at the right hand of God, [Col. 0655A] sent the Holy Spirit to the disciples. What it means to send Him is considered. It is said that the whole Trinity, as some maintain—or, more plausibly, the Father and the Son—sent the Holy Spirit; for only the third Person was sent. The nature of that visible appearance of the Holy Spirit is considered, as are what His coming and indwelling mean. It is also asked whether, when the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove above the Lord and in fire above the disciples, both things which were seen truly existed.

### Chapter V

It is then stated that what appeared above the Lord was not a dove but the appearance of a dove; likewise, that those fiery tongues were not real tongues of fire, but aerial forms which, like the dove and the human figure seen in an apparition, returned into the air when their office had been fulfilled. [Col. 0655B] It is also asked how one who appears can be a true human being; and why the Spirit appeared in a dove and in fiery tongues is explained.

### Chapter VI

Next, it is said that those whom life commended and doctrine enlightened rightly preached to others. It is also said that they preached first to the Jews—why this was so, and why they finally turned to the Gentiles. Finally, through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch, all Israel will be saved. The purpose of preaching and the origin of religion are considered.

### Chapter VII

God can bestow faith without speech; it is stated that He rarely, though sometimes, does this, as is explained shortly afterwards. It is also said that things necessary for all are apportioned individually, and why; and that faith is given neither for one’s own merits nor those of one’s parents, for it is God’s gift, lest anyone boast of it. [Col. 0655C] Faith, not born from works, gives birth to works, which before faith are nothing. No one is chosen or saved because of lineage, personal merit, or parental merit, but by grace alone.

### Chapter VIII

It is therefore asked why parents pray for their children—or indeed why the whole Church prays for those to be converted. This is explained through more careful examination.

### Chapter IX

It is said that children are miserably tormented to their parents’ sorrow, or gloriously exalted to their delight, and why. Although faith and salvation arise from grace, faith and correction of life are properly ascribed to grace, while salvation is truly ascribed to merits.

### Chapter X

Since righteousness proceeds from faith and blessedness from righteousness, it is asked how one who has not been reborn [Col. 0655D] of water and the Holy Spirit will not enter the kingdom of heaven. It is said that, just as Abraham was first justified by faith and afterwards received circumcision as a sign, so we receive baptism.

### Chapter XI

It is further stated that faith joined with charity must necessarily mourn over sins committed and guard against sins to be mourned, in proportion to its love, and thereby obtain forgiveness of sins. The great efficacy of faith is considered.

### Chapter XII

It is also maintained that righteousness and salvation accompany not baptism but the Spirit—that is, faith. Salvation comes through martyrdom without baptism. But if martyrs are said to be baptized in blood, it is asked what happens if they die in fire or in another violent death without bloodshed. Since martyrdom takes the place of baptism, it should not be surprising that faith itself, from which martyrdom receives its strength, also takes baptism’s place; for it is necessity, not will, that excludes a person from the washing. How, then, the saying is to be understood—“Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven”—is explained. [Col. 0656A]

### Chapter XIII

But if righteousness is obtained through faith and thus forgiveness of sins, it is asked what need there is, for the remission of sins, to be washed with water.

### Chapter XIV

It is rightly taught that baptism is received for the remission of sins; and what it means to receive the Holy Spirit, as it were, in certain stages, and what He effects, are considered. It is also explained how baptism was instituted.

### Chapter XV

It is said who is baptizer and who baptized; [Col. 0656B] and that the perversity either of the one washing or of the one washed does no harm to the perfection of baptism. Nothing harms the baptized person except what is his own.

### Chapter XVI

The outward sacrament is not diminished even if mockery or error occurs on either side. Yet inward error and one’s own error harm inward purity. If an error occurs outwardly, the sacrament is endangered; nevertheless, no harm is done to the soul healed by sincere faith. It is also asked concerning bathers who jokingly baptize themselves. Why the Holy Spirit descended upon Christ when He was baptized is stated, as are the meaning of outward washing; why fire is applied to washing; why water, rather than other liquids and elements, is assigned to this sacrament; and what the cleansing water and the washed body signify.

### Chapter XVII

[Col. 0656C] It is then considered what in baptism is to be compared to death, what to burial, and what finally to resurrection. It is asked why, before Christ, the day was counted together with the following night, but afterwards the reverse; and why, in the Lord’s burial, three days are followed by three nights. It is stated that water signifies the Holy Spirit.

### Chapter XVIII

Baptism is deferred until a festival, especially the Paschal festival, and the reason is given. It is also said why little children are catechized before baptism, and that the law of catechizing must stand.

### Chapter XIX

Because a child does not know how to believe, he is said to seek the sacrament of believing. The need for godparents at this age is shown, and that godparents must labor to ensure that what they pledged for infants comes to pass in adults. [Col. 0656D]

### Chapter XX

The discussion is directed to godparents, and it is said who and how they are to be understood. Just as catechization is necessary for adults but can be absent in infants, so adults can dispense with the office of godparents, which little children need. Baptism can also stand without any godparent at all.

### Chapter XXI

It is stated why this sacrament is deferred for catechumens until the solemn festival. Older persons, when being regenerated as catechumens, are first asked whether they renounce the devil. For unless they renounce him also in deed, they approach the washing unworthily and without benefit.

### Chapter XXII

Christ’s death, together with burial and resurrection, effects through baptism what it signifies in us. Therefore, just as death is not repeated, neither is baptism. It is stated to whom baptism is entrusted, and that confirmation too is not repeated. Why confirmation originated is shown. [Col. 0657A]

### Chapter XXIII

It is further stated that children ought to be confirmed in their childhood; hence negligence is charged when it is deferred. It is also asked what need there is for hands to be laid upon them promptly, now or in ancient times, when the sacrament already received suffices until the age of discernment. What confirmation confers is considered. It is said that confirmation is more worthy than baptism, and therefore granted only to bishops; and that a sacrament obtained with difficulty is more worthy and less necessary.

### Chapter XXIV

Just as certain sacraments may not be repeated, so some others do not suffice unless received repeatedly, such as confession and the Eucharist. It is also said that in the spiritual temple the strength of the building consists in baptism, as was indicated to us when Christ was baptized; the remaining things provide the sacrament’s adornment. [Col. 0657B]

### Chapter XXV

It is also shown what kind of persons the Holy Trinity, assisting at baptism, makes. Although adults possess virtues through faith, these are nevertheless increased through baptism. From the baptism of the Head it is understood what proceeds from it to the members. It is asked why heaven is opened to the baptized, and what sort of baptism it was—and how it surpassed circumcision—which, before the Passion, did not open heaven even to those baptized who died.

### Chapter XXVI

[Col. 0657C] It is said that after the resurrection the Lord ratified His decree concerning baptism, and earlier concerning catechization, when He said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit”; and why there is added: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age.” It is also considered why baptism was publicly celebrated before the Lord prior to the resurrection, and why, although baptism lacked something of perfection before the Passion, it nevertheless surpassed circumcision.

### Chapter XXVII

It is then asked what it means that heaven is opened to the baptized. The Holy Spirit, descending upon catechumens, removes guilt; descending upon the baptized, He remits punishment. [Col. 0657D]

### Chapter XXVIII

It is also declared that heaven lies open to the baptized, and not before, and why. Where believers who died between the resurrection and the ascension were is considered, as are when and to whom heaven is opened. Heaven is opened or closed not according to foreknowledge, but according to present merits.

### Chapter XXIX

It is said why, as in baptism, heaven is not said to be opened in confession. Although the opening of heaven is understood mystically, bodily eyes nevertheless saw it bodily opened; and what it means to see heaven opened is considered. Likewise, what it means that the Lord, coming up from the water, saw heaven opened, and first the Holy Spirit descending.

### Chapter XXX

It is added that after the covenant of baptism has been broken, confession is the second refuge. As sin must be vomited forth by the mouth, so it must be vomited forth by the heart; how this is done is shown. What becomes of one who confesses but does not repent, or who even delights in sin, is considered. It is asked who truly groans, whose groaning is foul before God, and why one who truly repents must retain no sin thereafter. [Col. 0658A]

### Chapter XXXI

It is also said that when God forgives, He remits sins not partly but wholly. The person whose fear produces repentance is evil, for a good person dreads guilt more than Gehenna. He who gives the fear from which repentance proceeds also gives love, so that the person may be worthy of forgiveness. Without charity and repentance, works are nothing; while iniquity is loved, no reward is gained. It is explained how one should distinguish what is good from what is evil. [Col. 0658B]

### Chapter XXXII

It is also shown that, although good things sometimes seem harmful and evil things beneficial, they are never truly so. Charity alone makes a person good, while the other virtues by their nature add strength to virtue. It is considered what vices one cannot yet be free from, and what remedies them.

### Chapter XXXIII

Next follows a discussion of concupiscence remaining after baptism; of venial sins, their guilt, forgiveness, origin, and unavoidable character; of how they increase; and of their relation to mind and body. In every sin, it is said, something is unavoidable and something venial. The disposition of the mind in the first motion is considered, as is deliberation and the condition of anyone who deliberates in doubt. [Col. 0658C] Consent is not always given: a good disposition endures unwillingly. But one who favors a wicked impulse, though he dissents from the action, is wicked. Had he restrained it immediately, he would have proved victorious, bearing only as much shame as comes from his yielding too gently. The condition of one who abstains from love of vice and from the will to sin is considered, as is the meaning of consent.

### Chapter XXXIV

There is also discussion of good persons who are dead and evil persons who are dead, and of the efficacy of the good tree and the evil tree. Neither appropriates the other’s fruits.

### Chapter XXXV

It is asked what good things avail here and what in the future; what things are not good; when a work is evil; when it is called neither good nor evil; and whether dead good works truly benefit.

### Chapter XXXVI

[Col. 0658D] It is also said which good things belong to reward and which are gifts; what place merits hold; and that merit is God’s gift and sometimes itself a reward.

### Chapter XXXVII

It is added that the righteous person falls, and whence a person is righteous; how one who has charity falls; how charity is then a fountain in which a stranger has no share; and how charity never fails.

### Chapter XXXVIII

It is further said that judgment sometimes proves to be alien one whom providence judges alien. It is considered how the saying “Charity never fails” is to be understood; what earthly charity is like, what charity that has attained maturity is like, and what degree perfect charity appears to merit here. [Col. 0659A]

### Chapter XXXIX

It is shown among whom perfect charity is found: even if it falls, it does not fail. When it flees, it leaves a root by which the sinner may return; and such a person is not alien. Though he staggers, he does not fall down. It is asked whether he would be damned if he died in the meantime, and concerning his merit.

### Chapter XL

There follows a discussion of sins deserving condemnation, some of which exist in the mind alone. Consent is said to incur greater guilt than negligence. It is considered what negligence is rebuked, whose work is more heavily accused, and when death is in the house, at the gate, or in the tomb.

### Chapter XLI

It is said how negligence is death even when it does not produce an act. [Col. 0660A] It is also considered how many dead persons the Lord raised, where, how, and why He did so.

### Chapter XLII

It is afterwards said why the Lord did not raise a fourth dead person; whence every guilt after baptism is judged deserving of condemnation; and concerning one who has no settled habit of sinning and is therefore delayed from evil; and one wholly attached to sin, impeded only by necessity. Perfect will is reckoned as an accomplished deed. It is said that actions are done outwardly both well and badly, and whence each receives its name.

## Prefatory Notices of the Sixth Part

[Col. 0659]

### Chapter I

[Col. 0659B] In the sixth part it is written that there is one consideration before baptism and another after it: before, with respect to the tinder of sin; and how it is imputed afterwards, and what the power of baptism effects.

### Chapter II

It is added that good things or evil things bring themselves to us in two ways, and how. Why one and the other exercise dominion is considered, as is whether a wicked will or its effect is more blameworthy. There is also discussion of ignorance which does not incur guilt, and of the fact that humans and beasts often commit the same acts: in the former they are criminal, in the latter natural. This includes those whom nature has deprived of understanding.

### Chapter III

It is also asked whether, just as nothing is imputed to brute animals, less is imputed to persons of lesser knowledge. There is discussion of our ignorance and its effect, of the more simple multitude, and of what the Lord said: [Col. 0659C] “To everyone to whom much has been given, much shall be required from him.”

### Chapter IV

It is also said that the Jews are not excused because they do not believe in Christ. It is asked whether Gentiles are excused and whether they displease God.

### Chapter V

It is added that ignorance does not provide a defense against guilt. Its cause, and the cause of forgetfulness, are considered; what accompanies them; when they come and when they depart; and which ignorance is more culpable, that proceeding from another’s vice or from one’s own. There is discussion of the ignorance of Gentiles and Christians, whether Gentiles should be accused for deeds done unknowingly, and of lack of knowledge arising from actual guilt, original guilt, and the burden of the flesh.

### Chapter VI

It is then said whence ignorance arises, [Col. 0659D] and whence it is aggravated. There is a distinction between hereditary and personal conditions, and also among personal conditions; and discussion of the weakness of inheritance, the corruption of bodily constitution, and the disintegration of the mind.

### Chapter VII

Next various cases are introduced to show that a human being is to be judged not according to the outcome of the deed but according to the intention of the mind. The first concerns parents killed by the act of their child.

### Chapter VIII

The second concerns a servant killed by a knife when his master called him.

### Chapter IX

The third concerns a son entrusted by his mother to a nurse and dying through an unforeseen mishap.

### Chapter X

The fourth concerns a husband unknowingly having intercourse with a maidservant substituted by his wife.

### Chapter XI

[Col. 0660B] The fifth concerns a son married to his mother, both being ignorant of their relationship.

### Chapter XII

By the example of blood relatives unknowingly joined in marriage, and by many other means, it is shown that, when the mind has not been deceived, the deed is not evil; conversely, a foul mind corrupts the deed. As the deed draws its quality from the heart, so too it draws its magnitude.

### Chapter XIII

It is also asked on what grounds the foregoing events and similar cases ought to be judged harmful; and it is shown that this cannot be established by arguments and examples. Good things should not be abandoned even though evil results from them.

### Chapter XIV

It is then shown how outcomes relate to those from whom they arise, [Col. 0660C] and it is carefully demonstrated, by the necessary uses of eating and sleeping and by the farmer who must labor to seek sustenance, that they can happen without those persons’ guilt. It is considered what misfortune may happen through neglect; when use and reason permit action; and when action should be omitted.

### Chapter XV

It is said when negligence arises; when ignorance is penal; when there is weakness; when weakness itself is culpable; and when it is absolved. It is considered whence this weakness and ignorance arise, that Christ’s grace meets them, whether they remain after faith, whether they harm as punishment or guilt, and whence they come. It is also considered how the first human being was made, sinned, and was punished.

### Chapter XVI

Ignorance and weakness are added to be punishments rather than faults. It is said how one falls into them, how a person burdened by origin is weighed down when he sins from himself, and why dullness and sickness have been given to humankind. It is considered how guilt proceeds from ignorance; which ignorance is not detestable; and ignorance and weakness before and after baptism. [Col. 0660D]

### Chapter XVII

It is then said that every kind of affliction comes from God; what evils are; and that what a human being pursues and receives badly, God grants well.

### Chapter XVIII

It is next shown how God provides a way of acquiring the things that we pursue wrongly, and how we possess them. It is asked whether God produces ignorance and weakness in us, and how; whether the sins we commit through them are imputed; what these are like when from God and when they arise naturally instead; and what we naturally do not know or cannot do. [Col. 0661A]

### Chapter XIX

It is shown in wars what is to be imputed to God and what to human beings, by the example of the Romans who devastated the Jews. Their suffering, not the Romans’ action, pleased Him.

### Chapter XX

The saying is introduced: “There is no evil in a city which God has not done.” It is also said that an unjust action is evil and yet is not from God. That this is not contradictory is carefully and subtly demonstrated.

### Chapter XXI

It follows, when God permits, whose ministry He employs. He works through both good and evil ministers, and how He does so is considered. It is also considered by whose ministry good souls and evil souls are conveyed.

### Chapter XXII

[Col. 0661B] It is stated how demons rage against their own people, how they behave toward the good, and why God permits them sometimes to harm the good.

### Chapter XXIII

It is added that the princes of demons send their followers, and that God sends the same; how this happens is considered. It is asked whether they can inflict death and what kinds of injuries they bring; they are often forbidden to harm as much as they wish. It is found that evil angels torment certain people, and that good angels torment evil people. A human being is not always tormented by a minister.

### Chapter XXIV

The causes for which the scourge of God comes are set forth. If it happens that a good person is struck by a good angel, the reason is considered. It is also considered how angels preside over souls and kingdoms. [Col. 0661C]

### Chapter XXV

It is stated that Michael, formerly the guardian of the Jews, migrated to us with those whom he guarded there. Likewise, individual angels are assigned to individual kingdoms, and how they behave in mutual conflicts is considered.

### Chapter XXVI

It is added that Raphael heals diseases, as is shown through Tobias and the centurion; and that he is an archangel, like the other two, under whom there is a host of physicians.

### Chapter XXVII

It is stated over whom Gabriel presides with his army.

### Chapter XXVIII

It is stated that the embassy of expiations has been entrusted to Michael.

### Chapter XXIX

It is stated that Michael’s office is to lead the souls of saints [Col. 0661D] into paradise and to carry the prayers of those under his charge to God, just as each of the others carries those of his own.

### Chapter XXX

It is shown that all the other good angels also serve God in human affairs.

### Chapter XXXI

It is said which orders cherubim and seraphim serve, and that one may infer from the interpretation of their names that they caused the bush to burn and those cities to perish.

### Chapter XXXII

The inference from Ezekiel that cherubim are devoted to offices is added, along with what may be understood from the words of Dionysius. It is said what the cherubim do in Ezekiel and that, in Isaiah, the seraph removes iniquity.

### Chapter XXXIII

It is said what names are common to all; whence they are called Spirits and whence angels; why all are called angels; and why all are believed to have been sent. [Col. 0662A]

### Chapter XXXIV

It is then said how many orders of angels God distinguished, to what offices He assigned them, and when their offices and actions will cease.

### Chapter XXXV

It is further stated how many angelic offices and names there are, why they are expressed in the plural, and what is meant when the plural or singular is used.

### Chapter XXXVI

It is said which angels are sent to announce and which to act; how and why they are called angels; who archangels are; and that more than three are called archangels.

### Chapter XXXVII

[Col. 0662B] It is said that the order of angels is subject to the order of archangels, that they sometimes have particular offices, how this is so, and what the rest do.

### Chapter XXXVIII

It is stated what the Virtues are and what their ministry is.

### Chapter XXXIX

The Powers are considered, and why they have been established.

### Chapter XL

It is shown why the Principalities are so called.

### Chapter XLI

It is said what the Dominions are and over whom they preside; and over whom both the Principalities and Dominions preside.

### Chapter XLII

It is also said who the Thrones are and what their office is.

### Chapter XLIII

[Col. 0662C] It is shown how cherubim and seraphim stand before God, and what should be thought concerning them according to Dionysius, Daniel, and the Apostle.

### Chapter XLIV

The interpretation of the names *cherubim* and *seraphim* is also provided, together with how, according to those interpretations, they watch over human welfare.

### Chapter XLV

It is said that it is not unreasonable to believe that demons fell from the nine orders, and that there are nine varieties of spirits.

### Chapter XLVI

It is afterwards shown that the individual malicious spirits serve the prince of demons in their respective orders: some as angels, some [Col. 0662D] as archangels, others as Virtues, Powers, Principalities, and Dominions; others as Thrones; some as cherubim; and some as seraphim. Demons harm in so many ways that it is scarcely possible, or impossible, to confine them to nine modes.

### Chapter XLVII

It is said whence the nine orders derived their names. In almost as many ways as human beings are helped or deceived, demons too help or deceive; and why “almost” is added is considered. Sometimes things done perversely by humans without a demon also occur without one. It may be believed that eternal generosity itself sometimes confers bodily benefits; sometimes it does so through human beings, sometimes by other means. Whoever helps or troubles a human being is God’s minister.

### Chapter XLVIII

[Col. 0663A] It is then asked from what multitude the prince of demons comes, and this is finally shown. Although he was great, he thought more highly of himself than he was. It is considered whom the others obey, why some rage more effectively than all others, how much they have been weakened, and, according to some, when he fell.

### Chapter XLIX

It is said that the enemy with his followers stains by foulness of thought and afterwards by action, and how this occurs. One who adds an evil work to an evil will becomes more harmful. There is discussion of one who is everywhere pleased with himself in evil, and one who lives badly but nevertheless regrets it after sober reflection. It is considered how many and what good things God bestows, and why. It belongs somehow to the nature of all beings to hate evil, which is good, and to love what is good. The character of this will is considered, as is the will inspired by God’s grace and how one should act while living in evil. [Col. 0663B]

### Chapter L

It is said that good will, speech, and action are from God, though something of the human being is present in these. God’s grace is offered to all; some reject it, others receive it. Of those who receive grace, some persevere in good while others depart. It is asked what comes to us from grace and what from free choice. There is some merit of free choice, and why; and every good thing we do is done not only by us but with God Himself.

### Chapter LI

It is afterwards shown how one who corrects life through God’s grace, repents, and abounds in virtues may be numbered among the fellow citizens of the saints. It is considered what will become of him if death overtakes him; of one who refuses to confess crimes; and of one who returns to sins confessed. It is asked whether the sins had been forgiven before his return. Confession itself is God’s gift. It is considered in whose power it lies for a deed to be done well or badly; repentance of heart and confession; how a priest should deal with those who have confessed to him; excommunication without naming a person; named anathema and when it should be imposed; the priest’s intention in this work; and that form of excommunication in which a secretly inflicted injury is struck without names being spoken. It is considered how a person’s way must be revealed to God, how an offense must be disclosed to the priest, what becomes of one who does not correct life and yet hopes for pardon, and why confession must be followed by penance. There is also discussion of the burden to be imposed by the presbyter. [Col. 0663C–D]

### Chapter LII

It follows how a priest should counsel a penitent, and that God must be appeased by some anxious satisfaction. It is considered how he should treat another’s sheep; those who, abhorring their own stain, seek unknown presbyters; and those who do this in order to receive better counsel. It is said what a penitent should do, whatever the priest may be like; and that whatever is lacking in the priest is supplied by God. It also considers the meaning of “charity covers a multitude of sins” and “almsgiving extinguishes sin.” [Col. 0664A]

### Chapter LIII

It is added that one must act differently with a sick person than with a healthy one, and among the healthy, differently with a worldly person than with one who fears God; and how this should be done. If a person rejects the priest’s fitting counsel and, being guilty, falls into perjury, it is considered what the presbyter should do.

### Chapter LIV

It is also said how one who, because of an injury done to himself, pursues the guilty person to destruction is guilty; and concerning one who swears against the accused so that the accusation may be thought similar. How he ought to repent is considered.

### Chapter LV

It follows that a judge or his minister must not consent to persecutors of the innocent, nor permit an impious person to live. Care must be taken that this is not done from hatred, favor, or some such motive. [Col. 0664B]

### Chapter LVI

It is also shown that the Church needs two swords, to whom they are assigned, how they should be divided between them, what end they should seek, and how they should regard injuries done to themselves. Justice is not for sale. The relation of each power to the other is considered.

### Chapter LVII

It is added how one should deal with a sick person who, terrified by sins, fears God alone; and with a presbyter who reassures those who do not cease to nourish some sin either in themselves or in another. It is considered what counsel should be given them; which sins are to be treated by a presbyter and which by a bishop; and why some are treated publicly and others secretly. [Col. 0664C]

### Chapter LVIII

It is connected with this that a burden owed by those who live is not to be imposed on the dying. It is considered how a person about to die should be addressed by a presbyter, how he should be addressed if he recovers, and what a priest must chiefly provide.

### Chapter LIX

It is afterwards said what work confession requires and, finally, what the fruit of penance is.

### Chapter LX

It is added how human beings are bound; what the punishment of sin is; when they are absolved; how long they are held fast by the bond of sin; how a person contracts a condition in which he cannot move himself toward life; and how he withdraws himself from evil. It is considered what one is like who returns from the death of sin to life, and that, restored to righteousness, he is prepared for the way of truth by priestly confession; [Col. 0664D] and why no one should be slow to confess.

### Chapter LXI

It follows whence binding and absolution come, and that the sacrament of binding and loosing belongs to priests. Since it belongs to God alone to forgive sins, it is considered what it means for human beings to forgive sins or absolve from them. The priest does nothing except bind one who ought to be bound and loose one who ought to be loosed.

## Prefatory Notices of the Seventh Part

[Col. 0663]

### Chapter I

[Col. 0663D] In the seventh part it is said what is required after confession and absolution, and by what means the vision of God is obtained. It is said how guilt is forgiven in two ways; how and why vices are quickly pardoned; [Col. 0664D] and concerning God’s forgiveness toward one who proposes to accuse himself before a priest. It also considers who are freed from punishment for sin now and who in the future; which sins obtain forgiveness after death; and the threefold participation in sins. [Col. 0665A]

### Chapter II

It is stated that discipline, together with prayer and almsgiving, deserves threefold forgiveness; how it does so, and how these advance salvation.

### Chapter III

Discipline is shown to be a work. There is external and internal discipline, and it is considered whence each comes to a person. The more severely a person bears them, the more splendidly he acts. What internal discipline is, when we possess external discipline, and why remedies of virtues contrary to contrary vices are appropriate are discussed. There is also discussion of the satisfaction of rods and fasting, and the manner of fasting.

### Chapter IV

[Col. 0665B] It is said what kind of prayer ought to proceed, what it means if meanwhile the mind wanders, and that one who strives to prevent wandering is blessed in that very struggle. It is also considered what the petitioner should be like, what he asks for, and why words are used.

### Chapter V

When we give alms, it is said what we provide for ourselves; that one ought not give what is not needed, or give so much as to exceed due measure; and that care for the soul’s health must be pursued more earnestly than care for the body. It is considered how we should benefit a living neighbor; for which dead persons we should pray; why, in rites for the dead, we pray for infants and penitents; and what those who wish to assist their neighbors bodily should do, how they should do it, and from what resources assistance should be given.

[Col. 0665C] CHAPTER VI. It is further explained why we offer a tenth and retain nine for ourselves; from what things the tithe must be paid; to whom, and why to them.
