It is also considered to whose judgment their manner of life is to be left; and that the clergy, whatever they may be like, must always be revered and not deprived of what is due to them; how tithes are to be paid, to whom they are to be rendered, and what is to be assigned to laymen and what to bishops.

CHAPTER VII. It is also stated why authorities are established by God; that He appoints them in a peaceful manner, and why; that authority must be obeyed; that one authority provides for the body and another for the mind, and why; why the king’s sword has been added to Peter’s sword; what a king owes to the Church; how far the bishop’s authority is to be preferred to that of the king; how necessary it is to kingdoms; and concerning the preeminence of each in relation to the other.

CHAPTER VIII. It is explained how a king ought to bestow care upon temporal authorities; what sort of persons grant things ambitiously; when the reward for a work increases; when a work has its reward from the Lord; what ministers a king ought to provide; and how he ought to instruct them.

CHAPTER IX. It is also stated why soldiers are under a king; why taxes are paid by men; what subjects owe their lords, and conversely; and how subjects ought to be faithful to their lords, and conversely.

CHAPTER X. It is shown that one wishing to enter the clergy ought to be free and literate; that he must abstain from military service, trade, and secular judicial business, and why; that nevertheless many such persons are not immediately to be admitted to the choir; that no one should presume to approach the ranks of God on his own authority; that each person ought to be ordained under a definite title; and how he is to minister there.

CHAPTER XI. It is stated that marriages may be contracted below the rank of subdeacon, and why they are afterwards forbidden; why this was not observed in the old law; that at times, even then, they practised continence, and why; and that priests of grace must by no means imitate the priests of old.

CHAPTER XII. It is further stated what one who seeks to live well in his own rank must do; what he deserves who usurps a rank; what one ordained in the Church, receiving a benefice, or placed over it must guard against; what recipient and giver must consider; what a prelate ought to consider in distributing the offices of the Church; what one being promoted must consider; and with what intention a cleric should conduct worldly affairs.

CHAPTER XIII. It is explained why Simon Magus offered Peter money; that spiritual power is neither to be bought nor sold, nor any possession that cannot be held without spiritual ministry; and what a minister who has wrongly entered Christ’s sheepfold must do.

CHAPTER XIV. It is stated how long a sacrament once conferred remains; concerning the suspension and degradation of the ordained; and concerning those who exercise an office from which they have been forbidden.

CHAPTER XV. It is explained what one with a good entrance must do; how a court chaplain ought to conduct himself; and how a parish priest ought to conduct himself.

CHAPTER XVI. It is further stated why a priest ought to excel in teaching and life; what he may be forbidden, and on what grounds; and what sort of teacher ought to be a judge, or to cease being one.

CHAPTER XVII. It is added what the instruction of a priest includes; what his study ought to be like; how infants are to be assisted when their lives are despaired of, by baptism; why, although formerly adults were baptized, now all infants are baptized; and that an offering ought to be made after baptism, but must not be extorted.

CHAPTER XVIII. It is shown what comes first and what follows in moral instruction; concerning teaching and the rod; when exhortation alone is needed; and that reason must moderate discipline.

CHAPTER XIX. It is shown that there are three parts of the Church—prelates, the continent, and the married—signified by Noah, Daniel, and Job, and represented in the field, the bed, and the mill; how these three orders are signified by these three men and in these places; and concerning the office and chastity of prelates.

24 CHAPTER XX. It is further stated what Daniel—that is, the continent—must do; that they can be neither fornicators nor married persons; that the counsel, “If you wish to be perfect,” etc., does not concern married persons; and how a married person ought to conduct himself toward his household and toward God.

CHAPTER XXI. It is then found that beneath prelates are the continent and the married; what they receive from them; that subjects must not rebuke prelates; what sort of teacher one ought to be, why he ought to be such, and what reward follows from this.

CHAPTER XXII. It is then considered where passage may take place between the mill, the bed, and the field, and where it may not; what happens if the transition to continence is made prematurely; that those dwelling in the mill may enter the bed; that from neither of these may one pass to the field unless the Church calls; under what necessity one raised up may return to a private station; and concerning the saying: “Two are in the field, two in the bed, two in the mill: one is taken and one is left.” It is also explained how all the good and evil remain only in these places.

CHAPTER XXIII. It is further stated what three kinds of life the three orders of the Church profess; what the active life is like and what the contemplative life is like; what action does and what contemplation does; that Rachel and Leah, Mary and Martha, signify these lives; and that the history of these women is suited to these lives.

CHAPTER XXIV. It is stated which is Noah’s part; that a prelate must have experience of both lives; that otherwise he is in no way fit; and that, being both active and contemplative, he ought to excel so greatly that he governs the people as though it were his wife.

CHAPTER XXV. It is then asked what the active life is, and to which life it is to be preferred; that the contemplative is better; that, when the labours and anxieties of Christ and of His own are considered, the active seems to excel; but that, with regard to future things, the contemplative is better; that here, just as the active is surpassed, so at times it surpasses the contemplative; and that a prelate ought to employ both.

CHAPTER XXVI. It is further stated that there are two loves, just as there are two lives, and how they relate to those lives.

CHAPTER XXVII. It is further stated that there is no life in which a human being can please God except one or the other of these; and therefore that one who shuts himself up in solitude does not thereby immediately enjoy the pursuits of religion. It treats of those who presumptuously enter, or having entered maintain, a solitary life; of those who do everything negligently; of those troubled by pride or envy; of those deceived by the appearance of sins who do not dare to rebuke their brethren’s excesses, or even foster them; of those disobedient to their superiors; of the good that will belong to those who are rightly subject; of who are good subjects; how authorities ought to be solicitous, since they must render account for their subjects; when one separated from secular society is good, and when he begins to be perfected. It also treats of one whom the mill of the world drives round; how each should exercise himself in his own office; of building upon the foundation with gold, silver, and precious stone; of building over it with wood, hay, and stubble; how a person should relate to worldly things; how they should be loved; how their loss should be mourned; of those who descended to hell; and that the divine judgment, sometimes changing custom, introduces unusual things—here, concerning the resurrection of the dead.

CHAPTER XXVIII. It is then stated that God created and gave the first wife to the first man; how the two are one flesh; that, if human beings had not sinned, the law of marriage would have joined only two persons; and that woman is subject to man. It also treats of the fact that several wives were granted to the patriarchs, and why; why wives were to be taken from kinship rather than from foreign peoples or idolaters; that wives were dismissed for many reasons, and why; and that concubines formerly permitted in the law were afterwards forbidden, though not multiple wives.

CHAPTER XXIX. It is likewise found that among the Gentiles there were concubines and wives. It is stated that Christ’s preaching called persons found in a union not away from it, but within it; that He came to abolish vice, not an office; concerning marriage between a believer and an unbeliever; what the law means in forbidding unbelievers to be taken or retained in marriage; and how the Apostle nevertheless advises retaining an idolatrous spouse.

CHAPTER XXX. It is shown in what decree of Christ the first law of marriage returns; why divorce occurs; what ought afterwards to be done; that a husband must provide for both the body and the soul of his wife; why, though the husband presides in other matters, both are equal in rendering the marital debt; why marriage is permitted although abstinence would be much better; and when intercourse is not imputed as sin. It is stated that it is better to incur the fault of such intercourse than to withdraw oneself from one’s wife; and it treats of those intent on satisfying lust and defiling themselves by mutual desire.

CHAPTER XXXI. It is further stated that sexual intercourse is a natural act and is corrupted only by accompanying circumstances; that, just as some acts can easily and others only with difficulty be performed without fault, intercourse cannot at all be so performed; that natural acts of this kind are good in nature but are disfigured from another source; that they are not commonly blamed except because of their accompanying circumstances; and that they involve no fault if those untimely accompaniments are excluded.

CHAPTER XXXII. It is further stated that married persons can always practise continence; how they may do so; and that this must not be altered. It treats of what is vowed secretly and what publicly; of vows made rashly and against reason; of what must generally be maintained concerning every vow; and of what married persons preferring continence must do.

[Col. 0668D] CHAPTER XXXIII. It is stated when a human being separates what God has joined; that it is lawful to retain or dismiss one who commits fornication; how the saying, “He who retains an adulteress is foolish and impious,” is to be understood; that neither adulterer can accuse the other; that one must not separate because of receiving [the spouse]; how the dismissing and the dismissed should live; and why God permitted separation on account of fornication of the flesh, but not for another reason.

CHAPTER XXXIV. It is also added that a union may freely be broken off, before consent is given, on account of the worship of demons or moral abomination, or if such a manner of life cannot be endured; yet that continence must be maintained. It also concerns persons arranging to dismiss wives, in the former case because of fornication of the flesh, in the latter because of fornication of the mind; and what it means that the Lord excepts one fornication, whereas here two are excepted.

CHAPTER XXXV. It is further stated that after marriage many things happen such that its use cannot continue, though marriage itself does not cease. It treats of many things done in marriage or beforehand because of which it either is not a marriage or ceases to be one; what those things are; and that the Lord taught some matters, leaving the rest to be taught by His Church.

CHAPTER XXXVI. It is further stated whom the ordinances of the Church exclude from marriage; concerning the connection between baptizer and baptized; why the manner of baptism is such; concerning affinity between man and woman; and what happens if causes that prevent marriage by preceding it arise after the marriage has been made.

CHAPTER XXXVII. It then concerns one who, after pledging faith to someone in promise of marriage, meanwhile marries another. It is stated that perjury is preferable to doing something contrary to law; what sort of oath it is good to swear; what sort is criminal; when it is good to abandon an oath; that no one sins in order to avoid another’s scandal; concerning an oath which cannot be made without sin nor abandoned without scandal; and concerning a marriage betrothal supported by an oath, while another marriage has meanwhile been contracted.

CHAPTER XXXVIII. Having shown which persons cannot be joined, nor remain joined after being so joined, it states which may remain together and may also separate. It treats of the marriage of a free person and a female slave, and of one unable to render the marital debt.

CHAPTER XXXIX. It is stated with what outlook marriage should be undertaken, and what good or evil it brings with it; what causes sometimes arise in marriage that greatly displease God; what consideration one about to marry should have; and what are the principal causes of matrimony. It treats of the three goods of marriage which persons entering into union should embrace, and why; that marriage cannot exist without fidelity and sacrament, but can exist without offspring; that spouses must never act so as not to receive children; that fidelity is sometimes without sacrament and sacrament without fidelity. It also concerns those who come together with the intention of committing fornication in every way; what would happen if those being joined rejected the goods of marriage; what if in marriage only wealth, pleasures, and such things are sought; one drawn to embraces by pleasure; one who, for his own desires and disregarding God’s will, consents to the goods of marriage; one who attends to God’s law but nonetheless pursues carnal pleasure; that while a spouse lives all things must be endured with her; and the freedom of the survivor after the other’s death.

## HERE BEGIN THE PRELIMINARY NOTICES OF THE EIGHTH PART

[Col. 0669]

[Col. 0669C] CHAPTER I. In the eighth part it is stated that Christ reconciles the world to His Father by the refreshment of His body and blood; why He chose to do this in this way; what this bread signifies; who eat it; concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood among the ancient people; and concerning figure, shadow, and the truth of the reality.

CHAPTER II. It is further stated what bread and what drink are, and why no other is admitted to the Lord’s table; why body and blood are consecrated; why many grains are gathered there; that by eating this bread people are joined to the Lord; that the body refreshes the flesh and the blood the soul, and why; concerning the efficacy of bodily and spiritual food; that spiritual food is received by some unto life and by others unto death; what must be done at the end for a criminal; what sort of good person may communicate; and what the Eucharist is to the worthy and unworthy.

CHAPTER III. It is stated why water is mixed in, what it signifies, that we who partake ought to remember the thing signified, and why; how priests and how lay people ought to partake, and why lay people do so in that manner; that flesh is not without blood, nor conversely; and that bread dipped in the cup is not to be distributed.

CHAPTER IV. It is added what kind of body the Lord gave His disciples to eat; that it was not yet to suffer anything; that in the Passion was fulfilled what had been enacted in Christ’s mortal body; that what is now performed at His table preceded in the Passion; that we are Christ’s temple while we receive Him; what the Lord’s table signifies; and that this sacrament is preeminent.

CHAPTER V. It is further stated how the Lord changes bread into His body and wine into His blood; what words should be used concerning this change; that no one should assert anything other than what the Lord’s words indicate He intended; that each is in the other and neither is without the other; that it cannot be received except whole; concerning the breaking by the teeth and contrition; that, though the substance is changed, the properties remain; that there is no deception of the senses there; and what those appearances present for consideration.

CHAPTER VI. It is stated by whom alone, though they be unworthy, the Eucharist may be consecrated, provided the prescribed form is observed; whose office it is to give or refuse it; to whom, when, and why; how one acting otherwise is guilty; what must be done for the unworthy; and concerning the secretly wicked.

CHAPTER VII. It is further stated how often the ordinances of the Fathers establish that communion should be received; that priests ought to partake more frequently; and that each should take care to approach with earnestness.

CHAPTER VIII. It is afterwards explained why the Lord did not reject our foods; that He did what He had determined that His own would do; how those who choose a solitary life should live; how those who migrate from place to place should live; and that no class of human beings harms one who conducts himself holily. It is also stated that, following the Lord’s example, we must live even among the wicked so that we may benefit them; and that one must change location where one cannot escape the death of the soul.

CHAPTER IX. It is likewise found that the Lord took the old supper with His disciples, and why; that it must not be restored; that its final part—namely, participation in body and blood—should be repeated more often; that the Lord washed His disciples’ feet and commanded them to do this for others; that He diminished and ended the figures; concerning His answer to the Jews accusing His disciples of plucking ears of grain; that the old observances are by no means to be retained after Christ’s new institution; why the Apostle sometimes returns to them; and that the Lord’s supper must by no means be reenacted.

[Col. 0671B] CHAPTER X. It is further stated when the Lord restored freedom concerning foods; that we ought not eat anything to a brother’s offence; concerning food sacrificed to idols; concerning certain foods that at times should not be used; and concerning the saying, “What enters the mouth does not defile a person,” etc. It also treats of what would follow if the Church forbade the freedom of foods restored by the Lord; of Jews who now set aside some things as though unlawful, add some new things as though most holy, and command abstinence from certain foods as though unclean—not for the sake of bodily discipline.

CHAPTER XI. It is added concerning the alternation of Jews and Gentiles in the faith; that certain distinguished persons from the Gentiles will resist Antichrist; that some Jews will obey; concerning those whom Antichrist will seduce to himself; and what is meant by “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then,” etc.

CHAPTER XII. It is further stated when Elijah and Enoch were taken up into paradise; what they await there; that they are believed to have a better state than ours and to be destined for a better one; what they are believed to do while preaching for three years and more; what will then happen to the Jews; what happens meanwhile; and the phrase, “He will no longer know us.” It also treats of the killing of Elijah and Enoch; why they will be forbidden burial; the condition of Antichrist after their death; for how many years they will preach; for how many years Antichrist will exercise his tyranny; why this is so; the shortening of his persecution; and where he will be slain.

CHAPTER XIII. It is further stated what will precede the coming of this most wicked one; why the Apostle spoke to those fearing that the day of the Lord was at hand; how the saying is to be understood, “Let him who now restrains continue to restrain until he is taken out of the way”; and that his coming is by the working of Satan, and according to what manner of working.

CHAPTER XIV. It is further stated how many days will be granted to the elect for repentance after he is slain, before Christ comes; that no deception will befall the elect; that no pardon is to be hoped for by Antichrist’s ministers; how and by whom sudden destruction will come upon them; that the Judge’s fire is thought to precede the Judge; how it will blaze in His sight after He has appeared; concerning running waters and our fire; that heaven and earth will be changed for the better; that fire and water will not exist at all; concerning birds that will perish; how high the fire will rise; concerning the higher heavens; why the world is mutable; whose immutability follows its change; and to what extent.

CHAPTER XV. It is further stated how long the final fire will last; that the living will die in it; through whom the dead will rise; that they will be incorruptible; concerning incorruption and transformation; what all will rise like and to what state; that every limb will return to its own proper name; and that Christ’s resurrection is the certainty, cause, and example of our resurrection.

CHAPTER XVI. It is set down from what source, according to the common opinion of all, the begetting of children derives its origin. It is stated that many hold bodily increase to come from another source; whence it comes in the unborn and in those already born; concerning the share in a human being received from parents according to this view; whence, accordingly, more distant fetuses arise; that others say parental seed grows to the full quantity of a male; that, according to these, internal nutriments are not converted into human substance; and what rises again according to this opinion and according to the other.

CHAPTER XVII. It is then asked whether we shall rise with all our limbs; whether the rib will return to Adam; concerning children, if seeds return to parents, or if children will have nothing in their own substance that their parents had in theirs; that all existed in Adam’s loins; that there is one origin; that children consist solely of the material of their parents; that some things in a human being remain and others depart, and what these are; that a human being will not resume in the resurrection superfluities cast off during life; that necessary things withdrawn by the human condition will then be resumed; concerning the saying that not a hair will perish; and what stature each person will have in the resurrection.

CHAPTER XVIII. It is further stated what sort of condition human beings will receive after the resurrection; that the Transfiguration was an example of future brightness; that the saints will lack clothing in it; that, just as Christ differs from them, so the saints differ from one another in splendour; that the resurrection of the dead is likewise so; and that there is a twofold brightness among those who rise.

CHAPTER XIX. It is further stated when fire will come and the Lord descend, and why only then; when the trumpet will sound, and why then; who will rise first and who afterward; how great the lightness of resurrected bodies will be; how the Lord will descend; why the voice that will be heard is called a trumpet; what delay there will be in rising; concerning the trumpet through which they will rise; how, in the twinkling of an eye, some will rise earlier and others later; and concerning the assertion of some that the remaining living persons will die in their rapture into the air with those raised earlier, and thus be raised. It is also asked how the dead will rise, in what body they will live, concerning the Lord’s descent and resurrection, and what will occur in the fire, and why.

CHAPTER XX. It then treats of the trumpet and the Lord’s coming, whether they will occur simultaneously; how, after the fire, He will judge the living and the dead and the world through fire; and that some hold that the Lord, descending with the trumpet, will bring in the fire and raise up in it the resurrected dead.

CHAPTER XXI. It is stated how long the final fire will last; what must be the case if souls are then to be purified outside their bodies as now; what those in bodies will suffer who sinned in bodies; what opinion is rather to be maintained if the resurrection of those already cleansed and those needing cleansing occurs together; that the Lord will wait in the air until His own are gathered to Him; and, if this seems absurd to anyone, what he will say of the judgment—why it is posited and what seems to oppose it.

CHAPTER XXII. Although the times of the conflagration and judgment are unknown, it is further stated that sudden destruction will certainly come, and why; that sun and moon will be deprived of light, and why; and concerning the saying, “There will be signs in sun and moon,” etc.

CHAPTER XXIII. It is further stated concerning the delay after the signs until the conflagration; that the resurrection will occur in it; that after this has happened the saints will ascend; that a cloud will receive them; why angels and clouds will minister although the capacity to rise will not be lacking in itself; that then all flesh will see the salvation of God, but not afterwards; and what it means that the Lord will be revealed in a flame of fire.

CHAPTER XXIV. It is further stated concerning the Lord’s words which follow the signs of the sun, moon, and stars: namely, “And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven,” etc.

CHAPTER XXV. It is stated which will first be received into their respective places, the good or the evil; that both will receive different dwelling places in the Father’s house according to their merits; concerning the state of the righteous; why all human beings and angels will be present there; how the Lord will come to judgment; concerning His kingdom over the Church; that eyes of flesh will see Him; from where and to where they will be gathered; and what is to be said concerning the unworthy.

CHAPTER XXVI. It is added that it is unknown over what part of the world the Lord will appear; nevertheless, what should be supposed; what He will do; and on what merit. It is also stated that we must help our neighbours both spiritually and bodily, which is greater, and concerning the usefulness of piety.

CHAPTER XXVII. It is further stated that on the day of judgment the good and evil deeds of all will be revealed to all, and why; concerning sins covered through repentance; and concerning good and evil deeds abolished.

CHAPTER XXVIII. It is stated how at that time the conscience of one person will contain the deeds of all; to what extent the hearts of the wicked will be enlarged; by whose power this will happen; and, since what belongs to each of the Three is common to all Three, how the Father gave all judgment to the Son.

CHAPTER XXIX. It is then found how the evil and the good will see God; and the meaning of Christ’s Transfiguration with Moses and Elijah is inserted.

[Col. 0674B] CHAPTER XXX. It is added that there will be a twofold order of those saved and those damned, and how this will be; and, although some saints will be judged, how all will judge, according to the saying, “The saints will judge the nations,” and, “The righteous will rule over them in the morning.”

CHAPTER XXXI. It is then asked what it means to judge the world; that the Lord will pronounce a judicial sentence after the manner of mortals and inflict punishment or reward through ministers; that the saints will be judges under the Lord, and how; and that the Lord will judge both good and evil, whereas the saints will judge only the evil.

CHAPTER XXXII. It is further stated that after judgment the evil will remain in punishment and the good in delight; that the state of the evil will not be hidden from the saints, and why; that the miserable will know the glory of the saints but will not see it, and why; and that no one can set forth the goods of the latter or the evils of the former, and why. It then treats of the misery of Gehenna; that in neither state will there then be works, and why; concerning the disposition of the mind; and that the evil will have no remedy, nor the good a fall.

# Robert Pullen, *Book One of the Sentences*

[Col. 0673]

31 CHAPTER I. First, it is shown that God exists.

[Col. 0673D]

[Note: [Col. 0673D] Master of the Sentences, book I, distinction 3.] The rational progress of irrational things, and their tireless return upon themselves, undoubtedly proves that a disposer presides over their mechanism. But did He who gave things their order Himself have a beginning of existence? Things which begin to exist necessarily require a cause of their subsistence. For who can understand how that which lacks existence could come to existence unless something of such a kind preceded it, from which it might have the beginning of subsisting? And who will deny that what is the cause of another’s being exists more excellently than that other? Therefore either God lacks a beginning of existence, or He has something more excellent and prior to Himself. Let it therefore be established that God exists and has no beginning of subsistence.

Whatever exists is either substance, if we follow Aristotle [Note: [Col. 0675D] *Categories*, chapters 2 and 4.], or accident. Which of these is God? If He is an accident, He exists through another, although He grants existence to other things. If He is substance, He is susceptible of contraries—whereas He is unchangeable and immutable. For substance is so called because it is subject to accidents. Shall we say that it is called substance not because it subjects itself to another, but because it exists through itself and not through another? If so, among things known to us no substances are found that we know otherwise than as subject to accidents. If so, He is designated by no name, because every name signifies substance together with quality; and therefore this disyllable, *Deus* (“God”), is not a part of speech, because that of which it seems most to be a name does not exist. Or, if it is a name, what is His substance subject to quality? For, as Aristotle declares concerning genus and species, a name determines a quality with respect to substance.

## CHAPTER II. Against the error of idolatry: there is only one God

The blindness of idolatry attempts with profane speech to assert a plurality of gods. But things that are several will be found either superior one to another or equal. God, however, cannot be subordinate to anyone. Therefore, if there are several gods, they are surely equal to one another. Certainly, because God lacks a beginning, He cannot have an end. For whatever is bounded by an end receives a beginning of existence. A thing may indeed begin to exist and, by the benefit of Him through whom it began, know no end. Yet that which hastens from being to non-being by an inborn defect also comes from non-being to being through the gift of its maker, since it could not attain this by its own effort. For if it had always existed, it would surely possess such power that it could never fail.

Accordingly, since God is extended through eternity, nothing befits Him except to be adorned with goodness, knowledge, immensity, and power that cannot be overstepped—indeed, cannot be approached. Therefore, if there are two gods or more, neither can be inferior to another while God’s majesty remains intact; without doubt, however many there are, all must be revered with the undifferentiated equality stated above. Let the vanity of idolatry therefore blush, which fabricates some gods as younger, others older, some greater, and others lesser.

But let those also be confounded who ascribe equality to several gods. For just as it seems fitting to the age of divinity that it never began, and to its mighty workmanship that it should bring every thing to completion in matter and form, so reason likewise approves, and the heart rightly accepts, that such great excellence should be regarded with uniqueness of majesty. For how can God be more than one if the Creator too is only one? But He is known to be one and the sole Creator because the fabric of the world is found to be one and sole.

For if there were several gods, just as the one God, besides whom there is no other, began a good work by innate goodness and completed it because He is most perfect, so the others too, for the same reasons, would each have begun and completed his own good work. For just as the holy and glorious Trinity, because God is one, performs works indivisibly by one will and the same power, so a plurality of gods would, through the plurality of the above-mentioned realities, produce divided works. For anyone self-sufficient and subsisting through himself would share work with another in vain, as though he needed another’s assistance.

For one assists another either by nature—as in the holy Trinity, in which there can be absolutely no difference of wills, knowledge, power, or indeed operation: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (Ps. XVII, 1)—or by beneficence, as “with the holy, the Lord is holy”; or by necessity, as when we need another’s help.

But you will say that mutual love demands this: that even where there is no need, it shares its operation. This is so between human being and human being; but it cannot be so between God and God. The Son assumed flesh; the Father loves the Son; yet, because there was no need, the Father declined to be incarnate with the Son. And just as the Father and the Son, with the Holy Spirit, perform one work because of the unity of divinity, so, if there were many gods, the multiplicity of divinity, since cooperation would not be needed, would produce multiplicity and division of operation. And because our understanding is too weak for investigating such matters, where reason fails, faith supported by authority comes to aid, affirming that God is one.

## CHAPTER III. There are three persons

[Note: [Col. 0676D] Master [of the Sentences], *Sentences*, book I, distinction 2.] But if God is one, as Moses testifies: “Hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one” (Deut. VI, 34), how is He three, according to the saying: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one” (John I, 5, 7)? Therefore the one thing—that is, God—is these three. Yet each one of these three is God, good and wise. Why, then, are they not three good, wise gods, but one? Each of the three—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—is likewise individually a good, wise man; yet three good, wise men are not one man.

We confess one substance in the Godhead, as the Lord teaches: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). How then are there three persons? Or, if there are three persons, why are there not as many substances, but only one? For in creatures unity of substance is accompanied by identity of person, and diversity of persons is followed by multiplicity of substances. As Peter is one substance, so he is one person; Peter, James, and John, as they are three persons, are also three substances.

The dialectician will say: The species is the whole substance of individuals, and the whole species, the same species, is found in each individual. Thus the species is one substance; its individuals are many persons; and these many persons are that one substance. For according to Porphyry, all human beings are one man through participation in the species.

By dialectic you seek to solve the obscure by what is obscure, and what is believed by something unbelievable; you accomplish nothing. For you see how that which is only one is three. Is not a house one, yet roof, wall, and foundation? Is God likewise one and yet Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? No integral part receives the name of its whole: neither wall nor roof is a house. But the Father is God, nor is the Father anything more than the Son, nor are both more than the Holy Spirit. Therefore no one has perceived the simple essence, God, as compounded of persons.

[Col. 0677B] Is it, then, as a genus which is one in itself, on receiving differences passes into many things and is those things, so that God, who is one substance, formed by fatherhood, sonship, and procession from both, is several—not gods, but persons—just as a genus is several, not genera, but species?

But if God is three from those three [relations], then from intelligence, immensity, beauty, omnipotence, sweetness, and the rest He becomes many more—indeed, from innumerable things innumerable.

But you will say: There are certain forms of genera which by no means bring them into the being of species. There are likewise properties pertaining to substance which do not constitute a person. Or you will say: These are the same as God, and therefore do not produce diversity of person; those are not the same as God, and therefore can do so. But what intervened, that these should be [something distinct], while those should be the same as God and not be [distinct]? Again, if the substance which is the one God, and is therefore one, is three persons because it is affected by those three [relations], it seems itself to be the matter of the persons; and they seem to be compounded out of it and the affecting qualities. Thus substance seems greater because prior, and the persons lesser because subsequent. And the Father, who is God, will be less than God, who is matter; less than fatherhood, which is God; and similarly the Son and the Holy Spirit. Again, if God and form are joined so as to constitute a person, who joined them? Are not all things that are joined capable also of being separated? Again, if, just as there are three persons, so there are three forms from which they are constituted, then, since these forms, like the persons, are eternal, and since, in order that the persons may be distinct, they are not God (for the same thing could not diversify itself, while the persons are one God), are there not, I say, three things found co-eternal with God, and six things coeval with one another?

Therefore God the Creator, one in substance and threefold in persons, is neither extended by parts nor varied by forms: so that He is admirable in His unity because of the Trinity, and inexplicable in His Trinity because of the unity. Even in unity, why do we confess three persons rather than more, except because we believe authority? For faith has no merit where human reason supplies proof. [Note: [Col. 0677D] Gregory, Homily 26.] For God says in Moses: “No man shall see [Col. 0678A] me and live” (Exod. 33:20). And in the Gospel it is said: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18). Therefore, while a human being lives in the mortal state, he cannot see God: certainly never with bodily eyes; with spiritual eyes he will be able to do so after this life. For the vision of God is promised to the mind alone, when it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). Observe the future tense: for now God is not open even to the heart. If no one knows God, neither does he know the Father; for if he knew the Father, he would certainly also know God, since the Father is God. But if he knows neither the Father nor the Son, does he nevertheless understand both to be God? Does he know that the Only-Begotten is begotten from the Unbegotten, as from looking at any two men you know that they exist, though you do not thereby know either inwardly? So too, often by some consideration of the one in relation to the other, [Col. 0678B] the Father is in some manner known; yet both are said to be unknown.

But against the first point the Lord says: “This is eternal life, that they may know thee, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent” (John 17:3), to be the one God. Therefore, if he knows how to recognize that the Father and Son are God, he already has eternal life. Against the second point the prophet says of the Only-Begotten: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8). If he knows Him to be begotten of the Father, let him declare His generation to us.

But someone will say: “I know each person separately to exist; I do not know all the persons together to be one God, but I believe it. Likewise, I do not fail to know that the Son is begotten; nevertheless, I believe Him to be God.” You truly believe: for we believe what faith conveys to us; we see what direct apprehension makes manifest to us. And, according to the Apostle, faith is “the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1); whereas direct apprehension is the comprehension of things known. He intends to define faith who says: “Now the Catholic faith is this” [Note: [Col. 0678D] Athanasius, in the Creed], etc.; and, after inserting certain matters, adds: “Christian truth compels us to confess each person separately to be God and Lord.” What is it to confess each person to be God except to acknowledge each person to be God? But whether this must be acknowledged by faith or by direct apprehension, the treatise itself indicates, since at its beginning it undertakes to expound the faith, and at its end concludes it when expounded. In the same place, lower down, it reads: “This, then, is the right faith: that we believe and confess that our Lord Jesus [Col. 0678D] Christ, the Son of God, is God and man.” Therefore, on faith’s assertion, we believe that the Lord Jesus is God and that the Lord Jesus is man. For just as the disciples knew by their senses Him whom by faith they believed to be God to be man, so after the Ascension we apprehend both by faith, neither by knowledge; yet, in absence, we hold them more firmly by faith than [they did] in presence by knowledge, and adhere unwaveringly to them by the assent of the mind.

Perhaps, defending the error stated above, someone will undertake to attack the foregoing chapter by an unfair explanation, as follows: “The Lord Jesus is believed to be God according to His humanity; according to His divinity He is known to be God.” But if He is truly believed, He is God according to that [humanity]. But if the Lord is, according to His humanity, God—whereby the Father Himself is other—then according to His humanity He is equal to the Father. For according to that whereby He is God, it is improper also to call Him lesser; contrary to the statement: “Equal to the Father according to divinity, less than the Father according to humanity.” Therefore He is wrongly believed to be God according to humanity, when according to humanity He is rather God’s servant, just as according to divinity He is Lord of the servant. Since, then, faith proves the Son of God to be God—for the Lord Jesus is God not insofar as He is Son of Man, but because He is Son of God—will faith persuade me that He was born of the Father, or will the thing itself show it us? But if we know that He was begotten of the Father, we cannot fail to know Him to be God. For, as Augustine testifies [Note: [Col. 0679D] *On the Words of the Lord in the Gospel of John*, feast 51, Homily 43; among [the works numbered] 50; Book II, *Against Maximinus*, ch. 6.], every [Col. 0679B] thing begets what it itself is: a horse a horse, a human being a human being; therefore God begets God. But because, while ignorant of the Lord Jesus, we believe Him to be God, while ignorant of His being begotten by the Father let us believe it, according to: “I believe in God the Father Almighty.” And a little later: “And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Only-Begotten Son of God; and born of the Father before all ages.” Therefore I believe, but do not know, that the Lord Jesus was born of the Father. For “who shall declare His generation?” (Isa. 53:8).

Similarly, no one can declare the procession of the Spirit from both. Therefore, if we firmly hold by faith not only that each person in itself, but also that all the persons together, are one God; and not only that the Father begot, but also that the Holy Spirit proceeded from both; and if faith is the evidence of things not seen [Col. 0679C] (Heb. 11:1), we are compelled to believe what will be permitted to appear to none of us on earth.

Let no one rebuke us as though ignorant because “knowledge,” “revelation,” and “cognition” are repeatedly used in matters pertaining to faith: “Know that the Lord”—that is, Jesus—“is God” (Ps. 119:3). Likewise: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed [this] to you” (Matt. 16:17). And again: “Now I know in part” (1 Cor. 13:12). But it is one thing to use words properly and another improperly, though never in a way condemned by authority. But if it is so that the persons are not affected by properties, how can that ecclesiastical statement stand: “That in the persons the property, in the essence the unity, and in the majesty the equality may be adored”; [Col. 0679D] and that authoritative statement concerning the Trinity [Note: [Col. 0679D] In the *Explanation of the Creed to Damasus*, among the works of Jerome]: “We confess not only the names, but also the properties of the names”? What are the properties of the persons, and what are those of the names? The unbegotten Father begot the Son; the Only-Begotten was born of the Father; the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. [Note: [Col. 0680D] Master, Book I, distinction 25, § M.] These are properties which the categories do not know and which wholly exceed our understanding. For whose intelligence can comprehend that the Father begot the Son from His own substance, when it is not permissible to assign a wife to the former or a mother to the latter? Since the Father’s and Son’s substance is one and the same, and thus the Son’s particular substance is not separated from the Father’s whole [Col. 0680A] substance to be shaped by natural increase; and since the Father does not precede the Son in eternity any more than in time. For if the Father is coeternal with the Son, how is He Father? But if, in order to be Father, He is prior to the Son, is not the Son God because He began? It is clear that God the Son is coequal with God; but what is equal is customarily called not the same as itself but one thing equal to another. Are there then two gods? For He is believed to be equal not because He is God, but because He is Son. For because He is God, He is the same as the Father; because He is Son, He is other than the Father, likewise God; and other He cannot be unless equal. For if He were unequal, one of two consequences would follow: either, if greater, He would have a Father who was not God; or, if lesser, the Son would not be God. For no one can be greater than God, nor can God be less than anything. Therefore there are not two gods, but the Father and the Son are two. Thus we believe: “Born of the Father before all ages, God from God.” God, then, was born from God, but only because He is Son. And if God born from God could not be born unequal, then beyond doubt God born from God is equal; therefore, just as God was born from God, so God is equal to God.

Each person, therefore, has what is so proper to itself as it is unknown to us. Names have properties, and separately have their meanings. The Father is God; but God is the Son: for whatever God is, the Son also is. Therefore the Father is the Son. Far be it! For it does not follow at all that, if Peter is a human being and Paul is a human being, Peter is Paul. But rather thus: the Father is [Col. 0680C] God; but whoever—not whatever—is God is the Son; therefore the Father is the Son. The consequence is true; the minor premise is false.

## Chapter IV. The unchangeable God is not subject to qualities and accidents.

[Note: [Col. 0680D] Master, Book I, distinction 8, paragraph 3 and following.] When we call God great or beautiful, we do not attribute these to Him—for He has no accident. But we call Him great and beautiful without relation, if this can be understood, and without quantity. For God is not understood to be qualified after the manner of a human being. For according to Isidore [Note: [Col. 0680D] Isidore, Book I, *Sentences*, ch. 1], just as in God greatness and beauty are the same as God, so in a human being they are other than the human being. For just as every creature, so also [Col. 0680D] a human being is insufficient to itself and in need of what is external; whatever greatness, beauty, or quality it possesses, it owes to forms and to the maker who impresses the form. But God, because He is the supreme good, is not from elsewhere but from Himself whatever quantity He has and whatever quality He has. Or, just as we call God great without quantity and good without quality, do we distinguish every human being and every thing that is truly formless by the discrimination of our thoughts rather than by diversity of forms? For this is the power of the mind: to conceive a thing in different ways even though it is not different in forms. What I say is difficult to see, more difficult to explain. For [Col. 0681A] by what do things of the same color agree with one another, and by what do they differ from things of different colors, if there are no accidents? Or, as some say, do they agree and differ, but in nothing—as white things resemble one another, but in what? In a participated species? But reason proves that universals do not exist. In an individual whiteness? But each is seen to possess its own whiteness, not another’s. Yet it is clear that they are like one another because, although they possess different whitenesses, they nevertheless possess whitenesses. But if we remove forms, whence comes likeness? If I speak thus, I speak in the customary manner; I seem to have both divine and secular authors against me.

Yet if it is proper to confess this, God is not varied by forms, nor is any work of God; then will not a work differ from its maker by the dissimilarity of variation? [Col. 0681B] A creature grows and diminishes, rejoices and suffers, hopes and fears, is now warm and now cold, and is altogether subject to change; and if any creature is more stable through the favor of its Creator, when deprived of that favor it is dissoluble. Is not, then, the strength and weakness of Creator and created thing manifest?

If a body changes because it was hot but is now merely warm, why is God unchanged when He first created the world and afterwards ceased from creation; when He first bestowed grace upon the Jews so that they might overcome their enemies, and afterwards withdrew that same grace so that they might be overcome? He who from eternity was only the Son of God became in time also the son of man—namely, He was not incarnate before and is incarnate afterwards—if that which is without form does not change when it becomes incarnate. Why is a human being changed from black to white, and from sick to healthy, without having acquired a form? Or is this the difference between maker and thing made: that an artisan, although distinguished from his work by acts, is nevertheless not changed in essence as his work is? For acts, accidental to the divinity in succession, come and go, while it remains unchanged in itself, because such things do not pass through it in such a way that it must thereby be altered, as pain greatly changes one who is joyful, sickness one who is healthy, and better [changes] what is less good.

If, therefore, God is capable of receiving acts and consequently accidents, so that they are now present in God and now absent, He begins to have within Himself what He formerly lacked and to lack what He formerly had, just as substances subject to corruption do. This is certain in all substances, but in many things accidental to them it is doubtful. If, I say, [Col. 0681D] the acts accidental to God remain what they are, then, since before the world He was wise, loved justice, hated the contrary, and was disposed in other ways, it is established that the Creator preceded the creature not alone, but attended by a household of acts.

But if this is so, are wisdom, goodness, beauty, and immensity in God nothing other than divinity itself? For authority so declares. [Note: [Col. 0681D] It points to the authorities of the Fathers; see them in the notes.] What cause, I ask, makes being wise in God one thing, while wisdom is the same as God? Therefore, just as neither the substance, which is one and the same for the three persons, nor the persons, which, though three, are nevertheless of one substance, [Col. 0682A] have in their nature anything different from the one possessing it—nor is anything done to them or possessed by them from which even the slightest changeability may arise—so a creature, whether formless, which is less, or formed, which seems more, is so disposed, or can be disposed, as to change.

## Chapter V. Though diverse things are attributed to God, He remains one and the same.

[Note: [Col. 0681D] Master, Book I, distinction 8.] Therefore let no one of sound mind suppose such apparent forms of God to be other than God Himself, regarded in one manner and another according to the incomprehensible vastness of His majesty. Indeed, whenever we call God omnipotent, just, or wise, we designate the divine essence alone, though we meditate upon it in different ways according to its modes [Col. 0682B] of being. Such meditation is displayed through various verbal expressions; and such expressions embrace not only those things which we understand concerning the unity of the divine immensity, but also those which distinguish the Trinity in persons. Although these are many and enter human minds in various ways, nevertheless, as has been said, God’s goodness can be nothing other than good God; nor can the rest—those which seem as forms to adhere to the simplicity of divinity—be anything other than God, marked by various dignities and yet simple and one.

What, too, shall we suitably call the properties by which we marvel at the distinction of the persons, except persons naturally distinct from one another—distinct, indeed, as other than one another, but not separated? For “the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, that of the Holy Spirit another.” [Note: [Col. 0682D] Athanasian Creed.] Yet they are always and everywhere together. The Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son; the Holy Spirit is in both, and both are in Him. For “such as the Father is, such is the Son, and such is the Holy Spirit.” [Note: [Col. 0682D] Ibid.] Therefore each is beheld in each, as most like in most like; whence: “Philip, he who sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9).

As was said above, we call these forms the same either as the unity of divinity or as any one of the persons, lest, if according to our manner each were something other than that in which it exists, the venerable [Col. 0682D] eternity of infinite greatness should be an exceedingly abundant multitude of things. It is impious to attribute this to any but God alone. Such a multitude of things, however, is denoted by a multitude of words, as I have said: some adornments comprehend the unity, others the marks of the Trinity. But just as the Trinity is one in Deity and in all its adornments, so it is threefold in persons and in all their marks. For the Father and Son with the Holy Spirit are one in Deity, and likewise one in wisdom, immensity, goodness, and all else; whence: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). But these same three, although distinguished [Col. 0683A] in very many ways, nevertheless do not constitute more than three properties. For however many they are, they intend only to distinguish three persons. The properties of the persons are denoted distinctly by certain words, and confusedly by others: distinctly, single ones; confusedly, two or three. These [Note: [Col. 0683D] This is drawn from Augustine, *Tractates on John*, tractate 9, about the middle.] are the water jars, each holding two or three measures (John 2:6). “Father,” “Son,” and “Holy Spirit,” these three words distinctly signify their own three properties; but “person” signifies the same three indiscriminately. For it does not attribute something common, such as “Omnipotent,” “good,” and the rest, to the three persons; rather, it indicates each as distinct from the others. Yet it does this indistinctly, because it establishes no certainty of differentiation. In a similar manner it is said of God: “Who weighs the mass of the earth with three [Col. 0683B] fingers” (Isa. 40:12): for the one divinity works in three persons. Thus, although each thing is other than, diverse from, and different from other things, and although it is common to every thing to differ, they derive from the difference by which they differ no community or agreement.

## Chapter VI. Two processions and principles.

[Note: [Col. 0684D] Master, Book I, distinctions 10–14, 29.] There are also two processions. One is that of the Son from the Father, according to: “For I proceeded from the Father.” The other is that of the Holy Spirit from both. For the procession which is from one alone and that which is from one and another cannot be one and the same procession. For if one procession common to the two existed, just as, for example, one omnipotence common to all three persons exists, then undoubtedly, just as omnipotence belongs without distinction to the three, so that they are one in it, procession also would belong to the two. But now, because it is possessed differently in one and the other, it is proved to be different in each. In omnipotence the Son is such as the Holy Spirit is. But in procession the Son is not such as the Holy Spirit is. For what is the Son’s procession but His generation? And what is the Holy Spirit’s procession but His distinction from the others? Therefore whenever something is attributed to persons, it either exists in them similarly and without any difference, and will be common to all; or differently, as “person” to the three, and “procession” or “principle” to two; and it will be something common in name only, not also in reality. Yet if, with respect to creation, we venerate the Creator with the prerogative of principle, principle is surely common to the whole [Col. 0683D] Trinity. For it is the principle of every creature, from which, as creator, the whole universe of creatures receives the gift of its own subsistence.

But if we contemplate the holy Trinity in itself, just as the Son and the Holy Spirit are each proceeding—the Son from the Father alone, the Holy Spirit from both—so the Father and Son are each a principle: the Son of the Holy Spirit alone, but the Father both of Him and of the Son. For, as they teach, the Father is origin in the Trinity. For whatever is from somewhere, not according to place but according to substance, has as its principle that from which it is; hence the Son from the Father is principle from principle—unless perhaps someone says that He is principle not of Himself but of creatures. But by the same reasoning the Holy Spirit is principle from principle. If the reasoning holds, usage does not.

Therefore, just as each of the three is a person, but because each is so differently not all are one person but three, so also each of the two proceeds and each is a principle; but because each does so differently, the two together are by no means one proceeding being or one principle, but two proceeding beings and two principles. The Father is principle only; likewise, the Holy Spirit proceeds only; but the Son both proceeds and is principle. He who has only one of the two has it in relation to two. But he who participates in both is related in one respect to one, in the other respect [Col. 0684B] to the other. The Father, as authority attests, is principle without principle, because there both is one who proceeds from Him and is none from whom He derives; and therefore He is principle to another and has no principle for Himself. But the Son is principle from principle because He both is principle to another and has a principle for Himself. [Note: [Col. 0684D] Richard of St Victor, Book V, *On the Trinity*, ch. 25.] Yet we can give this to unity: the Holy Spirit proceeds from another, but no one proceeds from Him; while the Son both proceeds from another and has one proceeding from Him. But to have one proceeding from oneself and to proceed from another is to be principle from principle; while to proceed from another and to have no one proceeding from oneself is to be from a principle but not to be a principle. To be principle without principle is to have one proceeding from oneself and to proceed from no one. Hence it is clear that “principle” and “proceeding” are relative to one another: for a principle is the principle of that which proceeds from it, and that which proceeds proceeds from its own principle. Therefore, because they are simultaneous by nature, like things must be maintained in both.

The Father, like the Son and Holy Spirit, has certain things because He is God and others because He is a person. From the unity of divinity, as was said, the Father has all the same things as the Son and Holy Spirit; but person requires distinction. Thus the Father, because He is God, has omnipotence, goodness, and very many other things; but the Son and Holy Spirit, because they too are God—not another God but altogether the same—have omnipotence and goodness, not one goodness and another, but altogether the same goodness. So also, because He is a distinct person, the Father has certain things other than the Son and Holy Spirit have. For from distinction of person the Father has a Son, is unbegotten, is principle, and lacks a principle. That He is Father requires that He have a Son. That He is unbegotten requires that He have no father. Yet the Holy Spirit lacks a father and is not unbegotten, because “unbegotten” is the name of the Father alone. But when I say “principle,” I indicate neither that He has a Son nor that He lacks a father, but that there is one who proceeds from Him. Now it is evident that being principle belongs to the Father not at all because He is God, since the Holy Spirit also is God and is not principle. Therefore, His being principle arises from some distinction of person. But in order that distinction occur—since from it no commonality results—the Father is principle in one way and the Son in another. For the Father is principle both of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, whereas the Son is principle of the Holy Spirit alone. But the Father is principle of the Son differently from His being principle of the Holy Spirit: of the Son as begotten from Himself, of the Holy Spirit as proceeding from Himself. Yet the Father and Son seem each to be principle of the Holy Spirit in one and the same manner, just as [Col. 0685A] the Spirit Himself seems to proceed without distinction from both. Then, because just as the Father and Son are each omnipotent in one and the same way—indeed, not two omnipotent beings but one—so too, because each is principle of the Holy Spirit in one and the same way, are there not two principles of the Holy Spirit but one? But it is established that the omnipotence, like the divinity, of the two is one and the same; and therefore I rightly say: “One is omnipotent,” just as [I say] “eternal God.”

Yet the relation, although similar, perhaps is not one: that between the Father and the Spirit, and that between the Father and the Son and that same Holy Spirit. Or if it is one, perhaps Father and Son are no longer two principles of the Holy Spirit but one; so that it may now be said that, just as certain things are common to all three, so others are truly common to two. One part of these belongs differently, as procession to the Son and Holy Spirit, or principle in whatever manner possessed, to the Son and Father. The other part, however, is possessed in one and undifferentiated manner—as “principle” in the Father and Son with respect to the Holy Spirit. Therefore, just as three are one God and one omnipotent being, so two are one principle. Likewise, two proceeding beings are one proceeding being—which does not seem very credible. For it is fitting that the persons be one in everything that they receive from the nature of divinity, and not one in what they assume from the nature of distinction. For divinity requires singularity, whereas distinction calls for plurality. The persons have many things from divinity, yet from those many things they are not many: indeed, they are three, but from another source. For from those many things they are only one [Col. 0685D] God. If there were no distinctions of persons, while now they are three because of those distinctions, then one alone would remain amid many things. And since He would be omnipotent, good, wise, and immense, He would indeed be those many things, because He had very many such things; yet He would not be several, because He alone would be one. Thus Caesar was all things, yet existed as one only. Therefore, if the holy Trinity, though it has very many marks of its substance, is nevertheless one nature in all of them because the substance is one, why should not two persons, although one personal property is granted to belong to them, nevertheless be two in it rather than one because it pertains to distinction? Thus Father and Son are not one principle but two, and likewise the Son and Holy Spirit are two proceeding beings, not one.

Certainly, the Son is principle just as the Father is; but whereas the Father is principle of two, the Son is principle of one. Again, the Father is principle of the Son as Son; but the Son is principle of the Holy Spirit not as Son; and therefore perhaps the latter is principle differently from the former, and thus there are two principles.

But although each seems to be principle of the Holy Spirit in the same manner, there can nevertheless be two principles of the Holy Spirit. Thus twins—if it may in any respect be permitted to compare great things with small—are brothers of their sister in the same way, and yet they are her two brothers. The Son is from the Father; the Holy Spirit is from both. And though the Son is other and the Holy Spirit other, is the former from the Father in one way and the latter from both in another? I see twins to be from their one and the same father in one and the same manner, yet nevertheless distinct from each other. If, then, just as the Holy Spirit seems to be from the Father and Son in one and the same manner, so also the Son is from the Father not in another but in that very same manner—if, indeed, one mode can belong both to Him who is from His principle by generation and to Him who is otherwise from His principle—nevertheless the Son and Holy Spirit are truly two, and can also be two proceeding beings; just as among us several things often proceed similarly from one or from several principles, yet are not one but several proceeding things, distinct from one another on a definite ground.

But if the Son is from the Father in one way and the Spirit from both in another—as perhaps seems more credible—then the distinction between the two appears clearer, and the procession of each ought to be seen more distinctly. So too, if the Father and Son are granted each to be principle in only one mode, they cannot in any way be denied to differ from each other in person, and may likewise be called two principles; just as among us there are certain things distinct from one another and separate principles, although things distinct from one another do not produce differently.

But if the Father is related to the nature of principle differently from the Son, as is thought truer, how much more must the one and the other, if matters are as they seem, be different principles? For if—the impossible being supposed—the unity of divinity withdrew and the Trinity of persons remained, then, since the persons would no longer be one God, they would certainly not be one omnipotent being or one omniscient being; nor would they agree in other things by that unity which the dispersed singularity of substance would undoubtedly carry away with it. Nevertheless, the persons would then be wholly whatever they now are from the nature of plurality. Hence it is clear that the Father and Son would then be two principles, and likewise the Son and Holy Spirit two proceeding beings, because then they could be one in nothing. But now, with the singularity of divinity preserved and likewise the plurality of persons preserved, why should each not retain its own full right: so that the persons, just as by the nature of singularity they are something one—for example, one God, one Omnipotent—may also by the distinction of plurality [Col. 0687A] be several: three persons, two principles, and two proceeding beings? Unless perhaps someone thinks that “principle” and “procession,” by their own nature, are consecrated to singularity. This is plainly false. For if there were one person in the one divinity, there could be no place there for principle and procession, each of whose nature requires a plurality of at least two.

## Chapter VII. On the mission of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0687D] Master, Book I, distinctions 16, 17.] The Father sends, and the Son sends; but the Father sends the Son and the Holy Spirit, whereas the Son sends the Holy Spirit alone. Conversely, the Son was sent, and the Holy Spirit also was sent; but the Son by the Father, the Holy Spirit by both. [Col. 0687B] Hence it is clear that the Father sends and the Holy Spirit is sent, while the Son alone has both roles. Therefore, as the three stand eternally in relation to principle and procession, so they also stand temporally in mission.

But what is it for the Son and Holy Spirit to be sent except for an invisible nature to appear in a visible effect? And what does it mean that the Father sent both, but the Son the one, except that the mission was accomplished by the will of the Father and likewise of the Son? But then the whole Trinity sent the Son and the Spirit, since the mission was made by the will of the whole Trinity. This pleases some, though the expression varies in order that the persons may be distinguished. Therefore, since it seems less fitting to say that the Son or Holy Spirit is sent by Himself, or that the Son is sent by the Spirit, it can surely be said—and not absurdly understood—that one is sent by another, the proceeding being by His principle. Therefore only He is sent who, appearing through some manifestation of His presence, is from another by whose will He is shown to human beings. But the Lord Jesus says in Isaiah: “And now the Lord God has sent me and His Spirit” (Isa. 48:16). What does “the Father sent” mean except “He ordained that He be incarnate”? And what does “sent by the Spirit” mean except “conceived by the Holy Spirit”? The assumed humanity may deservedly be said to have been sent also by the Spirit, just as a good teacher is said to be sent when confirmed by God.

## Chapter VIII. The Father is other than the Son, not another thing; and similar matters.

The Father is not He who is the Son. For the person of the Father is one, [Col. 0687D] that of the Son another. [Note: [Col. 0687D] Master, Book I, distinction 24, §9 and following.] Yet the Father is that which the Son is, because both are one God. For the Father is God, omnipotent, wise, good, and these and many other things; the Son is all the same things. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “All things whatsoever the Father has are mine” (John 16:15). As the exposition of that passage requires, He says this of matters which belong to the Father’s very divinity, in which He is equal by possessing everything that the Father has. Therefore whatever the Father is, the Son also is; hence He says: “I and the Father are one.” [Note: [Col. 0688D] Ordinary Gloss, on the same passage.] But the Father is begetter—this is one thing; unbegotten—this is another; principle without principle—this is a third. None of these is the Son. How, then, is whatever the Father is also the Son? Whatever the Father is from His divinity, the Son also is; but in His person the Father is something which the Son is not. For just as the Father is many things in common with the Son, so He is also many things in Himself apart from the Son. In the former matters, whatever the Father is the Son also is; in the latter, not whatever the Father is is the Son. Thus it is clear that the statement “Whatever the Father is, the Son is” is false in the breadth of its meaning, though it can be true when restricted.

Unless someone more subtly maintains that statements of this sort should be accepted: “The Father is someone who is not the Son,” but not, “He is something which is not the Son.” “The Father is other than the Son,” but not “another thing.” Again, the Father is not he or that one who is the Son, and is that or the thing [Col. 0688B] which the Son is. Finally, perhaps the Father should be called such a one as is not the Son, and not such a thing as is not the Son: so that the masculine gender indicates distinction of person, but the neuter unity of substance.

Yet it is not so in every respect. Hence: “And in this Trinity nothing is before or after,” etc. The Father is a principle without principle; that is not the Son, but something other. What? A principle from a principle. What follows from this? That the Father is one thing and the Son another? That the Father is some such thing, or something, or that which is not the Son? No. For Father and Son are one and the same. What then? In what respect is the Father other than the Son? In that the Father is not he who is the Son; likewise, the Father is someone—or, if it may be so said, such a one [Col. 0688C]—as is not the Son. According to the nature of his person, the Father is many things which the Son is not. Is he therefore something which the Son is not? No. Rather, for this reason he is another person than the Son; just as, according to the nature of his divinity, the Father is very many things which the Son also is. Is he therefore the very one who is the Son? No. Rather, for this reason he is the same as the Son. The Father is someone, or a certain person; the Father is something, or some thing: “something,” because he is God; “someone,” because he is a Person. Something other is said of the Father than of the Son; and if this is so, not everything said of the Father is said of the Son. Hence it seems to follow that the Father is called other than the Son, and that not everything called Father is also called Son. But however these matters stand, the Father is never, on this account, a different thing from the Son; rather, he is another person than the Son; and whatever [Col. 0688D] the Father is, the Son is—not the one who is Father.

Is not each thing, however, that which is truly said of it? Therefore, if the Father is truly called other than the Son, is he not what he is called, and consequently other than the Son? The Father is called begetter of the Son; the Son, begotten of the Father; and both are true. To be begetter and to be begotten are plainly different things; hence it seems that the Father is called something other than the Son. Unless it is to be understood more precisely that something other is said of the Father than of the Son, or that being begetter—which is said of the Father—is other than being begotten—which is understood of the Son. Conversely, although something other is said of the inner man [Col. 0689A] than of the outer man, the inner man is not therefore called another person than the outer, but another thing. For the rational soul and flesh are one human being; yet the one is something other than the other. But in whatever way anyone is said to be something, or something is said of someone, the Father is never thereby a different thing from the Son, though he is sometimes another person. That other thing which is predicated of the Father and not of the Son is indeed the Father and is called such; the Son, however, neither is nor is called it. Yet the Father is not thereby a different thing from the Son, nor is he called so. It is one thing to be omnipotent, another to be omniscient; thus one thing and another are said of God when he is called omnipotent or omniscient. Yet in no respect is God, or is God called, a different thing as omnipotent than as omniscient.

Likewise, severity is one thing and mercy another; and [Col. 0689B] although the latter properly belongs to the Savior and the former to the Judge, nevertheless the Judge is he—and is that—which the Savior is and is called, and is neither another person nor another thing.

**42.** The Holy Trinity says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). It is therefore rightly said that those three made man—indeed, the entire world. Hence it seems to follow that these same three were at some time makers of the same world. If at any time they were makers, how many makers then existed? More than one according to the plural nature of the number? And how many but three? But if three were creating or making the world, how is there one maker or Creator of the world? Therefore, while those three made the world, there was one making the world by one operation. [Col. 0689C] Thus those same three certainly exist, reign, and will what is good; nevertheless, because their essence of existence is one, there is one existing, one reigning with undivided dominion, one willing in the single immutability of will. Yet if on any ground, or by any authority, we are compelled, because of the plurality of persons, to speak of three who reign or three who create, we must by no means falsely speak of three kings or three creators, since unity of substance forbids it.

## CHAPTER IX. God is everywhere essentially.

Where is the Lord? Is it, according to the letter: “His seat is in heaven” (Ps. 10:4)? Or according to the statement: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” (Wis. [Col. 0689D] 1:7), because “the whole earth shall be filled with his majesty” (Ps. 71:19)? The Prophet says to him: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 138:8). [Note: [Col. 0689D] Master of the Sentences, I, dist. 37, §1.] Thus there is no place where God is not, not only potentially but also essentially; not divided into parts, but wholly everywhere; contracting neither purity in what is pure nor defilement in what is filthy.

But does not “the Spirit flee deceit” (Wis. 1:5)? In what is deceitful he is indeed present by substance, but not by indwelling grace. For if I locate God somewhere such that he is not elsewhere, he will seem enclosed and circumscribed by place—contrary to the Prophet: “There is no end to his greatness” (Ps. 144:3). Isidore says of him [Col. 0690A] [Note: [Col. 0690D] *Sentences*, I.2, sentence 3.]: “He is in the world, yet not enclosed; outside the world, yet not excluded.” Therefore, if, because he lacks parts, we deny that he fills the world—a magnitude unknown to us—let us assert that he occupies a simple place, since the Lord is simple.

But we would confine a great inhabitant within a small dwelling. For although he has no parts, “the Lord is great and exceedingly praiseworthy, and there is no end to his greatness” (Ps. 144:3). Nor does he need a place after it has been made, since he did not need one before it was made.

## CHAPTER X. In the body the soul is wholly everywhere.

Like the image of God, the soul is wholly everywhere in its own body, a lesser world. For the soul is either simple or composite. If composite, it consists of parts more numerous [Col. 0690B] than the body’s, fewer, or equal in number. But why more? Why fewer? It seems rather to consist of an equal number of parts. Why? So that individual parts of spirit may occupy individual parts of the body. Otherwise, whence keenness of sensation, constancy of growth, and finally continuity of wholeness?
