These cannot exist except with the soul, nor can the soul itself exist in the limbs except with them—unless some accidental violence has disturbed matters. Hence, because they follow it as it departs, they do not deny that they are its attendants.

But if this is so, as the body grows, the spirit too grows; as the body is mutilated, the spirit is shortened; the body is cut into pieces and is no longer a body; the soul is cut with the body and is no longer a soul, but a fragment. [Col. 0690C] This is allegedly proved when parts of an animal separated from one another by cutting are seen to leap. For the lifeless body lies motionless; therefore the soul perishes, while a fragment of it remains. Consequently the Scripture of truth is convicted of falsehood when it proclaims a spirit that is in fact mortal to be immortal. Again, if individual parts of the soul accompany individual parts in the body, so that part corresponds to part and whole to whole—for the body’s extent requires a corresponding extent of soul to animate it—it follows that the same conjunction of parts which first occurs in the body follows in the spirit. The spirit therefore has its own head and its other limbs. Are not, then, in each individual two heads, making them two-headed; four feet, making them four-footed; [Col. 0690D] and every limb doubled, making them multiple? But why is this seen neither in the whole nor found in what has been cut apart? Why, I ask, is the spirit invisible, why incorporeal? For we do not yet see how an incorporeal spirit can be extended through incorporeal parts. Let us therefore meanwhile maintain that it is simple; for this accords both with reason and with authority.

But if it is simple, while it is in the body it is either in it as wine in a cask—that is, so as to be in no part of it—or else it is in every part, in several parts, or in one part alone. And that part will be either divisible or indivisible. But if it adheres here and there to a divisible part, why would it not likewise adhere everywhere to the divisible whole? There is no reason why a simple and indivisible thing [Col. 0691A] should not inhabit wholly a composite and divisible thing, whether great or small; if reason does not deny it in the lesser, it has no ground for denying it in the greater. But if the soul, queen of the human organism, intending to convey the decrees of royal majesty to her subjects, mindful of her own simplicity chose for herself a single throne, how can she, if she is not in the other regions of her kingdom, perceive what happens there? How can she supply those same regions with growth and with stability in growth? For wherever life yields to death, no one doubts that the soul is absent. Why? Because the administrator of all vegetative life is lacking there. And if that royal emblem should—as happens—be shaken down by some violence, its ruling queen cast from her throne to the ground, will she go into exile? She had no other seat in the kingdom; [Col. 0691B] or, if she had one, by the same reasoning she has a third and a fourth. Either then, as a human being moves from place to place over the ground, so the soul moves through the human being from place to place; or, if it has only one, indivisible dwelling, then if it happens that the human being loses it, the soul likewise will be lost, for the human being will cease to be human.

But just as all that belongs to a human being increases in the succession of ages until maturity, so, when maturity slopes toward old age, it diminishes; and through repeated emissions in illness a human being is diminished everywhere, outwardly and inwardly, just as in recovery he is replenished.

Will it be said that the soul has some immovable particle in the whole body? But who knows this? What fixed seat, then, will the soul have in a human being? Or, if [Col. 0691C] the soul inhabits not one part in a human being but several, why not all? For just as we establish through sensation that it is present in these parts, so through growth or wholeness we must prove that the same soul is present in the others. It also happens that where the soul had previously been for sensation, it is no longer afterward, but remains only for continuance—as in those whose one limb dies beforehand while the rest are still alive. For it departs entirely from that limb and, if not immediately leaving it open, nevertheless leaves corruption behind: limbs already bloodless and therefore in a sense withering serve as a presage of the future dissolution.

How, moreover, can it be understood that the soul is in a human being as liquid in a vessel unless some emptiness within it is imagined? [Col. 0691D] But if it is held enclosed in the belly, a man will seem pregnant rather than ensouled; if it is in the mouth, one must fear that it will be expelled with spittle. Wherever it may be in such a manner, it must expect the violence of expulsion. Such absurdities are more pleasantly ridiculed, as though with laughter, than pierced straight through by the point of reason. Then, as has been said, it will exercise its powers where it is absent—perhaps as an archer works at a distance by instruments.

Someone will say: “The spirit is in the body as sensibility and rationality are in a human being, which, as they say, are so in the whole that they are in no way found in a part.” But however it may be with an accident, how can a substance be somewhere while it itself is nowhere there? How, I ask, can cold in the head feel heat in the foot unless it is in both? Yet the other points already made oppose this view. Therefore there will be no place in the flesh where the spirit of the flesh is not; and since it is indivisible, wherever it is, it is wholly there.

But how will one indivisible substance [Col. 0692A] occupy so many places distinct from one another? Perhaps as God himself, whose image it is, does? I wonder at both. A hand is cut off; when the soul is wholly in it, does the spirit not withdraw with it? No. For who withdraws unless he changes one place for another? One who leaves a place altogether and takes up no other rather perishes than withdraws. Thus, when its contrary comes upon it, it fails rather than flees. The spirit indeed departs from a severed hand, but goes nowhere, because, not having entered a new abode [Note: [Col. 0691] Better thus: “because, not having entered a new abode,” etc.], it remains in all the other limbs as before. Thus when a human being decreases, the soul departs from what is removed but enters nowhere; just as, when the human being grows, it enters what is added but departs from nowhere.

[Col. 0692B] But when a living creature is cut apart limb by limb, the parts themselves are seen to twitch. If the soul is absent, whence is the movement present? Is it because the soul has recently departed and leaves that movement behind? But if, while present, it gave rest, how did it cause movement when absent? Is not an animal rather agile when the soul is present, and without it lying motionless? Or does life remain for a little while after the soul’s expulsion, disturbed by violence and itself disturbing the limbs?

But if this is so, is there not life in the corpse because of movement, and death because of the soul’s departure [Col. 0692C], so that the same body simultaneously displays two contraries? For we often see, after skins have been torn from an animal, small pieces leap about here and there. Therefore the soul is in them, so that they live; and they live, for there is no other impulse by which they move themselves. Let an animal such as an eel be cut into many pieces; let the pieces be carried, with angelic swiftness—as Habakkuk was carried to Babylon—through the regions of the world. Though separated by so great an interval, they will, no less than if joined together, by their leaping demonstrate the soul’s presence. The soul therefore will be divided not by parts, which it lacks, but will be wholly at the same time in east and west, north and sea. What it does not possess of itself, then, it occupies throughout the whole world by means of flesh. Does it occupy the whole world, or only its own body? [Col. 0692D] It follows its body whether compressed or extended. Therefore, when a human being is—as happens—crushed and broken up by the sudden collapse of a mass, either in the twinkling of an eye the soul is separated from every tiny portion, because in the twinkling of an eye the body itself is scattered piecemeal; or we shall marvel at the force of its departure, since, bound to dying limbs, it is scarcely freed even by struggling. And, as we have said, we shall wonder whence motion comes to severed portions; or the soul, poured into every separate piece, will follow them when disjoined, producing the marvel that a soul divided from itself by so many and such great intervals simultaneously occupies them undivided, without filling the spaces between.

We see little people and those of medium size; we see giants as well. What if the body were extended still further in proportion [Col. 0693A] as the world expands?—for he who can do less can do more. Would the created spirit, made like God the Creator, contain the structure of the world within its own compass, just as the Creator does? Or rather, as God, the assessor of human growth, has set limits to nature beyond which it may not proceed, has he fixed bounds which it is unlawful to exceed?

## CHAPTER XI. On God’s love and hatred.

[Note: [Col. 0693D] Master, Book III, distinction 32.] God hates none of the things he has made. For if he hated them, who could endure the hatred of the Almighty? Or what could resist his will? (Wis. 10:25.) Clearly, then, anything he hated would perish; for what other fitting effect could the hatred of the All-powerful have? If, therefore, he hates none of the things he has made, does he not love them either? But [Col. 0693B] the continuance of a thing in existence is a sign of one who loves it. Therefore, does he not merely fail to hate what he has made, but also love it?

Accordingly, he loves both a converted and a fallen human being, as well as an angel. But does he love them equally or unequally? If unequally, he loves the good more and the evil less; for to say the reverse is quite unfitting. Therefore God loves more and less. But if more and less exist in God, inequality and diversity exist in him; and therefore he is not God if he is unequal and diverse in relation to himself. Therefore he loves equally those whom, lest he cease to be God, he cannot love unequally. Hence it is clear that God loves Judas as much as Peter, an enemy as much as a friend, the betrayer of the Son as much as [Col. 0693C] his confessor, the seller of the Son for a vile price as much as the one who poured out his precious soul for the grace of confession. It is clear, I say, that God loves Satan, his despiser and oppressor of his servants, no less than Michael, the worshiper of divinity and helper of the Church. But if he loves Satan, it follows that he also loves his only-begotten Son. Would he love an adversary and not the consubstantial Son? Therefore he loves the Son, but not more than his adversary—not more, I say, God than the devil—lest, if he loved more, he should not be God.

Either, then, he loves improperly under compulsion, deprived by impious compulsion of lordship and thus of divinity; or, acting freely, he badly orders within himself the love which he rightly orders in humanity, he who says: “He ordered love in me” (Song 2:4). For, though prudent, [Col. 0693D] he acts imprudently when he loves the devil and a holy human being—indeed, the Lord and a demon—equally. But if this is so, he is imprudent and unjust; and God cannot be such.

Does not one who knows more teach his own less? Or, lest there be more or less in him, shall we falsely say that he knows no more than he teaches? Or, in order that he may know more than he teaches, shall we falsely say that by “more” and “less” he is unequal to and different from himself? Therefore we shall admit that he knows more when he teaches his own less, gives more when he owes his own less. Thus he loves this person more when he loves that person less. Nor will he become greater or lesser because he does more or less in this regard; he is not thereby changed, but rather just. For as he is better than another, so he loves this one more than that one; that is, as he is more good, so he loves more. [Col. 0694A] Who would deny that a maker is better than his work? But if we cannot explain or disentangle what we perceive, shall we therefore rashly hurl down as ill-formed, novel, and unheard-of matters of our faith, when now we know in part and see through a mirror in an enigma? (1 Cor. 13:12). It is better to be devoutly ignorant than foolishly definitive; for faith, as I say, has no merit where human reason furnishes proof. [Note: [Col. 0693D] Gregory, Homily 26 on Ezekiel.] For, according to the Apostle, faith “is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1).

Can there not be things more secret in God than our sight is able to penetrate? Does a human being, who does not yet know earthly things, already comprehend heavenly ones? Does a soul that does not yet know itself recognize him in whose image it was made? [Col. 0694B]

If one human being holds one thing dearer than another, what change is this? He does not undergo alteration within himself because he holds this thing more dear. What if he has always held it dearer? Has he not always rested in intense love? And what has this to do with alteration, which occurs only when one moves from one affection to another? A human being, then, remains the same while loving this one more and that one less; and will God not remain? But if someone first holds a person less dear and afterward more dear, he undoubtedly changes, since he increases in love. Is God similarly changed? Healthy and injured eyes approach to look upon the sun: the healthy eye is delighted, the injured eye offended. [Col. 0694C] Is this difference in the sun, or rather in the eyes? The sun shines equally on both and warms equally; yet, from what warms equally, they are not warmed equally. Why? Because one matter is more capable of being warmed than the other.

Thus God, one and immutable in himself, accommodates himself to the variety of merits, so that he loves the devout more or less and hates the impious according to the character of their life—drawing love chiefly from what is his own, but hatred solely from what belongs to another. Scripture indeed records that he hates none of the things he has made (Wis. 11:35), while not being silent that he hates the wicked, addressing speech to him thus: “You hate all who work iniquity” (Ps. 5:6). This latter statement occurs very frequently in Scripture; [Col. 0694D] the former rarely.

Therefore, lest the sacred Scriptures, inspired by the Holy Spirit to sacred writers, be left in contradiction with one another—to God’s injury—we should temper the rigor of one statement by another, not the statement which shines by very frequent repetition and which, through the variety of its repetitions, teaches unambiguously what it means: “He hates none of the things he has made.” Rather, he loves the just person whom he made, both human and angel; but he hates the unjust person whom a human being or angel, wandering astray, bears. Injustice is nothing; therefore, according to authority, one who involves himself in injustice becomes himself nothing. And the Gospel says of God: “Without him was made nothing” (John 1:3). Either, then, we shall explain it thus: He hates none of the things he has made that persist in their appointed order; or thus: he who is hates none of the things he has made—that is, among the things he has made. For, since among the existing things he made nothing offends him, he excludes only that which, as alien to his love, [Col. 0695A] has fallen through error into non-being—unless at some time he chooses to call back to being what has erred into non-being, so that he may love it when turned toward him, but hate it when wholly turned away.

The punishment of the miserable is an indication of hatred; for he who hates is eternal God, and the miserable one who is punished endures perpetually. Whomever he hates eternally, because that person loves iniquity without end—he does not descend into hell for the sake of amendment—he punishes without end. For here, in hope of pardon and conversion, they in some sense love the one who converts them; there, despairing of an end or mitigation of punishment, they must, according to the nature of the affections, hate the one who inflicts it. [Col. 0695B] For if there are those here who hate, whence comes the saying, “The pride of those who hate you rises continually” (Ps. 73:13), how much more there? And if “he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than John” (Luke 7:28), is not the reverse true in hell: those lesser in wickedness exceed the notorious criminals who remain among us? Certainly; either it is true or very probable.

But if God so loves the just person as to hate the unjust, and if an unjust person becomes just only through God, how will he justify one whom he does not love? Or how does he love one whom he knows to be hateful? He certainly loves the evil person: “For he first loved us” (1 John 4:10). Otherwise, he would not make him good. He loves him, not because that person is evil, but because he himself is good; he loves the evil person in order to make him good. He loves him certainly, not only now, but from eternity. For what reason would he love the wicked now but not earlier? Or why now and earlier, but not afterward? Did not the Lord Jesus love those who did not yet exist—or, if they existed, did not yet believe—yet would believe, when he prayed not only for those who then believed but also for those who would believe? (John 17:20). [Col. 0695C]

As he loves eternally, so he appears to love equally the guilty person beforehand and the saint afterward. For he loves the guilty person in order to convert him, the converted in order to sanctify him, and the sanctified in order to save him. This he wills for an enemy; what more will he will for a friend? Thus “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Rom. 9:13). Both were equally defiled by the stain of the whole mass; one he chose through mercy, [Col. 0695D] the other he rejected through justice, and what was due to both he did not exact from the one through mercy.

But what if one whom he loves while still guilty were overtaken by death before reconciliation? It will not indeed happen; yet, as it can happen, if it did happen, what would occur? Would one of two things not be necessary: either that out of love he crown an impious person, or that because of impiety he condemn one dear to himself? He would certainly destroy the one who died beforehand; for he does not love him in guilt, but so as to sanctify him once absolved from guilt.

Yet if this happened, he would not save the person whom he now loves in order to save, because he would not then love him, since from eternity he would have adjudged him to damnation. For it is certain beyond doubt that divine foreknowledge is never mistaken and divine will is never frustrated. [Col. 0696A] If he loves the evil person because he will be good, does he likewise hate the good person because he will be evil and persist in evil? Or will it be said that such a person was never good, according to: “They went out from us, but they were never of us” (1 John 2:19)? They were never among the saints by predestination; but were they or were they not such by likeness? Yet Esau, whom God hates, is cleansed in circumcision from the original stain which alone he had; and every wicked person is cleansed in infancy through regeneration. But if he is cleansed wholly, how is the one whom God hates evil? Or if he is good, how does the just Judge hate him? Especially if he should die below the age of discretion—that is, while he is still good—and if God hates him now, then God would save him as one dear to him, because he is [Col. 0696B] just. Therefore the Lord hates a person to be damned not only while he shines in innocence, but even before he existed, because he always had the intention of damning him. Why? Because of the fault which he foresaw. For he does not respect persons, but foreknows merits and determines to damn according to them. Thus, before Esau existed, he hated him. Did he not hate the one whom he assigned to eternal punishments, whom, that is, he willed to damn? For unless he had willed it beforehand, he would not punish afterward.

Does he not himself punish? Certainly: “He will miserably destroy the wicked” (Matt. 21:41), because he himself says: “I will render vengeance to my enemies” (Deut. 32:41); for “he will avenge the blood of his servants, and repay vengeance upon their enemies” (Deut. 32:43). Certainly, as he foreknows, so he wills beforehand what he will do, because “what was made in him was life” (John 1:4). [Col. 0696C] He thus made the things that are to be.

Or did he in no way will concerning the wicked person before he existed, or concerning the good person while he stood in goodness; but, provoked by later evil merits, begin to will what he afterward did? For he does nothing unwillingly—indeed, he does it willingly. But now willing and now unwilling do not accord with divine constancy; for the Wise One does not repent.

Yet we shall seem thus to oppose Scripture, which maintains that God punishes no one before guilt and crowns no one before merit. Is not God’s hatred a grievous punishment and his love a desirable crown? Shall we say, then, that he neither hates anyone before merit nor has loved anyone before merit? But the Lord presses us when in judgment he will say to the good: [Col. 0696D] “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 5:25). How did he not love from the beginning one for whom he prepared a kingdom from the beginning? Or how did he prepare eternal fire for the devil and his members without hatred? Certainly, just as he destined heaven for the devout and hell for the impious, he would have done the reverse, except that “he has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills” (Rom. 9:18). Shall we answer the question stated above by asserting that punishment and crown belong only to one who exists and endures, whether lamenting in pain or rejoicing in delight?

Nevertheless, it is not absurd to say that God loves even one who is to perish while he remains in goodness. Would he not love one whose holy life pleases him? Does he not embrace a holy life even in one who perishes, just as in one who is saved he pursues an evil life? Yet how does he love one acting holily while he entertains the intention that, after that person is corrupted, he will destroy him? He loves him because he disposes himself toward him for the time being as he ought toward a good man; but this love passes away because wickedness comes in. Conversely, however, he does not always hate the unjust person, to whom he often gives milder recompense than his merits deserve. [Col. 0697A]

## CHAPTER XII. On God’s anger, wrath, and will.

Just as authority records God’s love and hatred, so it also makes known his anger and wrath. But anger and wrath are passion and disturbance in their possessor, lesser and greater respectively, according to: “My eye has been troubled by wrath” (Ps. 6:8) [Col. 0697B], and: “The anger of a man does not work the righteousness of God” (Jas. 2:20). Nor do hatred and love any less turn the mind’s gaze from the vision of rectitude. Hence Sallust [Note: [Col. 0697] Sallust, *On the Conspiracy of Catiline*, p. 58, Geneva edition, 1615.] considers that judges ought to be free from anger and hatred, friendship and pity; if the mind is distressed by anger, it is even more so by hatred. But God judges in tranquillity: he does not boil under any disturbances of the affections, subject to changeableness.

Therefore, in the manner familiar to us, he neither hates nor loves, neither is angry nor has pity. Yet he has pity, but without anxiety of heart, when he assists one who is miserable. He is angry, but without swelling of heart, when he inflicts punishment. He hates the one for whom he wills hell; he loves the one for whom he wills life, willing both as justly as secretly, [Col. 0697C] without agitation and with an unmoved will. For it is not sudden, but eternal. Times pass, but it does not pass: what he willed to be now, he wills to be now, and he will will to have been now.

But you will say: He previously willed many things which he does not now will; for example, he once willed the Lord Jesus to die, but now wills him not to die but to live. Yet he whom he once willed to die then, he now wills to have died then, not to die now. For he never willed the Lord to die now, but always willed him to die then. Thus the Lord always wills things that happen to happen when they happen; he never wills them to happen when they do not happen.

But does he so will things that happen that he also wills things that happen wickedly? For if we say that he does not will them, how can that which he did not will be, when he can do whatever he wishes by a nod alone [Col. 0697D]? Does not he, just as he made all things which he willed to exist, make all things which he does not will not to exist? If, then, the Almighty does not will something, why does he not prevent what displeases him from happening, and thus give occasion for grief? For how can anyone not will something unless it displeases him? And how will it displease him unless, when it happens, he regrets it more or less, according as it displeases him? Does not everyone who does not will something to be will it not to be? And do they not do what they will, if they can? Will accompanies one who does not will; for we should judge “not to will” to be nothing other than that to which “to will” pertains. Therefore, either there is no difference, or only a slight one, between not willing a thing to exist and willing it not to exist.

[Col. 0698A] But not willing and not willing-to are not the same. We rightly say that inanimate things do not will anything; but we do not rightly say that they refuse or do not will it. Therefore it is clear that God in no way does not will the wicked things done in the world; for if he did not will them, he would not permit them to exist. For if he did not will them to happen, he would will them not to happen; and because his will is never ineffective, without doubt they would not happen. Shall we then freely say that he wills things which we may not say that God does not will? Indeed, we pray to him daily: “And lead us not into temptation” (Matt. 6:13). This would by no means be requested unless he were feared as about to lead us into it. And in the Prophet it is said to him concerning a servant: “You have destroyed him from correction” (Ps. 88:45), that is, you have made him clean by scourges. Likewise concerning enemies: [Col. 0698B] “Set them as a wheel” (Ps. 82:14), that is, in proportion as they rise again backward, so do they fall forward: they advance in matters of the world, which ought to be put behind them; they fail in matters pertaining to the Lord, which ought to be preferred. And, “like stubble before the face of the wind” (ibid.), that is, make them such as do not resist the tempter. This would not be asked by a soldier if he knew it displeased his king.

If the foregoing is so, God wills evils to happen; and things which he wills to happen surely please him. Therefore those who act wickedly please God, since they fulfill his will so that in nothing do they dissent from it. Or are they blamed as contrary to God because, while fulfilling God’s will, they make no progress, since they seek to please not God but themselves? Yet to seek this is plainly to act wickedly. But those who act wickedly, according to what has been said, obey God who so wills. Therefore those who, while acting wickedly, do God’s will, [Col. 0698C] fulfill God’s will when they glory in their evil deed. Is God then—who cannot be unjust—unjust when he punishes those who act wickedly though they previously pleased him? Or do those who act wickedly among us act rightly before him, so that the wicked are falsely glorified as good?

But guided by authority and reason, we are certain that very many things are done unjustly. Things done unjustly cannot please God, for the Prophet says to him: “You are not a God who wills iniquity” (Ps. 5:5); and elsewhere he represents God rebuking the wicked: “You thought wickedly that I would be like you” (Ps. 49:21). Certainly God would be like the wicked person in this respect [Col. 0698D] if iniquity pleased him as one wicked. Therefore, whenever divine speech seems injurious to God because it is thought to associate wicked things with him, it must be reconciled by careful inquiry, so that it never disagrees with itself and accords in every respect with moral goodness. Therefore God, who tempts no one to evil, leads no one into temptation by assisting in evil, but by not assisting in good. For it is just that “he who is filthy should be filthy still” (Rev. 22:11). [Note: [Col. 0697] Augustine, Letter 105, Book I to Simplicianus, Question 2, etc.] He imparts wickedness to no one, but withholds grace, without which nothing but ruin remains. Thus we shall not deny altogether that our Lord wills our crimes, nor altogether that he does not will them. For although he does not refuse to let saints sin—which occurs for the growth of humility—nevertheless [Col. 0699A] he does not will them to persevere in sin. For just as, if he did not will it, sinning would not occur, so, if he wills it, escape from evil occurs. That the supremely good wills good things and that his will is effective, I think no one doubts unless he does not know that “every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17). Therefore, whoever falls when overthrown, that person’s rising again was not willed by him whose will cannot be frustrated.

But since we see that he does not will this at all, shall we say that he does not will it? Yet if he does not will the sinner to be converted, does he will him not to be converted? Both alternatives are most wicked; who doubts that both are devilish? For it is as unjust for a criminal not to be converted as it is just for him to be converted. The one who chose that the devout person should be converted [Col. 0699B] has, because he preferred that the impious person should not be converted, weighed the reversal of their lot in an equal balance.

It is therefore established that God does not will everything which, if it happened, would appear good; but those things which he wills and which do not yet exist he causes to subsist, or, if they already subsist, he does not permit to perish. Similarly, we know that he does not will only those evils from which, in his providence, he preserves his own so that they do not occur, or from which, if they occur, he himself mercifully delivers them.

Nevertheless, we know that whatever reason approves and whatever divine speech commands is pleasing to God; and that all else which opposes either reason or authority is to be judged displeasing, without condemning customs by a merely arbitrary judgment. These things indeed displease God because he forbids them and makes them displeasing to the minds of the saints; [Col. 0699C] those are called dear because he commands them and makes them lovable to the saints.

Was it not pleasing to God that Jesus should die, He who ordained that the world should be redeemed by his blood? Or how was he made obedient to the Father unto death (Phil. 2:8), unless, mindful of the Father’s will, he patiently endured all things even to the cross? But if it pleased the Father that the Son should die, then he willed that he should be killed only by the Jews, lest he should have willed something else in vain, since nothing else occurred. [Note: [Col. 0699D] The Master, *Sentences*, book I, distinction 48, §3.] [Note: [Col. 0699D] See Augustine on Psalm 93.] Shall we say that the Father willed concerning the Son only that he should die, but had no will as to how this was to take place? Yet that would belong to an improvident will, not a divine one—especially since not being killed, but killing, is more often reckoned a fault. Therefore, since he willed him to die, and there is no guilt in this, he also willed him to be killed. But if he willed Jesus to be killed by the Jews, did he not have to will that the Jews should kill Jesus? For how could the faithless have done this unless he himself had willed it, Jesus saying to Pilate: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11)?

Therefore God gives the faithless power to commit their crime; nor would he give it unless he willed it. Why, too, is the Father said to have handed over the Son, unless because he willed that he should be handed over? To be killed by persecutors, in whatever manner, is never a fault; indeed, it is often a virtue worthy of heaven, “because precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:15). But no one is ignorant that killing the saints is an outrage, who foresees the torments of those who kill them. Let God, then, will that Christ be killed, because this is most holy; but let God never will that anyone kill Christ, because this is utterly wicked. For just as he without whose will nothing good happens, while all evil things happen, wills that the good be killed by the evil, so that patience may be crowned, so he does not will that the evil kill the good, so that injustice may be exacted.

He does indeed will that a human being be able to do evil, because the ability to do evil is not a vice, just as the ability to do good is not a virtue. Rather, the ability to do evil is good in the one who was able to transgress and did not transgress; for one who did not act merely because he could not, is neither to be blamed in the good nor praised in the evil. Likewise, one who, although able, did not act is either happily good with respect to evil or wrongly evil with respect to good. Thus let the power of evildoers be pleasing—as a good power—while their will and its effect are displeasing.

## Chapter XIII. How God finds, judges, or rewards according to merits

We have said that one washed in the sacrament of baptism is free from guilt before attaining discernment; let us also say that an adult, though foreknown for Gehenna, is worthy of salvation while living well. That such a person at some time lives well Scripture attests, declaring that if the righteous man abandons his righteousness, “he shall die in his unrighteousness” (Ezek. 18:24). And that he is at some time good, and worthy of heaven so long as his goodness endures, the Lord openly teaches, saying: “Behold, your names are written in heaven.” Many of these afterward “turned back” (Luke 10:20).

Providence encompasses the outcomes of things; judgment measures the present life. [Note: [Col. 0700D] Ambrose on Romans, chapter 9.] Hence the Lord says: “Where I find you, there I shall judge you,” as though he said: “I shall consider, when I judge, neither what you have been nor what you will be, but above all what I find you to be.” Thus one whom foreknowledge assigns to hell according to future things, judgment often inscribes in heaven according to present things; for if he should happen to die in the meantime, he would unquestionably receive the reward due to salvation. Likewise, one whom God has predestined by right, if death should snatch him away while he remains uncorrected in wicked deeds, would be unworthy of his homeland and would live as an exile in hell with the devil, from whom, while he remains proudly uncorrected, the unceasing wrath of God exacts unending torments.

[Col. 0700D] Does the supremely good Creator, then, knowingly love his creature, though supremely evil, hating its Maker and every good thing, as though moved by fatherly compassion, when the very production of the deed is evidence of hatred? Or shall I say that he loves one whom he does not allow to perish, but rather that he hates one whom he preserves for torments? Or is love apparent in this: that he moderates by mercy the punishment which he inflicts by justice, according to the saying, “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:11)? But if he loves the one whose punishment he relaxes through gentleness, surely he hates still more the one whose eternal misery he prolongs through severity. For he imposes torments more strictly than he mitigates them gently: “Judgment without mercy [shall be] for him who has not shown mercy” (James 2:13).

But if “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth,” that is, judgment, how is this way—namely, punishment imposed upon the wicked—judgment together with mercy? Shall I say that mercy is present, but as though asleep, as though lukewarm, because divine severity burns watchfully against the wicked, and therefore the judgment is without mercy because mercy is so slight as to be practically nonexistent? Or rather, must this saying of the Lord be held plainly according to the letter? Hence in the Prophet: “When his wrath shall have been kindled shortly,” etc. (Ps. 2:12). [Note: [Col. 0701D] The Ordinary Gloss there, from Cassiodorus.] For, according to the exposition of this passage, the wrath of God against the reprobate is said to be kindled at judgment because there is then no patience in him. But if in punishing he will have no patience, what place remains for mercy? And how will he love one upon whom he does not have mercy? But if he does not love the lost human being, still less does he love the devil.

The authority commenting on the prophetic text which says, “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth,” explains the verse, “You are near, O Lord, and all your ways are truth” (Ps. 118:51), as follows: “Toward all whom God delivers and condemns, all his ways are mercy and truth; because where he does not show mercy, the truth of vengeance is deservedly given, since he condemns no one undeserving, but delivers many undeserving persons.” [Note: [Col. 0701D] Gloss there, from Augustine on Psalm 118.] Therefore all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, because none of his works exists except from one or the other of these: thus in this life the wicked are awaited through mercy and converts are corrected, and in the future [Col. 0701C] both receive an equitable recompense through justice, because “he will render to each according to his works” (Ps. 61:13).

But if “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18), since mercy supplies what works have not attained—“for his mercy is forever” (Ps. 135:1)—how does God render future goods according to works? No one would receive these goods in greater or lesser measure unless he had first merited differently. Thus the kingdom of heaven belongs not to the giver but to the receiver (John 14:2); thus, “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (ibid.). Yet, because no one’s merits, being small and temporal, would suffice, the merciful God completes what merit begins.

[Col. 0701D] But if the good life of this age, because it is both brief and small, would not be recompensed with eternity unless through the generosity of the giver, why is a worldly fault exacted by everlasting punishment? [Note: [Col. 0701D] Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 44.] Does justice supply what guilt did not merit? But this is not the character of justice, which renders to each what is his own, but rather of tyranny, which oppresses through violent domination. Yet just as present good acquires future good, through God’s mercy and through his judgment, though hidden, so the sin of the world, which will come to an end, claims for itself infinite torments when the supremely just Judge judges, while concealing his justice from us—unless the Lord testifies: “He who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than John” (Matt. 11:11). After this life charity and holiness are perfected, so that they may be worthy of blessedness, and may persevere perfectly, so that they may be worthy of eternity, according to the saying: “He who loves eternally merits eternally to possess what he loves”; consult this on the passage, “Your statutes [I have inclined my heart to perform] forever, because of the recompense” (Ps. 118:112).

[Note: [Col. 0702D] Ordinary Gloss, from Augustine.] On the other hand, malice begun here, accumulated there, and thereafter never to be diminished, merits punishment—and this without end. For just as goodness, by God’s gift, so also malice, by its own guilt, merits a greater recompense, both now and especially in the future, weighed according to the quantity of merits. Since we are inclined toward evil, guilt suffices for this; but because we are weak in good, merits do not suffice for it. The former suffices and the latter does not, because to the latter is repaid far more than is due, while to the former only what it deserves. If this is so, both the lost person and the saved person plainly have a recompense, not only for what each did in the body, but also for what each does after the body: one in heaven, the other in hell.

But the Apostle seems opposed to this when he asserts that at judgment “each shall receive the things proper to the body, according to what he has done” (2 Cor. 5:10). “Proper,” because no one will be judged for another’s acts; “to the body,” because not for things done outside it; “according to what he has done,” because God examines deeds already performed, not future ones.

In this examination the will is chiefly investigated, and whatever is done is assessed according to its nature. But it is very strange if the will of this age deserves recompense but the future will does not, although then it is shown to be much better in good and worse in evil. For if, like angels, human beings were never changed in will and were never to be changed by death, the latter would receive misery and the former happiness, and both continuously because of the continuance of their will. Surely everyone would say that what is properly done in human beings is what they do not deny to be properly done in angels. Now, because the will precedes death and the eternal will of which we speak succeeds it in both groups, will it therefore lack recompense? Or rather, will the temporal will obtain recompense for the eternal will? For the passing will is the cause of the enduring will.

## Chapter XIV. What we merit here we shall receive in the future

[Note: [Col. 0702D] See Isidore of Seville’s book *Differentiae*.] We must therefore know that this state of our mortality has found in this world a fitting middle place between sorrow and joy; and this world itself has been placed between heaven and hell. Here we are neither tortured by hell’s grief nor gladdened by heaven’s delight. Rather, in comparison with hell, we reign as though in heaven; in comparison with heaven, we live as exiles as though in hell. Hence descent and ascent lie before us: we descend through ourselves and ascend through God. Whichever of these two extremes you attain, you will remain there and will be unable to avoid either one. Therefore this life is for meriting; the future life is for receiving. We act in the body so that after the body, and again when the body has been received, we may receive things corresponding to our deserts.

Thus the apostolic statement mentions only those human merits that introduce either rest or misery, though those who have entered do not cease to merit the continuance of misery or of rest. What we worthily do in this life are called merits; what we will in the other life are more properly called rewards of merits. Present things are indeed the cause of future things. To this life I assign action; to the other, will. For after death, when the activity of works has ceased, thought alone will remain.

Therefore in adults punishment endures deservedly because guilt does not depart. But why will the little child, who has contracted a stain only from origin and none from personal act, be afflicted with everlasting torment? Is this also among the hidden things of the Son? But if one who has committed no sin is so crushed, what will happen to one who offends throughout the whole day? Before the severe Judge of original guilt, such a child is, though secretly yet justly, proscribed to the region of the perishing. And for those who perish, perpetuity of punishment, as I have said, entails perpetuity of guilt; perhaps this also applies to little children. [Note: [Col. 0703D] See the notes toward the end of chapter 6 of this part.]

For a little child, taken out of the prison of the flesh and now master of himself, either enters into free reason or, as though still in the flesh, will continue to lack freedom of choice. Shall, then, a rational spirit never have the use of reason? But “the body weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation burdens the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15). Therefore when the soul is stripped of body and bodily habitation, it will also be stripped of the burden which flesh brings; and, its intellect freed after the human condition, it will think of intelligible things. What is plainly so in the little child who is saved, must also plainly be fitting in the one who is lost. Either, therefore, he will have charity and, by merit worthy of heaven, will be held in hell; or he will not have it, and no one should any longer doubt that he is justly deprived of joy.

If these foregoing points are so, then beyond doubt God’s justice toward his saints is joined with clemency, while toward the reprobate there is justice alone without clemency. But if his mercy is never without justice, how is his justice found without mercy? For just as he does not show mercy unjustly, so it is unfitting that he should judge cruelly.

Yet it should be noted that when the Lord, in his goodness, converts an ungodly man who has regard for no good manner of life, and when he purposes in his mercy to save the innocence of infancy made at peace with God through regeneration, he appears not to follow the balance of justice but the sweetness of mercy. For if he attended to the scale of judgment, he would recompense the ungodly with nothing other than what is worthy of his merits—namely, hell—and he would not recompense infancy with heaven, since it has no power to merit anything. But now, weighing the goodness of both against their poverty, he prefers to employ mercy rather than judgment. Therefore it must be confessed, since it is truly so, that in some cases he does not punish as justice requires, because the matter is treated more gently by mercy; such is the case when the ungodly person is justified. For it was just that, since he is in filth, he should “be filthy still”; but mercifully he is cleansed from filth.

But just as the soothing consolations of mercy exclude this sort of severity of justice, so other cases admit the scale of justice and find no gentleness. Hence: “Judgment without mercy for him who has not shown mercy” (James 2:13). Yet some things proceed jointly from mercy and justice, as when something is given according to merits; but because merits do not suffice, grace assists. By this means the righteous attain eternal life.

Perhaps you will think it presumptuous to assert that God does something that is not a work of justice; then judge it presumptuous also to affirm that God does something that is not a work of mercy. For to consider him either harsh or unjust is impious in either case. But if he does that in which he employs not mercy but justice alone, what wonder if he does that in which he employs not justice but mercy alone? [Note: [Col. 0704D] The Master, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 46, toward the end.] He always possesses both, but in doing certain things he proceeds from one, certain things from the other, and other things, as has been said, from both.

What then shall we say? Is not whatever God does just, and whatever he does merciful? Certainly, indeed, he does nothing unjust and nothing unmerciful. Is it therefore also certain that whatever he does is just and merciful, as this appears to mean: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:4)? But if this is so, how was it said that one thing proceeds from justice alone and another from mercy? If, I say, every work of God is just and merciful, how is one produced by judgment and the other by piety, rather than both by both? Perhaps whatever is done by God is called just and merciful because it is holy and good, not because it is just in the sense that nothing happens except what judgment requires—lest the wicked should not be converted and little children should not be saved. Likewise, it is not merciful in the sense that he exercises piety everywhere—lest judgment without mercy never occur for the one who has not shown mercy.

When this takes place, he bestows no mercy, yet without cruelty, because through justice he tortures the wicked. For what harshness is there in rendering to merits their due? Or, if it is disgraceful that the guilty person should suffer while the judge does not show mercy, then surely the wrath which they have merited by their own wickedness is softened by his own goodness. It is softened, I say, because he is kind; but he punishes because he is just: with a very slight mitigation, because they did not show mercy; but with the greatest punishment, because they so deserved.

Certainly he could spare even the worst person, after first making him righteous. Yet it would not accord with equity unless he repaid the persistently wicked person according to merit. Nevertheless, he who gives precedence to justice could spare even this person through mercy, but does not will to, lest he be thought the author of the wicked; hence he says: “You wickedly supposed that I should be like you; I will rebuke you,” etc. (Ps. 49).

But in whatever way he shows mercy, what sort of mercy will it be where love is absent? Does he perhaps, as he is angry with the diligent persons whom he disciplines and yet does not hate them, so show mercy to the wicked persons whom he somewhat spares and yet does not love them? Certainly that penitent prophet fears this anger when he prays: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury”—that is, do not destroy me in judgment—“nor correct me in your wrath” (Ps. 6:1): do not, after this life, burn away the rust of my vices by purgatorial fire; cut and burn here instead; I cannot endure correction in the future. That anger is medicinal, for healing, from which salvation is expected; but that mercy is shown to the sick person whose cure is despaired of—not because the physician is powerless, but because the sick person is rejected as unworthy.

For if he willed, he would heal; but he would will it if he loved. For if he loved, he would will good to the beloved; otherwise, how would he love one to whom he willed either not-good or even evil? But if he willed good to him, good would also come to him; otherwise the will of the Almighty would be ineffective, and calamity would torment one who desired something but failed of its accomplishment. But “he has done whatsoever he willed” (Ps. 113:3). His will is not one thing and his action another, lest he be rightly charged with weakness if his will, without the support of action, did not suffice for accomplishing things. Yet it does suffice: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 32:9). It is therefore clear that if the supreme Judge willed good for the condemned person, the condemned person would also be well.

But how can one whose condition is always evil will him good, if, though able to deliver him, he never wills to do so? For if he cannot free from misery one whom he loves, how is he free from sorrow? Or does he will him good only to the extent, not of delivering him altogether, but of diminishing his affliction? Yet the evil that remains is still so great that one can hardly be well who perceives no good and never finds any good in himself, one whom death feeds upon. Or shall I say that he is well, though he himself never perceives it? But what good is such a good? Thus he is both well and ill: if well, let him rejoice; but because he is ill, let him grieve. Yet Scripture knows no rejoicing in Gehenna, but rather mourning: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 8:12). [Note: [Col. 0705D] The Master, book IV, distinction 46.] I therefore think it must be confessed that the miserable person is not well.

Yet I will neither stubbornly deny nor rashly affirm that the condemned person—especially one utterly wicked—is miserable, but less ill than his merits require. [Note: [Col. 0705D] He hesitates with Augustine on Psalm 105, “For his mercy is forever,” and with *City of God*, book XXI, chapter 24: they acknowledge the balance of rigorous justice even in the condemned. Jerome, at the end of book II on Ezekiel 7; the author of the homily on the words of David, “Who am I?” among the works of Chrysostom; nor do several scriptural authorities contribute little. Augustine, however, *City of God*, XXI.24, judges that God punishes less than is deserved.] [Col. 0705D] But if the wicked person is less ill, the good Judge has willed him to be less ill; yet not well, because his condition is only evil. What reasoning, however, compels us to confess that God either wills or makes the condemned person less ill, when he renders to each according to merits? For if he renders less, then in rendering he does not reach the full extent of merits; how, then, does he render according to them? He renders to the good according to their merits, because he gives as much as they have merited and adds from grace. Therefore, he has not loved the person to whom he has willed less ill—and thus ill. But as he has loved the one to whom he wills good, so he has hated the one to whom he wills evil. It is evident that he wills evil for one whom he has destined to the fires of Gehenna.

Will a human being, then, love one whom God hates? Indeed, evangelical authority says concerning the devil: “No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one,” that is, the devil, “and love the other” (Matt. 6:24), that is, God—and such a person is commended by the authorities; “or he will cling to the one,” namely the demon, “and despise the other,” namely the Lord—and such a person is censured. Therefore each person rightly hates the adversary of the human race, whom he knows God has consigned to hatred. It is therefore clear that the Lord hates one whom it is not permitted for the servant to love. For if the Lord loved him, a servant who knew his lord’s will yet did not do it would be beaten (Luke 12:47). The Lord himself would also deceive his servant wickedly, if he persuaded him to hate one beloved by himself, and enviously loved one whom he preferred others to hate.

Therefore I, a servant, will hate one whom the Lord hates; I will will evil for one for whom the Lord wills evil. For one whom he wills to be ill now and worse in the future, I too will will likewise. Hence in the Psalmist: “You who love the Lord, hate evil” (Ps. 96:10), namely, the devil. For how am I to love him? Shall I desire that, once converted, he be restored to heaven? Shall I knowingly resist the divine will? Shall I desire that his torments be eased even in part? In vain: hardened wickedness does not permit it. Shall I demand pardon for wickedness? He is unrepentant; I shall not obtain it. Rather, I shall provoke the Just One against myself, while, insofar as lies in me, by the abominable devotion of prayers and by the impious offering of devotion, I turn what is just toward injury. Certainly God can suspend the punishment of the unworthy, as he often does temporarily; but no pardon is due in any way to an unrepentant mind. I think this must be said of demons, and also of human beings—but of those whom we already know to have been received into hell, weighed down by crimes and overtaken by a most evil death.

[Note: [Col. 0706D] The Master, book IV, distinction 45, §2 and following distinction; Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 110, in reply to Dulcitius; the question of Damasus concerning prayer for the dead; Chrysostom, Homily 3 on the Epistle to the Philippians; Prudentius, etc., as in the notes.] For perhaps the merits of the living can alleviate in some respect the punishments of the lost, if, as some maintain in their opinion, the person merited this in his previous life. What shall I say about those who are wicked in this life and, because of their wickedness, are to perish after this life? God’s hatred toward them is certainly plain; but will ours also be plain? They are our brothers; we have a common Father in heaven, to whom together we cry: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. 6:9), namely God; and one common father on earth, from whom we all are born, namely the first human being. Shall I hate my brother? But “he who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). Shall I not love him? But “he who does not love his brother remains in death” (1 John 3:14). Shall I reject my brother, made an enemy to me? But the Lord commands us to love enemies (Matt. 5:44).

The Apostle instructs us in all things to discern what the will of God is (Rom. 12:2); for among all things this alone ought to please the servant: what he finds that his Lord wills. But the Lord wills to destroy evil persons miserably (Matt. 21:41); will the destruction of evil persons therefore not please the servant? But how will he love his brothers if he wills them to be condemned? Or if he does not will this for his brothers, does he not despise the Lord whose will he opposes?

While we live on earth, in the land of the living, we do not prejudge to destruction even the end of the most wicked, which is known to God but unknown to us; for we hope that their life may be changed for the better. [Note: [Col. 0707D] Augustine, *City of God*, XXI.24.] According to the Apostle, who says: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls to his own lord; but he shall stand” (Rom. 14:4). For if their end were not hidden, it would not be fitting to dissent from the divine judgment. Nor do we dissent from it in every respect, since he himself wills that we should dissent in this way: he “wills all persons to be saved and none to perish” (1 Tim. 2:4), [Note: [Col. 0707D] Augustine, *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 15; *City of God*, XXII.1, etc.] not in himself, since “he has done whatsoever he willed,” but in all those whom he causes to will in such a manner that a pious affection may move the pious Judge to pardon the ungodly, as we read that blessed Stephen, in the very slaughter inflicted by those stoning him, obtained pardon by prayer for his persecutor Paul.

God indeed foreknew from eternity that he would cleanse the unclean; but he also prepared within himself the means of amendment, the intercession of the saints.

Therefore, while the will of God is hidden, let us will what accords with love for our brothers. When the will of God has been revealed, let it draw all hearts to itself. Hence in heaven there will be perfect blessedness, where the Lord and the servant will not will different things, according to the saying: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 114:9). It is as though he said: “Here, in the land of the dying, I do not please him, where through both ignorance and weakness I will something other than he wills; but there I shall please him, because I shall not displease in my own will, which will be his.” Hence Father Abraham, at peace in rest, says to those troubled in fire: “A great chasm has been fixed between you and us” (Luke 16:26). This is not because the good there do not see the wicked, but because they do not pass over to them through compassion; because a father or mother in heaven will not grieve for a son or daughter in hell; because the most just vengeance of God will not displease the most just. Otherwise, how will God “wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Rev. 7:17), if misery does not cease even there? For grief is misery, which is customarily called the cause of tears. [Note: [Col. 0707D] Thus Augustine, *City of God*, XX.22; Gregory, *Morals*, XXXIII.19 and XXXIV.16; Thomas Aquinas, *Commentary on IV Sentences*, distinction 50, questions 2 and 4.] But there is there neither pain nor mourning.

“He who does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18). Hence it is clear that both Jews and Gentiles who depart this life without faith are assigned to torments without hope; as the Lord also testifies: “Many are called, few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16). Because among Christians they have multiplied beyond number, do we not hate those many whom we know the Lord has rejected?

But the above-mentioned position will no longer stand: that the Lord inspires the saints to will that “all persons be saved and none perish” (1 Tim. 2:4), and the text will require another explanation. Or shall we say that in the Church, from its beginning until its completion, many are called and few chosen; but whether all those living together are predestined to life or not will remain uncertain to us? Thus it is permissible—indeed necessary—to desire their salvation, and the aforementioned text requires no other explanation. But if, as seems more likely, throughout the whole time of the Church many are called and few chosen, we shall explain it thus: God wills all to be saved—that is, none to perish—not in himself, certainly, but, as has been said, in his own people. For there is no one whom they will to perish, since there is no one whose salvation they do not will.

But since the Church, although the time is unknown, is nevertheless not doubted to contain very many who are at last to be vomited out, if it happens that we love some of these—perhaps many—as our contemporaries, do we not unknowingly hate with the Lord the multitude of the reprobate whom, knowingly, we love? Thus, looking at an army from afar, I see persons known among unknown persons; but though I see them indiscriminately, I do not know that I see them. Thus, seeing meadows green with flowers and fields wave in the breeze, we marvel; and though we do not doubt that we see flowers here and ears of grain there, we doubt whether we have seen this particular flower or that particular ear. Thus we know many things without knowing that we know them, and can do things without knowing that we can do them—both of which we prove by experience. The ruin of the bodies of the ungodly unto the grave and of their souls unto hell has often been revealed to the godly by a prophetic spirit.

But did they not will what they perceived the Lord to will? Certainly they did, those whom we often read invoking curses upon persons destined for destruction—not through venom of mind, but in agreement with God. For I think that no one loves a sinner except when it is unknown that God hates him; for the good man wills to love all except those whom he knows God hates.

Thus he wills all human beings to be saved and no one of this age to perish; that is, he makes his saints will all, unless someone has become known to them as belonging unfavorably to that people. If someone loves persons foreknown by God for death, but while they live almost unknown to human beings, not in order that they be granted heaven but that, by the merit of charity, they may be tortured more tolerably—perhaps few will understand this. Yet it is a very slight love that neither bestows good nor removes evil, but merely lessens it; for the force of love must be reserved for the predestined. [Col. 0708D] But in this way it happens that the same persons are knowingly loved and hated.

For my part, I would find it difficult to believe that anyone loves one for whom he does not will blessedness but does will endless misery; but I would readily admit that one may feel compassion. For just as it sometimes happens that we are angry with friends, so we may have compassion on enemies. Hence the Lord, “seeing the city, wept over it” (Luke 19:41), a city to be destroyed by a twofold crushing.

## Chapter XV. On God’s omnipotence

[Note: [Col. 0708D] The Master, book I, distinctions 42–44.] God is omnipotent. Yet, as reason has it, although there are countless things he cannot do—such as lie, deny himself, and the like—he is omnipotent precisely because he cannot do these things. He is therefore omnipotent in such a way that he can do absolutely nothing that would be done irrationally and wickedly. Nor can he be unable to do anything that can fittingly be ordered by him. He is conspicuous in the prerogative of power: he can do whatever is fitting, lest he be marked as weak; he cannot do whatever is unfitting, lest in any respect the power for evil obscure the strength of good, and lest he diminish insofar as he approaches perversity. Hence every creature, compared with God, is weak.

But lest omnipotence should break out anywhere into unlawful acts, it is fitting that the Omnipotent should not only know all things, but also foreknow them: “his wisdom is without number” (Ps. 146:5). This wisdom is ignorant of a beginning just as it is of increase; for if it ever grew or began, it would have advanced in knowledge. But what reason could there be for his knowing something later but not earlier? As the Evangelist says: “What was made, in him was life” (John 1:4). [Note: [Col. 0709D] Augustine, tractate on Psalm 44, and elsewhere.] It is as though he said: Whatever comes to be in time lived in his knowledge before time.

Therefore it is necessary that whatever God’s providence comprehends together without beginning should also be carried out by his truth in its proper times. For if he neglected to fulfill something which, in foreseeing it, he promised would occur, then the Lord, who is “faithful in all his words” (Ps. 144:13), would become a liar. And because every ordinance of God is, by reason of his constancy, called an oath, if he changed anything he would be both a liar and perjurer, and therefore would not be God. Accordingly, whatever act done precipitately would nullify the integrity of divine providence would appear evil and irrational; but, as was said above, God cannot do whatever is done irrationally.

If, then, whatever was otherwise than God ordained would be irrational, and he can do nothing irrational, it is clear that he can do nothing except what the truth of providence contains. But he foreknew nothing except what occurs; therefore he can do nothing except what happens. Indeed, he can do nothing except what he wills and does. For he determined to do only what he brings about through his will. These four things, then, are bound together by such a bond that they neither abandon nor exceed one another: the power of divine action is equal to providence, and will is made equal to power together with action. Hence they say that God’s power is not greater than his will.

But if I say that God could have foreseen otherwise the things which he now foresees as they are, so that according to that providence he could freely will and do something other than he now wills and does—this indeed would, according to what that providence would then have contained, be good and rational; but according to what now is, it is evil and irrational.

You reply: No place for another providence could have preceded the one God now has, because he never existed without this one; nor is it fitting that he should have had both at once, since they would contend with one another. If, then, God’s ordering cannot either first ordain things otherwise than they occur, or later change what has been ordained, how are the zeal of the saints and salvation in return for their zeal, and the perversity of the ungodly and hell in return for it, rightly assigned respectively to grace and divine justice? What grace or justice is there when, whether he ordains or brings about what has been ordained, he can change nothing on either side? We would recognize grace and justice if, when he preferred this, he were no less able to prefer the other.

Do I see anything other than the force of necessity, when he could never give Peter the power to deny, nor Judas persevering grace? He found both in filth, but could not deliver either. He saw Judas fixed in the mire, but could accomplish nothing by drawing him out. He drew Peter to himself because he could not leave him in the mud. In regard to none of the things I have done or shall do, nor of those from which I have ceased or shall cease—whether they are good or evil—does he have any power either to assist them to be, or to prevent them from being.

How, then, is he omnipotent, if he lacks the power to be present to someone in such a way that the person, helped, does a good he was going to omit or omits an evil he was going to do? It follows that I have become either wholly ungrateful, or less grateful, to my Creator, since he bestows on me what he cannot withhold.

But you will say: “You ought to give thanks because, although he cannot do otherwise, he does not do what he can unwillingly.” Yet in that case I give thanks not so much for the deed, since he cannot avoid it, as for the will; but neither do I give thanks earnestly for that, because he cannot avoid even it. For we are accustomed to give thanks to one who confers a benefit on us in such a way that, if he wishes, he can withdraw his hand. For one who gives under compulsion has neither retained the thing nor earned gratitude.

Perhaps you will say: “God too, if he wills, may act otherwise than he does; but even if he wills it, he cannot be allowed to give his will effect; otherwise the order of providence in the soul would totter toward collapse, and God, stained by the mark of falsehood, could no longer be God. Nor would it be fitting for him to will anything of the sort which providence has ruled out as future; and it has ruled out whatever does not occur. Therefore he wills nothing except what will happen, concerning which it is established that ‘he has done whatsoever he willed’ (Ps. 113:3).” [Note: [Col. 0709D] Augustine, *City of God*, XIV.19; IV *Against Julian*, 14; *On Rebuke and Grace*, 11; *On the Gift of Perseverance*, 7; *Enchiridion*, 107; V *Against Julian*, 16. Likewise, *On Rebuke and Grace*, 12, and concerning the fifth article falsely attributed to him.]

Yet human nature was so created [Col. 0710D] that, though it is stirred toward vice by no incentive at all, it nevertheless has within itself the capacity for evil. But it can neither avoid evil, nor will good, nor, when it has willed it, bring it to completion, unless the Lord assists it. For because it is not sufficient for a person to avoid evil by himself, one who trusts in the Lord alone says: “Remove from me the way of iniquity” (Ps. 108:29). But that the inclination toward good comes from the Lord God, he adds: “Incline my heart unto thy testimonies” (ibid.). Already anticipated by good will, but still needing to be brought to completion in good work, he pours out prayer to God and says: “Establish thy word unto thy servant in thy fear” (ibid.). For the word is established [Col. 0711A] through the Lord when, through him, the meaning of the word is fulfilled in action; and when the Lord instills fear of himself, he applies it as a spur against sloth.

Thus the first man, abusing the freedom of his choice, transgressed. But could God protect him from transgressing? He could not, since he can do nothing except what happens. Therefore, since man does not have it from nature—unless God cooperates—to avoid guilt (for avoidance of guilt is a great power, especially where evil will is concerned), and since every power is from the Lord God, “coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17), the Lord saying to his disciples, “Without me ye can do nothing” (John 15:5)—nothing good, certainly, but only what is evil—why did Adam incur guilt when he admitted what was forbidden, though he never possessed from himself the effective power of avoiding [Col. 0711B] harmful things, unless God protected him? Yet God could not protect him, because he had foreknown otherwise. Therefore either human beings bear no guilt, or, if there is any, it must be thrown back upon the Creator.

But perhaps you will say: “Although divine power was unable to secure a sinner against sinning, nevertheless God bestowed grace by whose use he could remain unharmed.” A remarkable matter! God is able to begin a benefit, but unable to complete what he has begun. And what I consider monstrous: a little child, destined even then to reign, but destined in adulthood to sin and therefore finally to be damned, nevertheless received grace by which he was capable of living holily and, through holiness, of reigning with God. Consider the wonder: although God neither wills nor can preserve a saint, nor make one whom he has preserved blessed, lest, as has often been said, foreknowledge prove false [Col. 0711C], that little child can both persevere in innocence and obtain eternal life, whether God wills it or not.

The same line of reasoning may be applied to him who was made an angel by God and a devil by himself. God, the supremely blessed source of every good, against whose omnipotence nothing can stand, so endured the ruin of human nature in justice that he also provided its restoration in mercy: restoration through the incarnation of the Word. When by grace alone he predestined it, he showed himself merciful; more merciful when he consolingly promised what he had foreseen within himself; most merciful when, by redeeming, he fulfilled what he had promised. But if, as has been said, neither foreknowledge nor things foreknown can turn aside in another direction, God could not free man otherwise than by the Incarnation [Col. 0711D] from Satan’s yoke; nor could he defend the man whom he assumed either from the insults of mockers or from the cruelty of those crucifying him, though that man himself was able to escape these things.

Therefore let us be grateful to the servant rather than to the Lord. The servant could, the Lord could not, refuse us salvation. He who could because he willed it conferred the benefit; he who did not will it and could not, as though yielding to necessity, complied with necessity. For, just as it was necessary for God to exist, so it was necessary for him to redeem the world. He did indeed will both to exist and to redeem; but he could avoid neither the one nor the other.

What astonishing misery, if he who was God could not escape such a shameful passion [Col. 0712A], and finally such a disgraceful death. What astonishing impotence, if he could not restore lost man except by dying. Yet he could, since according to [Note: [Col. 0711D] Augustine, XXVIII *Against Faustus*; *On the Agony of Christ*, ch. 10 and following; XIII *On the Trinity*, ch. 18.] authority another way was possible to God, though none was more suited to our weakness. For, exercising most just power and stripping the devil of tyrannical dominion, he could by his command alone have recalled his servants, whom the devil had led away as fugitives by deceptive promises. [Note: [Col. 0711D] Athanasius, *Oration* 3 *Against the Arians*; Leo, Sermon 2, *On the Nativity*; Bernard, Epistle 190, etc.] But he preferred to display humility to those seeking power, and to reveal his affection to those who would serve him: made man as a vigorous traveler, offering guidance to his followers and preparing them beforehand by word and example.

Therefore God, who preferred this manner and had very many others ready at hand, and the Lord Jesus, showing the twelve [Col. 0712B] apostles that he had no need of them for his defense, testifies that he could ask his Father, who would supply him, in place of the twelve apostles, twelve legions of angels (Matt. 26:53) to fight on his behalf against the cruelty of the Jews. The Son says this in vain if his Father cannot do it. But if he can do it—as he truly can—he can do something which he never wills and never does.

Therefore, supported by evangelical authority and proceeding from one particular case to other particulars by analogy, let us maintain that God can do innumerable things which he does not will. Yet because in this life it is difficult, or altogether impossible, for us to explain by reasoning how God can be able to do something which he does not will, some great man said concerning the future life—not this present life: “Then we shall see how many things God can do and does not will.” [Note: [Col. 0712D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 95.]

For divine providence knows, and we also know on Scripture’s teaching, that Christ will destroy Antichrist. Therefore, if he were to save Antichrist, then, beyond doubt, given the present state of affairs, he would render his providence false. Hence it appears that, if he can save Antichrist, he can render his providence false. For to save Antichrist would be to render providence false; but he can save Antichrist, since it is established that he can do all things. Can he, then, deceive himself? Far be it! For the premise of this inference is both highly plausible and full of deception: a true antecedent produces a false consequent.

I think the answer should be this: whenever it is said, “If God can act otherwise than he has foreseen, then he can be deceived” [Col. 0712D], this seems to follow because to act otherwise would be to be deceived. He can indeed act otherwise, because he could also have foreseen otherwise. For if another providence could not exist, neither could anything happen otherwise; otherwise, if something could happen which could not beforehand be foreseen, then something could certainly be done by God without foresight and without prior deliberation. But every work of God begins, while his prior deliberation of the work precedes its beginning, because “what was made in him was life” (John 1:4). Therefore he can act otherwise by following another providence which has always existed; yet he cannot falsify this providence which now exists, which would then never have existed.

Therefore [Col. 0713A] he cannot act otherwise in such a way that this providence has existed and is left unfulfilled, which is impossible. But he can act otherwise in such a way that, without this providence, another existed and was fulfilled not as what actually is, but as what could be; and this is not impossible.

Therefore I think this distinction must be employed: none of those things which are known to be shameful in themselves is worthy of being within God’s power, such as pride, envy, gluttony, and lust. Rather, only things which could be done honorably are possible for him, although divine providence judges that very many of these should be passed over. Such is the case of granting Judas persevering grace and denying it to Peter: both could have been done well, and it was well that neither was done. God can will and do things of this sort, but he will never will or do them, because he would will and do wrongly, solely because he has firmly resolved within himself that he would neither will nor do any of them. Thus he can do such things because, considered in themselves, they could be done honorably; but he does not will them because they would be contrary to his resolution.
