He can indeed do them well and honorably, because from eternity he could have foreseen that they would be done well and honorably.

But if he can will and act contrary to his resolution—and to will and act contrary to one’s resolution is plainly to will and act wrongly—does it not follow that he can will and act wrongly? Far be this also! This argument, veiled in deceptive plausibility, reveals its foulness to one who examines it inwardly, because through true concessions it intends to secure the concession of something false.

Perhaps you wonder whether God can will or do anything [Col. 0713C] contrary to his resolution. But what is it to will or act contrary to a resolution, except to will or act something other than what has been resolved? It is established that God can do this. But if acting contrary to a resolution means nullifying the resolution, then this certainly does not befit God.

I shall say more boldly: even today God can pour compunction into the devil and grant pardon to him when repentant, and salvation to him when making satisfaction. I shall add, most boldly, that in the one person who is Christ, divinity can separate itself from humanity and [p. 59] withdraw its grace from the humanity thus separated, so that now a mere man, without God, may fall into vice, and from vice into hell. To prevent that from ever happening, God bestowed a benefit indeed, but did not enclose his power within that benefit. For, without prejudice to justice, he can revoke a benefit that is known to have been bestowed not through the recipient’s merit but through the giver’s affection. That man indeed merited much, but by God’s power, not his own; so that if God renders what the man has merited from himself, but retains what he himself has wrought in the man, that man will have nothing in which to rejoice.

If he could mercifully have granted salvation to his adversary, he denied it—and will deny it—with most equitable severity. Do you still call grace the glory which the only Son of God bestowed upon the Son of Man? But how is it grace if it cannot be withdrawn? Yet it can. For the Prophet introduces the humanity speaking thus to the divinity united to it: “My God, do not be silent to me, lest I become like those [Col. 0714A] descending into the pit” (Ps. 27:1). “Do not be silent: do not separate from me the divinity which, while I possess it with me, leaves me ignorant of nothing by its own teaching. For if you are silent, when you separate yourself from me, personally united to me, I shall become like those descending into the pit”—those descending into the depth of iniquity and hell—“so that I may not differ in punishment from those with whom I have agreed in guilt.”

Jesus, the man who knew all things, would by no means ask this if it were impossible for divinity; but because it could happen, he obtained by obedience that it should not happen. Never fearing a fall from the height of his estate, he undoubtedly foreknew the constancy which he did not at all doubt that he would merit by the most holy obedience of his service.

Therefore God’s power embraces more than his will; though this is by no means fully clear, because if God can do something [Col. 0714B] which he neither wills nor foresees, he seems, as was said, capable of being contrary to himself. Yet power is not greater than will: for power and will are the same, because each is what God is. Thus, though God knows more than he teaches, knowledge does not exceed teaching in him; for each is God.

## Chapter XVI. On God’s providence

[Note: [Col. 0713D] Master, I, distinction 35.]

He could also have foreseen otherwise, since it is clear that he could have done otherwise, and did so. For as power acts freely according to choice, so the freedom of providence freely chose this or that, so that, just as power is brought to this effect which we know by will alone [Col. 0714C], so foreknowledge, compelled by no necessity, preferred this order of events which we shall see. Hence the Lord says: “You have not chosen me, but I have chosen you” (John 15:16). For what is election except the choosing of one portion from among different possibilities, made at pleasure?

This voluntary ordering of foreknowledge, as we said above, had no beginning and will have no end. Foreknowledge and ordering indeed cease to be called thus once that which was foreknown has occurred and passed; but they do not cease to be what they are. For what are foreknowledge and ordering but knowledge beforehand assigning its order to future things? But foreknowledge is altogether knowledge; and it is impious even to think that the Lord’s knowledge could fail in the least degree or be brought to the end of its existence [Col. 0714D], since, while things change, it comprehends the unstable in stable fashion:

> Boethius: “Remaining stable, it gives all things to move.”

Indeed, itself preceding future things, it accompanies present things and pursues things past, embracing all at once, by penetrating investigation, everything. For the divine eye surveys with present vision the entire multiplicity of things which have been and will be, so that all things are present to God according to the authority [Note: [Col. 0713] Augustine, in many places, but especially *To Orosius*, ch. 8.]—not by actual existence, but by the penetrating clarity of knowledge. For things occurring at different times cannot all exist simultaneously even for God. You cannot at once stand and act [Col. 0715A], be awake and asleep, be healthy and sick, be a child and an old man, or, finally, be alive and dead at one time.

God, therefore, is not mistaken where man is certain, so as to believe or see simultaneously things which cannot exist simultaneously. For where or when could he see such discordant things mingled together? But you, Adam, long ago reduced to ashes in body outside Paradise and content in spirit in heaven: how, though mortal, do you still eat forbidden fruit in Paradise before God? How, I ask, without your knowing it, are you now in hell without pain, just as earlier, unaware, you were in heaven without delight? Therefore all things of every time are present to God, not in such a way that they exist, but in such a way that they do not lie hidden from God any more than present things do.

Thus he is said to have made things which are future, not because their nature already existed, but because knowledge preceded them. And this knowledge, since it does not impose necessity of existence on past or present things, will not impose it upon future things either. Thus the prophets, God revealing it, know future things: does such knowledge compel them to exist? Likewise we, instructed by the renewal of things when the year regularly returns, foresee many things; but by foreseeing them we voluntarily supply no cause whereby future things subsist.

Therefore God’s providence comprehends even all future things. It sees evils only; it does not also cooperate with the doer, because “without him was nothing made” (John 1:2). Yet it permits them to occur because of the good that results from them. Thus, “the wicked lives for the righteous, just as the wicked is proud and the poor man is set on fire” (Ps. 9:23): that is, the poor man is inflamed with charity.

But God not only knows good things; he also acts with the one acting [Col. 0715C]. Hence it is said to God through the Prophet: “With the holy man thou wilt be holy” (Ps. 17:26), that is, “you will work holiness.”

But the person whom he wishes to help in good, he does not wish to compel, lest there be no merit in the human being and free choice perish. He so foreknows scourges and the varied changes of nature that he accomplishes what he has foreknown without us, because “he will strike and heal” (Hos. 6:2). “Thou hast milked me as milk and curdled me as cheese” (Job 10:10). And because “neither he that planteth is anything, nor he that watereth” (1 Cor. 3:7), he gives the increase. God therefore knows future things either as things done without him, such as guilt; or as things done with him, such as counsels of reason; or as things done through him, such as the works of nature.

[Col. 0715D] If God foreknew these future things in such a manner that he began providence at some time, deliberation would precede that beginning: among many possibilities, what would he judge most worthy of choosing? But because reason does not permit him to be older than his own providence, it is difficult to find in God a place for another providence. Indeed he has never had another providence, but reason proves that he could have had one. For what necessity would compel the omnipotent one to remain fixed upon arranging this way rather than another? And if an angel, from the moment it exists, does one thing and can do another, why may not God also, who is without end, from the moment he exists, foresee one thing and nonetheless be able to foresee another?

But if he can foresee what he has never foreseen, and thus know what he has never known—which is even more known to him than to us, since he is ignorant of nothing in our manner among all the things he can do or know [Col. 0716A]—can he begin to foresee or know anything? But just as his power cannot begin, neither can his knowledge. Whatever he can foresee though he has never foreseen it, or know though he does not yet know it, he can do so not in such a way as to have begun, but in such a way as to have foreseen, known, and willed it from eternity.

If defenders both of reason and of authority—for the same authority which compels us to hold that God can do more and has done fewer things also requires us to hold that whatever he can do, he could have foreseen—if, I say, persuaded by such reasoning, we say that God has foreknown things which are, in such a way that he could nonetheless have arranged in providence things which never are, then he always possesses this power of assigning existence to things which never subsist, with an unchangeable discrimination of outcomes. Thus, while he assigns Antichrist to perdition, he also has the power to assign him to salvation. For since he incessantly assigns him to damnation, either he can never foresee his salvation, or, while he foresees damnation, he possesses at the same time, together with that providence, the power of a contrary providence. It is like your retaining in sleep [p. 61] the power of waking, though you have no power to be awake while you sleep.

Does God likewise lack the power, while he foresees someone’s damnation, to foresee that same person’s salvation? You lack the power to be awake while asleep—that is, to do both simultaneously—yet you have the power to be awake when you are going to sleep; for nothing but will draws you into sleep, not necessity. Thus God likewise does not have the power to foresee both simultaneously, for that could not honorably occur on any account; nevertheless, he has the power to foresee one then when he will foresee the other. For the freedom of choice by which he is led to foresee in this manner at this particular time could also have led him, at that same time, to foresee not in this manner but otherwise. I say the same confidently concerning a past moment and a future moment.

But, if he previously had the power to foresee now otherwise than he foresees, does he also retain now the same power of foreseeing now otherwise than he foresees? Yet, since he now has one providence, if he can have its opposite along with it, he can have two contrary providences simultaneously. Therefore what he previously could do, he cannot now do. Thus he could formerly have made me, now deprived, king; but he cannot do so now. For how can he bring it about that the same thing both is and is not at the same time—namely, that I should at this instant both be and not be king? Likewise, a little while ago it was possible for God to end my life now; but now and afterwards it is impossible that I should die now.

I grant that God is of such power that, before the present moment, he can at that very present moment bring about whatever he pleases. But once the present, ordered by God, already is or has passed, I deny that God can bring to actuality in that present moment anything which did not pertain to that same present. [Note: [Col. 0717B] Augustine, XXVI *Against Faustus*, ch. 5.] In saying this, I do not detract from divine power, but show it to be most orderly. For it would resemble confusion—indeed, chaos would seem well ordered—if, together with his own ordering, he could introduce a contrary state concerning what is or is not. Therefore what happens cannot fail to happen, and what has been done cannot be undone.

Hence, according to Jerome [Note: [Col. 0717] In the letter to Eustochium, *On the Keeping of Virginity*. It is read differently in the printed editions; consult the notes.]: “Though God can do all things, he cannot restore a virgin after her fall. He can indeed free her from guilt, but he cannot make it the case that she was not corrupted.” Why? Because, as has been said, what has been done cannot not have been done.

Yet I think God’s power must be discussed cautiously, and we should assert not what he is able to do in himself, but what we judge concerning him [Col. 0717B]. For because it is apprehended by faith, we conjecture in darkness what it is like in itself. What is farther from our perception than that Christ’s body should remain whole in heaven, and yet be received every day by the faithful on earth—not piecemeal, but entirely whole—upon many altars? What could be more incredible to human perception than this? Yet nothing is truer to faith.

Like God’s knowledge and will, his power too has no beginning and lacks no end [Col. 0718A]; therefore whatever he can do, he can always do. For as, before a thing exists, he has the power to bring it into existence, so after it has existed he retains the same power by which he brought that thing into existence. And as, before something happens, it is possible for him to prevent the event, so after it has happened he no less has the possibility of having prevented it before it occurred.

But you will say: “After a thing has happened, he cannot make it not have happened.” I answer: he has never had the power to nullify his own will or leave things foreseen unfulfilled. He never has that power; and he never lacks this other power: with eternal will and endless knowledge, to will, foresee, and do not this thing which happens simultaneously, but another thing alone.

Likewise it is never possible for him, after something has once happened, later to bring it about that the deed was not done. Yet he always has the power, before it happens, to prevent anything happening at any time, or already done, from occurring. Thus what has been done can, or cannot, fail to be done. How is divine will the cause of divine providence, as was maintained above, if neither precedes the other in existence? Just as life in the body is an effect of the soul, not something prior to its cause.

## Book II

[Col. 0717]

### Chapter I. Why, and in what manner, God created the world

[Col. 0717C]

[Note: [Col. 0717D] Master, II, distinction 12.]

Therefore God created the world when he willed, being able both to have created it earlier and to have added to it as many other worlds as one can imagine. For by what could the craftsman of supreme power have been bound to an earlier summons? Or, if he could create one world from nothing, by what would he have been prevented from making many? Therefore one God chose to fashion one world; the good God, a good world; the eternal God, an everlasting world—one which, the more ancient it was, the more immense and therefore the better it was. He himself, needing the world in no respect, existed before it blessed and incapable of being happier, just as before it the world was nowhere to be found.

It is therefore clear that God acted not in order that it might go well for himself, but that others might share in his goodness. According to Moses, he made in six days all that is contained within the circuit of heaven; according to another Scripture: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Sir. 18:1). Yet a temporal delay in the work was necessary, so that the earth, empty and void, covered with a vaporous thinness of waters, might be uncovered as dry land appeared, clothed with verdure, and adorned with living creatures. Nor could man rightly be said to have been made from mud unless mud had first existed from which man came forth. Therefore he first created the earth shapeless beneath the waters, and afterward uncovered it; afterward he portrayed it in manifold forms [Col. 0718C]. [Note: [Col. 0717D] Master, Book II, distinction 2, §7.]

Therefore he created all things together, because after his rest he added nothing dissimilar or from new matter. For things generated by a mixture of different species, such as a mule; or things that spring from corruption, such as a certain kind of worm; or things which, contrary to nature, emerge from God’s hidden purposes so as to recall God’s wondrousness—such as monstrous births—do indeed come later in form, but were among the first works in matter. Thus ancient matter is clothed in a recent form whenever something unusual is born into the world. Natural things, however, declare themselves akin to the first works, having derived thence their origin of substance and thence received their quality. Therefore all bodies come from first matter; but all souls are like those first things.

God therefore rested on the seventh day (Gen. 2:4) [Col. 0718D]: not from working, because “my Father worketh hitherto” (John 5:17), but from the novelty of works. For whatever he created before, he made previously either with matter already lying before him or by reproducing a likeness; or rather, he created all things together because, in the creation, he joined the unformed matter of bodies, Adam’s soul, and every angelic nature in heaven. [Note: [Col. 0718D] Augustine, VII *On Genesis according to the Letter*, ch. 24 ff.; the Master here.] These are called “all things” because whatever follows them—of substances I speak—derives from them [Col. 0719A] either origin or likeness: all bodies origin from unformed matter, all souls likeness from the first soul.

### Chapter II. Earth is the dwelling of human beings; heaven, of spirits

[Note: [Col. 0719D] Master, Book II, distinction 2, §6.]

Therefore he appointed earth as a dwelling for human beings, heaven for spirits, and finally heaven for human beings also. He created the angel immediately with heaven and in heaven, because “In the beginning God created heaven,” and because “the angel is the beginning of the ways.” Man could not describe the things God made simultaneously; hence Moses afterward set down separately how God established heaven between the waters, whence it deserved to be called the firmament.

[Col. 0719B] But if heaven revolves, do its inhabitants revolve with it? This belongs more to philosophers than to Christians. How can they be in something revolving unless they revolve together with it? It is not at all clear. Therefore the firmament stands still [Note: [Col. 0719D] Read Augustine, II *On Genesis according to the Letter*, ch. 10.], though the stars do not stand still, so that it may be a dwelling suitable for the saints. Reason does not deny that this can be so. Or certainly, if it is truer that heaven moves, let another, stable heaven farther beyond be sought, to which the Lord ascended, according to the Apostle, above all the heavens, in order to draw all the saints to himself (Eph. 4:10). For “wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matt. 24:28). The Lord says: “If any man serve me, let him follow me; and where I am, there shall my servant be also” (John 12:26). [Note: [Col. 0719D] At the beginning of the *Hexaemeron*.] For according to Bede, the heaven which was made in the beginning, immediately filled with heavenly citizens, was at once separated from every revolving thing.

But ought this homeland of spirits to be spiritual or bodily? For what need has spiritual nature of a bodily place? Or how can the bodies of those who are saints dwell in a spiritual region? Reason does not permit that the dwelling destined for angels and saints should be divided. For it is altogether unfitting that the saints, who will make up the angelic loss, should be separated from angels. No one could rightly deny that the angels themselves would be dishonored if the inner chamber in which the Savior is with the saints did not include them.

But who would say that heaven is spirit? Who would dare introduce so great a novelty—or rather, an error? Certainly no one is ignorant that both good and evil angels alike, and souls after God, are called by the name of spirits; but beyond these, neither usage nor Scripture remembers anything that ought to be honored with such reverence. It remains, therefore, that heaven is a body; to regard it as an accident is left to a madman. And if glorified flesh is a glorious dwelling for the soul, let not spirits complain when content with the heavenly hall, since God the craftsman has made its structure conspicuous with admirable diversity of adornment; or, if it cannot be seen, it is nevertheless not lawful to believe that such great inhabitants are assigned a dwelling less suitable than they deserve.

Therefore, if on this reasoning we confess heaven to be bodily, conversely let us not deny on equal reasoning [Col. 0720A] that hell is a bodily place. Otherwise, how could it contain torments of heat and cold? Thus we understand a prison below as we understand a palace above; hence the Apostles’ Creed says: “He descended into hell; he ascended into the heavens.”

### Chapter III. Some angels excel others

[Note: [Col. 0720D] Master, Book II, distinction 9.]

All angels were created good and wise; nevertheless, some excel others in both respects. Therefore those whom he had ennobled above the rest by the dignity of creation, making them venerable by the majesty of office, he set over the lesser angels, so that they might promote human beings and serve their leader in their legions, until the saints—being made equal to angels—are raised in marvelous beauty from the camp to the palace [Col. 0720B], from exile to the kingdom. Then, according to the Scriptures, every power of preeminence will cease (1 Cor. 15:24). And because preeminence is abolished when human beings are brought to completion, it is clear that it was established on account of the weak, for the purpose of their completion. Hence the Apostle says of angels: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent to minister for those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation?” (Heb. 2:14).

### Chapter IV. Greater freedom was given to angels than to human beings

[Note: [Col. 0720D] Master, II, distinctions 5, 7, and 23.]

The freedom of choice was granted to angels as to human beings: in human beings it is indeed very powerful, but in angels far more powerful. In order that freedom of choice may exist, discernment, will, and power are necessary [Col. 0720C]. Discernment, so that you may know what is good and what is evil, and may distinguish in your own manner what is preferable among goods and what is worse among evils. Will, so that you may incline your mind, as you please, toward either of the things discerned. Power, so that, if you please, you may attain without impediment what you have chosen.

Thus they speak of a judgment free in respect of will. For judgment, by which individual matters are weighed, is free in respect of will only when what the will embraces is delayed by no difficulty in being put into action. Therefore free choice does not exist without discernment; nor does it exist with discernment but without will; nor with both, but without the capacity to carry out the choice. It is freer in proportion as it finds these three things more unrestricted. Children lack this, and irrational beings lack it as brute animals do. There is no human being who does not lack it in some respect: now through a defect in examination of choice, now through the desire for the matter examined, and sometimes through the attainment of the matter desired.

This capacity is indeed present in all by nature; but the exercise of nature is absent in some. The first man flourished in this power: judging individual things truly, readily willing good things, and leaving nothing he willed undone because nothing opposed him. Such is man by the nature of his creation, though he can do nothing without cooperating grace. But he who flourished in these things at birth was grievously stripped of his bloom by transgression, so that, altered by a lamentable reversal, he experienced the powers of choice changed to their opposites [Col. 0721A]: rash in judgment, desiring what is forbidden, sluggish and weak for useful things, impetuous toward shameful ones. Therefore free choice was oppressed in a manner that left it unfree, but it was not extinguished.

For just as a spark buried under much ash, stirred by certain kindlings and as though struggling to break free, finally bursts into flame, so our mind is indeed weighed down by the burden of corrupt flesh. Yet when it attends to itself, it shows in its inquiry into things that a certain remnant of strength has remained for resistance. But when it is aided by divine help, though with difficulty, it nevertheless acts powerfully. For it is due to the punishment of sin that one who could easily have remained attached to good pursuits, because he departed voluntarily, should return with hardship and do good with labor; yet, through God’s mercy, he carries many great things through to completion [Col. 0721B]. Thus the vigor of nature is corrupted through man and corrected through God, especially in the time of grace, awaiting completion in the resurrection, where the body, wonderfully made whole, will not weigh down the soul.

For the earthly dwelling will have become heavenly: no longer a burden, but an honor to the soul; so that human nature will then be made equal to angelic excellence. Thus the first human being, created good on earth, is at last to be perfected in heaven. Great, therefore, is the human being sown on earth; greater is the angel created in heaven. The human being is indeed great, but earthly, since he needs earthly nourishment; the angel greater, because wholly spiritual and therefore free from the supports of external things. [Col. 0721C] Hence the erring human being deserved, through redemption, to be recalled. The angel did not deserve this: for no one gave him evil counsel, and he himself was far stronger. He had, indeed, in his nature the power to sin; for one who afterwards sinned plainly had, even before—namely, from the time he was created—the ability to sin. This ability is known to have been good both in God, who bestowed it, and in the angel who persevered. For he who could transgress but did not will to do so deserved to be confirmed. He would not sufficiently be called worthy of reward if fault were absent because he could not fall away. He would certainly be worthy of honor and reverence because of his own dignity, but deserving of little—or rather no—reward for his goodness. It was good, then, that he could sin; but evil that he did sin. For he had from himself that by which he sinned, but from the Creator that by which he was able to sin. Thus he himself was the cause of his evil, while the Creator was the cause of his good.

Why then are you surprised if that Spirit did what he could do? He could do evil; he did evil. What evil? Ungrateful to his exalted Creator, he swelled with pride because of his nature, to such an extent that he wished to be made equal to the Lord. Good as he was on account of the goodness of his nature, he raised himself up of his own accord; he was no longer good, because through pride he became evil—he who had formerly been good. [Note: [Col. 0721D] The Master, Book II, distinction 5, §§4, 5 and following.] And so, when grace stood offered to both, [Col. 0722A] he in his self-assurance rejected it, while the other gratefully embraced it. The one who despised divine assistance rightly fell; the other, reverently seizing it, stood firm in truth. Without it both would have fallen; with it both could have persevered. But he who persevered, because he rejected the example of the one who turned away, deserved, as one bound to his Creator, to be converted; and because of [Note: [Col. 0721D] Isidore, *Sentences*, Book I, ch. 12, sentence 12.] the other's ruin he himself was confirmed in the truth.

## Chapter V. The vision of God confirmed the good angels, which the evil angels lacked.

[Note: [Col. 0721D] The Master, Book II, distinction 4.] But what is this confirmation, and what this conversion? Did God, in making the angel, make him blessed by knowledge of Himself? This indeed appears to be so, because it is said of the devil: “He did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44). In what truth? In that in which he was, but did not remain. Here truth [Col. 0722B] seems especially to mean knowledge of that Truth who said of Himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). For just as this lower portion of the world is understood to be assigned to those who believe, so that higher region which they call heaven seems rather to be allotted to those who see.

There are two things that chiefly blunt the mind’s sight: the burden of the bodily dwelling, whence it is said, “The body weighs down the soul” (Wisdom 9:15); and iniquity, according to the words, “He broke my teeth by number” (Lamentations 3:16). For God diminishes the powers of understanding in proportion to the number of sins. Therefore why should a rational spirit—free from the burden of flesh and from the stain of wickedness, being well created and appointed to contemplate its Creator—not have seen God from the moment it came into being? Or, if it knew Him at once, ought it not [Col. 0722C] also to have known lower things, so that, according to one author, nothing in created things is hidden from one who knows the Creator?

But if this is so, how could one who saw God and foresaw his fall also foreknow his own damnation without either foolishness without grief, or grief without foolishness? Therefore, from the time he existed and saw God, he was either foolish or miserable. But how could he be foolish while beholding God, or why miserable through no fault? [Note: [Col. 0721D] Dionysius, *Celestial Hierarchy*, Book VII; the Master, Book II, [Col. 0722D] distinction 11, §5.] Perhaps knowledge of the Creator does not admit ignorance concerning created things along with itself? Yet it does not therefore make one certain about everything. [Note: [Col. 0722D] Jerome, on Ephesians, chapter 3.] For the day of judgment is hidden even from the spirits who behold the Trinity; and when Christ was ascending into heaven, He was hidden even from some of them, who asked: “Who is this King of glory?” (Psalm 8:10). Behold, some angels had not yet comprehended [Col. 0722D] Christ, the supreme excellence of all creation. [Note: [Col. 0722D] Augustine, *Literal Commentary on Genesis*, Book XI, ch. 17 and following; *On Rebuke and Grace*, ch. 10, after the middle; Anselm, *On the Fall of the Devil*, ch. 2.] Therefore, while he was still an angel, the devil could both fail to foreknow his own fall and nevertheless know God.

But if he knew Him, since knowing God is eternal life, one of two things must follow: either he lost by sinning the eternal life which he had received—but then how did he receive eternal rather than merely momentary life, unless perhaps he would have retained eternally through obedience that life which he had deserved to hold only for a moment? And though it passes away for him, it endures for another. But if, according to the Gospel text, eternal life is the vision of God (John 17:3), he who lost eternal life did not retain the vision of God: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). Or, if by admitting sin he did not lose eternal life, what harm did his fall do him, if he did not cease to be blessed? For it is wholly incongruous that anyone should see God and at the same time be miserable through impiety. Hence it is said: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isaiah 26:10). For one who sees God’s glory must at the same time become glorious through that vision. God is so glorious that one who beholds Him cannot be inglorious. Thus the Lord Jesus, while enduring the harsh paths of His Passion, [Col. 0723B] nevertheless enjoyed blessedness through the vision.

But if the vision of God is eternal life, and eternal life is nothing other than blessedness, and each is the unfailing enjoyment of the highest good, then demons—who plainly are miserable and are to become still more miserable—have never beheld God. To pass over their other punishments, they are more than sufficiently tormented by wrath and envy. For we believe that, together with the impious, they are in hell subject both to heat and to cold, according to the words: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 8:12)—weeping because of heat, gnashing because of cold. After the judgment, though incorporeal, they are immediately to be punished by bodily penalties. [Note: [Col. 0723D] Augustine, *City of God*, Books XIII and XXI; *On the Nature of the Good against the Manichaeans*, ch. 33. The Master, Book II, distinction 6, §§5–6; and Book IV, distinction 44, §6.] From this we are instructed to infer that, already grievously tormented amid the diverse conditions of the air, they are reserved to be tormented far more grievously afterwards, [Col. 0723C] and more grievously in proportion as hell is distant from the air. For they are bound in this air as in a prison, finally [Note: [Col. 0723D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 28; *Literal Commentary on Genesis*, Book III, ch. 10; *City of God*, Book VIII, ch. 22, etc.] to be delivered to hell, there to receive, as it were, in the place of the condemned, punishments proportionate to their guilt, though only after a long delay. [Note: [Col. 0723D] Jerome, on Ephesians, chapter 6.] Since they are plainly captives, they are plainly miserable, and therefore unfit to behold God.

Hence apostolic authority says: “The demons believe and tremble” (James 2:19). [Note: [Col. 0723D] Cassian, *Conferences*, VIII, ch. 12, etc.] Believing is far from seeing; and therefore the Apostle compares the demons’ faith to the idle faith of human beings, saying: “You believe that God is one; you do well” (ibid.). It is as though he said: “I do not reject your faith, O human being; but I reproach it because it is idle, since by such a faith you are like the devil.” Thus it follows: “The demons also believe.” Therefore, if the foregoing is so, spirits receive faith at their creation, so that, already believing, they may deserve also to become those who see. For it is greatly at odds with truth that they should not know God by faith at their creation, when there is no doubt that even after becoming demons they believed. If, then, being created, they believed, those who believed ought, as stated, to have merited the vision of God. For one who has even once [Col. 0724A] tasted the glory of God by beholding it seems thereafter to be strengthened against evil desire by that very taste [variant: “withdrawn”].

[Note: [Col. 0723D] The Master, Book II, distinction 5.] Therefore, if they were created in faith, they rightly exchanged faith for vision through perseverance. But because, while the others became proud, they preferred to be subject to their Maker, they deserved to be made steadfast in blessed subjection. Thus they were converted both from faith to seeing God and confirmed in seeing Him. But if by nature they saw Him, then, when the others fell, those more closely bound to the Lord were converted so as to cleave more tightly to their Creator by the bond of charity, lest perhaps they too should fall into such misfortune; and by the merit of this conversion they were confirmed in goodness, lest they any longer fear anything similar.

[Note: [Col. 0723D] The Master, Book II, distinction 3, §4 and following.] Yet it may be said more subtly that spirits were so made by God that they could at once and always be good, unless they drew corruption from elsewhere. Hence, from their very origin, one appeared most wicked, or at least evil—namely the devil and our soul; another best, or at least good—namely the angel, and likewise the soul, though the latter first. Thus the former did not first receive existence and then evil existence; they received existence from their Author, but evil from elsewhere: the one from himself, the other from its dwelling-place. The latter, as soon as they received existence, acquired a precious existence: one still to be perfected, the other perfected at once. Thus “in the beginning darkness was upon the face of the deep” (Genesis 1:2), in the devil; and light was made in the angel.

## Chapter VI. The good angel, though able, does not sin.

[Note: [Col. 0724D] The Master, Book II, distinction 5, §2, teaches the impeccability of angels; Augustine, *Literal Commentary on Genesis*, Book XI, chs. 7 and 13; Book XII, ch. 9; *On Rebuke and Grace*, ch. 10; *Enchiridion*, chs. 57 and 105; *City of God*, Book XI, chs. 11 and 13, etc.] Augustine reports that neither an angel after conversion or perfection, nor a human being after [Col. 0724C] resurrection, can be defiled by the stain of sin. Thus, just as the ability to die was assigned to the human being alone in creation, yet is to be changed into immortality in regeneration, so the ability to sin, which is certainly known to be natural, is already known to have been removed from one and is still awaited to be removed from the other.

Jerome says: “God alone is one in whom sin cannot occur; all other things, since they possess free choice, can be bent in either direction.” [Note: [Col. 0724D] Jerome on Luke 15, in Tome I, Epistle 21 to Pope Damasus, at the end of the tract *On the Prodigal Son*.] That is: God cannot sin; the other beings which possess free choice can sin. For beings lacking free choice necessarily also lack sin. Therefore either Augustine will be contrary to Jerome, or he maintained that heavenly beings cannot sin because it is certain that they do not will to sin. And since they are very, very far [Col. 0724D] from the will to sin, sin is reckoned among them as though impossible. In ordinary speech we are accustomed to say that we cannot do what we do not will to do at all. You will encounter this usage more than once even in Holy Scripture. [Note: [Col. 0724D] Mark 6 and 10:45; Genesis 34:4, etc. See Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration on Theology*.] It is clear, then, that before the fall they were naturally removed from a perverse will, and after the fall were made much more remote by the grace that established them firmly.

[Col. 0725A] Yet, while thus established, they can still sin, their nature remaining, according to the saying: “Those who serve him are not stable, and in his angels he finds perversity” (Job 4:18). For the angels who serve God are not stable: they can sin, as is evident in those who fell and sinned. But if we admit that angels can transgress, then consistently, as is fitting, we must not deny that they can also be damned. Shall we, in consequence, rightly deny that demons can be converted, and, once converted, can be saved? For if angels can without impropriety perish through themselves, though never destined to perish, why cannot demons fittingly be saved through God, though never destined to be saved? For as much as the latter are hardened in evil, so much are the former supported in good.

But if, according to the Apostle, “Every creature of God is good” [Col. 0725B] (1 Timothy 4:4), and the devil is God’s creature according to the words, “You created the north and the sea” (Psalm 88:13)—that is, the devil and evil human beings—how is he evil? Is he both good and evil: good by creation, but evil by his own will? But if he is truly good, how is he also evil? Then love as good the one whom you hate as evil; yet concerning that Gospel passage, “For he will either hate the one and love the other” (Matthew 6:24), [Note: [Col. 0725D] Ordinary Gloss.] the exposition says: “No one loves the devil.” Perhaps you will answer: “His substance is altogether excellent, but his will alone, together with his action, is perverse.” Yet his substance is nothing other than himself. Therefore the devil is altogether good, and consequently should be loved by God and revered by human beings because of his majesty. A strange thing! If one always acts wickedly and desires worse things, he is not evil. Then the just Judge ought not to condemn one who is altogether good—indeed, not even torture him for an hour. Rather, He should pour out all His wrath upon that which is evil: namely, the devil’s will and action. But what rational wrath can be directed against irrational things? And by what punishment can insensible things be injured?

But you will say: “Pure nature is indeed punished, but because of impure things joined to it.” Certainly the proximity of evil never rightly harms anything unless it infects what is near it with its own contagion. Therefore, if—as is truer—you call the devil evil, how do you assert that his substance or nature is good? Is there in him, besides himself, another substance or nature which is rightly good and called God’s creature? [Col. 0725D] But who would agree that there are two substances in him, and that one is not God’s creature? Indeed, I know with certainty that some good remains in him, such as knowledge; but I am speaking of his substance. If you trace the devil back to the beginnings of his nature, you will find not only a good work of God, but an excellent one; if you consider what followed, his substance is no longer good, nor is it God’s creature. Rather, it is his own work and consequently the devil. Why? [Note: [Col. 0725D] Consult the notes.] Because he who had been excellently fashioned by God in creation was most foully defiled by himself in sinning. Although Augustine [Note: [Col. 0725D] Augustine in many places, but particularly *Enchiridion*, [Col. 0726D] ch. 14.] seems to wish that one who is evil should always [Col. 0726A] remain good in nature, and that two contraries should be found in the same being. Let us pass over as acknowledged the point that, if the sense conveyed by Augustine’s text must be preferred, whatever seems contrary will be distorted through a virtually forced exposition.

## Chapter VII. Why one human being was formed, and when the soul is infused.

[Note: [Col. 0726D] The Master, Book II, distinctions 16 and 17.] The first-formed human being was provided against arrogance by being fashioned from mud; but, in being ennobled by his form, he was instructed to praise the skillful hand of the Potter, which added to the work what was lacking in its origin. God chose to fashion one human being from one, impressing upon the creature the seal of Himself, so that, just as God is the one origin of all things, so the human being, by a friendly imitation, should be the one origin of all human beings. For from the woman taken [Col. 0726B] from the man springs the whole succession of descendants. Since we all come from one, the authority of one principle is commended, so that many hearers may obey one teacher, and, joined through reciprocal bonds of kinship, may love one another as members of a family.

Once the man had been formed, the soul was breathed into him, perhaps in order that we too may learn from the beginning what ought rightly to be held concerning succession. For that a soul which is to rule ought not to be introduced before the palace is complete is indicated to the discerning by the Law, when it says that one who strikes a pregnant woman and causes a miscarriage by the blow must give life for life if the expelled fetus is fully formed (Exodus 21:22); but, if it is half-formed, he is to be fined money. Why, unless because the spirit is not infused before the body is formed? For only then is the presence of the soul declared, when what is born already feels and moves.

But how could liquid seed coagulate into a certain solidity and be differentiated into the variety of members unless it were brought to completion in these stages of growth through the ordering of a spirit? Does a woman about to give birth lend her own soul meanwhile to this mechanism? But if it is personally joined also to the little one, do not two human beings live by one common soul, so that the little one is a human being before receiving its own soul? If, however, it is not present united to it in its generation, what does it contribute to formation? And how can one soul be simultaneously present whole in two, indeed even in several—not merely members but entire bodies—if, as happens, a woman pregnant from a single intercourse has conceived not simply [Col. 0726D] one child? It is clear, then, that the seminal force of generation is separated not only from the substance but from the soul of each parent, so that what previously contained the soul in the body now subsists of itself without a soul. For just as what flows away in generation from a part is, without doubt, detached both from the father’s body and from the mind of his body, so, persuaded by the example of this likeness, we maintain that what the same generation draws from the mother is likewise separated, lest a portion of the mother’s spirit should inhabit the father’s alien addition.

But if every kind of herb and tree rises from a small origin to its natural height, [Col. 0727A] expands to the extent appropriate to its growth, and takes on the differentiation of colors suited to its condition, attaining complete development of itself, while disdaining to call for the aid of a soul, why should not the same force of nature provide both form and measure, before life, to the maternal conception? For if a soul is infused at once to give warmth to the seed once emitted, it is either personally united to what is not a human being, or, still remaining another person, gives no benefit to its growth—just as the mind of one not yet born does nothing for a pregnant woman who is dead. Why? Because, though it is contained in her, it is nevertheless personally distinct. Thus air contains a spirit, thus heaven, and finally hell; yet they are not moved in a living manner by the spirit, because they are not personally united with the spirit. Thus the soul seems to contribute nothing to growth if, placed in the seed, it remains another.

Therefore, either its union seems empty if it is not personal, or absurd if it is personal. For both reason and usage establish that soul and human being are reckoned one. But that a spirit and a nonhuman being should be one has neither reason nor proper usage behind it. Yet however the soul enters this liquid dwelling, if it is forcibly expelled from the receptacle before that receptacle has attained its completeness—as often happens, and we marvel at such half-formed births—what sort of body will it have in the general assembly of all? [Note: [Col. 0727D] The Master, Book IV, distinction 44, §7.] For it will have to possess a body; but what body except a human body? No other would be fitting. But how will it then be human, since it was not a human being in this world? [Note: [Col. 0727D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 85; *City of God*, Book XX, chs. 12 [Col. 0728D] and 13.] And what kind of human being will it be, unless it rises again with the rest? For according to [Col. 0727C] the Apostle, “We shall all indeed rise again” (1 Corinthians 15:51). But who can rise again unless he has first fallen in death? How, moreover, does one depart through death who never lived? For those are called dead which at some time lived. We confess by faith that the Lord will judge the living and the dead—that is, those whom that world-destroying fire finds either still alive or already dead. Will then this new and unprecedented human being be judged, one who will be found neither living among the rest nor dead? Judas also indicates in the book of Maccabees that resurrection occurs only where death has gone before, when he hopes that those who fell will rise again (2 Maccabees 12:44). Nor is the Apostle unaware of this, when he repeatedly speaks of the resurrection of the dead and, after other matters, adds: “If by any means I may attain to the resurrection which is from the dead” (Philippians 3:11). The same point is very frequently urged in both the Old and the New Testament.

A body that originally stains the soul infused into it is undoubtedly destined for death, as the primal cause of sin. For death is the proper punishment of the first sin; hence God said to the first human being: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Genesis 2:17). To everyone to whom guilt is transmitted from him by origin, the punishment of guilt is also transmitted, so that just as the soul draws defilement from the body, it may bear death in the body because of that defilement. The soul itself does not die, but suffers in that which is dying. That [Col. 0728A] punishment by death follows where original transgression has preceded is also attested by the Apostle: “The sting,” he says, “of sin is death” (1 Corinthians 15:59). Sin infects like poison; death stings like pain poisoned by that poison. Wherever, therefore, the poison of sin is infused, let the sting of death be expected. Hence, if a soul established in a seminal body is contaminated from the seminal body, it may rightly seem liable to be tormented by the death of its own body, so that, as has been said, it draws punishment from that from which it draws guilt.

But for that body itself to die, as has been said, it must first live; and everything that lives lives either sensibly or insensibly. Yet only that which adheres from the root to its own solidity ought to live insensibly. For how can what will live with a rational soul appropriately belong to insensibility? From where else would it receive life except from the soul that it contains? Even if someone should hold that its parts live an insensible life, feeling is nevertheless usually attributed to the whole itself because of the sentient soul. But whatever is sentient must be an animal. Therefore that origin of humanity is unquestionably an animal, if it lives so as not to be insensible.

But it seems wrongly called an animal, since it is not believed to feel. For who would attribute sensation to seed? Nor can it be an animal other than a human being, lest an animal that is not a human being become a human being, and every human being be an animal before being a human being. But it is not yet a human being either, since humanity is lacking; and therefore its members, form, and size appropriate to humanity are absent. Therefore, if it is neither sentient because it is not a human being, nor another animal, nor insensible because it is neither herb nor tree, it is plainly clear that it has no life, and consequently cannot die.

Perhaps someone will say: “A soul introduced into fluid matter is at first not defiled by its contagion, because, remaining in itself, it does not yet accept personal union. Hence, as though shut up in a filthy hut, it is not fouled, though it will finally be fouled when the palace of the human structure is completed.” If, then, before this mechanism has been brought to its full completion, the injury of a violent expulsion, as often happens, befalls its inhabitant, which was created rational and pure by God and is thereafter liable to no stain—thus escaping the one danger of bodily contagion—not only in the time of grace but even before it, [Col. 0728D] how can it be due to hell without guilt, or to heaven without the Redeemer’s advent? Why should one need a Redeemer who is held captive by no captivity conquered over him?

Attending to these considerations, therefore, we are instructed to confess that the soul is to be given to the body only when the human being, now endowed with sensation, can rightly be called a human being, so that the whole succession of procreation may represent the animation of the first parent. And this has been said concerning when the soul comes to the body.

## Chapter VIII. The soul is not derived by propagation, but is from God.

[Note: [Col. 0728D] The Master, Book II, distinction 17.] I think we must now add an inquiry concerning whence it comes: whether by propagation (*tradux*), or solely from God creating it. [Col. 0729A] The parents of our flesh are understood to be propagators, because the origin of our outward human being is propagated as a cutting taken from both parents by the pruning-knife of generation. But are the same parents likewise propagators of our inward human being, so that, just as body descends from bodies, one soul descends from two? I investigate whether a soul derives its origin from two, because I do not think that one parent alone provides its origin. For why should I call one and not the other a propagator? Should I consider the offspring closer, by the law of parental relationship, to one begetter, so that it is much more beholden to the one from whom it receives also its mind than to the one from whom it receives only its flesh? Nor can I say that body is born from one parent and spirit from the other.

For the Gospel’s statement concerning the elect says: “Who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God” (John 1:13). [Col. 0729B] It first sets forth the birth which is “of bloods,” according to which not the elect but the fallen are born; it then immediately adds the second, which is “of God,” by which the elect are reborn. But why is the first said to be “of bloods” rather than “of blood,” unless, as the authority [Note: [Col. 0729D] Augustine, *Tractates on John*, tractate 2, on this passage: “Who were born not of blood…”] attests, the blood of each parent, altered in color by carnal pleasure, comes together into one seed for producing offspring? Hence we see that offspring indiscriminately receive from both parents a likeness in stature, form, and constitution. [Note: [Col. 0729D] Bede, ibid.] Therefore, just as we know beyond doubt that one flesh flows from two, so I think it more probable that either both souls or neither produces the soul to be born. Thus two souls seem to be the underlying [Col. 0729C] matter of a third, just as before he is personally a son, he is materially known in his parents.

But all matter is transferred either whole or diminished into a new designation: bronze into a statue, a trunk into a beam, wood and stones into a house—although perhaps those things do not become the house, but rather the house is made from them. A soul, however, having no part, creates nothing from itself by a part. How, then, can two souls, each whole, become a third in forming it, especially when, after it has already been produced, the two remain such as they were before? And how can each come together as though a part, so that a third consists of both? According to the teaching of some, just as one candle lights another without loss to itself, [Col. 0729D] so a soul, unharmed, begets a soul. Yet I think this is put forward not as an assertion but as an opinion.

Again, if souls—namely two souls, as stated—pour forth one soul, this emission occurs either during generation, or afterward, or beforehand. For delay in this matter might perhaps seem incongruous. The Creator of all implanted original causes in His world, so that, when these came together, the progress of natural things might emerge. According to Augustine, [Note: [Col. 0730D] *Literal Commentary on Genesis*, Book IV, ch. 24; Book VI, chs. 10, 17, and 18; *City of God*, Book XI, ch. 27; and especially *Literal Commentary on Genesis*, Book VIII, ch. 7.] He also reserved within Himself certain hidden causes, by which effects would suddenly appear not through nature but through His power. But we are now not investigating how great the Craftsman’s power is, [Col. 0730A] but what nature can do. What force of nature, then, would require that those two souls, and not others, should produce a third after generation or before it, at one time rather than another? Perhaps it is more credible that, when bodies are relaxed by the pleasurable agitation of the generative organs and souls are seized by the delightful relaxation, the present integrity is fashioned from the one and the certain origin of future integrity from the other. Hence, through the incitement of lust, corruption is propagated to the body and concupiscence to the spirit, as suits each alike from a similarly infected beginning. This is what displeases none, or few, among those to whom the origin of the soul according to matter is pleasing.

Therefore integrity is either immediately mixed with the beginning of integrity—against which the argument has already proceeded—or kept apart until it is introduced when the [Col. 0730B] dwelling has been completed. For I consider no one so shameless as to deny either that the soul is to be embodied or that it is assigned to any body other than that with which it was born. But if it is kept apart, and meanwhile its parent is removed by some accident—as we undoubtedly know happens, since we see parents die before their children and half-formed births be born prematurely—then either it will remain destined to be embodied though its dwelling has been destroyed, and you will be surprised that there are far more souls than human beings, though a rational soul and flesh ought rather to be one human being; or it will be joined to the offspring of other parents, so that the same person has four parents: the mind of these, the flesh of those; indeed, so that it receives one soul from generation and another from elsewhere. Therefore the soul seems to descend by propagation neither during generation, nor afterward, nor beforehand—and much less by two of these, or by all three.

Yet if it does, perhaps someone may think that a mind is the child of a mind, as born from its substance; and that the absence of intercourse is no obstacle, knowing that a virgin gave birth (Isaiah 7:13), and that God begot His only Son from His own substance. If, then, a mind is plainly the offspring of a mind—indeed, of minds—how can one be from two unless we regard one as, so to speak, mother and the other as, so to speak, father? Nor perhaps without reason. For just as our flesh proceeds through the flesh of both parents when the union of the generative organs is mutually supplied from each side, so too our spirit is generated through the spirit of both. Therefore [Col. 0730D] our parents seem not without reason to be the generators in us both of bodily and incorporeal substance.

But the Apostle says to the Hebrews: “We had fathers of our flesh who disciplined us, and we revered them. Shall we not much more submit to the Father of spirits?” (Hebrews 12:9). Why did he distinguish the fathers of our flesh unless he wished another to be the Father of our spirits? Why did he call God the Father of spirits unless to prevent our thinking that there is another father of souls?

Therefore we receive flesh from our parents; but the soul does not descend by propagation. It is not subject to the concurrence of natural causes, but owes its existence to the powerful God. [Col. 0731A] That the child’s soul very often represents the parents’ soul in its dispositions does not prove that soul is propagated from soul. Rather, the body derived from body, retaining the nature of its origin, affects in its own manner the soul infused into it. And: “The judgments of God are a great deep” (Psalm 35:7).

## Chapter IX. The soul is created good and pure in the body.

[Note: [Col. 0731D] The Master, above.] I think a further inquiry is appropriate: whether the soul’s creation is to be understood as occurring within the body or outside it. If outside, where outside? Is it near the body? But what function would it have near the body? Is it to prepare a dwelling for itself before entering it? That is what we assign to others. For we presume nothing of the sort, since Job’s author says that we are milked out by God like milk, curdled like cheese, [Col. 0731B] clothed with flesh and skin, and compacted with bones and sinews. Although these are works of nature according to God’s decree, as we have said, they are in no way works of the soul. Why then should it stand beside the body? Does it wait so that it may enter easily, as though from nearby, when the time comes? But the spiritual agility of the mind, endowed with swiftness, is not delayed by any spatial distance.

Or does spiritual nature, not yet weighed down by the burden of flesh and [perhaps: therefore] equal to the angelic, share a place in heaven with the angel? But then every soul descends from heaven to be embodied, which belongs rather to the philosophers. For the Lord Jesus alone descended from heaven, but did not ascend alone, since He was crowned with the glorious spoils of captivity. Hence He said: “No one has ascended into heaven except the Son of Man who descended from heaven, who is in heaven” [Col. 0731C] (John 3:13). That is, except one united, as a member to the head, with Him who descended from heaven. To descend from heaven belongs to Him; to ascend there belongs to us. His descent is for our sake; our ascent is through Him. Let each of us therefore preserve what belongs to him, and not usurp another’s right.

Again, if the soul is believed to have been created outside the body, what sort of thing is it believed to have been when created? We understand all God’s works to be very good (Genesis 1:31). Rational beings, unless weighed down by earthly covering, we judge not only to employ reason—as they do even in the body—but to examine individual things with the keenest discernment. This was perceived by him who said: “The body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling [weighs down] the mind that thinks many things” (Wisdom 9:15). Once this burden is removed, if even with it the soul thinks many things, without it it penetrates and investigates countless things. Therefore, having attained angelic height, since it was made in the image and likeness of God, while it remains in the dignity of its creation, it will, I think, with no one dissenting, be reckoned both most excellent because of God’s likeness and most prudent because of God’s image.

After taking counsel concerning the rest of creation, the Holy Trinity said: “Let us make humankind in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26). It took counsel after the other things, as though turning to an outstanding work. It impressed its own likeness upon the human being. This is not to be understood according to flesh, but according to mind; for in relation to God it is impious even to think of any bodily members or anything corporeal. A created spirit, therefore, is made like the Creator Spirit. It has no source from which to corrupt this likeness [Col. 0732A] until it is defiled in its muddy dwelling. Infused into the body, then, it contracts guilt and imbibes forgetfulness. But how do the fictions of the Gentiles differ from this: that souls are made drunk from Bacchus’ bowl by the draught of Lethe so as to forget what went before? Therefore we learn nothing new by study; we merely recall what we knew beforehand.

Likewise, souls before their incarnation either do not know God; but how then, when they are freer than in the flesh, where they apprehend God at least by faith? Or, if they know Him, either they do not love Him; but then, ungrateful to the author of benefits, they are not defiled in the body—indeed, they were defiled far more basely before it; or they love Him, but then, obedient to their God, they are by no means idle. Rather, the more they know Him whom they love, the more ardently [Col. 0732B] they burn in His love, knowledge of the good itself imparting its sweetness. Therefore, while they are still to be embodied, they blaze with a more abundant charity than when, already burdened with flesh, they are impeded both from love and from knowledge. For they love less, while they know less why they should love.

If, therefore, amid the frailty of our mortality, charity, when well matured and perfect, scarcely ever—or never—allows one whom it has once seized to perish: for this is the fountain in which the stranger who is to be condemned, or rather the wicked man, does not share [Note: [Col. 0732D] Augustine, Tractate 6 on the Epistle of John.] (Prov. V)—how can souls which, as we have said, flourish much more excellently in charity before incarnation, after incarnation not only fall away from so great a charity, but even perish through their fall? For charity never fails (I Cor. XIII, 9), precisely because, as it is possessed more abundantly in the future, so too, once rooted now, it is never, or scarcely ever, plucked out. Though winds rush upon it and floods rush upon it, that house which has been founded upon it shall not be moved (Matt. VII, 25): certainly, one who leans upon charity is not moved—unless he slips away from it.

Therefore, souls that perish through the body did not possess charity before the body. For, if they had possessed it, as we said before, they would not, obedient to their God, have been idle. But, following the Apostle, we freely confess that souls before birth have done neither anything good nor anything evil. Speaking of Jacob and Esau, he says: “When they were not yet born, nor had done anything good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand—not of works, but of Him who calls—it was said: The elder shall serve the younger” (Rom. IX, 11).

[Col. 0732D] The Apostle intends to prove that Jacob was chosen by grace alone and Esau rejected, in no way on account of works. For no works had preceded, since they were not yet born; nor had they earned anything in the womb or beforehand, since they had done nothing good or evil. For if the souls of both, at least before the body, had done good, God would seem to judge one justly because of merits and the other unjustly; but if they had done evil, mercy would be shown to one and vengeance for evil work exacted from the other. If they had divided good work and evil between themselves, the good would rightly be accepted and the evil rejected on account of works. For if it were done in the opposite order, each would be held cheap in view of the other. Thus it is clear that, if they earned anything either in the womb or before it, the purpose of God might seem to have been fulfilled not according to election [Col. 0733A] but according to works, when it was said to her who still bore twins in the womb: “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. XXV, 25)—that is, “Your younger son shall be the better.”

These matters considered, someone might perhaps think that the soul is made within bodies. Hence perhaps in Genesis God is represented as having breathed into the man, once formed, the breath of life—that is, a soul. He “breathed in,” because He imparted it by breathing (Gen. II, 27); by breathing, because He brought it forth from the bosom of providence, whence it might be breathed. It is therefore clear that, although a spirit comes from one breathing, it is not of that breather’s substance; likewise souls proceed from their author and are of another nature. Nor is He said first to have breathed and afterward to breathe in. Why? Unless it is because souls are not first created in order that they may afterwards be introduced into their little dwelling. Therefore He breathed in when He created the spirit within.

[Col. 0733B] But if souls are made only in the flesh, and are pure from the stain of sin and clear from the cloud of ignorance—as seems more fitting for things made in the image of God—while they are such, what need have they of a mediator? Surely, where discord has arisen through guilt, there is need for the reconciliation of a mediator. But if, from the very beginnings of their subsistence, they are troubled in both respects because of the body which weighs down the soul, how can they be understood to have been well made? When a good craftsman works not-good material, the work derives one thing from its maker and another from its matter: from matter, whatever ugliness it has; from the maker, whatever beauty. In the same way, the Creator imparts nature, while the body imparts corruption to the soul. God gives being; the body gives bad being. So far as God is concerned, the soul is subtle and upright; but so far as [Col. 0733C] the body is concerned, it is dull and perverse. From the Creator it receives that by which it may deservedly be judged of conspicuous dignity—unless disgrace is violently forced upon it from elsewhere. This, indeed, is removed only from the first humans, since they did not receive corruption from the body but introduced corruption into the body.

## Chapter X. A human being is not something distinct from body and soul, but is body and soul themselves.

[Note: [Col. 0733D] Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, III, distinction 6, etc.]

Let us now see what the whole human being is like as created, and what he became through guilt; what belongs to the human being and what belongs to the mind. First, let us consider what a human being is. According to some, therefore, a human being is something composed of soul and a human body, distinct in nature from each and, numerically, a third thing. [Col. 0733D] This third thing is neither increased by the addition of one part nor equal in quantity to the other, although a part is ordinarily supposed to add increase to the wholeness of bodies; whereas the whole itself contains its own part within the compass of its extent. Consequently, in every individual there are two things: one a human being and the other not a human being, utterly alike with one another, since they have entirely in common both human form and the members of humanity. Yet they are alike in a manner unfamiliar to us, because in nothing can they be seen to be unlike. For how can unlikeness be perceived when identity presents itself everywhere to the gaze?

[Col. 0734A] How, then, do two appear, when those seeing them perceive them to be neither alike nor unlike one another? Perhaps what is hidden from outward eyes is not hidden from inner eyes. Yet how is one of the two pronounced not to be human, when the non-human is not seen—since it perfectly displays human form and, by sure indications, shows a soul infused throughout that form? Therefore either this alone is the human being, or, if the other is also present with it, then in each individual there appear rightly two human beings, not one spirit and one body, but both bodies.

Yet if it is truer to confess that the third thing, which we said consists of corporeal and incorporeal substance, is the human being in itself, then this too will be true: the one who is now a dead human being was not previously a living human being, but only a part of one. Thus a little child in the womb, inanimate before the soul, never passes into being a human being, but into being a part of a human being.

The Catholic faith holds [Note: [Col. 0733D] Athanasius, on the Creed.] that, as rational soul and flesh are one human being, so God and man are one Christ. Therefore, just as God and man are one, so soul and flesh are one; God and man are one, but not one thing. For creative and created substance are always two, though united personally. In the same way, soul and body cannot be one thing, but can be joined. Faith teaches that God and man come together personally in Christ. It is impious to make Christ a composite thing. For God, as Augustine testifies in Book [Note: [Col. 0733D] III, chapter 10.] III against the heretic Maximinus, can be part of nothing: for a part always lacks something of the perfection of its whole, whereas nothing can be lacking to God.

[Col. 0734C] Therefore Christ is not a thing composed out of diverse substances, but, as the same Augustine testifies in the same place, one person of double substance. Thus, just as God and man—complete man, soul and body—are one Christ, not three substances making a fourth but meeting in one person, so likewise soul and flesh are one human being by a union of natures [Note: [Col. 0734D] See notes.], not of parts. Setting aside such trifles, then, let us assert that two natures adhere personally in a human being; and let us reject as frivolous the claim that a human being, as though a third thing, consists of two natures. Thus the human being is not a third thing made from two, but subsists from a rational soul and human flesh. Yet human flesh, while it is animated, is customarily called a human being; it becomes a human being out of what was inanimate through animation, and remains so while it adheres to the mind [Col. 0734D] [Note: Better thus: “When animation finally returns, [it] will be dead,” etc.]; when animation departs, it will be dead until it eventually returns, and indeed is not then a human being.

## Chapter XI. Reason, anger, and desire give form to the soul.

Let us now see what belongs to the soul, that afterward we may more easily consider what properly belongs to the human being. God the artificer endowed the soul with three powers: reason, anger, and desire. It belongs to reason to discern between good and evil. Anger ought, with fervent zeal, to reject what has shown itself to be cowardly. [Col. 0735A] Nor would it perhaps be absurd to say that it is the office of desire that things worthy of pursuit should be sought; for care for nourishing the body undoubtedly belongs to its office, so that, while reason persists in investigation, desire may seek what the flesh needs. Nor, I think, is it improper to add that anger repels what would harm the body. For I consider it certain that anger should reject what harms the spirit and desire seek what benefits the body. Yet who would stubbornly deny that each has the duty of its own administration in respect of both?

But insofar as desire is bound to caring for the body, I think it is called sensuality, because it summons the service of the senses into its ministry. Sensuality, indeed, can of itself desire what is advantageous to the body, but cannot attain it except through the encounter of the senses.

[Col. 0735B] There are five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. How greatly desire is deprived when they fail is easily discovered. But if the spirit is unquestionably aided by the senses, which are corporeal, why should not sensuality, though bodily, also render useful service to the mind? We rightly declare this sensuality to be implanted in the soul, for while through it the soul enjoys carnal desires, it is not undeservedly tormented for those very desires. That it belongs not to the human being but to the mind alone is indicated by the exposition of the verse, “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V, 17). [Note: [Col. 0735C] In the Gloss on this passage of the Apostle.] There it is held that the flesh—that is, the spirit acting according to carnality—desires against itself acting according to reason.

For the spirit, consulting sensuality, [Col. 0735C] which has received the name “nourishment” because it feeds the flesh, seeks aberrant things that it condemns by reason. It desires unlawful things from what is alien, yet rejects the things desired from what is its own. Reason is its own, implanted by nature; sensuality is alien, contracted through the grace of the flesh. Such an exposition is futile if the outward human being desires. But where desire is, sense is also likely to be. For, as I have said, the senses obey desire. Hence reason declares that the soul will suffer punishment through the body whenever, through the body, it exceeds measure by the disordered stirring of the senses.

Moreover, when the wantonness of the senses ranges about, does not the one who desired enjoy what he desired once he has obtained it? And who is that one but the same person who now apprehends through sense what he previously sought by desire? For example: the spirit, to which desire alone belongs, itself desires food for its body; once it has obtained it, it follows that the same spirit takes pleasure, and no one else is affected by the taste of flavors. For whoever is gladdened by the incentives of flavors must himself possess the sense of tasting: to whom can a feast be savory unless taste is active in him? Therefore taste belongs to the spirit, and the other senses as well, since by nature they are directed [perhaps *ferri*, “borne”] toward the same subject.

Yet although the senses belong to the soul, the instruments of sense are assigned to the body. Hence the body receives one thing through its instruments, the soul another through the senses. The body, indeed, is exposed to the impact of any body; while the soul, according to the nature of the impact, either enjoys [Col. 0736A] pleasure or is tortured by distress. For example, while eating, it belongs to the body to be moved, to the soul to take pleasure; in a contest the body is worn down, the mind is distressed. You will find likewise through the other senses that one thing belongs to the human being and another to the spirit.

That the soul embraces the whole range of senses did not escape Plato. Indeed, he indicates this in his customary involved manner when asked about sight: he relates that an inner fire flows out through the eyes and, joined to the external fire, flies across to the opposing body; reflected from it, it returns through the same eyes to the soul and thus produces the sense called sight. What is meant by this except that sight is an inner fire—inner because it dwells in the soul, fire because it illuminates in seeing? Sight, I say, passes through [Col. 0736B] the eyes to external objects, not by a change of place but by the efficacy of seeing; and what it learns through the cooperating light it reports to the mistress that sends it, thereby informing her, who is herself the faculty of sense.

Thus, by such an outgoing and return, whenever the soul judges bodily things, it shows that the sense called sight is within it. In the same treatise Plato states beforehand that instruments assist the provident motions of the soul. He ranked the eyes first among these instruments. What are these motions with which the eyes cooperate together with the remaining instruments, except the five senses? Certainly those very five are the senses. Therefore, as I mentioned above, Plato explained how the eyes assist sight. He held that the instruments render a similar service to the senses, each remaining instrument to its corresponding sense. He therefore calls the five senses motions of the soul. [Col. 0736C] They are motions because the soul is moved by a certain motion of its own while external things are judged through the senses.

Yet we call these senses corporeal, although we have already established that they belong to the soul. For, as Aristotle testifies, the senses are concerned with the body and are in the body. We therefore call them corporeal not because they give form to the body, but because they cannot be present to the soul except through the body: once the living creature is destroyed, sensation is destroyed. Why? Because the living creature and sensation come into being together: a living creature comes into being through the soul, while sensation comes to exist in the soul through the living creature.
