Thus the senses are only in the body, because outside the body the soul lacks them; and they are concerned with the body because the spirit escapes the jurisdiction of the senses.

Accordingly, you may rightly call these motions of the soul—and sensuality, the ruler of those motions—corporeal for a double reason: only in the body do they obtain both dwelling and operation. If, then, the senses do not belong to the living creature, how is it sentient? And if they do not belong to the soul except in the body, how can it feel outside the body? Certainly a soul cast into Gehenna does feel punishment, but not through the affliction of the senses; rather, according to the quality of its sins. But whenever animals are called sentient, we must be content that what belongs to the contained is attributed to the container.

## Chapter XII. Reason presides over all the soul’s powers.

[Note: [Col. 0736C] Peter Lombard, II, distinction 24, §6.]

Below the soul, then, all the senses serve sensuality; sensuality and anger in turn serve reason, reason [Col. 0737A] directing everything, lest there be anything excessive or deficient—unless restless handmaids, unfaithful to their mistress, seize dominion for themselves. Where reason is, discernment must also be present there, and nowhere else. But whoever exercises discernment of good and evil surely, by consenting to one or the other, deserves either punishment or a crown.

Thus brute animals are also rational, but naturally without understanding; because they lack judgment of mind in what they do, they will also lack the reckoning of recompense. For God judges works only according to hearts, and therefore says: “A good man brings forth good from a good treasure; an evil man brings forth evil from an evil treasure” (Matt. XII, 33). When there is no treasure in the heart, there will be no judgment upon the deed. Unless it is truer that God, since He judges original sins even in those lacking sensation, much more rightly judges actual sins—but gently, because nothing is done contrary to the judgment of reason. Yet one who distinguishes thing from thing ought to be judged severely according to deeds.

But who is the one who distinguishes? Which of the two is it—the outward human being or the inward? Or both? It is certain that the soul has a discriminating power, which it doubtless derives when it is marked with the countenance of its God. Should we also maintain that the human being has a reason of his own?

But how can one and the same reason belong to things so different, or how can two reasons be asserted in things personally joined? For if reason is the same in the mind and in the human being, it follows that, when the human being perishes, reason itself remains in the mind. Thus the destruction of the foundation does not entail the destruction of what is founded upon it, if the reason of the two is the same and both must have the same rationality. [Col. 0737C] For rationality is the power to reason, whereas reason is the force and efficacy of that same thing. Thus even tender infancy has rationality, because it already possesses the capacity to reason in its due time; but it does not yet have reason, because it cannot yet use reason.

Moreover, as great as the vigor of any act is in number, so great usually is the power of that same act. For each person has one capacity for fighting and one power of fighting; one skill in wrestling and likewise one power; one expertise in disputation, and, in the same person, one power for that same activity. Therefore, where there is only one force of discernment, called reason, there will also be only one power of discernment, called rationality. Consequently, if the human being and his mind have one reason, they must also have one rationality.

But Aristotle says: “The species of opposite genera are opposite, and their differences are opposite.” Now body and spirit are opposite genera; human being and soul are their opposite species; therefore their differences will be opposite—differences dividing the genera and constituting the species. Thus rationality, which is substantial to the soul, is not substantial to the human being; or, if it is, it is another rationality, so that in each individual there are two rationalities and therefore two reasons, two angers and two desires. Thus, just as the soul is rational in its own right, so the human being himself would be rational and would discern, become angry, and desire. It is therefore pointless for these three powers to be called powers of the soul in itself and not of the human being.

[Col. 0738A] This doubling of powers would also entail a doubling, in each individual, of branches of knowledge, of guilt, and of thoughts in every matter: so that when I am believed to deliberate alone, two rather deliberate; two of us contract two sins in the same act; and I have acquired two grammars and two of every other science.

But if I grant that the human being is rational while denying that he has those powers, it may perhaps seem absurd to call rational one who cannot use reason and who, finally, does nothing either badly or well.

Yet I should soon judge it more consonant with reason to ascribe the three powers and their companions—namely thought and knowledge, virtue and vice—to the soul alone. Aristotle accordingly, in his *Categories*, after assigning its qualities to the animal, added the soul’s own qualities too: justice and injustice, anger and folly. Yet he applies their names to the animal when he adds: “According to them we are called irascible and foolish.” Therefore, because in accordance with ordinary usage he assigns all such things to the animal, even while recognizing them to belong not merely to the animal but to the soul, he does not err here. Since animal and soul are one person, it is customary in speech to ascribe to the animal what in reality belongs only to the soul.

Accordingly, when we say of someone, “He is a grammarian, a musician, chaste,” we ascribe to the human being what belongs to the mind. Our Lord Jesus also used this manner of speaking. When He says, “Before Abraham came to be, I am” [Col. 0738C] (John VIII, 58), His humanity speaks on behalf of His divinity. But when He says to the sons of Zebedee, “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” (Matt. XX, 22), His humanity speaks for itself.

But this may cause difficulty: if, as we have said, all vices belong to the soul, why do writers call some spiritual and others carnal—spiritual, such as pride and envy; carnal, such as fornication and drunkenness? They are called carnal because they are carried out only through the flesh. In murder, the sword pierces vital organs and cuts off the head; yet it is not the sword but the human being who sins. The sword does act, but the one who moved the sword is the offender. So the flesh drinks and fornicates, but the mind is guilty because it takes pleasure. Thus the act belongs to the flesh, but guilt to the mind; and not without reason, because it uses the flesh as an instrument.

Nor am I troubled by Scripture’s mention of carnal desires. They are carnal (I Pet. II, 11) because they are brought upon the spirit by the flesh and administered through the flesh. And because the soul is defiled both from itself and from the flesh, it is expected to be tormented both in itself and in the flesh. Yet since neither virtue nor vice belongs to the human being, neither pleasure nor misery should belong to him. Both, however, the soul will receive in greater measure for itself, even through the body, in the resurrection; for then the human being will be either far more beautiful and strong or far more ugly and corrupt than now. Our present state, being intermediate, will there rise or fall in a wonderful degree, and the soul, beyond what is proper to itself, [Col. 0739A] will pass into greater pleasure or greater pain.

## Chapter XIII. When reason arrives with its companions.

*Master, as above.* We have indeed already placed reason in the soul together with its company. But we must now inquire when reason itself, the leader, arrives with its subjects, anger and desire. Certainly, desire is proven to be present from a human being’s very birth, because immediately one seeks certain things and flees their opposites; but the advance of age brings anger with it. These two go before separately; reason at last follows. For just as anger is truly present in anyone from the moment he is capable, when occasions arise, of becoming angry, though it often lies hidden unmoved; so reason is rightly held to have arrived [Col. 0739B] when someone, even though he rests for a time, nevertheless has ready at hand the capacity to exercise judgment concerning things whenever need requires.

But if childish age has not yet acquired reason, how is such a soul meanwhile in the image of God? Or if it already has reason, why is it not yet able to use reason? How can dormant reason, idle reason, and therefore undiscerning reason conform anyone to God, especially since without understanding it cannot accomplish this? Therefore, whether reason is present in little children or absent, nothing will belong to the image of God. Yet we shall establish its arrival more certainly when it has shown us its presence through many signs requiring experience.

But how does this rational soul differ from the irrational spirit of brute animals? Does it declare itself quicker in every respect by sure indications? Certainly, if we attend to outward things, we find the latter far superior [Note: [Col. 0739] Hence that saying of the poet:

> “In hearing the boar precedes us, in sight the lynx, in taste the ape,  
> In smell the vulture, in touch the spider.”].

But if the nature of each is examined in a just comparison, the former will seem superior even to a person of little discernment. For it is born to understand and born to act well. And, so far as lies within itself, it does both not merely well but perfectly. Yet immersed in the dregs of flesh, as though half-choked, it is oppressed until its time and does neither: scarcely sufficient to animate the fluid beginnings of human nature, until, as the human being is gradually made firm and gradually fitted to it, it displays to us in part that for which it was born. It will complete its nature after the human being—if indeed it has merited this in the human being—when it plainly sees the author of things. And then, when it has brought itself into view in the nature of things [Col. 0739D] (for it is not uncertain that, before judgment, many things are hidden even from it), nothing will remain hidden.

## Chapter XIV. The souls of brute animals perish with them.

The irrational spirit subsists with the animal; after the animal it ceases to subsist. But even if it remained, it would remain the same, because, just as before, it would possess no reason. Someone, perhaps wandering from the path of authority, may maintain that even the souls of brute animals lose nothing when their deaths are overcome, being subject, of course, to perpetuity. (For I would judge the frivolity unworthy even of a hearing which, after first asserting the animal’s life, should finally deny that it will perish.)

[Col. 0740A] But where will they be, and for what purposes will they remain? Will they fare badly forever or well? But why either, when without reason they have merited neither? Who can conceive their condition? They no longer have bodily senses; perhaps they can still become angry, but they cannot desire.

But since they are assigned to so great and perpetual a punishment for a crime, do they rejoice or grieve? If so, whence comes this? Is it from expectation of future things, reception of present things, or recollection of past things? But what deeds performed in the flesh could they recall that would deserve either eternal rejoicing or mourning? How could they contract either of the two on the occasion of present things, when neither sensation, now absent, supplies it, nor reason, never present, judges it, nor a judge dispenses it according to the debt of merit—which does not exist without reason?

[Col. 0740B] And in regard to the future, how can they be exhilarated by pleasure or cast down by sadness? Do they always expect some new thing? But what reason is there for such unceasing novelty? And whence would irrational creatures obtain this reflection? Are their powers asleep, so that they are given over to unbroken drowsiness? But the nature of spirits perseveres in wakefulness, except when the need of the flesh brings sleep. Perhaps, just as a living animal is changed into an inanimate one and thereby deteriorates, so a soul previously irrational, driven out by death, improves by becoming rational, its nature changed into the image of God? But if so, that which guilt has not defiled remains to be made blessed by glory. And since the resurrection of human beings is believed to be forthcoming, why should the resurrection of beasts also be denied? Is it because they lack reason and merit? But very many human beings lack these as well, and yet they will rise again.

[Col. 0740C] Whatever clever answer may be given to these questions, let us reject them and hold to the teaching of the authorities, affirming that the souls of brute animals perish with them.

## Chapter XV. What imagination is, and of what kind.

Let us add imagination to the matters already mentioned. Imagination is a certain inward representation, marked by an imitation of absent things that are capable of being subjected to the senses. It is active even in dreams and in brute animals, bringing back to memory, whether asleep or awake, both things that are and things that are not, by presenting images of both to the soul. Since, apart from reason, no one doubts that irrational creatures often surpass us in the remaining powers of the soul, those are plainly mistaken who contend that no spirits preside over brute animals—unless bodies borrow for a time the prerogatives of spirit.

[Col. 0740D] But if those prerogatives are not granted to the human being himself, how can they fittingly belong to a beast? It may perhaps seem more fitting that, as such great endowments belong not to the human being but to the human being’s mind, so they belong not to the beast but to the beast’s ruler. That brute animals have souls is found in the words, “You will take away their spirit” (Ps. CIII, 29); and afterwards, “You will send forth Your Spirit” (ibid.); and elsewhere, “There is no spirit in their mouth” (Ps. CXXXIV, 17). We have already stated what belongs to the human being and what belongs to the mind.

## Chapter XVI. What a human being is by creation, and how many are to be recalled from error.

[Note: [Col. 0741D] The Master, II, distinctions 16 and 19.]

It remains to say what the human being is by nature and what he is through guilt. The first human being was born into a state as much higher than our present state as it was lower than the future one. Had he preserved his middle condition, he and his descendants would not have experienced our misery. Once access of death had been restrained and obedience fulfilled, he would soon have attained eternal glory [Note: [Col. 0741D] Gregory, *Morals*, IV, chapter 28.]. For just as his corruption has undoubtedly spread to all, so it is credible—and some, worthy of imitation, maintain—that, had it occurred, all would through that same person’s obedience have been confirmed in obedience, with only those then being born who are now the children of light [Col. 0741B] [Note: [Col. 0741D] Anselm, *Why God Became Man*, I, chapter 18.].

For it would not have been fitting for others to be born, nor for the same persons to be born in a greater or smaller number. For if Adam remained the same person after sin, to be finally led back through God’s mercy from exile to his homeland, would it not be more consonant with faith that, just as obedient persons would be born from one who obeyed, so transgressors would be born from a transgressor, persons hoping for redemption from one who was to be redeemed—from the same, that is, the same persons?

I do not deny the most certain birth of those who are to perish. I seek only to establish the identity of those to be saved, both through divine justice and through mercy. For [Note: [Col. 0741D] Augustine, Letter 157 to Optatus, before the middle.] unless they had been lost after the Fall, the elect would recognize God’s mercy toward themselves less fully; and they would be neither more numerous nor, as has been said, fewer. For if they were fewer, human ruin would be restored only halfway through the Redeemer; but if they were more numerous, the Fall would seem expedient, through which the heavenly court increased. Especially since it seems that precisely as many must be led back from error as would have had to be created for salvation if they had not erred—neither more in number nor fittingly fewer.

[Note: [Col. 0741D] The Master, *Sentences*, Book II, distinction 9, §7 and following; [Col. 0742D] and distinction 1, §9.] But because the losses in the angelic multitude were to be repaired by the number of human beings, both belief and widespread opinion strongly hold that the multitude of the fallen must be compensated by equality, so that however great the number of demons, an equal number among human beings and the good may be hoped for. Was human nature, then, not to be made unless angelic nature fell? Was the world not always without humanity? Was earth in vain, sea futile, air and stars for nothing, and the luminaries themselves superfluous? Surely all these things, according to authoritative testimony, are assigned only to our uses.

Yet because, once those uses have finally ended, they will remain improved for the beauty of the world, they could by the same reasoning have been made even apart from such uses: the world would indeed be less perfect without human beings, yet still honorable in its own adornment. But if, while the angel stood, the human being were made and then wholly perished—whence would the Fall come, when there was no devil? And why would the human being be made if he were wholly to perish?

[Col. 0742A] Either outcome could indeed have occurred; but this seems less likely and that more fitting: namely, that the heavenly Jerusalem would be made fruitful with a far greater number of citizens than it is now expected shortly to receive. For the human multitude added to them would increase the completeness of the spiritual hosts. Therefore, because that city hopes partly for reparation of the loss caused by its diminution, it should also partly rejoice. For it hopes to have as many citizens as it knows angels to have been created; but it does not hope for that number which it undoubtedly would have had if the angel had remained standing and the human being had adhered to the one who stood.

But the Apostle attributes imperfection to this present life and perfection to the future: “For we know in part and we prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be done away” (I Cor. XIII, 9). [Col. 0742B] [Note: [Col. 0742D] See Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 29; and *City of God*, XXII, chapter 1; Anselm, *Why God Became Man*, chapter 18.] Therefore in the future age there will be neither restoration nor diminished joy. Or must additions to the number of saints be owed for so long as the diminution of the angels is made whole, and, once restored, be heaped up with the additional human increase owing to it—so that the entire multitude of Sabaoth, however great it was when created, may be restored by the substitution of human beings, and, beyond that, those human beings not be lacking who perhaps ought not to have been lacking even if the angel had not fallen? For perhaps God’s creation would have been incomplete without humanity.

But now there is a greater multitude of saints than those who will fill the places of demons. This is in no way incongruous, except because it is contrary to common opinion. Nor perhaps is it wholly contrary even to common opinion; for Scripture, against which it is impious to speak, says: “He set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God” (Deut. XXXII, 8). [Col. 0742C] [Note: [Col. 0742D] Gregory, Homily 34 on the Gospels.] Someone whose authority in the Scriptures deserves assured confidence, explaining this passage, maintains that the multiplication of the nations to be saved will finally end when it has reached, in faithful equality, the number of the holy angels—that is, of those who remained standing.

Certainly it could have happened that more angels remained standing and fewer fell. Thus saints equal in number to the greater group can fill the places of the fewer by one portion of their number; while by the portion exceeding that number they can complete the number which, even if no angels had fallen, was to be completed from angels and human beings counted together as one. But this view required a smaller number of good human beings if the angels had remained; because they erred, it requires a greater number. Yet this is not absurd, for the Fall of angels demands it.

[Col. 0742D] I do not recall ever having heard that among angels the host of demons is the more numerous, as among human beings the host of the reprobate is known to be much larger. Nevertheless, on whichever view one settles, either the saints will be more numerous than the angels, if an equal number must be substituted in the place of demons; or the starry dwelling recovers an unequal compensation for its loss, if it receives only a human multitude equal to its inhabitants. But whichever of these two be the case, there would be lacking the total number of human beings and angels that would have existed without the Fall.

But if that opinion is preferred which makes human beings—saying nothing of the lost—as many as the angels, and likewise as many as the demons, then without doubt the number among angels and demons will be equal, as some indeed hold. Yet this doctrine of equality seems open to criticism because of the equality of citizens. For if the total number of heavenly spirits had not been diminished by any Fall, it would have increased by the addition of humanity; now, however, with the Fall restored by equality, the total just mentioned is restored, but the increase that would have come from humanity does not return. This perhaps does not displease one who says that each total is subject to perfection: both the earlier total of more citizens and the later total of fewer.

[Col. 0743B] But it would be quite surprising unless the total were so much more perfect as the reverence of its citizens were more abundant. Yet it would be more surprising still unless the most perfect God had also preferred the more perfect total, especially since, had subjection been preserved, it would have been such. For I am not unaware that God was able to create a total however much greater or smaller. But this, it seems, pleased Him: that which would have come to be had pride been removed—unless perhaps what will be lacking in number is to be supplied in merit. For a multitude may be smaller in number yet equal, or even greater, in merit.

## CHAPTER XVII. The angel sinned, and man, who immediately rises again equal to the angel.

For if angels, rather than human beings, had offended, those who remained standing would surely have filled the places of those who fell. And if it so pleased [Col. 0743C] God, by the merit of virtues to prolong both parties, so that, if not by number, then by worth they might equal that whole number which was to be gathered from human beings, and also those angels who sinned—had they not sinned. But human beings too sinned. Yet from their error the Redeemer rescued as many as He willed; and He not only made the number of those rescued equal to the total just mentioned, but even set it above it—perhaps not by equality of number, but by surpassing merit.

For if the saints are, as they say, to be made equal at the regeneration even to the angels confirmed in grace; and if the angels, as reason seems to show, deserved to be increased for their steadfastness, because they rejected the example of evil offered by the others stained by pride, just as the latter deserved to be diminished for their fall (these, certainly, being deprived of that increase unless [Col. 0743D] those had sinned), there is no doubt that human beings will attain a merit far more immense than the angels would have possessed had none fallen. For the angels are already so great, and human beings are hoped in the future, as has been said, to be made their equals. Why? Because human beings too deserted the way of righteousness through their own fault; but, restored by God’s grace and having now experienced their loss, they perhaps seized it again with far greater ardor. Certainly, had they not transgressed, they would have been happier; but now they have become no worse at all. Thus transgression brought misery, while God’s mercy restored holiness—or, if one ought so to believe, increased it. For according to the Apostle: “Power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9).

Therefore peaceful good conduct merits [Col. 0744A] life; but warfare, when it triumphs, merits glory. For warfare attacks from one side through the tempter’s enticement, and from the other through the madness of the persecutor. Yet one supported by strength, struggling against it, may be shaken by worldly frailty, but cannot be overthrown while God’s grace sustains him. Therefore there is no condemnation, even if one totters under suffering, provided that reason dissents; or even if, touched by human frailty, one falls—what harm is there, if afterwards he rises more cautious, indeed better through humility? For the Spirit works all things together for good (Rom. 8:29). [Note: [Col. 0743D] “And the palm is more glorious for one who, when tempted, did not consent, than for one who was unable to be tempted.” Augustine, *On Genesis*, I, ch. 6, [Col. 0744D].]

If, therefore, there had been no struggle, there would have been no palm of victory. Remove the arena and the prize too is removed; the athlete is no longer an athlete. His earlier caution has perished with humility; patience has withdrawn; and whatever other qualities depend upon exercise have disappeared—qualities without which, if you live in repose, you may be a good man, but cannot be a good soldier. [Col. 0744B] Take up these arms: now you are both, and therefore you are better.

These points aim to show that, just as human beings would have become perfect had obedience been preserved, so now, after it has been lost, they may hope through God’s compassion to become more perfect. Nor are we permitted to doubt whether holy Zion is of greater excellence after Adam’s fall, since [indeed (or: also)] we know that it has twice had its one—rather, its supreme—head, namely our Savior Jesus, and second, the queen of the angels, His undefiled virgin mother Mary. [Note: [Col. 0744D] Consult the notes.]

But if the mother, [as] adorned with such fruitfulness and redeemed at the price of such offspring, had not needed a Redeemer, she would not have been illumined by these luminaries as by sun and moon; and therefore, had she not been infected by sin and had needed no healing, she would have been far inferior, with salvation preserved, to what she is now with salvation [Col. 0744C] restored.

Nor does that city alone shine more brilliantly in itself; it also possesses more illustrious citizens. For the ever-virgin Mary, made the mother of the Savior, grew beyond all that can be said. Do not the saints, then, made Christ’s brothers, likewise grow? Certainly they grow—but as His mother herself grew, and as His brothers themselves grow. In what way as brothers? In honor alone? But what is honor except vanity without accompanying benefit? Therefore they appear to have become better in merit and more worthy of God as their brother. Indeed, He declared them to be His brothers when He said to the Father concerning His brothers through the Prophet: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers” (Ps. 21:23).

Furthermore, through Adam’s fault humanity seems to me to have increased, when I consider the origin of man and angel. Let us suppose [Col. 0744D] that each had preserved the state in which he was made. Then, if the angel is lesser than he is now, as was said—and it is not fitting that man should be greater than angel, which is plainly evident now, since at most man is only equal to the angel—without doubt man would be greatly equal to the angel and would appear less than he now does.

Conversely, if the human fall, through God’s mercy, brought increase to humanity, then the angel must also be considered to have increased through the angelic fall, God rewarding him—lest, if man increased and the angel did not, man should surpass him, although without this increase he had been equal. Yet I do not praise fault in angel or man, although majesty increased to both through fault. I accuse the fault; I proclaim God. God is wonderful: wonderful when He creates both wonderfully, more wonderful when He wonderfully repairs them after their creation and diminution. For if He had preserved in goodness those whom He had begotten good, that would indeed have been great. But now, because He turns wickedness into good, He has certainly done something greater. Although nothing is difficult for God, it nevertheless seems more possible for that which is not to come into being, because nothing resists its being brought forth, than for that which exists badly—and therefore resists—to be corrected.

O ineffable mercy! We deserted our Creator and turned aside to the betrayer; yet the merciful One, though provoked by our folly, is not made harsher toward us, but is proved more merciful, because He not only brings back fugitives, but redeems them by His own death. O [Col. 0745B] venerable Judge! An angel fell through abusing freedom. Another received the price for the one who fell. 82 What then have you done, Satan? You tore yourself away from your own fellowship; through deceit you seduced man. But whom did you harm? Human nature is better because of you; angelic nature is greater; heaven lost you—indeed, it expelled one unworthy of itself; one more worthy succeeded in your place. “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:11). Truth was displayed in the angel and in you; mercy shone forth in man.

For it belongs to justice to inflict punishment upon you and yours, unrepentant as you are—or rather, to speak more truly, upon you miserable ones with him. It belongs to mercy to confer glory on that angel who, in contemplation of God, rejected your ways; and it plainly belongs to mercy, in human nature, not merely to reconcile to Himself the fugitives, but by unusual loving-kindness, as it were after a triumph, to crown them. [Col. 0745C] All these things accrue through you to your pain, and to the honor of the Creator and those whom He has increased. Whom, then, did you harm? Yourself alone.

Indeed, for these reasons it serves the Creator’s praise that He decreed the heavenly Jerusalem, because through His working it was renewed to the highest degree, either by restoration of number or by the supplement of merit. If the number of its citizens must necessarily return to equality, and no more human beings can ascend than demons fell, then undoubtedly, unless that city were destined partly to fall, man would not have been made at all; indeed, nothing would exist which only man would require. And there would be perfection, but less than it is now, since God not only restores the fall of created things, but wonderfully exalts them, thereby clearly revealing both His power and His mercy.

[Col. 0745D] For God, in His providence, foresaw the losses of the spirits and planned their restoration; He created man, and whatever man required. As we said a little earlier, perhaps man ought not to have been created unless the heavenly court, emptied of its proper number and decreed to be restored by the supplement of human beings, had required it. But when this court was at last restored in number, how was it also made equal in dignity? Surely man is less than an angel in this age, though not in the age to come.

## CHAPTER XVIII. If man had not sinned, he would have been free from death and punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0745D] *Magister*, II, distinctions 19 and 20.]

Let us return from our lengthy digression and, as we began, [Col. 0746A] review the beginnings of humanity. Therefore, unless the first man had gone astray, he would, as I have said, have deserved no punishment for himself or his offspring. For why should innocence be struck, when there is no cause for striking—that is, sin? Just as death, “the sting of sin” (1 Cor. 15:55), is introduced, so too is the punishment by which death is anticipated. Hence, after transgression was committed, the woman is assigned labor in childbirth (Gen. 3:16), servitude in her activity; and the man, sustenance in sweat and a toilsome life, until he returns to the earth from which he was taken (ibid.).

Thus no affliction would have troubled human beings unless a hasty impulse of counsel had broken the covenant struck with the Creator by the benefit of creation. [Note: [Col. 0745D] Augustine, XIV, *On the City of God*, ch. 26.] And now a woman, married to a virgin man, would give birth without pain, having received the male seed [Col. 0746B] without ardor. For no act would occur with wrongdoing, none without delight. Religion, carefully observed on every side, would banish weariness too; for a life that was nothing but obedience would fail if it became burdensome to itself.

## CHAPTER XIX. What paradise was like, and what man was like when expelled from it.

[Note: [Col. 0746D] *Magister*, II, distinctions 17 and 29.]

Paradise of delight removed weariness from its inhabitants: shaded by fruitful trees and watered, like Egypt by the Nile, by an immense spring; situated in the East, as some say; raised so high above the rest of the world that it remained wholly untouched by the waters of the Flood. By its situation it defended the immense expanse of its native plain from every inclemency and rose above all the pestilential [Col. 0746C] changes of our atmosphere. It had fruit for food sufficient for whatever multitude it might contain, and also the fruit of the tree of life against disease, death, and old age. By God’s gift, its power is said to have been so great that even after sin it would have driven every affliction away from man, if its use had still been permitted. Therefore divine vengeance expelled the offender, lest he take from the tree of life and, by force imposed upon death contrary to his desert, live forever.

Therefore he was expelled so that he might die and the sentence of the One threatening might be fulfilled, according as He said: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2:17). Yet there is no doubt that he could have died within but lived outside, either if use of the tree had been forbidden or if the tree had been deprived of this power, unless the just Judge had provided one place worthy of righteousness and another place worthy of transgression. [Col. 0746D] Having been expelled, he seems to have lived in exile near the double cave—where he is believed to have been buried with the other patriarchs, and where some think he was also created—because he heard from the Lord that, after continual calamity, by dying he would return to the earth from which he was taken (Gen. 3:19), that is, the earth from which he was created. For Scripture seems to establish that he was formed outside paradise, when it says that God brought the man whom He had formed into paradise (Gen. 2:8).

And lest human presumption should entertain thoughts of return, that place is thought to have escaped our intercourse through a vast expanse either of sea or of desert. [Col. 0747A] And lest wicked labor, after overcoming the intervening obstacles—if indeed that is possible—should endeavor, as though now having attained its desire, to force its way through the difficult entrance, a revolving flame is maintained at the threshold by angelic ministry (Gen. 3:25), to frustrate every rash attempt. But what need is there for the way to the tree of life to be guarded by a fiery sword stationed before paradise, if no one can approach it as far as that?

Does the event concern mystery alone—namely, that there is no return to paradise, that is, to rest, except by passing through the sword, that is, anxiety? But if our effort is barred from access to that place by an interruption of intervening space, perhaps vast and rough but by no means insurmountable, why has no one, repelled by the flaming sword from entering, returned gloriously after setting out ingloriously? [Col. 0747B] Is it because paradise has not yet made its region known to any person of our condition?

But again, why is it guarded, if distance, by which it is separated and unknown, is sufficient for its protection? Or if, as most assert, it lies in the East, has no one dared undertake so long a journey? Or has someone, frightened by the harshness of the long interval and ignorant of paradise, condemned the rashness of the undertaking? Yet although God, by the understanding through which nothing remains unknown to Him, knew that no one would approach it through human effort, He nevertheless preferred, either for the sake of signification or to impress upon human minds the guilt of disobedience and the loss of paradise, both to fortify paradise with a watchful guard and to transmit its protection in writing for those who would read.

## CHAPTER XX. Adam was equally exposed to good and evil.

[Col. 0747C]

[Note: [Col. 0747D] *Magister*, distinctions 24 and 29.]

But let us return to man in paradise, not yet a transgressor. Thus he could die and not die; he could sin and remain free from sin. Certainly he was not incited to fault by any tinder of sin, nor was he restrained from fault by any force; free in either direction, he suffered difficulty in neither. He was sufficient for himself in illicit matters, while God’s help stood by him for honorable ones. [Note: [Col. 0747D] *Magister*, II, distinction 18, §2 ff.] But transgression made him prone to transgression and unworthy of God’s help, so that evil may sit in the heart and good become displeasing.

But death would come: either with sin, if he lacked life’s fruit, or even without sin, if he abstained from [Col. 0747D] eating. For just as the offender could no longer avoid death when deprived of the healing remedy of life-giving food, so before the offense he would not remain alive if he withdrew himself from the food of life. What does it mean, then, when I say “before the offense,” as though he could be innocent who does not eat and thereby dies? Clearly, then, he was animate (*animalis*), since he could not endure without food! For I was made animate, destined through obedience to become spiritual. For according to the Apostle: “What is spiritual is not first, but what is animate” (1 Cor. 15:46). Thus man might become more glorious, receiving blessedness as in some sense due to his own [Col. 0748A] merit, though increased by God’s grace.

Accordingly abstinence from one fruit is commanded; and, given the full grace of the One commanding, it is not difficult, since all the rest are allowed. For it was permitted to eat from every tree of paradise (Gen. 2:16), but He forbade eating from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 3:3). Even if a difficult command had been given, it would certainly not have been fitting to refuse it. How much more wickedly does he incur the iniquity of faithless servitude who both receives the Lord’s commands and, having received them, sets them aside without necessity. Therefore, the first man, the stronger in nature and the higher in place, was all the more shameful in his fall.

But to us is owed a glorious triumph over the enemy: though prone to falling through the tinder of sin and exiled among the Babylonians in his kingdom, we, with God as our author, reduce to nothing the poisonous cunning of the deceiver; and, breaking the bonds of captivity, joyfully return to our homeland.

## CHAPTER XXI. He could misuse freedom in various ways.

But could he who seized the forbidden fruit have misused freedom in another way as well? Before eating the death-bringing fruit, the woman, shamefully seduced, believed the serpent that the prohibition of eating had been made with evil guile and that the threat of death was not only false but envious, lest those who ate should attain the divine likeness. Therefore, after the crime had been committed, the Trinity employs bitter irony: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us” (Gen. 3:22). [Note: [Col. 0748D] *Magister*, II, distinction 22, §5.]

Yet Adam himself did not hope in that way, since according to the Apostle Eve alone, and not Adam in the same manner, was deceived, Adam having been created more discerning. [Col. 0748C] Thus either the man was taunted through the woman’s pain; or he was taunted because he did not restrain the rashness of the inferior sex; or finally—and this seems most likely—because he rashly desired what he knew to be impossible. And since “before ruin the heart is lifted up” (Prov. 16:18), he either arrogantly delighted, as I have said, in the serpent’s promise, though he knew it was empty; or, carried along by feminine impulse, a man excessively subject to his wife knowingly opposed his Creator. He first secretly stained himself in mind by arrogance, so that afterwards, once the crime had become manifest, he might deserve his fall.

[Note: [Col. 0748D] Augustine, XIV, *On the City of God*, ch. 11. “It must be believed that he made use of his woman—one human being joined to one human being, a wife to her husband—for transgressing God’s law; not because he was seduced into believing her as though she spoke truthfully, but because he yielded to the bond of companionship.”]

Therefore both sinned grievously, but the woman more grievously, before they fell. For both were wickedly defiled, corrupted inwardly; but their defilement was increased when it broke out outwardly.

[Col. 0748D] Yet if each offense is weighed more carefully in itself, the inward stain of yielding seems worse. The fruit itself was good; it was harmful only because it was forbidden. Taken insolently, it certainly produces offense because it despises the judgment of the One commanding. But Adam had earlier acted more foolishly and ruinously, if, as I have said, through evil desire he armed himself against majesty. Eve, however, raved far more madly when, in her ambition, she attributed to the Creator the devil’s lie and envy. Already ungrateful for His benevolence in creating her, [Col. 0749A] because she rivaled His majesty, she had experienced it; and the reason implanted in her, though now deceived by falsehood—yet previously illumined by native brilliance—held truth before her.

Hence, to one inferring some things from others, it is entirely clear that the first human beings sinned inwardly before their external offense, and in many ways; and that they could have done so in still more ways.

Why, then, was that eating alone to be forbidden? Were not other things harmful to experience because they were not forbidden? Did not He forbid all things together who enlightened man by reason to distinguish permitted from forbidden things? Would man, then, not fall by acting against conscience, when the angel fell by accusing conscience through ambition? Therefore, because things evil in themselves did not need to be forbidden, He forbade what was in itself permitted and would become illicit by being prohibited. Perhaps God wished [Col. 0749B] to suggest to us that the abstinence most pleasing to Him is that which not only avoids evil, but also takes some lawful things in moderation and wholly relinquishes others in contemplation of God. Or man was not forbidden from evil, lest it should seem to have harmed him because it was evil rather than because it was prohibited.

85 But since a law precisely laid down establishes a reward so that it may be loved, and a punishment so that fear may be instilled, the threat of death follows the prohibition of food. Perhaps this is so that reason may understand that, if what was not evil in itself was to be punished with so severe a penalty because it was forbidden, then what was naturally evil and likewise forbidden by intervening reason could much less be committed with impunity; rather, it must be punished by an equal or greater penalty. Thus perhaps the punishment of one fault is proclaimed so that the same thing may be feared in other cases. But the foretold punishment of the transgressor implies, conversely, the reward of the obedient. For divine speech customarily states one part and leaves the rest to be understood. Thus, in threatening death, it passed over the innumerable sufferings which precede it and was silent about the exile in hell which follows it. Similarly, it may be that He intended death, which He assigned to one fault, to be assigned to all others as well.

Unless someone replies that the repeatedly mentioned eating was to be punished by death only because of the weight of preceding crimes. Then, unless such crimes had preceded, would death not be inflicted upon the guilty person merely for the eating alone? Yet the words of the Lord’s threat appear [Col. 0749D] to have introduced the forbidden eating as though it alone were sufficient for death.

## CHAPTER XXII. The threat also applied to Eve.

[Note: [Col. 0749D] *Magister*, II, distinction 21, final section.]

If we consult the words, they seem to concern the man alone; if we attend to what follows, they concern the woman too. For she herself, responding to the serpent in the plural, made known that what had been commanded to the man was commanded to her as well. Unless she had shared with her husband in the command, she would not have remained immune from the penalty of guilt. Therefore the Creator, speaking to the man, spoke in the man to the woman also; perhaps even to the whole household, so that instruction poured into the head might then spread through the members. This indeed seems to be so. For just as obedience was necessary to the parents for an increase of merit [Col. 0750A] and as a sign of subjection, so it was also necessary to their children. Since disobedience is punished in children too, obedience likewise appears to have been set before them.

Perhaps this is why the tree of transgression, like the tree of life, is said to have occupied the middle of paradise: that its native inhabitants might recognize that use of the former was forbidden to them all alike, while use of the latter was granted. Therefore the Lord set no limit upon the duration for which this abstinence of obedience was commanded. For in heaven no food at all would be taken, nor was this food ever promised to be taken in paradise. Hence the Lord says to man concerning that food: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2:17), that is, from being mortal you shall become destined to die.

Therefore, because He substitutes death for the eater, it is evident that He forbids eating so long as man can die. And because He says, “on whatever day,” He excludes no time during which man can die. In the meantime death appears possible until, obedience having been completed, he passed from paradise into heaven, from the place of merit to the place of reward: putting off the mortal condition necessary to one who fights, and putting on the immortal condition appropriate to one who triumphs; once time had passed, to be rewarded with eternity, as free from every corruption as he would be removed from corrupting food.

But let us examine the words of the command further. By mentioning a day, He indicated time, not eternity; for the prohibition would be superfluous when the forbidden thing could not be pleasing. But when [Col. 0750C] He first put forward the sign of universality, He excepted no day. Therefore, when He added “day” to the universal expression, saying, “On whatever day you eat,” and so forth, He warned the hearer to refrain from eating as long as the return of day remained in his power. Accordingly, both the parents and all children, if they had been born in paradise, ought—as seems likely—to have kept this command for as long as they dwelt there, receiving the reward if, though able to transgress, they refused.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Even if Adam had persevered, he would not have imposed on his descendants a necessity of persevering.

For if the Creator’s grace had bestowed such strength upon free will that it had no capacity to bend toward forbidden acts, abstinence would be commanded in vain and [Col. 0750D] the reward of abstinence would not be deserved. Why, then, just as the voluntary vices of the parents rendered their children necessarily liable to vice, would parents freely persevering not have produced necessary perseverance in their children? Or was the law of abstinence directed only to themselves?

But this may perhaps seem absurd to someone. Perhaps it is more fittingly said that those born received no more strength than those created, and that both the begotten and the unbegotten were equally subject to the law. All obeying it would likewise all be rewarded. Then, according to the tradition of the authorities, only those would be born, as we have said, whom Christian salvation now adopts: by God’s power ensuring that those who are good, though born to reprobate parents, would be born not from those parents, who then would not exist, but from their good parents—and, as seems more likely, not from more remote ancestors but from immediate ones.

But if one part obeyed the law and another obeyed desire, the good appear to have needed an increase in number, so that the total foreseen by God might stand in complete fulfillment. The rebellious, however, would no longer be recalled but consigned to the exile of hell—unless perhaps the merciful condescension of the Creator, which attended the universality of our fall, guarding against the complete loss of so worthy a creature, brought back to their homeland those whom it was proper to bring back, and in its lavish benevolence preferred to complete the saints—whose small number could be filled by their own increase—from the return of the fugitives.

Yet if, before the divine judgment, that opinion prevails [Col. 0751B] which maintains that the innocence of the first human beings would have been transmitted to their descendants, just as through their crime all are held under inherited guilt, we may without absurdity say that the first parents, after the enemy was defeated and their merit of obedience advanced as God should provide, would obtain security for their own future perseverance and that of their descendants—not by receiving a necessity of doing good, but by having their will established in good.

Unless some more plausibly maintain that the same progress made by the parents was to be granted to their children: they would either, after obedience was completed, pass one by one after the manner of our own time; or rather, because their life was everlasting, wait a little while until the number of our fellow servants was completed (Rev. 6:11), and at last exchange paradise for heaven generally, as we hope will happen now.

## CHAPTER XXIV. God commands justly, although evil follows from it.

[Note: [Col. 0751D] *Magister*, II, distinction 23.]

But does God, foreknowing all things, rightly command that which, once commanded, results in evil? Why should the Lord not command His servant what ought rightly to be done, even though He knows that the servant will wickedly turn away from the law? The Lord, then, commands fittingly, as befits the Lord; the wicked servant pays the penalty of insolence, as befits one who is rebellious. What is unjust here? What is commanded is just; what is punished is just.

Or did that which was just in itself become unjust with respect to the future? Would He therefore not command His servant to render the Lord’s due obedience because He knew that the servant who had served his Lord would not serve Him? Is it not better that God command what is His due, and that the despiser of the command suffer what is his due? Finally, why should He not impose a duty upon one who would refuse it, in order that He might healthfully humble by afflictions one perniciously puffed up; might teach—[Note: [Col. 0751D] A word such as *doceret* (“might teach”) or something similar seems to be missing.]—the madman, stirred by suffering, to condemn his counsel and submit his own will to the divine will; and might make him, having experienced the highest danger, clearly recognize that it is supreme folly for a creature to strive against his Creator, who offers life to one moving toward Him and death to one moving away from Him?

Thus after his fall man was made not so much weaker as more certain in matters relating to God and more cautious in matters coming from the enemy. [Col. 0752A] For weakness, medicinally opposed to arrogance, nourishes humility; the grace of the healer, supporting one who totters, strengthens weakness, so that the one surrounded by weakness may neither be lifted up in boastfulness nor succumb in battle when sustained by the Lord’s kindness. Therefore weakness, when it restrains conduct and kindles charity—for, indignant at torpor, it rises as though spurred on—should be accounted not a deficiency of nature but an advantage. [Note: [Col. 0752D] Augustine, Letter 105 to Sixtus; Letter 157 to Optatus, before the middle; and Sermon 254, *On Time*.]

For what if certain persons, pursuing the allurements of desires, gradually become worse through illness, are entangled in most destructive crimes, and from sluggish persons become paralytics—indeed, from sick persons, dead persons? Does not the Judge of supreme equity and mercy either mercifully transform and renew such persons, or more sternly exercise His own people through the fallen, or finally prepare vessels of mercy in vessels of wrath? [Col. 0752B] Thus appear both what was owed to them because of fault and what is bestowed in praise of the One who shows mercy. Therefore He rightly permits evils to occur, because He knows how to make good out of evils.

## CHAPTER XXV. Before sin there was no need for clothing.

The first human beings had no need to be clothed, since they had nothing shameful about them and no intensity of heat or cold could harm them. Their nature, then fortified against such things, and the apparently temperate pleasantness proper to the place both repelled these changes of air. Nor did the Creator’s glory permit any ugliness in His work, especially in man, whom He set above the other living creatures even in bodily form.

But why, after sin, were they ashamed of their nakedness—especially their genitals? Because mutual lust, inflamed at the sight of one another, [Col. 0752C] then first assailed them: it would produce shame through the novelty of the experience and, through the titillation of the flesh, seek concealment.

Whatever deformity in the limbs forces itself upon our sight is undoubtedly derived from the anger of the Creator, according to the saying: “I am stricken like grass” (Ps. 101:5). For if peace had been preserved, all things would have proceeded more naturally for human beings—first the innocence of the first parents, followed by that of their descendants. Therefore the Creator either permits or causes defects to arise among the members in anger, defects that He would certainly have driven away had He been appeased. He causes them when, for example, He marks our flesh with leprosy or when any single incongruity discolors its otherwise remaining beauty. He permits them when, for example, through parental negligence women conceive while menstruating, [Col. 0752D] or when pregnant women injure in some manner a child rationally conceived and are to bear a fetus of that kind. Why? Because of the guilt of presumption in either parent; through God’s governance, altogether just in itself, though for us often hidden.

Therefore, if such afflictions, darkening the native appearance considerably, are inflicted upon the whole succession through God’s anger—either a filial blow to humble or a cruel blow to cast down—what is absurd in maintaining that the first source of our race also, by transgressing, dimmed the brightness of its creation, and so found itself as much more deformed as it was made worse?

[Col. 0753A] But you will say: “An offense spiritually stains a person, while the flesh nonetheless remains in the fullness of its beauty.” Certainly most offenses do no physical injury, though some do. Envy disturbs human serenity of appearance by emaciation, lust by pallor, arrogance by an angry expression, and other things in other ways; yet nature remains as it was before and afterwards. How much more, then, does the primordial offense—which, from the moment it entered, changed nature so greatly that one who shortly before could not die was now dead—seem also to have presented to the eyes the offense of deformity?

How can a person, irreparably transformed from life to death, from health to frailty, and finally from frailty to corruption, with the bodily constitution irreparably dissolved, be thought—when all else has been lost—to have kept only the beauty appropriate to a perfection subject to change? [Col. 0753B] How, I ask, can I quickly persuade you that man fell into so great a collapse and with so great a loss to himself, without any loss of his former beauty? Yet if it so pleased God, man indeed fell and his beauty remained. But if his appearance too withered when struck by sin, what wonder if the now guilty man was ashamed when he looked at himself, though he had felt no shame in his former beauty?

He was especially troubled when he looked upon his own genitals and those of his companion, fearing a shameful movement might be marked in the shameful parts. Hence he is reported to have woven a girdle of fig leaves, perhaps fleeing both the deformity of the genitals and their movement. That movement, itself most foul, perhaps made those members uglier than all the rest through its most foul and perhaps continual presence, intolerable to behold. [Col. 0753C] Thus the sight of sex offended for two reasons: importunate movement and the deformity arising from it.

## CHAPTER XXVI. In what form the Lord walked in paradise.

It would be surprising unless the Lord presented Himself to be seen in a visible and especially human form, since, after the offense, He addressed in human fashion those who feared the face of the one walking. For walking required something visible, and speech required a human being. Such conversation seems fitting, as though from a human being to human beings—although it is well known that not God Himself, but an angel in God’s place, appeared in human form to no one. For they could not yet understand that spiritual speech by which spiritual beings speak among themselves and to God; otherwise there would have been no need for the visible, audible [Col. 0753D] word of a human being.

They therefore walked by faith, not yet by sight: faith which original stain would darken and healing grace would later illumine; sight to be received when the allotted measure of obedience was fulfilled. Hence it is clear that paradise had inhabitants of an intermediate condition, far inferior to heavenly beings and far superior to exiles. Therefore, in consequence of sinning, they deserved to decline in age, strength of intellect, inner purity, and outward beauty; but through the gratuitous mercy of the Creator they are to be restored, as regards the soul even in this age, and as regards the body only in the age to come. This is the first and second resurrection. Yet in the second, the first too will be completed.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The man yielded to the woman in sins, and is subjected to sin’s punishment.

[Col. 0754A]

But let us still consider the fall of the parents. When the man lifted himself up in pride against his head, who is Christ, he yielded to his wife, whose head he ought to have been, while she devised evil. For unless they had inwardly corrupted themselves through pride, which was to be repressed by their fall, he would undoubtedly have vigorously resisted his wife when she tempted him outwardly, and she the demon. For it is true that “before glory the heart is humbled” (Prov. 18:12). Therefore, had humility been preserved, they would have gained the glory of victory.

If the man alone had acted manfully, then, after the woman had been condemned so that fear and caution might be instilled in others, another woman would have had to be formed and joined to the man as an image of the first. But if that was not at all fitting, then, according to the Lord’s judgment, once the penalties of death had been imposed, the first woman appears to have had to be raised for the man, so that a holy woman with a holy man might beget children in paradise, lest this should occur contrary to merit, either from an evil person there or from a good person elsewhere. For without marriage, how would those being born be propagated?

But because both sinned, both paid penalties. For since an impure spirit infected pure flesh with its own stain, the infected flesh continually repays its infecter in kind, and now, restless with its desires, incites the one who disturbed it while it was at rest by the deadly taste. For before this there had been complete peace between these natures: the flesh urged nothing unlawful because it had received no injury. But when the spirit broke the covenant which had been made and infused its defects into the flesh, then, because the inflicted sickness never ceases to burn, the flesh thinks itself always still to be avenged, as though not sufficiently avenged. [Col. 0754C] And not without reason: whoever withdrew his own obedience from his own ruler is justly enslaved to that over which he ruled. He refused to obey his Creator; he is compelled to serve a slave.

What is the point of these things? I shall state it more plainly. When the soul despised obedience to the Lord and misused the body as though it were an instrument, it pitiably undermined the body’s strength toward evil; and from that enfeeblement it incurred many disadvantages. The body is weakened, or even falls, because the mind, seized with madness, pours into it, seminally and causally, the poisonous draught of transgression—with its resulting defects—so that it may be brought under control and also tormented: namely, wasting through various diseases, sometimes diverse deformity, at other times the wearing away or amputation of limbs, and finally death itself of the whole body. [Col. 0754D] For by transgressing, the mind brought it about that, when occasion arises, the flesh cannot avoid the aforesaid evils and, what is most pitiable of all, is compelled to render impure the spirit infused into it. [Note: [Col. 0753D] See the notes on the following chapter.]

Certainly this is most pitiable, yet not unjust. For since of its own accord it summoned a stain upon the body, it now deservedly endures that stain even against its will; for not even an infant of one day is without sin: “For every man is a liar” (Ps. 115:11). After original sin has been committed, the possibility that a human being should be without sin is lacking to man, though not lacking to God. Man cannot do this, and often seeks it; God can do it [Col. 0755A] and never does it. Man beneficially strives toward it; he is not allowed to attain it, and this too is beneficial: while he labours, religious devotion is satisfied; while he is held back, humility is satisfied. [Note: [Col. 0755D] By the ordinary law.]

God gives his saints a burden, lest ease in acting make the soul insolent and it fall. For every human being is held under the sin they call original; and since no one ever frees himself from its yoke, no one wholly overcomes, down to the last detail, the oppression of actual sins, which serve original sin. By the expiation of charity you can indeed escape, even if only for an hour, the entire host of actual sins; yet even in so cleansed a state, recalled to its habitual manner by the original disease, you cannot stand long. But the harmful root of origin—from which the still more harmful growth of actual sins springs up—is eradicated by no force, [Col. 0755B] unless perhaps together with life itself. Therefore, although the liability of origin has no means by which it may be washed away, [Note: [Col. 0755D] See the notes on the following chapter, 31.] it has a ground upon which it may be excused. For the grace of the Mediator is a remedy for the infirm, so that the sickness harms not salvation but benefits humility.

Thus corruption was inflicted upon the body by a mind suited to it; and, in return, the flesh repaid the mind with a corruption not unworthy of it. Hence the soul both contracts contagion and loses strength; reason, which ought through prudence to provide for the whole household and through rule to govern it, is deprived both of its kingdom and of its counsel, so that truth often either remains hidden or, when known, grows numb. Anger, when unrestrained, throws into confusion; desire, when inflamed, enfeebles. Both, crossing the threshold of moderation, rise irreverently against their mistress; while they entice by consent, they bind in servitude.

[Col. 0755C]

The five senses also, together with their instruments, and imagination, born from them and commonly inclined to vanity, continually strive to take reason captive—and very often succeed—unless reason is strengthened by grace and the hostile party is restrained.

What am I saying? Hear the sum of it. Whatever good the spirit apprehends through reason, however great it may be, it rejects if it gives no pleasure; whatever evil it reaches through the other faculties, however great, it embraces if it gives pleasure. By the one it is covered with darkness; by the other it is made impure through excess—unless the aid of the Creator remedies human defects in both respects. It is clear, then, that the body is weakened by the spirit, and that from the weakened body very many disadvantages return upon the spirit.

## Chapter XXVIII. As the first were, so also were those begotten from them.

[Col. 0755D]

[Note: [Col. 0755D] Master, Book II, distinction 31.]

But since in the first parents the entire multitude of their children was contained and confined within a narrow compass—not because each individual then possessed a separate portion of them (for two human beings do not seem sufficient for so great a capacity), but because those two contained within themselves the seminal cause of all, though certainly a very small one (for they produced very few children from themselves), from which the propagated multitude of the rest is expanded—[Note: [Col. 0756D] Consult the notes on this and the following chapters, where original sin is discussed.] such as the first two were, such those born from them had necessarily to be. For a small portion taken from a corrupted [Col. 0756A] mass must itself also be corrupted; from it, as from corrupted seed, corrupted fruit rises up—a human being, yet one made like his parents. And this portion, though corrupted in its origin, becomes more corrupt through generation. For generation also draws from sin the stain of lust: the seed drawn forth and emitted in its heat supplies matter, discoloured by an evil passion, for procreation. Hence the Prophet says: “In sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. 50:7). And Job: “Who can make clean one conceived from unclean seed?” (Job 14:4). Therefore, if corruption is owed to the seed from the mass, it is increased through generation.

Since the portion of the mass seems more corrupt, may that which is born from the portion likewise rightly be called more corrupt, [Col. 0756B] so that each person is the more corrupt the farther removed he is from the first parent? For if, because the seminal cause is corrupt, it requires a corrupt effect, why should it not require a more corrupt effect because it is more corrupt? Indeed, the part which is seed appears more impure than its whole. For although the whole human being is shaken by lust, its chief force is seen to tend toward this: that the part separated from the whole may turn itself into another form. And because it is directed most especially to itself, it also wastes itself away most especially.

But if a human being, stained in other respects, were to beget without lust, would such offspring be conspicuous for purity because its conception proceeded without passion? Yet how could a solid structure stand upon unstable material? Especially since the Lord Jesus, uniquely begotten in the manner stated above, while granting to nature all its other defects, departed from nature and excluded nature’s stain, in order that he might thus assume true humanity without anything in man hindering the plan of human redemption. For when universal nature found no place for itself in the Lord Jesus, an unprecedented violence was inflicted upon it: not undeservedly upon its Author, but necessarily upon the sinner. [Col. 0756C] The Holy Spirit, coming upon the Virgin, kept her untouched and overshadowed her from the passion to which conception is subject; and he brought the conception forth to such a point that, though the cause of dying remained, the cause of sinning was expelled. Therefore that which was born holy deserved to be personally united to the Son of God.

If, therefore, the Son of Man was made immune from sin not by nature but by the power of the Most High, [Col. 0756D] and solely in order that he might become a worthy sacrifice for sin, how could anyone—even if he is supposed to have been begotten without sexual intercourse—be naturally pure, without cause, when begotten from the impure? And if he is granted to be free from guilt, let him also be granted to be free from punishment. For who is deservedly afflicted by punishment unless defilement through guilt has preceded? Hence the Lord paid what he did not seize, since he was struck not for his own deeds but for ours; [he is] a little less than him who, because he is granted to be free from defilement, ought also to remain untouched by punishment.

For as long as Adam stood rightly, all was well with him; when he bent himself toward wrongdoing, he immediately received punishment. To whomever parental guilt is transmitted, the punishment owed to guilt is also inflicted. But punishment is hoped to be removed when guilt finds no place in a man. If, therefore, someone were perhaps to be born without guilt, he would likewise be without punishment—unless death, by admitting Adam’s guilt, had also appropriated punishment.

Moreover, such a man, since he would not be struck by the incentives of vices, would surely remain in no respect unable to persevere forever in native purity. Since he possesses unending innocence, let him also possess life. Yet, situated outside Paradise and thus excluded from the tree of life, he has life without death within his grasp—a life which not even the first man in Paradise could have possessed without the benefit of that same tree. Surely, since the fiery sword guarded the entrance to Paradise after the first pair were expelled, I think that no one, barred by the first guilt, was borne into it as the first man had been, except perhaps the two, Elijah and Enoch, to whom the merit of their life, and especially the reason of divine dispensation, granted this.

[Col. 0757A]

Either, then, the man described lives without using the tree of life, or dies without deserving punishment. But because reason seems to grant assent to neither alternative, I think it must be admitted that this man of whom we speak drew to himself the nature of the whole mass, so that, although his conception issued chastely from his parents’ loins, it nevertheless contracted disease because it came forth from diseased persons. But what kind of disease? One by which a man is inclined to sin, [Col. 0757C] and is bound to death and to the signs that foretell death.

If unclean lust is added to this conception, whose chastity has just reproduced in the child the parental corruption, it makes that conception unclean. Thus, in accordance with Job’s complaint, one conceived from unclean seed cannot by nature be made clean; for, while he laments the uncleanness of the seed together with its germ, he indicates that lust, from which uncleanness flows, is to be blamed. Nature therefore brings one stain, lust another. For I do not know how it can properly be maintained, without damage to modesty, that both are the same stain, since reason has shown me one to be distinct from the other. [Note: [Col. 0757D] This is not the author’s opinion.] Nor, I think, should it be said either that an incorrupt portion proceeds from a corrupt mass, even if you remove lust; or that no defilement issues from the foulness of lust, even if you set aside the defect of nature. A particle, then, separated from its whole by the force of generation, receives, besides the stain it has from origin, another from generation. For reason does not allow us to suppose that lust supervenes without increasing the defect, or that nothing descends from origin while everything is derived from lust.

[Col. 0757D]

When I consider these things, the part appears more corrupt than its whole in its own respect, so much so that all the natural corruption of the parents pours itself causally into the seed, corrupting generation. For since parents are accidentally defiled—whether through choice, drunkenness, and wantonness, [Col. 0758A] or through a diseased bodily constitution, as in leprosy—reason does not compel the stain to be transmitted to descendants, although it often allows that this occurs. But a human being formed from seed twice corrupted is himself twice corrupted. These two defilements are reckoned either both as belonging to nature, or neither; or separately, so that one belongs by nature and the other does not, but belongs accidentally.

If both are naturally present in the child, it follows also that he will naturally beget offspring more corrupt than his parents and himself more foul in nature. For, besides the accompanying stain of parental nature, he receives, as we have often said, another from the uncleanness of conception. He transmits both as companions of his own nature, and as natural to him, to his own offspring. When a third is added, which lust inflicts, the original stain increases [Col. 0758B] and gains strength as it passes on. Hence, as we have already said, a person is shown to be naturally more corrupt the farther he is found to be from the first parent.

If this is true, perhaps this explains why human nature, just as it advances by succession, likewise declines in body—in age, strength, and size—while in mind it becomes daily more inclined toward forbidden things and slower in judgment: in our own age, indeed, astonishingly dull when it investigates what would profit it, but exceedingly ingenious when it handles vain things. Our nature of itself hastens toward ruin; and when God is angry, he precipitates it in its haste. Nevertheless there is no condemnation in the saints, for however infirm they may be, grace remedies them, and power is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor. 12:9).

[Col. 0758C]

And indeed, if both defilements are assumed into nature, the consequences we have stated will seem to follow. But if neither ought to be reckoned as belonging to nature, neither should be thought either to have been transmitted by predecessors or to be transmitted by successors. For it would be wrong that what alone is natural should leave nature’s propagation unaccompanied. Why, then, does not even one escape the sickness of those who beget, as though it were inherited by those begotten? But if one of the two claims for itself the right to subject the whole multitude of those born to its condition, which of the two is it? What lust produces was absent before lust; for if it had been present earlier, it would wrongly be declared to arise from lust. But what does not accompany nature and enters in time, since it does not flow from ancestors, [Col. 0758D] will not flow onward to descendants. Arising, however, from generation in those generated, it stains them in such a way that it does not carry the stain on to those generated by them—unless perhaps it has been declared universal for this reason: that no one is born who is not contaminated from unclean seed.

But the first human beings were not born under our law; since they lack generation, they also lack the defilement of generation. Yet the corruption of the human race, arising from and in them, had to be propagated into all posterity; and, as we also said above, besides the stain which lust produces, nature brings another. Thus, when we seek a single defect of the human race, we find it doubled. There is, therefore, one thing which depraves the first humans before intercourse and passes in its entirety into procreation. [Col. 0759A] For they themselves, to repeat briefly what has been said, withered in body; and their souls were weakened on both sides in their powers almost to the point of collapse, so that the spirit could not attain the purity it should seek in the body, because the body could not be cleansed so completely as to retain nothing by which it might harm its guest.

Hence a double contagion creeps into those born: one troublesome to the flesh, the other to the mind. The contagion is indeed double, but the sin is single: that which adheres to the flesh is only contagion, whereas the contagion present in the mind is both contagion and sin. Such were those born already; such also were those begotten by the born.

## Chapter XXIX. Whether the soul is guilty through the first original sin.

[Col. 0759B]

[Note: [Col. 0759D] Master, Book II, distinctions 30, 31, and following.]

Perhaps it is fitting that corrupt flesh should produce corrupt flesh. But whence the soul is corrupted may perhaps be sufficiently clear; yet whether it ought justly to be corrupted is not sufficiently clear unless it too proceeds from the parents. And even if someone contends that it proceeds from them, how is it justly contaminated by sin unless it is also punished for that contamination? But how, without reason, does it justly receive either guilt from a stain or punishment from guilt in infancy? If the stain of a child proceeds from fault of reason, whether by consenting or by neglecting, then the child sins not originally but actually; and this is rejected as contrary to authority.

For this reason, the soul, before it can distinguish actual sins, has no share in them but participates only in original sin, and from this is guilty, as justly as secretly: “The judgments of God are a great deep” (Ps. 35:7). But when he deigns to grant us his presence, the deep will be opened. For then, “Who shall seek mercy and truth?” (Ps. 60:8). And the Lord says: “On that day you will ask me nothing” (John 16:23). Meanwhile, piously acknowledging the ignorance owed to our frailty, let us not, as children, dispute over hidden matters, until he reveals the secrets of hearts and the things hidden in darkness.

## Chapter XXX. Whence evil comes, and what its reward is.

[Note: [Col. 0759D] Master, Book II, distinctions 34, 35, and 36.]
