But since God, the most certain author of all things desirable both for body and for mind, is their author, from where comes the origin of evil? God made angel and human being such that, if they willed, they could sin; and, when they sinned, they would undergo punishment: the angel, a fall; the human being, death and hell. [Col. 0759D] He gave the ability to sin so that whoever can sin and yet does not will to sin may deservedly be crowned. He set punishment before reason, so that the cautious may be frightened into guarding themselves, and the heedless may, as is fitting, be tormented for the warning of the just. Thus they were made able to sin and to receive punishment. Therefore it is not surprising, as has already been said, if they do what they can do. For from ability—which is surely a good of nature—they voluntarily proceed to willing, which is a defect of nature.

But an evil will shapes its own acts; such advancement is not from God. Yet punishment, which follows from fault, is not without God. Guilt is, indeed, like viper’s seed, from which a whole harvest of sorrows springs: both those brought by nature’s corruption and those brought by the Creator’s indignation. For it pleases God that we reap pain from both sources, because it did not displease us to sow iniquity.

[Col. 0760A]

Iniquity, because it is foul, never pleases God; punishment, because it is just, never displeases him. This is what it means that guilt is without him, but punishment through him. If, therefore, sin proceeds from power, which is God’s good, and punishment from sin, it is plainly clear that first evil has drawn its origin from good, then evil from evil. [Note: [Col. 0759D] Augustine, Book II, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, ch. 28, etc. [Col. 0760D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 14, toward the end.] Since the nature of the wicked is not incapable of action, but possesses its own will, when it freely turns of itself toward what is unlawful, it becomes liable to inevitable guilt. For by the Creator’s gift it possessed the capacity to remain in its own integrity and to be its own master. But if it preferred to slip headlong from the summit of perfection, it would not consider returning to be within its own power; rather, it would wish that it possessed this power rather than had created it. Therefore it is not surprising that one who entangled himself in sin without necessity should necessarily be held in sin. Yet for the guilty to escape unpunished would likewise conflict with the judge’s severity—not because he could not spare the guilty, but because it was more fitting that he punish. Thus guilt came from man; torment came from the Judge.

## Chapter XXXI. The whole multitude of human beings was defiled by one sin.

[Note: [Col. 0760D] Master, in the place cited above, on the transmission of sin.]

Since we said a little earlier that the sin of the parents was transmitted to all their [Col. 0760C] offspring—and for this reason is perhaps called original—we should inquire whether it is one sin or many by which the entire multitude of human beings, corrupted by hereditary right, is itself depraved as though from a root.

Consulting that passage of the Apostle in which, speaking of Adam, he adds, “In whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12), we seem to give the following answer: the entire mass of human beings was defiled together and at once when Adam sinned alone in Paradise—for all were still he. Did human beings, then, sin before they existed? Yet the first man sinned with his wife in Paradise; therefore all his offspring is held guilty outside Paradise. Thus all sinned together and at once, because he alone sinned in whom all were still confined causally and seminally, so that through his sin, once committed, all alike contracted guilt.

[Col. 0760D]

Accordingly, on the passage in John, “Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), the following exposition is found: [Note: [Col. 0760D] In the Ordinary Gloss.] “The sin of the world is called original sin because it is common to the whole world, by which all human nature, created together and at once, transgressed the divine laws through disobedience in Paradise; and the grace added to each individual remits that original sin.” What is therefore rightly called actual in the first human beings, as committed by themselves, is called original in those who follow, because it harms them from their origin.

[Note: [Col. 0761D] Master, Book II, distinction 33.]

But Adam sinned in many ways, both before and after the unlawful eating, while his children had not yet been begotten. Will all of this be imputed together to those born afterwards? If this is granted, will not those begotten after the sins of later parents be liable to the same sins? What things appear alike in reality, and what reason can rightly make them unlike—especially when Scripture testifies that God punishes the sins of parents in their children? If, therefore, we judge that all Adam’s transgression known to have preceded the generation of offspring is to be exacted from his children until the end—for how could what followed stain those already born?—why are the sins of parents punished in children only to the third and fourth generation? (Exod. 20:5) Unless perhaps the judge of supreme mercy, taking pity on his guilty people, set a limit to parental guilt, so that the punishment borne by children might be moderated even though their parents’ guilt was not.

But Scripture repeatedly declares that the eating of the forbidden fruit is detestable to those yet to be born. For since we consider children guilty because of their parents’ transgression, and the parents then committed either their only or their chief crime of transgression when they took the forbidden food, the eating harmful to their progenitors is rightly reckoned original sin to those begotten. Especially because death, which is known to have been inflicted upon the first-formed man as the punishment for that accursed eating, has been derived from him into all; this surely seems to require that all be held guilty of the aforesaid eating. [Col. 0761C] No one escapes that death, which unquestionably arose from the eating as punishment from guilt.

Thus the general guilt of the human race appears to be that eating alone, because it alone is demanded by the punishment of death owed to the whole world. But then the other sins of parents are not punished in children unless they imitate their father’s wickedness; hence punishment is fixed at the third or fourth generation. For parents who survive in wickedness so long commonly become instructors of their children; but when grown, the children, defiled by their own acts, perhaps deservedly perish.

But how does punishment reach little children whom no guilt defiles, and how are those who receive no defilement from themselves defiled from another, especially from one so remote? I should be less surprised if they received from Adam the sin itself from which contagion deservedly entered them. But now the wonder is increased for me because the whole guilt remained with him who alone ate wickedly, while the contagion from that evil eating nevertheless reaches his descendants. The parents alone sinned; why then are the descendants guilty? Do little children have in themselves some defect through which they have deservedly contracted guilt? But according to the Apostle, they have not yet done anything good or evil (Rom. 9:11).

[Col. 0762A]

Yet taught by the frequent tradition of the holy Fathers, we boldly confess that little children are bound by original sin alone, so that before the use of reason I judge it wicked to assign them actual faults.

Little children therefore draw a stain, and thereby guilt, from the first father. But what is the soul’s stain except guilt? How, then, can stain cling to one who lacks guilt? Or how can one free of stain rightly be guilty? Is the soul of a child then pure from every defilement? Is one entirely free from every crime deservedly assigned to torments? But authority testifies that not even an infant of one day is without sin. For example, one who has committed fornication but does not now commit it is certainly free from the act of fornication; yet if still unrepentant, he remains held by the guilt of a fornicator. However great the interval of place or time separating him from the act, he is rightly judged a fornicator, unclean, and finally guilty. So perhaps an infant is justly called a sinner, not because sin is present in him, but because it preceded in Adam.

[Note: [Col. 0761D] Augustine, Book I, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, ch. 26.]

For each person has sin as long as he lacks forgiveness for that sin. Therefore, although he does not have sin in act, he has it in guilt. But if baptismal remedy comes to the aid of an infant, is that infant not now without sin, since he neither has it in act nor remains liable to guilt? Likewise adults also, though not for long, are nevertheless for however brief a time entirely free from wicked acts through the compunction of a contrite heart; and, having obtained pardon for those acts, they are for the time being wholly cleansed and found to have no sin.

[Col. 0762B]

What then is meant when it is said that not even an infant of one day is without sin? Is this said not because a human being cannot be without guilt, but because he has not been without it? For although a little child may not have guilt, he has had it. An adult perhaps at some time drives the whole army of evils from the camp by the weapons of repentance; but such a person neither remained so before nor will always persevere so afterward. What, then, is the tinder of sin, the sickness of nature which will never leave mortals, except sin? Of this the Apostle says: “It is no longer I who do it, but sin which dwells in me” (Rom. 7:20). Is it called sin not as guilt, but as that by which one comes to sin?

But if it is truer that, after the fall of the first-formed man, no one in this state of mortality can be cleansed even for a moment so completely as to be subject to no sin whatsoever, then such guilt must be sought as can be excused by baptism or repentance but cannot be removed. [Col. 0762D] [Note: [Col. 0761D] See the Notes.] Perhaps this is what Scripture means when it grants that no infant of one day is without sin and declares that every human being is a liar (Ps. 115:11).

Thus the infant is guilty of two offences: he is implicated in original guilt and in his own. In original guilt, because, as the Apostle says of Adam, “In whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12). In his own, because Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0762D] Book VI, *Against Julian*, ch. 19; Book II, *On the Merits of Sins*, ch. 4; *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, ch. 26, etc.] that concupiscence is born with little children, is loosed from guilt in baptism, and is left for the contest. Since concupiscence needs forgiveness, it is clearly an offence; since it is born with little children and remains after baptism, [Col. 0763A] it is clearly continual.

But because reason does not permit, before discernment, either good or evil to be done, concupiscence must be understood as an offence—not indeed an actual one, but, since it is born with little children, a natural one. This is the tinder of sin, nourishing and advancing other sins. This is what lies in wait, as though in hiding places, during childhood, so that in its proper time it may leap forth openly, rendering people prone to evil action and causing them to incline downward toward vices. It makes contestants either honourable or inglorious, according as its evil prompting is resisted or consented to. When Adam wickedly desired, he brought this upon himself and left it to us as an inheritance.

It is therefore rightly called concupiscence, because it was produced through desiring and moves us to desire what is unlawful. If anyone, because it preceded in Adam and flowed from him to posterity, wishes to call it original, he may perhaps seem neither mistaken nor absurd—unless perhaps, because this too is called original sin, two original sins are introduced contrary to Scripture’s usage. Does Scripture, by mentioning one and passing over the other in silence, deny the other? The one is indeed original guilt, and is so called. Perhaps the other is also original, but is not called so to the same degree. Yet is it not in some way so called when it is said to be born with little children? For it would not be born with little children if the parents, and the first parents, had remained in native purity; nor would it be inborn in all unless it belonged to all. Is it not then proved to be original because it invades all to whom it flows even from the first parents? Yet the other has claimed this name for itself as though it were its own proper name.

[Col. 0763B]

But why? I do not know, unless perhaps because it was the origin both of concupiscence and of all evil. For although mortal eating came through desiring, concupiscence does not seem to have preceded the eating but to have followed it. If, after something had wrongly been desired, the mortal food had been abstained from, perhaps neither death nor concupiscence, its companion, would have had to be inflicted. For surely, like death, concupiscence is not the cause of disobedience but its punishment.

Yet when little children are called originally guilty, concupiscence seems either alone, or chiefly, to be blamed. For if a little child is guilty of two things, one in himself and the other in his parents, is it not reasonable that each is bound more by what is his own than by what belongs to another? How, however, can it be another’s, when “the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father”? (Ezek. 18:20). Perhaps descendants bear the iniquity of their ancestors, yet the son does not bear the iniquity of the father. From the time when one is called father and the other son, neither is bound by the other’s guilt; “the soul which sins, it shall die” (ibid.). But what does “it shall die” mean except that it alone, without another, is punished for its own offence? For the just Judge gives to each what is his own; he does not impose one person’s burden upon another. For, as the Apostle testifies, “Each shall bear his own burden” (Gal. 6:5).

[Col. 0763D]

[Note: [Col. 0763D] Master, Book II, distinction 33.]

If this conflicts with Scripture and does not please reason—to pursue in one innocent person the liability of another—then it is wrong also for Adam’s sin to be exacted from his descendants, unless perhaps the sins of parents are punished in children before baptism, while the son does not bear his father’s iniquity after baptism. Thus the prophetic utterance seems to have set a limit to the proverb in which it was said that the fathers ate sour grapes and consequently their children’s teeth are set on edge (Jer. 31:29). [Note: [Col. 0763D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chs. 46 and 47.] The fathers ate sour grapes when they admitted that by which nature would be harmed; the children’s teeth are set on edge if, through their parents’ guilt, they become slower in doing good. But if this proverb holds before baptism, it ceases afterward.

If this view is closer to truth than the other, it is nevertheless far beyond our understanding. Therefore concupiscence is either chiefly or solely the original stain in little children originally guilty: chiefly, if we are also held by another’s sin; solely, if we are bound only by our own. [Note: [Col. 0764D] Consult the notes.] For concupiscence, proceeding from the first origin and arriving even to the end, leaving everywhere behind it a foul trace, is more rightly reckoned the original stain of children than that which settled in the origin itself and defiled it alone.

[Col. 0764C]

But since death, known to be the punishment of forbidden eating, passed through all, perhaps no one appears destined to die deservedly unless he is held guilty of that same eating. Yet death is not unjustly owed to anyone who is weakened through that eating toward concupiscence. That first sin alone may properly be called the original sin of each individual—not because the son bears the iniquity of the father, but because they are judged guilty of it insofar as they are subject to the concupiscence born from it. It is said to be forgiven in the baptized [Note: [Col. 0764D] Augustine, Book I, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, ch. 26.] when the concupiscence arising from it is pardoned.

# Book Three

[Col. 0763]

## Chapter I. Sin turned the path owed to heaven toward hell.

[Col. 0763D]

Thus the human race, discoloured originally in little children and, in adults, actually depraved through the iniquity of origin, turned aside the path which nature owed to heaven by its prohibition, and passed with hurried step toward hell. It would never have returned home unless “the Dayspring from on high” had visited us (Luke 1:78): namely, the Lord visited his servants and the physician his sick patients—both alike a Dayspring from on high—and, when they had been healed, he opened heaven’s gate and led them home again. [Col. 0765A]

Not immediately, however. He delayed for a long time so that, having experienced their sickness, they might be less ungrateful toward their deliverer. For lest, trusting too much in free will, they should presumptuously attribute to themselves what it is exceedingly brazen to attribute to anyone but God—namely, the power of themselves to avoid evil, to do good, and to know both—they were left to themselves for a long time, that they might learn by experience what they could accomplish on their own. Thus, continually falling into worse things, they became astonishingly defiled in life and darkened in reason.

But lest, needing a healer, they should reject him when present through ignorance, prophets were sent beforehand, who often and in many ways explained him, his deeds, and his sayings by manifold description. Thus the sick might both hope for the one to come and eagerly receive him when he came; if they were unwilling to receive him, they would then have no excuse for their sin.

[Col. 0765B]

Likewise, lest man, though asleep in body, might seem able by himself easily to awaken to better effort when doctrine roused him, a law was given which taught rightly but gave no assistance. We always tend toward what is forbidden. What pleased less before the prohibition began to please more once prohibited. For it belongs to those deprived of grace to burn with desire for forbidden things, while those made gracious restrain themselves from them. The law is set before both. Those advanced by grace become better when they obey; those abandoned by that same grace necessarily become worse when they resist.

Therefore human beings, evil in the age of reason, became worse in the age of the law—not all, however. For the Lord reserved for himself some remnant in each age, illuminating their minds through faith in the one to come: fewer and to a lesser degree before the law; more and more fully under the law; and by far the most numerous and most abundantly in the age of grace.

Yet there were some before the Law, such as Abraham, and outside the Law, such as Job, who, although most were established under the Law, were far more receptive to the truth that was to come. Likewise, in the Law the chorus of prophets drank much more deeply of our truth than we, less instructed in our own Law, scarcely grasping even the sum of Christian doctrine. For God then spoke in a vision to His saints (Ps. 88:20), because the prophets understood what they foretold through God’s revelation. Hence the prophet says: “My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe” (Ps. 44:2), that is, of the Holy Spirit teaching me as I speak, without the labor of study.

Yet study was not entirely absent even from the prophets, as the same Prophet testifies: “My mouth shall speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart understanding” (Ps. 48:4). Thus, inspired by Him who “made known His ways to Moses, His wills to the children of Israel” (Ps. 102:7), they knew the mysteries—not by having study taken away from them, but by having its toil removed, so that the mind might apply itself to understanding and God might illumine the attentive mind with truth. Therefore, the people of these three periods, the nearer they come to the last, act either more foully or more enlightenedly according to the quality of their study. For “to whom more is entrusted, from him more is required” (Gregory); in each period faith triumphs, as the Apostle testifies: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6). And, according to the Prophet: “The just shall live by faith” (Rom. 1:17). In whatever period God chose a person, He distinguished that person by our faith, as has been said, so that the righteous person might through faith become blessed through righteousness. For there is no other way to life, at least for adults.

## Chapter II. What avails for infants and older children before and under the Law

[Col. 0766B] [Note: [Col. 0765D] The Master, IV, distinction 1.]

Surely, just as in our own time regeneration alone remedies infants, so before the Law—and also during the period of the Law among those to whom the Law was not given—either faith alone on behalf of infants, or sacrifice on behalf of somewhat older children, intervened, as circumcision did in Abraham’s household. This is what some writers relate:

[Note: [Col. 0765D] Gregory, *Morals*, book IV, ch. 3; Cyprian, *On Circumcision*; Augustine, book IV *Against Julian*, ch. 5; Bernard, epistle 77. [Col. 0766D]]

For although childhood before the use of reason commits nothing of that kind by which it incurs guilt, we wonder why one who has done no evil needs a remedy—so much so that, without it, eternal torments are owed. What we now indeed do not know, we shall know in the future: namely, that humanity was so defiled by original sin that, without any personal act, unless remedial help is given, Gehenna is justly due.

Even with the defect removed without remedies, the Author of nature could have saved nature; but He did not will this, lest the fault appear slight—or rather nonexistent—if no recompense were exacted for it. Yet if this were done, no one would perish, and it would be gain to the wicked and loss to the good: gain to the wicked because they would not perish; loss to the good because they would be less good than they are now. For, having experienced frailty, they become humbler; and, seeing the just destruction of the ungodly, they become more grateful to the Savior for their own deliverance. But the Lord’s counsel is rather to avoid losses to the good than to seek gains for the wicked. Therefore remedies were rightly established in the respective periods even for infants, by which, if they received them, they might attain salvation, and, if deprived of them, destruction.

## Chapter III. When circumcision was performed, and what became of one who died before it

[Col. 0766D]

[Note: [Col. 0766D] The Master, *Sentences*, IV, distinction 1.]

But circumcision is commanded to be received on the eighth day. For it is reckoned unlawful to circumcise earlier (Lev. 12:3). Therefore, does one who dies between birth and the eighth day, because he lacks the remedy, undergo punishment, as in our time does one who lacks baptism? Yet baptism may lawfully be administered whenever it is needed. Circumcision, however, as I have said, may be administered only on the eighth day. Therefore, just as after birth there is among us no salvation without baptism, because the time for the remedy is always present, so among them, before the eighth day, there was, as it seems, no condemnation, because the law of circumcision had not yet taken effect.

Baptism is universal because it is enjoined upon all; circumcision is not, because it is commanded only to Jews—and not even to all of them, since women are nowhere found to be circumcised. Therefore the male sex owes itself to circumcision, specifically from the eighth day. Hence one who dies before the eighth day is not held guilty of failing in this obligation.

[Note: [Col. 0767D] The Master, above, final section.]

But you will say: certainly he is not guilty of a future circumcision, but of the ancient transgression; and because he did not receive the remedy, he does not escape torment. I do not deny that this could be so; but I do not easily think it is so, especially since little girls do not perish although they lack circumcision. Why should boys perish when it is unlawful to circumcise them? If there is anything by which the former may be helped, let there likewise be something by which the latter may be aided. For who, if endowed with divine mercy, would consign such a multitude of boys and girls to destruction? It would be more permissible to presume a sacrament than to admit the peril of so many human beings.

Nor did circumcision pertain to a woman, nor to a man before the proper time, because it was performed sacramentally. For when every soul that has not been circumcised is declared to perish from the people, Scripture’s customary manner gives to the whole what belongs to a part: this is understood only of those males whom premature death did not carry off.

What then ought we to hold concerning those who could receive life in the womb but could not be born? Among us, indeed, the teaching of the holy Fathers establishes that for those born or unborn, yet deprived of baptism, nothing is to be hoped for except punishment. Hence children extracted from slain mothers, even if found dead, are, according to due custom, excluded by Mother Church from the common cemetery of the faithful. She does not judge worthy of her own bosom those whom, though they bear human form, she does not know to have received the sacrament; and, while she excludes them from her bosom, she does not regard them as hers.

If at times she buries a woman who died while pregnant, she does not thereby receive the unborn gentile. It belongs, surely, to ecclesiastical discipline not to honor with burial in the cemetery those removed from the maternal womb for whatever reason if they lacked baptism. Yet it belongs to maternal compassion not to pierce the womb of a pregnant daughter, even when she is already dead, unless perhaps there is hope that the offspring may be extracted alive. Necessity therefore compels the extraction from the confinement of a womb already dead of one who is about to die immediately; otherwise humanity does not permit one to search by cutting into the hidden recesses of the body. It judges it more tolerable to bury a dead child within a dead woman in a place not due to it than in an excessively inhuman manner to disclose nature’s secrets that wish to remain concealed. Justice requires that one already separated from its mother, and unworthy of its mother’s fellowship, be placed in its own proper place.

Since unborn children perish in the time of the New Covenant, did they also perish in the time of the Old? Why should unborn children perish when born children would not perish—neither among the Jews, since they were not yet to be circumcised, nor among the Gentiles, being excused by the faith of their elders? Why should not whatever efficacy there was from the womb benefit them in the womb, whether among Jews not yet circumcised or among Gentiles shortly before birth, unless perhaps you posit remedies for infants that could not be performed before birth? Otherwise, a remedy present within the womb will be thought to have had force no less than outside it.

If you judge that Jews now born need no assistance from any remedy because the time has not yet presented itself for that one remedy to which alone, by God’s command, they are bound—namely circumcision—and if you think it rash to invent during the interim another remedy not learned from Scripture, by what reasoning do you free the born from guilt while binding the unborn, unless being enclosed in the womb harms the latter and having emerged from it benefits the former? But why should the one benefit and the other harm, when neither is a vice nor the other a virtue?

If the faith of parents saves Gentile infants after birth, does it not follow that those prevented by death before their birth must likewise be delivered by that same faith from the second death? For if they possess in themselves nothing saving and await only their parents’ faith, how, though they have changed in no respect regarding themselves—for those being born change place, not themselves—how, I say, do they receive a faith which they awaited, now helpful and now of no benefit? Therefore, if Gentile infants perish without a remedy, why not Jewish infants also? But if parents’ faith is a remedy for the former, why not for the latter, especially since before the binding requirement of circumcision they are considered equal among themselves, because God does not show partiality among persons?

If parents’ faith pleads before the Judge for children, does it belong to immediate parents or also to more remote ancestors? For if any parent whatsoever is said to stand before God on behalf of those to be born, no child perished down to the Flood, because Noah, a man eminent in faith, preceded everyone in that work. Nor ought anyone to have perished before the Flood, since Adam himself was distinguished by faith. But if, as I think more likely, it belongs to contemporaries to help children by faith and somewhat older children by sacrifice, it is not surprising that help should have shone forth from the same source from which danger had arisen. Among the Gentiles without doubt innumerable children, and among the Jews perhaps some, were bound to misery by their parents’ unbelief—perhaps not because it harmed them, but because it did not benefit them. I have said that parents’ faith benefits children. Does one who shows himself a parent by care, though not by nature, help a foster-child whom he receives by believing? I do not know; yet I do not deny it.

## Chapter IV. A father’s purity benefits his child; his foulness does not harm

See how much a father’s purity avails for his offspring. God was about to destroy the children, abhorring their stain; but because He had regarded the father’s purity, He remitted the wrath owed by the children. Looking upon the nobility of the parents, He forgot the disgrace of their offspring. Do children’s reproaches similarly increase because of the foulness of their parents? Certainly not. For even a parent’s virtue is not now thought to add to the purity of a child procured by sacrament.

If, therefore, as most maintain, paternal virtue was useful to its little children, perhaps it was so lest the piety of fathers should be dismayed at the danger of innocents. It unquestionably availed enough that those innocent of personal sin, cleansed from original sin, should not perish; perhaps it did not avail enough that, once cleansed, they should excel by as much as they had been born from more excellent parents. For just as the equality of baptism most certainly makes infants of our own time equal to one another, and just as those under the Law could not differ from one another when the same circumcision cleansed them, so the logic of analogy seems to demand that, in the ancient period among the Gentiles, we should reckon nursing infants equal to one another through reconciliation, since we believe them not unequal through the contamination of origin.

Unless perhaps among us and under the Law the uniformity of the sacrament bestowed upon infancy produces equality, whereas among the Gentiles the diverse merits of the holy Fathers—upon seeing which God spared childhood—produced diversity. Thus the uprightness of parents was, as they say, once a cause of salvation for their little children.

## Chapter V. A child is punished for a father’s evil and rewarded for his good

[Note: [Col. 0769D] The Master, II, distinction 33.]

But now too, just as then, fathers’ crimes afflict children both young and grown, even good children. Therefore, grieving to see the undeserving tortured in miserable ways, we wonder until those entering the sanctuary of God receive the answer, upon consulting the book of life, that children are struck both to grieve their parents and to increase their own merit. For it is fitting that wicked fathers should be rebuked also through this; and it is salutary that heavenly children should be beaten by scourges for the benefit of patience. Thus perhaps it is said: “I shall punish the sins of the parents in the children,” which is understood of wicked children.

[Note: [Col. 0769D] Augustine on Psalm 108, on this verse, etc.]

Thus the Prophet says concerning the punishment of Judas’s children: “Let his children wander about and beg; let them be driven out of their dwellings” (Ps. 108:10). And again: “Let his offspring be for destruction” (ibid.). For the common opinion is that the torments of the dead increase through the sufferings of the living whom they loved; and those coming thence are permitted to learn this, so that their torments may thereby also be intensified. Or, if living loved ones do not at all perceive what the dead suffer, nevertheless the living perhaps endure scourges for their ancestors’ crimes in order to terrify the living. Therefore children are very often punished for the sins of their parents, either to add to their parents’ evils or to terrify others. Thus the sons of Eli perish under punitive judgment (1 Sam. 4:4), to their own ruin as well.

Conversely, parents’ religion sometimes appears to bring good things to children, for their encouragement and as an example to others. Why, under the Law, when prayer is poured out to God, do descendants ask that help be given them for Abraham’s sake, unless they perceive that God, in regarding a father’s good, bestows good upon his children? In the reverse order too, either the evils of good parents are allotted to children for their testing—thus evils are inflicted upon Job’s children, to Job’s own benefit as well—or the goods of bad parents are allotted to children to their detriment. For evil fathers are exalted through good children, and good fathers are exercised through evil children. When adversities press upon him, a strong person rises against the burden and is strengthened in contempt for mortal things. But when desired things abound, the intemperate person, captured by false delight, is twisted away from the contemplation of the true good toward evil desire as by an inextricable hook.

I have partly treated what good or evil in children produces, knowing that the same causes bring forth different effects in different persons. Yet those effects should chiefly be pursued which experience presents or reason demands. But when we refer the good or evil of parents to their children, that passage seems to object: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. 18:4). Likewise the declaration that God will render to each according to that person’s merits. Therefore, if we attend to the state of the age to come, every wicked person will bear his own burden, and no good person will lack recompense for merit. Turn your eyes to our present life, and you will see the good and evil of some people benefiting or harming others. From such an intermingling, wherever you turn your eyes, do not imagine partiality in God (Gal. 2:6). For God does not show partiality; rather, for the advantage of the commonwealth which He undertook to govern, He arranges now harsh things, now gentle.

For when, because of wicked parents, He chastises one child but honors another because of good parents, if He distinguishes solely the parents’ merits so as to embrace the one and reject the other, there may perhaps be partiality. But if, in distributing hard and gentle things, He looks not so much to the parents as He seeks an outcome, what room remains for accusation? Especially since partiality properly exists only when one, looking upon worldly splendor, admires the person whom one elevates and disdains the person whom one ignores.

That diversity in paternal merit does not produce diversity of condition in children is clear: children receive alternation from identity of paternal merit, and similarity from diversity of paternal merit—at one time similarity in misery or virtue, at another in vice or happiness. For from a father, whether good or evil, good and evil children, happy and miserable children, alike come forth.

Yet it must not be denied that it often turns out well for good children because of their fathers, or badly for bad children because of theirs. God, the dispenser of the highest justice, sets aside partiality, since, although He orders each thing according to merit in its own way, He never accommodates His favor to the disease of nobility. For worldly nobility, when it is foolish, commonly reverses the proper order by revering what belongs to pride and abominating what belongs to humility.

## Chapter VI. Why the old Law belonged only to the Hebrews and the new Law to all

[Note: [Col. 0770D] The Master, III, distinction 40.]

But we have wandered too far; let us return, asking why it was fitting for the Law and circumcision to be proposed to only one family, namely the Hebrews. For if there were no salvation without the Law, the promulgation of the Law would have been offered to all. But it was enough for some to receive instruction, so that all might learn from the few how great their weakness was. “For the Law brings no one to perfection” (Heb. 7:19); it was a burden “which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear.” Therefore they might eagerly flee to Him whose yoke is sweet and whose burden light (Matt. 11:30), whose purpose is to complete the beginnings of the Law. Thus Law followed Law—the new following the old—by so much the more perfect as it was enacted by one more perfect. Since there is no salvation without it, it is commanded to all.

For as salvation existed outside while the Old Testament stood, so after the New had been given salvation exists only within it. Therefore the first Law ought not to have been proclaimed to all, lest we seek in it the salvation of all, since it was assigned not to the whole world but to a part. But the second, being imposed upon the whole world, is shown to be saving for the whole world. Both before the Law and during the time of the Mosaic Law, salvation existed among the Gentiles. Whence? Certainly salvation did not come from the Law even for Jews, since, according to the Apostle, “It is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Heb. 10:4). Although the rite of sacrifices held primacy among legal observances, even Jews did not have salvation from the Law. Whence then? Both had it through faith; for, as the Apostle testifies, “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6).

But there is one faith, just as there is one baptism: without doubt, ours, which works through love. This is the new Law: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John 13:34). For charity does not exist outside faith. If a person has charity, that person is righteous; but the righteous person is righteous by faith. Hence: “The just shall live by faith” (Rom. 1:17). Therefore our Law is perfect, and through it there is salvation in every age—indeed, perfect salvation. For what the old Law began, the new Law completed.

## Chapter VII. How the Lord drew the people

[Note: [Col. 0771D] The Master, III, distinction 37.]

Because they were immature and would reject everything lofty, weak things were promised to the weak. Yet through the Creator’s beneficence they undertook certain corrections of life which were easy to carry out, while some vices remained which they were not yet able to prohibit. Hence they were commanded to love friends; they were not forbidden to hate an enemy. They could lend at interest to outsiders, though not to neighbors (Matt. 5:43). Those who suffered injury were permitted to exact retaliation, but not allowed to exceed equality.

For certain reasons it was lawful to dismiss a wife; indeed, it was not unlawful to have several wives at once. Separation was permitted lest homicide be committed. A wife was dismissed by her husband—certainly an evil, yet permitted—lest, compelled to keep a hated wife, he should kill her, which would without doubt be far worse. Accordingly, it was allowed that one man should take many wives, so that multiplied offspring might multiply the people whom the surrounding multitude of Gentiles pressed on every side. It was unlawful for one woman to marry many men, because one woman could not conceive by many men.

Thus the Lord, commanding things easy to do yet good, while also overlooking evils not yet to be cut off, drew a people still tender to His worship—now through fear, now through the promise of things judged among the weak either advantageous or disadvantageous.

## Chapter VIII. Whether they ought rightly to have been condemned or mercifully saved

[Note: [Col. 0772D] The Master, as above.]

Therefore, ought the people who served through terror of losses and desire for gains, doing few and slight good things while committing many great evils, to have been condemned according to merit or saved through mercy? But if the Judge is just, how can salvation come to the wicked? Yet since the Law does not forbid these crimes, and since they nevertheless do what it commands, how, if the Judge is just, can salvation be denied to the obedient? For if the previously mentioned vices endangered those who possessed them, did He not deceive badly who permitted them, either by silence or in writing, as though they would cause no harm? If it incurs guilt to worship God solely through fear or desire for temporal advantage or disadvantage, why did He wish to deter from impiety through losses and incite to piety through gains?

Indeed, the religion of perfection, which is certainly that of Christians, admits no such filth. Among them, “the one who is ignorant shall be ignored” (1 Cor. 14:38). It begins with another fear, namely that of Him “who can cast body and soul into Gehenna” (Luke 12:5), and is completed by another desire: that God of gods may be seen in Zion (Ps. 83). Different things must be set before the strong and the weak, for the same things do not benefit both. For the strong, salvation is strengthened; for others, sickness is either relieved or cured.

Were those under the Law, then, spiritually sick persons who received commandments not for the restoration of salvation but for the easing of condemnation, so that “the son of the slave woman may not be heir with the son of the free woman” (Gal. 4:30)—that is, the people of the Synagogue with the people of the Church? Was the Judge thus just when He destroyed the wicked, and merciful when He moderated punishment for offenders by moderation? But then that whole people must be reckoned among the lost, except perhaps for a very few among many who excelled in Christian perfection.

Yet the following seems contrary: that particular people of God, observing according to its institutions the Law enacted for it and not yet to be brought to an end, should rightly have perished, when an established judgment, examined and supported by favorable writings, maintains that the Law in its own time availed for the salvation of one who obeyed it. Hence the Apostle: “Circumcision indeed is beneficial, if you keep the Law” (Rom. 2:25). For if the circumcised who kept the Law had perished, it might perhaps have diminished evil, but it would not have benefited them.

The Lord also says to the apostles, and in the apostles to us: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:20). Therefore the righteousness of Christians must be greater than that of Jews. But if Christians’ righteousness is greater, there must necessarily also be some righteousness among Jews. Since righteousness is the cause of salvation, if those who kept the Law attained righteousness, they will without doubt also attain salvation. Otherwise hell would hold in misery even the patriarchs, whose salvation is not doubtful, although at the very height of religious observance they appear to have had not one wife but several—not successively but simultaneously, without repentance—contrary to the Creator’s ordinance: “The two shall be one flesh” (Matt. 19:5), and contrary to the law of Christian perfection.

Certainly men of even slight holiness would have admitted nothing of the kind if they judged that their souls were endangered by it. But it is impious to suppose that, while intent upon salvation, they were unaware of condemnable acts—or even that the Law deceived them—when it either passed over or allowed such actions.

[Note: [Col. 0773D] Chrysostom, Homily 56 on Genesis 30; Ambrose, *On Abraham*, book I, ch. 4.]

Thus what among us is punished as the gravest crime, so that Christian religion may be purified in every direction, divine judgment preferred to overlook among the ancients, administering to each age according to the measure of grace then given and appropriate, and not yet according to the life to come.

## Chapter IX. Grace was less for the Jew than for the Christian

For it was fitting that lesser grace should instruct lesser persons, while the greater grace brought by Christ would instruct greater persons. Yet, to reveal its own powers, before He came He sent beforehand some persons outstanding in dignity of merit and for that reason to be preferred to very many good baptized persons. Therefore our Lord was merciful when He imposed a bearable burden upon the ancients. Nevertheless, He showed Himself just when He did not punish vices which He had not forbidden.

[Note: [Col. 0773D] Augustine, epistle 163. Here he indeed saw what had to be seen: that certain things were then lawful for the righteous. For they did these things by prophetic spirit and God’s authority, who without doubt knows even for whom it is beneficial to be killed, etc. [Col. 0774D]]

Thus, although defiled by not a few crimes and not corrected by the accompanying life—indeed, neither foul nor requiring correction, since excused by permission—those who nevertheless fulfilled the Law as far as they could, because no one fulfilled it completely, were received into Abraham’s bosom through God’s mercy, and indeed now possess heaven. For the burden which, as Peter taught concerning his people, “neither we nor all our fathers were able to bear” (Acts 15:10), and concerning which Moses taught, “Cursed is everyone who does not do all the things written in the book of the Law” (Gal. 3:10; Deut. 27:26)—because no one could do this, it enclosed them under a curse. This occurred so that, in the time of grace, joyfully abandoning the exceedingly burdensome Law of works, they might flee to the light burden of the Christian Law, in which a holy will, even without a work, is endowed with blessed eternity; so that those begun through Moses might deserve to be completed through Christ.

“You have sat at the table of a rich man; know that you must prepare like things” (Ecclus. 31:12).

[Note: [Col. 0774D] Augustine, Sermon 45, *On the Saints*.]

The rich man is Christ, whose is the earth and its fullness; the rich man’s table is the refreshment of His body and blood; to sit is to cease from vices and rest in upright pursuits. This is the Christian’s holy leisure. Therefore you have sat at the rich man’s table when, as a worthy guest, you received the Eucharist. Receiving the Eucharist is a commemoration of the Lord’s Passion. Thus the Lord said to His disciples at that same table: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19).

[Note: [Col. 0774D] Gregory, Homily 22 on the Gospels.]

Therefore, when blood is poured for you from the chalice, remember that Christ poured out blood for you from His side; when you receive in your mouth Christ’s body, as if to be broken, remember that Christ suffered distress for you. But you truly remember if you imitate Christ’s hard path, since “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, that we should follow in His footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21). If, therefore, while receiving the Eucharist, you remember the Lord’s Passion in such a way that you also imitate it, then, sitting at the rich man’s table, you truly know that you must prepare like things.

Therefore, pursuing the hard and narrow way which leads to life, how is Christ’s yoke sweet and His burden light for you, if you consider the stumbling-blocks set along the road beyond number? The way through this valley of tears which leads to life appears narrow because it is at once laborious and dangerous. Yet that same road, scarcely endurable by reason of its own hardship, is a sweet yoke and light burden when one considers the boundless joy to which it leads.

And because “the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:41), what wonderfully delights reason greatly burdens the flesh. Charity, which bears all things, makes even the greatest burden bearable; sensuality, seeking pleasant things, dislikes whatever is different. Hence a person of great merit is proved when he hates, so far as he is concerned, what is unjust, and seeks what is just.

The old Law also, if you consider the totality of its commandments, is unbearable. If you contemplate their character—since many things are allowed to the weak which must be removed for those who are being perfected—it is now bearable. Thus our Lord burdened the Old Testament with a multitude of commandments so that the New might be sought; He tempered the burden of multiplicity through the quality of its precepts so that the Old might be maintained. He remitted what gives offense through multiplicity, and restored what is well done through accommodation to the times. He is the One “whose mercies are over all His works” (Ps. 154:9). For who will accuse the wise God if, introducing certain easy things to do, He proposed them, while passing over in silence certain things—whether valuable or foul—which were to be taught only to the advanced? What, for this reason, was not to be commanded by the teacher will certainly not be required by the judge. “Is your eye evil because He is good?” (Matt. 20:15). Does He not have mercy on whom He wills? (Rom. 9:18).

[Note: [Col. 0774D] Hugh of St Victor, *On the Sacraments*, book I, part X, ch. 6, etc.]

Perhaps, however, it should be read that those from that people whom God destined for salvation were also completed by evangelical instruction before the end of their lives. This may indeed be said, but it is not necessary. Whatever their condition while remaining here, when departing hence they were honored with the customs of that homeland toward which they tended. They would certainly never have attained this unless they had first kept the Decalogue; but it could not be kept unless three commandments were kept out of love for God and seven out of love for neighbor. Therefore the fulfillment of the Law is love of God and neighbor; hence those alone who had charity, fulfilling the Law, deserved Abraham’s bosom.

## Chapter X. Who perished, who were good, and who perfect

For among that people there were very many who worshiped God while attending to earthly things, not loving righteousness but merely fearing punishment. All these, because they did not embrace charity, deservedly perished. Among them, like roses among brambles, rare good persons gave off fragrance. Since they sought first the kingdom of God, whom they loved more, they were permitted to seek and love also the things of the world. Did they then serve both God and Mammon? (Matt. 6:24). Rather, they served God for His own sake, and they served God also for the world’s sake. They were good indeed, but not yet perfect.

Insofar as they served God for His own sake, they were good, because they loved God; insofar as they served God for the world’s sake, they were not yet perfect, because they loved vanity. Perfect among them were those who did not care to be temporally happy, such as the one who said to God: “Give us help in trouble, for human salvation is vain” (Ps. 59:13).

The less perfect, then, loved God and the world. But if they loved the world more, or loved both equally, they would serve God and Mammon. Yet now, whenever matters come to such a pass that one of the two must be offended, they plainly reject what they had judged pleasant before they offend God even in the least. Thus they serve God without ambiguity, not Mammon. This is the charity which “covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8) in the less perfect.

There is one charity in some persons of each Testament and another in others. For very many vices are required to be renounced by us which were not imputed to the ancients; and so charity must necessarily be different in us from what it was in them. They embraced God, yet, as I have said, were permitted to embrace certain vices:

[Note: [Col. 0775D] Namely, things which are already such among us.]

though even then the perfect preferred to reject them. “Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6). Loving a friend, they could hate an enemy without danger; yet even then a fully good person thought that enemy ought to be loved. We, however, are commanded not merely to love enemies but also to do good to them (Matt. 5:44).

Thus it is clear that, although Christians shine forth in religion, those obedient to the Law were nevertheless good. For the Law intimates the Law which the Gospel declares; the Law instructs in the morals required by that age, and our Law completes it. Therefore those who kept the law of circumcision must have been good, as instructed by faith and pure in morals—especially those who conformed themselves to Christ, whom they knew beforehand by prophetic spirit.

Why, then, was the old Law called the Law of slavery and death, but the new the Law of freedom and grace, according to the saying: “If the Son shall set you free, then you shall truly be free” (John 8:36)? In both Laws there are many slaves, to be rejected at last, while free persons to be endowed with the Father’s inheritance are few. For just as the words of the old Law, so also those of the new, sound in vain in the ears unless God’s grace works within. “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6).

But through Moses the Lord imposed the old Law upon the old people. In it He taught the beginnings of a good life, but did not bring the aid required for fulfillment. To whom did He not bring it? To almost all. For although the grace of reconciliation was bestowed upon all through circumcision, most, upon reaching the age of reason, broke the covenant begun; and to these the Lord deservedly did not bring help through the Law, except when, as happens, He recalled some from error. For all these, the Law was one of slavery and death.

It was a Law of slavery because through it they received both fear by threats, so that they might serve in whatever way they could, and desire by promises, so that they might do this under compulsion—yet through threats. God gave fear so that they might avoid evils, but promised many advantages to the obedient, so that, receiving the good things of the world dear to them, they might love the Giver and serve Him out of love. While good persons feared the One who threatened and loved the One who promised, the wicked, fearing only, despised charity and were seized by desire for advantage. Therefore, frightened by fear and carried away by desire—desire arising from God, fear from the Law—they endured the Law in slavery: a law of death, because those who act according to the Law but do not do so out of charity most rightly perish, seeking neither to please the Lord nor to benefit their fellow servant.

## Chapter XI. What fear comes from God, and why the Old Testament is one of slavery and the New one of grace

[Note: [Col. 0776D] The Master, III, distinctions 37 and 40.]

Fear is said to proceed from God. But what fear? Certainly not that which the Lord forbids, saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. 10:28). Is it then that which He adds, saying: “Fear Him who can cast both body and soul into Gehenna” (ibid.)? This is without doubt a gift of the Spirit; hence: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10), and: “He shall fill him with the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. 11:3).

God is also feared because He can inflict troubles in this present age. Is this fear too from God? But if God causes Himself to be feared because of future affliction, why not equally because of present affliction? For it is not unfitting to fear God because of the evils of this age merely because it is disgraceful to fear a human being because of worldly losses. Nor, because it is sinful to fear the devil lest he drag one into hell, is it therefore less good to fear God lest He send one into Gehenna.

One who fears Satan, or an evil person, because of adversities that can be inflicted, seeks a deadly peace with one with whom conflict ought to be maintained. Thus fear, foul in itself, prepares a peace more foul still. Yet there is a certain fear belonging to nature: we necessarily recoil from a torturer. This is not indeed to be blamed, but lamented.

The old law, therefore, is one of servitude and death; ours, however, of liberty and grace. For under the law of circumcision, although grace is bestowed, it is nevertheless far greater for the baptized, who are enabled to despise things passing away and prefer those that endure. Yet the former needed, at least in some way, to worship God: besides the grace of circumcision, they had to be frightened by loss of possessions lest they turn aside to what was forbidden, and attracted by temporal rewards so that they might thus love the Lord’s commands. We, therefore, freely serve gratuitously; they were slaves hired for a price. But if they do not love even in this way, they live under the law of death. We, however, can live most holy lives in our own law. For in it grace is given, by which one may live freely. For although fear of God precedes worship, charity brings it to perfection. Thus the Apostle, distinguishing between the people of the two Testaments, declared what we ought to be, saying: “You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but the Spirit of adoption as sons” (Rom. 8:15). He denies what belongs to the old order and then affirms what belongs to the new person. Then the Spirit disturbed them with fear, so that it might compel them even thus into service. But now He bestows charity, by which, instructed as sons, they may obey their Father. Since that people was not to be brought to perfection before Christ, You began religion among them by giving fear; among us, since we have now received Christ, You have brought what was begun to perfection. For that time was appointed for fear, ours for charity.

Yet at that time there were many good people, and among the many some were perfect. All of these, more or less according to the merit of their lives, drew faith, hope, and charity from the right belonging to our time, while under the right of circumcision they endured the legal decrees. These served under the law of grace; just as, conversely, very many who live in the time of grace are seen to belong rather to the time of the old order, since they serve God with their attention fixed on passing things. They do indeed what they ought, because they serve the Lord; but not as they ought, because not for His sake; and for this reason they are evil, though good in comparison with the worst. For the worst are those who do not worship God even thus.

## Chapter XII. Under the law, hell received the righteous.

But worshippers of God under the law also descended to the lower regions—whence the Lord too descended into the lower regions—not, certainly, to be tormented, unless something still remained to be burned away, but because they were to be deprived of the vision of God, and by that deprivation alone utterly cast down. For little or no concern need have been felt about the character of the place, if they could have seen God even from there and had awaited the Savior’s coming in unquestionably less distress. For there they received something better than those living among us receive; not indeed from the nature of the place—for ours, though evil in itself, is so much more tolerable as it is higher in situation—but from the quality of their merit. Since they had merited well here, they suffered no evil there, being free from sin and certain of their reward; and, being stripped of the flesh, they were also free from the obligations of the flesh.

## Chapter XIII. When and why Christ came as the end of the law.

Since, meanwhile, faith in Christ supplied these consolations and was at last to supply blessedness, and since that same faith was to bestow it upon the world once justified, Christ came when experience had already made clear that neither human nature left to itself nor nature instructed by commandments had strength enough even to cease from evil—much less, I would say, to do good. He came, therefore, to fulfill the oracles of the prophets and also to accomplish the desires of those who awaited Him. This is the Prophet of whom Moses said to his people: “God will raise up for you a Prophet from among your brethren, like me; Him you shall hear” (Deut. 18:15). He therefore came in the flesh, not because He could not save His own otherwise, but because He saved them more fittingly in this way. For thus His mercy, of which we stand especially in need, is especially shown to us; and we too, beholding the admirable—indeed astonishing—loving-kindness of our Author, are bound to our Author by humble, indeed indissoluble, devotion.

He came, moreover, to bring the law to its end, as He Himself testifies while speaking to the Father in the prophet: “You did not require holocaust or sacrifice for sin; then I said: Behold, I come” (Ps. 39 [40]:7). It is as though He said: When it pleased You that the sacrifices of the law should cease—together with which the priesthood, whose function lay in them, and the law placed between the two, which instructed the priests and regulated the sacrifices, also had to cease—then I came into the world to do Your will: one for many, the new for the old, the reality for the figures, introducing namely the sacrifice of My body, and a priesthood worthy of so great a sacrifice, and a law for priests fully teaching the ordinances of sacrifice.

When Christ came, therefore, the law had to be ended—not indeed all at once, since He Himself was circumcised according to the law, as the Apostle says, “made under the law” (Gal. 4:4), but gradually to pass away. Because it was good, He fittingly accepted it in order to defend it as authentic; because it was insufficient in merit, He ended it as less effective, in order to substitute the perfect law. Thus He set aside the figurative elements of the law, as it were by certain steps: provided that we read that He worked on Sabbaths contrary to the letter of the Sabbath law, [Note: Col. 0777D. Gratian, XXV, question 1, after chapter 116.] and that He freed the adulteress, who according to the rigor of the law was to be stoned (John 8:6); and other things of this sort. At last He fixed a boundary upon legal institutions altogether, saying near the end: “I will drink no more of this fruit of the vine until I drink it new in the kingdom of My Father” (Matt. 26:29). The vine is the people Israel, according to the saying: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:7). The fruit of the vine is the religion of that nation; to drink of the fruit is to delight in its religion; the renewed fruit is reformed obedience. [Col. 0778D] The sense, therefore, is this: Nothing of worship of this kind any longer pleases Me as it has hitherto; but the new obedience, which that old worship signified, does please Me. The former was thus given for a time and was honorably buried after a delay; it was not cast aside irreverently and as quickly as possible, like idolatry. For its observances cease, but not its teaching, so that we may strive spiritually to fulfill what that people performed figuratively.

## Chapter XIV. Both laws contain sacraments with promises, and commandments.

The old law—indeed, also the new—contains three things: sacraments with promises, and commandments. The sacraments foreshadowed things to come: for example, the various sacrifices in the law, circumcision, and wars against foreign peoples. By that unceasing conflict is signified our uninterrupted struggle against spiritual wickedness and vices. At one time we are victors, when, armed with virtues and with God as our helper, we defend for ourselves as true Jews the land of promise, that is, the region of the living, against those who attack it. At another time we are defeated, when God is angry because of our vices and we either yield to temptation or, as though exiled by nations, are carried captive by demons into hell. Circumcision, performed on the eighth day at the gateway through which the propagation of corrupt generation proceeds, foretells that in the eighth age of the common resurrection every contagion of the first birth will be circumcised away. In the sacrifices, sometimes the passion of our Redeemer is signified, as in the lamb and the holocaust; sometimes the destruction of different vices, as in the bull representing arrogance and the goat representing wantonness.

I know, however, that figures, like words, have different and differing interpretations. Thus the uncleanness of food is forbidden so that delight in sin may be avoided. The sacraments of the law therefore promised future things. But now promises must cease, because the reality of the promises has succeeded them. Whoever still promises lies, because he has already fulfilled what was promised. Let us not Judaize by distinguishing foods from foods, because under the law of Christ, as the Apostle testifies, “All things are clean to the clean” (Titus 1:15). Rather, as Christians, we ought through abstinence to chastise our body and bring it into subjection.

Let bodily circumcision also pass away, because the true circumcision of the inner person, begun in its good part through Christ’s death, completed in Him Himself, and therefore most certainly hoped to be completed also in us, has taken its place. How displeasing signs are after the things signified have appeared, the Apostle shows in one instance when he says: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2). The Lord likewise, rejecting all sacrifices by a part for the whole, says in the Psalmist: “I will not accept bulls from your house, nor goats from your flocks” (Ps. 49 [50]:9).

Indeed, if reason requires it, we may make war with Jews; but we can Judaize on no ground except at peril. For the Apostle did not Judaize when, compelled by a disturbance, he circumcised his disciple. For, assigning no reverence to the act, he cut off the foreskin as one might cut off a finger for the sake of peace. We must avoid Judaism so thoroughly that we also beware of Sabbatarianism, because we prefer the rest which it signifies—rest from vices, or rest of the soul after death.

The legal sacraments, therefore, are set aside; in their place succeed either other sacraments of, as it were, greater merit, such as baptism in place of circumcision, or the things signified, such as the sacrifice of righteousness and praise in place of animal sacrifices.

The law has promises, as I have said, of good things that do not yet exist, and also threats of present evils. The prophets likewise—though they concern us especially—often promise heavenly things, as: “The upright shall dwell with Your countenance” (Ps. 139 [140]:14); and again: “You will give them drink from the torrent of Your delight” (Ps. 35 [36]:9). For the Prophet directs his speech to God. They often threaten hell, as: “They have been set in hell like sheep; death shall feed upon them” (Ps. 48 [49]:15). But to Christians not good things, but evils, are promised now together with future goods, the Lord saying: “If anyone wishes to come after Me, let him deny himself and take up his cross” (Matt. 16:24)—behold the evils of this age; “Where I am, there My servant also shall be” (John 12:26)—behold the goods of the age to come. Hard things are imposed upon the perfect, lest, captivated by what passes away, they desire eternal things less. Therefore they make little of threats of present hardships. Hence they are shaken by fear of hell, but more by fear of offending God.

But we receive the commandments of Moses. Yet since the law brought no one to perfection, we reverently embrace Christ’s additions as is fitting; for He “came not to destroy the law, but to fulfill” it (Matt. 5:17). Christ, therefore, is the end of the law and the prophets; at His end He also ended the law, on the condition that its figurative elements should cease in practice but remain in teaching: “For whatever things were written were written for our instruction” (Rom. 15:4). The legal promises also are now rejected, because heavenly promises are preferred. Yet moral commandments are retained, except that certain things permitted to the immature are excluded for Christians, and certain things that should not be stated to little children are proposed to adults.

But if “the law and the prophets were until John” (Matt. 11:13), how did it remain until the Lord’s Passion? Certainly the law did not begin to be shaken before John, but from John onward, who publicly introduced, against paternal tradition, the new practice of baptizing unto repentance. He also indicated that the sacrifice of the Paschal lamb, which held first place among legal observances, was about to end and had never taken away sin; for, upon seeing the Lord Jesus, he said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold Him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). It was as though he said: Flee the old lamb together with the other victims, for behold the Lamb of God, who alone is to be followed. The old victim could not cleanse the world of sin, for behold Him who alone takes away the sins of the world. Nor did this belief arise from a rash impulse; for the Father’s voice was heard: “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear Him” (Matt. 17:5).

Therefore, that true Jews may consider who that Prophet is, born from among the brethren, whom Moses commands them to hear: the Father’s voice, now heard, thundered it forth, since when it says, “Hear Him,” He is heard. It is the same as if it were said: This is He whom Moses proclaimed should be heard; let Him be heard. Hence each commanded that He be heard. The law, therefore, was until John, but no less also until the Lord’s Passion. Thus, after John, when the cross was imminent, the Lord ate the old Passover with His disciples; at that supper He ended that Passover together with its accompanying ceremonies, substituting a new rite of His body and blood.

## Chapter XV. On the Son’s conception and incarnation.

[Note: Col. 0779. Master, *Sentences*, Book III, from the beginning; Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 41.]

Therefore the sacrifice of the old lamb ceased; that of the new began—the Lamb whom she, untouched by man, conceived by the Holy Spirit. Untouched by man, lest He who came to free the rest from corruption should necessarily be born corrupt through conception from lust. But if God is able—as indeed He is—to cleanse even now the union of male and female from every ardor of foulness, this is unusual for us, but was due to our first parents before guilt. Yet it is not fitting that He who is to be venerated as God the Father in His divinity should also have a human father in His humanity, and thus have two fathers; rather, He has one Father and another mother: a mother in the nature of humanity, but without the office of a father; a Father in the nature of divinity, but without a mother’s cooperation. Thus He is the same person: man from a mother without a father; God from the Father without a mother; wonderfully the Son of His mother, more wonderfully the Son of His Father. “Who shall declare His generation?” (Isa. 53:8). A chaste Father begets; a virgin mother bears; Isaiah’s prophecy is fulfilled: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7:14). What is it to conceive except to retain seed received from a man? Not thus, therefore, but otherwise did the Virgin conceive: certainly not from a man, but from the Holy Spirit.

[Note: Col. 0781D. Master, Book III, distinction 4.]

But how by Him? As from intercourse with a man seed is drawn forth from both parties, but shamefully, because passionately [Note: Col. 0781D. See Augustine, *Enchiridion* 38–41, and *On the Trinity*, Book XIII, ch. 18.]; so through the Holy Spirit that portion was personally set apart from the Virgin Mary which was to be formed into a human being—without doubt reverently, because without lust. Indeed, I say too little: it was also without every stain of original sin. Certainly this befitted Him who undertook this work. For that man was conceived by the Holy Spirit, not as by a father, but as the agent effecting the conception. The Holy Spirit did not beget that man, but brought about His begetting—indeed, the whole course of His humanity; yet not alone, but together with the Father and the Son. For the works of the Trinity are undivided, though they are customarily treated separately because of the distinction of the persons. Thus it is said: “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of His mouth all their power” (Ps. 32 [33]:6), as though the heavens were uniquely the work of the Word and their power that of the Holy Spirit. There are many statements of this kind, so that through works which are not respectively different for different Persons, yet while different things are assigned to different Persons, we may perceive distinct Persons, whom elsewhere we are taught are one in substance. Hence “Holy, holy, holy” is said three times because of the Trinity, while “Lord God of hosts” is added once because of the unity. Very many things are ascribed to the Holy Spirit, especially those saving gifts which the holy Trinity bestows upon us from love. Love in the middle joins distinct persons to one another, and the Spirit, the common Spirit of the Father and the Son, proceeds from both. Therefore things proceeding from love fittingly belong in a special way to the Holy Spirit, because He is likened to love.

[Note: Col. 0781D. Councils of Toledo VIII and XI.]

Accordingly, since the works of the Trinity must be the same, the whole Trinity effected the incarnation of the Son; yet none but the Son was incarnate. And because God the Trinity is everywhere, He was also in the Virgin’s womb—indeed, in the flesh that was there becoming human. Yet only “the Word was made flesh” (John 1:14). The Father and the Spirit were in that flesh as they are everywhere; the Son was in the flesh in a different way from His presence everywhere. He is everywhere, but nowhere else united; He is in the flesh and personally united to it.

But what is this being united, incarnate, or taking flesh, except a work of God? And how could it occur except by God’s action? If it belongs to God and therefore to the whole Trinity, why is the incarnation attributed to the Son alone? The whole Trinity established it; the Son alone received flesh. To make is one thing, to be in what has been made another. For God is in the creature that He has made—not now making it, because He has already made it—and each of these belongs to the individual Persons as it belongs jointly to the Three. Yet the Son is somewhere in such a manner that neither the Father nor the Spirit is there in that manner. For in the assumed humanity the Son is present through unity of person, in a way in which neither the Father nor the Spirit is there.

Humanity, therefore, is both the work and dwelling-place of the whole Trinity; but in humanity there is unity only with the person of the Son. This unity is the assumption of humanity, the mystery of the incarnation, the Word’s being made flesh, and whatever other expression designates the kindness and humanity of our Savior. All this means nothing other than that God is in a human being by unity of person. But this one thing must be excluded from the Father and the Spirit, and therefore the whole of it also: the Son alone, therefore, is united.

## Chapter XVI. On the union of the natures, Christ’s conception, and descent.

[Note: Col. 0782D. Master, Book III, distinction 2.]

But when is He united? Is it in conception itself—that is, while the original portion is separated from the mass—or only when the human form has been completed? If we maintain that divinity was united with the soul in the formed human being, reason would surely not oppose this, were it not that concerning that passage in which the venerable Virgin replied to the heavenly messenger, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38), many say—not absurdly—that with this assent the Son of God came. If, then, the Son of God came with the conception, which truly occurred when the Virgin assented to Gabriel, and united Himself to what was conceived, perhaps you will wonder that one person subsisted from the majesty of the Son and the seed of humanity. But cease to wonder when you reflect that, after the body and soul have been separated from each other, the divinity is united to both no less than before. Life therefore joined the body with the soul, but not with God; for death separated the body from the soul, but not from God. As after death, so before life, it is more easily believed that the living God is joined with what is not living, namely the body. Hence, in many places, the faithful begin their prayers for the general aid of our frailty as follows: “Holy Mother of God, who worthily deserved to conceive Him whom the whole world could not contain,” etc. Therefore the Mother of God conceived Him whom the whole world does not contain, who reaches from end to end and whose majesty fills the whole earth. From this it is clear that the Mother of God conceived God; for how would she be the Mother of God unless she had conceived God? What is it to conceive a human being except to receive the seedbed of humanity? What, then, is it to conceive God except to receive God personally united to that seedbed? Otherwise, how did she conceive Him whom she nevertheless already possessed before, since He could be absent from nowhere?

She therefore conceived a human being when a portion of her body, which she had possessed, began to be set apart as the material of another human being; and she conceived God when He whom she had possessed in the common manner of all others began to be possessed by her in the womb in a singular manner, incarnate. Hence in the Creed we also confess that the same Son of God was conceived of the Holy Spirit, because He was conceived of the Holy Spirit by His mother. Hence elsewhere we sing of the same One: “He came down from heaven, and was incarnate by the Holy Spirit of the Virgin Mary, and was made man.” Therefore, since the Virgin Mary conceived God, when did she conceive Him if not when He was incarnated? For what else is it for God to be conceived than to be incarnated? Hence perhaps where the Creed says, “Conceived of the Holy Spirit,” [Note: Col. 0783D. Constantinopolitan Creed.] elsewhere it has, “Incarnate of the Holy Spirit.” For from the moment He descended, the Virgin immediately conceived Him.
