But what does it mean that He descended, who remained afterward in heaven and had already filled the whole earth? How did He descend from heaven, from which He never departed? How did He descend to where He always remained? It is impossible for one who must be present in every place to be moved in place.

But He descended when He who was known in heaven through divinity began to be known on earth through humanity. Thus He did not descend in substance, but He descended in being known. This knowledge came about through the incarnation. Hence incarnation is added immediately after the descent mentioned above. Or rather, He descended from heaven when, by becoming incarnate, He humbled Himself to earth, as the Lord testifies: “I came forth from the Father” (John 16:28). Hence also the Apostle: “He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:7). For taking the servile form was, as it were, an abolition of majesty. He therefore descended from heaven to earth when He laid aside His majesty into flesh; yet He did not abandon what He was, but assumed what He was not. Thus descent is nothing other than incarnation. Therefore, after the Son’s descent is mentioned, the exposition, for clarity’s sake, treats of His incarnation, and then adds: “Made man” (John 1:14). Certainly He was first incarnate in being conceived and afterward made man. Perhaps the Evangelist understood this when he said: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.). The Word was made flesh from the time when He was incarnate; He dwelt among us after He was made man.

Yet He was not made flesh, any more than He was made man, through a changeableness of nature, but through union. For divinity was not changed into humanity, lest there be a confusion of substance; rather, humanity was united to it, so that there might be unity of person. Both authorities—the one by “conceived,” the other by “incarnate”—make known the same Son of God as dead and buried. This would never truly be said unless God and the one dead or buried came together in one person. In this way, in many passages you will find in reading that Mary the Mother of God conceived and bore God, that God suffered, and other expressions more properly fitting humanity. For whenever different natures are personally united, both Scripture and ordinary usage customarily attribute what belongs to one to the other. Thus any human being is rightly called wise or foolish when joined to a wise or foolish soul; but if the soul were absent, neither statement could truly be made. Therefore God would not rightly be considered buried, dead, incarnate, or conceived, unless He were understood to be joined personally to conception and flesh, and also to the dead and buried person. Likewise, you would never call the Son of God the son of man unless one person comprehended both God and man. God was made man; and although God and man are each one thing, He is one. Thus the Son of God was made the son of man; and although there are two essences, He is nevertheless one. Are they not also one Son? Similarly, the wise Son of God and wise son of man, and likewise Master, Redeemer, and Savior: are there not two natures, yet one person, so that there is one Redeemer and Savior, one Master and wise one, according to the saying: “One is your Master” (Matt. 23:8)?

## Chapter XVII. Why and how God is man, or conversely.

[Note: Col. 0784D. Master, as above.]

Since the union of divinity and humanity is far stronger than that of soul and body—for these come together in life and depart in death, whereas those can be united before life and cannot be separated by death—the expression of so great a union allows both “God is man” and “man is God” to be said, although neither is the body called soul nor the soul ever called body.

Yet beware of calling man God in such a way that you understand something corporeal to be incorporeal. Each nature remains what it is and never passes into the other, but joins itself to the other, so that there is one person of two—indeed, three—substances: God, soul, and body. For a true human being would not exist without a soul, nor is it the office of divinity to animate flesh.

If anyone should maintain that Christ did not have a soul and that God supplied the place of the soul, Christ never died, since He was never separated even personally from God. Christ, therefore, had a soul, by whose departure He might die and by whose return He might live again. Heretic, hear Him Himself: “I have power to lay down My soul and to take it again” (John 10:18). Hear the Catholic faith concerning Him: “Perfect God, perfect man, subsisting of a rational soul and human flesh.” [Note: Col. 0785D. Athanasian Creed.] Christ therefore subsists from divinity and humanity, not as a composite, because God can be the part of no thing. For if Christ were composed of God and man, He would be neither man nor God, since no whole is its own part. Yet Christ is most truly, in different respects, both man and God. When we say, “Christ is man,” the word used as subject signifies humanity. But when we say, “Christ is God,” it denotes divinity. When we say in this third way, “Christ is God and man,” the name Christ makes both natures manifest. Thus the language is explained so that the truth may be perceived; thus the expression varies, so that now this nature, now that, now both natures in Christ may be understood. Again, when you hear that man is God, do not understand that what was born in time existed before times, that what is contained in a place fills every place, or that what is body is spirit; for “God is spirit” (John 4:24).

But if God cannot exist without these things, nor man without those, how is man God or God man, since man may not be raised to these or similar rights of God, nor does it suit God to stoop to what is unfitting for Him? Therefore neither man is God nor God man by nature. Hence we say of Christ that He is equal to the Father according to divinity and less than the Father according to humanity. [Note: Col. 0785D. Athanasian Creed.]

There are two natures in Christ, one creating, the other created. Which of the two is equal to the Father? For it is impious to make both equal to the Father, because the created one is unquestionably less. Therefore the creating nature must be made equal to the Father, since nothing else remains that can be so equated. Accordingly, when we say that Christ is equal to the Father according to divinity, it means nothing other than that the Son of God is equal to the Father. But why is added, “according to divinity”? Is the Son equal to the Father according to divinity? The Son, insofar as He is Son, is equal to the Father; according to divinity, He is one and the same with the Father. What, then, does “Christ is equal to the Father according to divinity” mean except that Christ’s divinity is equal to the Father?

I think what follows must be interpreted in the same manner: “Less than the Father according to humanity,” that is, Christ’s humanity is less than the Father. But what is wholly equal is not what is wholly less; therefore Christ’s divinity is not Christ’s humanity. But divinity in Christ is the same as Christ God; Christ’s humanity is nothing other than Christ man. Therefore neither God is man nor man God by nature, yet by grace He is so. This grace made God and man one person, on account of which God and man are one Christ. For it is not as one nature is constituted from a head and other members that one nature is constituted from soul and flesh, or from God and the whole human being, whether called nature or substance; only the person is one. As there is one human being in the former case, so here there is one Christ. Hence we say: “As the rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ.”

If, therefore, “God was made man” is not understood so that substance appears changed into substance, the creating into the created—for such a change would empty the changed nature, because what it was before would not remain—what does it mean that God was made man, “not abandoning what He was, He assumed what He was not,” except that this nature never becomes that one, although this nature at some time binds that one to itself? Hence it is said: “One, not by conversion of the substance of divinity into flesh, but by the assumption of humanity into God.” Therefore God was not changed into man, and consequently was not made man—for He always remained God. What indeed is becoming except changing?

Yet God was most certainly made man: “not by conversion,” as has been said, “of divinity into flesh, but by the assumption of humanity into God.” God, I say, was made man, not by changing Himself into man, but by assuming man to Himself, so that nature might be joined to nature, but not changed into the other or mixed with the other after the manner of wine and water—lest there be confusion of substance rather than unity of person. Thus God is not man essentially, but He is man personally. God is not essentially man because, being spirit, He cannot be body; God is personally man because, though He is spirit, He is nevertheless united to a human body. He is united to man as soul is united to body.

What, therefore, does “God is man” mean except “God is united to man”? What does “man is God” mean except “man is united to God”? And what does “man is united to God” mean except “man and God are one”—indeed, soul and flesh and God are one? One, certainly, not one thing: for soul, flesh, and God are surely one because they are one person. They are in no way three, because they are not three persons; likewise they are in no way one thing, because they are not one nature. Without doubt they are three things, because they are three substances. Thus soul, flesh, and God are neither one thing nor three persons; they are one and they are three. [Note: Col. 0785D. “As in that singular divinity there is Trinity in the persons and unity in the substance, so in that special union there is Trinity in the substances and unity in the person. And as there the persons do not divide the unity, nor does unity diminish the Trinity, so here the person does not confuse the substances, nor do the substances themselves dissipate the unity of the person,” etc. Bernard, Sermon 3 on the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, about the middle, and *On Consideration*, Book I.] Conversely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one thing and are three; they are not one person and are not three things. Hence it is clear that the neuter gender must be used for substance and the masculine for person. There is now no doubt what should be understood when one hears “God was made man”; for what does “God was made man” mean except that God was made united to man, that is, made one with man?

## Chapter XVIII. Opposite predicates belong to Christ according to His two natures.

For Christ, who before time was God alone, at the end of time is also man; and therefore He who was of one substance only—and was that one substance with the Father and the Holy Spirit—is now of the same substance, not losing what He was, and also of another substance, assuming what He had not been. For Christ is one and the same, not one person and another: first the Only-begotten of the Father, and at last also the only-begotten of His mother.

Since there is only one Christ, and He is man and God not merely by title but essentially, it is evident that Christ, who is only one, is nevertheless of two substances—indeed, both substances. One always existed; the other began to exist. He who was uncreated was made: the Creator was made a creature. He who lives perpetually immortal in what is His own deigned to die in what is ours, remaining both that which could die and that which could not die. He who remained one thing from eternity began to be the other. He who is thus constituted, and who is Christ, is certainly the Son of God, and therefore the person of the Son of God. For how could He be Christ and not the Son of God? And how then could He be the Son of God and not the person of the Son of God? Christ, therefore, is the person not of the Father, not of the Holy Spirit, but of the Son alone.

It is therefore not surprising that what is rightly said of Christ may also be said of the person of the Son of God: among many other things, this also may be said: [Note: Col. 0787D. Master, Book III, distinction 6, §§4–5, etc.] the person who always existed of one substance—indeed, who still exists of one substance only with the Father—has, from the time when He assumed our body, been found to be of two substances. For if Christ is not one person and another, but one only—first God, afterward man-God—then similarly is not the person, then and now, not one and another but one only? For Christ, formerly God alone, was the person of one substance alone; now, also man, He is the person of two substances. If, therefore, Christ is one both then and now, why is the person not also one? One nature is not two, and yet Christ, formerly of one substance and not two—indeed, formerly one nature and now two—is only one. Thus the person, formerly of one nature and afterward of two, is itself also one.

If the usage of the Fathers contains these or similar expressions, whether more or fewer, we receive them reverently. Yet let us beware of understanding well-spoken words wrongly. If we hear that Christ, immortal without beginning, deigned for our sake to become mortal, let us not err by thinking that the divine nature was changed into the human. When divinity is asserted to be united to humanity, let us suspect no confusion of either through mixture. Rather, while the nature of both God and man remains its own, when we hear “made” or “united,” let the union of soul and flesh into one person be understood.

Since Christ was formerly God and afterward man and God, we must not therefore suppose that the name Christ denotes something common, first to one nature and afterward also to the assumed one. For Christ then was nothing other than the one nature, nor is He now anything other than that nature together with the assumed nature. What then? If Christ who was then is He who is now, is the nature which was then one now itself also the other? It was not made the other, but the other was joined to it.

I think the expression of this union is indicated when he who existed in one nature is asserted to exist in two natures. I understand the same thing if it is said that Christ was one substance and is two. Nor do I think otherwise wherever the person is declared to be of one substance before, and afterwards of two substances [Col. 0788B]. But whatever turn the customary use of words may take among orthodox authors, whether we adopt this manner of speaking or another, let us avoid profane novelties of language. Let the words vary; let the meaning remain sound. Divinity and humanity are truly two; therefore they are by no means one; they are united to one another in their own manner. Therefore He is truly One, not by confusion of substance but by unity of person; because, “as the rational soul and flesh are one,” etc. Thus, as in a human being we speak of the unity of person as belonging to the union of soul and flesh, so in Christ let us speak of it as belonging to the connection of divinity and complete humanity—a connection similar indeed, yet stronger. This connection, then, I judge to be properly called a person, while understanding the name “person” differently here and differently in the Holy Trinity. For there [Col. 0788C] the first, second, and third persons are one and the same substance; here, however, two or three substances are one and the same person. And since for these substances to be united to one another is nothing other than for there to be a person, it is certainly one thing for there to be a person in the Holy Trinity and another for there to be a substance.

Having considered these matters, the person which is one substance with the Father and the Holy Spirit seems perhaps more properly said to be in a person of three substances, or itself together with humanity to be a person of three substances, than it should be said that the person which was only God is now a person of three substances. For how can a person which was only one substance now be a person of three substances, if to be a person of three is nothing other than to be three things united to one another [Col. 0788D]?

How, then, is the person which was only one substance now three or two substances, rather than that which always was united to humanity? Nevertheless, we revere the usage of authors and embrace the sound meaning, however the words may stand; nor do we call improper what the usage of the saints approves, although we judge one formulation more proper than another.

When our Lord Jesus died, and consequently soul and flesh were separated from one another, yet remained united to the divine substance, it is clear that soul and flesh were two substances, the divine substance a third—indeed the first—and therefore that there was one person of three substances [Col. 0789A]. Yet both before death and after it, soul and flesh, though joined to one another, nevertheless remain two substances. For as God and man, so in man soul and flesh, cleave together into one person, not into one substance. Therefore, from the time that divinity assumed complete humanity, because no separation followed, the unity of person endures in three substances.

[Note: [Col. 0789D] He nevertheless mentions both forms of expression in *On the Trinity*, book XII, ch. 17. The designation “three substances” is also approved by the Eleventh and Fifteenth Councils of Toledo.]

Augustine, however, commonly says that it is the person of two substances, considering the divine and human natures. In the human nature, flesh and soul are customarily understood. But Scripture uses the name Christ without distinction, to designate the divine and human nature, whether each separately or the person subsisting from both. Yet that nature is properly signified [Col. 0789B] which “was anointed with the oil of gladness above its companions.” For *Christ* means “anointed.” Therefore Christ, first existing as the creating substance, afterwards both that substance and two created substances, at last died for us. For if Christ is God and man, and every man is soul and flesh, then certainly Christ is God and, because He is man, also soul and flesh. The divinity did not die, although God is said to have died. For Isaac was not sacrificed (Gen. III, 22); but the ram was sacrificed. This is death of the human nature, though not of it in its entirety, since the soul is immortal. Therefore, of the three substances in the person, the flesh alone died; the soul suffered with it; but the divinity remained untouched.

What, then, do the foregoing words mean—“Christ, first existing as the creating substance, afterwards both it and two created substances, at last died for us”—except that the flesh of Christ died, which was united to soul and divinity, whereas previously divinity had been foreign to this connection [Col. 0789C]? Let us examine kinds of expression as far as we can, so that we may discover what is appropriate to each and why it was said in one way or another.

## Chapter XIX. Why He Is Said to Have Suffered; and That, Though the Parts Were Separated, Christ Remained One Person

[Note: [Col. 0789D] Lombard, *Sentences*, book III, distinctions 21 and 22.]

But because God is united to the man who suffered and was buried, God is rightly said to have suffered and to have been buried. Is it then because He was united to the seed which was to be formed into a man that He could rightly also have been called seed? I see no danger in this as a matter of meaning. But in matters of faith it is faulty to employ even expressions which Catholic usage does not accept. God is united to flesh, so that He is called flesh; hence, “The Word was made flesh” (John 1:13), that is, God is united to man. He is united to the soul, yet is not called soul. Thus perhaps He was united to seed, yet was not called seed.

But since God is united first to flesh without a soul, then to flesh with a soul; likewise to flesh bereft of a soul, and finally to flesh raised to immortality: are there also four persons because the flesh has undergone four changes? Far be it! For the person remains one, however much the flesh may change. Likewise, soul and flesh are one human being in childhood, youth, and finally old age. But Christ’s death [Col. 0790A] separated the soul from the body. The body rested in the tomb; the soul descended to the lower regions. Hence we confess both that Christ was buried and that He descended to hell. Meanwhile, however, divinity and soul still subsisted even then as one person. Reason shows likewise that God remained one person with the body.

But since at that time the body was separated from the soul, were the persons also divided? Far be that as well! For body and soul were not then one person with each other. But God with the soul, though not with the soul alone, was one person; likewise God with the body, though not with the body alone, was one person—not one person and another, but one alone. For when flesh and soul are joined, God is not one person with them by reason of such a joining; otherwise there would be one person composed of God and any human being. Rather, because God is united to each nature, He is one person with both. Therefore the union of two natures with each other does not make one person with the Godhead; nor does the separation of the two cause a plurality of persons. Thus, when a body is divided, while the soul still remains with its divided parts, the same person remains from the soul and the divided parts as existed when the same parts were joined together [Col. 0790B]. In like manner, if any one spirit were united to many whole bodies, or conversely one body to many spirits, however the union of substances might be changed, the unity of person would seem to follow it.

I said that there is one person from the soul and the body united to it, whether its parts cohere or are separated. [Note: [Col. 0790D] This same opinion appears in Lombard, book III, distinction 5, §3.] But the same person would not retain the same name of person [Col. 0790C]. To speak of a human being: the person who, when his limbs are dissolved, is not called a human being, was called a human being when those same limbs were joined—the name of the substance that dies being transferred, in a special way, to that substance and, in common usage, also to the other which does not die. Conversely, the person consisting of God and flesh is now called Christ; but before the soul was infused He was not so called. Yet even then there was one person from God and flesh [Note: [Col. 0790D] See the notes.], though without soul; the same person afterwards from God and flesh joined to soul; and finally the same person from God and flesh separated from soul.

Therefore one and the same person subsists from substances—at one time two, at another three; with two of the three at one time joined to each other and at another separated, while the third is always joined [Col. 0790D]. So too a heap, now increasing in number, now decreasing, and now occupying one arrangement, now another, nevertheless remains one and the same heap; likewise one and the same human being and person while the body grows and diminishes.

## Chapter XX. On the Incarnation, Union, and Person of Christ Made Man

[Note: [Col. 0790D] Lombard, as above, and distinction 3, final paragraph.]

I said that God was united to flesh before it had a soul; and I not only said so but also advanced some little arguments and attempted to demonstrate it by authority. But reason, weighed down by the mass of flesh, is often deceived; and authority, though right in itself, is not rightly understood. Therefore I think that, except where something is held by faith on certain authority—and especially in matters belonging to faith—we should speak cautiously and more as an opinion, lest what could have been pardonable through ignorance be made unforgivable by obstinacy.

Accordingly, we earnestly affirm the incarnation of the Word. But the time of the incarnation either occurred, as we argued, together with conception; or, if that ought not at all to be held—although it seems that it ought—then certainly the Word was made flesh when the flesh itself was made man. But since the question has been raised when Deity was united to humanity, we must now inquire, so far as we are able, what this union itself is. For it is clear that the personal union of which we speak [Col. 0791B] is not a coming together of parts, since God and man, just as man and soul, are one person but not one whole. Where composition is absent but some association of diverse substances is present, a person does not immediately result; for a rider is fitted to a horse, and one hand to another hand, yet neither is united to the other.

There is another association of different things which is difficult to define. For who can explain the bond of soul and man, and finally of the whole human being and divinity? For it is impossible to narrate the generation of the Word, and most difficult to expound the incarnation of the Word. Yet whatever this bond may be, I judge it to be a personal union; and this I hold firmly: every living creature lives by it, and, when it is broken, perishes [Col. 0791C].

But since Catholic faith teaches us the Trinity, how is a quaternity of persons introduced? The three persons are Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; how then is there a fourth from the connection of the Son of God, the son of man, and the soul? But I do not think that this person is to be counted with those. For “person” is said here and there in a very different sense. There are three persons and one substance there; here there are three substances and one person. Here three substances are one person; there three persons are one substance. We venerate a Trinity of persons in one substance; in one person we marvel at a Trinity, if it may be so called, of substances. Grace joined this person; those persons are coeternal with one another by nature [Col. 0791D]. [Note: Here Pullus does not speak of Christ’s person insofar as it is the person, or personality, of the Word itself—as he stated above that the person of the divine Word and that of Christ are one and the same—but speaks of “person” insofar as he calls it a certain composite of two natures, divine and human; from this he does not depart. [Col. 0792D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, XIII, ch. 17; Sermon 8, *On Time*; and Tractate 99 on John.] Therefore neither count this person together with them nor regard it as one of them. For one nature of this person is one person in the Trinity; but to insert all three natures into the Trinity, or to count them among things external to it as equals, is impious. For neither the human being nor the soul is in the Trinity, nor is the Only-Begotten outside the Trinity; finally, it is wholly unfitting to add to the Trinity something inferior to it.

If, then, at some time there was one person from divinity [Col. 0792A] and animated seed, beyond doubt it was not other than the person which afterwards comprised three substances together, just as a heap is not different when it consists of fewer things than when it consists of more. And if one and the same person consists now of two and now of three natures, why could not the same person at some time also have had one nature in one person, so that it would be the same person now of one, now of two, and now of three substances? If it is granted that the soul exists before the human being just as it exists after the human being, before incorporation as well as after it, why should one person not be believed to be of one substance both before and after, but of two while the soul is contained in the body? Therefore one and the same person is, as I have said, at one time of one substance [Col. 0792B], at another of three, and at another of two.

And although such a person is nothing other than one substance at one time, that which is two natures at another time, and three at yet another, still there is no reason why three should be two or two another thing. Thus a smaller heap, later made larger, is said to be one and the same heap; nevertheless the number of the smaller is different from that of the larger. But how is that person which is one, and is now in the Trinity, and was formerly only one substance, now of three, when the Trinity itself is only of one substance? Because with the Father and the Spirit it is of one substance, but with the human being it is of three; or rather, it is not the person itself, but that which is from it and the human being, which is a person of two—or rather, three—substances. For how can one and the same person, at one and the same time, be of one substance only and also of several [Col. 0792C]? You have heard: with the Father and the Spirit, of one; with the human being, of several. Why do you cavil?

But because the person which, by itself, is of one substance is also, with the human being, a person of three substances, I am not mistaken when I say: the person is of one substance in itself, but of several with the human being. For it and the human being are several substances. Since you admit that a person of one substance is several things only together with the human being, or is a person of several substances, you do not rightly assert that this one is of one substance and that one of several, or that one and the same person is of one and of several, when what was formerly one remains always what it properly is. When it joins itself to the human being, there is not that person, but a person of several things from that person and the human being. For what is from diverse things is not one of those diverse things [Col. 0792D]. [Note: It should not be inferred from this that Pullus admits in Christ the composition called *ex his* (“from these”); above, in ch. 17 and elsewhere, he refutes it at greater length.]

A heap, indeed, which now consists of the first ten and of others added afterwards, was certainly formerly a heap of ten, and was those ten themselves; but now it is neither. Yet, according to you, the person of three both contains within itself the person which is of one and is that very person. Consider how that can stand.

It seems to me that we should speak more properly thus: one and the same person subsists from the person which is one in the Trinity and from humanity assumed in its entirety; therefore it subsists from one person and two substances. And because this person was not incarnate except with its own substance, by which it is personally united to the other two, that person is also a person of three substances [Col. 0793A].

## Chapter XXI. Apart from Sin and Ignorance, Christ Had Other Defects

[Note: [Col. 0793D] The Master, book III, distinctions 13–15.]

In order to assume true humanity suited to redemption, our Lord did not refuse the defects due to humanity apart from sin. Among these is the ignorance proper to those not yet born. Thus Christ, being born, seems to have assumed it also as a child, [Col. 0793B] so that ignorance might gradually diminish in the customary course of time and wisdom succeed in its proper stages—unless it is more credible that everything came sooner and more fully to the human being united with God. Hence at twelve years old He is said to have disputed with the teachers; for Luke testifies: “He advanced in wisdom and age and grace before God and men” (Luke 2:52). But one who advanced in wisdom abounded in it increasingly. Wherever wisdom increases, ignorance must previously have diminished. Surely ignorance ought to accompany the frailty of infancy, and wisdom to increase with advancing age.

Unless we should rather believe that the child was full of God, and already then also full of grace and truth (John 1:14), as though filled with the spirit of wisdom and understanding [Col. 0793C], the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and also the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. 11:2): so that He whom God assumed into one person with Himself was immediately filled with every fullness of grace. For God would deem unworthy of so great a dignity a human being who is called God and is God, if he were disfigured by any defect except those required either by the rationale of redemption or by the necessity of humanity.

But if infant ignorance be granted to have harmed nothing in redemption, how can it be shown to have been beneficial, when human nature does not seem to require it? For in Adam it was created intelligent and prudent. But you will say that it is natural for little children to know absolutely nothing. Yet ignorance appears to have arisen from fault. For although the body weighs down the soul, and by weighing it down makes it both dull and ignorant, a defect of transgression, not nature, produces such oppression. Otherwise, how would a well-created body render the spirit insensible? How could the soul, the image of God, free from all iniquity, become as though irrational and ignorant of all things, when certain irrational creatures are born with their own perception, in which they gradually advance as they grow [Col. 0793D]?

If humans had not sinned, it is credible that in being born they would either bring the use of reason with them from the womb or, if the pressure of the womb prevented this, receive it at birth, to advance with age—not perhaps because the smallness of their bodies made them slower, but because, by attending to individual things, they would learn them. Yet I think it should neither be obstinately denied nor shamelessly asserted that those bodies too would have been born with such constitutions that the less fit would receive a slower rational development and the fitter a keener one in due course. But this, more than anything else, I would believe: whatever their constitution, infants, age being no impediment, would be able and know how adequately to manage themselves.

For if this is readily available to the young of animals, how much more to those of human beings, especially at that time when there would have been no fault from which foolishness or punishment could arise? Otherwise the rearing of children would have been shameful and anxious for parents; and that certainly befell transgressors as a punishment, rather than being made by nature. For this reason too women give birth in pain—whereas, if they had not sinned, they would have reared their children in joy and given birth in tranquillity, certainly as infants [Col. 0794B]; for how could the narrowness of the womb contain the size of an adult?

Therefore neither the rationale of human creation nor that of infancy itself seems to require that the boy Jesus, who was free from sin, should have been childishly ignorant. For who doubts that the salvation of human beings stood not in wisdom but had need of great wisdom? Hence it is evident that the humanity of the Word drew something from each condition: from both that condition which shone before transgression and ours which withered after guilt, without taking either entire condition. For He assumed our hunger and fatigue, together with certain other of our defects—our capacity for suffering—so that, afflicted by many sufferings, He might release us from many sins. Thus He who came in order to suffer for His brethren showed Himself conformed to His brethren, that the kinship might be evident [Col. 0794C].

Yet the manifestation of assumed humanity rejected the contaminations of sin and, together with sin, the tinder of sin: folly. If you ascribe either of these to the Savior, you detract from salvation. For neither could a sinner take away sins nor could one less than prudent secure salvation. Therefore Christ the man, because He was God, rejected every ignorance just as He rejected every fault. Hence, as mediator for us, appealing to the threefold Majesty, according to the Apostle, “He was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5:7). Therefore He took punishment from us, but rejected the cause of punishment, sin, and ignorance, the effect of sin, as something that would lead to degeneration.

But from the first creation He received purity and keenness of perception in both respects, more illustrious and better than all created things, not only when an adult but even before He was born. Hence in the psalm He says in direct address to God: “From my mother’s womb you are my God” (Ps. 21:11). And again: “My hope from my mother’s breasts” (ibid.). He was wonderfully and extraordinarily wise and devout, recognizing his God from his mother’s womb and fastening his hope upon God from his mother’s breasts: “Having become so much better than the angels, as he inherited a more excellent name than they” (Heb. 1:4) [Col. 0794D].

Therefore, since He is and is called God and the Son of God, it is certain that, by as much as He is better than the angels, by so much He is greater. Hence, concerning the assumed human being, God says through the Prophet: “He subjected all things [Col. 0795A] under his feet,” so that nothing was not subjected, except Him who subjected all things to Him. Subject only to Him, and having all things subject to Himself, nevertheless during the time of His weakness He was made a little lower than the angels (Ps. 8:5; Heb. 2:8). Truly a little lower, because diminished only in passibility; otherwise, in all things He was made higher even than the heavens. Yet He was not lower for long, since by rising again He was crowned with glory and honor.

If, then, as born from the former condition He was pure and prudent, while from our condition He was also made mortal in our fashion, would He not, if no slayer had been present, have died by the law of mortals? For such is the condition of this life: unless some external force intervenes, it fails of itself as it grows old. We maintain, with Augustine as witness [Note: [Col. 0795D] Book II, *On the Merits of Sins*, ch. 29.], that this was the life of Christ the man [Col. 0795B].

## Chapter XXII. Whence Christ Had the Power to Emerge from the Closed Womb, and Similar Matters

If He received from our condition a life destined to end, and from the former condition a life of splendor, whence did He receive the ability to emerge from His mother’s closed womb? For just as among us the way for the child to be born is opened through intercourse, so it is clear that this ought to have been so in paradise. It is evident, therefore, that neither condition required birth from a virgin. Did Jesus, while still mortal, borrow from the condition of immortality that by which He also, transfigured in another appearance, presented Himself to the apostles to be seen before the Passion? For just as the resurrection is known to shine with every splendor, so it is not absurd to judge that it is held by no obstacle. Hence the Lord is read to have entered among His disciples after the Resurrection (John 20:19) [Col. 0795C].

Thus it may reasonably be said that not only two earthly conditions but also a third, heavenly one, were at work in our Lord while He was still passible. Was it not heavenly that, even before the Passion, He saw God face to face, and that He walked upon the waters with steady footsteps? For in heaven the human soul will have this clarity: that it knows God plainly; and the human body will have this lightness: that it can set foot upon water, indeed even through the air, as though on solid ground. Hence the saints are said to be destined to ascend, borne on clouds.

A marvelous thing: conspicuous in native purity, He was deprived of the tranquillity due to purity! A new thing: a human being within our capacity lacked our sin! A wonderful thing: a mortal human being with us on earth possessed by power what is promised to the saints in heaven to possess by nature [Col. 0795D]! For although these things are hoped to come from the generosity of the Creator, because they occur so as to remain without end, they are rightly reckoned as nature. How great was the power by which the mass of our body was born from a Virgin, walked upon waters, saw God in such a body, and possessed, even for an hour, the appearance of immortality!

## Chapter XXIII. The Child Christ Was Full of Wisdom

[Note: [Col. 0795D] The Master, book III, distinctions 13 and 14.]

Distinguished men defend, each for himself, one of the two opposing opinions stated above concerning the Savior’s infancy: some affirming the ignorance, others the complete wisdom, of our Lord Jesus as an infant. But on firm authority, reinforced by some reasoning, we have preferred the opinion of those who maintain that all things were known to Christ even in the womb [Col. 0796A]. Nothing that Luke says of Christ—“He advanced in wisdom and age and grace before God and men” (Luke 2:52)—will oppose this, if understood inwardly. For He advanced in age, as He grew by yearly increments not only before human beings but before God, who is not deceived. But wisdom and grace, which came together and at once to the human being from the very union with God, receiving absolutely no increase in themselves, advanced before human beings, to whom they became more and more apparent.

For as soon as God became man, the human being was raised so far that He could neither know more nor become better. This is intimated to the understanding reader by the authority explaining Luke: when Christ rose again, He did not increase in holiness, knowledge, or blessedness; rather, He gradually manifested, for God’s praise and human benefit, the grace which He had wholly received by the gift of the Trinity. He advanced in wisdom and grace before God and human beings, insofar as through both He obtained the glory of the former and the benefit of the latter [Col. 0796B].

For I think this passage must be explained so that Luke does not contradict himself, having previously said of Christ: “But the child grew and was strengthened, full of wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him” (ibid.). Hence it is clear that the nature which grew in Christ as a child was full of wisdom, and that the nature in which the grace of God was—which is certainly the humanity—was full of wisdom in Christ’s childhood [Col. 0796C]. But one in whom the fullness of wisdom dwelt lacked nothing of wisdom. Did He receive diminished grace, so that, being fully learned, He should be only half fully good? Far be it! For we recall, on the authority handed down to us concerning this passage of the Evangelist, that both were immediately poured into Christ in their fullness. Therefore, from the moment He began to be, the child Jesus immediately grew, by God’s gift, into such knowledge and such eminence of character that afterwards nothing increased in either.

## Chapter XXIV. Christ Was Not Increased in Merit or Made Better

[Note: [Col. 0796D] Lombard, book III, distinction 18.]

What am I saying? Did not the man Jesus, following the manner of human beings, as He devoted Himself to works of charity, increase His merit more and more and, through increased merit, make Himself better [Col. 0796D]? A merely human person is judged better by a few small increases; but Christ the man, having performed so many and such great acts for God’s praise and human benefit, is in no respect made better than He was before. He endured so much for God and did not become more pleasing to God. For if He became more pleasing, He certainly also became better. How, then, did God, according to the Apostle, exalt Christ because of what He did in his humanity (Phil. 2:9), when He did not thereby hold Him more pleasing? Or if He did hold Him more pleasing for such a cause—since He exalted Him for such a cause—how was He not better by as much as He was more pleasing to God?

Therefore, if because He became obedient to the Father unto death it is necessary to believe that He increased in merits and became better [Col. 0797A], more pleasing to God, then He did not receive perfection immediately upon the advent of God.

But how was the child Jesus already full of grace, if you consider knowledge and charity, and charity’s companion virtues, all of which have their place in the soul? Without doubt He was full of grace and immediately perfect, because He afterward received no increase in them. If you consider the works springing from the root of virtue, which accrued ever more abundantly day by day, He “advanced in wisdom and age and grace before God and men” (Luke 2:52). By this advance He became obedient to the Father unto death, for which God exalted Him. Therefore our Lord Jesus, even in His mother’s womb, was perfect in one respect, while in another He still had to be perfected [Col. 0797B].

But if He was immediately full of knowledge and charity, since He was most knowing, did He not survey with the eye of His mind His entire path of obedience? And since He excelled in highest charity, did He not also most earnestly desire that the things which He knew would occur concerning Him in service to God should occur then and in the manner in which it pleased the Father? If He had preferred otherwise or at another time, would He not have had either an evil or a less good will?

If, then, the man Jesus, our Lord, while still a child, most perfectly desired to fulfill, in obedience to the Father and for the benefit of His brethren, everything which God had arranged by the grace of redemption, when and how it ought to be fulfilled; if He was already in mind prepared for everything, and would have wished things which God willed to occur in the future to occur in the present—how, with so perfect a will, was He less good or less pleasing to God than He was later, when He fulfilled what He had willed? For, as I said, the delay in fulfillment came not from Him but from the Father [Col. 0797C].

But you will say: a will so worthy was certainly of great merit, yet merit accumulated when such great action was added to such a will. But according to Scripture, before God the perfect will to act is reckoned as the deed. You will say: the will is reckoned as the deed because the reward of the deed is apportioned to the will—not indeed every will, but that which is confirmed as perfect through consent; nevertheless it is not to be equated with the deed. Clearly, merely willing is less than carrying one’s will into effect.

## Chapter XXV. The Author Does Not Merit as a Human Being through Charity

[Note: [Col. 0797D] The Master, as above.]

But tell me: since every sin is voluntary, and likewise since your disposition gives your work its name, does not a work take upon itself from the will the character and name either of a good or an evil work? Clearly, according to the quality of the heart is the nature of the work. Hence the Lord says: “A good man brings forth good from a good treasure; an evil man, evil from an evil one” (Luke 6:45). Thus, when we judge a work good or evil, we very often err, because it is named otherwise from the heart. For the work itself, considered in itself, deserves neither name; hence the Lord never regards the work by itself, but according to the disposition of the mind. He requires a work [Col. 0798A], but only one that proceeds from charity. Thus charity is always pleasing in itself; a work is never pleasing except through charity. But in the saints charity heaps up good works, and a good work increases charity, so that each person is better through a good work by as much as he is more fervent in charity as a result of that good work.

But the Holy of Holies, even while still a child, shone with such charity that, as has been said, nothing increased in Him in this respect. The saints become better day by day because they grow in charity. But how did the Holy of Holies become better, since He was never made greater in charity?

Nevertheless, because He obeyed the Father, according to the Apostle He deserved to be exalted. Why? Was it on account of works, which are nothing except with charity? Or on account of charity [Col. 0798B], which is pleasing to God even in itself? Certainly God loved the charity perfected in Christ, on account of which He also accepted the works. For this charity produced its fruits in their proper times, yet before they were produced it always held them stored within itself in affection.

Hence He seems to have become obedient to the Father unto death not only when He died, but long before, when through charity He was ready to die; so that He would not become more worthy of reward by the execution of death than He had been previously by the will to die. For if the faithless, had they known, would never have crucified the Lord of glory, would the Lord Jesus—who, according to the Apostle, was exalted because of the suffering of the cross—have been the Lord of glory, or of lesser glory, or of no glory, because the Passion had been lacking? This would not have been because He was unwilling, since in Himself He was prepared for everything, but because the persecutor recoiled from cruelty [Col. 0798C]. I do not think so.

For if merit increased by the continuation of works, does He not still accumulate merits because He does not cease even now to do good? For according to the Apostle, seated at the right hand of the Father, He intercedes for us (Rom. 8:34). Because the Father works even now (John 5:17), works indeed exceedingly good, does He therefore become better even now? Do angels and human beings, after the resurrection when the consummation of all things is awaited, because they shall praise the Lord for ages of ages (Ps. 83:5), also increase their merit for ages of ages? Far be all this! For what is always growing never reaches its summit [Col. 0798D].

Therefore, if a rational creature brought to the very height of its perfection nevertheless still—indeed then more especially—does good without becoming better; if the Creator Himself does not cease to do good yet cannot increase; finally, if the humanity assumed by the Creator, now also received into heaven, does so much more good than others as it agrees more than all others with the divine will, yet acquires no increase—what wonder is it if, while passible on earth, it did good without becoming better thereby? For charity cannot be idle wherever it is; whenever it is present, the fruit arising from it is pleasing because of it. And because charity and its fruit extend forever, the saints are endowed with blessed perpetuity because of charity and its fruit; yet, once perfected in the resurrection, they hope to acquire nothing further [Col. 0799A].

## Chapter XXVI. What Is to Be Said Concerning Demons
[Note: [Col. 0799D] The Master, Book II of the *Sentences*, distinction XI, §4 and following.] It does not seem strange, therefore, if our Lord, perfected from the very womb, continued good works for himself in his due time and yet, though not thereby of greater merit, was granted exaltation according to the Apostle. But if men and angels who have attained perfection continually do good works and yet do not become better, what shall we say of demons? Is the malice of demons deferred to be perfected on the day of judgment, so that the perfection of wickedness comes with the completion of punishment? [Col. 0799B] If this is so, then, just as they act wickedly every day, they become worse every day—just as depraved human beings do. But if, in their very fall, the evil will of demons was perfected just as the good will of angels was, then, as angels continually do good yet do not become better through their good deeds because they are already perfected in disposition, do not demons likewise heap evil upon evil day by day, yet fail to become more wicked through this accumulation of evil because they already possess the wickedness of a depraved will in its completed form?

But if they are not worse for acting wickedly, how do they act wickedly, especially now, and on what ground are they to be punished for such deeds? Again, on what ground do they deserve impunity in the greater matter, when human beings are punished in the lesser? The Lord Jesus acted well and did not thereby become [Col. 0799C] better. Though he was not becoming better, he nevertheless acted well, to be crowned for such deeds; through his merits he was to become happier, not better. So the devil may act wickedly without becoming more wicked, and nevertheless act wickedly; he is finally to be punished for this, through his merits becoming more miserable, not worse. Thus angels indeed act well and perhaps are not made better; yet perhaps they will finally become happier than they now are, though not better.

But you will say to me: If the Lord Jesus, because he possessed a will perfected in goodness, would nevertheless have had the same reward that he now has even had there been no opportunity to fulfill so holy a will, would not a good and an evil angel, if they are already perfected—[Col. 0799D] one in love of good, the other in hatred of good—rightly receive the same reward even if some circumstance had prevented the fruits which love and hatred produce every day from occurring?

But Christ’s will sought to please God in all things, comprehending individually every thing in which it would please God. The will of an angel confirmed in goodness likewise desires to please God in all things, just as the will of demons desires in all things to displease him; but neither, because of ignorance of the future, can comprehend individually all the things in which it wishes to please or displease, upon the arrival of which a new act of will arises, so that, as by its general will, so also by its particular will [Col. 0800A] together with its effect, it appears worthy to procure them.

Hence an angel, made evil by seeking likeness to God, is seen to become worse when, through his fall, he is embittered so as to hate God supremely. He increases his malice when, thirsting without interruption for the ruin of all human beings, he does not cease wickedly to envy the kingdom of God. Since this appears to be so, it likewise appears fitting that, for what he did in heaven and in falling, he is now tortured in this air, and that, when his wickedness has been completed through what he does among us, he will finally be tortured completely in hell for all these things.

Likewise, perhaps some may think that, by equal stages in goodness, the merits of the holy angels have increased, until, when the number of saints has been completed, the merits of the angels too are completed together with it: so that, because they remained steadfast in their counsel, they would meanwhile possess much, though not the whole, of the glory in which they ought to have remained, diminished because of the number of the rest who fell; and, when the number has been completed, they would attain complete glory as their reward. [Col. 0800B]

Therefore the fall of the human race, though certainly evil, the good God turns to good: while he brings about the restoration of the fallen through the ministry of angels, he judges worthy of a crown not only the human beings who are restored, but also the angels through whose service they are restored. 122 Although I do not deny that it may be otherwise [Note: [Col. 0799D] See the Master, II, distinction 11, §4, whose erroneous opinion is noted at [Col. 0800D].], I nevertheless think nothing more credible than that the good and evil angel ascend, by different paths and as by certain steps, all the way to the summit: the one of righteousness and blessedness, the other of wickedness and perdition. Thus, once perfected, the one immediately in love of God, the other in hatred, they do not cease to increase—the one helping human beings in love, the other harming them in hatred. [Col. 0800C]

## CHAPTER XXVII. Christ assumed childhood, as he did the other conditions.

[Note: [Col. 0800D] The Master, III, distinction 15.] But how, according to the Gospel, was Jesus, even as a child, full of wisdom and grace, when complete wisdom and grace seem more fitting to a fully grown man? Did that which he was not appear in his outward appearance as a child, while what he was—a man in full stature—lay concealed; just as, when he rose again, he showed his disciples the old form which he had laid aside, so that he might be recognized, but concealed the new form subject to immortality, which mortals could not endure? Did he then possess the stature of a man in his mother’s womb, although, [Col. 0800D] when born, he presented infantile appearance to our eyes, according to the saying: “Behold, the Lord will make a new thing: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. XXXII)? For what is it to encompass a man except to have in the womb a human being already adult? This is certainly new and unheard of. But I think “man” is to be understood not in respect of stature, but of sex. Why, then, is it new? Because he was begotten from a mother alone, without the cooperation of a father. For Scripture very frequently calls him, and indeed understands him to be, little. Reason required that, the stain of sin and its attendant ignorance having been excluded, the Lord, who was truly to clothe himself in our nature, should assume the smallness of childhood which nature grants to those being born and necessity requires. [Col. 0801A] For he rejected guilt and ignorance, since they were in no way fitting for God; but he assumed our flesh even in its smallness, with its other deficiencies, because he judged it beneficial to redemption. This accords more fully with Scripture, agrees with human custom, pleases nature, and is approved by reason.

For it would indeed have been easy for Christ, just as at the Supper he offered himself sacramentally to each disciple, whole and entire although about to die, to have thirty years’ stature contained within the narrow confines of a womb—more marvelous, certainly, precisely because more incomprehensible to human reason. Yet this ought neither to have happened nor to be asserted, lest the crafty perversity of heretics, having found support, be most difficult to overthrow, while it lies that everything which faith most certainly affirms is to be understood not according to the truth of the thing, but according to what appeared and was outwardly seen. For if he is understood to have been little in the womb, little when born, little when growing, and to have reached adult strength by certain stages—not truly, but only as he appeared—why should heresy not similarly say that his miracles, his marvelous sayings, his crucifixion and death, his burial and resurrection, and finally his incarnation, merely appeared and were not true? [Col. 0801B]

Therefore, agreeing with reason and authority—indeed, fearing to oppose the catholic faith by which we are Catholics—we confess and most certainly affirm that our Lord grew small in his mother’s womb in the customary manner, proportionate to the capacity of the womb, and was born in an unprecedented manner. For a virgin conceived him and a virgin bore him: since she gave birth without passion; overshadowed by the power of the Most High, she conceived in chastity; and, by the working of that same power, gave birth unharmed. The barriers of virginity which received him intact also brought him forth intact.

But the prince, passing forever through the closed gate (Ezek. XLIV, 2), proceeding from his bridal chamber into that same bridal chamber—by what entrance did he enter? If I attend to the substance of his humanity, he plainly came out from the womb and did not enter into the womb; if I consider the substance of God, it is fitting for it neither to enter a place nor depart from one, since there is no place from which the Lord is absent. For the Son of God already existed in the Virgin’s womb; but afterward he began to be there in another way—not, certainly, by a different manner of dwelling, but by union with flesh. [Col. 0801C]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Whether the man who proposed good things, or God in the man, performed miracles.

[Col. 0801D]

He himself, for the sake of human beings, set before us the blessed life when it was fitting and in the manner in which it was fitting. But lest he benefit us by example alone, he added an authoritative teaching of the good life itself. And because he introduced things new and unheard of, he confirmed his wonderful teaching by miracles.

[Note: [Col. 0801D] The Master, III, distinction 14.] But must we judge the knowledge which we know to have been great in the man Christ equal to that which is in his divinity? Again, the miracles which Christ undoubtedly performed: did a human being perform them, or did God perform them in the human being? The Gospel testifies: “The Lamb of God, who takes away the sins [Col. 0802A] of the world” (John I, 29). What does it mean that the Lamb of God is said to take away sins, except that he takes away sins insofar as he is the Lamb? And what is he insofar as he is the Lamb, except insofar as he is sacrificed? Therefore not God alone, but also the man united to God takes away sins; for he redeemed us by his own blood and opened the gates of heaven. Does not the nature which poured out its blood for us also redeem us? And will not the same nature which redeemed us bring us into heaven, the mediator between God and human beings? For those whom it draws from the earth, it strives to bring into heaven to be united with God: the true Paschal Lamb, leading us out of the true Egypt of this world and bringing us back into the true land of promise, which is the land of the living.

Hence it is clear that created nature, which suffers, united to the creating nature, which does not suffer, offers the price of our redemption and has the merited power to forgive sins. Accordingly, by the miracle of the paralytic carrying his own bed, he proved that the Son of Man could forgive sins. For “he upon whom the Holy Spirit descends in the form of a dove, this is he who baptizes” (John I, 33). Upon whom did the Holy Spirit descend except upon Christ according to his humanity? For this in no way befitted his divinity. Therefore Christ baptizes according to his humanity. [Col. 0802B]

But what is baptism except the blotting out of sins by the sacrament of water? Therefore Christ, according to his humanity, blots out sins. [Note: [Col. 0802D] In the Gloss.] For on the passage already mentioned, where it is said, “This is he who baptizes” (John I, 33), you find when reading that the Lord Jesus, together with the sacrament of baptism which he entrusted to the ministers of baptism, [Col. 0802C] also could have entrusted the efficacy of baptism—namely, the abolition of sin—though he preferred to retain it for himself. If the Lord Jesus could confer upon his ministers such great power that they not only baptized but also blotted out sins, who would dare deny that the nature in Christ, even the human nature, has power to forgive sins? And if it cleanses from vices, it also illumines with virtues; for, “ascending on high, he gave gifts to human beings” (Eph. IV, 8). What does “ascending, he gave” mean except that the substance which ascended distributed those gifts? And what gifts? Under one name understand them all: faith, forgiveness, understanding, devotion.

But the humanity which, on earth, happily distributes these gifts to those justly made captive by it, will, as follows, render eternal goods in heaven. For humanity—since the Deity, which is everywhere, cannot come anywhere—will itself come to judge the living and the dead, because “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, because he is the Son of Man” (John V, 22). Therefore Christ, because he is the Son of Man—that is, in the nature of man—will judge. And what is it to judge except to render to each according to his works? Therefore Christ’s humanity will grant the good blessedness in heaven and hand the wicked over to endless torment in hell. If the substance of a human being can do these so great things, how much more can it perform miracles? Thus he satisfied a great multitude of people with a few loaves and little fish (Matt. XV, [Col. 0803A] 34; Mark VIII, 7), and walked with firm step upon the waters (Matt. XIV, 25). Did he then solidify the liquid so that it might bear the walker’s weight, or meanwhile remove weight from his body so that it could be borne by the waves? He could have done either, but then walking on the sea would no longer have been a miracle—rather, the waves’ solidity by congealing, or the body’s lightness by loss of weight.

We therefore marvel that the weight of a human body trod the fluid sea, since Scripture records his walking on the sea as a miracle. We do not prejudge that the water was thickened or the man lightened, since Scripture is silent about both; otherwise we must confess that the water was first solidified while Peter walked upon it (ibid.), then dissolved as soon as he sank, and immediately had to be solidified again when he was drawn back and walked upon the water. Or, if the water retained its nature, Peter, on falling into the water, recovered the bodily weight which he had previously lost, only to lose it again as soon as he was drawn out. [Col. 0803B]

But because such comings and goings of qualities do not accord at all with reason, we must confess that weight passed over the liquid by God’s power, which, when it withheld itself, allowed Peter to sink according to the nature of the thing—so that you may consider what accords with nature and what occurs by miracle. Likewise the Lord, breaking a few loaves and magnifying their fragments, multiplied them so greatly that such a large people were readily satisfied from so great a multiplication, marvelling that so few loaves had increased enough for many to be satisfied from a few. Therefore he who created all things from nothing, and who formed Adam’s rib (Gen. II, 22), with nothing brought in from outside, whole into a woman, likewise blessed the small number of loaves into a great abundance, not by transforming things distinct from bread into the quality of bread. Otherwise I would not marvel that bread was made from bread; but I would deny that many were satisfied after multiplication from a few loaves. Yet to deny this is contrary to Scripture, while to say that other thing is unheard of.

Christ’s humanity likewise strengthened the paralytic among the other miracles of its power (Matt. IX, 6), so that, through the miracle visibly done by it, the invisible forgiveness of sins might be believed to be done by the same humanity. For when the Jews doubted—indeed, what is worse, disbelieved—that the humanity which alone they understood could remit sins, he set before them an external cure, so that the inward healing of the paralytic might not remain hidden from them. [Col. 0803C] For since it had to be shown that humanity itself forgave sins, it was necessary that it perform marvels before human eyes. If healing of the soul is granted to it, healing of the body will much more readily be granted; for physicians too can heal bodies, but cannot heal souls. [Col. 0803D]

Considering these things, we rightly venerate not God alone but also the human being in Christ. From him, as from a most abundant fountain, there flows out upon us a most abundant flood of every good thing. And while we recognize in these goods the generosity of the human being, we also proclaim in them the beneficence of God; for, as the Apostle testifies, “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (II Cor. V, 19). Therefore God, through the passion of the human being united to himself, [Col. 0804A] redeemed the world, forgives sins, illumines with virtues, shines forth in miracles, and makes blessed with eternal life. God can do these things by his own power; the human being can do the same things, but by God’s gift.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Whether a human being can do whatever God can.

[Note: [Col. 0803D] The Master, III, distinction 14.] Can the human being united to God, by God’s gift, likewise do everything that God can, according to what he himself confesses concerning himself after the resurrection: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII, 18)? Was it not given to the human being, because before it was given he did not have it himself? It was not given to God, because he was never without it. Great in size, conspicuous in beauty, and altogether wonderful in the whole arrangement of its condition, this world is indeed a remarkable work; but because it is insensible and inanimate, the human being is far superior, because made in God’s image. Therefore, although it is glorious that God created the human being, it shines still more gloriously that he re-created one who had perished. For, because he fashioned the human being according to the body from clay and according to the soul from nothing, we venerate him as powerful. But because he deigned to restore both substances of the human being who departed from the Lord to the devil, miserably defiled by that departure, [Col. 0804B] we greatly admire the undeserved mercy of the powerful one.

Wonderful mercy: goodness recalled one who had despised his maker. Wonderful power: it changed into good a human being who had become wholly evil and therefore resistant to correction. Surely this is wonderful—indeed more wonderful than when he created the human being who did not yet exist and therefore could not resist the one working upon him. Hence it is clear that among God’s works redemption especially belongs to the praise of God. Therefore, since the humanity of the Savior has been divinely granted that greatest power, the power of redemption, what other power should be denied it? For, as it itself testifies: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII, 18). [Col. 0804C]

## CHAPTER XXX. Whether the human being has as much knowledge and goodness as God.

[Note: [Col. 0804D] The Master, above.] If God granted his whole power to the human being united to himself, it seems that we must confess that he granted him his whole knowledge as well. Why should he possess complete power but diminished knowledge, when omnipotence requires all knowledge, lest through ignorance it rush headlong into error in some respect? This is especially so because Gospel truth asserts that he was “full of wisdom” (Luke II, 40). For one who is full of wisdom possesses wisdom in such a way that nothing of wisdom is lacking to him; if anything were lacking, he would be empty in part and would lack fullness. And if he received from God such power and such understanding, ought he not to possess an equal goodness as a third alongside those two, lest, when that third moderates, seasons, and adorns the other two, they be displeasing to the degree that, exceeding the third, they refuse to have it as their companion? But so that we may understand that nothing of truth and nothing of goodness is lacking to him, the Gospel does not pass over the fact that he was “full of grace [Col. 0805A] and truth” (John I, 14). Grace, of course, is a good given freely.

Shall we then say that, as powerful, as wise, and as good as God is, so powerful, so wise, and so good is the human being because he is united to [Col. 0806A] God? But if this is so, how is he less than God, according to the statement: “Less than the Father according to his humanity”? Yet however great he is, the human being is nonetheless inferior to God—indeed inferior because he possesses everything by God’s gift.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0805]

## 126 CHAPTER I. The creature is in every respect less than the Creator.

[Col. 0805A]

But if this too is unfitting, namely, that in any respect a creature should be made equal to its Creator, then that human being who redeemed us, because he is a creature, ought not to be of the same power, wisdom, and goodness as his Creator. Though endowed with everything inferior, as one subject to God, he is nevertheless far higher than all created things because God became man. By as much as he surpasses inferior things, by so much—or more—is he surpassed by the one above him. For the Lord testifies: “No one is good except God alone” (Luke XVIII, 19). Therefore, if in the one person who is Christ you wish to distinguish God and human being, even so great a human goodness is not equal when compared with God, according to the saying: “No living being shall be justified in thy sight” (Ps. CXLII, 2). Therefore the humanity assumed by God does not appear righteous if you attend to the divinity. Humanity is indeed good and righteous, but when compared with divinity, [Col. 0805B] because divinity far surpasses it, it grows dim by comparison; yet when compared with all created children of men, it is found to surpass all in beauty. But because divinity is far higher, humanity is certainly small in comparison with it. For, if we believe Jerome [Note: [Col. 0805D] At the end of the treatise *On the Prodigal Son*.]: “Divinity alone is that into which sin does not enter; all other things, since they possess free choice, can sin.” But the Savior’s humanity is included among all other things. Therefore, since it has free choice, can it sin? [Col. 0805C]

It is certain that our Lord and Redeemer, the man Jesus, rejected nothing which human nature ought to possess; but God implanted in humanity by its very nature the ability to sin, so that it might be a human being’s merit to abstain from faults through the strength of free choice. [Note: [Col. 0805D] Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*, ch. 17 and following, where he calls the possibility of sinning—which he teaches there comes from God—a possibility.] Hence some judge that our Lord Jesus, made like his servants and brothers in all things except sin, ought to have been able to sin, so that greater glory might accrue to him for avoiding evils which he could commit than if he refrained from sin simply because he could not sin.

Let no one object concerning divinity, which is certainly so much more glorious because it is removed not only from sin but also from the possibility of sinning. For it is one thing to dispute concerning God the ruler, whose honor consists in the glory of majesty; another concerning the human being who is a servant, whose honor likewise consists in the obedience of subjection. But one obeys commendably who, as Scripture says, “Can transgress and has not transgressed” (Ecclus. XXXI, 10). Thus every servant, however devoted in service, [Col. 0806A] is good in such a way that he can be evil; but one who, established in goodness, can be moved from it is plainly inferior to one immovable in goodness. Therefore Christ the human being is good, but God is incomparably better. [Note: [Col. 0806D] Augustine, Book III *Against Maximinus*, ch. 12.] Yet although very many maintain that the human Christ could not possibly sin, God is far better by nature; the human being is good too, but by grace; and what is by nature is stronger than what is by grace. [Col. 0806B]

## CHAPTER II. As God surpasses the human being in goodness, so he surpasses him in power.

If God surpasses the human being in goodness, he also surpasses him in power. For the divinity itself created the human being whom it assumed and is powerful enough to create very many equal to him. The Father could, if he wished, become incarnate in another human being, and the Holy Spirit in a third. [Note: [Col. 0806D] The Master, III, distinction 1, §3.] This could have been done, but it was unnecessary for it to be done. For whether incarnation pertains to the power, humility, or mercy of the Word, the whole Trinity possesses these three alike; no difficulty held back the Father and the Holy Spirit from incarnation, but only will, lest it be less fitting that one who is not Son in the Trinity should become a son in a human being. [Col. 0806C]

Therefore, though the Son of God became the son of the Virgin Mary, could he not, just as he chose blessed Mary, have chosen another mother? Certainly; for the Almighty acted in this solely by grace and could have become human in any one of the holy virgins, unless it was because he found—or rather made—glorious Mary blessed among women. [Col. 0806D] But why he chose to prepare her, and not another, as a dwelling suitable for himself, he knows; perhaps he will reveal it to us when we shall be like him. He who knew how to become human even without a mother did so because likeness in birth befitted one living as a human being among human beings.

Likewise, just as he was united to the body in the tomb and to the spirit in hell, there would have been no difficulty in being united in any comparable way to human beings, unless the human being whom he assumed—indeed, whom he was preparing for himself by creating him—alone sufficed for the work of our restoration. Hence it is evident that he who was born from God the Father created one born from the Virgin mother, so that you may compare him with the very many whom he could create either from a mother or without a mother. Yet above all it is fitting that the Only-Begotten of the Father should also be the only-begotten of his mother, and that he who alone is God should also alone be human. But although he is one person with God, reason removes from the human being every power to make himself or beings equal to himself; for every work must necessarily be regarded as other than its maker by nature, and far inferior in dignity. Therefore, if you consider in Christ according to themselves the two substances, one creating and the other created, the created substance is manifestly inferior in power, just as in goodness. [Col. 0807A]

## CHAPTER III. The power of God and that of the human being are not the same but different.

[Note: [Col. 0807D] The Master, III, distinction 14.] But perhaps someone will object: If God and the human being, the one assuming and the one assumed, do not have the same power because God can do what the human being cannot, how is the power of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit the same? For whatever is natural can be; because the Father begets, it is possible for the Father to beget; because the Son is begotten, it is possible for the Son to be begotten; because the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, it is possible for the Holy Spirit to proceed. Yet each of these three can do what pertains to himself in such a way that he cannot do what pertains to the others. How, then, is there one and the same power of all, when each can do what the others cannot? [Col. 0807B]

But whoever can do more in acting is certainly more powerful; for to be able in evil is to be unable, since one who is powerful in vice is certainly vicious and powerless. Yet one who can transgress is not thereby either a transgressor or powerful. Whoever is more powerful, however, undoubtedly has a power as different as it is superior. Therefore Christ as God is plainly more powerful than Christ as human, because he can do more in acting; and consequently, because he has a greater power, he has not the same power but a different one. One and the same power—just as one and the same virtue or knowledge—can be greater at one time and lesser at another. But whenever two substances, one of which can or knows more, are considered, they are not usually said to have, much less actually have, the same knowledge or power. Even when they are called the same, each still has its own, equal to the other’s. Likewise, when someone has increased in knowledge or power, he is said to possess knowledge and power other than before; yet the power or knowledge that has increased is not another thing in itself but altered.
