Speech has its own modes and varies; truth remains the same. Let no one be deceived. [Col. 0807C–D]

## CHAPTER IV. The power of the Trinity is one and equal.

[Note: [Col. 0807D] The Master, Book I of the *Sentences*, distinction 7, §§6–7.] But no one of the three persons can do more than another, because whatever one can do in acting, another can do in the same manner. For to beget the Son, or to be begotten from the Father, or finally to proceed from both, is not to act, since authority testifies that the works of the Trinity are undivided. For if begetting and proceeding were acting, the maker would certainly precede his work, and generation would not be eternal. Likewise, to provide is not to act, but to know. What, then, is it in this case for the Son to be begotten except for the Father to be Father; to be begotten by the Father except to be Son; and to proceed from both except to be the Holy Spirit? [Col. 0808A]

But, in order to consider in one of the three the nature of each, to be Father is nothing other than to be God having a Son. Who would dare say that it is anyone’s operation to be Father, or to be God having a Son, especially since every agent is more worthy and better than his work? For what kind of agent could that be who would rightly have to be better than being God having a Son? As evil as injustice is, so evil is being unjust; as good as justice is, so good is being just, just as, in proportion as a human being is good, it is good to be a human being. Finally, whatever each thing is like, such is its being that thing. Therefore, as good and worthy as God having a Son is, so good and worthy is being God having a Son. [Col. 0808B]

For if you say that God is good in a greater sense, but being God is a lesser thing, then, inasmuch as being God is good, God has that much glory. Without doubt, in your view God is more good while possessing less good and glory. But reason proves that God’s glory and blessedness are equal to his goodness and worthiness. Therefore, as good and worthy as God having a Son is, so good and worthy is being God having a Son. But none can be better and worthier than God having a Son; therefore none can be better and worthier than being God having a Son. For what is it to be God having a Son coequal with himself except the glory and majesty of the Father, which it is impious for anyone to surpass? Likewise, to be God having a Father coequal with himself is the glory and majesty of the Son.

Hence, if we intend to distinguish the persons, we seem to find equal glory and coeternal majesty, yet one glory and majesty in one person and another in another. For unless they were one and another, whence would equality arise? Where distinction is absent, equality has no rationale; rather, along with existence, there is identity. [Col. 0808C]

But if we do not wish to distinguish the persons, but to consider the substance of the persons, which is surely one, then one divinity, one glory, and the same majesty are found. This is what he understood who said: [Note: [Col. 0808D] In the Creed.] “But the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one; their glory equal, their majesty coeternal.” For when he attributes one divinity to the three persons, he attends to what is one in them; when he adds equality of glory and coeternity of majesty, he recognizes one person as distinct from another. Without doubt, in mentioning equal glory he has regard to equality of persons, not of glories. For the three equal persons have one glory and majesty among themselves, just as they have one immensity, one omnipotence, one dominion and eternity, and finally one divinity. Just as there are not three gods but one God, not three immense, omnipotent, eternal lords but one, [Col. 0809A] so rightly there are not three divinities but one divinity; not three immensities, omnipotences, dominions, or eternities, but one. In the same way, just as there are not three glorious beings but one, so there are not three glories but one.

Nor is this without reason. Since God is one, every form or property of God, if one may so speak, is also one; just as, since there are three persons, the individual properties of the persons are three, each belonging singly to one.

But since every person, to speak only of the Trinity, is God, and God is likewise every person, the property of God is also the property of the persons; and conversely the property of the persons is necessarily God’s. Why is it that I attribute some properties to divinity and others to the Trinity? Every property common to the three persons I call God’s, because being God is itself common to the three persons; but the individual properties which belong severally to each one you may rightly call properties of the persons. Now these properties—to dwell upon two—I take the Father, who is God, to have, and likewise the Son, who is God, to have; each is certainly a great glory. Yet although these properties are one and another, they are not therefore one glory and another glory, but one alone. Thus both Father and Son are God; and although Father and Son are one and another, they are not one God and another God, but one alone. And just as the Son is equal to the Father, God to God—equal, indeed, because Son; one and the same because God—so the glory of the three persons is equal, but equality is said on account of the persons, whereas in glory there is identity. [Col. 0809B–C]

And indeed, if anyone judges begetting itself to be an operation, and grants that begetting itself is nothing other than being Father, he is refuted in the manner stated above. But if, to defend the claim that begetting is an operation, he denies that begetting is what it is to be Father, while admitting that begetting is the reason why he is Father: how can any operation be of such efficacy that from it the Father, who is certainly God, has being, when it is more fitting that the operation proceed from him rather than he from the operation?

[Col. 0809D] And perhaps someone will grant that the Son—who is indeed principle from principle—has the Father as his cause, since the Son is from the Father. [Note: [Col. 0809D] Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 16; Hilary, Book XII, *On the Trinity*; Victor the African, Book I *Against Arius*; Richard, Book V, *On the Trinity*, ch. 7; and the Greeks generally.] But how can the Father, who is principle without principle, have a cause why he is, since the Father is from no one? If he takes refuge in saying that begetting itself is the cause, not indeed why that person exists, but why he is Father, reply that among us to be a person and to be Father are different, because there is a person who is not, and one who is not, Father; but not there. For there, to be that person is to be Father, and conversely. Therefore begetting and being begotten, and finally proceeding from both, are fittingly called properties of the persons, not their actions. [Col. 0810A]

Therefore, so that there may be no division in the works of the holy Trinity, whatever one person can do in acting, another can do in the same manner. Hence, if you weigh the works of the three persons, one and the same power is found in the three; but if you contemplate the properties of the three persons, each without doubt can do what the others can in no way do. And just as God the Father is not God the Son—because there are two persons, yet not two gods but one God—so perhaps the power to beget God is not the power to be begotten by God, because there are two properties, yet not two powers but one. Accordingly, wherever you turn, the power of the three persons will be one and the same, just as their glory is. [Col. 0810B]

Unless someone says that the three have one power, majesty, and glory by reason of the unity of divinity—which is undoubtedly true—and again that each has his own by reason of the distinction of his own property—which may perhaps be true. But he adds that it follows from this that the three have three powers and as many glories; and that it thus proves them to be three powerful and glorious beings, just as from the one power and glory of divinity, one indeed is powerful and glorious. But the former way is less perplexing because the words are more customary. Yet if you compare the substance of the human being and of the Lord with the substance united to it, the greater and lesser power of the one and the other is certainly made evident.

## CHAPTER V. How all power was given to Christ as man.

[Col. 0810C]

[Note: [Col. 0810D] Master, III, distinction 14.] Nevertheless, all power was given to the Lord Jesus—certainly, as much as ought to be given to a human being. But to which human being? Certainly to that one whom God had assumed. But how is all power given, if a greater power is reserved to the giver? Greater indeed by an amount no one can estimate. Yet Scripture is accustomed to say more and mean less, and conversely to intend more and express less. The less the power, moreover, the lower too, it is understood, are holiness and perhaps wisdom; nevertheless our Lord, according to his humanity, was full of grace and truth (John 1:14). For anything said to be full of another thing is so called not because it comprehends the whole of it, but because it cannot receive more of it. Or, if in any respect the Lord and the servant must have an equal measure in relation to one another, I would sooner grant this of knowledge: that, through God’s far more abundant gift, he possessed more knowledge than holiness and power—after our usual manner, since, though we have little goodness, we nevertheless know much more than we are willing to do in life, or are able to do even when willing. But however much humanity knows, it still appears inferior, because it received the whole as a gift of divinity.

Yet that a creature should know as much as the Creator, or be equal to him in any respect, neither sits well with the mind nor pleases Scripture. Hence in the Prophet humanity says thus to divinity: “Your knowledge has become wonderful beyond me; it has grown strong, and I shall not be able to attain it” (Ps. 138:6). [Note: [Col. 0811D] See Cassiodorus on this passage.] Certainly, the knowledge of divinity, proclaimed through humanity, became wonderful to human beings, to whom so many mysteries were laid open, and it grew strong in human hearts. But when it adds, “and I shall not be able to attain it,” the truth of the human condition is disclosed: the assumed human being cannot be made equal to the divine substance. It is as though he said: “I indeed advance greatly in your knowledge, but I do not reach the point of comprehending it fully.”

## CHAPTER VI. On God’s will, power, and prayer in the Passion.

[Col. 0811B]

[Note: [Col. 0812D] Master, Book III, distinction 17.] But our Lord Jesus, even when he was still about to die, willed whatever ought to be willed and could do whatever he willed; so that not only according to his humanity, but also according to his divinity, his knowledge was greater than his power, and his power likewise greater than his holy operation. For does not each nature—the greater from itself, the lesser from the greater—know whatever it can do, though it cannot do everything that it knows? Certainly, it knows evils, yet cannot do evils. It is likewise established that it can do whatever it does, though it does not do everything it can do. For very many things, considered in themselves, could rightly be done; yet, considered in relation to the whole, it is better that they not be done. Indeed, God prefers some things which, if done, would shine forth, to remain undone, because in the order of things something else is fitting. Certainly God, who could have ordered things otherwise, deliberately chose, on the basis of his own reason, this order which exists: an order in which he so proportioned great things to small, and evils to goods, that the whole, when considered, delights the observer from every side, while a change in even the smallest detail would mar its appearance. For what we do without judgment, God deliberately disposes for the beauty and splendor of his creation. We never cease perversely acting, lest God cease bringing forth his own goods from our evils. Because a human being is evil, he works evil; because God is good, he turns it to good. Nor does he, being almighty, care to prevent evils, because goods arise from evils. Evils are undoubtedly despised by God; but because they produce goods, they are rightly tolerated. Therefore God rightly punishes evils in us because they occur contrary to his prohibition; but because he knows how to make good use of evil deeds, the deliberate severity of God permits evils to occur so that goods may result. But when evils have no place among goods, because God has ordained another course for things, evils are not permitted to occur through provident mercy, lest goods be darkened and defiled by their proximity. Thus divine dispensation ennobles the universe of things by a glorious order, while bringing only goods into actuality, and at the same time arranging all things in its own manner: so that, although you ought to revere goods for their native splendor, you cannot sufficiently marvel at evils because they produce so much good. Indeed, it also contributes to the increase of delight that each thing is suited to such a place and such a time as most accords with the honor of the universe.

Now let us return to the point at which it was said of our Lord that, even while about to die, he willed whatever ought to be willed and could do whatever he willed. For how did he will whatever ought to be willed, if, although he knew the will of the glorious Trinity—that he himself should be crucified for us—he nevertheless knowingly wished, contrary to God’s will, not to be crucified, saying in Mark: “Father, all things are possible for you; remove this cup from me” (Mark 14:36)? Why does he ask that this cup, that is, the measure of his passion, be removed from him, if he desires to suffer according to God’s will? He certainly understood this will of God when he said to Peter, who struck with the sword, in John: “Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me?” (John 18:11). But in saying this he not only knew God’s will, but also indicated that, at God’s command, he would drink the cup. How then, a little earlier, did he will what ought to be willed, if he knowingly desired, contrary to God’s command, not to suffer? How could he do what he willed, if he did not escape the passion he rejected? How, I say, did he later desire what he had earlier rejected, saying, “Father, remove this cup from me” (Luke 22:42), when shortly afterward he said, “Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me?” (ibid.)? Was he subject to bewilderment—was he and was he not? Far be it! For he certainly always desired to die for our salvation, being thus made obedient to the Father unto death. Indeed, if in foolish fashion he at one moment did not wish and at another wished to suffer, he would become not only obedient to the Father but disobedient as well. For bewilderment could have no place in him who “began to be afraid and troubled” (Mark 14:33). Our frailty errs through bewilderment, when fear and distress overtake us unawares. But the Lord Jesus was not bewildered by fear, because fear did not seize him unexpectedly as it does us. He feared by deliberate resolve, so that the support of deliberation might exclude the error which fear, without deliberation, would introduce. He voluntarily summoned the fear and distress which he was to undergo, lest the saints despair in suffering when they are overtaken unawares by distress and fear. Hence, when the Lord himself was in fear and distress, an angel from heaven appeared strengthening him, so that the saints may expect strengthening from heaven in anxiety. For the fact that, according to the Gospel, “he began to be sorrowful and distressed” (Mark 14:34), is certainly understood to mean that sorrow proper to him, originating from his will, was not imposed by an outward affliction; this is clear when it is said that “he began to be sorrowful” (Matt. 26:37). He was also to be strengthened by his own will, because he had no need of an angelic comforter. Therefore the angel strengthened him with words; but in reality he himself strengthened himself, as was necessary.

The voluntary fear and sorrow of which I have spoken, as the very order of the narrative indicates, most certainly gave rise to that prayer, “Father, remove this cup from me.” For such a prayer seems fitting to one who is sorrowful and afraid. Christ therefore shuddered at death, as nature requires; but voluntarily—something beyond nature—out of such horror he uttered such a prayer, that you need not wonder if saints, struck by the horror of death, suddenly break forth even into words prompted by trembling. The saints, repressing fear and sorrow naturally brought on by approaching death, confidently and rationally rejoicing, seek the palm of martyrdom: afraid from the frailty of the flesh, secure through reason’s deliberation. “For the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Mark 14:38). But far be it that the Holy One of saints, unwilling to suffer, should have prayed that the cup be removed from him—he who is the fountain of love, thereby offending against love for God who commanded the passion, and love for the neighbor who needed the passion. For in this prayer, which says, “Father, all things are possible for you; take this cup from me” (ibid.), he was not asking not to suffer. Rather, this is the meaning: “Father, all things are possible for you, and therefore, because this is easy for you, remove this cup from me—if nevertheless it ought to be removed.” That we should understand this meaning in these words, though the words do not say all this explicitly, is indicated by what immediately precedes and follows in the same passage of Mark. For it is prefaced: “He prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him” (ibid.); that is, he prayed that, if it ought to occur, the passion might depart from him—a passion which, though lasting but an hour, was bitter. For in our usage, what can happen is what ought to happen. This he prayed; but in what words? Certainly those immediately added: “Father, all things are possible for you; remove this cup from me; but not what I will, but what you will” (ibid.). What, then, is “Father, all things are possible for you; remove this cup from me,” except: “Because you can do all things, Father, take away the passion”? What is added, “not what I will, but what you will,” except: “if you will it”? Thus the total sense is: “Father, take the passion away from me, if you will.” This is what is read in Luke: “Father, if you will, remove this cup from me.” The same thing appears in Matthew thus: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. 26:39).

But since his humanity knew with fixed and unchangeable certainty that its passion pleased divinity, what was the point of praying that the passion might not come, if it pleased God? For what benefit is there in asking in any way for something which God is known not to will at all? Yet while he uttered the words of one praying, he took care to reveal to us the disposition of his mind, made fearful by horror at the passion. Such was that disposition that, unless he were bound to the passion through obedience to God and compassion for his neighbor, he would prefer, if God delivered him, to escape it as bitter. And through this he rightly became dear to God and pleasing to humanity, since what displeased him in itself pleased him in consideration of those others. Hence, after it has been said, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me”—words in which, beyond doubt, the disposition of mind we have just explained is made manifest—it is immediately added, as though in opposition: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” For the disposition of mind, born of the flesh and rejecting death, and the will of God and of reason, commanding death, seem in some fashion to oppose one another. Both wills—the one of God or reason, the other of the flesh, which in this passage is understood as nothing other than a certain horror and trembling at death—are contained in these few words: “not as I will, but as you will.” For when it says, “I will,” the horror of death is shown; when it adds, “as you will,” God’s will is revealed. The entire expression, “not as I will, but as you will,” makes clear that the Lord Jesus assented not to the horror of death but to the will of divinity. Moreover, the Lord used “will” in the sense of “shrink from” when he said to Peter: “When you grow old, another will gird you and lead you where you do not will” (John 21:18). The horror and fear of the one who was afraid occupied the first part of the prayer: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me”; the devotion and will of the one praying occupied the final part, namely: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” Not as horror and fear urge, but as pleases God. Although the inclination of the flesh, both toward itself and toward the misery of the Synagogue, urges another thing—“let this cup pass from me”—and does so with this qualification, “if it is possible,” nevertheless, though I will what you will, let it occur not as I will, but as you will. Let it occur not because I, a human being, will it—for human willing cannot be followed—but because you, God, will it; for divine willing ought to be followed, than which nothing more holy can be said. Here it is evident that in Christ one will was that of the human being, as though obedient, and another that of divinity, as though commanding.

## CHAPTER VII. Whether Christ feared being consigned to punishments.

[Note: [Col. 0813D] Master, III, distinction 15.] But he who feared death: did he also dread being thrust into the torments of Gehenna? For if he did not fear Gehenna, why did he pour forth this prayer to divinity in the Prophet: “Do not deliver me up together with sinners, and do not destroy me together with those who work iniquity” (Ps. 27:3)? Divinity would deliver up the human being it had assumed together with sinners if, in accordance with the desire of those crucifying him, it gave him over to death without his rising again. It would destroy him together with workers of iniquity if, as the Jews desired, it condemned our Lord. Why then would he pray thus if he feared neither that he would remain in death nor that he would be destroyed after death? Yet how could he fear this, since the truth could not be hidden from one endowed and filled with wisdom, especially in this matter? Hence, in the Prophet, addressing him directly, he says: “You will not abandon my soul in hell, nor will you give your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10). Since this Holy One was not to be corrupted in the tomb, he had said beforehand: “My flesh shall rest in hope” (ibid.); for his flesh rested in the earth in hope of the resurrection. And since his soul, brought back from the lower regions and restored to the body, was to be exalted as the whole human being at God’s right hand, therefore, because he was at his own right hand, his heart rejoiced. How then did he fear destruction, who was not uncertain of salvation? Or if he did not fear destruction, why did he pray that he might not be destroyed? How did the Spirit of the fear of the Lord fill him, concerning whom it is said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10)? And again: “Fear him who can cast both body and soul into Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28). For the beginning of wisdom is to fear him who can cast body and soul into Gehenna. How did that fear fill him? Was it as we often fear that something may happen which, having been taught by reason, we know will not happen at all? Thus at night we tremble at an encounter with a dead person, though we know that nature prevents it. Likewise, when standing on the summit of any place, a certain horror of falling commonly runs through us entirely; reason marvels that those firm in their footing should be shaken by empty fear. But if it is judged superstition that, when struck by such fear, we ask that what we know cannot happen may not happen, how did the prayer of our Lord proceed rationally—even if one grants that he was moved by horror of condemnation—when he earnestly prayed against his own condemnation and yet always remained certain of salvation? Our Lord Jesus, the head of the prophets, foreknew all things that were to happen, whether to himself from God or to his own people from himself; but these would happen only through the merit of obedience and the devotion of prayer. Therefore, by acting well and praying devoutly, he obtained what was not to be had by another way.

Thus he lived innocently and prayed holy prayers, not because he doubted he would obtain his request, but because it was certain that it could not otherwise be obtained. But since, all ambiguity removed, he was wholly certain of the salvation of himself and his own, how did the Spirit of the fear of the Lord fill him—that fear, I say, which, since it is the beginning of wisdom, makes a person fear him who can cast body and soul into Gehenna? Finally, how did he fear being cast into Gehenna by him from whom he knew with complete certainty that he and his own would be saved?

## CHAPTER VIII. How fear precedes love.

[Note: [Col. 0815D] Augustine, Epistle 120, *On the Grace of the New Testament*, and Tractate 9 on the Epistle of John.] This fear, coming first, prepares a place for love. For while we fear the Judge’s punishments, we avoid sins, the cause of those punishments. But while this is done from fear alone, vices are no longer committed outwardly in action, yet are not yet expelled inwardly from the mind. And since we abandon evils in deed but love them in mind, the beginning of wisdom is now present, while wisdom itself is still absent. But it will come when you no longer wish to do evil, even though you could do it without punishment. This heavenly will serves love. Whoever, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, has been anticipated by fear will, while preserving that for the sake of which fear came first, eventually be enriched with love, having become wise through the beginning of wisdom. For truly to love rightly is finally to be wise. Fear is therefore rightly called the beginning of wisdom, from which, as seed sown, love—which is wisdom—springs up. But as love grows, it diminishes fear; and when love is perfected, fear immediately is no more, because, as John testifies, “the one who fears is not perfect in love” (1 John 4:18). Thus you may fear and love at the same time; but while you fear, you cannot be perfect in love. Therefore, servant of God, while you live you fear, and while you live you are not perfect. While you live, you fear God, and therefore you continually say to him: “Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name” (Ps. 85:11). In the future you shall rejoice without fear. Now you rejoice in order that you may fear, because you enjoy the hope of blessedness through love in such a way that you fear, through frailty, to be deprived of the thing hoped for. Hence the Apostle says: “Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12). Love, kindled by desire for heaven, draws one toward righteousness; fear, pierced by horror of hell, draws one back from unrighteousness. Since you are not a good person unless you turn from evil and do good, fear and love rightly accompany one another in you: by the one you overcome the assault of wicked impulses; by the other you embrace the pursuit of good practices. Therefore, so long as you are destined to die, you love and fear without cessation—unless perhaps God at last reveals to you and makes you certain of your salvation, so that you who formerly disciplined your body and reduced it to slavery lest perhaps you should become reprobate, may at last know whom you have believed and be certain, saying with the Apostle: “Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the righteous Judge will render to me” (2 Tim. 4:8).

And because you now fear nothing but only love, love is now perfected in you: “For perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). Therefore, as love grows through its degrees, fear, as has been said, diminishes through corresponding degrees in this life, until love, having advanced after death to its height, no longer suffers fear to remain with it. For love and fear have such a nature that you love not at all the one whom you fear excessively, and fear not at all the one whom you love perfectly. Once you have loved someone even in part, you immediately cease to fear him excessively; certainly, love, when it comes, moderates fear, and as it advances, cuts it away. Therefore, since “the one who fears is not perfect in love” (ibid.), Christ could not possess this fear, because he excelled in perfection of love. Hence, when it is said, “The Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11:3), this must either be referred to his members or understood of another kind of fear. [Note: [Col. 0816D] The Master, Book III, distinction 34, §8; Augustine, as above.] Certainly there is another fear, holy and enduring for ever and ever, which is born in this age and reaches its fulfillment in the age of ages. It may perhaps be reverence, which is owed to superiors by reason of subjection; in heaven, certain of the incorruption of the flesh and secure of the Spirit’s honor, it is not distressed by dread but delights in love. Yet meanwhile it fears offending the one whom it loves, and fears being deprived of him, as though clothed, because of frailty, in the cloak of righteousness, until, unclothed, it rejoices in virtue.

## CHAPTER IX. On faith, hope, and love.

[Note: [Col. 0816D] Master, Book III, distinction 23 and following.] The Apostle shows us that the most excellent way to God consists in these three: faith, hope, and love. With these no one is evil; without them no one is good. Faith and hope are necessary before death, but love endures after death. Love is love of God and neighbor: it embraces God above all things and the neighbor above all else. Every living human being is called a neighbor, because all human beings are neighbors to us, since we are joined to one another by our common natural condition. Therefore, those whom nature associates, love should unite: begun in the state of mortality and perfected in immortality. Faith, according to Scripture, is “the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1). By faith, certainly, we are persuaded of things hidden from us; by faith we are not permitted to doubt concerning the eternal goods that are hoped for; and in this way they somehow subsist in us as certain and firm. We hope to attain by living well the goods which we expect to come by believing. Above all, faith is necessary, without which you understand neither what to hope for nor what to love. But what does it profit to believe, after the manner of the ungodly, that goods or evils will come, without hope of attaining the goods and escaping the evils? Hope is always vain unless, through the merit of love, it is worthy to obtain what it desires. Therefore, because through faith we see things not yet known, as through a mirror in an enigma, while through hope we await things not yet attained: when we see face to face and obtain the thing hoped for, then faith, because it is partial, and hope will undoubtedly be abolished in us—the one yielding to sight, the other to possession. But “love never fails” (1 Cor. 13:8), because, by its nature reaching from mortality to immortality, it does not reject perfection.

## CHAPTER X. Whether Christ possessed hope and love.

[Col. 0817C]

[Note: [Col. 0817D] Master, Book III, distinction 23, and resolved in distinction 27.] Therefore, since no one who is both good and mortal can be without these three, did our Lord Jesus, in whom were all treasures, also possess these three while he lived among human beings? Beyond doubt he hoped to rise after death and, after the ascension, to sit at God’s right hand—a hope not put to shame because he was poured out in love. But it is certain that he loved God, to whom he was obedient unto death; and he also loved those who would believe, for whom he even prayed. Did he not also love the children of perdition, when, seeing the city, he wept over it (Luke 19:41), and when he called even the betrayer “friend”—he in whose mouth no deceit was found (1 Pet. 2:22)? Otherwise, if he loved only those who would love him, what reward would he have, since the Gentiles do the same? For no person is supreme in love unless, together with friends, he embraces enemies also.

But how did the Lord Jesus, judge of the living and the dead, love those most utterly lost, unless, if he could, he freed them from perdition? But if he could not do this, did he not thereby make his desire foolish? How, I say, could he love those whom he knew were to be enveloped in endless misery, if he neither rescued them from it nor even took care to alleviate their evils? Or if he willed either of these things but could do neither, what sort of Lord should I call him? Or what sort of judge, who is able neither to absolve the guilty nor to aid his servants? Would he not necessarily be inglorious through impotence and desolate through a frustrated desire? Finally, how was it fitting for him to love, or to be concerned for the torment, of those whom he knew to be hateful to God and destined, as a sign of hatred, by God’s decree to torments that would never end and never be lessened even in the slightest degree?

But he who came to do the Father’s will ought not knowingly to dissent from that will. Hence he too hates the faithless, intending to render to each according to his works, so that he in no way spares those whom he ought not to spare: “Judgment without mercy, because they did not show mercy” (James 2:13). Therefore, he ought not to love the good together with the lost, because he himself foreknew what pleased God concerning each person. But we love any wicked person because we do not know what judgment God wills concerning him. Hence we withdraw our affection from those we know to be reprobate, whether already dead, as Nero, or still to die, as Antichrist; just as we wish good to all, whether already dead or still to die, whose salvation is uncertain to us. For once uncertainty has been removed—as will certainly occur in the future—and we are certain, then a great chasm will be fixed between us and the wicked, so that we cannot cross over to them in compassion.

But when our Lord called Judas “friend,” he expressed not what Judas was, but what he ought to have been. For the kind conduct of the Master toward his disciple deserved that the disciple should love the Master, and indeed that the Master should love the disciple in return. Hence, in the Gospel, God is represented under a parable as saying of the faithless Jews: “They will reverence my son” (Matt. 21:37). They did not reverence him, but they ought to have done so. And when he wept over the evils about to come upon the city, perhaps it was compassion at the ruin, though just, of the guilty—such as occurs in a judge still dwelling in a place subject to suffering. Or, just as he prayed for his persecutors, who afterward received forgiveness, so he wept because future good persons were among the wicked, whose evils he rightly lamented. [Note: [Col. 0817D] Augustine, Tractate 31 on John, and Sermon 49 in the Appendix to Volume X. See the notes.] Since it is certain that he was supreme in love and certain in hope, did he not also excel in faith, without which, according to the Apostle, it is impossible to please God? (Heb. 11:6.)

## CHAPTER XI. Christ enjoyed vision in place of faith.

[Col. 0818D] [Note: [Col. 0818D] The Master, as above.] But if the Lord Jesus also comprehended heavenly things by faith, since faith, according to the Apostle, is “the evidence of things not seen” (ibid.), then the Lord Jesus too saw through a mirror in an enigma. Thus even he who was the light of the world was hidden from the light of truth. But whoever has a lesser knowledge of God through faith, to be enlarged at last in vision, certainly has, because of that lesser knowledge, a lesser love—one which for the time being grows as knowledge grows, and which will finally be greatest when knowledge is greatest. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than John” (Matt. 11:11), because the least of the angels surpassed John—even though none among human beings was greater than John—while he still dwelt among human beings, since the more clearly that angel knew the highest good, the more closely he loved it; but John would eventually surpass him, when, brought into heaven, he would be reckoned among the greatest. To those considering these matters, it may perhaps seem that while he was mortal the Lord Jesus knew less, and would know much more and more clearly in immortality, if he did not yet comprehend by sight but believed by faith what was to come. But if, as necessarily follows, he thought more obscurely by faith concerning future things, he must have possessed a goodness appropriate to one believing, and would receive after the passion the goodness appropriate to one seeing, so that, by as much as sight differs from faith, he would be holier in sight. For if believing God is so delightful as to make you good, how much more will seeing him make you best, since it is more delightful?

If, then, before death our Lord could think of his God only as though in shadow, and possessed a goodness due to the darkness of such thinking, would not even the least of angels, since it was granted to him to behold God in clear light and since he must possess a goodness corresponding to that light, would not, I say, the least angel surpass the Lord of all in both wisdom and goodness? But he who, as the Prophet testifies, “was made a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:6), solely through the capacity for suffering belonging to our mortality, would now be far too much lower, if angels—not only greater angels, but even lesser ones—were conceded to be more eminent in holiness and more capable of truth. But a sound mind rejects both conclusions as contrary to reason and opposed to authority. Hence it is clear that, since our Lord never possessed faith, without which it is impossible for a merely human and mortal person to please God, he possessed instead vision, by which he most penetratingly beheld divinity as it is, as was fitting, and thereby was especially pleasing. Therefore we differ from Christ, and are as servants to the Lord through faith, because he, as was fitting, saw God as he is; through hope, because he already possessed by seeing God what we chiefly await in hope; and through love, because his love embraced only those whom divine goodness judges are to be saved.

## CHAPTER XII. Christ, though capable of suffering, possessed the first robe.

[Col. 0819D] [Note: [Col. 0819D] Master, Book III, distinction 27.] But if “no one has ever seen God” (John 1:18)—that is, no merely human being in this age—while Christ, although subject to suffering, nevertheless saw God as he is, since eternal life is “to know the Father and Jesus Christ whom he sent to be one God” (John 17:3), then clearly our Lord Jesus possessed eternal life while at the same time enduring the troubles of this life.

But what blessedness was there if he suffered pains along with it? Yet, just as a double affliction, one of body and another of soul, is believed on Scriptural testimony (Jer. 17:18), so a double robe is hoped for: one of the soul and one of the body. The souls of the saints, stripped of their bodies, immediately receive the first robe, namely the vision of God, while awaiting the second, which is the glorification of the body. Therefore the soul of Christ, not weighed down by the burden of flesh through sin or ignorance, was adorned even in suffering flesh by the first robe, as though united to God; the second robe was delayed for a time because of redemption. Thus the Savior’s soul rejoiced without interruption in the vision of God, but from the things done concerning the flesh it sometimes experienced distress. Hence it is evident that the second robe was still lacking, while the first was not yet wholly consummated. The capacity for suffering belonging to our mortality excluded the second; pain inflicted on the soul by evils occurring among human beings diminished the first. Hence it is clear that before death the Savior possessed in the greatest part eternal life, from which blessedness necessarily proceeds, because he beheld divinity face to face; yet he had not received it wholly, while dwelling in the valley of tears and keeping hard paths. Therefore there is no reason to wonder if he who possessed what is chief—indeed, almost the whole—and therefore was called by the name of the whole, in eternal life, was called blessed, though, because he was not yet fully blessed, it is not absurd that he endured adversities.

## CHAPTER XIII. Why he endured adversities, and such a death from those people.

[Note: [Col. 0820D] Master, Book III, distinction 20.] He endured adversities and acted well, both because this was fitting for our redemption and so that he might offer examples to our frailty; finally, he was condemned to a most disgraceful death. This was not because he could not redeem otherwise, but so that by the greatness of the price he might make known to us the greatness of his love and of our sin. He suffered in human nature, because divinity remained untouched. This is Isaac, whom the sacrifice did not touch, setting before the passion a ram.

But if Judaea had recoiled from sending its Lord to crucifixion, would God have become human in vain because he had not redeemed captive humanity by shedding blood? Surely the deficiencies of our mortality assumed by the Mediator could have sufficed to reconcile us to God. For the devil had no right in the human being whom he had deceived by evil deceit; having unjustly invaded another’s servant, he deserved to be stripped of his possession—indeed, to be judged also for that invasion. Thus there was no need for anything to happen through which he might justly lose the right he had none of in humanity—though God permitted humanity to be oppressed, because it had believed the oppressor. Although, in daring to tempt the Lord a third time, he may rightly seem to have been deprived of his usurped power. But, as was said, God could have freed humanity without the Incarnation, and, having become incarnate, without the passion. Yet, because he foreknew all things, he knew that the Jews’ mind was inclined toward his death; he permitted this evil to occur—to their destruction indeed, but to the world’s salvation—so that good might come, patiently enduring evils inflicted for the sake of goods. He was just, in that he still allowed those who willed it to become yet more defiled; merciful, in that from their defilement he wisely cleansed the whole world. Therefore the Redeemer did not come in vain, since he foreknew the utterly ready madness of the faithless for that deed.

Yet if, abhorring and rejecting so great a crime, since no necessity compelled it, they had refused it, God would have become human for this purpose in vain; indeed, he would also have provided redemption by this way in vain. But lest anything be done by him in vain, the mind aware of the future makes provision, deliberately foreseeing and arranging that to which the course of events never fails to conform. Therefore, if the Jews had refused to crucify Christ, it would be more correct to say that this had never previously been foreseen than that it had been foreseen in vain.

## CHAPTER XIV. Christ offered the price not to the devil, but to God.

[Col. 0821B] [Note: [Col. 0821D] The Master, above.] The Redeemer, then, in giving a price for captives so that they might be released to him—to whom did he make this offering? Was it to him who had led them away captive and held them in captivity? For surely the price of redemption must be offered to the one who holds the persons to be redeemed in captivity. But far be that utterly wicked impiety: that God the Savior, lowering himself before the treacherous devil, should have offered his precious death—which would indeed have been idolatry. Nor would the devil have accepted such a gift, by which he knew he would be deprived of his power; indeed, had he known, he would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2:8). Thus, once he learned it, he worked through Pilate’s wife to prevent the Passion. But the frenzy of the Jews, first spurred on by the devil, [Col. 0821C] could not subside even when he himself had now ceased to urge it.

Christ, therefore, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, offered the sacrifice of his Passion to the one whom he obeyed in suffering. For surely one ascribes obedience to the person whom one obeys. God was pleased, by means of this offering as a price, to bring back the captives and humble their accuser. Therefore Christ endured shameful and harsh things, so that you might fear to suffer neither of them for Christ’s sake, for your own benefit, when he did not disdain to suffer for another’s benefit. Hence he said: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John 12:26). Behold the labor. “And where I am, there shall my servant be also” (ibid.). Behold the reward.

Finally, in his Passion the man gave up the Spirit so that he might die, to take it up again on the third day and, restored to life, rise again, having power to lay down his life [Col. 0821D] and to take it up again (John 10:18). The man was able to do both through the soul that willed it. By becoming incarnate, God became man, and remained so until the Passion. Then, however, God—because he began to be dead—ceased for a time to be alive; yet not God, but the man. Likewise, when he ceased to be dead, he became alive again, and a new man, a change having occurred in relation to soul and body, while the divinity was in no way joined differently to either.

## CHAPTER XV. On the efficacy of Christ’s death and Passion

[Note: [Col. 0822D] The Master, Book III, distinction 19.] Christ’s Passion together with his death effected [Col. 0822A] the forgiveness of sins, both of those who came before and of the saints who followed. For in our own time, when the Passion came first and faith in the Passion followed, a righteous person is made righteous not by works but by faith; receiving baptism and good works as signs, preservation, and increase of faith and righteousness; now perfectly holy, as redeemed by the Passion and sanctified by faith. For either, without the other, would be of no benefit.

Hence the Apostle says of Christ: “Whom God put forward as a propitiation through faith in his blood” (Rom. 3:25). Therefore, since the saints of our time are fully cleansed by the merit of the Passion and by faith, the heavenly palace is immediately opened to them. The ancients too were justified by that faith; for “with the heart one believes unto righteousness” (Rom. 10:10). Yet they were to advance in righteousness by the stages of good works [Col. 0822B]—not perhaps because righteousness, which is not born from works, is increased by works. Rather, since righteousness of heart seems to be the cause of work, faith appears to produce righteousness, and righteousness good work. Faith, unless a person prefers to fail, continually increases: both so that one becomes more discerning in knowledge of the good, and more ardent in love of the good. This is the faith at issue—not the faith of demons, but the faith which, illuminated by charity, belongs only to saints. For this, as the Apostle testifies, is “faith working through love” (Gal. 5:6). A degree of righteousness and of works follows a degree of faith, so that, according to the Apostle, righteousness comes from faith, not from works (Rom. 3:20; Eph. 2:9). Thus the increase of faith is followed by an increase of righteousness and works. Hence the Apostle distributes gifts of the Holy Spirit according to the measure of faith [Col. 0822C] (Eph. 4:7).

Unless it is truer to say that, just as faith begins from grace, righteousness begins from faith, and from righteousness come both the beginning and continuation of good works, so faith and righteousness receive increase from a good work through the merit of obedience; God distributing gifts according to the increments of the measure. No one becomes righteous except by faith; yet by works one becomes more righteous.

But if faith without works is dead, how, according to the Apostle, does faith without works justify? It is faith without preceding works; even if these precede, since outside faith they are vain according to the Scriptures, they do not lead to faith. Faith, I say, makes one righteous even before works. Hence one snatched away before the time for working is saved by faith alone [Col. 0822D]; and not without reason, because necessity excludes good work, while the will desires and seeks it. A perfect will to act is reckoned as the act itself. Hence the Apostle maintains that faith works through love (Gal. 5:6). Faith, indeed, dead in itself because idle, always works through love: either, if it has time, it accomplishes many good things through love’s persuasion and power; or, if it lacks time, love is counted as a work. Faith without works, then, is dead: that is, faith empty of charity and necessarily idle. Or faith initially justifies without works; but if it has time to work, faith without works is already dead.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the perfection of the ancients

[Col. 0823A]

[Note: [Col. 0823D] The Master, Book III, distinction 25.] The saints of old, therefore, must have been perfect, as righteous by faith and advancing more and more in righteousness; equal to the righteous of our time, and many of them greater than many of ours—except that the sins without which one does not live were not yet forgiven, and the good things which they performed through the merit of faith were not yet received.

Their sins were not yet forgiven because the old sacrifices could not bring this about: for, according to the Apostle, it was impossible for sins to be remitted by the blood of bulls or of other animals (Heb. 10:4). This was accomplished at his coming by the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world. Therefore they descended to hell, as not yet having obtained pardon for their sins. There they endured no punishments [Col. 0823B]—except those needing purification—through the mercy of the sparing Judge, because they departed from this life in true repentance through God’s mercy.

Therefore they obtained there something better than here: assurance of the future blessedness which they hoped to obtain in heaven through Christ. For it was not permitted to see God among the dead; otherwise there would have been no such need to long for Christ’s coming.

## CHAPTER XVII. On hell, and how the righteous were there

Hell is indeed a place lower and worse than earth, which the power of God so adapted for his own that they were better off there than here, having only this anxiety: that they were excluded from the glory due to the inhabitants of heaven. For their merits did not have such power [Col. 0823C] that those whom evils had drawn down to hell should be lifted up by good deeds to heaven, until Christ should come, whose merits would make up the deficiency of the preceding fathers, so that the merits of the ancients, made acceptable to God through Christ, might at last become worthy of the reward of heaven.

Meanwhile, he neither bestowed good things, since they were not sufficiently worthy of so great a reward; nor forgave evils, because the price had not yet been paid; nor punished those whom faith in the coming one excused. Thus, as though a truce had been declared, he held over the sins of those who preceded, so that they might be forgiven in Christ’s death and that, in this time, the ancients might be illumined with full righteousness. Hence in the time of grace they returned from hell as having had their guilt forgiven, and ascended to heaven as having righteousness completed [Col. 0823D]. Thus the Apostle declares that Christ suffered “for the remission of preceding sins, in God’s forbearance, to show his righteousness at the present time” (Rom. 3:25).

The ancient saints, therefore, receive in the time of grace what they did not previously possess: namely, that perfection which our saints attain in our own time. While they lived, since Christ had not yet come, they were never such as to be worthy of heaven. Ours, since they are already redeemed, are now such as ought to ascend into heaven. Thus ours are made fully righteous, and so are at once honored with heaven. But the ancients were by no means fully justified in their own time, and therefore eternal life was deferred. For “the righteous lives by faith” [Col. 0824A] (Hab. 2:4; Rom. 1:17; Heb. 10:38); that is, one made righteous by faith is made worthy of life by righteousness. For the reward of righteousness, according to Scripture, is eternal life. Therefore, while the reward is withheld, the merit is judged only half-complete.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How the merit of the ancients was fulfilled

[Note: [Col. 0824D] The Master, Book III, distinction 25.] The merit of the ancients was fulfilled when it was assisted by Christ’s merit, so that, together with another, it now sufficed to obtain glory, whereas previously—namely, by itself—it did not suffice. Yet the ancients were righteous in a certain manner; indeed, some of them were very righteous. For how were those not righteous who, possessing faith in Christ, strove in every way to please God? Whenever they offended, they did not delay satisfaction [Col. 0824B]. God showed that their merits pleased him by performing many miracles at their prayer; by honoring them after death in the region of the wretched as exempt from misery; and by sending his Son to rescue them from there and make them blessed in the fellowship of angels.

Such great men, then, were undoubtedly righteous. Yet they were not as reconciled to God, but as sustained under a truce until reconciliation. Why, then, after honoring them so greatly during the truce, what did he confer upon them once reconciled?

## CHAPTER XIX. Why Christ descended into hell

Therefore, Christ’s soul, for a time separated from his body but no less united than before to the divinity, rested bodily in the tomb, while his soul descended into hell [Col. 0824C]. There would have been no need for it to descend unless the souls of the saints, as well as those of the impious, were held there. This seems in some measure required by that conversation narrated between the rich man buried in hell and Father Abraham.

But when the rich man, looking up, saw Lazarus in Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16:26), does this not seem to bear upon the idea that the lost occupy the lowest parts of hell, according to the saying: “A fire is kindled in my wrath, and shall burn unto the lowest hell” (Deut. 32:22)? Will, then, the fire of judgment be kindled here, and, blazing around the wicked, draw them to the lowest hell? And, lest this fire be tormented elsewhere, does not the following statement apply: “It shall devour the earth with her increase, and burn the foundations of the mountains” (ibid.)?

[Col. 0824D] But authority gives this passage a quite different explanation, one much more fitting to the entire sequence of the text. If, however, the lowest regions of hell are assigned to the lost and a separate dwelling was due to the saints, then beyond doubt they claimed for themselves the first—that is, the upper—regions of hell.

## CHAPTER XX. On the dwellings and location of hell, and the bite

That there are different dwellings among the dead Abraham does not deny when he speaks to the rich man: “A great chasm,” he says, “has been fixed between us and you” (Luke 16:26). Certainly, when this parable was spoken by the Lord, both parties were in hell. Yet the parable intends something else: the rich man is the Jewish people [Col. 0825A], Lazarus the gentile people, and Abraham’s bosom the rest of the saints, to which Lazarus is carried by angels through faith. The rich man is buried in hell because of unbelief. Between them a chasm is fixed, which neither the one party can cross by seeing nor the other by compassion. Each side perceives the condition of the other; but one knows it clearly, while the other believes it after doubt has been dispelled. If this is not wholly so now, it is certain that it will be so in the future.

Hell, moreover, is beneath, according to Isaiah, for it is situated in the lower regions of the earth (Isa. 14:9). Hence in the psalm: “You have delivered my soul from the lowest hell” (Ps. 85:13). On this passage the following appears [Note: [Col. 0825D] In the Ordinary Gloss]: “The heavenly dwelling is above; the earthly is hell; from this one goes to the lower hell.” Hence [Col. 0825B] the Lord rescued souls by sending his Son.

All of them? Far from it! For he himself says: “O death, I will be your death; O hell, your bite” (Hos. 13:14). By biting [Note: [Col. 0825] Gregory, Homily 22 on the Gospels; and in the Appendix, vol. X of Augustine, Sermon 52, *On the Diverse Subjects*.] one part is taken and another left. Some seem to have belonged to the part taken who still needed purification for some time: recently dead persons, not to be lost because they had departed from among men in repentance, yet not immediately to be placed in Abraham’s bosom because the fruits of repentance had not yet been accomplished.

Where then were they? Were they not in a place where punishments existed? Certainly in such a place. Were they, then, in the lower regions of hell, which are assigned to the wicked? But of that region the Prophet says to God: “Who shall confess to you in hell?” (Ps. 6:6)—that is, no one. Hence elsewhere: “For hell shall not confess to you” (Isa. 38:18) [Col. 0825C], that is, it shall not praise you. Why? “For those who go down into the pit shall not await your truth” (ibid.), that is, the advent promised by you who are true. Certainly, in our time they do not desire the second coming, nor in the old time did they desire the first, since it would bring them no advantage.

Yet kings David and Hezekiah, new men living in the time of the Old Testament, were by no means ignorant that both good and evil persons passed after death to hell. What, then, does it mean when they say that there is no confession in hell, when surely it was not fitting for the saints in hell to cease from confession—being already better than before and more secure of blessedness, as having been freed from the burden of the flesh?

## CHAPTER XXI. Where those to be purified were formerly

[Col. 0825D]

Although the whole extent of that dwelling is denoted by the name “hell,” its upper part is nevertheless often called Abraham’s bosom, and its lower part hell. Where, then, were those to be purified in ancient times? Were they in the penal region with the lost? But “who shall confess to you in hell?” (Ps. 6:6); whereas those being purified must praise God. Shall we then say that “For hell shall not confess to you” should be understood of those who remain there and will not depart, not of guests who will pass through it? For travelers derive their name not from the region through which they pass, but inhabitants from their residence. And although it can rightly be understood of all who were to be saved from those held in hell [Col. 0826A], the saying applies more closely to those being purified: “Those who go down into the pit shall not await your truth” (Isa. 38:18), for they needed God’s mercy, not truth.

But if they were held for a time in the region of the lost in order to be purified by torments, did they not, once purification was complete, ascend to Abraham’s bosom—that is, the upper region, where there was rest? So in our time those deceased in whom something remains to be burned away are tested after death by purgatorial punishments; once the testing is completed, they are raised to Christ. Indeed, expiation reconciles those whom guilt had separated from him.

For if those in whom present contrition and tribulation fully burn away their offenses, though they continually sin while among us, nevertheless deserve fellowship with the heavenly beings immediately upon leaving us, how much more should the saints in whom satisfaction is not yet complete, after death no longer sinning because the body no longer weighs down the soul, and therefore suffering contrition far more effectively than here, just as they are afflicted far more grievously than here, and thus corrected by severe chastisement, be granted heaven? For purgatorial fire, intermediate between our punishments and those of hell, surpasses ours by as much as it is surpassed by theirs. This the Prophet understood when he said: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury, nor chastise me in your wrath” (Ps. 6:2). By “fury” he means Gehenna, since, Scripture teaching it, every punishment is milder than Gehenna [Col. 0826C]; and he calls purgatorial fire, as less than fury, “wrath.”

The Prophet entreated against both, but was silent about punishment among men, as though saying: “I dread future evils; I do not fear present ones.” For he himself, desiring present afflictions in order to escape future ones, said: “Give us help in tribulation, for the salvation of man is vain” (Ps. 59:13).

## CHAPTER XXII. Where those to be purified are now

Therefore whoever in this age, which is assigned to repentance and full of miseries, disciplines himself too little, is deservedly corrected afterwards, when it is rather the time of recompense, by a severe and untimely discipline.

But where does this discipline occur? In heaven? In [Col. 0826D] hell? Yet neither heaven seems suited to tribulation nor Tartarus to correction, especially in our time. For if only the good are assigned to heaven, are not only the evil assigned to hell? And if heaven excludes every evil, how can hell receive any good? For just as God appointed heaven for the perfected alone, so likewise he appears to assign Gehenna only to the impious, so that this may be the prison of the guilty and that the kingdom of friends.

Where, then, are the repentant after death? In purgatorial places. Where are these? I do not yet know. How long are they there? Until satisfaction is completed. From there they go where they would immediately ascend if they had completed repentance in the flesh. Thus they remain below in order to complete repentance.

## CHAPTER XXIII. When the purified are granted heaven

[Col. 0827A]

Therefore, those whom repentance still to be performed holds back are restored to heaven once it has been completed. Unless someone places them in places of rest outside heaven, saying that repentance completed in the flesh, as in its proper place, has sufficient power to make one worthy of the vision of God, whereas repentance performed after leaving the body, as in an alien place, does not merit this before the resurrection. But are those who are for so long excluded from the sight of God and from Christ’s presence not, meanwhile, insufficiently reconciled to God because satisfaction is incomplete?

Perhaps in the time of the apostles some died who, had they survived only a few more days, would have completed their repentance. Is it fitting, then, that the punishment of a few days be prolonged until the resurrection? [Col. 0827B] Two people die: one has lived a long and intensely devout life, but little remains for expiation; the other has lived a less devout and shorter life, but has nothing left to be burned away. How, then, is the one who is less good immediately granted the vision of God, while one much better is held back from glory for so long? Therefore expiation is understood to correspond to the measure of guilt: greater or less, long or short. Yet it is always more severe, because satisfaction did not precede during its proper time in life.

Hence, when purification has been completed, the repentant—both ours, from purgatorial places outside hell to heaven, and the ancients, from purgatorial places in hell to Abraham’s bosom for refreshment—seem continually to ascend. But the great chasm fixed between the good [Col. 0827C] and the evil seems to have prohibited this passage (Luke 16:26), unless perhaps this chasm is understood as being between the inhabitants of heaven—which is not absurd—and those in hell.

If, however, the same chasm was also among the dead, then undoubtedly, according to Abraham’s words, there was no passage between good and evil. Did those to be purified, then, remain outside Abraham’s bosom from Adam until Christ in order to be tormented forever? But if they were almost purified in life, why such lengthy torments? Or did they at last rest there? But how could they rest without torment in a place assigned to torments? How were they in rest? Therefore, once purified, they seem to pass to the upper regions, if the truth of the matter permitted such passage. Otherwise, it seems necessary to say that even those to be corrected lived in the upper region.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How those to be purified were in hell

[Col. 0827D]

But just as rest is incompatible with the lower regions, so affliction is at odds with the upper regions; and in Scripture one does not easily find a third place among the dead assigned to those being purified. What then? Just as good and evil persons are mingled in one place on earth but separated in merit, were they also dwelling together in hell, differing in punishment and rest? This indeed pleases many.

Nor is it surprising that souls are tormented there by bodily fire and cold, since they endured the same in the body. Conversely, it is not surprising if, just as gold refined in the furnace suffers no loss, and just as saints rise in the fire of judgment and ascend through fire without burning, so pure souls were amid the fires of Gehenna without anxiety [Col. 0828A]. For it seems absurd to assign two dwellings to hell, one for rest and another for torments, and nevertheless to assert either rest amid torments or labor among those at rest.

Yet if those being purified had to be alongside those at rest, how could this be stated more suitably than by saying that punishment and rest are together, while division of places is set aside? Whatever in Scripture seems to require this division can be referred back to rest and punishment, which, although they do not differ in place, are separated by nature. Wherever salvation, confession, or other things due to saints after death are denied to hell, “hell” is understood as referring to the damned, or the statement is referred to our own time.

## CHAPTER XXV. What happened to those being purified when Christ descended

[Col. 0828B]

Christ, therefore, displaying his charity—he who could do all things without descending—descended from heaven to earth and likewise from earth to the dead, and brought the saints back from there. What did he do with those not yet purified? Did he leave them there for a time? But how could he, who had come for his own, abandon a part of them? How could the prison, suitable only for those still liable to punishment, now suit persons already reconciled? For by Christ’s death even those being purified were reconciled. One who is righteous through faith in Christ cannot rightly be called unreconciled after Christ’s death; the unrighteous person is an enemy, but one made righteous has been made reconciled to God. To the extent that purification still remains necessary [Col. 0828C], reconciliation is lacking. One will be fully reconciled; but before Christ there was no reconciliation. For the Apostle says of Christ: “Through whom we have now received reconciliation” (Rom. 5:11), as though saying, “Never before.”

For he is the true Solomon, mediator between God and human beings, joining both peoples into himself as one cornerstone, and reconciling both to God. But when did this reconciliation begin? With righteousness; and righteousness comes through Christ’s blood. Hence the Apostle says: “Now justified in his blood” (ibid.), as though saying, “Never before”; for according to the Apostle it availed “for the redemption of the transgressions which were under the former testament” (Heb. 9:15).

## CHAPTER XXVI. That Christ led the persons being purified away from the dead

[Col. 0828D]

Therefore, those whom he found among the dead still needing purification Christ led away from the dead, lest the enemies, maliciously claiming a half-complete power, should glory in those left behind. But where did he lead them? To purgatorial punishment? This could reasonably have happened; it was more reasonable [Note: [Col. 0827] See Augustine, Book XII, *On Genesis*, ch. 33; Epistle 99; and Book XVII, *The City of God*, ch. 2.] that they should be released.

For he who chose to visit them and deemed them worthy of his presence, being merciful, does not seem to have wished to grieve them by separating them from himself. As, while mortal among mortals, he did not separate himself from his own, so, once his soul had taken souls to itself, it does not seem fitting, I think, that he should separate them from himself. He who paid on the cross for the thief’s thefts, intending immediately to receive him into rest [Col. 0829A]—why would he not unite his own captives to the thief by the same price, and bring both with himself into the kingdom of blessedness?

But how far did he descend who descended to the dead? Truly, he who did not disdain to become incarnate in order to heal the sickness of the world joined good persons to himself in such a way that the physician did not avoid the sick. Therefore, since he judged it necessary to come to those who were at rest, perhaps he did not refuse to visit those who first needed cleansing. But when he liberated his own from there, he undoubtedly left the upper dwelling—if such a dwelling exists—empty.

But once emptied, for what necessary purpose was it? Was it so that torments might now spread through it? But if they are there now, it is more credible that they were there before. Was it so that persons being purified might descend there in the time of grace? But [Col. 0829B] since that place is free of punishments, how is it suited to those being chastised? Even if someone posits punishments there, how can hell be due to the righteous after redemption? Nor can those who have already been converted to righteousness be denied to be righteous. Since, then, after Christ’s coming the region of hell is not suitable for penitents, purgatorial fire is mentioned in their case while hell is passed over.

Thus, just as the gate of heaven, formerly closed to the human race through sin, is opened to the saints, sooner or later, when Christ ascends, so, when he returned from the dead, he shut after himself the entrance of that place, lest from that time onward any of his own should pass there. Hence in the Psalm: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O everlasting gates” (Ps. 23:7). That is, gates which formerly did not exist are raised at the Ascension, through which one enters eternal goods. What does this mean? The power to enter heaven is given.

But the rulers of hell, unwillingly, raised their gates—those through which people went to hell—at the Lord’s descent; that is, they lost the power by which they drew all people down to the dead [Col. 0830B]. Yet hell remains open to the impious, just as heaven remains closed to them.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0829]

## CHAPTER I. When and in what manner Christ rose

[Col. 0829B]

Christ’s soul, therefore, having come out from the dead with the whole multitude of holy souls, entered his body on the third day and granted it resurrection, just as, in leaving it, it had disfigured it by death [Col. 0829C]. Thus, by the soul’s return, the man became immortal and incapable of suffering: “Having risen from the dead, Christ dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9).

Moreover, he was glorified to such a degree that he shone like the sun, just as, before the Passion, he appeared at the Transfiguration with a radiant countenance through his omnipotence, showing beforehand to his disciples the form of the resurrection. But after the resurrection he concealed it; for if the appearance disturbed them, how much more would the reality itself have done so? Therefore, presenting his former appearance to the disciples, he accommodated himself to their weakness, so that they might recognize him and endure his company during forty days.

But how did one who was immortal assume the appearance of mortality? How, after death, did he show himself as if a mortal man? Did the splendor of majesty and the disfigurement of our mortality exist together? Or, while he displayed one, did he lack the other? Yet neither condition seems to be deprived of its own property; nor does either condition seem able to possess the nature of both, since they are so very different.

What then? Were the apostles’ eyes deceived, so that they thought they saw in Christ an appearance which was not there at all? Far be such illusion from faith! The appearance shown was presented to their eyes without deception. Thus, when the eyes of the two disciples were first prevented from recognizing him because they saw an appearance unfamiliar to them, they afterward recognized him in the breaking of bread (Luke 24:35), because at last a familiar appearance presented itself [Col. 0830B].

Christ, therefore, showed himself in one appearance and then another, yet did not abandon his own. He possessed his own appearance within himself and concealed it; he appeared in another appearance, yet did not possess it within himself. Thus, when he distributed himself to his followers, he set before their eyes the appearance of bread and gave their palate the taste of bread. He who changed bread into himself by his power preserved, by that same power, bread’s appearance and taste outside the bread, so that he might give himself to his own in the appearance and taste of bread—since they would shrink from receiving him in his own appearance. Thus he does not give himself in the appearance that is his own and which he possesses in himself; rather, he gives himself in an appearance not his own, which he never possesses in himself [Col. 0830C].

## CHAPTER II. What should be thought concerning those brought out from the dead

Since Christ rose, what should be thought concerning those whom he brought back with himself from the dead? It is indeed established that many bodies of saints rose [Col. 0830D] and appeared to many (Matt. 27:52). Did they, as many suppose, receive the twofold garment already, so that they might rise with the Lord as suitable witnesses to his resurrection?

But to whom would so great a restoration of witnesses have been more fitting than to David and the other prophets, and first to the patriarchs, of whom the Apostle says: “All these, approved by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promise, God having provided something better for us, lest they should be perfected without us” (Heb. 11:39). They have not, therefore, yet received the restoration of soul and body, so that the joy of all may be greater when they are perfected together.

Hence it is more credible that Christ alone rose in glory, while the others, once the testimony of their office had been performed, were again dissolved into earth without the pain of death [Col. 0831A], awaiting a little while until the number of their brethren should be fulfilled (Rev. 6:11).

## CHAPTER III. How and when Christ ascended, and when he will descend

During forty days, appearing frequently to his disciples (Acts 1:3) in order to establish them in faith, Christ remained under heaven, attended by a great multitude of saints, all of whom he brought with himself into heaven at the Ascension. For “when he ascended on high, he led captivity captive” (Eph. 4:8). “The tribes, the tribes of the Lord,” ascended there (Ps. 67:19). For before Christ it was permitted to be rescued from the dead but not to enter heaven.

Christ, however, is understood neither to have ascended before the completion of the forty days nor to descend after their completion except on the day of judgment [Col. 0831B]. Both are truly possible; but neither needs to occur, because neither reason requires it and authority disagrees: he “ascended into heaven, from where he shall come to judge the living and the dead” [Note: [Col. 0831D] In the Creed.]

Therefore, inventing nothing of our own, let us maintain that he who ascended will descend when he comes to judge, lest, if we assert that he ascends and descends again and again, transgressing the bounds of authority, we introduce not merely two but many comings. Thus he never ascended before the fortieth day, nor will he descend before the judgment. For if he had ascended and descended earlier, since he was to ascend on the fortieth day in the apostles’ sight, this descent [Col. 0831C], besides the first and last, would constitute a third coming; indeed, as the number of ascents increased, so would the number of comings.

I do not deny that after the Lord’s Ascension our Lord Jesus has sometimes appeared to saints; but it seems to me that he appeared either in heaven in person or on earth through angelic ministry. Thus saints themselves, or rather angels acting in their stead—especially those whom divine providence had assigned to guard the saints while they dwelt in the flesh—are sometimes recorded to have appeared to human beings. For it is fitting that they, as the very name “angels” suggests, be employed in such matters. The saints themselves remain with Christ, no less in place than in contemplation.

Although another account may be given, this one ought to be believed more readily. Yet although Christ and his saints have their own dwellings in heaven, nothing prevents them, if it should be necessary, from appearing below, as they will appear at the judgment and, as people say, have appeared rather often.

## CHAPTER IV. When and how Christ sent the Holy Spirit

Christ, therefore, seated at the right hand of God—that is, reigning in equality with the Father, or resting after labor in the higher goods—sent his own and the Father’s Spirit to perfect his disciples, whom he had previously infused with that Spirit in order to begin their formation. I do not think that for the Spirit, who is everywhere, to be “sent” to his own means anything other than that he is shown, though invisible, in a bodily appearance [Col. 0832A]. Yet it was not he himself, but the figure signifying him, that was seen.

Therefore the Father and the Son—or even, perhaps, the Holy Spirit, as some may think—sent the Holy Spirit when they displayed to observers something that signified the Spirit. The whole Trinity, or rather the Father and the Son, sent the third person; the third alone was sent, because no appearance of either of the others was visible. For that appearance offered itself to be seen only on account of the Spirit, just as only the Father’s voice was heard: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3:17), and just as only the Son was seen as a human being.
