Yet the Holy Spirit did not unite himself to that appearance in one person, as the Son did to humanity. Nor without reason did he alone appear, since he came to bestow sevenfold gifts. For his coming means making people good by generously bestowing gifts; his indwelling means increasing the gifts bestowed by preserving them. Therefore he rightly came to the disciples: those who had previously scarcely attained the beginning of goodness, hiding themselves as fearful persons, he now made truly good, as people trampling earthly things underfoot and pursuing eternal things alone, having been given the knowledge necessary for both.

But the Spirit, who appeared over the Lord in the form of a dove (John 1:32), showed himself to the disciples in fiery tongues (Acts 2:3).

But was that fire, and that dove—was each thing that appeared truly what it seemed? Yet we often read that angels appeared to saints in human form; but [Col. 0832C] is that which is seen when appearing as a human being truly, in reality, a human being? If it is, is it not as though one—indeed, truly one—of the sons of Adam? If therefore it is truly and solely a human being, that is, what is seen, how is the vision of angels said to be in human form? Does an angel clothed with a human being use him for certain functions, and for that reason is an angel rightly declared to appear in a human being? But I dare not, as a transgressor of authority, invent this from myself; nor do I understand how a human being may suddenly appear or vanish before human beings, especially while they are not yet immortal. And even if someone should maintain that this is so, it is nevertheless wholly unsuitable that an angel, immortal, should take to himself a mortal human being for earthly business, since that work could be performed [Col. 0832D] either by a human being himself or by an angel in bodily form.

But if craftsmen, devising various works, shape God's creatures in different ways; if magicians, imitating the signs performed through Moses, misused God's elements and by incantations produced signs themselves and certain similar secret effects, whether by an actual effect or merely by deception of the eyes, why should we not retain the tradition of the Fathers and believe that angels, being illustrious in knowledge and excellent in power, fashion for themselves from the air bodies suited to what they have to do, so that, having obtained a harmony with their subtle and agile nature, they are hindered by nothing whenever and wherever they wish suddenly either to appear or to vanish—to appear as soon as a visible form has been made, to vanish as soon as that same form has been dissolved? Unless perhaps it is truer that they may hide themselves at will, [Col. 0833A] even while in a body. Thus after the resurrection the Lord, although remaining in the flesh, nevertheless at one time showed himself to be seen, at another withdrew himself after having been seen. Yet this was a form, not a phantom—indeed, one truly presented to human sight—because it is taken from the air for human use and, when its use is finished, is laid down into the air. Thus the new king formed from pre-existing matter a new star, the herald of his birth; and when the time of its embassy was completed, he likewise resolved it into its own matter.

## Chapter V. That neither a real dove nor real tongues appeared

Therefore that which appeared above the Lord was not a dove, but the form of a dove, according to the statement: “The Holy Spirit was seen in the form of a dove.” As for the fiery tongues, [Col. 0833B] just as you know that they were not tongues in the ordinary sense, so perhaps you do not believe that they were fire, but rather the appearance of fire shaped in the manner of a tongue. For if that had truly been a dove and this a tongue, some animal—or rather, a human being—would have lost this one, while the parents of that one would have laid an egg and warmed it into a chick. [Note: [Col. 0833D] Augustine, *On the Christian Contest*, ch. 22.]

It nevertheless could have been a real bird, formed from the air by heavenly power, just as that herald of the Lord’s birth was perhaps a real star—except that, descending by a heavenly flight, it would not have cared to settle above the Lord. Indeed, for this reason it does not seem to have been a real bird: because neither is the one seen in an appearance a real human being; nor do I think the argument from resemblance should be despised. Therefore, just as that apparition is judged to be a rational animal and is not one, but is its likeness, so also this [Col. 0833C] irrational animal is seen, yet we do not suppose it to be a bird, although we see it as a bird. Heavenly power moves both forms—indeed, also the third form, that of the fiery tongues; both, and likewise the third, are taken from the air and return to the air when their task is completed.

But even if someone should posit this dove as real and that fire as real, how will the one who appears be a real human being? [Note: [Col. 0834D] The Master, II, distinction 8.] For it must not be believed either that human beings descended from Adam—indeed, human beings of many forms—are born who, by their own will or angelic manner, sometimes present themselves to be seen and sometimes withdraw themselves from human gaze; nor is it lawful to regard as human beings, though they look human, those produced from material other than Adam. For no human being of our race—being weighed down by mortal corporeality [Col. 0833D]—can have such power as to be seen unexpectedly and suddenly withdrawn from sight; nor can one who is such belong to our race, since, having no intercourse among human beings, he is found nowhere. Where he was born and reared, among whom he lived—there is no one who knows; indeed, there is no such person for you to know.

Likewise, then, the likeness of a dove and of a fiery tongue appears rather to be the thing under discussion, not the thing itself. For if it is a tongue, how is it fiery? But if fiery, how is it a tongue? Certainly, if it were fire—fire known to us, I mean—it would burn up each of those disciples on whom it rested, unless divine power, to which nothing is difficult, restrained its nature. Therefore, if this so pleased God, I do not deny that a real [Col. 0834A] dove flashed forth from the air and real fire shone above the apostles—yet fire not to burn but to give light, like that which, in the bush, certainly did not consume it. Such was the Spirit’s appearance at baptism, because he requires dove-like persons. But he manifested himself to the disciples in fiery tongues because, while he instructed those whom he was teaching through the diversity of languages on account of the diversity of nations, he kindled them with fire, so that, when the rust of vices had been consumed, they might both shine with knowledge and burn with charity.

## Chapter VI. To whom they preached first, and to whom afterwards, and why

Therefore those whom their life commended and their teaching enlightened rightly preached to others; yet first to the Jews, so that those among them predestined to life might be converted, while the rest would have no excuse for their unbelief. At last, however, when they would not endure the teaching, because they judged themselves unworthy of the Gospel (Acts 13:46), the apostles turned to the Gentiles, so that through them in the meantime the fullness of the Gentiles might enter into faith; and when that was completed, through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch all Israel might finally be saved (Rom. 11:25). For God appointed the apostles for converting the Gentiles; but he reserved Elijah and Enoch—translated into paradise, as they say, needing no refreshment of food, and known likewise not to use renewed clothing; happy beings, more blessed than we and less heavenly—for this purpose: that he might at last convert the Jews fully.

The aim of preaching is the religion of Christian conduct. The origin of religion is faith, since according to [Col. 0834C] the Apostle it is itself the foundation of the spiritual building (2 Tim. 2:19). It is not yet idle, for otherwise, as in demons, it is dead; rather, it is enlivened by charity. For this faith, when it loves God and neighbor, is surely active, since it is that which, as the Apostle testifies, works through love (Rom. 10:17). The Apostle also teaches that faith is born from hearing.

But how is it from hearing, if, according to the testimony of the same Apostle, it is not from ourselves but is God’s gift, not from works? (Eph. 2:8). Surely “flesh and blood has not revealed it,” but “my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16:17); that is, it is made manifest not by human nature but by the grace of God. What he had impressed upon the ancients, if not upon all, at least upon many, by inspiration, he declares to us by preaching. The preacher indeed pours forth words, but God pours into the mind the sense of the words—indeed, faith itself. For an understanding sharpened by practice in the Scriptures often discerns the meaning from the words; but it receives faith in that meaning only through grace.

## Chapter VII. Why things necessary to all are apportioned among individuals; and concerning faith and salvation

Therefore, although God could grant faith without speech, he does so rarely in the time of grace—yet sometimes, as in Paul—so that a teacher is needed. Thus things necessary to all are apportioned among individuals, so that [Col. 0835A] each person, finding in another what is lacking to himself, may be bound to that other by love. Therefore hearers should love their preachers, through whose office, God working inwardly, they are illuminated with faith—not because of the merits of their parents, whether past or future. For it is God’s gift, not from works, “so that no one may boast” (Eph. 2:8). The Apostle would not say this if God considered any work whatsoever of anyone whatsoever, so as to repay faith to someone as though from merit. For faith would then no longer be purely and properly God’s gift; rather, it would become a kind of recompense for merit, and a human being would have something of which to boast.

Therefore, so that no one may boast, faith is grace alone: it is not born from works, but gives birth to works. For works, however magnificent, are nothing before faith: “There is none who does good; there is not even one” (Ps. 13:2), that is, no one does good until he comes to Christ; for he is the one, that is, the only one, in whom good is done. Hence in Job: “Who can make clean one conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you alone?” (Job 14:4). Where the Apostle recalls the promises made to Sarah and Rebekah, this exposition is found: [Note: [Col. 0835D] In the Ordinary Gloss.] “The promise made to Sarah shows that no one is saved because of descent; likewise that made to Rebekah shows that no one is chosen because of any merit of his own or of his parents, but by grace alone” (Rom. 9:9). But if no one is either chosen or saved by parental merits, neither is anyone granted faith because of parental merits. For faith, occupying a middle place between election and salvation, is born from the former and gives birth to the latter.

Therefore, if parental merits produced faith in children, they would also confer salvation; for it is established that from faith comes righteousness, and from righteousness salvation. But if anyone has faith or righteousness through the merits of his parents or his own, then surely, according to the Apostle, “the one justified by works has glory, but not before God” (Rom. 4:2)—that is, he would attribute eternal life to himself or to his parents, not to God. Therefore no one obtains faith or righteousness through anyone’s merits, either his own or another’s; rather, “God has mercy on whom he wills” (Rom. 9:18).

## Chapter VIII. Why parents pray for their children, and the Church for those to be converted

What then is the meaning of parents praying for their children—indeed, of the whole Church praying for those to be converted, in imitation of the Lord Jesus praying for those who would believe? What, I say, does it pray for on behalf of those who do not yet believe or who are criminal, if it obtains neither faith for the former nor righteousness for the latter? Yet the supplication of the saints obtains faith for children—indeed, for others and for unbelievers—and righteousness for the wicked. Hence Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, falling at Jesus’ feet, asks for his only daughter (Mark 5:22), and the father of the dead girl is told: “Do not fear; only believe, and she shall be saved” (Luke 8:50).

[Note: [Col. 0835] Gratian, *Decree*, d. 1, *On Penance*, ch. 87, illustrates this passage with a not dissimilar commentary.]

The ruler of the synagogue is the choir of teachers; Jairus had as his only daughter the Jewish people, for whom he owed spiritual care. “Jairus” means “enlightening” or “enlightened”: enlightened by God in order that he might enlighten his only daughter by teaching and example. This man falls at Jesus’ feet when he sets him before himself [Col. 0836A] and apprehends by faith the one whom he awaits as Redeemer, to be preferred above all even according to his humanity. Endowed with this faith, he asks the supreme physician to heal one sick with sins and dead through unbelief; and the father is inspired to obtain by the supplication of paternal faith that his daughter may finally—after the calling of the Gentiles—be raised from the death of the soul.

Thus the centurion asks the Lord for his dying servant; and the Lord, having praised the centurion’s faith, answers him: “As you have believed, let it be done to you” (Matt. 8:5). This centurion, attended by a hundred soldiers, is the Christian people, who, while longing solely for eternal things, is fortified by progress in virtues. Distinguished by the prerogative of faith, he obtains through prayer the salvation of the soul for the lesser multitude [Col. 0836B] which serves God in fear and which would surely die unless charity came to its aid for righteousness. Hence Mary and Martha, living sisters, pray for their dead brother Lazarus (John 11:5): that is, the contemplative and active man procure from the Lord salvation for a neighbor lying numb in wickedness.

A person also benefits himself by praying: both the unbeliever unto faith and the one needing correction unto amendment. Hence Augustine, long uncertain what he should hold in faith, desiring the true way, finally deserved to find it. So one who lives in vices is delivered through prayer; God hears him “in the hidden place of the storm” (Ps. 80:8). For the storm is the slavery of sin, which rules in the hidden place of the heart; there, when Peter began to sink, he took him up as he cried out (Matt. 14:30), hastening him on amid multiplied weaknesses. If, then, a slave of sin is freed now by his own supplication, now by another’s, what does it mean that no one is aided toward faith or righteousness by his own merits or another’s?

But a supplication offered to God for someone’s amendment is sometimes accepted, whenever, being asked, he changes an evil person into a good one. Merits, however, when directed toward something else and not toward God’s giving someone faith or moral uprightness, never, so it seems to me, bring it about that God grants this. And it is certain that merits of themselves cannot in any way confer it. Thus faith, and righteousness together with salvation, are never obtained from merits of this sort, but are sometimes obtained through supplications. Yet each of the three [Col. 0836D] is received by grace. For grace itself draws a person to faith and leads one entangled in wickedness toward amendment. And in doing both, it is sometimes stirred toward this by its own native sweetness, sometimes prompted by supplications—which grace itself also produces. For no one’s supplications can merit before God that he should be obliged as a debt to bestow his grace either upon those about to believe or upon those to be cleansed from vice; for that would no longer be the giving of grace, but the payment of a debt.

Certainly, supplications do not demand anything as though owed to them. Rather, by certain inducements they implore mercy. Hence the whole pursuit of Christian religion ought to be called supplication rather than [Col. 0837A] merit, because “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come” (Rom. 8:18). Human merits therefore do not bind God under the strictness of judgment; rather, devout supplication moves the gracious judge to grant, by his free benefit, faith to the idolater, righteousness to the crooked person, and salvation to the person persevering in a good purpose. [Note: [Col. 0837D] These points are qualified in the following chapter.] And just as I know most certainly concerning the good things that you do, so I especially hold concerning the good that another does, that neither tends toward obtaining salvation for you, nor benefits you in possessing salvation. But if your works can in no way benefit your salvation, how could they benefit your righteousness or faith?

## Chapter IX. The source of children’s prosperity and adversity; and concerning faith and salvation

[Col. 0837B] But children are often, by divine dispensation, either tormented in miserable ways to the grief of their parents, or perhaps gloriously exalted to their delight. Does God crown or punish parental merits in their children? By no means. Rather, the severity and mercy of the steward console or afflict parents through their children.

Nevertheless, although both faith and salvation derive their origin from grace, the illumination of faith and correction of life are properly ascribed to grace; salvation, however, to the merits of a good life. For although a person’s faith and discipline sometimes arise through supplication, and although salvation often comes through grace alone in the case of little children, in adults the merit of a good life is required in order that they may be saved. Hence he “will render to each according to his works” (2 Tim. 4:14). Yet a person’s faith more often arises without his supplication, and very often an evil life is suddenly changed. Whatever a person does well while he is evil is reduced, as it were, to nothing, so that, if faith or a good life follows, it may be attributed not to merit but to grace. But whatever a good person does well, because it remains effective and is worthy of reward, is rightly called such that salvation may plainly be understood to be given on its account by merit.

Conversion, therefore, is rightly attributed to grace, because any good which precedes it is so lifeless that it ought not to be called the merit of conversion. Salvation, however, is rightly imputed to merits, because truly good things are brought forth from the treasure of a good person.

Yet, if we investigate the matter more deeply, not only faith but salvation itself is from grace; for if you weigh the price of faith and of salvation, whatever is done to obtain faith will be reckoned as virtually nothing, and whatever is done for salvation will be found utterly insufficient, so that the grace of the Almighty alone is worthy of such generosity. Therefore one who wishes to state the truth of the matter with precision should say: “Faith is from grace”; he should by no means say: “Faith is from merits.” For it is “God’s gift, not from works” (Eph. 2:8); reward is owed by merit from righteousness. But nothing of such a kind is done from which faith would be owed as a right. Therefore faith is not from merits: for it is God’s gift, not from works.

For although faith and righteousness often arise through human supplications, since God inspired even the will to pray—whence comes: “both to will and to accomplish [Col. 0838A] according to [his] good will” (Phil. 2:6)—faith and righteousness are by no means from our works, but from God. They would be from human works if they arose from those works themselves without grace; and then everyone justified by works would have glory, but not before God (Rom. 4:2). Therefore no one obtains faith, righteousness, or blessedness by merits either his own or another’s; rather, “God has mercy on whom he wills” (Rom. 9:18). Thus these three, according to one, admittedly less proper, manner of speaking, proceed from merits; and according to another, more proper, manner of speaking, do not proceed from merits.

## Chapter X. How no one is saved unless baptized

[Col. 0838B] No one who understands the Apostle or the Gospel is unaware that righteousness proceeds from faith and blessedness from righteousness. How then can it be said: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:4)? Since every righteous person is necessarily righteous from faith, and since one comes to baptism through faith, it is plain that before the washing the person was righteous; for he could not possess faith, which works through love, and be unrighteous. Since, moreover, after the age of discretion baptism derives its efficacy from faith—for without faith the washing would avail nothing—why should faith not also, before the washing with water, accomplish what belongs to its own power, namely righteousness, according to the Scriptures?

Hence the Lord declares Simon Barjona blessed (Matt. 16:17), but because of faith. For the same reason it is said to the thief: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). In both cases, embracing faith and not binding the thief to the sacrament of regeneration, he grants blessedness to the one and rest to the other. For the thief might have been baptized in prison or before, but this hardly seems to have been the case: both because the law of baptism had not yet been so widely published, and especially because he seems to have blasphemed with the other thief and then, amazed by what occurred on the cross, to have believed. [Note: [Col. 0838D] See Augustine, *Questions on Leviticus*, bk. [as printed], question 84.]

Therefore, just as Abraham, one of the holy Fathers, was first justified by faith and afterward received the sacrament of circumcision as a sign of the inward reality already received, so his children are first justified by faith, from faith, and afterward receive the sacrament of washing as a sign of the inward reality already received. [Col. 0838D] And just as he would not remain in righteousness already received if, neglecting God’s command, he refused circumcision, so these, righteous beforehand, would immediately become unrighteous if, contrary to obedience, they refused baptism. Thus forgiveness of sin is immediately granted to a contrite and humble heart, yet confession must afterward be made. But if someone with a contrite heart is overtaken by death before confession, contrition intervenes so that he may not perish. Therefore, one already righteous by faith must be baptized in faith, lest he perish from the righteous way; for if he despises the washing, he has already fallen away from the faith which works through love. But if he is prevented from the washing of regeneration by death overtaking him, because he is not outside the foundation, he cannot perish.

## Chapter XI. On the efficacy of faith mingled with charity

[Col. 0839A]

Faith mingled with charity, because it loves God and neighbor and remembers that it has offended both, necessarily mourns its sins as much as it loves, and avoids what is to be mourned as much as it loves; and thereby, through loving, obtains remission of sins, because “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8), according to the saying: “Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47). Faith, therefore, which works through love alone produces a good person, because it empties him of vices and adorns him with righteousness. For “he who does not love his brother remains in death” (1 John 4:20); how much more one who does not love God! For so long as anyone is such, because he remains in death, he does not deserve to revive—that is, to obtain forgiveness [Col. 0839B] of sin.

The Lord indicates that faith has such great power when he says to the woman: “Your faith has made you whole” (Luke 7:50). Again: “According to your faith, let it be done to you” (Matt. 9:29), which he said to the two blind men. And elsewhere: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done to you as you wish” (Matt. 15:28). It is not idle faith, which belongs to demons, that merits this, but loving faith, which belongs to the saints. Faith therefore fulfills the will and obtains salvation: for “with the heart one believes unto righteousness” (Rom. 10:10), and therefore unto salvation.

Thus faith saves even one whom baptism does not wash. Hence: “While Peter was speaking, the Spirit fell upon all who heard the word; and the believers of the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished, because the grace of the Holy Spirit had been poured out upon the Gentiles. For they heard them speaking in tongues and magnifying [Col. 0839C] God. Then Peter answered: ‘Can anyone forbid water, that these who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have should not be baptized?’ And he ordered them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ” (Acts 10:40). Therefore before baptism they received the Holy Spirit so that they magnified God, and thereby, already believing, they were righteous: “Wisdom shall not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. 1:4). “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding” (ibid.).

For just as the Holy Spirit is poured into some before baptism, so he is also poured in after baptism. Hence Peter and John prayed for the Samaritans that they might receive the Holy Spirit: “for he had not yet come upon any [Col. 0839D] of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit” (Acts 8:15).

## Chapter XII. As in martyrdom, so sometimes in faith: salvation without baptism

Therefore it is not baptism but the Holy Spirit, received through faith, that is accompanied by righteousness and salvation; salvation also comes through martyrdom where baptism has not preceded.

But you will say: martyrs are baptized in their own blood; what if they are burned by fire, or otherwise die violently without blood? Are they also baptized in fire and violence?

[Col. 0840A] The Lord handed down—and the Church customarily celebrates—baptism by water and Spirit, by a threefold immersion and invocation of the Trinity. How, then, do you assert baptism where there is neither water, immersion, nor invocation of the Trinity? If you cannot deny that certain people are glorified, yet do not dare say that they were baptized in water, you judge that they suffered martyrdom in place of baptism. Why, then, should you wonder if faith too takes the place of baptism, when it is not the will but necessity that excludes a person from the washing? For if martyrdom, which draws its strength from faith, fulfills the place of baptism, why not faith also?

Since, then, some enter the kingdom of heaven through martyrdom and perhaps some through faith, though not born again of water, when we hear, “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 0840B] (John 3:4), let us understand that “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). Did not the Lord Jesus, whose words these are, enter heaven without being born again of water? For he was washed not with his own baptism but with John’s baptism. His own baptism was performed for remission of sins and therefore had no relevance to him; John’s did not regenerate, and therefore suited him who, being free from sin, had no need to be born again.

That decree, then, excludes the ancients; it does not include the Lord Jesus, nor does it concern those distinguished in faith whom necessity separates from the sacrament. Thus, when it is said, “Everyone who asks receives” (Luke 11:10), those who ask neither piously nor perseveringly are excepted. Likewise, when it is said, “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16:16), it is understood only of those [Col. 0840C] who believe in such a way that they love, love in such a way that they persevere; and you will find many statements of this sort.

## Chapter XIII. Why baptism was instituted

But if righteousness is obtained through faith, and thereby remission of sins, what need is there to be washed with water? How is the washing itself received for remission of sins? The washing is needed because the Lord instituted it thus. It had to be instituted thus in order that pride might be broken, when a rational human being humbles himself before an insensible element. Hence the Jordan, which bears the figure of baptism, signifies a descent from pride.

Moreover, just as after contrition—when Lazarus is raised by the Lord himself—confession is necessary, when by the ministry of servants he is loosed from the bands of death, that is, from the body of sin; so after faith, by which death is driven away, baptism follows in order that life may be strengthened. [Note: [Col. 0839D] See the Master, IV, distinctions 17 and 18.] And just as charity at any time covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet. 4:8), so that they are no longer for condemnation; while contrition, which charity produces, and satisfaction, which contrition brings about, cover those same sins so that they are no longer exacted for punishment; so faith remits sins to a person so that he is not condemned, and baptism so that he is not punished. [Note: [Col. 0840D] Consult the notes.] What faith does, baptism shows; faith destroys sins, baptism teaches that they have been destroyed, whence it is called a sacrament.

## Chapter XIV. What baptism and the Holy Spirit accomplish; and how baptism is instituted

[Col. 0841A]

[Note: [Col. 0841D] The Master, IV, distinction 3, penultimate section.]

Baptism, then, is rightly received for remission of sins, because it frees from the penalty of sin, signifies that absolution, and strengthens the life born from faith. Therefore, one who receives the Holy Spirit through faith possesses him more fully in regeneration, and will possess that same Spirit especially in confirmation. For this is to receive the Spirit, as it were, by certain steps: to advance through increases in the good life. Hence the disciples received the Spirit more than once. For the Spirit gives life through faith, strengthens against vices in baptism, and makes fit for doing good in confirmation. Faith raises up in the manner of penitence; baptism heals in the manner of confession; [Col. 0841B] confirmation strengthens in the manner of satisfaction. First, alive after death; second, sound after sickness; third, robust after health.

Therefore those born from bloods—that is, from parents—unto guilt are born again in water through the Spirit from God unto life. They are born old, that is, children of wrath; they are born again new, that is, children of God. Yet regeneration, begun in faith, is advanced by water and is to be completed by confirmation.

But if remission of sins comes through the advent of the Holy Spirit, and regeneration itself is finally obtained even before the washing, why is it specially ascribed to the washing? Because whenever these things occur, baptism signifies that they occur; and therefore they are rightly judged to belong to baptism.

Baptism, however, receives no other liquid or [Col. 0841C] element besides water, on the authority of the Lord, who says, “Unless one is born again of water,” etc. (John 3:4). Nor does water suffice without invocation of the Trinity. Hence the Lord commanded all nations to be baptized “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 19:28). To baptize is to perform the washing by a threefold immersion, as by invocation of the Trinity. We know from the authority of Scripture that only washing with invocation of the Trinity is to be called baptism; but we accept the threefold immersion from use and reason. We deny that there is true baptism if the invocation of the Trinity is lacking; nor should we deny it even if the threefold immersion is lacking. Invocation of the Trinity must be present; it is not fitting that the threefold immersion be absent. Without what is necessary, baptism [Col. 0841D] does not exist; without what is fitting, it can exist, though negligence involves guilt.

## Chapter XV. The perversity of washer and washed does not invalidate baptism

[Note: [Col. 0841D] The Master, IV, distinction 5.]

Therefore only the person who baptizes or is baptized according to this tradition is regarded as either baptizer or baptized. Neither the perversity of the one washing nor of the one washed prevents it from being called baptism. The washed person is in no way harmed by another’s perversity, but is in some way harmed by his own—not so as not to be baptized, but so as not to be cleansed by being baptized.

What then? If one baptizes in jest and mockery and another is baptized, shall we call such a person baptized? [Col. 0842A] But if the one baptizes in jest while the other is baptized seriously, what does the latter lose thereby? Does he not do what pertains to him, receiving the washing according to ecclesiastical custom, even though the former sins in washing mockingly, provided he does not depart from the rule of baptizing? Thus, if a priest mocks someone confessing sins, he nevertheless rightly assists the mocked person; the guilty person, confessing discerningly and making satisfaction diligently, is nonetheless absolved from guilt.

Conversely, if someone baptizes in every respect according to Catholic practice, but the candidate approaches with a mocking intention, does not mockery, like pretense, remove the reality of the sacrament, while being unable to remove the sacrament itself? Thus the person seems baptized but not cleansed. Likewise, although someone contracted marriage as though in play, the objection of play will nonetheless not dissolve the marriage entered into. Thus, if the whole action of baptism on both sides is performed mockingly, provided only the order of the sacrament is duly observed, why should things which separately do no injury to the sacrament extinguish it when combined? For it is one thing to see the sacrament itself; another to consider what is done by the sacrament. The sacrament presents itself to the eyes; the reality itself is traced by the mind. The sacrament takes place in the body, but the power of the sacrament in the mind. Finally, the body is washed with water, but the soul is cleansed by the Spirit.

## Chapter XVI. On the nature and signification of the washing

[Note: [Col. 0842D] The Master, IV, distinctions 4 and 6, §5.]

Therefore the sacrament of baptism, which is wholly performed outwardly and possesses its complete nature in itself, seems to suffer absolutely no impairment from whatever mockery or any error may be present in the mind [Col. 0842C] of either the baptizer or the recipient of baptism. But the cleansing for which the sacrament is received, since it too takes place inwardly, is rightly harmed by inward error—not another’s error, but one’s own. Thus, if error occurs outwardly in the action of the sacrament, then the sacrament itself is endangered. But if danger to the sacrament does no harm to the soul when sincere faith entirely heals that soul, neither does corruption of the soul corrupt the sacrament when the sacrament itself is completed by its own absolution.

What then if bathers baptize themselves? If someone bathing completes the sacrament of baptism in the case of infants, I dare deny them neither the sacrament nor the fruit of the sacrament. What I concede to [Col. 0842D] infants, then, how can I deny to adults? And although I rightly deprive the latter, because they receive irreverently, of the benefit of the mystery received, nevertheless, because they receive it in whatever manner, by what reasoning could you exclude them from baptism? Therefore deny that persons have been baptized only when that which is baptism’s own and proper feature has been omitted.

The Holy Spirit descended upon Christ after he was baptized in the form of a dove (John 1:32), not because he had ever been absent from Christ, who was conceived by the Spirit, but in order that the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the baptized might be signified—whereby fire customarily accompanies baptism in its signification. Certainly, he willed to be baptized not for himself but for us, and to have the Holy Spirit descend and the heavens [Col. 0843A] opened above him. The outward washing signifies the inward, so that, as water washes the flesh, the Holy Spirit may be understood to cleanse the mind. Fire is usually joined to the washing so that complete purification may be understood. By these elements, surely, stains are customarily washed away; yet water without fire sometimes signifies the cleansing of spiritual stains. And because it belongs to water alone to wash, Scripture rightly employs water for people to be washed spiritually; it does not believe that other liquids—indeed, even the other elements—are sufficient for this business.

Water, while it washes, signifies the cleansing Holy Spirit; the body, while it is washed, signifies the cleansing of the soul. Water therefore signifies the Spirit, and washing signifies remission of sins. Certainly, the Holy Spirit acts in the manner of water, and [Col. 0843B] remission of sins occurs in the manner of washing, as Paul teaches: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6:3).

“We were baptized into the death of Christ,” that is, into the likeness of his death; or “through his death we were baptized,” that is, purified. For just as Christ died to mortal life, so Christ’s death causes us through baptism to die to our former manner of life: “For we were buried with him through baptism into death”—that is, through baptism dead to vices. In baptism too we are buried in the likeness of Christ, so that we may not only cease from our former manner of life as dead to it, but, as though buried and [Col. 0843C] removed farther away, may no longer even think of desiring it. But what benefit is there in lacking the old life unless we advance in the new: “So that, as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life”?

## Chapter XVII. On the correspondence of baptism and the Passion
But that we may examine the apostolic comparison more closely, let us see what in baptism is to be compared with death, what with burial, and finally what with resurrection. When the person to be baptized is immersed in water, Christ’s death is signified; when, plunged beneath the water, he lies hidden, Christ’s burial is represented; when he is raised from the waters, Christ’s resurrection is declared. The immersion is repeated a third time [Col. 0843D], not only in reverence for the Trinity, but also because of Christ’s three-day burial. In the Lord’s burial, day follows night for the third time; likewise in baptism, a threefold emergence accompanies the threefold immersion. Before Christ’s coming, a day was counted together with the night that followed it; in the Lord’s Passion the order of counting is changed, and the day is reckoned with the preceding night. The first reckoning ends from day into night, because the first Adam, falling from the day of creation, fell into the night of transgression. The second reckoning ends from night into day, because the second Adam, having driven away the darkness of the old transgression, illuminated the world with the light of his newness. Three days in the Lord’s burial follow three nights [Col. 0844A], because we who had been darkened in thought, speech, and deed, being corrected in those same three respects, now shine through the Lord’s death. The Lord has mercy on these, saying: “I have compassion on the crowd, because they have remained with me three days” (Matt. 15:32). The same meaning is presented to us in the threefold immersion and the emergence that follows in an equal number. For in the Christian order you must first die and be buried threefold to sin; afterward, rising in the corresponding threefold manner, you must advance in religious conduct. Thus water rightly signifies the Holy Spirit, because he puts sin to death and buries it. Immersion rightly signifies the remission of sins, because to be immersed is to die and be buried to sin. And what is it to die or be buried to sin, except that not only guilt is expiated, but also [Col. 0844B] the disturbances of an evil habit are calmed? Regeneration is likewise rightly declared through emergence, because, once sin is buried, nothing remains except that we rise to righteousness: that, having now died to sin, we may again live to righteousness, and thus, having been born to oldness, may be reborn to newness. In baptism the Spirit precedes after the manner of water. Remission follows in the likeness of immersion, imitating emergence. Regeneration holds the final place. The cause, indeed, comes first: first cleansing the dwelling of evil, finally reshaping it with good.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Why baptism is deferred until a feast.

[Note: [Col. 0843D] Lombard, IV, distinction 6, §6.]

But unless some necessity presses, baptism is customarily deferred until a festival, especially the Paschal solemnity [Col. 0844C], so that those meanwhile catechized—that is, instructed in the faith—may at length renounce the devil in church and be solemnly baptized by the priest. They are catechized first because without faith they either would not wish to be baptized or, even if they wished it, ought not to be baptized, since it would profit them nothing. Therefore, since adults are catechized necessarily, infants too are catechized by the rationale of custom, though not from necessity. For just as adults, if premature death prevents baptism, are saved by faith deriving from catechization alone, so infants, although catechumens, are certainly damned without baptism. Nevertheless, the rule of catechizing must stand even for infants, not only because it came first in adults, but much more because it is a certain preparation for driving out the devil [Col. 0844D], like a supplication on behalf of those to be baptized—effective indeed, but not sufficient for salvation. For in order that someone may be saved, necessary faith is required for adults, or the sacrament of faith, which is baptism, for infants. Without either, no one can be saved.

## CHAPTER XIX. Why sponsors are necessary for a child in baptism.

[Note: [Col. 0844D] Lombard, IV, distinction 6, §7.]

Therefore, because a child does not know how to believe, he requires the sacrament of believing. At this age sponsors are needed, through whose service the child is presented to the priest, and on whose testimony the child is baptized, lest a question about the baptism later arise. For whenever baptism is uncertain, if the person is a child, since without the washing [Col. 0845A] he would perish, he must in every case be baptized. For the saints [Note: [Col. 0845D] Pope Leo, letter to Rusticus of Narbonne; likewise to Leo, bishop of Ravenna, epistle 37; and the Council of Carthage, *On Consecration*, distinction 4.] do not judge as repeated that which is not known to have been performed. But if he is an adult and has faith, there is no danger if he has not been baptized, while either his household falsely says that he was reborn, or keeps the truth silent; for, like everyone else, he believes himself to have been baptized in childhood. It also belongs to sponsors both to answer on behalf of children and to stand as sureties of the covenant entered, through the response, between God and human beings. They must therefore take care that what they have pledged for little ones they labor to bring about in them as adults. For why would either the priest ask, or the sponsor answer for the child, that he believes and renounces the devil, unless the priest requires and the sponsor promises that, in due time, the child will believe and will avoid paths forbidden by faith? For in vain would the former [Col. 0845B] address speech to a child who understands nothing, and the latter, who is not yet capable of faith, answer as a believer.

## CHAPTER XX. How the speech is addressed to sponsors, and concerning sponsors.

[Note: [Col. 0845D] Lombard, III, distinction 6, §7.]

The speech, therefore, is addressed to the sponsors. But because it is done for the child, it is pronounced as though it were said to the child. Thus, when such a question is heard from the presbyter—“Child, do you believe in God? Do you renounce the devil?”—this is certainly understood: “Sponsors, do you guarantee on behalf of the child that, if life accompanies him, he will renounce the devil?” Augustine, however, explains the sponsors’ answer thus: “I believe,” that is, “I receive the sacrament of believing.” Therefore, when you hear the question, “Child, do you believe in God?” and the answer, “I believe,” you understand this: “Sponsors, through whose office the child is presented [Col. 0845C] to God, will he receive the sacrament of believing?” “He will receive it.”

Thus catechization is altogether necessary for adults, though it may be absent in infants; likewise adults can dispense with the service of sponsors, which infants require. Infancy needs sponsors, as many suppose, so that those lacking their own faith may be saved by another’s faith. Another’s faith does indeed benefit the child; for without it he would not be admitted to the sacrament. Yet even if no sponsor were present—indeed, if no one at all in the world believed—provided that even a most pagan person, observing the Church’s rite, baptized him, he would nevertheless be saved by the power of the sacrament and would find mercy with Christ, who alone baptizes. For one must not look to the quality, whatever it may be, of the person who performs the sacrament with voice and hand [Col. 0845D], since it is neither performed better by a good person nor worse by an evil one. Rather, let us look to him alone whose prerogative it is to confer power upon his own sacrament. Therefore, when a hypocrite or an unclean person approaches, he receives from a human being that sacrament which belongs to humanity; but he does not receive from God that purification which belongs to God. The adult anticipates this purification by faith before the sacrament; the infant, because he is without faith, receives it in the sacrament. [Note: [Col. 0846D] Consult the notes on chapter 13 of this part.] Thus in children the reality follows its sacrament; in adults it precedes it.

## CHAPTER XXI. Why baptism is deferred, and concerning the baptism of older persons.

[Col. 0846A]

The sacrament is customarily deferred for catechumens until the solemnity, that it may be received before the people, for honor to God and as an example to one’s neighbor. Nor is waiting dangerous for those who, through catechization, are righteous by faith. But for infants, upon whom hell nevertheless hangs even though they are catechumens, delay is exceedingly dangerous, since the infirmity that attends infancy compels uncertainty about their lives. Hence, among prudent people it is customary that they be baptized as soon as possible. Those who have become older are first made catechumens and, in due time, are regenerated by renouncing the devil. [Note: [Col. 0846D] Lombard, IV, distinction 6, final section.] Priests ask for this reason: that they themselves may answer by renouncing, [Col. 0846B] not merely in speech but much more in will; for this is the point of “the inquiry of a good conscience toward God” (1 Pet. 3:22). For if they prefer to persist either as fornicators, drunkards, or in any other shameful conduct, they are rejected as unworthy of the washing. Even if they are admitted to the washing, they are admitted without benefit; for pardon is rightly denied to those remaining in guilt whom impenitence hardens while they are bound by vice. Therefore they receive the sacrament but do not receive the sacrament’s fruit. They will receive it when impenitence departs with the softening of their mind, yet never by a repeated sacrament. For just as Christ’s death, burial, and resurrection are one, so too the sacrament taken in their likeness ought to be one.

## CHAPTER XXII. On baptism and confirmation not being repeated.

[Col. 0846C]

[Note: [Col. 0846D] Lombard, IV, distinction 7, final section.]

For Christ’s death is one, together with his burial, and likewise his resurrection is one; what it signifies in us through baptism it also accomplishes, whenever love of evil does not resist its operation. Therefore, since through the one death of Christ and the efficacy of the one baptism pardon is available to you whenever repentance is not absent, so Christ’s death is never repeated, nor is baptism, the likeness of that death, ever to be repeated. For “one faith, one baptism” is proclaimed (Eph. 4:5). Therefore, since baptism is never repeated (and it is now due only to presbyters, unless someone of whatever rank is called in an emergency [Col. 0846D], lest one depart this life without the sacrament—the Church now entrusts this sacrament to presbyters, whereas in the time of the apostles it was performed without distinction); since, I say, baptism is never repeated, neither should confirmation be repeated, because once received it likewise suffices. It is rightly called confirmation because, beyond remitting sins as well, it also confirms one in good and, as it were, equips an athlete in advance against the spiritual forces of wickedness. And [“better, but”] the sacrament of baptism is more necessary, without which there is no salvation for infants. Hence, when necessity [Col. 0847A] compels, the power to baptize is denied to no one. But the sacrament of confirmation is not so necessary for infants; indeed, they can lack it without danger to salvation. Yet they too ought to be confirmed, especially for the work to come. Thus, when little children were brought to the Lord so that he might touch them, he laid his hands upon them (Mark 10:13). He himself also, issuing a decree concerning the confirmation of little children, said: “Allow the little children to come to me.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. When and why little children should be confirmed.

Therefore little children ought to be confirmed while they are little. Hence it is judged blameworthy negligence whenever this sacrament is postponed through indolence for those who may meanwhile die.

[Col. 0847B] But why is it necessary for hands to be imposed promptly either upon those baptized in our own time or upon those circumcised in the past, when the sacrament already received suffices for attaining salvation until the years of discretion? For from that point confirmation is needed for the labor of struggle. Yet through the laying on of the Lord’s hands, or of his minister’s hands, it is credible that the glory of eternal life first granted is afterward increased. And confirmation is more dignified than baptism, insofar as becoming an athlete is more dignified than being cured of illness. For baptism heals; confirmation invigorates the one healed. Hence confirmation is now granted to the bishop alone, just as it was granted in the time of the apostles. Therefore confirmation given through the bishop’s laying on of hands, like the eucharist consecrated through the presbyter’s consecration, is regarded as more precious in proportion as it is [Col. 0847C] more difficult to obtain. For among the sacraments, that which we attain with some difficulty is more dignified and less necessary; the less difficulty anything involves, the more necessity it undoubtedly possesses. It was a provident institution that what is indispensable for salvation should be available everywhere, whereas that by which salvation is made more certain or more abundant should be rarer in proportion as it is more remote from the attainment of salvation.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On sacraments to be repeated, and the power of baptism.

But although it is not permitted to repeat certain sacraments, because once received they suffice for every time, there are others which, unless received more frequently, do not suffice for one who continues to live. Hence we repeat confession and [Col. 0847D] the eucharist often. For whenever we sin, we need confession for the sake of amendment; and because the weakness of the flesh does not cease to weaken the spirit, we do not cease to strengthen both by the help of the eucharist. Rightly received, it remits sin and imparts strength; wrongly received, on the contrary, it increases guilt and weakens the guilty person.

Let us therefore embrace the authority of the Christian law in its decrees that something be done either once or repeatedly. Roof, wall, and foundation: these three give strength to a house; what is painted and what is carved provide ornament. The former make the building; the latter make it visible. So too, in the spiritual temple, the power of the structure consists in the threefold immersion and invocation of the Trinity; the rest furnish the sacrament’s adornment. [Col. 0848A] For the power of the Trinity is present in the sacrament of baptism, as was signified to us when Christ was baptized. For when he was baptized: “The heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him. And behold, a voice from heaven saying: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’” (Matt. 3:16). The Son is baptized; the Spirit of God descends like a dove upon the baptized one; the Father’s voice makes known the baptized one’s dignity.

## CHAPTER XXV. What those baptized are like, and why the heavens are opened to them.

Behold, the blessed Trinity is present in baptism, making those washed dove-like and thereby beloved sons of God—now pleasing in proportion as previously they were displeasing—and to such persons the heavens are rightly opened. And although these things are first present in adults through faith [Col. 0848B], nevertheless, when they obediently humble themselves to the washing, these same things are infused more abundantly. But I refer these things to us through baptism because in Christ they neither originated nor grew through baptism. Rather, in the baptism of the Head it is signified what is due to the members from baptism.

But what is meant by the heavens being opened to the baptized? Is it that they are now worthy of the vision of God, so that however foul they may formerly have been, once cleansed by baptism, if they should happen to die immediately, they are without delay carried into heaven? But this cannot in the least be understood of those who, having received the washing before the Lord’s Passion, were overtaken by death; for heaven, previously closed, was opened by the Lord’s Ascension. Therefore they descended to the lower regions. What kind of baptism, then, is this which, ineffective in its power [Col. 0848C], does not open heaven? Or how does it surpass circumcision, when one who is baptized descends to the lower regions just as one who is circumcised does?

But the periods of circumcision and baptism are distinct. For the time of circumcision, like that of the Law, lasted until the Lord’s Passion, because, as the Passion approached, he said: “I will no longer drink of this fruit of the vine” (Matt. 23:33). The vine is the Jewish people, because “the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:7); its fruit is the fruit of observances. Thus the sense is: “Of this fruit I will drink nothing, but from now on”—that is, from the time of the Passion—“I reject it altogether.” “But I shall drink from now on,” that is, I shall pleasantly receive fruit—not this fruit, but a new one [Col. 0848D], and not alone but with you. Therefore from the time the Lord suffered no one submits himself to Jewish institutions, which the Apostle counts all as dung (Phil. 3:8), because those who handle them become foul and stinking. Only let every new person reverently take hold of those things signified through figures as new things, rejecting no decree of the new law. The time of circumcision, therefore, because it is set before the old person, ends in the Lord’s death; but baptism, as appointed for the new person, obtains its proper place once circumcision has ended. Hence, after the resurrection, the Lord said to the disciples: “Go therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (Matt. 28:19).

## CHAPTER XXVI. Whence baptism and catechization derive their authority.

[Col. 0849A]

By establishing after the resurrection a universal decree concerning baptism, the Lord assigns baptism its proper place after the resurrection. But because catechization prepares a place for baptism, he first says, “Teach all nations” (*ibid.*). Then, in a few words, he comprehends what the work of baptism is, saying: “Baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son,” and so forth. But because good life is required after the sacraments, he adds at the third stage: “Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you.”

But lest so great a task produce distrust in the weak, he supports the uncertainty of those who waver by the certainty of promises, saying: “Behold, I am with you [Col. 0849B] until the consummation of the age” (*ibid.*). But so that the authority of baptism, privately enjoined after the resurrection, might become clear, the sacrament of washing is publicly celebrated in the Lord’s presence before the resurrection. It is therefore no wonder if something was lacking from baptism received before its proper time. Yet even then it prevailed over circumcision, because, whereas circumcision did not suffice unless baptism followed after the resurrection, baptism received beforehand was not afterward to be repeated; for it had no less force after the resurrection because it had been received before the resurrection. Likewise baptism, as intended for adults, is received as a remedy also against actual sins—but only past sins—perhaps to the extent that after the washing they require no penalty by the grace of expiation. [Col. 0849C] Circumcision, however, as offered to children, excuses original guilt alone.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The question what it means for heaven to be opened to the baptized.

But let us return from our digression and inquire what it means that the heavens are opened to the baptized. Is heaven not opened for this reason: that the entrance to that place may be understood to lie open for the baptized? But to what purpose does it lie open if one is not permitted to enter? If someone is baptized and, because of former foulness, is kept from entering heaven until he has completed penitential satisfaction, is the gate not closed to him while he is kept away from it? But if, by the power of baptism, those who only shortly before had been most wicked while living in the flesh immediately enter heaven [Col. 0849D], how is no sin left unpunished? Hear the Apostle: “For the gifts of God are without repentance” (Rom. 11:29). An expositor explains it thus: [Note: [Col. 0849D] In the *Gloss*.] “The grace of God in baptism requires neither groaning nor lamentation nor any work, but faith alone, and freely pardons everything.” Therefore God’s gifts—that is, remission of sins effected in baptism—do not require repentance, that is, a purgatorial penalty after remission. Indeed, the contrite heart which precedes baptism, and the humbled heart which obediently submits to the sacrament, so cleanse the guilty person that they suffice in place of punishment. So great before God is compunction joined to humility through obedience. Therefore the Holy Spirit descends upon catechumens and pardons guilt. [Note: [Col. 0850D] See notes on chapter 13.] Likewise, he descends upon the baptized [Col. 0850A] and pardons punishment: catechization merits pardon but does not yet remove punishment, just as pure confession removes guilt indeed but requires satisfaction. Baptism, however, because pardon of sin has already been obtained beforehand, pardons satisfaction for sin; likewise martyrdom, with all sins remitted, also removes every subsequent burden from its dwelling-place. Hence, while the thirtyfold and sixtyfold fruit receive the left hand, the hundredfold fruit, which is martyrdom, provides passage to the right. Why? Because the martyrs’ reward is not deferred after death.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. For whom and when heaven is opened.

Therefore heaven is rightly said to lie open for the baptized, and not before [Col. 0850B], because satisfaction for offenses forgiven through catechization, not yet completed, would previously exclude them from the vision of God. But for those rightly baptized, only the condition of mortality separates them from glory. The water, fully reconciling us to God, extinguishes the turning flame which held us guilty persons back from entering paradise (Gen. 3:24), so that the entrance lies open.

It should nevertheless be noted that if any of the faithful happened to die between the Resurrection and the Ascension, he waited, associated meanwhile with the Lord Jesus, for the Ascension, before which the heavenly gate ought not to have been opened. Hence it appears that the heavenly gate is open not to those baptized before, but only to those baptized after the Ascension. Unless perhaps someone maintains that heaven is opened to the reborn, not because it is [Col. 0850C] immediately permissible to enter, but because in due time they will be permitted to ascend there. But on that reasoning heaven has been open to the righteous from the beginning of the world, when it is rather read to have been closed; and likewise to the most wicked who are nevertheless to be converted, and to penitents not yet reformed through worthy fruits. For heaven is opened to all, not by the clarity of foreknowledge, but by the worthiness of life obtained through the Redeemer’s death. For God does not close or open heaven by looking at his foreknowledge, but by looking at our life. Nor, when he does this, does he contemplate future things, but present things. For we are not now considering what providence judges concerning individuals, but what the judgment of God, assessing merits not as they will be but as they are, determines regarding each person. For if you look to providence, which measures the outcome of a matter, among the baptized few are those for whom heaven is open. Consider, therefore, the judgment that assigns to heaven everyone who rightly receives baptism, because it considers him presently worthy of heaven. Otherwise, if those whom providence judges are to be excluded are not considered worthy of heaven even in baptism by God’s judgment—though sanctified by the washing—because satisfaction still remains, how is heaven opened to such persons, who are neither now worthy to enter nor ever will be? For we are now speaking of those who become good through baptism but quickly return to their vomit. Are the heavens said to be open for that reason—that in baptism those who had previously lived wickedly obtain the grace which, if they pursue it to the end [Col. 0851A], will nevertheless grant them heaven, once the foulness of paganism has first been expiated through penitential amendment, whether in this age or the future? But on this account heaven is no longer asserted to be open to those mentioned above; rather, it is believed to be opened under a certain condition. By a similar rationale, heaven is opened in confession as well.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Why heaven is not said to be opened in confession, and concerning its opening.

Since, then, the heavens are said to be opened in baptism, why is this not also said in confession, unless because after confession the fruits of repentance remain, while after baptism they do not? Thus heaven is rightly said to be opened in baptism, something which Scripture teaches is likewise accomplished in martyrdom; for in each the kingdom of heaven is at hand. And although we understand the open heavens mystically, it does not depart from truth that bodily eyes saw them actually split open, just as they saw the Holy Spirit descend thence in bodily form. Thus in Mark the Lord immediately, “coming up from the water, saw the heavens opened and the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him” (Mark 1:10). And in John: “John bore testimony, saying: ‘I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven, and it remained upon him’” (John 1:32). What does it mean that, coming up from the water, he saw the heavens opened, except that at that time a bodily opening presented itself to bodily eyes? For the spiritual opening is always available to the spiritual eyes both of the Head and of the members. Again, what does it mean that, coming up from the water, he saw the heavens opened? What does this signify—that he sees them opened as he comes up—except that the opening occurred while he was in the water, and appeared already accomplished to him as he came up from the water? What does it mean that, after the heavens are declared to have been seen opened, the Spirit is then said to have been seen descending from heaven, unless that descent followed the opening? It is a fitting order: the opening precedes, from which the dove’s descent is seen. For since it is established that it descended from heaven, from where more fittingly would it descend than from the opening, when this accords especially with the mystery? To be sure, heaven is opened and the dove comes from there when grace is dispensed from on high to human beings [Col. 0851D], by which it becomes possible, after the man [Christ], to have fellowship with the citizens of heaven. The heavens are therefore opened so that this dove may descend upon the baptized and, returning, carry them through the open gate to the heights.

## CHAPTER XXX. On confession.

[Note: [Col. 0851D] Lombard, IV, distinction 14.]

Because, still subject to vanity, we do not keep the covenant of baptism, confession is established for us as a second refuge after shipwreck. Thus the Prophet, speaking of God, directs instruction to us: “Pour out your hearts before him” (Ps. 61:9), that is, confess your sins. And again in the same sense: “Reveal your way to the Lord” (Ps. 36:5). But before confession, in which poison is vomited out through the mouth, it is necessary that the poison itself be separated from the heart. For what is “pour out your hearts” except, “Pour outside yourselves those things which lie hidden in the conscience”? And what is “pour outside yourselves” except, “Having cast them out from within, declare them outwardly,” according to: “For I will declare my iniquity” (Ps. 37:19)? Therefore confession of the mouth has no force unless it derives its worth from the disposition of the mind. Before all else, then, the person about to confess evil deeds must groan over those evil deeds, because “God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. 50:19). But if contrition of heart is the origin of correction, one who does not yet grieve over his offense—or, what is worse, rejoices in what he has committed—does not yet, by confessing, accuse that which he does not yet hate; he condemns himself by his own judgment. For he does not confess his injustice against himself to the Lord, which he would do if he regarded what he confesses as opposed to his will. But one who truly groans resolves to cease from those things over which he would again groan, according to: “Have you sinned? Cease” (Ecclus. 21:1). Surely that groaning is foul before God which laments past foulness while desiring future foulness. This is not because lamentation in itself displeases, but because it cannot have force owing to what is joined to it. Thus Judas repented more than enough, but despair, his companion, defiled his repentance. For in each direction, what could be good in itself is contaminated by something external to it. Hence one must take great care that anyone intending to correct his life, while overturning his conscience by trustworthy examination, leave behind nothing [Col. 0852C] that might grievously weigh upon his conscience. For whoever “offends in one point” (Jas. 2:10), while unwilling to be corrected in that point, is guilty of all those things from which he thought himself freed through a contrite heart. He is guilty of all, because on account of the one thing he retains, God does not forgive him all the other things which he himself relinquishes. He makes known to the physician every sin from which he wishes to be healed; he conceals one injustice in which he prefers to remain ill, contrary to the Prophet: “I made my sin known to you, and I did not conceal my injustice” (Ps. 31:5). God will not hear one praying for his sins if he has looked upon iniquity in his heart (Ps. 65:18); for he himself says: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, I will not remember any of his iniquities” (Ezek. 18:22).

## CHAPTER XXXI. How and to whom sins are pardoned.

[Col. 0852D]

Therefore, when he grants forgiveness for crimes, he pardons not some but indeed all; for the one who repents of all obtains forgiveness for all, since God has already been made favorable to him. But the one who persists impenitent even in one matter does not obtain gifts from an angry God, gifts which ought rather to be given to those reconciled.

But repentance is often produced by fear in one who fears burning, not sinning. [Note: [Col. 0851D] See Augustine, Sermon 19, *On the Words of the Apostle*, near the end.] Such a man is certainly evil, since a good man abhors guilt more than hell. The former, foreseeing punishment, restrains guilt; if it were permitted with impunity, he would commit what he restrains. [Note: [Col. 0852D] “He who does not do evil through fear would prefer to do it, if it were permitted.”] Nor [Col. 0853A] can anyone be good who would desire unlawful things if he dared. [Note: [Col. 0853D] Augustine, on Psalm 32, middle; Augustine, Sermon 15, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] For in a certain way each person’s will desires whatever he refuses solely from necessity. What you do under compulsion, it is true that you do; it is false that you will it. The will, indeed, having surmounted every violence and defending intact the right of its own liberty, sets the body’s servitude against the injuries of its assailant [perhaps: “assailant”]. Thus one who repents from fear is still a slave, because he fears lashes; he is not yet a son, who, loving his father, hopes for an inheritance. But the slave is cast out from Sarah’s dwelling, since he will not be an heir (Gen. 21:19). Therefore whoever, while repenting, is distressed by fear alone does not yet merit pardon through repentance. But he who grants fear in order to impose, from fear, the necessity of repentance [Col. 0853B], will grant love together with repentance, so that the penitent person may be worthy of pardon—provided only that, having been anticipated by the beginning of wisdom, he proves duly grateful to his giver. For why is fear of the Lord called the beginning of wisdom except because whoever embraces fear of the Lord through the duties owed will subsequently be equipped by divine mercy with wisdom—without which love does not depart unaccompanied—to triumph over his former conduct? Indeed, both the tears of repentance and the brilliance of works are rejected as tasteless unless love supplies each with the seasoning of acceptability. Hence the Apostle judges a person without love to be nothing, even if he excels in knowledge, gives his body over to suffering, or distributes his possessions for the use of the poor (1 Cor. 13:3). Thus he wished us to know that everything which may appear however resplendent is unacceptable to God and therefore foul because it is not seasoned with love.

But “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:9); and one who hates his own soul plainly does not have love, for if he had it, he would surely love his own soul. For to love rightly is precisely to love one’s own soul for that end. Therefore one who loves iniquity no longer has love; but what is done outside love cannot profit. Thus, while one loves iniquity, one does not do that from which one receives a reward. Indeed, to love iniquity is to be an evil tree; but an evil tree cannot bear good fruit, just as a good tree cannot bear evil fruit. What then? Does one who loves even a single iniquity do no good at all in the meantime?

[Col. 0853D] Yet he is devout in prayer, diligent in fasting, observes discipline with the greatest strictness, and practices mercy with great affection, while stained only by one blemish that torments him with lust. Therefore, since on account of one vice someone is an evil tree, and an evil tree cannot bear good fruits, what shall we say? Where there is one vice, is there no good at all? Who would attempt to maintain this, when considered reason distinguishes otherwise and the evidence of experience proves it? It is established that a righteous person sins at least venially; why should it not also be established that an unrighteous person does much good? Therefore, where there is one evil, not everything there is evil; just as, where there is one good, everything is not immediately good. Rather, goods are often intermingled with evils, and evils with goods.

Yet goods and evils are weighed differently when we consider what they are in nature or what they can do in effect. Virtue and vice: if you consider the nature of each, virtue never ceases to be good, while vice is always evil. But if you measure the powers of each, then by sound reasoning each thing is good when it makes the person in whom it exists either good or better, now worthy of glory. Conversely, you rightly consider evil that by which anyone becomes evil or increases in evil, and is deservedly liable to punishment. [Col. 0854B] But when any virtue or vice is deprived of its proper efficacy, the former is no longer good because it benefits nothing, nor the latter evil because it harms nothing. The latter, by the same reasoning, does not employ its nature so as to harm; nor can it occur contrary to its nature so as to have power.

## CHAPTER XXXII. As no goods harm, so no evils help.

It should nevertheless be observed that good things appear to harm when someone is puffed up by them, and evil things to help when someone is humbled by them. Yet good never truly harms; rather, the vice that arises in a person from a good thing always harms. Conversely, what is evil can never be beneficial; but the Spirit of the Lord, who works all things together for good, brings good out of evil. Love alone is the virtue that makes a person good. Once love has begun, the addition [perhaps: “by the addition”] of the other virtues increases the goodness already born, with knowledge of the Scriptures taking the lead in all things. While love reigns, vice indeed exists in a person, but is without power. For then only that is admitted which either springs forth as an unconquerable shoot from the tinder of sin—what they call *propassion* (baptism remedies this, according to: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin,” Ps. 31:2)—or is venial, without which one cannot live. Against such daily evils there are daily goods: almsgiving, prayer, and confession, according to: “Confess your sins to one another, that you may be saved” (Jas. 5:16). Invisible sins are lesser evils because in this life they cannot be avoided or overcome [Col. 0854D]. [Note: [Col. 0854D] Book II, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, ch. 4; Book I, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, ch. 25; Book VI, *Against Julian*, ch. 19.] All these, together with the tinder from which they sprout as from an evil root, lead to condemnation before the washing, as Augustine attests concerning concupiscence; in baptism they are released from guilt, and after baptism they are left for the struggle.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On concupiscence, venial sin, and unconquerable sin.

Concupiscence, therefore, because it is itself unconquerable, is excused after baptism, being left behind in baptism along with all its offspring, because those too cannot be conquered. [Col. 0855A] Venial sins, however, because they can in some measure be avoided, are not, like unconquerable things, free from guilt when committed; rather, they await forgiveness through satisfaction, though a light one. Both venial and unconquerable sins, as also criminal sins, take their origin in the mind. Yet each of the three grows, while retaining its own name, whenever, as nature urges, it bends the bodily members to its service.

Human corruption, to be sure, instils diverse impulses into the mind; and the mind, stirred by the same diversity, weakens the body. In every individual sin there is something unconquerable: namely, the first movement, which either the devil’s suggestion or the tinder of sin, when an occasion is offered, arouses. There is something venial as well: namely, that same movement when pleasure, now lingering for a while over it, entertains and embraces it. Pleasure to which reason dissents, [Col. 0855B] yet does not extinguish it, exceeds the measure of pleasure and is close to a disgraceful act whenever it wanders so far as to deliberate whether what it suggests should be done. Inquiry that investigates what is good and what is evil is approved, according to the saying: “Test all things” (1 Thess. 5:21). But when what is seen through inquiry to be wicked is then deliberated upon—whether it should be done or not—that is rightly condemned, because of the saying: “Hold fast what is good” (ibid.).

One who deliberates in this way is no longer alive, yet not dead; for while he debates between the two, he does not know which he wishes, since he as yet wishes neither. For if he consented to either, there would no longer be deliberation. Such a person neither turns his mind away from evil nor directs it toward good. And because he knows both, yet remains uncertain which of the two to choose, neither immediately preferring good to evil nor at once rejecting evil in reverence for good, [Col. 0855C] he is undoubtedly unjust. For although reason has not yet consented to the vice over which he deliberates, nevertheless not immediately detesting such deliberation, lingering in it, and favoring it, is plainly to consent to wickedness.

Nor should you suppose that a person assailed on every side by evil impulses thereby gives assent to those impulses, even though he is in some manner affected by them. For a good man endures the insolence of impulses unwillingly, doing what he does not will. But whoever favors an evil movement and thereby cherishes it, although he dissents from its outward act, has already consented to its evil root; he has indeed become evil, because he loves evil. Had he immediately suppressed the onset of the evil movement, he would have triumphed over the enemy without a wound. [Col. 0855D] For as often as anyone suffers assaults of vices, so often, if he resists manfully, he emerges a victor, gaining as many crowns as victories.
