Conversely, the more softly anyone yields to an evil movement, the more shame he incurs.

Nevertheless, whoever, defended by God, refrains from love of vice and from the will to sin, saying with the Apostle, “What I do not will, that I do” (Rom. 7:20), and finally, aided and strengthened by grace, drives the hated sickness from his own bounds, obtains at last—though scarcely and after long desire—the trophy he has sought. These, then, are the *propassions* [initial involuntary stirrings], which, so long as they remain without consent, are venial. Once consent is applied, what is admitted becomes damnable.

Consent occurs whenever, [Col. 0856A] stirred either by pleasure or by bitterness, whether through deliberation or through impulse, we acquiesce in wickedness: no longer restraining the mind’s desire, but loosening the reins, so that the will lacks nothing for evil, even though it is sometimes frustrated in carrying it into effect. And this is what either makes a man evil or increases him in evil. While a man is such, he is an evil tree that does not bear good fruit. Yet in the meantime he often does many things which, considered according to their nature, are certainly good, but considered according to their effect are no longer so. For good things are enfeebled by their proximity to evil: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5:7), until repentance comes to the rescue, so that things which had been dead may live again.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On dead goods and dead evils

[Col. 0856B]

[Note: [Col. 0855D] The Master, IV, distinction 15, § 5.]

What benefit, then, do good works confer while they are corrupted—indeed, dead? Certainly they should no longer truly be called either good things or good fruits, since they neither make nor increase a good man or a good tree, nor are they worthy of reward, because, according to the Apostle, they profit nothing (1 Cor. 13:3). Thus neither is an evil man good because of his good works, nor is a good man evil because of his evil works. Therefore, one who follows exact speech will not deign now to call the former good, or the latter evil, because, stripped of their native vigor, they degenerate through their accompanying dispositions. Things which would reign by themselves lie numb and subjected when something stronger comes upon them.

The Lord rightly says to certain persons: “How can you speak good things, when you are evil?” (Matt. 12:34). For those who are evil cannot [Col. 0856C] speak good things. Thus an evil tree cannot bear good fruit, because “there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13:4). No one does good until he comes to the One—that is, to God. So too a good tree cannot bear evil fruit. Perhaps a good tree can become evil, since conversely an evil tree becomes good; but neither tree appropriates the other’s fruits.

[Col. 0856D] Perhaps this appears otherwise to human judgment. Yet God, who is not deceived, if he beholds iniquity in the heart, judges the heart itself corrupt; and therefore whatever is contained in a depraved heart, or is poured forth outwardly from it, however excellent it may be in its own nature, divine judgment declares corrupt because of even one stain clinging to the heart. Thus, whenever Pilate mingles the blood of the Galileans with their sacrifices (Luke 13:1), the Lord rejects their offering. What does this mean? Pilate, whose name is interpreted “the mouth of a hammerer,” is the devil, “the hammer of the whole earth,” testing the potter’s vessels. The Galileans are interpreted as “those who migrate”: these are Christians, whose purpose is to migrate from dwelling in this life into the kingdom to come. Blood, which as though bursting out from hiding-places defiles and weakens, is concupiscence; when it leaps forward as far as consent, it pollutes and undermines the spirit. The sacrifice is a good work.

But if good things done by evil persons are dead and, because charity is absent, profit nothing, what is [Col. 0857A] meant by the assertion that no good goes unrewarded? For the rich man, already condemned, is told: “You received good things in your lifetime” (Luke 16:25). Yet what could that rich man, unrighteous and given to luxury, have done in life that deserved recompense as a reward? How are the good works of the wicked said to be dead and to profit nothing, if they are rewarded even in this life? Shall we say that they are dead and profit nothing after this life, but live and profit in this life? Hence: “You received good things in your lifetime.”

Perhaps this bears upon the case of the Egyptian midwives, who, out of fear of God, preserved the males contrary to Pharaoh’s command, though afterward they also lied to the king through fear of death; God did them good. [Note: [Col. 0857D] Augustine, *Against Lying*, ch. 15.] “And because they feared God, he built houses for them” (Exod. 1:21), that is, he gave them some suitable means of maintaining a household.

166

## CHAPTER XXXV. Whence certain evils arise, and whether dead goods truly profit

[Col. 0857B]

[Note: [Col. 0858D] The Master, as above.]

Shall we say, then, that slight and corrupt good things are effective only briefly and in an evil life, while true goods are truly effective in life? Yet things that arise from no intention, or from an evil intention, are in no sense good. They may perhaps appear good; but either, without a good intention, they are not good, or through an evil intention they become evil. For your disposition gives your work its name. Thus the Lord says: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light; but if it is evil, your whole body will be dark” (Matt. 6:22). Therefore whenever the intention is evil, its work, though it seem good, is itself evil as well. Likewise, from the light of intention arises the light of action. [Col. 0857C]

For that which is truly done wrongly is sometimes produced not by a good intention, but by an intention deceived by the appearance of good. Often an intention is good, but, corrupted by an evil adjoining it, produces fruit that is indeed not evil, because the intention itself is good, yet is not even good, because it is corrupted. Of such an intention the Lord says: “See therefore that the light which is in you is not darkness” (ibid.); that is, let not an intention naturally shining be darkened accidentally.

Yet the good deeds which wicked persons do seem neither entirely without profit nor truly dead, if they ought in some manner not to remain unrewarded. [Col. 0857D] But what offering pleasing to his lord can a fugitive deserving the cross make if his mind is not turned back toward him? Who renders a welcome gift out of what he does not possess? For “the sacrifices of the ungodly are abominable to the Lord” (Prov. 15:8). Thus Isaiah represents the Lord as saying to the ungodly: “When you stretch out your hands, I will turn away my eyes from you; when you multiply prayer, I will not hear: for your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1:15). Since their hands are bloody—that is, their actions are disgraceful—even their outstretched hands, that is, works directed by intention, displease him. Unless one prefers to assert that outstretched hands displease precisely because they are bloody, and that these are the sacrifices of the ungodly which will be abominable to the Lord. But neither the designation “sacrifices” nor the stretching out [Col. 0858A] of hands—rather, their contraction—seems applicable to filthy actions.

Shall we say, then, that that rich man, evil at the end—for which reason he was buried in hell—had formerly been good for a time, whence the words, “You received good things in your lifetime” (Luke 16:25); and that therefore no good deed of the just goes unrewarded, not only of those persevering in good but also of those whose charity grows cold? Perseverance receives recompense both now and in the future because, as the Apostle testifies, “godliness has promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come” (1 Tim. 4:8). Hence Solomon says: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2:6). It is as though he said: God’s temporal benefits strengthen a mind fixed on heavenly things, whereas eternal benefits will make the whole person secure on every side. [Col. 0858B]

But one who acts well temporarily is rewarded temporarily; let him hope for nothing in the future. For hell, toward which he hastens, grants a reward to no one, nor does the heavenly dwelling grant punishment—the punishment toward which the devil, destined for torment, fell. The rich man, tortured in flame and desiring at least to be cooled by a drop, hears in the lower world that not only are gifts denied, but that punishments are not even mitigated on account of merits, when he is told, “You received good things in your lifetime.” For if he had, by means of previous good deeds, been spared torment in hell, he would in some manner have received good things after his life.

But the Lord denies that one resisting his commands will leave hell until he pays the last farthing, that is, the least sin. It is as though he said: You will leave hell when you have paid the punishments owed even for the least sin. Therefore, since it is certain that he will never leave, it is also certain that he will never pay what is owed. [Col. 0858C] Thus, for the sins which he carries with him from here without repentance, he does not hope for forgiveness in hell through the good deeds of his life, even for the least of them. For impenitence, just as it removes forgiveness, so it does not allow punishment to be softened.

Hence Ezekiel says: “If the righteous man turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity, he shall die in his sin, and the righteous deeds which he did shall not be remembered” (Ezek. 3:20). Why, after saying, “He shall die in his sin,” does he immediately add, “and the righteous deeds which he did shall not be remembered,” unless because, if one who was once righteous should happen to die in sin, the righteous deeds formerly done will afterward profit him nothing? Therefore, if they profit at all, they profit in life. [Col. 0858D] But how do they profit in life? For if later evils bring barrenness upon earlier good works, so that they profit nothing after death, how will they help a living person? For Gregory testifies that, after a righteous person falls away from righteousness and commits iniquity, his righteousness is immediately consigned to oblivion; this is not postponed until after death. Thus all a person’s righteousness appears to become fruitless when crimes follow upon good deeds, so that the righteous deeds he did are no longer remembered, neither in this age nor in the future—unless the dead works perhaps revive through repentance.

[Col. 0859A] Therefore, whatever good deeds profit those who look back and afterward persevere in wickedness profit them while they are good. It may indeed happen that persons who persevere in evil and are eternally damned nevertheless receive some reward in the meantime or in temporal matters. But if the Judge consigns to oblivion after death the righteousness of the righteous who fall away, how much more the good deeds of the unrighteous?

Gregory, on that passage, [Note: [Col. 0859D] Homily 11 on Ezekiel.] “Their righteous deeds shall not be remembered,” says:

> This is especially to be considered by us: when we commit evil, we recall past good deeds to mind without cause, because in the commission of evils there ought to be no confidence in previous good deeds.

For this reason later evils extinguish earlier good things. The excessive power of evil, like the worst leaven, corrupts and renders dead not only the good things done at the time, but also those which preceded them. Nor will they revive unless, through repentance, the leaven itself [Col. 0859B] from which evil originates is washed away.

However good the rich man may once have been, if in the end he was evil in faith, how did he receive good things in life? Perhaps, while he was good, things went well with him because of his good deeds; or, if he always remained evil, the lesson is that the wicked are never well off in hell, though they often are in this age—as conversely good persons are now ill off, as Lazarus was, but will be well off in the future. Perhaps the midwives too received their reward before their lie (Exod. 1:20); or, if, as the sequence of the text requires, it came afterward, the divine dispensation did not in the meantime see fit to answer the evils which followed, but rather strove by its beneficence to urge readers toward works of mercy.

[Col. 0859C] Therefore no good deed—provided only that it truly deserves the name of good, that is, that it is not contaminated either while being done by present wickedness or after it has been done by subsequent wickedness; or, if it happens to be defiled in this way, that it also happens to be cleansed by satisfaction—no good deed, I say, if it is of this kind, goes unrewarded.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On rewards and merits

There are some good things which are rewards only, such as eternal goods bestowed not on children but on adults. There are others which are gifts only, such as riches together with other bodily advantages, when they are given to the undeserving. Fear of Gehenna too, together with the other things granted by God so that people may depart from wickedness, belongs in this class. Between these two kinds of graces merits hold a middle place. [Col. 0859D] These, indeed, are the good things of which it is said, “No good deed goes unrewarded.”

For God gives certain initial good things, by which the guilty person, as though pleading, rises to reconciliation with God. Once reconciled, and with God cooperating, he does that for which he ought to be rewarded. Merits, therefore, are rightly placed between both classes: by gifts one comes to merit, and by merit to reward. Merit too is always God’s gift, though sometimes it is also a reward. But let the eye of reason distinguish among the benefits of the Author.

168

## CHAPTER XXXVII. That the righteous person can fall

[Note: [Col. 0859D] The Master, *Sentences*, book III, distinction 31.]

It must be noted that a righteous person can fall. [Col. 0860A] Thus in Ezekiel two righteous persons are found: one who perished because he did not heed the teacher, and another who, because he did heed him, lived on in life (Ezek. 3:18). But no one is righteous except through charity. Therefore one who has charity falls, and sometimes perishes. How? Because he loses charity. Thus the Lord says: “The charity of many shall grow cold” (Matt. 24:12).

But if one who had charity perishes, and everyone who perishes is alien to the condition of the heavenly Jerusalem, how is charity a fountain in which the stranger does not share? (Prov. 5:17). Yet one who perishes loses charity. How then does the Apostle say: “Charity never fails”? (1 Cor. 13:8). [Note: [Col. 0860D] Augustine, Tractate 6 on the Epistle of John.] You may possess other things and nevertheless be evil; but you cannot possess charity and be evil. Thus charity is the fountain in which the stranger does not share: [Col. 0860B] for while anyone is illuminated by charity, he is not denied citizenship in Jerusalem.

But what does the apostolic statement mean: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19)? If you consider the providence by which the outcome of things is weighed, evil and lost persons were never in the fellowship of the saints, nor did they ever go out from a place where they never were. But if you attend to the judgment whose examination considers only present things—hence, “Where I find you, there I will judge you”—then evil persons are sometimes seen to be among the good and to depart from the good, now inscribed and now erased from the book of the living.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On providence, judgment, and charity

[Col. 0860C] [Note: [Col. 0860D] The Master, above.]

Therefore, the person whom providence judges alien is often shown not to be alien by the sentence of judgment. [Col. 0860B] Perhaps the Apostle, because faith and hope and many other things precious in this world are abolished after this life, says in praise of charity: “Charity never fails” (1 Cor. 13:8), since it begins now and is perfected in the future. He did not mean it to be understood in such a way that, once possessed, it never departs, but that, once born here, it extends into the age to come.

Yet it may also be understood without absurdity that charity, at the beginnings of a good life, commonly has a certain tenderness: it is already worthy of heaven, but not yet fit for the severe warfare either of temptation or persecution. This is the charity of which the Lord says: “The charity of many shall grow cold” [Col. 0860D] (Matt. 24:12). One guided by this charity often falls and perishes. This is the person who goes out from the good and is alien to the kingdom.

But once charity has reached maturity, and has acquired, whether later or sooner, the strength of firmness, it is now the fountain in which the stranger does not share (Matt. 7:25). Whoever has this is founded upon firm rock. Let winds then rush upon it; let floods rush upon it: that house will not be moved. Why? Because it is fortified by charity that never fails. Hence charity appears even in this world to earn for a person that rank which, once anyone has reached it, he never afterward sins criminally or perishes. For because [Col. 0861A] “charity does not act improperly” (1 Cor. 13:4), one who always perseveres in charity never acts wrongly. For if he sinned willingly, he would drive away charity, which does not fail.

Who then is there who does not sometimes wound, or rather kill, charity? There is either no one, or one exceedingly rare, whose reason always resists wickedness and does not very frequently consent to it.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On perfect charity

[Note: [Col. 0861D] The Master, above.]

For this reason that charity which never fails, which “does not act improperly,” “is not ambitious,” “does not seek its own” (ibid.), and has the other qualities listed by the Apostle, belongs to very few, perhaps among the more devout only to the most devout. Unless one prefers to maintain that even mature charity often [Col. 0861B] falls, yet does not fail. It falls because it often departs; it does not fail because it departs only to return. Once it has departed, it is no longer charity itself; rather, its departure acts improperly, seeks its own, and admits similar things.

Thus David, Solomon, and Peter also—men whom it is not impious to think had attained that degree of charity, though neither is it right confidently to affirm it—are known to have sinned most grievously despite being excellent men.

But charity driven away by vice, because it was the charity which, once possessed, does not afterward permit a person to perish, may credibly have left behind some root of itself. From this root the conscience of the guilty, pricked and pricked again, never permits rest, [Col. 0861C] until charity, sprouting from its own root through grace, restores the disturbed person. Therefore whoever has attained the firmness of charity, although he often breaks away from it, is not a stranger, because he always springs back to the same charity. For, founded upon firm rock, he will not be cast down either by the blast of winds or by the onrush of floods. He is indeed very often driven so as to stagger, by the wind of temptations and the flood of pleasures; but he is never moved so as to fall, because “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16:18). They do prevail in many respects, so that we may acknowledge our frailty; but they do not prevail so that we may extol God’s goodness. They would prevail if one who fell did not rise again.

Of charity of this kind it is written in the Song of Songs: “Many waters could not extinguish charity, nor shall floods overwhelm it” [Col. 0861D] (Song 8:7). [Note: [Col. 0861D] Master, *Sentences*, III, distinction 31.] Under the name “charity” this does not speak of tender charity, but of mature charity, which a greater or lesser temptation can weaken but cannot wholly uproot. Yet it sometimes seems to be weakened so greatly that, if someone should die in the meantime, he might also be damned. But they say that charity has this merit from its maturity: it does not permit those who are its own to die in sin.

## CHAPTER XL. On damnable sins, consent, and negligence

But let us return to those sins which, after unconquerable and venial sins, we called damnable in the third degree. [Col. 0862A] Some of these are confined to the mind and are imputable because of consent. Consent, however, is a greater fault than negligence, because consent wills what is evil, whereas negligence does not foresee evil. It is far more corrupt to will evil than to be ignorant through carelessness.

Yet negligence, which is often understood together with consent—as though consent had taken place and had issued in an evil deed—is reproved whenever through it we fall into a fault that we could have avoided by exercising diligence. [Note: [Col. 0861D] The Master, as below.] But just as negligence is less than consent in vice, so a work of negligence is deservedly less blameworthy than works of consent. [Note: [Col. 0861D] Augustine, *The Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, book I, ch. 12, and Sermon 44, *On the Words of the Lord*.]

But while consent and carelessness do not break out into an evil deed, [Col. 0862B] this is death in the house. When they boil over from within to an outward act, this is death at the gate. When they extend from an act to a habit that harms by example, the dead person becomes foul-smelling, after the manner of Lazarus.

## CHAPTER XLI. On negligence and the force of death

[Note: [Col. 0862D] The Master, book IV, distinction 16.]

I said that negligence is death even when it does not produce a harmful act, because whoever, possessing greater understanding, commits something from which scandal arises so far as lies in him—even if it does not arise in the act itself—is deservedly proved guilty.

Jesus raises the first dead person privately and without difficulty; the second at the gate, that is, publicly, with some delay, as though with some difficulty; the third, while many are standing by, he calls back alive from the tomb with great delay and, as it were, great difficulty.

170

The Lord observes the places and distinguishes the modes; nor does he exceed the fixed number, seeing that these matters are not unsuited to signification. The first dead person, to be sure, is lightly raised by Christ in private. [Col. 0862C] By Christ, because through yourself you can be weakened by unconquerable things, burdened with sickness by venial things, and at last die through consent. It is not through yourself but through the one who raises you that you can return to life. The raising takes place privately because private matters should not be made public, but healed by private remedies; and what is confined to the mind alone is easily forgiven.

The Lord raises the second dead person at the gate before many people, with some delay, because a crime leaping from the house of the heart into the gate of action must be struck by a punishment certainly grave—as committed at the gate—and graver still if before many. To the third, already foul-smelling, life is granted where delay, labor, and tears are displayed. [Note: [Col. 0862D] Augustine, Sermon 44, *On the Words of the Lord.*] For where the disease of wicked imitation is prolonged by the stench of habit, punishment must be exacted doubly from the guilty person: both because he acted wickedly in himself, and because, by his long and foul conduct, he scandalized the little ones so far as lay in him. Therefore, because he did not avoid the gravest offense, he must be corrected by the gravest censure, delay, labor, and tears. [Col. 0863A]

And just as one who commits a hidden offense is treated with a hidden remedy, lest public medicine expose a child’s wound to the grief of mother Church while she sees some mock and others applaud him, recognizing in another what they find in themselves, so one who sins publicly must repent not privately but publicly. The person who has wounded holy Church by an open guilt must heal her wound by open satisfaction.

The degree of satisfactions must correspond to the degree of faults. Thus the first death, being lighter than the others, is treated more lightly. The second, because it must be imputed more than the first yet far less than the last, is treated more difficultly than the first but far more easily than the last. He who is omnipotent suffered no difficulty whatever in raising the dead in different ways; but he wished to express the nature of our failings, which, according to the degrees of their progress, take on two effects: they increase in guilt and cling to us more and more. [Col. 0863B] Hence at the beginnings of sin it is easier to recover one’s senses; but when it becomes a habit, recovery is more difficult.

## CHAPTER XLII. Why he did not raise a fourth person, and by what all fault is judged

[Note: [Col. 0863C] Augustine, Sermon 44, *On the Words of the Lord.*]

The Lord did not choose to raise a fourth dead person because a servant does not admit a fourth degree of sinning. Every fault after baptism that is judged worthy of damnation comes either through consent, deed, or finally habit. Fault begins in consent and gains strength as it proceeds. Thus, in the Lord’s testimony: “Whoever is angry with his brother”—that is, who from an inner stirring wills evil to his brother—“is liable to judgment; but whoever says, ‘Raca,’”—that is, who from anger and evil will breaks out into a voice of indignation—“will be liable to the council” (Matt. 5:22), which is more serious than judgment. For a judgment is when an assembly meets to hear a cause; a council is when, after the accusation has been proved, the penalty of the condemned person is debated. But whoever says, “You fool” [Col. 0864A] (ibid.), which is open insult, “will be liable to Gehenna,” when he undergoes punishment already determined.

Hidden hatred, then, is evil; the unrestrained outbreak of indignation born from it is worse; and refusing to spare insults is worst of all. This is evident because hidden hatred is punished by judgment, indignation by a more severe penalty, namely the council, and insult by the gravest penalty, namely Gehenna.

But one who has an intention to sin, yet does not wholly have it and therefore is held back from an evil act, plainly offends less than one who bursts forth from intention into deed. Yet one who clings wholly to the sin and is prevented from the deed only by necessity, because he does not do what he desires with his whole heart solely because he cannot or because he fears punishment—how is he, before God whom he does not revere at all, less guilty [Col. 0864B] of the obstinate persistence of his will than he would be by the act itself, which that will proposes, plans, and finally, so far as lies in it, wholly performs? He may perhaps dread punishment; but because he hates justice, he dishonors the Judge. Jesus made clear in one case what he wished to be understood in all, saying: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28).

Instructed by this saying, we maintain that a complete will to act is reckoned as the deed. Yet when the Lord binds one who desires and whose inclination tends toward adultery by the guilt of adultery in the heart, who, without transgressing the Lord’s decree, will bind him by the guilt of adultery in deed? A complete will to act is perhaps reckoned as a deed because it is liable to hell as the deed is, though not to the same extent as the deed.

[Col. 0864C] The Lord’s saying is true: “Out of the heart proceed thefts, adulteries, murders, blasphemies,” and other shameful acts (Matt. 15:19). For according to the nature of dispositions, the quality of actions is assessed. “A good man brings forth good out of a good treasure,” just as, conversely, “an evil man brings forth evil out of an evil treasure” (Matt. 12:36). Therefore good and evil actions are performed outwardly, but each receives its name from the inward good or evil.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0863]

## CHAPTER I. On reflection before baptism and after it

[Col. 0863D]

[Note: [Col. 0863] Augustine, book II, *On the Merits of Sins*, ch. 4, and elsewhere.]

It must be noted that reflection is one thing before baptism and another after it. Before baptism, the tinder of sin itself, with its filthy offspring, is judged a damnable offense. For an infant is condemned because he has natural concupiscence; how much more an adult, because he both has concupiscence and lusts? Therefore before the washing the tinder of sin itself is imputed, and evil movements born from that tinder are also imputed. Since these are very, very many, they heap up very great torment for those to be condemned.

But after baptism: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” [Col. 0864D] (Ps. 31:2). You indeed have the sin of concupiscence and its movements, but it is not imputed unless one strays as far as consent. For the power of baptism brings it about that such things are now only for weakness, whereas before they were also for death. Therefore God does not impute this to the baptized for damnation, though perhaps he imputes it for punishment. And fittingly, things designated by the name of death are punished with the penalty of damnation, while things designated by the name of sickness are punished with the penalty of distress.

Thus after the Apostle said, “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Rom. 7:25)—that is, “I commit only venial sins”—he added: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who do not walk according to the flesh” [Col. 0865A] (Rom. 8:1). For, avoiding crimes, they commit only unavoidable things; and while he removes only damnation from these, he perhaps permits punishment. He removes damnation from light sins now because he regards them as damnable in paganism.

## CHAPTER II. On an evil will, its effect, and ignorance

[Note: [Col. 0865D] The Master, II, distinction 42.]

But, as I said a little earlier, goods or evils come before us in two forms. The first are rooted in thought; the second spring from the root so as to become works. I rightly call them one and another, because what lies hidden in thought cannot be the same thing as what appears in action. Thus one sin is an evil will; another sin is the disorderly operation of its disposition. [Col. 0865B] These are the two deaths.

[Note: [Col. 0865] Compare chapter 49 of this part, and the notes on it.]

But which is more blameworthy? Certainly the second stain. For the first is almost always present together with the second; since the first is harmful in itself, the second harms only through the other. An action which comes second, however horrible it may appear, is without fault if the mind is innocent. For if the heart is pure—“Blessed are the pure in heart” (Matt. 5:8)—then shameful acts do not proceed from such a heart. Things that appear outwardly often seem shameful acts, but are not, because they do not proceed from the heart. For if they were truly crimes, they would have proceeded from the heart according to the Lord’s saying.

[Col. 0865C] The mind incurs a stain whenever it either consents, against conscience, to an unlawful thing, or through carelessness fails to resist because it is ignorant. Of this it is said: “The ignorant person shall be ignored” (1 Cor. 14:38). For one who is ignorant in such a way as not to be guilty through ignorance—because neither negligence produced it nor wickedness of life deserved it—incurs no guilt from what he does or leaves undone in ignorance. Conversely, one who does good without knowing it is judged unworthy of reward.

Humans and beasts commit many of the same acts, which in humans are called criminal and in beasts natural. Why? Anger and concupiscence drive them headlong without the guidance of reason; and they are not blamed because they lack discernment. [Col. 0865D] Human beings are to be accused because they act against conscience, or, if that is not the case, because through fault they do not know what they could have known. Hence the Lord says: “That servant who knew his lord’s will and did not act according to his will shall be beaten with many stripes; but he who did not know it and did things worthy of stripes shall be beaten with few” (Luke 12:47).

But what does “he did not know, yet did things worthy of stripes” mean, unless that he was ignorant through fault and therefore, while ignorant, did things worthy of stripes? For one who is ignorant by nature and creation appears to be without fault and without grace in what he commits ignorantly. Thus persons regenerated by Christ’s grace, whom nature deprived of the faculty of understanding—though the case differs for someone who once possessed that faculty but lost it through his own fault—appear like infants newly born. [Col. 0866A] They await the certain salvation appropriate to baptism, neither increased by merit nor diminished by vice, even though, driven by anger and concupiscence in the manner of beasts, they commit many foul and many cruel deeds.

If these had not been baptized, they would have had this fault; yet their evil movements and acts would not be imputed, because, like beasts, they lack understanding. But if concupiscence harms those born without understanding, why does it not harm those who have been born and are adults, even though unsound in an evil way? If concupiscence before the washing consigns the insane to Gehenna, how much more its own worse movements and still more wicked acts do so. Yet though such persons are somewhat advanced in age, because they remain infants in understanding, they undergo nearly the judgment of infants. In persons of this kind, whether washed or unwashed, [Col. 0866B] I consider either another’s benefit or another’s harm, because I do not know that any actual and personal goods or evils are found in them. For they do not possess the treasure of conscience from which a good man brings forth good and an evil man evil. They are therefore neither good nor evil from themselves, and yet they are such from another source.

## CHAPTER III. Whether less is imputed to those of lesser understanding
Post baptism, then, if nothing is imputed to persons who are altogether brutish because they make no use at all of reason, are not their harms imputed less to those who are less capable, because they use reason less? And just as natural ignorance wholly excuses the brutish, because they know nothing at all, does it not likewise excuse others wherever they are naturally ignorant, so that whatever natural ignorance conceals in anyone, whether done or left undone, neither benefits nor harms them? For ignorance introduced by carelessness or fault should seek pardon for what is done, saying to God: “Do not remember my ignorances” (Ps. 24:7). Plainly, our ignorance and each of its effects are blameworthy. But the ignorance of nature, and each of its effects, is to be lamented. For it conceals from simple people certain subtleties in faith and morals—namely, fragments of the Lord’s passion—things reserved for the perfect, while they must be fed with coarser food. Hence the simpler multitude is less strong in faith and less restrained in conduct; yet, while it faithfully employs the powers given to it, if it does not guard against what it does not know, it seems free from blame in that act in which a person of understanding would sin criminally. For the Lord says: “To everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required of him” (Luke 12:48). This is undoubtedly a general command, concerning not knowledge alone, but also virtues and money—in short, every human advantage, both inward and outward.

But if much is required of one to whom much has been given, is not less also required of one to whom less has been given? Finally, of one to whom nothing has been given in some matter, will nothing be required in that same matter—provided that it is not that person’s own fault that nothing has been given? Thus it seems certain that a person to whom no money has been given is not at all to be accused for not having given it; nor one to whom bodily health and strength have not been granted, for not having contended in the contest after the manner of a healthy and vigorous man. Therefore, if the Author of all things has denied someone understanding altogether, will He require of him what exceeds the conduct of a sensible person? Or if someone is naturally deprived, in some undertaking, of the counsel of foresight, will he be charged as guilty—especially if he is a Christian—because he did not sufficiently guard against himself?

## Chapter IV. That Jews and Gentiles Are Not Excused

The Jews have no excuse in their sin of not believing in Christ, because He came to them; therefore the Gentiles have an excuse, to whom nothing about Him was proclaimed. But how do they have an excuse? Is their not believing in Christ a sin, as it is for the Jews, yet they are excused in their sin whereas the Jews are not? Minor sins, for example, are customarily excused in the baptized and the married by the power of preceding sacraments, so that they are not imputed. But where there is no remedy—especially amid the darkness of the Gentiles—how can what is truly done wrong be excused? Do remedies excuse guilt among believers, while among unbelievers what is not guilt, though thought to be so, is excused?

But because “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 2:6), do the nations displease God because they lack faith? Certainly they do not please Him, because they are not righteous; plainly, without faith they cannot be righteous. Indeed, they displease Him because “those who sinned without the law shall perish without the law” (Rom. 2:12). They cannot avoid sinning because they lack the protection afforded by faith; for “this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith” (1 John 4:5). Therefore they do not please God because they are not righteous, and they displease Him because they have sinned—not perhaps because they do not believe in Christ. Certainly, although one may displease God without faith, this need not result from that cause but from another.

Thus, if an unmarried man, while begetting a son, offends God, he does not offend because he begets, but because he commits fornication. Similarly, perhaps one who lacks faith does not please God, yet not because he does not believe, but because, by not believing, he lives wrongly against conscience. But if not believing in Christ is no fault for those to whom nothing about Him has been communicated, because this cannot in any way be understood of itself, should not everything similarly hidden be free from blame? If, then, some fault is unknown in such a way and thus cannot be avoided, is guilt incurred by committing it? Thus, if someone is innocently ignorant of Christ, what fault is it if he does not honor Him with the worship due to Him?

Shall we therefore absolve such uninstructed persons, among the Gentiles, from idolatry, and among all people from liability for any stain whatever, so that no enormities of whatever kind are imputed to them whenever they know them neither through another’s communication nor can know them of themselves, being small in understanding—though they are nevertheless to undergo judgment for other matters in which conscience holds them guilty? Whoever affirms this will depart not so much from human judgment as from customary opinion. Whoever prefers to maintain it will say either that the ignorance by which Christ is neither believed nor honored in the ways due to Him is of one kind, while that by which crimes are committed is of another, so that the former defends the unbeliever and the latter deceives the wrongdoer.

But one who says this should show, by this reason or another, why he says it. If human understanding had not been corrupted, it would wholly grasp what accords with religion; and therefore, being deprived of its powers while it heaps up defilements, it is rightly reproved. Nevertheless, even if you suppose its original purity restored, it could not comprehend without revelation “the mystery hidden from the ages” (Col. 1:26); consequently, faith in the incarnation is innocently unknown while nothing is heard about it. Or else he will establish an equal principle in both cases: that here the ignorant person is not held liable for ignorance, while there the person who does not believe is already judged.

But how, then, is the Gentile excused in comparison with the Jew? Does being excused mean that guilt is imputed less: that the pagan is condemned because he does not believe, but the Jew more severely, so that, when the two are compared, the Gentile has no sin while the Jew has sin?

But how can an evil which cannot be known, and which therefore is not done against conscience—when thefts, murders, and other punishable things proceed from the heart—be charged? Does this too have a rationale, but lie hidden among the secrets of the Son? Or, just as at every time He mercifully enlightens some with faith, now through hearing, now through inward prompting, and, by the merit of faith, grants knowledge capable of salvation or capable of condemnation; just as, grace going before in all things and free choice cooperating, He strips the wicked and adorns the upright: so too, employing a hidden judgment, does He, because of evil merits, blind the mind, either so that it does not believe, or, even if it has believed, so that through failure to distinguish good from evil it becomes foolish; but in matters already examined does He at times deny the power of acting well? Why He has mercy on this person and hardens that one (Rom. 9:15), do not hope to know before you are blessed.

## Chapter V. On Ignorance

It is therefore established that ignorance caused by fault has neither defense nor power to excuse acts done rashly. The first transgression is also the cause both of ignorance of things to be known and of forgetfulness of things known; for each accompanies guilt, and comes when guilt comes and departs when guilt departs.

What then? Is nothing excused through ignorance when ignorance itself exists through fault? There is, however, a very great difference between being ignorant through another’s fault and through one’s own. For ignorance, like the stain inherited from parents, is certainly less blameworthy than that which comes from oneself. Therefore, just as both kinds of guilt are imputed before baptism, but only one’s own afterward, so perhaps neither kind of ignorance provides an excuse among the Gentiles, while one does among Christians: namely, that which is in you without arising from your own fault, but not the other, which is in you because of your own fault and which, as stated, plainly has neither defense nor power to excuse rash acts.

But although it is reasonable that ignorance should not defend one whom fault blinds, the question remains: why should pagans—ignorant in some matter, whether through parental inheritance or bodily burden, without any personal act of their own—rightly be accused for things done unknowingly? Yet just as grace comes to the aid of such ignorance, perhaps it likewise abandons it to evil because of its work. Unless it is rather necessary to suppose that the original stain and its companion, natural ignorance, are alike, and that both, by God’s hidden judgment, are sometimes charged in wrath and sometimes excused by grace. Ignorance produced by actual fault is charged, and more severely; why should that produced by original fault not be charged too, though less severely; and that born from the burden of the flesh occupy a middle position?

## Chapter VI. Whence Ignorance Arises and Is Aggravated

We are ignorant by hereditary right; we aggravate ignorance by earthly dwelling; and we heap up what has been aggravated through unrestrained transgressions. There is a difference between what is hereditary and what is one’s own. Likewise, among one’s own conditions, that which comes from bodily constitution, and is ascribed to nature—though corrupted—differs from that which comes from the mind’s deviation and is attributed to free choice. We are affected greatly by inherited weakness, more by corruption of constitution, and most of all by dissolution of the soul.

There is a conjunction of original stain with its own ignorance. There is another conjunction of impulses of the flesh, perhaps likewise with its own ignorance. Finally, there is a third—not merely perhaps—by which we do evil and, by doing evil, understand perversely. God imputes all three before conversion: the first two indeed by a hidden judgment, but the third openly. Afterward, once regeneration has been received, He seems to attend only to the third—unless grace is withdrawn through apostasy, by violation of the covenant.

## Chapters VII, VIII, IX, X, XI. Various Cases Are Related

Fearing thieves and enemies, I surround my house with a rampart; I conduct water through excavated ground for the necessary use of a mill. Here a father, there a mother, coming from afar to visit their son, falls in unwittingly. Am I rightly accused of parricide because I did not know of the parents’ arrival?

As I am about to eat, I prepare food with a knife for eating, as is customary. Meanwhile my master commands a servant to hurry swiftly to him, repeatedly shouting. The servant, rushing as the way lay, passes close by me and by chance falls upon the iron which I held in my hand while attending to the food; he dies. Which of the three is the murderer? Can not each defend himself from liability?

A mother, hindered by adequate reasons, cannot sufficiently care for her child; she obtains a nurse, sufficiently suitable so far as she herself can determine. Through the nurse’s negligence the little child dies; or misfortune obstructs the nurse even while she acts carefully. For example, while she is attending the child, either a rabid dog unexpectedly attacks and inflicts a mortal wound upon him, or a sudden storm arises and a collapsing part of the dwelling crushes the infant. What have the parents sinned here, and what has the nurse—who is not negligent, but intent on carefulness—sinned?

A man, having his wife with him in their bed, rises by night and goes out to relieve himself. Meanwhile she—such are women’s evil arts—hastens to adultery. To prevent her husband from discovering it, she substitutes for herself in her place a maidservant who is privy to the matter. He, suspecting nothing less than such a substitution, after returning embraces his bedfellow; and because no suspicion of such a thing, nor any distinction in touch, presented itself, the matter remains undiscovered. While the husband is heavy with sleep, the mistress returns at dawn and the maid slips away. What then? Shall we say that the man committed adultery? Or, if the woman was a relative by blood, that he also committed incest with a kinswoman? Or rather, that so far as lay in him, he had intercourse with his own wife?

Robbers secretly carry off a child from his cradle; they die, while the child survives. When he becomes a young man, he finds no indication of his native land. Nor does his mother, investigating what has become of her child, hear anything even giving rise to suspicion. By chance the two come together and, with mutual consent, finally enter into marriage under the authority of the Church. Mother and son celebrate marriage, being unknown to each other. But perhaps she should not have married anyone, nor he taken any woman, from whom either might have come to doubt that he was dealing with his mother or she with her offspring. Yet who will dissolve a marital union already made, when suspicion never does this, but only certain and proved knowledge?

But what will a man do whom his mother secretly abandoned and exposed? He cannot remain continent: “It is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. 7:9). For not all receive this saying which commends continence; only the one who can receive it should receive it. What then? Shall he marry no woman of an age from which he might doubt whether she is his mother? But on that reasoning he must avoid every age: he must not marry an older woman lest she be his mother or maternal aunt; one equal in age to himself, or younger, may be his sister. Thus he must marry no woman at all, since every woman can at least be suspected of belonging to his own kindred.

What then? Since one was abducted and the other abandoned, and each is uncertain who or whence he is, may neither obtain for himself a spouse from any place, for fear that the union be polluted by incest? But then no one should marry, for it may happen that a woman thought unrelated by birth is in fact a relative; and this is frequently corrected by experience, though marriages nevertheless continue in their ordinary course. For divine ordinance commanded celibacy upon no one except one who freely chose it. Therefore, one who knows his own lineage should provide for himself a woman whom he knows not to be related to his own kin. But one who knows nothing of his tribe—for all either are ignorant or conceal it from themselves—does not at all know whom to seek or whom to avoid. What shall he do? Let him act freely: let him marry, without doubt whether it is good or evil, whichever woman he finds suitable for himself. For one whose conscience accuses him in an act however good is guilty—not because he does evil, but because he thinks his action evil. For the Apostle says: “Everything that is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23); plainly, whatever you do, if you believe it is done wrongly, it is guilt.

## Chapter XII. A Work Is Judged from the Heart

[Note: [Col. 0871D] *Magister*, Book II, distinctions 40 and 42.]

Therefore, if Church ordinances have joined persons under the yoke of marriage, even though blood relatives have come together, so long as this is unknown, it is absolutely not imputed; I have offered certain examples. But innumerable similar cases are found, in all of which something customarily happens which, considered in itself, seems deserving of severe punishment. Yet because the soul, in whose keeping lie the praise and blame of all that is done, is conscious of no malice in itself, if it is not deceived, the work itself is not evil either. Surely, unless a house is laid desolate by death, how will a dead person appear at its gate?

[Note: [Col. 0871D] Augustine, *Sermon on the Mount*, Book I, ch. 12.]

If you remove the first death from the heart, how will you find the second in the deed, or the third in habit? And just as, when the soul is pure, the work is impure in no respect, so too, when the mind is impure, the action is necessarily defiled. A work therefore takes its quality from the heart, and also its quantity. For because the eye is single, the body is full of light; and as single as the eye is, so full of light is the body (Matt. 6:23; Luke 11:34). Thus the poor widow contributed more than the rich (Luke 21:3), because what was smaller in the thing was weighed by the will. The same reasoning applies conversely: very often an action is, by its own nature, either only slightly evil or even good; but because it proceeds from a most evil heart, the divine examination judges it most evil.

Sometimes too, what seems to us excessively cruel—as when a diseased son, distressed by the harsh but corrective beating of his father, throws himself into death—or excessively shameful—as when an imprudent mother, excessively bent over her work, miscarries a dead child, or while sleeping, without contemplating anything of the kind, smothers a child lawfully born—before God, who Himself is the examiner of affections, is imputed in one case to justice and in the other, at most, to negligence.

## Chapter XIII. Judgment Is Not to Be Made According to the Outcome of an Act

But if anyone tries to maintain, from the events mentioned above and similar ones whenever they occur, that those whom I considered free from blame above become sources of blame, I should like to know why. Is it because such things happen through ignorance arising from negligence, and the outcomes should therefore be imputed as faults of disposition? Or is it because, even though the purity of the soul remains untouched, such events are themselves of such a nature that they rightly cannot go unpunished?

But if accidental events are required of a person because of themselves, from whom they take whatever occasion they have for coming to be, certainly not even good men, while they act well, are free from blame, since evils very often arise even from actions well done. For when the apostles instruct the world with heavenly teaching and form it by saving examples, they are to some “an aroma of life unto life,” to others “an aroma of death unto death”; and in both, Jesus Christ is a good aroma to God (2 Cor. 2:13). As He Himself testifies, if He had not spoken to the Jews, they would have had no sin (John 15:22). His venerable teaching and wonderful life became guilt to those who despised them, just as the resurrection became a hanging for the betrayer.

[Note: [Col. 0872D] Author of the *Book of Questions on the Old and New Testament*, question 94, among Augustine.]

Therefore, let all who examine reality as it is with keen discernment hate evils for their own sake, regard good things with suspicion—or rather avoid them—lest evils follow from good things. This is a hateful decree, fit to be followed only by one whose mind is unsound. For when someone, guided by reason, “provides good things in the sight of all people” (2 Cor. 8:1), so that God may be honored thereby and the neighbor built up, if a foolish person nevertheless takes offense, the prudent person is not at fault. The latter does what he ought and benefits; the former takes offense at another’s good and harms himself. For if you act well and discerningly, whatever follows from it, you are not held guilty.

## Chapter XIV. No One Is Liable for Many Outcomes

Outcomes, then, are not stained with their own discoloring dye so as to infect with stain all those from whom they derive their origin; nor do they contract a plague as though from the negligence of the ignorant, so as to become destructive to them. For if things of this kind cannot happen without the fault of those whom we think absolved, because ignorance produces negligence and negligence produces guilt in outcomes, then a double tendency defiles a person: the first through a defect of the heart, the second through a defect of outcome.

It follows that whoever does something from which the aforesaid outcomes can arise is defiled twice if they occur, once if they do not. For, so far as depends on him, they occur when he permits that from which they can occur. He is certainly guilty because, deceived through ignorance as if by negligence, he does not guard against something from which evil could arise. Accordingly, let no one eat, lest he consume something that brings death upon himself; let no one refrain from eating, lest by abstaining he encounter certain death. A person who sleeps is foolish, because sleep offers occasion to dangers. He is more foolish if he avoids that which nature does not permit to be avoided. The farmer is foolish because he prepares in his field a hiding-place for an ambusher, and in his house provisions for gluttony; he is far more foolish if he lies idle through sloth, because he does not prevent hunger together with death. In short, everyone will be foolish whatever he does, since nothing can be done from which one should not fear danger. He will be foolish and mad if he gives himself to idleness, because in that way he also abandons what ought to be done. Rather, the person who strives not merely to begin but also to complete what reason and experience urge appears truly wise; he does not vainly and curiously foretell what misfortune may happen, but is attentive only to what ought to be done and to its being done. For no one can, by his own care, either foresee the varieties of outcomes in his actions or, having foreseen them, avoid them in any way, even in part.

What negligence, then, is mine if, while I conduct myself appropriately, I either do not know what nature does not allow me to prevent, or do not guard against what, if I am able to anticipate it, I am not able to escape? Many things do not occur even to the diligent, and it is superfluous to occupy the mind in investigating them. But if, while the mind wanders, someone has considered beforehand who, what, and concerning what matter something may occur, yet sees no reason why he should believe it will occur, will he, fearing what is necessary, pursue empty notions like dreams? But if he sees that the thing he judges ought to be done is of such a kind that he ought to fear future scandal—for “woe to the man through whom scandal comes” (Matt. 18:7)—then he should indeed avoid with all his strength another’s harm. Yet provided that he does not incur harm to his own salvation, he ought to do good, lest another be scandalized; he ought not to do evil.

## Chapter XV. On Negligence, Ignorance, and Weakness

Therefore there is no negligence unless, through your sloth, you either do not know what you ought to know or do not follow what you know. It can indeed happen that you do not know through fault, although you labor to know. I do not consider this properly negligence, but rather penal ignorance. It may likewise happen that your life does not accord with your judgment, not merely because you do not will it, but because you cannot accomplish it. Nor do I consider this negligence, but weakness.

But this weakness, if it arises from a habit of evil or from God’s wrath, is blameworthy; yet let it cry out to be healed: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak” (Ps. 6:3). If it comes from nature, it is absolved, as when you will not to lust, not to grow angry, and the like, yet cannot. The Apostle complains of these things because he does what he does not will; and he no longer does it himself, but the sin that is in him. For those who do not walk according to the flesh, there is no condemnation in these things (Rom. 7:15). Nature bears this weakness together with ignorance, the insuperable with the insuperable. I do not say that they follow nature because creation introduced them, but because our life never lacks them, born as they are from the first disobedience.

Ignorance conceals what is worthy of knowledge; weakness separates even from what is known. But what follows? The grace of the Redeemer unveils hidden things and restores weak things. To a great extent they remain even after faith, but no longer harm; indeed, what harm would they have done even in paganism? I know that they harm as punishments; but I ask whether they harm as guilt. Every guilt is either original or actual. A person derives original guilt from the first transgressor, and actual guilt from himself. But the ignorance or weakness now under discussion does not arise in a person from himself, but from the necessity of nature. Therefore it either is not guilt, or it is original guilt.

[Note: [Col. 0873D] Augustine, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, Book II, ch. 4.]

If it is original guilt, it is imputed to the pagan and forgiven to the Christian. I know well enough that it is original; but I investigate whether it is also guilt. Man was created prudent, knowing useful things, and strong to carry them out; he transgressed. He who sinned through himself was punished in himself; he swelled up against his Maker, lost what had been given by his Maker, abused knowledge, and is punished with ignorance; he abused his powers toward evil and is weakened toward good. Therefore man himself sinned in what he ought not. The Judge imposed the punishment that He ought. Guilt comes only from man; punishment only from the Judge.

## Chapter XVI. On Ignorance and Weakness

Since, therefore, it is established that God’s purity inflicts the impurity of sin upon no one, if it is likewise established that God’s wrath has imposed ignorance and weakness upon guilty man, it must necessarily also be established that these two are punishments of the guilty, and by no means sins. Guilt indeed renders one defiled; weakness, together with the rest, renders one miserable. I know that these were imposed because of Adam’s guilt both upon himself and upon his descendants; yet if the Judge’s hand pours them upon the guilty, I deny that they are sins.

[Note: [Col. 0873D] Augustine, *On Free Choice of the Will*, Book III, chs. 4, 19.]

But if God punished Adam for disobedience so that he became more ignorant and weaker than before, does not anyone who falls into sins likewise, through God’s punishment, fall into ignorance and weakness? In addition to the natural defects designated by these names, transmitted from Adam together with original sin, he receives accidental defects along with his own sin—burdened from his origin and cast down by himself.

Certainly, just as the keeper of the law is strengthened in good, so its transgressor is weakened in it. Likewise, just as the temple of the Holy Spirit shines through so great an indweller, so, when the Spirit flees what is feigned, the mind grows dark. You say to God in the Psalm: “From your commandments I have understood” (Ps. 118:104). Indeed, if you wish to understand the law, keep the commandments. Thus, conversely, it appears that one who does not keep the law does not understand the law. Yet it often happens that a transgressor understands the law in many matters. But the understanding of the transgressor is as nothing compared with that of the obedient person.

We therefore increase ignorance and weakness, which we received from Adam, in proportion as we sin. If we judge these in Adam not to be sins but punishments, why should we not maintain the same principle in ourselves: that apart from God each person is defiled both originally and actually, while from God each is punished for defilements both original and accidental?

[Note: [Col. 0874D] Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XV, ch. 9.]

Certainly, we have learned from the tradition of the Fathers and know by experience that, just as God, to curb human pride, after the Fall checked human beings both with dullness and with sickness—for they had raised themselves in vain conceit from the little advantage still remaining and therefore had to be humbled by a second persecution—so after the Flood He diminished their length of life and stature, and day by day wore down the powers both of mind and body. Therefore, while the body burdens the soul more or less, whether according to the nature of its constitution or, what is worse, according as the soul entangles itself in its desires, God is pleased to infuse into the soul, in different degrees, dullness and languor arising from such bodily burden—unless the grace of the Creator strengthens the inward person against the assault of the outward one.

But if all dullness together with all languor is not sin but punishment alone, what shall we say? Is it not sin and guilt to be ignorant of the good that ought to be done and of the evil that ought to be left undone? Is it not sin and guilt, finally, to be ignorant of Christ, not merely through a defect or lack of nature, but also through the wickedness of life? Shall we absolve from guilt the Jews and the pagans who, intoxicated with antiquity, disdain the cup of novelty? Far from it!

For some things are sufficiently good in themselves, or not evil at all, yet become evil through certain additions. Everyone praises prayer and almsgiving; no one condemns eating and sleeping. Yet when it is time to keep vigil, sleeping is sloth. To devour human flesh is inhuman; giving in pursuit of empty glory is a crime; worshipping idols is sacrilege. Thus we do not accuse ignorance and sickness as such, but lament them. Yet either being ignorant of what one ought not to be ignorant of through fault, or failing to resist when one ought, is certainly grave guilt.

Thus ignorance is from God in such a way that abominable ignorance is not from God; just as giving alms is from God, but giving them for vain glory is from the evil one. But abominable ignorance is not that which is natural; or, if ignorance that arises through fault is not itself guilt—or, more truly, if ignorance and weakness naturally inborn through the bodily burden are called not only punishments of sin but also sins, though not personal but original—shall we not say that they proceed in no way from God, but, just as what happens through one’s own fault, so natural defects happen through the fault of one’s origin?

If so, they undoubtedly pertain to the soul’s condemnation before baptism, and perhaps also the things that proceed from them. But if their possession itself makes a person guilty, they will either be counted among original sins—and each person will possess an excessive multitude of original sins—or among personal sins, and a person will be a sinner in many matters without an act of sin, or with an act but without sinning by reason, so that a person is evil without bringing evil out of an evil treasure. Whichever of the two is the case, these things, together with their causes, are imputed before baptism and forgiven through baptism. They always remain, yet never harm.

## Chapter XVII. What Evils Are from God

[Note: [Col. 0875D] *Magister*, Book II, distinction 37, and Book I, distinction 46.]

But the prophet, wishing to teach us that every kind of affliction proceeds from God, taught that there is no evil in a city which the Lord has not made. He did not say, “There is no sin in a city which the Lord has not made,” but “evil” (Amos 3:6), meaning that whatever is not sin and is evil has been made by the Lord. In this statement perhaps he includes ignorance and weakness, which perhaps differ from sins both in name and in reality, yet are evils. Perhaps the prophet understood that the Lord made these when he said: “Forming light and creating darkness” (Isa. 45:7). For light is made by God, and, if one is to believe it, He also makes the darkness of ignorance. Indeed, concerning other things which are evil but not sins, the prophet added: “Making peace and creating evil” (ibid.). That by “evil” you should understand disturbance is indicated to you by the preceding word “peace.”

God brings war, and man brings war: the one well, the other wickedly. Man commonly prepares war, yet it never occurs unless the Lord wills it; and His willing is to effect. A war takes place: God’s justice causes it, human madness commits it. Therefore, warfare itself, if you look to God, is justice; if to man, it is madness and therefore guilt.

I know that conflicts of combatants are sometimes undertaken by people justly and even holy; but I require here the manner in which war is wickedly undertaken. “Length of days is in God’s right hand, but riches and honor in His left” (Prov. 3:2). Two men alike pursue riches, honors, or powers through theft, plundering, fraud, perjuries, sacrileges, superstitions—in short, through every practice driven by greed or vexed ambition—with evil craft and unceasing labor. One obtains them; the other cannot. Why? He in whose left hand are riches and honor, He from whom, according to the Apostle, “all authority is” (Rom. 13:1), is pleased to give to one and deny to the other. The person pursues wickedly and obtains wickedly; God gives well.

## Chapter XVIII. Whether Ignorance and Weakness in Us Are from God

At times, therefore, we pursue worldly things wickedly; but God rightly opens the way to obtaining them. We possess what has been obtained wickedly; but God causes us to possess it, certainly not wickedly. Therefore possessing itself is from God, namely, in a good way; possessing wickedly is from ourselves, namely, in an evil way. For sin belongs to us, but holiness to God.

May it not similarly be the case that God produces ignorance or weakness in us, just as regards Himself, who punishes the guilty, it is just, while as regards us, who deserve it by wicked living, it is guilt? While we live wickedly, we hasten toward ignorance and weakness, so that we may not know what we ought to know or be unable to do what we ought to do. We indeed hasten toward these defects, and God confronts us with them and hands them over to us, unless in His mercy He checks the rush of our madness. Thus we have these defects from ourselves and receive them from the Lord: from the Lord as punishments, from ourselves as guilt.

Whatever we sin through the course of these defects is not excused by ignorance or weakness, because we arrive at both through our own fault. Since you have them from God, they are punishment; if you did not deserve to have them, they are no longer guilt to you. Therefore, while they are naturally present, they are punishment and not guilt.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] Augustine, *On Free Choice of the Will*, Book III, ch. 22.]

Whatever you do not know naturally through ignorance, or cannot do through weakness, if you wholly do not know and cannot do it, you do not sin at all in such matters, because the expiation of regeneration excuses invincible impediments. Before baptism, however, because original guilt is exacted, the proliferations of the aforesaid defects which it produces are rightly exacted as well. Hence the pre-voluntary motions of the soul which no one can overcome are punished before baptism; this is evident because they are remitted through baptism.

But I think that such punishment is the mildest of all. In what you do disorderly, you are undoubtedly more guilty in proportion to the knowledge you possess and the resistance you are able to make. Hence the first man was reproved with most severe punishment for his transgression, because he was plainly endowed with such intelligence and gifts that he could without difficulty recognize the truth and adhere to it once recognized.

Although some, preferring the easier opinion, maintain that riches and honor are in God’s left hand to give or permit according as people are worthy or unworthy. Therefore God, in anger, sometimes does not bestow what those who wickedly aspire step by step to the summit, or try to satisfy any perverse will, seek. When this occurs, God is said to do it, because it would not happen unless He permitted it. Thus God “turned the hearts of the wicked so that they hated His people and dealt deceitfully with His servants” (Ps. 104:25).

## Chapter XIX. In Wars, What Is to Be Imputed to God and What to Man
For we have said that God brings about wars: for through him they occur among human beings, just as famine and plagues do. Let us see what in wars is to be imputed to God, and what to man. Indignation, full of pride and avarice, moved the Romans against the Jews when they refused tribute; and their destruction and captivity, not undeserved because of the wickedness of their morals, the righteous Judge willed. But what he willed rightly, he saw the Romans will wickedly. For both were preparing for Judaea to be destroyed and carried into captivity: the one from justice, the other from insolence. Therefore it pleased God that his good will should be fulfilled through their evil will. Yet neither the evil will nor the evil execution of the deed could please the Just One, since both were unjust. But that good came about through their evil contrivance was pleasing to God. Thus the furious mind eager to destroy Judaea; the preparations of that furious mind; the warfare that pursued those preparations; finally, their laying waste the country and leading its devastated people into captivity—all this is surely detestable to God, since an evil action cannot please the good God. To be ignorant and to be weakened, finally to possess a thing and to be in another’s power, is not to act; it is God’s will. Yet the suffering produced by an action displeasing to God pleases God: so that what the Roman destroys and carries into captivity does not please God, while what the Jew suffers in defeat and captivity does please him. “There is no evil which God has not made” (Amos 3:6).

## Chapter XX. An unjust action, being evil, is not from God

[Note: Col. 0877D, *Magister*, II, distinction 37.]

But you will say: an unjust action is evil, and yet it is not from God. You are entirely right. But another kind of evil is at issue: namely, not that which defiles, but that which afflicts; not the evil belonging to the agent, but that inflicted by the agent. For what you do is plainly an action, perhaps an unjust one; but what results from it is generally an affliction, and never unjust. For while you rise against someone either cruelly or because it is right that it be done, you afflict and he is afflicted: to afflict, therefore, belongs to you; to be afflicted belongs to him. He receives torment from what is his own; you do not receive it from what is your own, unless perhaps the torturer happens to be wearied by torturing. But it is one thing to torture another, another to be wearied by the torture itself; for sometimes one action brings on two troubles, one for the afflicter and another for the afflicted. Yet reason distinguishes the intermingling of things and assigns to each what belongs to it. To afflict, then, is the cause of punishment, not punishment itself.

[Col. 0878B] These are the evils which the Lord always causes, but their causes only when they are just. For those things that seem evil and harsh to human beings proceed always from God, but only sometimes from man. You can always endeavor to inflict them, but what you desire will not occur unless God wills it. And just as you are never holy except with the holy God—for it is not through yourself that you yourself do good, but through God’s grace with you, so that you produce a good work, though God acts first—so too you think that you inflict penal evil, but God inflicts it through you. But pleasurable evil, which is sin, you do by yourself; yet you would not do it unless God—not, I say, willed it, but rather permitted it. God, creating penal evil in a human being, strikes either by himself or through a minister, with a fatherly scourge or a cruel punishment. But when the stroke is inflicted by the Judge, he is always either merciful or just in inflicting it. The man receiving the stroke is sometimes unjust in receiving it. For example, a worshipper of God, negligent in obedience and given over to vices, falls under them and is rebuked by the very severe correction of the scourge; stunned, he renders neither the care due to one subject to him nor worship to God. And because he is weakened through fault, and through weakness does not discharge what he owes, the weakness too is not undeservedly reckoned a fault. For whenever through your own vice you fall into a condition from which you cannot withdraw your foot without offending God, that very falling is also an offense. Such suffering, therefore, is punishment from the judge and fault from the accused.

## Chapter XXI. By whose ministry God strikes, and how

[Col. 0878D]

When God strikes, he employs now the ministry of angels, now that of human beings. Nor does anyone doubt that this is done sometimes through irrational animals, sometimes through inanimate elements; it also happens that a human being is struck within himself. But whether God does such things through angels as well, or even by himself, is perhaps not sufficiently known. God works through both good and bad ministers, angels and human beings. Through good angels he overthrew Sodom; through an evil destroyer, God the Judge killed the firstborn of the wicked. Thus, among us too, a good judge acts upon criminals through executioners—through evil persons—and sometimes also through good persons, acting well even through those who act badly.

The evil destroyer appeared when God passed over and freed his own people, teaching that, from the blood of the lamb, the figure of Tau should be applied to the doorposts (Exod. 12:24; Ezek. 9:4). It was certainly an evil spirit that strove to destroy the firstborn of each household, marked as they were by faith and love; from this attempt the form of Tau, an image of the cross impressed upon the forehead, restrains him. Therefore God torments evil people through evil angels, and likewise through good ones. For at the end of the world, when they gather the tares from the wheat, they, the reapers, “will remove from his kingdom all scandals,” binding them in bundles to be burned (Matt. 13:30).

Evil spirits daily draw down to hell souls which they also unwillingly extract from their bodies. [Col. 0879B] Hence the Lord says: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you” (Luke 2:20 [apparently intended: Luke 12:20]). These are indeed the exactors who commit sin and without interruption exact punishment for sin; they demand the soul in the night of this world—but where will they lead it except to hell? For if Lazarus’s soul is carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom, is it not fitting that the rich man’s soul should be buried by demons in hell? (Luke 16:22.) Surely holy souls are always transferred into rest by the ministry of angels, and wicked souls to Gehenna by the ministry of demons. These demons both draw them to the lower world and demand them from their bodies; the same demons torment them in their bodies, and are therefore thought to heal when they cease injuring them. They would truly heal if they cured not only the sickness inflicted by themselves, but also that found in the human being. Nor do they attack only the wicked, but [Col. 0879C] also the good, bringing with them loss of possessions, bodily injuries, and death itself.

[Note: Col. 0879D, Gregory, on the final passage of Job.]

Thus Satan, having shaken the banqueting hall, bereft the holier Job of his holy sons (Job 1). They were certainly holy; Job possessed them far better, because far more securely, dead in Abraham’s bosom than alive in the world. Accordingly, when children of equal number were afterward born to him, he recovered everything twofold (Job 42:10).

## Chapter XXII. What demons are like toward good and evil persons

[Note: Col. 0879D, *Magister*, book II, distinction 6.]

Demons use wicked people as they please, like cattle belonging to them by their own right, unless they are restrained by the mercy of him “who places the depths in his storehouses,” knowing with himself what good will come to us through evil persons. But they always wish to harm the good and can never do so unless God permits it, either for the testing of saints, so that they may recognize their own strength and become grateful to God, or so that they may recognize their weakness and seek to be strengthened. Thus Satan complains that the Lord has hedged Job about with his possessions (Job 4:10); but once he hears “Go” from God, he is sent against Job and immediately attacks. God says, “Go”: although he abhors the evil intentions of evil persons, nevertheless he embraces the good outcomes of their evil intentions. Evil persons act wickedly, but the Spirit of the Lord “works all things together for good,” since he turns even evil deeds toward good ends. He therefore permits evils to occur because he intends to bring good out of evils.

## Chapter XXIII. On the sending of evil spirits

[Note: Col. 0879D, *Magister*, above.]
