The prince of demons sends out his followers; hence they too are called angels of God, according to the words: “And the angel of the Lord pursuing them” (Ps. 34:6). The former sends them for the destruction of all; the Lord, for the testing of his own. They agree in the sending, but differ in the cause of the sending; and thus they do not fully agree, because they send in different ways and for different purposes. Each sends so that both evil and good persons may be tormented. They aim at the same thing and will the same thing, but they differ greatly. One is guided by reason; the other is driven by disturbed, unbridled frenzy.

Hence Satan is said to have gone out from the face of the Lord. When he took Job’s children and goods and afflicted Job himself most severely, the Lord’s prohibition prevented him from inflicting death. For to kill was no more difficult than to torment, unless the divine will had opposed it. Why, indeed, would the Lord forbid death if Satan either could not or would not inflict it? He who daily brings death upon saints through his members can bring it about also by himself; indeed, he sometimes does bring it about. For when a plague is inflicted upon many wicked persons, just as good persons may suffer distress among them, why should they not also perish among them? It is credible that the calamity of shipwreck and war, as also of plagues, famine, and similar things, is produced, if not always, at least frequently by evil spirits.

[Col. 0880C] These indeed are the visitations through evil angels by which the Lord sends the wrath of his indignation. Hence, on the passage, “He called famine upon the land” (Ps. 104:16), this interpretation is also found:

[Note: Col. 0880D, in the Gloss from Augustine on this passage.]

“He called” it as though it were an animate person, perhaps because he sends evil angels who are set over such things. Thus he called famine—that is, the angel set over famine. But lest they harm as much as they wish, they frequently hear: “Do not harm the earth or the sea” (Rev. 7:3). For in Job Satan is said to be mocked by the angels of God, who are set over the powers of the air, lest they harm us. This is the meaning found there:

[Note: Col. 0880D, in the Gloss.]

“This dragon which you formed to be mocked by him” (Ps. 104:27).

Therefore spiritual torturers as well as bodily ones—that is, demons as well as human beings—both indiscriminately afflict good persons and evil. Scripture sometimes says that holy angels torment wicked persons, and this perhaps occurs frequently and in various ways. Reason, however, does not compel us to conclude that whenever, or in whatever manner, a human being is struck, it must happen externally, either by an angel or by a human being. A person can waste away through a natural illness or an accidental injury, and can perish in other ways without the agency of a minister.

## Chapter XXIV. On God’s scourge and angels presiding over souls and kingdoms

[Col. 0881A]

[Note: Col. 0881D, *Magister*, II, distinction 11.]

But however God’s scourge comes, it seeks either to strike in order to correct, to torment one who is unrepentant, or, when it finds a good man, to advance him in goodness. Yet that a good man is struck by a good angel does not occur to me, except perhaps for this reason. It is certain that, while souls are pilgrims in the body, each is assigned to an individual angel. Hence, forbidding anyone to cause one of his little ones to stumble, the Lord adds that “their angels always behold the face of God” (Matt. 18:10). While they guard those entrusted to them, they both defend them from evils and aid them in good things; yet the right of free choice remains entirely intact, and the path of uprightness is nowhere abandoned. For they would not otherwise have willed to be present except as is fitting.

Just as every soul, so too all kingdoms are believed to have been entrusted to the guardianship of angels. Hence Moses, according to another translation, says: “He set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God” (Deut. 32:8). This is expounded as follows: just as we read that a guardian angel is assigned to each human being, so we should believe that angels have been appointed as princes of nations. For in Daniel we read of Michael, prince of the people—that is, of the Jews—and of the angel of the Persians or Greeks (Dan. 10:13). But after and through the Lord’s cross, the leader with his army, serving the people of God, is believed to have migrated from a non-people to the people of God, from the unbelief of the Jews to the conversion of the Gentiles.

## Chapter XXV. That Michael, having left the Jews, guards us

[Col. 0881C]

[Note: Col. 0881D, Isidore, *Origins*, V.]

Nor is there doubt about Michael himself, since he who is called Michael—that is, “Who is like God?”—rightly belongs to those who, being remade by grace in the inner person according to the image of God, have thereby become gods and sons of the Most High. Nor is it absurd to believe that those whom Michael held subject to himself while he guarded the Jewish people migrated with him. For Josephus relates that the angels presiding over the Temple cried out:

[Note: Col. 0881D, book VI, chapter 31 and following; book VII, chapter 12, *The Jewish War*.]

“Let us flee from these dwellings.”

Just as Michael has an army serving him for the guardianship of God’s kingdom, so it is credible that individual angels appointed over the individual kingdoms of the world hold primacy over all those who must provide for each kingdom under their authority.

But when one man contends against another, or one nation against another, it is possible for an evil conflict to be undertaken against a good one. Yet if the angel of the Lord stands beside his own charge, does he not oppose the adversary? Perhaps he strives to benefit his own side, not to harm the other; for that is his office—not to injure a good man, but to assist, as is proper, the one whose protection he has undertaken. For holy angels are bound to those entrusted to them by such affection that in Daniel a certain venerable contention between them is recorded, each standing for his own side while God’s will had not yet become known. Yet some hold that evil angels are assigned as princes over evil nations, and that they stir up wars among nations. Hence the good angel speaking with Daniel says: “Now I shall return, that I may fight against the prince of the Persians” (Dan. 10:20). For it does not seem appropriate to say that battles occur among good beings.

## Chapter XXVI. On Raphael’s office

[Note: Col. 0882D, Isidore, *Origins*, V.]

Just as evil spirits procure hardships, so benevolent ones procure good things for us. Raphael, whose name means “medicine of God,” heals illnesses. Thus, sent to Tobit, he restored sight. The faith of the centurion, commended by the Lord, bears on the same point: when he confesses that he is set under another’s authority, that he has soldiers under him, and that he says to one, “Go,” and he goes; to another, “Come,” and he comes; and to his servant, “Do this,” and he does it (Matt. 8:9), he believes all the more that he who pre-eminent in supreme authority over angels serving under him can command them, and through their ministry heal his absent servant, commanding illness to depart and health to come.

For it is fitting that he who, together with the other two, alone among the other spirits is honored with a proper name because of offices suited to our needs, should be an archangel together with those other two archangels. Thus, because the multitude of the sick is innumerable, the supply of physicians should also abound under the chief physician. Perhaps it belongs to their providence both to avert illnesses and to preserve health.

## Chapter XXVII. On Gabriel’s office

[Col. 0882C]

[Note: Col. 0882D, Isidore, *Origins*, V.]

Gabriel is interpreted “strength of God,” because he is set over undertakings requiring strength, such as wars. Thus he announces the incarnation to the Virgin, his mother, of the one who was coming to overthrow the powers of the air. An army of angels serves under this archangel. And who but he would cooperate in difficult undertakings under so great a prince? By their ministry, just wars seem to be begun, unjust ones impeded, wrongly begun ones mitigated, rightly begun ones administered, and brought now to victory, now to peace. Since their power seems to disperse seditions, they are also rightly thought to bind together covenants of peace.

## Chapter XXVIII. On Michael’s commission

[Col. 0882D] We also read that the commission of expiations and, therefore, of propitiations was entrusted to Michael. Hence he rightly presides over Mother Church, in whom is found the place of expiation and propitiation. Therefore, contemplating Michael’s office, let us say in wonder: “Who is like God, who dwells on high and looks upon lowly things?” He is free from sin and is merciful to expiate sins. He is an expiator when forgiveness of sin occurs, and propitious when reconciliation is granted through forgiveness.

## Chapter XXIX. Michael offers to God the souls and prayers of his own people

Michael, therefore, one of the chief princes, as is read in Daniel (Dan. 10:13), the prince of the angelic host, works with his forces so that human beings may become fit to pass, after this temporal life, into the heavenly one. To him has been given authority over the souls of the saints, to lead them into the paradise of rejoicing. I think that he too, together with his company—and especially each person’s own angel—brings each person’s prayers before the tribunal of the Judge. This is not because, without their ministry, he would be ignorant of the desires of the saints, but because they rejoice to obey their Creator and to benefit human beings, when they announce our prayers to the inhabitants of heaven and intercede with God on our behalf.

[Note: Col. 0883D, *Magister*, IV, distinction 45, §§6–7.]

Thus the angel of Daniel carried to the Lord the prayer Daniel made for the captivity of his people; he had Michael as his helper there, but complained that the angel—that is, the prince—of the kingdom of Persia had opposed him. While this angel acts for those entrusted to him, he believes that Israel ought not yet to be freed from their service, and before the Judge he accuses the sins for which Israel is held under the yoke of captivity. But Daniel’s side prevails.

## Chapter XXX. All angels serve God for human beings

[Note: Col. 0883D, *Magister*, II, distinction 10.]

Just as, Scripture teaching us, we know that the three aforementioned angels together with their subordinates have undertaken offices in the conduct of human affairs, so we judge that the rest—indeed, all alike—serve God in human concerns. Speaking of them, the Apostle says: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent in ministry for those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation?” (Heb. 2:14 [apparently intended: Heb. 1:14]). Ministering by office, and actually sent, they always stand before him who is everywhere. Hence Daniel says: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7:10). For those who range abroad in ministry always stand before him whom they serve by contemplation. Thus Raphael, sent to Tobit, says: “I am one angel of the seven who always stand in the sight of God” (Tob. 12:10). Some nevertheless maintain that some go about ministering, while others stand in contemplation.

## Chapter XXXI. On the cherubim and seraphim

But Scripture mentions the cherubim and seraphim, which are said to be the two orders that stand in attendance, as ministering. Thus one of the seraphim flies to Isaiah and, touching his mouth with a burning stone, cleanses him from fault and makes him fit to speak (Isa. 6:6). The seraphim, indeed, whose name means “burning fire,” is rightly thought to work through fire. Therefore it is not absurd to suppose—though perhaps presumptuous to assert—that by their ministry both the unburned bush burned and Sodom and Gomorrah utterly perished by fire and sulphur. But the same two seraphim who set the cities on fire first brought Lot out of danger (Gen. 19:16). That they were good is clear, since they justly destroy the wicked but mercifully lead the righteous man away from destruction. Hence I judge that those who have authority to punish also have authority to deliver from punishment.

The Prophet too, after saying, “Who makes his angels spirits,” adds: “and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. 104:4). “Burning fire” is the interpretation of *seraphim*. Therefore the seraphim minister to God.

## Chapter XXXII. On the cherubim and seraphim

In Ezekiel the cherubim are said to have lifted up their wings when raised from the earth (Ezek. 10:16). There are other grounds also from which one may infer that the cherubim themselves are assigned to offices. But, as they say, the tradition of the venerable man Dionysius is that the higher spirits enjoy contemplation alone, whereas the lower perform missions, having received the character of their names according to the nature of their offices.

[Note: Col. 0883D, chapter XIII of *The Celestial Hierarchy*, and elsewhere.]

But in Ezekiel a cherub stretches out its hand to the fire (Ezek. 19:7); in Isaiah a seraph removes iniquity (Isa. 6:6), although the name *seraph* belongs to fire while expiation belongs to Michael. Surely the Lord alone removes iniquity; and through whom, if not through him who, by interpretation of his name, holds the place of the Lord? Yet the seraph touched the prophet’s mouth with a coal, as Jerome says:

[Note: Col. 0884D, Jerome, 161.]

“Behold, this has touched your lips, that your iniquity may be taken away” (ibid.).

He admits that he worked in fire, which belongs to his office; he says that iniquity is to be removed, but does not ascribe this removal to himself. Perhaps because the fire was applied through his ministry, while expiation was entrusted to another. Or perhaps through the ministry of the seraphim not only is outward fire kindled, but also the inward fire which is charity; of this it is said: “Charity covers all sins” (1 Pet. 4:8). Thus one of the seraphim touches the prophet’s lips with fire; through fire God kindles charity; charity burns away sins, so that the prophet, no longer defiled in his lips, may become fit for the word of preaching. Hence perhaps hearts are cleansed by charity through the ministry of the seraphim; and expiation obtained through the fruits of repentance restores full propitiation through the ministry of Michael and his soldiers. But in Ezekiel perhaps the cherub is now associated with fire so that in such a matter, full as it is of knowledge, we may examine it inwardly; for *cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge.”

## Chapter XXXIII. Why they are called angel and spirit

[Col. 0884D] The common names of all are *angel* and *spirit*: they are spirits by nature, but angels by office. Hence the Prophet says: “Who makes his angels spirits” (Ps. 104:4).

[Note: Col. 0884D, *Magister*, II, distinction 10.]

For those who are spirits by nature become angels when occasion requires. *Angels* means “messengers”; and I think that all are called angels because there is none among them who is not sent. Hence the Apostle calls all spirits ministering and sent in ministry, in proclamation of Christ who sends them all, for those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation (Heb. 1:14). For he who sends all is pre-eminent over all, while they serve the Father in forming sons for the inheritance.

## Chapter XXXIV. How many orders there are, and to what they are assigned

For provident God, before humanity fell, having planned its restoration, distinguished nine orders of angels necessary for that restoration. For he who had resolved to send heavenly spirits to support our weakness assigned those whom he would send to various offices, undoubtedly suited to our restoration. For what does it mean that the Apostle calls all spirits ministering, except that he understood all to be assigned to ministerial offices? What does it mean that he declares all to be sent in ministry, except that they continually fulfill in action what is laid upon their office? And what does it mean that, after those two statements, he immediately adds a third—“for those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation”—except that both the offices and the exercise of those offices tend to this end, that the predestined may receive the inheritance of salvation? Therefore it is reasonable that offices established with their activities for the salvation of persons should cease after they have been saved, since, according to Scripture, “then every power shall be abolished” (1 Cor. 15:14).

## Chapter XXXV. What the offices are, and how many names they have

There are nine offices of angels, whose names are these: angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominations, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim. Usage expresses the names of these orders in the plural, because there are many who are denoted by these names. When, therefore, you hear the plural, you understand many of that order whose name you hear. But when the terms of the individual orders are uttered in the singular, the proper singular persons of those same orders are indicated. Since I find the designations of certain orders in both numbers, I do not think the same impossible for the remaining orders; and I say that the designation of each order properly signifies either individual persons in the singular or many persons in the plural.

## Chapter XXXVI. What they announce, what they do, and how

Angels and archangels move from place to place to announce; the other spirits, however, to act. [Col. 0885D] Yet the former announce in such a way that they sometimes act, and the latter act in such a way that they generally announce. But when both are sent, they sometimes borrow what is proper to the other so that they never, or only rarely, depart from their proper task. Angels are believed to be messengers of lesser matters; archangels, of greater matters. Perhaps archangels are so called not only because they announce principal things, but also because they rule those who announce lesser things.

Thus Zechariah says: “Behold, the angel who was speaking in me went out, and another angel went out to meet him; and he said to him: Run and speak to this young man, saying to him: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without walls” (Zech. 2:3). The superior angel teaches the inferior what he himself should teach the prophet. And perhaps the prophet’s own angel was the one instructing the prophet, since he spoke in the prophet. Therefore I judge all those to be archangels who have authority to command those who announce and themselves to announce the highest matters. And although we read only three names of archangels, we do not deny that very many others of that order are included without being named.

## Chapter XXXVII. Angels are subject to archangels

I think, therefore, that the order of angels is subject to the order of archangels, just as we see the rest subject to priests. These two orders, although sometimes—like all the others—they act separately, have their own offices of announcing: the one under others, the other over others. The other orders may perhaps instruct human beings by their speech concerning divine matters, but the task properly assigned to them seems to be action.

## Chapter XXXVIII. Which are the virtues, and their ministries

The virtues are those through whose ministry miracles occur. The saints say that angels are present at the sacrament of the Mass. I judge these to be from the order of virtues, since such work belongs not to nature but to God’s wondrous power. Thus we judge that the miraculous signs which we read were performed by Moses in leading the Jews, and by the apostles in converting the Gentiles, were performed through the ministry of the virtues.

## Chapter XXXIX. Why there are powers

[Col. 0886C] God established the powers for this purpose: that evil spirits, restrained through them, should not harm the world as much as they wish.

## Chapter XL. Why they are called principalities

They are called principalities because they hold principacy among the others.

## Chapter XLI. On dominations

Dominations are those to whom principalities too are subject. Perhaps, just as archangels preside among those who announce, so principalities are set over some, if not all, of those who act, and dominations over the orders. It may also appear that human beings are subject to principalities, and principalities to dominations. Why? “There is no power except from God” (Rom. 13:1); hence every human authority is subject either to the supreme domination or to an inferior principality.

## Chapter XLII. On thrones and their office

Thrones are those upon whom God sits, so that through them he may decree his judgments. Perhaps it belongs to their office to communicate God’s decrees. Thus, while Daniel beheld a vision and sought understanding, the likeness of a man appeared, saying: “Gabriel, make this vision understood” (Dan. 8:16). The appearance of a man appeared because it was not a man but an angel, seen in the form of a man. Perhaps he was one of the thrones, teaching Gabriel that God had judged that he should instruct the prophet concerning the vision. Although the Jews hand down, and very many agree, that this was Michael.

[Note: Col. 0887D. See Jerome on Daniel, chapter 8.]

But how does one archangel command another what he is to do? Perhaps the prince of the Jews, and therefore Daniel’s patron, asks the one set over wars to teach the prophet the outcome of the wars, which it was fitting for him to know. And perhaps judges are subject to the thrones, and by their assistance decree judgments without corruption.

## Chapter XLIII. On the cherubim and seraphim

The cherubim and seraphim, of which one order is last and the other next-to-last, are said to stand before God in such a way that they never withdraw for the performance of outward tasks. The lesser spirits, namely angels and archangels, are assigned to such matters; and these two orders, it is said, take the names of the others whenever what they do corresponds to those names. They say that this was the teaching of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite.

But in Daniel Michael is called one of the chief princes (Dan. 10:13). And the Apostle, wishing to prove Christ’s universal pre-eminence, ought to have shown the universal subjection of the angels. Thus he uses universal language: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent in ministry?” (Heb. 2:14 [apparently intended: Heb. 1:14]). And because, according to the Apostle, the names of the nine orders seem suited to ministries, let us assign administrative names to the two remaining orders.

## Chapter XLIV. They serve human beings according to the interpretation of their names

[Col. 0887C]

[Note: Col. 0887D, Isidore, *Origins*, V.]

For *cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge,” and *seraphim*, “burning fire.” Are they not full of knowledge because they are said to burn with the heat of love, since they contemplate the divine glory more closely than the others? Rather, the nearer they are to truth, the more capable of truth they ought to become. Do not those who abound in knowledge excel in charity in proportion to the knowledge they receive? But perhaps they are said to be full of knowledge because knowledge is gained among us through their ministry. And perhaps the burning ones are so called not only because they preside over fires, but also because they pour charity into the saints. Angels indeed watch over human welfare through these divisions of ministerial service; and it is credible that those who fell away from that number press upon human beings with dangers in just as many ways.

## Chapter XLV. That demons fell from the nine orders

[Note: Col. 0888D, *Magister*, book II, distinction 6.]

For we judge that the multitude of demons fell from the nine orders. Nor is this unreasonable, since, as the Apostle recalls, three orders seem to seek to separate the saints from the charity of God. Perhaps, as is his custom, he understands the whole through a part; elsewhere too he names the order of the saints through a part, while meaning all. For writing to the Ephesians, he places Christ above every principality, power, virtue, and domination (Eph. 1:21). In Colossians likewise there are subjected to him “whether thrones, or dominations, or principalities, or powers” (Col. 2:10). That he has expressed these orders with the sign of universality, in both plural and singular forms, clearly shows what I said above: namely, that a plurality indicates very many, while the singular indicates individuals. For whenever universality is added, individual things are designated by the singular and many things by the plural. Thus it is established that there are nine distinct kinds of spirits, because Scripture frequently mentions angels and archangels, cherubim and seraphim. To these four, add the remaining five orders which we found shortly before in the Apostle.

## Chapter XLVI. How evil spirits serve their prince

[Col. 0888B]

[Note: Col. 0888D, *Magister*, book II, distinction 6, §4.]

The individual evil spirits, therefore, appear to serve the prince of demons in their respective orders. Some are angels or archangels, insofar as they deceive more or less by making announcements; others are virtues, insofar as they perform deceptive miracles. Under their protection, magicians opposing miracle to miracle against Pharaoh seem to have competed. The Antichrist too, subject to corrupted virtues, seems destined to deceive the unwary by signs.

What of powers?

Perhaps powers restrain spirits less skilled in evil, lest they help when they intend to harm. For the same powers, insofar as they are able, oppose endeavors if these are good; but if they are evil, they assist them.

[Col. 0888C] What of principalities and dominations?

Principalities and dominations also rule over inferiors. Or perhaps the former trouble princes and the latter kings. Through their exertions the former are advanced and the latter humbled.

What of thrones?

Thrones weaken true judgments, strengthen false ones, and generally set certain false paths before judges.

What of cherubim?

Cherubim harm as virulently as they flourish in knowledge. That falsely named knowledge seems to be available to pagans, and likewise to heretics; finally, these very cherubim seem to be assigned to the Antichrist for things to come.

What of seraphim?

I judge that seraphim burn wickedly in evil just as they burn well in good. Perhaps they are ministers of conflagrations, and also of rancor, anger, envy, and lust. And although the nine orders appear to serve these pursuits, whether in good or evil, it may also be that the good help and the evil hinder in other ways. For although three alone, to whom proper names are assigned, are thought to be archangels by their common office, they are known also to be assigned to certain particular tasks. Demons too tempt in so many and such varied ways that it is either exceedingly difficult, or altogether impossible, to include the kinds of temptations within nine distinctions.

## Chapter XLVII. On the assistance and deception of human beings
[Note: [Col. 0889D] The Master, II, distinction 6, etc.] Since, then, there are nine orders, what prevents their names from having been taken from their better-known offices? Nevertheless, in however many other ways human beings are helped or deceived, in nearly so many ways demons may help or deceive. I say “nearly,” because each person is tempted by his own desire (James 1:14). And just as a person is spiritually harmed by himself, why should he not also be harmed bodily, so that, without the cooperation of demons, human beings may by conscience itself inflict upon each individual harm of both kinds? For whence would the faithless have crucified the Savior, although earlier—but no longer then—they had the devil as an assistant?

Moreover, things perversely done by human beings without diabolical suggestion sometimes occur without the demons’ knowledge. For just as they do not always know thoughts, unless they infer them from signs, so they sometimes do not apprehend actions either—namely, when, being absent, they are attending to other matters. Thus the Virgin, who was betrothed to a man, concealed her virginal childbirth from those who were deceived. David received the eye of prophecy, illuminated not, as others were, through figures or angelic agency, but by an inward vision, saying: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. 84:9). And thus it is read in the Book of Kings: “The spirit of the Lord was directed into David” (1 Sam. 16:13).

Hence there is a tradition of the Fathers that divine goodness infused the grace of prophecy into King David not through a subordinate creature, but through itself. But if the adorable majesty bestows a spiritual benefit not through a minister indeed, but sometimes directly through itself, it may likewise be believed—and not absurdly—that eternal liberality sometimes directly confers bodily benefits. For it itself stretched out the heavens, enclosed the earth within the heavens, and surrounded the dry land with the encircling Ocean. Finally, when incarnate, revealing what it was, while healing human beings inwardly and outwardly, it supplied no few proofs of its majesty.

Thus, through the activity of good and evil angels, good and evil are sometimes brought about for human beings; and sometimes they arise in other ways. For it not rarely happens that human beings either assist or harm other human beings in both ways. But that a person is harmed through vice is without God. Yet whoever acts so that a person is helped or bodily afflicted is a minister of God, whose rod of wrath Assyria also is (Isa. 10:5). He spares this rod for a time; indeed, he does much good through it, conferring both only so far as is expedient for the chastisement. Once that is accomplished, he breaks the rod, intending to give it fuel for the fire. Thus Isaiah, under prophetic obscurity, intimates that the Romans—certainly liable to destruction, yet preserved for the purpose of taking the Jews captive—received from God many great benefits suited to the uses of their ministry [Col. 0890A]. In the same prophet, the Lord arms Assyria, the rod of his wrath, against the Jews, fortifying it with strength and understanding (ibid.). Yet Assyria does not judge in this way, but attributes matters to its own powers; after the Jews have first been punished through it, it too is punished when God strikes it. This is not because God ever delights in the devices of wickedness, but because, in the counsel of justice, he desires to avenge the ungodly.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Of the multitude from which the prince of demons comes

[Note: [Col. 0889D] The Master, book II, distinction 2, final section, and distinction 6.] But since, corresponding to the nine orders of angels, we suppose that there are also nine multitudes of demons, whose names do not differ from the names of the holy orders: hence the Apostle says, “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers” (Eph. 6:12). From which multitude, then, is the prince of demons to be understood as coming? Certainly, in the view of most, he seems to have been created either the highest angel or rather among the highest. For to him belongs the saying: “You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom, perfect in beauty” (Ezek. 28:12). And shortly afterwards the same Scripture adds: “Every precious stone was your covering” (ibid.), arranging nine kinds of precious stones. What else does this mean except that, since there are nine orders of angels, every order adorned him who was set above all by the benefit of creation, so that, as another might glitter with gems, he himself shone with the nine orders?

If, therefore, as many maintain, the dignity of each order undoubtedly follows the numerical rank itself, then, since the seraphim are counted the ninth order, he who is the subject of our inquiry is included among the seraphim—unless it be because Ezekiel, who added this point also to the authorities already cited, has: “You are an outspread cherub”; and the prince of this world is more than once called a cherub.

[Note: [Col. 0889D] See Athanasius, *On the Letter to Serapion*, and Cyril, [Col. 0890D] book I of the *Glaphyra*.] Therefore he will more rightly be reckoned a cherub. Unless perhaps he is a seraph by order, but a cherub by interpretation.

But if equality makes the persons of each order equal to one another, how did Satan, even while he was good, surpass the others in his own order? Or, if one order admits inequality of merits, how is it one order? Yet things belonging to one order are often not equal among themselves [Col. 0890D]. And those known to be lower in rank are sometimes proved superior in merit. It may therefore be that among the seraphim or cherubim there are lesser and greater members, and that the prince of demons was one of the greater. For reason seems better satisfied by holding that God created those who would persevere equal to one who would fall—indeed, not a few greater than he—so that equals and greater beings might remain standing, and the one who fell might not be the greatest.

[Note: [Col. 0890D] See the notes for the authorities he follows.] Yet because it belongs to pride to prefer oneself to all, he judged himself the greatest, he who even compared himself with God. He was certainly great, but thought more highly of himself than he was. Therefore a great one fell [Col. 0891A], lest you glory in your own greatness or consent to evil counsel. Those who consented to the proud one fell with the proud one; those who clung to God deserved to have God as their prince; the demons who agreed with the adversary made him prince of demons. Since all of them have one perversity in harming human beings, and one will in obeying him who is stronger in this respect, each rages in evil more effectively in proportion as he surpasses others in the power of creation.

But I think that the nature of spirits is weakened in its corruption by as much as it is increased when confirmed; so that he who is least in the kingdom of heaven, exalted by the vision of God, surpasses the very prince of demons. Thus it came about that he who considered himself to be preferred—or perhaps truly was preferred by the benefit of creation—sank, irreparably overthrown, beneath even the greatest and the least alike. Hence in the same Ezekiel the address to him runs thus: “Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty; you destroyed your wisdom because of your beauty” (Ezek. 28:17). As though he said: Because you derived pride from beauty, you lost wisdom through beauty.

[Note: [Col. 0891D] Augustine, book XI, *On Genesis*, chapters XXIII and XXIV.] Others, however, believe that the devil was by no means of such great excellence, since he immediately turned himself away from truth, delighting in his own power. Therefore he did not taste the sweetness of the blessed life, which he did not disdain after receiving it, but lost by refusing to receive it. He could not, therefore, have foreknown his own fall, because wisdom is the fruit of piety. And he fell at once, not from what he had received, but from what he would have received had he been willing to submit. But what Isaiah says, “How you have fallen, Lucifer, who rose in the morning” (Isa. 14:12), etc., and Ezekiel, “You were the seal of likeness” (Ezek. 28:12), etc., applies in some respects to him and more extensively to his body.

## CHAPTER XLIX. That the devil defiles, and concerning those who are defiled

[Note: [Col. 0892D] The Master, book II, distinction 42.] The enemy of the human race, together with his attendants, while preparing snares for everyone, defiles them with a twofold foulness: first in thought, then in action. For unless the mind sinned, the law would not forbid desire; and if it alone sinned, it would not forbid theft, homicide, and the rest. For it would have sufficed to forbid desire alone.

But you will say: what is done outwardly is forbidden, not because it is a second sin arising from a perverse will, or because inner foulness itself gains an increase from it, but lest anyone will what he cannot will without fault. What then is the reason why the judgment of holy mother Church punishes the actual transgressions of her children with such severe correction if they are not blameworthy, while it forgives the will itself—which alone is guilty—either with no satisfaction or with one that is too easy? Therefore, if you will evil, you are guilty; if, while willing evil, you add an evil deed, you are more guilty. Thus our first parents, by willing to transgress, became evil; by transgressing, they were struck with death. Surely “the heart is lifted up before ruin” (Prov. 16:18). Mother Church, therefore, imitating her Creator, rightly accuses the perverse heart and scourges the evil deed [Col. 0892A].

Now an evil deed and an evil life exist where a wretched person pleases himself from every side. If such a person performs any good deeds, he profits little or nothing.

But there is another who nevertheless lives a defiled life, yet, having consulted reason, is distressed by his pollution and desires to do good. Nevertheless, recalled by the sweetness of habitual evil, he cannot accomplish the good that he desires. Having drunk of the cup of Babylon, while he is tossed upon the inextricable storm of this world, although he somehow longs for harbor, he nevertheless remains caught in shipwreck. For in his mind two wills struggle against each other: one good, the other evil; but the evil prevails and the good groans. Let him therefore cry to him who alone hears in the hidden place of the storm. When he is in tribulation, let him cry to the Lord and he will be heard; let him say: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak; heal me, Lord” (Ps. 6:3). The Savior’s declaration is: “Everyone who asks receives” (Matt. 7:8). Let him therefore ask continually, ask devoutly, flee to works of mercy, take hold of discipline; and he who gave him the ardent desire to depart will at last grant that he departs.

A bad person, therefore, who nevertheless wishes to become good, is regarded by God and delivered from evil on account of certain goods that are his own—indeed, also God’s goods. For God bestows goods in this world: either earthly goods, which happen more abundantly to the lost; or second goods, among which is fear of hell, by which the sinner is changed from his perverse way; or third goods, by which one already righteous may become worthy of a crown. The first are given so that life may be lived from them on earth; the second are supplications and a kind of path, so that one may attain those things which are worthy of reward [Col. 0892C]. Such goods, therefore, in a certain manner flourish and live. For although the one who does them has not yet become good, he has nevertheless done them so that, through lesser goods, room may be prepared for greater and rewardable goods, and thus he may become good.

But one who does not yet hate his own stain and prefers to remain in it, even temporarily, does not yet perform living goods. Since he loves the vice from which he presently does not care to depart, whatever good he does he renders dead; for this is the evil tree which cannot bear good fruit (ibid.). But that tree which, anxious over its own harmful shoot, grieves and meditates upon uprooting it, is no longer an evil tree, because it detests its evil shoot; it is not yet good, because, though unwillingly, it is burdened with an evil shoot. Holding a middle state [Col. 0892D], it considers what it is to be detestable and ardently desires what it is not, but is delayed by the sickness of its condition.

Therefore those things which are meanwhile done in some measure rightly bring neither punishment nor reward to the doer; yet, by the merit of their own worth, provided that such a person does not depart from his purpose, they rightly obtain for him that, once the vices have been overcome, he may finally possess those things from which he may hope for reward. But one unworthy of rewards is still alien from charity; and one who does not possess charity can derive no benefit from it (1 Cor. 13:13). Therefore, if someone lives shamefully, even though inwardly grieving, how can he prosper through his deeds—not only, I do not say, in other attainments, but even in attaining spiritual things—when he is deprived of charity, which “does not act perversely”?

[Col. 0893A] Yet one who is displeased with himself and strives to become good is not wholly alienated from charity. Hence, because he has been anticipated by certain first fruits of charity, he also performs certain first-fruit goods, so that, finally inflamed by charity itself, he may add better and truer goods worthy of charity. For where there is no charity at all—as happens whenever one stain is knowingly loved—there can be no living and effective good; rather, the merits of works increase in proportion to the increase of charity.

Whoever endeavors thoroughly to overcome the filth of his life, if he cannot at once wholly unburden himself, benefits by laying down part of it, so that the foul burden of crimes may at least be gradually diminished and thus finally nullified. For just as I do not think forgiveness for past deeds should be given to one who partly hates and abandons his pollutions, because he embraces them in another respect—although someone makes some progress when, while he acknowledges guilt, he does not extend punishment to himself—so I think that forgiveness should meanwhile be given to one who is wholly displeased with himself and strives to improve, even if he cannot thereby do what he desires, provided he hates and abandons those things. For “he draws near to God, and God will draw near to him” (Jas. 4:8).

But since “a little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5:6), and leaven is sin while the lump consists of good deeds, how can good deeds coexist with sin? Yet when the sharpness of the leaven fails, its corruption also fails. Likewise, when the love of sin is driven away, perhaps even its power to poison good things is expelled. Yet let no one be idle in sins that he hates [Col. 0893C], lest, overtaken by death, he perish before laying aside crimes which he does not sufficiently hate. For if he hated them perfectly, he would surely triumph over them as things trampled underfoot.

But now he both hates and loves: he loves when enticed by sensuality; but, having consulted reason, he hates both what he does badly and what he loves badly. Even so, oppressed under the yoke of slavery, he cannot free his neck; for he feels in his members a law resisting the law of his mind and captivity. Who, then, will free the wretched man from this body of death except Christ alone? (Rom. 7:24). Christ will indeed free him—but the one who perseveres in knocking and crying: “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13).

Some become so entangled in one such vice—or, worse, in many—that they neither escape nor desire to escape, caring either not yet, or, worst of all, never, to be corrected. “The worst of men, when they have descended into the depth of vices, despise escape” (Prov. 18:3). For such persons no hope remains, unless perhaps God’s regard instills a will in them either to desire to become better or at least to desire to desire it, according to the saying: “My soul has longed to desire your justifications” (Ps. 118:20).

By nature’s benefit, every person possesses a will of this sort, by which he somehow abominates what is unjust and embraces what is just; but it is so weak that no one advances through it, though everyone is accused by it [Col. 0894A]. Hence the Apostle says: “To will is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish it.” It is present because it is near and lies there; it lies there because I cannot accomplish what I will. But a will inspired by the grace of God is of such power that it is never without effect, unless the person himself fails that grace.

[Note: [Col. 0893D] Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 13: “For God, unless they themselves fail his grace, will, as he began the good work, so also bring it to completion,” etc.] Of this will the Apostle says: “For it is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish, according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13). Whoever feels himself endowed with such a will should rejoice in God’s gift, giving earnest thanks and asking to advance. Therefore, if one still living in wickedness desires at least to will the good, let him ask to will it. But if he already wills the good, let him hasten toward its accomplishment and strive to leave wickedness; once he has abandoned his sins, he should immediately ask forgiveness. When this has been received without difficulty from the merciful Judge [Col. 0894B], it is then time to seek a holy life and the reward of holiness. And this is the right order. For while you are evil, you cannot hope for pardon, nor may you rightly expect, before pardon, what belongs to the righteous. Therefore, crying from the depths of iniquities, because “with God there is propitiation” (Ps. 129:4), withdrawn by the law of mercy, we trust in pardon; and through pardon our soul will hope in the Lord.

## CHAPTER L. Although good things are from God, something belongs to man

[Note: [Col. 0894D] The Master, II, distinction 26.] It should be noted that, although divine generosity grants every good will, every pure word, and also chaste action, nevertheless in these first three there is something belonging to man. Thus, after the Apostle, speaking of his fellow apostles, had said, “I labored more abundantly than they,” he immediately added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10). For he did not labor alone, but with the help of God’s grace. This grace was offered alike to all the angels and to the first human beings, all created good; one rejected it, another received it by freedom of choice. But it was the first one’s own vice that he rejected the Creator’s assistance prepared for him; whereas the other clung to it both by his own will and, first, by the generosity of the giver.

What the beneficent giver offered, this one gratefully accepted; the ungrateful one neglected it. For free choice always languishes and lies dormant by itself unless God’s arriving grace awakens its insufficiency. Grace leaves some, entangled in sins, to themselves, as is fitting for them; but it resolves to visit others because it itself is worthy [Col. 0894D], doing in a person this: that one who by himself is capable of no good may now freely accomplish it, unless he himself prefers to fail grace. For whenever grace is pleased to offer itself to someone, that person either acts in cooperation with grace, in either direction, or, despising it, does not cease to act wickedly.

But when one lives well after receiving grace, one person perseveres happily in his purpose, while another, drawn back by habitual perversity, withdraws his foot. That the latter falls back occurs because he does not consent to grace, without which one never lives well; that the former perseveres in good is the work of grace, with which he agrees [Col. 0895A]. Hence it is clear that grace is the first and chief cause of all good deeds; for it goes before good beginnings, that they may endure, and follows them, that they may remain.

But some secondary authority for right action belongs to our own free choice. Certainly, it belongs to our capacity, when anticipated by grace, to act well through grace; and, when it follows grace, not to cease from good. Therefore free choice has some merit when, abhorring resistance to the commands of God, it begins now to worship God, and, once it has begun, wishing to please God, afterward perseveres. For although grace recalls the erring and leads the obedient onward, it draws one who is willing and does not compel one who is unwilling. It is so powerful and vigorous that whenever it pleases it can change even the will and life of the most perverse person to any degree of amendment, without any difficulty or compulsion.

Since such a person preferred to assent to conversion, which he could have resisted; since, established on God’s way, although able to turn aside he refused to do so; and since, finally, unlike many, he did not neglect cooperation with grace but embraced it and endeavored to follow it in all things—he is judged worthy of reward. For according to Scripture, “The kingdom of God is not of the giver but of the receiver”; that is, it arises not only from the gift of the benefactor but also from the labor of the servant.

Therefore, if you contemplate God, to whom whatever praiseworthy thing is found within our capacity is rightly attributed, since he himself awakens and advances the sluggishness of free choice, all our good is deservedly judged a gratuitous gift [Col. 0895C]. But if you consider the powers of free choice, which, compelled by no necessity, freely adapts itself only to the grace offered, then our good is in a certain sense judged due, so that each may rightly be judged according to his works. Hence the excellence of our actions is both grace and merit; yet grace, as leader, claims primacy for itself in every respect. Therefore whatever merit there is is rightly ascribed to grace, which both promotes it so that it may exist and accompanies it so that it may remain. For “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17).

Thus not only grace, sent from God, which pricks our sluggishness, but even the very assenting to and cooperating with grace—which is indeed from us, yet only in such a way that it could not happen without the aid of preceding grace and could not remain accomplished without the support of subsequent grace—is in a sense God’s work [Col. 0895D]. Therefore every good work that we do, we do not alone, but with God. Thus the Lord, speaking with a faithful man, says: “The works that I do, he also shall do” (John 14:24). For divine power, in a person, causes chaste faith, a pure will, and whatever springs from these as though from seeds cast into the ground; yet it does not work except with the person. For the Spirit invisibly and secretly—because “you do not know whence it comes or whither it goes” (John 3:8)—draws our mind toward will and faith with works, and by its own ways, largely unknown to us, works every good that is in a person.

A person also works his own good deeds [Col. 0896A], by means surely his own and more familiar to himself: what God teaches, the person believes; what God inspires, the person loves; finally, whatever good you do, you do with God acting. For “with the holy he will be holy, and with the innocent man he will be innocent” (Ps. 17:1); indeed, he is holy with the holy person whom, while living holily, he helps in holiness. This is what the Apostle meant when, after declaring how much he had done, he immediately added that he had labored not through himself but through God, saying: “Not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10).

## CHAPTER LI. Who deserves to be a citizen of heaven

By this [supplied: grace], if anyone strives to correct his life, he must before all else examine whether he grieves over committing vices—not some, but all of them—from fear of God, not fear of the world [Col. 0896B]; so completely that he would on no account wish to have done, or to do in future, those or any other such things. Whoever recognizes this condition in himself, comprehending with sincere knowledge the rule of faith and morals—because “in these things, one who is ignorant is ignored” (1 Cor. 14:39); for one holding an erroneous opinion in faith or a foul opinion in morals, as likewise a foul life, is rightly condemned—if he hopes and prays for pardon, possesses charity, is contrite in penitence, and is clear in the knowledge of saving things: that person, I say, and no other, now and not before, may rejoice that he has been enrolled with the saints as a fellow citizen of the heavenly kingdom. Hence the Lord says: “Rejoice in this, that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

If death should overtake such a person before confession, provided only that he has not rejected confession, then, however greatly he must be punished by purgatorial suffering, it is nevertheless known, once uncertainty has been removed, that he will finally be saved [Col. 0896C]. But whoever refuses to disclose his crimes to a priest, either terrified by worldly fear or ashamed at the dishonor of the matter, obtains pardon in no way; or, if he formerly desired to confess, he now acts so as to lose the pardon he had obtained. Thus whoever is made contrite by compunction of heart or purified by the disclosure of confession, if he returns to his vomit and rejects the covenant, binds himself anew by sins already abandoned.

[Note: [Col. 0895D] The Master, book IV, distinction 22; Augustine, book I, *On Baptism*, chapter 12.] For once the covenant has been broken, sins pardoned under the covenant are recalled, just as the many debts previously forgiven to the wicked servant are later exacted because, though he had sought pardon, he refused to have mercy on his fellow servant who owed less. Certainly, they were truly forgiven for the time being; this is clear because they would not have been demanded from someone who died in the meantime. But forgiveness has no force unless one does not act against its law. Hence it is clear that confession of sins is very necessary.

But let no rash person arrogate to himself what is not under his own control, imagining that it lies within his own power to confess whenever he chooses; for confession is God’s gift. Hence the Prophet says: “Confession and magnificence are his work” (Ps. 110:3). You can indeed proclaim your sins boastfully, like Sodom (Isa. 3:9). You can likewise disclose your foulness with a foul heart. But to disclose it savingly comes not from yourself, but from God’s gift. Thus it lies within you for any good work to be done badly; but for it to be done well does not lie within you [Col. 0897A]. And if oral confession is not from you, much less is contrition of heart from you—the source from which confession has force, and without which it has no value.

[Note: [Col. 0897D] Distinction 17, section 5.] One kind of confession may be made to equals; the other, unless extreme necessity presses, is owed to priests. If you are burdened by daily sins, and by those without which life is not lived, it is enough to confess such things to your peers, indeed sometimes even to inferiors. By this custom priests ordinarily and daily confess indiscriminately to those standing around them.

[Note: [Col. 0897D] The Master, book IV, distinction 27, section 5.] But if confession cannot be made individually, since this can rarely be done because of the multitude and because one to whom it might be made is not always present, then it is at least most useful to make it generally, and to do so fairly often. For diligent confession, especially when made to a priest and expressed by name, has such power not only to cleanse the guilty person, but also to blunt frequent assaults of vices and dull the violence of disturbance. James speaks of that reciprocal confession, saying: “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (Jas. 5:16).

[Note: [Col. 0897D] Book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 17, in the Gloss.] In accordance with this exposition, he gives the command concerning those sins without which life is not lived—namely, those committed through ignorance or human weakness. Forgiveness for all these is easy because there is no consent to guilt.

[Note: [Col. 0897D] In the Gloss, from Bede.] For, as the same exposition testifies, sins committed deliberately receive forgiveness only through penitence. Therefore, following the authority of the more serious leprosy, let us disclose our uncleanness to a priest, and take care to be cleansed for whatever length of time he commands [Col. 0897C].

Peter and Mary each obtained forgiveness of sin, yet neither by confession (Luke 7:47; Luke 22:61). Rather, she did so because she loved much; he, because the Lord looked upon him, through the bitterness of tears.

[Note: [Col. 0898D] *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 17, section 3; Ambrose, book X on Luke, chapter 22, Paris edition, col. 216.] Some, taking their example, believe that the distress of a penitent is sufficient even if he refuses confession. They suppose that the saying suits this view: “Tears erase the offense which shame prevents from being confessed.” Certainly, an offense which you are ashamed and reluctant to confess must be erased by tears. And it is true that laughter does not erase the offense which an impudent person confesses; rather, conversely, if someone confesses his offense with shame, it is erased not by pleasures but by tears [Col. 0897D]. Yet both Scripture earnestly commands confession and the Church establishes it. Who but one excessively bold changes this, or who but one excessively presumptuous overturns it, abusing the example of Mary and Peter? For since you must deal with a human being by speech, the accusation of conscience suffices before him who knows all things.

[Note: [Col. 0898D] Ambrose, cited above.] I read of Peter’s and Mary’s tears; I do not recall finding that they discovered any satisfaction other than this. What follows from that? Do the writings contain everything that happened? If, through the merciful presence of the Lord, one set of tears sufficed, will everyone expect the same? The woman caught in adultery was set free (John 8:10): will no guilty person afterward be punished? The thief was transferred from the cross to rest; nevertheless others are saved—yet “as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:15).

[Note: [Col. 0898D] In the rules of law.] For the privileges of a few do not make a common law. “Reveal your way to the Lord and hope in him, and he will act” (Ps. 36:5). You reveal it to the Lord when you reveal it to his vicar. If you could approach the Lord directly, you would accuse yourself before the Lord. But because this cannot at present be done, you make use of the Lord’s vicar in the Lord’s place. And the decrees of ministers, when prudently made, stand and remain valid before the Lord. For, as the Lord testifies, “Whose sins they forgive are forgiven, and whose sins they retain are retained” (John 20:23). And because you confess to the priest as though to God, he must conceal your secrets as though they had been disclosed not to himself but to God alone [Col. 0898B].

Therefore, when offenders in any crime and those aware of the offense are known to him through confession but unknown to others, he receives them, as though God alone knew their perverse and impenitent hearts and he himself did not, when they come with others to public assemblies, to refreshment at the altar, and to participation in the Eucharist. For he may not expose publicly by accusation those whom he knows through confession to be unworthy; nor is it fitting, to the scandal of all, to repel from communion those whom he judges guilty.

Therefore, when ministers are warned and asked to strike with an anathema someone wicked and aware of wickedness—both facts known to them by confession but unknown to others—because the offender does not care to approach satisfaction for the offense he has committed, nor the one who knows of it to the disclosure of what he knows, though summoned by the admonition of ecclesiastical custom, they do not hesitate to do what they are asked: that is, by an excommunication left indefinite and not specified under proper names, to bind under a curse the criminal and the person who knows of him. For they do not intend to anathematize demons, by whose effort the sin occurs; nor God’s angels, under whose knowledge it occurs; nor indeed God himself, under whose penetrating gaze all things are done; nor finally themselves, under whose awareness wrongdoing is also committed. The curse is poured out only upon human beings to whom the harmful action of guilt is imputed. To whom, then, is it imputed except to one who committed it, or assisted the doer, or, when able, did not deter him from the act, or finally to one who knew of it and, when he ought in justice, did not keep watch [perhaps: did not make it known]?

One kind of anathema is specified under proper names, as the authority of Scripture commends. Thus the Lord commands that one who will not listen when you rebuke him alone, then before witnesses, and finally before the Church, be regarded as a heathen and a tax collector. The Apostle also (Matt. 18:18) commands that a certain man, whose filth was manifest—indeed, as they thought, manifest—be handed over to Satan (1 Cor. 5:5). What is handing someone over to Satan except excommunicating him? Certainly an evil man, though he is a rotten member in the body of the Church, nevertheless, so long as he is in any way a member of the Church, is in some measure shielded from Satan’s attacks by the Church’s good deeds. But once, by the evangelical sickle of anathema, he is cut off from the bosom of mother Church, he loses that little share of life which he possessed in the body by being separated from it. Thus, when excommunicated, he is handed over to Satan, since he is now afflicted by the adversary with unrestricted power and by the adversary’s own right: either to be vexed by bodily punishment—as occurred when Paul handed someone over to Satan—or to be defiled by spiritual injury, as happens daily when the Church excommunicates [Col. 0899B].

But excommunication of this kind, directed against a third person, ought not to be carried out before the person accused of the crime has been definitively, and not merely on suspicion, judged worthy of anathema; indeed, not before, having been summoned according to ecclesiastical custom, he has evaded ecclesiastical jurisdiction. Thus the Lord commands that one who does not listen when you rebuke him first alone, second before witnesses, and third before the Church itself, be regarded as a heathen and a tax collector. Rightly, therefore, one summoned so often who does not heed his mother by making satisfaction alienates himself from his mother’s bosom through the fault of obstinacy.

From one thus alienated, until reconciliation, all communion and fellowship with the faithful are withheld by the authority of excommunication, for this reason: that, expelled on the one hand from the fellowship of the saints and more frequently afflicted than usual on the other by the power of demons, he may be ashamed and fear for himself, and thus, compelled by a certain necessity, flee to peace, descending into Babylon to be delivered there. For no priest of the Church, as minister and instrument, separates anyone from the Church except with the intention of restoring him better, following the Apostle’s practice of handing over the criminal man to Satan “that the spirit may be saved in the day of judgment.” Otherwise, if he anathematizes in order that it may go badly with the person anathematized, he harms himself before he harms another. Yet those who associate with excommunicated persons in such a way that they ought not, by the right of their condition, to be separated from them are by no means bound by the anathema [Col. 0899C].

[Col. 0899D] There is also another kind of excommunication, not so well known to the sacred page but very familiar to ecclesiastical custom—to which it is not lawful to object—by which an injury committed secretly is struck by the herald’s voice, while names are withheld because they are unknown. This species of anathema differs from the first as much as it is recognized as alien to its particular character. For since it names no one from whom it removes communion, it knows no such person; indeed, it removes communion from no one. Such persons and their accomplices are anathematized for correction after the threats of anathema. If they neglect correction, they themselves increase their condemnation, unless, before departing from here, they reveal their way to the Lord.

Good works are a way, because they lead to God.

This way, in order that pride may be avoided, should seldom be preached. [Col. 0900A] Hence the Lord, not so much guarding Himself as providing for us, commands that His great deeds be kept silent. Paul, however, himself disclosed the glorious things that had happened to him, though others did not know them—not seeking glory from men, but because they held opinions about his apostleship that were harmful to themselves. So far as lies in you, desire that your good deeds be concealed; but when, unless they are disclosed, scandal will arise against you, then unwillingly reveal what you had first wished to keep silent. Reveal it unwillingly, fearing vain glory, yet desiring the salvation of your brethren.

An evil life too is called a way, because those who follow it will be thrust into the fires of Gehenna; and unless you disclose it, though you are able to do so, you certainly cannot be reconciled to God. Therefore, “Reveal your way to the Lord” (Ps. 36:5), not in part but wholly. Wholly: so that you conceal nothing suggested by memory. [Col. 0900B] For so great a multitude of faults, not merely venial but even damnable ones, presses itself upon those who, through habitual sloth and indifference, have enslaved themselves to the service of wicked deeds, that it becomes either exceedingly difficult, or altogether impossible, to recount in confession the names and number of each individual vice. Therefore disclose to the priest every offence that occurs to your mind, confessing sorrowfully that through your negligence you keep silent about very many things which ought not to be kept silent; ask God not to remember your ignorances. Clearly, compunction of heart and confession of mouth ought to be general. Hence the Prophet says: “I made my offence known to you, and I did not conceal my injustices” (Ps. 31:5). Therefore make your offence known by confession so fully that you conceal none of your iniquity.

[Col. 0900C] For if, fearing its harshness, you conceal even one wound from the physician, although all the rest might be most fully healed, would not what remains prove ruinous for lack of treatment? [Perhaps “without treatment,” or “through neglect,” in a single word.] But even though, with your heart first broken, you have afterward vomited out by confession of the mouth the poison pressing upon your inner parts, and, by making satisfaction, have driven the vomited matter away from your vicinity, being in some measure relieved by the habitual disease, you nevertheless remain guilty, because you have not yet been absolved from guilt, though you have abandoned it, until you begin to lay aside any sin which you still embrace. You must plainly know that repentance of heart is never effective without confession of mouth; while confession without repentance is [Col. 0900D] always fruitless.

Whoever confesses truly and beneficially should recount matters as they occurred. He should neither exaggerate his shame beyond the facts nor excuse it, shrinking from it, through an accumulation of words. Excessive contempt is sought in one case and feared in the other, but in both truth is endangered. Therefore announce whatever you have sinned, and announce it as you sinned. Neither pass beyond nor fall short of this limit; beware of more and less; set forth what it is and of what sort it is. For often what occurs in the carrying out of an affair either outweighs the deed already done or adds guilt to it. For this reason: “Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in him, and he himself will act” (Ps. 36:6). For one who reveals his way in this manner ought to hope for pardon, and God will do what he hopes for. It is necessary to hope, because without hope there is no obtaining. Yet if anyone does not amend his life and hopes for pardon, he hopes in vain, because he does not obtain what he hopes for. Clearly, “Cursed is the man who sins in hope” (Jer. 17:5); for he sins securely, expecting pardon when he ought rather to fear Gehenna, saying, “The mercy of God is great” (Ps. 85:13). It is indeed great—but for the one who turns back, since wrath is owed to the one who turns away.

After compunction of heart and hope of pardon, and finally after confession, the fruits of penitence must follow. For as compunction is nothing without hope, and neither of them without confession, so these three together are ineffective if, when time and ability allow, you either do not receive from a priest the penitential observances [Col. 0901B] or think little of carrying them out once received. Although you have received pardon through the purity of confession, if afterward you neglect to make satisfaction, you lose what you received—just as one who does not forgive the offences of fellow Christians causes the forgiveness granted him by God not to remain.

Yet everyone should beware of assuming an unbearable burden, lest necessity force him to collapse beneath a load wrongly imposed by a priest. For while those who place unbearable burdens upon men’s shoulders are rebuked by the Lord (Matt. 23:4), those who accept such burdens are by no means commended; for what is unbearable ought altogether to be refused. Therefore, once you have undertaken what your strength can and ought to bear, do not lay it aside; indeed, undertake it [Note: [Col. 0901D] “May God behold your devotion even if a man does not suitably moderate your affliction.” Hugh of St Victor, *On the Sacraments*, part IV, book 3, chapter 3.], and do not lay it aside: “Lay hold of discipline, lest the Lord at any time be angry” (Ps. 2:12). Whoever [Col. 0901C] offends is liable to punishment; if he shuns punishment, the offence increases. Therefore God, angered at the person who dreads the distress voluntarily undertaken, inflicts upon him a far heavier distress which he endures unwillingly. For, as Scripture declares: “He who fears frost, snow shall fall upon him” (Job 6:16). That is, whoever, by taking precautions, protects himself from punishment humanly imposed for wrongdoing will be unexpectedly overtaken by the punishment due from heaven: avoiding the easy punishment, he falls into the grave one.

## CHAPTER LII. How counsel should be given to one guilty of sin.

And indeed, one hindered by sin should provide for himself in this manner. But one who must counsel the person hindered, when about to undertake a work which scarcely anyone performs sufficiently carefully [Col. 0901D] and well, should first fortify himself by invoking divine assistance; then he should consider:

> Who, what, where, with what aids, why, how, when

the person acted. For according to the quality of these circumstances, the quality of the matter itself is assessed, and the guilt is judged either lighter or heavier. Once the cause is known—because no sin goes unpunished, for “God does not spare all who work iniquity, taking vengeance upon all their devices” (Ps. 98:8)—the priest, about to impose a punishment proportionate to the guilty person, should devise it in accordance with: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke 3:8). He should consider what each person’s strength can accomplish, what it refuses to bear, and what is due to the fault in justice, so that he may humble the guilty person as is fitting, while imposing what can nevertheless be endured.

One person can bear fasting, another the rod, another cold, another labours; in short, one can bear this and another that. Let the physician provide the sick person with a kind of treatment able to be a remedy, not an increase of illness. Certainly, because we offend God through the sweetness of sin, we must appease Him by some anxious satisfaction. Thus our first parents, because they incurred offence amid pleasant things, expiated it by a severe judgment. Therefore, besides works of mercy, by which from our abundance we supply the needy without labour to ourselves, we need the heat of a furnace by which the rust of perversity may be consumed. This heat is either undertaken in the present life or will not be escaped in the future.

[Col. 0902B] Therefore let the priest provide present punishment for those for whom he must render an account, so that they may avoid future punishment. Other sheep do not belong to him; indeed, he should neither bind nor loose them except when reason and necessity compel it. For some, abhorring their own stain, are accustomed to seek out not their own priests but strangers, at whose hands they may either be more lightly burdened or less ashamed. I do not bind penitents of this sort to damnation, provided only that they abandon their crimes; but because they do not act as they ought, neither do I absolve them without the harshest chastisements.

But if they find insufficient counsel among their own priests, and for that reason flee to other men of better counsel, either with permission received or with penitential satisfaction enjoined by their own priests, so that under those men’s direction they may amend their lives or strive to perform what has been imposed, I not only do not accuse them but commend the alertness of their prudence. Yet whatever sort of priest he may be, and however he may have given counsel, let the penitent only grieve over his offences, disclose them to the priest, and undertake whatever the latter has religiously prescribed. But if the priest goes astray, let the penitent keep to the way, lest blind man offer guidance to blind man and both fall into the pit. I say: the error of a priest cannot harm a penitent who follows reason.

[Col. 0902C] Perhaps the priest treats the wound of sin too carelessly through the severity of the lash, but there is no danger to the penitent’s salvation in that. Let the priest beware for himself; whatever is lacking on the priest’s part is supplied by God. Thus, if a physician exceeds the measure in cutting, the King repays all to His soldier in heaven. If the priest does not punish as he should, God adds punishment, either in the future by purgatorial fires or in this world in various ways: now afflicting the penitent with shame, now striking him with suffering, sometimes taking away the things he held dear. For if a priest ignorantly looses or binds, does the just Judge carelessly preserve the decree? Or, if He preserves it, how does He deprive Himself of His own power in accordance with [Note: [Col. 0902D] Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, homily 26.] authority? Clearly, He would deprive Himself of it if the judgment did not stand: “Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke 2:8); “lay hold of discipline, lest the Lord at any time be angry” (Ps. 2:12); for “it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10:32).

But if penal discipline is so necessary, what does it mean that [Col. 0903A] “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8), and that almsgiving extinguishes sin (Dan. 4:24)? Perhaps—indeed certainly—charity accomplishes this: that sins do not lead to eternal punishment; it does not accomplish that they do not lead to purgatorial punishment. But perhaps almsgiving has the power to extinguish the incentives of vices. Thus it is prefaced: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. 3:33). What do “as” and “so” mean except that, just as water extinguishes the blaze of fire, so almsgiving extinguishes the inducement to guilt? Yet when the inducement has been removed, the punishment still due to sin remains. It may nevertheless be so—indeed it is permitted to believe so—that punishment is moderated through works of mercy. For “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” [Col. 0903B] (Matt. 5:7), not only in the future but also now.

Therefore I do not think charity and works of mercy, which rise from charity as from a good root, should be despised. Through charity there is forgiveness of sins; through these works, mitigation of the customary distress caused by sins that have been forgiven; and through both, the punishment due to sin is moderated in the present, while endless glory is owed in the future.

## CHAPTER LIII. How one should deal with the sick person and with the healthy person.

Whenever counsel must be given to a guilty person, the priest should know that he must act differently with one who is sick in body and, as it were, about to depart from the earth, and differently with a healthy person. Among the healthy, moreover, he must instruct differently one accused of a crime and fearing death or mutilation [Col. 0903C], and one who fears God but does not fear the world. For one accused person who fears the world should be admonished not to dread temporal punishment more than eternal punishment; he should be admonished not to fear man so greatly that he offends God; he should be admonished, when he must undergo the examination of the divine judgment, not first to provoke by perjury the One whose patronage he will afterward need at judgment. For one who despises the supreme Judge by perjuring himself, how will he afterward trust in His judgment?

Therefore no other counsel should be given to the accused person than that, abhorring perjury, he should rather accept temporal punishment from a temporal judge than, by delaying it briefly, deserve eternal punishment from the eternal Judge. He should know that “God will not judge twice concerning the same thing” (Nah. 1:9, according to the Septuagint). For one who, considering his former life, is contrite and humbled in heart, if he patiently accepts whatever punishment is offered him for his fault, escapes future punishment for the same fault [Note: [Col. 0903D] *The Master*, book IV, distinction 15, §§1–2.]. Thus He punished the Sodomites, those drowned in the Red Sea, and finally those struck down in the wilderness, in the present life, lest [Note: [Col. 0903D] See the notes.] He punish them eternally.

But if the accused person, suitably instructed by the priest, assenting to the flesh, chooses instead to plunge headlong into the uncertainty of peril and salvation by committing perjury, nothing remains for the priest—who should consider such judicial proceedings to be eradicated from Christ’s Church [perhaps *procuret*, “should seek/procure,” rather than *putet*, “should consider”]—except, after all things have been performed in the ecclesiastical manner, [Col. 0904A] to permit to be done what, although the guilt became known through confession, could by no means be corrected.

But if divine judgments also reveal the person who is guilty through confession—for “the judgments of God are a great abyss”—it does not seem to belong to the priest to approach persons of this kind. For once someone convicted by God’s judgment, or caught in the very act of wrongdoing, is handed over to a secular judge, he has the judge in place of a priest [Note: [Col. 0904D] See the notes.], since he must disclose the hidden deeds to the person from whom he will receive punishment for them. For if a priest visits such persons, the crimes of the wicked are strengthened by hope of confession and the Eucharist.

But if Christ is received by the penitent and confessing person, by what audacity, especially among Christians, is the temple of God violated by the disgrace of tortures?
