Or if the priest knows that he cannot defend Christ’s sanctuary from injury, why has he consecrated a dwelling-place to the dishonour of its inhabitant? If a guilty person flees to a temple built of stones, he is free; but if he himself is built up by repentance and confession, and by reception of the Eucharist is dedicated into a living and true temple, is he not free? Therefore judges must either keep priests away, or absolve the guilty and convicted persons—because they have received Jesus as their patron—lest they commit sacrilege.

[Col. 0904B] For those who commit crimes after receiving the Lord’s body do not gain protection from what they have received, but punishment; not honour, but condemnation. They act so that God, whom they had received in the sacrament, ought not in fact to remain their indweller. But those who formerly lived disgracefully and come, by God’s grace, to a happy end—cleansed by confession [Col. 0904C] and strengthened by the Lord’s body—how are they dragged to the scaffold by the faithful as though faithless, which they should no longer appear to be? “Will not God destroy those who violate the temple of God?” (1 Cor. 3:17).

But if those who are faithful in name but faithless in fact neglect to show honour to one in whom they know their Lord resides, it would have been better for the priest, in name, to avoid convicted and confessing persons. Then, provided only that they repented duly, no danger at all would threaten their salvation; judges would be free from violating the Lord’s temple; and despair of pardon would restrain those contemplating crime from an unlawful attempt, as they would say to themselves: “If I commit such an outrage and am caught, my salvation is endangered, because a priest will not be admitted in order that I may be saved.” Was this not, I say, better than that injury should be inflicted upon the Author through injury done to His servant?

But those who are to be tortured for martyrdom are not barred from the sacrament of the body and blood, nor does the person who strengthens them with viaticum consider that he has dishonoured Christ. Yet it is one thing to suffer disgrace for one’s crimes, another to suffer it for the name of Jesus (Acts 5:9). The former is shameful; the latter honourable. This is the cause of heaven; that, the image of hell. Therefore the Eucharist is fittingly bestowed upon the former as worthy, and withheld from the latter as unworthy of so great a sacrament. Perhaps a person is worthy of life because of penitential compunction, yet nonetheless unworthy of the Eucharist [Col. 0905A] because of the punishment of disgrace. For how is one rightly given Jesus as indweller who is denied burial in the Catholic cemetery? How can you give someone the Lord’s body and deny him the honour of burial? With what face do you associate with the Lord, by the merit of confession and communion, a person whom you separate from the fellowship of His servants? The souls of the saints await such a soul as their companion in heaven, and do you make the body of a holy soul an exile on earth from the bodies of its companions? You sin grievously against the Lord’s saint—indeed, against the Lord Himself.

## CHAPTER LIV. On the guilt of one who prosecutes an accused person out of hatred.

But one who, because of an injury done to him, pursues and accuses the accused person even to destruction: since in the faith of Christ it is not permitted to repay evil for evil, he is guilty toward his neighbour, inasmuch as he loves property or murderous vengeance more than his neighbour. Perhaps the accused person does not die, yet this man is held guilty as a murderer.

But one who swears, in order that an accusation against the accused may be considered credible, if the accused is afterward acquitted by divine judgment, plainly commits perjury. And because he seeks a capital sentence and, though grieved, does not accomplish it, besides the perjury he actually commits, he is a murderer in attempt and will. Because he sinned publicly, let him do public penance; or, if he neglects this, let him submit, as is fitting, to ecclesiastical discipline.

## CHAPTER LV. How a judge and his officer ought to act.

[Col. 0905C] Let a judge and his officer not agree with persecutors of the innocent, nor sit “with the council of vanity” or enter in with those who act unjustly (Ps. 24:5); rather, let him rescue the poor and free the needy from the hand of the sinner (Ps. 81:4). Yet let him not allow an impious man to live, for “he does not bear the sword in vain” (Rom. 13:14). Nevertheless, if he kills an innocent person or assists one who kills him, he is a devil and abuses the sword. But if he strikes with the sword one whom reason has proved guilty—for it is not lawful to condemn an uncondemned person—he is God’s minister. Only let him beware lest he do, through private hatred, favour toward another, or any earthly impulse whatsoever, what ought to have been done solely in view of divine justice and will, and human correction; otherwise he will be judged [Col. 0905D] not a judge of the guilty but a most cruel persecutor of men.

## CHAPTER LVI. On the two swords of the Church.

Our Lord Jesus judged two swords sufficient in His conflict. Clearly, the holy Church, which is the body of that Head and which has likewise undertaken a struggle against the world, needs two swords in battle [Note: [Col. 0905D] See Hildebert of Le Mans, bishop, in his letter to H., bishop of Sées; Hugh of St Victor, *Miscellanies*, book I, title 49, near the middle.], each expressing the sign of the cross. For nothing may lawfully be defended or attacked except that which it is fitting to do without injury to reverence for the cross. One sword is assigned to clerics, the other to laypeople. If both are entrusted to one person, neither is exercised as it ought to be.

Hence: “No one serving as God’s soldier entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2:4) [Note: [Col. 0906D] Thus Edgar, king of England, in his address to the assembled prelates of his realm.]. For Peter, cutting off Malchus’s ear with one sword, judged the other to have nothing to do with himself. Therefore priestly dignity and secular power should divide these two swords between themselves. The latter should judge the body, the former the spirit, to be subjected to its own jurisdiction. Thus one sword should strike the guilty person with bodily cutting, the other with spiritual correction when he refuses correction. Both should tend to this end, and no other: that their subjects, once corrected, may preserve peace with one another.

[Col. 0906B] Let no one placed in authority regard injuries done to himself or his loved ones in such a way as to exact vengeance—which belongs to God alone—according to: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord” (Rom. 12:22). Rather, let him regard whatever is done wrong to himself and his own as though done to strangers, so that he seeks not vengeance from anger but correction from charity. Let him not desire evil for the guilty person, but seek that person’s amendment through punishment and the Church’s correction through example. Thus let him return good for evil, not evil for evil.

Nor should he recover his own property or defend himself, because he is a Christian. Yet he should sometimes do both, because he is a judge: namely, when violence is inflicted or has already been inflicted upon his subjects by enemies; for then he fights rather for his people than for himself. Thus, when the need for correction requires it, he punishes thieves and robbers of his property who have been convicted and confessed—not serving vengeance but justice. Thus teachers punish pupils, parents their children, and masters their slaves, not only when they offend against others but also when they offend against themselves: each, as his authority requires, seeking to cut away the vices of his subjects, yet never seeking to avenge his own injuries except when he sins. Thus, with Abraham’s agreement, Sarah afflicted her rebellious maidservant (Gen. 16:6). Thus Joseph, when he imposes discipline upon his brothers, seeks to erase the fault of those who have sinned.

[Col. 0906C] Let no one associate himself with Judas, so as not to transact truth and justice—which is Christ—within his power for Christ, but sell it for a price. Let neither power despise what belongs to its own jurisdiction or usurp what belongs to the other’s. Let each, without exceeding its own limits, attend to correcting the other’s wrongs. While one pursues an enemy of justice and is unable to prevail, let the other, which has less power by itself, assist it with all its strength. Let the secular power, as reason requires, thrust such a person into prison, cut off limbs, or finally, if necessary, punish with death. Let the spiritual power, with Peter’s sword, cut off the right ear of one who rises against Christ, whether by acting against the Head or against the members: that is, let it bar him from hearing God’s word, either by suspension or by anathema. These, then, are the two swords assigned to ecclesiastical discipline.

## CHAPTER LVII. How one should deal with a sick person who fears God.

Since it has been said how one ought to deal [Col. 0907A] with a person who, because of guilt, fears an earthly judge, let us now add something concerning one who, terrified by sins, fears Him “who can cast both body and soul into Gehenna” (Matt. 5:30). As for one who repents while healthy in body, there is no need to repeat what has been said above; it is fitting only to add, to the foregoing, what counsel should be given to the sick person. Yet this must be added to the earlier points: the priest should not deceive, as it were by a trap, one who comes to him intending to amend his life.

For whoever reassures people who cherish and love even one sin, whether in themselves or in others, and do not wish to cease from it—whether by asserting that it will do no harm, or by maintaining that any amount of compensatory satisfaction is enough for an offence not abandoned—such a person gives life to souls that do not live; indeed, he overwhelms those dead in iniquity, as though buried under a mass after death, by his reassurance. [Col. 0907B] Therefore nothing but certain condemnation, which is due to the impenitent, should be promised to an impenitent person. Yet you may counsel such a person to implore repentance from God through works of mercy and divine worship. And if in the meantime it happens that he repents of some sin, do not deny him the opportunity for satisfaction—yet not prematurely, but when impenitence for that sin has departed from his heart. While it remained, it prevented the satisfaction for any sin from being effective.

Therefore let a numerous heap of crimes be taught to be scattered little by little, and let a great growth of thorns, if this cannot be done all at once, at least be uprooted from the field of our life through successive labour, so that the work may be accomplished more easily. [Col. 0907C] For it is rare that anyone suddenly becomes utterly base; but it is much rarer that anyone quickly becomes wholly good. Human frailty is more inclined toward unlawful things—except that sometimes, by God’s power, it happens that someone, “made perfect in a short time, fulfilled many years” (Wis. 4:13): that is, he ascends in a short time to the degree of religious life which is usually reached only after long delay.

Some crimes are private, others public. Some say [Note: [Col. 0907D] He seems, above others, to indicate Peter Damian in the notable book called the *Gomorrhianus*.] that both ought to be cut away by the bishop and chastised under his direction. But because public penance is known to be assigned to bishops, a sin requiring it rightly belongs to the prelate. And because a hidden fault avoids an open correction, both kinds of pastoral care rightly belong to priests; [Col. 0907D] otherwise neither could the prelate suffice for a multitude so great as requires counsel, nor would people be willing or dare to disclose themselves to those who, especially in this age, are devoted to the world. Therefore, as the prelate cures manifest crimes with manifest punishments, so let the priest strive to heal hidden offences with hidden remedies. In the latter case satisfaction is concealed, lest the Church’s weakness be scandalized by publicized penance; in the former, through public penance, the scandal born of public sin is removed.

## CHAPTER LVIII. How one should deal with those dying and with those recovering.

[Col. 0908A]

[Note: [Col. 0908D] *The Master*, book IV, distinction 20, §4.] But no burden owed by the living should be imposed upon those who have fallen ill and are now about to depart from among us. For we know both how to bind and how to loose upon earth; but how to burden, or when one should loose beneath the earth, is known to God, not to us. While they are upon earth, priests know their own parishioners; when they go beneath the earth, they pass into the diocese of the supreme Priest. Do not stretch out your hand into another’s jurisdiction.

If you burden people stupefied by death and terrified by the kind and quantity of their vices with the weight due to their offences, you compel them to despair. Therefore, when you address one about to depart, [Col. 0908B] say and do those things which lead him to grieve over the sins he has committed, and grieve in such a way that he nevertheless trusts in pardon. If the sick person happens to recover, then at last teach and impose the punishment due to his offences, but in such a way that neither condition supplies an occasion either for a faint-hearted person to despair or for one overburdened beneath the load to collapse. Thus the priest’s care should chiefly aim to induce the guilty person to grieve over his fault without despairing of pardon. For the entire force of the matter lies here: salvation does not exist without these things, and it does exist with them. For if a punishment less than the merits require is undertaken, the satisfaction must not be despised; certainly, for this reason the soul’s rest is delayed but not taken away.

## CHAPTER LIX. What need there is of confession and of penitence.

[Col. 0908C]

But if salvation can arise from compunction of heart and hope of pardon, what need is there afterward for confession? And finally, what need is there for the fruit of penitence [Note: [Col. 0908D] *The Master*, book IV, distinction 18.]? Because according to the ordinances of the Church, whoever can attain those two things and despises them loses salvation. They are also necessary because present punishment carefully undertaken protects against the far more grievous future punishment of purgatory. Therefore confession is necessary, not only because obedience must not be set aside, but also so that you may know what ought to be done; after knowledge, performance is necessary, lest you have known in vain what ought to be done. Confession is necessary also because, when it is worthily performed, absolution from sins takes place in it.

## CHAPTER LX. On the binding of sin and absolution.

[Col. 0908D]

[Note: [Col. 0908D] *The Master*, book IV, distinction 18.] But in order that the rationale of absolution may be set forth more clearly, one must first understand what it is to be bound, so that the necessity of being loosed may be foreseen. People are bound by spiritual bonds either of sin or of the punishment of sin. The punishment of sin, as we have just learned, consists either in the penitents’ lamentations or in the exclusion of excommunicated persons. But one who is held outside the Church—indeed, outside the Church’s benefits—by the bond of anathema is absolved when reconciliation is restored.

[Col. 0909A] Whoever loves sin and is thereby hindered from the right way is bound by the bond of sin; so also is one who has already cast aside vice but, like a person recently recovered from an illness, is newly healed from vice and is still held back by bad habit from freely doing what he ought.

[Note: [Col. 0909D] Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, book II, homily 20; Augustine, sermons 8 and 44, *On the Words of the Lord*, and elsewhere; Isaac of Langres, canon 11, etc.] But one who remains subject to punishment before fulfilling the fruits of penitence is absolved when he has completed them, so that he is now worthy of rest. A person contracts from himself such a condition that, weighed down by the death of transgression, he cannot move by his own power from death to life. This is Lazarus motionless in the tomb. But by divine power it comes about that a person oppressed by crimes withdraws himself from the deadly burden. This is Lazarus called out from the tomb by the Lord’s cry, who, with God’s help, returns from death to life (John 2:43).

Once life has been restored, he retains for some time, as it were, traces of his former death; he is in some way numb and dull, while through the deficiency of human frailty he sees inadequately, when considering what must be done, and is scarcely able to carry out as he should what he has considered and recognized. This is Lazarus raised up, his face covered and encircled with bands. But whoever has been restored to righteousness and is held back from the straight path by the trouble of past shame, as it were by certain grave-cloths, is prepared by priestly confession to keep the way of truth; and thus the difficulty of doing good which was previously present is gradually lightened through the habit of good. This is Lazarus loosed by the ministry of the disciples and permitted to go.

[Col. 0909C] It is therefore very necessary that no one be slow in coming to confession. For although anyone with a contrite and humbled heart rises again from the death of the soul, nevertheless, because of a certain residual numbness after death has departed, he is continually drawn back, even unwillingly, toward the things of death, and is kept sorrowfully from the offices of life. This continues until absolution through confession brings it about that the face of the mind, formerly veiled by the napkin of sin, may see the truth not—as before—as though through a napkin, but more fittingly, more and more clearly; and that the other members, previously constricted as by certain bands of illness and therefore, although restored to life, scarcely throbbing toward life, may now walk the unhindered path of life with free step—ever freer as they advance—with the faculty of reason giving guidance throughout, each in its own manner.

[Col. 0909D] Such impediments are brought by death, each chiefly in its own kind. When returning life struggles to overcome them, it does make progress, but little, until, aided by confession and the work of confession, it receives and increases the powers by which it may free itself and grow. Therefore let every person be swift to confess (Luke 1:19), for in this way he will become ready to do good.

[Note: [Col. 0909D] See the notes.] But whoever, through confession, devotes himself to the fruits of penitence—being now strengthened by the absolution which occurs in confession—is bound to punishment until those fruits have been completed. But how long punishment for sin ought to be prolonged and when it ought to end is known to Him to whom satisfaction is made by punishment. Therefore whoever thinks and rejoices that he has escaped the obligations of crimes by making satisfaction should always keep before his eyes how difficult and how scarcely deserved his deliverance was, and should shrink from falling back and returning to the vomit.

## CHAPTER LXI. On the power of binding and loosing.

[Note: [Col. 0909D] *The Master*, above, §§6–7, etc.] In all the foregoing, a person’s evil merit produces binding, while God’s merciful judgment produces absolution. Yet the sacrament of binding and loosing belongs to God’s own vicars, that is, the priests of the Church. Hence the Lord says: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20:23). And likewise: “Whatever you bind on [Col. 0910B] earth shall be bound in heaven” (Matt. 16:19), and so forth. The former is addressed commonly to all; the latter to Peter and, through Peter, set before all. Accordingly, by the Lord’s authority the apostles and their successors retain human sins and thereby loose persons from them.

But “who can forgive sins except God alone?” (Mark 2:8). It is He, certainly, who forgives sins: He who places virtues before forgiveness and grants eternal life to both [Note: [Col. 0910D] The same teaching in St Thomas.]. What, then, is it among human beings to forgive sins or absolve from sin, except to celebrate the sacrament of forgiveness and absolution? From the moment a person repents, God forgives; afterward, the minister of God forgives the sins of the person confessing by absolving him. And what does it mean that he forgives by absolving, except that he performs the sacrament of forgiveness and absolution? The absolution performed by a priest over a penitent after confession has been made is a sacrament, because it is the sign of a sacred reality [Note: [Col. 0910D] *The Master*, book IV, distinction 1.]. And of what sacred reality is it a sign, if not of forgiveness and absolution? Clearly, the absolution from sins administered by the priest to confessing persons signifies the remission of sins which contrition of heart had previously brought about. Therefore the priest looses from sins, not because he forgives sins, but because he reveals sacramentally that they have been forgiven. And why must this be revealed, except that consolation may be given to the penitent?

In another way also the priest absolves from sins: when the troublesome distress caused by a past and forgiven offence, repeatedly and intolerably resisting, is eased by the sacrament of absolution—indeed, by God through the priest—and, when fitting, cut off by the advance of promotion [Note: [Col. 0910D] St Thomas, *Summa theologiae*, III, question 86, article 5.]. This obstacle of frequent assault is gradually calmed and put to sleep by continual resistance; while it is overcome in some respects, it remains to be overcome in others. Indeed, it is never conquered to the last detail until we are removed from this world.

Once penance has been completed—not always such as a human being imposes, but such as God has foreknown; for if a person does less than is fitting, God makes it up by purgatorial punishments, either in this age (nor is our [Col. 0911A] satisfaction superfluous, since, if it is complete, it removes the punishment altogether; but if diminished, it partly lessens the scourge due from God for our transgression)—once penance, I say, has been completed, the guilty person is absolved by God: not only so that he need no longer be punished for sin, but also so that, purification having been made, he may be rendered fit for heaven. A human being does not effect an absolution of this kind, because no one knows when it is proper for it to take place. Hence the ordinances of the Church have decreed nothing to the effect that, just as completed confession is followed by absolution, so completed satisfaction should follow it as well. For the priest knows from the mouth of the confessor and from his manner of life whether he absolves him from guilt. But no means of experience has been discovered by which it may be certain when he ought to be released from the punishment of guilt, except perhaps from that which he himself imposed.

[Col. 0911B] 217 As the priest absolves, so also he binds, while administering the sacrament of both acts. Thus the priest binds to punishment, and binds to guilt, when after confession he burdens someone, for a time, on account of his offences. But he declares that a person unwilling to cease from evil cannot obtain pardon; and so he retains sins, which are retained also before God. Conversely, when one ceases and confesses, he remits sins by absolving him—sins remitted also before God. For he says to his vicar Peter: “What is expedient you shall bind; what is expedient you shall loose,” thus explaining the judgment of the Lord’s decree: that apostolic authority extends so far as to bind one who ought to be restrained by bonds, and to absolve one worthy of absolution. [Note: [Col. 0911C] Gregory, Homily 26 among the 40; Augustine, on Psalm 36; Jerome, on Matthew, ch. 16; and Gratian expressly, XI, question 3.] For one who looses or binds improperly deprives himself of his own authority. God does not consent that what such a person does should be so done. He binds by anathema upon earth one undeserving of it, and he is not bound before God; he absolves by anathema upon earth one unworthy of it, and he shall not be loosed [Col. 0912A] in heaven. The priest excludes one person from the Church, [Note: [Col. 0911C] Jerome, in Gratian, XXIV, question 3, ch. *Si quis*.] but God receives the excluded person. To another the priest opens entry into the Church: what good does that do one whom the divine judgment rejects? Therefore let no one bind the living with cords, nor absolve the dead; lest by binding he inflict death, or by absolving draw forth stench. From the one comes fear of despair; from the other, hope of security in sinning; and others are corrected by the example. Woe to those who kill souls by a sentence which do not die in life. Likewise, woe to those who make souls live by judgment which do not live by merit. [Note: [Col. 0912C] Gregory, cited above.] So far as lies in you, first know a man to be dead in sin before you hinder him with the bond of death; let him first be called forth from the tomb by Jesus’ cry before the binding is removed through the ministry of your office.

[Col. 0912B] Consult also the Lord’s words and observe that your care concerns only one whom you judge to be dwelling upon earth, not one already rotting beneath the earth. [Note: [Col. 0912C] Gratian, XXIV, question 2.] Under the Law, if a priest discovered anyone leprous within the camp, he cast out the person when detected; if, once expelled, he later saw him sound, he recalled him into the camp—making neither the leper nor the clean person, but merely distinguishing the two. [Note: [Col. 0912C] Lombard, *Sentences*, IV, distinction 18, §6.] By the same reasoning, the prelates of the Church consider that they have authority to distinguish sound members of the Church from rotten ones and, having made this discernment, to separate some from others. But although it is not the work of their ministry to make persons either clean or unclean, since the one is accomplished by God’s power and the other by the ugliness of the thing itself, nevertheless, when they loose or bind, this results in the accused becoming either better or worse: either because, like a leper, he is cast outside, or because, having been found sound, he is received within the camp.

## BOOK VII

[Col. 0911]

### 218 CHAPTER I. On the remission of sins

[Col. 0911C]

[Note: [Col. 0911D] Lombard, II, distinction 18.] After confession and absolution, discipline, prayer, and almsgiving are necessary—for the sake of satisfaction, indeed of religion itself. By these three are obtained [Col. 0911D] the vision of God, and beforehand pardon for sin. Certainly guilt is remitted in two ways: either so that it shall no longer lead to condemnation, or so that it shall not remain even for punishment. [Note: [Col. 0911D] Lombard, IV, distinction 17, §1.] In the first way sins are forgiven as soon as the heart is broken by compunction, according to the saying: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, I shall remember none of his iniquities” (Ezek. XXXIII, 12). And again: “I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord’; and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Ps. XXXI, 5). God therefore forgets our offences when, having turned back through compunction, we are no longer reckoned as belonging to Gehenna. He likewise forgives the person who intends to accuse himself before a priest not only the sin, but also the impiety of the sin: that is, both that he sinned, and that he sinned so often, at such a time, in such a place, in such a manner, and in whatever other like ways he committed offences.

Whenever this remission is made, it is made in this life; for pardon for an offence is vainly hoped for in the future if one is taken hence without pardon. But some are released from the punishment of offence now, others in the future: now, those who complete satisfaction before death; after death, those whose expiation is not completed until after death. [Note: [Col. 0912D] Augustine, Letter 50; Sermon 11, *On the Words of the Lord*; [Col. 0913D] Book I, *On the Sermon on the Mount*, ch. 22; *Enchiridion*, LXXXIII; and *On Rebuke and Grace*, ch. 12, etc.] To this release from punishment may not unfittingly be applied what the Lord says in the Gospel of [Col. 0913A] one who sins against the Holy Spirit: that it shall not be forgiven him either in this age or in the age to come (Matt. XII, 32). The punishment of this sin is sometimes deferred in this life, but is never remitted; for afterward it will be exacted by everlasting torments. Why? Because he remained impenitent in life. Therefore, just as the penitent are released, whether in the future, from sins—that is, from the bonds of sins—so conversely the impenitent will be absolved neither here nor in the future.

But perhaps the Lord’s saying is more fittingly understood of the sin itself than of its punishment. Certainly certain offences obtain pardon in the present, which I think must be understood of all serious sins, if they come to pardon. For sins committed venially perhaps obtain pardon after death, but not others. It sometimes happens [Note: [Col. 0913D] Lombard has the same passage, IV, distinction 21, §4.] that a righteous man commits a venial sin and is overtaken by death, without having time to reflect on it. Since after the fault he experiences no sorrow of heart through repentance for his error, it is not unreasonably believed that he has no pardon 219 for the offence until, returning to himself after death, he groans over his transgressions, whether generally or, as I consider more likely, individually. Hence there is a tradition among our teachers [Note: [Col. 0914D] Gregory, chiefly alluded to here, *Dialogues*, IV, ch. 39; XXV, distinction, ch. *Qualis hinc*.] that besides the remission of sins made in the present, another is granted in the other age, but only for light sins. For grave sins, unless they are forgiven in this age, [Col. 0913C] pardon is vainly awaited afterward. If the matter concerned the punishment due for sins, the distinction between grave and light would be made in vain, since, once expiation is completed, the punishment of both is remitted without distinction, both in this age and in the future.

Therefore it is a holy and salutary thought to pray for the dead, that they may be released from sins (II Macc. XII, 46): in two ways—either that any stains of human frailty which they may have contracted be blotted out; or, if all their sins have already been forgiven in life, that they be freed from the punishments remaining due after forgiveness. For anyone is released from sins by a threefold participation: either when the sins themselves are pardoned to a contrite heart; or when the burden arising from sins, which after the departure of sin vexes those bound in poverty and chains, is assuaged by the Lord’s aid; [Col. 0913D] or thirdly, when the discipline deserved by guilt ceases. But the first remission accomplishes that guilt shall not lead to condemnation; the second, together with the third, that the punishment of sin shall depart.

### CHAPTER II. What discipline together with prayer and almsgiving merits

The three good works set forth above—discipline, prayer, and almsgiving—merit this threefold remission, and not without reason. Prayer placates God; discipline chastises the penitent; almsgiving labours for the benefit of brethren. Rightly, then, to one diligently striving to emerge from sins in these three ways, the power to fulfil his vow is at length granted; after the vow comes pardon, and after pardon that poverty by which it is burdensome to a person both to leave familiar things and begin new ones is gradually lessened by the same three means, and health is restored. They likewise make satisfaction for sins; finally, they adorn this life with good character and grant and enlarge the life to come.

### CHAPTER III. On discipline and fasting

Discipline is necessary, because, as the Apostle testifies, those who are without discipline are adulterous children and not sons (Heb. XII, 8). But discipline is one thing inward and another outward. A person sometimes undertakes each himself, sometimes receives it from elsewhere. Yet although both may in some measure be displeasing to frailty because of distress, if a person, contemplating heaven, does violence to himself—for “the violent seize it” (Matt. XI, 12)—and by reason embraces what the flesh abhors, he acts all the more gloriously the more grievously he suffers.

Inward discipline is the manifold distress of the mind and the exercise of cares, both varied and frequent, when undertaken rationally. In the Apostle, “the care of all the churches” produced the consuming burden of cares. When he said, “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (II Cor. XI, 28), he indicated that distress of mind is necessary. We possess outward discipline when we patiently endure affliction arising from external things, from those dear to us, or finally from our own body. This, arising from externals and breaking into the inner chamber of the inward person, becomes inward; for how can that which does not afflict, more or less, the very inner recess of the heart by its force be either affliction or discipline? It is necessary that what we have sinned through pleasure be cleansed by the bitterness of chastisement; and nothing seems more fitting than to set contrary remedies against contrary evils. Let continence, since it is contrary to fornication, cleanse those whom fornication has defiled; let abstinence aid those harmed by gluttony; let silence make recompense for talkativeness; let the plunderer become generous; and let one who has injured others by insults or any other wrongs, peace being restored so far as lies in him, not delay to undergo what he inflicted. 220 Finally, whatever part of the body you have abused in evil, use that same part, if possible, to an equal extent in good. Thus, according to the Apostle: “As [Col. 0914D] you have presented your members to serve injustice, so they must likewise be presented to the service of justice” (Rom. VI, 19).

Yet if the transgressor’s frailty is so great that he cannot endure either the kind or the amount of satisfaction, some such practice must be sought as his strength will not refuse and which nevertheless torments the guilty person. There is therefore a kind of satisfaction which almost anyone’s constitution can endure, yet which is harsh and all the more pleasing to God the more humble it is: when anyone, prostrate at a priest’s feet, presents himself naked to be beaten with rods.

Above all kinds of punishment by which mother Church chastises her children, fasting is celebrated with a general veneration as though preferable to them all. The examples of the prophets have confirmed it; the abstinence of our Lord has established it; the devout practice of the saints of the New Testament has handed it down. Certainly among every people and in every place, restraint in eating and drinking is fittingly and appropriately observed. If it is frequent and constant, it especially subjects and reconciles the outward person to the inward person. [Note: [Col. 0915D] See Jerome’s dicta on Fasting in the Rule of Monks, vol. IX.] Although reason sometimes moves us to abstain from fasting on account of time and place, moderation—without which fasts themselves have no value—can and ought to be continual and perpetual. Fasts which weigh themselves down by gorging, or which weaken nature by depriving it of what is its due, must be assigned, on the one hand, to gluttony and, on the other, to superstition. Therefore the body must be chastised by constant mortification [Col. 0915B] (I Cor. IX, 27) and sustained by daily refreshment, so that mortification may bring the body into subjection and refreshment may supply strength for that subjection. This is what the Apostle teaches when he speaks of chastising the body and bringing it into subjection. This is also what he teaches when he warns that no one hates his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it. Hence, according to the tradition of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0915D] In Cassian, Book V of the *Institutes*, ch. or §9, according to [Col. 0916D] Dionysius the Carthusian.], daily hunger and daily dining are preferred to fasts of three days. One must dine in order to be able to bear the burden and heat of the day; yet with moderation, so that one endures something hard. Otherwise, what sort of fasting is it when no punishment makes recompense for the guilty pleasure opposed? One recompense is desirable: to fast until you are hungry. Another, further practice even beyond fasting, is to restrain [Col. 0915C] the appetite as it rushes headlong and put a bridle upon desire. Finally, whatever is undertaken for discipline, if it admits no bitterness, is rightly rejected.

### CHAPTER IV. On prayer

Prayer must proceed from a contrite and humble heart, for “God resists the proud” (Jas. IV, 9), and when the petitioner’s affection grows cold, he esteems it little. Prayer also requires that attention of heart accompany the utterance of the mouth; otherwise its affection is exceedingly weak if it does not steady the wandering mind. But if the mind, given over to vain things, wanders of its own accord, what good is it to move the lips? Certainly little, or rather nothing. When you speak to someone and turn your mind elsewhere, is not your speech contemptible if your distraction is noticed? But if you strive to bind your whole mind to the words, and nevertheless are distracted by unconquerable weakness, will this not be imputed not to you but to your frailty, so that it is no longer you who do it, but the sin dwelling in you? If the attention of devotion attended the constancy of prayers and equalled it, you would certainly be blessed. But now, while you labour to become attentive and devout and struggle against your sickness, you are blessed by the contest itself, and at last will receive the triumphant crown of the struggle. I judge the same to be understood of every struggle against infirmity: [Col. 0916A] for “strength is made perfect in weakness” (II Cor. XII, 9).

The petitioner also must be such, and what is requested must be such, that it is not fitting for a request of this kind to be refused to a petitioner of this kind. 221 For we often ask and do not receive because we ask wrongly. It also happens that, although we multiply prayers, God does not hear us because our hands are full of blood. Words are not necessary to disclose to God, who searches the heart, what we desire. For although devout meditation of the heart stirs up the Judge’s mercy, we nevertheless use words, both to instruct our neighbour by examples and to rouse the torpor of our natural heaviness to holy zeal by words as by certain goads. Finally, we use them so that [Col. 0916B] with our mouth also, as with our other members, we may serve God wholly, just as before we served sin wholly.

### CHAPTER V. How we ought to benefit body and soul

When we give alms to our neighbour, we provide what is necessary either for soul or for body. Whenever something is given that is not needed, if it is so inadequate as to be of no use whatsoever, is not the giver foolish or miserly? But if it is so much as to exceed the measure, is not the giver either improvident or wasteful? Yet what benefits the soul has greater merit than what is useful to the body, just as a master is superior to a maidservant. Thus the body must be cared for [Col. 0916C] so that each person may seek still more earnestly that the spirit may be well.

We can be useful to our neighbour’s soul both while he remains in the flesh and afterward. Let us therefore strive to benefit our neighbour while he is still living, praying to God and diligently aiding our neighbour, so that, if he is wicked, he may be recalled from error; but if good, he may advance in his purpose. After life, however, if we know certainly either that people have entered heaven—as the saints and infants washed in baptism—or that they have gone down to hell—as unwashed infants or any persons overtaken by sudden destruction while engaged in a shameful deed—what scope remains for our diligence? Is it that those held in hell may be rescued, or at least tortured less severely there? But there is no redemption in hell. For those who are there are regarded as so depraved that it ought not to be less ill with them. Although some [Note: [Col. 0916D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 110, etc.] say not dogmatically but conjecturally that benefits performed for such persons, if they are of any benefit, may perhaps avail to have them punished more lightly. And what shall we ask for those received into heaven? That they may fare well? But there no one can fare ill. That they may fare better? But for us to fare better requires their intercession. Do you not make yourself ridiculous whenever, still dwelling in exile, you presume to intercede for one already established in his homeland and glorying in the presence and familiar fellowship of the Lord?

What then is meant when we pray for the dead, “Grant them [Col. 0917A] eternal rest,” and so forth? But what use is it to request in prayers something which those who already have it, or those who never ought to have it, we know quite well to be so? Not only is it of no use, it is foolish: for it is known that the former will never lack the kingdom and the latter will never possess it. For whom, then, is such a prayer offered? Certainly for those who are thought not yet to possess it, but are hoped to possess it. And who are they, except those whom we know to have acted rather negligently in life, but whom we hope, from their signs, nevertheless to have reached a good end? Therefore our care seeks that those whom we consider afflicted by purgatorial punishments may be brought to rest through our intercession. Yet in the Offices for dead infants we pray for rest; and for penitents, that they may not fall into the dark places of darkness, but, rescued from the gate of hell, may be brought by holy Michael the standard-bearer into holy light: as though a regenerated infant could be kept from rest, or a penitent thrust into hell’s darkness, or anyone rescued from hell’s jaws. But since the Church does not expect penitents to be damned and hopes that both they and the regenerated will alike be saved, I think she is joyfully offering, under the form of fitting prayer, a kind of congratulation not unwelcome to its author.

But if we wish to help our neighbours in matters which can benefit the body, let us oppose, insofar as we can, dangers to their persons and losses to their goods, coming to the aid of the oppressed in whatever way, according to the saying, “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. VI, 2). Therefore, if we intend to visit those bound by sickness or prison—for if [Col. 0917C] we can do more, what merit is there in merely seeing?—and if we see naked, thirsty, hungry travellers or persons burdened by any necessity, let us consider them human beings, and therefore not despise our own flesh in a brother. Let us strengthen those bereft of counsel, or, whenever they need it and we have the means, aid them in deed. For if we know our brethren to be in need and can, out of what is sufficient for us—so that we ourselves do not lack—supply their want, yet, though we have two tunics, do not give one to one who has none, nor even from our surplus, after the manner of Magdalene, wipe the Lord’s feet, how do we possess charity, apart from which there is always death of the soul? One who possesses only what he or his household needs, and what he ought not to lack, is not required to bring assistance out of his own want. For just as a certain order must be observed in charity, according to the saying, “He ordered charity in me” (Song II, 4), so also in the effects produced by charity: first provide for yourself, afterward for others, for each person according as he is more or less closely joined to you. But since “a man’s own riches are the redemption of his soul” (Prov. XIII, 8), and “the sacrifices of the wicked are abominable to the Lord” (Prov. XV, 8), both things must be done: whatever you possess through wrong, restore in some manner to its rightful owner—if not fourfold after the manner of Zacchaeus, at least singly—and from what is rightfully your own aid the needy, as your resources permit and they require. For a man’s own riches are his redemption. Hence it is clear that we are not instructed to redeem our soul by giving away things necessary to us, but from what we possess and can do without; for this abundance is called riches. This is what the Lord means when he does not command one who has one tunic to give it away, but one who has two to give the other (Luke III, 11).

### CHAPTER VI. Why we offer a tenth, from what things, and to whom

We offer a tenth so that, together with the nine orders, we may be counted as a tenth order in place of those who fell. We offer a tenth to God and retain nine for ourselves, so that we may attribute to God what in us is perfect, though less in quantity, and to ourselves what is more abundant but weak. A tenth, moreover, of all that we possess—whether fruits of the earth, offspring of animals, or gains of any kind—must be paid to God for the support of clergy. [Note: [Col. 0917D] See the English Constitutions, Book III, title *On Tithes*.] For because they set aside secular business, according to the saying, “No one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs” (II Tim. I, 4), they need others’ labour all the more because they refrain from their own. Being devoted to divine service, they devote themselves to prayer and to the diligent correction of Christ’s flock, and give less attention to bodily necessities. Since they labour for the common good of all, it is equitable that they be supported by all in common, either by the obligation of offerings and tithes, or, if that is insufficient, by gifts, as the Apostle says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?” (I Cor. IX, 11). Therefore [Note: [Col. 0917D] This points, in Augustine’s customary manner, to his third discourse on Psalm CIII at this verse.] God planted the cedars of Lebanon so that sparrows might nest there (Ps. CIII, 17). That is, those lofty in the brightness of the world are rooted there so that Christ’s poor, raised above all earthly things on the wings of virtues, may have a place where, so far as nature’s needs are concerned, they may rest.

What sort of life priests lead is no concern of ours; let us merely provide what is owed to them as ministers of Christ. But let us leave to the Lord what they are like. For “who are you to judge another’s servant? Before his own master he stands or falls” (Rom. XIV, 4). Let us always remember how badly it went for Ham, Noah’s son, because he preferred to mock rather than cover his father’s nakedness (Gen. IX, 22). Therefore let us honour even clergy who conduct themselves rather negligently, on account of their dignity, lest they perish through an uncultivated life and we through immoderate speech.

But whoever is devoted to works of mercy must not withhold the tenth from ministers of the Church, but should provide from the remaining nine parts for the need of his own people and others. Although clergy may have sufficient for themselves, they must not on that account be despoiled of what is due by the plundering of laypeople. Therefore the tenth, if not the best among ten, should at least be that which the order of either birth [Note: [Col. 0918D] See the English Constitutions cited above.] [Col. 0919A] or counting has brought forth; and it must be paid in the parish to which it belongs, so that laypeople do not transfer it to a minister of another parish, though he be needy and more worthy. [Note: [Col. 0919D] Council of Worms, ch. 6; First Council of Orléans, ch. 19; Council of Meaux, ch. 46; Council held at Koblenz, ch. 8.] Whenever they confer it upon persons to whom it is not legally due, or cheat even those to whom it belongs when giving it, they incur the crime of sacrilege [Note: [Col. 0919D] XVI, question 7, ch. 1.]; for they make no invasion of human property, but by open robbery or stealthy theft presumptuously steal from God the rights of the Lord’s servants. Nothing else, therefore, belongs to laypeople except faithfully to render what they owe to those for whom it was instituted.

[Note: [Col. 0919D] XVI, question 1, chs. 55–57.] The ordering of ecclesiastical goods is a matter of episcopal care. For the bishop must see to it [Col. 0919B] that the priests under his hand each receive in his own parish only so much income that poverty need not compel them to pursue shameful gain, while sufficiency allows them to maintain those who will serve with them in the Church and their domestic servants. Hence, as an exemplary form of the flock, so that they may show examples of holy conduct to those subject to them, they must carefully receive guests and mercifully assist the destitute as their means allow.

But if the Church’s resources can extend further, the bishop’s administration should ensure that they are spent for good uses—if necessary, on ornaments of the same Church, or especially on the needy. If the Church’s resources are so abundant that they can suffice for its own needs and benefit others, it may reasonably be done—provided no violence is done to priests in their own possessions [Col. 0919C]—that from what overflows support be given to some community of brethren, either temporarily or in perpetuity; but with this reservation, that if at any time what gives benefit to another does not suffice for itself, it may freely retain for its own need what without it it either cannot exist at all, or must fare badly. But it is the work of episcopal oversight to ensure that the Church’s benefices are assigned or restored under secure legal title.

### CHAPTER VII. Why powers are established by God, and in what manner

[Note: [Col. 0919D] Lombard, II, final distinction.] Powers have been established so that, at their command, the things subject to them may be conducted in due order. But “all authority is from God; therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. XIII, [Col. 0919D] 1). Certainly all authority is from God, but in different ways. At one time he imposes it in anger—for he “makes a hypocritical man reign because of the perversity [Vulgate: because of the sins] of the people” (Job XXXIV, 30); at another, while tranquil. He is angry with one who usurps rank by wrongful accession; he is sometimes also angry with the people, to whom he sends a tyrant rather than the ruler they are unworthy to receive. [Col. 0920A] Yet whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance. Authority must therefore be obeyed, but never in such a way that assent is given to an error unlawfully introduced by its holder. Error commonly mingles itself with authority as evil with good. But they must be separated from one another by the judgment of the mind, so that you submit yourself to authority and reject error from yourself. If, fearing God, you submit to authority, then out of that fear withdraw yourself from the wickedness of the powerful. One authority has the care of the body, the other of the mind. Both are established by God so that the whole person may preserve his complete salvation; but above all peace and safety for the outward person are sought, so that repose may be secured for the inward person.

Therefore one power is established as auxiliary to the other. [Note: [Col. 0919D] See ch. *Solitae*, *Extra*, on greater and lesser authority and obedience, from Innocent III to Emperor Constantine; Chrysostom, Book III, *On the Priesthood*, and Homily 4 on Isaiah ch. VI and Homily LXXXIII on Matthew; Ambrose, *On the Dignity of the Priesthood*, ch. 2; Gelasius to Emperor Anastasius; Peter of Cluny, Letter 29, Book VI: “Although the Church does not possess the emperor’s sword, it nevertheless has authority over emperors themselves. Hence it is told under the figure of the prophetic name: ‘I have set you over nations and kingdoms, to root up, destroy, ruin, scatter, build, and plant.’”] Certainly, because priestly dignity cannot prevail to cut away continually recurring diseases of the Church by Peter’s sword, there is need of Christ’s other sword, entrusted to royal authority. For if the priest could secure and preserve the correction and peace of the Church by his own spiritual sword, no necessity would require the admission into the Church of the bodily sword of kings. Indeed, if no one outside the Church existed by whom Catholic peace could be disturbed, what need would there be of one who strikes? But now this authority is established so that none of those outside may presume to assail the Church, nor any within to disturb it by causing scandal. Or, if this has been begun, they may be corrected by bodily punishments and losses—unless the offence be one more properly subject to the justice of priests, who may neither shed blood nor strike kings with the spiritual sword. The king [Col. 0920C] therefore, because by the order of his ministry he owes the Church this: that, standing with equity, he support her children and utterly cast down her enemies in justice—if he so conducts himself, he is truly a king; otherwise he exercises tyranny under a false name.

[Note: [Col. 0920D] Damian, Letters, Book VII, Letter 3, to Henry, king of the Romans.] Since it belongs to the office of the bishop to labour for healing wounds of the soul, so that the inward person may be healthy, while the king’s care wholly labours to remove wrongs inflicted from without—except that often, when necessary, each assists the other’s office by his own—there can be no doubt that this authority must be preferred to that one as much as the body is inferior to the soul. Indeed, as the body goes astray unless directed by the rule of the soul, so kingdoms rush headlong unless supported by the guidance of priests. Saul stood in his kingdom while he obeyed Samuel (I Sam. XXVIII, 7); but as soon as he consulted the witch, he fell. King David had fallen grievously, but when Nathan rebuked him, he humbly accused himself and rose again (II Sam. XII, 13). Therefore the priesthood presides over kingship in matters concerning God, and kingship presides over the priesthood in matters [Col. 0921A] concerning the world. Let each, then, render what is due to the other. Let the king obey the priest in God’s commands; let the bishop know himself subject to the king in secular affairs. Thus let what is Caesar’s be rendered to Caesar, and what is God’s to God (Matt. XXII, 21).

### CHAPTER VIII. On earthly powers

[Note: [Col. 0921D] Lombard, cited above.] Above all, a king ought to devote his care to earthly authorities, so that those legitimately established may be followed by a sound order of conduct. For one who ambitiously climbs to a rank of dignity behaves in that rank always, or very often, greedily. Thus those who gain offices by gifts seek profit from the office once acquired. Since they did not receive it freely, neither do they give freely. While these thirst for money, they do not fear either to sell or destroy justice. Even when they are thought to act well, such people do not serve God, since even in well-conducted matters they attend not to what God commands. They admire only money, or reputation, or favour, or finally something of that sort which is not pleasing to God. Or if they act for God, because they mingle another cause with it, they corrupt their intention, wishing at once to serve two masters. For while they seek to please God, they displease him because they do not act sincerely in what they do for God, seeking together with God what it is wicked to seek in an act done for him. But when something is done from love of the Lord, its reward certainly increases if it is also done for a brother’s benefit. For that is done perfectly which whole charity promises. Just as what does not arise from charity is denied the dignity of reward. Therefore a work has no reward before God unless it proceeds from love of one or the other: God or neighbour.

A king, then, should by his diligence provide himself with ministers who come lawfully to the office of service. Once appointed to office, he should instruct them so that they either will not, or at least dare not, oppress justice, according to the apostolic saying: “Sent by the king for the punishment of evildoers and for the praise of the good” (I Pet. II, 14). Therefore let the king send such leaders as punish the wicked and honour the good, 225 remembering also that, as Scripture testifies, “An unjust king has all his ministers wicked” (Prov. XXIX, 12). Hence it is clear [Col. 0921D] that an equitable emperor cannot be one who permits wicked ministers to remain in his empire. Therefore let him say with King David: “My eyes are upon the faithful of the land, that they may sit with me; he who walks in the blameless way served me” (Ps. C, 6). If such judges are chosen by the king, each will say in truth with the judge David: “I did not sit with the council of vanity, and I shall not enter with those who do iniquity” (Ps. XXV, 4).

### CHAPTER IX. On soldiers and tribute

Under the king are soldiers, so that, if necessary, they may fight for their country either by driving back foreign nations or suppressing internal wars. In order that kings may suffice for this task, taxes are paid by all in common. Subjects therefore owe taxes to their lords, and lords owe their subjects protection against the assault of enemies. For he unjustly exacts taxes who does not defend taxpayers, to the extent of his ability, from injury. Those who serve through taxes—indeed all who are under a lord—should show themselves faithful to their lords, without prejudice to faith in Christ. In the same way lords should know themselves bound to their subjects. For both one who withholds from another what is owed by the law of his condition, and one who abandons for the sake of his condition what he owes to God, are abominable before God. Therefore let one person so favour another as not thereby to offend God. Let the farmer avoid greed; the merchant, fraud.

### CHAPTER X. On one who wishes to enter the clergy

[Col. 0922B]

Whoever wishes to pass from the laity into the clergy—for this lies within the choice and discretion of each person—must be free; lest, if he is a slave, he either be wrongfully taken from his master, or be drawn back into servitude to the shame of the clergy. [Note: [Col. 0921D] Pope Leo, Epistle 1, ch. 4; Gelasius, Epistle 9, ch. 16; First Council of Orléans, ch. 10; Fourth Council of Toledo, ch. 75; Council of Rheims, ch. 1; *De servis non ordinandis*, Extra, bk. I, tit. 18.] But if he is free and unlettered, he is not yet fit for the clergy. Such a person must also abstain, by reason of this vocation, from military service, trade, and secular courts, since a cleric engaged in trade pursues shameful gain. A cleric may neither shed blood nor pronounce judgment that blood be shed, because “no one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2:4). But whoever is free and learned, and has renounced those affairs proper only to laymen, is at last rightly admitted to the clergy when his life contains nothing for which he should deservedly be rejected. [Note: [Col. 0922D] Jerome, Epistle to Nepotianus; Ivo, part V of the *Decree*, ch. 6.] For a cleric ought to excel a layman in merit as well as in rank, so that he may rightly be called a cleric—that is, one allotted either to God or by God. Such a person is suited to the clergy; yet he is not immediately to be admitted to the choir if, perhaps, he is intolerable in appearance—not because on that account he is further removed from God, but because he is merely more unsightly in social fellowship.

One who voluntarily approaches the clergy must not therefore presume by his own action to attain clerical ranks. It belongs to you, if you wish, to choose the clerical life for yourself; but to ascend a rank within the clergy is not your office, but another’s. [Col. 0922D] To seek a manner of life, whether in the clergy or outside it, lies within your right; but once placed in the clergy, it is forbidden to seize for oneself the honour of ranks. As the Apostle says: “No one takes this honour to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was” (Heb. 5:4). Therefore archdeacons were established by God through the bishop, so that through them such persons might be chosen in the clergy by God—persons who, duly called, should come forward for ordination, each according to what suits him and what the ministry of the Church requires. For those who thrust themselves forward—since “no one takes this honour to himself”—must be rejected as presumptuous or covetous.

[Col. 0923A] [Note: [Col. 0923D] Council of Calchuth, canon 6, vol. I; English council of Isaac, in the canons, title specially concerning this matter.] But those called to orders under the title of a particular church, intending to minister to that same church and to transfer elsewhere only if necessity perhaps requires it, should be ordained. For those ordained without a title—how do they presume upon a ministerial rank when they have not undertaken a place in which to minister? They are servants of God’s household; but of whose household? They do not know. Since they profess themselves ministers of the Church, yet no church enrols them among its ministers, they are certainly not ministers but usurpers of ministry. They would truly be ministers if the Church knew them. Such men have never been ministers of the Church, and yet they have received ministry. Hence it is evident that one may not be ordained without a title. But what profit is there in being enrolled under a title while plotting something else? Indeed, it does very great harm: they receive the title deceitfully, because they do not wish to serve under that title. Do you not practise deceit when you accept the title with your mouth and reject it in your heart? So far as lies in you, are you not ordained without a title when you refuse the church to which you are enrolled and have no other? When, at a public hearing, you assent as the title of a particular church is read, do you not profess that, in the order received, you will be that church’s minister, as though by a herald’s proclamation? But when the undertaking of so great a promise is set aside through negligence, what else is sacrilegiously committed in the mind but the crime of apostasy?

## CHAPTER XI. Why marriage remains permitted below the subdiaconate

Marriage may be contracted below the rank of subdeacon; afterward ecclesiastical discipline forbids it. [Col. 0923C] For this reason the last three orders are called sacred: the nearer they approach the altar, the more strictly they bind themselves to a continent life. Hence it is said to them: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52:11). Therefore those who bear the Lord’s cup by virtue of their office must put aside the cup of demons; indeed, they must abstain even from embraces which are permitted to others.

Under the old law, because only the Levitical tribe was appointed to minister in the Temple, it was fitting for the ministers of the altar to contract marriages. Yet each, during his turn of ministry, lived a celibate life, so that he might more freely—indeed, more worthily—serve the figures and shadows of the ceremonies. Since the old law has reached its goal and its authority has ended, let it not restore marriage to the priests of grace unless it also restores the ceremonial figures. On what grounds can priests claim marital rights for themselves, when our law freely advances laymen’s sons to orders, but the sons of priests only after delay? [Note: [Col. 0923D] Extra, bk. I, tit. 17, *On the Sons of Priests*.] The ancients, when they ceased from Temple ministry, went to their wives; our priests, since they must often be ready for service, may never be free for embraces. [Note: [Col. 0923D] Jerome, bk. I *Against Jovinian*; Chrysostom, bk. VI *On the Priesthood*; Siricius to Himerius, chs. 7 and 12; Innocent I to Victricius, ch. 9, etc.]

Those men, while carrying the flesh and blood of animals, shunned the touch of their wives; our priests, whose office is daily to handle the Lord’s flesh and blood, whether for themselves or for the benefit of others, think even the embraces of prostitutes lawful. For among us no woman is joined to a priest in marriage, since he may dismiss her whenever he wishes. Moreover, such a union is transgressive, because it is forbidden by a general enactment. By the very habit of his life the monk, and by the rank of sacred order the cleric, each professes continence in deed without words. Clerics are in the choir; laymen are outside. The presbyterate comprises the sacred orders; and, in proportion as individuals differ from others in place and habit, so they should shine forth in moral uprightness. The prerogative of place and habit seems to promise something great. Let each take care lest the promise prove false in himself.

## CHAPTER XII. What must be done in order that one may live well in one’s rank

[Col. 0924B] Therefore, whoever seeks to conduct himself well among men in his own rank must first take care not to rise to that rank against God. For: “He who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold, but climbs in another way, is a thief and a robber” (John 10:4). Christ is the door, because he himself says, “I am the door” (ibid.). The sheepfold is the assembly of Christians. Therefore, one about to minister in the Church should enter through Christ, and he will minister well; but badly, if he climbs in by another way. He who approaches lawfully enters through Christ; from his entrance he has already received the means by which, unless he prefers to fail, he may act well under persecution. But he who usurps a rank of dignity deserves nothing other than to conduct himself wickedly in it; and if it happens otherwise, grace accomplishes it.

Therefore, he who enters by the door is shepherd of the sheep; [Col. 0924C] he who climbs in another way is a thief and robber. If you consider one entering here through a lowly gate and another climbing there in pride, what else should rightly be thought of each except that the latter falls from a height and the former rises to the heights? The one is to be praised in God’s flock; the other is destructive. Sometimes the reverse happens, but it departs from the nature of the beginning. The language used by us, and by the Lord himself, embraces as familiar what belongs to nature; but what is contrary to it is rejected as unusual.

Accordingly, whoever is ordained, receives any benefice in the Church, or is set over it, must beware lest he obtain this for himself, either directly or through another person, by some scheme. [Note: [Col. 0924D] Gregory, Homily 4 on the Gospels; I, question 1, ch. *Sunt nonnulli*.] If he approaches by entreaty, it is a gift from the tongue; if he has exerted himself by some form of service, it is a gift from the hand in the sense of service. But if money directed to that end has intervened, it is a gift from the hand. Yet: “Blessed is he who shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isa. 33:15). Therefore both recipient and giver must beware lest their right hand be filled with gifts. The one must see that he does not rise in honour only to fall through ambition, according to the saying: “You cast them down when they were lifted up” (Ps. 72:18). If, by his own or another’s petitioning or service, he contrives to be exalted, he gravely offends; but if he obtains it through money, he must be punished most severely. For “no one takes this honour to himself” (Heb. 5:4), and it must be received freely. The other, in turn, must ensure that he rejects as unworthy the man who thrusts himself forward.

But if, prompted by someone’s merits or persuaded by his friends, he promotes that person in the clergy, he does not sin—provided only that he does not promote an unsuitable person. Rather, after careful investigation into whether the person is worthy of promotion, once he has found him fit, I do not think it wrong if he more willingly advances him to honour because he has been asked on his behalf or has become obligated to him for a reasonable cause. Will you reject from an honour fitting to him a good man because you are indebted to him, or because someone has commended him to you? In the one case you will show yourself excessively harsh; [Col. 0925B] in the other, ungrateful for a kindness.

“But,” you say, “the Lord cast buyers and sellers from the Temple” (Matt. 21:12); indeed, he still casts them out. Do not be too righteous, so as to promote no one in the Church who has proved helpful to you, lest you be thought to sell promotion. For how do you sell, when neither he—as far as you can judge—has rendered you service in order to obtain it, nor have you accepted his service in order to confer upon him that which ought to be freely given? Perhaps you repay in this way what he has deserved well from you; yet you give freely, because you accepted no gift in order to give it. You have only promoted a person suitable for the office, for God’s sake. For you ought neither to promote an unsuitable person nor to promote even a suitable person except for God’s sake. The fact that many ask you, or that you are obligated to the man himself, urges you to promote him; yet do not do so unless you first recognize that it pleases God. And, in order to know this, fulfil not God’s will so as to satisfy your own, but your own will so as to satisfy God’s, so that your will may follow the divine will rather than precede it.

“Keep your heart with all watchfulness” (Prov. 4:22), lest you be cast down through fault while you are lifted up in honour. You must therefore look more keenly lest an evil intention reign inwardly while you are outwardly exalted in rank. Even though you obtain it honourably before men, you may nevertheless come before God with a corrupt heart. Thus it often happens that a bishop seems to promote someone well and lawfully, yet in the very deed acts badly and unlawfully because he considers some earthly consideration in his action. [Col. 0925D]

Therefore, when a prelate distributes the various offices, together with possessions belonging to those offices, for the ministry of the Church; when he performs ordinations and dedications; when, finally, he carries out anything requiring spiritual exertion, he must consider nothing except that in every respect there be done what ought to be done among neighbours and by which he may be pleasing to God—so that neither greed, vain glory, nor anything of that kind may usurp anything. In the same way, one who is promoted must consider nothing except how to carry out, with diligent care, what has been entrusted to him, so that both his intention and [Col. 0926A] his work may aim at the salvation of souls.

Certainly, many worldly affairs may be conducted so that the substance of this world may abound, provided only that worldly goods are not sought unjustly, nor kept or squandered unjustly when acquired. Yet the office of a judge, although in a certain sense a secular occupation, is administered for gain only at peril to the soul. For the sternness of justice must be exercised to correct wickedness and establish peace in the Church; in this he acts, as it were, in God’s place and is God’s minister; for this cause he does not bear the sword in vain (Rom. 13:14). Thus a cleric may undertake other work with the intention of providing necessities of life for himself and his household; but he must neither assume nor exercise an ecclesiastical office except in order to seek the welfare of souls. Surely, according to Scripture, “those who serve at the altar should live by the altar” (1 Cor. 9:13). But it is one thing to do something in order that you may live from it, and another to do something from which you live. Intend something other than merely living from it. Therefore, one preparing to enter the ministry of the Church must not climb in by another way, but enter through the door, especially—or among the chief things—guarding against simony.

## CHAPTER XIII. That spiritual power, or its possession, must not be bought or sold

[Note: [Col. 0925] Mag., bk. IV, distinction 4; Ivo, part V of the *Decree*, chs. 85, 91, 95, 122, 208.] Simon Magus offered money to Peter (Acts 8:18), so that, having received power, he might acquire both reputation and wealth for himself. Thus, so far as lay in him, he bought power in order to sell it. Therefore you must neither buy nor sell spiritual power, lest by either act you become a Simonist.

“But,” you will say, “I do not seek the dignity that proceeds from the gift of the Holy Spirit; I labour only to obtain an ecclesiastical possession.” If you seek for money any possession among the Church’s goods which cannot be held without a spiritual ministry, you are a Simonist by the attempt alone—not because you buy the possession, but because together with that possession you attain something which may not be attained in that way. [Note: [Col. 0925] Ivo, *Decree*, bk. II, ch. 84.] For according to the ancient tradition, whoever buys one of two things which cannot be possessed separately leaves neither unbought. Therefore, whatever you may think privately, you are without doubt a Simonist whenever by purchase you obtain something which you cannot obtain through any ecclesiastical possession without dignity. If Simon Magus is condemned by a curse for his intention alone, will you escape, contaminated with simony through action?

For Peter replied to the Magus: “May your money be with you unto destruction” (Acts 8:20). It is as though he said: “Had I received it, it would have been unto destruction with both me and you. But now, without me and with you alone, let it be unto destruction. I do not desire your destruction, but declare the fitting due of your merits: that the money wickedly offered by you and rightly refused by me may cast not me together with you, but you alone, into hell.” Therefore beware, giver; indeed, beware also, recipient, lest the same money drag both into [Col. 0927A] Gehenna—yet you lower down, who ought to have provided for both.

But if you have entered badly as a minister into Christ’s sheepfold, repent and minister—unless your detestable entrance has caused such scandal that nothing else can be thought except that you should be willing to abandon what you wickedly undertook; such is a rank obtained by the act of simony. Once the scandal has been corrected by satisfaction, ministry may be permitted, unless perhaps the matter is so execrable that one ought scarcely, or never, to be admitted to ministry; such are murder or treason, especially when committed for the sake of obtaining a dignity.

For it does not happen that a murderer or a twice-married man is promoted; and it rarely happens that one publicly disgraceful is promoted in the Church or retained after promotion. This is not because, after forgiveness of sin or a second marriage, he has less claim to salvation, but for the dignity of the sacrament. David was forbidden to build the Temple for the Lord because he was a man of blood (3 Kings 5:3); Solomon was admitted because he was peaceful. Both were good, yet the one rejected is better [than the one admitted]: why, unless by reason of sacramental grace? Surely a peaceful man, fitted to reconcile peace, ought rightly to be set over the spiritual building which is the Church. But one who has been a murderer, or has contracted a second marriage, is rejected as unworthy of so great a task: the one because he represents a violator of God’s Temple, the other because he does not represent the single marriage of Christ and the Church.

But one stained by the disgrace of his former life is promoted only with difficulty, or restored after removal, unless at some time a devout way of life, pleasing to all, has commended it. And although the persecution of the Church and the killing of Stephen did Paul no harm in becoming an apostle, nevertheless the strictness of Catholic institution must not be neglected; for, although it takes nothing away from salvation, it greatly increases caution.

## CHAPTER XIV. On a sacrament once conferred, suspension, and degradation

It must be noted that a sacrament once conferred remains as long as life remains: certainly for a good person unto good, but for a bad person unto evil. Therefore rebaptism and reordination are not permitted. Nevertheless, the ordained may be suspended, and, when the fault is very grave, degraded. The former does not fix an endpoint, but the latter does; neither deprives one of the sacramental power; both exclude one from exercising the office and remove one from its use—the one less severely, the other for longer.

When satisfaction and reason call for someone to be restored, the sacrament of ordination is not therefore repeated; rather, the operation of the power, previously interrupted, is exercised with the prelate’s favour. But while a sentence of suspension or degradation remains, what if the forbidden office is meanwhile performed? Certainly, because the power is not removed, both the good and those under prohibition seem able to use their own power; but it is to the harm of the latter and of all who are within [the Church] in such a way as to despise the prohibition.

## CHAPTER XV. On the chaplain and the parish priest

Whoever has a good entrance must carefully avoid a bad performance. For what profit is it to have begun the path of uprightness and to fail before it is completed? Therefore, having been advanced to the dignity of priesthood, whether the care of a tabernacle or of a temple has been laid upon you, act after the manner of the good shepherd. And what is a tabernacle except a movable dwelling, such as courts are? Likewise, what is a temple except a place fixed in one location, such as parishes are?

Therefore, as in ancient times among the Jews there were those who ministered in the tabernacle and afterward those who served in the temple, so in the Church, which contains the truth of the old shadow, why should not priestly guardianship be provided under the care of bishops for courts no less than for parishes? Yet this must be so arranged that, wherever the court may go, it never diminishes the rights of the parish presently concerned. Let the chaplain reap the revenues of the court entrusted to him; but let him leave to the parish priest whatever is enclosed within the boundaries of the parish. [Col. 0928B]

## CHAPTER XVI. What sort of priest one ought to be, and why

A priest must excel in learning and life, so that he may instruct his subjects by word and draw them by example to what he has taught.
