For one who speaks and acts contrariwise is either not believed or despised. Such a person may neither teach nor rebuke a sinner. He is hard pressed on every side: woe to him if he is inactive, because he has an office requiring action; woe if he is not inactive, because he is unworthy to act. He must speak by virtue of his office, yet it is altogether unfitting for him to do so because of his sin. For God says to the sinner: “Why do you recount my just judgments and take my covenant into your mouth?” (Ps. 49:16).

Note that neither reading nor prayer is forbidden to the wicked person; he is only forbidden to expound God’s law to others. Hence those convicted as guilty of crimes are excluded from the ministry of the Church. He who has a beam in his own eye cannot remove the speck from his brother’s eye (Luke 6:42). For when the woman caught in adultery stood in the midst, to be stoned under the law by those standing around, the Lord, asked for a judgment, said: “Let him who is without sin cast the first stone at her” (John 8:7). By this judgment he both mercifully freed the wretched woman and trained the minds of the faithful, so that one who judges the guilty may know no guilt in himself.

Therefore, one who is wicked and strikes the wicked with a judicial sentence both transgresses Christ’s ordinance and becomes worse than the Jews, who recoiled from it. Thus a teacher or judge must either be righteous—or, if not yet so, become righteous—and carry out his office; or, if he does not wish to be such, lay aside the office. For whoever professes himself a judge heaps up Gehenna for himself if he does not wield the sword, or if, unworthy, he strikes with it.

## CHAPTER XVII. On priestly teaching, learning, and baptism

The teaching of a priest consists in two things: purity of faith and, secondly, uprightness of conduct. Therefore, let the priest’s care first be directed to teaching his parish—for the subject here is not the priest who exercises a private priesthood among brethren—the mystery of the Trinity and the sacrament of the Incarnation. Let him also declare that without the washing there is no salvation, and that the age of little children is exceedingly frail, so that they may be brought to the Church for baptism as quickly as possible. [Col. 0929A] [Note: [Col. 0929D] Question XXX, question 1, throughout.]

But if there is despair of life, so that there is no need at all for delay: if a cleric is lacking, let a layman assist; if no one else is present, let the father help; if he too is absent, let no bystander hesitate, but rather confer the sacrament than allow a human being to perish. Nor, when extreme necessity compels, should parents be delayed from giving assistance on the ground that their marriage-bed fellowship must thereby be dissolved as unlawful. For, just as anyone seeking a rupture of marriage who deceitfully contrives to be present at the regeneration of his own child is frustrated in his purpose, because the union is not dissolved; so one who, with devout intention and in order to provide for a salvation which would otherwise perish, celebrates baptism for his children, ought not on that account to be separated from his spouse—lest he prefer the child to perish rather than lose his spouse.

[Col. 0929B] [Note: [Col. 0929D] Same question, ch. *Ad limina*.] The law, serving charity, decreed that no one should marry, or sleep with, a woman whose son or daughter he has received from the baptismal font. It judged such reception, like kinship together with affinity, sufficient to ensure that those thus joined should love one another. Hence it was decreed that those whom such a relationship does not unite should be bound to one another by the bond of marriage. Therefore, what charity has established must not work against charity, lest, while action contrary to such ordinances is avoided, a person’s salvation be neglected.

Thus, when help cannot otherwise be given, baptize your own offspring, or carry it to a baptizer if this can be done. But lest bitter death snatch away the little one, accompany it to be regenerated by water. And if there is no other person, you yourself should stand beside the priest while it is baptized. Nor, in so great a necessity, should you fear the Church’s custom by which parents are excluded from the church while baptisms take place there. This custom does not forbid what must necessarily be done; rather, as I think, it guards against a certain error: lest, when in the ancient manner, especially at the Paschal solemnity, little children are brought from all sides to the Church for baptism, someone through mistake receive his own child from the font as though it were another’s. All parents, therefore, are excluded so that no one may incur the error of such reception.

But when no error is possible, why is it necessary that parents be forced outside, unless perhaps so that the old custom may be recalled to mind? This is especially so when it occurs in a place where no multitude of persons for baptism now normally assembles. In former times this was done particularly for adults, for whom delay was not dangerous—having been instructed in the faith as catechumens, and since their being baptized together brought greater joy to the Church and proclamation of God. But it is not now usually done, since almost only little children are baptized. The bodily life of these is highly uncertain, but the death of their soul without washing is most certain; this compels baptism to be hastened and regeneration to be given individually.

Once regeneration has been accomplished, just as after confession, an offering is customarily made to God that what has been well begun may be brought to completion. It is fitting that the faithful make such offerings, but they must not be extorted by priests. For what is it to demand money for regeneration, confession, ordination, or dedication [Col. 0930A], except to sell doves? What is it to celebrate the solemnities of Mass with a view to temporal advantage, except to sell Christ with Judas—so much the more wickedly because Christ has been exalted by rising again? Likewise, what is it to sell a place owed to the dead except, by usurping another’s property, to rejoice over the death of brethren, when one ought rather to mourn? Finally, what is it to exercise for an earthly thing that which, by right of ministry and for the sake of salvation and charity, the clergy owe the laity, except to sell in God’s temple what ought more properly to be given than sold? Yet the Lord does not cease to cast buyers and sellers out of the Temple.

Nevertheless, if by money I obtain for myself and mine something without which either salvation is absent or scandal is present—something which ought to be bought even at the price of death if it could not otherwise be obtained—I am certainly not buying something in the Temple, but procuring the Temple itself for myself and mine. But whenever we can obtain the sacraments of our salvation according to ecclesiastical custom, we surely dishonour them if we strive to obtain them in the manner of traders: we ourselves act wrongly, but those who sell act most wickedly. Therefore clerics must conduct no commerce in the office entrusted to them, since even under secular law commercial dealing in court is accounted shameful gain for a cleric.

But even if a cleric should put up the rights of his rank for sale, a layman must not presume to buy them, lest he perish together with him—unless necessity perhaps compels it. For if, God forbid, a priest’s greed will confer upon you only for a payment that which is necessary in religion, let him rather perish with your money than your life be defiled through lack of the necessary act.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The teaching of morals begins

Once faith has been taught, it remains to teach morals. In moral teaching, the cutting away of vices comes first; the formation of virtues follows. For while a person devotes himself to vices, he is not yet fitted for virtues. The nature, development, and end of vices and virtues must be treated in turn. Let the teacher preach the word from knowledge and chastise the transgressor from authority. For teaching without punishment, and punishment without teaching, are almost the same thing; indeed, one without the other can rarely be useful.

Yet often the multitude or power of transgressors is so great that exhortation alone is needed, since persons of this sort ought not to be struck, lest, when they turn to sedition, correction become fruitless and the peace of the Church be disturbed. [Col. 0930D] [Note: Augustine, Epistle 50, near the end; and *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, bk. III, ch. 2; Innocent, Epistle 22, ch. 6.] Therefore let practical judgment be the teacher of discipline: at its direction, some matters must be punished and others overlooked. The Apostle forbids even eating with one called a brother who is criminal and incorrigible (1 Cor. 6:11), commanding judgment of those within and forbidding judgment of those outside. They are, as it were, outside and beyond the Church against whom ecclesiastical censure cannot be exercised because they rely either on secular power or on popular favour. Such people must be drawn in by the manner used for Gentiles, not exasperated. But those who behave disorderly should be punished if they are within—that is, if they belong to the Church—and either do not wish, or even if they wish are unable, to resist ecclesiastical decrees.

## CHAPTER XIX. On prelates, the continent, and the married

[Note: [Col. 0931D] Augustine, bk. II *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, ch. 10; on Psalm 132, and elsewhere.] There are three divisions in the Church: prelates, the continent, and the married. These are Noah, Daniel, and Job: in the field, in the bed, and at the mill. Noah, governing the ark amid the flood, represents prelates governing the Church in the world. They are also in the field when they break up the soil of our minds with the plough of their teaching and, in breaking it up, suitably sow the seed of God’s word, from which it may yield the fruit of good works.

Daniel the continent man signifies the continent. These are in the bed, because a quiet life removed from worldly care befits such persons. Job, because he had a wife, represents the married. [Col. 0931B] [Note: [Col. 0931D] Augustine, on Psalm 132.] Since the care and labour of a household rest upon them, the noisy and restless dwelling of the mill is suitable for them. Let each, therefore, persevere in his own pursuit. Let Noah cultivate the field and govern the ark, and flee women’s embraces—he who, apart from women’s companionship, has undertaken residence in the field or the ark. Hence Noah did not enter the ark with his wife, [Note: [Col. 0931D] Consult the notes.] nor, while governing the ark, did he know his wife.

What then does the Apostle mean when he says: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife” (1 Cor. 7:2)? If this is a general decree, does not anyone who embraces chastity do so with rash presumption? Why did he say this and not do it himself, he who, bearing witness to his own continence, said: “I wish all men to be as I myself am” (ibid.)? [Col. 0931C] [Note: [Col. 0931D] A notable passage for the celibacy of St Paul.] How can he wish all to be chaste if he commands each to have his own wife? But lest the order of the continent perish from the Church by the Apostle’s decree, we should understand that the Apostle did not command that each should have his own wife, but advised it. Nor did he offer this counsel indiscriminately to every person, but permitted each person who needs it to guard against fornication by marriage.

And, in order that those to whom the divine law removes marriage may be excluded, he did not say, “Let each have a concubine,” but “his own wife.” Yet, in order that those capable of continence might rather remain continent, he decreed that the incontinent should marry, precisely in order to avoid fornication. For [Note: [Col. 0932D] See above, on ch. 11, where we cited those who seem here to have anticipated Pullo.] if the priests of the law, during the time of their turn, did not return at all to the company of their wives—although they had to be married, since ministers of sacrifices and of the figure had necessarily to be taken from the priestly tribe—how shall the priests of grace have wives during the time of their ministry? They must always either baptize, visit the sick with the Eucharist, or do something of that sort; they are to handle not now the shadow of the figure but the body of the thing signified, the flesh and blood of Christ; and they may be taken from every human condition, especially since among us no union exists between priests and women unless it may be dissolved by either whenever he wishes, or, if it is otherwise contracted, the Church considers it void. [Col. 0932A]

Therefore the preacher of continence must avoid fornication and abhor women’s embraces. For among us priests who are not continent are, without ambiguity, fornicators. God will judge fornicators and adulterers all the more strictly in proportion as each one’s rank is higher.

## CHAPTER XX. On the continent and the married

[Note: [Col. 0932D] Augustine, on Psalm 132.] Let Daniel, hating the cares of the world, rest in bed and guard chastity with all his effort. For chastity is precious in the world and altogether necessary for those who have stripped themselves of the world. Such persons can neither be fornicators, lest they perish more grievously, nor spouses, lest they act against their vow by marriage or against marriage by their vow. Marriage draws one toward secular affairs, but the purpose of their vow forbids these things.

Therefore the Lord’s counsel, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor” (Matt. 19:21), is by no means directed to married people. Rather: “Let him who can receive it, receive it” (ibid.). For they can neither leave their possessions nor make themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of God. “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release” (1 Cor. 7:27). Since you must not dismiss your wife, neither can you do without your property. You are therefore divided by necessity. Surely you cannot devote your whole self to God because you are bound in part to the world.

Your soul is troubled within you; therefore remember God from the land of Jordan [Col. 0932C] (Ps. 41:8). Seeing the miseries that the care of marriage and the labour of the world bring upon you, you are troubled: take breath for a little while. Remember God, because marriage is from God and care for one’s household is not against God. For “whoever does not care for his own, especially those of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5:8). Therefore, lest you have believed in vain, give care to your own, unless perhaps they do not need your care, or the death of your soul certainly threatens you from that care. Hence the Lord says: “He who loves father or mother or other things more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37).

Therefore, while you are afflicted in the world, be consoled by remembering God. Consolation will by no means fail you if you remember God from the land of Jordan and Hermonim, from the little mountain. If, afflicted, you wish to be consoled in God, be a mountain through the height of your life, but little in opposition to the swelling of pride. You can be a mountain from the land of Jordan—that is, from the fruitfulness of humble descent—for you rise in the fruit of good works if you first descend through humility. You can descend from Hermonim if you prolong the *anathema*—the accursedness—of your life. [Col. 0932D] [Note: Augustine, on Psalm 41, verse 8.] Let the anathema, then, make you little, and thence rise by fruit. Thus, having become a mountain, remember God from the little mountain.

It remains, therefore, that those who have wives should be as though they had none [Col. 0933A] (1 Cor. 7:29): not that they should bestow no care upon them, but that they should not give more attention than is proper, for the time of our departure is near (2 Tim. 4:6).

## CHAPTER XXI. On the pre-eminence of prelates

Under the care of prelates are contained the other two orders of the Church, namely the married and the continent. From them each receives what suits his own life; from them they have instruction and examples of life, while the flood of worldliness overwhelms the world. Where would Daniel and Job have life except in the ark of the Church? How are they in the ark unless they are subject to the ruler of the ark, namely Noah himself—principally to Christ, and secondarily, indeed, to his vicar? Thus it is: the Lord makes his faithful people dwell amid the flood, and “the Lord will sit as king for ever” (Ps. [Col. 0933B] 28:9).

Whoever, then, desires to be governed by God even to the vision of God must not disdain to be subject to the vicar. For how can one live either in the bed or at the mill unless he is supported by the cultivator of the field? What does it matter to you what sort of farmer he may be, since life is to come to you from his hand, provided you do not neglect to receive it? If he is wicked, it will indeed be to his own detriment. But what harm arises for you from this, when, if you are good, even through an evil minister that which your soul needs is procured for you? Who are you to judge another’s servant—indeed, your own prelate? “Before his own Lord he stands or falls” (Rom. XIV, 4). To whom, surely, does it belong either to reward him while standing or to destroy him when fallen? Take care, however, lest the same wickedness [Col. 0933C] drag both you and him down to hell: him, because he admitted it; you, because you despise, more arrogantly than the Pharisee, one who admits it. Remember that Ham was rejected with a curse because he publicized the exposed nakedness of Noah his father (Gen. IX, 22); whereas Shem and Japheth were blessed because they covered their father’s shameful nakedness. Therefore, do not turn even the blameworthy life of your teachers into an occasion for mocking narration.

But you, teacher, understand that a twofold necessity of doing good rests upon you. Your life must be holy in yourself and circumspect toward those subject to you, so that you may rebuke the disobedient, instruct the ignorant, and strengthen the wise. You are debtor both to wise and to foolish persons: may all alike find in you a pattern of life and examples of holiness. In [Col. 0933D] you may all recognize what is fitting in themselves and what is unfitting; let such gracefulness govern the bearing of mouth and eyes, and indeed of all the members, that, on seeing you, each person may recognize what to approve and what to condemn in himself. If you conduct yourself in this way as a good imitator of your profession, you will be crowned with a double laurel: because you have not forgotten yourself and because you attend well to another. A private person may hope for one crown, because he attends only to himself. Yet it can be, indeed it sometimes is, that a private person endowed with much devotion becomes of greater [Col. 0934A] merit than one established in authority who occupies the lowest place among those governing well. Yet it is easier, and happens more often, that one who governs well is better than one who is well governed, just as one who understands well, if he has charity, is accustomed to love more; although one who knows less, aided by grace, often surpasses his superiors in love.

## CHAPTER XXII. On passing from one of these places to another

There can be a passage from the mill to the bed, and from either of these to the field; but not from the field to the bed, and indeed it is not permitted to return from either to the mill. For it is fitting that the cultivators of God ascend according to the ranks of their profession; they are not permitted to descend. Certainly the continent person is superior to the married person, and rightly so; but each of these two is inferior to the prelate. Yet it must be determined how one ought to ascend this ladder, or is not permitted to return by it.

[Note: [Col. 0933D] XXVII, question 2, Agath.] Those joined to one another by the law of marriage cannot undertake the rule of continence unless both first wish, by common consent, to abstain from marital intercourse. For they can be released from rendering the marital debt, if it pleases each of them to do so [perhaps: “if it pleases one or the other”], but they cannot be released from marriage. [Note: [Col. 0933D] Augustine, Epistle 199 to Edicius and 45; on Psalm CXLIX; on Numbers, question 59; Book I, *On Adulterous Marriages*, ch. 2; Gregory, Book V, Epistle 49; Jerome, *Apology against Jovinian*, etc.] Having undertaken continence, they may either still manage a household or enter the bed. But if someone prematurely enters the society of the continent and the bed of those at rest, what will happen? Unless both have given consent to continence—or unless he has done so secretly—if the one remaining in the world lodges a complaint, the other will be recalled from the cloister in order to render the marital debt [Col. 0934C] to that person, and will at last fulfill his vows if he survives his spouse.

If a servant has been imprudently admitted either to orders or to a community of brothers [Note: [Col. 0934D] Augustine, Epistle to Count Boniface; Council of Chalcedon, canon 15; Arles, canon 3, and Ivo, Part VII of the *Decretum*, ch. 44; Gelasius, Epistle 1, ch. 16, etc.], is he to remain in what he has begun without complaint from his master? Or, if silence cannot lawfully be imposed upon one who complains, ought an injury to be done? What then? Should the one be deposed from his rank, and the other stripped of the religious habit, and restored to his master, to whom loss was fraudulently inflicted? For such a person ought, with permission, to have passed from the mill either to the bed or to the field. Hence, one who presents himself for sacred orders without his wife’s knowledge, after this becomes known, will not, I think, be taken from his wife on account of the order; rather, the order, as though it had never existed, will be suppressed.

[Col. 0934D] But one occupied with the care of his own people, and especially of his household, lest he lose faith and become worse than an unbeliever (I Tim. V, 8), though desirous of a quiet life, should nevertheless not abandon his own, unless at some time they can do without him or are opposed to his salvation. But if it happens otherwise, what is to be done? Is he to be brought back? But that is unusual. Is he to be taken away from those who will perish? That is indeed harsh. What then should be said here and above? I do not know. [Note: [Col. 0934D] XXVII, question 2; Magister, IV, distinction 27, §8. See under the title *On the Conversion of Married Persons*, Extravagantes, Book III.] Perhaps this: let the brothers either provide a steward or, better, provide for the needy family. Let a servant likewise be restored [Col. 0935A] to his master—or rather, let redemption be made. For if a wife is to be restored to her husband, why should not a servant likewise be restored to his master? For he who decreed that a wife should not depart from her husband also commanded that the things which are Caesar’s be rendered to Caesar.

Those who live at the mill may, both on their own initiative and when instructed, undertake the bed. From neither place may you go forth into the field on your own; but when the Church calls, you are compelled, and do not heed one who compels you [Note: [Col. 0935D] Chrysostom, Book IV, *On the Priesthood*, ch. 1, etc. See the notes.] unless you are fit. Once raised to dignity, do not return to private life unless necessity presses: either because you entered contrary to God’s will or because after entering you cannot be useful. For a lamp lit upon a lampstand is not to be hidden under a bushel; nor is salt that has lost its savour useful for anything further except to be cast out.

[Col. 0935B] [Note: [Col. 0935D] Augustine, on Psalm CXXXII.] Only three men are known to be saved: Noah, Daniel, and Job. The Lord shows these three, together with those who are to perish, in three places: in the field, the bed, and the mill. For in each of these there are found two persons: one will be taken and the other left (Matt. XXIV, 41). Therefore, whoever you are, do not become sluggish through confidence in your place: from there one will be taken and another left. It may be provided for you that you are taken; it may be—and this is nearer to you—that you are left. But how do those who are to perish and those who are to be blessed all alike dwell only in the places mentioned above? Certainly not only married people but all who attend to worldly cares, whether good or bad, inhabit the mill. Whoever either sets aside the labours of the age and the restless pleasures [Col. 0935C] of the world, or assumes the appearance of one who has set them aside, is in the bed. And who among subjects—indeed, among all persons—does not either rest or attend to work, except children, whose unknowing tenderness is as yet unfit for either? Among workers some are set over others. Who, then, does not lead either a quiet or a laborious life? Even among the pagans philosophers preferred leisure. Who among active persons does not either obey a superior or provide for an inferior? This also exists among the pagans.

Therefore, one must be either a prelate or a subject; for one who is not a prelate and is not a subject is headless. A prelate is situated in the field; a subject is either in the bed or at the mill. Although some at the mill are set over others, it is by worldly power. [Col. 0935D] For one who presides spiritually is rather in the field; but though being headless is a fault, being many-headed is not. Those dwelling in one place can belong to one head—that is, one prelate. But those whose life is set in transition: what head do they have, except that they accept the head of each place in which they are? Nor is it absurd—indeed, it is necessary—to change many heads in this manner. For who is there who, under the one head Christ, does not have many heads: a priest, a bishop, and higher dignities as well?

Courtiers, unless they have obtained a prelate in the court, [Col. 0936A] and travellers, in whatever parish they may be, should obey that parish’s instruction. Yet it is good, and the practice of the Church provides, that those intending to travel abroad should travel with the counsel of the person whose parish they belong to, lest perhaps that which ought to appease the Lord provoke him. For a man who has a wife is not permitted to travel if she objects, or if, though consenting prematurely, she cannot do without the marital debt. Therefore let him preserve her to whom he owes faith. Likewise, neither may a servant leave his master unless the latter approves; nor may a prelate leave his subject, if it is dangerous, when he is intending to travel or to do something else. Merchants and students also travel about: while they are in their own place, they have their own advisers for their souls; while away, let them receive temporary ones.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the contemplative and active life

[Col. 0936B]

The three orders of the Church profess two lives: the first active, the second contemplative. These have their counterpart among the pagans as well: theoretical among philosophers, practical among the rest. [Note: [Col. 0935D] Augustine, Tractate 124 on John, after the middle.] The active life is in labour; the contemplative in rest. The active life persists in good works; contemplation applies itself to knowing faith and works. Action merits blessedness by worshipping God and helping one’s neighbour; contemplation, by searching out the condition of the heavenly life, tastes in advance the sweetness of that condition. The latter teaches; the former practises. The former exhausts; the latter refreshes. There is sadness with weariness there; here, breathing again through the perceived goodness of God. Hence contemplation is delightful and skilled in holy instruction. This is [Note: [Col. 0936D] Isidore, Book III, *Sentences*, ch. 15, and Book I, *Differences*, ch. 29.] [Col. 0936C] Rachel, beautiful in appearance and fair to behold, whom Jacob embraces [Note: [Col. 0936D] Ivo, Epistles 17 and 25, to Pope Urban.]. Action, however, is burdensome; and because it is troubled by many things, it is less acquainted with things of lesser use. This is Leah [Note: [Col. 0936D] Ibid.], whom Jacob disdains, weak-eyed. Leah marries before Rachel because action ought to precede contemplation. Certainly action accustoms the novice to goodness and advances him; contemplation then strengthens the one advanced by refreshing him with a certain sweetness. For one who rests before acting grows sluggish through idleness, wanders in mind, and perishes, rather than contemplating; since he has not yet discovered what contemplation is, so that he may behold its secrets and, captivated by sweetness, rejoice. Rachel is dear in herself; Leah too pleases, but through fruitfulness. For contemplation delights Israel by its own merit; [Col. 0936D] but Jacob would not endure the weariness of action unless the usefulness of labour strengthened him. This is Martha, who is anxious and troubled about many things [Note: [Col. 0936D] Augustine, Sermon 27, *On the Words of the Lord*, and above, 26.]; she prepares a banquet for the Lord in his members, so that in whatever way she may refresh either the human being or the human mind. She prepares it because the spirit is willing, but does so anxiously because the flesh is weak; she is concerned about the preparation—indeed, disturbed about the serving. She wills well but does not know how; she does not know from what source, and is troubled. What she has willed well, she finally accomplishes; but the outcome responds inadequately to her will, and she is troubled. But Mary [Col. 0937A] sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to his word (Luke X, 39). These two are in the house where the Lord feasts: contemplation and action are in the Church where the Lord is gladdened by a spiritual banquet.

For some time Lazarus was absent, dead in the tomb; but, restored to life through the intercession of both sisters, he remains sound among them. He is the one whom sin killed, but who now lives among the brothers formerly left behind through the intervention of the saints. While dead, he took no care of himself; yet he was restored to life through the prayer of the living: “For the prayer of a righteous person has great power” (Jas. V, 16). [Note: [Col. 0937D] Augustine, Sermon 27, *On the Words of the Lord*.] Martha labours in order to feed the Lord; Mary rests in order to be fed by the Lord. Yet, because no one is worthy to be fed unless he has imitated the Lord’s footsteps, Mary sits at the Lord’s [Col. 0937B] feet while each faithful person ceases from worldly cares so as to attend to fulfilling the Lord’s commands; and he hears the Lord’s word when he understands what the Lord wills. Do you wish to understand the law? Keep the commandments (Matt. XIX, 17); and likewise: “Be at leisure and see that I am” (Ps. XLV, 11), etc. Action and contemplation, like sisters and friends, are near one another and accompany one another for a time. But the elder, born first, will end with the world; the younger will reign after the world. For Mary chose the better part, which shall not be taken from her (Luke X, 43), as though he said: Martha’s part, which is anxious and troubled, is to be taken away; therefore let Martha console herself in her restlessness. But Mary’s part, subject to the Lord and enjoying his teaching, exists here in some manner, but truly remains [Col. 0937C] in the future. For there all shall be taught by God (John VI, 45); but now contemplation is joined to action. Hence Jacob has Leah together with Rachel. Action, however, cannot endure long because it is burdensome in itself unless it tastes something in advance, for its strengthening, of the sweetness of contemplation. Therefore Rachel was introduced after Leah; but this sweetness does not usually endure long. For just as serenity, as the cause of reward, is owed to the age to come, so hardship, for the sake of merit, belongs to the present age: “For judgment begins with the house of God” (I Pet. IV, 17), both that it may be purified from vices and that merits may be accumulated, and finally lest it delight in the pilgrimage of exile.

But lest the medicine exceed its measure, among dense thickets of bitter things sweet things are gathered here and there. Hence the Apostle, worn down by continual experience of evils, deserved to be carried up to the second heaven as a consolation. Therefore, as holy delight will be perpetual in the future, so now it is brief and lasting but an hour; while hardship is continual and only rarely interrupted. This is Leah: quick to be born, slow to die. Rachel, however, delays in being born and is soon to depart. For the history relates that Rachel was born later, and hastens to tell of her death; but it reports Leah as older in birth, while delaying—or rather, omitting—to report her death.

Whenever, while one labours in action, a certain holy savour is felt in the labour, contemplation strengthens action. But when you apply yourself to contemplation [Col. 0938A] and some distress from elsewhere intrudes, know that Martha has interrupted Mary’s rest. Thus whatever delights you according to God amid Martha’s anxious care is bestowed by Mary, her fellow-worker; but whatever disturbs you in Mary’s rest is introduced from Martha’s proximity. Certainly, because serenity is not yet complete, clouds sometimes—indeed, very often—burst in. Likewise, because present hardship has some good joined to it, pleasant things console amid harsh ones. The active life is assigned to Job at the mill; the contemplative life to Daniel in the bed.

## CHAPTER XXIV. What a prelate ought to be like

[Note: [Col. 0938D] Council of Orléans, canon 5.] What then is the part of Noah himself in the field, who labours in order to feed both? How will he feed contemplatives [Col. 0938B] if ignorant of contemplation? How will he refresh active persons if unaccustomed to action? Therefore, one who ought to preside must also have experience of both lives, lest scoffers mock him with the words: “This man began to build and was not able to finish” (Luke XIV, 30). For this reason, let no one presume to pass from the mill to the field unless, if not by habit or profession, at least by the maturity of his manner of life he has tasted the pleasantness of the bed. But scarcely anyone is fit to be taken from the bed into prelacy unless he has first been turned about by the rolling of the mill. “For we ought not to have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses,” but one tempted in every way, able to pity those who are ignorant and err, because he himself is surrounded by weakness (Heb. IV, 15). The one who has felt in himself, through experience of temptations, their troubles and conquered them by the spirit of strength; who, weighing human ignorance, has often laboured to find truth; who has repeatedly struggled against our weakness, prone to falling—such a person will finally know how to provide for our need and will desire to do so from compassion. One ignorant of this becomes errant through inexperience, hard toward subjects without affection, and unmerciful. Therefore, one who has learned rest around the mill and experienced labour in the bed will be able to make progress in either state. Hence Jacob, who was in labour, became Israel through a vision: he has Leah and Rachel. This is the person who, through the merit of a good life, excels others—both active and contemplative—to such an extent that, like a husband over a wife, he governs the people subject to him.

## CHAPTER XXV. Whether contemplation or action is to be preferred

[Col. 0938D]

But which is to be preferred to which: action to contemplation, or the reverse? Certainly, if we consider Leah and Martha on the one side, Rachel and Mary on the other, each appears good, but the contemplative life better. Thus Israel is better than the good Jacob. This is also indicated by the fact that Mary chose the better part, which will not be taken from her (Luke X, 43).

But Christ, and indeed his apostles, preferred to be exercised in the labour and anxiety of action; nor did contemplative fruits fail them while acting. Yet through action they became both more useful to the world and [Col. 0939A] more pleasing to God. By contemplation they would have benefited almost only themselves; by action they benefited everyone, including themselves. And one who loves his neighbour has fulfilled the law. The proof of love is the performance of work (Rom. XIII, 8). Because our Lord Jesus became obedient unto death, even death on a cross, therefore the name above every name was given to him (Phil. II, 8). Our Lord Jesus was certainly more contemplative than all human beings; nevertheless, not on that account but rather through exercise in labour did he deserve to be called the Saviour of the world. For the same reason, raised to the Father’s right hand, with all things subjected beneath his feet, he was granted the name above every name. For the same reason martyrdom joined martyrs—especially the apostles—more closely to God and set them even above holy contemplatives. Certainly, as they bear about Christ’s sufferings and act as ambassadors for Christ in teaching, as good imitators, they approach the Lord and Master as much in merit as in likeness. He whose kingdom was not of this world did good and taught well, and was thereby exalted. And you, although a private person—if you live holily and, when and as is fitting, teach—are you not to be exalted?

When these matters are weighed, the active life seems to excel. Certainly contemplation is always more pleasing and, if we look to the future, is found far better. For once action is ended, contemplation will then rise and will never cease; therefore Mary chose the better part, because it shall not be taken from her. Yet in respect of our present condition, just as action is very often surpassed, so it also sometimes surpasses contemplation. For action, through the good moral habits of private life, prepares in this age a place for contemplation; and this is common to the saints. But there are some, though few, who labour in active life beyond others in order to learn [Col. 0939C] the holy Scriptures. When they commit them to memory, they store fodder like holy animals in the belly; later, in contemplation, they chew over with delight what they had acquired by labour. In this way they are fitted for prelacy and for an active life beneficial to the community. Thus private action is inferior in merit and dignity to contemplation; but contemplation under our mortal condition is inferior in merits to the fruits of active prelacy, which may hope for the highest rank from God in heaven. [Col. 0939D] “He will set them over all his goods” (Matt. XXIV, 42), as authority teaches—not because they alone will possess them, but because they will possess them above others. Such is Jacob’s progress from Leah to Rachel, that he may find delight; then from Rachel back to Leah, that he may produce fruitfulness; and finally from Leah to Rachel, to end the alternation—now truly Israel.

Contemplation is suitable for those stripped of the world; action accords with those entangled in it. But both are incumbent on a prelate, so that by contemplation he may learn what to do for his subjects, and, wearied by action and therefore needing refreshment, he may flee [Col. 0940A] to the consolations of contemplation. Thus, by alternating, he may at one time endure Leah’s weariness and at another embrace Rachel’s delights, never forgetting that by the obligation of his profession he is bound to the most excellent concerns of the active life. Let him therefore provide for the salvation of souls; yet let not Christ’s vicar neglect bodily administration. For Christ himself was sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. XV, 24): he taught the instructions of salvation and supplied necessities of the flesh. The former is first; the latter second.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the two loves

There are, then, two lives; likewise, there are two loves. But how do these relate to those lives? For a life not adorned with charity cannot be good. [Col. 0940B] Each appears to operate in each life. For love of neighbour is very often love of God, and especially the cause of contemplation: certainly because we love our neighbours, we are gladdened by a certain sweetness while we labour for them. And because we love the Lord, we rejoice both in doing good to his servants and in praying to him, giving him thanks, serving him, and continually meditating upon him. What is this delight, born in us from each love, except a certain foretaste of future contemplation and blessedness, capable of refreshing us against the hardships of this exile? Indeed, this pleasure that accompanies works arises from charity and belongs to contemplation. But the works themselves, proceeding from love so that they may be good—whether God is worshipped or a neighbour helped—undoubtedly belong to the active life. Charity, therefore, wholly finds what it does in the contemplative life, just as it does in the active life.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the different kinds of people

There is no life other than one of these two by which a human being can please God in what he does. Therefore, whoever rests from the world, unless he is refreshed by the sweetness arising from love, how does he belong to the contemplative profession? And one who lives in the world, unless drawn by charity he does good and avoids doing evil, how is he active? Where can he hope for salvation? Therefore, one who, fearing the wickedness which the world openly contains, shuts himself away in solitude, even though he does not immediately, upon entering religious life, enjoy delights [Col. 0940D]—for at the beginning “the way that leads to life is narrow” (Matt. XIV, 7), but as one advances Christ’s yoke is sweet and his burden light (Matt. XI, 30)—nevertheless, because for the sake of fulfilling the words [Note: [Col. 0939D] Thus Bernard, on these words: “Behold, we have left all things,” etc.: “The Church cries to her immortal Bridegroom from the ends of the earth: ‘Because of the words of thy lips I have kept hard ways.’ These indeed are the words which persuaded human beings to contempt for the world throughout the whole world and to voluntary poverty. These are the words which fill monastic enclosures with monks and deserts with anchorites.”] of God’s lips he keeps hard ways, while the spirit is willing but the flesh weak (Matt. XXVI, 41), is surely not far from contemplation, because he has both entered a place of rest and persists in good works.

Such persons, however, must take great care lest, appearing in sheep’s clothing, they be inwardly ravenous wolves: outwardly displaying a good work while inwardly concealing a wicked heart, [Col. 0941A] or—what must especially be avoided—being most righteous in public but secretly also infamous in action. For some, seeking their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, usurp either the solitary life or the life which they have entered; often weary of the world, they seek to satisfy the flesh in the cloister. One who despairs of being exalted in worldly society sometimes seizes the religious habit, acting superstitiously in order to be elevated. Another, neither cold nor hot, follows custom like cattle and does everything negligently. Others, afflicted by pride or boiling with envy, despise everyone else alike; they interpret even good deeds maliciously. Some, deceived by an appearance of piety, do not dare to rebuke the faults of their brothers; but, what is far more intolerable, they sometimes even foster them unknowingly. Whoever, though able, does not correct another thereby consents; and the Apostle attributes guilt not only to those who act but also to those who consent (Rom. I, 32).

Some are disobedient to their superiors, contrary to the Apostle’s saying: “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers” (Rom. XV, 1). The soul is to be subjected not only in body but also in will—though not in things contrary to right, but only in the Lord. For a person ought to know that he owes obedience to no one against God; for God instituted powers not against himself, but toward himself. Thus every soul should be subject to powers, not in every manner, but to the higher powers—that is, in those matters in which it has them placed over itself.

[Col. 0941C] While authority is being sought, strive, so far as you can rightly do so, that an evil person is not appointed. But once he has been appointed, whatever he may be, do not blaspheme or curse the ruler (Exod. XXII, 28); only be subject, not merely to the good and gentle but also to the perverse. And do this from the heart. Why? Because “there is no power except from God.” Why, then? Because “he who resists authority resists God’s ordinance.” What harm follows? Hear what comes next: “Those who resist acquire condemnation for themselves” (Rom. XIII, 1). But what good will come to those well subject, and who are well subject? Let the Apostle teach us by speaking thus to servants: “Servants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, in the simplicity of your hearts, as to Christ; not serving only when watched, as those pleasing men, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, serving with good will as to the Lord and not to men, knowing that whatever good each person does, he will receive this from the Lord, whether slave or free” (Eph. VI, 8). Therefore superiors, even evil ones, must be obeyed in simplicity, so that as obedience is outwardly displayed, so it may be inwardly present in the will. I say, obey as Christ—not, indeed, that we may please people, but that we may do God’s will. For it is God’s will that we serve our superiors with good will and judge that this obedience itself is God’s worship. Therefore let anyone safely serve authorities who does not fail to know that in that service he serves God, knowing: [Col. 0942A] “Whatever good each person does, he will receive this from God.” To such authorities, as subjects, you pay tributes, as though to those who are to render an account. When they fight, they act for their country; you rightly pay taxes for judgments, “for they are God’s ministers, serving you for this very purpose” (Rom. XIII, 6), namely, on account of the taxes. “Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; customs to whom customs” (ibid.). Tribute is what regions pay to authorities; customs is what is paid when goods are carried through districts. Therefore, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s” (Matt. XXII, 17), etc.; for one without the other is insufficient.

Let authorities, however, be diligent, as persons who will render account to God for what has been entrusted to them and will be condemned or saved according as they have administered their office well or badly. [Col. 0942B] Therefore let them instruct the ignorant, rebuke wrongdoers, and not allow without punishment those who neglect to be corrected. “For they do not bear the sword without cause” (Rom. XIII, 4): Caesar bears the bodily sword, Peter the spiritual. A necessity rests upon both: upon Caesar to strike, upon Peter to teach. Caesar also teaches, but the laws of the world; Peter too strikes, but with the spiritual sword. Thus one lives well everywhere who keeps obedience, separated from worldly conduct. He is indeed good if he does good according to his profession; but he begins to be perfected when righteous living itself becomes sweet to him.

Whoever is turned about by the mill of the world—soldier or farmer, merchant or practitioner of any other lawful occupation—cannot otherwise be saved, since he does not hold the contemplative life, unless he has the active life. For, [Col. 0942C] as has already been said, there is no third life by which one who uses reason ought to hope for life.

But how do those pursuing different worldly occupations live the active life, if they seek their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ (Phil. II, 21)? If they seek to prevail in the world rather than to please Christ? Such persons, therefore, either are in no sense active, or, as they turn the mill, are subjected to vanity not because they wish it so but because of him who subjected them in hope. Thus neither the vanity of worldly life nor the circling of the mill is pleasing; rather, each should labour in the office to which God has assigned him, so that he may finally be freed and meanwhile render service to the Lord according to his station. Therefore, whatever your occupation, exercise yourself in it according to your capacity for God’s sake, so that you may lawfully acquire the means to live lawfully. Thus render an offering to God and aid to your neighbour. [Note: [Col. 0941D] Augustine, Book XXI, *City of God*, ch. 26, etc.] If you possess worldly goods for necessity rather than pleasure, you are among those who build on the foundation of faith gold, silver, and precious stones (I Cor. III, 12), who in the fire suffer nothing, or only little. These are those who possess all things as though possessing nothing (II Cor. VI, 10).

But if you possess your property with some love—which is proved when you lose it with some grief—yet in no way wish to offend God for the sake of your property, you do not yet destroy the foundation, since you love the property less than God; rather, you build wood, [Col. 0943A] hay, and straw upon it, which suffer in the fire as much injury as you have possessed love for worldly things. “For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (I Cor. III, 11).

God lays the foundation through the office of teachers; let each see how he builds upon it. Whatever you do, however splendidly you may live, if you depart from faith, what you do is vain, because you cannot build a temple to God outside the foundation. Therefore one must build upon the foundation either with gold, silver, and precious stones, or with wood, hay, and straw. You place gold, the most precious of metals, upon the foundation if you shine in faith with love of God pre-eminent among gifts. You work in silver, which holds second rank, if you love your neighbour, which is the second commandment. As much as gold surpasses silver, so much—indeed, more—must God be loved above one’s neighbour. Gold comes first in order and silver follows, because God is loved first; but this is insufficient unless one loves one’s neighbour. Love of God ought to be the reason that a human being is also loved; from love of neighbour love of God increases. If you love your neighbour otherwise than for God’s commandment, it is either a natural affection, which even beasts possess and from which evil often results, or plainly a vice, by which wicked people ally themselves in matters unfitting. But because charity cannot be fruitless, precious stones follow. If you perform things pertaining to the worship of God or the benefit of one’s neighbour [Col. 0943C] without charity, you have precious stones, but not placed after gold—indeed, you do not have them in gold and silver. Therefore you will set precious stones in gold and arrange them in silver, so that they may have power and be fitting. The contemplative person sets gems in gold; the active person in silver. Those who live in this manner will suffer little or nothing in purgatorial fire.

There are some who seek to see God and love God above all things; their spirit is willing, but their flesh weak. While they take some delight and glory to a degree in the things of the world—contrary to “Delight yourself in the Lord” (Ps. XXXVI, 4) and “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI, 14)—they act disorderly in proportion as they cling to the world in love. For love, whether good or bad, being unable to conceal itself, reveals by certain signs what sort it is and how great. But, just as holy love must expect its recompense, so also disordered love must expect recompense for itself and its offspring, more or less. Thus one builds straw upon the foundation because his attachment is slight; another hay because it is greater; another wood because he will suffer most in punishment. These persons are certainly good, but together with good—or before it—they have committed some unlawful acts. According to the Apostle, they “will indeed be saved, yet as through fire” (I Cor. III, 15): if they are not burned in this age, they will be burned in the future.

Perhaps someone wonders how he can seek, preserve, and use worldly things appropriate to necessity if he does not love them. [Col. 0944A] A farmer heaps up manure, keeps it, scatters it over the field, endures its stench, tolerates the work, and beholds its ugliness. He bears everything, not for those things themselves, but to make the field fruitful; he loves things that are not to be loved for their own sake, but for their usefulness. Conduct yourself likewise toward worldly things: love things not for themselves but for use, and thus you love the use of the thing, not the thing itself. Therefore seek the use of things; do not take delight in their outward form; rather, delight in the Lord (Ps. XXXVI, 4). When you admire the beauty of the world, let admiration for the creature be turned toward veneration of its Author. Hence: “Bless the Lord, all works of the Lord; praise and exalt him above all for ever” (Dan. III, 57). Inanimate and irrational things praise God when rational beings, considering them inwardly, are stirred to praise. Hence: “Let every spirit praise [Col. 0944B] the Lord” (Ps. CL, 6).

Carnal persons direct their attention elsewhere; spiritual persons, therefore, who are worthy of this, should themselves praise God. For among God’s works there is nothing so small, nothing that seems so neglected, that He should not be glorified from it without end. “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his purposes” (Ps. 110:2). Therefore, while the Creator is proclaimed from created things, or grace is referred back to its giver from good things, you derive benefit for yourself from worldly things and render honour to the Lord. Therefore use worldly things and take satisfaction in them; if it happens that you lose them, you may perhaps grieve, not over the loss of things which you did not love, but over the removal of a use which you needed—yet not even then except with moderation, remembering that this was God’s good pleasure.

In such matters Martha is careful, though not wrongfully so [Col. 0944C]; Mary, devoting her attention to better things, is more at rest. These two alone are at once with Christ: the one to be fed by him, the other to feed him. Meanwhile poor Lazarus lies numb outside and decays in the tomb; but the sisters earnestly entreat the Lord that he who was dead may be restored to life. This, then, is the Christian life: that you sit at the Lord’s feet, intending to follow his footsteps; that you may not wander, lend your ear to his teaching; and, as you have learned, you will be concerned not only for yourself and for Christ in himself, but will also labour to benefit Christ in his members.

As for those who are not members of Christ, you ought, so far as lies within you, to strive by your zeal to fit them into Christ’s body; thus, with God cooperating, restoring the dead to life. Or at least let us strive to bring out into rest those who are dead in body and, as we suppose, are detained for their sins in the fire [Col. 0944D], unless perhaps we know that they have descended into hell. For God’s decree concerning these is that no one can be delivered from there in our time. Will our Lord, who became their brother, not redeem such persons—that is, those whom impenitence, arising from their way of life, draws down to the lower parts of the earth—and will a human being redeem them? For such there is no propitiation, no ransom-price to be given to God: “they shall labour for ever” (Ps. 48:9); they will live and will have no remedy.

The decrees of the divine judgment distribute their course through the natural processes of things, providing each person’s merits with their due recompense. Yet they sometimes alter the customary course, so that, when God does one thing by following the ordinary course of things, it may also be proved that he can do another, often introducing what is unusual. Hence certain wonders present themselves to our minds; and among the chief of them is that the dead rise again. By the wondrous working of God in his saints, many dead people have risen; among them there may have been—indeed, it is credible that there were—some restored to life who, because of their former wickedness, had been liable to Gehenna. For the dead who were sought out were not those who had lived holy lives [p. 242]; rather, without distinction, as often and as many as was necessary, they were raised up. Who, then, would dare deny that among those who died in their sin, some at least, if not all, returned to life after death, were corrected by so great a benefit of God experienced in themselves, and, divine grace accompanying them, were preserved to the end? Thus a twofold miracle occurred: both that the flesh was restored to life and that the soul, contrary to the usual course, was lifted from Gehenna [Col. 0945B].

[Note: [Col. 0945D] Consult the notes.] Let no one object that, whichever way a tree falls, there it will lie—that is, whether a person dies good or evil, he will remain such—and that in hell there is no redemption; for those who descend into that pit will not further wait for God to be propitiated toward them. Let no one make such an objection. These statements were certainly spoken, not to define what God may sometimes do in his power, but to declare what God customarily does. For Holy Scripture relates what ordinarily happens in individual cases; things done rarely and contrary to ordinary practice it passes over as though they had not happened, except when it occasionally introduces some of them in a special discourse [Col. 0945C]. For what is said generally is customarily said according to ordinary practice.

## Chapter XXVIII. Begins concerning marriage.

[Note: [Col. 0945D] Lombard, book IV, distinction 26.]

God created and gave to the man a wife: first, the first woman; one wife to one man. What he established in fact, he confirmed in speech, for he said: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24). Marriage is one flesh, not only because woman was taken from man, but principally because through the marital act and sexual intercourse a certain natural union of both bodies comes about. Hence the Apostle: “He who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body” (1 Cor. 6:16). If human beings had not sinned and had continued multiplying in Paradise, this law of marriage would have joined only two persons to one another by an indissoluble bond [Col. 0945D]. For there would have been no need, as there is now when the bond has been broken by death, for a second or third union of two persons in the same flesh after the first; nor would there ever have been, as now sometimes happens, three or more persons successively in one flesh.

Eve was not made independently but was taken from Adam, so that it might be known that in marriage woman is subject to man. Hence it was said to the woman: “You shall be under the power of your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Gen. 3:6). Thus Sarah knew herself subject to Abraham, calling him lord. For according to the Apostle, “the head of the woman is the man” (1 Cor. 11:3) [Col. 0946A]. It is therefore sin for a woman not to be subject to her husband; it is an inversion for a servant to be set over a lord, a wife over her husband.

[Note: [Col. 0945D] Lombard, book IV, distinction 33.]

In the time of the patriarchs and of the Law, one man had several wives. Thus Abraham, a most holy man, had Sarah as his wife and Hagar as his concubine. But he had intercourse with the slave-girl at his mistress’s command, and at that same woman’s command he sent her away. His grandson Jacob likewise obtained two wives, Leah and Rachel, and two concubines, the maidservants of his wives; he used the maidservants with the consent of their mistresses.

At that time the whole world was given over to idolatry; the household of Abraham alone offered worship to the one true God. Religion and superstition divided Jews from Gentiles so greatly [Col. 0946B] that the latter could not cease to pursue the former with continual hostility and endless war. The former, defending their ancestral laws out of zeal for God, remained unconquered—indeed victorious—while God protected his soldiers, except that, when they frequently withheld from their God the worship due to him, they happened to be overcome by their enemies, so that they might learn both what they owed to God and what they were capable of by themselves. Therefore the very numerous and frequent slaughter of Jews required the multiplication of wives among the rest, just as did the signification of the mystery [Note: [Col. 0945D] Augustine, *Against Faustus* and Tractate 11 on John; etc. Ambrose, book I, *On Abraham*, chapter 4. Chrysostom, Homily 56 [Col. 0946D] on Genesis, chapter 30.] among the patriarchs, on account of the fruitfulness of children. Thus wives were multiplied for one man, so that, conception being multiplied, the restoration of the human race might follow.

Hence it was not permitted for one wife to have several husbands at once, because she cannot conceive by many [Note: [Col. 0946D] Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 17, and book III, *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 12.] as one man can beget children by many women [Col. 0946C]. Therefore at that time one man might have several wives, nor could it be a crime [p. 243] for something to be done among God’s people which God permitted.

A man ought especially to take a wife from his own kindred, lest any confusion of tribes arise. Yet it was not permitted either to marry foreign women and idolaters or to retain them when married, lest associations with Gentiles become a cause of unbelief. Those joined by the Law also had to be separated by the Law. This is the bill of divorce, by which a man dismissed a repudiated wife for many reasons—namely, whenever she displeased him because of some shamefulness. It was allowed because of the hardness of neck in that people, lest, if men were compelled to keep wives they hated, they might prefer to kill them.

Before the Law, the patriarchs made use of concubines; these were prohibited in the Law thus: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20:14; Deut. 5:18). For the whole is indicated through a part, since by adultery every carnal union outside the covenant of marriage is prohibited [Note: [Col. 0946D] See Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapters 14 and 15.]. The Lord himself also used this manner of speaking: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to lust after her has committed adultery in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). Thus concubines were allowed to the patriarchs before the Law for whatever reason; afterwards they were prohibited. Hence [Col. 0947A] Deuteronomy prohibits there being a prostitute among the people of Israel, or any male fornicator [Note: [Col. 0947D] Consult the notes.]. Therefore, according to the ancient custom, it was not permitted under the Law to have any concubine, but it was permitted to have more than one wife.

## Chapter XXIX. On the marriage of Gentiles.

[Note: [Col. 0947D] Lombard, book IV, distinction 39.]

Among the Gentiles there were concubines and wives, but wives who could be dismissed according to the law of the nations. Christ’s preaching found certain persons in this marital union, and called them to faith not out of it, but in it. Matthew was called from the tax office, Peter while engaged in fishing; therefore, one was permitted to return to fishing, which can be carried on without wrongdoing, while the other was not permitted to return to tax collecting, which can scarcely, or never, be conducted lawfully. So also with fornication and every defilement. But Christ’s faith calls human beings in marriage [Col. 0947B], and in every manner of life that is rightly administered. It came to remove unbelief, not status; vice, not office.

Hence the Apostle advises those called to faith in Christ while in marriage not to depart from their spouses, unless the unbelievers are unwilling to live with them. For if the unbeliever departs, the believer also may depart; indeed, the believer could freely depart even from an unbeliever willing to cohabit, because of spiritual fornication, namely idolatry. Yet the believer is advised to remain, so that the unbeliever may be sanctified through the believer’s continual exhortation. If this happens, the law of marriage, contracted and begun among unbelievers, is brought to completion in Christian faith, and a marriage begun according to Gentile custom becomes a marriage according to Christ [Col. 0947C].

But if a believer either dismisses an unbeliever or is dismissed by one, it is not a sin to unite with another. For a marriage contracted apart from the Church’s tradition cannot be valid; in like manner both Gentiles and Jews dissolve marriages they have contracted. It would also become an impediment to faith and impose a certain delay upon conversion if a converted spouse, dismissed by one not converted, were compelled to continence.

But why does the Law command that unbelievers neither be taken in marriage nor retained? Certainly the Law commands the idolater to be avoided, lest idolatry be incurred; the Apostle advises that the idolater be retained, so that idolatry may be destroyed. It is never lawful for a believer to marry an idolater; but, according to the Apostle’s dispensation, it is lawful to retain one already married. Plainly, the Law does not address those who enter marriage while unbelievers, but those who are believers beforehand [Col. 0947D]. Therefore the Law prohibits one thing; the Apostle advises another.

## Chapter XXX. Whence divorce arises, and how a husband should conduct himself toward his wife.

[Note: [Col. 0947D] Lombard, book IV, distinction 35. Augustine, book I, *On Adulterous Marriages*, chapters 8 and 9.]

By Christ’s decree, the original law of marriage in some manner returns: one person belongs to one person. For Christ’s command and the Apostle’s exposition make it plainly clear that a spouse [Col. 0948A] is not to depart from a spouse except because of fornication; and if one departs for that reason, one must remain continent or be reconciled to one’s spouse. For while one lives, the other is bound. As long as both live, marriage cannot be dissolved, though cohabitation can be. But if one has fallen asleep, the survivor should either remain continent or, if preferred, marry whom he or she wishes, provided it is “only in the Lord” (1 Cor. 7:39).

While spouses live together, the husband, as her head, should provide his wife with what is necessary both for soul and body, lest the flesh fail through hunger and the spirit through sin; for Adam’s failure to correct Eve was a sin. Let the wife be subject to her husband, a helper in all things belonging to a woman’s role. In other matters the husband presides; in rendering the marital due both are equal [Note: [Col. 0947D] Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 6, and book XXXII *Against Faustus*.]. Therefore let each render the due to the other, unless perhaps, by mutual consent, they prefer to abstain for a time. To render the debt of the marriage-bed when it is demanded is never a sin; but to deny it when it is sought cannot be good. For the Apostle commands wife and husband to render their respective dues because of incontinence (1 Cor. 7:3), lest Satan perhaps tempt them and they fall into the devil’s snare through fornication.

Therefore, unless incontinence compelled otherwise, it would be far better to abstain from the marital act by mutual consent; for purity itself has its reward, while the marital act is by no means wholly free from fault. [Note: [Col. 0947D] Lombard, distinction 26.] Hence the Apostle, wishing all to be like himself, nevertheless permits the use of marriage because of weakness [Col. 0948C]; he permits a pardonable evil lest it become condemnable—the intercourse of marriage, lest it become an assembly of sexual immorality. Marital intercourse is scarcely reckoned a fault, because it is not imputed as such, when intercourse occurs for the sake of offspring, or in rendering the due, or finally in order to avoid fornication. Although the use of marriage does not entirely escape fault even in these ways, it is nevertheless far better to incur fault in this manner than to withdraw oneself from one’s wife, lest one burn with lust, the wife be deprived of her due, or offspring fail to be born. It is better, therefore, to incur that evil which God does not impute, so that the associated good and necessary things are not abandoned, than to avoid that lesser fault and encounter grave offences.

But those who cherish one another in mutual embraces to satisfy lust [Col. 0948D], or are drawn by irresistible carnality, commit something much more serious than the preceding, though still pardonable; or they defile themselves with a foul desire, and this is an act to be washed away by the tears of repentance.

## Chapter XXXI. On intercourse and other natural acts.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] Lombard, book IV, distinction 26, §§4 and 4. See Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 16.]

Like eating, sleeping, and walking, intercourse too is a natural act and has nothing evil in itself [Col. 0949A], but is corrupted by accompanying circumstances; just as human beings and angels are good by nature but become evil by accident. Hence, if the first human beings had remained as they were made, neither they themselves nor their acts would ever have become evil. But now something corruptible intrudes upon both human beings and human acts, whereby both are corrupted.

Some acts can easily be performed without fault, such as sitting and walking; some are only with difficulty defended from guilt, such as eating and speaking; while some are never performed entirely without fault, such as intercourse. Acts of this kind are good in their nature; from elsewhere comes that by which they are discoloured. Thus it is lawful to will to be angry and to desire, but it is by no means fitting to direct these toward persons to whom they ought not be directed. It often happens that the utterance of a particular word denotes an action not as it is in its nature but as it exists wrongly in vice: for example, when someone is said to have committed adultery, rape, or blasphemy [Col. 0949B]. What is adultery except to have intercourse with another person’s spouse? Intercourse itself, in this case, is not condemned except because it is directed toward another’s spouse. Blasphemy is to speak evil concerning God; speaking evil is not evil, but it is evil where it ought not to occur. Concerning God, however, it is wicked. Nor will you easily find an act that is condemned otherwise than because of an accompanying circumstance. Therefore there is no fault in doing or commanding acts of this sort, unless what improperly accompanies them is not wholly repelled. Do the act; remove its companion; you have not sinned.

## Chapter XXXII. On the vow of marital continence.

[Col. 0949C]

[Note: [Col. 0949D] Lombard, book IV, distinction 27.]

Those living under the law of marriage may abstain for a time, or always, in order to live more excellently—unless perhaps incontinence prevents it. If they choose perpetual continence, they may establish it either privately between themselves or with the testimony of the Church. Once it has been settled with sound reasoning and firm resolve, it cannot be changed without danger to the soul. “Make vows and perform them” (Ps. 75:12).

But what has been resolved secretly, if it is harmlessly broken either by both or by one party imposing compulsion, God, who knows it, not the Church, which knows nothing of it, will judge the despiser of the vow. Vows made before the Church and confirmed in the Church’s manner—the vows which a man’s lips have uttered—if broken, are judged by the Church [Col. 0949D]. For vows proposed either through a certain levity or contrary to reason, the Church charges with imprudence and does not command to be kept. Indeed, this must generally be maintained concerning every vow: no one should neglect what has been rightly resolved with a firm mind, lest one become guilty of the vow either before God, if it was made secretly, or, if publicly, before the Church as well.

Therefore, if spouses prefer continence, they may carry it out either while living together, which is more dangerous, or by separating from one another, which is certainly safer. If they remain together, only carnal intercourse should be avoided; in all other respects the reciprocal obligations of marriage should be observed. But if they choose to separate from one another [Col. 0950A], it is the husband’s duty to provide a suitable place for his wife, where she lacks what is necessary neither for soul nor for body. Since he removes her from his own care, provision must be made for her to be able to exist on her own.

Since the husband is always the wife’s head, even if he himself prefers continence, he must consider again and again what the strength of the woman is, to whom he owes fidelity; nor should he draw her away from the right of the marriage-bed or from his care unless he clearly judges that it can be done thus. For if, according to the Lord’s teaching, “a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife” (Matt. 19:5), how great must be the care between spouses, for whose sake even parents are to be left? Therefore, “what God has joined, let no human being separate” (ibid.). But God separates when he himself puts one of them to death, or when he adorns both with continence [Col. 0950B]. Yet when death intervenes, the survivor may unite with whom he or she wishes, provided it is only in the Lord (1 Cor. 7:39); but this is not permitted when continence intervenes.

## Chapter XXXIII. That separation is possible because of fornication.

[Note: [Col. 0949D] Lombard, distinction 35.]

A human being also separates what God has joined whenever he brings this about by fornication; therefore those who, as can be seen, have lawfully come together may lawfully depart from one another. Certainly the Lord permits a spouse to be dismissed because of fornication; he does not command it. Thus it is lawful both to retain and to dismiss an adulterous spouse. Yet Scripture says: “He who retains an adulteress is foolish and impious” (Prov. 18:23). This is plain enough concerning an adulterer; but here for a husband to retain an adulteress means either not to be willing, though able, to correct her, or, worse still [Col. 0950C], to encourage her in sin. Such a person is foolish in one respect and impious in another.

But if someone does not consent to adultery, he may retain the adulteress; if there is need of an embrace, dismissal is not advisable. Yet he may dismiss her, unless perhaps he too is polluted by the same crime. For if both are adulterers, neither can accuse the other; but if one is innocent, that person may freely dismiss the adulterous spouse if he or she wishes—not, however, on suspicion, lest a spouse be dismissed as often as he or she displeases. For the judgments of the Church, by whose authority such matters are handled, condemn no one upon an accusation unless first convicted or confessing.

Let one who dismisses, just like one who has been dismissed, live continent; or, if unwilling or unable to do so, according to the Apostle [Col. 0950D], let that person be reconciled to his or her spouse and take back the dismissed spouse. Since the Apostle advises this, it is clear that retaining an adulteress is not foolish and impious in every manner. Let the dismissed wife be taken back, unless perhaps something has meanwhile happened such that she ought not be restored—for example, if in the meantime she has laid aside secular dress; this I think rather than affirm. It lies in the decision of the one dismissing whether to take back the dismissed spouse, as the Apostle understood when he made reconciliation depend upon that person’s choice. For one who has been dismissed cannot return without the authority of the one dismissing; plainly, one who was compelled to depart against one’s will cannot return at will.

Just as a husband may dismiss a wife, so a wife may dismiss a husband because of fornication [Col. 0951A]; while an equal spouse lives, one can in no way adhere to another union. For when spouses’ cohabitation is separated, marriage itself is not at all separated. The Lord permits division because of fornication, because fornication has separated from the spouse the person who ought to be one flesh with that spouse and joined that person to another. But if fornication is absent, other troubles must be endured—which certainly was not the case under the Law of Moses: if she is leprous, barren, foul-smelling, or badly behaved.

## Chapter XXXIV. Separation is possible because of unbelief and also intolerable conduct.

[Note: [Col. 0951D] Lombard, book IV, distinction 39.]

It should nevertheless be observed that if either spouse leads a life so shameful, whether through worship of demons or through abominable conduct [Col. 0951B], that the other is unwilling to endure cohabitation unless he or she consents to that person’s own shamefulness; or if the one does not demand this, yet the other cannot endure such a manner of life without incurring wickedness together with the wicked person—then that person may freely break every bond, lest he or she be separated from God. For whoever does not leave father, mother, wife, and so forth for Christ in so great a danger is not worthy of him.

For if carnal fornication can separate spouses, then surely separation must occur because of spiritual fornication, with continence preserved here also. Since they entered marriage under Christ’s law, they can never dissolve a marriage once concluded. You propose to dismiss your wife because of fornication of the body; another must dismiss his wife because of fornication of the mind [Col. 0951C]. You may retain your wife; the other must dismiss his. You may lawfully dismiss your wife even if she wishes to be corrected; the other must retain his wife if she wishes to abandon her error. For bodily fornication, which is an evil act against you, remains the very act for which dismissal is permitted; but mental fornication, which is sin against God, has itself departed—the man was fleeing it when he proposed to dismiss his wife.

But why has the Lord excepted only the one cause of fornication, while we assert two kinds of fornication, so different from one another, and also mutual consent to continence, each as a reason why marriage may be separated?
