Perhaps both ought to be understood under the name “fornication”; or rather, the Lord’s exception excluded only bodily fornication, intending to declare not what cause may separate spouses for God’s sake, but what cause may separate them because of a spouse. Elsewhere it is taught that one must withdraw from every manner of life in which danger to salvation is recognized; here, however, nothing else is said except for what shamefulness in a spouse one may lawfully dismiss that spouse under the New Testament [Col. 0951D].

For under the Old Testament a spouse could be dismissed for many shameful causes: certainly not because failing to dismiss that spouse would be a sin against God, but because the person to be dismissed displeased the prospective dismissing spouse. But under the Law the shamefulness of fornication is reserved, for which, without distinction, both wife may dismiss husband and husband wife if cohabitation is displeasing. For God’s sake, however, neither aggravation of troubles under the Law nor contamination by fornication among us removes the fellowship of the marriage-bed from the accuser [Col. 0952A]. Therefore neither a Jew is commanded to dismiss a shameful wife nor a Christian an adulterous one for God’s sake. Rather, let each consider which course is preferred and act at pleasure. For because your spouse, by committing adultery, has injured you—indeed has, contrary to the faith of marriage, separated his or her flesh from yours and, shamefully, defiled it by an unlawful union—you may rightly remove your shared life from one who has faithlessly removed your flesh from his or hers.

## Chapter XXXV. On certain impediments to marriage.

[Note: [Col. 0952D] Lombard, book IV, distinction 29 and following.]

It should be observed that after marriage many things already mentioned can happen so that the use of marriage cannot continue, while marriage itself does not cease to exist [Col. 0952B]. Many things also can exist in marriage, or before it, because of which either no marriage exists or it has at some time ceased to exist.

Since the consent of both parties is necessary for marriage, if either one or both object to marriage, or because of tender age do not yet know how to give consent, then marriage is absent as long as mutual consent is absent. But even if consent occurs on both sides, and the persons are such as ought by no means to be joined, there is no marriage on either side if both know this; or, if only one knows it, marriage exists on one side only. But if neither party knows it and their ignorance is without fault, marriage plainly exists—always, if it remains always unknown; or for as long as it remains concealed [Col. 0952C]. Once the defect has disclosed itself, if it has been established under ecclesiastical law, nothing remains except that those who ought to have been joined had it not become known must, now that the matter is known, separate from one another, so that each may adhere to another—unless at some point the Church’s dispensation exercises its own strictness.

But those who enter marriage so that no cause whatsoever intervenes for which the marital union should be annulled while both live may separate the fellowship of the marriage-bed only because of fornication; for the Lord’s judgment concerning marriage was pronounced concerning persons thus joined in wedlock.

Nevertheless, the Lord did not define what sort of persons were fit or unfit for marriage [Col. 0952D]; he entrusted that definition to his Church. He himself taught certain things and reserved the rest to be taught by his bride. He taught what he commanded to be observed under either the old or the new law, that is, the Gospel. These are the two denarii which he brought forth and gave to the innkeeper, saying: “Whatever more you spend, when I return I will repay you” (Luke 10:35).

For to the innkeeper—that is, to the prelate of the Church, to whose keeping have been entrusted the Lord’s beasts of burden, according to the saying, “I became as a beast of burden before you” (Ps. 72:23): simple animals wholly subject, with full devotion, to Christ’s burdens, so that he may strive through constant care to cleanse the Lord’s stable and restore it by the nourishment of word and example—he committed two denarii, that is, the two Testaments, in which the king’s image shines forth [Col. 0953A], so that by knowledge of both he might care for the wounded person in soul; and wherever Scripture proved insufficient for healing, he might himself supply what was lacking by diligent effort.

[Note: [Col. 0953D] Council of Trent, session XXI, chapter 2; and session XXIV, chapters 3 and 4.]

Therefore, by the Samaritan’s grace, he has two denarii; but if anything more must be spent, let him labour by the exercise of his intelligence. Among such additional expenditures is almost everything that the Church establishes concerning the contracting of marriage. Hence, in accordance with the authority of the Law, which permits one to be joined only to a spouse of one’s own religion, the Apostle says of a wife after her husband’s death: “Let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (2 Cor. 7:39). Therefore, in order that she may marry in the Lord, let her choose a man of Christian religion—not a Jew, not a Gentile. If this is done, it is condemnation of the soul, because the union is no marriage in any respect.

Among those known by the Christian name, however, one should be taken in marriage whose companionship does not endanger the life of the soul [Col. 0953B]. If this is done too negligently, the marital bond will not on that account be annulled; but if necessary, cohabitation will be dissolved.

## Chapter XXXVI. Whom the ordinances of the Church exclude from marriage.

[Note: [Col. 0953D] Lombard, book IV, distinctions 35, 37 and following.]

The ordinances of the Church exclude from marriage persons whose mode of life, as monks; rank, as subdeacons; or vow of chastity, confirmed by the testimony and judgment of the Church, requires continence. Likewise they exclude a man and woman whom the Church judges to be related by blood or affinity. They also exclude those bound by a connection of this kind: when, of one who is regenerated in baptism, one person becomes a parent according to the flesh, while another is the baptizer or the one who speaks for the baptized person, that is, the sponsor [Col. 0953C].

The same connection—indeed a greater one—exists between the person who immerses, or receives from the immersion, and the person who in regeneration takes on Christ’s yoke. Clearly, the ministers of baptism and the baptized person are more closely joined by reason than are the baptized person’s parents and the ministers of baptism; for that connection is primary, since the latter arose only from it. Both the person who asks in baptism and the person who answers the question are bound to the baptized person and to his or her parents, but especially the person who asks. For that person performs the sacrament of washing when, in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, he immerses three times and draws out the immersed person three times.

For if he did not immerse, he would deny the Lord’s death and burial. If he omitted anything from the number, he would contradict the three-day burial. But if he did not draw out the immersed person a third time [Col. 0953D], he would derogate both from the resurrection that followed the third day and from the Trinity. Therefore, because the priest completes the sacrament fully, he confers more upon the washed person than does one merely present and who touches the person for whom he stands surety: the former is called father; the latter, godfather.

A man and woman, though not blood relatives, can nonetheless in a certain way be joined by affinity: whenever either he has slept with one of her female relatives, or she with one of his male relatives. Affinity properly exists between a husband and his wife’s kindred, and [Col. 0954A] between a wife and her husband’s kindred. Yet the name “affinity” may improperly be used also in fornication. Therefore those devoted to divine service who have chosen a stricter life cannot enter into marriage.

But those joined by any of the three bonds of connection mentioned above may indeed marry, but not one another, unless in some case the Church has a different judgment [Note: [Col. 0953D] The Church can grant dispensations concerning certain impediments to marriage.]. These are the causes why certain persons cannot enter marriage; and if they do, everything is judged void once the fact has been discovered.

[Note: [Col. 0954D] See Council of Trent, session 24, *On Marriage*, canons 3 and 4.]

But if these causes, which prevent marriage from being contracted by preceding it, occur after marriage has been made, what is to happen? Will it be lawful for each spouse to separate from the other [Col. 0954B] and afterwards unite with whomever he or she pleases? If this is lawful, what remains except that whenever a spouse is displeasing, a cause of this kind may be alleged? But whether such things occur through an occasion of discord or by chance, so that the marriage is judged annulled, it must be wholly rejected that cohabitation be separated. And even this must be rejected unless perhaps the strictness of dispensation has so provided for the purpose of correction and precaution, and then only so that it may be beneficial.

I think, however, that this should be added generally: in matters entrusted as additional provisions to Mother Church by the firm and unshaken authority of the Old and New Law, the children ought to do nothing other than what their holy mother has ordained by sacred custom and venerable tradition.

## Chapter XXXVII. On a pledge supported by an oath, and marriage contracted elsewhere.

[Col. 0954C]

[Note: [Col. 0954D] Lombard, book IV, distinction 28, §2.]

Some also maintain that if someone promises marriage to another with a pledge confirmed by an oath, and this can be proved, a marriage contracted with someone else after the pledge has been given ought not to stand; rather, one must return to the first person. Others, however, hold that the consent of both parties, since it effects marriage, prevails over a promise, even one confirmed by an oath [p. 249].

Certainly such a promise should have been fulfilled if it could lawfully have been fulfilled; otherwise it was preferable to commit perjury rather than do something contrary to law. For to commit perjury concerning what has been sworn against God is certainly good; just as swearing lawful things, when necessary, is good—because one must not swear without necessity, and then our words should rather be “yes, yes; no, no” (Matt. 5:37), while perjury is wicked—so to swear what cannot otherwise be done except unjustly is a monstrous crime; to abandon what has been sworn, though that is certainly to commit perjury, is to avoid judgment, which is certainly good. Therefore repent in the former case not because you swore, but because you did not keep the oath; in the latter grieve because you swore, not because you left the oath unfulfilled.

Yet if what has been sworn is sinful to do, while abandoning it causes scandal, it must be carefully investigated which course can be borne more tolerably. Unless perhaps it is truer that no one ought to guard against another’s scandal by means of his own sin; for you ought not to act wickedly so that another may fare well. Therefore, whenever scandal arises for others through you, act rightly so that the scandal may be removed. For: “Woe to the man through whom scandal comes” (Matt. 18:7). But if you cannot otherwise remedy the scandal unless you defile yourself with the stain of sin, grieve over the harm done to your brethren only insofar as you meanwhile provide for yourself; for you are not a cause of scandal if another is scandalized by your innocent conduct. Yet, since by swearing what you ought not to have sworn you yourself caused the situation in which, if you abandon an ill-made oath, the weak may perhaps be scandalized: therefore, as has been said, if you do what you swore, you certainly sin, because it is evil; but if you abandon it, you likewise sin, because in abandoning it you scandalize the Church. Thus both to do it is to sin, and to abandon it is to cause scandal. Yet abandoning evil is nothing other than good; but from your good another’s evil arises, nor are you without fault—not because you abandon evil, but because you had sworn that you would not abandon it. Therefore the whole stain of sin returns to the very folly of the oath. You must plainly grieve, then, both because a foolish oath preceded, and because you see that scandal will follow from it. For you cannot increase the grief of an ill-made oath by the evil execution of the deed. Hence whenever you act in a way that produces scandal, if you cannot otherwise remedy the scandal unless first, by acting against God, you wound your own soul, grieve that you have harmed your brethren; but do not strive to cut away harm in another in such a way as to inflict upon yourself a wound of the soul.

[Col. 0955C] Remember, however, to make clear to those scandalized that you have changed your resolution, though they have been scandalized, because to persist in it would be to offend God, and because you cannot offend God in order to please human beings.

But let us return to their assertion that a betrothal pledge, supported by faith or oath, ought to be brought to fulfilment. If, however, a marriage is meanwhile contracted elsewhere, they think an injury must be done to the pledge: the law of marriage has been unjustly undertaken, yet it is not to be destroyed. Certainly many things are done which, once done, cannot be altered. And, lest we depart from the same subject: if all matters which ought to take place before marriage are transacted before the Church, but consent to marriage is not given, is it not an injury that the marriage agreement is disregarded—and a greater injury if marriages are contracted elsewhere? Yet no one dissolves the marital union.

Amid these contentions of the parties, I think that one must hold to what does not conflict with ecclesiastical decrees. Therefore, I think that the decrees of the Catholic Church should be consulted; if they answer that neither kindred persons ought to be joined nor persons bound by a pledge of faith may be separated, the custom of the Church must not be disregarded.

[Note: Col. 0955D. Augustine, as found in Cause 27, question 2, chapter “In Two Ways.”] But if the matter stands otherwise, who would dare alter a marriage that has been made, [Col. 0956A] since its making was never forbidden?

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. What persons may remain together or be separated?

[Note: Col. 0955D. Master, Book IV, distinction 36.] These, indeed, are persons who ought by no means to come together in the marriage-bed, or, after they have come together, to remain together. There are others for whom, after marriage, neither remaining together causes harm nor separation is sinful. For if a woman has married a slave as though he were free, once she discovers this, she either confirms the marriage if she prefers to cohabit, or, if she prefers to dissolve what was fraudulently done, the Church remedies it and, if it was thus constituted, dissolves it. Being therefore released from the law of her husband, “let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord.”

[Note: Col. 0956D. Question 33, question 1; and Question 32, question 7, chapter “Those Who.”] If one spouse is unable in any way to render the marital debt to the other, whether through the evil act of sorceresses or through a defect of the sexual organs, when this has long and carefully been examined—lest any fraud be practised upon the marriage—it is left to their choice, provided that they have never rendered the marital debt: either to live together continently, or, once separated, to join themselves in new marriages. Yet those whose capacity to render the marital debt has been wholly removed by a defect of nature are to be excluded from marriage.

[Note: Col. 0956D. The Master, distinction 34.] But if marriage has existed between persons of this kind, especially in the present time, how is the old marriage dissolved and a new one superimposed? If, however, there was no marriage, why are they not judged as in the case of fornication, when they are sometimes permitted to remain together? But just as Jews and Gentiles had marriages which could be dissolved; and just as, at the beginning of the Church, a marriage begun in paganism between a convert and an unbeliever is not forbidden to continue, yet neither is it compelled to continue—for when circumstances require, both its existence is permitted and its non-existence is proper—so among us there are certain kinds of marriages which are marriages for some time and which, when certain causes supervene, cease to be marriages. Some, however, call these rather quasi-marriages; for true marriages, especially in our own time, remain indissoluble while the spouses live: “while her husband lives, the woman is bound.”

And indeed we have briefly treated what persons ought to be joined in marriage and what, after marriage has been contracted, may occur to dissolve the union. For we judge ourselves wholly insufficient to treat marriage fully—as indeed almost any subject—since, once one question has been resolved, countless new ones arise from practice itself.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. What good or evil marriage brings.

[Note: Col. 0956D. Master, Book IV, distinction 31.] Now I endeavour to set forth by what standard I judge marriage ought to be undertaken, what good it brings with it, and likewise what evil—though only in part. You ought therefore to become a husband either in order to multiply the worship of God through the begetting of children, or in order to regulate the incontinence of your flesh. For if you seek an heir to your possessions, what has that to do with God? If you desire to satisfy pleasures, is that not against God? Other reasonable grounds may also occur, and likewise others which are by no means to be approved, which either please God not at all or greatly displease him. Yet the causes mentioned occur most frequently.

Marriage is from God; and what is from God ought to be done for God. But you take a wife admiring nobility of family, desiring the protection of power, enticed by excessive wealth, inflamed by the flame of lust: you either forget God altogether or, which is almost the same thing, think of him only after everything else. Therefore it is in no way surprising if those who unite in this manner live together miserably. Accordingly lift your eyes to God, and enter marriage with him in view.

[Col. 0957B] Nor is it harmful—indeed, it should be done—that after the first consideration you do not neglect the next: namely, that you provide yourself with a bride of such appearance that, while gazing upon her beauty, you will have no need to be provoked toward others. There is also reason to procure such a marriage connection as will provide you with protection in the world. Therefore undertake the matter as need requires; and, lest you be troubled by the low birth of one less noble, choose one from whom you may receive honour—honour not in order to swell with pride, but so that you do not incur contempt through the marriage connection. But since the two chief causes of marriage are the procreation of children and the avoidance of fornication, fornication especially prevails; to avoid it the Apostle commands each man to have his own wife (1 Cor. 7:2). Hence sterile persons and the aged unite without hope of offspring, [Col. 0957C] for the purpose of repelling fornication.

[Note: Col. 0957. Augustine, Book I, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapters 10, 11, 21; and Book VII, *On Genesis*, chapter 7.] Those who marry receive along with marriage these three goods of marriage: fidelity, offspring, and sacrament. Fidelity, so that the purity of marriage may not be defiled by an adulterous embrace; offspring, so that the Christian religion may increase; sacrament, so that the union may not be broken by any divorce. Without fidelity and sacrament there is no marriage; without offspring it can often exist. For, as has been said, no procreation is hoped for among the aged and the sterile. Those who, unwilling to have children, devise by any evil means that they should not be born, neither enter marriage as spouses nor remain spouses afterwards—unless perhaps it happens that they put this parricide out of their minds.

[Col. 0957D] But a spouse, if she truly wishes to be what she is called, although she does not value having children, must nevertheless not act so as not to have them. Otherwise, just as one who is baptized insincerely indeed has baptism in reception but not in benefit, so this woman is a spouse in sacrament but not also in reality. Such a spouse, therefore, should not hope for an excuse from the good of marriage in marital intercourse. Such persons cling to their wives in a condemnable manner, and yet they have marriage with one another. For who would separate them from each other as though they were not spouses, rather than call them back from error by correction? If this evil practice had been known beforehand in a wife, she should by no means have been taken from a sound head of judgment.

[Col. 0958A; Note: Col. 0957D. Augustine, cited above.] There may be marital fidelity without sacrament; likewise, sacrament is sometimes present without fidelity. This happens whenever those entering marriage either intend to preserve an undefiled marriage-bed between themselves but contemplate leaving one another, or wish to live together in the manner of spouses while desiring to commit fornication everywhere. Those who unite with such an intention, because they reject from themselves a good of marriage, are, if both are such, both fornicators with each other. If only one is such, the other alone is a spouse. Persons of this kind will never be spouses until, having removed the vices which prevent marriage from coming into being, they embrace the goods of marriage. But if there is no marriage between such persons, why are they not separated from one another and freely joined in new unions? Whatever may lie hidden in the mind, provided that what is fitting to marriage is done before the Church, it is certainly counted as marriage.

[Col. 0958B] For although the marriage is not yet present in benefit, it is nevertheless present in truth as a sacrament. What is contrary to marriage lies hidden in the heart; what belongs with marriage is spoken by the mouth. Before the Church, because he takes a wife according to the Church’s custom, whatever foolishness he conceals in his heart detracts nothing from the marriage. It may indeed be that it benefits him little or not at all; yet it cannot be that it is not a marriage.

There are also many other grounds for which, if marriage is undertaken, it may truly be marriage and yet benefit little or not at all. In marriage, however, the evils mentioned above are especially to be avoided, and their opposites are to be sought most earnestly as goods of marriage. For if the speech of those being joined rejects these goods, the Church’s dispensation opposes a fornicating union, just as it does not receive for baptism one unwilling to renounce the old life, though, when the sacrament has in some manner been conferred on either side, it exacts what is due. But if in marriage you seek nothing except riches, pleasure, or something of that sort, and even reveal this in your words, your error must be rebuked by the Church; yet for that reason you do not seem to me to be barred from marriage. For it is better even so to unite than, to the scandal of the Church, to serve promiscuous fornication.

But are those who unite in this way excused for the pleasure of the marriage-bed by the good of marriage? Certainly, one who, following Christ’s ordinance, takes a wife lest he commit fornication against God’s prohibition, or, should it so happen, that children may be raised for God with such an intention that no hardship may lead the person himself to separate what God has joined, is freed through the good of marriage from the evil of the marriage-bed. Indeed, because in order not to offend God he both takes a wife and does not seek to dismiss her, consulting not the flesh but God’s will, he undoubtedly obtains a reward.

[Col. 0958D] If he sleeps with his wife in order to beget children, to avoid fornication, or to render what is due to his companion, he truly governs himself in accordance with the Lord’s will; the evil of ardour that attends the good of his purpose is wholly forgiven. But if such a man—as is our frailty—is sometimes carried astray in desire toward embraces, [Col. 0959A] he will indeed be saved, but “as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:15). For one who holds and takes a wife according to God does not perish because of the pleasure of the marriage-bed: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Heb. 13:4). Even a good man, overtaken by frailty, is sometimes drawn by pleasure, both toward food and toward intercourse; but God forbid that a man wholly good in intention should be condemned for sins that cannot be overcome.

But one who consents to the goods of marriage for his own desires, setting aside God’s will, since they are not truly goods, how can they have their effects, so as to gain before God a reward of themselves or pardon for ardour? How could they obtain pardon at all, or—lest the soul be condemned—how could false goods bring this about, or rather, evils? Are not those things evil which are done not to satisfy reason but lust? The greatest goods of the Church, such as faith, baptism, confession, fasting, and almsgiving, if they are not exercised as reason demands, avail little and sometimes do very great harm.

[Col. 0959B] It therefore seems that, whatever reason you have for taking a wife, if you do not direct yourself toward what pleases God, you cause the goods of marriage to lack their effects. For you receive the goods of marriage not for God but for your own inclination; and, as has been said, they cannot properly be called goods, both because they are not loved for God and because they are either tolerated or sought for lust. How can things of that kind profit rather than harm? For it is certain that goods done for evil and evils done for good are both harmful. Therefore, whenever the goods of marriage vanish, the pleasure of the marriage-bed is not at all excused, except that a lighter condemnation follows, because sin is committed in such a way that the Church is not scandalized.

But I shall speak of that marriage in which, to be sure, God’s law is observed, but nevertheless the fulfilment of carnal desire is also sought, though secondarily. I dare neither judge it condemnable nor absolve it from punishment.

[Note: Col. 0959B. Augustine, on Psalm 80, and Book XXI of *The City of God*, chapter 26.] It is like one building upon the foundation with wood, hay, and stubble. For on what grounds shall I condemn the man who seeks God as far as he can, although frailty draws him—not so that he may in any degree commit fornication, but so that he may desire delight in marriage? He would even shrink from this unless God had permitted it to the weak. Frailty draws him not so that, despising God, he may seek a worldly possession or honour, but so that he may desire what has been granted to the weak.

But evils lie close to goods, so that, with God’s help, you may not be deceived solely in your inquiry into matters. So long as one’s spouse lives, however much hardship arises from life together, it must certainly be endured.

[Note: Col. 0960B. Jerome on Matthew 19, at “If such is a man’s case,” etc.] But after the spouse’s death, the survivor is free to marry whom he or she wishes, only in the Lord. The Apostle made no exception, nor does the Church. Yet it lies within each person’s choice, whenever released from marriage, either to remain continent or meanwhile to adhere to marriage; “but she will be happier if she remains as she is” (1 Cor. 7:40).

# BOOK EIGHT

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0959C]

[Note: Col. 0959D. Master, Book IV, distinction 8 and following.] In order through the folly of faith to save believers and confute the proud, the Lord was pleased to reconcile the world to his Father not only through the washing of regeneration but also through refreshment with his body and blood. He knew how to accomplish this otherwise; but he preferred thus to inculcate humility in his own people, so that faith, knowing that nothing is impossible for God, might declare the true way of salvation through that which the human mind judges foolish.

The eating of Christ’s body was prefigured by the eating of manna. This bread from heaven, this bread of angels, is rightly so called, because it signifies him who, being the refreshment and joy of angels, descended from heaven so that, having assumed flesh, he might become also the bread of human beings.

[Note: Col. 0959D. Augustine, Sermon 93 *On the Seasons*, and Tractate 26 on John.] Therefore, the angels, being stronger, eat him [Col. 0959D] in his divinity; weak humanity eats that same one in flesh. Moses struck the rock with wood; the rock itself poured out water; the water refreshed the thirsty people (Exod. 17:6). Thus the Jews fastened Christ, wounded on the cross, [Col. 0960C] to the wood. That is, the rock—which, according to the Apostle, is Christ (1 Cor. 10:4)—was struck by Moses with wood; and the rock poured out water when blood flowed from Christ’s wounds to give drink to the faithful.

[Note: Col. 0960D. Augustine, Tractate 26 on John, and especially Sermon 93 *On the Seasons*.] Thus the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood preceded among the ancient people, and, as the authorities acknowledge, were equally efficacious for believers—not because the figure of a thing can possess its power, but because God, who can do all things, wished then to give through shadow what he is pleased now to confer through truth. This is what the Apostle says: “All were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink” (ibid.), signs being imposed to signify the things signified.

Is, then, the popular practice confirmed by consideration of this matter: namely, that those who taste blessed bread on the Lord’s Day—or, if they are prevented, take even a herb as though it were the Eucharist—receive the same benefit and that it serves in place of the Eucharist? Who would dare introduce this without authority? Especially since, once the reality is present, reason requires the reality itself to exist on its own account; but before it is present, the figure has force. Once the truth of the thing has arrived and is active, shadow and figure ought to cease. Therefore, since the aforementioned things are neither the reality itself nor a figure of the reality, how can they produce what the reality itself is known to be able to produce?

But likewise, how can a figure either of baptism, such as the cloud and sea, or of the body and blood, such as manna and water, be judged to have had the same efficacy as the reality, when, according to the Apostle, it is impossible for sins to be removed by the blood of goats or bulls? [Col. 0961A] Certainly, by the sacrifice of the old victim the sacrifice of the new was prefigured. But if this figure did not accomplish what its reality accomplished, how can other figures accomplish what their realities accomplish? Figures, as has been said, do not possess the efficacy of the things figured; but what is impossible to the figure is possible to God in the figure.

But I think it truer that figures have the office of disclosing their realities; and that faith, concealed in the figures, when revealed by God to those who received the figures, bestowed through hope what is now conferred through the reality upon believers by the things signified. This indeed seems to have been intended by the person who thought that the figures had the same efficacy for believers as the reality. For how did they have the same efficacy for believers? What does “they are equally efficacious for believers” mean, except that faith in a future reality was as effective for the ancients as faith in a present reality is for contemporaries? And how the same, unless both peoples received the same thing by faith—one without delay, the other after delay? For neither figure nor reality profits anything without faith; but faith cannot lack fruit, because “the righteous shall live by faith” (Rom. 1:17; Hab. 2:4).

## CHAPTER II. On the bread and wine of the sacrifice.

[Note: Col. 0961D. Master, Book IV, distinction 10.] No bread other than wheaten bread, nor any liquid other than wine, is admitted to the Lord’s table—perhaps because he called himself the vine and compared himself to a grain of wheat; but chiefly because he consecrated bread and liquid of this kind into his body and blood, so that this might be understood as food and drink for rational beings, not for those living like beasts of burden. This sacrifice is celebrated with body and blood, so that one who shares in it may be made wholly alive by it.

Different grains come together for this sacrifice, [Note: Col. 0961D. Cyprian.] because it is prepared for the diverse persons of the Church: many grains make one bread, and the many persons to whom this refreshment is owed are one Church. For to others it is death—unless one is a true member of the Church. By eating this bread, we are joined to it, because, when the mystery is worthily received, we ought to be joined to our Lord. Hence the Apostle: “The bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of the Lord?” (1 Cor. 10:16). That is, through the body it causes us to have a certain communion with the life of the Lord.

The cup has the same meaning, except that blood, [Col. 0962A] by which the soul is sometimes signified, indicates that the soul is to be refreshed by that nourishment; while the body is signified by flesh, so that, because we consist of body and soul, we may be perfected in both by the power of heavenly food, and, as we are strengthened bodily by bodily food, so spiritually by spiritual food. We take the former in order to live in the world, but the latter in order to live in God. And just as the former cannot cause us to live according to God, so the latter does not cause us to live according to the world. Each follows its own distinct course: the one, while filling the belly, lessens the belly’s urgency; the other, while strengthening nature, persists in its integrity.

This food is received by some unto life and by others unto death. For “whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:29). And what is it to eat judgment except to become liable to condemnation through eating? How great a condemnation? As great as that of one “guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (ibid.). And what is it to be “guilty of the body and blood of the Lord,” except to pay the penalties of Christ’s death? And what is it to pay the penalties of Christ’s death except to undergo the punishment of those crucified in torment? Those who did not know God despised him as mortal; these people both know God and despise him as immortal. Do they not despise him whenever they approach unworthily?

But you say: “They do not know that they are despising him.” What follows from that? Ought they not to know it? “The ignorant person shall be ignored” (1 Cor. 14:38). It was certainly blameworthy for the Jews not to know that Christ was God, since his life among them made it such that they ought not to have been ignorant. Not to know that the unworthy must not communicate is intolerable negligence, especially among Christians, whose duty it is at least not to leave such great sacraments unexamined.

[Col. 0962C] But what Church is there in which the body of Christ is not proclaimed, and in which it is not proclaimed that those who are to receive it must be prepared? Hence the Apostle: “Let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup” (1 Cor. 11:28). Let a person therefore examine himself by scrutinizing his errors and correcting those discovered; and, according to the nature of the crime and as reverence for the Saviour’s table requires, let him abstain from such great food. Yet if death approaches, let him receive viaticum; for this banquet is necessary for those departing for the heavenly supper. Nevertheless, “if the righteous person is overtaken by death, he shall be at rest” (Wis. 4:7). For one who could have had this food and neglected it departs badly from this life: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54). Therefore, one who does not eat has no life; but one who eats unworthily has death. It is evil to lack life, but far worse to incur death. What then should be advised? Correct your life and communicate. But if you do not yet wish to be good, it is the lesser evil not to communicate. You are good, however, [Note: Col. 0962D. Hilary, in Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction 2.] if you have no deadly sins, even though you have daily ones—that is, if your mind is not disposed toward sinning.

[Col. 0963A; Note: Col. 0963D. Augustine, Tractate 26 on John, after the middle; *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 53.] Therefore recline confidently at the Lord’s table, so that, refreshed, you may become stronger against vices, more vigorous for good things, and more discerning in the knowledge of both. By this food the great person lives, while the small person is choked. This food belongs to the great; when the small appropriate it, because they have less capacity, they fail in receiving it. For as much as it benefits the worthy, so much does it harm the unworthy. Certainly, from it the good return better and the evil worse. As a sign of the inward sickness, which is never absent from those approaching unworthily, outward illness is sometimes added; so that one who sins against the sacrifice and salvation of the Church may, through receiving the good thing badly, suffer bodily sickness or death, because he does not discern the Lord’s body, rushing irreverently to it as though to bodily food, guilty even if not through wickedness of life, [Col. 0963B] by this alone: that he does not show due care for so great a matter. Therefore, as the Apostle says: “Among you are many weak and infirm, and many sleep. But if we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:30). For if we had corrected our perversity, we certainly would not have been punished. Yet punishment is inflicted only in order that life may be corrected. Hence the Apostle: “When we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with this world” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER III. Why water is mixed in, and how communion is to be received.

[Note: Col. 0963D. Master, Book IV, distinction 11, §7.] The Church directs that water be mixed into the cup, because blood flowed with water from the Lord’s side. Water, according to the manner of Scripture, signifies the people (Rev. 17:1); therefore blood is not without water, [Col. 0963C] because the Passion is for human beings. When the flesh is eaten [Note: Col. 0963D. Gregory, Homily 22 on the Gospels; Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter “When It Is Broken.”] and the blood is poured into the mouth, the Passion of the Lord, afflicted in body and drenched in blood, is signified. Hence the Lord said to his disciples, and through them to others: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). Therefore, as often as we partake of the sacrament, we ought to remember the thing signified. Why remember it, unless that we may consider what he bore for us and not neglect what ought to be repaid? Let us hear what this is: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21).

And indeed Christ declared to his disciples, and through his disciples to the remaining priests, how they ought to partake of the Lord’s table, saying: “Take and eat: this is my body” (Matt. 26:26); and afterwards: “Drink all of this; this is my blood” (ibid.).

[Note: Col. 0963D. The Master, distinction 11, §6.] Thus the body is first to be received by presbyters, and then the blood. Christ’s institution must not be altered, since it has been established in this manner by the sanction of his decree: “Do this in remembrance of me.” Therefore let not something else, but this, be done.

But he entrusted to the judgment of his bride [Col. 0964A] how the Eucharist ought to be received by laypeople.

[Note: Col. 0964D. Council of Trent, session 21, chapter 2, and its canons; Council of Constance, session 13.] By her counsel and practice it is rightly done that Christ’s flesh is distributed to laypeople. Certainly it would be dangerous [to distribute] the blood under its liquid species to a multitude of faithful persons in church, and far more dangerous to carry it through the parish to the sick. For since flesh is not without blood, nor is blood anywhere except in flesh, whoever receives either does not leave the other unreceived. Even if he believes rightly, he does not show that he believes rightly if, while distributing flesh, he dips it in blood, as though either flesh lacked blood or blood existed outside flesh. It must certainly be freely and confidently confessed that one cannot receive the one without the other. And there is no doubt that, if blood is administered to someone who is extremely sick in order that it may be received more easily, the requirements of communion have been met.

[Col. 0964B] For who would dare offer dipped bread, when the Lord offered bread separately and the cup separately?

[Note: Col. 0964D. Third Council of Braga, canon 1. See the Notes.] Who would dare join together what the Lord chose to administer separately?

But you will say: “Why should I not offer it dipped without the Lord’s example, when you do not hesitate to offer one without the other?” The Church’s dispensation does not customarily carry both about, lest something unsuitable arise; and, for the same reason, avoiding spillage, it fears dipping. Dipped bread was handed to Judas, a man of dipped and defiled mind. Nothing of this kind, nor in this manner, is to be offered to the faithful. Yet in many places dipped bread is offered, so that, as they say, both elements may be distributed according to the Gospel and the matter may thus be carried out more safely and expeditiously. But Christ acted otherwise, and Roman authority earnestly forbids this to be changed.

[Col. 0964C; Note: Col. 0964D. Pope Julius, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter “Since Every”; and Paschal II, in a letter to Cluny.] 

## CHAPTER IV. What body Christ gave to his disciples: one that would suffer nothing from it.

[Note: Col. 0964D. Master, distinction 11, final section.] The Lord offered to his disciples for eating a mortal body—and, what is more, one that was to die—when he said, “which shall be given for you”; as also of the blood “which shall be poured out for many” (Matt. 26:28). For how could he have handed over as immortal what was not yet immortal, rather than what it was? He certainly offered his mortal and passible body to be eaten. Yet it was neither to die through being eaten nor to suffer; for just as now, so also then that food appeared to be broken and crushed, but neither occurred. But reason dictates that an impassible body suffers nothing and is not broken. Yet what reason is there why a passible body should be eaten and not crushed? Human reason does not comprehend how flesh, whether mortal or immortal, can be eaten without being crushed. But God can do what humanity cannot understand.

Christ, immortal, entered among his disciples though the doors were shut; the same Christ, while mortal, came forth from his mother’s closed womb. And though he already had the size of an infant, [Col. 0965A] he required no opening. By the same power it comes about that he who is of adult size is contained in the mouths of the faithful, is eaten yet not broken, and is whole and at once in diverse places. This occurs wondrously both before his death and after his resurrection. We see neither, but venerate both, because faith has no merit where human reason supplies proof by experience.

[Note: Col. 0965D. Gregory, Homily 26 on the Gospels.] What was enacted in Christ’s mortal body by reception of the sacrament was afterwards completed in his Passion itself; but what is now represented at Christ’s table was enacted in his past Passion. That reception therefore signifies what was still future, but this refreshment signifies what is now past. There the future Passion is signified in mortal flesh; here the past Passion in immortal flesh. The union in receiving signifies the union of the mind; for when we receive Christ’s flesh into ourselves, what do we signify except that we are Christ’s temple? But then we are Christ’s temple when we flourish in conduct and faith under so great an indweller.

[Col. 0965B] If we sit at the Lord’s table in such a state, we certainly cleave to our Lord: “He who cleaves to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). But if we are separated from God in spirit, then by communicating before those present we lie, since we are not God’s temple, though by receiving the sacrament we profess ourselves to be such. The Lord’s table therefore signifies not only his Passion but also conformity and, as has been said, the unity of the Church. Have charity, and you will be bound by this bond both to the head and to the members.

[Col. 0965C] The sacrament is therefore rightly judged the Church’s chief sacrament, because it both signifies such holy things and, indeed, bestows them on those who participate rightly.

## CHAPTER V. On the conversion of bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood.

[Note: Col. 0965D. Master, distinction 11, §§1–2.] The Lord, by the power of his blessing, both himself and through his ministers converts bread into his body and wine into his blood, so that neither bread nor wine remains what it was before, but passes into another nature: bread into flesh and wine into blood. Certainly it passes into no other [nature] than that which he took into heaven for us. Nor is the blood into which wine passes any other than that which flowed from his side and which still remains in Christ’s flesh.

Of a small child it is said, “He will become and be an old man”; therefore, of one who has become an old man it is rightly declared that he was a child. Likewise, while consecrating, you rightly say of bread that it will be converted, that it will pass into Christ’s body, and that it will become Christ’s body. But does it follow that, after this has occurred, I should conclude that Christ’s body was bread, dough, or flour? For before consecration it was not that; since what now wholly exists and then existed—unless someone should dare absurdly, indeed dangerously, to say that the same body is at once flesh in heaven, dough in the kneading-trough, and wheat in the granary?

Bread passes into the body. Thus the Lord, having taken bread and blessed it, [Col. 0966A] said: “This is my body” (Matt. 26:26); likewise, having taken the cup, after thanksgiving he added: “This is my blood” (ibid.), as though saying: “Know that what you see under the appearance of wine is my blood, and let no one doubt that what still appears as bread is my body.” And because, just as it had been bread before the blessing, so after the blessing he called it his body; and just as it had been wine before, so after the thanksgiving he called it his blood. Let no one dare maintain anything other than what the Lord’s words indicate that he intended. Therefore do not deny that bread becomes flesh, nor think that it becomes something else. Believe that the wine, after thanksgiving, becomes blood; and do not maintain that it is changed into something else.

Therefore do not suppose that in blessing bread is converted into blood, wine into flesh, or either into a soul or the divine nature.

[Col. 0966B] The man born of the Virgin is personally united in the body to both the creating and created substance, and is converted into neither. What it is impious to believe concerning the man, let no one presume to suppose concerning bread and wine. Yet the wine becomes blood—the blood, indeed, which has been shed through flesh—because Christ has no other blood. And since blood exists only in flesh, it cannot at all be received except in flesh. Therefore, when you receive the blood, you also receive flesh, but only through the blood, which is not without flesh; for if it were, flesh would not also be received.

And when, as can be seen, the smallest amount is received, nevertheless nothing remains to be received. Far be it that, as in a butcher’s shop, flesh should be torn into pieces; so too that the communion of the body and blood of Christ should be diminished particle by particle—especially now that Christ has risen immortal and incapable of suffering. For Christ, rising from the dead, now dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him (Rom. 6:9). Those who said, “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” (John 6:61) recoiled from such eating. The Lord answered this error, saying: “What then if you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before?” As though he said: Since the Son of Man, whole and entire, is to ascend into heaven—where also he was formerly according to his divinity—it is clear that my flesh is not, as you wrongly suppose, to be distributed to believers morsel by morsel after the manner of bodily foods. Thus the body of Christ appears to be broken, yet is not broken; it appears to be crushed by teeth, yet is not crushed. Clearly, crushing and breaking accompany the appearance, not the reality.

[Note: Col. 0966D. *Magister*, distinction 12, §§ 1–3.] But when, by Christ’s power, bread is changed into flesh and wine likewise into blood, the substance of wine and bread certainly ceases to be what it was, and becomes what it previously was not. Yet the properties of both things that have passed over remain; hence after consecration our five senses find what they found before consecration. Sight sees the appearance of bread and the colour of wine; hearing distinguishes by ear the breaking of the bread and the pouring out of the wine; nose by smell and palate by taste discern the nature of each; by touch, roughness or smoothness, hardness or softness are perceived. The substance therefore passes away, but the form remains; you do not marvel at either, but contemplate the Almighty. Accordingly, it is not a deception of the senses but a true apprehension of the thing: although upon the Lord’s table there is only flesh and blood, nevertheless the nature of wine and bread is perceived. This is not because the flesh and blood are of such a quality, but because, after the substance of each has been changed, the quality of its nature is not changed. This quality is variously altered by breaking and crushing; but the reality hidden under the appearance is altered in no way. For when various modes of division disperse the appearance of bread, Christ is received whole under every portion of the appearance, just as he was received under the whole appearance.

[Col. 0967B] Clearly, just as in another appearance—not yet his own—he displayed himself to be seen, having temporarily assumed the glory of the resurrection, while still in the Transfiguration the old man (I mean as regards passibility), having laid aside mortality even after death, appeared already glorified, in the old form familiar and bearable to the disciples for an hour; so now the appearance of bread is set before the eyes, but under that appearance the Saviour of the world is held. In each of the two visions an appearance other than that which Christ then possessed was shown (unless perhaps for that hour he was such as he offered himself to be seen); but in the third vision Christ never had in form that which it [or: which] apprehends. Yet these three appearances display beneath themselves, and offer to be handled, nothing other than Christ’s body—indeed, Christ himself.

[Col. 0967C] For, to linger on that from which our discourse began: bread passes into the true body, not bloodless but full of blood; not dead, but quickened by a soul and united to God.

Bread must be changed into such a body, because Christ has no body of another sort [perhaps: “another mode”]. We maintain that bread is changed into that very body, because we dare not say that it is changed into a part of the body. For the Lord did not say, “Take; this is a portion of my body,” but, “Take; this is my body” (Matt. 26:26). If, therefore, as wine is changed into blood, though that blood is contained within a man, so bread were changed into a portion, though contained within the compass of the body, it would certainly have to be said, “This is a part of my body,” just as it is said, “This is my blood” (ibid.), rather than that a part should be called by the name of body; for neither is blood called by the name of man. Therefore, just as blood is called by its own name and not by that of what contains it, so also, if bread were changed into a part of the body, it would be called by its own name and not by that of what contains it. Therefore, however small or however constituted the appearance may be which presents itself to our eyes after the blessing, faith should venerate beneath the covering of that appearance not only flesh and blood but Christ’s wholeness, without which neither Christ’s flesh nor his blood exists, with due honour. Nor should it marvel that the words of eating and drinking remain along with the appearance and form. Under each appearance the whole Christ is certainly received, if words congenial to the appearance accompany that appearance.

### Chapter VI. Who may consecrate, and how ought they distribute?

[Note: Col. 0967D. *Magister*, distinction 13.] The sacraments of the altar are consecrated by none but priests, and not even by them when they approach contrary to the ordinance of the Church. Those unworthy in life can indeed consecrate; but they must observe the ecclesiastical rite. For the unworthy, though to their own loss, nevertheless consecrate; but never otherwise than by following the discipline of consecration. At least, this seems to me so.

[Note: Col. 0967D. Augustine, *Against the Donatists*, and Book V, chapter 20.] It belongs to priests to take care to whom the Eucharist should be given and from whom it should be withheld. It must be withheld, if this can be done peacefully, from all who publicly lead a wicked and shameful life, out of reverence for so great a sacrament: lest, if it is given to such persons, the weak be scandalized as by something given unworthily; lest the wicked themselves be deceived by the false hope that they are honoured with heavenly bread; and lest the priest be held guilty for improvident administration. And how, I ask, is he guilty? Like one who gives what is holy to dogs—indeed, the Holy of Holies. Thus among the Jews a second Passover was instituted: those who, because of uncleanness, could not celebrate the first Passover, celebrated the second after being purified. So also, if because of sins we cannot celebrate our Passover with others, delay is necessary until, purified, we can celebrate it a second time.

[Col. 0968C] But one who is however criminal yet concealed must be warned privately, lest he presume to make what ought to be for salvation into his destruction. If, however, he insists on this and demands that there be done for him what is done for the faithful, communion must be given, lest by refusing you expose his wickedness, or appear to hate one to whom you are unwilling to give life-giving food. Therefore, lest you expose him as unworthy or make yourself suspect, you will most certainly give him his own death, and by this sole means avoid scandal to the Church. If you refused, you would certainly offend gravely; when you give, you commit no sin whatever. For “he eats and drinks judgment to himself” (1 Cor. 11:29)—certainly to himself, not to you.

[Note: Col. 0967D. Augustine, Sermon 22, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] Let it be a consolation to you, when you distribute to evil persons together with good ones, that the Lord Jesus did the same by his example, since among his apostles he did not exclude Judas from his supper.

[Note: Col. 0968D. Augustine, Book III, *On Baptism*, chapter 10.] For this supper, purer than a ray of sunlight, passes through filth and does not contract defilement by passing through it; it illumines what is fair and exposes what is foul. A good man becomes better after the supper; a bad man returns from the supper more deformed.

### Chapter VII. How often one should communicate, at minimum.

[Note: Col. 0968D. Council of Aenham, in England.] Some customarily communicate more often, others less often. Yet the statutes of the Fathers prescribe communion three times a year: on the day of the Nativity, at Easter, and at Pentecost.

[Col. 0969A. Note: Col. 0969D. Augustine, Epistle 118, to Januarius; *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, chapter 53.] Priests, however, need to be strengthened more frequently; laypeople at least three times. The king’s household sits at his table, and they do so more frequently because they are nearer.

[Note: Col. 0970D. Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, IV, chapter 6.] But let each person, according to the custom of the faithful among whom he lives, earnestly see to it—whether more frequently or less—that he approaches worthily.

### Chapter VIII. That the Lord did not avoid human foods, nor should the company of evil people be avoided.

Because the Lord Jesus preferred to live among human beings, he by no means rejected the foods of ordinary human intercourse, thereby doing himself what he decreed would be done by his followers: in accordance with their Master’s command, wherever they lodged they ate and drank what was available there (Luke 10:7). For those who remain in one private place should lead the solitary life of abstinence of John the Baptist and the wilderness-dwellers—strict, as they choose, yet according to reason. But those who travel from place to place, or live among many people, should imitate the table fellowship of apostolic cheerfulness and moderation, if they wish neither to be scandalized nor to give scandal; knowing that “the kingdom of God is not food and drink” (Rom. 14:17), and that it is of greater merit to restrain desire amid abundance than to abstain through want.

[Note: Col. 0970D. See Jerome, *Dicta on the Rule of Monks*, vol. IX.] Yet if gluttony assails anyone, it is safer to flee abundance.

The Lord attended a wedding and did not shrink from the guests, thereby showing that desire, not provisions, is to be feared, and that no class of persons harms one who lives among them and behaves holily. The slander of grumblers did not reckon this when, because the Lord took food and drink without distinction—because the physician visited the sick—they accused him of being a drinker of wine and a companion at table of tax collectors and prostitutes (Matt. 11:19). Yet how much better it is to eat honeycomb and fish with the Lord (Luke 24:42) than red lentil stew with Esau (Gen. 25:34)! Let us follow the Lord’s example and not disdain association with evil people as though we should be defiled by them. For if you conduct yourself lawfully among evil people, you can help those who heed you both by word and example; the leaven of the evil does not turn you to its bitterness, but you gradually draw it out from them.

Therefore, why do you flee the company of evil people when they might become better through you and you would not become worse through them? You are certainly cruel: you are unwilling, though you can, to be of benefit. You hasten to good people who have no need of you; you abandon evil people who are safe from danger with you. Surely you act foolishly or arrogantly if either you abominate sinners as excessively righteous, or, while conducting yourself rightly, believe yourself defiled by proximity to evil people. But if what grieves you is that among the guilty you are not free from fault, examine your life and inquire whether the things of which you complain are daily faults or damnable ones. If they are daily faults, where on earth can they be avoided? Because such things are continual, groan continually; but because for the saints there is in them no condemnation—indeed, there is consolation—especially if you are devoted to works beneficial to the Church and, as though on a journey, fittingly gather dust.

[Col. 0970A] For whatever is unavoidably contracted through human frailty in works of charity is excused by the fruit of those works, since “charity covers all sins” (1 Pet. 4:8). Will you therefore avoid the goods of the journey because of the stain of dust? Great and heavenly goods because of small and venial evils? Is there, then, no good you can undertake because good things are always followed by evils that you fear?

But wherever you are, or whatever you do, if intolerable sins arise for you there, and by no means can you escape the death of the soul in that place or action, avoid danger to yourself altogether, however approved the place or action may be; and “whatever scandalizes you, cut it off and cast it from you” (Matt. 5:29). Yet I think it must be considered more keenly lest, while we walk “through a mirror, in an enigma,” the appearances of things deceive us, with Satan’s angel transformed into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11:14). Against this, God’s grace is necessary. Do not trust in your own strength, but “cast your care upon the Lord” (Ps. 54:23). And that it may be present with you, let your life deserve it, according to the saying: “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” (Jas. 4:8).

### Chapter IX. Concerning the Lord’s supper and other ancient rites not to be restored.

The Lord, born of a woman and made man under the law, received with his disciples the old supper, customarily celebrated with a lamb, unleavened breads, and wine. He received it in order to put an end to the old and introduce the new. For after the disciples had prepared the Passover and the Lord had reclined, he said: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22:15). According to its authority, he desired first to eat the typical Passover and thus disclose to the world the mysteries of his passion, so that he might both show himself an approver of the ancient Passover and teach that, now truth had come, the shadow should cease. Hence he adds: “For I say to you that from this time I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.” As though he said: I shall no longer celebrate the Mosaic Passover until it is fulfilled, spiritually understood, in the Church, which is the kingdom of God. To this day Christ eats in this kingdom when he spiritually performs in his members what Moses commanded a rude people to observe carnally. Therefore let the shadow cease, because truth has come; just as manna failed after the children of Israel ate the produce of the land and used that food no longer.

Then follows: “And having received the cup, he gave thanks and said, ‘Take and divide it among yourselves.’” This cup pertains to the old Passover, which he was bringing to an end; receiving it, he gives thanks, plainly because old things were about to pass away and all things were to become new. It follows: “For I say to you that I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.” Just as he declares that he will not drink the typical Passover drink, so also he declares that he will not eat the typical food of lamb and unleavened bread, until the glory of the resurrection has been shown and the kingdom of God—that is, the end [the text reads *fides*, “faith”] of the world—comes; so that through the change of these two sacraments, judged chief among the others, he may teach that the sacraments of the law are to be transferred to spiritual observance. Thus in the Lord’s supper a limit is set to the ancient Passover, both as to food and drink.

Therefore let no one restore the Lord’s supper either with wine or unleavened bread, any more than with the eating of lamb, because the Lord brought these things to an end; otherwise, he judaizes. The final part of the supper, which is owed to the new man as the first was to the old, in which the Lord distributed to his followers the sacraments of his body and blood, is itself to be repeated more often, by authority of the Lord, who after distributing the new supper and new Passover said to the apostles, and through them to others: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). The Lord therefore, when the solemnities of the old Passover were finished, passes to the new, which he desires the Church to celebrate in memory of his redemption, substituting for the flesh and blood of the Lamb the sacrament of his own flesh and blood in the form of bread and wine.

The Lord also rose from supper and washed the disciples’ feet; and when he had reclined again, he said to them: “If I, Lord and Master, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet; for I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you also should do” (John 13:15). Whether by washing feet with the hand, or by forgiving one another’s sins with the heart and praying for one another, there can be no error for one who understands. The Lord teaches what we should flee and what follow; for the figure of the law gradually diminishes. Thus he touches lepers and breaks Sabbaths: “the law and the prophets were until John” (Luke 16:16). At last he brings all these things to an end in the supper, declaring without ambiguity what displeases and what pleases him, when on the one hand he says, “From this time I will not eat it; I will not drink of the fruit of the vine,” and on the other adds, “Do this in remembrance of me; I have given you an example.”

When the Pharisees accused the apostles because on Sabbaths they plucked ears of grain and rubbed them to eat them (Matt. 12:1; Luke 6:1; Mark 2:23), the Lord answered: “If you knew what this means, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice,’ you would never have condemned the innocent” (Matt. 12:7). Clearly God ordained to save the world through the mercy of his grace, not through observances of the law. Again, the Lord says, as it were, that they are not to be reproved because “the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath” (Luke 6:5). Clearly, he who is Lord of other things is likewise Lord of ceremonies; rightly, he makes them stand when he wills and cease when he wills. If Christ’s institution does not suffice for you, you are excessively righteous; if you pass it by, you are a transgressor.

After the Lord, consult the Apostle. For he says: “If you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law” (Gal. 5:18). It follows that whoever is under the law lacks the Apostle as guide. But he is under the law who trusts in legal observances. Paul rebukes the Colossians because, in the manner of Jews, they admonished themselves thus: “Do not touch; do not taste,” things which all perish in their very use (Col. 2:21). For the Apostle disapproves of avoiding touch as one avoids a corpse, and shrinking from taste as one does from pork, after the manner of Jews.

[Col. 0972A] For not only these, but all things of this kind, tend to destruction if a person abstains from them and uses those things while believing that he is thereby justified. He says likewise: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2). Circumcision is one observance, and among great observances a chief one. For circumcision and Passover hold first place among figurative rites; and this makes clear that whoever places hope in observance of the law receives no benefit from redemption.

Again, the Apostle, commending Christ and disparaging legal observances, says: “For whose sake I have counted all things loss, and I consider them dung, that I may gain Christ” (Phil. 3:8). He does not say *some things*, but that all things are loss and to be counted as dung, because whatever good things are found in a human being immediately fail, corrupt by annihilating, and infect the one who touches them with their own stench. The Apostle avoids this in order to gain Christ. Why? Unless because salvation is not in such things? Therefore the man burning with zeal for God’s house disputes so often against the law, in order to uproot what is harmful from its roots, showing that worship of the law differs little from worship of idolatry. Thus he says to the Galatians: “Do not again be held under a yoke of slavery” (Gal. 5:1). Since the Galatians had never previously been under the law—for he calls it a yoke of slavery—how does he say, “Do not again be held under a yoke of slavery”? But they were previously under a yoke of slavery while oppressed beneath the burden of idolatry; and they in some way return to it when they subject themselves to the law, now compared with it. For the sacraments of ceremonies, still observed, because they promise as yet future the truth of grace which has already come, now serve falsehood. The law, being “a shadow of things to come” (Heb. 10:1), if still retained, falsely promises as future that which we know in the event itself to be past. But how does it differ from worshipping false gods to worship false sacraments—indeed, in the sacraments to venerate some Christ, I know not who, as one yet to be born?

But Paul humbled himself to the law by circumcising Timothy, so that the deception and scandal of the Jews might cease; for they were prepared to stir up disturbance and sedition if he received and ordained as bishop an uncircumcised son of a Jewish woman (Acts 16:3). And he himself, who had grown his hair by a vow like a Nazirite, shaved his head at Cenchreae according to the law (Acts 18:18). After many things, too, in Jerusalem, purified according to the counsel of James and the elders, he entered the temple according to the law and offered a sacrifice (Acts 21:26). Christ, the end of the law—indeed, the law itself—established that the law should cease, while Paul taught that it ought to be upheld, saying among other things: “For through the law I died to the law, that I might live to God” (Gal. 2:19). It is as though he said: By authority of the law, I abandon the law so completely that I do not approach it any more than if I were dead. Why? That I may live to God. For only one dead to the law lives to God and to God’s honour. Did the vessel of election then become so senseless that he judaized against himself and against the law—indeed, against God and his Lord—and introduced the law? Far be it!

[Note: Col. 0971D. Bernard, Sermon 66 on the *Song of Songs*.] A Jew abstains judaizingly from many foods; sometimes a Christian abstains from the same foods, but either for continence or because they are detrimental to bodily health, and he does well. A Jew judaizes when he rests on the Sabbath; a Christian too sometimes rests on that day, but observes his own solemnity when it falls on the Sabbath and conducts himself in a Christian manner. Thus we do many things with Jews, but not in order to observe their law. So the Apostle, when he yielded to legal observances, showed them no reverence, but, using a dispensation, found a remedy against scandal.

[Note: See Peter Abelard, Book V on the Epistle to the Romans.] Therefore in matters of this sort there is absolutely no danger, either when they are omitted or when they are done, if in what is done no hope is placed in them and no error of Judaism is introduced by habitual use; rather, what reason requires is done. Unless extreme necessity compels it, nothing of this kind should be done with Jews, nor for so long that they may boast, as it were, of our judaizing. Let us beware, therefore, lest we imitate the Lord’s supper so far as to judaize.

What reason, then, requires us—on the unusual day preceding the Lord’s passion in Lent—to eat supper after the midday meal, as though following the Lord, and, if resources permit, to consume unleavened breads together with wine? What necessity compels us—for without necessity it is sinful—to break the Lenten fast, which because of our frailty should be passed through with forty meals, precisely at the season when abstinence ought to have been more vigorous?

[Note: Col. 0973. See *On Consecration*, distinction 3, chapters “Non liceat” and “Non oportet.”] You answer: the custom of the Church must be observed. But among us this custom is either that of no laypeople or of few; most clerics do not observe it, and even the most religious communities avoid it. Therefore there appears to be no necessity of custom for preserving this practice, unless perhaps the Lord’s supper ought to be represented by such a celebration. For why do they call this the Lord’s supper unless by it they represent the Lord’s supper? But, as has been said, the Lord’s supper was partly old and partly new. Who, however, would dare represent its newness otherwise than as the Lord himself handed it down, saying: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19)? If then its oldness is repeated, why is it not repeated completely, so that lamb may also be joined with unleavened bread and wine? But do you shrink from eating meat during fasts? I too, when I am to fast, do not think it reasonable to eat twice in one day. But by not eating meat you follow custom; by celebrating the Lord’s supper you think yourself defended from the guilt of violating the fast.

The Lord who commanded that the final and new part of the supper be retained himself ended the first and ancient part of that same supper; and apostolic institution prohibited it to all together with legal observances. How, then, do you restore what was ended by the Lord and prohibited by the servant on the Lord’s behalf? And how does the observance restored by a wrong free you from the guilt of breaking the fast? Thus you make yourself a transgressor in two ways: while you observe not even the chief form of fasting, you judaize as an injurious imitator of the Lord.

[Col. 0974A] But you remain in such a Church that you will cause scandal unless, in Paul’s manner, you yield to Judaism? For an hour, to avert danger, reason seems to allow undertaking something legal; but to repeat it every year without interruption—is that not rather to introduce error than to allay scandal? Must one judaize without end because of the scandal of the foolish? Christ did not teach us thus; nor did the Apostle instruct us thus. Both accepted death, both accepted persecution, in order that the old law might cease and the new might flourish. Do you dare make customary use of that for ending which the Lord did not hesitate to end his life upon the cross? Therefore, if anyone is a new creation in Christ, old things have passed away, and behold all things have become new (2 Cor. 5:17). Where all things have become new, nothing of oldness can remain. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any power nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love (Gal. 5:6).

### Chapter X. On the freedom to take foods without occasion of offence.

When the Lord freed the world from the law, he also restored freedom concerning foods prohibited in the law, so that nothing which might lawfully be taken according to the law of nations should henceforth be unclean. Thus the Lord says: “Not what enters the mouth defiles a person” (Matt. 15:11; Mark 7:15). For there is nothing outside a person which, entering, can defile. Hence the Apostle says to the Romans: “I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is common through him, except to one who considers something common: to that person it is common” (Rom. 14:14). For this is confidence in Jesus: that nothing is common—that is, unclean—through him who, after he came, released us from the law.

[Col. 0974C] Hence the Apostle shortly afterward says: “All things indeed are clean; but it is evil for the person who eats with offence. It is good for a person not to eat flesh or drink wine, nor anything by which your brother is offended” (ibid.). He had shortly before added: “Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food” (ibid.). Again: “Do not destroy by your food the one for whom Christ died” (ibid.). Therefore, whatever can be eaten may lawfully be eaten, unless the weak are scandalized by it; and let one who eats contrary to conscience eat. For the Apostle testifies that one who distinguishes foods otherwise clean, if he eats, is condemned, because it is not from faith: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23)—that is, whatever is done contrary to the conviction that it is evil.

That even foods sacrificed to idols may be consumed, provided brothers need not be scandalized by it, Paul showed in writing to the Corinthians. He says: “Concerning foods sacrificed to idols, we know” (1 Cor. 8:1). What do we know, unless that it is lawful to eat because they have not been defiled by an idol? Yet: “See lest perhaps this freedom of yours become an occasion of stumbling to the weak. For if anyone sees one who has knowledge reclining in an idol-temple, will not his conscience, being weak, be encouraged to eat things sacrificed to idols, and will not the weak brother for whom Christ died perish through your knowledge?” (ibid.). Therefore, if things sacrificed to idols may be eaten in the idol’s presence, how much more may any foods elsewhere be eaten, unless scandal forbids it?

He says likewise to them: “All things are lawful to me, but not all things edify” (1 Cor. 10:23). For according to the exposition of the same passage:

[Note: Col. 0975D. Ordinary Gloss on this passage.] All things are lawful according to natural law, because all things are clean; the discussion concerns foods. They are lawful—that is, forbidden by no command of the Lord—but not all edify neighbours. And because they are lawful but are not always to be used, he determines how it is lawful to eat or not eat, saying: “Eat whatever is sold in the market, asking no questions for conscience’ sake” (ibid.). Whose conscience? That of the weak person standing by. Eat, because “the earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness” (Ps. 23:1). What belongs to the Lord cannot be unclean. Again: “If one of the unbelievers invites you to supper and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you. But if anyone says, ‘This has been sacrificed to idols,’ do not eat, for the sake of the one who informed you and for conscience’ sake; but I mean not your conscience, but the other’s” (1 Cor. 10:28).

Therefore animals found dead, killed by a fall, water, or wild beasts, whether sold in the market or placed upon the table, may nonetheless be eaten—indeed, rather than things sacrificed to idols. For if one of the two were to be avoided, what had been sacrificed to demons would certainly be avoided. Thus Christian law commands that no things which may be eaten, nor any things which can be drunk, be wholly abandoned—unless perhaps some circumstance arises on account of which it is fitting to avoid as unlawful what is lawful. Thus on Friday, when it falls among days of fasting, it is now not lawful to eat meat because the Church’s abstinence forbids it.

[Note: Col. 0975D.
