See Peter Abelard, Book V on the Epistle to the Romans, p. 705, where he cites St Ambrose.] Food may also become contemptible because of an accident or because it is unfamiliar; those prone to nausea cannot bear drink either if something occurs contrary to decency. There is no fault in taking such things, unless it causes scandal to onlookers; for this reason you should not eat butter among the Franks, or garlic among certain others. Hence the Apostle says: “If food scandalizes my brother, I will never eat flesh, lest I scandalize my brother” (1 Cor. 8:13). Food may also be unhealthy for the eater and therefore must be avoided. Thus cheese, permitted for food by the law of nations, is avoided by some almost as though it were a plague. In matters of this kind the instructions of a physician, not a teacher, are observed.

But if we incur offence while eating or drinking or abstaining—either generating scandal among the weak, or finally, by serving gluttony too greatly, bringing ruin upon ourselves—what does it mean that what enters the mouth does not defile a person? Certainly, it is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person; rather, according to the Lord’s saying, what proceeds from the heart does so (Matt. 15:11; Mark 7:15). For when we offend in the aforesaid ways, we either act against conscience or sin through negligence. If the heart is defiled in neither way, no sin is committed. Clearly, when no evil proceeds from the heart, what enters the mouth cannot defile. Indeed, nothing external is done wrongly, except perhaps among those of whom it is written: “Those who sinned without the law will perish without the law” (Rom. 2:12).

If the Church’s customary practices had prohibited the freedom concerning foods restored by the Lord, and practice had accepted this prohibition in such a way that what the Church had decreed and practice had strengthened by acceptance ought not be neglected, that would be one matter. Yet it is far better that freedom established by the Lord’s own mouth and confirmed by apostolic ordinance should endure forever, than that anyone should render it unlawful as though correcting it, and that we should have religion, alongside the Jews, in distinguishing foods and drinks. For, as the Apostle testifies: “Let the kingdom of God not be food and drink, and food does not commend us to God. Neither do we lack if we have not eaten, nor abound if we have eaten” (Rom. 14:17).

Let no one set the apostles against the Apostle as though they were opposed, because, while allowing other things, they prohibited what was strangled together with blood—not establishing a decree,

[Note: Col. 0976D. See Augustine, Book XXXII, *Against Faustus*, chapter 13.] but, as I think, accommodating the weakness of some.

Yet there are some for whom Moses is better known than Christ, who follow more closely the letter that kills than the Spirit that gives life; whom Moses’ veil overshadows, rather than the bright face concealed beneath the veil enlightening them; and consequently they neither understand Moses nor sincerely receive Christ. Hence the Lord says: “For if you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also, for he wrote concerning me” (John 5:46). Looking at the surface of the law, they except many things as unlawful in our time and, deceived by some novel resemblance of their own devising, add them and hand them down as though most sacred, though in the truth of the matter they are vain.

[Note: Col. 0976D. See Bernard, Sermon 66 on the *Song of Songs*.] The Apostle knows such people as those who give heed to spirits of error, because evil spirits speak in them; and to doctrines of demons—that is, of persons possessed by demons—who speak lies in hypocrisy, that is, under a feigned religion in order to deceive more effectively; having their own conscience seared, that is, burned and made conspicuous by the mark of concealed falsehood; forbidding marriage and commanding abstinence from foods as though unclean, not for bodily discipline, which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and those who have known the truth—namely, this truth: that every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if received with thanksgiving, for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer (1 Tim. 4:1), lest the devil, who tempts through food, should harm through food. The Apostle wrote this to Timothy.

Therefore, since it is a virtue of abstinence, and the teaching of the saints, to refrain from foods for a reason, see whether it is not monstrous madness to abstain from foods as though they were unclean—a teaching that is certainly of demons. For “all things are clean to the clean; but to the defiled [variant: *unclean*] and unbelieving, nothing is clean; but both their mind and conscience are defiled” (Titus 1:15). All things, certainly, are clean according to their natures. Hence: “And they were very good” (Gen. 1:31). Some things are unclean to Jews according to their signification; nor are all things suitable for us, whether because of bodily health or the custom of human society. All things are clean—but to whom? Certainly to the clean, who receive them in good faith and are righteous. But to those defiled through sin, and to unbelievers who do not believe, nothing is clean (Titus 1:15), because they are unworthy of God’s gifts. Yet defilement does not arise from food, but from the evil understanding and conscience of sinners. Hence it follows: “But both their mind and conscience are defiled.”

Woe to those who call good evil and evil good; who praise drunkenness, fornication, and certain other abominations as though due to nature, or excuse them on grounds of human frailty, or proclaim that they are not damnable. When their subjects are ensnared in such novel practices, they punish them with no correction or the slightest correction, as though only for trivial excesses. But if anything is done contrary to their own traditions, rather than God’s, they cry out that it is an intolerable evil and must be punished most severely, killing souls that do not die and making alive those that do not live. These people have made the commandments of God void because of their traditions.

### Chapter XI. On the alternation of faith among Jews and Gentiles.

When the Gentile world lay numb in idolatry, Judaea flourished in the worship of God [Col. 0977C]. From the time Judaea became foolish, the Gentile world rose to faith; when at last the Gentile world fails, Judaea will revive in faith. “O the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God, how incomprehensible are his ways!” (Rom. 11:33). Thus, in these matters as in others, since he could not, as it were, save both peoples simultaneously, he saves them in turn. He calls to himself the nations, sufficiently humbled by the foulness of idolatry; but he rejects the Jews—raised above the nations by the worship of God and made proud against Christ by the observance of the Law. At last, sufficiently subdued by the prolonged wearing-down of captivity and by persistence in evil living, they will be converted through the calling of Elijah and Enoch. But the nations, daily corrupted by errors both of faith and morals, will be overthrown, circumcision having been summoned, under Antichrist as their leader, of whom they are worthy. Except that certain distinguished persons among the nations will resist Antichrist, and some undistinguished Jews will obey him. Both groups will be few, because “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 2:21). For when those from the nations who have been foreordained to salvation have been received into faith, then through the faith that works through love the fullness of the Jews also will be received unto salvation; and yet some of them will adhere to Antichrist. [Note: [Col. 0977D] So Ambrose, Chrysostom, and Jerome himself, Question 11 to Algasius.] Hence the Lord, speaking to the Jews, says: “I came in the name of my Father and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John 5:45) [Col. 0978A].

Nor was it hidden from the Prophet that Antichrist would also seize the nations, or on what grounds. For he says: “Set, O Lord, a lawgiver over them, that the nations may know that they are human beings” (Ps. 9:21). For this reason they accept Antichrist, the giver of a perverse law: [Note: [Col. 0977D] Augustine, on this verse of the psalm.] because they behaved foolishly in the manner of human beings. Whomever Antichrist has seduced to himself, Christ, as they say, will not take care to call back; for “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:26)—as if he said: After the calling of the nations, and not before, the calling of the Jews will take place generally. And what does “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” mean, except that Israel will not first be saved completely [Col. 0978B], but then, when the calling of the Gentiles has been completed? Therefore, after the full calling of the Jews, no further receiving of Gentiles remains; for the receiving of the Gentiles has its own time before the receiving of the Jews. But if no Gentile is received after the common calling of the Jews, and the kingdom of Antichrist is to follow the calling of the Jews, none of those among the Gentiles whom Antichrist’s kingdom has seized will have salvation. And if we consult Holy Scripture where such matters are treated, we shall find that no one at all deceived by Antichrist returns.

## CHAPTER XII. On Elijah and Enoch

[Col. 0978C] [Note: [Col. 0977D] Augustine, *City of God*, XX, ch. 29; *On Genesis*, IX, ch. 6; *On Original Sin*, II, ch. 23; *On the Merits of Sins*, I, ch. 3.] Elijah and Enoch, one taken up into paradise after the Flood and the other before it, await the time when, just as John preceded and pointed out the coming of the Saviour, so they too may announce before the end of the world the coming of the Judge through their proclamation; so that all may hasten to prepare themselves, first for the conflict with Antichrist, and afterward for judgment. Since these two live without the support of food and drink—although they neither hunger nor thirst—indeed, since no affliction whatever touches them, they are believed to be in a condition much better than ours, though much inferior to that which they will have. They possess, certainly, a happiness worthy of so exalted a place; but they hope for one far more precious in heaven. [Note: [Col. 0978D] Augustine, *City of God*, XX, penultimate ch.; Question 83, q. 58; *On Genesis*, IX, ch. 6, etc.; *Questions on the Gospels*, II, q. 33; to Dulcitius, final question.] In accordance with Christ’s preaching [Col. 0978D], they are believed, by steadfastly proclaiming the word of God for three years and a little more, to bring back the hearts of the children to the fathers—that is, the Jews to the faith of the patriarchs—and to strengthen and fortify the Church of God against the transformation of the world now imminently to come.

Tradition holds that at that time the Jews, after their long captivity, will return from every quarter to their own land; [Note: [Col. 0978D] See Tertullian, *On the Soul*; *On Antichrist* cited by Augustine, etc.; Augustine, *City of God*, XX, ch. 29.] there they will hear and receive the word of faith, and there they will courageously endure torments from Antichrist, who will usurp the seat of his kingdom in that same place [Col. 0979A], like good athletes of Christ. Meanwhile, however, that nation which will finally obtain mercy will suffer evils. Hence the Lord says: “For there will be great distress upon the earth, and wrath against this people; and they shall fall by the edge of the sword, and shall be led captive into all nations; and Jerusalem shall be trodden down by the Gentiles, until the times of the nations are fulfilled” (Luke 21:24). This distress and wrath, certainly, continue to this day for that people scattered among all nations; yet they will not continue forever. Hence, after the sequence concerning distress, mercy is added: “Until the times of the nations are fulfilled,” that is, until the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, so that all Israel may thus be saved and may joyfully return, as it were, to the throne of its own birth.

[Col. 0979B] What, then, is the meaning of what the Jews say of God in the Prophet: “And he will know us no longer”? (Ps. 73:9). Certainly, he will not restore the Jews to their former kingdom, but will bring them back so that they may become Christians. [Note: [Col. 0979D] Tertullian, cited above, ch. 50.] Among the first, however, Elijah and Enoch, after completing the course of their office, will be killed by Antichrist as obstacles to his designs; and, lying in the streets, they will be forbidden burial, lest there be any confidence in the resurrection which they had preached, or any imitation of them, whether in doctrine or in life—since all see them as wretched. After their death—which is thought likely to occur near the beginning of Antichrist’s kingdom—he is believed to reign in peace for about three and a half years, having first subdued the world in various ways.

Therefore, for the same number of years during which Christ preached, he willed that the heralds of his coming should preach; and for the same period he will permit Antichrist to exercise tyranny [Col. 0979C], so that what Christ built up in three years he may confirm through true men over three years, and Antichrist’s perversity may likewise attack it for three years, though in vain. [Note: [Col. 0979D] See the book *On Antichrist* among Augustine’s spurious works, vol. IX.] For that twofold sifting, which draws people both by persecution and by false miracles, or by alluring them with the goods of the world—a trial such as there has been none since the beginning, and therefore those who resist will be especially great among the saints—will shake the chaff completely out, but will merely agitate the wheat within. But because, unless those days were shortened, no flesh would be saved (Matt. 24:22), the burden of persecution is moderated by its brevity. For soon after his kingdom, the Lord Jesus will kill him by the breath of his mouth (2 Thess. 2:8) [Col. 0979D], that is, by the power of his command, either in person or through Michael. [Note: [Col. 0979D] Augustine, cited above.] According to the doctors, he will be killed on the Mount of Olives, in his tent and on his throne, in the place opposite that from which the Lord ascended into heaven.

## CHAPTER XIII. What Will Precede Christ’s Coming, and the Apostle’s Teaching

Before the advent of this most wicked one, there will first come the departure [Col. 0980A]: first, so that the nations depart from the empire of the Roman rulers; afterward, from the faith, and thus from the spiritual sovereignty of the Roman Church. This departure will be a sign of the day of the Lord, but it will precede the time of Antichrist. Hence the Apostle spoke in this order to those who feared that the day of the Lord was imminent: “Let no one deceive you in any way, because unless the departure comes first, and the man of sin is revealed, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God or is worshipped, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God” (ibid., vv. 3–4).

Certainly, before the day of the Lord comes, when the accession has been completed in its own time, the departure will occur; once it has been fulfilled, that wicked man will come—the wholly sinful one, the son of perdition or of the devil, who destroys human beings [Col. 0980B], or because he himself is to be destroyed and destroys others; who opposes, indeed is called Antichrist, and exalts himself by raising himself above everything called god, such as the gods of the nations or the saints, or worshipped as God, such as the Trinity. He will sit in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God; that is, in the Church, or in the Temple destroyed by the Romans [Note: [Col. 0979D] So Theodoret on 2 Thessalonians 2, and Jerome to Algasius, q. 11.] which the Jews will then rebuild. [Note: [Col. 0980D] So Irenaeus, Hippolytus, Cyril of Jerusalem, John Damascene, book IV, ch. 28, etc.] And which Jews, if not those who at about that time will have gathered at Jerusalem from diverse parts of the world?

[Note: [Col. 0980D] Augustine proposes both interpretations, *City of God*, XX, ch. 19.] This alone, then, remains: “Let him who holds now hold, until he is taken out of the way; and then that wicked one will be revealed.” That is: let the one who now holds the faith hold it until it grows cold; this will be its being taken out of the way, that is, removed from the midst of the world [Col. 0980C]. Or: that which restrains him is the power of Rome, to which all still flock from every side as to a head; or the accession, not yet completed, restrains him until both are taken out of the way. Or until the iniquity which is now mystical and hidden—for “the mystery of iniquity is already at work” (ibid., v. 7)—becomes public, as though one of the ordinary things of life, so that a person is no more ashamed to commit adultery than to walk. Then, with a seat prepared for him, that wicked one will reveal himself to a world worthy of him. Of him, the Apostle testifies: “His coming is according to the working of Satan” (ibid.), because, prompted by the devil, he will do everything; yet not without awareness, like madmen, who, as the Doctors say, bear no blame for evil deeds. [Note: [Col. 0980D] Augustine, *City of God*, XX, ch. 19.]

According to that working of Satan, he comes “in all power and signs and lying wonders, and in every seduction of iniquity for those who perish”—in every power of human authority and riches [Col. 0980D]. Hence: “He shall rule over all his enemies” (Ps. 10:15). In signs and wonders, greater and lesser; “lying,” because they are not real, as seems likely, but fantastic productions of magical art; or, if real, they lead to falsehood by God’s permission because they confirm the lie—that he is God. In every seduction, because by threats, flatteries, and every means he will seduce people into iniquity. For he has said in his heart, “I shall not be moved from generation to generation without evil.” [Note: [Col. 0981D] See Augustine on this verse of Psalm 9.] As though he said: I can rise above all others only through evil arts. He acts wickedly without concern, because “God is not in his sight” (Ps. 10:4). Why is God not in his sight? “According to the multitude of his wrath, he will not seek.” His mind will be so disturbed that he will not inquire how greatly the sinner has provoked the Lord. “His ways are defiled at every time,” that is, throughout his life. “At every time,” that is, compared with all times: no time has ever been so defiled that one would not judge the carefully considered life of Antichrist more foul. And yet, “the judgments of God will be removed from his face”: for either he will not attend to them or he will not believe them [Col. 0981B]. In various ways in the same psalm, the varied wickedness of that most evil one is exposed—a wickedness that will seize and entice only those who perish, while it will attack those to be saved now gently, now harshly. Yet it will succeed in neither way; for the power of the divine purpose prefers to defend its own from the jaws of that wicked one rather than to draw them back after they have been deceived.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Elect and Antichrist’s Ministers

After he has been killed, Christ will not come immediately. Rather, as may be understood from Daniel, forty-five days will be granted for repentance to the elect who wavered but did not fall in that persecution; how long afterward is wholly unknown. But if every deception of Antichrist is directed toward those who perish, it is clear that none will be directed toward those who are to be saved [Col. 0981C]. Likewise, if time for repentance is granted only to the elect, no pardon should be hoped for by Antichrist’s ministers, who instead will rejoice during those empty days, marrying and feasting. “And when they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (1 Thess. 5:3). And what destruction except that of which the Prophet, speaking of the Lord, says: “Fire shall go before him” (Ps. 96:3)? And again: “Fire shall blaze in his presence” (Ps. 49:3), a fire which will devour the earth with its produce and burn even the foundations of the mountains (Deut. 32:27)—certainly even before the Judge appears.

Although some explain this passage differently: the fire of Judgment, as is thought, will precede; and after it has appeared before him and in his presence, the same fire will blaze [Col. 0981D], by which all the world’s produce and all the earth’s structures, together with animals, will be reduced to ashes. Then the streams of water which run through different regions of the world, whether for human use or for irrigating the earth, will cease; hence the saying: “The sea is no more” (Rev. 21:1). [Note: [Col. 0981D] Augustine, *City of God*, XX, ch. 16.] Then this present fire of ours, which serves our needs, will no longer exist; hence also: “The light of a lamp shall shine in you no more” (ibid., 18:23). Yet fire will truly remain, though not in this place nor for this function. Water likewise will be elsewhere and for another purpose.

[Col. 0982A] It is agreed, with this exception, that according to the Scriptures fire and water will be wholly dissolved by the final burning; the rest, however, will be changed into a better form. For Scripture says through Peter: “The elements shall be dissolved with heat” (2 Pet. 3:10): two, so that they may be better, whence, “I saw a new heaven and a new earth” (Rev. 21:1); two, so that they may not exist at all—namely fire and water. They say that the water’s departure is contained also in the words: “Because of the bewildering noise of the sea and the waves” (Luke 21:25); for the sea, when it goes away together with its waves, will make a confused sound from heaven. Hence there is no doubt that birds of the air perished in the Flood and will perish by fire. Therefore they say [Note: [Col. 0981D] Augustine, *City of God*, XX, chs. 16 and 18.] that the fire will rise into the air as high as the Flood rose.

But concerning the highest heaven of heavens, some ask [Col. 0982B] whether it too will perish by fire. [Note: [Col. 0982D] The Master, IV, distinction 47.] Yet whether by fire or otherwise, it seems destined to perish, because the Prophet seems to have spoken of it when he says, “They shall perish.” For the preceding words are: “And in the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands.” [Note: [Col. 0982D] Augustine on this verse of Psalm 101: “They shall perish,” etc.] He who founded the immovable earth also made the heavens with his hands, as something worthier. And what are worthier than the earth except the higher realms? Yet of these it follows: “They shall perish.” Why, then, will they perish? Perhaps because iniquity existed there also, and the whole world had to be changed for the better. The changeable world was created changeable for humanity; the change of humanity is followed by the change of the world—so completely that earth and air perish, the air either alone or together with heaven; that is, they lose the form familiar to us. As it says: “In the beginning [Col. 0982C], Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands; they shall perish”—eventually, indeed; meanwhile, however, “all shall grow old like a garment.” They perish, then, in respect of form, while the earth remains forever in respect of substance. But they do not merely perish into oldness; they also pass into newness. They pass, because the Lord says: “Heaven and earth shall pass away” (Matt. 24:35); into newness, because it is written: “I saw a new heaven and a new earth” (Rev. 21:1). Hence the Prophet says: “And like a covering you shall change them” (Ps. 101:27); for when a covering is changed, it is made new. It follows: “And they shall be changed” (ibid.), because once changed they will by no means be changed again. Such will be the renewal of the world as suits renewed humanity [Col. 0982D].

## CHAPTER XV. On the Final Fire and the Resurrection of the Dead

The final fire will last as long as the purification of the faithful is needed. In this fire the living will die, and through him who will then come to judge the living and the dead, the dead will rise, according to the saying: “We shall all indeed rise” (1 Cor. 15). Of what sort? Hear what follows shortly afterward: “The dead shall rise incorruptible.” “We shall all indeed rise” (ibid.) [Col. 0983A], because those who are found alive will die in the fire and, after death, will rise like the other dead. [Note: [Col. 0983D] Augustine, *City of God*, XX, ch. 20, and Letter 80; but he doubts in his response to Dulcitius, Question 3. Fulgentius, *On the Faith*, ch. 3.] But both good and evil will rise incorruptible; hence it follows: “And we shall be changed,” as if to say: incorruption is common to all, but the change is ours—that is, the saints’. Therefore the saints are changed in themselves unto glorification; together with the wicked they rise to bodily wholeness and the complete restoration of their members. For whether anything has been lacking to human bodily quantity through a defect of nature or through any occurrence in the world, the omnipotence of the one who raises the dead will restore it all. [Note: [Col. 0983D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 91; Sermon 4, *On the Words of the Lord*.]

The resurrection will do two things: it will supply what the living lacked, and restore what after death has been dispersed in whatever manner. Thus eye will return to eye [Col. 0983B], foot to foot; in short, every member which exists in this mortal state will then return to itself, and they will be in the same order and with the same completeness of their parts. Yet whatever is defective in the members here will certainly be corrected there; whatever accords with nature will then be made firm; and whatever a deficient nature now mars through the deformity or absence of any member, grace will doubtless then refashion, repairing what is missing either from the customary bodily excretions or, as I think more securely and certainly, from adjacent parts. Thus he who created all things from nothing—for now he does not will bodies to arise except from something—will himself form from the members and their nearest adjacent parts what does not exist, so wisely and powerfully that from what existed will be made what did not exist, while nonetheless, after it has been made, that from which it was made will recover its proper quantity. Thus, after the rib was taken from Adam’s side, the Lord filled in flesh in its place.

God is therefore wise, not as though ignorant, gathering again confusedly and without order the minutiae of corpses however widely scattered, and attaching one to another bodies and members. God is powerful, not as though unable to prevent what is mutilated and deformed here from remaining so. The tongue of the rich man, which here served his throat and its companion, talkativeness, is tormented in hell by the burning of flame. Why, except because each person is especially to be punished in hell in that member by which he especially offended God on earth? Thus each member pays in hell for what it sins here [Col. 0983D]. Conversely, perhaps the saints receive a greater crown from the Lord in that part of themselves in which they have laboured more for the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0983D] Augustine, *City of God*, book 22, ch. 20; *Enchiridion*, ch. 91.] [Note: [Col. 0984D] Ambrose, on Luke 24.] Thus the first reward is of the mind, the second of the body.

Far be it, then, that what is now a tongue should be an eye in the future, lest one seize what belongs to another and neither possess what is its own. Therefore each member will either return to its own name or will be assigned another’s name as a reward. [Col. 0984A] But even the least of its own members will not lose their names. For Job says of God: “Whom I myself shall see, and not another; and my eyes shall behold” (Job 19:27). “I myself”: the same soul in the same body. “And not another”: not different through a transposition or confusion of members—as he indicates in part when he adds, “And my eyes shall behold.” What does “my eyes shall behold” mean except that the eyes which I now have will then see? Thus what is an eye here will likewise be the same eye there, and not some other thing. Hence, by an argument from likeness, it follows that the remaining members also will resume their own names.

If Christ rose, we too shall rise. To establish the certainty of our resurrection, the Apostle adduces the Lord’s resurrection [Col. 0984B]. Therefore, just as by that resurrection we are certain of ours, so let us examine in it what ours will be like. Certainly, just as apostolic authority makes us certain that if Christ rose, we too shall rise (1 Cor. 15), so the truth of the matter seems to establish that, as Christ rose, we too shall rise; Christ’s resurrection is thus not only the cause but also the example of ours. No one would dare assert that Christ received through resurrection a body or members other than those he had before death, or differently arranged. For he died crucified; he was buried; the same person rose, resuming exactly the same substance, so far as the flesh is concerned, but altered in glory. Who can deny that the same will occur in those also [Col. 0984C] who are known to be destined to die in the final fire, and, as they say, to die and rise in the very act while they are caught up into the air to meet Christ? [Note: [Col. 0984D] Augustine, cited at the beginning of the chapter; Jerome to Minervius and Alexander; Fulgentius, *On the Faith to Peter*, ch. 3; Ambrose on 1 Thessalonians 4; the Master, IV, distinction 43, §5.] Does it not therefore especially fit that what has been fulfilled in the head, and is expected to be fulfilled in no small part of the members, should be assigned to all alike: that all alike should rise changed, rather than some, contrary to Job?

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Procreation and Growth of Human Beings according to Different Views

All agree that the procreation of children takes its origin from the seed of the parents—not of one but of both—so that they are children of human beings [Col. 0984D], not like Christ, the Son of Man, taking their material from both, not from one alone.

Most hold that growth comes from elsewhere, whether in the womb or after birth. In the womb, it comes from the humours of the womb; after birth, from nourishment. Thus the increase in growing persons is precisely as much as is converted from food into human substance. Consequently, in the whole human being only a very small portion comes from the parents, a very small portion from one’s own prior substance, and none from more remote ancestors. For it cannot possibly happen that the exceedingly few and tiny particles separated by generation from the bodies of Adam and Eve should be distributed to all human beings in such a way that every individual receives even an atom from them—especially since, according to this view, human seed remains in its smallness, merely taking into itself certain alien materials and, from what it receives, completing the quantity due to human beings. The first human beings, therefore, were made from earth; but their descendants, especially the more remote, were made neither from earth nor from the first human beings, but solely from food [Col. 0985A].

Others say [Note: [Col. 0985D] Hugh of St Victor, *On the Sacraments*, I, part VI, penultimate chapter; Lombard, *Sentences*, II, distinctions 30 and 18.] that just as Adam’s rib, certainly a small thing, was formed into the whole of Eve, certainly something far greater, while no external supports or additions from which a large thing could arise were taken on; so too the seed of parents grows to mature human size through the power of him who created all things from nothing, who multiplied a few loaves and little fishes to feed thousands. Yet all things are from nothing by power alone: the woman from the rib; whereas human procreation occurs by both power and nature. This view calls fire, baths, clothing, food, and drink the supports of childhood: food and drink nourish inwardly; fire, baths, and clothing outwardly. Nevertheless, just as the latter are not converted into human nature, neither are the former. Indeed, according to the Lord’s statement, “everything that enters the mouth goes into the belly and is expelled through the privy” (Matt. 15:17). Thus, just as whole Eve was formerly compressed within the rib, so the entire abundance of potentiality was contained in Abraham’s loins and in Adam’s loins. The rib was small and yet became large; likewise the small seed of parents, in propagating, became a multitude of children [Col. 0985C]. Eve is nothing other than what was Adam’s rib; nor is the whole human race anything other than what existed beforehand in the loins of the first parents. This view delights in saying that nothing but human substance rises again. The other view does not at all shrink from holding that swine’s flesh or similar food, though converted into human substance, either alone or for the greater part rises again.

## CHAPTER XVII. There Is One Origin, and on What Remains or Departs

[Col. 0985D] [Note: [Col. 0985D] The Master, cited above.] But if the resurrection restores each person’s own members, will Adam receive back the rib? But then Eve would no longer exist, so that the emission of seed might return to the parents, and there would no longer be any children. Thus Adam will be alone in the resurrection—which is unthinkable! For “we shall all rise” (1 Cor. 15:51). Or, according to the other view, children will have nothing in their substance which their parents previously had in theirs—which is likewise unthinkable. For, just as Levi was in Abraham’s loins when he paid tithes, according to the Apostle (Heb. 7:5), so all were in Adam’s loins when he sinned. Hence, to put it thus, just as Levi himself paid tithes to Melchizedek in Abraham, according to the Apostle [Col. 0986A], so, according to that same Apostle, all sinned in Adam. Therefore, in a certain manner all mortals existed in Adam’s loins—and are they to lose that in which they were immortal?

But the Lord made one man and formed from him a wife, so that all who succeeded by birth might recognize themselves as subject not to diverse origins but to one only; and thus human beings might learn, in their own nature, to honour the authority and unity of one origin, rejecting the example of the devil, who, by introducing schism, attempted to introduce another origin after God. But if Eve had been produced not from Adam but from another material, the unity of origin would not at all be commended to posterity. Likewise, if there are some who consist so completely [Col. 0986B] of the material of food that they contain nothing from Adam and Eve, would not diversity—indeed, a multiplicity—of origins be introduced in this way also? A very few would have derived their material partly from Adam; most entirely from elsewhere; some from one kind of food, others from another. For unless seed that proceeded from the first parents is increased in the manner of the rib, it can in no way be spread among all human beings. Thus, when the seed has failed, human beings are entirely made from alien material; and both now and in the future the unity of origin commended by the Lord perishes.

It is therefore much more reasonable, I think, that the seed of parents should, in imitation of the rib, gain from itself through God its own increase, so that human beings may consist neither partly nor wholly of material other than that of their parents [Col. 0986C], and thus all may have been entirely in the loins of the first parents and one origin may be established. But whether this is so or otherwise, it is nevertheless believed that some things in a human being are meant to remain, while others are meant to depart. For Adam had a rib so that a woman might be made from it, not so that he might receive it back again; for God put flesh in its place. Likewise seed departs from parents, not indeed to return, but so that the procreation of children may result from it.

Will all the other things that fall away from the bodies of saints be restored—whether through the shedding of blood, cutting off hair or nails, or the frequent exhalations of illnesses that often attack the body in vigour and leave it thin? But if, through exhalation, bodily parts pass into the air in sickness, then, upon recovery, food is converted into the body. Otherwise, just as food, when available, causes the body, without any external addition, to increase and remain within itself, so also, when such supports are lacking, it may perhaps cause the body to become thin and fail within itself—not cause any part to be expelled from it and to exist elsewhere [Col. 0986D].

They say [Note: [Col. 0986D] Augustine especially notes this, *Enchiridion*, ch. 89, and *City of God*, XXII, ch. 19.] that everything which departs must be brought back, though not in such a way that every item must return to that bodily part in which it previously was, lest there be an excessive density or length of hair or nails, and likewise lest a certain deformity through excess arise for those beholding themselves in the other parts. [Note: [Col. 0987D] The Master, IV, distinction 44, §2 and following.] Hence they consider that everything which formerly belonged to the mortal body will be present at the resurrection; yet in such a way that whatever would be unbecoming in its own place supplies the need of other members. But in some people there are excretions so numerous and so great that they could not merely furnish this, but would exceed the whole human being by far, far more. But if it is God’s purpose that nothing of the human body should remain in the earth, I would more credibly think [Note: [Col. 0987D] St Thomas holds the same view, as do those who wrote on the *Sentences* after him.] that every thing is restored to its own place: whatever any part of the body contained here, it will receive there, God bringing what is much and excessive, little and minimal, into a measure suited to the resurrection. Thus infants will rise large [Col. 0987B], and those of excessive size will be proportioned. Thus those whose members lack their proper number or measure will find an equal number and measure.

Yet it does not seem necessary that human substance which departed from us whole should resume its excesses, discarded even in life. Is it not better that what flows away through continual intercourse and the polluting illusions of the night should be absent, together with that seed which is formed into human nature? Is it not pointless to recover the teeth cast off in childhood for those who have received teeth more suited to mature age? Living persons also leave behind other things which do not seem necessary to those who depart this life whole. Especially since no one dares affirm—although no one dares deny it either—that the Lord Jesus, in rising again, took up more of the body than he laid down in dying on the cross, except perhaps that which was removed in circumcision. But apart from that, it is credible that many other things also were separated from the Lord’s body in the ordinary human way. It may indeed be, if God so pleases, that he restores everything to Christ and his people; but the resurrection will have nothing more than death had time for. Yet whichever is the case, the person who rises will have neither less than is fitting [Col. 0987C] nor more. But I affirm neither alternative; rather, I believe a third: namely, that from all that this mortal condition has taken away from human substance, what is necessary must be resumed, and what is superfluous left behind, so that resurrected bodies resume all that benefits completeness and leave behind all that need not be resumed.

[Col. 0987D] [Note: [Col. 0987D] Augustine, *City of God*, XXII, ch. 19.] Yet the saying that “not a hair shall perish” may perhaps seem to require that absolutely nothing be left behind. This should be understood to mean that greater things will not be lacking to the saints, for whom lesser things will not be lacking either. An eye perishes where a hair does not perish, in the sense that the resurrection is believed to retain hairs, yet not the superfluity of hairs. For all hairs are numbered, but they are not all preserved. What we judge concerning hairs, we judge also concerning the other members.

[Col. 0988A] [Note: [Col. 0987D] The Master, IV, distinction 44, §1.] At the resurrection, they say, each person will be of the stature which he would naturally have had at the age of thirty if prevented by death, or which he had at that age if he died in old age. [Note: [Col. 0987D] Anselm, or the author of the Commentary on Paul at Eph. 4, has this from Augustine; see Augustine, *City of God*, XXII, chs. 14–16, etc.] Human beings will therefore be unequal to one another—greater and smaller in different ways—as the course of the world has brought them forth differently. Hence the Apostle, discussing the resurrection, says: “Until we all come to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4:13). “All,” for all who are to be saved will come to meet the Lord in the air, not some; they will come not as children but “to a perfect man,” so that each may be perfect in the number of members and due bodily size. When he says “to a perfect man,” he does not deny the female sex [Col. 0988B]; rather, he teaches concerning men what must be understood as very similar concerning women. [Note: [Col. 0988D] Augustine, *City of God*, XXII, ch. 17.] [Note: [Col. 0988D] Fulgentius, *On the Faith*, ch. 3.] We shall attain the perfection of mature humanity, namely that which brings us to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ; not to Christ’s own measure, certainly, because some will be physically greater than he and some smaller. [Note: [Col. 0988D] Augustine, ibid., ch. 15.] The age of Christ’s fullness is thirty years, for then, as Christ did, every person receives the fullness of human nature. The resurrection will restore to all the measure of this thirtieth year.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the State of Human Beings after the Resurrection
[Col. 0988C] But what quality will a quantity of this kind acquire? A wretched one in the faithless, a glorious one in the saints. Hence the Apostle says: “We await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will refashion the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. III.20). What, then, is his, so that ours may become known? In the Transfiguration he displayed beforehand an example of the glory to come, when “his face shone like the sun, but his garments became white as snow” (Matt. XVII.2). No clearer or more brilliant example of the resurrection could be found. The garments are the saints, which became white as snow when his face had shone like the sun. For by as much as the sun surpasses snow in brightness and beauty, by so much is Christ more glorious than all the saints. The saints will be glorious, yet Christ is more glorious: for the saints are like snow, but the Holy of Holies is like the sun. Yet no one should suppose that the saints will be clothed in the resurrection.

[Col. 0988D] Christ left in the world the clothes that he had in the world. Adam existed naked before his sin, and would never have needed clothing had he never sinned. Hence it is apparent that one who, while still in paradise, had no need of an animal garment, would much less need clothing in heaven once made spiritual. For one who preserved obedience possessed so great a beauty, and was to possess a beauty far more excellent after its completion, that, if he had been clothed, the garment would rather have covered what ought to be seen than concealed what was shameful. Thus the dignity and sufficiency of the resurrection require no garment, whether for concealment or for protection. Nor did the Lord’s garments become white as snow in the Transfiguration so that anything of this sort should be understood to occur in the resurrection; rather, the brightness of the garments indicated the beauty of those who rise again.

[Note: [Col. 0989D] Lombard, IV, dist. 49, §1, 4, no. 5.] But as there is a difference in glory between Christ and the saints, so also, in the resurrection, some saints will surpass others. Hence the Apostle: “One is the glory of the sun, another the glory of the moon, and another the glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption”—that is, both immortal and impassible—“it is sown in dishonor; it will rise in glory; it is sown in weakness; it will rise in power” (I Cor. XV.41)—that is, in a state in which nothing can harm it. “It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body.” [Note: [Col. 0989D] Augustine, *On Faith and the Creed*, ch. 6; *City of God*, XIII, ch. 20; XXII, chs. 21 and 91; *Enchiridion*, ch. 91.] He does not say “spirit,” as though the body were to be changed into spirit, as some nevertheless suppose. [Note: [Col. 0989D] See Jerome, letter to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem.] Against this the Lord said to his disciples after the resurrection: “Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have.” I say, the Apostle does not say, “A spirit will rise,” but “a spiritual [body],” because it will be wholly subject to the spirit and will no longer resist it. Therefore it will rise spiritual, passing so into the nature of spirit that it becomes agile, light, and in no need of food or clothing (Luke XXIV.4).

In proportion to the glory of the outward person, glory will also be given to the inward person: so that whoever possesses more beauty of body may also possess more in the vision of God; and whoever perceives more of God [Col. 0989C] may also grasp more in the knowledge of things. Hence the Apostle: “Instructed in charity, and unto all the riches of the fullness of understanding, unto the knowledge of the mystery of God the Father of Jesus Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II.2). Certainly, instructed in the knowledge of God, they thereby arrive at all riches—that is, abundance—with an understanding made full, so that they may have perfect understanding of human and divine things, of the soul and of the heavenly spirits. In the knowledge of God—not, I say, as regards works, but of the mystery of God—so that what is secret and known by few concerning the essence of God the Father of Christ may be known: namely, that he is a person distinct from the Son, although the same as he in substance. Whoever strives toward this knowledge should have recourse only to Christ. [Col. 0989D] For the nearer anyone approaches Christ in faith, the more richly he is endowed from Christ’s treasure. And if knowledge increases in accordance with the increase of faith, how much more will those loftier in appearance become loftier in the knowledge of all things.

There is a twofold glory of those who rise again: one of body and one of mind, differing among different persons. These are the many dwelling-places in the house of Christ’s Father. There they shall be: “As is the heavenly one, such also are the heavenly” (I Cor. XV.48): as Christ is, so are Christians, just as here they are, “As is the earthly one, such also are the earthly.” As Adam is, so are those descended from him—provided that, “As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly.” Thus, as we formerly went before in Adam, may we consequently be renewed in Christ.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Lord’s descent, the trumpet, and those rising again

[Note: [Col. 0990D] Lombard, IV, dist. 43, §2.] But the fire in which the resurrection of all is to occur, as has been said, seems destined to come before the advent of the Judge. By its burning, after all who are found alive have been deprived of life, the time then seems to come for, according to the Apostle, “the Lord himself to descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God” (I Thess. IV.15). Why only then? It is agreed that he will descend from heaven with the trumpet of God. But the trumpet will then sound—if indeed it is to have a place—when the death of all has preceded it. But why then? Because the trumpet will sound in order that the dead may rise. Hence it follows: “And the dead who are in Christ will rise first; then we who live, who remain, shall together be caught up with them to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (ibid.).

Those dead who meanwhile are in Christ according to their souls—that is, rest in Christ—even if they have been cremated, since there could have been doubt concerning them, will rise first, so that the resurrection may be more marvelous. For we who live, who remain at the Lord’s coming, will not precede those who have fallen asleep; but rather, as was said, “They will rise first; then we who live, who remain”—that is, those of you who will be alive and will have survived all the preceding [Col. 0990C] torments of Antichrist, and are therefore most worthy and, as they say, like the apostles in their sufferings—“we,” I say, “who live, who remain, shall together be caught up with them.” What does “they will rise first; then we shall together with them be caught up” mean, except that their resurrection, being prior, will await ours, which is later? Certainly without difficulty, because [Note: [Col. 0990D] This is Augustine, *City of God*, XX, ch. 18, but in different words.] this conflagration of the world will be for the saints what the furnace was for the three children. And at last we shall together be caught up with them in the clouds.

[Note: [Col. 0990D] Lombard, dist. 47.] How great the lightness of the bodies of those rising again, who will ascend in a cloud from different parts of the world, coming to meet one another and also to meet Christ descending from heaven into the air! Hence after the words, “He ascended into heaven; he sits at the right hand of God the Father [Col. 0990D] almighty,” there follows, “From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.” [Note: [Col. 0990D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 55.] The living whom the fire of judgment finds, or the righteous dead before the fire, or the unrighteous.

Accordingly, as the Apostle says, the Lord himself—that is, in his own person—will descend from heaven, not humble as before, but “with a command”: that is, commanding with the voice of his own archangel, namely Michael, which will cause the dead to rise. This voice is called a trumpet, as though manifest; namely, because, as a trumpet in wars, so then it will defeat enemies; and as a trumpet at festivals, it will invite friends to the solemnity [Col. 0991A] of eternal glory. This same voice can thus be called a trumpet. For the trumpet will be the great voice of angels; and this will likewise be the trumpet of God because it is Christ’s, or because God will give it efficacy. What efficacy? [Note: [Col. 0991D] Augustine, letter 120; *On the Grace of the New Testament*, ch. 34. Lombard, IV, dist. 43, §2.] Hear the Apostle: “Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall indeed all rise, but we shall not all be changed. In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet; for the trumpet will sound,” etc. Therefore, as has been said, all, both good and evil, will rise; but not all will be changed into the glory of immortality and impassibility. What delay, then, will there be in rising? Certainly a small one. For, that the resurrection may be more marvelous, all will rise “in a moment”; but since there is delay in a moment, he adds, as if correcting himself, “in the twinkling of an eye”—that is, as quickly as an object is seen or perceived by the eyelid, [Col. 0991B] namely, with the greatest swiftness.

But through what will this exceedingly swift resurrection occur? Through the trumpet—that is, a great and manifest voice, after which there will be no other. This [Note: [Col. 0991D] Augustine, above, the same ch. 34.] trumpet is a cry; hence it is said: “A cry was made: Behold, the bridegroom comes” (Matt. XXV.6). By the name of trumpet some evident and illustrious sign is meant, which elsewhere is called the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God, and in the Gospel the voice of Christ, which the dead will hear and come forth. [Note: [Col. 0991D] Augustine, on this verse of the same psalm.] Hence the Prophet, speaking to God, says: “You caused judgment to be heard from heaven” (Ps. LXXV.9); and elsewhere: “He will summon heaven above and earth” (Ps. XLIX.5), that is, the righteous who are above and sinners. For what purpose? “To distinguish his people” (ibid., 4). What will result from that distinction? “The saints shall exult in glory” (Ps. CXLIX.5). And what of the wicked? “The earth trembled and was still” (Ps. LXXV.9). Certainly, earthly people will be afraid and will cease from those things which they held dear here.

But if all are to rise in the twinkling of an eye, how will some rise earlier and others later? Each individual’s resurrection will occur in the twinkling of an eye; yet it does not therefore follow that the resurrection of the later and the first must occur simultaneously. Both will indeed occur in the twinkling of an eye; but one in one instant, the other perhaps in another. It may also happen that the earlier and the later rise earlier and later within one and the same twinkling of an eye. One and the same twinkling has an earlier and a later. Nevertheless, some maintain, [Note: [Col. 0992D] See the authors cited above.] perhaps not unreasonably, that after the first have been raised and caught up, [Col. 0991D] the rest, still alive, will be caught up into the air together with those raised; and that in the very act of being caught up they will die and rise again. Perhaps the Apostle indicated this when he said: “The dead who are in Christ will rise first; then we who live shall together be caught up with them” (I Thess. IV.16). For what does “then we who live shall together be caught up with them” mean except that they will rise first? Then—that is, after their resurrection—while still living we shall together with those raised be lifted up, so that those already raised and those still about to die may ascend together. Thus the dead will rise before the living, [Col. 0992A] but will not ascend before them. [Note: [Col. 0992D] See Jerome, letter to Minerius and Alexander; Augustine, *City of God*, XX, ch. 20.] And since, according to the Apostle’s testimony, “we shall indeed all rise” (I Cor. XV.51), we shall all also die. For there is no resurrection except from the dead. Hence the Apostle says: “But someone will say: How do the dead rise? And with what kind of body [276] do they come?” (I Cor. XV.35). It is as though he said: Reason does not allow that one who has died should live again; or, if this happens, reason certainly does not allow that he become other than he was before.

The Apostle answers someone, and first the earlier question: “Fool, what you sow is not made alive unless it first dies” (ibid., 36). It is as though he said: Mortals are not quickened into immortality otherwise than by first dying. Certainly, the mortality of the seed is, as it were, the seed of future immortality.

That the resurrection will be of another glory but nevertheless of the same substance, [Col. 0992B] the Apostle declared when he continued: “And what you sow, you do not sow the body that will be, but a bare grain; but God gives it a body as he wills, and to each seed its own body” (ibid., 37–38). Likewise, certainly, the body of this lowliness differs greatly and is, as it were, bare in comparison with the beauty of future loveliness which God gives to each as he wills. Thus, as the grain differs from that which grows from it, so this body differs from that which rises again: it differs in glory, certainly, but not in substance. For as its own body is given to each seed—wheat’s to wheat, barley’s to barley—so our former bodies will be restored to us.

If, then, those not yet dead are caught up together with those already raised, while all must rise and there is no resurrection except from death, it is reasonably said that death and resurrection will occur in the very act of being caught up. For it is not fitting that this be delayed until they are already standing with Christ in the air. But if the resurrection of those who died long ago finds those presently alive, the resurrection itself must occur around the very beginning of the final fire. For if there were any delay, the resurrection of the first would not find the last living people; for mortal life cannot endure long in fire. But it is agreed that the resurrection will not occur before the trumpet that is to bring about the resurrection has sounded. And because the Lord is to descend from heaven with the trumpet, this will not occur before the Judge has arrived. Therefore the Lord seems destined to descend from heaven neither before the fire nor long [Col. 0992D] after the fire. Not before the fire, lest the trumpet in and with which he descends should sound before the fire and, by its life-giving sound, the resurrection of the dead take place—contrary to everyone’s opinion—before and apart from the fire; whereas they rather hold that the resurrection occurs in the fire, so that the purified may pass unharmed through the fire, while those needing purification, as the authorities relate, [Note: [Col. 0992D] See Augustine, *City of God*, XXI, ch. 26, near the middle.] remain in the fire as long as there is something in them to be purified. Hence the Apostle: “Each person’s work will become manifest, for the day of the Lord will disclose it, because it will be revealed in fire; and fire will test what sort each person’s work is. If anyone’s work, which he has built upon it, remains, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire” (I Cor. III.15).

Those who build virtues upon the foundation of faith depart this life, some wholly pure, others with certain deadly sins. But the day of the Lord—which begins after death—judging according to the merits of each person’s present conduct, will disclose through purgatorial fire, whether interim or final, what each one’s work is like. Whoever has work that remains unburned in the fire is wholly good, because he will receive a reward. But whoever has work that is combustible will suffer loss in the fire; yet he himself will be saved, but through fire. Therefore the Lord does not seem destined to descend before the fire.

## CHAPTER XX. On the trumpet, the Lord’s advent, and the fire

[Col. 0993B]

[Note: [Col. 0993D] Lombard, IV, dist. 43.] But someone may say that the trumpet will not sound before the fire, whereas the Lord will descend before its sound. But since the Lord’s descent aims at this: first, the dead rise; afterwards, they are judged—why would he come beforehand? Is it because he will come to judge not only the living and the dead, but also the world through fire? But since it is agreed that he will descend from heaven with the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God, his descent seems simultaneous with the [277] trumpet. But if the trumpet occurs with the advent, and both occur after the fire, how will he come to judge the living and the dead and the world through fire? If the fire has first overtaken the world, how will Christ, coming [Col. 0993C] afterwards, judge the world through fire? Is the preposition *per* (“through”) used in place of *in* (“in”), one preposition for another, as in the Apostle’s words: “For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who slept through Jesus”? “Through Jesus” (I Thess. IV.13), that is, “in Jesus.” For those who slept in Jesus—that is, died in the faith of Jesus—he will not only raise, but also bring with him into heaven, that they may be with him in the same blessedness. Or, while he has not yet descended bodily from heaven, by the sentence of the conflagration he will in a certain manner anticipate judging the world through fire.

Perhaps someone may be pleased with the view that the Lord, descending from heaven with the trumpet, then—and not before—brings fire upon the world; that in the fire he raises the dead; and that he lifts up the raised together with the living. Thus the Lord’s advent precedes, the conflagration immediately follows by the authority of the one arriving, and the resurrection of the dead promptly follows the trumpet sounding together with the conflagration—so swiftly that it finds alive the people of that time. And reason seems to require that the resurrection follow the trumpet without delay, since it is impious to deny the cause such supreme efficacy. Hence, after saying, “For the trumpet will sound” (I Cor. XV.52), the Apostle immediately adds: “And the dead will rise.” But if the trumpet is simultaneous with the fire, and the fire follows the advent, how can the judgment be through the advent? Therefore the Lord will descend first, and the trumpet’s sound will occur afterwards. But how then will he descend at the trumpet’s sound? Is it because his descent [Col. 0994A] will have its completion in the sound that it is rightly declared that the descent will occur in the sound?

## CHAPTER XXI. On the final fire and the purification of souls

But it is agreed that the final fire will last as long as the purification of the faithful requires. If souls outside their bodies are to be purified then as they are now, it is necessary either that the resurrection of all be commonly delayed until these souls too have at last been purified and, together with the others, resume their bodies at the trumpet of God, which by then will have been sounding long after the world’s conflagration; or that those raised first wait in the fire for those yet to be raised, or ascend before those who will ascend, I know not how long, later.

But if the satisfaction of penitents is otherwise ordered, [Col. 0994B] because the state of all things will then also be otherwise ordered—namely, so that, in the final fire, the souls of those already raised may pay in their bodies whatever sins they formerly committed in mortal bodies—then this will occur: from the resurrection onward they will be immortal, yet not immediately but only at last—perhaps, uncertainly, “not yet”—to become impassible; for a time they will endure torments in the manner of those damnably immortal. If this is so, how will the matter stand? Will they rise long before the others, to be wholly cleansed in the fire, so that the trumpet sounds twice? But whence will this be proved? Or will it sound without interruption from the resurrection of the penitents to that of the saints? But where is that found? Certainly, the trumpet and the resurrection seem to be joined to one another.

But if the resurrection of those already cleansed and of those still [Col. 0994C] requiring cleansing is to be celebrated together, what is more appropriate to hold than that the purified are immediately caught up to meet Christ in the air, while the others remain in the fire until their purification is completed, the Judge distributing to each group what it deserves? And since it is not credible that Christ, with one part of his own people while another part remains behind, should ascend into heaven—when rather the wicked will first go into eternal fire and at last [278] the good into eternal life, so that, just as all the wicked go together into fire, so all the good go together into life—we must confess that the Lord will remain with his saints in the air until the commander has gathered his whole army to himself, and the commander becomes a fellow banqueter, the soldier a guest. This is by no means an absurd thing to believe.

If, however, anyone judges it absurd for the Judge to come before he conducts judgment—as though it were not the beginning of judgment to set the world on fire, to raise the dead in the conflagration, to torture some of those raised in the fire as accused persons, according to the words, “He will kindle a fire round about his enemies” (Ps. XCVI.3), to purify others as penitents, and to lift others to himself through the pyre unharmed because of the holiness of their merit; and as though judgment consisted only in this, that one sentence be pronounced on this side and another on that: “Go, cursed ones, into eternal fire; come, blessed ones, receive the kingdom” (Matt. XXV.41)—if, I say, this seems absurd to anyone, namely that the Lord should wait in the air throughout the whole delay of the penitents, [Col. 0995A] as though it were shameful for God to be anywhere, and as though the Judge of almighty mercy could not, if it were fitting that this be done, purify his own people as swiftly as possible—what will he himself say concerning the Judge’s advent? Will he say that fire will go before him (Ps. XCVI.3), and after the fire has gone before for as long as is fitting, the trumpet will follow; that, when the resurrection has occurred through its power, all will remain alike in the fire—the good unharmed, the wicked in torment, and the penitents, as has been said, being burned free from the stain of sin—and that only then, after the cleansing is accomplished, will the Judge come? But this seems to be hindered by the fact that the Lord is said by the Apostle to descend with the trumpet and to come with all his saints: “at the advent of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints.” Unless perhaps the statement, “He will descend with the trumpet,” should be understood as though it said, “He will descend with a herald.” And what does “He will descend with a herald” mean except that he will send before him a herald of his descent?

[Note: [Col. 0995D] Augustine, letter 120, ch. 34.] Thus perhaps it may be said that he will descend with the trumpet because he will send before him the trumpet that announces his descent and judgment, in accordance with the words, “You caused judgment to be heard from heaven” (Ps. LXXV.9), and, “He will send his angels with a trumpet and a great voice” (Matt. XXIV.31). For perhaps he will send angels beforehand with a trumpet by which judgment is made heard.

It may also be said that the Lord will come with all the saints because he will come from heaven to judgment with all the saints—that is, as do all the saints. Yet they will first, at the sounding of the trumpet, immediately receive their bodies, and at last come to meet the coming Judge. Or “with all the saints” means that he will come to judgment as all [Col. 0995C] the saints do: he himself descending from heaven, while they, having received their bodies, ascend from the earth and meet the descending Lord. Thus, while the Judge is descending, the saints neither ascend before nor after him, but then ascend to meet the one who comes toward them. This seems to be the sense of the Apostle’s words: “Then we who live shall together be caught up with them to meet Christ in the air” (I Thess. IV.16). [Note: [Col. 0995D] Augustine, *City of God*, XX, ch. 20: “For one goes to meet one who is coming, not one who remains.”] He did not say, “We shall be caught up to Christ,” as though Christ were located somewhere, but “to meet Christ,” as though he were journeying. Hence elsewhere: “until we meet” (Eph. IV.13)—that is, we who come from different places meet Christ coming from heaven.

## CHAPTER XXII. On sudden destruction and the signs of judgment

[Col. 0995D]

But although the times of the general conflagration and judgment that will come through fire are hidden—because it is unknown when this will happen, in winter or summer, by night or by day, and though no one knows even the moments, because it is likewise unknown at what hour of day or night it will occur—yet through the Apostle it is most certain that “when they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden [Col. 0996A] destruction will come upon them, like pain upon a woman with child, and they shall not escape” (I Thess. V.1–3). For after Antichrist’s death, his ministers will promise themselves peace and security. And, according to the Lord’s testimony, “As it was in the days of Noah, so will be the advent of the Son of Man. For as they were in the days before the flood, eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day Noah entered the ark, and they did not know until the flood came and took them all away, so will be the advent of the Son of Man” (Matt. XXIV.37–39; Luke XVII.26–28). For, by a conflagration sudden to all, sudden destruction will come upon them. It is sudden because, as was said, they will attend only to their pleasures. Yet it will not be sudden for the saints, to whom Antichrist’s advent will be a sign.

And this too: after the tribulation has begun [Col. 0996B] or perhaps ended, “immediately after the tribulation of those days, the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven” (Matt. XXIV.29; Luke XXI.25; Mark XIII.24). Thus, after that tribulation has ended, of which the Lord says, “There will be great tribulation such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor will be”—for whose faith will not be shaken when the persecutor of piety is a worker of miracles? Yet this persecution will not endure long, because, according to the Lord’s teaching, “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved; but for the elect’s sake those days will be shortened” (Matt. XXIV.21–22). Certainly they will be shortened; for, as authorities relate, [Note: [Col. 0996D] Augustine, *City of God*, XX, ch. 8.] these evils will be so great for three and a half years. After, I say, that great tribulation has ended, a brief peace will follow: for the wicked, a deceptive security; [Col. 0996C] for the good, a testing. Immediately, according to Matthew, the sun, moon, and stars will for a time be deprived of their light. Why? That they may indicate to the saints the nearness of the Lord’s advent. But when the world is renewed, they will receive a greater light.

[Note: [Col. 0996D] Lombard, IV, dist. 48, §5.] Luke—or rather, the Lord according to Luke—says concerning the same matter: “There will be signs in sun and moon” (Luke XXI.25), etc. There will be signs in sun and moon: “for the sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes” (Joel II.31). “And on earth distress of nations” (Luke XXI.25), perhaps on account of heavenly as well as earthly signs. On account of which earthly signs? “Because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves” (ibid.), perhaps as they disappear from the midst. [Col. 0996D] Then people will wither from fear (ibid., 26) and from expectation of the unusual things that will come upon the whole world (ibid.).

But if expectation comes beforehand, how, according to the Apostle, will the destruction be sudden? Perhaps because of worldly fickleness: now, seeing the signs, people will be frightened; now, becoming more secure, they will give themselves up to pleasures in a mad security, to be overtaken by destruction. Or perhaps only those with sound minds will be frightened by the signs—for the signs are made for their sake—while others merely wonder and yet, blinded by their wicked life, proceed carelessly. Or the unfamiliar, because dreadful, roar of sea and waves, as their end now draws very near—as though they, together with the other elements, were afraid and tottering and were about to be changed in the fire that immediately follows, according to the words, “The elements will be dissolved with heat” (II Pet. III.10)—will make people wither from fear and expectation. Until then they are secure and say, “Peace and security” (I Thess. V.3); but now sudden destruction comes upon them and they wither. [Note: [Col. 0997D] Lombard, IV, dist. 48, §5.] Nor is it surprising that those who flourished in the world should wither in expectation of the strict examination, if the faith that had been green without works should fade. “For the powers of heaven will be shaken”: the angelic powers tremble at the sight of the Judge. [Note: [Col. 0997D] See Augustine, letter 80 to Hesychius, and sermon 130, *On Time*, in the Appendix.] Therefore Job says: “The pillars of heaven tremble and fear at his coming” (Job XXVI.11). If angels tremble, how much more human beings.

## CHAPTER XXIII. When the fire will come, and on resurrection and ascent

[Col. 0997B]

After the signs, however, little or no delay is believed likely before the conflagration. Hence in Matthew, the words immediately following the signs are: “And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven; and then all the tribes of the earth will lament; and they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty” (Matt. XXIV.30). But Luke, after recounting that people will wither and the powers of heaven will be shaken, immediately adds: “And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty” (Luke XXI.27). Hence one may judge that, when the signs are finished, judgment, which will occur in fire, will follow directly. The Lord’s power will bring about this fire, as he says: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath” (Deut. XXXII.22).

[Col. 0997C] In this fire—whether earlier or after a delay—the resurrection will occur through the trumpet. Once it has occurred, whether immediately or after some time, either the saints by themselves or all the saints and penitents together will ascend to the Lord Jesus in the air. Or the Lord may first descend only as they ascend; or he may have descended beforehand, so that the saints may descend together with him, while he waits in the air and they make their way to their bodies through the ministry of angels. A cloud will receive the renewed, as it received Christ. Hence the Apostle: “We shall together be caught up with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air” (I Thess. IV.16). For in clouds those changed will be caught up together by angels and separated from the fellowship of the wicked. Since “wickedness sits upon a talent of lead” (Malach. V.7), [Col. 0997D] the wicked, weighed down by the burden of sins, will remain in the torment of fire. Thus the capacity to ascend by one’s own power neither was lacking to Christ nor will be lacking to the Christian who rises again. Yet angels rejoice in service, and saints in honor. The cloud is employed not as proof of necessity, but of power.

In the very fire in which all will rise and the good ascend, all flesh together will see the salvation of God (Luke III.6). Hence the Apostle: “At the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of his power, in a flame [Col. 0998A] of fire giving vengeance” (II Thess. I.7). For the Lord Jesus will come from heaven with angels, through whose ministry the power of God will appear as they choose the good and cast out the wicked. He who was previously hidden in heaven will come in revelation in a flame of fire—that is, so as to be revealed in a flame of fire. Not, however, so that he himself will be surrounded by fire, because he will be with his own in the upper regions of the air, which the flame will not reach; for it is believed that it will rise only as high as the floodwaters rose. [Note: [Col. 0997D] Augustine, *City of God*, XX, ch. 16.] Rather, being beyond the flames, he will appear to those dwelling in the flames. If the wicked see him—for “they will see him whom they pierced” (John XIX.37)—how much more the good! This fire, as the Apostle testifies, will give vengeance to those who did not know God, that is, did not receive the faith, [Col. 0998B] and to those who do not obey the Gospel, that is, do not carry out what they received. But lest anyone suppose that only those people will be punished there, he adds: “They will pay eternal penalties in destruction from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his power” (II Thess. I.9). For after judgment they will not see the face of the Lord, nor the glory that his power will give to the saints. When the Apostle says that the Lord is to be revealed in a flame of fire, what else does he seem to imply except that he will not at all be seen before the world’s conflagration?

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the words of the Lord following the signs

But whenever he is to be revealed, in what form will he present himself to be seen? Hear the Lord’s words that follow the signs of sun, moon, and stars:

[Col. 0998C] “And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and then all the tribes of the earth will lament, and they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty. And he will send his angels with a trumpet and a great voice, and the elect will be gathered from the four winds” (Matt. XXIV.30).

Certainly, this will be after the signs, though not immediately, because the world seems first destined to be set on fire. “Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven,” that is, in the air: the sign [Note: [Col. 0998D] Augustine, sermon 40, *On the Saints*; sermon 63 to the brothers in the desert; sermon 130, *On Time*, in the Appendix, attributed to Chrysostom, homily *On the Cross and the Thief.*] of the cross, so that they may see him whom they pierced, the banner of the triumphant victory. “And then all the tribes of the earth will lament,” conscience accusing them too late. Nor is it surprising that they will lament, because they will see the Son of Man coming to judge in the clouds of heaven: for “thus he will come as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I.11). He who first appeared humble will come a second time with great power and majesty.

“And he will send”—whether after he has come, or rather before, since otherwise those who rise at the trumpet of the angels sent forth do not seem likely to see the Lord coming in the clouds, but rather to find that he has already come—he will send, I say, his angels with a trumpet and a great voice, so open and so intense that it will be heard everywhere by the dead, which voice the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0998D] See the passages from Augustine above.] calls the trumpet of God and the voice of the archangel. With this voice he will send his angels, or [Col. 0999A] perhaps bring it about through them. Hence [Note: [Col. 0999D] Lombard, IV, dist. 43, §2.] some call it the voice of angels.

What will occur through the ministry of the angels who are to be sent with the trumpet? The elect will be gathered for judgment from the four regions of the world: east, west, north, and south. Hence the Prophet says to the angels: “Gather his saints to him” (Ps. XLIX.5). [Note: [Col. 0999D] Lombard, IV, dist. 47, §4.] The angels’ office in judgment will also be to gather the wicked into hell. Hence the Lord says: “At the consummation of the age the angels will go forth” (Matt. XIII.49). Will they go forth on their own authority, or at the Lord’s command?
