Indeed: “The Son of Man will send his angels.” Why will he send them? “They will gather out of his kingdom all stumbling blocks.” What does this mean? They will separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous. What more? They will cast them into the furnace of fire. What will they suffer? “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” By the weeping of eyes and gnashing of teeth, recognize the reality of the resurrection of bodies. Teeth gnash in those who rejoiced here in gluttony. Eyes weep in those who wandered through lusts. Therefore each person will be punished in the members in which he sinned, so that by whatever part of himself he sinned, he may bear the penalty for that same sin in the same part. Thus it is also clear that there will be no transposition of members in the resurrection. Weeping is usually caused by burning, and gnashing of teeth by cold, because there they “will pass from snowy waters to excessive heat” (Job XXIV.19).

## CHAPTER XXV. Whether the good or the wicked will first be rewarded, according to their merits
[Col. 0999C] Which will come first: the casting down of the wicked into hell, or the admission of the good into heaven? Hear the order: “These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:46). For it is fitting that the judge should first strike his enemies before all, with the authority of all the saints—who, it is agreed, will judge with the Lord—cooperating [Note: [Col. 0999D] Lombard, IV, dist. 47, §2.], with an everlasting blow, and afterwards bring his friends into the palace.

But if the wicked are to go into eternal punishment by Christ’s authority, Origen promises release after many years to wicked human beings and even to the demons in vain [Note: [Col. 0999D] Augustine, *City of God*, XXI, ch. 17.]. Therefore, just as they will be damned without end, so they will be cast into hell before the saints are carried into heaven, the Lord saying: “At harvest time I shall say to the reapers: Gather the weeds first, and bind them [Col. 0999D] into bundles to be burned; but gather the wheat into my barn” (Matt. 13:30). The harvest is the day of judgment, because then good and bad alike will be taken together from our world, as weeds and wheat from a field at harvest. [Note: [Col. 1000D] See Augustine, Sermon 39, *On the Saints*.] For then, at Christ’s command, the angels—whose office will be to separate the wicked from the good and assign each party to its due place—will first gather the weeds and bind them into bundles for burning; not into a single bundle, because each person will be punished according to the measure of his iniquity. [Col. 1000A] But they will gather the wheat into Christ’s barn, that is, into the heavenly dwellings. Clearly, through the ministry of angels, the wicked will first be gathered into hell and the good afterward into heaven, so that the latter may receive diverse dwellings in the Father’s house, while the former receive diverse punishments in hell, just as the bundles differ.

“Then the righteous will shine like the sun” (ibid.), in the splendor of beauty and without decline. There, therefore, the sons of men will be beautiful. Yet the Son of Man is “fairer in form than the sons of men” (Ps. 44:3). The sons of men there will be mighty; the Son of Man, mightier, because he is the Lord.

At the judgment all human beings will be present, and each will receive according to his works. All the angels too will be present, [Col. 1000B] since they are witnesses of human actions, under whose guardianship people have acted well or badly. Thus the Lord says: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then [282] he will sit upon the throne of his majesty, and all nations will be gathered before him; and he will separate them from one another, and set the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left” (Matt. 25:31). He who first came humbly, as one to be judged, will return a second time in majesty, as one who is to judge. And all the angels will be with him as ministers with their judge. Then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty; that is, he will reign over the Church, in which his omnipotence will then appear.

And first, through the ministry of angels, human beings of every race, every age, every condition, and every sex will be gathered [Col. 1000C] before him. This is not, of course, so that they may be seen by him who sees everything, but so that they may see with bodily eyes him whom formerly they had seen either not at all or not with mortal eyes. [Note: [Col. 1000D] See Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, Homily 20; Bede, on Luke III; Augustine, Exposition 1 on Psalm 48 and Sermon 65 *On Various Subjects*.] For it is fitting that all flesh should see the salvation of God, so that those who in the flesh either despise or venerate the Savior may also behold in the flesh his manifest majesty; and may either be distressed that they despised one so great and such as he is, or rejoice that they magnificently venerated one who is great.

It is therefore certain that they will be gathered before him; but from where and to where? Each from that place where his body has been: the sea yielding up its dead, the earth yielding up its own. Everyone worthy of it will surely be gathered to Christ in the air, so that Christ may then at last sit upon the throne [Col. 1000D] of his majesty. But what shall I say about the unworthy? Will their being gathered together mean that all, remaining in their respective places, see the judge at once? But since all the saints are certainly to be gathered through the ministry of angels to that place where Christ will appear in the air, I think nothing more likely than that the wicked also will be assembled in one place, since all nations must be gathered, especially there where they may see Christ set above them with all the saints.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the place of judgment and the separation of those to be judged

[Col. 1001A]

[Note: [Col. 1001D] Lombard, IV, dist. 48, §4.] I do not know at all over what region of the world Christ will choose to appear. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “The kingdom of God does not come with observation; nor will they say, ‘Look, here,’ or ‘Look, there’” (Luke 17:20); that is, neither the time is certain nor the place determined when or where the last judgment is to be conducted. Yet I judge that, because he will undoubtedly come in the same manner as his own saw him go into heaven, that region of the air which the Lord’s Ascension adorned should be honored by the radiance of his coming. Thus he who comes to judge the whole world may occupy a place in the middle of the world, separating them from one another, so that he may set the sheep at his right hand—that is, establish [Col. 1001B] the simple in blessedness—and the goats at his left—that is, the wanton and those foul with depravity—in eternal misery.

For what merit will so great a separation be made? Because the former refreshed Christ, hungry and thirsty in his members; received him as a stranger; clothed him when naked; and visited him in prison (Matt. 25:37). But the latter neglected to do such things. That is, some are saved because they performed works of mercy, while others are damned because they did not concern themselves with such works. But if those perish who did not do good to the needy, what will become of those who unceasingly inflict great evils on their neighbors? Indeed, this account is demanded of those who possess worldly goods: that, in addition to care for their own lives, they should attend to the need of their brethren. But all alike are required, according to their abundance of spiritual resources, [Col. 1001C] to make up one another’s want, in accordance with the saying: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. 6:2).

It is a great thing to assist anyone oppressed bodily in whatever manner; it is far greater to be generous toward spiritual needs. There charity begins; here it is perfected. Therefore one who hungers and thirsts after righteousness must be refreshed with the bread of the word and cooled with the drink of wisdom; one who wanders must be called back into the house of mother Church; “receive one who is weak in faith” (Rom. 14); help one oppressed by some tribulation or by the prison of sorrow, through compassion or consolation. In short, every person must strive by every means, according to what befits his own person, to promote his brethren in whatever he is able. For “to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit [Col. 1001D] for usefulness” (1 Cor. 12:7). For godliness is useful for all things, having the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come (1 Tim. 4:8).

For one who works for the salvation of all thereby abounds here in spiritual goods and in the future in heavenly goods. Indeed, the entire sum of our discipline lies in the mercy of God; one who follows it and yet slips will be beaten. But if anyone has only bodily exercise, he will suffer everlasting punishments. Therefore, following the Apostle’s counsel, “exercise yourself unto godliness. For bodily exercise is useful for a little” (ibid.). For watching, fasting, working, or wearying oneself in other ways—which is bodily exercise—is useful only for this: that a bridle may be imposed upon lust, sin punished, and the future crown increased insofar as this small matter requires. [Col. 1002A]

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the disclosure of good and evil deeds

[Note: [Col. 1001D] Lombard, IV, dist. 43, §4.] On the day of judgment, all good and evil deeds will be made manifest to all, so that all may be judged in the general judgment of all: the saints unto salvation, but the wicked unto perdition. Hence the Lord says: “Nothing is covered that shall not be revealed, and nothing hidden that shall not be known” (Luke 12:2). Therefore, when the Lord judges the secrets of human beings, no wickedness now covered will then not be uncovered, and no righteousness now hidden will then not be known. For the Lord’s judgment permits nothing now concealed to remain concealed in the future.

Must this be understood so universally [Col. 1002B] that nothing whatever concerning creatures will be denied to the saints, to whom knowledge of the Trinity will be given, so that they comprehend both the natures and the events of all things? Certainly, after knowledge of God, I think it very easy, if need be, to have knowledge of every thing. Although in the meantime, even in heaven, while they possess less and know less, they nevertheless hope at last to be fully blessed and also fully instructed.

[Note: [Col. 1002D] Lombard, IV, dist. 43.] It is certain, however, as has been said, that all works, both good and evil, will be disclosed to all. But should the sins of those whose sins are covered by repentance, and the good works of those whose good works are discolored by final wickedness, be passed over in silence at the judgment, as lacking reward? It can rightly seem that the vices of the saints, even though removed by satisfaction, ought to be recalled in memory by themselves—who then seem least of all to be subject to forgetfulness—and understood by others, for whom not mouths but the consciences of all will speak. [Col. 1002C] For in order that the virtue and kindness of the Deliverer may appear to the delivered—and indeed to others—for the praise of God and thanksgiving; in order that it may be clear that the saints conquered their vices and broke the allurements of evil habit, to their own honor and to the accusation of the unworthy, because they did not act similarly: it does not seem incongruous that the faults of the saints should also be known at the judgment. [Note: [Col. 1002D] Against Lombard in the same place, who is criticized for this reason.] Indeed, the good deeds done by the wicked do not seem to be hidden at the judgment either, so that those who fell away, through persistence in their own fault, from the good which they had begun through God’s grace may be without excuse; those who did not advance to further things through the good they undertook, and did not overcome evils.

Having received strength, they yielded to evils. Thus the saints may rejoice that they did not fail as the failing did; and the Lord may be praised, because, while he grants the grace of salvation even to those who are to perish, he plainly shows a man of sound heart that the cause of perdition arises elsewhere, and not from him. Thus the day of judgment will make manifest what is now hidden. Hence the Apostle also says: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also illuminate the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of hearts” (1 Cor. 4:5). For the time of judgment will be the time for judging, when the Lord [Col. 1003A] comes to judge. He will also illuminate the hidden things of darkness: he will illuminate them because then all things will be known to all, and through this they will be able to judge themselves and others; they are “the hidden things of darkness” because then the deeds and thoughts of the wicked will become open. The judge will also reveal the counsels of hearts, that is, the good thoughts of the saints. “And then each will have praise from God.” Then there will be praise for one who thinks or acts well. Here it is not known who is worthy of praise.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How one consciousness will contain the deeds of all

[Note: [Col. 1003D] Lombard, IV, dist. 43, §3.] But since our mind does not perceive many things except slowly and successively, how will the consciousness of one person at the judgment contain the deeds of all? Will that day last so long that all things may come before the mind in succession according to our present manner? Yet innumerable cycles of years would scarcely seem sufficient. But then a thousand years will be as one day; for our mind, then made nothing more difficult, will run through a thousand years no more laboriously than one day, having become capable of all as of one, of many as of few. For our mind must be changed with us in a wonderful manner and made of such great capacity that it will contemplate the divine immensity in one unbroken and perpetual gaze. It will not marvel at all things in such a way that it cannot comprehend each individual thing wholly, simultaneously, and without limit [perhaps: “can”]. And the whole company of saints rightly awaits such breadth of soul in all things. The hearts of the wicked too must be enlarged so far that no one may be ignorant of good or evil. But how much more they must know, that day will not permit to remain unknown.

[Col. 1003C] [Note: [Col. 1003D] Lombard, IV, dist. 48.] Such disclosure of hearts will proceed from the power of the Trinity, which will also repay everyone according to his works. For if the Son is to do this, as indeed he is, and the works, will, and power of the Trinity are undivided, then what belongs to each is common to the Three. [Note: [Col. 1003D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, I, ch. 3; III, *Against Maximinus*, ch. 18; and Tractate 21 on John, after the middle.] Yet “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5:22). The Father does not judge so as to appear in the judgment. For the whole Trinity is to be seen only by hearts that are pure. But he gives judgment to the Son, not because he is his own Son, with whom he possesses all things equally, but because he is the Son of Man. Therefore the Father gives him authority and power to judge and to appear before all alike in judicial majesty: not as God, but as servant; not as the Son of the Father, but of the mother. Yet he is not one person here and another there, but one thing and another thing: for there is one person, but nevertheless one substance and another.

## CHAPTER XXIX. How the good and the wicked will see God

[Note: [Col. 1004D] Lombard, IV, dist. 48, §§1, 2, etc.] But if all will see Christ’s humanity at the judgment, what is to be said of his divinity? “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26:10). [Note: [Col. 1004D] See Augustine, *On the Trinity*, I, ch. 13; Augustine, *Against the Arian Sermon*, ch. 11, and Sermon 13 among the seventeen added at Paris: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the brightness of God.”] Let the wicked see only him whom they pierced. [Col. 1004A] What shall be said of the saints? Those who saw God in heaven—will they not see him when descending to the judgment? The souls of the saints saw him outside their bodies; why, then, when they have resumed their bodies—bodies now glorified—should they not see him?

But you will say: outside heaven there is no place for human beings to see God. Yet angels see God both outside and within heaven; why should human beings not do so too, especially those who by the glory of the resurrection appear already made equal to angels? Perhaps you will say that those who come down from heaven to the judgment will deservedly see the Trinity in the judgment because they had also seen it before while remaining in heaven. But others, though good, will wait, as some say, until Christ, passing from the judgment to heaven, ministers to them. Yet they are already completely [Col. 1004B] purified and adorned with resurrection glory; they will appear in the judgment glorified with the glorified Christ. This was signified by Christ’s glorification, shown for a time to Moses and Elijah in the Transfiguration. Moses, already dead, signifies the dead; Elijah, still alive, signifies the living who will be found at the coming judgment. Both were seen with the Lord in majesty, because those whom they signify are to be seen with the judge in glorification. But if glorification is shared with the others, why is the vision of God not given to them together with the others?

[285] But you will say: the Transfiguration celebrated on the mountain signified rather the glorious union in heaven of Christ and the saints. Let it be so. Yet, I think, you will not deny that all who are to be saved will be seen above with the Lord, just as those who are damned will be seen below. Will not all who will pass with the Lord into heaven be with the Lord [Col. 1004C] in the air? Is it not fitting that they appear in glory, just as the wicked appear in misery? For how can anyone be inglorious while among the glorious with the Lord? Is it not rather: “When Christ, our life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:4)? The apostolic sentence, addressed to the Colossians and through them to all, seems to exclude no one except one destined for perdition who either is not with Christ or is without glory. And when will this be? “When Christ appears.” But when will he appear unless, coming forth from concealment, he presents himself to be seen by all at the judgment? Therefore, how can those who at the judgment share in the glory of the others be deprived of the vision of God which the rest will possess, when Scripture excludes from it only the wicked, saying: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26:10, according to the Septuagint)?

Therefore something common must be asserted. And what more fitting than that those who are to be caught up into the air to meet Christ, once they have come to him, may together with him shine in body and be radiant in mind: possessing flesh visible in the beauty due to it, and spirit illuminated by the vision of God. Bodily eyes, although they are hoped to become far more penetrating than they are, will nevertheless retain their power within bodily things, leaving their proper domain to spirits: so that bodily things alone may be open to bodily eyes, while spiritual things too are made manifest to spiritual eyes. Thus the outward eyes will be great, yet unable to go beyond their limits; the inward eyes greater, since they fully retain their own right and nonetheless possess another’s. Therefore: “All flesh will see the salvation of God” (Luke 3:6). But: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8)—not only in heaven, but earlier at the judgment as well.

That saying seems contrary to this: “And, passing by, he will minister to them” (Luke 12:37), according to the exposition of some who maintain that, after the judgment, Christ the judge will pass from the knowledge of the humanity seen at judgment to the knowledge of divinity, raising his own to it after the judgment. The righteous, they say, will see this future brightness only after the wicked have been removed. Thus, according to them, the passing will be that of one ministering, as though going from one course to the service of another course. Clearly, the first course for the godly will be the great revelation of glorious humanity; the greatest, the manifestation of most glorious divinity. The former will happen at the judgment; the latter, they say, will happen in heaven after the judgment.

Yet, as I think, this is better understood as a passing not of service but of place: when, returning from judgment to the kingdom, he will satisfy the faithful with his brightness, as is also commonly said. The passage, then, will be from the air into heaven; but in passing he will not cease to minister to his own. And with what, if not with the banquet of eternal blessedness? Therefore, at the judgment and afterwards, let only the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God (Isa. 26:10, according to the Septuagint).

Perhaps in passing he will minister to his own by giving different things to different persons, that is, to each according to his works. There is indeed one [Col. 1005C] house of the Father; but “in my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” (John 14:12), because the vision of God is one for all, yet is increased and varied for individuals according to the increase of their merits.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the twofold order of the saved and the damned

[Note: [Col. 1005D] Lombard, IV, dist. 47, §3. See Augustine on Psalms 49, 86, and 121, and *City of God*, XX, ch. 5; Gregory, *Morals*, XXVI, ch. 20; Bede, Homily on St. Benedict.] Both among the saved and among the damned there will be a twofold order. For among the children of Gehenna, some are those of whom it is already said: “He who does not believe is already judged” (John 3:18). Others are those whose judgment is deferred until the end, of whom it will be said: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). Clearly, some are already foreknown for perdition; others will indeed perish, but this remains unknown until the examination. [Col. 1005D] For what is for the present partly hidden will at last plainly remain hidden in no respect.

Among the saints too, the salvation of some is already known, while that of others is unknown until the end. For we already know the salvation of those professors of the Christian faith who left everything for Christ. Hence the Lord says to those who followed him and left everything: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon thrones, judging,” and so forth (Matt. 19:28). That is, when those who are generated here for mortality are regenerated for immortality; when the form of a servant, which was judged, exercises judicial power, [Col. 1006A] then those who followed Christ after leaving all things will be judges with him. [Note: [Col. 1006D] Augustine, as above.] By the twelve thrones is understood the totality of those judging; by the twelve tribes, the totality of those being judged.

But those who possess worldly property and appear to use it rightly will be saved, though their salvation is at present hidden. Therefore, we know the salvation of those who left everything for Christ, but do not know that of those who retained their possessions. Yet we understand the salvation of the former not always, but more often; that of the latter sometimes, but more rarely. Thus more of the latter—but not all—and fewer of the former—though many—are destined for perdition. Hence the Prophet says: “A thousand will fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.” [Note: [Col. 1006D] Augustine, as above, on Psalm 90 at this verse.] At God’s side, as though belonging to his household, seem to belong [Col. 1006B] those who, leaving everything, have devoted themselves to divine service; at his right hand, those somewhat less intimate with his household, who possess lawful things and appear to use them rightly. Yet a thousand of these will fall, and ten thousand of those, because many from the former and more from the latter will fail.

So perhaps the number of those who possess worldly goods will be far greater, since salvation is due to far more among them than among those who leave everything, because the latter are much fewer. Yet among the fewer the judgment concerning salvation is more certain; among the greater number it is more uncertain, because the former customarily bind themselves more closely to God, [Note: [Col. 1006D] Note the excellence of monastic vows.] while the latter do so less. Therefore, among those who act rightly, one who leaves everything is in his own way already judged—that is, for salvation; one who retains his possessions is not yet judged, because [Col. 1006C] what can be known about the former in this life on account of his elevated way of life is unknown about the latter because of the multiplicity of worldly concerns. Thus it is said that those who leave everything and follow the Lord will be judges with the Lord; but those who possess lawful things and use them rightly will be judged. To the former he promises that they will judge with the Lord, because they left everything for him. To the latter, that they will receive the kingdom, because they devoted works of mercy according to their resources.

Each party, then, is great; but the first is greater. The first, which is to judge, is already known; the second, which is to be judged and examined to determine whether it belongs to salvation, is awaited. Therefore the Lord said in the present to those who had left everything for him that they would judge with him. But he promised that on the day [Col. 1006D] of judgment he would say to others: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat,” etc. (Matt. 25:35). It is therefore certain that those to whom he said they would judge with him will judge with him; concerning the others it is unknown until “Come, blessed” is heard. Thus, as stated, there is a twofold order of all human beings: one already judged, the other yet to be judged.

But if among the saints some will judge and some will be judged, why does Scripture, by divine intimation, seem to make the final judgment common to all saints? For it says: “The saints will judge [Col. 1007A] nations” (Wis. 3:8). And again: “The righteous will rule over them in the morning” (Ps. 48:15). For saints insofar as they are righteous will judge, indeed so completely that they will rule over those whom they judge—namely, those who remain nations, that is, as they were born, or indeed very often worse. When, then, will they judge? “In the morning,” that is, when the night of this ignorant and guilty age is ended. [Note: [Col. 1007D] Augustine, in the same place: “Morning will appear, that is, when the uncertainties of this age have passed.”] Scripture excludes none of the saints; who, then, will exclude them? Especially since the Prophet speaks here generally of judgment: “This glory is for all his saints” (Ps. 149:9). If all the saints will judge, how will some—even the greater part—be judged? [Note: [Col. 1007D] Lombard, IV, dist. 47, §2. See Richard of St. Victor, Pullus’s contemporary, *On Judicial Power*.] Will they judge and be judged? Certainly, but in different respects. For they will judge the nations by the authority of dominion; nevertheless, [Col. 1007B] they will be judged because they will then be known to belong to the order of judgment [or “of the judgment”].

Unless perhaps it is fitting that certain companions of the heavenly court, surpassing others by the merit of their prerogative, should be specially designated by the name of saints and righteous; and that these, rather than the rest, should be called judges with the Lord. [Note: [Col. 1007D] Thus Lombard, IV, dist. 47, §3, near the end.] This seems more consistent with the Gospel authority cited above.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the judgment of the Lord and of the saints

But whether all, or the greater saints, will judge the world, what does it mean for them themselves to judge the world? In human practice, judges are those whose office is either to pronounce the judicial sentence or, by the hands of ministers, inflict punishment upon the person against whom it has been pronounced. The Lord too will pronounce the eternal sentence, saying to some: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41); and to others: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (ibid.). This is not because a spoken utterance is needed, [Note: [Col. 1008D] Lombard, IV, dist. 47, §1.] but because it will happen by the judge’s authority. It will occur by the Lord’s command and through the ministry of angels. Therefore the Lord is rightly called judge, since he both pronounces the sentence of judgment and, through ministers, inflicts punishment or reward.

The saints will be judges with the Lord—indeed, under the Lord. “Two-edged swords are in their hands” (Ps. 149:6), because, receiving the power of the word of God, they will judge with the Lord “to execute vengeance among the nations, rebukes among the peoples” (ibid.). “Rebukes,” [Col. 1007D] so that each may rebuke the wicked with the Lord, saying: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). “Vengeance,” so that the poor who were mocked may take vengeance upon the proud, to the point that “the righteous will rule over them in the morning” (Ps. 48:15): “to bind their kings with fetters and their nobles with iron manacles” (Ps. 149:8). For, bound hand and foot, they will be cast into outer darkness (Matt. 22:8). Thus the saints, in the manner of judges, will both pronounce the judicial sentence with the chief judge [Col. 1008A] and inflict punishment through the ministry of angels. They are rightly called judges because, in virtue of their office, they alone will give the capital sentence, which others also will know; and because they will in a manner bind the feet and hands even of kings and nobles, and likewise in a manner cast them into outer darkness. For by the authority of their decree, those who are to lose the former use of their feet and hands—indeed of all their members—will be cast by angels into outer darkness.

But it should be observed that the Lord will judge both the good and the wicked, as one who will come to judge the living and the dead; that is, to render to each party according to its work. The saints, however, will exercise their judgment only upon the wicked, according to the Scriptures—namely, “the judgment written” [Note: [Col. 1008D] Augustine, on this passage of Psalm 149.]—that is, the judgment treated in many [Col. 1008B] Scriptures. Hence the Apostle says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6:3). Lest anyone attribute this judgment to the apostles alone, the Prophet adds: “This glory is for all his saints” (Ps. 149:9).

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the state of the wretched and the blessed after judgment

[Note: [Col. 1008D] Lombard, IV, final distinction, §§5 and 7.] After the judgment, the wicked will remain in punishment without end, just as the good will remain in blessed delight. The state of hell cannot remain hidden from the penetrating sight of the saints, so that from the wretched it may be learned how well things have gone for the saints. The wretched too will know the glory of the saints, though they will not see it: sight failing, so that they do not see the good things; awareness remaining, so that they grieve over what they do not possess. Each party will fully know its own [Col. 1008C] state, so that nothing may be lacking to one for joy or to the other for sorrow.

No mortal intellect can fully set forth the evils of the former and the goods of the latter, since those things exceed our understanding beyond measure—indeed beyond our capacity of sense—whether good or evil. Yet in Gehenna there will be heat and cold for the wretched: both excessive, both infinite. There will be envy, pride, and every other defilement of the inner person that preceded upon earth. For as each person is found at the end of his life, so he will remain after life: the tree will lie where it falls. Hence the condemned hear the Lord say: “You who work iniquity” (Matt. 7:23).

[Col. 1008D] [Note: [Col. 1008D] Lombard, IV, dist. 50, §1.] For in hell the evils produced here by the exercise of works are continually enacted in the mind. When one descends to hell, the disposition of a badly ordered mind becomes worse, just as the disposition of a well-ordered mind among us is improved in heaven. For in hell each must become as much worse as he becomes more wretched, just as, conversely, in heaven each becomes as much better as he becomes more blessed. The works which the disposition of the mind here brings forth through bodily instruments, whether good or evil, will not exist there. [Note: [Col. 1008D] Lombard, IV, dist. 49, §5.] Will the good, then, be less good in heaven [Col. 1009A] because they will possess goodness without works of goodness? Or the wicked less wicked in Gehenna because they will possess wickedness without works of wickedness?

Good works, because they are laborious, will not exist in heaven, lest anything diminish happiness, and because there is no need for merit to increase there. Likewise evil works, because they are pleasurable to the wicked, will not exist in hell, lest misery be lessened in any respect. Yet the disposition of the mind—that is, the wickedness or goodness of the heart—since it seems then to be brought to completion, seems no less vigorous than if it issued in action; for a perfect will to act is reckoned as a completed deed. Likewise, God is so good in himself that he cannot become better through action; and all beings in the future seem destined to be so complete in their state that no increase appears possible by adding action.

But now, through the merit of good or evil works, inward goodness or wickedness grows and is strengthened. For the disposition of the mind produces works from itself, and through them either raises a person to the highest point or plunges him into the depths of vices. Hence those devoted to vices and virtues continually become greater and firmer, each in his own purpose. To express this fact, the Lord Jesus—for whom nothing is difficult—after raising the first dead person, raised the rest with certain general powers; he, unlike other human beings, while still mortal shone forth with such goodness, because he was also God, that although he acted well unceasingly, nothing was added to his goodness. [Col. 1010A]

The wicked in hell, tortured by the opposition of snow and fires, because “their time will be for ages” (Ps. 80:16), will hope for no remedy at all. The good, whose times hasten unceasingly to be present (Deut. 32:35), like those whose participation will be “in the same thing” (Ps. 121:3), will fear no fall. Among them, “one thing and another” will find no place, because they will endure “in the same thing”: no one among them will think doubtfully of having been or of being to come, but will marvel only at being; because there nothing will pass away and nothing will be future. For what is there must always be so. But in hell let a variety of times be understood, where the changing misery of torments will endure. [Col. 1010B]

[Col. 1009]

**Observations of Dom Hugh Mathoud, Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint Maur, on the Books of Sentences of Robert Pullus**

**On Book I**

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 1009C]

“Adam,” according to Augustine’s witness, “every thing begets what it itself is: a horse a horse, a human being a human being, God God.” Pullus alludes to this passage of Augustine, volume X, *Sermons of the Lord’s Words in the Gospel of John*, Sermon 51, where he proves that those who deny the consubstantiality of the Son inflict an injury upon the eternal Father. “If, therefore, the Son is of a different substance from the Father, the Father begets a monster. For when a creature—that is, a woman—gives birth to what is not human, it is called a monster. But in order that it may not be a monster, what is born is what the one who begot it is: human and human, horse and horse, dove and dove, sparrow and sparrow.”

Epiphanius says likewise, *Heresy* 76, no. 6: “He has wholly begotten a Son; it cannot be that he is not equal and similar to the Father. For whatever begets, begets something similar to itself—not merely similar, but so equal that it is the same. For a human being begets a human being; God, God.” Augustine again presents similar statements in Homily 43 among the fifty. See further Book II *Against Maximinus*, ch. 6; Cyril, Book X of the *Treasury*, and Book II on John. [Col. 1009D]

“And in the Trinity we confess not only the names, but also the properties of the names.” The author indicates [Col. 1010C] that explanation of the Creed which has hitherto circulated among the works of St. Jerome under the title *Explanation of the Creed to Damasus*, and which Marius Victorinus rightly relegated to the corner among Jerome’s spurious works. In it, moreover, the following occurs in accordance with the author’s meaning [292]: “For we confess not only the names, but also the properties of the names—that is, the persons; or, as the Greeks express it, the hypostases, that is, the subsistences.”

Yet that it was neither written by Jerome nor sent to Damasus is sufficiently evident from the fact that Augustine openly attributes it to the heretic Pelagius, writing not to Damasus but to Pope Innocent. Thus, in chapter 30 of *On the Grace of Christ*: “Pelagius recently sent to Rome both letters and a booklet setting out his faith, writing to Pope Innocent of blessed memory, whom he did not know to be dead.” In chapter 32 and following he cites certain passages from this booklet of Pelagius which occur word for word in that *Explanation*. Nevertheless, I should think that Pullus, misled by the public error of his age, believed [Col. 1010D] this paraphrase of the faith to be an unquestionable offspring of Jerome, to whom it is found ascribed even before the age of Charlemagne, as is clear from those books *On Images* attributed to the said Charles. We also read it inscribed with Augustine’s [Col. 1011A] name in William of Paris, *On Sins and Vices*, chapter 10. Yet even if Pullus knew it to have been written by Pelagius, he would no less have cited it as authoritative, since it is certain that it was approved by Pope Zosimus, as the latter himself attests in his fourth letter to the Africans; see Baronius’s *Annals*. But it is certain that the author had Jerome in view. Our contemporary, the Master, was no sharper-sighted, in I, distinction 25, § M, attributing both these very words and the entire explanation to Jerome, as did many others, including St Thomas, *Supplement*, question 13, article 1, and elsewhere; and before him our Peter of Poitiers, chapter 4 of the first part or distinction, who also expressly cites Jerome. But who would not wonder that the Conimbricenses, II, *On the Soul*, question 3, article 2, and not a few modern writers should have been blind in this matter? The reader should note that, through a printer’s fault, the text of this explanation of the Creed quoted above from the author is mutilated.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 1011B]

“For thus authority cries out.” What authority he intends to indicate is not easy to conjecture. We think he had in view the common teaching of the Fathers of the Church proclaiming divine simplicity: Hilary, VIII, *On the Trinity*; Athanasius, *Letter to the Bishops of Africa*; Basil, letters 80 and 141 to his Caesareans; Gregory of Nyssa, *To Ablabius*, at the end; Marius Victorinus, I *Against the Arians*; Cyril of Alexandria, I *Treasury*, chapter 8, and XI, chapter 1; Leo, letter to Turibius, chapter 1 and especially chapter 5; Gregory, XVI *Morals*, chapters 20 and 21; and so forth. But above all, Dionysius, chapter 1 of *On the Divine Names*, and Augustine, V *On the Trinity*, chapter 11, seem especially to have illuminated the author’s way:

> Just as the Trinity is called one God, great, good, eternal, almighty, and selfsame, so its Deity may be called its very self, its greatness its very self, its goodness its very self;

and VI, chapters 4–7:

> This is what it is for God to be: to be strong, or just, or wise, and whatever one may say concerning that simple multiplicity or multiple simplicity.

## CHAPTER VI

The present chapter seems to involve three principal difficulties.

1. That the Father and the Son are two principles of the Holy Spirit.
2. That each receives the character of principle from being a person, not from being one God; or, if one prefers to hear the author’s own words, because this character of principle belongs to distinction, there are two in it rather than one; so that the Father and Son are not one principle but two; and likewise the proceeding Son and Holy Spirit are two.
3. That the Father in relation to the Son, and the Son in relation to the Holy Spirit, are likewise two principles in an equal respect and manner.

This analysis of the difficulties of the chapter was also recognized by the most celebrated Dom de Sainte-Beuve, royal professor of the most eminent house, renowned for learning and virtue. Rightly consulted by me, he reconciled my mind—long perplexed about the diagnosis of this chapter—with both truth and Pullus, in 293 letters, written to me [Col. 1011D] with the utmost kindness.

First, as regards the first difficulty: it is not of the greatest importance if one uncovers the hidden ambiguity of the word *principle*. For if that word is taken adjectivally—which the following passages show Pullus to have done—then no one can rightly deny that the Father and Son may be called two principles of the Holy Spirit no less than two spirators; and the school accepts the latter expression. As Robert of Melun observes, names of this kind are predicated singularly of the individual persons and perhaps plurally of the whole, whether they are taken with the force of nouns or participles; but it is otherwise if the word is uttered substantively. We need not labor to prove that the author uses it here in the former manner. For this statement most clearly indicates that the spirative power is the same in Father and Son, and that they produce the Holy Spirit in one undifferentiated manner:

> The Father and Son, each in one and the same manner, appear to be a principle of the Holy Spirit, just as the Spirit himself appears to proceed indifferently from each.

Once this foundation of friendly truth is established, no difficulty need remain except one of words. Nor should one hesitate to concede to the author that the Father and Son are two principles of the Holy Spirit, or two spirating supposita, provided he admits that the formal character of spirating is the same. Yet he would not judge it one unless he took *principle* adjectivally. For the most generally accepted rule among dialecticians is: “Numerical names added to substantives multiply not only supposita but also forms.”

Indeed, the author’s chief purpose in this difficulty is to prove that two supposita, the Father and the Son, are necessarily required for the production of the Holy Spirit, because he proceeds as the love and bond of both. Although their spirative power is the same, it nevertheless presupposes persons really distinct from one another, and Fatherhood and Sonship themselves as conditions necessary for this production. Moved by this consideration, St Thomas had formerly said in I, distinction 2, that the Father and Son are two spirators. Certain scholastic theologians subscribed to this view, such as Gabriel and Ockham, who hold that one and several principles of the Holy Spirit may there be asserted in different respects. So too Durandus, I, distinction 29, question 2:

> If the name *principle* is understood as that which acts, then the Father is one principle; but the Father and Son are two principles.

Accordingly, some theologians writing after the Councils of Lyons and Florence note that the Fathers did not say that the Holy Spirit proceeds “from one principle,” but “as from one.” This is a diminishing particle, and does not allow the proposition to extend further than the Council’s meaning. For when the Greeks contended that, if the Holy Spirit proceeded from the Son, he would proceed from two formally distinct principles, it was sufficient to answer that he is produced not from two, but as from one: that is, not indeed to deny two principles, but to deny a twofold power of spirating. Pullus adopts this way of explaining the matter, though he preceded that council, and illustrates it strikingly with the example of twins.

But why, you will ask, did he alone depart from the path and, rejecting the unity of principle which everyone asserts seriously, seek duality so anxiously and defend it so vigorously? Here is our conjecture. First—and this is certainly the chief point—because our most Christian doctor lived many years before the definitions of the Fathers at the Council of Lyons under Gregory X and at Florence under Eugenius IV, he could not be guided along this royal road, from which one now turns neither to right nor left. He would surely have willingly obeyed these determinations of the Fathers, more readily than many theologians later than the said councils, had it fallen to his lot, as to them, to write after their time. Here one should note Facundus’s rule, book V: “The manner and order of inquiry after the definition of a council confirmed by the consent of the whole Church ought not to be the same as it was before the definition.” Those who, through an excessively premature zeal for truth, wrongly and ignorantly accuse of error and rashness whatever singularity they suspect in the writings of the ancients, or whatever does not agree so closely with the tenets of the more recent school, depart from this rule. Yet learned persons everywhere proclaim that even the blemishes of those ancients ought not to be despised.

Second, if one removes the question arising from the name, Pullus has nothing at all discordant with the common opinion, as the other Robert of Melun rightly judges.

Third, he was not alone in dancing outside the chorus. Nearly six hundred years earlier, Rusticus, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, in his disputation against the Acephali, found in volume IV of the *Library of the Fathers*, confesses that he does not sufficiently see whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son in the same way as from the Father; and he says that some taught the contrary. Not to mention not a few moderns, concerning whom we shall shortly see.

[Col. 1013A] Finally, while the exceedingly difficult question between Latins and Greeks concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit—whether he proceeded from the Son—was scarcely yet settled, this Latin writer judged it more advantageous for the interests of faith, while preserving the unity of the formal principle, or active spiration, to defend against the Greeks the claim that not the Father alone but also the Son is a principle of the Holy Spirit. To show this more easily, he says that the notion of principle arises not from the fontal bosom of the divine nature but from the very distinction of persons, in the manner discussed above: namely, insofar as the Spirit himself proceeds as the notional love of both. Thus, since by the force of his procession and property he bears a relative relation to the Father and Son, he of himself requires both persons for his production. Augustine indicates this in VI *On the Trinity*, chapter 5.

This is the second rock of this chapter, and as it were the diaphragm of the difficulty: namely, that the Father and Son derive this character of principle from the force of their personal distinction. But here too Facundus’s other rule must be recalled, *In Defence of the Three Chapters*, IX, chapter 5: “It is customary for Catholic prudence and piety, from things indubitable and evident, both to confirm what is ambiguous and to make manifest what is hidden.” For, if the truth of the preceding assertion stands—that our author writes that the Father and Son produce the Holy Spirit in one and the same undifferentiated manner—then all else must be directed by this rule. Thus, when he argues in the present chapter 6:

> Persons ought to be one in everything that they receive from the nature of divinity, and not one in that which they take from the nature of distinction;

and again:

> Why should not two persons, even though one personal property is conceded to belong to them, be two rather than one in it, because it belongs to distinction? Thus the Father and Son are not one principle but two; likewise the proceeding Son and Holy Spirit are two;

and other similar statements, it is entirely certain that the unity of the formal principle is not undermined—for he repeatedly asserts that the power of spirating, which he calls a personal property, is one—but that only the plurality of the principle *which*, that is, of the supposita, is asserted. And it is clear that the distinction of persons follows from this. Likewise, when at the end of the chapter he continually maintains that the Father and Son stand differently in the nature of principle, he either speaks of the nature of principle as it is in the Father for generating the Son and in the Son for producing the Holy Spirit; or as it is in each for spirating the Holy Spirit. We reserve the former statement for the third part of this explanation. As to the latter, we judge it entirely free from blemish, briefly as follows.

It is certain that active spiration, although the same in Father and Son, connotes something in the Father which it does not connote in the Son, and conversely. Moreover, theologians agree that the production of the Holy Spirit requires both the suppositum of the Father and that of the Son. The only question they debate is whether this is required merely concomitantly or also formally and per se. Nor do they deny that something may formally and per se proceed from several supposita either solely on the side of the term, or solely on the side of the productive power, or on the side of both term and productive power together. In either case they concede that active spiration connotes certain things in the Father which it does not in the Son, and conversely.

In the first way, since it is certain that the Holy Spirit proceeds as the third person, he presupposes the other two as already distinct and prior by origin. Thus he proceeds through the spirative power, insofar as it connotes in the Father the character of the first person and in the Son the character of the second. Further, he proceeds through a power not communicated to the Father and communicated to the Son through generation. These two points suffice in Pullus’s teaching for him to say that the Father and Son stand differently in the nature of principle.

In the second way the matter is still clearer. For the Holy Spirit formally and per se proceeds from the mutual love of the Father and Son; but this mutuality does not exist through different acts. Therefore it arises from a different connotation of the active power in the supposita. From this it follows that the Father and Son stand differently in the nature of principle, not through diversity of the formal principle and productive power, but through diversity of the remote and connoted principle. This interpretation of Pullus’s mind is recommended by the familiar manner of speaking of the Fathers, especially the Greeks, when they say that the Father produces the Holy Spirit through the Son: that in such a production the Father participates more principally, or more immediately, than the Son, and other expressions of nearly the same pattern. Augustine expressed the same in XV *On the Trinity*, chapter 17:

> Not without reason in this Trinity is no one called the Word of God except the Son; no one the Gift of God except the Holy Spirit; and no one except God the Father is he from whom the Word is begotten and from whom the Holy Spirit principally proceeds. I added “principally” because the Holy Spirit is also found to proceed from the Son. Yet the Father gave this also to the Son, not when he already existed and did not yet possess it; rather, whatever he gave to the only-begotten Word, he gave by begetting him.

Nor do Bonaventure, Scotus, and Durandus—I, distinction 11, question 2—Gabriel, question 3, and Marsilius, question 15, article 2, hesitate to say that the Holy Spirit proceeds more principally from the Father. But this comparative expression should be avoided.

Yet, if I correctly grasp the author’s rather difficult mind, as is his custom, when he admits that the Father and Son stand differently in the nature of principle, and from this thinks he can infer that there are no less two principles in divinity than two proceeding persons—the point toward which the supposition that concludes the chapter tends—he seems to return to the former state of the question indicated above: namely, to employ that notion of principle by which the Father is related to the Son and the Son to the Holy Spirit. This is the third knot of the chapter, likewise to be untied by us briefly.

That this outlined sense of *principle* is especially pressed by the author is shown, among other things, by what he proposes about the middle of the chapter:

> It is clear that the Father is not a principle because he is God; for the Holy Spirit too is God, yet is not a principle. Therefore, whatever is a principle is so by some distinction of person. But in order that there be distinction—since in it there is no community—the Father is a principle differently from the Son. For the Father is a principle both of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; but the Son, of the Holy Spirit alone. Yet the Father is a principle of the Son differently from his being a principle of the Holy Spirit: of the Son, as begotten from himself; of the Holy Spirit, as proceeding from himself. But the Father and Son each appear to be a principle of the Holy Spirit in one and the same manner,

and so forth. By these words, as also by those quoted above from the latter part of the chapter, he very plainly shows that he is considering the aforesaid notion of principle.

Each of these statements may certainly be advanced by the author without any prejudice to truth.

First—and this is easier—they may be explained concerning the character of principle as *which*, or as taken connotatively. The following words, written shortly before, serve this interpretation well:

> Thus too, if it be granted that the Father and Son are each a principle in only one manner, they must nevertheless by no means be denied to differ from one another in person; and they may thus be called two principles, just as among us certain principles are diverse and separate from one another, although they differ from one another yet do not produce differently.

For although Fatherhood in the Father and active spiration in the Son are not really distinct from one another, it is nevertheless certain that the character of principle follows the person, not the nature, as Pullus shows; otherwise the Holy Spirit himself would also be a principle *ad intra*, or would not possess everything that the divine essence requires in the direct sense. And in this sense the Father and Son stand differently in the nature of principle: the former, as principle of the Son begotten from himself; the latter, as principle of the Holy Spirit proceeding from himself.

Furthermore, no one will deny that Fatherhood and active spiration as it is in the Son are at least distinct in reason. This virtual distinction, joined with the plurality of supposita, provides a sufficient foundation for saying that the Father as Father and the Son as spirator are two principles. This is enough for Robert’s meaning: that one stands differently here, the other there, in the nature of principle. For theologians admit—and this is surely the most immediate antidote to this chapter’s difficulty—that when the Father and Son are called two principles, if *principle* is taken as formally denominated from relation, such a proposition can be sustained no less than when they are said to be two related things.

Finally, even if these supports of reasoning accomplish nothing at all with an obstinate mind, the author ought no more to be accused of error than Durandus and Scotus. The former judges active spiration to be really distinct from Fatherhood in the Father and from Sonship in the Son; the latter judges that the Holy Spirit would be other than the Son even if he did not proceed from him, because, he says, being begotten and being spirated are really distinct. Robert, however, has asserted neither of these things anywhere. But enough—indeed more than enough—on this subject.

“Unless perhaps he says [the Son is principle] not of himself but of creatures; but [Col. 1015B] by the same reasoning the Holy Spirit is principle from a principle.” If the reasoning is valid, the expression is not customary. This is a genuine Pullian phrase, and let its meaning be this: in divinity the Son is an *ad intra* principle from a principle of himself, but not a principle of creatures and *ad extra* from a principle of himself. Otherwise the Holy Spirit in the same sense would be a principle from a principle, because he too is a principle of creatures and *ad extra* from a principle of himself *ad intra*. Yet our Robert warns that calling the Holy Spirit “principle from a principle” is contrary to usage.

An excellent discussion of this subject is supplied by the other Robert, namely Robert of Melun, our contemporary and also a survivor. Robert of Torigny writes in the Appendix to Sigebert, under the year 1163, that he was then already advanced in age when raised to the episcopate of Hereford in his native England. This author wrote a *Summa of Theology*, subtle indeed and, if one considers the question it discusses concerning medicinal grace, most desirable, especially in the present age; but it is not so rich in varied learning as the work which Pullus had composed a few years earlier. After these scholia had already been completed, we happened to obtain a hitherto unpublished manuscript of his from the Victorine library. Since we thought the teaching of an author contemporary with Pullus would benefit our observations on Pullus, we extracted a few passages from it, so that the following chapter might serve the present inquiry.

### Should it be said: “The Holy Spirit is principle from a principle”?

*(From Robert of Melun.)*

> Therefore we must discuss this distinction of the three persons more carefully and set forth concerning it those things which the Catholic faith holds, the holy Church celebrates, and the authority of the Fathers confirms. For here we do not promise that doctrine of the distinction of the three persons which is known as it will be known in the future; but that doctrine which may more properly be called faith, and is strengthened by the firmness of true faith. For one kind of knowledge is that which is prior to faith; another is the knowledge which belongs to faith. The former is possessed concerning the Trinity itself without creatures and apart from faith; the latter is possessed in the present state with creatures and with faith. Thus the Father, as Scripture says, is principle not from a principle; but the Son is principle from a principle. Scripture does not say whether the Holy Spirit is principle from a principle, or not from a principle, or from principles. Yet it does not leave unspoken that he is one and the same principle with the Father and Son. But if to be principle from a principle means to be from the Father and to be the same principle as the Father, how shall we deny that the Holy Spirit is principle from a principle, since he has his being from the Father and is the same principle as the Father? Nor can we deny this merely because we do not find Scripture asserting it; for it does not deny everything that it does not assert. Yet in matters pertaining to the distinction of the Trinity, we should say nothing unless we find it said, or can prove it from what has already been said. Hence we especially see that, although there may be a reason why some things seem capable of being said, they ought nevertheless to remain unspoken because no customary usage of saying them is found. Therefore, even if this expression has a reason why it might seem able to be said, it should not be said because it lacks customary usage. We can, however, say that the Holy Spirit is not principle from a principle—that is, that he is not the Son. For the phrase “principle from a principle” designates the person of the Son, just as “principle not from a principle” designates the person of the Father. For to be principle from a principle is the same as to be from the Father through generation, which belongs to the Son alone. Therefore, just as no customary usage is found for calling the Holy Spirit principle from a principle, so the reason for saying it altogether resists such language, because he does not receive being from the Father alone as the Son does.

These are Robert of Melun’s words in accordance with the thought of our chancellor.

[Col. 1016B] “But if the Son is from the Father in one way and the Spirit from both in another way,” and so forth. One might say that by these words Pullus sketches the opinion later held by Scotus, in order to prove that the Son ought rather to be called the second than the third person of the Trinity. Leaving aside that difficulty here, we make only this observation: nothing unfortunate should be inferred from the particle of doubt, *perhaps*, which Pullus inserts throughout this work more frequently than usual. He uses it habitually even in matters which he believes most certainly and with divine faith. Besides the passage cited from this chapter, see chapter 9 of part II, column 2, line 53: “Perhaps to someone it may seem that the soul comes to be in bodies”; chapter 52 of part VI, p. 211, column 1, line 2: “But perhaps—indeed certainly—charity brings it about that sins are not unto eternal punishment,” and so forth; chapter 1 of part VII: “Do those things which are committed venially—perhaps those and not others—obtain pardon after death?” There are many other passages. This is commonly used by theologians merely for the sake of disputation; and it is enough that he did not intend it otherwise even once.

## CHAPTER X

“If the soul is the queen of the human mechanism,” and so forth. From the author’s phrasing and manner, we probably conjecture that Aristotle is here tacitly attacked because of what he writes in chapter 7 of *On the Motion of Animals*:

> We must judge an animal to be so constituted as a city well furnished and regulated by laws. For in such a city, once the plan of administration has been established, there is no need for the ruler, being absent, to concern himself with each individual thing that occurs. Rather, each performs his own office as commanded, and one thing after another is administered and ordered by custom. But in living beings nature itself brings this about: each member is so constituted as to be properly disposed for carrying out its own functions. Therefore there is no need for the soul to be present in each individual member; rather, while it abides in a particular principle, the remaining members live and perform their functions because they are joined to it.

These statements strongly support the opinion of certain ancient philosophers against which Pullus shortly rises.

“Will it be said that the soul has some immovable little part in the whole?” For some placed the soul, as a watchwoman in a lookout-post, at the summit, as Xenocrates did; others in the brain, as Hippocrates did; Herophilus in the cavity of the brain, or around its base, as Tertullian notes; Strato and Erasistratus in the membranes. They were especially led by the consideration that only in the head, as in a citadel, do the internal and external senses keep watch, acting as the soul’s messengers and attendants in things to be done. Philo the Jew, in the book entitled *That the Worse Is Wont to Plot against the Better*, located it in the heart, following the Stoics. Parmenides and Epicurus placed it in the entire breast; why not also beneath the omentum, lest it grow thin—something that the latter feared so anxiously? I should think that some others also placed it [Col. 1017A] in the mouth; our Robert wittily warns them seriously to beware, for religion’s sake, lest they shake it out with their spittle. Whoever wants more should hasten to our sources: Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 15; Lactantius, *On the Workmanship [of God]*, chapter 16; Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Making of Man*, chapter 12; Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*; and so forth. In any event, throughout this chapter and in certain others of this work, the author’s disposition should be excused, since he occasionally indulges obscurity more than is proper.

## CHAPTER XI

“As he foreknows, so he forewills what he is going to do.” These words troubled some people, who thought that from them above all else it could be inferred that God predestines even the wicked to punishment. But there is nothing here different from Augustine, who in many passages, especially those published in his old age, consistently taught the doctrine of a twofold predestination. Remigius and the Church of Lyons therefore taught it in the book *On Three Letters*; Lupus Servatus, in his book *On Three Questions Controverted in His Time*—the second of which concerns twofold predestination—and another writer of Ferrières, in his collection *On Three Questions*, where he gathered on this matter various teachings of the saints, especially Augustine, Jerome, Gregory, Fulgentius, Isidore, and the Venerable Bede. So too the Council of Langres, chapter 3, and the Council of Valence, chapter 4:

> We confidently confess the predestination of the elect to life and the predestination of the ungodly to death. Yet in the election of those to be saved, God’s mercy precedes good merit; whereas in the condemnation of those who perish, evil merit precedes God’s just judgment.

To all these add the monk Ratramnus of Corbie, in the two books on predestination which he composed by order of King Charles the Bald.

Moreover, Pullus’s doctrine in sense and almost in wording accords with the third of the seven rules concerning predestination delivered by the Church of Lyons through Remigius.

[Col. 1017C]

> Certainly, just as he destined heaven for the devout and hell for the ungodly, so he would have done the reverse, had it not been that “he has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills.”

This is a striking statement, certainly worthy of notice by all who, serving both truth and Augustine, affirm the predestination of the good before foreseen merits. Nor could this Catholic doctor, ever devoted to Augustine’s teaching, have taught anything else than the faith of his age. His contemporary and countryman Robert of Melun judged that doctrine to be so religiously binding that he denied the contrary teaching could be defended without suspicion of heresy—though this was perhaps put somewhat harshly.

The Apostle’s saying (Romans 9:18), cited by the author—“He has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills”—must be understood in accordance with Augustine, Letter 105: “For the whole mass was deservedly condemned through sin; and he does not harden by imparting wickedness, but by not imparting mercy.” And in I *To Simplicianus*, question 2: “Therefore, ‘He has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills,’ can accord with the preceding statement in such a way that God’s hardening is his unwillingness to show mercy, so that nothing is inflicted by him which makes a human being worse, but only that which would make him better is not bestowed.”

## CHAPTER XII

“But if it pleased the Father that the Son should die,” and so forth. The Master, I *Sentences*, distinction 48, § C, proposes and resolves in almost the same words the objection which the author treats at length. Nor is Pullus’s and the Master’s teaching consonant here only, even word for word: it is so in several other places of this work as well, as we have sometimes indicated in the margins of the text, using asterisks on both sides. This appears very clearly in chapter 14 and following, where one finds this notable passage:

> For he always possesses both; but he produces some things to be done from one, some from the other, and others, as has been said, from both.

It occurs in nearly the same words in Lombard, IV, distinction 46, near the end. From this I should think, along with many others, that not the Master illuminated Pullus, but Pullus the Master.

## CHAPTER XIV

> “For perhaps the merits of the living may lessen in some respect the punishments of the lost, if, as some state by way of opinion, the latter had merited this during their previous life.”

He seems especially to allude to Augustine and Damascene. The former, in chapter 110 of the *Enchiridion* and in his answer to Dulcitius’s second question, seemed to the author to have held this opinion:

> The prayers of the faithful benefit some either so that there may be full remission, or at least so that the condemnation itself may become more tolerable.

And shortly before:

> They benefit those who, while they lived, merited that these things might afterwards benefit them.

The latter, in a certain sermon for the departed—also found in the *Lives of the Fathers*, as St Thomas writes in the *Supplement*, question 71, article 5—reports that a certain condemned man testified to Macarius that he and his companions [Col. 1018B] in hell were sometimes aided by the latter’s prayers. Yet this sermon, inscribed with Damascene’s name, is not of unquestioned authority.

Augustine again seems to have held this opinion in chapter 112 of the *Enchiridion*: “They think—so this pleases them—that the punishments of the damned are somewhat mitigated at fixed intervals of time. Even in this way it can be understood that God’s wrath, that is, damnation itself, remains upon them. For this is called God’s wrath, not a disturbance of the divine mind: so that in his wrath, that is, while his wrath remains, he nevertheless does not restrain his mercies—not by ending eternal punishment, but by applying or interposing relief amid torments.” The Christian poet Prudentius agrees in the fifth hymn of the *Daily Cycle* (*τῶν καθημερινῶν*, “of the daily [offices]”), for the lighting of the Paschal candle, where he teaches that a small repose was granted to the damned on the night when Christ rose victorious from the lower world:

> Often, for harmful spirits too, there are famous holidays from punishments beneath the Styx,  
> on that night when the holy God returned  
> from Acherontic pools to the world above—  
> not as, etc.  
>
> Tartarus grows languid under gentle punishments,  
> and the people of shades exults in respite from its prison,  
> freed from fires;  
> nor do the thunderbolts boil with their accustomed sulphur.

It is astonishing how uncertain and varied the school of ancient theologians was on this subject, as may be seen in St Thomas, *Supplement* to the Third Part, question 71, article 5, who argues against all their opinions. We refrain from setting forth his views and those of others cited by him, because they occur everywhere among theologians. Read Peter Damian’s letter to Dominic, chapter 5; he seems to have believed others too readily. At the end of book II of Isidore’s *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, the last two chapters appear to us to have been forged by some idle writer. In one of them that author stitches together a new opinion concerning relief for the damned in these words:

> Suffrages may benefit even the damned by way of diminution. For the more persons are saved through the Church’s merit, the fewer will be damned; and thus their punishment will be less through the removal of fellowship with those persons.

He perhaps invented this by alluding to this passage of the author in *On the Triple Habitation*, among Augustine’s works: “The sight of condemned human beings and demons, and above all of the devil himself, torments the ungodly and sinners.” And to Gregory, Homily 40 on the Gospels: “That sinners may be punished more severely in their torment, they are also tortured by the punishment of those whom they loved to no purpose.” Yet we have called the aforesaid two chapters spurious because they mention *opus operatum* (“the work worked”) and *opus operantis* (“the work of the one working”), expressions unheard of in Isidore’s age. Moreover, they are not found in the list of chapters of Isidore’s book VI, nor even in the manuscript in which those two chapters occur, although the remaining chapters are carefully listed.

That is, that no one perishes—not, to be sure, in himself, but, as has been said, in his own [people]. Pullus examines rather anxiously in this chapter the sense of that Pauline statement (1 Tim. [Col. 1019A] 2:4): “Who wills all men to be saved,” etc. It is strange that he does not recall that modern interpretation which so keenly occupies the studies of the parties: namely, that God, by an innate and proper will, so far as lies in himself, wills without distinction the salvation of all human beings, none excepted, although, in view of the foreseen final wickedness of the evil, he disposes effectively to save only those who will in fact persevere in charity. This common interpretation, I say, would have served his purpose. For he asks whether holy and faithful Christians—who ought to desire the salvation of all human beings—may dissent from the divine will, which does not will, in itself, that all be saved indiscriminately. He answers that they dissent because the outcome of the wicked is unknown to them; indeed, that they do not dissent in every respect, since God wills that they should dissent in this manner. “For if,” he says, “their outcome were not hidden, it would not be fitting to dissent from the divine judgment; nor do we dissent altogether, since he himself wills us to dissent in this way: he who wills all men to be saved and [Col. 1019B] no one to perish—not in himself, because ‘whatever he willed, he did’—but in the saints, whom he causes so to will.”

He would have freed himself from this difficulty and answer—which seem less to display the literal sense of the Pauline text—and would readily have reconciled the will of the saints, who desire without distinction the salvation of all human beings, with the divine will, had he approved the common and modern interpretation mentioned above, by saying that God also wills, so far as lies in himself, the salvation of all human beings; and that therefore the saints in so willing do not dissent from him in any respect. But whatever may be said of that interpretation, he adhered to those expositions which he knew had especially pleased Augustine.

Augustine, as he himself admits in *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 14, employed several explanations of this passage, where he recounts two. The first is that some persons from every class of humankind are saved; thus the distribution is made according to the several classes, not according to each individual in those classes, as St. Thomas teaches, *Summa*, First Part, question 19, article 6, reply to objection 1. He also sets out this mode of explanation notably in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 103; likewise the Fathers deported from Africa to Sardinia in their synodal letter; the author of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, book I, chapter 12; Fulgentius, *On the Incarnation and Grace*, chapter 31; Gregory, *On 1 Kings*, book V; and all those to be cited below for the second mode of explanation.

The other mode, especially pressed by Pullus, is taught by Augustine in the following chapter, 15: “It may also be understood thus: God wills all men to be saved because he causes us to will it; just as he sent the Spirit of his Son crying, ‘Abba, Father’—that is, causing us to cry.” And in book XXII of *The City of God*, chapter 1: “According to this will which God works in human beings, he is also said to will what he himself does not will; but he makes his own people will it, just as he is said to have known what he causes to be known by those by whom it was formerly unknown. According to this will, therefore, by which we say that God wills what he causes others to will—persons to whom future things are unknown—he wills many things and does not do them.” And at once, at the beginning of the following chapter (to which, we think, Pullus aimed): “His saints, inspired by him with a holy will, will many things to happen which he does not do; for they pray piously and holily for certain persons, and he does not do what they pray for.” Thus too Remigius, archbishop, with his clergy of Lyons, *On the Three Epistles*, chapter 11, from the same Augustine: “Or certainly, ‘who wills all men to be saved’ is understood thus: because he causes his saints through the Spirit to will this; that is, he inspires them to desire that all human beings, like themselves, should be saved.” Lupus Servatus has something similar near the end of his *Question on Free Will*.

All those cited under 301 put forward a third mode of explanation: namely, the Acts of the Church of Lyons, Lupus of Mainz, and others. Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, explains it thus from Augustine in *On Predestination against Scotus Eriugena*, chapter 2; or rather Augustine himself in *Enchiridion*, chapter 103: “‘Who wills all men to be saved’: as though it were said that no human being is saved except one whom he himself wills to be saved; not that there is no human being whom he wills to be saved, but that no one is saved except one whom he wills.” [Col. 1020A] “And therefore he must be asked to will it, because it must happen if he wills it,” etc. Augustine confirms this excellently in book IV *Against Julian*, chapter 8; *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 8; and Letter 107. Prosper, in his letter to Rufinus and response 8 to the Chapters of the Gauls, does likewise, etc.

In these three modes, as the Church of Lyons observes in chapter 13 of book I *On the Three Epistles*, “no absurdity and no incompatibility with the faith is found. For whether by ‘all men whom God wills to be saved’ all classes of humankind are understood; or whether ‘God wills all men to be saved’ is understood in this way, because all who are saved are saved only by his will; or whether it is believed to have been said in that sense that God wills all men to be saved because he himself wills this in his saints, inspiring in them such a will that they desire all human beings to be saved as themselves—in all these, I say, there is an interpretation altogether true and salutary.” Let all this be said in proportion to the importance of the matter and in favor of Pullus, to whom this truth was dear; for we wish to assert nothing rashly from our own judgment, which [Col. 1020B] is certainly most slender.
