The ruin of the wicked—the body’s descent to the tomb and the soul’s descent to hell—has often been disclosed to the devout by a prophetic spirit. On the former, among others, Gregory should be read, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapters 51–54, where he presents as many examples on this subject.

On the latter ruin, besides the same Gregory in the same place, one should read Sulpicius Severus, *Life of St. Martin*; Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book VIII, chapter 5; Vincent of Beauvais, book XXV of the *Mirror*, chapter 85; Matthew Paris, *English History*, under the year 1072; Peter Damian, Letter 5, chapters 13 and 24; Baronius under the years 507, 716, and 1054. I prudently refrain from citing them at greater length.

## CHAPTER XV

“Whatever happens in time lived before time in his knowledge.” This is a remarkable passage, and wonderfully favorable to the opinion of certain Fathers who refer the Ideas to Wisdom, and therefore to the divine Word. On this subject Tertullian speaks excellently in *Against Praxeas*, chapter 5 and following; Origen, on 1 John; and the author of *On the Incarnation*, among the spurious works of Augustine, book II, chapter 8. But Augustine himself treats it most fully in many places: *On the Trinity*, book VI, chapter 10; Tractate I on John; *Eighty-Three Questions*, questions 46; *The City of God*, book XII, chapter 20; *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book V, chapters 13–15; and especially his exposition of Psalm 54, which Pullus had in view. In sense and almost in words, the statements of Peter Abelard in book I of his *Introduction*, chapter 17, somewhat after the middle, agree with this exposition.

“It is clear that he can do nothing except what the truth of providence contains; but he foresaw nothing except what comes to pass; therefore he can do nothing except what happens; indeed, he can do nothing except what he wills and does,” etc. Robert, our author, raises these and many other objections from the teaching of his rival and contemporary Abelard, which seems almost to have been transcribed word for word from book III of Abelard’s *Introduction to Theology*, chapter 5, page 1117, etc.; and here he deliberately refutes them. Thus Abelard says, at the cited page: “So far as I judge, since God can do only what it is fitting for him to do, and it is not fitting for him to do what he omits to do, I certainly think that he can do only what at some time comes to pass. Although this opinion of ours may have few or no supporters, and may seem to disagree greatly with the sayings of the saints and somewhat with reason.”

Pullus, friendly even at the altars, strikes down the audacity of this man—otherwise very well known to him—point by point, and at almost every word carrying any force. Here we shall note only what seem to be the principal and decisive points of the controversy.

“That would indeed be good and reasonable according to the state of providence then; but according to what now is, it is evil and unreasonable.”

This utterly true pronouncement, on which the weight of the controversy depends, did not escape Abelard; but he prepared this evasion. Thus, on page 1114, about the middle: “But perhaps, you will say, that [Note: [Col. 1021] This seems to me the correct reading: ‘that just as one good thing is just, but what he now does is reasonable,’ etc.] just as one good thing is just, what he now does is reasonable; so it would be good and equally fair if he did that and left this undone.” Against this he wrongly directs his dart. “But if that which he omitted to do were equally good when he chose to do this, there was surely no reason why he should leave that and choose this.” Yet he again objects to himself Pullus’s argument, though expressed in other words: “There was, you say, a reason: because, since both ought not to be done, and it was equally good for this or that to be done, whichever of them was done was done reasonably.” Pullus sheds much light upon this reasoning; the reader should see it in the text, for it is highly worth reading, and perhaps such as persuaded the man of Nantes to retract.

“For what grace or justice is there when, whether he disposes or brings into effect what he has disposed, he can change nothing on either side?” This did not escape Abelard. Thus on page 1116: “Otherwise no thanks would be owed to him for what [Col. 1021B] occurs, since he acts to bring about things which he cannot omit, compelled by a certain necessity of his own nature rather than led by free will.” Yet he evades this by his customary subtleties, in the manner now set forth by Pullus.

“But you will say: thanks must be rendered to you because, though he cannot do otherwise, he does willingly what he can do.” This, I say, is Abelard’s very answer, page 1121, line 5: “The final objection—that no thanks should be rendered to God for what he does, because he cannot in any way omit it and acts through a certain necessity rather than by will—is altogether frivolous. For a certain necessity of his nature or goodness is not here separate from his will; nor should it be called compulsion, by which he would be forced to do it even unwillingly, for,” etc.

“Either, then, human beings have no fault at all; or, if there is any, it must be laid upon the Creator.” His adversary did indeed raise this argument against himself, but did not solve it. For he imprudently strengthened the second alternative, page 1115: “For if this person who is to be damned could not at all be saved, nor do the things by which he might be saved by God, he certainly ought not to be blamed or held guilty for not doing what he could not do.” But he judges that the cause must be attributed to God: “Since,” he says, “neither can happen except through God.” Robert replies to him more fully in the text.

“Therefore that little child can both persevere in innocence and possess eternal life, whether God wills it or not.” These follow from what he had immediately adduced. These are the absurdities flowing from Abelard’s teaching, whose view of divine omnipotence is excessively thin. For after objecting to himself on page 1115: “Who does not know that this man who is to be damned can be saved, or that this good man can become better than he will ever be?” he answers, page 1119: “When we say that God can save one who is by no means to be saved, we refer the possibility to the very nature [Col. 1021D] of divinity: that is, the nature of God does not oppose his saving him.” This is altogether false. Above, he grants that the man can indeed be saved by God, but refers the possibility only to the capacity of human nature. And on page 1120 he says: “Although a person’s being saved by God and God’s saving him are the same thing, it is not surprising if, though the former is possible, the latter is granted to be by no means possible.” Nothing is more absurd than this interpretation—or rather fabrication; and from it Pullus draws the arguments by which he rejects and tears Abelard to pieces.

“But if, as has been said, neither foreknowledge nor things foreknown can be turned aside otherwise, God cannot [act] otherwise than by the Incarnation,” etc. This is another stumbling-block in Abelard’s teaching, and the rock against which he struck on page 1121: “Yet some think that he can do certain things in another manner than he does, but that he always chooses the more fitting manner of doing them; which also wholly departs from reason.” Pullus replies excellently, in his usual manner. Hugh of St. Victor also noted this error in *On the Sacraments*, book I, part I, chapter 22, perhaps likewise pointing his finger at Abelard, his contemporary. But we judge that this should be added to Hugh’s reasoning: God can do not only better things, but also what is not simply better, by the innate liberty whereby he carries out whatever he wills. When he chooses it, whatever it may ultimately be, it cannot be evil; indeed, precisely because it so pleases God, it often seems to be preferred to a greater good, as Catholic faith and certain reason persuade us. We leave it to others to produce the abundant authorities of the Fathers proving this.

“He would provide himself, in place of the twelve apostles, with twelve [Col. 1022B] legions of angels.” Abelard miserably twists this effective argument drawn from sacred authority, page 1116 and following: “The Lord’s statement should be understood conditionally rather than absolutely: not that he could ask or obtain, but that he would obtain if he asked, since his prayer could in no way be in vain,” etc. Thus speaks the British sophist, but with an attitude toward truth far from fair; for surely nothing is so possible as that which Truth itself promises will occur if it so pleases him. For a conditional proposition concerning something to be done, such as that of Christ the Lord, does not create the possibility of its object, but presupposes it; and it indicates only the futurity, as they say, of the event, provided such a condition is attached.

For the crown of this disputation, one should read what Peter Damian elaborated expressly on this topic; but because it ranges rather far afield, and the book is no longer difficult to find, we refer the reader to Opuscule XXXVI, chapter 1.

[Col. 1022C] Yet we do not wish to grant to Abelard—who boasts so much of himself in the ambitious speech of vanity—that which he once vaunted as a young man, but corrected with groaning as wisdom matured and he approached old age: namely, that he was the sole or first defender of this mad opinion which we have examined. Certainly, while he was still half-blind amid the dust of the arena, he could not see that others before him were made of the same stuff, upon whom, among others, Jerome, Augustine, and Peter Damian cast a ray of truth. Among these Jerome mentions Diodorus disputing with Chrysippus in the first dialogue *Against the Pelagians*. Plotinus also spread this poison with sacrilegious mouth, *Enneads* V.5.12 and VI.8.21.

But at last Abelard, having become from a Dionysian monk a monk of Cluny, wearied of the subtleties of logic and disgusted with reason’s base servitude; as soon as the ray of faith freely revealed itself to him, published the apology conceived by his repentant mind, to the satisfaction of all learned persons’ hopes, under the fostering care and pious zeal of the Venerable Abbot of Cluny. In it he took thought for divine omnipotence, for truth, for his order—most deserving in relation to the Church and letters—and finally for his own salvation and reputation. “I believe that God can do only those things which it is fitting that he should do, and that he can do many things which he never does.”

## CHAPTER XVI

“That, according to the authority, all things are present to God, not by an act of existing, but by the penetrating power of knowing.” In the margin of the text we noted Augustine, who, as usual, seems to have illuminated the author in advance in this opinion. Thomists vigorously defend the contrary, swearing by the words of the Master, *Summa*, First Part, question 14, article 13, in the body of the article; Pullus, at least a hundred years earlier, neatly mocks them.

[Col. 1023A] “But when the present itself, by God’s ordering, already is or has passed, I deny that God can bring into present actuality anything which does not belong to that same present.” Without naming him, he strikes at Peter Damian, who throughout Opuscule XXXVI vigorously maintains the contrary. There he acknowledges such abundant divine omnipotence in every matter that he asserts God can restore a defiled virgin, not merely in respect of the fullness of merits, but even as regards bodily integrity; and he comes close to being angry with Jerome for teaching otherwise, in this celebrated statement, as Peter Damian expressed it: “I speak boldly,” says Jerome, “although God can do all things, he cannot restore a virgin after her fall. He can indeed free her from punishment, but cannot crown one who has been defiled.” Jerome says this to Eustochium. Others, however, read it differently.

Peter is angry with him thus, in that place: “I confess that this opinion could never please me; for I attend not to who says it, but to what is said,” etc. That the controversy was not yet asleep in Pullus’s age is clear, among other evidence, from Robert of Melun’s manuscript *Summa*, where he asks under a special heading: “How is Jerome’s statement to be understood: although God can do all things, he cannot restore a virgin after a fall?” There, though without naming names, he seems to allude to the celebrated dispute on this matter between Peter Damian and Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino. Desiderius explains Jerome differently from Pullus. The former denies that God can restore a virgin after a fall because he does not will to do so—a rich field for Peter’s dispute. The latter, adhering more closely to Jerome’s meaning, denies it because it is impossible for what has happened not to have happened.

## ON THE SECOND BOOK

[Col. 1023]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1023B]

“But all souls [are] similar to those first ones.” Pullus’s opinion will appear a Lesbian rule to all who, concerning the equality or inequality of souls, defend “truth” merely for party interests. For a most celebrated conflict has been fought among the foremost theologians over whether all souls are equal in origin. But setting aside all that we had diligently collected, sufficient for either side of the question, and wishing only to respect the authority of the University of Paris, we judge that Pullus spoke only of specific similarity. Thus the Parisians say in an article mentioned by Durandus, book II, distinction 32, question 5: “If anyone says that all souls are equal in origin, he errs; for otherwise Christ’s soul would not be more perfect than Judas’s soul.” Since this thunderbolt has been hurled from the citadel of truth, we should judge worthy of condemnation those who make light of that censure, as we have more than once read.

[Col. 1023C] “Or certainly he created all things simultaneously, because in creation he joined together the unformed matter of bodies, Adam’s soul, and every angelic nature in heaven.” He seems to mention the opinion—long since discarded, though once debated as a question—that Adam’s soul was contemporaneous with the creation of the angels. Augustine was uncertain on this matter, as is clear from chapters 24 and 25 of book VII of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis* and book XII, chapter 23, of *The City of God*. Hugh of St. Victor, Peter Comestor or the author of the *Scholastic History*, and this master likewise adhered to the doubt, who calls it a scrupulous question. Philastrius yielded rather more freely to his own view, branding as heresy 49 those who say that the creation of the first man’s soul did not precede the formation of his body. But Augustine rightly observes in *On Heresies* that Philastrius has included among heresies many things which nevertheless express sound doctrine. And among matters rashly and falsely suspected, Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca*, book V, note 27, mentions Philastrius’s opinion that the breath of life neither is nor represents the rational soul. As for our author, he defends the common opinion in the following chapter 9.

## CHAPTER II

“He created the angel immediately with heaven and in heaven.” We know that very celebrated authors, far superior both in antiquity and in number, have voted for the contrary opinion. But the author, wholly devoted to Augustine, steadfastly adhered to the position Augustine favored in book XXII *Against Faustus*, chapter 10; Sermon 251; and book II, chapter 19, of *The City of God*—though Augustine had been uncertain in the unfinished book *On Genesis*, chapter 3, and debated both sides. He also followed Epiphanius, heresy 65; Basil of Seleucia, Oration 1; and Junilius Africanus, book II, chapter 2. We may perhaps elsewhere prove that the decretal of Innocent III and the Lateran Synod neither harm this view nor favor with determinate certainty either side of the dispute.

[Col. 1024B] “The firmament therefore stands, though the stars do not stand, so that it may be a suitable dwelling-place for the saints.” Those who pursue curiosities with the ambitious arrogance of novelty rather than with the zeal to seek truth more deeply in the writings of the ancients will be angry here with the author, who seems—if one excepts the heaven called empyrean—to have admitted only one or two heavens. But none of the ancient Fathers whom I have read embraced that laborious sequence and number of celestial spheres, which the school of the Lyceum received almost by unanimous consent, up to the number two [an apparent textual or OCR uncertainty]. On the contrary, some of them accuse of error those who devise a number beyond two.

Thus Theodoret, *Questions on Genesis*, question 2: “He who does not believe that there is a second heaven departs from the straight path; but he who attempts to name more adheres to fables, abandoning the teaching of the divine Spirit. For Moses names only two heavens: one made before light, the other made after light, from the nature of waters.” Chrysostom likewise, both on Psalm 148 and in Homily 4 on Genesis, before the middle, says that those who multiply the heavens in this manner oppose the authority of the divine Scriptures. So Gregory of Nyssa, book I *Against Eunomius*; Ambrose, *Hexameron*, book II, chapter 2; and John Damascene, *On the Faith*, book II, chapter 6. We add Severian of Gabala, some of whose works appear in volume VII of the English edition of Chrysostom’s works. Pullus adhered most confidently to their opinions, though in a rather perplexed sense; we would expound it, were these matters not philosophical and nearly foreign to our purpose.

Yet there is one question which it would be ungrateful to pass over: namely, how, according to the author’s cited text, can the stars move while the firmament stands? Setting aside everything superfluous and plainly curious, which has nevertheless occupied pens elsewhere, I think it more probable that when Pullus raised these objections for himself, he had in view the opinion of certain persons who, although they admitted only the one heaven visible to us, nonetheless, because of the diverse motions suggested by the irregular sequence of the wandering stars, added certain spheres—called carrying spheres—in which the stars revolved. Thus that one heaven was a system of spheres inserted into one another by mutual embrace. A trace of this opinion is found in Basil, *Hexameron*, book III, and Ambrose, book II, chapter 2. But even assuming such a view and the immobility of the visible heaven, one would have to say either that these spheres, so linked together, and the stars fixed in them, were moved by certain intelligences; or one would have to adopt Plato’s opinion, who believed that the planets move by the motion called rotation, whereby they turn in a circle upon themselves. [Col. 1025A] Aristotle did not approve this motion in *On the Heavens*, book II, text 48.

More in accordance with the author’s thought, since he highly esteemed Augustine, one may answer that he alluded to the notable passage in *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book II, chapter 10, in which Augustine says that this controversy was current in his time, and that certain brethren had asked him what he himself thought of it: “Some brethren raise a question concerning the motion of heaven: whether it stands still or moves. For, they say, if it moves, how is it a firmament? But if it stands still, how do the stars, believed fixed in it, travel from east to west, the northern ones describing shorter circuits in orderly fashion, so that heaven, if there is another pole hidden from us, appears to turn from another summit like a sphere; but if there is no other pole, it appears to rotate like a disk?” After a few intervening words he replies: “Let them know this: the name ‘firmament’ does not oblige us to think that heaven stands still. For it may be understood to be called a firmament not because of standing still, but because of firmness, or because it is the impassable boundary between the upper and lower waters. Nor, if truth persuades us that heaven stands still, are we prevented by the circuit of the stars from being able to understand this. For even those who investigated this most curiously and idly found that, if heaven did not move and the stars alone revolved, everything could still occur which has been observed and comprehended in the revolutions of the stars.” Thus Augustine, and Robert after him, who, besides this heaven, recognized another as the seat of the blessed. This is clear both from this chapter and the preceding one, and especially from his saying that the angel was created in heaven and with heaven, although he writes that the angel’s creation preceded the formation of all visible things, and thus the formation of the firmament, which was created only on the following day.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 1025C] “That, according to one of the authors, nothing in creatures is hidden from one who knows the Creator.” This is Pope Gregory, near whose most sacred head—which has for eight hundred years been preserved and venerated with the greatest devotion and the most certain faith in this monastery of St. Peter the Living at Sens—we write these things in the present year 1651. In *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 35, both from the words cited and from others in the same place, he teaches that blessed Benedict, still mortal, was suffused with beatific light and raised to the intuitive vision of God. That Pullus subscribed to this friendly truth, and understood Gregory’s words in no other way than of the beatific knowledge of God, is most certainly inferred from his using them to commend the opinion he here examines: namely, that angels knew God clearly and intuitively immediately from their creation. For he shows that this is the state of the question in these words: “But truth in this place seems chiefly to mean the knowledge of that Truth which says of itself: ‘I am the way, the truth, and the life.’ For as this lower part of the world appears assigned to believers for knowledge, so that upper part—which they call heaven—appears rather to be allotted to those who see.” By these latter words he contrasts the angels’ knowledge under discussion with ours, which comes through faith, or as through a glass in an enigma. He immediately adds: “Therefore, since the rational spirit was free from the burden of flesh and the stain of sin, being well created and destined to behold its Creator, why should it not from the moment it existed see God? Or if it knew him immediately, was it not necessary that it should also know the lower things, so that, according to one of the authors, nothing in creatures is hidden from one who knows the Creator?”

The passage of Gregory assigning this intuitive knowledge of God to St. Benedict is in the cited place: “Hold firmly, Peter, what I say: for to the soul that sees the Creator, every creature is narrow. For however little it has seen of the light of the Creator, everything created becomes small to it, because by that very light of vision the bosom of the inner mind is enlarged; and it is so expanded in God that it becomes superior to the world. Indeed, the soul of the seer is raised even above itself: when it is carried above itself in God’s light, it is enlarged within; and, seeing itself exalted, it understands how brief is that which, when humbled, it could not comprehend, etc. When, therefore, it is said that the world was gathered before his eyes, heaven and earth were not contracted, but the mind of the beholder was enlarged; and, caught up in God, it could without difficulty see all that is beneath God.”

From this it appears that Pullus did not in the least doubt, because of St. Gregory’s authority, that Benedict’s mind, illuminated by this beatific light, had risen to an intuitive knowledge of the Creator, since he referred the saintly doctor’s cited words to exactly the same sense. We marvel at this at least to this extent, and believe that truth ought on this account to be congratulated: that a writer free from every monastic order, unprejudiced by any religious habit, and not otherwise by nature easily swayed, inclined to this opinion by the guidance of truth alone. He should therefore deservedly be enrolled among the other most distinguished defenders of this opinion. Among them we count Bernard, in the sermon on “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me”; Rupert of Deutz, *On the Glory of the Son of Man*, book XII; Bonaventure, *On the Luminaries of the Church*, sermon 20; Denis the Carthusian, sermon on St. Benedict; Benedict Haelten on Gregory’s cited passage in his monastic inquiries; Thomas of Jesus, the Carmelite, *On Divine Contemplation*, book VI; Maximilian Sandaeus, *Theologia Varia*, book III, commentary 40, exercise 2; likewise the theologians of Valladolid, and the Fathers of the College of St. Vincent at Salamanca, who, as some report, swear a celebrated oath upon these words of Gregory.

To these we should not hesitate to add—since those who deny that St. Benedict received this endowment generally wish to deny it to others as well—all those Fathers who earnestly assert that certain ancients possessed this divine *epiphaneia* (manifestation) and genuine vision of God, as Moses and Elijah did: Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book I, chapter 3, and book VIII, chapter 2, concerning Moses; Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 27, and Letter 112; Basil, Homily 1 on the *Hexameron*; and Ambrose, likewise in the first homily: “He spoke with God mouth to mouth, not in a vision or dreams; not in an appearance or through enigmas, but was deemed worthy of a clear and manifest knowledge of the divine presence.”

“Christ, even as he ascended to heaven, was hidden from some of them,” etc.—namely, from certain angels. Few in Pullus’s age will approve this opinion; but devoted to the ancient theology of the Fathers, he followed their tracks closely. For Dionysius, the most ancient among them, in book VII of the *Celestial Hierarchy*, portrays certain angels as hesitating at the sight of Jesus and seeking knowledge of his divine work undertaken for us; and Jesus himself teaches them personally, first revealing to them his graciousness toward humankind. So also Maximus the Scholiast on the aforesaid chapter 6 of Dionysius; Justin in the *Dialogue with Trypho*; Jerome on Isaiah 63; and especially Ambrose, *On Initiation*, book IV, chapter 7.

Besides others, Anastasius of Sinai—perhaps too strongly—in the first of his Anagogical Contemplations on the *Hexameron*, volume I of the *Library of the Fathers*, and Theodoret on Psalm 23, taught this as well. To these might be added all, especially Greeks, who testify that the angels had not seen the Son of God until he put on humanity, believing that the divinity could not be seen even by them. Thus Athanasius, near the end of his last book *Against the Arians*; Chrysostom, Homily II on the First Letter to Timothy, chapter 3: that angels began to see the Son of God with us, whereas previously they did not see him; Theodoret, in the first dialogue called *Atreptos* (“Unchangeable”); Gelasius of Cyzicus, in the preface to the Greek-Latin edition of *The Acts of the Council of Nicaea*, 1599: “Nor could he be seen by angels in the substance of divinity unless he had become incarnate.” These matters would, however, require explanation here, were Robert not at variance with them on this point.

“For we believe that those who are in the lower regions together with the wicked are to be punished together by heat and cold,” etc.—that is, after the judgment they are immediately to be punished by bodily penalties, though themselves incorporeal. This expression too displeases modern writers, especially since St. Thomas—who made the school’s course slippery—taught the contrary in the *Summa*, First Part, question 64, article 4, reply to objection 3: namely, that demons no less than the souls of the damned are already tormented by avenging flames. Yet Pullus’s doctrine pleased both Greek and Latin Fathers; but for brevity’s sake, it is enough to have pointed a finger toward them.

Among the Greeks: Origen, Homily 8 on Exodus, chapter 6; *On First Principles*; and book V on the Letter to the Romans; Nemesius, *On the Nature of Man*, chapter 1; Theodoret, *Against Heresies*, book V, chapter 9; Justin, in both *Apologies*; John Damascene, the final book and chapter of *On the Faith*; Tatian, *Oration against the Greeks* (printed at Paris, [Col. 1027B] 1618); Isidore of Pelusium, book II, Letter 90; and Didymus, *Treatise against the Manichaeans*, volume IV of the *Library of the Fathers*: all maintain with Pullus that demons have not yet been consigned to the infernal fires of hell.

Among the Latins: Minucius Felix, *Octavius*; Lactantius, the final book of the *Institutes*, chapter 26; Ambrose on Luke 12; Jerome on Isaiah 25; Augustine, Letter 49; *On the Nature of the Good against the Manichaeans*, chapter 33; *The City of God* near its end, and in several passages in book XXI; Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 29, and *Morals*, book IV, chapter 10; Fulgentius, chapter 8 *On the Trinity*; Chrysologus, Sermon 52; and Bernard, the author’s contemporary, in his sermon *On the Death of St. Malachy*, where he says that a sentence has indeed been pronounced against the demons but has not yet been promulgated. Scripture too favors this, in 2 Peter 2, as Augustine says in the cited passage of *On the Nature of the Good*, etc. Indeed, no trace appears in the sacred pages or in the councils that could oppose this opinion. For although the Council of Florence, later than Pullus’s age, defined this concerning the souls of the damned, it was silent concerning demons; and therefore Cajetan, in this matter, departed from his own side in commenting on 2 Peter 2.

They did not first obtain existence before obtaining a bad existence: their existence was from the Author; their evil condition from elsewhere. The words must be read cautiously, yet are free from blemish. Their meaning is owed to Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book II, chapter 23 (a passage which he transcribed verbatim in chapter 48 of the sixth part, though he does not adhere to it; from this one may infer that it was not the author’s settled view). There Augustine, speaking of the devil, says:

> But he was immediately ungodly, and consequently blind in mind; he fell not from what he had received, but from what he would have received had he been willing to be subject to God, etc.

And near the end of chapter 19 of the same book:

> Not without reason have I thought it possible to say that the devil fell from the Creator himself—that is, from the very beginning either of time or of his own condition—and never at any time stood in the truth.

The meaning, therefore, of Pullus’s words is that the apostate angels fell immediately upon being created, or after the first instant. This is also the opinion of St Thomas, article 6, question 63, who says:

> The more probable view, and that more consonant with the sayings of the saints, is that the devil sinned immediately after the first instant of his creation.

Pullus requires at least that instant in this chapter, since he says that all the angels received faith at their creation and were able to merit with it. From this we gather two points in his view: namely, that they were created in grace—without which there is no merit—and that they remained in it for a time.

We nevertheless admit that the author’s cited words, in which he yields not to his own opinion but to that of others, commend the view mentioned by the Master, II, distinction 3, § E, and rejected by St Thomas in article 5 of the cited question 63, with this condemnation:

> Some held that the demons were evil immediately in the first instant of their creation, not indeed by nature, but through the sin of their own will, because from the moment the devil was made, he rejected righteousness. Whoever agrees with this opinion, as Augustine says in *The City of God*, book II, chapter 13, does not think with those heretics—that is, the Manichaeans—who say that the devil possesses a nature of evil. But because this opinion contradicts the authority of Scripture—for it is said, etc.—it has reasonably been rejected by the masters as erroneous.

So St Thomas.

## CHAPTER VI

“If, then, you say that the devil, as is truer, is evil, how do you maintain that his substance or nature is good?” And, after a few intervening words: “Now neither is his substance good, nor is he God’s creature.”

Lest the unwary stumble upon this rock, a man of most approved learning and sounder theology—commended by me under many titles, yet sufficiently distinguished by his own light—shall hold out a torch from the shore. He is Jean de Launoy, Parisian theologian, who, in a letter to me full of varied learning, voluntarily removed what I had with difficulty suspected to be an obstacle in the author. His words ought to be transcribed here, lest I be ungrateful and unfair to the reader. Thus he writes:

> The school of theologians has now adopted the opinion that the substance of demons has remained intact, and that they have been deprived of no endowment belonging to nature. Yet it does not reckon this opinion among the fixed dogmas of the Church. For not every falsehood in scholastic teaching is such as to result in damage to the Christian faith. Indeed, William of Auxerre indicates, in book II of his *Summa*, treatise 26, where he discusses the question of evil angels, that four hundred years ago there were persons who without censure thought the contrary. “It has been said,” he writes in chapter 3, “that sin corrupts natural goods,” etc. He subsequently refutes these views by the right of one expressing an opinion, but attaches to them no mark of error.

> Moreover, the importance of this question also depends upon the opinion which establishes no distinction between created substance and its faculties. This is taught by John Scotus, or Eriugena, who lived in France under King Charles the Bald—that is, long before Robert Pullus was born. Scotus’s words are these, in *On Predestination*, chapter 8: “For it is far removed and laid up in the secret recess of profound understanding what distinction there is between the free will of man, which belongs to nature, and his free choice, which is manifestly the gift of the Creator.” And later: “God made man thus: namely, essence, will, and knowledge; and these three are one. For for rational life, being and willing are not different; nor are willing and knowing different. Rather, his being is a knowing will; his will is a knowing essence; and his knowledge is a willing essence. Therefore these three are one and one nature; indeed, the whole nature of the soul is will.”

> After Robert Pullus’s age, the Nominalists, a most distinguished school of philosophers, embraced this opinion, which does not distinguish a faculty from created substance. Therefore, if nature and its faculties are one and the same thing, and if Pullus held that the nature of demons was corrupted through sin, his assertion would not be so inconsistent. We lost free choice for loving God through the greatness of the first sin, as Augustine teaches in Letter 107. Likewise, the Second Synod of Orange decreed that the whole man—made of body and soul—was rendered subject to corruption and weakened through Adam’s assent, and even that man’s free choice was lost. These passages are understood variously by various authors; but this diversity of interpretation will include Pullus and preserve him from theological error.

Thus Jean de Launoy.

Nor do I find Pullus’s expression so unwelcome to Augustine that Augustine does not use it in more than one place, asserting that the devil’s nature, as soon as he sinned, was perverted by his evil will. He teaches this most plainly at the beginning of chapter 16, book XI of *On Genesis*:

> Scripture does not say how pride cast down the devil so that he perverted his good nature by his own wicked will; yet clear reasoning shows that this had already happened and that through it he envied man.

And in *The City of God*, book XII, chapter 3:

> A vice is called so for no other reason than because it corrupts the good of nature in them.

And below:

> For what do they do to those natures by harming them, except take away their integrity, beauty, health, strength, and whatever good is customarily removed or diminished from nature through vice?

What, however, should be held in this matter without any scruple is taught by the same Augustine, book I *Against Julian*, chapter 8:

> If it be asked what an angel or a human being of evil will is like, the most correct answer is: evil—taking the name of quality more from the evil will than from the good nature. For nature is substance itself, capable both of goodness and of evil. It is capable of goodness through participation in the good by which it was made; but it receives evil not through participation in evil, but through privation of good. That is, no nature which is something evil is mixed into it, because no nature, insofar as it is nature, is evil.

See also chapter 14 of the *Enchiridion*, to which Pullus expressly directs this chapter in the place where he cites Augustine.

For the sake of learning we shall add one point: Philastrius, chapter 59, mentions an opinion asserting that demons, after their sin, somehow changed their nature and substance. Certain later Greeks adopted it and openly taught it at the Council of Florence. Council of Labbe, volume XIII, column 29:

> That the devil and those who fell with him from the glory of God almost took on flesh; and those who were immaterial became partly material. For this reason they run toward material bodies and rest in bodies, as did the one who said, “If you cast us out, Lord, permit us to go into the herd.” And he permitted them, and the herd rushed down the steep bank. For this reason they also desire to dwell in human bodies, for they rest in them. Behold how they are partly fleshly and are to be punished; and the matter which they received they will burn in eternal fire.

That is: The devil and those who fell with him from God’s glory almost took on flesh; and those who had been free from matter became partly material. For that reason they run to material bodies and rest in bodies, like the one who said: “If you cast us out, Lord, allow us to enter the herd of swine.” And he allowed them, and the herd rushed into the precipice (Matt. VIII, 30). Therefore they also desire to live in human bodies, for they rest in them. See how they are partly fleshly; they are to undergo punishment, and the matter they received will be burned for ever in fire.

## CHAPTER VII

“So that what previously contained it in the body may now subsist by itself, without life.”

Some ancient philosophers, and not of the lowest rank, taught that semen is animated and alive—a view now unwelcome to almost everyone. Thus Plato in the *Timaeus*; Galen, *On Marasmus*, chapter 5; Themistius, *On the Soul*, book I, chapter 21. Among more recent writers: Theophilus Zimara, *On the Soul*, book II, text 43; Peramatus, *On Semen*; Valesius, *Controversies*, book II, chapter 9; etc.

## CHAPTER VIII

“Unless because an authority testifies.”

He indicates Augustine and Bede as familiar authorities. The former, in Tractate 2 on John, and the latter at the same Gospel passage, interpret “who were born, not of bloods” as “of male and female.” Augustine says: “For human beings are born from bloods, from male and female.”

The author appears to have taken not a little of this chapter from the *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, following the belief of his age, in which most people thought it a genuine work of Augustine.

## CHAPTER IX

“Souls are made drunk by Lethean draught unto forgetfulness of earlier things.”

These are very familiar poetic fictions, mentioned by Virgil in *Aeneid* VI; Lucan, book VIII; and Ovid, *Tristia* I, elegy 7. From this arose Jerome’s phrase, **λήθης πεδίον**, “the plain of forgetfulness,” namely from the river Lethe washing Africa near the furthest promontory of the Syrtis, where Berenice was situated. **Λήθη** means “forgetfulness,” and perhaps the fable arose from it.

## CHAPTER X

“Soul and flesh are one human being, by the coming together of natures, not of parts.”

Desiring to consult brevity rather than philosophy, we pass over many matters by which it might perhaps be welcome to reconcile Robert Pullus, who differs from the common opinion of philosophers, with modern thinkers. Certainly, in a human being fully completed in the final sense, he seems to recognize no true composition other than a personal one. We have been unable to find among recent writers any trace of this opinion except the material advanced on this subject by Domingo de Soto in his *Logic*, under the category of substance, question 1.

Yet, if correctly understood, these authors do not appear to deny some real and substantial union of body and soul, both in Christ the Lord and in other human beings. They deny only that from these things thus joined there arises a third substance, neither body nor spirit, but something composed of both. Thus they say that flesh and soul meet as natures possessing a mutual order toward one another, not as parts mingled together so as to generate some third thing from themselves. They therefore seem to admit union while excluding confusion.

Peter of Poitiers will provide more on this matter, though with somewhat greater freedom, near the end of Part, or Distinction, IV of the *Sentences*. So also will Robert of Melun in his treatise *On the Incarnation*. From that work, still unpublished, we have selected certain passages necessary for considering this difficulty, which we do not wish the reader to be unaware of, since in the twelfth century it was an exceedingly famous question among the scholastics. Thus he writes:

> Therefore Peter’s soul, even while it was in the body, was a person, etc.; when it departed from the body, it remained the same person that it had been in the body. But while it was in the body, Peter’s person was said to consist of soul and flesh, and to be a certain composite of soul and flesh. This ceased to be when it departed from the body; yet nothing that it was ceased to be, because that composition was not one of parts but a certain union of diverse natures. It follows that Peter’s soul and body were one person, yet not one substance. Therefore, because Peter’s person was no substance composed of Peter’s soul and flesh, the person which Peter was did not cease to be anything when the composite of Peter’s soul and flesh ceased to be. For just as in God several persons are one substance, so in man several substances can be, and are, one person. From this it is also taught that God and man could be one person.

Thus the Melun manuscript.

By these words he teaches the same opinion as Pullus: namely, that the entire account of personhood lies in the soul even when separated, as he proves under a title specifically devoted to this subject. The distinguished writers of that age agree with him: Peter Abelard, in his exposition of the Apostles’ Creed, p. 375, about the middle:

> If, then, in individual human beings there are two natures, bodily and incorporeal, but only one person, so also in Christ there are two natures, divine and human, but only one person. A person is said, as it were, to be one in itself; that is, any rational substance so separated in itself from other things that it does not constitute a substance with any other thing. Therefore, as long as the human soul is in the body, it cannot be called a person, because, joined to the flesh, it constitutes with it one human person and one rational substance.

So too Peter Lombard, III, distinction 5, final section; the other Peter of Poitiers, his pupil, cited above, of whom perhaps elsewhere; Hugh of St Victor, *Summa of Sentences*, tractate 1, chapter 15: “For the soul is a person, like an angel.” Read also the same author’s *Apology for the Incarnate Word*, against those who say that Christ as man is not something; and Peter Abelard at the cited place, pp. 383 and 1128.

## CHAPTER XIV

“Perhaps he affirms something that departs from the path of authority.”

Whom he alludes to, we do not know. It is certain that Plato was charged with this error by St Thomas, *Against the Gentiles*, book II, chapter 84. But Bessarion, book II *Against the Calumniators of Plato*, chapter 7, removes the stigma rashly fastened upon him and maintains that Plato taught the contrary in the *Timaeus*, nor did he hold such an absurdity elsewhere.

## CHAPTER XVI

“Only to those children of light who are now being born and who excel,” etc.

Some judge this worthy of imitation. We think he chiefly means Gregory, *Morals*, book IV, chapter 28—wrongly cited here in St Thomas as chapter 36—and Anselm, *Why God Became Man*, book I, chapter 18. Hugh of St Victor cites a certain Gilbert for the same opinion, *Summa of Sentences*, chapter 12:

> If man had not sinned, none of those to be damned would be born. But because he sinned, those to be damned are born together with those to be saved: the saved in the place of those who would then have been born; the damned in no one’s place, but for the exercise and crown of the good.

Hugh does not seem to dissent from this view. Read Augustine, *The City of God*, book XIV, chapter 10. For a fuller understanding of this chapter, one may read the author of the *Questions to Antiochus* among the works of Athanasius; Isidore, *Sentences*, book I, chapter 12; Moses Bar Cepha, Part I of *On Paradise*; William of Paris, in the first part of the second part of *On the Universe*, chapter 18. Again: Augustine, *The City of God*, book XXII, chapter 1, and *Enchiridion*, chapter 29; Anselm, in the cited book, chapters 16 and 17; etc.

## CHAPTER XVII

“But the mother, adorned with such great fruitfulness,” etc.

The text is corrupt, as the failure of grammatical construction, among other things, shows. We think that in place of the particle *sicut* (“as”), one should read *Sion* (“Zion”), so that the sense and grammatical construction are genuine and complete. For these words must be referred to that holy Zion mentioned above, namely the Church. He proves that Adam’s sin benefited it even from the fact that it is illuminated by Christ Jesus and his mother, these heavenly luminaries as though by sun and moon. Yet it would not be blessed by the sight of them had Adam not sinned. For Robert holds, with the sounder opinion of the Fathers and theologians, that, if Adam had not sinned, the heavenly physician would not have come.

## CHAPTER XXV

“It is agreed to have flowed from the wrath of the Maker.”

Permissively: insofar as he permitted such excessive movements in the sexual organs to flow from nature corrupted through sin.

“Vices grow together.”

Not moral vices, but natural defects.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

The context of this chapter, in which occur difficulties insoluble even for Augustine himself—as he admits in *On the Morals of the Church*, book I, chapter 22, and Letter 29 to Jerome—requires a prudent and attentive reader, lest one rashly stumble or suppose that the author asserts certain things which he certainly merely proposes as objections and finally rightly refutes. Having noted this solely for the benefit of beginners, we briefly explain Pullus’s view of the transmission of original sin and, as is our duty, reconcile it with earlier theology and our own.

Pullus appears, therefore, to hold the opinion commonly attributed to his contemporary, the Master, II, distinction 31: namely, that he recognizes in generative seed a certain diseased quality, through whose contagion and defect the soul is stained and acquires the blemish of origin. He says:

> The flesh itself which is conceived is polluted and corrupted in sinful concupiscence; by contact with it, when the soul is infused, it receives a stain by which it is polluted and made guilty—namely, the vice of concupiscence, which is original sin.

Both seem to have drawn support for this opinion from another principle peculiar enough to writers of their age, and even to themselves: namely, that nothing external enters into the reality of human nature, but whatever naturally exists in human bodies pre-existed materially in Adam; having been cut off from him by the seminal path, it is increased and multiplied in itself, with absolutely nothing external entering it. This is much like the way the same Master writes, II, distinction 18, that Eve was formed from Adam’s rib without any composition at all from an external thing. He defends this view in the cited book, distinction 30, § N. Our author teaches it at greater length in chapter 17 of the final part.

If this doctrine stands, it is not difficult for either writer to show the propagation of the primal stain: namely, that the rest, cut off from the corrupted seed of the first-created man and transmitted materially from him even to us, are likewise corrupted; and that souls are at last infected by the plague of that parental stain in corrupted bodies, just as a precious liquid is corrupted in a vessel already defiled.

Very few in this age are pleased by such an opinion; and, remarkably, some have branded it an error, supported by the authority of Anselm, who preceded the author by a few years. In *On the Virgin’s Conception*, chapter 7, Anselm reveals himself as defender of the contrary side:

> Although a child is carried in seed from sinful concupiscence, there is no more guilt in the seed than in spittle or blood if someone spits with an evil will or emits something from his own blood with an evil will. For it is not the spittle or the blood but the evil will that is blamed.

Thus Anselm. In his defense, an anonymous admirer of Anselm, apparently living not far from the age of Bernard and Pullus, vigorously attacked Pullus and his followers. This is clear from his short surviving work among Anselm’s writings, in which he says that in his own time there were persons teaching that in the seed itself there was a certain tinder of sin and a corruption of human nature, from which the blemish of origin was contracted. He inveighs sharply against them for Anselm’s sake.

But, with due respect to this writer and to the others who differ from our author, Pullus followed Augustine, as was his custom, not Anselm. For the vindication of his teaching it will suffice to point out the guide who preceded him in many places, especially *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book II, chapter 8:

> The question now is not about the nature of human seed but about its vice. The former has God as its author; from the latter original sin is drawn. For if the seed itself has no vice, what is the meaning of what was said, etc.?

Still more clearly, *Against Julian*, book VI, chapter 7, about the middle:

> That this vice of origin, which is not a body but an accident, could not remain in the seed after it has been remitted by forgiveness cannot be asserted by any most subtle person, since he is overcome by divine authority, through which that part of the body was commanded to be cut off precisely in order that this vice might be cleansed. If it were not in the seed, it could in no way reach infants, from whom it was to be removed by that bodily circumcision.

And *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book III, chapter 9:

> Believers transmit unbelief to their descendants; this does not belong to those who have been regenerated through the Spirit, but is the defect of the mortal seed by which they are generated in the flesh.

See also chapters 22, 23, and 24 of book I of *On Marriage*; and book V *Against Julian*, chapter 4, at which our author certainly seems to have aimed:

> Therefore, in order that soul and flesh may both be punished, unless what is born is corrected by rebirth, surely either both are drawn from man as corrupted, or one is corrupted in the other as in a corrupted vessel, etc.

Nor does the author of the commentary on the Epistle to the Romans among Ambrose’s works say otherwise on chapter 7, as he is also cited there by Lanfranc and by the Master, II, distinction 31, § D.

Guibert the abbot, *Against the Jews*, book I, chapter 5, and his short work *On the Virgin*, chapter 7 before the middle, likewise subscribed to this view. So did Peter of Poitiers, distinction 2, chapter 19:

> There is another defect of human nature after sin: namely, a certain foulness, a certain stain arising from the ardent intercourse of the parents, which is the cause of original sin and also original sin.

That is, causally, not formally, as he proves afterwards. Innocent III, in his exposition of Psalm 50:

> From defiled and corrupted seed a body is conceived which is likewise corrupted and defiled. The soul, finally infused into it, is corrupted and defiled—not from an integrity or purity which it possessed, but from that which it would possess if it were not united to a defiled and corrupted body; since it is infused in being created and created in being infused.

Likewise Albert the Great, II, distinction 30, article 1, etc., and distinction 31, article 2, where he gives extensive support to this opinion, which he states was common in his own time; and so do many others. Our author’s contemporary Hugh of St Victor had also taught it in explicit words, *On the Sacraments*, book I, part VII, chapters 24, 25, 28, 31, 35, and the final chapter.

Finally, among more recent writers we add to Pullus as a companion the most celebrated man of distinguished learning, William Estius, who casts most welcome light upon Pullus’s teaching through his commentaries on distinctions 30, 31, and 32 of book II of the *Sentences*, with the revived splendour of freer theology. What we ourselves think of this transmission of the primal stain is not our task to state here.

## CHAPTER XXXI

Lest the reader’s mind again waver on slippery ground in this chapter, it will help to note that here Pullus understands original sin in two ways: causally, as they say, and formally; that is, as it first existed in Adam and afterwards passed into all human beings from him, though not numerically the same; and then as it exists in each individual as something proper and internal. The latter he calls concupiscence itself, as we shall shortly see.

The Fathers of the Second Council of Orange seem to have spoken in the former sense in chapter 2, using words taken from Augustine, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book IV, chapter 4, as did Trent, session 5, canon 3. Augustine speaks in the latter sense in several passages soon to be cited. Although in them he recognizes Adam’s transgression itself as the cause of original sin, he does not hesitate to say that concupiscence itself is the original stain. Hugh of St Victor used this twofold understanding of primordial sin in the cited place, chapter 26. Having deliberately noted these points, any obstacles in the author’s text may now readily be removed.

For when he says: “Thus an infant is perhaps rightly called a sinner, not from what is present, but from what preceded in Adam,” everyone sees that this is said of the parental stain in the former sense. In this sense he denies that Adam’s actual transgression creeps into those being born so as actually to inhere in them, since it is false that that blemish is transmitted in such a way as to be an actual thing common to all; and it is otherwise certain that Adam’s sin itself was removed through his repentance. Therefore, as Pullus writes, although the infant does not have sin actually, he nevertheless has its liability.

He recognizes, moreover, another original sin, internal and radically adhering to each individual, which, he says, may be excused through baptism but cannot be removed. This passage must now be examined.

A fault, then, must be sought which can be excused by baptism or penance but cannot be removed. Given Pullus’s view that original sin is concupiscence itself, there is no difficulty in the cited words. Their meaning is this: concupiscence, in which the character of the primitive defilement is discerned, is in one respect removed by baptism and in another remains. Whatever in it has the true character of sin is removed:

> When, says Estius, § 2 on distinction 32 of book II of the *Sentences*, the dominion of concupiscence is removed, so that it no longer pleases the will or draws it toward unlawful desires.

Thus Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book I, chapters 26 and 27; *On the Merits of Sins*, book II, chapter 39; etc. The tinder of sin remains, however. Augustine writes in many places that in the regenerate this is not sin, but is left for the contest: for example, *On the Merits of Sins*, book II, chapter 4; *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, book II, chapter 14; *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book I, chapters 13 and 14; *Against Julian*, book II, chapters 3, 8, 9, and 10; and *The City of God*, book I, chapter 18; etc. The Council of Trent expressly teaches the same thing, session 5, canon 5.

Yet when infants are called guilty by origin, concupiscence alone, or above all else, seems to be blamed. He repeats this in the following chapter. Here Robert plainly teaches that internal original sin, properly understood, is concupiscence itself. Peter of Poitiers, Chancellor of Paris, in a passage soon to be cited, writes that this opinion was common in Pullus’s century, indeed almost universal.

Augustine was the most faithful defender of this opinion: *On the Merits of Sins*, book I, chapters 9, 10, and 19, and book II, chapter 4; *Against Julian*, book I, chapters 3, 5, 9, and 10, book V, chapter 3, and book VI, chapters 6, 7, and 8; *On Marriage*, book I, chapters 23, 24, and 25; etc. Those who followed him include Hugh of St Victor, part VII of *On the Sacraments*, as already seen; the Master, II, distinction 30, § G; Praepositinus—whose work in ancient handwritten parchments we preserve in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés—in his *Summa*, under the heading “On Original Sin”; Peter of Poitiers, distinction 2, chapter 19:

> Following the common highway, we say that concupiscibility, not ignorance, is original sin.

And in our own age William Estius, on distinction 30, § 8, who excellently proves his view by an argument drawn from the authority of the Council of Trent.

By the name “concupiscence,” moreover, Pullus understands not merely that which, by the impious itch of lust, stirs Venus; Augustine warns in *Against Julian*, book VI, chapter 7, that this is only a part of original concupiscence. He means rather that which ranges over all things that can be wrongly and disorderly desired by human beings, and which inclines them to every kind of sin, whether fleshly or spiritual, according to Paul’s enumeration in Galatians V. This is sufficiently gathered from the context of this chapter, in which he appears to have had in view Augustine, *The City of God*, book XIV, chapters 2, 3, and 4, and the *Enchiridion*, chapter 45.

## ON BOOK THREE

## CHAPTER III

“But you will say: surely he is not guilty of a circumcision yet to come, but of the ancient transgression; and because he has not received the remedy, he will not escape torment.”

This is the stone of stumbling upon which the Master struck. In IV, distinction 1, final section, persuaded by this reasoning and by testimony of Bede wrongly understood, he asserted either that the eighth day for circumcision must be anticipated in infants in desperate health, or that uncircumcised infants dying were damned. Pullus here condemns this opinion, which the Parisian school rejected; so too does Hugh, monk of St Victor, excellently, *On the Sacraments*, book I, part XII, chapter 2.

## CHAPTER IX

“Therefore, when blood from the chalice is poured into you, remember that Christ shed blood for you.”

He appears to have had in view the passage which Gratian cites from Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter “When It Is Broken”:

> When blood from the chalice is poured into the mouths of the faithful, what else is signified but the offering of the Lord’s body upon the cross and the outpouring of his blood from his side?

Related is Gregory’s statement in Homily 22 on the Gospels:

> For us he dies again in this mystery; for there his body is received, his flesh suffers for the salvation of the people, and his blood is poured no longer into the hands of unbelievers but into the mouths of believers.

See the same Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 58.

By these words, after the authorities cited, Pullus expresses the ancient practice of the Church whereby the deacon, in the morning assembly of the people, administered the Lord’s blood from the chalice to communicants. This rite—especially attested by Cyprian—is so frequently mentioned by authors that we voluntarily omit further remarks which might be made. For the sake of antiquity, we shall append one item which amply commends that custom. It is taken from a manuscript history of the Life of St Amator, bishop of Auxerre, written around 590 by Stephen the African. There, under the year 380 or thereabouts, he relates:

> There was a certain Heraclius by name, from the city of Autun, descended from a most distinguished family. His wife was named Palladia, a match for her husband in conduct and birth, and even more abundant in plentiful wealth. Having withdrawn from the worship of demons, she had committed herself to the faith of the true religion and to its doctrines and cleansing bath, while her husband remained [variant: dwelt] in his former errors. After completing holy baptism, she wished to travel to the city of Auxerre, near which she possessed an estate. When she had taken up lodging in the suburb, the Paschal day arrived. On the very day of the Lord’s Resurrection, being a neophyte, she proceeded to the holy church adorned with shining ornaments. The aforementioned Palladia glittered with such varied brilliance of jewels that she obscured the brightness of the sun and concealed the daylight with costly adornments. When the sacrifice had been completed, and she wished to be strengthened by the gift of the Eucharist and by drinking the Lord’s blood, she approached the blessed Amator, then a deacon, who offered the most holy chalice to the people unto eternal life. Seeing her adorned in sumptuous finery, he addressed her thus: “You shall not taste from this chalice of the blood of Jesus Christ the Lord unless you lay aside the burden of your adornment. For this night you committed the crime of defilement; you must put on mournful attire, wash away your nocturnal offense with a flood of tears, and then approach the most holy feast.”

Thus Stephen. It should nevertheless be noted in passing that the “crime” and “nocturnal offense” which the most holy deacon charged against the woman consisted solely in the work of marriage and intercourse with her husband. For she described it to her husband in no other way when she complained thus:

> Unless I had laid aside my garments together with my ornaments and humbly performed penance for the nocturnal act I had committed, I would by no means have communicated.

Moreover, although in Robert’s age the use of the chalice was commonly denied to the people, as he himself suggests in the final part, chapter 3, many nevertheless wish to infer from the cited passage that even in his age the contrary custom prevailed in many places: that laypersons received communion under both kinds. They complain greatly that, in their own time, communion under bread dipped in the chalice had not yet been universally extinguished, and they maintain that he alludes to this custom in this chapter.

Certainly, if one may consult his contemporaries, or those only a few years earlier—indeed, his equals—no one will deny it. For Hugh, throughout chapter 6 of the third treatise of the *Sum of Sentences*, seems to intimate this; as is also gathered from chapter 4, book II, part III, of *On the Sacraments*, where he speaks of monks. In the *Rule for Clerics* of Peter de Honestis (who died in 1119), book II, chapter 22, “On the Sick and Dying,” we read as follows: “But if the illness should grow more and more severe, let them be sprinkled by priests with blessed water, anointed with holy oil, and fortified by reception of the body and blood of Christ.” Our Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, speaking of Louis VI, says: “When, to the admiration of all, he had first made [Col. 1036A] confession of his sins, he communicated in the body and blood of Jesus Christ.” Hugh, bishop of Rouen and monk of Cluny, in his letter to Pope Innocent II, in which he informs him of the death of Henry I, king of England, says: “Under this assurance, in fulfillment of our office, we absolved him three times, over three days. He adored the cross of the Lord; he devoutly received the body and blood of the Lord.” One should read Ivo of Chartres, Letters 28 and 63; Rupert of Deutz, book II of *On the Offices*, chapter 9; and Lanfranc, primate of England, book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, chapter 15. Having set out the words which Berengar had adduced from Augustine’s letter to Boniface, Lanfranc adds: “Yet in the sacrament which the Church regularly celebrates in memory of this event, the flesh of the Lord is daily sacrificed, divided, and eaten; and his blood is drunk from the chalice by the mouths of the faithful.” He offers similar statements in Letter 33 to Domnaldus, which Dom Luc d’Achery published with other letters, accompanied by notes full of varied learning; yet, in the interest of brevity, he did not wish to dwell upon these words.  

[Col. 1036B] Still more clearly this rite is commended by canon, or decree, 317 of the Council of Clermont under Urban II, enacted in Pullus’s time, while he had not yet laid aside the toga praetexta: “Let no one communicate from the altar unless he receives the body separately, and likewise the blood—except in case of necessity and precaution.” Baronius says that this statute was issued by the Fathers (under the year of Christ 1095) in hatred and condemnation of the Berengarian heresy, which maintained that the figure was sufficiently fulfilled by receiving one symbol alone. We shall provide more on this matter in the final portion of chapter 3, where we discuss communion under bread dipped in the chalice.

Not only in Robert’s age—which alone was what we wished to show—but also for many years afterward, this custom continued: communicant laypeople received both symbols. Saint Thomas, in *Summa Theologiae*, III, question 80, article 12, throughout, is an unimpeachable witness. Indeed, Paludanus, who was living in 1337, attests that it still prevailed in certain churches: *Commentary on the Sentences*, book IV, distinction [Col. 1036C] II, question 1, article 1, conclusion 2. There, besides the Greek liturgies, in which this was done, he writes that in certain Western churches it customarily occurred without any privilege:

> “The Greeks communicate in the flesh and blood; and in certain churches there is a custom that they communicate under both species, and it is not a sin; for, when it was customary, it was not a crime. Thus they act carefully in churches or monasteries, so that they spill nothing.”

Yet this did not then prevail universally among all; Pullus, as we have seen, warns that the opposite custom was also ordinarily observed by others. Thus it is certain that, despite what theologians press against innovators, the rite of communion under both species never prevailed in such a way that every person not bound to sacred ministry was not free to abstain from reception of the precious blood. Perhaps one must except the times of Popes Leo and Gelasius, when the Manichaean heresy was spreading. Since its adherents deemed the use of wine wicked and impious, every one of the faithful communicated under both species, lest anyone give others grounds to suspect him.

[Col. 1036D] It will not be an unwarranted digression if we also note what we read in ancient English constitutions, gathered into one volume by William Lyndwood, official of the Church of Canterbury. Thus, under the title “On the Supreme Trinity”: “In such smaller churches, permission is granted only to the celebrants to receive the blood under the species of consecrated wine.” From this William himself infers, by the argument from the contrary—which is extremely strong in law, book I of the *Digest*, “On the Office of Him to Whom,” etc.—that in cathedrals and larger churches others had been granted the drinking of the Lord’s blood. “And this,” he says, “I should judge to be so, at least with respect to those assisting the celebrating priest, who, according to the custom of various churches, communicate with the priest himself by receiving the body and blood. Thus it is customarily observed when the pope celebrates solemnly. For after the pope has taken a portion of the blood through a reed, he hands the remainder to the deacon to drink.”

Indeed, that not only sacred ministers but also others, especially monks, were permitted to drink the Lord’s precious blood from the chalice through a tube, [Col. 1037A] is attested by Rhenanus in his notes on Tertullian’s *On the Soldier’s Crown*: “This is clear,” he says, “from the recently unearthed book of signs, which is common among the Benedictines.” And in the earliest constitutions of the Carthusian Fathers—which are known to have appeared while Pullus was alive—it is forbidden “that they should possess any precious vessels except a silver chalice and a tube through which laypeople may drink the Lord’s blood.” That this was likewise practiced among Cistercians and certain others is testified by Innocent III, chapter *Ex parte*, “On the Celebration of Mass,” and by William cited above:

> “The brothers communicate in the convent. The priest holding the chalice with the blood, seeing that the quantity of blood would not suffice for all the brothers, puts a little wine into it,”

in accordance with what is found in chapter 53 of the book entitled *The Beginning of the Cistercian Monastery*: “While the brothers receive the blood, wine is to be poured in by the deacon when necessary. But if any of that blood remains, [Col. 1037B] let him drink it with the chalice after he has returned the tube to the subdeacon; before returning the tube, he is, insofar as he can, by sucking from both ends, to empty it of the Lord’s blood.” The tube mentioned here is called by some a *canna* (“reed”), by others a *pugillaris*; this latter term occurs frequently in the author of the book *On the Roman Order*.

The use of this custom, long since obsolete, is retained in part even today by two most celebrated Benedictine monasteries in France: Cluny, in our diocese of Mâcon, and Saint-Denis near Paris, of the Congregation of Saint-Maur. In these monasteries, every Sunday and on rather more solemn feasts, after communion has been completed, it is customary—at Cluny, for the deacon, subdeacon, and lesser ministers of the altar, called candle-bearers; at Saint-Denis, for the deacon and subdeacon alone—to carry the celebrant’s chalice to a table specially prepared near the altar, and there alternately drink the remaining precious blood through a tube or silver reed. [Col. 1037C] I remember doing this many times while I lived as a monk at Cluny, though I had scarcely reached the years of puberty; and again at Saint-Denis for a full two years, though by then I had been initiated into holy orders.

## Chapters XV, XVI, XIX, and XX: On the Incarnation of the Divine Word

Some will be angry, others perhaps will laugh, and all will be astonished that this most Christian doctor of ours departed from the common path and from the almost unanimous judgment of all Catholics; that, rejecting the ancient opinion on the manner of the first mystery of the dispensation, he devised a new one in his zeal to investigate truth more deeply; and one which pleased only a few, and only in his own century, as his contemporary Robert of Melun writes in the chapter on the Incarnation in his treatise *On the Incarnation*, which we shall reproduce in full below.

[Col. 1037D] For until then the common understanding of the Church concerning the conception of the divine Word had been—as it is now—that the Son of God was united neither first to flesh nor first to soul, but to these parts united simultaneously, at that moment of time when they constituted a perfect human being, if one excludes a created subsistence. But Pullus, adhering more closely to the letter both of Scripture and of the councils, and also to certain opinions of the Fathers, especially Augustine—or, if one prefers, indulging rather too much in the logical subtleties which had great currency among theologians of his age—teaches that the mystery of the Incarnation took place in such a manner that the Word of God was first personally united with the seed-stuff of humanity supplied by the Virgin Mother of God; then with animate flesh, just as he remained personally joined to lifeless flesh in the tomb. If this doctrine stands, Christ’s conception was not instantaneous but in some manner successive. The Word assumed not only rational nature, but irrational, indeed even inanimate, nature: such as seed, or unformed blood, or something of that kind serving in the formation of the fetus.

[Col. 1038A] He endeavors to recommend this assumption of the seed-stuff, as he calls it, or of inanimate flesh, on the following grounds. First, because in the Constantinopolitan Creed the Fathers state separately: “And was incarnate of the Holy Spirit”; then, “And was made man.” Thus he wishes the first member of this clause to refer to the assumption of flesh alone, and the second to the whole humanity, that is, flesh already animated. “In conceiving,” he says in chapter 16, “he was first incarnate; afterward, made man.”

Next he urges it from the claim that it is no more incompatible for the Word to be united to flesh not yet animated than to flesh without life; but he was so united in the tomb—why then not in the Virgin’s womb? “Perhaps,” he says in the same place, “you will wonder that one person should subsist from the majesty of the Son and the seed of humanity; but cease wondering when you recall that, after the body and soul had been separated from one another, the divinity was no less united to each than before.”

Thirdly, Pullus and his followers prove this—as is gathered from Robert of Melun—by Saint Augustine’s authority. Although others explain it differently, [Col. 1038B] it was readily embraced by Pullus as favorable to his own opinion. Augustine alludes to John 2: “This temple was built in forty-six years,” in book IV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 5, and in *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 56. He applies the passage, as does the Gloss there, to Christ’s conception, interpreting the number of years as the forty-six days required for the complete conception and formation of a human being. He explains it thus, in the cited chapter:

> “Human conception is said to proceed and be completed in this way: during the first six days it has, as it were, the appearance of milk; in the following nine days it is changed into blood; then in twelve days it becomes solid; during the remaining eighteen days it is formed into the complete outlines of all the members; and after this, during the remaining time until birth, it increases in size. Therefore, forty days with one added, etc., are counted from the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on which day the Lord is believed to have been conceived—because on the same day he also suffered—to the eighth day before the Kalends of January, on which day [Col. 1038C] he was born. Therefore it is not absurd to say that the temple which signified his body was built in forty-six years, so that as many years as were spent in building the temple, so many days were spent in the perfection of the Lord’s body.”

These are Augustine’s words, and Pullus seems beyond doubt to have followed his lead.

Augustine was not alone in teaching this successive formation of Christ’s body, from which the author consequently infers that the Word was united to flesh not yet animated. Others mentioned by Theophylact taught it also, and he does not appear to dissent from them when, writing on the first chapter of Luke, he says:

> “Someone else perhaps will say that, just as a painter first sketches and lays in shadows, and then applies the finished colors, so the Lord himself, fashioning flesh for himself and forming the image of man, first sketched it in the womb of the Virgin, having compacted flesh from the blood of the Ever-Virgin, and afterward gradually gave it form. But this is doubtful. For some say that, as soon as the Lord overshadowed the womb of the Virgin, the child was immediately perfect. Others do not accept this. Hear what he says: ‘Therefore also the holy thing which will be born’—that is, what increases part by part in your womb and does not exist immediately as perfect.”

By this he seems at least to intimate that in his time the doctrine that Christ’s conception was instantaneous, and accomplished in the manner commonly accepted by all, was not altogether settled among orthodox writers. [Col. 1039A] Theophylact flourished in 1070; Pullus in 1130 and thereafter.

Indeed, if the mind of the councils and the more generous teaching of the Fathers are examined more deeply by all who customarily weigh every aspect of matters without any prejudice, Pullus certainly asserted nothing that appears to conflict either with decrees of councils or with that teaching of the Fathers which they proclaimed with ample labor and anxiety. On the contrary, it is certain that what the Fathers most strongly urged, whether defining jointly or writing individually concerning the *oikonomia* (dispensation) of the divine Word, is most clearly established by Robert’s very doctrine: namely, that the Word was not united to the soul before it was united to the flesh, and that Christ’s flesh was not conceived before it was assumed. They particularly urged the first point against the Origenists, who imagined that Christ’s soul, united to the Word, had existed for a long time before his Incarnation—as is gathered from Origen himself, book II of *On First Principles*, chapter 6; from Sophronius’s letter in the Sixth Council of Constantinople, session 11; from the First Council of Braga, chapter 6; and so forth.

[Col. 1039B] That this was the purpose of the councils which appear to define something concerning the priority of the parts assumed by the Word—and that they did not at all address the question now debated by Pullus—is clear both from the Fifth and Sixth Synods and especially from those passages commonly brought forward by writers opposed to Pullus: namely, the first and second canons of the Fifth Synod of Constantinople, as reported by Nicephorus, book XVII, chapter 28. The first is:

> “If anyone says or thinks that the soul of the Lord pre-existed and was united to God the Word before the Incarnation and birth from the Virgin, let him be anathema.”

The other is:

> “If anyone says or thinks that the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was first formed in the womb of the holy Virgin, and that afterward God the Word and the soul which had pre-existed were united to it, let him be anathema.”
