For by the first anathema it strikes only the Origenists; by the second it censures only those who wished Christ’s body to have been formed before its assumption by the Word. [Col. 1039C] When it adds, “and the soul which had pre-existed,” it does not deny that the Word was united to the soul after the union of the same Word with the body; it merely denies that he was united to a soul which had preceded the formation of its body by a long time, as the Origenists wrongly thought.

Robert, wishing to comply with this double canon, teaches that the Word of God was united neither to already formed flesh nor to a pre-existent soul, but to the seed-stuff of humanity itself; and then to animated flesh. Thus Sophronius says in the Sixth Synod:

> “The Word, therefore, and God is made flesh—that which is ours—not by being joined to flesh previously made, nor by being united to a body previously formed and at some time pre-subsisting by itself, nor by being joined to a pre-existing soul; but when these came into existence, then the Word himself and God was naturally united to them, their union being contemporaneous with their existence. They never came to be by themselves before their truest conjunction with the Word, nor ever existed at all as some other human being like us; rather, they came into existence together with their natural conjunction with the Word, and did not precede that conjunction even by the blink of an eye.”

The Latin reads: “Therefore the Word God is incarnate, that which is ours, not joined to already made flesh, nor united to a body preformed and at some time pre-subsisting in itself [variant: *counitus*, ‘united’]; nor joined to a pre-existing soul; but when these came to subsist [variant: *exist*, ‘come into existence’], then the Word himself and God was joined to them, naturally having union and subsistence contemporaneous; and they never existed in themselves before their truest conjunction with the Word, nor existed at all as some other human being like us, but came into existence together with their natural conjunction with the Word, and did not have one prior to the other even by the blink of an eye.”

It was therefore sufficient for those Fathers to teach that the soul was not assumed before the body, and that flesh did not exist before it was personally united to the Son of God. [Col. 1040A] But whether the assumption of the flesh preceded its animation or not, nowhere will one read that this was defined in councils. Or if they offer anything that seems to bear upon the matter, one will find that it was not enacted by any canon or decree, but stated in the manner of many other things which, though occurring in councils, are nevertheless certainly not counted among the dogmas of faith.

Concerning the two canons in Nicephorus—if they possess any authority—it has already been shown above that they are rather childishly pressed against Pullus, since they instead of themselves support his opinion. We said “if they possess any authority,” both because Nicephorus’s reliability wavers in many respects and because it is certain from Pope Gregory that the Fifth Synod dealt with no question of faith. Fourteen anathemas do indeed occur at the end of this synod, but Pullus is struck by none of them, not even by the fourth.

What is adduced from the Synod of Ephesus, or rather from Cyril’s letter to Nestorius, does not so clearly and distinctly attack [Col. 1040B] the author’s opinion as to seem to undermine it as a dogma of faith. Those who place that letter among Cyril’s anathemas as number 13 are seriously mistaken; still worse are those who call it the thirteenth Ephesian canon, such as Suárez and others. For although it says that the Word joined to himself flesh animated by a rational soul, and near the end says: “But because the sacred body born of her, the blessed Virgin, was animated by a rational soul, to which the Word of God was substantially united, he is said to have been born carnally”—these words suggest nothing other than what the author himself most sincerely admits: namely, that the Word united to himself flesh animated by a rational soul, because this is principally and of itself required for the truth of human nature.

But whether he assumed the soul at precisely the same moment of time or nature as the flesh—which is the point of Pullus’s disputation—Cyril, the Synod of Ephesus, Sophronius in the Sixth Synod, and others say absolutely nothing. They insist only that the Word of God was united to flesh animated by a rational spirit, insofar as they taught against Apollinaris, Arius, Eunomius, and kindred sectarians that divinity did not supply the role of a soul in Christ, but that he possessed a true intellectual soul like other human beings. [Col. 1040C] Cyril’s dispute with Nestorius, and his purpose in composing the aforesaid anathemas against him, was not this; it was only to declare that Christ does not have two persons; that he was not first a man and afterward united to God; and that the union was not merely accidental but substantial and hypostatic. Nestorius had craftily devised the first of these errors.

Accordingly Cyril says in the same place: “For a common man was not first born of the holy Virgin, and then the Word came to dwell in him; rather, in her womb and virginal uterus he joined flesh to himself, and underwent carnal generation, making the birth of his own flesh his own birth.” And again, writing to Nestorius, he says: “Therefore God is said to have been born and conceived of the Virgin, because in the Virgin’s womb, and in the very conception of the man, God was united to the flesh.” These statements certainly provide considerable support for Pullus’s opinion.

[Col. 1040D] It should indeed be noted, when testimonies of Fathers or councils are brought forward, that they should generally not be understood in the sense presented by a truncated and detached sequence of words—a frequent stumbling-block among scholastics, especially the less learned—nor reduced to those scholastic subtleties to which many wish to subject the doctrines of sacred teaching and the very dogmas of sincere faith, which know none of the hazards of slippery reasoning. Rather, their meaning must be derived from the whole context of the chapters, from the nature and mode of the matters then under discussion; moreover, one must investigate the intention of councils and Fathers, their reason for writing, and the heresies against which they chiefly directed their pen.

The first is obtained all too easily merely from authors’ indexes and tables; the second only by serious and prolonged reading. Since this has been rare among certain writers on theological matters, it is no wonder if they have [Col. 1041A] enclosed within the boundaries of faith many things which rest only on the authority of persons holding opinions; and branded others with the mark of heresy or error—as we have already seen Augustine once complain concerning Philastrius. Nor should every more expansive statement found in councils or Fathers be believed to be an oracle of faith, or an assertion of fixed truth and authority; only those statements should be so regarded which contain the substance of the matter under examination, or which are established by canons or by the unanimous judgment of all the Fathers.

Otherwise, because the Fathers of the Seventh Synod approved a dialogue between a pagan and John of Thessalonica, who contended that angels ought to be painted because they were corporeal, one would have to say that the holy and ecumenical synod believed angels to be corporeal. Likewise, though the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon had commended a letter circulating under the name of Ibas to Maris the Persian, every learned person knows that the Fifth Synod treated it more harshly. [Col. 1041B] From this you may see that not everything pleasing to, or approved in, councils proceeds from the treasury of faith or is always of unchangeable authority. Therefore, whatever one may find in them that at first sight appears contrary to Pullus is not sufficient for branding his opinion as heresy or error; for Augustine has rightly pronounced concerning propositions of this kind, in book I of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 19: “It is not contrary to faith until it is refuted by most certain truth.”

Finally, the passage brought forward as decisive of the entire controversy, and as a sort of authoritative oracle of faith—the celebrated period from Sophronius’s letter confirmed by the Sixth Synod—namely: “At the same time flesh, at the same time the flesh of God the Word. At the same time flesh animated and rational, at the same time flesh of God the Word, animated and rational”—a passage which Damascene also seems to have had in view in book III of *On the Faith*, chapter 2—creates no obstacle for Pullus. Indeed, one might not unreasonably conjecture that he drew support for his opinion from it. For the meaning of the cited text is this: as soon as Christ’s flesh existed, it was also the flesh of the Word; and as soon as that flesh was endowed with a rational soul, it was likewise united to God the Word. [Col. 1041C] The author wholeheartedly embraces both propositions. But no one, unless plainly divinely inspired, could infer from this that the flesh was not assumed by the Word before it was animated.

The Greek text itself confirms this, with the clauses and punctuation found in the Binius and Royal editions—the only editions I possess:

> “At the same time flesh, at the same time flesh of God the Word. At the same time rational animate flesh, at the same time rational animate flesh of God the Word.”

For the remainder of this letter we refer the reader to the text itself, from which he will gather more material favorable to Pullus’s opinion, or at least not unfavorable to it. For example: “He completed the time of lawful childbirth, and through every natural thing that does not transmit sin, was made like us human beings.” And in the same letter, while recounting the marvels of this conception and birth, Sophronius is perpetually silent concerning the instantaneous assumption of the parts, which we nevertheless rank among the principal matters. “The recital,” he says, “of marvelous works: conception without seed, John’s leaping in the womb, the birth itself without corruption, inviolate virginity—undefiled before birth, in birth, and after birth—the heavenly instruction of the shepherds,” etc. Although this is an argument from negative authority, it is nevertheless very strong in law when someone proposes to establish something through an enumeration of its parts but omits matters which, if true and adduced, would strikingly illuminate the question.

[Col. 1041D] Indeed, someone might infer the contrary from Sophronius, because more than once in the same letter he affirms that all things lowly and human were voluntarily manifested by Christ simultaneously and naturally, while he nevertheless remained God in them.

Furthermore, when Sophronius’s letter was read and approved, the council did not intend to declare the manner and circumstances of the mystery of the Incarnation. It was approved not for that end, but only that the [Col. 1042A] Fathers might show that Christ has two wills and operations; that was the council’s purpose. Nor would the letter surely have been introduced had it merely explained Christ’s conception while remaining silent concerning the doctrine then in controversy. Finally, the word *simul* (“at the same time”) in Sophronius’s words must be explained; theologians show that it can be understood in various ways when they examine this Scriptural passage: “He who lives for ever created all things together.”

As regards the Fathers, we readily admit that one reads in them many things which make Pullus’s opinion exceptional and therefore not to be rashly received in so difficult a matter. By this frank admission we spare ourselves much labor in explaining their authorities and reconciling them with Pullus. Yet, as we have already said, their intention, cause, and manner of writing must be examined; then it will be evident that by this consensus of minds they did not provide for faith, but for a certain propriety and fittingness. According to this, it was especially fitting that the Word should be united not to seed-stuff or inanimate flesh—though it is beyond controversy that this could be done—but only to a body formed by the due arrangement of its parts and animated *logikōs*, that is, by a rational soul. [Col. 1042B] For, as Hilary warns near the middle of book IV of *On the Trinity*: “The meaning of statements must be taken from the occasions of speaking; for the matter is not subject to the wording, but the wording to the matter.”

Indeed, even today believers, persuaded by arguments drawn from propriety and fittingness not unlike these, devoutly believe and embrace with better wishes than some others the immaculate conception of the Virgin Mother of God, free from original stain. Yet, from this universal agreement of the Church concerning that endowment of the Virgin Mother—which it rightly proposes and celebrates—no one would say that it is an unquestioned dogma of faith, or that those who contradicted it must be accused of error. One might suspect that the same reasoning applies to the question considered by Pullus, since the Church has nowhere distinctly pronounced the contrary, and since there are not lacking several defenders of Pullus’s side, as we learn from Robert of Melun and Theophylact.

Moreover, theologians agree, after Tertullian, [Col. 1042C] Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine, and others, that inanimate and insensible things could be assumed by the divine Word; and that the argument from fittingness and propriety should be given little weight in this mystery of the Incarnation. For it is certain from Gregory of Nyssa, *Catechetical Oration*, chapter 27, that all natures stand on the same footing with respect to their assumption by the Word. See also Augustine, *On True Religion*, chapter 16; Saint Thomas and his followers, III, distinction 2, question 1, article 1; Scotus, question 1, § “To the second article”; Durandus and Paludanus, question 1; Gregory of Valencia, disputation 1, question 4, point 1; and others, especially recent writers.

Bonaventure teaches the contrary in book IV against Marcion, chapter 21, distinction 2, question 1—but solely because of impropriety. “To effect a union,” he says, “by which an ass became God, or some other brute animal, would rather detract from than commend divine wisdom and power.” Yet Tertullian had already refuted that argument admirably in book *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 4, showing at length that such fittingnesses should be counted as nothing in matters of the Incarnation when they undermine rather than establish the truth of assumed flesh. He says of Christ:

> “He who is ashamed of me, I too shall be ashamed of him. Yet no matter for shame could be fitting except for my Christ, whose condition is the more shameful—as is clear even from the reproaches of heretics, when they declaim with all the bitterness they can against every ugliness of birth and upbringing, and even against the indignity of flesh itself. But how can he be subject to shame who does not undergo it? Not coagulated in the womb—though it was the womb of a virgin, yet of a woman—and, if not from seed, nevertheless according to the law of bodily substance, from a woman’s fluid; not flesh before form; not called an animal after taking shape; not delivered after the torment of ten months; not cast suddenly to the earth, shaken by the pains of birth, together with the filth of so great a body, through the bodily sewer; not immediately inaugurating light with tears and the first wound of his restraint; not thoroughly washed, not treated with salt and honey; not initiated into swaddling-clothes, the wrapping of a future burial; [Col. 1043A] not thereafter rolled amid uncleanness in bosoms; troublesome at the breasts; long an infant, scarcely a boy, slowly a man—but sent forth from heaven, once full-grown, once complete, immediately Christ, Spirit and Power, God only,” etc.

By these final words, and those following, he attacks Marcion. And in book *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 4, he says:

> “Begin, indeed, from birth itself: come now, declaim the filthy features of the elements of generation in the womb—the foul clots of fluid and blood; describe the flesh, nourished for nine months from the same filth; describe the womb swelling daily, heavy, anxious, unsafe even in sleep, uncertain in its cravings, disgust, and appetite. Now launch into the very shame of the woman in labor, which ought to be honored either because of the danger or revered because of nature. You surely shudder at the infant poured forth with all its encumbrances, and certainly filthy. You will disdain its being straightened in swaddling-clothes, shaped by ointments, made ridiculous by caresses. You despise this veneration of nature, Marcion; and how then were you born?” etc.

[Col. 1043B] And after some further remarks: “For what is more unworthy of God, what more shameful: to be born or to die? To bear flesh or a cross? To be circumcised or to be nailed up? To be brought up or to be buried? To be laid in a manger or to be placed in a tomb? You will be wiser if you do not believe these things either; but you will not be wise unless you have been foolish in this world, believing the foolish things of God.”

Jerome, closely following Tertullian’s discussion, argues thus in his book *Against Helvidius*, not far before the end:

> “Add, if you please, the other indignities of nature: the womb swelling for nine months, nausea, childbirth, blood, swaddling-clothes. Let the infant himself be described to you, wrapped in the customary covering of membranes; let hard mangers be pressed upon you, the crying of the little child, circumcision on the eighth day, the time of purification, that he may be proved unclean. We are not ashamed; we do not keep silence. The lower the things he suffered for me, the more I owe him; and when you have recounted everything, you will bring forward nothing more disgraceful than the cross.”

The venerable Abbot Guibert urged something similar against the Jews. Among other things, he answers them thus in chapter 3 of book I: “Do not attend to the corruption of flesh and the stench of the womb; do not suppose that anything stinks to God except sins.” [Col. 1043C] You will read more in the separate book *On the Nativity of Christ*, which Ratramnus, monk of Corbie, published against certain innovators of his time who denied that Christ was born and came forth through the womb of his immaculate Virgin Mother. Our Luc d’Achery made this book public together with many others.

Thus one must not concede so much in this mystery to many arguments from propriety and fittingness—on which we do not wish to determine anything whatever—that heretics may attack its truth on their account, or orthodox believers be hindered by them. Therefore, at Rome not long ago, namely about the year 1490, the supreme pontiff refused to approve the proposition which Pico della Mirandola had asserted among his nine hundred propositions: that irrational nature cannot be assumed by the divine Word. Pico could scarcely clear the assertion of error in chapter 4 of his *Apology*, though he was moved by the arguments on account of which others perhaps will take offense at Pullus.

[Col. 1043D] Let the reader consider why the holy pontiff was so severe in this thesis—otherwise not dishonorable to Christ—and so angered against a man who had earned great merits in letters, whom he would surely have spared more readily on this account, unless it were established that the Word assumed many things devoid of soul, or at least assumed them without any reference to their being informed by a rational soul: blood and the other bodily fluids, nails, teeth, and so forth. Certainly, no one can fail to see how little these differ from the author’s opinion. For the same reason Clement VI, as appears in the *Directorium Inquisitorum*, part II, question 10, commanded the retraction as heretical of the opinion of someone who had asserted publicly at Barcelona that Christ’s shed blood did not remain united to the Word during the three days of death.

Although very many of the Fathers teach the opinion opposed to Pullus’s, yet because they rest upon no arguments other than those drawn from a certain fitness and propriety [Col. 1044A]—arguments which most of them willingly admit ought not always to be followed, as we saw above from Tertullian, Jerome, Gregory of Nyssa, and Guibert—it follows that this consensus ought not to brand the author with the mark of error. Nor should anyone say that those writers are themselves stained by this blemish: namely, Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus* III, ch. 1, and *Stromata* I, III, and VI; Origen, book VI *Against Celsus*; Tertullian, in *On Patience*; Irenaeus, book I, concerning the Carpocratian heresy; Epiphanius, book I, *On the Same Heresy*; Cyril, book I of the *Glaphyra on Exodus*, on the words of Psalm 44, “Fair in beauty,” etc.; Augustine, on that same psalm and on Psalms 118 and 127. These think that Christ, among the other defects of nature, assumed even ugliness of countenance—although all the remaining Fathers without exception, as also the common sense of the Church, seriously resist this, and expound literally of his bodily beauty those words of the Psalmist: “Fair in beauty above the children of men.”

How many more things will you find in those writers [Col. 1044B] that breathe an altogether individual opinion! Yet, because the ray of faith or the Church’s definition had not yet shone forth, no one except rashly would blame them, though they depart from the common track and sometimes seem dangerous in matters of faith. Are there not difficulties in Augustine, especially concerning the creation and propagation of souls? Are there not some singular statements in Jerome concerning the punishment of the Sodomites? And so forth. Are there not, in Bernard, writing in Pullus’s age, certain things inserted obscurely and rather inadequately concerning holy and righteous souls not yet admitted to the intuitive knowledge of God? Yet at the same time almost everyone had gone over to the opposite side; and nevertheless that common view did not impute the stain of error to those who thought otherwise in certain respects. For, as the bishop of Hermiane warns in writing against Mutianus, the Church has always shown this reverence to those who have died in the bosom and peace of her communion: that she condemns neither those who perhaps [Col. 1044C] erred in such questions through the ignorance of human weakness, nor even their statements themselves, as she condemns those of heretics. For a man is made a heretic not by ignorance arising from human weakness, but by obstinacy.

As regards more recent theologians, Pullus’s cause would indeed be lost, unless they judge more fairly that some things must be pardoned in antiquity and that ancient authors are not now free to display the manners and genius of a recent academy. We admit that the schools of modern theologians resound with more subtleties, distinctions, and arguments—especially concerning this mystery—which consume the greater part of their studies, though these were unknown or unwelcome to the ancients. Certainly, in Pullus, Abelard, Gilbert of Poitiers, Richard and Hugh of Saint Victor, Lombard, Peter of Poitiers, Robert of Melun, Peter the Chanter, and the rest who were our author’s contemporaries or near-contemporaries, you will not find that forest of difficulties and questions which throws our theology into diversities in every direction [Col. 1044D] and not infrequently drives it into such straits that it must, even unwillingly, invent many things.

And, lest we step outside the chorus, how varied and difficult is that web of questions: Did the Word assume an intellect? Besides the union with the parts of humanity, is there another distinct union of the Word with humanity? Were the assumed parts informed by accidents? Did the gathering of blood at the place of generation, and the organization of Christ’s body, take place instantaneously through local motion? In what order of suitability and dignity were the parts assumed? Was the soul assumed through the mediation of the spirit? Was the blood assumed immediately? And many similar matters, for the establishment of which in whatever fashion the whole scholastic enterprise labours. Nor can it safely obtain what it seeks unless it humbly has recourse to priorities of nature—language unfamiliar to the ancients—and divides within one instant of time several instants of nature, thereby enclosing ecclesiastical simplicity amid the thorn-thickets of philosophers, as Jerome says of similar matters in book I *Against the Pelagians*.

Again, as though it still pressed down a road made uneven by many scruples [Col. 1045A], it introduced the celebrated distinction between the order of intention and that of execution: demonstrating that in the former order flesh was first assumed by the Word, while in the latter the soul was first united to it. Pullus himself grants this same thing without any verbal entanglements, confessing that the body was assumed first and the soul afterward.

The old should therefore not be regulated by the exact rule of the new scholasticism; otherwise we should have to scoff in many places at the teaching of certain men whom we nevertheless rightly reckon among the foremost theologians. Let Albert the Great serve as an example: speaking of eucharistic transubstantiation, he says, “Subject to better judgment, it seems to me that nothing of the substance of bread and wine remains.” And Cardinal Peter d’Ailly considers that same dogma, as it is now explained by theologians, among the more probable opinions; whereas an opinion is a habit to which the existence of falsity is not repugnant. Yet who would fairly be angry with them for their manner of speaking, which others freely excuse because the age so required, theological matters not yet having been fully clarified? Much more at fault are those [Col. 1045B] professors of present-day theology—certainly very celebrated men—who say that the proposition opposed to Pullus is an article of faith, although they produce no passage of Scripture and no canons of councils except those two from Nicephorus discussed above, which plainly favour Pullus more generously; as do likewise the epistle of Sophronius, the passage from Fulgentius’s *On Faith to Peter*, ch. 18, and Gregory, *Morals* XVIII, ch. 27, which they likewise cite but twist into an altogether contrary meaning—especially if those canons are mentioned.

For Nicholas Ysambert, in his treatise *On the Incarnation*, question 6, article 1, asks: “Was flesh assumed earlier in time than the soul, or conversely? Or were both assumed simultaneously?” He answers in his first proposition:

> “The soul of Christ the Lord was not assumed by the Word earlier in time than the flesh, nor conversely; rather, soul and flesh were assumed simultaneously and at the same time by the divine Word. The whole proposition is of faith; for we have it defined [Col. 1045C] in the Sixth Synod. For in its eleventh session the epistle of Sophronius was read, and in the thirteenth session approved; in it it is expressly stated that neither the soul of Christ the Lord nor his flesh pre-existed union with the Word. ‘Simultaneously,’ says Sophronius there, ‘flesh; simultaneously, flesh of God the Word. Simultaneously, rationally animated flesh; simultaneously, rationally animated flesh of God the Word.’ And in Nicephorus, book XVII of the *History*, ch. 28, this second canon of the Fifth Synod is reported: ‘If anyone says or thinks that the soul of the Lord pre-existed and was united to the Word of God before the Incarnation and birth from the Virgin, let him be anathema.’”

Thus Ysambert; and he adduces nothing further, whether from Scripture or councils, to prove that his whole proposition is of faith. Yet who does not see that in both passages, whether Sophronius’s or Nicephorus’s—or the Fifth Synod’s, if this latter is not spurious—the sole issue is against Origen, who thought that the soul of Christ the Lord had pre-existed its union with the Word for a very long time? Further [Col. 1045D], nothing else can be concluded from Sophronius’s epistle than that soul and flesh did not exist before they were united to God the Word. Nor did Ysambert cite it to prove anything else, when he says: “In it it is expressly stated that neither the soul of Christ the Lord nor his flesh pre-existed union with the Word.” Pullus himself freely admits precisely this, and fully agrees with both Sophronius and the Fifth Synod: against Origen he maintains that neither the soul nor the body existed in itself before being united to the Word, but that the Word was united first to flesh and afterward to the soul—not merely to flesh, but also to the seminal beginning of that flesh.

Ysambert therefore ought to have asserted as of faith only the first part of his proposition, against Origen: namely, that Christ’s soul was not assumed by the Word earlier in time than the flesh; not the second part, which concerns the priority of the flesh’s assumption. Everything he adduces proves only the former; concerning the latter he brings forward absolutely nothing in the whole chapter. Indeed, in the following article, article 9, he freely admits that [Col. 1046A] in the order of execution and existence flesh was by nature assumed before it was animated by the rational soul. Pullus simply admits this, without any regard for the order of execution or intention—terminology, as we have said, unknown or unfamiliar to the ancients.

Suárez had poorly led the way for Ysambert, becoming a stumbling-block to that most learned man. He likewise teaches that the other part of his conclusion is of faith: namely, that the body was not assumed before it was united to the soul; *Disputation* 16, question 6, article 4, section 3, first conclusion. But why is it of faith? Suárez replies:

1. Because it was defined in the Fifth Synod, according to Nicephorus. But the canons cited from Nicephorus prove the contrary, and are of doubtful authority.

2. It was defined, he says, in the Sixth Synod, in the epistle of Sophronius. But was Sophronius an arbiter of faith? Does Suárez intend the genuine sense of that epistle? Was the epistle read and approved to prove this point? And so forth, as above.

3. It was defined, he says, in the Council of Ephesus, canon 13. But there is no thirteenth canon of that council [Col. 1046B], for only twelve are read; and perhaps Suárez did not notice that the passage he had in view was taken from Cyril’s epistle to Nestorius. In what sense it should be understood has been indicated above.

But who would not wonder that William Estius also, even in this light, remained in darkness? In III, distinction 2, §6, he objects against Pullus only the Nicephorian canons and the passage from Fulgentius, *On Faith*, ch. 18, which are altogether irrelevant. Enough has already been said concerning the canons. Here is Fulgentius’s passage:

> “Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that the flesh of Christ was not conceived in the Virgin’s womb without divinity before it was taken up by the Word; rather, God the Word himself was conceived by the taking of his flesh, and the flesh itself was conceived by the incarnation of the Word.”

Since Pullus admits each of these points in the very same terms, could they seriously have been urged against him? For if “flesh” is taken in its proper sense, as Pullus contends that it must be, could Fulgentius have more clearly supported him [Col. 1046C]? So too in *On the Incarnation*, ch. 3: “The very taking of flesh was the virginal conception.” And below: “Nor could flesh, without union with God the Word, having been sown by no intercourse with a man, in any way arise in the secret recess of the virginal womb. Therefore no interval of time is to be imagined between the beginning of the flesh conceived and the coming of the Majesty to be conceived.” If these statements differ from the author’s meaning, let others confess that light is distinct from the sun.

Estius further adduces one passage from Gregory, *Morals* XVIII, ch. 27, near the end—wrongly cited by him as ch. 35, elsewhere 36—but it supports Pullus’s opinion all the more. It is therefore no wonder if Pullus hurls at his opponents that convenient saying of Deuteronomy: “Our enemies are judges.” For Gregory there, arguing against Nestorius, treats the very question treated by our author and teaches that there was nothing human in Christ which was not immediately personally united to God the Word; this is the constant aim of Pullus’s disputation. Gregory says:

> “He was not conceived and born as a mere man, and afterward received, through merit, that he might be God; but upon the angel’s announcement and the Spirit’s coming, immediately the Word was in the womb, immediately within the womb the Word was flesh.”

This is all Gregory says there. Does the author differ from this? Does he not constantly insist on the same thing? Is Pullus not as friendly to Gregory as both are hostile to Nestorius? Must his opinion, then, be condemned as error, heresy, and blasphemy when, O theologians, you assert the opposite opinion as an article of faith and do not prove it? I pass over Canisius, Vásquez, Maeratius, and many others who have counted this theological tenet—though I think it entirely true—among the dogmas of faith, going in a body after the opinion of their predecessors.

Indeed, in this year 1651 we have seen theologians of a gentler disposition toward Pullus, both from the most eminent house and from the royal College of Navarre. Having properly grasped and understood his doctrine, they found in it nothing worthy of an obelus or of the lesser critical mark, provided that for a while the haughty brow of novelty be lowered and the prejudice caused by the language in which the school luxuriates [Col. 1047A] be set aside, and that all things be interpreted more generously—as is fitting in ancient authors, especially those who deserved exceedingly well of letters and the Church, as Pullus did among the leading men of his age, without anyone dissenting. They nevertheless admit, as we do with them, that his doctrine is not the common one and that it would have been better to refrain from it.

Nor should this be omitted: if this distinctive doctrine of Pullus had produced any suspicion of error, theologians would not then have been lacking—especially at Paris, where he taught for a long time—who would not have allowed the unleavened bread of truth to be corrupted by the leaven of falsehood. They would certainly have censured the author, attacked the error, convicted him of obstinacy, and condemned him by their own or by a Roman anathema. But until now no one has even dared to mutter against him. On the contrary, when his reputation for learning summoned him to Rome, at a time when all resounded with fierce denunciations of Abelard, everyone welcomed and congratulated him as another Apollo of the Muses; and the Supreme Pontiff himself appointed him to a dignity [Col. 1047B] of the highest rank among the purple-clad Fathers. Surely that winged messenger of truth—I mean Bernard—would not have spared him; Bernard attacked our Abelard somewhat harshly, so that he was almost driven into exile from the very sanctuary of faith.

Nor would others have kept silent about him, men for whom even the slightest shadow of error that they suspected in the *Sentences* of the Master was enough to make them contrive many measures against him and compel Pope Alexander to safeguard Lombard’s reputation and teaching.

Moreover, we read that Walter of Saint Victor wrote a book against the four labyrinths of Gaul, as he calls them: Peter Abelard, Gilbert of Poitiers, Peter Lombard, and Peter of Poitiers. In their books certain obstacles stand out and delay the unwary. But concerning Robert’s errors there is a profound silence among all. We know indeed that Robert of Melun censured his opinion, though without naming him; but he does not accuse its defenders of heresy or error, content with this single rejection:

> “[Col. 1047C] Thus they say that God the Word assumed flesh before the soul. This has neither authority, nor reason, nor the common assertion of the Church.”

Enough has already been said concerning the Church’s faith and authority; let us briefly satisfy the objection from reason.

The prudent reader will observe that Pullus was not devoid of reason when he held that God the Word was personally united to the seminal beginning of humanity, if he remembers the rule accepted by all theologians: all actions, passions, and other predicates which belong to Christ but not by reason of his divinity are attributed to the divine Word only insofar as the Word was first united to the nature to which such predicates belong—namely, to be conceived, begotten, born, to suffer, to be buried, and so forth, which are said of the Word only because of the communication of idioms. Therefore, since “to be begotten” and “to be conceived,” which councils and Fathers frequently affirm of God, do not belong to him by reason of the divine nature, the author judged [Col. 1047D] it necessary that the Word should first be united to those parts whose union constitutes generation, in order that he might rightly be said to be begotten and that the Blessed Virgin might truly be called *Theotokos*, “God-bearer.”

By the same reasoning, since “to be conceived” is not said of the Word insofar as he is Word and God, but only by reason of that nature which is properly and immediately conceived, he consequently taught that the Word must first and immediately be united to that nature, so that he might truly be said to be conceived and it might be true that the Blessed Virgin conceived him.

It remains only to understand what “to be conceived” means, and what is the nature immediately conceived. Pullus calls it “seed,” or “the seminal beginning of humanity.” But he explains thus in chapter 16 what it is for God to be conceived:

> “What is it to conceive a human being except to receive the seminal beginning of humanity? What, then, is it to conceive God except to receive God personally united to the seminal beginning?”  

And after some intervening remarks:

> “When was he conceived, except when he was incarnate? For what else is it [Col. 1048A] for God to be conceived than to be incarnate? Therefore, to be incarnate is nothing other than for some nature to become flesh when it was not formerly flesh.”

In Pullus’s view this cannot be said of the Word unless he is first united to that nature which, while it was flesh only imperfectly—say, seed, or gathered blood, or something of that kind—becomes perfect flesh. We readily believe that Robert was persuaded by this line of reasoning, because he discusses the matter extensively in chapter 16 after the middle.

Lest anyone be troubled because Pullus more than once asserts that Christ was conceived from the seed of the Blessed Virgin—a statement which at another time offended a certain Louvain theologian no little—it should be known that Bede stated this distinctly and that Pullus had him in view. Thus Bede, book IV, ch. 49, on Luke 11:

> “But if the flesh of God the Word, born according to the flesh, is declared foreign to the flesh of his Virgin Mother, then in vain would the womb that bore him and the breasts that suckled him be pronounced blessed. For what consistency is there in believing that he was nourished by the milk of her from whose seed he is denied [Col. 1048B] to have been conceived, when, according to physicians, both fluids are shown to flow from the source of one and the same origin? Therefore he could be conceived from her seed from whose milk he could be nourished,” etc.

John Royard the Friar Minor, in his *Apology against the Zealot*, learnedly and sharply turns this passage of Bede, together with others, against his opponent. The latter had judged a similar proposition—“The most blessed Virgin conceived her son Christ from her own seed”—worthy of being marked with the nail, saying: “The proposition itself is not heretical, but it is an unusual opinion; indeed, I think it impure and unworthy to be preached to the common people.” Royard proves that this censure is ignorant; but we pass over his little work, which has been committed to print. Indeed, the opinion of John Eck is noted by many as excessively singular and altogether untenable: in his Sunday homilies he teaches that Christ was conceived from the blood of the heart of the Virgin Mother of God. It is certain that the material supplied by the gracious Virgin [Col. 1048C] was of a nature similar to that which other mothers furnish for the formation of offspring, whether it is called seed or blood. Hence Bernard excellently says in the sermon *On the Sevenfold Spirit*, considering Isaiah’s words, “And a flower shall rise from his root”:

> “If Christ’s new flesh had been created in the Virgin out of nothing, as some have thought, the flower could not be said to have risen from the root. But now, since he came forth from the root, he is without doubt proved to have had matter in common through a common origin.”

Yet although Pullus holds these views, in a matter of such importance and manifest difficulty the Catholic doctor, wholly without contention or stubbornness of mind, has taken himself captive in obedience to the faith. With a disposition generous toward the faith, he begins chapter 20 thus:

> “I said that God was united to flesh before the soul; and I not only said it, but also brought forward some little arguments and attempted to establish it by authority. But reason, weighed down by the mass of flesh, often goes astray; authority, right in itself, is not rightly understood. Therefore, except for what is held by certain authority [Col. 1048D] from faith—and especially in matters belonging to faith—I think one ought to speak cautiously and rather by estimation, lest what might through ignorance be pardonable become unforgivable through obstinacy. We therefore firmly affirm the Incarnation of the Word; but as to the time of the Incarnation, either it took place simultaneously with conception, as we argued—or, if this was by no means fitting, though it seems that it was fitting—then certainly the Word became flesh when the flesh itself became man.”

Thus Pullus himself is his own strict censor and Aristarchus. In this we follow him as well. Though we freely admit that Christ’s assumption of humanity took place in an instant, yet if anything harsh or unsound has entered into this defence of the author—which God avert—we willingly reject it and sincerely submit it, together with all else in this our work, whatever its worth, to the judgment of holy Mother Church and her doctors. If, after this, some unskilled censor should appear, I ask him to recall Gregory Nazianzen’s saying in the *Apology*: “We all wish to appear learned and [Col. 1049A] Catholic whenever we criticize others and judge them impious.” And that of Facundus, book X, defending the Council of Chalcedon’s Three Chapters:

> “We ridicule the cruelty of those who are cowardly in defending their own party but swift to condemn, and who seek from criticism of their elders a dishonourable glory shared with heretics.”

Now, to keep our promise and make the opposing views more evident, we give here the entire chapter from Robert of Melun’s unpublished treatise *On the Incarnation*.

## Whether the Word assumed flesh and soul simultaneously

> “It is customary to ask whether the Word assumed flesh and soul simultaneously, or flesh before soul, as happens in the conception and formation of other human beings. For first seed is conceived in a woman’s womb and formed into the figure of a human being; then, after forty-six days, when the body has been formed, the soul is infused by the operation of God alone. Both physical reasoning affirms this and divine authority confirms it. For blessed Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1049D] See Augustine, book LXXXIII, question LVI, and book IV *On the Trinity*, ch. 5.] on the passage of John [Col. 1049B], ‘This temple was built in forty-six years,’ etc., that the human body is formed in this number of days, and that the soul is joined to it when it has been formed. He also seems to hold that this occurred in the man Christ: that is, that his body was formed in the Virgin’s womb within this number of days, and that the soul was afterward joined to it.
>
> “Unless this were so, as some suppose, the truth of human nature would by no means have been preserved in the conception of that man; yet he who assumed the whole of human nature in truth ought to have observed this. ‘The Word,’ they say, ‘could indeed have been in that substance of flesh without a soul, because in the three days of his death he was in it without a soul.’ Thus they say that God the Word assumed flesh before the soul. This has neither authority, nor reason, nor the common assertion of the Church. For when Augustine says that that number of forty-six accords with the perfecting of the Lord’s body, he understands this of the formation of Christ’s body, not of the time at which it was animated. For the lineamental [Col. 1049C] composition and shape of human nature were not yet so developed and visibly apparent that they could be discerned and distinguished.
>
> “But the claim which they advance, concerning the truth of human nature needing to be observed in conception, is nothing. For whether the soul is joined to the body at the stated number of days, or is not joined to it, does not pertain to the integrity of human nature. Whether it is joined sooner or later, there will no less come to be a human being possessing the integrity of human nature. Again: does not being born from the union of male and female pertain more to the integrity of human nature than the soul’s being joined to the body at such a number of days? For although within such a period the human body becomes fit to receive and retain the soul, yet in that process the number is not as necessary as generation itself. Generation itself supplies the matter in which the substance of a human being is formed and is the material cause. But the period of forty days, if it is in any way a cause why the body is made fit to receive the soul, is only an external cause: a cause not from which the thing is made, but one without which perhaps it is not made. Therefore, if Christ possessed everything that belonged to human nature, even though the union of male and female was no cause of his human generation, much less could it prevent him from possessing the integrity of humanity that his body was not animated under the same procedure, law, and number of days as the bodies of other human beings are animated.
>
> “But what they say—that the Word could well have been in Christ’s flesh without a soul because he was so during those three days in which he lay in the tomb—is nothing. For blessed Augustine says that the soul was the bond between the Word and flesh, because the Word was united to flesh through its mediation. But if you ask how, after the soul had been separated, the Word remained with the flesh [Col. 1050A], we say that there are many such things which cannot in any way be joined except through some intermediary, yet after that intermediary is removed, they remain joined. This often happens in artificial things and can especially happen in spiritual things. Very often two persons come to love, through the mediation of a third, and become of one mind; nevertheless, after that third has been separated from both, those two remain bound together.
>
> “But where it is written, ‘The Word became flesh’ (John 1:14), the name ‘flesh’ signifies the whole human being, as in: ‘All flesh shall see the salvation of God’ (Luke 3:6). Blessed Augustine likewise explains it in this way, because he seems to have meant that the Word assumed the whole human being simultaneously. For immediately upon the Word’s being incarnate, he was man; this is conceded by all, and it would not at all be true if the Word had communion only with flesh. For in the three days in which the flesh lay in the tomb, the Word was united to both, that is, to soul and flesh; and indeed perhaps [Col. 1050B], not even then was the Word man. For by flesh alone or by soul alone the Word could not be called man, since human nature does not consist in either one alone. Therefore, if the Word was man immediately after he was incarnate, it is clear that he assumed not flesh before soul but soul and flesh simultaneously.
>
> “For it was not with respect to flesh alone that it was said to the Virgin Mary: ‘The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you’ (Luke 1:35). By the overshadowing of the power of the Most High is signified the fullness of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which was in the assumed human being. For the Word could not receive gifts from the Holy Spirit; for in the Trinity, for one person to receive something from another is to be from that other. Indeed, the Word can have nothing from the Holy Spirit from whom he does not have being. Therefore, with respect to the soul, the fullness [Col. 1050C] of good things was in the assumed human being, or it was in him in no way. Hence, if in the very Incarnation of the Word the angel’s promise was fulfilled—that is, that the power of the Most High overshadowed him—the Word assumed soul and flesh simultaneously.
>
> “Again, the whole Church sings that the Creator of the human race took an animated body from the Virgin. This cannot in any way be true if, when he assumed it, it was inanimate and if, after being assumed, it remained inanimate for forty days. For he then assumed it such as it was when it was assumed. If he is first said to have assumed an animated body because after the assumption, when so many days had elapsed, it came to be animated, then let it also be said that he assumed a man of ten years because he later was such a man. Jerome says: ‘The Word never laid aside the man whom he once assumed.’ But he did not assume him when he assumed flesh, for then he could not truly be called either perfect or true man; nor when he assumed the soul, for then he assumed only a part of man, not a perfect or true man. [The particle *nec*—“nor”—seems to need adding.] He was incarnate before he assumed man. We must therefore confess [Col. 1050D] that Christ assumed flesh and soul simultaneously, that he was a true and perfect man, and that immediately after the assumption he consisted of a rational soul and human flesh.”

Thus Robert of Melun, whose arguments it would nevertheless be neither unwelcome nor difficult to answer—and perhaps to satisfy—if Pullus’s opinion were ours.

## CHAPTER XVIII

The unity of person persists in three substances; Augustine, however, customarily speaks rather of the person of two substances. This question was once of greater importance than it is today: whether Christ ought to be said to subsist in only two natures or substances, or rather in three. Pullus treats it here not lightly; for his sake we offer a few observations.

It is certain that the latter manner of speaking pleased many among the ancient Fathers: namely, that Christ subsists in three substances. The author therefore follows them: Justin in the First *Apology*; Theodoret, book V of the *Heretical Fables*; Ferrandus the deacon, in his letter to Severus; Pope Gelasius, near the end of *On the Two Natures*; Pope Leo, Epistle 11; Isidore of Seville, book I *On Differences*; Etherius and Beatus, book I *Against Elipandus*; Bernard, book V *On Consideration*, chs. 9 and 10, and sermon 3 for the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord; Stephen of Autun, in *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, ch. 17; and especially the bishops of Spain under Charlemagne, both when writing separately and when assembled in the Eleventh and Fifteenth Councils of Toledo. Pope Benedict II, however, disliking their opinion, endeavoured to recommend the opposite. But the Spaniards reply to Pope Sergius that they had not defined it rashly. We also showed in the margin of Pullus’s text that Augustine is not opposed to the author, since [Col. 1051B] he more than once employed both modes of expression, as in book XIII *On the Trinity*, ch. 17, and elsewhere.

On the other hand, the bishops of Italy, Gaul, and Germany vigorously fought against the Spanish bishops at the Council of Frankfurt under Charlemagne in 794. Thus the Italians, in the booklet against Elipandus sent by the council’s decree to the Spanish prelates, say:

> “There are many who maintain that the one person of the Mediator consists of three substances: Word, flesh, and soul. Yet in a matter of faith it does not seem necessary to scatter the counters of syllogistic reasoning with the hand of sophistical secular learning. It would have sufficed, according to the teaching of the most salutary proclamation of the preceding Catholic Fathers, to confess in the sincere language of simplicity one person from each nature: Christ, true God and true man,” etc.

The Gallic and German bishops, in the synodal epistle of the same council, argue at length that only two substances or natures ought to be said to be in Christ. They confirm this with testimonies from Augustine [Col. 1051C], Ambrose, Cassiodorus, and others. We add John Damascene, book III *On the Faith*, ch. 16; Rusticus the deacon, *Against the Acephali*; Paulinus of Aquileia in the *Sacrosyllabus*, praised at the Council of Frankfurt; and Leontius, book I *Against Nestorius and Eutyches*.

Both opinions, however, are safe in faith, and each was necessary in its own time. When certain heretics denied that the Word had assumed a soul or true flesh, the Fathers most wisely said that Christ was composed of three substances: God, flesh, and soul. But when this genuine expression gave others occasion to doubt whether flesh and soul were naturally united with one another in Christ, they judged it safer to proclaim only two natures, divine and human. But there is now no reason for theologians to dispute about these matters.

## CHAPTER XXIII

Two opinions concerning the Savior’s infancy, [Col. 1051D] stated above and opposed to one another, are respectively defended by distinguished men: some defend ignorance, others complete wisdom, and so forth.

Among the defenders of the first opinion, besides others, the author seems to indicate Ambrose, *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation*, ch. 7, and book V *On Faith*, likewise ch. 7; Epiphanius, heresy 77; Cyril of Alexandria, Paschal Oration 17; Vigilius, book V *Against the Monophysites*, vol. IV of the *Library of the Fathers*; Eustathius of Antioch, book *Against the Arians*, cited by Pope Gelasius in *Against Eutyches and Nestorius*, printed in the same volume of the *Library of the Fathers*; Cyril again, book II *On Faith*, ch. 3; Proclus, in the letter to the Armenians; Fulgentius, book I to Trasamund, ch. 7, and book III, ch. 18; Rupert, book I *On Genesis*, ch. 21; and Richard of Saint Victor, book I *On Emmanuel*, chs. 15 and 16.

Among defenders of the latter opinion, which he supports, are Jerome on Isaiah 7, “He shall eat butter and honey,” and on Jeremiah 31, “A woman shall encompass a man”:

> “According to the advances of age, through crying and infancy he seemed to advance in wisdom and age; but as a perfect man he was enclosed for the customary months in the woman’s womb.”

There are also Augustine, book II *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, ch. 29—the passage chiefly intended in the preceding chapter 21, where the author named him expressly—John Damascene, book III *On the Faith*, ch. 22, and many others.

The author nevertheless will not deny that the Lord Christ possessed, from the beginning of his conception, that human knowledge called experiential, consisting in the use and experience of things. Accordingly, he advanced in it, acquiring certain intelligible species anew which he had not received from the beginning. This opinion greatly pleases both ancient and modern theology.

## CHAPTER XXX. (G)*

[Col. 1052B] From a letter of William of Mauritania, which we have here in manuscript together with certain others, it is clear that Hugh of Saint Victor, monk and prior near Paris, taught the opinion contrary to Pullus’s concerning the knowledge of the soul of Christ the Lord. We freely produce this most noble fragment of antiquity, thereby satisfying the wishes of learned readers.

### Letter of William of Mauritania to Hugh, Prior of Saint Victor

**WILLIAM sends greetings to HUGH, Prior of Saint Victor.**
Arnulf, archdeacon of Séez, told us that, concerning a question previously debated among us, he had discussed it with you. The question is this: whether the soul assumed by the Godhead in the person of Christ possesses, without any limitation, as much knowledge and wisdom as the Godhead possesses. And he said that you had answered that Christ’s soul has, concerning absolutely everything, as much knowledge as the Godhead has. He added that you had confirmed your answer quite ingeniously by authorities and subtle arguments.

[Col. 1052C] I, however—if it were permissible to differ from your wisdom—would prefer the contrary view. For I judge that that soul, although most worthy of all creatures, nevertheless in no way attains equality with divine wisdom. This seems demonstrable by the following reasoning. Christ, speaking to the Father, says: “Eternal life is to know you, the one God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John III, 17). It is therefore clear that eternal life, that is, supreme blessedness, consists especially in the knowledge of the Trinity. It is also evident that Christ’s soul would possess blessedness equal to that of the Godhead if it possessed equal knowledge of the Holy Trinity. For if it had equal knowledge, there would be no reason why it should not have equal charity and equal measure of the other things in which blessedness consists—something which perhaps you too concede. But who would dare say that that soul, from the moment it existed, possessed blessedness equal to God’s, when in God there can be no misery whatsoever [perhaps: “the same misery”]? [Col. 1052D] Yet that soul was involved in many and great miseries. For concerning the miseries of the human nature assumed by the Godhead, the Prophet says: “I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the despising of the people” (Ps. XXI, 7). And elsewhere: “Tribulation is near, and there is none to help” (ibid., 12). Likewise: “The reproaches of those who reproached you have fallen upon me” (Ps. LXVIII, 10). Christ himself also says: “My soul is troubled; and what shall I say?” (Ps. VI, 4). Likewise: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. XXVI, 38). Since, therefore, it is evident that Christ’s soul was miserable before the Passion, it was impossible for it then to have blessedness equal to God’s. For it could not be possible for misery and God’s supreme blessedness—which cannot be increased or diminished—to coexist in the same soul. Therefore it is not true that Christ’s soul has knowledge of the Holy Trinity equal to God’s, and the other things in which blessedness consists.

Likewise, by another argument it is evident that Christ’s soul has wisdom less than that of the Godhead. Since wisdom is a great spiritual good, if the soul has wisdom equal to God’s, it will be false that God has a greater sufficiency in every good than his creature. But this does not agree with reason. For just as a creature cannot be equal to the Creator, so the good of one cannot equal the good of the other, nor can the sufficiency of one equal the sufficiency of the other.

Nor is this confirmed only by these arguments, but also by the authority of the Apostle, who says: “For who knows what belongs to a man, except the spirit of the man which is in him? So too no one knows what belongs to God except the Spirit of God” (I Cor. II, 11). Nor should certain words of Ambrose move anyone, when he says that Christ’s soul possesses by grace all that God possesses by nature. This must not be interpreted so universally as to mean that all things which belong to God by nature are now in every respect equal in Christ’s soul by grace. [Col. 1053B] For no one is unaware that this is false, since God is eternal and lacks beginning and end, whereas the soul has a temporal beginning. Ambrose therefore meant to affirm by these words that, just as in God there is a sufficiency of every good, so almost all these same goods are in Christ’s soul and abound in it beyond all other creatures; yet they do not abound equally in it and in God. A similar kind of expression occurs elsewhere, as in: “Who enlightens every man coming into this world” [Col. 1054A] (John I, 9); and in the Apostle’s words: “All things are lawful to me, but not all things are beneficial” (I Cor. VI, 12).

But if anyone objects against my assertion that the soul has lesser wisdom and God greater wisdom, saying that it follows from this that Christ’s person has two kinds of knowledge, 334 I answer that he possesses not only two, but every kind of knowledge, as the Apostle testifies: “In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II, 3).

To state my view briefly concerning these matters: I affirm that, just as Christ is equal to the Father according to his divine nature, so according to that same nature he possesses everything that the Father possesses, and possesses everything in the same manner as the Father. But just as, according to his humanity, he is less than the Father, so according to his humanity he has lesser wisdom, just as he has lesser power. For according to the assumed humanity he is neither Creator nor omnipotent. [Col. 1054B] For although Christ, according to his divine nature, is Creator—as John says, “All things were made through him” (John I, 3)—he himself, according to his humanity, was made in time, as the Apostle says: “Who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. I, 3). Thus far I have written to you only with the intention that, if anything displeases you in what I think, you may reply by instructing me through arguments and authorities. Farewell.

## TO BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1053]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1053B]

“Whence some suppose,” etc. No one will deny that Pullus recognized the impeccability of Christ the Lord. Yet lest the doctrine of this chapter seem excessively meagre in asserting that dogma, it will not be burdensome to bring in here what he sets forth in Part One, chapter 15, as useful for this question. There, having examined and affirmed the rights of divine omnipotence, he declares, under this supposition, what it can ultimately do by the full force of its unrestricted power:

> I would say more boldly that even today God can infuse contrition into the devil and grant pardon to the repentant. I would say most boldly that, in the one person who is Christ, the Godhead can separate itself from the humanity and, once separated, withdraw its grace, so that now a mere man without God might fall into sin, and from sin into hell.

By these words he explains Christ’s impeccability in precisely the way more commonly found among theologians: they assign as its proximate cause the union of the Word with humanity, together with a certain special grace and protection by which God so governs it that it cannot fall into sin.

But the fact that he seems to suppose that the power of sinning should be reckoned among the functions of freedom, and therefore that Christ, endowed with the attributes of true freedom, did not lack it, is true only of that power of sinning insofar as he says that the will, in first act, has the power to incline itself in either direction—by virtue of which it could truly fall into sin at will if it were left to itself alone in a state of pure nature. It is not true, however, of a faculty somehow and immediately disposed for sinning, such as exists in us. For St Thomas seems to me to have observed correctly in the *Disputed Questions*, question 22, article 6:

> “To will evil is not freedom, nor a part of freedom, although it is a certain sign of freedom; but the ability to will evil is accidental to the nature of freedom, for it indicates a defect of nature which freedom itself does not intend.”

Before Thomas, Robert of Melun had defended this point no less learnedly than carefully in his manuscript *Summa*. It will not be burdensome to read here his view, which explains the nature of freedom in general.

> “Free choice is not to be defined, as some suppose, as ‘the power of inclining oneself both to good and to evil.’ For if this were an adequate definition of free choice, neither the confirmed spirits nor the damned spirits would have free choice—which is false. For it is a natural good of creation, of which neither confirmation by grace nor obstinacy in evil deprives anyone. Therefore the former have not been deprived of freedom of choice through malice, nor the latter through grace. Yet the former can incline themselves by free choice only to evil; the latter only to good. 335 Hence it is clear that free choice is not the power of inclining oneself to either alternative. Even though it cannot incline itself to evil, it is not thereby less free; rather, the less it can turn toward evil, the freer it is. From this it appears that the ability to do evil is not a part of free choice, although evil can be done from freedom of choice.”

Such is his statement.

## CHAPTER IV

For a fuller understanding of that difficulty which Pullus, in this chapter, as was his custom, subtly expounds—namely, the question then highly celebrated among scholastic writers, whether in the Godhead the Father’s being Father, or begetting the Son, denotes some operation—we add the opinion of the other Robert, from the aforesaid *Summa*, folio 32, reverse side.

> “Some say that it is in no way true that the Father can do anything which the Son cannot do, although the Father can beget the Son and the Son cannot. They maintain that when it is said, ‘The Father can do many things which the Son cannot,’ this is to be understood of works subject to the Father’s power; for he can perform no work which the Son cannot perform. This is true with respect to things which have been, are, and will be. But what the Father can do, namely beget the Son, is not among those things which can be a work of the Father. For if begetting the Son were a work of the Father, either some work of his resulting from such an operation would be coeternal with him; or nothing would result; or the Son too would be a work of the Father. But it is unfitting either that some work should be coeternal with the Father, or that the Son should be the Father’s work, or that nothing should result from such an operation. Therefore it is not true that the Father can do something which the Son cannot do, namely beget the Son.
>
> “‘But,’ someone says, ‘when the Father is said to be able to beget the Son, he is said to be able to do something which he can do, or something which he cannot do. If he is truly said to be able to do something which he cannot do, then it will be true that the Father can do something which he cannot do. I very much doubt whether any rational mind can assent to this. Therefore, if it is true that begetting the Son is something which God the Father can do, then begetting the Son appears to be something which God the Father can do—indeed, which he did and does. For the Father begot and begets the Son. But if the aforesaid ability has an act with an effect, then undoubtedly the Son will be a work of the Father. Thus the Son will be one of the Father’s works, and so he will not only be begotten but also made: the work of himself and of the Father, since nothing is the work of one which is not the work of the other.
>
> “Since these things do not sit well with the palate of Faith—that is, that begetting the Son is something which the Father can do and that the Son was made—we must consider what the Father is said to be able to do when he is said [Col. 1055B] to be able to beget the Son. To understand this, we must inquire whether the word *can* is taken in the same way in these statements: ‘God the Father can beget the Son,’ and ‘God the Father can create the world.’ If it is taken in the same sense in both, then the sense it has in both can also belong to the Son. Therefore, if it is true that the Father can do nothing which the Son cannot do because the Father can create the world, neither will the Father seem able to do anything which the Son cannot do because the Son can beget. For God is not said to be able to do something in a qualified sense which it is not true that he is simply able to do. Therefore, if nothing is said to be within the Father’s power, when he is said to be able to beget the Son, which it is not true that he can do, then begetting the Son is one of those things which God the Father can do. But since the Father can do nothing which the Son cannot do, by the same reasoning begetting the Son is one of those things which the Son can do. Since this is false, that from which it follows must necessarily be false: namely, that begetting the Son is something which God the Father can do. [Col. 1055C] Therefore, since from the Father’s ability to beget the Son it does not follow that the Father can do something which the Son cannot do, begetting the Son does not appear to be something which the Father can do.
>
> “Therefore *can* does not seem to be taken in the same way when the Father is said to be able to beget the Son as when he is said to be able to create the world. For from the Father’s ability to create the world, it follows that the Father can do something which the Son can do; and therefore, from God the Father’s ability to create the world, it follows that he can do something. Since this does not follow from God the Father’s ability to beget the Son, either *can* is taken differently, or begetting the Son is not something which the Father can do. But *can*, in the judgment held here, is not taken in the same manner. Although this difference cannot be explained in words, it can easily be understood from what follows from it. For from the Father’s ability to beget the Son, it follows that the Son can be from the Father’s substance; indeed, the very generation of the Son—that is, the Son—is from the Father’s substance through generation. [Col. 1055D] But from the Father’s ability to create the world, it follows that the Father can make what must come to be in time, and the creation of the world is subject to this power.
>
> “Similarly, when it is said, ‘God the Father can be God; can be unbegotten; can be Father,’ God is not said to be able to do these things by that power by which he can do all things. If he were, these would be thought to belong among those things [subject to divine power]; but this cannot be unless the Son could do them also, since the Son is equally powerful with the Father. Hence these are not among the things encompassed by divine power. From this it is certain that *can* is taken differently when God is said to be able to do these things, and differently when he is said to be able to do things which occur in time.
>
> “The same difference in the use of this word *can* is found with regard to creatures. Thus, when it is said, ‘Paul can be a man,’ this does not show that Paul can do anything that may or may not be done by him, because it does not then show that he can do anything contained under his power. [Col. 1056A] But when it is said, ‘Paul can preach to the Romans,’ it shows that he can do something which may or may not be done by him; and this is one of those things subject to his power.
>
> “From these points the matter for which they were introduced is easily resolved: namely, that God the Father can do absolutely nothing which the Son cannot do, although he can beget the Son and the Son cannot. For by ‘can beget the Son’ nothing is shown except that the Father can be Father, because begetting the Son and being Father are altogether the same. Therefore, just as the Father is nothing which the Son is not merely because he is Father—although he is a different person from the Son—so neither is it true that the Father can do something which the Son cannot do because he can beget the Son, which the Son cannot. For the ability to beget the Son distinguishes the person of the Father, to whom alone it belongs to beget the Son. Therefore, because this is proper to the Father, it does not designate the power which he has in common with the Father [read perhaps: with the Son] and the Holy Spirit; [Col. 1056B] rather, it designates the singular property of his relation. It does not follow from this that the Father can do something which the Son cannot.”

Thus Robert of Melun—whose position is highly suited not only to Pullus’s doctrine, but also to that of our Peter of Poitiers.

## CHAPTER VIII

“Which perhaps is reverence,” etc. Peter Abelard had stumbled seriously over this point. He wrongly devised that there would be no fear in Christ or in the blessed, until Bernard rebuked him and urged better things. As appears from his Letter 190 to Innocent II, Abelard subsequently set forth, in his *Apology*, this testimony of Christian truth, agreeing in sense and almost in words with Pullus’s present doctrine:

> “Many things are said of Christ which must be understood not so much of the head as of his body, which is the Church; 337 for example, that spirit of fear—which is the beginning of wisdom—which perfect charity casts out. Therefore one must believe that the spirit of this fear was never in Christ’s soul, which possessed the most perfect charity; yet it is not absent in the lower members. For by the union itself with the Word that soul possessed such perfection and such security that it knew itself utterly incapable of committing anything by which it might incur punishments or offend God. Yet I acknowledge that chaste fear, enduring for ever and ever, which is properly called the reverence of charity, always exists both in Christ’s own soul and in the elect angels and human beings. Hence it is also written of those heavenly spirits: ‘Dominations adore; Powers tremble.’”

So Abelard.

## CHAPTER X

“Or just as he prayed for his persecutors, from which they subsequently obtained pardon.” It is not the intention of the author, who is most devoted to Augustine’s teaching, that Christ prayed indiscriminately for all his crucifiers and that all of them obtained pardon. Rather, he prayed only for those—as Blessed Thomas explains, *Summa theologiae*, III, question 21, article 4, reply to objection 2—who were predestined to attain eternal life through him. He seems to have gathered this from Augustine’s words in Tractate 31 on John, where the herald of divine grace writes:

> “Amid many who were strangers, he saw some who were his own. For them he was already asking pardon from those from whom he was still receiving injury. For he did not attend to the fact that he was dying at their hands, but to the fact that he was dying for them. Great indeed is what was granted to them, both by them and for them, so that no one may despair of the remission of his sin, when those who killed Christ deserved pardon.”

Thus Blessed Thomas in the cited place: “The Lord did not pray for all his crucifiers, nor even for all who would believe in him, but only for those who were predestined,” etc. The following words prove that this is the sense of Pullus’s expression, for by them he affirms that Christ had compassion upon the city of Jerusalem when he wept over it in the same way as he prayed on the cross for his persecutors. For he has compassion on the city, [Col. 1057A] he says, because among the wicked were future good persons, whose evils he rightly lamented. Indeed, Augustine writes in the cited place that these were the very persons for whom the Lord prayed while hanging on the cross. Among Augustine’s works there appears, in the Appendix to volume X, Sermon 49, ascribed to John Chrysostom, where you will find a similar commentary on this passage.

## CHAPTER XIII

“Indeed, the devil had no right in the man whom he had deceived by wicked fraud; since, as one who had invaded another’s slave, he deserved to be stripped of his possession and even to be judged for the invasion. Therefore there was no need for anything to be done by which he might reasonably lose the right which he had no right in man—though God permitted man to be oppressed because he believed the oppressor.”

A nearly similar opinion in Abelard greatly angered Bernard. Yet the Doctor of Truth would not have censured it as it stands in the author’s words, unless he had seen it mixed with some leaven in his opponent. For though Abelard seems to have uttered some sound and unadulterated statements on this matter, he nevertheless rashly intermingled other statements by whose contagion he infected what otherwise might have seemed clean. Let the reader consult Bernard’s Letter 190 to Innocent. But let him remember that Abelard repudiated, as a child falsely attributed to him, that book of *Sentences* which the abbot of Clairvaux pressed especially against him as a workshop of falsehood. The other things which Abelard comments upon in his exposition of the Epistle to the Romans concerning this disputed right of the devil over human beings—provided only that one separates those points which he subsequently adds with little fairness—do not seem to me worthy of Bernard’s pen. Since they differ neither in meaning nor almost in wording from Pullus’s teaching here, it will not be useless briefly to make clear their genuine sense, especially as I know that this view displeased not Bernard alone but was also censured by the Parisian doctors:

Abelard judges that the devil acquired no right over the person whom he deceived, although by the most just right a human being becomes, through sin, liable to eternal punishment and to the tormenting devil. Therefore, having investigated the matter more closely, Abelard declares in his *Apology* that Christ by his death freed humankind from the devil’s yoke.

Certainly, a human being is bound through sin to eternal punishments and handed over to the devil as torturer, as the Parisians assert. The author would not rightly deny this, nor would Abelard himself deny it; for in his exposition of the Epistle to the Romans, p. 550 and following, he freely grants it:

> “What right could the devil have in possessing a human being, except perhaps because, with the Lord’s permission or even by his delivery over for torment, he had received him?”

And in the middle of p. 551:

> “By these arguments it seems proved that the devil acquired no right over the person whom he deceived by deceiving him, except perhaps, as we said, insofar as this concerned the Lord’s permission, who had handed the man over to him for punishment as though to his jailer or torturer.”

[Col. 1057D] These words readily accord with what we cited above from the author: “God permitting the man to be oppressed, because he believed the oppressor.”

But though these statements savour of truth and breathe the genuine doctrine of faith, Pullus’s opinion, which denies that the devil had any right of legitimate dominion over human beings, cannot be rejected.
