Rather, the devil exercised a sheer usurpatory tyranny, one which could not yet become stable unless supported by divine command or will. “For,” he says, “one who had made an invasion as against another’s slave deserved to be stripped of his possession and even to be judged for the invasion.” This reasoning is agreeable to many of the Fathers, who recognize here the devil’s tyranny grievously harassing human beings but nowhere attribute to him a power of just lordship. They do indeed acknowledge that human beings are justly tormented, but by a right restored to God, as the legitimate lord punishing a runaway slave, and not by a right belonging to the devil, who only performs the office of jailer or [Col. 1058A] torturer. Among others, Blessed Thomas demonstrates this learnedly throughout *Summa theologiae*, III, question 48, article 4, where he presents the entire doctrine of this and the following chapter. Having examined the truth of the matter, he thus resolves the principal objection:

> “With respect to punishment, man was bound principally to God, as supreme Judge, but to the devil as torturer, according to Matthew V: ‘Lest perhaps your adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer’; that is, as Chrysostom says, to the cruel angel of punishments. [Note: [Col. 1057] Homily 12 on Matthew, *Unfinished Work*, near the end.] Therefore, although the devil unjustly, insofar as lay in him, held in servitude the human being deceived by his fraud, both with respect to guilt and with respect to punishment, it was nevertheless just for the human being to suffer this: God permitted it with respect to guilt and ordained it with respect to punishment. Therefore, in relation to God, justice required that the human being be redeemed, but not in relation to the devil.”

Such are Blessed Thomas’s words, than which nothing is more suited to the author’s meaning. Further, they agree in this: each says that Christ paid the price not to the devil but to God the Father alone. Peter of Poitiers likewise expressly asserts this in Part IV, chapter 19.

But, surprisingly, Bernard himself, in the letter cited above, concedes precisely this to Abelard, perhaps unwillingly:

> “Moreover, although we call the devil’s power just, we do not call his will just. Thus it was not the devil who invaded, nor the human being who deserved it, but the just Lord who exposed him. For one is called just or unjust not from power but from will. Therefore this certain right of the devil over the human being, although not acquired by right but wickedly usurped, was nevertheless justly permitted.”

What then, most excellent Doctor, is this right of the devil over human beings, if it was not acquired lawfully but wickedly usurped, other than that man is oppressed by God’s permission because he believed the oppressor? Pullus certainly admits this, and Abelard with him, as we saw above.

Robert of Melun shed considerable light on this difficulty under the special heading: “On the claim of some that the devil did not hold humanity justly, though humanity was held justly by the devil.” Although he seems, in deference to Bernard, to have undertaken a defence of Bernard’s opinion, he nevertheless wished to make provision also for the other position:

> “It can also truly be said that the devil held humanity justly. Yet those who deny this are, as it seems to me, considering the devil’s fraudulent deception and unjust will. Things fraudulently acquired are said to be possessed unjustly.”

Let these remarks made in the author’s favour suffice. No one will deny that it has been our purpose to rescue him unscathed from the censure of Bernard and the Parisian doctors.

## CHAPTER XVI

“As though they had not yet obtained pardon for their sins.” Someone had thought that this opinion of the author, concerning the patriarchs detained in hell, should be marked with the lowest anchor, as though it recommended the opinion, now rejected by everyone, of those who asserted that charity could coexist with liability to eternal punishment. But whatever may be said of that opinion—which I do not deny pleased certain ancient writers, and of which perhaps we shall speak in Part Six—the two chapters immediately following splendidly show Pullus wholly free from suspicion of this doctrine. There he treats the matter more fully and in accordance with the mind of the Church: the patriarchs and the other righteous persons of that time had not yet obtained full pardon before Christ’s coming because they could obtain nothing except through Christ’s merits and his death. Had this not occurred, they would have obtained absolutely nothing. Therefore, Pullus says, while the reward is withheld, the merit is reckoned only half-complete.

Richard of St Victor expressed this truth somewhat more harshly in chapter 19 of the book entitled *On the Power of Binding and Loosing*. In a manner sufficiently consistent with what he had said above—namely, that the sinner is freed by God from guilt and, through the ministry of priests, from liability to punishment by reason of the efficacy of the sacrament of which they are ministers—he judged as follows concerning the patriarchs:

> “Without any doubt the patriarchs and prophets possessed charity, and yet they were held under the debt of eternal damnation; otherwise they would neither have descended to the lower regions nor needed Christ’s death or any redemption. Therefore, without any ambiguity, they were held under the debt of eternal damnation—not because it was eternal for them, but because it would have been eternal for them unless Christ’s death had absolved them from this debt.”

Bellarmin, however, vindicates these statements from error in Book II, chapter 14, *On Penance*.

## CHAPTER XX

“By biting, a part is taken.” He alludes to this passage of Gregory, Homily 22 on the Gospels, which is found in the Appendix to Augustine, volume X, and is Sermon 52, *On Various Subjects*:

> “For he drew all things when he left none of his elect in hell. He took away all things—that is, all the elect. For in rising again the Lord did not restore to pardon all unbelievers who, on account of their crimes, had been handed over to eternal punishments; but he snatched from the prison-houses of hell those whom he recognized as his own in faith and deeds. Hence it is rightly said through Hosea: ‘I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O hell’ (Hos. XIII, 14). What we kill, we cause to cease utterly. But by what we bite, we take away one part and leave another,” etc.

Augustine considered this difficult question from both sides; in his own age it had not yet been fully resolved. See Letter 99 to Evodius, where he also touches upon the more important question whether Abraham’s bosom was in hell or, as he there thinks, very far removed from it. You will easily perceive that Pullus had Augustine’s discussion in view in what follows, although he preferred to adhere to Augustine’s contrary opinion in Book XX of *The City of God*, chapter 15, and in the exposition of Psalm LXXXV. There, following the Church’s common understanding, Augustine teaches that the limbo of the Fathers was in hell, but distant from the places assigned to the punishment of the damned.

## CHAPTER XXIII

“Unless someone places them outside heaven in places of rest, saying that penance performed in the flesh, as in its proper place, has such power as to make one worthy of the vision of God; whereas penance after the body, as performed in an alien place, does not merit this at all before the resurrection.”

We have so far been unable to discover any trace of this opinion, which the author refutes, among writers prior to or contemporary with Pullus. For although certain Fathers seem to have admitted the view—at least verbally—that the souls of saints had not yet attained the intuitive vision of God, which they would receive only after the general resurrection of bodies (a view which, in Pullus’s age, the Church had not yet condemned), no one mentions the distinction he refers to: namely, between souls to be blessed in heaven, or already blessed there—the former because satisfaction for sins had been deferred into the next life, the latter because recompense had been fully and seriously completed here.

Yet a tradition reported by Bede, *History*, Book V, chapter 13, to which the most learned Doctor himself does not dissent, seems related to this opinion: that a certain separated soul, later returned to the body, was shown a fourth place besides heaven, purgatory, and hell—a kind of most delightful meadow, in which dwelt souls free from every pain but not yet fit for heaven. Dionysius the Carthusian collected many similar accounts in the *Dialogue on Particular Judgment*, article 31. And, remarkably, distinguished men of recent theology have readily given support to this opinion.

While this work of Pullus was already going to press, there came into my hands a little book published by Thomas Anglus of Albiis, East Saxon, entitled *An Account of His Stewardship concerning the Intermediate State of Souls*. In it this new writer contends that there is indeed an intermediate place or state assigned to the souls of the dead: namely, to those candidates for heavenly glory who will nevertheless not possess it until after the general conflagration of the world, because they departed this life either with venial sins or under an obligation to undergo temporal punishment. But he contends in vain that this place should, properly speaking, be called purgatory, since no purification of souls will take place except on the day of judgment; likewise, that it is vain to believe that souls remaining there suffer any discomfort from fire or any other external agent. Accordingly, with considerable labour and anxious care, he proves and defends the claim that no one who, at death, is not immediately fit for heaven can be called from that intermediate state to heaven before the day of judgment, whatever the Church prays or earnestly petitions for such a person, and whatever pious works it offers on his behalf. He writes that the Church’s intercessions, prayers, Masses, alms, and other offices of maternal devotion are useful only insofar as they move Christ the Judge to hasten his coming and the final day of judgment, in the prelude to which alone [Col. 1060B] he thinks souls will be purified. We have mentioned all these points precisely because they agree strikingly well with the words cited above from our author, although Pullus himself consistently teaches throughout his work the Church’s common understanding concerning purgatorial fire and souls there paying punishments to the last letter of the law.

But whatever may be thought of that recent opinion—whose censure we willingly leave to others much more learned than ourselves—it is certain that many things may be read in that writer which undermine the Church’s common practice, delay the most devout service rendered to the souls of the dead, distort many passages of Scripture and canons of councils into a peculiar sense, and at the least cause scandal to many, especially the less educated. Not to mention that the path to vices, already steep and slippery, and the approach to virtue, would become more sluggish if the common belief that punishments in purgatory must be terribly endured—a belief that strikes terror even into holier men—were so lightly to disappear.

## CHAPTER XXIV

“Thus also they dwelt together in hell; they differed in punishment and rest,” a view which indeed pleases very many, especially Robert of Melun, Pullus’s contemporary, in the penultimate chapter of his manuscript *Summa*. But because in the final chapter he seems to hold a different opinion concerning Abraham’s bosom from others, we now first bring his view to light.

### What is meant by Abraham’s bosom, and how could the souls of the righteous be in hell and yet at rest?

> “A bosom (*sinus*) is customarily called a secret place of great spaciousness; hence it often signifies Charity, such as are the bosoms in vestments prepared and consecrated for ministry at the altar. Therefore Abraham’s bosom seems to me to designate no place, but the reward given for the merit of faith—a faith which, although it was first found in Abraham, nevertheless shone forth especially in him. [Col. 1060D] Therefore all who have imitated Abraham in the faith especially commended in him, because ‘he believed in hope against hope,’ are deservedly received into his bosom and joined with him in blessedness. For there seems to be no reason whatever to grant that hell, or any place in hell, was Abraham’s bosom, in which Lazarus with the other righteous persons was comforted, even though before Christ’s coming they were held in hell and were comforted in Abraham’s bosom. For through Christ’s death righteous souls were not snatched away from Abraham’s bosom, as though they were no longer there after Christ’s resurrection. Indeed, in the rites for burying the dead, the Church still prays daily that they may be led by angels into Abraham’s bosom. For Blessed Martin is recorded to have said at his death, with the devil standing nearby: ‘You will find nothing deadly in me, but Abraham’s bosom will receive me.’

But this reward which is given for the merit of faith is rightly called a bosom, because it is spacious and hidden. [Col. 1061A] It is spacious, because it holds as many as heaven holds; it is hidden, because thieves do not come near it, nor steal anything from it. It is hidden because “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9). This bosom is called Abraham’s because he who held primacy in the merit of faith should also hold it in the reward. Before Christ’s coming this bosom was one of consolation; now, one of joy. Hence, concerning Lazarus’s reward before Christ’s coming, Abraham himself replies to the rich man: “Now he is comforted here, but you are tormented” (Luke 16:25). He does not say, “He enjoys blessedness,” but “he is comforted,” because, for the merit of faith, he possessed the repose of consolation, in hope of sharing that eternal blessedness which he now possesses in actuality.

But because that expectation itself involved a long delay, the postponement of the future reward may, I think, be called a punishment for him, if considered in comparison with the full sufficiency of eternal blessedness, which neither can be possessed nor possess [Col. 1061B] any deficiency. Since the [p. 342] saints preceding Christ’s coming did not possess this, they wished to have something which they did not have, and not to have something which they did have. Wherever this is so—that is, wherever they desire to be present what is absent, and absent what is present—there is undoubtedly some sort of punishment; for where this is so, there is neither full joy nor perfect satisfaction, but a certain hunger and thirst, and an imperfect will. Hence also those who enjoy the blessedness of the eternal vision are perfectly blessed, because they wish to have nothing which they do not have, and to lack nothing which they do have. For this reason all the saints preceding Christ’s coming, so long as they lacked this fullness of blessedness in their reward, are said to have been [Note: [Col. 1061D] Perhaps: in Abraham’s bosom, or in hell.] [lacuna] just as they were also in darkness, so long as they lacked that eternal light. It was therefore possible [Col. 1062A] for them to be in hell and in Abraham’s bosom: that is, outside the vision of eternal brightness, and in the repose of consolation, which was rendered to them for the merit of the faith which shone forth in Abraham.

But it must not be granted concerning souls now undergoing—even the most grievous—purgatorial punishments that they are in hell, although they are outside the vision of eternal brightness. For this would signify that the gate of paradise had not been opened to them, which is false. For it is open to them, but they themselves are not yet worthy to enter.”

Such is Robert, who grants much to Augustine’s opinion discussed above.

## CHAPTER XXV

We restore from our manuscript the title of this chapter, missing in the manuscript, as follows: What was done to those to be purified when Christ descended? In the following chapter he grants, not without a certain pious feeling, that they were brought forth by Christ himself and generously endowed with heavenly glory. Although this view displeases St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* III, q. 52, art. 8, and many theologians after him, Augustine is testified to have taught it by what he says in Book XII of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, ch. 33: “That Christ’s soul indeed came even to those places where sinners are tormented, in order to release from their torments those whom his justice, hidden from us, indicated were to be saved, is not without reason believed,” etc. Since these words would be wrongly understood of the damned, they must have been said of those detained in purgatory. Epistle 99 to Evodius and Book XVII of *The City of God*, ch. 11, seem again to recommend this interpretation, as does also the author of the *Elucidarium* attributed to Anselm. Not to mention quite a few modern writers, encountered everywhere in all authors.

## ON THE FIFTH BOOK

[Col. 1061]

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 1061C]

Hence it is more credible that Christ alone rose into glory. This is no new or trivial controversy, which we find debated on both sides in the writings of the ancient Fathers, with very celebrated defenders on either side: namely, whether Christ alone now possesses the twofold robe. Very many modern writers embrace the negative position, together with Origen in his exposition of the first chapter of the Epistle to the Romans; Ambrose, at the end of his exposition of Psalm 1; Sophronius, in his synodical epistle; Epiphanius, *Heresy* 75, near the end; and Clement of Alexandria, Book VI of the *Stromata*, shortly after the beginning. And, lest I conceal anything, this view certainly relies on the support of more Fathers than the other; yet the other rests upon a stronger foundation of arguments and adheres more closely to Scripture than the preceding view.

Augustine taught this latter position in Epistle 99, and supplied Pullo with its chief argument, which I do not wish to write out again here. So too [p. 343] Augustine, ch. 32, Book II of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins* [Col. 1061D]; Jerome, Epistle 150 to Hedibia; Chrysostom, Homily 89 on Matthew, with his followers Theophylact and Euthymius; and St Thomas, who, after weighing the force of arguments and authorities on both sides, settles the dispute thus, III, q. 53, art. 3, reply to objection 2: “Nevertheless, Augustine’s arguments seem much more effective.” I had almost omitted Justin, *Questions to the Orthodox*, question 85.

Yet the author does not judge this endowment of flesh assumed into immortality to be so peculiar to Christ that he wishes it denied to the Virgin Mother. For although this is not an unshaken dogma of faith, the common sense of the Church agrees in that direction. Pullo maintains, in Part VII of this work—and more expressly in Part VI, ch. 51—that it is sinful to depart even slightly from that consensus when the Church agrees universally upon a matter; and he teaches that it is not lawful to oppose ecclesiastical custom. [Col. 1062C] Moreover, it was piously believed by very celebrated authors contemporary with him: Richard of St Victor, in his commentary on the *Song of Songs*, ch. 42; Bernard, in several places; Hugh of St Victor, Book III of *Theological Instruction*, ch. 125; and Peter of Poitiers, Part IV, ch. 19. They believed that she ascended bodily, glorified, into heaven; as did also the saints who slept and rose with Christ. A little earlier Anselm, ch. 8 of *On the Excellence of the Virgin*; Rupert, Book VI on the *Song of Songs*; and Guibert, abbot of Nogent, Book I of *On the Relics of the Saints*, ch. 3, had taught the same. Guibert’s works were published this year through the devoted labor and assistance of Dom Luc d’Achery, who illustrated them with notes rich in varied learning.

Walter, the Victorine monk of Paris, appears to have written something distinctive on this matter in a separate manuscript work, *Against the Four Labyrinths of France*, etc. There, on folio 70 verso, he speaks thus concerning the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin:

> “It is therefore evident from the foregoing [Col. 1062D] that she, who seemed to have neither an equal before her nor one to follow her, led a life without sin by singular merit—not merely for thirty-five years after conception, but, as is read, for the preceding fifteen, amounting altogether to about fifty years of her life. For, says Jerome, it befitted the Virgin to be endowed with such gifts, she who gave glory to heaven, God to earth, faith to the nations, an end to vices, order to life, and discipline to morals. For, while still in her mother’s womb, she was singularly filled with the Holy Spirit; and not only did she fill Elizabeth from the abundance of her blessing, but she also compelled John to leap in her womb through the Holy Spirit—John, than whom no greater has arisen among those born of women. From this fullness, as is read, when the angel revealed it after the assumption of her most holy soul, her most holy body also—remaining untouched by corruption in the tomb for forty days, just as it had been untouched by sin—on the ninth day before the Kalends of October [23 September], was made conformable to the brightness of that body which God took from her and raised into heaven. And we do not deny, says blessed Jerome, that this was done to blessed Mary; that is, we do not deny what many doctors both believed and left in their writings.”

Thus Walter, or Galterus.

Pullo, therefore, would not alone have departed from the path, surrounded as he was by so many guides and companions on every side. But why delay? This is not the purpose of the chapter: it concerns only those who appeared as witnesses of the Lord’s Resurrection. It would indeed be almost divinely perceptive for someone to suppose that Pullo, at that time and in that passage, had the Mother of God in view. Yet even if this be granted, there is nothing to blame in the author, who presents only an opinion, and does so quite fairly, without any obstinacy whatever.

## CHAPTER III

At the present time, the teaching of this chapter will seem unusual to some, in that our cardinal refuses his support to the pious credulity of the faithful. Yet he offers [Col. 1063B] [p. 344] several ways by which such very frequent apparitions may safely be believed without this real descent of Christ and the saints to earth. You may see that these explanations were not unwelcome to more recent theology in scholastic writers on St Thomas, Part III, q. 58, although they extended the credibility—and the deception—of visions and apparitions of this kind further.

Several passages of Scripture favor the author, and Bede seems to interpret them in his sense in the *Retraction on Acts*: “This is what the Psalmist testifies was said by God the Father to the same Lord Jesus Christ: ‘Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool’” (Ps. 109:1 [Vulgate]). “For he was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God; in that seat, surely, of paternal majesty he remains continually in his divinity.” Likewise Chrysostom, Homily 9 on Acts: “Christ must remain in heaven until the times of the restoration of all things.” And Augustine, considering the word *until* [Col. 1063C] in the preceding psalm, says: “The Lord is above until the age comes to an end.”

Pullo nevertheless wished to guard himself against certain other Scriptural passages seemingly to the contrary, excluding all stubbornness from his own view. For his position would be rather inconvenient, especially in the passages of Acts 9, 22, and 26, and 1 Corinthians 9 and 15. But concerning other apparitions of Christ and the saints, commonly circulated here and there, his teaching does not seem contemptible; for in this matter, as in most others, he showed sober judgment. Robert of Melun supports his view in a few words, in his manuscript *Summa*, fol. 68: “If apparitions are ever said to occur of such souls, or of the dead persons themselves, there is no doubt that they are made by spirits.”

## CHAPTER V

As though their parents had laid that dove as an egg. He may have had in view Augustine’s passage, [Col. 1063D] ch. 22 of *On Christian Combat*: “For they say that that dove too was not born from an egg, and yet it could appear to human eyes”; Augustine here objects to himself while maintaining that the dove which alighted upon Christ’s head as he received baptism was a real dove. Persuaded by this author, St Thomas, III, q. 39, art. 7, subscribed to the same opinion. Yet Augustine himself seems to think otherwise in Epistle 102 to Evodius, to which, I suppose, Pullo gave much attention; as also to ch. 5, Book III of *The Wonders of Sacred Scripture*—which he regarded as a genuine work of Augustine—where its author maintains that Christ did not take the dove from birds, but made it solely from the air. The genuine Augustine says the same in Book II of *On the Trinity*, ch. 5, writing that there was made “a certain temporal appearance of a creature, in which the Holy Spirit might be visibly manifested; whether when he descended upon the Lord himself in bodily form as a dove, or when, ten days after the Ascension had elapsed, on the day of Pentecost,” etc. Others will supply more evidence, such as Pamelius on ch. 3 of Tertullian’s Book *On the Flesh of Christ* [Col. 1064A], etc. But let these matters be set aside, having been debated with excessive scrupulosity among Fathers and theologians.

The teaching set forth in the following, eighth chapter requires an attentive reader; yet in the ninth chapter he seasons and tempers it with Christian salt, besides what he has elegantly said concerning merit in ch. 36 of this part and in the final chapter of the last part, etc.

## CHAPTER X

Thus his children are first justified by faith; afterwards they receive the sacrament of washing as a sign of what has already been received inwardly.

We shall more suitably examine the shadow of error which he seems here to raise in relation to the following ch. 13, where he treats wholly of baptism. In any case, he owes almost the entire teaching of this chapter to Augustine’s *Questions on Leviticus*, question 84. For brevity’s sake, we refer the reader to it.

## CHAPTER XIII

[p. 345]

[Col. 1064B]

Several things are read in this chapter which may cause no little difficulty for the less learned, or for those who have not yet grasped the character of ancient theology, unless they are first taught what was the view of ancient writers—especially those flourishing in the twelfth century—regarding the force and efficacy of the sacraments of the new law, particularly penance and baptism received by adults.

One must know, then, that in that century—to which we trace the cradle of scholastic theology—there were many who, neglecting the storehouse of firmer and holier teaching, gave themselves almost wholly to the genius of reason. And since an uncultivated field is fertile in thorns, wearied of another’s hand and delighting only in fruits which grew spontaneously, it is not surprising if they produced many things either rustic or of thin and unwholesome sap. They especially infected the unleavened bread of truth with this ferment of novelty when they brought the doctrines of sacred teaching down strictly to the subtleties of the Lyceum and logic. Thus Walter, in the work mentioned above, *Against the Four Labyrinths of France*, etc., complains concerning his contemporaries [Col. 1064C], writing that they were animated by one Aristotelian spirit. What the venerable grayness of the Fathers had hitherto established upon the foundation of its authority was not indeed rejected by them, but was divided into so many parts, assailed by so many sayings of rival reason, or mingled and confused with new inventions—as mortal minds rarely rest—that the native brightness of truth was obscured by that spurious brilliance, or vanished altogether. Hence arose dissensions in the schools; hence disputes of minds, back and forth; and, remarkably, especially concerning those matters on which salvation uniquely depends, and which faith—knowing none of reason’s distinctions—had hitherto, without all discursiveness and with ease, instilled into everyone’s minds.

Never, however, was there a sharper or more useless conflict than in explaining the efficacy of the sacraments. You will see it represented by so many opinions of the ancients [Col. 1064D] that you will plainly not know who struck the mark or who strayed farther from it. It would be too laborious and foreign to my purpose to recount here individually the opinions which I was once permitted to read in their papers while frequenting ancient libraries—especially since some have now appeared in print with their authors’ names, while others, with their authors suppressed, are identified by not a few modern writers.

But the view which most prevailed, and seems to have endured down to the time of the *Praepositivus*, is that which Hugh of Lotharingia made especially slippery in the *Summa of Sentences*, treatise 6, ch. 11, and in Book II of *On the Sacraments*, Part XIV, ch. 8; as did his fellow-initiate Richard in his special treatise *On the Power of Binding and Loosing*, almost throughout, but especially ch. 19. It is this: in a sinful person—here the discussion concerns adults only—a twofold obligation arises in relation to baptism; and in a penitent after baptism, a threefold obligation. [Col. 1065A] The first concerns the guilt of sin, the second the liability to damnation or eternal punishment, and the third a certain compensation or satisfaction for that punishment, to be imposed both by confessors and by God himself, which the guilty person is bound to perform.

They say that the first is removed before any administration of the sacraments, God alone forgiving sins when he observes the penitent’s sincere contrition. Therefore these authors repeatedly indicate that this contrition must precede reception of the sacraments, when they answer affirmatively this question: “Must confession useful for salvation be made in charity?” The author sufficiently indicates in this chapter that the same must be said of baptism.

The second is removed by the actual reception of the sacrament itself, performed in charity. From their words it also seems possible to say that a twofold absolution takes place having the character of a sacrament: one merely declarative of that primary absolution which God alone bestows when he [p. 346] forgives sin; the other additionally effective, by which God together with the priest remits liability to eternal punishment.

From the [Col. 1065B] third, however—which belongs solely to penitents after baptism and entails sacramental satisfaction—God alone, properly speaking, seems to release. For although the guilty person must undergo it here or in purgatory, unless perhaps it is compensated in some other way, as by a most intense act of charity, still, because the priest does not know whether he has imposed an adequate satisfaction or how far it must extend, it is necessary that this be left to God’s knowledge alone. Pullo plainly attests this in the following words in the final chapter of Part VI: “A human being does not effect absolution of this kind, because no one knows when it is fitting for it to occur,” etc.

Thus, in this opinion God alone forgives sin; but God and the human minister of the sacrament forgive the liability to punishment. God remits punishment only conditionally: namely, provided that the guilty person, if able, will approach the sacrament duly disposed. The priest, however, remits it absolutely when he bestows the sacrament of absolution, knowing that the penitent has already satisfied his own duty and the law established by God.

[Col. 1065C] Pullo seems to have held this opinion—whose most celebrated defenders we mentioned above—and did not teach it superficially: both in this chapter on baptism, and in ch. 27 of this part; and also in Parts VI and VII, where he treats confession more extensively, especially chs. 59, 60, and 61 of Part VI and ch. 1 of Part VII. If ch. 13 of this part and ch. 59 of Part VI are compared, the author’s mind will plainly appear to have been no different from what we have just indicated.

Richard, in the cited ch. 19, seems to have examined this entire business of sacramental reconciliation most thoroughly, though not most correctly:

> “To what was said above,” he says, “some [Col. 1065D] object and say: Those who truly repent of their crimes certainly already possess charity; otherwise, how can what is written be rightly understood of them: ‘At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved’? For no one capable of charity can be saved without charity. But, they think, one who has charity cannot be held liable to eternal damnation. How then does the priest absolve him from such liability, if before priestly absolution, with charity intervening, he has already deserved to be absolved? Yet patriarchs and prophets undoubtedly possessed charity, and nevertheless were held by the bond of eternal damnation; otherwise they would neither have descended to the lower regions nor needed any redemption.”

From this he concludes that in penitents contrition excludes sin and introduces charity, whereas the priest’s absolution completely abolishes the debt of eternal damnation. But more explicitly, he had previously said in ch. 7:

> “Behold, from what we have already said, we can plainly [Col. 1066A] understand, in the loosing of sins, what the Lord does by himself; what he does through his minister; and what he does both by himself and through the office of his ministers. By himself, indeed, he looses the bond of hardening; by himself together with his minister, the debt of eternal damnation; and through the minister, the debt of future purgation.”

Peter Abelard—or rather, the author of the book *Against Heresies* among Abelard’s works—ch. 13, p. 479, understood the administration of this sacrament no differently when he says: “After Christ raised Lazarus, he said to his disciples: ‘Loose him’; the Lord wished those whom he had raised to be loosed and shown to be loosed by them.” Explaining this loosing on the following page, he says: “It is evident that God alone forgives sins by inwardly giving life through grace; and that the priest forgives, not by inwardly giving life, but by absolving from the debt of eternal punishment through the satisfaction which he imposes.”

Peter Lombard stumbled on the same slippery ground, and in my opinion came nearer to a fall than the others. Although he very rightly held that liability to eternal punishment cannot be separated from forgiveness of sin, and ascribed the remission of both to God alone, as is clear from distinctions 17 and 18 of Book IV of the *Sentences* [Col. 1066B], he nevertheless held that liability [p. 347] to eternal punishment cannot be separated from forgiveness of sin, and struck more grievously against another stone when he discoursed far too meagerly on the power of the keys. For in §6 of distinction 18 he grants priests of the new law only the bare and simple ministry of declaring the absolution already effected by God. “But he did not grant this to priests, to whom nevertheless he gave the power of binding and loosing—that is, of showing persons to be bound or loosed.” Nor does he bestow upon them any greater power for this than upon legal priests. “Therefore,” he says, “in loosing or retaining sins the evangelical priest acts and judges just as the legal priest once did in the case of those defiled with leprosy, which signifies sin,” etc. His chief disciple, Peter of Poitiers, ch. 16 of the third distinction, adhered immovably to this position.

The authors of the former opinion, however, [Col. 1066C] though they have less sober judgment, do not so diminish the power of the keys that they fail to ascribe, together with God, the release from liability to eternal punishment to them. Indeed, they hold that nothing whatever is accomplished in this business of justification except in relation to the keys, whenever the opportunity is granted to use their ministry. The author frequently asserts this, as in ch. 51 of Part VI, not far from the beginning and near the end: “Plainly knowing,” he says, “that repentance of heart without confession of mouth never avails, but confession without repentance is always fruitless.” And in ch. 59 of the same part: “Confession is also necessary, because in it, when worthily celebrated, there is absolution from sins.”

From these words and others soon to be cited—so that we may now attend briefly to the author and his followers—I think certain arguments may be drawn which soften this position somewhat and easily reconcile it with the Church’s understanding and the teachings of the Fathers.

The first point which we perceive, [Col. 1066D] and not on conjecture alone, as the cited texts attest, is that which all recent writers unanimously employ as a most present antidote for curing similar maladies which they discover in writers of Pullo’s age, and sometimes in works assigned even to earlier centuries: namely, that by the benefit of contrition preceding the reception of the sacraments, liability to guilt and punishment is remitted in such a way that it nevertheless includes, at least implicitly, the intention of receiving the sacrament. For this sacrament was instituted by Christ the Lord in such a way that its reception perfects the disposition and satisfaction required on our part for the forgiveness of sin. It follows that, although sin is remitted at the presence of perfect contrition alone, this nevertheless always occurs with the intention of confession and in relation to the keys of the Church, as Trent declares, Session 14, ch. 4. Certainly, even the strictest critic will find nothing in the author which conflicts in the least with this explanation; indeed, he supports it [Col. 1067A] in several places, as we have sampled above, and especially because he says in the first chapter of Part VII: “Therefore God forgets our offenses when, seeing us converted through compunction, he does not reckon us as belonging to Gehenna. He forgives the person who proposes to accuse himself before the priest not only sin, but also the ungodliness of sin—that is, both that he sinned, and that he did so many times, at such a time, in such a place,” etc.

The second point which removes suspicion of error from the author—and which one scarcely notices in other contemporary writers—is that he attributes some imparting of sanctifying grace to the sacrament, even when received by adults who approach it truly contrite. If this truth is assumed, he differs hardly at all from the opinion of many modern writers who, according to what we judge the more probable and safer view, hold that the efficacy of the sacraments of baptism and penance is sufficient, as to their principal effect, if they confer an increase of sanctifying grace upon those who must necessarily have contrition before receiving them.

Pullo plainly recognizes this fuller influx of grace in the real reception of the sacraments [Col. 1067B] [p. 348] throughout this work, especially in the following ch. 14, where he asks under a special heading: “What do baptism and the Holy Spirit effect?” He answers himself: “Baptism is therefore rightly received for the remission of sins, because it frees from the punishment of sin, signifies one who has been absolved, and strengthens the life born of faith. Therefore, one who receives the Holy Spirit through faith possesses him more fully in regeneration,” etc. And after a few intervening words: “Those therefore who were born from bloods—that is, from parents—unto guilt are born again from God, through the Spirit in water, unto life: they are born old, that is, children of wrath; they are born again new, that is, children of God. Regeneration, however, begun in faith, is advanced by water and is to be completed by confirmation.” Let the same judgment be made concerning sacramental confession. Moreover, in the following ch. 27 he grants it remission of guilt.

A third point by which Pullo’s view should be moderated is the [Col. 1067C] judicial power which he acknowledges in priests of the new law, as one will find in several places in Part VI, especially in the final chapter immediately after the middle. This is further supported by his constant assertion that priests, as true judges, always loose from liability to eternal punishment, and sometimes bind persons guilty of sin, as in the chapter just cited:

> “Therefore the priest binds to punishment; he binds to guilt, when, after confession, he burdens one person for his offenses up to a time, while he declares that another, unwilling to cease from evil, cannot obtain pardon; and thus he retains sins, retained also before God. Conversely, by absolving the person who ceases and confesses, he remits sins, remitted also before God,” etc.

[Col. 1067D] Richard of St Victor, who adopted the same view as the author, fortified himself with this defense, sharply attacking the Master, defender of the contrary doctrine, as is clear from his Book *On the Power of Binding and Loosing*, ch. 12—incorrectly numbered 21 elsewhere:

> “There exists an opinion of some persons so frivolous that it seems more laughable than refutable: for they think that priests have no power to loose, but only to show persons as loosed.”

His fellow-initiate Hugh, mentioned above, likewise waged war with no unequal weapons against the same opponent. Yet many agreed with the Master: Bonaventure, on the same distinction, art. 2, q. 1; Gabriel, q. 1, art. 2; Major, question 1 and distinction 14, q. 2; Medina, treatise 2, in his special question *On the Effects of Penance*; and many others. Thus it is true—as I observed at the beginning of this discussion—that minds entered into many intricacies, windings, and most obstructed whirlpools of solitary reason when each wished to abound in his own opinion and to investigate by his own light the dogmas of faith, though God “makes darkness his hiding place.”

Let these few remarks suffice concerning the author’s teaching about the effect of the sacraments upon penitents. It will be enough to point to them when we say something about confession, which he discusses near the end of Part VI, but without the windings of controversy and dispute.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 1068A]

Whatever error of mockery or of any other kind is present in the mind. And a little later: “Interior error, not another’s but one’s own, rightly causes harm.” These and similar statements in this chapter and the preceding one are true, provided that the minister does not lack at least the intention of doing what the Church does. Although this intention is inward, and the author does not express it when he adds: “Thus, if there is error outwardly in the action of the sacrament, then at last the sacrament itself is endangered,” and at the beginning of the chapter: “Therefore the sacrament of baptism is carried out wholly outwardly,” he nevertheless sufficiently understands it in this statement: “Therefore he denies baptism only when that which is baptism’s own and proper element is omitted.” And in the preceding chapter: “Provided, however, that he does not exceed the rule of baptizing.” A minister would exceed it if he acted apart from or contrary to the mind of the Church.

In the designation of baptism, fire is usually involved. Gregory Nazianzen, [Col. 1068B] in his oration *On the Holy Lights*; Gregory of Tours, Book V, ch. 11; Nicephorus Callistus, Book III of his *History*, final chapter; and [p. 349] Honorius of Autun, Book V of the *Gem of the Soul*, *On Holy Saturday*, describe this rite. Augustine, however, gives another explanation of this ceremony from the author’s, in his exposition of Psalm 65, on the words: “We passed through fire and water”:

> “For this reason, fire is first used both in the sacraments and in catechizing and exorcising. For why do unclean spirits commonly cry, ‘I am burning,’ unless there is such a fire? After the fire of exorcism one comes to baptism, so that from fire one comes to water, and from water to refreshment,” etc.

Yet the cited authors, especially Honorius, speak of a lighted candle given to the baptized as a sign of faith and of the grace of the Holy Spirit, who then especially dwells within them. Anyone wishing for more may consult Tertullian *On Baptism*; Cyprian’s letters, especially Letter 13; Augustine in many places; Alcuin, Burchard, Rabanus, Gratian *On Consecration*, Amalarius, Ivo of Chartres [Col. 1068C], in a special treatise on this subject; Pamelius, Joseph Vicecomes, etc.

## CHAPTER XXII

He also, laying down a decree concerning the confirmation of little children, says: “Allow the little children to come to me.” Among ancient writers few refer this saying of Christ the Lord to the sacrament of confirmation, whose institution they rather maintain took place at the Supper. Pope Fabian writes that this was handed down to him by his predecessors, and Melchiades does likewise in an epistle to the bishops of Spain. But we have already noted [Col. 1068D] elsewhere that those decretal epistles of supreme pontiffs down to Siricius are regarded by learned persons as of questionable authenticity; and perhaps from this arose that invention of the heretics of this age, who falsely claim that the sacrament of chrism was instituted not by Christ but by Melchiades, or even by the Fathers of the Council of Meaux under Charlemagne.

Pullo’s opinion is nevertheless generous and not unwelcome, especially in that age, when we know that not all persons—even among the orthodox—thought so catholically concerning the institution of this sacrament. Among these are noted Alexander of Hales, Part IV, q. 24, no. 1, and Bonaventure on distinction 7, art. 1. Yet one may also suppose that the author believed that this sacrament was not instituted, but simply prefigured and indicated, by Christ’s laying of hands on children, mentioned in Matthew 19 and Mark 10. In the Council of Sens we read that some held the same view as Pullo and cited the same passage from Mark to prove it.

## CHAPTER XXXI

Therefore, whoever, while repenting, is distressed by fear alone, does not yet merit forgiveness through repentance. But he who gives fear in order that through fear he may impress the necessity of repenting, will together with repentance grant love, so that the penitent may be worthy of pardon.

The author is speaking of fear of Gehenna and the torments of hell, for he had previously said: “But fear generally produces [Col. 1069A] repentance in the person who fears to burn, not to sin.” He clearly shows below that this fear is a gift of God and a certain beginning of salvation; and likewise in ch. 49 of Part VI, where, dividing the goods bestowed by God into three kinds, he enumerates them thus:

> “For in this age God gives goods either earthly goods, which more abundantly fall to the lost; or other goods, among which is fear of Gehenna, by which a sinner is turned from his crooked path; or thirdly, goods by which a person already just may be made worthy of a crown. The first are given so that one may live from them on earth; the second are aids and a certain path by which one may attain those things that are worthy of reward,” etc.

Robert nevertheless maintains that this dread of Gehenna, though generously imparted by God, which some call *attrition*, does not contribute to justification except remotely, and, taken by itself, is not a genuine part of true [p. 350] repentance, but only a disposition. It is a preliminary movement and stirring [Col. 1069B] by which God rouses the sinner, so that, terrified by the image of the infernal punishments which he most justly deserves, he may flee to the lamentations of repentance. For, as the author teaches, “God gives fear in order that through fear he may impress the necessity of repenting.” Therefore, one struck by that fear alone does not yet truly repent but, as he suggests above, “is certainly an evil man; for a good man dreads guilt more than Gehenna.” Read the remainder of the chapter, in many passages of which he had Augustine in view, but especially Sermon 19 *On the Words of the Apostle*, near the end: “Even if through fear of Gehenna you do no evil, you are not yet perfect. I dare to say: if through fear of Gehenna you do no evil, faith is indeed in you, because you believe that God’s judgment will come; I rejoice in your faith, but I still fear for your wickedness.”

From these words of the author and from the others cited above on ch. 13, it is clear that attrition conceived from fear of Gehenna alone—for we are here speaking only of it as so described—was not known to ancient writers contemporary with Pullo as a true part [Col. 1069C] of a sacrament, whether in name or in meaning. Lopez therefore rightly wrote in the first part, ch. 9, of his *Guide of Conscience* that the fathers of that opinion were Melchior Cano and a certain Henry of the University of Salamanca. They think that the sorrow by which a sinner is shaken through fear of hell alone, so understood and not elevated further, is a sufficient disposition for receiving justifying grace when the sacrament is added. But as this opinion is new, so it is dangerous, and it detracts from Sacred Scripture as much as it thinks it grants to the sacrament.

Indeed new, since it is certain that it emerged only after the Council of Trent; dangerous also, and—what is remarkable—so confessed spontaneously by those whom we read to have yielded to it in part. These have no doubt that contrition and love of God above all things are a divine precept, to which one ought to conform at least once; and moreover that, in matters which principally conduce to salvation, one ought not to prefer what is less probable, [Col. 1069D] and rests upon no support other than the authority of those who hold the opinion. They judge and advise that one should trust contrition rather than attrition joined to the sacrament, especially when one is reduced to such straits that death seems imminent. For nothing has yet been clearly and explicitly determined by the Church on this matter; and this is enough for all who, in a difficult matter where the whole issue is at stake, are commanded to let all doubtful points give way, and cling tenaciously only to those things which have come down to us through the tradition of faith or have been established by the unanimous agreement of the Fathers, not to regard Cano’s opinion as rashly suspect.

Among others, Sánchez recommends this in his *Summa*, Part I, Book I, chapter 9. For there, while showing that the benefit of absolution may be bestowed upon one who is merely attrite, he nevertheless gives this warning to himself and his reader: “Yet I would understand this with the exception that the penitent is at the point of death and is able to have contrition. For then it would be mortal sin both to receive, and to administer to him, the sacrament of penance with only known attrition, because of the grave danger of eternal damnation [Col. 1070A] to which he would be exposed, should this opinion perhaps not be true, whereas, aided by God’s grace, he might obtain the secure remedy of contrition.”

The same witness to Christian sincerity was elicited by truth from Domingo de Soto. Although he denies that attrition, as such and clearly recognized, suffices with the sacrament, allowing it only when it is in good faith thought to be contrition, he nevertheless rightly warns, for the sake of security, that one ought not rest there: Distinction 18, question 3, article 2: “This teaching that attrition becomes contrition in the sacrament, although true, is nevertheless not very ancient. For the ancient Fathers recognized contrition alone as necessary for confession. Indeed, if someone told me that he did not repent on account of God, I would not dare absolve him.” You will read similar statements in Suárez, Part III, question 9, article 4, disputation 15; Becanus, Part II, tract 1, chapter 4; and many other more recent writers, 351 who seem to have indulged novelty more than is fitting.

That this opinion of Melchior and Henry detracts from Scripture [Col. 1070B] in proportion as it grants more to the efficacy of the sacrament is attested by that numerous collection of texts from sacred Scripture in Bellarmine and others who have written on penance. They exhort penitents to no sorrow other than the sorrow of contrition proceeding from sincere love of God above all things. Nor should it be said that the power of the sacraments will thereby be ill provided for if the necessity of prior contrition is admitted. For the answer is ready.

First, granted the institution of the sacrament of penance, contrition receives its adequate efficacy from the desire for the sacrament, which one must never neglect when it is available. Secondly, although contrition, or sorrow for having offended God, ought to precede, it is not always so thoroughly pure and intense, or so inflamed with most ardent charity, as by itself, outside the sacrament, to cleanse away the rust of vices. And it seems that the Fathers of Trent, in chapter 4 of the cited [Col. 1070C] session, spoke of contrition thus imperfect—namely, such as includes love, but love not so fervent that it reaches toward God as to be loved above all things. Thirdly, when, with divine aid, charity has attained that degree of ardour—though the corruption of nature does not often permit this—the sacrament is still not without its influence, on account of the increase of grace which all grant it, even though it does not in fact effect grace’s first production. By this final principle nearly all the ancients understood the generation of grace through the sacraments; nor can even their opponents think otherwise while they assign the first place to contrition. Finally, not only does the sacrament lose nothing, but it gains greatly from a prior movement of contrition. Even the doctors of the opposing party admit this, saying that justification by contrition is a nobler mode than by attrition; for contrition receives a more generous pardon and a more abundant increase of grace than attrition, just as the way to God through love is readier than through fear.

Moreover, the occasion for ingeniously devising this mask of such wan and meagre attrition, nourished solely by [Col. 1070D] the flames of hell, seems to have been given—but wrongly—by chapter 4 of the aforesaid fourteenth session of the Council of Trent. There the Fathers, describing the movements of sorrow that precede justification, approve those commonly conceived from fear of hell and punishments, and write that they dispose a person to receive grace in the sacrament of penance. Hence arose Cano’s invention in his *Relections on Penance*: “Attrition formed from fear of hell alone suffices with the sacrament for a person to obtain the grace that remits sins.”

But, with due respect to Cano and to those who commonly employ this assertion, I would say that they have either not followed or not understood the mind of the Council. For the purpose of the Fathers in that chapter is to silence the mouths of those speaking iniquity, who accused such movements of sorrow—or rather of fear—as though they either produced hypocrisy or increased sin. Against them they teach that these movements are impressed by God and are impulses of the Holy Spirit—not indeed indwelling, but [Col. 1071A] only moving from without—and indeed dispositions for obtaining grace with the sacrament. But who, unless he were altogether divine, would dare infer from this that the Council spoke of an immediate and proximate disposition, or that it granted to servile fear those endowments which in that chapter it ascribes by right to filial fear alone? For, as Augustine, the most celebrated defender of grace, says in Letter 144: “He is an enemy of righteousness who does not sin through fear of punishment.”

Further, suppose the Council declared that this imperfect contrition, which they call attrition, sometimes comes nearer to the cradle of grace. Yet it did not intend that it should burn with the fire of hell alone; it intended some charity—by which alone a good person is made—to be mingled with it, when it attaches to it, as companions, turning away from and hatred of sin, and hope of pardon; all concede that this hope can win no one over without love of God.

Moreover, those who more fully champion the sufficiency of attrition maintain that one must speak no differently of an adult’s justification by baptism than of the justification [Col. 1071B] of the ungodly in the sacrament of penance, chiefly because of the authority of the Council of Trent. Yet that the rationale is the same in each case is repeatedly conceded, among others, by the most learned Nicolas Isambert, on question 68 concerning baptism, disputation 6, article 4. But it will be perfectly clear to one reading that synod, Session 6, chapters 6 and 7—where it sets forth the sequence of dispositions toward justification—that it always required true love of God as a disposition preceding the sacrament.

But so that the mind of the Council may be more clearly evident from the Council itself: when, in the aforesaid chapter 4 of Session 14, it takes sorrow conceived from fear of hell as a useful disposition, with the sacrament, for justifying the sinner, it must be said to have spoken there in the same way as it discusses the matter in the present chapter 6 of Session 6, where it expressly treats the conditions required for justification. There it certainly appears to attribute nothing to such fear except that the sinner is shaken by it and, thus terrified, disposes and raises himself to the true parts of penance—hope of pardon, hatred of sin, and love [Col. 1071C] of God—not that it should influence justification itself proximately and immediately, much less alone with the sacrament. But let us examine the meaning of the Fathers of the Council as expressed in their own words, Session 6, chapter 6:

> “They are disposed toward that righteousness when, aroused and assisted by divine grace, receiving faith by hearing, they are freely moved toward God, believing true the things divinely revealed and promised; and especially this: that the ungodly are justified by God through his grace, through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus. And when, understanding themselves to be sinners, they are usefully shaken by the fear of divine justice, turning themselves toward consideration of God’s mercy, they are raised into hope, trusting that God will be propitious to them for Christ’s sake. They begin to love him as the fountain of all righteousness, and therefore are moved against sins by a certain hatred and detestation.”

From this it is evident that the following serve the work of justification in this sequence:

1. Faith in God as justifying.
2. Fear conceived from apprehension of his divine justice.
3. Confidence and hope of obtaining pardon.
4. Sincere love of God.
5. Hatred and detestation of sin.
6. Finally, reception of the sacrament, actually or in desire.

With this sequence of dispositions thus set out, who can fairly say that the Council’s intention was that, with the other, nearer dispositions removed, fear alone—which is nearly the most remote of all—could influence justification together with the sacrament? Is confidence in obtaining pardon one of the dispositions required by the Council, and, to use the words of the cited chapter 4 of Session 14, which are the sole support of the opposing opinion, a disposition “which disposes the sinner to obtain the grace of God in the sacrament of penance”? Yet who would assert that confidence alone, by itself with the sacrament, procures remission? Rather, it should be tempered by that fear through which we receive the spirit of salvation, so that, “passing through fire [Col. 1072A] and water,” as Augustine says on Psalm 65, “we may be brought into refreshment.”

Therefore, from the fact that the Fathers of Trent elevated fear born from consideration of the punishments of hell to the business of justification, it must not be thought that they determined that it alone, with the sacrament, would suffice while the act of charity and its other companions were absent. They only declared against the heretics that it is not a counterfeit of penance, but a genuine, though remote, disposition toward it. Throughout the whole context of that fourth chapter, or elsewhere, a prudent reader will observe nothing capable of opposing even the slightest obstacle to this our exposition, provided that, as we demand, setting aside for a while partisan zeal and free from prejudice, he weighs more attentively the issues in this controversy.

353 But that a supernatural act of love for God, immediately accompanied by hatred of sin, always holds first place in the justification of the ungodly and must never be absent, the same Council taught more than once. Thus, in that cited and repeatedly celebrated chapter 4 of Session 14, where it describes the character and nature of contrition—which we here maintain as necessary—it declares its necessity as follows: “This movement of contrition was necessary at all times for obtaining pardon of sins.” Yet contrition is especially vigorous through love of God above all things. It had previously mentioned this same act of love as the proximate disposition to grace in chapter 6 of Session 6, as we have just seen; and canon 3 of that same session identifies the same love of God as a necessary preliminary to justification by this anathema:

> “If anyone says that, without the prevenient inspiration of the Holy Spirit and his assistance, a person can believe, hope, love, or repent as is necessary for the grace of justification to be conferred upon him, let him be anathema.”

I have said these things at greater length, but not to satiety, since I have always hated novelty. And this concession should be made both to a languid stomach that rejects everything raw and insufficiently tested, and in favour of the author, who, sacrificing to friendly truth, I have thought should be commended also to the Fathers of Trent, among whom truth received most distinguished approval. Yet let these things be said in such a way that I by no means wish perfect contrition to be required before the sacrament as absolutely necessary. For I consistently acknowledge, after the Council of Trent, that imperfect contrition suffices, provided it does not exclude love of God; I have spoken only of that contrition which admits no degree of love.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

“A fountain is there in which the stranger does not share.” All the author’s contemporaries cite it similarly: Hugh of Lotharingia, Peter Lombard, Richard, Robert of Melun, Peter of Poitiers, etc. They allude to Proverbs 5:16: “Let your fountains be dispersed abroad, and divide your waters in the streets; possess them yourself alone, and let no strangers share in them.” Yet they followed Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, chapter 14, who, although he understands this passage as concerning baptism, cites it similarly.

[Col. 1072D] By the name of that mature charity, of which Pullus speaks in this chapter, we believe he understands nothing other than the very grace of predestination, by whose benefit, although the righteous sometimes fall, they nevertheless rise finally, as he intimates near the end of chapter 39. At the beginning of that chapter he also suggests another understanding of the charity which never fails, which we call the grace of confirmation. “That,” he says, “belongs to very few, and perhaps, among the more religious, to the most religious.”

## CHAPTER XXXIX

“Whence it is established that David and Solomon, and Peter also—whom it is not unlawful to believe had already attained that degree of charity, though neither is it lawful confidently to affirm it—men most excellent, sinned most grievously.” The interpretation of this passage can be uncertain and varied, although it is certain that the author speaks in all these words of those three as still remaining on the way. He seems [Col. 1073A] in this passage neither to establish nor to deny Solomon’s salvation, knowing well that the Fathers held differing opinions on this matter. We have now gathered these opinions without hasty labour; but, lest we linger over superfluities, it will suffice to touch upon them here.

Tertullian subscribes to Solomon’s condemnation in Book II *Against Marcion*, chapter 23; *On Prescription*, chapter 3; Book III *Against the Same Marcion*, chapter 20—though there he does not exclude final repentance. So do Cyprian, Letter 7 to Rogatianus; Augustine, Book XVII *City of God*, chapter 20: “He had evil ends after good beginnings”; and Book XXII *Against Faustus*, chapters 81 and especially 88; Chrysostom, Homily 66 to the people of Antioch; Cyril, Book VII *Against Julian*; Bede, in Book 30 of *Questions on Kings*; and the Gloss there, on chapter 11 of Book III.

But that he repented and attained salvation—leaving aside authors of the medieval and more recent periods—is written by the most distinguished Fathers, Ambrose and Jerome. The former, in the preface to his exposition of Luke, calls him holy. In the *Apology of David*, chapter 3, he repeats the same: “What shall I say of David, and what shall I say of holy Solomon?” The latter commends Solomon’s repentance in many places, as in the exposition on Ecclesiastes, chapter 2; in the letter to Salvina on the death of Nebridius; and repeatedly in Ezekiel. On 2 Maccabees, chapter 4, he records this noteworthy statement:

> “The Hebrew books assert that Solomon was led five times through the streets of Jerusalem as an act of repentance, and say that he came into the Temple which he had built carrying five rods. Four of these he gave to the interpreters of the law in order to be beaten by them; but they said by common counsel that they would not lay hands upon the Lord’s anointed, and so he was beaten by himself.”

These are the words of St Jerome, to which St Thomas seems to subscribe in Book III *On the Government of Princes*, chapter 8. Let the curious hasten on to the rest.

## CHAPTER XL

[Col. 1074A]

“This death is in the house,” etc. Pullus owes this allegory of the three kinds of sin—namely, of the heart, deed, and habit—applied to the three kinds of dead persons raised by the Lord, which he develops with a copious array of words and ideas, to Augustine, Sermon 44 *On the Words of the Lord*, and Book I *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, chapter 12 (incorrectly chapter 23 in Gratian, chapter 21, distinction 2, *On Penance*). The author also borrowed it from Augustine in the book *On True and False Penance*, chapter 11, or from Pope Gregory, Book IV *Morals*, chapter 25, near the end.

Abelard develops it excellently in his manner, Sermon 2 *On Palm Branches*, where, among other things, he explains thus:

> “The dead girl, who was still kept shut in the house when she was raised, signifies those sinners whose sins were conceived only in the mind and had not yet advanced outwardly into action. But the young man carried outside the gate signifies those whose sins have already burst into effect, so that they can now [Col. 1074B] be seen by all. Lazarus, however, not only buried but also four days dead, signifies those who are burdened by a long habit of sinning and a great mass of sins, and who, by the example of long-standing custom, corrupt others as well; hence they are said to stink. Therefore these three dead persons signify, as we have said, three deaths of the soul: sin of thought, that is, contempt of God still hidden in the mind and not yet advanced into action; sin of action, that is, sin now appearing through action; and sin of habit, already long established in action, etc.”

No differently does Hugh of St Victor, in the *Miscellanies* of the second codex, Book IV, title 33; the Master of the Sentences, distinction 16 of Book IV; Peter of Poitiers, Part III, chapter 4; and many others, before whom Jonas of Orléans should have led the way in Book I *On the Instruction of Laymen*, chapter 17. Dom Luc d’Achery, most devoted to the cause of letters, plans to bring to light that work, not yet published.

## ON BOOK SIX

[Col. 1073]

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 1073C]

“As also the resurrection [came] to the traitor for hanging.” Here Pullus seems to have yielded too much to the author of the *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, who in the entirety of Question 94 strives to persuade readers that Judas did not die by hanging until Christ’s resurrection was announced. I should think Pullus seriously supposed this book to be a genuine work of Augustine, since not a few later writers distinguished for learning—among them Baronius, in the year of Christ 34, no. 74—attribute it to Augustine. But the school of Louvain, following Jerome, cast this offspring, unworthy of such a parent, into a corner. Jerome, if I am not mistaken, loathing the trivialities of this work, writes to Evagrius that its author was unskilled in language and learning. Not a few conjecture it was written by a certain Hilary, a Roman deacon who ardently supported the Luciferians.

Maldonatus writes that some held this opinion that Judas was hanged after the resurrection. [Col. 1073D] Whether he read any besides this Hilary, we do not know. The true Augustine teaches the opposite on Psalm 108: “‘Let his days be few’ means the days of his apostleship, which were few, since before the Lord’s Passion they were consumed by his crime and death.”

## CHAPTER XXI

“Whom the rival form of the cross bars from his attempt, Tau impressed upon the forehead.” A notable passage concerning Exodus 13:24 and Ezekiel 9:4: “Pass through the midst of the city, in the midst of Jerusalem, and mark Tau upon the foreheads of the men who groan.” Not a few ancients observed that this letter, last among the ancient Hebrew letters, resembles a cross: Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 11, and Book III *Against Marcion*: “For it is the Greek letter Tau itself, but our T, the form of the cross, which it foreshadowed would be upon our foreheads in the true and Catholic Jerusalem.” Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, and Book II of the *Testimonies against the Jews*, chapter 22: “That in this sign of the cross there is salvation for all who are marked on their foreheads, God says through Ezekiel: ‘Pass through the midst of Jerusalem and mark a sign upon the foreheads,’ etc.” Jerome in the commentary of the author of the book *On the Disputation of Church and Synagogue*, about the middle, among Augustine’s spurious works in volume VI, etc.

In very ancient Missals also, not infrequently—for example, among the Cluniacs—we find, in place of the initial letter of the canon, *Te igitur*, etc., the figure of a cross drawn by the ancients. The Samaritan alphabet also—whose users retained the ancient Hebrew characters—depicts its last letter in the form of such a cross.

“Certainly by the ministry of angels holy souls are always transferred into rest; by the ministry of demons, wicked souls into hell.” Jerome on chapter 7 of Daniel and Ambrose, Letter 21 of Book VII, think that both are done through the ministry of demons. But the more numerous party among the Fathers and theologians, together with prayers prescribed in ecclesiastical Rituals, favour Pullus’s opinion. Among them is Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* IV, by whom the angels are called τῇ ἀνόδῳ ἐφεστῶτες, “those set over the ascent of souls.”

## CHAPTER XXIV

“Thus all kingdoms also are believed to have been entrusted to the guardianship of angels.” The views of nearly all the Fathers concur in this opinion, persuaded by the same testimony of Moses as Pullus. See especially Dionysius, chapter 9 of *The Celestial Hierarchy*; Origen in many places, but notably Homily 35 on Luke and Book V *Against Celsus*; Eusebius, Book IV *Evangelical Demonstration*, chapter 6; Chrysostom’s homily on the archangels; Theodoret on Daniel 10; Isidore of Pelusium, Letter 85; Clement, *Stromata* VI: “The offices of angelic rulers are distributed among nations and cities”; Epiphanius, Heresy 51; and Basil, Book III *Against Eunomius*.

Many Latins agree, likewise following the Seventy Interpreters: the author of the *Recognitions*, Book II; Jerome on Daniel 7; Rufinus, *On the Apostles’ Creed*; Gregory, Book XVII of the *Morals*, chapter 8 throughout; Isidore, Book I *On the Supreme Good*, chapters 12 and 7; Origen, chapter 5: “Hence it appears,” he says, “that there is no place over which angels do not preside.” Aureolus should be read in the *Flowers*, title 33, §6.

That presiding angels are also present with churches, oratories, and sacred [Col. 1075B] gatherings and buildings of religious persons is so frequently mentioned by the Fathers and writers of ecclesiastical history, and is now so commonly encountered, that it is tiresome to rehearse it here. Consult the same Aureolus, title 34, chapter 3, sessions 1, 2, and 3.

“Whence Moses according to another translation.” He means the Septuagint version:

> Ὅτε διεμέριζεν ὁ Ὕψιστος ἔθνη, ὡς διέσπειρεν υἱοὺς Ἀδάμ, ἔστησεν ὅρια ἐθνῶν κατὰ ἀριθμὸν ἀγγέλων Θεοῦ.

> “When the Most High divided the nations, as he scattered the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God.”

The Greeks greatly approved this reading, although they also mention the other. Nor do we find few Latins to whom it was likewise pleasing: Jerome on the cited Daniel 7; Gregory, Homily 34 on the Gospels; Victorinus of Pettau in his work on Revelation; etc. Incidentally, it may be useful to note that Pullus owes the greater part of those writers whom he here cites at such length to Gregory and Isidore in the cited passages, to Cassian in Conference 8, and to Dionysius, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, who held the torch before them all.

## CHAPTER XXV

[Col. 1075C]

“For Josephus relates,” etc. In Book VII, chapter 12 of *The Jewish War*: “Before sunset, chariots were seen carried through the air over all the regions, and armed battle-lines passing through the clouds and surrounding the city. But on the festival day called Pentecost, when at night the priests entered the inner Temple, according to their custom, to celebrate the divine rites, they first perceived a certain fear and noise; afterward they heard a sudden voice saying, ‘Let us depart from here.’” Hegesippus also mentions this, Book V of *The Destruction of Jerusalem*, chapter 44; Tacitus, Book V of the *Histories*; Eusebius, *History*, Book II, chapter 8; and St Jerome writing to Paula and Eustochium.

Josephus writes that this voice was heard at Pentecost and foretold the destruction of the city. Jerome does not agree, teaching in Letter 17 that it was a mournful lament for the Lord’s Passion. Whether Hilary aimed at this when, in the final canon [Col. 1075D] on Matthew, he writes that the rending of the veil in the middle signified the departure of the angels guarding the Temple, we do not know. “The honour of the veil,” he says, “together with the guardianship of the protecting angel, is removed.” Spondanus, the illustrious bishop of Appamia, thought the angels uttered this voice more than once in the Temple at Jerusalem, in his abridgment of Baronius, under the year of the Lord 34, no. 38; and we readily agree with him.

Some, however, think angels are appointed over nations—evil angels over evil nations—as princes. Cassian himself, among others, in Conference 8:

> “It is manifest that opposing powers wage discord, conflict, and hostility against one another, which the nations conduct among themselves at their instigation; that they rejoice in the victory of their own nations and are tormented likewise by their diminution; and that, for this reason, they cannot be at peace with one another, since each continually strives with restless rivalry on behalf of those over whom he presides against the ruler of another nation. From this we may evidently infer that, apart from the reasons and opinions set out above, those unclean spirits are called principalities or powers, etc.”

Thus he speaks in chapter 13, holding precisely this view of the government of kingdoms through angels as he does of the guardianship of each individual person. In chapter 17 of the same Conference he assigns to each person two angels, one good and one evil.

Origen should also be consulted, Homily 9 on Genesis, and Jerome on Isaiah 25, who inclines toward the opinion that the princes mentioned in Daniel are those who “did not keep their own principality,” etc.

“I will visit upon the kings and princes of the earth, the rulers of this darkness and the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.” Of these princes presiding over different provinces it is also written in Daniel: “The prince of the kingdom of the Persians came out to meet me; and the prince of the Medes, and the prince of the Greeks.” Some others, later than Robert, [Col. 1076B] subscribed to this opinion; we therefore pass them over.

The opinions of the other Fathers, however, turn elsewhere. They aptly describe, and set forth at length, the sense in which the most blessed spirits wage disputes and conflicts with one another. Among them see Isidore of Pelusium, Letter 85, Book II; Gregory, *Morals*, Book XVII, chapter 8; and Chrysostom—but I do not presently recall where.

## CHAPTER XXX

“Although some think that some go about ministering, while others stand by contemplating.” No minor question was debated among the ancients: are all angelic spirits without distinction sent by God, or does this belong only to the lower orders? Or, at least, do some stand by while others range hither and thither, endeavouring to procure human salvation? Saint Dionysius, chapters 8 and 13 of *The Celestial Hierarchy*, firmly asserts that the highest [Col. 1076C] spirits are never sent down to these lower things. Thus he says: “Those higher ranks never depart from the inner mysteries, because, insofar as they excel, they never perform an external office.”

Gregory follows him, as cited above, in Homily 34 on the Gospels, and finally many other theologians of the middle and later ages: specifically Hervaeus of Bourg-Dieu, among the works of St Anselm, on chapter 1 of the Epistle to the Hebrews; and St Thomas, Part I, question 112, article 2 and following. He allows that the five lowest orders are sometimes sent; but he denies that the Dominations and the three other orders of the first, or higher, hierarchy ever depart at all, or serve in these lower matters. But how little fairly disposed toward antiquity he is in this point—if Dionysius is excepted—appears from the fact that among the ancients who treated angels more carefully, scarcely one can be found who did not cast his vote for the contrary opinion. Thus you see that Pullus, most devoted to the venerable antiquity of the Fathers, rightly conceded to their views.

For, to select a few from many: the author of the *Questions to the Orthodox*, among the works of Justin, question 30; Eusebius, Book VII *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 6:
