> “We are taught by Scripture to believe that the ministering powers and spirits sent for service on behalf of those who are to receive the inheritance of eternal life—I mean the holy angels of God—enjoy the divine light and for that reason are compared with the lights of heaven; whereas certain perverse spirits, unable through their wickedness to receive the divine light, became darkness. The first of these, etc.”

Athanasius, in Orations 2, 4, and 5 against the Arians, proves at length, in accordance with the author’s mind, the divinity of the Son from the sending of all angels to earth. And in Oration 3: “There are many archangels, many thrones, dominations, and powers; thousands upon thousands and ten thousand times ten thousand ministers stand by and appear, offering themselves ready to be sent.” No less explicitly Didymus proves the divinity of the Holy Spirit by this same argument in the first book bearing this title, where, discussing the Apostle’s passage to [Col. 1077A] the Hebrews, he declares among other things:

> “Speaking of all invisible creatures, he says that they are ministering spirits; for which reason he adds: ‘Are they not all,’ etc. For although not every invisible creature has been sent individually, yet because others of the same kind and rank have been sent, they too have in a certain manner been sent in possibility, being companions of those sent and of equal substance.”

Ambrose, Book I *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 10; Chrysostom, Homily 8 on Genesis and at the same passage in Hebrews; Pseudo-Ambrose on the same passage; Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 34 near the end; Jerome, Letter 142; Gregory of Nyssa, Book I *Against Eunomius*; and, most fully of all and most in accordance with Pullus’s thought, Primasius in his exposition of the Apostle’s aforementioned passage to the Hebrews, also tend in the same direction. For he mentions the very spirits who stand by, 358 and contends with the author that they sometimes go forth to minister. Some of his works are extant in volume I of the *Library of the Fathers*.

These things have been said rather more fully, both because of the importance of the matter and in favour of Pullus, to whom this opinion was especially pleasing. He relied principally upon Paul’s argument in Hebrews 1: “Are they not all ministering spirits,” etc. From the universal deputation of all heavenly spirits to earth for the sake of those who receive the inheritance of salvation, the Apostle proves most forcefully that Christ is to be preferred to them all. The force of Paul’s argument would be diminished if some angels were perpetually at leisure or, as they say, stood by immovably. Radbertus of Corbie did not sufficiently perceive this force of the argument, nor did very many later writers who introduce prejudice against truth in their commentaries on this passage.

## CHAPTER XXXII

“But it is the tradition, they say, of the venerable Dionysius.” He teaches this at length in *The Celestial Hierarchy*, especially chapter 13. When its author saw himself pressed by the authority of Isaiah 6, which testifies that one of the seraphim came from heaven to purify the prophet’s lips, he wished the passage to be understood in such a way that not someone of that highest order, but another angel of the lower hierarchy, performed that office. He did so in a mode of speech not alien to the genius of Scripture, which even applies the name of God to those angels who carry out his commands concerning us. Above we praised Gregory, who likewise defended himself by this interpretation of Dionysius.

But adhering more closely to the letter, Gerson, Chancellor of Paris, in the *Trilogy*, denies that it can be said without suspicion of heresy: “Not all angels are ministering spirits, given for service on behalf of those who are to obtain the inheritance of salvation.” Gerson speaks somewhat harshly, but generously in favour of Pullus’s opinion. Not ill suited to it are the words which the aforementioned Jerome, writing to Damasus in his own name and that of others, declares thus:

> “A certain Greek, very learned in the Scriptures, explained that the seraphim are certain powers in heaven which, standing before the tribunal [Col. 1077D] of God, praise him and are sent on various ministries, especially to those who need cleansing and deserve, because of former sins, to be purified in some measure by punishments.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

“The Virtues are those through whose ministry miracles are performed.” Dionysius, cited differently, says:

> Τὴν δὲ τῶν ἁγίων δυνάμεων ἀῤῥενωπόν τινα καὶ ἀκατάσειστον ἀνδρείαν εἰς πάσας κατ’ αὐτῶν θεοειδεῖς ἐνεργείας πρὸς μηδεμίαν ὑποδοχὴν τῶν ἀνδιδομένων αὐτῇ θεαρχικῶν ἐλλάμψεων ἀδρανῶς ἐξασθενοῦσαν, δυνατῶς ἐπὶ τὰ θεομίμητα ἀναγομένην.

That is to say: “By this designation of the Virtues is signified a certain virile, manly, and unshaken courage, by which, endowed for the performance of all their God-like operations, they are not weak or sluggish in receiving any of the divine illuminations bestowed upon them, but are powerfully raised to imitation of God.”

Gregory, Isidore, and Bernard, however, write with the author that miracles are performed by them. Thus Bernard in Book V *On Consideration*, chapter 4: “Let us suppose that above these archangels are the Virtues, at whose command or through whose operation signs and wonders occurring in the elements or made from the elements appear for the admonition of mortals,” etc. And Peter Abelard, Book III of the *Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans*, p. 643: “Those through whom signs and miracles are more frequently performed are called Virtues.”

“They say that angels are present at the holy sacrament of the Mass.” From Tertullian’s passage *On Prayer*, chapter 12—“while the angel of prayer is still standing by”—Pamelius says that the holy Fathers Ambrose, Augustine, and Chrysostom infer that a multitude of angels is present at our Christian sacrifice. Hence is confirmed that part of the Canon: “Humbly we beseech thee, almighty God, command these things to be borne by the hands of thy holy angel,” etc. And the author of the liturgy circulated under James’s name says: “Christ our God goes forth [Col. 1078B] to be sacrificed and given as food to the faithful. Before him proceed choirs of angels with every principality and power; the many-eyed cherubim and the six-winged seraphim, veiling their faces,” etc.

Nilus, a monk of Constantinople and disciple of Chrysostom, reports in a letter to Anastasius that, while he was serving as teacher in a church, angels familiar to him were accustomed to be present and to stand bowed around the altar. King Canute of England attests a similar multitude of angels attending the sacred mysteries in chapter 4 of his ecclesiastical laws. But others say more on these matters.

## CHAPTER XLII
Although the Jews maintain, and very many agree with them in this, that this was Michael. Jerome seems among others to have held this view, for in chapter VIII of Daniel he endorses the Jewish opinion on the matter: “The Jews say that this man, who commanded Gabriel to make Daniel understand the vision, was Michael. Accordingly, because the vision concerned battles and the contests of kings—indeed, the succession of kingdoms—Gabriel, who is set over battles, is assigned to this office, etc. But where prosperity is promised to the people, and *hilasmos* [ἱλασμός], [Col. 1078C] which we may call God’s propitiation or expiation, is required, Michael is sent, whose name means ‘Who is like God?’—so that it may be understood that no one except God can offer [or: effect] propitiation or expiation.” See this passage in the gloss at that place and in other writers who followed Jerome. Yet Theodoret and Isidore Clarius, on the same passage, think it more probable that this was not any angel but the Lord Himself. “From what has been said,” says Theodoret, “it may be inferred that it was the Lord.” And Isidore: “According to the Hebrews, a certain great angel is signified, whose name was wonderful and hidden. He is Christ, the master also of the angels.” But Jerome’s interpretation is preferable.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

“Therefore he will more properly be reckoned next to the cherubim.” Athanasius seems to have held this opinion in his Letter to Serapion: “But the devil, who was among the cherubim [Col. 1078D] and was the seal of likeness, fell from heaven like lightning.” Cyril too seems to have held it in Book I of the *Glaphyra*, on the basis of the very testimony examined by the author; Saint Thomas adopted Cyril’s answer to it in *Summa Theologiae*, I, question 63, article 7, reply to objection 1.

“Nor was he the greatest who fell.” In his customary way, Pullus follows Augustine, who discusses this matter in scholastic fashion in Book II of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 18 and following. Yet he inclines to that side of the question which denies that the highest of all the angels fell. Although this view was unwelcome to many of the ancients, and today has, so far as I know, not even one defender, I shall nevertheless not allow the author to proceed alone—as is my duty. First, I shall join to him John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith*, Book II, chapter 4. Writing that those heavenly powers which presided over the earthly order as governors were banished from the number of heavenly powers, he judges that not the prince of all spirits fell away: “Of those angelic powers, that one which presided over the earthly order, and to whom [Col. 1079A] the guardianship of the earth had been entrusted by God, etc., was the first to fall away from good and to be established in evil.” Likewise Maximus, the scholiast on Dionysius, on chapter 11 of *The Celestial Hierarchy*; and Gregory of Nyssa in his catechetical discourse, etc. Wishing to accommodate their view, Saint Thomas, already cited, does not strike that opinion with any theological anathema.

“Others, however, etc.” From this point through the end of the chapter, the author copied word for word from Augustine’s Book II of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapters 23 and 24.

## 360 CHAPTER XLIX

“He stains it with a twofold foulness.” This is sound doctrine, and as it were an antidote to that poisonous evil which at that time was swelling in Peter Abelard, Robert’s rival. Abelard denied that the malice of sin becomes more serious through the accompanying outward act. As an example he gave the eating of some forbidden food, which would effect absolutely no evil in one already inwardly and determinately inclined to such food. Thus, [Col. 1079B] near the end of his answer to Heloise’s twenty-fourth question: “When we wrongly take something as food because we believe it forbidden to us, that food which enters the mouth does not at all defile the soul; rather, our preceding conscience had already done this. Nor does what we now take by mouth matter at all for sin, but rather the fact that we consented to eat it.” Pullus refutes this admirably in this chapter. The University of Paris also judged that this blemish of Abelard should not be passed over, and rubbed it away with this pumice-stone: “Abelard contends that our taking forbidden food by mouth does not matter at all for sin; but in this way he entirely removes the greater gravity of sin arising from the accompanying outward act.” Abelard would not, however, seem simply to be condemned on this ground, unless in maintaining it he relied upon another principle. Perhaps more will be said in the notes on Peter of Poitiers. In this chapter Pullus owes much to Augustine.

“Whatever good he does, he renders dead.” That is, deprived of grace or charity, and having no right [Col. 1079C] to eternal life. Yet no one doubts that such works ought not therefore to be abandoned. First, because they obtain grace and greatly serve the work of justification. Then because they restrain a person already fallen, lest he plunge further headlong into vice, and enable him to perform those duties whose omission would again inflict a deadly wound upon him. Thirdly, they help lest, if the sinner—careless of his salvation—grow sluggish in idleness, those very habits which obey the will for the sake of acquiring virtue should perish or be weakened. Thus Augustine rightly says on Psalm CXVII [117]: “When, through fear of hell, a person restrains himself from sin, a habit of righteousness develops; what had been difficult begins to be loved; fear begins to be excluded by charity; and a chaste fear succeeds, by which we fear lest the bridegroom delay.” See other incentives of this kind, which the Fathers commonly employ to impel sinners not yet restored to righteousness toward good—while the grace of God always goes before and moves effectively.

## CHAPTER L

[Col. 1079D]

“For whenever grace is pleased to offer itself to someone, that person does one of two things: either, cooperating with grace, he acts; or, despising it, he does not cease to act wickedly. But when, grace having been received, a person lives well, one perseveres with Felix in his resolve, while another, drawn back by habitual depravity, withdraws his foot. But the reason this latter falls back is that he does not consent to grace, without which one never lives well.”

Let the author not be thought singular—unless he is understood otherwise—in what he writes concerning rejection of inward grace. As usual, we shall briefly show Augustine as his guide. In *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 34, discussing at length God’s external and internal calling, Augustine precedes the author thus: “To consent or dissent belongs to one’s own will.” A few words later: “Certainly God works even the willing to believe in a person, and in all things His mercy goes before us. But to consent to God’s calling or dissent from it, as I have said, belongs to one’s own will.” Add what he teaches, not cursorily, in the immediately preceding chapter [Col. 1080A]. And in *On Nature and Grace against the Pelagians*, chapter 67: “Since He who calls back one who has turned away is everywhere present, in many ways through creation serving its Lord; since He teaches the believer, consoles the hopeful, exhorts the loving, assists the striving, and hears the praying, you are not charged with guilt because you involuntarily do not know, but because you neglect to seek what you do not know; nor because you do not gather up wounded limbs, but because you despise one who is willing to heal.”

Pullus’s view is supported no less by what Augustine says in Book XII of *The City of God*, chapter 6, where he proposes and investigates the matter thus: “If two persons alike in disposition of soul and body see the beauty of one body, and, upon seeing it, one of them is moved to enjoy it unlawfully while the other remains firmly established in a chaste will, what, we suppose, is the cause that an evil will occurs in the one and not in the other—the same object having caused it in the person in whom it occurred?” After setting out answers which might wrongly be made on either side, and even [Col. 1080B] excluding the devil’s temptation as a moving cause, he answers the point as follows: “For, to remove this obstacle also from the question: if both are tempted by the same temptation, and one yields and consents to it while the other remains what he was, what else appears except that one willed and the other did not will to fall away from chastity? Whence could this arise except from their own wills, when the disposition of body and soul had been the same in both?” etc.

These words of Augustine must certainly be understood suitably of an impulse of the will then to elicit an act of perfect continence, and therefore toward some pious and saving good which needs supernatural help; not of mere temptation to evil, which can be overcome without grace—as someone gratuitously comments upon this passage. The author also follows Augustine in *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, Book II, chapter 26, *On God’s Aid*: “That it is rejected by many belongs to their own wickedness,” etc. To all this may be added what Saint Thomas, on chapter XII of the Epistle to the Hebrews—“See to it that no one lack the grace of God”—sets forth in lecture 3: “The grace of God is lacking to no one, but, as far as it is concerned, it communicates itself, just as the sun is not lacking to blind eyes.” Yet this grace very often suffers rejection. And the Fathers of Trent, session 6, chapter 5: “Nor does man himself do absolutely nothing in receiving that inspiration, since he can reject it.” And the Council of Sens of 1528, chapter 15: “Nor, finally, should the assistance of God who draws be of such a kind that it cannot be resisted.”

Others, especially those who seek merely, out of party zeal—from which we are very far removed—to prepare support for truth, will supply more.

“If, returning to his vomit, he repudiates the covenant, he who has now abandoned his sins binds himself anew.” Augustine had this passage in view in Book I of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 12: “That sins which have been forgiven return where brotherly charity is absent, the Lord most plainly teaches in the Gospel concerning that servant whom, when He found him a debtor,” etc. These words long caused considerable difficulty, [Col. 1080D] for Hugh of Saint Victor in the final chapter of Book II of *On the Sacraments*, part XIV, and for William of Paris near the end of his treatise *On the Sacraments*—although the former held another view too in his *Summa sententiarum*, tract 6, chapter 13.

The Master mentions this opinion in Book IV, distinction 22, and says that many very celebrated writers maintained it. He therefore judges it probable and not to be rashly proscribed, although he embraces the opposite opinion. Approved doctors support both sides. “Therefore, prejudging neither side, I leave the judgment to the reader, adding that it will be safe for me and near to salvation to eat crumbs beneath the table of the lords.” Thus speaks Peter, wisely and soberly. Yet his pupil, the other Peter of Poitiers, dissents from him in Part III, chapter 12, where he likewise mentions both opinions.

I know, however, that this view has today been dismissed as worthless and banished from theological schools, and cannot safely be received since it was condemned by Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, III, question 88, especially articles 1 and 3, where he reconciles in his customary way the divergent authorities of the Fathers. Nor can an answer otherwise be made for the author—if he is to be summoned before the tribunal of revisions—than by the solution through which Saint Thomas dissolves the objections, and which he borrowed from the Master in the distinction cited, §53: “Forgiven sins are said to return [Col. 1081A] and be imputed because, on account of ingratitude, the person is made guilty and sinful as he had been before. For what had been forgiven is said to be exacted because one ungrateful for forgiveness received becomes guilty as he had been before.”

## CHAPTER LI

“But one confession may be made to equals.” Namely, as he immediately adds, the confession made of daily sins, without which, Augustine says in many places, people do not live. The Venerable Bede, first of all—to whom Pullus alludes below—is said to have indicated this remedy for venial sins. For although Augustine often speaks of their expiation, as in Sermon 41 *On the Saints* and Sermon 119 *On Time*; Book I, chapter 7, *On the Creed, to the Catechumens*; chapter 71 of the *Enchiridion*; Book I, chapter 33, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*; Homily 19 among the fifty, and 27, and the last homily, chapter 3, cited by Gratian, *On Penance*, distinction I, chapter *There Are Three*—nevertheless he nowhere openly mentions this mutual confession made to equals, which would suffice for cleansing venial sins.

The passage of Bede which the author had in view is his comment on chapter V of the Epistle of James, on the words “Confess to one another,” etc.: “But in this injunction the following distinction must be made: daily and light sins should be confessed mutually to equals; and we should believe that they are forgiven through their daily prayer. But the uncleanness of a more serious leprosy should, according to the law, be disclosed to the priest; and we should take care to be purified according to his judgment, as often and for as long a time as he commands.” Strabo transcribed these words, with only slight alteration, in his comment on this passage, and Pullus took them from him.

All who taught a similar confession of lesser sins appear likewise to have intended this, including in the author’s time Hugh, monk of Saint Victor, of whom below; the Master of the Sentences, Book IV, distinction 17, §E; and his particular adherent Peter of Poitiers, Book or distinction 3, chapter 13; likewise the other Peter, cantor of Paris, in the *Summa on the Counsels of the Soul*, which we possess in manuscript together with the earlier Peter’s work. But he lived half a century after Robert. Accordingly, while listing useful means for cleansing lesser sins, he adds: “Likewise the Lord’s Prayer, and the beating of the breast, with general confession made to equals concerning such slight offenses as arise through some sudden intrusion. For more serious sins must be confessed to priests and superiors.”

The Benedictine order, most tenacious of the ancient customs of the Church, does not permit this long-obsolete rite of mutual confession to disappear entirely. In its monasteries restored to regular observance, monks customarily disclose their lesser faults in turn before all the brethren twice every week. We read that this was often done by the ancients—indeed daily, as Jonas, bishop of Orléans, writes in Book I of *On the Instruction of Laymen*, chapter 16: “It is the Church’s custom to make confession of more serious sins to priests, through whom people are reconciled to God. But as to daily and light sins, there are those who confess mutually to one another, except monks, who do this daily. That mutual confession ought to be made concerning light and daily sins is made clear by what follows,” etc. This author flourished in 818, under Louis the Pious. I had drawn from him several things that would be useful to these observations, since he had not yet been published, as I thought; but while these commentaries of ours on Pullus had languished for two whole years—which it is irrelevant to explain here—another edition, unexpectedly, is being hurried to the press through the diligence and labor of Dom Luc d’Achery. I have therefore deleted much, because it has now been published.

[Col. 1082A] This daily mutual confession of lesser faults was familiar not only to monks but also to the canons of cathedrals—and still more to those clergy later called, in a not meager phrase, regular canons—as is expressly found in their rule, whose author was Chrodegang, or Crodegand, bishop of Metz. Thus chapter 18 says: “When the clerics come together in church to sing Prime, and the office itself has been completed, before Psalm 50 let them offer their confessions in turn, saying: ‘I confess to God and to you, brother, that I have sinned in thought, word, and deed. Through my fault. Therefore I ask you: pray for me.’ And the other responds: ‘May almighty God have mercy on you and forgive you all your sins; may He deliver you from every evil, preserve you in every good, and bring you to eternal life.’ And he says: ‘Amen.’ With humble heart, competing in prayer for one another, they do this for each other. When this is completed, let them assemble daily for chapter.”

When they have gathered there: [Col. 1082B] “Whoever is guilty shall ask pardon and receive judgment according to the measure of his fault. But whoever asks pardon for a fault, the more deeply he humbles himself and acknowledges himself guilty, the more mercifully and lightly shall he be judged by the superior. For it is necessary that all our negligences—that is, those of thought, tongue, or deed—should always be judged in this present life through true confession and humility, lest after death they make us guilty.” Considering this passage, the Fathers of the Council of Aachen under Louis the Pious prescribe this most salutary practice to the same cathedral canons: “Let them come daily to conference, where they shall read through both this rule and readings from other holy Scriptures; ask pardon for offenses committed; and receive a sentence according to the nature of the offense,” etc.

But these and other exercises of regular life prescribed in the same chapter to the aforesaid canons—and in which, save perhaps for their habit, they differed little from monks—have, by the common fate of mortal things, fallen into disuse. Whereas formerly, living together, dining together, and by their very place, dwelling, and cloistered exercises, they breathed monastic life itself, they now gather only for choir and capitular business, living, as it were, outwardly (*hōsei exōterikōs agontes*, ὃσει ἐξωτερικῶς ἄγοντες).

Moreover, it is sufficiently clear from the cited authors that this confession was not customarily made in a uniform manner. Some exposed every single atom of their sins to examination. Others thought confession satisfied if they acknowledged generally that they had indulged human frailty too much—for example, that their tongue had been too wanton; that they had been too inclined to gluttony in food; that their gaze wandered over individual objects; and many similar things which reading the ancients will furnish. Pullus, however, as we shall see below, judges sufficient for this purpose the confession which the Church has hitherto retained in the entrance of the Mass, and by which priest and choir confess to one another at Prime and Compline.

“The other [confession], unless extreme necessity presses, is owed [Col. 1082D] to priests.” Namely, that which is sacramental and which includes mortal sins as the necessary matter of confession. From this it seems possible to infer that the author did not depart from the proper path but taught the common doctrine of his age: namely, that when danger of death is imminent, confession should be made to a layperson if legitimate ministers of the sacrament are unavailable, provided it is always made with the desire to confess to priests should they arrive. Before the Council of Trent, the more recent school of theologians had not yet sufficiently and consistently rejected this doctrine.

All who devote special attention to Augustine trace the beginnings of this opinion to the famous tenth chapter of the book *On True and False Penance*, persuaded that it contains his genuine teaching—although chapter 17 of the same book clearly proves it spurious. This is the chapter cited by Gratian, *On Penance*, distinction 1, chapter *He Who Repents*; by the Master, *Sentences*, Book IV, distinction 17, §E; and by Peter the cantor of Paris [Col. 1083A]—whose book has been published, though I possess it only in manuscript—who, after citing the same authority, concludes: “From this authority we have that in necessity confession must be made to a layperson if a priest is lacking, and not merely of venial sins but also of mortal sins.” But here is the passage of Pseudo-Augustine:

“Such, therefore, is the power of confession that, if a priest is lacking, one should confess to one’s neighbor. For it often happens that a penitent cannot confess before the priest whom he desires, because neither place nor time provides him. And though the person to whom he confesses lacks the power to absolve, he nevertheless becomes worthy of pardon through his desire for a priest, when he confesses to his companion the shamefulness of his crime. For the lepers were cleansed while going to show their faces to the priests, before they reached them. Hence it is clear that the Lord looks upon the heart when necessity prevents people from reaching priests. Often indeed they seek them while healthy and cheerful, but while seeking them, before they reach them, they die. But God’s mercy is everywhere: He knows both how to spare the righteous and how to do so, though not as quickly [Col. 1083B] as if they had been absolved by a priest. Therefore, whoever confesses wholly to a priest should confess to the best priest he can.”

Some further approve this practice, customary at that period, on the authority of the genuine Augustine writing to Fortunatus, whose words Gratian reports in *On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter *It Is Holy*.

That this duty, in the absence of a priest and in a case of necessity, fell especially to deacons in the Latin Church—for the Greeks did not approve this custom—is attested, among others, by Cyprian in Letter 13, unless Pamelio must be granted that Cyprian there speaks only of absolution from excommunication; though this may rightly be questioned. It is further evident from chapter *Thieves*, *Extra*, *On Theft*; from Stephen of Autun, chapter 8, treating the ordination of deacons; from Burchard, Book XIX of the *Decrees*, chapter 153; etc. And among English constitutions, under the title *On Penance and Remission*, Archbishop Edmund says: “Concerning penance, we command that deacons shall not presume to impose penance except in those cases when a priest cannot do so, or is absent, or foolishly or indiscreetly refuses, and death threatens the sick person.” This canon is repeated under the title *On Baptism and Its Effect*. Finally—leaving unmentioned almost countless pronouncements on this point—I infer it not obscurely from this couplet of Raymond’s metrical *Summula*, written in an old hand, which I possess. Under the title *On the Office of Deacons*:

> When no presbyter is present, let a deacon  
> Give the Lord’s body to the sick, and also hear their sin.

Moreover, Blessed Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, in his little book *On Concealing Confession*, writes that, in the absence of priests, this office of hearing penitents’ confessions belongs to ecclesiastical persons. He wishes rank among them to be observed according to the grades they hold in the Church: deacons before subdeacons, subdeacons before acolytes, these before exorcists, and so forth among the rest. He then concludes: “In this we recognize that concerning hidden matters we ought to confess to every ecclesiastical [Col. 1083D] order; but concerning open matters, it is fitting to confess to priests alone, through whom the Church—which knows publicly—both looses and binds. But if you find no one in ecclesiastical orders to whom you may confess, seek out a pure man [Note: [Col. 1083D] A “pure man,” that is, a faithful layman.], wherever he may be,” etc.

Saint Thomas most expressly taught that laypeople too could be granted this prerogative, in his commentary on distinction 17 of Book IV of the *Sentences*. He was certainly led by the reasoning found in other authors of the preceding age: namely, that since the necessity of the sacraments of Baptism and Penance is equal, they also wished the status of the minister of each to be equal, and that in a case of necessity laypersons might rightly be summoned as ministers of penance, since the canons do not exclude them from the ministry of Baptism in such a case. Indeed, in his answer to the first objection, article 3, question 3, of the cited distinction, he teaches that sacramental character ought not wholly to be denied even to this confession: “Nevertheless, a confession made to a layperson from desire for a priest [Col. 1084A] is sacramental in some way, although it is not a perfect sacrament,” etc. He holds that its deficiency is to be supplied by the supreme priest, that is, Christ.

Yet it seems more advisable, and more consistent with the mind of such authors, to say that they placed confessions received by persons other than priests not among true sacraments but only among those things which our writers call sacramentals. This we certainly believe concerning Pullus; nor will those who read what follows in his work deny it, where he writes that the power of the keys was granted to priests alone.

We shall add one point, which especially commends this custom: the ancients observed it with such religious seriousness that they thought confession should be made even to devout women, if others were lacking. Peter the cantor, writing at the end of the twelfth century, was uncertain on this question. Nevertheless, he finally agrees that it may be done if there is no danger of scandal—even to a Jew or heretic:

> “And likewise, may one confess to a woman who will not be scandalized [Col. 1084B] by such confession? Again, if a faithful man in service to a Jew is dying on the road, with only his master present, and has no sins on account of which that Jew might wish or be able to disparage the confessing man or the Church; and if, before he dies, he confesses to that Jew and adjures him by God and by the fidelity he owes him to report his penance and confession to the Church—will he be believed when afterward he reports this? Will he not nevertheless report the confession to the Church, since no danger follows from it? I answer,” says Peter, “that I believe the Lord who gives contrition to the penitent in such a case will teach him by inward inspiration what he ought to do. For, I believe, because of such great necessity, he may confess even to a Jew or heretic. He may also commendably refrain from confessing to such persons if conscience dictates this to him.”

Albert the Great, his contemporary, resolves this knot less anxiously. Considering this difficulty in Book IV, distinction 17, article 58, he concludes: “A layperson has this power in a case of necessity, and likewise a woman.” But he is by no means to be forgiven for adding in the following article that such confession and the absolution applied to it are sacramental, no less than Baptism administered by laypeople. There is no doubt that Saint Thomas, as we saw above, drew this doctrine from his teacher, though he moderates it with Christian salt. Raymond sang no differently. In the metrical *Summula* mentioned in the column immediately above, the poet, himself deceived, thus plays upon the verse:

> Let the sick person seek any priest he can,  
> When his own is absent. If he has no priest  
> To whom he may confess, let a layperson or woman be confessor.  
> For baptizing, or confessing the shame of the heart,  
> In the hour of death every human being suffices.

Yet we regard as most true the opinion of Scotus, writing on the aforesaid distinction of the Master: such confessions made to laypeople are neither necessary nor usually useful, perhaps are not even lawful, and much less sacramental. See matters of greater weight in Dom Luc d’Achery’s notes on Blessed Lanfranc’s treatise *On Concealing Confession*.

“The manner in which priests customarily and daily confess indiscriminately in the presence of those standing around.” Here the teaching of the other Peter of Poitiers, the Victorine monk, should be noted. In distinction 20 of his book on penance, he says there are two kinds of confession: general and special. “Special confession,” he says, “is that in which every sin is stated; general confession is that in which the Church confesses generally twice a day, namely at Prime and Compline. It is made for venial sins and for criminal sins which have been consigned to forgetfulness.” Hugh, a monk of the same Asceterium, had previously taught the same in Book II of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 1, part XIV, but mentioned only light and daily faults. So too does our Peter of Poitiers, distinction 3, chapter 13: “Confess your sins to one another.” Yet we believe [Col. 1085A] this was said concerning the confession of venial sins made twice daily, at Compline as well. His Master, however, distinction 21, §E, ascribes to that general confession made in the Church a cleansing from sins not only venial but also mortal sins which have blamelessly slipped from memory: “Here it is implied that general confession also removes mortal sins of which one has no awareness.”

We judge that Pullus chiefly spoke of this confession when above he holds that daily and light sins should be disclosed to equals; and that he had it in view again when shortly afterward he adds: “But if confession is not made one by one, since because of their multitude that can rarely be done,” etc. Yet it is most useful for it to be made at least generally, and rather frequently. We do not deny, however, that these words also express that confession of sins made to God alone, of which Chrysostom often speaks and which was very familiar to the penitent king, as is evident from the Psalms.

[Col. 1085B] It should not be passed over that some in England, Pullus’s nation, were so ignorant and willingly credulous that they thought themselves sufficiently relieved of the guilt and consciousness of mortal sins by the general confession recited at the beginning of Mass. To remedy this evil, then widely spreading, the English Fathers decreed as follows in their constitutions under the title *On the Celebration of Masses*: “We also forbid any priest who has fallen into mortal sin to presume to approach the altar to celebrate before he has confessed. Nor should he think, as certain persons mistakenly believe, that mortal sins are removed through general confession.” That is, the confession made at the entrance of Mass, or at Prime or Compline, as William Lyndwood notes there. He recognizes another general confession, and calls it sacramental: that which is sometimes made privately, generally as to venial sins while some more serious sins are specifically enumerated. He asserts that both remove venial sins, and cites several authors on the matter.

[Col. 1085C] There was another general confession of penitents, in a somewhat longer form and with a catalogue of sins that scarcely even the most wicked could commit. There was another, little different from this, which parish priests made publicly in church for instruction; on Thursday of the Lord’s Supper it was followed by a general absolution through the bishop’s hands in cathedral churches, and by abbots or others in Benedictine abbeys which enjoy the rights and privileges of a see—as we have frequently seen, especially at the royal church of Saint-Denis near Paris. Finally there was another general confession, likewise comprising many kinds of vices, which even bishops of most approved life and others publicly uttered near the end of life, for the sake of humility and devotion. Examples of it will be supplied by Hugh Menard, formerly most highly esteemed by me for two reasons, in his observations on the Gregorian Sacramentary, pages 224, 225 and following.

By way of a concluding ornament, we shall append the as-yet unpublished formula of that general confession at Mass which the Cluniacs used with great devotion in Pullus’s age. In their principal constitutions—written under Saint Hugh the abbot by his faithful disciple Saint Ulrich, of which we have a manuscript copy here—it is prescribed that not even the smallest word be added to that formula. In those *Constitutions*, page 70, where the rites of the greater liturgy are treated, it reads: “Likewise, bowing, he says the confession. Its form is prescribed in such a way that neither at Mass nor at the Hours when it is to be said may it be said with more words than these:

> I confess to God and to all His saints, and to you, Father, that I have sinned in thought, word, and deed. Through my fault. I ask you to pray for me.”

It resembles the form used by regular clerics—later called Augustinians—and cathedral canons, when, in monastic fashion, they stated their faults in turn, as is found in Chrodegang’s Rule, chapter 18, discussed above.

[Col. 1086A] “Or he is to be afflicted by bodily punishment,” as occurred when Paul handed someone over to Satan: “To hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians V). The author of the Commentary on the Epistles of Paul, ascribed to Jerome, seems to have guided the author in this passage: “That he may have power to take him bodily. When he sees that he will have rest neither here in the flesh nor hereafter in spirit, may he repent in deed so that he may be saved.” Ambrose teaches the same interpretation in Book I of *On Penance*, chapter 12 and following, understanding “destruction of the flesh” as chastisement of the flesh, not its annihilation. Pacian likewise in Letter 3 to Sempronianus; Primasius in his Commentary; Haymo and Cajetan on the same place. This opinion pleased the Greeks generally, Chrysostom teaching it in many passages. Augustine, however, was undecided in this matter. For in Book I of *The Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, chapter 20, and in *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, [Col. 1086B] Book III, chapter 1, he speaks thus, yet affirms nothing certain or definite: “What, then, was the Apostle doing except providing for spiritual salvation through the destruction of the flesh, whether by some punishment or bodily death—as Ananias and his wife fell before the feet of the apostle Peter—or through penance,” etc.

Yet the more numerous party of the Fathers understands this passage otherwise: namely, as the mere expulsion and separation of that person from fellowship with the faithful, which we call major excommunication. Augustine does not deny this, for in the cited Book *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, chapter 2, he calls the punishment inflicted by the Apostle an anathema. Chrysostom himself supports it, when treating the words in 1 Timothy I, “whom I handed over to Satan.” Comparing this with 1 Corinthians V, he says: “That sinner was expelled from the common assembly of the faithful; he was cut off from the flock, made naked; and thus, left without protection, he lay exposed and was delivered over to the attacks of wolves,” etc.

## CHAPTER LII
[Col. 1086C] Considering what each person’s strength can bear, what they refuse to endure, and what is rightly due to the fault, he should show this (so that the guilty person may thus be humbled); yet he should impose what can be borne. The words he writes again in the following Part, chapter 3, aim at the same point. This opinion is certainly worthy of notice, since it aptly commends the Church’s practice now in use and points, as it were, to its cradle. For it is certain that the discipline of imposing the more severe canonical penance was not generally relaxed before the beginning of the twelfth century. That it still persisted diligently to the end of the eleventh, although not a few resisted it, is attested by what one finds throughout Peter Damian and throughout the book entitled *Gomorrhianus*, in which he repeatedly urges upon Leo IX the ancestral strictness of this practice, and obtained from him an apostolic ruling in accordance with his wishes.

Nor should it be inferred from Damian’s approval of certain commutations of penances that had long since arisen—namely, that some might pay money for what ordinarily had to be undergone in the flesh—as he shows in the eighth letter of the fifth book [Col. 1086D], that the severity of the canons had in his own day been abolished or moderated for the majority. Rather, one may infer that their rigor remained unimpaired. Since most people judged themselves unequal to it, they earnestly begged to have recourse to the aforesaid commutations through their confessor—commutations which the Church had received already four hundred years before Peter. Moreover, this practice concerned only a few laymen, and those wealthy ones. The English Fathers judged that it should no longer be tolerated with impunity at about the time when such commutations first appeared, namely, around the middle of the eighth century, at a general council of England presided over by Cuthbert, bishop of Canterbury. For thus the Fathers assembled at Clovesho in 747 decree against certain rich persons who mitigated the canons by payments of money:

> “This matter must be discussed at greater length, because recently a certain man, rich according to this world, seeking to have reconciliation granted to him more quickly for some grave offense of his, asserted in his letters that this same wickedness had, according to the undertakings of many persons, been expiated to such an extent that, if he should thereafter be able to live, the fast of three hundred years would have been fully paid for it by modes of satisfaction—namely, by the psalmody, fasting, and almsgiving of others—apart from his own fasting, although he himself might in some fashion fast, even if only a little. 368 Therefore, if divine justice can thus be appeased through others, why are the rich—O foolish promisers!—who can redeem fasts by countless rewards given to others for their own crimes, said, in the words of Truth, to enter the kingdom of heaven with greater difficulty than a camel passes through the eye of a needle?”

Read also the canons issued under King Edgar, about the year 967.

Other examples are available of this rite, declining indeed but not yet dead in the century mentioned, both from Gregory VII, who sharply directed his pen against false penances—that is, penances departing from the exact observance of the penitential canons—and from various [Col. 1087B] councils and penitential books issued at that time, in which we always read that penitents were punished seriously and according to the strict letter of the law.

But in the following century, in which Pullus was writing, the relaxation of this sacramental discipline had already begun for a time—the Church always providing what was more suitable. This is shown not only by what he repeatedly urges in this Part and in the following one, but also by what we read in Peter of Blois’s treatise *On Penance* and in certain others. Yet the most lenient of all was William of Paris, who lived later. Although he writes that knowledge of the penitential canons is necessary for a priest, he held that it should be theoretical rather than practical; satisfaction should either be diminished or imposed to the exact measure of the law, according to careful consideration of each penitent’s character and the circumstances, which for the most part determine the gravity of a matter. Yet this was to be done in such a way—as the age now allowed—that the laws should yield to the priest’s discretion.

He grants much else of this kind in the second treatise he published *On Penance*. And in chapter 13 of *On the Sacrament of Orders* he writes to this purpose:

> He whose office it is to impose penitential satisfactions also has the office of increasing, diminishing, and changing them, as he sees expedient for the honor of God, the salvation of souls, and public and particular benefit.

Our poet mentioned above expressed the same at folio 124 in verse:

> Let the priest be circumspect while he hears crimes,  
> Concerning the persons: which is poor, weak,  
> Sound or sick, wealthy or in sacred orders,  
> Strong or frail in body; which is a pilgrim,  
> Which is devout; which is less fit to bear  
> Punishment for vices. In their cases let the priest  
> Regulate the whole matter, hastening to deal with their faults,  
> Applying remedies against them and sending them to purgatorial penances;  
> If he cannot do so more usefully, let him bring them to further measures.  
>
> Let not the priest conceal the manifest crimes of the people  
> Until they repent and themselves pay, as is fitting.  
>
> [Col. 1087D] Let the priest show a compassionate countenance, and to some  
> Propose light burdens, if he grants a dispensation; to others  
> Let him propose sweet things, for whom strong things are easy to bear.

Finally, Raymond, flourishing about the year of Christ 1225, declares that this remission of canonical penalties had by then generally prevailed everywhere—as human nature, always desiring easier things and indulging itself, tends to do. In book III of the *Summa*, chapter “On Penance and Remission,” he writes:

> Others call all penances, without distinction, arbitrary; and custom seems to embrace this last opinion. Yet the first is safer, though more difficult.

For this devout man, most firmly attached to antiquity and to the sacred canons, endured with difficulty this distaste for a stricter discipline. He was convinced that its force would be of no small benefit if administered prudently. This, indeed, we know has always been the Church’s aim, although that most kindly mother has decreed that many things should be granted to her children according to the diversity of times and circumstances—as most wisely, so also most piously.

[Col. 1088A] Let these remarks, however, be understood only of hidden sins, although sometimes more serious ones. For the author’s intention was no other, as he sufficiently teaches near the end of chapter 57 of the following Part, when, dividing crimes into public and private, he judges that the former should be remedied thus: “Therefore, just as the bishop cures manifest crimes with manifest scourges, so let the priest endeavor to heal hidden offenses with hidden remedies.” It would not be burdensome to show by many proofs that this practice of seriously punishing grave and public sins was religiously preserved in the Church, were brevity not required. We shall append just one point: the cited poet aptly dealt with this matter. Writing on the penance of women, customarily performed for sins not only public but also hidden, when these carried a certain gravity with them, he omits absolutely nothing of canonical penalties, except pilgrimages, which were then very familiar to men but rightly denied to women as a precaution. Thus, at folio 135:

> If such a woman has committed adultery not publicly,  
> Let her not pay for it publicly, lest she be suspected by her husband.  
> After the death of one, let her sufficiently pay for it.  
> Young matrons can fulfill the *carenae*  
> In their own homes, although they do not go out.  
> Let them fast, pray, lie on straw, go  
> With bare feet, and walk clad in haircloth.  
> Moreover, there are many labors for amendment;  
> Let them employ these: such a path is honorable for them.

“I do not bind such penitents to condemnation, provided only that they abandon their crimes.” The statement seems obscure to me and must necessarily be reconciled with the author’s subsequent words: namely, that penitents fleeing their own priest must have his permission to confess to another, unless recourse is had to superiors; thus confession must always be made to a priest holding ordinary or delegated jurisdiction. Although parish priests and religious delegated by the supreme pontiff may confer the benefit of absolution upon travelers, authors rightly deny that persons traveling solely in order to evade the jurisdiction of their own parish priest merit this favor, and judge that absolution in such a case is invalid. Bonacina, disputation 5, question 7, point 2, proposition 4, no. 6:

> “Yet limit this to cases in which they travel in good faith—that is, provided they do not make the journey in fraud of the law, solely so that they may confess to others. Thus, one who makes a journey only for this purpose, to avoid his own parish priest and confess to another, cannot validly confess before the parish priest or priest of the place to which he arrives; as Coninck well observes in the place cited; Vasquez in the place cited, no. 6; Suarez, disputation 25, section 2, no. 9; Reginald, book I, no. 80; and other recent writers,” etc.

These are Bonacina’s words, though perhaps all those who enjoy the privilege of hearing confessions everywhere will answer him.

That this is the author’s meaning is indicated both by what precedes [Col. 1088D] and by what follows. For he first stated that a priest ought neither to bind nor loose another’s sheep except when reason or necessity compels him, and he denies that either is present in the case mentioned. Then he requires, in one who legitimately judges that he should leave his own priest because the latter lacks sufficient learning, that he provide himself, with that priest’s knowledge, with another better qualified. This proves all the more strongly that such a deceitful flight from one’s own priest is not lawful, since it indicates a lack in the penitent of sufficient contrition and disposition. Yet if these are present from another source, and a minister equipped with the requisite qualifications is not lacking, Pullus does not dare decide whether the shame which commonly suggests that flight will impair the integrity of the sacrament. Our poet thought likewise, at folio 133:

> If your priest is unlearned, with his consent you shall approach  
> Another who is wiser than he.  
> If he does not consent, seek one higher than him.

[Col. 1089A] Yet Bernard’s opinion should be noted and safely accepted. In sermon 3 on St. Andrew, he judges that, through the pursuit of a more deeply rooted humility, one should not depart even from unlearned pastors and prelates:

> “Nor let it move you,” he says, “if he is illiterate or undiscerning, 370 because this itself is a sign of the humility that produces confession. Remember that there is no authority except from God. ‘The Scribes and Pharisees sit,’ he says, ‘upon Moses’ seat.’ Notice that he says not the one sitting, but the seat—not the person, but the chair. What if permission is granted to flee to another? Yet first disclose to him the secret of your heart, because salvation is not complete if he is avoided or despised, though you ought to have adhered to or honored him. What if his instruction seems insufficient to you? The way to freedom lies open: pour out your heart before another learned and eloquent person, while preserving the privilege of the one to whom you entrusted your soul.”

It would be better for this most friendly truth to prevail everywhere among all persons than for those soul-markets of our age, by which nothing anywhere is gained less than the salvation of souls. I say nothing of the harm to ecclesiastical peace, which that disorderly wandering of penitents, generally with contempt for their own pastor, must endanger—indeed, I might say, destroy. Yet here we wish to leave untouched the practice of regular clergy, provided that what must be observed is observed; the Apostolic See has sent them as auxiliary forces into the camps of the Lord.

“How does he act according to authority,” etc. Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, Homily 25, before the middle:

> It often happens that he either condemns the innocent or looses others while he himself is bound. Often, in loosing and binding subjects, he follows the impulse of his own will rather than the merits of the cases. Hence the person who exercises this power of binding and loosing according to his own wishes and not according to the conduct of those subject to him deprives himself of that very power.

Read also Jerome on Matthew chapter 16; Augustine on Psalm 37; Hugh of St Victor, treatise 6 *On the Sacraments*, chapter 14.

## CHAPTER LIII

[Col. 1089C]

“Thus he punished the Sodomites, thus those drowned in the Red Sea, and thus finally those struck down in the wilderness in the present life, lest he punish them eternally.” This is a difficult passage, as it has seemed to most who always prefer sounder interpretations. Anyone wishing to adhere more closely to the letter could escape the difficulty with this brief comment: the author’s meaning is not that the Sodomites and the others mentioned, overtaken by sudden death through God’s vengeance, escaped eternal punishment by that temporal death. Rather, it is only that these punishments were inflicted on them by God with the intention that, if they had wished to use them for salvation and repent properly, they would beyond doubt have escaped the punishments of hell due to their sins.

The aim Pullus pursues in this chapter supports that interpretation: namely, that those who piously assist persons condemned to capital punishment should teach them to undergo death willingly and with true repentance, because God is sometimes appeased by that satisfaction and exchanges for a temporal penalty—received with patient and contrite spirit—the punishment that would otherwise be paid in the other life. If this repentance is lacking, the result will be that they undergo not only the punishment imposed by the earthly judge but, in addition, are punished eternally by the avenging flames to which God assigns them. In this sense Isidore says in book I, chapter 30: “For some, condemnation begins here, so that complete destruction may be hoped for there.” Nor should God then be thought to judge twice for the same thing: for he punishes the condemned only once, though the punishment begins here and never ends after this age. Isidore himself excellently says this in book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 2, sentences 3, 7, and 8.

But although these points have the flavor of sound doctrine, and scarcely any other ray of truth could illuminate this passage, there seems to be a difficulty in the fact that the author borrowed it from Jerome—though, as is his custom, without naming him.

For, treating Nahum 1:9 according to the Septuagint version—“The Lord will not take vengeance twice for the same thing in affliction”—Jerome seems to judge that the Sodomites, etc., paid in this world every punishment due to their sins because God does not judge twice for the same thing. For Jerome expounds as follows:

> “If it seems to you cruel, harsh, and bloody that he destroyed the human race in the flood; rained fire and sulphur upon Sodom and Gomorrah; drowned the Egyptians in the waves; and struck down the bodies of the Israelites in the wilderness: know that he rendered punishments in the present life for this reason, lest he punish eternally. Certainly, either what the prophets say is true or false. If what they seem to say concerning his severity is true, they themselves said: ‘The Lord will not take vengeance twice for the same thing in affliction’ [Nahum 1:9, according to the Septuagint]. But if it is false, then this saying is false [Nahum 1:9, according to the Vulgate]: ‘A double affliction shall not arise.’ Therefore the faith described in the Law is also false. But if it is true—as they cannot deny, since the prophet says, ‘The Lord will not take vengeance twice for the same thing in affliction’—then those who have been punished will not be punished afterward. But if they are to be punished afterward, Scripture lies, which it is impious to say. Therefore those who perished in the flood, the Sodomites, the Egyptians, and the Israelites in the wilderness received their evils in their own lifetime.”

These are Jerome’s words. They undoubtedly present a rather difficult meaning and one insufficiently compatible with many passages of both Testaments, such as 2 Peter 2:6; Jude, the one chapter, verse 7; and especially Matthew 10:15: “It shall be more tolerable for the land of the Sodomites and Gomorrheans on the day of judgment than for that city.” By these words Christ indicates that the Sodomites too, although more mildly, are to be punished in the future age. Jerome’s words can nevertheless be reconciled with the truth and somewhat softened from his own words. It would now be neither laborious nor, for Pullus’s defense, unnecessary to do so, had not our contemporary Master, in *Sentences* IV, distinction 15, §§ A and B, undertaken to defend doctrine against Jerome’s error.

[Col. 1090C] “He regards the judge as his priest, since he must reveal to him the hidden things of his crimes.” He speaks of a person condemned to capital punishment, to whom he says that a priest should not go in order to administer the sacraments of Penance and the Eucharist.

It is not surprising that the author, for the sake of religion and of maintaining stricter discipline, adhered to the custom of his age. For even in later centuries—when we know that the rigor of ecclesiastical censure was somewhat relaxed—the contrary custom could scarcely prevail, namely, that even the sacrament of Penance should be administered to those liable to death. In former times the Church denied this favor to all who, while in desperate illness, after crimes frequently repeated and after renouncing the faith, first requested penance when already near death. Among other witnesses, the Fathers of the First Council of Arles, final canon, and Cyprian in his letter to Antonianus testify to this:

> “Therefore, dearest brother, we have judged that those who do not do penance and do not testify to sorrow for their sins with their whole heart and with a manifest profession of lamentation should be altogether barred from hope of communion and peace if they begin to entreat while in illness and danger. For it is not repentance for their offense but the warning of pressing death that compels them to ask; and he is unworthy to receive comfort in death who has not reflected that he is going to die.”

Similar evidence may be gathered from the Council of Elvira, chapter 46, and from Innocent I, *Letter to Exuperius of Toulouse*, chapter 2.

But that those condemned to death had not yet been granted the comfort of sacramental penance in 1396 is proved by the edict of King Charles VI, issued at Paris on the fourth day before the Nones of February in that year. It appears in the book of ancient ordinances, folio 124, in our manuscript. The most Christian king decrees that guilty persons condemned to death are to be admitted to the sacrament of Penance. This was done in view of Clement V’s decree in the Council of Vienne, found in book V of the *Clementines*, title 9, chapter 1:

> “Since, according to canonical statutes, the sacrament of Penance ought not to be denied, if requested, to those assigned to their final punishment, we, wishing altogether to abolish a condemnable abuse introduced in certain regions against this rule, exhort all officers of justice and temporal lords in the Lord to desist from such abuse,” etc.

Nevertheless, that the former practice still persisted, at least in France, in 1515 can sufficiently be gathered from the synodal acts of Stephen de Poncher in that year. Under the title “On the Sacrament of Penance,” they read as follows:

> “Likewise, in accordance with the Council of Vienne, under penalty of excommunication, admonish the ordinary judges of your places that they shall cause the sacrament of Penance to be administered by a suitable person to those condemned to death before they suffer, abolishing the contrary custom. Nor do we wish the sacrament of the Eucharist to be denied to the same persons if they are truly penitent and request it.”

These are the words of the Synod of Paris, which we have here printed in contemporary type.

[Col. 1091B] What could scarcely be abolished in France, even though a conciliar decree and a royal edict had preceded it, is not surprising if it likewise occurred with equal difficulty in England after laws had been enacted by Kings Alfred, Edward, and Cnut. These likewise provided that no one should bar persons condemned to final punishment from the sacrament of Penance. Thus, among the laws enacted by Alfred the Great, king of the English, and Guthrum, king of the Anglo-Danes, in the council where they made their treaty, law 8 reads: “If anyone guilty of a capital offense wishes to make confession to a priest, let it never be denied him.” And law 8 of Edward the Elder reads: “If anyone condemned for a capital offense wishes openly to confess his sins to a priest, let this be granted him. But let all zealously and diligently promote every divine law, so that they may obtain divine mercy and avoid these punishments imposed upon guilty persons by wise men.”

Therefore, the punishments which wise men had imposed upon guilty persons—which had made the custom unstable—namely, the denial to offenders of permission to confess, so that they might be restrained by that severity and not rush headlong further into vice, the most gracious king remits. And lest some judges might perhaps resist to the contrary, as occurred in France, Cnut adds penalties: “If anyone condemned for a capital offense wishes openly to confess his sins, let this be granted him. But if anyone denies it, let him pay the king one hundred and twenty shillings, or at least clear himself of guilt with five men joined to him.”

A certain writer celebrated in this age understands this fine otherwise, and certainly in Pullus’s favor, as is evident from his letters sent to me on this matter. He judges that Cnut moderated Edward’s law. For, he says, Cnut allows permission to confess to be denied to those condemned, provided two conditions are met: either that one pay the king one hundred and twenty shillings, or that, with five men joined to him, one clear oneself of fault.

Yet it is certain that these laws were either not received in common practice or had fallen into disuse by Pullus’s age, ancient customs having returned, as we read happened in France, though under the third dynasty of our kings. Under the second dynasty, however, the custom had become established of admitting public offenders, soon to suffer death, to the sacred practice of confession, as is clear from chapter 27 of the Council of Mainz in 848, the Council of Worms, chapter 80, and the Council of Tribur, chapter 31.

Boniface, archbishop of Canterbury, likewise complained of this among the English in the English Constitutions under the title “On Penance and Remissions.” Establishing there the same provisions as Clement V at the Council of Vienne, he says:

> “This is especially urged on account of prisoners, to whom this sacrament is frequently denied inhumanely—indeed, lest we say unbelievingly. And if at times an opportunity to confess is granted to offenders, it is granted to them so briefly and so inopportunely that it turns rather to the danger of desolation and despair for the wretched than to the joyful consolation of the spirit.”

But when Pullus says, “The accused regards the judge as his priest, because he must reveal to him the hidden things of his crimes,” he rather strongly commends the custom then in use and discussed above [Col. 1092A]: namely, that laypeople, in a case of necessity and in the absence of priests, conferred the benefit of absolution. Scotus testifies that this was observed especially in the case of those condemned to death, although the practice displeased him considerably, as is clear from what he says in IV, distinction 17, article 3. Today, however, just as the Eucharist is commonly denied among us to persons accused of capital crimes, so the sacrament of Penance is everywhere administered to them. Hear briefly at last what our poet thought of this matter in the *Summula of Raymond*, folio 39:

> You may lawfully be confessor to thieves and criminals,  
> To those whom the just sentence of a judge has condemned,  
> And those whom public custody binds in fetters.  
> But take care not to behold the death of robbers, the hanging of thieves,  
> Or slaughter of whatever kind; for by law  
> Your power to sing Mass is thereby removed.

The author strives by many arguments to persuade that the Eucharist too should be denied to the condemned; or, if this by no means pleases, he urges judges not to compel to death those whom they judge not unworthy of heavenly life, which far surpasses natural life. This is an opinion worthy of a most Christian teacher; yet, as regards the final part of the statement, we nowhere read that it was put into practice among those accustomed to grant the sacred viaticum to persons punished by final execution.

France judged more religiously that communion should nowhere be administered to them than that, to Christ’s dishonor, one refreshed with life-giving food should be handed over to the executioner to be killed. The Constable of France, the Count of Saint-Pol, earnestly requested it from Louis XI, king of the French, but could not obtain it, as Gaguin reports, book X, chapter 20:

> “Having completed confession in the Christian manner, he asks that the viaticum of Christ’s body be administered to him, but he did not obtain it. Nevertheless, the divine service which we call Mass was performed before him, and blessed bread was brought, which he devoutly ate.”

Yet it is certain that bishops sometimes protested against this custom [Col. 1092C] and attempted to introduce the contrary practice, as is sufficiently shown by the acts of the Synod of Paris under Stephen de Poncher, related above. Pius V also confirmed that synod by a *motu proprio* issued in 1569, and Spain adopted it with the support of a royal charter; as, not so long ago, several cities of Germany did likewise under a ruling of Emperor Charles V, as is evident from article 79 of his constitutions—provided, however, the emperor says, that the wishes of the accused concur in it.

Thus he wished to guard against the bad custom of certain persons who, led by a feeling of compassion, gave unmixed wine to offenders until they were sated, so that, with their senses dulled, they might suffer less pain. But these belong to new law; that custom was not in force in Pullus’s age, indeed not even from the year of Christ’s birth one thousand onward.

“But those who are to be tortured for martyrdom are not forbidden the sacrament of the body and blood.” This was a very well-known practice of the Church both at its birth and in its sufferings: those destined for martyrdom fortified themselves with the divine viaticum. Hence, because the faithful could not hold synaxes—that is, Eucharistic assemblies—through fear of persecution, they carried the Eucharist with them and preserved it more reverently at home in a chest or another suitably adorned place, so that, when the sword of persecution threatened, refreshed by that heavenly bread, they might fight more courageously. Tertullian should be read, book II *To His Wife*, chapter 5; *On Prayer*, near the end; Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*, etc.

The story of Tarsicius the acolyte also shows this. At the end of the Acts of Pope Stephen and Martyr, he is said to have been killed by raging pagans while carrying Christ’s body with him. So too the deed of Lucian, martyr of Antioch: with his feet placed in stocks, his hands bound to a piece of wood hanging over his head, and lying stretched out on his back, after the signs of the sacred mystery had first been placed upon his breast, he offered the unbloody sacrifice and partook of it on the day before his death.

“To whom you give the body of the Lord, how do you begrudge the honor of burial?” etc. Here is another complaint of Pullus against the denial of burial rights to the condemned. Yet this custom did not prevail equally everywhere. In most places we read that they were commonly buried according to ecclesiastical custom; elsewhere, dispensations were sometimes granted, especially for nobles. Thus the Synod of Paris in 1515 decreed on this subject, under the title “On Burials”:

> “Likewise, since those who are hanged on gibbets for their crimes are not forbidden to receive the sacraments of Penance and the Eucharist, we permit them to receive these, and afterward, once their penance has been completed, to be buried in churches or cemeteries and prayers to be poured out for them; because it is written: ‘The Lord will not judge twice for the same thing.’”

Almost the very same words are reported by the Second Council of Mainz under Rabanus and are found in *Decretum*, XIII, question 2, chapter *Quaesitum*. But what is stated there in the gloss is noteworthy and necessary for the point we discussed a little above. Mention is made of persons condemned to death: although the Eucharist is offered to them, it does them no good in escaping death; churches or sanctuaries to which they generally flee, however, provide them security and protection.

> It is customary to ask why the person who flees to a church is freed, while the person who receives Christ’s body is not, though Christ’s body is greater than all things. Answer, *De consecratione*, distinction 2: because Christ’s body is food for the soul and not for the body; therefore it frees the soul, not the body. Or say that it is a privilege of the Church and ought not to be extended by inference, etc.

From this we again learn that the Eucharist was sometimes offered to those soon to suffer execution, a practice which the author vehemently rejects in this chapter.

## CHAPTER LIV

“He is afterward absolved by a divine examination,” etc. He mentions this examination also in the preceding chapter. He alludes to the solemn purgations customarily performed in order to rebut an imputed suspicion or accusation of crime. Authors of individual ages show at length that these were frequently employed in ancient times: by an oath made at the tombs of martyrs; by touching fire or red-hot iron; by swimming in hot or cold water; by single combat; or, finally, by receiving the Eucharist. Single combat and other such practices are mentioned in the capitularies and in the constitutions of the Lombards, Visigoths, book VI, title 1, chapter 3; and the Frisians, title 3, chapters 4, 5, and 6, and title 14, etc.

Pope Stephen, chapter *Consuluisti*, and Celestine III, chapter *Cura suscepti*, *On Purgations*, etc., condemned purgations by boiling water and red-hot iron, and similar practices. Ivo, letter 74, advises Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, that one ought not obey a king proposing such things, because that wicked judgment had been rejected by ancient canons and decrees of most holy pontiffs. Yet that it was customary in Pullus’s time is attested by his contemporaries: Ivo, in the place cited and several others, and Abbot Guibert, book III of his *Life*, chapter 14. Indeed, not a few thought it lawful and a true judgment of God, as Pullus suggests; Agobard, archbishop of Lyons, wrote a special treatise against them. For much more on this rite, see Martin Delrio, *Magical Investigations*, book IV, chapter 4; Juret, in his notes on Ivo’s letters; and most recently Luc d’Achery, in his annotations on Guibert’s works, pp. 660 ff.

In monasteries, if some concealed crime was to be detected, Mass was said by the abbot or by another in his name; and at the end each individual communicated with these words: “May the body of the Lord be to me for proof today,” as we learn from the Council of Worms in Gratian, in the cited cause, chapter *Saepe contingit*. Supreme pontiffs and other bishops likewise sometimes administered this communion for that purpose: Pope Adrian to Lothair, king of the Franks; Gregory VII to Henry, king of Germany; Frederick, archbishop of Mainz; and others.

Another examination, namely by the judgment of the cross, is mentioned in the ancient formulas at the end of Marculf’s formulas, chapter 12: “Notice concerning vindication by the cross.” As Bignon notes, the form of this purgation seems to be described in the title 14 of the laws of the Frisians cited above: namely, two lots were prepared, one plain and the other marked with the sign of the cross. The two were unrolled upon the altar on a linen cloth; then, after various prayers, they were to be drawn by a priest or a boy. If the lot of the cross was drawn first, they judged innocence sufficiently proved. Yet, out of reverence for the cross, this was prohibited by the *Capitulary*, book I, chapter 108.

Although, as we have said, many examples of these purgations survive, we give here the complete formula of examination by red-hot iron, omitting only the litanies: both because it has not yet been printed and because it seems to differ from others in certain noteworthy points; and also because it appears to have been written under Pope Eugenius III, in Pullus’s lifetime, as the heading of the manuscript states. The saints invoked in the same litanies show that it was in use in the diocese of Amiens.

## THE JUDGMENT OF IRON BEGINS

[Col. 1094B] First let the priest sing the prescribed Mass. After this, let him cause a fire to be kindled; let him bless water and sprinkle it over the fire, over those standing by, and over the place where the judgment is to be performed. Then let this prayer over the fire follow.

Lord God, almighty Father, unfailing light, hear us, you who are the creator of all lights. Bless, Lord, this light, that it may be sanctified and blessed to you. You have illuminated the whole world, so that from this light we may be kindled and illumined by the fire of your brightness. As you illuminated Moses with fire, so illuminate our hearts and minds, that we may be worthy to attain eternal life. Through the Lord, etc. Then let the litany be performed, as it follows in the manuscript.

Then let the priest approach the fire and bless the ploughshares, saying:

**Prayer**

God, righteous judge, author of peace and judge of equity, we humbly beseech you that you may deign + so to bless these ploughshares [Col. 1094C], or this iron appointed for conducting this examination of whatever uncertainty, that, if this man is innocent of the aforesaid matter for which purification is now sought, he may appear unharmed when he takes this heated iron; but if he is guilty and culpable, may your most just power be revealed in him in accordance with truth, so that injustice may not prevail over justice, but falsehood may always be subject to truth. Through you, Christ Jesus.

Bless, Lord, holy Father, through the invocation of your most holy name, through the coming of your Son our Lord Jesus Christ, and through the gift of the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, these ploughshares, or this kind of metal or iron, for the manifestation of your true judgment. Let it be sacrificed by you and sanctified by us, so that, with every falsehood removed far away, the truth of your judgment may be made manifest to your faithful. Through the same our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in unity.

[Col. 1094D] Almighty God, we humbly implore you concerning the examination of this matter now before us: let injustice not prevail over justice, but falsehood be subject to truth. If anyone should wish to cover over or obstruct this present examination by some evil practice or herbs, may you, most righteous Judge, deign to render it void by your most holy right hand. Through Christ our Lord.

May the blessing of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit descend upon these ploughshares, or upon this iron, for discerning the true judgment of God. Amen.

Then, for the person to whom the crime is imputed, let the psalm be sung: “Lord, hear my prayer; give ear to my supplication,” etc.

Our Father. And lead us not. Save your servant, O my God, who trusts in you. Send him help, Lord, from the sanctuary, and defend him from Zion. Let no enemy prevail against him, and let not the son of iniquity continue to harm him. Be for him, Lord, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy. [Col. 1095A] Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you. The Lord be with you. And with your spirit.

**Prayer**
Hear, we beseech thee, O Lord, the prayers of thy suppliants, and spare the sins of those who confess to thee, so that in thy kindness thou mayest grant us alike pardon and peace. Then let those who are to be examined be catechized in these words:
