I adjure you, man, by God the almighty Father, who created heaven and earth, the sea and all things that are in them; and by Jesus Christ, his Son, who was born and suffered for us; and by the Holy Spirit, who came in divine fire upon the apostles; and by holy Mary, Mother of God; and by all the choirs of angels, by apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins: if you know yourself guilty of the aforesaid crime laid to your charge, do not presume today to take this iron into your hand. But if you are so rash as to presume to take it while defiled by that same crime, may you depart conquered and confounded by the power of our Lord Jesus Christ and by the triumph of the cross. But if you are secure and innocent, then, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and by the triumph of the holy cross, we give you leave to approach confidently to receive this iron. May the Lord, the just Judge, deliver you, as he rescued the three youths from the burning fire and freed Susanna from a false accusation, so that you may appear safe and unharmed. And may the power of our Lord Jesus Christ be shown today in you unto a right judgment, he who lives and reigns. Then let the person who is to be examined say:

Behold, for that examination and security which I must today make for a true judgment, I believe more in God the almighty Father—that he is able, in this matter for which I have been accused, now to show both justice and truth in me—than to believe in the devil and in evil arts, or to thwart the justice and truth of God.

Then let him take the oath and carry the iron to the designated place. When this has been done, let the dean seal his hand; and afterwards, until the judgment has been verified, it is good for him to mix blessed salt and water into all his food and drink.

## CHAPTER LVI

“Let priestly dignity, therefore, and secular power divide between themselves these two swords,” etc. Thus aptly to the purpose spoke Edgar, king of England, in an address to Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury, and the other assembled prelates: “Emulate, O priests, emulate the ways of the Lord and the judgments of our God. It is time to rise up against those who destroy God’s law. I hold Constantine’s sword in my hand; you hold Peter’s. Let us join right hands; let sword be joined to sword; and let the lepers be cast out of the camp, that the sanctuary of the Lord may be cleansed.”

Although shortly before this Pullus asserts that, of the two swords mentioned in Luke 22, Peter did not judge the other—the temporal sword—to belong to himself, and therefore wishes it to be assigned only to laymen, as Emperor Frederick maintained in his letter to the imperial party against Pope Adrian IV, it is nevertheless certain that both swords, the spiritual and the temporal, belong to the Church, and most especially to Peter. Bernard himself acknowledges this in *On Consideration*, book IV, chapter 3:

“Why do you again attempt to seize the sword which you were once commanded to put into its sheath? Yet whoever denies that it is yours does not seem to me sufficiently to heed the Lord’s saying: ‘Put thy sword into its sheath.’ Therefore it too is yours, perhaps to be drawn at your command, though not by your hand. Otherwise, if it in no way belonged to you, when the apostles said, ‘Behold, here are two swords,’ the Lord would not have answered, ‘It is enough,’ but rather, ‘It is too much.’ Therefore both belong to the Church: namely, the spiritual sword and the material sword. The latter, indeed, is to be wielded for the Church; the former, by the Church. The one is in the hand of the priest, the other in the hand of the soldier; but certainly at the priest’s direction and the emperor’s command.”

Boniface VIII transcribed these words in Extravagant *Unam sanctam*, *De maioritate et obedientia*, to prove that the Roman pontiff possesses authority over both swords. He then adds, in conformity with what Pullus has here:

“But it is necessary that sword be under sword, and that temporal authority be subject to spiritual power. For since the Apostle says, ‘There is no authority except from God; and those which are from God are ordered’ (Rom. 13:1), they would not be ordered unless sword were under sword,” etc.

The two powers, united in alliance but not confused, assist one another mutually. And, when it comes to the truth of the matter, as Nicholas I says in his letter to Michael, the emperor did not arrogate to himself the rights of the pontificate, nor did the pontiff assume the imperial title.

## CHAPTER LVII

There are private crimes and public crimes; some say that both are to be disclosed to the bishop and punished at his direction. This distinction between public and private crimes, insofar as concerns confession and the penance to be performed for them, began to be heard only about the year of Christ 700, as may be gathered from the penitential books of the Venerable Bede, Ecgbert archbishop of Canterbury, and Rabanus Maurus; and from the canons of Isaac, bishop of Langres, and of certain councils held after the aforesaid period. It is therefore not surprising if writers of an earlier age—whom Pullus perhaps means in this chapter—wrote that both private and public sins were subject to the cognizance of bishops and to public penance, if they so ordered: provided that the sins were grave, and with due regard also to the practice of the nascent and growing Church, in which public penance was imposed only at the bishop’s direction.

Why should we not also say that Pullus intended to indicate, besides the more ancient Fathers, Peter Damian, who seems to argue at length in the book called the *Gomorrhianus* that certain most secret crimes ought to be punished by public penalty and by none other than prelates? Unless one says that his opinion concerns cases reserved to the bishop; for there he deals chiefly with the most shameful crime, although committed most secretly. But this is only our own conjecture, such as it is.

Although after the aforesaid time, that is, after the year 700, solemn penance for public crimes was reserved to the highest priests, while private penance for hidden sins was for the most part left to presbyters, it is nevertheless certain that bishops in many places diligently sought out the disclosure of hidden crimes. Lest anything remain concealed through fraud, they appointed rural deans for this purpose, who, after first requiring an oath from them—of which you have an example in Gratian, Causa 35, question 6, chapter *Episcopus*—were to investigate the depraved habits and vices of individuals, report them afterwards to the bishop himself, and have them seriously punished at his direction.

We learn this from Regino, abbot of Prüm, at the beginning of book II of his *Collection of Canons*—on which Trithemius, in *Ecclesiastical Writers*, under “Regino,” writes—and likewise from Burchard and Isaac of Langres in their own collections of canons. Yet there “hidden crimes” are understood not as crimes known only to the offender who committed them, but as those known also to certain others, however few. On this assumption, we judge that Pullus spoke only of those hidden crimes of which no one else is conscious unless the guilty person himself gives signs of his wrongdoing. For he calls them “concealed offences,” which, he says, flee open correction.

For this custom of the Church has survived intact down to our own time: bishops may safely take cognizance of the depraved conduct and hidden crimes of their subjects if these come to their knowledge without violating the seal of secret confession.

Still less would the author have denied the “reservation,” as they call it, of certain cases, because of which recourse must be had to higher prelates, especially to the supreme pontiff. For in the time when he was living at Rome—having been summoned by Innocent II to the insignia of the second rank, namely in 1139—the Lateran Council was held, and canon 15 reads as follows:

“If anyone, at the devil’s instigation, incurs the guilt of this sacrilege, namely by laying violent hands upon a cleric or monk, let him be bound by the bond of anathema. Let no bishop presume to absolve him, except in danger of death, until he has been presented before the apostolic presence and received its command.”

Nor do we wish to understand what he likewise adds—“A hidden fault flees open correction”—as referring to those public penalties which necessarily follow censures established by law and incurred by the very fact. The Church always had jurisdiction over these, even though the crimes themselves were internal, as some say, or rather most secret, and never to be spread abroad. It is certain that such penalties continued publicly for a long time after Pullus’s death; and that the Council of Trent restored them one by one, although in this age we know that they very rarely come into public view, both because of the carelessness or ignorance of certain priests and because they are too easily commuted into other secret penalties.

Pullus, therefore, speaks only of ordinary confessions, to which no reserved case of conscience is attached. It would be superfluous to prove this at length, since he himself sufficiently discloses his meaning. Thus, speaking of the multitude of penitents, he says: “Otherwise the bishop will not be able to suffice for such a great multitude requiring counsel; nor will the people themselves wish or dare to reveal themselves to those who, especially in this age, are devoted to the world.”

These words make it plain that he does not speak of sins which might be reserved by the bishop, or which were already reserved, since these are not sins of the multitude but occur rarely. He also says this in order to relieve the shame of penitents, which shows that there is mention only of internal or merely hidden sins, as we said above—sins which involve liability to no canonical penalty, as the age then prescribed.

Moreover, what sins required the hand of the supreme pontiff and what the hand of the ordinary bishop, our poet, so often praised, shows thus at folio 130—though his simplicity of style is readily pardoned on account of its antiquity:

> There are certain crimes that fall under the authority  
> Of a bishop or pope; of these no power is given to you.  
> One committing incest, a seducer of virgins, or a murderer,  
> A sacrilegious person, one who strikes his father, or a Sodomite—  
> Seek a bishop. Seek the pope if you have set fire,  
> If you have struck clergy, or have been a Simonist,  
> Or if you have forged a papal bull: you will go likewise.  
> One who smothers an infant at birth, or a mother who has neglected  
> Her child, however it may die;  
> If a father or mother is violently harmed; or one  
> Who commits bestial wickedness, or who, in treachery  
> [perhaps “betrayal”], kills his own lord; or one who  
> Gravely violates sacred things in church; or an adulterer; and one  
> Who defiles his mother, female relative, or sister—  
> These, though secretly committed, are subject to the bishop’s judgment.  
> If your friend can have another confessor,  
> Let her not confess her shameful acts to you.

And at folio 142, on the reverse page:

> Do not absolve an enormous crime of vice without the pope:  
> A sacrilegious person, one who strikes clergy or parents;  
> The killer of a brother, children, or women;  
> A violator of holy Church by fire or sword,  
> Or by a double sexual offense: incest and every adultery.  
> Let them teach more fully; let a murderer also be joined to these,  
> And a perjurer. What do those who act shamefully  
> With the Lord’s body and with chrism do? They undergo graver penalties.  
> Such persons, or persons like them, go to Rome, unless female sex  
> Prevents it, or infirmity, or old age.  
> Then a dispensation is granted on the counsel of elders.  
> Let the Church punish a manifest crime more than a hidden one.  
> Let those said to be capable of absolving what belongs to the pope absolve it.  
> Let certain of their superiors absolve these by their own key.

This has been set out rather more fully, for the sake of antiquity, so that the diligent reader may learn what practice of the penitential forum then prevailed in the Church.

## CHAPTER LX

“This is Lazarus,” etc. It is remarkable to what straits the Gospel account of Lazarus’s resurrection reduced both Pullus and nearly all the theologians of that age. Following its exposition in a purely literal and verbal fashion, they commonly held that God alone, by himself and excluding all ministry of priests, restores sinners to life through the remission of guilt, though a movement of contrition must precede; while priests, as dispensers of the sacrament of penance, loose persons from the bonds of sins—that is, from liability to punishment—as Lazarus was bound with bandages, as was shown above at chapter 13 of the fifth part.

So teaches the author of *Against Heresies*, among the works of Abelard, chapter 13; Hugh of St Victor, book IV of the second *Miscellanies*, title 26; Richard, his associate, in his particular treatise on this matter; the Master of the *Sentences*, book IV, distinctions 17 and 18, § F; and Peter of Poitiers, ours, who adopted both his opinion and formulations in chapter 16 of part III of his *Summa*.

The author seems to have derived the allegorical meaning of this history, with others, from Augustine in several places—for example, tractate 49 on John, homily 27 among the fifty, etc.—but especially from sermon 8, *On the Words of the Lord*:

“Someone therefore says: ‘What good is the Church if the one confessing, now raised by the Lord’s voice, comes forth? What good is the Church to the one confessing, to whom the Lord says, “What you shall loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven”?’ Consider Lazarus himself. He came forth with his bonds; he already lived by confessing, but he did not yet walk free, entangled in his bands. What, therefore, did the Church do, to which it was said, ‘What you shall loose shall be loosed,’ except what the Lord immediately said to the disciples: ‘Loose him and let him go’?”

And in sermon 44, likewise *On the Words of the Lord*:

“He came forth from the tomb alive and could not walk; and the Lord said to the disciples: ‘Loose him and let him go.’ He raised the dead man; they loosed the bound man, etc. It is therefore necessary that he who has returned to life be loosed and permitted to go. He gave this office to the disciples, to whom he said: ‘What you shall loose on earth is loosed also in heaven.’”

Thus Augustine. After him also Gregory, homily 26 on the Gospels and *Morals*, book XXII, chapter 13; Bede, on the Gospel of John at this passage; Isaac of Langres, canon 11; and before them Ambrose, *On Penance*, book II, chapter 7. See what we noted on chapter 40 of the fifth part.

“Who has now been strengthened by that absolution which takes place in confession.” And still more explicitly in the following chapter. These words of the author deserve notice. From them we infer that the practice in the sacred forum of deferring sacramental absolution—until the fruits of penance had been completed, or until the satisfaction imposed by priests had been performed—which had hitherto persisted with sufficient religious seriousness, began in his age, that is, the twelfth century, to decline into old age, not to say to die.

For that the priestly absolution was not commonly separated in time from the act of penance in that age is sufficiently declared not only by Robert, but also by his contemporaries whom we cited at chapter 13 of the fifth part: among others, Richard of St Victor, especially chapters 9 and 22 of the treatise *On the Power of Binding*, etc.; Hugh, his companion, *On the Sacraments*, book II, part XIV, chapter 1; and the *Summa of Sentences*, treatise 6, chapter 10 and following. In the first place he says:

“We disclose the liability of a graver fault to a priest in individual confession; and, according to his counsel, when the duty of satisfaction has been offered, we obtain pardon of sin.”

He says “offered,” not “completed,” as though he meant that it was then sufficient for one to accept the penance or satisfaction offered by the priest. This, however, was subject to the safeguard that the priest should be assured, from external signs, of the penitent’s inward disposition and contrition, which the cited authors require to precede the sacrament. Since, in their view, this contrition removes guilt before the actual reception of the sacrament, they were not readily persuaded that absolution ought to be deferred, guilt having already been remitted, provided that the penitent promised to satisfy God as soon as possible.

Peter of Blois, writing in the same century as the author, was led by precisely this reasoning to urge priests to show such indulgence to penitents, in his treatise on penance and the satisfaction to be imposed by priests. There he writes:

“What do you know whether he has not already been cleansed by tears and contrition? Perhaps he has been delivered by the very intention of confessing. ‘I said: I will confess,’ and thou hast forgiven. Lazarus was raised by the Lord before his bandages were loosed by the apostles. Lepers were cleansed by the Lord before they showed themselves to the priests,” etc.

But if they observed no signs of sorrow, or only weak signs, they did not wish absolution to be premature; Pullus earnestly advises that it then be deferred in the preceding chapter 57: “If meanwhile it happens that he repents of some sin, do not deny pardon to one making satisfaction; yet not prematurely, but when impenitence for that sin has departed from his heart. So long as it remained, it allowed no satisfaction for sin to have force.”

Accordingly, the practice restored by certain recent writers from ancestral custom seems to us worthy of approval: where there is no inconvenience, they defer absolution until the labours and fruits of penance have been completed, or until the period fixed by the confessor, in which he may ascertain the penitents’ condition and whether they have truly kept their promises. Would that the wishes and efforts of all might indeed unite in that most salutary custom of the advancing Church, which would be deadly to growing vices and would keep very many from frequent relapse into sins. It would moreover serve the dignity, usefulness, and efficacy of the sacraments, which are for the most part harmed by that premature rite of absolving penitents indiscriminately—a practice which judges of the external forum would regard as disgraceful, not to say harmful, in dealing with defendants marked even by a lighter crime. Yet this is said without prejudice whatsoever to those who think otherwise.

## CHAPTER LXI

“And what is the need of opening up, except that consolation may be given to the penitent?” Lest innovators wrongly abuse this passage, who wish to acknowledge no other effect of confession than that alleviation of conscience and assistance which arises from mutual conversation with a most faithful friend, when we voluntarily disclose to him whatever deeply wounds the mind, one must have recourse to what we carefully assembled at chapter 13 of the fifth part. There we set the stage for this doctrine of Pullus and held a light from the shore, lest anyone unwarily stumble.

For we showed at length that Pullus’s teaching in that age—also regularly proclaimed, not superficially, from the lectern by the other leading theologians—was safe concerning the power and efficacy of the sacraments of baptism and penance. In particular, we proved more than sufficiently, both from the author’s quoted words and from the statements of other contemporaries, what those sacraments effect: how they sometimes increase the abundance of grace; how they chiefly free from liability to punishment; and finally how they raise priests to the tribunal of judicial authority. Thus they do not rest merely in that bare and excessively meagre relief of conscience. It would be tiresome to repeat here what has already been written.

For Pullus’s sake, let it suffice to say one thing: few writers of his age have expressed the nature, necessity, and circumstances of sacramental confession, down to its smallest details, and likewise its various effects and offices, either more clearly or more elegantly. The kindly reader will observe this with appreciative attention.

“Consulting also the Lord’s words, consider that only this belongs to your care: judging one who dwells upon the earth, not one rotting beneath the earth.” The author alludes to the statement of Gelasius I in the Roman Council, where he declares in these words that absolution must be refused to a certain deceased Vitalis:

“So far as human ability allows, we provide remedies to one who desires them, as the Lord admonishes us, leaving wholly to the divine judgment whatever lies above the measure of our capacity. Nor can they charge us with the question why we remit the offense of transgression to the living, since this is possible to the Church by God’s gift. Let them not demand that we now grant pardon to the dead: it is manifest that this is not possible for us. For since it has been said, ‘Whatever you shall bind upon earth,’ he therefore reserved to his own, not to human, judgment those who are clearly no longer upon earth. Nor does the Church dare to claim for itself what it sees was not granted even to the apostles, because the case of the living is one thing and that of the dead another.”

And he alludes to Leo’s words in letter 91 to Theodore: “What one remaining in the body has not received, he cannot obtain once stripped of the flesh.” Nor is it necessary for us to examine the merits and acts of those who have died in this way, since our Lord God, whose judgments cannot be comprehended, has reserved to his own justice what priestly ministry could not accomplish; wishing his authority to be feared, so that this fear may benefit all,” etc.

The same opinion is read in the *Commonitorium* of the same Gelasius, which he handed to Faustus when sending him to Constantinople concerning Acacius, bishop of Constantinople. Since Acacius had died in this state after condemnation by the Apostolic See, the senators of that city earnestly asked that the anathema be removed and that they be allowed to communicate with their bishop. Gelasius declares, in the aforesaid *Commonitorium* and in his letter to the bishops of Dardania, or those established throughout Illyricum, that their absurd petition must not be granted and indeed could not be granted.

Pope Vigilius explains at length, near the end of his *Constitutum on the Three Chapters*, that it is the custom of Roman pontiffs to dare to determine nothing concerning the dead. Gratian, agreeing with them and likewise with our author, writes in Causa 24, question 2:

“That no one can be excommunicated or absolved after death is shown from the words of the Gospel, where it is said: ‘Whatever you shall bind upon earth,’ etc. ‘Upon earth,’ he says, not beneath the earth; showing that we can loose or bind the living according to the diversity of their merits, but cannot pronounce sentence concerning the dead.”

But, as Gratian says in the same place, this is not to be understood of every crime. There are certain crimes for which anyone may be accused or condemned even after death, such as heresy. This is most clearly proved from the Fifth General Synod, where, after the question had been debated at length—whether heretics ought to be condemned after death—the Fathers decreed that anathema should be pronounced even against the dead.

Some especially commend and uphold this decision by the multiple authority of Augustine, Rabanus Maurus, and several bishops who condemned heretics after their death. Thus Origen, Theodore bishop of Mopsuestia, and not a few others are recorded as having been condemned after death, both at the Sixth Synod and at the Seventh; and, by the same right, some were also absolved.

“As Sextilianus, bishop of Carthage, says at session 8 of the Fifth Ecumenical Synod: ‘In former times, many bishops gathered in our province and, making decisions on certain matters belonging to ecclesiastical order arising from various causes, decreed concerning deceased bishops who leave their property to heretics that they should be subject to anathema after death.’”

A famous example, in Pullus’s century, is that posthumous absolution which, at the request of Heloise, deaconess of the Paraclete and former wife of Abelard, the venerable abbot of Cluny sent her for her husband. It was composed in the following words and written and sealed by his own hand:

“I, Peter, abbot of Cluny, who received Peter Abelard as a monk of Cluny, and granted his body, secretly conveyed, to Abbess Heloise and the nuns of the Paraclete, by the authority of almighty God and of all the saints absolve him, by my office, from all his sins.”

It appears among his works, folio 345.

Yet this excommunication or anathematization after death, as likewise absolution, neither newly determines nor accomplishes anything with respect to the salvation or damnation of those whom it concerns. For, as the author admirably observes in the preceding chapter 58: “While they are upon earth, presbyters know their own parishioners; when they go beneath the earth, they pass into the diocese of the supreme Priest. Do not stretch out your hand into another’s jurisdiction.”

But to subject a dead person to anathema is to deprive him of ecclesiastical burial, to offer neither prayers nor sacrifice for him, and to deny him the other offices of piety by which Mother Church, in her devout religion, is accustomed to aid her children. To absolve, on the other hand, is to grant a share in fruits of this kind. We say this only for the instruction of the less learned. Saint Gregory recounts a notable instance of this matter in book II, chapter 23, of the *Dialogues*, concerning Saint Benedict, and in book IV, chapter 55.

In the time of Saint Leo, however, and before the Fifth General Synod, no such practice of posthumous absolution existed in the Roman Church, especially with respect to penitents who died before reconciliation had been granted them. We are taught this by chapter 6 of Leo’s letter 92 to Rusticus of Narbonne, besides the passages quoted above. Leo says: “We who did not communicate with them while living cannot communicate with them when dead.” Alcuin, at the end of his book *On the Divine Offices*, if he is its author, uses and follows this canon word for word.

But certain other churches preferred to subscribe to the contrary opinion, which advised indulgence toward the dead: the Gallican Church, in the Second Council of Arles, chapter 12; the Council of Vaison, chapter 2; and the Capitularies, book V, chapter 77; the African Church, especially at the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 79; and the Spanish Church in the Second Council of Toledo, canon 12.

## ON THE SEVENTH BOOK

## CHAPTER III

“There is, therefore, a kind of satisfaction which the nature of almost anyone can endure, though it is harsh, and so much the more pleasing to God the more humble it is, when anyone, prostrate at the priest’s feet, presents himself naked to be beaten with rods.”

Here mention is made of a scourging accepted not under compulsion but voluntarily; not privately, but before the confessor. We think this should be noted, so that you may know that the use of this rite was unknown to the ancients—as the complaining Florentine clerics observe in Peter Damian, book V, letter 8—and that it emerged in Pullus’s age, or a few years before it: namely, toward the end of the tenth century, about the year 980.

That punishment by rods imposed, rather than voluntarily accepted, was familiar to the ancients—at least with regard to religious, nuns, clerics, tenants, and servants—we learn from the canons of Isaac of Langres, title 4, chapter 13; from the first council held at our Mâcon in the year of Christ 581, chapter 8; from the Third Synod of Soissons, chapter 9; the Synod of Lestines, chapter 6; and the Second Synod of Duzey. There Duda, who had suffered adultery, and her accomplices Bertha and Erpeda, are punished with rods. We learn it likewise from the penitentials of Theodore, Bede, and Romanus—unless this seems to have been newly sewn into them by others—and especially from the Capitularies inserted in the volumes of the councils of Gaul.

We need not mention the many monastic rules in which frequent reference is made to beatings, disciplines, blows, rods, thrashings, slaps, strokes, scourgings, and other such things. Among others, our Menard in his *Harmony of Rules*, and Haeftenus in his *Monastic Investigations*, will supply abundant material.

But we infer that the practice of desired scourging, or at least voluntarily undergone scourging—which the author here commends—began in Damian’s time, or, as we said, around the year 980. Apart from the Florentines’ complaint against Damian quoted above, this is because before this period no, or at least very few, examples of it are available among ecclesiastical authors; whereas afterwards this practice of disciplines was frequent not only among monks, but also very pleasing to many secular persons. It took place not merely in private but also at the crossroads of cities, when the spur of genuine sorrow and compunction impelled penitents to it. We read that it was especially practiced in the age of Saint Vincent the Dominican.

In that age flourished those famous companies of self-flagellants, to whom that eminent preacher seemed favourable, as may be inferred from the closing words of Jean Gerson in the treatise he issued at Constance, *On the Sect of the Self-Flagellants*; or at least whom he did not effectively condemn, as Gerson himself says in the letter addressed to him.

Yet because many things had entered that sect, whether through the occasion of this public flagellation or rather from elsewhere, which the Church rightly rejected, it was not allowed to continue for long. This is so, however, only if it is certain that those who freely submitted themselves to that public scourging under Saint Vincent should be counted among those condemned in this way. That this is not credible the reader will infer from many things in Surius’s *Life* of him.

From this, however, it came about that the aforesaid chancellor of Paris, then at Constance, inveighed somewhat harshly against popular disciplines of this sort. There, as already mentioned, he published a special treatise on this subject, in which, among many other matters, he says:

“In this matter it must be feared that, among clerical persons and in holy places, this shedding of blood may cause excommunication, irregularity, defilement, or profanation in those same holy places. Christ’s law prohibits the careful imposition of public penances upon clerics, priests, and prelates, out of reverence for the clerical state. How much less ought such persons to undertake public penances of this kind, as, it is reported, many among the number of self-flagellants do; for though they seem to conceal themselves, they are nevertheless sufficiently recognized. The same would be said of distinguished persons of either sex; likewise concerning the preservation of the modesty of young women and young men who there strip themselves, and concerning the need not to impair the dignity of men or diminish the authority of parents.”

Yet although Gerson perhaps becomes more heated than is proper against public penances of this kind, we do not think that his censure condemns the use of the scourging which Pullus here commends, because of what he immediately adds, from which our author does not differ:

“If Christ’s law seems to permit scourges, according to the saying, ‘Behold, I am ready for scourges,’ nevertheless circumstances must be added by which our service may be reasonable: first, that such flagellation take place by the judgment of a superior imposing such a penance; that it be done by another, moderately, without scandal or ostentation, and without blood, according to the tradition of Saint Paris; as this sort of flagellation is performed in approved religious orders and by certain devout persons.”

Thus Gerson, in words very much in agreement with Pullus’s. Yet we do not believe them universally correct, especially when he says that rods were nowhere canonically inflicted or to be inflicted upon clerics, nor that clerics were punished through public penances, even after the time of Constantine the Great. For we read the contrary in the canons of Isaac of Langres, title 4, chapter 13:

“But if he is a servant or an ecclesiastic, let him be publicly scourged and shaved; and, by command of his own bishop, let him undergo public and canonical penance.”

And in book VII of the Capitularies of Charles the Bald, chapter 311:

“But if a cleric or monk falls into this sin, after the third beating, having been sent to prison,” etc.

Likewise, veiled nuns are to be bound by the same penance. The same is stated beforehand concerning a fornicating presbyter:

“Let him remain in prison for two years, and let him appear first whipped [Note: [Col. 1103] Perhaps *scuticatus*, from *scutica*, French *escourgée* (‘whip’).] and scourged.”

Similar provisions appear in the Synod of Lestines, held in 742. And in the *Register*, book IX, letter 66, Saint Gregory commands Bishop Paschasius:

“First deprive Hilary of the office of subdeacon, which he exercises unworthily; then, after he has been publicly punished with beatings, have him transported into exile,” etc.

The aforesaid Synod of Mâcon restricts this canonical punishment, as regards younger persons, to thirty-nine strokes.

Yet if anyone should stubbornly maintain that these provisions are to be understood only of the lesser clerics, not of the higher orders, unless degradation had first occurred (which perhaps Gerson seems to have understood, guided by the authority of St. Leo writing to Rusticus of Narbonne, and of the Fifth Council of Carthage, canon 11), we do not dispute it. But even if this be freely granted, Gerson will gain nothing advantageous for his position: namely, that public penance, or the infliction of rods (which among some was a part of it), was therefore excluded from the priesthood because those who underwent it became infamous and could consequently not be restored to their former rank; from which he concludes that clerics ought much less to scourge themselves publicly. For such infamy did not arise from the penalties of public penance themselves, but from the accompanying grave crime, which was commonly notorious when such public or solemn penance was imposed. If, however, awareness of a hidden offense, or otherwise the very ardor of compunction, compelled priests to undergo it, and they were permitted to do so by their superiors—which certainly happened not infrequently, especially in Spain, as we learn from the Thirteenth Council of Toledo, about the year 683—then no stigma of infamy was attached to them. On the contrary, they continued, as before, in the public ministries of the Church, provided the bishop so directed.

The Fathers of the cited Council of Toledo prove this very notably. Having first shown that such penance serves as a remedy for committed sin, they subsequently add that it is no detriment to priests who perform penance in this manner: “Is the gift of penance, which is given as a remedy for sin, to be turned into a prohibition of the sacrament?” Accordingly they decree: “While the enactment of the ancient canons remains in force, any bishops or priests who henceforth receive the gift of penance through the laying on of hands, and who have not branded themselves by the confession of mortal sins, shall not lose the right of retaining their governance; but, after receiving through the metropolitan reconciliation in the customary manner of penitents, they shall perform the usual duties of their order, or the other sacraments of the mysteries entrusted to them.”

That truly public and solemn penances are here under discussion is clear from the question of the bishop of Valeria, which gave occasion for framing that canon, and from the Fathers’ own manner of speaking. To the same effect are canon 53 of the Fourth Council of Toledo and canon 12 of the First Council of Orléans, which includes both priest and deacon. One should also read the chapter *Quaesitum*, Extra, *On Penance and Remission*; the chapter *Presbyter*, distinction 28; and *Si quis presbyter*, distinction 30, etc. From these it is evident that priests, and even bishops themselves, sometimes devoted themselves to public penance, always without violation of the canons; and consequently—as we press against Gerson—they could scourge themselves publicly without any irregularity or impairment of ecclesiastical discipline. This was one mode of undergoing public penance.

And lest anyone perhaps call this final point into doubt, we offer as a witness, among others, the man who composed glosses on Raymond’s metrical *Summula*. On folio 129, after setting out rather carefully the rites of public penance, he concludes their sequence thus: “After this he must again remain outside the church until Ash Wednesday, and he does this every year for so long as the bishop mercifully dispenses with him. And on Sundays he publicly scourges himself before the doors of the church; and in the city he is to do the same before the cross,” etc. He indeed admits that this solemn penance brings irregularity with it, but with an exception most welcome to us and certainly highly useful to the matter under consideration. “It should be known,” he says in the same place, “that anyone performing solemn penance will be irregular; and this is true if such penance is imposed upon him by a judge. But it would be otherwise if someone performed such penance of his own motion,” etc. This, on the contrary, opposes Gerson’s opinion above; for he does not condemn this kind of scourging provided it be done by the judgment of a superior imposing such penance—although it is certain that penance thus imposed by another incurred irregularity.

We are even less persuaded by Gerson’s further assertion: that the scourging should be administered by another, as is done in approved religious orders and by certain devout persons. For though by this exception he does not oppose Pullus, and though we do not condemn the practice of those who prefer to be beaten with another’s assistance, we nevertheless take it ill that those who harmlessly inflict violence upon themselves with their own hand should be censured. Peter Damian protects and vindicates them from the taunts of their rivals in Book V, letter 8, and Book VI, letter 27, adducing effective arguments to persuade men of this point and strongly defending voluntary scourging inflicted by oneself. “If,” he says in letter 8, “the discipline of rods seems new, and therefore blameworthy, to those who do not practice it, and if it is judged the destruction of the canons and the abolition of decrees through the foolishness of envious persuasion, is the venerable Bede therefore to be reproved, who, following the judgment of the ancient canons, declares that certain penitents ought to be bound with iron circles,” etc. Let the remainder of both letters be read.

Further, the above-cited glossator on Raymond contradicts Gerson himself, writing that penitents scourge themselves: “On Sundays he publicly scourges himself before the doors of the church.” Thirdly, the Apostle’s action in 1 Corinthians 9 argues the contrary: “I chastise my body”; in Greek, ὑποπιάζω, “I strike,” “I beat.” And, as Henri Estienne observes, that word denotes the bruise arising from a blow, which was visible in the Apostle’s flesh from the actual infliction of rods; Gretser discusses this clearly in Book I of *On Discipline*, chapter 4. But Paul’s scourging was voluntary and undertaken without anyone’s direction. Indeed Chrysostom himself, Homily 34, recommends daily bodily chastisement administered by oneself: “Thus continually bring it”—the flesh—“back to this fear,” etc. “Strike it; tear it with blows and scourges.” Hesychius too, who flourished in the fifth century, teaches the same as Chrysostom, in *Centuria* I, chapter 331, as useful for subduing the flesh. Finally, almost all religious orders approved by the Apostolic See preferred this practice of scourging oneself, both publicly and privately, to having it done by another.

We pass over those associations of laymen, even of nobles, called penitents, established by Henry III, king of France. Their custom is, on set days, to administer “discipline,” as they call it, to themselves with their own hand, as is still done today at Toulouse, Bordeaux, Aix-en-Provence, etc.

From this one may further judge whether the legal proposition that Gerson again raises is immovable: that it does not befit eminent men, for the sake of devotion and of their own accord,

> To tear their tender backs with a knotted scourge,

when, on the contrary, the voluntary chastisements of so many illustrious men and women, which we read with astonishment in Damian and Surius, establish and prove the opposite. I dislike repeating what Busaeus wrote on this matter in his notes on Peter of Blois’s commentary on Job [Col. 1105A]. Whether Gerson can rightly call such practices “a pollution of blood,” we cannot readily say. We have treated this matter at greater length than usual, but in consideration of the author, who commends the practice of disciplines in the Church, certain obstacles raised by Gerson’s cited words had to be removed.

But to return more closely to Pullus’s text: in discussing this kind of penitential satisfaction, he writes that penitents freely prepared for it were customarily beaten by their confessors. We have selected here several examples of this voluntary scourging.

Osbert—or rather Osbern—the Benedictine monk and precentor of the church of Canterbury, who flourished under Dunstan about the year of Christ 1074, relates that a certain count, punished with an anathema by Dunstan for incest, made the following satisfaction: “Therefore, while Dunstan was holding a general council of the whole kingdom concerning the observance of Christianity, the count, forgetful of himself, barefoot, with his body clothed in torn garments, carrying rods in his hand, forced his way into the midst of the council, and fell at Dunstan’s feet, groaning and wailing,” etc. Matthew Paris, explaining how deeply Henry, king of England, was pierced by grief of heart over the murder of St. Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, describes it thus: “He sought absolution from the bishops then present; and, exposing his naked flesh to the discipline of rods, he received three or five blows from each of the religious men, of whom a great multitude had assembled.” Herbert likewise says so in Book IV of his *Four-Part History*, chapter 5; but he adds that the king received at least eighty-three blows from the monks of Canterbury Cathedral.

The Roman Church retained some trace of this rite of scourging penitents: penitentiaries still hold long rods in their hands while standing before the tribunal. In this sense, some think, the passage of Optatus of Milevis, Book I against Parmenian, should be understood: “Let him go out from here as though hands were laid upon him in the episcopate and his head were shaken in penance.”

Lancelot Ducsac, an old French writer, mentions this customary satisfaction—and one more in keeping with the author’s meaning—in the first part of his work. We print his words in French, lest anything be lacking to antiquity:

> Confession is worth nothing if the heart is not repentant; and if you are far removed from the love of our Lord, you cannot be reconciled except through three things. First, by confession of the mouth. Second, by contrition of heart. Third, by sorrow of heart and by works of almsgiving and charity. Such is the right way of loving God. Now go and confess in this manner, and receive discipline from the hands of your confessors; for it is a sign of merit.

Which is said in Latin: “Confession profits nothing unless the mind is moved by repentance. If you are far removed from the love of our Lord, you cannot return to favor with him except through three things: first, confession of the mouth; then contrition of heart; and finally sorrow of heart and works of charity and almsgiving. This is the right way of loving God. Therefore go, confess as you ought, and receive the discipline of rods from your confessors; for it is a sign of merit.”

From this method of making satisfaction, we believe arose what Nangiacus records in his *Life* of St. Louis, king of France: “After his confession, he always received discipline from his confessor.” And later: “Nor do I think it should be omitted concerning a certain confessor whom he had before Brother Geoffrey of Beaulieu, of the Order of Preachers, who was accustomed to give him disciplines too excessive and severe; his tender flesh was greatly afflicted by them. He never wished to reveal this suffering to that confessor during his lifetime. But after the said confessor’s death, as if joking and laughing, he humbly acknowledged this to another of his confessors.”

Reginard, in his account of the deeds of St. Ammon, then archbishop of Cologne, writes that this most devout exercise of a contrite heart was also familiar to the Emperor Henry, who flourished in the eleventh century: “He never presumed to put on the royal insignia unless, secretly, through confession and penance, and moreover through satisfaction by blows, he had humbly obtained permission from some priest,” etc. Surius, 4 December.

Peter Damian likewise reports this of Rudolph, bishop of Gubbio, in Book I, letter 19, to Pope Alexander II: “He was continually girded around the breast with an iron circle. Yet, when he undressed before the Fathers, he carefully concealed the circle sunk beneath his flanks. For he was never present at chapter as confessor without receiving discipline.”

The poet of our metrical *Summula* of Raymond likewise alluded to this on folio 122, where, enumerating those branded with the charge of sacrilege, he excepts confessors, although they strike those confessing:

> You are a sacrilegious man if you have violated sacred things;  
> if you have struck a religious person  
> or one of the clergy—unless the blow is holy.  
> A teacher strikes a pupil; a confessor, one confessing shameful deeds,  
> and is permitted to do so.

We pass over many others because they are well known; the reader may find them abundantly enumerated in Peter Damian, Book I, letter 29 to Pope Alexander; Book V, letter 8; Book VI, letter 34; and Book II, letter 14. In the latter he sets forth the celebrated custom, in the Benedictine order—and thence among others—of scourging oneself every Friday, already flourishing in his time: “On Friday all our brethren, whom the monastic order indeed binds together, add this also to the fullness of their own salvation: they offer themselves up in chapter to reciprocal blows of brooms, and furthermore keep a fast on bread and water.”

The reason for introducing this scourging into the Church, insofar as the penitential forum is concerned, seems to have been the severe punishment imposed by the canons upon penitents. Since they saw themselves unequal to bearing it, they redeemed it through other pious works, as our author not obscurely indicates in this chapter. Hence the frequent journeys of penitents to holy places; hence the rise of a more extensive use of indulgences; hence departures for Rome and Jerusalem; hence the companies of those marked with the cross; hence the construction of churches, bridges, and similar public buildings from money collected person by person—such as that most celebrated church of the Mother of God, built under Maurice, bishop of Paris, from the alms of penitents with remarkable speed and no less magnificence. Hence finally arose the practice of voluntary scourging, which we have described, and that dreadful crash of scourges repeatedly striking upon shoulders. Peter Damian, already cited, treats at length of this redemption of canonical penalties by disciplines; and before him the venerable Bede does so in the final chapter of his book *On Remedies for Sins*, provided that there is no suspicion of some later addition, as we have already said.

## CHAPTER V

“In the *agendis* [rites] of dead children.” A more recent hand had added *exsequiis* (“funerals”), but wrongly and ignorantly. For in ancient codices and ritual books the word *agenda* is read alone and without an addition. Canon 9 of the Council of Carthage: “It was said by all the bishops: Whoever, being a priest, should wish to celebrate the *agenda* in any place without consulting the bishop acts contrary to his own honor.” In the final title of St. Jerome’s Lectionary: “In the *agenda* of the dead.” Grimald, in the *Sacramentary*, title to chapter 102: “Masses in the *agenda* of the dead.” The same, in the title to chapter 11. See Menard, Haeftenus, and others on the Rule of St. Benedict; Pamelius on liturgical matters, etc.

## CHAPTER VI

“But the ordering of ecclesiastical affairs belongs to episcopal care,” etc. Whatever be the case concerning this disposition of ecclesiastical property or revenues, which certainly belonged to bishops according to the canons, it will not be unwelcome to many students of antiquity to indicate the definite date at which the conventual table, as they call it, of the canons was separated from that of the bishop. By benefit of this separation it was thereafter lawful for each canon to possess property of his own, notwithstanding the protest of the most holy discipline of the canons.

We learn this from a most noble fragment of the Council of Aachen under Pope Gregory IV, preserved in the very ancient chronicles of our monastery of St. Peter-le-Vif at Sens. I had hesitated for a while about its authenticity because it was not found in the printed copies of this council. But another transcript of this fragment then came into my hands, liberally sent with its assessment by the most learned Nicholas Camuzat, canon of Troyes; it maintains the unquestionable authority of our text. Moreover, from other authors it is certain that benefices were first established by Gregory IV, of whom this passage speaks, as, among others, Vicecomes notes in Book IV, chapter 2, *On Baptism*.

[Col. 1107B] **On the Council of Aachen; on canons**

> “About this time, in the reign of Louis the Pious, Gregory IV came from Rome to the palace at Aachen, summoning a council of nearly all the eastern prelates and all the western ones. There they enacted very many regulations useful to the Gallican Churches, with the Roman pontiff confirming them. They decreed concerning the canons, who then lived under provosts—because the provosts administered temporal matters badly and the nobler and more powerful canons usurped possessions—that every canon, after the number of persons had been reduced to a fixed limit, should possess his own temporal property; and that from the common treasury each should receive distribution according to his attendance in choir at the divine offices.”

So it stands there. The canons, having hitherto embraced this decree with all their wishes, observe it with such unimpaired vigor that they regard it as a sin to depart from it even by a fingernail’s breadth.

And lest what follows in the same manuscript be lost, we add, for the benefit of these same canons, the likewise enacted provision concerning the liberty of their houses. After the bishops had also made a few regulations for monks, the following occurs in sequence under a special heading.

**On the liberty of the houses of canons**

> “In these times Louis the Pious granted the canons, with the lord pope’s agreement, liberty and judicial authority in their houses. And he wished them to be clothed in grey and variegated garments, because the Church in Gaul had grown so greatly that kings, dukes, and barons had sons, brothers, and uncles in churches of canons and monasteries of monks; and the stronger submitted themselves to the obedience of the humble.”

We have recorded these several matters because they have not yet been published in print.

## CHAPTER X

“It is not lawful to ordain without a title.” The author seems to have had in view not only the ancient canons which prohibit ordaining anyone without a title—for example, canon 6 of the Council of Chalcedon, in Ivo, third part of the *Decree*, chapter 102, from Leo III’s letter to King Charles; and the Council of Nantes, in the same author, third part, chapter 169, etc.—but especially the decree of Urban II, issued at Piacenza only a few years before the author’s time. It declares an ordination made without a title not merely unlawful but invalid: “By an enactment consonant with the statutes of the holy canons, we decree that an ordination performed without a title shall be deemed invalid. And each person titled in a church shall remain there permanently,” etc.

Yet Innocent III mitigated this severe censure of the canons in the chapter *Cum secundum*, Extra, *On Prebends and Dignities*, and in the chapter *Tuis quaestionibus* of the same title: he teaches that a title of patrimony suffices. The author sufficiently indicates that this was not in force in his own age; indeed the holy Council of Trent, session 21, chapter 2, *On Reform*, does not wish persons to be promoted even on that title unless the bishop judges that they should be received for the need or benefit of his churches. Read further the chapter *Non liceat*, the chapter *Episcopus* under the cited title, and the chapter *Si Episcopus* in the same title, in the Sixth Book; also the Lateran Council under Alexander III, Part I, chapter 9.

But lest anyone be troubled by the fact that the cited pontiffs declare ordination without a title to be invalid, note the Gloss on the word *irritas*: “invalid as regards exercise, not as regards validity”; for they do not lose their order.

“Do you not assent when, in a public hearing, the title of a certain church has been read,” etc.? Here Pullus very strongly commends the ancient custom of the Church not to promote anyone to sacred orders who was not assigned to the ministries of a particular church. Such a person was accordingly entered on its list or register, commonly called the *canon*; from this, it is held, priests called *canonici* derived their name—the men now called simply canons. Those who wandered and did not remain in fixed residences were called fugitives and supernumeraries, as in canon 15 of the Council of Clermont.

Therefore Basil of Caesarea directs that several registers of the Church should be kept: one with the bishop, another with the chorepiscopi or rural deans, and a third kept by the clerics of each church to which a man was enrolled, lest any fraud creep into that most select body of clerics. Basil calls such clerics *canonici* in his letter to Amphilochius, canon 6, because their names were read in the canon. In Zonaras, commenting on the Council of Nicaea, canon 17, “to be enrolled in the canon” is the same as “to be ordained in the clergy”; and a mark or sign of degradation was the striking of a criminal cleric’s name from that canon. Filesac, *On the Sacred Authority of Bishops*, chapter 13, §5, also observes that those now called canons, assigned to a particular college or church as to a title according to the canon of Chalcedon, received this name in the age of Charlemagne, whereas previously they were called clerics. Hallier likewise, *On Sacred Elections*, Part II, section 6, chapter 2, article 1, no. 3, judges that everything found in ancient law as said of priests is to be understood as said of cathedral canons: “The matters found in the old law concerning canons of the greater church to be summoned for ordination,” he says, “are consonant with these things.”

## CHAPTER XI

“For this reason, the last three are called sacred orders.” Some hold that the subdiaconate began to be regarded as a sacred order only from the time of Urban II. Innocent III seems to suggest this in the Extra, *On Servants Not to Be Ordained*: “For although it was not regarded as a sacred order in the primitive Church, yet from the constitution of Gregory and Urban it is beyond doubt, according to modern times, to be a sacred rank.” Urban’s constitution reads thus: “Let no one be elected bishop unless he has been found to live religiously in sacred orders. By sacred orders we mean the diaconate and priesthood; for the primitive Church is read to have had these alone. But because subdeacons also minister at the altars, we admit them when necessity requires,” distinction 60, final canon.

Yet whether this constitution permits one to infer that the subdiaconate is a sacred order, we can scarcely determine. In the *Summa* of Peter the Chanter of Paris—extant in manuscript at Paris in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés—chapter 54 reads: “The first laying on of hands is due to those being ordained deacons. For it has newly been instituted that the subdiaconate is a sacred order.” That Peter flourished at the end of the twelfth century. But our Peter of Poitiers, who lived at that time, seems to judge that subdeacons were not yet bound by a vow of continence. For, inquiring whose duty it is to abstain by force of sacred ordination, he does not mention them, when he says in chapter 25 of the third distinction: “The perfection of an order is complete continence, whose sign is to show it in deed. Every priest is bound to this, whether he has care of a flock or not, and likewise the deacon. This perfection is nothing other than the vow of continence, concerning which it is said: ‘He who can receive it, let him receive it’” (Matthew 19:12).

Others, however—and we agree with them—more conveniently refer this to the time of Gregory I, whom they say is the Gregory mentioned by Innocent. For in Book I, letter 42, on the occasion of certain subdeacons of Sicily who were unwilling to practice continence or to abstain from the wives they had married, he directs that the following precaution be observed thereafter: “It therefore seems to me that from the present day all bishops should be instructed not to presume to make anyone a subdeacon unless he has promised to live chastely,” etc.

Our Ratramnus, monk of Corbie, also notably demonstrates the antiquity of clerical celibacy among subdeacons in both the Greek and Latin Church, at the end of his treatise *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit against the Greeks*. There, replying to their various objections against the Latins, particularly against celibacy, and having first enumerated the canons of the Councils of Nicaea and Neocaesarea, etc., and the constitution of Emperor Justin, he continues:

> “The present enactment is known to remove every cloud of doubt, clearly forbidding marriage not only to priests and deacons, but also to subdeacons and to all others whatsoever in the clergy. It forbids them to permit anyone at all to live in their house except their mother and persons free from the stain of suspect indecency. It decrees that transgressors, if convicted, shall be expelled from the clergy and that such persons shall be assigned to the duties of the curia as a penalty of disgrace.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Let, therefore, the glorious princes of the Greeks say, relying on what arrogant presumption, they are unashamed to act against the ordinances of their forefathers, against the laws of the Church, and against the custom hitherto observed, reproaching Romans and Latins because they do not permit bishops, priests, Levites, and subdeacons to take wives. For behold, they are convicted by imperial laws, which, since they enact measures for Romans and Latins, undoubtedly condemn those who act contrary to them.”

This author exists in manuscript in the celebrated Library of Thou, that storehouse of antiquity so richly furnished that it has hitherto satisfied the wishes of all learned persons.

“For among us no woman [is joined] to a priest,” etc. Here, and in the text of chapter 19 cited below, Pullus seems to have indulged obscurity more than is fitting. Since I reasonably distrusted my ability alone to grasp his genuine sense, I consulted several persons to shed light upon my blindness. Among them, I think, the royal professor of the most eminent house, Monsieur de Sainte-Beuve, happily illuminated the matter. Removing the obstacles I had feared in the author, he thus briefly explained Pullus’s meaning and his own:

> “By the words ‘For among us,’ etc., the author gives the reason why he immediately called women who endure priests’ embraces prostitutes: namely, because among us—that is, in the Roman Church—none of them is joined to a priest in marriage. He proves it because a priest may dismiss her whenever he wishes. It is as though he argued thus: a woman who has intercourse with a man outside lawful marriage is a prostitute; but a woman who has intercourse with a priest has intercourse with a man outside lawful marriage. This is shown because a woman whom a man may dismiss whenever he wishes has intercourse with him outside lawful marriage. But a priest may dismiss whenever he wishes the woman with whom he has intercourse; therefore,” etc.

Thus he.

“A monk by the very habit of his life, and a cleric by the rank of sacred order: each professes continence in fact, without words.” Pullus was not ignorant of the monks’ custom of making solemn profession; but because the Rule of Benedict—which the Cluniacs, Cistercians, Camaldolese, and almost innumerable other monasteries of Benedictine monks and sacred virgins professed—was universally known in his age, and because chastity is not vowed in it except implicitly, he consistently wrote that monks profess continence without words. “For,” says Basil, letter 2 to Amphilochius, chapter 19, “we know no profession of men except those who have attached themselves to the order of monks; they seem silently to have accepted celibacy.” Innocent III declares this continence so proper to the monastic state, in Extra, *On the State of Monks*, chapter *Cum ad monasterium*, that he asserts no one, not even the supreme pontiff, can dispense from it.

The form of solemn profession to be made among the Benedictines is as follows, as observed in the French Congregation of St. Maur:

> “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen. In the year from his Nativity, N., on the Nth day of the month N., I, Brother N., of such-and-such place in the diocese of N., promise stability, conversion of my manner of life, and obedience according to the Rule of our Holy Father Benedict, before God and his saints whose relics are kept in this monastery N., in the diocese of N., under the Congregation of St. Maur of the Order of St. Benedict, in the presence of the Reverend Father Dom N. and the monks of the same monastery. In witness whereof, I have written this document, or petition, with my own hand, on the day and in the year stated above.”

The Carthusians use it as well, with a few omissions; nowhere is a vow of continence expressed.

“Clerics are in the choir; laymen are outside.” In former times rails were set around the altar and choir to keep back the crowd of laymen, especially from the place open to clerics alone: chapter 1, Extra, *On the Life and Honesty of Clerics*. The imperial and royal majesty is excepted; for Balsamon argues, on canon 69 of the Sixth Synod, that in reverence for anointing and royal power, the emperor or king has free and open access even within the altar rails, unless he is found bound by some crime or evil deed. St. Ambrose charged this against the Emperor Theodosius, in Theodoret, Book V, chapter 18.

That altar rails belonged to the earliest and most ancient structure of churches is sufficiently clear from the panegyric of Paulinus, bishop of Tyre, where Eusebius calls the enclosure a latticework fence of wood: “The sanctuary is enclosed on every side in a square form by lofty columns, the spaces between whose middles are filled with wooden latticework or transennae, extending in a moderate and uniform length.” Book X of the *History*, chapter 4.

From such rails the chancellors of princes were formerly so called, because they performed the functions and duties of their office stationed within the rails—that is, enclosed by a wooden barrier—which kept away a troublesome crowd pressing in, while allowing them to be seen by everyone without inconvenience or distress. This is stated more plainly in Agathias, Book I of the *History*, and Cassiodorus, letter 6, Book X of the *Variae*. The Church too employed this office of chancellor—distinguished among the Fathers clothed in purple—and our Robert held it for some years. But when the office, or rather its authority, had grown to a degree that could be feared, vice-chancellors were created, the office of chancellor having been suppressed.

## CHAPTER XIII

“For according to ancient tradition.” We find it in Ivo, Part II of the *Decree*, chapter 84, from a letter of Paschal—or, as others read, Paschasius:

> “But if anyone should object that consecrations are not bought, but rather the things themselves that arise from consecration, he is proved utterly to speak foolishly. For since a corporeal church, or a bishop, or an abbot, can in no way prosper in such things without corporeal and external goods, just as the soul cannot live bodily without the body: whoever sells either one of them, without which the other could not be had, does not fail to sell both. Yet the sacred canon utterly eliminates this objection,” etc.

## CHAPTER XV

What Pullus means by “chaplain” and “parish priest,” and by “courts,” “tents,” and “parishes,” is not easy for me to conjecture—unless, as I readily concede, he means by courts and tents the very chapels or oratories of kings over which the chaplain presides, and which are frequently mentioned by our authors under the kings of the first and second dynasties; and by parishes, the parish and rural churches themselves, in which the sacred baptismal font is found.

The former are mentioned in the Council of Agde, canon 21, and the Third Council of Orléans, canon 7: “That in the oratories of estate-holders, they shall by no means admit foreign clerics against the will of the bishop to whom the privilege of that territory is known to belong, except perhaps approved men whom episcopal authority has ordered to be retained there.” And in the Council of Chalon, canon 14: “Certain of our brethren and fellow bishops, while we were sitting in holy synod, brought forward a complaint that oratories built long ago on the estates of powerful men, and the resources bestowed there, are claimed against the bishops by the owners of the estates; and that they no longer permit even the clerics who serve at those oratories to be disciplined by the archdeacon.” The Fathers of the Council of Meaux, canon 75, likewise address Charles the Bald concerning these chapels and courts.

Mention of a priest-chaplain is also frequent in English constitutions. There William of Lyndwood, together with the Archdeacon, notes that *tabernaculum* is sometimes taken to mean a church, chapter *Sicut non alii*, *On Consecration*, distinction 1; and that *parochia* may mean the mother church of the diocese itself, or even the whole diocese; and *parochiani*, bishops—usages very frequent in ancient law.

The name *chapel* was not heard before the time of Gregory of Tours. Many derive it from the cloak (*cappa*) of St. Martin—called a cowl (*cuculla*) by others—which, having come into the possession of our kings, they ordered to be carried with them everywhere out of devotion and religion, especially when going to war, so that with it spread out before them beneath the royal tent they might pour out prayers and perform the other customary offices of piety and religion. Those who carried or guarded it, they say, were called clerical chaplains. Thus Walafrid Strabo, in *On the Beginnings and Growth of Ecclesiastical Things*, chapter 38: “Chaplain was first derived from the cloak of blessed Martin, which the kings of the Franks used to have with them in battle as an aid to victory; and the clerics carrying and guarding it together with the other relics of the saints began to be called chaplains.” So also the monk of St. Gall, Book I, *On the Deeds of Charlemagne*, chapter 4; and Vicecomes, Book II, *On Ancient Rites of the Mass*, chapter 28.

But others more plausibly judge that the name *capella*, from which the priests or clerics called chaplains derive, came from the sacred reliquary chest, which was also called a *capella*, because it contained the relics of saints. Hence Evodius, Book I, *On the Miracles of St. Stephen*: “a silver *capella* in which was a portion of relics.” And Eckehard, in the *Life of Notker the Stammerer*, chapter 15, speaking of the archchaplain Solomon, who had brought with him a *capella* of sacred relics dedicated to St. Gall, writes that the following verses were inscribed upon it:

Behold the cross, and the pious shrine of Mary with the saints.

Charles chose this to be the chief chapel. The priests who bore those sacred relics were called chapel-priests (*capellani presbyteri*), as is often found in the ancient councils of Gaul. Indeed, that very reliquary shrine of St Martin—at which purgations and oaths were performed—was called a *capella*, as Marculf the monk testifies in Book I of the *Formulas*, chapter 38:

> It was adjudged that, of the five persons named, the same man, together with three others and three others, making seven by his own hand, should then swear in our palace upon the chapel of Lord Martin, where the remaining oaths are performed.

From this passage Strabo and the monk of St Gall must be corrected: where they print *cappa*, one must write *capella*. For it is not credible that so many distinguished men who deliberately wrote on the deeds and miracles of St Martin—namely Sulpicius Severus, [Col. 1112A] Paulinus of Nola, Venantius Fortunatus, Gregory of Tours, and others—would have been perpetually silent about this cloak of his, if they had known or believed the things others write about it.

Whatever may be the nature and derivation of the word, from this chapel or cloak of St Martin arose those famous chapels of our kings, filled with many relics of saints—to which they were most devoted—and which they wished to have carried with them wherever they went. In them flourished the most celebrated sacred rites, varied furnishings, a larger body of ministers, enriched by royal gifts, enlarged by privileges, and raised to so lofty a summit of honours that even today the noblest magnates, indeed the chief ecclesiastical dignitaries themselves, compete individually to be enrolled in them.

Honorius of Autun, near the end of Book I of the *Gem of the Soul*, adds another explanation of the word *capella*:

> “The greater churches are called *templa*; the lesser, *capellae*, from goatskins. The ancients, and even nobles, had little travelling churches made of goatskins, and called their guardians *capellani*. A *capenum* is called a house to which the poor flock to seek alms; hence a church is called a *capella*, in which Christians, poor in spirit, assemble to seek the alms of the soul. There are also chaplains called from the cloak of St Martin,” etc.

This author has been published, but to me he belongs merely among the many writers of the same stamp, among whom Robert Pullen stands out: a canon of the Church of Amiens, flourishing in 1170, who wrote excellently on ecclesiastical offices, persons, sacred vestments, and so forth.

## CHAPTER XVII

**He who exercises a private priesthood among the brethren.** Pullen did not have in view the practice customary in the monasteries of his own time; rather, he meant that ancient practice of which frequent mention occurs in old councils, where it is forbidden [Col. 1112C] that public Masses be celebrated in monasteries. Thus in Ivo, Part VII of the *Decree*, chapter 13 (otherwise 12), and in Gratian, Question XVIII, distinction 2, chapter *Luminoso*, the words of St Gregory are quoted:

> “We also prohibit altogether the celebration of public Masses in monasteries, lest any occasion of popular gathering be afforded in the retreats and dwellings of God’s servants; for this is not expedient for their souls. Nor may a bishop there presume to establish his chair, or exercise any authority of command, or perform any ordination, however slight, unless asked by the abbot; so that monks may always remain subject to their abbots, and, freed from vexations and every burden, may perform the divine work with the fullest devotion of mind for ever.”

So speaks Gregory.

Indeed, from the same Book V of the *Register*, epistle 46, and Book VII, epistle 15, we learn that in earlier centuries there were few priests within cloisters. This must chiefly be understood of monks dwelling far from cities and [Col. 1112D] from the concourse of people, upon whom no care of souls at all rested: such as we still see in greater number today—the Cistercians, Camaldolese, Carthusians, and so forth—who inhabit forests or retreats of more sacred solitude, are less exposed to the sight of secular people, and are not compelled to discharge the duties of a public priesthood.

But if one may consider the other orders—for example, the Augustinian clerics, who were emerging under Ivo of Chartres in Pullen’s age, and especially the Benedictine order, which was best known of all—although constant contemplation of heavenly things is implanted, or rather inborn, in it, it is nevertheless certain that from the very cradle of the Benedictine family not merely some of its members, called to the foremost mitres of ecclesiastical dignity, but entire communities of monks publicly laboured for the salvation of souls, celebrated sacred rites before the people, taught the people from the pulpit, and fulfilled the other offices of apostolic care [Col. 1113A] which, by ancient right, fell to those priests whom the populace call secular, summoned to the governance of souls.

Witness to this are the many famous colonies of monks, the many companies of martyrs, the many bands of apostles, whom the Roman See sent out from the innermost recesses of monasteries into the vast regions of the two Germanies, Poland, Norway, England, and so forth: very small bands, for the purpose of spreading the Gospel, baptizing, and establishing churches and dioceses—of which they themselves were the principal founders, without contradiction—and discharge the remaining works of pastoral care to which the hierarchical order has hitherto applied itself. Thus Pope Gregory repeatedly attests in his letters to Augustine, Laurence, Mellitus, Justus, and the other Benedictine bishops, concerning England—which, since we have selected Pullen’s nation here, was newly to be brought to the faith through Benedictines. The Venerable Bede, Polydore Vergil, Raynerius, and other writers of the English Church likewise testify; it would be superfluous to excerpt anything from them.

The very construction of monasteries of this order, whether beside cities or in their very centre, likewise bears witness: their vast churches, renowned rites of worship, the very splendour of ceremonies, the modulation of chant, the exceptionally famous sound of bells, the use of sacred vestments after the manner of the Roman Church, to whose rites it constantly adhered, [Col. 1113B] and similar things, in which even today it yields nothing to cathedral churches. Surely none of these things could ever have grown up with the order unless it had been assigned, however reluctantly, public functions of the priesthood.

For how many monasteries in every province of the Christian world still enjoy cathedral rights and privileges, over which clergy and people are subject, and in which the most extensive authority flourishes in spiritual and temporal matters? The Council of Trent recognizes and approves this, Session 25, *On Regulars*, chapter 11. And, that we may not travel farther in search of testimony to the truth, but remain within the boundaries of recent France: do not the monks of St-Germain-des-Prés at Paris; those of St-Denis near Paris; those of St-Corneille at Compiègne; Corbie; Cluny; Fécamp; St-Médard at Soissons; Rebais; St-Valery at the mouth of the Somme; Vézelay; and so forth—not to mention the nuns of Jouarre—still possess cathedral rights and authority, labour at the foremost pastoral responsibilities, and exercise a public priesthood? Not out of an alien desire to dominate clergy, but from maternal affection—indeed, one might say necessity—to bring up the spiritual children whom they once begot in Christ Jesus through the Gospel.

Hence the splendour of pontifical insignia flowed from the Apostolic See into many abbeys of this order: the tiara and mitre heavy with gold and jewels, rings, gloves, sandals, and the remaining ornaments of the highest dignity. Pullen, writing at the time, could not have been ignorant that many abbots used them, and those most holy men, such as Hugh and Peter [Col. 1113D] of Cluny.

But, returning more closely to the author’s text: when he speaks of private priesthood among brethren, he refers only to Cistercians, Camaldolese, Carthusians, or certain other most devoted inhabitants of the wilderness—for the new offspring of mendicant orders had not then made the Church fruitful—not to Benedictines. For it is entirely certain that at that time they were devoted to the higher ministries of the Church, and even possessed several bishoprics as founded by themselves, as Robert of Torigni, an eyewitness, reports in the appendix to Sigebert’s *Chronicle*, in the year of Christ 1151, the second or third year after Pullen’s death:

> “In Wales there are four bishoprics; in England, seventeen. In eight of these, monks occupy the episcopal sees.”

And after a few intervening words:

> “This is found in England because the first preachers of the English—namely Augustine, Mellitus, Justus, and Laurence—were monks. In eight other episcopal sees there are secular canons; in one, regular canons.”

Meanwhile, the statement deserves notice, since it blunts the pen of Gabriel Pennot and the other regular clerics of Ivo’s institution, to whom the Benedictines’ apostolate in England is welcome only if [Note: [Col. 1113D] Author of *The Triumph of Thomas à Kempis*, article 10, §2.] they renounce monasticism; indeed, they would have the whole succession of metropolitan and episcopal sees erected either by the apostles or by their disciples entered on the register of their own Augustinians. Among these—mentioning only a few out of all those appropriated to themselves—Pennot lists [Note: [Col. 1114D] Book II of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 11 and following.] the Roman Church itself, mother of all; and among the churches of Gaul the metropolitan sees of Lyons, Sens, Besançon, Bourges, Bordeaux, Narbonne, [Col. 1114B] Reims, Rouen, Toulouse, Tours, and so forth, for no other reason than that they sought to observe rules handed down to them by Christ and the apostles. If this is most readily conceded, we do not begrudge their now summoning into their own camp, by this trumpet-call, every religious order established anywhere in the Christian world, old and new, and Christianity itself, if they please. But let us continue.
