These points are further confirmed by the Venerable Bede, Book IV of the *History of the English*, chapter 27, where, speaking of Aidan, bishop of Lindisfarne, he writes as follows for our purpose:

> “For Aidan, who was the first bishop of that place, came there himself a monk together with monks and instituted there a monastic manner of life, just as the first blessed father Augustine is known to have done in Kent, as the most reverend Pope Gregory wrote to him, as we have set out above,” etc.

The apostolate in England of Augustine and the others of the Benedictine family—from which the honours of public priesthood in Benedictine England itself proceeded—is attested by Æthelhelm, or Aldhelm, bishop of the West Saxons, flourishing in 690. Thus in his *Poem in Praise of Virgins*, at the beginning of Volume VIII of the Cologne edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, pages 8 and 9, where he speaks of St Benedict the Father:

> In those same times blessed Benedict shone forth,  
> Whom God, the merciful Creator, had granted to Asconia,  
> That he might lead the people of the Lord walking the right path  
> To the footprints of the eternal kingdom’s Guide.

And shortly afterwards:

> Gregory the bishop, unfolding his distinguished life from its beginning,  
> Had once described it in writings,  
> Until he happily passed into the heavenly citadel.  
> We rejoice to be gathered in the number of his disciples,  
> Whom fruitful Britain bears in her bosom as citizens;  
> From him the grace of baptism has now flowed to us,  
> And the venerable company of teachers has come running. [Col. 1114D]

These are his words; he was a contemporary of Augustine himself, bishop of Canterbury, or only a few years later.

For abbots performed the functions of bishops, and monks those of canons; hence in ancient documents of our monasteries the latter may sometimes be seen called regular canons, because they discharged the duties of cathedral canons while not departing by a nail’s breadth from observance of the Rule. That this long continued in Canterbury itself, the metropolitan see of the English, especially in 1170, when blessed Thomas of Canterbury fell beneath the swords of the wicked, is attested by Roger and, after him, Baronius under that year, when recounting the martyrdom of this most illustrious bishop. There is nowhere any mention of canons, but rather of monks, whom he accordingly calls “cathedral monks” in the same place. Baronius says:

> “In the same year, after St Thomas had been removed from their midst, the Church of Canterbury began to be tossed about, when the cathedral monks of that church were choosing a successor.” [Col. 1115A]

They adhered, of course, to the precepts of the Benedictine Rule, which gives monks the right to elect an abbot, although, as Baronius notes, the provincial bishops then claimed that office for themselves, whether rightly or wrongly. When these bishops had been excluded from the monks’ chapter, the smouldering tinder of hatreds broke out into fresh sparks.

See Bede, in his *Cuthbert*, chapter 26, and Book I of the *History of the English*, chapters 26 and 27; Marcellinus in Surius, 1 March, Volume II; William of Malmesbury; William of Newburgh, Book I of the *History*; Matthew of Westminster, under the year 1170; Vincent of Beauvais, Book XXIX of the *Mirror of History*; Polydore Vergil, Book V; Jacobus Meyer, under the year 1208; and so forth; Innocent III, Book I of the Letters, on the Benedictine archbishop of Monreale in Sicily; and so forth.

Monks were also sometimes intermingled with cathedral canons and together occupied themselves in the divine offices in choir. Platina, in Gregory the Great’s life, testifies that this arrangement was established by Pope St Gregory:

> “He further ordained that, almost without interruption, the divine offices should be celebrated in the church of St Peter by the weekly priests and by monks. From this it is clear that in many places the dwellings of monks and secular priests were adjacent; stirred by emulation, they served God as diligently as possible.”

So says Platina. This still flourishes today in the Ambrosian Church at Milan, where canons on one side of the choir and Cistercian monks on the other sing the divine praises together. The custom also continues to the present in the Church of St Peter in Ciel d’Oro at Pavia, where the holy body of St Augustine rests, with Augustinian hermits and regular clerics of the same name chanting together in alternating choirs.

Nor was this custom strong only among the English: episcopal sees were erected in Benedictine monasteries, and monks themselves, retaining their habit and the unviolated discipline of regular observance, performed the office of canons. To speak only of our own countrymen: in France alone we find at least as many Benedictine bishoprics as Robert of Torigni listed in England. For in 1317, while the Roman pontiffs were seated at Avignon, John XXII endowed several monastic churches of this order with an episcopal see; in them monks bound by religious vows retained the regular habit until almost our own times. Thus those of Castres were clad in secular dress in 1535; those of Sarlat and St-Pons-de-Thomières were stripped of monastic dress only in 1615, Paul V allowing looser practice; those of Tulle were released from vows in 1517; Vabres in 1577; Alès in 1530; Condom in 1540; Luçon in the time of Paul II; Saint-Flour in 1476 by Sixtus IV; while those of Maleac have not yet suffered any lapse from the Rule. These examples are within the limits of recent France; beyond them, were we inclined to range further, we could recount more and older memorials of pontifical [Col. 1115D] dignity received by our monasteries.

We can readily believe that those who forced me—though I was unwilling—to bring forward these few facts did not know them. From the very etymology of “monk,” which suggests solitude, they judged that our monks must relinquish these functions and cares of public priesthood; that the jurisdiction over clergy and people which still prevails in most places must be abolished; that the apparatus of worship must be removed from the order; that mitres and titles of dignity must be proscribed; and that anything which rivals cathedral rights, privileges, and honours must be surrendered with the greatest readiness. They were plainly unaware that these were not badges of ambition, but the inherited rights of piety, the very foundations of an order most deserving of the Church, and either ornaments or dues of its service lavished in obedience to the faith, as has been indicated above.

When these matters had already been sent to press and were nearly appearing [Col. 1116A] in print, it happened that I read a certain little book, an emblem of most sincere charity and a genuine offspring of cloistered modesty, entitled *The Triumph of Thomas à Kempis*. Its author, a regular cleric of Ivo’s institution—whom out of reverence I shall not name here—was eager to prove that the rights of public priesthood had come to his own cloistered brethren, and had come much more generously than to monks, for whom he anxiously supposes that ecclesiastical distinction to be merely adventitious. He therefore supplied a new explanation of the dignity introduced into his cloisters, which will serve our purpose, though contrary to its author’s intention. [397] He derives it from the nobility of fur garments, or almuces, which regular clerics borrowed from cathedral canons—or rather from the foremost monks and hermits:

> “The canonical habit of the Augustinian clerics is especially noble because of its fur garments or almuces, which supreme pontiffs, cardinals, kings, doctors, jurists, and other men of more eminent rank use. This undoubtedly flowed from those primitive kings, who, since they were for the most part shepherds, used garments and staffs of fur; hence the purple of kings—who also carry a sceptre in place of a staff—is of fur. Such fur garments were granted to canons, first because they enjoy a royal priesthood by their institution; secondly because they are shepherds of souls; and finally because they occupy themselves almost continually with divine praises and songs. For it was ancient custom that one who devoted himself to singing songs should put on a fur garment, in imitation of shepherds clad in fur, who commonly steal leisure for singing songs.”

So he writes on page 140, in order to prove that his Ivoine brethren should be exalted to the Church’s throne. [Note: [Col. 1115D] Page 138, line 18, of the *Triumph of Thomas à Kempis*.]

This explanation, drawn out at length and not without hauteur, if it has any force, will benefit us rather; this has already been suggested above.

For those fur garments which our countrymen call almuces are called *armilausae* by others, as by Paulinus, bishop of Nola, in Letter 7 to Severus; by Isidore, *Origins*, Book XIX, chapter 22; and by Cassian, *Institutes*, chapter 8, *melotē* (μελωτή), following the Septuagint at 3 Kings IX and 4 Kings I, and the Apostle at Hebrews XI. No one who attends to these passages will deny that they belonged properly to monks. The chief of the ancient monks was Elijah, who wore such a covering; Jerome says of him in Letter 28: “Elijah, carried up to heaven in a fiery chariot, left his *melote* on earth.” Concerning him and the other prophets the Apostle writes above: “They went about in *melotai* and goatskins, destitute” (Heb. IX, 37), and so forth. Anthony, who closely imitated them in piety as also in dress, is likewise said to have possessed a *melote*. Athanasius reports in his *Life* of Anthony, speaking of the *melote* and cloak given by Anthony to him, a most holy man:

> “Give Bishop Athanasius the *melote* and the worn cloak on which I lie; he himself brought the new one.”

Palladius bears witness in the Rule of St Pachomius’s monks that they also wore sheepskins over their garments: [Note: [Col. 1116D] In the *Lausiac History*, chapter 38.] “Let each have one worked white sheepskin; [Col. 1116D] without it let them neither eat nor sleep.” Pope Gregory plainly reports, in his usual manner, that St Benedict the Father likewise used the *melote*, in Book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 7, in this statement of Placidus: “When I was being drawn from the water, I saw the abbot’s *melote* over my head, and perceived that he himself was bringing me out of the waters.”

But before proceeding further, the reader may perhaps ask what the *melote* itself was and what shape it had. Eucherius answers in Book II, chapter 10, of his *Instruction to Salonius*: “The *melote* in the Book of Kings is a simple skin, which Egyptian monks still use, hanging down from one side.” The Glossary of Cambron calls it “*melota*, woollen garment, and bag.” “It is a goatskin, hanging from the neck and girded down to the loins.” And Simeon Priscus, in Theodoret’s *Religious History*, chapter 6, explains it as “a small piece of cloth woven from goatskin, over the shoulders.” From these statements Laurence Landtmeter concludes, in Book I of *On the True Dress of Clerics and Monks*, chapter 27, that the almuces of canons, or those fur garments formerly worn over the shoulders, derived their origin from this skin. Until a few years ago they covered the head with them, in accordance with the decree of the Council [Note: [Col. 1117D] “Let them enter churches holding almuces or birettas on their heads.” Council of Basel, Session 21.] of Basel, Session 21; whereas now, in most places, they merely burden the arms.

The use of this *melote* or almucium was not introduced solely by private laws of monasteries. Rather, perhaps because it had fallen into disuse, it was restored to our Gallican monks by the Fathers assembled at Aachen in the council discussed above under chapter 6 of this part. Since another fragment of that council has not yet been published, we set it out in full, although, because of the excessive age of the characters, it is marred by some errors.

### Concerning the monks of Gaul

> “At that time Gallican monks were permitted [Col. 1117B] to use woollen breeches, shirts, fur garments, boots, fur hoods [perhaps *de pellibus*, ‘of skins’], almuces, gold-bright coverlets, and mattresses for the sick. They were also permitted, on great feasts, to have several dishes, with bread *farinulis* [otherwise *ferinulis*], and *sciatis* [another manuscript: *fialis*] of spiced wine, for the honour of the feasts and the nobility of the Franks—not for gorging the belly, but for the restoration of strength. Since the Franks have no olive oil, the bishops wished them to use bacon-fat. They further wished, with the agreement of the most illustrious Louis, that monks should remain without disturbance from laypeople in the monasteries which they possess in villages, fortresses, boroughs, and cities. The bishops decreed, with the agreement of the lord pope, that monks should abstain from heavy work and labour for the dignity of the priesthood; and that, in place of labour, they should sing at the Hours certain appointed psalms for the living and departed faithful, with prescribed prayers. They also wished that at Easter and Pentecost monks should maintain the Roman custom in divine worship.”

This occurs in our older chronicles of St-Pierre-le-Vif at Sens and in the notes of the most learned Camuzat.

From these things it is apparent that the use of almuces or fur garments, so much approved by our Ivoine religious, was older and more common among our monks; nor is it even now wholly rejected. It certainly still survives among the monks of St Nicasius at Reims when they attend divine offices and perform sacred rites, and at Fécamp at least in the precentor. Others, such as the monks of St-Denis near Paris and Corbie, wear almuces of another material on the left arm, after the fashion of cathedral canons, while vested in albs and attending divine service: they are made solely of black cloth, according to the constitution of Clement V at the Council of Vienne, *Clementines*, Book III, title 10, *Ne in agro*, at its beginning. In it the holy pontiff decrees that monks’ almuces should be made [Col. 1117D] either of skins or of black cloth:

> “Let them be content, in place of hoods, with almuces of black cloth or skins, together with the hoods of the habit which they wear.”

The monks of Bursfeld—an exceptionally noble and extensive Benedictine branch among the Germans—still retain this use of the habit, as Haeftenus observes in Disquisition 4, Book V, treatise 3, under the special title “Whence the monks’ almucium?” This is finally conceded by Gabriel Pennot himself, the leading writer of the regular clerics, in Book I, chapter 22, no. 5, of the *Tripartite History* of his canons: although not all bishops drawn from regulars use a linen tunic, nevertheless all have customarily used an almucium, because the almucium is not a peculiar dress of clerics, but common to clerics and monks alike. In the passage cited, no. 3, he further reports that Augustine of Hippo used it, on Baronius’s authority, *Annals*, Book II, under the year 261, no. 90 and following; *birrus* and *almucia* having the same meaning in Baronius. If, then, the Ivoine monk above constructed so elaborate an argument from the wearing of almuces or fur garments to access to hierarchical dignities, what rank, I ask you, is worthier of their summit than monasticism? But let a very weak faith avail its author, to whom perhaps the reason why the use of the fur hood entered clergy and cloisters was either unwelcome or not readily accessible. For this manufacture of skins does not display the trappings and glitter of vanity, but our unceasing shame arising from the fault of our first parents and the remembrance of death, to which sin has bound us. Durandus, bishop of Mende, argues no less learnedly than devoutly in his *Rationale*, Book III, chapter 1, explaining the reason and derivation of the word *superpelliceum*:

> “It is called a *superpelliceum* [Note: [Col. 1118D] But better *subpelliceum*, as Andreas Du Saussay, cited below, observes.] because in ancient times it was worn [Col. 1118B] over fur tunics made from the skins of dead animals; and this is still observed in certain churches, recalling that Adam, after sin, was clothed in such skins.”

And before him Cassian, *Institutes*, Book I, chapter 8:

> “Of them the Apostle says: ‘They went about in *melotai* and goatskins, destitute, distressed, afflicted—of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts and mountains and caves and holes of the earth’ (Heb. III, 37). Yet this garb of goatskin signifies that, with every wantonness of carnal passions mortified, they ought to stand in the utmost seriousness of virtues, and that nothing wanton or heated from youth and former instability should remain in their bodies.”

Therefore, my Tityrus, the use of fur coverings in church was not introduced from the singing of songs. Rather, clerics and monks took them from the first-created human beings as a sign of mournful penitence.

And lest his assertion again remain unsupported, it will not be unwelcome to note, by the way (ὡς ἐν παρέργῳ), that these almuces [Col. 1118C] were not a burden for the arms, as they now are among most of our canons and monks, but a covering for the head: according to the more renowned lexicographers and decretists, a lined hood hanging from the neck across the shoulders to the arms, approximately to the elbow. Coriolanus writes this in his *Defence*, chapter 5, in answer to the third argument. Gabriel Pennot himself considers it more probable that almuces succeeded in place of that garment which was formerly called a *maforte*, or short little cloak—the model of our Augustinian and the other clerics of his family—in the book and chapter cited above. A little earlier he says:

> “Hence it seems to me probable and certain that the ancient *birri* were either hooded or caped. First, this follows from the very name *birrus*, from which no one doubts the name *birretum* is derived, by which people cover their heads. Secondly, from the Theodosian Code we know that the use of *birri* and hoods was almost the same; now hoods served to cover the head. And thus those who take *birrus* and *almucia* as the same must necessarily say this as well—among them Baronius himself, as Pennot admits. For Molanus proves, in Book III, chapter 5, *On Canons*, that the *almutia* or *almutium* was formerly used to cover the head.””

These are Pennot’s words. In §3 of the same chapter, he shows that this hooded *birrus*, or, in Baronius’s language, Augustinian garment, was extremely ancient in Spain, Gaul, Italy, and other places. He also shows that he and the regular clerics of his Congregation of the Lateran—so called from the Lateran Church, to whose ministries they were for some time attached before being compelled to withdraw—used such almuces in churches when attending divine service about twenty-five years earlier. We have seen above that the force of this ecclesiastical custom was confirmed by the Council of Basel, Session 21, and by the Council of Sens under Antoine du Prat in the year of the Lord 1528. Thus chapter 18 of its moral decrees states:

> “Those who are to say the canonical Hours shall enter the church in a full-length tunic, clean surplices, and copes according to the diversity of the seasons, holding hoods, almuces, or birettas on their heads.” [Col. 1119A]

But some years ago the almuces were removed from the head; now, though the votes of the chapter members differed among themselves, they support them only as far as the arm, retaining hoods conveniently in winter, the only season in which they, like many others, go about hooded.

The companions of the metropolitan Church of Lyons were more religious and more equitable toward antiquity. Bernard of Clairvaux once congratulated that church because it knew no novelties. Among them, so far as I know, this praiseworthy custom of covering the head with fur hoods while engaged in sacred offices has not become obsolete except perhaps in recent years. The same is true at Rouen, in the greater church, as Andreas Du Saussay, a most learned writer of this age, says in Part I, Book V, chapter 5, of his *Clerical Panoply*: its canons, when attending ecclesiastical offices in choir, are clothed in their almuces, which hang from the head upon the shoulders and below, nearly to the hem of the cope, and so forth. To these we add the canons of Laon, most tenacious of the Church’s ancient rites, who even today—as appears from their *Ritual*, soon to be published through the efforts of their most learned venerable dean Bellot—have in winter, according to ancient custom, the use of a rochet and a lined cope of red silk, while their heads are covered with an *armilausa* of grey furs, and so forth.

Nor has this use yet been wholly proscribed from the very famous monasteries of St Victor at Paris and St John in the Vines near Soissons. There novices still cover their heads with fur garments, though professed monks today wear their *forcaturae* flowing only about their shoulders; perhaps this has been so since the time [Col. 1119C] when Gabriel Pennot wrote. He attributes the fur hood as characteristic of his own order in Book II, chapter 69, of the *Tripartite History of Regular Canons*:

> “Some”—he is speaking of his own regulars—“use woollen hoods borne over the shoulders, like the ancient canons of St Frigdian; this custom is still kept among our brethren there. Others use skins, or fur hoods, or fur scapulars, which in the constitutions of Benedict XII are called *forcaturae*: such are the Victorine canons in Gaul, those of Windesheim, and certain others in Belgium.”

By the name Victorines, Pennot includes all the clerics of Sainte-Geneviève—of whom the Victorines are founders and archetypes—in Book II, chapter 57, §3, in the middle. But these men, being ordered to obey the cathedral canons under whose stipends and banners they sometimes serve, assume only a winter hood in those churches where it is no longer customary to cover the head with a fur garment, in imitation of the cathedral canons.

But enough now of these matters. I would certainly never have lingered over them had not our aforesaid regular-cleric author interposed with his clever fiction, just when I was about to demonstrate—while meanwhile satisfying Pullen’s phrasing—that the honour of clerical rank and the very ornaments of public priesthood had been granted to our people almost from the cradle of the order. From the nobility of fur garments he supposed that this hierarchical splendour had been conveyed to his own order and must be removed from monastic hoods; as though Mother Church, when appointing her children to preside over divine offices, were to summon tailors to ask what difference there is between hooded men and mitred men wearing *forcaturae* and covering their heads in shaggy *melote*. [Note: [Col. 1119] “The outer habit of regular clerics according to Gabriel Pennot and others, as above.”] Let him only remember what Honorius of Autun wrote in honour of hoods, near the end of Book I of the *Gem of the Soul*, chapter 237:

> “The monks’ hood was taken from the apostles’ *colobium*.”

The Church’s practice by which parents are removed from the church [Col. 1120A] while children are being baptized there—supply: “children.” The occasion for introducing this custom into the Church was provided by certain cases like that concerning which Pope Deusdedit wrote back to Gordian, bishop of Seville, in 30, question 1, chapter 1:

> “Your deacon has come to us, bringing the letter of your Holiness, [which reports] that certain men and women, on the preceding Easter Saturday, because of the great press of people, unknowingly received their own children from the sacred font.”

This is forbidden by the Council of Mainz, chapter 55:

> “Let no one receive his own son or daughter from the font of baptism; nor let him marry his child’s godmother, his goddaughter, or the woman whose son or daughter he has presented for confirmation.”

Yet we learn from Book VI of the *Hypognosticon*, attributed to Augustine, that the contrary practice once prevailed:

> “We know,” he says, “that even little children, who do not possess the use of free choice, so that we may judge concerning their good or evil merits, are carried in their parents’ arms to the grace of holy baptism.”

And Augustine himself [Col. 1120B], in Letter 23 to Boniface:

> “What is that which happens when children are presented for baptism: their parents, as though speaking on behalf of their faith, answer for them and say that they do what that age cannot even think?”

And certainly the reason for that custom deserves notice, the point at which Augustine there aims: namely, because parents, through carnal intercourse and generation, are the cause of eternal condemnation for their children, which the stain of original sin brings with it, they should therefore cooperate in obtaining their salvation through the benefit of spiritual regeneration, which takes place through holy baptism.

Such offerings ought to be made by the faithful, but they ought not to be extorted by priests. What the faithful, regenerated, freely offered at once, either for the construction of the church or for the support of the ministers, then poor, later began to be extorted from them. To prevent this Simoniacal blemish from spreading with impunity, provision was first made by the Synod of Elvira, chapter 40:

> “It has been resolved, for correction, that those who are baptized shall not, as used to be done, put [Col. 1120C] coins into the basin.”

The Fathers of the Third Council of Carthage confirm this canon, chapter 1:

> “It has been resolved that every bishop shall do this throughout his churches: when those who present their children for baptism voluntarily offer anything according to their vow, it shall be received from them; but if, through the necessity of poverty, they have nothing to offer, no pledge shall be violently extracted from them by clerics. For many poor persons, fearing this, keep their children from baptism.”

For at that time not only the rich but also the poor regarded it as a sin to omit this offering. Hence many poor persons were distressed, not merely from devotion, but especially lest they be marked by the fault of poverty. Gregory Nazianzen rebukes them for this in Oration 40, *On Holy Baptism*:

> “It is shameful to say: ‘Where is the gift that I am to offer because of baptism? Where is the splendid garment in which I shall shine? Where are the things required for receiving my initiators, so that in these matters too I may gain celebrity for my name?’”

By these latter words he indicates that bishops and ministers of sacred things were also customarily entertained with a banquet and lavish table [Col. 1120D]. Among others, Cujacius discusses this from a novella of Leo, in the law *Universos*, Code *On Decurions*. This banqueting pomp especially flourished at funerals, as Augustine states in Letter 64 and Paulinus in Letter 31 to Aleth. But both practices were abolished, or at least their use was moderated, by the canons. For, as an example of sobriety, clerics ought to do everything at a wholly even level of expense and distribution, except that on the Kalends of each month they might present themselves a little more generously and splendidly by some slight addition. This is the “Calendar of the canons,” concerning which see the synodal acts of Laurence, metropolitan of Esztergom, etc.

What is demanding money for regeneration or confession? [Col. 1121A] Hincmar, chapter 13, *To His Suffragans*, forbids money to be given for administering the sacrament of penance. Likewise Herard, bishop of Tours, chapter 87, forbids anything whatever to be demanded for confessions.

Or for ordination or dedication. The canonical censures concerning these things are very well known. Yet nothing prevents the one who has consecrated a place from rightly accepting, without the fault of simony, anything offered through voluntary generosity. This was customarily done by the liberal payment called an *eulogia*, in the canon *Eleutherius*, 18, question 2. Likewise, although a bishop is obliged to ordain clerics without the necessity of any exaction, nevertheless, as aid for travel and expenses, he may receive with impunity and without the disgrace of simony a certain number of solidi from each of those ordained. Such is the canon concerning ordinations in the Constitutions of Isaac Angelus, Book of Eastern Law. Likewise Cedrenus records under Justinian that Evagrius the philosopher, having been baptized, gave thirty pounds of gold to Bishop Synesius, without disgrace to either party.

What the Church chiefly intends, therefore [Col. 1121B], is wholly directed to preventing anything from being demanded by a legal contract or through the necessity of any agreement—not to remove the faithful’s voluntary generosity toward the ministers of the Church. Thus nothing can be owed them by agreement, nor can any fixed stipend be prescribed, as some think—although the contrary practice, which has become established in many dioceses, is not to be condemned by me. Hence Apollonius reproaches Montanus the heretic, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chapter 17, because he assigned fixed salaries to ministers of the sacred word:

> “He appointed collectors of money; under the name of offerings he contrived to receive gifts; finally, he furnishes salaries to the preachers of his word, so that the teaching of that same word may be strengthened by the sordid belly and gluttony of the stomach.”

Since, moreover, no reason invalidates customs approved and praised which arose from simple generosity, they are indeed commanded to be preserved intact and inviolate by Innocent III, canon *Ad Apostolicam*, *Extra*, *On Simony*; and more fully by the rescript of Pope Gregory, Book I of the *Register*, Letter 64.

What is celebrating the solemnities of Mass for the sake of temporal gain [Col. 1121C], if not selling Christ with Judas? Alas, how many priests of this age Pullus strikes with this anathema! Yet ancient and praiseworthy is the pious custom of the faithful of giving to priests who celebrate for them either money freely counted out or a sum fixed by the ordinaries. This seems to have succeeded those offerings of bread, wine, produce, and other foodstuffs of that kind which were once made to individual priests at Mass and are frequently mentioned by the Fathers. It also replaced banquets less becoming to Christians—Augustine himself advising and urgently demanding this, as may be gathered from his Letter 64—both those customarily held on saints’ feast days and especially those prepared for the funerals of the dead at no ordinary expense.

But although receiving money for celebrating Mass was lawful, every agreement to take it—this alone being what Pullus attacks in this chapter—was always forbidden. After his death, namely in the year [Col. 1121D] 1196, it was again condemned by the Fathers assembled at York:

> “We have also decreed that it must be forbidden for any priest to enter into an agreement, at a stipulated price, for the celebration of Masses; but he may receive only what is offered at Mass.”

Likewise, what is it to sell a place due to the dead, etc.? Thus too the Fathers of the Council of Tribur, chapter 16, to whom Pullus here most plainly alludes:

> “An abhorrent ancient custom, to be avoided by all Christians, has crept in: selling for a price the burial owed to the dead and making the grace of God a thing for sale, though nowhere under evangelical grace do we remember finding or reading this, etc. Why do you sell earth to earth? etc. Remember that the earth belongs not to man but to the Lord. If you sell earth, you will be held guilty of invading another’s property. You received it freely from God; freely give it for His sake. Therefore let it be forbidden to all Christians without exception to sell earth to the dead and to deny them their due burial.”

Lest, as Theodoric writes in Cassiodorus (*Variae* III.19), “[Col. 1122A] the wretched should be compelled, amid the bitterness of grief, to lament grievous losses of property; and, constrained by impious devotion, either be driven to sell their patrimonies for the dead or, sorrowing, to cast their beloved bodies into the meanest graves.”

Yet the praiseworthy custom of the faithful again escapes these censures: by it a fixed sum of money, together with offerings, is generously given, or even required, as the stipend of ministers of the Church, who are chiefly supported by the funeral expenses of the dead. This is especially so because, at their anniversaries, offerings—at least those of thirty days—are not matters of mere generosity but are governed by a certain legal obligation, as is clear, among other sources, from the constitution of Charlemagne, Book VI of the *Capitularies*, title 195; *V.*, chapter *De quarta de Praescriptionibus*; the final chapter of the *Extra*, *On Wills*; and the sole chapter, final section, *On Resident Clerics*, in the *Sixth Book*.

I had almost omitted to observe that Pullus attacked the Simoniacs here with more than cursory effort [Col. 1122B] because, in his age, the poisonous offspring of that evil was spreading far and wide, especially among the English, his own nation. Wishing to guard against it, the prelates of the Church assembled at London in 1138 by command of Innocent II and decreed:

> “Following the canonical institutions of the holy Fathers, by apostolic authority we forbid any price whatsoever to be demanded for chrism, oil, baptism, penance, the visitation of the sick, the betrothal of women, anointing, communion of Christ’s body, or burial. Whoever presumes to do this shall be subject to excommunication.”

By “demanded,” understand: with a prior pact or agreement assumed.

To close this chapter, as with a crown—in which Pullus instructs parish priests—we shall append the most important part of the synodal letter of Ratherius, bishop of Verona, a writer celebrated in his own age. We possess it here in manuscript with certain other of his works not yet published, but shortly, God willing, to be committed to print. They were most kindly sent to us by Antony Bellottus [Col. 1122C], dean of the venerable Church of Laon, a man most renowned for piety and learning. This letter is learned and worth reading; but because it runs somewhat long, we did not wish to copy here its first part, which discusses the Paschal solemnity. Ratherius flourished around the year 950; Baronius discusses him in Volume X of the *Annals* and lists his works under the year 954.

## Synodal Letter of Ratherius, Bishop of Verona, to the Priests Established throughout His Diocese

We also admonish and entreat your brotherhood, as we find written elsewhere, that, thinking of our common salvation, you listen more attentively to our admonition, commit to memory what we suggest to you, and diligently strive to put it into practice.

First, we admonish you that your life and conduct be blameless: namely, that your dwelling be beside the church and that you have no women in it. Rise every night for the night office; chant your office at fixed [Col. 1122D] hours; perform Masses reverently; receive the body and blood of the Lord with fear and reverence; wash and wipe the sacred vessels with your own hands. Let no one sing Mass unless fasting. Let no one sing who does not communicate; let no one sing without amice, alb, stole, fanon, and chasuble. Let no one do so with knives hanging outside his garments, nor with spurs; and let these vestments be clean and serve no other use. Let no one presume to sing Mass in an alb which he uses for his ordinary purposes. Let no woman approach the altar or touch the Lord’s chalice.

Let the corporal be most clean, and the altar covered with clean linen cloths. Let nothing be placed upon the altar except reliquaries and relics, or perhaps the four Gospels and a pyx containing the Lord’s body for the viaticum of the sick; let the rest be stored in a clean place. Every church should possess a complete missal, a lectionary, and an antiphonary. In the sacristy, or beside the altar, let there be a place prepared where water may be poured out when the sacred vessels are washed [Col. 1123A]; and there let a clean vessel containing water hang, and there let him wash his hands after communion. Let no one sing Mass outside a church, in houses, or in unconsecrated places; let no one sing Mass alone.

Make the sign of the cross over the chalice and the offering correctly: that is, not in a circle or with the crossing of fingers, as very many of you do, but with two fingers held straight and the thumb enclosed within, by which the Trinity is signified. Strive to make this sign, +, correctly; for otherwise you cannot bless anything.

Visit the sick and reconcile them; according to the Apostle anoint them with holy oil; administer communion with your own hand; and let no one presume to hand communion to a layman or woman to carry to a sick person. Let none of you demand payment or a gift for baptizing infants, reconciling the sick, or burying the dead. See to it that through your negligence no infant dies without baptism. Let none of you be drunken or quarrelsome, “for the servant of the Lord must not quarrel” (2 Tim. 2:24). Let none of you [Col. 1123B] bear arms in a disturbance, for our weapons ought to be spiritual. Let none serve the amusements of dogs or birds. Do not drink in taverns. Care for the poor, orphans, and pilgrims, and invite them to your small meals. Be hospitable, so that others may take good example from you.

Every Sunday before Mass make holy water, with which the people may be sprinkled, and have a vessel for this purpose alone. Do not give sacred vessels and priestly vestments in pledge to a merchant or tavern keeper. Let none of you bring one unworthily doing penance to reconciliation for the sake of anything whatsoever, or bear him a certificate of reconciliation. Let none of you exact usury or become the author of an interest-bearing loan. Know that the goods and property which you acquire after the day of your ordination belong to the Church. Let no one acquire a church without our knowledge and consent. Let no one obtain a church through secular power. Let no one, by money, supplant another in his church. Let no one leave the church [Col. 1123C] to which he has been assigned by title and migrate to another for the sake of gain. In another’s parish let no one sing Mass without the consent and request of the parish priest, if he is present. Let no one receive a tithe belonging to another. Let no one invite a penitent to eat meat and drink wine unless he has at once given alms on his behalf. Let no one presume to baptize except at the vigils of Easter and Pentecost, unless because of danger of death. Let each have a font; and if he cannot have one of stone, let him have another vessel prepared for this purpose, in which nothing else is done.

See that you teach all your parishioners the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer. Teach your people by every means that the fast of the Ember Days, the Rogation Days, and the Greater Litanies must be observed. On the Wednesday before Lent invite the people to confession and impose penance according to the character of the offense—not from your own heart, but as [Col. 1123D] it is written in the penitential. Four times a year—that is, at the Nativity of the Lord, the Lord’s Supper, Easter, and Pentecost—admonish all the faithful to approach communion of the body and blood of the Lord. Exhort married persons to abstain from their wives at fixed times. Distribute *eulogiae* after Mass to the people on feast days. Let no one travel without a stole. Let no one put on lay clothing. Let no one presume to sell, exchange, or alienate by any device any property, possession, or serf belonging to the Church.

Teach them to observe the Lord’s Day and other feasts, from evening to evening, without servile work. Forbid, under the invocation of almighty God, the devilish songs which the common people customarily sing over the dead at night, and the loud laughter which they practice. Do not communicate with the excommunicated. Let no one presume to sing Mass for them; and announce this also to the people committed to you. Let none of you go to weddings. Announce to all that no one may take a wife [Col. 1124A] unless the marriage is celebrated publicly. Forbid abduction in every way; ensure that no one approaches a blood relative and that no one takes another’s betrothed. Make swineherds and other shepherds come to Mass even on the Lord’s Day. Let godfathers teach their godchildren the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, or have them taught. Let chrism always be under lock or seal, because of certain unbelievers.

We wish also to know concerning every priest whether he was born of free parents or in servile condition; whether he was born in our parish, or ordained there, or to what place he was previously assigned [perhaps *praetitulatus*, “pre-titled”]. If he was a slave, let him show his charter of freedom; if from another parish, let him show letters of commendation, which they call *formatae*.

We also take care to admonish you concerning the ministry entrusted to you: let each of you, if possible, possess in writing an exposition of the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer according to orthodox tradition, understand it fully, and, if he knows how, diligently instruct by preaching [Col. 1124B] the people entrusted to him; if not, at least let him retain it or believe it. Let him understand well the prayers of the Mass and the canon; or, if not, at least be able to recite them from memory and distinctly. Let him be able to read the epistle and Gospel well, and would that he might at least be able to explain their literal sense. Let him know how to pronounce regularly from memory the words and divisions of the Psalms, together with the customary chants. Let him know by heart the discourse of Bishop Athanasius on faith in the Trinity, beginning *Quicunque vult* [“Whoever wishes”]. Let him be able to recite distinctly the exorcisms and prayers for making a catechumen, for consecrating the font, and the remaining prayers over a male and a female, both plural and singular. Likewise, let him know the rite of baptism; the rite for aiding the sick; likewise, the rite of reconciliation according to the manner canonically reserved to him, and of anointing the sick; and let him at least know how to read well the prayers suited to that need. Likewise, [Col. 1124C] let him know the rite and prayers for conducting the funerals of the dead; likewise, let him retain by heart the exorcisms and blessings of salt and water. Let him know the night and day office; let him understand, if possible, the lesser computus—that is, epacts, regular concurrents, the Paschal limit, and the rest. Let him have a martyrology, a penitential, and the other necessary books.

Know for certain concerning those to be ordained that they shall in no way be promoted by us unless they have spent some time in our city, or in a monastery, or with some learned person, and have received some instruction in letters, so that they may appear fit for ecclesiastical dignity. Since ecclesiastical authority also provides that four portions ought to be made from ecclesiastical goods—one for the bishop, another for the fabric of the church, a third for the clerics, and a fourth for the poor and guests—if you possess your own portion in full, have no resentment concerning those things belonging to the bishop, the fabric, or the poor. [Col. 1124D] Remember that the Lord commanded: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. 20:17); and do not be concerned about what does not belong to you. But regarding what does belong to you, keep faith among yourselves and divide it in common, whether it be great or small, knowing that the Apostle said: “Let no one defraud his brother in a matter [that is, in any cause], because the Lord is the avenger in all these things, as we told you beforehand and testified” (1 Thess. 4:6). Know also that it is better for every Christian to suffer fraud than to inflict it.

Keep Lent uniformly, excepting Sundays. For if you fast one day and feast excessively the next, you have observed not a forty-day fast but a twenty-day one. In Advent, unless a feast intervenes, know that you must abstain from meat and intercourse for four weeks. At the Nativity of the Lord, abstain entirely, even from lawful intercourse, for twenty days and nights. Likewise abstain during the octaves of Easter and Pentecost, the litanies, and the vigils of all feasts; also on Fridays [Col. 1125A], but especially on every Sunday, day and night.

By the compelling authority of the Paschal feast, we admonish your charity, brothers sincerely to be loved in Christ, that you fast on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday of Holy Week until the ninth hour, excepting little children, those worn out by advanced age, and the sick. On Thursday at the ninth hour, all who are to be reconciled should come to the mother church. On Friday fast until the ninth hour, and longer if anyone wishes. On Saturday let no one presume before the tenth hour to sing Mass or conduct the general baptism. If anyone cannot fast because of illness, let the fasting which the universal Church performs benefit him; for we are all one body in Christ. Only let no one through personal importunity compel the whole of our Church to sin against God or violate in any respect so glorious a feast. Know that you may impose penance for hidden sins [Col. 1125B]; recognize that public sins must be referred to us. Let none of you make a cleric without our permission; let no one make one who stammers or is excessively lisping; let no one make one whose understanding of letters is dull. If a feast not belonging to the holy Mother of God Mary or to the apostles occurs during Lent or the Ember fasts, know that the fast should be kept rather than the feast celebrated—unless it is the feast of that saint who lies in that parish. For God delights in no solemnity more than in that fast by which one abstains from foods and vices. Idleness too is the enemy of the soul. Consider whether, without knowledge of the matters we have set forth, you can perform your ministry, lead to life the people entrusted to you, and present them to Christ.”

Thus Ratherius. It will also be fitting to append a few things which the cited poet wrote in verse in the metrical *Summula of Raymond*, folio 92 and following. A manuscript also exists in the Library of Saint-Germain [Col. 1125C] des Prés.

## On the Life and Honesty of Clerics

We do not wish suspicious persons to be in priests’ houses:

their mother, sister, a sister’s daughter,  
or the nieces of a brother may be in them or nearby.

According to their ability, let them give what is theirs  
to the wretched, their companions, and the needy,  
and provide the benefits of hospitality  
to Christ’s servants. Let them not be players  
of forbidden games, such as dice, ball-games, and *deciorum* [an uncertain game-name].

Let them apply themselves to books, sermons, and reading  
the lives of the saints, and to doing what is honorable.  
Let them watch over the care of souls night and day.  
If need be, let them give body and soul for Christ’s flock.

Let them do nothing unworthy of them. Let them be moderate  
in clothes and adornment; let them so live outwardly  
that they may be teachers and examples to their own people;  
and what the tongue cannot do, let a good life at least teach.

We forbid them sparrowhawks, hawks, and falcons.  
Let them not be noisy or drunken, nor keep hunting dogs.  
They may undertake necessary work:  
[Col. 1125D] binding books or writing for payment, if  
they are poor in possessions or lack means.

We permit them nets and snares for catching birds,  
hares, or small beasts, or hunting that is not noisy.  
They may fish lawfully; but let there be no public fishing,  
only private. When they meet, let their activity be devout;  
let them pursue such permitted joys among themselves,  
but not omit the Hours or any part of the Office.

We forbid their presence at the dances of maidservants;  
let them flee the uproar of laypeople and taverns.  
And let them give more to Christ’s poor, restrain  
their own expenses, and avoid taking what is superfluous, etc.

## Chapter XIX

“There are Noah, Daniel, Job”; “in the field, in bed, and at the mill.” The author owes this excellent allegory, which greatly pleased writers of Pullus’s age, to Augustine [Col. 1126A] in several places, but especially Book II of the *Questions on the Gospels*, chapter 44; the exposition on Psalm 132, “Behold, how good,” etc.; and Book II, chapter 10, of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*. See Cassian, illustrated by Gazaeus, Conference 18, chapter 16. Among Pullus’s contemporaries, Peter of Poitiers, Part III, chapter 27, should also be read.

“Therefore Noah did not enter the ark with his wife, nor, while governing the ark, did he know his wife.” He undoubtedly consulted John Damascene, final book of *On the Orthodox Faith*, chapter 25. We give that passage here, lest less learned readers stumble at Pullus’s foregoing words and suspect that, contrary to Scripture’s text, he denied that Noah’s wife entered the ark. Damascene says:

> “Noah was commanded to enter the ark and preserve the seed of the world; and he received this command: ‘Enter,’ He says, ‘you and your sons, and your wife and your sons’ wives.’ And he separated them from their wives, so that in chastity they might escape the sea and that shipwreck of the whole world. But after the flood had ceased [Col. 1126B]: ‘Go out,’ He says, ‘you and your wife, and your sons and your sons’ wives.’ Behold, marriage is again permitted for multiplication.”

This is Damascene, and Pullus after him. They subtly note that the words of Scripture, when recounting entrance into the ark, immediately list Noah with his sons, thereby representing the continence which they would maintain in the ark. But when speaking of their departure, Scripture immediately mentions Noah and his wife, representing the permission to have intercourse again.

“Especially since among us,” etc. Thus again Dom de Sainte-Beuve briefly explains this passage, a difficulty not unlike the one mentioned above on chapter 11: “Especially since among us,” etc. By these words the author proves that priests of the New Law cannot have wives whom they approach with marital intention, because among us there is no union of a priest and a woman unless it can be dissolved at the pleasure of either; or, if it is otherwise, the Church considers it void. That is: because in the Catholic Church the bond of marriage [Col. 1126C] ought to be perpetual and indissoluble; but such is not the bond between a priest and a woman, since they may separate at either person’s pleasure. Or, if they do not wish to separate but wish to retain an undivided companionship of life, the Church does not regard such a union as valid.” Thus the most learned professor, who wished by this to guard the terms *libet* and *libuerit* in the author—terms which have caused much trouble for many, especially for me—although throughout his work the author notably commends and more clearly proves the celibacy of the Church’s sacred ministers.

## Chapter XXII

“You are not to go out into the field on either [ground] by yourself; but, when the Church calls, you are obliged [to go], and do not heed the one compelling you unless you are fit.”

The last period of this passage in Pullus may seem slippery to some, especially among religious, who, bound most strictly [Col. 1126D] by a vow of obedience, would think it an immense sin not to comply with the wishes, admonitions, commands, or chapter decrees of their superiors when they summon some subject to prelacies. This applies not only to one who freely resists from humility, but especially to one who knows certainly before God and without any scruple that he is unequal to bearing such a burden—one which Jerome writes is frightening even to angelic shoulders.

Yet, although it is not ours to determine anything in this difficult matter, nor either to prick or be pricked by the thorns—of which the present-day field of cloisters is most fertile—we shall nevertheless sufficiently discharge the task imposed upon us of defending Pullus by briefly showing that his teaching is safe and exact to the finest points of law. Or, if confidence in the assertion must waver, we should first blame its guarantor, Chrysostom, whom he chiefly followed, Book IV of *On the Priesthood*, chapter 1.

For Chrysostom writes there, instructing his intimate friend Basil, that a person whose conscience is free from scruples [Col. 1127A] regarding his own insufficiency—by which he might fail to provide adequately for the Church’s dignity or the salvation of souls, and might even do much harm—is neither bound nor ought to be placed over ecclesiastical titles; indeed, those promoting and those promoted sin gravely. The whole chapter of that book ought to be copied out, but because it is accessible to everyone, we shall extract only the passages on which the weight of the matter rests.

He had first said that all those who ascend to the priestly mitres through fraud or ambition, or who misuse them when obtained, are to be punished most severely. He then adds that those who are dragged to undertake these offices, while knowing themselves unprepared for them, are no less inexcusable:

> “Nor does any ground of excuse for their negligence remain to those who seem to have been compelled. For even if, as they say, a thousand persons urge and compel them, they ought not to look to their number and authority, but each person should first examine the powers of his own mind; and, after carefully investigating everything, only then consent to those who compel him.”

And after some intervening remarks [Col. 1127B]:

> “Therefore the one who ordains must first investigate everything carefully, and much more the one being ordained; for even though he has as partners in his condemnation those who compelled him, he himself will not be spared punishment, but an account will be required from him much more severely than from them,” etc.

He gives the reason:

> “For the one who ordained could be deceived by the opinion of many, so as to believe that the ministry belonged to one unworthy of it; but he who is taken up cannot say, ‘I was unknown to myself as I was to others.’”

He confirms this thus:

> “To avoid loss in small matters, we exercise such care and do not yield to the will of those driving us; but where eternal condemnation must be undergone by priests who do not administer rightly, without any preceding examination we are, as they say, blindfolded, putting forward compulsion by others—which certainly will carry little weight before our Judge.”

But Chrysostom says again [Col. 1127C], most aptly:

> “I pass over the fact that no one can compel an unwilling person at all. But suppose that he has suffered an unjust necessity and many deceptions in order that he might be caught: will this nevertheless save him from punishment? etc. Certainly, since you did not hasten to assume this dignity, being conscious of your weakness, you acted rightly and well. Therefore you ought, with the same resolution of refusal, to have resisted even those by whom you were elected.”

These are Chrysostom’s words, not merely concerning simple priesthood but especially concerning that office to which care of souls is attached, as is clear from the subjects he discusses in those six books published on this matter. The apologetic treatise of Saint Gregory Nazianzen on his flight should also be read.

We would indeed give more, and more willingly, than most might demand; but what has been said for the author’s sake is sufficient. Nor do we wish these remarks to prejudice the authority of prelates, much less their pastoral care: just as they strive, especially in our age, that no one may be employed in governing souls who is not furnished with the required qualifications [Col. 1127D], so neither would we wish anyone chosen by them for ecclesiastical titles to resist obstinately, if the most praiseworthy practice of the nascent Church still prevailed—of inviting, compelling, and drawing persons to prelacies.

Religious subjects are even less subject to the statements of Chrysostom and Pullus: not by reason of a vow of obedience, which rejects all unlawful things, but because of that examination by which superiors diligently investigate the abilities and character of their subjects before assigning them to public ministries and ranks of religion. It ought to be sufficient for each person—especially if troubled by scruples—to comply most readily with those under whose rule he lives. But if a certain obstacle to salvation threatens both himself and others, one which prelates cannot or will not perceive—the former sometimes happens—who would then deny that refusal of a prelacy is not only meritorious but necessary?

## Chapter XXVII

[Col. 1128A]

> “Therefore a double miracle has occurred: both that the flesh should be restored to life, and that the soul, contrary to what is usual, should be lifted from Gehenna.”

In this most difficult question—whether some of the damned can be saved and have in fact attained salvation—Robert taught the view which is less open to scruples, although we know for certain that it too has been rejected by many. Theologians ask in Book IV, distinction 46, whether a damned person who has not been resurrected can, without receiving any sacrament at all, be made blessed; or whether at least, if restored to life and fortified by the sacraments, first of baptism or penance, he can obtain that grace.

Pullus prudently kept silent about the first part of the question; he strongly adhered to the second. For although elsewhere he confesses that there will be no redemption in hell, he teaches that this must be said according to the general rule and without any exception. If God wishes to exempt someone from that general rule, He can rightfully do so and sometimes does; but He does so by those means [Col. 1128B] which He has freely granted for restoring human salvation: namely, that the one restored to life receive baptism if he died with original sin, or obtain forgiveness for actual sins by salutary repentance.

Those who embrace the former part of the question lend abundant support to Pullus; for it would not be difficult to believe that God raised some persons back to life so that they might afterwards secure salvation through the benefit of the sacraments—provided, moreover, it be established that some obtained this without prior disposition and without receiving any sacrament. This latter position is asserted by those who do not regard as doubtful the story of Trajan, emperor of the Romans, recalled from hell by the prayers of Saint Gregory the Great and attaining salvation; as Damascene, or the author of the sermon *On Those Who Have Fallen Asleep in the Faith*, first of all believed. Saint Thomas, *Sentences*, I, dist. 43, q. 2, art. 2, and IV, dist. 45, q. 2, art. 2, with many from his school; Altissiodorensis, book IV, chapter *On the Damned* [Col. 1128C]; Godfrey of Viterbo, part XV of the *Pantheon*; Abulensis—though not very fair to the sanctity of Gregory IV—in his book on Kings, chapters VII and LVII; Vincent in the *Speculum*, book XXII, chapter 22; John Stella, in the life of St Gregory; Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca Sancta*, book VI, note 47, near the end; Vigerius, in the *Institutions*; Navarrus, in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 22; Alphonsus Chacon, Dominican and confessor to the Supreme Pontiff, in a work specially written to prove this; Bartholomew de Medina, III, p., q. 52; and others.

Thus the cited Sixtus of Siena, from St Thomas, *Supplement*, question 71, article 5, reply to objection 4:

> “To the report of Damascene that the souls of Falconilla and Trajan were helped at the prayers of Thecla and Gregory, St Thomas replies that such aids were special dispensations granted to each by singular privilege; and that things granted by grace to certain persons outside the common law ought not to be drawn into an example for others.”

Augustine seems to have preceded all these in book I *On the Soul and Its Origin*, chapter 10 [Col. 1128D]. There he writes that, through the prayers of St Perpetua, her deceased brother Dinocrates was released from the bonds of damnation. “Who then knows,” says Augustine, “whether that boy, after baptism, was estranged from Christ by his impious father through idolatry in the time of persecution, and for that reason went to the death of damnation; and whether he did not emerge thence except through the prayers of his sister, who was about to die for Christ?” Thomas of Strasbourg, I, dist. q. 41, writes that the virgin Ottilia did the same for the soul of her father.

But setting aside all those matters, for the proof of which no necessity is imposed on us by the author’s words, the other part of the question, which he himself defends, is accepted by many theologians: namely, that certain damned persons, restored again to life and reformed, attained salvation through certain efficacious means. Augustine taught this in sermons 32 and 33 *On Various Subjects*; Eulogius in book I *On the Miracles of St Stephen*; Gregory of Tours, *On St Arnulf, Bishop*; Sulpicius, *On St Martin*; Lipsius [Col. 1129A], book *On the Miracles of Blessed Mary*; Halensis, chapters 10 and 22; Anthony, *On St Thomas Aquinas*; and others. All report that, through the prayers of those saints, certain persons who had died in mortal sin returned to life for a time, in order to procure for themselves the means necessary to salvation. Since such miracles, which one encounters everywhere in the histories of the saints, must be accepted and embraced piously and generously, everyone can see that the author’s opinion ought safely to be received as free from stain; but with the caution which most theologians wish to be added: namely, that those who died in this manner were not damned absolutely, but merely had their sentence suspended by God the Judge, who foresees the future prayers of his people for them.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

Therefore concubines were permitted to the patriarchs before the Law for some reason or other. This author, although in chapter 8 of the third part he calls not the women joined to the patriarchs concubines or mistresses but wives, here nevertheless seems to say that they were concubines, and that this carnal union was not marital but fornication—though without fault by reason of a divine dispensation. Peter of Poitiers asserts the same, part V, chapter 17: “At that time it was permitted to have several wives; yet marriage belonged to one of them. The others were concubines, for the increase of God’s people.”

Pope Leo, in answer to the fourth inquiry of Rusticus of Narbonne, Epistle 92, opened the way for this opinion:

> “Not every woman joined to a man is that man’s wife, just as not every son is his father’s heir. The bonds of marriage are lawful among freeborn persons and among equals; and this was established by the Lord Himself long before Roman law came into existence. Accordingly, a wife is one thing, a concubine another; as a female slave is one thing, a free woman another. Therefore, in order to show the distinction between these persons, the Apostle adduces testimony from Genesis, where Abraham is told: ‘Cast out the slave woman and her son,’ etc. [Gal. IV.30].”

Ambrose, book I *On Abraham*, chapter 4, seems likewise to imply this, as do all who condemn Lamech’s polygamy. One should also read Augustine, book XXII *Against Faustus*, chapter 3; book II *Against the Opponent of the Law*, chapter 9; book XVI *On the City of God*, chapter 25; and elsewhere. In these places he defends Abraham against the Manichees, who charged him with the heat of unrestrained lust, maintaining that he took another companion of his bed not to satisfy lust [Col. 1130A], but from the desire to increase his offspring. Augustine would have considered this statement superfluous if the multiplication of wives had been lawful without a dispensation.

He especially suggests this in *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 14, where he asks whether, in his own time, it might be lawful to take a concubine, at least temporarily, for the sake of begetting children if one’s own wife were barren. “Thus, perhaps,” he says, “what I do not know whether it can be done, and rather think cannot be done—yet perhaps, if a concubine were employed temporarily, he might seek children alone from that union,” etc. By these words he properly means a concubine, not a woman who was indeed a wife but of servile condition, or taken without a dowry, or brought in merely as a partner of the bed, as most recent writers explain. For in that case Augustine would have had no room for doubt, since the First Council of Toledo, canon 17, assumes the lawfulness of such union, in a sense not inconsistent with the phraseology of Scripture in many places.

In the following chapter Augustine makes his meaning clearer and writes that concubines were permitted to the patriarchs:

> “Certainly, with the wife’s consent, to take another woman, so that common children might be born—by the union and seed of the one, but by the legal right and authority of the other—was lawful among the ancient fathers. Whether it is lawful now, I would not rashly say. For there is not now the necessity of propagation that existed then, when even to married women who were bearing children it was permitted to introduce other women for the sake of more numerous offspring; which certainly is not permitted now.”

This is Augustine’s teaching, together with much else elsewhere; he held that the ancient Fathers were granted, for a time, the use of mistresses and concubines.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

“Some also assert,” etc. He may have had in view the Novella of the emperor Justinian—or rather of Julian’s predecessor—which Gratian canonized, 30, q. 5, chapter *If Anyone*: “If anyone, having touched the divine Scriptures, swears to a woman that he will have her as his lawful wife [Col. 1130C], or if he gives such an oath in an oratory, she shall be his lawful wife, although no dowry and no other written instrument has intervened.” The Master also raises this text as an objection against himself, IV, distinction 28, § B. See his solution there, or Hugh of St Victor, *Summa of the Sentences*, tract 7, chapter 7. Both agree with Pullus. Finally, this was established in law by Alexander III, *Extra*, *On Betrothals*, chapter *Concerning Those*, and by Gregory IX, in the same title, chapter *If Between*.

# ON THE EIGHTH BOOK

[Col. 1129]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1129C]

“And they availed the believers likewise, as the authorities admit.” Among others Augustine does so most notably; Pullus consulted not only him, but also his contemporaries Hugh, the Victorine monk, and Robert of Melun.

> “Whoever,” says Augustine, “understood Christ in the manna ate the same spiritual food as we do. But the fathers of unbelievers, who sought in the manna only satisfaction, ate and died. So also they drank the same drink. For the rock was Christ. Therefore they drank the same drink as we do, but spiritual: that is, a drink received by faith, not one drawn with the body. You have heard, ‘the same drink.’ The rock was Christ; for Christ was not one then and another now.”

And after a few intervening words:

> “Therefore, the same food, the same drink—but for those who understood and believed.”

Hugh’s opinion in this matter was somewhat more liberal. In book II *On the Sacraments*, part VIII, he says: “Some sacraments belong to the Law, others to nature, others to grace, yet they have the same effect of healing.” This must be seasoned with Christian salt, and understood in the manner in which Pullus here answers Augustine.

Is the popular decree, then, confirmed by consideration of this matter—namely, that those who taste blessed bread on the Lord’s Day, or, if prevented, take even an herb as though it were the Eucharist, receive the same benefit and that it counts for the Eucharist?

Whether some persons, deceived, ever falsely believed that blessed bread—of which there is frequent consumption among us—confers upon those who receive it the same gifts of grace which the Eucharist bestows upon the rightly disposed, is not altogether known to us. Yet there are very many examples among the ancients showing that it was commonly given in place of the Eucharist, both to catechumens at baptism and before baptism, as a sign of union and peace. Hence one may see that this blessed bread is sometimes called a sacrament in Innocent, Epistle I, chapter 5, and in Augustine, book II *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 26. Speaking there of catechumens, he says: “What they receive, although it is not the body of Christ, is nevertheless holy, and holier than the foods by which we are nourished, because it is a sacrament.” In the same passage he proves from the Apostle that even ordinary foods are sanctified, implying that blessed bread possesses a greater sanctification and is consequently called a sacrament because it was a sign of a sacred thing: that is, of the catholic union and benevolence with which the Church treated her catechumens before baptism.

This accords with what Gaguin reports in book X, under Louis XI, chapter 20, concerning the constable of St Paul, as we have already seen and write here again. When he was soon to be punished with the final penalty, he earnestly begged the king to give him the symbol of ecclesiastical peace and communion, namely the true body of the Lord; but the king refused him this grace. Yet, says Gaguin, the divine service which we call the Mass was celebrated before him, and blessed bread was offered, which he devoutly ate. Here it should incidentally be noted whether Wolfius was not certainly deceived by the popular decree of which Pullus speaks here, when, beside himself, he so foolishly comments on Gaguin’s words: “See the contradiction: Christ’s body is said to have been refused and yet meanwhile given. Wonderful theology.” For the sake also of that sanctification which resides distinctively in blessed bread above ordinary foods—or because of a certain analogy which it has with the consecrated species and particles—it is sometimes called host, *eulogia*, offering, morsel, and so forth. By these names the very sacrament of the most holy Eucharist is frequently denoted among ancient writers [Col. 1131B], as will now be observed.

No one can fail to see that the use of this bread was frequent from the very birth of the Church, not merely among catechumens but among all the faithful. A decree of Pope Pius concerning this rite survives in Burchard, book III, chapter 27, and one of the Council of Mâcon in the same author, chapter 32. But the custom was not the same everywhere. In some places—for example, in the West—the people offered these loaves individually to the priests during the solemnities of Mass, in order that they might be blessed. This is clear from the chapters of Herard of Tours, chapter 114: “Let the faithful be admonished to offer lights, incense, morsels, and first-fruits.” And in the chapters of Hincmar of Rheims to the priests of his parish, chapter 7:

> “Of the offerings brought by the people and left over from consecration, or of the breads which the faithful bring to church, let the priest suitably have portions cut and kept in a clean and suitable vessel, so that after the solemnities of Mass those who have not been prepared to communicate may receive *eulogiae* from them every Lord’s Day and on feast days. Before distributing to those who are to receive them, the priest shall bless those from which he is about to give the *eulogiae*, in these words; and he shall so distribute them, taking care that crumbs do not fall carelessly: ‘Lord, holy Father,’ etc.”

The same is found in the Council of Nantes, canon 9. From this religious practice and caution of sanctifying or blessing the bread and distributing it to each person, we perhaps believe with the author that the unlearned people sometimes came to think that bread so blessed counted in place of the Eucharist.

But in the Eastern Church among the Greeks, the priest himself—when acting with a deacon, or alone without a deacon—took the one great whole loaf which was offered and, with a sharp implement or small lance, traced upon it the sign of the cross. Cutting with the lance the seal or marked portion of the loaf into four parts in the form of a cross, he removed from it the particle called the seal, together with the core of bread adhering beneath it and the lower part of the figure representing the sign of the cross; he placed it in a most clean vessel [Col. 1131D], and afterwards consecrated it. At the end of Mass, however, he broke into pieces the remaining bread from which he had cut out the sacrificial offering and gave it to the faithful.

That these loaves were leavened—as such loaves are still today distributed every Sunday in many places throughout France at the morning assembly of the people—is clear from the above-cited Pope Innocent and from the decrees of Melchiades and Siricius, as is read in the book *On the Roman Pontiffs*. There these loaves are designated by the name *fermentum* (“leaven”); the pope sent them, after blessing them, through acolytes to bishops in his communion and even to secular princes. Thus Pope Formosus sent one to Charles the Simple, king of France, in 894, when the king had asked that it be sent to him as a pledge.

But among the Benedictines these loaves, whose use was more frequent, were unleavened, and entirely like those which were employed daily for the sacrifice of Christ’s body. This we learn from the ancient customs of Cluny, mentioned above at p. 366. Their practice was that the Armarius, or keeper of sacred things, prepared in a pyx as many hosts as there were brothers in the monastery expected to come to communion. Yet the priest consecrated only those that would be used for communion; the remainder he merely blessed during the solemnities of Mass. The *apocrisarius* then supplied these in the refectory to brothers who had been unable that day to refresh themselves with the sacred bread. They called them unconsecrated or non-consecrated hosts. Thus one reads in the office of the *Apocrisarius*: “He carries the pyx with the non-consecrated hosts into the refectory, from which, as I have said above, each tastes who did not wish or could not communicate.” Chapter 34 of book I, speaking of the blessing of new grapes, directs that they should be supplied to the brothers in place of unconsecrated hosts or blessed bread [Col. 1132B]: “Afterwards they are distributed in the refectory by the priest in place of hosts; and this is not omitted even if it is the Lord’s Day.” And chapter 26 of the same book specifically notes that they are not to be set out on the fast-days of the Ember seasons: “Nor are unconsecrated hosts given in the refectory, as they usually are on other ordinary days.” This had also formerly been forbidden by the Fathers of the Council of Laodicea, canon 49, lest the Lenten fast be broken on the pretext of *eulogiae*. Likewise, canon 14 provides that they should not be offered on Easter weekdays or sent to other parishes, because on those days everyone ought to attend the Eucharistic assembly. But the Cluniacs prohibited them for another reason.

They decreed that the distribution of these *eulogiae* or hosts should take place in this manner:

> “On ordinary days, non-consecrated hosts are carried into the refectory and distributed by the priest’s hand to those who have not communicated that day. This is usually done in the following order: he first gives from those hosts to Lord Abbot; then, since there are three tables, to one table on either side at the right of Lord Abbot; then to all on the other side; and so he returns again to the right, and each person kisses the hand of the distributor.”

In the Constitutions of Fleury, p. 398: “When Mass is ended, let a non-consecrated host be given to each person.” These matters concerning the Cluniacs have been treated somewhat more fully because they have not yet been published. The distribution of similar *eulogiae* is ordered by the Fathers at the assembly of abbots gathered at Aachen, capitulary 68: “Let *eulogiae* be given to the brothers by the priests in the refectory.” We think this passage should be understood in this sense, with better reason than the scholiast of that council, at the end of volume III of the *General Chronicles of the Order of St Benedict*, French edition of 1647.

## CHAPTER II

“Sometimes an outward sickness is added.” Cyprian discusses at length this bodily punishment of those who communicate unworthily with the most sacred body of Christ in his sermon *On the Lapsed* [Col. 1132D]; so do Pacian, *On Penance*; Chrysostom, homily 5 on I Timothy; and before them Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*. Regino also tells the astonishing story of King Lothair of France and many others accompanying him: after perjuring themselves and receiving the Eucharist unworthily from the hand of Pope Adrian II in 868, they were struck with various punishments and disasters, and all died within the year. Jonas, bishop of Orléans, also noted in his book *On the Instruction of Laypersons* [Note: [Col. 1131D] Book III, ch. 14]:

> “Many are punished with sickness or even death because of sins committed in the soul. Hence the Apostle says to the Corinthians that, because they were accustomed to receive the body of the Lord unworthily, ‘there are many sick and weak among you, and many sleep.’”

Jonas understands this “sleep” as death.

## CHAPTER III

“Therefore the blood is not without water, because the Passion is for humankind.” The appropriate and, as we think, genuine interpretation of this passage is this: if there is no water in the chalice to be consecrated, there is no blood—not indeed with respect to the truth of the thing, but with respect to the meaning of the mystery. Pullus seems to have had in view the decretal of Pope Alexander, if it is of unquestioned authenticity, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter 1:

> “In the sacramental offerings which are offered to the Lord during the solemnities of Mass, the Passion of the Lord must be mingled, so that the Passion of Him whose body and blood are made may be celebrated, etc. For, as we have received from the Fathers and reason itself teaches, neither wine alone nor water alone ought to be offered in the chalice of the Lord, but both mingled together, because both are read to have flowed from His side in His Passion.”

There one may see several other canons, but they may properly be explained as concerning only the necessity of precept, as they say, and not the necessity of the sacrament.

Yet if anyone should obstinately maintain that the author, by the cited words, thought that the sacrament would be invalid if water were absent from the chalice—which, however, we should never concede—he would certainly not be alone in saying so, as Pamelius indicates in his notes on Cyprian’s epistle to Caecilius.
