Considering Cyprian’s argument, “Thus the Lord’s chalice is not water alone, nor wine alone,” he supports Pullus in this way: “Hence the opinion of those who hold the mixing of water to be so necessary that without it the consecration of the Lord’s chalice is invalid seems probable,” etc. Peter Lombard shows that this opinion pleased many in his time, near the end of distinction 11 of book IV of the *Sentences*. Nor should it be passed over that Hugh of St Victor wrote on this matter at the same period, *Treatise 6 of the Summa of the Sentences*, chapter 9:

> “It is customary to ask whether, if water were not added through forgetfulness or negligence, the sacrifice would be invalid. But since we have no authority on the matter, we dare assert nothing from our own judgment. Yet we can say that a person guilty of such a thing ought to be punished severely.”

By this Hugh declares that those who judged the mixing of water necessary with the necessity of the sacrament would be violators of no decree [Col. 1133C].

Indeed, it should be noted that Bellarmine himself, a most diligent student of the rites of the ancient Church, considers that opinion probable, book IV *On the Eucharist*, chapter 10: “Whether the sacrament can subsist without water is not altogether certain; yet the common opinion inclines to the affirmative side.” The scholiast of Raymond’s *Poetic Summula*, fol. 24, second page, instructs priests concerning this case:

> “If the priest himself finds nothing in the chalice, he must then pour in wine with water. If he finds wine only, there are two cases: either before receiving Christ’s body or after receiving it. If he finds wine only before receiving Christ’s body, then the priest must pour in water and say the words of the canon which pertain to the consecration of the blood,” etc.

But in all these matters, and especially those concerning the sacraments, one must abide by the judgment and practice of holy mother Church, apostolic and Roman.

[Col. 1133D] These authors rest upon the act of Christ the Lord Jesus, whom, in consecrating the chalice, they teach to have mixed water with it. Besides others, they are: James the Apostle in the liturgy, if he is its author; Clement of Rome, *Apostolic Constitutions*, book VIII, chapter 17; the cited Cyprian; Basil in the liturgy; the Third Council of Carthage, canon 24; Theodoret, in the first dialogue; Damascene, book IV *On the Faith*, chapter 14; and, most recently, the Council of Trent, session 22, chapter 7. Indeed, the aforesaid Council of Carthage adds that the Lord “handed it down.” Yet if the word *handed down*, which the council employs, were to be adhered to literally, there would now be no room for doubt. Read Bernard, Epistle 69, and Armagh, book IX of the *Questions on the Armenians*, question 9, etc.

Here is what Peter Pictor, canon of St Omer, formerly wrote on this subject in his manuscript poem *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, chapters or divisions 10, 11, and 12. [Note: [Col. 1133] From a Corbie manuscript, preserved in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.]

> This is the blood shed from Christ’s wound,  
> Which by the priest’s mouth passes to the soul’s benefit.  
> And so that nothing may be lacking to the sacrament,  
> The living spring must be present in the wine upon the altar.  
> Water is mixed with wine, by which we are signified,  
> We who are given life by life-saving nourishment.  
> The peoples whom grace protects are signified by water,  
> Whom Christ’s blood joins to their head as members.  
> Further, if wine is offered to the Lord without the spring,  
> It is denied that Christ’s Passion was for humankind.  
> For if the creature that had to be redeemed were lacking,  
> Why did God become human, or why did He die?  
> Conversely, if there is a spring without wine mixed in,  
> It is shown that the people remain alone without Christ.  
> Wine works nothing here without the sacred spring,  
> Nor is the saving spring made propitious without the blood.  
> As both flowed from the sacred wound of Christ,  
> [Col. 1134B] so both must together be set forth in the offering.  
> God is held to be the true vine, Christ the fountain of life;  
> The spring appears to come from the Fountain, the blood from the vine.  
> Therefore one is not sacrificed without the other,  
> Since in this way the sacred Passion is commemorated in its fullness.

“This”—that is, the mixing of water with wine [Note: [Col. 1133D]]—“was not celebrated at the birth of the chalice, when the new Passover was consecrated after the old Passover. For the Lord, changing only bread and the liquid of wine into His own flesh and sacred blood, is read to have given them to His disciples at supper.”

“But He committed to the judgment of His Bride how the Eucharist should be received by laypeople,” etc. This is an observation worthy of attention and an ample reply to the complaining voices of innovators. It notably commends the Church’s remarkable power and authority in the common ordering of the sacraments—which the Council of Trent teaches in many places—and also sets out the principal reasons why the use of the chalice at the sacred table was commonly denied to the people. See Trent, session 13, in the decree of prorogation; session 21 throughout, and after canon 4; session 22 near the end; and the decree on the petition for concession of the chalice. See also the Council of Constance, session 13, etc.

But, as we observed above on chapter 9 of the third part, although communion under both kinds was not so frequent among laypeople before Pullus’s time, we nevertheless said there many things which sufficiently show that its use had not been wholly suppressed in most places. Indeed, it was restored for a time, at least in France, by a canon of the Council of Clermont under Urban II, which we also produced there. This will become still clearer from what we are about to set forth concerning communion under bread dipped in the wine, against which the author vehemently inveighs as prevailing in his own time.

“It would indeed be dangerous for the blood under a liquid species to be distributed in church to a multitude of believers; and far more dangerous for it to be carried through the parish to the sick.” Here Pullus touches upon certain reasons why the drinking of the Lord’s blood was withdrawn from laypeople [Col. 1134D]. Gerson, the most learned, records many other highly noteworthy reasons in his treatise *On Communion under Both Kinds*, which he published at the Council of Constance, where he was present in 1417. It will not be unwelcome to recount them here:

> “Most of those gathered to consider this matter”—he speaks of the theologians, especially the Parisians assembled at that same council—“say that the custom of not communicating laypeople under both kinds was lawfully and reasonably introduced, especially after the multiplication of the faithful. And this was done to avoid the many dangers, irreverences, and scandals surrounding the reception of this blessed sacrament. The first danger is spilling; the second, carrying it from place to place; the third, the defilement of vessels, which ought to be consecrated and not handled everywhere or touched by laypeople. Much less should consecrated wine be sold to apothecaries, as is said to happen among such persons [Note: [Col. 1135D] He speaks of the Bohemians]. The fourth danger lies in the long beards of laymen. The fifth lies in preserving it for the sick, because vinegar might form in the vessel, and Christ’s blood would then cease to be present; it ought neither to be received nor newly consecrated without Mass. It could happen that pure vinegar would be given as Christ’s blood. Add to this that in summer gnats or flies might breed, however tightly the vessel were closed; at times it might even rot or become as though abominable to drink. This reason is very forceful. There is also another reason when many others have drunk from it. And one asks in what vessel the consecration could take place of as much wine as would be required at Easter for ten or twenty thousand persons. The sixth disadvantage would be the expense of wine, at least in many regions where wine for celebrating is scarcely found, and elsewhere is bought dearly. There would also be danger of freezing,” etc.

This is the testimony of the Parisians reported by their chancellor.

And there is no doubt that if, to facilitate consumption, the blood is poured into the mouth of someone extremely ill, the requirement of communion is satisfied.

For the Fathers of the Ninth Council of Toledo decreed that those who, through excessive weakness, cannot swallow Christ’s body should be content with a draught of the blood alone. Paschal II made nearly the same decree at about that time in his letter to his fellow clergy at Cluny, which Baronius extracted from old documents of the same monastery and prints in his Appendix to the year 1118, fol. 618 of the Pavia edition; we shall give it in full below. In it the Supreme Pontiff condemns communion under bread dipped in the wine, which had become rather obstinately established among the Cluniacs, and orders that everyone receive Christ’s body and blood separately. Yet he excepts the sick and children: “Except children and those altogether infirm who cannot swallow bread [Col. 1135C]; for them it is sufficient to communicate in the blood.” Gilbert of Poitiers, bishop and author, writes that a different practice was common even in Pullus’s age, at least among most people, in a letter to Matthew, abbot of St Florentius, which Dom Luc d’Achery published this year: “Baptized children often communicate in the sacrament of the chalice alone; and the sick in the sacrament of bread alone.”

Formerly, however, it was customary for the sick—we shall shortly consider the healthy—to be fortified with the holy viaticum by being given, in a silver spoon, the species of consecrated bread dipped in the blood. This was both because of the danger of spilling, since it was most dangerous to bring the holy chalice to the sick in this condition, and so that for their comfort they might receive both Eucharistic symbols. Isaac of Langres, canon 20, appears to allude to this: “If he is believed to be about to die immediately, let him be reconciled by the laying on of hands, and let the Eucharist be poured into his mouth.”

This is clear from a manuscript of the monastery of St Remigius at Rheims, dealing with the visitation of the sick [Col. 1135D]. It specifically notes that, if the sick person’s strength permits, he should receive alternately the body and blood of the Lord, with the formula for each communion given there. But if he is weaker, only one formula is used, as follows: “May the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve your soul unto eternal life,” because then the Lord’s body, dipped in the blood, is given to the sick person in a spoon.

The Fathers of the Council of Clermont under Urban II seem to have intended this by the canon which Baronius reports, volume II, from the ancient monuments of Antonio Agustín: “Let no one communicate from the altar unless he receives the body separately and the blood likewise, except by necessity and for precaution.” By the final words—which do not, however, appear in Orderic Vitalis, book IX of his *Ecclesiastical History* for the year 1095, who gives the canon thus: “Let the Lord’s body and the Lord’s blood be received separately” [Col. 1136A]—nothing else is indicated than that the mixed species may be given when the necessity of communicating is present and danger of spilling is feared, as was done among the Cluniacs. This was accustomed to occur with sick persons near death who requested both symbols of communion; because of the extreme dryness of the palate and danger of spilling, it did not seem safe to administer them otherwise than together and mixed. In this sense must be understood the canon of the Council of Tours, reported by Burchard, book V, chapter 9, and Ivo, part II of the *Decree*, chapter 19: “Yet this sacred offering must be dipped in the blood of Christ, so that the priest may truly say to the sick person: ‘The body and blood,’ etc.”

With this precaution in mind Paschal II judged it sufficient for the sick to communicate in the blood, because, he says, “they cannot swallow bread,” as is clear from his letter to his Cluniacs, shortly to be cited. Yet we gather from their statutes, mentioned above, that they observed the contrary custom [Col. 1136B]. Thus chapter 26 states: “The Lord’s body itself is dipped in wine mixed with water, so that the sick person drinks it from the cup; he also drinks the ablution of the chalice and, if possible, the ablution of the priest’s fingers and again of the chalice. If he cannot, another drinks it.” Would that this rite of communicating the sick were current today for the reason given above by the Supreme Pontiff. In that chalice there was only the host, as is expressly stated a little earlier; but out of reverence and for greater caution, they wished it to be purified two or three times.

Our frequently praised old poet expressed this communion of the sick somewhat differently, fol. 30:

> If he suffers only because he cannot chew, then  
> Let him receive nothing but water touched by Christ’s body.  
> Yet however great a portion of Christ’s body  
> The sick person receives, he is proved to have received the whole.

As the scholiast there observes, he alludes to a practice then used in certain places: when sick persons were so weak that they could not be fortified by the holy viaticum, the priest nevertheless brought them Christ’s body so that, stirred by its presence, they might at least eat spiritually.

> “Formerly it was the practice,” he says, “that when a sick person was unable to eat the Lord’s body through excessive weakness, the priest showed him Christ’s body, instructing him concerning the dignity and efficacy of this sacrament. The priest washed in water the hand with which he had touched Christ’s body, and offered such water to the sick person to drink.”

Yet he warns that this was no longer customary in his time, indeed not even necessary. “For,” he says, “by believing alone the sick person eats Christ’s body spiritually and receives the effect of the sacrament. Hence blessed Augustine: ‘Why do you prepare your stomach? Why do you prepare your teeth? Believe, and you have eaten.’”

The cited poet had written the same:

> When the sick person vomits, he ought not to receive Christ’s body;  
> [Col. 1136D] if he believes, he eats faithfully by believing.

But all this must be read cautiously and not rashly brought into practice, although not dissimilar things are reported of Hugh, the Victorine monk, by Blessed Antoninus at the beginning of the third part of his *History*, and by John Gerson in his treatise *On Communion under Both Kinds*: namely, that when near death he ordered the Eucharist brought to him, although he was not going to receive it because of nausea of the stomach. Thus far concerning communion of the sick; now let us consider the other kind, which concerns the healthy.

Nevertheless, in most places bread dipped [in the wine] is offered, so that, as they say, both elements may be distributed in accordance with the Gospel, and the matter may thus be carried out more safely and expeditiously. But Christ acted otherwise, and Roman authority earnestly forbids this to be changed. Hugo of St Victor—though repudiating it—mentions this communion under dipped bread, that is, the mingling of the species of consecrated bread with the likewise consecrated species of wine, which the author here strongly censures as having become widespread in his time, in the *Summa Sententiarum*, tract 6, ch. 9; in Part VIII, *On the Sacraments*, bk II, ch. 4; in bk II, *On the Offices of the Church*, ch. 11; and also in the treatise *On the Mirror of the Church*, ch. 7. After him the Master of the Sentences likewise mentions it, bk IV, dist. 11, final section. Cardinal Humbert too, in his work *Against the Slanders of the Greeks*, writes that this dipping of the eucharistic bread prevailed among them, and censures it in almost the same words as Pullus. Gervase, in his *Chronicle* under the year 1175, likewise attests that its use was condemned by the fathers of a certain English council held in that year; this is clear from canon 15, which he reports with the others.

Hugo everywhere invokes the authority of Pope Julius, found in *On Consecration*, dist. 2, ch. *Cum omne*, from that pope’s letter to the bishops of Egypt. Since all twelfth-century writers—Pullus, Hugo, Gratian, Lombard, and others—regarded it as a genuinely authentic offspring of the Apostolic See, it is unsurprising that they wrote that communion by dipped bread had been earnestly forbidden by the Roman Church. But we have already noted above that this decretal of Julius, like a great many attributed to his predecessors, is of suspect authenticity: namely, forged by Isidore Mercator and rather rashly, if I may say so without offence to Gratian, inserted into the body of canons.

This rite and practice of a moist Eucharist—as the Third Council of Braga calls it, canon 1—had long prevailed and continued in most places down to Pullus’s time. This is asserted not only by him, an eyewitness, but by several others, either his predecessors or nearly his contemporaries. Among them was John, bishop of Avranches, in his little work *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, sent to Maurilius, archbishop of Rouen, about the year of Christ 1072. There he describes the rite and custom of communion by dipped bread as follows: “The priest divides the Lord’s body in three ways,” and, a little later: “[Col. 1137C] ‘Let the priest, or one of the ministers, receive the third portion; but not with dipped bread. Rather, according to the decree of the Council of Toledo, the priest is to communicate separately with the body and separately with the blood. Except for the people, who are permitted to communicate with dipped bread, not by authority but because of the extreme necessity arising from fear of spilling Christ’s blood.’” In place of the Council of Toledo, whose canon in question does not exist, one would apparently have to read the Third Council of Braga, canon 1.

> [Note: [Col. 1137D] Uldaric was still living at the beginning of the twelfth century.]

During Pullus’s lifetime this custom of dipping the sacred bread had become very prevalent among the Cluniacs, though they expressly acknowledge that it was contrary to the practice of other Churches. In bk II, ch. 38 of the *Customs* of that monastery, on “The Priest of the Week,” St Uldaric outlines the rite of this dipping. Since the matter is especially worth knowing, since that chapter contains much that strikingly commends the ancestral splendour of our order in matters concerning divine worship, and since the manuscript has not yet been printed, it will not be unwelcome to begin a more detailed account. Thus, on p. 72 of our manuscript:

> “The subdeacon carries the hosts to the deacon standing beside the altar and covering himself, so that he may choose from all of them the three he wishes to consecrate. Therefore, after the paten with the hosts has been left upon the altar, the wine which has been offered is poured by the same deacon into another chalice; and he leaves only as much as suffices for the consecration. Yet he does not himself mix water into it, because he is permitted neither to pour wine nor [Note: [Col. 1137D] He is perhaps speaking of one not yet initiated into sacred orders, but merely performing the office of subdeacon, to whom the handling of sacred vessels and the pouring in of water are not usually permitted.] water; rather, he gives the deacon the water-cruet together with the chalice, so that the latter may mix it. He gives him a linen cloth so that the outside of the chalice may be carefully wiped, lest any wine or water perhaps remain on the exterior and what has been consecrated be lost.
>
> “On this occasion the deacon does not take care to separate the fingers mentioned above, because he has already placed the hosts which he was to place. Then at last, when the chalice has been set upon the altar, the subdeacon returns with the paten and cruet; he sets the paten full of hosts upon the cupboard, and puts the cruet where it is usually kept. He takes another silver paten, stored inside a golden dish, and carefully wipes it with a very white cloth continually hanging near the cupboard for this very purpose; afterwards he wraps it fittingly and reverently in a linen cloth. Meanwhile the priest, censing the chalice and host, makes three crosses with the incense over them both, and one sort of circuit. He likewise censes toward both the right and left corners of the altar as far as he can extend his hand, though keeping his feet together. When, before the Preface, the priest has said, ‘For ever and ever,’ the deacon stands behind the priest and the subdeacon behind the deacon, holding the covered paten aloft as stated above. They stand upright until the point at which the *Sanctus* is sung; thereafter they ought to be bowed and intent upon prayer until the Lord’s Prayer has been completed by the priest. [Col. 1138B] The deacon nevertheless notes when the priest bows during the Canon, and washes the aforesaid four fingers again. After the Lord’s Prayer he receives the paten from the subdeacon, intending to give it to the priest; nevertheless, he does not separate his fingers when he elevates the chalice together with the priest. The priest sets the paten at the foot of the chalice; and after breaking the host, he puts one small portion into the chalice, as is the general custom, and leaves two upon the paten, covering both with the corporals. But first he carefully shakes his fingers over the chalice itself, lest some fragment of the Lord’s body have adhered to them during the breaking. Still keeping them closed with all care and held to his breast, he first gives the peace to the deacon and subdeacon, and then goes down again to give the same peace to the brethren.
>
> “Meanwhile the deacon breaks and divides the two hosts which the priest did not divide. The subdeacon carries the paten belonging to the chalice back to the cupboard, [Col. 1138C] sets it on the altar together with the linen cloth, and then stands bowed in supplication at the right-hand corner of the altar until the priest returns. On returning, the priest dips in the blood the portion of the Lord’s body which he is to consume, and thus consumes it.
>
> “One of the attendants mentioned above takes the dish from the cupboard and holds it, when brought forward, upon the rail—made, I suppose, chiefly for this purpose—between the two columns of the ciborium. The deacon puts upon the dish the paten on which lies the divided body of the Lord. He also hands the chalice containing the blood to the subdeacon standing inside between the rail and the altar; the subdeacon holds it slanting, as closely as possible, against the dish. The dean communicates first, and after him all the others approach from the outside; except those in albs, before communicating they ask pardon. Each must place himself so close to the dish that, should the Lord’s body happen to fall while being received—whether from the mouth of the recipient or from the hand of the minister—it cannot fall anywhere but back into the dish.
>
> “Before the priest gives the body itself to each person, he dips it in the blood, although this is contrary to the practice of other Churches; for some persons, especially our novices, are so untrained that, if they received the blood separately in this way, it would be impossible for them not sometimes to incur serious negligence.
>
> “When all who wish have communicated, and finally the subdeacon and, if thought proper, the man holding the dish, the dish itself is covered. Its holder does not move from his place until the priest has consumed the blood and the wine with which he afterwards washes down the blood. The subdeacon receives the chalice from the priest, and [Col. 1139A] the deacon receives from the altar the paten of the chalice, lifted together with the corporal. Both he and the holder of the dish go behind the priest: he with the chalice behind the right corner of the altar, and he with the dish opposite the left. Yet at their approach the whole community asks pardon, in reverence for the Lord’s body and blood.
>
> “The remaining attendant comes with another chalice outside the rail, so that the priest may wash over it with wine the fingers with which he handled the Lord’s body—as the deacon also does immediately after he has communicated and before unfolding the corporals. The priest then drinks this wine, which a second attendant pours, so that the chalice may be washed on both sides. After the priest has returned from giving the peace, the man carrying the candlestick holds it raised aloft and does not set it down until the first collect after Communion has begun to be concluded. Immediately afterwards the paten and chalice are carried back together to the cupboard, where, no matter how bright the day may be, both are most carefully examined by the subdeacon and another attendant with a candle, [Note: [Col. 1139D] A remarkable vigilance concerning the divided elements.] [Col. 1139B] lest even the tiniest particle of the Lord’s body remain. If he sees anything remaining, he does not touch it with his hand, but lifts it only with his tongue and consumes it, etc.”

Thus far the manuscript.

Although he had himself formerly practised this communion in the moist species, Paschal II disapproved of it and wrote to Pontius, abbot of Cluny, that they should desist from it and that communicants should receive the body and blood separately. We give in full the letter already mentioned above:

> “PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son PONTIUS, abbot of Cluny: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “Writing to Caecilius, blessed Cyprian says: ‘When something is prescribed through God’s inspiration and command, it is necessary that the faithful servant obey the Lord; he is excused before all men because he arrogantly assumes nothing to himself.’ Nor ought anything else to be done by us than what the Lord first did for us. Therefore, in receiving the body and blood of the Lord, according to the same Cyprian, the Lord’s tradition must be observed; nor must a human and novel institution depart from what Christ the teacher both commanded and performed. For we know that bread by itself and wine by itself were handed down by the Lord himself. We teach and command that this practice be preserved always in the holy Church—except in the case of little children and persons wholly infirm, who cannot swallow bread: for them communion in the blood is sufficient.”

Among the Greeks, the manner of receiving dipped communion was such—even in the author’s time, as may be gathered from Cardinal Humbert’s treatise *Against the Slanders of the Greeks*—that they first cut the offering with an iron lance in the form of a cross and mixed it in the chalice with Christ’s blood, then served these moistened particles to each person standing by with a spoon. Severus, patriarch of Alexandria, mentions this spoon in *On the Order of the Offering*: “He uncovers the covering of the mysteries, [Col. 1139D] places the paten on the left side, the chalice on the right side, and the corporal and spoon with the paten.”

In some other Churches, not the people but only ministers of the altar, or even the subdeacon alone, communicated with dipped bread. This is clear from an order of Mass discovered in the Palatine Library and published by Matthias Illyricus. It reads: “But while giving the chalice with the most holy commingling to each of the ministers, let him say: ‘May the reception of the body and blood of the Lord,’ etc.” On these words our Menard notes on p. 302 of his *Observations on the Sacramentary of St Gregory*: “Secondly, it should be noted in this Mass of Illyricus that not merely the blood is given to priests and deacons, but blood mingled with Christ’s body.” This agrees with the rite of the Roman Church observed 131 years after Pullus, [Col. 1140A] and still partly retained today when the pope celebrates solemnly, as may be seen in Durand’s *Rationale of Divine Offices*, ch. 54. When the Supreme Pontiff reaches Communion, he leaves the altar and returns to his own seat; the deacon brings him the sacred host with the paten, and the subdeacon the chalice. There the host is divided by him into three parts. He reverently consumes one, gives another to the deacon, and puts the third into the chalice. After the pope has drunk part of the precious blood through a sacred *pugillaris*, that is, a silver and gilded tube, the subdeacon likewise consumes the third part dipped in the remaining blood. We learn that this was also practised among ourselves from the Ritual of Ratold, abbot of Corbie in Gaul: “Let the bishop communicate the priests and deacons with the kiss of peace, yet with the dry sacrifice; and the subdeacons with the mixed sacrifice. And let deacons and priests taste in turn from the chalice, held by the subdeacon, of that blood itself.”

[Col. 1140B] No Church in France, so far as we know, still practises such dipping of the sacred bread for priestly clerics, except that royal and world-famous Church of the monastery of Saint-Denis near Paris, of the Order of Saint Benedict and the Congregation of Saint-Maur. There the deacon and subdeacon—whichever of the two it may be, it does not matter—who receive the use of the chalice, draw to their mouth with a silver tube the fragment of the most sacred host left by the celebrant before they alternately drink the precious blood, as we have repeatedly discussed and observed. At Cluny, however, where such use of the chalice is again found, the priest consumes it in the manner of the others, but first draws it out of the chalice with the end of the *pugillaris* or tube—unless, during the last fifteen years, the ministers of the altar have imitated those of Saint-Denis.

Moreover, from what has been set out above—especially from Pope Paschal’s letter to the Cluniacs—two points may be observed, to fulfil our promise. First, communion under both species, even when received separately, was quite firmly established in Pullus’s century. Hence Baronius, after the letter just cited: “But because even thus they did not cease from the use of forbidden dipping, the holy Church afterwards began to practise communion under the single species of bread alone.” The point is also clear from a reason other than that offered above by the Cluniacs and John of Avranches for offering dipped bread: namely, lest an uncultivated and disorderly people spill the sacred liquid. That reason would have no force if use of the chalice had then generally been denied to laypeople; yet later, led by sounder counsels, the Church declared that it ought no longer to be administered.

The second point is that infants themselves also communicated at that time, but only in the blood, as the holy pontiff notes in the cited letter. Correspondingly Hugo of St Victor, in ch. 20 of *Theological Instruction on the Sacraments*, or Robert Paululus, canon of Amiens—under whose name that book is also inscribed in a manuscript of the Library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés—writes: “If it can be done without danger, according to the Church’s original institution the sacrament of the Eucharist should be given to children under the species of blood. Hence the ignorance of priests, still retaining the form but not the reality, gives them wine in place of blood. I should judge this altogether superfluous, if it could be omitted without scandal to the simple. But if there is danger in reserving Christ’s blood or administering it to children, it seems preferable to refrain.” Thus they write.

Our poet of the *Summula*, cited above, held otherwise. He thinks that viaticum should be administered to children only when they are at least seven years old, know the distinctions of reason, and are in danger of death. Thus, fol. 29:

> Do not give the Lord’s body to children remaining under twice five years of age,  
> though they be pure in body:  
> nevertheless, they do not know what they receive. Therefore it is forbidden.  
> [Col. 1141A] Give it to those whom cruel death presses, even if they are  
> eight or nine, or seven years old, when it is established that they know  
> the *Our Father*, and their life has been tested.

## CHAPTER VI

And indeed this seems right to me. Pullus modestly supports the truth, not unaware that some men of his age, Catholics and revered for their reputation for learning, taught the contrary: the Master [of the Sentences], bk IV, dist. 13; Peter of Poitiers, his disciple, Part V, ch. 13; and Hugo of St Victor in the *Summa*, tract 6, ch. 9: “Others think that not even manifest heretics consecrate. For no one says in the consecration itself, ‘I offer,’ but ‘we offer,’ in the person of the whole Church. Whereas the other sacraments may be performed outside the Church, this can never be so; and this view seems the more deserving of assent.” So says Hugo. Concerning the sacrament of penance, some others taught that schismatics and heretics could not be its ministers. Bernard notes and erases this error with his pumice-stone in Sermon 66 on the *Song of Songs*, attacking those heretics who, under the name of apostolics, troubled Gaul in his time with various errors. There is no doubt that Bernard persuaded Abelard himself to adopt sounder views; from him Bernard elicited this testimony in his *Apology*, where Abelard acknowledges that the power of binding and loosing belongs to bishops both unworthy and worthy, as long as the Church tolerates them. The Donatists and Luciferians had formerly stumbled upon this rock, as Augustine attests concerning the former and Jerome concerning the latter in books expressly written against them. Their cause was later adopted by the Waldensians, as Antoninus writes, Part IV, title 11, ch. 7, §2; by John Wyclif, as is clear from the Council of Constance, session 8; and finally by the filthy herd of Innovators.

## CHAPTER IX

What reason, then, requires that, contrary to the custom of Lent, on the day preceding the Lord’s Passion, after dinner, [Col. 1141C] we should dine, as it were, in imitation of the Lord, and, if resources permit, consume unleavened loaves together with wine, etc.? Pullus was troubled to see this custom, still prevailing in many monasteries, and censures ecclesiastics and religious more sharply than usual—for few laypeople, he notes, practised these things. On Maundy Thursday these drinking parties were quite familiar to them, since they broke the fast, which should then be completed with only one meal; and they seemed also to indulge Jewish rites excessively through such a custom.

At that time it was customary among monks and among clerics and canons who had not yet abandoned common living that, on Thursday, at the Lord’s Supper, after the afternoon washing of feet performed in the chapter-house by bishop and abbot, they would go to the refectory. There, after wine had been blessed with solemn ceremony, while the deacon chanted from the lectern the Gospel reading for that day, and all had taken their seats in order, the table officials distributed in portions and sparingly cakes, unleavened loaves, or—especially in our times—sweetmeats made with sugar; and the bishop, abbot, or dean himself offered unmixed wine to each person. I can adequately testify that this rite continued at Cluny Abbey down to the year 1633, and that I myself, though still a boy, was more than once refreshed by those provisions. It long flourished also in many other most renowned monasteries of France, doubtless encouraged by emulation of a friendly custom; but it is now dying out everywhere, since the Congregation of Saint-Maur happily arose for the Benedictine Order in France.

One may infer from canons 23 and 24 that this custom was introduced by the fathers of the Council of Aachen, but for a pious reason. In the latter canon the fathers direct that the *mandatum* be performed after supper; in the former, that on Maundy Thursday the abbot, if able, wash and kiss the brethren’s feet and offer them a cup. But later monks, wishing to safeguard health lest drinking should cause harm, added those unleavened loaves mentioned by the author, or something similar, contrary to the council’s intention. For in the ancient customs of the monastery of Fleury, printed at Lyons in 1605, pp. 398 ff., where Maundy Thursday is treated, those unleavened loaves were set before the brethren at dinner so that they would not break the fast. The rule is as follows: “After Mass, when all have assembled in choir and the lord abbot has arrived, they shall go to the refectory to celebrate supper. The boys shall go first with their masters; then the lord abbot; next the priors; lastly the novices. And the brother in charge of the bakers distributes unleavened loaves to the brethren. The refectorian must see beforehand that wine is poured into each person’s cup before the community arrives.” On p. 400, however, where foot-washing or the *mandatum* is mentioned, only wine is offered, in accordance with the council’s statute: “After the *mandatum*, the abbot shall offer drink in the refectory to each brother, kissing his hand, even to children.” This sort of practice may be seen in Lanfranc, metropolitan of Canterbury, in his decrees for the Order of Saint Benedict, which—as is noted there from the title of a manuscript of the Church of Canterbury—monks were required to observe both in monasteries and in the cathedral churches over which they presided. There, in section four of the first chapter, Lanfranc describes this rite at greater length and permits wine alone. From this one may suppose—since drink does not break the fast—that the author here censures not monks of that time adhering to most holy laws, but only those who had already added unleavened bread, sweetmeats, little cakes, or such round trifles of a third course to the drink. He thus exempts the former: “The greater part of clerics do not observe this custom, and the most religious communities avoid it.” Such in that age were many of our own countrymen in England who flourished under Lanfranc and Anselm, particularly those who performed canons’ duties in eight episcopal churches, as we reported above from Robert of Torigni.

[Col. 1142C] Indeed, the most ancient canons prohibited this breaking of the fast on Maundy Thursday. Thus the Council of Laodicea, ch. 50: “It is not proper that the fast be dissolved on Thursday of the last week in Lent, and that the whole of Lent be dishonoured,” etc. And in Gratian, *On Consecration*, dist. 3, ch.: “It is not permitted to break the fast on Thursday of the last week, and dishonour all Lent; rather, by sincere abstinence to complete the whole of Lent.”

Moreover, for the benefit of those to whom the works of blessed Lanfranc, published only a few years ago, are scarcely known, I shall describe here the manner of the foregoing ceremony from a very ancient manuscript of the monastery of Fleury on the Loire, almost ruined by the ravages of moths and cockroaches, a manuscript that seems to have escaped the pen and eyes of Jean du Bois. On fol. 31 ff. it reads:

> “The deacon, having silently received a blessing from the lord abbot, begins the reading at the words, ‘Before the feast day.’ When he comes to the words, ‘He who loves me,’ the lord abbot signals to the prior to strike the board. On hearing, ‘Arise, let us go hence,’ he strikes the board; when they hear it, all rise and, with the deacon leading the procession, go to the refectory in the same manner as they came to the chapter-house, as is done on Saturday for the charity-meal. Then, with the prior seated in the abbot’s place, the lord abbot and the person who washed feet with him enter the refectory, take glass vessels full of spiced wine, and carry them to the step, as is customary. The refectorian strikes his board gently until they reach the step. All silently say, ‘Bless [us],’ and the priest, rising, gives the blessing silently with uplifted hand. Then the lord abbot hands the prior a flask, kissing his hand. Next he gives [drink] to everyone on one side, and his companion to everyone on the other, kissing the hand of all those to whom they offer it [lacuna] They receive it while standing, the assistants who helped wash the feet offering each of them drink in other flasks.
>
> “When they have done this for everyone, including the children, the lord abbot alone, with those ministering to him, comes to the step where the deacon is reading with his attendants. Other brethren bring the cups of the deacon and those same attendants, and he hands them the flask, kissing their hands; but they do not drink [nonnisi: except] until the end of the reading. Those who brought them carry the cups back to the abbot’s table. Then the lord abbot, the other person who served with him in the drink, and the man whose hand has been kissed, having made a bow forward and backward [Note: [Col. 1143] ‘Forward and backward,’ that is, an act of reverence, as may be seen in Lanfranc’s *Decrees* and the Cluniac *Customs*.] at the step, go to their places. All rise after making that bow forward and backward until the lord abbot takes his seat. The prior withdraws to the other side, remaining at the same table beside the lord abbot. The other two who are said to have washed the lord abbot’s and his assistants’ feet rise and offer drink to him and his companions, kissing their hands. When the address is finished, the lord abbot strikes the board once, and [Col. 1143B] the deacon brings down the folded stole, etc.; and, taking their seats, they drink; etc.”

Thus far the manuscript; nor is Lanfranc substantially different. This custom diligently continued among the Cluniacs down to the year cited above, provided one removes the sweet treats in which they delighted, or the cakes or unleavened breads preferred by others.

It is certain, however, that these drinking parties—with no other food of any kind added—were permitted, especially on fast-days, solely to relieve thirst, which is then usually more intense, particularly among ecclesiastics and religious who, in addition to the exertion of fasting, still bear the continuous chant of psalmody. Church prelates, wishing with pious moderation to provide for this natural necessity while leaving the force of the fast unimpaired, allowed those after-supper drinks. We read numerous examples of this custom in ancient Church records. It still flourishes today in this very ancient Benedictine abbey of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif at Sens, where we write, when the celebrated body of canons of the metropolitan and primatial church comes to its church to sing Vespers on the eves of the feasts of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, Saint Remigius of Reims, the most blessed first bishop and martyr of Sens, and Savinian, apostle of Gaul, who rests in that Church of Saint Peter. When Vespers has been solemnly sung by those venerable canons, all enter the monastery cloister. Seated here and there, at the edge of the sacristy and chapter-house and on the platform of the colonnade, with the superior of the monastery, or his deputy, seated together at the right of the precentor or of those holding the chief dignity, near the door of the said sacristy, they are presented in glass cups with wines of three kinds or colours—white, red, and a third of a somewhat clearer colour—by the parish priests of churches dependent on that monastery. Kneeling before the monastery superior, they intone the versicle, “Bless [us]”; and when the choir replies in harmonious chant, “The Lord,” he blesses the wine with a distinct blessing for each kind. Immediately all alike, canons and clerics, taste or drain it, while those parish priests and other ministers of the lower choir offer the cups in turn. But lest the fast—especially strict on the vigil of Saint Peter—be broken, and also out of regard for antiquity, which that most noble college of canons has always cultivated, they add neither cakes, sweetmeats, nor unleavened bread, as others mentioned above did and as Pullus censures. Content with drink alone, they deserve, we have thought, to be declared exempt from his censure.

“And I do not think it reasonable for one intending to fast to eat twice in the day.” For that after-supper meal, or slight provision of an evening table—which some call a little supper and others a *collatio*—had not yet crept into Christian fasts, [Col. 1144A] by which some corruption began to be brought into their very strict observance: food that used to be served only toward evening was now taken at noon, after the office of the evening synaxis had first been anticipated, so that at least ecclesiastical custom might thereby be accommodated. Bernard writes, Sermon 3 in Lent, that at that time the faithful took their meal on fast-days, especially in Lent, only at Vespers: “Until now,” he says, “we alone have fasted until None; now all will fast with us until Vespers—kings and princes, clergy and people, noble and lowly, rich and poor together as one.” And Peter of Blois, Sermon 11: “In Lent too the Mass office is postponed until after None, so that the meal also may be postponed until after Vespers.” Ratramnus, monk of Corbie in Gaul, testifies in his unpublished treatise *Against the Greeks* that this was the practice every day except Sundays and feast-days among monks and also among the canons of Ireland, who then lived in community: “The Scottish people inhabiting the island of Ireland have the custom in monasteries of monks, canons, and all religious persons, at every time except Sundays and feast-days, of fasting and permitting food to the body only at None or at Vespers: at None on summer days, but at Vespers on winter days.”

Although St Thomas, some 130 years after Pullus, writes in *Summa Theologiae* II–II, q. 157, art. 7, that it was customary, through the custom of the people, to break the fast about the ninth hour, neither he nor the others mentions a light supper. Bellarmine therefore rightly wrote in his treatise *On Fasting*, ch. 3: “The Church does not command but tolerates the practice of breaking fast about noon and taking a little supper at night. Nor are there lacking among Catholics those who, content with one meal, taste absolutely no food except at the ninth hour or toward evening.” He congratulates and agrees with them as follows: “Although those who break their fast at the sixth hour have a probable reason for their custom, nevertheless it must be admitted that those act better who, according to the old practice, take food not before the ninth hour, and in Lent not before Vespers.” The ninth hour is our three o’clock in the afternoon, and Vespers, or sunset in spring, is our six o’clock. Let the haters of ancestral custom therefore depart, to whom the highly praiseworthy practice of some persons of our age is nauseating—being already full, no doubt—who, during Lent and days of similar fasting, taste no food whatever until the sun declines toward setting. Yet let this be said in such a way that we do not wish rashly to pronounce anything against the contrary custom.

## CHAPTER X
Since on Fridays, as on fast-days, it is now by no means permitted to eat meat. By this he seems to imply that in former times the eating of meat on those days was optional and not unlawful, although the laws of fasting then remained unchanged. [Col. 1144D] Pullus’s opinion will be quite pleasing to the wishes of many modern writers, especially to the very learned Jean de Launoy, who in a separate treatise maintains that abstinence from meat is not so essential to an ecclesiastical fast, such as the Lenten fast, that, when prelates dispense from it for legitimate reasons, the fast itself must immediately be abandoned.

Indeed, it is certain that the Church, at least in most places, has altered several practices concerning the choice of foods in fasts—matters no less important than abstinence from meat itself—while the observance of fasting has everywhere remained unimpaired. From this one may infer that, even if the eating of meat were now permitted on those days, the most holy observance of fasting would not thereby be abolished. The present custom of taking the meal six hours earlier; the *excoenium*, or evening collation [Col. 1145A] or light supper; the permission to use wine; the modern use of dairy products; and other such things, from which ancient Christians most religiously abstained, do not prevent the solemn observances of fasting from still flourishing in the Church. Nothing is held more ancient, nor anything more religious. Thus I should not reluctantly agree with the wishes of that writer: namely, that the same reasoning should apply to meat if, because of a general scarcity of Lenten foods, its use were permitted with the Church’s consent.

Certain examples of saints support this: while they observed the law of fasting to its very letter, eating meat was sometimes customary for them. Thus it was for the most holy man Spiridion, who ordered pork to be served to a guest coming to him during Lent. “When it had been cooked,” says Sozomen, *History*, book I, chapter 11, “he made the guest recline with him and began to eat the meat which had been set before them. He urged the guest to imitate him. When the latter refused and said that he was a Christian, Spiridion said that for this very reason [Col. 1145B] he ought to refuse the less. For, as Holy Scripture declares, ‘all things are clean to the clean.’”

Here it should be noted that, if abstinence from meat had then been imposed by a general decree, Spiridion—who was most observant of the Church’s canons—would certainly not have used it contrary to those canons. Still less would he have urged his guest to eat what the Fathers had forbidden, had that prohibition stood throughout all the Churches. Nor, what is important to me in this matter, would he have sealed his judgment with the authority of Scripture if that selection of foods, afterwards accepted by the general agreement of peoples, had already prevailed among all who fasted.

At that time, however, the laws governing fasters were various and left to discretion, provided that all agreed in preserving intact the observance of fasting, which consists principally in one bodily meal per day, taken soberly. Yet it must be admitted that only very few used meat, and that even they did so with other foods. Epiphanius shows this variety in the practice of fasting at greater length in his exposition of the Catholic faith, found [Col. 1145C] at the end of his books against heresies; and after him Socrates, *History*, book V, chapter 21.

> “They differ not only in the number of the days of Lent, but also follow diverse rules of abstinence from foods. Some abstain entirely from every kind of animal; others, among animals, eat fish alone; others eat birds also with fish, asserting, as Moses has it, that birds are born from water. Others abstain from fruits enclosed in hard coverings and from eggs; others live on dry bread alone; others not even on that. There are some who, after fasting until the ninth hour, use various kinds of food. Different nations fast in different ways, and the causes of this are almost innumerable. Since no one can show a command concerning it handed down in written records, it is plain that the apostles left freedom in this matter to each person’s mind and discretion, so that each might do what is good neither from fear nor from necessity. [Col. 1145D] We know that this diversity in fasting exists in the Church.”

Ratramnus says nearly the same in book IV of his work against the Greeks, except that, more in keeping with the author’s thought, he adds that many who fast in this manner refresh themselves without distinction of foods.

Further, that abstinence from meat had not in his time been imposed by the Church seems to follow from Theodoret, *Fables of Heretics*, book V, chapter 29:

> “The Church does not embrace abstinence from wine and from eating meat, and the rest of continence, in the same manner as heretics do. For they command abstention from these things as though they were abominable; but the Church commands nothing concerning them. For it does not forbid their use,” etc.

He proves this from the Apostle’s words, also quoted above by Spiridion. But later the Church established by many canons that abstinence from meat and that selection of foods. Therefore the Faculty of Theology at Paris counted this law among ecclesiastical, not apostolic, constitutions, in the articles it issued concerning certain doctrines of the Christian [Col. 1146A] religion disputed in the preceding century:

> “Ecclesiastical constitutions—such as those concerning fasting, the selection of foods, abstinence from meat, and many other matters—truly bind in the court of conscience.”

Nor should it be passed over that Erasmus favored Pullus’s words rather excessively in a letter to the bishop of Basel:

> “Little by little there crept in the custom which made Friday a fish-day for us. Then, once this had succeeded, Saturday was added; now Wednesday too is in danger. On account of observances of this kind we see people afflicted and finally dying, yet considering themselves Christians when they are Jews.”

See the chapter *Jejunia* and the chapter *De esu*, *De consecratione*, distinction 3. On the latter the Gloss notes: “Wednesday is counsel; Friday is command.”

Pullus is silent about abstinence from meat on Saturday, because in his time it had not yet been imposed, nor observed everywhere, but had been received only as optional, or by the force of custom alone, in certain [Col. 1146B] dioceses. There is indeed a canon of the Roman synod under Gregory VII, chapter 8, cited by Gratian, *De consecratione*, distinction 5, chapter 31, in which the faithful are exhorted to abstain from meat on Saturdays. Yet, as the Gloss there notes, it is the pope’s counsel, not a command, except in places where a different custom has taken root.

Nevertheless, that several bishops attempted to introduce this abstinence, especially in Gaul, is attested by Glaber, book IV, chapter 5, around the year 1000, speaking of councils held in Aquitaine:

> “This in particular is worthy of record: it was agreed by all in common that, in every week and by a perpetual ordinance, people should abstain from wine on the sixth day and from meat on the seventh, unless perhaps serious illness compelled otherwise or some very great solemnity intervened. But if any circumstance occurred such that this rule was somewhat relaxed, then three poor persons should accordingly be maintained with food.”

Sigibert, in his *Chronicle* under the year 1032, notes the penalties imposed by such councils upon offenders:

> “Whoever refused would be deprived of Christianity; [Col. 1146C] and, when departing this life, no one should visit him or commit him to burial.”

But Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, protested against these measures and resisted somewhat more vigorously:

> “He could be induced by no urging, as Sigibert notes in the same place, to accept these things; but he refuted each article, saying . . . . . ‘A fast on the sixth or seventh day should not be imposed uniformly on all, because all do not have the same capacity; nor are all satisfied with this one fast, because the character of penitence is not the same for everyone. To establish these things by an oath, or to aggravate the violation of an oath by perjury, is not beneficial. To excommunicate those who oppose them, to deny visitation to the sick or burial to the dead, is detestable. The authentic decrees of the Fathers suffice; and for neglect of these matters an appropriate form of penance should be imposed.’”

Thus Gerard. From this it appears, especially from the penalties enacted by the Fathers, that the practice of this abstinence was neither attempted superficially nor introduced negligently. Yet, although immediately [Col. 1146D] accepted by laypeople, it could scarcely be admitted by the Cluniacs, even though they had elsewhere sworn by solemn oath to the words of the Rule which prohibited every consumption of meat. Therefore their venerable abbot Peter Mauricius became greatly angry with them, calling them raven-like, in book VI, letter 15:

> “Even mimics and camp-followers abstain from meat every Saturday for God’s sake; moreover, most laypeople abstain every Wednesday; some of them even every Monday. But our brethren of the holy order, monks of the heavenly profession—and these Cluniacs—despising God and casting off shame, spend, as they say, the entire year in consuming meat, with no day except Friday omitted; and they do this not even secretly, but openly and publicly,” etc.

In other regions, however, that practice did not prevail so strongly. This we infer from Innocent III’s rescript to the archbishop of Braga in Spain, *Extra*, *De observatione jejuniorum*, chapter *Consilium*. When the supreme pontiff was asked what should be done with persons who, on account of a certain but rather slight weakness, had eaten meat on Saturday, he answered that the custom of the region should be observed. This sufficiently indicates that no general decree of the Church then existed [Col. 1147A] requiring abstinence from meat on Saturdays.

Indeed, in 1336—about two hundred and fifty years after Gregory VII’s constitution—the renewed and common practice of *xerophagy* on Saturday is demonstrated by the bull of Benedict XII. In the Benedictine Rule, chapter 26, while allowing sick monks the eating of meat on certain days of the week, he excepts the following other days:

> “We establish and ordain that throughout the entire year, on Wednesday and Saturday; and from the first Sunday of Advent, etc., all regulars of the same order or religion shall everywhere abstain from eating meat.”

There would have been no need to except Saturday expressly if abstinence from meat had already been general among all on that day, as it was on Friday; this is why the pope does not mention [Col. 1147B] Friday. Moreover, Saint Antoninus, writing a hundred years later, in part II, title 6, *On Gluttony*, chapter I, §1, mentions Friday alone:

> “By the Church’s law, eating meat is forbidden on Friday throughout the year and in fasts; and dairy products in Lent.”

And in chapter II, §3 of the same title:

> “To eat meat on Saturdays in places where there is a universal custom of not eating it is a mortal sin, etc.; otherwise it is not so if the custom of the country is that it is eaten, as in France, Catalonia, and other regions, because then one must follow custom, distinction 12, *Illa*.”

“Therefore do not eat butter among the Franks either,” etc. The passage is difficult to understand and cannot be reconciled with any historical records, especially since butter was unquestionably in very common use among the French, particularly at Paris, where Pullus taught for a long time. This is sufficiently proved by many canons of French councils which enjoin abstinence from butter in Lent, such as chapter 40 of the capitularies of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, etc.

Therefore, with the most learned men Jean-Baptiste Souchet, Jacques Sirmond, and Denis Petau, whom I have consulted orally or in writing, I think (although the author’s words appear to aim at something else) that he is alluding [Col. 1147C] to that Lenten abstinence from butter which then prevailed in Gaul and has not yet been wholly extinguished everywhere among the French. Charles Guillard, bishop of Chartres, testifies that it was most ancient among foreign peoples as well, in his synodal statutes of 1555:

> “Abstinence from the use of butter and dairy products belongs to the common and ancient institution of the Church.”

Indeed, others maintain that it was promulgated by Pope Telesphorus, who was very close to the apostles, and that his decree was renewed by the Fathers of the Sixth Synod. Since in Armenia the faithful ate eggs and butter during Lent only on Saturdays and Sundays, the Sixth Synod of Constantinople enacted that, if anyone ate eggs or butter in Lent, a cleric should be deposed and a layperson excommunicated, as Cardinal Hosius relates, chapter 91, *On Ceremonies Taken from Time*. Gregory, replying to Augustine, teaches that this too ought to be observed by the English recently converted to the faith as a general statute of the Church: namely, that on the days on which they must abstain from meat, they should abstain also from butter.

Yet in many provinces its use was permitted on fast-days outside Lent; in others it was not. Hence perhaps arose the scandal mentioned here by Pullus, because of the diversity of usages; and he wished to guard against it in the preceding heading. Antoninus treats this fittingly in part II, title 6, §3, “Whether Dairy Products May Be Eaten in Lent?”:

> “Note,” he says, “that if anyone, during fasts established by the Church outside Lent, eats dairy products in places where it is customary not to eat them, it is a sin. But where it is customary for such things to be eaten generally, or by the greater part, they may be eaten: distinction 76, chapter *Utinam*, etc.”

But for a fuller explanation of these matters Peter de Palude teaches as follows in book IV, distinction 15:

> “The eating [Col. 1148A] of dairy products in Lent is forbidden, as in distinction 4, chapter *Denique*. But it is not forbidden in other fasts unless custom so provides; and Augustine, Ambrose, and Jerome say that this custom must be observed everywhere in fasts: distinction 12, *Illa*, and distinction 76, chapter *Utinam*. Hence one who is simply ordered to fast is obliged only to abstain from meat, and may therefore fast while using dairy products. The Britons, however, who eat butter in Lent seem excusable, because in matters in which the Church can dispense, it dispenses by knowing and tolerating; provided that it tolerates in such a way that it neither punishes with excommunication nor forbids by word,” etc.

Thus Antoninus and Paludanus, implying that none but the Britons admitted butter in Lent. This abstinence still persists in Occitania; and when it is temporarily relaxed in favor of certain persons, the condition is always imposed that it be done secretly and without scandal. The synodal acts of Stephen de Poncher, their bishop, testify that in 1515 the general use of butter had not yet been permitted among Parisians [Col. 1148B]:

> “I exhort and admonish you to fast at the suitable season during Lent, as also ordained by the Church, and, as the sacred canons have judged, to abstain from meat, milk, cheese, butter, eggs, etc.”

When dispensation in the eating of butter began, it was granted on condition that some payment be made toward the fabric and benefit of the Church: namely, ten denarii by the poor, twenty by persons of moderate means, and thirty by the rich. Witness is the custom still prevailing in certain dioceses of Gaul, especially Chartres: on Easter Day itself, after the morning and evening synaxis, the Church’s collector calls out at the church doors, *Payez vos beurres*—“Pay your butter dues!”—so that each person pays individually the appointed denarii according to his condition. They say that the tower at Rouen, called in the vernacular *La tour de beurre*—“the Butter Tower”—was built from money thus collected.

[Col. 1148C] From these facts we infer that, since this abstinence from butter prevailed more religiously in Gaul than among neighboring peoples, it is not surprising that Pullus, wishing to safeguard their consciences, should carefully warn foreigners visiting among them to refrain temporarily from eating butter in order to avoid scandal, just as the Apostle judged concerning certain other foods for the same reason.

“Or among certain others, garlic.” We think that the eating of garlic is condemned by no law; yet because of its persistent and not very agreeable odor, it is certainly commonly rejected. Hence Horace, *Epodes*, ode 3:

> If anyone with impious hand has ever broken  
> His aged father’s throat,  
> Let him eat garlic more harmful than hemlock.

Nor does Peter Abelard disagree with our author. Following Ambrose, and likewise writing concerning the avoidance of scandal, he says in book V on the Epistle to the Romans, p. 705:

> “If we examine more carefully, in the fundamental intention itself, those things in the apostles and apostolic men which seem contrary, we shall find that these and those must sometimes be forbidden and sometimes permitted according to time [Col. 1148D] and place; and that in forbidding certain things, regard has sometimes been had more to the decency of life than to the religion of faith. Thus in the *Hexaemeron* blessed Ambrose permits garlic to be taken as medicine but forbids its use as food, because respectable persons may easily be scandalized by its smell. And we believe the same is done concerning certain other cheap foods for the sake of preserving decency.”

Thus cheese, though permitted for eating by the law of nations, is avoided by some almost as though it were a plague. In old English constitutions, under the title *On Tithes*, we find this praise of cheese, taken from another source:

> Unskilled physicians call me harmful,  
> Yet they do not know why I bring injury.  
> Those with experience, I think, know well the benefit  
> By which cheese brings aid to a failing stomach.  
>
> [Col. 1149A] Cheese taken before food helps if the bowels are loose;  
> If they are bound, it ends the meal.  
> While it drives the food that has been eaten to the bottom of the stomach,  
> It helps digestion no less.  
> If the stomach is weak or has little appetite,  
> It becomes welcome to the stomach and stimulates food intake.

“While they permitted the other things, they prohibited what was strangled together with blood”—not, however, by establishing an immutable decree, but, in my opinion, by accommodating the weakness of some persons. Understand by “decree” one which would remain unalterably in the Church until the end of the age. In this sense abstinence from blood and strangled animals, as also from things sacrificed to idols, was not an apostolic decree; for it is quite certain that it was later removed.

Indeed, some have not been lacking who wished to hold that the canon of the Council of Jerusalem had been abrogated before Paul wrote to the Corinthians—although we judge that this must by no means be granted—because Paul allows food offered in sacrifice to be eaten if this can be done without scandal. [Col. 1149B] This seems to be the author’s meaning: he thought that Paul could not so quickly have dispensed from a law in the making of which he himself had participated, had it possessed the force of a decree—that is, of immutable law. And indeed, when he writes that the apostles decreed this only in order to accommodate the weakness of Jews, for whom Gentile neophytes eating sacrificial or strangled foods would have been a scandal, he seems to follow Augustine, book XXXII *Against Faustus*, chapter 13:

> “If the apostles then commanded Christians to abstain from the blood of animals, so that they should not eat meat from strangled creatures, they seem to me to have chosen for the time a thing easy and by no means burdensome to those who observed it. In this matter, Jews and Gentiles observed something in common for the sake of that cornerstone joining the two walls into itself, etc. But when that time had passed, in which those two walls—one coming from circumcision, the other from uncircumcision—although agreeing in the cornerstone, yet stood forth more distinctly in certain [Col. 1149C] peculiarities of their own; when the Church of the Gentiles became such that no carnal Israelite appeared in it: what Christian now observes this, so as not to touch thrushes or smaller birds unless their blood has been shed? Or not to eat a hare if it has been killed by a blow of the hand to the neck without a bloody wound? And those perhaps few who still fear to touch these things are mocked by the rest. Now that saying of truth has taken hold of all minds in this matter: ‘Not what enters your mouth defiles you, but what comes out,’ etc.”

This is Augustine’s teaching in accord with Pullus’s thought.

Nevertheless, it is certain that this law concerning the non-permission of blood and strangled animals, etc., long remained in the Church, as is clear from the Council of Gangra, chapter 2, and from the penitential books of Bede and Rabanus. Yet from the authority of Augustine just quoted we have that in his own time the law was not of the strictest obligation, which accords sufficiently with Pullus’s opinion. See Saint Thomas, I–II, question 103, final article, at the end.

[Col. 1149D] “They except many things unlawful in our time.” He tacitly attacks the innovators of his age, who were called Apostolics, against whom Saint Bernard also inveighs sharply in Sermon 66 on the *Song of Songs*; we omit Bernard’s words for brevity’s sake. See Genebrard’s chronology at the beginning of book IV. He also notes, under the year 1052, that Emperor Henry, at Goslar in Saxony, ordered certain heretics to be hanged, with the consent of all, because among other errors they abominated the eating of every animal, like the Manichaeans.

## CHAPTER XVII

“Therefore I judge it much more reasonable that parents’ seed, in the likeness of a rib, should receive from God its own growth from itself,” etc. Hugh of Saint Victor says no otherwise in book I, *On the Sacraments*, part VI, penultimate chapter; likewise the Master of the Sentences, book II, distinction 30 near the end, and distinction 18; Peter Comestor, *History*, chapter 73; Peter of Poitiers, part V, chapter 19; etc.

These authors consider that there is no other matter in human beings [Col. 1150A] properly called that of human nature than that which existed in Adam at the first origin of things. Conveyed in fragments to descendants by seminal propagation, it is propagated in them without the addition of any extraneous thing. They further maintain that only that flesh is human which will someday be raised to immortality and the other endowments of resurrection. Consequently, they assert that bodies are nourished not in order that some determinate portion of matter—which others suppose to have been consumed by the force of innate heat—may be restored, but only that they may be sustained by an external juice, or that the original heat may have something upon which to expend its violence. It is as goldsmiths, when refining gold, add a little lead lest it evaporate into the air and perish entirely.

This opinion seemed advantageous to those writers, both in order that the unity of the origin of all human beings might be preserved, and in order that the truth of human nature—insofar as it is posited as flesh or matter—might be shown in the general resurrection. Pullus discusses both matters more fully, as we shall dwell on them [Col. 1150B]. Yet that this opinion pleased few and rests upon no stable foundation, so that it has been rejected and rightly refuted by almost all theologians, and finally put aside by the Parisians and marked with an obelus in the Master’s works, may be seen in the authors who wrote on the second and fourth books of the *Sentences*. We mentioned the same opinion above when discussing the transmission of the original stain, at chapter 28 of the second part.

“Unless perhaps that which was removed in circumcising the foreskin.” Here Pullus seems modestly to hesitate, since he was not unaware of the reports commonly circulated in his time concerning the foreskin, navel, tooth, and other such relics of Christ the Lord. Guibert, abbot of Nogent, could scarcely endure their claimed physical presence on earth, in many passages of books II and III of *On the Relics of Saints*, for example book II, chapter 1:

> “There are those who claim to possess the Lord’s [Col. 1150C] own foreskin from his circumcision; concerning which the great Origen says: ‘There were some who were not ashamed to write books on the Lord’s very circumcision.’”

And chapter 2, §1:

> “But if the question concerns this physical presence, assuredly whoever claims for himself his tooth, or navel, or that which is said to have been cut off in circumcision, lies altogether.”

Finally, in book III, in a special work against the people of Saint-Médard:

> “I should like you to deign to answer into the possession of what body, at the resurrection, you think the Lord’s tooth and all the other things will pass. For we are dealing among us no less with the navel and the other things said to be possessed from him than with the tooth; what is said clearly of one applies to the rest. Where then will the things preserved from the Lord the Savior go when that last day comes upon us? If they are to return to the original body, where will they enter? What places will open themselves to receive them? Or has the glorified Savior remained toothless until now, in order to reserve a place for the tooth yet to arrive? Surely no suitable place for so small a tooth could possibly belong in the manly throat of the Lord. Let that be granted. Where, I ask, will the navel be put back? Are two glorifications celebrated in the same body, [Col. 1150D] etc.?”

Thus Guibert, printed in this year. But, burning with zeal for truth, he did what Pullus prudently refrained from doing, as did Innocent III after him, in book IV, chapter 30 of *On the Mysteries of the Mass*, in Bollandus:

> “What shall be said of the foreskin from the circumcision, or of the cutting off of the navel? Did it likewise return, at Christ’s resurrection, to the integrity of human substance? For it is believed to be kept in the Lateran basilica; though some say that Christ’s foreskin was brought from Jerusalem by an angel to Charlemagne, who transferred it and placed it at Aachen; but afterwards Charles the Bald placed it in the Church of the Savior at Carosium. Yet it is better to entrust the whole matter to God than rashly to define anything,”

as do very many modern writers who, whether from party zeal or an innate desire to pronounce on every question, contend with one another to transfer relics of this sort to the Romans, the people of Anizy, the people of Antwerp, the people of Carosium, and now to Calcata in Latium.

## 432. CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 1151A]

“He did not say that the body is changed into spirit, as some nevertheless think.” The author had in view this passage of Augustine, *City of God*, XIII, chapter 20:

> “Flesh serving the spirit will rightly be called spiritual, not because it will be changed into spirit, as some think because it is written, ‘A natural body is sown; a spiritual body shall rise’; but because,” etc.

Augustine says similar things in book I, *On Faith and the Creed*, chapter 6, but especially in letter 146 to Consentius, where he discusses this difficulty expressly.

## CHAPTER XXV

“Origen promises in vain liberation after many years to wicked persons and even to the demons themselves.” Epiphanius treats this false doctrine of Origen—or rather of the Origenists—in heresy 6 and in his letter concerning Origen’s errors to John of Jerusalem; Jerome in letter 61 to Pammachius and in another against [Col. 1151B] the same John; Augustine, *City of God*, book XXI, chapter 17, and *On Heresies*, chapter 43; and Gregory, *Dialogues*, chapter 44.

That this error was condemned by the Church is testified by the same Augustine in the cited passage of the *City of God*; Jerome in his *Apology against Rufinus* and letter 78 to Pammachius; and the Fifth Synod under Pope Vigilius and Emperor Justinian, in which several doctrines of Origen were condemned. Theophilus likewise condemned it in the Alexandrian synod. Yet our Genebrard, in his collections concerning the life and writings of Origen, chapter 6, attempts to remove from Origen the stain of the error that the punishments of the damned and demons will someday end, maintaining that he wrote such things more for the sake of disputation than assertively and from his own opinion. For in homilies 1 and 14 on Ezekiel, homily 14 on Joshua, books XII and XIV on Numbers, book V on the Epistle to the Romans, and homily 9 on various matters, he writes the opposite. Thus not a few reasonably suspect that Origen’s writings were sprinkled with such blemishes by his adversaries.

## CHAPTER XXVII

[Col. 1152A]

“It does not at all seem incongruous that at the judgment the sins of the saints too should be understood.” The Master stumbled over this point in following the contrary opinion, book IV, distinction 43, §4:

> “If it is asked,” he says, “whether the sins committed by the elect will then come to the knowledge of all, just as the evils of the damned will be known to all, I have not read this expressly stated in Scripture. Therefore it may not unreasonably be thought that sins covered and removed here through penitence will be covered there also, while the others will be disclosed to all.”

For this reason this opinion is rightly noted among his selected errors. It conflicts with many passages of Scripture: Matthew 10; Mark 4; Luke 8 and 12; I Corinthians 4; Revelation 20; Daniel 7; etc. These generally prove that at the judgment there will be a public disclosure of all the secrets of conscience. Further, the repentance of the saints will be distinctly known by all no less than their other virtues; but such knowledge cannot exist without disclosure of the sins on account of [Col. 1152B] which it was performed, since these are related both in knowledge and in nature. Very many Fathers teach this; but we refrain from listing their judgments in so easy a matter.

But now there has been more than enough—especially for me, to whom not only superfluities but also things offered somewhat too freely in this kind of writing have always been distasteful. Others will desire more: both those who wish for greater fullness and those who delight in fewer words. Yet let them pardon these slender offspring of my intellect when they recognize the barrenness of the subject. And lest I sin with impunity, I am the first to vent my severity upon the faults of my pen. Others, who have experienced the cares, labors, and annoyances which printing brings with it, will readily reject any further attempts at finding fault with a press that has failed in its duty. If, moreover, the reader notices any blemishes of my dim-sighted intellect that detract from the dignity of sounder learning, we earnestly ask him to erase them with his pumice-stone; and we here already condemn as worthy of the obelus whatever is such, sincerely submitting everything to the censure of the learned and to the judgment of the holy mother, the Apostolic and Roman Church.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1152. SUGER, ABBOT OF SAINT-DENIS

[Col. 1151]

## NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. VII, p. 368)

[Col. 1151C] Suger [Note: [Col. 1151] *Life of Suger*, bk.
