I, no. 3; part II of the documentary proofs for the *History of Saint-Denis*, p. 195], born of humble stock to a father named Helinand, first saw the light in 1081, as all agree in France; indeed, according to the conjecture of a recent author in the second volume of the French work entitled *Historical and Literary Curiosities*, pp. 48 ff., he was born in the province of Belgium, and specifically in the territory of Arras, namely in the town of Saint-Omer, then comparatively recent and little distinguished. The author infers this from two letters found among the documentary proofs for the history of Saint-Denis. One, no. 138, is from Louis VII, written about 1148 from Asia, informing Suger of the death of Alvise, bishop of Arras, in these words: “Your venerable brother, the bishop of Arras, has departed to the Lord in a blessed consummation.” From this he concludes, and not rashly, that Alvise, bishop of Arras, was Suger’s brother. Since Alvise was of Flemish descent and had first been a monk of Saint-Bertin, he should be believed to have been a native of Saint-Omer, and consequently Suger also. For there is another letter, no. 137, of Alvise himself to Suger, from 1147, quite consistent with this, which begins: “Dearest brother Suger, venerable abbot . . . . . we grant,” etc. Certainly it would not have been fitting for Alvise to use so familiar an address if he had not really been Suger’s brother, when other bishops and even princes addressed Suger with such reverence, as will subsequently be seen.

Moreover, when about ten years old, Suger began his novitiate among the monks of Saint-Denis [Col. 1153A] [Note: [Col. 1153D] Documentary proofs for the *History of Saint-Denis*, part II, p. 180]. Endowed with remarkable natural ability and polished by study, he attended the synod of Poitiers in 1106. He was then appointed provost of Berneval in Normandy, and subsequently, about 1109, of Toury, a famous town in the Beauce [Note: [Col. 1153D] Pagi, vol. IV, p. 419]. Already renowned, he undertook embassies on behalf of King Louis to the supreme pontiffs Paschal II, Gelasius II, and Callixtus II; one embassy to the latter pope took him to Italy in 1121. Having discharged it splendidly, he was, by the unanimous vote of all, requested to become abbot in 1122, or 1123 according to the present reckoning, while absent and without the king’s knowledge. Because the election had been made without his permission being sought [Note: [Col. 1153D] Duchesne, vol. IV, *Historical Writers of France*, p. 311], the king ordered that the messengers who had brought him the decree of election for confirmation be committed to the prison of the castle of Orléans.

While returning to France, Suger learned of all this through the legate and thus expressed his feelings:

> “I was distressed by a threefold danger: whether, by accepting an election contrary to the will of my lord the king, I should have to endure that the mother Church be despoiled on my account through the rigor of the Roman Church and through the authority of Lord Pope Callixtus, who loved me.”

But he was soon freed from this anxiety, when the two men whom he had sent in the two directions brought favorable news. He adds:

> “When, with God’s help, we had arrived at the mother Church (on Friday, 10 March, that is, in 1122), she received her prodigal son so sweetly, so filially, so nobly, that we found the king, who had formerly met us with a stern countenance but now with a serene one, the archbishop of Bourges, and the bishop of Senlis [Col. 1153C], waiting there and rejoicing over us. They received us most speedily with great veneration, together with the rejoicing assembly of brethren. On the following day, namely Saturday in Mid-Lent, he ordained me, though unworthy, priest; and on the following Sunday, Passion Sunday, he consecrated me there, before the most sacred body of the blessed Dionysius, as abbot, though undeserving.”

This ordination is recorded in the short chronicle of Saint-Denis under the year 1122. The chronicle of Nangis says of it:

> “Suger, monk of Saint-Denis in France, famous for his knowledge of the Scriptures, although he had been advanced only to the order of deacon, was, on returning from Rome, whither he had been sent by Louis, king of France, elected abbot upon the death of his abbot Adam. On his return he was first ordained priest, and afterward, in the presence of the king, was blessed as abbot by the archbishop of Bourges in his church of Saint-Denis.”

This occurred in the third year of the pontificate acquired by Archbishop Vulgrin, as is found in vol. II of the new Library of Labbe, p. 82.

Suger himself still speaks thus of his election in an instrument from the cartulary of the library of Saint-Denis belonging to Thou, copied by Félibien from the original among the documentary proofs for the *History of Saint-Denis*, no. 128:

> “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, amen. I, Suger, humble servant of the church of the blessed martyrs [Col. 1154A] Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius. Since it is clearly established that, by the abundant favor of almighty God, contrary to the expectation warranted by our merits [reading uncertain: *meriti, morum*] and the lowliness of our birth, I, even while absent and conducting business at the Roman curia, came to the administration of this holy church, and that the divine power laudably and wonderfully delivered me in this same holy Church from the hands of enemies seeking my life: it is fitting and altogether expedient for our lowliness to commend and exalt it with all the affection of our heart, and to honor and cherish our brethren who serve the Lord God,” etc.

Suger went to Rome in 1123. There he was received by Callixtus and the entire company of the purple-clad Fathers with an exceedingly honorable proclamation of praise, and attended the Lateran council on the question of investitures [Col. 1154B] as King Louis’s envoy. Suger had won the king’s favor while studying with him at Saint-Denis [Note: [Col. 1153D] *Universal History of Paris*, vol. II, p. 94], so much so that the king declared in his councils that Suger was his faithful and intimate adviser. In a diploma of 1124, by which he confirmed for him the privilege of holding annual fairs, when war with the king of the Germans was imminent, the king took the banner from the altar of the blessed martyrs Dionysius and his companions [Note: [Col. 1154D] Documentary proofs for the *History of Saint-Denis*, no. 124]:

> “To this banner the county of Vexin, which we hold from them in fief, is known to owe service, according to the ancient custom of our predecessors, and by right of bearing the standard, as the counts of Vexin were accustomed to do.”

Suger accompanied the king on this expedition [Note: [Col. 1154D] Duchesne, vol. IV, *Historical Writers of France*, p. 548]. In the following year, 1125—the third of his administration and the seventeenth of Louis’s reign—on the Sunday of the Ides of March, in the third indiction, he exempted the townsmen and householders of the town of Saint-Denis from the exaction called “dead hand,” which had become established since the time of his predecessor Abbot Ivo.

In the same year, with the consent of Maynard, count of Morspeck, of his wife Matilda, and of his sons, he concluded a peace settlement concerning several possessions that Count Adalbert, Maynard’s predecessor—whose daughter Maynard had married—had taken from the monastery of Saint-Denis [Note: [Col. 1154D] Documentary proofs for the *History of Saint-Denis*, no. 125]. When Maynard restored or compensated for them, Suger, in the presence of Adalbert, archbishop of Mainz, and Gerard, cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, absolved him and his predecessors from the bond of anathema. This was done at the celebrated conference held at Mainz concerning the election of the emperor. Among others, Peter, Suger’s clerical brother, subscribed on Suger’s behalf.

To this matter belongs Suger’s Letter VII, published in vol. IV of Duchesne, p. 554. From it we learn that Albert, count of Morspeck—undoubtedly the man mentioned above—had been excommunicated for retaining the aforesaid property, but subsequently, when he repented, was absolved by Suger. The condition of his guilt and anathema was annulled on the understanding that thereafter, every year on the feast of St Martin, he should pay five ounces [Col. 1155A] of refined gold to the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius. If he should be found to violate this custom and return to his former rapacity and wickedness, like a dog to its vomit, he would incur the wrath of almighty God and could no longer be released from the bond of anathema. This indeed appears to have happened to him.

About this time Suger was one of the arbiters of a settlement between Stephen, bishop of Paris, and the chapter of that church. From the beginning of his office, he had resolved to restore monastic discipline, which had fallen into decay, both in himself and in his brethren. Accordingly, the reform of the monastery of Saint-Denis by Suger is assigned to the year 1123—perhaps prematurely—in the chronicle of Nangis, where the following is added under that year [Note: [Col. 1155D] *Spicilegium*, vol. XI, p. 411]:

> “For through the negligence of the abbots who had preceded him [Col. 1155B], and of certain monks of that monastery, the regular observances had been so cast aside in that place that the monks scarcely retained even the appearance of religious life.”

Yet, impeded by various affairs, he could not fully carry this out until about 1127. For this he was praised by St Bernard in Letter LXXVIII; see Mabillon’s notes thereon. He is again adorned with the highest praise by St Bernard in Letter CCCIX, the first among the Sugerian letters in vol. IV of the *Historical Writers of France*, p. 493, addressed to Pope Eugenius:

> “If any vessel for honor in the house of the great King is held in esteem in our Gallican Church; if any man, like the faithful David, entering and going out at the command of the Lord—then, in my judgment, that man is the venerable abbot of Saint-Denis. For I know the man: in temporal matters he is faithful and prudent; in spiritual matters fervent and humble; and in both—which is most difficult—he conducts himself without reproach. At Caesar’s court he is as one of the Roman curia; before God, as one of the court of heaven . . . . . for to love and honor his person especially is to honor your ministry” [Note: [Col. 1155D] Documentary proofs for the *History of Saint-Denis*, no. 126].

In 1129—not 1128, as in the short chronicle of Saint-Denis and vol. II of the *History of the Church of Paris*, p. 69, nor, still less, 1127, as read in vol. II of the *History of the University of Paris*, p. 103—he secured the restoration of the abbey of Argenteuil to its mother house of Saint-Denis at a council held in Paris at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, presided over by Matthew, bishop of Albano and legate of the Holy See. Suger’s charter on this matter appears in our appendix, no. 63, col. 52, and there also no. 64, a letter of Pope Honorius II to Suger confirming the preceding charter. Kings Louis VI, in the twentieth year of his reign, and his son Philip, in the first year of his, likewise approved this by their diploma, issued at Rheims in the solemn Easter court, at the anointing of the most glorious Lord King Philip, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1129, indiction VII.

In the following year, 1130, with the consent of the chapter [Note: [Col. 1155D] Ibid., no. 128], he ordered that the commemoration of the Blessed Virgin [Col. 1156A] be solemnly celebrated every Saturday, as on the last three days of the octave of Pentecost; nevertheless, he forbade the omission of the seven psalms with the litany and the Office of the Dead. He likewise ordered the commemoration of St Dionysius and his companions every Thursday, and accordingly increased the general daily allowance to the brothers’ refectory from six solidi by four solidi, making ten. “And lest,” he says, “this ordinance should ever be allowed to lapse under any pretext of avarice, from those revenues increased by our labor—namely, from the toll collected from the Road—we establish and confirm ten pounds and ten solidi for this Thursday meal, and ten pounds and ten solidi for Saturday, from our revenues in Vexin,” etc. Furthermore, he ordered that certain feasts be celebrated with greater honor and devotion than usual, assigning a specified number of solidi to each.

This charter was issued in 1130 and was approved and confirmed by Peter, priest-cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, and Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Sant’Angelo and legate of the Apostolic See. In the same year Suger went to Cluny to meet Pope Innocent II in King Louis’s name and greet him. When the pontiff came to Saint-Denis in 1131, he was received there with the highest honor by Suger and the convent. After celebrating Easter there, Innocent departed for Rouen and, in letters written to Suger in that city on 9 May, confirmed the privileges of the monastery [Note: [Col. 1155D] Documentary proofs for the *History of Saint-Denis*, no. 130], first congratulating the abbot on the restoration of regular discipline [Col. 1156C] there.

On 17 June 1137, the sixteenth year of his administration, Suger caused his testamentary dispositions to be approved in chapter [Note: [Col. 1155D] Ibid., no. 131]. In the same year he appended, as it were, letters concerning numerous donations made to the church of St Paul [Note: [Col. 1156D] Documentary proofs for the *History of Saint-Denis*]. Also in 1137, he attended Louis VI at the castle of Montrichard in Touraine, when the king was thought soon to die and was receiving the sacraments of the Church. But the king recovered his health; to render thanks to the holy martyrs Dionysius and his companions, he came to the monastery, and thence proceeded to the castle of Béthisy in Valois. There he completed the marriage of his son Louis with Eleanor, the only daughter of the duke of Aquitaine. The younger king immediately went to his new bride, accompanied by Abbot Suger, who about 1140 increased the stipends of the monks [Note: [Col. 1156D] Ibid., no. 133].

He was elsewhere a man of such probity and distinction that Henry, king of England and duke of Normandy, did not hesitate to have him as arbiter of peace between himself and the king of France, and thereafter held him in high honor [Note: [Col. 1156D] Letter CLIII among Suger’s letters, Duchesne, vol. IV, p. 141]. His piety toward God was so conspicuous that he magnificently constructed, almost anew, the basilica through his care and at his expense [Note: [Col. 1156D] Documentary proofs for the *History of Saint-Denis*, part II, p. 181].

Suger began this arduous work at the very first entrance of the doors. There he removed [Col. 1157A] an addition said to have been made by Charlemagne to enclose the tomb of his father Pepin, who had ordered himself to be buried prostrate rather than lying on his back, outside at the entrance of the doors, on account of the sins of his father Charles Martel. Suger then enlarged the body of the church, built three doors, repaired and heightened the towers. When the lower part of the basilica had been completed and adorned with cast-metal doors, he invited Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, Odo of Beauvais, Manasses of Meaux, and Peter of Senlis to dedicate it.

The short chronicle of Saint-Denis says of this dedication:

> “In 1140 the new work of the church of Blessed Dionysius, in its front portion, was dedicated by Lord Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, in the nineteenth year of the administration of Lord Abbot Suger, who constructed that same work.”

To ensure that the year of consecration should not be forgotten, Suger caused it to be marked by this distich:

> The year of the Word was one thousand, one hundred, and forty,  
> When it was consecrated.

He then turned his attention to rebuilding the upper portion of the basilica also, assigning two hundred pounds annually for the expenses of the fabric; of these, one hundred and fifty pounds were spent from offerings made at the altar and to the relics during the period of the proclamation. The foundations of the building were laid in that same year, 1140, on the day before the Ides of July, a Sunday, in the presence of the king, who laid the first stone. In 1143 [Note: [Col. 1157D] Documentary proofs for the *History of Saint-Denis*, part I, no. 134], Suger, whom St Bernard calls the king’s counselor in Letter CCXXII, was granted a diploma of protection.

Meanwhile, that great and remarkable structure was built with such speed [Note: [Col. 1157D] Ibid., part II, p. 182] that, within three years and three months, he had it dedicated as complete and finished in every respect on 2 June, the feast of St Barnabas, which fell on a Sunday in 1144. This was recorded in the distich:

> The year of the Word was one thousand, one hundred, and forty,  
> The fourth, when it was consecrated.

Yet the preceding year, 1143, is recorded in the short chronicle of Saint-Denis in these words:

> “1143: dedication of the chief portion of the church, and translation into that chief portion of Blessed Dionysius and his companions, and of other saints whose bodies are contained there, in the twenty-third year of the administration of Lord Abbot Suger” [Col. 1157D] [Note: [Col. 1157D] Vol. VI, *Benedictine Annals*, p. 377].

He also richly furnished this basilica with countless gifts of vessels, relics, gems, and other objects of exquisite value, as he himself explains at length in a separate book on the deeds performed during his administration—or perhaps it was Brother William, Abbot Suger’s secretary [Note: [Col. 1157D] Documentary proofs for the *History of Saint-Denis*, part II, no. III, p. 172], whose name, according to their editor François Duchesne, appears in some manuscripts as the author of this book and another concerning the dedication of the church of Saint-Denis [Col. 1158A] (*Historical Writers of France*, vol. IV, p. 331). Nevertheless, these books seem rather to be attributed to Suger, since he speaks in them in his own name.

The king and queen attended this dedication, accompanied by many magnates and a large assembly of archbishops and bishops. On this occasion, in favor of the venerable Abbot Suger, his friend and intimate, the king in 1144 granted, as an endowment for the continuing lights of the church, the customary dues he possessed in certain villages of Saint-Denis, for which eighteen pounds were paid to him annually.

Moreover, Suger founded the priory of Blessed Mary of the Fields near Essonnes, close to Corbeil, establishing there twelve monks with a prior. In 1145, he converted into a priory of twelve monks and a prior the abbey of Chaumont in Norman Vexin, which had been given to him by the king, who held it in his own domain; and he took care that its church should be consecrated by Hugh, archbishop of Rouen. He built the village of Vaucresson [Note: [Col. 1157D] Vol. IV, *Historical Writers of France*, p. 554], granting numerous privileges in that same year, 1145, the twenty-third of his government, to those wishing to settle there.

Two years later, in 1147, the year in which Suger was chosen to administer the kingdom during the king’s absence, he received from Alvise, bishop of Arras, the altar of Anchin as a gift to augment the lighting of the church of Saint-Denis, as is read in the documentary proofs for the *History of Saint-Denis*, no. 137. In that year, I say, when King Louis the Younger departed upon the holy expedition, the administration of the kingdom was entrusted, by the choice of all the estates of the realm, approved by the king and pope, to Abbot Suger and Count William of Nevers [Note: [Col. 1158D] Vol. IV, *Historical Writers of France*, pp. 495–496]. But the count refused this office, pleading a vow to enter the Carthusian order, which he fulfilled shortly afterward. Suger was therefore compelled to take the whole weight of the kingdom upon his shoulders, apart from Ralph, count of Vermandois, the foremost prince of royal blood himself. Ralph calls Suger his lord in Letter XI to him.

This letter, with many others by the same Ralph to Suger, is found in vol. IV of the *Historical Writers of France*, in the section on Suger’s letters, pp. 493 ff., namely nos. 9, 17, 41, 86, 100, 115, and 160; and conversely two of Suger’s letters to Ralph, nos. LXXXIV and CLIX [Note: [Col. 1158D] Ibid., pp. 493 and 499]. Hence Ulger, bishop of Angers, addresses Suger by the title “Majesty”; the convent of Saint-Riquier calls him “most serene lord and father” in Letter XXIII; Goslenus, bishop of Chartres, calls him “Excellency” in Letter CIV; and the chapter of Autun commends to his excellence the election of its bishop, Henry of Burgundy, in Letter XLIII [Note: [Col. 1158D] Ibid., pp. 507 and 527]. St Bernard adorns him with the titles of greatness, sublimity, and prince in Letters LXX and LXXII [Note: [Col. 1158D] Ibid., p. 517]:

> “I beseech and advise your sublimity, because you are the greatest prince in the kingdom.”

Peter the Venerable, bound to Suger by the closest friendship, gives the name of royal government to his administration [Note: [Col. 1159D] Martène, vol. I, *Anecdota*, col. 416]. Geoffrey, duke of the Normans and count of Anjou, says in Letter VIII to Suger [Note: [Col. 1159D] Vol. IV, *Writers of France*, p. 495]: “I do not wish your authority to be unaware,” etc. Count T. of Flanders entreats “the excellence of his holiness” in Letter LXII [Note: [Col. 1159D] Ibid., p. 514]. The commune of Beauvais calls him “Holiness” in Letter LXXXVI; P., archbishop of Bourges, calls him “Sublimity” in Letter LXXXI [Note: [Col. 1159D] Ibid., pp. 519–520]; and the dean of the church of Noyon addresses Letter XLIV to “Suger, vicar of the kingdom” [Note: [Col. 1159D] Ibid., p. 508].

There are also many letters of King Louis VII to Suger [Note: [Col. 1159D] Ibid., pp. 494–544], namely nos. 6, 22, 39, 48, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56, 58, 59, 60, 68, 69, 70, 94, 96, 139, 148, and 161. In four of these, nos. 53–56, addressed to Count Ralph of Vermandois as well as Abbot Suger, nothing is found from which one may infer what Gerard Dubois writes in vol. II of the *History of the Church of Paris*, p. 94: that this count was joined to Suger in the administration of the kingdom, except perhaps merely as an assistant, together with Samson, archbishop of Rheims.

Not only Gallican bishops, princes, magnates, and the king himself paid Suger such great honor; foreigners also held him in the highest esteem [Note: [Col. 1159D] Ibid., p. 503]. Among them, Jocelin, bishop of Salisbury, in Letter XXXVI addressed to “the beloved and deservedly beloved Father and Lord Suger, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, ruler of the realm of the Franks,” says:

> “The fragrance of your reputation, which spreads everywhere, has made us hasten from lands beyond the sea toward your fragrance. We have come, therefore, from the ends of the earth to hear your wisdom, namely the wisdom of the Solomon of our time. We have heard the wisdom; we have seen the temple that you built; we have viewed the ornaments which you offered and which are being offered; we have considered the order of the ministers and their ministries; and deservedly we burst into the words of that queen of the South: ‘The half was not told me,’ and, ‘Your wisdom and works are greater than the report in our land.’ For who would not marvel that one man should sustain so many and such great affairs: preserving the peace of churches, reforming their condition, defending the kingdom of the Franks by arms, adorning it with morals, and correcting it by laws? . . . But may your serenity pardon us because, when we departed from Gaul, we were unable to see your face as we wished,” etc.

Robert, bishop of Hereford, writes similarly in Letter XXVI to Suger [Note: [Col. 1160D] Vol. IV, *Writers of France*, p. 500]:

> “More abundantly do the gifts of so many graces and virtues, which are widely proclaimed concerning you for the benefit of many, draw me into love of you and gladden my soul. For if wisdom or foresight is sought, such is found in Suger that whatever affairs depend upon your counsel proceed more cautiously and succeed more happily. If recourse is made to religion, from the mirror of your life shines forth both what gives light outwardly and what is profitable inwardly. Added to this is the praise of liberality, which delights to anticipate requests with benefits, and, unasked, asks one who is about to ask,” etc.

From these many letters no doubt remains that Suger performed his office splendidly for the good of king and kingdom. Although occupied by the business of the whole realm, he nevertheless did not turn his mind away from care for the monastery. For, as the author of his eulogy says [Note: [Col. 1160D] Documentary proofs for the *History of Saint-Denis*, part II, p. 195]:

> “While he presided over the monastery, he also presided over the palace, and he so managed each office that the court did not prevent him from caring for the cloister, nor did the monastery excuse him from the counsels of princes.”

Thus, possessed of supreme authority, Suger successfully carried out what the king and pope had proposed concerning restoration of discipline in the abbey of Sainte-Geneviève, then administered by extremely lax canons. He introduced there twelve canons of Saint-Victor in Paris and Prior Odo, whom he appointed abbot on the feast of St Bartholomew in 1147. Suger’s letter of that year to Pope Eugenius on this matter may be found in our appendix. I refrain here from mentioning other letters on the same affair, both from Suger to that pontiff and conversely, and from St Bernard to Suger; they will be more suitably treated below when we discuss the abbey of Sainte-Geneviève.

In the following year, 1148, Suger attended the council of Rheims, at which, under the presidency of Eugenius III, Gilbert of Poitiers, bishop of Poitiers, was condemned. By the pope’s command, in 1149, he replaced the canons of the church of Compiègne, whose abbot was Prince Philip, with monks. Numerous letters on this matter appear in the often-cited fourth volume of the *Historical Writers of France* [Note: [Col. 1160D] pp. 542–546].

I add, from cols. 414, 415, and 416 of vol. I of Martène’s *Anecdota*, that Roger, first abbot of Saint-Evroult at Orléans, calls Suger “a man of lofty counsel and outstanding prudence”; that Geoffrey, count of Anjou, thanks Suger for laboring to restore peace between himself and the king; and finally that Peter, archbishop of Bourges, asks him to excuse him before the king because he cannot come to him at Meudon.

At last, consumed by a lingering fever contracted after so many labors borne for Church and kingdom, at the time when St Bernard wrote Letter 266 to him [Note: [Col. 1160D] Mabillon’s edition of the works of St Bernard, 1690, col. 262], Suger departed this life in 1151, in the twenty-ninth year of his office and the seventieth of his age. “A beloved father and excellent shepherd,” he died “amid the words of the prayer and the Creed, on the day of the Ides of January,” etc., as the circular letter announcing his death states [Note: [Col. 1160D] Documentary proofs for the *History of Saint-Denis*, part II, p. 201]. This year is read as 1152 in the chronicle of Nangis, [Col. 1161A] vol. II of the *History of the University of Paris*, p. 262, and in Mabillon’s fuller notes on St Bernard’s Letters LXXVIII, col. 28, and CCLXVI, col. 74, owing to differing methods of beginning the year.

King Louis, though then far away, came in person to honor Suger’s funeral; many bishops also attended it. His tomb may be seen in the transept of the church, within the southern wall near the great door by which one descends to the cloister. Before it was placed a tombstone bearing the words: “Here lies Abbot Suger.” To this place Abbot Matthew of Vendôme caused Suger’s body and those of five other predecessors to be transferred in 1259.

The Sammarthani appended an extract from an old manuscript codex of Saint-Denis in place of an epitaph, “not wishing,” they say, “to omit it, because it seems in some measure to illuminate Suger’s memory.” Nor should we omit it, who profess rather to increase than diminish things worthy of remembrance. It is as follows:

> “This is the final year of the life of Suger, abbot of the royal monastery of Saint-Denis in France, of happy memory: a man of great prudence and eloquence, and among the distinguished men of the Gallican Church most learned and most eloquent. How earnestly, during his prelacy, he strove to raise his church in every glory and honor, to order it religiously, and to render it rich in revenues, larger in buildings, and adorned with ornaments, is evident to all. Through the cooperation also of the heavenly mercy of Him who raises the humble on high, He so exalted this man from humble common birth that he not only spoke with praise, by the wisdom with which he was endowed, from the throne and tribunal of judgment in the royal Parliament, but also, as a man of great counsel and resource, esteemed and of proven fidelity in the whole royal household, he sat with exalted princes and especially directed the helm of the kingdom itself. Keenness of intellect, elegance of speech, learning, and skill in composing and writing always shone in him. He stood in such high regard with Pope Eugenius that whenever more serious matters arose in the realm and were brought to the pope’s hearing, he entrusted them for settlement to Suger’s proven discernment.

> “When the glorious King Louis of France departed for Jerusalem, he especially entrusted the government of his kingdom, by the counsel of bishops and magnates, to Suger’s fidelity and diligence. With God’s help, Suger administered and governed it in such a way that, upon the prince’s return, he restored to him what had been entrusted, in peace and unimpaired. But since no one is exempt from the condition of dying, when he began to be afflicted by the illness of which he died, he asked to be carried by the brethren’s hands into the chapter house. There, after words of edification, he cast himself with tears and groans at the feet of all and humbly submitted himself to their judgment, tearfully begging that, whatever offense he had committed against them or whatever he had done too negligently, they would forgive him out of regard for mercy. All the brethren did this most willingly, with the utmost devotion and abundant shedding of tears.

> “This venerable father passed away amid the words of the prayer and the Creed, on the day of the Ides of January, in the year of the Lord 1152, in the seventieth year of his age, nearly the sixtieth since receiving the monastic habit, and the twenty-ninth of his prelacy. Six bishops attended his burial and funeral, together with many abbots and Louis, the most Christian king of France. Mindful there of his piety and forgetful of royal majesty, the king wept most bitterly while he was buried. The whole royal household wept, and also the people, who mourned him as a most prudent counselor and the wisest governor and administrator of the entire kingdom.”

Félibien reports two epitaphs of Suger [Note: [Col. 1161D] *History of Saint-Denis*, p. 572]. One says that he died on the seventh day of Theophany, that is, 12 January; the other, on the eleventh. The thirteenth day, or the Ides, should be retained, as found in the ancient necrology of Saint-Denis and that of St Peter of Chartres, as well as in the martyrology of Sainte-Geneviève in Paris, in these words:

> “On the Ides of January, the anniversary of Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, through whose assistance and industry, at the command of Lord Pope Eugenius of holy memory and the illustrious king of the Franks Louis, our church was changed from the condition of secular canons to the order of regulars.”

The necrology of the Church of Paris says:

> “On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February died Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, for whose soul William, his nephew and our fellow canon, gave us sixty Parisian pounds.”

The ancient necrology of Saint-Denis also reads [Note: [Col. 1161D] Documentary proofs for the *History of Saint-Denis*, part II, p. 207]:

> “On the day before the Nones of January and on the day before the Nones of February, and thus in every month except October, the commemoration of Lord Abbot Suger.”

He wrote the deeds of Louis VI. He had also begun to write the history of Louis the Younger, but death prevented him from completing what he had undertaken. He also wrote many letters to the supreme pontiff [Note: [Col. 1162D] Vol. IV, *Historical Writers of France*, pp. 493–546], to kings, and to every most noble magnate, especially while he most worthily administered the kingdom during Louis the Younger’s journey to the Holy Land. Conversely, there survive many letters to him from great men, especially Peter, abbot of Cluny, and Bernard of Clairvaux, who flourished in learning and religious life in that age. Finally, William, his intimate associate and a monk of Saint-Denis, wrote Suger’s life, which may be seen among the documentary proofs for the *History of Saint-Denis*, part II, p. 194.

[Col. 1163]

## SECOND NOTICE

(*Literary History of France*, vol. XII, p. 361.)

### § I. History of Suger’s Life

The birthplace of the illustrious Suger is a problem upon which various conjectures have been offered, none of which, in our view, produces complete conviction. The one which seems to us to come nearest the truth makes him a native of the territory of Saint-Omer. [Note: [Col. 1163]

Félibien, *History of Saint-Denis*, p. 152.—It is thus that Dom Liron (*Historical Curiosities*, vol. II, p. 48) attempts to establish this opinion. Alvise, he says, who was made bishop of Arras after having been abbot of Anchin, was born in the territory of Saint-Omer. Now Suger was Alvise’s brother.

1. This is proved by a letter of King Louis the Younger. Informing Suger of Alvise’s death, he says to him: “Your venerable brother, the bishop of Arras, has departed to the Lord in a blessed consummation.” This is the only bishop of whom that prince, writing to Suger, said: “your brother the bishop.”

2. Alvise himself gives Suger the same designation in a charter issued in favor of the abbey of Saint-Denis (*History of Saint-Denis*, documentary proofs, p. CVI): “Dearest brother Suger, venerable abbot.” Add to this the great esteem in which Alvise, a subject of the count of Flanders, was held at the French court; the lively interest shown by King Louis the Fat in his election to the bishopric of Arras (*Literary History*, vol. XI, pp. 673–674); the urgings the king made to him to accept that dignity; the satisfaction which he expressed to the people and clergy of Arras at this choice; and Alvise’s attachment to the abbey of Saint-Denis. If this convergence of probabilities, carefully weighed, does not wholly persuade the mind, it should at least, it seems, shake it.

We possess a short letter of Alvise published by Baluze in addition to his charters (*Miscellanies*, vol. V, p. 405). This document did not appear to us to warrant giving this prelate a separate article in this history.]

The date of his birth is more certain. All critics agree in placing it in 1081. Suger’s father was Helinand, a man of the common people, whose sole distinction in the world was his integrity. From his tenderest youth he was offered by his parents to the religious life in the monastery of Saint-Denis in France. A thousand fine qualities, whose seeds were perceptible in the child, caused him to be received with open arms by Abbot Yves, then head of that house. A few months after his admission, he was sent to the priory of L’Estrée, a quarter of a league away and a dependency of Saint-Denis. [Note: [Col. 1164] Suger, Epistle 88.] There must have been religious there capable of instructing him, for he himself acknowledges that he was always carefully brought up. [Note: [Col. 1164] “He spent his time there singing, sleeping, and doing nothing,” says M. Dauvigni (*History of Illustrious Men*, vol. I, p. 6), following the unfaithful and partisan Dom Gervaise, of whom he is merely a slavish abridger.] The terms of his testament state that he spent ten years in this retreat. [Note: [Col. 1164] Duchesne, *Script.*, p. 282.]

Abbot Yves having died in 1094, Suger was recalled to Saint-Denis at about the same time. The occasion for this recall was as follows. King Philip I had just entrusted his son Louis, later surnamed the Fat, to this abbey, to be trained there in letters and virtue. [Note: [Col. 1164] Duchesne, ibid.] Adam, Yves’s successor, wishing to stimulate the young prince’s emulation and provide him with a companion of his own age, thought it fitting to place near him the young Suger, whose agreeable character, open mind, and application to work suited this purpose very well. The result went further than the abbot had hoped. Suger had the good fortune to please Louis exceedingly; and from that point there arose between these two persons of such unequal rank the constant friendship whose consequences were no less useful to the king and the State than honorable to the favorite.

Philip having recalled his son to court about 1098, [Note: [Col. 1164] Duchesne, ibid., p. 522.] Suger went to perfect his abilities in a celebrated school situated on the borders of Touraine and Anjou, near the abbey of Fontevraud. History does not name this school; but the location just indicated, on Suger’s own authority, [Note: [Col. 1164] Epistle 88.] cannot be that of the academy of Poitiers, as Duboulay maintains (vol. II, p. 7). It seems to us much better suited to the abbey of Saint-Florent of Saumur, where learning truly flourished at that time under Abbot William, successor to Sigon. [Note: [Col. 1164] Manuscript history of Saint-Florent of Saumur, by Dom de Guines, ch. 21.]

Having completed the course of his studies, Suger returned to Saint-Denis toward the end of 1103; he was then in his twenty-third year. The progress he had made during his absence drew his brethren’s attention upon his return. His abbot especially, who had spared nothing for his education, congratulated himself on having succeeded so well. With satisfaction he observed all the advantages united in his person: a short stature indeed, but enhanced by an agreeable and intelligent countenance; polished manners, without affectation or servility; liveliness without thoughtlessness; a mind fitted for business and fertile in resources; a remarkable facility in expressing himself in both languages; together with an air of propriety and a regularity of conduct that had never belied themselves. Adam did not judge that a man of such merit ought to remain in obscurity. [Note: [Col. 1164] William of Saint-Denis, *Three Books on the Life of Suger*, bk. I, no. 4, among the proofs in Dom Félibien’s *History of Saint-Denis*.] He himself took him to court to pay his respects to Prince Louis, who for four years had shared the throne with his royal father. From the summit of greatness Louis had not forgotten his fellow student. He saw him again with joy and gave him fresh assurances of his friendship.

The success of this first visit opened the way to court for Suger. His abbot ordinarily took him along whenever he was obliged to go there, whether for the interests of his house or affairs of State. [Note: [Col. 1164] Suger, *Life of Louis the Fat*, p. 288.] Sometimes he even sent him to represent him there, as well as at ecclesiastical assemblies, so greatly did he rely upon his prudence and ability. Suger himself tells us [Note: [Col. 1165] Suger, *Life of Louis the Fat*, p. 288.] that he was chosen to attend the Council of Poitiers, held in 1106 concerning aid requested by the Christian armies in the Holy Land. Again, it is from him [Note: [Col. 1165] Ibid.] that we learn that two years earlier he had attended the council of State which deliberated concerning the marriage of the only daughter of Guy Trussel, lord of Montlhéry, to Philip, son of King Philip and Bertrada, countess of Anjou.

One of his principal occupations at Saint-Denis was the study of the archives—a study much neglected before him—by which he enabled himself to defend the abbey’s possessions and privileges against those who wished to attack them. [Note: [Col. 1165] Egasse du Boulay, *History of the University of Paris*, vol. II, p. 18.] Galon, bishop of Paris, found in him a formidable adversary when, in 1107, he challenged the exemption of Saint-Denis. The dispute was heard in the presence of Pope Paschal, who was then at La Charité-sur-Loire. Suger, whom his abbot had brought there, pleaded his house’s cause in such a manner as to win the case and the pope’s esteem. He then had the honor of accompanying Paschal to Châlons-sur-Marne and of being admitted to the council which the pope held there concerning his disputes with Emperor Henry V.

Suger had no less courage and firmness of soul than liveliness, flexibility, and sagacity of mind. [Note: [Col. 1165] Félibien, ibid., p. 152.] This led the monastery to entrust him with the administration of the estate of Berneval in Normandy, which the officers of the king of England were plundering with impunity. His conduct there fulfilled his brethren’s expectations. He stood up to the usurpers, checked their violence, and even compelled them to restore the property they had seized. Another estate of Saint-Denis was exposed to like depredations: [Note: [Col. 1165] Ibid., p. 138.] namely Toury, on the road from Étampes to Orléans. Hugh du Puiset, the terror of the whole surrounding country, [Note: [Col. 1165] Duchesne, ibid., p. 299; Mabillon, *Annals*, bk. 22, p. 365.] ravaged it through the ransoms he exacted from the inhabitants and strove in every way to make himself master of the castle. When Suger became provost there, he first attempted gentler and persuasive means of winning over the tyrant, but in vain. Hugh was of a character that could be overcome only by superior force of arms. [Note: [Col. 1166] Duchesne, ibid., p. 300.] He did not expect our provost to make him experience this. Events undeceived him. Having put himself in a state of defense, Suger repelled his attacks, pursued him in turn, and carried devastation into his own lands. These successes, indeed—although Suger often personally performed the duties of a captain, so ill suited to his profession—were less his own work than that of King Louis the Fat. Within four years the prince came no fewer than three times to lay siege to the castle of Le Puiset. The place, captured as often, was at last reduced to ashes. After this defeat Hugh fled and went to expiate his crimes in the Holy Land.

During this war, a truce granted upon the rebel’s feigned submissions gave our provost leisure to attend the Lateran Council held in 1112. The object of that assembly, as is known, was to free the pope from the bonds in which the emperor had placed him by forcing him to surrender the investitures.

On returning to France, he continued to govern his provostship of Toury. He likewise continued to make frequent journeys to court, each of which brought him an increase of favor in the prince’s esteem.

After Paschal’s death, on 18 January 1118, Louis deputed him to convey his congratulations to Pope Gelasius II, whom the persecution of Bourdin, his rival claimant, had compelled to take refuge in France. Suger met the Holy Father at Maguelone in a situation in which the monarch’s homage, assurances of protection, and gifts sent through his ambassador could not have arrived more opportunely. At the audience granted him, a day and place were agreed for a meeting between His Holiness and the king. But Gelasius’s sudden death prevented him from fulfilling this engagement. His successor Calixtus II likewise needed French support to maintain himself upon the Holy See. Again Suger was charged, in 1119, with carrying to him the good wishes of Louis and of France. In the same year he attended the council held by this pope at Reims. What role he played there is unknown; and the role ascribed to him on this occasion by the modern historian of his life [Note: [Col. 1166] Gervaise, *Life of Suger*, vol. II, p. 157.] belongs among those multiplied fictions which have rightly caused that history to be called a romance. [Note: [Col. 1166] Vaissette, *History of Languedoc*, vol. II, p. 559, no. 14.] All that appears certain is that Calixtus from then on conceived a particular esteem for the deputy of Saint-Denis. Two years later the pope saw him again at Bitonto, in the territory of Bari, at the head of an embassy which the king had sent him on business whose object history does not specify. [Note: [Col. 1166] Suger, *Life of Louis the Fat*, p. 310.] Suger stated the matter that had brought him with a wisdom and grace that made the pontiff wish to keep him for some time, so as to enjoy his conversation at leisure. But having sounded him out on this matter, he could obtain nothing. His master’s affairs being concluded, he at once took leave of the pope and departed.

Eagerness to see his brethren again, together with some presentiment I know not what, made him hasten his return. But on the road, and even in Italy, he received news which somewhat slowed his journey. A messenger sent by the monks of Saint-Denis came to tell him of the death of his abbot, who had died on 19 January 1122, and of the chapter’s choice of Suger himself to replace him. [Note: [Col. 1166] Ibid.] He added that, since this election had taken place without the king’s participation, the prince, far from confirming it, had become so enraged against the delegates who brought him the decree that he sent them to prison in the castle of Orléans. [Note: [Col. 1166] Ibid., p. 311.]

This account produced the most vivid and varied impressions upon Suger’s mind and heart. The death of his abbot, to whom he owed what he was, moved him to tears; the honor his brethren had done him in choosing him to govern them filled him with gratitude; but the haste with which they had acted in this affair threw him into the most cruel embarrassment. What resolution should he take in so delicate a situation? To acquiesce in his election seemed rashness capable of bringing the whole weight of the king’s indignation upon himself and his house; to renounce it for this reason was to incur the pope’s displeasure, who would not have failed to brand such conduct as weakness and pusillanimity. At last, after much reflection, he resolved to detach part of his people: some to consult the pope as to what he ought to do, [Col. 1167] and others to precede him into France and learn whether it was safe for him to appear again at court.

As the first group were preparing to leave, there arrived a churchman of the Roman court, a man of rank and Suger’s friend, who generously undertook his commission to the pope. His anxiety did not last long. The delegates whom he had sent to France returned in haste to tell him that the monarch’s anger had passed; that he had released the prisoners of Saint-Denis; and that he himself would see Suger again with joy. He then quietly continued his journey. Arriving at Saint-Denis, he found the king awaiting him at the gate, accompanied by several bishops and followed by the whole community. Louis and the prelates, by their caresses, and his brethren, by the expression of their affectionate respect, made his entry resemble a true triumph. The very next day, a Saturday, the bishop of Senlis ordained him priest—for he had until then been only a deacon—and on the following Sunday he received the abbatial blessing from the hands of the archbishop of Bourges. This was proceeding somewhat quickly, as may be seen; but the king wished it so, in order to witness the entire ceremony, and it was thought proper not to deny him that satisfaction.

The new abbot devoted all the rest of the year to examining the condition of his house, which his long and frequent absences had in some sense made unfamiliar to him. But in the following year he took up a rather misplaced devotion, whose motives and object it is proper to give in his own words:

> [Note: [Col. 1167] *Life of Louis the Fat*, p. 312.] “In the second year after our ordination,” he says, “we set out to pay our respects to the Roman Church, lest we seem ungrateful by failing in this duty. For what claims had not this common mother of the Churches acquired upon our gratitude? She had graciously admitted us, before our promotion, to various councils held at Rome and elsewhere; she had honored us with applause when we pleaded before her, whether for the interests of our house or for other affairs; and, finally, she had rendered numerous judgments in our favor.”

He then relates the gracious manner in which Pope Calixtus and his whole court received him on this new journey, and the six months he spent at Rome, during which he attended the Lateran Council where the great question of investitures was settled.

> “After this,” he says, “we went to offer our prayers at Monte Cassino, at Saint Bartholomew’s of Benevento, at Saint Matthew’s of Salerno, at Saint Nicholas’s of Bari, and at Saint Michael’s on Mount Gargano. From there we returned to France with papal letters praising us and assuring our monastery of the protection of the Holy See.”

Nothing could have been less equivocal than these demonstrations of esteem and goodwill with which the pope had honored the abbot of Saint-Denis. Subsequent events made this still clearer. About eighteen months after Suger’s departure, Calixtus, impatient to see him again and wishing to attach him permanently to his person, wrote to urge his return, promising to raise him to a higher dignity—which seems capable only of referring to the cardinalate. Suger accepted this invitation, doubtless after arranging the matter with the king. He departed with a numerous retinue and the sums of money needed both for travel expenses and to prepare himself for the honors he was to receive. But Calixtus’s death, which he learned at Lucca, caused all the fine hopes he entertained to vanish. “At this news,” he says, “we turned back, avoiding the Romans’ old and new avarice: *Romanorum novam et veterem avaritiam devitando retrocessimus*—‘we withdrew in order to avoid the Romans’ new and old greed.’” [Note: [Col. 1167] Ibid., p. 313.]

Suger was amply compensated for the pain caused by this reverse through the favorable reception the king gave him upon his return. Louis had already felt the injury he had done himself by allowing him to depart. To remove from him the temptation of a repetition, he involved him so deeply in affairs that it was no longer possible for him to withdraw. History records no particular title with which the monarch invested him; but it tells us that he exercised great influence in every operation of government. These cares caused very troublesome distractions in the administration of his house. Wholly occupied with the public good, his neglect of everything else allowed confusion to follow the affairs that besieged him at Saint-Denis. This monastery, having become, as it were, the seat of justice and the office of war, stood continually open to litigants, soldiers, and even women. [Note: [Col. 1168] Saint Bernard, Epistle 78.] The cloister, a place specially consecrated to silence, echoed with the cries of litigation and the noisy conversations of those who came to solicit favors and offices. The result was that the monks, distracted from their observances, abandoned themselves to idleness.

The abbot’s personal conduct was by no means fitted to conceal these disorders. His luxury seemed to rival his influence. His table, clothing, and equipages proclaimed rather a great secular lord than a superior of monks. But God, who had merciful designs for this extraordinary man, did not permit him to persevere in a way of life so little suited to his state. The external means employed to touch him and bring him back to himself are unknown. Common opinion gives Saint Bernard credit for his conversion. However this may be, it was as sudden as it was sincere and lasting. At the very time when it was least expected, the abbot of Saint-Denis embraced reform and had it adopted by his community so promptly and peacefully that he seems not to have met the slightest opposition. This happy event coincides with the year 1127. When the abbot of Clairvaux learned of it, he wrote to Suger in the name of all good people to congratulate him. Yet far from suggesting in his letter that he had contributed to this marvel, he asks Suger who had proposed such perfection to him, and declares that he received the news with the same surprise as everyone else: *Quis tibi hanc perfectionem proponebat? Ego tanta, fateor, audire de te, etsi desiderabam, non tamen sperabam*—“Who was proposing this perfection to you? I confess that, although I desired to hear such things of you, I nevertheless did not hope for them.”

Upon reforming himself, Suger would gladly have left the care of the State in order to devote himself wholly to retirement; but the king would never consent. He was therefore obliged to combine a new way of life with his former commitments: the austere observances of the monastic profession with the duties of a courtier, the maintenance of regular discipline with the immense detail of public affairs. Our abbot, renewed by grace, faced everything and won applause on all sides. In his cloister, a monk full of fervor and a vigilant superior, he seemed occupied only with his salvation and that of the souls entrusted to his care. To remedy the inconvenience of his frequent and unavoidable absences, he took care to appoint a deputy capable of replacing him. This was the monk Hervé, whom he named grand prior, a man indeed of only moderate ability but of prudence and zeal upon which Suger could rely. At court, humble and stripped of all the pomp that had formerly surrounded him, he was only the more esteemed by the great. His merit, in which they no longer perceived any blemish, subdued them—however unruly they were—[Col. 1169] to the point of choosing him as arbiter of their disputes with the king. The monarch himself did nothing without Suger’s counsel.

It was doubtless after consulting him that Louis held the assembly of Étampes in 1130, to decide between Innocent and Anaclet, who were contending for the papacy. When the decision favored the former, Suger was appointed to carry him the news at Cluny. [Note: [Col. 1169] *Life of Louis*, ibid., p. 1315.] This was the place which Innocent, expelled from Italy, had chosen for his retreat, awaiting more favorable circumstances that would permit him to appear openly. One may easily imagine the joy caused him by this embassy and the marks of affection with which he overwhelmed the bearer of it. On taking leave of His Holiness, the abbot of Saint-Denis begged him to honor his monastery with his presence. Innocent promised, and kept his word the following year.

Philip, son of Louis the Fat, then sat upon the throne with his father. When this young prince died tragically on 13 October 1131, Suger needed all his intelligence and the ascendancy he held over his master’s mind in order to console him. After drying the monarch’s tears, he suggested that he promptly give the deceased a successor. This counsel was all the wiser because the king’s health was beginning to decline, and there was reason to fear that the throne would become unstable and lie exposed to the ambitions of the great if his death left it vacant. Louis readily adopted his minister’s views. Accordingly, he associated Louis, his second son, later surnamed the Young, in supreme power; and, to make this association more solemn, he brought him to the Council of Reims, where he had him anointed and crowned by the pope in that assembly.

The father’s sentiments toward the abbot of Saint-Denis passed into the son’s heart, where they grew stronger and increased with age. Suger had the honor of accompanying this young prince on his journey to Bordeaux to marry the heiress of Aquitaine. When the joy of that illustrious union was disturbed by the news of Louis the Fat’s death, our abbot was among those who persuaded Louis the Young to hasten to Paris—a wise precaution which thwarted the schemes of several lords ready to rise in revolt.

Amid the political and military affairs that occupied Suger during the first years of the new reign, he conceived and carried out the design of rebuilding the church of Saint-Denis. The merit of this undertaking, whose principal details will be given below, may be characterized in one phrase: it was worthy of Suger’s wealth and genius. But here is a striking contrast. Beside this monument of his magnificence, he built another in which his modesty shone no less brightly. It was a cell ten feet wide and fifteen long, intended as this great man’s retreat for his spiritual exercises. [Note: [Col. 1169] William, *Life of Suger*, bk. II, no. 10.] A saying of Peter the Venerable on this occasion is reported. Looking at this small room after admiring the beauties of the church, the abbot could not refrain from saying to those who accompanied him: “Here indeed is a man who condemns us all. If he is lavish, it is for the Lord’s house. But how far he is from permitting himself the expenditure that we make in housing ourselves!”

The delights Suger enjoyed in this solitude increased day by day his distaste for the employments that drew him to court. [Note: [Col. 1170] William, ibid., bk. I, no. 2.] He was on the point of freeing himself from them when a convergence of unforeseen circumstances cast upon him alone the whole weight of government. This deserves some detail.

In 1145 the envoys of the crusading princes of the East arrived in France with letters from Pope Eugenius III exhorting the faithful to a new crusade. Louis the Young, inconsolable for having put the town of Vitry to fire and sword two years earlier, believed he had found an opportunity to repair this wrong by taking the cross himself and dedicating himself to the journey to the Holy Land. Suger, consulted on this matter, was not of this opinion. He represented to the monarch what France had to fear from his absence, full as it was of vassals no less restless than powerful, and therefore very apt to profit from the occasion in order to stir up disturbances. Seeing that Louis’s conscience resisted these political considerations, he begged him at least to see Saint Bernard before deciding. The king consented; but, far from censuring his design, the abbot of Clairvaux regarded it as a divine inspiration and made it a matter of religion for him to follow it. From that time the matter was settled. In 1146 Louis solemnly received the cross from the saint’s hands at Vézelay.

When he was ready to depart, in February of the following year he convoked the prelates and barons to arrange with them the manner in which the State would be administered during his absence. Saint Bernard, charged to speak in the name of the assembly, proclaimed the count of Nevers and the abbot of Saint-Denis regents of the kingdom. Both, equally surprised, protested that so weighty a burden exceeded their strength. The former also alleged a vow to enter religious life, and on this ground obtained his release. It was not so with Suger. Far from heeding his remonstrances, they did not even think it appropriate to give him a new colleague. The only favor granted him was to ask Samson, archbishop of Reims, and Ralph, count of Vermandois, a close relative of the king, to lend him their assistance, but in subordinate positions and under his authority. Such a favor was scarcely likely to bend him. He persisted in his refusal. Fortunately, the pope was then in France. Recourse was had to him in order to overcome the abbot of Saint-Denis’s resistance. This expedient succeeded: Eugenius spoke and was obeyed. As the reward for this compliance, the pontiff joined the spiritual sword to the temporal sword which the prince had placed in Suger’s hands, giving him authority to excommunicate all who opposed his will.

We reserve for the following paragraph the account of the principal events that marked his regency. Here we shall confine ourselves to saying that, despite the frequent opposition he had to endure, the reins of State never wavered in his hands; that he always knew how to maintain the authority of the laws, prevent or suppress uprisings, check usurpations, and watch over the security of frontier strongholds; and, in a word, that he exercised the sovereign authority entrusted to him with all the prudence and wisdom that could be desired. This is the testimony which Frenchmen and foreigners alike eagerly rendered him. Indeed, some of the latter journeyed to France in order to verify for themselves what fame proclaimed concerning his merit. Among them was Joséel, bishop of Salisbury. It is well to set before the reader part of the letter which he wrote to the regent upon his return to England. [Note: [Col. 1170] Duchesne, ibid., p. 503.]

> “Your reputation, spread everywhere,” he tells him, “determined us to cross the sea solely out of the desire to know you; and we have come from so far away only to witness the wonders related of you, as of the Solomon of our age. Our curiosity has been fully satisfied. We have had the pleasure of hearing the words of wisdom that proceed from your mouth; we have considered the magnificent church which you have caused to be built, the ornaments with which you continually embellish it, the order and [Col. 1171] harmony reigning among those who serve it; a thousand other things contributing to your glory have engaged our attention. Certainly we have every reason to say with the Queen of the South that not half of what we see with our own eyes had been reported to us, so greatly does the truth surpass the report of fame. For indeed, who would not be astonished to see one man sustain the weight of so many important affairs: maintain the peace of the Churches, reform the clergy, defend the kingdom of France by arms, cause virtue to flourish there, and order it by laws?”

The king of Scotland, David, was moved by the same curiosity as the bishop of Salisbury. Since his dignity did not allow him to come personally to France, he sent ambassadors there with gifts for Suger and a letter asking for his friendship. [Note: [Col. 1171] William, *Life of Suger*, bk. I, no. 9.]

Yet, however wise Suger’s regency was, secret enemies succeeded in making it suspect to the king through letters which they wrote to him as he was preparing to return. [Note: [Col. 1171] Ibid., bk. III, no. 7.] But the delusion did not last long. The pope, whom Louis saw while passing through Rome, entirely disabused him concerning the regent. On his return, the testimony of his own eyes did still more than that of the Roman pontiff. He was astonished by the good order Suger had established in the kingdom and found no better means of discharging his obligation toward him than by honoring him with the noble title *Father of the Fatherland*—a title ratified by the unanimous consent of the great and the people.

Louis brought back very little glory from the crusade. On leaving the Holy Land, he had left matters in nearly the same confusion in which he had found them. He felt this misfortune keenly, and intended to repair it at the first opportunity. [Note: [Col. 1171] Ibid., no. 8.] But what redoubled his own zeal had so chilled that of the French lords that it was impossible to bring them into his plans. Suger then conceived a resolution for which there had been no precedent before him in a private person, and which has had only one imitator since: [Note: [Col. 1171] Cardinal Ximenes, who financed the expedition to Oran at his own expense.] namely, to raise an army at his own expense and lead it himself into Palestine. He had already made considerable preparations for this expedition when a lingering fever, combined with his great age, warned him to think only of the great journey into eternity. He prepared himself for it by every means that religion places in the hands of the faithful. [Note: [Col. 1171] Félibien, *History of Saint-Denis*, p. 189.] Feeling his end approach, he assembled his brethren in chapter and, after asking their forgiveness for the faults he had committed in his abbatial ministry, restored to their ranks and offices those whom he had deprived of them.

Saint Bernard, informed of his condition, wrote him a very fine letter exhorting him toward death. [Note: [Col. 1171] Bernard, Epistle 266.] Three bishops, his friends, received his final breath. He died at the age of seventy, on 12 January 1151. [Note: [Col. 1171] This is the date given in the short chronicle of Saint-Denis, and not the year 1152, as [Col. 1172] several modern writers maintain. Add to this: first, that Odo, Suger’s successor, reckoned 1152 as the second year of his administration; second, that Joscelin, bishop of Soissons, one of the three prelates who attended Suger at his death, himself died on 24 October 1151. (Félibien, *History of Saint-Denis*, proofs, p. CCVI; *New Gallia Christiana*, 2nd ed., vol. VII, pp. 376–377.)]

No minister was ever more universally regretted, or deserved better to be so. He united in an eminent degree moral, Christian, and political virtues. It may be affirmed that he was one of the best abbots of his century and the most accomplished minister France had possessed since the establishment of the monarchy. His example is a good answer to the arguments of those false sages who imagine, and try to persuade others, that the exact practice of Christian obligations cannot be reconciled with the conduct of public affairs.

The funeral of this great man drew a large concourse of prelates, lords, and people. The king himself honoured it with his presence. It is said that, seeing the body lowered into the tomb, the monarch could not restrain his tears. This feeling was probably not fleeting: the subsequent events of his reign must often have recalled to him bitterly the void which Suger's death had left in his council. “Alas!” said a contemporary author [Note: [Col. 1171] William, *Life of Suger*, bk. I, no. 5.], “if that great minister were still alive, we should not have lost half the kingdom (through the repudiation of Queen Eleanor), nor should we continually have arms in our hands to preserve the other half.” The original place of his burial is unknown; but it is known that in 1259 Abbot Matthew of Vendôme had his body transferred into the thickness of the wall at the crossing of the church, on the south side, where it remains today, bearing externally this simple inscription: *Here lies Suger, abbot* [Note: [Col. 1171] Félibien, *ibid.*; *Gallia Christiana*, new ed., *ibid.*]. This abbot apparently did not know the epitaph composed for him by Simon Chèvre-d'Or, a regular canon of Saint-Victor and Suger's contemporary, since it was not unworthy to be engraved upon his tomb. We transcribe it here after the historian of Saint-Denis.

> The flower, jewel, crown, and pillar of the Church has fallen;  
> Its banner, shield, helmet, light, and summit—  
> Abbot Suger, an exemplar of virtue and justice,  
> Weighty with devotion, devout with gravity;  
> Great-hearted, wise, eloquent, generous, honourable,  
> Present in judgment in body, in mind self-possessed.  
> Through him the king prudently governed the affairs of the realm;  
> He who governed the king was, as it were, a king ruling a king.  
> And while the king lingered beyond the sea for many years,  
> This man presided over the kingdom, acting in the king’s stead.  
> What scarcely any other man could unite in himself, he united:  
> Good toward men, and good toward God.  
> He adorned, repelled, and increased the noble Church—  
> Its see by praise, its losses by vigour, its choir by men.  
> Small in body and in birth, constrained by a double smallness,  
> Yet in his smallness he refused to be small.  
> The seventh day after Epiphany took light from him;  
> The true Epiphany gave him to the true God.

[Col. 1173] Since the introduction of the Congregation of Saint-Maur into the abbey of Saint-Denis, Suger's tomb has been adorned, in 1645, with a copper plaque three and a half feet high and two and a half feet wide, set in a marble frame. At its four corners are emblems intended to express the principal virtues of this abbot. An epitaph is engraved on the plaque, setting forth his praise in a most elegant manner, though somewhat too diffusely to be inserted in this history. It may be found in Dom Félibien’s history.

Suger's disciples likewise did not fail in what they owed to his memory. As soon as he had closed his eyes, they published news of his death, his virtues, and their mourning in a very fine circular letter addressed to all the faithful. Elsewhere we shall discuss this letter, as also the *Life of Suger*, both composed by his secretary William [Note: [Col. 1173] See below under William of Saint-Denis, who follows Suger immediately in our edition. EDITION OF THE FATHERS.].

## § II. His writings

Writings bearing Suger's name naturally command favourable expectations. It is indeed scarcely likely that a man whose whole life was an uninterrupted succession of great occupations amused himself by writing things useless or of little worth. The truth bears out this presumption. Everything that issued from Suger's pen has genuine merit and evident usefulness. His works are of several kinds. In the survey we are about to make, we shall begin with his letters.

Duchesne collected sixteen of them in the fourth volume of his great Collection, together with a large number of letters written to Suger. Since most of the latter belong to authors whom we have discussed or shall discuss later, we shall mention them here only insofar as is necessary for understanding the letters of the man with whom we are concerned.

The collection is preceded by an extract from Saint Bernard’s 309th letter, addressed to Pope Eugenius. Recommending to His Holiness the envoys whom Suger was sending him, Bernard speaks of the abbot as follows: “If there is in our French Church any precious vessel capable of adorning the palace of the King of kings; if the Lord has among us another David, faithful in carrying out His commands, it is undoubtedly the venerable abbot of Saint-Denis. This great man, whom I know personally, joins prudence and fidelity in the administration of temporal affairs with fervour and humility in matters spiritual; and, what is rare, he is equally irreproachable in both respects. At court he lives as a wise courtier, and in his monastery he is a model of regular observance. I beg you to receive kindly the envoys of so estimable a man.”

At the head of these envoys was John, Suger's nephew and a monk of Saint-Denis. But death overtook him before he reached Rome, and his companions, either discouraged or unaware of the purpose of the mission, decided to turn back. Eugenius, informed of this misfortune, wrote to Suger to console him, promising favourably to hear all those who should come in his name.

In the article on Ulger, an account has been given of the letter addressed by that prelate to Suger on behalf of the monks of Bourgueil, concerning the election of an abbot which they had made during Suger's regency without informing him beforehand; of the letter which those monks themselves wrote to him in sending the elect for confirmation; and of the favourable yet cautious answer which Suger made to the bishop of Angers.

The division which arose in the chapter of the Church of Paris in 1147 gave Suger business to attend to at the beginning of his regency [Note: [Col. 1174] Egas. Bul., vol. II, p. 248; Dubois, *Ecclesiastical History of Paris*, vol. II, p. 115.]. The question was that of replacing Dean Bartholomew of Senlis, who had been raised to the episcopal see of Châlons-sur-Marne. Since the canons could not agree on this matter, the regent offered them his mediation. He then proposed that they submit to the pope’s decision. They agreed. He himself undertook to write to His Holiness, and did so in at least two letters, of which the first is lost to us.

In his response to this first letter, dated at Auxerre on 6 October, Eugenius informed the regent that he would devote his attention to restoring peace in the Church of Paris. The same letter goes on to thank Suger for offering him any place he might choose in France for holding a council. The pope concludes by promising the regent that he will grant him justice against the duke of Lorraine, “whom,” he says, “we have already excommunicated for other offences.” This duke, of whom Suger had complained to the Holy See, was Matthew I.

As for the deanery of Paris, Suger's second letter to the pope shows that, after the election had been held in accordance with his orders by four arbitrators, it had fallen upon one of them, named Clement. Our abbot represented to the pontiff that the election appeared invalid. “For,” he says, “either the four arbitrators agreed in their choice, in which case the elect gave himself his own vote, which is contrary to the rules; or only three were unanimous, in which case the election is not in accordance with your intention, since you promised to approve only the man whom all four should elect. But further,” he adds, “the candidate is unworthy of the office because of his brutal character and incapacity.”

As evidence he relates the scandal which Clement had caused in choir on a feast day, loudly ordering the cantor, Albert, to be silent while the latter was speaking to one of the choristers in order to show him what he ought to sing. “This outburst,” he says, “is all the more blameworthy because the cantor ranks equally with the dean, both in choir and in chapter, and, if he has committed any fault, it is for the chapter to rebuke him. The bishop of Paris has tried in vain to settle this quarrel, although the cantor has offered to make every suitable advance. The case is presently pending before your tribunal. I beg Your Paternity to remedy this disorder, so that the Church of Paris may suffer no diminution thereby.” Despite this letter, the dean remained in office, and his dispute with the cantor was amicably settled.

Suger stood very high in the favour of Roger, king of Sicily. A false report having reached that prince that Suger was to come to Sicily, he undertook part of the journey to meet him, and turned back only when he had been undeceived. Another proof of his favourable sentiments toward our abbot is found in the following letter which he wrote him:

> “Roger, by the grace of God king of Sicily, duke of Apulia, and prince of Capua, to his dearest friend, the venerable Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis. It is the duty of friends to congratulate one another upon their prosperity. We have therefore considered it proper to inform you, as our intimate friend, that, thanks be to God, we are at peace and in health. In return for what you owe us, we ask you frequently to give us news of yourself, so that we may have occasion to rejoice in your good fortune, just as we are assured that you rejoice in ours.”

Suger answered the monarch in these terms:

> “We render thanks to Your Majesty—not such thanks as we ought, but such as we are able to render—for the graciousness with which so great and wise a prince has remembered our smallness and asked us ourselves for news of our condition. It is indeed a favour which binds us wholly to you, and of which we shall never lose the memory, that you have deigned to communicate to us your prosperity and to inquire into ours. In replying to Your Majesty on this latter point, we initially intended to speak to you of several matters worthy of your interest. But, fearing the weariness which too lengthy a letter might cause you, we have entrusted our envoy to tell them to you orally.”

We possess a letter from Stephen, king of England, to our abbot, very much like that of the king of Sicily. He thanks him for the good offices he renders at the French court, asks him to continue them, and assures him that he takes particular care of the estates of Saint-Denis situated within his dominions. Suger's answer has not survived. But what deserves notice as an example of his rare prudence is that he knew equally how to preserve the friendship of this prince and, as will shortly be seen, to retain that of Stephen’s two rivals, Geoffrey, count of Anjou, and the Empress Matilda, his wife.

Although Suger had wished to dissuade the king from going personally on crusade, he was nonetheless zealous, as has already been seen, for that expedition; here are fresh proofs of it. When the estates had been summoned at Chartres to consider means of organizing into an army the multitude who had taken the cross [Note: [Col. 1175] *Councils*, vol. X, p. 1102.] and maintaining them on the march, the abbot of Saint-Denis wrote to the abbot of Cluny, inviting him to attend this assembly [Note: [Col. 1175] Peter the Venerable, bk. VI, letter 19.]. Nothing is more moving than the picture he gives in this letter of the unhappy state of affairs in Palestine, nor more urgent than his arguments for the necessity of working to restore them. The abbot of Cluny replied [Note: [Col. 1175] *Ibid.*] that he was ill and had appointed a general chapter for the very day on which the estates were to meet: two reasons which prevented him from accepting Suger's invitation. Neither Suger's letter nor the other’s reply appears in Duchesne’s collection; they are found only in the sixth book of the latter’s letters.

Suger wrote on the same subject to Humbert, archbishop of Lyons, and that prelate likewise excused himself from being unable to attend the estates at Chartres. The principal reason he alleged was that the archbishop of Sens, who disputed his primacy, was to be present; it was therefore unsuitable for him to meet him, lest he compromise the dignity of his Church. Duchesne preserved this reply, but Suger's letter no longer exists.

After the death of Alberic, archbishop of Bourges, in 1141, the see of that Church was disputed between Peter de la Châtre, descended from an ancient house, and Cadurc, the king’s favourite. The former, formally excluded by the monarch, who had decided in favour of his rival, appealed to Pope Innocent, who did not hesitate to consecrate him. Louis the Young, angered by this proceeding, seized the temporalities of the Church of Bourges and declared that Peter should never have either that Church or any other within his dominions. This gave rise to an open breach between the court of Rome and that of France.

Saint Bernard fortunately succeeded in settling the affair by inducing the king of France to yield to the pope. Peter de la Châtre was therefore confirmed in the archbishopric of Bourges. Before departing on crusade, the king invested him with the temporalities of that Church; but most of those in possession of them refused to surrender them. Cadurc, master of the tower of Bourges, maintained himself there through the connivance of the royal provosts of Berry. Renaud de Crécy, to whom custody of the castle of Saint-Palais, four leagues from Bourges, had been entrusted during the troubles between the two rival candidates, claimed it as his own property. Both men, summoned by the regent to submit, sought the protection of the count of Vermandois.

Suger, informed of their activities, was not alarmed.
