He wrote to the count that what he had ordained concerning the two towers conformed to the king’s intentions and that he would change absolutely nothing. “This,” he says in closing, “is what we wish you to command them in writing through the bearer of this letter: *Quod per praesentem nuntium vos ipsis praecipere scribendo volumus*—‘which we wish you, by writing, to command them through the present messenger.’” The authoritative tone with which Suger speaks to the count clearly shows that the latter did not share the regency with him. The two castles were in fact restored, as is attested by the letter of thanks which the archbishop of Bourges wrote to the regent on the matter.

After serving Peter de la Châtre so well, Suger had occasion to request his protection for the monks of Chappes-Aude, a priory dependent upon Saint-Denis, three leagues from Montluçon. Other neighbouring monks were troubling them and had taken from them a church of which they were in possession. In the letter which the regent wrote to the prelate on this subject, he recalls the services he had rendered him at the expense of his own interests; for his zeal on Peter de la Châtre’s behalf had, he says, brought him several harsh treatments from the king and others.

When Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, died on 24 January 1149, Suger sent commissioners to take possession of the regalian rights until the see of that Church should be filled. This he notified to the canons in a first letter addressed to them. The chapter soon made its election, which fell upon the archdeacon Goslen. It immediately informed Suger, asking him to confirm the election and restore the regalian rights to the elect. The regent’s answer states that he approves the election, but cannot surrender the regalian rights before the prelate has appeared at court to take, according to custom, the oath of fealty.

Suger granted no dispensation in this respect. Peter, abbot of Massay, near Vierzon in Berry [Note: [Col. 1175] This may help to establish approximately the date of the election of this abbot, whom the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, together with his two predecessors, merely place before the middle of the twelfth century.], had excused himself from appearing at court after his election; the regalian rights of that abbey consequently remained in the king’s hands. The abbot recognized his fault, and, having come to request investiture, obtained it with a letter from the regent to the royal provosts and sergeants of Berry, ordering them to release the temporalities into his hands.

When Suger saw the lords who had accompanied Louis the Young returning from the Holy Land, he knew the dispositions of most of them and was greatly alarmed by the king’s delay in Syria, where they had left him. His first concern was to write and urge him to return.

> “The disturbers of the public peace,” he told him, “have returned, while you remain, as though captive in a foreign land, when you are bound to defend your subjects. What are you thinking of, my lord, to leave the sheep entrusted to you thus at the mercy of wolves? How can you conceal from yourself the danger with which the plunderers who have preceded you threaten your dominions? No, you are not permitted to remain any longer away from us. Everything here calls for your presence. Therefore we entreat Your Highness, we exhort your piety, we appeal to the goodness of your heart; finally, by the faith which mutually binds prince and subjects, we implore you not to prolong your stay in Syria beyond the feast of Easter, lest a longer delay make you guilty before the Lord of failing in the oath you took when you received the crown. As for us, impatient to see you again, we await you as an angel of God. You will, I think, have reason to be satisfied with our conduct. We have deposited with the Knights Templar the money which we had resolved to send you. Moreover, we have repaid to the count of Vermandois the three thousand pounds which he lent us for your service. Your land and your men now enjoy a happy peace. We reserve until your return the reliefs from the fiefs held of you, the tallages, and the provisions of food which we levy upon your domains. You will find your houses and palaces in good condition, through the care we have taken to repair them. I am now declining in age; yet I venture to say that the duties I have undertaken for God’s love and out of devotion to your person, without any regard to myself, have greatly hastened my old age. With regard to the queen your wife, my advice is that you conceal the displeasure she causes you until, once restored to your dominions, you can deliberate calmly upon this matter and others.”

The fears which dictated this letter were soon realized. Robert of Dreux, having left the Holy Land very dissatisfied with the king, his brother, wished to profit from his absence to seize the government. His measures were so well laid, and so large a number of barons had entered into the plot, that he saw himself on the point of succeeding. To defeat his plans, the regent saw no other resource than to summon the estates. Soissons was designated as the place of meeting. When the abbot of Clairvaux learned of Suger's resolution, he wrote congratulating him upon it.

We possess a letter of the regent to Samson, archbishop of Reims, asking him, as “a precious jewel from the head of the crown of the kingdom” (*tanquam pretiosam de capite coronae regni gemmam*), to attend that assembly with his fellow-provincial bishops. He wrote similar letters, now lost, to the other archbishops and the great men of the realm. The assembly was indeed held, and there Suger triumphed completely over the enemies of the state.

One of the crown’s great vassals who showed the greatest zeal and fidelity during the king’s absence was Geoffrey, count of Anjou. On every occasion he openly declared for the regent. Having agreed to meet at Beaugency regarding affairs of the kingdom, the count’s health did not permit him to be present, and he wrote to excuse himself. In a second letter he informed Suger that, being much better, he was ready to employ his person and all that depended upon him in service of the state—indeed, he says, “with much greater diligence than if the king himself were present” (*et multo diligentius quam si rex praesens adesset*).

The count’s devotion to duty did not go unrewarded. Upon his return to France, Louis placed Henry, Geoffrey’s son and later king of England, in possession of Normandy by force of arms, retaining Norman Vexin for himself. It is true that shortly afterwards they quarrelled concerning Girard de Berlai, or Bellai, whom the count had stripped of the castle of Montreuil [Note: [Col. 1177] The siege of Montreuil, undertaken by the count of Anjou, began toward the end of 1148 and lasted three years. The *Chronicle of Normandy* speaks thus under the year 1148: “Duke Geoffrey besieged the castle of Montreuil in Poitou [Col. 1178] and built there three stone castles; and that siege lasted for three years, until Berlai, lord of the castle, surrendered himself to the count. The count then utterly demolished the tower and castle.”].

As they were on the point of taking up arms, Suger intervened between the two parties to reconcile them. He first addressed the king in a letter exhorting him not rashly to undertake war against a vassal whose power he had recently greatly increased by investing him with Normandy. Above all, he begged him to consult the great men of the kingdom. “For,” he says, “I fear that you will fail in this undertaking if you enter upon it on your own initiative and without counsel. Thus, although you have already summoned your men for this expedition, I take the liberty of telling you that it is appropriate to suspend hostilities until you have deliberated with your vassals—that is, the prelates and the great men—upon the matter. In that event you may expect everything from them; for I do not doubt that the fidelity which they owe to the kingdom and to your crown will lead them to contribute all their strength to the success of a war which they have unanimously planned with you.” This letter proves that the king’s vassals then believed themselves strictly bound to assist him only in wars upon which he had taken their advice.

Suger likewise wrote to the count and to the Empress Matilda, his wife, exhorting them to satisfy the king. He recalls to them the tokens of esteem and affection which King Henry, Matilda’s father, had shown him on every occasion: “So far,” he says, “that this prince, great as he was, did not disdain to come out to meet us and, when he was at war with France, to communicate to us, in preference to his own advisers, his plans for restoring peace. Hence it happened that we often caused him, by our counsel and with divine help, to desist from several wars into which troublesome spirits had led him and which they did everything in their power to maintain. I do not even remember—I dare say it—that during twenty years he made any peace with the king without our contributing to it by our efforts, since we possessed the advantage of sharing equally the confidence of both monarchs. It is therefore the memory of the kindnesses of the great King Henry which leads me to advise you seriously to work to calm the mind of our sovereign while there is still time, and before he has entered into engagements with your enemies. Consider that nothing is more necessary to you than peace in the circumstances in which you stand. For if the kingdom of England, which cannot escape you, should fall to you in time of war, all the great riches contained in the royal treasury, instead of turning to your advantage, would become the prey of greedy plunderers or the pay of the troops which you would be obliged to maintain.”

Dom Martène published, in the first volume of his *Anecdotes*, an answer from the count to Suger, thanking him for the effort which His Highness (*Sublimitas*) had taken to work for his reconciliation with the king. But he warns him that, since the monarch’s army is on the march against him, he cannot refrain [Col. 1179] from putting himself on the defensive. Nevertheless, he assures him that if the king will kindly suspend hostilities, he will abide by whatever Suger and the count of Vermandois decide.

Suger replied to this letter with another which Dom Martène likewise brought to light. In it he tells the count that, while he was conferring with Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux and confidant of that prince, concerning means of settling his dispute, the count of Vermandois unexpectedly came upon them; that they joined with him and with other well-intentioned persons to go and find the king; and that at last they obtained from the monarch a truce for the count of Anjou until means could be devised for establishing a firm peace between them. “I do not doubt,” he adds, “that the count of Vermandois has informed you of the same thing.”

Although Suger makes no mention of any hostilities exercised up to that time between the king and the count, it is otherwise certain that Louis had entered Normandy with armed force, where he found the young Henry ready to defend his duchy; that some castles were besieged on either side; and that the war would have been carried on more vigorously had not an illness obliged the king to return to Paris. This may be seen in detail in our modern historians. Yet certain circumstances are absent from their account which they ought not to have neglected. They are as follows: that Girard de Bellai, from the depths of the prison in which the count of Anjou held him, invoked the protection both of the pope and of the king; that the thunders of Rome were launched against the count of Anjou; that this prince, having come to the French court to treat for peace, agreed to restore the land of Montreuil to Girard, whom he had brought with him, but refused to receive the absolution from ecclesiastical censures which was offered him, maintaining that he had done nothing but what was just toward his vassal. On this occasion Saint Bernard, witness to the scene, is reported to have said: “I do not doubt that this man will soon be punished for his obstinacy, either by death or by some other great misfortune” [Note: [Col. 1179] Geoffrey, *Life of Saint Bernard*, bk. IV, ch. 3.]. The prediction, it is added, was fulfilled by the event, the count dying within a fortnight.

During his stay in Paris, Pope Eugenius had agreed with the king and Suger to establish a regular community in the church of Sainte-Geneviève, in place of the secular canons who served it [Note: [Col. 1180] Egass. Bul., vol. II, pp. 226–231.]. The motive for this change was the dissolute life led by those canons; but the occasion was a very violent and almost bloody quarrel between the pope’s attendants officiating at Sainte-Geneviève and the canons, concerning a carpet which had covered His Holiness’s prayer desk (*prie-dieu*). The former claimed it forcibly by virtue of custom, and the latter defended it in the same manner; nor could the king’s presence restrain either side.

At first it was proposed to substitute for the canons monks from Saint-Martin-des-Champs. Such was the tenor of the commission which Eugenius issued from Langres to Suger on 29 April 1148. But at the former canons’ representations, the pope changed his mind and instructed Suger instead to choose canons from Saint-Victor to replace them. Under this new order, Suger, accompanied by the abbots of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Saint-Maur, and Ferrières, went to Saint-Victor to ask its abbot Gilduin for Odo, his prior, together with twelve of his canons.

The proposal initially met serious difficulties. Gilduin pleaded his need of Odo to help him bear, in his old age, the burden of government. At last, after resisting throughout the day, he allowed himself to be overcome. On the following day, the feast of Saint Bartholomew, the new colony was led to Sainte-Geneviève. The bishop of Meaux, who awaited it, celebrated Mass, during which Odo received the abbatial blessing from his hands. The new canons were then put in possession of the regular buildings. The next day the regalian rights were granted them, and the men of Sainte-Geneviève came to swear fealty to them.

This whole account is recorded in a letter from Suger to the pope, reporting his actions. Since most of the former canons had obeyed with very poor grace, Suger foresaw that at the first opportunity they would trouble their successors through lawsuits and quibbles which would entail appeals to the court of Rome. In this same letter he asks His Holiness to prevent that inconvenience, since, he says, like young plants, the new reform requires rest and tranquillity in order to take root and become established.

Eugenius made a very obliging reply to this letter, exhorting the abbot of Saint-Denis to crown a work which he had begun with such success. But what Suger had foreseen soon occurred. The dispossessed canons, repenting of their compliance, subjected the reformers to several affronts. Then they went together to Rome to complain of Suger, whose threats had checked their misconduct. Our abbot had scarcely learned of their departure when he informed the pope by letter, asking him not to be misled by these rebels’ calumnious accounts.

He drew a highly unfavourable picture of their conduct. Their principal excesses were these: instead of faithfully surrendering the Church’s treasure, they had taken four marks from the shrine of Saint Geneviève and a quantity of other reliquaries; they retained the lands and estates of that church; they disputed the regular buildings with the new canons; and they sought every opportunity to disturb them in the divine service. “We could,” he says, “have employed against these mutineers the royal authority of which we are the depositaries; but we thought it more respectful to report them to you and await fresh instructions from Your Paternity.”

This letter did not produce all the effect Suger had hoped from it. Eugenius, naturally inclined to gentleness, believed that he should grant something to the dissatisfied party. And because they insisted that he remove their affairs from Suger's jurisdiction, he adopted a middle course by appointing the bishop of Auxerre as Suger’s colleague in the commission. The letter in which he notified this arrangement to our abbot contained nothing but honourable expressions concerning him. “It is not,” he says, “that we entertain any distrust concerning you. The conduct which you have pursued hitherto has sufficiently demonstrated your prudence and firmness. But we have judged it proper to associate a new commissioner with you, in order to silence the murmurs of the former canons and remove every pretext for gratifying the particular hatred they bear toward you.”

Suger had only cause to be pleased with the conduct of the bishop of Auxerre. They worked in concert and in a short time set the final seal upon the reform of Sainte-Geneviève.

This was not the only undertaking of this kind entrusted to the Abbot of Saint-Denis. Louis the Young likewise had at heart the reform of the secular chapter of Saint-Corneille at Compiègne. Passing through Rome on his return from the Holy Land, he had obtained from the pope a bull dated 13 March 1149, appointing Suger and Baldwin, bishop of Noyon, to replace the canons with monks of Saint-Denis. This affair provoked great disputes. The king, who had foreseen them, went first to Compiègne [Col. 1181] to await Suger, who was to bring there twelve of his monks, with Odo, intended to be their abbot. The bishop of Noyon joined them on the way.

At their arrival the chapter was summoned to hear the papal letters read. Since none of the canons appeared, the king, who was present, nevertheless had the bull read before several other clerics and a multitude of townsmen, who all raised their voices in approval. On the following day, at the king’s urgent solicitation, the canons appeared in chapter, headed by Philip of France, their abbot; but this was only in order to overwhelm the two commissioners with insults, without regard for the royal majesty. In vain were they promised the enjoyment of their prebends: they were determined to listen to nothing. Enraged, they ran from the chapter to the church; having shut themselves in by closing the doors, they seized the ornaments, plundered the treasury, and carried off, among other relics, the Holy Thorn and the Holy Shroud. The monks, meanwhile, having entered the church by an outlet, sought to take possession of the choir. The uproar then redoubled to such a point that, without the assistance of the people, who flocked from every direction, the holy place would have been bloodied. The relics were wrested from the canons’ hands, and they themselves were ignominiously expelled.

It is highly probable that the townsmen undertook to maintain the monks in possession, since on the very next day the king and Suger departed, leaving the bishop of Noyon to settle what remained to be done. Upon his return, Suger wrote to the prelate, exhorting him to bless the new abbot on the patronal feast-day, 14 September, or on the following Sunday. Baldwin did what Suger wished, though not without encountering vigorous opposition. He informed him by letter, stating that it was important to send to Rome to obtain confirmation of all that had been done. “For,” he said, “that is the sole foundation upon which a solid building can be raised, since whatever rests only upon the commands and threats of a prince has nowhere near the same firmness as that which is established upon apostolic authority.” Suger followed this advice and sent off the new abbot of Saint-Corneille with a letter to the pope, in which he set forth the facts just related and begged His Holiness to ratify what he had done by virtue of his orders.

He also wrote to the Abbot of Cluny, with whom Odo was to stay, asking him to give Odo letters of recommendation for the pope. At the end of this letter one reads: “To the venerable lord and father, Abbot of Clairvaux by the grace of God, Suger, abbot of Blessed Dionysius, sends the same greeting”; words suggesting that Odo was also to pass through Clairvaux, and that this letter was common to Saint Bernard and the abbot of Cluny. It is also found in the Library of Cluny (cols. 960–961), among the letters of Peter the Venerable.

The count of Vermandois had been admitted to the council at which the reform of the chapter of Saint-Corneille was resolved upon. The abbot of Saint-Denis thought himself all the more obliged to give him an account of what had just occurred because this prince was better able than anyone else to restrain the canons by seizing the great estates which they possessed in his territories. Suger exhorts him to this in a letter in which he recalls the constant friendship that had prevailed between them and the mutual assistance which they had given one another on every occasion. He calls the count to witness that he had undertaken the task of reforming the Church of Compiègne only reluctantly.

Suger had a particular affection for the abbey of Fontevraud. He gave evidence of it in a dispute which it had with Gilbert de la Porrée, bishop of Poitiers. This prelate, wishing to subject the monastery to himself, refused to bless Abbess Matilda, elected in 1150, unless she acknowledged his jurisdiction. The abbot of Saint-Denis wrote to the pope to complain of this conduct. He begged the Holy Father to favor a house so famous and so edifying, “a place of such great religious observance, which, when we were studying in those parts, we saw newly begun, and which, by God’s will, we hear and rejoice has now grown to nearly four or five thousand nuns.”

This letter was reproduced from Duchesne by Father Sirmond in his notes on the thirty-second letter of Book VIII of the letters of Geoffrey of Vendôme.

We do not know who this Robert de la Bove (*de Bova*) was, on whose account Suger wrote to Thierry, bishop of Amiens, reproaching him for having received him into his diocese. He calls this Robert a criminal, an apostate, and an infamous man, and exhorts the prelate to expel the wretch without delay.

The following four letters, written by Suger during his final illness, were published by Dom Martène in the first volume of his *Anecdotes*.

The first is addressed to Henry, bishop of Beauvais and brother of the king, to the chapter, clergy, and people of that city. Its purpose is to dissuade them from a revolt which they were plotting against the king. Suger employs all his eloquence to make them feel the atrocity of the crime they are about to commit, the rashness of their design, and the extremity of the misfortunes they are preparing for themselves. He calls God to witness that this news grieves him much more than the fever by which he is afflicted. At one point he addresses the bishop, setting before him what is demanded of him by his capacities as the king’s brother, a shepherd of souls, and a citizen; at another, the chapter, which he entreats not to stain the glory of the Church of Beauvais by a sedition as criminal as it is senseless; and at another, the people, whom he exhorts to have compassion on themselves, assuring them that it would be as impossible for him to prevent the city’s utter ruin, should they persist in their fatal disposition, as for an ant to drag a cart. He concludes with these remarkable words: “See to it, discerning men, that on another occasion there not be written what was once found inscribed upon the marble column of this city, spoken by the emperor: ‘We order the town of Pontius to be rebuilt.’”

The second letter is a reply to one Saint Bernard had written to our abbot, exhorting him to bring his course to a Christian end. The saint had enclosed some small gifts with his letter, including a valuable towel and blessed bread. Suger thanks him for all this, expresses great contempt for life, and declares an ardent desire to return to his Creator. He commends himself to the prayers of the holy man and of his entire community, declaring that he would dearly have wished to enjoy Bernard’s presence before dying.

The third is addressed to Joscelin, bishop of Soissons, who had excused himself, on account of his infirmities, from being able to come and see him. Our abbot presses him to grant him this consolation; and, as the prelate had told him that he did not expect to survive him for long, Suger prays that this may not happen. Joscelin yielded to his friend’s entreaties.

Finally, the fourth is written to the king. This letter breathes the sentiments of the tenderest piety. Suger warns the monarch that he feels the moment of his dissolution approaching; that, filled with confidence in divine mercy, he is preparing without disturbance to appear before the tribunal of the sovereign Judge; and that his friends, [Col. 1183] astonished to see him suffering for so long, are persuaded with him that God thereby wishes to grant him time and means to expiate his faults. He commends the king and his realms to divine providence, and wishes that, after a happy reign on earth, he may share in the eternal crown. He begs him to continue his protection of the abbey of Saint-Denis, “which,” he says, “is one of the noblest portions of your kingdom. Love,” he continues, “the Church of the Lord; defend widows and orphans; be the avenger of oppressed innocents. By this you will obtain heaven’s aid against visible and invisible powers, against the attacks of your declared enemies, and against the snares of your secret enemies. Such is my counsel. Keep this letter carefully, since you cannot keep me much longer, and make it a law to observe faithfully what it contains. It is for your own interest that I speak to you.”

Such are the letters of Suger which time has spared. We flatter ourselves that your readers will not disapprove of the detailed account we have given of them. It hardly seemed permissible to pass rapidly over monuments so precious and so interesting for our history.

Part of these letters, and of those written to Suger, had been known to J. Baudouin before they were published. He translated forty-six of them into French, and had them printed in 1640 at Paris, by Augustin Courbé, in the second part of an octavo work entitled: *The Faithful Minister Represented under Louis VI, in the Person of Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis in France and Regent of the Kingdom under Louis VII, Drawn from the Latin Manuscript of Brother William.* At the head of the work is a portrait of Suger, below which one reads these two verses:

> The delight of kings and of the kingdom, Abbot Suger,  
> Whom scarcely did Rome ever bear an equal; such was his countenance.

Secondly, Suger composed the *Life of Louis the Fat* [Note: [Col. 1183] Duchesne, vol. IV, pp. 281–321.]. No one was better placed than he to execute such a work. It may therefore be affirmed that he fulfilled all that could have been expected of him in this respect. The history of his own life was so closely bound up with that of the monarch that he could not refrain from mingling into the latter a number of incidents concerning himself. This work is dedicated to Joscelin, bishop of Soissons, the man most capable, by the obligations he had at court and by the intimacy in which he lived with our abbot, of bearing witness to the truth of his narrative. Among the anecdotes found there, the following seemed to us most worthy of the reader’s curiosity.

Bouchard de Montmorency, having been summoned before the tribunal of King Louis the Fat by Adam, abbot of Saint-Denis, to answer for the wrongs he was doing to the abbey, received an unfavorable judgment. This lord, present in person, loudly protested that he would not submit to it. Nevertheless, says Suger, he was not arrested for this, because it is not the custom of the French, but withdrew freely: “When, having lost his case, he refused to carry out justice and the judgment, he was not detained—for that is not the custom of the French—but departed,” etc.

Speaking of the stay which Paschal II made at Saint-Denis, our author says that, by the manner in which he conducted himself, that pope left posterity an example of moderation unknown and unexpected among Romans. For, having been conducted to the treasury, he not only took nothing, he says, of the gold, silver, and precious stones before his eyes, but did not even deign to look at them, contenting himself with asking for a little of the garments of Saint Denis.

William III [Note: [Col. 1183] And not Robert, as Dom Montfaucon says (*Monuments of the French Monarchy*, vol. II, p. 42).], count of Auvergne, twice in succession, in 1126 and 1131, brought upon himself the arms of Louis the Fat because of the vexations he inflicted on the bishop of Clermont. Having been badly handled the first time, he invoked the aid of the duke of Aquitaine, whose vassal he was. But when this duke came into Auvergne, he was so disconcerted at the sight of the king’s formidable army that, on the point of giving battle, he sent deputies to say to him:

> “Sire, the duke of Aquitaine, your vassal, wishes Your Majesty every honor and prosperity. What he asks of Your Majesty is that you may be pleased to accept his service and preserve him in the enjoyment of his rights. For the same justice which imposes the law of service on the vassal requires equitable lordship from the lord. If the count of Auvergne, who holds of me as I hold of you, has committed any excess, I am bound to produce him before your court. This is an obligation which I acknowledge and have never refused to fulfill. I come today to repeat my submission in this matter, begging you to grant me the favor of accepting it. If Your Majesty doubts my sincerity, I am ready to provide hostages of suitable rank and in sufficient number. It belongs to the great men of the kingdom to judge; I will abide by whatever they decide.”

The king, says Suger, having deliberated on this with the great men, received, as equity required, the duke’s offers, oath, and hostages; restored peace to Church and country; and appointed a day on which the parties, with the duke at their head, would come to Orléans to plead before his court. Our historian does not say what judgment the court rendered. But what he has just told us well deserves notice. This admission by the duke of Aquitaine that he was obliged to produce his vassal before the king’s court to answer for his wrongs is clear testimony to the extent of that court’s jurisdiction and its authority over the great vassals of the kingdom.

When Pope Innocent II came to Saint-Denis on the Wednesday of Holy Week in 1131, Abbot Suger and all his monks went out in procession to meet him, singing hymns and canticles. The following day the pope celebrated the Lord’s Supper there with the ceremonies practiced at Rome, not omitting that called the *presbyterium*, that is, a distribution of gold coins to the clergy. On Good Friday he adored the Cross, and on Easter Day he attended Matins with the community. That same day there was a sort of cavalcade which our author took care to describe in these terms:

> “The pope, followed by several cardinals, left the abbey early in the morning and withdrew to the priory of L’Estrée. There they put on their richest ornaments, as they are accustomed to do at Rome during great ceremonies. Upon the pope’s head was placed a diadem consisting of a mitre surmounted by a gold circlet in the form of a helmet. The Holy Father then mounted a caparisoned white horse. All the cardinals, clothed in long mantles and mounted on horses of different colors, all of whose housings were white, went before him two by two, singing hymns. The barons and other vassals of the abbey went on foot, leading the pope’s horse by the bridle. Others went before and scattered a great quantity of coins to clear away the crowd. All the streets were hung with rich tapestries and strewn with greenery. Besides several companies of soldiers who came out in honor to meet the pope, there was an immense concourse of people. Even the Jews of Paris flocked to [Col. 1185] this spectacle and presented the pope with the book of the Law in a scroll covered with a veil. To this homage the Holy Father replied in words full of compassionate tenderness: ‘May almighty God deign to remove the veil which covers the eyes of your heart.’ At last the pope came to the basilica of the holy martyrs, all resplendent with the brilliance of gold crowns and precious stones far more precious than gold and silver. He celebrated the divine mysteries with us, and together we sacrificed the true Paschal Lamb; after which we went down into the cloister, all covered with carpets upon which tables had been set. There the pope and all his company, reclining in the ancient manner, first ate the material lamb. Then they sat down, and the remainder of the feast, which was most splendid, proceeded as usual.”

From Suger’s testimony it is known that Louis the Fat abdicated into the hands of his son before dying. “As the body and blood of Our Lord were being brought to him as viaticum,” Suger says, “he rose, dressed, and left his chamber, to the astonishment of everyone, in order to go out to meet his God. Having adored him, in the presence of clerics and laymen he put off the royal ornaments, relinquished the kingdom, confessed that he had committed many faults in government, placed his ring in his son’s hand as a sign of investiture, and charged him, under oath, to protect the Church, the poor, and orphans; to maintain every citizen in his rights; and above all not to cause anyone to be arrested in his court unless caught there in the act.” This prince survived his abdication by nearly two months. He died upon ashes, in the arms of Stephen of Senlis, bishop of Paris, and Gilduin, abbot of Saint-Victor.

Suger was simple enough to believe Merlin’s prophecies, calling him “the marvelous observer of the everlasting events of the English.” He cites one which he applies to Henry I, king of England. It is wholly to the glory of the man who is its object—assuming that the alleged prophet had any fixed object in his visions.

The *History of Louis the Fat* was first published in a folio collection of historians of France, printed in 1596 at Frankfurt by the heirs of Andreas Wechel. André Duchesne republished this work in a much more corrected form, from various manuscripts, in the fourth volume of his great collection of writers who dealt with our history.

Besides this full-length life of the French monarch, our author had composed his legend, divided into three lessons, to be read each year at the night office on the day of the king’s anniversary. It was published through the care of Dom Martène in the preface to the fourth volume of his great Collection.

Thirdly, Suger is the author of a book containing the details of his abbacy’s administration. Duchesne, the first editor of this work, doubts that it is by our abbot because, in the Saint-Denis manuscript by which he guided his edition, it bears the name of William, author of the *Life of Suger*. But Suger speaks there in his own name on every page; moreover, despite what the editor says, it is easy to recognize his style. In 1144, the twenty-third year of his administration, he was induced to undertake this work, not on his own initiative, he says, but by the prayers of his monks. One day when they were assembled in chapter, they urgently pressed him to put in writing what he had done for the good of the abbey: whether by new acquisitions; by recovering alienated property; by improving possessions enjoyed by the monastery; or by construction, decoration, and furnishings of the church. They gave two reasons for their request:

1. The memory of his benefactions would lead those coming after them to pray fervently for the repose of his soul.

2. His example would inspire his successor abbots to emulate him in making divine worship flourish.

This book may be divided into two parts. The first includes what he had done in the religious establishments, lands, and dependencies of the monastery; the second is entirely devoted to an account of the rebuilding and embellishment of the church. The following seemed to us the most remarkable matters in both parts.

Speaking of the French Vexin, situated between the rivers Oise and Epte, the author says that ancient records establish it to be a fief held from Saint-Denis; and that King Louis the Fat, who had acquired it, when about to go to war against the emperor, came to the abbey chapter and there declared that he held this fief from Saint-Denis and that, in his capacity as the abbey’s standard-bearer—a rank attached to this fief—he would be bound to render homage for it, if royal dignity did not exempt him: “In the full chapter of Blessed Dionysius, he professed that he held it from him and, by right of standard-bearer, would owe him homage if he were not king.”

Thus our kings already believed themselves [Note: [Col. 1185] A learned man says (*Abridged Chronology of the History of France*, year 1100) that, when Philip I acquired in 1061 the viscounty of Bourges, part of which was held from the county of Sancerre, this prince caused the count of Sancerre to render homage for what depended on his fief. We have carefully sought proof of this fact without being able to discover it. A person who has worked for several years on the history of Berry has assured us that he has likewise been unable to find it.

[Col. 1186] The same is true of the charter of investiture alleged to have been granted to Fulk, count of Anjou, by Louis the Fat, a charter in which, it is said, liege homage first becomes known (*ibid.*, year 1135, etc.). This document is wholly unknown to persons who claim to have carefully studied the monuments concerning Anjou. We regret that the author’s plan does not permit him to cite it.] exempt, by the right of their crown, from homage for fiefs which they held from their vassals. It is true that M. Brussel [Note: [Col. 1186] *New Treatise on Fiefs*, p. 152.] reports two documents, one from 1185 and the other from 1193, which show that Philip Augustus had himself dispensed by the Church of Amiens and that of Thérouanne from the homage which he owed the former for the city and county of Amiens, and the latter for the fief of Hesdin, on condition that these two Churches should be exempt toward him from the right of provision or lodging. But it does not appear that Louis the Fat gave any compensation to the abbey of Saint-Denis for the homage of the French Vexin.

Advocacies, in their original institution, were intended for the defense of Churches. But when they were made hereditary fiefs toward the end of the second dynasty of our kings, they became, through the tyranny of those invested with them, the scourge of the very Churches they had been intended to protect. The advowson of the land of Toury had always been attached to the lordship of La Ferté-Baudouin, and until Suger’s time it had always greatly harassed the provost and inhabitants of Toury.

“It happened,” he says, “that this advocacy came by inheritance to the daughter of Adam of Pithiviers. When we learned this, we sought, on our friends’ advice, to marry her according to our own wishes, whatever it might cost us. Therefore, wishing to secure [Col. 1187] this land and deliver it from the oppression of its advocates, we gave a young man from our household as husband to the young woman, with one hundred pounds of silver, both for her dowry and for her father and mother. We further gave thirty pounds of silver to King Louis [the Fat], from whom this advocacy was held, and by this means, with that prince’s consent, obtained that both the newly married couple and their successors should render to us and to those who should come after us homage, feudal service, and justice whenever summoned; and that if they should fail in this, we should be permitted to seize the fief of the said advocacy until they had given us full and complete satisfaction.”

It was in 1140 that Suger began building his church. The old one had two defects:

1. It was too narrow for the crowds who gathered there on the great feast-days; so much so, says Suger, that, in order to reach the relics of the holy martyrs, women walked over men’s heads [Note: [Col. 1187] Doubtless by means of a wooden gallery erected on those days.].

2. In several places it threatened ruin.

Moreover, the low portal, opened by a single door, was obscured by a kind of portico which Charlemagne had caused to be built over the tomb of King Pepin, buried, by his express wish, outside the church in expiation, he said, for the excesses of his father Charles Martel. Suger demolished this monument with the court’s permission, had Pepin’s tomb transferred elsewhere, and built a new portal opened by three doors and flanked by two large towers, equally suitable as an ornament in peace and a defense in war. The door-leaves were made of gilded bronze with bas-reliefs representing various mysteries, and Suger himself at the feet of Jesus Christ, with this distich addressed to him:

> Receive the prayers of your Suger, strict Judge;  
> In your mercy, let me be counted among your own sheep.

From there he proceeded to the east end of the church, which he rebuilt from the foundations together with the crossing, and finished with the nave, completed in 1144. The king laid the building’s first stone, and several prelates considered it an honor to lay others after him. We shall not enumerate the ornaments with which Suger enriched the new church: such as a gold altarpiece weighing forty-two marks, adorned with precious stones and placed on the altar of Saint Denis; three tables of the same material surrounding the high altar; a gold crucifix weighing eighty marks, made by seven goldsmiths whom Suger had brought from Lorraine; and an infinity of other riches [Note: [Col. 1187]

Among these riches, Suger mentions a chair of King Dagobert, on which, he says, the kings of France, according to an ancient tradition, used to sit at their accession to the crown in order to receive the homage of the great men of the kingdom. It was greatly damaged in Suger’s time, and he had it repaired both because of the work’s value and in consideration of the noble function it had served. This chair of Dagobert is probably not the one shown today at Saint-Denis.

It is said (*ibid.*) that he had the eagle in the middle of the choir regilded. This proves the antiquity [Col. 1188] of such lecterns.

He further tells us (*ibid.*) that in his time Saint-Denis possessed a kind of diptych, or ivory tablets, on which ancient secular stories were represented. He used them, he says, to adorn a gallery.]

, some of which came from the liberality of kings, princes, and prelates, whom Suger took care to name. On most of these works he had verses of his own composition engraved. He also had verses placed on the stained-glass windows [Note: [Col. 1187] One of these windows represented the Apostle Saint Paul turning the millstone, and prophets bringing sacks of wheat to the mill, with these verses providing the key to the allegory:

> By your working, Paul, you take flour from bran as you turn the millstone;  
> You make known the inner meaning of the Mosaic Law.  
> From so many grains comes the true bread, without bran,  
> Our perpetual and angelic food.] to explain the histories or allegories represented in them.

This magnificent edifice, in which painters, sculptors, metal-casters, and architects had exhausted all their skill, and which was admired in the twelfth century, nevertheless endured for no more than one hundred and twenty years. Eudes Clément, abbot of Saint-Denis about the middle of the thirteenth century, undertook a new church upon the ruins of Suger's, and his successor Matthew of Vendôme gave it its finishing touch. All that was allowed to remain of our abbot’s work was the portal and part of the circuit of chapels around the east end. Even today, in the stained-glass window of the central chapel, one sees a representation of the First Crusade in ten panels, with Suger’s image below. Dom Montfaucon provided an explanation of these ten panels in the first volume of his *Monuments of the French Monarchy* (p. 84).

Since Duchesne, this book has reappeared among the documentary proofs of the *History of Saint-Denis* published by Dom Félibien.

Suger, not satisfied with the detail into which he had entered concerning his church in the work just discussed, wished to compose a separate book on the dedication of this monument. After a long, very edifying preface, he says that, knowing of no fine quarry in his vicinity, he had at first thought of bringing marble columns from Rome to adorn his church. But while he was turning this plan over in his mind, he was informed that at Pontoise one of the finest quarries ever seen had been discovered. Once excavation had begun in this quarry, the inhabitants of the district and neighboring places came in crowds to offer their services in extracting the stones, applying themselves to the work with extraordinary zeal and success. In this connection he relates several miracles which testified to how pleasing this good work was to God.

We cannot follow our author in his description of the ceremonies observed at the dedication of his church and at the translation of the relics of the holy martyrs. Let it suffice to say that Louis the Young and the queen his wife attended, along with seventeen prelates, a great number of abbots and clerics, and an immense multitude of people. This writing is mutilated in Duchesne’s edition; but what is missing is supplied by Dom Mabillon in the first volume of his *Analecta* (p. 218). Dom Félibien reprinted it from the editions of these two editors in the proofs of his *History of Saint-Denis*.

Suger’s other writings are various charters, of which it is fitting to note the principal ones.

In 1125, the inhabitants of Saint-Denis came to our abbot to ask to be freed from mortmain. Suger granted them this favor all the more willingly because, [Col. 1189] he says, he recognized the defect of this servitude at its origin, since it had been established by his predecessor Abbot Yves without authorization from any title. Moreover, Suger was disposed to favor these inhabitants in recognition of a sum of two hundred pounds which they had given him to restore the entrance to his monastery. He likewise exempts from the same servitude all those dwelling within the territory of Saint-Denis; and “when the said burgesses,” he says, “marry their children outside it, should these children die without heirs begotten of their bodies, their inheritance shall return to their relatives settled at Saint-Denis, even though they may have other, closer relatives settled outside the town and territory of Saint-Denis.” The act, drawn up by Gregory, Suger’s chancellor, was sealed with the king’s seal and that of the abbot, and signed by Prior Gausbert, Christian the treasurer, Vivien the cantor, and several others.

By another charter or constitution, of approximately the same period, he established:

1. That forever, every Thursday and Saturday of the year, commemoration should be made of the Blessed Virgin;

2. That during his lifetime Psalm *Ad te levavi* (“To you I have lifted up [my soul]”) should be sung for him;

3. That after the death of King Louis the Fat, the anniversary of that prince should be observed forever.

Fear of the judgments of God, uncertainty concerning his last hour, and awareness of his own weakness led our abbot, in the year 1137, to make his will. For this purpose he assembled his brethren in chapter on 16 June; and, having prostrated himself at their feet, he begged them to grant him, for every day of his life, a Mass of the Holy Spirit, and after his death a perpetual anniversary observance. On that anniversary he wishes the ornaments, gold, silver, and precious stones which he had acquired for the church to be displayed publicly; and this, he says, not from any motive of ostentation, but for the same reasons which had led him to set down in writing what he had done during his administration. He further directs that the *chevecier* provide the brethren with two extraordinary portions: *Non qualescunque, sed plenarias et aptas*—“not of whatever sort, but full and suitable”—with *piment*, *pigmentum*, that is, a kind of hippocras. Nor are the poor forgotten. Suger assigns them, for that same day, two muids of wheat and two muids of wine. This will, printed by Duchesne and Dom Félibien, is signed by all the officers of the monastery, by two former abbots, by eight priest-monks, ten deacons, ten subdeacons, and ten boys, *pueri*—that is, young religious not yet in orders; after these follow the names of seven bishops, and of Robert, abbot of Corbie and pupil of Suger. [Note: [Col. 1189] It is noteworthy that all these witnesses did not subscribe at the same time. The proof lies in the signature of Samson, archbishop of Reims, who did not ascend that see until 1140 (*Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. X, p. 84). A disciple of Fr. Germon will infer from this that the act is forged. But there are a thousand examples [Col. 1190] to confound his ignorance and destroy his rash inference.] By this same act our abbot had founded his anniversary observance in the church of Saint-Paul, a collegiate church within the enclosure of Saint-Denis. In the following year he issued another charter, by which he granted several estates and various immunities to that church, on condition that the canons should come to pray before the body of every religious newly deceased, before his burial, and should celebrate a Mass for the repose of his soul.

Albert, count of Morspech in Germany, had long lain under anathema when Suger became abbot, because he had seized certain estates of the abbey located near his own lands. Moved by repentance, he came to Saint-Denis to ask absolution. Suger granted it upon the condition that he should pay every year, to him and to his successors in perpetuity, five ounces of gold. At the end of the act in which this is stated, Suger declares irreversibly excommunicated those who fail to fulfil this obligation.

It appears that Albert did not remain faithful to it; for after his death Mainard, his son-in-law and successor in the county of Morspech, had to seek both his own absolution and that of his father-in-law, for the unjust possession of the same estates just mentioned. This is learned from an act executed in 1125 between him and Suger in the city of Mainz, after the diet held there for the election of Emperor Lothair. [Note: [Col. 1190] Dom Gervaise (*Life of Suger*, vol. II, p. 296) built upon this journey a story drawn wholly from his imagination.] History does not state on what occasion Suger went to this assembly. But it is highly probable that he came as ambassador of France and in the interests of the nation. Be that as it may, it is certain from the names of those who subscribed the charter on his side that he came there in great state. There appear his chaplain; a clerk named Peter, his brother; Ansolde, his cup-bearer; and several knights, among them one named Suger. If this man, as is claimed, was related to our abbot, one asks whence his nobility could have come. Dom Gervaise learnedly decides that the king ennobled him in consideration of the services of the abbot of Saint-Denis, as though there were proof that ennoblements went back to the reign of Louis the Fat. To return to the subject of the charter before us: Count Mainard surrendered to the abbey the land of Celle-Neuve which he possessed in the territory of Metz, in exchange for the estates which the count, his father-in-law, had taken from it. Thereupon Suger absolved him and his predecessors from the excommunication which they had incurred, and did so in the presence of the archbishop of Mainz and the cardinal-legate Gerard: *In praesentia domni Adalberti Moguntini archiepiscopi, et Girardi venerabilis cardinalis et sanctae Romanae Ecclesiae legati*—“In the presence of Lord Adalbert, archbishop of Mainz, and Gerard, venerable cardinal and legate of the Holy Roman Church.” One may be surprised at the authority with which a mere abbot binds and looses persons who are not under his jurisdiction, before the very eyes of their own pastor and of a legate of the Holy See. But it must be observed that Suger, as he himself says in the book of his Administration, had repeatedly appealed to the pope for justice against the counts of Morspech; and doubtless His Holiness had entrusted his powers to him in order to proceed against these usurpers.

Dom Félibien reports a constitution of Suger by which he increased the revenues assigned to the maintenance of the community, and especially to the needs of the sick. To understand this document, one must know that, from the ninth century onwards, the *manse* of the abbots of Saint-Denis had been separated from that of the religious. We possess two acts concerning this division: the first, which did not take effect, made under Abbot Hilduin in 832; the second, made thirty years later under Abbot Louis, kinsman of King Charles the Bald, who confirmed it by his authority. [Note: [Col. 1190] Félibien, *History of Saint-Denis*, preliminaries, nos. LXXII and XCIII.] The quantity of provisions which the abbots bound themselves by these agreements to furnish the religious for their food would be astonishing if compared with the measures of our own day. What, for example, should one say of the clause according to which, if the vineyards ceded to the religious did not yield two thousand five hundred muids of wine, the abbot was to supply the remainder? Yet it is certain that the muid of that time was much smaller than ours, and we do not know its exact measure. Thus the [Col. 1191] declamations made by Dom Gervaise on this point and on others like it [Note: [Col. 1191] Who would not be indignant at the following unfaithfulness of the same author? In an agreement which Abbot Louis made in the ninth century with his religious (Félibien, *History of Saint-Denis*, preliminaries, p. LXX), he undertakes to give them five fat pigs, eleven hundred eggs, and poultry for the feasts of Easter and Christmas: *Tres siquidem porci et mille ac centum ova per tres festivitates . . . item alii duo porci per duas festivitates, ad volatilia eorum praeparanda*—“namely, three pigs and eleven hundred eggs for three feasts . . . likewise two other pigs for two feasts, for preparing their poultry.” Dom Gervaise, transforming the eggs into oxen, says that the monks, although bound to abstain from meat, demanded eleven hundred oxen, proportionately fat pigs, and an almost infinite quantity of poultry. The quantity of this poultry is not specified in the act. Moreover, poultry was formerly permitted on certain days in the best-regulated monasteries of the order, as was the pork fat called *oleum lardinum*, “lard oil.”] prove only a blind passion for slander, the excess of which had deprived him of reflection.

Besides these writings, Suger began the Life of Louis the Younger, which death prevented him from completing. [Note: [Col. 1191] William, *Life of Suger*, p. 195.] *Regis Ludovici splendido sermone gesta descripsit, ejusque filii itidem Ludovici scribere quidem coepit; sed morte praeventus perficere non potuit*—“He described in splendid style the deeds of King Louis, and likewise began to write those of his son Louis; but, overtaken by death, he was unable to complete the work.” But does this work still exist? We do not venture to affirm it. In Duchesne’s collection there are indeed two histories of this prince, composed by contemporary authors: the first under the title *Gesta Ludovici VII, qui Junior dicitur* (“Deeds of Louis VII, who is called the Younger”); the second under that of *Historia gloriosissimi regis Ludovici filii Ludovici Grossi* (“History of the Most Glorious King Louis, Son of Louis the Fat”). Both declare from the outset that they are continuations of the history of France from Louis the Fat onward. Nevertheless, there is reason to doubt not only that both came from Suger's pen, as a learned academician maintains, [Note: [Col. 1191] *Memoirs of the Academy of Inscriptions*, vol. XV, p. 580.] but that either belongs to him, wholly or in part. Here are our reasons, submitted to the judgment of our readers.

We ground the first doubt upon two striking differences observable between the two writings. The author of the *Deeds* gives Saint Bernard the title of saint, which the author of the *History* does not give him, and which he did not in fact possess until his canonization in 1174. Moreover, the former places Louis the Younger's departure on crusade in 1146, while the latter places it a year later. It is unusual for one and the same writer to contradict himself in this way.

The second doubt rests on the following considerations. The book of the *Deeds* begins with the reign of Louis the Younger and continues to the second marriage contracted by that prince in 1152—after Suger's death—with Constance of Castile. The editor adds that it went further still, but that the remainder was lacking in the manuscript which guided him. Indeed, it must have gone as far as the hero's death, since this is announced in the second sentence, which says that he is buried in the church of Barbeaux: *Qui abbatiam de Sacro Portu quae nunc Barbehel dicitur, in pago Meledunensi juxta littus Sequanae fundavit, ubi mausoleo mirifici operis feliciter requiescit*—“He founded the abbey of the Sacred Port, now called Barbehel, in the district of Melun beside the bank of the Seine, where he happily rests in a mausoleum of marvelous workmanship.” These words show that neither the beginning nor the end of this book can be Suger's. With regard to the *History of Louis the Younger*, we observe first that it is very concise down to this monarch’s divorce from Queen Eleanor. The principal events occurring during that interval are scarcely touched upon, whereas those following it, down to 1165, where the work ends, are treated more carefully. Further, Suger—the soul of the affairs of state under this reign—is not named a single time, though in the *Life of Louis the Fat* he had omitted almost no occasion to speak of himself. [Note: [Col. 1191] Bouquet, *Writers of France*, vol. III, p. 146.]

Is it not natural to conclude from these observations that the two writings under examination are equally foreign to our author? Yet it may be presumed that both issued from the abbey of Saint-Denis: first, because, as already observed, they are presented as continuations of Suger's work on Louis the Fat; secondly, because from time immemorial there had been religious at Saint-Denis charged with writing the history of our kings. This institution is wrongly credited to our author. [Note: [Col. 1191] Before Duchesne, the *Deeds* had already been [Col. 1192] printed in Pithou’s collection, though rather inaccurately. They are also incorporated in the Chronicles of Saint-Denis and translated fairly literally. “The compiler,” says M. de Sainte-Palaye (*Memoirs of the Academy of Inscriptions*, vol. XV, p. 571), “followed this work so exactly that he says nothing of the life of Louis VII beyond what is reported in the *Deeds*, and leaves a gap of twenty-four years in his Chronicle, until the reign of Philip Augustus, son and successor of that prince, where he resumes the course of the general history of the kingdom from a new historian.” With regard to the *History of Louis VII*, Duchesne likewise was not the first to publish it. Since the continuator of Aimoin incorporated it into his work, it appeared in all the editions thereof; the best is that issued at Paris in 1602 by Du Breuil. Yet it must be admitted that this piece is neither as full nor as correct there as in Duchesne’s edition.] It is certain that it goes much farther back. We have proof in an old manuscript, brought to notice by Lambecius [Note: [Col. 1192] *Bibliotheca Caesarea*, I, p. 957.] and overlooked in Father Le Long’s researches. In it appears the history of our kings in the vernacular language down to the reign of Charles the Bald. The preface begins in these terms: “He who begins this work sends greeting in Our Lord to all who shall read this history. Because many people doubted the genealogy of the kings of France, etc.” Shortly afterwards it is added that this history is drawn chiefly from the ancient annals of the abbey of Saint-Denis; and at the end of the history of Charles the Bald one reads: “Here end the deeds of Charles the Bald; and afterwards the chapters of King Louis the Stammerer, his son, and of the other kings thereafter, as far as the great King Louis, ought to begin.” Lambecius infers from this that the historical work consisted of several volumes. But it follows even more plainly that the abbey of Saint-Denis, long before Suger, possessed the practice of writing the history of our kings.

[Col. 1193]

# LIFE OF SUGER, ABBOT, BY WILLIAM, MONK OF SAINT-DENIS, HIS DISCIPLE

(Dom Félibien, *History of the Royal Abbey of Saint-Denis in France*. Paris, 1709, folio. Proofs, p. CXCIV.)

[Col. 1193A] WILLIAM TO HIS GAUFREDUS, HIS OWN.

Since, while you were present, no time seemed free to me for writing, immediately after your departure, mindful of your prayers and of my promise, I took up the pen and set about, as I could, to write something concerning our Suger which might be pleasing to you and useful to many. For as often as I contemplate with myself the virtues of that venerable man, so often I recall his words and deeds. He seems to me surely to have been set forth as an example, so that posterity to come may draw from both his words and his works a pattern of life. Since for some time I shared his life with you and observed his secrets, I greatly fear that I may deservedly be charged with ingratitude if I do not celebrate, in such words as I can, those things which came to my knowledge—especially since, beyond my deserts, I enjoyed [Col. 1194A] his favor and experienced his benefits. Although such is the nature of virtues that they cannot remain hidden, even if envy should impose silence upon all who know of them; nor is their remaining hidden any loss to them. For there will come, yes, there will come a day that shall bring into the light those good things concealed and suppressed by the malice of the age.

One thing, therefore, I must obtain from you: do not expect me to follow any fixed order in the things I shall recall concerning him. I have resolved to write, as they may occur to me, a few things out of many, scarcely any out of innumerable things. You yourself know everything better, and these matters ought rather to have been written by you. But because you so wish, because you command it, I shall do what I can, since I judge that nothing ought to be refused you.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 1193]

[Col. 1193B] I. This man therefore appears to have been divinely directed for the purpose not merely of enlightening the one place over which he presided, but the whole empire of the Franks; raised to this end, not that he alone might advance one order of monks, but that he might singularly promote every order of the Church. One gladly wonders of this man that nature placed in so small a body a spirit so fair and so great—unless it intended plainly, through him, to show that beneath any skin a most beautiful soul may lie concealed and that virtue may arise in any place; and that we might know that the soul is not weakened by the shortness of the body, but the body is adorned by the strength of the soul.

But because I know that a false opinion concerning him has become established in the hearts of some, it must be understood that, absent and far away, he was called to government, suspecting nothing of the kind, and that he came unwillingly. Nor was he able to resist, or to pass his life in obscurity, since the vigor of his intellect and learning, or the distinguished friendships of great men—or rather, above all these, the divine dispensation which had prepared this vessel of its Church for honor—had already brought him forth into public view. For such renown had seized upon him that, even if he had been concealed in the uttermost place, his former uprightness would nonetheless have revealed him, and the virtues in which he had been trained from childhood would have made him known. Such a light shone around him because of his early and unblemished counsels that, even if he had wished to possess darkness, he could not. All marvelled at a mind in him that was restrained and elevated, that trampled underfoot all worldly pride and laughed at everything which the multitude is accustomed either to fear or desire: established indeed in the world, yet by the better part of himself aspiring to heavenly things.

II. When he presided over the monastery, he presided also over the palace; and so he administered both offices that neither did the court prevent him from caring for the cloister, nor did the monastery excuse him from the counsels of princes. Because of his splendid and upright counsels, the prince revered him as a father and feared him as a tutor. Bishops rose when he arrived, and among them he sat first. For whenever bishops had assembled at the summons of urgent affairs of the kingdom, and the prince consulted them, they unanimously compelled this man, because of his tried and proven prudence, to give one answer for all. They dared add nothing to his words, as Job testifies of himself (chapter 29), “when his speech distilled upon them.” Through him the cry of the orphan and the cause of the widow reached the prince; he always intervened for these, and sometimes even commanded. Who, when oppressed and suffering wrong, did not have him as advocate, provided only that his cause was just? When he pronounced judgments, he never departed from what was right for any price; he regarded no person in judgment, loved no gifts, and followed no rewards. Who would not admire in him such a spirit: untouched by desires, humble amid prosperity, calm amid the tempests of the world, undaunted by dangers? He was indeed greater than one would believe could be suited to so small a body.

III. But because rivals reproach an illustrious man with the lowliness of his birth, they—blind and dull—do not consider that it belongs more to his praise and glory to have made his own people noble than to have been born of nobles. Plato also says that no king is not descended from the lowly, and no man of royal descent is not lowly. The long succession of time has mixed all these things and fortune has turned them upside down. The soul makes men noble; and his soul was plainly such that the man who wrote the following is believed not without reason to have described him:

> A soul beholding truths, skilled in what must be avoided and sought, assigning values to things not from opinion but from nature, entering into the whole world and casting its contemplation upon all its actions; most beautiful in its dignity, sound and vigorous in strength, untroubled and fearless: one whom no force could break, whom chance could neither lift up nor cast down.

This was indeed his soul. How often did that sincere and pure man attempt to leave both the court and every administration, that he might withdraw to greater things! But his fortune, which had raised him on high, did not permit it, nor did it allow him to grow old within the station of his birth—though, as he confessed, he would have preferred this to have happened to him.

IV. Although the chief business of the realm rested upon him, neither public nor private occupation ever drew him away from divine worship. Whether he attended the assembly of the brethren or celebrated the divine office with his household, he did not, as some customarily do, listen silently while others chanted psalms; rather, he himself was always most ready to chant or read. What I often marvelled at in him was that he retained in memory whatever he had learned in youth so thoroughly that no one could equal him in the whole monastic office. You would have thought that he knew nothing else, had learned nothing beyond these things—though he was so accomplished in the liberal studies that he sometimes argued with great subtlety from books of dialectic or rhetoric, to say nothing of sacred matters, in which he had grown old. He was so full of the reading of Holy Scripture that, wherever he might have been questioned, he had a suitable answer ready without delay. Because of his tenacious memory, however, he was quite unable to forget the poets of the gentiles; he would often recite to us from memory twenty, and sometimes even thirty, Horatian verses containing something useful. Thus, through a penetrating intellect and happy memory, whatever he had once grasped could never afterwards escape him.

V. Why should I recount what all know: namely, that he shone forth as the foremost orator of his times? For in truth, according to the saying of Marcus Cato, he was “a good man skilled in speaking.” He possessed such charm of eloquence in both tongues—his native tongue and Latin—that whatever you heard from his mouth, you would believe not that he was speaking, but that you were reading. His knowledge of histories was so complete that, whichever king or prince of the Franks you named to him, he would immediately run through his deeds with unfailing speed. He himself described in splendid style the deeds of King Louis, and likewise began to write those of his son Louis; but, overtaken by death, he did not bring the work to its end. For who could have known those matters better, or written them more faithfully, than one who had been most intimate with both kings and from whom no secret was hidden? Without him the kings entered into no counsel; in his absence the palace seemed deserted. From the time when he was first admitted to the royal councils to the end of his life, the realm is known always to have flourished and advanced for the better and more widely: its boundaries enlarged and its enemies subdued. When he was taken from their midst, the sceptre of the realm immediately felt a grievous loss through his absence, being known to have been mutilated by the loss of no small part of itself—namely, the duchy of Aquitaine—through want of counsel.

VI. Among his other virtues, this excellent man had especially this: if any one of his dependants was ever accused before him, he did not immediately lend an ear, but, being most prudent, held accusers suspect. He judged it unworthy to seek vengeance upon anyone before careful inquiry had fully established the matter; and he punished offenders not so much because they had sinned as lest they should sin. In exacting punishment, moreover, he showed himself such that no sensible person could doubt that he was compassionate and unwilling to exact it. He rebuked as a shepherd and was indulgent as a father. He did not readily remove his officials from their administrations unless there were definite and serious grounds and manifest faults. For he said that nothing was less advantageous to the commonwealth, since those who are removed take away what they can, while their replacements, fearing the same fate, hasten to plunder.

VII. Yet many, either ignorant or envious, who knew him less well, attempted to distort the excellent character of the man by hostile interpretation. Because, according to Solomon, his words were “as goads, and like nails driven deep” (Ecclesiastes 12), and likewise, like blessed Job, “the light of his countenance did not fall to the ground” (Job 29), they judged him too harsh and rigid, attributing to savagery what belonged to constancy. But to those who came nearer and were more closely joined to him, he appeared quite otherwise. Although he was very humane and pleasant with his intimate associates, cheerfulness never made him lax, just as sorrow never overwhelmed him. His practice was that of good parents, who are accustomed sometimes to rebuke their children gently, at other times threateningly, and sometimes even to correct them with blows. He disinherited no one for a first offence unless many and grave crimes were present, unless what he feared would happen outweighed what he punished; nor did he ever proceed to inflict penalties until he had exhausted remedies. Thus this prudent man administered mildly and beneficially the right entrusted to him, so that his name is celebrated today not only in Gaul but among foreign nations as well.

VIII. For which Christian king, having heard of his greatness of spirit, did not marvel, or desire to enjoy his conversation and be instructed by his counsel? Did not Roger, the most renowned king of Sicily, send him humble, supplicatory letters and gifts? Did he not, after learning of Suger's pious desire to make a pilgrimage, prepare to meet him? Did not Henry, the most powerful king of England, glory in this man’s friendship and rejoice in his intimacy? Did he not appoint him mediator and bond of peace with Louis, king of the Franks? Whenever he came to him concerning the peace of the two kingdoms, the king, contrary to his own custom, met him outside the palace and hastened into his embrace, preferring his conversation to any riches whatever. David also, the pious king of the Scots, sent him gifts together with friendly letters—namely, the teeth of a sea-creature, of remarkable size and no small value. I saw—God is my witness, I saw—the king of the Franks once standing reverently beside him while he sat upon a low footstool, with a circle of magnates surrounding them; Suger gave directions as though to inferiors, while they hung with every care and attention upon what was said. When the conversation had ended and Suger wished to escort the king, the king would not permit him to move from his place or rise from his chair. I have said these things so that rivals may know and detractors may hear what standing he held with kings and how great was the respect paid him by magnates.

IX. The religious Count Theobald of Blois honored him in every way and put him forward as his sole advocate before the kings of the Franks. How often did Geoffrey, count of Anjou and duke of the Normans, send him messengers who flattered and begged alike; how often did he write him humble letters in his own hand! Though Geoffrey was keen of intellect, fierce and exceedingly powerful in spirit, he often placed Suger’s name before his own. Thus both dukes named above, being the most powerful men of their time, gave this man thanks for their peace and especially ascribed to him the harmony of their realms. And indeed, I do not know whether this reading is more fittingly applicable to any of the Fathers of former times: “And in the time of wrath he became an author of reconciliation.”

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 1197]

[Col. 1197B] I. Perhaps I already seem to have written more about the venerable man than his rivals would wish; nor are there lacking persons to whom these things, though entirely true, cause disgust. I foresaw that this too would happen, but I shall not be content with them. For I shall most gladly add more, because I am with difficulty torn away from his memory: so that those who did not know him may, if possible, know him wholly; and those who did know him may know him again. For I know that whatever I attempt in his praise will be most welcome to very many. Not that I could know all his deeds and excellent virtues—nor could any of those who clung to him long before me, of whom today very few seem to survive. His head was already white with age when he deemed me worthy of sharing in his exalted companionship. Why should I not return thanks to him according to my ability? Why should I not always rise in honor of so great a name? He admitted into his intimate household a man who was a stranger, a newcomer, and utterly unworthy; and often received me at his table. From this one may sufficiently perceive that with him there was no respect of persons.

II. Because this glorious man was often compelled to be absent from the monastery for public interests, whether of the kingdom or of the Church, he appointed from among the brethren men of proven character and inflamed with divine zeal, to take the absent man’s place in the flock entrusted to him, by teaching and example. In promoting them he regarded neither birth nor country; but those whose life he had tested, these he promoted. This may be inferred from the fact that he set Hervé—a man of great holiness and remarkable simplicity, though not highly learned—over the congregation of brethren, knowing well that knowledge often puffs up, but charity always builds up.

III. Whether he was at home or abroad, one saw crowds of every rank and religious order hastening to him. Some of them received assistance for their bodies, others for their souls. None left him sorrowful; none empty-handed. Remote as well as nearby monasteries testify how lavish he was toward the poor and how merciful toward the sick. No one could adequately recount how liberal he was to all—to strangers and to his own people. Is not that remarkable work in glass in the church of Paris a plain indication of his extraordinary generosity? It is one example, but not the only one. For many works of this kind remain, which in many places he performed not so much from obligation as from generosity. Who ever approached him to request something just and did not leave him more cheerful? Either he fulfilled the petitioners’ wishes by aid, or appropriately soothed them with better hope; for he judged it most beautiful to grant everything and demand nothing.

IV. Although he was called, and was, shepherd of only one monastery, he bore continual concern and no small care for all the churches established anywhere throughout the kingdom: governing some by counsel, assisting others with the means of life. Above all, he took care that religion should nowhere appear to have grown lukewarm. To those in need he supplied provisions; for others he built workshops. It was a most beautiful spectacle in the sight of angels and men, when all leaned upon one man as upon a most firm pillar, and all drew from him as from a most abundant fountain. All knew him to be both for them and above them, and knew that his concern watched daily for the salvation of each and all.

V. Good Jesus, how great was his vigor, how great his spirit! At his advance tyrants fled, the sons of darkness hid themselves, and the sons of light and sons of day flocked eagerly to him. When the realm was disturbed and wars arose, as they commonly do, he was the chief seeker of concord and the most vigorous restorer of peace. In spirit he was Caesar; in speech, Cicero. He tamed rebels and conquered the obstinate. Of this man one might rightly say:

> While he was safe, all had one mind.  
> When he was lost, they broke faith.

And, to speak something boldly but truly, his prudence and courage were so great that I do not think the whole world could have sufficed for his government. I am mistaken if his purpose and aspirations do not bear witness to this assertion of mine: things which, as he had begun them, he would have completed in deed, had death, jealous of his prosperous actions, not thwarted him. For what the two most powerful kings, namely of the Franks and Romans, were unable—by what judgment of God I know not—to accomplish with their armies united and forces gathered from the whole West, this man, supported by divine help and by the exceptional intellect in which he excelled, had already vigorously undertaken to supply, as the following narrative will show.
