But I fear that the majesty of these matters would be wronged if they were described with so rustic and slender a pen. Meanwhile, however, we shall add some things concerning his manner of life and character, although it is certain that his daily life, and almost every one of his words, deserves commemoration.

VI. He had indeed been allotted a short and slight body, and continual labor had greatly diminished his strength. Yet moderation in food, restraint in foods that provoke the appetite, and careful watchfulness over himself carried him, with God’s help, into old age. His food was neither too cheap nor too refined. He never complained about its quality or its manner of preparation. Of everything placed before him, he tasted a small amount; the rest he sent to the poor, without whom I never saw him take refreshment. He never ate meat unless bodily illness compelled him and the persuasion of friends constrained him. He did not taste wine unless he had first mixed in a very generous quantity of water. In summer, moreover, he more frequently drank pure water. Though he possessed many kinds of grace, he lacked only this gift: after assuming government, he never appeared stouter than he had been as a private man—whereas nearly all others, however lean they may have been before, are accustomed, immediately after the laying on of hands, to grow fat in cheeks and belly, not to say in heart.

At every season, summer or winter, because he was content with very little sleep, after supper he either read, listened for a long time to someone reading, or instructed those seated with him by illustrious examples. The reading came from authoritative books of the Fathers; sometimes something was read from ecclesiastical histories. Being most pleasant in conversation, he recounted now his own deeds, now those of other brave men, which he had either seen or learned, sometimes until midnight. Then he rested a little in a bed which was neither excessively rough nor overly luxurious. He took the greatest care to avoid appearing to do anything notable in dress or manner of life. For he considered pretence unworthy of a good man, and judged it less honorable, as the Stoic says, to pursue ambition by a crooked path.

VII. Awaking from sleep after his rest, once he had celebrated the customary office of Matins, he hurried every day at first light to the church. There, before approaching the altar, he humbly cast himself down beside the tombs of the martyrs; offering his whole self to God in prayer, he moistened the pavement beneath him with tears. Thus the venerable priest proceeded, as devoutly as solemnly, to offer the saving sacrifices. But at the hour of the most holy sacrifice, who could worthily recount with what contrition he was kindled, with what abundance of tears and groans he was accustomed to pour himself forth, as one truly having God present? [Col. 1200B] At the Nativity of the Savior, the Resurrection, and the other chief solemnities, he was wonderfully festive in devotion and devout in festivity—swift of utterance, devout in heart. So completely did he allow no worldly business to enter into him, nor, so far as lay in his power, admit any mention of sad matters; for he maintained that the day ought to be passed joyfully and wholly spent in God’s praises. On those days, if, as often happens, the coming night found him most solemnly intent upon the evening praises, he said that it made no difference whether the divine praise were completed by night or by day, since both night and day belonged to Him—provided only that, contrary to custom, the solemn celebration should not appear diminished in any respect. He, as he had read in Scripture, “stationed the singers [Col. 1200C] opposite the altar, made sweet melodies in their sound, bestowed splendor upon the celebrations, and adorned the seasons until life’s end” (Ecclus. 47).

VIII. Toward sick brethren he was disposed no differently than if he had physically begotten each one whom he had spiritually begotten in Christ Jesus. For their care he himself provided physicians at no small expense, and, to put it briefly, by his own exertions he left their annual revenues doubled. Of this fact there are witnesses; and among them am I, the least of the brethren, more beholden than the rest to his kindness. For no one experienced his compassion more abundantly or more lavishly. I do not therefore recount all these things in sequence, lest I seem either vainly to boast of the favor of so great [Col. 1200D] a man, or lest a rough and lengthy discourse bring weariness to its hearers. May the Lord repay him on my behalf and graciously regard his works of mercy. Yet the Lord must be believed already to have rewarded His servant and cleansed his sins, since He has exalted his horn forever and enlarged his glory.

IX. Among the other things which he carried out nobly and vigorously, he summoned craftsmen of every kind from all parts of the kingdom: masons, carpenters, painters, smiths and founders, as well as goldsmiths and gem-cutters, each most skilled in his own craft, so that they might adorn the memorial of the martyrs with wood, stone, gold, gems, and every precious material, and make the church new from old, very spacious from cramped, and splendid from rather dark. In these undertakings neither hope deceived him nor fortune [Col. 1201A] failed him. For those wishing to know how resources aided his desire and success followed it need only look at the conspicuous works, which proclaim it. He also adorned the church with every abundance of precious furnishings: vessels of gold and silver; bowls of onyx, sardonyx, green stone, crystal, and every precious gem; purple hangings, gold-woven cloaks, and garments wholly of silk. To these he added works of no slight value in glass and marble, and multiplied the sacred vessels.

X. Very many letters of great men to him survive. Among those who wrote to him most frequently were Peter, Abbot of Cluny, and Bernard of Clairvaux, both illustrious in life and learning and, beyond these, in eloquence. Their testimony sufficiently shows how distinguished he was, and what reputation he possessed among all, whether near [Col. 1201B] or remote. The same God-beloved Father Bernard also wrote a brief letter to the supreme pontiff Eugenius, but one containing no brief praise of this man. In it he declared that, before Caesar, he was as though one of the Roman court; before God, as though one of the heavenly court—like David, most holy, “entering and going out” in every respect in the house of God. Likewise, when the Abbot of Cluny had at some time considered his works and buildings, and looked upon the very small cell which this supremely philosophical man had built for his own dwelling, he is said to have burst out, with a profounder groan, into these words: “This man condemns us all, because he builds not for himself, as we do, but only for God.” For throughout the whole time of his administration he built nothing for his personal use except that humble cell adjoining the church, scarcely ten feet wide and fifteen long. In the tenth year before his death [Col. 1202A] he had established it for himself, so that he might gather together there the life which, he confessed, he had long scattered among worldly affairs. There, in the hours permitted him, he devoted himself to reading, tears, and contemplation. There he avoided the tumults and crowds of secular affairs. There, as is said of the wise man, he was never less alone than when [Col. 1202B] alone, since he directed his mind toward every one of the best men, in whatever age they had lived. With them he conversed; with them he studied. There, when he rested, straw served him as a feather-bed; instead of soft linen, there was spread beneath him a somewhat light woolen *lena* [the reading is printed thus], which by day was covered with decent tapestries. I warn the reader that, while I strive for brevity, I pass over much from the multitude of his virtues; and I hasten to relate briefly what I remember having promised somewhat above.

## Book Three

[Col. 1201]

[Col. 1201C] I. Therefore, at the time when Louis, the most Christian king of the Franks, bearing the cross after the Lord, set out for Jerusalem, the bishops and magnates of the kingdom convened a general council, to determine to whom, above all among the nobles or ecclesiastical persons, the chief direction of affairs and government of the realm ought to be entrusted. By divine prompting it came to pass that all unanimously agreed upon this glorious man. Though unwilling and strongly resisting, he was compelled to assume the administration and care of the commonwealth. Since he judged this dignity to be a burden rather than an honor, he refused it as far as was lawful and did not consent at all to undertake it until at last he was compelled by Pope Eugenius, who was present at the king’s departure and whom it was neither lawful nor possible to resist. Yet let no one suppose that the king undertook the journey of pilgrimage by this man’s will or counsel. Although its outcome proved far otherwise for the king than he had hoped, he nevertheless embarked upon it from pious desire and zeal for God. But this prudent man, foreknowing the future, neither suggested it to the prince nor approved it when he heard of it. Rather, when at the very outset he had vainly tried to oppose it and could not restrain the royal impulse, he judged that one must yield to the times, lest he seem either to injure the king’s devotion or uselessly incur the hostility of its supporters.

II. Once the king had thus departed abroad and this eminent man had assumed control of affairs, brigands began to break out everywhere through the kingdom and bring into public the factions long conceived; from the prince’s [Col. 1202C] absence they inferred, as it seemed to them, a license for violence. Some openly plundered the property of churches and the poor by force; others carried on robberies in more hidden places. To punish them, the new leader at once girded himself with a double sword: one material and royal, the other spiritual and ecclesiastical, both divinely committed to him by the supreme pontiff. In a short time he suppressed the reckless audacity of the former and reduced the schemes of the latter to nothing by a strong hand. Thus divine favor accompanied him in all things, so that he won bloodless victories over the enemy and not the slightest part of the kingdom’s integrity was lost. In this manner, outwardly a lion and inwardly a lamb, this man of strength, with Christ as his leader, fought the kingdom’s battles peacefully. You could see men from distant parts of the realm—[Col. 1202D] Limousins, Berrichons, Poitevins, and Gascons—resorting to his protection in times of need. He satisfied them in every respect, now by aid and now by counsel, so that they hoped for nothing further from any king.

III. He moreover acted as a good householder, making larger those things which he had undertaken to preserve. Thus he restored royal residences and raised up the ruins of walls and towers. What palace or royal building was there which the prince, upon returning, did not find improved in some part? And lest the kingdom lack any honor because of the king’s absence, the soldiers received from him their customary pay, and on appointed days clothing and royal gifts. It is clear that he bestowed all these things from his own generosity [Col. 1203A] rather than from the king’s treasury or public funds. For all the money paid from the royal fisc he either sent to the king on pilgrimage or kept for him, reflecting that one far away had many necessities and that what was reserved would not be superfluous when he returned.

IV. By his decree ecclesiastical honors were bestowed upon or removed from individuals; indeed, elected bishops obtained consecration with his assent, and abbots were appointed at his direction. Without any envy or shame the bishops submitted themselves to him, deferred to him, and obeyed him. At his summons they assembled; when he dismissed them, they returned to their own places, rejoicing that such a man had been found among the clergy as could suffice, single-handedly, to bear the care of the realm on behalf of all.

V. The supreme pontiff rejoiced in such integrity and prudence in him, [Col. 1203B] so that whatever this man decreed in Gaul was held ratified at Rome, and whatever had begun before him received confirmation there. Pope Eugenius wrote to him with exceptional familiarity. He often strengthened him with exhortations, laying no commands upon him any longer but, to speak truthfully, humbly entreating him. This man confidently fulfilled what had been entrusted to him; the other assisted through the authority granted him. Matters which could not be settled at Rome often received an appropriate resolution in this man’s presence. Whoever reads their reciprocal letters and the writings frequently exchanged will readily understand how great was the reverence, honor, and trust which each had for the other.

VI. Then, before the king’s return, it happened that his brother returned from Jerusalem. Certain common people, readily stirred by novelties, immediately began to meet him and wish him life together with sovereign power. Some clergy as well, because certain things in the kingdom were being done otherwise than they wished, began to flatter him with disgraceful adulation and to incite him, relying on his royal blood, to seek unlawful things. We suppress their names here, lest we seem deliberately to injure anyone. But this man, righteous and bold as a lion, having learned of this presumption, acted so that the authority entrusted to him should not be disturbed. Just as he is said to have thwarted the guile of the Greeks against the camps of God, so, after taking counsel with the faithful men of the realm, he did not cease to oppose the other’s attempts until he prudently [Col. 1203D] repressed all his arrogance and compelled him to make fitting satisfaction. Such, indeed, were his faith and constancy that, for truth or justice, if circumstances required it, he would gladly meet death. When I weigh his mind from his deeds, I consider that both the prince’s safety and his return ought above all to be attributed to him. For he arranged that alms be distributed by clergy and people for the king’s safety, and instituted frequent litanies. Concerned for his return, he did not cease to recall him by both private and public letters; and, making known the common longing and anxious prayers of all, he rebuked the useless delays.

VII. Meanwhile, let no one be surprised if this man suffered what is accustomed to befall all good men. Let no one, I say, wonder if he encountered wicked lips and the deceitful tongue of informers, from which not even the Savior was immune. For as rumor ran about—a thing which daily, by its own facility, invents evils about good men and good things about evil men—certain accusations concerning him were brought to the king’s ears, and for a while disturbed the king’s simple mind and the affections of others, who lied according to their own dispositions. But when the prayers of the faithful, both of this man and of others, had secured the king a prosperous return, and the aforesaid Roman pontiff met him as he approached Rome, the pope, among the first words of their mutual conversation, took pains to commend this man to the king magnificently according to his merits. Thus he utterly pierced the tongues of the detractors and exposed as liars those who had attempted to stain this excellent man and dim his splendor. Thus it happened that envy not only did him no harm but even contributed an increase to his praises. For once the king had learned the truth and recognized the man’s fidelity both from his works and from the pope’s testimony, although he had loved him greatly before departing, now that every suspicion was removed, after his return he loved and honored him still more, as was fitting. Why should he not love him? Why should he not deem worthy of every honor one who had vigorously and faithfully governed the charge entrusted to him and restored it with peace and integrity? Why should he not entrust himself to him above all others, when he had proved him more faithful than the rest? He truly did love him, and the outcome proved how greatly. For, as very many know, he showed him favor both living and dead. From that time he was called Father of the Country by people and prince alike, and all together extolled him [Col. 1204C] with the highest titles of merit. Many believed that this degree of happiness should suffice him and that he could not rise higher by further advancement. But just as there is no final step of descent for the worst of men, so for men of virtue there is no end or limit to progress.

VIII. Therefore every day the distinguished man was troubled in mind because no traces of virtue resulted from that expedition of pilgrimage. He was also indignant that from so great a force of Franks some had miserably perished by sword or hunger, while others he saw returning without glory. Hence he was greatly concerned lest, on account of this misfortune, the glory of the Christian name should perish in the East and the holy places be handed over to be trampled by unbelievers. He had received letters from overseas from the king of Jerusalem and the patriarch of Antioch, tearfully inviting him to bring them aid. They declared that, after the prince had been slain, the cross of the Savior was shut up within Antioch by the Saracens, and that the city was near surrender unless help came more swiftly. In the same days Pope Eugenius sent him apostolic letters, both entreating him by reverence and commanding him by authority to use the wisdom granted him by God in providing aid to the Eastern Church and in removing, by whatever means he could, the reproach of the Christians. Moved therefore by this necessity, especially as apostolic command pressed him and authority strengthened him, he piously considered how he might bring aid to those in danger [Col. 1205A] and turn the injury done to the cross back upon the wicked.

Judging that the king of the Franks and his army, recently returned and scarcely able to draw breath a little, ought to be spared, he convened the bishops of the realm concerning this matter, exhorting and encouraging them to undertake with him the glory of a victory that had not been granted to the mightiest kings. When he had vainly attempted this three times, having tasted their fearfulness and cowardice, he nevertheless judged it worthy to fulfill the praiseworthy vow himself while the others stood idle. He had preferred to conceal this magnificent devotion for a time, either because outcomes were uncertain or to avoid boasting. Yet his great preparations revealed it. For he began to take care that, through the Knights of the Temple, funds necessary for so great an undertaking should be sent ahead to Jerusalem, from those revenues which he had added to the monastery by his own labor or skill. No one can rightly be indignant at this if he considers how much, through this man’s diligence, all the Church’s possessions had grown in revenue, how many estates were acquired, and how many churches added to the monastery in his time. He did everything, indeed, under the appearance that he was preparing to send others on his behalf; but in truth, if life were granted him as a companion, he himself intended to set out and undertake the plan. He hoped that the Almighty would be his helper, who is accustomed to grant victory to the worthy in few no less than in many, considering that in such matters counsel is needed rather than force, and prudence more than arms. [Col. 1205C]

IX. Meanwhile, while he deliberated concerning the departure and continually longed for the pious contest, the Most High, the searcher of hearts, with whom the will is counted as the deed, decreed—yes, decreed—to crown His athlete before the contest and spare the glorious old man, who had already fought many and varied struggles for Him. Thus, when the Lord summoned him to Himself, he was seized with a slight fever. We saw, my Geoffrey, we saw the old man, vigorous and fresh in spirit, struggling for some time with illness and a frail body. We saw him, frequently supported by the hands of others, offering the sacred victims, until the illness grew worse and his strength diminished, and he was confined to bed. I did not see this without pain and cannot speak of it without groaning. When he understood that this was his summons and that his final day was at hand, he bore the judgment of his Creator with even and cheerful mind: glad, as he said, that he would at last escape from this, as from a pit, into that free and lofty realm. Did he not foresee this in spirit when, in the same year, he traveled to Tours to pray at the tomb of the outstanding confessor? He was surely going to seek permission to depart and, as he told us, to bid him a final farewell. There too, at the saint’s tomb, he was seen, in his customary generosity, to offer a silk cloth of excellent workmanship.

X. One thing alone seemed painful to him: that another would take up the purpose of his devotion and, as he feared, carry it out too slowly. Therefore, lest he leave his vow altogether unfulfilled, he chose from among the noblest French magnates a man experienced in warfare, both in courage and strength, suitable to send in his place, since he himself, called to the heavenly Jerusalem, was going on before. Having imposed upon this man his work and vow, marked with the cross, he also granted him the expenses that he had sent ahead. These would suffice that man and no small number of soldiers for a long time to attack the faithless and avenge the injuries done to heaven. [Col. 1206A]

XI. From that day he began to await his final hour more cheerfully, and he did not tremble at the end, because he had completed life before death. Nor did dying trouble him, since living helped him. He went out willingly, since he knew better things remained for him once he had been sent forth. Nor did he think that a good man ought to go out as one goes out when expelled, driven away against his will. Thus in death’s presence he was cheerful; and, I call God to witness, he was more indignant at those promising him life than at death itself. With the same expression and disposition with which one commonly looks upon another’s end, he looked upon his own. He would not have welcomed it so gladly had he not long prepared himself for it. As some are accustomed to beg for life, so he desired departure, because by living well he had ensured that he had lived enough; and he had always attended not to how long but to how well he lived.

During this illness, which held him for four months or more, he gave thanks to the Almighty because he was being led gradually, not suddenly torn away, to the rest necessary for a weary human being. When, around the Nativity of the Lord, he felt himself more sharply oppressed, he began urgently to ask the Lord that his passage might be delayed a little, until [Col. 1206C] the feast-days had passed, so that because of him they should not be changed from festive into mournful days. In this he was plainly heard by the Lord: for, once the sacred days were completed, he passed to the Lord on the eighth day after Epiphany; and with Him, as we ought to believe, he now keeps an unbroken octave. And rightly: he who beyond other mortals had been accustomed to delight in the feasts either of the Lord or of the saints must be believed to take part in everlasting feasts.

XII. Behold, Geoffrey: while I wish to obey you, I have exposed myself to be torn by the bites of many and mocked by many. I know, of course, that there will be no lack of those who accuse me of presumption because I have undertaken a noble subject, one to be illuminated by outstanding heralds. Indeed, I waited long, hoping that someone would repay, through his merits, the debt owed to so excellent a man. But since some act too sluggishly, I have chosen to write as best I can rather than incur the charge of ingratitude or negligence. If anyone thinks I have written little in comparison with his merits, let him consider that by this very brevity I have provided for modern readers. But whoever complains that I have exceeded measure in writing, let him read the same man’s *Royal Deeds*; let him read, if he wishes, the writings sent to him from the whole world; and he will recognize that I have stopped far short of the eminence of the facts. I judge that I have merely laid foundations upon which loftier structures may one day rise. In a denser forest I have thrown down unshaped and scant material, to receive form one day at the hands of chosen craftsmen.

XIII. The remaining matters concerning his death—namely, how gloriously he passed away after living so praiseworthily, how praiseworthy were his funeral rites, and what distinguished persons attended the burial—will be shown more fully to those who wish to know by that letter concerning his death which I issued at your request. Finally, how happy you are, and happy I too, to whom it was granted to serve him both alive and dead, and by whose hands precious balsams were poured upon his now lifeless body! What remains to be wished is this: may he remember us and pray for us, he who was accustomed to pray with us, so that we, who rejoiced in his companionship, may be sustained by his prayers. And indeed, if I know him well, now that he is joined to eternal joys, he does not cease to fulfill the office of his name. For he who, while still among us, interceded with the exalted rulers for those subject to them, now also stands before the sight of the Godhead, Suger interceding for the devout and suppliant. If, while still burdened by the weight of the body, he bore such concern for the brethren, what is he to be believed to do now, when, with the bonds of flesh broken, he has escaped into complete freedom? There can be no doubt that the Lord now graciously receives his prayers—he who listened attentively to the Lord’s commands and fulfilled them diligently.

[Col. 1207]

## Circular Letter of the Convent of Saint-Denis on the Death of Abbot Suger. A Poem on His Death by William, a Monk of the Same Monastery, Is Added.

(Dom Félibien, *History of the Abbey of Saint-Denys*, Documentary Proofs, p. CCI.)

[Col. 1207B] To all the faithful established everywhere in Christ, the humble convent of Blessed Dionysius sends greeting, and the consolation which is sought in the present life, to be attained eternally in heaven. We have thought it fitting to notify your holy fellowship of the glorious departure from this world of the most reverend Abbot Suger, of pious memory, so that in the grief by which we are immeasurably overwhelmed we may receive from your charity some remedy of consolation. Since all of us, together and individually, are members of one head, it is clear that we owe one another mutual compassion. Therefore, although this Father, remembered and to be remembered in every age, became known to nearly the whole world for his singular wisdom, energy, and industry, we are nevertheless concerned, so far as concerns ourselves, lest we appear ungrateful and forgetful toward the immense benefits and merits of so great a Father.

Not that we could fully comprehend in this brief little letter all his excellent deeds and praises; for their exposition requires no small volume and no ordinary talent. Indeed, fame is less than his merits, and praise unequal to his virtues. Who could extol his life with worthy acclaim? Who could sufficiently marvel at his magnanimity from youth and at his prudence in both ecclesiastical and secular affairs? No one can adequately recount his vigilance in divine worship or his diligence in adorning the Church. His principal and constant purpose was to exalt the noble monastery of Blessed Dionysius with every glory and honor, to order it religiously, and to make its church rich in revenues, more spacious in buildings, and adorned with ornaments. The proofs of this are clearer than light and will endure to the end of the age. [Col. 1207D; 1208B] Therefore he can now truly and confidently sing to the Lord: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of Thy house and the place where Thy glory dwells” (Ps. 25:8).

Sharpness of intellect, elegance of speech, learning, and skill in composition and writing shone in him jointly and individually, so that scarcely anyone could know which of these excelled most in him. Yet what might seem more remarkable was that he wrote neither slowly nor anxiously, but with almost the same speed with which he spoke. In him flourished not only a happy natural memory, but also the highest art of grasping what was necessary and retaining it, so that whatever excellent things he had at any time heard or himself said, he had ready at hand in their proper place and time. Such sobriety flourished in him that no one could discern whether he was more sober before eating or [Col. 1208C] after taking food.

But, to gather much into few words, one fact testifies to the virtue and reputation in which this man was held throughout the whole kingdom: when King Louis set out for Jerusalem, on the counsel of bishops and magnates he specially entrusted the government of the realm to this man’s tested fidelity and skill. With God’s help he so administered and governed it for almost two years that, upon the prince’s return, he restored to him intact what had been committed to his charge. Whenever more serious matters arose in the kingdom and were brought to Pope Eugenius’s attention, the supreme pontiff also repeatedly referred them for settlement to this man’s proven discretion. Although unwilling and compelled to take part in the counsels of kings and princes, he bore this, as he confessed, with great burden of mind: so that he might aid orphans, widows, every sort of poor person and sufferer of injury, and above all that he might, at the proper time, support before the prince the Church entrusted to him [Col. 1209A] and the other churches established in the kingdom.

Lifted, therefore, by such great and extraordinary virtues in this magnificent man into a kind of transport of mind, we always wished him to survive; we believed him worthy of life, and therefore we have received a blow which we shall scarcely be able to bear. If we could command affection, we ought rather to rejoice that we had had such a Father than grieve that we had sent before us one whom we do not doubt that we shall someday follow. For he has not been taken away from us, but from dangers; nor has he so much lost life as happily exchanged it. Yet since no one is exempt from the condition of dying, when the venerable man began to be afflicted by the illness of which he also died, he asked to be led, supported by the brethren’s hands, into the chapter meeting. There, after words of exhortation, he threw himself at everyone’s feet amid the tears and groans of all. Since he feared the judgment of the common Lord, he humbly submitted himself to the judgment of the brethren, tearfully begging them, in consideration of mercy, to forgive whatever wrong he had done them or had performed too negligently. All the brethren most gladly did this, with the greatest devotion and abundant outpouring of tears.

He also of his own accord and most mercifully absolved all those who were somewhat negligent, whom he saw bound under any sentence for any offence whatsoever; and he was reconciled to all, whether absent or present, restoring them to their former offices and ranks. Finally, so far as lay in his power, he earnestly desired and requested, with many prayers, to be entirely released from pastoral care. But he was altogether unable to extract the brethren’s assent to this request. After some time, however, when he saw that illness was afflicting him more sharply, and understood from his own judgment and that of the physicians that his end was at hand, he summoned to himself his intimate associates: namely, the venerable bishops of Soissons, Noyon, and Senlis. By their testimony and counsel he arranged his own house, and fortified by their assistance he might depart this world more safely. As they sat with him daily, he humbly confessed to them—now severally, now all together—whatever his conscience feared, with many tears. He repeatedly professed the whole faith to them; he devoutly fulfilled whatever was imposed upon him by them; and from their hands in turn, for about fifteen days before his death, he received without interruption the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood. [Col. 1209D]

Thus wholly turned toward the Lord, he devoted careful attention both by day and night to psalms and to the invocation in order of the saints’ names. He also continually exhorted all the brethren to pursue peace and preserve unity above all else; he carefully admonished them to flee with all diligence scandals, seditions, and schisms, and to devote themselves to preserving the Order, divine worship, and veneration of the saints. This same beloved Father and excellent shepherd passed away amid the words of the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed, on the Ides of January, in the seventieth year of his life, about the sixtieth since assuming the monastic habit, [Col. 1210A] and the twenty-ninth of his prelacy. He passed away, I say, full alike of days and virtues: in heaven the saints rejoicing, but on earth the faithful of every sex and age, every rank and order, sorrowing and weeping.

At his burial and funeral rites, most celebrated for the dignity of the person and place, there were present by God’s will six venerable bishops, very many abbots and other religious men. With devout prayers they solemnly commended his spirit to God and his body to the earth. The most Christian King Louis, though far away, upon receiving the most sorrowful news of his death, hastened—setting aside all business—to attend the funeral with the foremost magnates of the kingdom, because of the close friendship and love they had long held for one another. There, mindful of affection and unmindful of royal majesty, he did not cease to weep most bitterly as Suger was buried. One thing is undoubtedly clear: he could not but come gloriously to his end, since his whole preceding life had been glorious. It was therefore divinely provided that bishops should consecrate his passing and that the king should honor his burial by his presence. The master of the Temple was also present with no small force of his Order, commending to the Lord by prayers, tears, and every means in their power the soul dear to them.

But we who survive him in this life—what comfort shall we find without him, who alone was accustomed to console the grieving, awaken joy, and banish sadness? How shall we be able to do without so great a companion in life, so great a relief from cares and labors? Illness shows what good health possesses; we feel more deeply what we had once we cease to have it. He alone was for us the one in whom domestic concern rested and public care found repose. He alone was both our comfort at home and our honor abroad. Yet we must not be ungrateful concerning one who has been translated, because he paid what was due to common nature and received from Christ what belonged to singular grace. How, indeed, can we ever cease to think of him, or remember him at any time without tears and grief—though he is to be attended with the joys of all, he who, having trampled death, has now received the crown of security? Can we ever either fail to remember so great a Father or remember him without a certain grace of tears? Yet, although these recollections renew our pain, they also bring delight. If we begin to mourn him, we may perhaps appear to hope too little for his salvation; if we restrain our tears altogether, we shall deservedly be accused of impiety and ingratitude.

We could not even prepare our minds for his death so that it might be more tolerable to us. So greatly did the mind dread to think anything of the kind concerning him—not because we were ignorant of the human condition, but because we had learned to think of nothing but favorable things concerning him. Yet he was taken away lest evil change his heart, because his soul was pleasing to God. He fell asleep in the Lord and was gathered to his fathers, nourished into a good old age. The earth returned to its earth, but his spirit sought the stars, to be crowned by Him and joined to the number of the elect, whom, while in the flesh, he served and for whom he fought with an undivided faith.

[Col. 1211A]

> When I recall the man’s merit, character, and life,  
> As one aware and mindful of his virtues,  
> Though I myself remain silent and keep back what I know,  
> Yet one day will bring these things to light.  
>
> Such is the nature of good: its power is not to be hidden;  
> Things long concealed come into public view.  
> I judge that he was rightly sent and given from heaven to mortals  
> As a pattern for living.  
>
> I marvel at so great a spirit in such a body,  
> And at such great and many goods enclosed in a small vessel.  
> But by this one example Nature wished sufficiently to prove  
> That virtue can be concealed beneath any outer skin.  
>
> A Cicero in speech, a Cato in merits, and a Caesar in spirit;  
> By counsel he ruled kings, by aid kingdoms.  
>
> [Col. 1212A] What Cato did at Rome, what Scipio once achieved,  
> This man alone achieved in his native land.  
> What praises, what titles, what triumphs  
> Can your flock sound forth for you, Father Abbot?  
>
> Best Suger, what worthy thing can be said  
> In view of your merits? This praise will be brief.  
> Yet heaven applauds you according to your merits, and the world,  
> And all Gaul celebrates your praises.  
>
> Seven stars smiled upon you at your birth,  
> And their aspect and power were beneficent.

Thesauris tibi larga suos natura paravit,  
Expanditque tibi philosophia sinus.  
Nec tibi successus laetos fortuna negavit.  
Fata dedere boni quidquid habere solent.

Bountiful Nature has prepared her treasures for you,  
and Philosophy has opened her bosom to you.  
Fortune has not denied you happy success;  
the Fates have granted whatever blessings people are wont to possess.

[Col. 1211]

# The Book of Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis, on Deeds Accomplished During His Administration, in Which Many Matters Relevant to the History of Louis the Fat and Louis the Younger Are Recorded

(Duchesne, *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. IV, p. 331, from a manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint-Denis. [Note: [Col. 1211C] Certain copies of this book name as its author William, a monk who composed the Deeds of his abbot Suger in Suger's name. That this is more likely is readily demonstrated by the style, which differs utterly from Suger's style.])

## Chapter I

[Col. 1211B]

In the twenty-third year of our administration, when on a certain day we sat in the general chapter, conferring with our brethren concerning both persons and private affairs, those same most beloved brethren and sons began earnestly and lovingly to entreat us not to allow the fruit of so great a labour to pass over in silence. Rather, they urged that the increases which the abundant bounty of almighty God had bestowed upon this church during the time of our prelacy—both through the acquisition of new properties, the recovery of lost ones, the enlargement of improved estates, the construction of buildings, and the provision of gold, silver, most precious gems, and excellent vestments—should be preserved by pen and ink for the memory of posterity [Col. 1211C]. From this they promised us two results: first, that through such knowledge all succeeding brethren might earn for the salvation of our soul the unceasing urgency of their prayers; secondly, that by this example they might be stirred to a zealously attentive concern for the worship of the Church of God.

Therefore, yielding assent as devoutly as possible to their devout and reasonable [Col. 1212B] request, neither from any desire for empty glory nor demanding any recompense of human praise or transitory reward, we have judged it fitting, lest after our death the Church be diminished in revenues by fraud of whatever kind or by whomever committed, and lest the abundant increases which the bountiful munificence of God bestowed in the time of our administration perish through silence under evil successors, to begin in its proper place with the founding of buildings and the augmentation of treasures belonging to the body of the church of the most blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius—a church which most sweetly nourished us from the breast until old age. We have likewise resolved to make known, for the information of both present and future generations [Col. 1212C], the increase of revenues from its castle—namely, its first seat—and from the surrounding neighbourhood.

The office of that castle, commonly called the toll and the exchange, amounted to sixty shillings every week. But Ursellus, a Jew of Montmorency, held ten shillings of this in pledge, together with the village called Molignum, [Col. 1213A] for twenty-four marks of silver and another large sum of money, as he said. At considerable cost we recovered both the village, worth twenty pounds or more, and the ten shillings themselves: we paid three thousand shillings to Matthew of Montmorency, who was willing to seize it for his Jew; and we paid the Jew's wife ten pounds and ten measures of grain. From ten other shillings, through improvement of the village, we caused that office to be increased without exaction.

Thus, the ten shillings formerly held by the Jew and the ten newly increased shillings yield, every week of the year, an increase of twenty shillings, amounting to fifty-two pounds; while the village yields twenty pounds. The rent of that same village was twelve pounds at the octave of Saint Denis [Col. 1213B], whereas it now amounts to twenty and more; hence there are eight pounds of increase from this source, and eight from a certain house which, after establishing a butcher's stall through the purchase of another house, we assigned to the use of the butchers for the support of infirm brethren. The total is therefore ninety pounds.

From the toll, moreover, there are twenty pounds, whereas formerly there had been forty pounds. Yet we have often received seventy pounds from it; and we could easily receive much more every year, were we not to condemn robbery and the proceeds of robbery with anathema.

From the *indictum*, which Lord Louis gave to blessed Denis, we receive three hundred shillings peacefully and without dispute; thirty-five shillings from the rent of bakers' stalls in the pantry, which we assigned for the brethren's refreshment on the feast of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul; ten [Col. 1213C] shillings from Gerard, our nephew—five from his house and five from the toll-guarantee. From the plots of the house of William of Cormeilles, which I bought for eighty pounds, there is a rent of fifteen shillings from three dwellings, the other two standing vacant.

In the brethren's small court, formerly vacant, we receive seventy shillings of annual rent from new tenants. From the court outside the village, where not even one tenant had ever lived, but which had been kept at the servants' expense, we receive an annual increase of twenty pounds: in it and in another new court adjoining it, more than eighty new tenants have been settled. There also, namely at Saint-Lucian, at great cost because the Church greatly needed these things, [Col. 1213D] we caused an enclosed vineyard of almost eighty *arpents*, as they call them, to be planted and cultivated. For its proper cultivation, to the Church's great advantage, we assigned to it those same twenty pounds. We did all this deliberately because of the shortage of wine, for crosses, chalices, and vestments were often pledged in many places, even at Latiniacum.

The increase from the mills of the same castle is such that, whereas formerly they used to supply the brethren's refectory with five *minae* of grain daily, they now continually supply eight every day. Calculated precisely from each week, their increase yields forty measures less one half. The increase in money amounts to one hundred and forty-six pounds and ten shillings.

We bought the house standing [Col. 1214A] beyond the Paris gate toward Saint-Médéric for one thousand shillings, because, since we frequently attended to affairs of the realm, we considered it fitting that we, our horses, and our successors should lodge there more honourably. From the Paris gate, which used to yield twelve pounds, we receive fifty; thus the increase is thirty-eight pounds.

## Chapter II. On Tremblay

Since the same village suffered many oppressive services from the count of Dammartin—namely, the exaction of a *taille*, five measures of grain which I had granted him for peace, although he had been accustomed to impose a *taille* as he pleased; the exaction of rams; and lodging in the village many times a year at the peasants' expense—we made this peace with the count concerning all these matters: the whole village should remain to us in peace, free of every exaction and customary due, while we should pay him from our own purse ten pounds each year at the octave of Saint Denis for his homage.

For this reason we rebuilt the village more willingly. At its entrance we caused a new court with a new barn to be erected, so that in it might be stored the general field-share and that of four ploughs, while in the other court, situated in the township, the tithes of the lands might be stored; and in both courts straw might be reserved for our uses. Whereas formerly we could scarcely, or never, obtain ninety measures of grain from that village, we brought matters to such a point that we receive from our reeve one hundred and ninety measures, apart from what they sow [Col. 1214C], what they supply as necessary to the ploughmen and oxen, and all the oxen and necessities furnished for the ploughs; for this reason they possess the revenue of the ovens. We retain our rent, *tensamentum*, mortmain dues, fines, and such *taille* as we choose to impose. Here the increase amounts to ninety measures of grain.

We enclosed the old court with a wall and erected there a nearly defensible house adjoining the church. With this fortification our successors will be able, if they wish, to defend themselves and their possessions against every enemy.

## Chapter III. On the Recovery of the Abbey of Argenteuil

When, in the teachable years of my youth, I turned over the ancient charters of possessions in the archive [Col. 1214D] and consulted the books of immunities because of the wickedness of many claimants, a charter of the foundation of the monastery of Argenteuil, by Hermenricus and his wife Numma, frequently came into my hands. It stated that the abbey had belonged to Saint Denis from the time of King Pippin. But on some occasion, through an unfavourable agreement in the time of Charlemagne, Pippin's son, it had been alienated.

For that emperor had obtained it from the abbot and brethren in order to establish there as abbess of nuns one of his daughters, who refused human marriage, on the condition that after her death it should return to the use of the church. But amid the disturbance of the kingdom under the sons of his son, namely Louis the Pious, the arrangement could not be completed while she remained alive [Col. 1215A]. Therefore, since our predecessors had often laboured in this matter with little success, after taking counsel with our brethren we sent our envoys to Rome, together with the ancient charters of foundation and donation and the confirming privileges, to Pope Honorius of blessed memory, asking him to investigate and restore our right by canonical examination.

Being a man of counsel and a guardian of justice, he restored to us that place and its appurtenances, both because of our right and because of the outrageous conduct of the nuns living there wickedly, so that the order of religious life might be reformed there. King Louis, son of Philip, our dearest lord and friend, confirmed this restoration and, by command of royal majesty, confirmed to the church whatever royal rights he possessed there [Col. 1215B]. Whoever wishes to know more fully the terms of this recovery may find them set out more clearly in the charters of kings and the privileges of the Apostolic See.

How great is the increase of this abbey and its appurtenances—Trappe, Herencurtis, Chaveniacum, Burdeniacum, Cerisiacum, the land of Montmélian, Bunziacum, Mosteriolum near Melun, and others—those who administer them wisely will recognize as worthy of a great prelate.

The increase from the old rent of Argenteuil, which does not belong to the abbey, is twenty pounds: formerly we had only twenty pounds, whereas forty are now rendered. Formerly we received six measures of grain; now, fifteen.

## Chapter IV. On the Vexin

[Col. 1215C]

In the noble county of the Vexin, situated between the Oise and the Epte, which the immunities of the church declare to be the proper fief of blessed Denis, and which King Louis, son of Philip, hastening against the Roman emperor who was rising against the kingdom of France, professed in the full chapter of Saint Denis that he held from Saint Denis and owed him homage by right of standard-bearer if he were not king—we laboured, with God's help, to enlarge the demesne through the following increase.

We obtained from the same King Louis the church of Cergy and the freedom of its court. From his son Louis we obtained, at the dedication of the church, by royal liberality for the remedy of his soul and for the protection of his person and kingdom, the road through that village [Col. 1215D] and all its revenues except wine and oats. No less devoutly he granted to the holy martyrs what he held at Cormeilles and at Oenitum, as well as everything he held at Trappes except the lodging-right.

By these and many other increases, especially through continual diligence and unremitting supervision—restraining the greed of reeves and servants in cultivating the lands and vineyards, and repelling the troublesome assaults of wicked advocates, for which in the early days of our administration we spent much on military needs—we have, with God's consent, brought matters to the point that, whereas in the time of our predecessors our brethren had been content with five shillings each day for the kitchen, they now receive beyond that increase another five each day, and fourteen on Thursday and Saturday together, without dispute, for the brethren's refreshment [Col. 1216A]. What remains beyond this is accustomed amply to exceed an increase of one hundred measures of grain. After Easter we judged this should be distributed for our own needs, the churches, the poor, or whatever necessities might arise. For in the final months of the year, the high price of grain sometimes punishes the improvidence of communities. The annual increase in money amounts to one hundred and fourteen pounds and twelve shillings.

## Chapter V. On Cormeilles in the Paris District

At Cormeilles in the Paris district, the increase [Col. 1216B] in rent is eight pounds: whereas formerly we had twelve pounds, we now have twenty. In grain we had ten or twelve measures; now, eighteen. At Centinodium, four pounds from the increase of the new rent, and one hundred shillings from the old. At Francorum-villa, forty shillings from new increase and forty from the old, apart from the fief. The tithe of our fief, which we bought from Paganus of Gisors and gave to the matricular clergy for the love of God, excepting the tithe of our own enclosed field, which we retained.

## Chapter VI. On Montigny

At Montigny, fifty shillings from the new rent and seventy from the old.

## Chapter VII. On Cergy

[Col. 1216C]

At Cergy, forty shillings of rent from the wood, the homage of the knight Theobald of Puteaux, and forty donkey-loads.

## Chapter VIII. On Louveciennes

At Louveciennes, whereas we and our predecessors were accustomed to render annually fifteen pounds for everything we possessed there—rent, grain, and wine—after certain pleas concerning ancient demesne lands, by which we prevented the peasant cultivators of the vineyards from retaining the revenues, while preserving the annual money-rent and grain due, we acquired almost one hundred measures of wine.

## Chapter IX. On Vernouillet

[Col. 1216D]

From Vernouillet, which had been in pledge for forty years, we receive ten pounds after paying its redemption, whereas before we had only sixty shillings. We assigned the revenues of this place belonging to us entirely to the infirm brethren.

## Chapter X. On the Valley of Crison

At the Valley of Crison we built a village, established a church and a house, and caused uncultivated land to be broken with the plough. Those who strive to build it up will better know how much it ought to be worth, since there are now almost sixty tenants there and many others would choose to come if someone were available to provide for them. For that place [Col. 1217A] had been like a den of robbers, with more than two miles of wilderness; it was entirely unprofitable to our church and, because of the neighbouring woods, suitable for robbers and armed followers. Therefore we decided that our brethren should serve God there, so that in the dens where dragons had formerly dwelt there might spring up the green growth of reed and rush.

We freed the possession of Saint Denis—including Mesnil-Saint-Denis, Dampierre, and the other villages of the castle called Cabrosa—from oppressions which had almost wholly ruined it through the greed of three *tailles* levied from ancient times: those of the lord of the castle of Cabrosa, the lord of the castle of Nielpha, and Simon of Ville-Aten. We remitted only those things which rightly belonged to their advocacy. We likewise recovered the hunting-right in Yvelines within the boundaries of the estate, which they had taken from Saint Denis for many years.

So that this should not be forgotten in future, we went there and remained for an entire week in tents, accompanied by approved friends and our men—namely Amalric of Montfort, count of Évreux, Simon of Nielpha, Ebrard of Villaperosa, and very many others. Every day of the week we caused an abundance of stags to be conveyed to Saint Denis, not from frivolity but to restore the Church's right; and we had them distributed to the infirm brethren, to guests in the hospital, and to the knights throughout the village, lest the matter be forgotten [Col. 1217B].

To the lord of Cabrosa, besides the ancient fief—namely, the advocacy of our land and half of the wood—we pay one hundred shillings yearly from our own funds, as to our vassal, so that he may not lay his hand again upon a *taille* or oppress the land. We are able, without opposition and at our discretion, to collect those one hundred shillings within that same land [Col. 1217C].

Lest the fruit of our labour be rendered void through forgetfulness, we have also taken care to commit to writing what, with God's help, we laboured to increase in Belsa.

The first village of Saint Denis, called Guillelvallis, near Sarclidas, which is listed in King Dagobert's catalogue among the places granted by that king to Saint Denis, had for many years—or indeed always—been so entirely unprovided for that there was neither a house in which even the abbot could lay his head [Col. 1217D], nor any barn, nor any demesne property in the whole village. Each year its inhabitants paid only twenty-five small measures, which do not exceed four of our measures, as rent for the land they cultivated, together with a small rent from their houses.

To restore it, out of love for our lords the holy martyrs, we came there and acquired for the Church, at great expense from both parties, a tract of land in that village amounting to three ploughlands. Over this land a great war had been waged for more than forty years between John of Étampes, son of Paganus, a noble and valiant man, and another knight of Pithiviers [Note: [Col. 1217D] Perhaps *Pithverensis*, “of Pithiviers.”]. What each sought so that neither might possess it, we retained for ourselves; thus ending their war, we caused the property to be secured to us by charter, through the favour of relatives and friends, namely Baldwin of Corbeil and many others [Col. 1218A].

In this new land, in the middle of the village, delighting in the pleasantness of the site and taking advantage of the neighbouring living springs and running streams, we caused an honourable court to be enclosed by a wall. At great expense we had a strong and defensible house built within the court, together with barns and every necessity. To relieve the dryness of upper Belsa, we also laid out, almost around it, a fishpond abundantly stocked with many fish. We established two ploughs on this estate, one in the new land and one in the old. We increased an estate which had yielded so little that it may now render fifty or more measures of grain annually [Col. 1218B].

Indeed, remitting the former rent which they had paid, though it was very small, we retained for ourselves the field-share of the whole land, except the ploughland held as the reeve's fief. On this account he promised to calm entirely the talkativeness of the peasants and their complaints about the changed custom.

## Chapter XI. On Monarville

There follows another village of Saint Denis near that one, called Monarville, made the most wretched of all villages. Trampled beneath the yoke of the castle of Méréville, it was reduced to beggary no less than if under Saracen oppression. Whenever he wished, the lord of that castle seized lodging there with whomever [Col. 1218C] he wished, devoured the peasants' goods with open mouth, carried off the *taille* and grain at harvest-time as a customary due, assembled his wood supplies two or three times a year to the loss of the village ploughs, and exacted as customary dues every intolerable burden of pigs, lambs, geese, and chickens.

Since under so great an oppression it was over a long period nearly reduced to desolation, we chose boldly to resist and resolutely to extirpate such burdens from the holy inheritance. When we brought him to suit, he defended those customs as an hereditary right received from his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather. Yet, by God's help and through the counsel of our men and friends, affairs reached the point that Hugh, lord of the castle [Col. 1218D], with the favour of his wife and sons and the consent of King Louis, his lord from whom he said he held, recognizing his injustice, wholly and forever relaxed and remitted to Saint Denis all these customs. With his own hand, under oath, he abjured them, as is more fully found in the charter of King Louis.

To retain his homage for our church, we granted him in our court two Étampes measures of grain, one of wheat and the other of oats, to be delivered through the hand of our monk or servant. Once the aforesaid village was freed from this torment, whereas it had scarcely been worth ten or fifteen pounds to us, it has been accustomed to render annually, through the hands of officials, one hundred Étampes measures of grain—often worth one hundred pounds, according to the price of grain [Col. 1219A].

Likewise, seeking to restore the possession called Rubridum, which had been entirely abandoned under the oppressive services of the castle of Puteaux, Hugh, lord of Puteaux, after the ruin of the castle, came to us one day concerning this matter. He proposed that he and I should cultivate, sharing the profit equally, the untilled land which the oppression of the castle had reduced to wilderness. Although some approved this as expedient, we refused, and laboured to accomplish for the Church's benefit by ourselves what we did not wish to do with him. We would not admit as partner in restoring the land one whom we had experienced, following the custom of his predecessors, as a most grievous destroyer.

For he had seized from that land, following his predecessors' custom, the very exactions [Col. 1219B] which we listed for Monarville: *taille*, grain, pigs, sheep, lambs, geese, chickens, young fowls, and wood. Thus he had rendered it wholly useless, lying unproductive both for us and for himself. Therefore, yielding to the misery of the land and the loss suffered by our church, we built a court on that barren ground and raised a tower above the gate to repel robbers. We stationed three ploughs there, restored the village called Villana, and put the disordered affairs of the land in order. We improved it so far that, whereas it had scarcely been accustomed to yield twenty pounds annually, it afterward yielded one hundred pounds, and often one hundred and twenty.

In rightful devotion to the holy martyrs for such benefits [Col. 1219C], from the profit of this labour we assigned every year eighty pounds, by charter and seal, to the building of their church until the work should be completed. We also removed from that land an evil customary due of the viscount of Étampes, called *palagium*.

## Chapter XII. On Toury

Toury, then, the renowned village of Saint Denis, head of the others and the proper and special seat of Saint Denis, providing food in the middle of the road for pilgrims, merchants, and all travellers, and restful repose for the weary, was so miserably burdened by the intolerable oppressive services of the lords of the aforesaid castle of Puteaux [Col. 1219D] that, when in the time of our predecessor, Abbot Adam of blessed memory, I came there while still quite young to oversee the land as provost, it already languished, almost deserted by its cultivators. Given over as prey to the rapacity of the men of Puteaux, it lay wholly open to “the peoples of Ethiopia.”

Not even the house of Saint Denis itself could at any time defend itself: the lord would break into it through his retainers, sacrilegiously carry off whatever he found, disturb the neighbouring villages by frequent lodging-visits, and compel the peasants' grain and *taille* to be carried to his castle, first for himself, then for his seneschal, then for his provost. Those who remained scarcely lived beneath the weight of so abominable an oppression.

Therefore, after staying there nearly two years and being wearied by these and other evils, by the pains of human compassion, and by the damage to our church, we joined together—not we alone, but all the churches possessing lands in those districts and equally burdened—and deliberated carefully how we might escape the unbearable yoke and tyranny of that most wicked castle [Col. 1220A]. From this came about, through our effort, that the venerable bishop Ivo of Chartres for his part, the chapter of Blessed Mary for its part, the abbot of Saint Peter for his part, the church of Saint John of the Valley for its part, the bishop of Orléans for his part, the church of Saint Anianus for its part, the abbot of Saint Benedict for his part, the archbishop of Sens for his part, and we for ours, approached the glorious King Louis. We tearfully set before him the despoiling of the churches, the lament of the poor and orphans, and the disinheritance of the alms bestowed upon the churches by his predecessors and by himself.

He, being a man of most noble energy, full of piety and an illustrious defender of churches, promised aid and confirmed by oath that he would in no way permit the churches or their goods henceforth to be destroyed by that wicked man [Col. 1220B]. By what labour, at what expense, and with what difficulty this excellent deed was accomplished may be found more fully in the deeds of the aforesaid king.

When the castle of Puteaux had been razed to its foundations, as its wickedness deserved, the lands of the saints—ours as well as the others—having recovered their former liberty, flourished in peace after withering in war; laying aside sterility, they restored the fruitfulness of cultivated land. After the death of our predecessor, Abbot Adam of blessed memory, when I was appointed, as unworthy as I was absent, to the seat of this holy administration, I remembered my former effectiveness and labour, for I had long served in that provostship, and devoted myself more earnestly to enlarging it.

Within the court which I had fortified with stake and wattle, I erected a well-walled castle; I had a tower-bastion raised above the principal gate, established suitable and defensible houses, and preserved inviolate the liberty of the village—indeed, of the entire land [Col. 1220C]. Accordingly, it once happened to me that, while I was hurrying with an armed force to Orléans after my lord the king and found the provost of Puteaux reviving his former evils, I seized him disgracefully and sent him in chains and dishonour to Saint Denis.

But because the possessions of churches ought to grow and be fostered in peace through the diligence of prelates, we made the inhabitants of our demesne lands there into rent-paying tenants, retaining the tithes of those lands. We order their rent to be committed to writing, lest it be forgotten. To show the increase in the value of this possession produced by our labour, we receive annually eighty pounds from the provostship, which had formerly been worth no more than twenty pounds. The daily use of the other customary dues, greatly improved, can readily demonstrate the increase in resources.

The ancient advocacy of that land extended in former times to the fortress of Baldwin, by which the land itself had been cruelly oppressed through long duration of time. Since no other means of resisting remained, it happened that this advocacy descended by hereditary right to a certain girl, daughter of the daughter of Adam of Pithiviers [Col. 1221A]. When we learned this, at great expense and by the counsel of our friends, we sought to marry her as we chose. Thus, to quiet the disturbances of that land and unwilling that it should suffer, as usual, from the molestations of its native lords, we arranged for the girl, with the advocacy-rights, to be given to a young man of our household. With the favour of King Louis, from whose fief the advocacy derived, we bestowed one hundred pounds of Saint-Denis money on the marriage and on the girl's father, on this condition: in return for this money and another thirty pounds which the king received from it, both they and their successors should perform homage, service, and justice, whenever we summoned them, for us and our successors [Col. 1221B]. If they failed in this, it would be lawful for us to retain the entire fief of the advocacy in full, as though it were our own, until they gave us satisfaction, with the consent of themselves and their relatives and the favour of the king.

We have taken care to list below the fiefs which we purchased from our own treasury, for maintaining garrisons each year for two months in the same castle of Toury.

## Chapter XIII. On the Village of Poigny

Likewise, we arranged that Berard of Essenuilla, as our man, should hold in fief from us the village of Poigny which Geoffrey Rufus held from his kinsman Berard [Col. 1221C].

## Chapter XIV. On Feins and Vendrovillare

We also bestowed upon the alms of Saint Denis another possession called Feins and Vendrovillare, together with the other dependent villages. We had purchased or recovered it at great expense—nearly one hundred and fifty marks of silver—from Galeran of Breteuil, his wife Judith, and their son Ebrard, a valiant man who died on the Jerusalem expedition. For it was said that in ancient times it had belonged to Saint Denis through the gift of Hubert of Saint-Galaric. We hoped in the mercy of God that this alms, granted to the poor, would mercifully obtain for us from almighty God the benefit of divine recompense [Col. 1221D]. For he said: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin.” And, so that it might serve the necessities of the poor more securely and perpetually, we caused it to be confirmed by a command of King Louis, preserved in the public archives.

## Chapter XV. On Belna

Among the other possessions of Saint Denis, Belna is recognized as one of the better ones in the district of Gâtinais. Extending almost four leagues, rich in wheat and wine, wonderfully capable of every kind of produce, it abounds in all good things if it is not vexed by the servants [Col. 1222A] of the king or by ours. Through the negligence of its inhabitants, who rarely cultivated it, it had declined to such poverty that, although it belonged to the chamber responsible for the footwear of this church, it could not in any way meet that obligation. Hence, when it remained in the abbot's hands because of default on its payment, he leased it out yearly, in its entirety, to the servants of that land for thirty pounds.

When at the beginning of our prelacy we found it ruined and almost reduced to wilderness, we set before our dearest lord Louis, king of the French—whose nobility we strove to serve as devoutly as faithfully—so great a loss to the Church. He too possessed on that land intolerable and nearly ruinous customary dues: three provisions [*procurationes*] annually [Col. 1222B], one supplied from the peasants' collective contribution, sufficient both for himself and for those serving him, and two supplied from Saint Denis's own revenues. By this calamity the land was utterly consumed. But because he was of exceptional generosity, and because he pitied so great a loss to the Church and the burdens borne by the poor, and was well disposed toward our love and service, he remitted to the church's demesne and to us forever that provision. The provision made from the peasants' collection he fixed at an annual obligation of eight pounds, under a command of royal majesty.

Encouraged by this benefit, we recovered for ourselves lands usurped and alienated by the reeve and by others. We caused enclosed vineyards at Saint-Loup, which for twenty years had been turned into ploughland, to be replanted; restored other vineyards near Belna which had been almost destroyed; bought still other vineyards from one of our men for twenty pounds in Orléans currency; and caused villages wholly emptied by predatory lodging-visits to be resettled [Col. 1222C].

## Chapter XVI. On the Tithe of Barville

Among other things, we recovered for the Church, as best we could, a certain tithe at Barville which certain knights had held for a hundred years, as they said, at an annual rent of two shillings and which is worth to us each year twenty or thirty measures of grain; likewise, we recovered whatever else had been lost.

Since the demesne buildings, exceedingly poor as they were, had wholly collapsed, the following incident especially stirred us to build the present pleasant and defensible structures. When I had arranged one day to settle our cases in that house, it collapsed so miserably by divine disposition in my absence that, had I been present, it would have utterly crushed the bed in which I would have lain, the flooring of the upper room, the casks in the lower storeroom, and the wine vessels [Col. 1222D]. Under so great a ruin it gave everyone proof that divine favour had spared me.

There we constructed an excellent barn and two ponds which, if well maintained, will provide for a long time an abundance of fish sufficient for those coming there. How greatly that estate has been improved with God's help and from what misery it has been raised is clearly shown by the certain increase: whereas formerly it rendered thirty pounds, it now frequently renders more than two hundred.

## Chapter XVII. On the Borough of Axone, Now Corbeil

[Col. 1223A]

The borough of Axone, belonging to Saint Denis and situated on the river Essonne, was granted to the holy martyrs by the ancient liberality of kings, as is recorded in their old charters. The violence of a certain tyrant transferred it to the castle of Corbeil and endeavoured, by dispossessing the holy martyrs on earth, to dispossess himself of heaven.

## Chapter XVIII. On the Cell Built at the Place Called Campis
Thus, after the lapse of many years—nearly two hundred or more—when the mother church of Axon, which is the parish church of Corbeil, had remained almost alone like a statue in the same place, the bishops of Paris also took it from blessed Dionysius, out of jealousy of the monastery’s inherent liberty; and, in order that this seizure might be stoutly defended, they granted it to Cluny and to Cluny’s dependencies, namely Saint-Martin-des-Champs and the church of Gournay. But the very tyrants of the castle of Corbeil, frozen in their wickedness, so miserably subjected everything to themselves that they left scarcely anything remaining except the bare ground of the land; and with sacrilegious audacity they reduced it to their own use, as though it were their lawful property.

There also remained a certain chapel, in honour, as was said, of blessed Mary—the smallest I have ever seen—half-ruined, in the place called Campis; and in it stood an ancient altar, upon which sheep and goats often grazed the grass that had grown over it from long desolation. There, according to the testimony of many persons, candles were often seen burning on the Sabbath day, signifying the holiness of the place. Moved by this occurrence, sick natives, and afterwards many foreigners as well, flocked thither in hope of healing, and were cured. Since, by divine ordinance, that place began to be visited by many from near and far, our brethren were sent there: the venerable men of good memory, Hervé the prior and Odo of Torcy, to serve our Lord and His blessed Mother, and to devote themselves to adapting and raising up that little place for divine worship. At once such an abundance of miracles blossomed forth there, to the wonder of all, that it was loved by all, proclaimed by all, and enlarged by whomever could do so. For there were brought there multitudes of the sick, of those afflicted by unclean spirits, and likewise sufferers who were blind, lame, or withered. Since countless miracles performed by the blessed Mother of God made the place famous, I have taken care to set down in this present page, for the honour of that place, two which we learned by sight or hearing.

## Chapter XIX. The Miracle of the Mute Girl

There was a noble matron, widowed for many years, namely the mother of the venerable man Robert, abbot of Corbie, who was our monk. As she was accustomed to visit holy places for the remedy of her soul, she came there with a girl of about twelve years, who had never spoken.

On the night of the Sabbath, while she spent the night in that little church with the mute girl [Col. 1224A], and was earnestly invoking the divine ears for herself and her people, when the brethren began the *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise thee, O God”), it seemed to that girl—as she related it—as though she had been carried into ecstasy: a certain glorious queen, fair as the moon and chosen as the sun, clothed in royal robes, crowned with gold and precious gems, passed before her, going from the left side of the altar to the right. When that queen compassionately called her by her own name—for she was called Lancendis—the girl, heard by the aforesaid matron and many others, answered aloud, in a tongue hitherto unused: “Lady.” Thereafter she knew how, and was able, to speak no less than if she had spoken throughout her whole life.

Those present raised this astonishing miracle to the highest public acclaim and spread it through the surrounding regions. We, however, who had known her mute for five years and afterwards speaking for five years, were rightly bound both to exalt and to love that holy place.

## Chapter XX. The Woman with Dropsy

We thought it fitting to add another miracle, as we promised. A certain woman suffering from dropsy, swollen like a pregnant woman and no less frenzied with cries of pain—for she was unbearably oppressed by watery fluid—was carried by her friends to Saint Mary at the aforesaid place. After she had lain concealed before the holy altar for many days, she repelled many visitors by the stench of her own corruption and of the decayed element. And when all hope of health had now failed [Col. 1224C]—for the swelling and discharge had already almost distorted even her face beyond recognizable form—many persons, healthy and sick alike, murmured and humbly requested that she be removed from that little church. But our brethren, venerable men, preferred mercifully to endure her unwelcome presence rather than mercilessly to endure her absence.

It happened, therefore, on a Sunday night—for it was especially at such times that the divine hand worked—that the dropsical woman, contrary to her custom, fell asleep. Suddenly the glorious Empress, the Virgin Mary, invisibly restored her womb, emptied of its flowing moisture, swiftly to a state as slender as it was sound. You might have seen—and those present, both our brethren and many others, did see—such an abundance of effused fluid and discharged phlegm upon the ground [Col. 1224D] that it was immediately necessary to carry it away in bowls, pails, and pots. When those present were astonished at the magnitude of the event, they rendered praise all the more devoutly to almighty God and His Mother. Weeping, they sang the *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise thee, O God”), and humbly implored almighty God, as He had begun, to continue there the honour of His Mother.

Therefore, embracing the task of honouring and exalting the aforesaid distinguished place, by divine appointment, for love of the Mother of God, through these and other signs of miracles and wonders, we immediately began to have it built. We established twelve brethren there with their prior, that a community of brethren might serve God there; we built a cloister, refectory, dormitory, and the other regular buildings [Col. 1225A]. We suitably furnished the church with ornaments, priestly vestments, hangings, and copes made from such hangings. We caused two books to be brought there from the mother church: namely, the old daily service-book and the gradual of Emperor Charles. We provided a respectable library of three volumes.

No less concerned for the brethren’s provisions, we established two ploughlands on land belonging to us near the place. We planted for them an enclosed vineyard, suitable for a great abbey and in good condition; by many means we acquired an abundance of vineyards. We built for that place, at no expense to it, four wine-presses of its own, worth nearly twenty-four measures of wine; we provided so abundantly that they sometimes hold two hundred and fifty, sometimes three hundred, measures of wine. We also had sufficient meadows enclosed by ditches on their own turf; we made adequately serviceable gardens, with sufficient seeds for vegetables.

There was another estate of blessed Dionysius, long deserted and reduced to wilderness, lacking even a single cultivator. Perhaps it had been accustomed to yield from neighbouring villages, through cultivation by outsiders, a measure of grain or less, or two or three sextarii of nuts. There we established for them three ploughlands in a new farmyard and a new grange. Because of the abundance of pasture and the improvement of the land, we placed there sheep, cows, and young stock for their use.
