We also assigned from our own resources another possession of blessed Dionysius near Brunet, from which they often receive ten measures of grain [Col. 1225C], nearly ten of wine, and hay for fodder of draft animals. Whatever we recovered from a mill lost for nearly sixty years, we left to them, on condition that on the day following the feast of blessed Dionysius they pay twenty solidi to the refectory of Saint-Denis. In the same village they have one hundred solidi in rents and tallage. At Corbeil, moreover, they possess seventeen pounds from their own fixed rent, besides other revenues from sales, fairs, and other customary dues; likewise a mill and an oven, eight measures of oats with chickens, and the whole prebend of Saint Exuperius.

## Chapter XXI. Marogil

[Col. 1225D]

In the district of Meaux, a village called Marogil was grievously troubled by reason of a right of passage which Ansold of Cornelio possessed almost up to the very houses of the village. Neither peasants nor any others dared leave the village safely without being seized, on many pretexts connected with that right of passage, by Ansold’s servants and carried off under arrest to his court; likewise, livestock leaving the village were made subject to ransom. Therefore, as he was setting out on the Jerusalem expedition, we gave him one thousand solidi for the peace of that village, so that he might surrender that right of passage to us. We caused this to be confirmed as belonging henceforth to blessed Dionysius, by the hand of Manasses, bishop of Meaux, and of that church, and by the seal of Count Theobald, with the consent of his wife and son. For, as he confessed, he had unjustly usurped it.

Wishing also to make known to our successors the terms of a certain exchange, in case, by God’s help, this might some day be changed for the better, we took care to record it. While the noble realm of the Franks stood under a monarchical order, everywhere that royal power extended, throughout the four divisions of the kingdom—namely Italy, Lotharingia, Francia, and Aquitaine—the church of blessed Dionysius abounded in many great possessions through the liberality of kings. But what unity had preserved intact, filial division strove both to corrupt and diminish. Hence blessed Dionysius, having lost Herelingas, Herbertingas, Salona, and many other possessions, also lost the estates situated in the district of Metz: namely the castle of Gomundas, Blistetot, and Cochilingas. When we repeatedly pressed this claim before the Apostolic See, those who had taken them away—both because of their injustice and because of the peril to themselves, for they died wickedly and most wickedly without confession—granted to blessed Dionysius, as if by exchange, the place called Cella with its dependencies, named in the charters of Emperor Louis, in full liberty. There we placed our brethren to serve God, in hope of increase and of eventual recovery.

## Chapter XXII. Calvomont

We also laboured to obtain the church of Saint Peter at Calvomont [Col. 1226C], both the abbey and the canonries themselves as the canons died off, from Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, and from Lord Louis, king of France. We reverently established there twelve brethren with a thirteenth as prior, for the exaltation of that church and the extension of divine worship. By God’s favour we obtained from that same reverend archbishop the consecration of the church and the blessing of a cemetery before it.

This new foundation, joined like a noble member to its head, the church of blessed Dionysius, will be as useful and suitable to our successors travelling from the Vexin into Normandy, or staying in that district for the safeguarding of the remaining possessions, as they shall find it to be. So much the more, therefore, it will rightly strive to enrich and foster it from its own resources or acquisitions, as a new planting. Since the brethren serving God there lack vineyards, we confirmed to them each year twenty measures of wine from the tithes which King Louis gave us at Cergy; and half of the tithe which we acquired at Ableiges.

## Chapter XXIII. Berneval

On the estate called Berneval, on the Norman seacoast, where I received from my predecessor my first obedience in some provostship, and where in the time of the most vigorous King Henry, while I was still quite young, I had freed it from the oppression of the royal tax-gatherers called *graffiones*, through much labour and many lawsuits [Col. 1227A], we recovered for the lordship of the church, at the beginning of our prelacy, the parish churches which Roger the priest and his brother Geoffrey claimed for themselves by hereditary right. We granted these churches and their revenues in perpetuity to the treasurer, to renew and increase the hangings of this church.

And because he had almost no income for meeting this expense, we added another village in those parts, called Quadraria, recently established. It yields four marks, while the church yields seven pounds, unless it can be improved. We also caused the other customary revenues of the aforesaid village of Berneval, both rents and others, to be increased, as we believe, to nearly fifteen pounds [Col. 1227B]. The customary due commonly called the *aquaria*, which in the time of our predecessor of good memory we helped recover from our provost who had seized it, we assigned to the brethren’s annual feast-day meal on the anniversary of the most pious King Dagobert. We laboured to make the villages Moriniacum, Liliacum, and Floriacum, which had not been accustomed to yield more than seven or ten pounds, yield thirty, or at least twenty-five. The same was done with Monte-Fusceoli.

## Chapter XXIV. The Ornamentation of the Church

With these increases of revenue thus assigned, we turned our hand back to the memorable enterprise of construction, so that for this also thanks might be rendered to almighty God [Col. 1227C] by us and by our successors, and that their zeal might be encouraged by good example to continue—and, if necessary, bring to completion—this work. For neither any lack of resources nor any impediment from any power whatsoever need be feared, if, for love of the holy martyrs, they are securely served from what is their own.

The first work which, by God’s inspiration, we undertook in this church was occasioned by the age of the old materials and their threatening collapse in some places. Summoning the best painters I could find from various regions, we devoutly had them restore and honourably paint it with gold and precious colours. Since I had learned this even while at school, and had desired to do it if ever I could [Col. 1227D], I completed it the more gladly.

## Chapter XXV. The First Enlargement of the Church

But when this was already being completed at great expense, divine prompting moved us, because of the crowding which we often saw and experienced on feast days—namely on the feast of blessed Dionysius, at the Indiction, and on many other occasions. The narrowness of the place compelled women to run over men’s heads, as though over pavement, toward the altar amid much distress and noisy tumult. Therefore, to enlarge and extend the noble monastery consecrated by the divine hand, aided by the counsel of wise men and the prayers of many religious persons, lest God and the holy martyrs should be displeased, I undertook to begin the work [Col. 1228A]. In both our chapter house and the church, I supplicated divine mercy: that He who is beginning and end, that is, α and ω—alpha and omega—might join a good end to a good beginning while preserving the middle, and might not reject from the building of the temple a man of blood, who desired this work with all his heart more than he would choose to possess the treasures of Constantinople.

We therefore approached the earlier entrance of the doors; removing a certain addition which was said to have been made by Charlemagne, we set our hand there. This was done for a sufficiently honourable reason: his father, Emperor Pippin, had caused himself to be buried there, at the entrance of the doors, lying prone rather than on his back, for the sins of his father Charles Martel. As is apparent, we laboured vigorously both in enlarging the body of the church and in trebling the entrance and doors, and in raising lofty and handsome towers.

## Chapter XXVI. The Dedication

We obtained the dedication of the oratory of Saint Romanus, for the service of God and His holy angels, from the venerable Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, and many other bishops. Those who serve God there know how secluded, devout, and suitable the place is for celebrating divine worship—as though, while they sacrifice, their dwelling were already in part in heaven. At the same celebration of dedication, in the lower vault of the church, two oratories were dedicated on either side: that of Saint Hippolytus and his companions on one side, and that of Saint Nicholas on the other, by the venerable men Manasses, bishop of Meaux, and Peter of Senlis [Col. 1228C].

When their single and glorious procession came out through the door of Saint Eustace and crossed before the principal gates, amid a great throng of clergy singing and people rejoicing, the bishops leading and attending to the holy consecration, they entered for the third time by the exceptional gate of the atrium, transferred from the old work into the new. When the festive work had been completed to the honour of almighty God and we prepared to labour on the upper part, they refreshed us somewhat in our weariness and most gladly encouraged us, lest fear of work or any lack should dishearten us.

## Chapter XXVII. The Cast and Gilded Doors

[Col. 1228D]

We erected the principal doors, summoning metal-casters and selecting sculptors, in which are represented the Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension of the Saviour. At great expense, and with much outlay upon their gilding, as befitted the noble porch, we raised them. We also provided other new doors on the right side, while retaining ancient ones on the left beneath a mosaic, which we laboured to have made here, contrary to custom, and set into the arch of the doorway. We also ordered that the tower and the upper defensive works of the façade be embellished, both for the beauty of the church and for use if necessity required; and we commanded the year of consecration to be inscribed in gilded copper letters, lest it be consigned to oblivion, in this manner:

> For the glory of the Church which nourished and raised him,  
> Suger laboured for the glory of the Church.  
> And, sharing in your possession, martyr Dionysius,  
> He prays that you may pray for him to share in Paradise.  
> The year was one thousand, one hundred, and forty  
> From the Word, when it was consecrated.

The verses on the doors are these:

> Whoever you are that seek to exalt the honour of these doors,  
> Marvel not at the gold or the cost, but at the labour of the work.  
> The work shines nobly; but may the work which shines nobly  
> Brighten minds, so that they may go through true lights  
> To the true Light, where Christ is the true door.  
> The golden door defines in these things what is within.  
> The dull mind rises to truth through material things,  
> And, first submerged, rises again at the sight of this light.

And on the lintel:

> Receive the prayers of your Suger, stern Judge;  
> In your mercy, let me be counted among your own sheep.

## Chapter XXVIII. The Enlargement of the Upper Part

[Col. 1229B]

In the same year, rejoicing in so holy and fortunate a work, we hastened to begin the sanctuary of divine propitiation in the upper part, where the continual and frequent sacrifice of our redemption ought to be offered in secret, without disturbance from crowds. As is found in the inscription of dedication for this upper work, by God’s cooperation and by His prospering of us and what was ours, we deserved mercifully to obtain, together with our brethren and fellow servants, the bringing of so holy, glorious, and renowned a work to a good end. We are so much the more indebted to God and the holy martyrs because He reserved for our times and labours what had been so long delayed.

For who am I [Col. 1229C], or what is my father’s house, that I should have dared either to begin so noble and welcome a building or to hope to complete it, unless, trusting in divine mercy and the aid of the holy martyrs, I had devoted my entire self to that work in mind and body? Yet He who gave the will also gave the power; and because the will concerned a good work, it endured unto completion through God’s help. A sure proof of how much the divine hand protected this glorious work, so active in such matters, is that in three years and three months that whole magnificent work—varied by so many divisions of arches and columns, in the lower crypt and in the soaring height of the upper vaults—received even the complete addition of its roof.

Therefore the epitaph of the earlier dedication, with a single word removed, also marks the yearly limit of this work:

> The year was one thousand, one hundred, and forty-four  
> From the Word, when it was consecrated.

To the verses of that epitaph we chose to add these:

> When the new rear part is joined to the front,  
> The hall shines, made bright in its middle.  
> For what is joined brightly to bright things shines,  
> And the work which new light floods shines nobly.  
> This work, which was enlarged in our time, stands complete—  
> While I, Suger, was its leader as it was made.

Eager, therefore, to press forward with my successes, since beneath heaven I preferred nothing to advancing the honour of the mother Church—which had nursed me as a child with maternal affection, endured me in my offending youth [Col. 1230A], strongly fortified me in mature age, and solemnly placed me among the princes of Church and kingdom—we devoted ourselves to executing the work and strove to raise and complete the lateral transepts of the church, joining them to the design of the earlier and later works.

## Chapter XXIX. The Continuation of Both Works

When this had been done, we had, at the persuasion of certain persons, directed our efforts toward carrying on the towers of the western part. But the divine will, as we believe, drew us back after the work on the other part was accomplished, so that we might undertake to renew the middle vaulting of the church, called the nave, and make it conform and equal to the two renewed works. We preserved, however, whatever portion we could of the ancient walls upon which the supreme pontiff, the Lord Jesus Christ, had laid His hand, according to the testimony of ancient writers, so that both reverence for the old consecration and a fitting coherence with the new work, according to the plan begun, might be preserved.

The chief reason for this alteration was that, if work on the nave were interrupted because of the towers, it would be completed more slowly—or perhaps never—whether in our time or that of our successors, through some misfortune. No pressure of circumstances would force the builders onward; rather, the joining of new and old work would endure a long delay. But because work has now begun in the spreading of the wings, it will be completed, with His aid, either by us or by those whom the Lord chooses. The recollection of past things is the assurance of future things. For He who, among other greater matters, has supplied even workers for the admirable windows, an abundant stock of sapphires, and ready expenditures of nearly seven hundred pounds or more, will not permit the most generous Lord to fail in providing what remains to be done. For He is the beginning and the end.

## Chapter XXX. The Ornaments of the Church

We judged it fitting to record the description of the church’s ornaments, with which the divine hand, during our administration, adorned His Church called His bride, lest forgetfulness—the enemy of truth—creep in and remove the example for future action. We both confess and proclaim our thrice-blessed lord Dionysius to be so generous and gracious that we believe he has accomplished and obtained so many and such great things with God that we might have advanced his Church a hundredfold beyond what we have done, had human frailty, the changes of times, and the inconstancy of customs not stood in the way. Nevertheless, by God’s gift, these are the things we have reserved for it.

## Chapter XXXI. The Upper Gold Panel

We estimate that we placed about forty-two marks of gold on the panel which stands before his most sacred body. We found a multiple abundance of precious gems—hyacinths, rubies, sapphires, emeralds, topazes—and also pearls arranged in dividing patterns, in a quantity we had never dared hope to find. You might see kings, princes, and many eminent men following our example: removing rings from their fingers and commanding the gold of the rings, together with gems and precious pearls, to be fixed on that panel for love of the holy martyrs. Archbishops and bishops likewise placed their very rings of espousal there in safekeeping, offering them most devoutly to God and His saints. Such a crowd of gem dealers from diverse kingdoms and peoples flowed to us that we did not seek to buy more eagerly than they hastened to sell under every form of administration. The verses on that panel are these:

> Great Dionysius, open the gates of Paradise,  
> And protect Suger with gracious safeguards.  
> You who, through us, established a new sanctuary for yourself,  
> Make us received into the chamber of heaven;  
> And let us be satisfied at the present table of heaven.  
> Things signified delight more through that which signifies.

Because it was necessary to place the most sacred bodies of our lords as nobly as possible in the upper vault, certain side panels of their most holy sarcophagus having been removed, for what reason we do not know, we restored fifteen marks of gold and caused its outer front and upper covering to be gilded throughout, below and above, with nearly forty ounces. We also had it enclosed with cast and gilded bronze panels, polished stones set into them because of the inner stone vaults, and continuous doors to ward off the disturbance of crowds [Col. 1231C]. Yet venerable persons can, as is fitting, behold the vessels containing the saints’ bodies with great devotion and an outpouring of tears. These are the verses on the tombs of those saints:

> Where the heavenly company watches over the saints’ ashes,  
> The people pray and weep; the clergy sing upon the ten-stringed instrument.  
> To their spirits the prayers of the devout are brought;  
> And, when those spirits are pleased, their evils are forgiven.  
> The bodies of the saints lie here buried in peace;  
> May they draw us after them, as we pray with many prayers.  
> Here this place stands as an outstanding refuge for those who come;  
> Here is safe flight for the guilty, though the avenger has power over them.

## Chapter XXXII. The Golden Crucifix

[Col. 1231D]

We strove with all devotion of mind, if possible, to have adorned all the more gloriously the adorable, life-giving cross—the saving banner of the eternal victory of our Saviour—of which the Apostle says: “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.” It is the sign of the Son of Man, glorious not only to human beings but even to the angels themselves, appearing at the end in heaven. We continually greeted it with the apostle Andrew: “Hail, cross, consecrated in the body of Christ and adorned from His limbs as with pearls.” Yet because we could not do as we wished, we wished what we could do better, and by God’s gift laboured to carry it out.

Accordingly, seeking an abundance of precious pearls and gems everywhere, both personally and through our envoys, we prepared the most precious material we could find in gold and gems for so great an ornament, and summoned the most skilled craftsmen from various places. They were to fashion it carefully and painstakingly, raising the venerable cross behind in the wonder of those very gems, while displaying in front, in the sight of the priest celebrating sacrifice, the image of the Lord Saviour for prayer, in remembrance of His Passion, as though He were still suffering on the cross. Blessed Dionysius had indeed lain in that same place for five hundred years and more, from the time of Dagobert down to our own.

We did not wish to pass over in silence one amusing but noble miracle which the Lord showed us concerning this. For when I was hindered by a shortage of gems and could not adequately provide for the matter—for scarcity makes them more expensive—behold: representatives of two orders and three abbeys, namely Cîteaux and another abbey of the same order, and Fontevraud, entered our little treasury adjoining the church and offered us for purchase such an abundance of gems—hyacinths, sapphires, rubies, emeralds, and topazes—as we had not hoped to find in ten years. Those who had them had obtained them from Count Theobald as alms; he, in turn, had received them through the hand of Stephen, his brother, king of England, from the treasures of his deceased uncle King Henry, which he had amassed throughout his life in wonderful cups. Freed from the burden of seeking gems [Col. 1232C], we gave four hundred pounds for them, though they were worth considerably more. And we added not only those, but also a great and costly abundance of other gems and pearls, for the completion of so holy an ornament.

Of refined gold, if I remember correctly, we placed about eighty marks. The base, adorned with the four Evangelists; the column upon which the holy image sits, enamelled with the most delicate workmanship; the history of the Saviour, depicted with testimonies from allegories of the Old Law; and the upper capital, representing in astonishing images the death of the Lord—all this was completed only with difficulty in two years, by several Lotharingian goldsmiths, sometimes five and sometimes seven.

The mercy of our Saviour, hastening to honour and exalt still more the ornament of so great and holy an object, brought Pope Eugenius to us to celebrate holy Easter, as is customary for Roman pontiffs staying in Gaul, in honour of the holy apostolate of blessed Dionysius. We had seen the same in the cases of his predecessors Callixtus and Innocent. On that day he solemnly consecrated the crucifix. From the title of the Lord’s true cross, which surpasses every and all pearls, he assigned a portion from his chapel to it. Publicly before all, he anathematized, with the sword of blessed Peter and the sword of the Holy Spirit, whoever should steal anything from it or sacrilegiously lay hands upon it [Col. 1233A]. We caused that same anathema to be inscribed below upon the cross.

We also hastened to have the principal altar of blessed Dionysius ornamented. Previously it had had only one splendid and precious front panel, given by Emperor Charles the Bald, the third Charles; since we had been offered to that altar for the monastic life, we set golden panels on both sides and raised a fourth, still more precious panel, causing the whole altar to be encircled so that it appeared golden on every side. Along the sides we placed candlesticks of twenty marks of gold, belonging to King Louis Philip, depositing there hyacinths, emeralds, and every sort of precious gem, lest they be taken away on any pretext; and we decreed that gems should diligently continue to be sought and added. The verses on them are these:

On the right side:

> Abbot Suger set these panels upon the altar,  
> Apart from that which King Charles gave before.  
> Make those unworthy of pardon worthy, Virgin Mary.  
> May the fountain of mercy cleanse the evils of king and abbot.

On the left side:

> If any impious man despoils the splendid altar,  
> Let him perish equally condemned, joined to Judas.

We also exalted the older panel, remarkable in workmanship and lavish expense, since foreign craftsmen were more lavish than ours. It was wonderful both in form and material, executed in relief work, so that some might say that the workmanship surpassed the material. We caused many things from our acquisitions, and still more from the church ornaments which we feared might be lost, to be fixed upon it: namely a gold chalice with its foot cut short [Col. 1233C], and certain other things. And because the diversity of materials—gold, gems, and pearls—is not easily known by the unspoken knowledge of sight without explanation, we caused to be set down in written letters a work open only to the literate, shining with the radiance of delightful allegories. We also added verses speaking of the same thing, so that it might be understood more clearly:

> With a loud voice the people cry “Hosanna” to Christ;  
> The true victim, given at the supper, took away all offerings.  
> He hastens to bear the cross, who saves all upon the cross.  
> What Abraham sacrifices for offspring signifies Christ’s flesh.  
> Melchizedek makes an offering when Abraham triumphs over the enemy.  
> Those who seek Christ with the cross carry the cluster upon a pole.

Thus, while we frequently considered these distinctions between ornaments, both new and old [Col. 1233D], from the very affection of Mother Church herself, as we gazed upon that admirable cross of Saint Eligius with its smaller crosses, and upon the incomparable ornament commonly called the *crista*, placed above the golden altar, we sighed from the depths of our heart: “Every precious stone was thy covering: sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald.” Of these stones, except for carbuncle alone, none is lacking—as is manifest, to the great amazement of those who know the properties of gems—but rather they abound most copiously.

Therefore, when at times, out of love for the beauty of God’s house, the many-coloured loveliness of gems drew me away from outward cares, and worthy meditation persuaded me to pass from material to immaterial things, through the diversity also of holy virtues, I seemed to see myself dwelling, as it were, in some strange region of the earthly world, which existed neither wholly amid the dregs of the earth nor wholly in the purity of heaven; and, by God’s gift, I seemed able to be transferred from this lower to that higher world in an anagogical manner.

I used to compare these things with those at Jerusalem, and gladly inquire of people to whom the treasures of Constantinople and the ornaments of Hagia Sophia had been accessible whether these ought to have any value in comparison with those. Since they acknowledged that these were greater, it seemed to us that the remarkable things we had formerly heard about had been prudently concealed out of fear of the Franks, lest the newly admitted intercourse of Greeks and Latins, through the impetuous greed of certain fools, should suddenly stir up sedition and the scandals of war [Col. 1234B]. For cunning is especially characteristic of the Greeks. Thus it may have happened that the greater things are those which appear here, stored safely away, rather than those which appeared there, left insecurely because of disturbances.

For we had heard from very many truthful men, and from Hugh, bishop of Laon, during the celebration of Mass, wonderful and almost incredible things concerning the pre-eminence of the ornaments of Hagia Sophia and of other churches. If these things are so—or rather, because we believe them to be so on their testimony—they would, in the judgment of many, be pronounced as inestimable as they are incomparable. Let each abound in his own judgment.

For my part, I confess that this above all pleased me: that whatever is more precious, whatever most precious, ought above all things to serve the administration of the most holy Eucharist [Col. 1234C]. If golden libation-vessels, golden bowls, and golden mortars for gathering the blood of goats, calves, or the red heifer served at the command of God or of the prophet, how much more should golden vessels, precious stones, and whatever among all created things is most precious be continually devoted, with full devotion, to receiving the blood of Jesus Christ. Certainly neither we nor what is ours suffices for this service. If we were changed by a new creation into the substance of the holy cherubim and seraphim, we should nevertheless render insufficient and unworthy service to so great and ineffable a sacrifice. Yet we possess so great a propitiation for our sins.

Those who disparage this also object that a holy mind, a pure heart, and faithful intention are sufficient for this administration [Col. 1234D]. We indeed approve that these are chiefly, properly, and specially required. Yet concerning the outward adornment of sacred vessels, we profess that nothing whatsoever ought to serve as fittingly as the service of the holy sacrifice, with every inward purity and every outward nobility. For in all things universally we ought to serve our Redeemer in the most fitting manner: he who did not refuse to provide for us universally in all things, without any exception; who united our nature to his own in one wondrous individual; who, setting us at his right hand, truly promised that we should possess his kingdom—our Lord, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages.

[Col. 1235A] We also undertook to renew the altar which, by the testimony of the ancients, is called the holy altar. For the glorious king Louis, son of Philip, was accustomed to say that, while he was brought up here from childhood, he had learned from the elders of the place that it appeared insufficiently well adorned because of age, because faithful custody had failed, and also because it was frequently moved on account of the most noble furnishings which are set up for different persons on different feasts, the more splendid for the more splendid feasts. We undertook this work out of reverence for the holy relics.

The consecrated porphyry stone remaining upon the altar, suitable enough no less in the quality of its colour than in its considerable size, was surrounded by hollow wood covered with gold, which had become very broken through the very patching of its age. By the ingenious arrangement of this hollow structure, the arm of Saint James the Apostle was believed to lie at the front [Col. 1235B], as the inner inscription itself testified, visible through an opening of the purest crystal. Likewise, on the right side, the appearance of a corresponding inscription declared that the arm of Stephen the protomartyr was enclosed; and on the left an inscription within similarly proclaimed the arm of Saint Vincent, levite and martyr.

Desiring, therefore, to be fortified by the protection of relics so great and holy, I was for a long course of time most gladly carried away by the wish to see them and kiss them, if I did not fear that this might displease God. Taking boldness, therefore, from devotion, while preserving due honour for antiquity and truth, we chose a manner and day for uncovering the holy relics: namely, the most sacred day of martyrdom of our blessed martyrs and lords, the eighth day before the Ides of October.

There were present archbishops and bishops from different provinces, who had come most gladly, as though by a duty owed to the apostolate of Gaul, to offer pious vows at the celebration of so great a solemnity: the archbishops of Lyons, Rheims, Tours, and Rouen; and the bishops of Soissons, Beauvais, Senlis, Meaux, Rennes, Aleth, and Vannes [Col. 1235C]. There was also an assembly of abbots, monks, clerics, and nobles, as well as an innumerable throng of people of both sexes.

Accordingly, when Terce had been sung on the same day of the feast and the most celebrated procession for so great a day was already being arranged before all those present, we summoned the archbishops and bishops, abbots, and other authoritative persons present to carry forth the altar. With such confidence in the truth of the matter, supported only by the testimony of the Fathers and by the inscription, as though we had already seen everything, we explained that we wished to open it and see the treasure of the most holy relics [Col. 1235D].

Certain members of our household said—prudently indeed—that it would have been safer for both the persons involved and the Church’s reputation to see secretly whether matters were as the inscriptions stated. To them, at once stirred by fervour of faith, I replied that, if things were as they were read, I preferred that all who beheld should know it, rather than that, if I inspected it secretly, all who did not behold should remain doubtful.

Therefore, having brought the aforesaid altar into the midst, and having summoned goldsmiths to open carefully the little receptacles containing the most holy arms, on which crystal stones rested and which bore their inscriptions [Col. 1236A], we found, as we had hoped, everything in full, God consenting, before the eyes of all. We also discovered why the relics had been placed in those receptacles: namely, because the Emperor Charles the Third, who lies gloriously buried beneath the same altar, had by imperial decree directed that they should be taken for him from the imperial shrine and deposited with him, for the protection of his soul and body. There too we found the proof marked by the impression of his ring, which pleased everyone greatly.

For not without reason had he established that seven lamps in silver vessels should burn continually before that holy altar, by day and night, forever—lamps which we, indeed, report as having been taken down—unless he had placed his greatest hope for both body and soul in the deposition of the holy relics [Col. 1236B]. For the support of these lamps and for the refreshment on his anniversary and those of his people, he confirmed with golden seals his estate called Ruoilum, together with its dependencies. Hence also it is that on nearly sixty different feast days six great and handsome candles, such as are rarely or never set up elsewhere in the church, are lit around that altar. Hence too, whenever the altar of blessed Dionysius is adorned, this altar also is adorned with noble furnishings.

We also caused to be raised a cross of remarkable size, placed between the altar and the tomb of the same Charles. In its middle, tradition held, was fastened the very noble necklace of Nantildis, queen and wife of King Dagobert, founder of the church; another necklace was set upon the forehead of Saint Dionysius—though the most skilful craftsmen testify that none equals this smaller one [Col. 1236C]. This was done especially out of reverence for the most holy iron *hoja* [perhaps “collar”], which, fastened around the most sacred neck of blessed Dionysius in the prison of Glaucinus, has deserved worship and veneration both from us and from all others.

For his part, the venerable Robert, abbot of Corbie, of good memory, professed in this holy church and brought up here from childhood—whom, by God’s grant, we had appointed abbot over the monastery of Corbie—caused to be made a finely gilded silver panel, in acknowledgment of his profession and in thanksgiving for the many benefits of the church.

We also changed the choir of the brethren, which those constantly occupied in the church’s service found very burdensome and somewhat unhealthy because of the coldness of marble and bronze [Col. 1236D], into the form now visible, in compassion for their labours; and, with God’s help, we worked to enlarge it because the community had increased.

We also caused the ancient pulpit to be repaired. Its marvellous ivory panels, with their exceedingly delicate carving—irreparable in our age—and their depiction of ancient histories exceeded human estimation. The panels, which had long lain defiled in the storage of chests and beneath chests, were gathered up; bronze animals were restored on its right side; and, lest material so great and so wonderful should perish, we caused it to be raised for the public reading above of the holy Gospel [Col. 1237A]. At the beginning of our tenure we had caused a certain obstruction to be removed from the middle, by which the centre of the church had been divided by a dark wall, lest the beauty of so great a church should be obscured by such barriers.

We likewise caused the noble chair of the glorious King Dagobert to be repaired. According to ancient report, the kings of the Franks, on assuming royal power, were accustomed first to sit in it to receive the homages of their nobles. It had become old and broken, and we restored it both because of the excellence of so great an office and because of the value of the work itself.

We caused the eagle in the middle of the choir, whose gilding had been worn away by the frequent touch of admirers, to be gilded again.

[Col. 1237B] We also caused a splendid variety of new windows to be painted by the skilful hands of many masters from different nations, from the first, beginning with the Tree of Jesse at the head of the church, as far as the one above the principal door at the church entrance, both above and below. One of them, leading upward from material to immaterial things, represents the Apostle Paul turning a millstone and the Prophets bringing sacks to the mill. Its verses are these:

> By working the mill, Paul, you take flour from the bran;  
> You make known the inner meaning of the Mosaic law.  
> From so many grains comes true bread without bran,  
> Our everlasting and angelic food.

Likewise, in the same window, where the veil is taken from Moses’ face [Col. 1237C]:

> What Moses veils, Christ’s teaching reveals;  
> They uncover the law who strip Moses.

In the same window, above the Ark of the Covenant:

> From the Ark of the Covenant Christ’s altar is shown through the cross;  
> In the greater covenant, Life wills to die there.

Likewise, in the same window, where the Lion and the Lamb open the book:

> He who is the great God—the Lion and the Lamb—opens the book.  
> Lamb or Lion, he becomes flesh joined to God.

In another window, where Pharaoh’s daughter finds Moses in a basket:

> Moses, that boy, is in the basket;  
> The royal maiden, in pious thought, cherishes him—the Church.

In the same window, where the Lord appears to Moses in the fire of the bush:

[Col. 1237D]

> As this bush is seen to burn, yet is not consumed,  
> So, filled with God, it ventures upon this fire, yet is not consumed.

Likewise, in the same window, where Pharaoh and his cavalry are submerged in the sea:

> What baptism does for the good,  
> A like figure, though from an unlike cause, does for Pharaoh’s army.

Likewise, in the same window, where Moses raises the bronze serpent:

> As the bronze serpent kills all serpents,  
> So Christ, raised upon the cross, kills his enemies.

In the same window, where Moses receives the law on the mountain:

> When the law was given to Moses, Christ’s grace aids it.  
> Grace gives life; the letter kills.

Since these windows, clothed in glass and in sapphire material, were made at great expense and with marvellous workmanship [Col. 1238A], we appointed for their protection and repair a master craftsman in charge, just as we appointed a skilled goldsmith for the gold and silver ornaments. They are to receive their prebends and what was assigned to them for this purpose—namely, money from the altar and provisions from the common granary of the brethren—and they are never to withdraw themselves from their oversight.

We also caused seven candlesticks to be made in enamelled work and excellently gilded, since those which the Emperor Charles had given to blessed Dionysius appeared ruined by age.

We acquired with fitting devotion, for the service of the Lord’s table, vessels both of gold and of precious stones, in addition to those which kings of the Franks and persons devoutly attached to the service of this church had assigned to blessed Dionysius [Col. 1238B]. We had restored a great golden chalice of one hundred and forty ounces of gold, adorned with precious gems, namely jacinths and topazes, in place of another which had been lost in pawn during the time of our predecessor.

We also offered to blessed Dionysius another most precious vessel, carved from green prase stone in the shape of a ship. When it had been offered to us for inspection, it was bought, with the permission of King Louis son of Philip, for sixty marks of silver, since that king had lost it in pawn for nearly ten years. We offered it along with certain flowers from the Empress’s crown. The vessel is marvellous both because of the quality of its precious stone and because of its unbroken size, and it is known to be adorned with enclosed work by Saint Eligius [Col. 1238C]; in everyone’s judgment it is considered most precious.

Another vessel, which seems to be of pure beryl or crystal, the newly married queen gave to King Louis, her lord, on the first expedition into Aquitaine, as a great token of love. She gave it to us, and we in turn most affectionately presented it to our holy martyrs and lords for use in the libation of the divine table. We inscribed the account of this gift upon the same vessel, adorned with gems and gold, in these little verses:

> The bride Aanor gave this vessel to King Louis;  
> Mitadolus [gave it] to his grandfather, the king to me, and Suger to the saints.

We also acquired for the service of the aforesaid altar a precious chalice of a single, continuous sardonyx [Col. 1238D]—that is, of sardius and onyx—in which the red of the sardius is so distinguished from the blackness of the onyx by the variation of its natural character that each appears to encroach upon, and lean upon, the character of the other.

We added another vessel of the same material, though not at all similar in form, in the likeness of an amphora. Its verses are these:

> Since we ought to make libation to God with gems and gold,  
> I, Suger, offer this vessel to the Lord.

We also gratefully assigned to the same service a splendid flask which Count Theobald of Blois sent us in that very vessel in which the king of Sicily had sent it to him, along with other objects.

We also deposited there the crystal vessels which we had assigned to the daily service of the altar in our chapel [Col. 1239A].

Likewise, a porphyry vessel, admirably made by the hand of a sculptor and polisher, had lain unused in a chest for many years. Transforming it from an amphora into the form of an eagle, we adapted it to the altar’s service with gold and silver material, and caused verses of this kind to be inscribed upon it:

> This stone deserves to be enclosed in gems and gold:  
> It was marble, but in these it is dearer than marble.

For all these things we give thanks to almighty God and to the holy Martyrs, because he did not refuse to grant abundantly to the most holy altar—to which, under the command of the holy Rule, he willed that we should be offered from childhood [Col. 1240A], so that we might serve him honourably.

Therefore, because we have recognized it as useful and honourable not to conceal but to proclaim divine benefits, we have recorded the increase of the liturgical cloths which the divine hand bestowed upon this holy church during the time of our administration. We pray that they may be displayed on the anniversary, to win the favour of the divine majesty, to enlarge the devotion of the brethren, and to provide an example for successor abbots. For neither such late nor such infrequent penitence suffices to make satisfaction for so many and such great offences committed by me, or for the enormity of my sins, unless we lean upon the suffrages of the universal Church.

[Col. 1239]

# Little Book of Abbot Suger of Saint-Denis on the Consecration of the Church Built by Him and the Translation of the Bodies of Saint Dionysius and His Companions, Performed in the Year 1140

(Dom Félibien, *History of the Royal Abbey of Saint-Denis in France*, Paris, 1796, folio, Proofs, p. CLXXXVII.)

[Col. 1239B] The admirable power of one single and supreme Reason, harmoniously tempering the disparity of divine and human things, makes them equal; and by the pleasing concord of one higher, ordered harmony alone joins together things which seem to oppose one another through the inferiority of their origin and the contrary character of their nature.

Those who strive to become glorious through participation in this supreme and eternal Reason frequently sit, as though in a tribunal, upon the throne of an acute mind. They labour at the continuous contest of like and unlike things, at discovery and judgment; from the fountain of the reason of eternal wisdom, with charity as its minister, they beneficially draw that by which they may resist inward warfare and internal sedition. Preferring spiritual things to bodily and eternal things to perishable things, they set aside the vexations and most grievous exactions of the outward senses of bodily sensation [Col. 1239C]. Raising themselves from their oppression, they fix the firmest gaze of the mind upon hope of eternal reward and zealously obey eternity alone. They forget carnal desires, exposed to the amazement and spectacle of others; and, in this manner, through the fellowship of supreme Reason and eternal blessedness, they rejoice to be joined by the merit of a glorious conscience, the only-begotten Son of God promising: “By your endurance you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

Yet humanity, crushed and grievously wounded by the corruption of its first condition, embracing present things rather than awaiting future things, could in no way endure this, unless the abundant ministry of reasonable human reason and of divine charity mercifully supplied what was needed to bring this very thing into effect. Hence it is written: “His mercy is over all his works” (Psalm 144:9).

Accordingly, together with others, we boldly and truthfully profess that, just as mercy alone saves us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, so we ought to labour—with the most grateful holocaust of a purified mind—to offer to him in suppliant devotion all our righteousness, insofar as he himself grants it, with all our will and ability [Col. 1240C]. Thus may he who can do so as God, and ought to do so as Creator if we do not resist, make equal in us this dangerous disparity. May he dissolve the enmities of inward opposition which we incurred through the first transgression, in losing his friendship [Col. 1241A], by that ineffable love through which he ineffably and inseparably united his divinity to our captive humanity. When the most grievous vexation of carnality is lulled and the tumult of vices stilled, may he bring the warring inward elements into peace within a tranquil dwelling-place, so that, free in mind and body and offering him acceptable service, we may be able to recount and proclaim the immeasurable generosity of his benefits toward us and toward the noble church which he deigned to set above us. Otherwise, should we prove mute in his praise, we may incur a deficiency of his benefits for this reason and hear that terrible voice: “No one was found who returned to give glory to God” (Luke 17:18).

Therefore, justified by faith and having, according to the Apostle, peace with God through our inward peace [Col. 1241B], we have worked to commit to writing for the knowledge of our successors one singular benefit among many bestowed by divine generosity. Like those who freely return gifts granted to them to their donors in order to give thanks, we set forth the glorious and God-worthy consecration of this holy church, and the most sacred translation of our most precious lords and apostles Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, and of other saints upon whose ready patronage we rely. We record for what cause, in what order, how solemnly, and by which persons this was done, so that we may both return, to the best of our power, worthy thanks to divine mercy for so great a gift, and obtain from God the timely intercession of our holy protectors [Col. 1241C], both because of the care expended upon so great a work and because of the record of so great a solemnity.

The glorious and renowned Dagobert, king of the Franks, though conspicuous for royal greatness of spirit in governing his kingdom, was nonetheless devoted to the Church of God. When he fled to the village of Catulliacum to escape the intolerable anger of his father Clothar the Great, he discovered without delay, in word and deed, that the venerable images of the holy martyrs resting there—appearing as most beautiful men clad in snow-white garments—asked for his service and promised help. With marvellous devotion he commanded that a basilica for the saints should be built with royal magnificence.

Having constructed it with a wonderful variety of marble columns and enriched it beyond estimation with abundant treasures of purest gold and silver, he caused cloths covered in gold and richly adorned with varieties of pearls to be hung upon its walls, columns, and arches [Col. 1241D]. Thus it seemed to surpass the ornaments of other churches and, flourishing with incomparable brilliance in every respect and adorned with every earthly beauty, shone with inestimable splendour. One thing only it lacked: it did not admit the size that it ought to have had. This was not because anything was lacking from his devotion or his will, but perhaps because at that time in the early Church there was as yet none either greater or equal; or because, being shorter, it reflected the brightness of flashing gold and gems smiling upon nearby eyes more keenly and delightfully, and thus shone more than sufficiently, as it might not have done had it been larger.

Because of the welcome opportunity offered by this remarkable shortness, when the number of the faithful increased and people frequently flocked to seek the saints’ aid, the aforesaid basilica was accustomed to suffer such inconveniences that, especially on solemn feast days, being extremely full, it often poured back through all its doors the excess crowds pressing against it [Col. 1242A]. It compelled not only those entering not to enter, but even those who had already entered to depart, driven out by those following them.

At times you might see, a wondrous sight, that people striving to enter for the veneration and kissing of the holy relics of the Nails and Crown of the Lord were met with such resistance from the amassed multitude that amid innumerable thousands none could move a foot. In their compression none could do anything but stand, like a marble statue, be stupefied, and cry out—the one thing still possible.

The crush among women was so great and so intolerable that, pressed among strong men as in a winepress, they displayed bloodless faces as though death were imagined, cried out terribly in the manner of women in labour, and many of them, miserably trampled underfoot, were lifted above the heads of men by the compassionate help of other men and moved along as though clinging to the pavement. Many, too, gasping their last breath, lay panting in the meadow of the brethren, while all despaired of them [Col. 1242B].

The brethren, displaying the tokens of the Lord’s Passion to those approaching, gave way before their crowding and contention; having nowhere to turn, they often escaped through the windows with the relics. I heard of this while I was a schoolboy being educated among the brethren; I grieved at it as a young man outside the community, and as a mature man earnestly desired its correction.

But when it pleased him who “set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me by his grace,” despite merits that opposed it, to appoint my smallness to the administration of this great holy church, drawn by the ineffable mercy of almighty God and by the aid of our holy martyr-lords, we resolved to hasten with all our heart and all the affection of our mind toward enlarging the aforesaid place [Col. 1242C]. We should never have presumed either to put our hand to it or even to conceive it, had not an opportunity so great, necessary, useful, and honourable required it.

Therefore, since the portico before the principal entrance on the north side, at the main doors, was constricted on either hand by paired towers—narrow, not high, not very suitable, and threatening ruin—we began, God working with us, vigorously to labour in that part upon the material foundation of a straight vault and twin towers, very strong indeed, but upon the spiritual foundation still stronger, of which it is said: “No one can lay another foundation than that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians 3:11) [Col. 1242D].

Relying on his inestimable counsel and irresistible aid, we advanced so far in a work so great and costly that, having first expended little and then, through accomplishing much, requiring nothing at all, we even confessed in abundance: “Our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5) [Col. 1243A]. By God’s gift there came to hand a new quarry of stone of such strength and such quantity as had never been found in these regions. A skilful abundance of masons, stonecutters, sculptors, and other workmen followed, so that through this and other means the divinity delivered us from what we feared, strengthening our resolve and providing unexpected help.

I compared the least things with the greatest: not even Solomon’s resources could have sufficed for the Temple more than ours could suffice for this work, unless the author of that work himself had abundantly prepared the means for its executors. The identity of author and work produces the sufficiency of the worker.

In works of this kind I was especially concerned with the suitability and coherence of the old and new work [Col. 1243B], wondering, examining, and searching throughout the remote regions of many lands where we might obtain marble columns, or columns equal to marble. Since we found none, there remained only this for our labouring mind and heart: to have them brought from the city—for we had often seen wonderful ones at Rome, in the palace of Diocletian and in other baths—at great expense, by a safe ship across the Mediterranean Sea, then through the English Channel and up the winding course of the River Seine, with the assistance of friends and even of nearby Saracen enemies. For many years and long periods we were troubled by thinking and searching about this.

Then, suddenly, the generous bounty of the Almighty, condescending to our labours, revealed what we were neither permitted to think nor to imagine: columns fitting and most desirable, to the astonishment of all, through the merits of the holy martyrs [Col. 1243C]. And the more, against hope and human expectation, divine mercy deigned to grant them in a place suitable and nowhere more pleasing to us, the more we judged it worthwhile to return greater thanks for relief from so great a labour.

For an admirable quarry lay near the fortress of Pontoise, bordering the confines of our lands: a deep valley hollowed not by nature but by human industry, which from ancient times had provided employment for stonecutters making millstones. Having hitherto produced nothing remarkable, it had, as we supposed, reserved the beginning of so great a usefulness for so great and divine a building, as first-fruits for God and the holy martyrs.

Whenever the columns were drawn up from the foot of the slope by ropes tied round them, both our own people and devout persons from nearby places, noble and ignoble alike, fastened to the ropes by their arms, chests, and shoulders, hauled them out in place of draught animals [Col. 1243D]. Through the slopes in the middle of the fortress, different officials, leaving the tools of their offices, came to meet them, contributing their own strength to the difficulty of the journey and serving God and the holy martyrs with whatever aid they could. Thus there occurred a noble miracle worthy of reporting, which we ourselves learned from those present and resolved to commit to pen and ink in praise of the Almighty and his saints.

One day, when dark gloom had covered the sky troubled by the pouring out of rain, the carts coming to the quarry were without the helpers customarily engaged in the work, for they had kept themselves away because of the assault of the downpour [Col. 1244A]. The ox-drivers complained and protested that they were left idle while the workmen were being awaited. They pressed their protests so insistently that certain feeble and weak persons, together with some boys, seventeen in number, hurried to the quarry, with a priest present, unless I am mistaken. Taking one rope, they tied it round the column and left another stake lying in the earth; for there was no one who undertook to pull it.

Then the little flock, encouraged by pious zeal, said: “Saint Dionysius, taking for your own sake this idle stake, help us, if you please. For you cannot blame us if we are unable.” Immediately, exerting themselves strongly, they drew out of the deep valley what one hundred and forty, or scarcely fewer than one hundred, had customarily drawn out with difficulty. They did so not by themselves, which would have been impossible, but by the will of God and the assistance of the saints whom they invoked [Col. 1244B]. They sent it on a cart for the building of the church. Thereupon it was proclaimed throughout the whole neighbourhood that this work greatly pleased almighty God, since he had chosen to bring help to its workers by these and similar signs, for the praise and glory of his name.

There follows another noble deed, worthy of memory, conspicuous in its account, and deserving proclamation by its authority. When a great part of the work had been completed, and the roofs of the new and old structures joined together, we were relieved of the great fear we had long felt because of the wide fissures of the ancient walls and the breaking of the columns supporting the great capitals and bases [Col. 1244C]. We accordingly set about fitting the buildings together.

When we had consulted both our own carpenters and the Parisian craftsmen in timber about finding beams, we received the reply—which was true according to their judgment—that in these regions they could by no means be found because of the scarcity of forests, and that they would necessarily have to be brought from the district of Auxerre. Since all agreed upon this, we were distressed both by the magnitude of the labour and by the long delay to the work.

One night, after returning from the office of Matins, I began to reflect in bed that I myself ought to travel through all the forests of these regions, search them all around, and lessen these delays and labours if the beams could be found here. Therefore, casting aside other concerns, we set out very early in the morning with carpenters and beam-measures, hastening to the forest called Iveline [Col. 1244D]. As we crossed our land in the valley of Capreolus, we summoned our servants who guarded our woods, as well as men knowledgeable about other forests, and adjured them by faith and oath to advise us whether beams of that size could be found there by any labour whatsoever.

They smiled; indeed, if they had dared, they would rather have mocked us, amazed that we plainly did not know that nothing of the kind could be found in the entire region. This was especially so because Milo, castellan of Capreolus, our man, who held half the forest from us with another fief, had endured wars for a long time from both the lord king and Amaury of Montfort, for the construction of defensive platforms and ramparts, and thus nothing of the sort had remained uncut or untouched [Col. 1245A].

But rejecting whatever they said, with a certain boldness of faith we began to search the forest. By about the first hour we found one beam of adequate measure. What more need be said? By the ninth hour, or earlier, through thickets, the darkness of the woods, and the density of thorns, we marked out twelve beams—for that was precisely the number needed—to the amazement of everyone, particularly those standing nearby. Brought to the holy basilica, they were set in place with rejoicing as the covering of the new work, to the praise and glory of the Lord Jesus, who had preserved them, as he willed, from the hands of plunderers for himself and for the holy Martyrs. Nor, therefore, was this divine generosity either superfluous or insufficient: it had ordained to govern all things in weight and measure and to give all things, since no further beam beyond what was needed could be found [Col. 1245B].

Firmly encouraged by such great and manifest signs attending such great works, we hastened urgently to complete the aforesaid building. Deliberating how, by what persons, and with what great solemnity it should be consecrated to Almighty God, we summoned the distinguished man Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, and other venerable bishops—Odo of Beauvais and Peter of Senlis—and, to accomplish this, amid manifold praise and a great gathering of various ecclesiastical persons, clergy, and people, we sang.

In the midst of the new addition, after blessing the water previously prepared in the cask standing there, they went out in procession through the chapel of Saint Eustace [Col. 1245C], by the street anciently called Panteria because all buying and selling is conducted there, and returned by another way through the bronze gate opening into the sacred cemetery. In the imparting of eternal blessing and most holy chrism, and in the offering of the true Body and Blood of Jesus Christ, the supreme priest, they most devoutly completed everything fitting for so great and holy a structure. They dedicated the most beautiful upper chapel, worthy of an angelic dwelling, in honour of Saint Mary, ever-virgin Mother of God; Saint Michael the Archangel and all angels; Saint Romanus, who rests there; and many other saints whose names are inscribed there. They dedicated the lower chapel on the right side in honour of Saint Bartholomew and many other saints; and the chapel on the left, where Saint Hippolytus is said to rest, in his honour and in that of Saints Lawrence, Sixtus, Felicissimus, Agapitus, and many others, to the praise and glory of Almighty God.

Desiring with all our heart, by God’s gift, to become a participant in so great a blessing as the fruit of our labour, we bestowed upon these chapels, as it were as a dowry, as is customary, a street adjoining the cemetery beside the church of Saint Michael. We had bought it from William of Cornel for eighty pounds, to provide for the expense of purchasing lights, so that they might possess from it a perpetual rent. The exact date is established by this truthful inscription, as may be read—if it has not been obscured—on the golden epitaph over the doors [Col. 1246A], which we caused to be gilded in honour of God and the saints:

> The year one thousand, one hundred, and forty  
> Was the year of the Word when it was consecrated.

Therefore, after that consecration celebrated, with the aid of supreme Majesty, in the eastern part, for the chapel of Saint Romanus and the others, our devotion—encouraged both by its own success and by the constriction which had for so long oppressed the saints so intolerably—turned our vow in this direction: while attending to the aforesaid work and postponing the continuation of the towers in the upper part, we should strive, to the full extent of our ability and resources, to enlarge the mother church. In thanksgiving, because divine condescension had reserved so great a work for one succeeding to the nobility of so many kings and abbots, though so insignificant himself, we would have it made as fittingly and gloriously as reason could devise [Col. 1246B].

Having taken counsel with our devout brethren—whose hearts burned within them while Jesus spoke to them on the road—we chose, under God’s inspiration, that because the divine operation itself, as venerable writings attest, had laid its own blessing upon the ancient consecration of the church by a proper and manual extension, we should honour those consecrated stones as relics by giving them an addition necessitated by so great a need, and should endeavour to ennoble it by the beauty of its length and breadth.

It was wisely decreed that the vault, unequal in height to the higher one, which covered the apse containing the bodies of our holy lords the saints, should be removed down to the surface of the crypt to which it was attached, so that the same crypt might offer its upper surface to those ascending by both stairways as a floor, and might display in a more elevated place to the gaze of visitors the saints’ biers adorned with gold and precious gems. It was also prudently provided that, by means of geometrical and arithmetical instruments, the midpoint of the old church’s roof should correspond to the midpoint of the new addition, where upper columns and intermediate arches, founded below in the crypt, were to be placed above; and that the size of the old aisles should be adapted to the size of the new ones. The exception was that approved and urbane enlargement around the circuit of the chapels, through which the entire interior beauty might shine forth, illuminated by the wonderful and uninterrupted light of the most sacred windows [Col. 1246D].

But, in order that what we proposed to undertake might be set out in a clear sequence by wise counsel, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, whose anointing teaches concerning all things, we assembled a gathering of distinguished men, bishops as well as abbots, and summoned also the presence of our lord, the most serene Louis, king of the Franks. On the Sunday before the Ides of July, we arranged a procession splendid in ornaments and distinguished by its persons. Indeed, bearing in the hands of bishops and abbots the emblems of the Lord’s Passion—namely, the Lord’s nail and crown, the arm of the holy elder Simeon, and other protections of holy relics—we humbly and devoutly descended into the places prepared for digging the foundations [Col. 1247A].

Then, after invoking the consolation of the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, that He might bring the good beginning of God’s house to a good end, the bishops themselves, having with their own hands made mortar from the blessed water of the dedication performed on the fifth day before the Ides of June, laid the first stones, singing to God the hymn “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” [Psalm 86], solemnly chanting through to the end of the psalm. The most serene king himself descended within and laid his own stone with his own hands; we also, and many other abbots and religious men, laid our stones. Some even offered gems out of love and reverence for Jesus Christ, singing: “All your walls are precious stones.” Rejoicing in so great and festive a laying of such a holy foundation, yet anxious about carrying the work through [Col. 1247B], fearing the changes of time, the loss of persons, and my own failure, we established, by the common counsel and persuasion of the brethren present and with the king’s assent, an annual income for completing these things: namely, one hundred and fifty pounds from the treasury—that is, from the offerings at the altar and the relics—one hundred at the Indiction and fifty on the feast of Saint Dionysius; and fifty from an estate in Beauce called Villaines, formerly uncultivated but, through God’s help and our labour, improved and made worth eighty or one hundred pounds annually. If through any misfortune that estate should fail to provide what was needed, another of our Beauce estates, whose revenues we had increased twofold or threefold, should make up the deficiency [Col. 1247C].

We confirmed that these two hundred pounds, apart from what the devotion of the faithful might bring to the treasury-chest or whatever might be offered for either work, should be continually assigned to these works until both the eastern and upper structures, together with their towers, were wholly and honourably completed without any question.

Thus, for three years, at great expense and with a populous gathering of workmen, in summer and winter, we pressed on toward the completion of the work, lest we might rightly have to complain to God: “Your eyes saw my imperfect state” [Psalm 138:16]. With His cooperation we made great progress; and there was founded, like an image of divine things, “Mount Zion, the joy of the whole earth, the sides of the north, the city of the great King,” in whose midst God shall not be moved [Col. 1247D]. Yet, stirred by the provocations of sins, He will not disdain to be appeased and made propitious by the fragrant holocaust of penitents.

For the central twelve columns represented the number of the twelve apostles, while the same number of columns in the side aisles signified the prophets; these suddenly raised the lofty building in accordance with the Apostle who builds spiritually: “Now therefore,” he says, “you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone,” who joins the two walls, “in whom the whole building, whether spiritual or material, grows into a holy temple in the Lord” [Ephesians 2:19]. And in Him, the higher and more fittingly we strive to build materially, the more we are taught that through ourselves we are being built spiritually [Col. 1248A] into a dwelling-place of God in the Holy Spirit.

Meanwhile, being especially concerned for the translation of the bodies of our most holy lords the martyrs and of the other saints who were venerated in various chapels throughout the church, we were earnestly encouraged to have their most sacred biers, especially those of our lords, ornamented and moved to a place where they might be more gloriously and visibly displayed to those who came. With God’s cooperation we laboured to make them very splendid by the elegance and skill of goldsmiths and by an abundance of gold and precious gems. On the outside, indeed, we prepared that they should be nobly adorned with these and similar ornaments; inside, for security, that they should be protected all round by a strong wall of most durable stones. On the outside, moreover [Col. 1248B], lest the place should be made cheap by visible building stone, we prepared for it to be decorated with cast and gilded copper plates—though not yet as fittingly as it ought to be.

For the magnificence of such great Fathers, proven to us and to all, requires that we most wretched people, who experience and need their patronage, should cover their most sacred ashes, whose venerable spirits stand before Almighty God shining like the sun, with the most precious material we can: namely refined gold and an abundance of hyacinths, emeralds, and other gems. Yet we chose to accomplish this one thing especially: before the bodies of the saints, we would erect a most celebrated altar for offering libations to God, which had never previously stood there, so that supreme bishops and distinguished persons might be worthy, through the saints’ intercession—these saints who offered themselves as a fragrant holocaust to God—to offer sacrifices pleasing and acceptable to God.

When I had proposed to place before it a gold frontal, though of moderate quality because of the poverty of our resources, the holy martyrs themselves supplied us with so great and unexpected an abundance of gold and of the most precious gems—such as scarcely existed even for kings—that they seemed to speak to us mouth to mouth: “Whether you wish it or not, we wish it to be the finest.” Thus we either did not dare, or were unable, to make it other than wonderful and exceedingly precious both in workmanship and material. Nor did the bishops themselves, who possess such things in distinction appropriate to their office, refuse to set upon the frontal, while present, their own pontifical rings set with a marvellous variety of precious stones [Col. 1248D]; and, though absent in overseas lands, they were moved by love for the holy martyrs voluntarily to send them.

The famous king himself offered emeralds bright and marked with spots; Count Theobald, hyacinths and rubies; nobles and princes from various places and ranks, precious pearls—thus inviting us voluntarily to carry out the work gloriously. Moreover, so many gems for sale were brought to us from nearly every region of the earth, and, by God’s gift, the means to buy them were offered, that we could not leave them without great shame and offence to the saints. Here and elsewhere we could experience that, if a good work exists in the will, it will, by God’s help, exist in completion. Therefore, if anyone in rash presumption should attempt to remove or knowingly diminish this ornament, lent by the devotion of so many and protected by such great patrons, may he deserve the offence of Lord Dionysius and to be pierced by the sword of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1249A].

We also judged it worthy not to pass over in silence that, while the aforesaid work of the new addition was being carried up with its capitals and upper arches toward the summit of its height, and before the principal arches were individually joined together, as though by the massing of vaults, a sudden storm arose: terrifying and scarcely bearable through darkened clouds, flooding rain, and a most violent force of winds. It grew so fierce that it shook not only sturdy houses, but even stone towers and wooden scaffolds. During that storm, on a certain anniversary of the glorious King Dagobert, while the venerable Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, was festively celebrating at the principal altar, before the community, Masses of thanksgiving for his soul [Col. 1249B], such was the force of contrary winds striking the aforesaid arches, unsupported by any platform and with no aid resisting them, that they trembled pitifully and seemed to sway from side to side, suddenly threatening a ruinous collapse.

Alarmed at the movement of those arches and roofs, the bishop repeatedly stretched out his hand in blessing toward that place and persistently opposed to it, in the sign of the cross, the arm of the holy elder Simeon. It was thereby plainly apparent that they escaped collapse through no stability of their own but through God’s mercy alone and the saints’ merit. Thus, although the storm caused much ruinous damage in many places to buildings thought exceedingly strong, when its force had been repelled by divine power it could inflict no harm upon the newly made arches, which alone were swaying high in the air [Col. 1249C].

Another memorable event followed, not by accident, as those judge who agree with that school which holds that Fortune wanders uncertainly abroad, carries and brings back turns of change, and that mortal things have chances; but by divine bounty, which provides abundantly in all things for great and small who hope in it, and which administers what it knows will be useful. For when, on a certain day, we were making arrangements for the court at the forthcoming consecration, which we expected to be very large, and were dealing with our friends, officials, and stewards, and had made fairly fortunate provision for other matters despite the hardship of the season—for in June almost every kind of food was expensive—this alone greatly troubled us: because sheep had died in that year, we had to seek mutton in the region of Orléans and toward Burgundy [Col. 1249D].

When orders had been given that a thousand solidi, or whatever sum was necessary, should be given to those travelling there, with urgent insistence that they not return late because they had set out late, on the next morning, as I was hurrying from my chamber according to custom to the celebration of the holy sacrifice, a certain monk in white from among the brethren suddenly drew me back, against my inclination, to the chamber. Somewhat provoked because he was hindering us from so great a task, I answered him less graciously than I should have. “My lord father,” he said, “we have heard that you need mutton for the imminent solemnity of your consecration. Sent by our brethren for this purpose, I bring to your fatherhood a very large flock of rams, so that you may keep what pleases you and leave to us what does not.”

Having heard this, we ordered him to wait for us after Mass; and, Mass ended, we reported to our people, in his presence, what he offered. They attributed this very thing to divine bounty: that what alone was lacking, and which had wearied us in seeking it, had unexpectedly been supplied by the delivery of religious brethren [Col. 1250A].

Thereafter the laborious completion of the work and our own devotion, long held in suspense and yearning for this, pressed for the consecration of the new church. Since we ardently desired that both the consecration itself and the translation of our holy lords the saints should take place with the greatest splendour, as thanksgiving and as the most welcome fruit of our labour, we carefully appointed, with the gracious favour of the most serene Louis, king of the Franks—for he most ardently desired to see his patron saints the martyrs—the second Sunday of June, namely the third day before the Ides, the feast of the Apostle Barnabas, as the day for the ceremony [Col. 1250B].

We therefore sent letters of invitation by many messengers, runners, and heralds through almost all the regions of Gaul. In the name of the saints and by the duty of their apostolic office, we earnestly invited archbishops and bishops to take part in so great a solemnity. Though we would gladly have received many and diverse persons for the performance of this rite—indeed, all of them, if possible—the lord King Louis himself, his queen and wife Eleanor, his mother, and the magnates of the realm arrived two days beforehand. Of the nobles of various peoples and kingdoms, and of troops of knights and foot-soldiers, both noble and common [Col. 1250C], no number can be given.

The following are the recorded names of the archbishops and bishops present: Samson, archbishop of Reims; Hugh, archbishop of Rouen; Guy, archbishop of Sens; Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury; Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres; Josselin, bishop of Soissons; Simon, bishop of Noyon; Elias, bishop of Orléans; Odo, bishop of Beauvais; Hugh, bishop of Auxerre; Aluif, bishop of Arras; Guy, bishop of Châlons; Algar, bishop of Coutances; Rotrou, bishop of Évreux; Milo, bishop of Thérouanne; Manasses, bishop of Meaux; and Peter, bishop of Senlis. When all these came in glory with the higher clergy of their churches for so great and noble an occasion and spectacle, the inward devotion of their minds and hearts was displayed by outward worship and dress.

As for us, we had ordered that not only external matters—for these had been abundantly provided without complaint—but also the saints’ bodies should be made ready. On the Saturday before, we took the bodies from their chapels and, according to custom, placed them most fittingly in draped tents at the exit of the choir. We prepared the sacramental instruments of consecration, awaiting so great a joy. We arranged matters so that the procession of such great persons, intent upon so holy a purpose, might readily move throughout the church inside and outside. Therefore, when we humbly asked the glorious and most humble Louis, king of the Franks, to keep back by means of his magnates and nobles the crowd that would meet the procession [Col. 1251A], he answered, with still greater humility, that he would gladly do this himself and through his men.
