Thus, through the whole night we kept vigil in the evening and morning office, most devoutly beseeching Jesus Christ our Lord, made propitiation for our sins, that for His own honour and love of His saints He might mercifully visit the holy place and deign to be present at the sacred rites not only in power but also in person. Therefore, at earliest morning, the archbishops and bishops, coming from their lodgings with archdeacons, abbots, and other honourable persons, arrayed themselves episcopally in the church and stood, very fittingly and reverently, beside the cask for consecrating the water, above [Col. 1251B], between the tombs of the holy martyrs and the altar of the Holy Saviour.

You might have seen—and those present saw it with no slight devotion—so many and such great bishops forming a circle, splendid in white vestments, richly adorned with pontifical mitres and rounded bands of very precious gold embroidery, holding pastoral staffs in their hands, encircling the cask, invoking the Lord’s name in exorcism, and celebrating so piously the nuptials of the eternal Bridegroom. It appeared to king and noble assistants alike more like a heavenly choir than an earthly one, more a divine work than a human. Because of its overwhelming multitude, the people were kept outside. And while the aforesaid choir sprinkled the church walls outside with blessed water by means of hyssop [Col. 1251C], the king himself and his officers held back the tumultuous press and guarded with rods and staffs those retreating toward the doors.

When, according to the established order, the mysteries of the holy consecration reached the repositioning of the holy relics, we approached the ancient and venerable tombs of our holy lords the saints—for they had not yet been moved from their place. The bishops themselves, the lord king, and all of us, so far as the narrowness of the place allowed, prostrated ourselves. Beholding the venerable shrines made by King Dagobert and covered in this manner, in which their most holy and God-beloved bodies were contained, they sang psalms and wept with inestimable joy. Calling upon the king, so devout and humble [Col. 1251D], they said: “Come, and with your own hands help carry here our lord and apostle and protector, that we may venerate the most sacred ashes, embrace the most sacred urns, and rejoice that throughout our lives we have received and held them.

“For these are the holy men who gave up their bodies for God’s covenant; who, kindled by the fire of charity for our salvation, left their land and kindred; who by apostolic authority taught all Gaul the faith of Jesus Christ; who fought manfully for Him; who, naked, restrained rods, and, bound, subdued fierce and hungry beasts; who endured unharmed the stretching of the rack and the heating of the furnace; and who at last suffered a blessed beheading by blunted axes [Col. 1252A]. Come then, most Christian king, let us receive our blessed receiver, Dionysius, humbly begging that he may ask for us from Him who faithfully promised: ‘The love and kindness which you have always shown will obtain whatever you ask.’”

Immediately arms were set in motion, hands stretched out; so many and such hands were extended that not even a seventh hand could touch the holy shrines themselves. Therefore the lord king himself thrust himself into their midst and, taking the silver bier of his special patron from the hands of the bishops—apparently from the hands of the archbishop of Reims, of Sens, of Chartres, and others—went out before it as devoutly as honourably. A wonderful sight! No one could ever have seen such a procession, except that procession of the heavenly host seen at the ancient consecration. The bodies of the holy martyrs and confessors came from the draped tents to meet Saint Dionysius and his companions at the ivory door, borne on the shoulders and necks of bishops, counts, and barons [Col. 1252B]. They proceeded through the cloister with candlesticks, crosses, and other festive ornaments, with many chants and praises; they carried their lords as intimately as they did tearfully for joy. Never in anything could they have been raised to greater joy.

Returning then to the church and ascending by the steps to the upper altar appointed for the resting-place of the saints, the pledges of the saints were laid upon the old altar. The principal new altar, in front of their new tomb and to be consecrated, was then dealt with; we entrusted its consecration to the lord Samson, archbishop of Reims. We also undertook the glorious and solemn consecration of twenty other altars. The altar in the centre, assigned to our Saviour, the holy choir of angels, and the Holy Cross, we entrusted to the lord Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury; that of the blessed and ever-virgin Mother of God Mary, to the lord Hugh, archbishop of Rouen; that of Saint Peregrinus, to the lord Hugh, bishop of Auxerre; that of Saint Eustace, to the lord Werdon, bishop of Châlons; that of Saint Osmanna, to the lord Peter, bishop of Senlis; that of Saint Innocentius, to the lord Simon, bishop of Noyon; that of Saint Cucuphas, to the lord Aluif, bishop of Arras [Col. 1252D]; that of Saint Eugenius, to the lord Algar, bishop of Coutances; that of Saint Hilary, to the lord Rotrou, bishop of Évreux; and that of Saint John the Baptist and Saint John the Evangelist, to the lord Nicholas, bishop of Cambrai.

[Note: [Col. 1251] Here the Chesnian manuscript ends; the remainder is supplied by the manuscript of Saint Victor in Paris.]

In the lower crypt, we entrusted the consecration of the greater altar, in honour of the Virgin Saint Mary, Mother of God, to the lord Geoffrey, archbishop of Bordeaux; the altar of Saint Christopher the martyr, on the right side, to the lord Elias, bishop of Orléans; that of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, to the lord Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres; that of Saint Edmund the king, to the lord Werdon, archbishop of Sens; and that of Saint Benedict, to the lord Josselin, bishop of Soissons. On the left side, we assigned the altar of Saints Sixtus, Felicissimus, and Agapitus to the lord Milo, bishop of Thérouanne; that of Saint Barnabas the Apostle [Col. 1253A] to the lord Manasses, bishop of Meaux; likewise that of Saint George the martyr and the virgin Gauburga to the same bishop; and that of Saint Luke the Evangelist to the lord Odo, bishop of Beauvais.

All of these carried out the solemn celebration of Mass in the consecration of the altars above and below so festively, so solemnly, so diversely, so harmoniously, so near together, and so joyfully that, from their unanimity and the pleasing melody of their coherent harmony, it was judged an angelic rather than a human concert. All acclaimed with heart and voice: “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from His place; blessed, praiseworthy, and supremely exalted be Your name, Lord Jesus Christ, whom God the Father anointed as supreme priest with the oil of gladness beyond Your companions [Col. 1254A]. By the sacramental imparting of most holy chrism and the reception of the most sacred Eucharist, You unite material things with immaterial, bodily things with spiritual, human things with divine, and sacramentally restore them, purified, to their source. By these and similar visible blessings You invisibly restore all things, and wonderfully transform even the present order into the heavenly kingdom, so that, when You deliver the kingdom to God the Father, You may powerfully and mercifully make us, the angelic creation, heaven, and earth one commonwealth; You who live and reign as God through all ages of ages. Amen.”

[Col. 1253]

# THE LIFE OF KING LOUIS VI, CALLED “THE FAT,” BY SUGER, ABBOT OF SAINT-DENIS IN FRANCE

[Note: [Col. 1253C] How much weight Suger's name adds to this history is known to everyone. For he must be regarded not only as a witness to the events he relates, but also as a participant in the counsels by which they were decided, and indeed repeatedly as their author. Yet anyone will readily recognize that he is excessively inclined toward his hero, and that his narrative approaches a panegyric rather than history. He is so occupied with the praises of Louis the Fat that he conceals all the blemishes with which his life was at times stained. Yet we do not say this in order to lessen the credibility of so weighty a writer, since it is one thing to keep silent about something true and another to assert something false.]

(Dom Bouquet, *Recueil des historiens*, vol. XII, p. 10.)

# THE PROLOGUE TO THE DEEDS OF KING LOUIS, SURNAMED THE FAT, BEGINS

[Col. 1253B]

To the lord Goslenus, bishop of Soissons, worthy of deepest reverence:

Suger, called by God’s forbearance abbot of blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, a servant of Jesus Christ of whatever sort he may be, wishes episcopal union in episcopal fashion to the bishop of bishops.

[Note: [Col. 1253C] “To the lord … Goslenus.” Josselin or Joslenus, bishop of Soissons, after commendably fulfilling the office of teaching in the Academy of Paris, was appointed in 1125. He was most closely joined to Suger in friendship and, admitted with him to the intimate counsels of both Kings Louis—namely Louis VI and Louis VII—frequently took part in court deliberations, without injury, however, to his pastoral office. The following epitaph is recorded as inscribed to him at the monastery of Longpont, founded by him, where he lies buried: “Joslenus, appointed bishop of Soissons in the year 1125; formerly archbishop of Bourges; most celebrated master in Paris; father of justice and of many monasteries; enemy of vices and outstanding cultivator of chastity. He died in the year 1151.”]

[Note: [Col. 1254C] “Suger … of blessed Dionysius the Areopagite,” etc. The opinion which confused Dionysius the Areopagite with his namesake, the apostle of Gaul, has long since become obsolete.]

It is fitting to submit both ourselves and our affairs to the deliberation and judgment of those whose universal judgment will pronounce a different verdict—hateful or welcome according to different persons—when “the noble man sits in the gates with the elders of the land.” Therefore, best of men, even if the chair had not bestowed this upon us—for I am wholly devoted to him to whom you are wholly devoted, nor, if you seek more, do I possess more—we entrust the deeds of Louis, the most serene king of the Franks, to the discretion of your approved learning. Since the Lord was most gracious to us jointly, both while we advanced and after we had advanced, let me by writing and you by correcting together celebrate and lament him whom we both loved [Col. 1254B].

For friendship even when acquired by benefits is not contrary to charity, since He who commands us to love enemies does not forbid friends. Therefore, by a twofold obligation, of benefaction and of charity—unequal indeed, but not opposed—let us carve for him a monument more lasting than bronze, once we have committed to writing both his devotion toward the worship of God’s churches and his remarkable energy in preserving the realm. Thus neither any change of times may destroy his memory, nor may the Church that benefits from his gifts cease, from generation to generation, to offer earnest prayers for him. May Your Highness prosper in episcopal office among the senators of heaven.

## CHAPTER HEADINGS

[Note: [Col. 1255B] These chapter headings are absent from the royal manuscripts.]

[Col. 1255]

I. How vigorous he was in youth, and with what valour he repelled the most powerful king of England, William Rufus, when he disturbed his father’s kingdom.  
II. How he restrained the nobleman Burchard of Montmorency, together with all his accomplices, from harassing Saint Dionysius.

[Note: [Col. 1255B] “Of Montmorency.” Saint-Germain manuscript: “of Monmoriac.”]

III. How he compelled Matthew, count of Beaumont, to restore the castle of Luzarches to Hugh of Clermont, after Lord Louis himself had assaulted that same castle by force of arms.  
IV. How, when he besieged another castle of the same Matthew, Conflans, a sudden disturbance of the weather forced the army into flight; how the army would almost have been destroyed had Louis himself not stood firm bravely; and how Matthew humbly made satisfaction to him.  
V. Concerning Count Ebles of Roucy.  
VI. Concerning the castle of Meudon.

[Note: [Col. 1255B] “Of Meudon”: Saint-Germain manuscript, “of Madun.”]

VII. Concerning the castle called Montaigu.  
VIII. Concerning Milo, and how he entered the castle of Montlhéry.  
IX. Concerning Bohemond, prince of Antioch.  
X. Concerning the capture of the castle of Gournay.  
XI. Concerning the capture of the castle of Sainte-Sévère.  
XII. Concerning the death of King Philip.  
XIII. Concerning his elevation as king.  
XIV. Concerning the capture of La Ferté-Baudouin and the liberation of the count of Corbeil and Anselm of Garlande.  
XV. Concerning the conference held at the Nympheal Bridges between King Louis and Henry, king of England.  
XVI. Concerning the treachery committed at La Roche-Guyon by William, Guy’s brother-in-law; the death of Guy; and the swift vengeance upon that same William.  
XVII. How he took from his resisting brother Philip the castle of Meudon and Montlhéry.  
XVIII. How, after capturing Hugh, he destroyed the castle of Le Puiset.  
XIX. Concerning his release.  
XX. Concerning the assault on Toury and the restoration of Le Puiset.  
XXI. Concerning his reciprocal treachery.

The remaining chapter headings are missing.

# THE LIFE OF THE MOST GLORIOUS AND ILLUSTRIOUS LOUIS, KING OF THE FRANKS, HAPPILY BEGINS

[Note: [Col. 1255B] This title is absent from the Saint-Germain manuscript; it is found in two royal manuscripts and in the Saint-Denis manuscript.]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1255A]

The glorious and renowned king of the Franks, Louis, son of the magnificent King Philip, still in the first flower of youth, scarcely twelve or thirteen years old, graceful and handsome, was advancing in such venerable diligence of approved character and such pleasing stature of body that he unmistakably promised in reality an honorable enlargement of his future sceptres and inspired a hoped-for confidence in the protection of churches and the poor. A tall boy, he attached himself at Saint-Denis with such great and almost inborn affection to the holy martyrs themselves and to their church—according to the ancient custom of kings, attested by the imperial charters of Charlemagne and other most eminent rulers—that throughout his life he continued the friendship, innate from childhood, which he bore toward their church [Col. 1255B], with much generosity and honor; and at the end, placing his highest hope in them after God, he most devoutly resolved [Col. 1256A] to commit and assign himself, body and soul, to them, so that, if it were possible, he might become a monk there.

Indeed, at the aforesaid age his native courage, ripening in youthful spirit, was vigorous and impatient of hunting and childish amusements, by which persons of that age are accustomed to grow wanton and to unlearn arms. [Note: [Col. 1256B] “Augtiva” in Royal MS 59, book 5; “nativa” in Royal MS 6265; “activa,” active.] And while he was stirred by the harassment of many magnates of the kingdom and of William, the exceptionally high-spirited king of the English, the still more high-spirited conqueror of the English, the strength of his worth glowed forth; virtue smiled upon exercise; he cast off idleness, opened the eye of prudence, dissolved leisure, and quickened vigilance. [Note: [Col. 1256B] “Virtus,” virtue: thus the Saint-Denis manuscript. The edition has “virtutis,” of virtue.]

For King William of the English, suited to warfare, greedy for praise and eager for fame, having disinherited his elder brother Robert and happily succeeded his father William, and having acquired the duchy of Normandy after that same brother’s departure for Jerusalem, strove by every means in his power to attack the famous young man wherever the duchy of Normandy extended along the borders adjoining the kingdom [Col. 1256B]. Their contest was alike and unlike: alike, because neither yielded; unlike, because William was mature and Louis a youth; William wealthy, lavish with English treasure, a remarkable purchaser and paymaster of soldiers; Louis without funds, while his father, sparing his resources, enjoyed the revenues of the kingdom, compelled military service only by the vigor of his good natural disposition and resisted boldly.

One might see the very swift young man fly now to the borders of Berry, now of Auvergne, now of Burgundy, with an armed force; nor, if he was spared, was he slower to return to the Vexin, and there, with three hundred or five hundred knights, to oppose most courageously the aforesaid King William with ten thousand men, and—as the uncertain outcome of war turns—now to yield, now to put him to flight. In such engagements many men on both sides were taken. The famous youth and his men held captive, among others, Count Simon, a nobleman; Gilbert of Laigle, a noble baron equally distinguished in England and Normandy; and Pagan of Gisors, who first fortified that castle. On the other side, the king of England held captive the valiant and noble Count Matthew of Beaumont, the illustrious and renowned Baron Simon of Montfort, and Pagan, lord of Montjay. [Note: [Col. 1257D] “Gislebertum”: Saint-Germain MS and Royal MS 5925 have “Gillebertum”; Royal MS 5265, “Gilbertum.”]

But anxiety for their military pay hastened the English captives toward a prompt ransom; the long duration of prolonged imprisonment wore down the French captives. They could by no means be released until, having entered the service of that king of England and bound themselves by homage, they swore to attack and disturb the kingdom and king.

It was commonly said that this proud and violent king aspired to the kingdom of the Franks, because the famous youth was his father’s sole son by his most noble wife Bertha, sister of Count Robert of Flanders. The two surviving sons, Philip and Florus, had been born of Bertrada, countess of Anjou, whom Philip had subsequently married; nor was their succession considered of value should the sole first-born die by any misfortune whatever. But because it is neither right nor natural that Franks should be subject to Englishmen—or rather Englishmen to Franks—the outcome frustrated the hope of this undertaking. For after he had tormented himself and his followers with this madness for three years or more, and could not, through Englishmen or Frenchmen bound to him by homage, achieve his will, he desisted.

When he had crossed to England, given over to luxury and the desires of his heart, and one day was engaged in hunting in the New Forest, he suddenly perished when struck by an unexpected arrow (A.D. 1100) [Col. 1257D]. It was believed that the man had been struck by divine vengeance, this evidence of truth being adduced: he had been an intolerable oppressor of the poor, a cruel extortioner from churches, and, whenever bishops or prelates died, a most irreverent withholder and squanderer of their goods. Some charged a certain most noble man, Walter Tirel, with having pierced him with an arrow. Yet, since Tirel neither feared nor hoped in him, we repeatedly heard him swear—and assert as though under a sacred oath—that on that day he had neither come to that part of the forest in which the king was hunting [Col. 1258A], nor seen him anywhere in the forest. [Note: [Col. 1257D] “Viderit,” seen him. Nevertheless almost the entire body of English writers, with scarcely anyone excepted, attributes William’s death to Tirel.]

Thus it is evident that divine power so suddenly reduced such great madness to ashes, so that he who needlessly troubled others might himself be troubled infinitely more severely, and he who coveted all things might ingloriously be stripped of everything. For kingdoms and the rights of kingdoms are subject to God, who unfastens the belt of kings.

William was succeeded in the kingdom with the utmost speed by his younger brother Henry—for Robert, the elder, was engaged in that great expedition to the Holy Sepulchre—a most prudent man, whose courage and learning of mind and body would furnish material as admirable as it is worthy of praise. But this does not concern our work, unless on some occasion we must briefly touch upon something that bears upon our subject, as also upon the kingdom of the Lotharingians. For we have undertaken to commit to written memory the deeds of the Franks [Col. 1258B], not those of the English.

Louis, therefore, the famous young man, pleasant, agreeable, and kindly—so much so that some even regarded him as simple—now grown up, an illustrious and spirited defender of his paternal kingdom, provided for the interests of churches and devoted himself to the peace of ploughmen [probably *aratorum*], laborers, and the poor, a concern long unfamiliar. [Note: [Col. 1258D] “Paterni,” paternal: Saint-Germain MS has “Patris,” father’s.]

## CHAPTER II

At that time certain disputes arose between Adam, the venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, and Burchard, a nobleman, lord of Montmorency, concerning certain customary rights. They boiled over into such troublesome hostility [Col. 1258C] that homage was broken between the confederates and they fought with arms, war, and fires. When this reached Lord Louis’s ears, he was indignant and took it badly. Without delay he summoned the aforesaid Burchard before his father at the castle of Poissy to answer the charges. When Burchard, losing his case, would not submit to justice by judicial decision, he was not detained—for that is not the custom of the Franks—but departed, and swiftly learned what damage and calamity the contumacy of subjects merits from royal majesty.

For the handsome young man immediately took arms against him and his confederate accomplices—for Burchard had enlisted Count Matthew of Beaumont and Drogo of Mouchy-le-Châtel, valiant and warlike men. Ravaging Burchard’s land, he destroyed and overthrew the towns and manors outside the castle, crushing them with fire, famine, and sword (A.D. 1101) [Col. 1258D]. Since they strove together to resist from the castle, he surrounded it with a siege force of Franks, Flemings belonging to his uncle Robert, and his own followers. Humbled by these and other blows of devastation, Burchard was bent to Louis’s will and pleasure; the cause of the quarrel was settled with satisfaction and peace was restored.

Louis then attacked Drogo of Mouchy for these and other wrongs, especially injuries inflicted upon the Church of Beauvais. Meeting him outside the castle, not far away, with a large force of mounted archers and crossbowmen, as Drogo was returning by what he thought the shorter route, Louis rushed upon him and did not permit him, under pressure of arms, to retreat and enter the castle without himself entering too. Rather, he charged among them and through the gate with them. As a most powerful wrestler and conspicuous swordsman, in the middle of the castle, often struck and often striking, he deigned to suffer no repulse and would not withdraw until he had burned the entire castle, with its furnishings, almost up to the tower’s enclosure [Col. 1259A]. Such was the man’s courage that he did not trouble to avoid the fire, although it was dangerous both to him and to the army and caused him severe hoarseness for a long time. Thus, humbled by the arm of God’s power, which was at work in the matter, Drogo was subdued as though bedridden beneath the dominion of Louis’s will.

## CHAPTER III

Meanwhile Count Matthew of Beaumont, in a long-standing rancor against Hugh of Clermont, a noble but fickle and simple man, whose daughter Emma he had married, sought to occupy wholly the castle called Luzarches, of which he had received half by reason of the marriage, and strove to fortify its tower for himself with arms and armed men. [Note: [Col. 1259D] Saint-Germain MS: “occupat,” occupies.] What could Hugh do except hasten to the defender of the kingdom and, prostrate at his feet, plead through tears that he should condescend to an old man and bring help to one burdened most grievously? “My dearest lord,” he said, “I would rather you possessed my whole land, because I hold it from you, than that my degenerate son-in-law should possess this part. I desire to die if he takes it away.”

Moved in spirit by his tearful calamity, Louis extended a friendly hand [Col. 1259C], promised assistance, and sent him away rejoicing in hope. And hope does not disappoint. For men promptly left the court to summon the count and order him, in the defender’s name, to clothe in the ordinary manner the man whom he had stripped in an extraordinary manner, and to contend on a fixed day by legal argument in Louis’s court. When the count refused to make amends, the avenging defender hastened to raise a great army and fell upon him. Assaulting the aforesaid castle, now with arms and now with fire, he captured it after much fighting, fortified the tower itself with a military guard, and restored it, fortified as it was, to Hugh as he had promised.

## CHAPTER IV

He likewise moved his army against another castle of the same count, called Canliacum [Col. 1259D], pitched camp, and ordered siege-engines to be prepared. But events turned out very differently from what he had expected. For the pleasant moderation of the weather changed into unpleasant and stormy violence; such great and terrible rain, thunder, and lightning disturbed the whole land by night, afflicted the army, and struck down the horses, so that some scarcely hoped to survive.

When, under this intolerable terror, some of the army at dawn were preparing a morning flight [Col. 1260A], while the defender still slept in his tent, fire was treacherously applied to the tents. Because this was a signal for departure, the army immediately hastened out as rashly as confusedly, fearing an unexpected retreat and paying no attention to what they ought to communicate to one another. Astonished by their precipitate rush and loud uproar, the lord asked what was happening, mounted his horse, and hurried after the army; but since they had already scattered in all directions, he could not in any way bring them back.

What else could the famous youth do but run to arms, retreat with the few men whom he could, place himself as a wall before those going ahead, often be struck, and often strike? Yet although those before whom he stood as a wall could flee quietly and safely, many who fled in groups and scattered far from him were captured by the enemy [Col. 1260B]. Among these were Hugh of Clermont himself, the more distinguished captive; Guy of Senlis; Herluin of Paris; very many common soldiers of obscure name; and many of the infantry.

Provoked by this injury, the more inexperienced and ignorant he had hitherto been of such misfortune, the more, when he returned to Paris, did he swell with the unrestrained passion of an agitated mind. And, as is the way of that age—provided that it is an imitation of valor—he acted and was stirred to action. [Note: [Col. 1259D] “Imitativa,” imitative: as in the Saint-Denis manuscript. The edition and manuscript *d* have “mutativa,” changeable; the Saint-Germain manuscript, “innutiva,” uncertain.] Burning to avenge the injury quickly, he wisely and prudently trebled his army from every side and repeatedly sighed that it was more fitting to endure death than disgrace.

When Count Matthew learned this from his friends’ reports, being an elegant and witty man, impatient of his lord’s accidental disgrace [Col. 1260C], he earnestly sought, through many mediators, a way of peace. With much sweetness and many flatteries he labored to soothe the youthful mind. He excused the injury, asserting very plausibly that it had occurred not through any deliberate intention but by chance; and he offered himself ready to make satisfaction at Louis’s command. At the prayer of many, the counsel of intimates, and even his father’s repeated entreaty, Louis’s spirit, though late, softened. He spared the repentant man, forgave the injury, restored the recoverable losses when the count returned them, freed the captives, and restored to Hugh of Clermont, under firm peace, what had been his in the castle that had been preoccupied.

## CHAPTER V

The noble Church of Rheims was being harassed by the plundering of its goods and of those belonging to churches subject to it, through the tyranny of the most powerful and turbulent baron Ebles of Roucy and his son Guiscard. The more he was exercised in warfare—for he possessed such high spirit that at one time, with a great army, he set out for Spain, an undertaking suited to kings alone—the more madly and greedily he pursued these depredations, robberies, and every sort of wickedness. [Note: [Col. 1259D–1260D] Anselm, vol. VIII, p. 864, records that Ebles went to Spain against the Saracens to bring assistance to the kings of Castile and Aragon. He says that Ebles undertook the earlier expedition at the urging of Pope Alexander II and the other under Gregory VII. Spanish historians are entirely silent concerning both.]

Therefore, after grievous complaint concerning so great and criminal a man had been laid a hundred times before King Philip and twice or three times before his son, the son promptly assembled a moderate army of nearly seven hundred knights, selected from the nobler magnates of France, hastened to Rheims, and for almost two months, in many engagements, punished the former sufferings of the churches. [Note: [Col. 1261D] “Nobilioribus,” nobler: four manuscripts add “et validioribus,” and stronger.] He ravaged the lands of the aforesaid tyrant and his supporters, gave them to the flames, and exposed them to plunder. [Note: [Col. 1261D] “Fautorum,” supporters: Saint-Germain MS and Royal MS 5925 have “factorum,” deeds.] It was excellently done: those who plundered were plundered, and those who tortured were tortured in like manner or more harshly.

Such was the courage of the lord and army that, while they remained there, they rested scarcely, or never, except on Friday and Sunday, without either engaging in hand-to-hand combat with lances and swords [Col. 1261B] or avenging by the destruction of lands the wrongs inflicted. The struggle was not against Ebles alone, but against all the barons of those regions, whom even kinship with the greatest men of Lotharingia drew in great numbers toward the renowned army.

Meanwhile many discussions were conducted about peace; and because various concerns and dangerous affairs in other regions urgently called for the new lord’s presence, he consulted his men and obtained peace for the churches from the aforesaid tyrant, causing it to be confirmed by oath after hostages had been received. [Note: [Col. 1261D] “Et impetravit,” and obtained: two Royal manuscripts and the Saint-Germain manuscript add “et imperavit,” and commanded.] He dismissed him thus greeted and chastised. He deferred to another day the matter which he was pressing concerning Château-Neuf.

## CHAPTER VI

He also brought no less celebrated military assistance to the Church of Orléans. He forcibly restrained Leon, a nobleman, the vassal of the bishop of Orléans for the castle of Meung, who was taking away the greater part of that castle and the lordship of another belonging to the aforesaid church. [Note: [Col. 1261D] “Leonium”: Royal MS 5925 has “Leonum.” “Mauduni”: Saint-Germain MS has “Maduni” (Meung).] He shut him up in the same castle with many others. After recovering the castle, Louis erected defensive works in the church nearest Leon’s house, and Leon strove to defend himself. But, as the strong man is subjected to the stronger, he was intolerably overwhelmed by an assault of weapons and flames. Nor did he alone pay the penalty of a long anathema: he and nearly sixty others, as the flames prevailed, fell from the tower, were pierced by the points of raised lances and incoming arrows, and, breathing out their last breath, carried their wretched souls in pain down to hell [Col. 1261D]. [Note: [Col. 1261D] “Transtulerunt,” carried: Royal MS 6265 has “transmiserunt,” sent across.]

## CHAPTER VII

The exceedingly strong castle called Montaigu, in the district of Laon, came into the possession of Thomas of Marle through a certain marriage. [Note: [Col. 1261D] Thomas had married first Ida, daughter of Baldwin II, count of Hainaut. After her death about 1101, he entered a second marriage with his kinswoman, the daughter of Count Roger, who brought him the castle of Montaigu as dowry.] He was a thoroughly depraved man, hostile to God and humankind. Since all the neighboring inhabitants feared and abhorred his intolerable rage, which, like that of a most savage wolf, grew with the confidence inspired by an impregnable castle, his supposed father, Enguerrand of Boves, an especially honorable and distinguished man, planned, more notably than the rest, to expel him from the castle because of his malicious tyranny, about A.D. 1104. [Note: [Col. 1261D–1262D] Enguerrand denied that he was Thomas’s father because of the suspected fidelity of Ada, his former wife, who had borne Thomas to him.] [Note: [Col. 1262D] “Engeirrannus”: Saint-Germain and Royal MS 6265 have “Engerannus”; Royal MS 5945, “Engenrannus.”] [Note: [Col. 1262D] Lord of Coucy.] [Note: [Col. 1262D] “Fautiosam,” factious, that is, malicious; it derives from *fauctio* or *factio*, meaning a wicked deed.]

It was agreed among Enguerrand, Ebles of Roucy, and all those whom they could draw to their side that they would besiege both the castle and Thomas within it [Col. 1262B], encircle him on every side with palisade and wattled fence, compel him to surrender by prolonged hunger, destroy the castle if possible, and condemn him to perpetual imprisonment. But the wicked man saw this; having now secured his fortresses, and before the enclosure from one fortification to the other had yet been completed, he secretly slipped out by night. Hastening to the famous youth, he corrupted the latter’s associates with gifts and promises and most quickly obtained military aid.

For Louis, pliable in age and character, assembled an army of seven hundred knights and hastened toward those parts. [Note: [Col. 1262D] “Flexilis”: in two Royal manuscripts and Saint-Germain, “flexibilis,” pliant.] When he approached the castle of Montaigu, the men who had surrounded the castle sent envoys to him as to their designated lord, beseeching him not to bring disgrace upon himself by removing them from the siege [Col. 1262C]. They urged that he should not lose the service of so many men for the sake of a thoroughly depraved man, declaring truthfully that it would be more disastrous for him than for them if the wicked man remained secure. But when they could not turn him from his purpose by flatteries or threats, they feared to act against their designated lord. Proposing that, after he withdrew from the siege, they would return to war anew, they yielded and reluctantly endured whatever he wished. [Note: [Col. 1262D] “Ab obsidione,” from the siege: two Royal manuscripts and the Saint-Denis manuscript have “ad obsidionem,” to the siege.]

Louis, by force of arms, broke up and dug down all the surrounding fortified places, relieved Montaigu, and, defeating their schemes both in arms and provisions, made it abundantly supplied. Therefore the magnates, who had yielded from love and fear of him, were angered and grieved because he had spared nothing; they threatened on oath that they would no longer submit to him [Col. 1262D]. When they saw him depart—Saint-Germain and Saint-Denis have “return” [Col. 1263A]—they broke camp, formed their battle-lines, and followed him as though intending to engage him. Only one thing prevented a mutual encounter: a stream, which offered a difficult crossing, kept the two armies apart. [Note: [Col. 1263D] “Prohibeat,” prevents: two Royal manuscripts and Saint-Germain have “prohibebat,” prevented.]

Thus on the first and second day both armies viewed one another, their trumpets sounding and their threatening missiles opposed. Suddenly a certain minstrel, a worthy knight, came to the Franks from the opposing side, announcing that at the first opportunity they found, the enemy would certainly engage them and avenge with lances and swords the injury inflicted upon their freedom; he had left them in order to join his natural lord and fight for and with him. The report resounded through the camps, and the soldiers’ boldness exulted. They adorned themselves with the shining splendor of mail-coats and helmets, stirred up their courage [Col. 1263B], and, should a crossing present itself, hastened to leap the stream, judging it more worthy to attack their enemies than to defend themselves.

When the most noble men Enguerrand of Boves, Count Ebles of Roucy, Andrew of Rameru, Hugh the White of La Ferté, Robert of Cappy, and other wise and discerning men saw this, they admired the designated lord’s courage, chose prudently to submit to him, and came peacefully to him. They embraced his youth, gave him the right hands of friendship, and pledged themselves and their men to his service. [Note: [Col. 1263D] “Ruciaco”: since the capture of Montaigu occurred later than 1101 and not earlier than 1104, Anselm plainly errs in placing the death of Ebles of Roucy in 1100.] [Note: [Col. 1263D] “Rameru”: Saint-Germain and Royal MS 5925 have “Ramerii.”] [Note: [Col. 1263D] “Contradentes,” giving: in two manuscripts and Saint-Germain, “contendentes,” striving.] Not long afterwards, so that the overthrow of the wicked may be ascribed to the divine will, Thomas lost both the castle and the marriage, polluted by the incest of consanguinity, through divorce. [Note: [Col. 1263D–1264D] In his third marriage, after this divorce, Thomas married Melisende, daughter and heiress of Guy, lord of Crécy and Nouvion.]

## CHAPTER VIII

Rising through these and other advances in virtue, the designated lord diligently strove, as circumstances required, to provide wisely for the administration and commonwealth of the kingdom, to subdue rebels, and by every means either seize or force into submission troublesome castles.

Thus, when Guy Troussel, son of Miles of Montlhéry, a turbulent man and disturber of the kingdom, had returned home from the road to the Holy Sepulchre, broken by the hardship of the long journey and the suffering of various afflictions, and had utterly collapsed in body because he had extraordinarily descended from the wall at Antioch through fear of Corbaran and left God’s army besieged within, he feared that his only daughter, Elizabeth, would be disinherited. [Note: [Col. 1264D] “Trusellus” in the Saint-Germain manuscripts and Royal MSS 6265.] [Note: [Col. 1264D] “Corboranni”: two Royal manuscripts have “Corborani.”] At the will and persuasion of King Philip and his son Louis—for they greatly desired the castle—he gave her in marriage to Philip, the king’s son by the subsequently married countess of Anjou (A.D. 1104). To bind the elder brother, Lord Louis, firmly to his interest, he confirmed the marriage, at his father’s request, with the castle of Meduntense [Col. 1264A].

When they received the castle into their custody on this occasion, they rejoiced as though they had removed a splinter from their eye or broken down enclosing barriers. Indeed, we ourselves heard the father say to his son Louis that Miles had burdened him most grievously by his vexations: “Come, my son Louis; keep watch over the tower whose oppression has almost made me old, and because of whose fraud and deceitful wickedness I could never possess good peace and quiet. His faithlessness made the faithful faithless and the faithless utterly faithless; it joined traitors near and far, and no evil anywhere in the whole kingdom was done without their consent or their action.”

Since the district of Paris was enclosed from the river Seine to Corbeil, with Montlhéry midway along the route and Châteaufort to the right [Col. 1264B], so vast a chaos of disorder had been established between the Parisians and the Orléanais that neither these could pass to those nor those to these without the judgment of traitors, unless they could do so by force of arms. But the aforesaid marriage broke the barrier and restored pleasant access in both directions.

To this was added that Guy of Rochefort, an experienced and veteran knight, paternal uncle of the aforesaid Guy Troussel, returned from the Jerusalem journey with fame and abundant resources and attached himself favorably to King Philip. Since, by old familiarity, he had already once before been the king’s seneschal, both the king and his son Lord Louis appointed him seneschal for the conduct of public affairs, in order that henceforth they might possess the aforesaid castle of Montlhéry peacefully [Col. 1264C], and might claim from their neighboring county—namely Rochefort and Châteaufort—and from other nearby castles both peace and service, which had been unusual.

Their mutual intimacy proceeded so far that, at his father’s persuasion, his son Lord Louis received in solemn marriage the daughter of this Guy, still unmarried (A.D. 1104). But he did not have as wife the woman whom he received as betrothed: before the marriage bed, the impediment of consanguinity intervened and dissolved the marriage after several years. [Note: [Col. 1264D] Pope Paschal II dissolved, at the Council of Troyes in 1107, the contracted marriage between Louis the Fat and Lucienne, daughter of Guy the Red of Rochefort, on the pretext of consanguinity, but in fact because of complaints from magnates offended by the excessive inequality of the spouses. Lucienne afterwards married Guiscard of Beaujeu.]

For three years their friendship continued in such a manner that father and son placed the utmost trust in him, while Count Guy and his son Hugh of Crécy devoted all their strength to the kingdom’s defense and honor. But because:

> A newly fashioned jar will long retain  
> The fragrance with which it was once imbued.

(Horace, *Epistles* 2.69)

the men of Montlhéry, imitators of their habitual treachery, treacherously devised a scheme through the Garland brothers, who had then incurred the hostility of the king and his son. Miles, viscount of Troyes and younger brother of Guy Troussel, came with his mother, the viscountess, and a great force of knights. Received into the castle by all with welcome but perjured intent, he repeatedly recalled his father’s benefactions with tears, displayed their noble and natural devotion, praised their remarkable fidelity, offered thanks for his recall, and, prostrate at their knees, humbly begged them to bring their good beginning to a good completion [Col. 1265A].

Moved by such a tearful kneeling, they ran to arms, hastened to the tower, and attacked its defenders most fiercely with swords, lances, fire, stakes, and stones. They pierced the outer wall of the tower in several places and wounded many of its defenders to death [Col. 1265B]. In that tower were the wife of the aforesaid Guy and the daughter betrothed to Lord Louis.

When this reached the ears of Guy the seneschal, being a man of one purpose, he promptly set out and boldly approached the castle with as great a force of knights as he could muster; he also sent the swiftest messengers so that men might follow him quickly from every side. [Note: [Col. 1265D] “Unanimis,” of one purpose: all manuscripts have “magnanimus,” high-spirited.] But the attackers of the tower, seeing him from the hill and unable as yet to overcome the tower, feared the sudden coming of Lord Louis as though it were a knife at their throats. They withdrew and began to hesitate whether to stand or flee.

Guy, however, being valiant and prudent in action, wisely summoned the Garland brothers away from the castle, confirmed by oath the peace and favor of the king and Lord Louis [Col. 1265C], and thus diverted them and their accomplices from their undertaking. [Note: [Col. 1265D] Royal MS 5265 adds “complices,” accomplices.] With their failure Miles too failed, and, weeping and lamenting over his frustrated plot, took to swift flight. When Louis heard this, he hastened most rapidly to the castle. Having learned the truth and finding that he had lost nothing, he rejoiced; but he was grieved that he had not found the conspirators in order to hang them on the gallows. Toward those who remained, however, because Guy had confirmed peace by oath, Lord Louis kept the peace. Yet, lest they devise anything similar thereafter, he demolished the whole fortification of the castle except the tower.

## CHAPTER IX
At about this time the illustrious prince of Antioch, Bohemond—whose prowess had won him the fortified city itself after that mighty siege [Col. 1265D]—came down into the regions of France (1106). He was a distinguished and famous man among the eastern peoples, and even among the Saracens there was celebrated a certain noble deed of his, one which could never have been accomplished without the divine hand.

For when, together with his father Robert Guiscard, he had once besieged the overseas stronghold of Dyrrachium—“almost,” in two Royal manuscripts and the Saint-Germain manuscript, rather than “once” [Note: Col. 1265D]—neither the treasures of Thessalonica, nor those of Constantinople, nor Greece itself in its entirety could drive them away. Suddenly, after they had crossed the sea, legates of Pope Alexander appeared before them, solemnly urging them by the love of God and by the obligation of homage, and most devoutly begging them to rescue the Roman Church and the lord pope, shut up in the tower of Crescentius by the emperor. They declared on oath that the City and the Church—indeed, the pope himself—would be shipwrecked unless aid came quickly.

The princes hesitated, uncertain what to choose: whether irrevocably to abandon so great and costly an expedition, or to suffer the pope, the City, and the Church to be reduced to servitude—indeed, to be shipwrecked. [Col. 1266B] As they agonized over this deliberation, they resolved upon the most excellent course: to do this and not to abandon that. Bohemond was therefore left at the siege, while his father crossed back into Apulia. Gathering men and arms wherever he could, from Sicily, Apulia, Calabria, and Campania, he hurried with the utmost promptness and boldness to Rome.

By the divine will, and in what was almost a miraculous portent, it happened that, while he was approaching Rome and the emperor of Constantinople, having heard of Robert’s absence, had assembled a Greek army and advanced against Bohemond at Dyrrachium by land and sea, on one and the same day Guiscard the father engaged the emperor at Rome, and Bohemond fought vigorously against the Greek emperor. Each prince, wondrous to relate, [Col. 1266C] triumphed over his respective emperor.

[Note: Cols. 1265D–1266D. “Triumphed.” Here Suger appears to have suffered a lapse of memory. It was not Pope Alexander II, but Gregory VII, his successor, whom Guiscard rescued when besieged by Emperor Henry IV; this occurred in 1084, namely two years after Dyrrachium had been captured by Guiscard. That capture took place on 8 February 1082.]

The reason for the aforesaid Bohemond’s arrival in these parts was that he sought by every means to join in marriage the most noble Constance, sister of the lord Louis-designate: charming in manners, elegant in figure, and most beautiful in face. For such was the celebrated prowess both of the kingdom of the Franks and of Lord Louis that even the Saracens were frightened by dread of this alliance. The lady was free, having rejected Hugh, count of Troyes, as a suitor, and she desired a second union with a husband not unworthy of her.

[Note: Col. 1266D. “Having rejected.” Constance, daughter of King Philip, had first married Hugh, count of Troyes; in 1104 she was thereafter separated from him on grounds of consanguinity.]

[Note: Col. 1266D. “Not unworthy.” Thus all manuscripts. The edition reads “worthy.”]

The prince of Antioch, shrewd and abundant alike in gifts and promises, successfully secured a most splendid marriage with that lady at Chartres, in the presence of the king and Lord Louis, with many archbishops, bishops, and magnates of the realm standing by (1106). Present there also was the apostolic legate of the Roman see, Lord Bruno, bishop of Segni, sent by Pope Paschal to accompany Bohemond in urging and strengthening the expedition to the Holy Sepulchre. Accordingly, he held a full and celebrated council [Col. 1267A] at Poitiers, at which we too were present, since we had recently returned from our studies.

[Note: Col. 1267C. “We were present.” The chronographer of Maillezais attests that this council was held in 1106, on 26 June, the sixth day before the Kalends of July.]

There, dealing with various synodal matters and especially with the Jerusalem journey lest it grow lukewarm, both he and Bohemond encouraged many men to go. Relying on the large company and numerous armed force of those men, Bohemond himself, Lady Constance, and the legate all returned prosperously and gloriously to their own lands.

Lady Constance bore Lord Bohemond two sons, John and Bohemond; but John died in Apulia before reaching the years of military service. Bohemond, however, a handsome young man fitted for warfare, became prince of Antioch. When he was vigorously pressing the Saracens with arms, and their jealous attacks gained nothing, he pursued them with insufficient caution. Caught in their ambush, though more high-spirited than was prudent, he was unhappily beheaded with one hundred [Col. 1267B] knights and lost Antioch along with his life in Apulia.

[Note: Col. 1267C. “Lost.” Sanudo, under the year 1130, p. 162, thus recounts the death of Bohemond, prince of Antioch, second of that name and rank: “After … Bohemond returns to Antioch, Rodoan, prince of Aleppo, enters the land of Antioch with a large army. But while Bohemond, suspecting no danger, rested on a certain plain of Cilicia, his enemies, having learned his position, suddenly rushed upon the Christians and slaughtered the prince with the rest who were unable to flee.” William of Tyre, p. 850, reports the same.]

In the year following the aforesaid Bohemond’s return home (1107), Paschal, supreme pontiff and pope of universal and venerable memory, came into the western regions, together with many most wise men—bishops, cardinals, and a retinue of Roman nobles—to take counsel with the king of the Franks, his son King-designate Louis, and the Gallican Church concerning certain troubles and new disputes over ecclesiastical investiture. On these matters Emperor Henry, a man possessing his father’s disposition and devoid of all humanity, was harassing him and threatening to harass him still more. Henry had cruelly persecuted and disinherited his own father Henry; and, as was reported, holding him under a most wicked captivity, he had most impiously compelled him, by the beatings and insults of his enemies, to surrender the royal insignia—namely the crown, sceptre, and lance [Col. 1268A] of St. Maurice—and to retain nothing as his own in the entire realm.

[Note: Cols. 1267C–D. “Came.” Added in the margin of Royal MS 6265; absent from the edition.]

It had indeed been decided at Rome, because of the treacherous unreliability of Roman mercenaries, that the affairs just mentioned—indeed all disputes—of the king, the king’s son, and the Gallican Church should more safely be debated in France than in the City.

[Note: Col. 1267D. “By aid/support” (*suffragio*). Thus all manuscripts; the edition has “by shipwreck” (*naufragio*).]

He therefore came to Cluny, and from Cluny to La Charité, where, amid a most celebrated gathering of archbishops, bishops, and members of monastic orders, he performed the sacred dedication of that noble monastery.

[Note: Col. 1267D. “Performed the dedication.” This dedication was carried out on 9 March, the seventh day before the Ides, according to the Chronicle of Fécamp.]

The nobler magnates of the kingdom were present as well. Among them, the royal seneschal of France, the noble count of Rochefort, came to meet the pope as his envoy, in order to serve him throughout the kingdom according to the pope’s pleasure, as a spiritual father. We ourselves were present at that consecration [Col. 1268B], and, standing firmly before the pope, we satisfied by clear reasoning and canonical judgment the complaints against the Church of St. Denis which Bishop Galon of Paris had been pressing.

[Note: Cols. 1267D–1268D. “We satisfied.” Having crossed the Alps in a most severe winter, Paschal arrived in 1106 shortly before Christmas, which, according to the Chronicle of Ursperg, he celebrated there. He then made for Lyons, where on 29 January of the following year he dedicated the new basilica of the monastery of Ainay (*Gallia Christiana*, new ed., IV, col. 236). He was at the village of St. Hippolyte on 8 February (*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 537). At Beaune in Burgundy he issued, for the benefit of the recently mentioned monastery of Ainay, a diploma dated at Beaune, 12 February, indiction XV, year of the Incarnation 1106, and eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II (*Gallia Christiana*, new ed., IV, Instruments, col. 13); here the year of the Incarnation is reckoned according to French custom. The pope then turned from Beaune to Dijon, and there, on 16 February, dedicated the church of St. Bénigne (Pérard, p. 210). Proceeding thence to Bèze, he addressed the brethren of that monastery and consecrated its high altar on 18 February (*Spicilegium*, quarto ed., vol. I, p. 638). After spending three days there, he went to Langres, where Bishop-elect Galdric of Laon and envoys of the Church of Laon were awaiting his arrival. Altolinus, abbot of St. Clement at Metz, also met him there; Paschal received that monastery under his protection and issued letters at Langres on 24 February. From that city he directed his journey to Auxerre, as we learn from a diploma issued there in 1107, indiction XV, without designation of the month (Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. V, p. 500). From Auxerre he therefore went to the cell of La Charité, where Suger met him in the king’s name.]

When, at Tours, at Saint Martin’s, he had celebrated *Laetare Jerusalem*, according to Roman custom, wearing the *phrygium*—the papal crown—[Note: Col. 1268D: “Phrygium.” The chief ornament of the supreme pontiff’s head is also called a “kingdom” by writers; now it is distinguished by a triple crown, whereas then it was encircled by a single one. Historians dispute which pope first used one crown, which two, and which finally three; the issue remains unresolved. Certainly the six statues erected either during Boniface VIII’s lifetime or shortly after his death depict him with one crown, although most writers assert that he added the second crown to the first; see Marengoni, *Chronicle of the Supreme Pontiffs*.]—on the fourth Sunday of Lent, 22 March that year [Note: Col. 1268D], he came kindly and devoutly to the venerable place of St. Denis, as though to the very seat of Blessed Peter.

Received gloriously and with full episcopal honor, he left to posterity this one memorable and, for Romans, unusual example: he not only did not covet the monastery’s gold, silver, and precious gems, as was much feared, but did not even deign to look upon them. Prostrating himself most humbly before the pledges of the saints, [Col. 1268C] he offered tears of contrition; he offered himself wholly in heart as a burnt offering to the Lord and [Col. 1269A] His saints; and he humbly begged that some small portion of the episcopal vestments of St. Denis, stained with blood, might be given him for protection. “Let it not displease you,” he said, “if you return to us even a little of his vestments, for we sent him to you, adorned with the apostolate of Gaul, without complaint.”

[Note: Col. 1269D. “Without complaint.” Thus all manuscripts; the edition has “with a gift.”]

King Philip and his son Lord Louis also met him there gladly and with reverent devotion (1107), bowing the royal majesty at his feet for love of God, just as kings are accustomed to bow at the tomb of Peter the fisherman with their diadem laid aside. Raising them by the hand, the pope made them proceed before him as most devout sons of the apostles. As one acting wisely and prudently, he conferred familiarly with them [Col. 1269B] about the state of the Church; and, gently persuading them, he begged them to bring aid to Blessed Peter and to himself, Peter’s vicar, to uphold the Church by their hand, and, as had become customary among their royal predecessors—Charlemagne and the other kings of France—to resist boldly the tyrants and enemies of the Church, especially Emperor Henry.

They pledged hands of friendship, aid, and counsel; they placed the kingdom at his disposal; and they appointed archbishops, bishops, and Abbot Adam of St. Denis, with whom we too were present, to hasten with him to Châlons to meet the emperor’s legates.

[Note: Col. 1269D. “They placed the kingdom at his disposal, and …” From this it is clear that Philip had already been restored to ecclesiastical communion and had at last obtained from the supreme pontiff the dispensation concerning his marriage for which Ivo of Chartres and other bishops had petitioned.]

When the pope had remained there for some time, the legates of Emperor Henry arrived by prior arrangement. They were not humble, but stiff-necked and obstinate. Having taken lodgings at Saint-Memmie—Royal MS: Saint-Memmius [Note: Col. 1269D]—they left there Chancellor Albert, by whose unity of speech and heart the emperor himself acted. The others came to the court in a great train, with great pomp and magnificently adorned. They were the archbishop of Trier, the bishop of “Alvertat” [uncertain reading], the bishop of Münster, several counts, and Duke Welf, before whom a sword was borne everywhere: a corpulent man, astonishing in the entire expanse of his length and breadth, and loud-voiced. They seemed to have been sent in an uproar more to terrify than to reason.

The archbishop of Trier alone, an elegant and agreeable man, rich in eloquence and wisdom and trained in the Gallic manner of public speaking, delivered a polished address. On behalf of the emperor he conveyed greetings and service to the pope and court, [Col. 1269D] saving the rights of the empire. He proceeded to state his instructions:

“This,” he said, “is the business of our lord emperor for which we have been sent. In the times of our predecessors, the holy and apostolic men Gregory the Great and others, it was recognized as belonging to the right of the empire that, in every election, this order be observed: before the election is made public, it must be reported to the ears of the lord emperor; and, if the person is suitable, his assent must be obtained before the election is made. Then, in the assembly, according to the canons, the election is to be proclaimed upon the petition of the people, the election of the clergy, and the assent of the patron. The consecrated person is then freely, and without simony, to return to the lord emperor concerning the regalia, so that he may be invested with ring and staff and perform fealty and homage.

“Nor is it strange that cities and castles, marches, tolls, and everything [Col. 1270B] belonging to imperial dignity should be possessed in no other manner. If the lord pope accepts this, the empire and Church will prosperously cleave together in good peace, to the honor of God.”

The pope then replied thoughtfully through the spokesman, the bishop of Piacenza:

“The Church, redeemed by the precious blood of Jesus Christ and established free, ought by no means to be reduced again to servitude. If the Church cannot elect a prelate without consulting him, then Christ’s death is nullified and she is subjected to him as a slave. If he invests with staff and ring—though these belong to the altars—he arrogates them to himself against God. If they subject hands consecrated to the Lord’s body and blood to lay hands bound to the bloody sword, they derogate from their own order and sacred anointing.”

[Note: Cols. 1269D–1270D. “Church.” The spokesman here uses “clergy” in the sense of the whole Church, after the custom of his time, playing upon the ambiguity of the word. Had the emperor’s legates answered this a little more acutely, the whole reasoning of the bishop of Piacenza would have vanished into smoke.]

When the stiff-necked legates heard these and similar arguments, they ground their teeth in Teutonic fury and raised an uproar. Had they dared safely, they would have spewed insults and inflicted injuries. “This dispute,” they said, “will be settled not here but at Rome by swords.”

But the pope sent several approved and experienced men to the chancellor, to confer with him calmly and peacefully on these points, to hear and be heard, and earnestly to entreat him to work for peace in the realm. When they had departed, the pope came to Troyes (1107), honorably held the universal council which had long been announced, and returned prosperously to the see of St. Peter, with the love of the Franks, who had served him greatly, and with fear and hatred of the Germans.

[Note: Cols. 1270D–1271D. “Returned.” Paschal’s journey through Gaul, which we began to describe above, continued as follows. Leaving the cell of La Charité, he was still at Marmoutier near Tours on 5 April, as letters issued there by him for the monastery of St. Laumer of Blois attest (Mabillon, cited work). From Tours he proceeded to Vendôme, where, according to Geoffrey, abbot of that place, he stayed eleven days (Geoffrey of Vendôme, bk. II, ep. 18). After these days he went to the monastery of St. Denis, where he stayed until the end of April, perhaps somewhat longer. For, in letters issued there on the day before the Kalends of May, he confirmed the possessions of the monastery of St. Martin-des-Champs (*History of St. Martin-des-Champs*, p. 154). He was lodging at Lagny on 3 May; on that day, by a diploma issued there, he confirmed the possessions of the monastery of Crépy (Mabillon, cited work, p. 501). From there he proceeded to Châlons. Since the business for which he had come to that city remained unfinished, he went to Troyes for the council he had summoned there. Mabillon mentions letters issued in that city by the pope on 24 May for the monastery of Saint-Amand of Elnone and believes Paschal did not leave before the penultimate day of May. But the most learned man is mistaken on this point. There survives a diploma of Paschal issued at Lurcy-le-Bourg in Nivernais, written through the hand of John, cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on 31 May, indiction V, year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1107 (*New General History of Christianity*, vol. IV, Instruments, cols. 85–86). Mabillon more correctly states that the pope was at Sauvigny on 9 and 5 June. Paschal was at Celsinaires on the vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul, and at Valence in July (ibid.). Finally, he stayed at Aiguebelle in Savoy on 4 August, whence he had reached Parma by 3 November.]

About the second year after the pope’s departure, the emperor, having assembled an extraordinary enemy force of thirty thousand soldiers [Col. 1271A]—all manuscripts read *millium*, “of thousands”; the edition reads *millia*, “thousands” [Note: Col. 1271D]—was pleased to have no paths except those opened by shed blood. He set out for Rome; pretending that he knew how to make peace, he laid aside the dispute over investitures, promised many good things, these among others, and, in order to enter the City, since otherwise he could not, he flattered. He did not fear to deceive the supreme pontiff and the entire Church—indeed, the King of kings Himself.

Because the Roman citizens heard that so great and ruinous a dispute of the Church of God had been laid to rest, they rejoiced exceedingly—Royal MS 6265 reads “knights,” not “citizens” [Note: Col. 1272D]—the clergy exulted beyond measure, and, in their delight, all strove to receive him with the greatest honor and elegance (1111). When the pope, surrounded by a company of bishops and cardinals in formal dress, riding horses covered in white trappings—“covered,” not “open,” in all manuscripts [Note: Col. 1272D]—and followed by a troop of Roman people, hurried out to meet him, men had been sent ahead to receive from the emperor, upon the holy Gospels having been touched, an oath of peace and a renunciation of investitures. At the place called Monte Gaudio, where the thresholds of the blessed apostles first come into view for arrivals, the same oath was repeated.

Then, in the portico, before the marvelous and universal spectacle of the Romans, the oath was made threefold by the emperor and the magnates themselves. Thereupon, far more nobly than if an arch of triumph had smiled upon him after he had won an African victory, he was crowned with the diadem by the pope’s most sacred hand, in the manner of the Augusti. With hymns and a manifold triumph of praises, he was led to the most sacred altar of the apostles in most celebrated and solemn devotion, while the melodies of chanting clergy and the terrible shout of singing Germans [Col. 1271C] pierced the heavens.

When the pope, celebrating the Mass of thanksgiving, had consecrated the body and blood of Jesus Christ, the emperor communicated, receiving the divided Eucharist as a marvelous hostage of the Church, pledged in the covenant of indivisible love and preservation of the agreement.

[Note: Col. 1272D. “Hostage.” Thus all manuscripts; the editions read “for faith.”]

The pope had not yet removed his episcopal vestments after Mass—“vestments” in all manuscripts; the editions have another synonym [Note: Col. 1272D]—when, upon the pretext of an invented dispute, Teutonic fury burst out in unexpected wickedness. With swords drawn, they ran about as though full of madness—thus all manuscripts; the edition reads “insanity” [Note: Col. 1272D]—and attacked the Romans, rightly unarmed in such a place. They shouted by oath that the Roman clergy, all bishops as well as cardinals, must be seized [Col. 1272A] or slaughtered. What no madness can possibly go beyond, they did not fear to lay impious hands upon the lord pope.

With inexpressible grief and heartfelt pain, both the Roman nobility and the people themselves bewailed the betrayal. Though they realized it late, some ran to arms while others fled like men stunned; and in the unexpected warfare of their enemies, they could not escape except by pulling down beams from the portico, causing their fall to serve as a defense. [Note: Col. 1272D. “Serve.” Royal MS 5925, Saint-Denis, and Saint-Germain read *fecerint*; Royal MS 6225 reads *fecerunt*; the edition reads *facere*.]

The aforesaid emperor, terrified by the torment of his most wicked conscience and criminal deed—“criminal” in the Royal and Saint-Denis manuscripts; Saint-Germain has the erroneous *factinorosi*; the edition reads “crime” [Note: Col. 1272D]—left the City as quickly as possible. Carrying off a spoil unheard of among Christians inflicted by a Christian upon Christians—namely the lord pope and all the cardinals and bishops he could seize—he withdrew to the city of Castellana, a place most strongly fortified by situation and art.

There [Col. 1272B] he shamefully stripped the cardinals and treated them dishonorably; and, what is unspeakable, he did not fear to lay hands on the anointed of the Lord. He proudly stripped the pope himself of his cope, mitre, and whatever insignia of the apostolate he wore—“wore” in four manuscripts; the edition reads “wears” [Note: Col. 1272D]—and inflicted many injuries, a phrase supplied by four manuscripts but absent from the editions [Note: Col. 1272D]. He did not release him or his followers, afflicted by much disgrace, until he compelled them to grant the settlement of the aforesaid pact and to issue the resulting charter.

He also extorted from the pope’s hand a fraudulent privilege, allowing him henceforth to invest. The same pope, before a great council of three hundred and more bishops, in a judgment of the Church which we heard, shattered this privilege and, by perpetual anathema, declared it null and void.

[Note: Col. 1272D. “Declared it null and void.” From the Royal and Saint-Germain manuscripts; absent from the edition.]

But if anyone asks why the pope acted so weakly, let him know that, when the shepherd and those at his side had been struck down, the Church languished; and the tyrant, reducing her to servitude, was almost occupying her as his own because there was no one to resist (1112). This he gave as a certain proof by his action: when he had somehow secured the release of the brethren, the pillars of the Church, for her protection and restoration, and had restored whatever peace to the Church he could, he fled to a desert solitude and would have remained there permanently, had not the violence of the universal Church and the Romans compelled his return.

[Note: Col. 1272D. “To whom.” Royal MS 5925 reads “indeed.” The printed *quod* should be read *quoniam*, “because.”]

But the Lord Jesus Christ, Redeemer and Defender of His Church, did not suffer her to be trampled down any longer, nor the emperor to go unpunished. Those who were neither captive nor bound by oath took up the cause of the imperiled Church; with the support and counsel of Lord Louis-designate, and with the Church assembled at a famous Gallican council, they bound the tyrant emperor with an anathema and pierced him with the sword of Blessed Peter.

[Note: Col. 1273D. Namely at the Council of Vienne, held on 16 September 1112.]

Afterward, the magnates of the German kingdom—his own supporters—stirred up the greater part of the realm against him. They deposed Burchard the Red, bishop of Münster, and did not desist from harassing or dispossessing him until the fitting extinction of his wicked life and tyrannical rule.

[Note: Col. 1273D. “Did not desist.” Two Royal manuscripts and the Saint-Germain manuscript have *supersederunt*; the editions read *desuper sederunt*.]

The empire was deservedly transferred from him by God’s vengeance: when he had been driven out, Lothair, duke of Saxony, succeeded, a warlike man and an unconquered defender of the commonwealth. [Col. 1273B] Having subdued recalcitrant Italy, Campania, and Apulia as far as the Adriatic Sea by devastation, accompanied by Pope Innocent and with Roger of Sicily present—“king” in the edition, “count” in four manuscripts [Note: Col. 1273D]—because Roger had made himself king, he returned victorious in a most noble triumph and yielded to death and burial.

[Note: Col. 1273D. “Pope.” All manuscripts read *papae*, “to/with the pope”; the edition reads *papa*.]

Let their own writers depict these and other such deeds. We, since we have proposed to do so, shall resume the thread of the deeds of the Franks.

## Chapter X

The aforesaid Count Guy of Rochefort, since—thus all manuscripts in abbreviation; the edition wrongly reads “whom” [Note: Col. 1273D]—through the machinations of his rivals the marriage being contracted between the lord-designate and his daughter had been challenged on grounds of consanguinity and dissolved by divorce in the pope’s presence, namely at the Council of Troyes [Note: Col. 1273D], conceived resentment in his heart and fed a slight spark into stirred-up flames. Nor did the lord-designate feel less hostility toward him, when the Garlande family suddenly broke off their friendship, violated their alliance, and intensified their enmities.

The lord-designate therefore found an occasion for war because Hugh of Pomponne, a valiant knight and castellan of the castle of Gournay, situated on the River Marne, had unexpectedly seized the horses of merchants upon the royal road and carried them to Gournay.

[Note: Col. 1273D. The Saint-Germain manuscript has the erroneous reading “unexpected horses.”]

Nearly beside himself with indignation at this presumptuous outrage, Louis gathered an army [Col. 1274D] and swiftly surrounded the castle in a sudden siege, so that the defenders might lack abundant supplies.

[Note: Col. 1274D. Daniel wrongly assigns this expedition to 1100, although it followed the Council of Troyes, held around the Feast of the Ascension in 1107.]

Beside the castle lay an island delightful for the abundance of its pastures, rich in horses and livestock. Stretching out somewhat in breadth but more in length, [Col. 1273D] it brought the townspeople the greatest advantage. It offered to those walking there the bright refreshment of running waters and the delightful beauty of grass now flowering, now green; and the encircling river gave its inhabitants security.

[Note: Col. 1274D. “And.” Royal MS 6265, Saint-Denis, and Saint-Germain read: “and, to those walking …”; the editions read: “when it …”]

Louis therefore prepared a fleet and hastened to attack the island. He stripped some of the knights and many foot-soldiers so that they could enter more freely and, should they fall, recover more swiftly. Others he ordered to occupy the island boldly: some by swimming; others by riding their horses, though perilously, through the depth of the waters; and he himself entered the river in the same way. The townsmen resisted stoutly. Higher up on the steep bank and lower down in the waves and against the fleet, they fiercely drove the attackers back with stones, lances, and stakes.

Yet, driven back, the attackers recovered their courage and pressed on to drive back those who had repelled them. They compelled crossbowmen and archers to shoot; they fought hand to hand as far as they could reach; armored and helmeted, they joined battle from the fleet with the audacity of pirates. They repelled their repellers, and, as valor impatient of disgrace is wont to do, they recovered by arms the island they had occupied [Col. 1274B] and compelled the defenders to withdraw shut up within the castle.

When after some time he could not force the tightly besieged men to surrender, impatient of delay he was carried away by a fit of daring. One day he summoned his army and attacked the most strongly fortified castle, nearly impregnable above because of the narrow, steep rampart called the *glande*—the upper part of the castle [Note: Col. 1274D]—and below because of the torrent’s depth. Climbing through the torrent, waist-deep in the ditch, he pressed toward the *glande*, commanded them to fight by fighting, and struggled most fiercely and bitterly with the enemy.

The defenders, on the other hand, quickly exerted themselves in defense, preferring boldness to life itself. They did not spare even the lord; they used their weapons and hurled the enemy back from above—indeed, cast them downward into the torrent below. Thus, on that occasion—“on that occasion” in four manuscripts; the edition reads “by that route” [Note: Col. 1274D]—the former gained glory, the latter suffered repulse, though unwillingly.

Thereafter siege-engines were prepared for destroying the castle. A three-storied tower was erected, an immense engine rising above the combatants, which, from its supreme [uncertain: *superlativa*] first fighting-platform, prevented the castle’s archers and crossbowmen from moving about or appearing. [Note: Col. 1274D. *Superlativa* is the reading to be adopted from three manuscripts.] Since they were constrained by these defenses without interruption day and night and could not attend to their own defense, the defenders protected themselves prudently in covered shelters; lying in wait for their opponents’ archers’ blows, they forestalled the men above on the first fighting-platform with the danger of death.

A wooden bridge was attached to the high engine; extending outward at a greater height, when lowered somewhat over the *glande* it would provide an easy entry for those descending. But the defenders, skilled in such matters, placed separate wooden platforms opposite, so that both the bridge and the men entering by it might fall on either side into underground pits armed with sharp stakes and deceptively covered with straw lest they be noticed, and thus face peril to life and a heavy toll of death.

[Note: Col. 1274D. The Saint-Germain manuscript reads “on both sides.”]

Meanwhile the aforesaid Guy, a shrewd and valiant man, stirred up relatives and friends, appealed to lords with entreaties, and hurried relief to the besieged. He therefore arranged with Count Theobald the Palatine, a man of most distinguished youth and trained by diligence in the discipline of arms, that on a fixed day—since provisions were failing the besieged—he should bring reinforcements and, by force of arms, deliver the castle from siege. Meanwhile Guy labored by plundering and burning to make the siege be lifted.

On the appointed day, when the aforesaid Count Theobald was both to bring relief and remove the siege by military force, the lord-designate assembled all the army he could, not at a distance but close at hand. Remembering the royal excellence of his inherited valor, he left the tents and their defenders and joyfully went to meet them. Sending a man ahead to announce that they were coming and wished to fight, [Col. 1275B] he summoned his barons, drew up his battle lines, and assigned the cavalry, infantry, archers, and lancers to their respective positions.

When they came in sight of one another, trumpets sounded; the spirit of riders and horses was stirred; battle was joined with the utmost speed. But the Franks, continually trained in war, attacked the men of Brie, softened by long peace. They struck them down with lances and swords, pressed their advantage, and did not cease courageously to assault them with both mounted and foot forces until the enemy, turning their backs, sought safety in flight.

[Note: Col. 1275D. The Saint-Germain manuscript reads *arripuerint*, “have seized.”]

Count Theobald himself, preferring to be found first rather than last in flight, lest he be captured, abandoned his army and hastened home. In that encounter some were killed, many wounded, and very many captured—“more” in all manuscripts [Note: Col. 1275D]—and they made the victory renowned and most celebrated throughout all lands.

Having won so great and opportune a victory, Lord Louis returned to the tents, drove out the townsmen disappointed of their vain hope, retained the castle for himself, and entrusted it to the Garlande family.

## Chapter XI
Thus, just as sloth, attended by indolence, makes noble men ignoble and glorious men inglorious [Note: Cod. St. Germ.: “more inglorious”], indeed casts them down; so strength of spirit, stirred by bodily exercise, raises noble men to greater nobility and glorious men to greater glory. It repays the vigor in which it delights by offering men splendid deeds from every quarter of the earth for their enjoyment. There were indeed those who petitioned him with magnificent supplications [Note: Cod. St. Germ.: *exorent*; the other manuscripts: *exorrent*; printed edition: *exhorrent*.] [Note: That is, petitions. Varro, Sallust, Tacitus, and other finest authors of Latin use *supplicium* in this sense.], to cross with a large and costly force into the region of Bourges, where the borders of Limousin adjoin it, namely against the very noble castle of Sainte-Sévère, famous by hereditary possession of knighthood and populous with many foot-soldiers; and either compel its lord, the nobleman Hunbald [elsewhere Hunbaud], to execute justice, or make him forfeit the castle, by Salic law, as right for wrong.
