When requested, Louis entered those districts not with a hostile force but with the military following of his own household. As he hastened toward the castle, the aforesaid castellan, accompanied by many knights—he was of noble [Note: Cod. Reg. 6265: “of noble birth.”] blood, generous and prudent—met him. Setting a certain stream before him, fortified with barriers and stakes, since there was no other approach, he resisted the French army. And while both sides remained there, separated by the stream, Lord Louis, angered that one of them had more boldly than the rest come out beyond the barriers, spurred his horse. Being, as he was, a man of greater courage than the others, he leapt upon him, struck him with his lance, and overthrew not only him but, through him [Note: “Through him.” Thus all manuscripts; printed edition: “besides.”], another with a single blow. He then made for himself in that same stream—unworthy of a king—a plentiful bath up to his helmet. Nor did he delay to press his advantage: where the other had come out through a narrow passage, Louis entered, and did not cease in hand-to-hand combat to drive the enemy back.

When the French saw this, they were wonderfully encouraged: they broke through the barriers, leapt across the stream, and, pursuing the enemy with great slaughter, drove them back, forced as far as the castle. The report flew abroad and struck the townsmen and the whole neighborhood with alarm: Lord Louis and his men, like most valiant soldiers, would refuse to withdraw until they had utterly overthrown the castle and either hanged the more noble inhabitants or torn out their eyes. Therefore prudent measures were taken: the lord of the castle should not delay to surrender himself to the royal majesty and subject both castle and land to his authority. Louis accordingly returned, made the lord of the castle his prize, left him at Étampes in a sudden triumph, and came back to Paris with happy success.

## Chapter XII

As the son advanced day by day, his father King Philip [Col. 1276C] declined day by day. For after bringing in the Countess of Anjou, he did nothing worthy of royal majesty, but, seized by desire for the woman he had carried off, devoted himself to satisfying his pleasure. Hence he neither looked after the commonwealth nor spared, with due restraint, the health of his distinguished and elegant body, being too indulgent toward it. One thing alone remained: through fear and love of his son and successor, the stability of the kingdom endured.

When he was nearly sixty, Philip laid aside kingship at the castle of Melun on the river Seine, in the presence of Lord Louis, and ended his final day (A.D. 1108). At his noble funeral were present the venerable men Walo [elsewhere Galo], bishop of Paris, the bishops of Senlis and Orléans, Adam, abbot of Saint-Denis of blessed memory, and very many religious men. Carrying the noble body of the royal majesty to the church of Blessed Mary, they kept vigil over it with solemn funeral rites.

On the following morning, the son placed the bier, fittingly adorned with cloths and every sort of funeral ornament, upon the shoulders of his chief servants [Note: “Servants.” Thus in four manuscripts; omitted in the printed editions.]. With filial affection, as was fitting, now on foot, now on horseback, he strove, weeping, together with the barons whom he had, to help bear the bier. Here too he showed remarkable nobility of spirit: throughout his life he had taken care neither to offend his father in any respect because of the repudiation of his mother or because of the brought-in Countess of Anjou [Note: Cod. Reg. 6265 adds “countess”], nor, as young men commonly do, to disturb his father’s rule in any respect by diminishing it.

When they had carried him with a great escort to the noble monastery of Saint Benedict on the Loire—for he had dedicated himself to that place—those who had heard it from him said that he had wished to absent himself from the burial-place of his royal fathers, which is held in the church of Saint-Denis almost by natural right, because he had behaved less than well toward the Church and because, among so many noble kings, his burial would not be esteemed highly.

[Note: Philip gave the leading men and his friends a somewhat different reason for choosing the church of Fleury as the burial-place of his body, if we believe Orderic Vitalis (book II, p. 325): “I know,” he said, “as this chronicler testifies, that the burial-place of the kings of the Franks is at Saint-Denis; but because I feel myself to be too great a sinner, I do not dare to be buried beside the body of so great a martyr. I greatly fear lest, in punishment for my sins, I be handed over to the devil and suffer what Scripture relates once happened to Charles Martel. I love Saint Benedict; I humbly entreat the pious Father of monks, and I desire to be buried in his church on the Loire. For he is merciful and kind, and favorably receives all sinners who seek a more reformed life and endeavor, according to the discipline of his Rule, to be reconciled to God.” This final passage is moreover worthy of notice, since it seems to allude to Philip’s intention of professing the Benedictine Rule—an intention once suggested to him by Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, as we learn from one of Hugh’s letters to this king, printed in its proper place.]

In that monastery, having laid him before the altar, they commended his soul to the Lord with hymns and prayer, as fittingly as they could, and received his body beneath solemn stones [Note: Otherwise: “they honorably buried the body.”].

## Chapter XIII

The aforesaid Louis, because in his youth he had earned the friendship of the Church by generous defense, upheld the cause of the poor and the orphaned, and subdued tyrants by powerful valor, was, with God’s assent, being raised to the summit of the kingdom according to the desire of the good; and likewise, if it were possible, was to be excluded by the deliberate machinations of the wicked and ungodly. It was therefore prudently resolved, chiefly at the urging of the venerable and most wise Ivo, bishop of Chartres, that they should assemble at Orléans as swiftly as possible to defeat the machinations of the ungodly and hasten diligently to effect his elevation.

Accordingly Daimbert, archbishop of Sens, was invited and came with his fellow provincials [Note: In two Royal manuscripts and Cod. St. Germ.: “provincials.”], namely Galo, bishop of Paris; Manasses of Meaux; John of Orléans; Ivo of Chartres; Hugh of Nevers; and Humbald [elsewhere Humbaud] of Auxerre. On the feast-day of the Invention of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, he anointed Louis with the most sacred oil, celebrated masses of thanksgiving, stripped off the sword of secular knighthood, girded him with the ecclesiastical sword for the punishment of evildoers, and gladly crowned him with the royal diadem. He also delivered to him the sceptre and rod [Note: Coins of the third dynasty of our kings, which display both, show that the rod must be distinguished from the sceptre. Some modern writers wrongly confuse it with what they call the royal hand. That, which succeeded the simple rod, first appears on the coins of Louis X.], and thereby, with clergy and people approving, most devoutly entrusted to him the defense of churches and the poor and all the insignia of the kingdom.

He had not yet put off the festal vestments after the celebration of the divine offices when evil messengers suddenly arrived from the church of Reims, bringing letters of protest and threatening, by apostolic authority, that the royal anointing must not take place if they had arrived in time. For they said that the first-fruits of a king’s first crown belonged by right to the church of Reims, and that this prerogative had remained inviolate and unshaken from the first king of the Franks, Clovis, whom Saint Remigius baptized; whoever should venture rashly to violate it was liable to perpetual anathema.

On that occasion they hoped either to obtain peace for their archbishop, the venerable and distinguished man Ralph the Green, who had incurred the king’s most grievous and dangerous enmity because he had been elected and enthroned in the see of Reims without the king’s assent, or to prevent the king from being crowned. But because they arrived too late, they were mute there and returned home talkative; or, whatever they may have said [Note: Cod. R. 5925: “whatever nevertheless they said”; Cod. St. Germ., St. Denis, and Reg. 6265: “may have said.”], they brought back nothing useful.

[Note: In A.D. 1106, upon the death of Manasses, archbishop of Reims, those entitled to vote in choosing his successor were divided into two parties. Some elected Ralph, surnamed the Green, provost and treasurer of the church of Reims; others, favoring the king’s wishes, elected Gervase, son of the count of Rethel and archdeacon of the same church. When the former was confirmed by Pope Paschal and occupied the see without awaiting the king’s consent, Louis refused to be anointed and crowned by him, regarding him as a rebel and usurper. This was perhaps the principal reason why Louis was so favorably consecrated at Orléans by the archbishop of Sens. Ralph later returned to the king’s favor and was confirmed in the see by him.]

## Chapter XIV

*(A.D. 1108.)* Louis, therefore, by God’s grace king of the Franks, could not abandon what he had been accustomed to do in youth: namely, to protect churches, defend the poor and needy, and devote himself to peace and the defense of the kingdom.

The aforesaid Guy the Red and his son Hugh of Crécy, a capable young man, vigorous in arms, suited alike for robbery and arson, and the swiftest disturber of the entire kingdom, did not cease, their resentment swollen by shame over the loss of the castle of Gournay, to disparage the royal majesty. Therefore Guy even chose not to spare his brother Odo, count of Corbeil, because Odo had given him no assistance against the king. Laying a trap for his brother’s simplicity, when Odo had confidently arranged one day to hunt with him, he learned what thing and what hope an unwise kinship corrupted by envy can produce.

Odo was seized by this same brother Hugh at the castle called La Ferté-Baudouin and bound in fetters and chains; nor, even if the opportunity arose, was he to be released except by making war upon the king. At this unprecedented madness, many townsmen of Corbeil—for the castle was being besieged by the veteran nobility of many knights—fled to the public refuge of the royal majesty. Falling at his knees with tearful sobbing, they announced the captured count and the cause of his capture, and with repeated prayer urged the king to rescue him by force. When he pledged the hope of rescue, they moderated their anger, eased their grief, and strove to recover their lord by whatever art and strength they possessed.

Thus it came about that certain men of La Ferté-Baudouin [Note: The location of this La Ferté-Baudouin is admitted by John de la Barre, historian of Corbeil, to be wholly unknown. Valois considers it quite probably identical with La Ferté-Adélaïde, La Ferté-Alais.], which belonged to Guy not by hereditary right but through his marriage to Countess Adelaïde [Note: Guy the Red of Rochefort, the first of that name, had married Adelaïde, widow of Burchard of Corbeil, who had borne him Odo. By her Guy had Guy II, thus Odo’s uterine brother. He repudiated and rejected her while retaining the castle.], agreed with certain Corbeillais [elsewhere “Corboilensians”] under oath to admit them cautiously into the castle.

Persuaded by them, the king hastened with a small body of courtiers, so that the undertaking should not become public. In the evening, while those previously sent ahead were still talking by the fires—namely Anselm of Garlande, the seneschal [Note: The three brothers of Garlande, sons of William de Garlande—Anselm, William, and Stephen—one after another bore the dignity of seneschal.], who, as a valiant knight, was admitted through the appointed gate with nearly forty armed men—he strove to seize it by force. But the townsmen, astonished at the clatter of horses and the unexpected murmur of riders, sprang up against them. Since the way was narrowed by opposing doors, and the entrance permitted neither advance nor retreat at will, the natives, bolder before their own gates, slaughtered them more readily.

Unable any longer to endure both the darkness of night [Note: “Of darkness.” Thus in four manuscripts; printed edition: *tenebrati*.] and the misfortune of the confined place, they made for the gate. Anselm, courageous as he was, retreating and struck down, could not reach the gate because the enemy had seized it first. He was trapped and took possession of the tower of that same castle with the count of Corbeil—not as lord, but as [Note: *ut* is absent from all manuscripts.] prisoner. Their pain was equal but their fear unequal: one feared death, the other only disinheritance [Note: In four manuscripts: “feared.”]. To them might be applied this verse:

> … Carthage and Marius endured  
> the consolations of fate.

When the cry of the fugitives reached the ears of the hurrying king, he scorned to be delayed by the hindrance of dense night. He leapt upon his swiftest horse and, attempting to burst through the gate and boldly bring aid to his men, was driven back by the shut gate and a hail of missiles, lances, and stones.

Then the brothers and kinsmen of the captured seneschal, overcome by grief, fell at the king’s feet. “Glorious king,” they said, “valiant in action, have mercy. If that accursed Hugh of Crécy [Col. 1280A], a most depraved man thirsting for human blood, should in any way be able either to come here or take our brother elsewhere and lay hands on him, he will very swiftly cut his throat [Note: Thus all manuscripts; printed edition: “will cut.”], nor will he care what punishment awaits him if, more savage than the most savage, he kills him by a sudden death.”

Fearing this, the king swiftly surrounded the castle, blocked the approaches to its gates, enclosed it with four or five fortified posts, and devoted himself to recovering the captives and the castle for the kingdom and for himself. But the aforesaid Hugh, first exultant at their capture and then greatly terrified by their rescue or the loss of the castle, was anxious and labored to devise, now mounted, now on foot, how he might enter the castle, under the varied false disguise of a minstrel or a prostitute.

While one day his whole attention [Note: Thus all manuscripts; printed edition wrongly: “invention.”] was occupied with this, he could not withstand the murderous attacks of those rushing out from the camp and took to flight for safety. Suddenly, among and ahead of the others, William, brother of the captured seneschal—a witty knight and vigorous in arms—tried, in pursuit, to hinder him with the speed of courage and horse alike. When Hugh saw him alone because of his own speed, he repeatedly aimed his shaken ash-wood spear at him. But because fear of those following prevented him from daring to delay, he resumed his flight. He understood admirably and cleverly that, if he could engage alone with the one man for any time, he would make his boldness of spirit famous either by the trophy [Note: Cod. Reg. 6265: “triumph.”] of single combat or by the risk of death.

It also often happened that he could by no means escape villages [Note: Cod. Reg.: “roads.”] situated on the road and the unavoidable assaults of enemies coming from them, unless, by feigned trickery, he deceived William of Garlande himself and cried out that the William pursuing him was Hugh; and, claiming to be on the king’s side, called upon them to stop him as an enemy. Escaping by these and other such devices, by caution of tongue no less than valor of spirit, he alone mocked many men.

The king, however, did not desist from the begun siege for this or any other reason. He tightened his grip on the castle, wore down the townsmen, and did not cease attacking them until, after soldiers had secretly forced their way in—though through the contrivance of certain townsmen—he compelled them by superior strength to surrender. In the uproar the knights fled to the keep, seeking safety of life, not escape from capture. Shut up there, they could neither protect themselves adequately nor leave the keep by any means, until some had been killed and more wounded. Yielding to the royal majesty’s discretion, they surrendered both themselves and the keep, not without consulting their lord.

Thus, by one act, equally pious and terrible [Col. 1281A], he restored the seneschal to himself, a brother to the brothers, and the count to the people of Corbeil, as prudently as he did mercifully. Of the knights of the castle, he disinherited some by devastating their property; others he resolved to punish most severely, wearing them down by prolonged imprisonment in order to frighten men like them. By such a victory, with God’s noble gift, he gloriously ennobled the first-fruits of his crown, contrary to his rivals’ expectation.

## Chapter XV

At that time (A.D. 1109) Henry, king of the English, a most valiant man, renowned in peace and war, happened to come into Normandy. Even that rustic prophet Merlin [Note: Ambrosius Merlin, whom medieval English writers relate to have flourished near the end of the fifth century, and to whom many prophecies full of absurdities are attributed, was long celebrated among the English and also among the French.], the marvelous observer and reporter of the English people’s everlasting fortunes, commends Henry’s remarkable excellence—proclaimed almost throughout the whole world—with the highest praise, as elegantly as truthfully. Bursting out abruptly in prophetic speech in his praise, as has become the custom of prophets, he says:

> “The lion of justice shall succeed, at whose roar the Gallic towers and the island dragons shall tremble. In his days gold shall be drawn from the lily and the nettle, and silver shall flow from the hooves of lowing beasts. The curled-haired shall clothe themselves in varied fleeces, because outward dress shall signify inward things; the feet of barking creatures shall be cut off; wild beasts shall have peace; humanity shall grieve at punishment; the form of commerce shall be split; the half shall be round; the rapacity of kites shall perish; and the teeth of wolves shall be blunted. The lion’s cubs shall be transformed into fishes of the sea, and his eagle shall nest above the mountains of Aravium.”

The wheel [Note: In four manuscripts: “whole.”] of this prophecy, so extensive and so antiquated, fits the man’s vigor and the administration of his kingdom so exactly that not one iota, not one word, can differ from its correspondence. Even what is said at the end about his cubs plainly shows that his sons and daughter were shipwrecked, devoured by sea-fish, and physically transformed in a reciprocal manner, thereby certainly fulfilling the prophecy.

The aforesaid King Henry, succeeding happily to his brother William, arranged the kingdom of England, with the counsel of experienced and upright men, according to the law [Note: Corrected from three manuscripts; printed edition: “kingdom.” Cod. Reg. 6265 reads “good men” for “upright men.”] of the ancient kings. To win their good will, he confirmed by oath the kingdom’s ancient customs [Note: Cod. St. Germ.: “had confirmed”; printed edition: “would confirm.”]. He then came to the harbor of the duchy of Normandy and, relying on the aid of the lord king of the Franks, set the land in order, restored its laws, and imposed peace by compulsion, threatening nothing less than the gouging out of eyes and the height of gallows for those who should plunder.

By these and similar promises, and by frequent fulfillment of his promises, he brought men under control; for anyone can be rich in promises. The land was silent before him. The Normans, strangers to peace through the fierce descent of the Danes, kept peace unwillingly, and in this very matter fulfilled the rustic prophet’s oracles. For the rapacity of kites perished and the wolves’ teeth were blunted [Note: All manuscripts read “are being blunted”; printed edition: “shall be blunted.”], since neither noble nor commoner presumed, with any boldness, to despoil or rob.

As for the words, “At the roar of the lion of justice the Gallic towers and island dragons shall tremble,” this too occurred: nearly all the towers and all the strongest castles of Normandy, which is a part of Gaul, he either caused to be destroyed, or subdued to his own will by installing his own men and maintaining them from his own treasury, if they stood ruined. The island dragons trembled when none of the magnates of England dared even to mutter throughout his rule.

In his days gold was drawn from the lily—that is, from sweet-smelling religious persons—and from the nettle—that is, from stinging secular persons: his purpose was that, as he benefited all, all should serve him. For it is safer that one person should receive from all in order to defend all than that, by receiving nothing, all should perish through one person. Silver flowed from the hooves of lowing beasts when rural [Note: All manuscripts: “rural”; printed edition: “tower.”] security produced full granaries, and full granaries supplied abundance of silver to full coffers.

On this occasion he also happened, by blandishments and threats alike, to wrest the castle of Gisors from Payen of Gisors: a strongly fortified castle, advantageously situated, which, with the river called Etta—pleasantly fertile in fish—flowing between, marks the boundary at both ends between the Franks and Normans, according to an ancient geometric cord jointly measured by Franks and Danes. It afforded the Normans a convenient route for invading France and denied it to the French. If the opportunity to possess it had been available, the king of the Franks no less than the king of the English ought, by right of his kingdom, to have sought it because of the advantage of the place and its immunity.

The demand for this castle therefore suddenly supplied tinder for hatred between the two kings. The king of the Franks sent to Henry concerning its surrender or demolition; when he achieved nothing, he charged him with breach of treaty, fixed a day for action, and appointed a place. Meanwhile, as usually happens in such affairs, the kings’ hatreds, inflamed by the slanders of their rivals, increased; and, before peace was even possible, they enlarged their military forces so as to meet one another at the conference with pride and hatred.

Having gathered a great part of the magnates of the French kingdom—namely Robert, count of Flanders, with nearly four thousand knights; Count Theobald the Palatine; the count of Nevers; the duke of Burgundy; and very many others, together with many archbishops and bishops—the king of the Franks passed through the land of the count of Meulan, because he adhered to the king of England, ravaging it and giving it to the flames, thereby paying flattering compliments to the coming conference.

But when very great armies had been assembled on both sides, the army encamped at a place commonly called Planches-Nympheul [Nympheoli, Neaufle], near a castle unfortunate in reputation, where local tradition says that those who met there were either scarcely ever or never reconciled [Note: Four cited manuscripts read “fed” rather than “pacified.”], upon the bank of a river flowing between them and preventing common passage. The most noble and prudent Frenchmen were selected and sent to the English king, crossing a shaky bridge which, through its very age, threatened sudden ruin to one man or many.

The spokesman charged with stating the grounds of their action, a skilled orator, addressed the king in the following speech, without greeting him [Note: Thus in four manuscripts; perhaps “with a greeting.” It is scarcely credible that the manners of that time were so uncouth that an envoy dared address a king without any preliminary greeting.]:

> “When, through the glorious generosity of the lord king of the Franks, your vigor received the duchy of Normandy as a fief from that same king’s munificent hand, it is established that, among and beyond the other provisions, this was specially confirmed by oath concerning Gisors and Bray: by whatever agreement either of you might obtain them, neither should retain them, but within forty days of taking possession the holder bound by the agreement should utterly destroy the castles themselves. Because you have not done this, the king commands both that you do so even now and that you repair your failure by the proper law. It ill becomes a king to transgress the law, since king and law possess the same majesty of command. If your men should deny any of these things [Note: Cod. St. Germ.: *dedicerint*; Royal and other manuscripts and St. Denis: *dedidicerint*.], or by evasiveness refuse to state them, we are ready to prove it by the law of judicial combat, with the full testimony of two or three barons.”

Before these men had finished and returned to the king of France, the Normans followed them [Note: All manuscripts: “following.”] and appeared before their king, shamelessly denying whatever could damage their case and demanding that the complaint be pursued in judicial order. Their chief concern was simply that, by whatever delay, while the business of the prepared [Note: Four manuscripts: “unprepared.”] action remained unfinished, the truth of the matter should not become evident to so great an assembly of the kingdom’s magnates.

The foremost men were sent back with the first envoys. Through Robert, count of Flanders, a distinguished combatant of Jerusalem, they boldly offered to prove the matter and, by rejecting the exaggeration of words through the law of judicial combat, to reveal in battle to which side justice should yield. When the Normans neither accepted nor suitably rejected this, King Louis, great-souled and eminent in spirit and body, swiftly sent men to put this alternative to the king: either destroy the castle or personally defend himself against Louis for the treachery of broken faith.

“Come,” he said, “the punishment of the contest ought to belong to him to whom the glory of truth and victory ought also to belong.”

He also made the most fitting arrangement he could concerning the place:

> “Let their army withdraw [Note: Cod. St. Germ.: *seccedat*, that is, *secedat*, “withdraw.”] from the riverbank, so that we may cross the ford, and a safer place may offer them [Note: Four manuscripts: “him.”] greater security; or, if it pleases them more, let the noblemen of the whole army have hostages for single combat [Note: Four manuscripts: “of fighting”; printed edition: “by fighting”], provided that, after our force has moved away, they permit us to cross to them. For otherwise the ford cannot be crossed.”

Some men, in ridiculous boasting, shouted that the kings should fight upon the aforesaid shaky bridge, though it would collapse at once. King Louis desired this with equal recklessness and boldness. But the king of the English said: “My pipe is not worth so much [Note: Cod. St. Germ.: “My *tabia* is not worth so much.”], that I should needlessly lose for these and such matters a castle famous and highly useful to me.” Rejecting this and other taunts, he said: “When I see the lord king in a place where I ought to defend myself, I shall not avoid him”—while he rejected what the inability of the place to accommodate it had offered.

Moved by this ridiculous answer, the French, as though the fortune of places waged wars, ran to arms; the Normans likewise. As both sides hastened to the river, only the impossibility of access prevented the loss of a very great slaughter and calamity. Since they had consumed the day in talk, at the approach of night the English returned to Gisors and our men to Mont Calv.

But when dawn, at the first light of heaven, drove away the stars, the French, mindful of the insult of the preceding day and further fired by the morning ardor of soldiery, raced ahead on their swiftest horses and attacked near Gisors. They fought with marvelous pride and marvelous boldness, endeavoring to show the Normans—wearied and driven in through the gate—how greatly men trained by much warfare surpass those relaxed by long peace.

The war thus begun from these and similar beginnings and continued for nearly two years harmed the king of England more severely, because he surrounded almost the whole march of Normandy, as far as the duchy extended, with many troops and costly payments for defense of the land. The king of the Franks, however, with the ancient and natural castles and fortified places of his realm, and with the freely offered vigorous attacks of the Flemings, men of Ponthieu, Vexin, and other neighboring peoples, did not cease to ravage the land with fire and plunder.

When William, son of the king of England, had performed homage to King Louis, Louis augmented the fief attached to the aforesaid castle by a special favor and grant [Note: Cod. Reg. 5925: “by special favor and grant he increased the aforesaid castle and its fief”; Cod. Reg. 6265: “by special favor and grant, the aforesaid castle, fief, etc.”; Cod. St. Germ. and St. Denis: “by special favor and grant, etc.”], and by this occasion restored Henry to his former favor. Before this occurred, however, the remarkable occasion of that same dispute and the dreadful destruction of men were punished by a remarkable vengeance.

## Chapter XVI

Upon a promontory of the steep bank of the great river Seine stands a hideous and insignificant [Note: Royal manuscripts and printed edition: “undistinguished.”] castle, called La Roche-Guyon. It is invisible on its surface, hollowed out within a lofty rock. There, on the slope of the mountain, the rival hand of a craftsman has enlarged, through a narrow and wretched entrance, a dwelling of vast extent cut into the rock: a cave thought to give oracles, in which Apollo’s responses are received, or of which Lucan says:

> … For although the Thessalian prophetess  
> compels the fates, it is uncertain what drew her there,
“...whether he looks upon the Stygian shades, or because he has descended to the shades. Perhaps from here there is a way to the dead.”

The lord of this gorge-bound [Note: [Col. 1285D] The Royal manuscripts: *fauciosi*, “gorge-bound.”] town, hated by gods and men, was Guy, a young man of good disposition, untainted by the inherited stock of his forebears’ wickedness. Having resolved to live honourably and without the greedy gluttony of wretched rapacity, he was overtaken by the calamity of that ill-fated place; cut down by the treachery of his most wicked, worse-than-wicked father-in-law, he lost both his place and his life by an unforeseen death.

For William, his son-in-law [read: father-in-law], a Norman by birth, a traitor without equal—thought to be his intimate and closest friend—having conceived sorrow and brought forth iniquity, found an opportunity for treachery at twilight on a certain Sunday. With those who, more devout than the rest, gathered first at the church beside Guy’s household, by the divided rock, he too came—though differently equipped: armoured, yet hooded—together with a band of traitors. While the others were at prayer, he at times pretended to pray; and, having watched for the way by which he might enter to Guy, he burst in through the doorway by which Guy was hastening to enter the church. Drawing his sword, he raged in an outburst of his own wickedness with his most villainous companions; he struck down, slaughtered, and destroyed the unsuspecting man, smiling though he did not perceive the sword.

[Note: [Col. 1285D] *Domui* (“household”). Thus corrected from four manuscripts. The edition has *domni* (“of the lord”).]

When his noble wife saw this, frantic with womanly grief, tearing her cheeks and hair, she ran to her husband. Caring nothing for death, she fell upon him and covered him with her own body. “Strike me down instead,” she cried, “me, unhappy woman, who deserve to die thus, you most vile executioners!”

Receiving upon herself the blows and wounds of the swordsmen that were directed at her husband, she said: “What have you done wrong to these men, dearest spouse? Were not son-in-law and father-in-law inseparable friends? What madness is this? You are full of frenzy.”

[Note: [Col. 1285D] “She said”: Royal manuscript 6265; absent from the edition.]

When they had dragged her about by the hair, cut her to pieces, stabbed her [Note: [Col. 1285D] *Punctam*, “stabbed.” This is the reading of the St-Germain manuscript and Royal manuscript 5265. The word is omitted in Royal manuscript 5925. The edition has *punitam*, “punished.”], and slashed nearly her whole body, they put her husband to death by a most shameful killing. The children whom they found they destroyed, dashing them against the rock with Herodian wickedness.

As they raged wildly here and there, the woman, lying on her back, raised her wretched head and recognized her husband’s mutilated body. Carried away by love, crawling with such strengthlessness as she could, in the manner of a serpent, touching herself all over, covered in blood [Note: [Col. 1285D] *Contrectans*, “touching”: in four manuscripts. The edition has *contorquens*, “twisting herself.”], she came to the lifeless corpse. She offered it whatever most loving kisses she could, as though he were alive [Note: [Col. 1285D] *Vivo*, “alive.” So read in four manuscripts; the edition also has *vivo*.], and, bursting into a mournful song and rendering such funeral rites as she was able, she cried:

“What have you left for me, dearest spouse? Did your praiseworthy continence beside me deserve this? Did the abandonment of your father’s, grandfather’s, and great-grandfather’s wickedness earn this? Did your renounced rapacity, which stored up at home relief for the want of neighbours and the poor, earn this?”

So she spoke, and, exhausted by her frenzy, lay deserted. There was no one to separate the wholly dead man and the half-living woman, entwined in one blood. [Note: [Col. 1285D] *Involutos*, “entwined”: so in four manuscripts. The edition has *involutans*.]

At last, after the criminal William [Note: [Col. 1286D] The St-Denis manuscript has “Guy.”] had exposed them like pigs, he sat down, sated in beastly fashion with human blood. Admiring more than usual the strength of the rock, he considered, though too late, how powerfully he might plunder all around, and how he might inspire fear in Frenchmen and Normans as he pleased. [Note: [Col. 1286D] Read *pro velle*, “as he pleased,” from four manuscripts; the edition has *procellae*, “of a storm.”] Then, thrusting his crazed head out of a window, he summoned the native inhabitants of the land; destitute of goodness, he promised them good things if they would join him. Not one of them entered.

In the morning, the flying report of so great and wicked a deed [Note: [Col. 1286D] *Volans*, “flying”: in four manuscripts; absent from the edition.] disturbed not only the neighbourhood but even those far away. Therefore the men of the Vexin, vigorous and most valiant in arms, greatly stirred up, each gathering to the utmost of his power forces of cavalry and infantry from every side, hastened to the rock, fearing that Henry, the most powerful king of the English, might bring assistance to the traitors. They stationed many horsemen and foot soldiers on the slope of the rock, so that no one might enter or leave; and, placing an army on the Norman side, they blocked the road, lest reinforcements should arrive.

Meanwhile they sent to King Louis, informed him of the treachery, and asked what he commanded concerning these matters. By the authority of royal majesty, he ordered that the traitors be punished with an exquisitely contrived and most shameful death [Note: [Col. 1286D] “And”: in Royal manuscript 6265; absent from the edition.] [Note: [Col. 1286D] *Puniri*, “be punished.” Thus to be corrected from four manuscripts; the edition has *muniri*, “be fortified.”], and directed that assistance be given if necessary. [Note: [Col. 1286D] The St-Germain manuscript has *mandato*, “by command.”]

After the army had remained encamped for several days, that abominable man began to fear as his force increased day by day. Realizing, under the devil’s prompting, what he had done at the devil’s instruction, he summoned certain of the more noble men of the Vexin and laboured with many promises to secure an agreement: that he might remain in the rock in peace, be allied with them, and serve the king of the French most faithfully.

They rejected his proposals and reproached him with the punishment due for treachery; yet they induced him, now softened to this point [Note: [Col. 1286D] *Ipsum*, “himself,” is absent from the Royal and St-Germain manuscripts.], to agree that, if they made some land swear allegiance to him and gave him safe conduct to depart, he would surrender the fortress which he had seized. When this oath had been confirmed, several Frenchmen were admitted. [Note: [Col. 1286D] In four manuscripts: “A few Frenchmen were admitted; many were admitted.”]

But their departure having been delayed, and on the pretext of the aforesaid land [Note: [Col. 1286D] Read in four manuscripts: “on the pretext of the aforesaid land.”], when, in the morning, some persons besides those who had sworn entered and others followed others, the shouting of those outside grew strong. They cried out terribly that the traitors must be handed over, or else those who consented to their protection must suffer a punishment like that of traitors.

The oath-bound men resisted with boldness and fear; but those who had not sworn, overpowering them, fell upon them with swords. They piously butchered the impious, mutilated their limbs, brutally disembowelled others [Note: [Col. 1287D] The St-Denis manuscript incorrectly has *dulcissime*, “most gently.”], and inflicted upon them every cruelty, considering anything milder insufficiently cruel.

Nor should it be disbelieved [Note: [Col. 1287D] “Is” is added in four manuscripts and absent from the edition.] that the divine hand hastened so swift a retribution: living or dead, they were thrown from the windows; bristling like hedgehogs with countless arrows, they were hurled about in the air on the points of lances—as though the earth itself rejected them. [Read: *vagantes*, “wandering about,” for *vacantes*, “being empty.”] Thus, by an unprecedented deed, they found an unprecedented punishment. [Note: [Col. 1287D] *Inusitatam*, “unprecedented”: so read in the manuscripts; the edition has *inusitate*, “unprecedentedly.”]

Because he had been senseless while alive [Note: [Col. 1287D] *Vivus*, “alive.” Thus to be corrected from four manuscripts; the edition has *unius*, “of one.”], he was made heartless in death. They tore from his entrails his heart, swollen with fraud and wickedness, set it upon a stake, and fixed it for many days in a conspicuous place as a display of vengeance upon iniquity.

They lowered the corpses both of him and of some of his companions into the river Seine, bound with fitted hurdles, rakes, and ropes, so that, if the current did not prevent them from floating as far as Rouen, they might display the punishment of treachery. Those who had defiled France with a momentary stench, they would not cease, now dead, to defile Normandy as though it were their native soil.

## Chapter XVII

The scarcity of faith causes evil to be returned for good more often than good for evil. The latter is divine; the former is neither divine nor human—yet it happens.

Marked by this wickedness, Philip, brother of King Louis, had obtained from the aforesaid Angevin woman the lordship of Montlhéry and the castle of Meudon, in the very heart of the kingdom, both through his father’s persuasion—which he never resisted—and through the seductive influence of his most noble and well-behaved stepmother. [Note: [Col. 1287D] Philip, son of King Philip and Bertrada, obtained the lordship of Montlhéry in 1104 by marrying Elizabeth, daughter of Guy Troussel, lord of that castle; his brother Louis, at their father’s urging, arranged this marriage.]

Yet Philip, ungrateful for such great benefits, presumed, in reliance on his most noble lineage, to kick against the goad. For his uncle was the distinguished knight and most powerful baron Amalric of Montfort; his brother was Fulk, count of Anjou and later king of Jerusalem. Their mother was more powerful still than all of them: a spirited and witty woman, most skilled in that remarkable feminine art by which bold women are accustomed to bring underfoot husbands provoked even by their wives’ injuries. [Note: [Col. 1287D] *Suppeditare*: that is, “to put beneath the feet, oppress, overcome.”]

She had so softened her former Angevin husband, although she had been wholly repudiated from his bed, that he revered her as his lady, often sitting at the footstool beneath her feet and, as though this came about by magic, obeying her will in every respect.

This one thing also exalted the mother, her sons, and all their proud offspring: if the king’s downfall should occur on any occasion, one of the brothers would succeed him, and thus the whole line of their kindred would most gladly raise its neck to the royal throne through a share in honour and lordship. [Note: [Col. 1288D] “Thus”: in four manuscripts; absent from the edition.]

When, therefore, the aforesaid Philip, repeatedly summoned, had proudly rejected both a hearing and the judgment of the court, the king, provoked by his plundering of the poor, destruction of churches, and ruin of the entire district, hastened there, though unwillingly. Although Philip and his men had repeatedly promised with great boasting to resist with a most powerful force of knights, they themselves withdrew timidly from the castle.

The king then rushed in without delay; armoured, he hastened through the middle of the castle to the tower and enclosed it in siege. As he began to set up engines of attack—mangonels and slinging machines—he compelled them to surrender, not immediately, but after many days, when they had despaired of life.

Meanwhile the mother and her uncle Amalric of Montfort, fearing the loss of the other lordship, namely Montlhéry, bestowed that same lordship upon Hugh of Crécy by joining him in marriage with Amalric’s daughter. They hoped thereby to set before the king one decisive obstacle [Note: [Col. 1288D] “To the king”: in two Royal manuscripts and the St-Denis manuscript; the edition has “and.”]: so that a route, continuously extended by the castles of this lordship, by those of Guy of Rochefort, his brother, and by Amalric’s own power as far as Normandy, might be blocked to him. [Note: [Col. 1288D] “So that”: thus read from four manuscripts; the edition has “from.”] Besides the other injuries which they could inflict every day as far as Paris, he would not even be permitted by any means to go to Dreux. [Note: [Col. 1288D] “Besides”: thus corrected from four manuscripts; the edition has “through.”]

For when Hugh hurried there swiftly after the marriage had been contracted, the king followed him more swiftly [Note: [Col. 1288D] *Subsecutus*, “followed closely”: in four manuscripts; the edition has *secutus*, “followed.”] and, at that same hour and moment when he learned of it [Note: [Col. 1288D] *Comperit*, “learned”: written without abbreviation in Royal manuscript 6265; the edition has *competit*, “is fitting.”], hastened most boldly to the town of Châtres belonging to the aforesaid lordship.

There, winning over the better inhabitants of the land by hope in his generosity and proven gentleness, he freed them from fear of the notorious tyranny and cruelty. [Note: [Col. 1288D] *Nota*, “notorious”: all manuscripts; the edition has *vota*, “vows.”]

For several days Hugh contended alternately to possess the place and the king to prevent his possessing it. But since one deception drives out another, Hugh was deceived by the following stratagem. Milo of Bray, son of the great Milo, appeared prudently. Claiming the lordship by hereditary right, he threw himself at the king’s knees [Note: [Col. 1288D] In four manuscripts: “throwing himself at the king’s feet”; the edition has “throwing himself at [his] knees.”], weeping and lamenting. With many prayers he appealed to the king and to the king’s counsellors, humbly begging that the royal generosity might restore the lordship to him and return his paternal inheritance; that the king might thereafter hold him as a servant or tenant and use him as he wished.

The king yielded to his mournful petition. Summoning the townsmen and now presenting Milo to them as their lord, he made them so peaceable and joyful despite every injury previously inflicted that it was as though he had sent down the moon and stars to them from heaven. [Note: [Col. 1288D] In four manuscripts: *exhilaravit*, “made joyful.”]

Without delay they suddenly ordered Hugh to leave; if he did not depart with the utmost speed, they promised him very swift destruction. Against their natural lord, they declared that neither faith nor oath had force, but only power or powerlessness. Hugh, astonished [Note: [Col. 1289D] *Stupefactus*, “astonished”: all manuscripts; the edition has *stupatus*.], took flight. He reckoned that he had escaped rather than lost his own possessions [Note: [Col. 1289D] “Himself”: present in four manuscripts and absent from the edition.]; for the fleeting joy of marriage he bore away the long disgrace of repudiation, and, not without great loss of horses and household goods, learned through shameful expulsion what advantage there is in making common cause with enemies against one’s lord.

## Chapter XVIII
As the most welcome fruit of a tree that bears well restores its fragrant flavour either by transplantation of the stock or by grafting of branches, so the propagation of wickedness and malice, which must be rooted out, issuing from a lineage of many evil men, is compacted in one man, as though serpent joined to serpent, goading amid little serpents, and gives drink of native bitterness like wormwood. Such was Hugh of Le Puiset, an evil man, enriched only by the tyranny of his own house and of his forebears. When he succeeded his uncle Guy in the lordship of Le Puiset—for his father, of extraordinary pride, had taken up arms at the beginning of the expedition to Jerusalem—he did not cease to outdo his father in every evil, the wicked seed proving true to its stock; those whom his father had beaten with whips, he, worse than his father, beat with scorpions. Swollen with pride because he had cruelly oppressed poor churches and monasteries with impunity, he advanced so far as to reach the place of which it is said: “There fell the workers of iniquity; they were cast out and could not stand.” Since he held neither the King of all nor the king of the Franks in great account, he attacked the most noble countess of Chartres and her son Theobald, a very handsome young man and vigorous in arms, ravaging their land as far as Chartres and delivering it over to plunder and fire.

The noble countess and her son sometimes attempted, though late and inadequately, to avenge themselves as best they could; yet they never, or scarcely ever, came within eight or ten miles of Le Puiset. So great was Hugh’s boldness, so ample the power available to his lordly arrogance, that few loved him while many served him, though many longed to defend themselves against him and very many indeed longed to destroy him. He was feared more than he was loved.

But when the aforesaid Count Theobald perceived that he could achieve little against Hugh by himself but much through the king, he hastened with his most noble mother—who had always been accustomed to serve the king nobly—to him, urgently entreating him with many prayers to give aid and representing that her abundant service had earned his help. She recounted certain disgraces of Hugh, of his father, grandfather, and great-grandfathers.

“Remember, lord king,” she said, “as befits royal majesty, the insult and dishonour which Hugh’s grandfather, breaking his oath, inflicted upon your father Philip. When Philip sought to avenge the many injuries done to him, Hugh’s grandfather shamefully drove him back from Le Puiset; in the arrogance of a most wicked kinship, he drove Philip’s army in factional conspiracy as far as Orléans, and dishonoured in his prison the captured count of Nevers, Lancelin of Beaugency, nearly a hundred knights, and—what had until then been unheard of—certain bishops.

“Add, further, as a reproach, by what right or origin the castle built in the midst of the land of the saints by the venerable Queen Constance for its protection has not from ancient times belonged to it; and how, after making everything his own, he has left the king nothing except injuries. Now, if it please you, since the force of the armies of Chartres, Blois, and Châteaudun, on which he has been accustomed to rely for resistance, would not merely fail him but would also oppose him, you could easily avenge both your father’s injuries and your own by destroying the castle and disinheriting Hugh. But if you do not wish to punish your own injuries, however just and well deserved, then either take upon yourself or remove the oppressions of churches, the plundering of the poor, and the utterly impious harrying of widows and orphans, by which he was despoiling both the land of the saints and its inhabitants.”

Pressed by these and many similar pleas, the king appointed a day to deliberate on the matter, and we met at Melun. There many archbishops, bishops, clerics, and monks gathered, because he devoured their lands more ravenously than a wolf. They cried out and lay at the feet of the king even against his will, imploring him to restrain Hugh, that most rapacious brigand; to rescue from the dragon’s throat their prebends, established by the munificence of kings in Beauce, fertile in grain, for the servants of God; to strive to free the lands of priests, no less oppressed under Pharaoh’s cruelty; and, as vicar of God, whose image the king bears for the giving of life, to restore God’s portion to freedom.

Receiving their request favourably, and undertaking nothing improperly, the king, after the prelates of the Church had departed—namely the archbishop of Sens, the bishop of Orléans, and the venerable Ivo of Chartres, who had been held in prison and whom Hugh had forced to be confined in that same castle for many days [Note: “Confined” (*pingi*), that is, shut up (*compingi*).]—with the consent of Abbot Adam, of blessed memory, our predecessor, sent me back to Toury, which I governed in Beauce. It was an estate of Saint-Denis, useful and fertile in grain [Note: “In grain” in four manuscripts; absent from the printed edition.], but wholly unfortified. He ordered me, while he was still to summon Hugh to answer the charges, to see to the strengthening of the estate as far as possible by the military force of his men and ours, lest Hugh destroy it by fire. For he would fortify it and, as his father had done, attack the castle from there.

[Note: Ivo condemned in speech and writing the unlawful marriage of King Philip and Bertrada. About the end of 1092 Hugh of Le Puiset, viscount of Chartres, wishing to curry favour with the king and break the bishop’s spirit, captured Ivo and confined him in his castle at Le Puiset, while the king’s retainers meanwhile plundered the estates of the Church of Chartres.

Admire Ivo’s constancy, gentleness, and prudence. When he learned in prison that the clergy and people of Chartres were considering securing his release by force of arms, he wrote them a very grave letter in order to deter them from this plan:

> “For you cannot please God by burning houses and plundering the poor; rather, you greatly provoke him. Without his good pleasure neither you nor anyone else will be able to set me free. Therefore I do not wish you, by acting against me, to fill God’s ears with the cries of the poor and the laments of widows. For it is not fitting that I, who did not come to the bishopric by weapons of war, should recover by weapons of war what belongs not to a shepherd but to an invader. If the Lord’s hand has touched me and still lies heavily upon me, allow me alone to drink my misery to the dregs; bear the wrath of God until he vindicates my cause, and do not heap upon my tribulation the misery of others. For I am resolved not only to be shut up or deprived of ecclesiastical rank, but even rather to die than to cause through myself a slaughter of men. I therefore admonish you through the surpassing love of Christ’s knowledge that neither you do this nor permit it to be done. Yet if you do it, it is certain that you do not wish to have me any longer as bishop. For in departing once already, as the outcome proves, you did not take good counsel either for me or for yourselves. Henceforth, then, be content with the bounds your fathers set.”

These are his words in Epistle 20. William, abbot of Fécamp, consoled Ivo as he lay in chains by letter; the most pious bishop returned thanks in Epistle 19. At last Hoel, bishop of Le Mans, secured his release by sending letters to Pope Urban II. Moved by these, Urban wrote to Renaud, archbishop of Reims, and his suffragans, that they should press for the rescue of the bishop of Chartres: “If he who seized him,” he says (*Councils*, vol. X, col. 463), “scorns to obey your admonitions, subject both him to excommunication and the castles in which he keeps him, together with his land, to an interdict on divine service, so that hereafter no one may presume to commit like acts against men of this order.”

By the force of these letters Ivo was restored to liberty. Yet he relaxed none of his constancy, but attended every council dealing with the marriage of Philip and Bertrada, advanced its condemnation by his arguments, and confirmed it by his vote. Nevertheless, from his letters we learn that he was eventually reconciled, since the king thereafter ceased continually harassing him and sought from Paschal II some dispensation concerning that marriage.]

With God’s help, we maintained this undertaking for some time well enough with a force of knights and foot-soldiers. When Hugh’s case had been concluded in his absence, the king came to us at Toury with a great army and demanded back from Hugh the castle adjudged against him.

[Note: “… demanded it back …” On this expedition Suger says much in his book *On the Deeds Accomplished in His Administration*.]

When Hugh refused to come out, the king hastened to attack the castle. He brought up against it both cavalry and infantry, many crossbows, bows, shields, and swords, and war itself; you might have seen and marvelled in turn at the rain of arrows, at the fire flashing above from the many blows upon shining helmets, at the sudden and astonishing breaking and piercing of shields. And when they had forced their way through the gate into the castle, the defenders from within, from the battlements, hurled upon our men an extraordinary and almost intolerable hail of stones; by casting down beams and thrusting out stakes, they began, but could not complete, the repulse.

The royal forces, fighting fiercely with the strongest courage and bodily strength, when their shields were broken, set splinters, doors, and every sort of wooden object before themselves and pressed upon the gate. We had also caused carts, heavily loaded with a great heap of dry wood, to be brought up for quickly kindling flames, grease, and blood—for the defenders were excommunicated and altogether devilish. The royal troops placed these carts before the gate with strong hands, so that they might offer even the carts an unquenchable fire and shield themselves behind the barrier of wood. While some dangerously struggled to set fires and others to extinguish them [Note: MS Royal 6265: “were struggling” (*concertarent*)], Count Theobald attacked the castle from another side, namely the side facing Chartres, with a large force of cavalry and infantry. Mindful of injuries, he hastened to storm it; and while he urged his men to climb the steep slope of the rampart, he grieved to see them swiftly descend—indeed, tumble down. Those whom he carefully compelled to creep upward, as though on our account, he saw recklessly hurled backward downhill; and he sought to learn whether they breathed their last under the weight of their pursuers.

For the castle’s knights rode about its defences on very swift horses; relying on hand-thrown stones, they unexpectedly fell upon their opponents, struck and maimed them, and hurled them grievously down from the height into the bottom of the ditch [Note: Saint-Germain manuscript: “grievously injured” (*graviter laesos*), perhaps intended.]. By now slackened hands and weakened knees had almost brought the assault to a halt, when the strong—indeed all-powerful—hand of almighty God, wishing the cause of so great and so just a vengeance to be attributed wholly to itself [Note: Saint-Germain manuscript: “so unjust” (*tam injustae*).], since the parish communities of the district were present, stirred up the stout spirit of a certain bald priest. Contrary to human expectation, what was possible was granted to him, though it had proved impossible for the armed count and his men.

Quickly placing before himself a most worthless little plank [Note: *Ascella*; Saint-Germain incorrectly reads *asella*. *Ascella*/*asserculus* = our *aiscelle*, “small board.”], and climbing with bare head, he reached the hedge. Concealing himself beneath the coverings attached to the hedge, he gradually removed them. Delighted that he could do this freely, he signalled to those hesitating and standing idle in the field to bring aid. Seeing the unarmed priest bravely pull down the enclosure, armed men leapt forward. Setting axes and every kind of iron instrument against the barriers, they cut and broke them apart; and, by a marvellous sign of heavenly judgment, as though another wall of Jericho had fallen, in that same hour the armies both of king and count entered through the shattered barriers.

Thus very many of the defenders, unable to escape in either direction the assaults of enemies rushing together from both sides, were quickly caught and severely afflicted [Note: The words “were … afflicted” occur in all four manuscripts and are absent from the printed edition.]. The rest, including Hugh himself, since the castle enclosed by its wall could not provide sufficiently secure protection within, withdrew into the upper part of a movable wooden tower [Note: All manuscripts read *in mota*, “into the movable [tower]”; the edition reads *immota*, “immovable.”]. Soon, terrified by the threatening missiles of the pursuing army, Hugh was struck down, yielded to surrender, and was taken prisoner in his own house with his men. Most miserably shackled, he learned what ruin pride brings forth.

When the victorious king had led out the captured nobles as booty worthy of royal majesty, he ordered all the castle’s furnishings and wealth confiscated and the castle itself burned. He delayed burning the tower alone for a few days [Note: All four manuscripts read “delayed for a few days”; the edition wrongly has *debuit*, “ought,” for *diebus distulit*.], because Count Theobald, forgetful of so great a benefit—which he could never have obtained by himself—was plotting to enlarge his march by building a castle in the territory of Le Puiset, which was held from the king, near the estate called Allonnes. When the king absolutely refused, the count offered to have this agreement argued by Andrew of Baldement, administrator of his land. The king replied that he had never entered into such an agreement and that he would defend this point, by reason and the law of judicial combat, through his seneschal Anselm wherever they wished safely to do so. These vigorous men sought many courts for this contest, but found none.

The aforesaid castle having therefore been wholly destroyed, and Hugh also being confined in the tower of Châteaulandon:

[Note: The year in which the castle of Le Puiset was captured with its lord and destroyed, and in which security was thereby restored to the Church of Saint-Denis, is learned from a diploma of Louis the Fat. For brevity we give only its principal portion:

> “In the name of the most holy and undivided Trinity … I … Louis … king of the Franks … to all worshippers of holy mother Church … We wish it to be held certain that Abbot Adam of the most holy and blessed martyr Denis, with the monks, brothers of the same monastery, came many times before our serene presence with tearful sobs. Compelled by the utmost necessity, he humbly and repeatedly begged that we, relaxing with a strong hand certain vexations of evil custom and tyranny and arbitrary exactions imposed upon the lands of the aforesaid Saint Denis subject to a certain town situated in the territory of Chartres, called Le Puiset, by the possessors of that town from their predecessors down to the time of our rule, should endeavour to restore to the Church of God and our own Church what had been taken away. Assenting to this sound petition … and seeing also that the town, which he had so long held as his own, could not be taken from him except by powerful force, we summoned knights from our kingdom and attacked it together. Not only by our own labour, but also through the manifest help of God alone and the effective intercession of the holy martyrs whose benefices he was devastating, its lord was captured with many others, and we demolished and destroyed that castle for ever. Finally, after the Lord God had overcome all resistance, we freely and peacefully remitted in perpetuity to God and Saint Denis all the revenues of customs which the sons of perdition had imposed in every manner upon the lands of Blessed Denis; and, in remitting them, we ordered this act to be marked and confirmed by the inscription and seal of our name, committing it to the record of letters. Done publicly at Orléans in the palace, in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1111, in the fourth year of our consecration, in the presence of those whose names and seals are subscribed and who bear witness to the truth.”

(DOUBLET, *Antiquities of Saint-Denis*, p. 843.)]

Count Theobald, relying upon the aid of his uncle, the illustrious King Henry of England, made war upon King Louis and his companions, disturbed the land, detached the king’s barons by promises and gifts, and plotted every measure most harmful to the commonwealth, hateful as he was [Note: Saint-Germain manuscript: *machinabatur*, “was plotting.”]. But the king, being a man suited for warfare, repeatedly attacked him in vengeance and, having called together many other barons and also his uncle Robert, count of Flanders—a remarkable man, famous in arms among Christians and Saracens from the beginning of the expedition to Jerusalem—laid waste his territory.

One day, when he had led an army against the count into the city of Meaux, he caught sight of him, sprang upon him and his men with fury, and, not fearing to pursue the fugitives across a bridge, overthrew them and plunged them, with Count Robert and the other great men of the realm, as they fell willingly beneath the swords, into the waves [Note: “With” occurs in four manuscripts and is absent from the edition.]. You might have seen the active man move arms worthy of Hector, make giant assaults upon the trembling bridge, press forward through dangerous access [Note: Four manuscripts read *periculoso*, “dangerous”; the edition has *periculo*, “danger.”], and, despite very many resisting, seize the town. Even the great river Marne flowing between would not have prevented this, had not a closed gate on the far side of the river stood in the way.

He won no less renown by a conspicuous feat of valour when, advancing his army from Lagny, he turned his arms against the opposing force on the pleasant plain of meadows beside Pomponne, compelling it with repeated blows to seek speedy flight. Fearing the narrow entrance of the nearby bridge [Note: *Artum*, that is, *arctum*, “narrow,” in four manuscripts; the edition reads *arcuum*.], some, seeking safety for their lives, did not fear to fling themselves into the river at the gravest risk of death. Others, trampling themselves underfoot as they rushed toward the bridge, threw away their arms; more hostile to themselves than the enemy, because all wished to go at once, scarcely one could enter the bridge. And while a tumultuous rush threw them into confusion [Note: Four manuscripts read *tumultuosus*; the edition has *tumultuosos*.], the more hastily they hurried, the more of them were delayed; so that the last became first and the first last [Note: Four manuscripts: “so that the first become last, and the last become first.”].

Yet because the bridge entrance was surrounded by a ditch, it afforded them protection: the royal soldiers could pursue them only one after another, and even so not without heavy loss to themselves, since while many tried, few could take the bridge. Those who entered by whatever means often involuntarily bent the knee, thrown into confusion by the crowd either of their own side or ours, and in falling back compelled others to do the same. But the king and his men pursued them, inflicting great slaughter; whomever he encountered he crushed, and those whom he crushed he plunged into the river Marne, both by the stroke of the sword and by the charge of his very powerful horse.

But just as his unarmed men floated lightly on the waves, so those armed in mail, heavy with their own weight, once submerged were dragged out by their companions before a third immersion, thereby incurring, if such was the occasion, the reproach of “rebaptized” men.

[Note: Orderic Vitalis, Book XI, p. 837, gives a considerably different account of the battle at Meaux:

> “Once the king made an attack upon Theobald in the district of Meaux and had with him Robert, lord of Flanders, and other nobles. There he was unexpectedly attacked by the comital household; the enemy’s greater number prevailed, and he was put to flight. While the king fled with his men, the margrave of Flanders fell upon a narrow path, was trampled by the iron-shod hooves of horses, and could not rise; his limbs badly broken, he was carried away with difficulty and died a few days later.”

Meier, partly agreeing with Suger, writes:

> “After defeating and putting the English to flight, King Louis the Fat led his army into the territory of Meaux, which was then under English allegiance. When Robert attempted to drive the men of Meaux, who had sallied out, back into the city, his horse was hamstrung before the gate; he fell and was crushed, dying on the third day, on the day before the Nones of December, or, as others report, on the third day before the Nones of October.”]

By these and similar troubles the king harassed the count, demolishing his lands both in Brie and in the district of Chartres, and valuing neither the count’s presence more than his absence nor his absence more than his presence. Since the count feared the weakness and indolence of his own men, he knew how to steal the king’s barons away, enticing them with gifts and promises and pledging, before making peace with the king, the hope of redress for various grievances. Among these he bound to his cause Lancelin of Bulles, lord of Dammartin, and Payen of Montjay, whose lands, situated as though at a crossroads, afforded a secure route for operations toward Paris [Note: In the fourth manuscript and the edition: *alligavit*, “bound,” rather than *obligavit*.].

For the same reason he enticed Ralph of Baugency [Note: Saint-Germain manuscript: *Rodulfum*.], whose wife was the full sister and kinswoman of King Hugh the Great’s daughter, Matilda. Preferring advantage to honour, and, as the proverb says, “the goad hastens the old woman,” driven by much anxiety, he irreverently joined the noble sister in an incestuous marriage to Milo of Montlhéry, to whom, as we mentioned above, the king had restored the castle.

[Note: On this marriage Ivo, bishop of Chartres, wrote to Pope Paschal in Epistle 238:

> “Moreover, should the case of Milo and the daughter of Count Stephen reach your ears, let your fatherhood know that Milo did not canonically dismiss his former wife, and did not canonically marry the daughter of Count Stephen, as has been proved by the judgment of bishops.”

This daughter of Stephen was named Adelaide. The Milo who married her was the second or third son of Milo the Great, lord of Montlhéry, lord of Bray-sur-Seine, and after his father viscount of Troyes.]

By this act he interrupted the freedom of movement and, as it were in the very middle chamber of France, established the old nuisance of storms and wars. By detaching with him his kinsmen Hugh of Châteaufort, lord of Crécy, and Guy of Rochefort, he exposed the districts of Paris and Étampes to war unless military action prevented it. And while open access was granted to Count Theobald and the men of Brie, and to Hugh, uncle of Troyes, and the men of Troyes, against the Parisians and the men of Senlis on this side of the Seine, and to Milo beyond it, the country was deprived of the ability of one group to aid another. Likewise, the men of Orléans were prevented from receiving aid when the men of Chartres, Châteaudun, and Brie were shut out by the support of Ralph of Baugency, with no opposition. But the king frequently built upon their backs; neither the lavish expenditure of English nor of Norman wealth spared him, while the illustrious King Henry attacked his land with all his strength and every effort. He was struck by these forces as though all rivers threatened to draw their sources away from the sea.

## Chapter XIX

Meanwhile it happened that Odo, count of Corbeil, died: a man who was not a man, because he was not rational but bestial [Note: “Bestial.” It would be difficult to conceive a judgment more insulting than this. Perhaps out of resentment at injuries recently inflicted by Odo upon the monks of Saint-Denis, established in the priory of Blessed Mary near Essonnes, Suger hurled this weapon against him. Indeed, Odo had behaved so unjustly in this matter, to remove this charge, that the abbot and community of Saint-Denis, unable to restrain him otherwise, removed him from communion with the faithful by a formal sentence. Nor was this without effect. Shortly afterward Odo was struck by a serious illness, begged pardon, and took care to make ample restitution for the injuries he had inflicted upon the monks. He himself attests this in the following charter, transcribed by Doublet (*Antiquities of Saint-Denis*, p. 845):

> “I, Odo, count of Corbeil, wish it to be known to the whole body of the faithful that, lured by the greed of human frailty and by the prompting and counsels of certain enemies, I unjustly attacked the cell of Saint Denis situated near Corbeil, newly built in honour of Saint Mary ever-virgin; entered the monks’ court and dormitory; and there violently took the revenue of Saint Denis placed in a chest. For this reason I was first summoned by the abbot and monks, and afterward excommunicated. Not long after, a serious illness befell me. In it, recognizing and fearing God’s judgment, I sent for the brothers whom I had offended and, through them making amends to God and his saints, sought and obtained absolution. Finally, for the salvation of my soul and body and in recompense for the revenue that I had taken, having taken counsel with my men, I decreed, granted, and relinquished in perpetuity to Saint Mary, Saint Denis, and the brothers dwelling and to dwell in that cell—I relinquished, I say—certain customary dues that I received there, namely *frescengagium* and *fenatores*. Done in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1111, indiction 5, epact 20, concurrent 2, in the year of Louis VI, king of the Franks. This act was granted by the wife of Count Odo, daughter of Andrew of Baldement; and witnesses to the matter are,” etc.

Here note that the custom concerning *friskingi* is a tax upon a certain kind of vehicle; *fenatores* are the same as *foenices*, French *faneurs* (“haymakers”) (CANGIUS).

Nor should one wonder that the abbot and his community claimed for themselves the right of excommunication against a count wholly free from their lordship. It is probable that they had received this power from the Roman pontiff or his legate. If they exercised that authority over a layman subject to them in any way, even without consulting the pope, they would have done nothing contrary to the custom of that age. For Ivo of Chartres’s letter to the dean and clergy of the Church of Paris, among his published letters, no. 112, teaches us that the chapters of many churches were accustomed thus to avenge injuries done to their subjects.]

He was the son of Burchard, a most arrogant count. Tumultuous, of extraordinary high spirit, and chief of criminals, when one day he aspired to the kingship and took up arms against the king, he refused to receive the sword from the hand of the man offering it, and addressed his wife, the countess standing by, with this taunt: “Offer the noble count a splendid sword joyfully, noble countess; for the count whom you receive from you will today render you king.” But, on the contrary, by God’s ordering, it happened that he departed this life neither as what he was nor as what he wished to be. For on that same day, struck by the lance of Count Stephen fighting for the king, he secured peace for the realm and, by utterly defeating them, transferred himself and his war to the lowest depths of hell.

[Note: This passage, somewhat obscure, misled later writers into inferring that not Burchard, Odo’s father, but Odo himself was killed by Count Stephen. But the charter quoted just above proves that Odo lived long after the battle discussed here. Although neither Suger nor another source records the year in which it occurred, it cannot have happened later than 1101, when Stephen went to Palestine and was killed there the following year. Odo therefore was still alive at least ten years after Stephen’s death.]

After the death of Count Odo, the son, Count Theobald and his mother, through Milo and through Hugh, by every gift, grant, and promise they could offer, made every effort to obtain the castle with the collateral heirs and thereby utterly to disembowel the king. On the other side, although the king and his men strove with much costly effort to obtain it by defeating them, he could by no means do so without the decision of the aforesaid Hugh, because Hugh was the count’s nephew. We therefore met on a day and at a place openly ominous of evil, namely at the estate of the bishop of Paris, Moussy [Note: In the fourth manuscript and edition: *Mosaicum*.]. Since Hugh’s decision would be harmful in one respect and helpful in another, because we could not do what we wished, we wished what we could [Note: In the third manuscript; the edition reads *noluimus*, “we did not wish.”].

For Hugh renounced before us the castle of Corbeil, to which he laid claim as heir, and renounced all forced services, all tallages, and all exactions levied upon the possessions of every church and monastery. Having given hostages for all these promises, and for the promise that he would never fortify Le Puiset without the will of the lord king, we returned, deceived by treachery, not by skill.

## Chapter XX
No delay: although the oath was not yet frozen but still fluid and fresh, Hugh made light of it. Exasperated by his long captivity, like a dog long chained which, when released, rages intolerably from the madness conceived and retained for a long time in bonds [Note: “retained.” Royal MS 5925, Saint-Germain, and Saint-Denis; Royal MS 5265, “received.” In the edition, “held”], he bites and tears when unchained. In the same way Hugh, melting his frozen wickedness, incites, agitates, and hastens toward treachery.

Having therefore made common cause with the foes of the realm—namely Count Theobald of Blois and the illustrious Henry, king of the English—when he learned that Lord King Louis was about to leave for Flanders on affairs of the kingdom, he gathered whatever force of knights and foot-soldiers he could and resolved to restore the castle of Le Puiset. He hastened either to destroy the neighboring settlement or to subdue it to himself. Passing one Saturday through the ruined castle, where, nevertheless, a public market stood open by the king’s permission, he swore by a herald’s proclamation, with astonishing deceit, that security was assured; there he unexpectedly cast into prison such of the wealthier people as he could identify [Note: Saint-Germain MS: “claim as his own”], and, like a raging beast, tearing apart whatever came in his way, he hurried with Count Theobald utterly to overthrow Toury, the fortified village of Saint-Denis [Note: “Overthrow” in four manuscripts and the edition; “destroy” in the text].

The day before, when he met us, knowing his own deceit and wickedness, he had obtained by much entreaty that we should go that very day to intercede for him with the lord king. He supposed that in our absence he would enter the village without difficulty, or, if resistance were made, destroy it altogether. But those who had entered the fortification in the cause of God and Saint Denis resisted as manfully as they did boldly, protected by God’s aid [Note: Royal MS 6265: “with God’s aid”] and the stronghold of the place.

When we had come this side of Corbeil and met the lord king, who had already learned the truth of the affair from Normandy, he very quickly asked why we had come. He laughed at our simplicity; then, indignantly exposing Hugh’s treachery, he sent us back with all speed to aid the village. While he himself collected an army by way of Étampes, we headed for Toury by the straighter and shorter route [Note: Royal manuscripts: “we head”; edition: “we head”]. From afar, with anxious and repeated looks, we fixed our gaze only upon this sign that the fortification had not yet been taken: the lofty three-storied tower rising above the broad plain from it was visible; once the fortification was captured, it would immediately be destroyed by hostile fire.

Since the enemy were plundering, ravaging, and occupying the whole neighborhood, we could induce none of those we met to accompany us, even by gifts or promises. Thus, the fewer we were, the safer. When the sun was already declining toward evening, and the enemy, unable all day to overcome our men whom they were attacking [Note: “Were unable.” Thus the four manuscripts; the edition has “being able”], had paused briefly from fatigue, we, as though we belonged to their company, seized the opportunity and burst through the middle of the village, not without great danger. For our people in the defensive works, to whom we had given the signal [Note: Thus in the four manuscripts and edition; “we had fortified”], opened the gate [Note: Royal MS 6265: “had opened”], and, with the Lord’s favor, we entered very swiftly.

Cheered by our arrival, they mocked the enemy’s Sabbath and, provoking them with many insults and reproaches, called them back to a counterattack, though I resisted and forbade it. Yet, as in my absence, so in my presence, the divine hand protected both the defenders and the defense.
