Though a few of our few and many of their many fell wounded, some were carried away in litters by several of their comrades; others, thrust into a scant and most wretched mound of earth, were laid aside to be exposed to wolves’ teeth on the morrow or the day after.

The enemy had not yet been driven back to Le Puiset when William of Garland, together with many of the readier and stronger armed men of the king’s household, hastened to the village’s assistance. They were most eager with all their hearts to find the enemy nearby, so as to display the courage of the royal soldiery [Note: “To display.” Thus all manuscripts; edition: “to show”]. The lord king himself followed at dawn, and, hearing that they were quartered through the town, prepared the vengeance he desired against the enemy. He was as joyful and exultant as he hoped vigorously to avenge their unexpected injury by a sudden slaughter and unlooked-for retaliation.

But when the enemies learned of his arrival, they wondered that a plot so carefully concealed had become known to him, that he had suddenly set aside his journey to Flanders, and that he had come to help not so much with speed as by flying. Since they dared nothing else, they pressed on with restoring the castle. The king gathered such an army as he could nearby, for war was pressing upon him in many places.

When Tuesday came, he led out his army, formed the battle-lines, placed commanders over them, stationed archers and crossbowmen in their proper places, and advanced step by step toward the still unfinished castle. Since they had heard [Note: Royal and Saint-Denis manuscripts: “he had heard”; Saint-Germain: “he was hearing”; edition: “they had heard”] that Count Theobald had boasted that he would fight him in the open field, the king, with his customary greatness of spirit, dismounted in armor among the armed men. He ordered the horses removed, encouraged those whom he had made dismount with him to be bold, urged them not to yield, and cried out that they should fight with the utmost courage.

When the enemy saw and feared him advancing so vigorously, they were afraid to leave the castle’s precinct. Timidly but cautiously, they chose to form their line within an old ditch of the ruined castle and wait there. Their calculation was that, when the king’s army attempted to climb out of the ditch, they could resist them there, throw their ordered ranks into disorder, and make their disordered ranks waver [Note: “Resist there, [their] ranks being ordered.” Thus the four manuscripts. Perhaps “they might resist”]. And this happened to a great extent.

For at the first onset of battle the king’s soldiers, with much slaughter and astonishing daring, drove them from the ditch as though defeated. But, pursuing them indiscriminately with their own ranks disordered, they pressed them hard. Meanwhile Ralph of Beaugency, a man of great [Note: Saint-Germain MS: “extraordinary”] intelligence and courage, fearing beforehand precisely what occurred, had concealed an army on one side of the castle, hidden by the height of a church and the shade of neighboring houses. When he saw his fugitives already passing out through the gate, he set his rested force against the exhausted royal soldiers and attacked them very fiercely.

Those who had been scattering the enemy in groups, weighed down on foot by the heaviness of their mail and armor, were scarcely able to withstand the ordered line of cavalry [Note: Thus all manuscripts; edition: “infantry”]. Through the occupied ditch, with the king fighting on foot, they withdrew after countless blows and a long reciprocal struggle. Too late they perceived how much wisdom surpasses boldness: had they waited for them in the field in ordered formation, they would have brought them altogether under their will.

But, dispersed in the confusion of the ranks, unable to find their horses [Note: The four manuscripts have the infinitive, “to find”], and not knowing what to do, the king, mounted not on his own horse but another’s, resisted bravely, called loudly for them to return, and personally urged the bolder men not to flee. With drawn sword he moved among the enemy’s formations, aided whom he could, drove back the fugitives, and, more than befitted his majesty, fought singly as a veteran soldier performing a soldier’s duty, not a king’s.

When, his horse exhausted, he could not alone prevent the army’s collapse, his squire came up and brought back his own warhorse [Note: “His own.” Thus all manuscripts; edition: “the first”]. Mounting it at once, bearing the banner before him, he returned against the enemy with a few men, rescued many of his own who had been captured with astonishing valor, struck down some of the enemy in a most forceful attack, and drove back the fugitives lest they do further harm to the army—as though they had encountered the Pillars of Hercules or been barred by the great Ocean. Before they could return to Le Puiset, an army of five hundred Norman knights, or more, met them. Had they come earlier, while the army was collapsing, they might perhaps have inflicted greater damage.

As the king’s army scattered in every direction—some heading for Orléans, some for Étampes, others for Pithiviers—the exhausted king came to Toury. Like a bull, driven from the first encounter, which tests his horns against tree-trunks and, gathering strength again in his mighty breast, unafraid of a great wound, rushes through the steel against his enemy [Note: “Driven like cattle.” Thus all manuscripts; Vergil], so the king summoned back his army, restored its vigor, and renewed its courage. He attributed the army’s disaster to folly, not lack of foresight. He declared that such things must sometimes inevitably befall soldiers, and he labored, with both inducements and threats, to stir them to fight all the more fiercely and boldly if opportunity permitted, and to punish the injury inflicted.

While both French and Normans persisted in restoring the castle—for with Count Theobald and the Norman army were Milo of Montlhéry, Hugh of Crécy, and his brother Guy, count of Rochefort [Note: “His brother” is absent from Royal MS 6265], and thirteen hundred knights were threatening a siege of Toury—the king was not bent by any fear. Day and night he strove to harass them by every means in his power and prevented them from seeking provisions far away.

When the castle had been restored in a single continuous week, certain Normans withdrew, but Count Theobald remained with a large army. The king, having recovered his strength, made ready for war, returned in force to Le Puiset, crushed the enemy who met him, shut them into the castle by fighting through the gate and avenging the injury done, and stationed guards of soldiers so they could not come out. He occupied an old abandoned *motte* of his predecessors, a stone’s throw from the castle, and built up a castle upon it.

[Note: “Motte”: a hill or mound upon which a castle is built. In former times castles were never built except in elevated places. In Flanders, however, a low and very flat region, mottes were customarily made by piling up masses of earth from every quarter, and strongholds were placed upon them. On this subject John of Collemedio should be heard, in the *Life of Saint John, Bishop of the Morini*, in Bollandus, January, vol. II, p. 799, col. 2: “It is the custom,” he says, “of the richer and nobler men of this region, especially because they are accustomed to engage in enmities and killings, to make themselves safer from enemies in this manner, and by greater power either conquer equals or oppress inferiors: they heap up an earthwork to whatever height they can manage; around it they dig a ditch, spreading very widely and of great depth; and they surround the upper edge of the same mound on every side, in place of a wall, with a rampart of closely joined wooden planks, made as strong as possible. They arrange towers around it as circumstances allow, and within the rampart build in the middle either a house commanding a view of everything or a citadel. Thus the gate of entrance to the village can be approached only over a bridge, which begins at the outer lip of the ditch, rises gradually as it proceeds, rests upon pairs or even triples of posts planted on either side at suitable intervals, and rises transversely across the ditch with such a graded ascent that, becoming level with the top surface of the mound, it reaches the outer edge and, at that point, the threshold.”]

With astonishing labor and anxiety, they raised it, enduring missiles discharged by slingers [Note: Royal manuscripts: “fundibaliarii”], crossbowmen, and archers, unless they erected beams joined [Note: Thus all manuscripts; edition: “bound”] with barriers against them. They suffered grievously because those who harassed them, safe within the castle enclosure, shot outward and did not fear any retaliation for the enemy’s wrongdoing.

A perilous contest for victory blazed between those inside and outside. The king’s soldiers who had been wounded strove most fiercely, mindful of their injuries, to wound in return. Nor did they cease from their undertaking until they had fortified the suddenly erected, as though fabricated, stronghold [Note: “Fabricated.” Thus four manuscripts; edition: “fated”] with many soldiers and much armor—certain that, as soon as the king withdrew, they must either defend themselves most boldly against the vexations of the neighboring place or perish most miserably by the enemy’s savage sword.

Returning to Toury and gathering his strength, the king carried provisions to feed the army in the aforesaid motte—now secretly with a few men, now openly with many—through the middle of the enemy’s battle-lines, as dangerously as boldly. At last the men of Le Puiset, pressed intolerably by the annoyance of their proximity, threatened a siege [Note: Thus four manuscripts and the edition; “sedition” in the alternative reading]. The king therefore moved his camp and occupied Yenville, scarcely a mile from Le Puiset, unexpectedly surrounding its inner court with palisade and wickerwork.

While the army pitched its tents outside, Count Palatine Theobald, gathering whatever strength he could from both his own men and the Normans, fell upon them with a most powerful charge while they were unprepared and not yet fortified, bent not merely on repelling but on overthrowing them. When the armed king met him outside, the battle in the field was severe on both sides. Lances and swords alike were employed without distinction; it was a contest more for victory than for life, more for a trophy than against death.

There one might see an example of astonishing courage. Though the count’s army was three times as numerous as the king’s and had driven the king’s soldiers back into the village, the king himself, with only a few men—namely his kinsman Ralph, the most noble count of Vermandois, Drogo of Monchy, and two or three others—disdained to retreat into the village through fear. Remembering his former courage, he chose rather to endure the most violent charges of armed enemies and almost countless blows [Note: “To endure” is absent from the edition, present in four manuscripts] than, if forced to enter the village, to be compelled to diminish the reputation of his own prowess and of royal excellence.

When Count Theobald, now considering himself victor, boldly endeavored to cut down the tents of the aforesaid count of Vermandois, that count came up with remarkable speed. Reproaching him that the men of Brie had never before dared such things against the men of Vermandois, he rushed upon him and, repaying the injury with great exertion, drove him back most courageously. Cheered by his courage and his shout, the royal soldiers leapt upon the enemy, attacked them eagerly thirsting for their blood, struck them down, disgraced them, and drove them back as far as Le Puiset. Even though the gate was filthy, they thrust them in by force, holding many captive and killing more. And such is the uncertain outcome of war: those who had earlier believed themselves victorious now blushed as defeated, grieved for the captured, and lamented the slain.

Thereafter the king prevailed against them, while the count, as though falling from the summit of Fortune’s wheel, declined and failed after long exhaustion of himself and his men, after intolerable and draining oppression of both. Since the strength of the king and his men increased daily, as did the gathering of magnates of the realm indignant with the count, the said count found an opportunity to depart. Pleading the wound received the day before, he sent messengers and intercessors to the king, humbly begging that the lord king allow him to return safely to Chartres.

The king, sweet-tempered as he was and gentler than human expectation, yielded to his request [Note: “Yielding.” Four manuscripts and the edition; alternative: “ascending”], though many advised him not to release an enemy trapped and lacking provisions, lest he later endure repeated injuries. The castle of Le Puiset and Hugh himself were left to the king’s discretion. The count departed for Chartres, frustrated in his vain hope, and what he had begun with happy promise he ended with an unhappy outcome.

The king, moreover, not only disinherited Hugh of Le Puiset, but also razed the castle of Le Puiset itself: tearing down its walls and digging out its wells, he overthrew and leveled it as a place exposed to the divine curse.

## CHAPTER XXI

At another time, long afterward, Hugh had been restored to the king’s favor upon giving many hostages and taking many oaths. But, again resisting through renewed treachery, and proving himself an apt pupil who had surpassed Scylla, the teacher of crimes, he was again besieged by the king and again disinherited. After he had pierced with his own lance the king’s seneschal Anseau of Garland, a valiant baron, he could not unlearn his inborn and habitual treachery until the road to Jerusalem, as with many other wicked men, extinguished by taking his life the wickedness inflamed with every poison.

[Note: “Extinguished.” William of Nangis records the death of Seneschal Anseau in 1115. On his authority we append the following letters of Louis VI, copied from the cartulary of Saint-Martin-des-Champs:

“In the name of Christ, I Louis, by God’s grace king of the Franks, wish it to be known … that Lord Matthew, prior of Saint-Martin, and the whole convent of that church came before us, requesting … that we grant to the church of blessed Martin a certain servant of ours named Ansold. Mercifully embracing their petition, we granted him to that church … in perpetuity. And in order that this may remain ratified and firm forever, we have ordered that the present charter be made and confirmed by the authority of our seal … Done at Paris, in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1117, the eighth of our reign, the third of Queen Adelaide; those present in our palace whose names and signs are written below. Sign of Anseau the seneschal; sign of Gilbert the butler; sign of Hugh the constable; sign of Guy the chamberlain. Given by the hand of Stephen the chancellor.”

Anseau, therefore, was still alive in 1117. Moreover, it should not be supposed that Hugh took up the journey to Jerusalem immediately, or within a brief interval, after killing Anseau. For Suger relates in his book *On His Administration*, p. 337, that when he was already abbot—a dignity he acquired in 1123—the following occurred: “It once happened to me,” he says, “that when I hurried after the lord king to Orléans with an armed force and found the provost of Le Puiset repeating his former evils, I seized him shamefully and sent him to Saint-Denis in disgrace.” Since Le Puiset passed into the king’s power after Hugh’s departure, it is altogether likely that Hugh was still living in Gaul when his provost, repeating his former evils, was captured by Suger.]

When the magnates of the realm and religious men were working to establish peace between the king of England, the king of France, and Count Theobald, those who had bound both the king of England and Count Theobald, conspiring against the kingdom, to recover their private grievances, finally learned by a just judgment [Note: In two Royal manuscripts and Saint-Denis: “by a just judgment”] what men worn out by war and gaining nothing through peace had done.

Count Lancelin of Dammartin lost, without hope of recovery, his claim to the *conductus* of Beauvais [Note: “Conductus.” Loisel interprets the *conductus Belvacensis* here as the right to enlist the communes of Beauvais for warfare, which was not without profit: certain communes paid taxes expressly for this purpose to their official. Perhaps these were called *conductus*. But perhaps nothing other than the right of lodging, the more common meaning of the word, should be understood here]. The pagan of Montjay, deceived in his claim to the castle of Livry [Note: Royal and Saint-Denis manuscripts: “Livry”; Saint-Germain: “Livrici”; edition: “Livraci”], deeply lamented that the same castle, demolished with its enclosure in one month, was restored much more strongly in the following month by the money of the king of England. Milo of Montlhéry, moreover, lost with grief and lamentation the highly welcome marriage to the count’s sister which he had gained through kinship. He received not so much honor and joy in contracting it as dishonor and sorrow in its dissolution.

This was, in the judgment of men, an excellent action, derived from the authority of the canons where this ruling is found: “Obligations made against peace are to be rendered wholly void” [Note: Thus all manuscripts; edition: “led back”].

The strongest right hand of kings is bound by the rightful obligation of its office to restrain the audacity of tyrants whenever it sees them endlessly provoking wars, joyfully plundering, crushing the poor, and destroying churches. When their license is interrupted, they are always inflamed to greater madness, like evil spirits: they slaughter more cruelly those whom they fear losing, cherish utterly those whom they hope to retain, and add fuel to the flames so that they may devour with infinitely greater cruelty.

Thomas of Marle, a most depraved man, while King Louis was occupied with the wars mentioned above and many others, had so devastated the regions of Laon, Reims, and Amiens—with the devil prospering him, since the prosperity of fools is accustomed to destroy them—and so devoured them with wolfish fury, that he spared neither clergy through fear of ecclesiastical vengeance nor people through any humanity. Slaughtering and destroying everything, he took from the convent of nuns of Saint John at Laon two excellent villages. He fortified the very strong castles of Crécy and Nouvion with an extraordinary rampart and high towers, as if they were his own; making them a dragon’s lair and a den of thieves, he exposed almost the whole land without mercy to plunder and fire.

Worn down by his intolerable oppression, the Gallican Church met at Beauvais in a general council [Note: This council of Beauvais was held on 6 December 1114], in order also here to begin the first acts of judgment against the enemies of the true Bridegroom Jesus Christ and to pronounce a sentence of condemnation. Conon, bishop of Palestrina, venerable legate of the holy Roman Church, beset by countless complaints of the oppressions he inflicted upon churches, poor people, and orphans [Note: “His.” Thus all manuscripts; absent from the edition], cut off his tyranny with the sword of Saint Peter—that is, by a general anathema. Though absent, Thomas was stripped of his military belt and, by the judgment of all, deposed from every honor as a criminal, an infamous man, and an enemy of the Christian name.

Moved by the complaint brought before so great a council, the king swiftly marched against him. Accompanied by the clergy, to whom he always adhered with the greatest humility, he turned aside to the very strongly fortified castle of Crécy. With a most powerful armed force—or rather, a divine one—he unexpectedly took the castle. He stormed its strongest tower as if it were a peasant’s hut, confounded the wicked, piously slew the impious, and, because he found them merciless, cut them down without mercy.

One might see the castle as though it were ablaze with hellish fire, so that one would not hesitate to confess: “The whole world will fight with him against the senseless” (Wisdom 5:21). Having gained this victory and eager to press his success, he proceeded to another castle called Nouvion. There someone reported to him:

“May your serenity know, my lord king, that in this wicked castle dwell those most wicked men who deserve only the place of the damned—those, I say, who, on the pretext of the Commune lost by your command, set fire not only to the city of Laon but also to the noble church of the Mother of the Lord, together with many others; who made martyrs of almost all the noble cities, both in cause and punishment, because they sought to assist their lord bishop in true faith; who, not fearing to lay hands upon the Lord’s anointed, most cruelly killed Bishop Gaudry himself, the venerable defender of the Church [Note: Other historians recognize in Gaudry nothing venerable except his clerical character. Guibert, abbot of Nogent, portrayed his character, clothed in all its shadows and colors, in his *On His Own Life*]; who exposed him naked to beasts and birds in the street, cut off his finger with the episcopal ring, and, with their most wicked instigator Thomas, strove to occupy your tower so as to disinherit you [Note: Thus all manuscripts; edition: “inheritance”].”

Thus doubly incited, the king attacked the wicked castle in 1115. He broke open those penal and sacrilegious places as if they were hell, released the innocent, and punished the guilty most severely. One man avenged the wrongs of many. Thirsting for justice, he made a common feast for kites, ravens, and vultures of every one of the most wicked murderers whom he caught; ordering them hanged on gibbets, he taught what those deserve who do not fear to lay hands upon the Lord’s anointed.

After overthrowing those adulterous castles and restoring the same villages to Saint John, he returned to the city of Amiens. There he besieged in that city the tower of a certain tyrant, Adam, despoiler of churches and of the whole neighborhood [read: “of one despoiling”]. After constraining it by a siege of almost two years and forcing its defenders to surrender, he captured it; having captured it, he utterly destroyed it. By its destruction he most gladly restored peace to the country, performing the office of a king who does not bear the sword without cause, and he permanently disinherited both the aforesaid most wicked Thomas and his followers from the lordship of that city.

In 1117, lest royal power seem to be confined by the narrowness of places in any part of the world—for kings are known to have long hands—a man came quickly to him from the territory of Bourges, Alard Guilebald, skilled and silver-tongued. Setting forth quite rhetorically the complaint of his stepson, he most humbly begged the lord king to summon to judgment with sovereign authority [Note: Thus all manuscripts; edition: “one”] a noble baron named Haimo, surnamed Varivacca, lord of Bourbon, who refused justice; to restrain the presumptuous audacity with which he was disinheriting the son of his elder brother, namely Erchembald; and to determine by the judgment of the Franks what each party ought to possess.

[Note: “Varivacca.” Haimo was so surnamed from the variegated color of his hair.

“Restrain—Erchembald.” Erchembald V, lord of Bourbon, who died about 1115, left an underage son of the same name. The boy’s mother soon afterward married Alard Guilebald in a second marriage. Haimo, brother of the deceased Erchembald, had deprived the latter’s son of his paternal inheritance. Alard complained of this to King Louis and stirred him to avenge the wrong.]

The king, from love of justice and compassion for churches and poor people alike, did not wish the poor, as the evil of war sprang up on this occasion, to pay the penalty of another’s pride. Having vainly summoned Haimo to court—for he refused, despairing of justice—the king, deterred by no pleasure or indolence, marched with a great army toward Bourges.

Turning aside to Germigny [Note: Saint-Germain and Royal MS 5925: “Germiniacum”; Royal MS 6265 and Saint-Denis: “Germaniacum”; edition: “Germanicum”], Haimo’s very strongly fortified castle, he sought to attack it in a hard struggle. Haimo saw that he could in no way resist and that hope for both his person and castle was already gone. Finding this the sole way of safety, he threw himself at the lord king’s feet and, repeatedly rolling over in the sight of many in amazement, begged that the king deal mercifully with him. He surrendered the castle, put himself wholly at royal discretion, and, in proportion as he had proudly withdrawn himself, was taught by these events to return himself humbly to justice.

The king retained the castle and brought Haimo himself into France for trial [Note: In Freher: “for litigation”]. By the judgment of the Franks or by a settlement between uncle [alternative: paternal uncle] and nephew, he settled their dispute as justly as mercifully, and put an end, at costly expense, to many oppressions and hardships. He habitually performed these and similar acts frequently in those regions, most mercifully, for the peace of churches and poor people; but since recording them in writing would create tedium, we have thought it fitting to refrain.

Unbridled pride has this further trait of arrogance: while the former disdains superiority, the latter no less disdains equality. To it applies that poetic saying:

> “Caesar can endure no one before him,  
> Nor Pompey an equal …”  
> —Lucan

Since all power is impatient of a partner, Louis, king of the Franks, by the superiority in which he surpassed Henry, king of the English and duke of the Normans, always behaved toward him as toward his feudal vassal. The king of the English, however, unable to endure inferiority in nobility of realm and astonishing abundance of wealth, strove, with the support of his nephew Count Palatine Theobald and of many rivals in the kingdom, to stir up the realm and trouble the king in order to diminish his lordship.

Thus the recurrent evil of old wars was renewed between them. The king of England and Count Theobald, joined by kinship through the Norman and Chartrain regions, combined to attack the king’s nearest frontier. They sent Count Stephen of Mortain, brother of one and nephew of the other, with an army to another region, namely Brie, fearing that the king might suddenly occupy that land in the count’s absence.

The king could not endure to spare Normans, Chartrains, or even men of Brie. Situated in the middle of both parties, as though at the center of a compass, he showed the spirit of royal majesty now against these, now against those, by wasting their lands and often by battle [Note: Thus all manuscripts; edition: “had shown”].

But the Norman frontier had been encircled, beyond the other defenses, by the noble foresight of the kings of England and dukes of the Normans, by the construction of new castles, and by the course of rivers that could not be crossed. Since the king knew a passage there into Normandy and desired access through it, he went with a small body of soldiers toward that frontier, in order to arrange matters more secretly. He cautiously sent men ahead, who, dressed as travelers but armored beneath their cloaks and girded with swords, went down the public road in 1118 to the village called Vadum-Nigasii (the Ford of Nigas), an old village ready to afford the Franks an open and welcome access to the Normans.

The river Epte flowed around it and gave security in its middle, but prevented passage at a distance both downstream and upstream. Suddenly they threw off their cloaks and drew their swords. Attacking the inhabitants vigorously with arms, they drove them back by most resolute resistance. Then the king, hastening dangerously down the mountain slope to bring timely help when his men were already almost exhausted, seized both the court of the village and the church fortified with a tower, though not without loss among his own men.

When he learned that the king of England was nearby with a great army, as was his usual practice, he summoned his barons and urged them under oath to follow him. Count Baldwin of Flanders, an outstanding soldier, an elegant and charming young man, Count Fulk of Anjou, and many magnates of the realm hurried to arrive. Breaking the barrier of Normandy, while some fortified the village, others exposed the land—prosperous from long peace—to both plunder and fire. What had been unheard of, they devastated everywhere in the presence of the king of England and afflicted the people intolerably.

Meanwhile the same king of England made preparations for a castle with great urgency, pressed the laborers on, and, while the king of France left his own position fortified by a guard of soldiers [Note: “Fortified.” In four manuscripts; edition: “messenger”], he raised his own castle on a neighboring hill. From there he intended, with a military force of crossbowmen and archers, to drive them back and cut off the provisions of the countryside, thereby forcing them to afflict their own land under continual necessity.

The king of the Franks returned this challenge in kind without delay. Suddenly gathering an army, he returned at dawn, like a man playing dice, and vigorously attacked that new castle, commonly called Malesès. With great effort and much giving and receiving of very heavy blows—for at such a market such toll is commonly paid—he manfully overpowered it, plundered it, and threw it down. For the honor of the kingdom and the humiliation of his opponent, he dissolved by genuine valor every design that had been contrived from it.

And because Fortune at some time spares no man in power, as the saying goes:

> “If Fortune wills it, you will become a consul from being an orator,”

If he wishes these same things, you will become an orator from a consul.

[Col. 1308C] **(A.D. 1118.)** After the long and remarkable successes of a most tranquil prosperity, the king of England, as though descending from the summit of Fortune’s wheel, was harassed by a strange and disastrous turn of events. On one side the king of France, on another the count of Flanders, related by marriage to the people of Ponthieu, and on another Fulk, count of Anjou, on behalf of the people of Le Mans, strove with all their strength utterly to trouble and assail him.

[Note: [Col. 1307D] “Of the people of Le Mans”: thus the Royal and Saint-Denis manuscripts. The edition reads “and of the Normans.”]

Nor was he attacked only by outsiders, but by wrongs and wars raised by his own men: Hugh of Gournay, the count of Eu (Henry I), the count of Aumale (Stephen), and many others besides. To complete his misfortune, he was afflicted by the inward loss caused by treachery: terrified by the private conspiracy both of his chamberlains and bedchamber servants, he often changed his bed, often multiplied armed watchmen against nocturnal fear, and commanded that a shield and sword be set before him every night as he slept. One of these, named Henry—his most intimate household servant, enriched by the king’s generosity, powerful and renowned, but more renowned as a traitor—was caught in so horrible a conspiracy that, though he had deserved the strangling noose, he was mercifully sentenced to the loss of his eyes and genitals.

[Note: [Col. 1308D] “And bedchamber servants”: from four manuscripts; absent from the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1308D] “Henry”: Royal MS 6965. In the other manuscripts, as in the edition, “II.”]

Beset by these and similar troubles, nowhere secure, yet conspicuous for the energy of his native greatness of spirit, prudent in adversity, he even wore a sword at the doorway; and he endured with impunity the many people whom he held [lacuna] outside the houses to gird themselves with swords, as though it were a game.

[Note: [Col. 1309D] “To gird themselves”: thus all manuscripts. Edition: “from gird themselves.”]

At this time one Enguerrand of Caumont, a vigorous and resolute man, boldly advancing with an armed force, stoutly seized the castle called Andely, whose battlements had secretly been fortified by a faction. Trusting in the king’s protection, he most boldly strengthened what he had occupied, so that he compelled the land from the river called Andelle, from the river Epte as far as the bridge of Saint Peter, to be wholly subject to him. Supported also by the company of many great men, he even met the king of England openly, pursued him disrespectfully as he withdrew, and used the king’s land from the boundary mentioned above as his own.

[Note: [Col. 1309D] Royal MS 6265: “in the palace.”]

[Note: [Col. 1309D] “Disrespectfully”: thus all manuscripts. Edition: “respectfully.”]

[Note: [Col. 1309D] Three manuscripts—Saint-Germain, Saint-Denis, and Royal MS 3325—read “used the land from the aforesaid boundary.” Royal MS 6365 reads: “used the land within the aforesaid boundary as his own.”]

On the side of Le Mans as well, when the same king had resolved, after a long delay and together with Count Theobald, to bring relief to those besieged in the tower of Alençon castle, he was repulsed by Count Fulk; he lost many of his men and, with that castle rendered inglorious, lost the tower. Harassed for a long time by these and such events, he had nearly sunk to the lowest point.

[Note: [Col. 1309D] “Lowest”: thus all manuscripts. Edition: “one.”]

But when divine favour had resolved mercifully to lift him up from so great a depression—after he had been harshly scourged and chastised for a time, for he was a generous benefactor of churches and a lavish dispenser of alms, but excessive in indulgence—the adversity of his humbled condition was unexpectedly and suddenly restored to the highest turn of Fortune’s wheel. His more formidable disturbers either bowed before the divine hand rather than his own or failed altogether, as the Godhead is accustomed mercifully to extend the right hand of mercy to those nearly desperate and deprived of human assistance.

For Baldwin, count of Flanders, by whose most grievous attacks the same king was severely harassed, frequently invaded Normandy. While, with the unbridled spirit of war, he was engaged in fighting the castle of Eu and the neighbouring coast, he was suddenly struck in the face by a lance—a rare but fatal blow. Scorning to take precautions for so slight a wound, he did not scorn to die, and chose to put an end to his attacks not only upon the king of England but thereafter upon everyone.

[Note: [Col. 1309D] Baldwin VII, count of Flanders, was severely wounded in the face in September 1118, in a battle near Eu or Auga, against Bretons supporting Henry’s side. The wound was neglected—indeed aggravated by excess—and he died the following year, on 17 June.]

The aforesaid Enguerrand of Caumont, a most daring man and presumptuous enemy of the same king, did not shrink from the prospect that the territory of the archbishopric of Rouen, belonging to Blessed Mary the Mother of the Lord, would be devastated. Stricken by a most grave illness after long vexation of himself and after the long and intolerable, deserved suffering of his own body, he learned, though late, what was owed to the Queen of Heaven and departed this life.

Fulk, count of Anjou, although bound to King Louis by personal homage, many oaths, and the giving of numerous hostages, preferred greed to loyalty. Without consulting the king, disgraced by treachery, he gave his daughter Matilda in marriage to William, son of the king of England, and by this fraudulent marriage alliance dissolved the enmities confirmed by oath which had been agreed with him.

[Note: [Col. 1310D] “Disgraced”: Saint-Germain, Saint-Denis, and Royal MS 5925. The edition and another Royal manuscript read “inflamed.”]

**(A.D. 1119.)** King Louis, having compelled the region of Normandy on that side to be quiet in his presence, now with a large force and now with a small one indiscriminately exposed it to plundering. By the long habit of harassing them, he utterly despised and held cheap both the king and his people. But one day the king of England, having assembled the forces of many men and observed the imprudent boldness of the king of France, secretly directed ordered ranks of soldiers against him. He set incentives—*incentiva*, “incitements”—so that they might rush upon him in an irregular manner; he placed armed soldiers so that they might engage more fiercely; he dismounted the cavalry; and he sagaciously strove to provide for himself by every military precaution possible.

[Note: [Col. 1310D] “Irregular manner”: Royal MS 6265. In the edition and remaining manuscripts, *exordinarie*; perhaps *exordinate*, “without order.”]

But the king and his men, deigning to make no preparation for battle, rushed out against them indiscriminately but most boldly. Those who first joined battle—the Vexin men, with Bouchard of Montmorency and Guy of Clermont—striking down the first Norman line with a very strong hand, wonderfully drove it from the field of Mars; and they repulsed the foremost cavalry formations against the armed infantry with a most powerful force. Yet the French who had intended to pursue them, disorderedly pressing upon lines exceptionally well ordered and formed, as happens in such cases, were unable to bear their sustained, organized assault and gave way.

The king, astonished at his routed army, as was his custom in adversity, sought steadfastly to aid himself and his men with arms as fittingly as he could. Not, however, without great loss to his scattered army, he returned to Andely.

[Note: [Col. 1310D] “Returned”: thus all manuscripts. Edition: “hastened.” Orderic Vitalis likewise describes the battle of Brémule here in question and its subsequent events, but in a very different style. Suger seems excessively favourable to the king of France; the other writer inclines too immoderately toward the king of England.]

Slightly shaken by the misfortune of this sudden event, lest his enemies insult him longer as though he dared not enter Normandy again, he showed himself, as usual, far more spirited in adversity and, as befits so great a man, more steadfast. He summoned back his army, called in the absent, invited the great men of the realm, and informed the king of England that on a fixed day he would both enter the territory and undertake a most celebrated contest. What he promised him as though under oath, he hastened to perform.

For, invading Normandy with a remarkable army and ravaging it, he caused the very strongly fortified castle called Jouy to be stormed after much fighting and consumed by fire, and advanced as far as Breteuil.

[Note: [Col. 1311C] “Consumed by fire”: Royal MS 6265. The edition and three other manuscripts read *conflari*, “to be melted/fused.”]

After remaining a while in the country, finding neither the king of England nor anyone upon whom he could adequately avenge the injury inflicted upon him, he returned to Chartres so that the punishment might also fall upon Count Theobald. Assaulting the city with the strongest force, he strove to burn it. But suddenly clergy and citizens alike, carrying before them the tunic of the Blessed Mother of God, most devoutly begged that, for her love, he should mercifully spare them as the chief protector of the Church, and implored him not to avenge upon his own people an injury done by another. The king, bowing the height of royal majesty to their entreaties, ordered Charles, count of Flanders, to withdraw the army and, out of love and fear of the Church, to spare the city, lest the noble church of Blessed Mary together with the city should be destroyed by fire. When they had returned home, they did not cease to punish their momentary misfortune with long, unbroken, and most grievous revenge.

[Note: [Col. 1311C] “Lest the church be destroyed by fire.” Nevertheless, the Chronicle of Morigny, Book II, attests that part of the city was burned by the king—plainly before the clergy approached him—in these words: “When Pope Calixtus learned that King Louis, arriving at Chartres with an army from Normandy, had burned part of the city,” etc.]

At this time, in 1118, Paschal, the supreme Roman pontiff of venerable memory, passed from this life to everlasting light. He was succeeded by Pope Gelasius, canonically elected from John of Gaeta, the chancellor. But Gelasius was intolerably harassed by the violence of the emperor Henry, who had intruded a certain Burdinus, the deposed archbishop of Braga, into the Apostolic See, and by the hired attacks of the Roman people; shut out from the holy see by their tyranny, he fled, as popes had formerly been accustomed to do, to the guardianship and protection of the most serene King Louis and to the compassionate support of the Gallican Church.

[Note: [Col. 1311C] “Fled.” Forced to leave Rome, Gelasius embarked on 2 September 1118 and reached Pisa some days later, remaining there for a time. Embarking again for Gaul, he first arrived at Genoa, where on 10 October he dedicated the cathedral church, and then at the harbour of Marseilles. He was in that city on 23 October, as is shown by the rescript confirming the possessions and churches of the monastery of Nobilly near Poitiers, issued at Marseilles on 23 October, indiction XII, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1119, and the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gelasius II (Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. VI, pp. 16–17). It should be noted that in his diplomas Gelasius, following Pisan practice, reckoned the civil year as beginning nine months and seven days earlier, and customarily began the indiction in September (Pagi, under 1118, no. 15). Shortly thereafter he departed Marseilles and, with sails set, was carried to the port of Saint-Gilles.

Soon bishops, abbots, and men of the highest nobility of those regions assembled there. Among them was Pons, abbot of Cluny, who presented the pope with thirty equipped horses and small gifts; the abbot of Saint-Concordius, or Saint Peter of Besalú, in the diocese of Girona, gave ten. Both accompanied the pope through that province. The pontiff was at Saint-Gilles on 7 November; a few days later at Maguelone; at Lattes, as Mabillon notes (*ibid.*), on 10 December. Letters cited by Baronius under this year show him at Avignon on 16 December. A bull of his for the monastery of Saint Andrew of Avignon, issued at Orange on 20 December, indiction XII, in 1119, the first year of his pontificate, shows that he then came to Orange (*ibid.*). The anonymous author of the Saxon Chronicle and Abbot of Ursperg testify that he held a council at Vienne before the end of that same year. Proceeding thence to Lyons, he began to fall ill; he was carried from Mâcon to Cluny and there exchanged life for death on 29 January.]

Having arrived, with naval aid—for he was oppressed by great poverty—at Maguelone, a narrow island in the sea, a city lonely and private, with only its bishop surviving, its clergy and sparse household neglected, yet very strongly fortified by a wall against attacks from Saracens crossing the sea, we delivered to him the messages sent by the lord king, since he had already heard of his arrival. With his blessing, because we had offered him the first fruits of the kingdom, we gratefully received back a fixed day and place, at Vézelay, for a mutual conference.

[Note: [Col. 1312D] “Wall”: thus all manuscripts. Edition: “indeed.”]

When the lord king was hastening to meet him, it was announced that the same supreme pontiff, long afflicted by gout, had spared both Romans and Franks by laying down his life, in 1119. Many religious men and prelates of the Church hastened to attend his Apostolic funeral rites. Present was the venerable Guy, archbishop of Vienne, nobly descended through collateral kinship from imperial and royal eminence, but far nobler in character.

[Note: [Col. 1312D] “Nobly descended through kinship.” Guy was son of William the Great, also called “the Bold-headed,” count of Burgundy; grandson of Renaud; and great-grandson of Otto-William. Otto-William’s wife Ermentrude had as parents Renaud, count of Roucy, and Alberada, daughter of Gilbert, duke of Upper Lorraine, and of Gerberga, whose father was Henry the Fowler, king of Germany.]

On the preceding night he had seen in a dream, by a sufficiently apt though unknown portent, that the moon, placed beneath a cloak, was entrusted to him by a very powerful person. Therefore, lest the cause of the Church be endangered by the Apostolic See’s vacancy, he was elected supreme pontiff by the Roman Church there present, and perceived more clearly the truth of his vision. Raised to the dignity of so great an eminence, he gloriously, humbly, but vigorously ordered the affairs of the Church. Through love and service toward Lord King Louis, and toward Queen Adelaide, his niece, he more suitably provided for ecclesiastical business.

[Note: [Col. 1312D] Adelaide was born of Humbert II, count of Maurienne, and Gisela, sister of Calixtus.]

Thus, holding a most celebrated council at Reims, and postponing a meeting with the legates of Emperor Henry concerning peace for the Church, he went to meet them at Mousson, toward the march. Since he achieved nothing, as his predecessors had done, he bound the emperor with the bond of anathema before a full council of Franks and Lotharingians.

[Note: [Col. 1312D] “Bound.” After his election on 1 February 1119 at the monastery of Cluny, Calixtus II, son, as stated, of William the Great, count of Burgundy, returned to Vienne, his archiepiscopal city. There he was crowned on Quinquagesima Sunday, which in that year fell on 9 February (Pagi, under 1119, no. 6; Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictines*, vol. VI, p. 36). Having arranged the affairs of that church, he travelled through Auvergne. Thence he went to Toulouse and held a council there on 8 July—not, as the printed acts erroneously state, on 7 June (*History of Languedoc*, vol. II, pp. 384–385).

Leaving Toulouse on 17 July, the pope went to the village called Fronton, three leagues north of Toulouse; then to the village of Saint-Audard in the district of Cahors, now Montauban; and then to Divona, the chief town of the Cadurci, where on 27 July he consecrated the high altar of the cathedral church (*ibid.*). He was at Poitiers on 27 August, when he granted letters of Apostolic protection to Elizabeth, abbess of the monastery of the Holy Trinity in that city. Leaving Poitiers, the pontiff went to Angers, where on 7 September he likewise consecrated the altar of the Lord at the Parthenay of Blessed Mary of Ronceray (Mabillon, *ibid.*). He did not leave before 9 September, as is attested by a diploma issued by him at Angers on 9 September in favour of the monastery of Savigny (Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, col. 659).

Proceeding thence directly to the monastery of Saint-Florent at Glanfeuil, he dedicated its church (Mabillon, *ibid.*, p. 37). Before reaching it, however, he appears to have visited the Parthenay of Fontevraud. In letters issued on 15 September at Marmoutier near Tours for the nuns of Fontevraud, he declares that he had dedicated their church. He could, however, have done this while presiding over the church of Vienne and acting as Apostolic legate. In any case, from Glanfeuil he came to Tours, where he was stripped by thieves during the night. When Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, learned of it, he gave the pontiff a grey fur garment and various furs, as Geoffrey himself testifies in his letter to Calixtus (Book I, epistle 12).

He had not yet left Tours on 24 September, when he granted the brethren of Marmoutier two privileges in their own buildings (Mabillon, *ibid.*). Leaving Tours, he directed his journey toward Chartres. Learning on the way that part of that city had been burned by King Louis, because of hostility toward Count Theobald, he changed his plan and arrived unexpectedly at Orléans. He then went to Étampes, was received in the palace, and, in the presence of King Louis and Adelaide his wife, dedicated the church of Morigny in the suburbs of that town on 3 October. This dedication, Mabillon says, is wrongly assigned in the printed works to the following year, when Calixtus was no longer in Gaul.

Leaving Étampes, the pontiff made for Paris, then went to Reims, where he held a council from 19 to 30 October. On the fourth day after it began, namely Wednesday the 23rd, as Orderic says, he proceeded to Mousson with a notable company; on the following Sunday he collapsed from exertion and fear and returned ill to Reims. From there he came to Gisors for a conference with the king of England; soon afterward to the monastery of Saint-Denis, where on 27 November he confirmed all the possessions of Saint-Martin-des-Champs. Passing then beyond Paris and preparing to enter Burgundy, he went first to Corbeil and then to Melun. The king and queen accompanied him and together escorted the pontiff to Ferrières, a royal abbey.

He was at Sens on 5 December, according to the monk Clarius; thence he celebrated Christmas at Auxerre. Subsequently received at Saulieu in the territory of the Aedui, he confirmed there the Charter of Charity of the Cistercians near the end of that year, 1119 (Mabillon, *ibid.*). From there he again visited the monastery of Cluny, where he renewed the privileges of that church for Bruno, archbishop of Trier, by a diploma issued on 3 January 1120 (*ibid.*, pp. 45–46). We learn from a bull issued there for the monastery of Vézelay that he was at Tournus on 12 January (*ibid.*).

The pontiff then held a council at Vienne, summoned by himself for the feast of Blessed Mary called the Hypapante, the Presentation (Councils, vol. X, p. 862). He was at Valence on the Rhône on 22 February, when he granted a new privilege to Pons, abbot of Cluny. He was still there on 25 February when he granted the church of Vienne a very extensive privilege reported by Baronius. Thereafter he proceeded to Montpellier, through the city of Viviers, where on 26 February he dedicated the cathedral church (*History of Languedoc*, vol. II, p. 386), and thence to Saint-Gilles. Then, after traversing Provence and crossing the Alps, he went to Saint Ambrose—that is, if I understand correctly, to Milan, says Mabillon. This is the brief sequence of Calixtus’s journey in Gaul.]

When, enriched by the votive benefactions of churches, he had gloriously arrived at Rome and was received with splendid welcome by both clergy and Roman people, he administered the Church’s care more successfully than many of his predecessors. He had not yet stayed long in the Holy See when the Romans, favouring both his nobility and generosity, captured the schismatic Burdinus, intruded by the emperor. He was seated at Sutri and compelled clerics passing to the thresholds of the Apostles to bend the knee. Having conquered him, they placed the crooked antipope—or rather Antichrist—upon a crooked beast, a camel, clothed in raw and bloody goatskins. Avenging the dishonour of God’s Church, they led him through the midst of the city along the royal road, so that the spectacle might be more public; at the command of Pope Calixtus they condemned him to perpetual imprisonment in the mountains of Campania near Saint Benedict, and, to preserve the memory of so great a vengeance, painted him trampled beneath the pope’s feet in the chamber of the palace.

Thus, while Lord Calixtus presided gloriously and subdued the robbers of Italy and Apulia, the lamp of the pontifical chair—the Church of Saint Peter—shone brightly, not under a bushel but set upon a mountain. Recovering what they had lost, the other churches, both in the city and beyond it, enjoyed the most welcome protection of so great a lord.

When I met him in Apulia at the city of Bitonto, sent by King Louis concerning certain affairs of the realm, the Apostolic man received us honourably, both out of reverence for the lord king and for our monastery. He would have kept us longer had we not been recalled by love for our Church and by the persuasion of our companions: the companions and fellow pupils of Hugh, abbot of Saint-Germain, and others.

[Note: [Col. 1314D] Hugh IX, monk of Saint-Denis.]

Having completed the affairs of the realm which we had undertaken, we hastened successfully homeward. Received, as is the custom of travellers, in lodging at a certain village, after Matins had ended, I lay down clothed upon the bed while awaiting dawn. Half awake, I seemed to see myself wandering alone in a small boat over a vast expanse of sea, entirely bereft of every oar; tossed perilously by the frequent motion of the waves, now rising and now falling, and, struck by the dreadful fear of shipwreck, importuning the ears of God with loud cries. Suddenly, through divine mercy, a gentle and calm breeze, as though raised in clear weather, turned straight the trembling and already endangered prow of the wretched little vessel and, more swiftly than expectation, brought it to a peaceful harbour.

[Note: [Col. 1314D] Observe this ancient custom of monks: even while travelling, they celebrated the night watches at the proper hours.]

[Note: [Col. 1315D] “And already”: from four manuscripts. Edition: “vain.”]

Awakening at daybreak and setting out upon the journey begun, I laboured in much meditation as I travelled, trying both to recall the vision and its interpretation and to explain it—for I feared that the assault of the waves signified some grave misfortune to me. Suddenly a household boy came upon us. Recognizing me and my men, joyful and sorrowful, he uttered a solitary sob and announced the death of our lord, Abbot Adam of blessed memory, my predecessor, in 1123, and the unanimous election concerning my person made by the full convent.

But since it had been done without consulting the king, he reported that the better and more religious brethren, together with the nobler knights, had offered the election to the lord king for his assent, but were met with many insults and shut up in the castle at Orléans. Then tears arose. Compassionating my spiritual father and humanly loving fosterer with affection of humanity and pity, grieving deeply at his temporal death, I most devoutly implored divine mercy to rescue him from eternal death.

When, through the consolation of many companions and through my own reflection, I had returned to myself, I was tormented by a threefold loss: whether, by accepting an election contrary to the lord king’s will, I should allow the mother Church to be despoiled and drained by both destroyers—by the severity of the Roman Church and by the authority of Pope Calixtus, who loved me—though she had never ceased most sweetly to cherish me from the breast and gracious bosom of her liberality, and though they had never sought such a thing, merely because of the occasion furnished by me; whether I should allow my brothers and friends to be disgraced and dishonoured in a royal prison for love of me; or whether, setting her aside because of these and like considerations, I should incur the reproach of so great a refusal.

As I was deciding to send one of my people to the lord pope to consult him about these matters, a noble Roman cleric and intimate acquaintance suddenly came to us. He willingly undertook to do in person what we had wished to accomplish through our own men at costly labour. We also sent one of our own men with him, who was going to the king, so that they might report to us what outcome the confusion of the troubled business had found. For we would not rashly expose ourselves to royal vexations.

Thus following on, as though we were tossed upon a great sea without a helmsman, troubled and uncertain of the outcome, and grievously anxious, we unexpectedly received, by the abundant mercy of almighty God and the calm breeze bringing the shipwrecked vessel to harbour, those who brought back the lord king’s peace, the release of those imprisoned, and confirmation of the election.

Taking this very event as an indication of God’s will—for it was God’s will that what we desired should promptly occur—we arrived, with God’s help, at the mother Church. She received the prodigal son so sweetly, so filially, so nobly that we found there, rejoicingly awaiting us, the lord king, who at first had met us with a stern but now with a serene countenance; the archbishop of Bourges; the bishop of Senlis; and many ecclesiastical persons. They received us with great reverence and very swiftly into the joyful assembly of the brethren. On the following day, namely the Saturday of Mid-Lent, he ordained me, unworthy though I was, priest. On the following Sunday, *These Are the Days*, he consecrated me there, before the most sacred body of Saint Denis, as abbot, though unworthy.

When Almighty God had accomplished this customary work, raising the poor man from the dunghill to make him sit with princes, he exalted me from the lowest place to the highest. In proportion to that exaltation, he made me more humble and, if human frailty does not prevent it, more devoted in all things to a hand both most sweet and most powerful.

[Note: [Col. 1315D] “More devoted”: Saint-Germain MS and Royal MS 6265. Two other manuscripts, with the edition, read “devotion.”]

Since that hand has prospered our smallness mercifully in everything—for it knows the insufficiency of our birth and learning—among the recovery of the Church’s ancient estates, the acquisition of new ones, the Church’s enlargement on every side, and the restoration or establishment of buildings, it has bestowed, in its mercy, this foremost and most welcome privilege, indeed its greatest: it fully reformed in that place the holy order of its holy Church, for the honour of the saints, indeed for its own honour; it peacefully established, without scandal or disturbance among the brethren, though they had not been accustomed to it, the religious purpose by which one comes to enjoy God.

[Note: [Col. 1316D] “By which”: Royal MS 6265 and Saint-Denis manuscript. Edition: “which.”]

This effectual divine will was followed by such an abundance of good repute, liberty, and earthly prosperity that even now, in order to stir our faint-heartedness more strongly, it is in some measure evident that it recompenses us even with temporal reward. Apostolic rulers, kings, and princes delight to rejoice in the Church’s prosperity; an abundance of precious gems, gold and silver, cloths, and other ecclesiastical ornaments flows forth from it, so that we may rightly say: “All good things came to me together with her” (Wisdom 7).

By the experience of this foretaste of God’s future glory, we adjure our brother successors, through God’s mercy and his terrible judgment, not to permit the holy religious life—which reconciles human beings and God, strengthens what is broken, restores what has been lost, and enriches poverty—to grow lukewarm. For just as those who fear the Lord lack nothing, those who do not fear him lack everything, even kings; they themselves also fail themselves.

Accordingly, in the year following our installation (1123), lest we be charged with ingratitude—for the holy Roman Church, before our promotion, had kindly received us both at Rome and elsewhere in many and various councils, while acting both for our church and for others; had listened favorably to our arguments; and had raised our affairs [Col. 1317A] higher than I myself had done—we hastened to visit her. Received with great honor by Pope Calixtus and the whole curia, we stayed with him for six months. While there, we attended the great Lateran council of three hundred or more bishops concerning the settlement of peace in the dispute over investitures. Having visited various holy places for prayer—namely Saint Benedict at Cassino, Saint Bartholomew at Benevento, Saint Matthew at Salerno, Saint Nicholas at Bari, and the holy angels at Gargano—we returned prosperously, with God’s help, the pope’s favor and affection, and letters of recommendation.

> [Note: “Higher.” So all the manuscripts. The edition has *alternis*, but wrongly. The sense, therefore, is: the Roman Church had raised our affairs—that is, the affairs of the church of Saint-Denis—higher than I myself had done.]

But when, on another occasion some years later, he summoned us back to the curia at Lucca, a Tuscan city, in order to honor us still more sweetly and, as his letters stated, willingly to exalt us, we learned the truth of his death and turned back, avoiding the new and old avarice of the Romans. He was succeeded by Honorius, a man of approved character, formerly bishop of Ostia, grave and severe.

Having learned of our rightful claim concerning the monastery of Argenteuil, disgraced by the most wretched manner of life of its nuns, through the testimony both of his legate Matthew, bishop of Albano, and of the lord bishops of Chartres, Paris, and Soissons, and also of Lord Renaud, archbishop of Reims, and many other men; and having read the ordinances of the ancient kings—Pepin, Charlemagne, Louis the Pious, and others—concerning the right to the aforesaid place, presented by our messengers, he, at the persuasion of the whole curia, both because of our justice and because of the women’s foul enormities, restored and confirmed it to blessed Denis [Col. 1317C].

> [Note: “Confirmed.” Alternatively, “reformed.” Our author treats more fully of the recovery of the monastery of Argenteuil in his book *On the Deeds Accomplished during His Administration*.]

But to return to our purpose, the recollection of the king’s history: before the death of Pope Calixtus (1124), Emperor Henry, having gathered a long-standing rancor in his heart against King Louis, because at Reims, in a council of Pope Calixtus held within Louis’s kingdom, he had been bound by anathema, assembled, as far as he could, an army of Lotharingians, Alemanni, Bavarians, Swabians, and Saxons, although they were hostile to him. Pretending, by the counsel of Henry, king of England, whose daughter he had married—and who was also making war upon the king—to be marching elsewhere, he planned a surprise attack on the city of Reims, intending either suddenly to destroy it or to besiege it with such disgrace and oppression as the pope had there inflicted upon him by the council he held against him.

> [Note: “There.” Saint-Germain manuscript; absent from the editions.]

When this became known to King Louis through the report of his intimates [Col. 1318B], he summoned, vigorously and boldly, a levy which he did not await; he enlisted the nobles and set forth the cause. Since he had learned both from many reports and from frequent experience that blessed Denis was the special patron and, after God, the singular protector of the kingdom, he hastened to him and, with prayers and benefactions alike, appealed to him from his heart: that he might defend the kingdom, preserve his person, and resist the enemies according to his accustomed manner.

And because they have this prerogative from him: if any kingdom should dare invade the kingdom of the French, the blessed and wonderful defender himself, together with his companions, is to be placed, as it were, upon his altar for its defense. This was done, in his presence, as gloriously as devoutly. The king, receiving from the altar the banner belonging to the county of the Vexin, which he held as a fief from the Church [Col. 1318C], received it devoutly as from his lord. With a small force he flew out against the enemies, to provide for himself, and powerfully invited all France to follow him.

> [Note: “Belonging.” The counts of the Vexin were formerly dependent upon the church of Saint-Denis by right of clientship. Therefore, when that church was attacked by enemies, they were bound, as its advocates, to take its side and, whenever a dispute had to be decided by arms, to lead its forces into battle under its banner. Philip the king succeeded to their place and office when he acquired the Vexin, and this was before 1087; for, according to William of Jumièges (*History of Normandy*, book VII, chapter 41), William the Great, king of England and duke of Normandy, in that very year furiously burned a certain town called Medan, part of this county and property of Philip, king of the French.
>
> Therefore, once the kings of France had become standard-bearers of the church of Saint-Denis through this acquisition, they took care, in most serious wars waged against enemies of the kingdom, down to the time of Charles VII, solemnly to receive its banner from the abbot’s hands, to bear it before them, and, after the wars were concluded, to bring it back to the same place. This standard, called in Latin *Auriflamma* and in French *l’oriflamme* by historians, consisted of a cloth of fiery-colored silk, divided below into three parts and ending in three green points, hung from a gilded spear.
>
> The counts of the Vexin owed not only protection but also homage to the church of Saint-Denis. Louis the Fat himself acknowledged this, for, hastening—as Suger says in his book *On the Deeds Accomplished during His Administration*—against the emperor who was rising against the kingdom of France, he declared in the full chapter of Saint Denis that he held the Vexin from him and, by right of standard-bearer, would owe him homage if he were not king.
>
> Indeed, we have a published diploma of that king concerning this matter, in which he calls himself a dependent of the church of Saint-Denis and shows himself grateful and munificent toward its most holy patrons:
>
> “When word had reached us that the king of the Alemanni was preparing an army to enter and oppress our kingdom, after taking counsel with our palatines we hastened, according to the custom of our predecessors, to the most holy basilica of the martyrs. There, in the presence of the chief men of our kingdom, we caused those same patrons of ours to be raised upon their altar, with pious feeling and love, for the defense of the kingdom.
>
> “Therefore it pleased us, as was fitting, to embrace and exalt with every affection in our own times the basilica of the most glorious martyrs, enlarged and adorned by the generosity and munificence of the ancient kings. In the presence, then, of the venerable Suger, abbot of the church set over it, whom we had as faithful and intimate in our counsels, and in the presence of our chief men, we received, from the altar of the blessed martyrs, the banner to which belongs the county of the Vexin, which we hold from them in fief. Observing and imitating the ancient custom of our predecessors, we received it by right of standard-bearer, as the counts of the Vexin had been accustomed to do.
>
> “We also granted to those holy martyrs, for perpetual possession, under their guidance and protection, both for the salvation of our soul and for the governance and defense of the kingdom and the preservation of our wife and children, the vicariate and every kind of jurisdiction and full liberty which, in former times, the power of many kings of France and our own had occupied near the town of Saint-Denis toward Paris. We have delimited it by a definite distinction of boundaries: from the river Seine, namely from the mill commonly called Bayard, to the upper end of the town called Aubervilliers.
>
> “Moreover, we granted in perpetuity every authority, all jurisdiction, and all the customs of the fair of the Indictum, because the aforesaid Indictum was established by apostolic authority, by the confirmation of archbishops and bishops, and by the ordinance of our predecessors, the kings of France, in honor and reverence of the holy relics—namely the Lord’s nail and crown. . . .
>
> “Done publicly at Paris, in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1124, the eighteenth of our reign and the tenth of Queen Adelaide.”
>
> (Félibien, *History of the Abbey of Saint-Denis*, Documents, p. 93, no. CXXIV.)

Thus the king, receiving the banner from his lord [Col. 1319A] as a votive offering, went out with a small force against the enemy to look after his own safety, and vigorously called upon all France to follow him. France’s accustomed courage, indignant at the enemy’s unprecedented audacity, summoned a military levy on every side, choosing forces and men mindful of their former valor and ancient victories.

When we had assembled in strength from every quarter at Reims, such masses of cavalry and infantry appeared that they seemed, like locusts, to devour the surface of the earth—not only along the courses of rivers, but in mountains and plains as well. While the king waited for a whole week for the German attack, this deliberation was made among the magnates of the kingdom:

> “Let us boldly cross over to them, lest they return unpunished after daring so arrogantly against France, mistress of lands. Let them feel the desert of their contumacy, not in our land but in their own, which, by royal right, lies subject to the French and has often been subdued by the French. What they planned furtively to attempt against us, let us openly turn back upon them.”

But the stern demand of others urged that they should wait longer; that, once the invaders had entered the borders of the march and could no longer escape after being cut off, they should overthrow them when defeated, slaughter them mercilessly like Saracens, expose the unburied bodies of the barbarians to wolves and ravens for their everlasting disgrace, and justify by the defense of their own land the cause of so many killings and such cruelty.

The magnates of the kingdom then arranged the battle-lines in the palace before the king, determining which forces were to be joined to which support of the kingdom. They formed one division, of more than sixty thousand horse and foot, from the men of Reims and Châlons; a second, of no smaller number, from those of Laon and Soissons; and a third, from the men of Orléans, Étampes, Paris, and the abundant army of blessed Denis, devoted to the crown. The king also arranged to take his place in it, hoping for the help of his protector:

> “In this line,” he said, “I shall fight as safely as vigorously; for beyond the protection of their holy lords [Col. 1320A], those who brought me up more familiarly as fellow-countrymen will either help me alive or bring me back dead, preserving me.”

Count Palatine Theobald, too, with his noble uncle Hugh, count of Troyes, having come after renouncing France—for with his uncle, the king of England, he was making war upon the king—formed a fourth division; and he placed in advance a fifth, belonging to the duke of Burgundy, Hugh II, and the count of Nevers, William II.

> [Note: “Renouncing.” The edition has this reading. Royal manuscript 5995 and Saint-Denis manuscript have *ajuratione*; Royal manuscript 6965, *adjuratione*.]
>
> [Note: A recent glossator in the Saint-Denis manuscript adds: “with eight thousand men.” But he does not say this on his own authority; he borrows it from another chronicle, as he warns in these words: “NOTE. This is an addition drawn from a chronicle concerning this matter.”]
>
> [Note: The glossator adds immediately: “a fifth, which contained ten thousand valiant men.”]

The excellent count Ralph of Vermandois, conspicuous by his close kinship with the king, relying on the best soldiery and on a large armed force from Saint-Quentin and all his land, equipped with hauberks and helmets, was appointed to hold the right wing; he approved the placement of the men of Ponthieu, Amiens, and Beauvais on the left.

> [Note: The glossator: “With seven thousand men.”]

The most noble count of Flanders, Charles, with ten thousand most battle-worthy soldiers, would have tripled the army had he learned of the crisis in time; he was being assigned to complete the rearmost line.

> [Note: The glossator: “In so great a number—that is, with seven thousand.”]

Duke William of Aquitaine, a near neighbor by situation; the excellent count Conan III of Brittany; and the warlike Count Fulk of Anjou greatly regretted that the length of the journey and the shortness of time prevented them from increasing the forces and punishing the injury done to the French most severely.

It was also provided that wherever the armies should engage, provided the place were suitable, wagons and carts carrying water and wine for the weary and wounded should be arranged in a ring like castles, so that men weakened by battle and wounds might there drink and tighten their bandages, gain strength, and fight more stoutly for the winning of victory.

> [Note: “Should engage.” Thus three manuscripts: Royal 6265, Saint-Germain, and Saint-Denis. In Royal manuscript 5925, as in the edition, “should find.”]

When the deliberation concerning so great and terrible an undertaking had been proclaimed, and such a strong levy had appeared, this very news reached the emperor’s ears. Pretending and concealing, he withdrew under a disguised pretext, choosing rather to bear the disgrace of failure than to expose both empire and person, endangered by ruin, to the very heavy vengeance of the French.

> [Note: “Appearance.” Perhaps for *apparatus*, “preparation.” The glossator adds: “They had already set foot beyond the kingdom with the king; advancing in squadrons against the disordered Alemanni, they had already killed as many as two thousand.”]
>
> [Note: The glossator has “thundered forth.”]
>
> [Note: The glossator adds: “and immediately withdrew,” etc.]
>
> [Note: Robert of Torigni, under the year 1124, relates the affair summarily in these words: “Emperor Henry, having assembled an innumerable multitude of an army, planned to invade the borders of the kingdom of the French. But when Louis, king of the French, was likewise hastening to meet him with an infinite army, Henry abandoned his useless purpose, by the counsel of princes and bishops; and this occurred in the month of August.” German historians indeed relate that Henry, having heard of the sudden rebellion of the inhabitants of Worms, was compelled to abandon his undertaking and lead the army back into those parts, lest the fire spread further and in order to suppress it at its very beginning.]

When the French learned this, only with difficulty could they restrain themselves, at the prayer of the archbishops, bishops, and religious men, from devastating that kingdom and oppressing its poor inhabitants (1124).

> [Note: The glossator: “when the king and the French.”]
>
> [Note: The glossator: “from the devastation of the German kingdom.”]

Having obtained so great and famous a victory—indeed, it was the same as, or no less than, if the French had won a triumph on the battlefield and returned home—the king rejoiced. Not ungrateful, he came most humbly to his protectors, the most holy martyrs, and, rendering them great thanks after God, most devoutly restored his father’s crown, which he had unjustly retained—for by right all the crowns of deceased kings belong to them.

> [Note: The glossator adds: “and not very bloody.”]
>
> [Note: “Or.” Thus two Royal manuscripts and the Saint-Denis manuscript. The edition has “not.”]
>
> [Note: “Retained.” Thus all manuscripts. The edition has “held.” The glossator adds up to this point.]
>
> [Note: The glossator adds: “of deceased kings.”]
>
> [Note: The glossator adds: “And, in satisfaction for its unjust retention, he generously granted to their church, for perpetual possession, the town of Cergy with all its appurtenances.”
>
> Nevertheless Louis himself testifies, in the following charter transcribed from the cartulary of that place, that he had restored this crown to the church of Saint-Denis already in 1120:
>
> “Louis, by the grace of God king of the French, to the archbishops, dukes, counts, and all the magnates of our kingdom: Since by the abundant mercy of almighty God the kingdom stands, etc. . . . After taking counsel with our palatines, we hastened with our wife to the basilica of the most holy martyrs; and, in the presence of the venerable bishop Lord Conon, legate of the apostolic see, since by right and custom the insignia of the kingdom of departing kings of France are returned to that holy martyr as their leader and protector, we rendered our father’s crown to him and made satisfaction for the delay in rendering it, etc.
>
> “Done publicly in the year of the Incarnate Word 1120, the twelfth of our reign and the sixth of Queen Adelaide. With the assent of our son Philip, present in our palace were those whose names and signs are subscribed: the sign of Stephen the seneschal; the sign of Gilbert the cupbearer; the sign of Hugh the constable; the sign of Guy the chamberlain. Given by the hand of Stephen the chancellor. Adam being abbot of Saint Denis.”
>
> It is remarkable that the consent of the royal boy Philip, who had scarcely reached his fifth year, is mentioned in this diploma. Moreover, one must observe in the chronological notices of this diploma the sixth year of Adelaide, combined with Louis’s twelfth and Christ’s year 1120; from this it follows that Adelaide married Louis in 1115, and indeed before 29 July, on which date Philip was succeeded by Louis.]

He also most willingly restored the Indictum—the outer fair in the marketplace, for the inner fair belonged to the saints—and, by confirmation of a royal ordinance, established the entire roadway extending over the spaces marked by marble crosses and columns, as though they were Pillars of Hercules barring every enemy (1124).

> [Note: What the Indictum is—now called in French *le Lendit*—and whence it derived, is explained more fully by Nangis in his *Chronicle*, in these words:
>
> “King Charles [the Bald] himself brought from Aachen to the church of Saint-Denis in France the Lord’s nail and the crown of thorns, which Charlemagne had formerly deposited there in the church of Saint Mary which he himself had founded. And he ordained that the fair of the Indictum should be held every year, on the second Wednesday of June, in the square called the Indictum; and that, by the bishops and pontiffs of all Gaul, remission and release of one-third of sins should be granted to those who came for the blessing of that fair, just as Charlemagne had earlier commanded at Aachen.”
>
> We are not unaware that Robert Gaguin and Dublet derive the origin of the Indictum from much earlier times—that is, from Dagobert’s generosity. But we judge them to be as far from the truth as they are removed from Dagobert’s age, since Nangis testifies that he drew from an old parchment of Saint-Denis what he reports concerning this institution.
>
> Moreover, the bishop of Paris used to consecrate the fair of the Indictum by a solemn blessing when it was held in the open field. But after it began to be held within the town walls, the abbot or prior claimed this office for himself. Hence the distinction between the outer and inner Indictum. Parisian students flocked to these fairs, not without order and ceremony, their masters preceding them with the rector; and later, after they were instituted, with the procurators of the nations, the scribe, and beadles. Nor was anyone permitted to offer parchment for sale until the rector had approved it and selected the bundles necessary for the schools.]
