The king himself, with his own neck, in a flood of tears and with filial devotion, carried his lords and patrons back to their place: the venerable silver shrines of their most sacred bodies, which had stood upon the principal altar throughout the time of the military assembly. There, while the brothers continually celebrated the most solemn offices of day and night, a great multitude of the most devout people and religious women had gathered, with manifold prayer, to support the army. The king rewarded them for these and other benefits bestowed at such expense, with many gifts of land and other advantages.

The German emperor, therefore, thus humbled by the event and declining from day to day, ended his life within the year, confirming the saying of the ancients: that no noble or ignoble disturber of kingdom or Church, because of whose cause or dispute the holy bodies are raised up, will survive a year, but will perish within it.

> [Note: Emperor Henry V died at Utrecht on the Rhine on 23 May 1125, in the forty-fourth year of his age.]

The king of England, aware of the German’s plot, since he had conspired with Count Theobald in making war upon King Louis, attempted, during the king’s absence, either completely to devastate or to occupy the adjoining March. But he was repelled by a single baron, namely Amaury of Montfort, a man most fierce in unceasing war, and by the valor of the army of the Vexin; achieving little or nothing, disappointed in his vain hope, he withdrew.

By this act France, in the memory of our own age and not even in the antiquity of many ages, did nothing more illustrious, nor displayed the glory of its power more splendidly through the combined strength of its members, than when, at one and the same time, it triumphed, though the king was absent, over the Roman emperor and the king of England. Thereafter the enemies’ pride was crushed; the land was quiet before him; and almost all the enemies whom he could reach voluntarily returned into favor and gave the right hands of friendship. Thus he who denies what is just gives everything to one who bears arms.

> [Note: “Nor.” Thus all manuscripts. The edition has “or.”]
>
> [Note: “Combined.” Thus four manuscripts. The edition has “assisting.”]

(1121.) In that same favorable season, Aimeric, bishop of Clermont in Auvergne [Col. 1323A], a man of honorable life and an eminent defender of the Church, himself assailed and driven out by the new and ancient arrogance of the Auvergnats—of whom it is said,

> “The Auvergnats dared to feign themselves brothers of the Latins”—

fled to the lord king and laid before him the Church’s tearful complaint: that the count of Auvergne, William, had occupied the city and, through the treachery of his dean, had fortified the episcopal church of blessed Mary with much tyranny. Falling at the king’s feet, he implored him to rescue the enslaved Church from further enslavement and to restrain the unbridled tyrant by the sword of royal majesty.

The king, as he was accustomed most readily to help churches, gladly but at great expense undertook God’s cause. Since he could not correct the tyrant by words or by the seal of his majesty [Col. 1323B], he hastened to action, gathered military forces, and moved a large French army into rebellious Auvergne. When he approached Bourges, the chief men of the kingdom—the warlike count Fulk of Anjou, the mighty count Conan of Brittany, the excellent count William II of Nevers, and many other magnates of the realm—met him with a great military force, as vassals bound to the kingdom, hastening to avenge upon the Auvergnats the injury done to Church and kingdom.

> [Note: “At Bourges.” Thus all manuscripts. The edition has “at Bourges” in a different form.]

Devastating the enemy’s land, they drew near Clermont. The Auvergnats entrusted themselves to the defense of the city, because it was exceptionally well fortified, abandoning their very strong mountain castles. The French, wisely mocking their simplicity and delaying their advance toward the city so that the enemy must either abandon the city lest they lose the castles, or remain and meanwhile consume their provisions, turned aside to a most excellent castle called Pont on the river Allier. Pitching tents all around, they plundered plains and heights alike. They seemed in their giant-like audacity to reach the sky as they seized the most fortified mountain summits, driving off not only herds of animals but also a superfluity of human cattle. Applying siege engines to the tower of that castle, they compelled the defenders, by the force of millstones and a rain of arrows, to surrender after great slaughter.

When the men holding the city heard this, struck with fear and expecting something similar or worse, they prepared flight, left the city [Col. 1323D], and abandoned it to the king’s discretion. The king, victorious in every respect, restored the Church to God, the towers to the clergy, and the city to the bishop, after confirming peace between them and the count by oaths and a multitude of hostages.

But when five years had passed (1126), the recurrent faithlessness of the counts of Auvergne brought back the bishop’s and Church’s calamity; he brought the renewed complaint to the king [Col. 1324A].

> [Note: Since this second expedition of King Louis into Auvergne followed the first after five years had already elapsed, and since Charles, count of Flanders, who was killed on 2 March 1127, took part in it, the first expedition must be assigned to 1121 and this one to 1126.]
>
> [Note: In Freher: “treachery.”]

The king, indignant that he had been so exhausted by fruitless labor, gathered at once a much larger army and returned to the land of the Auvergnats. Now heavy in body and weighed down by the mass of his fleshy bulk, although any other man, even with so grave and dangerous a bodily infirmity, would neither wish nor be able to ride, he, contrary to the dissuasion of his friends, was carried along with wonderful spirit. What even young men dreaded, he endured—the summer heats of June and August—and mocked those unable to bear the heat, although he often had to be supported by the very strong arms of his men in narrow marshy places.

> [Note: Alternatively, “any [woman]”; “dangerous [condition].”]
>
> [Note: In four manuscripts: “of many.”]

In his expedition were the very powerful count Charles of Flanders, Count Fulk of Anjou, the count of Brittany, the army of Normandy tributary to Henry, king of England, many barons and magnates of the realm—men sufficient even to subdue Spain. Passing through the difficult approaches of Auvergne and the castles that opposed him, he reached Clermont. When he brought his army against Montferrand, a castle rising before and opposite the city, the soldiers charged with defending it, fearing the marvelous French army unlike their own and marveling at the brightness of the sun reflected from hauberks and helmets, stood rooted by the mere sight. Rejecting the outer refuge, they scarcely even withdrew into the tower and its defensive enclosure.

> [Note: “Abortive.” Thus all manuscripts and the edition. Perhaps one should read *ab ortivo*, as from *ortus*, “the east,” that is, “eastern,” as Freher notes.]
>
> [Note: Four manuscripts have “they withdrew themselves for themselves”; but in Royal manuscript 5925 the word “there” has been restored.]

Fire, devouring in flames the houses of the abandoned refuge, reduced to ashes everything except the tower and its enclosure [Col. 1324C]. On the first day, because the town was burning fiercely in the sudden conflagration, we pitched our tents outside; on the next day, when the flames had died down, we returned inside.

> [Note: Alternatively, “within”; “they returned.”]

Early the next morning the king both distressed them and encouraged us by this single act. Since all night long they had not ceased to harass our tents, which were nearer to the tower on one side, with much fighting and many flights of arrows and javelins—so much so that, after armed guards had been placed between us and them, we had to be covered by shields—he instructed Amaury of Montfort, a soldierly man and excellent baron, to set an ambush for them from the flank and ensure that they could not return unharmed to the enclosure.

> [Note: “Of Montfort.” Thus all manuscripts. The edition has “from.”]
>
> [Note: The manuscripts have *intemtoriis* and *intemptoriis*; perhaps for *intentamentis*, “among the encampments,” as Freher has.]

Skilled in such matters, Amaury took up arms in the camp and, with the speed of horses, while our men impeded them, unexpectedly intercepted some of them from the flank [Col. 1324D] and quickly sent them to the king. When they begged urgently to ransom themselves at a great price, he ordered them to be mutilated and sent back inside to their comrades, bearing maimed fists in place of fists. Terrified by this, the others thereafter left us in peace.

While the construction of machines and engines was delayed, all Auvergne lay open to the army’s will and discretion [Col. 1325A]. Duke William of Aquitaine arrived, supported by an Aquitanian army. When, having pitched camp in the mountains, he saw the French ranks gleaming in the plain, he marveled at the army’s great size and regretted having come in his inability to resist [alternative reading: “to suffer shipwreck”]. Sending peaceful envoys to the king, he came to speak to him as to his lord, making this address:

> “Your duke of Aquitaine, lord king, wishes you much prosperity and the possession of every honor. Let not the exalted royal majesty disdain to accept the service of the duke of Aquitaine and preserve for him his right. For as justice requires service, so it also requires rightful lordship. Since the count of Auvergne holds Auvergne from me, and I hold it from you, if he has committed any offense, I have him to present to your court under your command. We have never prevented this; we now offer it likewise and humbly beg that you accept it. And lest Your Highness deign to doubt this, we are ready and have ready many sufficient hostages. If the magnates of the kingdom so judge, let it be done; if otherwise, ‘as’ [the text breaks off].”

> [Note: In Freher: “We are ready and have ready.”]
>
> [Note: These words concerning the authority of the royal court over the greater vassals of the realm deserve notice.]
>
> [Note: This punctuation is that of the manuscripts. Perhaps one should read, as Freher has: “as they shall judge concerning these matters.” Thus, therefore, the king, etc.]

Therefore the king, taking counsel with the magnates of the kingdom, as justice dictated accepted the duke’s pledge, oath, and sufficient hostages; restored peace to the country and the Church; fixed a day at Orléans for proceedings between them, in the presence of the duke of Aquitaine—which they had hitherto refused to do—and, gloriously leading the army back into France, returned victorious.

Nobly was it done—an act more distinguished than any he performed from his youth [Col. 1325C] to the end of his life. [Note: *Sua* (“his”) is absent in four manuscripts.] To avoid tedium, although the matter requires much, we have resolved to recount briefly not how, but what he did. (A.D. 1127.) The renowned and most powerful Count Charles, son of the king of the Danes and of the maternal aunt of Lord King Louis [Note: Charles was born to Canute IV, king of Denmark, and Adela, daughter of Robert the Frisian and Gertrude of Saxony. Gertrude had previously married Count Florentius I of Holland, by whom she bore Bertha, Louis’s mother.], having succeeded by the strongest right of kinship to Count Baldwin, son of Robert of Jerusalem, governed the very populous land of Flanders as vigorously as he did diligently: an illustrious defender of God’s Church, conspicuous for generosity in almsgiving, and a distinguished guardian of justice.

As one bound by the honour he had received [Note: Freher reads “by the debt” (*debito*).], he suitably sought before the judgment of his court satisfaction from certain men humble in birth but exalted in wealth, who proudly endeavoured to remove themselves from the reach of his lordship on the ground of kinship (for they were of the dregs of servile [Col. 1325D] condition). They—the provost of the Church of Bruges, namely, and his associates, men most proud and notorious traitors—laid most cruel snares for him. Accordingly, when one day (2 March) he had come to Bruges and, early in the morning, was attending the church of God, he lay prostrate on the pavement, [Col. 1326A] praying with a book of prayers in his hand. Suddenly one Burchard, nephew of the aforesaid provost, a savage henchman, with others from the same most criminal stock and other accomplices in the basest treachery, moved stealthily behind the praying man—indeed, one silently speaking with God—and, cautiously drawing his sword, very gently [variant: very lightly] touching the count’s neck as he lay on the ground, so that when it was raised a little it might unexpectedly meet the assailant’s sword, struck him with the blade. In one blow the impious man most wickedly beheaded the pious; the servant, his lord.

Those who stood by as accomplices in the impious murder, thirsting for his blood, rejoiced to tear the innocent man to pieces, like dogs raging over abandoned corpses. They gloried exceedingly that they had been able to complete [Col. 1326B] the grief which they had conceived and the iniquity which they had brought forth. Adding iniquity to iniquity, blinded as they were by their own malice, they butchered, unprepared and unconfessed, in the most wretched manner of miserable death, any castellans or more noble barons of the count whom they could attack, whether in that church itself or outside in the castle. Yet we judge it greatly beneficial to these men that they were found praying in church when they were slaughtered for loyalty to their lord, since it is written: “Where I find you, there I shall judge you.” [Note: These words do not occur in Holy Scripture.]

The fierce men buried the count in the church itself, lest he be mourned and buried honourably outside, and lest the devout people, stirred by his glorious life and still more glorious death, be incited to avenge him. Making the church itself [Col. 1326C] a den of thieves, they fortified both it and the count’s house adjoining the church; and, having prepared every sort of provision, they resolved in their utmost arrogance both to protect themselves there and to draw the land to their side.

Therefore, stunned by horror at so great and so criminal a deed, the barons of Flanders who had not consented to it [Note: “Had consented.” Thus all the manuscripts; the edition has “had assented.”], while paying tearful funeral rites, avoided the stigma of treachery by reporting this to their lord King Louis—and not to him alone, but, as rumour spread, to the whole world. The king, stirred to avenge so great a betrayal both by love of justice and by kinship, was detained neither by the war of the king of England nor by that of Count Theobald. Boldly entering Flanders in a burning desire to destroy the wicked men most severely, he exerted every effort of mind and action.

[Col. 1326D] He installed as count of Flanders William the Norman, son of Robert of Jerusalem, count of Normandy—for the succession belonged to him by right of kinship. [Note: William was the son of Robert, duke of Normandy; through his father he was grandson of Matilda, wife of William the Great, or the Conqueror, and daughter of Baldwin V, or the Pious, count of Flanders. Among several rivals he had Thierry of Alsace, to whom the county of Flanders belonged by a stronger right of kinship. For Thierry was born of Thierry of Alsace, duke of Lorraine, and Gertrude, daughter of Robert the Frisian and aunt of Baldwin VII, whom Charles had succeeded immediately. Indeed, the wishes of Flanders’ prelates and nobles inclined toward Thierry; but Louis’s authority intervened, and William the Norman’s cause prevailed. The king thus intended to compensate William for the duchy of Normandy, of which he had been deprived.]

When he came down to Bruges, fearing neither the barbarity of the land nor the foul kinship-line [Col. 1327A] of the traitors, he hemmed in the traitors themselves, besieged in church and tower. He prohibited food supplies other than their own [Note: “Other than their own.” Thus all the manuscripts, that is, supplies stored in their possession. Or perhaps one should read: “He prohibits supplies other than those …,” as in Freher.], which by God’s dispensation resisted even their use to their disadvantage. When for some time he had worn them down by hunger, pestilence, and the sword, they abandoned the church and held only the tower, so that the tower might hold them. Now despairing of life, when their harp had already been turned to mourning and their organ into the voice of weeping, the most wicked Burchard, escaping with his companions’ consent, sought to leave the land [variant: Flanders], but could not, hindered by his own iniquity alone. Having returned to the stronghold of a certain friend and intimate, he was seized by royal command and, after an exquisitely devised form of miserable death, bound high upon a wheel and exposed to the rapacity of ravens and other birds. His eyes were gouged out from above, [Col. 1327B] his whole face torn apart, and his lower parts pierced a thousand times with arrows, lances, and javelins. He was most miserably killed and thrown into a sewer.

But Bertold, the head of wickedness, having likewise resolved to flee, wandered about freely enough here and there; then, returning through pride alone—for he said, “Who am I, or what am I?” [Note: “Am” is absent from three manuscripts. In its place, outside the parentheses, they read *suis*, that is, “by his own people” or “with his own people.” We conjecture that copyists read *sum* in place of *cum*. Freher has “I did.”]—he too was captured. Handed over to the king’s judgment, he was condemned to a deserved and most miserable death. Suspended on a gibbet with a dog, whenever the dog was struck it turned all its rage upon him, devouring his whole face by chewing [variant: biting]; sometimes even, horrible to say, it defecated. [Note: Freher reads: “even upon him.”] Thus he ended his wretched life with an everlasting death—more wretched than the most wretched man.

Those whom he had shut up in the tower he compelled, by many hardships [Col. 1327C] to surrender; one after another he threw them down before their companions with their necks broken. One of them also, named Isaac, had been tonsured in a certain monastery through fear of death; having stripped him of monkhood, he fastened him to a gallows.

Having thus won the victory at Bruges, the king hastened with his men to Ypres, an excellent castle, in order also to take vengeance upon William the Bastard, a supporter of the treason. [Note: This William, called of Ypres, was the illegitimate son of Philip, second son of Robert the Frisian, here mentioned. Robert of Jerusalem’s widow strongly supported his aspiration to the county of Flanders.] He drew the people of Bruges to his side by threats and inducements, sending them messengers [Note: Freher: “He draws them into an alliance.”]. While William met him with three hundred knights, one part of the royal army attacked him, while another boldly seized the castle obliquely through another gate. Having retained it, the king expelled William, disinherited by all Flanders; and because he had aspired through treason to possess Flanders, he deservedly obtained nothing in all [Col. 1327D] Flanders. Flanders thus washed, and as it were [Col. 1328A] rebaptized, by these and various modes of vengeance and by the shedding of much blood, and Count William the Norman installed, the king returned victoriously to France with God’s aid (A.D. 1128).

But he also performed another comparable, God-pleasing, and on another occasion celebrated act of vengeance, when he swiftly extinguished in a strong hand, like a smoking firebrand, the utterly depraved Thomas of Marle, who was boring into God’s Church and reverenced neither God nor man (A.D. 1130). Compelled by the plaintive lament of the churches, when he had arrived at Laon to exact vengeance, it was decided, by the counsel of bishops and the leading men of the realm—and especially by that of the distinguished Count Ralph of Vermandois, who after the king was more powerful than the others in those regions—that an army should be led against Coucy. [Note: Ralph had urged this expedition upon King Louis not only to avenge the injuries of the Church of Laon but also his own: for his brother Henry, count of Chaumont in the Vexin, had been treacherously killed at Thomas’s command.]

As the king hurried [Col. 1328B] toward the castle, those sent to reconnoitre a suitable approach reported that it was wholly unsuitable and inaccessible; and since many pressed him to alter his plan in accordance with their report, “The king,” it is said, “indignant in his own courage, declared: ‘This plan was settled at Laon. What was there resolved we shall change neither for death nor for life. The splendour of royal majesty would deservedly be cheapened if we were mocked as men who fled in fear of a criminal.’” Having said this, with remarkable spirit—though heavy in body—he penetrated with his army through steep ground and paths blocked by woods, dangerously though it was. When he had come near the castle, the valiant Count Ralph was informed that, from another side of the castle, an ambush was being prepared for the wandering army and that their ruin was being pressed most urgently.

Immediately armed, Ralph made for the place by a shady way with a few companions. Seeing that some of his knights, sent ahead, had already struck the man and that he had fallen, he spurred his horse, charged him, and boldly struck him with his sword, inflicting a mortal wound—one which, unless prevented, he would have repeated. Thomas was captured, wounded unto death, and presented to King Louis; by the king’s command he was carried to Laon, to the praise of almost all, both his own people and ours. On the following day, after his open land had been made public property [Note: That is, as it seems to us, his fields were transferred to the public domain or fisc. Here *terra plana* means cultivated land; *publicare* means to assign to the fisc or confiscate.] and his ponds breached, the lord king Louis returned to Laon, sparing the land because it had a lord. He could not compel this utterly depraved man—by wounds, prison, threats, or entreaty—to release the merchants whom he held in prison after treacherously stripping them, while under safe-conduct, of all they possessed.

After he had taken a wife by royal permission, he seemed more distressed at the loss of the payments demanded from the merchants than at the loss of his life. When, almost forced to death by the extremely severe pain of his wounds, he was urged by many to confess and receive viaticum, he scarcely consented. But when the body of the Lord had been carried in the priest’s hand into the chamber inhabited by that wretched man, it was as though the Lord Jesus himself could in no way endure to enter the most miserable vessel of a wholly unrepentant man. As soon as that villain raised his neck, he immediately twisted it back broken and breathed out his foulest spirit, deprived of the divine Eucharist. [Note: “In the year 1130 Thomas of Marle, treacherously seizing merchants under his own safe-conduct, was attacked by King Louis with an army; wounded and captured by Count Ralph of Vermandois in vengeance for his brother Henry, he died at Laon.” From the appendix to Sigebert. The Chronicle of Saint-Médard records Thomas’s death in the same year. Nangis, however, wrongly places it in the year 1120.]

The king, disdaining further to pursue either the dead man or the dead man’s land [Note: *Aut* (“or”) is read in four manuscripts and is absent from the edition.], extorted from his wife and sons the merchants’ liberation and the greater part of his treasures. Peace having been restored to the churches by the tyrant’s death, he returned victoriously to Paris.

At another time also (A.D. 1127 or 1128), when a major dispute concerning the seneschalship had arisen between the lord king and the distinguished Amalric of Montfort, instigated by Stephen of Garland, and was supported by the aid both of the king of England and of Count Theobald, the king swiftly laid siege to the castle of Livry. Erecting siege engines and attacking repeatedly with frequent assaults, he captured it most forcibly. And because the distinguished count and his close kinsman Ralph of Vermandois, most prompt in attack with a crossbow-bolt, had lost an eye, he utterly destroyed the very strong castle. He afflicted them also with so great a war that they renounced, under a sound peace, both [Col. 1329C] the seneschalship and the inheritance of the seneschalship. [Note: The edition reads “to him” (*ei*); four manuscripts read “and” (*et*).] [Note: Stephen of Garland, archdeacon of the Church of Paris, dean of Orléans, burdened with other ecclesiastical benefices, and moreover chancellor of the kingdom, was not ashamed to succeed his brother William, who died in 1120, in the seneschalship. All religious men viewed with indignant astonishment the assumption by one devoted to sacred affairs of an office utterly at variance with his profession. When, about 1127, Queen Adelaide—whom he had offended—secured his expulsion from court, Stephen transferred the seneschalship, which he regarded as inherited by right, without consulting the king, to Amalric of Montfort, who had married Agnes, daughter of Stephen’s brother Ansel. This caused Louis’s anger and the wars between him and Amalric. When these were at last brought to rest, as Suger relates, both Stephen and Amalric returned to the king’s favour no later than 1130.]

In that war the king himself, a military man ever ready against enemies, was pierced through the leg by a crossbow-bolt. Though severely wounded, he made light of it with great courage, and, as if the throne of royal majesty disdained the pain of a wound, sternly endured the suffering as though he did not endure it.

[Col. 1330A] At that time (A.D. 1130), the Roman Church was struck most grievously, almost to its very heart, by a dangerous schism. When the supreme pontiff and universal pope Honorius, of venerable memory, had entered upon the way of all flesh [Note: Honorius died on 14 February 1130; this is agreed by all. Scholars disagree, however, whether Gregory was appointed to succeed him that day or the next. Fulk of Benevento and the Chronicle of Monte Cassino support the first view; the authority of the anonymous annalist of Margam Abbey, published in the Oxford collection, vol. II, supports the second. Pagi considers this author to have recorded most accurately both the date of Gregory’s election and that of his consecration. His words for 1130 are: “In this year, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, Pope Honorius died at Saint Gregory’s; and on the next day, that is, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of the same month, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, was elected to the apostolic office and was called Innocent. On the sixth day, namely on the Saturday following next, that is 22 February, he was ordained priest, on the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter; and on the next day he was consecrated supreme pontiff at Santa Maria Nuova. On that same day Peter Leo was consecrated to the apostolic office at Saint Peter’s.”], the senior and wiser members of the Roman Church had agreed that, in order to prevent tumult in the Church, a solemn election should be held at Saint Mark’s—and nowhere else—and jointly, according to Roman custom.

But those who, through continual attendance and intimacy, had been closest to the pope, did not dare to gather there for fear of the rioting Romans. Before the pope’s death was publicly announced, they elected as supreme pontiff the venerable person Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo. Those favouring the party of Peter Leo, meanwhile, summoned others to Saint Mark’s in accordance with the agreement; once they learned of the pope’s death, they enthusiastically elected that same Peter Leo, cardinal-priest, by the consent of many bishops, cardinals, clerics, and Roman nobles. Thus, establishing a ruinous schism and tearing apart the seamless tunic of Christ the Lord, they divided God’s Church. And while each party relies upon itself as a great judge, they draw persons away from one another, bind one another with anathema, and heed no judgment but their own.

Since Peter Leo’s party prevailed through the support both of his relatives and of the Roman nobility [Note: Three ancient manuscripts—Saint-Germain, Saint-Denis, and Reg. 5925—read “of Rome.”], Pope Innocent resolved to leave the city with his followers, in order that he might succeed in gaining the world. Going down under naval protection to the regions of Gaul, he chose as a safe and tested refuge, after God, for the defence of his person and Church the most noble kingdom of the Franks. Sending messengers to King Louis, he urgently requested aid for himself and for the Church.

The king, being a most devout defender of the Church, was quickly moved. He summoned at Étampes a council of archbishops, bishops, abbots, and religious men [Note: The Council of Étampes, held in April 1130, submitted the whole dispute concerning the two elections to the judgment of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. Bernard, already committed to Innocent’s party, pleaded for him with such force of eloquence that he persuaded everyone that Innocent should be regarded as the legitimate pope. The principal arguments on which his speech rested, apparent from his various letters, were these: although Innocent had been elected by a smaller part of the cardinals, secretly and without the others, he had been elected by the sounder party; and he was far superior to Anacletus in character and learning. The seeming haste of Innocent’s election, moreover, had been caused by Peter Leo’s ambition, since he was openly grasping for the pontificate. To this it was easy to reply that votes in elections ought not to be counted but weighed, and that the ambition of one man could not deprive the larger number of electors of their voting right. Yet we judge that it occurred through divine providence that Peter Leo, a man abandoned to luxury and negligent in divine matters, was deprived of the Roman see; he appeared all the less fit to discharge its offices properly in proportion as he sought it more ardently.]. Investigating by their counsel the person rather than the election—for amid every disturbance caused by the riotous Romans, the Church’s election may often be conducted less regularly—he gave his assent to the election on the counsel of these men [Note: Thus, without addition.] and promised thereafter to uphold it.

When he had delegated to us at Cluny the first fruits of his reception and service, they, cheered by such support, conveyed through us their thanks to the lord king with grace and blessing, and returned home. When Innocent came as far as Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire, the lord king met him with the queen and his sons. Bowing his noble head, often crowned with a diadem, as before Peter’s tomb, he prostrated himself at Innocent’s feet and promised him and the Church a Catholic devotion and the effective fulfilment of devoted service.

Following his example, Henry, king of England, met him at Chartres; most devoutly prostrate at his feet, he promised a willing reception of him and his followers in his land and the full measure of filial obedience. Visiting the Gallican Church as circumstances required, Innocent then passed into the regions of Lorraine. Emperor Lothair met him at Liège in the most solemn fashion, attended by a great assembly of archbishops, bishops, and nobles of the German kingdom. In the square before the episcopal church, offering himself most humbly as his *strator*—that is, attendant leading the horse—he hastened to the pope’s feet through the midst of the holy procession. With one hand he took the staff for defence, and with the other the bridle of the white horse, and led him as his lord. As the entire station descended, he conveyed him while supporting him, and made the loftiness of his [Col. 1331C] fatherhood known to those familiar and unfamiliar alike.

With the peace of Empire and Church thus joined, Innocent desired to celebrate the approaching holy Easter at our church of blessed Denis, as with a special daughter. Receiving him gladly on the day before the Lord’s Supper, out of fear of God and of the Church, mother and daughter, we conducted a most solemn procession before God and men and embraced his arrival, rejoicing in songs of exultation [perhaps *collaetantes*, “rejoicing together”]. Thus, after the Lord’s Supper had been celebrated among us in the Roman manner and with the costly gift called the *presbyterium*, he observed the venerable Passion of the Lord with due veneration and kept vigil through the night before the most holy Resurrection with fitting honour.

Early in the morning he passed by an outer way, almost secretly, to the church of the martyrs along the road, with a large company of attendants. There, preparing themselves in the Roman fashion and arraying themselves with abundant and wonderful ornament, they placed upon his head the Phrygian imperial ornament, like a helmet encircled with a golden band. They led out the pope riding a white, caparisoned horse; themselves likewise caparisoned, riding horses variegated with white coverings, they proceeded in doubled festive ranks, singing songs. The feudal barons of our church and the noble castellans, most humble *stratores* on foot, led him as he rode by the bridle. Some forerunners scattered a great quantity of coin to clear away the obstructing crowd. The Royal Road gleamed with willows and fixed posts adorned with precious hangings.

As squadrons of knights and a great throng of people came to meet him most honourably, even the blinded Synagogue of the Parisian Jews was present. Offering the letter of the Law—namely, a veiled scroll—it obtained from his lips this prayer of mercy and piety: “May almighty God remove the veil from your hearts.” [Col. 1332B] Arriving at the basilica of the saints, gleaming with golden crowns and flashing with the brilliance of silver, gold more than a hundredfold, precious gems, and pearls, he celebrated the divine rites divinely and, cooperating with us, offered the most holy victims of the true Paschal Lamb.

After Mass had ended, hangings were raised in the cloister and tables laid; reclining as though upon couches, they consumed the material lamb and received the remaining dishes of the noble table in the customary manner. On the following day they likewise returned the procession from the church of Saint Remigius to the principal church. When three days after Easter had passed, he crossed to Paris with thanksgiving and promises of aid and counsel. Thereafter, visiting the churches of Gaul and supplying from their abundance the deficiency of his own poverty, after travelling for some time by land, he chose to stay at Compiègne.

Meanwhile (A.D. 1131), an exceptional and thereafter unheard-of misfortune befell the kingdom of France. King Louis’s son Philip, a handsome and charming boy, the hope of the good and terror of evildoers, was riding one day through a suburb of Paris. His horse, startled by a devilish pig crossing its path, fell heavily; and its most noble young rider, thrown down upon the paving stones and grievously crushed beneath its weight, was left almost dead. [Note: King Philip was crowned on Easter Day, 14 April 1129, and died on 13 October 1131, at approximately sixteen years of age.] The city and all who heard of it were overwhelmed by grief—for on that day he had summoned an army for an expedition. Shouting, weeping, and wailing, they gathered up the tender boy, nearly dead, and carried him into the nearest house. As night approached, alas for grief, he breathed his last.

No Homer himself could adequately tell how great and astonishing was the grief and mourning that afflicted his father and mother and the leading men of the kingdom. After he had been buried in royal manner in the church of blessed Denis, in the tomb of the kings, on the left side of the altar of the Holy Trinity, amid a great gathering of bishops and nobles of the realm, his wise father, after mournful lamentations and miserable imprecations against his own surviving life, permitted himself to be consoled by the counsel of religious and wise men.

We who were his intimates and familiar associates, fearing that the constant burden of his weakened body would bring on a sudden collapse, advised him to establish alongside himself as king his son Louis, a most handsome boy, crowned with the royal diadem and anointed with the sacred oil, in order to repel the disturbances of rivals. Yielding to our counsel, he came to Reims with his wife, son, and the magnates of the realm. There, in the full and most solemn council which Pope Innocent had convened, he provided the realm with a fortunate successor, raised to kingship by the anointing with holy oil and the bearing of the royal crown. [Note: Louis the Younger was anointed on 25 October 1121.] Hence many people thought, as though by some presage, that his power ought to be enlarged, since he received the abundant blessing of so many and such great and diverse archbishops, bishops, Franks, Germans, Aquitanians, English, and Spaniards.

When the father, relieving the grief for the dead by joy in the living, returned to Paris, the lord pope, after dissolving the council, chose to remain at Auxerre. Finding an opportunity to return home through the company of Emperor Louis [read: Lothair]—for he had promised to bring him by force to Rome and depose Peter Leo—he went there with him. [Col. 1333B] [Note:

In attempting to describe Innocent II’s journey in Gaul, several knots present themselves which can scarcely be untied. Ancient accounts of his acts, cited by Baronius under 1130, no. 56, and Anselm of Gembloux in his *Chronicle*, attest that he set out by ship from Pisa and landed at the port of Saint-Gilles. “Having crossed the sea,” says the latter, “he at last landed at Saint-Gilles.” “Then he was received by the people of Arles,” are the words of Orderic Vitalis, book XIII, p. 895, “and from there sent envoys to the Franks.”

From Arles he came to Avignon, whence he wrote an apostolic brief to William, lord of Montpellier, dated at Avignon, the ninth day before the Kalends of April, in the first year of our pontificate (*GARIEL*, *Series of the Bishops of Maguelonne*, p. 170). Hence it is clear that Innocent reached the shores of Gaul much earlier than shortly before August, as Pagi thinks. Proceeding onward, the already-cited acts say, he entered the borders of Auvergne by way of Viviers and Le Puy, and first held a council at Clermont. But before reaching the borders of Auvergne, Anselm of Gembloux teaches us that he had arrived at Cluny in Burgundy, adding immediately after the words just quoted: “Afterward he came into Burgundy and was received at Cluny.”

In what month he visited this monastery, and what the pope did there, we learn from his charter issued at Valence, the eighth day before the Ides of March, 1132, and reproduced in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 1381: “We ourselves visited that monastery of Cluny, which belongs especially to the right of Saint Peter and of the Holy Roman Church; and on the same day on which, after the passage of many years, our predecessor Pope Urban of happy memory had consecrated there the high altar, with the archbishops and bishops who had assembled with us, and through the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit, we solemnly dedicated that same monastery.” But the high altar of the church of Cluny has been shown above to have been consecrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, or 25 October; therefore the dedication of the basilica occurred on that recurring day.

Orderic, in the passage already cited, records the days Innocent remained there: “Then,” he says, “the Cluniacs kept the pope and his companions for eleven days.” Leaving Cluny, the pope went to Clermont, stopping meanwhile at Roanne on the Loire, where he issued a charter in favour of Drogo, abbot of the monastery of Saint John of Laon, dated at Roanne on the day before the Nones of November (*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. X, Instruments, col. 194). At last entering Clermont, he held a council there at the end of November. Once it was concluded, he wrote an apostolic brief to Guilencus, bishop of Langres, to settle the dispute between the abbots of Saint Stephen of Dijon and Saint-Seine concerning two churches, dated at Clermont on the third day before the Nones of December (*PERARO*, p. 103).

[Col. 1334B] So far, reader, this sequence of the journey seems to proceed well. But two documents especially disturb it. The first, copied by Mabillon (*Annals of the Benedictine Order*, vol. IV, Appendix, p. 654, no. 26) from an autograph, is a record of Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, concerning the excommunication and absolution of the count of Ramerupt. It is dated in the year of the Incarnate Word 1123, indiction VIII, in the twenty-second year of the reign of Louis, most glorious king of the Franks, the first year of his son Philip, and the fifth year of our archiepiscopate—that is, of Rainald of Reims. These chronological indications agree completely with one another, provided that the year of the Incarnation 1129 is understood in the old style, that is, as 1130 before Easter. The record further reads: “When Pope Innocent was at Laon, the count of Ramerupt presented himself before him.”

What then? Was Innocent at Laon before Easter 1130—that is, before 30 March—when on the twenty-fourth day [Col. 1334C] of that same month he had not yet left Avignon? This surely exceeds all credibility. The other document creates no lesser difficulty: namely, Innocent’s charter for the monastery of Fos in the province of Arles, dated at Saint-Gilles, the third day before the Ides of November, indiction VIII—that is, in the first year of his pontificate, as Mabillon rightly interprets it (*Annals of the Benedictine Order*, vol. VI, p. 186). From his letters, we saw above that the pope had departed Saint-Gilles before 24 March; yet this new charter represents him as staying there on 2 November of the following month. Truly, here we need, to speak with Plautus, an Oedipus as interpreter—one who interpreted the Sphinx.]

Be that as it may, let us trace Innocent’s journey after the Council of Clermont, whose date cannot be moved. What places he visited on his way to Fleury, on what day he arrived there, and how long he stayed, is unknown to us. When he had proceeded thence to Orléans, Geoffrey of Chartres came to meet him and led him into his own city. Leaving Chartres, he turned aside to Étampes, and was lodged in the nearby monastery of Morigny, where he dedicated the high altar on 20 January 1131 (Gallia Christiana, new ed., vol. XII, col. 179). From there he directed his route to Liège, intending to greet Emperor Lothair, and there, on 22 March, held a council of thirty-six bishops, the emperor and his wife being present.

“Before he came to Liège, however, he turned aside to Lobbes, where he was honorably received, with a great gathering of neighboring abbots and certain bishops who had come there with him; he celebrated Mass at the altar of St. Peter and addressed the brethren in chapter” (*Spicilegium*, quarto ed., vol. VI, p. 619).

“Returning from Liège into Gaul, he came to Paris. He was then received at St. Denis on the day before Maundy Thursday [15 April]; after spending the days following Easter there, he returned to Paris.”

Nor should the Chronographer of Morigny be heeded when he writes that, after returning from Liège, Innocent stayed a long time at Auxerre and then went on to Tours in order to win over Geoffrey Plantagenet, count of Anjou, before coming to Paris. Certainly all this, as Mabillon observes (*Annales Benedictini*, vol. VI, p. 198), could scarcely have occurred after the council at Liège, held in mid-Lent, so as to allow the pope to be present at St. Denis in due time to celebrate Easter.

From Paris Innocent went to Rouen. From that city he wrote to Abbot Suger, confirming the privileges and possessions of St. Denis:

> Given at Rouen . . . on the seventh Ides of May, indiction IX, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1131, in the second year of the pontificate of lord Pope Innocent II.  
> (*Félibien, History of St. Denis*, p. 98)

Leaving Rouen, he went to Beauvais, as is testified by the diploma in which he confirmed Henry, king of England’s gift of one hundred marks of silver to the monastery of Cluny:

> Given at Beauvais, in the year 1131, on the Kalends of June.  
> (*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 1393)

After visiting various churches, especially those of Noyon and Laon, he chose, according to Suger, to remain at Compiègne until the Council of Reims, which he opened on 19 October [Col. 1335D]. When the council had been dissolved eleven days later, he went to Auxerre and stayed there until the following year. A diploma by which, at Abelard’s request, he received under apostolic protection the possessions of the convent of nuns of the Paraclete in the diocese of Troyes shows that the pope was in that city toward the end of November:

> Given at Auxerre . . . on the fourth Kalends of December, indiction X, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1131, and in the second year of the pontificate of lord Pope Innocent.  
> (*Bulaeus, History of the University of Paris*, vol. II, p. 127)

He left Auxerre in January 1132, intending to return to Italy, and reached the monastery of Cluny on the Kalends of February, as he himself writes in a letter to King Louis given at Cluny on the fourth Nones of February (*Councils*, vol. X, p. 955). He had not yet left there on the tenth of that month, when he gave a letter to Stephen, abbot of the Cistercians, forbidding any bishop or archbishop to compel abbots of the Cistercian Order to attend a council or synod except on a matter of faith:

> Given at Cluny, on the fourth Ides of February [Col. 1336B], indiction X, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1132, and in the second year of the pontificate [Col. 1336C] of lord Pope Innocent II.  
> (Manrique, *Annals of the Cistercians*, under 1132, ch. 1)

When he subsequently arrived at Lyons, he issued there a rescript whose conclusion reads:

> Done at Lyons, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1132, and in the second year of the pontificate of lord Pope Innocent II.  
> (*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 1394)

Therefore, as Pagi observes, this was before 16 February, when he entered the third year of his pontificate.

“Proceeding thence to Valence, where Pagi shows from letters given by him there that he remained from 22 February to 16 March (under 1132, no. 11), he descended to Saint-Gilles and, by way of the mountain of Geneva [the text reads *Genuae*],” says the anonymous writer cited by Baronius, “entered the borders of Lombardy; and, after celebrating the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection at Asti, came to Piacenza.”

But although he had made him Emperor Augustus, he could not obtain peace while Peter Leonis lived, because the Romans resisted. But when Peter Leonis had been removed from the scene, peace having been restored to the Church, by God’s help, after long instability and protracted, almost wasting sicknesses, the lord pope with happy success ennobled the most holy chair by the merits of his life and office.

Now King Louis, weakened somewhat by the burden of bodily heaviness and the continual strain of his labors, as is the way of human nature, was failing in body, though not in spirit. Yet if anything troublesome to royal majesty arose anywhere throughout the kingdom, he would by no means allow it to pass unavenged. For even at sixty years of age [Note: [Col. 1336C] The St. Germain manuscript reads “fifty years of age,” through a copyist’s error.] he possessed such knowledge and energy that, if the constant inconvenience of his overgrown body did not stand in his way [Col. 1335B], he would have crushed every enemy everywhere by overcoming him.

Hence he often lamented with inward groans: “Alas,” he said, “for the wretched condition that scarcely, if ever, allows knowledge and ability to coexist! For if I had known when young, or if now in old age I could act, I would most effectively have subdued many kingdoms.”

Yet, weakened by that bodily burden [Note: [Col. 1336C] The St. Germain and St. Denis manuscripts read “weakened,” *debilitati*.], even while most rigidly confined to bed, he resisted the king of England, Count Theobald, and everyone else so vigorously that all who saw him and heard of his distinguished deeds proclaimed the nobility of his spirit and lamented the weakness of his body.

Harassed also by this affliction, when, in a campaign against Count Theobald, his leg injured and himself scarcely able to be carried, he had caused Bonneval [Note: [Col. 1336C] Royal MS 6265: “the monastery of Bonneval.” [Col. 1336D] St. Denis MS: “Benis-vallis”; Royal MS 5925: “Bonavallis,” Bonneval.] to be burned, except for the monks’ cloister which he protected; and when on another occasion, though absent, he had through his men destroyed Château-Renard, a fief of Count Theobald; in the final expedition which he undertook, with a most noble army he destroyed by fire the castle of Saint-Brice on the Loire, because of its rapacity and its plundering of merchants, and compelled both its tower and its lord to surrender.

On his return from that expedition, at the new castle of Mont-Treherii [Note: [Col. 1336D] Thus four manuscripts. Félibien interprets that new castle of Mont-Treherii, together with the French Chronicles of St. Denis, as the castle of Mont-Tricard; but the readings formerly customary on the anniversary of Louis’s death, and composed from Suger’s own words, give “the new castle of Mont-Eherii.” We frankly admit that we are at a loss here. For the direct route from Saint-Brice to Paris does not pass through Mont-Tricard; indeed, it would be a very great detour. It is highly probable that the sick prince returned home by a shorter route. Should not “the new castle of Mont-Treherii” rather mean Châteauneuf-sur-Loire, to which the king was carried by boat and from which he could readily reach Paris? Or perhaps the castle commonly called Triguaire, not far from Château-Renard, for no more direct road leads to Paris from Saint-Brice? This is conjecture.] he began to suffer severely from a copious diarrhoeal discharge, as he had sometimes suffered before.

Being prudent in counsel, provident for himself, compassionate toward his own soul, and pleasing to God, he made provision for himself through the devotion of frequent confession and prayers. With all his heart he desired one thing above all: somehow to be conveyed to the holy martyrs, his protectors Dionysius and his companions; and there, before their most sacred bodies, to lay aside kingdom and crown, exchanging crown for crown, royal insignia and imperial ornaments for the humble habit of blessed Benedict, and to profess the monastic order.

Let those who disparage monastic poverty observe how not only archbishops, but kings themselves, preferring eternal to transitory life, flee in the greatest security to the singular protection of the monastic order.

As from day to day he was disturbed by severe diarrhoea, he was afflicted by so many and such troublesome physicians’ draughts and by the taking of various most bitter powders to check it [Note: [Col. 1337D] “Was infected,” *infectabatur*. Thus three manuscripts: St. Denis, St. Germain, and Royal MS 6265. The other Royal manuscript, with the edition, has “is afflicted,” *infestatur*.], that even healthy and strong men could not have endured them. Yet amid these and similar troubles, gracious toward all through an innate sweetness, he spoke kindly to everyone, admitted everyone, and soothed everyone, as though he suffered no discomfort.

Therefore, worn down by the most painful force of the flux and the long exhaustion of his emaciated body, disdaining to die meanly or unexpectedly, he summoned religious men, bishops and abbots, and many priests of the Church. Casting aside every shame out of reverence for the Godhead and the holy angels, he sought to make confession openly and most devoutly, and to fortify his passing with the most certain viaticum of the Lord’s body and blood.

While they hastened to prepare this, the king himself unexpectedly rose and prepared himself. Clothed, and to the wonder of all, he came out of his chamber to meet the body of the Lord Jesus Christ and stood by most devoutly. There, before all alike—clerics and laity—he divested himself as king, laid aside his kingdom, confessed that he had governed the kingdom sinfully, and invested his son Louis with the ring. He bound him by faith to protect God’s Church, the poor, and orphans; to preserve to every person his right; and to seize no one in his court unless that person committed an offence there in person (in 1137).

There also, distributing for the love of God to churches, the poor, and the needy gold and silver, desirable vessels, tapestries and tapestry-covered quilts, and every movable thing that he possessed or that was used in his service, he spared neither cloaks nor royal garments, down to his shirt. His precious chapel, a most precious cloth of gold and gems [Col. 1337C], a golden censer weighing forty ounces, candlesticks of one hundred and sixty ounces of gold, a chalice most costly in gold and most precious gems, ten precious silk copes, and a most precious hyacinth of his ancestress, daughter of the king of the Ruthenians [Note: [Col. 1337D] *Atavae*. Thus four manuscripts; the edition reads “Anne.” We may believe Suger means Anne, wife of King Henry and grandmother of Louis the Fat, who gave this hyacinth to her husband, King Henry, a nephew of the church of the holy martyrs. [Col. 1338D]]—this he delivered from his own hand into ours, directing that it be set in the Lord’s crown of thorns [Note: [Col. 1338D] This does not mean the entire thorn-crown of Christ, which is demonstrably known to have been brought into Gaul only in the following century, but merely a portion of it, taken by Charles the Bald from the treasury of the chapel at Aachen and given to the church of the holy martyrs.], and sent it to the holy martyrs through us; he most devoutly vowed that he would follow them if he could possibly do so.

Thus relieved of these things and filled with God’s mercy, kneeling humbly before the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ—which those who had just celebrated Mass had devoutly brought to him there in procession—he broke out in this utterance of true and Catholic confession, of mouth and heart, not as an unlettered man but as a most learned theologian:

> “I, Louis the sinner, confess one true God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and one person of this holy Trinity, namely the only-begotten Son of God the Father, consubstantial and coeternal with him, incarnate of the most holy Virgin Mary, who suffered, died, and was buried; who rose on the third day, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father, and will judge the living and the dead at the last and great judgment.
>
> “And we believe that this Eucharist of his most sacred body is that same body which was assumed from the Virgin and which he entrusted to his disciples for their being bound together, united, and abiding in him. And we firmly believe, and confess with mouth and heart, that this most sacred blood is that same blood which flowed from his side as he hung on the cross. We desire that our departure be fortified by this most certain viaticum and defended, against every power of the air, by the surest protection.”

Then, to the wonder of all, after first making confession of his sins and most devoutly communicating in the body and blood of Jesus Christ, he returned to his chamber as though beginning immediately to recover. Rejecting every display of worldly pride, he lay down upon a simple linen quilt.

When he saw me, in human fashion, grieving for one so great reduced to so little, one so exalted made so humble, he said: “Do not grieve for me, dearest friend; rather, rejoice exultantly that God’s mercy has granted me, as you see, to prepare for his coming.”

As he gradually began to recover strength, he descended, by whatever conveyance he could use, near Melun on the River Seine. From castles and villages, leaving their ploughs behind, most devoted people to whom he had preserved peace came down to meet and accompany him along the road, commending his person to God. And so, out of love for the holy martyrs whom he desired to visit and thank [Col. 1338C], he arrived with all speed and, God granting it, came to them on horseback.

He was received by the brethren and almost the whole country, as a most pious father of the Church and noble defender, with solemnity and utmost devotion. Prostrating himself most humbly before the most holy martyrs, he tearfully rendered the vowed and devoted thanksgivings for benefits bestowed, and most humbly entreated them to provide for him thereafter.

When he had arrived at the castle of Béthisy, messengers of William, duke of Aquitaine, quickly followed him, announcing that the duke, having set out on pilgrimage to St. James, had died on the road; but that before undertaking the journey, and also while dying on the journey, he had decided and left that his most noble daughter, the young woman named Eleanor [otherwise Aanor], should be married, and that she should retain and govern all his land.

Having taken counsel with his household, the king, with his customary magnanimity, gladly accepted what was offered. He promised that she should be joined in marriage to his beloved son Louis, and thereafter prepared a noble array to be sent there. He gathered an army of five hundred or more knights, chosen from the best men of the realm [Col. 1339A], and appointed over it Count Palatine Theobald and the eminent count of Vermandois, his kinsman Ralph [Note: [Col. 1339C–D] Ralph was the son of Hugh the Great, brother of King Philip.]. He joined to them us, his household officers, and all those whom he could find of sounder judgment.

Thus, as he took leave of his son at his departure, he said: “May the mighty right hand of almighty God, through whom kings reign, protect you and yours, dearest son. For if I should lose you and those whom I send with you through any misfortune whatever, I should care neither for myself in person nor for the kingdom.”

Also assigning abundant treasures and a sufficient store of wealth, he enjoined by royal authority—without hesitation—that a welcome daily allowance [Note: [Col. 1339D] The four manuscripts read “a welcome,” *gratam*; the edition has “welcome,” *gratum*.] be provided from the royal treasury for the army, lest they plunder anywhere in the whole duchy of Aquitaine, injure the land or the poor of the land, or make friends into enemies.

When we had reached the territory of Bordeaux through the region of Limoges, we pitched our tents before the city, the great River Garonne lying between us. There we waited and crossed to the city with naval assistance, until, on Sunday, the leading men of Gascony, Saintonge, and Poitou having assembled, he joined the aforesaid young woman to himself in marriage, crowned with the royal diadem. Returning through the district of Saintonge, overthrowing any enemies there were, we reached the city of Poitiers amid the rejoicing of the whole land.

At that time the summer heat raged more harmfully than usual; exhausted by its wasting force, we were somewhat weakened and greatly worn down. When King Louis, at Paris [Col. 1339C], was most severely afflicted by a recurring dysenteric flux, he was utterly failing. Never improvident in such matters, he summoned the venerable Stephen, bishop of Paris, and the religious Gilduin, abbot of St. Victor, to whom he made more intimate confession because he had built his monastery from its foundation. He repeated his confession and most devoutly sought to fortify his death with the viaticum of the Lord’s body.

As he was having himself carried to the church of the holy martyrs in order humbly to fulfil the vow he had so often made, he was overtaken by the urgency of illness; what he could not accomplish in deed, he fulfilled in heart, mind, and will. Therefore he ordered a carpet to be laid on the ground and ashes to be placed upon it in the form of a cross. Laid there by the hands of his attendants, fortifying himself with the sign of the holy cross, in the thirtieth year of his administration of the kingdom and about the sixtieth year of his life, on the Kalends of August, he breathed out his spirit [Note: [Col. 1339D] That is, in the year of Christ 1137, to which all historians assign his death. If one subtracts from that year-number the sixty years which Suger attests Louis lived, the year of his birth will be 1077, not 1081, as Lisiard, bishop of Soissons, incorrectly asserts in the Life of his predecessor St. Arnulf, in these words: “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1340C] 1081, the future King Louis was born, obtained by the prayers [Col. 1340D] and merits of St. Arnulf; and may he, in order to attain a good end, be aided by the intercessions of that same saint!”].

When at that same hour his body, wrapped in precious silk, was carried for burial to the church of the holy martyrs, and men had gone before to prepare the place of burial, one event occurred which does not seem worthy of being passed over in silence. For when the aforesaid king, in conversation with us, sometimes—or perhaps often—spoke about the burials of kings, he used to declare that the man was blessed who deserved to be buried between the most sacred altars of the Holy Trinity and of the holy martyrs, because he would obtain forgiveness of sins both through the intercession of the saints and through the prayers of those who came there. By this very statement he silently indicated his own wish [Col. 1340B].

Before the king and his son departed, we had arranged with Hervey, the venerable prior of the church, for his burial before the altar of the Holy Trinity, opposite Emperor Charles’s tomb, with the altar between them. But the place was occupied by the burial of Carloman, king of the Franks [Note: [Col. 1340D] “Burial”: St. Germain manuscript; omitted in the edition and the other manuscripts.], and because neither law nor custom permits kings to be dislodged, what we had proposed could not be done.

But in the very place which he had, as if by some presentiment, preferred, they searched contrary to everyone’s expectation—for everyone thought the spot blocked—and found a space reserved exactly, neither more nor less, suited to the length and breadth of his body [Note: [Col. 1340D] St. Germain manuscript: “they found,” *repererunt*.]. There, laid down with a multitude of prayers and hymns, and with a most solemn and devout royal funeral office, he awaits fellowship in the resurrection to come [Col. 1340C], nearer in spirit to so great a company of holy spirits because in body he lies buried close to the holy martyrs, ready to receive their intercession.

> Blessed is he who, while the world’s ruin totters,  
> could know beforehand the place where he was to lie.

May the Redeemer himself, through the intercession of the holy martyrs, raise up his soul, most devoted to those martyrs, and deign to place it among the saints—Jesus Christ our Lord, who laid down his life for the salvation of the world, who lives and reigns, King of kings and Lord of lords, through all ages of ages. Amen. [Note: [Col. 1340D] Royal MS 6265: “Here end the deeds of Louis, king of the Franks, surnamed the Fat.”]

[Col. 1341]

# THE LESSONS BEGIN FOR THE ANNIVERSARY OF KING LOUIS

(Martène, preface to vol. IV of the *Amplissima Collectio*, p. XXXVI.—The Benedictine authors of *Literary History of France* attribute this Legend to Suger. See above, col. 1186.)

## MARTÈNE’S NOTICE

. . . But since some mention has here arisen of the kings of France, it seems not inappropriate to add a few words, as it were incidentally, about their anniversaries. First, we observe that at their nocturnal vigils the last three lessons from their lives were recited. This is especially inferred from an old customary book of St. Denis in France, in which, among the various rites for the anniversary of King Dagobert, the following is found:

> For each nocturn the treasurer shall provide two priests, who shall incense the altars, the king’s tomb, and the community, and shall provide the three final lessons from his Life.

Likewise, in a very ancient manuscript of the same monastery, an abridged Life of Louis VI, surnamed the Fat, to be read at the third nocturn on the day of his anniversary, is found with this title: “Lesson VII begins for the anniversary of King Louis.” Although this rite may now seem unusual and wholly unused, it was then no less fitting than those funeral orations for princes which today are customarily delivered in the very midst of the sacred mysteries, and which are ordered for this sole purpose: that everyone present may be stirred to entreat divine mercy for the deceased prince.

On the second anniversary day of King Dagobert, the monks of St. Denis sang not only, as customary, Vespers together with nocturnal vigils and Lauds, but also the other daytime hours: Prime, Terce, Sext, None, second Vespers, and Compline. They retain this practice even now, along with many others, not without praise. And lest anyone suppose that we have asserted without grounds what we just said about the reading of the Life of King Louis VI on his anniversary, it is useful to set out here the lessons themselves from a manuscript of St. Denis.

## LESSON SEVEN

[Col. 1341A] Therefore the glorious and renowned king of the Franks, Louis, son of the magnificent King Philip, a noble scion of the ancient kings Charlemagne and other more illustrious rulers—as imperial charters themselves attest—clung to the holy martyrs and to their church at Saint-Denis with such great and almost native affection that, throughout his life, he continued the friendship toward their church, innate in him from childhood, through much liberality and honor. At the end, placing his highest hope in them after God, he most devoutly resolved to entrust himself to them body and soul, so that, if it could be done, he might become a monk there.

After thirty years’ administration of the glorious kingdom of the Franks, distinguished defence of the churches, and continual protection of the poor and orphans [Col. 1341B], he was, as is the way of human nature, somewhat weakened by the burden of bodily heaviness and the continual strain of his labors, failing in body though not in spirit. Yet if anything troublesome to royal majesty arose anywhere throughout the kingdom, he would by no means allow it to pass unavenged. For at sixty years of age he possessed such knowledge and energy that, if the constant inconvenience of his overgrown body had not stood in his way, he would have crushed every enemy everywhere by overcoming him. Hence he often lamented with inward groans: “Alas,” he said, “for the wretched condition that scarcely, if ever, allows knowledge and ability to coexist. For if I had known when young, or if now in old age I could act, I would most effectively have subdued many kingdoms.”

[Col. 1342A] Yet, though weakened by that bodily burden, even while most rigidly confined to bed, he resisted the king of England, Count Theobald, and everyone else so vigorously that all who saw him and heard of his distinguished deeds proclaimed the nobility of his spirit and lamented the weakness of his body. Harassed also by this affliction, when, in a campaign against Count Theobald, with his leg injured and himself scarcely able to be carried, he had caused Bonneval to be burned, except for the monks’ cloister which he protected; and when on another occasion, though absent, he had through his men destroyed Château-Renard, a fief of Count Theobald; in the final expedition he undertook, with a most noble army he destroyed by fire the castle of Saint-Brice on the Loire because of its rapacity and its plundering of merchants, and compelled both its tower and its lord [Col. 1342B] to surrender.

On his return from that expedition, at the new castle of Mont-Eherii, he began to suffer severely from a copious diarrhoeal discharge, as he had sometimes suffered before. Being prudent in counsel, provident for himself, compassionate toward his own soul, and pleasing to God, he made provision for himself through the devotion of frequent confession and prayer. With all his heart he most ardently desired one thing: somehow to be conveyed to the holy martyrs, his protectors Dionysius and his companions; and there, before their most sacred bodies, to lay aside kingdom and crown, exchanging crown for crown and royal insignia and imperial ornaments for the humble habit of blessed Benedict [Col. 1343A], and to profess the monastic order. Let those who disparage monastic poverty observe how not only archbishops but kings themselves, preferring eternal to transitory life [Col. 1344A], flee in the greatest security to the singular protection of the monastic order.

## LESSON EIGHT

[Col. 1343]

[Col. 1343A] As day by day he was disturbed by the force of severe diarrhoea, he was afflicted by so many and such troublesome physicians’ draughts and by the taking of various most bitter powders to check it, that even healthy and strong men could not have endured them. Yet amid these and similar troubles, gracious toward all through an innate sweetness, he spoke kindly to everyone, admitted everyone, and soothed everyone, as though he suffered no discomfort.

Therefore, worn down by the most painful force of the flux and the long exhaustion of his emaciated body [Col. 1343B], disdaining to die meanly or unexpectedly, he summoned religious men, bishops and abbots, and many priests of the Church. Casting aside every shame out of reverence for the Godhead and the holy angels, he sought to make confession openly and most devoutly and to fortify his passing with the most certain viaticum of the Lord’s body and blood.

As they hastened to prepare this, the king himself unexpectedly rose and prepared himself. Clothed, and to the wonder of all, he came out of his chamber to meet the body of the Lord Jesus Christ and stood by most devoutly. There, before clerics and laity alike, divesting himself as king, he laid aside his kingdom, confessed that he had governed the kingdom sinfully, invested his son Louis with the ring, and bound him by faith to protect God’s Church, the poor, and orphans; to preserve to every person his right; and [Col. 1343C] to seize no one in his court unless that person committed an offence there in person.

There also, distributing for the love of God to churches, the poor, and the needy gold and silver, desirable vessels, tapestries and tapestry-covered quilts, and every movable thing that he possessed or that was used in his service, he spared neither cloaks nor royal garments, down to his shirt. His precious chapel, a most precious cloth of gold and gems, a golden censer of forty ounces, candlesticks of one hundred and sixty ounces of gold, a chalice most costly in gold and most precious gems, ten precious silk copes, and a most precious hyacinth of his ancestress, daughter of the king of the Ruthenians—this he delivered from his own hand into ours, directing that it be set in the Lord’s crown of thorns [Col. 1344A], and sent it to the holy martyrs through us; he most devoutly vowed that he would follow them if he could possibly do so.

Thus relieved of these things and filled with God’s mercy, kneeling humbly before the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ—which those who had just celebrated Mass had devoutly brought to him there in procession—he broke out in this utterance of true and Catholic confession, of mouth and heart, not as an unlettered man but as a most learned [Col. 1344B] theologian:

> “I, Louis the sinner, confess one true God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and one person of this holy Trinity, namely the only-begotten Son of God the Father, consubstantial and coeternal with him, incarnate of the most holy Virgin, who suffered, died, and was buried; who rose on the third day, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father, and will judge the living and the dead at the last and great judgment.
>
> “And we believe that this Eucharist of his most sacred body is that same body which was assumed from the Virgin and which he entrusted to his disciples for their being bound together, united, and abiding in him. And we firmly believe and confess with mouth and heart that this most sacred blood is that same blood which flowed from his side as he hung on the cross [Col. 1344C]. We desire that our departure be fortified by this most certain viaticum and defended, against every power of the air, by the surest protection.”

Then, to the wonder of all, after first making confession of his sins and most devoutly communicating in the body and blood of Jesus Christ, he returned to his chamber as though beginning immediately to recover. Rejecting every display of worldly pride, he lay down upon a simple linen quilt. When he saw me, in human fashion, grieving for one so great reduced to so little, one so exalted made so humble, he said: “Do not grieve for me, dearest friend; rather, rejoice exultantly that God’s mercy has granted me, as you see, to prepare for his coming.”

## LESSON NINE
[Col. 1343D] As he gradually began to recover his strength, he made his way, by whatever conveyance he could, to the Seine near Melun. People came out and flocked together to meet him along the road; from castles and villages, leaving their ploughs behind, the most devoted populations—whose peace he had preserved—commended his person to God. And so, desiring for love of the holy martyrs to visit them and give thanks, he arrived with the greatest speed; by God’s gift he reached them on horseback. Received solemnly and most devoutly by the brethren and almost the entire country as the Church’s most loving [Col. 1344D] father and noble defender, he humbly prostrated himself before the most holy martyrs, and in tears rendered the prayers he had vowed and devout thanksgivings for benefits bestowed; and he most humbly implored them to provide for him henceforth.

When he had reached the castle of Béthisy, messengers of William, Duke of Aquitaine, swiftly followed him, announcing that the duke himself, having set out on pilgrimage to Saint James, had died upon the journey; but that, before undertaking the journey, and even while dying on the road, [Col. 1345A] he had resolved and directed that his most noble daughter, a young woman named Eleanor, should be married, and that all his land should remain hers. Having taken counsel with his household, he accepted the offer gratefully with his customary greatness of spirit, promised to unite her in marriage to his dearest son Louis, and then prepared a noble expedition to dispatch there. He assembled a most distinguished army of five hundred or more knights, chosen from the best of the realm; over it he appointed Count Theobald of Blois and his kinsman, the eminent Count Ralph of Vermandois. He also attached to them his own household and all whom he could find of sounder counsel. Thus, as his son departed, he bade him farewell: “May the mighty right hand of almighty God, through whom kings reign, protect you and yours, dearest [Col. 1345B] son; for if through any misfortune I were to lose you and those whom I send with you, I should care neither for my own presence in life nor for the kingdom.”

He also allotted abundant treasures and sufficient funds; and, lest they plunder anything throughout the whole duchy of Aquitaine, harm either the land or its poor people, or make friends into enemies, he solemnly charged them with royal authority not to hesitate to order a daily allowance for the army, agreeable and drawn from his own treasury. When we had passed through the region of Limoges and reached the borders of Bordeaux, we pitched our tents before the city, the great river Garonne lying between us, waiting there and crossing to the city by the aid of ships. [Col. 1345C] Then, on Sunday, with the leading men of Gascony, Saintonge, and Poitou assembled, he united the aforesaid young woman to himself in marriage, crowned with the diadem of the kingdom.

Returning through the district of Saintonge, overthrowing whatever enemies there were, we reached the city of Poitiers amid the rejoicing of the whole land. At that time the summer heat raged, more harmful than usual; weakened for some time and sorely worn out by its exhausting force, we were fatigued. When, as a result of this intolerable exhaustion, King Louis the lord was most severely afflicted at Paris by a recurrent diarrhoeal dysentery, he utterly failed. Yet he was never unprepared in such matters. Summoning the venerable Stephen, bishop of Paris, and the devout Gilduin, abbot of Saint-Victor—to whom he confessed more intimately because he had built [Col. 1345D] that monastery from its foundation—he made his confession again and strove with deepest devotion to fortify his departure with the viaticum of the Lord’s Body.

And when he had arranged to be carried [Col. 1346A] to the church of the holy martyrs, in order humbly to fulfil the vow he had so often promised, overtaken by the distress of his illness, he accomplished in heart, mind, and will what he could not accomplish in deed. He therefore ordered a carpet to be spread upon the ground and ashes to be placed on the carpet in the form of a cross. There, laid down by his attendants and fortifying himself with the sign of the holy cross, he yielded up his spirit on the Kalends of August [1 August], in the thirtieth year of his administration of the kingdom and about the sixtieth year of his age.

When, at that same hour, his body, wrapped in a precious pall, was carried to the church of the holy martyrs for burial, and those who were to prepare the burial-place had gone ahead, one occurrence took place which seems unworthy to pass over in silence. For when the aforesaid king had sometimes, indeed often, spoken with us concerning [Col. 1346B] the burials of kings, he used to declare blessed the man who deserved to be buried between the most sacred altars of the Holy Trinity and of the holy martyrs, since by the intercession of the saints and the prayers of those who came there he would obtain forgiveness of sins; by this very statement he silently indicated his own wish.

Before setting out with his son, we had provided with the venerable Hervé, prior of the church, for his burial before the altar of the Holy Trinity, opposite the tomb of Emperor Charles, with the altar between. But because the place of Carloman, king of the Franks, was occupied—and because neither right nor custom permits kings to be dispossessed of their lodging—what we had proposed could not be done.
