Yet, in the very place where he had, as it were prophetically, earnestly desired it, they searched contrary to [Col. 1346C] everyone’s expectation—for all believed the spot obstructed—and found a space reserved precisely suited, neither more nor less, to the length and breadth of his body. There, laid to rest in royal fashion amid a multitude of prayers and hymns, and the most celebrated and devout office for the dead, he awaits fellowship in the resurrection to come: nearer in spirit to so great a company of holy spirits, insofar as in body he lies buried closest to the holy martyrs, standing by to intercede.

> Happy he who, while the world’s ruin wavered,  
> Was able to know beforehand the place where he would lie.

May the Redeemer himself, through the martyrs’ intercession, raise his soul—most devout toward the holy martyrs—and deign to place it among the saints: Jesus Christ our Lord, who laid down [Col. 1346D] his soul for the salvation of the world, who lives and reigns, King of kings and Lord of lords, through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1347]

# Letters of Abbot Suger of Saint-Denis

To Pope Eugene III, King Louis VII, and other leading men of France; and letters to him, written concerning more serious affairs while he administered the kingdom. (A.D. 1147–1150.)

(Duchesne, *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. IV, p. 491, from a manuscript copy belonging to the illustrious Putean brothers. [Note: [Col. 1347B] The letters are prefaced by the following encomiastic poem:

### Verses in Praise of Abbot Suger

> Great Suger, Father, to whom the supreme height of merit  
> Gives the foremost place among the chief gods,  
> I offer you a poem newly drawn from the anvil;  
> I pray you, correct my writings with your file.  
>
> Though they be unpolished, though mean, though ill-arranged,  
> Yet, when you read them, you make them precious.  
> Therefore, I pray, hear my praises of your praise.  
> [Col. 1347C] My Muse urges me to praise you.  
>
> When Nature, mother of things, had created all things well,  
> She resolved to fashion you wondrously.  
> And whereas all else is fashioned from coarse material,  
> The goddess brought you forth from a nobler mass.  
>
> Long did the Artist’s reasoning remain uncertain  
> Whether to make you mortal or a god.  
> The material, powerful for the work, so suited either result  
> That from it a man or a god might be made.  
>
> And the goddess would have made a god, had not the heavenly ones forbidden it—  
> By whose counsel she does all that she does.  
> Indeed, they greatly feared that, were you wholly a god,  
> You would humble the other gods by working marvels.  
>
> At last, mingled with the envy of the gods, you are made both:  
> At once a half-man and a demigod.  
> Retaining with you half the substance in each nature,  
> You are neither man without god nor god without man.  
>
> From one part you desire divine things and deal in divine things;  
> [Col. 1348B] from the other you accomplish what belongs to man.  
> From your divine nature comes your painting in the Church  
> Of heaven and the gods of heaven.  
>
> From your human nature comes your defence of the realm by arms,  
> And the commonwealth is increased by your efforts.  
> Now, a demigod, you handle heavenly things in the temple;  
> Now, a man, you perform brave deeds in war.  
>
> Thus in each sphere you govern both the cause of man and that of God,  
> So that this matter accords with God, that with man.  
> While you govern the Frankish peoples with the king,  
> After the king, you hold the second sceptre almost as king.  
>
> [Col. 1348C] Never does the king accomplish anything great without you,  
> Nor do you accomplish anything great without the king.  
> So great is the harmony of action in you both  
> That neither differs from the other in what is done.  
>
> Each is so bound by love to the other  
> That one’s heart seems to hang upon the other.  
> Finally, mighty Rome, before whom the whole world bends,  
> Bends her proud neck to obey you.  
>
> Nor does she grant the great Caesars greater honour  
> Than she grants you, though enriched by Caesar’s gifts.  
> At your nod she binds and looses the guilty,  
> And does not permit him whom you justify to remain accused.  
>
> And, added to your titles, whatever you command in the city  
> Cannot long remain undone.  
> Thus king, thus Caesar, thus one among demigods,  
> Thus man, you strive to be a god greater than man.].—We have collated it with Bouquet’s edition.)

## Letter I. The Abbot of Clairvaux to Pope Eugene: In praise of Lord Abbot Suger

[Col. 1347A]

To his most beloved father and lord EUGENE, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, the little that he is.

If any vessel of honour from the great house of the great King is held in esteem in our Gallican Church; if anyone, like David, faithful in the Lord’s service both in going out and in coming in—then, in my judgment, that man is the venerable abbot of Saint-Denis. For I know the man: in temporal matters he is faithful and prudent; in spiritual matters fervent and humble; and in both—what is most difficult—he conducts himself without reproach. Before Caesar he is as one of the Roman court; before [Col. 1347B] God, as one of the heavenly court. We ask and earnestly entreat you graciously to receive the messengers of so great a man and, as befits you and as he is altogether worthy, to write back to him good and friendly words, full of familiarity and affection, favour and grace. For to love and honour his person in a special manner is to honour your own ministry. [Note: [Col. 1348C] Extract from Letter 309 of Saint Bernard.]

## Letter II. Pope Eugene to Suger: A Letter of Consolation

EUGENE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Concerning the death of our son John, your nephew, etc. See under Pope Eugene III, for the year 1153.

## Letter III. Ulger, Bishop of Angers, to Suger

Having announced the death of Peter, abbot of Bourgueil, he asks Suger to receive Peter’s successor Robert favourably.

To SUGER, by God’s election most reverend abbot of Saint [Col. 1348B] Denis, his dearest friend and lord, ULGER, by his permission—though unworthy—styled bishop of the Church of Angers: wholly his, offering the zealous service due in reverence, honour, and duty.

The noble Church of Bourgueil, situated in our bishopric, seated upon the estate and within the jurisdiction of the duke of Aquitaine, is known beyond doubt both to have been founded and to be supported almost solely by the benefactions of the dukes of Aquitaine. But this church, by God’s ordering, in whose hand are the death and life of men, was recently bereaved [Col. 1349A] and desolated by the ruinous misfortune and lamentable death of its lord abbot Peter, a great, venerable, and distinguished man. [Note: [Col. 1349D] “Bereaved …”: Peter, abbot of Saint Peter at Bourgueil, died on the eighth day before the Kalends of July [24 June] in 1148, as Mabillon thinks, *Annals*, vol. VI, p. 440. But since Ulger died in the same year, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November [17 October], according to the chronicle of Saint-Albin, this letter was certainly written in 1147 or 1148.]

Now the venerable and religious community of that place, to relieve so great a grief—and because these times, which would more properly be called tempests than times, threaten hardship, indeed the very worst afflictions, in our regions to holy places, especially those without protectors—assembled the brethren who had come, even from the remotest dependent houses, for the feast of that place, and hastened [Col. 1349B] to elect as father and shepherd one from the bosom of their monastery: Robert, a great man, whose conduct is proclaimed and held to be honourable, whose life commendable and religious.

They now come, namely the elected man and his electors, to the feet of your majesty, so that the elected may be presented to your favour, as he would be presented to the king were he present—the king to whom the duchy of Aquitaine has passed. King Louis, undertaking the celebrated pilgrimage, joyfully committed that duchy to your hands and treasury of wisdom, employing prudent counsel. We therefore, trusting in the excellence of your generosity, beseech your graciousness that, when they come to you, you receive them honourably and hear their petitions favourably; and that what you would do even unasked, you who stand in the king’s place [Col. 1349C] may perform in royal fashion, and send them back to us and to their own people in great joy. For we are wholly yours, and would serve you more willingly, if place and time allowed, than receive others’ services. We remember—and always shall remember—the benefits and honours which you have been accustomed most generously to bestow upon us. We pray for you at Mass before the Body of God and our Lord. Farewell, that we too may prosper.

## Letter IV. The Community of Bourgueil to Suger

They present to him, in the king’s absence, Robert, their abbot-elect.

To their venerable lord and father SUGER, by God’s grace and by his own merit abbot of Saint [Col. 1349D] Denis, the humble community of the Church of Bourgueil: greeting and the service of devotion.

Our revered father Peter, remembered not without groaning, having been taken from human affairs, our church has been ruinously bereaved. Since it could not remain long in its widowhood without diminution of its property—for the times are increasingly burdensome and dangerous—the brethren gathered universally for the feast of blessed Peter, [Col. 1350A] their patron. Taking wiser counsel, they discussed appointing a shepherd and elected, by unanimous election without any dispute, Brother Robert here present, a most honourable man whose life is proclaimed and held honourable among us. Therefore, since the king, undertaking his celebrated pilgrimage, has left ecclesiastical affairs in your hands, we present him to you as we would to the king were he present; and we humbly beg you to receive him graciously and honour him with the honour which such a great man deserves.

## Letter V. Suger to Ulger, Bishop of Angers

He gives his assent to the election of the community of Bourgueil, preserving the right of the crown, lest the Church of Bourgueil be troubled longer.

[Col. 1350B]

To Lord ULGER, venerable by God’s grace bishop of Angers, SUGER, by the same grace abbot of Saint Denis: devout prayers in Christ and the service of sincere devotion.

Having received the revered contents of your most welcome letter, we ought to have been moved so far—even had we been more unyielding—that we almost consigned to oblivion our duty toward the kingdom, which we wish faithfully to serve, and lent an ear to your pleasure. Therefore, unwilling that the Church of Bourgueil be troubled longer, yet unwilling that the dignity of royal majesty be diminished by doing the one and omitting the other, for the love of God, at your request—whom we greatly love—[Col. 1350C] and at the petition of the community of Bourgueil, we have given our assent to their election, reserving the right of the realm, on this condition: if anything in the matter has been done inadequately against the dignity of royal majesty, then, when God willing the lord king returns, they shall answer, just as if he were now present, before the judgment of his court, if it please him; or before us, who act in his place, should we wish to proceed against them concerning it.

## Letter VI. King Louis to Suger

He reports that he has safely reached the gates of Hungary and urges Suger to procure and send money.

LOUIS, by God’s grace king of the Franks and duke of Aquitaine, to his dearest SUGER, venerable abbot of Saint Denis: greeting and sincere affection.

[Col. 1350D] We write to you from the gates of Hungary. [Note: [Col. 1350D] “From the gates of Hungary”: King Louis entered Hungary in July and made the crossing there over fifteen days, as Odo of Deuil relates in Book II of *On the Journey of King Louis to the East*, p. 22.] Advancing straight to this place by divine direction, we and our princes have arrived joyfully, in complete safety, honour, and gladness. Everywhere, with the Lord aiding us, the princes of the lands come forth rejoicing to meet us, gladly receive us, willingly render service, and honour us devotedly. In all these things we bless the Lord, who has directed our feet and made our ways prosper.

Thereafter the state of affairs itself warns us—indeed, urges and reproves us—[Col. 1351A] to remember your admonition concerning the procurement of money to be brought after us for the needs of our expenses. While we were present, immense impediments of business prevented us from speaking and making arrangements with you as we should have done. But now, bearing heavy daily expenses, we turn to your proven fidelity, that with the charitable affection by which you always burn wholly for our honour in us, you may relieve our needs by aid that follows after us. How you are to do this—whether you send us money taken from ours or from yours—your discerning prudence knows better, judges more wisely, and can perform and determine better than our own foresight. For all that we have committed throughout the kingdom to your disposition and care, as if it were your own, is in your hand; and therefore your affection may fittingly do what we ask, whether from ours or yours, [Col. 1351B] because our necessity so requires. Farewell.

## Letter VII. Pope Eugene to Suger

EUGENE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your messenger and your letter, etc. See under Eugene, for the year 1153.

## Letter VIII. The Count of Anjou to Suger

He writes that he is barely recovering from a serious illness and cannot attend the meeting to be held with Suger at Beaugency.

[Col. 1351C]

To SUGER, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Saint Denis, GEOFFREY, duke of the Normans and count of Anjou: greeting, reverence, and service.

I do not wish your authority to remain unaware that I have suffered a most serious illness; but now, by God’s grace, as health returns, I am recovering. Therefore my friends, attending upon me and providing for my health, dare not advise me to undertake any great matter requiring negotiation. I therefore refer to you the conference which was to be held between us at Beaugency, since I could in no way attend it. For I do not at all expect to be fit for undertaking any long journey before Christmas.

## Letter IX. Count Ralph of Vermandois to Suger

He directs Suger to attend the assembly convened at the port of Verberie for peace in Beauvais, so that, returning thence to Paris, they may jointly discuss the affairs of Poitou.

[Col. 1351D]

To SUGER, by God’s grace abbot of Saint Denis, R. [Ralph], count of Vermandois: greeting.

The count of Anjou has postponed the conference. [Note: [Col. 1351D] “Has postponed the conference,” etc.: see the preceding letter.] You know that I have often laboured for peace in Beauvais, but have been unable to obtain it, and it is not readily at hand. If war prevails, unforeseen harm may result. But I am confident that, if your presence can be there, there will be peace. Therefore I direct you to come promptly on Sunday to the port of Verberie, where I have summoned them. Then, returning to Paris, [Col. 1352A] we shall hasten with you to the king’s affairs. There we shall also discuss together the words of the messengers from Poitou.

## Letter X. Count Theobald to Suger

He asks Suger to come and meet him at Corbeil.

To SUGER, by God’s grace abbot of Saint Denis, his dearest friend, THEOBALD, count of Blois: greeting and blessing [perhaps: affection].

I wish you to know that I shall shortly go into the country of Chartres. Therefore I direct you [Col. 1352B] to send Baldwin of Corbeil to meet me at Roset on New Year’s Day; he will accompany me. On the following Friday I shall lodge at Corbeil. [Note: [Col. 1351D] “On Friday”: in 1148, New Year’s Day, reckoned from the Kalends of January, fell on Thursday. Therefore this letter was written near the end of 1149.] And I ask you to come to meet me at Corbeil on that Friday, so that I may see you there and speak with you. Farewell.

## Letter XI. Count Ralph of Vermandois to Suger

He asks on what day Suger wishes to come to Paris to speak with Samson, archbishop of Rheims, concerning knights captured by Ralph’s brother.

To SUGER, by God’s grace abbot of Saint Denis, his lord, R., count of Vermandois: greeting.

The archbishop of Rheims, Samson, sent me word through the bishop of Soissons, Goslen, that he will come [Col. 1352C] to Paris on the fourth day after Christmas and will speak with his brother concerning the captured knights, and will do all in his power. And since perhaps he cannot come before Monday, [Note: [Col. 1352D] “Before Monday”: in 1147 Monday was the fourth day after Christmas; therefore this letter seems to belong to 1147.] send me word on what day you wish me to come, whether Sunday or Monday.

## Letter XII. Hugh of Lusignan to Suger

[Note: [Col. 1352D] Hugh VII of Lusignan went to Palestine in 1147 and is believed to have died on that expedition.]

He asks Suger to give complete credence to Wiormand, whom he sends to him, and to write back through the same man concerning the affairs of Poitou.

To his venerable friend and lord SUGER, abbot of Saint Denis, H. [Hugh] OF LUSIGNAN: greeting and the bond of heartfelt affection.

Faithfully obeying in all things especially your affection and your commands, we send to your presence Wiormand, faithful to us and to you. [Col. 1352D] Give him complete credence faithfully, and kindly write back to us through him, as becomes so great a friend, concerning the affairs of Poitou, with the vigour and prudence which distinguish you.

## Letter XIII. Manasses, Bishop of Orléans, to Suger

To SUGER, venerable abbot of Saint Denis, his lord and friend, MANASSES, by God’s grace humble minister of the Church of Orléans: greeting.

Because divine providence has placed the kingdom of the Franks under the direction and [Col. 1353A] protection of your judgment, as is fitting, we rejoice not a little. Therefore, when we departed from your presence on account of the necessity of our causes and proceeded to the lord pope, we entrusted our affairs with great confidence to your guardianship and the protection of your affection. Meanwhile, during the Advent season, certain of our parishioners violently and unjustly seized the property of Bernard, our liege man, who does not evade justice in our court. With the Lord’s assistance we shall take fitting counsel concerning them.

But, as has been reported to us, you compel the aforesaid Bernard, who holds from our fief, to come into suit in your court; though he firmly promises to carry out in our court whatever justice shall prescribe. We therefore kindly ask [Col. 1353B] your prudence not to trouble our liege man, whom we know to be just, on this account, and that we may have you as a ready helper and friend against the aforesaid plunderers concerning the injury they have inflicted.

## Letter XIV. Suger to the Chapter of Chartres

He sends envoys to them, bereft of their shepherd, to receive and preserve the regalian rights in the king’s name.

SUGER, by the grace of God abbot of Saint Denis, to the venerable chapter of the Church of Chartres: greeting and affection.

Your discretion knows that Louis, glorious king of the Franks and our dearest lord, undertaking his renowned pilgrimage for the love of God, entrusted to us the care of administering his kingdom by the counsel of archbishops, [Col. 1353C] bishops, and the leading men of the realm, and not without the lord pope’s assent. Since it is our duty, by reason of our office, diligently to seek out and faithfully preserve what belongs to the kingdom, we appoint the bearers of this letter as our messengers on the lord king’s behalf, to receive and preserve the regalian rights, asking you to assist them faithfully, as loyal subjects of the realm, in matters where assistance is required, until divine mercy comforts your Church—bereft of so great and glorious a shepherd—with a worthy successor through the customary procedure. [Note: [Col. 1353D] “Bereft of its shepherd,” etc.: Geoffrey, who, according to the necrology of the Church of Chartres, died on the ninth day before the Kalends of February [24 January] in 1148, is to be understood as having died in 1149, as we prove thus. Among the documents in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 331, one reads a charter for the monastery of Josaphat beginning: “In the year in which Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, died, when fourteen days had elapsed after his death—namely, in the year from the Incarnation of the Word 1148—William of Mécherol and his wife Itta, in the second week of March, the third week of Lent, on Thursday [Col. 1354D] of that same week,” etc. But in 1149, not 1148, the second week of March was the third of Lent, since in 1149 the first Sunday of Lent fell on 20 February. Therefore the second week of March was the third week of Lent; this cannot be said of 1148.]

For the more diligently it strives for the enlargement of the eternal kingdom, the more especially does it deserve to have its own wholly preserved for itself.

## Letter XV. The Community of Saint-Riquier to Suger

They ask him to confirm the election of Arnulf, prior of Corbie, as abbot of Saint-Riquier in Ponthieu.

[Col. 1353D]

To the most reverend lord and friend SUGER, abbot of Saint Denis, the entire community of Saint-Riquier [Col. 1354A] in Ponthieu: greeting and every due reverence.

We wish your fatherhood to know that all of us—the whole community of the monastery of Saint-Riquier at Centula—by the counsel and assent of religious persons and certain of our men, have canonically elected as our shepherd and abbot Lord Arnulf, prior of the church of Corbie, a most religious and honourable person, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. [Note: [Col. 1354D] Gelduin, abbot of Saint-Riquier at Centula, had gone to Jerusalem in 1147, apparently after resigning his office.] We therefore earnestly entreat your discretion not to allow the liberty and integrity in the election of our abbots, which we have hitherto possessed for the dignity of our Church from our lord Louis, king of the Franks, and from his predecessors, to be shaken or disturbed by any suggestion of evil [Col. 1354B] men. Rather, for God’s sake and ours, support and confirm our elected man with your great counsel and aid; through him, with God’s help, we hope that the calamity of our Church may be relieved. Farewell.

## Letter XVI. The Bishop of Orléans to Suger

To SUGER, by God’s grace reverend abbot of Saint Denis, and to RALPH, count of Vermandois, MANASSES, by God’s patience humble minister of the Church of Orléans: greeting and service.

We have learned that the misfortune of the murder of William of La Chambre, which recently occurred among us—that [Col. 1354C] his murderers, fleeing in fear of death to God’s church, the refuge of sinners, were violently dragged from it, where they clung both to the cross and to the image of the Crucified One, and were afterward committed to prison in a tower—has reached the ears of your highness. We, indeed, together with the whole city of Orléans, were most deeply moved, as was fitting, by so great and sacrilegious a violation of God’s church; and because they had been seized in defiance of God and the Church’s honour, we demanded that they be surrendered to us. When we could by no means obtain this, we placed the city under interdict, by the counsel of religious men. Yet it has pleased you, as we hear, to order their removal from there.

It does not seem to us that the interdict which we imposed upon the city by counsel should be lifted without the greatest deliberation while those prisoners remain in custody. There is also one matter by which both we and the whole city are utterly terrified and disturbed: that, on the very day when they were removed from the city, something happened among us by God’s hidden judgment. An image situated at the head of our church, fixed to a cross behind [Col. 1355A] a certain altar not far above the ground, was seen to weep, in the presence and sight of many clerics and laypeople. Tears were seen to drip and flow from its eyes, and from the ninth hour until midnight the abundance of tears did not appear to cease. Know that we have received this report from most honourable men who saw it.

Whether this happened because the sins of the people or our own sins demanded it, we do not know. Yet many judge that the miracle signifies the grief and sorrow of God’s Church, because it could not preserve in its bosom those prisoners and sinners who had taken refuge with her. Whatever the occasion of it may have been, we, who cannot neglect what belongs to our office, entreatingly beseech [Col. 1355B] your prudence to ensure that what was wrongly done in God’s Church be corrected by the counsel of your discernment, so that due and fitting reverence may be shown to her, and that the city, which grieves and suffers with its weeping mother, may be released from the bond of interdict.

## Letter XVII. Count Ralph of Vermandois to Suger

He writes that he has come to Rheims to the pope concerning his own affairs and those of the countess of Flanders; he then excuses his absence and asks to know Suger’s wishes.

To SUGER, by God’s grace abbot of Saint Denis, R. [RALPH], count of Vermandois: greeting.

Let your prudence know that I have come to the apostolic lord at Rheims, and that the countess of Flanders brought me here concerning her business; [Note: [Col. 1355D] Countess of Flanders: Sibylla, while her husband was travelling among the crusaders, administered the county of Flanders. “Meanwhile Baldwin, count of Hainaut,” says Lambert of Wattrelos under the year 1147, “broke the treaty made between himself and the count of Flanders, and devastated everything with arms, plundering, and slaughter. But when the countess of Flanders strove with many prayers to recall him from such conduct and could not obtain it, she at last, having been delivered from the childbirth which was imminent, raised arms against him, restrained and put him to flight, and afflicted Hainaut with many disasters.” But she seems first to have presented [Col. 1356D] her complaint at the council held at Rheims by Eugene III in mid-Lent, 1148.] and there we are discussing both her business and mine. Know also that the lord [Col. 1355C] pope and the whole court show me a good and cheerful countenance, but I do not at all know what they intend to do with me. [Note: [Col. 1356D] Ralph was then bound by the sentence of excommunication for repudiating his wife and taking Petronilla, sister of the queen of the Franks, as another wife, as Odo of Deuil testifies: “Yet I do not know whether Count Ralph, since he was then excommunicated, ought to be excluded from fellowship in our discourse,” etc.]

I know this for certain: my affair will never have a good outcome except through you. I had already received leave from the lord pope, but he himself detains me. Therefore, if it pleased you to conduct or postpone affairs at Paris, I should greatly wish it, and it would be good. For I do not know when I shall be able to come away from the court. But if it pleases you that I come to you, abandoning all else I shall come quickly. Therefore write to us your wish in everything, for whatever you command me, I shall do.

## Letter XVIII. The Countess of Nevers to Suger

She asks that a certain sum of money be restored to a man of Auxerre, which Geoffrey the Fat of Étampes and his brother Ralph refused to pay.

[Col. 1355D]

To her lord and friend SUGER, by God’s grace abbot of Saint Denis, I., countess of Nevers: greeting and service.

[Col. 1356A] Your prudence is not unaware that I have remained under your protection. For my lord is in the service of God and of the king; if anyone wrongs me or the men who belong to the protection of my husband, it concerns him. A man of the city of Auxerre complains concerning certain men of Étampes, Geoffrey the Fat and his brother Ralph, who owe him ten and a half pounds in Orléans currency and refuse to pay. When the lord king ordered that this money be paid, they likewise scorned his command. Therefore I ask you, as I would my lord, to have it restored. Send me word what you intend to do in this matter. The sureties for this money are Harduin, Felperius, and Jachelin.

## Letter XIX. The Dean and Chapter of Chartres to Suger

They ask him, acting in the lord king’s place, to approve the election of Goslen as bishop of Chartres and restore the regalian rights.

[Col. 1356B]

To their dearest lord and friend SUGER, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Saint Denis, R. [ROBERT], humble dean, and the whole chapter of the Church of Chartres: abundant greeting and affection in the Lord.

Your discernment, dearest lord, should know that, having received from you royal permission in the king’s stead, we assembled in our chapter on the appointed day; and, after invoking the grace of the Holy Spirit, by equal vote and unanimous consent we chose as bishop for ourselves and our Church our lord Goslen, our archdeacon [Col. 1356C], a man indeed generous, suitable, and learned. The religious men—the abbots who were present—approved this choice, while all the people applauded and gave thanks to God for the election of such a person, who is believed to be useful to the Church and faithful to the kingdom. We therefore ask your affection, most dear to us, that you may deign to give assent to this our election, which, as we believe, has been made by the Lord, and which we have taken care to present to you both orally and in writing; and that, in the king’s stead, you may restore the regalian rights to our elect. Farewell.

## LETTER XX. SUGER TO THE CHAPTER OF CHARTRES

A reply to the preceding letter.

[Col. 1356D] SUGER, by God’s grace abbot of Blessed Denis, to the chapter of Chartres—to ROBERT, namely, the dean, and the others—greetings and affection.

That you have unanimously and in common peace elected as your bishop Lord Goslen, the archdeacon, [Col. 1357A] greatly pleases us. Indeed, we have heard, and believe, that he is honourable and generous. For our part, insofar as pertains to Lord King, whose office we discharge, we gladly give our assent to this election. But concerning the regalian rights: as is known to have been the ancient custom in the court of the lords kings of France, when the bishop has been consecrated and has been introduced into the royal palace according to canonical custom, then all things shall be restored to him. For this is the order and custom of restitution: that, as we have said, once he has been established in the palace, he shall make fealty to king and kingdom, and only then receive the regalian rights.

## LETTER XXI. WILLIAM OF MAUZÉ TO SUGER

As he is about to depart for Jerusalem, he writes that Suger should send to Le Bourdet a wise provost from among his men, and a man to whom he may entrust the tower of Talmont, which Eblo of Mauléon had threatened to take away.

[Col. 1357B]

To SUGER, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, W[ILLIAM] OF MAUZÉ, his friend and seneschal of the king of the Franks, greetings.

We know indeed that your affection and intelligence have always been earnestly devoted to the affairs of the king’s land; and your discernment knows well enough how faithfully mine has been devoted, to the extent of its power, to the affairs of Poitou. Therefore we direct your kindness, lest any deceit remain hidden after my departure, to send as promptly as possible, without excuse or delay, to Le Bourdet a wise and upright provost from among your men [Col. 1357C]. Unless you do so, know in very truth that Le Bourdet and all that district will, unless God intervenes, be lost beyond recovery. For the faithful men of that region have written to me that enemies and townsmen were killing people in that town itself.

Moreover, as to my lord and friend, I report that I have hitherto guarded the tower of Talmont as faithfully as I could, for the king’s honour. But now Lord Eblo of Mauléon utterly deprives me of the revenues of the tower, and has told the bishop of Poitiers (Gislebert) that he will no longer allow me to have those revenues. Therefore I direct and entreat your highness to send such a man as I may hand over the tower to, one who will preserve it faithfully. [Col. 1357D] For I am going to Jerusalem, and I cannot guard it, nor indeed shall I guard it any longer. Farewell. If it please your friendship, I ask for your gift as a pilgrim.

## LETTER XXII. KING LOUIS TO SUGER

He writes concerning his arrival at Constantinople and the raising of money to be sent to him.

LOUIS, by God’s grace king of the Franks and duke of Aquitaine, to his dearest SUGER, venerable [Col. 1358A] abbot of Saint-Denis, greetings and abundant favour and affection.

Pursuing under divine aid the arduous journey of the most sacred pilgrimage, amid scarcely tolerable hardships and countless dangers we have passed through sound and joyful, and, with every prosperity and rejoicing, under the Lord’s guidance arrived at Constantinople on the Saturday before the feast of Saint Denis.

> [Note: [Col. 1357D] Odo of Deuil, Book IV, relates what was done at Constantinople on 4 October.]

From this city, where we halted for several days, we wrote to you, announcing all things concerning us as joyful and prosperous. A great many of our army had already crossed over or were crossing; and both they and we were prepared for the crossing. Let your diligence therefore be watchful in directing our steps through the aid of prayers; let it be prudent and circumspect in the administration of the kingdom entrusted to you [Col. 1358B].

As for obtaining money, which your prudence does not fail to know is most necessary for our daily needs, we ask you and beseech you with all the urgency of prayer we can; and through the affection and loyalty due to us we implore you to labour, with vigilant solicitude, to collect diligently by every means you can the money which is to be sent to us, and, once collected, to send it promptly and without delay. We commend ourselves to your holy prayers and to those of the Church of Blessed Denis. Your venerable brother, the bishop of Arras, has passed to the Lord in a blessed end.

> [Note: [Col. 1357D] Alvisus died in holy confession on 6 September 1147 at Philippopolis, while carrying out an embassy to Constantinople; from Odo of Deuil, Book III, p. 29 [Col. 1358D].]

Your beloved son, the monk Odo, sends you greetings.

> [Note: [Col. 1358D] Odo of Deuil, who became abbot of Compiègne in 1150, and afterwards abbot of Saint-Denis after Suger.]

For reverence toward Blessed Denis, we keep him honourably with us.

## LETTER XXIII. THE CONVENT OF SAINT-RIQUIER TO SUGER

They again ask that he grant them the prior of Corbie as abbot, and not permit them to remain longer without a shepherd.

[Col. 1358C]

To SUGER, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, their most serene lord and father, the humble convent of Saint-Riquier: greetings, and participation in every good that God is.

“Deal kindly with us who hope in the Lord, that we may dwell in the land and be fed upon its delights.” For, as though placed among nations which ravage and plunder, we are driven about like sheep without a shepherd—indeed, like a people without a king, and as [Col. 1358D] orphans without a father. Grieving and lamenting the so prolonged widowhood of our mother, we again cast ourselves at the knees of your piety in prayer, asking, for the love of God and for the salvation of your soul—and also because the administration of the churches of Gaul has been entrusted to you by the Lord in such affairs—that you may exert yourself so that our election and the steadfast consent in the Lord which we have and have had concerning the prior of Corbie may take effect, for the honour of the Lord and the restoration of our Church. This is what we, [Col. 1359A] the clergy, the knights, and the whole people ask of your most serene fatherhood. Let therefore the most gracious mercy of your dignity condescend to your sons and servants, and, lest we be thus afflicted any longer, extend a hand of consolation.

## LETTER XXIV. THEODERIC, BISHOP OF AMIENS, TO SUGER

He writes that his resources are insufficient to pay the money for which he has again been entered in Suger’s book.

To Lord and Father SUGER, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, T., by God’s mercy humble priest of Amiens, heartfelt service.

I beg you, my lord, erase me from the book in which you have entered me. For you wrote to me concerning the royal expedition,

> [Note: [Col. 1359D] This letter is to be understood as concerning the money which Suger was raising in support of the Jerusalem expedition.]

for which I am in no way able to provide sufficiently. I speak the truth [Col. 1359B] to my friend; I do not lie. Therefore may my lord spare me. For the service both of the lord pope and of the lord king has made me very poor and has put me daily into the frying-pan. Farewell, and take heed.

## LETTER XXV. GEOFFREY, ARCHBISHOP OF BORDEAUX, TO SUGER

He asks that nothing be changed in the territory of Bordeaux until he has learned the state of the land.

To his dearest lord SUGER, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, brother GEOFFREY, called bishop of the Church of Bordeaux, greetings and the affection of sincere love.

It had been our intention, lord, to travel by way of you on [Col. 1359C] our return. But the illness of our brother, the bishop of Saintes (Bernard), compelled us to return by a shorter route. We therefore now send to you the bearer of this letter with our own letters, wishing to be informed whether your proposed descent into our regions with Count Ralph of Vermandois, as you said, has still been determined upon by you, and what certain decision you have made about it. If your resolution is not yet settled, then, as we return to our own place with God’s help, we shall learn the state of our land and take care to inform you of what we learn, so that you may act according to what you hear and find expedient. Meanwhile, however, it does not seem advisable to us that you should alter anything there. On this matter we await from you, through the bearer of this letter, [Col. 1359D] whatever may please you. Our brother of Saintes, who labours as far as he can for the peace of the land, makes and awaits the same request of you.

## LETTER XXVI. THE BISHOP OF HEREFORD TO SUGER

He commends Suger highly; then asks him for relics of Saint Denis which he intends to send, requesting that they be designated by reliable inscriptions and entrusted to a trustworthy carrier.

ROBERT, by God’s grace humble minister of the Church of Hereford, to SUGER, venerable [Col. 1360A] abbot of Blessed Denis, greetings and such assistance of prayers as he may accept.

The offices of your generous favour, shown to me long ago and frequently offered, make me your debtor: if my indebted will cannot repay in kind, at least it can offer such thanks as it can. And although our own troubles often tear us apart, they draw us more abundantly into love for you; and the gifts of such great virtues, widely proclaimed of you for the benefit of many, gladden my soul. For what can one say? If wisdom or foresight is sought in Suger, it is found in such abundance that whatever affairs rest upon your counsel proceed more cautiously and succeed more happily. If one has recourse to religious devotion, from the mirror of your life there shines forth both what may give light outwardly and [Col. 1360B] what may be fitting inwardly. The renown of generosity is added: it delights to forestall petitions with benefits, before the petitioner has even asked.

Trusting in this renown for generosity, I approach more confidently with prayers as devout and humble as I can make them: that, for the honour of God and Mary the Mother of God, and for the protection and reverence of the holy Church over which, though a sinner, I preside, I may receive from your precious and abundant treasury some relics—especially relics of the precious martyr of Christ, Denis. When, therefore, you have prepared these gifts, as welcome as they are precious, which abundant charity cannot refuse to begging piety, your caution knows by what sure labels they ought to be identified, by what secure seal protected, and to what trustworthy carrier committed. The reward awaiting you for this requested charity [Col. 1360C] will be bestowed more abundantly by Charity itself, who is God: He gave us not one finger or limb as a price, but gave His whole self for redemption.

> [Note: [Col. 1359D] Since Robert, bishop of Hereford, died overseas while attending upon the apostolic lord, not in 1149, as John, prior of Hexham, has it in Twysden, vol. I, col. 277, but in 1148, on 22 April, this letter, written after the Council of Rheims, at which Robert was present, seems to be assignable to the year 1148 [Col. 1360D].]

## LETTER XXVII. POPE EUGENIUS TO SUGER

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis, greetings and apostolic blessing.

“The authority of our office exhorts us,” etc. See Pope Eugenius III under the year 1153.

## LETTER XXVIII. POPE EUGENIUS TO SUGER

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1360D] sons, the canons of Saint Geneviève, greetings and apostolic blessing.

“Whoever the truth of the Catholic faith …,” etc. See the same place.

## LETTER XXIX. SAMSON, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS, TO SUGER

He asks him to make efforts to assist him against the burgesses of Saint-Remi, who had hired knights to harass the churches of Blessed Mary and Saint Remi.

SAMSON, by God’s grace archbishop of Rheims, [Col. 1361A] to his dearest and most heartfelt friend SUGER, venerable abbot of Blessed Denis, greetings, and whatever is better and whatever is more delightful in both lives.

Relying upon your affection and energy, which we have often experienced, we humbly entreat your kindness with much urgency of prayer, that now, in our great necessity, for God’s honour and yours, and for the liberation of the churches of Blessed Mary and Blessed Remi, you may strive to aid us with a strong hand and without further delay. For the burgesses of Saint-Remi, who have inflicted grievous injuries and heavy losses upon the aforesaid churches and upon us, have now at last risen proudly against us and hired knights to assail us and plunder what belongs to us.

> [Note: [Col. 1361D] “Plunder.” This letter seems to be assigned to the year 1147, from the chronological indication in the following letter. Moreover, Louis VII, on returning from the Jerusalem expedition, made provision for the peace of the monks of Saint-Remi by a charter quoted by Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, col. 815, in which, among other provisions:
>
> “Following the custom of our predecessor kings, by our royal command, as it was decreed by them, we decree,” he says, “and establish by public authority, that the castle in which the same Blessed Remi rests in body, together with the borough adjoining it, shall be free from every foreign jurisdiction and authority; and that, apart from the abbot and [Col. 1362D] his monks, no one shall exercise there any judicial coercion. The abbot and brethren there may have brewhouses, ovens, strongholds, mills, fisheries, judicial rights, and a market whenever circumstances require it, and whatever seems suitable to their wishes and uses; and we freely permit and grant these things,” etc.
>
> “Done publicly at Paris, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1151, epact XII, concurrent VII, and in the nineteenth year of our reign [fourteenth from the first coronation, or from the death of our father], those present in the palace,” etc.]

[Col. 1361B] Farewell.

## LETTER XXX. THE ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER TO SUGER

He asks what the envoys of the king of France have reported to him concerning the Jerusalem expedition.

ALBERO, by God’s grace humble minister and servant of Trier, to SUGER, his dearest friend, abbot of Saint-Denis, prayers and the affection of intimate love.

When the gracious remembrance of your kindness presents itself to our mind, my heart and soul rejoice more gladly; and we are certain that such a man ought deservedly to be revered, whom the renown of his merits teaches us to honour far and wide. Therefore, since I ought by right to embrace this bond, [Col. 1361C] I desire to devote myself to your service; but because absence greatly hinders its accomplishment, good devotion fulfils its affection in prayers. We have been told, father and lord, that envoys have come to you from the lord king of France, who ought to convey reliable news of the expedition. If this is so, write back to us what you can; and if anything of ours pleases you, we are prepared for every service to you with a good heart and good will. Farewell. May your kindness kindly instruct and cherish the boy whom we entrusted to you.

## LETTER XXXI. PETER, ABBOT OF CLUNY, TO SUGER

To our venerable and dearest lord SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis, brother P., humble abbot of Cluny, greetings and sincere affection in the Lord.

We recently conveyed to you in other letters, and we repeat again in this present writing, as it is in our heart, that above all the prelates of your regions [Col. 1362A] we love your person especially, and reverence you with a fuller affection of charity as a particular friend of the Church of Cluny. Hence we are grieved beyond measure that we are not permitted even occasionally to see your reverence, whom we love so earnestly, and that the long-desired opportunity for conversation with you is prevented by the importunate occupations of our many affairs.

We therefore send to your affection our dearest brother and intimate friend, Lord Hugh of Crécy, through whom you may make known to us your wish. For if there is anything we know or can do which we recognize to be useful and advantageous to you, we are ready to render it in your service, in temporal matters no less than spiritual. Furthermore, we have placed in Lord Hugh’s mouth [Col. 1362B] a certain secret matter which we were unwilling to entrust to writing; we have conveyed it for this reason, that you may keep it secret and deal with it cautiously as you judge expedient.

## LETTER XXXII. POPE EUGENIUS TO SUGER

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis, greetings and apostolic blessing.

“Since our Lord and Redeemer,” etc. See Pope Eugenius III under the year 1153.

## LETTER XXXIII. PETITION OF THE CONVENT OF SAINT-RIQUIER TO SUGER FOR THE ELECTION OF AN ABBOT

I, STEPHEN, prior of the monastery of Centula, and the whole [Col. 1362C] convent of that place.

We wish all sons of the holy Church to whom these letters may come to know that we, all the monks of Saint-Riquier, with the counsel and assent of the religious persons of our province, and of our knights and nobles, as well as clerics and burgesses, have regularly and canonically elected for ourselves as shepherd Lord Peter of Bourges, monk of Saint-Denis.

## LETTER XIV. THEODERIC, BISHOP OF AMIENS, TO SUGER

He warns him privately to be vigilant about choosing a religious man as abbot of Saint-Riquier.

To his dearest lord and father SUGER, venerable [Col. 1362D] abbot of Saint-Denis, T., by God’s grace humble priest of Amiens, heartfelt service.

I speak into your ear, because, though I am troubled by many and continual evils, my spirit is afflicted above all by the disorderliness of my monasteries. [Col. 1363A] The monastery of Saint-Riquier must now be put in order, but the monks seek evasions and delays. We therefore forewarn you: unless they are constrained with a strong hand, they will choose a person according to their own depraved will, being men who have never learned discipline. This monastery needs a resolute and religious man; and, as it seems to me, either Bernard, prior of Anchin, or Drogo, prior of Lihons, is needed there. Farewell, and be watchful concerning this matter.

## LETTER XXXV. THE MAYOR GAUFRID AND THE ENTIRE COMMUNITY OF SAINT-RIQUIER TO SUGER

They ask him not to delay sending his monk Peter, elected abbot of Saint-Riquier.

[Col. 1363B]

To SUGER, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, their lord most worthy of every honour, G., mayor, the vavassors, and the entire community of Saint-Riquier: greetings in the Lord and due service.

We entreat your serenity to come to the aid of the desolation of our Church, which has languished so long without a ruler. Do not delay sending, as soon as you can, with your favour, Lord Peter, your monk, canonically elected by the counsel of our monks, the religious persons of our province, knights, and burgesses.

> [Note: [Col. 1363D] “Canonically elected.” See Letter 33 above.]

It is necessary for our house. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVI. THE BISHOP OF SARUM TO SUGER

He first praises him highly; then requests relics of Saint Denis, and excuses himself for having been unable to visit him after travelling into Normandy, before his return to England.

[Col. 1363C]

To the beloved and deservedly beloved father and lord SUGER, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, governor of the kingdom of the Franks, JOSEELUS [otherwise JOSCELINUS], by the same grace bishop of Sarum: the hand of a man beneath the wings of the cherubim.

The fragrance of your reputation, spread abroad everywhere, has made us run from lands beyond the sea into love for you.

> [Note: [Col. 1363D] After the Council of Rheims, held in mid-Lent in 1148, at which Joscelin was present with Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury.]

We came, therefore, from the ends of the earth, namely to hear the wisdom of Solomon of our time in you. We have heard your wisdom; we have seen the temple which you built; we have seen the ornaments which [Col. 1364A] you have offered and are offering; we have observed the order of the ministers and ministries. And deservedly we break out into the words of that southern queen: “Not even half was told us,” and “your wisdom and works are greater than the report in our land.” For who would not wonder that one man bears so many and such great affairs: preserving the peace of churches, restoring their condition, defending the kingdom of the Franks by arms, adorning it with morals, and reforming it by laws? We deservedly ought therefore to have entered the sea, entrusted our lives to sail and winds, and experienced the innumerable difficulties of a long journey, in order to come into your acquaintance.

But may your serenity pardon us because, at our departure from Gaul, we were unable to see your face as we wished. Inevitable necessity, imposed obedience, drew us away. For when we had crossed into Normandy on the affairs of our Church, which we had partly explained to you, our metropolitan, the lord of Canterbury, summoned us to the affairs of our mother Church of Canterbury and, without granting us time to draw breath, sent us to England.

> [Note: [Col. 1363D] “Sent us to England.” Theobald was then staying at Saint-Omer, an exile from England. For, as Gervase of Canterbury relates in Twysden, col. 1364:
>
> “When the Council of Rheims had been dissolved, Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, having received the lord pope’s blessing and permission to return, arrived prosperously at Canterbury and was honourably received by his convent and the citizens of Canterbury. On hearing this, the king, who happened then to be staying in London, moved by anger, came swiftly to Canterbury; and, after many communications through envoys between himself and the archbishop, which made less progress toward peace than was fitting, he finally compelled the archbishop to leave England. [Col. 1364D] After a truce of a few days, the latter crossed the sea at Dover and withdrew into France. After staying there for some time, he was recalled by the queen of England and William of Ypres to Saint-Omer, so that envoys of the kingdom might more easily approach him because of its proximity. There, on the Nones of September, he consecrated Gilbert, bishop-elect of the Church of Hereford, with the bishops from overseas, Theodoric of Amiens and Nicholas of Cambrai, present and assisting. Thereafter envoys, bishops, abbots, clerics, and laymen frequently came and went on both sides, but came little nearer to the good of peace; and, having sent letters to the various English churches, the archbishop proclaimed that the sentence of interdict was to be observed on the appointed day, namely the day before the Ides of September.”
>
> We thought it necessary to copy these words in order to demonstrate the date of this letter.]

Let, therefore, your kindness excuse us to itself, whom so evident a necessity excuses. Moreover, we send you our archdeacon, both to excuse us more fully and to bring us back some fruit of the love we bear toward you: namely, relics of the outstanding martyr Denis, through which a perpetual remembrance of your name may live not only in us but in the Church of Sarum. We have entrusted the other matters which we ask of you to the spoken report of the bearer of this letter [Col. 1364C]. May your excellence flourish, dearest Father.

## LETTER XXXVII. THE COUNT OF ANJOU TO SUGER

He declares that he is well and prepared to serve the king just as if the king himself were present.

To his dearest SUGER, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, GEOFFREY, duke of Normandy and count of Anjou, greetings and affection.

Know that, by God’s grace, I am sound and well, and prepared to carry out the command of my lord king. Therefore I inform you, as my dearest friend, that should it be necessary for you to summon me to the king’s service, you shall certainly find me prepared for everything you may wish [Col. 1365A] in the king’s service, and more diligently than if he himself were present.

## LETTER XXXVIII. COUNT THEOBALD TO SUGER AND COUNT RALPH

He asks them not to demand the capicery of the Church of Chartres by right of regalian authority, since he himself holds the regalian right of the bishopric of Chartres as a fief from the king.

To SUGER, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, and Count R[ALPH], his friends, THEOBALD, count of Blois, greetings and affection.

We have been told that you are demanding from the bishop of Chartres the capicery of the Church of Chartres, which you assert belongs to the regalian right and which Geoffrey, the bishop of blessed memory, held in his hand when he departed from [Col. 1365B] this world. I therefore wish to make known to you that I hold the regalian right of the bishopric of Chartres from the king as a fief together with my other fief, so that, upon the bishop’s death, the regalian right of the bishopric is my own property until another is installed. Therefore I ask you not to demand the capicery from the bishop on account of the regalian right, which is mine. But if you request it from the bishop by entreaty, I do not involve myself in that. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIX. KING LOUIS TO SUGER

He writes concerning his journey as far as Antioch, and directs him to hasten in collecting and sending money. (Year 1148.)

LOUIS, by God’s grace king of the Franks and duke of Aquitaine, to SUGER, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, greetings [Col. 1365C] and favour.

Your affection has compelled us to inform you, as soon as we could, with reliable news from the East concerning our condition. For we know—indeed we know—that you eagerly long with all your soul’s desire to hear of it, and that nothing could be more pleasing to you than to receive joyful news of us. Since we crossed the boundaries of our kingdom, the Lord has prospered our way well; and divine mercy brought us sound and unharmed as far as Constantinople, with great rejoicing and with the safety of the whole army. There we were joyfully and honourably received by the emperor.

> [Note: [Col. 1365D] “By the emperor”: Manuel.]

After remaining a little while, in order to prepare what seemed necessary, we crossed over to the Brachium and directed [Col. 1365D] our journey through the regions of Romania. In those regions we suffered no few losses, both through the emperor’s treachery and through the fault of our own people, and were grievously afflicted by many dangers. We did not lack continual ambushes by robbers, severe difficulties of the roads, and daily warfare from the Turks, who, with the emperor’s permission, had come into his land to persecute Christ’s army and were exerting all their strength to our injury. Because in many places necessities for food could not be found, the people were severely afflicted by hunger [Col. 1366A] for some time; and on one of the days, as divine judgment permitted because our sins required it, most of our barons fell.

> [Note: [Col. 1365D] “Our kinsman”: William.—For the disaster suffered by the army after it left Laodicea in January 1148, see Odo of Deuil, Book VI, p. 63 and following.]

Those who died on the ascent of the mountain of Lesser Laodicea, amid the straits of the terrain, included our kinsman, the count of Warenne; Rainald,

> [Note: [Col. 1366D] Rainald, son of William II, count of Nevers.]

of Tonnerre; Manasses of Bulles; Gaucher of Montjay; Evrard of Breteuil; and very many others, of whom the bearer of this letter will give fuller information, because grief does not permit us to speak at greater length. We ourselves were often in danger of death; nevertheless, freed from all these things by God’s grace, we vigorously escaped the persecutions of the Turks and, with our army safe under the Lord’s protection, arrived at Attaleia.

> [Note: [Col. 1366D] At Attaleia Louis celebrated the Purification of Blessed Mary, according to Odo of Deuil, Book VII, p. 69.]

There, after we had long and carefully deliberated about [Col. 1366B] continuing the journey, the common counsel of bishops and princes advised us that, since our horses had failed from the exhaustion of long hunger and labour, and a still greater difficulty of route remained, we should hasten by sea in ships to Antioch. Following their counsel, we arrived by a fortunate voyage, with the greater part of our princes, at the aforesaid city on the Friday after mid-Lent, 19 March; and from there we have taken care to send you this present letter.

Henceforth all our undertaking is in God’s hand. As we trust in Him, He will not abandon us who hope in Him, but will bring His own cause to a glorious outcome. Know this most certainly: either we shall never return, or we shall return with glory for God [Col. 1366C] and the kingdom of the Franks. It remains, therefore, for you often to keep us in remembrance and everywhere and always to commend us earnestly to the prayers of religious persons. And because our money has been very considerably diminished by many and various expenses, it is altogether necessary that you apply yourself more diligently to collecting it, and hasten to send us, through faithful messengers and as soon as possible, whatever has been gathered. For we cannot pursue Christ’s cause at all except at great expense and with much labour. Farewell.

## LETTER XL. SUGER TO POPE EUGENIUS

He relates that regular canons have been introduced at Saint Geneviève, and indicates what is necessary for completing the undertaking. (August 1148.)

[Col. 1366D]

> [Note: [Col. 1366D] See the letters of Pope Eugenius III issued at Langres, 3 Kalends of May, 1148.]

To his dearest lord and universal father, EUGENIUS, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, SUGER, humble minister of Blessed Denis: devout prayers in Christ, and fullness of obedience and service.

Having received the venerable letters of the apostolic command concerning the establishment of monastic religious life in the church of Blessed Geneviève at Paris, we embraced with the greatest joy this undertaking, so great and so pleasing to God, as though entrusted to us from heaven. For on this very matter the exalted holiness of your fatherhood had first asked our lowliness in person, though it ought only to have commanded. We have laboured with all the strength of our soul to bring it to effect. Although, because complaining canons were travelling to you—and because the Roman curia has sometimes been accustomed, without disgrace, discreetly to change its counsel according to circumstances—we had delayed; nevertheless, no opposition from hostile noble or low-born clerics or laymen would have made us grow cool or less resolute in this matter.

But suddenly, almost on the third or fourth day before that on which we intended to install the designated abbot and monks in the same church, [Col. 1367B] behold: the aforesaid canons, namely the cantor and the others, returned from your presence and delivered to us your altered ruling, for the good of peace, establishing regular canons.

> [Note: [Col. 1367D] These later letters were issued at Vercelli on 16 Kalends of July of the same year. See under Eugenius III.]

We received the second ruling as devoutly and gladly as if it had been the first. Taking with us venerable and wise men—the abbot of Saint-Germain (Hugh), of Saint-Pierre-des-Fossés (Ascelin), of Saint-Magloire (Baldwin), of Saint-Pierre-de-Ferrières (John), and other leading persons from among the neighbouring attendants—we hastened to the place of Saint Geneviève. In their chapter we held a deliberate meeting to determine what they wished to pursue concerning either the latter or the former decision, in accordance with the tenor of the letters which they had brought us. Since, being divided and holding differing opinions [Col. 1367C], they would not unanimously follow either ruling, or neither ruling, we persisted in much prolonged rebuke, because they rejected both what they had asked for and what had mercifully been granted. At length those of sounder counsel and the sons of light promised to receive regular canons peacefully.

We rejoiced in this, because some of their leading men asked that an abbot be appointed for them and that canons should be obtained from Saint-Victor. After consultation with those present, we turned to them: partly because we knew no church more religious in its observance, and partly because its proximity made it the most convenient for all their inward and outward necessities. We earnestly besought the venerable abbot of Saint-Victor (Gilduin), a man proved in works of piety, sometimes privately and sometimes in his convent, to help them; and, as an assistant of the Godhead, to uproot and destroy, to build and plant, in the Lord’s name.

But when, as a seasoned father and provident ruler of that place, he urgently declined the request, and learned that we were asking that his prior, a venerable and religious man, be made abbot, tears arose. With weeping and anguish of heart, setting before us his old age and infirmity and lamenting the loss of that prior’s counsel and aid if he were deprived of him, he detained us until the next None, almost the entire day, by refusing and protesting that it should never happen.

> [Note: [Col. 1367D] Therefore the writer of the *Life of Saint William, Abbot of Roschild*, is not to be heeded where he says:]

“Therefore the abbot of Saint Victor, having learned of their plan to change their order, importuned the lord pope and King Louis with earnest prayers, [Col. 1368D] that the Order of Saint Augustine might be established in that church, in honour of God, the Apostles Peter and Paul, and the Blessed Virgin Geneviève, under their patronage; maintaining with many arguments that those obstinate men would more readily be converted to their regular life than to the habit and customs of monks.”

At last, overcome by the prayers of many—indeed, by your authority, with which we adjured him insistently, in season and out of season—and enduring his own inconvenience, out of mercy and piety for another’s benefit, he entrusted to us the same venerable prior, Odo, together with twelve brothers, honourable religious men. On the feast of Saint Bartholomew, 24 August, we solemnly conducted them to that same church, with the clergy and people of the city; and, with the venerable bishop of Meaux, M. [Manasseh], whom we had brought with us for these proceedings, and with the assistance of your holiness, [Col. 1368B] we had him solemnly blessed as abbot that same day before the altar of Saint Geneviève herself. When Mass for that office had ended, we assigned them the cloister, chapter house, and refectory; and on the following day, acting on behalf of the lord king, whose office we exercise, we granted them royal authority and caused the men belonging to them to render fealty and swear oaths of security.

Accordingly, most holy Father, we judged it proper briefly to report to your exaltedness the execution of the business entrusted to us, so that you may be pleased that what you commanded has been done, and that our smallness may be known to be prompt in fulfilling your obedience. Henceforth, prostrate in spirit at the knees of your holy apostolate, [Col. 1368C] we earnestly and humbly beseech you to uphold and protect this work, the work of your hands; to draw the sword of Saint Peter at close quarters against every importunity of its rivals. We also ask you mercifully, if it please you, to forbid the vexations of appeals, by which they continually and indiscriminately disturb the brethren’s peace; and to extend by frequent propagation the same church, renewed for God, like a new plant, until it is perfectly rooted.

You will be able to offer the greatest assistance in all these matters if, as has been begun, you cause the fullness of the office to be maintained in that church, according to the observance of their order, down to one iota and one stroke, lest discord in the office and diversity in reading and singing become a scandal to regular and irregular clergy alike; lest the opening of doors on this pretext disturb the brethren by night and day; lest through these same rivals some disgrace steal upon them. Thus, in peace there, they may be able to render fitting service to almighty God, to the praise and honour of your holy apostolate and for the eternal reward of your person. For what should I not hope from your fatherhood? I myself, a sinner, trust that through this work of yours I shall gain some share of God’s mercy.

There is another point which we wish to make known to your fatherhood: as you first commanded, while preserving only their prebends, let the provostship and the custody of the lands remain with the regular canons. For if these are left in the hands of outsiders, they will squander everything and appropriate it to themselves, and perhaps will cruelly bring matters to a shortage of provisions, so that the order may be endangered even in this way. There is also another matter in which your sons especially need help at this beginning of their labour. Restrain a certain Ralph, who envies and disparages their religious life, by striking him with the sword of blessed Peter so that he may be converted; and, lest the impunity he enjoys produce the contumacy of others, repress his folly. May almighty God crush every enemy beneath your feet. We commend to your holy prayers those men, ready for your service, and our Church, and also your dearest son, [Col. 1369B] Louis, king of the French, who labours so strenuously in God’s work; asking that, if you have heard anything certain concerning him, you will inform us. May your holiness, most loving Father and lord, prosper for ever.

## LETTER XLI. THE COUNT OF VERMANDOIS TO SUGER

He asks that, at the queen’s request, money be granted to the clergy of Beauvais from the revenues of the bishopric of Beauvais, for the expenses of their journey to the pope concerning Henry’s election as bishop of Beauvais.

To Suger, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, R. [Ralph], count of Vermandois, greetings.

The clergy of Beauvais are hastening to Rome to the Apostolic See concerning the election of Lord Henry, and money is necessary to accomplish [Col. 1369C] this business. The lady queen asks both you and me that we grant them some portion of the revenues of the bishopric.

> [Note: [Col. 1369D] The queen: Adelaïde, mother of Henry, bishop-elect, and of King Louis VII.]

Therefore I ask you, since I strongly desire and approve this, to grant her request to such an extent as may please the lord king and preserve his honour and ours; for he is our lord, and we owe him what we would not do for another. Farewell.

## LETTER XLII. GEOFFREY, BISHOP OF BORDEAUX, TO SUGER

He reports the condition of his territory and the harassment of the king’s land by the viscount of Gabarret.

To his reverend and most dear lord in Christ, Suger, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis by God’s grace, brother Geoffrey, called bishop of the Church of Bordeaux, greetings, affection, and such service as he can render in the Lord.

As agreed, we ought to have informed you of the condition of our land. But we delayed this until now because, while circumstances were changing, only matters certain and known ought to have been reported to you. Know that at Menusanum [Mansan], on the Assumption of Blessed Mary, where the archbishop of Auch [William] [Col. 1370A] and nearly all the bishops and nobles of the whole of Gascony had assembled, we summoned the viscount of Gabarret before all present concerning the injury and harassment inflicted by him and his men upon the lord king’s land, as also concerning the siege by which he held the city of Dax—property of the king—under siege.

> [Note: [Col. 1369D] The viscount of Gabarret: Peter, son of another Peter, viscount, and of Guiscarda, who succeeded her brother Centule in the viscountcy of Béarn. From her name Peter’s successors were called viscounts of Béarn and Gabarret, as Pierre de Marca demonstrates in his *History of Béarn*, p. 441 [Col. 1370D].]

The letters of the lord pope were also read aloud and explained to him by us. They contained a sentence of excommunication against him and his entire land unless he ceased troubling the king’s land.

> [Note: [Col. 1370D] Letters of the lord pope, etc.: We do not possess these letters of Eugenius. But they are perhaps those by which, for the benefit of those signed with the cross, he forbids any question thereafter to be raised concerning all things which, when they took the cross, they had peaceably possessed, until certain knowledge is obtained of their return or death.]

It was very grievous for him and his men to hear this; yet there was one who perhaps spoke publicly words as harsh as these and harsher. Although not everything turned out as we wished, we nevertheless brought matters, not without great difficulty, to this point: [Col. 1370B] on the octave of Blessed Mary in … [supplemented from the manuscript: “September”], a day for a conference between the parties was appointed. There, following the advice of the aforesaid archbishop and of ourselves, he promised that he would act upon the inquiry which we had made of him on the pope’s behalf and for the lord king.

We do not know what he will do in this matter. Yet it is said that he will not be able to endure the sentence for long if it is strictly enforced. Therefore it seems necessary that the lord pope should again command, under every form of coercion, if anyone from your region approaches him, that the same sentence, or a graver one, be maintained; for perhaps there are persons who hesitate and are not quickly moved by the voice of a single command. The rest of our nobles, by God’s grace, appear more inclined than usual toward the good and toward peace in our land.

Martin, [Col. 1370C] who had been appointed keeper of the tower of Bordeaux, has lately entered upon the way of all flesh. The tower itself, as we learned from Martin and have certainly ascertained through our men whom we sent to inspect it, is wholly unprovided for in fortification and even in provisions. For, as Martin himself frequently complained to us, neither he nor the other retainers with him could obtain the maintenance they required. He said, accordingly, that he had faithfully spent the fourteen pounds promised to him in the preceding year, both for fortifying the tower and for supplying the needs of himself and those with him.

Now that he has died, those remaining there appear less fit [Col. 1370D] to keep watch. Moreover, the house of which we believe you have heard has not yet been built there, though it is most necessary. Since counsel and provision for the realm rest upon you, we ask you to convey these same matters to the lord count Rod. [Ralph] and to greet him for us. Let it be your concern and his, after considering these things diligently, if you love the honour of the realm and wish to preserve the land for it, without delay to provide for the urgent need: for the fortification of the tower, the rebuilding [Col. 1371A] of the house, the dispatch of suitable and vigorous guards and a good provider for them, and the means by which necessities may be supplied to them.

As to the officials of Aquitaine appointed by the lord king, and the provosts subject to them, the bearer of this letter, Brother N., will explain these matters and others known to him. We wish you to believe him as you would us. For he is one whom you know and who will tell you the truth, being, to the best of his ability, faithful and friendly in all matters pertaining to the king. Send us your reply through him, as you see fit.

## LETTER XLIII. THE DEAN AND CONVENT OF AUTUN TO SUGER

They request that he approve the election of Henry, brother of the duke of Burgundy, and commend him to the pope.

[Col. 1371B]

To Suger, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, father and lord, W. [William], dean of the Church of Autun, with the whole convent, greetings and due reverence.

Preserving in every respect, as is fitting, the honour and dignity due to royal excellency, we present to you, to whom our lord king has committed his office by the providential mercy of God, our election, lawfully and canonically performed. For, with the counsel and assent of religious persons and of all the clergy and people, we have elected Henry, [Col. 1371C] brother of the duke of Burgundy, our archdeacon and a man of royal lineage. We therefore beseech your excellency to give your assent to this election of ours and to commend the person of the elect to the lord pope by your letters.

> [Note: [Col. 1371D] Henry was the son of Hugh II, duke of Burgundy, by Matilda of Turenne; brother of Duke Odo II, of Robert, likewise bishop of Autun, and also of Walter, bishop of Langres. At Cîteaux he received the pallium from Eugenius III in 1148, while the pope presided over the general chapter of the Cistercians. These facts are given by the authors of *Gallia Christiana* from Mabillon. In fact Eugenius presided over the Cistercian chapter not in 1148 but in 1147, as we have shown in the life of Eugenius to be published below [Col. 1372D].]

## LETTER XLIV. THE DEAN OF NOYON TO THE SAME SUGER

Concerning the election of Baldwin, abbot of Châtillon, as bishop of Noyon, asking him to grant approval on the king’s behalf.

To Suger, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Saint-Denis and vicar of the realm, B. [Baldwin], dean of the Church of Noyon, and the whole chapter, greetings.

We notify your discretion that Baldwin, abbot of Châtillon, a religious man of honourable reputation, has been elected bishop for us by the counsel of religious men and the common assent of the chapter. We beseech you, [Col. 1371D] on the lord king’s behalf, readily to grant your assent to so suitable and honourable an election.

> [Note: [Col. 1372D] “Elected bishop for us.” Robert of Torigni, in Pistorio’s edition, under the year 1148, says: “Simon, the glorious bishop of Noyon, ended his days at Seleucia; Baldwin, abbot of Châtillon, succeeded him.” *Patrology*, vol. CLX.]

## LETTER XLV. POPE EUGENIUS TO SUGER

Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1372A] “Since it pertains to the office of religious persons,” etc. See Eugenius III under the year 1153.

## LETTER XLVI. THE ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX TO SUGER

To his most beloved father and lord, Suger, venerable abbot of Blessed Denis by God’s grace, Brother Bernard of Clairvaux, greetings and prayers.

Blessed be God, who has wrought salvation in your hand in the church of Saint Geneviève, so that the house of God might be restored to order and discipline. Apostolic authority itself gives you thanks because you have faithfully and effectively begun this magnificent work. We too give such thanks as we can, as do all who love the Lord in truth. Therefore we ask and most earnestly request that, in accordance with the tenor of the apostolic [Col. 1372B] letters, you extend your right hand to the work of your hands, so that what has been magnificently begun may day by day be brought to completion and happily consummated by the activity of your greatness.

We judged it superfluous now to urge your charity concerning the church of Saint Victor, since the guardianship of all churches is known to have been entrusted to you. Yet you ought to give greater attention to those whose religious life is known to stand in greater need.

## LETTER XLVII. ABBOT SUGER TO POPE EUGENIUS

He reports what has been done against the canons of Saint Geneviève, who were flocking to Rome in fear lest any alteration be made in their way of life and their property.

[Col. 1372C]

To his dearest lord and father, Eugenius, universal and supreme pontiff by God’s grace, Suger, abbot of Blessed Denis, fullness of obedience and service.

My mouth speaks the Lord’s praise, because the exaltedness of so great a father and universal lord has not disdained to render thanks to our smallness, which is almost nothing, for carrying out the obedience due at Saint Geneviève. Certainly, among other things, this especially encourages us toward an undifferentiated fullness of obedience and equips us, as piously as boldly, for the execution of all your commands to the utmost of our power.

The affair of Saint Geneviève now in hand is a divine work, a holy work, a work God has wrought through you in our days. Those wretched seculars, persecutors not so much of canons [Col. 1372D] as of Saint Geneviève, unable to obstruct us here, are hastening in crowds to Rome. They strive with all the force of mind and body to move Peter’s steadfastness by any occasion whatever, bend the Roman curia by petitions, deceive its familiars and, through them, others, by any seemingly honourable or dishonourable mode of persuasion, lest anything be changed concerning their life, their morals, or whatever property they possess.

[Col. 1373A] But since the cause of the Church is God’s cause, entrusted through Peter to Peter and Peter’s vicar, we trust in the Lord Jesus that he who began the work will complete it. Men who offend God and betray themselves will not prevail against religious life in the chief court of religion. We judged it worthy to inform your fatherhood how indiscreetly and irreverently they have behaved against your command.
