Before the archbishop of Reims [Samson], the bishop of Soissons [Goslenus], and many other religious persons, we showed your letters of command and demanded, on your behalf, the treasures which you ordered us to assign to the abbot and regular canons. Blinded by malice and wrapped in iniquity, they utterly refused to restore either the treasures secretly removed—namely, fourteen marks of gold, they say, from the shrine [Col. 1373B] of Saint Geneviève—or her relics, namely the chasuble of Saint Peter. Had we not spared them out of reverence for your exaltedness, we would have held them by royal authority as thieves or robbers.

Since, by these and similar injuries, they insult God, his saints, and apostolic reverence, we most humbly implore that, having incurred ecclesiastical punishment for contempt, disobedience, and sacrilege, they may soon feel the retribution which they deserve under the strictness of justice. For in pride they have risen to that place from which you can most easily cast them down by just judgment and preserve God’s servants in peace.

They had often hurled many insults and dreadful threats at them; had caused their boys to enter the same church of Saint Geneviève by night [Col. 1373C] and break down its doors; and had incited them to shout against the canons beginning Matins so that one could not hear another. When we were summoned there by the regular canons because of these injuries, we hastened there and sternly threatened such gluttons with blinding and mutilation if thereafter they committed anything similar. We repeatedly dispatched servants by night, should any be caught; and so, by God’s grace, with zeal for obedience and through fear of royal majesty, we most willingly protect them in peace as servants of the Most High God. In this devotion alone to God and holy religion we have persevered steadfastly as long as it pleased you.

Yet this great good, by which the Church of God rejoices and by which the renowned blessedness of your holy apostolate will be proclaimed until the end of the age, [Col. 1373D] can be brought to such a peaceful and tranquil conclusion if you cause the choir, chapter house, cloister, and refectory to be assigned to those religious men, according to the order of Saint Victor, for the preservation of holy religion, with those men excluded. Care must also be taken concerning the external revenues and custody of the lands, lest you leave them in those men’s hands, since out of complete hatred for religious persons they would destroy it. For it is certain that irregulars never agree with regulars except under a strong hand; nor, unless God’s mercy brings it about, will they be united with them in true peace for the extorted pleasure of sinners.

## LETTER XLVIII. KING LOUIS TO SUGER

He orders him to see that the possessions of Reginald of Boule, who remained in the East, and the inheritance of the deceased Drogo, are preserved.

Louis, by God’s grace king of the French and duke of Aquitaine, to Suger, by the same grace venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, greetings and favour.

Concerning Reginald of Boule, who has remained with us in the regions of the East in service to God and to us, we command you to give the care of your protection to his land—which, after the death of his brother Manasseh, he ought to hold by patrimonial right—and to all the men belonging to him, as if they were our own.

> [Note: [Col. 1373D] Manasseh of Boule died in January 1148, on the ascent of the Laodicean mountain, according to the letter of King Louis above, no. 39.]

If anyone wishes to harass them in any way, give them your assistance to the extent of your power. Concerning Drogo of Muncy, who has died, we likewise command you to ensure that his inheritance is preserved as our own, indeed for our benefit. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIX. HENRY, THE KING’S BROTHER, TO SUGER

Having been sought as bishop of Beauvais, he requests that another be elected.

To his most beloved father and lord, Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis by God’s grace, Henry, unworthy monk of Clairvaux, eternal greeting in Christ.

It grieves me that the Church of Beauvais is troubled on my account. Therefore from the beginning I had warned [Col. 1374C] the clergy not to undertake useless labour or burden the Church itself with harmful delay. Would that even now this vexation may have given them counsel or understanding, so that, cutting off every futile delay, they may hasten to provide for Christ’s Church by electing another person suitable for so great a ministry.

I most earnestly and affectionately ask your fatherhood, dear to me in Christ, to command that this be done quickly and altogether to forbid their labouring in vain thereafter, should they perhaps attempt it. For I wish you to believe this without doubt: the more labour is undertaken in this matter, the more will be lost. Farewell always in the Lord.

## LETTER L. KING LOUIS TO SUGER AND OTHERS

He orders them to arrange payment of money which he had borrowed through Ebrard, master of the Temple.

[Col. 1374D]

Louis, by God’s grace king of the French and duke of Aquitaine, to S. [Samson], archbishop of Reims; Suger, most renowned abbot of Saint-Denis; and R. [Ralph], count of Péronne, our dearest kinsman and friend: greetings and our favour.

We command your affection to regard as certain the matters which Ebrard, master of the Temple, shall communicate to you.

> [Note: [Col. 1373D] The administration of the realm had been committed to Suger alone at the assembly of Étampes; but after the king’s departure [Col. 1374D] from Saint-Denis, the archbishop of Reims was given to him as colleague. “And lest the secular sword be lacking to you two,” says Odo of Deuil, “a third was added, so that a threefold cord might not easily be broken.”]

For we sent him from Antioch to Acre on the sixth day before the Ides of May, to borrow money necessary for us.

> [Note: [Col. 1375D] Accaron: Acre, or Ptolemais.]

Therefore, on God’s behalf and ours, we command you to cause the money to be paid to them as quickly as possible—the money which you learn from the letters sent to you has been borrowed for us through them.

## LETTER LI. POPE EUGENIUS TO THE BISHOPS OF AUXERRE AND SOISSONS, AND TO SUGER

Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers H., bishop of Auxerre, G., bishop of Soissons, and his beloved son Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis: greetings and apostolic blessing.

“Our beloved son L.,” etc. See Pope Eugenius III under the year 1133.

## LETTER LII. KING LOUIS TO SUGER

He orders him to repay to Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, 104 marks of silver which Arnulf had lent to the king.

[Col. 1375B]

Louis, by God’s grace king of the French and duke of Aquitaine, to Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, his beloved and faithful servant: greetings.

Know that Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, in my great need lent me as much of his own gold and silver as he could; I still owe him one hundred and four marks of silver. Therefore I command you, setting aside every excuse and delay, to repay him that amount from my funds within a month after receiving this letter, so that for no reason [Col. 1375C] may he be offended against me or troubled.

> [Note: [Col. 1375D] Arnulf is said, in the *Deeds of Louis VII*, ch. 18, to have attended the council of Acre held on 20 May 1148, where it was resolved to besiege Damascus. After the siege was abandoned, many Frenchmen returned home, bringing back the king’s letters issued in this year.]

Know also that I have caused the aforesaid money to be secured to him.

## LETTER LIII. THE SAME TO THE SAME AND THE COUNT OF VERMANDOIS

After the deaths of Albert Dalvolt and his son Hugh, he orders them to preserve until his return the tower of Andresel, which Albert had built with the king’s permission.

Louis, by God’s grace king of the French and duke of Aquitaine, to Suger, by the same grace venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, and to R. [Ralph], count of Vermandois, his dearest kinsman and friend: greetings and our favour.

We wish it to be known to you that Albert [Col. 1375D] Davolt, one of our household, has died in the service of Christ and of ourselves. Since we have learned by reliable report that Hugh, his son, has also died, we have taken care to command you as our friends to ensure that the tower of Andresel, which the aforesaid Albert had fortified with our consent, be preserved according to the command [Col. 1376A] of our will until our return, guards having been appointed and established on our behalf, lest anything detrimental to us occur.

> [Note: [Col. 1375D] Andreselles, approximately three leagues from the city of Melun.]

As for the other possessions belonging to him, we command you to exercise the care of your protection by arranging them honourably as your discretion sees fit. Farewell.

## LETTER LIV. THE SAME TO THE SAME

He orders them to take greater care to preserve his house at Gisors.

Louis, by God’s grace king of the French and duke of Aquitaine, to Suger, by the same grace venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, and R. [Ralph], count of Vermandois: greetings and our favour.

[Col. 1376B] We have communicated our affairs to you, and again make them known to you, that you may hasten to fulfil them to the extent of your power according to the command of our will.

> [Note: [Col. 1376D] Louis appears to have written this letter immediately after his departure.]

Furthermore, we command you, as our most beloved faithful men and friends, to ensure that our house at Gisors is preserved for our benefit and henceforth cared for more diligently. Farewell.

## LETTER LV. THE SAME TO THE SAME

He orders them not to refuse his friend Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, sixty measures of his best Orléans wine.

Louis, by God’s grace king of the French and duke of Aquitaine, to his beloved friends Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, [Col. 1376C] and R. [Ralph], count of Vermandois: greetings and favour.

We command your affection that you do not refuse to give sixty Orléans measures of my best Orléans wine to my beloved and heartfelt friend A. [Arnulf], bishop of Lisieux. Farewell.

## LETTER LVI. THE SAME TO THE SAME

They are not to refuse the service of Archambault of Sully; his complaint is to be decided after the king’s return.

Louis, by God’s grace king of the French and duke of Aquitaine, to his beloved faithful servants Suger, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, and R. [Ralph], count of Vermandois: greetings and favour.

[Col. 1376D] Archambault of Sully has informed us that he is ready and devoted in all things to pursue our service at the will of our faithful men.

> [Note: [Col. 1376D] Odo Archambault was the son of William, eldest son of Stephen, count of Chartres, and Adela, daughter of William the Conqueror, king of England. William, having married Agnes, daughter and heiress of Gilo of Sully, left numerous lands and honours in the region of Bourges.]

He asks that, if he has committed anything against us, the complaint may meanwhile be deferred until our return and that, at our return, his position may stand at our pleasure. Since it is incumbent on you to provide in all things for our honour, [Col. 1377A] we command you to act in these matters, saving our honour, as the consideration of reason shall suggest to you, and not to refuse to accept his service for our honour.

## LETTER LVII. SUGER TO KING LOUIS

He adjures him not to remain in the East even briefly after Easter; he then writes about money paid to the Knights Templar and the count of Vermandois, and about concealing resentment against Queen Eleanor.

To Louis, glorious king of the French and duke of Aquitaine by God’s grace, our dearest lord, Suger, abbot of Blessed Denis, with the whole flock of brethren entrusted to him: the devotion of prayers and entire fidelity of service.

By what great and tearful sighs we accompany your most grievous absence from us, and by what great and devout petitions of prayer we commend your prosperity and safety, dearest lord, to the Lord God, we cannot possibly express. What mind could be so hard, what breast so iron, as not to be moved by the long and intolerable absence of so great and most merciful a lord? An absence which begins in sorrow endures in fear and terrifies by the horror of ruin. For whenever we remember the native nobility of royal majesty, the venerable excellence of your character, and your courage, merciful toward all and especially toward us, we desire either to fail before you or to fail with you. For if we survived you, [Col. 1377C] what change from one state into another could compare with it except falling from heaven into the abyss?

Let, therefore, the habitual compassion of your inborn goodness return to your heart. Love those who love you, as even beasts do by nature; be ashamed to destroy faithful and heartfelt friends; so that those whom, by leaving, you have crushed with excessive terror, you may at least revive with sufficient consolation by returning, after so many dangers and so many innumerable sufferings of various deaths.

And, that I may speak to you in the voice of your whole kingdom: why, dearest king and lord, do you flee us? “Did I not hate those who hate you, and waste away because of your enemies?” Since you ought to love both yourself and us who are yours as yourself, yet seem to love neither, we grieve the more. Since you have laboured most fiercely in the eastern regions and endured many almost intolerable evils, with what hardness—or rather cruelty—have you presumed, after the return of the barons and magnates of the kingdom, to remain among barbarians? The disturbers of the realm have returned, while you, who ought to defend it, live in exile as though captive; you have delivered the sheep to the wolf and exposed the kingdom to plunderers.

We therefore beseech your exaltedness, appeal to your mercy, adjure your kindness, and implore you by the faith which binds us together: do not remain there even briefly after Easter has passed, lest you appear in God’s eyes guilty of the profession and oath which you made to the realm when receiving the crown. Awaiting you as God’s angel, [Col. 1378A] we shall be ready to go wherever necessary and to prepare everything needed. May the King of kings and Lord of lords preserve your person safe for himself and for us.

We have delivered to the brothers of the Temple, according to your command, the money which we had intended to send you. Likewise Count R. [Ralph] has received in full all that he had lent you—namely, three thousand pounds, less two hundred. Your land and people rejoice, with God’s help, in good peace. We reserve for your return your cases and pleas, tallages and feudal reliefs, and also provisions. We ensure that your houses and palaces are kept intact and repaired where ruined; they lack only their lord. I was old, but have grown older especially through these affairs; in all of them I have worn myself out from no cupidity and by no motive whatsoever except love of God and of you.

Concerning your wife the queen, we dare to advise you, if it please you, to conceal the resentment in your heart, if there is any, until, by God’s will, you have returned to your own kingdom and have made provision concerning these matters and others.

## LETTER LVIII. KING LOUIS TO SUGER

He declares that he owes much to the Knights Templar and orders that the money he borrowed from them be restored without delay; he then writes of the postponement of his return.

Louis, by God’s grace king of the French and duke of Aquitaine, to his beloved and most faithful friend Suger, [Col. 1378C] most reverend abbot of Blessed Denis: greetings and favour.

I do not wish your discretion to be unaware of the great honour, reverence, and support which the brothers of the Temple have given to me and mine since I came to the eastern regions. For I do not see, nor can I see, how I could have remained or delayed there even for a short time without their prior aid and support, which has never failed me from the first day I was in those regions until this day when these letters left me—and at that moment they were most especially continuing it.

Therefore I earnestly entreat your affection: if formerly you loved them for God’s sake, now do not refuse to love and support them especially for the love of God and of us, so that they may perceive that I have interceded for them. Furthermore, I notify you that they have borrowed, and assumed upon themselves, a considerable sum of money on my behalf. For its repayment, lest their house be disgraced or ruined, it is not fitting that I make them liars, lest I too be found shamefully false with them. Therefore, commanding and begging you, I ask that without delay you repay them two thousand marks of silver.

I have ordered G. [Geoffrey] of Rancon [Col. 1378D] not to delay diligently repaying them the remaining debt; he has graciously promised me that he will do so.

> [Note: [Col. 1377D] See below the letter of Geoffrey of Rancon, no. 71.]

He must repay them thirty thousand shillings in Poitevin currency. Although he has given me a satisfactory answer, nevertheless, if he should perhaps refuse to repay them, I command you to admonish and compel him to do so. I commanded this of him so that you might not be excessively burdened with so great a debt.

Farewell, knowing and understanding that on this first crossing I believed that I would return home. But, observing the oppression of the Eastern Church and the urgent need of that land, moved by compassion and overcome by the prayers of the whole Eastern Church, I have promised to remain until Easter to support that Church. Then, with all uncertainty removed, I have resolved and firmly determined in my mind, with God’s favour and permission, to return home and to return to the kingdom granted me by God. I have written similar letters to Count R. [Ralph] concerning this money.

## LETTER LIX. THE SAME TO THE SAME

He recounts the many services rendered him by the Knights Templar and urges him to exact severe vengeance upon the goods and persons of those who had presumed to mutilate a cleric coming to their chapter.

[Col. 1379B]

Louis, by God’s grace king of the French and duke of Aquitaine, to his dearest Suger, abbot of Blessed Denis: greetings and intimate affection.

It cannot be said how great the services and how much affection the Knights of the Temple show us everywhere in the East. Therefore we bear their losses and injuries as though they were our own—indeed, more heavily than our own. Since, then, we owe them our assistance everywhere in avenging their injuries, we owe it especially and wholly in the matters which, to our disgrace, we have heard were inflicted upon them in our kingdom [Col. 1379C]. Accordingly, by the faith which exists between us, yours and ours, we ask, warn, and entreat your belovedness to exact, with every diligence and according to what you understand to be our will, a fitting, severe, and public punishment upon the property and persons of those who presumed to mutilate and dismember a cleric coming to their chapter.

## LETTER LX. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME AND TO THE COUNT OF VERMANDOIS

He orders them to ensure that money which he had borrowed from the brethren of the Order of the Hospital be repaid before Mid-Lent.

[Col. 1379D]

LOUIS, by the grace of God king of the Franks and duke of Aquitaine, to SUGER, by the same grace venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, and to R. [RALPH], count of Vermandois, greeting and our favour.

We do not doubt that it is evident to you that the Eastern Church, laid waste by the daily persecutions of Saracens and unbelievers, has raised its voice so high as to summon us inhabitants of the western regions, by its cry, to avenge it. And since difficult undertakings can by no means be accomplished without great labour and expense, in pursuing so great a cause we have been driven by the various waves of secular storms [Col. 1380A], and have spent our money on many and diverse expenses.

Therefore, although our own funds had failed, we nevertheless desired to fulfil Christ’s cause according to the purpose of our devotion, and we sought counsel in this matter from the brethren of the Order of the Hospital. Since they had always loved us, they fulfilled their love in action by coming to our aid in our necessity. For the perfection of love is the rendering of service. Accordingly, to supply our need, they lent us a thousand marks of silver acquired from foreign peoples; certain of our barons stood surety for us, on our behalf, for the aforesaid silver.

Wherefore we command you, as our dearest friends, to have the revenues of our lands assembled, [Col. 1380B] provided nevertheless that the term fixed by us—namely Mid-Lent—does not pass without our debt being paid to the aforesaid brethren, all excuse set aside.

## LETTER LXI. FROM SUGER TO POPE EUGENIUS

Against Clement, dean of the Church of Paris, who had indiscreetly ordered the cantor of that church to be silent in choir.

To his most loving father and lord, EUGENIUS, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, SUGER, humble servant of Saint-Denis, fullness of obedience and service.

Holy Father, invited by charity and at the request of many, we earnestly commend to your discretion the noble Church of Blessed Mary at Paris; because [Col. 1380C] it now needs assistance more than usual, we humbly ask you to aid it more than usual.

[Note: [Col. 1379D] *We humbly ask.* See Eugenius’s letter, given at Auxerre on the day before the Nones of October, 1147, in which he replies: “We have kindly received your messenger and letter [Col. 1380D], and have carefully considered what they contained. We are grateful that we perceive you to be concerned for the Church of Paris,” etc.]

For although it has hitherto customarily shone by the nobility of its venerable standing and the illustrious lamp of learning, it is now seriously faltering through the inadequacy of the holder of the deanery, and, unless aid is given, is hastening toward decline. For when the man who ought to lead others by teaching and the example of his life does not even know how to follow, surely the discipline of those subject to him, through his ignorance, strays from the path of learning and prudence.

Indeed, while we enjoyed in Gaul your presence, welcome to God and men, after B. [Bartholomew], dean of that church, had been made bishop of Châlons, the differing factions of the chapter of Paris—who, though frequently assembling locally, were unable to agree upon the choice of a person as dean—received from your fatherhood an order to entrust that election to the more honourable persons of the same church, through whose industry the controversy might be peacefully settled to God’s honour. Ready to obey, they entrusted the election to four canons of that church, one of whom was this Clement; they suspected no evil in or from them. But these men, refusing to confer upon others that which they had once undertaken among themselves, and instead keeping it among themselves, perhaps chose this man from among themselves as their dean.

We were greatly astonished at this: since the election had been entrusted to four by your authority, if three elected the fourth, they obeyed imperfectly. But if the fourth elected himself together with the others, your fatherhood’s discretion knows infinitely better than we what he did. Yet if what is deficient in the election were supplied by the integrity of the person, it might be endured as a compensating consideration. But, as those who know him report, he possesses neither discretion, nor good conduct, nor a good reputation. Publicly and privately, they say, he is inclined toward every worse course, devoid of counsel and aid, nearly useless in every need of the Church; under him the Church is more likely to languish than prosper.

You may recognize evidence of his indiscretion in the affair concerning the dispute which, as you may hear, he has initiated against the cantor of the same church, and which the bishop of Paris sends to your fatherhood [Col. 1381B]. For, by the custom of the Church and the authority of apostolic immunity, the aforesaid cantor is so equal in status to the dean that the dean has no authority, whether in ecclesiastical or civil affairs, in chapter or outside it, to decide anything without the cantor’s counsel.

One day, while they were in choir singing the canonical hour, and the cantor was speaking to a certain cleric—as is his custom in giving everyone instructions about what is to be sung or read—the dean seized this occasion for an attack, leapt upon the cantor, and shamefully ordered him to be silent. When the cantor continued what he had begun to say to his hearer, amazed at the dean’s indiscreet vehemence, the dean himself, Clement, raging like a possessed man, ordered the singing choir [Col. 1381C] to be silent. He did not consider that, if even the least of the canons—still less this man, who by the Church’s custom is equal to him, so that the dean may establish nothing without him either in choir or chapter—had committed some offence in choir, he ought to be corrected canonically in chapter.

From this arose between them the complaint whose accusation the lord bishop of Paris took care to write to your fatherhood. This was its beginning; this was the disturbance.

[Note: [Col. 1381D] *This was the disturbance.* Thus the printed editions. Perhaps one should read: “This was the beginning of this disturbance.” “He,” etc. For we found no manuscript to use.]

He agitates the Church with feet and hands, disturbs it so that he may himself be disturbed, being ignorant of peace and quiet. The aforesaid cantor, bearing the injury rather patiently, repeatedly offered himself for the doing and receiving of justice—lest he appear unreasonable—through the lord bishop of Paris, Theobald, through the chapter of the Church, through the lord of Auxerre, Hugh, and the lord of Soissons, Goslen, through us also, and through many others [Col. 1381D]. We heard that the man who suffered the injury was readier for a settlement of peace and execution of justice than he who inflicted it.

Nor is this the only or the first act by which he has been accustomed, as he is carried away by indiscretion, to harass the Church of Paris now generally, now personally. If all these acts were reported to you, [Col. 1382A] they would produce weariness. May it therefore please your holy fatherhood—to whom belongs the correction, alteration, and removal of all things (“the eyes of all hope in thee, O Lord”)—to provide for that Church in such a way that it may not perish within and without through the dean’s deficiency; that the noble Church of Paris, afflicted, may not degenerate; and that, when there is no need, it may not utterly decline on account of that man. Perhaps you will put forth your hand too late for its restoration.

[Note: [Col. 1381D] What Eugenius did, we do not know. Clement, however, remained dean until at least 1164.]

## LETTER LXII. FROM THE COUNT OF FLANDERS TO SUGER

To his lord and dearest friend SUGER, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, T., count of Flanders, greeting and the fullness of all affection.

Having the fullest confidence in your goodwill, with much devotion and with all the affection of my heart I beseech the excellence of your holiness [Col. 1382B] steadfastly to carry through to a good end what you have graciously undertaken for the support of the Church of Arras; and, for the love of God and of us, to make the election of our beloved Master Hugh, made by that Church with pious devotion and, as we believe, by God’s will, remain confirmed and inviolate. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIII. FROM THE COUNT OF NEVERS TO SUGER

He asks him to be present at Saint-Denis on a specified day for conversation.

To his dearest lord SUGER, reverend abbot of Saint-Denis, W. [WILLIAM], count of Nevers, greeting, service, and due reverence.

[Col. 1382C] As I have learned from your letters, I understand that you would gladly see me and speak with me, and I likewise desire to see you.

[Note: [Col. 1382D] *Your letters,* etc. We do not possess those letters of Suger.]

Behold, I have arranged to be at Saint-Denis in prayer on the coming Wednesday. Therefore, lord, I inform and earnestly entreat you to be present there by your favour, because I very much wish to speak with you. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIV. FROM THE ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX TO SUGER

To his dearest father and lord SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis, brother B. [BERNARD], called abbot of Clairvaux, greeting and affection.

You ought to work the works of Him who left you in [Col. 1382D] His place—or rather, the works of the Lord your God, who chose you for such a ministry. Among His works is the fact that the church at Mont has put on religious observance and beauty, where that new plantation has found in you a great counsellor and helper. We beg you to complete better what you have well begun, and to set yourself as a wall for the house of Israel, that man may not prevail. Deign also to console the abbot of that place, because [Col. 1383A] he is faint-hearted; for this befits the honour of your person, the salvation of your soul, and especially this present time.

## LETTER LXV. FROM THE COUNT OF FLANDERS TO SUGER

He writes that Robert, the king’s brother, had by no means withdrawn from the king with hostile intent or without brotherly feeling; he declares himself ready to defend the honour of the kingdom against Robert.

To SUGER, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, T. [THIERRY], count of Flanders, greeting and undivided affection.

I would long ago have come to you and discussed with you in person what you requested of me, had I not been occupied with my own affairs, and especially with paying my creditors what I owed them. [Col. 1383B] As for the disposition which Lord Robert, the king’s brother, displayed toward my lord the king of France during the pilgrimage expedition, believe the reports of others. But I tell and command you this: before his return, Lord Robert, having been summoned by the king to come to Nazareth for the king’s business, entirely absented himself; yet, as it seemed to me and to the other princes, he did not withdraw from my lord with anything but brotherly and friendly intention.

Accordingly, as befits your prudence and holiness, preserve in good faith to the king of France the towns and fortresses entrusted to you. And if any adversity should come upon you, resist manfully, with me as your helper and with God’s power as your defender.

[Note: [Col. 1383D] *Resist manfully,* etc. On disturbances stirred up in the kingdom, see Eugenius’s letters to Suger and to Hugh, archbishop of Sens, given at Tusculum, on the eighth day before the Ides of July, 1149.]

Therefore, whenever you please that I should come to you and confer concerning the affairs of the land entrusted to you, summon me without hesitation, and instruct me whether I should come with few or with many men [Col. 1383C]. For I am prepared in every respect to defend the land for the honour of my lord the king, and to evade no dangers or labours in faithfully serving him. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVI. FROM POPE EUGENIUS TO SUGER

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Since, as the inspected sequence of your letters has made clear to us,” etc. See under Eugenius III for the year 1153.

## LETTER LXVII. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis [Col. 1383D], greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Let it be known to your discretion,” etc. See the same place.

## LETTER LXVIII. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Having the fullest confidence in your goodwill,” etc. See the same place.

## LETTER LXIX. FROM KING LOUIS TO SUGER

Concerning the postponement of his return until after Easter, and Chancellor Baldwin’s dispatch; the king directs that Baldwin be summoned to conduct affairs of the kingdom.

[Col. 1384A]

LOUIS, by the grace of God king of the Franks, to his dearest SUGER, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and inward [perhaps *intimate*] affection.

We recognize that it is superfluous to stir your solicitous care in matters concerning either us or our kingdom by any entreaties whatsoever. For we know and are certain beyond doubt that your whole attention is always watchfully directed to that end, and that you await absolutely no prompting concerning these matters either from us or from elsewhere.

Nevertheless, [Col. 1384B] because we have postponed our return until Easter, after our princes, and fear the machinations of wicked men, we have especially thought it necessary now to write to you: in the meantime, above all things, since the care and guardianship of the kingdom chiefly belong to you, apply yourself more attentively to guarding it, and by your accustomed vigilance utterly frustrate every effort of malicious men, should they attempt to devise anything against our crown. For, with the Lord’s help, immediately after Easter we shall without doubt hasten to cross the sea and return to defend our kingdom.

Furthermore, we have permitted our faithful and beloved Chancellor Baldwin to return with our gracious leave [Col. 1384C], because we recognized that he would be useful and necessary to us in the regions of France.

[Note: [Col. 1384D] *Chancellor Baldwin.* Odo of Deuil in many places calls him Bartholomew, not Baldwin.]

His devoted fidelity deserves from us greater favour, honour, and distinction among our friends, because amid labours and dangers he did not in any way fail us in foreign parts. We therefore wish him, as one most dear to us, to be summoned for the conduct of the kingdom’s business, and for those matters which must be arranged to be arranged by his counsel. From his report you will learn everything certain about our condition.

## LETTER LXX. FROM THE ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX TO SUGER

To the venerable father and lord SUGER, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, greeting and prayers.

“Now is the time and work for you to take hold of the sword of the Spirit,” etc. See among the letters of Saint Bernard, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXII [Col. 1384D].

## LETTER LXXI. FROM GAUFRED OF RANCON TO SUGER

[Note: [Col. 1384D] See above, Letter 58.]

He declares that the king entrusted the land of Poitou to him and ordered him to distribute its revenues according to the king’s pleasure.

To his venerable lord and spiritual father SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis, GAUFRED of Rancon, greeting.

Your prudence does not fail to know that our lord [Col. 1385A] the king entrusted the land of Poitou to us and commanded what we should do with its revenues. He ordered us to pay thirty thousand solidi to the Knights of the Temple; thereafter its towers and castles were to be fortified. We are therefore greatly surprised that we have not yet had your counsel on this matter, but you have ordered us to pay G. Berlai four thousand solidi, to Fontevr[au]lt five hundred solidi, to the son of W. [William] of Mazières one thousand, and ten pounds elsewhere. This is burdensome to carry out.

[Note: [Col. 1385D] “…that we should pay G. Berlai,” etc. Giraud, lord of Bellay, whom Louis had invested with the seneschalship of all Poitou as a member of his most beloved household, according to John, monk of Marmoutier, in his *History of Geoffrey the Warlike, Count of Anjou*.]

Let your friendship know that we were recently in the Bordeaux region and spoke with the lord archbishop [Geoffrey] and with the barons of that land, which we found greatly disturbed. Let your friendship know that I would never tolerate in peace the provost whom you sent; but the lord archbishop and I took counsel that we should appoint one of the nobles of that land, who would restore the houses—which are greatly ruined—and the defensive walls. As for men-at-arms in the fortress, you may decide how many to send, whether from our land or yours, provided they are maintained from royal revenues.

Your friendship ordered us to come and speak with you at the city of Bourges. This is very burdensome for us, for I cannot yet recover from the journey [Col. 1385B], and, on the other hand, I believe you know another reason.

[Note: [Col. 1385D] From the journey which he had begun with the king and the crusaders. Odo of Deuil, Book VI, attributes to Gaufred the disaster suffered by the army near Laodicea after Christmas or at the beginning of January: “In this,” he says, “Gaufred of Rancon earned an everlasting resentment; the king himself had sent him first, together with his uncle, the count of Maurienne.” And in Book VII: “Meanwhile all the people judged Gaufred worthy of hanging because he had not obeyed the royal command; and perhaps his uncle, whom he had as a companion in guilt, was also his protector against punishment, because, while both were guilty and the king’s uncle had to be spared, one ought not to be condemned without the other.”]

But if it pleased you to come to Blois around Pentecost, we would most willingly come to you there. We inform you that C. [Cadurc], the chancellor whom you sent into that land, greatly disturbed it and acquired a very large sum of money for himself [Col. 1385C]. Know that we shall fulfil the lord king’s command to the best of our ability.

## LETTER LXXII. FROM THE ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX TO SUGER

To his dearest father and lord SUGER, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, brother B., called abbot of Clairvaux, the spirit of counsel and consolation.

“Having seen certain of your letters,” etc. See in Saint Bernard, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXII.

## LETTER LXXIII. FROM HENRY, SON OF COUNT THEOBALD, TO SUGER

He seeks advice concerning Anseric of Montréal, captured in a tournament by Rainald of Pomponne.

To SUGER, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, HENRY, son of Count Theobald, greeting.

[Col. 1385D] Perhaps it has not escaped your attention that Rainald [Col. 1386A] of Pomponne, your man, captured Anseric of Montréal in this tournament.

[Note: [Col. 1386D] *In this tournament,* etc. Saint Bernard’s Letter 376 to Suger appears to concern this tournament. He says: “Those men who returned fixed those accursed fairs for after the feast of Easter, and Lord Henry, son of the count [Theobald], and Lord Robert, the king’s brother, determined, with reins let loose, to rush upon and kill one another. Consider with what intention they undertook the road to Jerusalem, who returned with such an intention,” etc.]

I therefore entreat your goodwill not to find it burdensome, for my sake, to come to me at Meaux on the Sunday eight days hence. For I know that you are my most faithful friend and that, in this present affair, more than all those whom I know, you can help me both through the affection which I believe you bear toward me and through your proven discretion. Therefore, with your prudent counsel, I desire to settle the matter of the aforesaid Anseric with Lord Rainald, at a place and time agreed upon.

## LETTER LXXIV. FROM SUGER TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

He summons him with his suffragans to a general assembly to be held at Soissons, in order to establish the peace of the kingdom against the movements of insurgents.

[Col. 1386B]

To the venerable SAMSON, by God’s grace archbishop of Reims, SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and affection.

Since the glory of Christ’s body, namely the Church of God, rests upon the indissoluble unity of kingdom and priesthood, it is surely clear that he who provides for one assists the other; for it is plainly shown to all discerning persons both that the temporal kingdom stands through the Church of God and that the Church of God prospers through the temporal kingdom.

Therefore, since we see the kingdom seriously disturbed by the evasions and troubles of wicked men during the long absence of our most dear lord Louis, king of the Franks, upon pilgrimage [Col. 1386C], and fear that the Church of God will be more gravely disturbed together with the kingdom, and since prompt counsel is needed, we entreat and invite you as a precious gem in the crown upon the head of the kingdom; and by the mutual faith between you and us, ours and yours, and by the bond which binds you to the kingdom, we earnestly summon you to assemble with your suffragans at Soissons with us on the Sunday preceding Rogationtide.

[Note: [Col. 1386D] *The Sunday preceding Rogationtide,* etc. The fifth Sunday after Easter, which in 1149 fell on 8 May.]

For we have summoned, at the same time and place, the archbishops and bishops and the higher magnates of the kingdom, so that according to the profession of our fidelity and the oaths by which we are bound to the kingdom, we may prudently provide for the kingdom and the Church of God.

[Note: [Col. 1386D] *We may prudently provide,* etc. Saint Bernard praised the counsel in Letter 377: “May the Dayspring from on high visit you who propose to visit the kingdom of our most glorious king. Certainly it was God’s counsel that you should call to counsel both the princes of the court and those of the Church, so that all who dwell on earth may know that there remain both for kingdom and king a gracious friend, a prudent counsellor, and a strong helper,” etc.]

Let us bear one another’s burdens and set ourselves as a wall for the house of Israel [Col. 1386D]. For if we are steadfastly found to belong to that community of which [Col. 1387A] it is written, “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul,” both the Church of God will be endangered and a kingdom divided against itself will be altogether laid waste.

## LETTER LXXV. FROM S. OF CHÉZIAU TO SUGER

He asks whether he ought to restore the tower and territorial jurisdiction to Gaufred of Rancon.

To SUGER, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, S. of CHÉZIAU, provost of Oléron, greeting.

I inform you that G. [Gaufred] of RANCON, because of a feudal rent which I do not wish to render him—and which your sealed letters forbade me to render him—has sent his provost into the territory. He urgently demands that I surrender the tower and the territorial jurisdiction. But I defend the tower and territorial jurisdiction [Col. 1387B] as far as I can, and do not wish to surrender them. I therefore seek your advice as to what you wish me to do in this matter: whether to surrender the tower and territorial jurisdiction, or wholly to refuse them according to my ability. Yet it seems to me that, if I paid the feudal rent, I would have peace with him.

## LETTER LXXVI. FROM THE COMMUNE OF BEAUVAIS TO SUGER

They request that he do justice upon Waleran, lord of Levesmont, who had captured and despoiled a man sworn to the commune during the days of the Lord’s Resurrection.

To their lord SUGER, reverend abbot of Saint-Denis, the peers and whole commune of Beauvais, greeting [Col. 1387C] and service as to their lord.

We cry out and complain to you as to our lord, since we have been entrusted to the lord king’s hand and protection under your care. A certain man of ours, sworn to our commune, had heard that two horses which had been his in Lent were at Lenesmont [Levemont], and he went there on the Wednesday of Easter Week to seek them. But Waleran, lord of the aforesaid town, paying no honour to the Lord’s Resurrection, seized that man though he had committed no offence; he compelled him to pay ten Parisian solidi for himself, and to redeem his horses for fifty-six solidi. Since the man is poor and owes this and much other money at interest, we beseech your holiness in the Lord [Col. 1387D] to exact, by God’s grace and your own, fitting justice from the aforesaid Waleran, so that he may restore the stated money to our sworn man and may not hereafter presume to disturb anyone entrusted to you. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVII. FROM KING LOUIS TO COUNT THEOBALD

He writes of the gracious services rendered during the pilgrimage by Henry, his son; of his own return deferred until Easter; and asks Theobald meanwhile to watch over the kingdom.

[Col. 1388A]

LOUIS, by the grace of God king of the Franks, to his dearest THEOBALD, count, greeting and abundant affection.

The inward love which we hold in our heart toward your beloved son HENRY compelled us to write to your faithfulness from distant regions, for the glory of his name. His devotion, which he displayed toward us in every respect, and his gracious services have deserved greater favour from us and have won for him with us the affection of a more ardent love.

[Note: [Col. 1387D] *Won for him with us,* etc. Henry’s valour is praised by Odo of Deuil, Book VI, for defending the crossing of the river Maeander: “But the distinguished counts—Henry, son of Count Theobald, Thierry of Flanders, and William of Mâcon—rushed after them, the Turks, like a whirlwind, and more swiftly than words can tell forced their way through the steep bank, the rain of arrows, and the multitude of Turks.”]

In this matter, while offering rich thanks to your affection, we inform you concerning him so that you may promote him with more affectionate favour [Col. 1388B].

Let your affection know that our desire had been, in accordance with our will, to return with our princes to our kingdom. But the need of the Eastern Church compelled us to remain until Easter. Since the honour of our crown and the defence of our entire kingdom belong especially to your fidelity, we earnestly ask your valour to exercise vigilant diligence in guarding our kingdom, lest in the meantime the malice of wicked men be able to devise anything against our crown. For, with divine help, we shall without doubt take care to cross the sea immediately after Easter and return for the defence of our kingdom.

## LETTER LXXVIII. FROM THE ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS TO SUGER

He asks whether Suger will come to the assembly proclaimed at Soissons for affairs of the kingdom, because, if Suger cannot attend, he will order the count of Flanders and the bishops whom he had summoned not to come.

[Col. 1388C]

SAMSON, by God’s grace archbishop of Reims, to his dearest and heartfelt friend SUGER, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and sincere affection in the Lord.

As we had agreed, we have summoned the bishops and the count of Flanders, Thierry, to meet with us at Soissons on the Sunday on which “The voice of joy” is sung, in order to deliberate on the affairs of the kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 1388D] *“The voice of joy” is sung,* etc. This is the fifth Sunday after Easter, mentioned by Suger in Letter 74.]

They willingly promised that they would obey our summons. But because we do not know whether it will then be permitted and possible for you, we have decided to write to your affection, asking what you wish concerning this; for if you cannot come then, we shall have to direct the bishops and the count of Flanders not to come [Col. 1388D]. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIX. FROM THE ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX TO SUGER

To his most beloved lord SUGER, by God’s grace venerable [Col. 1389A] abbot of Saint-Denis, brother B., abbot of Clairvaux, greeting and prayers.

Our brethren of the House of God in the archdiocese of Bourges lack bread. We have heard that the grain of the lord king is abundant there and seems scarcely to be available for sale there. Therefore we ask you to order that they be given from that grain as much as seems fit to your prudence. For the lord king, while he was in this land, was accustomed to benefit them.

## LETTER LXXX. FROM KING LOUIS TO SUGER

He orders him diligently to protect and defend A. of Villerum and all those dependent upon him, because he had found him devoted to himself in foreign lands.

LOUIS, by the grace of God king of the Franks, to his dearest [Col. 1389B] SUGER, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and abundant affection.

We request and command your affection to take care diligently, in our place, to protect and defend our faithful A. of Villerum, together with all those who depend upon him, because he always strove to stand by us devotedly in foreign lands.

## LETTER LXXXI. FROM THE ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES TO SUGER

Concerning Juvenetus of Bourges and Arnulf, his son.

To the venerable and dearest lord SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis, P., humble servant of the Church of Bourges, greeting in the Lord.

Your eminence has summoned Juvenetus of Bourges and Arnulf, his son, to plead a case before [Col. 1389C] your presence. But because they are our friends and because we trust you, as we believe you trust us, we ask your affection to have the case for which you summoned them heard in the court of the lord king at Bourges, or to defer it until you come to Bourges. For Juvenetus is an old man and cannot endure the labour of riding. Let your prudence also know that each has a good reputation in the city, and that what has been reported to you against them, we believe, was done not from truth but from hatred. Write back to the provosts of Bourges what seems good to your prudence in this matter.

## LETTER LXXXII. FROM SUGER TO THE PROVOSTS OF BOURGES

He orders them to support Peter, abbot of Micy, who has been invested with the royal fief.

[Col. 1389D]

SUGER, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, to the provosts of Bourges and the servants of the lord king, greeting and affection.

Our venerable brother P., abbot of Micy, came before us; and because he appeared to have absented himself in accordance with our wish, he made satisfaction to us for it. We therefore invested him with the royal fief in such a manner [Col. 1390A] that, when the lord king returns by God’s grant, if he appears to have done anything against him, he shall present himself to make satisfaction according to the king’s pleasure.

We therefore command you, on behalf of the lord king and ourselves, to cherish, honour, and support the aforesaid abbot and those matters which concern him; and, wherever necessary, to extend to him a hand of help and counsel. We reserve for the lord king these and similar matters, which he will more suitably arrange for his honour and advantage.

## LETTER LXXXIII. FROM THE ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES TO SUGER

Concerning the tower of Saint-Palladius to be handed over to the king’s provosts.

To his venerable and most beloved brother SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis, P., humble servant of the Church of Bourges [Col. 1390B], greeting in the Lord.

What your prudence commanded, namely that the tower of Saint-Palladius be surrendered to the provosts of the lord king, was not burdensome to us, because we know that you provided this for our benefit. But Rainald of Craciac, unwilling to surrender it, said that he would send to Count R. [Ralph] and would act in the matter according to his command. We would not have delayed immediately to attack him after summoning the commune, except that we first wished to inform you. Let your affection therefore provide that he receives no support from Count R. For the harm might be greater not only to us but also to the lord king than to us. If we write too little concerning this affair, Master Audebert, a prudent and discreet man [Col. 1390C], whom we are sending to you, will inform you more fully.

## LETTER LXXXIV. FROM SUGER TO COUNT RALPH

Concerning restoring the stronghold of Saint-Palladius to the archbishop of Bourges, and entrusting the tower of Bourges to Guy of Herembrachen.

To the distinguished RADULF, by God’s grace count of Vermandois, SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and affection.

This young man, Rainald of Craciac, is hastening to you so that you may alter justice to the prejudice of the Archbishop of Bourges, by stripping him of the stronghold of Saint Palladius, with which he had been invested when the lord king set out for Jerusalem. But we, justice itself dictating it, ordered that the aforesaid archbishop be reinvested; this we shall in no way alter, and we wish you likewise to command it.

[Note: [Col. 1389D] “We wish you likewise to command it,” etc. Peter, Archbishop of Bourges, replies in the following letter: “We wish your affection to know that the tower of Saint Palladius has been surrendered, as you ordered.” He then adds: “Moreover, your brotherhood instructed us . . . that we should meet you [Col. 1390D] and together go to meet the lord king.” From these words it is clear that both letters were written in 1149, shortly before the king’s arrival.]

Concerning Guy of Herembrachen,

[Note: [Col. 1390D] In Letter 97 below he is called Guy of Rebrache.]

whom we had sent to fortify and guard the tower of Bourges, we inform your affection that the provosts of Bourges and Cadurcus have denied him the tower, although, after we had spoken with you, we again gave them that same order. [Col. 1391A] By means of the present messenger we wish you to order them this in writing.

## LETTER LXXXV. THE ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES TO SUGER

On the surrender of the tower of Saint Palladius.

To his dearest lord and friend Suger, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, P., humble minister of the Church of Bourges, greeting.

We wish your affection to know that the tower of Saint Palladius has been surrendered as you ordered. And although we do not yet possess it, we nevertheless render you manifold thanks for it, because we know for certain that you ordered it surrendered for our good and advantage. Yet, on the day after receiving your letters, we intended to proceed against Rainald with a large force of knights and foot-soldiers. [Col. 1391B] The more he threatened us on behalf of certain persons, whom for the present we do not wish to name, the more we armed ourselves against them and gathered strength.

Moreover, through Master Audebert, our messenger, your brotherhood instructed us to meet you and together go to meet the lord king. We shall gladly do this, both because the lord king’s arrival is most welcome to us, and because we wish and desire to honor your person, which is exceedingly dear to us. Moreover, we wish you to know that at Limoges we exhorted the Lord of Bordeaux and the bishops of Aquitaine, as we had discussed among ourselves, to remain faithful to the lord king; and, as they promised us, by the Lord’s help they will remain faithful to him. [Col. 1391C] Write back to us through the bearer of this letter whatever may please you.

## LETTER LXXXVI. THE COUNT OF VERMANDOIS TO SUGER

He writes that, while coming to Suger, he fell grievously ill at Crépy, even to the point of death; that, on the advice of the Archbishop of Reims and the Bishop of Soissons, he has fixed a day for dealing with his dispute with the Bishop of Noyon; and he asks Suger to be present at this meeting.

To Suger, by the grace of God Abbot of Saint-Denis, his beloved, R. [Ralph], Count of Vermandois, greeting and affection.

I had hastened on my journey to come to you as far as Crépy, and there, suffering a relapse, I was ill unto death, so that I despaired of life. But [Col. 1391D] by God’s grace I am better. Therefore, since I cannot come to you, pursue whatever seems good to you concerning the lord king’s affairs, and reserve whatever seems good; and I shall send to [Col. 1392A] you such of my men as you summon.

The Archbishop of Reims, Samson, and the Bishop of Soissons, Goslen, came to visit me. There we fixed a day for dealing with that dispute between myself and the Bishop of Noyon,

[Note: [Col. 1391D] “Between myself and the Bishop of Noyon . . . ,” etc. The dispute concerned the village of Laciniac, in which the Count of Vermandois was building a tower. Samson, Archbishop of Reims, brought this dispute to an end by an amicable settlement, in letters issued at Reims in the year of the Incarnate Word 1140, in the fourteenth year of the reign of Louis, most glorious king of the Franks, and the tenth year of our archiepiscopate. Among the Documents, vol. IX of *Gallia Christiana*, col. 380.]

namely, the fifteenth day from next Tuesday, at Causiac. And because you are greatly necessary to me in this matter, I ask your affection to come to us then, if you can. When that business has been completed, we shall proceed thence to royal affairs.

## LETTER LXXXVII. THE ARCHBISHOP OF BORDEAUX TO SUGER

He asks what Suger wishes done concerning the provostship of the city of Bordeaux, then vacant.

To his most beloved lord Suger, venerable by God’s grace Abbot of Saint-Denis, brother G. [Geoffrey], styled Bishop of the Church of Bordeaux, greeting and the service of devoted charity.

At the command of our lord the Roman pontiff, we had to go down as far as Limoges on account of the affair of the Archbishop of Bourges,

[Note: [Col. 1391D] “The lord of Bourges,” etc.: Peter, Archbishop of Bourges, who was in litigation with his archdeacon Bartholomew, a man of evil life and the worst reputation, as appears [Col. 1392D] in Peter’s Letter 136 among the Sugerian letters. We do not possess Eugenius’s letters on this matter.]

and then to proceed to Fontevraud, because of the need of that church.

[Note: [Col. 1392D] “The church of Fontevraud . . . ,” etc. In 1149 Petronilla, abbess of Fontevraud, died on 24 April; but Gilbert, Bishop of Poitiers, refused to bless Matilda in the place of the deceased unless she professed submission. Suger wrote to Eugenius on behalf of the nuns in Letter 88 among those published, in which he says concerning the Bishop of Poitiers: “You know, if it please your fatherhood, that the aforesaid bishop is accustomed to harass those subject to him.”]

Your messenger, the bearer of this letter, found us at Poitiers, where affairs of the land required us to remain. We therefore thought it proper to write to your prudence, so that, if it please you, we may learn from you—through the report of the bearer of this letter—the condition of the Gallican Church and the kingdom, whatever instructions you know should be given, and what you wish us to do.

We stand ready, therefore, lord abbot, and desire to stand at your command and good pleasure, as that of one whom from long ago we have loved with true charity in the Lord, [Col. 1392C] and in whom we have resolved, life permitting, to persevere. But what is to be done about the provostship of the city of Bordeaux? The office is vacant and the land is suffering. In this as in other matters we await your will, which we ask you to communicate to us in writing.

## LETTER LXXXVIII. SUGER TO POPE EUGENIUS

He asks him to favor the sisters of Fontevraud, whom the Bishop of Poitiers was harassing by demanding obedience from them and refusing to bless their abbess.

To his dearest lord and father, Eugenius, by God’s grace supreme and universal pontiff, Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis, the fullness of obedience and service.

On behalf of the sisters living at Fontevraud in holy religion acceptable to God, whom the Bishop of Poitiers, Gilbert, harasses by demanding their submission and refusing to bless their abbess, Matilda, we entreat as earnestly as we can the exalted authority of your holy apostolate. [Col. 1392D] As it belongs to your discernment to sustain the weakness of the weak by cherishing them, and to provide what is expedient for each, condescend to the frailty of their sex; and, because they rest upon your authority, retain them under your protection

[Note: [Col. 1393D] See Eugenius’s letter issued at Tusculum, on 26 August or 13 September.]

and do not wish them to be subjected to another, but grant them peace from this harassment.

For your discernment knows that it is not expedient for their souls to leave their monastic enclosure, nor under this or another pretext to join themselves to the world. You know, if it please your fatherhood, that the aforesaid bishop is accustomed to harass those subject to him. May it therefore please your excellence to free them from these troubles, and, in the abundance of your mercy, provide for them so that they may serve God in peace; cherish and protect them under the protection of God in heaven and your apostolic authority. [Col. 1393B] This is, indeed, so great a place of such great religious observance—a place which, when we were studying in those regions, we saw newly begun, and which, by God’s will, we hear and rejoice has now grown to nearly four or five thousand nuns.

## LETTER LXXXIX. POPE EUGENIUS TO SUGER

On the return of King Louis.

Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Blessed be God, who does not forsake those who hope in him,” etc. See Eugenius III, under the year 1153.

## LETTER XC. THE BISHOP OF AUXERRE AND THE ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX

They ask him to accept a truce between Hugh of Marigny and Hugh Borno. They then report that the king has landed in the nearer regions from Palestine.

[Col. 1393C]

To their dearest father and lord Suger, by God’s grace Abbot of Saint-Denis, Hugh, Bishop of Auxerre, and Bernard, called Abbot of Clairvaux, greeting and affection.

May it be the good pleasure of your condescension to hear our petition on this occasion. Hugh of Marigny, father of our most beloved brother, the Abbot of Trois-Fontaines, is at war with Hugh Borno, and many evils are either occurring or have occurred as a result. We beg and earnestly entreat you, so far as we can, to accept a truce between him and the aforesaid Hugh, [Col. 1393D] and his other adversaries, until the Advent of the Lord. Know that in this matter you will render us a great service.

Moreover, the lord pope has informed us certainly that, thanks be to God, the lord king has landed in the nearer regions.

[Note: [Col. 1393D] Pope Eugenius had previously informed Suger of this same fact [Col. 1394D] in the preceding letter.]

It is for you, and for those whom you judge appropriate, to hasten to meet him, as you know best.

## LETTER XCI. POPE EUGENIUS TO SUGER

Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1394A] “The letters which you sent us,” etc. See Eugenius III under the year 1153.

## LETTER XCII. POPE EUGENIUS TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS AND HIS SUFFRAGANS

Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers H., Archbishop of Sens, and his suffragans, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“With what devotion our dearest son Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, undertook the journey to Jerusalem,” etc. See above.

## LETTER XCIII. THE ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX TO SUGER

To his dearest lord and father Suger, by God’s grace reverend [Col. 1394B] Abbot of Saint-Denis, brother B., called Abbot of Clairvaux, greeting and devoted prayers in Christ.

“We send a poor abbot to a wealthy abbot,” etc. See among the letters of Saint Bernard, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXII.

## LETTER XCIV. KING LOUIS TO SUGER

He writes that he landed in Calabria on 29 July, and sets out the causes that delay his imminent return.

Louis, by the grace of God King of the Franks and Duke of Aquitaine, to the venerable Abbot of Saint-Denis, his dearest, by the same grace, greeting and abundant affection.

[Col. 1394C] From the desires of our own soul we also measure your feelings. For they reveal to us, by secret but sure promptings, how impatiently you have long borne our absence and how eagerly you await our presence. The letters of your summons bear witness to this,

[Note: [Col. 1394D] See Letter 57 above.]

in which your feelings burn with prayers for hastening our return, while your hearts labor more heavily through a friendly and indeed sympathetic sharing in our afflictions. For this reason we have taken all the more pleasure in sending you letters announcing our return, because we know that you will rejoice in them the more greatly.

In the regions of Calabria, according to God’s ordering, the first harbor of the desired safety of our return presented itself to us, and we landed on the fourth day before the Kalends of August [29 July]. There [Col. 1394D] we were received devoutly and reverently by the men of our most beloved Roger, King of Sicily; and we were most magnificently honored by him, through letters and messengers frequently sent to us. For nearly three weeks we awaited the arrival of the queen and our people. She had been carried by ship separately from us, and, after many circuits by land and sea, had at last, by God’s grace, reached Palermo in Sicily in a prosperous voyage, and was hastening thence to us in complete safety and joy.

The grave and uncertain illness, poised between death and life, of the Bishop of Langres, Godfrey, was also no slight cause of delay for us; and our intended conference with the aforesaid king likewise delayed the speed of our return. [Col. 1395A] Once we have seen him and prepared the other things that seem necessary for our journey, we shall take care to hasten our way, so that, by the Lord’s favor, you may rejoice in our embrace and we in yours.

## LETTER XCV. THE ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES TO SUGER

In the case of R. of Montfaucon.

To his dearest lord and friend Suger, venerable Abbot of Saint-Denis, P., humble minister of the Church of Bourges, greeting and true affection in Christ.

We do not know at whose instigation you ordered the provosts of Bourges to seize R. of Montfaucon unless he should first come before you at Paris for the execution of justice concerning one of his men, as he asserts—a matter in which he has presented, and still presents, himself ready to submit to justice in the lord king’s palace at Bourges, according to the usages and customs of that city. You also added that fixed and specified terms exist, on which, when summoned by you, he will gladly be ready on a suitable day to undergo judgment at Bourges.

Yet, for the preservation of the king’s fidelity and peace in our regions, since we know a great deal about the affairs of our land, we advise your prudence either to postpone that case for a time or to order him to appear for judgment before the court of the knights and servants of Bourges. Should it happen [Col. 1395C] that you travel into those regions on affairs of the kingdom, he will be prepared to abide by your judgment, command, or counsel.

## LETTER XCVI. KING LOUIS TO SUGER

He commands Suger to meet him secretly before his other followers as he approaches, so that he may become certain of rumors spread concerning the kingdom and know how he ought to conduct himself toward each person.

Louis, by the grace of God King of the Franks and Duke of the Aquitanians, to Suger, by the same grace Abbot of Saint-Denis, our most beloved and most faithful friend, greeting and our favor.

With what earnest desire we long to see the presence of your affection, we cannot set forth in this letter. [Col. 1395D] Now, however, we wish you to know the cause of our delay. After landing in Calabria, we waited fully three weeks for the queen, who had not yet landed. When she came to us, we directed our journey through Apulia by means of King Roger, who kept us with him [Col. 1396A] for three days. After we departed from him, the queen began to fall gravely ill. When she recovered from the illness, we immediately made for the apostolic lord,

[Note: [Col. 1395D] “To the apostolic lord,” etc.: in October. For in the short chronicle of Cassino one reads under the year 1149: “King Louis, returning from the regions of Jerusalem and honorably received by King Roger at Potenza, came to this monastery on 4 October; having been honorably received, he departed after the third day, conferred with the apostolic lord at Tusculum, and returned to France.”]

with whom we stayed for two days, and likewise for one day at Rome.

As we are hastening to come to you sound and safe, we command you not to delay coming secretly to us one day before our other friends. For, receiving many rumors about our kingdom and knowing no certainty concerning them, we wish to learn from you how we ought to act or conduct ourselves toward each individual. Let this be done so secretly that no one but your person may know what is contained in this letter.

## LETTER XCVII. CADURCUS TO ROTROU, COUNT OF THE PERCHE

Concerning the tower of Bourges entrusted to him and ordered by the Abbot of Saint-Denis to be surrendered: he asks him to procure from the Count of Vermandois that it be entrusted to Cadurcus and Rotrou for guarding.

[Col. 1396B]

To his lord Rotrou, Count of the Perche, Cadurcus, his friend and faithful man, and E. of Sal., greeting and affection.

We instructed you through your servant that we wished to speak with you. We had ordered that the Abbot of Saint-Denis should deliver the tower of Bourges to Guy of Rebrache,

[Note: [Col. 1395D] Above, in Letter 85, he is called Guy of Herembrachen.]

and to his knights and servants; and he had ordered me to surrender it promptly. We therefore inform you that we went to Count Ralph, and thence to the abbot, and spoke about the affair; and he replied to us that the abbot [Col. 1396C] was not doing this on his behalf or by his command.

Therefore we instruct you to notify Count Ralph by your letters, and to instruct your friend that the count himself should send privately to me, Cadurcus, your friend, his seal, bearing this: “I, Count Ralph, command you, Cadurcus, not to surrender the tower of Bourges to any man, as you swore to me, except to me or to my men.” Furthermore, know that we are your friends, and the city of Bourges is yours if you do this and if you wish to support us; and if you were soon to come to Bourges to see the Countess of Bourbon, you would act wisely.

[Note: [Col. 1396D] “You would act wisely.” From this letter it is clear who were the disturbers of the kingdom about whom Suger complained: (1) Robert, the king’s brother, from Letter 65; (2) Rotrou, Count of the Perche, his stepson; (3) Alix, Countess of Bourbon, wife of Archambald VII; (4) Cadurcus, the king’s cleric and chancellor; and perhaps Ralph, Count of Vermandois, Suger’s associate in the administration of the kingdom.]

Therefore, as quickly as you can, [Col. 1396D] send greetings in your name to me and to the knights and burgesses, and show them your service, your power in every place, and your goodwill.

## LETTER XCVIII. ODO, BISHOP OF BEAUVAIS, TO SUGER

He asks Suger to arrange Peter of Miliac’s absolution from anathema. Peter had been excommunicated for marrying the niece of Manasses of Bulles, although Manasses had had Peter’s aunt as his wife. The ground for absolution was that Peter, who was afflicting the district of Beauvais with evils, promised to take the cross if absolved.

[Col. 1397A]

To his lord and dearest friend Suger, by God’s grace venerable Abbot of Saint-Denis, Odo, by the same patience humble minister of the Church of Beauvais, greeting and affection in the Lord.

Your discernment does not fail to know with how many evils P. of Miliac afflicts the district of Beauvais. The maliciousness of this plague has also reached the king’s ears, and the report carried there has greatly angered the king. But now we have found a way by which both our country may be freed from so great a plague and his soul saved. For he promises the way of the Lord and that he will take the cross [Col. 1397B] if, by a dispensation of the Church, he is absolved from the bond of anathema under which he lies on account of the niece of Manasses of Bulles, whom he has as his wife.

Our Church judged that this sentence should be imposed upon Peter because the aforesaid Manasses, having this Peter’s aunt as his wife, repudiated her, on account of the woman’s frivolous breach of faith, and caused the marriage to be dissolved, as we think, unjustly. Therefore let your prudence approach the king on these matters and, by careful counsel, persuade him to request and command that the Lord of Clairvaux, Bernard, should, if it please him, absolve Peter by apostolic authority, just as he absolved Drogo of Monciac in a similar matter.

[Note: [Col. 1397D] “Matter.” Saint Bernard treats the affair of Drogo of Monciac in Letter 178 to Innocent II, written in 1139: “Would not the sword of Phinehas have been drawn forth most promptly and most justly to condemn the incestuous union of Drogo and Mili? But it was put to shame and thrust back, indeed by the obstacle of apostolic protection. Shame! What laughter this affair has aroused and still arouses among the enemies of the Church—and even among those very persons through whose fear or favor, perhaps, we have been diverted from the straight path! Friends are put to shame, the faithful are insulted, bishops are brought into reproach and contempt; and while their righteous judgments are despised, great injury is also done to your authority.”]

Thus our country will be freed from this diabolical tinder and contagion of public evil; for, if he remains, [Col. 1397C] as we suppose, he will breed the unrest of every sort of sedition.

## LETTER XCIX. HUGH, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS, TO SUGER

That he should receive the church of Saint Columba at Sens under his protection.

To the venerable Suger, by God’s grace Abbot of Saint-Denis, Hugh, Archbishop of Sens, greeting and affection.

It is our duty to reveal to you, to whom responsibility has been entrusted, the offenses of the enemies of the kingdom and of God’s Church; it is yours to correct them. We therefore complain to your prudence concerning R., the mayor of Sarmasie, in regard to the church of Saint Columba at Sens, because he is a man who, unless he fears the censure of the court, despises justice. [Col. 1397D] For he oppresses in every way he can the church of Saint Columba, whose servant he is; and, forgetting his service and servile status under a certain wrongful hereditary mayoralty, he has risen against the monks and makes himself, as it were, lord of their land.

Having been summoned by us, he evades justice; he even grievously harasses our priest with threats because that priest had excommunicated him. Therefore we command and ask your prudence to extinguish at one stroke, by the breath of your mouth, the so many and such great offenses of one peasant; and, correcting what he has done wickedly, [Col. 1398A] restrain him with vigorous force, lest hereafter a servant should presume so greatly against a lord, a criminal against holy persons, one man against many.

## LETTER C. COUNT RALPH TO SUGER

He reports that the king will not arrive before the feast of All Saints; he advises him in the meantime to call the king’s servants to account.

To his beloved Suger, by God’s grace Abbot of Saint-Denis, Ralph, Count of Vermandois, greeting and affection.

[Col. 1398B] The king’s messenger Bartholomew came to me, bringing his letters; and, insofar as I gather from his words, the king will not come so soon—perhaps not until the feast of All Saints, or even Saint Martin’s. It is therefore fitting that in the meantime you summon the king’s servants to render accounts, so that you may know what certain answer to give the lord king. But if you do not wish to do this without me, I shall come eight days from Monday.

## LETTER CI. ODO, BISHOP OF BEAUVAIS, TO SUGER

He reports disturbance arisen in the city and says that Count Ralph of Vermandois intends to expel the Count of Clermont from it. He therefore asks Suger to appoint a conference for restoring peace.

[Col. 1398C]

To his lord and father Suger, by God’s grace venerable Abbot of Saint-Denis, Odo, by the same grace humble Bishop of Beauvais, greeting, in an abundance of peace, to one who bears salvation to those in need.

By writing and by the spoken words of our clerics, we have previously made known to your fatherhood the misery that we suffer, and we still await the remedy we hoped for from you. We perceive the intention and design of Count R., namely that through this disturbance and the delay of peace he seeks to expel our friend, the venerable and pitiable Count of Clermont,

[Note: [Col. 1398D] “To expel the count”: Rainald, Count of Clermont, who had earlier married Adelaide, mother of Ralph, Count of Vermandois. But we nowhere discover what dispute was at issue between them.]

For if he labored for peace, he could have calmed all the sedition, [Col. 1398D] since, if he himself spoke, it would be done, and no one would disregard his command. But since they have a truce until next Sunday, let your discernment take pains to name a place and day for a conference which you can and will attend. We trust in God’s goodness that in your presence this tumult will be pacified, [Col. 1399A] and that reconciliation will not escape the hand of your wisdom; or, if it is wholly impossible to provide for peace, they will bind themselves mutually to a long truce.

Nor is it surprising if we seek peace so earnestly and complain of war for many reasons, which the bearer of this letter, a member of our household, will explain credibly to your gracious counsel no less fully than from our own lips.

## LETTER CII. THE BISHOP OF CHARTRES TO SUGER

He complains of the provost of Yenville, who had risen against him, and asks that Suger not refer the case to be tried by another.

To his dearest friend Suger, by God’s grace Abbot of Saint-Denis, G. [Geoffrey], humble minister of the Church of Chartres, greeting and affection in the Lord.

Your prudence knows that the lord king’s kindness has received our affairs under its protection, lest malicious persons should be allowed against us anything beyond what right requires. And since, by God’s will, you have been appointed to restrain the excesses of the wicked, we confidently hope that under such a judge our cause will not be endangered and the dignity of the Church will not be diminished.

We have said this beforehand because the provost of Yenville rises violently against us, harasses our men with false accusations, and is more intent upon greed than obedient to justice. When we asked him to grant us a delay, he refused, fearing that something might be lost from his gains if our case should come to be examined before you. [Col. 1399C] We therefore implore your discernment in this matter: do not place the examination of this affair before anyone other than yourself; and until it can be investigated by you, order a complete truce.

## LETTER CIII. HUGH, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN, TO SUGER

That he should restrain the depredations of Hugh Brostin.

To his venerable father and lord Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis, Hugh, humble minister of the Church of Rouen, greeting and favor.

The abbot and convent of Saint-Wandrille complain, and we complain with and for them, concerning Hugh Brostin. He harasses and takes away the ancient alms of the kings [Col. 1399D] of France at Calceium, which has been undisturbed and free since the time of Saint Ausbert, our predecessor. Now therefore, because you are charged to provide for matters of this kind in the lord king’s place, we command and beseech you to order the aforesaid Hugh to leave the said tithe in peace and not presume in any way thereafter to lay hands upon it.

As we have heard, he commits this injury because he has been excommunicated. It is necessary, venerable father and lord, that your hand restrain his robbery and tyranny when ecclesiastical justice does not recall him to the way of truth.

## LETTER CIV. GOSLEN, BISHOP OF CHARTRES, TO SUGER

He excuses himself for being unable to attend the solemnity of Saint-Denis, though summoned by Suger, because of the unexpected arrival of the Bishop of Auxerre.

[Col. 1400A]

To the lord Suger, by God’s grace venerable Abbot of Saint-Denis, Goslen, by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Chartres, greeting and devoted service.
