Out of reverence for the precious martyrs, blessed Dionysius, apostle of the Gauls, and his companions, and because of the command of your excellence—to whom we desire in every respect to render obedience with all our power—we had resolved to attend the most celebrated solemnity to which you summoned us. We ought to venerate and observe it, above other solemnities, with a more abundant devotion, almost as by hereditary right, because of our lord predecessor. But the unexpected arrival of the lord Bishop of Auxerre, Hugh, [Col. 1400B] has kept us against our will; having received word of it, we expect him on the coming Sunday. For we fear that he will hereafter suspect us of acting against him if he should see that we had avoided the presence which he is now for the first time offering us.

## LETTER CV. PETER, ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES, TO SUGER

On the return of King Louis.

To Suger, by God’s grace venerable Abbot of Saint-Denis, Peter, humble minister of the Church of Bourges, greeting and affection.

We render boundless thanks to your exalted person because you informed us of the lord king’s return and gave us advance warning to meet him with you. We would most gladly meet him, and earnestly ask [Col. 1400C] your affection that, if he comes by Saint-Gilles, you may come by way of us and pass through our province. For we desire to serve you and offer whatever honor we can. But if he comes by Cluny, we shall gladly go there with you as well. When you learn that he is approaching, inform us, so that we may know when we ought to join your journey. If we ourselves learn anything certain, we shall report it to you. Write back through the bearer of this letter whatever may please you.

## LETTER CVI. POPE EUGENIUS TO SUGER

Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and [Col. 1400D] apostolic blessing.

“Our sons A. and Her., clerics of the Church of Meaux,” etc. See Eugenius under the year 1153.

## LETTER CVII. THE SAME TO THE SAME

Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Certain priest R.,” etc. See the same place.

## LETTER CVIII. THE SAME TO H., ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son H., Archbishop of Sens, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1401A] “One of your priests, coming to Rome before our presence,” etc. See the same place.

## LETTER CIX. THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF CHARTRES TO SUGER

They complain of Hugh of Brétigny and Ebrard the viscount.

To the venerable Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis, R. [Robert], dean, and all the clergy of the Church of Blessed Mary at Chartres, greeting and true affection in Christ.

We have considered it fitting to complain and make known to your provident prudence that Hugh of Brétigny, obstinate and insolent, shamefully disregarding the king’s commands and yours, has never kept any of the agreements which he made in our presence with our Church and ourselves; [Col. 1401B] nor has he wished to restore anything of what he took away. Moreover, the lord E.,

[Note: [Col. 1401D] Ebrard, son of Hugh of Puteaux.]

the viscount, glorying in his perverse persistence in wickedness, is unwilling to make any reparation at all for the wrongs he committed against the Church of Blessed Mary and ourselves.

Therefore, trusting in your kindness and justice, so frequently shown to us in our necessities and in the affairs of Blessed Mary—and all the more because our most loving lord king entrusted us to your guardianship when he departed—we have recourse to you as to a father and patron. We most earnestly request that, continuing the care you have rightly undertaken for our Church and ourselves, you strike these obstinate and presumptuous men with the rod of correction, so that they may be compelled to restore what they took away [Col. 1401C] and deterred from doing the like thereafter. Farewell; and, if you please, report to us through the bearer of this letter what you decide in this matter.

## LETTER CX. THE ABBOT OF SAINT PANTALEON TO SUGER

He thanks him for the kindness shown to a certain boy, his nephew.

To his lord and most loving father Suger, by God’s grace Abbot of Saint-Denis, W. [Wolbero], Abbot of Saint Pantaleon at Cologne, whatever he can offer most devotedly in body and spirit.

It is written that charity is kind; and indeed you showed clearly enough that such charity dwells in you through your display of kindness and compassion, when, as I entreated your excellence on behalf of my boy-nephew while you were at Reims, [Col. 1401D]

[Note: [Col. 1401D] Namely, at the Council of Reims, held in mid-Lent in 1148.]

you granted my request with such fatherly kindness. Although for this reason I owe you abundant thanks, I would nevertheless like to learn from your own heart what service, among those things that touch your concerns, I ought especially to render you in return for this kindness. If anything must be done through your messengers in the city of Cologne which concerns your wish or advantage, I and the boy’s father are ready to serve you and yours in every affair. Farewell in the Lord, and show us, your servants, in the boy the work of compassion which you have begun.

## LETTER CXI. THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS TO SUGER

On the return of King Louis.

[Col. 1402A]

Hugh, by God’s grace Archbishop of Sens, to his dearest Suger, venerable Abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and affection.

We had written to you concerning the lord king’s arrival; but, having afterward received more certain news of it, we write to you again. For we saw Brother Galeran, who keeps the house of the Temple at Paris, returning from the lord king; he left him at the Forum Novum near Piacenza. We can no longer delay, but have already set out to meet the lord king. For the knight told us that on this very coming Sunday he will lodge at Cluny.

Therefore, if it please you, [Col. 1402B] we shall wait for you at Auxerre until the following Monday. For we greatly desire to have you as lord and companion on the journey. But if this is agreeable to you, send your messenger ahead, so that on Monday morning at Auxerre he may make your intention known to us.

### LETTER CXII. PETER, ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES, TO SUGER. On the same subject.

To his venerable brother and dearest friend Suger, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, Peter, humble servant of the Church of Bourges, greeting and affection in the Lord.

Certain persons came to Bourges and said that the lord king was drawing near and would arrive shortly. But we could not learn from them with certainty by what route he would come. We were awaiting your messenger, and still await him, as you informed us, so that, according to what you command us, we may hasten to meet him. May it therefore please your Highness to write back to us whether you have received any certain news concerning him: by what route you are to meet him, and where and when you wish us to meet him with you.

### LETTER CXIII. THE SAME TO THE SAME. On Bartholomew the archdeacon.

To his venerable and dearest brother Suger, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, Peter, humble servant of the Church of Bourges, greeting and affection in the Lord.

We received letters from your Highness, in which you directed us to be at Vézelay on Thursday, or at Corbigny on Friday. But after we had sent our messenger to you, we were told that the lord king had received our archdeacon Bartholomew, who came to meet him, into his favor, and had interceded for him with the lord pope; and that he also intended to address us on his behalf and urgently request that we desist from what we have begun for the honor and dignity of God’s house.

Trusting therefore in you—not because of our merits, but because you love God and His honor—we wish to forewarn your prudence, so that you may secure from the lord king that he will not wish to uphold that notorious man, of whose disreputable conduct you have heard much, nor intercede with us for him. For we fear that it would occasion offense if he were to address us concerning a matter that would have no effect. We can neither tolerate nor ought to tolerate his criminal life, nor indulge his offenses. For what we are doing concerning him we undertook on the advice of many religious persons, who would be deeply ashamed if we desisted, and would judge the countenance of God’s Church to have been, as it were, dishonored if they saw such a man prevail against the holiness of their counsel. May it therefore please your affection to write us your advice. For if you approve, we shall be at Corbigny next Friday, if we can possibly do so.

### LETTER CXIV. COUNT THEOBALD TO SUGER. He wishes to know whether Reginald of Courtenay has made satisfaction for money taken from merchants.

To Suger, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, his dearest friend, Theobald, count of Blois, greeting.

Reginald of Courtenay informed me that he had satisfied your will and pleasure concerning the merchants’ money. If this is so, and if he has made satisfaction to you concerning it, be pleased to inform me by your letters through this messenger. Farewell.

### LETTER CXV. THE COUNT OF VERMANDOIS TO SUGER. He asks him to obtain the longest possible truce concerning certain disputes, and to order the king’s servants to assemble at Paris.

To Suger, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, R. [Ralph], count of Vermandois, greeting and affection.

Because I am seriously inconvenienced, I cannot come to you on Tuesday or Wednesday; and on Thursday I must conduct some business which I cannot possibly leave. Therefore I ask you to obtain as long a truce as you can concerning the wars and disputes about which you wrote to me. On the coming Sunday or Monday, however, I shall certainly come to you; and the lord king’s servants, as I instructed you in other letters, can conveniently be ready to meet us at Paris. Then we shall be able suitably to settle the lord king’s affairs. Whatever you wish concerning these matters and others, command, and I shall do it.

### LETTER CXVI. COUNT THEOBALD TO SUGER. He reports that Reginald of Courtenay despoiled merchants under the king’s protection, and promises assistance in avenging the injury.

To Suger, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, his dearest friend, Theobald, count of Blois, greeting and affection.

[Col. 1404A] I wish it to be known to you that Reginald of Courtenay [Note: [Col. 1403] Reginald of Courtenay, or of Mont-Aroi, had departed for Palestine with King Louis; hence this letter must be assigned to the year 1149.] has inflicted a very great dishonor upon the king and upon you, who are guardian of his realm. For he seized the king’s merchants, who had paid their tolls at Orléans and Sens and all their customary dues throughout the king’s land, and took away their goods. Therefore I order you to direct him, on behalf of the king and yourselves, to release and restore the king’s merchants with all their goods in full. If he refuses to do so, and you wish to exact vengeance from him and march against him with an army, notify me; and I shall assist you in taking vengeance upon him.

### LETTER CXVII. THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS TO SUGER. On the return of King Louis.

[Col. 1404B] Hugh, by God’s grace archbishop of Sens, to his dearest Suger, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and affection.

We wish your affection to know that, the day after I came to you at Château-Nanton, a boy passed through Sens whom the lord of Beauvais was sending to his mother, in order that he might announce to her the arrival of the lord king. This boy said that the lord king had drawn so near that he would lodge at Cluny on the coming Wednesday. The boy spoke thus to our servants, and they reported it to us. We have therefore taken care to inform you of this, so that you may inquire into the certainty of the matter; and we ask you to report to us what you learn and send word what we ought to do.

### LETTER CXVIII. CADURCUS, CLERK, TO SUGER. On money which he had lent the king and which was to be paid him from the revenues of Poitou.

[Col. 1404C]

To his patron and protector Suger, by God’s grace his dearest and venerable lord, abbot of Blessed Denis, Cadurcus, clerk and his man, styled chancellor of the king of the Franks, greeting and service.

You know, master and lord, with what pious regard the lord king, at his departure from Reims, left me under your protection and safeguard; how mercifully, through my hand and not without an abundance of tears, he entrusted me to you. Therefore, trusting in the holiness of your goodness, I write to you confidently and am not ashamed to disclose to you what is necessary for me. For after God and the lord king, I have no one to whose protection I can or ought to flee except the refuge of your generosity, from whom and through whom I am certain of receiving consolation and attaining the fruitful result of my petition.

Remember the lord king’s command, which he gave principally to you and secondarily to Count R. [Ralph] at Reims: namely, that the money which I had lent him should be paid me in full from the revenues of Poitou. Since you do not doubt that this has not yet been carried into effect, I ask you, master and lord, that if any of the men of Poitou comes to you on the affairs of that land, it may please you to detain them until I meet you at Reims. Thereafter, if you command it, as soon as I come to you—or after the council has ended—I shall be ready, with God’s help, to go to Poitou according to your advice. Farewell in Christ; remember me.

[Note: [Col. 1405D] The Council of Reims, in the year 1148, as we have said, was held in mid-Lent.]

### LETTER CXIX. R. OF MONTFAUCON TO SUGER. He states that he is ready, on a suitable day, to submit to judgment according to the customs of Bourges concerning a man who denied him his service.

To his most reverend lord Suger, venerable abbot of Blessed Denis, R. [Rainald] of Montfaucon, greeting and due reverence.

It pleased your dignity, as had been represented to you, to summon me to Paris on the Sunday following the Assumption of Blessed Mary [Note: [Col. 1405D] “Following the Assumption . . . .” This day may be understood in the years 1147, 1148, or 1149, during which Suger administered the kingdom; to come nearer to the true year, we select the middle one.] concerning one of my men, who denied both himself and his service to me. On this matter I was ready, and still am, to submit myself to judgment in the palace of the lord king, or before the lord archbishop, according to the usages and customs of the knights and servants of Bourges. Nevertheless, for your affairs and those of the kingdom, you may draw me, at your pleasure, even to the furthest boundaries of the realm.

Indeed, if it pleases your Excellency to summon me concerning any controversy, we men of Bourges have fixed and definite limits, beyond which we are not compelled except by legal warrant [Note: [Col. 1405D] “We are compelled,” etc. Peter, archbishop of Bourges, attests the same in his letter to Suger, among the Sugerian letters no. 95, printed above.]. But I shall be ready, at one of the specified limits, to undergo judgment on a suitable day according to the usages and customs of Bourges. Farewell always in the Lord.

### LETTER CXX. THE COUNT OF BLOIS TO SUGER. He reports an injury inflicted by Guarin, son of Salomon, viscount of Sens, upon money-changers of Vézelay coming to his fair at Provins.

[Col. 1405C]

To Suger, by God’s grace abbot of Blessed Denis, his dearest friend, T. [Theobald], count of Blois, greeting and affection.

I inform you of the injury and dishonor which Salomon, viscount of Sens, has inflicted upon the king and upon you, who hold his land in guardianship, and of the loss and dishonor inflicted upon me. For Guarin, his son, seized money-changers from Vézelay who were coming to my approaching fair at Provins, on the king’s road between Sens and Bray. Salomon himself and the king’s provost of Sens had placed them under the king’s security by oath; yet he took from them goods worth, as they assert, seven hundred pounds and more.

Therefore I command and ask you to take offense at the breach of the king’s road, and to command Salomon firmly that, without any pretext or delay, he restore and cause restored whatever has been taken from the money-changers. For Salomon is in your power and can resist you no more than any man-at-arms. When you have so decided, report to me through the bearer of this letter what you have done in the matter. I would not allow this injury, which tends toward the destruction of my fairs, to remain unavenged.

Moreover, you know that you informed me, and I instructed you, that I should speak with you if you sent me word that this was your wish, on the Monday before Pentecost [Note: [Col. 1406D] “Before Pentecost,” etc. Since King Louis embarked upon the journey to Jerusalem after Pentecost in 1147, this letter, written before Pentecost, belongs to 1148, or perhaps the following year.] at Lagny; yet you sent me no word concerning it. Therefore I instruct you to tell me through this messenger whether you will come to Lagny on the aforesaid day, so that I too may go there to meet you, if you wish to come.

### LETTER CXXI. THE BISHOP OF AUXERRE TO SUGER. He commends to him the wife and children of his late friend Robert the physician.

[Col. 1406B]

To his dearest lord and father Suger, by God’s grace abbot of Blessed Denis, Hugh, called bishop of Auxerre, greeting and affection.

We have both seen and heard that you held Robert the physician very dear during his life. Since he has entered upon the way of all flesh, we trust in your kindness and ask that you extend to his wife and children the same affection which you had for the aforesaid Robert: treat them kindly for the father’s sake, and preserve intact for your service those things which Robert held.

### LETTER CXXII. THE COUNT OF NEVERS TO SUGER. On the same subject.

[Col. 1406C]

To his lord and friend Suger, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, G. [Note: [Col. 1406D] This Count G. who calls Suger his friend appears to be none other than William II of that name. Since he withdrew to the Charterhouse in 1147, we assign this letter and the two following letters on the same subject to 1146 or 1147.] count of Nevers, greeting and service.

We do not doubt that it is known to you and plain to us that R. [Robert] the physician, who has entered upon the way of all flesh, was a kind man and of good service. May his wife and children experience the benefit of his service and kindness, through the assistance and counsel of his friends. Therefore we command and ask you to love his wife and children for the love of God and of ourselves, and to do them good.

### LETTER CXXIII. THE ABBOT OF FERRIÈRES TO SUGER. He asks for a respite in paying the balance of money obtained from the monastery of Ferrières for the holy expedition.

[Col. 1406D]

To the reverend father and lord Suger, abbot of Blessed Denis, John, servant of the monastery of Ferrières, submission and obedience.

We must very frequently have recourse to your Fatherhood and your Excellency. Most severely pressed by the lord king’s assessment, we have paid, as best we could, twenty pounds since you left us. But owing to grievous poverty, we cannot at present obtain the remainder at all, because [read perhaps: *quia*, “since”] they are still detained in their harvests and other occupations. Therefore I humbly beseech your reverence to grant a suitable respite and time to me and to the provost, who threatens to seize our men on this account, so that we may obtain it. Farewell. May the strong hand of almighty God govern you.

### LETTER CXXIV. THE COUNT OF NEVERS TO SUGER. He writes of a conference held at Orléans with Geoffrey of Donzy, and of a day for battle appointed by the king for Geoffrey and one of the count’s knights.

[Col. 1407B]

To his dearest son Suger, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, William, count of Nevers, greeting in the Lord.

I have received the outcome of that conference which, as you know, was arranged at Orléans with Lord Geoffrey of Donzy [Note: [Col. 1407D] This controversy of the count of Nevers with Geoffrey of Donzy preceded in time that mentioned by the anonymous author of the *History of Louis VII*: “At that time Geoffrey of Gien gave one of his daughters in marriage to Stephen of Sancerre; this he did by cunning counsel, for he thought that Stephen could protect him from the attacks of the count of Nevers. Geoffrey even bestowed Gien upon that daughter as her marriage portion,” etc. “But Geoffrey had previously married the same daughter to Ancel of Traînel, giving him as marriage portion Nully and everything he held there, together with what he held in the borough of Ulchay.” The controversy seems to have arisen from the diminution of the fief without consultation of the overlord, who was then in Palestine.] with the king acting as intermediary. But matters were handled at Bonneval very differently from what I had hoped. I make no complaint against my lord the king, but I do not approve the counsel which he had with him; when I see you, I shall relate it to you more fully.

I command you, my lord, and urgently ask you by every means to come, for my sake, to Étampes on the vigil of the Chair of Saint Peter. For on that day my lord king has appointed a day for battle between Geoffrey of Donzy and one of my knights. Farewell.

### LETTER CXXV. POPE EUGENIUS TO SUGER.

Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Concerning the controversy and disagreement,” etc. See Eugenius III, under the year 1153.

### LETTER CXXVI. THE ABBOT OF CLUNY TO SUGER.

To his venerable and intimate friend, Lord Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, greeting and sincere affection.

[Col. 1407D] How greatly you are in our heart we would more gladly show you in person than communicate in your absence. But since hostile fortune has begrudged us your bodily presence—which we greatly hoped to see among us, especially at the king’s arrival—we now say this briefly to you. It falls short of the love which we have for your person if we say that all that is ours is yours, since we ourselves are yours more fully than you believe.

As to the present matter, we commend to you the prior of Nogent and his affairs, and earnestly ask you to write, concerning the matters which he himself will explain to you, to the lord bishop of Chartres.

### LETTER CXXVII. THE SAME TO THE SAME.

To his venerable and dearest lord and friend Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, greeting and the sincere affection of love in the Lord.

Because we have loved your reverence from long ago, and love it in the charity of Christ, we do not doubt that we too are loved by you. Therefore we do not hesitate frequently to ask you concerning the various circumstances of our affairs. Now we ask your affection on behalf of our house of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, which, because of the weakness of our most beloved brother Lord O., has been greatly diminished both spiritually and temporally and is daily more and more diminished.

Accordingly, yielding to his infirmity, we have, according to our custom, released him from the care of the aforesaid house and substituted in his place our beloved brother and son Lord Simon, formerly subprior of that same place, because he is greatly loved by us and our brothers for his honorableness and excellent character. We ask your prudence, for God’s sake and out of love for us, to regard him with affection and give him your assistance and counsel.

### LETTER CXXVIII. THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS TO SUGER.

[Col. 1408C]

Hugh, by God’s grace archbishop of Sens, to his dearest son Suger, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and affection.

Blessed be God, who has placed our cause in your hands and has appointed as judge the very man whom we would choose, if the choice were granted us. For although we do not at all doubt our archdeacon’s innocence, we nevertheless prefer your judgment, whose fairness we know, whose loyalty and gracious favor we have experienced. Farewell.

### LETTER CXXIX. THE BISHOP OF CHÂLONS TO SUGER. He asks him to act as his advocate and intercessor with the king.

[Col. 1408D]

To Suger, father and lord, by God’s grace the worthily reverend abbot of Saint-Denis, Bartholomew, by His patience priest of the Church of Châlons, the affection of sincere love.

Since the affection of your love toward us is abundant, we rejoice greatly because we have experienced its fullness in our past necessities and expect it in future ones. We therefore ask the mercy of your fatherhood to be for us a merciful advocate and intercessor with our most gracious lord the king. Before his arrival we endured many anxieties, as you know, in which we received counsel and remedy only from your clemency; after his return, moreover, being no less hindered by the frequent invasions of enemies, we have been unable to visit his magnificence as the due right of our humility required [Note: [Col. 1409D] “We have been unable to visit,” etc. Bartholomew had been elected bishop of Châlons while the king was on pilgrimage.].

Trusting greatly therefore in your generosity, we most devotedly beseech you to report to the lord king the injuries and persecutions we have suffered, and the losses of our goods which we have unjustly sustained. We are ready shortly to approach his presence, as our desire longs to do; and, according to the ability of our resources—however little that may be in comparison with the fullness of our will—we shall serve him from what is ours as our father and lord. Farewell.

### LETTER CXXX. A., BISHOP OF RENNES, TO SUGER. He writes that he had necessarily to go first as far as Nantes before coming to him, but will come in the first week of Lent.

To his dearest lord Suger, by God’s grace the reverend abbot of Saint-Denis, A. [Alan], humble servant of the Church of Rennes, greeting and dutiful affection.

We render abundant thanks to your holiness because you invited us, as though you were greatly indebted to us, to support the poverty of our exile. We therefore wish your fatherhood to know that, before coming to you, necessity required us to travel as far as Nantes, owing to the needs of that land and our own affairs. But, God willing, we shall come to you in the first week of Lent, as to our lord and patron [Note: [Col. 1409D] “God willing, we shall come.” Perhaps to attend one of the several assemblies which Suger convened for the restoration of the Jerusalem expedition, as his biographer testifies. Hence we judge that this letter may be assigned to the year 1150.]. Farewell.

### LETTER CXXXI. THE CLERGY OF BLESSED MARTIN OF TOURS TO SUGER. They ask him to attend a matter to be conducted at Meaux in the legate’s presence against the clerks of Saint-Maurice.

To Suger, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, the entire clergy of the church of Blessed Martin, greeting and the integrity of friendship.

It is a common and worn proverb that human things vanish with the passage of time. In time the joy of every pleasure dies; in time a mother forgets her sorrow. In this single respect the power and worth of friendship readily shines forth: time does not diminish its strength, nor age consume it. Nothing more splendid than this blessing gives the church of Blessed Martin cause for glory—that it has deserved to obtain your friendship.

But because there is no shame in seeking from the secret heart of a dear friend what one needs, the church of Blessed Martin, needing your counsel, humbly entreats and asks you, its special friend, to set aside your occupations and be willing to attend a matter to be handled in the legate’s presence [Note: [Col. 1409D] The legate was Alberic, bishop of Ostia, who in 1145, on the Sunday *Isti sunt dies*—that is, Passion Sunday—dedicated the monastery of Faremoutiers, as is recorded in an instrument cited by Duplessis among the proofs of his *History of Meaux*, p. 40: “Alberic, by God’s grace bishop of Ostia and legate of the apostolic see, to all the faithful, etc. We wish it to be known that, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1145—or 1146, if the year is reckoned from the Kalends of January—while exercising apostolic legation throughout the whole kingdom of France, and with our venerable brothers, namely the bishops of Paris, Meaux, and Troyes, present with us, on the Sunday *Isti sunt dies* we solemnly, by God’s grace, dedicated the venerable monastery of Faremoutiers, where a religious congregation of more than a hundred women is seen to serve God. The same monastery,” etc.] in the city of Meaux, against the clerks of Saint-Maurice, on the third day after the Sunday on which is sung, *Isti sunt dies* (“These are the days”).

### LETTER CXXXII. THE ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX TO SUGER.

[Col. 1410B] To his most loving father and lord Suger, by God’s grace abbot of Blessed Denis, Bernard, called abbot of Clairvaux, greeting and such prayers as he can offer in the Lord.

“I received most gladly the message brought by the master of the Temple and Brother John,” etc. See among the letters of Saint Bernard, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXII.

### LETTER CXXXIII. THE ABBOT OF CLUNY TO SUGER.

To our venerable and heart-dear friend, Lord Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, fullness of present and eternal salvation.

I grieve—and grieve beyond what I can express—that I cannot attend your sacred assembly, which the lord king has summoned at Chartres on the advice of your wisdom and that of other wise men. Believe an intimate friend, believe one who speaks the truth: I truly wish to attend but cannot; and because I cannot, I grieve. For who would not grieve at being unable to attend so holy an assembly, where no one will seek private gain, no one what is his own, but what belongs to Jesus Christ?

For no ordinary matter is being undertaken, but discussion concerns that matter than which none is greater—indeed, which is greatest of all. Is it not the greatest of all matters to provide and labor lest what is holy be given to dogs; lest the places where stood the feet of Him who worked salvation in the midst of the earth be again trampled by the feet of the wicked; lest royal Jerusalem, consecrated by prophets, apostles, and the Savior of all Himself, and that noble Antioch, metropolis of all Syria, again be subjected to blasphemous and impious men; lest the saving Cross itself, now, it is said, besieged by the impious, be captured as it was formerly by Chosroes; lest the very Lord’s sepulcher, which hitherto, according to the prophet, had been glorious throughout the whole world, perhaps be torn up by the roots, as they threaten to do?

Therefore I would most gladly, as I have said, have taken part in this undertaking, so holy and so necessary, to which you, venerable man, wished to invite my humility, if I could have done so in any way. Many things impede this journey of mine; but among them two are special. One is the manifold infirmity of my body, which I have suffered almost continuously from Christmas until this time. The other is a great assembly of priors, whom, before I knew anything of the matters you communicated, I had ordered to come to Cluny at almost the beginning of Lent, on the very day appointed for your assembly at Chartres, for deliberation about an unavoidable matter.

May your united reverence, so dear to me, therefore receive calmly, if it please you, my excuse—not feigned but true—and regard my absence as excused both in your own eyes and in those of others.

### LETTER CXXXIV. THE ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS TO SUGER. He excuses himself for being unable to attend the conference summoned at Chartres to assist the Eastern Church, because the archbishop of Sens was not ashamed to diminish his primatial rights.

Unibert, by God’s grace archbishop of the holy Church of Lyons, to his dearest and venerable Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, eternal salvation in Christ Jesus.

No faithful and God-fearing person is unaware with what grief and tears we ought to sympathize with the Eastern Church, now placed amid so many and such great miseries. The calamity and affliction it suffers itself makes clear with what vigilance and zeal every religious person and worshiper of God ought to labor for its assistance.

But because, by reason of our office and the right of our primacy, you have invited us, on behalf of the lord king and the magnates of the realm, to the conference to be held at Chartres, let your charity know that, so long as the archbishop of Sens is not ashamed, in this very cause of primacy, to derogate from our rights and to remain contumacious and rebellious against apostolic commands, it would shame us to proceed to those parts where the pope is opposed and the Church of Lyons is deprived of its due honor.

Moreover, we are detained by another great and unforeseen impediment: Lord Ylio [Note: [Col. 1411D] Ylio, or Hilio, abbot of Saint-Just outside the walls of Lyons—the church formerly dedicated to the Holy Maccabees took the name of Saint-Just from the time this saint was buried in that basilica.]—a truly great man and, as it were, preeminent in the Church of Lyons—is gravely ill and seems, as his disease worsens daily, to be nearing his end. Since the castles and fortifications of our church are in his hands, we have deferred going farther away for the present at the request and advice of our clergy, lest perhaps in our absence the children of this world, who always oppose churches, find an opportunity for malice and inflict an incurable wound upon the Church of Lyons.

For these reasons we send to you this venerable brother of ours and beloved son of our church, Lord Stephen, formerly archbishop of Vienne, a man indeed religious and experienced in the greatest affairs. As far as possible, he will assist you in God’s cause in our stead; and if anything is settled, through the efforts of the lord king and yourselves, concerning the affair of Sens in a manner conducive to the honor of God and the Church of Lyons, he will report it competently to us. For once the thorn of this discord has been removed and peace restored between the churches, we are prepared to meet the lord king and the persons of the Church wherever necessary, and to devote our counsel and assistance to this cause of God.

### LETTER CXXXV. GEOFFREY, ARCHBISHOP OF BORDEAUX, TO SUGER. He desires to be excused for being unable to attend the assembly at Chartres at Suger’s summons.

[Col. 1412B]

To his dearest and deservedly reverend lord Suger, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Blessed Denis, Brother Geoffrey, called bishop of the Church of Bordeaux, greeting and whatever service he can offer with affection.

Lord, we received the letter of your graciousness with due reverence. Having examined it carefully, I recognize that you, whom I formerly knew to be inflamed with zeal for God’s house and love of fraternal charity, have now, especially in a time of necessity, undertaken to advance Christ’s cause. We judged that your requests and summons—made by you on behalf of yourselves and the venerable lords and fathers, archbishops and bishops—ought to be accepted and fulfilled, both because of the matter itself and because of the petition of such great men, if ability had been present to us in accordance with our will.

Nevertheless, because “it depends not on him who wills or runs, but on God who shows mercy,” we have had to desist from the journey already begun, owing to bodily illness. Further, Lord Theoderic Galeran [Note: [Col. 1411D] Theoderic Galeran, mentioned below, occurs after Suger and Ralph, count of Vermandois, in a charter of King Louis VII for the monastery of Bonne-Nouvelle at Orléans, given in 1149: *Annals of the Benedictines*, vol. VI, p. 465. In the letter of Hugh, archbishop of Sens, to Suger, we read of Brother Galeran, who oversees the house of the Temple at Paris.] had summoned, on behalf of the lord king, both us and our brother bishops, and generally all the magnates of our land, to Saint-Jean-d’Angély on the Sunday *Ego sum Pastor bonus* [Note: [Col. 1412D] The second Sunday after Easter.], to establish the peace of the land and settle in our region those matters which concern the honor of the kingdom.

We therefore earnestly request that your serenity, so dear to us, consider our request granted: since we are impeded by the matters aforesaid and cannot attend so great an assembly [Note: [Col. 1412D] “So great an assembly,” etc.: the assembly at Chartres mentioned in Suger’s letter to Peter of Cluny.], may this not seem burdensome to you, lord; but may your charity regard us as excused both before yourself and before those who ought to assemble, our lords and fathers. Although absent in body, we shall nevertheless be present with you in spirit, praying that Christ may supply you with the spirit of counsel in His cause. Farewell.

### LETTER CXXXVI. THE ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES TO SUGER.

[Col. 1413A]

To his dearest brother and friend Suger, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, Peter, humble servant of the Church of Bourges, greeting and true affection in Christ.

Because we have great confidence in your religious devotion and friendship, we write to you more freely, especially concerning matters which we know pertain to honor. For Bartholomew, our archdeacon, a man of evil life and the worst reputation, obtained through the lord king’s entreaties with the lord pope that the case between us and him, which by command of the lord pope was being tried before the lord of Bordeaux, should be heard at Rome during the octave of Pentecost, to our detriment. Therefore we must shortly go or send there, unless we wish to fail justice and honor.

We therefore most urgently entreat your affection to secure from the lord king a letter to the lord pope on our behalf, and to write yourself, as our faithful Constantine will explain to you more fully.

### LETTER CXXXVII. THE ABBOT OF PONTIGNY TO SUGER. He commends to him the case of the treasurer of Auxerre, entrusted to Suger’s judgment by the Roman pontiff.

To his venerable lord and dearest father Suger, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, Brother Guy, called abbot of Pontigny, greeting and prayers.

Our treasurer of Auxerre is a friend of our house of Pontigny, and he believes that the petition of our lowliness has some weight with your eminence. Nor do we ourselves distrust your kindness, that, when we intercede for him, you will deign to grant us some small concession. If, therefore, the intercession of a poor man has any place with you, let our friend find you favorable in his cause, which the lord pope has committed to your discretion for determination. [Note: “Has committed to your discretion,” etc. His case was, if we are not mistaken, concerning the provostship of the Church of Auxerre. On this the author of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Auxerre*, ch. 55, vol. I of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca Manuscriptorum*, p. 465, says, when speaking of Hugh of Mâcon: “Finally, since in the judgment of the wise he was held among all the fellow bishops of the Gallican Church to be a man of exceptional integrity and great counsel, and since he had shown himself greatly solicitous for the common good of his Church, he nevertheless gave the provostship of that same Church to a certain nephew of his—the provostship which Hugh, his predecessor of venerable memory, with the most kindly affection of charity, had given for the common good of the brethren upon the table of Saint Stephen through the hand of that same protomartyr; and this was confirmed both by the authority of the supreme pontiff and by his own.” This being established, the present letter must be assigned to the year 1150, as is clear from St Bernard’s Letter 276.]

He is also summoned by the lord king in a case in which, nevertheless, for the love of God and of us, may it please your holiness that your support not be lacking to him. Since we did not have our own seal, we affixed the seal of the lord of Auxerre.

## LETTER CXXXVIII. POPE EUGENIUS TO SUGER

[Col. 1413D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1414A] “We do not believe that your prudence is unaware,” etc. See under Eugenius III, for the year 1153.

## LETTER CXXXIX. KING LOUIS TO SUGER

That he should put an end to the complaints of the poor people of Chartres against Ralph Malveisin, which the king had entrusted to his discretion for settlement.

LOUIS, by the grace of God king of the French, to our beloved SUGER, by the same grace venerable abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and abundant affection.

Your discretion heard with us at Chartres the complaints of poor persons crying out to us against R. Malveisin; and we charged you with settling them by your discretion. [Note: [Col. 1414D] Ralph, brother of Samson, archbishop of Reims, who in 1148 founded an anniversary observance in the church of Saint Geremarus at Flavigny for the souls of his father and mother, with the consent of his wife Brita, his sons Ralph, William, and Manasses, and his daughters Agnes, Joan, and Regina. Among the documents in vol. X of *Gallia Christiana*, col. 258.] But because we cannot attend to this matter on the Thursday immediately after Pentecost, we write, commanding your affection to give the poor such diligent attention [Col. 1414B] that God may be honored through justice, and that we may gain praise before God and all good people. Farewell.

## LETTER CXL. J., CARDINAL OF SANTA MARIA NUOVA, TO SUGER

He commends to him the case of Master Peter, entrusted to Suger’s judgment by Pope Eugenius.

To SUGER, by the grace of God venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, J. [JOHN], by the same grace cardinal-deacon of Santa Maria Nuova: greeting and affection.

We earnestly ask your affection on behalf of the bearer of this letter, Master Peter: in his case, which the lord pope commits to your prudence, let him find you compassionate and gentle, and sympathetic in mercy toward his great labors. He indeed maintains that he is free from the charge laid against him, although, even if he were found guilty, it ought surely to be mitigated because of the customary impunity of students’ offences. Yet because this case has been brought before the Roman court and remitted to you, let gravity be preserved, but let mercy also be applied; let folly be restrained, learning honored, instruction shaped, and charity restored. And, with the labors on both sides weighed, let an end be imposed in such a way that curiosity and a restless spirit may find no place whatever with you. Let this man answer for himself before a merciful judge; and whoever is convicted of having committed prohibited violence, let each bear his own burden.

## LETTER CXLI. HUGH, CARDINAL-PRIEST OF THE TITULAR CHURCH IN LUCINA, TO SUGER

On behalf of the same Master Peter.

[Col. 1414D]

To his dearest brother and friend SUGER, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, HUGH, cardinal-priest of the holy Roman Church of the titular church in Lucina: greeting and affection.

The bearer of this letter has undergone very great labor in coming to the feet of the lord pope. Bound by the bond of excommunication for his offences, we absolved him by the command of that same our lord. We have learned that his case, as is contained in the lord pope’s letters, is to be committed to your discretion; and because we have known him as a learned man, greatly concerned for the pursuit of discipline, we willingly intercede for him in his affairs. Therefore we entreat the prudence of your charity to support and treat kindly, insofar as justice permits, this man answering only for himself.

## LETTER CXLII. HUGH OF ROME TO SUGER

On behalf of the same Master Peter.

[Col. 1415B]

To SUGER, by the grace of God venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, his lord and friend, Brother HUGH: greeting.

Since it especially belongs to the duty of compassion, we cannot refrain from interceding with our friends for our own associates. Therefore, for the love of God and of us, support the bearer of this letter, Master Peter, whose case the lord pope remits to your discretion, insofar as justice permits. The study to which he has always applied himself in the liberal arts, and the uprightness of his character, so far as we know, ought to earn no small favor with the prudence of your kindness. He has also already suffered the greatest [Col. 1415C] hardship in this matter—and unjustly, as he himself and certain others maintain. He also endured a long time in the Roman court and worked to obtain permission for two of his companions, accused in the same case, to demonstrate their innocence in your presence. Since he could not obtain this, he must answer for himself alone.

## LETTER CXLIII. ROGER, KING OF SICILY, TO SUGER

He asks that Suger reciprocate by more frequently informing him through travellers of his condition.

ROGER, by the grace of God king of Sicily, of the duchy of Apulia and the principality of Capua, to SUGER, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, his dearest friend: greeting and affection.

It is the part of friends [Note: [Col. 1415D] “It is the part of friends,” etc. From the writer of the *Life of Suger* we know that Roger, king of Sicily, held him in high esteem: “Did not Roger, the most renowned king of Sicily,” he says, “send him supplicatory and entreating letters, and dispatch gifts? Did he not, when he afterward learned of Suger’s pious desire to make a pilgrimage, prepare to meet him?”—“And indeed at that time King Roger of Apulia was vigorously and successfully attacking Emperor C. P. and capturing many places. Had he been able to ally our king with himself against that ruler, he would have poured out all the abundance of his treasures for them,” says Odo of Deuil, book IV, p. 46.] that one should rejoice in the prosperity of the other. Therefore we have deemed it fitting to inform your affection that, by God’s grace, we are sound and well. We ask you, indeed, to render us the reciprocity owed to friends, and not to hesitate frequently to inform us through travellers of the condition of your beloved self, [Col. 1416A] so that, as you rejoice in our health, we too may rejoice in yours.

## LETTER CXLIV. POPE EUGENIUS TO LORD SUGER

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“The immense work of compassion which divine mercy inspired in our dearest son Louis, the illustrious king of the French,” etc. See under Eugenius III, for the year 1153.

## LETTER CXLV. NICHOLAS, ABBOT OF CORBIE, TO SUGER

He asks to be excused before the king for having sent no one to Orléans on the appointed day to answer regarding his dispute with the burgesses of Corbie.

[Col. 1416B]

To his lord and father SUGER, by the grace of God venerable abbot of Blessed Denis, NICHOLAS, humble minister of the Church of Corbie: abundant greeting and affection.

From all my dangers and necessities I confidently flee to your serenity as to the safest and most tested harbor of my safety. After I returned from you, hindered by the serious business being conducted between us and the count of Flanders, and having set out last Sunday for those regions at the summons of the bishops of Tournai and Thérouanne because of a mutual settlement, I was unable to send anyone to the lord our king at Orléans on the day he had appointed for us. I therefore earnestly entreat your affection, which I have often experienced, [Col. 1416C] to excuse me before the lord king and to see that he is not angry, because I did not dare entrust so important a matter, while absent, except to a most trustworthy messenger, and therefore refrained from sending one. I myself, without doubt, or my messenger, shall be present before you concerning this on the Sunday immediately following the feast of the Apostles. Since I greatly fear that I have offended your fatherhood by not sending someone on the aforesaid day, I ask to be assured by your letters of the remission of your anger. I ask also that we be informed whether what I have heard is true: that the lord king must come directly from Orléans to us. I further ask that, if you know the lord king will effectively prosecute both his own affair and ours against our burgesses, [Col. 1416D] you inform us, and I shall await his mercy. But if you perceive that he is being bent and acting more mildly, indicate the same to us, because unless his help is at hand for me, [Note: [Col. 1416D] “Unless his help is at hand for me.” Louis wrote letters contained in the manuscript cartulary of Philip Augustus and in the black cartulary of Corbie, fol. 34: “Louis, by the grace of God king of the French and duke of Aquitaine, to the elders G. of Hesly and Gilo, to the sworn members of the commune of Corbie, and to all the burgesses: greeting and our favor. It belongs to our right and office to preserve and defend the possessions of the churches of our realm and their people from private and foreign enemies. Compelled by this consideration, we command and order you to leave in quiet and peace the servants of the monastery of Corbie, both those belonging to the abbot and those belonging to the chapter; and to exact nothing from them for your commune, nor inflict any exaction upon the said servants or their property. For, both on account of the Church’s right and on account of the abbot, whom we strive greatly to love and honor, we will and confirm that they be free and undisturbed. Whoever proves contrary to this command of ours, let him not doubt that we shall be contrary to him, and let him know with certainty that we shall avenge the injury done to our crown and majesty.” Farewell.] I shall accept whatever peace may be offered. Farewell, and assist the honor of the Church.

## LETTER CXLVI. TO ROGER, KING OF SICILY

He thanks him for not disdaining to report his prosperity to Suger and inquire after Suger’s well-being.

To the glorious ROGER, by the grace of God king of Sicily, of the duchy of Apulia and the principality of Capua, SUGER, abbot of Blessed Denis: may you reign in Him who gives salvation to kings.

To the excellence of your royal majesty we return thanksgivings—not such as we ought, but such as we can—because the highness of so great, so wise, so renowned a lord has not disdained to remember our lowliness and inquire after our welfare. For such an inquiry has made me wholly and entirely the purchased possession of your serenity; nor throughout the whole time of our life can it fall from our memory that a lord of such nobility and power has informed us of his prosperity and asked to be assured of ours. Certainly, while informing your highness of our well-being, we deemed it fitting to write much to your excellence about many matters; but lest prolixity produce weariness, we have directed that these things be reported to you mouth to mouth by our messenger. May your highness prosper.

## LETTER CXLVII. POPE EUGENIUS TO SUGER

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1417C] “That priest R., who had come to us against Stephen, archdeacon of Sens,” etc. See under Eugenius III, for the year 1153.

## LETTER CXLVIII. KING LOUIS TO ABBOT SUGER

He entrusts to him the matter of the election of the bishops of Laon and Arras.

LOUIS, by the grace of God king of the French and duke of Aquitaine, to our dearest friend and faithful man SUGER, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and abundant affection.

The clerics of Laon came to us, lamenting the desolation of their Church and showing also what great disadvantages the Church would suffer if it long lacked the care of a pastor. [Note: [Col. 1417D] “The care of a pastor,” etc. Pseudo-Robert of Monte, who is known to have been a member of the Premonstratensian order, says under the year 1150 concerning Bartholomew: “Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, in the thirty-eighth year of his episcopate, despising the habit of the world, received the habit at Foigny.” Nangis and others, however, place this in 1151. But this letter, given before the death of Suger, proves that Robert’s date must be followed.] They therefore requested from you a free election; and because the Church could not endure delay, we were compelled immediately to yield to their just petitions. Yet, lest the matter be carried out entirely without your counsel, [Col. 1418A] we have sent these same men respectfully to your affection. We thus command you by request: as you know you ought, and as you know to be expedient for the Church, give them counsel, and let your prudence labor for the Church’s benefit and the realm’s honor. You surely know that through the weakness and failure of those set over them, the honor of Churches is impaired and the dignity of the realm diminished by the sloth of persons. It indeed concerns the honor of the realm that this Church be quickly aided, because there is war also in those parts and almost all the barons there have perished. Speak to the clerics of the Church whom we send to you as seems good to you; counsel them as seems good to you. For your will is ours, and we have placed our counsel in you. The clerics of Arras will shortly come to you; [Col. 1418B] [Note: [Col. 1418D] “The clerics of Arras will come to you,” etc. The matter concerned a new election of a bishop of Arras, although a certain Hugh had been appointed in place of Alviso, as may be seen in the letter of Thierry, count of Flanders, above. In the end Godescalc, abbot of Mont-Saint-Martin, was elected and consecrated at Reims by Archbishop Samson on 21 September, in the year 1151, according to Lambert of Watrelos.] advise them in our stead; and, if it seems fit to you and is not burdensome, bring them into our presence.

## LETTER CXLIX. THE ABBOT OF VÉZELAY TO SUGER

He writes on behalf of the widow of Robert, Suger’s former friend and physician, and of his deceased son.

To the venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, Lord SUGER, Brother P. [PONTIUS], however unworthy a minister of Vézelay: greeting, with the service of veneration and affection.

We consider what we write to you idle and superfluous, since the anointing of the Holy Spirit teaches you concerning all things. Your particular friend Robert has died, [Col. 1418C] and his son Matthew; the widow, a mother, remains alone, together with her only son. What then? But, as the abundance of your compassion knows and is accustomed to do, let them, if you please, feel that you bear tender mercies toward persons of this kind, and let mercy triumph over judgment. For you know that whoever shows mercy shall obtain mercy.

## LETTER CL. SUGER TO KING LOUIS

He begs him not to rush into war against the count of Anjou, whom he had made duke of Normandy, without the counsel of the magnates whom he had convened.

To his dearest lord LOUIS, by the grace of God king of the French and duke of Aquitaine, SUGER, abbot of Blessed Denis: devoted prayers in Christ and faithful service.

[Col. 1418D] We earnestly beseech the highness of your royal majesty, in which we have always been accustomed to place confidence, not to rush prematurely into war against the count of Anjou, whom you made duke of Normandy, [Col. 1419A] without the counsel of your archbishops, bishops, and magnates. [Note: [Col. 1419D] “You made duke of Normandy,” etc. On what conditions Louis handed Normandy over to the count of Anjou, the anonymous writer of that history teaches. He says: “Geoffrey, count of Anjou, and his son Henry, who afterward acquired the kingdom of the English, approached King Louis and complained to him about Stephen, king of the English, showing that he was unjustly taking away their rights. The king, therefore, wishing to maintain all persons justly and reasonably, as befits royal majesty, and to preserve to each his own right, invaded Normandy with a great army and took it by force; he restored it to Henry, son of the count of Anjou, and received him into homage for that land. Then, in return for the assistance granted him, with the consent of his father Geoffrey, he gave King Louis in full and free possession the Norman Vexin, which lies between the Epte and the Andelle,” etc. But the king’s dispute with the count of Anjou concerned another matter, namely the castle of Monasteriolum of Gerard of Bellay. On this the Angevin chronographer of Saint-Aubin, under the year 1150, says: “Geoffrey, count of Anjou, began to besiege Monasteriolum, constructing many castles around that fortress. Hence war arose between him and the king of France.”] For if you undertake anything with insufficient deliberation, it can neither be abandoned with honor nor accomplished without very great labor. But since you have summoned your men for this purpose, we advise and request that, after hearing their counsel, you wait by postponing the matter for a while, until you hear the counsel on this from your faithful men—namely, bishops and nobles—who, by the right of fidelity which they owe to the kingdom and crown, will help with all their strength to carry out what they recommend to you.

## LETTER CLI. POPE EUGENIUS TO SUGER

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“The monastery of Blessed Medard at Soissons is not unknown to you to be of the right of Blessed Peter,” etc. See under Eugenius III, for the year 1153.

## LETTER CLII. BALDWIN, BISHOP OF NOYON, TO SUGER

Concerning a meeting to be held with the archbishop of Reims over the pressing business that he had with Ralph, count of Vermandois.

To his dearest lord SUGER, venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, Brother BALDWIN, unworthy minister of the Church of Noyon: service and affection.

Blessed be God, who has made our desire prosper, leading us forth and bringing us back in safety and joy, and who has granted an effect corresponding to our petition. I myself would rather have come to you than sent this letter; but we judged it necessary first to turn aside to the lord of Reims, and afterward to see you, whom we greatly desire. It would be necessary for you and the lord of Reims to meet before the day of the conference, that we might confer about the pressing matter. Arrange for this to be done. Farewell.

## LETTER CLIII. SUGER TO G., COUNT OF ANJOU

He declares that the dispute between Geoffrey and the king of France greatly displeases him, and asks that the possessions of churches not be harmed on the pretext of war.

To the distinguished G. [GEOFFREY], count of Anjou and duke of the Normans, [Col. 1420A] and to the noble Empress MATILDA, SUGER, abbot of Blessed Denis: greeting and affection.

Let the highness of your nobility know that the dispute which has arisen between you and our lord the king of France greatly displeases us: both because of the love of God, who is the author and lover of peace; because of the oppression of the poor, which grieves us; and because of your peace and honor, which we greatly cherish. [Note: [Col. 1420D] “That dispute,” etc. The dispute concerned homage for Normandy, which Geoffrey transferred to his son Henry in 1149, as is recorded in the Angevin Chronicle of Saint-Aubin and in Robert of Monte’s appendix to Sigebert.] We cannot forget the honor and affection which the glorious King Henry showed us throughout his life. While he flourished wisely and powerfully in the administration of the kingdom of England and the duchy of Normandy, he ensured that the possessions of Saint-Denis were honorably and faithfully protected in every time of war and conflict; he treated me as an intimate friend. Whenever I came, that powerful and discerning man met me, and often disclosed to me what he concealed from many of his own men concerning the restoration of peace. Thus, with God’s aid, it often happened through our efforts that, out of many wars and the tangled schemes of many rivals, he reached a good settlement of peace. If he had deigned to trust us, we do not recall that during twenty years he ever made any peace with the lord king of France in which we did not faithfully and, beyond all others, give continual and loyal assistance, as one trusted by both lords. And we shall still gladly pursue this, opportunely and inopportunely alike, whenever we can, as befits an abbot and priest. Therefore, mindful also of the ancient benefits of the glorious King Henry, [Col. 1420C] we advise your nobility to strive vigorously and diligently, through friends and intimates, [Note: [Col. 1420D] “Through intimates,” etc. Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, was chosen as envoy for peace. See his letter to Suger below.] to seek the affection of the lord king and peace, while it can still be recalled and while he has not yet entered into alliance with your enemies. [Note: [Col. 1420D] “Alliance with your enemies,” etc. With Stephen, king of England, who was also seeking from the king investiture of Normandy. See Arnulf’s letter.] For even if the kingdom of England and an abundance of ancient treasures should accrue to your peace and prosperity, they would be fruitlessly consumed by the expenses of long wars, by plunderers, retainers, and hired soldiers. May the Almighty grant you the peace of heaven and earth. Concerning the land of Blessed Denis at Berneval [Note: [Col. 1420D] “At Berneval,” etc. Suger discusses it in his book *On the Deeds Accomplished during His Administration*, ch. 23.] and at Boscage, which the glorious King Henry caused to be kept wholly unharmed, even more diligently than usual in time of war, [Col. 1421A] we earnestly ask you to do the same. For on the pretext of wars, whether French or Norman, the possessions of churches or abbeys, wherever situated—whether in Normandy or in France—are not customarily injured or diminished.

## LETTER CLIV. SUGER TO T., BISHOP OF AMIENS

He rebukes him for having received Robert of Boves, a thoroughly wicked man, into communion in sacred things.

To the venerable T. [THEODERIC], by the grace of God bishop of Amiens, SUGER, abbot of Blessed Denis: greeting and affection.

True friendship is accustomed, when necessary, to rebuke friends more severely. Therefore we seriously reproach your affection because you have either received—or allowed to be received—Robert of Boves, a diabolical man and notorious apostate, into your Church, over which by God’s ordinance you preside. It is greatly to be feared for your discretion lest such a reception, hateful to God and men, if indeed it has occurred, [Note: [Col. 1421D] “If indeed it has occurred …” This is proved from letters cited by André Duchesne from the cartulary of the church of Saint-Acheul among the proofs of the *History of Coucy*, p. 341. The letters of Theodoric, bishop of Amiens, dated 1147, indiction X, contain the following: “It should also be known that in the castle of Boves that same church had from ancient times possessed, from the revenues of the mills, four measures of wheat by alms of Count Enguerrand. But stirred by the words of ill-wishers, Thomas, son of that Enguerrand, and Robert, son of that Thomas, had violently taken that alms away from the same church. More recently, however, that same Robert, count of Amiens, as he was setting out for Jerusalem, admonished by the counsel of religious men, was moved to compunction; and, in the presence of his mother Lady Milesende and of religious men standing by, he acknowledged his fault before the abbot of the aforesaid church. Having sought and obtained absolution, he confirmed to that same church in perpetual possession, through our hand and under the testimony of his men whose names are subscribed, those four measures of wheat to be received from the revenues of the mills.” It is otherwise uncertain whether Robert of Boves completed his journey to Jerusalem, since he is not counted among the crusaders.] may produce for you present ruin and eternal Gehenna. Strengthen, then, the feeble hands and make firm the weak knees; recover your strength; wield the sword mightily against that diabolical man, so that what occurred through insufficient caution may swiftly be corrected to the honor of God and yourselves. For it befits episcopal eminence voluntarily to correct what was done less well, just as it would be unbecoming to correct it under compulsion. Farewell.

## LETTER CLV. GEOFFREY, ARCHBISHOP OF BORDEAUX, TO SUGER

He reports that illness has detained him at Fontevraud and that he cannot attend the appointed assembly.

[Col. 1421C]

To the most reverend and deservedly beloved lord SUGER, by the grace of God venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, Brother GEOFFREY, called bishop of the Church of Bordeaux: greeting and ready service with devotion.

“Desire upon desire I desired to see your face, lord.” Therefore, summoned by you to the council at Chartres, [Note: [Col. 1422D] The council of Chartres was held in 1150, on the twenty-fifth day after the octave of Easter, according to Suger’s letter to Peter, abbot of Cluny.] we had intended to come, unless the impediments concerning the necessities of our land and other matters, of which we wrote to you, had intervened. And when we had already undertaken and largely completed the journey to come with our brother bishops to this holy assembly, [Note: [Col. 1422D] We have found nowhere written where this other assembly was held. From the author of Suger’s *Life* we learn that Suger assembled bishops three times concerning the business of the Holy Land.] the Lord so ordered that, because of an unexpected illness, we had to remain at Fontevraud. [Col. 1421D] [Col. 1422A] It has not therefore been granted us from above to accomplish at present what we desired: namely, to attend the holy gathering and enjoy the desired conversation with you. What charity can do, therefore, it performs. I embrace my lord and friend in the depths of Jesus Christ; with all the devotion I can offer, I acknowledge that I am wholly his, and in my small measure I should wish in all things to comply with your will. Through the bearer of this letter, Brother N., lord, who can explain the rest to you, deign, if it please you, to inform us of the matters being conducted around you and of whatever you may wish.

## LETTER CLVI. POPE EUGENIUS TO SUGER

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Because you bear attentive concern over the deficiency of the Eastern Church,” etc. See under Pope Eugenius III, for the year 1153.

## LETTER CLVII. SUGER TO B., BISHOP OF NOYON

He asks him to bless the abbot of Compiègne on the feast-day of Saint Cornelius, if this can be done without great scandal.

To the venerable B. [BALDWIN], by the grace of God bishop of Noyon, SUGER, abbot of Blessed Denis: the effect of sincere charity with affection.

Regarding the business which apostolic authority has entrusted to your eminence and our lowliness—the establishment of religious observance in the Church of Compiègne—[Note: [Col. 1422D] See Eugenius’s letters on this matter, issued at Albano, 19 June 1150.] let us render immense thanks to almighty God, because he has deigned to grant so good a beginning to so great and glorious a work. Trusting in his mercy, we believe that he who began the good work will himself bring it to completion with a mighty hand and outstretched arm. For we have, for the protection of our undertaking, the authority of the Gospel’s reply: “If anyone says anything to you, say, ‘The Lord has need of them,’ and immediately he will let them go.” Therefore, hearing and knowing this, let us press manfully on with the task laid upon us; let us utterly overthrow the camps of the devil which, through the sins of men, had been built in the aforesaid place; let us establish there the camp of Almighty God; and, once established, let us foster and maintain it with every diligence. Concerning the blessing [Col. 1422D] of the elect, Odo, we inform your affection [Col. 1423A] that, if it can be done without great scandal—for the canons are accustomed to gather on the feast of Saint Cornelius (16 September) more than at any other time of year—you should bless him at the altar of the aforesaid martyr on that feast itself, so that by offering these first fruits of your labor you may receive from Almighty God the fruit of eternal reward. But if it cannot be done without great scandal, we ask you to perform the same on the coming Sunday.

## LETTER CLVIII. B., BISHOP OF NOYON, TO SUGER

He announces that the abbot of Compiègne has been blessed and advises immediate recourse to the pope.

To his lord and friend, the venerable abbot of Saint-Denis SUGER, B. [BALDWIN], unworthy minister of the Church of Noyon: affection and service according to our ability and beyond it.

It has been done as you commanded, and blessed be God: the abbot has been blessed. Care and concern for his subjects have been placed upon him, but anxious concern binds a needy hand. For how shall a naked man clothe the naked, or a hungry man satisfy the hungry? Clearly counsel is needed where no creditor can be found and nothing is available from which a purchaser may pay. This counsel lies with you; it belongs to you to provide that those whom we have cast amid the waves may not be unable to reach the harbor. Our entire counsel is that a journey be made to the lord pope without any delay, so that, as the beginning came from him, so confirmation may also come through him. For he must be relied upon as a support, since whatever pressure or threat the king’s command brings is far less than what apostolic authority ordains and confirms.

## LETTER CLIX. SUGER TO R., COUNT OF VERMANDOIS

Concerning the sacrilegious irruption of Philip, the king’s brother, into the church of Compiègne, from which he forcibly carried off relics.

To the distinguished R. [RALPH], count of Vermandois, his dearest lord and friend, SUGER, abbot of Blessed Denis: greeting and affection.

Your discernment knows that the lord pope, by apostolic authority, imposed upon us, though unwilling, the burden of establishing religious life in the church of Compiègne. For one who fears for his own possessions is not without reason grieved to be burdened with another’s charge. But now it is evident that what had been determined by us in obedience to the command laid upon us has been irreverently violated; and that what the lord king discussed with you and with the lady queen (Adelaide) concerning the same matter has profited little or nothing. For immediately after we had departed, Lord Philip [Note: Philip was treasurer of the church of Compiègne, dean and chief keeper of the keys of St Martin’s at Tours, archdeacon of Paris, and moreover abbot of certain royal abbeys—namely St Mary of Étampes, St Mary of Corbeil, St Mary of Pincey, and St Mellon of Pontoise—in which he had succeeded his brother Henry, as may be seen in the documents published by Duchesne among the proofs of the *History of Dreux*, p. 228 ff.], the king’s brother, came with a sacrilegious and armed band both of laymen and clerics, violently broke into the monastery, and seized and carried off the casket in which no small portion of the relics was kept. Nor content with this rash act, he soon returned with his accomplices, shut the doors of the church upon himself, and attempted to carry off the venerable crown of our Saviour together with the precious and celebrated shroud of that same our Lord.

But when the townsmen heard of so great a crime, they hastened bravely under arms, both for the venerable relics, by which that place is renowned throughout the whole world, and also for the fidelity which they had already pledged to the abbot and brethren. Learning also that those sacrilegious men, so that the brethren might not ring the bells, had cut the ropes and, after inflicting insults on them, threatened them with death, they found the doors of the church bolted on the inside; yet they entered the church as best they could. And, had they not judged that deference was owed to the royal majesty in the case of his brother, they would, inflamed with zeal, have shamefully punished those found with him. Having therefore retained the relics and preserved our brethren, they drove back Philip himself and put his followers to flight, though these barely restrained themselves from vengeance.

Since therefore their audacity and the contumacious disobedience of the clerics summon us to administer justice, we invite your united support, in which we have great confidence, by apostolic authority. And, as our most faithful friend—for we have never failed one another in times of need—we ask and require you also on behalf of the lord king that, by your command, all that the criminal clerics seemed to possess under your protection be placed under sequestration. Indeed, by the deserts of their own offences they have deprived themselves alike of office and of the benefice of the Church. It will therefore be a certain proof of our mutual affection if, in the present work of God, we have you as a faithful and valiant helper.

## LETTER CLX. R., COUNT OF VERMANDOIS, TO SUGER

On the grain and goods of the monastery of Compiègne carried away by the canons: he writes that he will place under the king’s hand what remains.

To SUGER, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, his lord and friend, R., count of Vermandois: greeting and affection.

When your letters came to me concerning placing under seizure the grain and goods of the clerics of Compiègne, the canons had caused the greater part of them to be carried away. But all that remains I shall cause to be seized.

## LETTER CLXI. LOUIS, KING OF THE FRANKS, TO SUGER

He writes that after the feast of St Remigius he will settle the affairs of Compiègne with him; meanwhile he has ordered his mother and Counts Ralph and Theobald not to inflict any injury upon the monastery of Compiègne.

LOUIS, by God’s grace king of the Franks and duke of Aquitaine, to our beloved SUGER, by that same grace venerable abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and abundant affection.

You instructed us to go at present to the region of Compiègne in order to quiet the discord at Compiègne. But, as you well know, for a very long time now we have been unable to accomplish anything in our affairs. Therefore, our affairs now calling us, we have resolved to go to the district of Orléans and remain there until the feast of St Remigius. We ask you, therefore, meanwhile to bear with us patiently, since we do not wish to go there without you. Then, taking H. [Note: Henry, bishop of Beauvais.] with you, we shall go to the district of Beauvais and, according to your counsel, settle both those matters and the affairs of Compiègne.

We also wish you to know that we have sent our letters to Queen Adelaide, our mother, ordering her to leave the abbot of Compiègne and all his people in peace and to inflict no injury upon him or his men; and that she defer discussion of the wrong done by her son [Note: Philip, concerning whom see Letter 159 above.] and herself patiently until the octave of Blessed Denis. We have likewise ordered Count Ralph and Count Theobald to cause the abbot of Compiègne to be put in possession and invested, throughout all their lands, with those things that pertain to the church of Compiègne.

## LETTER CLXII. BALDWIN, BISHOP OF NOYON, TO LORD POPE EUGENIUS

He asks him to ratify the election of Hugh, bishop of Arras.

To the most holy Father and lord EUGENIUS, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, BALDWIN, unworthy minister of the church of Noyon: whatever good prayer or affection can accomplish.

As lord and master, you have burdened weak shoulders so greatly that, under the pressing anxiety of carrying out the work enjoined, strength was almost exhausted and failed. For, etc. See under Eugenius III, among the various letters addressed to him.

## LETTER CLXIII. SUGER TO LORD POPE EUGENIUS

He relates how, amid troubles and insults, he introduced religious monks into the church of Compiègne in place of canons of infamous life.

To the illustrious Father and universal lord EUGENIUS, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: the fullness of obedience and service.

Among all the matters granted to our smallness, most holy Father, whether by apostolic authority or by command of royal majesty, I have especially embraced these two: namely, the establishment of religious life in the church of Blessed Geneviève at Paris and in the noble church of Compiègne, which by right of Blessed Peter rests upon your authority, and which would be one of the noblest in Gaul if the infamous depravity of the canons inhabiting it had not stood in the way. We wonder with astonishment why or how this memorable deed could have been brought to effect, unless because we have known that the hand of the Lord is not weakened, and have recognized Peter’s strength in these and like matters and in all things.

Dearest Father, the strongholds of wickedness have been overthrown in execution of your holy command; there have been raised there the strongholds of piety and holy religious life, so that “in the lairs where dragons formerly dwelt, there may spring up the green growth of reed and rush.” We judged it fitting indeed to write to your holy fatherhood, in due order, the course of this action; but the abbot of that church, lately elected and lately blessed—a venerable man and a person of approved character—is hastening to you as to his lord and Father, to whom he wholly belongs. He will set forth both the whole affair and his own conscience, insofar as it concerns himself, and will show himself an executor of your will and of full obedience.

Yet we do not wish to conceal from your holy discernment, even in summary, the troubles and insults which the utterly depraved canons inflicted upon the lord bishop of Noyon and upon us even in the presence of the lord king: especially that most wretched dean, the bolder because he was the baser through the very infamy attaching to him; and another, Giraldus of the Port, no less wretched through the stench of his infamy; as well as other most miserable men deploring the evils within their own household and the filth of their domestic affairs.

On the first day, when summoned to hear your command, those canons scorned to come. But when we clearly saw that they kept themselves away and refused to hear your command, we caused your mandate concerning the establishment of religious life in that church to be publicly proclaimed before other clerics and many thousands of people, and declared that thereafter monks would serve there under religious observance. With the lord king standing by, we promised that the canons should peacefully possess their prebends, according to your pleasure, until you should decide what was to be done concerning them.

But those canons, in sacrilegious daring, rushed into that same church and carried off its most holy relics—the Lord’s crown of thorns and holy shroud—as well as its treasures, books, and priestly vestments, so that the monks might have nothing with which to serve God. While we protested against their disobedience on your behalf, they sang louder than usual, until the lord king and all who were present, clerics and laymen alike, astonished at their madness, restrained them.
