[Note: See the letter of Baldwin of Noyon cited above.] But when on the following day they had heard the full contents of your command, they persisted in their wickedness and the audacity of their disobedience.

## LETTER CLXIV. SUGER TO P., ABBOT OF CLUNY

He asks him to write to the pope that he may graciously receive the abbot of the church of Compiègne.

To the venerable PETER, by God’s grace abbot of Cluny, SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and devout prayers in Christ.

An honourable subject of petition is accustomed to compress an abundance of words. Therefore, concerning the church of Compiègne, which by command of the lord pope has been changed from its old state to a new religious order, we earnestly ask your holiness to assist it before the Lord by your prayers, and to write to the lord pope that he may graciously receive the abbot of that church, a venerable man and a person of approved character, and, as a pious Father and lord, provide in every way for the work of his hands. Farewell.

To the venerable lord and Father, by God’s grace abbot of Clairvaux, B., Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, sends the same message.

## LETTER CLXV. SUGER TO PETER, ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES

From the cartulary of the church of Blessed Mary of La Chapelle.

To the lord and venerable PETER, by God’s grace archbishop of Bourges, SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and affection.

Your predecessors, the archbishops of Bourges, greatly loved and supported Blessed Denis and his places. Therefore, because we place the fullest confidence in your affection—for which we have often laboured and have endured many grave things from the lord king and many others—we ask that, following the path of your predecessors, you too love Blessed Denis and defend and support his places.

But we especially beg, concerning the church of Stivalicules, that you restore it to us. In this time of disturbance, the monks of Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire belonging to the church of Bourges violently took it, through secular agency, from our brethren of La Chapelle. If those who have been invested claim a right in it, our brethren are prepared, at a suitable time which you appoint for them, to answer canonically concerning the matter with our counsel. But if it pleases you to hear the action, learn more fully through those same brethren what was done concerning it in the days of the venerable archbishops of blessed memory, Vulgrin and Alberic. Nor should it burden you to labour on our behalf, for, should occasion require, you would find us ready for your honour and service. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXVI. SUGER TO PETER, ABBOT OF CLUNY

[Note: This letter was published by Dom Martin Marrier in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, col. 918, among the letters of Peter the Venerable, book VI, letter 19.]

To his most beloved lord and venerable Father, PETER, by God’s grace abbot of the Cluniacs, SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: devout prayers in Christ, and the fullness of affection and service.

From letters recently brought from those regions, we have learned of the calamity of the Eastern Church and of the siege of the Lord’s Cross, the king of Jerusalem, the brethren of the Temple, and the other faithful in the city of Antioch; and we do not doubt that it has reached your ears as well. [Note: “In the city of Antioch,” etc.: after the death of Raymond, prince of Antioch, who fell in battle on 27 June 1149, the land of Antioch was ravaged by many disasters, as William of Tyre recounts, book XVII, ch. 9. This is also attested by the letter of A., seneschal of the knighthood of the Temple, to Ebrard des Barres, master of the same knighthood, printed in vol. III of the folio *Spicilegium*, p. 501: “After you departed from us,” he says, “by the demands of our sins it happened that we lost the prince of Antioch, together with all his barons and men, slain in a certain battle. When he was dead, the Parthians immediately invaded the land of Antioch; with no one resisting, they took all of it, fortified the castles, and held those which had been fortified; they hold them and will hold them unless divine mercy comes to our aid,” etc.]

Accordingly, archbishops and bishops, and indeed the lord king, the magnates of the kingdom, and ourselves have met at Laon concerning this matter. And the affair has advanced so far that we have resolved, fifteen days after the octave of Easter, to hold a general assembly at Chartres on this cause; to summon archbishops, bishops, and abbots from many provinces; to set ourselves as a wall for the house of God; to provide deliberately against so nearly inconsolable a grief; and, lest the faith be exterminated from those most holy places from which it was brought to us, to employ every possible effort, with God’s mercy going before and following after. [Note: “We have resolved to employ,” etc. What was done at that assembly is taught by the author of the *Life of Suger* published by us above.]

And because your presence would be exceedingly necessary for so great a work, we invite, summon, and humbly entreat your highness to be present at the aforesaid time and place for this most noble undertaking: on behalf of God, whose cause it is, and for whom we ought always to be ready to go even to prison and death; on behalf of the archbishops and bishops, who laid upon us this summons; and on our own behalf. Furthermore, we ask that you send these other letters with all speed to the lord of Lyons, lest delay give him an excuse for not coming.

The following letters were published by Dom MARTÈNE in *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, col. 413, from a manuscript of the Coislin Library.

## LETTER CLXVII. GEOFFREY, COUNT OF ANJOU, TO SUGER

He gives thanks that Suger is working to restore peace between the king and himself.

To SUGER, by God’s grace venerable abbot and his beloved friend, G., count of Anjou: greeting and affection.

I render great thanks to your eminence because the anger and discord that has arisen between the king of the Franks and me neither arose at your prompting nor gained strength through your counsel. I also give you great thanks because you take care to labour for the restoration of peace between us. I have learned this from the report of several persons, and especially through the exhortation of our friend Ar. [Arnulf], bishop of Lisieux.

But at present I have no opportunity to discuss the matters which you conveyed to me through that same bishop. For the deadline of the king’s enterprise is so near that I must prepare my affairs carefully, in order that, having gathered my forces, I may be able to resist the king’s approaching army. But if the king’s undertaking should be delayed or abandoned, or should already have passed, then, according to your counsel and that of Ralph, count of Vermandois, I would carefully consider the matters which you sent me, and whatever I could do concerning them, without prejudice to my honour, I would do willingly, according to your counsel and that of Count Ralph.

## LETTER CLXVIII. SUGER TO GEOFFREY, COUNT OF ANJOU

Reply to the preceding letter.

To the distinguished G. [GEOFFREY], by God’s grace count of Anjou, SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and affection.

While we were speaking concerning your affair, as the bishop of Lisieux and we had discussed it, the count of Flanders [Theoderic] unexpectedly arrived. By himself and through every means available to him, with our own urgent support, he scarcely obtained from the lord king, after much entreaty, that the army which had been summoned should be deferred, that there should be a truce between you, and that negotiation should proceed from truce toward peace. [Note: “That negotiation should proceed toward peace.” Negotiation did indeed take place, but in the following year, 1151, when Suger had already departed this life. The war was renewed for several causes related by Robert of Torigni (*Patrologia*, vol. CLX): “For, after Duke Geoffrey had besieged for three years with three stone castles the little monastery which he had destroyed—an unprecedented thing since Julius Caesar—and had also captured Girald Berlai, lord of the castle, against even King Louis’s will and prohibition, King Louis and Geoffrey, duke of Normandy, became enemies of one another . . . Discord having thus arisen between the king and the count, the king came with a great army, and Eustace, son of King Stephen, came with him; they entered Normandy before the castle of Arques,” etc.]

We do not doubt that you have received envoys from the same count and that they have explained the matter more fully to your nobility. We wish your serenity most certainly to know that, in arranging your peace and in all matters in which we can, we shall strive to earn the friendship of you and your people. For the bishop of Lisieux knows that we have laboured and continue to labour faithfully in your affair.

## LETTER CLXIX. PETER, ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES, TO SUGER

He asks that he be excused before the king because he cannot come to him at Mantes.

To the reverend Father and lord SUGER, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, P., humble minister of the church of Bourges: greeting and sincere affection in the Lord.

By divine mercy we have returned safely and prosperously from the thresholds of the apostles, except that we have lost some of our companions, for whom we are afflicted with heavy sorrow. We ourselves, and those who were able to escape with us the excessive heat of Italy and the vast unhealthiness of the land, have been worn out beyond measure. Moreover, our horses have entirely failed.

Since therefore we have received the lord king’s summons to meet him at Mantes, and this is impossible for us, we ask your kindness—which we have experienced as a most ready aid in many matters—that you hold us excused in this business before the lord king, lest he take it ill that we cannot come to him because of so many impediments. For we should wish to hasten to see his face even without a summons.

## LETTER CLXX. POPE EUGENIUS III TO SUGER

He commends to him Mo., a subdeacon.

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The prudence and devotion of your affection, etc. See under Eugenius, year 1153.

## LETTER CLXXI. POPE EUGENIUS III TO SUGER

Concerning the violence of the count of Anjou toward his brother Robert.

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

As in the letters of our most beloved son, etc. See in the same place.

## LETTER CLXXII. PETER, ABBOT OF CLUNY, TO SUGER

On their mutual friendship.

To the venerable, beloved, and intimate lord SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis, brother P., humble abbot of the Cluniacs: greeting, and all that he can offer.

If my tongue said one thing and concealed another, I should be one of those who “speak with a heart and a heart,” and of whom truthful Scripture says: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood.” Because I take care not to incur this judgment, for a long time I have shrunk with horror from speaking falsely not only to you but to all people under heaven. Therefore place faith in my words securely, not only now but always. For one who would not wish to deceive even an enemy by lying could by no means lie to a friend and intimate companion.

My affection toward you is so great, and has been so not only now but for very many years, that—not to mention any others—even brothers by blood themselves could not prefer themselves to you in love; my conscience, carefully and often questioned, has answered this or something like it. It often seems superfluous to submit this to your reverence, unless the affection of a friend’s heart, burning with such great love for you, compelled him to write even these things a thousand times; and rightly so. For I have often experienced your friendship, and would that—without injury to your honour or advantage—you too might someday experience mine.

We are sending into your region our most beloved son G., a helper of the Cluniac order, on certain business of ours. We have also sent him to your reverence, asking that you believe whatever he tells you on our behalf as though it were ourselves, and that you convey or write back your will and response either through him or by letter.

## LETTER CLXXIII. HUGH, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN, TO SUGER

He writes to him concerning his churches of Pontoise, Chaumont, and Gisors, which the king retained by usurpation.

To his most beloved Father and lord SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis, HUGH, archbishop of Rouen: greeting and peace.

Your kindness toward me gives me courage to set forth what my humility requires. The churches of Pontoise, Chaumont, and Gisors have in past times belonged by right and possession to the archbishop of Rouen. The king holds them. We protest, but receive no regard for mercy’s sake and are not restored for justice’s sake.

At last, having taken counsel, we wish through you, as the kingdom’s most faithful friend, once more to petition the king concerning the said churches. And for these matters, from our poverty, we shall endeavour to serve our lord as you think fitting, lest the almighty Judge someday see this sin, now long established, as demanding vengeance, and lest it become a scandal to those who occupy those churches through the king. We therefore pray and humbly beseech you to labour vigorously concerning this matter with our lord king, for the salvation of your soul and of the king’s; and, through the bearer of this letter or another person, as your grace judges best, hasten to write back to us while we still remain at Cluny, so that, knowing the state of the matter, we may know what we ought to do.

The king himself gave us this response about Gisors: that he would act toward us in such a way that he would not have it as a sin. We waited, and received nothing. I know how many and how great affairs occupy you, but may our petition, dearest Father and lord, find a place among so many things because of your generosity.

## LETTER CLXXIV. HUGH, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN, TO SUGER

Again he writes to him concerning the church of Gisors.

To his reverend Father and lord SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis, HUGH, priest of Rouen: greeting and the favour of grace.

Concerning the synod of the church of Mont-Girol, about which you wrote us through the priest of that same church, asking that we should, in consideration of the poverty of the place, make a peaceful claim, we defer the matter until we speak with you. For, since the ordinances of the sacred canons are not unknown to you, and our goodwill toward you is by no means unknown to you, we shall comply with this request of yours and with the rest according to your pleasure when we confer with you in person. You know indeed that, when due right is rendered to spiritual Fathers, the remaining portion is enlarged by divine blessing.

We seek your counsel concerning Gisors. For the church of Rouen cries out that in our days it has been despoiled of its fief. Moreover, it accuses us of silence and complains with astonishment that we do not enforce strict justice to the extent of our power, until Gisors or an equivalent value is restored to us. But because we know you to be most faithful to the king, whom we too love and wish to love, kindly suggest to him that he prudently provide for himself lest he incur the penalty of excommunication in this matter. For every Sunday the church of Rouen places under anathema those who plunder and diminish its goods, unless they make amends and restore what they have unjustly occupied. May your holy discernment fare well.

## LETTER CLXXV. ARNULF, BISHOP OF LISIEUX, TO SUGER

Concerning certain affairs between the duke of Normandy and the count of Anjou.

To the venerable and beloved Father and lord SUGER, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, ARNULF, humble minister of the church of Lisieux: greeting.

With the lady empress and her son, the duke of Normandy, I have conceived good hope, God willing, concerning the matter of which I discussed with you insofar as it pertains to Normandy. They immediately sent envoys in haste to the count of Anjou concerning the other point, which pertains to that side, begging him to frame that point toward peace and likewise to lend kindly counsel and assent to the point that pertains to Normandy. Since they have resolved to comply greatly with your counsel, they promise with much gladness that they will not prove ungrateful for your goodwill.

Therefore let your holiness do what it so kindly and sacredly promised us, and do not hesitate to indicate by a personal letter through this messenger the day to which the royal replies to the petitions of the English have been deferred through your efforts.

## LETTER CLXXVI. HENRY, BISHOP OF WINCHESTER, TO SUGER

He asks him to send an envoy to the countess of Flanders to request safe-conduct from her on his behalf.

HENRY, by God’s grace minister of the church of Winchester, to his venerable brother and dearest friend SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting.

We give you thanks concerning the matters which you conveyed to us through Henry our chancellor and Brother Savar, and ask you, when necessary and when you have our messenger, to carry your undertaking into effect. And since excessive caution does no harm, and all the authority of Flanders as far as the sea is in the hands of the countess [Sibyl], while the count [Theoderic] is absent, it seems to us advisable that you send your messenger and the messenger of Count Ralph together with your letters and our messenger to the countess of Flanders, and ask her that, when it becomes necessary for us to travel into those regions, she grant us and our people, for love of you, safe-conduct to pass through her land and authority, both going and returning; and that, if we request from her any of her men to escort us, she send them to us; and that, concerning all these matters, she send us letters sealed with her seal appended, containing these provisions.

Furthermore, we ask you to inform us whether you have received anything concerning our lord the king of the Franks or his people; and, if you have received his letters, to send us the letters themselves, or copies of them, if it please you. Farewell; and act so toward the countess through your letters and messenger that she grants me safe-conduct firmly. [Note: Henry requested a difficult thing, since access to Normandy was not safe for him. The countess of Flanders was the sister of Geoffrey, count of Anjou, who had taken the duchy of Normandy from her brother Stephen, king of England, by force of arms.]

## LETTER CLXXVII. THEOBALD, ARCHDEACON OF MEAUX, TO SUGER

He commends to him the poor nuns of Fontaines.

To his dearest Father SUGER, by God’s grace more than most reverend abbot of Saint-Denis, THEOBALD, called archdeacon of the people of Meaux: the horn of eternal salvation and the service of sincere affection.

I have not forgotten—indeed, I carefully recall—the well-known and widely proclaimed fact that you gladly make yourself a participant in every good work, and strive day by day to devote your attention to good works, recalling the saying of the Apostle: “While we have time, let us do good to all, especially to those of the household of faith.” With this assurance, your daughters, the religious women of Fontaines, compelled by the necessity of their poverty, flee to you as to a merciful father, supplicating and entreating you to deign to extend the hand of your customary charity toward the head of their church, which is now being built, and to take care to bring to completion the good work that you began for them.

For from their Bridegroom you will receive into your bosom “a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing,” entering into the joy of your Lord. So be it, so be it. May your holiness prosper; may God preserve it in health for his Church and for the kingdom of France.

## LETTER CLXXVIII. G., PRIOR OF LA CHARITÉ, TO SUGER

That, through the favour of the abbot of Clairvaux, he may restrain the oppressions inflicted upon him by the bishop of Auxerre.

To his most reverend lord SUGER, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, Brother G. [WILLIAM], humble minister of the brethren of La Charité, and the entire convent of that church: devout prayers in the Lord.

Seek in the secret recesses of your heart how greatly the eminence of your fatherhood flourishes in our memory, and judge it from the affection which you bear toward us. Since it belongs to sincere affection neither to be absent in place nor to yield to forgetfulness with time, our minds, refreshed by your presence and trusting not a little in your devotion, promise themselves much from your concern while they are placed in tribulation. And although the care of the office you have undertaken reminds your fatherhood that it ought with every effort to help the poor of Christ, especially those labouring in adversity, it is nevertheless not improper if the speech of our letter should stir your concern; for just as fire grows greater when the breeze blows, so the endeavours of a good mind advance.

Since therefore the lord of Auxerre [Hugh] is neither softened by our patience nor recalled by any pity from the injuries he inflicts upon us, and does not cease to harass us—not even because of a day for settlement fixed or accepted between us, nor meanwhile until it is observed—justice itself and equity compel you, as a son of truth and friend of fairness, to have compassion on us who are unjustly oppressed, though we say nothing. If we were refusing justice and he compelled us by force, and did what was his right, then we ought not be heard if we wished to complain further. But although we not only do not prevent justice but always offer every justice, he takes away everything belonging to us, both in tithes and in churches which are within his authority. He has not only seized our oxen, but has even sold them.

Now, after the appointed day for making peace—which he too set through the hand of the abbot of Clairvaux—not only is he not softened, but, lest he leave us any hope of a peaceful settlement, he is now more troublesome and severe than he used to be. For now he not only takes away what lies under his own authority, but also compels the lord of Nevers, the lord of Donzy, and every other person whom he can induce, to take away what we hold under them, as though by pontifical right. [Note: “As though by pontifical right,” etc. The bishops of Auxerre had granted the estate of the monastery of La Charité to the Cluniacs, as is recorded in a diploma of Louis VI, issued in 1119, where there is listed the priory of Blessed Mary of La Charité upon the Loire, which Geoffrey, bishop of Auxerre, William, count of Nevers, Bernard of Chailant, and other faithful men of our kingdom—to whom that place of La Charité, with its town and all its appurtenances, wholly belonged in spiritual and temporal matters—gave and granted, without any reservation on their own part, to Abbot Hugh, the monastery of Cluny, and their successors, etc.; vol. XIII of the quarto *Spicilegium*, p. 302.]

Afflicted therefore by such great oppressions, we cast ourselves mercifully at your knees and ask that, through the intercession of your prayers, we may deserve to obtain the favour of the lord abbot of Clairvaux to soften him toward us, so that by this proof we may perceive that the remembrance of our lowliness continues to flourish with you.

## LETTER CLXXIX. STEPHEN, KING OF ENGLAND, TO SUGER

He gives thanks for Suger’s friendship and for the services rendered him before the king of France.

STEPHEN, king of England, to SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis, his beloved friend: greeting.

I render you many thanks because you show me constant and unceasing affection, and have always taken care to be available and to intercede in all my business that I might wish to pursue before the king of the Franks, as I have learned from those who returned to me from there. And know that I am greatly indebted to you, and shall most willingly repay to you and yours the kindness which you have so often shown me. I shall cause your lands situated in my territory to be guarded and defended; and, as soon as I can, I shall restore to you that land which I gave you and which is still in the power of my enemies. [Note: “My enemies”: that is, Geoffrey, count of Anjou, who had acquired Normandy by arms and taken it from him.]

## LETTER CLXXX. HENRY, BISHOP OF WINCHESTER, TO SUGER

He commends to him the affairs of the king of England.

HENRY, by God’s grace minister of the church of Winchester, to his venerable brother and friend SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting.

I entrust my brother the king’s business to your affection with particular earnestness, asking you to support it as you are accustomed to do and, insofar as you know it to be expedient for him, not to delay bringing it to completion. The reason why I have sent neither greater envoys to the king nor to you is that I could scarcely return safely, and scarcely anyone on our side can cross over to you securely.

[Note: [Col. 1435C] *Can cross over.* For, as Gervase of Canterbury says under the year 1149: “Henry, son of the Empress, in the middle of May returned to England with a great retinue of chosen knights and foot-soldiers, and by his arrival stirred up the minds of many against King Stephen. For the earls and magnates of England were unwilling to raise any sedition against King Stephen . . . unless he himself, to whom all things rightly belonged, should return to England. Thus, on this occasion, he returned to England and, setting aside literary studies, began to pursue military exercises. Taking with him, therefore, the noble Ranulf, earl of Chester, and Roger, earl of Hereford, together with several others besides the renowned knights whom he had brought with him from Normandy, he visited David, king of Scotland, his kinsman. Received by him with the greatest joy and honour, he was also girded with the military belt, together with some of his contemporaries, on the sacred feast of Pentecost. From that day Henry began, for many reasons, to provoke against himself the mind of King Stephen and of his son Eustace . . . In the following year, at the beginning of January, he crossed over into Normandy. In those days all England was thrown into confusion by the din of war and exposed to fires and plundering,” etc.]

Therefore I send to the king and to you this man, who is faithful both to the king and to me; and give credence to whatever he may tell you orally on our behalf which is not contained in writing.

## LETTER CLXXXI. BALDWIN, BISHOP OF NOYON, TO SUGER

He excuses himself for not having come when summoned to him.

To the lord and venerable friend Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, Baldwin, unworthy minister of the Church of Noyon, wishes the spirit of fortitude.

That we did not come to the feast and at your summons, the repeated requests of our dearest brother and fellow bishop, the lord of Châlons, which had preceded them, compelled us; we do not put this forward as an excuse, but disclose the truth to a friend. As for the letters which followed, in which we received word of your illness, God knows how grievous the tidings they brought were to us. But we first saw them at Châlons, when we were already on the journey; and until the undertaking we had begun was concluded, we could not depart from the bishop. Yet we trust in the Lord, who has not forsaken those who hope in him. For who has hoped in him and been confounded? We trust that he will not allow our lowliness to be disappointed of its hope in him; but though for a time he has saddened us by your affliction, he will much more gladden us by your speedy recovery to health. We believe, God willing, that we shall see you shortly, and this is our request. This is what we desire with all our prayers: that the Lord Jesus may swiftly restore you, sound and cheerful, to us and to all your other household and friends, as he knows to be expedient for his Church and kingdom. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXXII. SUGER TO HENRY, BISHOP, CHAPTER, CLERGY, AND PEOPLE OF BEAUVAIS

He recalls them from the sedition planned against the king.

[Note: [Col. 1436C] Among the letters of Abbot Suger published by us, this is especially noteworthy, since from it we learn that Bishop Henry, the chapter, clergy, and people of Beauvais had planned sedition or rebellion against the king, and that Henry himself, the king’s brother, was a participant in this rebellion. Suger, out of his loyalty to the king, eloquently dissuades them from this crime. What Suger’s words, so urgent and so piercing, accomplished in Henry, the clergy, and the people of Beauvais, we do not know; their intended rebellion has become known to us from this letter of Suger alone. It does not seem far from the truth that they humbly obeyed the salutary warnings of so faithful a minister. Moreover, perhaps from these agitations of Bishop Henry against his brother the king arose adverse rumours concerning him at the Roman court, from which Saint Bernard strives to clear him in Letter 305 to Pope Eugenius, in these words: “He, namely Henry, and his brother the king do not walk in one spirit . . . Do not ask me whose fault it is; it is not mine to accuse anyone. It is enough for me to excuse the bishop, whom we have seen displaying, in his own person, every possible humility and submission, yet accomplishing nothing.” —Martène.]

To the venerable Bishop H., and to the chapter, clergy, and people together of the noble Church of Beauvais, Suger, by the grace of God abbot of Saint-Denis, wishes peace above and below from the King of kings and the king of the Franks.

From that familiarity by which, in the times both of the present lord king and of his father, when complaints arose, I was accustomed faithfully to labour for your peace, accepting no payment from anyone, as you know better than anyone—now also, though held by a serious illness, I ask, persuade, and advise you in every manner, while commending this course, that you do not stubbornly raise the heel, to your own disadvantage, against the lord king and the crown, upon which all archbishops, bishops, and barons depend and to which we are bound by right of fidelity.

For such daring is new and unheard of in this age, and you will not be able to endure it longer without the destruction of city and church. How ruinous and dangerous it is for arms to be raised by a bishop, or by the people committed to him, against their common lord—especially without consulting the supreme pontiff, the bishops of the realm, and the magnates—you yourselves will easily perceive. One thing ought above all to call you back from this presumption: up to this time you have nowhere heard that your predecessors attempted anything of the kind, nor will you be able to find an example of so wicked a deed in the records or reports of the ancients.

Why have you raised your heel against the lord king, that is, the pious friend of churches and most zealous promoter of every good, when he has absolutely no wish to take anything unjustly from you or from anyone else? If, through the persuasion of evil men, he had perhaps acted somewhat less well toward you, he ought certainly first to have been approached through the bishops and magnates of the realm, or rather through the lord pope, who is the head of the churches and could easily have brought all matters to peace.

Let the nobility of the new bishop therefore return to his heart. Although clothed in a commoner’s garb and unaccustomed to speak privately, he has gravely stirred up the king, his lord and brother, whom he ought rather to appease. If he does this from love of his Church, let him have zeal according to knowledge. If he strives to advance it well, let him divide more rightly. By conciliating royal clemency and submitting himself to its will, let him reconcile both himself and his Church and citizens to it, lest by diabolical craft there arise either the infamous disgrace of treachery against the crown, or of fratricide, or something of that kind.

And what shall I say of you, my dearest friends—the dean, the archdeacons, and the noble clergy of the chapter—if I hear that the noble estate of your Church is being overthrown and that, on this occasion, the abundance of God’s churches is being consumed by fire? He who knows all things knows that, though grievously ill and suffering from a quartan fever, I am at present afflicted more severely by this illness, and that I would willingly surrender myself for the calming of this sedition.

And what shall I say to you, most unhappy citizens, whom I have been accustomed to love greatly without any desire for gain—for I do not remember ever having received even one coin from you—if I hear of the overthrow of your city, of the plundering and exile of your sons and wives, and of the mutilation of many men? If these things happen now, then, the more they are delayed for any reason, the more swiftly, fiercely, cruelly, and miserably will they happen; for hatred increases through delay of vengeance.

Have pity on yourselves. Let the noble pontiff have pity on himself; let the clergy have pity on itself. For just as an ant cannot draw a cart, so in no way will they be able to defend the city of Beauvais from destruction against the strength of crown and sceptre. If I know anything, if I have retained anything—I who have now grown old in such affairs—you will spend what you acquired through long labour upon robbers and thieves; you will heap upon yourselves the anger of the lord king, indeed of all his successors; you will generate everlasting hatred for your descendants; and by the memory of this most wicked deed you will forever drive away from all churches throughout the realm the royal devotion and remarkable generosity by which they enriched this Church and others.

See to it, see to it, discerning men, lest there be written once again what was once found inscribed on a marble column of this city, spoken from the mouth of an emperor: “We command that the town of bridges be rebuilt.”

[Note: [Col. 1437D] The city of Beauvais is thus called, being even now spanned by many little bridges over its river, or because it is believed formerly to have borne the name *Bratuspontium*.]

## LETTER CLXXXIII. GOSLEN, BISHOP OF SOISSONS, TO SUGER

Concerning his desire to see him.

To the lord Suger, worthy of reverence, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, G., by the same patience called bishop of the Soissons people, wishes greeting in the Lord.

There is no greater desire on earth than to see you; nevertheless, I am so weak that I cannot manage to travel either on horseback or on foot. Yet, God willing, I shall hasten to come to you on whatever days’ journey I am able; nor do I think that I shall survive you for long.

[Note: [Col. 1437D] *Nor do I think that I shall survive you for long.* Pseudo-Robert of Torigni, published by Pithou, relates that Goslen died in 1151. If this is true, he did not survive Suger long. For in the necrology of Fontenay, under 25 October, one reads: “The most reverend Goslen, bishop of Soissons, of pious memory, departed from this world; he was our benefactor and a most noble teacher.”]

Farewell in the Lord.

## LETTER CLXXXIV. SUGER TO GOSLEN, BISHOP OF SOISSONS

Reply to the preceding letter.

To his most loving lord and friend, the venerable G., by God’s grace bishop of Soissons, Suger, still the humble minister, such as he is, of Saint-Denis, wishes that he may happily exercise the episcopal office among the blessed bishops of Jesus Christ in Almighty God.

I desire to see you, my friend, as much as you desire to see yours—or more, if I can. But since I have no strength of my own, I beseech Almighty God, with such prayer as I can, that I may deserve to see you before my death. As for your message that you will not long survive me, I desire with all the intention of my heart, and earnestly implore divine mercy, that God may preserve both your life and prosperity, because this would be most advantageous to me. I await the sight of your face and rejoice in expectation of so great a friend.

## LETTER CLXXXV. GOSLEN, BISHOP OF SOISSONS, TO SUGER

Reply to the preceding letter.

To the lord S., worthy of reverence, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, G., by the same patience called bishop of the Soissons people, wishes greeting in the Lord and the gift of a longer life.

Behold, I am coming, carried onward more by the desire to visit you than by my body’s ability. Pray therefore to Saint Denis, to whom nothing can be refused, that he may obtain from God that I find you alive. May the Lord grant you good health until I come to you, and thereafter.

## LETTER CLXXXVI. SUGER TO KING LOUIS

He commends the king and kingdom to God, and commends the Church of Saint-Denis to the king.

To L., the glorious king of the Franks and duke of Aquitaine by God’s grace, our dearest lord, Suger, least of all the abbots of Saint-Denis, offers devoted prayers in Christ and faithful service.

Worn away by the long wasting of a most severe illness, I considered it fitting to inform Your Excellency that my dissolution is near, while with good hope and good faith I await with all my heart the mercy of God, which he never denies to those who hope in him.

[Note: [Col. 1437D–1438D] *My dissolution,* etc. The Short Chronicle of Saint-Denis and Robert of Torigni report that Suger died in 1151; it is otherwise known that he was taken from life on the Ides, or 13 January. Some think this year should be understood as 1152 according to the French manner; but Pagi refutes them in his note on the year 1151, no. VI. Indeed, the name of Odo, Suger’s successor, is found subscribed to a charter of King Louis VII, whose closing reads, in vol. I of the *Amplissima Collectio*, col. 817: “Done publicly at Paris, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1151, epact XII, concurrent VII, and the nineteenth year of our reign, those present in the palace,” etc. All these chronological marks suit the year 1151, but not 1152.]

All wonder that, worn down by so great and prolonged suffering, I have survived, thinking that this has been granted to my lowliness by the bounty of divine mercy, so that, having had so much time for repentance, I might recall my years in the bitterness of my soul and make provision for myself. For, placed in so great an honour, I could not live without many [added: sins].

I earnestly commend to the Lord God your person, the prosperity of your person, and the state of the kingdom; and I beseech divine mercy with such prayer as I can, that among blessed kings you may obtain the unfading crown of eternal glory. But in all things, among all things, and before all things, I earnestly beseech Your Nobility on behalf of the noble Church of Saint-Denis, which is a very great part of your kingdom and crown: cherish and uphold it as a good and pious lord, and extend to it the hand of counsel and aid.

Let the loftiness of royal majesty remember how, when you departed as a young man from your land, you left the noble kingdom of the Franks in the hand of the Church; through so many dangers and deaths you visited the Eastern Church. See and consider, lest you lose so great a labour. Love the Church of God; defend orphans and widows. Thus, with God’s help, you will be able to resist every power, both aerial and worldly, and the snares of your rivals, of whom you have many.

For this is my counsel. Since you cannot keep me with you, keep this letter always with you, and endeavour to fulfil what is written in it; for I speak to you for your own sake. May Your Highness prosper.

## LETTER CLXXXVII. ABBOT SUGER OF SAINT-DENIS TO SAINT BERNARD

He gives thanks for the consolation given him in his last days and commends himself to Bernard’s prayers.

[Note: [Col. 1439C–1440C] Suger wrote this letter when near death, after receiving Saint Bernard’s Letter 206, in which the holy abbot encourages him to meet death without fear in these words: “Man of God, do not tremble to put off that man who is of the earth . . . What have you to do with earthly coverings, when you are about to go to heaven and will soon be clothed in the robe of glory?”]

To his most loving lord and venerable father Bernard, by God’s grace abbot of Clairvaux, Suger, still the humble minister of Saint-Denis, wishes greeting and the affection of sincere love.

You have visited us by your letter; may the Dayspring from on high visit you. You sent to me, a miserable sinner, your little gifts—or rather very great gifts: the precious napkin, the bread of your blessing, and the letter of consolation, containing good and holy words, overflowing with honey and milk; and you have given me the greatest consolation as I stand at my end.

For if I could have seen your angelic face even once before my death, I would depart more securely from this most miserable world. Know for certain, however, that if I had deserved to live a thousand years or more, I would not care to remain except in God’s good pleasure. For I trust not in works of righteousness, but in the mercy of God alone, which he always shows to those who hope in him; and with all my heart I desire to return to him. Therefore I devoutly commend my soul into your holy hands; and, prostrate at the knees of your holiness, I earnestly entreat you to win divine favour for my soul by your prayers and the prayers of your holy communities.

[Col. 1439]

# TESTAMENT OF ABBOT SUGER  
*(A.D. 1137)*

(Dom Félibien, *History of the Royal Abbey of Saint-Denis in France*, Proofs, p. XCIX, from the original.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen. Suger, by God’s forbearance humble minister of the Church of Saint Denis.

Since the great multitude of the Lord’s sweetness, which he hides for those who fear him and accomplishes for those who hope in him, was pleased through the abundant flow of his mercy to restore me to myself, making me mindful of my former iniquities, so that his mercy might quickly come before me—after the shifting and violent rocks of this unclean world, after the long exhaustion and almost consuming waste of body and soul through the cares of the Church and other matters—I fled in longing prayer to the suffrages of the saints in whose service I had laboured, though not as I ought, and to the prayers of our brethren serving there in a holy religion acceptable to the Lord. In the chapter-house, with them, as I was accustomed to do, I sat down in good peace.

Trusting in them and through them after the Lord, like a sick man before a faithful physician I began to unfold anxiously the ailments of my weakness, laying up my years in the bitterness of my soul, lamenting and inwardly abhorring them. I set before myself my long ingratitude for the abundance of divine benefits: how the mighty hand of the Lord raised me, poor as I was, from the dung heap; how even before this honour he caused me to sit with the princes of Church and kingdom; how he exalted me, unworthy and absent, to this holy seat, with the peace of all; and by what generosity of our lords the popes, our lords the kings, princes, and peoples, he calmed the snares of rivals, won goodwill for us, and prospered us utterly in all things, spiritual as well as temporal.

And while I am bound under so many debts, I am shaken by fearfully crying out concerning repayment: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. 115:3.) Therefore, wounded inwardly by grief of heart and preparing for flight, I most humbly beseech the true protector of life, with all the affection of mind and heart, prostrate at the knees of our brethren, of each and all, in the charity by which Christ loved us, pouring out his blood to unite us, that he may bring aid. For their peace, indeed, I expose myself now to labours, trembling and devoutly claiming a small share, however small, of future rest to be prepared for me.

And because those who walk with the Lord cannot be without charity—for their heart burns within them concerning Jesus while he speaks to them on the way—that venerable choir, near to the Lord, whose conversation is already in heaven, suddenly descended from on high into the valley of my sorrow. As fathers, brothers, and sons, in age, charity, and obedience, they stretch forth a generous hand of mercy and determine both orally and in writing what suffrages they will provide while I live and after I die.

For they establish for us by the unshaken law of truth, which is Christ, and ratify by this present charter of memorial, that throughout my lifetime Mass of the Holy Spirit shall be celebrated every day, so that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, who is the remission of all sins, may forgive us our sins, grant consolation, and pour in the dew of mercy. The continuous observance of this holy sacrifice shall proceed daily in chapter: begun and recommenced by the senior priests, it shall continue without failure through the younger brethren of the same order, and return to the seniors. This shall be done as long as I survive by the Lord’s mercy.

But when I have put off the most miserable man of this life, throughout all the courses of every year and season, for the remedy of my soul and of the brethren and benefactors of the Church, they shall, in the order stated, pronounce and chant the Mass of the Holy Spirit and “Eternal rest,” and by such perseverance reconcile to us the divine favour through the saving sacrifice.

Every year they shall make the anniversary day of my funeral—the day of terror, calamity, and misery—manifest by such and so great a suffrage in works of mercy. All those in priestly orders shall perform the full office in the convent, mercifully offering sacrifice to the Lord God for us on that day. The remaining brethren shall aid us before the Lord by the offering of fifty psalms. Those who do not know them shall mercifully assist us by whatever offering they can make. For our lowliness needs both great and small assistance.

And because, as dearest and sweetest brethren, they faithfully promised whatever good things I requested of them, we have also obtained from the whole chapter that the capiciarius brother, whoever he may be, shall provide from the capicium, on the day of our anniversary, that the brothers in the refectory receive a carefully furnished meal: namely, two shared dishes for all, not merely ordinary ones but full and suitable portions. The cellarer also shall provide his customary general allowance. The brethren shall have spiced wine from the wardrobe and cellar.

We humbly ask that this brother, whether he has seen us or not, should not bear these expenses grudgingly, since we were attentive to meeting many expenses in a great part of his office: namely, in enlarging the new and great building of the church; in constructing the great and charitable guesthouse; in repairing and renewing the dormitory and refectory; in increasing the treasury’s endowment; and in many other costly works, both of the church and its workshops, which we refrain from enumerating lest they be imputed to us as empty glory or some form of arrogance, which my soul does not need. Above all, we set these things down in order to acquire the goodwill and devotion of succeeding brethren.

But because sins are redeemed by the giving of alms, our dearest brethren, providing also for me in this regard, establish by firm ordinance that every year, on the day of my anniversary, the prior of this church and the almoner monk shall cause to be distributed in their presence two modii of wheat bread, four modii of wine, and sixty solidi-worth of meat, so that they too may share in this benefit—namely, in the great guesthouse itself, so that both place and work, by the Lord’s mercy, may cooperate for our good.

And when the poor canons in the house of Saint Paul, for whose benefit I also acquired something for the remedy of my soul, and the other clerical chaplains have rendered us the due of the anniversary either in the church of Saint Paul or at the place of my burial—if God’s mercy grants me this in that place—they shall assemble in their refectory and receive from the prior and almoner, from the alms above determined, one modius of wine and a hundred loaves, of the same weight and quality as those of the brethren.

We have taken care to determine from what source and where they shall have the wheat, wine, and money: wheat at harvest-time from Tremblay. For we greatly enlarged that estate, both by the building of the outer court and barns and in every other way. Likewise, at vintage-time, five modii of wine from Rueil, from the new acquisition which we made at Louveciennes. For we acquired there almost sixty modii of wine each year. The money shall be twenty solidi from Franconville; likewise forty solidi from the purse of the money-changer and toll-collector, in compensation for our withdrawing from the hand of Ursellus, the Jew of Montmorency, ten solidi which he seized every week from that same purse by reason of a pledge. For we spent three thousand solidi to redeem this money and the estate called Molignon, which that same Jew held in pledge.

We also asked our brethren that on the same day they should display, either at Mass or as they please, the ornaments of cloth, gold, or silver which divine munificence bestowed upon the same church during the time of our administration; so that the devotion of the brethren may be increased by holy prayers for my most wretched and hungry soul, and that the diligence of succeeding abbots concerning the worship of God’s Church may be encouraged.

And because all members ought to cooperate with their head, we requested that our anniversary be observed in all the dependent houses throughout the world, according to the means and capacity of the places.

At Argenteuil, in particular—a place alienated from this Church for nearly three hundred years and almost ruined by the unrestrained frivolity of the nuns—we laboured to restore it, Pope Honorius of blessed memory presiding and confirming it by privilege, and the illustrious King Louis reigning and granting his consent. There, on the same day, the brethren shall receive ten solidi from Sarterville for their refectory; and every year, without refusal, they shall distribute to the poor from the same source bread from one modius of wheat and two modii of wine, for the remedy of my soul and for the welfare of our brethren, both living and dead. Every Monday and Tuesday they shall celebrate Mass for me and for the other dead.

At Estrée, where our lord, after the thrice-blessed Denis, rested for the entire period of three hundred years—and where also, both for the exaltation of the praise of God’s saints and because of the many offences which I committed there while dwelling for ten years in my youth, both in age and habits—we have decreed that twelve monks, with a thirteenth as prior, shall reside under the Rule in service to God and the holy martyrs. To their refectory we have also assigned the estate of Molignon, which, as stated above, we had recovered from the hand of Ursellus the Jew; and we have devoutly requested and obtained continual prayer before the Lord, our anniversary, and a Mass for the dead every Wednesday.

At Corbeil, at Saint Mary, Mother of God—a most holy place which we have begun to build and enlarge, and which, if the Lord gives us life, we most firmly intend to complete—we have likewise devoutly requested our anniversary and a Mass for the dead every Thursday.

At the dependent house which we acquired in the bishopric of Metz, at the court held at Mainz, we likewise devoutly sought continual prayer, our anniversary, and a Mass for the dead every Friday.

Likewise, at the venerable place of Saint Alexander at Lebraha, we have implored a Mass for the dead every Saturday, our anniversary, and the stirring of divine ears on our behalf. No less earnestly have we requested and obtained in all the houses of Saint Denis, both near and distant, our anniversary, the earnestness of prayers, and a Mass for the dead once each week.

And since our dearest brethren, humbly asked by us and knowing that we need great assistance, willingly consented to our petitions, we appeal to them by prayer; we appeal also by the command of fatherhood; and, adjuring them by that obedience in which Christ offered himself to God the Father upon the altar of the cross, we entreat them that henceforth, throughout every course of time and in the successive generations of succeeding brethren, they may not cease from the suffrage which they have guaranteed to us, but may render what was promised and pay what was vowed, as those who must answer on the final day of strict judgment, when we shall see one another in him who sees us and all our deeds in every respect, and who may deign that we live for him through all ages of ages. Amen.

Done at Saint-Denis in the common chapter, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1137, indiction XV, epact XXVI, concurrent IV, moon XXIV, and the sixteenth year of our administration.

Mark of Lord Hervey, prior. Mark of Teuvin, subprior. Mark of Bernard, precentor. Mark of William, charter-writer. Mark of Stephen, treasurer. Mark of Geoffrey, capiciarius. Mark of John, infirmarer. Mark of Henry, cellarer. Mark of Albert, formerly abbot. Mark of Vincent, formerly abbot. Mark of Christian, priest. Mark of Ralph, priest. Mark of Adam, priest. Mark of Wildric, priest. Mark of Philip, priest. Mark of Robert, priest. Mark of Peter, priest. Mark of William, priest. Mark of John, deacon. Mark of Gerard, deacon. Mark of Hugh, deacon. Mark of Arnulf, deacon. Mark of Theobald, deacon. Mark of Richard, deacon. Mark of Solomon, deacon. Mark of William, deacon. Mark of Gerard, deacon. Mark of Rainier, deacon. Mark of William, subdeacon. Mark of Hugh, subdeacon. Mark of Ralph, subdeacon. Mark of Arald, subdeacon. Mark of Hubert, subdeacon. Mark of Eustace, subdeacon. Mark of Winebert, subdeacon. Mark of Gilbert, subdeacon. Mark of Radulf, subdeacon. Mark of Peter, subdeacon. Mark of Hemelin, boy. Mark of Ernald, boy. Mark of Warner, boy. Mark of Ilbert, boy. Mark of Philip, boy. Mark of Peter, boy. Mark of Cono, boy. Mark of Berner, boy. Mark of Guy, boy. Mark of Amblard, boy. Mark of Goslen, bishop of Soissons. Mark of Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres. Mark of Hugh, archbishop of Tours.
