[Note: [Col. 1445A–1446A] This testament and several others like it seem to prove that the canons which remove from regular abbots the power of making wills have not always been observed equally in every age, and that discipline has varied in this respect. It may nevertheless be said that such testaments ought to be regarded merely as confirmation of the first disposition which abbots had made of their goods while they were still masters of them. Moreover, if attention is paid, it will be observed in most of these testaments that the abbots who made them used them only to request prayers from their religious, to have certain alms distributed to churches dependent upon them, or finally to secure certain practices which they had established during their lives. They did not doubt that their disciples would comply with these provisions when they saw their abbot’s last will expressed in an authentic act, often approved by bishops and other persons of the highest rank.]

[Col. 1445]

# CONSTITUTIONS OF ABBOT SUGER

(Duchesne, *Writers on French Affairs*, IV, 546.)

## I. Concerning the commemoration of Blessed Mary at Saint-Denis every week, namely on Saturday and Thursday, and concerning the meal of the brethren on those same days

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. I, Suger, by the grace of God humble minister of the church of the blessed martyrs Denis, Rusticus, and Eleutherius.

Because, by the abundant propitiation of Almighty God, contrary to any expectation based on the merits of my conduct or birth, it is manifest that my lowliness—even while absent and engaged in business at the Roman court—was raised to the administration of this holy Church, and that divine power truly delivered and rescued me, in this same holy church, praiseworthily and wonderfully, from the hands of enemies seeking my life [Col. 1445C], it is fitting and altogether expedient for our littleness to commend and exalt it with all the affection of our mind, and to honor and cherish the brethren serving our Lord God; so that by the offering of divine worship in the present we may be able to please the divine gaze, and in the future may obtain some small share of divine recompense in the bosom of eternal blessedness.

Therefore, to the honor of Almighty God and of the blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, as we sat in our chapter in general assembly, we have decreed to continue, exalt, and adorn the commemoration of that holy Mother of God, under this provision: henceforth and for ever it shall be celebrated solemnly every Saturday, according to what is set down in the catalogue of this ordinance, just as on the last three days in the octave of Pentecost; except that we forbid the omission of the seven psalms, with the litany and the office for the dead. Since, indeed, we cannot sufficiently serve that most sacred Mother of God [Col. 1446B], queen of angels and men, owing to the distractions of the present age and the shortness of this wretched life, we encourage our brethren, with such prayer and favor as we can, to her most holy worship, worthy of God; and by both prayer and the stipulation of this privilege we continue for our successors for ever that most holy and pleasing service of God.

Moreover, we observe the commemoration of our most glorious and sweetest patrons, the most holy Dionysius and his companions—by whose wonderful and ineffable benefit we have been reared, taught, and aided—on Thursday, in the same order and with equal solemnity as that of this most holy Mother of God. For we have deemed it worthwhile to serve so holy and apostolic a lord of ours without ceasing, in life and after death, at least in this manner [Col. 1446C]: so that, mindful of his so many benefits, we may attain in him an inclined and propitious advocate before the strict Judge on the last and terrible day of judgment; and, as we share in his benefits in the present, so also in those to come, may happily obtain at least some outermost portion of eternal blessedness at the feet of our lord and master.

And since our brethren, like dearest sons obedient to our commands, have devoted both themselves and their successors to this service, we augment their daily general allowance of six solidi by four solidi, so that it becomes ten, for their refectory meal every week, on those most celebrated days of holy commemorations; whether they observe them, or suitably transfer them because of some principal solemnity of Vigils or of Lent [Col. 1446D]. And we earnestly beseech Almighty God and the terrible examination of the strict judgment that this augmentation may remain unfailingly. Therefore, lest it should ever be suppressed through anyone’s greed, we assign and confirm for it, from the revenues increased through our own labor—namely, from the toll collected on the highway—ten pounds and ten solidi on the seventh day of the week, from our revenues of Vilcassinum and from tithes granted by Louis, glorious king of the Franks [Col. 1447A].

Furthermore, devoted to the service of Almighty God and the support of our brethren, exchanging transitory things for eternal ones, we have decreed that certain solemnities be celebrated twice over, more honorably and more devoutly than usual, in compassion for their labors and for their consolation: namely, the Epiphany, the Ascension of the Lord, the Nativity of St. John the Baptist, the departure of blessed Mary Magdalene, the Nativity of the most blessed and ever-virgin Mary, and the feast of the most precious Theban martyrs. For each of the aforesaid solemnities we firmly confirm one hundred and twenty solidi for the exaltation of such feasts and the refectory meal of our brethren: sixty solidi of these are to be paid from the aforesaid toll, and sixty from the provostship of Vilcassinum. But if, by any chance or circumstance—which God forbid!—the aforesaid revenues should be greatly diminished or altogether fail, we likewise command, by the authority of Almighty God, that they be supplied from the other revenues of this Church and restored by the abbot.

For their evening meals also, which they call suppers, since from childhood and from the daily official recitation concerning them we have learned that they require some increase [Col. 1447C], we have granted them the tithe of St. Lucian, which served our own uses, on this condition: that from it they shall in perpetuity observe our anniversary after our departure from this life, and on that occasion receive ten solidi for their refectory meal from my supper-officer.

Therefore, from our dearest brethren and sons, with whom we earnestly desire to escape divine indignation and attain mercy, we have obtained, besides their individual prayers, while we enjoy this present light, a most faithful and irrevocable promise for myself and my successors: on every Thursday and Saturday on which the aforesaid commemorations may be celebrated, for the ordering of my sins and the direction of this most wretched life, they shall mercifully say in all the nocturnal and diurnal hours one psalm, “Unto thee have I lifted up”; and, after the dissolution of this wretched body [Col. 1447D], on those days of holy commemorations, “Out of the depths have I cried,” throughout all the courses of time. In this one special and continual provision we hope, through the aid of the holy Mother of God and the other saints, and through the successive intercession of our brethren, to lay aside the filth of our offences and to obtain mercy, at least on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, in some outermost region of Paradise.

We also command and establish that the anniversary of the most glorious Louis, king of the Franks, be observed every year after his most vigorous administration of the kingdom; and we direct that on that day they shall have twenty solidi for their own refectory meal from the aforesaid tithes of Vilcassinum bestowed upon us by him. [Col. 1448A] And lest this ordinance of ours and of the brethren, and the permanence of the present charter, be diminished or destroyed by any presumption or rashness, as we sit in our chapter in general assembly, by the nail and crown of the Lord, the arm of St. Simeon, and the authority of Almighty God and of all the saints, we impose and pronounce perpetual anathema and the fires of Gehenna upon violators; but upon the preservers and defenders of this privilege, eternal life.

I, Peter, priest-cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, approve and confirm.

I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Sant’Angelo and legate of the Apostolic See, approve and confirm.

## II. Concerning the men of the town of Saint-Denis, granted freedom.

[Col. 1448B] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, Suger, humble minister of the church of Saint-Denis.

Since it has pleased the divine dispensation to advance our lowliness to the administration of the church of the most glorious martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, we ought and desire, as far as we are able and as is fitting, with the filial affection of devotion to provide in every way for the honor and freedom of this our mother. Therefore we wish it to be made known openly both to those now living and to future posterity that the townsmen and residents of the town of Saint-Denis, severely burdened and afflicted by the levy of a most evil custom called *mortua manus* (“dead hand”), which truthful inquiry shows to have become established from the time of our predecessor Abbot Ivo [Col. 1448C], approached us with humble vows and prayers, begging that we rescue them and their heirs from the yoke of so wicked an exaction and oppression—not a charge due by ancient custom, but an ambitious introduction of a new levy.

Accordingly, having as customary taken counsel with our brethren, we unanimously assented to their request. For we judged it fitting to honor more highly and generously than the rest the town of Saint-Denis, which among all the possessions of the aforesaid church rightly holds a pre-eminent position and singular privilege, and is distinguished in a special manner by the presence of the most precious martyrs, with the special prerogative that it claims by right. Therefore, by the terms of this document and as a most firm memorial of permanence, we have for ever remitted the aforesaid exactions to all dwelling in the aforesaid town on the land of Saint-Denis or under its jurisdiction, because they gave us two hundred pounds, to be spent by our decision and provision upon renewing and adorning the entrance of the monastery of Saint-Denis [Col. 1448D].

Further, we have admitted to this release and alleviation from the levy certain persons of Saint-Marcel: Fulk, son of Elynand, and Herlewin the money-changer, with their heirs. But when it happens that the aforesaid burgesses give their offspring in marriage, after the death of those offspring, should they die without heirs, the parents residing in the town of Saint-Denis shall have the right of dead hand, even if there be some nearer relative who has no dwelling in the aforesaid town on the land of Saint-Denis or under its jurisdiction. And if it should happen that they marry their daughters to men subject to another lordship, we grant them no exemption from dead hand at all, but expressly require and command that they be recalled to their legal obligation.

For just as, by evident reason, we judge it just to remove in pious consideration unjust exactions from those whom they afflict and oppress, so we judge it unworthy to share the grace of voluntary remission—as benefits with the ungrateful—with those who are shown to evade the lordship of our church by withdrawing themselves and their property from us. Yet we have been pleased to grant this remission for the salvation of my soul, of our predecessors and successors, for the honor of our church and our fellow servants, and from the affection of goodwill [Col. 1449A]. Lest anyone hereafter, led by a similar example though not by an equal intention, presume rashly to do the same concerning the other estates of the church of Saint-Denis, we forbid it, under imposition of anathema, by the authority of Almighty God and the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius.

What we have accomplished from zeal for goodwill and feeling of compassion we have caused to be confirmed and strengthened, as a perpetual memorial, by the protection and consent of the royal seal together with our own seal, with the authorities and witnesses subscribed below, so that it may henceforth remain unviolated.

Done in the monastery of Saint-Denis in a general assembly, with Lord Suger, venerable abbot of the same monastery, presiding [Col. 1449C], in the third year of his administration, in the year 1125 of the Lord’s Incarnation, on Sunday, the Ides of March, the seventh lunar day, in the third indiction; epact XIV, concurrent III; in the seventeenth year of the reign of Louis, glorious and illustrious king of the Franks, who confirmed the present grant.

I, Abbot Suger, have subscribed and placed the violators of this privilege under anathema. The burgesses have promised, for my soul, to provide one alms from every household on the day of my death.

Witnessed by Gausbert the prior, Christian the treasurer, Vivian the cantor, Ralph son of Anthelm, Gregory and the other priests, and Philip the deacon.

[Col. 1449D] Witnessed by William of Saint-Cloud, Frederick, Herbert, Henry, subdeacons; Garnier, Robert, Peter, Fortin, acolytes; Geoffrey, Godfrey, laymen; William of Cornillon with his son William; Ivo son of Suger with his son Adam; Hugh of Saint-Denis, Hilduin, Seherius, and Itherius.

I, Gregory, chancellor of Lord Abbot Suger, have reread and subscribed.

## III. Concerning several properties granted to the Church of Saint-Paul by Abbot Suger, and concerning a measure of wine and one hundred loaves on the day of his death.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father [Col. 1450A], Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen. I, Suger, by divine grace abbot of the church of Saint-Denis.

Because by the abundant mercy of Almighty God our lowliness has been advanced and it has fallen to us to be raised to the government of this Church, we must serve the interests of God’s servants with much solicitude and continuous care, honor the Catholic Church and the servants of the Church, so that on the terrible day of the strict final examination we may deserve to hear from the Lord God: “Well done, good and faithful servant.” Therefore let the diligence of both present and future generations know that I, Suger, abbot of the church of Saint-Denis, with the consent of our brethren, have decreed and undertaken to honor and exalt the church of Saint-Paul, which adheres to our church like a limb to its head. This is both because through the preaching of blessed Paul, teacher of the Gentiles, we have obtained our lord and protector St. Dionysius [Col. 1450B], and because whatever honor and benefit we confer upon it, since it is ours, will wholly redound to our honor and advantage.

We grant the cloister of that church, the workshops in the cloister, and the cloister houses which they possess or may possess around the cloister, for building dwellings belonging to the church and houses for the canons, with inviolable freedom and exemption from every exaction. Nor do we grant this only there: wherever they have their houses, so long as they inhabit them, we free their houses, possessions, and household servants. But if these pass from their hands to other persons, they shall return under judicial power according to the law of the town. No freedom shall protect the property of our townsmen or other persons in their houses. This only shall be done: the property of others shall be handed over to our authority by the clerics of St. Paul [Col. 1450C].

They shall have jurisdiction to administer justice upon thieves of their own household and upon those who have stolen from them. Other fugitive thieves they shall hand over to our authority; likewise other accused persons who have fled to them. But if a dispute over anything arises between them and us, whatever the clerics can swear concerning it, either themselves or through a legally qualified person, they shall hold without further contradiction.

So that throughout all succeeding ages they may pray that the Lord be propitious to us—for me, a sinner, and for our brethren past, present, and future—we have wished to relieve somewhat their poverty from our abundance (for they are servants of God as we are, and are our fellow servants). They shall take annually forty solidi, which they had inviolably from Duolio, from the rent of Arnulf’s holding, and one measure of grain from a mill located by the town called Ulmechon [Col. 1450D]. We also grant each year, for the refreshment of the canons, one measure of wine from the cellar and ten solidi from the wine-dues of the criers at each of the two feasts of St. Paul, so that they may serve God and St. Paul more joyfully and devoutly.

Moreover, we grant to the same church of Saint-Paul the church of St. John, situated in the precinct of Saint-Denis; half the tithe of a certain town called Hablegias; a fourth part of the tithe of Barcheniac; and half the tithe of another town called Campiniac [Col. 1451A]. We also ask our brethren, for God’s love and ours—we who, so far as bodily weakness permits, labor in the service of the Church—to grant to the same church of Saint-Paul, for the refreshment in the refectory of Saint-Paul both of the chaplains of this town and of the canons, on the day of my anniversary, one measure of wine and one hundred loaves according to the pound and measure of our bread in the Refectory, as is written in the charter of our testament. This is on the condition and agreement that, on the day of my anniversary, if God’s mercy permits me to be buried within the enclosure of this church, they shall gather every year at my grave and make an offering for my soul; otherwise, in the church of Saint-Paul.

We have also granted these things to them so that, for these and other benefits, at the death of each of our brethren, monks of this church, they may assemble by their bodies before burial, make there the commendation of the soul, and celebrate Mass for it at Saint-Hilaire. If one of our monks should die outside this church while on obedience, they shall similarly assemble at Saint-Hilaire when they hear of our brother’s death, make the commendation of his soul there, and celebrate Mass for him. As for chanting the Psalter, which they declared that they were unable to perform after our Matins, it has been established that after our deceased brother has been buried, on the next day or within three days after his burial, they shall meet in the church of Saint-Paul and together chant the commendation of the soul and a Mass for his soul with recitation of the Psalter [Col. 1451B].

Nor should it be omitted that Abbot Adam, of pious memory, at the dedication of the church of St. Peter enlarged its endowment for the chanting of Matins on the vigil of St. Dionysius. He also fully restored the prebend, under the authority and anathema of Lord Coni, cardinal, the archbishop of Eurohic [uncertain reading], and Clarembald, bishop of Senlis, which King Robert of great piety had obtained from the chapter by his prayers. After the Matins of St. Dionysius, that same king continued works of mercy and prayers in the church of Saint-Paul; and, seeing that the humility of the church and its clerics kindly devoted themselves to God’s service, he gave to that church, so that God might be propitious to him, from his fisc the mill of Saint-Lucian and the mill by the spring near Pont-Malbert [Col. 1451C].

The common body of benefactors, moved by the entreaties and merits of the clerics, bestowed with wholehearted compassion the third, small mill—which long lies unproductive at uncertain times because of excessive water—the oven of Saint-Marcel, and the oven at the gate of Basuin. The enclosure of Strata, the enclosure of Cormelles, and the enclosure of Montmorency; the enclosure of Diogilo; and whatever small portion of rent lies around and within the town, the brethren, joining themselves to God’s service and almsgiving by the entreaties and merits of the same persons, have mercifully bestowed upon the same Church.

Done and confirmed in the chapter of Saint-Denis, in the year 1138 of the Incarnate Word, indiction XV, epact XXVI, concurrent IV, and the sixteenth year of our administration.

[Col. 1452A] Mark of Lord Abbot Suger; mark of Hervey, prior; mark of Bernard, precentor; mark of Stephen, treasurer; mark of Geoffrey, keeper of the cope; mark of Christian, priest; mark of John, priest; mark of Garnier, priest; mark of John, deacon; mark of Theobald, deacon; mark of Hugh, deacon; mark of Rodulf, subdeacon; mark of Bernerius, subdeacon; mark of Peter, subdeacon; mark of Ernald, boy; mark of Guy, boy; mark of Philip, boy.

## IV. Concerning the cultivated land of Indictum.

We wish it to be known to those present and to posterity that I, Suger, by God’s forbearance humble minister of Saint-Denis, with the common approval of our chapter, have granted in perpetual alms for the maintenance of Christ’s poor, for the remedy and salvation of my soul, the cultivated land near Indictum, which Louis, glorious king of the Franks, gave to St. Dionysius [Col. 1452B]. And, in order that this may be held ratified, we have caused it to be confirmed by a written mandate and our seal.

## V. Concerning the plot purchased from Gerard the Hospitaller.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, Suger, by the grace of God abbot of Saint-Denis, commit to the memory of both present and future generations that Robert the goldsmith, with my consent and that of our entire chapter, bought from Gerard the Hospitaller one plot of land for building a house before the monastery of Saint-Denis. After he had bought it, I enlarged it for him by some space; and, with the consent of the chapter, I granted, gave, and confirmed it to him thus enlarged, with this liberty: that both he and his heir shall have free power to exchange it, give it, sell it, or dispose of it in any manner they wish to anyone, whether burgess, peasant, or servant under the authority of Saint-Denis [Col. 1452C].

In order that under this agreement it may be less readily alienated, he shall give each year within the octave of Saint-Denis one silver spoon weighing one ounce. And lest anyone presume to invalidate this statute, we authorize it by the testimony of our seal.

And I, Matthew, by the grace of God bishop of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See, confirm with our seal what the abbot has granted.

The witnesses of this agreement are Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres; Odo, prior of St. Martin-des-Champs; Josbert, prior of Saint-Denis; Arveus, keeper of the cope of Saint-Denis [Col. 1452D]; and the entire convent of the same place.

## VI. Concerning towns of Saint-Denis taken away, namely Blitestorp and others.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, Suger, abbot of the church of Saint-Denis.

Let all present and future persons know that Count Albert of Morspec, a man of the highest discretion and prudence, recalled to the way of truth by the spirit of fear, which blows where it wills, approached us and our brethren both personally and through his representatives, earnestly pleading and urgently demanding that we deal mercifully with him and free him from the ancient and continuing bond of anathema. For this most noble count had taken as wife a most noble woman, namely the daughter of Theoderic, most illustrious lord of Montbéliard [Col. 1453A], through whose marriage he had acquired certain possessions from the inheritance of Saint-Denis: namely Blitestorp, Tatingum, Sulces, Fardulviler, Fehingasviler, Hoenchirche, Torneswile, and Precene.

But gathering this venerable man, who had in part come to repentance, by the bowels of mercy into the bosom of Mother Church from which he had strayed, because we have resolved to walk with God, and with Him desire not the death of a sinner but rather conversion and life, we freed the aforesaid man from the bond of anathema and the charge of sacrilege—upon this condition that the charge and anathema are removed: henceforth, every year on the feast of St. Martin, he shall pay five ounces of refined gold to the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius [Col. 1453B]. But should he—God forbid!—be found a violator of this custom, returning to his former plunder and wickedness like a dog to its vomit, let him incur the wrath of Almighty God, never again to be released from the bond of anathema.

## VII. Concerning the increase of the religious’ provisions and the first foundations of the church of Saint-Denis built by him.  
*(About the year 1140.)*  
[Dom Félibien, *History of Saint-Denis*, Documents, p. cij.]

In the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

I, Suger, however unworthy abbot of Saint-Denis, judge it honorable and useful before God, for all the faithful but especially for the prelates of the Church, to provide for those dedicated to the service of Almighty God, to relieve the labors and sweats of their struggles by every remedy, whether spiritual or temporal, and to sustain them with provisions so that they do not fail on the way [Col. 1453C]. For it has been marked out for such persons, by the Lord’s command, how they ought to shelter and cover with hides of oxen and cows the ark of the Lord’s covenant against violent rains and every affliction. In this they express what those who hold active prelacies by the obligation of their office must themselves do in place of hides: cherish and protect against every affliction contemplatives, who truly are the ark of divine propitiation.

Therefore I, Suger, by God’s forbearance thrice called abbot of Saint-Denis, a transgressor of God’s commandments, hastening through mercy to return to the heart of God, reflecting in fear and bitterness of soul whence I have come [Col. 1453D], what I have done, and where I must go, flee trembling to the protection of God’s servants. Though irreligious myself, I embrace their religious life with all my heart, humbly implore the intercessions of the religious, and take most devout care that they may provide for us more devotedly and effectively in spiritual things, while we sustain and cherish them with temporal provisions.

For from the provostship of Vilcassinum—which before our time was so reduced that it could scarcely provide five solidi for the brethren’s daily general allowance—we have, at the beginning of our prelacy, with God’s help, much expenditure, a strong military force, and, what even weighs upon my conscience, freed it from the oppression of advocates and other evildoers [Col. 1454A]. As it seems to us, we have arranged it for the better, increasing it twofold or threefold. We add five solidi on five days of every week to the brethren’s general allowance, so that on those days they always have ten solidi. On the other two days, Thursday and Saturday, in reverence of our commemorations—of the holy Mother of God and the holy martyrs—we have established fourteen solidi in another ordinance. Whatever exceeds five solidi, however, in this and in the other ordinance, is known, through God’s mercy, to have been secured by our labor for the love of God and observance of the holy Rule, as the number of brethren has increased. With the common consent of our brethren, we forbid this charter of augmentation ever to be diminished or defrauded in any respect, under perpetual anathema and perpetual curse. This concerns the general allowance.

Concerning the pottage: because for some reason it was withheld from the brethren from Indictum until the octave of St. Dionysius, we will and establish that henceforth it be supplied continuously throughout the whole circuit of the year, through the hands of monastic or lay servants. And lest they lack the means for it, we have added to this increase a new rent of fifty solidi or more from the newcomers whom I caused to be lodged on vacant garden land [Col. 1454B]. We likewise establish by sanction that this rule concerning pottage be firmly observed without interruption, both for the brethren themselves and for the support of poor persons from outside who need these and other things. Thus far concerning the first meal.

Concerning the second meal, called supper, we have made a third provision so that it may be more ample and more fittingly abundant than usual. It was formerly increased by certain additions from us: namely, the tithes of St. Lucian, which belonged to us; a grant of twenty solidi, which the gardeners themselves paid us from their surplus; and the grain which was rendered to us from Petraficta. But now, for the love and reverence of holy religion and for the devotion of our brethren, we have also granted and confirmed indissolubly under perpetual anathema the rent of that same town—one hundred solidi, or more if it shall be greater [Col. 1454C]. This is retained, however: by the decision and attestation of that monk who is the supper-officer, collection shall there be made from the same rent of our vineyards, insofar as pertains to us; for half the costs belong to the vineyard-shareholders.

Furthermore, we have heard from the most sacred mouth of Him who will say at that universal and wondrous hearing, “I was sick, and you visited me” (Matthew 25:36), and the opposites to those who did the contrary, how great is the value of pursuing works of mercy and caring for the sick. He taught still more clearly that this pertains especially to prelates, when he carried the sick sheep back to the flock upon his shoulders. Compelled, therefore, by this vowed solicitude, we admonish and command by the authority of God the brethren who are officers of this ministry, both those now serving and those who shall succeed them as our vicars in this very matter, that cheerfully, piously, and gently they accommodate themselves to the varying desires of sick brethren, elderly men, and all infirm persons, according to their different infirmities, and minister to them as to angels of God [Col. 1455A], because charity is the height of monastic religion.

They shall first serve these persons—yet with one intention—who for any reason have entered the infirmary buildings by command of the guardian of the order, namely with one dish at every table, in addition to what will be brought to them from the refectory. So that this may always continue, we have added six pounds to the ancient revenues of that same provostship, acquired by our labor in the borough—not through any evil contrivance, but by purchase of a certain house and the establishment of stalls, from which this rent is unquestionably due.

We also admonish and advise the brethren serving in this office that, apart from what ought to be devoted to the outward care of the lands, they expend the usufruct of the entire provostship upon the brethren’s necessities, and that no pretext of buying cloaks or other ornaments should creep in, but that the whole be entirely reserved for the brethren’s needs [Col. 1455B]. To provide warmth for those weakened and elderly persons, which they greatly needed, we have confirmed to it, under perpetual anathema, our holding of Garsonisville, which was from their own town.

Moreover, since we earnestly commend the remembrance of our lowliness to the love of brethren present and future, without any preceding merits on our part, so that it may benefit the salvation of our soul, we have deemed it worthwhile to revive, restore, and establish for the salvation of souls the commemorations of our emperors and great men, which they deserved to have observed through great liberality and abundant munificence, but which had been lulled to sleep through the long course of time. Among them we have judged that the solemn commemoration of the illustrious and most noble Emperor Charles III should be renewed and restored in this manner [Col. 1455C].

The manner is the same as that contained in the testament of the imperial majesty, by which that same glorious emperor bestowed with royal liberality upon St. Dionysius the noble estate of Ruoilum with its appurtenances and the forest waters. He established a noble command, worthy of an emperor: whereas the anniversary day of death is customarily commemorated yearly among others for other kings, he decreed that his own be observed every month, on the day before the Nones of the month [Col. 1455D], announced in chapter, celebrated in the monastery, and provided in the refectory with a worthy meal for the brethren from the revenues of the aforesaid estate.

No less noble is the command attributed to so great an emperor by which he decreed that seven lamps should burn without failing through succeeding ages before the most holy altar of the Holy Trinity, from the usufruct of the aforesaid estate. And because, wherever the need of imperial government called him in the world, he nevertheless always with full affection of heart planned and intended to be buried there, he fortified the place of his burial with the safest safeguards of holy relics. Retaining them from the imperial treasury of his chapel, he placed in the front part of the blessed altar the bone of the arm of St. James the Apostle, brother of the Lord [Col. 1456A]; on the right, the arm of St. Stephen, the first martyr; and on the left, that of the blessed martyr and levite Vincent, as we ourselves saw with our own eyes in the company of the venerable archbishops of Lyons, Reims, Tours, and Rouen, and the bishops of Soissons, Beauvais, Rennes, Senlis, Aleth, Meaux, and Vannes. We held the impression of his ring as evidence of the truth, so that, buried near the altar and surrounded on every side by pledges of the saints, he might avoid every spiritual and temporal affliction. These relics of the saints were displayed by them with us for the people of God to seek their protection; and, after the altar had been repaired with the same precious gold and suitable workmanship, they honorably replaced them there.

But since these ordinances of so great an emperor, though sanctioned by golden bulls, had through the hostile vicissitudes of long time in some respects grown weak and in others altogether failed, we, for the love and honor of God and of the holy relics, and no less for the remedy of the soul of Lord Charles, most serene Augustus, after taking counsel with our brethren, have labored diligently to revive and restore them [Col. 1456B]. We decreed that the lights of the seven lamps which had perished should burn continually; we honorably restored the worn-out silver vessels of those lamps; and we joined to the candle burning there—which alone had previously burned before the altar of St. Dionysius—a second candle, so that two might burn unfailingly, just as we had already established that two should burn continually before the bodies of the saints.

We have most firmly determined that every month, on the day before the Nones, the obsequies of his anniversary shall be celebrated more solemnly than usual, and we have inviolably restored the refectory meal on those same days. So that suitable resources may not be lacking for the continual lights and appointed meals, we have assigned inviolably ten pounds from the aforesaid estate of Ruoilum, which he added to these purposes in his testament, to be taken in the octave of St. Dionysius [Col. 1456C]. We have established that this be given to the sacristan, who is keeper of the cope, through the hand of the master prior, who shall ensure the provision of oil for the lights and continually supply ten solidi each month for the funeral meals.

For what is there that so great an emperor, and so intimate and heartfelt a friend of St. Dionysius, could not deserve—he who ennobled that church with so many and such great possessions, adorned it with so many ornaments of gold and precious gems, and, to crown all its blessings, most gloriously distinguished it with the eminent tokens of the Lord’s Passion, namely the nail and crown of the Lord and the arm of the holy elder Simeon, shining forth as with the most splendid ray of the true Sun [Col. 1456D]?

Therefore, all of us, well-disposed in these and similar matters, assembled in our chapter, after deliberating slowly and carefully upon this charter of renewal, approved it by the authority of God Almighty and of the blessed martyrs Dionysius and his companions, and also by the common and unanimous confirmation of our chapter. We enacted it as an unshaken law, beseeching and adjuring by the blood which Jesus Christ shed upon the cross [Col. 1457A] that this institution should not be abandoned on any pretext; that the present charter should not, through any person or for any reason, suffer again the disaster of falling into disuse, after the fashion of the former ancient provisions; but that it should always stand sound and unimpaired in its institutions and chapters, most firmly, through the unshaken ages of ages.

Moreover, for the four matricular clerics, who labour continually in that same church, we have given, that they may remember us, a certain tithe which, because it belonged to our fief, we bought from Paganus of Gisors at Franconville: since the provision of their prebends had grown somewhat scant. We gave it in both bread and wine, excepting that portion drawn from the enclosed vineyard belonging to the church itself.

There remains, indeed, another worthy chapter which, although it may appear to end with the execution of the things [Col. 1457B] promised, nevertheless—because we both desire and hope that it may profit us toward an eternal recompense—we have judged worthy to insert in this document. In the nineteenth year of our administration, when we had gladly and faithfully laboured upon the new work in the front part of the church, and had fittingly joined that new work to the old by the beautiful harmony of new columns and arches; and when, together with the same new church, we had caused the upper oratory of Saint Romanus, the lower one of Saint Hippolytus, and, on the other side, that of Saint Bartholomew, to be consecrated by Hugh, venerable archbishop of Rouen, and other venerable bishops; and when we had permanently assigned to the lights of those oratories, as a Catholic endowment, the land of the royal demesne which we bought from William of Cornillon, with the favour of his children and relatives, for eighty pounds, to be leased and occupied [Col. 1457C]—then the love and devotion we bore to the holy martyrs, our lords and protectors, suddenly drew us to enlarge and extend the chief upper part of the church.

Nor could the incompleteness of the former work turn us aside from undertaking this one, since we hoped in the Lord that the omnipotence of God could provide a complete supplement both to that earlier work and to this subsequent one, either through us or through those whom it pleased Him to employ. Our devotion was further stirred because that place within the Holy of Holies, suitable for the Divinity and most pleasing to the frequent presence of holy angels, was so cramped that, at the hour of the holy sacrifice [Col. 1457D] on feast days, the brethren receiving the most sacred Eucharist could not remain there, nor could they often endure the troublesome crowd of arriving pilgrims without great danger. You could see some grievously trampled by others; and—what many would not believe—rash little women, stepping over men’s heads as though over a pavement, striving to rush to the altar, at times struck and driven back, and retreating for a while into the cloister with the aid of pitying men, nearly half-dead and gasping with almost their last breath.

Therefore, hastening with all the fervour of our soul to resist these and similar disturbances, we gathered an assembly of illustrious men, both bishops and abbots, and also secured the presence of the lord and most serene king of the French, Louis. As had been resolved in our chapter, on the day before the Ides of July, a Sunday, we arranged a procession splendid in its ornaments and distinguished by its persons. Indeed, bearing before us in the hands of bishops and abbots the emblems of the Lord’s Passion—namely the Lord’s nail and crown, the arm of the holy elder Simeon, and other protections of sacred relics—we humbly and devoutly descended to the site prepared for laying the foundations. Then, after invoking the consolation of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, that He might bring the good beginning for the house of God to a good conclusion, the bishops themselves, having first with their own hands mixed the mortar from the blessed water of the dedication performed on the fifth day before the Ides of June immediately preceding, laid the first stones, singing a hymn to God and solemnly chanting “His foundations” through to the end of the psalm [Col. 1458B].

The most serene king himself descended inside and laid his own stone with his own hands; and we, together with many others, both abbots and religious men, laid our stones. Some also laid gems, singing, for the love and reverence of Jesus Christ: “All your walls [shall be] precious stones.”

Exhilarated, then, by so great and festive a laying of so holy a foundation, yet anxious about carrying the work through—fearing the vicissitudes of time, the dwindling of persons, and my own failing—we established, by the common counsel and persuasive urging of the brethren present and with the lord king’s assent, an annual revenue for completing these works: namely, 150 pounds from the treasury, that is, from the offerings of the altar and relics—100 at the Indict and [Col. 1458C] 50 on the feast of Saint Dionysius—and another 50 from the property situated at Belsa called Villana, formerly uncultivated but, by God’s help and our labour, improved and made to yield eighty pounds each year. If this should fail in the completion of these works through any misfortune, our other Belsa, whose revenues we have increased twofold or threefold, should make up the deficiency. We have decreed that these 200 pounds, apart from what the devotion of the faithful may bring to the treasury-chest, or whatever may be offered to either work itself, shall be continuously devoted solely to those works, until both the buildings—the front and upper portions, with their towers—are wholly and honourably completed, without any question whatsoever.

[Col. 1458D] Done in the common chapter of Saint Dionysius, in the presence of the persons subscribing below, whose authority, under anathema, confirmed the aforesaid chapters.

The sign of Milo, bishop of the Morini. The sign of Guarinus, bishop of Amiens. The sign of Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres. The sign of Hugh, archbishop of Tours. The sign of Samson, archbishop of Rheims. The sign of Goslinus, bishop of Soissons. The sign of Odo, bishop of Beauvais. The sign of Robert, abbot of Corbie.

## VIII. On the Immunities of the Village of Val-Cresson. (A.D. 1145.)

[Again from Duchesne, as above, as are also the following charters.]

[Col. 1459A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen.

We wish it to be known to both present and future persons that I, Suger, by the grace of God abbot of the church of the blessed martyrs of Christ Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, with the common consent of our chapter, have granted that whoever may wish to live in a certain new village which we are building, called Val-Cresson, shall hold a measure of land—namely one arpent and a quarter of an arpent—for an annual rent of twelve denarii, and shall be free from every tallage and exaction [Col. 1459B]. Thus they shall not, on the summons of any person—whether king, prince, or servant of Saint Dionysius—go forth from or undertake military service or an expedition from their village, except by the abbot’s own command and in his person, or with the prior if the abbot be absent. Nor shall they plead outside their village for anyone except the abbot. From an arpent of Saint Dionysius’s land, wherever they receive it, they shall pay us four denarii in rent and the tithe; nor may anyone undertake to cultivate land adjoining that village unless he is a resident in it. We have fixed the popular laws—which they call *plenae* among themselves—at ten denarii. Done at Saint-Denis, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1145.

## IX. On the Tithe of Saint Brice. (A.D. 1148.)

[Col. 1459C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen.

Since it is unambiguous to those who know the Law that, by God’s own command established in the Law, tithes ought to be paid to the Levites set apart for God’s own service, whenever a lay hand usurps them it plainly runs counter to divine decrees. And not only do the impious invaders of them incur the greatest peril to their souls, but so also do those who, thereafter retaining them as though by hereditary right, do not cease to possess them until death overtakes them.

Accordingly I, Suger, by God’s permission servant and unworthy abbot of the monastery of Saint-Denis in France, often asked by Matthew surnamed the Fair that I should grant to Saint-Martin-des-Champs, to hold and possess, the two parts of the tithe of Saint-Brice which he held in fief from Saint-Denis, have graciously granted this with all my chapter [Col. 1460A]. For in our presence and that of our whole chapter, the aforesaid Matthew granted the aforesaid tithe of Saint-Brice to the house of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, while we willingly and amicably gave our assent and bore witness to the act, because of the great affection of mutual love between ourselves and that house. Many other suitable witnesses of this confirmation were also present; their names are subscribed below:

Clement, dean of the Church of Paris; Wermundus, archdeacon; Albert, precentor; Hugh, archdeacon of Arras; Philip, brother of the king; Nevelon, his master; Walter, son of Mainburgis; Herluin, canon; Simon, nephew of the abbot; Matthew, lord of Montmorency; Ruricus of Andilly; Guy of Groela; [Col. 1460B] Walter of Aulnay; John of Vincelles; Philip, his brother; Godard of Saint-Brice; Arnulf of Hoxae; John of Gonesse; Theodoric, mayor; Evrard, hosteller; Henry, vintner; Tigerius; Ewrard, servant.

This was done, and this charter made, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1148, while Louis, king of the French and duke of the Aquitanians, was reigning, in the eighteenth year of his reign and the twenty-seventh year of our abbacy.

## X. On John, Bernard, Peter, and Gerald, Hermits. (Year uncertain.)

I, Suger, by God’s grace abbot of the church of Saint-Denis, wish to make known to all faithful persons, future as well as present, that John, Bernard, Peter, and Gerald, living the eremitic life, came before [Col. 1460C] our highness and devoutly petitioned that we receive them into our fraternity. They granted to God and Saint-Denis their place and church, built by themselves in honour of the Blessed Mary, situated in the parish of Parciac, and all their possessions, both acquired and to be acquired; and they submitted themselves, by our command, to the jurisdiction of the Church of La Chapelle, so that they might no longer receive other brethren into that place without the permission of the prior of La Chapelle. We, for our part, granted them that they might remain in their own habit as long as they wished. But if they wished to enter the monastic order, they should be received as brethren of the monastery [Col. 1460D]. While Louis, king of the French, was reigning and Wlgrin was archbishop of Bourges. This was confirmed at La Chapelle, into the hand of Ralph the prior, before monks, clerics, and laypersons.

[Col. 1461]

# PRIVILEGES GRANTED TO SAINT-DENIS IN THE TIME OF SUGER’S ABBACY.

(Dom Félibien, *History of the Abbey of Saint-Denis in France*, Proofs, Part I, p. xciii.)

## I. King Louis, Sixth of That Name, Enlarges and Confirms the Privileges of Saint-Denis on the Occasion of Receiving the Banner from the Altar of the Blessed Martyrs. (A.D. 1124.)

[Col. 1461A]

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Louis, by the grace of God king of the French, to the archbishops, bishops, dukes, counts, and all magnates of our realm.

Since we have manifestly recognized that, through the abundant mercy of God Almighty, our kingdom stands, and that what is earthly can never truly prosper except through what is heavenly, we must, with utmost diligence and continual care, apply ourselves to the worship of God’s churches, lavish works of kindness from the munificence of royal majesty, and exchange earthly things for heavenly by a happy commerce; so that by these means the administration of our kingdom may be glorious in time, and, when these temporal things fail, those heavenly things may receive us into everlasting dwellings.

Therefore, giving especially earnest attention both to churches far and wide and above all to the noble monastery of thrice-blessed Dionysius and his companions, with that first affection by which, receiving our whole realm through the lot of apostleship, he restored it to the Lord God by the shedding of his own blood, and also because our predecessors were bound to him by the benefit of both spiritual and bodily assistance, we are sufficiently devoted. When word reached us that the king of the Germans was preparing an army to enter and oppress our kingdom, after taking counsel with our palatines [Col. 1461C], we hastened, according to the custom of our predecessors, to the basilica of those most holy martyrs. There, in the presence of the magnates of our kingdom, we caused those same patrons of ours to be raised upon their altar, in pious affection and love, for the defence of the realm.

It therefore seemed fitting to us, as indeed it was, to embrace and exalt with every affection in our own time the basilica of those most glorious martyrs, enlarged and adorned through the liberality and munificence of ancient kings. Accordingly, in the presence of the venerable abbot of the aforesaid church, Suger, whom we held to be faithful and close in our counsels, and before our magnates, we received from the altar of the blessed martyrs the banner to which the county of the Vexin—recognized as held by us from them in fief—pertains; following and imitating the ancient custom of our predecessors, we received it by right of standard-bearer, as the counts of the Vexin had customarily done [Col. 1461D].

We also granted to those holy martyrs, our guides and protectors, to possess forever, in devotion for the salvation of our soul, the governance, all manner of jurisdiction, and full liberty which the authority of many kings of France and our own had in past times occupied near the town of Saint-Denis toward Paris. Its boundaries, as we have fixed them by a certain demarcation of limits, extend from the River Seine—namely from the mill commonly called Bayard—to the upper end of the village called Halbervillare. Furthermore, we have granted in perpetuity all authority, all jurisdiction, and all customs of the fair of the Indict, since that said Indict was established in honour and reverence of the holy relics—namely the Lord’s nail and crown—by apostolic authority, by confirmation of archbishops and bishops, and by the ordinance of our predecessors, kings of France [Col. 1462B].

For we have judged it fitting to render thanks to the Lord God in these and such other ways as we can, because on the day of the Indict He has deigned to exalt our kingdom with the emblems of His Passion, namely the nail and crown; and because He has deigned to place the protection of ourselves, our predecessors, and our successors at the head of the realm, namely with the holy martyrs. But if anyone attempts to violate this command of our grant, let him incur the wrath of God and the displeasure of Lord Dionysius, and let him be judged guilty of offence against our majesty [Col. 1462C].

That this decree promulgated by us may obtain fuller force, we strengthened it by the sign placed below in our own hand, delivered it to be confirmed by our faithful persons present, and ordered it additionally to be marked with the seal bearing our image. We committed it to writing lest it be erased by forgetfulness; and, lest it be infringed by posterity, we confirmed it below by the authority of our seal and the monogram of our name.

Done publicly at Paris in the year of the Incarnate Word 1124, the eighteenth of our reign, the tenth of Adelaide [probably a dating formula; uncertain], with those present in our palace whose names and signs are written below.

The sign of Stephen, seneschal. The sign of Gilbert, cup-bearer. [Col. 1462D] The sign of Hugh, constable. Given through the hand of Stephen, chancellor.

## II. Privilege of the Same King Louis and His Son Philip for the Monastery of Saint-Denis. (A.D. 1129.)

> [Note: [Col. 1463D] Since this King Philip, the eldest son of Louis VI, did not survive his father the king, he is not ordinarily included in the catalogue of the Kings of France. Nevertheless, he has sometimes been counted with the others, as may be seen in the old inscription on a reliquary enclosing a relic of King Saint Louis, which is visible in the treasury of Saint-Denis. On one side one reads: “Philip IV, King of France, son of the blessed King Louis”; and on the other [Col. 1464D]: “Philip V, King of France, son of King Philip IV.” This is intended to designate the kings Philip the Bold and Philip the Fair, his son, further identified by the arms of their queens, their wives, which are on the base of this reliquary. Thus, according to the reckoning of the author of this inscription, the eldest son of Louis VI was Philip III, whereas the name is commonly used for the successor of Saint Louis.]

[Col. 1463A]

In the name of the Lord God and of our Saviour Jesus Christ, Louis and Philip, his son, by divine providence ordaining, kings of the French.

If things solemnly given or granted by God-fearing persons to places dedicated to divine worship are afterwards known to have been taken away on any pretext, and we restore them by our authority to their former state and confirm them anew by the decree of our command, we confidently believe that this pertains beyond doubt both to obtaining eternal blessedness and to strengthening the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore let the industry of all our faithful, present as well as future, know that the venerable man Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, greatly beloved and close to us, represented to our clemency how he had learned that the monastery called Argenteuil [Argentolium], situated in the district of Paris on the River Seine, ought to belong by right to blessed Dionysius, the most glorious martyr of Christ; and he asked that, for the increase of our merit, we should cause it to be restored to its former state.

For he showed us for rereading the charter of the most serene emperors Louis the Pious and his son Lothair, in which he gave our knowledge most evident satisfaction concerning the first donation of that place by its own founder, named Hermenricus, and his wife Mumma; concerning the confirmation which Lothair, formerly king, ordered to be drawn up for that same donation; and concerning the complete restoration by the same emperors in the time of Abbot Hilduin [Col. 1463C]. Having frequently examined these matters in the presence of religious persons—namely Matthew, bishop of Albano and legate of the apostolic see; Stephen of Paris, in whose diocese the place lies; with the counsel and assent of Rainald, archbishop of Rheims; Goslinus of Soissons; Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres; and other good men and magnates of our realm—we restore in full the aforesaid place of Argenteuil to those sacred martyrs whom we love most highly, with whom we wish and have vowed to be buried: both because of the right of that church, which we have recognized, and because in that monastery, in our time, more than among other monasteries of Gaul, the order of monastic religion shines forth through God’s mercy and the merits of the holy martyrs.

For the remedy of our soul, the administration of our realm, and the preservation of our wife and offspring, we grant them whatever is ours there, retaining absolutely nothing for ourselves from all things belonging to royal dignity. Rather, whatever is now seen there shall be restored to be held under the right and donation of that monastery, with all its integrity and appurtenances; and at no time hereafter may any person, of whatever rank or power, presume to make any claim against or bring any suit upon the governors of the aforesaid monastery and of the most blessed martyr of Christ, Dionysius [Col. 1464A]. Instead, let the aforesaid monastery of Argenteuil be permitted peacefully to hold and administer it, just as it holds the other possessions granted and belonging in like manner to the authority of Saint Dionysius; and let it have complete freedom to do whatever it wishes for the need or advantage of that church.

We adjure all our successors by the holy and undivided Trinity and by the coming of the just Judge, God and our Saviour Jesus Christ, that they in no way presume to violate this command of our authority. Rather, just as we devoutly restore the aforesaid place by granting it to those holy martyrs, so let them diligently and devoutly strive to preserve it. And so that the holy congregation itself may more earnestly entreat the Lord’s mercy and those saints for us, Queen Adelaide, all our offspring, and the stability of our kingdom, and so that this confirmation of our ordinance may have fuller force, we have, in God’s name, signed this our authority below by the counsel of the bishops who were present and ordered it to be marked with our seal [Col. 1464C].

The sign of Louis, most glorious king. The sign of Philip, king. The sign of Adelaide, queen. Rainald, archbishop of Rheims, drew it up. Vulgrin, archbishop of Bourges, assented. Aimeric, bishop of Clermont, assented. Yelendus, bishop of Langres, assented. Stephen, bishop of Autun, assented. Hatto, bishop of Troyes, assented. Simon, bishop of Noyon, assented. Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, assented. Stephen, bishop of Paris, assented. Goslinus, bishop of Soissons, assented. John of Orléans. [Col. 1464D] The sign of Ralph, count of Vermandois. The sign of Chludovicus, cup-bearer. Simon, chancellor, authenticated it.

Done at Saint-Germain-des-Prés in the presence of Lord Matthew, bishop of Albano and legate of the apostolic see, and Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres [Col. 1465A], and the other bishops named above.

Given and confirmed at Rheims, in the solemn court of Easter, at the anointing of Lord Philip, most glorious king, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1129, the seventh indiction, the twentieth year of the reign of the lord and most serene king of the French Louis, and the first of Philip his son. Happily, in God’s name. Amen.

## III. Privilege of Louis VII. (A.D. 1143.)

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

It belongs to royal dignity and office to fear God, through whom kings reign, as the King of kings. For He has power [Col. 1465B] to loosen the belt of kings and to repay, for temporal benefits, the crown and reward of eternal glory. Therefore I, Louis, by the grace of God king of the French and duke of Aquitaine, instructed by these and other teachings of faith, fearing and anticipating the strict judgment of the strict Judge, make known to present and future persons that Suger, venerable pastor and abbot of the church of the most blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, came before us, humbly and devoutly imploring that, for the love of God and the holy martyrs, for the remedy of the soul of my father Louis of pious memory, and for the safety of our person and preservation of our kingdom, we ourselves should confirm what my father granted to that church and secured by charters of royal majesty granting immunity.

Accordingly, to this just petition and pious devotion we gave our assent, as was fitting, in hope of heavenly recompense; and whatever my father’s generous munificence granted, or whatever granted by his predecessors he confirmed, we ourselves grant and confirm with equal will and equal love: namely, an increase of the dust-toll (*pulveraticum*) or passage-toll (*pedagium*) at the customary places of Saint-Denis; five dwellings in its borough of Jews, with their households; also the house situated at Saint-Denis which Robert, king and great-grandfather of my father, gave, and which my father confirmed, together with the court of that house, its residents, and everything belonging to the same house; the free and untroubled emancipation of the church’s own serfs, without any claim by ourselves or our successors [Col. 1465D]; and all jurisdiction and coercive authority over usurers and counterfeit coinage.

Upon an abbot’s death, no recovery shall be made of any of the movable or immovable goods whatsoever which he possessed. We also grant the complete removal, from the aforesaid borough as far as the church of Saint Lawrence near the bridge of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, of dwellings or inhabitants not belonging to that church; and on the other side of the royal road, from that same town of Saint-Denis to the other bridge near Paris beside the house of lepers; likewise toward the Seine from the same town of Saint-Denis to Montmartre, except Clichy; and on the other side from that same town of Saint-Denis to the royal road leading to the Louvre [Col. 1466A].

We grant the church of Cergy with all its appurtenances; likewise its court and the houses of the court, free and immune from every exaction; and all road-rights, as he himself granted them. In the village called Belna, the two provisions which my father remitted because they belonged to the monks’ own resources, we too willingly grant; and, concerning the third, we prohibit, just as he prohibited in his liberality, the exaction from the collective payment of the peasants of more than eight pounds in any year. Furthermore, if my father’s generous munificence granted or confirmed any other things to that church, we too, for the love of God and the holy martyrs, grant the things bestowed and confirm them by the authority of royal majesty. But that these provisions may remain forever untouched and unimpaired, we have strengthened them by the impression of our seal and the monogram of our name [Col. 1466B].

Done at Paris in the year of the Incarnate Word 1143, the seventh of our reign, with those present in our palace whose names and signs are written below.

The sign of Ralph, count of Vermandois, our seneschal. The sign of Matthew, chamberlain. The sign of Matthew, constable. The sign of William, cup-bearer. Given through the hand of Cadurcus, chancellor.

## IV. Privilege of the Same King. (A.D. 1144.)

[Col. 1466C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Louis, by the grace of God king of the French and duke of Aquitaine.

Since we have manifestly recognized that, through the abundant mercy of God Almighty, our kingdom stands, and that the earthly can never truly prosper except through the heavenly, we must, with utmost care and continual diligence, apply ourselves to the worship of God’s Church, lavish works of kindness from the munificence of royal majesty, and exchange earthly things for heavenly by a happy commerce; so that by these means the administration of our kingdom may become glorious in time, and, when these temporal things fail, those heavenly things may receive us into everlasting dwellings.

Therefore, giving especially earnest attention to churches far and wide, and above all to the noble monastery of thrice-blessed Dionysius and his companions, with that first affection by which, receiving our whole realm through the apostolic lot, he restored it to the Lord God by the shedding of his own blood, and also because our predecessors were bound to him by goodwill and intimate friendship—having bestowed much upon him and received far greater things through him—we hastened, with our wife Queen Eleanor and a company of many of our magnates, to the dedication of the basilica of those most holy martyrs, which had been most splendidly performed in the new enlargement of the church, namely in its chief part [Col. 1466D].

There, after the consecration of that church, we approached the old place in which the sacred bodies of our particular patrons—the most blessed Dionysius and his companions—were contained, with a great assembly of archbishops and bishops. After the shrines had been opened, the holy pledges taken out and carried on our own shoulders through the church, we laid them down in the most glorious place prepared above, with joyful tears [Col. 1467A]. Finally, touched by the inspiration of God Almighty and love for the martyrs themselves, we summoned the archbishops and bishops who were present, together with Suger, the venerable abbot of that church, our friend and familiar, and bestowed by right of endowment, for maintaining the lights of that church, certain customary dues which we possessed in some of their villages and for which eighteen pounds were paid to us annually: namely, at Cergy and at Cormeilles, whatever we had there, whether in vicariate or advocacy, and everything whatsoever belonging there to us, except our wine and oats, except our lodging-right, military service, and riding-service at the summons of the servant of Saint Dionysius.

At Osny likewise, whatever we possessed, except the press and our lodging-right, military service, and riding-service at the summons of the servant of Saint Dionysius. At Trappes and Herencourt, likewise everything which we possessed, except our lodging-right, military service, and riding-service at the summons, as we have said, of the servant of Saint Dionysius. Finally, in the infirmary’s cultivated land near the borough of Saint-Denis, whatever we possessed, we granted along with the aforesaid gift. That this may obtain the safeguards of perpetual stability, we ordered it to be committed to writing, marked with the impression of our seal [Col. 1467C], and strengthened by the monogram of our name inscribed below.

Done publicly at Paris in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1144, the eighth of our reign, with those present in our palace whose names and signs are written below.

The sign of Ralph, count of Vermandois. The sign of Matthew, chamberlain. The sign of Matthew, constable. The sign of William, cup-bearer. Given through the hand of Cadurcus, chancellor.

## V. (A.D. 1145.)

[Col. 1468A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Louis, by the grace of God king of the French and duke of Aquitaine.

Our predecessors, the kings of the French, always sought to venerate and enlarge the noble and glorious church of Saint Dionysius with such special devotion as they found greater protection in the aforesaid martyr of Christ. Most willingly following in their footsteps, we make known to all persons, present and future alike, that our most dear brother Philip, with our assent and will, gave to Saint Dionysius and to the church of Blessed Mary of the Fields one prebend in the church of Saint Exuperius of Corbeil, in which church he himself holds the office of abbot, to possess forever in its entirety [Col. 1468B].

Moreover, the monks of Blessed Mary of the Fields shall perform the service owed for the prebend in the church of Saint Exuperius during the appointed weeks, just as each of the canons does; and on the day of that saint’s feast, every year forever, they shall come in solemn procession to his church and shall take part, together with the college of canons, in the celebration of the Sunday Mass. That this may obtain the safeguards of perpetual stability, we ordered it to be committed to writing, secured by the authority of our seal, and strengthened by the monogram of our name inscribed below.

Done publicly at Paris in the year from the Incarnation [Col. 1468C] of the Lord 1145, the ninth of our reign, with those present in our palace whose names and signs are written below.

The sign of Ralph, count of Vermandois, our seneschal. The sign of William, cup-bearer. The sign of Matthew, chamberlain. The sign of Matthew, constable. Given through the hand of Cadurcus, chancellor.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1152: WILLIAM, MONK OF SAINT-DENIS, DISCIPLE OF SUGER

[Col. 1467]

# NOTICE

(*Literary History of France*, vol. XII, p. 545.)

Under Abbot Suger there lived at Saint-Denis a religious named William [Note: [Col. 1467C] Félibien, *History of Saint-Denis*, p. 136], who, by clearly marked merit, won Suger’s confidence and became his secretary. In that capacity he accompanied him on his journeys and at court. Having had the misfortune to lose him, he did not find the same feelings toward himself in Suger’s successor, Odo of Deuil. Certain disagreements which he had with that abbot at the beginning of his administration caused him to be relegated to the priory of Saint-Denis-en-Vaux, near Châtellerault in Poitou. This retirement pleased him, and he settled there, despite efforts made at the abbey shortly afterwards to induce him to return [Note: [Col. 1469] Martène, *Anecdota*, vol. I, p. 441]. We have no information concerning the other circumstances of his life or the year in which it ended.

A witness and admirer of Suger’s conduct, William preserved its memory for posterity in three writings. The first is the circular letter of the religious of Saint-Denis concerning Suger’s death; the second is his Life in three books. In both works, much more effort is devoted to extolling Suger’s virtues than to describing his actions. But William does not offer his hero insipid and extravagant praises, nor does he pile up commonplaces in his favour. Sound sense, love of truth, and religious feeling visibly seem to have guided the panegyrist’s pen. Moreover, his style is noble, elegant, florid, and, as perfectly as the age allowed, suited to the genre he had chosen. The *Life* is dedicated to Geoffrey, William’s fellow monk. We shall gather here several details from it that are not found in the article on Suger which we have already given.

“Among the great qualities of this illustrious personage, his memory was not one of those that caused the least admiration. He seemed to have forgotten nothing that he had learned. Whenever occasion arose, he would recite as many as twenty or thirty verses of Horace or Virgil. He possessed a thorough knowledge of the history of all our kings, so that, as soon as one was named to him, he related the particulars of his life as though he were reading from a book. He knew almost all Scripture by heart, and had meditated upon it so well that he immediately explained every difficult passage proposed to him” (Book I, chs. 4–5).

We have spoken above of the esteem in which Suger was held by sovereigns and great men. Here is a further trait confirming what we have said on this subject. “I have seen,” says our author—and I call God to witness it—“I have seen the king of France standing respectfully before him, with all the great men surrounding him in the same posture, while he, seated on a small bench, dictated his orders to them as to inferiors, and all that court listened with the greatest attention to the words issuing from his mouth. When the council was over, if he wished to set about escorting the king out, he was not free to do so: the monarch would not allow him to leave his place, nor even to rise from his seat” (*ibid.*, II.8).

“Being accustomed to sleep little, he regularly spent a considerable time after supper, whether in summer or winter, either reading or hearing someone read, or recounting notable incidents from history to the company. The reading concerned the authoritative writings of the Fathers, and sometimes ecclesiastical history. As for his stories, since he was very cheerful in disposition, he sometimes made them turn upon what had happened to himself, and sometimes upon the exploits of brave men which he had witnessed or learned from others; and the conversation sometimes continued until midnight. He then went to rest in a bed that was neither too luxurious nor too hard. For he took great care not to draw attention to himself by any singularity, whether in his clothing, furnishings, or food. He regularly interrupted his sleep to attend Matins, and at the first break of day rose again to return to church. But before approaching the high altar, it was his custom to go and prostrate himself before the tombs of the martyrs. There, without witnesses, he offered up his whole self to the Lord, and in the fervour of his prayer watered the pavement with his tears. Thus did this venerable priest prepare himself to offer the saving victim with as much splendour as devotion. But while he celebrated the holy sacrifice, who could worthily recount with what compunction, what abundance of tears, what groans, he discharged that awe-inspiring office?” (Book II, no. 7.)

These two writings form part of the Documentary Proofs for Dom Félibien’s *History of Saint-Denis*. They had already appeared in Baron d’Auteuil’s *History of the Ministers of State* (pp. 276–297); and before the original of the second had appeared, Baudouin had published a French translation of it in 1640.

William’s third work in Suger's honour is an elegy in the form of an epitaph. It is likewise found in the cited work of M. d’Auteuil (p. 297).

After leaving Saint-Denis, William, as has been said, was earnestly urged to return. With the abbot’s approval, his brethren ceased not for a year to send him both letters and messengers to recall him. It appears that he long remained without answering them. At last he wrote to four of them to indicate the reasons preventing him from yielding to their entreaties. [Note: [Col. 1469] *Ibid.*] These four religious were the precentor, cellarer, the abbot’s secretary, and physician; all four bore the name William. After amusing himself over the identity of their names, he says that either he must have been deceived or have lost his wits to abandon the new dwelling in which Providence had placed him. He proves that he had found there what he hoped for and more, by a description of the place, whose substance is as follows.

It is a pleasant and fertile valley, in which fruits of every kind grow abundantly. A river, the Vienne, divides it, separating the monastery from the town; he enjoys the town’s advantages without feeling its inconveniences. A charming forest borders the surrounding hills, which are neither too high nor too low, so that they leave the winds enough free course to renew the air of the plain, but not enough to cause devastation there. With little labour the soil receives every kind of seed and returns it a hundredfold. Everything grows much earlier there than elsewhere. The vineyards covering all the slopes produce a wine comparable to Falernian. “There,” says our author, “a wonderful thing! I have seen red wine made from white grapes, and white wine from black grapes”: *Hic mirum in modum ex albis botrionibus vinum vidi rubrum, et ex nigris e converso hic conficitur album*—“Here, in a wonderful manner, I have seen red wine from white clusters of grapes, and, conversely, white made here from black ones.” Apples grow in such quantity that one tires of seeing them and grows weary of gathering them. There, among other trees, pines rise so high that they equal the cedars of Lebanon in height; and they bear so much fruit that their nuts are used instead of almonds for the needs of the sick. [Note: [Col. 1469] *Ex quibus (pinubus) tanta nucum colligitur* [Col. 1470] *abundantia, ut in usus infirmantium non quaerantur amygdala*: “From these pines such an abundance of nuts is gathered that almonds need not be sought for use by the sick.”] The ground is also well suited to walnut-trees; there are not men enough to gather all their walnuts, nor cellars enough to store them. One sees there also fig-trees, pear-trees, chestnut-trees, and finally everything that nature produces of herself and that human skill customarily causes her to produce. In the middle of the monastery is a spring, warm in winter and cold in summer; outside it divides into two streams which, after watering the gardens of the local inhabitants, flow into a large pond carefully stocked with fish. “Finally,” he adds, “this place has so many advantages besides those I have just mentioned that the testimony of one’s eyes is required to be convinced of them; and whoever has once arrived there never leaves except reluctantly. And you want me [Col. 1471] to leave this abode and exchange it for another! What! Shall I leave here to go back to you and expose myself anew to the danger of a thousand disagreeable mishaps?”

William then thanks his brethren in very courteous terms for the affection they show him. He declares that he is most sincerely concerned for their welfare, their standing, and the other prerogatives they enjoy. “For my own part,” he says, “I have now become accustomed to my poverty; I love it, I am content with it, and it suffices me at least as much as Croesus’s great treasures sufficed that prince.” This letter is one of the wittiest and most agreeable that we have encountered among those of the century with which we are concerned.

According to M. d’Auteuil, it was not Suger, as we stated above, who authored the book concerning his administration, but William, who composed it at Suger's command and under his direction. The proof offered is the difference between the style of that book and that of the other works of this abbot. But this difference does not seem to us sufficiently great to outweigh the authority of the oldest manuscripts, in which this book bears Suger's name at its head, nor that of the book itself, in which Suger always speaks in his own name.

[Col. 1471]

## LETTER OF WILLIAM, MONK OF SAINT-DENIS, TO CERTAIN OF HIS FELLOW MONKS

He praises the solitary dwelling he had chosen in Aquitaine and excuses himself from returning to the former honours that he had left.

(MARTÈNE, *Anecdota*, vol. I, p. 441, from the Coislin manuscript.)

[Col. 1471A] To his lords and worthily venerable brethren, WILLIAM the precentor, WILLIAM the cellarer, William the notary, and WILLIAM the physician, fellow retainers of my lord, likewise WILLIAM.

[Note: [Col. 1471A] William, the writer of this letter, appears to be that William, monk of Saint-Denis, intimate of Abbot Suger and author of his *Life*, as also of the circular letter on the death of the same Suger. That letter was formerly read on Suger's anniversary, as we learn from the Coislin manuscript, from which we have drawn this letter following the circular letter. For among the various distinctive ancient rites of the renowned abbey of Saint-Denis, especially noteworthy is the custom by which the *Life* of Dagobert [Col. 1472A] and the virtues of Abbot Suger were publicly read in church on their anniversaries, so that, on hearing of their good deeds, the monks might be more encouraged to entreat the divine power on their behalf. This practice, at least as regards the reading of Dagobert’s *Life*, endured until 1633, when the reformed Congregation of Saint Maur was introduced into the aforesaid monastery of Saint-Denis and, on the judgment of learned men, abolished it.]

There were too few namesakes for you in Gaul unless one were added from Aquitaine as well.
