What did it seem good to my lord abbot and to your united fraternity to do, that you should trouble me with so many frequent messengers and letters, and urge me to leave the place [Col. 1472A] where one day is better than a thousand, where I seem to have obtained some small measure of liberty and joys that come almost too late? Either I was deceived in choosing the place, or I am mad if I leave it. And may I perish if the place itself does not invite me to write, for its excellence supplies material for writing. May I perish if, after spending a year in it, I have not convinced myself that I shall desire no longer to change it.

For it is a valley [Col. 1473A] walled about with delights, a valley endowed with nature’s riches. Whatever fruits are found almost anywhere on earth seem here to have been gathered together by nature. Here one who wishes to devote himself to leisure and wisdom is neither assailed by commotion nor impeded by a crowd. No sound, no noise is heard here except what the singing of birds makes or the breath of the breeze stirs up. Yet this is its consolation in solitude: beyond the river it has a town, whose conveniences it enjoys and whose inconveniences it lacks. The place is cheerful and pleasant, enclosed by woods and hills, yet neither too low or sunken nor exposed to the troublesome blasts of winds. The soil is fertile and faithful to what is entrusted to it: whatever is committed to it, it returns to the cultivator with a hundredfold increase. Here every crop and every kind of fruit grows more abundantly [Col. 1473B] and ripens more quickly.

Here I have seen such an abundance of apples that they weary those who look at them and tire those who gather them. And lest anyone suppose that the fruits are inferior, some are sweet as honey, others pleasantly sharp, and most will keep for a year. There is no agricultural work to which the fertile soil does not adapt itself and faithfully respond. Besides other things, one especially excellent product grows here, one that might make cities and towns envious and is thought more precious than Falernian wine. For it delights the taste and charms the smell. Here, in a wonderful manner, I have seen red wine from white clusters of grapes, and conversely white wine made here from black ones. When pure, it is such that it ill suits one who professes moderation, so that those who have drunk it must be bound—except that they are bound more strongly by the wine itself.

Here, among the other trees, pines rise [Col. 1473C] to such a height that they equal what are called the cedars of Lebanon. Such an abundance of nuts is gathered from them that almonds need not be sought for the use of the sick. Moreover, this place seems especially suited to those nuts called walnuts, so much so that there are often not enough people to gather them, nor storehouses enough to put them away. Pears are not lacking here, nor figs, nor quinces, nor chestnuts; and whatever nature produces spontaneously or cultivation is accustomed to provide is contained in this very small corner of earth. Finally, whatever is usually sown in gardens, or grafted or grows in thickets, the most pleasant valley produces, provided that the cultivator’s diligence be applied.

Here water is not drunk for money, nor is firewood bought at a price. [Col. 1473D] For a grove stands at the very doors, and in the innermost precincts a spring bubbles forth, gentle, pleasant to the taste, wholesome to drink, warm in winter and very cold in summer. It first meets the needs of the inhabitants, being protected with such diligent care that, above all, welcome solitude is not lacking and one may come to draw water with dry feet. Then it is very eagerly received outside by the common people, but first it is diverted into two streams that water the shrubs and moisten the gardens; flowing gently thus, it is gathered [Col. 1474A] into a nearby fishpond, constructed for maintaining a multitude of fish.

There lies below it a meadow, stretching lengthwise, pleasant, fertile, and so famous that, believe me, it received its name from its length. Little streams trickling from fish-filled pools wash both its sides in generous flow; hence the grass remains luxuriant at every season and, in the midst of summer heat, does not need rainwater. In this meadow, after the harvest of June, I saw hay gathered in August in such abundance that one could scarcely know whether the crop of the first season or the later one was greater.

Not far from here—namely, at a distance that an arrow may be shot twice—the river Vienne flows by, displaying various fish delicacies, so that we rarely need resort to the fishponds, unless perhaps a guest arrives late or weather drives the fishermen away from the river. [Col. 1474B] Moreover, our valley has caves cut out of rock, in which the inhabitants shelter themselves and their possessions from cold amid snow and from heat in summer. In them wine does not spoil, grain does not become tasteless, fruit does not rot, and no housebreaker is feared.

Finally, its chapel is such that, vaulted with light stone, it permits neither the cold of Capricorn nor the heat of Cancer to be felt. In it neither the healthy sleep without consequence nor the sick without hope of recovery. There, as the inhabitants testify, whoever enters to steal is punished either with blindness or with a graver vengeance. There are, beyond these, so many and such great endowments of the place that they can scarcely be made credible to anyone who has not seen them; scarcely can anyone who has once arrived here depart except [Col. 1474C] unwillingly.

Do you then wish me to abandon this place? Do you urge me to exchange it? Shall I leave here and return there, to plunge myself into the dangers of a thousand scandals? Epicurus advises Idomeneus to flee as far as he can and make haste before some greater force intervenes and takes away his freedom to depart. Yet he adds that nothing should be attempted unless it can be attempted fittingly and at the proper time. But when that long-awaited time comes, he says one must leap forth, and he hopes for a safe escape even from the greatest difficulties, provided that we neither hurry before the time nor delay when the time has come.

I know that you suffer from excessive longing for me, that you wish me to share in your joys. I embrace the love you bear for your own glory, rejoice in your affection, and do not fail to recognize [Col. 1474D] the kindness of spirit in which you summon me. But I have become accustomed to my poverty; it now suffices me no less than Croesus’s own wealth sufficed him. For, now made unaccustomed to honours, I have abandoned those honours by which my lord blesses his friends and honourably rewards those who deserve well of him. To confess the truth—to speak in your ear—my flute is not worth so much. I yielded my position, renounced my office, fearing Fortune, lest, if anything should happen, it be laid to my charge.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1152: JOSCELIN, BISHOP OF SOISSONS

[Col. 1475]

## NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. IX, col. 357.)

[Col. 1475A] Joscelin, or Goscelin (of Vierzy), called Rufus by Orderic Vitalis, had first been master of the schools in the Parisian academy, then archdeacon of Bourges and of Soissons. During that period he composed the epitaph of St Godfrey, bishop of Amiens. He succeeded Lisiard in 1126; attended the Council of Troyes in 1127 and that of Rouen in 1128, which he identifies as the second year of his episcopate in a privilege granted that year to Humbert, abbot of Igny. In the same year he attended the assembly at Arras and the blessing of Fulk, abbot of Épernay; and he subscribed to a gift made by Archbishop Rainald to the monks of St Maurice in the suburb of Reims, and to letters of John, bishop of Orléans, granting the church of St Anianus of Biliac to Ralph, prior of Celle in Berry. [Col. 1475B] In that year a wasting disease carried off many people in the district of Soissons; see Alberic’s *Chronicle* on this matter.

In 1129 Joscelin attended the anointing of King Philip and subscribed to the charter of father and son concerning the restitution of Argenteuil to Saint-Denis. In the same year he gave the monks of St Crispin the altar of Billy-sur-Ourcq. In 1130 he subscribed to the charter of Geoffrey, dean of Compiègne, granting Trois-Fontaines in the forest of Laigue to Abbot Guy, and to the confirmation of the foundation of Igny Abbey. In 1131 he was sent with St Bernard by Pope Innocent to meet both Gerard, who had seized the archbishopric of Bordeaux with the count’s support and held at once the churches of Bordeaux and Angoulême, and the count himself. They did so, but without success. [Col. 1475C] He founded Longpont Abbey in 1132. On the feast of SS Peter and Paul that same year, he showed the relics of St Geremarus to the people in the church of Beauvais and enclosed them in a shrine. On the same day he attended the translation of the relics of St Just by Bishop Peter, and was present at the gift of the land of Gland to the Premonstratensian church.

In 1133, called the eighth year of his episcopate in the charters of Silvamajor, he dedicated in the church of St Crispin the altars of SS Crispin and Crispinian; SS Simon and Jude; SS Marcellinus and Peter; SS Philip and James; and the chapel over the wall. In 1134, the ninth year of his episcopate, he caused Rainald, count of Soissons, to restore the altar of Terny to the monks of St Paul. [Col. 1476A] In the same year he confirmed the foundation of Val-Chrétien, made certain gifts to Odo, abbot of Marmoutier, and subscribed to Archbishop Rainald’s charter for Cuissy and Sélincourt. In 1135, the ninth year from his consecration, he secured for the people of Braine the tithe of the village of Blanzy. In a notice of a judgment of that same year for the monastery of St Crispin the Greater, though still alive, he is called “of pious memory.”

In 1136 he gave to Marmoutier the church of the Basiliques, which had once supported seventy-two canons but then barely sufficed for twelve; and he obtained a royal diploma declaring the exactions of the commune of Soissons null and requiring their correction. In 1137, the eleventh year of his episcopate, he confirmed the tithe of St Albin given to the church of Braine, and in the twelfth year gave them certain things in the territory of Hostelle. [Col. 1476B] In the same year he subscribed to the testament of Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, and to Archbishop Rainald of Reims’s charter for the church of Blangy.

On the Nones of April 1138, he translated the body of Godfrey, bishop of Amiens, from the chapter of St Crispin, where it had lain buried for twenty-three years, and placed it before the high altar in a vaulted tomb. In the same year he approved the foundation of Lieu-Restauré; was present at the grant by Garin, bishop of Amiens, of the church of St Gervasius of Encre to Theobald, prior of St Martin-des-Champs; had a dispute with Hatto, bishop of Troyes, concerning a certain cell, for the settlement of which they selected arbitrators that year; and subscribed to the letters of Archbishop Samson for St Theoderic.

In the same year, the thirteenth of his episcopate, he approved gifts made in his [Col. 1476C] diocese to the monastery of St Vincent of Laon. About that time Innocent II appointed him, among others, judge in the dispute between the bishop of Arras and the abbot of St Vaast. In 1139, the thirteenth year of his episcopate, he gave the canons of St John the altar of Laticy, and to Ernaud, abbot of St Crispin, the altars of Besny with all their tithes. In the same year he confirmed all that the monastery of Coincy possessed in his diocese and upheld the foundation of St Leodegar. In 1140, the fourteenth year of his episcopate, he confirmed the gift made by Rainald, count of Soissons, to Braine. In that same year he reconciled the canons of St Mary of Mont with the Premonstratensians of Braine; attended the Council of Sens, whence Letter 191 among Bernard’s letters was written in his name and in that of the other bishops of the province of Reims to Innocent II, concerning Abelard’s errors and their condemnation; was present with the king and other bishops when the foundations of the choir of Saint-Denis were laid; and attended the satisfaction rendered to St Remigius by Hugh, count of Roucy.

In the same year, the fifteenth of his episcopate, he confirmed the transfer of the Premonstratensians from Château-Thierry to Val-Secret. He subscribed to the charter of Blessed Mary of Saintes on Saturday, the feast of the Holy Innocents, the fifth day before the Kalends of January, 1140. In 1141 he received the homage of Ivo of Nesle, count of Soissons; subscribed to the judgment given by Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, between the abbots of Nogent and Prémontré; attended the agreement made between Manasses, bishop of Meaux, [Col. 1477B] and Riscendis, abbess of Faremoutiers; and gave the church of St Anianus to the church of Viviers.

In the same year, the sixteenth of his episcopate, he confirmed Braine’s possessions. In 1142 he sealed with his seal a gift to the monastery of St Crispin at La Caverne, consisting of certain fields and vineyards, by the dean and chapter of St Frambald of Senlis. In the same year he subscribed to the letters of Archbishop Samson confirming the foundation of the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu, and to his letters of 1143 confirming the church of St Mary of Château-Porcien to St Nicaise. In the same year, the seventeenth of his episcopate, he confirmed the possessions of the monasteries of St Crispin and St Sulpicius. In 1144, the eighteenth year of his episcopate, he confirmed the possessions of the monastery of St Ghislain situated in the diocese of Soissons.

In the same year he attended the dedication of the basilica of Saint-Denis [Col. 1477C] and consecrated the altar of St Benedict. With Archbishop Samson he dedicated the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu and subscribed to the latter’s letters for St Mary, St Remigius, and the monks of Rejet. He is mentioned in the same year in a charter of Nicholas, bishop of Cambrai, for Saint-Denis. In 1145, the eighteenth year of his episcopate, he confirmed the possessions of the Carthusians; and in the nineteenth year the possessions of the Premonstratensians whom he had established in the church of St Mary and St Evodius within the walls of Braine.

In the same year he subscribed to Archbishop Samson’s charter concerning the agreement between the abbot of St John of Valenciennes and Hugh, prior of Savy. In 1146, the twenty-first year of his episcopate, he gave Odo, abbot of St Remigius, a third part of the tithe of Dhuys; in the same year he exempted from tithes the parish place of Longpont, [Col. 1477D] almost reduced to a wilderness. In the following year he subscribed to Archbishop Samson’s letters for St Remigius, and in that same year attended the Council of Paris, in which he was chosen, among others, to examine the propositions of Gilbert of Poitiers.

In 1148 he attended the Council of Reims convened for the same cause. In the letter of Geoffrey, monk of Clairvaux, concerning the events of this synod, Joscelin is described as endowed with both secular and literary learning. Indeed, there survives in Martène’s very extensive *Collection*, vol. IX, col. 1101, his exposition of the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer. In 1148 he subscribed to Archbishop Samson’s instrument confirming a gift to the monastery of St Lucian by Theobald, archdeacon of Beauvais, and to the same archbishop’s letters for St Quentin in the Island. He attended the dedication of the churches of Hasnon, performed on the fourth day before the Kalends of June 1149, and of Vaucelles.

In the same year he confirmed, in the chapter of Longpont, gifts made to that monastery, and subscribed to the charter of Manasses, bishop of Orléans, giving Marmoutier the church of Blessed Mary of Bonne-Nouvelle. In 1150, the twenty-fifth year of his episcopate, he confirmed the possessions of the church of Charmes, and subscribed to Archbishop Samson’s charter reconciling Baldwin, bishop of Noyon, and Ralph, count of Vermandois. In 1151, the twenty-sixth year of his episcopate, he approved the agreement concerning a tithe in the territory of Raroy, made between the monks of St Martin-des-Champs at St Gemma and those of Igny. [Col. 1478B] About that time there survive three letters of Joscelin and Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis (*Anecdota* of Martène, vol. I, cols. 424–425), concerning their mutual desire to see one another; from these it is clear that both were friends, both ill, and both near death.

Finally, Joscelin, “father of justice and of many monasteries, enemy of vices and most eminent cultivator of chastity,” as he is called in the *Life* of Blessed Godfrey, bishop of Amiens, after many illustrious achievements, rendered his soul to God on the ninth day before the Kalends of November, 1152. By his agency, says the writer of the *Annals of Prémontré*, five abbeys of that order had been built in his diocese. He was buried [Col. 1478C] before the altar of the holy apostles Peter and Paul in the nave of Soissons Cathedral, beneath a tomb; thence he was transferred, as founder and principal benefactor, to a mausoleum within the apse-wall of the presbytery of Longpont church, on the epistle side. There may be seen the effigy of the bishop, adorned in pontifical dress, with this inscription:

> Here lies Joscelin, bishop of Soissons, who first brought the community of this house from Clairvaux in the time of Blessed Bernard the abbot.

This bishop possessed great influence with the king. Consequently St Bernard’s zeal burned against him for a while because he did not better direct the royal mind. Angered by the saintly abbot’s letters, Joscelin prefixed to the letter in which he replied to him: “Greetings in the Lord—and not the spirit of blasphemy.” On this matter see St Bernard, Letter 223, who addressed other letters to him as well; so too did Pope Eugenius III and Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis. Suger also dedicated to Joscelin his *Life of Louis the Fat*, under which king Joscelin and that abbot held the foremost roles in governing the kingdom, as is proved by the many letters written to him, especially those of St Bernard.

He is commemorated in the necrologies of Fontevraud, Artonne, and St Just of Beauvais on 25 October. On that day the necrology of Fontaines reads: “The most reverend Joscelin, bishop of Soissons, of pious memory, departed from this world; he was our benefactor and a most distinguished teacher.”

[Col. 1479]

## EXPOSITION OF THE CREED AND THE LORD’S PRAYER BY JOSCELIN, BISHOP OF SOISSONS

(MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, from a manuscript of Marchiennes monastery.)

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATION

We have transcribed the following exposition of the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer by Joscelin, bishop of Soissons, from a very ancient manuscript of Marchiennes monastery. Joscelin was endowed with both secular and literary learning, as Geoffrey, monk of Clairvaux and secretary of St Bernard, writes in his history of the Council of Reims. He was counsellor to Louis VII, king of the Franks, together with Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis; he was sent as legate by Pope Eugenius III, together with St Bernard, to William, duke of Aquitaine and count of Poitiers, for the suppression of the schism. Several letters of Eugenius, St Bernard, and Suger addressed to him survive. Nicholas the monk, in the *Life* of St Godfrey, bishop of Amiens, honoured him with this commendation:

> Joscelin, formerly archdeacon of Bourges and most celebrated master of Paris, father of justice and of many monasteries, enemy of vices and most eminent cultivator of chastity.

And certainly, if we believe the annalist of the Premonstratensian Order, five abbeys of that order were built through his agency in the diocese of Soissons. The very renowned Cistercian monastery of Longpont likewise acknowledges him as its founder.

## HERE BEGINS THE EXPOSITION BY JOSCELIN, BISHOP OF SOISSONS, OF THE CREED

[Col. 1479A] **I.** Your fraternity has asked me to send you an exposition of the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, such as I am accustomed to preach in churches. You have indeed exercised fitting moderation. For who can fully understand or expound the Lord’s Prayer, which divine Wisdom itself dictated in its own words—not through a prophet, not through an apostle? The mysteries of the Creed also are profound and covered by a sacred veil. Yet when we drink from a spring, we quench our thirst, even if we do not swallow the entire spring. Therefore, as we are accustomed to expound these things to the people for their understanding, and as you request, we shall attempt to speak with the Holy Spirit as our guide. First, it seems, we must deal with the Creed.

**II.** In the Creed we show both the faith that we have toward God and our own faithfulness to him, so that we may ask more boldly through the Lord’s Prayer. For Jesus entrusts himself only to the faithful, and grants great things only to them. The unbeliever, however, is an importunate petitioner and will soon suffer refusal.

The name *symbolum* is compounded from the Greek preposition *syn* and *bolo*. *Syn* means “with”; hence what we call a yoke-partner, the Greek calls a *synjuga*, “one yoked together.” A *bolus* is a mouthful, that is, as much bread or food as the mouth takes in at one time. Therefore, just as many guests make a *conframa*, that is, a common banquet, and each contributes his own share, so the holy apostles are known to have done. After the Lord’s Ascension and the coming of the Holy Spirit, who had taught them all truth, being about to fulfil Christ’s command—“Go into all the world, preach the Gospel; whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved, but whoever does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16:15)—they met together before dispersing, lest the preaching of faith among so many apostles should be discordant. They made a spiritual common banquet, [Col. 1480B] that is, the *confram*, the Creed. In it they did not set forth every article of faith in detail, but only twelve statements, since they themselves were twelve, Matthias having now been substituted for Judas, so that each might contribute his own. I do not remember ever having read this anywhere in canonical Scripture.

These statements, however, are altogether necessary: if one believes them and does not err in other matters, one can be saved; without them, no one who has reached the age of understanding can attain salvation. Athanasius says: “This is the catholic faith, which unless everyone believes faithfully and firmly, he cannot be saved.” For faith is the foundation of all good things, the messenger of human salvation; and it is impossible for anyone to please God without faith. But if anyone does not walk by faith, he will not arrive at sight. Therefore, whoever is baptized should learn the Creed when he reaches years of understanding. Godparents too should take pains that their little children know it. For they became sureties for them before God when they answered for them at baptism. In whatever language they are taught or learn it is of no concern, provided that they believe firmly.

## The Twelve Articles of the Creed

**III.** The twelve statements constituting the Creed seem to be distinguished as follows.

The first: “I believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth.”

The second: “And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.”

The third: “Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.”

The fourth: “Suffered under Pontius Pilate, died and was buried, descended into hell.”

The fifth: “Rose from the dead.”

The sixth: “Ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty, from there he shall come to judge the living and the dead.”

The seventh: “I believe in the Holy Spirit.”

The eighth: “The holy catholic Church.”

[Col. 1481C] The ninth: “The communion of saints.”

The tenth: “The forgiveness of sins.”

The eleventh: “The resurrection of the flesh.”

The twelfth: “Eternal life.”

The faith manifested through the Creed has its foundation in the believer’s heart; and there it is fully known by him who searches hearts and inner dispositions. Yet you have read: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10)—not, however, for the person uttering it, but for those who hear. For when many people make their faith known to one another by words, charity increases and the multitude of believers becomes one heart and one soul. Therefore faith must always be preserved in the heart and, when fitting, proclaimed with the voice, according to the saying: “You shall not appear empty before God” (Exodus 23:15). Faith must always be offered to God, if not with the voice, at least with the heart.

Let him therefore who dares say, “I believe in God.” If he speaks truthfully, he is blessed; for “the righteous lives by faith” (Romans 1:17).

## The Difference between Believing That God Exists, Believing God, and Believing in God. Unity of Essence and Trinity of Persons in God
IV. He does not say, “I believe God” (*Credo Deum*), that is, “that God exists”; nor does he say, “I believe God” (*Credo Deo*), that is, “that he is truthful.” For believing in this manner is insufficient for righteousness, since the demons also believe in this way and tremble. Rather, he says, “I believe in God.” This expression signifies a certain progress of the faithful soul, desiring to cleave to God through love and to be brought to completion in him through good action and will. If one bound by criminal sins says this, he lies; while serving such sins, he does not advance toward God but falls away from God. He cannot please Truth through falsehood; indeed, by lying he brings ruin upon himself. “For a lying mouth kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11). Therefore, before saying this, let each person examine himself; and, if he finds himself in sin or in the will to sin, let him rather keep silent. But if he immediately repents and turns himself toward God with every good will, let him confidently say, “I believe in God.”

He says “God” in the singular, to distinguish him from idols, which the Gentiles believed to be gods. For there is only one God, as Moses says: “Hear, Israel, your God is one” (Deut. 6:34). But because that one God is three persons, he further distinguishes by saying “Father”; as though he said: I believe that the one God is Father; I believe that the one God is Son; I believe that the one God is Holy Spirit—that is, that the one essence is three persons, and that those three persons are one essence, not several. If you do not yet understand, believe, and you shall understand. Understanding does not come before believing; rather, “from thy commandments I have understood” (Ps. 118); nor does that faith advance to justification which is first understood by human reason. For faith has no merit where human reason supplies proof. If, when someone narrates something, you understand what he says, he owes you no thanks if you believe it. But if you have not yet understood, and esteem the author so highly that you cannot disbelieve what he says, he is rightly deserving of your gratitude.

This is the fountain in which no stranger shares. Jew or Gentile shudders even to hear of Trinity in unity and unity in Trinity, and therefore refuses to believe it. Hence it comes about that in the present age he does not attain the justification received through faith, nor in the age to come possess eternal life, so that we may repeat: “The righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17).

But let us return to the exposition. He says “Father” because before time he begot the Son, coeternal with himself. “[I believe] in the almighty Creator of heaven and earth,” that is, in him who by his omnipotence is the maker of heavenly and earthly things, that is, visible and invisible things. If you ask, since the Son is almighty and the Holy Spirit is almighty, why “almighty” is joined to the Father and cannot be said of the Son or the Holy Spirit: a certain infirmity of old age is commonly suggested by fatherhood, so that younger sons are stronger than elderly parents. But he is not such a father; he does not diminish power, who preserves omnipotence for himself.

### The second part of the Creed is expounded

V. It follows: “And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.” The conjunction *and* indicates that “I believe” must be repeated, so that one says: “And I believe in Jesus Christ.” In exactly the same ways in which we distinguished above what it is to believe in God the Father, understand that one must believe in the Son; for, since he is equal to the Father in majesty, he ought not to be lesser in honor. Thus, to believe in the Son is to advance toward him through good action and will, so that we may be united to him through love.

Nor are the names preceding and following “Son” empty words; rather, they are, as it were, goads urging our advance toward the Son. It is as though he said: We ought rightly to believe in the Son just as in the Father, because he is Jesus—that is, our Savior, saving us from the power of the devil—and Christ—that is, our anointed one. Two persons are anointed: king and priest. The Son of God is our king, ruling us over “this great and broad sea,” that is, the world; and he is high priest, making his cross a bridge for us, by which we may pass from this world to him, according to the saying: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross,” etc. (Matt. 16:24).

“His only Son”: as though he said, although there are many sons of God, according to what is said in John’s Gospel: “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12), this Son alone is consubstantial and coeternal with him, uniquely begotten. Thus no part of the Godhead flows from the Father into the Son while another part remains in the Father; rather, the whole Son is in the Father, and the whole Father in the Word.

If you distinguish it thus—“his only Son, our Lord”—the meaning is fitting. It is as though he said: This Son in whom one must believe is our Lord, not merely by that common lordship by which the Father is Lord, the Son is Lord, and the Holy Spirit is Lord, but by a certain singular and unique lordship, by which he purchased us with his own blood, according to the saying: “For you were bought at a great price” (1 Cor. 6:20). For the Father was not incarnate, and therefore could not shed blood; nor was the Holy Spirit [incarnate], and therefore could not endure the Passion.

### The third article of the Creed. Original sin. Pleasure as the penalty of original sin. Christ conceived through the cooperation of the whole Trinity

VI. “Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, of the Virgin Mary.” Without interruption it might fittingly seem that “I believe in the Holy Spirit” ought to follow; for, since one must believe only in the Trinity, which is one God, and not in anything else, after saying “I believe in the Father, I believe in the Son,” it would appropriately be said, “I believe in the Holy Spirit,” who is the third person of the Trinity. Yet the order of the words would be unsuitable. For if, after “I believe in the Holy Spirit,” there followed “who was conceived by the Holy Spirit,” the conception would seem to refer rather to the Spirit, of whom mention had most recently been made, than to the Son, of whom mention had been made more remotely. Therefore, after “I believe in the Son” has been said, without inserting anything else: “who”—understand, the Son—“was conceived by the Holy Spirit.”

Everyone conceived from the intercourse of man and woman is conceived in sin. For the very pleasure felt in intercourse would never have existed either in the first parents or in their offspring, had those first parents not sinned. Once they sinned, this pleasure was propagated as the penalty of sin. Hence those conceived in it are so infected with original sin—of which that pleasure itself is the penalty—that they are damned forever unless aid is first given them through the sacrament of baptism, as the Gospel says: “Unless one is born again, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5). David too was born of lawful marriage, and yet says: “And in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. 50:7).

Therefore, lest that conception in sin occur to you when you hear “who was conceived,” he immediately adds “by the Holy Spirit”: that is, not “of bloods,” nor “of the will of the flesh,” nor “of the will of man,” but of the Holy Spirit. Thus was he conceived, so that the Virgin suffered in that conception no pleasure—which is the penalty of original sin—just as Eve would not have suffered it had she conceived before sin. Yet this cannot be compared with that divine event, which is far more magnificent.

When one says, “a wife conceived by her husband,” do not understand “Mary conceived by the Holy Spirit” in the same way. Rather, understand that the Holy Spirit was the author of this conception: by his illuminating and sanctifying the Virgin’s heart, Christ’s flesh was conceived from the flesh of blessed Mary alone, with no origin of seed-flesh operating from without. For just as a worm is born from pure mud when the sun warms it, so Christ’s body was propagated from the Virgin’s flesh alone. Thus, comparing himself to a worm, he says through the Psalmist: “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21:7): that is, conceived after the manner of a worm from earth alone, not from the admixture of another seed, and not after the manner of a human being, who is ordinarily conceived only through the mingling of male and female seed.

Observe that he is not said to have been conceived by the Holy Spirit so as to exclude the Father and the Son from this operation. For where there is one nature and the same essence, there cannot be a different operation. Therefore, the whole Trinity cooperating, this conception took place, so that by an ineffable principle of generation the Son himself was in the Virgin the creator of himself, he who brought about his own creation through the Father and the Holy Spirit. Although the whole Trinity performed this sacrament, mention is nevertheless made of the Holy Spirit, because through him who proceeds from both, those two from whom he proceeds could fittingly be understood.

### Christ born with his mother’s virginity intact

VII. “Born of the Virgin Mary.” Just as the singular conception did not infect the Virgin with sin, so the singular birth did not corrupt her virginity. For as conception did not open the mother’s womb, neither did birth open it; but just as she was a virgin before conception and birth, so she remained the same after conception and birth.

One may ask why God, when he was to assume human nature, wished to take it from the mass corrupted in Adam, rather than create it new, neither from father nor mother, as he had made Adam. But it was much more wondrous to assume it incorrupt from a source preceded by corruption than to have created it incorrupt with no preceding corruption. He assumed it from woman alone because the female sex seemed less worthy of mercy and redemption on account of Eve, who first drew man—and his posterity that was to follow him—into death. She drew him, however, not through seduction. For the woman was deceived; Adam, however, was deceived knowingly, but preferred to obey his wife in evil rather than offend her. This is the third part.

### The fourth part, embracing Christ’s ignominious sufferings

VIII. “Suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried; he descended into hell.” Christ’s ignominious sufferings are placed in the fourth part, according to the Apostle’s saying: “We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block indeed to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, but to us the power of God and the wisdom of God. For the weakness of God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. 1:23).

Pilate is mentioned not to confer any dignity upon the person, but solely to determine the time. For there were many men named Jesus; but, in order to specify which Jesus is the one in whom we are to believe—the one conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary—it adds, “suffered under Pontius Pilate,” as though it said: He is the one who endured the Passion while Pontius Pilate governed Judaea. For times are customarily determined by rulers.

Therefore the God who is impassible by nature suffered in the assumed passible nature, in order to restore the human race, which was subject to suffering, to impassibility, as it is said: “It was necessary for Christ to suffer and so to enter into his glory” (Luke 24:46). That is: Christ’s Passion was fitting in this respect, that through it it was brought about that, when all the faithful rise again, they rise immortal and impassible; and this is the glory of the resurrection.

### The punishment of the cross was most ignominious. Why Christ wished to die on the cross

IX. “Crucified.” The kind of death inflicted by the cross was most ignominious. Hence it is written: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death” (Wis. 2:20). Therefore he wished to be crucified in order to free us from eternal torments and transfer us to eternal life.

For since the devil presumptuously stretched out his hand against him over whom he could have had no right—since he committed no sin, nor was conceived in it—he rightly lost the dominion which he was thought to have extended and exercised over the human race. Jesus could have died by another kind of death, but none was more fitting than the cross. For because unbelievers regarded Christ’s death as useless, like that of another condemned man, the very manner of his Passion showed that it was most beneficial: it prepared joy for heaven, a remedy for hell, and redemption for the whole world.

For when he drew from hell the souls of the blessed who awaited him, he opened paradise; and he provided a remedy even for the angels, increasing the joy of their fellowship. This could be signified by the height of the cross, on which the inscription was written, and by the portion fixed in the depths of the earth. That it would benefit the whole world could be indicated by the fact that one part of the cross faced east, another west, another south, and another north, so that through this it might be understood to what extent it would bring sufficient redemption to all who inhabit the various regions of the world, unless it remained in them [antecedent unclear]. We fear to set forth the mysteries of the cross, for they are exceedingly profound and harmful when abbreviated.

### By Christ’s three-day burial three kinds of sin in us are destroyed

X. “Dead.” He truly died a real death, just as he was born in a real birth, in order to free us from eternal death and through temporal death grant us eternal life. “And buried.” He wished to be buried so that he might bury us with himself in respect of our vices and concupiscences. Hence the Apostle says: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through grace, so we too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6:4).

That is, having laid aside all oldness, let us be conformed to Christ’s likeness, so that through the threefold mention of baptism and Christ’s three-day burial, the three kinds of sin in us—consent, act, and habit—may be destroyed. In this respect our old man was crucified with him.

### Christ, descending into hell, opened paradise’s gate to the saints

XI. “He descended into hell.” That three-day delay between death and resurrection was not idle. While the body lay in the tomb, the soul descended into hell in order to lead with itself into paradise the souls of the saints who awaited this redemption. The gate of paradise, which from the beginning had been closed to all as a penalty, was then opened when the cherub stationed at paradise’s entrance with a flaming sword was removed. Thus the good entered together, and John the Baptist and the Holy Innocents did not precede the thief who had heard from the Lord: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

Observe that although Christ’s soul was separated from his body by as much distance as lies between hell and the tomb, the union in the person of Christ of divinity and humanity, once entered into, did not cease, does not cease, and will not cease. Nor could the divinity, which is everywhere, be separated from the body by the removal of its covering, according to the Psalm: “If I ascend into heaven, thou art there; if I descend into hell, thou art present” (Ps. 138:8). If you do not yet fully understand, believe. Thus these infirmities of Christ surpass all the strength of the world.

### Why Christ is said to have risen on the third day after death

XII. “On the third day he rose from the dead.” Crucified on Friday, he gave up the spirit about the ninth hour. Thus, through the final part of Friday, the whole following Sabbath, and about the first part of Sunday—which is called the first day of the week—the Lord rose. Hence the statement is true: “On the third day he rose from the dead,” not because three full days had elapsed, but because parts of three days had elapsed.

Many had risen before Christ, but afterwards returned to death. Lazarus was raised and became bishop; he governed the Church of Jerusalem. [Note: [Col. 1485] Joslenus therefore did not suppose Lazarus to have been bishop of Marseilles.] But he died again. Christ, however, “having risen from the dead, dies no more” (Rom. 6:9), and is therefore the witness of a true resurrection. For that resurrection is true which is not undone by death. God promises this to his own according to the Apostle: “For if we have been made one with him in the likeness of his death, we shall likewise be one with him in his resurrection” (Rom. 6:5). This is the fifth part.

### In what sense Christ is said to sit at the Father’s right hand

XIII. “He ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the almighty Father, and thence shall come to judge the living and the dead.” Forty days intervened between Easter and the Ascension, during which the Lord associated with his disciples. As he rose at Easter, so on the day of Ascension he placed above the heavens the condition of our nature, which he assumed when born of a human mother. According to his divinity, however, he who was everywhere could not previously have been absent from there.

When he is said to “sit,” do not refer this in your mind to a position of limbs, as though he were in such a posture; understand judicial authority, because “the Father has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). “He sits at the right hand of God the Father.” God the Father is not something bodily that has a right or left hand. He is the most simple nature, wholly everywhere, incapable of being bounded by dimensions, so that one part of him is on the right or left, before or behind, above or below. Rather, understand by “right hand” the highest blessedness, in which the Son is always equal to the Father; just as, conversely, by “left hand” understand the utmost misery, according to the saying: “But the goats on the left” (Matt. 25:33).

“Thence shall he come to judge the living and the dead.” The Apostle says: “We shall all be caught up to meet [him] in the air” (1 Thess. 4:17). For judgment is believed to be there. But “he shall come” is said according to his humanity, because those who crucified the Lord will see him whom they pierced—that is, his humanity. Yet the wicked person will be taken away lest he see the glory of God; nor could anyone remain wholly miserable to whom God reveals himself.

Understand by “the living” those whom his coming, which will come “as a thief in the night,” finds living for this purpose, though they will die at that coming; and if anything in them still deserved long punishment, it will be purged in a moment, through the terror, horror, and anguish of his coming. Or understand by “the dead” those whom his coming finds already dead and raises again; by “the living,” the righteous destined for life; and by “the dead,” those condemned to eternal death.

Let those who profess this faith attend to the fact that in this Creed Christ’s humanity and humiliation, by which they were reconciled, are commemorated so carefully, lest they be found ungrateful for their Redeemer’s benefits. Through his humanity he reconciled them; through his divinity he absolved them, lest they be justly deprived, through ingratitude, of the paternal goods allotted to them.

XIV. “I believe in the Holy Spirit.” The Holy Spirit is the third person in the Trinity, true and one God with the Father and the Son. Therefore one must believe in him just as in the Father and the Son: consubstantial with Father and Son, he proceeds equally from both. What it is to believe in God, as stated above, recall here. Faith in the Holy Spirit, who is called sevenfold, is fittingly placed in the seventh part because of the seven graces read in Isaiah.

XV. “The holy catholic Church.” “I believe” must be repeated, while the preposition *in* must be omitted. For one must believe in nothing except the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit alone, nor does the rational creature find rest elsewhere. Hence in the Psalm: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain” (Ps. 41:3); and elsewhere: “My soul has desired and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83:3).

Therefore distinguish it thus: “I believe that the catholic Church is holy.” Church means a congregation of the faithful; *catholic* means universal. That congregation of the faithful, then, is to be believed holy which rests on the common faith—namely, the faith preached by the apostles, which endures firmly among the rulers of the churches and remains inviolable among the multitude of peoples—and not that which is whispered by heretics in private rooms or behind curtains. This is the eighth part.

### What is the communion of saints?

XVI. “The communion of saints.” Repeat: “I believe [in] the communion of saints,” that is, the truth of the Church’s sacraments, in which the saints who departed this life in the unity of faith shared. To understand more fully: if anyone questions you in order to entrap you in conversation, asking what you think about baptism, the Lord’s body and blood, or the other sacraments, do not gape like an oven; reply briefly: “I believe about these and the other sacraments what the saints truly believed.”

“I believe [in] the communion of saints,” that is, that the saints hold heavenly gifts in common—not that one does not have more than another, since “star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 15:41), but that they so burn together in glory that neither the lesser envies the greater nor the greater despises the lesser.

XVII. “The remission of sins.” Repeat: “I believe [in] the remission of sins”—not only of those remitted through baptism, but also of those cleansed through humble confession and worthy satisfaction. This is the part.

XVIII. “The resurrection of the flesh.” Repeat: “I believe.” Human flesh that was once animated shall rise again on the day of judgment; and every soul shall in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, be assigned to the body which it governed, however putrefied or scattered it may be. Thus the good may be made blessed in a double robe—that is, in soul and body—and the evil crushed by a double affliction. This is the eleventh part.

XIX. “Life everlasting.” “I believe” must be repeated. Death followed the resurrections of the dead celebrated before and after Christ; but this general resurrection will not be subject to a separation of soul from body. Rather, whether the good receive eternal life or the evil endure eternal punishments, they shall endure forever. Here the twelfth part is completed. Amen. “Amen” is, as it were, the seal of the whole Creed, as though it were said: Whatever is contained in these twelve propositions is necessary for the faith that leads to sight.

## The exposition of the same author on the Lord’s Prayer begins

### The Lord’s Prayer: brief in words, long in meanings. How to pray. What to pray for

I. As your brotherhood requested, we have for a little while explained the meaning of the Creed, the deeper things of truth. Now we turn to the depth of the Lord’s Prayer, not seeking a bottom in the abyss, but desiring only to swim upon its surface. For the Lord’s Prayer is at once very brief and very long: brief in words, long in meanings, so that there is no one who does not grow dim-sighted in contemplating it.

Every rational petition concerns either goods to be desired, evils to be avoided, or sins committed to be forgiven. Whatever lies beyond or short of these is either imperfect or excessive. The diligent reader will find all this comprehensively contained in this very concise discourse. For when we pray that God’s name may be sanctified, his kingdom may come, his will be done as in heaven so on earth, and daily bread may be given us, this concerns goods to be sought, whether of the future or the present life. When we say, “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors,” it concerns forgiveness of sins committed. And when we entreat that he not lead us into temptation but deliver us from evil, it plainly concerns avoidance of evils.

Therefore one should pray more devoutly with this prayer, in which nothing necessary is left out and nothing superfluous requested. It is credible that God will not readily deny what is asked through the words he taught, if the affection of the mind accords with the voice. For Jesus Christ, who taught us prayer, taught humility also, saying: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29); he taught sobriety, saying: “Let not your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness” (Luke 21:34); he taught us to fast, saying: “When you fast, do not become sad like the hypocrites” (Matt. 6:16); and he taught almsgiving, saying: “When you give alms, let not your right hand know what your left hand does” (ibid.).

He who taught these things ought not to have passed over instruction in prayer, which is very powerful for attaining and preserving the things mentioned above. Thus he said: “But when you pray, enter into your chamber, and when you pray, pray to your Father” (Matt. 6:6). First he teaches how one should pray: namely, that, having excluded the fantasies of earthly desires which descend through the doors of the senses into the heart, signified by the chamber, heart and tongue may so come together as one in prayer that what belongs to one may be said of the other, according to the Psalmist: “My heart spoke to thee” (Ps. 26:8); and elsewhere: “My tongue too shall meditate on thy righteousness” (Ps. 34:28), although speech more properly belongs to the tongue and meditation to the heart.

Yet it is of little use to know how one should pray unless we also know what we should pray for. Unless we are taught it, we cannot know it, as the Apostle says: “For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought, but the Holy Spirit intercedes for us” (Rom. 8:26): he teaches, causes us to ask, and with him the Father and the Son, because the three have one teaching and operation.

### Some petitions of the Lord’s Prayer concern the present life, others the future life

II. He says: “Thus shall you pray: Our Father.” Notice what a careful teacher he is, who in words so concise—seven little phrases, or petitions—comprehended everything that ought to be sought. Otherwise, if he had done this through a prolixity of words, the crooked and unstable human heart could not have been held by a long discourse. For one who does not have the meditation of the heart with “Our Father” will scarcely have it even with the entire Psalter. Yet five words with understanding are better than ten thousand words without meaning.

Of these seven petitions, the first three can be practiced and requested in the present life, but are perfected only in the blessed life. The final three are necessary in the present life in order that one may attain the blessed life; but once that life has been attained, they are not at all necessary. The middle petition—“Give us this day our daily bread”—is partly necessary in the present life and ends with it; but partly it pertains to the future life and will endure and be perfected only there, as, God willing, we shall show in the exposition of each petition. Now let us come to expound the body of the Lord’s Prayer itself.

### How great is God’s condescension, who wished to be our Father

III. “Our Father, who art in heaven.” It is the custom of secular orators, when they intend to persuade a judge of some great matter, to use an introduction especially to win his goodwill. In accordance with this practice, this spiritual petitioner is taught by his Creator, Redeemer, and fellow-brother, Jesus, before making his petition, to win the goodwill of the one from whom he desires to obtain it. Thus he says, “Our Father,” as though saying: Great indeed is what I wish to ask, but I ask it from a Father, not from a stranger. By nature I was a child of wrath; but by grace going before and following after, cleansing the heart through faith, you willed that I should be an adopted son, your heir, and a co-heir with Christ. How, then, can you deny anything, you who gave so wondrous a gift, that you should be their Father?

Under the Old Testament, who presumed to call God Father? “The Lord is his name. And I am the Lord” (Isa. 42:8). They served in fear, as slaves, not in love, as sons. But the people of acquisition are subject to him not so much through fear as through love.

Still, let one who says “Father” while praying to God take care not to lie. For if God is his Father, he is God’s son. But the Gospel says: “Whose works you do, his son you are.” If you do the works of the flesh, you are a son of the devil—works which are manifest: fornications, uncleannesses, sensual excesses, etc.; those who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God. If you find yourself in any act or will of the kind mentioned above, do not presume to call God Father. He will rightly be indignant against the devil’s son who falsely claims to have God as Father.

And who is there who has not done works of the devil in act or will? “For we have all sinned; and if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). Shall no one, then, say “Our Father” for his salvation? Far from it. Attend closely. Wisdom spoke wisely: it did not say, “Whose works you have done,” for then we would all be sons of the devil; rather, it says, “Whose works you do,” adding as though to say: When you are about to say “Our Father,” consider beforehand whether you are engaged in a criminal act or a criminal will. If you find yourself such, be silent: you are a son of the devil, and God will not hear you under the name of Father, because you are not his son but rather a stepson. Yet do not despair: descend into your heart; repent that you have sinned; change your evil will; seize hold of the desire for good. Now you are a son of God. For by willing you now do his works; the perfected will of the mind is counted as the deed performed. Therefore say boldly, “Father.” Nothing ought to be dearer to a son than his father, nor to a father than his son. The love of God is in you.

### God is Father of all, not of one alone

IV. “Our.” This petitioner recognizes that God is not the Father of one person alone, but of all the faithful; and the sons of the same Father must be brothers. Since you know them to be brothers, you ought to love one another; for “if you do not love the brother whom you see, how can you love God whom you do not see?” (1 John 4:20). Do you love God and your neighbor? You are perfect in love. He who is love denies you nothing.

Let not the rich person despise the poor, if he recognizes him as a brother. And see how gracious is this prayer, which never prays for oneself alone but for all fellow-brothers. Prayer is more effective when all pray for all than when individuals pray for themselves alone, according to the saying: “Woe to him who is alone, for when he falls he has none to lift him up” (Eccl. 4:19).

V. And lest this prayer be thought directed to a carnal father, it adds: “Who art in heaven,” that is, who have your dwelling in those whose conduct and desire are in heavenly things—in your lovers—according to the saying: “If anyone loves me, my Father will love him, and we shall make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). This does not mean that the Divinity is more confined in heaven than on earth, for he is everywhere. But the righteous are very fittingly signified by the name “heavens,” as in: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:2). Sinners are called “earth,” as in: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:6), as though the spiritual distance between the righteous and the sinner were as great as the bodily distance between heaven and earth.

### The first petition of the Lord’s Prayer

VI. Having won goodwill, he asks, “Hallowed be thy name.” This is the first petition, concerning those things which are perfected only in the blessed life. A more rational order might seem to require that he first ask for those things which make progress in the present life and are necessary for attaining rewards in the blessed life. But observe that this petitioner burns so ardently with love that, forgetting things later and transient, he longs with the whole desire of his soul for things prior and everlasting. He says: This I ask, this I request: that thy name may be sanctified—not that it may be holy, since it cannot possibly fail to be holy; for that would be an idle request—but that it may be recognized as holy by all.

“God is known in Judaea” now—that is, among the faithful and those who confess him. But the Gentiles do not know God. When the day of judgment comes, however, and the righteous receive eternal blessedness while the unrighteous receive utter misery, then God will be known by all, and no one thereafter will believe an idol to be God.

Or otherwise: “Hallowed be thy name”—namely, “Father.” Jews and Gentiles who do not believe Jesus to be the Son of God do not believe that God is his consubstantial and coeternal Father. Nor do they believe in the regeneration of baptism, in which we are adopted by God the Father as sons and daughters; instead, they call us dogs. Thus the name of fatherhood in God seems to them not holy but abominable. But when the blessed life has been attained and all see that every judgment has been given to the Son, they will be unable to deny that God is Father to God the Son. For when they see those reborn in the sacrament of baptism placed at the right hand to enjoy the good of the paternal inheritance—as heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ—then the name of fatherhood in God will undoubtedly appear holy.

Or thus: Christ is the name and glory of the Father. Christians are named from this name. Therefore he prays that the Christian name, now detestable to Jews and Gentiles, may be recognized by them as holy. This will happen in the blessed life, according to the saying: “We fools thought their life madness and their end without honor” (Wis. 5:4). How then are they among the children of God?

### The second petition
### VII. Second Petition: “Thy kingdom come.”

[Col. 1492D] Whither will that come, or whence will that come which is everywhere? For there is nowhere where God does not reign, according to the saying: “If I ascend into heaven, thou art there; if I descend into hell, thou art present,” etc. (Ps. 138:8). A madman does not know where he is, or who he is; yet he is somewhere, and is someone. A blind man does not know the nearby light; likewise, though he serves sin, he does not recognize that God reigns over him, because God is not before his eyes. He therefore prays that the kingdom of God, which is lacking to those who are ignorant, may be known by all.

Or, more plainly: God reigns especially in those in whom sin neither reigns, nor is present, nor can be present. Sin reigns in the devil and in his members, to whom sin is pleasing and who do not resist it at all. Sin is present but does not reign in those who, having sinned through the frailty of the flesh or the devil’s suggestion, immediately repent and confess without delay. [Col. 1493A] Sin can be present but is not, as in the newly baptized and as in Adam before he had transgressed. But God is said to reign in the blessed angels, who, after the fall of the others, have been so confirmed that they can no longer sin, and in the souls of the saints. Therefore he asks that God may reign in us in that excellence in which he reigns in the angels: namely, that sin may be wholly alien to us—neither reigning, nor present, nor able to be present.

### Third Petition

### VIII. Third Petition: “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.”

Who resists his will? Yet he prays that the concordant will of the faithful still dwelling on earth may be as concordant with God’s will as is the will of the holy angels, to whom nothing displeases that pleases God, and nothing pleases that displeases God.

[Col. 1493B] Or thus: now the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. He therefore prays that, when this discord has been quieted, the whole soul may agree with God in its sensual faculty, by which it is burdened by the flesh, just as it agrees with him in reason; according to the saying, “My heart and my flesh rejoiced in the living God” (Ps. 83:3). This will be accomplished only in the blessed life. And this is the third petition.

### Fourth Petition — Under the Name of Bread All Necessities Are Requested. The Kiss of Peace before Communion

### IX. “Give us this day our daily bread.”

[Col. 1493C] Grammarians say that *panis*, “bread,” is derived from the Greek πᾶν (*pan*), “all.” Hence, under bread is fittingly requested every substance necessary for passing through the present life: that is, food and clothing necessary for the body, according to the Apostle: “Having food and coverings, let us be content with these” (1 Tim. 6:8); and also the teaching of God’s word and participation in the body and blood of the Lord. These are provisions for the soul in the present life, lest it fail on the way and so not reach the blessed life.

Let the bread, then, be called “ours,” as explained above, and not another’s. For whatever is superfluous is foreign to us and belongs by right to someone else who needs it. It is “daily,” because it is needed daily. Temporal bread, once received, does not suffice forever, but is needed day by day. But if we receive the body and blood of the Lord really, we are united with those who communicate spiritually and by faith. Hence, at communion, the priest proclaims the kiss of peace to the people.

[Col. 1493D] “Give us this day.” The petitioner moderates his request and does not extend it far into the future, being content with what is for today. He follows the evangelical precept: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow itself will be anxious for itself” (Matt. 6:34). Note that reflection and anxious concern about tomorrow are prohibited, not foresight. For the former seem to imply a certain distrust of God, as though we would not have necessary things from God’s goodness unless they were prepared by effort and human ingenuity. But one who believes that much good comes through man, yet all comes from God alone, may provide for the future. Otherwise monks and hermits, who lay up provisions for their communities for the whole year, would be outside the scope of the *Our Father*.

[Col. 1494A] Although some explain “today” as meaning “this year,” so that one may without sin provide from harvest to harvest and from vintage to vintage. Thus explained, the fourth petition seems to belong to the three following petitions. For it asks for the necessities of the present life, not of the eternal one; because then neither the body will need food and drink nor the soul preaching or the real reception of the Lord’s body and blood, when God will be all in all.

Another reading is: “Give us this day our supersubstantial bread.” The refreshment that surpasses every substance is God, who is rightly called supersubstantial. Material bread can ease hunger and thirst, but cannot abolish them. For one who is full today, unless he is filled tomorrow or the day after, becomes hungry and thirsty. Therefore this petitioner, weary of this alternation, prays to be fed by that bread which is above every creature; when fed by it, he shall hunger and thirst no more, according to the saying: “Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 14:15).

[Col. 1494B] It is “daily,” because we cannot exist even for a moment without God; and he asks that it be given “this day.” But in the blessed life there will be a “today” which no night will interrupt, because there will always be one everlasting daily day. Therefore on that day he desires to be fed, according to his measure, with the bread of angels, so that, like them, he too may hunger no more. According to this interpretation, the petition seems to belong to the preceding three and asks for that which will be fulfilled only in the blessed life. Therefore above we called this petition the middle term, because, according to one interpretation, it seems to share in the three preceding petitions, and, according to the other, in the three [Col. 1494C] following.

### Fifth Petition — If You Wish to Be Forgiven, Forgive

### X. “And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.”

This fifth petition, concerning the forgiveness of offenses committed, belongs to the present life. For in the blessed life no one will sin, and therefore no one will need forgiveness of sins. Thus the petitioner, who in the first petitions had so ardently stretched himself toward the goods of the blessed life, returns to himself and recognizes that he still lives in this miserable life, full of miseries and sins. He prays that our debts may be forgiven us; unless they are forgiven, we do not attain the kingdom of heaven.

[Col. 1494D] But he asks this with the addition: “As we forgive our debtors”; that is: if we forgive, forgive us; if we do not forgive, we do not presume to ask that you forgive. A grave condition: “He who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 2:11). You kill your brother if you do not forgive him, but desire his death, and then say, “Forgive, as we forgive.” You are mad.

But perhaps this condition ought to be omitted, and one should say simply, “Forgive us our debts.” If you wish to correct the *Our Father* and seem wiser than Wisdom itself, which dictated it, you are most foolish. If you wish to be forgiven, forgive. According to the Gospel: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke 6:3). Otherwise, “he who stops his ear at the cry of the poor will himself cry and not be heard.” God does not even receive your gift unless you have first forgiven your offenses, according to that Gospel saying: “If you offer your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then, when you come, you shall offer your gift” (Matt. 5:23).

[Col. 1495A] He asks that debts be remitted. Sins seem to be called debts because satisfaction is owed for them; for just as no good goes unrewarded, so no evil goes unpunished. He therefore seems to ask that sins may be wholly forgiven when we repent, that satisfaction for sins may be made lighter, and that pardon may be granted more quickly. For even the souls of those who have died well, whose sins were forgiven in penitence and confession, are purified in purgatorial places if they did not make full satisfaction in the present life. For them, even after death, the sacrifice of the body and blood of God is offered and alms are given, so that the punishment by which they are purified may be lighter and may end more quickly.

[Col. 1495B] Someone lends money or any of his goods without interest to a needy brother. It would have been better had he given it; nevertheless he does good if, by lending, he assists one in need. Will God forgive him if he too has not forgiven this debt? Far from it! Yet if the debtor is so poor that he cannot repay, it is better to forgive than to exact payment harshly, according to the saying: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all that debt because you asked me. Should not you also have had mercy on your fellow-servant, as I had mercy on you?” (Matt. 18:32).

It follows: “And lead us not into temptation.”

### Sixth Petition

### XI. The sixth petition concerns the removal of future evils.

[Col. 1495C] For it is not enough for past evils to have been forgiven us unless God preserves us from those into which we have not yet fallen. And he says this thus: “Lead us not,” etc. To be tempted is not sin, but produces a crown. “He shall not be crowned unless he has striven lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5). We read: “God tempted Abraham” (Gen. 22:1), and “The Lord your God tempts you” (Deut. 13:3). Unless you give consent to a perverse temptation inflicted either by the flesh, which desires against the spirit, or introduced by the evil spirit, according to the saying, “Sendings by evil angels” (Ps. 77:49), you do not sin but advance toward what is better.

But if you have the full will to carry out in deed that by which you are tempted, if [Col. 1496A] you could, you have died the first death. You must fear lest you plunge into the second death, that of the deed, and the third, that of habit. [Note: [Col. 1495] St Augustine, *Sermon* 98, *On the Words of Luke*, chap. 6.] He therefore prays that God may not lead us into any sin. Yet because we cannot refrain from sin without him, God seems to lead us into temptation when he does not defend us and does not grant grace; nevertheless, he gives that grace only gratuitously, because we have not merited it—indeed, we have justly lost it.

Note that, when he asks not to be led into consent to perverse temptation, he prays that every kind of sin may be kept far from him; because he who does not consent does not act, and he who does not act does not become habituated. These are the three deaths of the soul into which he prays not to be led.

### Seventh Petition

### XII. The seventh is: “But deliver us from evil.”

[Col. 1496B] The present life does not subsist without some sin, according to John: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8). Yet there are light sins, which easily obtain pardon if only we repent, and which are believed to be wiped away in the common confession, “I confess to God.” He therefore asks to be delivered also from those evils without which the present life, owing to the frailty of the flesh, is not lived.

Otherwise: “Deliver us from evil,” that is, from the devil. For the devil is especially called evil, just as, conversely, “no one is good except God alone” (Mark 10:18). Therefore, since the devil lies in wait for our end and does not care what we have been, but what we are at the end of life, he asks at that moment to be delivered from the devil, so that then the devil may find nothing evil in him, just as he found nothing in the blessed Martin.

### XIII. Amen.

[Col. 1496C] “Amen” is, as it were, a seal of confirmation, so that, if he asks faithfully, he may not suffer rejection. Luke comprises these seven petitions in five. For, passing over “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth,” he understands it to be contained in the two preceding petitions. He does not add the last, “But deliver us from evil,” as though it were contained in the preceding words, “And lead us not.” Hence “And deliver us” is not added, but rather “But deliver us,” so that it is not a petition in itself but depends upon the preceding one.

Some strive to apply to these seven petitions the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit and the eight beatitudes; but because these do not seem very useful for the instruction of the simple, we have deliberately passed them over.

[Col. 1495]

## Charter of Joslen of Soissons for the Monastery of La Sauve-Majeure

(Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, VI, 664.)

[Col. 1495D] In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. G., by God’s forbearance called bishop of Soissons, to P., venerable abbot by the same grace of the monastery of La Sauve-Majeure, and to all his successors to be canonically appointed forever.

The see over which, by God’s ordering, we preside brings more anxiety than repose, more labor than tranquility. For it is a divine oracle that a good shepherd ought to oppose himself to the vexations suffered by the sheep entrusted to him and, by his own intervention, repel their injuries; for Christ, the good shepherd, laid down his very soul for his sheep. Therefore, dearest brother in Christ, we wish those now living and those to come to know how we resisted the injurious harassment which Count Raynaud of Soissons was inflicting upon the monastery of St Paul, belonging by right to the abbey, concerning the altar of Terni, and how we finally restored peace.

For, as we learned from the sealed charter of our predecessor of good memory, Bishop Lisiard, the altar of Terni with its appurtenances was bestowed upon the monastery of St Paul by our predecessor, Lord Hugh IV. The account of this matter is contained in the same charter in these words:

“May the prudence of both those to come and those now present know that the altar of Terni was given to the church of Blessed Paul, which belongs to the church of St Mary of La Sauve-Majeure, by Lord Hugh, bishop, my predecessor. Raynaud, son of Tescio, intervened, who held that same altar as a benefice from Ingelran of Coscia; and the same Ingelran likewise assented and granted that the conveyance of that altar should be made to the aforesaid place through the hand of the aforesaid Bishop Hugh, from whose benefice it had descended. And it was done; and that altar, with the chapel of Neuville and its appurtenances, was possessed by the church of Blessed Paul for a long time.

“But afterward, when the aforesaid Raynaud, setting out for Jerusalem, had fallen there among the Lord’s warriors, and when by his death the church of St Paul had been deprived of its benefactor and defender, John, count of Soissons, violently took that altar of Terni from the monks of St Paul and appropriated it to his own uses. But Guy the castellan, nephew and heir of the aforesaid Raynaud, took grievously the violent seizure, and could not endure that the alms and gift of his uncle, a most distinguished man, should be altered or diminished. He therefore repeatedly approached that count through friends and kinsmen, and obtained an agreement in this matter: the aforesaid Count John was to hold the altar only during his lifetime; after his death, without delay or any objection, it was to return free and undisturbed to the monks of St Paul, from whom he acknowledged that he had unjustly taken it.”

It happened not long afterward that this same count died. After his death, before his body was given burial, the count’s wife and his son Raynaud, weeping, rendered it into my hands and asked that I restore it through myself to St Paul; and with many sighs they begged that the sin which their father had incurred by taking it away might be forgiven. Many of the clerical and lay orders were present at this surrender and restoration. We have transcribed these matters from the charter of our predecessor Lord Lisiard for knowledge of what was done.

But after Raynaud, son of Count John, had been equipped as a knight, at the prompting of evildoers he seized that same altar and reduced it to his own use, although the monks of St Paul had held the same altar peacefully for many years after the death of Count John. When we summoned him to account and he evaded justice, we kept him outside the Church for almost two years. Finally, since he could obtain no relaxation from us in this matter except by submitting to our judgment, he restored the altar with all its revenues to the monastery of St Paul through our hand, on the condition that neither he nor any successor should lay a hand, by any device or under any injury whatsoever inflicted by the monks, upon the aforesaid altar or its revenues.

Ilgerius, prior of St Paul, promised that every year, so long as he lived—to him alone, that is, and in no way to any of his heirs—he would give Count Raynaud three measures of oats, by a heaped measure, and seven half-measures of grain, that is, grain not less than a half-measure of wheat, wherever the prior should choose; but not from the revenues of the altar of Terni, lest perhaps that altar should at some time appear to the count to be subject to a rent.

Finally, so that the monastery of St Paul might be more securely fortified in the future against the troubles and harassments of the count or his heirs, on the solemn day of the Nativity of the Lord, when, after the Gospel, we had ascended the pulpit to address the people, we set forth the account of the matter in the presence of the count, clergy, and numerous people assembled there. The count acknowledged and granted all these things; and in the presence of the whole church he declared the altar of Terni to be free and unencumbered for the monastery of St Paul, to such a degree that neither he nor his heirs should henceforth lay a hand upon any revenues belonging to that altar or arrogate anything from them to themselves.

Batildis, countess and wife of the same Count Raynaud, renounced the altar with its appurtenances insofar as it concerned her; and she granted and approved her husband’s renunciation. We, clothed as we were for the celebration of Mass, excommunicated before the eyes of the whole Church and pronounced a sentence of anathema upon the count, the countess, and any ecclesiastical or secular person who should appropriate to himself the aforesaid altar or its revenues, or alienate them from the church of St Paul, unless, after a second or third warning, he should restore and make amends for what had been taken within fifteen days. And so that this memorial charter of the transaction might possess inviolable force, we commanded it to be confirmed with our seal.

This was given in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1134, the ninth of our episcopate, while Louis the father reigned in France and Louis the son, anointed king, was in the fourth year of his kingship, as we have indicated. This was done before the eyes of the Church; nevertheless, it pleased us to add a few witnesses out of the many.

Present at the count’s act were: Arnulf, provost; Roard, dean; Nivelo, archdeacon; Adelard, archdeacon; Tetbald, archdeacon; Ebalus, archdeacon; John, priest; Galterus, priest; Theobald, priest; Gaufridus, deacon; Ingelbertus, deacon; Yvo, deacon; Ingenulfus, subdeacon; Rorigo, subdeacon; Arduinus, chancellor; Guislebertus of La Ferté, knight; Giraldus of Châtel, knight; Germundus of Châtel, knight; Robert of the Market [M.]; Hugh of Vieux-Marché [M.]; Wido of St Medard [M.]; Peter, son of Walter [M.]; Ingelrannus Matifart; Dietus of Val-Balmer; Theodericus of Neuville; Arnaudus of La Chaîne.

Present at the countess’s grant were: Ebaldus, archdeacon; Peter, son of Guerin, knight; Robert of the Market.
