What power of sinning did Christ possess? 334. Whether Christ’s tooth or foreskin is preserved on earth, and where, 431.

Freedom in foods restored through Christ, 265. What was formerly the selection of foods in Lent? 426.

The necessity of circumcision; upon whom and at what time was it enjoined? 98.

Clerics are to be honored, and their lives are not to be judged by laypeople, 222, 232. Who are to be admitted to the clergy, and how? 225. The celibacy of clerics, 226, 252, 390, 407. The place of clerics in the Church, 226, 391. They are to engage in no trade in their ministry, 231.

Clerics ought to make an alternating confession of their lighter faults in chapter, according to the prescription of the Council of Aachen, 363. What the life, morals, and exercises of clerics, privately and in church, ought to be, 403, 406. Whether heaven rotates, and whether its inhabitants rotate with it, 63, 305. The number of the heavens, 305.

The Lord’s Supper is not to be restored according to Jewish custom, 261, 422, etc.

The Church’s various rites concerning communion under both kinds, 316. In Pullus’s age it was practiced in some churches and not in others, 316, 421. In cathedrals and major churches laypeople received communion under both kinds; it was otherwise in smaller churches, 317. Communion under both kinds was granted especially to monks, 317. How the communion of the sick was formerly administered, 416. See more, 416. Communion under bread dipped in the chalice, 417. The manner of receiving it among the Greeks, 420. Among the monks of St-Denis near Paris, 421. What was the communion of little children? 421.

How the conception of Christ occurred according to Pullus’s opinion, 318, 331.

Decree of the Council of Clermont concerning communion under both kinds, 317; of the Councils of Basel and Sens concerning wearing almuces on the head, 399.

How texts of councils are to be cited, 321. Whatever is read in councils or Fathers is not always an undoubted dogma of faith, 321.

What is concupiscence? 94. It is original sin, 95. Why it remains after baptism, 95, 94. See 314.

Who are confessors who deceive those coming to them by fishing for gain? 214, 370. They ought not to absolve rashly, 214.

Why confession and penitence are especially necessary, 215. The necessity of confession, 152. On confession, 162. Nothing is to be concealed in it, 162. It is necessary for salvation, 206. Confession of venial sins is to be made to equals, 206, 362. Among Benedictines it is made twice weekly, 362. Whether it should be made by laypeople, 363. It was also made to women in a case of necessity, 365. Public confession of sins was formerly made in more than one rite, 363. What force belongs to the general confession at Prime, Mass, and Compline, 365. The benefit of frequently repeated confession, 306. The seal of confession, 207. Confession must be complete, 208. We must also confess notable circumstances, 209, 210. Confession is to be made to one’s own priest, and when it is permitted to make it to others, 210, 369. The formula of general confession used by the Cluniacs, 366. Cathedral canons and regular clerics of St Augustine used a similar formula, 366.

The sacrament of confirmation increases grace, 158. Its dignity and excellence, 158. When was it instituted? 349.

How celibate and married persons ought to live, 232.

Contrition does not impede the efficacy of the sacraments, 351. See more there.

The body of Christ is entire in heaven and on many altars, etc., 61. See under “Eucharist.”

The cup of Bacchus, intoxicating souls with Lethean drink into forgetfulness of former things, 72, 310.

Whether the creation of the world occurred in six days or all at once, 62. God created all things at once, because after resting he added nothing unlike them or from new matter, 62.

The existence of creatures shows that God exists, 31. The existence of creatures proves that they are loved by God, 44. How are there three creators and one Creator? 42.

### D
Demons not yet confined in hell, 66, 309. Demons were evil from the outset, 308. Pullus seems to maintain that the nature or substance of demons is no longer good, 67, 308. Whether the nature of demons was changed through sin, 308. By the fall of the demon human nature became better, and the angel was made greater, 82. He had no right over the man whom he had deceived by evil fraud, 137, 337. Demons fell from the nine orders, 199. How do the demons, each in their respective orders, serve their own princes? 200, etc. To which order did the prince of demons belong? 201, 359. Pullus holds that certain damned persons, or persons detained in hell, attained salvation, 242, 409. Their condition in hell after the Judgment, 287. Whether the suffrages of the faithful benefit the damned, 299. David received the grace of prophecy not through a subject creature but immediately through God himself, 201. Tithes are to be paid by laypeople to their own parish priests: why and how, 222. In this life we must not despair of the salvation of sinners, 54. There is only one God, 32. God’s existence is demonstrated, 31. He is receptive neither of acts nor of accidents, 36. He is extended by no parts and altered by no forms, 33. God is great and beautiful, but without quantity or quality, 35. In what sense is God the author of good and evil? 190. How does he will all people to be saved? 54, 300, 301. Another form, with names expressly stated, 207. To excommunicate is to hand over to Satan, 208, 367. What was the excommunication pronounced by the apostle Paul? 208, 366. Of the two denarii entrusted to the innkeeper, 247. Noah, Daniel, and Job in the field, the bed, and the mill, 232, 406.

What has happened cannot not have happened, 61, 303, 304. God “called” a famine, that is, the angel appointed over famine, 194. We hold more firmly by faith in absence than by knowledge in presence, 34. How faith justifies without works, 139. Faith is not born from works, but gives birth to works, 149. Faith is God’s gratuitous gift, 151. See more, 151. Its efficacy when joined with charity, 152. On faith, hope, and charity, 139. The children of the righteous are sometimes struck by God, to the grief of their parents and for the increase of their own merit, 99. The firmament stands, though the stars do not stand still, so that it may be a habitation suited to the saints, 63, 305. The sect of flagellants condemned by the Church, 383. What does the turning flame placed before the gate of paradise signify? 83. The water of baptism extinguishes it, 160. “Perhaps” does not always denote doubt among theologians, 39, 297.

## G

The office of the archangel Gabriel, 145. Galter, otherwise William, of Mauritania. See below under “William.” The book of Galter of St Victor against the Four Labyrinths of France, 327. Christ’s eternal generation is believed, not known. Pullus gives an allegorical exposition of “the fruit of the vine,” 106. The Genevieve community, or Canons Regular of St Augustine, 400. They sometimes serve cathedral canons, 400. Why do they not wear almuces on their heads? 400. See under “Augustinians.” Every thing begets what it itself is: a horse a horse, a human being a human being, God God, 34, 291. The two swords of the Church: to whom and for what they are assigned, 213, 376. The will inspired by God’s grace is of such power that it is nowhere without effect unless the human being himself fails grace, 204. God sometimes withholds grace, but gives malice to no one, 48. God’s wonderful ordering of medicinal grace toward human beings, 53. “If God willed it, he would heal; and he would will it if he loved; for if he loved, he would will good to the beloved,” 53. Grace was so necessary to the first human being that without it he could do nothing, 64. The grace of the Mediator is a remedy for the infirm, so that weakness may not hinder salvation but may benefit humility, 89. Grace was less for the Jew than for the Christian, 102. Pullus seems to have acknowledged the rejection of inward grace, 204, 360. A passage of St Gregory the Great is explained, in which he suggests that intuitive knowledge of God was granted to St Benedict the Father while still mortal, [Col. 1504] 65, 306, 307. The head of the same St Gregory is preserved with the highest devotion and most certain faith in the abbey of St Peter-le-Vif at Sens, for nearly eight hundred years, 306. The cause and rationale of ideas in God, 55, 56, 301. Pullus excellently demonstrates the communication of idioms between soul and body, 76. God is immutable while loving human beings more or less, 45. The immutability of God, 35. He alone is sent who, appearing through some manifestation of his presence, is from another, 40. Death in the house, at the gate, and in the tomb, 169, 354. The torments of the dead increase through the sufferings of the living whom they loved, 100.

What is the disease of nobility? 100.

An offering customarily made after baptism, 231. After confession, 231, 401, where there is more. An occasion of sin is sin, 192. Blessed bread in place of the Eucharist, 253, 411. More concerning it, 411. Its use was once more common among Benedictines, 412. The Church forbids dipped bread to be given in Mass, 256. The earthly paradise, and more concerning it, 82. Parents baptizing their children in necessity are not thereby forbidden the rendering of the marital debt, 230. Peter Lombard’s opinion concerning advancing the day of circumcision for infants in desperate health, 315. Peter of Poitiers, Chancellor of Paris, disciple of the Master of the Sentences, 365, 389. Another Peter of Poitiers, monk of St Victor at Paris, 365. Peter Pictor, canon of St Omer, 414. His poem on the Eucharist, 414. Pico della Mirandola, 324. The principle of the Holy Spirit: Pullus’s unusual opinion on this matter, 40. See page 292. Whether the Father and Son are two principles of the Holy Spirit, 38, 293. Various kinds of proof for refuting a false accusation in court are listed: trial by combat, water or red-hot iron, the Cross, and receiving the Eucharist, 374. How were prophets taught by God? 97. Personal properties are nothing other than persons distinguished from one another, 37. There are only three properties, 37. God’s providence, 59. The office of the archangel Raphael, 195. Under the chief physician there is an abundant supply of physicians, 195. The synodal letter of Ratherius, bishop of Verona, to be read by all priests, clerics, and especially parish priests, 405. What do reason, anger, and concupiscence accomplish in a human being? 74. The prerogative of religious persons at the general Judgment, 286. We know the salvation of those who have left everything for Christ, but do not know that of those who retained their possessions, 286. Ecclesiastical burial is not to be denied to persons guilty of crimes who are fortified with holy viaticum, 212, 373. What will the general resurrection be like, and what will happen to our bodies? 269. See more. At the Resurrection, what will be resumed and what left behind? 272. At what bodily stature will human beings rise? 273. They will rise at the stature which each had, or would have had, in the thirtieth year of life, 273. Robert of Melun, 296. His opinion concerning Christ’s conception, 325. On Abraham’s bosom, 341. On free will, 334. Robert Paululus, canon of Amiens, 393, 421. Robert Pullus. See the Preface and the material immediately following it. His modesty, 250. His opinion concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit is explained, 293. He seems sometimes to have indulged in obscurity, 298. Robert Pullus seems to have preceded the Master of the Sentences in doctrine, 299. He is defended from suspicion of error concerning the mystery of the Incarnation, 320, 327. Nothing indicates that he wrote from stubbornness in his own opinion, 329. He is again defended from error concerning the efficacy of the sacraments of the New Law, 347. He held the office of chancellor in the Roman Church, 391.

## S

How does a priest loose and bind? 216, 217. He has no power over the dead, 217, 381. The office and life of the priest, 229, 405. His life must be blameless, or he should abstain from sacred ministry, 230. See under “Clerical Celibacy.” Certain sacraments are to be repeated, others are not, 158. The less difficulty a sacrament has, the more necessity it carries, 158. What virtue and efficacy the sacrament of the New Law has according to writers of Pullus’s age, 345. Which Fathers taught Solomon’s salvation or damnation? 353. Whether God wills the salvation of all human beings without distinction, 54, 300, 301. The souls of the saints enjoy the vision of God immediately after death, 137, 138, 140, 142. The faults of the saints, even those removed by penance, are to be revealed at the Judgment, 283, 432. Their condition after the Judgment, 287. St Savinian, apostle of the Gauls and first bishop of Sens, 424. He rests in the church of St Peter-le-Vif at Sens, 424. The canons go there on his feast day, 424. Whether human seed is ensouled, 67, 310. The seed of both parents is required for the formation of offspring, 70, 310, 270. The parents’ seed is multiplied in likeness of Adam’s rib so that human procreation may occur, 272, 430. Ecclesiastical burial is not to be denied to those who die fortified with holy viaticum, 212, 373. It is not lawful to sell a burial place, 402. [Col. 1509] Whenever divine discourse seems injurious to God, it must be adjusted by careful investigation so that it may never be inconsistent with itself and may accord in every respect with propriety, 48. The stain of simony is to be avoided, 227. The simplicity of the divine essence, 36, 292. Whether the punishment of Sodomites, etc., was only temporal, 370. The principle of the Holy Spirit. For more on this subject, see both Pullus’s text, 38, and the *Observations*, 292. Christ was conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit, and how? 108. On the conception of Christ himself. See more there and at 318–331. To send the Holy Spirit is to display the invisible Spirit in a bodily form, 147. His coming on the day of Pentecost, 147. Why did he appear in the form of a dove and of tongues? 148. Evil spirits daily drag souls to hell, 193, 355. God generally afflicts human beings through their ministry, 355, 192. That there are three or two substances in Christ: either may be said, 113, 331. Suspension from the exercise of orders, 229.

## T

What does the letter Tau signify? 192, 355. Temptation is useful to human beings and leads to greater reward, 81. Why is the Old Testament one of servitude and the New one of grace? 105–106. The opinions of old and recent theology differ from one another; the old ought not to be corrected by the file of the latter, but rather the reverse, 325. The character and nature of scholastic theology described, 345. Certain theologians are excused because of the time in which they wrote, 325. Some of them, however—more recent writers, such as Ysambert, Suárez, and Estius—are criticized, 325. A fairer judgment of the Parisian theologians, 327. The opinion of ancient theologians concerning the efficacy of the sacraments of the New Law, 327. A distinctive opinion of Thomas of Alby, of the East Saxons, concerning the intermediate state of souls, is reported, 340. The various kinds of fear, 105. How do fear and charity mutually endure one another? [Col. 1510] 134. The spirit of fear with which the Lord Christ was filled was reverence toward God, 134, 336. Christ’s Transfiguration, a model of our resurrection, 273. The doctrine of transubstantiation explained, 258. How did the Trinity accomplish the Incarnation, and why was the Son alone incarnate? 109. In the Trinity we confess not only names but also the properties of the names, 35.

## U

St Ulrich, monk of St Hugh of Cluny and writer of the customs of that monastery, 366, 418. The multiplication of wives, even successively, would not have existed in the state of innocence, 242. Why did it exist among the Jews? 242. Whether the patriarchs were permitted to have several wives or even concubines, 242, 243, 410.

## V

The truth in which the angel did not stand is the knowledge of God itself, 65. The comparison of the active and contemplative lives with Leah and Rachel, 235; and with Mary and Martha, 235. This life is for meriting; the future life, for receiving, 51. “Many are called, few are chosen”: how? 54, 55. God’s will, 47. God’s will is never ineffective, 48. God’s will is not one thing and his action another, 53. The transitory will of this life is the cause of the enduring will in the other life, 51. While God’s will remains hidden, let us will what accords with love for our brethren, 54. What are the conditions of a vow? 245. A vow of continence, 245. Benedictines and many others do not express it in their profession, 390. The excellence of monastic vows, 286. God wills many things both now and formerly without change, 47. God wills all people to be saved and none to perish: Pullus teaches how these statements should be understood, 54, 300, 301.

## LETTERS OF SUGER, ABBOT OF SAINT-DENIS

1347

LETTER I.—From the abbot of Clairvaux to Pope Eugenius.—In praise of Lord Abbot Suger. 1347  
[Col. 1521] LETTER II.—From Pope Eugenius to Suger.—A letter of consolation. 1348  
LETTER III.—From Ulger, bishop of Angers, to Suger.—Having announced the death of Peter, abbot of Bourgueil, he asks that Suger receive favorably Robert, his successor. 1348  
LETTER IV.—From the community of Bourgueil to Suger.—They present to him, in the king’s absence, Robert, their abbot-elect. 1349  
LETTER V.—From Suger to Ulger, bishop of Angers.—He gives assent to the election of the community of Bourgueil, subject to the rights of the crown, so that the church of Bourgueil may not be troubled longer. 1350  
LETTER VI.—From King Louis to Suger.—He reports that he has happily reached the gates of Hungary, and bids him seek out and send money. 1350  
LETTER VII.—From Pope Eugenius to Suger. 1351  
LETTER VIII.—From the count of Anjou to Suger.—He writes that, scarcely recovering from a serious illness, he cannot attend the conference which he was to hold with him at Baugé. 1351  
LETTER IX.—From the count of Vermandois to Suger.—He directs him to attend the assembly convened at the port of Verberie for the peace of Beauvais, so that, after proceeding thence to Paris, they may jointly deliberate concerning the affairs of Poitou. 1351  
LETTER X.—From Count Theobald to Suger.—He asks him to meet him at Corbeil. 1352  
LETTER XI.—From Ralph, count of Vermandois, to Suger.—He asks on what day Suger wishes to come to Paris to confer with Samson, archbishop of Rheims, concerning the knights captured by Ralph’s brother. 1352  
LETTER XII.—From Hugh of Lusignan to Suger.—He asks him to trust in all matters Wiormand, whom he sends to him, and to reply through the same man concerning the affairs of Poitou. 1352  
LETTER XIII.—From Manasses, bishop of Orléans, to Suger. 1352  
LETTER XIV.—From Suger to the chapter of Chartres.—He sends envoys to them, bereft of their shepherd, to receive and preserve, in the king’s name, the regalian rights. 1353  
LETTER XV.—From the community of Saint-Riquier to Suger.—They ask him to confirm the election of Arnulf, prior of Corbie, as abbot of Saint-Riquier in Ponthieu. 1353  
LETTER XVI.—From the bishop of Orléans to Suger. 1354  
LETTER XVII.—From the count of Vermandois to Suger.—He writes that he has come to Rheims to the pope on business of his own and of the countess of Flanders; he then excuses his absence and wishes to learn Suger's pleasure. 1355  
LETTER XVIII.—From the countess of Nevers to Suger.—She asks that a certain sum of money be restored to a person of Auxerre, which Geoffrey the Fat of Étampes and his brother Ralph had refused to repay. 1355  
LETTER XIX.—From the dean and chapter of Chartres to Suger.—They ask him, in the lord king’s stead, to approve the election of Goslin as bishop of Chartres and restore the regalian rights. 1356  
LETTER XX.—From Suger to the chapter of Chartres.—A reply to the preceding letter. 1356  
LETTER XXI.—From William of Mauzé to Suger.—Setting out for Jerusalem, he writes that Suger should send to Bordeaux a wise provost from among his own men, and a man to whom he may entrust the tower of Talmont for safekeeping, which Ebles of Mauléon threatened to take away. 1357  
LETTER XXII.—From King Louis to Suger.—He writes of his arrival at Constantinople and of the money that must be sought and sent to him. 1357  
LETTER XXIII.—From the community of Saint-Riquier to Suger.—They again ask him to grant them the prior of Corbie as abbot, and not permit them to remain any longer without a shepherd. 1358  
LETTER XXIV.—From Theodoric, bishop of Amiens, to Suger.—He writes that his resources are insufficient to pay the money for which he had again been entered in Suger's book. 1359  
LETTER XXV.—From Geoffrey, archbishop of Bordeaux, to Suger.—He asks that nothing be altered in the territory of Bordeaux until he learns the condition of the land. 1359  
LETTER XXVI.—From the bishop of Hereford to Suger.—He commends several persons to him; then asks that the relics of Saint Denis which he is to send be identified by certain labels and entrusted to a reliable bearer. 1359  
LETTER XXVII.—From Pope Eugenius to Suger. 1360  
LETTER XXVIII.—From Pope Eugenius to Suger. 1360  
LETTER XXIX.—From Samson, archbishop of Rheims, to Suger.—He asks Suger to endeavor to help him against the burgesses of Saint-Remi, who had hired knights to harass the churches of Blessed Mary and Saint Remi. 1360  
LETTER XXX.—From the archbishop of Trier to Suger.—He asks what the envoys of the king of France have communicated to Suger concerning the expedition to Jerusalem. 1361  
[Col. 1522] LETTER XXXI.—From Peter, abbot of Cluny, to Suger. 1361  
LETTER XXXII.—From Pope Eugenius to Suger. 1362  
LETTER XXXIII.—Petition of the community of Saint-Riquier to Suger concerning the election of an abbot. 1362  
LETTER XXXIV.—From Theodoric, bishop of Amiens, to Suger.—He privately urges him to be watchful in choosing a religious man as abbot of Saint-Riquier. 1362  
LETTER XXXV.—From Geoffrey the mayor and the entire community of Saint-Riquier to Suger.—They ask him not to delay sending them his monk Peter, elected abbot of Saint-Riquier. 1363  
LETTER XXXVI.—From the bishop of Sarum to Suger.—First he lavishly praises him; then he requests relics of Saint Denis, and excuses himself because, having crossed into Normandy, he was unable to visit Suger before returning to England. 1363  
LETTER XXXVII.—From the count of Anjou to Suger.—He declares himself well and ready to serve the king, just as though the king himself were present. 1364  
LETTER XXXVIII.—From Count Theobald to Suger and Count Ralph.—He asks them not to demand the capicery of the church of Chartres under right of regality, since he himself holds the regality of the bishopric of Chartres from the king as a fief. 1365  
LETTER XXXIX.—From King Louis to Suger.—He writes of his journey as far as Antioch, and directs Suger to hasten to collect and send money. 1365  
LETTER XL.—From Suger to Pope Eugenius.—He recounts that regular canons have been introduced into Saint-Geneviève, and indicates what is necessary to bring this undertaking to completion. 1366  
LETTER XLI.—From the count of Vermandois to Suger.—He asks that, at the queen’s request, money from the revenues of the bishopric of Beauvais be granted to the clergy of Beauvais for the expenses of their journey to the pope concerning the election of Henry to the bishopric of Beauvais. 1369  
LETTER XLII.—From Geoffrey, bishop of Bordeaux, to Suger.—He reports the condition of his land and its ravaging by the king through the viscount of Gavarrat. 1369  
LETTER XLIII.—From the dean and community of Autun to Suger.—They ask him to assent to the election of Henry, brother of the duke of Burgundy, and to commend his person to the pope. 1371  
LETTER XLIV.—From the dean of Noyon to the same Suger.—Concerning the election of Baldwin, abbot of Châtillon, to the bishopric of Noyon, asking him to give assent in the lord king’s stead. 1371  
LETTER XLV.—From Pope Eugenius to Suger. 1371  
LETTER XLVI.—From the abbot of Clairvaux to Suger. 1372  
LETTER XLVII.—From Abbot Suger to Pope Eugenius.—He states what must be done against the canons of Saint-Geneviève, who were hurrying in crowds to Rome because they feared that something might be changed in their manner of life and their property. 1372  
LETTER XLVIII.—From King Louis to Suger.—He directs Suger to see to the preservation of the affairs of Reginald de Bulis, who remained in the East, and of the inheritance of the deceased Drogo. 1374  
LETTER XLIX.—From Henry, brother of the king, to Suger.—Though sought as bishop of Beauvais, he asks that someone else be elected. 1374  
LETTER L.—From King Louis to Suger and others.—He directs them to arrange payment of the money which he had borrowed through Ebrald, master of the Temple. 1374  
LETTER LI.—From Pope Eugenius to the bishops of Auxerre and Soissons, and to Suger. 1375  
LETTER LII.—From King Louis to Suger.—He directs him to repay to Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, one hundred and four marks of silver which Arnulf had lent to the king. 1375  
LETTER LIII.—From the same to Suger and the count of Vermandois.—After the deaths of Albert Dalvolt and his son Hugh, they are to ensure, until the king’s return, the preservation of the tower of Andelys, which the aforesaid Albert had constructed with the king’s permission. 1375  
LETTER LIV.—From the same to the same persons.—He directs them to take particular care to preserve his house at Gisors. 1376  
LETTER LV.—From the same to the same persons.—He directs that they not refuse to give his friend Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, sixty measures of his best Orléans wine. 1376  
LETTER LVI.—From the same to the same persons.—They are not to refuse the service of Archambald of Sully; the complaint against him is to be settled after the king’s return. 1376  
LETTER LVII.—From Suger to King Louis.—He adjures him not to remain, even briefly, in the East after the Easter deadline; he then writes about money paid to the knights of the Temple and to the count of Vermandois, and about concealing resentment toward Queen Eleanor. 1377  
[Col. 1523] LETTER LVIII.—From King Louis to Suger.—He reports that he owes much to the knights of the Temple and directs that the money he borrowed from them be repaid without delay; he then writes concerning his delayed return. 1378  
LETTER LIX.—From the same to the same.—He declares the many services rendered him by the knights of the Temple, and directs him to exact severe vengeance upon the goods and persons of those who dared to mutilate a cleric coming to their chapter. 1379  
LETTER LX.—From the same to Suger and the count of Vermandois.—He directs them to arrange repayment, before Mid-Lent, of the money that he had borrowed from the brothers of the Order of the Hospital. 1379  
LETTER LXI.—From Suger to Pope Eugenius.—Against Clement, dean of the church of Paris, who had indiscreetly imposed silence in choir upon that church’s cantor. 1380  
LETTER LXII.—From the count of Flanders to Suger. 1382  
LETTER LXIII.—From the count of Nevers to Suger.—He asks him to be at Saint-Denis on a fixed day for the sake of a conference. 1382  
LETTER LXIV.—From the abbot of Clairvaux to Suger. 1382  
LETTER LXV.—From the count of Flanders to Suger.—He writes that Robert, the king’s brother, has in no way departed from good will and brotherly feeling toward him, against whom he declares himself ready to defend the honor of the realm. 1383  
LETTER LXVI.—From Pope Eugenius to Suger. 1383  
LETTER LXVII.—From the same to the same. 1383  
LETTER LXVIII.—From the same to the same. 1383  
LETTER LXIX.—From King Louis to Suger.—Concerning his return delayed until after Easter, and Baldwin the chancellor whom he has sent and orders to be summoned for the conduct of the kingdom’s affairs. 1384  
LETTER LXX.—From the abbot of Clairvaux to Suger. 1384  
LETTER LXXI.—From Geoffrey of Rancon to Suger.—He declares that the king entrusted the land of Poitou to him and ordered him to distribute its revenues according to the king’s pleasure. 1384  
LETTER LXXII.—From the abbot of Clairvaux to Suger. 1385  
LETTER LXXIII.—From Henry, son of Count Theobald, to Suger.—He seeks advice concerning Anseric of Mont-Royal, captured in a tournament by Reginald of Pomponne. 1385  
LETTER LXXIV.—From Suger to the archbishop of Rheims.—He summons him and his suffragans to a general assembly to be held at Soissons, for securing the peace of the kingdom against the uprisings of rebels. 1386  
LETTER LXXV.—From S. of Chézy to Suger.—He asks whether he ought to surrender the tower and the district of the land to Geoffrey of Rancon. 1387  
LETTER LXXVI.—From the commune of Beauvais to Suger.—They ask him to do justice against Waleran, lord of Levesmont, who had captured and despoiled a man sworn to their commune during the days of the Lord’s Resurrection. 1387  
LETTER LXXVII.—From King Louis to Count Theobald.—He writes of the gracious services rendered during the pilgrimage by Henry, Theobald’s son; then of his own return delayed until Easter; and asks Theobald meanwhile to be vigilant in guarding the kingdom. 1388  
LETTER LXXVIII.—From the archbishop of Rheims to Suger.—He asks whether Suger will come to the council called at Soissons for the affairs of the kingdom, since, if he cannot be present, the archbishop will direct the count of Flanders and the bishops whom he had summoned not to come. 1388  
LETTER LXXIX.—From the abbot of Clairvaux to Suger. 1388  
LETTER LXXX.—From King Louis to Suger.—He directs him to endeavor to defend A. of Villerum, with all those dependent upon him, because the king had found him devoted to himself in foreign lands. 1389  
LETTER LXXXI.—From the archbishop of Bourges to Suger.—For Juvenetus of Bourges and his son Arnulf. 1389  
LETTER LXXXII.—From Suger to the provosts of Bourges.—He directs them to support Peter of Mâcy, invested with the royal right. 1389  
LETTER LXXXIII.—From the archbishop of Bourges to Suger.—Concerning the tower of Saint-Pallais, to be surrendered to the king’s provosts. 1390  
LETTER LXXXIV.—From Suger to Count Ralph.—Concerning the stronghold of Saint-Pallais, to be surrendered to the archbishop of Bourges, and the tower at Bourges, to be entrusted to Wildo of Herembrache. 1390  
LETTER LXXXV.—From the archbishop of Bourges to Suger.—Concerning the surrender of the tower of Saint-Pallais. 1391  
LETTER LXXXVI.—From the count of Vermandois to Suger.—He asks him to deign to attend a meeting with the archbishop of Rheims and the bishop of Soissons in his dispute with the bishop of Noyon. 1391  
[Col. 1524] LETTER LXXXVII.—From the archbishop of Bordeaux to Suger.—He asks what Suger wishes done concerning the then-vacant provostship of the city of Bordeaux. 1392  
LETTER LXXXVIII.—From Suger to Pope Eugenius.—He asks him to favor the sisters of Fontevraud, whom the bishop of Poitiers was troubling by demanding obedience from them and refusing to bless their abbess. 1392  
LETTER LXXXIX.—From Pope Eugenius to Suger.—On the return of King Louis. 1393  
LETTER XC.—From the bishop of Auxerre and the abbot of Clairvaux.—They ask him to accept a truce between Hugh of Marigny and Hugh Born; they then report that the king has landed in nearer regions from Palestine. 1393  
LETTER XCI.—From Pope Eugenius to Suger. 1393  
LETTER XCII.—From Pope Eugenius to the archbishop of Sens and his suffragans. 1394  
LETTER XCIII.—From the abbot of Clairvaux to Suger. 1394  
LETTER XCIV.—From King Louis to Suger.—He writes that he landed in Calabria on the fourth day before the Kalends of August [29 July], and explains the causes delaying his imminent return. 1394  
LETTER XCV.—From the archbishop of Bourges to Suger.—In the case of R. of Montfaucon. 1395  
LETTER XCVI.—From King Louis to Suger.—He directs him to meet the king secretly before anyone else upon his arrival, so that he may be informed of rumors circulated about the kingdom and know how he ought to conduct himself toward each person. 1395  
LETTER XCVII.—From Cadurcus to Rotrou, count of Perche.—Concerning the tower at Bourges entrusted to him and ordered by the abbot of Saint-Denis to be surrendered: he asks that the count of Vermandois be induced to entrust it for safekeeping to Cadurcus and Rotrou. 1396  
LETTER XCVIII.—From Odo, bishop of Beauvais, to Suger.—He asks him to arrange absolution from anathema for Peter of Miliac, excommunicated because he had married as wife the niece of Manasses of Boulogne, while Manasses had married the aunt of that same Peter. The reason for absolution was that Peter, who was afflicting the district of Beauvais with evils, promised to take the cross if absolved. 1397  
LETTER XCIX.—From Hugh, archbishop of Sens, to Suger.—That he receive the church of Blessed Columba of Sens under his protection. 1397  
LETTER C.—From Count Ralph to Suger.—He reports that the king will not arrive before the feast of All Saints, and advises him meanwhile to take an account of the king’s servants. 1398  
LETTER CI.—From Odo, bishop of Beauvais, to Suger.—He reports a disturbance that has arisen in the city and says that Ralph, count of Vermandois, intends to expel the count of Clermont from it. He therefore asks Suger to summon a conference to restore peace. 1398  
LETTER CII.—From the bishop of Chartres to Suger.—He complains about the provost of Hienville, who had risen against him, and asks that Suger not refer the case for hearing to another person. 1399  
LETTER CIII.—From Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, to Suger.—That he restrain the robberies of Hugh Brostin. 1399  
LETTER CIV.—From Goslin, bishop of Chartres, to Suger.—He excuses himself because, though summoned by Suger, he cannot attend the feast of Saint Denis on account of the unexpected arrival of the lord bishop of Auxerre. 1400  
LETTER CV.—From Peter, archbishop of Bourges, to Suger.—On the return of King Louis. 1400  
LETTER CVI.—From Pope Eugenius to Suger. 1400  
LETTER CVII.—From the same to the same. 1400  
LETTER CVIII.—From the same to the same. 1400  
LETTER CIX.—From the dean and chapter of Chartres to Suger.—They lodge a complaint concerning Hugh of Bretigny and Ebrard the viscount. 1401  
LETTER CX.—From the abbot of Saint Pantaleon to Suger.—He thanks him for kindness shown to a certain boy, his nephew. 1401  
LETTER CXI.—From the archbishop of Sens to Suger.—On the return of King Louis. 1402  
LETTER CXII.—From Peter, archbishop of Bourges, to Suger.—On the same matter. 1402  
LETTER CXIII.—From the same to the same.—Concerning Bartholomew the archdeacon. 1402  
LETTER CXIV.—From Count Theobald to Suger.—He wishes to know whether Reginald of Courtenay has made satisfaction for money taken from merchants. 1403  
LETTER CXV.—From the count of Vermandois to Suger.—He asks him to secure the longest truce he can concerning certain disputes, and to direct that the king’s servants assemble at Paris. 1403  
LETTER CXVI.—From Count Theobald to Suger.—He reports that Reginald of Courtenay despoiled merchants of the king whom he had captured; he promises aid in avenging this injury. 1403  
LETTER CXVII.—From the archbishop of Sens to Suger.—On the return of King Louis. 1404  
LETTER CXVIII.—From Cadurcus the cleric to Suger.—Concerning money which he had lent to the king and which was to be paid him from the revenues of Poitou. 1404  
LETTER CXIX.—From R. of Montfaucon to Suger.—He declares himself ready, on a suitable day, to undergo judgment according to the customs of Bourges concerning a man who denied him his service. 1405  
LETTER CXX.—From the count of Blois to Suger.—He reports an injury inflicted by Guarin, son of Salomon, viscount of Sens, upon the money-changers of Vézelay coming to his fair at Provins. 1405  
LETTER CXXI.—From the bishop of Auxerre to Suger.—He commends to him the wife and children of his friend Robert the physician, now dead. 1406  
LETTER CXXII.—From the count of Nevers to Suger.—On the same matter. 1406  
LETTER CXXIII.—From the abbot of Ferrières to Suger.—He asks him to grant a delay for payment of the remaining money which had been obtained for the monastery of Ferrières for the holy expedition. 1406  
LETTER CXXIV.—From the count of Nevers to Suger.—He writes concerning a conference arranged at Orléans with Geoffrey of Donzy, and concerning a day for battle appointed by the king for that same Geoffrey and one of his knights. 1407  
LETTER CXXV.—From Pope Eugenius to Suger. 1407  
LETTER CXXVI.—From the abbot of Cluny to Suger. 1407  
LETTER CXXVII.—From the same to the same. 1408  
LETTER CXXVIII.—From the archbishop of Sens to Suger. 1408  
LETTER CXXIX.—From the bishop of Châlons to Suger.—He asks that Suger be his patron and intercessor with the king. 1408  
LETTER CXXX.—From A., bishop of Rennes, to Suger.—He writes that he had to travel as far as Nantes before coming to Suger, but will come in the first week of Lent. 1409  
LETTER CXXXI.—From the clergy of Saint Martin of Tours to Suger.—They ask him to attend a matter to be dealt with at Meaux in the presence of the legate against the clergy of Saint Maurice. 1409  
LETTER CXXXII.—From the abbot of Clairvaux to Suger. 1410  
LETTER CXXXIII.—From the abbot of Cluny to Suger. 1410  
LETTER CXXXIV.—From the bishop of Lyons to Suger.—He excuses himself for being unable to attend the conference at Chartres, convened to aid the Eastern Church, because the archbishop of Sens did not hesitate to derogate from his primacy. 1411  
LETTER CXXXV.—From Geoffrey, archbishop of Bordeaux, to Suger.—He wishes to be excused for being unable to attend the assembly at Chartres in response to Suger's summons. 1412  
LETTER CXXXVI.—From the archbishop of Bourges to Suger. 1413  
LETTER CXXXVII.—From the abbot of Pontigny to Suger.—He commends to him the case of the treasurer of Auxerre, entrusted to Suger's discretion by the Roman pontiff. 1413  
LETTER CXXXVIII.—From Pope Eugenius to Suger. 1413  
LETTER CXXXIX.—From King Louis to Suger.—That he put an end to the complaints of the poor people of Chartres against Ralph Malvoisin, the settlement of which the king had entrusted to Suger's discretion. 1414  
LETTER CXL.—From J., cardinal of Saint Mary the New, to Suger.—He commends the case of Master Peter, entrusted to Suger's judgment by Pope Eugenius. 1414  
LETTER CXLI.—From Hugh, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, to Suger.—For the same Master Peter. 1414  
LETTER CXLII.—From Hugh the Roman to Suger.—For the same Master Peter. 1415  
LETTER CXLIII.—From Roger, king of Sicily, to Suger.—He asks him, in return, to inform him more frequently of his condition through travellers. 1415  
LETTER CXLIV.—From Pope Eugenius to Suger. 1416  
LETTER CXLV.—From Nicholas, abbot of Corbie, to Suger.—He asks that he be excused before the king for not sending anyone to Orléans on the appointed day to answer concerning his dispute with the burgesses of Corbie. 1416  
LETTER CXLVI.—To Roger, king of Sicily.—He thanks him for not disdaining to report his prosperity to Suger and inquire about Suger's welfare. 1417  
LETTER CXLVII.—From Pope Eugenius to Suger. 1417  
LETTER CXLVIII.—From King Louis to Abbot Suger.—He entrusts to him the case concerning the election of the bishops of Laon and Arras. 1417  
LETTER CXLIX.—From the abbot of Vézelay to Suger.—He writes on behalf of the widow and son of Robert the physician, formerly Suger's friend, who has died. 1418  
LETTER CL.—From Suger to King Louis.—He entreats him not to break into war against the count of Anjou, whom he had made duke of Normandy, without the counsel of the magnates whom he had summoned. 1418  
LETTER CLI.—From Pope Eugenius to Suger. 1419  
LETTER CLII.—From Baldwin, bishop of Noyon, to Suger.—Concerning a conference to be held with the archbishop of Rheims about an urgent matter between him and Ralph, count of Vermandois. 1419  
LETTER CLIII.—From Suger to G., count of Anjou.—He declares that the conflict between Geoffrey and the king of the Franks greatly displeases him; he asks, however, that ecclesiastical possessions not be damaged under pretext of war. 1419  
LETTER CLIV.—From Suger to T., bishop of Amiens.—He rebukes him for admitting Robert of Boves, a thoroughly wicked man, to communion in sacred things. 1421  
LETTER CLV.—From Geoffrey, archbishop of Bordeaux, to Suger.—He reports that illness has detained him at Fontaine-Ebrald, so that he cannot attend the appointed assembly. 1421  
LETTER CLVI.—From Pope Eugenius to Suger. 1422  
LETTER CLVII.—From Suger to B., bishop of Noyon.—He asks him to bless the abbot of Compiègne on the feast day of Saint Cornelius, if this can be done without great scandal. 1422  
LETTER CLVIII.—From B., bishop of Noyon, to Suger.—He reports that the abbot of Compiègne has been blessed and advises that recourse be made to the pope without delay. 1423  
LETTER CLIX.—From Suger to R., count of Vermandois.—Concerning the sacrilegious incursion of his brother Philip into the church of Compiègne, from which he forcibly carried off relics. 1423  
LETTER CLX.—From R., count of Vermandois, to Suger.—He writes that, grain and the goods of the monastery of Compiègne having been carried off by the canons, he will place what remains under the king’s authority. 1424  
LETTER CLXI.—From Louis, king of the Franks, to Suger.—He writes that after the feast of Saint Remigius he will settle affairs at Compiègne with Suger; meanwhile, he has ordered his mother and Counts Ralph and Theobald not to inflict any molestation upon the monastery of Compiègne. 1424  
LETTER CLXII.—From Baldwin, bishop of Noyon, to Lord Pope Eugenius.—He asks him to ratify the election of Hugh as bishop of Arras. 1425  
LETTER CLXIII.—From Suger to Lord Pope Eugenius.—He recounts how, amid troubles and insults, he introduced religious monks into the church of Compiègne in place of canons whose lives were infamous. 1425  
LETTER CLXIV.—From Suger to P., abbot of Cluny.—He asks him to write to the pope so that he may receive the abbot of the church of Compiègne favorably. 1426  
LETTER CLXV.—From Suger to Peter, archbishop of Bourges.—From the cartulary of the church of Blessed Mary of La Chapelle. 1427  
LETTER CLXVI.—From Suger to Peter, abbot of Cluny. 1428  
LETTER CLXVII.—From Geoffrey, count of Anjou, to Suger.—He gives thanks because Suger is working to restore peace between the king and himself. 1428  
LETTER CLXVIII.—From Suger to Geoffrey, count of Anjou.—A reply to the preceding letter. 1429  
LETTER CLXIX.—From Peter, archbishop of Bourges, to Suger.—He asks to be excused before the king because he cannot come to him at Meudon. 1429  
LETTER CLXX.—From Pope Eugenius III to Suger.—He commends to him Mo., a subdeacon. 1429  
LETTER CLXXI.—From Pope Eugenius III to Suger.—Concerning the violence of the count of Anjou against his brother Robert. 1430  
LETTER CLXXII.—From Peter, abbot of Cluny, to Suger.—On the mutual friendship between them. 1430  
LETTER CLXXIII.—From Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, to Suger.—He writes to him on behalf of his churches at Pontoise, Chaumont, and Gisors, which the king was retaining after usurping them. 1430  
LETTER CLXXIV.—From the same Hugh to Suger.—He writes to him again on behalf of the church of Gisors. 1431  
LETTER CLXXV.—From Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, to Suger.—Concerning certain affairs between the duke of Normandy and the count of Anjou. 1432  
LETTER CLXXVI.—From Henry, bishop of Winchester, to Suger.—He asks him to send an envoy to the countess of Flanders to seek a safe-conduct from her on his behalf. 1432  
LETTER CLXXVII.—From Theobald, archbishop of Meaux, to Suger.—He commends to him the poor nuns of Fontaines. 1433  
LETTER CLXXVIII.—From G., prior of La Charité, to Suger.—That, with the support of the abbot of Clairvaux, he restrain the oppressions inflicted upon him by the bishop of Auxerre. 1433  
LETTER CLXXIX.—From Stephen, king of England, to Suger.—He gives thanks for Suger's friendship and for the benefits shown to him at the court of the king of the Franks. 1434  
LETTER CLXXX.—From Henry, bishop of Winchester, to Suger.—He commends to him the affairs of the king of England. 1434  
LETTER CLXXXI.—From Baldwin, bishop of Noyon, to Suger.—He excuses himself for not having come to Suger when summoned. 1435  
LETTER CLXXXII.—From Suger to Henry the bishop, the chapter, clergy, and people of Beauvais.—He recalls them from a sedition planned against the king. 1435  
LETTER CLXXXIII.—From Goslin, bishop of Soissons, to Suger.—Concerning his desire to see him. 1437  
LETTER CLXXXIV.—From Suger to Goslin, bishop of Soissons.—A reply to the preceding letter. 1438  
LETTER CLXXXV.—From Goslin, bishop of Soissons, to Suger.—A reply to the preceding letter. 1438  
LETTER CLXXXVI.—From Suger to King Louis.—He commends the king and kingdom to God, and the church of Saint Denis to the king. 1438  
LETTER CLXXXVII.—From Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, to Saint Bernard.—He gives thanks for consolation given to him in his final illness and commends himself to Bernard’s prayers. 1440  

Testament of Abbot Suger. 1440  

## CONSTITUTIONS OF ABBOT SUGER

1445

I.—On the commemoration of Blessed Mary at Saint-Denis every week, namely on Saturday and Thursday, and on the refreshment of the brothers on those same days. 1445  
II.—On the inhabitants of the town of Saint-Denis granted freedom. 1448  
III.—Concerning several properties granted to the church of Saint Paul by Abbot Suger, and a measure of wine and one hundred lambs on the day of his death. 1449  
[Col. 1528] IV.—On the cultivation of Indictum. 1452  
V.—On a plot of ground bought from Gerard the Hospitaller. 1452  
VI.—On the estates of Saint Denis taken away, namely Blitestorp and others. 1452  
VII.—On increasing the provisions of the religious and on the first foundations of the church of Saint-Denis built by Suger himself. 1453  
VIII.—On the immunities of the village of Val-Cresson. 1459  
IX.—On the tithe of Saint Brice. 1459  
X.—On John, Bernard, Peter, and Gerald, hermits. 1460  

## PRIVILEGES GRANTED TO SAINT-DENIS DURING THE ABBACY OF SUGER

1461

I.—King Louis, sixth of that name, enlarges and confirms the privileges of Saint-Denis on the occasion of taking up the banner from the altar of the blessed martyrs. 1461  
II.—Privilege of the same King Louis and of his son Philip for the monastery of Saint-Denis. 1463  
III.—Privilege of Louis VII. 1465  
IV.—Privilege of the same king. 1466  
V.—Privilege of the same king. 1468  

## WILLIAM, MONK OF SAINT-DENIS, DISCIPLE OF SUGER

Notice. 1468  

LETTER OF WILLIAM to certain of his fellow monks.—He praises the solitary dwelling which he had chosen in Aquitaine and excuses himself from returning to his former honors, which he had abandoned. 1471

Notice. 1475
